[THE COMPLETE WORKS OF ZENO.]

PROLEGOMENA TO THE WORKS OF SAINT ZENO.

[Col. 0009]

[I–VIII] DEDICATORY EPISTLE.

[Col. 0009A] To the Most Eminent and Most Reverend Prince, Domenico Passionei, Cardinal of the Holy Roman Church: Peter and Jerome Ballerini, brothers and priests of Verona.

We present before you, Most Eminent Prince, the collection of sermons of Saint Zeno, Bishop of Verona—the most ancient, among all the Latin Fathers whose homilies survive. It has always been wonderfully commended among learned and cultivated persons on many grounds, not only among Catholics but even among heterodox writers. Now, so far as our resources and diligence have allowed, we offer it cleansed of many errors through the assistance of several ancient manuscripts which we were fortunate enough to discover and collate; supplied in certain lacunae; restored to its original and native integrity by separating the genuine works from the spurious; and at last conspicuously vindicated from the censures of certain persons. We repeatedly ask and entreat you graciously to cast your eyes upon it and to receive it under your protection and guardianship.

If it is permitted to disclose the rationale of our undertaking, we reflected that editors of books of this kind seek patrons who, no less by reason of their dignity and authority than by their learning and knowledge, may be able to examine and judge a new edition and, if necessary, give an account of the patronage they have undertaken. Yet, although it is easy to desire this double distinction in one person, it is most difficult to hope for it or to find it. For human affairs are generally so constituted that those who, owing to outstanding natural gifts, might advance in the best studies, and owing to their rank might patronize them, readily supply the latter qualification, which concerns patronage; but, occupied with the management of public affairs, cannot equally supply the former.

[Col. 0009C] But when we diligently inquired whether anyone in our own age had attained both distinctions, you immediately came to mind: in you, together with the highest dignities, an exceptional love and cultivation of learning has always shone forth. Indeed, from your earliest youth you devoted yourself with the highest praise to humane studies, and especially thereafter to sacred disciplines. In these, offering many proofs of your talent and learning, you gained for yourself the commendation and affection of learned men of various nations with whom you associated familiarly. Since you were found exceedingly suitable for the discharge of the greatest offices, a most difficult commission was immediately entrusted to you by the Roman Pontiff, and you were sent to the Netherlands. There, having not merely fulfilled but surpassed the great expectations already conceived of you, you were entrusted first with the apostolic legation among the Swiss, and then with that to Charles VI, Augustus Emperor.

[Col. 0010A] It can scarcely be said how many labours you underwent in that office, how many proofs of prudence and diligence you left behind, and finally how many affairs—most unlike one another in kind, most difficult in their magnitude, and most obstructed by the circumstances themselves as they arose—you conducted with the greatest ease and success. For in these offices you set before yourself not honour or leisure, but work, anxiety, and cares; and you continually pondered by what means you might each day accomplish something that would redound to the honour and benefit of the Roman See, the Catholic Church, and religion.

Anyone who attentively reads the *Acts of the Apostolic Legation to Switzerland*, published at Zug in 1729, will find in them a sufficiently fitting example of what we mean: there shine forth the zeal, gravity, holiness, and discipline of the ancient Fathers, cultivated by you with especial devotion.

[Col. 0010B] Nevertheless—who would have believed it?—so many prolonged and almost unceasing concerns did not distract you to such an extent that you granted nothing to studies, which demand a tranquil and unoccupied mind. Rather, whatever time remained from public duties, you diligently endeavoured to devote entirely to study, always advancing in some respect, now through reading, now through reflection and writing. This may be inferred from the funeral oration on the death of the great Prince Eugene of Savoy, composed by you through nocturnal labour and received with the highest praise by literary and learned men; and likewise from the recently mentioned *Acts* of the Swiss legation, which contain several notable monuments of your talent, eloquence, and learning.

Hence also, sparing neither effort nor expense, you assembled a distinguished and immense library, continually enlarged, of carefully selected manuscripts and printed books of every kind, from every quarter; it had already been exceptionally praised thirty years earlier by Bernard de Montfaucon especially on account of its two hundred excellent Greek manuscripts.

> [Note: Col. 0009D] In the Paris edition of the *Greek Palaeography*, year 1[.....]08, book IV, chapter 5, p. 290, the following is read: “The first plate presents seven specimens from the library of the most illustrious and our most friendly friend, Domenico Passionei. Though scarcely twenty-four years old, he shines with an incredible knowledge of things and disciplines; he is excellently learned in Greek and Latin literature, and has assembled a numerous library of manuscript and printed copies, worthy to be ranked among very few for the selection of its books. He watches over the interests of scholars in such a way that he offers, even unasked, to all who devote themselves to literary pursuits whatever he possesses himself or can obtain through the assistance of friends.”
>
> Likewise, in the preface, p. XXII, where various libraries containing Greek manuscripts are listed: “The library of the most illustrious Abbot Domenico Passionei, notable for the quantity and selection of its books, contains about two hundred Greek manuscripts; we have given specimens of some of them in book IV and, in the Appendix, several subscriptions of calligraphers.” Similar remarks are read in the Appendix, p. 510.

[Col. 0010C] You assembled this library not for display and ornament, as most men of high rank did at that time, but so that in hours snatched from sleep rather than from duty you might spend your life in it. From it, in accordance with the extraordinary power of your mind, you display a truly remarkable knowledge—not so much of books as of the matters contained in them. Thus, as we have learned from the testimony of serious men, you seem in some manner to have transferred the library you assembled into your own mind: so readily and abundantly do you indicate not merely the books treating any subject, but discourse and argue even upon the subjects themselves.

[Col. 0011A] After you were summoned to Rome and raised to that most eminent summit from which you shine over the whole Church—a station to which you were advanced not by the nobility of your most ancient and celebrated family, nor by services rendered (for you, so excellently furnished with the learning of the Fathers, had no need of recommendations which are by no means acceptable to you), but by your merits toward the Christian commonwealth—after, I say, you had been placed in this rank of dignity, although you have been continually burdened by more public cares than ever before, you have not therefore wholly taken leave of learning. Retaining your former habit, you are frequent in the library and in reading; and nothing gives you greater pleasure than to learn and write concerning books and the humane, learned, and sacred disciplines.

[Col. 0011B] All these considerations, therefore, moved us to judge that this edition of Saint Zeno ought to be dedicated to you. We hope that, because of your distinguished love for the best studies and especially for ancient books, you will most gladly accept this gift and be willing to show yourself such a patron as, by your authority, may afford it protection and, by your learning, may read and understand an ancient, eloquent, and most elegant author, and, should occasion arise, give an account also of your patronage.

[Col. 0012A] One thing causes us no small anxiety: that you will become not only the reader and judge of the author, of whose worth we entertain no doubt, but equally of those materials which we have added in his defence or for his elucidation. Yet your kindness and that noble disposition of yours—which sharpens the minds of those of excellence to do all that they can, and provides them with help and support—both revives and reassures us in this fear. Moreover, there is no doubt that whatever, owing to our weakness, may be lacking in this edition for the defence or explanation of the holy Bishop can, through your consummate expertise, be recognized and supplied.

Receive, then, Most Eminent Prince, this work which we offer you as a witness of our devotion and of our most devoted goodwill toward you. If it is less worthy in our name, it is certainly worthy in the author’s name and by his merits to receive your approval as Most Eminent Cardinal, just as it was formerly approved by Pope Sixtus V, to whom it was first dedicated.

[IX–XXVI] PREFACE OF THE BALLERINI BROTHERS.

[Col. 0011B] I. Among the ancient Fathers of the Church whose works have come down to us only in small quantity, very few indeed are praised by learned and cultivated men as highly as Saint Zeno, Bishop of Verona. In his sermons some admire the force of his eloquence and his abundance of expression; others extol the purity and elegance of his Latin style; but almost all commend the keenness of his intellect, his antiquity, gravity, piety, and the excellence of his thoughts and doctrine.

Yet, among critics who dissect every individual matter to the quick, there is no one whose works—especially as regards the determination of their author—have had so many difficulties raised against them as we find advanced from various quarters against this collection of sermons. Thus, although some learned men have worked diligently to resolve them, they seem not only to have achieved nothing but almost to have cut off from others all hope of establishing anything sound.

This, however—a point which, as far as we can discover, has hitherto occurred to no one as a suspicion—arises from the lack of an accurate edition. Zeno’s treatises were indeed first published at Venice in 1508 from a very ancient manuscript, which the celebrated Guarino had long before found in the library of the episcopal palace at Verona. For these words are read on the title-page of that edition:

> “The most elegant sermons to the people of the eminent and excellent man, the most illustrious doctor Saint Zeno, Bishop of Verona, extracted from a most ancient volume found at Verona by Guarino of Verona, a most eloquent man, in the library of the episcopal palace of Verona.”

[Col. 0011D] That edition was divided into three books. The first comprises seventeen sermons on virtues and vices; the second, thirty-eight sermons on matters of the Old Testament; the third, fifty sermons on matters of the New Testament. Each book bears its own title in this form.

Furthermore, homilies of Saint Caesarius of Arles and certain other small works were appended to Zeno’s treatises in the same edition. The following concluding statement must by no means be omitted, since it reveals the true editor of the edition. Guarino was nevertheless mistakenly judged to have been the editor by many who had not seen the edition itself because of its rarity, although it could otherwise be established that he had died nearly fifty years earlier:

> “To the praise and glory of the supreme and undivided Trinity, of the most blessed Virgin Mary, and of the blessed pontiffs Zeno and Caesarius and of all the saints: the sermons placed in this volume, and never previously printed elsewhere, most carefully revised and most studiously corrected by the venerable Father Albertus Castellanus of the Order of Preachers, and most diligently printed at Venice by Master Jacobus de Leuco at the expense of Lord Benedictus Fontana, happily come to an end in the year of the Lord 1508, on the twenty-fourth day of January.”

[Col. 0012C] This edition was immediately accepted by many, so long as it was not carefully examined. But when Sixtus of Siena, preparing his *Bibliotheca*, in which he rendered judgment on individual ecclesiastical writers, subjected Zeno’s published sermons to close scrutiny, he brought forward so many difficulties that, suspecting nothing of the defects of the edition, he maintained that Zeno ought to be removed from the catalogue of ecclesiastical authors.

For that edition presents several treatises by other writers inserted and intermixed among Zeno’s works, in such a way that it not only supplies no distinction by which one might be recognized from another, but even represents all alike as Zeno’s productions, with the single exception of one which bears the name of Saint Gaudentius, Bishop of Brescia. Thus a strong—or rather evident—argument arose for denying Zeno’s authorship of certain sermons. This provided sufficiently just cause, once all the rest also had been called into question, for raising the issue whether Saint Zeno of Verona was truly the author of any sermons worthy of being listed among ecclesiastical writers, or which works ascribed to this saint’s name were truly his—as Father Mabillon puts it in the *List of the Chief Difficulties of the Third Century*, appended to his outstanding work *On Monastic Studies*.

[Col. 0013A] II. To dispel these difficulties, first published by Sixtus of Siena and subsequently adopted and reiterated by others who followed his opinion, another edition of the same works was afterwards prepared at Verona in 1586, under Cardinal Agostino Valerio, the eminent Bishop of Verona. Raphael Bagata and Baptista Perettus, authors known for other works, considered that it should be corrected in certain places from the exemplar of an old manuscript, which they call “ancient” three times in the preface, and fortified by fairly extensive defences.

It was soon reproduced, though somewhat more negligently, in four editions of the *Library of the Fathers*, and finally reprinted more fully in a separate volume at Padua in 1710. Yet, although much was written in defence, the edition itself presents nothing new except a different arrangement of the sermons, in which they appear divided into two books. All the treatises remain equally disordered, intermixed, and marketed as Zenonian, including those which Sixtus’s arguments had clearly shown to be foreign.

[Col. 0013C] Consequently, whatever could be said in defence of so bad a cause not only achieved nothing, but rather stirred some people to indignation and persuaded them that a cause which needed to be buttressed and upheld by very weak arguments was far weaker and worse than it had previously been.

A further accumulation of difficulties arose in this edition from the date at which its editors placed Saint Zeno’s floruit. Since this plainly conflicts with the testimony of several sermons, the editors, instead of calming the minds of dissenting critics, sharpened them into still greater disagreement.

To all these matters concerning the question of authorship, add several others which contribute greatly to diminishing the credit of the edition itself. The old manuscript, which we noted as being mentioned three times in the preface, seems to be that same manuscript which the editors, among their testimonies, call “the ancient manuscript codex of the monastery of Saint Zeno,” when they cite from it the fragment of an Anonymous author in praise of Verona.

[Col. 0013D] This manuscript, preserved until now in the library of the same monastery, is much more recent in date, having been written in the fifteenth century. It is evident that it was of so little use to the editors that, content to correct a few passages which were extremely corrupt in the first edition, they achieved nothing in others. Indeed, having decided to imitate the editorial method used by those who recently published the works of Saint Ambrose under the auspices of Sixtus V—a method whose character is now known to all learned men and may be recognized from the most recent edition of Saint Ambrose—they thought the authority both of the manuscript itself and of the first edition should in some places be abandoned, as will become clear from the notes in their proper place.

[Col. 0014A] Therefore, in the Veronese edition and all those derived from it, besides the confused and disorderly mixture of foreign treatises with Zenonian ones, several arbitrary interpolations of passages should greatly offend us. So far as we have seen, no one has noticed them because of the rarity of the first edition.

Finally, certain features repeatedly occur in the first and all later editions alike which, although they concern neither identifying the author nor reproaching the editors—if indeed the latter were not at fault—nonetheless greatly detract from the credit of an accurate edition: namely, some errors of no slight importance, easy to recognize but exceedingly difficult to correct in accordance with the author’s intention; and numerous dislocations which at one point convey an obscure, at another an incomplete, and perhaps even a sense foreign to the author. Hence one may rightly say that, among all the editions bearing Zeno’s name, none has yet appeared which truly is or ought to be called an edition of Zeno.

[Col. 0014B] III. To remedy all these defects, a new edition had to be prepared in which, as the method of accurate editions demands, foreign sermons would be separated from Zeno’s genuine ones, lacunae would be supplied, errors corrected, and the holy Bishop restored to his own works and his authority vindicated.

For several years, therefore, we had been contemplating the preparation of an edition of this kind, long desired by learned men and absolutely necessary for restoring Saint Zeno’s honour unimpaired. But since nothing can be accomplished in such matters without manuscripts, and since in reading we had learned of a most ancient manuscript presented nearly nine hundred years before by Archbishop Hincmar to the library of the Benedictines of Reims—a manuscript mentioned by Father Ruinart in the *Acts of Saint Arcadius*, by Father Constantius in the *Vindications of Ancient Manuscripts*, p. 293, and in the Verona edition of Hilary, p. 463, as well as elsewhere by others—we thought that whatever diligence we might devote to other, much later manuscripts would be held of no account, or of very little account, if we passed over so ancient a manuscript already known to the scholarly world.

[Col. 0014C] We therefore thought it necessary to postpone our intended work until an opportunity should arise to consult and collate that manuscript through someone. Meanwhile it happened that Marquis Scipio Maffei, the most illustrious ornament of the entire republic of letters, undertook a learned journey to France. Considering this a most opportune occasion, we hoped that the manuscript would be collated with the printed editions as carefully as possible, and that its variant readings and other noteworthy matters would be transcribed.

Accordingly, this distinguished scholar, the outstanding patron of every humane art and discipline, and a most devoted admirer of Saint Zeno, to whom our plan was very pleasing, on arriving at Paris immediately dealt with the learned and noble Jean Levesques de Burigny. The latter secured, through François Maillefer, librarian of the monastery of Reims, permission to inspect the manuscript.

[Col. 0015A] When the permission to read it had been most kindly granted, our Maffei, with Jean assisting in the collation, transcribed from the manuscript with the greatest diligence its variant readings and other matters deserving attention. As soon as he returned to Verona, he communicated everything to us and strongly urged us finally to put our hands to the work.

It can scarcely be said with what eagerness we immediately took up the undertaking which had long been laid aside and almost abandoned. We promptly arranged for other manuscripts, which, though much more recent, nevertheless often provide no small assistance, to be sought out from various places and collated with the printed editions. It fortunately happened, through the favour of many people toward this edition, that we received, beyond all expectation, collations of eight further manuscripts, mostly of considerable value, from various regions. Since these will add great distinction to this edition, they also stimulated our eagerness to labour diligently upon it.

But before we state what we ourselves have accomplished, something must be said concerning the manuscripts themselves, as learned persons usually expect in such works. Since the most ancient among them, the manuscript of Reims, is to be as it were the basis and foundation of the whole structure, we understand that a more careful description of it ought especially to be given.

[Col. 0015B] IV. It is a parchment manuscript in small folio, of 140 pages, written in a script approaching printed type and by two hands. One hand copied the whole first book and also the second as far as Treatise XXX, in letters of larger size; the other added the remaining eleven treatises in letters of somewhat narrower size.

On the first folio the following words are written in capital letters of larger size: “Hincmar, Archbishop, gave [this] to Saint Remigius”; yet the first two words were written at the bottom of one blank page, while the remaining three were written at the bottom of the facing page, which is likewise written upon. The same formula, in the same script and arrangement, is found repeated four times elsewhere: three times in the course of the work, and for the last time at its end.

[Col. 0015C] At the beginning of the book, in a more recent hand and smaller letters, there appears: “Book of Saint Remigius of Reims, vol. XXXI”; and then in another, perhaps older, hand: “Let him who removes the book of Saint Remigius from it be anathema.”

There precedes a sermon of the venerable notary Coronatus concerning the Life of Saint Zeno, Bishop and Confessor, which we shall give among the documents. At its end, another and later hand has added: “His translation remains.” These words indicate the translation of Saint Zeno’s body, performed at the beginning of the ninth century and not described by Coronatus in the Life.

There follows the title of Zeno’s work in these words: “Treatises of Saint Zeno, Bishop of Verona.” The treatises are divided into two books, each preceded by a table of contents. The first contains sixty-two treatises, the second forty-one; of these, the final eleven were added by another, later writer in a script of smaller size, as we have just observed. The titles are painted in capital red letters.

[Col. 0015D] At the end of the manuscript is read the already-mentioned notice, written in capital letters: “Hincmar, Archbishop, gave [this] to Saint Remigius.” This is the description of the manuscript.

V. We now make some observations on the manuscript’s antiquity and importance. It is especially important to consider certain marginal rubrics added to several treatises by an ancient but second hand. Although each will be quoted and explained in the notes appended in its proper place, we think it both agreeable to readers and highly useful to our purpose to set their catalogue before their eyes here.

For these notes are such as to make it certain that, before the manuscript came into Hincmar’s possession at Reims, it belonged to the Church of Verona and had long been in use there in public ecclesiastical offices. This contributes greatly to establishing the manuscript’s antiquity and demonstrating the distinguished character of its origin.

[Col. 0016A] We shall set down these notes not in the order of the treatises to which they are attached, but in the order of the feasts and weekdays on which certain of Zeno’s treatises are marked to be read during sacred offices. We shall identify the treatises to which you will find them appended in their proper places and elucidated by commentary.

Treatise III, Book II, has this in the margin: “To be read to the brethren on the Nativity of the Lord, in the chamber, after the entrance of the deacons and before the bishop.”

Treatise XIII, Book I: “On the octave of the Lord, the bishop’s ninth lesson.”

Treatise LXXII, Book II: “To be recited on the first Saturday of the first month, before the bishop and before the procession.”

Treatise XXX: “At the first scrutiny, to be recited in the ambo by the bishop to the children.”

Treatise XXXVI: “To be recited by the bishop to the children before baptism.”

Treatise XXXVIII: “At Easter, to be recited by the bishop to the children after baptism.”

Treatise LV: “At Easter, to be recited before the bishop in the chamber after the entrance of the deacons, on Easter Day itself.”

Treatise XLV: “To be recited in the assembly by the deacon, on Easter Day itself, before the bishop, after he has come down from the chamber with the deacons and taken his seat, when apples have been offered in accordance with the custom and peace has been given, the bishop saying: ‘Christ has risen.’ R[esponse] of the others: ‘And ill. [incomplete]’”

Treatise XLIV: “To be recited from the ambo by a subdeacon, while the bishop sits in the assembly with the brethren.”

[Col. 0016D] Treatise LII: “On Easter Monday, to be recited in the assembly to the brethren before the bishop, before the station.”

Treatise XLIII: “To be read from the ambo at Saint Stephen’s, at the Martyrs, on Easter Monday, before the bishop begins to celebrate the sealing of the Holy Spirit.”

Treatise L: “On Easter Tuesday, to be recited in the assembly to the brethren before the bishop, before the station.”

Treatise LI: “At Easter, on Wednesday, in the assembly to the brethren, etc., as in the preceding rubric.”

Treatise XLVII: “On Easter Thursday, in the assembly, etc., as above.”

Treatise XXXV: “To be recited by the bishop to the children before baptism at Pentecost.”

[Col. 0017A] Treatise LXX: “On the feast of Saints Firmus and Rusticus, to be recited to the brethren.”

From these rubrics it is certainly clear that the Reims manuscript was for the public use of some church, from which the sacred reading to be delivered in religious assemblies on certain fixed days was to be taken. That the church for whose use it served was none other than the Church of Verona is shown, beyond conjecture drawn from Zeno himself, bishop of that city, especially by two rubrics: one attached to Treatise XLIII, Book II, where the church of Saint Stephen “at the Martyrs” is mentioned; the other attached to Treatise LXX, where the feast of Saints Firmus and Rusticus is mentioned.

These two together apply uniquely to the Church of Verona, in which there is a celebrated and ancient church of Saint Stephen at the Martyrs, and where the feast-day of the holy martyrs Firmus and Rusticus, whose bodies rest here, is solemnly observed, as we shall show more fully in the observations on these marginal rubrics in their proper place.

[Col. 0017B] It is therefore evident that this manuscript served the Church of Verona for a long time before Hincmar acquired it. From this its antiquity may be inferred. For if this manuscript was in use by the Church of Verona before Hincmar, it is plainly older even than the archbishop’s own age; for it would not have been necessary to add those marginal rubrics in another hand to a manuscript recently copied for Hincmar’s benefit, just as indeed they are not found added in other manuscripts.

Accordingly, the same manuscript appears to have been written at least a century before Hincmar’s time, and may therefore rightly be believed to belong at least to the eighth century. This perhaps explains why, after the Life of Saint Zeno written by the notary Coronatus, mention is made of the translation omitted by him in the words, “His translation remains.” It is sufficiently credible that this addition was placed at Verona by a second, but still ancient, hand at the beginning of the ninth century, when the translation had scarcely been performed and before the manuscript came into Hincmar’s hands. The manuscript itself must therefore be said to have been copied in its first hand at least in the eighth century.

[Col. 0017C] Moreover, since it was in such extensive use in the church in which Saint Zeno held office, it must certainly be believed to have been copied with the greatest care from older exemplars. This especially commends its excellence when joined to so great antiquity.

So much concerning the most ancient manuscript of Reims. We now turn to the others individually, though more briefly.

VI. Having found in Giacomo Filippo Tomasini’s *Venetian Manuscript Libraries*, p. 57, mention of a Zenonian manuscript preserved in the library of the Regular Clerics of Tolentino, as they are called at Venice, we informed Jean-François Séguier of Nîmes, the inseparable companion of Marquis Maffei on his learned journeys. Since he had recently been in that city, he collated it most carefully with the printed editions, with the assistance of Father Francesco Berlendis, a regular cleric of that place.

[Col. 0017D] It is a parchment manuscript, in a most beautiful hand, thought to belong approximately to the thirteenth century. Its readings come very close to those of the Reims manuscript, but it appears to have been copied by a less skilled and less careful scribe, since frequent omissions occur when the same word recurs in a passage.

Its beginning is as follows: “Chapters of the first book of the most holy Zeno, Bishop of this nourishing city of Verona and outstanding Doctor.” The word “this” reveals that the manuscript itself was either written at Verona or derived from some ancient Veronese manuscript.

The first page of the first treatise, *On Chastity*, is lacking, and it begins with the words “slippery advantage.” In the treatise *On Patience*, a long fragment of four pages from the treatise on Psalm 128 has been inserted continuously into the text. This fragment is subsequently omitted from that treatise when it is copied near the end of the manuscript.

[Col. 0018A] This seems to have happened because the manuscript was copied from an exemplar in which a quire of the treatise on Psalm 128 had been displaced from its proper location and, by some error, bound into the treatise *On Patience*, without the copyist of the Tolentino manuscript noticing it. We shall shortly see that precisely the same thing occurred in the Vatican manuscript.

The second book, written throughout in the same hand as the whole manuscript, contains the addition of the eleven treatises which we observed as added in the Reims manuscript by another hand. Only in these is the treatise *On Envy and Jealousy* divided into two; the same feature is found in the Vatican manuscript. These eleven treatises, which become twelve because of the division just mentioned, are followed by the treatise *On the Sign of the Holy Cross*. This is an eight-stanza hymn, which we shall show in the preface to the Appendix to have been excerpted from Prudentius’s longer hymn; and this addition is found in two other manuscripts, the Vatican and the Pompeian.

[Col. 0018B] The second book then ends with this clause: “Here end [the works] of Saint Zeno, most holy Bishop of the city of Verona and most diligent shepherd of that city.” This clause is read only in another manuscript of the monastery of Saint Zeno.

Finally, two treatises are added in that manuscript, which are likewise copied in two other Zenonian manuscripts: one on the Life, the other on the Translation of Saint Zeno. They are the two documents composed by a certain monk of Saint Zeno’s monastery, which Marquis Scipio Maffei published among other materials appended to his diplomatic history, p. 320; and both likewise appear in the Pompeian and Zenonian manuscripts.

VII. We learned that there are four manuscripts of Saint Zeno in the Vatican Library. But since the shelfmarks of only two were available, we obtained from Father Giuseppe Bianchini collations only of Vaticanus 1235 and Vaticanus Urbinas 150. These had been identified in the edition of Saint Gaudentius by Paolo Galeardi, Canon of Brescia, who further stated, on the testimony of Francesco Bianchini and Carlo Majello, most learned Roman prelates, that they were written in the thirteenth century.

[Col. 0018C] It was especially important to have these carefully collated. Both contain an inserted sermon of Saint Gaudentius which, in the first edition of Saint Zeno also, occupies the penultimate place in the third book. From this we recognize that the manuscript found by Guarino in the library of the episcopal palace at Verona closely resembled these two. We particularly wished to see whether the order of treatises in those manuscripts was the same as, or different from, that in the other manuscripts; and determining this was highly relevant to deciding without rashness the chief controversy in this matter.

The Vatican manuscript, which Father Giuseppe Bianchini also considers to have been written in the thirteenth century, is parchment and much more correct than the Venetian manuscript of the Regular Clerics of Tolentino. Yet, because it likewise contains the same four pages wrongly transferred into the sermon *On Patience*, and likewise divides that same Basilian treatise into two, it appears to have derived from the same source as the Venetian manuscript.

[Col. 0019A] In other respects it has the same order of treatises as the remaining manuscripts. Only after the eleven treatises copied by another hand near the end in the Reims manuscript, and after the treatise *On the Sign of the Cross*, there follows on p. 197 the aforementioned sermon of Saint Gaudentius of Brescia, *On Peter and Paul*; then on p. 198 another addition, as follows:

> “Here begins [the work] of Saint Vigilius, Bishop, on the praises of the most blessed martyrs Sisinnius, Alexander, and Martyrius, whose relics came through James, an illustrious man, to Bishop John of the city of Constantinople.”

This is the letter of Saint Vigilius, Bishop of Trent, written to Saint John Chrysostom, which the Bollandists published from another Vatican manuscript, no. 5374.

The beginning of our Vatican manuscript is: “Treatises of Saint Zeno, most holy Bishop and Shepherd of this most noble and magnificent city of Verona.” From this it is recognized that the manuscript was either Veronese or once copied from an older Veronese manuscript.

VIII. The Urbino manuscript 150, somewhat later than the Vatican manuscript described thus far and, in Father Joseph Blanchini’s opinion, perhaps written in the fourteenth century [Col. 0019C], is likewise on parchment. It begins as follows: “Sermon I of Zeno, Bishop of Verona, a most holy and learned man, On Chastity.” Some pages are missing here and there; but the order of the treatises is precisely the same. There is no addition of the Hymn on the Sign of the Cross; but on p. 163 verso is the sermon of Saint Gaudentius, and on p. 148 the letter of Saint Vigilius of Trent, with the same titles that we transcribed from the Vatican manuscript. In addition, there are five short works bearing the name of Saint Jerome, partly his genuine productions and partly spurious; then, at the end of the volume, this closing formula is appended: “The end of the work of Saint Zeno, Bishop, and of certain other matters.”

Two rubrics prefixed to two treatises of Saint Zeno in this manuscript ought not to be passed over. The first, before Treatise 14 of Book II: “Third Sunday in Lent, Lesson I, II, III: Treatise on Judas.” The other, before Treatise 15 of the same Book II: “Treatise on Job, Lesson of Blessed Zeno, Bishop of this See.” Since this latter rubric makes clear that this manuscript also belonged to the Church of Verona, or rather was copied from some older manuscript intended for the use of that Church, both titles plainly show that these sermons were at one time publicly read in that Church during the sacred offices. This usage was introduced later than the rubrics of the Rheims manuscript were written; for, among its many annotations of this kind, they contain nothing of the sort. Perhaps for this reason Ratherius, bishop of this see, drew a certain testimony of Zeno three times from the sermon on Judas, as we shall observe more fully in note 32 on that treatise [Col. 0020A].

To these two Roman manuscripts must be added a manuscript written for the Basilica of Saint Peter in the Vatican at the beginning of the thirteenth, or of the fourteenth, century, marked F. 33. Since Joseph Blanchini most graciously supplied it to us only at the very end, when the edition was already advancing and time did not permit us to await a collation of the whole work, we requested and obtained variant readings only for several treatises and difficult passages. In other respects, the same order of treatises appears in this manuscript as well, and the same Appendix as in the Rheims manuscript; only the titles differ here and there. Enough concerning the external manuscripts.

IX. To say something now concerning the Veronese manuscripts: among the manuscripts of the monastery of Saint Zeno, that manuscript was not found which Peter Calo of the Order of Preachers, at the beginning of the fourteenth century, testifies in the manuscript Collectanea cited by Henschenius that he had seen there. We did, however, find in the library of that monastery one somewhat later manuscript, made and written on parchment, apparently in the fifteenth century. It is the very manuscript which the Veronese editors call “ancient,” as we indicated a little earlier in this preface. The order in this manuscript is the same as in the others; the number of added treatises is the same as in the Rheims manuscript; only the titles or headings of the treatises vary here and there, several such titles being found in the first edition but not in the manuscripts mentioned.

The treatises are followed by the Life of Saint Zeno and the history of his Translation, written by a monk of Saint Zeno; then by the closing formula of the kind we mentioned at the end of the Venetian manuscript; and finally, in another hand, a fragment is appended of the Rhythm on the Praises of Verona, which, as we shall state elsewhere, was written by an anonymous author in the time of Pippin [Col. 0020C]. Father Vareschi, a monk and librarian of the same monastery, provided a copy of the manuscript and assisted in collating it.

X. Another paper manuscript, written in a very poor hand toward the end of the fifteenth century and containing various miscellaneous works by different authors, presents first seven sermons excerpted from some Zeno manuscript. Six of these name Zeno as author; the other was taken from the Appendix. They are written in this order: “On Attend to Yourself,” from the Appendix; “On Chastity”; “On Continence”; “On the Nativity of the Lord”; “On Humility”; “On the Prophet Jonah”; “On the Resurrection.”

XI. We did not examine the manuscript which we shall call the Sparaverian manuscript. But the most celebrated and noble Francesco Sparaveri once collated it with the printed editions and recorded its variant readings in observations on Zeno’s sermons. While planning a new edition of this writer, he laboured on these observations toward the end of his life; death interrupted him, leaving them incomplete [Col. 0020D]. We do not know whose manuscript it was or where it now is, unless perhaps it ought to be identified with the manuscript reported to have been among the books of the younger Sebastian Pisani, bishop of Verona and a contemporary of Sparaveri; yet we have been unable to discover where it passed after his death.

Sparaveri’s manuscript seems to have been of nearly the same type as the parchment manuscript of the monastery of Saint Zeno, since it often bears the same titles of treatises [Col. 0021A]. Yet, because it differs in certain respects and gives different readings in some places, as we shall note in the annotations to be supplied in their proper places, it clearly derives from a different exemplar. We owe its variant readings to Sparaveri, and have excerpted them from his observations, which will be printed at the end of the present volume.

XII. Finally, Count Alessandro Pompeo supplied a manuscript of a more recent age indeed, but written by a more accurate copyist; it should accordingly henceforth be called the Pompeian manuscript. From the pedigree of the Pellegrina family, artistically depicted at its front with the inscription “Peregrino Peregrini,” it is known that it once belonged to that distinguished man of the family, who flourished after the middle of the fifteenth century; and the manuscript appears to have been written about the same time [Col. 0021B]. The order and number of treatises are the same as in the Rheims manuscript.

The hymn on the Sign of the Cross is added, though without any title: written in the same continuous sequence as the final added treatise in the first hand, it is set apart by a second hand. Moreover, the final pages contain the Life and Translation of Saint Zeno, composed by a monk of Saint Zeno, and the fragment of the Pippinian Anonymous, as in the manuscript of the monastery of Saint Zeno. It may seem surprising that in the excellent library of the chapter of Verona, where so many ancient manuscripts are carefully preserved, no manuscript of Saint Zeno could be found. But since not a few others, whose former presence there is recorded, have perished through the vicissitudes of time, we do not doubt that manuscript books of Saint Zeno likewise disappeared among them.

That some manuscript of this kind was indeed there may be inferred not merely from John, priest and mansionary of the Church of Verona, who— as we shall note more fully in Dissertation I, chapter 3, §1—quite probably saw and read Zeno’s manuscript nowhere else; it also seems plainly established by the Venetian edition of Saint Zeno. Since it mentions a manuscript discovered by Guarino in the library of the Veronese episcopal palace, and since no other episcopal library is recorded except that of the chapter of the cathedral church, we judge beyond doubt that the manuscript was found in that library [Col. 0021C].

XIII. Thus there are nine manuscripts which we had the opportunity to possess. They were all the more useful because, except for the paper Zeno manuscript, each contains all the sermons of Saint Zeno individually; thus it was possible to compare all the sermons with eight manuscripts, except for several treatises for which neither the late-reported manuscript of the Vatican Basilica nor Sparaveri, who left his work unfinished, supplied variant readings [Col. 0021D].

Although all these manuscripts follow not only the same order of sermons seen in the most ancient Rheims manuscript, but also present in one hand copied treatises which in the Rheims manuscript are written in two hands, no one should therefore imagine that all the others flowed from this Rheims manuscript as from a source. On the contrary, since in the Rheims manuscript the copyist has repeatedly passed over, by inadvertent leaps, certain sentences—besides variant readings and varying titles—which ought each to be noted in their proper places and which we have found supplied in the other manuscripts, it is evident beyond doubt that some ancient copyist used other complete manuscripts, older than the Rheims manuscript, from which those sentences were supplied [Col. 0022A]. How much this contributes both to proving the antiquity of this collection and to showing the number of ancient exemplars, no one can fail to see.

XIV. If one may make a highly probable conjecture concerning the very origin of the collection—a matter that will be useful in many respects—we believe that it was drawn up and copied shortly after the holy bishop’s death, at the end of the fourth or beginning of the fifth century, from the papers he left at Verona. Certain imperfect, repeated, and wholly mutilated sermons strongly persuade us that the author neither compiled nor published it himself.

For among the ancient Fathers of the Church, one principal, perhaps the principal, concern was to commit to writing and publish works composed against pagans or heretics, as well as historical, catechetical, and other works useful or necessary under various titles [Col. 0022B]. But sermons familiarly delivered by any bishop to the people were not given such attention. For they generally delivered these extemporaneously, without committing them to writing; or, if they committed them to writing, they did not polish them with such care as to judge them fit for publication. Hence, among the almost countless bishops whom antiquity commends even for eloquence, very few written sermons have reached us; and not all of these were collected and published by their authors. Some were left among papers; others had persons who, after the authors’ deaths, took care to gather and publish them.

There is, however, this difference between sermons collected and published by their authors and those collected by others. Sermons of the first kind are found complete, proportionate, worked out, and highly polished, since no one customarily publishes anything except what is perfect and more thoroughly elaborated. Discourses of the other kind, by contrast, often appear rough and sometimes mutilated and incomplete [Col. 0022C]. Therefore, although Saint Zeno is the first among the Latin Fathers whose sermons were published, as will be shown in the prologue to Dissertation II, he should nevertheless not be thought to have compiled and published this collection himself. Rather, the materials which he left in papers after his death for use in the very numerous sermons that he delivered to the people were found by others; and, because of the outstanding reputation of the holy man, they were judged worthy of diligent collection. This was done with such care that whatever could be found, whether complete or less complete, was judged worthy of collection and publication—even if it were a slight fragment, a mere opening, or even a single period [Col. 0022D].

This observation was altogether necessary for defending quite a few passages which we have noted in Zeno’s treatises as incomplete or repeated word for word, with only a few additions or changes. Had the author himself intended to publish them, there is no doubt that he would have suppressed the repetitions and brought the rest to completion and polished them. From this also arises a conjecture regarding certain corrupt passages which no manuscripts could remedy: this did not occur through the fault of all copyists independently falling into the same error, but perhaps through a necessity confronting the first collector. Since he had undertaken to gather every work of Zeno, whatever it might be, even fragments, from papers partly erased or containing overwritten words or lines, as commonly happens in a first draft, he was at times obliged to copy what could not be read well, or where perhaps something was missing [Col. 0023A]. In such circumstances the same collector necessarily erred in some places, read one word for another, and even produced a mutilated sense. Later copyists reproduced these defects, so that there is no hope that any other manuscripts which perhaps exist somewhere will cure certain passages.

Therefore, if a few passages in this edition prove less than satisfactory, let no one blame either the author—as though he were not the most eloquent and lucid speaker whom we know from his other treatises—or us, who, when the manuscripts gave no help, ought by no means to have imposed corrections upon the text at our own discretion [Col. 0023B]. Rather, let him recall the nature of the collection which we have described, and render a fair judgment both concerning the author and concerning us, indeed even concerning the ancient collector himself.

XV. Once these facts concerning the manuscripts are known, how much progress we have nevertheless made from them in distinguishing the genuine sermons of Saint Zeno from the spurious, in correcting many passages, and in recording the more important variant readings in the annotations appended to each treatise, will be evident from the dissertations and annotations themselves. Now, in speaking of the division and order of the entire edition and of our other contributions, let no one take offence if we have followed neither the division and order of the manuscripts [Col. 0023C] nor that of the printed editions.

Had we followed the arrangement and order of the printed editions, spurious works would have had to be published intermingled with genuine ones; and, if these were separated, the size of the books would have been less even. Moreover, the headings of the treatises, altered in the printed editions, when restored exactly according to the manuscripts’ authority, sometimes seemed to require a different order. We were deterred from retaining the manuscript order, the same in all of them, because the manuscripts not only intermingle short treatises with long ones, which seemed no small inconvenience, but even scatter and separate in various places treatises having the same title and subject, which should have been published together. No sufficient reason occurs for this arrangement, except that the first collector copied down whatever came into his hands in whatever order, having no other principle in writing than to record in a manuscript everything Zenonian found among the papers [Col. 0023D].

Thus this deliberation long held us in no slight uncertainty. Whatever alternative arrangement came to mind soon began to displease us as various difficulties arose from every side, and no sufficiently safe principle of division and order presented itself that was free from every objection. Since some decision had to be made, the course that seemed least open to criticism was this: repeating in general the manuscript headings prefixed to each treatise, and gathering together treatises of the same heading, we divided all the sermons into two books [Col. 0024A].

Into the first we placed the longer treatises. If we inserted among them one very short treatise On Avarice, we did so because it was not right to separate it from two others of the same subject. These comprise all the treatises on virtues and vices, together with four other longer works to be given at the end of the same book. In the second book the shorter treatises will be set out. Though more numerous, they are, because of their brevity, nearly equal in bulk to the longer ones. First will be placed those concerning Christ as God and man; then those concerning the saints of the Old Testament; and finally the treatise on Saint Arcadius, the only martyr of the New Testament whom Saint Zeno is found to praise.

Several treatises on a passage of Scripture will follow; and lastly will be appended many short Paschal treatises, which we judged should be prefaced by a particularly important warning to readers [Col. 0024B]. So that no one may miss the order of the manuscripts and of the commonly cited Veronese edition, we shall provide both, compared with the new arrangement, in separate tables before the sermons themselves.

XVI. These two books, containing Zeno’s genuine treatises, will be followed by an Appendix, into which we have relegated eleven treatises wrongly ascribed to him and restored to their true authors. You will learn about these from a special preface. We have placed over the sermons themselves the title “Treatises,” rather than “Sermons,” which was used in earlier editions, because all the manuscripts consistently bear that title, and because this designation is proper to ancient ecclesiastical usage and is found more frequently employed [Col. 0024C].

For although *tractatus* formerly meant discussions by bishops concerning some matter of the Church, as is clear from Cyprian’s Letters 51 and 52, and although in Zeno *tractatus* sometimes denotes discussions on the faith written and published in those times, as will become plain from note 26 on Treatise 1 of Book I; nevertheless, just as *tractare*—which, as Optatus attests in Book VII against Parmenianus, belongs to bishops—is first used by Cyprian in Letter LVI, and thereafter often by others, to mean delivering a sermon in public assemblies of the Church, so the word *tractatus* became established as the formal term for an episcopal sermon solemnly addressed to the people. In the same sense it is commonly prefixed to the sermons of very many ancient Fathers, as we learn from the manuscripts of Saints Gaudentius, Augustine, Leo the Great, and others, and also from some editions accurately based on the authority of manuscripts [Col. 0024D].

Concerning the annotations which we have appended to every treatise, we warn readers that we did not propose merely to provide grounds for corrections, record selected variant readings, or explain more difficult passages. We also considered several other matters necessary both for establishing the author’s age and for defending the purity of his Latin expression. Thus, for the sake of certain persons held captive by several entrenched prejudices, it was necessary in some places to cite parallel statements from other Fathers of the fourth or even a later century, in order to prove that certain formulae or passages of Zeno, commonly supposed to be much older, may likewise belong to the fourth or even a later century [Col. 0025A].

We have sought to justify several less common words or modes of expression, which might appear exotic or characteristic of debased Latin, by citing examples from approved writers, where possible. Thus the very few expressions that we found in no other author remain sufficiently defended by the rest, especially since not all Roman and ancient words occur in the books of ancient writers. We have also occasionally touched upon certain matters which, though known to the learned, someone might perhaps judge should be passed over. But whoever he may be, we ask him to consider that we also had to consult the interests of the less learned, among whom there are likewise those who desire an edition of Zeno [Col. 0025B].

XVII. The plan of the three dissertations which constitute the Zenonian preliminaries is as follows. In the first, after the author’s genuine treatises have been separated from the spurious, a defence and vindication of the genuine ones will be supplied against the objections raised by critics. At the same time, the author’s certain date—whence the principal difficulties urged against him arose—will, in our judgment, be proved so clearly that no one but an excessively captious judge will refuse assent.

In the second, after certain matters have been set forth in the prologue concerning the usefulness and importance of these treatises for knowing some chief points of doctrine and ancient discipline—matters which, unless they had found a suitable place there, ought not to have been omitted here [Col. 0026A]—certain of the author’s somewhat harsher statements will be defended. Above all, the suspicion of Arian heresy brought against Zeno by Petavius will be most clearly refuted and demolished, through the explanation, by a new interpretation, of several of his passages not properly understood hitherto.

The third dissertation will set forth in four chapters whatever bears upon placing the life, death, and cult of the most holy bishop in clearer light. We omit, lest we become too tedious, an account of the remaining contributions that we have made toward completing this edition, since they will be apparent from their reading. One thing remains: that, for honour’s sake, we name our most deserving bishop Giovanni Bragadin and Giovanni Francesco Muselli, archpriest of the cathedral church. They gave this edition the fullest support and wished it to appear from the press of the seminary, recently established and equipped through the counsel and assistance of them both. We pray that God, the Best and Greatest, may preserve them long in health and safety, no less for the good of this Church than for that of learning [Col. 0026B].

[Col. 0025]

# DISSERTATIONS ON THE WORKS, ACTS, CULT, AND AGE OF SAINT ZENO

[Note: [Col. 0025D] In the Ballerini edition, indexes contained between pages XXVI and XXXIII precede this section; we have deliberately omitted them, since they contribute nothing useful to our edition. EDS.]

[XXXIII]

# FIRST DISSERTATION. ON THE GENUINE TREATISES OF SAINT ZENO AND HIS AGE

[Col. 0025]

## PROLOGUE

In this prologue, after recounting various critical judgments and difficulties, and then separating by the certain evidence of the manuscripts the spurious treatises that were the source of the chief difficulties, we set forth what must be determined in this dissertation concerning the remaining genuine works.

[Col. 0025C]

Before separating Saint Zeno’s genuine works from those wrongly attributed to him and establishing him as their certain author, we understand that we must set forth what learned men have thought on this matter and the arguments that moved them. We must begin with Sixtus of Siena, who first raised difficulties of no small importance and held the torch before the rest.

Accordingly, after listing in Book IV of his *Bibliotheca* the sermons contained in the Venetian edition of 1508, he rendered this judgment concerning them: “It is established that these sermons have for the most part been collected from different authors who lived nearly two hundred years later.” Giving the basis for this judgment, he says: “For the sermons that expound the psalms enumerated by us—79, 100, 126, 127, 128, 129, and 130—were copied from Hilary’s commentaries without the alteration of a single word. The sermon *On Attend to Yourself*, together with another sermon *On Jealousy and Envy* that follows it in the same volume, belongs to Saint Basil. The remaining sermons, or rather fragments of sermons, by their diversity of style indicate various authors. Moreover, the author of the sermon On Continence contained in this work affirms that more than four hundred years had elapsed from Christ’s birth.”

Further, relying on the authority of Peter de Natalibus, bishop of Equilio, who describes Zeno’s life in his *Catalogue of Saints*, Sixtus did not doubt that the same saint flourished under the emperor Gallienus. On that hypothesis, he judged the aforementioned sermons should, for the reasons already stated [Col. 0026D], be denied to him.

After Sixtus, Cesare Baronius, later cardinal, held the same conviction in the first edition of the Roman Martyrology. Thus, following the opinion of Galesinius, he did not hesitate to number Zeno among the martyrs who suffered under Gallienus in that Martyrology. Yet he judged the author of these sermons to be not this Zeno but another Zeno, known, as he thought, to the Church of Verona, who lived shortly before Saint Ambrose—so he believed could be inferred from Ambrose’s letters. Especially, in Sermon 5 of Book III in the first Venetian edition, now Treatise 7 of Book II, the Arian heresy is expressly denounced; this shows that the author must be assigned no earlier than the fourth century [Col. 0027A].

Such being the situation, Saint Zeno’s sermons were again published at Verona by order of Cardinal Agostino Valier, through the efforts of Raffaele Bagata and Battista Peretti. Recognizing that the perpetual tradition of the Church of Verona had never known any bishop Zeno other than Zeno the bishop and martyr, they attempted in their preface to refute openly the arguments of Sixtus of Siena and, without naming him, those of Baronius, in order to defend as author of the sermons this Zeno, who was said to have suffered martyrdom under Gallienus.

To Baronius’s objection from Ambrose’s letters, they replied that nothing proves the Zeno there mentioned to have been bishop of Verona [XXXIV]. As for Arian errors, they said that Zeno could readily have attacked them against Origen, who, according to Epiphanius, was Arius’s father. Regarding the reference to four hundred years in Treatise 5 On Continence, from which Sixtus of Siena drew his conclusion, they had no doubt that an error had entered the number. Accordingly, in that treatise they substituted two hundred for four hundred [Col. 0027B].

As for the four sermons found written in Greek among Saint Basil’s homilies, they said they lacked no arguments by which it might be shown that those Greek sermons also belonged to their Saint Zeno, namely because they believed him to have preached in the East long before Saint Basil. But abandoning this matter, since they did not wish to be contentious, they turned to the five treatises that occur word for word in Saint Hilary’s commentaries. Besides these five, there is another treatise on Psalm 130, so titled by them—by us, however, *On Humility*, Treatise 7 of Book I—which is beyond doubt Zenonian, since it is not found among Hilary’s works. Therefore, they did not at all doubt that another similar treatise on the same psalm was also Zenonian, because it presents the same thoughts and sometimes the same words. They inferred that, just as this one, so also the other four, must be ascribed to the same author; and they believed all of them had been inserted by someone into Hilary’s commentary [Col. 0027C].

They declared that they had not dared to deprive Saint Zeno of the possession of praise due to him, because they had found all the treatises called Basil’s and Hilary’s by the critics in the “ancient” manuscript, as they called it, together with the Zenonian works. The objection urged by Sixtus from style and brevity was also sufficiently well refuted. Finally, to establish that the holy Zeno, an author of the third century, wrote these sermons, they sought to gather from the works themselves certain indications of antiquity, foremost among them references to persecutions and martyrs; and they cited the testimony of Peter de Natalibus, bishop of Equilio, and Flavio Biondo, both of whom preceded the first edition. Peretti, moreover, in the Latin scholia on Zeno’s Life, published subsequently in 1597, added the support of Guglielmo Pastrengo and Michele Fossati—all of whom had mentioned Zeno’s sermons before that edition [Col. 0028A].

When Baronius read this preface and understood that the Church of Verona acknowledged only one bishop Zeno, the same man who was venerated as a martyr under Gallienus and held to be the author of the sermons, he abandoned his earlier view and decided to correct the notes of the Martyrology in that respect. He promised Cardinal Valier, then residing at Rome, that he would do so, as appears from Valier’s letter to the Veronese editors dated 17 January 1587, a fragment of which Peretti published in the scholia on Zeno’s Life.

Baronius indeed fulfilled what he promised in the additions to the notes on the Martyrology inserted into the second edition. There he did not hesitate to vindicate for Zeno, martyr under Gallienus, all the treatises inscribed with his name, except only those which demonstrably argue against the Arians. He judged that these had been wrongly inserted among the Zenonian works by copyists, since it is not unprecedented for something by one author to be mingled in the works of another ancient writer [Col. 0028B].

This opinion so clung to Baronius’s mind that he wrote that those certainly seemed to him mistaken who, maintaining that there was only one Zeno, wished him to have lived in Ambrose’s time. His chief reason was that the author in the sermon On Chastity—more correctly, On Continence—reckons from the time of the Apostle Paul’s writing the First Epistle to the Corinthians “nearly four hundred years and more,” as he says. In answer to the objection, he adds: “Certainly, if anyone counts four hundred years from A.D. 57, in which year we demonstrated in the *Annals* that Paul wrote that epistle, the author must have written in A.D. 457, after Ambrose’s death, who, as Marcellinus records in his *Chronicle*, died in A.D. 397. Therefore, since that numerical indication cannot, as they wish, be fitted even to Ambrose’s time, I think no one can rightly deny that it is corrupt.” Thus he approves the Veronese editors’ correction to two hundred.

He further strives to establish by three arguments that Zeno was a writer of the third, not the fourth, century. First, he argues that the author violently attacks women who marry pagans, and reveals that temples of idols were then open and sacrifices customarily offered—things forbidden by the laws of Constantine and Constantius, and therefore, in Baronius’s judgment, alien to Ambrose’s age. Next, from Sermon 2 On Avarice, now Treatise 10 of Book I, he infers that symbols of idolatry and idols themselves were engraved on coins. This he decidedly assigns to an age in which pagan emperors ruled [Col. 0028D], for, he says, Sozomen, Book I, chapter 8, testifies that Constantine the Great ordered the sign of the Cross to be stamped upon coinage; and Baronius declares that this is shown much more clearly from extant coins of various successors of Constantine.

Finally, he presses this observation as a third argument: “Since the author, in the sermon On the Spirit, ‘The House of God Is Built,’ plainly demonstrates that in his time no church, or only very few, had been erected that could be compared with the temples of idols, he clearly indicates that he flourished before Constantine’s time. By Constantine’s agency it is certain that most magnificent basilicas were erected in the West, especially at Rome, as well as in the East, at Jerusalem, Antioch, Constantinople, and other places” [Col. 0029A].

Such was Cardinal Baronius’s final opinion. It is therefore especially surprising that Father Labbe should count him among those who thought these sermons falsely attributed to Zeno of Verona. Vossius, in *De Historia Latinitatis*, Book III, part 4, chapter 2, knowing the matter to be settled, says: “Yet this Baronius does not deny that at least several sermons are genuine.”

Leaving aside Possevino, who copies almost everything from Sixtus, we come to Bellarmine. He first observes that Zeno is mentioned neither by Eusebius in his *History* nor by Jerome in his book *On Ecclesiastical Writers*. Then, after identifying the sermons of Hilary and Basil, he says he has nothing to say about the rest except their brevity, the repetitions in some, and the obscurity of others. Finally, he declares that what carries the greatest weight with him is that there is no mention of these sermons among the ancients, and that Guarino, the Veronese orator, was the first to discover them [Col. 0029B].

Barthius, who had read Zeno’s sermons and valued them highly, judged in *Adversaria*, Book XLII, chapter 18, that their diversity was so great that he believed many pieces in that work were not only not by that most eloquent bishop, but were even far more recent than any of the body of the other sermons.

August Buchner, who also read Zeno, in Dissertation 389, p. 257, not only praises his treatises but also argues at length that they must be defended. Among other testimonies he adduces not only those of Bagata, Peretti, and Cardinal Baronius, but also that of Casaubon himself, who calls this Zeno a most ancient Father and expressly states that he wrote in the time of Decius [Col. 0029C].

Robert Cooke, an English heterodox writer, in a book published at London in 1623, entitled *A Censure of Certain Writers Commonly Cited under the Names of Holy Fathers and Ancient Authors*, p. 84, pronounced dictatorially concerning Zeno’s sermons: “Zeno of Verona is spurious.” He repeats the difficulties of Sixtus, Baronius, and Bellarmine.

André Rivet, likewise heterodox, in Book IV of his *Sacred Critic*, having not properly understood the opinion of Sixtus of Siena, added only this of his own: that none of the writings of this Zeno existed before the year 1508, when many sermons were published under his name at Venice by Guarino, the Veronese orator—as though Guarino, living in that year, had been the author and publisher of such sermons. Others subsequently copied this opinion [Col. 0029D].

Ughelli, in volume V of *Italia Sacra*, repeating Baronius’s earlier opinion in his account of the bishops of Verona, listed two Zenos: one flourishing under Gallienus, the other in Ambrose’s age. He judged the latter to be the author of the sermons.

Father Labbe—leaving aside the remaining intermediate writers, who for the most part followed Sixtus, Baronius, and Bellarmine and contributed nothing new—although he foresaw that these treatises were assigned by some learned persons to Zeno of Verona, nevertheless, hindered by the opinion that Zeno lived during Gallienus’s reign, confessed that the Veronese editors had wasted their effort in ascribing the sermons to him before competent judges and that he could not accept their opinion. He says there are ninety sermons, though there are far more, repeats the judgments of other critics, and reaches his conclusion chiefly because of the preconception that Zeno died a martyr in the third century. Then he observes, correctly, that Zeno, bishop of Verona, appears to be the man named in Ambrose’s letter and therefore cannot be placed in the third century—a point also proved, with nearly all later writers, by Father Henschenius under 12 April [Col. 0030B]. But having established this with sufficiently probable arguments, though irrelevant to his own position, he seems to forget his proper purpose and leaves untouched the controversy whether the sermons can and ought to be attributed to this Zeno.

Cave follows Labbe in all things. Only after writing with him, “No mention whatever, even the slightest, was made of these works until Guarino first published them,” he adds this on his own authority: “Very recently I learned from the notice of Monsieur Alix that a sermon of Zeno, Bishop of Verona, is cited by Ratherius of Verona, a writer of the tenth century, in Monsieur d’Achery’s *Spicilegium*, volume II.” Yet he then leaves undecided whether this sermon belongs to the number of those now circulating under Zeno’s name.

Louis Ellies Dupin’s exceedingly harsh criticism [Col. 0030C] must be transcribed word for word from the Latin translation:

It is certain that the discourses extant under Zeno’s name cannot be by the man whom they suppose to have undergone martyrdom under Gallienus. For their author, in the fifth discourse (he seems to have cited this from Baronius; it is now Tractate 7, Book II), speaks of Christ’s divinity against heretics who, while admitting that the Word is God, did not believe him coeternal with the Father and thought that there had been a time when he did not exist. This plainly shows that the Arian heresy was already prevalent in his time. Nor can these discourses even be by Zeno of Verona, who lived under Constantius and Julian, because they are excerpts drawn from many authors. Four of them are entire works of Basil. All the homilies on the Psalms are drawn word for word from Hilary’s Commentaries [Col. 0030D]—a point which he explains in the accompanying notes. “The discourses,” he says, “on Psalms 126, 127, 128, 129, and 130 are Hilary’s. The discourses on Psalms 49, 79, and 100 may also be his, because this Father’s commentaries on those psalms have perished.”

The text then continues: “It is therefore clear that these discourses attributed to Zeno of Verona are a disorderly collection of sermons by a great many authors. Some are extremely short, while others are long; some are written in a full and polished style, others in a low and uncultivated manner; some are clear, others obscure; in short, nothing could be more uneven. In the discourse On Continence he counts more than four hundred years from the time when Paul wrote his epistle to the Corinthians; and yet in other homilies he mentions churches, [Col. 0031A] martyrs” (this is the proper rendering—not “churches of martyrs,” as is read in the Paris translation because of a missing comma in the French edition; what relevance that would have here no one can guess), “and catechumens” (as though catechumens had not continued beyond the fourth century). “From all this it is evident that these discourses, unknown to all antiquity, are an undigested collection, made by some unskilled copyist from sermons of several authors belonging to different periods and regions.”

In the accompanying notes he adds that certain longer discourses were drawn from Greek authors, while other very brief ones came from Latin authors and fragments of homilies.

Father Coutant, the Benedictine monk and celebrated editor of Hilary’s works, in the warning which he prefixed [Col. 0031B] to the five Hilarian treatises printed among Zeno’s works (p. 463, vol. I of the Verona edition), does not deny that the collection of treatises attributed to Zeno is ancient. Yet he maintains that it is later than Hilary’s age; or at least, he says, if anyone insists that it belongs to that Zeno who lived during Gallienus’s reign, he must certainly concede that it was subsequently enlarged with works by others, since no prudent person will deny that it consists not only of Hilary’s writings but also of several treatises by Basil.

Tillemont acknowledged that the most learned Protestants set a very high value on these treatises because of their author’s piety and elegance, and that they contain evident marks of antiquity. Yet, because certain discourses have Hilary and Basil as their assured authors, he likewise doubts the author of the rest; and he says that there is nothing persuading him that any treatise should certainly be vindicated for [Col. 0031C] Zeno of Verona. Thus he writes in *The Persecution under Valerian*, art. 7, vol. IV, p. 16. Moreover, in his notes, p. 587, note 6, after setting forth at length the opinions of Baronius, Bellarmine, Labbe, and Sixtus, he is astonished that the Verona edition changed “four hundred” into “two hundred” without the support of any manuscript; and he decisively refutes Baronius’s argument, based on the public sacrifices of pagans, offered in support of that correction. Yet he concludes that these sermons are a collection from various authors of the fourth and fifth centuries, some of which may be Zeno’s, although it is not possible to distinguish or identify them.

[XXXVII] Finally, the last of all, Johann Albert Fabricius, vol. III of the *Bibliotheca Latina*, Book IV, ch. 3, p. 420—although he briefly indicates the conflicting opinions of critics [Col. 0031D] and inclines to the view of Sixtus of Siena, namely, that these sermons were for the greater part collected from various authors—nevertheless does not hesitate to affirm: “Certainly, it seems highly credible that some of them are by that Zeno.”

Accordingly, among so many and such severe judgments of very celebrated critics concerning the Zeno treatises—apart from the extreme and opposing positions, which contend that either all the sermons or none must be attributed to Zeno—the much fairer and more probable view appears to be that of those who judge the treatises to be a collection put together from various authors, yet do not therefore deny that Zeno is at least the author of some of them. How close this judgment comes to the truth will appear from what is to be said in this dissertation. Thus [Col. 0032A] anyone who tries to deprive Zeno of all the treatises will always labor in vain, no less than one who wishes to assign them all to him. Meanwhile, however, the doubt cast by so many critics’ judgments has led many persons, since they cannot distinguish genuine treatises from spurious ones, to doubt each individual work.

But the reason why the genuine offspring of Zeno could neither have been nor can now be distinguished from the supposititious works is the fault of the editors. As we noted in the preface, they did not publish separately the spurious pieces, which were placed after the Zeno works at the ends of manuscripts; indeed, they did not even mention that they stood at the ends of the manuscripts—information which would have been sufficient for scholars to settle the whole dispute. Rather, they presented them mingled with the genuine works, without any distinguishing mark, and indiscriminately circulated them as Zeno’s. Since these cannot have Zeno as their author [Col. 0032B], they also cast all the Zeno writings into doubt. To avoid this fault and at the same time cut off the gravest prejudice, we turned to the eight manuscripts of Zeno’s works which we could find, both in Italy and in France, merely to consult them. We immediately discovered that not only the five treatises thought attributable to Hilary and the four to Basil, but also two further treatises situated between the Hilary and Basil pieces, are consistently found at the end of all the manuscripts, appended to the rest, which we regard as undoubtedly Zeno’s.

Although this may suffice to persuade those skilled in manuscripts that an addition was made by a later hand—since it often happens in other codices too that blank leaves left after copying an author are filled with writings by others—[Col. 0032C] nevertheless, lest any doubt remain concerning this addition in the Zeno manuscripts, the most ancient Rheims codex presents it written in a different, later script. This will be evident to anyone from the specimen of hands inserted in the preface, which begins the Basilian treatise. Moreover, in the Vatican and Urbino manuscripts, after the addition of the treatises just mentioned, there is a sermon of St. Gaudentius of Brescia. It is therefore found inserted among the Zeno works in the Venetian edition of Zeno. Other writings by other authors are subsequently found added toward the end in both manuscripts, as we noted in the preface; there too we mentioned another addition, namely, another treatise or a hymn on the sign of the Cross, found in three manuscripts. It is therefore quite certain that manuscripts of Zeno’s works were not [Col. 0032D] free from additions of this kind.

We have relegated to the Appendix those treatises by various authors appended at the end of all the codices, eleven in number. Their authors will be identified and established most clearly in the preface that we shall prefix there. Therefore, since we are now speaking of Zeno’s genuine treatises, there is no further difficulty concerning these eleven, which we set aside from him on the evidence of the codices themselves. Controversy can remain only concerning the rest.
