In order to establish and prove that these are entirely Zeno’s, since everything alleged or capable of being alleged against them reduces to three questions—whether all are by one author; to what age or century they belong; and finally whether the author, whatever [Col. 0033A] the century in which he lived, is St. Zeno, bishop of Verona—we undertake to establish these three points most fully in three distinct chapters: first, that all ninety-three remaining treatises, apart from the eleven relegated to the Appendix, are by a single writer; then, that this writer is shown from the treatises themselves to belong to the fourth century; and finally, that this fourth-century writer, the author of all these treatises, is none other than St. Zeno, bishop of Verona. If, after refuting everything [XXXVIII] which critics have objected against each of these points, we demonstrate these three matters clearly, nothing further, it seems, will be needed to vindicate the writings of St. Zeno. At the same time, the question concerning St. Zeno’s date will be resolved—a question which had produced the greatest prejudice among scholars in this matter, being almost settled by the contrary and commonly held interpretation of the tradition, as it is reported, of the Church of Verona.

[Col. 0033B] # CHAPTER I. IT IS ESTABLISHED BY MANY ARGUMENTS THAT THE NINETY-THREE TREATISES WHICH WE HAVE SEPARATED FROM THE ELEVEN ADDITIONS HAVE ONE AUTHOR.

## § I.—Arguments drawn from the manuscripts are proposed.

Several indications in the same codices suggest that the ninety-three treatises, divided in all manuscripts into two books and copied one after another, are by one author. There are, namely, titles prefixed to the individual treatises with certain closing formulas, as well as tables of the individual treatises in the most ancient Rheims manuscript, from which this conclusion is plainly established. For in the titles and tables [Col. 0033C], where the titles of the individual treatises are listed, the last five treatises of the second book—the ones immediately preceding the additions—are alternatively headed as follows: “Treatise by the author mentioned above.”

Here are the words of the table itself:

XXVI. Likewise, *Treatise on Easter by the author mentioned above*; now Tractate LIV, Book II.  
XXVII. *Treatise on Daniel at Easter*; now Tractate LXIX.  
XXVIII. *Invitation to the Font by the author mentioned above*; now Tractate XXXI.  
XXIX. *Paschal Treatise*; now Tractate XLII.  
XXX. *On Genesis by the author mentioned above*; now Tractate XX.

The formula “by the author mentioned above” plainly indicates that not merely these but also the intervening treatises, even though they bear no such formula, are by the same author mentioned above—that is, the one expressly named either at the beginning of the books or in the closing formulas, of which we shall speak shortly. Thus they all have one and the same author.

Perhaps it will seem strange why this formula is appended only to those final works and occurs in none of the preceding eighty-eight. But this appears to have been done by the first copyist deliberately, not by accident, because these treatises marked the end of the works by one author. So that no one might thereafter doubt whether they all had the same author, or whether some had, as often happens, been added from other authors, he judged that these last should be marked with a formula cutting off every doubt.

Moreover, this same formula is found repeated in the actual titles immediately prefixed to the final [Col. 0034A] treatises, not only in the Rheims manuscript but likewise in others. Nor does it occur again in the eleven subsequent treatises, which are headed thus: “Interpretation of Psalm 126,” “On Psalm 127,” and likewise for the rest. This is sufficient indication that scribes did not recognize these as by the same author, as they did the preceding works; accordingly, the first copyist marked the latter with that relative formula both in the titles and in the table of titles.

What is more, Discourse XXX of Book II, which we have just noted as the very last before the additions, ends in the Rheims manuscript, besides the aforementioned title-form, “On Genesis by the author mentioned above,” with this other entirely similar formula: “Here ends *On Genesis* by the author mentioned above.” In other treatises bearing this same closing formula, the author’s very name is sometimes added after it [Col. 0034B], as we shall note in due place from the annotations on the individual treatises. This closing formula, wonderfully confirming the same authorship, does not occur in the following pieces [XXXIX]; for they conclude with these words: “Psalm 128 ends”; “Psalm 129 ends”; “Psalm 130 ends, happily.” No closing formulas of this sort may be found attached to the preceding works.

Finally, something especially noteworthy must be observed in the Pompeian codex. In the title of Treatise XXX—the final treatise of Book II before the additions—it uses this singular formula, not otherwise customary: “St. Zeno of Verona, On Genesis.” By this the copyist seems to have wished to indicate that all the treatises copied up to this point belong to the author named at the beginning.

Indeed, among the following eleven treatises, which, as we shall see in the preface [Col. 0034C] to the Appendix, belong to three authors—two to Potamius, five to Hilary, and four to Basil—the manuscripts place all the works of each author together, rather than inserting one author’s works among another’s. If this order was consistently observed in the additions themselves, it is much more probable that the remaining works, also divided into two books and continuously copied according to the same arrangement, were assigned to a single author.

## § II.—The argument from style is pressed. Examples are offered, especially from the treatises which Coutant assigns to Hilary. The author is shown to have imitated Hilary in places. Examples of distinguished writers who imitated others and at times copied the very same words.

[Col. 0034D] All this is fully confirmed by the similarity of style that runs through the entire collection. Those who objected a difference in style in order to assign several authors were indeed right, and justly pressed this argument, so long as they thought that the Appendix treatises too had to be assigned to a single author. The manner of writing in those eleven treatises is not so much very different from the style of the other ninety-three as it is readily perceived to vary even among themselves. For these are the productions not of one but of three authors: Hilary delighted in a plain and easy style; Rufinus, whom we shall prove to be the translator of Basil’s four homilies, used a freer and more careful pen; and Potamius, author of the two treatises, labors in a wholly uncultivated, obscure, and difficult style, such as may be recognized in the letter published by Acherius and to be reprinted in the Appendix [Col. 0035A].

Thus, when some attempted, following the editors’ arrangement, to assign and claim all these treatises by such very different writers for one author, the objection based on stylistic difference was justly made. We are astonished that some made light of it, or thought it might be evaded on the flimsiest grounds. But if the eleven treatises mentioned are separated, as we have now done in this edition, there remains absolutely nothing to object concerning the style of the rest. If anyone applies himself for a while to turning these works over and over, so as to begin to taste and distinguish the author’s genius and manner of writing, he will surely find nothing that does not everywhere exhibit one and the same author, whether in thought, words, or syntactic construction.

Let us offer, for example, two treatises formerly on Psalms [Col. 0035B] 100 and 130, now Tractate 21, Book II, and Tractate 7, Book I. Father Coutant, in the warning to Hilary’s Commentary on the Psalms, no. 23, suspected that they should be ascribed to the bishop of Poitiers, because they contain thoughts expressed by Hilary at times in the same and sometimes in exactly the same words, as are found in his Commentary on those Psalms. From this, he says, one may judge what sort of treatises Hilary—that is, Hilary—delivered to his people, and what sort he later reworked into a commentary.

For, since two treatises on Psalm 130 were listed in the Verona edition, we relegated to the Appendix and restored to its author one of them, which is expressed in the same words as Hilary’s Commentary and is copied at the end of our manuscripts together with other Hilarian works. But Coutant thought the other, which likewise contains similar material, should also be claimed for the same author. He conjectured that Hilary first wrote this one in the style of an address to the brethren, while the other was the same work, enlarged by Hilary when he arranged the various discourses delivered to the people on the Psalms into the body [Col. 0035C] of his commentary. The same, he thinks, happened in the other treatise on Psalm 100.

But as regards the similarity of thoughts and words between Hilary’s Commentary and our author’s treatises on Psalms 100 and 130, we shall demonstrate clearly in the following chapter that our author lived somewhat after Hilary in the fourth century. Coutant never even considered this, because the prevailing assumption concerning Zeno’s antiquity prevented him from foreseeing or suspecting that our author could have had Hilary’s Commentary on the Psalms before his eyes and drawn something from it, so as to express in his own treatises not only certain thoughts but sometimes the very same words.

In fact, the author is found to have imitated Hilary in this fashion not only in the treatises just cited, Tractate 7, Book I, and Tractate 21, Book II, but also in two others: Tractate 8, Book I, entitled *On Fear*, and Tractate 17, Book II, entitled *On Jonah*. This will be plain from the annotations appended to each treatise, where we have reproduced Hilary’s words. Yet no one has ever supposed these treatises to be Hilary’s. And since they do not expound the Commentary on the Psalms, but merely touch in passing [Col. 0036A] on something from the Psalms that occurs in Hilary’s Commentary, they cannot plausibly be regarded as the kind of treatises which Coutant supposed Hilary first delivered to the people and then incorporated into his Commentary.

Likewise, we have observed four other treatises of our author—Tractates 3, 12, and 16 of Book I, and Tractate 2 of Book II—in which he expressed certain thoughts from Lactantius, and in places the very same words. Yet no one would say, or even dream, that these were written by Lactantius himself. If this sufficiently reveals an authorial disposition that does not at all shun such imitation, who can further doubt similar imitation from Hilary’s Commentary?

So that there may be no further doubt that all are by one and the same author, the same style affords abundant testimony [Col. 0036B] throughout. This is the matter proper to the present chapter and must now be discussed more fully. Father Coutant, wishing to vindicate Hilary, who is known to have drawn some material from Origen into his Commentary on the Psalms, employs this defense in the warning to the same Commentary, Psalm CLXVII, no. 13: “For it is one thing to imitate, another to translate or copy; nor does a person act as a translator who adds some things, cuts away others, and turns the rest into his own style.”

He further observes that Jerome, on this very ground, cleared Hilary from that criticism: namely, that he had set forth Origen’s books in such a way that, pleasing in his own style, he was “rather the father of the word than its translator.” Our author is found to have done exactly this when he drew certain things from Hilary or Lactantius. Adding some things, omitting others, and converting only certain and few things into [Col. 0036C] his own style, he pleased in his own style and was rather the father of the expression than a slavish copyist. What we have said of additions and omissions will be sufficiently clear from our comparisons and annotations.

As for the style, anyone who, having read Hilary’s Commentary on the one hand—for it alone occasions the difficulty—and our author’s treatises on the other, does not immediately distinguish them, wholly lacks any feel for Latin expression. Hilary’s style is plain, easy, and generally concise; ours is sometimes lofty, sometimes florid, falling into definite rhythmic cadences, readily indulging in allegorical language, and above all marked by a certain peculiar syntax, which we have so far found not only absent from Hilary but from every other Latin writer as well.

With regard to ornaments in the expression of words and thoughts, allegories, and a much greater abundance of speech [Col. 0036D], no better way of recognizing this exists than by comparing the literary works of both writers. We think that we have sufficiently indicated this in the annotations placed beneath the author’s text itself. Concerning syntax, however, we shall here append a few clauses that exhibit the author’s distinctive syntax, frequent in his other treatises.

In Tractate 7, *On Humility*, Book I—formerly the discourse on Psalm 130—no. 1:

> *De quibus Scriptura divina quid pronuntiet, audiamus, cujus ista sunt verba.*

“Let us hear what Holy Scripture pronounces concerning these matters, whose words these are.”

No. 2:

> *Ut possimus merito mereri, Scriptura quod dicit.*

“That we may be able to merit worthily—what Scripture says.””

Here *Scriptura quod dicit* stands for *quod Scriptura dicit*, “what Scripture says.”

Again:

> *Dominus ipse vos pro promisso quid hortetur accipite.*

“Receive what the Lord himself exhorts you concerning the promise.”

And again, a little later:

> *De quibus Joannes discipulis quid praedicet, omnibus est in usu.*

“What John teaches the disciples concerning these matters is familiar to all.”

But especially to be considered is no. 5:

> *Intonat lingua, caret quae numquam veneno serpentis.*

“The tongue thunders forth, which is never without the serpent’s poison.”

Here the relative *quae* is placed after the verb which governs it, just as elsewhere it is frequently placed after another word. Thus Tractate 3, no. 2:

> *Utraeque cujus exaggerare opulentiam velocitate mira contendunt.*

“Both strive with remarkable speed to exaggerate whose wealth,”

instead of *cujus opulentiam utraeque contendunt*, “whose wealth both strive to exaggerate,” etc.

[Col. 0037A] Thus Tractate 4, no. 6:

> *Quavis versutia qui fallitur numquam.*

“He who is deceived by no trickery whatever.”

Tractate 5, no. 4:

> *Observantiae qua perfectione Dei cultus debeat custodiri.*

“By what perfection of observance the worship of God ought to be maintained.”

Tractate 12, no. 6:

> *Mortemque ipsam, perennis cui beatitudo succedat.*

“Death itself, to which everlasting blessedness succeeds.”

Tractate 7, Book II, no. 4:

> *Nec tamen desiit esse, ante quod fuerat.*

“Yet it did not cease to be what it had been before.”

A similar phrase occurs in Tractate 16, Book I, no. 4:

> *Odit jam sine causa, ante quod amaverat.*

“He now hates without cause what he had formerly loved.”

Tractate 62, Book II:

> *Propter vos qui est occisus.*

“He who was slain for you.”

We omit the rest. See further, in the same Tractate 7, Book I, now [Col. 0037B] under discussion, the extremely rare syntax near the end, which in the annotations we shall show to be distinctively Zeno’s. You will find some similar instances in Tractate 21, Book II, on Psalm 100, such as this immediately after the beginning:

> *Igitur in praesenti psalmo propheta cum dicat...*

“Therefore, although the prophet says in the present psalm…”

And especially in Tractate 8, Book I, *On Fear*, and Tractate 17, Book II, *On Jonah*, the same kind of syntax and the same authorial genius are seen everywhere. If, to this very distinctive syntax, you add the remaining peculiarities of expressions, allegories, and thoughts, wholly unlike Hilary’s, do you not immediately recognize a style and an author for those treatises different from the Hilarian author, yet the same as the style and author of the remaining treatises, in which the same character, diction, and syntax continually shine forth?

[Col. 0037C] From this, then, Dupin’s bold opinion surely vanishes: his assertion that the discourses on Psalms 49, 79, and 100 might be Hilary’s because that Father’s commentaries on those Psalms have perished. For, apart from the fact that the first two treatises—formerly on Psalms 49 and 79, now Tractate 15, Book I, and Tractate 27, Book II—are not entitled “On the Psalm” in any manuscript, though Dupin’s argument rests on that title; even if we granted that St. Hilary wrote commentaries on all the Psalms which perished through the injuries of time, as Coutant argues on sufficiently probable conjectures, still all the treatises mentioned display another manner of expression and another syntax so unmistakably that anyone who does not recognize how far they are from Hilary’s has plainly not read the works of either author.

[Col. 0037D] But perhaps someone may here raise a difficulty, not concerning imitation of thoughts—which is frequent among other authors—but concerning the copying of the very words known in places to have been excerpted from Hilary. Such a person may not therefore establish Hilary as the one author of all treatises of this kind, since, where the style differs too plainly, every imitation and copying of words is useless for claiming one author; yet he may at least judge this practice unworthy and unbecoming in our author. But those versed in reading the ancients will know that it is by no means new or alien even to the practice of weighty writers.

Porphyry, in Eusebius’s *Preparation for the Gospel*, Book X, ch. 3, noted that among the Greeks Dinarchus [Col. 0038A] transferred many passages verbatim from Demosthenes’ speech *Against Conon* into his earlier speech *Against Cleomedon*. We pass over the many passages from Greek writers, without naming them, translated and inserted verbatim into their own works by Tertullian, Jerome, Ambrose, and other Latin authors; these are identified in the careful editions of those writers.

To speak, however, of Latin writers who similarly drew profit from other Latin authors: the ancient author of the books *On the Sacraments* drew from Ambrose’s book *On the Mysteries* not merely thoughts but often words as well, as the Benedictine editor observed in his prefixed warning. The same Benedictine editor of Ambrose observed, in the warning to sermons ascribed to this Father, that St. Maximus of Turin, having diligently studied the works of the celebrated Ambrose, inserted large fragments drawn from them—especially from the Commentary on Luke—into his own [Col. 0038B] sermons.

What more need be said? Although St. Cyprian was eloquent and learned, did he not copy some things verbatim from Minucius Felix’s little book in the works which he composed against the Gentiles? This is displayed to view by setting out the passages from both writers in vol. II of the *Apparatus to the Great Library of the Fathers*, pp. 34–37. Who, then, should any longer wonder if our most elegant author sometimes took a few things from Hilary—from that great and celebrated bishop who, to use Jerome’s words in Epistle 34 to Marcella, “in his own times was everywhere renowned throughout the Roman world for the merit of his confession, the labor of his life, and the brilliance of his eloquence”?

[Col. 0038C] [XLII] ## § III.—Other objections refuted.

Another objection must be answered here. It exaggerates a certain remarkable diversity in these ninety-three treatises and seems to prove multiple authors. Certain critics have thought that nothing could be more uneven than these treatises: some are long, others short; many are repetitive; some are clear, others obscure. Dupin judged that the longer ones had been translated from Greek authors, while the shorter were put together from Latin authors and fragments of homilies.

But if someone insists upon the brevity of some or the length of others, does this establish different authors? Does not St. Leo, who wrote several fairly lengthy sermons, also have brief ones nearly equal in length to our author’s? See Sermons 5, 6, 7, and 12. Are not brief works likewise found in Augustine, who otherwise composed mostly long works? Perhaps someone will say that works as brief as some of ours have no parallel anywhere else. What then? If this proves anything, it proves not only that they are not by our author, but that they can be attributed to no ancient writer at all—nothing could be more absurd.

Who would believe that the apostle St. John, already an old man and hindered by age itself, gave sermons so brief that he said only, “Little children, love one another,” and repeated the same thing often, unless St. Jerome had committed this to writing from ancient tradition? Why might not others, prevented for some reason from preaching at greater length, have delivered brief sermons to the people? If these are not found collected [Col. 0039A], as are our author’s treatises, perhaps the reason is that the others wrote nothing of the kind, whereas our author did write these. We see them to be full of the gravest matters and worked out with especial care. Having been found among his papers, they were judged by an ancient collector worthy of being placed in a codex together with his other works and transmitted to posterity, especially because of the esteem which the writer enjoyed.

Why the author adopted so unusual a brevity in these treatises, we shall discuss at greater length in the warning to Tractate XXX, Book II. There we have offered several conjectures on the matter, and from the annotations of the Rheims manuscript we shall show that these treatises in particular, more than the others, are Zeno’s. For the present, we add only what serves our purpose: since the subjects contained in these admittedly [Col. 0039B] brief treatises indicate an ancient writer, there is absolutely no reason to take them away from the author of the rest when they display most plainly the same style.

Some are fragments of sermons, not sermons themselves. We readily admit this, and it has been observed in the annotations. But what follows? Do they therefore have another author? What argument, I ask, is that? Among the works of St. Peter Chrysologus there are some mutilated sermons, yet no one has therefore suspected that they should be assigned to another author.

What should we add concerning repetitions found in several treatises of this kind? [Col. 0039C] Many examples of similar repetitions are available in other Fathers too, yet no one has used them to establish multiple authors. The Benedictine editors long ago observed that St. Ambrose sometimes repeats the same things, p. 1045, vol. II: “we observe that this happens to him from time to time.” And on p. 1048 they mention that he sometimes repeats the same matters in almost exactly the same words.

Did not St. Leo the Great sometimes transfer whole chapters verbatim from one work to another? The celebrated Letter to Flavian, chapters 3 and 4, contains several passages which the most recent editor noted in the margin to have been taken verbatim from various sermons on Christ’s Nativity. In Epistle 97, to the monks of Palestine, there are seven chapters which, apart from a few words, are read in exactly the same language in Epistle 134, to the Emperor Leo. In both these letters is found a long passage from Sermon 61, *On the Passion of the Lord*, comprising two entire chapters. [Col. 0039D] Finally, and most remarkably, the two letters to Pulcheria, Epistles 27 and 30, contain mostly repeated material, as do the two to Emperor Theodosius, Epistles 39 and 40, although they were sent to the same persons and at a very short interval.

If, because of these repetitions, no one has supposed another author than Ambrose, Leo, or other writers of this kind—whom we omit for brevity—to be responsible for the repeated writings, then neither should anyone press the repetition and similarity in certain of our author’s short treatises. On this see further what we observe in the warning to Tractate 30, Book II, p. 238.

We now come to the distinction inferred from the clarity of some treatises and the obscurity of others. [Col. 0040A] But this proceeds wholly from a difference in subject matter, not in the author. It is one thing to treat virtues and vices, and other subjects of morals or sacred history, where a broader field of speech lies open and freer scope is granted to the pen; it is another to treat mysteries which the author chose to expound briefly, not in simple language but through allegories and scriptural figures.

In treatises of the first kind, the author’s speech is more open. In the second kind, however—concerning which the readings and ceremonies of Paschal feasts, as well as the author’s own genius, seem to have required that the mysteries, already familiar to all hearers, should be expressed through figures and allegories, so that they would not grow weary if such mysteries were delivered in a plain manner—the author judged that these mysteries should be represented by figures and allegories to hold and delight his hearers. From this, some obscurity at times results.

Thus obscurity resides in the things themselves, not in the words or the style, which is everywhere uniform. Diversity is inferred from style, as we have often said, not from a difference in subjects. Finally, among these more obscure—or, to speak more properly, allegorical—treatises are many which, no less than others of a clearer and more polished kind, we noted in the preface as having been read in this Church of Verona during sacred services before the ninth century, as works of the same author.

One objection remains, drawn from matters contained in these treatises. Some of these matters seem incapable of fitting not only one century, but also one writer. But the task of resolving this very wide-ranging objection belongs to the next chapter. There we shall show that the author of all these treatises, whom we have hitherto maintained to be one, belonged to the fourth century; there it must be established that whatever has seemed to some persons to indicate another time may suitably fall within that same century.

# CHAPTER II. IT IS DEMONSTRATED THAT THE AUTHOR WROTE IN THE FOURTH CENTURY, AND THAT EVERYTHING CONTAINED IN ALL THE TREATISES ACCORDS WITH THAT CENTURY.

## § I.—A remarkable passage in which the author reckons almost four hundred years is examined. The arbitrary correction of the Verona editors is noted. Cardinal Baronius’s objection is answered by other examples; and the testimony of St. Philastrius, likewise arbitrarily corrected in Fabricius’s edition, is shown to require restoration from the authority of the manuscripts. Certain other words of the same passage are considered.

Since the author’s date can be learned from no other source than certain testimonies found in the treatises themselves, and since these can be brought forward and considered only one by one, we fear that, when arguments are drawn from some particular treatise which plainly indicate the fourth century, readers may object that the inference is invalid if we then conclude that the author of all the treatises must be assigned to that same century. We therefore wish at the very outset to warn such readers that they should remember, first, that in the preceding chapter we have already demonstrated that all the treatises have one author, so that whatever is proved concerning the author of one treatise [Col. 0041A] is sufficiently proved concerning the author of [XLIV] all; and, secondly, that our purpose is to construct the full demonstration of this chapter not from the testimony of one treatise alone, but from that of several mutually concordant treatises, which we shall successively bring forward. Yet we do not intend the demonstration itself to be considered entirely complete until, near the end of the chapter, we have shown that certain testimonies thought to be referred to another period are in no way inconsistent with that same century.

Accordingly, the reference to nearly four hundred years which are reckoned from the delivery of Paul’s Epistle to the Corinthians down to the Author’s own time, in Treatise 5, Book I, is an evident argument that he wrote in the fourth century. For the passage reads thus:

> But since this apostolic decree has been operative for nearly four hundred years, or even more—and when human beings were more vigorous and Christians exceedingly rare—why should I, when almost the entire world itself is now Christian, and human vigor, as the world grows old, is worn away, blunt the edge of truth with soothing words, etc.?

This chronological statement appears openly and distinctly both in all the manuscripts and in the first Venetian edition. Only in the later Veronese edition, from which the others proceeded, was it independently altered by the editors, who alleged an error in the number; they were moved by the sole preconception that the Author had lived in the third century. “It is objected,” they say, “that the discourse On Continence cannot be by St. Zeno the martyr, since in it the Author is said to have been separated from the promulgation of St. Paul’s teaching by four hundred years and more . . . . . We say that the text, as it is corrupt in many places, is here likewise depraved—as often happens with numbers.” Tillemont, considering this method of correction in note 6 on the persecution under Valerian—a method supported by no manuscript and indeed employed contrary to the evidence of the manuscripts (which, moreover, express the number not by the numeral letters CCCC but by the word *quadringentos*, “four hundred”)—remarks that it is a sufficiently certain and safe method for readily withdrawing and extricating oneself from very grave difficulties.

To support and uphold a correction so arbitrary and unstable, Cardinal Baronius, in his second revision of the *Martyrology*, advanced the objection that, if “four hundred and more” is retained, the Author’s date must be extended not merely to the fourth century but to about the middle of the fifth; for Paul wrote the First Epistle to the Corinthians around the middle of the first century. You will find Baronius’s own words quoted in the preface to this dissertation. But those who press this point along with Baronius show that they have not sufficiently observed monuments of the fourth century in which the same chronological designation is used in the same sense as by our Author.

Arnobius, who flourished under Diocletian—that is, at the beginning of the fourth century, according to Jerome—introduces a pagan speaking against Christians in Book II, p. 94, as follows: “Was not your religion nonexistent four hundred years ago?” In the creed composed by the pseudo-synod of Antioch in A.D. 345, and quoted by Athanasius in his book *On the Synods*, the following is said of the Paulianists:

> They maintain that Christ himself, the Son of God, the Mediator, and the Image did not exist before the ages, but that he became Christ and Son of God only from the time when he assumed our flesh from the Virgin—not a full four hundred years ago.

Eusebius of Caesarea, a writer of the same century, who died in A.D. 340, speaks thus in Book II against Marcellus of Ancyra, chapter 1: “First of all, it is paradoxical that this Word should have begun not four hundred full years ago.” The pseudo-synod of Sardica, in the decree preserved in Hilary, Fragment 3, no. 2, vol. II, p. 648 of the Veronese edition, reproves the same Marcellus of Ancyra, among other things, because “he says that the Lord received the beginning of his reign four hundred years ago.” This pseudo-synod, moreover, was held in A.D. 347.

St. Hilary of Poitiers, in Book II against Constantius, written in A.D. 355 or 356, says, no. 5, p. 537: “Four hundred years after the Only-begotten of God deigned to come to the aid of the perishing human race . . . . . a new and most foul pestilence, the Arian, has now been poured forth.” St. Philastrius, bishop of Brescia, a contemporary of St. Ambrose who wrote before A.D. 391, gives the following in all editions prior to the Hamburg edition prepared by Johann Albert Fabricius, chapter 3: “And from the Lord until now, four hundred and thirty years or more.”

“But Philastrius,” Fabricius immediately adds in the accompanying note, “indicated in chapter 83 that he wrote before A.D. 391, and he attended the Council of Aquileia in A.D. 387 . . . . . Hence Latinius Latinius, with whom other learned men agree, judged the number manifestly corrupt and to be restored thus.” Accordingly, Fabricius emended the text of the Hamburg edition [XLV] to read: “And from the Lord until now, three hundred and eighty years or more.”

Yet this depends upon an insufficiently observed custom of that age in reckoning years. Philastrius is found to use this chronological notation not only in that chapter, but also in chapter 106, p. 206, where it is written:

> This is found to be contrary, if any have thought thus; for we know that more than four hundred years have now passed since the Lord came, and have been completed.

Here Fabricius thinks one should read, very arbitrarily, “about four hundred years”; yet, if the holy bishop had meant this, he would not have added “and have been completed.” This very explicit addition confirms that the earlier chronological statement should likewise not be corrected; indeed, it sufficiently suggests that the opinion commonly prevailed at that time that four hundred years counted from Christ’s birth were considered completed before the year 390.

For in the ancient Corbie manuscript, whose variant readings, carefully transcribed, are reported at the end of the latest Brescia edition, p. 163, one plainly reads: “And from the Lord until now, four hundred and thirty years, more or less.” The expression *plus minus* (“more or less”) both eliminates Fabricius’s correction and wonderfully establishes our interpretation. We may now add another testimony, from Jerome’s Epistle 129 to Dardanus, no. 7. Although it belongs to A.D. 414, when that letter was written, it nevertheless comes to the same result, since it reckons slightly fewer than four hundred years from the year 70 after Christ’s birth:

> After the destruction of the Temple—namely, under Titus, after A.D. 70—the ruin of both city and Temple has remained for somewhat less than four hundred years.

From all these texts, and others which might be adduced to the same effect, it is clear that this designation of four hundred years exceeds the actual total by about fifty years. We find that such an excess was not peculiar to this fourth century alone, but common to other ages as well. Tertullian, in *Against the Nations*, Book I, written around the beginning of the third century, claims nearly three hundred years for the Christian religion instead of two hundred, chapter 7: “Thus not yet three hundred years [this is how it should be written from the testimony which follows, rather than the CCL found in the editions, where C has been changed to L] have passed to our time”; and in chapter 9: “As we said above, not yet three hundred years have passed to our time.”

St. Peter Chrysologus, who flourished about the middle of the fifth century, in Sermon 145, *On the Generation of Christ*, at the end, reckons about five hundred years from Christ’s birth:

> Human laws settle disputed questions within thirty years; yet Christ, after about five hundred years, is still called upon to furnish the grounds of his birth, suffers litigation over his origin, and endures inquiries into his status.

In the ancient Collection of Canons which St. Leo’s editor published from two manuscripts, this chronological notation is prefixed to chapter 35, a canon of the Council of Chalcedon held in A.D. 451: “In the five hundredth year from the Incarnation of the Lord, in the fifth indiction.” Felix III, in his treatise or letter against Acacius, first published by our Marquis Maffei in vol. V of the Venetian edition of the Councils, says: “They wish to overthrow institutions of Christ established five hundred years ago, when the law of men cannot be annulled after thirty years.”

We may add testimony of another kind from Procopius, who, writing the history of the Gothic War about the middle of the sixth century, reckons nine hundred years elapsed from Appius the consul to the time of Belisarius, although only 863 years had passed:

> Belisarius led his army along the Latin Way, leaving on the left the Appian Way, which Appius, a Roman consul, constructed nine hundred years earlier and gave his own name.

After the testimony of so many writers, and indeed of different centuries, who agree in this computation of years by an excess of about fifty years, what force can Baronius’s objection retain, such that he would have “four hundred years” in Treatise 5, *On Continence*, regarded as written through some gross error? In an age when years were reckoned by consuls, not from a fixed epoch based on Christ’s birth, no very exact calculation was used in identifying that epoch. Rather, a round number was employed, which we know from common opinion or tradition to have exceeded the truth by nearly fifty years.

Moreover, in our Author, besides the round number “four hundred,” which very often is not written as wholly exact, the phrases “nearly” and “or even more” must also be noted. At first sight they may seem contradictory: for if the years are nearly four hundred, they would be understood to be not more, but rather somewhat fewer. Yet, lest we believe that a contradiction crept into the Author within the bounds of a single sentence, the particle “or” sufficiently indicates that he wrote “nearly” and “or even more” in the sense of “about,” so as to signify that he did not intend to mark an exact number of years, but that, using what they call a broad brush, he recorded approximately the years commonly reckoned—years which, as we have seen, eminent writers too assigned as four hundred in the fourth century according to a certain popular epoch.

Before passing from this text of the Author, however, another observation of no lesser importance must be added, by which his same date and the same century are confirmed. We must note, namely, the words by which he declares that almost the whole world was Christian in his own age. Understood of the Roman Empire, as we have shown in the annotation, this can belong only to the fourth century, when, after peace had been granted to the Church by Constantine, the Christian faith, openly propagated throughout the Roman Empire, made its greatest increase everywhere.

If anyone requires a striking proof of this matter, he may consult the pagan author Ammianus Marcellinus, who in Book XXI, chapter 2, reveals that even the soldiers of the Roman Empire were Christians. Hence Julian, when acclaimed emperor in Gaul, “in order to draw all men without obstruction to his favor, pretended adherence to Christian worship; for,” Zonaras says, Book XIII, no. 11, “he feared the soldiers, whom he knew to be almost universally Christian.” Nor should it move us that Tertullian, in the *Apology*, chapter 37, testifies that all Roman cities were filled with Christians in his time. For there it is clear from the context that he is speaking rhetorically: he does not affirm that almost the whole Roman world, as our Author says, was Christian, but suggests that throughout the Roman world there were so many Christians, though dispersed, that an army could have been formed from them against the pagans, had they wished to employ force and arms.

In the same sense, in Book *Against the Jews*, chapter 7, when he affirms that Christ’s name reigns in the various provinces which he enumerates, he does not say that those provinces were wholly Christian, but indicates that Christians were in them, among whom Christ’s name reigned. The same interpretation must be applied to the passage of Serapion of Antioch in Eusebius, Book V, chapter 19, where the Christian faith is said to have spread throughout the whole world; and likewise to the testimony of Bardesanes in the same writer, Book VI of the *Preparation for the Gospel*, chapter 8, where Christians are reported to be found in almost every city.

Accordingly, the forced interpretation of the Veronese editors appears worthless. In order to destroy—or rather evade—the argument derived from our Author’s text, they say in their preface: “Now, when the Gospel had been disseminated through all the provinces and received by many, the Author here puts, as often happens, the whole for the part.” The Author’s words admit no such explanation, especially since he is known to have said “almost the whole world” strictly, not figuratively, in order to signify the multitude of Christians then flourishing throughout the world, and to contrast it with the exceedingly rare Christians, as he calls them in the same passage, of earlier times.

## § II.—The Author, in arguing against the Arians, is proved by several testimonies to belong accordingly to the fourth century. The worn-out response of the Veronese editors.

A second argument, exceedingly strong for the fourth century and common to several treatises, concerns expressions and propositions which, “as no one acquainted with the events of those times can fail to know,” in Baronius’s words from his first notes on the *Martyrology* for April 12, “had never been heard before the emergence of Arius’s heresy.” They are of such a kind that, although the same author altered his opinion in his second revision of the *Martyrology*, he still declared that for this reason it could not be denied that certain sermons printed among the minor works of St. Zeno could not belong to the martyr crowned under Gallienus—namely, those which, in his judgment, plainly refute Arius’s heresy. “This,” he says, “could, if I am not mistaken, be proved by many arguments and the best conjectures, if the limits of a note permitted it.”

To make the force of these principal expressions and terms clearer, it will be very useful to set forth under certain headings what the Arians held on the one hand and what the Author replied against them on the other. Thus even those who are not fully learned in these matters may recognize that the Author is deliberately arguing against the Arians.

These heretics, speaking of the Son of God, according to Athanasius, *On the Decrees of Nicaea*, no. 18, p. 223, used formulas of this kind: “From things that did not exist”; “He was not before he was begotten”; “There was once when he was not.” By these they meant that the divine Word was created from non-existent things—that is, from nothing, like the other creatures—that he did not exist before he was begotten, and consequently that there was once when he was not.

To oppose these claims, our Author, together with the Catholics, first taught in Treatise 3, Book II, that God the Father had begotten another from himself—that is, God the Son—from his own unbegotten substance, in which, remaining blessed forever, he brought forth the Son, possessing all things equal to those possessed by himself. And in Treatise 2, Book II, he says: “The Father reflected back his whole self into the Son.” By these expressions he openly reveals that the divine Word was begotten not from nothing, or from non-existent things, but from the very substance of the Father.

Then, to reject the second formula, “He was not before he was born,” or the equivalent formula, “There was once when he was not”—by which the Arians denied eternity to the divine Son—he repeatedly insists on the term *coeternity*: in Treatise 2, Book II, “one original coeternity”; and in Treatise 6, Book II, no. 4, “with whom there is one possession of the original and everlasting kingdom, one substance of coeternity and omnipotence, one equality, one power of august majesty.” To this belong also the words in Treatise 55, where he acknowledges the Son as “alone privy to the Father’s antiquity,” that is, coeternal with the Father; and, to omit other examples, in Treatise 7 he identifies with the greatest precision that heresy which, though more modest in speech, is more mordantly harmful: it does indeed call the Son of God God, but denies that he was begotten from the Father by the perpetuity of nobility, and says that there was a time when he was not.

These words especially moved Baronius, since they strike directly at the Arian heresy. For no one taught such things before Arius; no one before this time so explicitly identified and refuted such a heresy, nor indeed could anyone have identified and refuted it.

The Arians denied the equality of the Son with the Father and proclaimed the Son inferior to the Father. The Author declares the Son equal to the Father in all things in Treatises 3 and 4, Book II; and in Treatise 6, no. 4, he presses the single equality of both. He does so in formulas so explicit, repeated, and reinforced by other phrases that he indicates these were not accidental assertions, but deliberate professions against an error already dominant. Thus, in Treatise 1, Book II, he distinctly affirms that Catholics proclaim the Son, God from God, equal to the Father—a proclamation which belongs only to the fourth century in opposition to Arius’s heresy.

Nor did the Author merely assert this equality; he wished at times to establish and confirm it in entire treatises, rejecting objections raised by the Arians alone. See Treatises 1 and 6 of Book II in their entirety.

Nothing was more habitual with the Arians than to reject the Greek term **ὁμοούσιον** (*homoousion*, “of one substance”) and its Latin counterpart, “one substance,” since it cut down their error at a single blow. Hence their famous rule, recorded by Phoebadius, p. 301, vol. IV of the Lyons edition of the *Library of the Fathers*: “Let no one say ‘one substance.’” Catholics, on the contrary, distinguished themselves from Arians among the Greeks by the term **ὁμοούσιον**, and among Latins by confession of one substance; and in opposing them they pressed no formula more strongly.

You will frequently read this Latin confession and formula in the Author, and will find the single substance of Father and Son expressed in decisive terms: for example, Treatise 6, Book II, no. 4, in the words quoted a little above; and Treatise 7, no. 2, where he writes:

> For if the Word is in God, and the Word is God, and that which is in him is what he is who is present within, there are two persons and two names; but there is one substance of original perpetuity and deity.

Again, in Treatise 12, no. 1: “one substance, power, deity, majesty, and will of Father and Son.” Finally, to omit other instances, in Treatise 2, in order somewhat to explain the matter, he offers an analogy of two seas communicating with one another through a strait between them. Although, by their own nature, they are distinct in places and names, nonetheless there is “one power, one substance, one nature of flowing, of the vapor of the threefold deep.”

If you do not find the word *consubstantial* in the Author, it makes no difference. For in the century to which we assign him this word is scarcely found, or perhaps not found at all, among Latin writers except in Marius Victorinus, vol. IV of the aforementioned *Library of the Fathers*, whom we find to be the only and first writer of all to use it. The others, however, consistently said in Latin “one substance” throughout that period; this was rendered and accepted as the equivalent of the Nicene Greek term **ὁμοούσιον**, as may be seen in the Latin translations themselves of the Greek creedal formulas published by St. Hilary in his fragments.

Hence the statement of Lucifer of Cagliari in the book *On Not Sparing Those Who Sin Against God*, p. 237, vol. IV of the same edition of the *Library of the Fathers*: “What the Greeks call *homousion*, we Romans call ‘of one substance with the Father.’” He repeats this at p. 243 in the book *That One Must Die for the Son of God*. Hilary likewise says in Book IV *On the Trinity*, no. 4: “Of one substance, which in Greek is called *Homousion*.” Similar statements are made by the author of the treatise *On the Orthodox Faith Against the Arians*, vol. II of the Appendix to Ambrose, p. 345, and by others, whom it would take too long to cite.

Accordingly, since the Author vigorously insists on the one substance which other Fathers of his age, deliberately contending against the Arians, likewise insisted upon, he sufficiently reveals himself to be fighting against that heresy, even though he does not employ the word *consubstantial*. But let us proceed to further matters.

To eliminate this one substance, the Arians objected that something must have been taken away from the Father’s substance in order for the Son to be begotten, and so they claimed that Catholics must admit the Father to be diminished and imperfect. To oppose them, the Author in Treatise 2 uses this expression: “While the Father’s state remains entire, he reflected his whole self into the Son, so that he might detract nothing from himself.” And in Treatise 5:

> God is born from God, possessing the whole Father and detracting nothing from the Father; the one shines in the other, and the glory of each is a shared honor, because what belongs to the Son belongs to the Father, and what belongs to the Father belongs to both.

Repeating this in Treatise 3, he presents other formulas diametrically opposed to the Arians: “Whole from whole, true from true, perfect from perfect. Possessing the whole Father, detracting nothing from the Father.” Likewise, in Treatise 13, Book II, no. 3: “The Father’s substance and will of undiminished deity.” And at the end of Treatise 2, Book I:

> You, though one in three, are in no way divided; you are moved by no slander of human curiosity. From the paternal fountain you are wholly poured forth in the Son; and yet, when wholly poured forth, you do not depart.

Moreover, anticipating the other Arian objection, by which they charged Catholics with Sabellianism—as though those confessing one undiminished substance of Father and Son must likewise confess one person of both—he explained himself nobly against Sabellius in Treatise 7, Book II, no. 9. After citing John 10:30, “I and the Father are one,” he adds:

> He certainly did not say this in such a way as to confound two by reducing them into one, but so as to teach us that the two have one omnipotence of deity and power.

Do not these formulas, together with many others of the same kind which we omit for brevity’s sake, exceedingly frequent in several treatises where they are deliberately directed against Arians, and almost all issued together in Book II, plainly prove that our Author lived after the birth of Arius’s heresy? Some expressions of this sort may indeed be found in the ante-Nicene Fathers; thus among Latin authors Tertullian alone once wrote “one substance” and “coeternity,” yet not with such force as to indicate that he intended to strike at any particular error. But who can point out in any ante-Nicene writer so many formulas together, so directly and diametrically opposed to Arian errors, and repeated so often?

The Veronese editors believed that they had answered this objection when they declared these writings directed against the errors of Origen, whom Epiphanius calls the father of Arius. Was our Author alone to identify in Origen a heresy which no one whatever is found to have identified in him before the Arians? And was he to identify it in so many passages, and in sermons, as if Origen or the Origenists openly maintained in the West a manifest heresy against which Catholic bishops had to inveigh sharply?

This is surely incredible, especially when one considers that the works of Origen, a Greek and ancient writer, were unknown to Westerners until the celebrated controversy over Origen’s books arose near the very end of the fourth century. It is certain, moreover, that only at this period did not merely Epiphanius but also Theophilus of Alexandria and many others begin to denounce Origen as Arius’s father. Before that time, since not one person has been found who attributed this error to Origen, the excuse offered by those who defended Origen seemed sufficiently plausible to some: namely, that Origen’s books had been corrupted by Arians. Thus Photius testifies, codex 223, that they altered St. Methodius’s *Symposium* and inserted Arian opinions into it. We suspect that the same happened to Theognostus, whom Photius found in his own day abounding in Arian expressions, although Athanasius, citing his words, had invoked him as one of the fuller ancient witnesses to Catholic doctrine against the Arians.

Indeed, if Origen had sounded the note in advance for the Arians, how could authors who wrote much against him before the outbreak of the Origenist controversy, and who accused many things in his works—such as Methodius, Eustathius of Antioch, and Apollinaris (the latter two being among the fiercest opponents of the Arians)—how could they, I say, have noted nothing of the sort tending toward Arian errors? “They did not at all criticize him,” says Socrates, Book VI, chapter 13, “as holding wrong opinions concerning the Holy Trinity,” because, as the same writer says in Book VII, chapter 6, “Origen throughout his books confesses the Son to be coeternal with the Father.”

What if Origen taught Arianism? Aetius, Eunomius’s teacher and a most violent Arian, despised him, according to the testimony of the same Socrates, Book II, chapter 35. And if certain Arians attempted to cite his books in confirmation, as they thought, of their own heresy, Basil and Gregory Nazianzen immediately refuted them, says the same Socrates, Book IV, chapter 26, and demonstrated that they did not understand Origen’s doctrine at all. Indeed, Athanasius, in his Epistle *On the Decrees of Nicaea*, no. 27, p. 232, did not hesitate to appeal to Origen as holding the view opposed to the Arians; there he cites a passage of his which utterly uproots the foundation and basis of Arianism, also identified by our Author in Treatise 7, Book II, no. 1:

> Let the one who dares to say, “There was once when the Son was not,” understand.

These are Origen’s words quoted by Athanasius.

From this testimony of Origen alone we rather understand that even at that earlier time there was some other person who said what the Arians later taught. In Egypt, indeed, there was St. Dionysius of Alexandria, a disciple of Origen. Not in order to sound the note in advance for the Arians, but in order to oppose the Sabellian heresy then spreading in Libya and neighboring regions, he incautiously used that expression, as is clear from a fragment of his letter to Euphranor and Ammonius, quoted by St. Athanasius in the Epistle *On the Opinion of Dionysius*, no. 4, p. 246: “For, since it is a thing made, it was not before it was made.”

For this reason Dionysius of Alexandria was reported to St. Dionysius, bishop of Rome, who immediately wrote a letter in which he strongly condemned that expression:

> It is therefore no slight but supreme impiety to say that the Lord was in any manner made by hand; for if the Son was made, there was once when he was not. But he always existed.

Thus Dionysius of Rome speaks in the fragment preserved by the same Athanasius, *On the Decrees of Nicaea*, no. 26, p. 232. The Alexandrian soon issued an *Apology*, in which, making clear his purpose against the Sabellians and proving himself free from the error which the Arians later seized upon, he wrote many things that were of great use to Catholics against the Arians.

From this history, therefore, it is established that in the third century that formula was used by certain persons only in Egypt—whence it is found only in a few records concerning the Alexandrian Church—and that they used it in order to refute the Sabellian heresy in a Catholic sense, not in order to introduce and defend a new one. When Dionysius of Alexandria was warned that the expression was displeasing, he confirmed Catholic doctrine so clearly in his *Apology* that among the ancients no one can be found who rejected Arius’s error more forcefully or more brilliantly than Dionysius.

Who, then, would suppose that in these Western regions our Author alone repeatedly and sharply preached against Dionysius or some other person of the same type and place as though he were defending Arius’s errors? Would one not rather understand that he openly attacks the Arians, who in the fourth century raged everywhere, and especially within these regions of Italy under the leadership of Auxentius? This is particularly so because he attacks deliberately and repeatedly not that formula alone—which had been censured in St. Dionysius of Alexandria—but many other expressions never heard from anyone before Arius.

For Socrates, Book I, chapter 6, calls Arius’s assertions new and unheard of; and Sozomen, Book I, chapter 15, says: “He dared to preach in the Church what had never been said by anyone.” Before both of them, Rufinus, *Ecclesiastical History*, Book X, chapter 1, says: “He began to advance certain perverse doctrines concerning faith in Christ, doctrines which had never previously come into question.” Hence Hilary calls Arianism “a new heresy,” Book VII *On the Trinity*, no. 3; “a novel heresy,” no. 5; and “a novel plague, newly discovered after nearly four hundred years,” Book I to Constantius, no. 5—meaning a heresy which no one taught or defended before Arius, whatever may be the case if some similar formula had slipped from someone in another, yet Catholic, sense against the Sabellians.

[L] But in order to demonstrate with complete clarity that our Author attacked Arians and not some ancient error, it will suffice to read the first treatise of Book I and its annotations. There he unmistakably condemns the curiosity of Arians who dispute by philosophical reasoning concerning the most lofty mystery of divine generation—a characteristic peculiar to no other sect (on this, see Dissertation II, chapter 2). He notes various “faiths,” or formulas of faith, and various treatises which divide faith into many sects; this can refer only to the formulas and treatises of the Arians. He clearly indicates the services performed by heretics at the courts of kings—that is, emperors, and Christian emperors, as we shall infer from the context—before judges, that is, magistrates, before the rich, and occasionally only before pagans. How these points suit Arians alone will be learned from the annotations taken together. What further need is there to show that an Author speaking so precisely against the Arians flourished in the fourth century?

## § III.—Other fourth-century heresies attacked by the Author confirm his date.

We shall now add further confirmation from other heresies which the same Author attacks, heresies arising only in the fourth century. First, in Treatise 1, no. 5, Book I, besides those who disseminated errors concerning the Son of God, he also rebukes those who sinned by subtle reasoning concerning the divinity of the Holy Spirit:

> Under the sound of law and faith, inflamed by the worldly love of ostentation, you presume that by arguments you are able to compel, examine, measure, and distinguish the inestimable and incomprehensible perpetuity of the divinity of God born from God, and of the Holy Spirit, by the very law through which he exists from himself.

And against those who prejudged the equality of the Holy Spirit, he issued that splendid profession in Treatise 13, no. 1, Book II:

> The Holy Spirit . . . . . possesses one substance, power, deity, majesty, and will with the Father and the Son.

Among earlier heretics, however, there is not a single one who detracted from and diminished the Holy Spirit together with the Son, as the Author’s text states. The Arians were the first who, erring concerning the Son, were bound by the same reasoning consequently to err concerning the Holy Spirit. Yet the earliest Arians, content to dispute concerning the Son alone, did not press this consequence; hence they were not charged with having erred on this point, nor was this error condemned at the Council of Nicaea.

Only the later Arians, or rather the Semi-Arians, introduced this error. Thus it may be seen refuted in Hilary, Book II *On the Trinity*, and in Ambrose, Book III *On the Holy Spirit*, and condemned at the Council of Constantinople in A.D. 391. Sozomen expressly affirms that this heresy arose in the same fourth century as Arianism, and from Arianism, Book VI, chapter 23:

> At the same time—that is, during the reign of Valens—there again arose the question whether the Holy Spirit should be regarded as of the same substance as the Father and Son. Although this question had begun long before, that is, from the rise of the Semi-Arians, it then received its greatest development. The Anomoeans, that is, the pure Arians, and the Semi-Arians agreed. For both asserted that the Holy Spirit was a minister, third in order and honor, and unlike in substance.

Accordingly, since our Author openly attacks these persons in the words cited from Treatise 1, he could in no way have written before the middle of the fourth century.

There is another heresy which he distinctly identifies in Treatise 7, Book II, in these words:

> Finally, one [heretical view] asserts that Jesus Christ took his beginning from the womb of the Virgin Mary, and that he thereafter became God by reason of righteousness, not by birth.

Indeed, after attacking the Arians, he subsequently refutes this view near the end of the same treatise in such a manner as sufficiently to show that both heresies were active in the same age. Therefore, before he attacks the Arians, he speaks against this heresy again in Treatise 6 of the same Book II:

> If, as some suppose, he took his beginning as a mere man from the womb of the Virgin, what hope is there, etc.?

Here the words “as some suppose” especially must be observed, since they indicate this error to be present, as much as the Arian error.

Moreover, although several ancient heretics taught this error (concerning whom see annotation 3 on Treatise 6), none defended it in the same century as the Arians except the Photinians. In order to depart far from the Arians, they fell into this heresy; consequently, Arians detested Photinians no less than Photinians detested Arians. Catholics, situated between the two, refuted both errors. Thus our Author, in rebuking together both parties who taught contrary doctrines, reveals that he lived in the period when both heresies were simultaneously contending after the middle of the fourth century.

The author of the error which located the image of God not in the soul but in the body, through a mistaken application to this matter of the Genesis testimony, “Let us make man in our image,” etc., is identified by Epiphanius, *Heresy* 70, as Audius or Audaeus, who lived in the fourth century. The same error is rejected in that century by St. Hilary on Psalm 129 and by Philastrius, ch. 97. Therefore our author too, since he refutes this error not cursorily but deliberately and at length in Treatises 19 and 20 of Book II, is proved beyond doubt to have lived in the same century.

[Col. 0051C] Finally, in Treatise 8 of Book II he affirms that Mary was a virgin before childbirth, in childbirth, and after childbirth, in formulations so definite that they cannot be found in anyone before the virginity of the Blessed Mary was attacked in the fourth century. On this matter see more in note 5 on Treatise 5 of Book I, where other testimonies of the Author concerning the same subject, repeated elsewhere, are also indicated. These appear to have been spoken in order to defend or advance Catholic doctrine against a rising heresy.

§ IV.—A new argument drawn from a public church in the city. The objections of the Veronese editors and of Baronius refuted. Further inferences from the Bishop’s public sermons, at which Gentiles also were present, and from the great number of catechumens baptized annually at Easter.

[Col. 0051D] Treatise 14 of Book I supplies a notable testimony relevant to the present question. Entitled “On the Building of the House of God,” it was undoubtedly delivered by the Author when a newly built church in the city was first opened. Hence that festive opening: “I should wish, most beloved brethren, to employ a certain triumphal manner of speech, and to redouble in praise the sacred summit of this new work.” Again, at II.2, he mentions this new church and calls it “your building,” because, as he says in no. 5, it was owed to the frequent benefactions of the wealthy. Finally, in no. 6, it is called “this new place of sacred prayer,” which toward the end he terms an earthly dwelling-place.

Now, although during the first three centuries of the Church Christians held sacred assemblies in certain private places, which they called churches, they were nevertheless not permitted to build new public buildings for that use. Only through the Emperor Constantine, who professed Christ, was permission first granted in the fourth century to construct public churches. Accordingly, one would wrongly say that an Author who speaks so unequivocally about a new public church lived before that century.

We are astonished, however, that the Veronese editors wrote in their preface: “The Author shows, from the spiritual building of the house of God, that churches had not yet been constructed for Christians at that time.” Had they said merely that the Author did not employ the single term *templum* (“temple”), we should not object; for Christians, since that name was customarily applied to the edifices of idols, were hesitant to transfer it to churches before St. Ambrose and Theodosius the Younger, who are first found using that word to signify Christian churches, as we observed more fully in note 26 on Treatise 5 of Book I. But since those editors mean a material building, of which such explicit mention is made in the three testimonies just cited, we are greatly astonished that they pressed as an argument the very point from which they should plainly have confessed themselves defeated.

What, moreover, if these other words of the same treatise, no. 1, are considered: “Throughout the whole Church of God there is either no place of prayer, or only a very rare one, which can in any degree even now be compared, amid the ruins swallowing them up, with the edifices of idolatry”? The Author does not deny that there was absolutely no place of prayer, that is, no Christian church, or only a very rare one; rather, he presupposes that Christians possessed many places of prayer, or churches, among which nevertheless none, or very few, could be compared with the edifices of idolatry in magnificence.

[LII] [Col. 0052C] In his annotations on the *Martyrology*, Baronius infers from this testimony that the Author flourished before Constantine’s time, since it was through that emperor’s works, especially at Rome, that the most august basilicas were erected. This would be excellent reasoning if the Author had asserted only that no place of prayer could be compared with the buildings of idols; but he adds “or very rare.” Thus he sufficiently indicates that somewhere there was a church not at all inferior to the most magnificent temples of idols. Meanwhile, since he here shows that many churches, though not magnificent ones, had been built in various places, the error of the Veronese editors is now much more apparent: in this treatise they saw that no churches had then been built by Christians. Had they seen otherwise, they would very easily have recognized that the Author could not be placed before the fourth century.

That these churches were public is evident also from the fact that they were openly built for the purpose of being churches, whereas formerly private houses had secretly been assigned for the use of ecclesiastical assemblies, lest anything outwardly become known to the Gentiles. At least those churches were public—though perhaps few—which could anywhere be compared with temples of idolatry; and this suggests that other public churches also existed, though inferior in size and magnificence. Moreover, Treatise 7 appears certainly to have been delivered by the Author when that new church, first opened, was dedicated; this strongly supports its public character.

This is further supported by a passage from Treatise 10 of Book I, no. 3, where women are said openly to have proceeded to the church of God with their whole bodies adorned in gold; and likewise by another passage from Treatise 5 of the same book, no. 8, in which the Author, speaking of Christian wives married to pagans, marks no less explicitly the latter’s open resort to a temple of idols than the former’s open resort to church on the same day, so that both are understood to have been equally public.

Finally, we submit one point beyond all possibility of doubt from Treatise 3 of Book I. At its very beginning, the Author, calling learned men present while he preached, means Gentiles. In note 2 on that place we have shown that, captivated by his eloquence, they frequently attended him while he delivered sacred sermons; and at the same time we infer the Author’s period, when he did not fear the presence of Gentiles. This occurred only in the fourth century, when, after persecutions by the Gentiles had been removed by Christian emperors, it was permitted to profess the Christian religion publicly in churches without any fear, so that Gentiles themselves might also be admitted to sacred sermons.

Nor should it trouble anyone that in Treatise 5, no. 8, he calls the pagan husband’s sacrifice public but that of the Christian wife secret. For it is clear from what we noted there that the word “secret” is not to be applied to churches, but refers solely to the sacrament of the Eucharist, which, by ancient discipline, could be seen not merely by pagans but not even by the catechumens themselves. All catechumens were excluded from the church after the reading of the Gospel and the sermon. Hence the Author there immediately explains himself, adding: “The sacrifice of that man,” that is, the pagan husband, “may freely be handled by anyone whatsoever; yours”—he addresses the Christian wife—“cannot, without sacrilege, be seen even by Christians themselves who have not been consecrated,” that is, catechumens.

[Col. 0053C] The Veronese editors, whom we have seen greatly deceived in denying the construction of a sacred temple, or church, add error to error by declaring that the Author in the same Treatise 7 shows that Christians were few in number: “He shows that churches had not yet been constructed for Christians, but that they constituted a new people and were very few in number.” Nothing is more false. For in that place, although he acknowledges that the newly built church, constructed at great expense for the convenience of the faithful, was very spacious, he openly affirms that it was nevertheless found still too narrow because of their incredible multitude: “Rejoice therefore, brethren; recognize in this newly built church your own building, whose capacity you have made narrow by your blessed number.”

Such a multitude of believers also fits well in the fourth century, since earlier persecutions had created the greatest obstacles, both to the public dissemination of preaching and to the conversion of sufficiently many persons to the faith. Another weighty confirmation is supplied by those treatises which report that the Author simultaneously washed in holy baptism at the Paschal festival numerous catechumens of every class, age, sex, condition, and even nationality. See Treatises 33 and 38, 42 and 43 of Book II. Since each repeats approximately the same thing, they imply that such a number was customarily immersed in the baptismal washing every year at Easter; and this can credibly have occurred only after peace had been restored to the Church.

§ V.—The prohibition upon the Gentiles’ construction of temples, and yet the public practice of idolatry, both mentioned by the Author, define his date more certainly as after the middle of the fourth century. Baronius’s objection dismissed. What was decreed concerning pagan worship from Julian’s death down to the year 391.

To the argument drawn from the public churches of Christians must be added another, taken from temples of idols. Although they were open, they could by no means be built in the Author’s time. In the same Treatise 7, no. 1, after saying that it is not especially praiseworthy to celebrate the construction of a new church, since that may be common to Gentiles or Jews, he gives this reason for the latter statement: “For they too, if it should be permitted, or if they should wish, might perhaps build more splendid synagogues and erect more splendid capitolia.” In note 3 on this treatise we proved that *capitolia* is written for “temples.”

Now observe the two clauses set forth disjunctively: “if it should be permitted,” or “if they should wish.” The first cannot apply to Jews, since the Jewish sect is said to have been forbidden by no law under Theodosius, Law IX, *On the Jews*, A.D. 393; and only in A.D. 421 did Law 21 of the same title provide that they should thereafter not cause any synagogues to be founded. This was confirmed, it is recorded, in A.D. 423, Laws XXV and XXVII. Therefore the second clause, “if they should wish,” concerns the Jews; but the first, “if it should be permitted,” plainly concerns the Gentiles. It is consequently certain that in the Author’s age Gentiles were not permitted to build temples. This can belong only to the fourth century, since under Christian emperors temples of idols were either closed before Julian or, after Julian, tolerated in such a way that new ones were nevertheless not permitted to be built.

That the Author has in view this latter period, after Julian’s death, is clear from Treatise 5, where churches were publicly attended by Christians no less than temples by pagans, and the pagans’ sacrifice is described as public in no. 8. No other period under Christian emperors can be assigned in which temples of idols stood open while their construction was prohibited.

[Col. 0054D] Yet this mention of open temples and public sacrifices led Baronius, who took no notice of the prohibition on building those very temples, to maintain that the Author flourished before the fourth century: “While the Author most openly shows that temples of idols were then open and that victims were customarily sacrificed, he plainly indicates that that age was altogether different from Ambrose’s time, since it is established that already long before, not only by Constantine . . . and by Constantius . . . victims had been forbidden and temples ordered closed, but that at that time the Romans could not even obtain the erection of a single altar of Victory, as Ambrose writes at length to Valentinian and argues against Symmachus.”

[Col. 0055A] But although under Constantine and Constantius it was not permitted to open temples or offer sacrifice, the situation was otherwise after Julian, who fully restored the worship of pagan superstition, until Theodosius the Great and Valentinian the Younger again abolished every pagan cult. In order that neither the matters concerning the altar of Victory, which moved Baronius on the authority of Ambrose and Symmachus, nor material that might also be adduced from Socrates and Theodoret should trouble us—of whom the former, *History*, Book III, ch. 24, and the latter, Book V, ch. 20, expressly write that temples everywhere were closed under Jovian, Julian’s successor—we understand that this proposition must be clearly established: namely, that after Julian’s death pagan worship was still permitted for some time, contrary to Baronius’s hypothesis. This is especially necessary because the more certain delimitation of the Author’s age depends greatly on it. To establish it, we must briefly collect and consider whatever was decreed concerning temples and sacrifices from Julian’s death to Theodosius the Great.

[LIV] Jovian, an excellent Christian, was proclaimed emperor immediately after Julian. Having learned from experience, says Sozomen, Book VI, ch. 3, that calamities had been brought upon the Roman Empire by God’s wrath because of his predecessor’s impiety, he lost no time in writing to the governors of the provinces that they should assemble in churches, zealously worship the divine power, and recognize the Christian faith alone as deserving veneration among the Romans.

Consistent with this testimony of Sozomen is what is reported concerning this same edict of Jovian in the history dealing with Athanasius and Alexandrian affairs, written in the fourth century and published from a manuscript of the Chapter of Verona by our fellow citizen Maffei in vol. III of *Observations on Literature*, no. 8, p. 71: “In the following month, Toth 18—that is, 14 September 363—the letters of the Emperor Jovian arrived for Olympius the prefect, directing that God Most High and Christ alone be worshipped, and that the peoples who assemble in churches celebrate their religion.”

These letters of Jovian, though issued in favor of Christians, cannot nevertheless be called a law enacted against pagans; hence nothing from them was inserted in the title *On Pagans* of the Theodosian Code. Yet, because the emperor’s disposition was sufficiently known from this—how greatly, namely, he preferred the Christian faith alone to pagan worship—it could happen that the Gentiles feared that the same emperor would shortly enact laws against them or restore earlier laws. Perhaps from this arose the event, recorded by Socrates, Book III, ch. 24, that all temples of the Gentiles everywhere were closed at the same time, and that the priests of demons hid themselves in various places wherever each could. This should nevertheless be understood with some exaggeration; “all” and “everywhere,” if taken strictly, are utterly false, as will be clear from what follows.

For the same reason it seems that Christians were held in honor, pagans in contempt, and temples of the pagans in some places were destroyed through the zeal of certain Christians, as we suppose, as Libanius recorded in Oration 12. But that no law against the edifices of idols was enacted by this emperor is clear from the fact that the pagan orator Themistius, in Oration 5 delivered before Jovian shortly before he died, includes among his praises that he promulgated a law granting each person liberty to follow whichever religion pleased him most; and that, having prohibited only magical rites involving evil deeds, he did not forbid the other sacrifices.

The same Socrates, whom we heard testifying that temples were closed under Jovian, repeats this opinion and further gives this reason: in Book III, ch. 25, he says that Jovian had made it his object to extinguish the quarrels of dissenters by mildness and gentle verbal persuasion; and that he said he would cause annoyance to no one whatsoever, whatever his faith might be.

Before a year had elapsed Jovian died, and Valentinian succeeded him, taking his brother Valens as colleague in the empire.
