At the beginning of his reign, according to Zosimus, Book IV, ch. 3, Valentinian forbade nocturnal rites—as indeed we see was done in the first year of his reign, A.D. 364, by Law 7, *On Magicians and Astrologers*, of the Theodosian Code—but, at the urging of Praetextatus, permitted them to be performed lawfully, suspending the force of his own law, provided that everything should be done according to ancestral customs, as they had existed from the beginning.

Socrates, Book IV, ch. 29, indeed reports that Valentinian troubled no sect or religion. The contemporary writer Ammianus Marcellinus states the same more expressly, Book XXX, ch. 9: “Finally, his reign became distinguished by this moderation: he stood neutral amid religious differences, troubled no one, neither ordered the worship of this nor of that, nor bent the necks of his subjects by threatening prohibitions toward the religion which he himself worshipped; but he left these matters intact as he found them.” The emperor himself likewise says in Law 9 of the Theodosian Code, *On Magicians and Astrologers*: “I judge that divination by the entrails has no association with the causes of evil arts; and I do not consider it a crime either in itself or in any other religion besides which was permitted by our ancestors. The laws issued by me at the beginning of my reign are witnesses, laws by which free permission was granted to everyone to worship whatever he had embraced in his mind.”

Hence he is praised by the Gentile Symmachus in his *Relation to Valentinian the Younger*, nos. 3 and 17; and St. Ambrose, Epistle 17, no. 16, reports that Valentinian the Elder was reproached because he had shown indulgence to the Gentiles. In Epistle 18, refuting Symmachus’s relation, which had proposed to Valentinian the Younger that he imitate the indulgence of his predecessors, Ambrose says, no. 39: “For if they have proclaimed, solely for their own side, the forbearance of those emperors who, though Christians, nevertheless did not remove the decrees of the Gentiles, how much more ought you to be bound by brotherly love?” The brother here mentioned of Valentinian the Younger is Gratian; and the Christian emperors are named in the plural, ruling the West, which was the question at issue. They can surely be none other than Jovian and Valentinian the Elder, both of whom are said not to have removed the decrees of the Gentiles. Thus they are proved, since they did not prohibit Gentile worship, to have permitted temples and sacrifices.

[LV] Valens, to whom his brother Valentinian assigned the eastern empire, followed his brother’s policy for some time, until, pressed especially strongly by Christian monks, he abolished sacrifices in such a way that he nevertheless did not entirely shut temples in the East or forbid the burning of incense. Hence Libanius, in his Oration *For the Temples* addressed to Theodosius the Great, who at that time ruled only in the East after Valens, p. 473 among the *Minor Works* of Jacobus Gothofredus, says: “When Julian died among the Persians . . . the use of sacrifices certainly remained for some time. But when certain innovators arose, it was prohibited by the two brothers”—Valens and Valentinian—“but not the burning of incense.” He adds that this practice was confirmed by law even under Theodosius himself.

Indeed, at the beginning of Theodosius’s reign in the East, the Gentiles still had freedom, according to Zosimus, Book IV, ch. 29, to enter sanctuaries and propitiate the gods by ancestral rites. Referring to this in the oration just mentioned, Libanius addresses Theodosius: “Therefore you ordered neither that temples be closed nor that anyone be excluded from entering them; you expelled neither fire nor incense nor the other honors of fumigations from temples and altars.” This is not contradicted by Laws 7 and 9 of Theodosius, title *On Pagans*, in which only sacrifices are said to have been prohibited, and those who entered temples and shrines with the intention of sacrificing were punished severely.

But let us return from East to West. After the death of Valentinian the Elder, the western empire passed to Gratian and Valentinian the Younger. Gratian enacted a law praised by Honorius, Law 20, *On Pagans*, by which, leaving temples and sacrifices untouched, he prohibited only the expenditure of public funds upon that most shameful superstition. Hence St. Ambrose, Epistle 18 to Valentinian II, no. 16, speaking of Gratian’s law, testifies that nothing was taken from pagan superstition by it except the revenues derived from estates: “Yet no one denied votive offerings to shrines or legacies to soothsayers; the estates alone were taken away.” And in no. 31 he openly teaches that sacrifices were everywhere celebrated during Gratian’s reign.

If Gratian removed the altar of Victory from the Roman senate-house, Ambrose reveals in the same passage that this was done because sacrifice could not be tolerated in a place where many Christians assembled; for most of the senators had professed Christ. Thus under the brothers Gratian and Valentinian in the West, temples of idols stood open, and not incense-burning only, as happened in the East, but sacrifices too were celebrated in them. Hence Libanius, in the oration cited, p. 484, affirmed to Theodosius, emperor of the East, that sacrifices remained at Rome, the metropolis of the West.

[Col. 0057D] Thus the whole objection of Baronius collapses. From the single altar of Victory removed at Rome by Gratian’s order, of which we have just spoken, he inferred that even in Ambrose’s time temples were closed and sacrifices forbidden; and he declared with absolute certainty that our Author, who mentions temples and sacrifices, must be excluded from that period.

The first person in the West to declare war upon temples and sacrifices was Valentinian the Younger, after his brother Gratian had already perished, by Law 10, title *On Pagans*, issued A.D. 391, on the third day before the Kalends of March [27 February]. In the same year, on the fifteenth day before the Kalends of July [17 June], Theodosius the Great, who seems to have been the author of that law’s enactment, decreed the same thing in Law 11 of the same title. Both laws may be read in the Theodosian Code.

These laws were confirmed in the following year, after Valentinian the Younger had died and Theodosius ruled the entire Roman Empire; they were strengthened by new and very severe penalties, under which no one could enter edifices of idols either in cities or in villages, nor could anyone offer sacrifices even while traveling. Since these laws were not everywhere wholly observed—as occurred in certain most remote villages of Africa, in which sacrifices were clearly celebrated, as is evident from Augustine and Canon 3 of the Council of Carthage, A.D. 401—new laws are found to have been repeatedly issued, ordering the destruction of rural shrines. On these see the Theodosian Code, title *On Pagans*.

[Col. 0058B] These details concerning the fate of pagan temples and sacrifices required lengthy discussion, not so much that Baronius’s error might be exposed as that the more certain date of our Author might be determined. For, on the one hand, he wrote Treatise 14 of Book I at a time when Gentiles were not permitted to build new temples—a condition fitting only the age of Christian emperors. On the other hand, he wrote Treatise 5 when Gentiles could with impunity both enter temples and celebrate sacrifices; he also mentions sacrifices performed in the countryside in Treatise 15 of the same book, no. 5. Under Christian emperors, at least in the West, permission for these acts existed only from Julian’s death until A.D. 391, when temples were closed and all sacrifices everywhere forbidden. It follows that the Author wrote the cited treatises during this intervening period, from which his date may be determined with the greatest certainty.

If anyone objects that sacrifices took place in African villages at the beginning of the fifth century, as we have just noted from Augustine and the Carthaginian synod, we reply at once—lest someone perhaps suppose that the Author’s date may therefore be extended beyond A.D. 391—that, although after that time the license of certain pagans in some village may have gone so far as to despise even the emperor’s repeated laws, still no one could be found to litigate about the legal right of pagan temples, since not merely the legal right to temples but the temples or shrines themselves, along with sacrifices, had already been abolished.

Yet in the recently cited Treatise 15, besides sacrifices celebrated in rural shrines, the Author testifies that disputes concerning the legal right of temples arose daily, as may be seen from note 15 on the words: “You litigate daily lest anyone take from you the legal right of temples.” Therefore, although the date of another author who mentioned sacrifices might be extended beyond A.D. 391, that of our Author certainly cannot.

§ VI.—The Author, imitating not so much Lactantius as Hilary also, is shown to have lived after the middle of the fourth century.

The chronological limits which we assigned to the Author in the preceding paragraph—from Julian’s reign to A.D. 391—fit admirably with what we add concerning his imitation of Hilary. This must be regarded as a new and invincible argument for assigning the same Author to the fourth century. From the annotations on Treatise 8 of Book I and Treatises 17 and 21 of Book II, which we believe we have demonstrated in chapter 1, § 2, to be genuine works of our Author, it is quite clear that, when he wrote these treatises, he had before his eyes Hilary’s Commentary on the Psalms, from which he excerpted not merely several thoughts but sometimes the very same words.

[Col. 0059A] Now this Commentary, as the Benedictine editors establish, was Hilary’s final work, written after A.D. 364 and before A.D. 368, when he had already died. At the least, that Commentary was certainly composed after the books *On the Trinity*, published in exile before A.D. 360, after he had been released from exile and returned from the East to the West; this occurred in A.D. 360 itself. Therefore our Author, who read this Commentary so conveniently that he sometimes extracted certain thoughts from it in precisely the same words, must be placed after the middle of the fourth century. This corresponds wonderfully with the chronological limits established in the preceding paragraph.

What we suggested in the same chapter 1, § 2 concerning the imitation of Lactantius would also support assigning the Author to the fourth century, since Lactantius too belongs to that century. But because the imitation of Hilary points to a narrower and later period, we judged that the argument should chiefly be drawn here from it. It is so evident that no one can offer a probable reply unless he rejects the three treatises from the Author and assigns them to Hilary—although we have shown there that they differ too openly from Hilary’s style and must be vindicated for our Author. By the same reasoning, four other treatises listed there, in which the Author similarly imitates Lactantius and sometimes follows him in exactly the same words, would have to be denied to the same Author and attributed to Lactantius. Yet if anyone said this, in order not to place the Author after Lactantius’s period, he would make Lactantius, a layman writing against the Gentiles, into a bishop preaching sermons, and would be met with the laughter of scholars.

[LVII] § VII.—A notable passage of the Author concerning the redemption of captives, wonderfully consonant with two passages of St. Ambrose, is shown to concern persons captured by barbarians after the battle of Hadrianople, A.D. 378. Several arguments establish that the Author’s date cannot be extended beyond the fourth century.

What has been said thus far proves that the Author flourished not only in the fourth century, but also after A.D. 360 and before A.D. 391. Finally, we propose for consideration another historical event indicated by the Author, by which that same dating will be admirably confirmed. At the end of Treatise 10 of Book I, commending the generosity of his hearers, the Author says: “But this is not addressed to you, brethren, whose generosity is known in all the provinces, whose pious seed is scattered, as it were, through the members of the whole world; through you many have been redeemed, many have been freed from deadly edicts, many stripped of harsh conditions give thanks.”

Here he speaks of the redemption of captives. Some, unless redeemed, were oppressed by harsh conditions; others were compelled to undergo death because they were subject to deadly edicts issued against them, as we have established in the notes there. These captives had to have been dispersed through so many and such great regions that the generosity of those contributing to their redemption was known in all the provinces, and their pious seeds—that is, alms—were scattered through the members of the whole world, namely through the provinces of the Roman Empire.

Under Constantius, Valentinian the Elder, and other emperors of the fourth century, barbarians are indeed recorded to have repeatedly invaded the frontiers of the Roman Empire, and there is no doubt that Christians were carried off into captivity by them. But among the various incursions of this kind, none can at all fit the events indicated by the Author except that which followed the battle of Hadrianople, in which the Emperor Valens himself most miserably perished along with two-thirds of his army.

For the other incursions, as we learn from Marcellinus, who carefully describes each, were slight and limited in scope; they did not ravage whole provinces, were more quickly suppressed by the Romans, and generally compelled the barbarians to seek peace on the condition that they restore all captives, as Zosimus expressly reports, Book III, ch. 5, concerning one incursion under Julian. But it was not so with that invasion which we called fatal to Valens. Let us briefly describe the event from Ammianus Marcellinus, Book XXXI.

[Col. 0060B] When the Huns had brought devastation upon the Gothic people, the Goths, wishing to escape the assault of the Huns and seek a dwelling beyond all their reach, resolved to withdraw into Thrace. They sent envoys to Valens with many promises, and the emperor consented, provided that they entered that Roman province without carrying weapons. This was done in A.D. 376. But afterward, oppressed by hunger through the greed of officials and driven to revolt, they assumed a savage temper and ravaged all Thrace not only with slaughter and fire but also with an immense number of captives.

When Valens heard this, he hastily settled matters as best he could with the Persians and hurried into Thrace. In A.D. 378, at Hadrianople, he joined battle with the barbarians, and the outcome was most disastrous. “For,” says Marcellinus, “it is established that scarcely a third part of the army escaped. Nor, apart from the battle of Cannae, does any event appear in the annals to have been fought with such utter destruction.” In this victory it can scarcely be said how many soldiers from various provinces suffered captivity. But why mention soldiers alone? For afterward, elated by this success and more terrible to the Romans, the Goths ranged widely through the northern provinces and freely traversed them as far as the roots of the Julian Alps, which antiquity called the Veneti—these are Marcellinus’s own words.

In this devastation of so many provinces they subjugated not only Macedonia and Thessaly, mentioned by Zosimus, Book IV, ch. 31, but, besides destroying very many people, carried away innumerable captives from other provinces also mentioned by Marcellinus, profiting by their slavery, sale, or ransom. The calamity of captives who could not be redeemed by their own people was such that they were consigned to harsh slavery or even to death. Such compassion for their suffering arose among Christians that money was collected from all quarters; some bishops of churches did not hesitate even to melt down sacred vessels, so that from their sale they might raise money to redeem more captives.

[LVIII] The following two testimonies of St. Ambrose from Book II of *On the Duties of Ministers* must be cited here, for they certainly speak of this redemption; and they will show both how great the captives’ misery was and how closely that writer agrees with our Author. First, St. Ambrose, ch. 15, no. 70:

> “It is also the highest generosity to redeem captives, to snatch men from the hands of enemies, to rescue human beings—and especially women—from death and from disgrace; to restore children to parents, parents to children, and citizens to their native land. These things are too well known from the devastation of Illyricum and Thrace: so many captives were for sale everywhere throughout the whole world that, if you called them back, they could not fill the number of one province! For,” he continues in no. 71, “the barbarians brought nothing of humanity to mercy, except what greed had preserved for ransom.”

The other testimony, ch. 28, no. 136 of the same Book II, is expressed in these words:

> “We have sometimes incurred reproach because we broke up the sacred vessels in order to redeem captives . . . But who is so hard, cruel, and iron-hearted that he should be displeased because a man is redeemed from death, a woman from the impurities of barbarians—which are worse than death—or young women, boys, or infants from the contamination of idols, by which they were defiled through fear of death?”

Have you observed: captives throughout the whole world, whom one who redeemed them would rescue from death? What could agree more closely with our Author’s words? Therefore, to return at last to the main point of the argument: since our Author, in commending the most generous liberality displayed by his hearers in redeeming captives, has in view the redemption of the same captives of whom Ambrose wrote—the only event by which it could truly happen that generosity of this kind was known in all the provinces and its pious seed scattered, as it were, through the members of the whole world, as the Author declares—it is beyond doubt that Treatise 10 of Book II was delivered after A.D. 378, when the barbarians carried off so great a number of captives, partly from the defeated Roman soldiers and partly from the subjugated Roman provinces.

But since there must at last be some end to the arguments for establishing the Author’s date, how wonderfully do all the chronological indications gathered, though from various treatises, concur in the fourth century—and indeed [Col. 0061D] in such a way that some of them plainly prove that the Author wrote no earlier than the middle of that century, while others prove that he did not write in a later century! For the former part, which alone has been more disputed, most of the evidence has been assembled from several treatises. As for the latter, which no one has challenged, the points we alleged from the laws of the Theodosian Code in § 5 are clear; from them we have determined that the Author wrote the seventh treatise of the first book before the year 391. Although this evidence, especially in a matter least open to dispute, ought to be more than sufficient, nevertheless I should like briefly to offer two observations from other treatises, so that you may see that all cohere and all point to the same period.

First, the Author vehemently condemns second marriages in Treatises 5 and [Col. 0062A] 16 of Book I. Although this was common in ancient centuries, you will not readily find it censured so sharply beyond the fourth century. Then, in Treatise 4, no. 1, and Treatise 5, no. 6, of the same book, he mentions virgins then flourishing among the pagans, whom there is no doubt were Vestals. In our notes we have shown from other authors that these were still flourishing in the fourth century; but there were none in the fifth, since, after their revenues and likewise their estates had been taken away by Gratian, and after Theodosius the Great’s victory over Eugenius in 394, Zosimus, Book V, chapter 38, records that under the reign of Theodosius himself only a single old woman remained among the Vestal virgins. From this Lipsius proves, in his *Syntagma on the Vestals*, chapter 14, that the Vestals survived to the very end of the reign of the elder Theodosius, but were then wholly extinguished. But perhaps we have already said too much concerning the arguments which we have been able to discover for defining or limiting the Author’s date. Let us proceed at once to the objections.

[LIX] § VIII.—The objection concerning persecutions and martyrs is refuted. A brief history of fourth-century persecutions.

The matters that moved Baronius, since they concern subjects dealt with in the preceding paragraphs, have there been rejected by us, with the single exception of that concerning signs of idolatry on coins; yet this too, drawn from Treatise 10, you will find sufficiently answered in note 11. The arguments which the Veronese editors introduced into their preface in order to persuade readers that the Author was most ancient all fit not merely the first three centuries of the Church, [Col. 0062C] but also the fourth, and some likewise the fifth. This is in part clear from what has already been said, and in part will appear from the notes to be appropriately added. Only one argument, derived from the persecutions and martyrs mentioned by the Author, may seem to someone more forceful; and what we have collected in our notes may not suffice to overthrow it. Accordingly, something must be said concerning this point.

Not only in the two passages cited by those editors, but in three passages, explicit mention is made of persecutions or of martyrs then dying in the present time. In Treatise 6, *On Patience*, Book I, no. 8: “You are the daily mother and crown of martyrs.” In Treatise 27, Book II, no. 3, he depicts at length persecution under the allegory of the vintage and mentions martyrs “upon whom,” he says, “a violent hand is laid, and who are led away to the place of punishment . . . mocked by persecutors with every conceivable insult, they are slaughtered,” etc. Finally, in Treatise 45 of the same book: “Autumn too is the season of martyrdom, in which not the blood of the vine but that of the digger is shed.” Since in these passages persecutions and martyrs are indicated as present, indeed daily occurrences, which are thought in no way to fit the fourth century occupied by Christian emperors, it is inferred that the Author’s date must be raised to the time of the persecutions.

But first it should be observed that expressions of this sort are found in other fourth-century authors as well. Among them is this passage from Hilary’s *Commentary on Psalm* 122, no. 10, speaking of the injuries suffered by the faithful: “We are beaten, reviled, driven into flight, put to death by sword, flame, [Col. 0063A] and the deep; cruelty is wreaked upon our honour, cruelty upon our bodies: our pain lies in these wrongs.” See other testimonies in note 20 on Treatise 27, Book II.

Moreover, what if the opinion has taken root falsely that there were no persecutions and no martyrs in the fourth century? While Constantius was emperor, that great patron of the Arians, did not a dreadful persecution rage against Catholics defending the Nicene faith, in which some were carried off into exile, others tortured on the rack, and still others punished with death? Hence Hilary, in his book *Against Constantius*, no. 1, exhorts Catholics to martyrdom; and Liberius, in the letter to the Confessors written before his own exile, preserved in Hilary, fragment 6, uses these words in no. 1: “You have now been marked out as martyrs for future glory.” Likewise Athanasius, in the *Apology to Constantius*, no. 32, p. 316: “For if those who refused to sign against me suffered so many and such great evils; if laymen who refused communion with the Arians were condemned to death,” etc. Reporting similar matters, Hilary in his book *Against Constantius*, no. 11, testifies that clerics of the Church of Toulouse were beaten with clubs and deacons crushed with lead.

To this must be referred the massacres perpetrated in the Alexandrian Church when George invaded it. Considering these, Athanasius says in his Letter to the Orthodox: “Not to be lengthy in writing, persecution is at hand such as has never before arisen against the Church.” Therefore the most eminent father of the *Annals*, Cardinal Baronius, having set forth the matters relating to Constantius’s persecution, rightly concludes, no. 87, under the year 353:

> From what has been said concerning the affliction of certain Churches, it is permissible rather to imagine than to write what the others suffered. [Col. 0063C] For if so many and such great things are recorded as those which we have recently enumerated after collecting them from fragments of writers of different periods, what and how great must the remaining events be thought to have been, which have remained buried in silence? If the affairs of even one Church, over whose Catholic clergy and people a bishop presided in Catholic communion, had been recorded, a diligent historian would without doubt have produced a great volume from the disasters inflicted by the Arians.

Then, under the same Emperor Constantius, Sapor, king of the Persians and hostile to the Romans, stirred up a great persecution against Christians, in which many thousands of Christians died, as Jerome testifies in his *Chronicle*. Sozomen, Book II, from chapter 1 through chapter 13, describes this persecution at length and names several of the martyrs. His sole error is that he refers it to the age of Constantine, whereas, from the earlier testimony of Jerome and other evidence adduced by Valesius in his note on chapter 13, it is established that this kind of persecution began in 347 and continued until the death of that king, who died in 380. Ruinart most correctly proves this in the *Sincere Acts*, where, besides the acts mentioned by Sozomen, he supplies the acts of other martyrs who suffered in that persecution.

Constantius was succeeded by Julian. Although Julian decreed no open persecution against Christians, nevertheless not a few are proved to have gained the palm of martyrdom during his reign from those acts which the aforementioned Ruinart published among the genuine acts. Accordingly, Augustine rightly included him [Col. 0064A] in the catalogue of persecutors, in *The City of God*, Book XVIII, chapter 52. After Julian was killed in 363, Valentinian succeeded, following Jovian’s brief reign, and soon admitted his brother Valens to a share in the imperial power. This latter was far more vehement than Constantius in maintaining the Arian heresy and attacking the Catholic faith in the East, which he governed. Of this persecution Augustine left the following written in the same work, chapter 52: “Finally, in our own memory Valens . . . an Arian, did he not devastate the Catholic faith throughout the regions of the East with a great persecution?” And in Book II *Against the Letters of Petilian*, no. 206: “Let them inquire what the Catholic Church suffered in the East when Valens the Arian was emperor.”

Hence, without doubt, Saint Ambrose, in Book II *On the Faith*, chapter 16, calling persecutions those which Catholics suffered from Arian treachery—namely under Constantius and Valens—speaks thus in no. 140: “I have no desire to recall the slayings of confessors, tortures, and exiles”; and in no. 141: “But now, almighty God, enough and more than enough: by our destruction and by our blood, we have expiated the slayings of confessors, the exiles of priests, and the wickedness of so great an impiety”—that is, in the Gothic war, from which so great a ruin flowed into the Roman Empire. And in Book III *On the Faith*, chapter 15, no. 128: “Which of us would dare to unseal the priestly book”—that is, the Nicene faith—“sealed by confessors and already consecrated by the martyrdom of many? Those . . . who did not dare to violate it became confessors and martyrs. How can we deny their faith when we proclaim their victory?”

While Valens the Arian persecuted Catholics in the East, [Col. 0064C] Athanaric, king of the Goths, fought against them in the West. We still possess the most excellent letter of the Gothic Church to the Church of Cappadocia, written in 372, in which the martyrdom of Saint Saba is described. Concerning this persecution, confirmed by various contemporary authors whose testimonies Ruinart cites in the acts of Saint Saba the martyr, Augustine wrote in *The City of God*, Book XVIII, chapter 52:

> Is the persecution not to be counted when the king of the Goths persecuted Christians in Gothia itself with extraordinary cruelty, when there were there only Catholics, of whom very many were crowned with martyrdom?

Furthermore, from Ambrose, Book II *On the Duties of the Clergy*, chapter 28, we have learned that Christians captured by those barbarians were defiled by the contagion of idols through fear of death; and from this we understand that those who did not renounce the Christian faith or sacrifice to idols were put to death.

Finally, when pagans saw either by imperial command or through Christian zeal that temples of idols were being overthrown, statues broken to pieces, or even that relatives were abandoning their old superstition, professing the name of Christ, and being, as it were, snatched away from them, did they not, driven by a certain madness, raise a riot, attack whatever Christians they found, and kill many? Let the acts of the martyrs of Anaunia and of Vigilius, bishop of Trent, be read; toward the end also of the fourth century, he was killed by pagans in the neighbouring district of Trent. To this belong the words of Saint Ambrose, [LXI] Book I *On the Duties of the Clergy*, chapter 42, no. 17:

> I think it must also be guarded against lest some persons, through an excessive desire for glory, abuse their authority too insolently and often arouse and inflame the minds of the Gentiles, already alienated from us, into zeal for persecution and into anger. Thus, that they may be able to persevere and overcome punishments, how many do they cause to perish!

Here you see persecutors and martyrs indicated. These words undoubtedly concern persecutions stirred up by certain Catholic clerics or monks who, while moving the authorities against temples of idols, especially in the East, through excessive zeal for the Christian religion, provoked the indignation of the Gentiles against Christians. The sacred *Annals* testify that in these times some Christians were killed by tumultuous gatherings of pagans. After so many testimonies to fourth-century persecutions, who would now dare to press the persecutions or the few martyrs mentioned in our Author’s treatises in order to maintain, against the most evident arguments set forth in the preceding paragraphs, that he must be excluded from the fourth century?

# CHAPTER III. IT IS PROVED THAT THE AUTHOR OF THE TREATISES, WHOM WE HAVE SHOWN TO HAVE LIVED IN THE FOURTH CENTURY, IS SAINT ZENO, BISHOP OF VERONA.

## § I.—It is shown that the treatises in question have always been attributed to this Zeno by manuscripts, ancient witnesses, and the tradition of the Church of Verona.

But it is now time to proceed to the third head of the controversy, which is chiefly relevant to our purpose: namely, whether he whom we have thus far demonstrated in Chapter I to be the sole author of all the treatises under discussion, [Col. 0065C] and in Chapter II to be an author of the fourth century—whether he, I say, is Saint Zeno, bishop of Verona.

To prove this, we understand that two things must be proved: first, that the treatises in question have always been attributed to this Zeno alone; and then, that his lifetime properly falls in the fourth century. As regards the first point, all manuscript codices ascribe these treatises to Zeno by name—not merely through the general title prefixed to the codices, but also through certain formulae placed at the beginning or end of several treatises. In these formulae Saint Zeno is expressly named as the sole author of them all, as we established in Chapter I; this may be gathered from what was said there in § 1.

Only because the first edition, taken from Guarino’s papers, appeared in 1508 when the manuscripts were not known, some persons—who had seen not only no manuscripts but not even the edition itself—wrongly concluded from misunderstood words of Sixtus of Siena that Guarino himself had attached these treatises to Zeno and procured their publication; consequently, they claimed, there was no mention of them among the ancients. This latter observation seemed very weighty to Cardinal Bellarmine, since among others he named Eusebius and Jerome, who are entirely silent concerning Zeno of Verona.

But there is no need to say anything about the fantasy that the forgery and publication of the treatises are to be charged to Guarino, since, apart from the evidence of the manuscripts, the very words of the edition, quoted in the general preface, sufficiently demolish it. As to what moved Bellarmine—the silence of Eusebius and Jerome—it is easily [Col. 0066A] removed. Eusebius could not have written about Zeno, since Zeno flourished somewhat after Eusebius’s time. Jerome himself, who composed his catalogue of ecclesiastical writers in 392, shortly after the death of our Author, gives a sufficiently suitable answer in the prologue to the same work. Foreseeing that several writers, especially of that age, would be omitted and wishing to avoid incurring odium on that account, he excuses himself in these words:

> But if any of those who continue writing to this day have been omitted by me in this volume, they must blame themselves rather than me. For I could not know the writings of persons who concealed them, living far away; and what may perhaps be known to others may have been unknown to me in this corner of the world. Certainly, when they have become renowned through their writings, they will not greatly lament the loss caused by our silence.

Indeed, who has ever pronounced the works of Athenagoras and Commodianus spurious because Jerome says nothing of them? He likewise passed over the books of Julius Firmicus Maternus and Philastrius, famous on account of their subject matter and written in the same century and age as our Author; yet no one has called them into doubt. Add that the authors of treatises or sermons are seldom named by the ancients. Who mentioned Saint Gaudentius, bishop of Brescia, Zeno’s contemporary, although he himself collected and published in his lifetime treatises more carefully worked out? Who ever remembered the sermons of Saint Peter Chrysologus before the Anonymous of Melk was published by Father Pez, that single ancient author who for this reason included him among ecclesiastical writers? [Col. 0066C] Gennadius, who lavishly gives testimony to the letters of Saint Leo, says not a word about his sermons. We pass over many other matters of this sort, since no lengthy discussion is needed to refute similar objections.

It is, moreover, most astonishing that persons have been found to write that no mention had been made of Zeno’s sermons before they were published at Venice in 1508, when the Veronese had already long produced several witnesses older than that edition. In the Latin scholia to the Life of Saint Zeno which he himself composed in Italian, Baptista Perettus published a poem composed by Michael Fossati in 1482, containing these verses:

> Sacred Zeno, father of your country, the codex of your sermons teaches how great your muse was.

Lest the rarity of that little work be objected, the Veronese editors, in their preface—which is also prefixed to Zeno’s works in the *Libraries of the Fathers*—adduced two other witnesses: Flavio Biondo, a fifteenth-century writer, in *Italia illustrata*, region 9; and Peter de Natalibus, a fourteenth-century bishop and writer, Book I of the *Catalogue of Saints*, chapter 43. Perettus, moreover, in the scholia mentioned above, added William Pastrengo, who flourished about the middle of the fourteenth century.

In a very rare work printed under the title *On the Origins of Things*—incorrectly, however, because, as Scipio Maffei rightly observes in Book II *On Veronese Writers*, that title belongs only to Pastrengo’s second little book, while the first, prefixed to it, should from the author’s purpose [Col. 0067A] and from its subject matter have been entitled *On Illustrious Men*—Pastrengo, I say, in this little work *On Illustrious Men*, p. 77, after listing Saint Zeno’s treatises, adds:

> The memorable John, priest and mansionary of the greater church, testifies that he saw and read all these little works.

Besides those witnesses cited by the Veronese, there are others much older and beyond every exception. Peter Calo, of the Order of Preachers, who compiled two volumes *On the Lives of the Saints* at the beginning of the fourteenth century and is cited by Peter de Natalibus, at the end of the *History of the Elevation of the Body of Saint Zeno*, published by Henschenius from the Barberini manuscript, vol. II for April, p. 76, not only mentions Zeno’s treatises, but testifies that he saw them, composed in a beautiful and subtle style, in two volumes [Col. 0067B]—that is, divided into two books, as they appear in the manuscripts—at Saint Zeno of Verona, that is, in the monastery of Saint Zeno at Verona.

At the same beginning of the fourteenth century, a certain John, called by Panvinius a deacon of Verona and by Pastrengo, his near contemporary, a priest and mansionary, wrote the Imperial History from which our Panvinius derived no little assistance in composing the *Antiquities of Verona*. In Book I of that [LXIII] history—some manuscript excerpts from which Jerome Tartarotius has very kindly sent us—he compiled the same list of Zeno’s treatises which both William Pastrengo and Peter de Natalibus are known to have copied word for word, and he adds: “These writings and treatises of his I myself read and saw.”

Opposite this list, the following marginal note is found in the same codex, providing another testimony concerning our Author:

> I, Leonardus Judex de Quinto of Verona, possess all the above-written books

—meaning the sermons of Saint Zeno indicated by John the priest—“which are in a most elegant style.”

This Leonardus Judex de Quinto, who is named in a document of 1379 in Ughelli, vol. V, p. 885, possessed a most flourishing library at Verona, which, as Mazagagia reports in a manuscript work in the Muselli library entitled *On Modern Deeds*, Book III, chapter 8, he transferred to Venice in 1388. Before this time, in a very ancient manuscript of the Veronese chapter containing Jerome’s and Gennadius’s catalogue *On Illustrious Men*, Zeno’s name is found added in a later hand, [Col. 0067D] because even then he was being reckoned among ecclesiastical writers.

In the eleventh century, or at latest in the twelfth, an anonymous monk of the monastery of Verona, writing the Life of Saint Zeno, openly shows that he had read Zeno’s sermons. For he introduces Zeno speaking in two discourses: one of them gives in the same words the beginning and end of Treatise 6, *On Patience*, Book I; the other is similarly drawn from Treatises 32 and 42, Book II. See the documents appended to *Diplomatic History* and published by Marquis Maffei, p. 326.

In the tenth century Ratherius, bishop of Verona, an eminent writer of many works in his time, openly recognizes Saint Zeno, his predecessor, as the author of sermons. He cites four times testimony from Zeno’s own treatise on Judah, which now appears as Treatise 14, Book II; and this is the treatise which, as we observed in note 1 on the Urbino codex, was formerly publicly read in the Church of Verona on the third Sunday of Lent. Ratherius calls Zeno by the following expressions. First, Part I *On Contempt for the Canons*, p. 352, vol. I of the latest edition of Acheri’s *Spicilegium*: “Here I shall use the authority of blessed Zeno, namely in the sermon which, in his accustomed most eloquent manner, he composed on Judah the patriarch and Tamar his daughter-in-law, saying,” etc. Again shortly thereafter: “As Saint Zeno affirms.” Thirdly, at the end of Sermon 1 *On Lent*, p. 391: “That blessed Zeno says to the contrary.” Finally, more expressly, in the Synodical Letter to the Presbyters, p. 377: “Since our special teacher [Col. 0068B] and protector, namely blessed Zeno, says,” etc.

But why should we linger longer in enumerating ancient witnesses, when the oldest and most excellent testimony of all is available from the Reims manuscript, which, as we saw in the preface, bears the name of Archbishop Hincmar and was given to the monastery of Saint Remigius? There we also observed that this codex had long been in use in the Church of Verona before it came into Hincmar’s hands, and so must be considered somewhat older than Hincmar’s own age, that is, the ninth century. In this codex, just as in other manuscripts of later date, Saint Zeno is repeatedly declared to be the author of the treatises, both in the title and in the formulae cited a little earlier.

What is more, since this very codex was formerly used in the Church of Verona, it supplies the ancient tradition of that Church concerning Saint Zeno as author. For in many annotations in an ancient hand placed in its margins, which we described in the preface, it is recorded that several treatises were long ago publicly read from that codex by our bishops or deacons during sacred ecclesiastical offices. Who, then, would fail clearly to recognize in so ancient and well-established a rite of the Church of Verona that the same Church always regarded as the author of these treatises—which were adopted so especially into the ancient and solemn use of the Veronese liturgy—Saint Zeno the bishop? His merits gave him to this city as patron, and so commended his sermons to his successors that several of them passed into certain formularies of sacred mysteries to be recited annually [Col. 0068D] on fixed days. Surely, if they had been the work of another bishop, an outsider or one less worthy, it is wholly incredible that they could have entered, under Saint Zeno’s name, the liturgy in some sense proper to this one Church and have been publicly read in that Church for so long.

Who, then, can any longer doubt that the ninety-one treatises [LXIV] which we showed in Chapter I to be by one author have no other author than Saint Zeno, bishop of Verona? To him they are assigned both by manuscripts from so many different cities and provinces, by the testimonies of so many writers, and also by the tradition of the Church of Verona.

## § II.—The common prejudice concerning Saint Zeno’s age under Gallienus, the sole objection so far raised against the conclusions established, is reconsidered. Baronius’s and Ughelli’s opinion of two Zenos—one flourishing under Gallienus, the other, in the fourth century, author of the treatises—is wholly novel. All documents recognize only one Zeno as bishop of the Church of Verona; therefore Baronius retracted his opinion. The origin and basis of the prejudice in question.

Once the Author has been determined by these arguments, nothing further need be added concerning his date. For if it has been evidently demonstrated for us in Chapter II that the author of the treatises flourished in the fourth century, it plainly follows that Zeno—whom we have thus far shown, by so many manuscripts and witnesses and by the ancient tradition of the Church of Verona itself, to be the author of those same treatises—must likewise have flourished in the fourth century, and certainly within those limits [Col. 0069A] of that century which we have already fixed from the most certain marks in the treatises.

Yet against this most well-established argument stands the one common prejudice by which Saint Zeno is believed to have lived under Gallienus, that is, in the third century. This prejudice is promoted by some under the name of the tradition of the Church of Verona. In order not to oppose it, Cardinal Baronius in the first edition of his *Martyrology*, and Ferdinand Ughelli in vol. V of *Sacred Italy*, judged that two Zenos, bishops of Verona, must be admitted: one who, as was handed down, died under Gallienus; the other, author of the treatises, who flourished in the fourth century. But if we establish beyond all doubt that the Church of Verona always recognized a single Zeno to whom the sermons can and ought to be attributed, and that he flourished not in the third but in the fourth century, nothing further can be objected.

Before Baronius—who first introduced two Zenos without any documentary evidence, led solely by the argument that he knew with certainty that one Zeno, the author of the sermons, was a fourth-century man, but had learned from Veronese sources that another Zeno was venerated by the Church of Verona as having lived under Gallienus—no one had ever heard of two Zenos as bishops of this city. The very tradition of the Church of Verona openly opposes this opinion, since it has always recognized only one Zeno, in such a manner that the same man whom it venerated as the holy and great patron of the city it has perpetually held to be the writer of the sermons. This is clear from all the authors of different centuries whom we cited a little earlier, and likewise from all the manuscripts, three of which were written in the thirteenth century, while one was produced before the ninth, in order to be used by the Church of Verona itself in public offices.

Among these testimonies of the Church of Verona, those of Ratherius and of the Reims manuscript deserve particular notice, because they display greater antiquity and authority. Ratherius, as we indicated above, cites Zeno three times as author of the same treatise, and everywhere calls him either Blessed or Saint, because he was then regarded as the author of the sermons who was venerated among the saints by that Church. Most particularly to be noted is the passage in the Synodical Letter: “Since our special teacher and protector, namely blessed Zeno, says in the sermon which he composed most elegantly on Judah, son of Jacob, and Tamar his daughter-in-law.” Now this Zeno, “our special teacher and protector,” has always been and still is Saint Zeno, whom Ratherius, using a similar phrase in his *Apologeticus*, p. 366, vol. I of Acheri’s *Spicilegium*, where he mentions Zeno’s basilica, calls “our particular patron.”

Moreover, from the Reims manuscript, which records that several treatises were read by bishops or deacons among the sacred mysteries of the Church of Verona, do we not plainly learn that the Church regarded their author as both a bishop of Verona and a saint, as he is there entitled? Nor should Ferdinand Ughelli be heard, who, perhaps to reconcile these facts, also enrolled among the saints a second Zeno, supposedly the author of the treatises. The Church of Verona has always listed, and still lists, only one Zeno among its sainted bishops. [Col. 0070B] Indeed, it is most astonishing that, although he introduced this other Zeno, unknown to the Church of Verona, into the succession of Veronese bishops under the guidance of Baronius—who was the first and only person to state this opinion in the first edition of the *Martyrology*—and moreover arbitrarily invented him as a saint, he did not rather follow Baronius as his guide when Baronius, warned of the Veronese tradition by those responsible for the Veronese edition of Zeno, had long since abandoned and retracted his earlier opinion concerning two Zenos in his second revision of the *Martyrology*, in these words:

> But since, as we have learned, the Church of Verona does not accept two Zenos, we willingly withdraw from our former opinion.

Yet another tradition of the same Church of Verona seems opposed to the Veronese tradition which we have thus far demonstrated: namely, the tradition by which the same Zeno is reported to have been a martyr under Gallienus. This cannot be reconciled with the date of the Author of the sermons. It is not our intention here to eliminate Zeno’s martyrdom, concerning which more will be said in Dissertation 3, chapter 2, but rather to eliminate the date which is elevated to Gallienus’s reign.

One Coronatus, a notary and writer of the seventh or eighth century, laid the foundation for this tradition—or rather prejudice. From him others subsequently proclaimed an antiquity honourable not only to Zeno but also to the Church of Verona. To overthrow Coronatus’s foundation, we shall first propose for consideration two ancient monuments beyond every exception, proving that Zeno—whom the Church of Verona recognized as one only—lived in the [Col. 0070D] fourth century. Then, after examining Coronatus’s own little work, we shall diminish the credibility of the present tale also by showing his several errors in this history; and, if possible, we shall seek out and indicate its occasion or origin.

## § III.—Zeno is proved to have lived in the fourth century from Saint Ambrose’s letter to Syagrius. The same is established by the ancient list of bishops of Verona, which plainly derived from the diptychs.

Let the first document be Letter 5 of Saint Ambrose to Syagrius, whom the context of the letter plainly proves to have been bishop of Verona at that time. In this letter, no. 1, Ambrose mentions the virgin Indicia, whom he testifies had been approved by the judgment of Zeno of holy memory and consecrated by his blessing. This virgin, who is shown throughout the letter to have been subject to Syagrius’s jurisdiction, was certainly a virgin of Verona; and Zeno of holy memory, who approved and blessed her, was undoubtedly Saint Zeno, bishop of Verona, since it is certain that at that time no one except a man exercising the highest priestly office blessed and consecrated virgins.

Nor should anyone object with the Veronese editors that Indicia, a citizen of another city, could have been veiled by another Zeno, and afterward come to Verona to spend her life with her sister, who had married Maximus of Verona. It is easy to say such things, but not similarly easy to prove them. If, when some clear document is produced against certain prejudices, it were permissible to introduce inventions in favour of the prejudice, what could ever be so firm and certain that it could not by this method be uprooted and evaded? Therefore, after Father Labbe, this argument drawn from Ambrose’s letter has rightly appeared altogether compelling and evident to everyone, so that learned men have judged the reply of the Veronese editors to be worthless and not even worthy of mention.

What if we confirm still more plainly, from the very things narrated in Ambrose’s letter, that the virgin Indicia was a Veronese? For Maximus, the husband of her sister, after initiating litigation against Indicia concerning certain property, was greatly distressed that the virgin had withdrawn from association in the estate of his kinship. He therefore ordered that the dwellings of his wife and of the virgin be separated by a wall [Col. 0071C] interposed between them—surely in the same house—and that the fellowship of sisterhood between the sisters be divided, as is reported in no. 17, p. 769. This is clear evidence that one part of the shared house belonged to Indicia. For if she had come to Verona from another city, Maximus, given his hostile and alienated disposition toward her, could have expelled her from both house and city and sent her back to her native country. But let us proceed to other matters.

A second proof is drawn from the ancient succession of the first eight bishops of Verona, which we have carefully learned was preserved in several records, until, owing to the preconceived opinion about Zeno’s age, more recent writers did not hesitate on their own initiative to fabricate another succession. According to Panvinio, *Antiquities of Verona*, book IV, chapter 3, this succession was read in the Imperial History of John [Col. 0071D], mentioned by us in § 1. The part especially relevant to our purpose, which sets out the order of the last five bishops, is contained in the fragment which Jerome Tartarotius excerpted for us from that manuscript Imperial History, in these words:

> Blessed Zeno, bishop of Verona, an outstanding teacher, was the eighth bishop of that city. For after St. Proculus, who was the fourth bishop, St. Saturninus received the episcopate; Lucillus succeeded him; after him came St. Gricinus, a teacher; and Blessed Zeno succeeded him.

We read the same order in an older author who wrote a rhythmical poem in praise of Verona. This little work, found in a manuscript of the monastery of Lobbes—where it may be believed to have been brought by Bishop Ratherius, when, exiled from Verona, he returned to that monastery from which he had come—was first made public by Mabillon in prose form in his *Analects*. Later our Marquis Maffei reprinted it in its rhythmical form among the records appended to his *Diplomatic History*. This poem was also complete in a manuscript of the Celestine monastery at Rimini; and a fragment of it, concerning Zeno and the succession, is transcribed at the end of a codex containing the treatises of St. Zeno in the monastery of St. Zeno. It was likewise preserved complete at Verona in another codex formerly held by the Jesuates dwelling at the monastery of St. Bartholomew on the Hill, written at the end of a Pentateuch. Bagata and Perettus attest that this Pentateuch was written in a parchment codex in very ancient lettering, in their book entitled *Ancient Records of the Holy Bishops of Verona*, p. 14 [Col. 0072A–B]. From the same codex Jerome a Curte transferred the earlier part of this poem into book I of his *History of Verona*.

In the manuscript of St. Zeno this poem is said to have been taken from the writings of Isidore; Jerome a Curte, as well as the aforementioned Bagata and Perettus, sufficiently imply that they believed this. The error appears to have been occasioned by the fact that Isidore is named in the second verse of the poem. Yet the context openly shows that the poem was written long after Isidore, since Pepin was then residing at Verona—that is, at the end of the eighth century, or at least at the beginning of the ninth. For Pepin was called king of Italy in 781 and died in 810. We shall therefore henceforth call the author of this poem the Pipinian Anonymous. Accordingly [Col. 0072C], this Anonymous sets out the order of the first eight bishops of Verona in these verses:

> Euprepus, bishop, first preached at Verona;  
> Dimidrianus was second, Simplicius third;  
> Proculus, a confessor, an excellent shepherd, fourth;  
> Saturninus was fifth, and Lucilius sixth;  
> Gricinus, teacher and bishop, was seventh;  
> Zeno, the renowned martyr, shepherd and confessor, eighth.

[LXVII] This succession of bishops deserves the highest regard. The Churches took the greatest care to preserve such lists, since ancient discipline required them to write the bishops in order in the diptychs and to recite all of them, even the saints, at the second *Memento* during the solemnities of Mass, both in East and West, in approximately the form that we learn from the Book of Sacraments of St. Gregory, edited by Menard from a Corbie manuscript. There, in the Mass for a deceased bishop, below the action, vol. III of the Works of St. Gregory, p. 215, are these words [Col. 0072D]:

> Over the diptychs. Remember also, O Lord, thy servants N., who have gone before us and sleep in the sleep of peace.

After this, the names written in the diptychs were recited; hence follows: “Likewise after the reading,” namely, of the diptychs: “To these, O Lord, and to all who rest in Christ,” etc.

This rite continued in force after the age of the Pipinian Anonymous, as is clear from testimonies cited by Father Martène, vol. I, *On the Ancient Rites of the Church*, book I, chapter 4, article 7, no. 24, p. 408. Especially noteworthy is the passage from the Roman Order of the Church of Amiens in the year 1120, where one reads: “Remember, O Lord, also those,” namely, Firminus, etc.; thirty-one bishops of that city are there listed by name [Col. 0073A]. Another is from Cardinal Ximenes’s Mozarabic Missal, in which a long succession of bishops of Toledo is recorded in Martène, article 12, p. 460.

Nor should it cause difficulty if the names of all the bishops of each church are not written at the *Memento* in every canon of ancient missals. For elsewhere the inserted notation “Remember N. and N.”—formerly written “Ill. and Ill.”—usually meant that all the bishops of that particular see were named from the diptychs themselves or from some similar record. Thus, in Colbert manuscript 2585, Martène adds after the words, “Remember also, O Lord, thy servants, male and female, Ill. and Ill.”: “the bishops of the present church.” From an order of diptychs of this kind the Pipinian Anonymous could have learned and recorded the genuine succession of the earlier bishops of Verona. We believe that Bishop Rampert of Brescia similarly recorded such a succession in a later age, when, in his sermon on the Translation of St. Philastrius, he set forth by names alone a much longer list of the bishops of Brescia, doubtless known from the diptychs [Col. 0073B].

Thus, lists from records of this kind, arising from so ancient and simple a rite, are not to be regarded as lists found in catalogues of a later age, but as though taken from the ancient diptychs themselves. They should be believed to contain the true succession of the ancient bishops as they followed one another. From them many errors may be corrected with complete safety; indeed, we seem to have corrected the later succession of the bishops of Ravenna, vol. IV of Cardinal Noris’s Works, p. 976 [Col. 0073C]. We have already corrected other matters in other episcopal successions in our work *On the Origins of the More Ancient Churches and Metropolitan Sees of Italy*, composed many years ago, which, when permitted, we shall complete and publish. There you will find a fuller discussion of the authority and use of such catalogues and diptychs.

Nor, indeed, should falsehoods inserted in later catalogues be objected to in order to undermine confidence even in the succession of bishops. The names of bishops alone, arranged in order, could have been taken from the diptychs, in which nothing besides their names was read. Hence this succession must be considered sufficiently secure and true. But as regards historical events and chronological notices, since these had to be taken from elsewhere [Col. 0073D], they could be inserted among the episcopal succession as true or fabulous according to the nature of the records from which they were drawn. Often certain things have been introduced from the opinion of the populace, lightly assenting to fables, which learned persons demonstrate to be utterly false. We particularly wish this warning to be noted, lest anyone think that credence must be given to everything said by the Pipinian Anonymous besides the succession of bishops. For what he inserted about the daughter of the emperor Gallienus is false, as we shall show in the following paragraph.

Moreover, lest anyone any longer doubt that this Anonymous’s succession was derived from the diptychs, we should like to confirm it by an argument which seems to us very clear. In this succession St. Proculus is placed before St. Zeno [Col. 0074A]; but according to the opinion of more recent writers, if Zeno is to reach the age of Gallienus, he must be placed before St. Proculus, since the age of St. Proculus is otherwise fixed later than Gallienus, as we shall soon see.

It is clear from many other records of this church that St. Proculus was always recognized as preceding Zeno. St. Proculus is constantly named before St. Zeno in all ancient canons of the Mass, prayers, epigrams, and litanies. Thus, for example, in the canon of four very ancient codices of our Veronese church: “of Proculus and Zeno”; while in the litanies of another capitular manuscript of the same church: “St. Proculus, St. Zeno, St. Theodore,” etc. The same saints are listed in the same order in certain prayers contained in this latter capitular codex, and also in a Roman Order of the ninth century [Col. 0074B], which Francis Blanchini published from another manuscript of the chapter of Verona in the Prolegomena to Anastasius, vol. III, p. 51. Finally, the same order occurs in an inscription of the same age still existing in the church of St. Helena, which anyone may read in Ughelli, vol. V, p. 781. The same order is found in ancient litanies from a nine-hundred-year-old Fleury manuscript, published by Father Martène, part 3 of *On the Ancient Rites of the Church*, book III, chapter 15, p. 592.

No other reason can be found for this than that St. Proculus preceded St. Zeno in time. Otherwise Zeno, being the great patron of the city of Verona and much more renowned throughout the Church, as we shall show in Dissertation III, ought to have been named first, unless chronology prevented it. We shall give relevant fragments from these Mass canons [Col. 0074C] and litanies in the same Dissertation III, chapter 4, where the discussion of Zeno’s cult will more properly belong. This argument, arising from ancient tradition and the true order, wonderfully confirms the genuineness of the Pipinian Anonymous’s succession and convicts of manifest novelty and error those who, abandoning or despising this ancient order, thought another new one should be introduced to sustain preconceived opinions.

To proceed from this Anonymous’s succession to the determination of Zeno’s age: St. Proculus is there fourth, and St. Lucillus sixth; the age of both is established from other records. St. Proculus was alive at the beginning of the fourth century, when Saints Firmus [Col. 0074D] and Rusticus were brought to Verona under Maximian and soon afterward crowned with martyrdom. This is plainly evident from their ancient Acts, published by Marquis Maffei at the end of his *Diplomatic History*, p. 303.

In some manuscripts of the Acts, Maximinus is read instead of Maximian, and some have therefore thought that Proculus’s age should be raised to Maximinus’s reign. But the Acts show that the emperor was then at Milan; Maximinus was never in that city, since, having scarcely entered Italy, he met death at the siege of Aquileia. This was rightly proved by our Father Peter of Padua, of the Conventual Order, in Ughelli, vol. V of *Italia Sacra*, p. 685. Moreover, many examples show that the names Maximian and Maximinus were written indiscriminately in codices [Col. 0075A] and easily confused. Thus the reading “Maximian,” found in other codices, appears not only preferable but genuine. It was found in the ancient manuscripts seen and cited by the Bollandist Fathers under 24 March, in the entry for St. Proculus. For it is well known that Maximian was at Milan and intensified the persecution of Christians; therefore St. Proculus and Saints Firmus and Rusticus are rightly assigned in all ancient martyrologies, as also in the Roman one, to the persecution of Diocletian and Maximian, which began to rage in 303. Thus the fourth bishop of Verona flourished at the beginning of the fourth century.

Let us turn to the sixth, named Lucillus—or Lucillius, as the Pipinian Anonymous wrote it for the sake of the metre of the rhythmical poem. Likewise, our Maffei shows that Isidorius must be written for *Isidorus* in the third verse for the same metrical reason [Col. 0075B]. In Fragment 2 of St. Hilary, p. 632, after the Sardican synodical letter to Pope Julius, there are subscriptions of fifty-nine bishops, among which, in twentieth place: “Lucius, from Verona in Italy.” The same occurs among the subscriptions attached by the same Sardican bishops to St. Athanasius’s letter to the clergy of Mareotis, which our most distinguished and learned fellow-citizen recently published from a most ancient manuscript of the chapter of Verona, vol. III of *Literary Observations*, p. 38.

The name Lucius instead of Lucillus should not disturb anyone. St. Athanasius called Lucillus the very man who subscribes in the synodical letter as Lucius, in two places: in the *Apology to Constantius*, no. 3, p. 297, “Λούκιλλος ὁ ἐν Βερωνὶ”—“Lucillus at Verona.” Though he does not identify the city in the other *Apology*, no. 50, p. 168, Lucillus is there [LXIX] named ninth among the bishops who either attended or agreed with the Council of Sardica; he is known to be the bishop of Verona, distinct from Lucius, listed in sixtieth place, bishop of another city, just as in the Sardican synodical letter another bishop of the same name subscribes separately from the bishop of Verona.

Therefore this Lucius—perhaps popularly called Lucillus, diminutively, because of his small stature—was among the Fathers of Sardica in 347. Indeed, from the words of Athanasius’s *Apology to Constantius*, he appears still to have been alive when Athanasius wrote that work, that is, in 356; or at least Athanasius, calling him living at that time, had heard nothing of his death:

> Fortunatianus, bishop of Aquileia, is a witness to this fact. The same may be confirmed by the testimony of Father Hosius. Crispinus of Padua, Lucillus of Verona, Dionysius of Leiden, and Vincentius, bishop in Campania, are likewise witnesses. And since Maximinus, etc., are dead …

By distinguishing Lucillus from the dead, Athanasius plainly believed him to be alive [Col. 0075D]. Now, if the fourth bishop of Verona, Proculus, flourished at the beginning of the fourth century, while the sixth, Lucillus, was still alive after the middle of that same century, in 356, who does not immediately understand—since, from what has been said, there can be no doubt about the order of the catalogue—that Zeno, listed as eighth, ascended the see of Verona some time after that year, so that some time, however brief, may be assigned to Gricinus, the intervening seventh bishop? This dating accords perfectly with the age of that Zeno [Col. 0076A] mentioned by St. Ambrose, and with that which we demonstrated in the preceding chapter must most evidently be assigned to the author of the treatises. Therefore the error is manifest by which the age of this same Zeno is raised to the reign of Gallienus.

Since, as we noted above, Coronatus the Notary, from whom the others received it, first disseminated this error, we should like to examine his relevant history, lest anyone be influenced even slightly by his authority. Although what we have established by the documents so far presented should be sufficient, nevertheless, for greater confirmation, we wish to submit his account to examination. If we show it plainly fabulous and false in other respects, it will certainly become evident that he drank from some muddy source, so that we are compelled to give him no credence in his chronological dating, especially since in this matter all the ancient records already considered openly contradict him.

### § IV. The account of Coronatus the Notary, by which the age of the emperor Gallienus is assigned to Zeno, examined and shown to abound in fables.

We shall see in the notice prefixed to the *Monuments* that Coronatus the Notary wrote the *Life of St. Zeno* in the seventh or eighth century. Yet he reports almost nothing properly concerning the life of St. Zeno, so that he seems to have received nothing about Zeno’s own deeds transmitted in writing. But just as Ratherius, tenth-century bishop of Verona, when intending to say something about St. Metrone—concerning whom he complains that nothing had been written—was forced to say what the unlearned populace sang, as is clear from Ratherius’s work recently published at the end of the *Book of Civil Law of the City of Verona* [Col. 0076B–C], so Coronatus, intending to write something about St. Zeno, of whom he had found nothing set down by the pen, could only report what, impressed on people’s minds by its fame and wonder, circulated in a kind of popular tradition: namely, certain remarkable miracles. Memory of these tends to endure longer; yet they themselves, through the disposition of the populace, commonly fall far from their original form by many additions, omissions, and alterations, and are so contaminated by false additions that it is very often impossible to distinguish and determine what is true and what false.

You may read Coronatus’s account concerning Gallienus in nos. 4 and following of the *Life* itself, which we shall give complete in the first place among the *Monuments*. To make clear to everyone how many improbable things it contains [Col. 0076D], we think it proper now to note the following. First, the remarkable event by which Gallienus’s only daughter is said to have been wonderfully freed from a demon after Zeno was summoned to the emperor by messengers ought to have been so notable and celebrated that it is utterly incredible that for approximately five centuries no one recorded anything about it, and that Coronatus the Notary, in the seventh or eighth century, was the first to mention it.

Next, in no. 5, the monastery in which St. Zeno is said to have lived with several others, all indeed called by Zeno’s name, is indicated to have been public at Verona. This is wholly unbelievable concerning the first three centuries, when Christians, concealed because of persecutions, displayed nothing in public buildings [Col. 0077A]. Further, when Zeno, at the emperor’s request, had set out to heal his daughter troubled by a demon and had expelled the demon, he is said to have received from Gallienus the emperor a royal crown which Gallienus himself wore on his head, and immediately distributed it to the poor. Yet before Aurelian an ornament of that kind was not in use among Roman emperors.

Who, further, could plausibly maintain that a pagan emperor permitted Zeno to destroy all idols and build churches in Christ’s name, and that this happened after Zeno had returned to Verona? Thus, though Christians possessed not even a single public church anywhere else, several would have been built at Verona through Zeno by order of that emperor, as is reported in no. 7. But let us omit many other things that could be considered; these are more than enough for competent judges to demonstrate that this narrative is fictitious.

If anything true lies hidden among these improbabilities, we can conjecture only this: that Coronatus committed these matters to writing from popular tradition without any examination. Perhaps it had anciently been handed down that Zeno freed the daughter of a certain Gallienus from a demon; and since the emperor Gallienus was well known to the populace, people began to relate that the daughter of the emperor Gallienus had been freed by Zeno. Such mistakes occur frequently in writers of a later age. For example, when they found certain names of governors resembling names of emperors, they made emperors out of governors. Perhaps that Gallienus whose only daughter St. Zeno healed lived at Palatium—[Col. 0077B–C] a place between Trent and Verona mentioned in the Itinerary of Antoninus—as Marquis Scipio Maffei observed in his letter to Coletus, inserted in vol. V of *Italia Sacra*, p. 675. When, through resemblance of name, this same man had been transformed into an emperor by popular addition, other improbable details were subsequently added to his story, which Coronatus adopted and wrote down. But we consider it utterly vain and unworthy to spend further effort on such conjectures.

Whatever the origin of this fable which insistently invokes the emperor Gallienus, all the many later writers who are known to have received it from Coronatus—so that it is often repeated in precisely the same words, and has even migrated into antiphons, responsories, and hymns—deserve no greater credence. Thus you see that the foundation upon which the ingrained prejudice that Zeno’s age reached the reign of Gallienus rests has at last been uprooted and utterly overthrown [Col. 0077D]. With this established, who, disregarding this narrative and prejudice, would not think that greater assent should be given to the documents by which St. Zeno is proved to have lived in the fourth century? Thus, with the other Zeno excluded—whom the Church of Verona never recognized—that Zeno should be considered the author of those treatises to whom they are most consistently attributed in manuscripts, by many writers, and by the tradition of the Church of Verona itself.

### [LXXI] § V. The age of St. Zeno delimited by certain bounds, with which all things are shown to agree.

From what has been established so far, it is possible to circumscribe our author’s episcopate within more certain chronological bounds [Col. 0078A]. In § 3 we proved clearly that Lucillus, the sixth bishop of Verona, lived in 356, or at least—if he had died shortly before—was considered alive by Athanasius in that year. Gricinus, or Grichinus, according to the order of the catalogues, succeeded Lucillus as seventh; St. Zeno succeeded him as eighth. Andrea Dandolo also states in his *Chronicle*, book IV, chapter 5, vol. XII of *Italian Matters*, p. 35, that Zeno was the successor of Brichinus, as he calls him.

In § 3 we also showed that Zeno had already died when St. Ambrose wrote to Syagrius. The Benedictine editors assign this letter of Ambrose to about 380; yet in their chronological ordering of the letters they observe that those who propose and insist on that year give no reason for their opinion. We infer that Ambrose sent this letter somewhat later than that year, but not earlier, because Zeno’s death seems, for other reasons, to be placed later rather than earlier.

It cannot be placed earlier, if adequate time is to be allowed for the notable generosity of the bishop of Verona in redeeming captives, which St. Zeno could commend in Treatise 12, book I. Such a celebrated redemption could not have been carried out except some time after the battle of Adrianople, in which Valens died in August 378, as anyone may infer from the discussion in chapter 2, § 7 [Col. 0078B]. That Zeno’s death occurred in the later part of 380, or in the following year, is not implausibly suggested by the fact that no bishop of Verona appears at the very numerous Western council held at Aquileia in 381, at which several bishops, especially from neighboring cities, were present. Although this could have happened for other reasons without referring it to death—for several others were likewise absent—it may have occurred because, after Zeno’s death, the see was vacant at that time. Thus sufficient time is left for the mentioned redemption. Whatever the case, there is no doubt that Bishop Zeno’s age must be placed between 356 and about 380.

Before we show how admirably all the matters that we have especially observed in the treatises marked by some indication of time in chapter 2 agree with this date, allow us, I ask, without any charge of presumption, to indicate by a certain conjecture that occurs to us the beginning of his episcopate. Concerning its end, indeed, we have supplied more certain records [Col. 0078C–D]. We do not wish to affirm anything, but only to propose what others may more prudently examine and, better instructed by records if they find them, either reject or confirm.

It is clear from no. 21 of the mentioned letter of Ambrose that the virgin Indicia, already blessed by Bishop Zeno, had lived with Marcellina, Ambrose’s own sister, at Rome, “in our house,” as Ambrose says, “while we were absent.” That is, she lived there when Ambrose, not yet a bishop, regarded his Roman residence as “our house,” where he customarily lived. Otherwise he would have omitted the expressions “in our house” and “while we were absent,” since a bishop’s house is none other than his episcopal residence. By the latter words he seems to indicate that at that time he was absent from that house as it were by chance; this can apply only to the period before his episcopate. Now St. Ambrose entered upon the episcopate in 374. Therefore Indicia, consecrated by Bishop Zeno, had been at Rome before 374.

Thus the beginnings of Zeno’s episcopate must be placed before 374. Moreover, in order that adequate time may be allowed both for Indicia’s journey to Rome and her stay in Ambrose’s house, and also for her consecration and probation by Zeno at Verona—so that she was not tested and blessed with the virginal veil only a few months after Zeno’s creation as bishop, which Ambrose’s words and meaning do not permit—Zeno must be said to have obtained the episcopate some time before 373 as well [Col. 0079A].

Then, in all ancient books of the Church of Verona, three days are marked on which Zeno’s memory was celebrated by sacred offices: the day before the Ides of April, the deposition of St. Zeno; the twelfth day before the Kalends of June, the translation of St. Zeno; the sixth day before the Ides of December, the dedication of the church of St. Zeno. All the surviving records in the monastery of the basilica of St. Zeno, though not very ancient, mark four feast days. For they add the feast of St. Zeno’s ordination. With this one difference: whereas other books mark the dedication of the church of St. Zeno on the sixth day before the Ides of December, these books belonging to that basilica—which ought to celebrate a more solemn office for its dedication and to give it preference over others—mark St. Zeno’s ordination for celebration on that day, and designate the dedication of the basilica two days later, that is, on the fourth day before the Ides of December.

See the movable solar Paschal Cycle composed in 1455, visible in the ambulatory of that monastery; the manuscript monastic breviary preserved in its library; and the parchment books used in the choir, which appear older than the other records [Col. 0079B–C]. Why, I ask, did the monks of St. Zeno alone, to whom that basilica belonged, transfer the feast of its dedication—which should have been preferred above all others—to another day in order to make room for the office of St. Zeno’s ordination, while others observed no such celebration? If this proceeded from some ancient and distinctive rite, and was not recently invented—as what follows strongly implies it was ancient—then the dedication of the church of St. Zeno must surely be placed on the sixth day before the Ides of December in such a way that his ordination too fell on that same day. The Church of Verona now indeed celebrates it on that day according to the latest recension of the Roman Martyrology.

Indeed, on the wall of the choir of the recently demolished ancient and distinguished parish church of St. Zeno at Brescia, which from ancient times down to our own memory celebrated its patron’s feast on the sixth day before the Ides of December with the rite of a Confessor and Bishop, there was a painting of about the fourteenth century representing the consecration, or ordination, of St. Zeno, with these verses below it:

> Zeno is consecrated; the church renews its solemn rites.  
> Offer incense, devout ones: let your devout incense be prayers.

These two testimonies—the painting and the verses—plainly signify that, by ancient tradition, this day was held sacred to St. Zeno’s ordination [Col. 0079D–0080A].
