Moreover, in the old Book of Sacraments of the Ambrosian Church published by Pamelius, when the Mass of St. Zeno is prescribed for the sixth day before the Ides of December, there is read in it a prayer, p. 438, which very explicitly mentions the ordination of the same holy bishop:

> Almighty everlasting God, who hast adorned thy blessed confessor Zeno with pontifical insignia, etc.

The feast of his ordination was also marked on the same day in a manuscript martyrology of the Church of Verona from 1274, cited by Bagata and Perettus in *Ancient Records of the Holy Bishops of Verona*, p. 16. Further, even in the older records of this church which mark the dedication of the basilica on that same day, not everything in the sacred offices concerns the dedication of a church, as is almost customary in other books when they prescribe the celebration of a church’s dedication. This may be seen in the records published by the Venerable Thomasius and in the Sacramentary of St. Gregory. Rather, most elements—and especially the Mass appointed and recited on that very day—concern the feast of Bishop Zeno, as will be clear from the documents to be supplied after the dissertations [Col. 0080A–B].

The Mass of St. Zeno—I say of St. Zeno, not of the dedication of the basilica—for December is mentioned in two charters: one of 922 [LXXIII], p. 732, in Ughelli, vol. V; and another of 1038, p. 754. The feast of St. Zeno in December is mentioned in another charter of 865, p. 721. Finally, what is of greater value than all else: in the Book of Sacraments which, as we shall see in the notice to the *Monuments*, was written under King Otto, and likewise in Vatican manuscript 3806, of about the ninth century, of which we shall speak there, two prayers assigned to the eighth day of December similarly mention the beginning of Zeno’s pontificate, or ordination [Col. 0080B–C]. In the Secret, for instance, we find:

> O God, who bringest a bright light into the world through shining pearls, and who hast prepared for the blessed pontificate [thus in the cited manuscripts; but in Angelo Rocca’s Roman edition of the Gregorian Sacramentary, which contains this same Mass, “for the pontificate”] of Zeno an eternal crown of glory in heaven, etc.

More explicitly, in the prayer at Communion:

> O God, who hast made for such a church a bishop—namely, who hast consecrated St. Zeno as bishop.

You will read these prayers in full below, in the Masses to be set out. From this someone may conjecture that formerly, perhaps before the basilica of St. Zeno was dedicated in the ninth century, the commemoration of his ordination was made in the sacred offices on the sixth day before the Kalends of December. But once the basilica was subsequently consecrated on the same day, of which annual mention had to be made, the solemn celebration of both feasts seems to have been joined in such a way that something was said in the offices concerning the dedication of the basilica, while most elements concerning ordination, or Zeno as bishop, were still retained. Meanwhile the feast of the dedication, being later, began to be marked in ritual books, so that mention of the ordination gradually disappeared from titles and calendars [Col. 0080C–D].

In the basilica of St. Zeno itself, however, because the principal office of the dedication, rather than a simple commemoration, had to be performed, the ancient office of ordination was retained on that day and the office of the dedication was transferred to another day, as we could show had customarily been done in other instances. If this conjecture is approved, then, given that St. Zeno’s ordination fell on the sixth day before the Ides of December, one may infer that he was ordained bishop of Verona in 362. For it is established that episcopal ordinations were performed on Sundays. Between 356 and about 380—the interval within which, from what has been said, Zeno’s episcopate may be placed—the sixth day before the Ides of December fell on a Sunday three times: in 356 itself, in 362, and in 373. Zeno could not have been ordained bishop in 356, since Lucillus was then living, or, if he had died, Gricinus could scarcely yet have succeeded him. Nor in 373, since, as we showed above from Ambrose’s letter, he had consecrated Indicia some time before that year. Therefore it is quite credible that St. Zeno was consecrated bishop on the sixth day before the Ides of December in 362, the final year of Emperor Julian [Col. 0081A–B].

But this, as we said a little earlier, is by conjecture, which we leave to others to examine, reject, or confirm. So long, however, as what we set down at the beginning of this paragraph stands—namely, that Zeno’s age, established by several records, must be placed between 356 and about 380—all things agree admirably, so that nothing could agree better.

The reign of Julian may have extended to the beginning of Zeno’s episcopate. At that time the temples of idols were open and disputes concerning the law of temples were permitted, as is related in Treatise 15, book I. This could nevertheless also have fallen in the age of other emperors, down to 391, when, as we saw in chapter 2, § 5, the worship of idols was everywhere wholly abolished by most severe laws [Col. 0082A]. After Julian’s death, under Christian emperors, a new church could openly be built and opened; at its dedication or inauguration, whatever it was, St. Zeno delivered Treatise 14, book I. Pagans could attend Zeno’s preaching without any fear thereby being introduced, as we saw stated in Treatise 3 of the same book I. The immense multitude of catechumens of every age, sex, rank, and nation, whom several treatises testify were washed each year in the waters of baptism, and the immense number of Christians growing daily, for whose accommodation a new and spacious church was still too narrow, according to Treatise 14, book I, no. 2, are not incredible.

[LXXIV] Compare the remaining matters that may bear some chronological indication. If not all agree with this age, though others do agree, then reject our opinion about Zeno’s period and, if you please, assign another author to all the treatises. But if everything agrees with this period and does not agree with another, we understand that nothing remains to prevent you from recognizing and acknowledging St. Zeno, bishop of Verona, flourishing in that same age, as the true author of the treatises which we have distinguished as the genuine offspring of one author. Thus an end may at last be put to those controversies which, for so many years, have occupied the minds of scholars concerning Zeno’s writings and age.

## [LXXV] SECOND DISSERTATION, COMPRISING A DEFENCE OF ZENO’S DOCTRINE

[Col. 0081]

### PREFACE [Col. 0081C]

In which a few preliminary remarks are made concerning the excellence of the Zenonian treatises.

Although, when the sermons of the Fathers are under discussion, the work is customarily regarded as of no great importance, nor indeed as such as can arouse the attention of scholars and profitably hold their minds: nevertheless, since the sermons especially of the ancient Fathers are those in which both the ancient discipline and the teaching of morals and faith handed down to ancient Christians are preserved (and nothing can be more excellent than these things), anyone who considers the matter more carefully will surely judge that nothing is more illustrious than sermons of this kind. And if this estimate must be made of all treatises of that class, it must undoubtedly be made in the highest degree [Col. 0081D] of those composed by a more ancient writer and presenting the first and oldest collection of sermons. That the treatises which we now publish are of this kind, reader, you may ascertain from the following consideration: although from the time of the Apostles onward all bishops diligently laboured to feed their sheep with the divine word, nevertheless no collection of sermons of this sort is available which you can show to be older than ours by reason of its author’s date. For the discourses of the ancients were delivered extemporaneously, [Col. 0082C] not written down, or at least taken down by shorthand writers. Or, if they brought forward something carefully elaborated which could be collected, they themselves composed one or more books from several of their own sermons treating some subject, so that the old form of the sermon entirely disappeared. Thus the works of Clement of Alexandria consist of many sermons successively woven together and published by their author; and similarly the commentaries of St. Hilary on the Psalms, most of St. Ambrose’s works On the Duties of Ministers, On the Mysteries, and so forth, are known to have been arranged from various treatises by the same method. These treatises of Zeno of Verona are therefore the oldest of all among Latin writers; and on that account this collection is to be valued above the rest.

If you think attention ought also to be paid to the matters themselves contained in any work, [Col. 0082D] to say nothing of matters belonging to secular learning, many of which will from time to time be considered in the notes: in these treatises there stand forth a splendid image of ancient discipline and remarkable testimonies to the most excellent doctrines, from which both writers on ecclesiastical discipline and defenders of the faith may derive no slight benefit. How notable are those points of discipline by which he discloses that confession of sins, and likewise a certain penitence, were formerly [Col. 0083A] customarily required before the sacrament of baptism; and by which he indicates heated baptismal water, continually running through channels into the sacred font, and the coin (*denarius*) handed to the baptized with altogether singular testimony—besides many other matters relating to the examination of catechumens fixed at a definite number of days, to salt, oil, milk, the white garment, and other things celebrated elsewhere in the rite of baptism. We pass over the Eucharist administered under both species and, even in that century, carried home under the species of bread; the ceremonies of the Paschal solemnity skilfully described; the observance of the Lenten fasts; the continence of married persons at that time; the bodies of Christians laid out openly in churches while the sacred offices were performed; and many more such matters, which you will very easily gather from the Index. See especially [Col. 0083B] what is set forth in Treatise 50, Book II, concerning [LXXVI] the rite of ordaining ministers and reconciling penitents at Easter, by testimony altogether the oldest of all—indeed, unique. From it is drawn a hitherto unknown piece of information concerning ecclesiastical discipline, by which certain otherwise common opinions of learned men are overthrown, or must be qualified by some exception.

But the testimonies contributing to the establishment of notable doctrines are more numerous. He speaks so expressly, though by figures, in support of original sin that, if St. Augustine had possessed a copy of these treatises, there is no doubt that he would have cited this Father, of most weighty authority and tradition, against the heresy of Pelagius. See Treatise 16, Book I, no. 3, note 16, where he most plainly refers the cause of all temporal punishments [Col. 0083C] to the fault of the first parents; and Treatise 15 of the same book, no. 12; and especially Treatises 39 and 42, Book II, where, by affirming that those who approach baptism are first dead and then made alive in baptism, and by mentioning the old man slain in baptism, he plainly testifies to the original fault which kills the soul. Still clearer testimonies are available concerning the power of baptism, in which all sins whatsoever are entirely wiped away; concerning the character impressed upon the soul in baptism, which can never be erased (whence that sacrament cannot be repeated); concerning grace, which in baptism is conferred not equally upon all but greater or less according to the differing measure of merits; concerning the baptism of boys and infants; the communion of saints; the power of the keys of the Church; sacrifice for [Col. 0083D] the dead; *exhomologesis*, that is, confession and penitence for sins; the perpetual virginity of the Blessed Virgin Mary; and many other doctrines of the Church of the same sort. Their testimonies are so frequent and clear that it is already tiresome to enumerate them. But it is enough to have indicated these; whoever reads will find more.

Yet among so many and such distinguished testimonies to the Catholic faith, it cannot be denied that some rather harsher expressions occur, which may have offended certain persons. But this is common to all the ancients. For, since different words and expressions were used at different times and places, and since the heresies had not yet arisen that made the Fathers more cautious and introduced fixed formulas of speech, certain things fell from those speaking more freely [Col. 0084A] which offended no one at the time, but, after heresies and fixed formulas had arisen, became displeasing and can be twisted into a bad sense. Hence, while Catholics have always taken great care in defending and explaining expressions of this kind, this is also judged the chief duty of editors—so much so that anyone who fails in it where necessary may rightly be accused of producing an imperfect edition. Accordingly, it will be the task of this dissertation to defend certain expressions and propositions of Zeno; and in proportion to the matters requiring defence, we have divided it into ten chapters.

[LXXVII] CHAPTER I. CERTAIN FORMULAS OF ST. ZENO CONCERNING THE ETERNAL GENERATION OF THE WORD OF GOD ARE DEFENDED AGAINST PETAVIUS’S CENSURE, AND THEIR MEANING IS EXPOUNDED.

[Col. 0084B] § I.—Petavius’s censure is presented.

If Father Denis Pétau, S.J., an eminent ornament of the Society of Jesus, had found the expression according to which the divine Word is said to have proceeded from the Father when the plan for creating the world was adopted in one or two ante-Nicene Fathers, it should still, as far as possible, have been interpreted so as not to appear to contain an Arian meaning. Or, if there could have been doubt whether one or two men had given some support to the Arian position by certain expressions, since not all the formulas by which Catholics spoke of the generation of the Word had been defined and fully expounded in those earliest times, we should have thought Petavius excusable if, without excusing the error or danger of error but exposing it, he had warned that caution was necessary. But since not one or two, but several of the most eminent ante-Nicene Fathers are found to have employed that expression, he ought altogether to have refrained from a censure which, if it had any force, would greatly detract from the authority of tradition and the Fathers; nor should he have opened an entrance for heretics, so that, on the testimony of this most learned Catholic theologian, they might rise up against tradition and the Fathers, not without great prejudice to Catholic doctrine. Moreover, since not only several ante-Nicene Fathers but also some later than the Council of Nicaea, who fought most vigorously against the Arians for the true faith, are found to have used the same formula of speech, he should surely see that the expression must contain a sound Catholic sense, very far removed from Arian heresy; and he ought to have laboured [Col. 0084D] to extract that sense, whatever it was, and then to interpret the many ante-Nicene Fathers in the same sense, rather than to denounce nearly all of them as forerunners of the Arian error. But Petavius, after unfairly attacking several ante-Nicene Fathers, when he comes to St. Zeno, bishop of Verona—whom he indicates as flourishing after the Council of Nicaea, and elsewhere cites as giving testimony against the Arians—does not hesitate, together with Marius Victorinus, a writer of the same century, to bring him under suspicion of the same error because of several expressions of this sort. Let us quote his entire censure, though lengthy, lest we appear to import anything into it, especially since we must refute it in this chapter. Thus, [Col. 0085A] after considering the testimonies of the earlier Fathers whom he censured—Athenagoras, Tatian, Theophilus of Antioch, Tertullian, and Lactantius—he immediately adds the following concerning Zeno, who speaks similarly, in Book I, *On the Trinity*, chapter 5, no. 7:

> With respect to these earlier writers, indeed, it is less surprising that they entertained such views concerning the production of the divine Word. I cannot sufficiently wonder at Zeno, bishop of Verona, who in his third sermon on the eternal generation of the Son of God (now Treatise 5, Book II) seems to have thought the same as those ancient writers. “The beginning, brethren,” he says, “is assuredly our Lord Christ: whom, before all ages, God the Father, still somehow within Himself, enveloped by some consciousness of His own, in the undivided fullness of the Spirit of blessed eternity, embraced as Son, not without affection, yet without distinction. [Col. 0085B] But, in order that He might establish the order of the things He had conceived, that ineffable power and incomprehensible wisdom brings forth the Word from the region of the heart; omnipotence propagates itself. God is born of God, possessing all that belongs to the Father and detracting nothing from the Father,” etc. “But it is the opinion of a madman to suppose how He who proceeded was generated. For the Son tempers Himself on account of the nature of things, lest the limited capacity of this world be able to sustain the Lord of eternal majesty. When the [LXXVIII] Father commands that the world be made, the work is completed by the Son together with the word.” Here Zeno shows that the Word of God had from all eternity clung and lain hidden in the bosom and essence of the Father, as though undivided from and attached to Him; but afterwards, when He wished to fashion the universe as designed by Himself, he says that He propagated and begot that very Word from Himself. And this is the first of the two [Col. 0085C] births which he explains in the following sermons (now Treatises 7 and 8, Book II). He makes the same point also in the two preceding sermons (now Treatises 3 and 4 of the same Book II), which are entitled *On the Eternal Generation of the Son of God*. For in the first (now Treatise 3), with the words slightly altered, after saying that Christ is the beginning, he speaks thus: “Whom before all ages the Father embraced as Son, not without affection, yet without disclosure, in the unfathomable secret of His sacred mind and in a consciousness known to Himself alone. Therefore that ineffable and incomprehensible wisdom propagates wisdom, omnipotence omnipotence. God is born of God; the only-begotten of the unbegotten; the sole from the sole; the whole from the whole; the true from the true; the perfect from the perfect; possessing all that belongs to the Father and detracting nothing from [Col. 0085D] the Father. He proceeds into birth, He who was in the Father before He was born.” Therefore he indicates that the Son existed in the Father before being begotten by the Father; but the generation and birth occurred when He wished to create all things, as he declares in the second sermon (now Treatise 4): “From whose mouth, that the nature of things which was not might be formed, proceeded the only-begotten Son, the noble inhabitant of His heart, hence made visible because He was to visit humankind,” etc. This is the view of the ancients which we have explained.

Thus far Petavius’s censure. By “the view of the ancients” in those final words, he means the view of the Fathers just mentioned, according to which they, as he had said in the same no. 7, judged the Father superior to the Word in age, dignity, and power; and although they asserted that the Son was of the Father’s substance or nature—wherein alone they made His condition different from that of the others properly called creatures—they nevertheless thought that He had a beginning no less than creatures did; that is, they thought that He was by no means a hypostasis distinct from eternity. [Col. 0086A] Thus Petavius interprets those ancient Fathers, and Zeno agreeing with them, as having handed down that the Son of God was begotten in time.

But what he says he wonders at concerning Zeno, who seems to have thought the same as the ancients—or, as he says in no. 8 when about to consider Victorinus’s passages, that there are also some Catholic writers later than the Council of Nicaea who seem to be in the same case—we should more reasonably say that we wonder at in Petavius: that he should denounce as guilty of the very error which they oppose [Col. 0086B] Fathers who even attacked Arian heresy. Nor is the explanation which he inserted in his Preface, chapter 1, no. 12, sufficient to clear this censor of so many Fathers altogether: there he maintains that the Fathers whom he thus criticizes differ from the customary rule not in substance but only in their manner of speaking; and he professes the same more fully in Book I, chapter 6, no. 4. For what good was it to say this once and again, if, when adducing their very testimonies, he does not add the principle for interpreting those expressions, but recites and urges them in such a way as though they could appear to differ in substance and not merely in manner of speaking? Indeed, the recent heretics who in these last times have revived the Arian heresy long buried do not use the explanation which Petavius gave in the cited passages, in order to represent the same Fathers as substantively opposed to them and [Col. 0086C] favourable only in manner of speech; rather, they seize upon the Fathers’ expressions themselves, which Petavius set forth in full light, in order to persuade people that those Fathers thought as they did, on Petavius’s own testimony. It would indeed be enough for our purpose merely to rescue Zeno from their hands and defend his expressions; and it would suffice to set this forth briefly, if what others have written in his defence, when defending the tradition of the Nicene faith, had been written according to Zeno’s thought. But since those writings do not precisely represent the Author’s meaning, nor altogether defend all his expressions, we must employ a longer discussion. Moreover, because the expressions of the other Fathers whom Petavius attacks are nearly the same, once Zeno has been defended [Col. 0086D] from the interpretation we shall give, you will have the others defended at the same time. And so that this may be perceived more clearly, something must be said about each of them at the end, so that the testimonies may, by comparison, illuminate and confirm one another.

[LXXIX] § II.—The testimonies of St. Zeno in which the Nicene doctrine is expressly asserted against Arian heresy are indicated.

With respect to Zeno, then, we first wish to ask Petavius why he did not preface his discussion with Zeno’s clear testimonies, by which it is evident that he held Catholic doctrine, but brought forward only those three which create difficulty. For if anyone, after reading many collected passages revealing [Col. 0087A] his manifestly Catholic mind, encounters one or two somewhat more difficult testimonies, he will not be disturbed, because he understands that these must be explained from the others. But if only these three are read, and someone infers from the omission that no clearer passages are available, the Author’s opinion is immediately rendered highly doubtful, and the suspicion that he favoured the Arians is forced upon him. Therefore, before we defend Zeno’s more obscure propositions, we think that his plain testimonies, by which he agreed with the Nicene Fathers, should be quoted here. Yet, in order to establish the Author’s date, we collected the greater and more remarkable part of these in the first dissertation, chapter 2, § 2, so that we might establish that the Author, openly fighting against the Arians, flourished in the fourth century. Therefore, lest we do the same thing twice, reader, we ask you again and again [Col. 0087B] to consult and reread them in that place; for they plainly demonstrate not only his date but also his Catholic position, which we have undertaken to defend here. You will find him setting against the chief assertions of the Arians their opposites; among these you will especially find most expressly stated those propositions that are diametrically opposed to the suspicion of error raised by Petavius—namely, those by which, defending the Son as begotten eternally from the Father, he confesses Him not only coeternal and coequal with the Father but also of one substance with the Father. He establishes this so expressly and deliberately that he openly refutes and dissolves objections even as raised by the Arians. We shall add here one testimony omitted there, than which nothing is more conspicuous for showing that Zeno is altogether remote from the imputed suspicion of Arian doctrine. [Col. 0087C] Petavius, that is, appears to suppose that the Author intimated that the Son of God was not begotten from eternity, but in time—before, that is, He created any other creature whatsoever. But does he not, in Treatise 7, Book II, while about to refute those who handed down this very notion, those who, as he himself says in no. 1, “indeed call the Son of God God, but [say that He was] not begotten from the Father by the perpetuity of nobility, [and that] there was a time when He was not,” expressly identify that opinion as heresy? Does he not, I say, openly reject in no. 3 this very time attributed to the Son’s birth in these words: “Let us now see, excellent Christian”—thus he calls the Arian ironically—“how you thrust time between the Father and the Son”? Is it credible that this same time, which he so expressly reproves as heresy, was asserted anywhere else by Zeno? If to this testimony [Col. 0087D] you add the others collected in chapter 2, § 2 of the preceding dissertation, by which the Author rejects from a Catholic standpoint both this error and other Arian expressions, it will then become manifest from them all that he taught and defended Catholic doctrine against the Arians most expressly. No one can now rightly suspect that the passages which Petavius alone enumerated contain a meaning foreign to that doctrine and tending toward the Arians, unless he judges the same author to be opposed to and contradicting himself. Rather, since a few obscure passages generally ought to be explained from many clear and manifest ones, and not the reverse, it must be evident from so many and such explicit testimonies of St. Zeno that an entirely different meaning lies beneath them from that which Petavius attributes to those three passages [Col. 0088A]—a meaning which we now undertake to discover and explain.

[LXXX] § III.—The texts objected by Petavius are examined. Bull’s interpretation is proposed and assessed.

Petavius’s accusation was that Zeno’s opinion was as follows: the Word of God had from all eternity clung and lain hidden in the bosom and essence of the Father, as though undivided from and attached to Him; but afterwards, when the Father wished to fashion the universe designed by Himself, he says that He propagated and begot the Word from Himself, and that this was the first of two births which St. Zeno explains in the following sermons. So he says. This censure comprises two points: first, that Zeno did not acknowledge the eternal generation of the divine [Col. 0088B] Word, since he taught that the same Word had indeed existed in the Father from eternity, but so undivided that He was one and the same with the Father not only in substance but also in person; second, that the same Author thought that the divine Word proceeded from the Father only when He undertook to create the world, in order to employ Him as an instrument of creation. This was the opinion of Arius and the Arians. Petavius thinks that this temporal procession of the Son from the Father, which concerns created things alone, is that birth of the Son which Zeno calls the first especially in Treatise 8, where, distinguishing Christ’s two births, he says:

> Therefore the first birth of our Lord remains within the consciousness of the Father and the Son alone; nor has it anything interposed or conscious, because it proceeded in one accord from the affection of the Father’s mouth.

But these two points of the censure, although they seem distinct, are connected in fact, and one so depends upon the other that whoever refutes the first from Zeno himself has sufficiently refuted the second also, and has established that the holy bishop’s mind and doctrine are defended from the Arian dogma. For if you establish and prove that Zeno sufficiently declared an eternal and proper generation of the divine Word when he affirmed that the same Word was still veiled and hidden in the Father’s consciousness, it will immediately follow that the other generation attributed by Zeno to that same Word is not the first, and must accordingly be explained in such a way that it conflicts in nothing with the first eternal generation and lends the Arians no support.

Accordingly, as regards the first point, the very [Col. 0088D] testimony from Treatise 8 which, because it speaks of Christ’s first birth, Petavius cited as temporal, contributes strikingly to establishing it as eternal. For when Christ’s first birth is there said to be that which remains in the consciousness of the Father and Son alone, and has nothing interposed or conscious, the birth indicated is surely that of the divine Word in that eternal state when, before all ages, as Zeno says in the first text objected by Petavius, the Father, still God somehow within Himself, embraced Him as Son, veiled by some consciousness of His own, in the undivided fullness of the Spirit of blessed eternity, not without affection but without distinction; or, as he says in the second text from Treatise 4, when before all things there remained one God, [Col. 0089A] and the same other God from Himself into Himself, alone conscious of His own secret. In both passages you see the same doctrine of hidden generation being inculcated which appears in Treatise 8, where consequently he says: “You are not permitted to seek this earlier birth”; because, namely, it remained in the consciousness of the Father and Son alone in Treatise 8, with the Son veiled by the Father’s consciousness in Treatise 5, and with God alone conscious of His own secret in Treatise 4. Thus St. Zeno, in Treatise 8, explaining the words of Treatises 4 and 5, as Petavius himself indicates the passage, acknowledges in those words the first birth of the Son, which Petavius does not recognize in Zeno. Nor does he indicate the first birth which Petavius understands as first, namely, when, “in order that He might establish the order of the things He had conceived, that ineffable power and incomprehensible wisdom brings forth the Word from the region of the heart”; [Col. 0089B] rather, he indicates that birth in which the Son, though veiled in the Father’s consciousness, is nevertheless expressly said to be embraced by the Father as Son, not without affection. An invincible argument against Petavius is then drawn from these words. For since the divine Word, in that eternal state (“before all ages,” he says), certainly before the order of things conceived was established—that is, before the decree for creating the world was made (understand a priority of reason, as the schools call it)—since, I say, in this eternal state the divine Word is affirmed to be Son, although veiled in the Father’s consciousness, He is undoubtedly asserted to be truly begotten and to have a true generation. For, as Petavius himself admits in Book V, *On the Trinity*, chapter 9, no. 11, “there is no Son without generation”; or, as Augustine says in Book V, *On the Trinity*, no. 7, “He is Son precisely because He is begotten; and because He is Son, [Col. 0089C] He is certainly begotten.” Therefore, if the divine Word existed as Son from eternity, and indeed as Son begotten according to Zeno’s thought, He was certainly also distinct from the Father. Hence Zeno himself openly admits in Treatise 4 that there were already then the one and the other—that is, two persons, Son and Father; we treated these words more fully in note 2. These points are sufficiently plain from the very passages objected by Petavius. And if you add to them the remaining testimonies indicated in the preceding paragraph, in which the Author strikingly defends the divine Son as coeternal and equal with the Father and of the same substance, you will now [Col. 0089D] need nothing further to confirm—or rather, to demonstrate—this sufficiently evident interpretation of the texts, from which we have proved that the same Son was begotten from the Father eternally and only hidden in the Father’s consciousness.

But the difficulty for Petavius arose from the statements in the same Treatise 5 that the Father embraced the Son in the undivided fullness of the Spirit and without distinction. Yet these do not imply unity of person in that eternal state—or rather, in that priority of reason—as Petavius’s argument would require. Otherwise Zeno could not have called Him Father and Son, unless perhaps he had adopted the opinion of the Sabellians and Patripassians, who maintained that Father and Son are distinct in words, not in reality. In that case Petavius would accuse St. Zeno, in one and the same treatise, of supporting two mutually conflicting heresies, Sabellianism and Arianism—something that seems impossible and cannot be proved ever to have happened to anyone by any example. [Col. 0090A] Rather, these expressions indicate only that this generation of the Son was so hidden and veiled that, in that priority of reason, before deliberation concerning the creation of the world, the Son could not yet emerge outwardly with any distinction. Therefore, what is expressed in Treatise 5 by the words “without distinction” is precisely explained in Treatise 3 by these words, “without disclosure.” This is more strikingly confirmed from Treatise 4, where he acknowledges the divine Son as hidden in the Father from eternity at that point of reason for no other reason than that, since no decree had yet been conceived to create the world, He could not be visible; whereas, from that decree, He necessarily had to become visible:

> “From whose mouth,” he says, “that the nature of things which was not might be formed, proceeded the only-begotten Son, the noble inhabitant of His heart, hence necessarily [Col. 0090B] made visible because He Himself was to make the earthly world and visit humankind.”

Thus we have given the complete text from all the manuscripts and the first edition. From this a broader way is opened for explaining the second point of Petavius’s censure and for disclosing Zeno’s thought and doctrine. For since in these words he attributes a certain birth to the divine Word in connection with the plan of creating the world, saying, “The only-begotten Son proceeded,” etc.—words with which others from Treatise 5 agree: “In order that He might establish the order of the things He had conceived, that ineffable power and incomprehensible wisdom brings forth the Word from the region of the heart; omnipotence propagates itself”—since, I say, a certain new birth is attributed in these words to the divine Word in connection with the plan for creating the world, in addition to the one which he had acknowledged in the preceding words [Col. 0090C] as hidden in the Father’s bosom, Zeno seems to have acknowledged, in a certain manner, two births of the Word.

Accordingly George Bull, in his *Defence of the Nicene Faith*, section 3, chapter 9, § 6, maintains that Zeno asserts the eternal generation of the Son of God in the earlier words, but considers that the later words describe that birth in time by which the Son proceeded from the Father to create the universe:

> “And this,” he says, “is nothing other than the revelation of the Son, whom the Father, so to speak, embraced within Himself and for Himself alone from eternity, or His going forth and procession from the Father . . . in order to bring into being things which did not exist and to manifest Himself to created beings, namely angels and human beings.”

We cannot deny that this temporal manifestation of the divine Word was also called a kind of birth and [Col. 0090D] procession by other Fathers even after the Council of Nicaea. Among them, most clearly of all, is the author of the treatise *On the Orthodox Faith against the Arians*, inserted in the Appendix to Ambrose’s Works, who is probably believed to be Gregory of Baetica. Explaining Proverbs 8, “The Lord created,” or “founded, me in the beginning of His ways,” he writes in chapter 2, p. 349 of the Appendix, vol. II of Ambrose:

> God did not so create His wisdom as though He had at some time been without wisdom; but, when He says “the beginning of His ways,” He shows the beginning of the movement of some work, so that the wisdom of God has as its beginning this: that it proceeded from God to create all things . . . [LXXXII] Therefore Wisdom was created—indeed, begotten—not for itself, which always existed, but for those things which had to be made by it.

And similarly Prudentius, [Col. 0091A] in Hymn 11, openly discussing the creation of the world itself, says:

> Although you arose from the Father’s mouth  
> and were brought forth by the Word,  
> yet Wisdom had been warm before  
> within the Father’s breast.

Since in these lines he designates the divine Word by the name Wisdom, and indicates that it existed already from eternity in the Father’s breast before arising from the Father’s mouth and being brought forth in the creation of the world, he appears to agree entirely with Zeno according to Bull’s interpretation.

Yet we cannot agree with Bull that this generation or external manifestation was so called by Zeno in the passages from Treatises 4 and 5 cited by Petavius. For anyone who reads the entire texts—especially as we have published them complete from the manuscripts—will certainly see most clearly [Col. 0091B] that in both Treatise 4 and Treatise 5 Zeno speaks of a certain eternal generation of this same Word, which does not conflict with the other, hidden generation affirmed in the preceding words and demonstrated by us thus far. For first, Treatise 5 deals with that nativity of the Word by which not only omnipotence propagates itself—or “re-propagates itself,” as other manuscripts read—but also by which God is born from God, possessing all that belongs to the Father and detracting nothing from the Father, etc. These things do not suit a merely external and temporal manifestation, and they correspond exactly with what is stated in almost the same words concerning an undoubtedly eternal generation in Treatise 3: “Therefore that ineffable and incomprehensible wisdom propagates wisdom, omnipotence omnipotence. God is born from God; the Only-begotten from the Unbegotten; [Col. 0091C] the Only One from the Only One; the Whole from the Whole; the True from the True; the Perfect from the Perfect, possessing all that belongs to the Father, detracting nothing from the Father.” For these words and formulations, proper to the Catholic Fathers and openly declaring the identity of substance of Father and Son, cannot apply to a creature created before all things for the creation of the world, as the Arians thought. For the same reason, they cannot apply to an uttered word (*verbum prolatitium*), which—even if it had been uttered in creation, as some seem to have thought (on which see what will be said at the beginning of the following paragraph)—was nevertheless something created. Neither, therefore, can they apply to a temporal and external manifestation of the eternal Word. Although this indeed signifies something external, so that through that external thing the Son of God could be said to have proceeded [Col. 0091D] to create the universe, it could not likewise be affirmed that God was born from God, the Whole from the Whole, possessing all that belongs to the Father, etc. Such expressions, and the meaning underlying them, were employed by Catholics to establish the Son’s intimate and consubstantial equality with the Father; as we showed in note 6 on the same Treatise 3, they undoubtedly concern the internal, eternal, and properly so-called generation of the divine Word. On this matter see more in Petavius, *On the Trinity*, Book VI, chapter 10.

Secondly, that Zeno speaks of that generation by which the same Word came forth in order to establish the order of things conceived is evident from Treatise 5. That this generation was eternal is indicated not only by the word “might establish” (*instrueret*), which sufficiently suggests not the actual creation of the world, occurring in time, [Col. 0092A] but the counsel and decree concerning the world’s creation, which was certainly formed from eternity. It is proved more clearly by the words of Treatise 4, where, after the divine Son is said to have come forth through this generation—“that the nature of things, which did not exist, might be fashioned, the Only-begotten Son came forth, the noble inhabitant of His heart”—the same Son is not immediately said to have been manifested for that reason, as Bull’s hypothesis would require (if that generation were identical with manifestation). Rather, it is added: “thereafter He was necessarily made visible, because He Himself was going to make the earthly world,” etc. The words “thereafter visible” declare a manifestation consequent upon this; while “was going to make” declares that the manifestation would occur later, in the creation of the world, at the appointed time.

Indeed, if a generation is here asserted from which the Son of God had subsequently to become visible in creating [Col. 0092B] the world—and “visible” and “manifested” are the same—then undoubtedly a generation is asserted from which that external manifestation subsequently proceeded, and which therefore occurred before the manifestation itself accomplished in the creation of the world. For the Son of God could not be manifested or be visible before created things existed, but only once things had been created. Referring, indeed, to this same generation, the Author says in Treatise 6 of Book II: “The Only-begotten, by coming forth from the Father before the origin of things,” etc. Here the word *before* (*τὸ ante*) openly shows that the generation of the Word, whatever it may be, preceded the origin, or creation, of things. [LXXXIII] Therefore the Author understood by “generation” not the manifestation itself, but something distinct from it.

If any Arian, denying the eternal generation of the Son of God, [Col. 0092C] had asserted these things, they would readily be understood as referring to the creation of the Word. Since the Arians denied that He was eternally begotten and consubstantial with the Father, they did indeed proclaim Him a creature—but one created as firstborn before the origin of every other thing. But in a Catholic bishop who establishes by explicit testimonies both the Word’s eternal generation and His consubstantiality with the Father, as we have seen in our Author, there is no further place for a nativity of this sort—or, more properly, a creation. For the same Word, eternal and consubstantial with the Father, with no assumed nature, could not at the beginning of time also be created; for, as true and eternal God, just as He cannot cease to be what He is, so He cannot begin in time or be intrinsically changed and generated into a creature. Therefore, by this nativity [Col. 0092D] the Author undoubtedly understood something alien to the Arian sense; but since it preceded creation and consequently external manifestation, it must also be distinct from manifestation itself. Further, if from these statements you exclude not only the Word’s creation, imagined by the Arians, but also the external manifestation implied by Bull, no temporal thing remains to which this generation asserted by Zeno, which, as we observed shortly above, does not accord with an uttered word, can be assigned. We must therefore understand something eternal, and in some respect different from that first, concealed and hidden generation; and such a thing that the same divine Word, although truly begotten as the Father’s Son, could nevertheless come forth into the counsel for creating the world, so as thereafter necessarily to become visible in time, when He Himself was to make the earthly world.

[Col. 0093A] If you add to this that the Son of God is said necessarily to have become visible because He came forth from the Father, no less because He was going to make the earthly world than because He was going to visit the human race, when He assumed human nature, then you will certainly recognize that in that by which the Son of God came forth from the Father nothing was generated, uttered, or manifested in the world’s creation; rather, something eternal must be established from which no less the creation of the world than the incarnation of the Word derived. And since this eternal reality especially concerns the world’s eternal creation—of which St. Zeno speaks more expressly and repeatedly; around which the chief controversy with the Arians turned; and from which Petavius drew the principal difficulty [Col. 0093B] urged against Zeno—we shall endeavour in the following paragraphs to investigate and establish what that eternal reality is, advancing an interpretation drawn from the teaching of the ancient Fathers, but insufficiently explained by others and requiring a somewhat fuller exposition from us.

Yet, lest we speak overconfidently on this matter, we recognize that some may find it somewhat subtle, and may at first sight believe that it did not enter Zeno’s mind when he wrote. But if, reader, you consider more closely not some technical and elaborate mode of declaring this explanation, more suited to the formulas and method of modern theologians than to the simplicity of the ancient Fathers, but the thing itself designated under this explanation—which alone, though in other words, we shall show Zeno to have conceived and sufficiently indicated [Col. 0093C]—you will perceive that this eternal reality, looking toward the creation of the world, which gave occasion for external manifestation but is distinct from that external manifestation, was known to the ancient Fathers and regarded as the divine Word Himself and as a certain divine generation of the Word. This will become clear partly in the following §4, especially from Augustine, and partly in §§7 and 8 from other Fathers. There can then be no difficulty in persuading yourself that St. Zeno thought and taught the like, since his words in particular cannot be explained otherwise, as we have just said and will shortly show still more plainly. Nevertheless, should anyone still prefer Bull’s interpretation, since it sufficiently safeguards the Catholic opinion of the Author, we shall not resist stubbornly. Yet our explanation will not be useless for those who judge that Bull cannot at all be accepted in view of the difficulties we have set forth.

[LXXXIV] § IV.—The true interpretation of Zeno’s expression is set forth.

Two formulas used by St. Zeno to explain this second, so to speak, nativity may shed light upon this interpretation: one in Treatise 4, “He came forth from the mouth of the Father”; the other in Treatise 5, “The Father, from the region of His heart, belches forth the Word.” These formulas, also common among other Fathers when speaking of the divine Word, derive from a twofold testimony of Holy Scripture, [Col. 0094A] which Zeno himself expressly cites to his purpose in Treatise 7, no. 1: the first from Ecclesiasticus 24:5, “I,” that is, Wisdom, “came forth from the mouth of the Most High”; the second from Psalm 44:1, “My heart has uttered a good word.” The holy Fathers commonly interpret both passages of the eternal Son of God, who is the Father’s Wisdom and Word; and they frequently refer both to the creation of created things, of which Ecclesiasticus especially speaks plainly.

And indeed, since all things were created through the Father’s divine Word, as the sacred writings testify in many places, this Word is rightly said to have come forth from the mouth of the Most High: through it the Father said, and things came to be. This word “Let there be,” which He uttered from His heart, is that Word in which and through which all things were made. [Col. 0094B] Further, the holy Fathers must be understood to have taken this Word to be the Son of God Himself, not that uttered word, “Let there be,” which some have supposed God spoke in creating the world—an external, created, and time-bound word—as Petavius rightly noted and proved, *On the Trinity*, Book VI, chapter 1, no. 7. For this was the heresy of Paul of Samosata: he called the Son of God an uttered rather than a subsistent Word, as is clear from Philastrius, chapter 64; Epiphanius, *Heresies*, 65; and Marius Mercator, in the letter *On the Difference between Paul and Nestorius*. Rather, they must be understood to have meant another Word, inward and subsistent, as Phoebadius calls it in his book *Against the Arians*, p. 304, vol. IV of the *Library of the Fathers*: namely, that Word by which the Father, speaking with Himself in the Son, deliberated from eternity concerning the creation of the world. [Col. 0094C] By the utterance of this eternal command it came about that the world was created at the appointed time and that God Himself and the Word of God were manifested to that world.

This Word of the eternal decree is said by analogy with other words to have come forth from the mouth of the Most High; but there can be no doubt that it was uttered from the inward mouth, so to speak, of the mind—from that mouth of the divine mind to which Wisdom belongs—when the Father, about to create the world, in some manner sent forth that Wisdom which shone forth most fully in the world’s creation, pronouncing, if it is lawful to speak thus, that decree: that the world should be created from those eternal principles and in that order which divine Wisdom, especially attributed to the Word, brought forth. On this subject read Origen, vol. II, *On John*, p. 165. This decree of divine Wisdom is also rightly said to have been uttered from the heart, since all divine decrees concerning contingent things proceed from the free will of God and are therefore attributed to the heart. [Col. 0094D]

But lest you regard this as our arbitrary invention, reader, when we interpret this divine command as understood by Zeno to be the Son of God, consider first that, in our view, nothing better explains what is repeatedly stated in Scripture: that all things were made in the Word and through the Word, which many Fathers together with Zeno affirmed, on the basis of the indicated scriptural testimonies, both to have come forth from the mouth of the Most High and to have been uttered from the Father’s heart. Secondly, theologians know that not only those things which belong to [Col. 0095A] wisdom are especially attributed to that divine Word, called in Holy Scripture the Father’s Wisdom—hence many interpret the words of Psalm 103, “You made all things in Wisdom,” as meaning “in the Son,” whom they understand to be called “Wisdom, the artificer of all things” in Wisdom 7:21—but also those things belonging to power are claimed for the same Word. Accordingly, Scripture says that all things were created not only in Him, as He is God’s Wisdom, but also through Him, as He is God’s Power; and for this reason the Apostle Paul, in 1 Corinthians 1:24, gives Him the distinctive name “the power of God and the wisdom of God.” For many patristic testimonies confirming both titles, see Petavius, *On God*, Book V, chapter 8, no. 3, where he treats power, and Book IV, chapter 2, as well as *On the Trinity*, Book VI, chapter 9, where he discusses [Col. 0095B] Wisdom. There too you will gather why these two attributes of the divine nature, common to the three Persons, are especially attributed to the divine Word.

Further, if that eternal command concerning creation of the world was established in Wisdom and possessed the power by which all things were created in time, it is certainly easy to understand that the divine Word, which is called in a special sense the Power and Wisdom of God, can likewise in a special sense be called that command. Since the Father issued it from eternity, He may in some way be said to have issued and begotten the divine Word. Indeed, Augustine, Sermon 120, no. 6, proves that the Son of God is the Father’s command itself—not a command given in time, but a command begotten. “For,” he says, “how is that which is the Word of the Father not the command of the Father?” And in *Tractates on John*, Treatise 21, [Col. 0095C] no. 4: “For by speaking in the Son what He was to do through the Son, He begot the Son Himself, through whom He would make all things.” Again, in *Against the Sermon of the Arians*, chapter 3, he testifies that the Father’s command that all things should be made is nothing other than the Word through whom all things were made. And in *On the Trinity*, Book I, chapter 12, no. 26: “The Father’s command is not one thing and the Father’s Word another”; and in *Against Faustus*, Book II, chapter 5: “Christ is the Word of God, in whom all things were spoken before they existed”; and in *Against Maximinus*, Book II, chapter 24: “The Son Himself is the command of the Father, because He Himself is the Word of the Father.” We pass over other passages of the same kind, in which this same holy Doctor declares both that the divine Word is the Father’s command and that He is begotten by the Father.

With this in view, [Col. 0095D] the Synod of Antioch against Paul of Samosata, in its synodical letter, declares that the divine Word was begotten by the Father as a living and subsistent operation, effecting all things in all; and this plainly pertains to the command of which we have spoken. In the same manner St. John Chrysostom, Homily 2 on the Epistle to the Hebrews, affirms that the Father begot the Word Himself as Creator. And St. Gregory the Great, *Morals*, Book XXIII, chapter 19, says: “God’s speaking is His begetting the Word”; without doubt he embraces that utterance by which the Father commanded the creation of the world and, in commanding it, begot the Word. To the same effect are the sayings of other Fathers carefully collected by Petavius, *On God*, Book V, chapter 8, from no. 5 onward, in which, looking to the creation of the world itself, they very often call the Son of God the very willing and counsel [Col. 0096A] of God—in Greek, *βουλή* (*boulē*, “counsel”). Both terms indicate that eternal decree, called by them a command, by which all things were created at the appointed time in the Son and through the Son. And as this decree, so the Word Himself could be said both to have been uttered from the heart and to have come forth from the mouth of the Most High.

Whichever formula one uses, a certain procession and generation of the Word is signified, because through this decree the Son of God had a relation to creatures which, as the mere Son lying hidden in the Father’s bosom, He did not have, or is not conceived to have had. More on this follows in the next paragraph. Since by the power of this eternal decree the divine Word was manifested to us in His own time, other Fathers judged that this external manifestation too should be called a certain generation and nativity of the Word. Chrysologus writes in Sermon 62 on the Creed: “The Father begets the Son for us when He reveals Him to us.”

[Col. 0096B] Therefore, to return to the Author: by the expression in which St. Zeno teaches that the Father’s Son, though begotten by the Father, nevertheless came forth into the counsel of creating the world from the Father’s mouth and heart, so that He thereafter necessarily became visible because He Himself was going to make the earthly world, he appears to have referred to this decree for creating the world. And indeed, since the world was created not through the power of an uttered word—which in all probability was not issued in the world’s creation—but through the power of the eternal decree, as we observed shortly above, the word “thereafter” (*exinde*) can refer to this decree alone. This decree itself appears, according to the opinion of the Fathers explained thus far, to have been understood by Zeno as the Word of God. [Col. 0096C] Therefore, this decree, spoken by the Father in the Word and committed through the Word to execution in its own time—from which the same Son necessarily became visible in creating the world—attributes a certain nativity to the same Word; yet it is an eternal nativity intrinsic to God, by which Zeno could say that God came forth from God, since this eternal divine Word is truly God.

From this one may further understand how aptly the Author, surely with this in view, wrote in Treatise 4 that the same Son of God, thereafter—that is, because He came forth from the Father—was necessarily made visible not only because He Himself was going to make the earthly world, [LXXXVI] but also because He was going to visit the human race, when, namely, He became man, as we indicated in the preceding paragraph. [Col. 0096D] In the other explanation and opinion, especially advanced by Bull, no one will understand this equally well; in ours, it is very easy and proper. For in that eternal decree, by which we said the Son came forth, all future things were spoken: no less the creation of the world than the very incarnation of the Word. Thus this one eternal procession of the same Word, explained through the decree, is recognized as that from which, as Zeno teaches, both things derived.

One point from Zeno himself may be objected to this interpretation—one which seems to vindicate and confirm Petavius’s observation—namely, that if the Author had wished by the expression we have considered to signify this eternal generation of the divine Word, he would not, in Treatises 7 and 8, have enumerated only one eternal nativity of the Son in the first place, [Col. 0097A] but two: one by which He lay hidden, veiled in the Father’s consciousness; the other by which He came forth into the counsel of creating the world. It is concerning this latter alone that Petavius raises his difficulty. Nor would he have placed second, in both places, that nativity by which He was born in time of His mother. Since, therefore, in each Treatise he consistently enumerates only one nativity of the Son from the Father and another from the mother, he does not know the two nativities of the same Son from the Father described thus far; rather, he seems to have acknowledged and called the first only that one by which He is said to have come forth from the Father’s mouth into the deliberation to create the world and to have been uttered from the region of His heart.

Although these objections have little, or rather no, force against Zeno, since they are sufficiently and more than sufficiently dissolved by his other statements expressly establishing Christ’s eternal nativity hidden in the Father’s bosom, [Col. 0097B] nevertheless, lest anything be lacking to our argument, let us proceed to another way of explaining his expression. This will not indeed destroy the first explanation, but will rather establish and explain it more clearly; and thus every difficulty will be entirely removed.

§ V.—The same interpretation of Zeno’s expression is explained more clearly and established on another basis.

Among the several terms by which the second Person of the Trinity is called in a special sense by the Fathers on the authority of Holy Scripture, only these three are so proper and singular to that Person that they cannot belong to either of the other divine Persons: namely, Son, Word, and Image. Augustine expressly establishes this in *On the Trinity*, Book V, no. 14, and Book VII, no. 1 and following. The case of the name Son is plain, since “Son” is the relational term so proper to the second Person that it fits none of the others. The same must plainly be thought of the names Word and Image, because Image and Word are no less relational terms than Son. “Word,” Augustine says in *On the Trinity*, Book VII, no. 3, “is not said with reference to itself, but only relatively to Him whose Word it is.” Likewise Hilary, speaking of Image in *On the Synods*, no. 13: “No one is an image of himself; rather, an image must show the one whose image it is.”

These three names by which the second Person is designated are one and the same in reality, not only because He who is called by these three names is one and the same, [Col. 0097D] but also because the second Person of the Trinity is the Father’s Son precisely because He is the Father’s Image and Word; He is Image because He is Word and Son; and finally He is Word because He is the Father’s Son and Image. For when the Father begot the Son, He begot nothing other than this Word and this Image; accordingly, nativity belongs no less to Son than to Word and Image.

Further, the Son is called Word insofar as the Father, in begetting Him, spoke all things in Him; and this Word, which He spoke when He spoke all things, is that Son whom He begot. The same Son is the Father’s Image insofar as, with a perfect likeness—one which cannot apply to created things—He expresses and represents all that belongs to the Father. This Image, which so perfectly represents and expresses everything belonging to the Father, [Col. 0098A] is the begotten Image-Son, as St. Basil says in Book II *Against Eunomius*—or the born Image, as Augustine says in *On the Trinity*, Book VII, chapter 7. Finally, this Word, by which the Father spoke all things, likewise represents all things perfectly; consequently this Word is Image, and this Image is Word; and both are the Son begotten of the Father.

After these preliminaries, the question may now be asked whether this Son is the Father’s Word insofar as all divine things are spoken in Him, or also insofar as things to be created were spoken in Him. This may likewise be transferred to the Son as Image representing divine and created things. If we omit mention of possibilities, let no one object; for besides the fact that the holy Fathers, disputing against the Arians, are not found to have spoken [Col. 0098B] so expressly and distinctly about possible things as about divine and created things, possible things, known and spoken, necessarily derive from the divine attributes themselves and may in some measure be reckoned under the notion of the divine attributes.

Concerning the Son as Word, Augustine replies in Question 63 of the *Eighty-Three Questions* that all things had to be spoken by the Father in the Word, not so much those things which belong to the Father as those concerning created things. For this reason, he testifies, it is better that the Word of God be called Son than Reason, so that there may be signified not only His relation to the Father but also His operative power in relation to those things which were made through the Word. “Reason,” however, although it makes nothing through itself, is rightly called reason. Therefore there is nothing which the Father has not spoken in the Son, whether it concerns the essence, attributes, and other divine notions, [Col. 0098C] or things to be created. Otherwise, if He had not spoken something in the Son, the Father would have begotten another Word distinct from the Son, in which the things not spoken in the Son would be spoken; and He would thus have had another Son, not an only Son. For “if there are many words, there are many sons,” says Ambrose, *On the Incarnation of the Lord*, chapter 2.

Further, although in eternity there is no before and after, nevertheless for the understanding of our mind something prior and something subsequent must be conceived. Before the Father spoke in the Son the things to be created—things established by a free decree of the whole Trinity—the Father must be conceived to have begotten the Word, in whom, when He begot Him, He spoke all divine things and represented all divine things. At this prior moment of reason, the Son, Image, and Word of the Father was truly born, but lay hidden within the Father’s consciousness, [Col. 0098D] because He represented and spoke no external thing to be created. Afterwards, when the decree to create the world was made, the Father spoke what He willed to create; and then the Word came forth from the Father’s bosom, in which He lay hidden, speaking and beholding the things to be created, in whom all things to be created were represented. The former was the Father’s Word, born to God alone; the latter was likewise the Father’s Word, but in some manner begotten for us, to use the formula of Gregory of Baetica quoted in §3.

Yet since this prior and subsequent—which, according to our capacity, we have described as a twofold Word, one regarding divine things and the other created things, a twofold distinction of relations suggested by the Augustine just cited—does not make two Words in the divine Son, who is utterly simple, but one Word, “because the Word by which He speaks Himself and the Word by which He speaks the creature are of one substance,” as Anselm says in the *Monologion*, chapter 31, now 33, [Col. 0099A] therefore one Son and one eternal, not twofold, nativity are rightly and strictly mentioned by Zeno in Treatises 7 and 8, though, speaking according to human capacity, he may seem in Treatises 4 and 5 to employ a certain distinction.

Now, if you please, apply here what we collected in the preceding paragraph from Augustine and other Fathers concerning the divine decree to create the world. You will find that for this reason that decree is called the Son and Word of God: because in the Word and Son of God all things that were to be created were spoken. Thus this paragraph does not contradict the preceding one, as it appears to do at first sight, but offers a better explanation of it—though each may be illuminated by the other in light of what was said there.

[Col. 0099B] Nor should you object that this divine decree, in which we recognized the properly so-called generation of the divine Word, was begun indeed in knowledge but completed in love, so that it shines forth not so much in the representation of the Word as in the Word and Father breathing forth, as they say, notional love, and in the Holy Spirit Himself, who is notional love. For, apart from the fact that the Fathers, when dealing with Arians attacking the Son of God, attributed certain things common to the other Persons to the Son Himself, as if they were proper to Him, in order to establish His equality—as Scripture itself says in a particular way that the world was made through the Word—although that decree truly concerns the three divine Persons, nevertheless insofar as it is a begotten decree [LXXXVIII] or signifies notional generation, [Col. 0099C] it can apply to the Son of God alone, because He alone was begotten. Hence the Fathers rightly attributed to the Son alone those things which, in the decree, signify the properly so-called generation of the Son or Word.

But setting these matters aside, since the Word by which created things were spoken by the Father is the same Word by which the Father spoke all divine things, and the nativity of both Words is the same—although, by a certain human mode of reasoning, a twofold Word and a twofold nativity are distinguished—you will now certainly understand why St. Zeno, recalling the generation of the Word as regarding created things, said in Treatise 5: “God is born from God, possessing all that belongs to the Father, detracting nothing from the Father,” etc. These words suit equally the generation of the Word speaking divine things.

[Col. 0099D] Finally, we may inquire into a point that contributes to a fuller confirmation or explanation of the present subject: why St. Zeno, touching in Treatises 4 and 5 upon both relations of the Word, to divine things and to created things, nevertheless insisted more strongly and expressly upon establishing the generation of the Word insofar as He looked to created things, so that some could think he spoke only of this. We believe this arose from the attacks of the Arians, whom he had especially undertaken to refute. For they often used to proclaim, as Hilary testifies in Fragment 2, no. 26, that God the Father begot the Son for the purpose of establishing the world and, by His own power, made a new and other God from nothing, into a new and other substance. [Col. 0100A] Athanasius recalls the same things in *Oration 2 against the Arians*, nos. 24 and 25.

Therefore, since the Arians laboured to insist on the purpose of establishing the world in order to deny that the Son of God was eternal and equal to the Father, Zeno thought he should insist especially on explaining the divine Son’s generation in relation to the establishment of the world, so as to oppose them directly. He was certain that if he defeated the Arians on this point, he would have nothing further to fear from the other point, concerning the generation of the Word hidden in the Father’s bosom. With regard to the former point, the matters most to be noticed last are those added in both Treatises after the assertion of the divine Word’s generation into the counsel to create the world. For they are such that the Author expressly asserts and defends the equality and consubstantiality [Col. 0100B] of the Son with the Father—precisely those things which the Arians particularly maintained were impaired thereby. Thus it is shown that his purpose in urging this generation especially was to overthrow the Arians’ principal endeavour.

Read the Author’s own words, and what we say will be plain; at the same time it will become far more certain that this same Author, who in asserting that nativity of the Son deliberately defends His equality and consubstantiality with the Father, is very far from establishing there, as Petavius believed, a nativity in which the Son would be neither equal to the Father nor of the same substance. Rather, it is clear that he asserts a nativity by which the same Son is begotten into the counsel of creating the world and is shown as executor of that counsel, in such a way that no prejudice thereby accrues to His equality and consubstantiality.

[Col. 0100C] Thus, in Treatise 1, Book II, no. 2, having raised the same Arian objection by which they declared the Son inferior to the Father because the world was created through the Son, the Author says: “But he to whom a command is given is inferior, you say.” He does indeed acknowledge the Son as executor: “He is the executor of the paternal heart, from which He came forth.” But while defending Him as nevertheless equal, he adds this reason: “For it is no less to do great things than to say them.” And he further adds: “Although that which was spoken by the Father is, or may be called, because the Son is the Word, not without the Son,” etc. In the former words, in which the Author grants that the Son is executor of the paternal heart from which He came forth, the phrase “from which” (*unde*) indicates the Son’s procession or nativity from the Father’s heart. This is recognized as nothing other than that in the eternal decree [Col. 0100D] by which God spoke in the Son, or in the Word, whatever things were to be created. Thus our writer also implies that the decree or eternal saying itself is the Son of God. The Son thereafter executed that decree, by the power of which He proceeded from the Father’s heart, at the appointed time: what the Father had said in the Son or Word was to be done, the Son Himself, as executor, did; for all things were made through Him.

Then observe the reply by which the Author proves that this Son, though executor of the work, is not inferior to the Father. He relies not so much on the reason that it is no less to do great things than to say them, but on the point especially relevant here: [LXXXIX] “that which was spoken by the Father is, or may be called, because the Son is the Word, not without the Son.” By these words it is sufficiently implied that the Son, as the Father’s Word, is the Father’s very eternal saying or decree, and is one and the same God with the Father. [Col. 0101A] These words entirely blunt and refute every assault of Arian quibbling, and fully confirm that the interpretations hitherto set forth by us express Zeno’s mind.

§ VI.—A difficult expression of Zeno is explained, by which the proposed interpretation will be remarkably confirmed.

Add now a somewhat harsh formulation of Zeno’s, from Treatise 3 of Book II, speaking of the eternal generation of the divine Word, which is contained in another of the testimonies adduced by Petavius. Like others, this expression appears difficult to explain within that view and seems to involve a contradiction; in ours, however, it is not only readily explained [Col. 0101B], but wonderfully establishes and confirms the interpretation hitherto advanced, with which alone it plainly agrees. These are the words of St Zeno concerning the divine Son: “He proceeds into birth, who was, before he was born, in the Father, equal in all things.” Some have thought that the discourse here concerns that birth of Christ by which he was born of the Virgin, so that he is understood to have been in the Father from eternity before being born, namely, of the Virgin. But since throughout that whole treatise, both before and after the words quoted, there is discussion of the one birth of Christ by which he proceeded from God the Father, there can be no doubt that the words “he proceeds into birth” refer to the same generation of the Word from the Father, and thus leave no place for birth from the Virgin.

But here lies the difficulty. For what can this mean: “he was before he was born”? If the Son of God [Col. 0101C] was, then he was born; and is it false that he was before he was born? But if he was not yet born before he was born, then he was in no manner in the Father. Yet these matters are readily reconciled in Treatises 4 and 5 according to the interpretation we have set forth. For he is said to have proceeded into that birth by which the only-begotten Son came forth from the mouth of the Father, in order that the nature of things, which did not exist, might be fashioned—when, that is, the Father, to arrange the order of the things conceived, “belched forth the Word from the region of his heart,” as we explained in the preceding section. Nevertheless, before he was thus born, the same Son was in the Father, insofar as, as Zeno says in this very Treatise 3, “before all ages the Father embraced him in the depth of his sacred mind, in a secret beyond conjecture and in a consciousness known to himself alone, as Son—not without affection, but without revelation.” Similar words are quoted at the beginning of Treatises 4 and 5.

Thus you see indicated by this formula the two births of the Word which, as we noted above for common understanding, Zeno distinguishes in Treatises 4 and 5: the one in which he was the true Son in the Father’s consciousness, revealed to God the Father but not to us; the other in which he is subsequently conceived as born to us for the creation of things, when the Father spoke the Word concerning the creation of the world. And he was in the Father by the first birth before he was born—that is, before he was conceived as born by us through the second birth. Although these are distinct according to a certain manner of our reasoning, they are in reality one birth; just as the Word by which, in the former birth, if we may so speak, all divine and necessary things were spoken, and the Word by which, in the other birth, [Col. 0102A] all things to be created were spoken, is one and the same—as we have shown above at greater length.

But in order that it may be understood ever more clearly with what intention and in what sense St Zeno employed this formula, and that it may be made fully certain that this very testimony has very great force for declaring Zeno’s Catholic mind, wholly remote from the dogma of the Arians; and also in order to cut off every suspicion which might perhaps arise in anyone—that the Author said “he was, before he was born, in the Father” because he believed the Son at first to have been in the Father’s bosom so undifferentiated that he was not yet born or distinct, and then to have been born in time for the Father to employ him in creating things, which was Petavius’s judgment—all this, I say, requires notice that among the Arians there was a customary formula concerning the divine [Col. 0102B] Son: “He was not before he was born,” as is read in the Nicene anathema.

By the words of this formula they meant that the Son of God did not exist from eternity, but existed only when, in the creation of the world, he was made or begotten by the Father. This they explained by another celebrated formula likewise cited in the same anathema: “There was once when he was not.” Thus Arius says in Athanasius, *First Oration against the Arians*, no. 5, p. 409: “Nor was he before he was made, but he also had a beginning of creation. For God was alone, and the Word and Wisdom did not yet exist. But when afterwards he wished to create us, then indeed he made a certain one, whom he also named Word, Wisdom, and Son, in order that through him he might create us.” Eunomius agrees with this in the Confession of Faith published in vol. I of the latest edition of Canisius’s *Antiquae Lectiones*, p. 178: “He did not name the Son without generation before he existed.”

Nor did they hesitate to affirm that he was begotten before all ages; but they did not understand this as though he had been begotten from eternity, but as though he had been made before the establishment of the world, namely at the beginning of time. “A thing made did not exist before it was made,” they objected from a letter of Dionysius of Alexandria, a fragment of which Athanasius considers for this purpose in his *Letter on the Opinion of Dionysius*, no. 4, p. 246.

Eusebius of Caesarea did not hesitate indeed to pronounce anathema upon this formula, upon which the Nicene Synod had pronounced anathema, in the letter quoted by Athanasius at the end of the book *On the Decrees of the Nicene Synod*; but he then explained himself in such a way as to say nothing alien to the Arians. “Nor,” he says in no. 9, “did we think it absurd to pronounce anathema on the words, ‘He was not before he was begotten,’ since all confess that the Son of God existed before he was born according to the flesh.” This could stand together with the Arian view that the same Son was not co-eternal with the Father, since they too maintained that he was begotten before all creatures in order that the Father might employ him as an agent in creating them.

Emperor Constantine, by another line of reasoning, is reported by the same Eusebius in the cited letter to have assented to the proscription of that Arian formula. Eusebius states in no. 10 that Constantine affirmed the Son to have been in the Father before he was born, because before he had actually been begotten, he existed potentially in the Father, although he was not begotten.
