This expression, signifying that the Son of God did not always exist [Col. 0103A] actually and therefore was not begotten from eternity, openly favors the Arians—unless perhaps that proposition is understood of the former order of origin, in which the Son is conceived as first existing potentially in the Father and then actually, while both are from eternity.

Others, by contrast, in order to oppose the Arians, advanced the same formula which Zeno uses here: “He was, before he was born, in the Father.” But they used it in an interpretation by which, while attempting to escape one heresy—as Philastrius noted in chapter 124—which denied eternity and unity of substance to the divine Word, they fell into another, affirming him unbegotten and therefore not Son from eternity. Augustine, following the same Philastrius, describes this heresy more briefly in *Heresies* 80, p. 23, vol. 8:

> Another, not understanding that the Son is born eternally, thinks that that birth took its beginning from time; and yet, wishing to confess the Son co-eternal with the Father, supposes that he was with him before he was born from him. That is, he thinks that he always existed, but did not always exist as Son; rather, that he began to be Son from the time when he was born from him.

Therefore, for a Catholic man making a Catholic profession against the Arians, this mode of expression ought either to be entirely omitted, even though it might appear opposed to them—as Hilary judged in Book XII of *On the Trinity*, no. 31—or, when the dispute with the Arians concerned birth, it ought to be professed concerning that birth with such precision that it admitted no suspicion or ambiguity.

In this matter two points above all had to be guarded. First, the Son had to be declared to have been in the Father from eternity in such a way that he was at the same time distinct from [Col. 0103C] the Father and openly shown to be the Father’s Son. Further, he had to be affirmed equal to the Father and of the same substance as the Father, so that no one could infer that the Son was inferior to the Father. The Author accomplishes both in the very treatise into which this formula is inserted.

He sufficiently secured the first point in the opening period, when he affirmed that the Son, though still hidden in the Father’s bosom, was truly Son, writing that before all things the Father embraced him as Son, “not without affection, but without revelation.” By this formula he surely taught that the Son’s being in the Father was truly that of a Son, and therefore that he was Son actually, not potentially; likewise, that the Son was truly begotten and distinct from the Father, since the Father could be said to embrace him as such.

He guarded more than sufficiently against the second error by declaring that the same Son was, before he was born by the second birth, “in the Father equal in all things.” [Col. 0103D] These final words, pertaining to the first birth and omitted by Petavius, not only affirm, in declaring the Son equal to the Father, that he is distinct from the Father—for no one can be called equal to himself, since equality necessarily regards another—but also, in adding that he is equal to the Father in all things, unquestionably ascribe to the Son the Father’s very eternity and the same substance, without which he could not here be equal to the Father in all things.

Indeed, because this was the goal and chief point of the Arian controversy, St Zeno immediately added a copious ground for the equality he had asserted: “For the Father begot in him another self from himself,” namely, from that unbegotten [Col. 0104A] substance of his, in which, remaining blessed forever, he brought forth a Son possessing all things equally with himself. Do you hear Zeno openly confessing that the Son is distinct from the Father and exists as one substance with the Father? For the Father begot another self from himself—namely, from the Father’s unbegotten substance. If that substance is unbegotten, and nevertheless the Son was begotten from it by the Father, that same substance undoubtedly had to be communicated to the Son; another neither ought nor could have been communicated. Thus the Father is understood truly to have begotten another self: “another,” namely, not “another thing.” The former expression, *to alium* [τὸ alium], indicates distinction of person; the latter, *to se* [τὸ se], asserts the identity, as they call it, of the divine nature.

Accordingly, the Father is also said to have brought forth a Son possessing equally all things which the Father possesses. Here “equally” is said for “the same”; and this is plainly to confess the same substance of Son and Father, which, as we have shown elsewhere, Zeno expressly declares in other testimonies.

Moreover, since this whole argument and splendid profession of Zeno’s confession concerns that birth of the Son of which he had said, “He was, before he was born, in the Father equal in all things,” and since this state is the same as that which Zeno sets forth in other words in Treatises 4 and 5, when he declares the Son veiled and hidden in the Father’s consciousness, it is now finally clear that in these treatises also Zeno asserted that the Son, even in that state, was truly begotten, distinct from the Father, equal to the Father, and of precisely the same substance—the Author himself here explaining this abundantly.

Let Petavius now go and, after quoting the text [Col. 0104C], “He proceeds into birth, who was, before he was born, in the Father,” press this inference: “Therefore he signifies that the Son existed in the Father before he was begotten by the Father; but generation and birth occurred when he wished to create all things,” and so forth. Had he quoted and considered the whole text, and not omitted the words pertaining to the state in which the Son existed in the Father, namely “equal in all things,” nor immediately passed over the reason subsequently given for this equality, “For the Father begot in him another self from himself,” he would easily have recognized a true and properly so-called generation even in that state in which the Son was in the Father. Nor would he have understood either the words “He proceeds into birth,” or the words “before he was born,” to signify the first birth of the Son, but rather another birth, which we have explained and which does not conflict with the first.

But if anyone should be unwilling to take the words, “For the Father begot in him another self from himself,” together with the rest, as the reason—as we have hitherto assumed—of the final words pertaining to the Son’s first and hidden birth, “He was, before he was born, in the Father equal in all things,” but rather as the reason of the words, “He proceeds into birth,” namely the other birth, by which, in the plan for creating the world, the Son is said in the other two Treatises, 4 and 5, to have proceeded from the mouth or heart of the Father: since the first birth has been sufficiently defended from other words, this causes no difficulty; indeed, it favors our position much more. For it will become plain that the same Son, whom from the first birth we otherwise find to be no less distinct from the Father than equal to the Father in all things [Col. 0105A], is also acknowledged by the Author in this second birth to be eternal, equal to the Father, and of the same substance with the Father, as the words and meaning of the argument just observed declare. Nothing could be adduced more clearly to refute Petavius’s entire judgment and establish our interpretation.

[XCII] § VII.—Brief Vindication of the Ante-Nicene Fathers from Petavius’s Criticisms

Enough, and more than enough, has now been said about Zeno. The plan of our undertaking would not require us to add anything further about the other Fathers merely because Petavius censures them with a similar judgment. But since our interpretation will generally serve also for explaining the other Fathers; and since from the similar language of so many Fathers, containing almost the same formulas as Zeno’s and repeatedly admitting no explanation other than ours, it will become fully apparent both from what source Zeno’s language flowed and that our interpretation is not a product of ingenuity but is in fact conveyed—if not in precisely the same words—by the testimonies of several Fathers, and is highly fitting, not to say necessary, for explaining them: it seemed proper to make a few observations about each, as briefly as possible.

Petavius’s accusation against the Fathers preceding the Nicene Synod rests almost upon the same formula as that which was censured in Zeno. Hear him speaking of them all together in Book I of *On the Trinity*, chapter 5, no. 7, after considering their testimonies:

> Therefore, some of the ancients . . . said that the Son was brought forth by the supreme God and Father when he resolved to create this universe, in order to employ him as a kind of minister; some express this opinion more clearly, others more obscurely. Such are chiefly Athenagoras, Tatian, Theophilus, Tertullian, and Lactantius.

For Athenagoras, the very text which Petavius objected in Book I of *On the Trinity*, chapter 3, no. 4, speaks sufficiently. For there he expressly asserted that God has a Son, who is the Father’s Word in “idea” and “efficiency.” “Idea” is here said of the Word insofar as all things were spoken in him from eternity; “efficiency,” however, refers to the external act by which all things were created through that same Word.

But the passages which Petavius presses, in which Athenagoras calls this Son “the first offspring of the Father,” not as though he had been made—“for God, who is eternal Mind, had from the beginning within himself the *logos* [λόγον], that is, reason, since he is eternally rational”—but as though, when all things, along with concrete matter, formless nature, and earth as a kind of vehicle, had been subjected, and denser elements had been mingled among lighter ones, he came forth to be their idea and actuality: these, I say, wonderfully favor us.

For first, he affirms that this Son, called *logos*, which he interprets as “reason,” was in the Father from eternity, so that the Father may be called eternally rational. Athanasius, Gregory of Nyssa, and other Fathers used this same argument to demonstrate to the Arians that the divine Word was eternal. But then, he says, the Word came forth for the creation of the world, as the idea of the things to be created—an idea which certainly existed from eternity, since the Father spoke in the Word from eternity whatever things he resolved should be created—and without which there could be no actuality of those things, since nothing could attain actuality, or be created, without the Word, through whom all things were to be spoken from eternity and created in time.

What in these points does not wholly agree with what was said above? When Athenagoras writes that the Son, the *logos*, was in the Father from eternity so that the Father was rational, he certainly understands the Son according to that state in which the Father knew himself and all divine things in the Son. Accordingly, he interprets *logos* as “reason,” not “Word,” because in this state the Father is considered as rational, or as knowing all things that concern God; but as regards things to be created, nothing has as yet been conceived. For this reason alone Augustine judged that *logos*, where created things are concerned, should better be translated “Word” than “reason,” as we saw in § 5.

When Athenagoras, moreover, refers the same Son to created things, he calls him the idea in which the things to be created were pre-conceived and eternally spoken in the Word. By the force of that utterance, when they were afterward brought into effect at the appointed time through the Word, he rightly calls the Word himself their efficient cause. If you keep these matters in mind, you may read Petavius’s objections and will immediately find that all collapse of themselves, so that nothing further need be added.

[XCIII] The same point may be gathered quite plainly from the testimony of Tatian, whom Petavius renders in Latin in the same chapter, no. 5, as follows:

> God was in the beginning; and we understand the beginning to be the power of reason. For the Lord of all, being himself the substance of the whole universe, insofar as no creature had yet been made, existed alone. But insofar as he himself was all power and potency, and the substance both of things visible and of things invisible, all things were with him. For with him, through rational power, the *logos* itself which was in him brought them forth. Moreover, by the will of his simplicity the *logos* burst forth; and though it did not issue into a void, it was the first-begotten work of the Father.

Since Tatian defines “beginning” in the Greek text as *logou dynamin* [λόγου δύναμιν], while the word *logou*, which Petavius renders by *ratio* (“reason”), signifies Word itself—whence the ancient translator rendered “power of the Word,” rather than “power of reason,” and did better, since the Greek word *logos*, where it concerns created things, should be rendered “Word” rather than “reason,” according to Augustine just cited—it is plain that by the name “beginning,” as Tatian explains it, the Word itself must be understood. By its power or virtue—for the Greek word *dynamis* [δύναμις] can signify either—all things were created, as Scripture relates. Hence it is most correctly called the beginning of all things; Petavius himself observes that this name refers to the origin of things.

Therefore, when Tatian says that God was in the beginning, since the beginning is the Word itself, he means the Father by “God,” and plainly confesses that the Father was in the Word; just as immediately afterward he expressly declares that the *logos*, that is, the Word, was in God the Father. By these statements he plainly implies both that they always existed and that they were of the same substance.

Thus Tatian says that both the Father in the Word and the Word in the Father have always existed through the power of the Word, just as Athenagoras above proved that the Father always had the *logos* because he was always rational. The Father was always in the Word, of course, because without the Word he would not have been Father. And he was the beginning of things through the power of the Word, speaking in the Word all things to be created. Had he lacked the Word, he would have said nothing to be created, and consequently would never have been the beginning of things to be created.

Tatian, as we said, speaks in this text of the Word as the beginning of things to be created; and therefore presupposes that everything to be created was spoken from eternity in this Word. Thus one understands how apt is the reasoning of his statement, “All things were with him,” that is, with God, when he says: “For with him, through rational power, the Word itself which was in him brought them forth.” He brought forth, namely, all things which were therefore with God from eternity, as the Author had undertaken to prove. This is correct: since through rational, or speaking, power, all things that were afterward made were spoken by God the Father and thus in some manner brought forth in this Word, all things were with God in this Word; and together with God were both the Father, who spoke all things, and the Word, in which all things were spoken.

If these things concern eternity, Tatian consequently presupposed that this Word was born of the Father from eternity; without it not only could nothing be created, but neither Word nor Father would exist. This eternal bringing forth of things in the Word also indicates that generation of the Word which is not the generation of things but belongs properly to the Word. For it is not so much the Word of divine things as the Word of things to be created which the Father properly begot from eternity, when he spoke both divine things and things to be created. Although both were spoken simultaneously from eternity, yet according to the human manner of speaking one is conceived as spoken earlier and the other later, as we explained in Zeno.

Since, moreover, this generation belongs properly not to things but to the Word, although things brought forth or spoken in the Word by it from eternity then existed not actually but only virtually, insofar as they were to be created in time through the power of this Word actually and truly brought forth from eternity, Tatian nevertheless considered the Word itself to have been brought forth by the Father from eternity not merely virtually, as Petavius thought, but actually—as is clear from the whole context explained thus far.

But let what he next adds not disturb anyone: “Moreover, by the will of his simplicity the *logos*, or Word, burst forth.” For here he contemplates that external utterance of the Word which some thought was made in creating the world through a certain sensible voice, by which God himself said, and things were made. That belongs to another question. If the same Tatian adds that this Word, “not issuing into a void,” was the first-begotten work of the Father, this seems to refer to that sensible utterance of the Word, which, if it was the cause of all things, was God’s first work.

But if he believed that not the uttered but the Father’s inward Word somehow issued outwardly, he ascribed to the same Word an external [XCIV] generation, which is nothing other than its external manifestation: the divine power, hidden inwardly in God from eternity, at length came forth outwardly. Consequently he afterward affirmed that the Word was born “by participation, not by cutting-off”; for *merismos* [μερισμὸν], as Petavius himself says, does not, I think, mean “division,” as the translator renders it. By these words Tatian confirms that he believed the Father always to have been with the Word and not to have been left without it when it communicated itself to so many created things. For that communication of the Word, by which it flowed outwardly into so many created things, was not a cutting-off of the Word from the Father or a division of its inward substance—by which the Word always existed in the Father and the Father in the Word—but was merely its participation, by which the Word itself, and through the Word God himself, shines forth in created things. But perhaps too much has been said about Tatian.

We shall dispose more briefly of Theophilus of Antioch, whom Petavius comments upon in his own manner in the same chapter 3, no. 6. For he openly confesses that the Father had the inward *logos* in his own inner being. If he adds that he begot this *logos*, bringing it forth together with his Wisdom before all things, he did not therefore consider that first *logos* unbegotten, or undifferentiated in the Father and begotten only when, in the creation of the world, all things were spoken in the Word, as Petavius interprets. Rather, he understood the former *logos* as the Word inward in the Father, in which the Father spoke all divine things; and the latter as the Word speaking things to be created, as we explained more fully in Zeno.

Furthermore, Theophilus affirms another kind of generation of the uttered *logos*, which we considered in Tatian and which does not impair eternal generation, as we there indicated. This is also confirmed by what Theophilus himself adds: “The Father begot this uttered *logos*, the first-born of all creation, not so that he himself might become devoid of Word, but so that he might beget Word”—that is, uttered Word—“and might forever converse with his Word,” that is, his inward Word.

The passages from Tertullian, Book *Against Praxeas*, chapter 5, quoted by Petavius in chapter 5, no. 2, bear upon the same matter. For when Tertullian testifies that the *logos*, or reason, was with God from eternity, he plainly declares the inward Word of God to have been begotten from eternity, in which the Father, rational before the beginning—that is, from eternity—spoke with himself concerning the things of God. This, we think, is the reason which Tertullian calls his own.

Further, when the same God, deliberating about the creation of the world, thought and arranged speech with his reason—that is, with the Son or Word—or, as he had stated a little before more explicitly, when with and in that very reason which he had within himself he silently thought and arranged with himself what he was to say through the Word, namely when he commanded the world to be created: when, I say, God is said to have thought and arranged these things with himself in reason or the Word, that generation of the Word is surely indicated in which the Father silently spoke and decreed from eternity in the Word the things to be created.

Finally, Tertullian indicates in chapters 6 and 7 the uttered word produced in the act of creation itself; and by this formula he signifies nothing other than the external manifestation of the Word, which we explained in Tatian. Yet Petavius thinks that Tertullian asserts this final and external birth of the Word, which occurred at the beginning of time, as the first and sole one. He believes this follows from these words in chapter 6:

> For when God first willed to bring forth into their substances and forms the things which he had arranged within himself with the reason and Word of Wisdom, he first brought forth the Word itself, having within itself the inseparable Reason and Wisdom, so that through it the universe might be made—the universe which had been thought and arranged through it, indeed already made insofar as it was in God’s mind. For they lacked this: that they might also be known and held visibly in their own forms and substances. Then, therefore, the Word itself too took on its form and adornment, sound and voice, when God said, “Let there be light.”

We greatly wonder that these words could have troubled a learned man. For first, already in chapter 5 Tertullian had expressly confessed that God, before creating the world, had not been alone from eternity. He adds this reason: “For he had with himself that Reason which he had within himself,” namely his own Reason. By these words he plainly implies that Reason, that is, the Word, was distinct from God the Father from eternity; otherwise God would have been alone from eternity, which Tertullian judged must be denied for this reason.

Hence, concluding that chapter, he says: “I can therefore without rashness have laid down in advance that God, before the constitution of the universe, was not alone, having within himself Reason, and in Reason the Word, which he made second from himself”—that is, a second person—“by revolving it within himself.” Here he most expressly mentions a second person, distinct from the Father and begotten before the constitution of the world.

Moreover, we do not know whether Petavius, in writing these things, noticed the following words of Tertullian, which occur immediately after the testimony objected by him and which we find Petavius himself quoting in the same no. 2 of chapter 3:

> This is the perfect birth of the Word”—namely, Petavius comments, the birth by which he brought forth the Word itself in its own form and adornment when he said, “Let there be light”—“when it proceeds from God, first established by him for thought under the name of Wisdom: ‘The Lord created me as the beginning of his ways’; thereafter begotten for effect: ‘When he prepared the heaven, I was with him at the same time.’ From then on, making him equal to himself, from whose proceeding he became Son: first-born, as begotten before all things; and only-begotten, as alone begotten from God, properly from the womb of his own heart.”

Did he observe the explicit distinction: “first established by him for thought under the name of Wisdom; thereafter begotten for effect”? Tertullian here plainly distinguishes a twofold birth of the Son of God. The one is that by which the Father, in thinking within himself about the things to be created—as he calls it—brought forth the Word under the name of Wisdom: “it proceeded, having been established,” he says. This is the properly so-called birth of the Word, which he calls the first, when all things to be created were spoken from eternity by the Father in the Word. The other is that by which God brought forth the Word for effect in the actual creation of the world. Although this is a generation of the Word in a less proper sense, it is nevertheless called a perfect birth because the former birth, although a proper birth, lay hidden within God; whereas this one, coming forth outside God, in some manner brought the former hidden birth forth, since it made the Word itself manifest to creatures. For this reason the Son of God in the creation of the world received form and adornment, or a certain sound and voice; and thus his birth was perfect, not with respect to God, in whom it had always been most perfect [Col. 0110A], but with respect to us, to whom it then first began to be known.

Tertullian also not obscurely indicates this same distinction of a twofold birth in Book II *Against Marcion*, chapter 27, speaking of this Word “whom, by bringing him forth from himself, he made Son, and thereafter set over his plan and will.” When he says that by bringing him forth from himself he made him Son, he certainly signifies the eternal bringing forth, or birth, of the Son; otherwise he would have asserted two Gods, one eternal and the other not eternal, and thus would have fallen into the error which he rebukes in Marcion.

Contemplating this birth, he says in chapter 21 of the *Apology*: “We have learned that this one was likewise brought forth from God, begotten by bringing-forth, and therefore called Son of God and God by unity of substance.” These final words especially show that the subject is that internal bringing forth and birth of the Son by which he obtained one substance with the Father, not the external one, to which this unity of paternal substance does not belong.

By the other words, “and thereafter he set him over his plan and will,” we have no doubt that the external birth, just discussed, is indicated; and Tertullian sufficiently distinguishes it from the former by the adverb “thereafter.” In other passages mentioned by Petavius in no. 4, and explained more fully by Fr Le Nourry, vol. II, *Apparatus to the Library of the Ancient Fathers*, Dissertation 4 on Tertullian, chapter 8, Tertullian affirms so unmistakably that the Son is distinct from the Father and yet of no less one substance with the Father that our explanation, given for the more obscure testimonies hitherto considered, should be entirely secure. At the least, these clear passages ought to have moved Petavius not to think that certain more obscure testimonies should be interpreted in an alien and utterly contrary sense.

Finally, Lactantius, Petavius’s last target of accusation (chapter 3, no. 6), when in *Institutions*, book II, chapter 8, he teaches that a spirit like himself was brought forth by God the Father before he began this work of the world, so that from that good one it might arise like a stream and flow forth forever, is plainly speaking of that generation of the Word by which the Father eternally spoke in the Word whatever things were afterwards made through that same Word by participation in divine goodness. Indeed, when he testifies in the same place that the Word was employed by the Father as counsellor, he certainly signifies that this Word was eternal, since God’s counsel and decree were eternal. Moreover, if he had that counsellor from eternity, [Col. 0110D] before he determined anything concerning the creation of the world, he presupposes that that Word existed as the true Son in the Father before the Father determined in the same Word that anything should be created; and consequently he presupposes that generation [XCVI] of the Word by which the Father spoke himself in the Word before he spoke in it the things to be created.

If he calls this Word a spirit like the Father, no one should take offence; for he calls it a similar spirit in the sense in which that Word is called in Scripture the image of God and the impress of his substance. This in no way conflicts with the unity of substance affirmed by Lactantius himself in other testimonies. Further, in book IV, chapters 8 and 9, he adds something concerning a certain uttered discourse, or “vocal spirit,” as he calls it, which Petavius took to mean an external sound. But since Lactantius plainly affirms that this vocal [Col. 0111A] spirit was conceived not in a womb but in the mind, and conceived by the Father through a certain unimaginable force and power of his majesty, he undoubtedly and plainly signifies not the external but the inward generation of the same Word—the generation proper to the eternal Word. He calls this a spiritual birth in chapter 13 and contrasts it with bodily birth; and at the very beginning of chapter 8 he warned that it is wholly unimaginable. Hence also, in book II, chapter 8, he declares that the Word was eternally begotten ineffably by the Father.

Further, from book IV, chapter 25, it is evident that Lactantius understood this one—whom he thought could be generated through the utterance of voice and spirit—to be God from God. It is also clear that he called him “voice” and “spirit” in the manner of the prophets, who indicated the Son of God by the names of Word and Spirit. Therefore nothing prevents us from understanding the Son of God, God from God, truly under the name “vocal spirit” as well, which Petavius took as a sounding voice, in the writings of Lactantius, especially in book IV, chapters 8 and 9. There he ascribes to this vocal spirit, whom the Father conceived not in a womb but in his mind, the likeness or image of God the Father, in accordance with Paul—and indeed a substantial image, since, he says, it is endowed with its own understanding and wisdom. Such predicates do not apply to a sounding voice in Petavius’s sense.

That comparison of two human spirits, one of which men silently emit through the nostrils, while the other they send forth noisily from the mouth when they speak, does indeed explain the distinction Lactantius intended between angelic spirits—created silently, like breath drawn through the nostrils, not to teach but to minister [Col. 0111C]—and the spirit of the Word, which, like breath proceeding from the mouth, was to teach human beings. But it has no force in other respects. Lactantius did not intend there to establish a complete and adequate comparison; Petavius therefore ought not to have ridiculed it on account of this comparison. Nor does Lactantius transfer to the Word the vocal sound which he employs in the comparison, insofar as the Word was eternally begotten from the Father’s mind. Rather, he says this because the Word was to employ his voice toward the people—that is, because he was to be the teacher who conveyed to humankind the doctrine of God and the heavenly mystery. This concerns that teaching which the divine Word, afterwards clothed in human nature, delivered in explicit speech.

But enough concerning the ante-Nicene Fathers. Since you have heard that they all employed the same formula [Col. 0111D] used by Zeno, you will understand these two conclusions: first, that he used not a new formula but an ancient one, received from so many Fathers and learned from their books; secondly, that they did not use it in the sense which, as Petavius thought, would give the Arians their cue, but in the sense in which Zeno—the most vigorous opponent of the Arians—judged them, upon reading them, to be understood so rightly that he did not hesitate to use the same formula himself.

## § VIII.—Marius Victorinus Vindicated from Petavius’s Censure

What need is there to speak of Marius Victorinus, whom Petavius thought to be in the same case? Throughout all four books *Against Arius* he so deliberately defends Catholic doctrine in explicit words and arguments that anyone who, because of some formula censured by Petavius, thinks he held that the divine Word came forth by external generation when God created the world—as the same author infers from passages he has cited—either has not read Victorinus’s books or, if he has read them, has certainly failed to understand his position, perhaps hindered by the prejudgments scattered by Petavius. That position seems sufficiently explained by other, very clear testimonies.

For Victorinus most expressly confesses the eternal generation of the Word in many places. Thus, wherever he calls the generation [XCVII] of the Word “manifestation,” or “the disclosure of inward power,” so that the Father is the one who is within and the Son the one who is without—these being substantially the formulas noted by Petavius—either these formulas must be understood of the same eternal generation, or they must be understood of an external generation in such a way that this outward generation in time, which is a manifestation, causes no prejudice to that inward and eternal generation. This writer understands the formulas in both ways.

In the first sense, he calls the inward and eternal generation of the Word a manifestation, because God, willing to see and know himself, begot an image of himself in which he might see himself; and he calls this image, which is certainly the Word, a manifestation. He held it to be outside the Father—that is, distinct from the Father—as the person of the Son is distinct from the Father, although the Son was always in the Father. He expressly teaches this in book I, p. 269, letter h, vol. IV of the *Bibliotheca Patrum*: God, whom he defines as perfect life, “willing,” he says, “to see himself, that is, his own power, namely the Father” (for he had called the Father “power”), “there came to be this manifestation of himself”—where he plainly calls the manifestation the image of the Father, in which the Father’s substance becomes manifest to the Father himself—“which is and is called generation, and accordingly exists outside. For every act of knowing, precisely insofar as it is knowing, is outside the one who desires to know. But I say ‘outside’ as in the act of inspection, insofar as it is seeing oneself.”

He therefore acknowledges this inward and eternal manifestation and generation, just as the Father’s knowledge was inward and eternal, by which he knew himself in the Son. He proves this very clearly in many places, especially in book II, p. 273, letter f. He develops the same point more fully in book III, p. 275, letters f and g, from which we transcribe a few words:

> “What understanding understands is outside, and that which it understands is within.”

Accordingly, he places the Father, who understands, within; but the Son, whom he understands, or in whom he understands himself, without. For this reason he acknowledges in the Father a certain inward movement turned back upon itself, from which the Son is generated. He explains this in the present connection as follows:

> “Movement is always from substance and in substance—or rather is itself substance. When it looks outward—and to look outward is to be movement or motion—this itself is to will to see, understand, and know oneself. But when it sees itself, it exists as twofold, and is understood both as the one seeing and as that which is seen: the very one who sees, and the very thing which is seen. Because it sees itself, that is, looking outward, it is begotten or exists outwardly, in order that it may understand what it is.”

Therefore, if he is outside and if he is begotten, he is the Son—yet Victorinus shows him to be endowed with the same substance as the Father. Finally, he calls this movement by which the Father begot the Son “operation” and “action,” and adds: “This is the begetting; this is the birth.” Many more statements of the same kind could be produced, especially from book IV, pp. 287–288. But these seem sufficient for anyone to understand that the manifestation and operation by which the Father is said to be within and the Son without must, in Victorinus’s judgment, be referred to the eternal and inward generation.

In the second sense, when Victorinus refers manifestation and action to the creation of things, it must be observed that he does so in such a way that the Son of God was from eternity the *logos* [λόγος] of all things that are, according to book I, p. 260, b and f, since the Father decreed all future things in the Word. For, he says on p. 262, h, *logos* is not a mere utterance, but “a power communing concerning the creation of something with those things which are to be.” See p. 270, d. Accordingly he calls the Son, in relation to creatures, the *logos* and will of the Father in the same place, while asserting at p. 263, a, that he was eternal and of one substance with the Father. Finally, he teaches that this will of God proceeded at the appointed time into active power, in the same place, namely when it proceeded into the bringing-about of the things that exist, p. 266, e.

Since in this matter the Word has been manifested to us, this manifestation, or “appearing,” as he calls it, is reckoned by Victorinus as a certain outward birth and generation. Thus he says in book IV, p. 284, d:

> “Appearing is a birth from hidden things; and a birth from hidden things is also a nativity—and the nativity of one who existed even before he arose in this way.”

Here he expressly attributes a metaphorical generation to the Word in the very creation of things; and by saying that the Word existed before he thus arose, he affirms that the Word existed from eternity by that eternal and inward generation of which enough has been said above.

It cannot be denied that Victorinus wrote these matters with greater subtlety and obscurity, deriving them from the rules of dialectic, in which he took particular delight—a feature for which St Jerome reproached him. But it is one thing to criticize the obscurity and dialectic of his books against the Arians, and another to twist certain obscure formulas into a meaning which he combats in the clearest terms throughout all four of those same books. This Petavius did, as though he had not even considered interpretation. Meanwhile, excellent reader, you see [XCVIII] with what caution one must deal with ancient volumes, lest we be deceived by some expression of theirs that we suppose must be explained according to our own or common usage, when they have sometimes attached to it another meaning proper either to their age or to a particular school. This is especially to be suspected when the obvious explanation produces something unworthy, resulting in the error and discredit of exceedingly wise, or even most holy, persons. Guided by this principle, we, having examined St Zeno more carefully—whom we had read was summoned by Petavius into suspicion of a dangerously grave error—seem to ourselves to have drawn out and explained sufficiently his genuine opinion. This has contributed no little also to the vindication of the ante-Nicene Fathers and Victorinus.

# CHAPTER II. FOR WHAT REASON ST ZENO JUDGED THAT THE ETERNAL GENERATION OF THE SON OF GOD SHOULD NOT BE WRITTEN ABOUT, AND WHAT TREATISES ON THE FAITH AND WHAT FORMULAS HE CENSURED

[Col. 0114A]

Certain statements in Treatise 1 *On Faith* cause no small difficulty for some readers. At first sight, St Zeno seems both to deny instruction in the faith and to censure, indeed attack, those who expound faith in treatises and establish it by arguments. But anyone thoroughly acquainted with St Zeno’s mind and the occasion for writing his treatises will easily understand whatever harsher things occur on this subject.

At the Council of Sardica, in order to restrain the audacity of the Arians, who, not content with the formula of Nicene faith, continually invented new explanations, additions, and corrections, the following provision was made, as St Athanasius reports in the *Tome to the Antiochenes*, regarded as the synodal letter of the Council of Alexandria:

> “Although,” he says, no. 5, p. 772, “some requested that something be written concerning the faith, as though something were lacking to the Nicene Synod, and rashly attempted to obtain this, the synod assembled at Sardica nevertheless took the matter indignantly and decreed that no further written statement concerning the faith should be issued, but that the faith promulgated by the Fathers at Nicaea should suffice, since it was deficient in nothing but was full of piety. It decreed that no second profession of faith should be issued, lest what had been written at Nicaea be judged imperfect and an opportunity be given to those who continually wish to write and define concerning the faith.”

But when the Arians disregarded this restriction, daily effort was made so that each person might enlarge his own party—into which they themselves were also divided among themselves—and deceive the simpler people by issuing various creeds or treatises on faith, in which each established his own opinion and error through many reasonings and arguments.

The multiplicity and conflict of these formulas and treatises is excellently depicted by the contemporary author St Hilary in book II *To Constantius*, no. 4, p. 545. After affirming that the Arians, when asked about faith, write their own doctrines and, while proclaiming the things of God, have brought upon the world “an eternity of error and of conflict forever returning upon itself,” he continues:

> “Under the seemingly unreasonable pretext of this necessity, the practice of writing and innovating the faith afterwards became established. Once it began to create new things rather than retain what had been received, it neither defended what was old nor established what was new. Thus faith became a matter of times rather than of the Gospels, since it is drafted according to years and is not held according to the confession of baptism. It is exceedingly dangerous and even pitiable for us that there are now as many faiths as wills, as many doctrines as dispositions, and as many causes of blasphemies springing up as there are vices. For creeds are either written as we wish, or understood as we do not wish.”

[XCIX] “And although, according to one God, one Lord, and one baptism, there is also one faith, we depart from the one faith that alone exists; and while many are made, they have begun to be so many that none remains.”

And in no. 5, where he gives examples of contradictions:

> “For we are mutually aware that, since the synod of the Nicene assembly, nothing other than creeds has been written. While there is conflict over words, question over novelties, occasion from ambiguities, complaint about authors, contest over parties, difficulty in agreement, and one begins to anathematize another, scarcely anyone now belongs to Christ. For we wander amid the uncertain wind of doctrines: either, while we teach, we disturb; or, while we are taught, we err. And indeed, what alteration does the creed of the preceding year now contain within itself? First comes one which decrees that *homoousion* be kept silent; next another, which decrees and proclaims *homoousion*; then a third, which excuses, by indulgence, the term *ousia* simply adopted by the Fathers; finally a fourth, which does not excuse but condemns it.”

And shortly afterwards:

> “We decree annual and monthly creeds concerning God”—for they were altered so frequently, and new ones continually issued—“we repent of decrees; having repented, we defend them; having defended them, we anathematize them. We either condemn what is another’s in our own formulations, or what is ours in others’; and, biting one another, we have now been consumed by one another.”

There were, indeed, many formulas of faith: some issued in the various synods of Arians and Semi-Arians, others promulgated by certain bishops in defence of their own faction. These, therefore, are the many treatises, the many creeds, indeed new ones, “nourished by the toil and favour of controversy,” which St Zeno mentions in Treatise 1, book I, no. 3.

The great subtlety of intellect and force of argument that heretics employed in these writings, to the grave danger of readers, is clear from Athanasius’s letter *To the Bishops of Egypt and Libya*, p. 278, no. 8, where he seeks to deter Catholics from reading such writers in these words:

> “Even if, while writing, they borrow expressions from Scripture, nevertheless reject them, though they may have brought forward words of orthodox faith; nor should you wish to heed those who speak thus. For they do not speak with a sound mind, but, clothed in these words as in a sheep’s skin, inwardly hold the same views as Arius. . . . Therefore, if what they wrote were written by orthodox men, such as the great Hosius,” etc.—he lists other Catholics—“. . . If they,” that is, the Arians, “were like these,” that is, the Catholics, “there would certainly be no ground for suspicion in their writings; for the character of apostolic men is simple and candid.”

And in no. 9:

> “Since these writings have as their authors men hired for payment to defend the cause of heresy, . . . brothers, you must be watchful and cautious . . . lest some deception arise from elegance of language and cunning.”

Other Fathers also testify to this Arian cunning in philosophizing wrongly concerning matters of faith. See the numerous testimonies of Gregory of Nyssa, Gregory Nazianzen, Basil, Epiphanius, Faustinus, Cyril, and Ambrose collected by Petavius in the *Prolegomena*, chapter 3, from no. 3 onward. Catholic Fathers considered this sophistical cunning and human reasoning in argument—which had divided the Arians into so many errors and opinions—to be especially dangerous and to be avoided. From this it is now clear why St Zeno forbade the production of treatises on the faith.

The brother whom he addresses in Treatise 1 was trying, by philosophical arguments, to exhaust the very fountain of divinity, no. 5. Under the sound of law and faith, inflamed by a worldly love of display, he presumed that by arguments he could compel, examine, measure, and distinguish the immeasurable and incomprehensible eternity of the divinity of the God begotten from God and of the Holy Spirit, by the very right whereby it exists of itself. Therefore, although perhaps he intended to undertake this disputation with no bad motive, Zeno set before him the danger of such discussions in order to draw him away from this curious pursuit. On this occasion he brings into disrepute the treatises on faith which the Arians issued daily through similar reasonings, because they were convicted of tearing apart and destroying the faith which they had undertaken to expound and confirm by arguments.

For this purpose he commends credulity, or simple faith, above subtle teaching, because simple faith alone is universally necessary, whereas subtle teaching is full of presumption and danger. Hence he says in no. 1:

> “I think it most evident that one who is simple is better than one who is excessively clever; for the simple person simply believes all God’s words, whereas the clever person, made foolish by excessive wisdom, confounds himself in vain inquiries.”

St Zeno, therefore, does not here censure simple instruction in the faith, which he does not deny to be necessary in order that one may know whatever one ought to believe. Rather, he uniquely condemns ingenious disputations concerning the faith, excessive subtlety in matters of faith, curiosity, and dialectic, which are ruinous to many. “For disputation,” he says in no. 2, “just as it cultivates faith, so, if it is crafty, uproots faith,” as experience demonstrated in Arian disputations and treatises. Thus St Zeno taught the same things as other Fathers, whether in this first sermon *On Faith*, which we have considered thus far, or elsewhere in many passages which it would take too long to enumerate. Seeking to restrain the insolence of the Arians and repress excessive curiosity in investigating the mysteries of faith, he taught that whatever is handed down concerning the birth of the Son must indeed be believed, but affirmed that to wish to form opinions through vain arguments belongs not to one who worships but to one who is mad. See Treatise 8, book II, no. 1.

If St Zeno was truly opposed to treatises on the faith even when written by Catholic men, he did what the other Western bishops did, who consequently thought ill of the Easterners when they heard of creedal formulas or treatises issued by them. Thus, in order to reconcile the Catholic Easterners to Westerners indignant on this point, St Hilary sought in his book *On Synods*, addressed to the bishops of Gaul, no. 63, to clear their mind and purpose by reference to necessity:

> “Nothing should seem strange to you, dearest brothers, in the fact that creeds have begun to be expounded so frequently: heretical frenzy imposes this necessity.”

Immediately afterwards:

> “Would that they did not know them at all! For they would be excused more readily if they were ignorant than if they were hostile.”

Yet the grief of these bishops, unable to confine itself in silence, seeks the unity of this faith which it has long since lost through others. Meanwhile Hilary nevertheless commends the Gallican bishops themselves as blessed in the Lord and glorious, because, he says, “retaining the perfect and apostolic faith in the profession of their conscience, you have hitherto remained ignorant of written creeds.” Thus Zeno’s mind is recognized as shared with the Westerners and approved even by Hilary while he argues on behalf of the Easterners.

Perhaps, however, someone will object to what is stressed near the end of the treatise *On Faith*, where Zeno seems to disapprove not only every investigation and discussion of divine mysteries, but also their defence against heretics:

> “Avoid disputation. Whoever asserts”—that is, vindicates and defends—“God in some manner denies God; for defence is offered only to what is weak.”

But here he censures no defence other than that which this brother wished to undertake, in the manner of the Arians, through philosophical arguments. He by no means rejected the defence which, setting aside such reasonings, devoted all its effort to vindicating the faith and expounding sacred authority. For in no. 5 he says:

> “If you desire to display knowledge of the law, dispel the clouds of the readings. Teach that it is not contrary to itself. Teach that everything it sings must be believed.”

In the treatises which he approved, he wished reliance to be placed upon sacred authority alone; he rejected only the philosophical reasoning customary among the Arians and the source of errors. As Ambrose observed in the same connection in book I *On Faith*, chapter 5, no. 42, such reasoning “has power not to establish but a zeal to destroy.”

If some subtler reasoning had been necessary to blunt Arian weapons, we would find St Zeno no more favourably disposed even in that case, because of fear of the danger. We see that this very fear was impressed upon Hilary when necessity compelled him, the first among Westerners, to compose books *On the Trinity*. “We are compelled,” he says in book II *On the Trinity*, no. 2, “by the faults of blaspheming heretics to do unlawful things, to scale arduous heights, to utter what is ineffable, and to presume what is not permitted. Although what is commanded ought to be fulfilled by faith alone—namely, to adore and venerate the Son together with the Father, and to abound in the Holy Spirit—we are compelled to stretch the lowliness of our speech to things that cannot be narrated, and, by another’s fault, are driven into fault: things which ought to have been contained within the reverence of minds are now brought into the peril of human speech.”

And in no. 5:

> “Their unbelief drives us into uncertainty and danger, so that it is necessary to say something beyond the heavenly prescription concerning matters so great and so hidden. . . . What is demanded is immense; what is dared is incomprehensible: that discourse concerning God should go beyond God’s own definition. He has given the names proper to his nature: Father, Son, Holy Spirit. Whatever is sought beyond the meaning of this discourse lies beyond the reach of language, beyond the aim of perception, beyond the grasp of understanding. It is not uttered, attained, or comprehended. The nature of the thing itself exhausts the meaning of the words; impenetrable light blinds the contemplation of sense; whatever is bounded by no limit exceeds the capacity of understanding. But, begging pardon for this necessity from him who is all these things, we shall dare, inquire, and speak.”

[CI] If Hilary confesses that by this writing he is doing something unlawful, falling into fault, and being drawn into uncertainty and danger, and if, though pressed by ecclesiastical necessity, he nevertheless judged it must not be undertaken without asking pardon or without so long an apology, who can fail to see on what grounds St Zeno tried to deter and turn away his brother from such writing? That brother was not driven by the same necessity that pressed Hilary, but, as appears, by curiosity alone. Zeno did not believe it truly unlawful to discuss divine mysteries with sound judgment; rather, taught by the daily experience of Arians, he saw the danger of falling into heresy arising from such disputations. No prudent person would merely refrain from blaming this, but would judge it worthy of praise—especially for the reason suggested by Zeno himself in no. 5: it is safer, indeed, to seem unlearned than to be sacrilegious.

We know that bishops of these regions also followed this policy after Zeno, from many sources, and especially from St Gaudentius, who governed the Church of Brescia shortly after Zeno’s death. In Sermon 14, p. 169, he left these words:

> “We ought, therefore, to believe God to be no other than he himself has revealed by his own Word that he ought to be believed. Nor should we examine his works in a rebellious spirit, but admire them with faithful devotion, because the word of the Lord is upright, and all his works are in faith. . . . Let us therefore cease, neglecting faith, to assail the divine mystery with insulting questions.”

St Peter Chrysologus, Archbishop of Ravenna, says in Sermon 62 *On the Creed*: “Attend, O human being, with what reverence faith is conveyed and entrusted to you. Hear the Father, that you may perceive, understand, and believe; do not scrutinize the Son. Confess that he is; do not rashly inquire whence, when, or how he is.” Many more statements of this sort occur, which there is neither leisure nor need to cite, since Zeno’s view seems sufficiently explained and vindicated by what has been said.

# CHAPTER III. VARIOUS FORMULAS OF ZENO CONCERNING THE INCARNATION OF CHRIST ARE VINDICATED

The formulas of Zeno concerning the eternal generation of the divine Word which seemed harsher have been explained in the first chapter. It remains to explain those concerning its temporal generation. They are, broadly, three.

The first consists in his repeatedly saying that the Son of God clothed himself with, took up, bore, or assumed “man.” This way of speaking is censured because by “man” one commonly understands not so much human nature as a human person; and no one but a Nestorian affirms that the latter was assumed by the divine Word. A second formula seems related, from Treatise 16, book I, no. 14, where there is mention of “the person of the man”: “The Lord from the person of the man whom he had assumed.” The second main formula occurs in Treatise 6, book II, no. 1, where he calls the Son of God “mingled with man,” as though divine and human natures had coalesced into one mixture—the heresy of Eutyches. To this expression is added that in Treatise 8 of the same book II, no. 2: “Thus, mingled with human flesh, he fashions himself as an infant.” The third is found in Treatise 2, book I, no. 9, where the author says that God was changed into a human being; and in Treatise 12, that he was enclosed in a human being, or enclosed in the covering of flesh, as he says in Treatise 9 of the same book, no. 1.

Yet, if the first two formulas are taken rigidly, they are found to be contradictory and to favour the entirely opposed Nestorian and Eutychian heresies. This itself sufficiently indicates that they were pronounced in a sense wholly different from that conveyed by the words when rigidly understood. This is especially established by the antiquity of our writer. Since the heresies of Nestorius and Eutyches, to which those formulas seem to lend support, had not yet arisen in the fifth century, the holy Fathers spoke more freely and safely—as Augustine frequently observed, albeit in another connection—without even considering the heretical sense later attached to the same phrases. Hence they used now this, now that apparently contrary formula more freely, yet always in the same Catholic sense.

The first expression, “he assumed man,” “he took up man,” and so forth, became objectionable only after Nestorius. Before then, it was used in a sound sense by the holy Fathers, as Agobard observes *Against Felix*, no. 8:

> “It seems to me that your charity should also be warned about this: Felix frequently delights in saying ‘the assumed man’ or ‘the form of a servant.’ Although this could be said piously, and is found very frequently to have been said by the holy Fathers, nevertheless it must be considered that in Nestorius these words displeased our people.”

This is certainly most true, with the exception of Victorinus, who before the age of Nestorius, in book II *Against Arius*, p. 272, vol. IV of the latest Lyons edition of the *Bibliotheca Patrum*, wished it to be said that the Word assumed not a man but flesh. Otherwise, if we wished to list all the ancient Fathers who employed the same formula in a Catholic sense, it would take too long. It is sufficient to name Tertullian, Lactantius, Hilary, Jerome, Augustine, and—what is more significant—St Leo himself, who, though a most vigorous opponent of the Nestorian heresy, nevertheless wrote “the assumed man” in Sermon 94 *On the Transfiguration*, chapter 2, and “united to man” in Sermon 33, or 4 *On the Epiphany*.

All these Fathers understood “man” to mean human nature, not a human person. Thus St Augustine, in *On the Predestination of the Saints*, no. 31, after saying “the assumed man,” immediately adds “the assumed nature of man.” Similarly Hilary, who in his commentary on Matthew, chapter 3, no. 2, wrote “the man whom he had assumed,” elsewhere speaks of “the nature of flesh assumed from the Virgin,” in Psalm LXV, no. 12; “the assumption of our flesh,” in Psalm CXXIV, no. 4; and “the material of the assumed body,” in Matthew, chapter IV, no. 14. Zeno likewise says at the end of Treatise 8, book II, no. 2: “For this reason he deigned to clothe himself with flesh.”

Moreover, the expression “the assumed” or “the received man” is even less to be censured in ancient authors because it is found, after Nestorius, still used in the sound sense just described, even in formulas of faith themselves. Such is the formula published by Martene, vol. I, *On Ancient Ecclesiastical Rites*, p. 163; in the hymn *Te Deum*, commonly attributed to Ambrose and Augustine; and in many authors, as is evident even from the single testimony of Facundus of Hermiane, writing near the end of book IX:

> “The ancient Doctors said that God the Word is, principally and according to essence, the only-begotten Son of God; but the assumed man received, by the unity of his person, that he might always be and be called the only-begotten Son.”

Here he understood “the assumed man” so plainly as human nature alone that he expressly affirms that there was one person in Christ. When Zeno says “from the person of the man,” he takes the word *persona* not in its scholastic sense but in the common sense customary among Latin sacred writers: what is elsewhere expressed by “as a man” or “in the manner of a man.” This we have established by examples from other Fathers in note 75 on Treatise 16, book I.

The second formula, expressing mixture, was common among the Fathers before Eutyches. They found no heresy in it, so much so that Augustine did not hesitate to define the incarnation of the Word in Letter 137, formerly 3, no. 11, as “God and man mingled.” But the verb “to mingle” here signifies not a confusion of the divine and human natures but their union or conjunction in the person of the Word. Accordingly, after replying to the question raised there—how God is mingled with man, for he uses this word—by another question, namely how soul is mingled with body, Augustine, continuing the same comparison, gives this second answer:

> “Just as in the unity of person the soul is united to the body, so that there is a human being, so in the unity of person God is united to man, so that there is Christ.”

Here he substitutes the word “united” for “mingled,” which had been used in the proposed question, as though they were one and the same. He then warns that, upon hearing this word, one must depart from the customary notion of bodies, in which two liquids are mixed in such a way that neither retains its integrity, and so forth.

Leporius, understanding this conjunction to be denoted by the word “mingling,” says in the booklet *Correction*: “For he knows how to be mingled without corruption and yet to be mingled in truth.” Irenaeus, Tertullian, Cyprian, Firmicus, Hilary, and, to omit the rest, St Leo—the condemner of Eutyches—used the same word in the same sense: in Sermon 22, *On the Nativity*, 3, chapter 1, “that one nature might be mingled with the other”; and in Sermon 33, *On the Epiphany*, 4, chapter 4, “mingled with the nature of flesh.” So too did Vigilius in book I *Against Eutyches*, even after the rise of that heresy, from which the word “mixture,” understood in a different sense, had begun to acquire an evil reputation.

That Zeno understood mixture as conjunction which did not injure the integrity of divine and human nature is clear even from Treatise 8, book II, no. 2 itself. There he teaches indeed that the Son of God was mingled with human flesh, yet in such a way that each nature remained whole: “There also, preserving what he was, he purposes to become what he was not.” He says similar things in Treatise 9, no. 2, and at the end of Treatise 7. Finally, in Treatise 6, book II, no. 1, he plainly calls Christ “man mingled” in order to teach neither a mere man nor mere God—the positions of the two heresies there noted—but a composite reality arising from the conjunction of both natures; or, as Lactantius says in book IV, chapter 13, that he was both God and man, “mingled from both kinds.” Cyprian had said “compacted from both kinds” in book II of the *Testimonies*, chapter 10. In this is contained an excellent profession of the Catholic faith.

Third-class formulations, although each separately may seem somewhat harsh and in some degree opposed to one another, are nevertheless not to be said, in the author’s mind, to conflict with the profession now set forth, [Col. 0121A] by which that which was is declared to remain intact in the Incarnation. Certainly they cannot tend to suggest that the divine nature, which is immutable and, according to Zeno himself, remained safe—that is, whole—was changed into the human; nor that it was enclosed in a human being, whereas the world and the world’s vastness cannot contain it, as he himself testifies in Tractate 9, Book II, §1. They serve only to make us understand that the Son of God truly became man, as though he could be seen as a mere man, the divine majesty being in some manner hidden beneath the covering of flesh—a majesty which, as Tractate 5 of the same book indicates, the limited capacity of this world cannot sustain.

In this same sense, together with the Apostle Paul, he called the divine Word “shortened,” in Romans 9:28: “You caused him, shortened for a little while from the immensity of his majesty, [Col. 0121B] to sojourn,” Tractate 2, Book I, §9. And in Tractate 8, Book II, §2: “At the appointed time the Son of God, his majesty meanwhile concealed, set forth from the heavenly seat; in the temple of the predestined Virgin he marks out for himself a camp, into which he is secretly poured, about to be generated as a human being; and there, while preserving what he was, he devises to become what he was not.” These statements are so clear that nothing further need be added.

## CHAPTER IV. WHAT THE AUTHOR TAUGHT CONCERNING THE SIN OF THE FIRST PARENTS

That Saint Zeno, in agreement with the common opinion of the Fathers, which entirely accords with the literal interpretation of Genesis, placed the sin of the first parents in the eating of the forbidden fruit, is clear from Tractate 6, Book I, §3, where he affirms that Adam wickedly tasted the sweet fruit of the sacred tree. He confirms the same point in Tractate 13 of the same book, when he teaches that death was brought upon Adam and Eve through the deadly tree, which the woman alone touched.

But in this same Tractate 13, §5, he indicates that Adam sinned through the male member which is circumcised: “For Adam,” he says, “when he plucked the forbidden fruit with this member, thereby introduced into the human race the rule of death.” He adds that circumcision was therefore commanded to the Hebrew people, so that, when it marks the seat of the maternal—that is, original—fault, it might teach them also that other crimes are to be avoided. He explains the same point more forcefully in Tractate 2, §8, when speaking of desire: “This one,” he says, “set Eve’s breast aflame with his torches.” By these words he quite plainly suggests [Col. 0121D] that the guilt of the first parents lay in the pleasure of sexual union, as though the tree and fruit forbidden them by God were that very union; and as though, by engaging in it against the prohibition, they sinned gravely and brought the whole human race into sin.

No one fails to see how foreign this is both to the literal sense of Genesis and to the interpretation of the Fathers. It ought to seem all the more incongruous because it is certain that carnal concupiscence had no place in the earthly paradise, as Augustine lucidly demonstrates at length in several books against the Pelagians. While pondering these matters and seeking the origin of Zeno’s opinion, we discovered something similar in Clement of Alexandria, [Col. 0122A] *Stromata*, Book III, p. 466. There, attacking a certain Cassian, a disciple of Valentinus and leader of the Docetists, and several others devoted to the same heresy, who with Tatian condemned marriage, he left the following in writing:

“It is certain that the Lord also came . . . to those who had gone astray in their perceptions or thoughts; he came, I say, to us—those things which were corrupted by our disobedience to the commandments, while we pursued pleasure too eagerly, perhaps because our first-created ancestor anticipated the time and sought the grace of marriage not at the proper time, and went astray.”

And shortly afterwards, p. 470: “Even if,” he says, “the serpent, having derived the scheme of its treacherous counsel from brute animals, persuaded one to say that Adam with Eve consented to union—namely, because the first-created humans had not otherwise made use of this nature, as some think—then creation is again assailed with curses, as though it had made human beings weaker than creatures devoid of reason, whereas those first formed by God surpassed them. But if nature indeed led them, like brute animals, to the procreation of children, yet, deceived by fraud, they were stirred earlier than they should have been, while they were still young, then God’s judgment upon those who did not await his will is just.”

Clement therefore teaches, following the opinion of certain unnamed persons, that Adam and Eve sinned in this: that, seeking pleasure too eagerly, they did not await the divine will by which union would be commanded, but sought the grace of marriage sooner than was proper. Perhaps those who advanced this opinion were the very heretics whom he refutes. Yet he does not wholly reject them on this point; by the word “perhaps” he does not deny that the same opinion may be defended, and maintains only that no conclusion can be drawn from it by which they may prove marriage to be evil.

Whence either they or Clement derived this opinion is wholly unknown. Yet it appears to have flowed from some apocryphal book, or rather from the interpretation of certain Hebrews, whom we think are indicated by Moses Bar-Cepha, Syrian bishop, when, in Part I of his *Commentary on the Site of Paradise*, chapter 19, p. 464, vol. XVII of the Lyons edition of the *Bibliotheca Patrum*, he writes:

“There are some who think that what Adam tasted was not a tree, but a sexual embrace, by which he united his body with his wife . . . and that the command, ‘Do not eat of that tree,’ meant nothing else than ‘Do not have intercourse, but live holy lives, without all sexual pleasure’; and that, ‘On the day you eat from it, you shall die,’ means, ‘On the day you unite your bodies.’”

We gather sufficiently that certain Rabbis of a later age also subscribed to this interpretation from *Dialogue 3 on Love*, near the middle, published in Italian in the sixteenth century by Leo the Hebrew of Modena. That this interpretation was more probably drawn by our author from Hebrew books, or at least from contemporary Hebrew views, is suggested by the fact that in Tractate 13, Book I, he argues concerning circumcision against the Hebrews and seems to endeavor to refute circumcision chiefly by means of their own opinion.

Indeed, if he had here put forward not an alien opinion but his own, how could he, in Tractate 6, [Col. 0123A] Book I, §3, have endorsed, as we noted at the beginning, the common explanation according to which Adam wickedly tasted the sweet fruit of the sacred tree? How could he, in the same Tractate 13, Book I, §10, have said that the deadly tree was touched by the woman alone, if both had touched the tree and fruit in the supposedly forbidden marital union? Therefore, we judge it credible that Saint Zeno employed this interpretation in order to convict the Hebrews more strongly by their own hypothesis. Since, however, he hints at this same view in Tractate 2, Book I, where there is nothing against the Hebrews, it may be acknowledged to belong not only to Hebrews but also to some Christians. Thus Saint Zeno did not consider it to be passed over when he undertook to speak of the destructive effects of sexual love, although he himself followed another and true opinion.

## CHAPTER V. HOW CORRECTLY SAINT ZENO THOUGHT CONCERNING DIVINE GRACE

This is the chief point at which Saint Zeno seemed, in certain places, to have spoken rather harshly to those who prepared the Verona edition. They therefore took the liberty of inserting certain words into the text in order to make a Catholic sense evident, thereby softening or explaining several passages—as happened around the same time with the Roman editors of Saint Ambrose, whom they acknowledge in their preface that they took as an example.

Foremost among the passages deemed harsh were the words in Tractate 1, Book I, §1, where he testifies that the nature of faith is such and so great that it is not lent to any human being by another, [Col. 0123C] but arises from that person’s will. Since this appeared to attribute everything to the will, so as not even to affirm divine grace, the Verona edition printed: “so that it arises in each human being not from another, but from that person’s will, preceded by the inspiration of the Holy Spirit and aided by him.” Likewise, in Tractate 2 of the same book, §3, the statement, “Thus faith is above all a thing belonging to us,” was thought to require completion in that edition as follows: “Thus faith, the gift of God, is above all a thing belonging to us.” Finally, in Tractate 12 of the same book, §4, distinguishing the twofold life of body and soul, he says: “This life we ourselves obtain for ourselves in this life by faith from the living stream of the sacred font.” Since these words were feared to be understood as excluding grace and attributing the whole power of justification to ourselves, they were similarly published with the addition: “we ourselves, God moving and helping us, . . . obtain.”

But these emendations bring Catholics into disrepute. For we have often seen heretics reproach us with corrections of this kind, in which a few editors indulged through vain fear, as though we had corrupted the works of the Fathers; and this has greatly prejudiced Catholic truth. Such corrections, I say, were unnecessary, since the question under discussion at that time allows these passages to be conveniently explained without injury to grace; moreover, from other passages Zeno reveals that his view of grace was sound.

The sense in which the first testimony was uttered will become clear from the question then at issue. In that place, Tractate 1, Book I, on Faith, the question was not whether faith is from grace or from the will—or whether it is not. Such a question never even entered Zeno’s mind; it was raised much later by the Pelagians. The holy bishop’s entire contention was against the Arians. Thinking that faith had to be expounded by many treatises and arguments, they labored so hard in composing, publishing, and reading them, as though faith could not be conceived without this study. To refute them, Saint Zeno declared that faith is not lent to a human being by another—that is, another human being—through the treatises mentioned, but arises from that person’s will. His intention and purpose was to exclude that single improper and dangerous devotion to treatises, as the rest of the discourse makes clear; he intended to affirm nothing against the necessity of grace.

A person who praises the will, which indeed cooperates in the conception of faith, is not thereby to be judged to exclude grace; just as one who affirms grace does not thereby exclude the will. Saint Zeno mentioned the will alone and not grace because no question and no error on this point then existed; and it is danger from error that usually sharpens the mind so greatly that we speak and write more cautiously. The interpretation of the third testimony is similar: in it, the life of the soul is said to be obtained by ourselves, just as above faith was said to arise from our will. The same holds for the second testimony, in which faith is affirmed to be especially our own possession. Yet he called it ours in order to contrast it with what belongs to another; for he immediately adds: “Therefore, if it is ours, let us preserve it as ours, that we may rightly hope for what belongs to another.” This has no bearing on the controversy concerning grace.

Moreover, other Fathers who flourished before the Pelagian era, not yet having been warned by their adversaries’ fury to speak more cautiously, sometimes used similar formulations, as Augustine noted. Although these formulations mention the will alone, they cannot be used to crush heretics; but since they do not thereby exclude grace, they cannot support them either. Did not Augustine himself testify concerning himself that, before the Pelagian heresy broke out, he had used a similar expression, which could indeed be understood in a sound sense but seemed to speak like the Pelagians? Thus, having written in his *Expositions of Paul’s Epistle to the Romans*: “Therefore what we believe is ours, and believing and willing are ours,” when the Pelagian heresy subsequently arose, to which these expressions might seem favorable, he both declares them insufficiently well written in *Retractations*, Book I, chapter 23, and notes there that they may nevertheless be rightly explained and understood. For, as he says in §2, both believing and acting are ours because of the freedom of the will; yet both are given through the Spirit of faith and love. And in §3: “It is indeed true, but according to the same rule: both are his, because he prepares the will; and both are ours, because they do not occur unless we are willing.”

That the other Fathers, and Saint Zeno in particular, commended the power of the human will in this sense is clear from other passages in which grace is commended and preferred. Most notable indeed is the passage found near the end of Tractate 6, Book I. After the author has praised the outstanding works of many saints, he plainly acknowledges that all must be referred to God’s gift—that is, divine grace—in these words: “All those who have been mentioned, and all who are blessed, are such by his—that is, God’s—gift.”

But most excellent of all, and equivalent to a thousand testimonies, is the passage from the same Tractate 1, Book I, where he attributes the origin of faith to the will in these words, §1: “We are not under law,” he says, “but under grace, which compels us to love God and to serve him alone in the sacrament of the one Trinity once believed—not by arguments, not by necessity, but by will.” As many words, so many propositions. This testimony embraces faith, love, and all Christian works by which we serve God; and it attributes all these to grace, which compels the will to perform them.

Yet by the word “compels,” lest he seem to attribute too much to grace, as though a necessity imposed upon us took away freedom of will, he explained himself by saying: “not by arguments, not by necessity, but by will.” These words indicate the efficacy of grace while leaving freedom untouched. Since the same tractate concerns faith, this testimony too, excluding arguments and necessity and affirming the will, speaks especially of faith: faith, he understands, is to be received not by arguments—that is, not by a reason or knowledge that introduces necessity—but by will. This is precisely the sense in which he said at the beginning that faith is not lent by another through arguments but arises from the will.

Therefore, since Saint Zeno calls grace that which compels the will to faith without necessity or rational demonstrations, the first text must be interpreted in exactly the same way. Grace should not be thought omitted as though Saint Zeno had not recognized it as necessary; rather, it was not always necessary to introduce it, as occurred also with other Fathers.

We may add another point, perhaps not of slight weight. Whenever the holy bishop uses antitheses, he always opposes will to necessity; consequently, he appears to have understood “will” as freedom, so that for him “by will, not by necessity” means the same as “freely, not necessarily.” Besides the passage just cited from §1 of Tractate 1 on Faith, where grace is said in this sense to compel to faith “not by necessity, but by will,” in Tractate 8, Book I, on Fear, [Col. 0125D] §1, he distinguishes two fears: one which is necessarily stirred by natural force in view of impending dangers, death, and the like; the other, which is the fear of God, conceived by us freely, not in natural trembling but in the rational exercise of instruction. To signify that the former is necessary and the latter free, he uses these words. Of the former, in §2: “What is feared is not a matter of devotion, but of necessity.” Of the latter, in the final section: “One fears by skill, not by chance; by will, not by necessity.” Here will is plainly understood as the freedom contrary to necessity.
