The author is rightly recognized to have taken will in the sense of freedom, insofar as free acts arise from the motion of one’s own will. Hence, to express this concerning that same free fear of God, he had said a little earlier: “He who begets himself by his own will”—that is, one is compelled by no external force and driven by no necessity. Similarly, therefore, when he taught that faith arises from the will, he wished only to indicate that it is freely generated. His testimony may consequently be adduced not to deny grace, but rather to establish freedom of choice.

## CHAPTER VI. WHETHER SAINT ZENO, IN SPEAKING OF FAITH OR LOVE, WENT TOO FAR

There are three other tractates in which he seems at times to have written somewhat harshly concerning faith and at times concerning love, and almost to have adopted contrary opinions. Lest these passages offer an occasion for error, the Verona editors judged that they should be explained by changing or adding terms.

First, in two tractates he extolled faith alone as though it alone were sufficient for salvation. For in Tractate 12, Book II, on Abraham, §2, he says: “Faith alone is to be preferred.” And in Tractate 33, as though faith alone sufficed to attain blessedness, he adds: “As much as one has believed, so much blessedness also shall one have.” In each passage the editors inserted an addition explaining that works also are necessary, so that the faith meant would be understood to be living faith which, as the Apostle says, works through love. Thus they published the first text: “Faith alone is to be preferred—that is, faith adorned with works, such as Abraham’s was”; and the second: “As much as one has believed and acted, so much blessedness also shall one have.” We wonder, however, that they added nothing also in Tractate 31, Book II, where the author seems to attribute the increase of grace to faith alone: “Whoever has believed more will make himself nobler.”

Yet if in these passages Zeno may seem to extol faith too highly, as though it alone has saving power, in Tractate 2, Book I, he exalts love in an entirely opposite manner. He not only affirms that neither faith nor hope can avail anything without love—which could rightly be said insofar as they contribute nothing to salvation unless adorned with love—but twice declares that neither can stand without it. Speaking of faith and hope, he says in §1: “If you deny them love, both will cease”; and in §5: “Neither will stand.” The Verona editors, however, with a rather freer hand substituted “they will be useless” for “they will cease” in the first passage, and “they will not profit” for “they will not stand” in the second.

But such a free correction or addition by the editors does not vindicate Zeno; it rather accuses him, as though his thought could not be fairly explained without additions or correction. It gave heretics, from whom the editors believed they were removing an occasion for error, the greatest opportunity for accusation against us, as though we had deliberately corrupted the Fathers whom we found opposed to ourselves, lest they seem opposed. Therefore another approach must be taken, by which Saint Zeno may sufficiently explain himself.

First, this very apparent conflict of his statements—he seems now to attribute too much to faith, now too much to love—should be sufficient evidence that neither faith nor love is given what it appears at first sight to be given; something else is implied, so that no contradiction follows.

To speak first of faith: Tractate 3, Book I, §4 makes it certain that Zeno attributes the reward of immortality only to those who cultivate true righteousness and, trampling down worldly pleasures, keep God’s commandments. Then Tractate 1 of the same book clearly shows that Zeno commends as useful for eternal salvation no faith other than that which works through love. For, in §2, speaking of faith, he testifies that those found without works are condemned by faith: “Those who come to her,” that is, to faith, “she requires of them the profession of belief alone, because she cannot see their faith; but if she discovers from their conduct that it is absent, she immediately punishes in anger, as faithless, the one whom she instructed.” Shortly afterward in the same section, he commends a faith which provides not only outward works but also inward purity of conscience: “Faith cleanses the conscience to its depths, so that it owes nothing even inwardly to guilt.”

One should consider the end of the same tractate, where he indicates that whenever he commends faith, he always commends that faith by which one faithfully serves God and places confidence in God alone. For, he says, a person should know that he is called *fidelis* (“faithful”) from *fidelitas* (“faithfulness”) and *fiducia* (“confidence”). Therefore, if he regards as truly and perfectly faithful the person who makes himself faithful by confidence—that is, hope—and faithfulness—that is, faithful observance of the commandments—he plainly praises and prefers only the faith which is not separated from confidence or hope and from faithfulness or works. Thus in Tractate 13, Book I, §11, he most expressly affirms that only observance of the will of God is necessary for those who live faithfully.

Moreover, in Tractate 2, Book I, §4, writing an encomium of love, he affirms that it is so endowed with, or preferred above, all things that it is by right the queen of all things—shortly afterward, in §5, he calls it “the substance of all divine virtues.” This could not have been said of faith in the tractate on Abraham unless he had there understood a faith surrounded and clothed with love. He speaks similarly of this same faith in Tractate 16, Book I, §12, when he attributes victory, or reward, to faith alone, as in Tractate 2, §2. Thus in Tractate 12, §4, in the very period in which he testifies that life is obtained through faith, wishing faith joined with works to be understood, he adds this reason for his statement: “Because the soul which has conquered the world by recognizing and observing true religion and true righteousness must necessarily enjoy immortal blessedness as the immortal reward of its labor.”

As for his apparent excessive exaltation of love in Tractate 2, Book I, when he declares that without it the other virtues—especially faith and hope—cease or cannot stand, this can be explained in two ways. First, Zeno’s statement that both—that is, faith and hope—will cease does not mean that he thought they invariably perish if love departs; rather, when love fails, they sometimes fail. He proves this in the same tractate, §6, by the example of Judas, who lost both hope and faith because love did not remain in him. See also what is added there on the same subject in §4.

Moreover, the author well knew and taught from Paul that faith and the other virtues can exist without love, though they profit nothing for salvation. In the same way, in discussing the praises of hope, he did not deny that, when hope fails, faith can remain; rather, he says that faith is of no use and can scarcely be found in one who is convinced that there will be no reward of eternal blessedness. For, in §1, he asks: “What Christian, in proving the necessity of hope, believes in Christ if he does not believe that the time of everlasting happiness promised him by Christ will come?” Read what follows there, where you will find Zeno at greater length speaking of the hope of the eternal reward known through faith. If this interpretation of Zeno’s thought is correctly maintained, many other passages that are rather obscure will thereafter be easily understood.

Second, another explanation, entirely fair to Zeno’s view, may be offered for why hope and faith truly do not stand, cease, and die without love; for he uses all these terms. Since nothing can subsist in the human mind without some love, faith and hope cannot stand unless they are loved; consequently, without every form of love they will cease and die. They will surely stand if they are loved, and there is always some love or affection in the heart. In this sense Saint Ambrose says, Sermon 9 on Psalm 118, §3: “Who hopes except one who desires and loves what he hopes for?”

Zeno speaks in this sense and with this meaning: by *charitas* (“love”) he does not understand narrowly that love by which God or neighbor is loved, but something much more extensive, by which we accept and in some degree love anything at all—even faith and hope themselves, while accepting them. Indeed, he uses the term still more broadly, so as to include a certain metaphorical love of things incapable of any genuine love. We demonstrate this plainly from the same tractate, beginning with a statement which would present no slight difficulty without this principal meaning of love. Thus he writes in §4: “Faith belongs to few; love belongs to all.”

Sparav., thinking this passage had to be understood of Christian love, judged it ought to be corrected so that it read with exactly the opposite sense: “Faith belongs to all; love belongs to few”; for Christian love is found in fewer people than faith. But, besides the fact that faith could not be said to belong to all, since not all hold the Christian faith—and Zeno speaks of all human beings, without a single word suggesting that he speaks only of Christians—no manuscripts and no editions support this correction. We therefore judge that Zeno spoke most truly under another meaning: faith is truly found in few because Christians are few in comparison with other unbelievers; although they lack faith, they nevertheless have some love, since no one can exist without some affection. Thus even the Gentiles are often reported to love one another and do good to one another.

Therefore Zeno is not speaking of true Christian love, but of *charitas* understood in the broadest sense as some kind of affection. That this sense was present in the author’s mind while writing is decisively shown by the fact that, intending to expound the praises of love at greater length, he displays how widely it extends. Using the name *charitas* throughout, he first praises those qualities of it that shine out in Christian love; but then he adds those that accord with a certain love belonging to all nations, indeed even to beasts and likewise to inanimate things. Thus, in §5, after mentioning a kind of love conceived as existing even in the elements themselves insofar as they hold together, he concludes with this general statement: “There is absolutely nothing which without this love can be pleasing, without it peaceable, without it faithful, without it secure, without it glorious, without it united to God, without it capable of being perfect.”

From this one recognizes how carefully ancient writers must be explained, lest by transferring into their times the meanings which words possess in ours, and judging that their words are to be interpreted by these meanings, we imagine that they erred or that the manuscript text is corrupt and must be corrected according to our own usage. Therefore, if Saint Zeno understood *charitas* so broadly as to mean any affection common even to beasts and inanimate things, he rightly affirmed that the other virtues—that is, faith and hope—fail without love, since it is evident that they cannot be accepted or cherished without some love for them. In this sense of *charitas*, Saint Zeno, speaking like Saint Ambrose, can incur no charge of error.

## CHAPTER VII. ON SECOND MARRIAGES AND THE MARRIAGE OF CHRISTIANS WITH UNBELIEVERS

Among the errors which some heterodox writers endeavor to pile up and object from the writings of the most holy Fathers, if possible in order to undermine their authority, not the least is that second marriages—and still more fourth and further marriages, though successive—seem to be represented by some Fathers as criminal. Since Saint Zeno is among these Fathers, having argued sharply against such marriages, especially in Tractate 5, Book I, a defense of this chapter must not be omitted. Above all, because something new may be brought forward from the reasons he gives, from which the sound intention not only of Zeno but also of the other Fathers, and sufficiently fair defenses of them, may be gathered—defenses in which all may rest who are guided not by prejudice against the Fathers but by reason.

But to speak first and chiefly of our author: in Tractate 5, having undertaken to commend continence, and disregarding the objections of many persons which we explained in Note 2, he first endeavors to persuade his readers to virginity. Then, intending to promote the continence of widowhood, he argues in §§4 and 5 to some extent against second marriages; yet he presses only reasons showing that such marriages are less fitting and unnecessary for a widow who has children and who has loved and sincerely mourned her husband from the heart—not reasons establishing them as unlawful.

Indeed, at the beginning of §4, citing one passage of Paul in which nothing is prescribed except as counsel, he commends the preservation of a single perfection of observance in divine worship. And at the beginning of §6, he expressly classifies second marriages among things nearly sound, on which he did not wish to dwell longer. Let the word “nearly” trouble no one, since it does not concern the fault of such marriages themselves but the defect of incontinence, which, being commonly the cause of marriages of that kind, prevents them from being wholly sound. For the same reason, even first marriages, if undertaken as a remedy for incontinence, are not altogether free from some defect, as Saint Augustine plainly proves from Paul’s epistles. Therefore Saint Zeno advances nothing against second marriages that does not contain a sound judgment.

In this respect several other Fathers are found to have spoken much more harshly. For Athenagoras, in the *Plea for the Christians*, a little before the end, after saying of the Christians of his age: “Each one of us remains, as he was born, either unmarried or in a single marriage,” adds, against second marriages as alien to Christians: “For second marriages are a specious [Col. 0130B] adultery.” For he says: “Whoever dismisses his wife and takes another commits adultery.” Nor are you permitted to dismiss her whose virginity you have taken away, nor to take another; for he who deprives himself of his first wife, even though she be dead, is a secret adulterer.

Saint Irenaeus seemed no less severe toward second marriages to some when, in Book III, chapter 19 of *Against Heresies*, he wrote: “That Samaritan transgressor, who did not remain with one husband, but committed fornication through many marriages.” But this is mistaken. The passage concerns the Samaritan woman in the Gospel, who did not enter several successive marriages, but had several men at once, none of whom she had married; and consequently it does not censure second or multiple marriages, but a woman guilty of multiple fornications. Yet the author of Question 59 to Antiochus, among the works of Saint Athanasius, considers her first five husbands legitimate. Moreover, some manuscripts read “wicked men” (*impiis*) instead of “marriages” (*nuptiis*), which removes the difficulty still more thoroughly.

Clement of Alexandria seems to agree more closely with Athenagoras. In Book II of the *Stromata*, p. 421, he says: “Marriage is the first union of man and woman according to the law”; and in Book III, p. 457: “Each of us, if he wishes, has power lawfully to take a wife—in a first marriage, I mean.” From these passages it appears that he regards only the first union as lawful marriage, not the second. Hence, at p. 464: “Fornication is a falling away from one marriage into several.”

Minucius Felix likewise seems to reckon among the adulteries of the pagans the several marriages which some among them contracted. Thus, in the *Dialogue*, after the middle of chapter 24: “One kind of sacred rite crowns a woman of one husband, another a woman of many husbands; and with great religious zeal they seek out the woman who can count the more adulteries.” And in chapter 31 he testifies that Christians use one marriage, or none.

To these should be added the ancient author of the incomplete work on Matthew, Homily 32 on chapter XIX, who calls second marriages true fornication, or respectable fornication. For he says: “The Apostles commanded men to enter second marriages because of human incontinence. For to take a second wife is indeed according to the Apostle’s command; but according to the rule of truth it is truly fornication. Yet, since it is committed publicly and lawfully with God’s permission, it becomes respectable fornication.”

Origen also ought not to be passed over, in Homily 17 on Luke, where he declares that successive bigamists and polygamists are excluded from the kingdom of God, saying: “But now second, third, and fourth marriages, to say nothing of more, are found; and we know that such a marriage will cast us out of the kingdom of God.” But if the remainder is read, it immediately appears that by “the kingdom of God” Origen means that perfection and crown proper to virgins and continent persons who have kept one marriage. For he continues: “For I think that the monogamist, the virgin, and the person who perseveres in chastity belong to the Church of God; but that he who is a bigamist, even if his conduct is good and he abounds in other virtues, nevertheless does not belong to the Church, nor to that number which has neither wrinkle nor blemish nor anything of the sort, but belongs to the second rank and to those who call upon the name of the Lord and are indeed saved in the name of Jesus Christ, [Col. 0131B] yet are by no means crowned by him,” etc. Hence, in Homily 19 on Jeremiah, he teaches that a bigamist is not to be assigned to eternal punishment, but will share in some salvation—though not so great a salvation as that attained by one who has lived continently. See also Homily 27 on John.

Finally, among Catholic Fathers we have not cited Tertullian, who openly condemns bigamy in his book *On Monogamy*. For, as Saint Jerome observed [CXI] in his commentary on chapter I of the Epistle to Titus, Tertullian wrote that book when he was a Montanist heretic; and among the errors of that sect was the view, Jerome likewise testifying, that second marriages should be excluded from communion with the Church. Besides, Catholic Tertullian must be set against heretical Tertullian: in Book II *To His Wife*, he advised his wife, should she be unable to remain continent after [Col. 0131C] his death, to enter a second marriage—provided that she married a Catholic, not a pagan.

Some may be troubled by what Ratramnus relates in Book IV, chapter 2, *Against the Greeks*, vol. I of Acherius’s *Spicilegium*, pp. 109 and 111. Citing Socrates, he says that the people of Constantinople “do not think alike concerning the reception or rejection of those married twice, but are divided: some considering their reception valid, others dissenting.” But those mentioned by Socrates, Book V, chapter 22, as hostile to second marriages are not Catholics but Novatian heretics, who did not receive those married twice.

Thus among Catholics only those four Fathers whom we have mentioned are found to have spoken somewhat more severely against second marriages; yet we shall say something further below concerning their opinion. The remaining Fathers, together with the Catholic Church, did not regard second marriages favorably; and, by every argument they could, sought to deter Christians from them, as Saint Zeno did. Yet they never judged them in themselves unlawful or dishonourable. Indeed, they regarded and proscribed as heretics first the Montanists and then the Novatians, who condemned them.

Many Fathers, like Saint Zeno, thought that much harsher treatment was called for in the case of those who pursued third and further marriages. Saint Zeno himself, in section 6, says: “But I linger over matters almost sound”—namely, second marriages—“as though truly execrable crimes [Col. 0132A] had already been corrected,” where he begins his discussion against third and further marriages, which, as you see, he calls truly execrable crimes.

Not very differently, Saint Basil, in his First Canonical Epistle to Amphilochius, canon 4, calls whatever marriage is contracted after bigamy not marriage but “disciplined fornication”; and in canon 50 he calls such multiple marriages defilements of the Church. Saint Gregory Nazianzen, in Oration 37, on the Gospel text, “When Jesus had finished these sayings,” considering the Apostle’s words at Ephesians 5, “This is a great mystery; but I speak concerning Christ and the Church,” says: “By this discourse he seems to me to dissuade from second marriages. For if there are two Christs, there are also two husbands; but if there is one Christ, one head of the Church, let there also be one [Col. 0132B] flesh, and let the second be rejected. But if he forbids the second, what is to be said of the third? The first is law; the second pardon and indulgence; the third iniquity; but whoever exceeds this number is plainly swinish.”

Do you see that he censures second marriages, but considers them worthy of pardon and indulgence; while he treats third marriages as iniquity, and judges the rest far more severely? From this testimony of Nazianzen we do not doubt that Leo the Wise drew the saying in the law entitled “A Woman,” in the Code *On Second Marriages*: “First marriages are law; second marriages, indulgence; third marriages, swinish illegality; fourth marriages, bestial life.”

Nor should Herard, Archbishop of Tours, be omitted. Among chapters extracted from ancient writers, in the year 858 he records this third chapter: “No layman is to have more than [Col. 0132C] two wives; what is beyond this belongs to adultery.” Saint Ambrose himself, who cast his vote for second marriages against the Novatians, appears to disapprove of repeated marriages in *On Widows*, chapter 11, section 68: “For we do not forbid second marriages, but we do not recommend them … I say more: we do not forbid second marriages, but we do not approve of their frequent repetition.”

We see, indeed, that not to approve is one thing, and to disapprove is another: the former applies to a thing not altogether good, the latter to a thing plainly evil. Yet this sufficiently shows with what feeling third and repeated marriages were received in the Church. Even those who defended their lawfulness could not refrain from declaring them less approved by themselves.

Here, then, is the way to grasp the Fathers’ meaning when they classed such marriages as adultery or fornication. By those terms they did not intend them to be understood as evil in themselves [CXII]; hence they did not accuse them absolutely of adultery or fornication. Rather, they seemed to discern in them a certain immoderate desire, which, so long as it remained within marriage, could not be called true adultery or fornication; yet because of its unrestrained appetite for pleasure, it seemed to bear some resemblance to such conduct. Thus, with Athenagoras, it could be called adultery, but seemly adultery; with Basil, fornication, but disciplined fornication; and with the author of the incomplete work, honourable fornication. We should not therefore suppose that bigamy or repeated marriages were truly condemned by these Fathers. For if they had considered them evil and condemned, how could they have called them seemly, disciplined, [Col. 0133A] and honourable?

This is a clear argument that they used the words “fornication” and “adultery” according to an ancient customary expression, which did not always signify a true offence of the kind usually understood when those terms are taken strictly, but sometimes denoted a marriage not highly approved. For the same reason even first marriages were called adulteries when someone, while observing the legal formalities, contracted one with a woman of lower rank. Such private women are also found called concubines, even though men had taken them as wives.

Before anyone gives judgment on the testimony of the ancients, he must consider and understand their words, rather than imposing upon them the sense which those words bear today. He must carefully observe what meaning they had formerly, when uttered by the writer, and for what purpose they were written. Unless this is done, we must necessarily fall into many errors and understand absolutely nothing, while imagining that we have understood everything.

That the whole matter may become entirely clear for our purpose, Clement of Alexandria above all others must be considered. We recently gave his testimonies against second marriages; in the last of them, a falling from one marriage into several is expressly called fornication. First, it is certain from Book I of the *Stromata*, p. 428, that he does not condemn second marriages. After praising the honourableness of monogamy, he says of second marriages: “If you burn, says the Apostle, enter into marriage.” And on p. 461 he explicitly admits that a second marriage is permitted by the Apostle because of intemperance and burning: “For here too he does not sin according to [Col. 0133C] the Testament, for it is not forbidden by law; nevertheless, he does not fulfil that entire perfection which is pursued according to the Gospel.” What clearer evidence could be produced to establish that second marriages may be contracted without sin?

When, therefore, he calls them fornication, he indicates by the word “fornication” something other than what is commonly meant. What that is may be learned from the entire context. Thus he says on p. 464: “For shaming and restraining those who are inclined to second marriages, the Apostle suitably speaks in a certain lofty tone. For he says: ‘Every sin is outside the body; but he who commits fornication sins against his own body.’ But if anyone dares call marriage fornication, he in turn attacks the law and the Lord with curses. For just as greed and the desire to possess more are called fornication, because they oppose contentment; and just as idolatry is the attribution of deity to many instead of one God; so fornication is a falling from one marriage into several.”

What could more plainly show that the meaning of fornication is taken here broadly rather than strictly? The same must be thought concerning “adultery,” for, as Clement himself notes, fornication and adultery are mutually used by the Apostle in the same sense. According to Clement, the Apostle calls three things fornication: first, greed, by which a person not content with what suffices covets more; secondly, idolatry, by which a person not satisfied with the one God establishes several gods; [Col. 0134A] and finally, for the same reason, bigamy is called fornication, because someone slips from one marriage into several. Do you see the broad meaning of fornication which the Fathers employed in this matter when they called second or multiple marriages fornication or adultery? They did so without condemning them as evil and unlawful in themselves, just as the Apostle did not condemn them, although he is said to have given them the name of fornication.

But let us return to Saint Zeno, from whom we have digressed a little. Since he reckoned repeated marriages beyond bigamy among truly execrable crimes, he may seem to have spoken with the greatest severity, so that we can interpret him only with difficulty. Yet he called them execrable crimes in the same way that Gregory Nazianzen called them iniquity; and it is clear from Oration 39, entitled *On the Holy Lights*, that Gregory nevertheless did not condemn them, since there he openly defends them against the Novatians.

Similarly, anyone reading Jerome’s discussion of second marriages in Epistle 79, section 11, to Salvina—where he calls them “precepts of bigamy not good” and “very bad justifications”—will judge that he regarded bigamy as a genuine crime. But did he not expressly add that he did not condemn it in his *Apology for the Books against Jovinian*, or Epistle 48, pp. 228–229 of the Verona edition? Did he not, on chapter I of the Epistle to Titus, identify as Tertullian’s heresy the view that bigamy should be condemned? And in Epistle 123 to Ageruchia, does he not suggest that he said so much against bigamists in order to recommend continence, not because he considered multiple marriages evil?

That Saint Zeno had the same purpose, although he does not state it in express words, may readily be inferred from his own statements. After he had argued more sharply in section 7 against marriages contracted with unbelievers, in order to deter Christian women from them, he finally urges them to continence in such a way that, if they cannot remain continent and must marry—even marry repeatedly—they should marry a Christian, not an unbeliever: “Therefore henceforth flee, virgin; flee, widow, marriages of this sort”—that is, with an unbeliever. “If you cannot be continent, at least do not make your marriages bear interest”—that is, multiply them beyond two—“lest, on that day of resurrection, among many husbands you cannot recognize whose wife you were.”

These words oppose multiple marriages, yet without any mark of criminality. He then lays down this one rule for multiple marriages, should they be contracted: that women must avoid marriage with unbelievers. “Do not be sacrilegious; do not betray the law. Why marry a profane man when you can marry a Christian?” This, therefore, was the one thing Zeno considered unlawful and particularly warned against. Indeed, if we consider what he said in section 6 concerning multiple marriages, nothing appears from which a crime in the proper sense can be charged.

Above all, it should be noted that Zeno does not address younger women. Just as Paul himself permitted them second marriages because of the danger of incontinence, so third and further marriages should be permitted them all the more fairly if, while still in the vigour of life, they are bereaved of two or more husbands and face the same danger of incontinence. On this ground Saint Jerome, in his commentary on chapter I of the Epistle to Titus, excuses them and proves that they may sometimes be found more worthy of praise than those who have had only one marriage until old age. Rather, our holy bishop addresses old women, who often appear as newly married brides. In their case the danger of incontinence is not ordinarily considered, but only a sheer love of sensual pleasure, which is undoubtedly to be condemned; and on this account such marriages could in a sense be called truly execrable crimes. The further reasons he adds do not exceed the limits of a fitting and plausible argument, by which a certain civil decency—not divine law—is shown to have been violated by them.

One point at the end deserves especially to be considered, because it opens a notable avenue for defending the Fathers. After the holy bishop had argued against repeated marriages of this kind, suddenly stirred by a certain feeling, he breaks out in section 6: “What shall I do? Where shall I turn? I do not know. For I do not see what I am to preach to the Gentiles in exhortations to divine and true worship. Shall I proclaim the blessedness of virginity? They too have their virgins; though not blessed, they nevertheless have them. Or shall I summon them to the glorious toil and palm of widowhood? Perhaps they may mock us because our sacred virgins and widows labour greatly for the great reward of immortality, whereas theirs labour without reward. But this alone is where we surpass them: Christian women marry more often for the sake of their holiness.”

These words seem to show us why the holy Fathers of those times declaimed with such zeal against bigamy and multiple marriages, and why they laboured to oppose them with many canons: by these, they excluded bigamists from the priesthood [Note: [Col. 0135D] Thus pagan priests also could not be bigamists. Servius on *Aeneid* IV; Tertullian, *On Monogamy*, chapter 17.]; subjected them to penance [Note: [Col. 0135D] Council of Neocaesarea, canon 3; Basil, Second Canonical Epistle to Amphilochius, canon 4, section 7.]; and, as we learn from Jerome [Note: [Col. 0135D] *Against Jovinian*, section 14, p. 263 [Col. 0136D], vol. II, Verona edition; and Epistle 123 to Ageruchia, section 7.], barred them from the Church’s relief-fund, distributed for the support [CXIV] of Christians. Moreover, priests were forbidden to attend their banquets [Note: [Col. 0136D] Council of Neocaesarea, canon 7.], and the sacred offering, blessing, and crown or veil by which the marriages of women who had had one husband [Note: [Col. 0136D] Tertullian, Book II *To His Wife*, chapter 9; Ambrose, Epistle 19.] were sanctified were forbidden to be used for them.

Among the pagans, to be sure, the chastity of the marriage bed was observed so religiously that women regarded it as a matter of religion not to marry another after the death of their first husband. A striking example is Penelope, who, solicited by many to enter a second marriage, firmly resisted, fearing both violation of faith toward her husband and public reproach, as is clear from her own words in Homer, *Odyssey* XVI.

In this sense Dido in Virgil, *Aeneid* IV, to signify that she would not marry again after the death of her first husband, first utters many imprecations against herself, verse 27:

> Before, O modesty, than I violate you or dissolve your laws.

Then she adds concerning her husband, verse 28:

> He who first joined me to himself  
> Has taken away my loves; let him keep them with him and preserve them in the tomb.

And she was so steadfast in this resolution that, although she ought voluntarily to have desired marriage with a king, she nevertheless preferred, rather, to be consumed than to marry, lest she experience second [Col. 0136A] marriage; so Tertullian recalls from historians cited by Servius, *On Monogamy*, chapter 17. He further adds that there were other pagan women who preferred to die for their husbands rather than marry another. See also Saint Jerome, Epistle 123 to Ageruchia, Verona edition, section 8.

Among the ancient peoples of Germany, though barbarian, Tacitus records several communities in section 6 of *The Customs of the Germans* in which only virgins married and no second marriages were heard of. For, he says, “They receive one husband as they have one body and one life: there is no thought beyond him and no longer desire.” Jerome, in the cited passage, gives a notable example bearing on this matter: German women took their own lives rather than be compelled to marry a second time. Valerius Maximus likewise testifies to this, Book VI, chapter 1.

Pausanias, in the *Corinthian Affairs*, Book II, chapter 21, reports that it was once holy and customary among Greeks for women, after the death of a first husband, to abstain from second marriage. Similarly Euripides, in the *Alcestis*, verse 464, shows that among them it was shameful and hateful if a husband, after his wife’s death, took another. Thus the chorus is introduced as speaking:

> But if her husband should choose a new bed,  
> He would surely become most hateful to me.

Valerius Maximus reports that the same custom prevailed among the ancient Romans, Book II, chapter 1, section 3: he says that the ancients placed upon women of one husband the crown of chastity, while those who proceeded to second marriages incurred the stigma of intemperance and wantonness. “Those who had been content with one marriage were honoured with the crown of chastity; for they thought that especially uncorrupted in loyal devotion was the mind of that matron who, after the bed in which she had laid aside virginity, did not know how to go forth into public, believing experience of many marriages to be a sign of a kind of lawful intemperance.”

Publius Syrus sufficiently indicates that Romans of his own time thought the same, in verse 284:

> Frequent marriages have a place among reproaches.

And in verse 482:

> A woman who marries many men pleases many men not.

That Romans considered these women less chaste may be inferred from their forbidding them to touch the statue of Chastity set up at Rome. For Festus, under the word *PUDICITIA*, says: “It is unlawful to touch the emblem of Chastity except for a woman who has married once.” Martial more openly did not hesitate, in Epigram 5 of Book VI, to brand the intemperance of women who married repeatedly with the mark of adultery:

> She who marries so often does not marry: by law she is an adulteress;  
> I should be less offended by a more straightforward adulteress.

Likewise Quintilian, *Declamation* 306, calls multiple marriages a certain shamelessness in marrying.

Since, then, this opinion against multiple marriages prevailed among pagans, it seemed exceedingly shameful to the holy Fathers—who understood that righteousness far more perfect than pagan righteousness was to be cultivated from the Christian law [CXV]—if second and repeated marriages, regarded unfavourably even by pagans, should flourish among Christians. Therefore, especially in the first four centuries of the Church, when Christians were intermixed with pagans, they strove much more vigorously by speech, writings, and even canonical penalties to dissuade Christians from such unions, lest they seem—to the great scandal of the Gentiles—to approve and encourage the intemperance of multiple marriages, or, as they called them, adulteries.

Thus we believe it is at last clear what Saint Zeno and the other Fathers intended in restraining repeated Christian marriages, and in what sense they used names current among the pagans—adultery, fornication, or crime. But perhaps too much has been said about second marriages.

What Saint Zeno more vigorously presses in the same Treatise 6, Book I, section 7, concerning contracting marriage with unbelievers needs no defence. For it was not only the constant opinion of the Fathers that such unions could not be contracted after baptism, since in them the danger of sin—especially emphasized by Saint Zeno—usually threatens; but such unions are also forbidden because of that danger in the Old Law itself, Deuteronomy 7:3: “Neither shall you make marriages with them. You shall not give your daughter to his son, nor take his daughter for your son; for she will turn your son away from following me.” The same is found at Exodus 24:16.

Indeed, some considered such marriages absolutely forbidden by the Apostle, both when he says in 1 Corinthians 7:39, “Let her marry whom she will, only in the Lord”—that is, as most explain it, only to a Christian; on this point Jerome, Book I *Against Jovinian*, section 10, should be read—and when he commands in 2 Corinthians 6:14: “Do not draw the yoke with unbelievers. For what sharing has righteousness with iniquity? Or what fellowship has light with darkness? What agreement has Christ with Belial? Or what part has a believer with an unbeliever? What harmony has the temple of God with idols? For you are the temple of the living God,” etc. Saint Zeno certainly envisaged this interpretation, as we noted in annotation 25.

With this also in view, Saint Cyprian, in *On the Lapsed*, reckoned among the crimes for which God, angered, permitted the Church to be afflicted by persecution that Christians entered into marriage with unbelievers. Augustine, in *On Faith and Works*, chapter 19, observes that Cyprian declared this to be nothing other than prostituting the members of Christ to pagans. Add that councils had forbidden such marriages even before Zeno’s time: Elvira, canons 15 and 17; Laodicea, canons 10 and 13; and Arles I, canon 11.

Only in Africa, and perhaps elsewhere as well, from a certain simplicity, ignorance, or whatever other cause—not indeed on the part of bishops but of the people—an opinion gradually prevailed long after Saint Cyprian that these unions were permitted. Thus, as Augustine testifies in the cited place, they were either not thought sins at all or the issue was left undecided. In this period Saint Monica married an unbelieving husband, by whom she conceived Augustine himself.

Nevertheless, the same holy doctor opposed such marriages in Book I of *On Adulterous Marriages*, chapter 21, although in chapter 25 he did not venture to define them as prohibited by divine law. Soon thereafter the Council of Carthage in 397, canon 12, prohibited them for the sons and daughters of clerics; this was ratified by several other synods, especially Chalcedon, canon 13; and at length a universally operative diriment impediment to marriage was established from this, though its beginnings cannot be precisely determined.

In these regions, in the age of our author, this kind of marriage so displeased bishops that Saint Ambrose, asked by Saint Vigilius of Trent to advise him, for the government of his Church, what seemed necessary or useful, replied in Epistle 19 that, among other matters, particular care must be taken that Christians not be joined in marriage with unbelievers. Thus, when Saint Zeno preached vehemently on this subject and set before their eyes the dangers to which such unions are liable, he did what we find the other Catholic bishops to have done.

[CXVI] CHAPTER VIII. EXAMINATION OF SAINT ZENO’S SINGULAR TESTIMONY CONCERNING CERTAIN POSSESSED PERSONS.

How freely the Verona editors treated Treatise 16, Book I, section 3, *On the Resurrection*—deleting some things, adding others, transposing and emphasizing others as they pleased—we have carefully noted in its place. What offended them, it seems, or what they believed might offend others, was that Saint Zeno here advances an altogether singular opinion: the spirits that possess the bodies of the possessed are not always true demons, but are sometimes souls of human beings whom, he says, “we remember to have died recently, and especially by some violence, while persisting in idolatry.”

That this disturbed the editors is evident from their thinking that the testimony had to be softened so as to suggest a fiction created by demons, removing or altering the passages by which Saint Zeno indicated that he did not at all think the event fabricated by demons. But we do not know what offence this contains.

We would not suppose that they feared someone might think that, if certain souls of evil persons were reported to invade the bodies of the possessed, they were not punished by the pains of hell before the day of final judgment. For the same difficulty would apply to demons, who are reported to have confessed that they burn by Lactantius, Book II, chapter 5, and Book V, chapter 21, and also by Firmicus, *On the Error of Profane Religion*, p. 100; yet they burn through the fires of prayer, as Minucius says in the *Octavius*, chapter 27, and burn without fires, as Hilary affirms in *Against Constantius*, section 8. This does not mean that they lack their own punishment as well, which Saint Cyprian, *On the Vanity of Idols*, p. 451, reports to be increased by exorcisms.

Therefore, if certain souls of the impious, by God’s permission, invade certain bodies, they may there, like demons, suffer punishments corresponding to their own offences, even though they do not yet dwell in hell. Or did those editors fear that Zeno would be thought to hold the opinion which Saint Augustine lists among Tertullian’s heresies in *On Heresies*, chapter 86: “He also says that the worst human souls after death are changed into demons”? This opinion seems derived from Platonists—for Plotinus taught something similar, according to Augustine, *City of God*, Book IX, chapter 11. Though I have not been able to find it in Tertullian, it is in some manner attributed to Origen by Saint Jerome, Epistle 59 to Avitus.

It is indeed an error if evil souls after death are thought to put off and reject their own nature and be transformed into the nature of demons. In this sense the proposition is condemned as heresy by Philastrius, chapter 121, for the nature of a soul is not changed into another nature. But Zeno’s words suggest nothing of the kind. Indeed, he is so far from the opinion that the souls of the wicked are changed into demons that his argument clearly rests on their being truly souls, rather than demons, while they occupy possessed persons. From this he infers the immortality of souls and consequently the resurrection. Yet he does not wholly deny that this could be a fabrication of demons pretending to be souls, writing: “But you say: ‘These demons feign such things.’ The proof is all the better,” etc.

But if he held that genuine souls of the impious may sometimes invade possessed persons in the place of demons, what error, pray, is involved in this opinion? We know that sacred writers dispute greatly whether, in those visions in which the souls of the pious are reported to have appeared to the living, the souls themselves showed themselves under another appearance, or whether all occurred through the agency of angels. Augustine, discussing this controversy in *On Care for the Dead*, chapters 10, 11, 15, and 16, does not dare deny the reality of the vision. For, he says, if we answer that these things are false, we will seem to oppose rashly the writings of certain faithful persons—for example, Saint Ambrose’s account of the discovery of the bodies of Saints Gervasius and Protasius, and Lucian’s account of the body of Saint Stephen—and the experiences of those who affirm that such things happened to them. After much discussion on both sides, he leaves the matter uncertain and does not deny that both may occur: sometimes through the souls of the righteous themselves, sometimes through angels.

Therefore, who could without rashness deny an event so definitely attested by Zeno—an event which had as witnesses the very persons present while he spoke? For, just as the souls of the pious, by God’s will, could, according to Augustine, appear to people for the benefit of the living and say, confirm, or show certain things, [CXVII] why could not certain souls of the impious, by God’s same permission, perform the role of demons, so that the truth of faith itself might be confirmed by their testimony? Saint Zeno indeed confirms the truth of the resurrection from these very cases. At least the event cannot be denied; and consequently no blame can be attached to Saint Zeno for drawing a most powerful argument for his case from a fact established among his hearers, particularly since at the end of the section he raises the suspicion of a demonic fabrication. On this matter see also, if desired, Aeneas of Gaza, in the dialogue entitled *Theophrastus*. There, discussing most clearly the state of souls and certain acts performed near tombs in the name of souls, he contends, p. 66, vol. VIII of the Lyons edition of the *Library of the Fathers*, that those performing them are evil demons representing human souls. This confirms Saint Zeno’s suspicion.

CHAPTER IX. WHAT THE AUTHOR THOUGHT CONCERNING THE LAST JUDGMENT.

From Treatise 21, Book II, on Psalm 100, Zeno may seem not to have thought correctly concerning the final judgment, since there he exempts both believers and unbelievers from that judgment. Having cited Christ’s words from John 3:18, “He who believes in me shall not be judged; but he who does not believe has already been judged,” he adds: “By saying this, he exempts believers from judgment; he does not admit unbelievers [Col. 0140B] to judgment.” He then confirms this more clearly: first, concerning believers: “For what need is there to judge the believer? Judgment arises from matters of uncertainty; once uncertainty is removed, the examination of judgment is not required.” Then, concerning unbelievers: “Hence there is likewise no need to judge unbelievers, because they are already condemned by their unbelief.” He proves this from Psalm 1: “The wicked shall not rise in judgment, nor sinners in the council of the righteous.” He then argues at greater length that judgment remains only for those who stand between unbelievers or wicked persons and believers or saints, whose hidden secrets of crooked and ambiguous life must necessarily be examined.

But lest these points offend anyone, it must first be observed that several ancient writers handed down similar views. Nor shall we mention those whom Origen accuses of simplicity [Col. 0140C], because, from the words of Psalm I, “The ungodly shall not rise in judgment,” they denied that the wicked would attain the resurrection or be deemed worthy of God’s judgment. We mean the most learned Fathers of the Church, whom we do not think should be charged with such simplicity, and who either lived before Zeno, were his contemporaries, or even later taught similar things. Lactantius must first be mentioned. In *Institutes*, book VII, chapter 20, after affirming that all will rise at the end of the world, and that the same King and God will render the great judgment upon them, he adds, no. 5: “Yet not all will then be judged by God . . . for those who have not acknowledged God, since no sentence of acquittal can be passed concerning them, are already judged and condemned; the Holy Scriptures testifying that the ungodly shall not rise in [Col. 0140D] judgment.” St Hilary, on Psalm I, says almost the same things as Zeno; indeed, we have observed in the notes that Zeno transferred into his own discourse much material of this kind from Hilary. Likewise St Ambrose, on the same psalm, commenting on the words, “For the ungodly shall not rise in judgment,” similarly says in no. 51: “For he did not say, ‘They shall not rise,’ but says, ‘They do indeed rise, but not in judgment.’ Now one who rises certainly exists and remains; but because he did not believe in Christ, he has already been judged, and therefore does not come into judgment—the punishment of an already completed judgment awaits him. . . . But concerning the statement, ‘The ungodly shall not rise in judgment,’ according to the Gospel the sentence is absolute, because not all will be judged.” Having cited Paul’s text, “We must all stand before the judgment-seat [Col. 0141A] of Christ,” which seemed contrary to this, he replies that Christ spoke of unbelievers, who did not believe in the Lord Jesus; while the Apostle, though he said “all,” undoubtedly spoke of those who believed. Jerome, in his *Dialogue against the Pelagians*, no. 28, having cited the text of the same psalm, says: “For they have already been prejudged unto perdition.” The author of the *Breviary on Psalm I*, among Jerome’s works, vol. VII of the Appendix to the Veronese edition, chapter 4: “Not because they do not rise, but [CXVIII] because they do not rise in judgment: for judgment concerning them has already been pronounced.” The author of another Commentary ascribed to Jerome in the Bobbio manuscript, in the same vol. VII, p. 27, in the preface to the aforementioned *Breviary*: “He did not say absolutely, ‘They shall not rise,’ but added, ‘In judgment.’ Although they will not rise for examination, they will rise in order immediately to receive the sentence of condemnation [Col. 0141B]; he gave the reason shortly before: the ungodly, rising unto punishment, will not have that delay which the force of judgment is accustomed to introduce in investigations.” St Paulinus of Nola, *Poem* VII, p. 346 of the Veronese edition:

> Therefore the scattered multitudes of humankind  
> Throughout the world will be divided in this order:  
> The ungodly, who denied due worship to God,  
> Will not rise to be judged,  
> But to be punished; for, seeing its own crime,  
> It will have no need for questioning to expose it,  
> Since they will bear the impending mark of death,  
> Not carrying on their foreheads the sign of salvation.  
> But the sinner who is nevertheless not ungodly—  
> And this is a great multitude—will not rise unto glory,  
> But will rise to be assigned to examination.  
> For he cannot sit with the righteous as judge,  
> Being about to render account of his own deeds  
> And, according to his varied conduct, be either approved or condemned.

Finally, to omit others, St Caesarius, sermon 77, [Col. 0141C] Appendix to Augustine, no. 4: “For neither pagans, nor heretics, nor Jews come to judgment, because it is written concerning them: ‘He who does not believe has already been judged.’”

Who would dare accuse of error so many Fathers who handed down similar statements, rather than understand that their testimonies should be interpreted in such a sense that they truly did not exempt the ungodly or unbelievers from the last judgment—whom they acknowledged would stand before God as judge—but indicated something else that does not conflict with Catholic doctrine? This meaning is readily derived from comparing all the testimonies. First, they deny neither the resurrection of the godly nor that of the ungodly; rather, they say that they will rise, but not for judgment, which they expressly affirm concerning the ungodly. Moreover, our author clearly [Col. 0141D] affirms the resurrection both of righteous persons and of criminal persons in book I, tractate 16, no. 11. When they deny judgment, they do not deny that the righteous and the ungodly will stand before Christ’s tribunal on the day of the last judgment, nor that in it the former will enter eternal glory and the latter eternal punishment. Rather, taking “judgment” to mean an examination of a doubtful case, they affirm only this: that in the certain case both of righteous believers and of unbelieving ungodly persons, no judgment or examination will be needed. Zeno’s reasoning clearly proves this: “For judgment arises from doubtful matters,” etc. Hence, in no. 2, affirming that from death onward the righteous are destined for everlasting life and the ungodly for eternal punishment, he says that “no further inquiry awaits them”; by *inquiry* he plainly means that kind of judicial investigation which he denies to be necessary. [Col. 0142A] This is further confirmed by what is said of intermediate sinners, whom he declares must necessarily be examined because of their equivocal life: “For unless ambiguity is resolved, it cannot rightly deserve a sentence.” The statements of the other Fathers likewise bear upon this point.

Accordingly, in the judgment of these Fathers and of Zeno, all indeed will rise, and all will also stand before Christ’s tribunal—righteous, ungodly, and intermediate persons—and all likewise will receive either eternal reward, acquired according to their merits, or punishment. But not all will require judgment and examination in order that this most just sentence may stand: certainly not the righteous, nor the ungodly, whose case is entirely clear, but only the intermediate persons, whose life, though doubtful—not doubtful to God, from whom nothing can be hidden, but to human beings—will require a distinct judgment, examination, and inquiry, so that the justice of the divine sentence may be vindicated before [Col. 0142B] all. Meanwhile the Judge will give to each his due: to the righteous, whom he will honor as sons; to the ungodly, whom he will immediately assign to the executioner, not to be heard but to be consigned to their appointed punishments; while he will weigh the intermediate sinners. This is not because their deeds were not weighed immediately after death, nor because they did not then receive the sentence due to them—for in tractate 16, book I, no. 2, he teaches that our souls, stripped of the remains of their bodies, are, according to the character of their deeds—which surely presupposes a judgment concerning deeds—some banished to penal places and some refreshed in peaceful abodes—but because, before the eyes of the whole world, this same equity of divine justice must become manifest through a public examination of judgment. Thus, St Zeno himself concludes, on [Col. 0142C] the very day of the last judgment, a crown will be given to the righteous; pardon to sinners who are either excused or amended; and eternal punishment to the ungodly.

If only sinners are mentioned here, to whom, if excused or amended, pardon is said to be granted, no one should therefore infer that Zeno thought intermediate sinners between the righteous and ungodly—or, as is clear from the context, Christian sinners—would obtain pardon on the day of judgment. That would fall into another error held by others. For the Author plainly shows in tractate 16, book I, no. 11, that among these same sinners, or intermediate Christians, there will be many who, neither excused nor amended, will meet the end of the ungodly or unbelievers; for, speaking of the resurrection of the unrighteous, he says that it consigns the ungodly together with sinners and all unbelieving nations [Col. 0142D] to everlasting punishment. Equally clear are the things which elsewhere he teaches concerning works and charity, to be joined with faith by the Christian if he is to enjoy immortal blessedness. Since we have noted these in chapter 6 of the present dissertation, we refer the reader there.

## CHAPTER X. ST ZENO’S VIEW OF THE STATE OF RIGHTEOUS SOULS AFTER DEATH

From the conclusions established in the preceding chapter one doubt may arise: whether the Author, who so affirms in tractate 21, book II, no. 3, that a crown will be bestowed on the righteous on the day of judgment, and who in tractate 16, book I, no. 2, teaches that their souls are refreshed after death in peaceful abodes—whether, I say, he has adopted the view revived by certain heterodox persons of our own time, who teach that the righteous are to receive their eternal reward in heaven, with the vision of God, only after the resurrection, while meanwhile their souls rest in some peaceful dwelling until the day of the last judgment opens heaven to them. [Col. 0143A] Another testimony of Zeno from tractate 12, book I, at the end, may also seem relevant: “There is no doubt,” he says, “that our will, to whichever side it has joined itself, will bring victory, and that in the resurrection it will either enjoy eternal reward or be punished with a like punishment.” But this latter passage is easily rescued from the hands of heretics if we consider, first, that he writes of the reward of the righteous in the same manner as of the punishment of the ungodly, whose souls nevertheless the Author most plainly declares in tractate 16, book I, no. 2, to be banished to penal places immediately after death. [Col. 0143B] Secondly, in order to understand his meaning and purpose, it must be observed that tractate 12 speaks not of the soul but of the flesh or body; and he affirms that in the resurrection our will—that is, the will of the body—will either suffer punishments or obtain reward. This is because before the resurrection the body has not experienced in the body the punishment or reward due to it; before then, without the body, it has experienced torments only in the soul, or has enjoyed reward, as the Author plainly teaches in other passages shortly to be indicated.

[Col. 0143C] As for the other passage, in which he wrote that the souls of the righteous, freed from the remains of their bodies, are refreshed in peaceful abodes, it was customary for very many ancient Fathers, when they assigned Abraham’s bosom, peaceful abodes, and other such things to the souls of the righteous after death, to understand Paradise, as Ludovico Muratori establishes at length in his latest work on Paradise. Indeed, that these peaceful abodes in Zeno mean in the same sense a place of delights is sufficiently suggested by the word *refoveri*, “to be refreshed.” Moreover, in no. 5 he indicates that they are Paradise, where he relates that Christ promised Paradise after death to the thief hanging on the cross with him; and in no. 6, when, intending to rebuke those who mourn the dead, he warns that those passing to better things—that is, to a place of blessedness—should not be accompanied with lamentations. Add that in tractate 21, book II, he declares that righteous and ungodly persons immediately after death receive and undergo, according to their merits or sins, either reward—and indeed eternal reward—or eternal punishment. “From this [Col. 0143D] [CXX] life,” he says, “each carries with him either a crown or punishment”; and lest anything be thought deferred, he adds shortly afterward: “The righteous are destined for everlasting life, the ungodly for eternal punishment.” More clearly still, at the end of tractate 27, book II, setting forth what happens to martyrs after death, he uses these words: “The martyr is received into the hidden place of the Lord’s dwelling, so that, there transformed from a human being into an angel, he may glory in the eternal blessedness of life.” The same point can be confirmed from tractate 18 of the same book, [Col. 0144A] where St Arcadius the martyr is said to have ascended into heaven after death:

> O end worthy of a glorious departure! About to ascend to the height of heaven—when, as the context shows, he was on the point of dying—he sends ahead the impediments of his body and himself goes before the funeral rites of his own death. . . . The most blessed martyr Arcadius still lingers in the world, namely in the body, and already the martyr is enrolled in heaven.

These final words seem to refer to Paul’s words at Romans XII, 23, where the firstborn—that is, the elect—are said to be enrolled in heaven while they live on earth; but when they ascend hence through death to heaven, their names do not cease there to be recited and celebrated. But lest anyone think Zeno held this only of martyrs, as others have wrongly supposed it to be a privilege peculiar to martyrs, let us hear the same bishop speaking universally of all righteous persons and explaining himself clearly in tractate 12 of the same book II, no. 4. There he interprets the angels whom Jacob saw ascending to heaven by the ladder as righteous persons ascending to heaven:

> “Those ascending are the righteous, who by upright morals, through the steps of obedience to the divine commandments, are daily borne by the glory of their spiritual journey into heaven.”

Here the adverb “daily” must especially be noted; it must surely be understood of those righteous persons who from day to day depart after death into heaven—unless an unjust judge should deny it. Therefore there can be no doubt that, in Zeno’s thought, the peaceful abodes in which the souls of the righteous are refreshed are the heavenly homeland itself, in which God is seen. In support of this understanding, in tractate 3, book I, [Col. 0144C] no. 4, he declares that the souls of those who keep God’s commandments—that is, of all the righteous—when freed from the bonds of flesh, namely after death and before the day of judgment and resurrection, will enjoy the promised blessedness, which will surely arise in heaven from the vision of God:

> “Keeping God’s commandments, and by offices of this sort crushing worldly pleasures, when he has become victorious and is free from the bonds of flesh, he will enjoy the inestimable blessedness of promised immortality.”

And most clearly, in the same tractate 16, book I, which contains the disputed testimony, no. 14:

> “But when death, which is thought to be feared, is tasted, then promised happiness is bestowed upon it—that is, upon the soul—destined to enjoy the blessed abodes of glory remaining forever and to feel thereafter none of the world’s troubles.”

There the blessed abodes of glory remaining forever are undoubtedly the place of heavenly [Col. 0144D] glory, not that bosom of Abraham in which souls must remain until the day of the last judgment; and these abodes are indicated as to be entered immediately after death has been tasted. The Author had given the reason for this shortly before, in the same no. 14: “For otherwise that robe of immortality is not assumed unless first this fleshly spoil, the soul’s pleasant poison, is, according to God’s sentence, returned to the place from which it was taken.”

[CXXI] **THIRD DISSERTATION: ON THE DEEDS OF ST ZENO AND HIS CULT**

[Col. 0145]

## PREFACE

[Col. 0145A]

Although two fairly lengthy Lives of St Zeno have been published—one written by Coronatus the Notary, who flourished before the ninth century, and the other by a Zenonian monk, who lived about the eleventh century—nevertheless, anyone who declares that we know little, almost nothing, of the deeds of our Author cannot be blamed. For among the matters which Coronatus committed to writing, he certainly sets forth vividly many wondrous miracles which God performed through Zeno; but he touches upon very few matters concerning his life and virtues. Thus it is plain that he drew nothing from ancient monuments, but merely wrote down what popular report, impressed upon memory because of the fame of the miracle, handed down. [Note: [Col. 0145D] See the Admonition to the *Monuments*, no. 1, at the end, and note 3 on the Life itself.] Hence these same accounts are also found surrounded with several false additions, as will become clear from the notes on that Life, to be placed below among the monuments. The Zenonian monk, published by Marquis Maffei, received everything from Coronatus, though he does not name him, and added nothing except other miracles, which contribute nothing to knowledge of the life.

Among the Lives of Zeno we have not included the poem of Jacob, priest of Verona, composed in 244 hexameter verses and published by Fr Henschenius from a manuscript of the Zenonian monastery, in volume II for April, p. 76. For he did not propose to describe the life of the holy bishop, but his miracles: precisely those which are read in prose in the anonymous Zenonian monk, except for three further miracles there appended. The anonymous writer of Pipino, a ninth-century author, in his *Rhythm on the Praises of Verona*, sang in a few verses a few things about Zeno, but things which may be valued more highly than the aforementioned Lives, as will be clear from what follows. Accordingly, amid such a scarcity of probable monuments, let no one demand from us a Life of Zeno. For we have no wish to imitate Baptista Perettus, who, in a Life written in Italian and first published at Verona in 1597 with Latin scholia, then appended to the Paduan edition of St Zeno in 1710, achieved nothing other than to render the Zenonian monk into Italian and add other matters from invention or popular report, resting on a weaker foundation. Yet, lest the reader’s desire be entirely disappointed, we shall undertake to set forth whatever it has been possible to collect from Zeno’s tractates and other ancient documents.

[CXXII] **CHAPTER I. ON THE DEEDS OF ST ZENO UP TO HIS DEATH**

[Col. 0145D]

### § I.—Conjectures concerning Zeno’s birthplace

First, it is fitting to conjecture concerning Zeno’s birthplace. In the first Latin scholium to the Life just mentioned, Baptista Perettus maintains that he was a Veronese, from Peter de Natalibus, bishop of Equilium, book I of the *Catalogue of Saints*, and from the lessons read at Milan in the cathedral church on the feast of his Ordination, 8 December. But since these later testimonies prove nothing concerning ancient matters, as Cardinal Baronius rightly noted, no. 12, volume I of the *Annals*, p. 59 of the Cologne edition, and since no one before Peter de Natalibus has been found to have suggested this, no prudent person will acquiesce in Perettus’s opinion. We are therefore free to submit our conjectures to the eyes and judgment of learned persons.

Zeno’s name, received and frequent among the Greeks, seems to show him to have been Greek. Tillemont, together with Buchner, judged him Greek in note 5 on the persecution of Valerian, volume IV, p. 587. Before them Blasius Roseltus, in Saibantean manuscript 658, containing a history of bishops, thinking this true, added the following reason—which Panvinio wrote in the same words in *Antiquities of Verona*, book IV, chapter 6, when he reported the view of some persons—“for,” he says, “the phraseology of his sermons seems to have a certain Greek and foreign flavor.” Indeed, someone might infer from the anonymous writer of Pipino from which province he came, namely Syria, where Greek speech was certainly current at that time. For he says:

> I cannot recount the deeds of this saint,  
> The marvels which almighty God displayed  
> Through him, from Syria in his journeying as far as Italy.

The author of the hymn seems to have had this opinion in view—a hymn which the Veronese editors published from two manuscript Benedictine breviaries—when it is there related that St Zeno traversed maritime nations.

We too would readily cast our votes for this opinion, unless two considerations stood in the way. A Greek author could not speak and write Latin as correctly and purely as St Zeno, whose style, although it sometimes swells and is sprinkled with many little flowers, nevertheless falls in no respect short of purity of Latin expression. Whether one considers individual words, the arrangement of words, or syntax, he appears to have been trained from earliest childhood in Latin authors, educated among Latin speakers, and cultivated in Latin schools. He displays himself thoroughly conversant with Latin poets, using their expressions and verses so aptly that they are seen to have become part of his very substance and blood, not forced in by violence. He is shown to have been accustomed to reading Virgil; verses of Virgil may sometimes be understood to have fallen from his pen. Authors of that sort were expounded and read by boys in order that they might acquire Latin of greater purity and a livelier diction. Certainly among Latin writers of the fourth century no one is found equal to him, or more Latin, in purity of Latin; so much so that several learned men have deservedly praised his Latinity, and Casaubon and others have called it most elegant. Basilius Faber, moreover, who compiled the *Treasury of Learning* with the utmost zeal and an almost limitless reading of Latin authors, in order to offer students of Latin a careful and highly useful method by presenting every Latin word excerpted from approved Authors and restored to its roots, did not hesitate frequently to cite Zeno, and on the authority of that Author alone to include several words among approved usage. Among the many Greeks who wrote anything in Latin, not merely is there not one who can be compared with Zeno; but, since they wrote in an acquired rather than native language, all are found to have written poor Latin. There can be no doubt that St Zeno would similarly have written poorly had he possessed the same Greek origin and education. This first argument seems sufficiently strong to prove that the Author was born of Latin parents, or at least educated and trained among Latins.

Let us now add another argument by which his province may be more certainly determined. There exists a tractate by the Author concerning St Arcadius the martyr, whose remembrance is found in no other ancient writers. But the Zenonian manuscripts make clear that he suffered at Caesarea in Mauretania. Why, among all the bishops of Verona, would Zeno celebrate Arcadius’s feast-day with such religious devotion unless he was attached to him by some special devotion and perhaps derived his origin from the same province in which Arcadius met death? Those who have studied the Author’s tractates with greater care have discerned the style of African writers in him. Among them, Gaspar Barthius thought he perceived a Christian Apuleius in Zeno, as book XLIII of the *Adversaria*, chapter 10, p. 1944, and book V on Statius’s *Silvae*, p. 446, attest. In fact, many expressions of the African Apuleius, and likewise many words peculiar to him and to other Africans—Tertullian, Cyprian, and others—are found in Zeno’s tractates, which one would seek in vain among writers from other Latin provinces. Nor should one wonder that an African was made bishop of Verona, for in that period bishops and clergy were often supplied from foreign provinces. From Jerome we learn that Fortunatianus, bishop of Aquileia in the same century, was African. Was not Donatus, African by birth, a presbyter of the Church of Milan even after Ambrose’s death, as Paulinus testifies in his Life of Ambrose, no. 54? Nor should the opinion of the anonymous writer of Pipino move us: although Zeno was African, he could have journeyed from Syria to Verona, since travel to the East was common at that time. St Philastrius, bishop of Brescia, while still a presbyter, is likewise said by St Gaudentius, in his tractate on St Philastrius, p. 241, to have “travelled through almost the whole extent of the Roman world, preaching the Lord’s word.” Gaudentius himself also plainly states that, while he was in the East, he was appointed Philastrius’s successor in the same Brescian see, both in his sermon on his own ordination, p. 181, and in his sermon on the dedication of the Basilica, p. 191. Finally, although the name Zeno was frequent among Greeks, it was by no means alien to Africans. We find among Africans Zeno a martyr under Decius, whose body, after it was translated to Byzantium, is recorded to have been commemorated among the Greeks. See the Bollandist *Acts of the Saints*, 10 April, volume I.

### § II.—The beginning of St Zeno’s episcopate; his ordination is placed on 8 December. His success in converting Gentiles to the faith. How greatly he labored to refute and suppress Arians. Verona converted to Christianity by him.

Accordingly, after a journey to the East, which Zeno must be believed to have undertaken before his episcopate—for bishops did not leave their own sees except for very weighty reasons—he was placed over the Church of Verona after Cricinus, on the sixth day before the Ides of December, A.D. 362, in the final year of Julian, as we have conjectured with sufficient probability in Dissertation I, chapter 3, § 5. Since the year is evident if the day is established, as we showed there, it is fitting here to add in confirmation other arguments, drawn successively from new documents and considerations, besides those previously brought forward for establishing that day.

First, in chapter 4 we shall see that many churches in Italy and elsewhere dedicated in St Zeno’s name celebrate his feast on the sixth day before the Ides of December. We shall show in § 3 that this was not the day of the holy bishop’s death. Since, when Saints’ feasts were transferred, care was taken that, if the day of death was impeded, the feast should be moved to another day upon which either the translation of the Saint’s body, the dedication of a basilica, or his ordination was celebrated, as we shall note in that paragraph: although our books mark the dedication of St Zeno’s church on 8 December, it is nevertheless highly probable that his feast in other churches was assigned to that day chiefly because of his ordination rather than because of the church’s dedication. For, from Rabanus and Wandalbert, ninth-century writers, and from Vatican manuscript 3806 of the same century, that day appears already from the ninth century to have been celebrated in various places, whereas the Basilica of St Zeno had scarcely then been dedicated. If one considers that at Cesena and Pistoia St Zeno was chosen as great patron, or as they call it, titular saint, before the ninth and even before the eighth century, and was worshipped on the same day by a single or principal feast—such as is now celebrated by the immemorial custom of those churches—then that day was already famous before the ninth and even the eighth century, certainly not because of a dedication which occurred later, but because of an ordination. It is therefore clearly demonstrated by this argument that the ordination was celebrated at Verona on that day as well.

Add another observation from the books of our own church, by which the same point is confirmed. Although in some calendars the dedication of the church of St Zeno is noted on that day, the ecclesiastical books themselves appoint and describe both Mass and Office for St Zeno the bishop, not for the dedication of the church. We have touched sufficiently upon the Mass in Dissertation I, chapter 3, § 5, and the point will be clearer from the Admonition to the Monuments, no. 5. To speak now of the Office: in a thirteenth-century capitular manuscript, containing the prayers, lessons, and antiphons used throughout the year for Saints in the Church of Verona, and entirely agreeing with other older manuscripts, the same antiphons which in three other books are assigned as proper to St Zeno for recitation at Lauds are also prescribed for the Hours. They are indeed set down in December, together with the prayer *Deus qui nos*, likewise proper to St Zeno the bishop. Hence one may infer that in the Church of Verona, for whose public services that codex was used, not only Mass but also an Office for St Zeno the bishop, not for the church’s dedication, was celebrated in December; so that it appears that the Church of Verona itself celebrated on 8 December the ordination of St Zeno, not the dedication of the basilica, just as we have noted at the cited place in Dissertation I that the Zenonian monks distinctly celebrated it on that day.

Therefore, since it cannot be proved that the dedication of St Zeno’s basilica, even though marked on that day in certain manuscript calendars, was celebrated by any special Office in the Church of Verona, either it was celebrated only by the monks two days later—or, as other codices read, on the following day—or it was celebrated by the Church of Verona that day only by a commemoration. To this commemoration alone can belong the antiphon and responsory which are noted in the *Carpsus* thus: “At the dedication of St Zeno, antiphon and responsory for the dedication.” If this does not please, since the rubric of the *Carpsus* conflicts with another ritual book of the Church of Verona and does not agree with the Masses of the others, which on 8 December present both Office and Mass for St Zeno alone, not for the dedication of the church, the error of the *Carpsus* is manifest—of the sort that is elsewhere noted in the same book. If it is thus established that St Zeno’s ordination was celebrated and performed on 8 December, it will be altogether plain, from what was said in Dissertation I, chapter 3, § 5, that St Zeno was ordained on that day in A.D. 362, Julian’s final year. Let us proceed to other matters.

After this emperor died in the following year, 363, the Roman Empire came into the hands of men who, although they did not entirely abolish idolatry, nevertheless themselves practiced the Christian religion alone and zealously favored it. This opened to Zeno a broad way to cultivate that religion openly at Verona; and by both piety and teaching he made marvelous progress in its cultivation. At that time there were many pagans; among Christians, moreover, there were not a few Arians because of the persecution which Constantius, Julian’s predecessor, had pressed so vigorously against Catholics through offices, deceits, and threats, at the prompting of the Arian bishops Valens and Ursacius, that he shook the whole world, corrupted Fortunatianus of Aquileia in these regions, and intruded Auxentius into the see of Milan. Auxentius not only occupied that Church until A.D. 374 for twenty years, but also endeavored to infect and rend the faith of all Italy with his heresy. Seated on the episcopal throne of Verona, St Zeno opposed himself by frequent sermons and instruction to the impiety of pagans and Arians alike.
