How vigorously and successfully the holy bishop labored among the Gentiles is clearly proved by the immense number of persons who were washed in baptism every year. From tractate 3, book I, note 1, we infer that persons attracted by his eloquence and zeal even attended while he himself preached. In tractates 33 and 42, book II, persons diverse in origin, age, sex, and condition—and, as tractate 38 adds, nationality—are mentioned as being cleansed together in the sacred waters at the Paschal feasts. Since these and other tractates delivered in different years repeat nearly the same thing, they show that in every year there was a great multitude of persons to be baptized. This contributes remarkably to setting forth the bishop’s labor and diligence in securing this result. The same conclusion also follows from the church which, as we shall say, he built at Verona. Although it was sufficiently large and spacious in itself, it had become too small because of the exceedingly increased number of Christians, as he himself states in tractate 14, book I, no. 2. Thus the tradition which the anonymous writer of Pipino committed to writing, when he wrote of Zeno,

> “Who by preaching led Verona to baptism,”

is shown by these tractates to be ancient and genuine. The same anonymous author adds: “He destroyed many idols.” Although it is probable that he did this in the city which he won for Christian faith, it is much more probable that he did so in the rural districts, where there were more private shrines and images, against which we read that he declaimed in tractate 15, book I, no. 5. Nor did he diligently seek merely to extirpate pagan worship from those whom he converted to the faith; he also sought to eradicate the depraved habits which they had contracted from pagan education, as may be learned from many of the tractates.

Moreover, he deliberately delivered frequent sermons against the Arians, several of which still survive. See the first tractate of book I and several at the beginning of book II. It is evident from tractate 77 that some of them attended these sermons; the same may also be inferred from tractate 1, book II, and tractates 7 and 8 of the same book. Although some Arians nevertheless remained at Verona under Syagrius, Zeno’s successor—for Ambrose, in Letter V, no. 1, to Syagrius himself, relates that after Zeno’s death heretics stirred up hostility against the virgin Indicia, whom St Zeno had consecrated—it is highly probable that Zeno recalled the greater number of them to the faith. Thus it may be said of him what St Gaudentius testifies concerning St Philastrius in his sermon on his own ordination, p. 183: “The voice of Zeno, flowing abundantly through the grace of the Holy Spirit, founded this Church in faith in the Trinity to be adored and established it in true hope and perfect charity.” For just as St Philastrius, seventh bishop of Brescia, according to the same Gaudentius in his sermon on the life of Philastrius, p. 241, “fought not only against Gentiles and Jews, but also against every heresy, and especially against the raging Arian perfidy of that time,” so St Zeno, eighth bishop of Verona and a contemporary of Philastrius, fought no less fiercely against idolatry than against heresies, especially Arianism. Thus he is known to have purified Verona from errors and led it to the true religion, just as Brescia is recorded at the same time to have been purified from errors through Philastrius and brought to the Catholic faith.

That this may not seem surprising to those who suppose that the cities of Italy, especially, had embraced the name of Christ in the earliest centuries of the Church, let them consider, I pray, without ranging more widely, the neighbouring cities of Como, Modena, and Trento; they will find that the same thing happened to them which, as we have said, befell Verona and Brescia. St Felix, almost a contemporary of Zeno and the first bishop of Como (as we learn from the hymn on St Abundius, the second bishop of that city, [CXXVI] in Ughelli, vol. V, p. 258, and from another ancient hymn on St Amantius, the third bishop of Como, in the same author, p. 259), was likewise the first to build churches at Como, and the first to sow the faith of Christ there and win people for Christ. This is evident from Epistle IV of St Ambrose to the same man, where at no. 7 you may read:

> “The harvest of Christ is great,” he says, “but the labourers are few, and it is difficult to find those who may help. … Certainly, in that order of the people of Como, most have already begun to believe through your teaching and have received the word of God through your doctrine; but He who gave believers will also give helpers,” etc.

Of St Vigilius, bishop of Trento, who lived for some time after Zeno, do not the Acts, in the Bollandists, vol. V for June, p. 165, report this?

> “There he converted the whole city to Catholicism and placed a church for the Lord within the city walls—where previously there had been none.”

Does not the author of the Life of St Geminianus, bishop of Modena, published [Col. 0151C] from a Verona manuscript in vol. II, part II, of *Rerum Italicarum*, leave us these words concerning him, who was plainly contemporary with Zeno, at p. 691?

> “Assuredly, while the whole world was flocking to the worship of Christ, the aforementioned city [Modena], receiving the Lord’s faith through the successors of the Apostles, rejected the vain foulness of idols and, through the preaching of holy priests, began to receive again the inheritance of heaven which it had long lost. In the catalogue of these confessors, the city of Modena, at the Lord’s command, received the most blessed Geminianus … in the times of the Emperor Jovian, ruler of the whole commonwealth. Refreshed by him with the nourishment of heavenly life and purified at the font of holy cleansing, it abandoned its superfluous slavery to idols and bowed its neck beneath Christ’s sweet yoke.”

Had the distinguished editor, in commenting on these words, considered at the same time examples from other cities [Col. 0151D] in which precisely the same thing is found to have occurred, he surely would not have written in the preface, p. 687:

> “The statement that the people of Modena renounced the superstition of the pagans only under the Emperor Jovian, through the work of Bishop Geminianus, rests on no support of truth or probability and must be relegated to fables.”

If the author of the Life had stated that the people of Modena first embraced the Christian religion through Geminianus only under Jovian, he would indeed rightly be reproved by the editor. But that is not what he suggests. Rather, he relates that the people of Modena received the faith through other bishops, successors of the Apostles; and he recounts only that under Jovian’s reign they abandoned idolatry through Geminianus’s labours. This solely implies that Modena, [Col. 0152A] which long before had received the faith among some few persons, in this period—when there was freedom to embrace the Christian profession—gave its name to Christ almost wholly, after idols had been entirely overthrown, as had not previously happened. This is the less open to criticism because it is confirmed by the churches of very many other cities, to which the same thing happened.

Moreover, fables of this kind, introduced and handed down by popular report, tend to enhance rather than diminish the antiquity and renown of a church. Thus reports concerning any church that are more restrained and less glorious arouse no suspicion of popular fable and ought, beyond others, to be considered most reliable.

### § III.—A New Church Built at Verona. Zeno’s Clergy. Two Classes of Virgins at Verona. The First Monastery in the Entire West Founded at Verona by Zeno. Revelry and Drunkenness at Martyrs’ Festivals Abolished.

Furthermore, that our Zeno built a new church from its foundations in this city, and that, when it was first opened, he held the assembly of Christians with great solemnity, is evident from Tractate 14, Book I. It may perhaps have been the first church in the city built for that purpose; for before this, sacred rites were performed in private houses adapted to the use, or at least outside the city’s sacred boundary. The generosity of wealthy Veronese showed itself in this work, since it is mentioned in no. 3 through frequent and large contributions of theirs. [Col. 0152C] Yet they showed themselves generous not only on this but on other occasions as well, especially when urged by the bishop. This was particularly the case in the redemption of captives, which Zeno himself extolled in a public address with exceptional praise; see Tractate 10, no. 5, Book I.

Moreover, the bishop professed poverty, as appears from Tractate 44, Book II. From the same passage it is also clear that he had clergy; for he calls certain persons witnesses: “the workmen who are with me,” he says. Thus, in Tractate 16, Book I, no. 6, he mentions priests who used at solemn divine services to commend to God the souls of the departed; and in Tractate 50, Book II, he refers to ministers who assisted the bishop in sacred rites, and also to sacred ordinations, by which lower ministers were promoted to a higher rank at Easter. By affirming that recompense was rendered to devout priests at that same time, he plainly indicates the diligence of devout priests who worked with him, whether in instructing catechumens or preparing penitents; their recompense was baptism itself and reconciliation, which were solemnly performed at Easter. [Col. 0152D]

A passage of St Ambrose’s Epistle V to Syagrius, Zeno’s successor, also bears upon this question. Since it is related there that priests visited Indicia after she had been blessed by him, this appears to be no obscure testimony to priests ordained in Zeno’s time. It is also quite credible that the author praises the chastity and celibacy of these priests in Tractate 5, Book I, no. 7.

[Col. 0153A] But who could doubt that Zeno established his clergy in sound discipline, when it is manifest from the same letter of Ambrose that he also cultivated the discipline of virgins? From it we plainly gather that in Zeno’s time there were at Verona not only virgins who, bound by a vow of virginal chastity and veiled after probation, lived chastely in their own homes—such as Indicia, concerning whom we have said more in Dissertation I, chapter 3, § 3—but also virgins who, having professed virginity, lived a common life in a monastery. For, as Ambrose relates, when Indicia was falsely accused through calumny, her accusers spread the alleged crime as follows, at no. 19:

> “Common women ran to the monastery, declared that a virgin had given birth and that the child had been killed; a rumour from the monastery was spread among the people.”

Although by the end of this fourth century there were some monasteries of virgins in the West, as may be inferred from other passages of Ambrose himself, yet this monastery, apparently founded at Verona by Zeno, we believe to have been the first of all, or at least the first among those whose memory has been transmitted in writing. From this great number of Veronese virgins, some cultivating virginity in a monastery and others in private homes, we further recognize the fruit of Zeno’s sermons, in which virginity was especially commended, as in the present Tractate 5, Book I. We consider that this bishop should be counted among those bishops of Italy praised by St Augustine in Epistle XXII, no. 4, who, seeing that the *agapae*—love-feasts—established for the relief of the poor and the honouring of martyrs had gradually become occasions of revelry, drunkenness, and licentiousness, preached against them so successfully that they banished them from their churches and from all Italy. We observed this in note 18 on Tractate 15, Book I, where the author inveighs against persons who, in order to indulge more often in feasting, drunkenness, and impurity, invented martyrs for themselves in whose cemeteries they might hold love-feasts. [Col. 0153C]

Nor does it seem proper to omit here what three authors of the sixteenth century reported: Paul of Middelburg, bishop of Fossombrone, in the preface and also in Book I of his work entitled *Paulina on the Correct Celebration of Easter*, published in 1513; Johannes Stoeffler in the *Roman Calendar*, published in 1518, proposition 17; and, from these authors, Onofrio Panvinio, *Antiquities of Verona*, Book IV, chapter 6. They report that a Paschal canon was issued or restored by Zeno; but on what evidence we are wholly ignorant. Indeed, we do not hesitate to count this among fables.

[CXXVIII] ### § IV.—St Zeno Celebrated for Miracles. The Day of His Death.

Not only Coronatus but also the Anonymous Author of Pipino relates that Zeno had great power over demons:

> “And indeed he freed many from the pestiferous enemy.”

Coronatus describes two miracles which, among the many accomplished through him, appear to have been the more famous. Being more deeply impressed upon the minds of the people, they were subsequently surrounded with idle additions, as happens with matters that, not having been written down by anyone, are transmitted among the people. Coronatus himself received them with these additions and committed them to writing. Yet they are not to be rejected because of false additions in such a way that the truth itself, which usually has some place in miraculous accounts—even though it cannot easily be distinguished—should thereby be entirely discarded. The Anonymous Author of Pipino repeats the same accounts, adding a third remarkable miracle. If one removes a single word, “Caesar,” his account describes them much better than Coronatus’s, briefly and without any additions that create difficulties for critics. Here are his complete words, as they are found at the end of the Zenonian and Pompeian manuscripts; for in the Lobbes manuscript, from which Fr Mabillon published this little work of the same Anonymous Author, there is an evident lacuna, as Marquis Scipio Maffei rightly observed, p. 179 of his *Diplomatic History*. We supply it from the aforesaid manuscripts.

> The eighth shepherd and confessor, the illustrious martyr,  
> Who by preaching brought Verona back to baptism,  
> Healed the daughter of the Emperor Gallienus from an evil spirit;  
> He brought back oxen, together with a man who was sinking, from the sea.  
> And indeed he freed many from the pestiferous enemy;  
> He raised a dead man taken from the river;  
> By frequent fasts he destroyed many idols.  
> I cannot recount the many works of this holy man,  
> Through whom, coming from Syria as far as Italy,  
> Almighty God showed wonders.

These and Zeno’s other miraculous deeds—although we suppose there were more, even if they were not preserved and handed down as the people’s memory faded—made him renowned from ancient times in many cities, provinces, and nations beyond his own, concerning which more will be said in chapter four. [Col. 0154C]

Now, for him to have brought the Church of Verona, despite the opposition of pagans and Arians, to the state we have described, he certainly must have governed it for some time. From what we conjectured in Dissertation I, chapter 3, § 5, it is not improbable that he presided over that Church for eighteen years, namely from the year 362 until about 380. At that time, translated to heaven and rewarded for his labours, he was present as protector to the Verona which he had nourished in the Christian religion. Hence it came about that the city, not unmindful of his benefits, soon chose him as its great Patron and invoked him. [Col. 0154D]

We consider that no further labour need be spent on the year, nor anything added, unless perhaps someone wishes to indicate the opinion of certain modern writers who, without producing any evidence, state that Zeno died in 301; on this see more in the Admonition to the monuments, no. 3. Coronatus the Notary, the most ancient of all who mentioned his death, does not specify the day of his death at all. Recalling only the celebrated miracle in which the water of the river Adige, suddenly flooding to a great height, did not enter the open door and windows of the Church of St Zeno—a miracle described by St Gregory the Great, *Dialogues*, Book III, chapter 19, as having occurred five years earlier, namely in 589, and reported to that pontiff by the tribune John, who had witnessed it with Count Pronulfus—Coronatus, I say, by recalling this miracle not obscurely assigns the saint’s death to the same day as that miracle. At no. 9 he says: “While, on the holy day of his birthday [that is, Zeno’s] … they were assembling for the solemn celebration of Mass,” etc. [CXXIX] [Col. 0155A]

Rabanus Maurus, who flourished about the middle of the ninth century, records the following in the Martyrology published by Canisius, vol. II, part II, of the latest edition:

> “8 December. In the city of Verona, the natal feast of St Zeno, martyr, when the waters of the river Adige rose as high as the upper windows of the roof of his church and could not enter it, thereby displaying the power of the martyr.”

But Paul the Deacon, earlier than Rabanus—for he wrote under Charlemagne at the beginning of the same century—in Book III of *The Deeds of the Lombards*, chapter 23, assigns the same miracle to the sixteenth day before the Kalends of November, that is, 17 October. Although the Meda manuscript and Lindebrog’s edition read merely “the Kalends of November,” it is evident that the numeral letters XVI, found in other manuscripts and editions, were omitted. This is confirmed by Landulf in the Addition to the *Miscellany*, recently published in vol. I of *Rerum Italicarum*, p. 181, who followed—or rather copied—Paul the Deacon and wrote XVI Kalends of November.

Yet the day on which the miracle of the Adige occurred cannot possibly be St Zeno’s day of death, as Coronatus implies; for no documents designate that day as Zeno’s feast-day, whereas they do commemorate other days dedicated to Zeno’s memory and observed as feasts. [Col. 0155C] From this too one may recognize what authority should be granted to Coronatus. Nor should it be surprising that the Zenonian monk who wrote that the holy bishop rendered his soul to his Creator on the day before the Ides of April (*Maffei, Diplomatic History*, p. 329) shortly afterwards called the day of the restrained Adige his natal feast; for it is certain that, like many other things, he took this from Coronatus.

In many martyrologies and calendars, and in many churches that annually celebrate Zeno’s feast, 8 December is assigned to this feast. But he should not therefore be believed to have died on this day, as the aforementioned Rabanus seems to indicate; for in the same Martyrology Rabanus had entered Zeno’s day of death as the day before the Ides of April. Nor is this Rabanus’s only repetition: after recording the Translation of St Zeno on 21 May, the day on which all other monuments record it, he marked it again, through an obvious slip, on 21 July, a feast entirely unknown to all Veronese monuments.

All the documents of the Church of Verona, together with those of other authors and churches, constantly place St Zeno’s death on the day before the Ides of April, a day now also celebrated by our Church as the death-day of our Protector. On 8 December, however, most ancient Veronese manuscripts and the small Martyrology—which Francesco Maria Florentini published from the Lucchese manuscript of the Hieronymian Martyrology—record the dedication [Col. 0156A] of the Church of St Zeno. A few record “the dedication of St Zeno” or “the consecration of St Zeno.” Only documents of the monastery of St Zeno, none later than the fourteenth century, mark on that day Zeno’s ordination and, two days later, the dedication of St Zeno’s church. On this see more in Dissertation I, chapter 3, § 5.

Therefore, the churches which observe Zeno’s feast on 8 December present no difficulty. Since 12 April very often falls during Lent or the Easter feasts, days on which the natal feasts of saints were formerly not celebrated, such feasts customarily were transferred to another day assigned in the particular church to the saint’s translation, ordination, or dedication of his church. Thus, according to Radulfus, *On Canonical Observances*, chapter XVI:

> “The solemnity of St Gregory was formerly accustomed to be transferred to the day on which he had been ordained.”

The same is confirmed both by the author of the Life of St Rupert, bishop of Salzburg, written in the twelfth century, and by the author of chapter XXIV added to the treatise *On the Donations of the Same Church*. Both, speaking of the feast-day of St Rupert himself, who died on 27 March, state that St Virgil established it for the diocese on 24 September, [CXXX] the day on which he had translated Rupert’s body, but in the city on 25 September, since 24 September was occupied by the feast of the dedication of the church in which the saint’s body rests. They assign this reason for the feast’s removal from the day of death: that, because of the offices of Lent or Easter itself, that day rarely could be celebrated as worthily as it should be. These are the words of the author of the Life, who then adds:

> “It is also fitting and religious that whatever another observance of that celebration, on the days of his death, has taken away out of reverence for the Lenten office or regard for the joy of Easter, should at least be supplied here, in the house of his repose, when the day of translation has been assumed—he who was the founder of this see and apostle of its religion.”

Finally, to offer an example close at hand and altogether parallel: St Proculus, the fourth bishop of Verona, for the same reason of concurrent Lent or Easter, is recorded on 9 December in the martyrologies and calendars of many other churches, as also in the Roman one, and at Venice, where a church dedicated in his name stands. Yet ancient monuments record on 23 March “the deposition of St Proculus, confessor,” while on 9 December they record “the dedication of the Church of St Proculus.” [Col. 0156D] For precisely the same reason—to add this also—the feast of St Ambrose, who died on the day before the Nones of April, is celebrated everywhere except in the Church of Milan on 7 December, the date of his ordination.

Hence the excellent and entirely true admonition of Cardinal Baronius in his notes to the Martyrology for 18 March:

> “Nor should it be surprising if, as often happens, the same saint is treated on one day in the Roman Martyrology and on another day elsewhere, since in one place his translation, in another the dedication of his church, or, as happens with bishops, his ordination is celebrated.”

Thus, since the practice of foreign churches celebrating St Zeno’s natal feast on 8 December creates no obstacle, there can be no doubt that he died on 12 April, as all the monuments of the Church of Verona and the annual observance of his cult testify. We must now turn to the question whether St Zeno died a martyr or a confessor; since this requires a longer discussion, it must be treated in a separate chapter. [Col. 0157A]

## CHAPTER II. THE CONTROVERSY OVER ST ZENO’S MARTYRDOM EXAMINED ON BOTH SIDES.

In undertaking to discuss the title of martyr customarily given to St Zeno, we enter upon a matter full of odium. If you affirm that he was a martyr but do not prove it with sufficiently appropriate testimonies, you will seem to have wished to uphold a received opinion; you will not escape the criticism of learned persons, still less that of religious persons, to whom it is almost sacrilege to advance as certain a doubtful matter concerning prerogatives of saints of this kind. If, conversely, you deny that he was a martyr, you may provoke a still greater offence, not only among the common people but among very many devout persons, who will accuse you of hostility to the cult of the holy Protector, to the tradition, as they call it, of many centuries, and to the offices of the Church of Verona; they will charge you with rashness, favouring novelty, and perhaps even violating religion and piety. [Col. 0157B]

Carefully considering these dangers threatening on either side, we initially hesitated for some time whether we ought to refrain from this controversy. But when we realized that the celebrated question could not be left untouched and that a dissertation on the life of the holy bishop would otherwise appear incomplete, we judged at last that, in order to avoid both dangers, we should take this course: to present the documents available for both sides and set them fully in the light, while deciding nothing ourselves, but referring everything to the judgment of readers, which will not be difficult to bear. [Col. 0157C]

[CXXXI] ### § I.—Arguments for Upholding St Zeno’s Martyrdom Are Set Forth, and Contrary Arguments Refuted.

First let the documents supporting martyrdom be considered. St Gregory the Great, the most ancient of all the witnesses, twice calls St Zeno a martyr in *Dialogues*, Book III, chapter 19, where he describes the miracle of the overflowing Adige, which stood at the open door of the Church of St Zeno. First, in these words:

> “At the city of Verona, the swelling river Adige came to the church of the blessed Zeno, martyr and bishop.”

Then:

> “But as it stood before the door, to show all the merit of the martyr, the water also …”

This is the reading of all printed and manuscript witnesses. Among the codices, especially worthy of mention is the very ancient one in our Capitular Library, in which the word “martyr” is plainly read.

Coronatus the Notary, who inserted some false and incredible things in other matters, is not comparable with St Gregory either in antiquity or authority. His testimony—by which he not only does not call Zeno a martyr but states that he was “received in peace,” a formula usually signifying the death of confessors—has no force against Gregory. Consequently, arguments that might be drawn and pressed from a similar expression in the Zenonian monk, Peter de Natalibus, or others who plainly took their material from Coronatus, are likewise worthless. [Col. 0158A]

Paul the Deacon, who wrote at the beginning of the ninth century, describes the same miracle of the Adige in Book III of *The Deeds of the Lombards*, chapter 23. Following the authority of St Gregory the Great, whom he cites, he also calls St Zeno a martyr. Likewise John the Deacon, in his Life of Gregory, written after the middle of the ninth century, Book I, no. 35, calls St Zeno martyr and bishop in Gregory’s very words. Rabanus mentions Zeno four times in his Martyrology and four times calls him martyr. Wandelbert, in the metrical Martyrology written in 842, printed complete in vol. II of Acheri’s *Spicilegium*, calls our Zeno a martyr on 8 December. In the same century Notker, in the Martyrology published by Canisius, vol. II of *Antiquities of Readings*, part III, latest edition, always adds the title of martyr when mentioning St Zeno, both on the day before the Ides of April and on 22 May.

Usuard also calls him a martyr in the manuscript of St-Germain, though the Bollandists object to this with arguments of no small weight. They maintain, first, that that manuscript is not, as commonly asserted, Usuard’s autograph book; then, on the basis of another, older codex, they argue that additions were inserted by others into the St-Germain manuscript. Among these they count the name of St Zeno and the title “martyr” added to Zeno. They think that Usuard made no mention of this saint, just as Florus, the genuine Ado published by Rosweyde in vol. XVI of the *Library of the Fathers*, and the authentic Martyrology of Bede published by the same Bollandists make none. This is confirmed by the ancient codex of the Chapter of Verona containing the same Martyrology of Bede, in which St Zeno’s name plainly appears to have been added by a second hand. [Col. 0158C]

Nevertheless, the name “martyr” is found in the author of the Martyrology commonly attributed to Bede, in additions to the Martyrology of Ado on 8 December, and in most codices presenting the enlarged and interpolated Martyrology of Usuard. In the Calendar of the monastery of Monte Cassino, published in vol. VII of *Rerum Italicarum*, p. 936, in April, Zeno is said to have been “crowned by martyrdom”; and likewise in another Calendar prefixed to a ninth-century manuscript Gregorian Sacramentary, Vatican no. 3806, one reads in the same month: “of St Zeno the martyr.”

Against the points so far established, a major objection is commonly raised, seeming stronger than the rest. It is said that the Church of Verona, which above all others ought to know whether its Patron and bishop died a martyr, always called him a confessor, not a martyr, and honoured him as a confessor in offices and Masses down to Bishop Aloysius Lippomano, who about the middle of the sixteenth century first altered the ancient rite and instituted offices and Masses to be celebrated for a martyr. A number of foreign churches, to be indicated in chapter 4, §§ 2 and 3, following that old rite, likewise at that time celebrate the annual feast of St Zeno with the offices and Masses of a confessor, not a martyr. [CXXXII] [Col. 0159A]

But there is an easy response to this objection drawn especially from the rite of the Church of Verona, which other churches evidently followed. Besides the fact that the manuscript *Carpsum* of the Church of Verona, just mentioned, specifies as the antiphons to be recited at the Introit, Offertory, and Communion in the Mass for St Zeno’s feast those which are now also customarily said in the Masses of martyrs in Eastertide; and likewise that the Lectionary of St Euphemia, cited in the scholia of Battista Peretto, assigns for the day of the Translation of St Zeno the Gospel “I am the true vine,” which today we likewise read in the same Eastertide Masses of martyrs; and that we learn from another manuscript Missal of the monastery of St Zeno that the same Gospel was read whenever one of the same saint’s feasts fell in Eastertide—besides these facts, I say, our Church of Verona appears to have maintained the ancient rite observed by Micrologus in the book *On Ecclesiastical Observances*, chapter 45, as Battista Peretto notes in the same scholia on the Life of St Zeno. It is printed in vol. XVIII of the *Library of the Fathers*, p. 485:

> “Note,” he says, “that Pope St Gregory first instituted pontifical offices in the Gradual book for these martyrs—the Roman Pontiffs—as for confessors, as for St Marcellus the antiphon ‘He established,’ and for St Felix the antiphon ‘Priests’; and this was altogether fitting because of the excellence of the apostolic dignity. Observing this also, our elders are read to have kept offices of confessors for the same saints in the daily and nightly office; these likewise indicate episcopal dignity in the same manner and nevertheless do not prejudice the martyrdom of any of them. The Gradual book shows that the same must be observed concerning St Apollinaris.”

So far Micrologus. Indeed, that this rite prevailed particularly in the Church of Verona is shown by the fact that in its ancient liturgical books bishops, though martyrs, are nevertheless called confessors, and an office of confessors is prescribed for them. To omit the few Roman Pontiffs listed there whose martyrdom is not established by certain documents, we shall mention only bishops certainly known to have been martyrs. Rather than survey every liturgical book of this Church, it will be sufficient to consider the manuscript called the *Carpsum*, which, after an authorial preface published by Scipio Maffei in the Additions to the final part of *Verona Illustrata*, provides a calendar and records from time to time the rite of offices to be celebrated in this Church, as well as the opening words of antiphons, responsories, and psalms suitable to each office. This *Carpsum* was written by Stephen, priest and cantor of the same Church, before the middle of the twelfth century, since the following five chronological notes, in another hand, are found in the margin of the Calendar between 24, 25, and 26 June: [Col. 0160A]

> Here Oprandus the Archpriest was promoted, 1166.  
> 8 August: Beatrix, 1171.  
> 11 October: Nativity of St Placidus, V.; and in the margin: Foundation … 1175.  
> 10 April: Election of Adrian the Archpriest, 1186.  
> 7 June: Consecration of Adrian the Archpriest as priest, 1186.

Accordingly, the following entries bearing on our subject are written in the Calendar of this *Carpsum*:

> 2 February: St Blaise, confessor.  
> 24 April: St Adalbert, confessor.  
> 5 June: St Boniface, bishop and confessor.  
> 26 June: Nativity of Saints John and Paul, martyrs, and St Vigilius, confessor. [Col. 0160B]

[CXXXIII] Thus all these, who are unquestionably martyrs as we otherwise assume, are called confessors in the Calendar of the *Carpsum* itself. Further, although the Calendar reads: “8 August: Nativity of Sixtus, Felicissimus, and Agapitus, martyrs,” nevertheless in the *Carpsum* the office of St Sixtus is marked as that of a confessor bishop, while the antiphons of the other two are those of martyrs. Thus it appears that the rite prevailed in the Church of Verona whereby those otherwise true martyrs were called confessors, and offices for them were celebrated not as for martyrs but as for confessors.

Learned persons could have suspected and inferred this same fact from Ughelli himself, p. 781, where he reports a Veronese inscription. In that inscription, erected in the ninth century, in the time of Andrew, Patriarch of Aquileia, as a memorial of dedication in what was formerly the church of St Gregory and is now commonly called St Helena, and still visible there, the relics of saints contained there are listed as follows: “of St Vigilius, confessor; of St Proculus, confessor; of St Zeno, confessor.” Here you see that not so much St Zeno together with Proculus, as surely St Vigilius, bishop of Trento, who indisputably died a martyr, is equally called “confessor”; and this designation was followed by the rite of offices and Masses. From this rite of the Church of Verona it seems, moreover, to have resulted that St Zeno is called confessor, not martyr, in other monuments of the same Church as well, so that this cannot be construed as a denial of his martyrdom. [Col. 0160C]

Although in most Veronese monuments the title of confessor alone is asserted for him, some documents do not fail expressly to declare him a martyr. Emperor Henry, in the privilege granted in 1055 to the abbot of the monastery of St Zeno, Ughelli, *Italia Sacra*, vol. V, p. 763, twice calls him a martyr. In another privilege, conveyed in 901 by Berengar to the same monastery of St Zeno at the request of Vitalis, bishop of Vicenza, although he is twice called a confessor, he is also once named martyr. See Ughelli on the bishops of Vicenza, vol. V, p. 1031. The Anonymous Author of Pipino, who composed a rhythm on the praises of Verona, knew well enough the Veronese rite described above; did he not nevertheless think St Zeno should be called both confessor and martyr together?

[Col. 0161A]

> The eighth shepherd and confessor, Zeno the illustrious martyr.

William Pastrengo of Verona, one of the most learned writers of the fourteenth century, to whom it is utterly incredible that this rite was unknown, did he not write openly of Zeno: “He suffers martyrdom”?

Nor should it be objected that St. Zeno could not have been crowned with martyrdom if he lived after Julian’s reign, as we showed in Dissertation I. For although it is granted that after Julian there were no persecutions in Italy against Christians—a point sufficiently discussed in the same dissertation, chapter 2, final section—St. Zeno might nevertheless have been killed in some disturbance raised by pagans, against whom he had fearlessly set himself. For a similar reason, not many years later, the three holy Anaunian martyrs, and soon afterward St. Vigilius, bishop, met a glorious death for Christ in the neighboring valleys of Tridentum. Or he may have endured and suffered as many and as great persecutions for the propagation of the faith as his contemporary, St. Philastrius, bishop of Brescia, suffered. His successor St. Gaudentius recorded the following concerning him in his sermon on the life of St. Philastrius, pp. 241–242:

> Against the Gentiles and the Jews . . . and especially against . . . the Arian faithlessness, he fought with such vigor that he was even subjected to blows and bore in his body the stigmata of our Lord Jesus Christ.

In agreement with this view, John, mansionary priest of the Church of Verona, writes the following concerning Zeno in the manuscript *Imperial History*: “After many torments he rested in Christ on the second day before the Ides of April.” Even if he did not die amid those persecutions and torments, this does not prevent him from being called a martyr. For St. Cyprian calls martyrs those confessors who, having suffered much for Christ, had not yet died under tortures; and St. Paulinus calls Felix of Nola both martyr and confessor. Likewise, the same St. Felix of Nola, St. Eusebius of Vercelli, and others—who otherwise suffered only certain things for the faith and afterward died in peace—are proclaimed martyrs and honored with the office of martyr. [CXXXIV]

Accordingly, when in 1554 Aloysius Lippomano (as Peretto attests in his Latin scholia on the Life of St. Zeno) ordered all the clergy of the diocese of Verona to celebrate the office of one martyr-bishop, whereas previously that of one confessor-bishop had been celebrated, he is not to be blamed. Nor should those Churches be reproached which, in order to conform themselves to the Veronese example, are quite credibly believed later to have adopted this same rite; concerning them we shall speak in chapter four. These are all the points which we have been able to gather in favor of the view that Zeno was a martyr. You see, reader, that they have been set forth and pressed with all the force available to us, so that nothing might be taken away from the strength of the side now followed by the Church of Verona. We now turn to the evidence supporting the opposite view.

## § II.—Arguments for the Opposite View Set Forth

The most ancient witness of all those who mention Zeno is St. Ambrose, archbishop of Milan, an author of the greatest accuracy and reliability in many respects, and indeed a contemporary of Zeno. Therefore Zeno’s martyrdom could not have escaped Ambrose’s notice, if Zeno had met a glorious death for the Christian faith while Ambrose himself was already bishop. When the case of the virgin Indicia, formerly approved and blessed by St. Zeno, was brought before him, Ambrose wrote much in her defense to Syagrius, Zeno’s successor; and, in adducing the judgment of this saint who had approved her, he would undoubtedly not have omitted the title “martyr,” which would have contributed greatly to its authority. Yet he calls Zeno only “the bishop of holy memory,” not a martyr, saying:

> But you, without the counsel of any brother, have made this judgment a prejudgment: you have thought that a girl approved by the judgment of Zeno of holy memory and sanctified by his blessing should, after so many years, be brought into danger of condemnation without an author of accusation, without an accuser, without a declarant of the charge.

Thus it plainly appears that Ambrose knew nothing of his martyrdom; and if Ambrose had learned nothing of it, it is highly probable that Zeno died peacefully a natural death rather than by martyrdom—unless Ambrose’s testimony is refuted by evidence of equal age and authority.

Compared with Ambrose’s testimony, the authority of St. Gregory the Great, the oldest evidence available for the martyrdom, is far too late. Since he lived two centuries afterward, it may be that, when recounting the miracle of the Adige and calling Zeno a martyr, he mistakenly believed him to have been called a martyr, whereas John, from whom he had learned of the miracle, had described him merely as a bishop and confessor—unless perhaps John himself is more plausibly thought to have erred in that title.

Indeed, defects of this kind are not without precedent in St. Gregory. As Molanus observes in the second edition of Usuard, St. Juvenal, bishop of Narnia, whose feast is marked on the fifth day before the Nones of May in the Roman Martyrology, is called a martyr by St. Gregory, Book IV, chapter 12, although he was merely a confessor. We add another example from Epistle 73 of Book IX in the old arrangement, now Epistle 62 of Book VI, where the same pontiff calls St. Leucius, bishop of Brindisi, “most blessed martyr.” Yet in the cited Martyrology, and also in a manuscript Calendar of the Casanatensian Library, written at the beginning of the ninth century and formerly belonging to a monastery of Benevento, he is called, on the third day before the Ides of January, “bishop and confessor”; and he is still honored as a confessor in his own Church of Brindisi.

It is true that in editions after the Roman one he is called Leontius, not Leucius. But since his body is said to rest at Brindisi, while the city of Brindisi has never acknowledged the resting there of the body of any Saint Leontius, as it once possessed that of St. Leucius, bishop, before it was transferred to Benevento, the reading of the earlier editions of Gregory seems preferable. Together with the five manuscripts cited in the Benedictine edition, they read *Leucius*. From these two errors of the holy pontiff, in which he bestowed the title of martyr upon confessors, there arises no unwarranted suspicion of a similar error when the same pontiff wrote that Zeno was a martyr, though St. Ambrose did not recognize him as such.

The Life by Coronatus, abounding in several improbabilities which we have considered elsewhere, is admittedly of very slight authority. Yet this cannot be denied: when it says of Zeno, “He was received in peace,” it shows that, amid the many improbabilities which the author had gathered from popular report to magnify the glory of the holy bishop, he had heard nothing of Zeno’s martyrdom. Nor was anything of that kind reported at that time—namely, in the seventh or eighth century, not long after St. Gregory’s death—in this very Church of Verona. [CXXXV]

Add that in the Life of Coronatus, read in a very ancient Rheims manuscript, where the miracle of the Adige is recounted, the very words of St. Gregory appear to have been inserted, as we shall say in note 10 on the same Life. There, instead of the words found in St. Gregory, “to show the merit of the martyr,” the text reads, “to show the merit of the confessor.” Hence there is reason to suspect that the Veronese writer—whoever he was—who once inserted that addition in the manuscript then at Verona and now at Rheims, altered “martyr” to “confessor” in Gregory’s words, and considered the holy pontiff mistaken in this matter because St. Zeno was regarded at Verona as a confessor, not a martyr.

For the same reason, the Zenonian monk, when naming Gregory and quoting his words, omitted the designation “martyr” and substituted “saint,” writing: “to show the merit of the saint”; or, as is read in a manuscript lectionary of Brescia mentioned by our Maffei in the preface to the Zenonian Monk, p. 317 of *Historia diplomatica*, “to show the merit of the confessor.” Unless perhaps this Brescian manuscript lectionary contains the very Life of Coronatus, taken from a similar Rheims exemplar; certainly another manuscript lectionary of the Church of Trent contains it, and it likewise gives this addition and wording in preference to Gregory’s words.

If, therefore, it is probable from these considerations that St. Gregory, in calling Zeno a martyr, fell into an error involving a single name, the testimonies of Paul the Deacon, John the Deacon, Rabanus Maurus, and Notker are of no assistance. For it is evident that, just as they derived the miracle of the Adige which they mention from St. Gregory’s *Dialogues*, so also they derived the title of martyr which they attach to Zeno. The same reasoning disposes also of later writers—Wandelbert, Usuard, or rather the authors of additions to Usuard and to Ado, and others commonly cited—who may quite credibly be thought to have drawn from Gregory or from other followers of Gregory.

Only two manuscripts seem especially worthy of consideration in confirmation: Vatican manuscript 3806, cited in the preceding section, and another Veronese manuscript from the monastery of the Holy Spirit. The Vatican manuscript, which mentions St. Zeno the martyr in its Calendar in April, says nothing of him in its Sacramentary in that month; and only in December, when the Calendar notes nothing concerning this saint, does it provide his Mass—the same Mass which is read in our manuscripts. In it he is called only confessor-bishop, as you will see from the third Mass. These facts seem to have arisen solely because the name “martyr,” inserted in the Calendar in April, was taken from St. Gregory or from another copyist of his; whereas the Mass derived from a Veronese source, to which, as we shall shortly see, this designation was unknown.

By precisely similar reasoning, in the manuscript Martyrology of the Veronese monastery of the Holy Spirit there is, in April, a brief account of St. Zeno’s martyrdom in the form of martyrologies, in almost the same words as those found in the printed Usuard. Its testimony to martyrdom was derived from St. Gregory’s authority, adopted by other writers of martyrologies. Yet later, in two other feasts of St. Zeno in May and December, recorded only from Veronese books, he is called solely confessor-bishop.

The argument drawn from the ancient rite of the Church of Verona—that St. Zeno’s feast was celebrated down to Lippomano with the office and Mass of a confessor, not a martyr, and is still celebrated according to ancient custom in several outside Churches, as we shall see in chapter 4—this argument, I say, especially drawn from the rite of the Church of Verona, is indeed not sufficient to deny Zeno martyrdom to the extent that many, with Henschenius, have made it sufficient, as we showed more fully in the preceding section. Nevertheless, the points then advanced are not such that, because certain definite martyrs were honored in this Church according to the rite of confessors, St. Zeno may therefore be proved a martyr unless it is demonstrated from another source.

It cannot indeed be denied that the antiphons indicated in the *Carpsum* for St. Zeno’s Mass in Paschal time, and the Gospel of the same season written in two other manuscripts, are of the sort commonly said during that season concerning martyrs. Yet in ancient times these appear to have belonged to Paschal time, not to martyrs specifically. For in the ancient books of Masses published by the venerable Cardinal Thomasius, the rubric “In the common of one martyr or confessor” is found both in the Antiphonary, p. 281, in the Lectionary, p. 80, and in the *Capitulare Evangeliorum*, p. 217. The same is also noted in the Responsory-book and Antiphonary for the office of Paschal time, p. 314, and for the common office, p. 361. Thus, an argument drawn from antiphons and Gospels of this sort cannot be used to establish the cult of a martyr rather than a confessor. [CXXXVI]

What can yield certain evidence of cult from the Masses are the prayers, or the gradual responsory if it bears the saint’s proper name. There the title “martyr” or “confessor,” added to the proper name, safely indicates whether he was regarded as confessor or martyr. But all the prayers which may be read in the six manuscript books of the Church of Verona, and indeed in every Mass of St. Zeno to be described below, consistently use the single title “confessor-bishop,” never that of martyr. The gradual responsory placed after the Epistle and indicated in the *Carpsum* calls the same saint by no other title: “Holy confessor Zeno,” and so forth. Who, then, would wish to argue from antiphons and a Gospel—shown to have been formerly common to martyr and confessor alike—in favor of martyrdom against the express testimony of the prayers?

Indeed, from this it may rather be confirmed that the antiphons and Gospel of St. Zeno’s Paschal Mass, which are now regarded as proper to martyrs, were formerly common also to confessors. This is especially clear since the same *Carpsum* and other ritual books present the whole Paschal office of St. Zeno as to be recited for a confessor-bishop. They certainly would not have done so if the Paschal Mass, which had to agree with the office, had been judged proper to a martyr.

From this it also becomes wholly clear that the objection advanced in the preceding section from the *Micrologus*—which writes that the offices of Roman pontiffs otherwise martyrs were performed for confessors because of the excellence of apostolic rank—is empty. For those martyrs were explicitly called martyrs in the prayers; moreover, as the *Micrologus* itself notes in the same place, in their office the hymn, invitatory, and verses “Glory and honor,” “Thou hast set him, O Lord,” and “Great is his [glory]” are sung as for martyrs. In contrast, in the office of St. Zeno among the monuments to be cited, the hymn itself, invitatory, verses—in short, everything—spoke of a confessor.

Certainly those pontiffs who are known to be martyrs are also named martyrs in the prayers of the Sacramentaries of our Church of Verona. Thus St. Sixtus, in the prayers distinct from those of the martyrs Felicissimus and Agapitus—as the *Carpsum* likewise separately sets down their antiphons—is called a martyr, not a confessor, among the others. Similarly, St. Blaise, who is called a confessor not so much in the Calendar of the *Carpsum* as in another Calendar of a twelfth-century Sacramentary book, and who, besides, is designated a martyr in other manuscript Calendars, is nevertheless consistently given the title of martyr in the prayers of all the books.

As for the other three martyrs—Adalbert, Boniface, and Vigilius—whom the Calendar of the *Carpsum* counts among confessors, and whom an inscription in St. Helena’s church so designates in the case of Vigilius, we can offer no explanation whether they were called martyrs in the prayers or not, since they occur nowhere in the three mentioned books of Sacramentaries.

Nor should it be omitted that in the *Carpsum*, upon which the whole argument depends, there occur several errors which somewhat diminish its credibility. Let us give one example suited to the present issue. In the preceding Calendar: “The fifteenth day before the Kalends of August: the nativity of St. Mammas and Philastrius, martyrs.” And in the *Carpsum* itself: “On the nativity of Saints Mammas and Philastrius: antiphons and psalms and responsories; and the whole office from that for several martyrs.”

In these texts it must surely be strange that St. Philastrius—who both at Brescia and everywhere has always been honored with the cult of a confessor, who is likewise called confessor by St. Gaudentius his successor and by Rampert, bishop of Brescia, and also in the recently mentioned inscription of the Church of Verona in St. Helena’s, where one reads “St. Philastrius, confessor”—that this same St. Philastrius, I say, should nevertheless be counted among martyrs in the *Carpsum*, and in that very *Carpsum* which designates as confessors certain pontiffs who were certainly martyrs. No one can say that this is free from error. But if the author of the *Carpsum* erred in this point, who does not immediately see that he could similarly have erred in other matters? [CXXXVII] But let us proceed to other things.

Who would compare the two documents of the Church of Verona cited in the preceding section in support of the title of martyr with the very numerous documents to the contrary? By those same documents, which seem most clearly to establish the contrary tradition of that Church, the authority of the Veronese writers Anonymous Pipinianus and William Pastrengo is likewise weakened—or rather refuted. It is credible that in applying the title “martyr” they followed St. Gregory alone.

Indeed, because Anonymous Pipinianus calls St. Zeno both martyr and confessor, it is evident even from this that, uncertain whether St. Zeno was martyr or confessor, he wished to satisfy both designations then current so as not to err. He therefore adopted the title “martyr” from St. Gregory, but did not think that the name “confessor,” grounded in the ancient tradition of his Church and confirmed by so many testimonies, should be omitted. For the same reason one may suppose it happened that both names were joined together in the Meda manuscript of Paul the Deacon, *Rerum Italicarum*, vol. I, p. 447, and in one of the two documents raised in objection.

There are many monuments of the Church of Verona that bear the single title of confessor and thus witness to the tradition of that Church: several may be found in Ughelli, *Italia Sacra*, vol. V, from p. 705 onward, and many others could be added from the archives. More ancient than all is a charter of the year 769, written in the village of Campiglione in the diocese of Milan and published by Marquis Maffei among the documents useful to him in illustrating Veronese history, part I, p. 375. It mentions “the basilica of the most blessed Zeno, confessor of Christ.”

Add inscriptions. Besides the one in St. Helena’s church cited above, the same Scipione Maffei published another in vol. II of *Verona Illustrata*, p. 515. Set up in 1123 in the monastery of St. Zeno itself, it calls Zeno only a confessor. Another may be added, located in the church of Monte Aureo in the diocese of Verona. It has not yet been published; having once been carefully copied by Fr. Joseph Blanchini, we think it should be appended here:

> In the year of the Lord 1060, in the thirteenth indiction, this church was consecrated on the sixteenth day before the Kalends of September, in honor of the Holy Cross and St. Michael, and of the holy martyrs Castorius and Victor, and of the holy confessors Martin, Zeno, and Remigius, by Theobald, bishop of Verona.

Furthermore, in the lessons read on St. Zeno’s feast before Lippomano, no mention of martyrdom occurs; there one reads only, “He rested,” or “He was received in peace.” In the statutes of the city of Verona, including those still in force, when St. Zeno is named as the great patron of the city, he is called only Confessor. The same happens in the other civic decrees issued for his cult. In all the litanies, both of our Church and of others which we shall indicate in chapter 4, he is consistently counted among confessors.

The same was true in the litanies still customarily recited after Lippomano in the commendation of the soul in the Church of Verona. These were first printed in 1536 by Giovanni Matteo Giberti in the book for catechumens for the use of Verona Cathedral, and reprinted in 1573, when Bishop Agostino Valerio made no alteration. The change was made only in 1609 under Alberto Valerio, as we read in the Ritual of the Church of Verona: St. Zeno was transferred from the confessors to the martyrs in those litanies, p. 86, and again in others after the Penitential Psalms, p. 209.

Moreover, four books of Sacraments of the Church of Verona—three Capitular books and one of the Confraternity of St. Mary of the House—place St. Zeno among confessors in the Canon of the Mass. Three of these, namely the Capitular books, add St. Zeno among confessors while listing Saints Firmus and Rusticus among martyrs as follows:

> Communicating . . . [with] Lawrence, Firmus and Rusticus, Chrysogonus, John and Paul, Cosmas and Damian, Hilary, Martin, Augustine, Gregory, Jerome, and Benedict, Proculus and Zeno, etc.

No one, we think, will be able to produce an example in which any martyr is shown placed among confessors either in litanies or in the Canon of the Mass. If our St. Zeno had truly been a martyr, then, just as they did not hesitate to place Saints Firmus and Rusticus among martyrs, they would much more have judged that St. Zeno, the great Patron, should be counted among them.

In the same way, in the suffrages formerly recited between the offices in this Church, Theobald in 1305, in the very constitution confirmed in the same century by Bishop Peter Scaliger, ordered these suffrages and made first an especially honorable mention of St. Zeno, Father and Patron of this City, and then of the holy martyrs George and Firmus and Rusticus. Yet, in assigning the order of the suffrages, he indicates that the commemoration of the holy martyrs should be made first, then that of St. Zeno. This certainly would not have been done unless St. Zeno was regarded in this Church as confessor, not martyr; for commemorations of martyrs always precede commemorations of confessors.

Thus, also in an older Capitular manuscript of about the thirteenth century, containing prayers, lessons, and antiphons throughout the year, both proper and common for saints, the following suffrages are prescribed in the same order at Matins and Vespers: first of the Cross, then of peace, then of St. Mary—whose antiphon changed daily—afterward of St. George, of Saints Hermagoras and Fortunatus, Firmus and Rusticus, then of St. Zeno, and finally of All Saints. In these suffrages themselves, which we shall give from that manuscript, St. Zeno bears only the name of Confessor.

Add that neither Ratherius, who mentions St. Zeno in his works and with honorable titles, nor manuscript treatises containing his works—among which the most ancient Rheims manuscript served this very Church in sacred offices—nor Calendars, whether ours or foreign, of which Fr. Henschenius saw and indicates several in chapter 1, no. 3, p. 70, calls him a martyr; rather, all distinguish him by the title of confessor alone.

It also seems difficult that St. Zeno, who died when Gratian, Valentinian the Younger, and Theodosius were emperors, after persecutions had already ceased, should have suffered martyrdom. If it had befallen him through an uprising of pagans, as it did the Anaunian martyrs and St. Vigilius, bishop of Trent, the event would have been no less celebrated than it was in the case of those Tridentine martyrs; and some record relevant to the manner of his death would have been handed down to posterity.

It is indeed probable that, while bringing Verona to the faith and vigorously opposing pagan superstition, arranging for the destruction of idols and the overthrow of temples, he suffered many things at the hands especially of rural pagans; perhaps he also suffered from Arians, while zealously laboring to expose their schemes, restrain their assaults, and exclude their plague from his diocese—as St. Gaudentius records happened to St. Philastrius, bishop of Brescia. But just as St. Philastrius was never therefore regarded as a martyr, neither was St. Zeno; hence Ambrose did not call him martyr. Nor should the authority of the *Carpsum*, which declares that Philastrius was a martyr, be raised in objection. As we saw shortly above, that is a manifest error; it may not be used to establish Philastrius’s martyrdom, and much less that of St. Zeno, [CXXXIX] who in that same *Carpsum* is described only as a confessor.

But to set some limit to this discussion, these are the arguments that may be brought on either side. Do not seek our judgment among them, reader. From the outset we have proposed in this controversy only to gather and explain all that is available for each side, not to pronounce a decision. Accordingly, following the prudent counsel of Father Henschenius, we conclude with these words which he left written at the end of chapter 2, p. 73, after setting out several arguments on both sides:

> We leave everything to the judgment of prudent men.

For historical information alone, we add that Francesco Maria de Aste, archbishop of Otranto, who published at Benevento in 1716, under the patronage of Cardinal Ursini—later Benedict XIII—his most extensive discussions on the Roman Martyrology, stated in that work, on the express authority of the then reigning Clement XI, that, moved by Henschenius’s arguments, he had not wished to decide the controversy. Meanwhile he proposed this safer formulation: that the Martyrology should say, after the manner of Molanus, “At Verona, St. Zeno, bishop, who governed that Church amid the storms of persecution, and, having suffered much, ended his life.” By these words he thought that both the term *passio* (“suffering”) and the statement “he was crowned with martyrdom in the time of Gallienus” should be omitted, while not denying that our saint suffered much. But we too submit these matters to the judgment of sounder minds, together with the same archbishop.

## CHAPTER III. ON THE MORE NOTABLE EVENTS REPORTED AFTER ST. ZENO’S DEATH

Having thus far pursued those events which occurred up to the death of St. Zeno, we must now set forth those which followed upon his death. When the saint had departed this life, his great renown had been won not so much by the merits of his former life as by the prodigies and signs wrought both while he lived and after his death. Immediately after his death, therefore, a church was built in which his body rested, by a certain person whom Coronatus, no. 8, calls “of the family of Gallienus”—that is, of the Gallienus whose daughter, afflicted by a demon, St. Zeno had healed.

This is sufficiently plausible if the man is understood as a kinsman of that Gallienus who lived in the fourth century, concerning whom we offered some conjectures in Dissertation I, chapter 3, § 4. But if he is understood as a kinsman of the emperor Gallienus, whom Coronatus wrongly names, it would be wholly incredible to those who know from Aurelius Victor that the entire line of that emperor was exterminated with him.

In Coronatus’s own time, namely the seventh or eighth century, this church stood not far from the river Adige and outside the walls of the city of Verona, as Paul the Deacon relates in Book III of *The Deeds of the Lombards*, chapter 23. Some think it was the church now called St. Zeno in Oratorio, but, as we shall see below when discussing the Translation, they are mistaken.

At that church, which we have learned from Coronatus was near the Adige, there occurred about two centuries after the holy bishop’s death the famous miracle that St. Gregory the Great inserted in *Dialogues*, Book III, chapter 19, on the testimony of John the Tribune, who had been present with King Authari and Count Pronulfus. On a certain day, when a large crowd had assembled in that church, the Adige suddenly rose above its banks and burst forth, reaching the church itself with great force. Yet it did not enter through the open doors. Rather, rising gradually as high as the church windows, the water occupied and blocked the entire doorway, but did not flow inside at all, as though it had been solid.

We shall give a full description of this miracle in the very words of the holy pontiff among the selected testimonies. Furthermore, Paul the Deacon establishes for us in this dissertation, chapter 1, § 4, that the day of this miracle was the sixteenth day before the Kalends of November, a time when river floods commonly occur.

To determine the year: since St. Gregory, in describing the miracle, states that it occurred “about five years ago,” it is certain that the miracle took place approximately five years before he published the books of the *Dialogues*. For that reason, because Father Henschenius thinks that the *Dialogues* were published in 593, he assigns the miracle of the Adige to the year 588. Yet, even if one grants that the books of the *Dialogues* were completed and published in 593, we do not doubt that the miracle of the Adige occurred on the sixteenth day before the Kalends of November in the year 589. From that date to 593 runs approximately a five-year period—that is, a five-year period begun, not completed.

Another detail of Gregory’s description fixes this year with complete certainty. He relates that the flooding of the Adige occurred when, at Rome, the Tiber left its channel and rose so high that its water flowed over the city walls and then occupied large districts. We clearly establish the year of this flooding of the Tiber from the contemporary author Gregory of Tours, who in Book II of the *History of the Franks*, chapter 1, assigns it in explicit chronological terms to the ninth month, that is, November, of the year 589. Therefore, since Gregory the Great places the flood of the Adige at the same time, it must undoubtedly be assigned to the sixteenth day before the Kalends of November in the year 589.

This miracle of the Adige, and many others performed daily, rendered the holy bishop ever more renowned [Col. 0170B]; and they moved King Pippin of Italy, son of Charlemagne, and our bishop Rotaldus to consider transferring his body to a more fitting place. This we learn from the Zenonian monk, author of the little work *On the Translation of St. Zeno*. For when both had one day entered the church of St. Zeno together and were speaking of his miracles, both those they had heard of and those they had seen, they reasonably and worthily proposed to place more suitably and more loftily the great treasure which lay in a position humbler than was fitting, and to enlarge the narrowness of the church. Accordingly, they began a spacious and more magnificent church; and in it they constructed a dark crypt—for so the same author calls the *Confession*, or that underground place in which the holy body still lies—supported by columns and paved with stones. There they raised a prominent mound—so he calls the tomb itself—of polished marbles, and dedicated it as the tomb of the most sacred body. When this subterranean construction had been completed, but before the church itself was finished (for Ratherius, nearly two centuries later, testifies in his *Apologeticus*, p. 366, vol. I of Acheri’s *Spicilegium*, that some money had been given them by the Emperor with which they were to complete the Basilica of St. Zeno), the translation of the sacred body itself was carried out.

Although the writer of this translation is somewhat later, since he lived at the end of the eleventh or the beginning of the twelfth century, as we shall establish in the Preface to the monuments, and although he may have inserted no small amount of falsehood in describing it, as happens very easily in writings of this kind: nevertheless, the substance of the matter itself [Col. 0170D] proceeds from an ancient document, in exactly the same manner as the Life of St. Zeno compiled by him was taken for the most part from Coronatus the Notary, though he nowhere mentioned him. Indeed, a manuscript book of Reims suggests that the same translation was written by someone in ancient times. It passed into Gaul after the middle of the ninth century, that is, about fifty years after the translation. There, after the Life of St. Zeno composed by Coronatus has been copied, these words, in another hand, are added: “His translation remains.” These words sufficiently indicate that an account of St. Zeno’s translation had at that time been written, that it was lacking from the Life composed by Coronatus and copied there, and that it remained to be appended.

Accordingly, the date of the translation [Col. 0171A], fixed by that author as during the reign of Pippin and the episcopate of Rotaldus, is confirmed by certain documents in Ughelli. One of them, dated 865 and fully quoted on p. 721, mentions the feast of St. Zeno “in the month of May,” and undoubtedly refers to the translation, which all the calendars and ritual books of our Church assign to 21 May; Rabanus and Notker, ninth-century authors, likewise mark it on that day in their martyrologies. Hence what is related about Pippin and Rotaldus concurring in this undertaking is also probable. What the author recounts, moreover, concerning Benignus and Carus, pious and holy men living near Lake Benacus in a narrow and precipitous place, who were summoned to transfer the sacred body [CXLI], seems to derive from an ancient monument. But the remaining details [Col. 0171B] with which his story is clothed, since they display certain fabulous interpolations improperly inserted, we have judged should here be omitted. Anyone may, however, read them in the monument itself, to be printed below.

The Zenonian monk’s words concerning the actual elevation of the sacred body—“While it was being carried about near the church”—suggest that the body was brought from some nearby place into the new church; and thus they refute the common opinion that it was transferred from the church of St. Zeno called *in Oratorio*. This opinion, or rather this error, seems to have prevailed at the beginning of the fourteenth century, since John of Verona writes as follows in Book I of his manuscript *Imperial History*: “His body was first buried in a monastery near the city of Verona; then, in the time of King Pippin of Italy, son of the Emperor Charlemagne, it was laid with glory in the church of St. Zeno Major.” This arose from the preconception that the Basilica of St. Zeno had been erected entirely anew from its foundations, where previously no church had stood. Yet it is clear from the privilege of Louis and Lothair of the year 847, in Ughelli, p. 718, that it was renovated, not newly built: “How the glorious King Pippin, together with Rotaldus, bishop of that see, had renovated the church of St. Zeno, confessor of Christ.” This agrees remarkably with the words of the Zenonian monk, who writes that Pippin and Bishop Rotaldus conceived the plan of building a church, not in order to construct a new one somewhere else, but to enlarge the narrowness of the church—certainly an old church.

Moreover, not only the church but also the adjacent monastery is reported to have been rebuilt and renovated, as appears from another diploma of Louis the Pious, Pippin’s brother [Col. 0171D], p. 705. From these documents we learn that a monastery had been attached in ancient times to that old church in which Zeno’s remains first rested—a fact which no one can suspect concerning the church of St. Zeno *in Oratorio*. Nor should one press the difficulty arising from the miracle of the Adige, as though no church other than that called St. Zeno *in Oratorio* could be thought to have stood near the Adige and been exposed to the floods of that river. For, apart from the fact that a document in Ughelli, p. 699, names a monastery of St. Zeno situated outside the city of Verona beside the bank of the Adige—which document, though considered false, is nevertheless believed to have been fabricated and written before the eleventh century—the Adige, which with swift course erodes much and slopes somewhat to one side [Col. 0172A] while receding from the other, could without difficulty, ten or eleven centuries ago, have flowed close to the old church of St. Zeno, when the city walls had not yet been extended so far. Furthermore, the old church itself, in which St. Zeno’s body first lay, may have stood upon ground lower and more depressed than that on which the present new basilica stands, so that, in a great inundation, the waters of the Adige could readily have reached the windows of that church.

It is, moreover, credible that the church of St. Zeno *in Oratorio* is the one enumerated in Pacificus’s inscription among churches founded or renovated by him:

> Founder of churches, excellent renewer  
> of those of Zeno, Proculus, Vitus, Peter, and Lawrence, etc.

Pacificus, the very famous archdeacon of our cathedral church [Col. 0172B], died in 846, whereas the translation of St. Zeno had occurred at the beginning of that same century. It should also not be omitted that this translation of the sacred body, since it was made from the same but lower place to a higher and more magnificent one, ought more properly to be called an elevation. Thus Father Henschenius entitled it in Peter Calo’s *Miscellanies*, p. 75: “History of the Elevation of the Body of St. Zeno.” Yet examples are not lacking in which a mere elevation of a sacred body was termed a translation. Finally, it is clear from several ancient calendars—of which enough has been said in Dissertation I, chapter 3, §5, and in this dissertation, chapter 1, §2—that the church to which the holy bishop’s body was transferred was dedicated in the same century as the translation, or a little later, on the very day, the sixth day before the Ides of December, on which the Saint’s ordination was celebrated. Here we omit some miracles said to have occurred either during the translation itself or afterward; for anyone may read them, partly in the Zenonian monk and partly in Jacobus [CXLII] the priest, among the monuments to be appended to this dissertation.

We shall add only a few matters concerning St. Zeno’s body. First, Panvinio, who read many monuments now lost through the vicissitudes of time and drew not a few things from the *Imperial History* of John of Verona, says in Book V, chapter 25, of his *Antiquities of Verona*: “Under this bishop—that is, Adelbert—the nation of the Hungarians ravaged Italy, attacked Verona with great force, and, after destroying its suburbs by sword and flame, burned among them the basilicas of the saints Zeno, Proculus, Stephen, Nazarius, and Celsus. In this alarm, the abbot of St. Zeno and his monks carried the body of that saint, buried in their keeping—which they greatly feared might be stolen away—together with a chalice and cross of gold of the greatest value, granted to the monastery as a gift of Pippin, into the church of St. Mary Major, to be kept in its sacristy. But after Verona’s affairs had been restored to tranquillity a few years later, they brought them back to the former basilica, against the wishes of the canons, where they are preserved whole in their places to this present day.” Jerome della Corte likewise records this event in Book IV of his *History of Verona*, p. 209.

Now three Hungarian incursions into Italy are described by the contemporary author Liutprand [Col. 0173A]. The first occurred in March 900, according to Book II, chapter 4, of his *History*, vol. II of *Rerum Italicarum*, p. 345; for he relates it after the death of Arnulf, which happened at the end of November 899. The second occurred two years later, according to chapter 11 of the same book of Liutprand; for he states that it followed immediately after the blinding of Louis, son of Boso, which occurred at Verona in 902. The third followed the death of Berengar I, who died in 924; in that year he reports, in Book III, chapter 2, that the Hungarians burned Pavia. Since the first of these incursions is by far the most famous—the one mentioned for the year 900 by the Annals of Bertin, in the same vol. II of *Rerum Italicarum*, p. 576, and by other writers cited by Pagi under the year 900, nos. 17 ff.—and since Liutprand himself testifies that the Hungarians reached Verona in it, we believe that St. Zeno’s body was brought to the cathedral church in that year, 900. Whether Adelbert was then governing this Church as bishop, as Panvinio reports, is not for us to investigate and determine.

But it is not possible to establish when the same sacred body was restored to its place. Several monuments in Ughelli provide ample testimony that it was there a few years later, and that from then until these times it has been devoutly preserved in the same place. It will not be useless to indicate them. On p. 728, in the will of Bishop Notker, dated 922, the monastery of St. Zeno is mentioned, “where his buried body rests.” On p. 727, in a diploma of Hugh, King of Italy, dated 926, rights granted to the same monastery are confirmed, “where his holy body rests buried.” A similar formula is likewise found in a document of 1021 in Muratori, *Este Antiquities*, p. 129, and in many others mentioned by Marquis Maffei, vol. I of *Verona Illustrata*, p. 670; so much so that the missal of the monastery of St. Zeno, written in the fourteenth century, bears witness concerning the same Saint “who rests in the present church.” At the beginning of a book of Civil Law written at Verona in 1228, and recently published from a manuscript of the Chapter of Verona by Bartholomew Campagnola, archpriest of St. Cecilia, are these words: “To the honour of God and of His most glorious Mother, and of most blessed Zeno, in the consolation of whose most sacred body we rejoice,” etc. The same thought is repeated in other words in the prologue to the Statutes of Verona, written in 1450 by Silvester [Col. 0173D] Lando, chancellor of the city of Verona—to pass over other testimonies which carry down to our own age the constant tradition that this body has been preserved at Verona in the church of St. Zeno.

Yet none of this prevents some relics of St. Zeno from having reached other places. To pass over those which Bagata and Peretti mention in several Veronese churches in their work entitled *Ancient Monuments of the Holy Bishops of Verona*: Herman the Cripple says in his *Chronicle* under the year 1052, vol. III, part I, p. 272 of Canisius’s *Antique Readings*: “Relics of the blessed confessor Zeno were brought by Waltharius, bishop of Verona, into Alemannia, to the village of Ulm, and in these times shone forth by very many miracles.” So writes that contemporary German author [CXLIII], who died two years later, in 1054. Certainly more credit should be given to his testimony than to any later writer who, enlarging his account, alleged that Zeno’s very body, rather than relics, had been brought to Ulm.

In the church of St. Saviour of Monte Amiata in the diocese of Chiusi, relics of St. Zeno, together with relics of St. Proculus and other Saints, are said to have been deposited in the dedication of that basilica in 1036, in a document in Ughelli, vol. III, p. 624. In an inscription of Treviso dated 1082, published by Ughelli, vol. V, p. 515, relics of St. Zeno the confessor are also listed among the relics of many Saints deposited in the church of St. Nicholas near Treviso. In the inventory [Col. 0174B] of relics kept in Prague Metropolitan Church, Father Henschenius notes, in the additions to vol. II of April, p. 958, “a notable fragment of St. Zeno the bishop,” brought by Emperor Charles in 1370. At Pavia, relics of St. Zeno the bishop—who, as will be clear from what follows in the next chapter, was undoubtedly St. Zeno of Verona—are said by Father Romuald of St. Mary in *Sacred Pavia*, part III, p. 85, to be preserved among other Saints’ relics in St. Thomas’s. At Cesena, an arm of St. Zeno is said to be preserved in the most ancient parish church called by his name, in Bernardino Manzoni’s *Chronology of Cesena*, p. 62. We have not had leisure to note and investigate other instances of this kind. But for demonstrating the distinguished cult of the most holy bishop, we have employed more careful attention and inquiry; and since it will be especially glorious for our Author, it seemed proper to establish it more fully in a separate chapter.

## CHAPTER IV. ON THE MOST ANCIENT AND WIDESPREAD CULT OF ST. ZENO

### § I.—How much the antiquity and dissemination of a cult contribute to recognizing the outstanding merits and renown of Saints. The cult of St. Zeno in the Church of Verona is first set forth.
