If anyone wishes to gather by other means the virtues and merits of ancient Saints, which cannot in the least be known from their deeds themselves because of the lack of Acts, no more certain or distinguished evidence is available than [Col. 0174D] if one can demonstrate their ancient and widely diffused cult. For although holy men have always been held in veneration throughout the whole Church, and especially in those places where they performed noble labours for God and the Church, and although the days of their deaths were celebrated with solemn rite, yet in ancient times their cult was not ordinarily so exceptional that it became established immediately after their death and spread far beyond their native soil, unless their holiness and renown were very great indeed. This greatness must be judged proportionately greater where their cult is found to have spread both sooner after their death and more widely.

Hence the memory of many bishops, whom every ancient see venerates among the Saints, was formerly confined within narrow limits; and it was granted only to very few, who were more celebrated, to be honoured also in other cities and provinces. Lest anyone among the Saints suffer injury by comparison, we name no one; but what we have affirmed is most well established among those learned in ecclesiastical antiquities. The one conclusion relevant to our subject, and injurious to no one, of this chapter is that St. Zeno was among those whom antiquity honoured far and wide with every indication of exceptional cult [CXLIV]. This tends the more to his glory if he was only a confessor, not a martyr, since scarcely any confessor—but only certain martyrs—was ordinarily granted in ancient times a cult extending beyond his native land.

Among the several witnesses to a cult which may be enumerated, the chief are: the dedication of churches in the Saint’s name; proper offices and Masses; the insertion of his name into the Canon and litanies; and other things of that kind. If, by certain ancient and reliable documents, we establish that all these things concerning our Zeno were widely diffused from ancient times both at Verona and elsewhere, nothing will be lacking for demonstrating the distinction of his cult and holiness. Let us first speak of his cult at Verona.

Very many churches, both in the city and in the diocese of Verona, are above all called by the title of St. Zeno; it would take too long to enumerate them. Moreover, three feast days commemorating this Saint are recorded for several centuries in ancient monuments, and the Church of Verona annually observed them with solemn rite: the deposition of St. Zeno on the day before the Ides of April; his translation on the twelfth day before the Kalends of June [Col. 0175C]; and, on the sixth day before the Ides of December, in some monuments the dedication or consecration of St. Zeno, but in most the dedication of the Basilica of St. Zeno. In that basilica a fourth feast, of his ordination, was added; it is now celebrated in place of the feast of dedication. On this matter see more fully Dissertation I, chapter 3, §5, and this Dissertation, chapter I, §2.

Proper Masses, hymns, antiphons, blessings, commemorations, and responsories are found in the manuscript books of our Church, to be described among the monuments below. In three tenth-century sacramentaries, moreover, there is a proper Mass of St. Zeno with his own proper preface. One of them, written in the reign of King Otto and Bishop Wolfgang, displays the Mass of St. Zeno in first place, written in golden letters. Four sacramentary books, mentioned by us in chapter 2, §2, place Zeno’s name among the confessors in the Canon; and three of these, belonging to the Chapter, invoke him not so much in the *Communicantes* as after the Lord’s Prayer, as follows: “Deliver us, we beseech thee, O Lord, etc., and by thy holy apostles Peter and Paul and Andrew, and by thy blessed confessors Martin, Proculus, Zeno, and Benedict, with all the Saints, etc.” In the litanies likewise, which we have read in several thirteenth- and fourteenth-century manuscripts in the Library of the Chapter of Verona and elsewhere, as well as in certain prayers and blessings contained in the same manuscripts, St. Zeno is invoked among the other holy confessors.

In the Roman Capitular Order written in the time of the Emperors Louis [Col. 0176A] and Lothair and the Empress Ermengard, published by Francesco Bianchini in the *Prolegomena* to Anastasius, vol. III, p. 51, these words occur: “Hear us, O Christ . . . [for] our N., bishop chosen by God. ‘Give him life, St. Firmus’ [the transmitted text reads ‘Vita. III. S. Firme,’ and is materially uncertain].” The response is: “Help him.” “St. Proculus.” The response is: “Help him.” “St. Zeno.” “Help him.” The Veronese of old chose him as their greatest patron. Hence Bishop Ratherius, in his *Apologeticus*, p. 366, vol. I of Acheri’s *Spicilegium*, calls him “our particular patron”; and in his synodal letter to the priests, p. 377, “our special teacher and guardian.” He is likewise called patron and governor of the city of Verona in an imperial privilege of Otto, dated 988, in Ughelli, p. 745, and another of 996, p. 749. In both, the bishop of Verona is called “Vicar of St. Zeno” as a mark of honour. In the prologue to the Statutes of Verona he is designated by the titles patron, protector, and defender; and great cult was always decreed for him in several chapters of the same Statute and in other sections, as they are called, which may be seen in the city chancery.

Finally, it is worth noting a principal rite of the Church of Verona, still in force: secular clergy and religious of both sexes commemorate St. Zeno at Matins and Vespers when the commemorations are recited, and also in the collect *A cunctis*, after the commemoration of the Apostles Peter and Paul. This rite, prescribed by Bishop Gian Matteo Giberti in the Constitutions, title 2, chapter 2, is found prescribed more than two centuries earlier in the manuscript synodal constitutions of Bishop Theobald, confirmed in another synod by Peter Scaligero, as will appear from the monuments to be appended. From these facts, we believe, one may sufficiently gather how greatly St. Zeno was formerly honoured by the Veronese. Even now they cherish the same cult: on fixed days they make processions with offerings to his basilica, where the sacred body rests; and the whole city repeatedly gathers there in great numbers, that their great patron may intercede with God for help in their necessities.

### § II.—How widely the cult of St. Zeno spread in other churches of Italy

But St. Zeno was honoured with exceptional cult not only at Verona, to which he had rendered most distinguished services, but also from ancient times in other cities and provinces, not merely neighbouring but remote. Nothing could more strikingly establish the greatness and renown of his holiness. When Coronatus the Notary, having described the miracle of the Adige elsewhere mentioned by us, writes, “Thus reverence and awe toward Christ’s priest increased,” some may perhaps think that his cult began to spread beyond Verona after that miracle was made known by Pope St. Gregory in the *Dialogues*.

At Pistoia in Etruria, indeed, the cathedral church is said by Ughelli to have been dedicated to St. Zeno after the year 595, when the river of that city overflowed and, upon Zeno’s invocation, was wonderfully restrained. See vol. III of *Italia Sacra*, p. 284. The people of Pistoia seem to have been moved to invoke St. Zeno in that event by the recent and widely publicized miracle of the Adige. But the author from Pistoia from whom the additions to Ughelli were excerpted did not hesitate to affirm that Ughelli’s opinion rested on no foundation. While he criticizes certain parts of Ughelli’s account, which it is of no importance to recount here, he especially declares that the church had been dedicated to Zeno considerably earlier. It subsequently came about that the people of Pistoia chose St. Zeno as their patron and still honour his memory on two days: the day before the Ides of April, and with a more solemn feast on the sixth day before the Ides of December. How honourable this is to our bishop, everyone sees.

Certainly, although there can be no doubt that St. Zeno’s cult was promoted much more after the miracle of the Adige, which occurred in 589, yet that his memory and cult had spread widely beyond Verona before that time is demonstrated by what Agnellus relates in his *Ravennate Pontifical*, first published by Father Bacchini and recently included in the second volume of *Rerum Italicarum*. To remove all doubt, the matter must be taken from the beginning. The Goths, adherents of the Arian sect, occupied Ravenna in 493. Although Belisarius recovered the city in 540, it soon returned to Gothic power and remained under their rule until 552. In the following year Agnellus, a champion of the Catholic faith, ascended the episcopal throne of that city; and Emperor Justinian granted and conceded to him whatever could belong to the rights or rites of the Goths. Among other things, he enumerates altars and churches. Then the historian adds the following in chapter 2, p. 113: “Therefore that most blessed man reconciled all the churches of the Goths which had been constructed in the times of the Goths or of King Theodoric.” Enumerating these churches, both urban and rural, he includes among the rest a church of Blessed Zeno in Caesarea.

That this is the same as the church which Urban IV, in a bull of 1262 to the Cardinal Canons of Ravenna, published by Rubeus, Book VI of the *History of Ravenna*, p. 438, second edition, calls the church of St. Zeno at the Well, is indicated by the fact that there is still a road called “of the Wells” at the place where Caesarea formerly stood. Although no documents known to us have thus far definitely stated that the St. Zeno after whom this church was named [Col. 0177D] was St. Zeno, bishop of Verona, this may nevertheless be inferred from the fact that all other ancient churches elsewhere in the neighbouring provinces of Italy called after St. Zeno recognize no patron other than the bishop of Verona, as will appear from what follows. Furthermore, in the same diocese of Ravenna another church of St. Zeno once stood outside the Hadrian Gate; and John Ferretti of Ravenna, bishop of Lavello, expressly testifies that it had our bishop as patron. He died about the middle of the sixteenth century and left in manuscript decades of a History of Ravenna, read and mentioned by Ughelli, vol. VII, p. 743. Of these, so far as we know, nothing now survives except an index kept in the Vatican Library, codex 5833. In the index to the second Decade, p. 281, there is: “On the churches of St. Mercurialis, bishop of Forlì, and of Zeno of Verona, outside the Hadrian Gate.”

If, then, these facts make it probable that the church of St. Zeno in Caesarea was also named after the same bishop of Verona, and if Agnellus reports that it was reconciled by the archbishop, it was undoubtedly under Gothic power and among those churches which the Arian Goths—and especially Theodoric, the first king of the Goths in Italy—are said to have built. Therefore, between 493, when the Goths first occupied Ravenna, and 552, when they were completely expelled from that city, a church was dedicated to God at Ravenna in Caesarea in honour of St. Zeno of Verona [Col. 0178B]. Perhaps this building should be attributed to Theodoric himself, who ruled for a time at Verona and captured Ravenna in the same year, 493. Nor should one object that it seems incredible for an Arian king to have built a church in the name of one who had most vehemently opposed the Arians. For Agnellus likewise relates in the same chapter 2 that a church of St. Martin—also a most distinguished opponent of the Arians—had been built at Ravenna by the same king and was similarly reconciled.

Thus, a hundred years and somewhat more after St. Zeno’s death, and before the miracle of the Adige itself, the cult of St. Zeno had spread widely outside Verona. Since this happened to no other confessors except St. Martin of Tours—whose cult was, it is credible, greatly promoted by the Life written by Sulpicius, so that no relics of any other confessor, but only of martyrs, are said to have been dedicated in the churches of Ravenna—it may already be understood that St. Zeno, especially if he was solely a confessor, was of great renown in himself, having attained a comparable cult without being advanced by the commendation of any Life. This seems to be what Ratherius refers to in Book V of the *Proloquia*, p. 330, vol. IX of the latest collection of ancient writers by Father Martène, where he introduces certain persons wishing to name a very celebrated Saint and reports that they used to name St. Zeno and St. Martin, as if both were equally current in popular speech: “This is, they will say, a new prophet, a recent apostle, suddenly made an angel. This is holy Martin; this is holy Zeno, just now sent down from heaven.”

But let us pass from Ravenna to another place. For many churches dedicated to St. Zeno are read of elsewhere. Although their beginnings are not equally certain with what we have established concerning Ravenna, yet, since most were founded from time immemorial, it is sufficiently credible that at least some reach back to nearly the same period.

At Cesena, a monastery of Saints Lawrence and Zeno is named by St. Gregory, and we consequently learn that it was built before the seventh century from Letter 6 of Book XIV of Gregory, written in 604 to Marinianus, bishop of Ravenna. There, p. 1264, occurs: “Fortunatus, the bearer of the present letter, asserts that the office of abbot was committed to him by the late Bishop Natalis in the monastery of Saints Lawrence and Zeno, situated in the fortress of Cesena,” etc. This same monastery of Saints Lawrence and Zeno is likewise mentioned in certain documents written in the eleventh century and later, in Ughelli’s *Italia Sacra*, under the Bishops of Cesena, vol. II. That this St. Zeno, associated with St. Lawrence, the most celebrated martyr—which greatly contributes to demonstrating his renown—was none other than Zeno, bishop of Verona, is suggested not only by the argument advanced a little earlier concerning the Ravennate church of St. Zeno in Caesarea. In addition, a parish church at Cesena dedicated to our Saint still exists, mentioned by Bernardino Manzoni in his *Chronology of Cesena*, p. 62. Since several Cesenate monuments report that it was formerly a monastery, it is surely identical with the one celebrated in St. Gregory’s time and called after Saints Lawrence and Zeno. There was also another church of St. Zeno outside the gate leading to Cervia, subject to the parish church mentioned; it was later called by the title of the Visitation of the Blessed Virgin Mary. Three feast days of St. Zeno are still celebrated in the said parish church, the chief, however, being observed on the sixth day before the Ides of December.

At Pisa, we learn that there was formerly a very wealthy monastery bearing the title of St. Zeno, in an eleventh-century document, vol. III of Ughelli, p. 364. The church of this monastery later became a parish church, which still bears the same title. To make clear that it belongs to our Zeno, it celebrates his feast on the sixth day before the Ides of December with the rite for a confessor-bishop; that day is sacred to our bishop. Nor was Zeno’s memory honoured, or is it honoured, at Pisa only in that monastery—now parish church—but throughout the Pisan Church. It is now celebrated on the following day with the semidouble rite, his bishop’s office having been transferred in order to make room for the feast of the Conception of St. Mary. This surely derives from the most ancient cult of St. Zeno in that Church.

A chapel of St. Zeno located in the castle of Monte Casuli, in the diocese of Reggio in Emilia, is named in a document of Anselm, archbishop of Ravenna, dated 1156, vol. II of Ughelli, p. 37.

At Chiusi, it is likely that St. Zeno was honoured in the old church of the monastery of St. Saviour of Monte Amiata, since we observed at the end of chapter 3 that relics of this Saint were deposited there in 1036. Moreover, Ughelli published from a manuscript lectionary of that monastery the Life of St. Zeno composed by Coronatus the Notary; from the arrangement of the codex, it appears to have been read among the lessons of the sacred office.

Father Romuald of St. Mary states in *Sacred Pavia*, part III, p. 86, that at Pavia there is a church of St. Zeno built at least in the Lombard age: “Where,” he says, “an ancient shrine is seen standing at the Palace Gate. Although Breventano, *History of Pavia*, fol. 95, considers it to have been the work of the noblemen of Pavia, the Mediabarba, this must be understood of a restoration . . . for it is established in the manuscript history of Jerome Calcagnini [Col. 0180A] that it existed in Lombard times and was frequently visited with devotion.” He further observes that this church was formerly called by the title of Saints Zeno and Vitalis, but “is now called only by the name of St. Zeno.” Finally, he proves that a distinguished college of canons, presided over by a provost, existed there, and cites charters of the tenth century which mention this church. In the diocese of Pavia, moreover, there still stands in the place called Lardirago a church of St. Zeno, whose feast is celebrated on 8 December.

From the churches we must begin, in order to set forth the veneration in the Church of Milan. From the archive of the Cistercian Fathers of St. Ambrose at Milan, our Marquis Maffei published in Part I of *Verona Illustrata* two documents, IV and V [Col. 0180B]. One was written in the eighth year of Aistulf, king of the Lombards—that is, A.D. 757—and the other in the thirteenth year of Desiderius and the eleventh of Adelchis—that is, A.D. 769. Both mention the basilica of the most blessed Zeno, confessor of Christ, in the village of Campellione, commonly Campione, which Magnerada’s parents had built in the Milanese diocese and which Magnerada herself and Valderata had subsequently enriched with certain revenues.

It was moreover fortunate that a parchment codex was found in the library of the metropolitan Chapter, entitled: *On the Lives, Churches, and Memorable Things of the Church and Diocese of Milan*, by Goffredo de Bussero, parish priest of Rodello in the parish district of Appiano, who is said to have lived about the year 1300. In this codex, no. 456, there is a “Record of the Churches of St. Zeno” [Col. 0180C], listed in these words:

At Decino, the church of St. Zeno.  
In the parish district of Rosate, at Vermezzo, the church of St. Zeno.  
In the parish district of Corneliano, at Albignano, the church of St. Zeno.  
In the parish district of Olzate, at Cairate, the altar of St. Zeno; and the church of St. Peter and Syrus.  
In the parish district of Vatisio, at Lixago, the church of St. Zeno.  
In the parish district of Gallarate, at Crenna, the church of St. Zeno.  
At Gerenzano, the altar of St. Zeno.  
In the parish district of Vimercate, at Usmate, the church of St. Zeno and Margaret.  
At Vanzate, the altar of St. Zeno in the church of St. Paul.  
At Marliano, the church of St. Zeno.  
At Calugo, the church of St. Zeno.  
In the parish district of Agliate, at Zuccone, the church of St. Zeno.  
In the parish district of Dairago, at Castano, the church of St. Zeno.  
In the parish district of Travaglia, at Locimo, the church of St. Zeno.  
In the parish district of Incino, at Serzana, the church of St. Zeno.  
In the parish district of Brivio, at Porchera, the church of St. Zeno.  
In the parish district of [Col. 0180D] Missaglia, at Masciago, the church of St. Zeno.  
In the parish district of Bollate, at Garbagnate, the church of St. Zeno.  
In the parish district of Pontirolo, at Osio, the church of St. Zeno.  
At Trezzo, the altar of St. Zeno in the church of St. Protasius.  
Likewise, at Milan, two churches.

[CLXVIII] Thus, besides four altars, there were at that time two churches in the city of Milan dedicated to St. Zeno, and twenty in the diocese. Since then, however, the titular saints, as they are called, have occasionally been changed—as sometimes happens in new construction or restoration—so that now only one church is found in the city and nine in the diocese. Of these, one was built later and is not included in the catalogue just cited; nor is the one situated in the village of Campellione, attested by the two eighth-century documents. From this [Col. 0181A] one may infer not only how great and how ancient was the veneration of this saint, after whom so many churches in one diocese were formerly named; we also have no doubt that, had comparable codices of other churches been transmitted to us, we would likewise be able to discover more churches dedicated to our Zeno than are now called by his name.

But besides churches, Milan affords other monuments of ancient veneration. In vol. II, part II, of the *Rerum Italicarum*, Ludovico Muratori published two calendars of the Milanese Church, and the feast of St. Zeno is marked in both: in the first, p. 1029, “On the Ides of April: St. Zeno, bishop”; in the other, p. 1041, “Six days before the Ides of December: St. Zeno.” In vol. I, part II, p. 107, of the *Museum Italicum*, Father Mabillon, mentioning a manuscript antiphonary [Col. 0181B] of the Ambrosian Library in which are listed the feasts of all saints to be celebrated in the Church of Milan, testifies that he read among other entries the following:

“On the seventh day of December: the Ordination of St. Ambrose; afterwards St. Zeno, St. Syrus, St. Thomas.”

This sufficiently indicates that St. Zeno’s feast was celebrated at Milan on the sixth day before the Ides—that is, 8 December—as is marked in one of Muratori’s published calendars; after it was celebrated the feast of St. Syrus, five days before the Ides of December. Since only these four feasts before Christmas Day were marked in that antiphonary for December, and similarly only a few are recorded for the other months, Mabillon judged it worthy of notice that very few saints’ feast-days were formerly celebrated in the Milanese Church:

“These are minor matters,” he says, p. 109, “and perhaps some will consider them unworthy of report; but from them alone one may readily understand how greatly, in later times, the solemnities have increased—solemnities which were far fewer in the Milanese Church five hundred years ago, when that codex was written with a pen.”

But is it not an outstanding testimony to St. Zeno’s particular renown that he is found among those very few? Likewise, in the ancient breviaries of the same Church, the office of our Zeno is prescribed on the sixth day before the Ides of December, with three lessons. Ancient missal-books, both those published at Milan in 1522, 1548, and 1560, and that published by Pamelius in vol. I of his *Liturgica*, which is highly esteemed, as well as Vatican-Palatine manuscript 506, written in the thirteenth century, all exhibit the same proper Mass of St. Zeno [Col. 0181D], with its own preface. See p. 438 of Pamelius’s edition.

At Rome, however, in the library of the Cistercian Fathers of Holy Cross, there is an Ambrosian Missal printed by Christophorus of Regensburg in 1482. In it, likewise, on that December day, the proper prayers and preface of our Bishop are read; but the preface, at least as memory now suggests, differs greatly from the one published by Pamelius, since it says nothing about Gallienus’s daughter.

Yet this deserves notice: in the Ambrosian Breviary printed in 1549, the following is read on p. 129 for the seventh day before the Ides of December, after the second Vespers of St. Ambrose:

“Then commemoration is made of St. Zeno. Others make it of the Conception of the Virgin, as at her Nativity, with the psalmody of St. Ambrose and the psalmody of St. Zeno; let each act according to his own devotion.”

Hence it is clear why the office of St. Zeno, formerly performed on the sixth day before the Ides of December, gradually became a commemoration when room began to be given to the office of the Conception of the Blessed Virgin Mary. The same happened in other churches; consequently, in later offices and in the Mass only the commemoration of St. Zeno is noted, as is still read in the Milanese Missals and prescribed in the Ordinary of the same Church. This too has recently been altered, in that St. Zeno is distinguished by the title of martyr.

The diocese of Como now counts three churches of Zeno: the first, a parish church, at the place called Monte Olimpino; the second at Mandello; and the third, a parish church [Col. 0182B], at Salorino under Swiss rule. There, on the sixth day before the Ides of December, the feast is celebrated with great solemnity under the rite of a bishop-confessor, with the canons of Balerna assembling.

[CXLIX] If we wished to speak at length of the city and diocese of Brescia, what a broad field would open before us! Fifteen churches of the diocese acknowledge St. Zeno as their patron: namely, the churches of Ono, Odolo, Heno, Goglione Inferiore, Brione, Borgo San Zeno, Maclodio, Boldeniga, Monticelli di Brusati, Caino, Paitone, Ronco, Scarpizzolo, Gratacasolo, and Sale Marasino. Of these, the first nine celebrate his feast on the sixth day before the Ides of December under the rite of a confessor; the rest, under the rite of a martyr, on the day before the Ides of April. In the city of Brescia itself there are two churches of St. Zeno. One was formerly an ancient parish church [Col. 0182C]; the other is still an important parish, where his office, celebrated under the rite of a confessor on the sixth day before the Ides of December, is said to have been transferred a few years ago to 12 April, the rite of confessor being changed to that of martyr.

Yet although that parish church changed its rite not long ago, after the example of the Church of Verona, nevertheless the cathedral church, when proceeding there in the Rogationtide stations, still recites the collect and antiphons of a confessor. The body of St. Rusticianus, bishop of Brescia, who died in 585, is said to be buried in this church. If he was buried there immediately upon his death, this church was exceedingly ancient, and the veneration of St. Zeno there was very ancient indeed.

In the diocese of Trent seven churches venerate [Col. 0182D] our Zeno as patron: one at Tassullo in the Val di Non, in the village named after its patron; the second at Lomaso, in the village of Fiavé; the third at Tenno, in the village of Cologna. All three celebrate the feast on 8 December with a solemn Mass and a large procession of the people. There are, moreover, two churches in the parish of Muri; and to one of these, in the place called *il Palù*, the people of Muri flock in great numbers when any calamity threatens, and especially when rain is needed, a procession being proclaimed during the summer; they experience the Saint’s patronage to be present for them.

Finally, in the village called Nomi, and also in the parish of Nogaredo near Rovereto, two other very ancient churches of St. Zeno, bishop of Verona, may be seen. To the latter [Col. 0183A], the rector of Pomarolo proceeds on St. Zeno’s day, with the people entrusted to him, in the sacred rite of procession. Father Benedict of Cavalese, of the Strict Observance of St. Francis, who communicated these notices to us, also informed us that in the village called Aldeno, not far from Trent toward the west, although its church now has another titular saint, it nevertheless formerly acknowledged and venerated St. Zeno, bishop of Verona, as its chief patron, as the recent rector of that church declared when consulted by letter. It is highly probable that this happened also in other churches, as we noted in the Milanese churches.

The same Father Benedict, after making a careful search in the episcopal library, further affirmed that there is found there a manuscript breviary bearing this note:

“This book formerly belonged to Lord George of Liechtenstein, bishop of Trent, 1420.”

A calendar is prefixed to this breviary, in which St. Zeno is mentioned twice in a second hand: “On the day before the Ides of April, St. Zeno, bishop of Verona: the day of his death or deposition”; and “on the sixth day before the Ides of December, the translation of St. Zeno, bishop of Verona.” Here *translation* was written in error for *ordination* or *dedication*. The same is read in another manuscript breviary belonging in 1449 to Johannes Hinderbach, bishop of Trent, and also in other manuscript breviaries and missals preserved in the library just mentioned. In a manuscript martyrology for the use of the church of St. Vigilius, written in 1435, the feast of St. Zeno, bishop and confessor, is marked on the same days, but no mention at all is made of a translation.

[Col. 0183C] From two documents it is clear that St. Zeno’s feast was celebrated in the Church of Trent. The first is a manuscript lectionary from the Chapter archive, in which the Life of St. Zeno is read divided into nine lessons, with this heading: “On the feast of St. Zeno, bishop and confessor.” The second is the perpetual calendar for the use of the Church of Trent, published in 1554 by Donato Faeti at the command of Cardinal Christopher Madruzzo, bishop of that Church. It is composed and arranged in thirty-five tables, and in every table, from fol. 11 to fol. 250, repeatedly gives the following for 16 December: “Zeno, bishop and confessor, the eighth of this month,” namely December, indicating that his feast was to be transferred from 8 to 16 December. Finally, a codex of the episcopal library attests that the memory of the holy Bishop was observed in the litanies of the same Church among the holy bishop-confessors [Col. 0183D].

[CL] We have recently learned of five churches at Bergamo dedicated in honour of St. Zeno: four parish churches, at Cene, Trescore, Albino, and Cenate; and a fifth, an oratory in the parish of Curnasco.

In the diocese of Vicenza, three parish churches—at Colzè, Resecco, and San Zeno in the Bassano district—have from time immemorial been dedicated to the same Saint. There are also two oratories bearing the same title: one very ancient, hewn into the rock of a mountain at Costa Fabrica; the other in open country, dependent on the parish of Arzignano.

[Col. 0184A] Nor does Padua lack veneration for the holy Bishop; for in the Paduan diocese we find five ancient churches dedicated in his name: at Molvena, Montagnana, Zovon, Altichiero, and Monselice. The parish church of the last place, dedicated to St. Thomas the Apostle and St. Zeno, confessor of Christ, is mentioned in several documents relating to the Venetian monastery of St. Zacharias; the oldest of these, from 994, is cited by Ludovico Muratori in *Antiquitates Estenses*, p. 128. Throughout the Paduan Church, moreover, the office of St. Zeno, under the rite of a bishop-confessor, is still celebrated on account of his unquestionably ancient veneration, assigned to 8 December; but because of the feast of the Conception of Blessed Mary, it is transferred to the first unimpeded day.

At Mantua there is a parish church of St. Zeno [Col. 0184B], said by Father Donizone, in his *History of the Church of Mantua*, part I, book IV, p. 225, to have been built by Matilda. He also observes that before Matilda—that is, before the eleventh century—there was in that place an oratory named for the same Saint, in which the monks of St. Andrew celebrated the offices.

From monuments of the Church of Treviso, published by the distinguished Canon Antonio Scotti in the additions to Ughelli, we learned that three churches in the Trevisan diocese were formerly dedicated to St. Zeno. Subsequently the same Canon, who was to illustrate the succession of the bishops of Treviso with many new documents, informed us that two additional churches of St. Zeno are found in the same diocese; he also supplied other documents pertaining to each of the five churches of the same Saint, which [Col. 0184C] must not be omitted.

In the letter of Pope Eugenius III to Boniface, bishop of Treviso, A.D. 1152, in Ughelli, p. 527, is mentioned the parish church of St. Zeno at Ruvico, a village on the banks of the Anasso, which from time immemorial has celebrated the feast of St. Zeno its patron on 12 April, under the rite of a bishop-confessor. Another church mentioned in the letters of the same Eugenius III is situated in the Asolo district and gave its name to the castle of San Zeno. There Alberic da Romano, brother of Ezzelino, was besieged and captured, as Rolandino relates, book XII, chapters 13, 14, and 15. It is a parish church dedicated in honour of our Zeno. Its solemn feast-day is observed on the sixth day before the Ides of December under the rite of a bishop-confessor. On 12 April, however, a feast called one “of devotion” is celebrated in memory of the death of the same patron; likewise, on the twelfth day before the Kalends of June, a similar feast is celebrated in memory of his translation. Formerly, on both days, both the office and Mass were performed with solemn rite.

In a brief of Alexander III of 1170 for the Chapter of the Church of Treviso, in Ughelli, p. 526, are named “the neighbouring lands which,” he says, “you possess at San Zeno”; but no memory of this church now remains. Within the boundaries of the parish church of St. Martin, nearly a thousand paces from Treviso, there is still a small church sacred to St. Zeno. That it is very ancient, and was formerly a monastery of nuns subject to the abbot of the great monastery of St. Zeno at Verona, is inferred from a charter of 1238 indicated by the aforementioned Canon. In it Lady Agnes, a nun of that Trevisan monastery [Col. 0185A] of St. Zeno, with the consent of the same abbot, gave to Brother Matthew, Prior of the entire Order of Hermit Friars, all the rights that she possessed in that church of St. Zeno, retaining for herself, for as long as she lived, only the usufruct; the Hermit Friars were thus to enter possession of those rights only after her death. That this indeed took place in his own time is apparent from another charter discovered and collected by the same Canon.

In this church, moreover, sacred rites in honour of the bishop-confessor are still performed. At Postioma, likewise in the Trevisan diocese, there survives a church of St. Zeno, where the feast is celebrated on the day before the Ides of April. There the same Saint is honoured with special reverence and a distinctive devotion of the neighbouring peoples. For on the fourth Sunday of every month during summer [Col. 0185B], a procession having been proclaimed, very great crowds flock to that church in order to pray for his intercession with God for the produce of their fields.

A document from a manuscript, published in the most recent edition of Ughelli, vol. V, p. 1102, testifies that a church of St. Zeno had long since been built at Grado in the ninth century. Fortunatus, Patriarch of Grado, who died in 826, recounting what he bequeathed and did, lists among other things: “At St. Zeno, an altar all around, and one platform above it.”

At Torcello, the veneration of St. Zeno is demonstrated by a church called by his name in a diploma of Frederick I, issued to Leonardo, bishop of Torcello, in 1177, p. 3 of the *Prodromus* prefixed to the *Diplomatic Codex of the Law of Nations* [Col. 0185C] published by Leibniz.

Here we shall also add an observation which should not be omitted, drawn from a parchment manuscript of St. Mary *de Domo* in the city of Verona. Although this codex was found at Verona and, as clear indications show, was written in the eleventh century, the saints mentioned in its prefixed calendar and litanies show that it belonged specifically to the Church of Torcello, or to another of those located in the Venetian lagoons. Thus this book reveals not only that St. Zeno’s feast was celebrated in that church—whether at Torcello or another Venetian lagoon city—on the sixth day before the Ides of December; it also presents his name among the confessors in the rite for administering penance:

“St. Augustine, St. Nicholas, St. Zeno, St. Proculus,” etc.

Since the chronological order is by no means observed in these litanies in listing the other saints [Col. 0185D], it is not surprising that St. Zeno is placed before St. Proculus contrary to the ordering of other litanies. Since, moreover, the feast of Zeno the bishop is entered in the calendar just mentioned on the sixth day before the Ides of December, we believe this led Peter de Natalibus, bishop of Equilio, living in those regions, to think, after observing that the commemoration of this Saint was marked on that day in churches known to him, that the same day was Zeno’s date of death. Accordingly, in his *Catalogue of Saints*, book I, chapter 43, he wrote: “He passed in peace to the Lord on the sixth day before the Ides of December.”

At Canale in Friuli, a village under imperial jurisdiction, there is a church of St. Zeno. A fourteenth-century manuscript breviary belonging to the Church of Cividale has this entry in its calendar for the sixth day before the Ides of December [Col. 0186A]: “The Conception of St. Mary the Virgin; Zeno, bishop and confessor.” From this it is known that, after the introduction of the feast of the Conception, that church made a commemoration of the same Saint, whereas formerly—as happened elsewhere—it celebrated the office of St. Zeno.

What shall we say of the Church of Aquileia? Father Henschenius observed, p. 70, that in its ancient calendar the feast of St. Zeno, bishop and confessor, is entered for 8 December, to be celebrated with three lessons at Matins. Something similar was formerly done at Venice until the sixteenth century, as is clear from Peretto, who cites printed Venetian calendars in his Latin scholia on the *Life of St. Zeno*, p. 81, edition of 1598. There he likewise cites other printed calendars from Brescia and other cities which listed, on 12 April, “St. Zeno, bishop of Verona.” Canon Scotti, whom we mentioned recently, reported in letters that in a manuscript calendar of his Church of Treviso from 1525, which he notes was copied from an earlier one, the following is read on 8 December:

“St. Zeno, bishop and confessor, ninth lesson; the Conception of Blessed Mary, double feast.”

The calendar of the Church of Modena, written at the beginning of the eleventh century, published by Bacchini after Agnellus and most recently reprinted [CLII] in vol. II, part I, of the *Rerum Italicarum*, p. 218, marks on the sixth day before the Ides of December the feast of Dalmatius and Zeno, sufficiently indicating that offices for them were held at Modena. In the monastery of Monte Cassino too, the memory of our Saint was made in the sacred offices, as may be known from the calendar belonging to that monastery [Col. 0186C] and published in vol. VII of the *Rerum Italicarum*, p. 936, where his feast is marked.

Indeed, we learned that the memory of the same Saint was observed throughout the whole Congregation of Monte Cassino from the calendar prefixed to the monastic psalter of the Order of St. Benedict, Congregation of Monte Cassino of St. Justina of Padua, printed at Venice in 1606. There, under 8 December, we read:

“The Conception of the Blessed Virgin Mary, greater double; and commemoration of Zeno, bishop and martyr.”

The same commemoration, but with the title only of priest and confessor, is likewise read on the same day in a manuscript Benedictine breviary, written about the beginning of the fifteenth century, which belonged to a monastery at Pavia. We do not wish to omit here that the calendar of a manuscript breviary of the Friars Minor, held in the library of the Church of Trent, similarly reads [Col. 0186D]:

“8 December: the Conception of St. Mary the Virgin, and St. Zeno the confessor.”

From this we know that the holy Bishop was venerated outside Verona even by the Order of Friars Minor. Since that manuscript breviary was bought at Augsburg by the most celebrated Bernard Clesius, cardinal and bishop of Trent, it is probable that it belonged to a convent of Friars Minor in Germany. Thus this testimony bears more directly upon establishing the spread of St. Zeno’s veneration outside Italy, which will be discussed in the following section.

But, to return to our purpose, we have cited breviaries and calendars, not martyrologies. For in the calendars and breviaries of churches or religious orders, the names were generally entered only of those saints whose offices were performed there—as is clear from the fact that most days are vacant in them, so that ferial offices might be said. Conversely, martyrologies listed very many saints to whom no special veneration was rendered. Since, then, St. Zeno was venerated not only in those churches or cities of which he was patron, but generally in other cities and churches and in congregations of religious orders, either by a proper office or at least by a proper commemoration—which it is credible was substituted for the old office of St. Zeno in favour of the Conception of Blessed Mary—who would not at once understand the special veneration and astonishing renown of so great a bishop? [Col. 0187B]

These are the facts concerning the veneration of St. Zeno throughout Italy which we were able to gather partly from published Italian monuments and partly through letters from certain friends. We do not doubt that, had it been possible, through time or friends, to apply greater diligence in investigation, other churches of Zeno and other testimonies of ancient veneration would have been found in other cities and provinces as well, where no opportunity of inquiry and no suitable time was available. For among the cities from which we sought information, none has yet been found that did not furnish some monuments of this kind. Therefore, from what we have touched upon concerning a few Italian cities, readers should infer the rest for themselves; and, when they recognize that the veneration of St. Zeno was ancient and widely spread throughout all Italy [Col. 0187C], let them also admire the ancient, very rare, and only seldom shared renown of our Patron.

## § III.—On the Veneration of St. Zeno as Spread beyond Italy

What if the fame and veneration of holy Zeno, not merely within the otherwise very extensive boundaries of Italy, but beyond them, had from ancient times spread far and wide? It is indeed regrettable that it was not convenient, through correspondence, to seek information from various regions, by which we have no doubt we would have found him both patron of many more churches and inserted in many more calendars or litanies. Yet from the few things collected from some published books, anyone may judge how much more we could have adduced if it had been permitted to inspect the monuments of more churches outside Italy [Col. 0187D].

Certainly, we learn especially from the Church of Freising that Zeno’s veneration formerly spread into Germany. St. Corbinian, first bishop of Freising, who died in 730, according to Aribo, the fourth bishop of Freising, in the eighth century, in his *Life* of St. Corbinian, published by Mabillon, *Acts of the Saints of the Third Century*, part I, chapter 20, p. 48 of the Venetian edition—St. Corbinian, I say—built a basilica at Mais, in the diocese of Freising in Bavaria, and “placed there the patronages of Valentinus and Blessed Zeno, and dedicated it in their honour.” Hence, as Father Meichelbeck observes in vol. I of the *History of Freising*, in the *Life of St. Corbinian*, § 8, p. 16, St. Zeno, bishop of Verona, chosen by Corbinian as his *Evergetes* (“benefactor”), has been venerated down to this day by an annual office in the Church of Freising.

Nor was St. Corbinian the only person in Germany to honour St. Zeno with such special veneration. Joseph III, bishop of Freising, elected in 749, founded the monastery of Isen in honour of St. Zeno, bishop of Verona, as the same Father Meichelbeck relates, pp. 50 ff., where he cites two pages of donations made to the church of St. Zeno. Concerning the place, he observes on p. 52: “In our age Isen is a municipality of Freising; and secular canons have possessed for many centuries the collegiate church, as it is called, of St. Zeno.”

Next, at Halle in the diocese of Salzburg—the place now called Reichenhall—there is the celebrated monastery [Col. 0188B] of St. Zeno. Viguleius Hundius treats of it at greater length in vol. I, p. 9, of the *Metropolis of Salzburg*, and vol. III, p. 505; likewise Fathers Francis and Paul Mezger in the *History of Salzburg*, book IV, chapter 10, p. 383, and book VI, p. 1255; Father Hansiz treats it more briefly in vol. II of *Germania Sacra*. It was formerly a parish, which afterwards, upon the establishment of a provostship, was entrusted to Regular Canons by Conrad I, Archbishop of Salzburg, who died in 1147, as Hansiz demonstrates.

In this monastery three feast-days of St. Zeno are still celebrated with distinctive prayers, to be described among the monuments. These derive from three ancient proper Masses. There is also there a silver statue of St. Zeno, made in 1480, in whose breast is contained a noteworthy portion of the sacred relics of the same bishop, bearing this inscription:

“Jawbone, with one tooth, of St. Zeno the Bishop.”

The name of our Bishop reached the Swiss as well. Hartmann, a monk of St. Gall who flourished in the ninth century, wrote in verse litanies to be sung in procession on Sundays. Henry Canisius first published them in vol. V, p. 732, of *Antique Readings*, and in the most recent edition in vol. II, part II, p. 193. Not only does Ekkehard mention these same litanies in the *Life of Notker*, but Metzler, also a monk of St. Gall and a friend of Canisius, testifies that in his own time they were used on stated days:

“Pope Nicholas III canonized these litanies, and our people—the monks of St. Gall—publicly sing them on the Rogation Days.”

The venerable Cardinal Tommasi published them again under the name of a hymn from a Vallicellian manuscript codex, in his work entitled *Ancient Books of Masses of the Roman Church*, for Monday in the Lesser Litany, p. 118. In these litanies St. Zeno is listed among the confessors together with our St. Proculus, likewise a bishop. If St. Proculus is placed after Zeno, no one should doubt that this was done for metrical, not chronological, reasons. Here are the words of the litanies themselves:

> Sylvester, Damasus, Gregory, and Ambrose,  
> Hilary, Zeno, Maximus, and Leo,  
> Martin, Proculus, Caesarius, and Eusebius,  
> Pray for our many sins.  
> Sacred order of the chief confessors,  
> By your aid make your people safe on every side.

[Col. 0189A] Nor did Zeno’s renown escape the Gauls. In the monastery of St. Benedict at Fleury there is a codex more than nine hundred years old, from which Father Martène, part III of *On the Ancient Rites of the Church*, book III, chapter 15, published an order among various rites for aiding the dying; it contains litanies prescribed to be recited at the agony of death. In these litanies Zeno is found entered together with Proculus, his predecessor. That the codex was for the use of the Gallican Church is shown by the listing among the bishops of Gaul in this order:

“St. Remigius, St. Proculus, St. Zeno, St. Anianus, St. Audoenus,” etc.

For the remainder, if desired, see Martène, p. 592.

Since a manuscript missal belonging to the Church of Angers and intended for its use contains a special Mass [Col. 0189B] of St. Zeno—the fuller account of this codex will be given in the Notice to the *Monuments*—it is not improbable that St. Zeno’s veneration was propagated there.

Other documents from other regions which we might consult either have not yet been published or have not reached our hands. Since we first conceived the plan of treating this subject, moreover, we have not been able, owing to pressure from the printers, to examine all the documents that are in Verona itself. We add this in assistance to those who may someday wish to add other material to this chapter: wherever a church of St. Zeno or any document of his veneration is found in the West, anyone wishing to conclude with certainty that it concerns our Zeno should attend not only to the fact that the very many churches of St. Zeno throughout the West thus far discovered by us are not to be referred to anyone other than St. Zeno, bishop of Verona, and likewise that no other Zeno has been found inserted in litanies. With regard to churches, he should also investigate, if possible, the feast-day celebrated in them; he will find that it falls either on 12 April, or on 8 December, or perhaps somewhere on 21 May—three days sacred to no Zeno other than ours. In litanies or similar prayers, moreover, he will generally be listed among the confessors together with St. Proculus, bishop of Verona; or, if [Col. 0190A] mention is found only of St. Zeno, bishop or confessor, it may not rashly be inferred from the whole body of monuments concurring in the veneration of one Zeno of Verona that he too must be regarded as no other Zeno. By the same reasoning, we do not hesitate to affirm this concerning the altars named for St. Zeno which we have learned of in various churches, although we thought it necessary to refrain from investigating and reporting them, lest the chapter become excessively long.

Meanwhile, that the discussion may return whence it began—or rather, may come to an end—if the veneration of St. Zeno is so ancient that it has been possible to find its monuments transmitted about a century after his death, and if these have been found not at Verona alone but in other cities and provinces of Italy, in Germany, in Switzerland, and in Gaul [Col. 0190B], where we have found very celebrated churches, outstanding monasteries, colleges of canons named for St. Zeno, his patronage invoked with God in litanies and public prayers, and himself adopted from ancient times as the special patron of villages and even cities; where he has been venerated by offices, processions, and other expressions of devout religion not only in churches dedicated in his name but in whole dioceses—things found to have fallen to the lot only of very celebrated and very few other saintly confessors—who would not form the highest opinion of the holiness and renown of St. Zeno of Verona, proved by so many testimonies of ancient, widespread, and manifold veneration?

And if one recalls that in the tenth century Ratherius, in the testimony cited in the preceding section, joined him by a customary formula to St. Martin, bishop of Tours, who was always reckoned among the most celebrated saints [Col. 0190C], one will by no means think that excessive honour was attributed to him by the people. Our concern in considering these things more carefully and proposing them for consideration has been not to diminish in any respect the glory and veneration of any of the other saints, but to awaken and promote the veneration of so great a Patron, which has gradually grown cold among some, as often happens with ancient things, because they are less aware of his former renown.

[CLV] **MONUMENTS CONCERNING ST. ZENO, BISHOP OF VERONA**

[Col. 0189]

**NOTICE**
[Col. 0189D] I. Before presenting the monuments relating to the life of St. Zeno, together with the Masses, hymns, and other liturgical documents proper to the same Saint which we have found in ancient books, it is desirable to preface a few remarks concerning some less well-known matters. Coronatus the Notary, author of the first monument, was the first to commit the Life of St. Zeno to writing. Perettus, in his Latin scholia on the Life of St. Zeno [Col. 0190D], numbered him among the more recent writers, and made him almost contemporary with Peter de Natalibus, who flourished in the fourteenth century. Yet that he lived before the translation of St. Zeno’s body, which took place at the beginning of the ninth century, is inferred not only from his making no mention whatever of that translation, but especially from the fact that, in no. 8, he reports the sacred body of Zeno as still resting in his own time [Col. 0191A] in the basilica in which it had first been laid after death; and the Life written by him is found in a Rheims manuscript which, as we have shown in the general preface, was written before the ninth century.

Moreover, since he relates the miracle concerning the inundation of the Adige described by St. Gregory the Great, which occurred in the year 589, it must be held with Fr. Henschenius that he flourished in the seventh or eighth century. He is styled “Venerable” not so much in the Rheims manuscript as in the Lobbes manuscript seen by Molanus; and in the latter he is additionally called “most Christian,” as also by John, priest and Mansionary of the Church of Verona, who mentions him in book I of the manuscript *Imperial History* in these words: “Coronatus, a most Christian man, flourished at Verona; he composed the Life of blessed Zeno in a moderate [Col. 0191B] style.”

This Life is read as inserted in ancient lectionaries, as in the parchment capitular manuscript at Trent and in two Vallicellian manuscripts, III and VII; and it was in use before the Zenonian Monk, of whom we shall shortly say more, wrote a fuller Life. Molanus testifies in his annotations on Usuard that he saw it at Lobbes: “At Lobbes there survives the narrative of the venerable Coronatus, the most Christian notary.” Perhaps it was brought there by Ratherius, bishop of Verona, who withdrew to Lobbes in the tenth century. Indeed, after we had written this, letters came from Lobbes to Scipione Maffei reporting that, in a codex written in Ratherius’s own hand, there is included among much else a *Sermon on the Life of St. Zeno, Bishop*. Peter Calo had included the same work in his *Collectanea*, as Fr. Henschenius noted in the Barberini manuscript, [Col. 0191C] p. 73. Boninus Mombritius first published it, about twenty years before the beginning of the sixteenth century, in vol. II of the *Lives of the Saints*. Then, in 1653, Ferdinand Ughellius reprinted it from a manuscript of the Abbey of St. Saviour of Monte Amiata in vol. V of *Italia Sacra*. Finally, from seven manuscripts, [CLVI] Fr. Henschenius included it in vol. II for April, p. 70. We have generally followed the reading of the most ancient Rheims codex.

In this manuscript, however, as also in the Lobbes manuscript written by Ratherius, this Life is entitled a *Sermon*, though improperly. That in Coronatus’s time exceedingly little about the life of St. Zeno—of which no older document had given an account—was generally known and preserved in popular memory is more than sufficiently proved by the fact that he writes almost nothing of Zeno except a few miracles, and those [Col. 0191D] themselves derived from common tradition, as you will sufficiently gather from note 3. Thus, after scarcely touching in the first chapter upon the Saint’s life, he immediately passes to miracles, writing near the end of that chapter: “Let all peoples who desire his miracles hear”; and again at the end, according to the manuscripts of Henschenius, Ughellius, and Mombritius: “Behold, of his many miracles, I, the useless Coronatus the Notary, have set down what I have learned,” etc. Such accounts, however, as preserved and reported by the people, are often stuffed with added little tales. While older and more genuine documents are lacking, we could not omit this one. Finally, we shall give briefly the notes which, in the proemium to Dissertation III, we undertook to append to this Life; from them certain incredible or false things, derived from [Col. 0192A] popular rumor and mixed with true matters, will be recognized, and it will at the same time become clear how slight is the authority of those who, from this monument, insist that St. Zeno was contemporary with the emperor Gallienus.

II. This Life of St. Zeno, written by Coronatus, as soon as it first came to light, immediately captivated and attracted the minds of men, who until then had read nothing concerning the holy Bishop committed to writing. They accordingly judged it worthy not only of insertion in lectionaries and of having antiphons for the sacred offices extracted from it, but also of being rendered into rhythm by some unknown writer. Bartholomew Campagnola, chancellor of that same chapter, communicated this rhythm, found in a capitular manuscript of the ninth century, in which, although no distinction of verses is observed; he also showed us other items from the capitular manuscripts. But since this Rhythm repeats the same matters as Coronatus, and since its author, often bending Coronatus’s very words into rhythmic form, employed a pen of little success, and met with a most careless copyist, who seems to have corrupted some things and perhaps even omitted two strophes—so many are lacking for the strophes to correspond to the same number of letters of the alphabet prescribed to himself by the author while composing the Rhythm—[Col. 0192B] for these reasons, I say, the Rhythm did not appear worthy of publication.

Nevertheless, so that it may become evident that everything committed to writing concerning Zeno in the age of Gallienus was taken from Coronatus, we judged that this ancient document, hitherto unknown, should not be omitted. Its author will appear to have followed Coronatus exactly, [Col. 0192C] and the same judgment must therefore be made concerning other monuments of later ages. The reading *Ignōtas Patrias* in Coronatus, as we shall print it from the Rheims manuscript, is confirmed by this hymn. It will also be useful to detect there certain seeds of the Italian language, such as the particle *perque*, which we pronounce in Italian *perché*. Certain principal peculiarities will further be noteworthy: for instance, *imperii*, *imperium*, etc. are consistently written in place of *imperatoris*, *imperator*.

[CLVII] III. There will follow the history of the Translation of St. Zeno, carried out at the beginning of the ninth century. The author of this history, who prefaced it with a Life of St. Zeno, seems to identify himself as a monk who lived for some time in the monastery of St. Zeno itself. For shortly after the beginning of the Life he says: “Nor must those things be passed over which religious men with whom we stood saw with faithful eyes”; [Col. 0192D] and from this he also shows himself conversant with documents which he could have read only in that monastery. Nor is it credible that he digressed into praises of that same monastery for any other reason than that it concerned him very closely. Only the words “with whom we stood,” and the passage in which he means the very monastery of St. Zeno, suggest that, when writing, he was no longer in that monastery. Yet these facts can be reconciled with the foregoing observations if we say that he was indeed a monk of the Zenonian monastery, but later moved to one of the smaller monasteries subject to it, where he composed this little work.

Led by these arguments, we have judged that the author of the work in question should, for purposes of distinction, be called the Zenonian Monk; though we do not wish anyone to trouble himself over this if he thinks otherwise. Two characteristics guide us in determining this author’s date. In first calling the emperors “our Emperors,” if he wrote the work at Verona, as we probably believe, he reveals that he lived when Verona was under imperial dominion, from which it was removed toward the end of the twelfth century. Then, in recounting the final miracle, he mentions the discovery at Mantua of Christ’s blood, which is reported to have been discovered twice: first in 804, and again in 1049. See Donesmondi, *Ecclesiastical History of Mantua*, book III, p. 139 ff., and p. 195 ff. Since that miracle cannot belong to the first occasion—when perhaps St. Zeno’s translation had not yet taken place—as a miracle performed after the Translation [Col. 0193B], nor by much can the Monk’s lifetime be assigned so early, since he recalls gifts made to the monastery of St. Zeno by several emperors after Pippin, the final miracle concerns the second discovery of the blood.

Indeed, while narrating this miracle, the author mentions a lofty tower which was being built. The time when construction of this tower began is clearly taught by an inscription placed at the foot of the same tower, in which it is recorded as begun in 1045. This accords very well with 1049, while construction was still proceeding. Thus the monk’s lifetime must be placed between the middle of the eleventh century and before the end of the twelfth. If, however, at least that final miracle was among those which the religious men with whom he had lived saw with their own eyes, it seems fairer to assign his lifetime to the end of the eleventh century.

[Col. 0193C] These two little works of the monk are copied in a manuscript lectionary of the twelfth century owned by Bartholomew Campagnola, archpriest of St. Cecilia. But if that Zeno, provost of the monastery, who was surnamed Solomon on account of his merit in religion and wisdom—as is reported in one of the miracles—is the Solomon mentioned in the inscription carved in the basilica of St. Zeno in 1178, situated in the wall where the notable porphyry vessel is kept, then the age of this monk would at some point have to be placed later. Yet this Solomon may be someone other than Zeno the provost. And if the miracles were reported by the author in chronological order, Zeno Solomon, mentioned by him, must have lived before 1049, when Christ’s blood was discovered at Mantua and the final miracle occurred through Zeno’s intervention. [Col. 0193D] But enough about the monk’s age.

The author of the history of the Translation prefaced it with a Life of St. Zeno, largely taken from Coronatus the Notary, which in the manuscripts of St. Zeno and in the sacred offices almost took the place of Coronatus’s Life. It is read, namely, in many manuscripts after the sermons [CLVIII] of St. Zeno: in the Tolentino, Zenonian, and Pompeian codices; likewise in the two Vatican manuscripts 1233 and 1234, of which we have recently learned; and, besides, in manuscripts of another class, the Musellian, Saibantean, and Maffeian; and, to omit other codices, in Bartholomew Campagnola’s lectionary and another belonging to the nuns of St. Mary of Campo Marzo.

In Campagnola’s lectionary, since eight numbers appear in the margin, the Life is divided into eight lessons. But in the manuscript of the nuns of the Order of St. Francis, the Life is divided into nine lessons, and the Translation likewise into the same number. Yet it should be noted that in books of this kind, the author’s prologue, which is read in other manuscripts, is omitted; the beginning of the Life is one thing in the nuns’ manuscript and another in Campagnola’s. The beginning found in the nuns’ manuscript is found exactly the same in another Brescian lectionary mentioned by Scipione Maffei, p. 316 of the *Diplomatic History*, also in Vallicellian lectionary no. III, thought to have been written in the thirteenth century, and in a very ancient parchment lectionary kept in the archive of the chapter of the Church of Trent. These three lectionaries, however, contain the Life of St. Zeno written by Coronatus, not by the monk.

[Col. 0194B] It would be excessively tedious to reprint the monk’s Life, which repeats the same material from Coronatus. It will therefore suffice to point out what the monk added beyond Coronatus. He represents Zeno as flourishing not only in the time of the emperor Gallienus but also in that of St. Dionysius, Roman pontiff. In relating the miracle by which Gallienus’s daughter was freed from a demon, he adds certain details with a more expansive pen: for example, the three fish which the holy Bishop, returning from fishing, gave as a gift to envoys sent by the emperor, and the fourth which they took away, which could not be cooked with the others. He records that a dead man carried off by the river was restored to life; though Coronatus omitted this miracle, the Anonymous Pipinian bears witness to it, as we have restored from two manuscripts.

Then he introduces the Saint speaking: for the first sermon he transcribes all of tractate 32, book II, and a fragment of tractate 42 of the same book; for the second, the beginning and end of tractate 6, book I. Finally, he recalls at length many things said by him to his followers near the end of his life, and declares that he—whom he made contemporary with Gallienus—died, according to the Maffeian edition, on the day before the Ides of April, in the three hundred and first year of the Lord. [Col. 0194C] But since this year-date is absent in Bartholomew Campagnola’s codex and in the Musellian manuscript, while in the Pompeian manuscript it is read in the margin in a later hand, it is quite credible that it was not written by the monk-author himself, but crept from a marginal note into the text of certain manuscripts, as it is read in the manuscript used by Maffei and in Vatican 1233.

Here it is worth noting in passing that, even if this date was added by others, as seems more probable, and although we recall reading it also in other codices of later authors of comparatively lesser age—for instance, in Saibantean manuscript work 658, which Blasius Rossetus, writing on the bishops of Verona, dedicated to Peter Lippomano, where under Zeno he has: “The eminent pontiff and father of his country died on Saturday, the day before the Ides of April, in the year 301 from Christ’s birth”; and similarly, in an older manuscript of the monastery of St. Zeno, written around the middle of the fifteenth century, in a catalogue of the holy bishops of Verona this note by another later hand is read: “He died in the year 301, whose body rests in it”—the opinion that St. Zeno’s lifetime reached into Gallienus’s reign was therefore not so universally fixed that others did not think differently.

Hence also, in a manuscript of the Musellian Library [Col. 0195A], which among other things contains Ferreto’s poem, later published in vol. IX of *Rerum Italicarum*, St. Zeno, eighth bishop of the Church of Verona, is said by the author of the work [CLIX] providing a brief account of two hundred cities to have lived about the year 322. There a certain Lexicon and Chronicle of Irenaeus Pacificus are cited—not that ancient archdeacon, as some have believed, but another, much later man, whom the author calls mansionary of the greater Church of Verona. It is not sufficiently clear whether what is related concerning Zeno belongs to the testimony there quoted from the Lexicon or not.

Furthermore, we have found two fifteenth-century authors who represent St. Zeno as living in the fourth century and as a contemporary of Ambrose: namely Flavio Biondo, who in region 9 of the *Italia Illustrata* declares that his writings breathe the Ambrosian eloquence which he imitated; and St. Bernardino of Siena, who, in sermon 47, article 2, chapter 3, p. 244, vol. I of the Lyons edition, recounting a certain amusing anecdote which he attributes to St. Zeno, calls him a cleric [Note: [Col. 0195D] We judge that Bernardino’s words should be set down here, since they produce an anecdote attested, so far as we know, in no other document—not because credence should be given to it, founded as it is at least on the false hypothesis that he was St. Ambrose’s disciple, but lest we omit anything concerning St. Zeno mentioned by others.

“St. Zeno, bishop of Verona,” he says, “when he was a cleric of Blessed Ambrose, a holy and pure young man, and was following blessed Ambrose through the city, though he was mature in gravity of character, laughed with unusual lightness. When the holy bishop noticed this and wondered, he asked the reason for the levity. The innocent young man said to him: ‘I saw, Father, a demon sleeping upon the train of that woman who went before us. And when she lifted the train so that she might not be soiled in that muddy crossing, the sleeping demon rolled down into the mud; and I see him wholly defiled.’ When St. Ambrose considered this, recognizing purity of heart and keenness of understanding in his cleric, he gave thanks to God and humbly acknowledged that he had not possessed such keenness in seeing a demon. Hence perhaps Bishop St. Zeno is customarily carved and painted with a smiling face.”] of St. Ambrose before his episcopacy. Although these two testimonies make Zeno younger than is proper, they nevertheless contribute greatly to showing that the fifteenth-century opinion concerning St. Zeno’s age was not that which proclaims him to have lived under Gallienus.

But to return to the Zenonian Monk: if anyone wishes to read in that monk what we indicated a little earlier and what is not found in Coronatus, he may consult Maffei’s *Diplomatic History*. There Maffei published entire, among several monuments, this monk’s work comprising the Life and Translation of Zeno [Col. 0195C], omitting the final miracles which Henschenius had published from Peter Calo’s *Collectanea*. We shall give only the history of the Translation, absent from Coronatus, collated with and supplemented from the two Musellian and Pompeian manuscripts. We have spoken more fully of this Translation in Dissertation III, chapter 3, where we conjectured that the monk used some older document, although he added certain less credible or fabulous matters from popular report, such as the story of the blackbird. Marquis Maffei has quite plausibly inferred, p. 319, that the occasion for this little tale was given by an ancient Christian metal lamp in the form of a dove, preserved underground in the church of Melsine, concerning which the populace still spins tales.

[Col. 0195D] IV. Since, moreover, after the Zenonian Monk, the priest Jacob wrote the miracles of St. Zeno in hexameter verse, adding three other miracles which occurred later besides those recounted by that Monk, we shall append that fragment containing these three miracles, so that nothing relating to [Col. 0196A] Zeno may be lacking. That this priest Jacob was an author of the fifteenth century is clear from the second miracle which we shall present, where he mentions a lawsuit pursued by a Veronese before the Venetian Senate, in which he obtained victory. It is therefore clear that Verona was already at that time under the dominion of the Venetian Republic, which occurred only in the fifteenth century.

From these things it may also be conjectured that Benedict and Catharina Saracena, whom the third miracle mentions, were parents or relatives of that Antonio Zeno Saraceni, whom Sixtus IV appointed archdeacon from being a Veronese cleric in 1475, according to a document in Ughellius, p. 945. Jacob’s complete poem, consisting of 244 verses, was once inscribed upon a tablet; it was then published by Father Cherubino Lazzaroni in the book entitled *The Shepherd of Verona*, and by Henschenius in vol. II for April, p. 76.

V. To these monuments relating to the life and miracles of St. Zeno we shall add Masses and other matters concerning the day and night office which we have found proper to St. Zeno in liturgical books; a few comments on them are necessary. We have obtained six Masses. The first is read in three ancient manuscript sacramentaries of the Church of Verona kept in the Capitular Library. One of these, complete above the rest and composed with the utmost care, is recognized as written before the eleventh century because in one prayer it names “our king Otto”; it presents the Mass of St. Zeno in first place, written most elegantly in golden letters [Col. 0196C].

The same Mass, but without the preface and final prayer, is also found in another sacramentary of a certain school called St. Mary of the House, p. CIII, on 12 April. From certain characteristics this book appears to have been written in the eleventh century. For on p. II an Easter table is described which begins with the year 1064; it can therefore be considered written about that same year, just as, by similar reasoning, the venerable Cardinal Thomasius determines on p. 40 the date at which the manuscript antiphonary of the Angelica Library of the Augustinians was composed.

Indeed, in the margin of the same page there is a note in a later hand mentioning Pecorarius, who was podestà of Verona in 1223, in these words: “The years of the Lord will be one thousand two hundred and twenty-three when he rules Verona.” This Mass is likewise contained, without preface and final prayer, in another missal of the chapter of Verona written near the end of the twelfth century. It is placed on 8 December under this title: “Dedication of St. Zeno.” Nor are any other Masses for St. Zeno found anywhere else in that Missal, because this day—the sixth day before the Ides of December—is the first of the three dedicated to St. Zeno, since the Missal begins with Advent; the same Mass was therefore read on the other days as well.

There is also a manuscript Missal of about the fourteenth century belonging to the monastery of St. Zeno Major, in which four Masses of the same Saint are presented: three for the three feast-days, one for the day of his deposition, another for the day of his Translation, a third for the day of his ordination, while a fourth, assigned to no feast, is shown to be fairly general. In it, however, this first Mass is assigned to the day of deposition under the title “Deposition of St. Zeno.” Thus this first Mass is contained in manuscripts in six sacramentary books of the Church of Verona, and is consequently recognized as the one generally used in our Church.

[Col. 0197B] The second Mass, for the Translation of St. Zeno, we have found only in the manuscript missal of the Zenonian monastery. But the third Mass is read in the tenth-century sacramentary written in the reign of King Otto, as stated above, on the sixth day before the Ides of December [CLXI], and is prefaced by the heading: “Sixth day before the Ides of December, birthday feast of St. Zeno.” Yet in the prefixed Calendar for that day is noted: “Dedication of St. Zeno, confessor and bishop.” It is also found, much corrected, in the aforementioned missal of the monastery of St. Zeno, with the heading: “On the feast of St. Zeno in the Advent of our Lord Jesus Christ.”

The same Mass, through an error assigned to the fifth rather than sixth day before the Ides of December, and bearing the same title as in the Capitular manuscript, is also found in Vatican codex 3806, written in gold and vermilion, which is judged to date from about [Col. 0197C] the ninth century. It bears this title: “Book of Sacraments set forth by St. Gregory, Roman pope, published from the authentic copy in the library of the bedchamber.” We believe this is the codex used by Angelo Rocca when he published the Gregorian sacramentary from a manuscript Vatican copy which he calls most ancient, in the Roman edition of St. Gregory; there indeed the same Mass of St. Zeno is read, with the same error, on the fifth day before the Ides of December, vol. V, p. 265. It may therefore be inferred that this Mass, though corrupted by certain errors, is very ancient and was adopted also by other churches where St. Zeno was venerated. In this Mass it is especially to be noted that St. Zeno’s episcopate is mentioned, as though the ordination of the holy Bishop were celebrated on that day.

The fourth Mass is supplied by the same Missal of the monastery of St. Zeno and is recognized as common, both because it is marked by no title and assigned to no day or feast, and because its first prayer, *Propitiare*, is attributed in another manuscript of the same monastery to St. Lupicinus, bishop of Verona, buried in the basilica of St. Zeno. In a thirteenth-century capitular manuscript containing lessons, prayers, and antiphons to be recited for Saints and through the year, the same prayer is read before the Common of Confessors with this heading: “Prayer of St. Zeno or another.” The fifth Mass, written in a manuscript of the school of St. Mary of the House among the saints of December, is recognized as pertaining to the eighth day of that month.

Before proceeding from the Masses of the Church of Verona to other things, we shall append [Col. 0198A] the remaining items to be said in Mass, which are placed after the first three Masses in the frequently praised Zenonian manuscript and seem to have been common to them. They appear, however, to be proper to the monks. The Church of Verona is known to have used another introit and so forth from the frequently mentioned *Carpsus*, which for the day of deposition has the following: “At the introit: a. [that is, antiphon], ‘You have protected me, O Lord’; p. [that is, psalm], ‘Hear, O Lord, when I cry’; alleluia of the Resurrection; alleluia, alleluia; R\. [responsory], ‘Holy confessor Zeno’; off. [offertory], ‘You have set, O Lord’; co. [communion], ‘The righteous shall rejoice.’”

This will be followed by the Ambrosian Mass, which we have extracted from the Ambrosian Missal published by Jacobus Pamelius, vol. I of the *Liturgicon of the Latin Church*, p. 438, and also from three other Ambrosian Missals printed in 1522, 1548, [Col. 0198B] and 1560. Father Joseph Blanchini, who, from his exceptional devotion toward our Patron, worked diligently to procure and send us various documents from certain sacred codices, especially Roman ones, informed us that this sixth Mass is found in Vatican Palatine manuscript 506, written around the thirteenth century. Its title is: “Ambrosian winter and summer missal in honor of blessed Maurice, who was Milanese by nation and is said to have been a disciple of St. Ambrose.”

Two facts suggest that this codex belonged to the Church of Angers. First, in the prefixed Calendar, on 13 September, these words are read: “Deposition of St. Maurice, bishop and confessor. And he lies in the city of Angers, which is on the borders between France and Brittany, and to which this Missal belongs.” Then, at the end of the book, a later hand has appended this note: “I, Gervasius, priest of Bruzano, chaplain [CLXII] of the Church of St. Maurice, and Maziconius of St. Mary Major, donate this my Missal to the Church of St. Maurice for the usefulness of singing Mass, on condition that the official priests of this church always remember this small benefaction done by me, and that no bishop, priest, or neighboring persons have permission to give, sell, pawn, or transfer it,” etc. From this it appears that this Missal was in use in the Church of Angers.

Here it is further worth noting that the first two prayers of this sixth Mass are read in the Ambrosian Breviary of 1549. Finally, we shall add three prayers which are still recited on the three feasts of St. Zeno in the College of Canons Regular of St. Augustine called Reichenhall, and which seem to have been excerpted from ancient Missals, as we noted in Dissertation III, chapter 4, §3.

[Col. 0198D] VI. Thus far concerning the Masses. With regard to the Office, we shall first give antiphons with responsories from a capitular manuscript of about the tenth century; the same are contained in the fifteenth-century manuscript of the nuns of St. Mary of Campo Marzo and are also listed in the *Carpsus*.
