Any variations will be indicated in the notes below. Then, from another tenth-century capitular manuscript, we shall add short lessons and two hymns proper to St. Zeno and used in our Church. Next, from a fifteenth-century manuscript of the monastery of St. Zeno, we shall add three hymns used by the Benedictine monks [Col. 0199A]; these are those now used in the Veronese office with a few alterations.

Barthius wrongly believed that the third hymn, already published by the Veronese editors from two manuscript breviaries of the nuns of St. Lucy, had been prefixed to the codices of St. Zeno’s tractates: book II, *Adversaria*, chapter 12, and book XIV, chapter 20. We shall subsequently publish another hymn read after St. Zeno’s tractates in Vatican manuscript 1235. We shall not give the prayer customarily recited in the office of the Church of Verona. Although it is not indicated in the manuscripts praised above, it is gathered from another capitular manuscript containing prayers for the Hours, and from the Martyrology of the nuns of Campo Marzo, that the prayer was *Deus qui nos*, described in the second place in the first Mass [Col. 0200A]. From two manuscripts concerning the sacred offices of the Zenonian monastery, however, we learn that Zenonian monks used, in the offices for each feast, the first prayer of each Mass as the proper prayer for that feast. Finally, we shall give ancient suffrages concerning St. Zeno and some other matters; we shall state in their proper place from where these have been taken.

[Col. 0199]

[CLXIII] SERMON OF THE VENERABLE CORONATUS THE NOTARY ON THE LIFE OF SAINT ZENO. (C)

[Col. 0199B] I. In those days [Note: [Col. 0199C] The prologue in Ughellius and Henschenius differs from this; the latter observes that in most manuscripts the same material is presented with different phrasing but without any harm to the history. The prologue’s reading in Mombritius generally approaches the Rheims manuscript.] in the province [Note: [Col. 0199C] In Mombritius, incorrectly, “of Tuscany.”] of Italy, in the city of Verona, in which the acts of blessed Zeno shone forth, [Note: [Col. 0199C] Take care not to suppose from this word *evolvimus* (“we unfold”) that anything concerning Zeno’s deeds had been written before Coronatus, from which he drew what he committed to writing. For, apart from the uncertainty whether this prologue belongs to Coronatus himself, since nothing of the sort is read in other manuscripts and editions, *evolvimus* seems to be used for *descripsimus* (“we described”) in a certain barbarous manner of speaking, as may be inferred from the context. Moreover, in the proemium in Ughellius, vol. V of *Italia Sacra*, p. 680, it is made quite manifest in a wholly different fashion that nothing had been written except in the minds of the people; from these alone were extracted—or, to use the aforementioned word, “unfolded”—the things which Coronatus put into this Life. We append here the complete words of that proemium, since they sufficiently suggest and confirm what we have said elsewhere: that nothing concerning St. Zeno’s virtues had been handed down, but only concerning his miracles, of which popular memory alone nevertheless remained:

“Although we are not found capable of handing down to you in a fitting narrative all the miracles by which Zeno, bishop of the Veronese, shone forth, yet it was judged more right that, despite the offense to the sequence of discourse, we should say something about him, rather than that he, who once shone sufficiently through his silent virtues, should remain obscure in the darkness of ignorance. For we know that he is rightfully owed the company of the Saints, but is much more honored by human observances when his deeds, which ought to be recited, have been written for the understanding of the peoples.”] we unfold the virtues of so great a man. For the human mind is thus disposed to investigate the lives of Saints: as one who, thirsty and scorched by the heat of the sun, longs for streams of springs; or one who desires to hear most welcome news; or again one nourished on feasts of delights, placed on a distant journey, who longs to reach the satisfaction of his mind. So also I, though I am unable to set forth everything which so great a man did, whether in his manner of life or in miracles, nevertheless do not cease to relate as much as I can attain in part, lest some reader should disparage it, or a hearer listening to the reader should detract with an idle mind, since it is written: “Those who return evil to me [Col. 0199C] for good speak ill of me.”

And because the Lord himself said to those who do good: “Before I formed you in the womb, I knew you; and before you came forth from the belly, I sanctified you.” For he was blessed from the cradle [CLXIV] and [Note: [Col. 0200C] These words are absent in Ughellius; similar words, however, are read in others, though we trust that no learned person will be persuaded by them.] sanctified from the womb, and deserved to attain this: that through a holy life he might deserve to be a shepherd among the people. [Col. 0200B] And therefore, because the sound of his manner of life went forth into all the earth and his holiness shone out, let all peoples who desire his miracles hear.

II. For he was dwelling in [Note: [Col. 0200C] This monastery, of which mention will be made several times below, if Coronatus is to be believed, was thronged with many monks living together with the holy Bishop. But monasteries did not begin until the fourth century and are therefore incompatible with Gallienus’s reign. Nor do we believe that St. Zeno lived in a monastery in the fourth century. For although a women’s monastery at Verona was founded through Zeno at that time, as we have shown in Dissertation III, chapter I, §3, we have received no tradition of a men’s monastery. Nor can it be said that the bishop acted as abbot of a monastery; at most, he may have existed with his clergy.

Nor should anyone object that the Acts of SS. Firmus and Rusticus mention a monastery in which St. Proculus, predecessor of St. Zeno, is said to have hidden during the very persecution of Diocletian and Maximian. For there *monasterium* means a remote place in which one person lived a solitary life; Du Cange confirms this ancient meaning from St. Jerome, Cassian, and others. Marquis Maffei also observed from Agnellus that private oratories were called *monasteria*. Here, however, Coronatus perhaps introduced the name “monastery” because a monastery had in his own time been added to that church in which the sacred Body rested before the Translation. As the populace is prone to claim antiquity for things, it would be said that St. Zeno himself had founded and inhabited it. And because, in a later age, several of those who devoted themselves to this monastery were called Zenos in honor of the holy Bishop, Coronatus shortly afterwards, certainly from common report, declared that several monks bearing the same name lived with St. Zeno in that monastery in no. 12.] a monastery, in a more secluded place, in the town of Verona, beseeching the Lord through continual fasts and frequent prayers that He might deign to open for him an entrance for preaching to the peoples. Finally, day by day he devoted himself to turning the minds of men toward the love of Christ.

Truly, because the Holy Spirit was a teacher within him, as Truth itself speaks through itself, saying: “For it is not you who speak, but the Spirit of your Father who speaks in you.” And again: “I am the good shepherd, and I lay down my life for my sheep.” Thus he was gracious in speech, gentle in meekness and bearing, [Col. 0200C] so that God was praised in him by all who came to him; and he was so ardent that they promptly abandoned idols and believed in the Lord Jesus Christ.

### III.

At the same time, when the same man had gone out from the monastery and was fishing in the river Adige near the city of Verona, which lay at no great distance,

> [Note: Hence the holy bishop is usually portrayed with a fish hanging from his pastoral staff or from a fishing rod. This need not be rejected altogether. For perhaps, cultivating poverty, as appears from Tractate 44, Book II, no. 2, he procured his livelihood by fishing, as Paul did by the labor of his hands, perhaps recalling that even after Christ’s resurrection the apostles devoted themselves to catching fish, with the Lord himself approving.]

he raised his eyes and saw opposite him a certain man seated in a cart, with oxen yoked to it, being submerged in the river. For he was borne along with such speed that it was evident to all that this had been effected by the devil’s craft. And indeed, when the holy man lifted up his eyes and saw it, he recognized that this was the devil’s work. Raising his hand aloft, he repeatedly made the sign of the holy Cross, saying: “Get behind me, Satan; do not destroy the man whom God created.” When the devil saw this sign, he vanished like smoke, uttering cries and an impious shriek, as though he had plunged down from a high cliff, saying: “Although now you do not permit me to win the souls of men, nevertheless I am prepared to go into the unknown lands which lie all around, to hinder you.”

> [Note: “Unknown” in Mombritius, Ughelli, the Zenonian monk who copied Coronatus, and in all the manuscripts cited by Henschenius. In the Reims manuscript it was indeed *notas* (“known”), but *ig.* was added above in the same hand, so that it should be read *ignotas* (“unknown”).]

Then Saint Zeno of God said: “May the Lord not permit you to act against his servant.”

> [Note: Is it not incorrectly written in the Reims manuscript? We have corrected it from the other editions.]

### IV.

When these things had taken place, he departed with howling and shouting. Hastening on, the demon entered the house of Gallienus at Palatium,

> [Note: We conjectured in Dissertation I, chapter III, §4, that the Palatium mentioned in Antoninus’s itinerary between Trent and Verona, over which a certain Gallienus presided, may be meant here. The house of Palatium will therefore be the house of that Gallienus who governed in that Palatium.]

seized his daughter, who at that time was her parents’ only child, and began cruelly to torment her.

> [Note: Many writers mention that the emperor Gallienus had two sons; but we have learned of a daughter only from an inscription in Gruter, p. 275. Yet Coronatus calls this daughter “only” three times, as though Gallienus then had no offspring besides her. This certainly cannot be true of the emperor Gallienus, who, from the time he became emperor until his death, had sons mentioned in writers, coins, and inscriptions. Therefore this designation of an only daughter, if it rests on any true foundation, plainly establishes that this Gallienus was someone other than the emperor.]

Then the miserable father, together with the entire royal household, was afflicted and turned to grief because she was being so cruelly suffocated. While she was seized by this harsh torment, the demon began to cry out through the mouth of the emperor’s little daughter, saying: “I shall not depart from this body unless Bishop Zeno comes and I depart by his command.”

> [Note: In the other manuscripts and editions it is generally written “the king’s daughter,” and thereafter “the king,” and so forth.]

As soon as the emperor Gallienus heard this, he sent officers to seek out the holy man and began anxiously to search for him. Then, by the emperor’s command, soldiers went to the man of God. He was sitting upon a stone near the monastery and fishing in the river. When the soldiers came, since he was unknown to them, they earnestly began to question the holy priest of God, saying: “Who are you, man of God? Tell us whether you have seen Bishop Zeno, whom we seek by the emperor’s command.”

He answered them: “Although there are many men in our monastery bearing the name you mention, nevertheless tell me for what purpose you have been sent. For I, though very insignificant, am nevertheless a servant of Christ; I am called Zeno.”

> [Note: In Ughelli: “there are many men.” See note 5.]

Then the soldiers, consulting one another, said among themselves: “Why do we converse at length? Let us tell this man why we have been sent.” They answered and said: “The emperor asks for you and wishes to see you.”

Zeno answered: “Why does the emperor, who never ceases to be the enemy of all Christians, wish to see my lowliness?”

But they said: “The emperor asks you to restore to health his daughter, who is tormented by a demon and is his only child.”

He said to them: “The Lord Jesus Christ is almighty. Go; behold, I shall follow you, because it is fitting that the wonders of God should be made known to all.” Having said this, the soldiers departed.

### V.

> [Note: “The holy priest rose . . . and went to the palace,” as though it were a short distance from the city of Verona; this confirms our conjecture indicated in note 9.]

The holy priest then rose, prayed, and went to the palace, where the emperor was tortured and afflicted on account of his daughter. The holy bishop of God, while making his journey there, arrived before the soldiers who had been sent.

> [Note: The Reims manuscript read *quia*; we have corrected it from Ughelli.]

When the sign of the Cross had been made and Christ’s priest entered the palace, the demon immediately began to cry out through the mouth of the little girl: “Behold, Zeno, you have come to drive me out, and because of your holiness I cannot remain.” Having said this, the priest took the girl’s hand

> [Note: Thus from Henschenius; in the Reims manuscript: “saying.”]

and said: “In the name of the Lord Jesus Christ I command you: come out of her, demon.”

But he began to cry aloud, saying: “Although I am driven out from here by you, I shall go to Verona. You will find me—and those in whom I dwell—standing in the square awaiting you.” Thus Christ’s priest restored the emperor’s daughter to health.

### VI.

When the emperor Gallienus saw what had happened, he was seized with amazement and offered to the holy priest the royal crown which he wore upon his head, saying: “I can please such a physician, who has restored my only daughter to health, with no other gifts unless I offer him the crown which I possess.”

> [Note: In Gallienus’s age emperors had not yet adopted a precious crown, much less wore one upon their heads. See the cited Dissertation I, chapter 3, §4.]

While this was taking place, the multitude of people who had assembled at the palace turned from pagan error and believed in Christ Jesus our Lord. They begged Christ’s priest to teach them the way of salvation and that they might receive baptism for the remission of sins. But when the priest received the emperor’s crown, he immediately distributed it to the poor, saying: “If the Lord performs lofty deeds, glory must be rendered to him.”

### VII.

After these things had happened, the most blessed Zeno requested that permission be granted him to destroy all idols and to build churches in Christ’s name. The emperor agreed to all that he asked.

> [Note: Is it credible that a pagan emperor consented to this? In the same Dissertation, paragraph 4, we have shown it to be a fable.]

> [Note: Thus in Henschenius; in the Reims manuscript: “which.”]

After this, the priest entered the city of Verona and fearlessly preached the word in Christ’s name, so that the idols of the devil might be destroyed and churches built in Christ’s name. When this was done, the raging multitude of pagans continually acted so as to bring suffering upon Christ’s servant. But Christ, watchful in his servants, conquered the falsehood which pure faith held in the heart (*sic*).

### VIII.

When these things had been completed, he performed acts of salvation by interceding for the people, as from his earliest age he had been accustomed to do in love for Christ. While he was doing this earnestly, by God’s will he was received into peace not long afterward. Because he had become renowned among all the people through miracles, a certain man of Gallienus’s family built a basilica in honor of God and of the holy priest himself, not far from the river, where his holy body now rests; and that venerable place also shines with miracles in Christ’s name.

> [Note: Some text had to be added from Mombritius and Henschenius. The latter notes on these words: “Thus most manuscripts. Some read: ‘A certain man of Gallienus’s family’; or, with Mombritius, ‘A certain God-fearing man’; or, ‘A certain most noble man of Gallienus’s family.’ But Ughelli’s copy and the sole manuscript read: ‘King Gallienus built a basilica.’” Yet either account is equally false, whether this deed is understood of the emperor Gallienus or of one of that emperor’s kinsmen, since all his relatives were killed after his own death, as Aurelius Victor recorded.]

### IX.

After some time, when at the same city of Verona the people, together with clergy and priests, had devoutly assembled on the feast-day of his birth for the solemnities of the Mass, the river Adige—upon whose bank his body is known to have been buried—suddenly swelled in such a great flood that the water of the river rose to the windows, or even to the roof.

> [Note: Mombritius and Ughelli read “on the holy day of his Nativity”; Henschenius, “on the holy day of Nativities”: an obvious error, since the holy bishop died on 12 April and this miracle occurred in October. For more on this see Dissertation 3, chapter 1, §4. Moreover, in the margin of the Reims manuscript, beside this account of the miracle, three letters appear—G. P. C.—with a line over each. We have no doubt that the first two, G. P., signify Pope Gregory; let others conjecture concerning the third. For the account is frequently found expressed in almost the same words in his *Dialogues*. Yet those words, insofar as they derive from Saint Gregory, are absent from the other manuscripts of Mombritius, Ughelli, and Henschenius and may seem to have been inserted into Coronatus’s text. Nevertheless, the same addition, in precisely the same words, is likewise found inserted in an ancient lectionary of the Church of Trent, which presents this same Life of Coronatus divided into nine lessons.]

Although the doors of that church stood open, the water did not enter it at all; thus the standing water closed off the church door, as though that liquid element had been transformed into the solidity of a wall. When the people who had assembled there in honor of God and the holy priest saw this event, they cried out that they were perishing from hunger and thirst.

Since many were enclosed inside, the entire church was surrounded by a mass of waters, and they had no direction by which they could escape, fearing that there they would fail from thirst and hunger, they came to the church door to drink. They drew water which, as I said, had risen to the windows, and yet did not flow at all within the church. Thus it could be drawn as water, but could not flow as water. Standing before the door to display to all the merit of the Confessor, it was water for assistance and, as it were, not water for invading the place. Although there was so great a flood of water, a wall seemed to have risen all around the church, and no water entered inside.

How great, we may suppose, was the power of his prayer before God, when the water itself stood in the appearance of a wall and did not dare enter the venerable place. Therefore reverence and fear concerning Christ’s priest increased, so that, if faith requires it, the sick may be healed and the possessed may come and be set free. And if anyone invokes his holy name with true faith, his petition is granted without doubt. For many, coming from distant regions, lay bodies oppressed by illness at his tomb and, through his intercession, return to their homes with health and joy, through the grace of our Lord Jesus Christ, to whom be honor and glory unto ages of ages. Amen.

> [Note: In Mombritius, Ughelli, and Henschenius the following is added: “Behold, of his many miracles, I, Coronatus the notary, though useless, have briefly included what I have learned with certainty, lest I create weariness for readers or hearers.”]

[CLXIX]

## RHYTHM CONCERNING SAINT ZENO

From a capitular manuscript of approximately the ninth century.

Let princes hear, let peoples hear,

How great are the deeds performed by the holy man,

How great the things God grants to those who believe in him.

> [Note: **RHYTHM.**—Manuscript: “Let princes hear, let peoples hear.” Coronatus, at the end of no. I: “Let the peoples hear who desire his miracles.”]

Kind and gentle Bishop Zeno,

Confessor of the Lord and shepherd of the people:

How many graces he deserved from God!

> [Note: Manuscript: “Kind, dismiss Zeno Bishop.” We have corrected *gentle* from Coronatus, no. 2.]

Bishop Zeno remained chaste,

Sitting on a stone, fishing in the Adige.

> [Note: Manuscript: “on a stone.”]

How great the things God—

Opposite, he sees oxen with a cart,

And also a man drowning in the river.

> [Note: In the manuscript: “Opposite he sees oxen with a cart.” We transposed *he sees* for the sake of rhythmic metre, for the verse always ends with a dactyl.]

How great were the things he—

Raising his eyes, he made the sign:

“Back, Satan, do not win souls.”

> [Note: Perhaps *Retrocede*, “withdraw.”]

How great the things God—

He cries out strongly in a voice most great;

In a most great voice the demon had foretold.

> [Note: Manuscript: “in what voice.”]

> [Note: *Praedixerat* (“had foretold”) for the sake of rhythm.]

. . . . *(The repetition “How great were the things he—” is missing.)*

[Col. 0205B]

Wandering, I shall wander through unknown lands;

And because of me it is not permitted to win souls.

> [Note: *Girans giravi* in the manuscript.]

> [Note: *Perque* is written for *quoniam*, “because,” as is evident from Coronatus’s narrative.]

How great the things God grants: thanks to God.

> [Note: Here the copyist made one verse from two repeated verses, taking the first part from the first and the second part from the other.]

[CLXX]

Wailing, he cries out from a very great height

As far as the imperial throne—the daughter [text fragment uncertain].

> [Note: Manuscript: “crying out.”]

> [Note: “Daughter of the Empire.” The author of the Rhythm consistently uses *Imperii* in place of *Imperatoris*, “of the emperor”; this shows that he read *Imperatorem* in Coronatus, from whom he extracted this, as it is read in the Reims manuscript.]

. . . . . . . . . . . . .

Into whom he enters in the chaste body

. . . . . . . . . . . . .

How great—

The daughter of the Empire had remained chaste;

From the throne she calls upon Zeno.

> [Note: Manuscript: “into whom.”]

> [Note: “To the throne.”]

How great were the things he—

“I was harmed by this body;

If Zeno comes, then the demon will go out.”

> [Note: Manuscript: *Lesus*, “injured.”]

> [Note: “Whom the demon [will leave].”]

How great the things God—

He sent soldiers through unknown lands

To seek the man named Zeno.

How great [deeds] were performed—

[Col. 0206A]

N . . . . . . . . . . . . .

. . . . . . . . . . . . .

Man, who sits upon a stone, fishing in the Adige,

> [Note: “On a stone, in the Adige.”]

Tell us Zeno by name.

How great the things God—

There are many names through the monasteries,

> [Note: Manuscript: *Plure*, “more.”]

For if he wishes to say it, “Here is the man whom you seek.”

How great were the things he—

“What do we say, or why do we languish away?

Why do we not state the command of the Empire?”

> [Note: *Perque* for that which in Italian is said *perché*, “why/because”; nevertheless we have written *perque* here, as above in verse 20.]

Then the demon cries out through the mouth of the little girl:

“Zeno is now near, and I flee.”

How great are the deeds—

The bishop, a most holy man, came;

By the sign he put the phantoms to flight.

How great were the things he—

[X?] Still hastening, he came to Verona,

> [Note: Coronatus, from whom the author of the Rhythm drew, recounts that, when the demon was cast out of Gallienus’s daughter, it threatened the holy bishop that it would go to Verona and there would be found by Zeno, standing in the square, when he returned; and then, after the demon’s expulsion, that the emperor gave Zeno a crown. But the author of the Rhythm, confusing the order of the story, incorrectly reports that Zeno, as he approached Verona, found the demon standing in the square and was then given a crown by the emperor.]

How great the things God—

[Y?] To Christ let praise be given in the south placed [reading uncertain],

[Col. 0207]

## HISTORY OF THE TRANSLATION OF SAINT ZENO, APPENDED TO THE LIFE OF THE SAME SAINT, WRITTEN BY AN ANONYMOUS AUTHOR

[Col. 0207A]

It now seems necessary to make known the course of the translation of Blessed Zeno, because in the conduct of this affair certain things worthy of remembrance became manifest. This translation took place when Rotaldus, a man most distinguished by the qualities of his person, exercised pastoral care at Verona, and King Pippin, son of Charlemagne, whom Pope Adrian baptized, ruled the kingdom of Italy.

The king loved Verona, endowed with a royal site, more than other cities, and often conversed with the bishop whom he loved. When they entered Saint Zeno’s church together one day and spoke of his wonders, both those heard of and those seen, they reasonably and worthily resolved that they should place more fittingly and more loftily the great treasure which lay more humbly than was proper, and enlarge the narrow church.

Therefore, as they built the church, they constructed a dark crypt, supported by columns and paved with stone. There they raised an elevated mound of polished marble, which they dedicated to the tomb of the most sacred body. Then the king and bishop, having assembled priests and other sacred orders, in whose regard they hoped for divine favor, first sought to propitiate the Saint through manifold prayers, lest he should be angered by being moved by them. With immense fear they opened the chamber; and they were so terrified that no one in that great assembly dared touch the holy bones. For something divine and greatly fearsome seemed to breathe forth from it, inspiring horror and leaving all those standing around faint.

> [Variant: *tumulum*, “the tomb.”]

> [Variant: In two manuscripts *ab* (“by”) is absent.]

They immediately closed the sepulchre and departed. Then, while the king and pontiff were uncertain what they should do, among the many considerations which they discussed this course pleased them: for forty days, three times each week, the entire body of secular and ecclesiastical persons of both sexes, together with the king and bishop themselves, should come reverently and solemnly to the holy crypt and with one common desire beseech the mercy of God and of the Confessor, that he might inspire them with the manner in which so reverent a removal ought to be undertaken.

While these things were carried out with diligent care, word reached the king of a certain solitary man who lived on little herbs, water, and a small amount of bread. When he heard this eagerly, he promptly summoned the bishop. They therefore chose energetic and prudent messengers,

> [Variant: *industres*, “distinguished.”]

to whom they entrusted this task. Reaching the lake called Benacus, they made their way to the secluded man’s hiding-place, situated at a lofty lookout, by a narrow and dangerous path. When they saw the man, whose name was Benignus, and his disciple, who was called Carus, they rejoiced with great joy.

When he had heard the king’s and bishop’s message, he said to the messengers: “Return in peace, greeting again your lords, beloved friends; I rejoice greatly that I have been summoned to that solemnity, and in a little while I shall follow you.”

> [Variant: “your lord.”]

Immediately afterward he entered the little shrine of the Oracle and implored divine aid; then he prepared himself for the exertion of the journey.

> [Variant: “While.”]

When he had proceeded not far from the cell, behold, a blackbird began to flutter its wings noisily, chirp, and fly repeatedly across the path, as though signifying an ill omen in order to turn the man of God back from his undertaking. But the man, not unaware that this was the devil’s contrivance, adjured the blackbird to make no movement until he himself returned. There the blackbird stood motionless, as if it were without sensation.

> [Variant: “Afterward.”]

When he drew near and the king, bishop, and honorable men came to meet him, he was received honorably and learned what the king desired. Then he said: “Since your vows depend on a righteous purpose, you will find God gracious and granting success to your good petition.”

> [Variant: *opinionis*, “opinion.”]

Then they entered with chosen men, removed the stone, and no one spared prayers, whether those who were inside or those who remained before the doors. But the hermit, although aided by his own merits and by the prayers of all, entered trembling, carried the most blessed bones, and placed every one of them in order in a most clean receptacle prepared for this purpose. Then such a force of fragrance poured forth that none of them had ever before perceived anything so sweet.

Then the king, moved by his own urging and that of his companions, requested some portion of the relics, but the bishop refused to allow it. The king began to press more and more and promise great gifts. At last the bishop, overcome by prayers neither few nor small, consented. Preserving the integrity of the limbs, he granted particles of sinews, ashes, and garments; but enclosed the rest securely and deposited them under the seal of a ring.

At the sound of those singing psalms, the bank of the Adige resounded; the open fields thundered; and we believe that the very court of the Almighty rejoiced. While the aforementioned praises echoed around the church, as commonly occurs, many long-afflicted bodies were freed from their illnesses. Great joy arose that day, such as no one of that time had seen, because various kinds of healings were accomplished in a short time; and the procession became longer because of the sight of the signs.

> [Variant: *reliquerunt*, “left.”]

But the king, bishop, and inhabitant of the rock, in awe, brought in the holy limbs and placed them in the prepared mausoleum. After the pontiff reverently celebrated Mass, the king enriched God’s bride with a noble endowment. By right of ownership he gave her the monastery of Saint Peter called Mauratica, with all possessions pertaining to it; likewise the church of Saint Andrew the apostle, called Incavi or Incafi, with households, mountains and woods, meadows and vineyards, fields and sowing-lands, and all appurtenances. He also subjected to her the church of Saint Zeno near the lake, with all its revenues. He gave also the wood of Mantico; many embossed vessels of silver and gold; a Gospel-book adorned with an arrangement of gems and pearls and a beautiful engraving in gold; and other things in which royal dignity abounded. Following his example, our emperors have always loved the aforesaid place and offered their gifts.

[CLXXIV]

Bishop Rotaldus, rich in possessions, made the church heir to all his property. Indeed, very many nobles also eagerly contributed great portions of their wealth,

> [Possibly *adtribuerunt*, “assigned.”]

so that before the sun set that church had become exceedingly rich. But the man of God, eager to return to his hermitage, hastened his journey. As he approached his dwelling, he saw the blackbird lying on a sheer cliff. Thinking it was resting and awaiting his arrival, he approached to awaken it and give it leave to depart; but it had already died. The good man, pitying it, said: “This little bird failed through the devil’s prompting; and because it was irrational and offended unknowingly, it deserved pardon, not death.” On this account he imposed upon himself a most rigorous fast of forty days; hence a bronze image of a blackbird, made by casting, hangs there to this day.

When the king and pontiff saw Zeno’s miracles increasing and his resources growing like a river swollen by melting snow, they strove with all their strength, as guardians and promoters of faith, lest the place, fortunate in abundance, should become meagre through poverty of prayer. Therefore, with one purpose, like twin brothers, they decreed that the monastery once increased

> [Variant: *actum*, “done/made.”]

should be enlarged. They shared the concern to advance toward greater things the monks dwelling there in a proved manner of life, just as an artisan preparing a crown adorns it with excellent gems and pearls in order to complete the work begun. Not long afterward, with the same [thing] guiding the helm

> [Variant: *Deo*, “God.”]

that same discipline and moral gravity made those elders, together with the abbot, such men that the governance of the monastic rule was wonderfully maintained by them, and that they were a model

> [Variant: *formulae*, “models.”]

and mirror for their followers, and, like good fathers, produced good heirs.

The king rejoiced; the bishop rejoiced, beholding the abundant fruit of the sprouting crop. The city and its suburbs alike rejoiced in such a fellowship. Hence many, fleeing the shadowy breeze of the deceitful world, strove to become neighbors

> [Variant: *conterini*, perhaps “companions.”]

of such great men. It was not want that compelled them to do this; rather, yearning with hunger and thirst for holy life, they brought no small wealth to Zeno and put on the monastic habit.

> [Variant: *induerunt*, “put on.”]

Thus that place became more fortunate and more religious, protected under the wings of each emperor. But the most blessed Confessor, often putting into action the powers granted him by the Lord and accomplishing many memorable deeds, had drawn many people from distant parts—

> [Manuscript variant: “nations”; others: “regions.”]

some moved by religion, others compelled by the necessity of sickness. And (variant: “But”), lest we pass over everything, let us recount in this little work some of his miracles.

A demon entered a certain man of Trent and claimed for itself the powers of his body and mind. No limb performed its proper function; his foaming mouth uttered not human speech; and though his eyes were open, he did not see. When his raging enemy darted toward them, it made them bloody and terrible. He confessed people’s secrets and did many things not belonging to human nature; he was a wondrous spectacle to all.

When (variant: “While”) a priest, as is customary, adjured him, the demon called that priest a eunuch, a defect not yet known to those present. Then he blushed at the shame of the reproach laid upon him and departed.

> [Variant: *turpitudinem*, accusative for *turpitudine*.] Behold, a certain deacon approached the demon and, as if to avenge the priest, adjured him more severely. The demon recognized him as though very well known, called him by name, and, a ridiculous informer, revealed many things which the Levite had committed. Thus several who knew themselves implicated did not dare approach; and the demon, as if triumphant, stirred up its mockeries.

Then a certain Zeno, provost of the monastery, whom they surnamed Solomon for the merit of his religious life and wisdom, unable to bear the demon’s pride, grieved by the disgrace of the disclosure and still more by the wrong suffered by the created person who had been possessed, embraced Saint Zeno’s altar. Moved in his inmost being and bathed in tears, he poured out a prayer that this demonic insult should not go unpunished. Immediately the demon felt the force of the prayer and reluctantly left the vessel it had long abused. The man, rendering great and distinguished thanks to God and Saint Zeno, rejoiced that the harmful guest had been driven away.

Moreover, William, dried up and contracted, who, bent over like a quadruped, had pressed the ground with his hands, after hearing reports of many healings, asked to be carried there on a litter. As he approached the entrance of the church, he was borne in others’ arms and laid on the ground. He beat his breast with his fists, filled his voice with sobs, and said that he was worthy of something worse. Then he had lights lit,

> [Variant: “commanded [them] to be lit.”]

and, bent like a beast because he could not stand erect, began to crawl on knees and palms toward the altar. Immediately divine power entered his bones and sinews and touched his arthritic disease. He fell to the ground as if lifeless and lay for a long time as though without breath, so that he was believed already dead. Suddenly the form, joints, supports, and all knots of his body were strengthened and restored. At once he rose and quickly went to the altar. The people gathered; there was spiritual praise and jubilation. Glory and omnipotence were rendered to God, and mercy and magnificence to illustrious Zeno.

When the report of this miracle went abroad everywhere, a considerable crowd hastened from every side, as flocks are wont to gather in a pasture-field full of richness. Two men, one named John and the other Calvus, were brought there and lay paralyzed—companions in journey, suffering, and healing—whom their long stay had already made known and commended to many. They constantly kept watch at the church doors and implored Saint Zeno’s aid, now with shared prayers, now in turn.

When night and sleep overcame them, both saw a very beautiful old man, of bright complexion, whose snowy hair made him radiant. He came out from the entrance of the inner church carrying a staff in his hand. He raised it, struck both men, and said: “You have lain long enough in these little chambers; rise and praise God the Savior.” He immediately departed. When they awoke, they told one another what they had seen. They at once agreed that they had been restored to health. Rising swiftly, they celebrated God with resounding praises. Fearing that if they returned home too soon God might charge them with ingratitude, they remained for several days and faithfully related what had happened to them.

Nor shall we pass over a memorable event which befell Albert of Ceneda. When fierce enemies captured him, not content with the glory of taking him captive nor satisfied by other outrages inflicted against right and justice, they burned out his eyes with heated iron. Bereft of light, he sat in the darkness of sudden deprivation, lamenting; night and day, with incessant weeping, he appealed to God the Judge. When familiarity with his misfortune had at last diminished his shame, he began to emerge from hiding, guided by another’s direction, and for no short time followed his guide. He had become burdensome and hateful to his own people and often prayed God to cut short his unhappy life.

Suddenly he conceived the desire to hasten to Saint Zeno’s protection; then he sought travel assistance from relatives and friends. But they called him mad and mocked him for such a request. Omitting the rest, he pitifully begged his guide, once his tutor, to consent to his undertaking. The man immediately obeyed and promised that he would do whatever his master wished. He began the journey joyfully; and others of his household, acting humanely, went with him. He was led to the crypt in which Zeno had formerly rested. Prostrate on the ground, he invoked with tearful prayers the one to whom he had come, asking him to provide the aid of his accustomed medicine.

As he repeatedly said the *Miserere*, he unexpectedly saw those standing around him. Suddenly he cried out that he could see. Those who had come with him did not believe him, so he identified each person in turn, examining who he was and what he was wearing. When he proved to be an accurate identifier of those questioned, all began to applaud and praise God and his faithful Zeno. When his torturers heard of this, moved by repentance, they boldly approached him and asked him, for the love of the one from whom he himself had received mercy, to grant them pardon. He readily forgave their fault and accepted no compensation. He approached the abbot of Saint Zeno, took on the habit—the “cuirass”—of Saint Benedict, and served faithfully there for four periods of five years.

Nor shall I be silent concerning Wezilla, a girl possessed by a demon. While the demon lay hidden at one moment and raged at another beneath her tender limbs, she became a young woman. She ought to have been a comfort to her parents, but she was an inconsolable sight to them. The demon had often deceived them, swearing that it would depart if she were led to the altar of this or that saint. Thus for a long time it mocked their hope and exhausted their diligent care.

But at the time when Christ’s blood was said to have been discovered at Mantua, as her parents were taking her there, they turned aside to Zeno’s church. As she entered, the demon shook the girl more violently than usual, like an east wind shaking a young tree. Since it was the time for the Rogation prayers, a large crowd was proceeding there in psalmody. Seeing her head roll, her hair fly, her hands and arms shake, her feet leap, and several men labor to hold one small woman, all raised their hands into the air and cried with one voice: “Help, O God!” No one among so great a multitude withheld himself from such concern. You could see some bowing down in prayer, others weeping compassionately, and priests urging one another to their office; with such emotion the whole palace resounded.

Immediately the stronger armed one came and violently expelled him from his own house. O demon, with how much pain, how great a cry, and how sulphurous a stench he departed! The girl stood amid the people, pale, terrified, trembling, and exhausted. She could scarcely speak, though shortly before she had surpassed all others in voice; her feet and all her limbs shook, though shortly before she had exhausted strong men. Gone was he who had tormented her and breathed mighty strength into her. O how great was the praise and glory, and how great the acclamations uttered there!

[CLXXVII] When that wicked spirit departed, going about [Col. 0212B] seeking whom he might devour, he saw a monk standing beside a lofty tower then under construction. From its high pinnacle he rolled down a stone upon him and gravely wounded him on the head. The monk was carried off by the brothers as if dead; and this is held in memory, that so gaping a wound did not prove fatal. Immediately, like an arrow, he hurled himself upon the table of a certain native, and scattered from a distance, like a stormy whirlwind, everything that was upon it. Then, swifter than speech, he rushed upon a cart laden with thorns, which neither animal was moving nor any force of wind affected. Then the perverse driver turned it this way and drove it that way, as though fierce and untamed bulls had been yoked to it. Having performed these mockeries, he at once impelled the helmsman of a vessel carrying stones for the splendid building of St Zeno, intending both to drown the man in the river [Col. 0212C] and to wreck the ship. But the man fell beneath the stern, and the ship reached harbour without loss.

At the same moment he went from the Adige to the stream called Flubius (that is, the river Fibius), where ploughmen were taking their midday rest near a pleasant bank. While they peacefully attended to their affairs and there was no quarrelling among them, Satan began to tickle their hearts; consequently, some of them spoke insolently and arrogantly and hurled insulting words at their companions and intimate friends. Straightway, stirred up in a hostile spirit, they fought fiercely with sticks; and, had military weapons been at hand, they would have perished by mutual slaughter. But priests happened to be present there, and they separated the men, cruelly wounded, as mediators. Coming to themselves, they washed one another’s still-bleeding wounds which they themselves had inflicted, and, cutting bandages from their garments, [Col. 0212D] bound up the wounds with charity and tears. Thereafter the dreadful artificer did harm more secretly than openly, he who trusts more in tricks and devices than in force. The priests immediately recognized that Satan had come openly among the sons of God.

### Fragment of a poem on the miracles of St Zeno, written by the priest Jacob

A distinguished man, when Zeno’s festal day was at hand,  
lavishly provided yearly dinners for twice six poor persons.  
Behold, they brought word to that wretched father, doing such things,  
that his son had gone to Acheron through grievous wounds.  
But the father did not abandon what he had begun, although that son  
was his only child; nor did he abandon it because of such a death.  
Rather, he declared that Zeno would always be at hand to help him,  
and the father joyfully concluded the banquet.

[Col. 0213A] Having offered boundless praises  
to God, to Zeno, and to the noble citizens, immediately Zeno,  
by his own death—as by sleep—recalled the youth to his parent.

What of the man who, defeated by an enemy, fled from a castle  
at Verona to the Venetian city,  
and saw that everyone dealt cruelly and unjustly with him?  
As a suppliant he offered vows to Zeno, saying thus:

“Kind Zeno, I pray, be present to me as Patron by right,  
[CLXXVIII] whom Verona reveres in the foremost rank as her leader.”

Behold, suddenly the Venetian people and the entire Senate,  
seeing his rights, at last with gracious countenance  
made Zeno’s servant the victor. He himself  
reported orally that Zeno had written those things  
which lawyers and learned men had maintained  
[Col. 0214A] could not have been foreseen by him, though they had long sifted every particular.  
Thus he gained what he had vowed for, remembered his vow, and received it.

I pray you, Catharina Saracena, tell the inquirer  
what welcome gifts Zeno brought you, sick as you were,  
for many months. Benedict himself also  
is a witness that, appearing to him, he removed  
his fever and pain in the head, saying: “Rejoice, faithful one;  
you shall be safe if you make a fitting covering for Zeno’s bare  
head; for he appeared to you thus unclothed, he to whom all things  
shine in their purity. You shall leave  
your bed unharmed, while the whole household rejoices,  
as soon as may be.” Not in vain did the mother, cured of gout,  
pour out vows into Zeno’s ears with her prayers.

[Col. 0213]

## [CLXXIX] MASSES OF ST ZENO

FROM THE ANCIENT MANUSCRIPT SACRAMENTARIES OF THE CHURCH OF VERONA.

### MASS I

[Col. 0213B]

**Prayer.**  
[Note: [Col. 0213D] MASS I.—The monks of the monastery of St Zeno used this prayer in the cursus, or office, on the day when the feast of his deposition was celebrated, as we learn from two manuscript ritual books of the same monastery.]

Rejoicing in celebration, O Lord, enlightened by the venerable feast of your priest and confessor St Zeno on this day, grant in your mercy, being entreated by his worthy prayers, that, refreshed by the joy of spiritual nourishment, we may follow by imitation the way of salvation which he taught. Through the Lord.

**Another prayer.**  
[Note: [Col. 0213D] It appears from a Capitular manuscript and another belonging to the nuns of St Mary of Campo Marzio that the Church of Verona used this prayer in the offices on each feast of St Zeno.]

O God, who gladden us by the annual solemnity of the blessed confession of your priest and confessor St Zeno, grant, we pray, that, relying upon your power and having overcome the crafty assault of the enemy, we may deserve through his intercession to attain eternal joys. Through.

**Secret.**  
We pray you, God the almighty Father, look favourably upon the gifts offered to you; and, through the intercession of [Col. 0213C] your priest and confessor, blessed Zeno, may they preserve our frailty unharmed from the hidden prompting of the plotter; and, received devoutly by angelic hands, may they be joyfully borne before the sacred sight of your glorious and awe-inspiring majesty as an odour of sweetness. Through.

**Preface.**  
It is truly worthy. You deigned to lead blessed Zeno, abundantly filled with the copious sweetness of love for your holy name, to contemplate the desired brightness of your Godhead. By the invincible clemency of your compassion and piety, you made him so strong and unharmed amid worldly splendours that he was neither puffed up by the flattering greatness of prosperity nor bent by the billowing assault of stormy falsehood in adversities. For he was steadfast in faith, patient in charity, adorned with the vigorous purity of chastity, [CLXXX] and most renowned as a worker of salvation in miraculous virtues. Moreover, in carrying out the teaching of the divine dignity entrusted to him, [Col. 0213D] he daily refreshed the peoples whom he instructed with the nourishment of the divine word of life; and what, as a heavenly soldier, he faithfully preached ought to be followed, this admirable and devout steward took unceasing care to fulfil in deed. Therefore, almighty Lord, author of all things and of all good, we humbly beseech you: since on this day’s feast we recall the most celebrated day of his precious death, grant, being entreated by his most sacred prayers, that, freed from the bonds of our sins and defended from the fierce, crafty attack of our enemies, we may deserve, with you as our guide, to attain the kingdoms of heaven. Through Christ.

**At Communion.**  
Having received, O Lord, the mysteries of holy redemption, we pray that [Note: [Col. 0213D] The word *et* (“and”) is missing in the manuscript Missal of Zeno.] strengthened by the fullness of this saving remedy, and [Note: [Col. 0213D] In other manuscripts it reads: “And supported by the protection of the most wholesome blessed intercession of St Zeno.”] supported by the most wholesome protections of the blessed intercession of your priest [Col. 0214C] and confessor St Zeno, we may deserve to attain the eternal joys of the full feast. Through.

**Another.**  
Guard us, we pray, O Lord, as we celebrate the feasts of your Saints, and continually stir our wills to carry out the saving commands of your precepts. Through.

### MASS II

**Prayer.**  
[Note: [Col. 0213D] MASS II.—This prayer was used not only by the Zenonian monks in the cursus of the feast-day of the Translation of St Zeno, as is clear from their manuscript ritual books, but also by Benedictines of a monastery at Pavia on the sixth day before the Ides of December, as is evident from a fifteenth-century parchment Breviary manuscript. There, at second Vespers of the Conception of the Blessed Virgin Mary, one reads: “And commemoration is made of Saints Zeno and Syrus. For St Zeno, bishop and confessor: prayer, ‘O God, who art,’ etc.” The Capitular manuscript shows that this prayer, with slight changes, was used by the Church of Verona in prayers, or suffrages of the Saints, at the commemoration of St Zeno.]

O God, most mighty enlightener of your bishops, grant, we pray, that, formed by the glorious examples of your most blessed priest and confessor Zeno, we may pass without peril through the darkness of this age. Through.

**Secret.**  
Let the welcome prayer of blessed Zeno obtain from you, almighty God, forgiveness of our sins. [Col. 0214D] Through.

[CLXXXI] **Postcommunion.**  
Grant, we pray, almighty God, that we who keep the venerable Translation of your glorious [Col. 0215A] confessor Zeno by annual vigils may, by worthily following his manner of life, deserve to be sharers in his joys. Through.

### MASS III

**Prayer.**  
Celebrating today with holy devotion the venerable day of blessed [Note: [Col. 0215C] MASS III.—This Mass is full of errors in the Vatican and Veronese manuscripts. It is found corrected in certain places in the Roman edition of the Sacramentary of St Gregory, but much more correctly in the manuscript Missal of the monastery of St Zeno. This prayer likewise is more correct in two other manuscripts of the same monastery, since it was used by the monks of that cenobium in the cursus on the feast-day of St Zeno’s ordination. Thus, in the Zenonian manuscripts it reads here: “of the blessed bishop and confessor.”] your confessor Zeno, let us faithfully beseech you, O Lord, [Note: [Col. 0215C] In the Zenonian manuscripts: “the author of all good things we faithfully beseech”; the Roman edition likewise has the corrected reading “we beseech.”] the guardian of all, that in your kindness you may breathe upon our prayers, [Note: [Col. 0215D] The word *clemens* (“merciful”) is supplied from the Vatican manuscript and the Roman edition.] mercifully and favourably, just as you also [Note: [Col. 0215D] “That, being entreated by his prayers, you may grant us your mercy here and for ever” in the Zenonian manuscripts.] grant mercy to him. Through.

**Secret.**  
O God, who [Note: [Col. 0215D] In the Zenonian Missal: “O God, who, as with shining pearls.”] bring to the world a bright light [Note: [Col. 0215D] There: “the light of priests, bringest into the world.” The Roman edition likewise has “bringest.”] in shining pearls; [Note: [Col. 0215D] “And who to blessed Bishop Zeno,” in the Zenonian Missal.] who prepared for blessed [Note: [Col. 0215D] “Episcopacy,” in the Roman edition; but “by his episcopate” in the Veronese manuscript.] Zeno’s episcopate an eternal crown in heaven, [Note: [Col. 0215D] “A crown of glory hast bestowed,” in the Zeno manuscript.] and [Note: [Col. 0215D] The conjunction *et* (“and”) is absent in that manuscript.] deign also to be present to us your servants standing before the sight of your majesty. [Note: [Col. 0215D] “Grant us to enjoy the light of the grace of your majesty. Through,” thus in the Zenonian Missal.] [Col. 0215B] Through.

[CLXXXII] **At the Completion.**  
[Note: [Col. 0216C] “At Communion” in the Veronese manuscript; “Postcommunion” in the Zenonian manuscript.]

O God, who [Note: [Col. 0216C] “O God, who hast made such a bishop for your Church,” in the Zenonian Missal.] made such a bishop for your Church, [Note: [Col. 0216C] The Roman edition has *vitalem* (“life-giving”); the Zenonian Missal has *et talem* (“and such”), very rightly.] that you appointed such a priest in our times, who might offer a most pure and immaculate [Note: [Col. 0216C] The Zenonian Missal: “who might offer thee a most pure and immaculate.”] sacrifice. [Note: [Col. 0216C] The same Missal adds this, which these omit: “Make us to be aided by the patronage of this bishop and priest. Through.”] Through.

### MASS IV

**Prayer.**  
Almighty everlasting God, wondrous splendour of your Saints, who on this day raised up your blessed confessor Zeno to the glory of eternal blessedness: mercifully grant that we who venerate his feast on earth may be strengthened in heaven by the help of his intercession before your mercy. Through.

**Secret.**  
“With the gifts offered to you,” etc., as in the Secret of the first Mass.

**At Communion.**  
“Of your priest St Zeno,” etc., as in the first prayer of the first Mass, with this sole difference in the final words: “by imitating the way of salvation which he taught, may we obtain pardon.” Through.

### MASS V

[Col. 0216A]

**Prayer.**  
[Note: [Col. 0216C] MASS V.—This Mass follows the three preceding ones in the cited Zenonian Missal. But another manuscript of the same [Col. 0216D] monastery shows that at least the first prayer was used in the Mass and cursus on the feast-day of St Lupicinus, bishop of Verona, whose body rests in the same basilica. The same prayer is also found in the Capitular manuscripts before the Common of Confessors, under this rubric: “Prayer of St Zeno or another: Be favourable,” etc.]

Be favourable, we pray, O God, to your servants through the glorious merits of your confessor and bishop St Zeno, [Note: [Col. 0216D] This clause is absent from the Capitular manuscript, since it is peculiar to the basilica of St Zeno, in which St Zeno’s sacred body rests.] who rests in this present church; and by his pious intercession may we be protected from all adversities. Through.

[CLXXXIII] **Secret.**  
May your mercy, almighty God, receive the offering from our hands, and through the prayers of this your confessor and bishop St Zeno absolve us from all sins.

**Postcommunion.**  
Having partaken, O Lord, of the divine mysteries which we have offered to your venerable majesty for this holy Zeno, your confessor and bishop, grant, we pray, that through them we may deserve pardon for sins and be refreshed by the gifts of heavenly grace.

## OTHER MASS PROPERS RELATING TO ST ZENO, FROM A VERONESE MANUSCRIPT OF THE MONASTERY OF ST ZENO

[Note: [Col. 0216D] OTHER COMMUNION.—See the preceding warning, no. 5.]

[Col. 0216B]

**Introit.**  
The Lord made with him a covenant of peace and made him a prince, that the dignity of the priesthood might be his for ever. Psalm: I will sing for ever of the mercies of the Lord. V\. Glory.

[Note: [Col. 0216D] In a Missal of the chapter of Verona, written toward the end of the twelfth century, in which the Epistles and Gospels are written in their proper places, the Mass of St Zeno contains the reading from the Epistle of the blessed apostle Paul to the Hebrews: “Brethren, every high priest,” up to “Thou art a priest for ever according to the order of Melchizedek.”]

**Reading from the book of Wisdom.**  
“Behold a great priest,” up to the words “as an odour of sweetness,” which, for the sake of brevity, we have judged should be omitted.

R\. Behold the great priest who pleased God in his days.  
V\. None was found like him, who kept the law of the Most High. Alleluia.  
V\. Behold, Zeno the confessor, shepherd of the Lord, intercede [Col. 0216C] for the devout people of God.

[Note: [Col. 0216D] In the same Missal, which contains a single Mass [Col. 0217C] of St Zeno, the Gospel is according to Luke: “A certain man,” up to the words “shall be taken away from him.” [Col. 0217D] Peretto reports in the scholia to the Life of St Zeno that the same Gospel was in the parchment Lectionary of St Euphemia.]

**According to Luke.**  
At that time Jesus said to his disciples: “No one lights a lamp,” etc., up to the words, “and as a shining lamp will give you light.”

[Col. 0217A] [LXXXIV] [Note: [Col. 0217D] The same Gospel was appointed for reading in Paschal time in the Lectionary cited by Peretto.]

**In the Paschal season of the Lord. According to John.**  
At that time Jesus said to his disciples: “I am the true vine,” etc., up to the words, “and your joy may be full.”

**Offertory.**  
My truth and my mercy are with him, and in my name shall his horn be exalted.

**Communion.**  
Lord, you entrusted five talents to me; behold, I have gained five more. Well done, good and faithful servant: because you have been faithful in a few things, I shall set you over many; enter into the joy of your Lord.

### MASS VI

*(From manuscript and printed Ambrosian Missals.)* On the feast of St Zeno, bishop, 7 December.  
[Note: [Col. 0217D] MASS VI.—This title is found in the Ambrosian Missal edited by Pamelius. Vatican Palatine manuscript 506 reads: “Sixth day before the Ides of December, the nativity of St Zeno, bishop and confessor.”]

[Col. 0217B]

**Over the people.**  
Almighty everlasting God, who adorned your confessor Zeno with the mitre of the episcopate, grant, we pray, that through his example and glorious intercession we may despise in mind the glory of the world and ever seek heaven. Through the Lord.  
[Note: [Col. 0217D] After this prayer the Vatican Palatine manuscript has this rubric: “Seek the Epistle and Gospel under Confessors.” The 1548 edition of the Milanese Missal adds: “After the Gospel: Zeno, a good and most holy bishop, sat upon a stone and fished in the Adige.”]

**Over the shroud.**  
O God, who made this present day solemn by the glorious [Note: [Col. 0217D] “Departure” in the Vatican Palatine manuscript and in the printed editions of 1548 and 1560.] passing of your bishop Zeno, grant that we may continually be helped before you by his suffrages and cherished by his glorious [Col. 0218C] intercessions. [Note: [Col. 0218C] Printed editions: “continually comforted by his intercessions.”] Through the Lord.

[CLXXXV] **Over the offerings.**  
May the splendid intercession of blessed Zeno be present with your Church, O God, so that it may make our gifts acceptable in the eyes of your majesty and render you gracious toward us. Through the Lord.

[Col. 0217C]

**Preface.**  
Eternal God, recalling the merits of your blessed bishop and confessor Zeno, [Note: [Col. 0218C] The same manuscript with the printed editions: “the merits of Zeno to be set forth.”] whom in your free kindness you deigned to exalt in the office of bishop and the ministry of faith, so that he shone with immeasurable virtues and did not abandon his purpose of holy humility. For he rescued the daughter of the Emperor Gallienus from the power of a demon and healed the illnesses of many by mighty power. The river Adige itself bears witness to the strength of so great a bishop’s virtue: when, rising beyond its customary bank, it did not dare to enter the doors of the sacred church. Worthily, therefore, we do not keep silent concerning his praises in your name; worthily we proclaim his miracles in festive praises; worthily, together with him, we render vows of thanksgiving to you, O Lord, [Col. 0218A] giver of all good things. Through Christ our Lord.

**Postcommunion.**  
We pray, O Lord, may the glorious merits of your blessed bishop and confessor Zeno always protect us from every evil, on whose solemnity we joyfully receive your holy things. Through the Lord.

## THREE PRAYERS

[Note: [Col. 0218D] THREE PRAYERS.—We print these prayers as they were transmitted by a Regular Canon of the monastery of Halle to Father Benedict of Cavalesio, of the Strict Observance of St Francis at Trent, and by him to us: that is, as they are recited today at three feasts of St Zeno in that monastery. We have no doubt that the title “Martyr” was introduced recently, as also in the Church of Freising, after the Church of Verona introduced the cult of St Zeno’s martyrdom. We observed in Dissertation 3, chapters 2 and 4, §2, that some other churches conformed themselves to its example. Whoever consults the codices of that monastery, from which we believe with certainty that these prayers derive, will discover the matter more fully.]

*(From records of the monastery of St Zeno at Halle in the diocese of Salzburg.)*

### 12 April. On the feast of St Zeno, bishop and martyr

**Prayer.**  
Almighty everlasting God, who sanctified blessed Zeno, bishop of the Church of Verona, from the womb, and granted him victory everywhere over the enemy of the human race, [CLXXXVI] mercifully grant [Col. 0218B] that we sinners may be converted to you by his merits and prayers, and may deserve always to gain victory over the hidden enemy. Through the Lord.

### 21 May. On the feast of the Translation of St Zeno, bishop and martyr

**Prayer.**  
Celebrating with holy devotion the venerable day of the Translation of your martyr and bishop, blessed Zeno, we humbly ask your mercy: as you granted him glory according to his merits, so, with him interceding for our sins, deign to grant us pardon. Through the Lord.

### 9 December. On the feast of the Ordination of St Zeno, bishop

[Note: [Col. 0218D] The Ordination of St Zeno was transferred to this day, as in our own Church, because the eighth day was impeded by the feast of the Conception of the Blessed Virgin Mary.]

[Col. 0218C]

**Prayer.**  
O God, who deigned to choose blessed Zeno, your confessor and bishop, as an eminent teacher and preacher of the Catholic faith, grant, we pray, that through his intercession for us we may be stripped of the stains of our sins and deserve, O Lord, to please you with sincere hearts. Through the Lord.

## [CLXXXVII] SELECTED PASSAGES FROM THE OFFICE OF ZENO

### I.—ANTIPHONS AND RESPONSORIES

*(From two Veronese manuscripts.) On the Nativity of St Zeno.*

**At Vespers.**  
[Note: [Col. 0218D] ANTIPHONS AND RESPONSORIES.—In the manuscript of the monastery of St Zeno, in which his proper office is found, the responsory, verse, and antiphon at the Magnificat differ from those in the Capitular Antiphonary. It is fitting to transcribe them here. Responsory: “Most high bishop of God, blessed Zeno, protect your flock, for we believe that by your praises we are always to be saved.” Verse: “You who freed the daughter of Caesar Gallienus from demonic possession, preserve the people intent upon your praises.” Antiphon at the Magnificat: “Most merciful confessor of Christ the Lord, most blessed Zeno, we humbly beseech you: do not abandon us, but ever be for us a kind intercessor before the Lord, so that, with your help, we may deserve to attain the joys of eternal life.” The same antiphon [Col. 0220D] is read in the manuscript of the nuns of St Mary of Campo Marzio at second Vespers.]

While Zeno flourished greatly in the honour of the episcopate, by merits [Col. 0219A] not few he healed through God’s power the daughter of Caesar Gallienus from a ruinous affliction. Alleluia.

Holy confessor, great priest, blessed Zeno, intercede for us.

**Before the *Venite*.**

The King of Confessors.  
[Note: [Col. 0220D] In the Zenonian manuscript and the manuscript of the nuns mentioned in the preceding annotation, this Invitatory occurs:

> Let us praise the eternal, triune, and one God,  
> who bore holy Zeno into the heavens for himself.]

Psalm: Come, let us rejoice.

Antiphon. Blessed Zeno was sanctified from his mother’s womb and blessed from the cradle. Alleluia.  
Psalm: Blessed is the man.

Antiphon. By continual increase in uprightness and knowledge he deserved to attain such a degree that, through his most holy life, he became a shepherd among the peoples.  
Psalm: Why have the nations raged?

Antiphon. By continuous fasts and frequent prayers he asked the Lord to open to him an entrance for preaching among the peoples. [Col. 0219B] Alleluia.  
Psalm: O Lord, why are they multiplied? Verse: With my voice.

Responsory. This is Zeno, the holy bishop, whom the Lord adorned with the twofold virtue of holiness and wisdom. His splendid miracles shone forth into the world, and in heaven he obtained fellowship with the Angels. Alleluia.  
V\. This is he who performed great works before God, and the whole earth was filled with his teaching. And in heaven.

R\. Blessed Zeno, sanctified from the womb and blessed from the cradle, deserved to attain such a degree that, through his most holy life, he became a shepherd among the peoples. Alleluia, alleluia.

[CLXXXVIII] V\. The sound of his manner of life went out into all the earth, and his holiness shone brightly. Through his most holy life.

R\. In the more secluded part of the oratory, by continual fasts and frequent prayers, he asked the Lord to deign to open to him an entrance for preaching among the peoples. Alleluia, alleluia.

V\. He was devoted day and night to converting human souls in the love of Christ. To deign to open.

Antiphon. He was so gracious in speech and gentle in demeanour that God was praised in him by all who came to him.  
Psalm: When I called.

While engaged in the practice of fishing in the river, he saw a man sitting in a cart plunging headlong into the stream. Alleluia.  
Psalm: My words.

The man of God, lifting his hand on high, made the sign of the cross, [Col. 0219D] saying: “Turn back, Satan; do not destroy the man whom God created.” Alleluia.  
Psalm: O Lord, our Lord. Verse: The Lord guided the righteous man.  
[Note: [Col. 0220D] In the *Carpsus* another verse is indicated thus: “Thou hast placed, O Lord, upon his head.”]

[Col. 0220A]

R\. He was so gracious in speech and so gentle in meekness and demeanour that God was praised in him by all who came to him. Alleluia, alleluia.  
V\. He was so cheerful that they hastened to him at once and, leaving idols behind, believed in the Lord Jesus Christ. That God.

R\. While engaged in fishing in the river Adige, blessed Zeno lifted his eyes on high and saw a man seated in a cart, with oxen harnessed to it, being plunged into the stream. Alleluia, alleluia.  
V\. For it was carried with such speed that it was shown to all to have been done by the craft of the ancient enemy. He saw.

R\. Blessed Zeno, lifting his hand on high, made the sign of the holy cross and said in a loud voice: “Turn back, Satan; do not destroy the man whom God created.” Alleluia, alleluia, alleluia.

[Col. 0220B]

V\. When the demon saw that sign, he vanished like smoke amid impious cries and shrieking. Turn back.

Antiphon. Blessed Zeno said: “The Lord does not permit you to do anything against his servant.” Alleluia.  
Psalm: Lord, who shall dwell?

The wretched father and the whole royal household were afflicted with grief because the girl was being violently suffocated. Alleluia.  
Psalm: O Lord, in thy strength.

Zeno, priest of God, sat upon a stone and, following the teaching of the apostolic craft, fished in the river. Alleluia.  
Psalm: The earth is the Lord’s. V\. The Lord loved him.

R\. The demon then hastened into the palace of Caesar Gallienus and, seizing his only daughter, began cruelly to torment her. Alleluia, alleluia.

[Col. 0220C] [CLXXXIX]

V\. The wretched father, together with his entire household, was afflicted with anguish and sorrow. And seizing her.

R\. When Christ’s priest entered the palace and made the sign of the cross, the demon immediately began to cry out, saying: “You, Zeno, drive me out, and because of your holiness I cannot remain. Alleluia, alleluia, alleluia.”  
V\. “And if I leave here, I shall go to Verona, and there you will find me.” And because of your holiness.

[Note: [Col. 0220D] In the Capitular Antiphonary: “Holy Zeno, seek [this] under St Martin.” But in the *Carpsus*: R\. “Holy Zeno.” V\. “O holy Zeno.” We have supplied it from the manuscript of the nuns of St Mary of Campo Marzio.]

R\. Holy Zeno, confessor of Christ, hear your beseeching servants, and, O God, bring us the forgiveness obtained from heaven.  
V\. O holy Zeno, golden star, by the Lord’s grace receive with your accustomed mercy the groans of your servants.

**At Matins, in the Lauds.**

Antiphon. The Lord Jesus Christ is almighty; for it is fitting that the wonderful works of God be made manifest. [Col. 0220D] Alleluia.

Blessed Zeno the priest arose, made prayer, and went to the palace where the King was afflicted on account of his daughter. Alleluia.

[Col. 0221A]

When Christ’s confessor entered the palace and made the sign of the cross, the demon cried out through the girl’s mouth, saying: “Zeno, you have come to drive me out, and because of your holiness I cannot remain.” Alleluia.

Blessed Zeno took the girl’s hand, saying: “In the name of my Lord Jesus Christ, I command you: come out of her, demon.” Alleluia.

For Christ’s priest restored the King’s daughter sound from every mocking assault of demonic attack. Alleluia.

V\. He chose him.

**At the Gospel.**

Blessed Zeno distributed among the poor the crown he had received from the King, saying: “If the Lord works exalted deeds, to him let perpetual praises and glory be rendered.” Alleluia.

[Col. 0221B]

[Note: [Col. 0221] The same *Carpsus* shows that this antiphon was recited at second Vespers; for it reads there: “At Vespers, antiphon: Holy Confessor Zeno.”]

Antiphon. Holy confessor Zeno, shepherd of the Lord’s flock, we beseech you: intercede for us, that we may deserve to be with you in heaven. Alleluia, alleluia, alleluia.
