#### [CXCVI] V.—CONSTITUTION OF THEOBALD, BISHOP OF VERONA, EXCERPTED FROM THE CONSTITUTIONS ISSUED BY HIM IN 1305, AND LATER REPUBLISHED BY BISHOP PETER SCALIGER

(From manuscripts of the Chapter of Verona.) Chapter LXI, concerning the feasts of Saint Zeno and the celebration of Saints Fermo and Rusticus.

Desiring that the glorious Confessor, blessed Zeno, Father and Patron of this city and diocese of Verona, and the blessed martyrs George, Fermo, and Rusticus, should be venerated by the flock entrusted to us with fitting devotion and due honors, so that we may be aided before God by their merits, we command that their feast be solemnly celebrated every year throughout the city and diocese of Verona by people and clergy; and that in all churches of the same city and diocese their commemoration be made on each weekday at Matins and Vespers, with their antiphon and collect to be read in the aforesaid churches. Accordingly, for the three martyrs one common Antiphon and prayer shall be said: “O God, who grantest us to celebrate the memory of thy holy martyrs George, Fermo, and Rusticus,” etc.

The same commemoration was subsequently prescribed by Giovanni Matteo Giberti, bishop of Verona, in the *Constitutions*, title 2, book II, chapters 2 and 3, not only at Lauds and Vespers but also in Masses, in the collect *A cunctis* (“From all [dangers]”); and this is observed even today.

## SELECTED TESTIMONIES CONCERNING ST. ZENO, BISHOP OF VERONA

### St. Ambrose, Letter I to Syagrius, Bishop of Verona, §1

But you thought that this judgment ought to be claimed for yourself alone, without the counsel of any brother; and yet, before the trial, you rendered a prejudgment, in judging that a girl approved by the judgment of Zeno of holy memory and sanctified by his blessing should, after so many years, be brought into danger of accusation without an author of the charge, without an accuser, without one who avowed the denunciation.

### St. Gregory the Great, *Dialogues*, book III, chapter 19

Recently John the Tribune informed me by his testimony that Count Pronulf, when present with him, declared that he had been in that same place at the same time with King Authari, when the wondrous event occurred, and that he knew the matter.

For the aforesaid Tribune related as follows: “About five years ago, when the Tiber, leaving its channel here at the city of Rome, rose so high that its flood flowed over the city walls and already occupied extensive districts, the river Adige, swelling near the city of Verona, came to the church of blessed Zeno, martyr and bishop. Though the doors of that church stood open, the water did not enter it at all. Rising for a while, it reached the windows of the church, which were close to the roof; and, standing thus, the water shut the church door, as though that liquid element had been changed into the solidity of a wall. Many people were inside; but, with the whole church surrounded by such a mass of water, they had no way of getting out. Fearing that they would perish there from thirst and hunger, they came to the church door and drew water to drink from that flood which, as I have said, had risen as high as the windows, yet in no way flowed into the church. Thus it could be drawn as water, but could not flow as water. Standing before the door to show everyone the merit of the martyr, it was water to bring assistance, and, as it were, not water to invade the place.”

#### [CXCVIII] The Anonymous Pipinian, in the *Rhythm on the Praises of Verona*

Zeno, the illustrious martyr, the eighth pastor and confessor,

Who by preaching brought Verona back to baptism,

Healed Gallienus’s daughter of an evil spirit,

And restored from the sea oxen sinking together with a man.

Indeed, he freed many from the deadly enemy,

Raised a dead man rescued from the river,

And destroyed many idols through frequent fasts.

I cannot recount the many works of this Saint,

The wonders which almighty God, through him,

Displayed in coming from Syria as far as Italy.

[Note: After the third dissertation, chapter 1, in which we had published this testimony of the Anonymous Pipinian, we received from Lobbes a carefully transcribed complete *Rhythm* from a manuscript written in the very hand of Ratherius, bishop of Verona. In it one plainly reads not *Galli*, as Mabillon had printed, nor “of Emperor Gallienus,” as we had written from two later manuscripts in the place cited, but “Gallienus’s daughter.” We have therefore preferred this reading of an older manuscript and a known writer; it at the same time removes the one difficulty which we had thought existed in the Anonymous Pipinian, namely, that he seemed to have swallowed the fable of Emperor Gallienus. From this it may also seem possible to confirm what we conjectured in Dissertation I, chapter 3, §4: that the Gallienus whose daughter St. Zeno truly healed of a demon was some person who, through certain writers, was transformed into an emperor. We have corrected a few other points in accordance with the authority of the same manuscript.]

### Ratherius, Bishop of Verona, *On Contempt for the Canons*, part I, p. 352, vol. I of the latest edition of Acheri’s *Spicilegium*

Here I shall employ the authority of blessed Zeno, namely in the sermon which he composed, in his customary most eloquent manner, on Judah the patriarch and Tamar his daughter-in-law, saying: “The Devil is the father of all who live corruptly.”

### The Same Ratherius, in the Synodal Letter to Priests, p. 377, col. 2

And since our own special teacher and overseer, blessed Zeno, says in the sermon which he composed most elegantly on Judah the son of Jacob and Tamar his daughter-in-law, etc.

### John the Priest, Mansionary of the Church of Verona, writing in 1320, *Imperial Histories*, book I, manuscript

Illustrious teachers flourished in the Church of God, among them Blessed Zeno, bishop of Verona, an outstanding teacher, the eighth bishop of that city. …

This outstanding teacher Zeno wrote three treatises on Chastity, Patience, Faith, Hope, and Charity; one treatise on Justice; one on Fear; one on Spirit and Body; one discourse on the text, “When he shall have delivered up the kingdom to God and the Father”; a most beautiful exposition on Solomon’s building of the house of God; one treatise on Continence; three treatises on Baptism; one on the Nativity and Majesty of the Lord; on Daniel at Easter, [treatises] …; seven treatises on Psalms 40, 41, 126, 127, 128, 129, and 130; one treatise on Envy and Jealousy; one very lengthy treatise on the saying, “Take heed to yourself, lest perhaps an iniquitous word be hidden in your heart”; one treatise on the fast of the four seasons, on Psalm 80; one on the Miser and the Rich Man; three on Avarice; one on Circumcision; nine treatises on Genesis; nine on Exodus; seven on Isaiah; three on Daniel; one on Job; eight on the feast of Easter; five treatises entitled *Invitation to the Font*; one discourse on Jacob’s Dream; one treatise for neophytes on the Twelve Signs of Heaven; likewise two for neophytes; two on Faith; one on Jonah; a short treatise on the History of Susanna; two treatises on the Lord’s Day; two on Abraham; two treatises on the Nativity of the Lord; a Letter on the passion of the martyr Arcadius, who suffered at the same time, on the second day before the Ides of January, in Mauritania. … I myself have read and seen these writings and treatises of his.

[Note: By error, the treatise on Psalm 80 is cited in place of the treatise on Psalm 100, which is found among Zeno’s treatises but is not listed in this index of John of Verona.]

[Note: Pastrengo and Peter de Natalibus, in the index which they likewise copied from John of Verona, report eight, not nine, treatises on Genesis, although in the manuscripts no more than six bear this title. But it is plainly evident that John did not compile an altogether exact index of treatises from the manuscripts, since, even including spurious works, he lists only eighty-seven treatises, whereas the genuine ones themselves are more numerous; and, among others, he omitted the treatise on Judah, which Ratherius cited four times. Since he undertook to collect treatises bearing the same title scattered here and there in the manuscripts, it was easy for him to err in counting. For this reason, just as he recorded fewer treatises of the same title—for example, on Exodus—than occur in the manuscripts, so conversely he listed more on Genesis, perhaps counting the same treatise twice or three times while running through the titles of a codex.]

### Peter Calo, of the Order of Preachers, in manuscript *Miscellanies* at Henschenius, p. 76, vol. II for April

St. Zeno wrote more than eighty treatises on the Psalms, the prophets, the Nativity of the Lord, and various other subjects, as well as letters and several expositions, and a Life of St. Arcadius the martyr, who suffered at the same time, which I have placed on the day before the Ides of January. I myself saw these treatises, letters, and expositions, composed in a beautiful and subtle style, in two volumes at St. Zeno’s in Verona.

### William Pastrengo, Judge of Verona, in the Book *On Illustrious Men*, p. 77

Zeno, bishop of Verona, is regarded as distinguished in the time of Emperor Gallienus, and suffers martyrdom. This venerable bishop of God wrote three books on Patience, Chastity, Faith, Hope, and Charity, etc.

For he copies the cited John of Verona, and then adds: “The memorable man John, mansionary-priest of the greater church of Verona, testifies that he himself saw and read all these little works.”

### Peter de Natalibus, Bishop of Equilio, *Catalogue of Saints*, book I, chapter 43

Zeno, bishop and teacher of Verona, flourished in the time of Emperor Gallienus. … This venerable bishop wrote books on Patience, and all the rest in precisely the same words as in William Pastrengo.

### James the Priest, in the Poem *On the Miracles of St. Zeno*, in Henschenius, no. 4, p. 76, vol. II for April; for the age of this writer, see the prefatory notice to the documents

But when he first courageously delivered God’s holy words to the people, he was regarded as Verona’s worthy patron, though he was the eighth bishop in that city. For our Father taught sacred laws to hearts; indeed, he flourished in polished speech, and constantly urged by fatherly counsels that he might unite all persons to God himself, one and threefold. From the living font of Jesus he redeemed countless peoples, and this Father consecrated great temples to the honor of God.

And no. 17, p. 77:

O Verona, how exceedingly bright are the many and great deeds of your bishop, to whom you owe so much! For who is regarded as the first founder of your faith? What first light drives darkness from your hearts? What father in speech was more pleasing to his children than he? In whom did the splendor of expression and eloquence shine more greatly?

#### [CCI] Flavio Biondo, *Italia Illustrata*, region 9, Basel edition

Zeno—just as Christian religion and his own holiness require—shall be the first [mentioned]: a bishop of Verona renowned for sanctity, who wrote many extant works explaining the sacred writings of both Testaments and breathing the eloquence of Ambrose, whom he imitated.

### Michael Fossatus of Verona, in the Poem *On the Praises of Verona*, composed in 1482 and published by Baptista Peretto in the Latin scholia to the *Life of St. Zeno*, p. 60

Holy Zeno, Father of your country, the book of your sermons teaches how great your Muse was.

### Onofrio Panvinio, *Antiquities of Verona*, book IV, chapter 6

He was a man exceedingly vigorous in the conduct of affairs and eloquent in explaining the divine Scriptures. So long as he lived as bishop, he devoted himself constantly to this care: to turn and inflame the minds of the citizens toward embracing the true piety of Christ, after rejecting the worship of images. … He published eloquent sermons filled with great learning.

### The Same, book VI, p. 152

He was held to be most eminent both in piety, faith, and religion, and in manifold learning. For he wrote many works worthy of a Christian bishop, of which the following have come to our knowledge: three books on Patience, Chastity, Faith, Hope, and Charity, and the rest, almost as in John of Verona, whose manuscript history he used.

### Isaac Casaubon, on Spartianus, p. 34

Zeno of Verona is, in my judgment, the most elegant of the Latin Fathers.

### The Same, *Exercitations*, 16, §43

Zeno of Verona, a most ancient and most elegant writer.

### Caspar Barth, *Adversaria*, book XLII, chapter 15

Zeno, a writer to be admired for learning and piety.

### The Same, book XLIII, chapter 10

When I read the sermons of Zeno, once bishop of the Veronese, I seem to myself to be reading a Christian Apuleius: so learned and compact is that most noble writer in signifying much by few words.

He is called by the same Barth “a most learned bishop” in book XLII, chapter 5; “a most elegant bishop” in book XLII, chapter 18; “a most learned writer” in book XLII, chapter 15 and book XLVI, chapter 7; and “most acute” on Papinius Statius, *Thebaid* II, verse 231.

#### [CCII] Augustus Buchner, Dissertation CCCLXXXIX, p. 528

Zeno’s style is learned, florid, and elegant. It reveals the reading of the most excellent authors, especially Virgil; it is painted and variegated with diverse colors, and is composed moreover of distinctive and highly expressive words. It contains many ingenious and acute sayings, so that nothing could seem to be expressed more pointedly.

And p. 529: No one will waste his labor who undertakes to read his sermons, at once most learned and most holy. For, besides the fact that everywhere they instruct minds through brilliant and excellent sentiments concerning religion and invite and lead them toward true piety, one may there observe many things said with the utmost elegance and grace, which can wonderfully increase and enrich the resources of eloquence.

### Claude Saumaise, on Lampridius, p. 193

Zeno of Verona, an elegant and pious author.

### Emmanuel Schelstrate, *On the Discipline of the Secret*, chapter 4, single article, §5

Zeno, bishop of Verona, a most ancient and learned author.

### Marquis Scipione Maffei, book II, *On Veronese Writers*, Part II of *Verona Illustrated*: “ST. ZENO”

Of this our bishop we possess many sermons, through which he deservedly holds a place among the holy Fathers. Not a few learned foreigners cite and approve these sermons: Paul, bishop of Fossombrone; Boulenger; Saumaise; Valois; Buchner; Daumius; Barth, to whom our author seemed a Christian Apuleius; the great Casaubon, who judged him the most elegant of all Latin writers; and many others.

Father Bolland adduces his sermon on St. Arcadius as an authentic Life of that martyr; Father Ruinart does the same in the *Selected Acts*. But just as the time, rank, deeds, and even existence of this Saint are disputed, so, above all, are the sermons disputed; for they have been sharply rejected by a long line of capable critics.

Sixtus of Siena was the first, since he frankly wrote that Guarino had issued as Zeno’s sermons works for the most part taken from various authors: some being by St. Hilary and St. Basil, while the others, whether sermons or fragments, plainly show by their diversity of style that they are by different authors. All this was copied exactly first by Possevino, Bellarmine, Baronius, Molanus, and Miraeus; afterward by Rivet, Cocus, Vossius, Cave, Labbe, Oudin, Placcius, Dupin—who doubts whether this Zeno ever existed in the world at all—and many others, although they generally presented such views as their own opinions and did not even name Sixtus of Siena.

The later writers press particularly the point that these sermons were assembled, fabricated, and published by our Guarino, and that no prior knowledge or mention of them ever existed. How erroneous and false this is, despite the agreement of so many, we shall show in a few words.

First, it is false that Guarino produced the edition of these sermons: they were not published until 1508, that is, about fifty years after his death. Rather, they are said to have been transcribed for publication from a very ancient volume found at Verona by Guarino in the episcopal library (p. 1). But, to see how far from the truth it is that no one mentioned Zeno’s sermons before Guarino, it is enough to read the little work of William Pastrengo, Petrarch’s contemporary. For he not only includes Zeno among writers, but recites a catalogue of his sermons and cites a witness older than himself, namely John the priest, mansionary of the cathedral church, who attested that he had read them all (p. 77).

A contemporary of this man was Peter de Natalibus, who likewise enumerated the sermons when speaking of our Zeno; and somewhat earlier was Peter Calo, who collected and epitomized the lives of the Saints in two large volumes. The Bollandist Fathers drew from his writings a legend of the translation and miracles, at the foot of which he noted as follows, under 12 April: “St. Zeno wrote more than eighty treatises,” etc.; and then: “I myself saw these treatises, letters, and expositions, composed in a beautiful and subtle style, in two volumes at St. Zeno’s in Verona.” Therefore Guarino was neither alone, nor first, nor was the codex later found by him in the Chapter library the only one; another was in the library of the monastery of St. Zeno.

James the priest too—whose verses drawn from a Zenonian manuscript were published by the Bollandists—particularly praised the Saint in those times for his eloquence. We ourselves have newly published a Life of him at the foot of the *History of Diplomas*; its author may be conjectured to have lived in, or around, the twelfth century. In it the holy bishop is introduced speaking to the people, and he is made to utter some passages from these very sermons of his.

But this is not enough. In the tenth century flourished Ratherius, our bishop, celebrated both for his writings and his life. In three of his little works he cites a passage from the Sermon on Judah the Patriarch; and in the Synodal Letter he cites it after prefacing these words: “And since our own special teacher and overseer, blessed Zeno, says in the sermon which he composed most elegantly on Judah the son of Jacob and Tamar his daughter-in-law, etc.”

There is still better evidence. Hincmar, created bishop of Reims in 845, gave to the library of St. Remigius a codex containing these sermons under the title *Treatises of St. Zeno, Bishop of Verona*. Learned Benedictine editors of St. Hilary, as well as Father Ruinart, testify that this precious codex is preserved even today. Thus, Zeno of Verona’s sermons were known even in distant lands as early as the ninth century; nor should it be believed that they were then suspected at all of being apocryphal—that is, stolen and falsely titled—since a prelate of such learning as Hincmar thought them worthy of his gift to an eminent library.

See, then, how many testimonies there are, and how much earlier they are than Guarino. Nor do I doubt that we would possess testimony still earlier and clearer, if the book found by him in the Chapter library had not been miserably lost; for Father Castellani, the first editor of the sermons, says that it was very ancient, and it came from a library in which almost all the codices were in majuscule script and many were considered ancient even several centuries ago.

I believe, therefore, that the authenticity in general of our bishop’s sermons has been sufficiently justified. That some among them are not his is common to collections of sermons; that some are shapeless fragments may have arisen through scribes’ confusion and discretion, and because sometimes only a few periods spoken by him on some occasion were collected from his voice. The celebrated diversity of style is not generally verified, because in a great part of these documents the same genius and the same manner appear.

Difficulties concerning certain passages are resolved by abandoning the error of those who have considered him a man of the third century and the age of Gallienus; on this see our Letter to the Bishops of Verona in the new edition of Ughelli. That he lived toward the end of the fourth century becomes evident to anyone who properly considers, first, the condition of those times in these regions and the uniformity of events in neighboring countries. It is then made indubitable by the fact that St. Zeno succeeded Gricinus, and Gricinus Lucillus, who subscribed to the Council of Sardica in 347.

No less strong is the argument drawn from St. Ambrose’s Letter to our Bishop Syagrius, because Ambrose rebukes him for not holding innocent a sacred virgin already acquitted and sanctified by the blessing of Zeno of holy memory. This makes it entirely clear that Zeno had been his predecessor. But why are other proofs needed, when Zeno himself says in the Sermon on Continence that apostolic teachings had already been circulating for almost four hundred years? Thus the manuscripts read, and so does the first reliable edition.

This number need not be taken too strictly, as Vossius took it (*On Latin History*, book III, chapter 2), since the use of round numbers is well known and has countless examples. Felix III said simply, “After five hundred years,” in a letter which we have now republished and inserted in volume five of the Councils, although, as we have there demonstrated, it was written before the year 489. Nor does St. Zeno there calculate from the time of the Letter to the Corinthians which he mentions, but from Christian times in general and from Christ’s birth.

To refute the objection from the silence of the ancients; to enter into a particular examination of each sermon; to address the question whether he was a martyr or not; and other such matters, are not the purpose of the present undertaking. They will be the task of whoever finally undertakes a sound edition of this Father. No other author has greater need of one: to reunite, distinguish, identify the sources, explain, and correct. Whether this Saint was native to our land cannot either be affirmed or denied. His name indeed points rather to Greek origin, and the Anonymous writer, of whom we shall shortly speak, seems to indicate that he came here from the regions of Syria.

## DEDICATORY LETTER OF AUGUSTINUS VALERIUS, CARDINAL AND BISHOP OF VERONA, TO SIXTUS V, SUPREME PONTIFF, PREFIXED TO THE VERONESE EDITION OF 1586

[Col. 0237]

[Col. 0237B] When, last April, Most Blessed Father, Your Holiness, in accordance with the custom and institution of the ancient Roman Pontiffs, consecrated in the first year of your pontificate the wax *Agnus Dei* medallions, whose wonderful power, as instruments, so to speak, of divine mercy, has often been observed by mortals amid fires, floods, and storms; and when you entertained the sacred College of Cardinals, because of its goodwill and charity toward this order, with a banquet lasting three days, I remember that on the final day of the banquet, to which I myself was invited, Your Holiness mentioned St. Zeno, bishop and martyr of Verona. For, after the sacred reading and after the weighty table-discourses, you turned your eyes toward me and said: “Tomorrow will be celebrated the feast-day of St. Zeno, bishop and martyr, who amid the storms of persecutions governed the Church of Verona with wondrous steadfastness and was crowned with martyrdom in the time of Gallienus.” This commemoration was followed by mention of the sermons written by that most holy bishop.

[Col. 0237D] Since the words of Christ’s Vicar had been fixed in my mind, I regarded the commemoration of St. Zeno—whom, though unworthy, I had succeeded in this office after many years—as a silent yet urgent exhortation. Therefore, when, with the permission of Your Blessedness, I returned to Verona, more eager and ardent than ever before to discharge my pastoral duties, I first exhorted the entire clergy in the diocesan synod to venerate more devoutly the Patron of this city as an example of the proper governance of the Christian flock and as an excellent teacher, and to imitate him more diligently in character and life. Then, because the sermons of St. Zeno, which had been printed and published many years earlier, were exceedingly corrupt, and scarcely any copies of them any longer remained, I determined that they should be printed anew with much greater accuracy, so that the Veronese clergy and other learned and devout men might not be deprived of the useful reading of this most ancient and holy writer.

[Col. 0238C] The zeal of certain Veronese priests was added to this, men who lacked neither talent nor devotion in bringing honour to the Church of Verona. Accordingly, after they had been collated, corrected, and purged with me by many learned men, they were entrusted to the press by my command. Verona, Most Holy Father, is indeed famous for many splendid gifts of nature: for the mildness of its climate; the charm of its hills and of the Adige flowing through it; the size and antiquity of the city; and the excellence of its talents. It flourishes in works of art for adornment and defence, in arches, bridges, an amphitheatre, and sacred churches. Yet it is far more flourishing and fortified by the number and relics of its saints, especially the bishops who ruled it most wisely and holily.

[Col. 0238D] The first among these, Euprepius, was sent to Verona by St. Peter, prince of the apostles and Vicar of Christ; he had thirty-five successors who were holy bishops. Their memory is carefully preserved both in the book *On the Holy Bishops of Verona*, in several churches, and in the episcopal palace, where their painted images and inscribed names appear in a distinguished place; it is also most devoutly honoured in the divine offices, according to the decrees of diocesan synods and ancient custom. This city ascribes to their protection the great blessing that, throughout the course of so many centuries and amid so many waves of heresies, it has retained the Catholic faith in complete purity and with great constancy, [Col. 0239A] and has therefore obeyed with the highest reverence that holy Roman Apostolic See—its own See and the mother of all Christian faithful—from which the rule for right belief and right living must be sought.

Among these bishops Blessed Zeno the martyr holds the eighth place. Scarcely had he passed to heaven when the city of Verona adopted him as its patron and has perpetually honoured him as such, because it has very often experienced his protection in its calamities. The judgement of devout persons held it fitting that, since Zeno both lived and wrote in the time of Pope Sixtus II, his writings, almost dead, should happily revive while another Sixtus, Sixtus V, governed the universal Church; and that he who had been the silent author and instigator of their publication should also have as their eloquent patron and defender.

[Col. 0239B] Finally, just as the bishop of Verona ought to illuminate at Verona the little works of Zeno, bishop of the Church of Verona, so a cardinal ought to send them to the Roman Pontiff—whom the sacred College of Cardinals and the whole Christian commonwealth acknowledge and venerate as high priest, prince of bishops, heir of the apostles, Peter in authority and Christ in anointing, to use the words of St. Bernard. Thus Augustine, Cardinal of Verona, ought to send them to Sixtus V, whom he honours with the greatest reverence and from whom he has received many honours and great benefits.

[Col. 0240A] I do not doubt that Your Holiness will approve this pastoral labour of mine, though slight, undertaken in the summer heat, and will derive great pleasure from the writings of this bishop and martyr. Meanwhile may God, the author and giver of all good things, enrich Your Blessedness ever more abundantly each day with his gifts, as he does; and may he preserve you in health for a very long time for our College and for the whole Church, [Col. 0240B] so that justice, peace, the authority of that holy See, and every virtue may daily grow stronger and flourish.

## PREFACE OF RAPHAEL BAGATA AND BAPTISTA PERETTI TO THE SAME VERONESE EDITION OF 1586

[Col. 0239]

St. Zeno, bishop and patron of Verona, governed the Church of Verona with admirable constancy in most difficult times and amid great storms, and was crowned with martyrdom in the time of the Emperor Gallienus. He flourished not only in holiness of life and pastoral vigilance, but also in learning and eloquence, as his sermons, composed with the utmost gravity and with a certain apostolic spirit of that age, abundantly attest.

[Col. 0239C] The same St. Zeno must be counted among the most ancient writers of the Church, since he was contemporary with the most learned Origen and the most glorious martyr Cyprian. At Verona he is called Father of his Country and distinguished Teacher; with the title of Teacher he is honoured also in the Church of Milan. In Greece, too, he preached Christ’s Gospel. We possess sermons of this St. Zeno in an ancient handwritten parchment codex. The same sermons were discovered by Guarino, learned in Greek and Latin letters, in a very ancient volume of the bishopric; and in 1508 they were published at Venice by a certain bookseller, under the name of St. Zeno, in crude and exceedingly faulty type, so that there can in no way be doubt concerning their author.

[Col. 0239D] But now, after exact collation, correction, and purgation in more elegant type, they have been printed and distributed by command of the most illustrious and most reverend Augustus Valerius, likewise bishop of Verona and cardinal of the Holy Roman Church, in accordance with his diligent, watchful, and customary pastoral care. They have been arranged according to that learned order followed by the man of outstanding learning and judgement, Cardinal Felix of Montalto—now our Most Holy Lord Sixtus V—in his edition of the works of St. Ambrose: the first place was assigned to sermons explaining passages of the Old Testament; the next to those explaining the New; and the final place to those treating virtues and vices.

Nor should anyone object that the title “martyr” has been added to this edition, whereas the cruder edition lacks it. For it was proper to attribute to the holy author of these sermons the glory of martyrdom which—leaving aside the very ancient testimonies of Blessed Pope Gregory, the Venerable Bede, Usuard, and others—the most recent Martyrology published by command of Pope Gregory XIII attributes to him.

[Col. 0240B] Perhaps someone will object that these sermons belong to another Zeno, a martyr’s later namesake and likewise bishop of Verona, whom St. Ambrose mentions in his first letter to Syagrius. But that passage first contains nothing by which it may be proved that that Zeno was the author of these sermons. Secondly, it does not establish so clearly that he was bishop of Verona as to prove it conclusively. For when St. Ambrose had begun to preach—so we read in the life of St. Eusebius, bishop of Bologna, Book I of *On the Bishops of Bologna*—consecrated virginity to God, the people of Bologna, moved by his preaching, according to the same author Eusebius, were everywhere sending their daughters to Milan to receive the veil. St. Ambrose himself also mentions this in Book I *On Virgins*, where he testifies that virgins had even come from Mauritania to Milan in order to be veiled and consecrated.

[Col. 0240C] By the same reasoning, we must believe that the virgin named Indicia, mentioned there, was entrusted at Milan by St. Ambrose to that same Zeno, a man of holy memory, for approval and blessing. This may readily be gathered from the same letter. For St. Ambrose’s own sister, while she was at Milan, testifies that Indicia lived at Rome in her house while Ambrose was absent. A certain woman named Paterna, whom St. Ambrose calls his daughter, had never left Indicia. But Indicia seems to have lived at Verona, whither she had gone with her sister when the latter was newly married, with that sister, though separated by a wall, for only a short time. It is therefore evident that Indicia was distinguished by the consecrating blessing of virginity somewhere other than Verona, especially since, after so many years from her blessing, as St. Ambrose says, the mark of corruption was branded upon her.

[Col. 0241A] Moreover, there is the perpetual tradition of the Church of Verona, which we must uphold as secure by definite arguments in accordance with the prescription of the Canons. Apart from Zeno the bishop and martyr—concerning whom fuller treatment has been given in the little book *On the Holy Bishops of Verona*—that Church has acknowledged no other Zeno as bishop. This tradition is also attested by the sequence of Veronese bishops painted in the episcopal hall, in which only one Zeno, the eighth bishop, is seen.

Another will say that the errors of Arius are refuted by the author of these sermons, though Arius did not yet exist in the lifetime of Zeno the martyr. We reply that, since Epiphanius writes that Origen was the father of Arius, and St. Thomas the source of the same error, the errors disseminated by Arius existed before Arius was born, just as Luther’s errors were refuted before Luther disseminated that pestilential heresy.

[Col. 0241B] If he maintains that these errors are falsely attributed to Origen, as Pamphilus the martyr and other distinguished writers thought, he does not thereby prove that there was no reason why St. Zeno should have needed to refute that plague—the claim that the Son is not coeternal with the Father.

It is objected that the sermon *On Continence* cannot belong to St. Zeno the martyr, since in it the author is said to have been separated from the teaching promulgated by St. Paul by more than four hundred years, and since nearly the whole world was then Christian. We say that the text, as it is corrupt in many places, is also corrupted there, as often happens with numbers. Moreover, since the Gospel had been disseminated through all provinces and received by many, the author there uses “the whole” for “a part,” as is customary.

[Col. 0241C] It is an indication of a most ancient author that he frequently delivered sermons to Jews; invited catechumens to immerse themselves in the sacred font; and reproved Greeks who had then converted to the faith of Christ because, with their vain wisdom, they introduced vain notions about God even into the Church of God, as in Sermon I on Psalm CXXX. The same is shown when, in the sermon *On the Spiritual Building of God’s House*, the author demonstrates that churches had not yet been built for Christians and that the new people were very few in number. Again, in Sermon IV *To the Neophytes*, he mentions those who had bestowed their whole property upon the poor and who were God’s temple, although they had previously been temples of idolatry.

[Col. 0241D] The same may further be seen in Sermon V *To the Neophytes*, when the author exhorts them to flee idolatry and no longer seek omens. What then? Is it not plainly evident from Sermon I *On Easter* and from the sermon *On Patience*? In the former he interprets autumn as signifying the martyrs of his own time; in the latter he calls patience the daily crown of martyrs. Blessed Thecla, disciple of St. Paul the Apostle and the first female martyr, is adduced in the sermon *On Fear* as an example of fear of the Lord. In the sermon *On the Resurrection* he mentions some who had died in idolatry in his own time, and he rebukes certain Christians for not believing in the resurrection of bodies. Moreover, he described the life of St. Arcadius, a martyr who, as Peter bishop of Equilium testifies, was crowned with martyrdom in Mauritania in his own time.

[Col. 0242A] From these and very many other such indications, the author of these sermons is shown to be most ancient. As to the fact that three or four sermons are found among them which some think cannot be ascribed to St. Zeno—namely, the one entitled *On the Precept “Attend to Yourself”*; the sermon on the Gospel according to Luke, *On the Twofold Kind of Temptations*; the sermon *On Malice and Envy*; and the sermon *On Fasting*—which are found written in Greek among the homilies of St. Basil: although arguments are not lacking by which it would be permissible to prove that these too belong to our Zeno, since by preaching in Greece, long before St. Basil, with great zeal and most weighty labours he converted many to the faith of Christ, we do not wish to be contentious in this matter.

[Col. 0242B] But to the claim made by the author of the *Sacred Library*, namely that the seven sermons on the Psalms which he enumerated were copied from St. Hilary’s commentaries, we say that he erred as to their number; for the sermons on Psalm LXXIX and Psalm C are not found in St. Hilary’s commentaries. As to the other five, since two sermons on Psalm CXXX occur among these sermons, while the second resembles the first in certain vocabulary and in almost the same thoughts, and since the first is not found in St. Hilary’s commentaries, we say that the second was repeated by St. Zeno in his usual manner with some variation and therefore belongs to him; but it was inserted into St. Hilary’s commentaries by someone else, just as we see sermons and little treatises by authors of no small distinction having crept among the works of Jerome, Augustine, and certain holy Fathers.

[Col. 0242C] Whether the other four were inserted in the same commentaries by the same means or not is for others to judge. But we, finding in the same ancient handwritten codex these sermons also together with the four which, as we have said, we find written in Greek among St. Basil’s works, have not dared to deprive St. Zeno of the possession of praise due to him. Nor ought we to deprive the reader of so useful and agreeable a reading.

As to the objection from style—that the sermons are composed in varied modes of expression—whoever considers them properly will find, with very few exceptions, that they are of one style. For the same words, the same arrangement and connection of words, often occur in them. Nor is it safe always to make a judgement about an author from diversity of style, especially in a small number of writings; for not every author has always composed his writings in the same idiom. Indeed, as Aloysius Lippomanus, bishop of this Church of Verona, says in the preface to the reader in Volume II of the *Lives of the Saints*, we sometimes find this to have happened to Augustine, Jerome, and other holy Fathers, and even to St. Paul the Apostle: according to the character of places, times, and persons, they speak now more loftily, now more humbly.

[Col. 0242D] The incomplete sermons, which St. Zeno probably wrote at different times, were faithfully collected by one of his disciples, especially since some matters in them are nearly identical; this the author himself would certainly not have done, nor would anyone else who had wished to collect them from different authors. From these facts, therefore, it is possible to recognize how grievously the outstanding teacher St. Zeno has been deprived of his honour in that same place in the *Sacred Library*, stripped of his most excellent writings. Against this opinion and judgement, insufficiently discerning in this matter, stand Flavio Biondo, in the ninth region of *Italy Illustrated*; Peter, bishop of Equilium, in the life of St. Zeno; and the mathematician Johannes Stoeffler of Justingen, in the Roman calendar, who attribute the sermons to St. Zeno before they had been printed, in the preceding century.

[Col. 0243A] In our own age, besides Brother Leandro Alberti of Bologna, of the Order of Preachers, in his description of Italy, and Onofrio Panvinio in his handwritten chronicle, the same Aloysius Lippomanus and Laurentius Surius the Carthusian refute that man’s empty weighing and judgement. They are men distinguished for judgement, piety, varied and recondite learning, and especially profound knowledge of sacred history. They demonstrated not only in words but also in practice that the sermons are St. Zeno’s: one of them interwove, under Zeno’s name, sayings gathered like little flowers from these sermons into his chain of commentaries on Genesis; both inserted complete sermons bearing the name of Blessed Zeno among the Lives of the Saints which they collected with supreme prudence and incredible labour.

[Col. 0244A] To these weighty authorities is added the life of St. Zeno, written many centuries ago, in which several passages from certain of these disputed sermons are found. We further note that the sermon of St. Gaudentius, bishop of Brescia, which had been added to the printed sermons of St. Zeno, has been omitted because it is not found in the ancient handwritten codex.

This is what we have to say concerning the sermons of St. Zeno, in order that we might obey, with the reverence we owed, the command of our most devout and gracious shepherd and father. Enjoy, then, candid reader, these sermons of the martyr-bishop, which have been left to us by God’s great gift. When you read them attentively, you will perceive yourself wonderfully stirred to the pursuit of virtue and piety, and you will plainly recognize a man in whom Christ spoke.

## LITERARY NOTICE ON ZENO

*(From Schoenemann, vol. I, pp. 312–328.)*

### § I. Life

Bishop of Verona, concerning whom very few matters have been handed down with certain authority and continuous historical record. Some, led by his name and relying on the testimony of a certain anonymous versifier, have thought him Greek and a native of Syria. Their divination, besides being in itself rather frivolous and poorly supported, is completely undermined by a manner of expression far purer and more appropriate than a Greek man would seem likely to have attained through private study.

[Col. 0243C] On the contrary, from the same character of his style, the very learned Casaubon, Barthius, and others who have repeatedly praised his diction appear, not without reason, to have considered him African. The Ballerini brothers, his editors, added their support to this opinion from the treatise *On Arcadius the Martyr*, who suffered at Caesarea in Mauritania. Since his commemoration is wholly unknown among the ancients, they judge that it could not have been possible for a bishop of Verona to celebrate the day of his birth into heaven with such devotion unless he were attached to him by some special reverence, and therefore perhaps was himself a native of the same African province. They show at the same time that it was not contrary to the customs of Western churches to appoint Africans distinguished by merit as bishops and clergy, and that journeys to Eastern lands were likewise customary.

[Col. 0243D] The same writers state that he was ordained bishop on the sixth day before the Ides of December, in the year 363, the last year of Julian. Thus, after Julian died in 363 and the empire had once again passed to Caesars favourable to the Christian religion, Zeno began under most favourable auspices the duties of his new office. He attacked partly the pagans, who were probably still numerous at Verona then, and partly the Arians, who under Constantius, Julian’s predecessor, had almost crushed the Catholics in those regions. Some he converted to the faith by his eloquence; others he all but utterly defeated by vigorous attacks. Hence he was said to have cleansed Verona of errors and led it to the true religion.

[Col. 0244] He also accomplished, by distinguished zeal, the construction from the foundations of a new church at Verona; and when it was opened, he celebrated the first Christian assembly there with a sermon that still survives (*Treatise* XVI, Book I). From this same sermon the previously mentioned authors reasonably infer that this was the first church built at Verona for these purposes.

[Col. 0244C] He was a most vigilant guardian of morals and of the earnest conduct of life. There survives a treatise (*Treatise* XV, Book I) in which he inveighed with great force, by the example of bishops then prevalent throughout Italy, against those who misused the name of *agapae*—love-feasts—for banqueting, drunkenness, and indecency. Above all, we learn chiefly from Ambrose (*Letter*) that he fostered the discipline of virgins to such an extent that at Verona there were not only virgins who, bound by the vow of virginal chastity, lived in seclusion in their homes, but also women who had professed virginity and lived a common life in a monastery.

[Col. 0244D] The year in which he died, like most of his deeds, is uncertain. The Ballerini brothers preferred 380 or 381, so that he would have held the government of the Church of Verona for eighteen years—a period which they think scarcely long enough for accomplishing all that has been handed down to us so obscurely. There is no need here to speak of miracles and martyrdom. Whoever is concerned with the former should consult his editors and the sources from which they drew; the latter the Ballerini themselves undertook to prove to be a fable, with more labour than was perhaps necessary.

### § II. Writings

There survive of his works sixteen longer sermons and eighty-seven shorter ones.

### § III. Editions

Before the Ballerini brothers, no one could be said to have rendered good service to Zeno. For the sermons published under Zeno’s name quite early, namely in 1508, from a manuscript discovered by Guarino of Verona, not only did nothing to advance this author’s reputation, but also served to confuse scholars’ judgments concerning him. This was especially owing to John Sixtus of Siena (*Bibliotheca Sancta*, IV, Cologne, 1626, p. 391). Having encountered certain treatises which partly named Hilary or Basil as author, and partly displayed an author much later than Zeno—whose date Sixtus himself, following Bishop Peter Equilinus, had carried back as far as Gallienus—he readily allowed himself to be drawn into such doubt as to deny credibility even to all the rest, deciding that they had for the most part been collected from various authors nearly two hundred years later than Zeno.

Hence it came to be seriously doubted for some time whether Zeno ought to be numbered among ecclesiastical writers (Mabillon, *De Studiis monasticis*, part I, p. 277, 2nd Venetian edition, 1729, quarto). And although the authors of the Verona edition of 1586 composed a fairly lengthy defence:

> Yet since in the edition itself, apart from a different arrangement of the sermons, whereby they are seen distributed into two books, nothing new occurs, and all the treatises are equally disordered, intermixed, and sold as Zenonian—even those which Sixtus’s arguments had manifestly shown to be foreign—whatever could be said in defence of so bad a cause not only achieved nothing, but rather provoked some persons to indignation, and persuaded some that the cause itself, which had to be propped up and sustained by very weak arguments, was much weaker and worse than it had previously been. Moreover, to increase the difficulties, this edition also fixed the period in which St. Zeno flourished; since this plainly conflicts with the evidence of certain sermons, instead of calming the minds of dissenting critics, it sharpened them into greater disputes.

If to this you add the perverse method they followed in presenting the text itself—a method sharply censured by the same Ballerini, whose judgment has also just been quoted—and then observe that Zeno was subsequently copied from it, you will necessarily perceive with what right we asserted that before the Ballerini no one had deserved anything in this matter.

Toward the end of the preceding century a new edition was being prepared, but was interrupted by the author’s death. The following is said of it by the same Ballerini:

> Francis Sparaverius, a Veronese nobleman, thoroughly versed in Latin and Greek authors and an outstanding devotee of elegant letters and learning—concerning whom Scipio Maffei has reported more fully in Part II of *Verona Illustrata*—after producing several works with the highest praise, in his later years contemplated a new edition of St. Zeno, for which he prepared many annotations. But overtaken by death in 1697, he left the work unfinished. Following the Veronese order, he carried his commentary as far as the middle of the sermon *On the Building of the House of God*. After it, more than ten sermons remain in that edition without any commentary. Yet certain annotations indicate that he had prepared one, although it was not copied out, or at least had conceived it in mind; for in them he refers the reader to observations upon those later sermons as well. In these annotations he attempted to correct certain more corrupt passages and diligently and learnedly endeavoured to explain some more difficult expressions. He used one manuscript, which he seems even to have received late, and often wished for others by which he might restore the genuine reading. He clearly recognized certain spurious treatises; but, since he had not yet uncovered the received prejudice concerning the age of Gallienus, he hesitated in some places to regard certain added treatises as foreign, and in other places thought that a genuine sermon of Zeno, inconsistent with that period, should nevertheless be assigned to him. Thus it is not certain whether he would have changed his view had time remained for completing the edition and for longer reflection.

This unfinished commentary of Sparaverius has now also been added to the Ballerini edition. It is therefore through their immortal labour that one to whom scholars had previously denied the honour of authorship and even the standing of a learned man now shines forth in his office, merits, and writings, adorned with the honour of a most splendid edition. Gallandius followed the Ballerini recension and arrangement. The most recent labours on Zeno are those of Bartholomew Perazzini and James, Marquis Dionisi. Now for each in turn.

#### 1508

Venice, Benedetto Fontana. *Selected most elegant sermons to the people of the eminent, excellent, and most illustrious Doctor, Saint Zeno, Bishop of Verona, from a very ancient volume discovered at Verona in the library of the bishopric of Verona by Guarino of Verona, a most eloquent man.*

At the end:

> To the praise and glory of the supreme and undivided Trinity, of the most blessed Virgin Mary, of the blessed pontiffs Zeno and Caesarius, and of all the Saints, the sermons contained in this volume, never before printed, most carefully revised and most diligently corrected by the venerable Father Albertus Castellanus of the Order of Preachers, and most diligently printed at Venice by Master Jacobus de Leuco at the expense of Master Benedictus Fontana, happily come to an end in the year of the Lord 1508, on the twenty-fourth day of January.

From this fuller title it is readily apparent that, wrongly, for many years down to the Ballerini—who first corrected the error—the credit for this edition was attributed to Guarino of Verona. He had already died in the sixtieth year of the fifteenth century, and was entitled only to the credit for discovering the Zenonian manuscript. The work is divided into three books. The first contains seventeen sermons on virtues and vices; the second, thirty-eight sermons on matters of the Old Testament; the third, fifty sermons on matters of the New Testament. At the end are appended homilies of St. Caesarius of Arles and certain others, not distinguished from Zeno’s genuine treatises either by title or inscription, except for one sermon bearing the name of St. Gaudentius of Brescia.

#### 1586

Verona, Hieronymus Discipulus, quarto. *Sermons on very many passages of Holy Scripture and subjects of divine things*, with a dedicatory letter by A. Valerius (to Sixtus V, Supreme Pontiff).

This edition, produced at the instigation and by the design of Cardinal Augustine Valerius, bishop of Verona, through Raphael Bagata and Baptista Perettus, has nothing distinctive except that all the sermons are distributed into two books. For although they cite an ancient manuscript by which Zeno was made more correct in certain places, the Ballerini have shown that the manuscript was of quite recent date, written in the fifteenth century, and that its usefulness scarcely extended beyond correcting a few passages that were extremely corrupt in the first edition. Nor did they use it as they should have done. Rather, following the worst example of those who, under the patronage of Sixtus V, published Ambrose’s works, they repeatedly abandoned the authority both of the manuscript and of the first edition. Thus, in the judgment of the Ballerini, in this Verona edition and all those derived from it, besides the confused and disordered mixture of foreign treatises with Zenonian ones, what ought especially to offend is the arbitrary interpolation of certain passages—otherwise unnoticed, as they themselves observe, because of the rarity of the first edition.

It has a prefixed Life of Zeno, reportedly written by Raphael Bagata.

#### 1589

Paris, folio. *Sermons of Zeno, Bishop of Verona, on very many passages of Holy Scripture, etc.* In the second edition of Bigne’s *Bibliotheca Patrum*, vol. III.

#### 1618

Cologne, folio. *Sermons of Zeno of Verona.* In the *Bibliotheca Patrum*, vol. III.

#### 1644

Paris, Gilles Morel, folio. *Sermons of Zeno, Bishop of Verona, martyr and eminent doctor, on many passages of Holy Scripture, etc.* In the *Bibliotheca Patrum*, vol. II, col. 359. Reissued there in the same collection in 1654.

#### 1657

Lyon, at the expense of Laurent Anisson and Jean-Baptiste Devenet, folio. Various sermons of Zeno in Aloysius Lipomani’s *Catena on Genesis*, and likewise in the *Catena on Exodus* issued by him in the same place and year.

#### 1662

Paris, at the expense of Antoine Bertier, folio. Various sermons of Zeno in François Combefis’s *Concionatory Library of the Fathers*.

#### 1677

Lyon, Anisson press, folio. Sermons of Zeno in the *Maxima Bibliotheca Patrum*, vol. III, p. 359, with a prefixed Life, p. 356.

#### 1710

Padua. *Sermons of St. Zeno.* Reprinted from Raphael Bagata’s edition.

#### 1739

Verona, Seminary Press, Augustine Carattonius, folio—rather, quarto. *Sermons of Saint Zeno, Bishop of Verona. Now for the first time published with the diligence required*: foreign works, that is, having been separated and relegated to an Appendix, and several manuscripts consulted, among them one written about a thousand years earlier, collated in France by Marquis Scipio Maffei. Edited and elucidated by dissertations and continuous annotations by Peter and Jerome Ballerini, Veronese priests and brothers.

It was certainly no slight undertaking to produce such an edition of Zeno’s remains, in which the labour to be expended concerned the author no less than the text itself. Love of their native city could accomplish this: they were about to vindicate its bishop, illustrious in the memory of deeds and writings. But two things in particular had prevented earlier learned and acute men from discerning the truth: the inveterate opinion from the martyrology that St. Zeno lived and suffered martyrdom under Gallienus, and the prejudice of Sixtus of Siena that the sermons attributed to Zeno were a medley drawn from many authors widely different both in condition and in time.

Baronius alone had suspected that the author lived shortly before St. Ambrose, both from Ambrose’s letters and because the Arian heresy is mentioned in the treatise which in this edition is Book II, no. 7. Yet, wishing also to preserve the status of Zeno whom he had assigned among the martyrs under the Emperor Gallienus, he made this man distinct from the Veronese author of the sermons, thus positing two Zenos. But when he learned from the Veronese editors that the perpetual tradition of the Church of Verona knew no other Zeno besides Zeno the bishop and martyr, who was said to have suffered martyrdom under Gallienus, and whom they defended as the author of the sermons, he rejected his earlier opinion and subscribed to theirs. He therefore supposed only those treatises in which Arians are mentioned to have been inserted by Zenonian copyists.

After him, learned men were indeed not unaware that the bishop of Verona could not be carried back to the third century; yet none was prepared to examine and resolve the difficulties by which the matter seemed entangled. We rejoice that the Ballerini at last disentangled them so successfully.

In this connection one must first mention the defence written for the author and his sermons in the Zenonian prolegomena, comprised in three dissertations. The first treats of the genuine treatises of St. Zeno, bishop of Verona, and of his date; the second, of his doctrine; the third, of the Acts of St. Zeno and his cult. At the end are appended Documents concerning St. Zeno and selected testimonies. The second does not concern us; to the third belongs the brief account of Zeno’s Life which we gave above. Let us here present only an overview of the first, which sets out the method and foundations of the whole edition.

In the preface, after recounting various critical judgments and difficulties, the spurious treatises are finally separated from the genuine by the certain evidence of the manuscripts; and by that very fact the source and seat of the chief difficulties is overthrown. They observe that the genuine treatises of Zeno had been impossible to distinguish from the spurious through the fault of earlier editors. The latter had not separately presented the spurious treatises appended at the end of the manuscripts, nor even noted that they were placed at the end of the manuscripts—a notice which would have been sufficient to settle the entire controversy for scholars. Instead, they presented them intermingled with the genuine works and marked by no distinction, publishing them indiscriminately as Zenonian. Since these could not have Zeno as their author, they cast all the genuinely Zenonian works into doubt as well.

There are eleven such treatises, and they are consistently appended at the end of all the manuscripts; the editors likewise added them at the end of their edition. When these are removed, eighty-three remain, of which they maintain that there is one author. They demonstrate this by arguments drawn from manuscripts and from style, and by refuting the various objections made by learned men from differences of subject, character, and length. This is treated in chapter I, §§ 1–4.

In chapter II they proceed to establish that the author of these treatises wrote in the fourth century, and that everything contained in all the treatises agrees with that date. They first adduce a noteworthy passage from Treatise V, Book I, where the author counts four hundred years backward from his own time to the age of the Apostle Paul. The Veronese editors had rashly changed this to two hundred, and Baronius had later attempted to establish it by other arguments; each of these points is refuted. Then they press the weighty argument that an author arguing against the Arians must be assigned to the fourth century, reinforced by another argument: several fourth-century heresies are attacked in these treatises.

They add a public monument in the city of Verona: a church built under his auspices, opened and dedicated by him for common use (*Treatise* IV, Book I), something which could not have occurred before the fourth century. Likewise, the prohibition laid upon pagans against building temples, while public idolatrous worship nonetheless continued—matters mentioned by the author—define his period within more certain limits, after the middle of the fourth century and after Julian’s death. Further, the author seems to have imitated not Lactantius only, but Hilary as well.

Finally, a remarkable passage by the author on the ransom of captives, wonderfully agreeing with two others in St. Ambrose, is shown to refer to those captured by barbarians after the battle of Hadrianople in 378. At the same time, it is established that the author’s date cannot be extended beyond the fourth century, but that he flourished before 391. Lastly, the objection concerning persecutions and martyrs is removed by a brief history of fourth-century persecutions, chapter II, §§ 1–8.

With these points established, in chapter III they endeavour to prove that the author whom they had shown to have lived in the fourth century was St. Zeno, bishop of Verona. They appeal first to the manuscripts, ancient witnesses, and the tradition of the Church of Verona, all of which attribute these treatises to that Zeno. They then re-examine the common prejudice concerning St. Zeno’s date under Gallienus—the sole point which had seemed capable of being opposed to their conclusions—explain its origin and basis, namely the narrative of Coronatus the notary, and prove from the certain evidence of St. Ambrose’s letter to Syagrius and the ancient list of bishops of Verona that Zeno lived in the fourth century. Further, they scrutinize the narrative of Coronatus the notary, written in the seventh or eighth century, and show it to abound in fables. Finally, they define the age of St. Zeno, with which all the evidence agrees, within certain limits, between the years 356 and 380, chapter III, §§ 1–5.

Moreover, these most learned editors touched upon and discussed many matters of ecclesiastical history and literature—as they later did in their edition of Leo’s works—which are familiar to the memory of all scholars. But we must now describe the remaining merits of this edition.

They succeeded in obtaining nine manuscripts, eight of which contained all the sermons; the ninth, the most ancient, the Rheims manuscript, seemed to be the source of the rest. With their help they not only separated the spurious treatises from the genuine, as has appeared from what was said above, but also corrected the text remarkably in many places or established the ancient reading.

As regards the division and order of the sermons, they judged it inappropriate to follow either the earlier editors or the manuscripts. In both, the longer and shorter sermons were indiscriminately combined, those alike in subject and title scattered apart; and, in the editions, the genuine were also confused with the spurious. Accordingly, having assembled together the treatises with the same title, they divided all the sermons into two books. The first contains the longer sermons, nearly all prescribing concerning vices and virtues; the second, the shorter sermons, more numerous and diverse in subject. So that no one might miss the order of the manuscripts and the commonly cited Verona edition, they displayed both, compared with the new arrangement, in separate tables before the sermons themselves.

In their annotations they aimed not only to give the rationale of their corrections, record selected variant readings, and explain more difficult passages, but also to show more extensive care in elucidating diction. This was done both to confirm the author’s date and to vindicate the purity of his Latin expression:

> For the benefit of some who are held bound by certain now-ingrained prejudices, it was necessary sometimes to cite corresponding statements of other Fathers of the fourth, or even a later, century, by which it might be proved that certain expressions of Zeno, or certain testimonies, commonly thought to belong to a much earlier period, also fall within the fourth or even a later century. We have endeavoured to clear certain less common words or manners of speaking, which might appear foreign or of debased Latin, by indicating examples from approved writers, where possible; so that those very few which we have found in no one else remain sufficiently justified by the rest, especially since not all Roman and ancient words occur in the books of ancient authors.

The eleven treatises by other authors, appended as an Appendix, did not receive a comparable degree of care, but are nevertheless not without critical annotation. After the Appendix follow, with preface and dedicatory letter, the Verona edition of 1586; then Francis Sparaverius’s *autoschediasma*—“improvised sketch”—of annotations, with a preceding editorial notice, from which we excerpted certain things a little earlier. Broad reading in authors of both languages, as well as in ecclesiastical writers, and a ready talent for explanation and correction shine everywhere in these observations.

Moreover, this excellent edition lacks neither a suitable index nor a careful preface nor the ornament of typography worthy of it, nor a patron in whom it might glory in that age and to whom it is dedicated: Cardinal Passionei.

#### 1769

Venice, press of Giovanni Battista Albrizzi, folio. *Treatises of St. Zeno, Bishop of Verona*, from the splendid Ballerini Verona edition of 1739, edited by Andrea Gallandius in vol. V of the *Bibliotheca Patrum*, pp. 107–157. The text alone was transcribed. It was scarcely worthwhile to mention the observations appended in a few places which, as he writes, appeared to have escaped the Ballerini. He discusses Zeno in the *Prolegomena*, chapter 12, pp. 19–20.

#### 1784

Verona, folio. *The Works of St. Zeno translated into the vernacular by Marquis Giovanni Jacopo Dionisi, canon of Verona.* At the end: Dionigi Ramanzini.

It is not ours to judge the quality of the translation. But I think its author held a more magnificent view than Zeno deserved of the force and rhythms of Zeno’s eloquence, and of reproducing them in translation. In his preface he discusses this at length, matters which concern the common precepts and rules of translation as much as this Zenonian rendering. He declares that he laboured more to convey Zeno’s meaning and character generally than his words and the colouring of his diction.

But this edition has a special service that perhaps concerns more people: the critical and exegetical annotations of Bartholomew Perazzini, archpriest of Verona, appended to the individual treatises. In them one finds, partly punctuation and partly the words themselves, corrected with acuteness and outstanding judgment, as the consensus either of the Ballerini or of all editions whatsoever, or some consideration weightier than all these, seemed to recommend; and one also finds interpretations of passages different from those previously customary. These are by no means few, although abbreviated by the author of the translation, who also adapted the style. There is the additional advantage that, in an index not carelessly compiled, the new readings, readings restored after exclusion, other supplied readings, and changes in punctuation may be seen at a glance. After the preface, moreover, a Life of Zeno is added. The work is dedicated to Pius VI, Supreme Pontiff. The brilliance of the type and paper is altogether exceptional.

### Manuscripts

Here it is worth noting what the Ballerini observed concerning the collection of the sermons of St. Zeno: that shortly after the holy bishop’s death, at the end of the fourth or beginning of the fifth century, it was drawn up and transcribed at Verona from papers he had left behind. They deny that the author himself prepared and published it because several pieces occur unfinished, repeated, and mutilated. Hence they judge it probable that the materials which he had left in papers after his death for use in the very numerous sermons he delivered to the people were discovered by others and, because of the man’s exceptional reputation, diligently collected. This was done with such care that whatever could be found, whether complete or incomplete, was all judged worthy of collection and publication—even if it was a small fragment, a brief opening, or even a single period. But let us hasten to our purpose.

Mention has already been made above of Guarino’s manuscript. No trace of any manuscript of Zeno now remains in the library of the chapter of Verona. Among the Ballerini manuscripts, none was older or superior to the following.

**The Rheims manuscript**, given almost nine hundred years earlier by Archbishop Hincmar to the library of the Benedictines of Rheims. Father Ruinart mentioned it in the *Acts of St. Arcadius*, and Father Coustant in the *Vindiciae Veterum Codicum*, p. 293, and in his edition of Hilary, p. 463; it is also mentioned elsewhere in the Verona edition and by others. Since in it, as the most ancient witness, lay as it were the base and foundation of the whole structure, the editors gave an exact description of it with two specimens in the preface, pp. VI and IX. From certain indications they note that manuscripts older than it had been available to its scribe. Besides it, they had the following.

**The Tolentinate manuscript.** A parchment manuscript in the Venetian library of the Tolentine Regular Clerics, of very beautiful handwriting, thought to belong approximately to the thirteenth century. Its readings are very close to the Rheims manuscript, though it appears to have been written by a less skilled and careless scribe, since frequent omissions occur where the same word recurs in a passage.

**Vatican manuscript no. 1235**, a parchment manuscript written in the thirteenth century, proceeding from the same source as the Venetian manuscript, although more correct. The editors observe that the manuscript found by Guarino seems to have been very similar to it.

**Vatican Urbinas 150**, also a parchment manuscript, but somewhat later than that just described, perhaps copied in the fourteenth century.

> **Note [Col. 0252D].** Two manuscripts of Zeno besides these exist in the Vatican; but since the identifying numbers were available for only two, Father Joseph Blanchini could provide the editors with collations of only two.

**The manuscript of St. Peter’s Basilica in the Vatican**, written at the beginning of the thirteenth or of the fourteenth century, marked with the letter F. 33. Apart from the sermon titles, it agrees throughout with the Rheims manuscript. The editors requested and obtained, when their edition was already underway, not a complete collation of it, but variant readings of only certain treatises and difficult passages.

**The Verona manuscript of the monastery of St. Zeno**, of more recent date, unquestionably fifteenth-century, bound from parchment leaves: this is the very manuscript which the Veronese editors in 1586 called “ancient.” It agrees with the Rheims manuscript also in the order and number of treatises, except only for titles. The Ballerini affirm that this is distinct from the manuscript which Peter Calo of the Order of Preachers, at the beginning of the fourteenth century, testified in manuscript *Collectanea*, cited by Henschenius, that he had seen there.

**The Sparaverius manuscript.** The manuscript book which Francis Sparaverius once collated with the printed editions, and whose variant readings he recorded in the observations cited in their proper place. Its identity is unknown. The Ballerini observe that for the most part it agrees with the manuscript of the monastery of St. Zeno, though it differs from it in some points.

**The Pompeian manuscript.** A recent manuscript, but one supplied to the editors by Count Alessandro Pompeio and written by a more careful scribe. It was copied about the middle of the fifteenth century. The order and number of treatises are the same as in the Rheims manuscript.

[Col. 0253]

## TREATISES OF SAINT ZENO, BISHOP OF VERONA (C)

> **Note [Col. 0253B].** They are called “sermons” in the printed editions. We have preferred the designation of our manuscripts, which is also very common among other Fathers and more frequent in their manuscripts, as we observed in the Preface.

### BOOK ONE

## TREATISE I

> **Note [Cols. 0253B–0254B].** We have retained the title of the Verona edition and of the manuscript of the monastery of St. Zeno. Indeed, this is one of the two treatises on Faith which John, a priest of Verona and historian of the early fourteenth century, recalls as having been written by St. Zeno, as also do William Pastrengo and Peter de Natalibus, who followed the same John. The first Venetian edition of 1508, and the table or index of Book II in the same manuscript of St. Zeno, bear this title: *On the Commendation of Faith*. In all the other manuscripts, however, it is entitled *Treatise of Faith*; and only in the index prefixed to the Pompeian manuscript is this title recorded: *On the Treatise of Faith*. This title is not wholly to be disregarded, since St. Zeno’s purpose in this first treatise is not to commend or explain faith, but to insist that treatises on Faith should not be written. He understood this of treatises in which someone might dare to explain the mystery of the Trinity by human reasonings, as we have shown more fully in Dissertation 2, chapter 2, which must certainly be read for understanding the present treatise.
>
> The one point which gave us pause about numbering this first among Zeno’s treatises was that it appears to have been handed down rather as a letter to someone whom he calls “Brother” than as a discourse delivered to the people. For he addresses him continually and endeavours with many arguments to deter and dissuade him from writing such treatises, a practice full of danger. It is added that Peter Calo of the Order of Preachers, who lived at the beginning of the fourteenth century, in the manuscript *Collectanea* cited by Henschenius, vol. II, April, p. 76, when mentioning the works of St. Zeno which he says he saw in manuscript in the monastery of St. Zeno at Verona, affirms that he read there not only eighty treatises but letters as well. Among the works of St. Zeno, the designation “letter” could suit no work better than this treatise.
>
> Nevertheless, we did not think that the authority of the manuscripts should be abandoned. It is well known that in discourses to the people the holy Fathers sometimes addressed an individual person, so that, while reproving a fault in one person, they might spare the multitude and sufficiently provide against a common danger. Meanwhile, this should not be passed over: this treatise was translated into German by Gottfried Arnold and published among other more select works of the Fathers, especially Greek Fathers, likewise translated into German—first at Leipzig in 1696, then twice at Goslar in 1702 and 1716, as we learn from Fabricius, vol. VII of the *Bibliotheca Graeca*, p. 493.

### On Faith
1. 3 The greatest blessedness of Christian fidelity is to know the nature of faith: it is of such a kind and magnitude that it is lent to no individual [Col. 0254B] by another, but arises from that person’s own will.

[Note: [Col. 0254B] The Pompignan manuscript, together with the Urbinate, reads “blessedness” (*felicitatis*); but in the margin of that same Pompignan manuscript it has been corrected to “fidelity” (*fidelitatis*), which is the reading found in the other codices.]

[Note: [Col. 0254B] We have restored the text thus from the manuscripts and the Venetian edition, since in what follows it is plainly presupposed that faith arises in a person not from another, but from his or her own will, through the preceding inspiration and assistance of the Holy Spirit. We have sufficiently discussed the reason for this presupposition in Dissertation 2, chapter 5. Only some codices add *suo* (“his own”) after *homini* (“to a person”). The holy Bishop therefore says that faith is not lent to any of the faithful by another—that is, by one who proposes and proves faith to that person—but arises from each person’s own will. When St. Zeno said this, his sole intention was not to exclude grace, which was not then under discussion and which he affirms quite clearly both shortly afterward and elsewhere, but to refute those who tried to expound faith by arguments and treatises, as though by such effort faith were implanted in hearts. See Dissertation 2, chapter 2, from which must be drawn the occasion and subject of this treatise, as well as the explanation and defence of certain expressions in it which may seem harsher. St. Zeno speaks similarly in Treatise 2 of this book, §5, when discussing charity: “For it is learned from the law”—that is, from doctrine, as will be clear from Note 5—“but is born in minds.”]

But if, as some suppose, it depends upon the mouth of the teacher, then undoubtedly, when that same teacher falls silent or teaches otherwise, it is consumed.

[Note: [Col. 0254C] If anyone rightly grasps Zeno’s purpose, indicated in the preceding note, nothing in these words will cause offence. The holy Bishop does not condemn those who insist on the necessity of preaching for the reception of faith; indeed, we read that he admits the communication of the law, or the instruction (*didaskalia*) of faith: see below, Note 49. He attacks only those who laboured to establish faith by arguments, as though faith’s implantation and propagation depended on such activity. In this sense he had shortly before said that faith is not lent by another but arises from one’s own will; if such assent is absent—for not all obey the Gospel, Rom. 10:16—every effort of the teacher will be futile.]

Moreover, unless faith, preceding it and girded with every devotion, embraces the communication of the law, and produces its effect both for itself and for the one to whom it gives credence, [Col. 0255A] the communication will be fruitless; for it cannot confer the fruit of faith upon an unbeliever.

[Note: [Col. 0254D] In this treatise “law” is sometimes taken in its proper sense, for the commandments of the law, as when §2 says: “Through it God’s will is communicated to peoples; through it heavenly discipline is gathered,” etc. But it is more often taken for the dogmas and doctrine of faith themselves, as where he writes: “Whoever thinks that disputation about the law is faith is mistaken.” Here “disputation about the law” is plainly the same as disputation about the dogmas of faith, from what follows: such disputation, if crafty, uproots faith, because faith surely is not present where faith is sought—that is, where a question about faith is raised through disputation. Similarly, the holy Bishop calls the doctrine of faith “law” when in §5 he says: “Why do you restrict law by law? Why, under the image of faith, do you lay faith aside?” and elsewhere of the same kind.

This meaning of “law,” perhaps derived from Paul’s expression in Romans 3:27, where he calls it “the law of faith,” is also indicated by St. Augustine, *On the Proceedings of Pelagius*, §4. Considering Pelagius’s statement about knowledge of the law, Augustine says: “If perhaps Pelagius answered that he meant this very knowledge of the law . . . which is handed down through the doctrine of faith to neophytes and little ones in Christ, and by which those about to be baptized are catechized so that they may know the Creed, this is not ordinarily meant when someone is said to possess knowledge of the law.” By these words he does not mark as contrary to ordinary usage the taking of “law” for the doctrine of faith, but the calling of the doctrine of faith handed down to catechumens “knowledge”; for, he adds, “knowledge” is that according to which experts in the law are called learned.
