In this treatise also St. Zeno, in accordance with the opinion of those whom he attacks, generally understands “law” not so much as the simple doctrine of the dogmas of faith as the knowledge and expertise of faith itself—namely, the expertise in faith which those declared necessary who tried to explain in treatises the more obscure dogmas concerning the Trinity and to establish them by arguments suited to their intellectual capacity.

Accordingly, he refutes them, as Augustine refuted Pelagius, by bringing forward the multitude of simpler persons, who would still lie under the dominion of death if only experts in the law deserved justification. Concerning them he says in §4: “Therefore those who do not know letters do not have faith”; and similarly in §5 he praises those unskilled in the law and does not hesitate to profess himself less skilled—not because he lacked knowledge of faith in the Trinity, but because he believed himself unable either to publish treatises concerning it or to investigate and explain it by reason, as the Arians dared to do.

This law, which he shortly opposes to faith and distinguishes from it when he says in §4 that law cannot exist without faith whereas faith can exist without law, he calls “doctrine”; and he sets it in opposition to *credulitas*, that is, simple faith, in precisely the sense explained above. Thus here “law” is what there is “doctrine,” and here “faith” is what there he calls *credulitas*, on which term more is said in the following note. It is of the greatest importance to observe and distinguish this varying use of “law,” employed indiscriminately in this treatise.

Thus, in this place, “the communication of the law” appears to mean the instruction of faith; and it must be embraced by antecedent faith for this reason: unless someone shows himself teachable to one who hands down the precepts of faith, every effort of such communication or instruction will be wholly fruitless. St. Zeno emphasizes this for his purpose, not in order to deny the necessity of instruction, but in order to confirm—as he had said shortly before—that faith is not lent from another but born from one’s own will.]

Finally, Abraham pleased God by *credulitas* without law (Gal. 3:6), while the Jewish people displeased God by unbelief with law.

[Note: [Col. 0255D] *Credulitas*, frequently mentioned by our author, is not used for an excessive readiness to believe, which is not without fault; nor for a weak and feeble opinion, which has no place in the dogmas of faith without grave blame; but for simple faith, which gives assent to authority without law—that is, without rational argument. Such indeed was Abraham’s faith: he believed God not merely without demanding any argument, but, as the Apostle observes in Romans 4:18, he believed God against the hope which natural reason would suggest.

Yet in this passage, where faith properly so called is being discussed, Abraham’s faith seems rather to be commended under the name *credulitas* in that he believed by divine faith that Christ would be born from his seed before any treatises concerning this dogma—which the author calls “law”—had been published by Arians or anyone else. For this reason St. Ambrose, *On Abraham*, Book I, chapter 3, §21, praises him because “he did not seek a reason, but believed with most ready faith”; this is altogether the same as *credulitas sine lege*, “belief without law,” in our Bishop. More on Abraham’s faith below, Note 34.

Moreover, other writers too used this same term *credulitas* in the sense of faith. The martyrs Nemesianus, Dativus, and Victor write to St. Cyprian in Epistle 78: “Since you do not cease by your treatises to uncover hidden mysteries, you make us grow in faith and bring persons from the world to *credulitas*.” Arnobius, *Against the Nations*, Book II, p. 47: “You have become accustomed to mock our faith and this very *credulitas*.” The Council of Elvira, canon 42: “They first come to faith by *credulitas*”; and canon 44: “If afterward they come to *credulitas*.” Sedulius, *Paschal Work*, Book I, chapter 2: “This is true faith and firm *credulitas*.” In ancient Ordines there survive formularies of faith entitled “Formularies of *credulitas*.” And, to omit many further testimonies of this kind, our Bishop Ratherius says in his synodal letter to the presbyters: “Faith, that is, *credulitas* in God.” These matters had to be said at greater length, not because this passage itself requires it, but so that by this preliminary warning the reader may understand matters that would otherwise be more obscure when the same word is repeated below in a less certain sense.]

Hence there is no doubt that law cannot exist without faith, while faith can exist without law; otherwise that innumerable multitude, happier in its simplicity, would still remain under death’s dominion if only experts in the law had deserved to be justified.

[Note: [Col. 0256C] Thus the Pompignan manuscript; other codices read *ista* (“those things”). We judged *isthaec* preferable, so as to avoid ambiguity and make clear that the pronoun refers to the multitude.]

But since it is written, “The letter kills, but the Spirit gives life” (2 Cor. 3:6), and since we are not under law but under grace, which compels us to love God and serve him alone in the sacrament of the one Trinity, once believed—not by argument, not by necessity, but by will—I consider it most evident that the simple person is better than the excessively cunning. For the simple person simply believes every word of God; but the cunning person, made foolish by excessive wisdom, confounds himself through vain inquiries.

[Note: [Col. 0256D] The Pompignan and Zenonian manuscripts read *unitae*, “united.”]

[Note: [Col. 0256D] This reading of the Pompignan manuscript seems better, as the context shows, although the same codex offers *acute* (“shrewdly”) as a marginal correction, which is found in the editions and manuscripts.]

## II

But someone will say: “If this is so, then the law benefits no one.” Far from it. It benefits greatly indeed. For through it God’s will is communicated to peoples; through it heavenly discipline is gathered and retained (Rom. 3:20; 7:7); through it, I say, every kind of sin is made known, lest anyone perish through ignorance. It never ceases to warn, lest anyone excuse guilt by ignorance. Now severe, now gentle, it sets forth [Col. 0257A] the reward and also the sword, ready to assign to each what that person has chosen, so that each may rightly carry out what he undertakes.

[Note: [Col. 0256D] Here he takes “law” properly for the teaching of the law; for it is through this that God’s will is communicated to peoples, heavenly discipline is gathered, every kind of sin is made known, and so forth. But shortly afterward he again takes it for the doctrine of faith—indeed, even for both.]

[Note: [Col. 0256D] The Venetian edition and the Pompignan and Tolentine manuscripts wrongly read *corrigitur* (“is corrected”), although this was amended in the margin of the Pompignan codex to the reading written in the text from other manuscripts and editions. Every kind of sin is said to be made known through the law in the sense of Paul’s statement in Romans 3:20: “Through the law comes knowledge of sin.”]

[Note: [Col. 0256D] We approve the entirely Zenonian repetition of the verb *demonstrat* (“it sets forth”), found in the Urbinate manuscript and the Venetian edition.]

From those who come to it, it demands only a profession of *credulitas*, because it cannot see their faith. If it discovers from their conduct that faith is absent, it immediately punishes in anger, as faithless, the person whom it taught; and it declares that it was promulgated for no other reason than that faith may be vindicated against unbelievers.

[Note: [Col. 0257B] That is, those who come to faith. Here he takes “law” for the Catholic faith, which demands from those who come to it a profession of *credulitas*, that is, of simple faith.]

Finally, remove sin, and the dominion of the law ceases. For, as it is written, “Law is not laid down for the righteous but for the sinner”; because the righteous person lives by faith (1 Tim. 1:9; Gal. 3:11), while the unbeliever lives unrighteously.

Therefore whoever regards disputation about the law as faith is mistaken: whoever confounds two different things into one.

[Note: [Col. 0257B] From the most ancient Reims, Tolentine, and Vatican manuscripts and the Venetian edition we have added *quisquis* (“whoever”), though *quippe qui* (“indeed, whoever”) may seem preferable. The Pompignan codex, with different punctuation, writes: “The unbeliever was living unrighteously. Therefore whoever considers disputation about the law to be faith confounds two different things into one.” This punctuation is so pleasing that, were it not contrary to the reading of the older codices, we should gladly have inserted it into the text.]

For disputation cultivates the law, but if it is crafty, it uproots faith; [Col. 0257B] for faith surely is not present where faith is sought.

[Note: [Col. 0257B] The crafty disputation concerning law named here consists in those treatises on faith, to be mentioned shortly in Notes 26 and following, by which the Arians, made foolish by excessive wisdom, confounded themselves with vain investigations, as Zeno says in §I. These were treatises which did not cultivate faith, but uprooted it.]

[Note: [Col. 0257C] He attacks the Arians mentioned in the preceding note. While they sought through various treatises to determine which faith, among the multiple formularies of faith issued by themselves, should be maintained, he proves that they had no faith.]

Further, because law is common but faith private: because law always flows from the ancestral book, [Col. 0258A] whereas faith clings steadfastly to its own single purpose. Law passes from one person to another; faith perishes if it ever departs from its own standing or from another's. Law can address a person’s conscience, but cannot see it; faith cleanses the conscience to its very marrow, lest it owe anything to guilt even inwardly. For the one who does not fear his own conscience is the one who does not fear God.

[Note: [Col. 0257C] Two manuscripts read: “Finally, because,” etc. He calls “law” the instruction of the law, which is given in the public assemblies of the Church and is therefore common to all; he contrasts with it faith of the heart, and accordingly calls the former common and the latter private.]

[Note: [Col. 0257C] The “ancestral book” means that book of the law which the Jews received as handed down to them from their forefathers and which subsequently passed to us Christians together with the sacred writings. Hence it is added: “Law passes from one person to another.”]

[Note: [Col. 0257C] The Pompignan manuscript reads *ab suo* (“from its own”). Shortly afterward the Vatican manuscript has *in aliquo* (“in some respect”) instead of *vel aliquo* (“or from something”), and the Venetian edition has *in quo* (“in which”).]

[Note: [Col. 0257C] That is, faith purifies so thoroughly and inwardly that no guilt is owed, or sin committed, not only outwardly through words or deeds but inwardly through thoughts.]

Add that law is both learned and taught in parts.

[Note: [Col. 0257D] The Reims manuscript writes *Addo* (“I add”) here and in the following repetitions.]

[Note: [Col. 0257D] That is, it is handed down and learned part by part.]

Add that it is neither wholly understood nor retained. Add that anyone establishes it by arguments according to the capacity of his intellect. Add that all desire it, but no one completes it. Add that it is an indication of God’s will, not of God’s origin or nature.

[Note: [Col. 0257D] The Venetian edition reads *docetur* (“is taught”), but this is less satisfactory, since it produces an inept repetition of the preceding sentence. He affirms that the whole law, here understood as the doctrine of faith, is neither understood—because many matters in faith are obscure—nor retained—because the Arians did not believe all the dogmas. This is urged against the Arians; hence in §5: “If you approve one part, you disapprove another . . . since you do not believe the whole.”]

[Note: [Col. 0257D] The Veronese edition has *ut* for *et*; the Venetian edition has *complectitur* for *completur*. Since the whole context concerns law, or knowledge of faith, we would prefer *complectitur*, because all desire this knowledge but no one embraces it, even though one strives to attain it through treatises and reasonings. Yet we were unwilling to alter the text without manuscript authority, since perhaps St. Zeno intended to speak of the moral law, which he shortly calls the indicator of God’s will. Nevertheless, he could also have said that knowledge of faith itself is completed by no one, in the sense in which he says in §4, speaking of Arians who professed knowledge of the law, or faith, and attempted to acquire it through treatises: “They cannot by any arguments bring knowledge of the law to perfection.” This is the same as saying here, “It is completed by no one”—that is, brought by no one to perfection.]

[Note: [Col. 0258B] The indicator of the divine will is law properly so called, which contains moral precepts; but it can also be understood as the law of faith, insofar as it indicates what God wills us to believe, though it does not disclose the origin and rationale of the things to be believed, which the Arians tried to expound through treatises and arguments.]

## III

It follows that we must know whether we ought to assert that a treatise belongs to faith, or that faith belongs to a treatise.

[Note: [Col. 0258C] Since bishops engaged in ecclesiastical business were said to “treat” (*tractare*) matters—as is established from St. Cyprian’s Epistles 51 and 52, which mention proceedings held among bishops—expositions or formularies of faith issued by bishops deliberating in council were customarily called *Treatises on Faith*, or simply *Treatises*. The formulary of Nicene faith is called the “Treatise at Nicaea” in the definition of the Synod of Rimini, Fragment VII, in Hilary, §§3–4, as also in that synod’s letter to Constantius, Fragment VIII, §1; in Ambrose, *On Faith*, Book III, chapter 15, §125; and by the author of the treatise *On Orthodox Faith against the Arians*, chapter 8. Referring to Marius Victorinus speaking of the term Ὁμοούσιον (*homoousion*, “of the same substance”), he says: “But because it is not understood and causes scandal, it ought to be removed from Faith and from the Treatise, or at least . . .” See vol. IV of the *Bibliotheca Patrum*, Lyons edition, p. 273.

Here, however, St. Zeno does not mean the Nicene treatise, but those written by Arians after Nicaea, which he shortly calls “many treatises,” because many were then issued both in pseudo-synods and separately by individual bishops. These Arian treatises are mentioned by St. Hilary, *To Constantius*, Book II, §§4–5; Marius Victorinus, in his address *On Receiving the Homoousion*, p. 295; Phoebadius, in his book *Against the Arians*, p. 300; and others. It should be observed that the simple formularies of faith issued by Arians are not here called “treatises”—we shall shortly see them called “faiths”—but rather the fuller expositions of faith, in which each person tried to establish his own position about faith by arguments and reasoning, as the context makes clear.]

If we say that a treatise belongs to faith, we shall be grievously mistaken; for the nature of faith does not permit itself to be subjected to the artifice of verbosity, since it seeks nothing except to approve itself by its own powers alone. For that cannot be perfect which expects from elsewhere something necessary to itself.

[Note: [Col. 0258D] He calls “faith of the treatise” that faith which someone wishes to conceive by the force of treatises or arguments, because the person is unwilling to believe anything except what has been persuaded by arguments and treatises.]

But if we begin to speak of the faith of a treatise, then it will surely be neither ours nor its own, nor even that of the one whose faith it is said to be. For when a treatise establishes faith, it destroys it by that very act whereby it establishes it. It will give to no one what it does not possess; rather, it is itself still inquiring how it may fail to possess it.

[Note: [Col. 0259A] He shows that the faith of treatises is nowhere to be found. Since faith is sought in treatises, it cannot be in them and belong to them; it cannot be implanted in us through treatises and belong to us; nor can it be found in the author of the treatise himself, who has raised a question in doubt. Thus he declares that the faith of treatises destroys faith; for, as he said shortly before, “faith surely is not present where faith is sought.” Hilary says similarly in *To Constantius*, Book II, §6: “Then faith is sought, as though there were no faith.”]

Moreover, I see, as the names of their defenders indicate—remove these names, and perhaps there is no dispute—that there have been many treatises and many faiths, indeed novel ones, nourished by the exertion and favour of controversy. Since the true one can scarcely be found, I think they were offered for sale, lest they suffer from a shortage of adherents.

[Note: [Col. 0259B] The names of defenders written upon the treatises are, it is credible, the names of Arians and Semi-Arians written upon pseudo-synodical formularies of faith, or treatises, which they themselves issued. Marius Victorinus speaks thus in his book *On Receiving the Homoousion*, p. 295, where he bears witness not merely concerning Arians but Semi-Arians also; for he names Basil of Ancyra, who was at one time among the Semi-Arians. It also appears that certain treatises were published outside synods by individual heretics under their own names; such was the letter of Potamius, which, Phoebadius testifies, p. 301 of the cited volume, was circulated through East and West.]

[Note: [Col. 0259B] “There is perhaps no dispute,” he says, “if you remove the names of the defenders,” that is, of the authors, because certain formularies of faith issued by Semi-Arians could be understood correctly and would arouse no suspicion of heresy, were it not for the suspicion flowing from their authors’ names. It was known that they had deceitfully employed certain words and omitted others. Hence Hilary certainly suggests throughout his book *On the Synods* that some of these same formularies may be understood in a Catholic sense.]

[Note: [Col. 0259C] “Faith” means the same as a formulary of faith. Hilary says, Fragment II, §27, and *On the Synods*, §84: “The faith itself then written in a religious manner,” speaking of the faith composed at Nicaea. See also the *Book of Petitions* of Marcellinus and Faustinus to Theodosius, vol. I of Sirmond, where “faith” is repeatedly used in the same sense, as also in the confession of faith of Faustinus, vol. II of St. Leo’s Works, p. 138.

In the plural, it means Arian formularies in Hilary, *Against Constantius*, §7: “You, living, compose faiths against faith.” There “faiths” means the several formularies of faith written by Arians under the favour or in the presence of Emperor Constantius, or perhaps also those books which Lucifer of Cagliari reports as written, as it were, by Constantius against Catholic faith in *On Not Sparing Those Who Sin against God*. Again Hilary, *To Constantius*, Book II, §4: “It is miserable that there are now as many faiths as wills.” St. Athanasius, in *On the Synods*, mentions eleven formularies of faith promulgated by Arians down to the Antiochene synod of 361. Socrates, noting their multitude, *Ecclesiastical History*, Book II, chapter 41, calls it a λαβύρινθος (*labyrinthos*, “labyrinth”) and lists their chief forms. St. Zeno calls them “novel” because new formularies were issued from day to day. As for his statement that these faiths were nourished by the exertion and favour of controversy, see Notes 38 and 39.]

[Note: [Col. 0259D] He calls Arian formularies “saleable” because the Arians used rewards in order to increase the number of their adherents and draw more people to subscribe to, or assent to, their heresy. Hilary indeed reveals in *Against Constantius*, §5, that Constantius promoted the foulest persecution by riches and stirred it with gold: “But now we fight against a deceiving persecutor . . . who does not strike backs, but strokes the belly; who does not proscribe for life, but enriches for death; who does not thrust into prison for freedom, but honours within the palace for slavery; who does not torment the sides, but takes possession of the heart; who does not sever the head by the sword, but kills the soul by gold.”

Many, putting gifts first, as Liberius says in Theodoret, *Ecclesiastical History*, Book II, chapter 6, were corrupted in this way. Gregory Nazianzen consequently calls them, in Oration 21, §14, *In Praise of Athanasius*, persons ensnared by gain and lovers of gold more than of Christ. Among these, Faustinus and Marcellinus in their *Book of Petitions* to the emperor, in Sirmond, vol. I, p. 142, include Potamius, once a defender of the Catholic faith, who betrayed the faith in return for the reward of an imperial estate which he had desired to possess. Gregory Nazianzen makes similar statements in the cited Oration 21, *In Praise of Athanasius*, where he testifies that the Arians consumed the property of the poor for such evil use. Hence St. Zeno again relates that they summoned the patronage of the rich in aid; and in Note 39 we shall show that many were corrupted by their resources.]

Yet from all these it cannot be known or grasped what ought to be chosen. For that which has an ever uncertain condition will have neither a proper nor a firm standing. Indeed, the choice of one is the rejection of another; or, if all must be embraced, so that one has as many faiths as one does not have words, one will all the more possess nothing. For the treatise which generated them—or generates them daily—can still generate further ones; when provoked by its opposite, it again consumes them by reconsidering and refuting them according to the strength of minds and arguments.

[Note: [Col. 0260C] *Nec* (“nor”) is not absent from the Pompignan and Zenonian manuscripts. To understand what is here said about the shifting and uncertain condition of Arian faith, and at the same time to confirm clearly that St. Zeno’s statements closely agree with the history of his own time—so closely that nothing comparable can be brought from earlier centuries, in which some believe him to have lived, to which these statements would correspond equally—we consider it necessary to cite some notable passages of the Fathers that wonderfully accord with the present passage.

First, Athanasius, *Letter to the Bishops of Egypt and Libya*, §6, p. 275, vol. I: “Thus they disturb and throw everything into confusion, yet they themselves are not content with their own decrees. For every year, like those who draw up agreements, they too meet and pretend to define matters of faith, so that even from this they gain nothing but laughter and disgrace; for their decrees are annulled not by others but by themselves. If they considered what they had previously determined, they surely would not wish to determine other things, nor, after abandoning the former, would they now determine what, as they certainly intend, they will change after some time . . . Hence they never cease writing, and so, continually changing their own positions, they possess an uncertain faith—or rather, a certain and manifest unbelief and perversity.”

Further, in *On the Synods*, §14, p. 727: “For they mutually disagree among themselves; and, having departed from the Fathers, they are by no means of one and the same mind, but fluctuate amid various and differing opinions. Disputing against the Nicene Synod, they themselves held many synods; though in each of them they set forth a faith, they stood by no confession. Nor will they ever act otherwise; for by badly seeking the wisdom which they hate, they will never find it.”

Finally, Hilary, *To Constantius*, Book II, §4, declares it peculiar solely to his own time and unheard of among the ancients that so many faiths should be written: “Under what implausible pretext of necessity did the practice hence arise of writing and renewing faith?” And in §5: “For we are mutually conscious that, after the Synod of the Nicene gathering, nothing has been done except writing faith . . . We decree annual and monthly faiths concerning God, repent of decrees, defend what we have repented of, anathematize what we defended,” etc.

What Hilary says about annual and monthly faiths being decreed, St. Zeno calls “treatises” which generated them or generate them daily. This also makes clear that faiths are distinguished from treatises: treatises were disputations by which, as Zeno says, each person defended his own faith and refuted another’s according to the force of his intellect and arguments; “faiths,” meanwhile, were the formularies of faith generated from the opinions of opposing treatises and issued in multiple forms by various synods. For this conflict of Arians and Semi-Arians among themselves, see also Ambrose, *On Faith*, Book I, chapter 6, §§44–45.]

But if, as is necessary, there is that one noble and ancient faith, older, I shall say, not merely than the treatise but than its very inception, [Col. 0261A] and moreover older than the law—faith which by believing God won God, and which did not learn to believe but took belief beforehand—let this ruinous invention of its treatise tell me: what does the conflict achieve? “So that faith may not perish,” it says, “when it is wrongly believed or taught.” We shall shortly see how evil this reasoning is.

[Note: [Col. 0261B] These remarks concern Abraham’s ancient faith, which Paul praises in Romans 4 and Galatians 3 and which preceded not merely Arian treatises but even the law of the Decalogue itself, or the promulgation of Christian faith, which St. Zeno seems here to call “law.” Hence he adds: “Which did not learn to believe but presumed beforehand.” For *praesumo* means “I take beforehand.” That Abraham possessed the true faith which we Christians possess is certain from the Apostle, who on account of this faith calls Abraham “the father of us all”—that is, of those who follow the steps of faith (Rom. 4:12, 16)—and calls all who hold that same faith Abraham’s children: “Those who are of faith, these are sons of Abraham” (Gal. 3:7).

Accordingly, the Fathers demonstrated against the Arians from Paul that Abraham had the same faith in God and the Trinity as we do. Finally, the Apostle appeals to Abraham’s faith and proves, by the authority of Sacred Scripture, that Abraham believed as Paul himself then believed. So Lucifer of Cagliari, in Book I *For St. Athanasius*, p. 198, vol. IV of the Lyons edition of the *Bibliotheca Patrum*, and elsewhere repeatedly says the same; especially in *On Not Sparing Those Who Sin against God*, p. 228, where he holds that all the patriarchs after Abraham cultivated the same faith: “For if the Apostles did not believe as the patriarchs believed, why does the blessed Apostle summon everyone to embrace Abraham’s faith?” For more on Abraham’s faith as emphasized against Arian error, see Hilary, *On the Trinity*, Book IV, §27 and following. On the same faith of all righteous persons before Christ, read Philastrius, chapters 108–109, and Augustine, *City of God*, Book XVIII, chapter 47.]

[Note: [Col. 0261D] The Venetian edition reads *magis* (“more”) for *major* (“greater”), *quamque* for *quaeque*—where the Pompignan manuscript reads *quae*—and *promeruit* (“obtained”) for *praesumpsit* (“presumed beforehand”), as also in Jerome on Galatians, chapter 3, vol. VII, p. 423, Veronese edition: “Having surpassed the works of the law, he obtained God not through fear but through love.” Zeno used this word in nearly the same sense in Book II, Treatise 10, which is the first treatise on Abraham, §3. Here, however, *praesumpsit* should be read, since the subject is the faith which Abraham received before the promulgation of Christian faith; as we have noted, *praesumo* in approved writers means “I take in advance,” or “I take earlier.”]

IV. I now wish to know whether faith consists in doctrine, in simple belief, or in both.

[Note: Here “doctrine” means knowledge or expertise concerning the mystery of the Trinity, which the Arians boasted that they possessed and expounded in treatises. This is precisely the same as what we observed above, note 5, to be called the “law of faith.” Concerning *credulitas*, simple belief—that is, faith which, without doctrine or rational inquiry, defers to authority—enough has been said in note 6. A little later, where the text reads “if from simple belief,” the printed editions had “but if from simple belief.” We judged the particle *vero* (“but”), absent from the Pompeian and Zenonian manuscripts, to be omitted, since it is immediately repeated. In the Toledo manuscript this period is incorrectly placed after the following one.]

If it consists in doctrine, then those who do not know letters have no faith; nor even do those who do know them, because by no reasoning can they bring knowledge and observance of the law to perfection. If it consists in simple belief, it has no need of any interpretation; for, just as it is believed once for all, so faith is, by the very fact that what is believed has been believed, complete once for all, and is neither diminished nor increased. But if it consists in both, then the faith of the patriarchs was half-measured (*semensa*): and consequently books of our constitution must evidently be decreed for them, so that they may be perfect.

[Note: *Semensus*, like *dimensus*, *emensus*, and so forth, derives from *mensura*, “measure,” and is used of things which represent a half-measure; as *semodiale* derives from *semodius*, a vessel containing half a modius. So far we have been able to find this word, unquestionably good Latin, only in Zeno, unless in Ambrose, *On Penance*, II.1, one should read *semensas epulas* (“half-prepared banquets”) instead of *semesas*. He there speaks allegorically of a banquet to which not half-consumed fare from the preceding day was to be brought, but fresh provisions added, so that the banquet might be complete from both; hence, without these, the food brought the previous day would have been half the banquet, and “half-measured.” Zeno calls the faith of the ancient patriarchs *semensa* because, of the two parts of faith posited by the Arians—namely simple belief and doctrine—they had only one, and thus only half-faith: they believed by simple belief alone, not by the doctrine of the treatises later written by the Arians themselves. This is said ironically. Athanasius turns the same point, with a not dissimilar meaning, against the Arians in *On the Synods*, I.4: “If, according to their understanding, faith takes its beginning from the present consulship”—by which the formula of Rimini had been dated—“what will the Fathers and blessed martyrs do? Indeed, what will those men themselves do regarding those who, having been instructed by them in the Christian religion, fell asleep before this consulship?” etc.]

O how wretched is the faith that words compose! O how weak, whose limbs are daily scattered by diverse arguments! O how undefended, which seeks the patronage of emperors, judges, rich men, and sometimes even—what is worse—of pagans at every moment!

[Note: That emperors were called “kings” even in Zeno’s age is clear from almost countless testimonies. See the petition of Marcellinus and Faustinus to Theodosius; the works of Lucifer of Cagliari throughout; Hilary, *On the Synods*, 78; Ambrose, *Apology of David*, 6.26; Sulpicius Severus, book II; Philastrius; and others who frequently call the emperor a king. Likewise Justina, wife of the elder Valentinian, is called queen in Ambrose’s *Life*, 11, written by Paulinus to Augustine; and other wives of emperors are also called queens by Lampridius in *Alexander Severus*, Ammianus Marcellinus, XIV and XV, etc. Similarly, Greek Fathers very frequently use the name *Basileus* (Βασιλεύς), “king,” rendered in Latin *rex*, to signify these emperors.

Concerning this patronage of kings or emperors, eagerly sought by the Arians, Ambrose speaks splendidly in *On Luke*, VIII.17: “Set now before your eyes Arians intent upon worldly pursuits, who seek an alliance with royal power, so that they may attack the truth of the Church with military arms.” The kings mentioned by Zeno were Christians, as the context makes clear: he distinguishes them plainly from the pagans, writing that heretics had sought, besides the support of kings, also the patronage of judges, rich men, and sometimes even, what is worse, pagans. Thus he indicates plainly that he does not count kings among pagans; otherwise pagan aid would already have been sufficiently included under them. In using the plural “kings,” he seems to indicate not only Constantius but also Valens, both known to have strongly favored the Arians. If this is accepted, this first treatise would have been composed after 29 March 364, when Valens began to reign.]

[Col. 0263A]

[Note: The Reims manuscript has *judicium* (“judgment”). If that reading were genuine, it would refer to the emperors and concern what Hilary relates in *On the Synods*, 78: “For they deceived the ignorant king, so that, while occupied with wars, he might set forth the faith of such perfidy and, before beginning to reign, impose upon the Church a formula for belief.” Sulpicius Severus explains this more fully in book II. Yet, since the Arians summoned not only the authority of emperors but also that of magistrates of every kind in support of themselves—for, as Hilary says there, “What powers of the world has she not employed by the enticement of false religion?”—we preferred to retain *judicum*, “of judges,” from the other manuscripts and printed editions; especially since otherwise Zeno’s enumeration, once begun, would seem excessively defective and interrupted.

“Judges” were called all magistrates and provincial governors, who are commonly so named in the Theodosian Code. See also Ambrose, *On the Death of Satyrus*, II.58; Paulinus, *Life of Ambrose*, 8; etc. Hilary clearly shows in *To Constantius*, I.1 how the Arians employed the authority of such judges against Catholics: “Let your Clemency provide and decree that all judges everywhere, to whom provincial administrations have been entrusted and to whom alone the care and concern of public affairs ought to belong, abstain from religious observance; and that they thereafter do not presume or usurp, or suppose that they have authority to hear cases involving clergy and to crush and harass innocent persons by various afflictions, threats, violence, and terrors.” And in §2: “Command that governors of places offer neither zeal, favor, nor patronage to the most grievous heretics,” where he calls “governors of places” those whom above he had called judges. Finally, in §6 he describes at length the violence inflicted upon Christians through these judges, when he mentions the assistance of judicial proceedings.

Athanasius too, in the *History of the Arians to the Monks*, 15: “They brought with them as tutors and advocates the Easterners Musonianus the Count and Hesychius the Imperial Officer; trusting in their aid, they came forward boldly, thinking that thereafter they would accomplish everything by their power. For in that manner, sustained by such helpers, they made themselves terrible to whomsoever they wished, and laid snares for whomsoever pleased them.” Since large sums of money were needed to carry out these acts, the patronage of rich men too was summoned. Thus Zeno says that those many faiths, of which we spoke in note 31, were nourished by the toil and favor of litigation and offered for sale. Hence Gregory Nazianzen also says, in *In Praise of Athanasius*, 12, that George the Arian, who seized the Church of Alexandria, purchased the support of influential persons with money; and in §13, speaking of the Arians and their formulas, he says that they hired sycophants for payment and had judgments pronounced for a fixed wage.]

O how shameful and slippery a faith, whose secrets the opinion of another makes sport of!

[Note: It is said that “another’s opinion plays” with it because some Arians, writing mockingly against others whom they had condemned with anathema—for many, holding different views and subscribing to different formulas, struck one another with anathema—were making sport, in the gravest matter of faith. Or perhaps because, through these dissensions, faith was made a laughingstock among pagans; see note 44. Perhaps the work of Arius entitled *Thalia*, composed in effeminate and ridiculous modes, is also intended here. Athanasius testifies in his letter *On the Opinion of Dionysius*, 6, that it was not unlike Sotadic songs; Socrates, I.9, and Sozomen, I.20, report the same with Athanasius. Athanasius indicates in *Against the Arians*, I.2 and 4 how shameful and hateful to pagans themselves that mode of writing was. Thus Arian faith could be called shameful and slippery—or, if one prefers the reading, ludicrous—because perhaps the populace made sport of it in such loose songs.

Philostorgius, II.2, records in Photius that Arius’s *Thalia*, or writings of the same kind, was spread among the people in common songs: “When Arius withdrew from the Church,” he says, “he composed sailors’, millers’, and travelers’ songs, and composed other such pieces, which he adapted to particular tunes.” Eunomius the Arian likewise used a shameful, impure style of speech tending toward ridicule, in a sermon delivered at Constantinople before the people on the very feast of Theophany, according to the same Philostorgius, VI.2; and someone might likewise have mocked him for this.]

[Col. 0264A]

O how adulterous, which does not recognize by what author it was born! O how ridiculous, which, when two Christians contend, is called perfidy by one of them if it is not transferred to him, but, once transferred, is called faith!

[Note: Thus restored from five manuscripts, whereas previously *perfida* was read. We preferred the word *perfidia*, not only on the authority of the more numerous and excellent codices, but because whatever put forward a formula of faith yet was alien from the true faith was customarily called so. Hilary says plainly in *To Constantius*, 24: “Whatever is outside the one faith”—understand the Nicene faith—“is perfidy, not faith.” Hence, Fragment II.29, speaking of the formula of faith composed by Arians at Sirmium: “This is perfidy,” he says, “not faith”; and Fragment VI.7 calls the same formula “the perfidy written at Sirmium.” Phoebadius, preparing to attack this same formula in his book *Against the Arians*, says: “Beginning from the very head of perfidy, not faith,” p. 300, col. IV of the Lyons edition of the *Library of the Fathers*, letter D; and shortly afterward: “They are wholly absorbed in this their perfidy, not faith.” Saint Hilary calls the Arian formula published by Arian bishops in the name of Constantius—the formula mentioned by Sulpicius in book II—“the faith of perfidy” in *On the Synods*, 78. See also Fragment VIII.4; Ambrose, *On Faith*, III.129; and Chrysologus, Sermons 48, 52, 61, 64, and 87, where faith and perfidy are opposed, as also in Ambrose’s exposition of Psalm XXXVI, 28. Here, however, *perfidia* is taken more broadly of every error, even that of philosophers and pagans, opposed to Catholic faith. Comparing sophists with Catholic bishops, Ambrose says: “The former speak perfidy in many words; the latter assert faith in few.”]

O how untrue, if it flourishes by factions! O how like a public prostitute, whose secrets even the profane discuss!

[Note: The Reims manuscript reads *publica*; the other codices and printed editions, *publicana*. Besides the fact that in Zeno *publicana* has the same meaning as *publica*—thus in Treatise I.15.4 he uses *publicanas mulieres* for women publicly exposed—it seems better suited here, since he is speaking of faith, about which profane persons openly talked as though it were a public woman. That the Fathers called pagans “profane” is sufficiently suggested, to omit much else, by our author’s testimony in Treatise I.5.9, at the end, where, addressing Christian women, he says: “Why do you marry a profane man when you can marry a Christian?”

It is well known how cautiously Catholics formerly acted to prevent the sacred mysteries and more difficult articles of faith from coming to pagans’ knowledge; indeed, many things were not revealed even to catechumens. See Schelestratius’s dissertation *On the Discipline of the Secret*. On the occasion of the disputes which had arisen between Catholics and Arians, the latter, to enlist pagan patronage, violated the discipline of secrecy. They did not hesitate to disclose the whole case to pagans, both by publishing treatises in which the hidden and chief mystery of the Trinity was explained to pagans for mockery, and by admitting them to churches, where they might see and investigate every secret thing.

Thus Athanasius, in his *Apology against the Arians*, 72, p. 189, complains of Philagrius, prefect of Egypt and an apostate, and of pagan soldiers who were admitted to investigate things which even catechumens ought not to have seen. The synodal letter of Pope Julius to the Eusebians, quoted by Athanasius in the same *Apology*, p. 149, mentions sacred mysteries plundered and thrown to the ground by pagans at the ordination of Gregory of Alexandria against Athanasius. Gregory Nazianzen, in his *Oration in Praise of Athanasius*, 13, laments “profane judges of holy persons,” that is, of believers, and a new and unprecedented mixture: questions concerning mysteries publicly discussed before spectators. How great a scandal this was to catechumens and pagans alike may be gathered from Athanasius, *On the Synods*, 2, p. 717: “This gave catechumens no slight occasion of offense, and to pagans not merely ample but overflowing material for laughter: that Christians, as though only now awakened from sleep, should ask in what manner they ought to believe in Christ.”

When Saint Zeno says *fabulantur*, “they discuss as tales,” he seems to indicate not merely that pagans commonly talked about the secrets of Christian faith and ridiculed them among themselves, but perhaps also that, with great contempt for religion, they staged dramatic tales concerning these mysteries. It is reported that this happened at Alexandria before the very Council of Nicaea. Eusebius writes in *Life of Constantine*, II.61: “The spectacle of what was being done reached such a height of indignity that the venerable teaching of divine proclamation was exposed to laughter and mockery in the very theatres of unbelievers.”]

O how presumptuous, which prefers that men should believe its novel tradition rather than antiquity, rather than God the Lord saying: “You reject the commandment of God in order to establish your traditions” (Mark 7:9)!

[Note: In the Pompeian codex *magis* is absent. But just as in Plautus, *Stichus* I.2.13, and Terence, *Adelphoe* II.2.14, *malo* occurs pleonastically with *potius*, so Zeno could use it with *magis*. For *magis* seems sometimes to be used by approved authors for *potius*: Catullus, poem 67.30, “It is not shameful, but rather pitiable”; Virgil, *Eclogues* I.11, “I do not indeed envy; I rather wonder.” We omit other examples that might be cited of the same kind. A little later *adaeque* is read for *peraeque* four times in Plautus and in Livy, IV, first decade.]

But I do not say this in order to make the benefit of doctrine unwelcome; rather, so that everyone may know that faith is one thing and a treatise another, and that faith can neither be given, known, nor destroyed by a treatise. It cannot be given; for if it can be given by words, it can also be taken away by words. Neither can it likewise be known; for it may happen that someone bears one thing on his lips and another in the inner chambers of his heart.

[Note: The Toledo and Zenonian manuscripts read *labris*, “lips.” In the following member, at the words “cannot be another thing,” the infinitive *esse* is missing from the Reims codex.]

Nor, similarly, can it be destroyed; for if faith is true, it cannot be other than what it is. Therefore, since it does not lie within human capacity to see the secrets of faith, brother, your curiosity nowhere advances, nowhere does your struggle make progress. For the man whom you consider the most faithful even among your own adherents is here unfaithful; and the man whom you considered unfaithful is here faithful.

[Note: The Vatican and Urbino manuscripts, and the Venetian edition, read perhaps “nor in this.” The Pompeian codex omits *se*. We have printed *aestimet*, “may suppose,” for *aestimat*, on the authority of four manuscripts.]

Perhaps someone thinks himself more faithful if he speaks cleverly; whereas the truer believer is the one who, in preaching sacred things, has not stretched the keenness of his mind beyond what is permitted. For matters have come to such a point that our faith is required to the dishonor of God.

[Note: The Arians evidently required professions and subscriptions to formulas of Arian dogma, which resulted in dishonor to God.]

Solomon foretold that this would happen, and taught in these words what must be avoided: “Better is one deficient in understanding but fearful, than one abounding in cunning and transgressing the law” (Ecclus. 19:21). And again: “Do not be excessively wise, and do not argue beyond what is fitting” (Eccles. 7:17). Likewise Paul: “Do not be high-minded, but fear” (Rom. 11:20).

[Col. 0266B]

V. Since these things are so, why do you strain law by law? Why, under the appearance of faith, do you lay faith aside? Why do you attempt to drain dry the very fountain of divinity with philosophical arguments?

[Note: From Zeno’s present testimony we learn that among Catholic Fathers the work of those skilled in the law of faith, of which he speaks here, was threefold: to explain obscure passages of Scripture read among the sacred mysteries; to reconcile and harmonize statements that seemed contrary; and finally, to show and establish that the articles which faith “sings,” that is, proclaims, though surpassing the understanding of the human mind, are necessary to believe. The whole care of bishops in matters pertaining to faith was indeed occupied in these three things; and Zeno indicates that he would not at all disapprove of the labor if any qualified person undertook it. For he reproves only the audacity of those who, as he shortly says, inflamed by the desire of worldly display under the sound of law and faith, presume that they can compel, examine, measure, and distinguish by argument the incomprehensible mystery of the Trinity.

We have translated *canit* as “proclaims,” as in Martial, *On the Spectacles*, epigram I: “Whatever fame proclaims.” It may also be taken as “prophesies,” since the Latin verb *cano* is often so used because the Sibyls, thought to be endowed with prophecy, were said to have delivered all their prophecies in verse. It is more credible that Saint Zeno intended the prophecies of sacred Scripture containing more difficult matters, since elsewhere he twice calls a prophetic book a *carmen*, “song” or “poem.” If, however, someone, distinguishing the readings indicated in the first part of the author’s sentence from what is said to be “sung,” wishes to hold that Zeno meant by the readings sacred Scripture read in church assemblies and by the singing tradition preached orally; or if another prefers to understand in the first place that part of Scripture read in sacred assemblies and in the second that which was sung, we shall not contend further.]

If you wish to display skill in the law, clear away the clouds from the readings. Show that it is not contrary to itself. Show that everything it proclaims must be believed. But if you approve one part of it and reject another, how do you seek faith through that faith which you yourself accuse of unfaithfulness, since you do not believe it in its entirety?

[Note: The Vatican and Toledo manuscripts read: “when you do not believe the whole of that which proclaims.”]

But if you know the faith of the Spirit, display some power. Command mountains to move themselves. Let the fury of lions, their jaws fawning in admiration of you, vanish. Let the swelling wave of the sea beneath your feet harden into marble-like solidity. Let a whale serve as a boat, faithfully carrying your faith among the troubled bays of the surging sea. Restrain the course of the sun and moon from the prison-enclosure of the west by the bridle of prayer. Let the blazing fire of a roaring furnace, nature conquered, feel refreshment through you also. Breathe back into the souls of the dead restored to the homeland of life. Drive diseases from the afflicted; heal infirmities; rejoice in temptations and under tortures for the Lord’s name. If hard things occur, show that you possess faith like a grain of mustard seed.

[Note: The Urbino codex reads: “let it faithfully carry your faith from the western regions.” If genuine, this reading seems to indicate that faith is to be received not from the Arians occupying the East but from the westerners, who were for the most part Catholics. Yet *ab occiduis*, “from the west,” is absent from the other manuscripts and appears to have been repeated through a copyist’s carelessness from the following clause, where *ab occidui* likewise occurs. A little later the Pompeian and Zenonian codices have *Solis currus*, “the sun’s chariot,” for *Solis cursus*, “the sun’s course.”]

But if instead—and this is worse—under the sound of law and faith, inflamed by the desire of worldly display, you presume that by arguments you can compel, examine, measure, and distinguish the inestimable and incomprehensible everlasting divinity of God born from God, and of the Holy Spirit, by the very right whereby it exists from itself, I do not dare to answer you. For it is sometimes safer to seem unlearned than to be sacrilegious.

[Note: That Arians erred not only concerning the Son of God but also concerning the Holy Spirit is affirmed generally by Hilary, *On the Trinity*, II, and Ambrose, *On the Holy Spirit*, III.101; and it is especially clear from the heresy of Macedonius, condemned at the First Council of Constantinople in 381. See Philastrius, *Heresies*, 67, on the Semi-Arians—by which name he means the Macedonians—and 68, on the Eunomians. Yet Philastrius says in Heresy 67 that the Macedonians thought rightly concerning Father and Son, and declares that they erred only regarding the Holy Spirit, whom they proclaimed not true God but made and created. Since Saint Zeno here attacks those who erred not only in the doctrine of the Holy Spirit but also in that of the Son, it seems that he is not attacking Macedonians here but Arians, who sinned in both doctrines at once. Philastrius’s testimony concerning Macedonians is true of the later period, not of the earlier Macedonians contemporary with Zeno. These truly were Semi-Arians, and the first to pour forth heretical doctrine concerning the Holy Spirit no less than concerning the Son; consequently this testimony of Zeno properly applies to them.]

[Note: The Reims and Urbino manuscripts read *exinanire*, “to empty.” Below, the Pompeian codex has *tum tutius*, “then safer,” for *cum tutius*, “when safer.”]

And yet I have one who will oppose you on my behalf. For the law through which you perhaps compel me to sin as one less learned will itself, striking and exposing you severely, refute you, Solomon saying: “Do not seek what is higher than you, and do not investigate what is stronger than you. Always think on those things which God has commanded you, and do not be curious in the multitude of his works; for their speculation has deceived many, and has detained their understanding in vanity” (Ecclus. 3:22 ff.).

[Note: The Reims, Pompeian, and Zenonian manuscripts support *ne*, “do not,” while the printed editions had *non*. The words “and has detained their understanding in vanity,” absent from the Verona edition and those following it, have been restored from the manuscripts and the Venetian edition.]

Likewise Paul writes in reply to curiosity: “O the depth of the riches of the wisdom and knowledge of God! How unsearchable are his judgments, and how untraceable his ways! For who has known the thought of God?” (Rom. 11:33–34). And do you seek his nature? In another place too he clearly expressed the matter now under discussion, when he spoke these words in instructing Timothy: “I urged you to command certain persons not to employ perverse doctrine nor attend to fables and endless genealogies, which furnish controversies rather than the true dispensation of God which is in faith. But the end of the command is love from a pure heart, a good conscience, and simple faith” (1 Tim. 1:3–4).

[Note: *Inquit*, “he says,” had been inserted, but we deleted it as superfluous on the authority of the Pompeian and Zenonian manuscripts.]

VI. Therefore, if you are God’s servant, avoid foolish and unlearned questions, knowing that they generate quarrels. But a servant of God ought not to quarrel, because quarrelling is an enemy both of love and of faith; whoever loses these certainly knows neither divine things nor human things. Preserve these things if you are religious; guard them if you are truly reverent; avoid disputing about that which exceeds the measure of human understanding. Whoever undertakes to vindicate God, in a sense denies God.

[Note: Here *asserere* means not “to affirm,” but “to claim” or “vindicate”—and to vindicate by arguments devised against the Arians, as was evidently the intention of the person whom Saint Zeno the bishop is here trying to turn away from so great a venture by setting its danger before him. Hence he immediately adds: “For a defense is offered only for one who is weak; nor can he reverence him whom he thinks to be an object of his own intellect,” etc. The editors of the Verona edition thought the word *asserit* might offend and accordingly substituted words expressing Zeno’s meaning without the danger of ambiguity: “Whoever attempts to measure God by human arguments: defense,” etc. We have restored the genuine text from the manuscripts and the first edition.]

For a defense is offered only for one who is weak; nor can one reverence him whom one thinks has been assessed by one’s own intellect. But the true nobility of faith is this: to serve God faithfully (Prov. 10:10); to place confidence in him alone; to recognize that one is called “faithful” from faithfulness and confidence; to live with blameless morals; to presume to know him by a good conscience, not by talkativeness—which is surely the mother of sin—and neither to violate but to honor the one fullness of power of the Trinity, which is conceived by one mind and one simple belief.

[Note: The Pompeian manuscript reads *fidem*, “faith.” The Vatican manuscript reads “with good wisdom.” The Urbino manuscript, together with the Pompeian codex and the first edition, adds “Amen.”]

19. TREATISE II. On Hope, Faith, and Love.

[Col. 0269C]

I. The foundations of Christian perfection consist in three things: hope, faith, and love.

[Note: In the Pompeian and Zenonian manuscripts the word “and” is absent from the title; conversely, *invicem*, “mutually,” is absent from the Vatican and Toledo manuscripts. A little later, the Urbino, Vatican, Reims, and Pompeian codices and the Venetian edition read *aliis aliae necessariae*, “some are necessary to others,” instead of *alii alia necessaria*, retained after the Verona edition.]

These appear so mutually connected that some are necessary to the others. For unless hope comes first, for what does faith labor? If faith is absent, how will hope itself arise? If you deny love to these, both will cease; because neither can faith operate without love, nor hope without faith. Therefore, if a Christian desires to be perfect, he must be built upon these three things; for if any one of them is lacking, he will not possess the perfection of his work. Hence, first of all, hope in things to come must be set before us; without it we clearly see that even present things themselves cannot stand.

[Note: The Reims codex reads “is from God.”]

Indeed, remove hope and all humanity grows numb. Remove hope and all arts and virtues will cease. Remove hope and everything is destroyed. What is the point of a boy’s going to a schoolmaster if he does not hope for the benefit of letters? Why does a sailor entrust his vessel to the deep whirlpool if profit never comes to him, if the longed-for harbor never appears? Why does a soldier disregard not merely the hardships of harsh winter or blazing summer, but himself, if he does not carry hope of future glory? Why does a farmer scatter seed if he does not gather the harvest as the reward of his labor? Why does a Christian believe in Christ if he does not believe that the time of everlasting blessedness promised to him by Christ will come?

II. But hope comes from faith; and although it is set in the future, it is rightly subject to faith. For where there is no faith, neither is there hope; for faith is the substance of hope, and hope the glory of faith, since faith earns the reward which hope possesses. Faith indeed fights for hope, but wins it for itself. Therefore, brethren, we must cling to it tenaciously and guard it by every kind of virtue; we must press on toward it courageously. For it is the immovable foundation of our life: alike a bulwark invincible against the assaults of the devil and a weapon; the impenetrable breastplate of our soul; a concise and true knowledge of the law; the terror of demons; the strength of martyrs; the beauty—or wall—of the Church; the handmaid of God; the friend of Christ; the companion of the Holy Spirit. Both present and future things lie beneath it: the former, because it despises them; the latter, because it confidently anticipates them as its own. Nor does hope fear lest they fail to come, because it always carries them with it in its virtues. This is what it means that Abraham, “against hope, believed in hope” in God, so that he might become the father of many nations (Rom. 4:18). Now that which is against hope is what is impossible and not seen; but by this hope it becomes possible, when God’s word is believed firmly and without doubt. For the Lord says: “All things are possible to one who believes” (Mark 9:22). Hence Abraham believed God, and it was reckoned to him as righteousness (Gen. 15:6). He was righteous because he was faithful; “for the righteous lives by faith” (Gal. 3:6). He was faithful because he believed God; for unless he had believed, he could have been neither righteous nor the father of nations. It is therefore clear that hope and faith have one inseparable nature: for if either of them fails in a person, both die.

> [Note: Col. 0270C–D. The passage in view is Paul’s at Hebrews 11:1: “Faith is the substance of things hoped for, the evidence of things not seen”; and in what follows, faith earns the reward, while those things are foreseen for which faith in Christ is established as the beginning of all merit.]

> [Note: Col. 0270D. Vatican and Toledo manuscripts: “hope, the guardian of virtues.” Then the Pompignan manuscripts: “in this”; Vatican: “and in this.”]

> [Note: Col. 0270D. Here and elsewhere *praesumo* is often used by our author in the sense “I most certainly hope” or “I know beforehand”; as is shown by the words in §6: “God commends love of neighbour, because he confidently knows that it alone can preserve what he commands”—that is, certainly knows. Similarly, *praesumptio* is sometimes used for anticipated certain knowledge and confidence, as in Spartianus, *Life of Hadrian*, ch. 2: “He had an expectation of imperial power from Jupiter’s response.” For “lest they fail to come,” the Pompignan manuscripts have “that it may not come”; but another hand has written *ne* (“lest”) in place of *ut* (“that”).]

> [Note: Col. 0271C. The printed editions add after “not seen”: “to be possible”; but these words are absent from all the manuscript codices we examined, and should also be absent if St Zeno is here referring to Paul’s words at Romans 8:25: “What we do not see, we hope for; for what a man sees, why does he hope for it?” In keeping with this meaning, above St Zeno said that faith is the substance of hope and affirmed that hope is subject to faith, because we pursue by hope those things which we believe will be future, though they do not yet appear [ibid., v. 24].]

> [Note: Col. 0271C. The phrase “both die,” like the earlier “both will cease,” is discussed at length in Dissertation II, ch. 6.]

III. Faith, therefore, is above all our own proper possession, the Lord himself saying: “Your faith has made you whole” (Mark 10:52). Therefore, if it is ours, let us preserve it as our own, that we may rightly hope for things belonging to another. For no one entrusts his property to a bankrupt, nor will he honour a deserter with triumphal rewards—especially since it is written: “To him who has, it shall be given, and he shall abound; but from him who has not, even what he has shall be taken away” (Matt. 13:12).

By this, brethren, Enoch merited from God to be translated bodily, contrary to the law of nature. By this Noah escaped and found no one with whom he might compare the Flood. By this Abraham attained friendship with God. By this Isaac shone forth above the rest (Heb. 11:5, 7, 8, 20). By this Jacob prevailed in wrestling with God. By this Joseph brought Egypt under his dominion (Gen. 32, 41). This made dry ground, like glass, for Moses in the Red Sea (Exod. 14:22). This, setting aside their customary course, put reins on the sun and moon, so that Joshua’s desire might be obeyed (Josh. 10:13). This brought David, unarmed, triumphs over armed Goliath (1 Sam. 17). This did not despair in Job amid frequent and immense evils (Job 1–2). This was a physician in Tobit’s blindness (Tob. 11). This bound the mouths of lions in Daniel (Dan. 6). This turned the sea-monster into a little boat for Jonah (Jonah 2). This alone conquered in the army of the Maccabean brotherhood (2 Macc. 7). This made flames delightful for the three youths (Dan. 3). This confidently expected that Peter could walk upon the sea (Matt. 14:29). By this the Apostles stripped many people of deforming leprosy, with its contagious and scabby protuberances of festering sores, restoring them to clear skin. By this, I say, the blind saw, the deaf heard, the mute spoke, the lame ran, paralytics were restored, demons fled from the possessed, and even the dead were often commanded to return from their tombs with their own funeral processions—so that all might marvel that tears, which had lately been those of bereavement, became tears of joy.

> [Note: Col. 0271C. In the Verona edition: “Faith, therefore, is the gift of God.” On this addition, absent from the manuscripts and the first edition, see what we noted in Dissertation II, ch. 5.]

> [Note: Col. 0271C–D. Namely, heavenly things, which belong to God, which through faith we believe and await as future.]

> [Note: Col. 0271C–D. Thus the Reims, Pompignan, and Urban manuscripts and the Venetian edition; elsewhere “to a debtor” is read, and that word is also noted in the margin of the Pompignan codex.]

> [Note: Col. 0271D. Vatican and Toledo manuscripts insert: “concerning the faith of Enoch and Noah and Abraham with the body,” etc. But this seems to be a gloss which crept into the text from the margin, where it had been noted that this passage concerns the faith of Enoch, Noah, and so forth. In fact, Enoch alone was translated bodily.]

> [Note: Col. 0271D. The Pompignan manuscript reads *pervaluit* (“was fully strong”), as in Lucretius, book 6, v. 956, where some nevertheless judge that *praevalet* should be read.]

> [Note: Col. 0271D. “Scabby” occurs in the Pompignan and Zeno manuscripts. But the margin of the Pompignan manuscript notes “scabious.” “Contagious” is said of leprous eruptions because it is contracted by contact; “scabious,” however, appears to refer to eruptions of ulcers.]

> [Note: Col. 0271D–0272C. Sparaviero would prefer to read *exuviis* (“remains”) instead of *exsequiis* (“funeral procession”); but *exsequiis* must be retained, as is clear from Arnobius, *Against the Nations*, book 1, p. 30, who, speaking of the Apostles’ miracles, uses a similar expression: “They commanded the dead to return from their tombs, with the funeral procession turned about.” Zeno uses *exsequiae* in the sense of a funeral escort, as is evident from what follows, where he recalls that the attendant procession’s mourning was changed into joy. Ambrose likewise, *On Luke*, book 5, ch. 7, expressly uses *exsequiae* for the crowd accompanying the widow’s son’s funeral. In ancient funerals people followed the corpse, accompanying the funeral procession; hence Terence’s phrase: “Meanwhile the funeral goes forward; we follow.” Donatus notes that *exsequiae* takes its name from the people’s following. In this passage St Zeno is recognizably imitating Arnobius.]

> [Note: Col. 0272C–D. Cicero, *Letters to Atticus*, book 2, says “now he was accused”; and in *Brutus*, “now I saw.” Similarly, Ovid has “now he was” in *Tristia*, book 1, elegy 3. Again St Zeno, Tractate 5, book 1, §4: “now you cried out, now you gave back,” etc.]

IV. But it would take too long, brethren, to go through every instance—especially since love itself brings forward stronger claims. It is endowed above all things in such a way that it is by right the queen of all. Let faith triumph in whatever virtues it wishes, and let hope put forward many great things; yet without love neither can stand: faith, first of all, if it does not love itself; hope, if it is not loved. Add that faith benefits itself alone, while love benefits all. Add that faith does not fight without reward; but love is accustomed to confer benefits even on the ungrateful. Add that faith does not pass over to another; love—not merely does it pass over to another—it passes into the people. Add that faith belongs to few; love to all. Add that hope and faith have their time, but love has no end (1 Cor. 13): it grows at every moment, and the more loving persons entrust themselves to one another through it, the more they owe one another.

It loves no one for rank, because it cannot flatter; not for honour, because it is not ambitious; not for sex, because both sexes are one to it; not for a time, because it is not changeable. It does not envy, because it does not know what envy is; it is not puffed up, because it cultivates humility; it thinks no evil, because it is simple; it is not angry, because it gladly embraces even injuries; it does not deceive, because it itself keeps faith; it lacks nothing, because, beyond what it is, nothing is necessary to it. This preserves the settled compacts of peace among countryside, cities, and peoples. This makes the swords at kings’ sides safe. This suppresses wars, removes lawsuits, renders laws unnecessary, restrains courts, roots out hatreds, and extinguishes angers. This traverses the sea, circles the world, and supplies through trade the necessities of nations. Brethren, I shall quickly declare its power. Whatever nature has denied to places, love supplies. This compels two human beings, through the venerable covenant of marital affection, into one flesh. This ensures that the human being is truly what is born. It is love’s gift that a wife is dear, children noble, and fathers true. It is love’s gift that others are neighbours or friends to us, like us or more than ourselves. It is love’s gift that we love slaves as sons, and that they willingly honour us as masters. It is love’s gift that we love not merely acquaintances or friends, but often even those whom we have never seen. It is love’s gift that we recognize either the virtues of the ancients from books, or books from virtues.

> [Note: Col. 0272D. “Pre-eminent” is read in the Pompignan, Toledo, and Vatican manuscripts. But the margin of the Pompignan manuscript notes “endowed.” *Praedita* (“endowed”) is found in the sense of *praelata* (“preferred”) in Apuleius, *On the God of Socrates*, and in ancient glosses cited by Du Cange.]

> [Note: Col. 0272D. The Verona edition emended the text to “will not benefit,” concerning which see note 2.]

> [Note: Col. 0272D. Love is said to “pass into the people” because it benefits everyone; faith, however, benefits only the person who conceives faith, as he had said a little earlier: “Faith benefits itself alone; love, all.”]

> [Note: Col. 0272D–0273C. We think that the statement that faith belongs to few but love to all could truly be made in this sense: faith is found in few, because Christians are few in comparison with the other unbelievers; yet, though they lack faith, those unbelievers have some love, since no one can exist without some affection. Hence nations too are reported to love one another and to do good to many. Therefore this passage is not about true and Christian love; otherwise Sparaviero’s emendation would have to be admitted: “Faith belongs to all, love to few.” But since no manuscript and no edition supports this emendation, the passage seems to be understood and interpreted concerning love in its broad sense. See further Dissertation II, ch. 5.]

> [Note: Col. 0273C–D. This follows the Reims, Vatican, and Pompignan manuscripts. In the margin of the last, and in the Venetian edition, *pacesque* (“and peaces”) stands for *pacisque* (“and of peace”); the Verona edition has *paceque*; the Padua edition *pace*, with *-que* deleted, apparently by Sparaviero’s emendation, whose note is given below. That reading too would please us if it rested on any manuscript or edition. But because *-que* is everywhere read, we have preferred the reading of four manuscripts to the others, since it does not depart from Zeno’s syntax; for the author sometimes attaches the conjunction *-que* to the second word after a comma. He also said *composita pacis* elliptically for “peace agreements concluded in establishing peace,” like Horace’s *amara curarum* (“the bitter things of cares”), *abdita montium* (“the hidden things of mountains”), and many similar expressions in Lucretius, Tacitus, Apuleius, and others.]

> [Note: Col. 0273D. “Deceives” is read in most manuscripts and in the Venetian edition. Only the Pompignan and Zeno manuscripts and the remaining editions have “makes,” which we have retained.]

> [Note: Col. 0273D–0274C. “City” in place of “world” was wrongly written in manuscripts and editions through the easy change of one letter. The sense required the emendation. We have restored “through trade” from the Reims and Pompignan manuscripts and the Venetian edition; otherwise the text read: “it circles the city; it supplies trade necessary for nations.”]

> [Note: Col. 0274C. *Reddit* means “supplies” rather than “gives back”; for, as Celsus the jurist observes, *On the Meaning of Words*, law 20, Digest, “although the word *reddendi* has the sense of giving back, it also takes by itself the sense of giving.” Thus one frequently finds *reddere epistolam* (“to deliver a letter”) and *jus reddere* (“to administer justice”) among approved authors. Yet, since trade is under discussion here, *reddo* could be understood strictly: in trade, when goods are exchanged, one gives back one thing for another received.]

> [Note: Col. 0274C–D. Here “noble” children means children not degenerate, who preserve the honour of their lineage by right actions; and this is especially achieved through love, insofar as it impels them to preserve the honour of that same lineage.]

> [Note: Col. 0274D. The Reims and Urban manuscripts read “strangers or enemies”; “strangers” is also found in the Pompignan codex, but wrongly, since strangers are included in the following clause. A little later, for *demorer* (“may I linger”), the margin of the Pompignan manuscript and the Venetian edition have *demoror* (“I linger”), and *sunt* (“are”) for *sint* (“may be”).]

V. But why should I linger longer among human beings, as though they alone were endowed with this affection? Do we not see every kind of living creature testifying to love through association and concord? Thus all their movements are directed, as it were, by one common sense under love’s guidance, so that anyone may understand that this cannot happen without the instruction of natural friendship.

What they do for one another in emergencies is made plain to everyone by the almost daily examples of the delightful contest among pigs. If one of their number, tossed about by the rage of a bold wolf, begins to be led into present danger by tyrannical attacks, all suddenly run together; they aid the distressed one; they vie in repeatedly throwing themselves before the enemy’s very weapons; they confound him with a mighty din; and, baring their filthy tusks, resist like some tortoise-formation. By love they overcome more easily what, separately, they could scarcely conquer by bare strength.

The very elements also, brethren—sufficiently different and sufficiently opposed—would long ago have met destruction, had beneficent love not bound them together by the faithful offspring of a perpetual marriage, mutually endowed with equal gifts of moderation. There is absolutely nothing which, without this, can be pleasing; without this, peaceful; without this, faithful; without this, secure; without this, glorious; without this, joined to God; without this, perfect.

Finally, when the Lord was asked which was the greatest commandment of the sacred law, he spoke thus: “You shall love the Lord your God with all your heart, with all your soul, and with all your strength. And the second is like it: You shall love your neighbour as yourself. On these two commandments hang all the law and the prophets” (Matt. 22:37, 39–40). Hence it is clear that love is the substance and natural teacher of every divine virtue. For it is learned from the law, but born in minds: the law depends on love, not love on the law, as Sacred Scripture says: “The law is not laid down for the righteous, but for the sinner” (1 Tim. 1:9). The sinner, however, is one who does not have the love of God, and therefore is rightly subject to the law which produces wrath. But perhaps someone will say: “The law is to be despised, because it is unnecessary to the righteous and burdensome to the sinner.” Far be it, brethren! Rather it must be venerated, because it is a mirror of truth, because it is a certain rigid form of love. Whatever it has learned from the righteous, it compels the unrighteous also to do: glorious in a twofold way, glorifying one person and correcting another.

> [Note: Col. 0274D. Vatican and Urban manuscripts: “marked”; Zeno, Pompignan, and Sparaviero: “devoured”; Toledo: “is marked,” followed shortly by “when he begins” for “when he has begun.”]

> [Note: Col. 0274D. *Infestatio* occurs in Tertullian, *Apology*, ch. 1.]

> [Note: Col. 0274D. The Venetian edition and the Pompignan manuscript’s margin have “head.”]

> [Note: Col. 0274D. Printed editions and the margin of the Pompignan manuscript read “commandments”; but the text itself and the Reims, Toledo, and Zeno codices read “precepts.”]

> [Note: Col. 0274D–0275C. The Padua edition has “producing,” but wrongly: Paul’s passage at Romans 4:15 is intended—“for the law produces wrath.” We have emended from the manuscripts and the other editions. The Urban codex alone has “of those producing.” The Toledo manuscript shortly afterward has “because also to the righteous.”]

> [Note: Col. 0275C. Latin writers of the best standing use such forms as *bifariam*, just as *trifariam*, *quadrifariam*, *multifariam*, and so forth. Yet Diomedes the grammarian has *trifarie*, Pliny, book 18, ch. 7, and Solinus, ch. 18, have *multifarie*, from which Zeno’s expression seems sufficiently vindicated. The Toledo and Urban manuscripts read “endowed” for “glorious.”]

VI. It is therefore established that the whole of Christianity is deposited more in love than in hope or faith. The evident example is Judas Iscariot, the Lord’s betrayer: he lost both hope and faith because love did not remain in him. Thus heresies and schisms too are scattered abroad, when faith and hope, swollen with pride, are torn away from the foundation of love.

But learn from Paul, as your guide, what not only these but other virtues are without love: “And if,” he says, “I have all faith so as to remove mountains, but have not love, I am nothing. And if I distribute all my goods as food to the poor, and if I hand over my body to be burned, but have not love, I gain nothing” (1 Cor. 13:2–3). For love, brethren, loves all things, believes all things, hopes all things, endures all things. Love never fails (ibid., vv. 7–8). Therefore the Lord God rightly commends love of neighbour, because he knows with certainty that it alone can preserve what he commands.

> [Note: Col. 0275C. The Pompignan and Zeno manuscripts write “Schariotes,” as do Jerome’s manuscripts at Matthew 10, p. 57, and Hilary on Psalm 128; most of our manuscripts have “Scarioth.”]

> [Note: Col. 0275C. Here *praesumo* plainly means “I know certainly,” as we observed in note 6.]

VII. The first duty of love, therefore, is to render back to God the fact that we have been born, and to owe our life to him alone; to retain absolutely nothing in the inner chambers of our heart which we keep under another’s claim. But when, at the invitation of this same devotion, we begin to be inhabited by him—or to dwell in him—as John says, “God is love; and he who abides in love abides in God, and God abides in him” (1 John 4:16), then at last, brethren, we shall worthily render love to him through himself. For, when the exchange has been made, what is his becomes ours in accordance with our share.

It follows that we should also love our neighbours with the affection with which we love ourselves, especially since the very laws of kinship require this. For the prophet cries: “One God created you. Is not one father the father of you all?” (Mal. 2:10). Whoever retains consciousness of his own nobility loves his brother, and waits to hear nothing from the law lest admonition diminish piety. He so loves himself in his brother that he hates himself without him.

To complete the matter: God made the human being in his own image and likeness so that, in contemplating the image, we might feel reverence for the truth. The condition was thus established that whatever evil or good we do to anyone, we may seem to have done to God. Therefore John, the Lord’s special counsellor in his hidden mysteries, firmly declares: “If anyone says, ‘I love God,’ and hates his brother, he is a liar. For he who does not love his brother whom he sees cannot love God whom he does not see” (1 John 4:20).

Let us therefore strive, brethren, with the noble rivalry of mutual love; and, by venerating the image of God as worthily as possible, let us show what we owe to Truth itself, knowing that whoever injures the image provokes Truth to the destruction of his own soul. Nor is proof far from the statement.
