If anyone should violate in any way the portrait of some illustrious king—though merely a human being—does he not immediately pay the capital penalty as if for sacrilege committed? How much more carefully and vigorously must one guard against this in the cause of God, whom alone whatever is feared even by kings among the powers of nature itself fears?

> [Note: Col. 0275D. Not that we ought to love nothing besides God, since God commands us also to love our neighbour; but that nothing should be loved except by the right and rule which God himself has established for us, so that in all things which we love we may love God himself.]

> [Note: Col. 0275D–0276A. Sparaviero would prefer to read “ours.” In what follows, “duty” is understood—that is, the second duty; for he has spoken hitherto of the first.]

> [Note: Col. 0275D. Toledo, Urban, Zeno, and Pompignan manuscripts: “waited for.”]

> [Note: Col. 0275D. In the margin of the Pompignan manuscript: “destruction.”]

> [Note: Col. 0275D–0276D. “Portraits” are called *vultus* (“faces”) by Trebellius Pollio in the *Life of Claudius*, by Vopiscus in the *Life of Probus*, by Capitolinus in the *Lives of Maximus and Balbinus*, and also in the Code, “On the Public Announcement of Rejoicing,” where it is clear that imperial images were displayed for public veneration. From this testimony we learn that the practice prevailed among Christians too in St Zeno’s age; for he calls emperors “kings,” as we have shown in Tractate 1, note 38. This is also clear from Ambrose, sermon 10 on Psalm 118, §25: “He who crowns the emperor’s image certainly honours him whose image he has crowned; and he who despises the emperor’s statue certainly seems to have inflicted injury upon the emperor whose statue he has spat upon.” And in *Hexaemeron*, book 6, ch. 9, §57: “The bronze-cast heads of rulers, and faces fashioned in bronze or marble, are worshipped by human beings.” Zeno’s statement concerning capital punishment for violators of images refers to the Julian law of treason, cited in Digest 48, title 4, laws 5 and 6. St Methodius, cited by Damascene in the final testimony after *Oration 3 on Images*, vol. 1, p. 390, testifies that those who cast insults upon the images of rulers were condemned as though they had sinned against the rulers themselves. Basil says similar things in his exposition of Isaiah 13, in the same Damascene, p. 366. Spartianus too, in the *Life of Caracalla*, p. 87: “At that time, those who urinated in a place where there were statues or images of the emperor were condemned.” Famous likewise is the history of the imperial statues cast down at Antioch, which there aroused great disturbance through fear of extremely severe punishment; on that occasion St John Chrysostom delivered several addresses to the people, entitled *On the Statues*. We omit many further examples.]

> [Note: Col. 0276D. The “powers of nature” here are called lightning, earthquakes, diseases—or, to use the Psalmist’s words, to which St Zeno seems to have referred: fire, hail, snow, ice, storm-winds. The sense is that no one fears these powers of nature, which themselves inspire fear even in kings, except God alone, whose commands they obey; for they perform his word.]

VIII. But everyone must necessarily know the distinctive nature of sincere love, lest the rule of truth be put at risk through the sound of a name. For there is another love, indeed contrary to our salvation, to which human form is rightly assigned, because it is known to be temporal and fragile. Therefore it is depicted with a boyish outline, because its wanton slipperiness is not restrained even by old age. Therefore it is naked, because its will is shamefulness. Therefore it is winged, because it rushes swiftly into whatever it has conceived. Therefore it is equipped with arrows and torches, because a sword is always joined to illicit passions. It is blind, moreover, because once it has flared up, it considers neither age, nor beauty, nor sex, nor rank, nor even that sacred affection of at least sound piety.

This love set Eve’s breast on fire with its torches. This killed Adam with its arrows. This tried either to subject Susanna to the monstrous fires of two elders or to slaughter her with a parricidal sword. This accuses Joseph to the woman of having been violent, though, when she stripped him, she found him not shameless. This stormed the synagogue when it granted arms against her to its own. This is turbulent everywhere, everywhere driven in frenzy. It promises, deceives, gives, takes away: now sad, now cheerful; now humble, now exalted; now drunk, now fasting; now accuser, now accused. It jokes, plays, grows pale, wastes away, sighs, conceals, complies; it either tempts or deceives, and flatters more wickedly than it rages. It passes over no opportunity whatsoever to harm. Do you wish to know what evil it is? Even in its own fruit it hates itself. The whole world seethes daily with its poisons; and all things are so corrupted by its pestilential pleasures that whatever is done in the world—while sacred utterances command us not to love it—seems rightly accursed to those who think rightly. For John says: “Do not love the world or the things which are in the world. If anyone loves the world, the love of the Father is not in him; because everything which is in the world is the lust of the flesh, the lust of the eyes, and the ambition of this age; this is not from the Father, but from the world’s lust” (1 John 2:15–16). Through this the devil captures and deceives the diverse minds of human beings, and thus began to be called Cupid by his own luxurious worshippers.

> [Note: Col. 0276D–0277C. Things are said to be *committed* when they are thrown into a certain risk or contest. Thus Juvenal, *Satires* 6.435, has *committit vates*, “the poet brings [them] into comparison,” because comparison exposes them to danger. Therefore, “lest the rule of truth be committed under the sound of a name” means “lest, because of similarity of name, it be thrown into risk and danger.” Yet perhaps someone may prefer the reading of the Urban manuscript, which has *commutetur* (“be exchanged/confused”).]

> [Note: Col. 0277C. Vatican and Pompignan manuscripts: “at least”; the Urban manuscript: “of its own.” In the margin of the Pompignan codex: “at least, indeed.”]

> [Note: Col. 0277C–D. What St Zeno hints at here is explained more fully in Dissertation II, ch. 4, where we have expounded at greater length a similar passage from Tractate 13, book 1.]

> [Note: Col. 0277D. *Flagitare* in the sense “to defame and accuse” is found in approved writers. See Festus under *intercutem* and Tacitus, book 1, ch. 53. It is especially used of the infamy of shameful acts, just as it is also used for seeking or committing sexual disgrace; similarly *flagitium* means sexual disgrace. Love defamed Joseph with the charge of an attempted shameful crime, as though he had inflicted upon the woman the violence which he had suffered. The Vatican manuscript has *flagitasse* (“to have accused”) for *flagitat* (“accuses”).]

> [Note: Col. 0277D. Sparaviero judges that the history indicated here is that described in Numbers 25 and Judges 20–21.]

> [Note: Col. 0277D. We restore “deceives” from the manuscripts and the first edition; the word was absent from the other editions.]

> [Note: Col. 0277D–0278C. The Urban manuscript has “is jealous,” a verb used by Tertullian in his poem *Against Marcion* and by the Vulgate translator at Psalm 73:3. But Zeno wrote *zelatur* for *zelat* in Tractate 4, §2.]

> [Note: Col. 0278C. The Pompignan manuscript has “and earlier.”]

> [Note: Col. 0278C. The same manuscript has “diverse”; then the Urban manuscript: “deceives captured minds.”]

> [Note: Col. 0278C. “His own” is absent from the printed editions; we retain it from the Reims and Pompignan manuscripts.]

IX. Let us now see whence true love comes, where it abides, and to whom it is chiefly due. Certainly to him who made the human being; who gave him his own likeness as the gift of perpetual love; who bestowed the earth upon him; who subjected all the elements of the world with their living creatures to his power; who commanded years, seasons, months, nights, days, and the two most brilliant chariots of the royal spheres to serve him with the ever-beneficent delight of their changing succession; who, when he had been killed by the perniciously sweet poisons of the love mentioned above and submerged in the infernal dwelling-place, restored him to life through the sacrament of his majesty and, beyond this, enriched him with participation in the heavenly kingdom.

O love, how devout and how rich! O how powerful! Whoever does not have you has nothing. You were able to change God into a human being. You caused him, diminished, to sojourn for a little while away from the immensity of his majesty. You bound him in a virginal prison for nine months. You restored Eve in Mary. You renewed Adam in Christ. You provided the sacred cross as salvation for a world already lost. You emptied death by teaching God to die. It is your work that, when God, the Son of almighty God, is killed by human beings, neither of the two is angry.

You hold the soul of the heavenly people when you adorn peace, preserve faith, embrace innocence, cultivate truth, love patience, and present hope. You make human beings diverse in customs, ages, and condition into one spirit and one body from one nature. You do not allow glorious martyrs to be separated from the confession of the Christian name by any tortures, any novelty of death, any rewards, any friendships, any affections—things indeed worse than every torturer in the biting force of affection. You are content to be naked in order to clothe the naked. For you, hunger is satiety. If a needy and hungry person eats your bread, your wealth consists in possessing all that you have as mercy. You alone do not know how to be asked. You rescue without hesitation the oppressed, even at your own loss, when they are placed in any distress. You are the eye of the blind, the foot of the lame, the most faithful shield of widows, a parent better than either parent to orphans. Mercy or joy never permits your eyes to be dry. You love your enemies in such a way that no one can distinguish what separates them from those dear to you. You join heavenly mysteries to human things and human things to heavenly. You guard divine things. You rule in the Father. You obey yourself in the Son. You rejoice in the Holy Spirit. Though one in three, you are divided in no manner; no cavilling of human curiosity moves you. From the paternal fountain you are wholly poured forth in the Son; yet, wherever you are wholly poured forth, you do not depart. You are rightly called God, because you alone set in motion the power of the Trinity.

> [Note: Col. 0278C. The text read “number-bearing”; but the reading of the Pompignan, Toledo, and Urban manuscripts was preferred, since the sun and moon, while giving delight, also confer benefit.]

> [Note: Col. 0278C. Vatican manuscript: “very sweet.”]

> [Note: Col. 0278C–D. The holy Fathers often call the incarnation of the divine Word a *sacramentum* or mystery, following Paul at 1 Timothy 3:16. Thus our bishop, Tractate 12, book 1, §1, speaking of Christ, who is called both Son of God and Son of Man, says: “Son of God pertains to his ineffable origin; Son of Man, to the sacrament,” that is, the incarnation. Likewise Chrysologus’s sermon 147 is entitled “On the Sacrament of the Incarnation.” We shall show at Tractate 9, book 2, note 12, that *sacramentum* means “mystery.”]

> [Note: Col. 0278D. This formula, excluded after the Eutychian heresy, could in Zeno’s age be used without fault and in a catholic sense, as we explained more fully in Dissertation II, ch. 1, §3. *Breviatum* is the participle of *brevio, -as*, a verb used by Quintilian, book 1, ch. 9; Manilius, book 3, v. 461; Lactantius, *Epitome*, ch. 8; and Sidonius, book 2, letter 2: “to ascend by shortened steps.”]

> [Note: Col. 0278D. The Pompignan manuscript and Venetian edition have “restored”; the whole sentence is absent from the Vatican manuscript.]

> [Note: Col. 0278D–0279B. The Reims manuscript adds “in the world”; but this is a dative governed by *providisti* (“you provided”). Then the Vatican manuscript has: “You [taught] the death of the Lord to die.”]

> [Note: Col. 0279B. “To you” restored from the Reims, Vatican, Pompignan, and Zeno manuscripts. How the Father rules and the Son obeys is explained by St Zeno in book 2, Tractates 1 and 6. The Father is said to obey himself when ruling in the Son insofar as the Father performs the same things that the Son does: John 14:10, “The Father abiding in me, he himself does the works.”]

> [Note: Col. 0279B. St Zeno seems to have said “in the Son” for “into the Son.” See note 7 on Tractate 16, book 2.]

> [Note: Col. 0279B–0279C. Reims manuscript: “power.” Toledo manuscript: “the power of the Trinity alone.” The Vatican codex has the same, and writes “you have come together” for “you set in motion.” This passage appears corrupt and obscure. That God is called power by reason of operative power is evident from several patristic statements, which may be seen in Dionysius Petavius, *On Theological Dogmas*, vol. 1, book 8, ch. 8. But why love is called God by reason of a power which love alone “sets in motion” is not entirely intelligible unless explained thus: namely, that love alone, by which God loves himself and us, effected that he, about to communicate himself outwardly, should exercise power in the creation of the world, so that there might be beings in whom the divine perfections would shine forth and whom he would make participants in his goodness.]

## TRACTATE III. On Justice.

I. Perhaps someone among the learned bystanders may burst into laughter because a most unlearned and inarticulate man dares to say something about justice—a subject concerning whose proper nature men outstanding in talent and learning have published nothing certain in enormous books.

[Note: **Tractate III.**—We infer from this that persons learned in Zeno’s discourses were present; let us conjecture briefly who they were. Since in this sermon the holy bishop commends that justice which, according to the tenets of philosophers, was called folly by the Gentiles, while he reproves that secular justice which, though unjust, was proclaimed wisdom by the Gentiles, one may suppose that the learned persons who received Zeno’s discourse with laughter were Gentiles themselves. For, from the false justice which they cultivated, they believed themselves truly wise, and Christians—enemies of this justice—to be foolish and ignorant.

But perhaps the Gentiles themselves should here be thought to be called learned for another reason: he fears laughter from these learned men because of his unadorned discourse, such as they demand, but which he declares absent from himself, an inarticulate and most ignorant man. Indeed, the Gentiles commonly believed that they alone who cultivated more polished letters and philosophy were learned; Christians, however, they called strangers to such studies, rude and ignorant. Hence the Gentile Caecilius, in Minucius Felix’s *Octavius*, p. 32, is represented as speaking thus against Christians: “All ought to be indignant and deeply offended at hearing certain persons—untrained in learning, strangers to letters, inexperienced even in the common arts—make some definite pronouncement concerning the sum of things and the divine majesty, concerning which philosophy itself, through so many ages and among so many sects, still continues to deliberate.”

Celsus heaps up similar charges in Origen, book III, p. 144, calling Christians utterly unlettered and rustic; Julian the Apostate is reported to have written the same, from Nazianzen’s fourth oration *Against Julian* and from Cyril of Alexandria, book VI *Against the Same*. Read also, if you wish, what Arnobius reports as the opinion of the Gentiles, book II, p. 45. Meanwhile consider, reader, how great Zeno’s eloquence and learning must have been, since learned Gentiles also assembled to hear him.

From this, moreover, it is plainly demonstrated that the church stood open to all—not only catechumens and heretics, but Gentiles also—while the sacred sermon was being delivered. This is expressly established by other monuments of the same and later age. See the Council of Valence, canon 1; Carthage IV, canon 84. Yet in Tertullian’s age this seems to have been less approved among Catholics, as appears from *On Prescription*, ch. 41. Rebuking the practice of heretics as foreign to Catholic discipline, at least in Africa, he says: “First of all, it is uncertain who is a catechumen and who a believer: they enter alike, hear alike, pray alike; even if Gentiles happen to arrive, they will cast what is holy to dogs and pearls before swine—though not real ones. They wish simplicity to mean the overthrow of discipline; the care for discipline which belongs to us they call pandering.”

But the discipline which displeased Catholics in the first three centuries, while concealment was necessary because of persecutions, became acceptable after peace had been restored to the Church, when there was nothing to fear from arriving Gentiles and it was permissible to distinguish and exclude them at a fixed time together with catechumens, so that what is holy might not be given to dogs. Likewise, the Jews interpreted the Law before everyone; on this see Valesius at length in his notes on Eusebius’ *History*, book II, ch. 6. Moreover, in this Zenoian sentence manuscript Pomp. has *audeat* (“may dare”) for *audeam* (“I may dare”).]

[Note: We possess no solid and exact image of true law and genuine justice; we make use of shadows and images. Thus Cicero candidly confessed in book III of *On Duties*, speaking in the character of a Gentile philosopher. Although Gentile philosophers handed down much concerning justice, Lactantius demonstrates at length, *Divine Institutions*, book V, that they nevertheless attained nothing solid or true. From him St. Zeno drew not a few things for this tractate, as we shall shortly see.

Gentile poets too understood this; and therefore, says Lactantius himself, book IV, ch. 5, they invented the fiction that Justice, offended by human vices, withdrew from earth and migrated to heaven. In the following sentence the Venetian edition has *non curo* (“I do not care”) for *non curem* (“I shall not care”), and manuscript Urb. has *jocatur* (“he jokes”) for *jocetur* (“he may joke”).]

But I shall not care how anyone may mock me. For in the Church of God an embellished discourse is not sought, but pure truth—a truth from which all those men wandered far, and not undeservedly, who thought that God’s justice consisted in the powers of eloquence.

[Note: Here St. Zeno marks Gentile philosophers and orators. Gentile philosophers taught philosophy in public schools even in Ambrose’s time, as we learn from book I of *On Faith*, ch. 13. “They are rich in speech,” says the same author, *Exposition of Psalm XXXVI*, no. 28; and in book VII *On Luke*, no. 66, he observes that most of them parade their supposed wisdom in glittering speeches.

Sophists especially are indicated. Their custom was to be always ready to speak extemporaneously on any subject whatever, as Cicero testifies in book II of *On Ends*. In this they displayed a certain counterfeit and empty appearance of wisdom, professing it for display or profit, as he says in book IV, ch. 23, of the *Academic Questions*. Since among the Gentiles whatever tended to one’s own advantage and benefit was called justice, as will become clear below, St. Zeno is not without reason in declaring that their justice consisted in this sophistical babble.

Accordingly Ambrose, mentioned above, says in book II of *On Abraham*, ch. 10, no. 76: “The sophists of this world have framed the following definition: that the wise man is a good man skilled in speaking.” Here you see that “wise” and “good” are taken as identical, and that sophists place both in skill of speech. Concerning Gentile orators trained in the schools of sophists, who professed the wisdom of eloquence while pursuing unjust gains, see what our author says in no. 2. The Venetian edition has *in eloquentia et viribus* (“in eloquence and powers”) for *in eloquentiae viribus* (“in the powers of eloquence”).]

Finally, because they could not comprehend it—for they could not do so without instruction in the divine wisdom of which they had no knowledge—they asserted two kinds of justice: one civil, the other natural.

[Note: That is, because only that wisdom and justice which are learned through faith are true. Hence St. Zeno, no. 4: “Unless you believe, you shall not understand”; and Lactantius, *Institutions*, book VI, ch. 9: “Whoever does not know God must necessarily fail to know justice itself.”]

[Note: Among sophists Carneades was famous—the man who delivered two speeches at Rome concerning justice: one in which he endeavoured to establish it, another in which he tried to overthrow it and prove that it did not exist. For the highest glory of sophists was to argue on either side.

The speech which he gave against justice contained the seeds of the distinction indicated here by Zeno. After Lactantius had quoted several fragments of this speech, *Institutions*, book VI, ch. 16, he says: “Thus, having divided justice into two parts, calling one civil and the other natural, he overthrew both: because that civil justice is indeed wisdom but is not justice; while natural justice is indeed justice but is not wisdom.” We have no doubt that St. Zeno drank from this source.

Carneades called civil justice—which he admitted to be wisdom, but not justice—the laws which human beings established for themselves on grounds of advantage: namely, when they cared more for their own interests, safety, and life than for those of others, indeed even when, if necessary, they injured others in their property and life. He called this wise, even though it could not be called just. Natural justice, however, he said, was that by which a person harmed no one, gave each person his due, and chose himself to suffer loss of goods and life rather than inflict force and injury on anyone. This was regarded by Carneades as the height of folly, although he could not deny that it was truly justice.

These matters had to be set out more fully from the remembered fragments, so that what Zeno has built upon this foundation may be more readily understood.]

The Apostle made the distinction quite openly when he spoke to the Romans, saying: “For, being ignorant of the justice of God and wishing to establish their own justice, they did not submit to the justice of God” (Rom. 10:3).

But, since they expected nothing from the future and considered only the advantages of the present life, they defended the false as true against the true; and thus, with open eyes, they lost both out of their very hands: God’s justice, because they regard it as foolish, since it labours to benefit others more than itself, at the cost not merely, I say, of property but even, if necessary, of life itself; their own justice, because, although it is falsely clothed in the name of wisdom, nevertheless, by pursuing its own advantages—which cannot at all be secured without the disadvantages of others—it cannot be denied to be unjust by anyone, however truly foolish.

[Note: The Gentile philosophers against whom the argument is directed say, when speaking of virtue, that it is to be pursued for its own sake; for they do not at all see its rewards, which are eternal and immortal (Lactantius, book V, ch. 17). Indeed, they thought that no eternal reward would follow virtue apart from the honour given it.

Hence in Cicero—as Lactantius observes from the now-lost dialogue *On the Republic*, book V, ch. 18—the same Laelius, defender of justice, says: “Virtue plainly desires honour, and virtue has no other reward.” This is the whole reason why they did not know true justice and wisdom, but judged it the greatest folly. “For if after death we are nothing,” says Lactantius, “then surely it is the mark of a most foolish person not to provide for this life, that it may be as long as possible and full of every advantage.” See also ch. 15. Shortly afterward manuscript Urb. has *utraque* (“each”) for *utramque* (“both”).]

[Note: This passage has in view those arguments of Carneades in his speech against justice. Having undertaken to prove either that justice did not exist, or that, if there were any, it was the height of folly because it harmed itself while serving the interests of others, he attempted to establish this by arguments relating partly to the loss of external goods and partly to the loss of life. It is quite credible that Zeno read these in Lactantius, ch. 16, and had them in mind when he wrote this; therefore, lest the author’s meaning not be fully understood, it is worth setting them out.

First, concerning external goods: “If a good man has a runaway slave or an unhealthy and pestilential house, defects known to himself alone, and he offers them for sale in order to sell them: will he declare that he is selling a runaway slave and a pestilential house, or will he conceal this from the buyer? If he declares it, he will indeed be good, because he will not deceive; yet he will be judged foolish, because he will sell at a low price or not sell at all.”

He then gives another example: a person finds someone who thinks that he is selling brass, when it is gold; and, having posed the question, asks: “Will he remain silent in order to buy it cheaply, or disclose the fact in order to buy it dearly?” He answers: “You plainly wish him to seem foolish for preferring to buy it dearly.”

Concerning the goods of life he says: “Justice is not to kill a person and not to touch what belongs to another at all. What then will the just man do if he is shipwrecked and someone weaker in strength has seized a plank? Will he not thrust that man from the plank in order to climb aboard himself and, supported by it, escape—especially when there is no witness in the midst of the sea? If he is wise, he will do it, for he must perish unless he does. But if he prefers to die rather than lay hands upon another, he is not unjust, but foolish, because he does not spare his own life while sparing another’s.” Having added another similar example, he concludes: “If the just man does not do this, he must nevertheless be foolish.” Thus far Lactantius from Carneades’ speech.]

[Note: Carneades himself, in the speech by which he intended to attack true justice and defend the other, civil justice—which he called wisdom—did not dare deny that injustice was joined with it. Indeed, he freely conceded it, saying of a man who conceals a defect in an article and sells it for a higher price: “If he conceals it, he will indeed be wise, because he will look after his own interests; but he will also be bad—that is, unjust—because he will deceive.” Similar remarks occur in another fragment in Lactantius.

Cicero speaks more plainly in the dialogue *On the Republic*, where he introduced Furius arguing for Carneades and Laelius arguing against him. Although Furius most vigorously defended that civil justice of the world which St. Zeno calls “their own,” nevertheless, Lactantius says in ch. 16, he conceded that it was wisdom indeed, but unjust.]

II. Yet if they could have known true justice, whose reward is immortality, and which is for this reason covered with the veil of apparent folly—that a great thing might be sought by great virtues and great labours—they would unhesitatingly choose to be judged foolish but just, rather than wise but unjust. Especially so because all their fraud is now exposed: they did not have the power to alter the realities, but only the names, branding justice with the term “folly” and injustice with the term “wisdom.” If you correct these terms and restore them to their proper places, you will find that folly agrees more with injustice, wisdom with justice.

[Note: Similarly Lactantius, book VI, ch. 16: “They change only the names; the things themselves remain.”]

Nor shall I cease to prove this by the testimonies of sacred Law, whose words are these: “Since the world did not know the wisdom of God through wisdom, God judged it best to save believers through the folly of preaching” (1 Cor. 1:21). And again, more clearly: “If anyone among you seems to be wise in this age, let him become foolish so that he may be wise; for the wisdom of this world is folly with God” (1 Cor. 3:18–19). For this reason the same God thus declares through the prophet: “Let not the wise man glory in his wisdom, nor the strong man glory in his strength, nor the rich man glory in his riches; but let him who glories glory in this: in understanding and knowing that I am the Lord, who exercise mercy, judgment, and justice upon earth” (Jer. 9:23–24).

Oh, in how few words he has fully set forth this whole business so earnestly conducted in the world! For by these three things, which are the foundations of all vices, the whole human race is driven, shipwrecked at every moment as if by violent storms, toward destruction. For wisdom, boiling over with dense arguments, adorned with the persuasive and pleasing falsehood of brilliant speech, armed with the trumpet of voice and the sword of the tongue, draws all actions to itself, gathers crowds, and harangues. It decides lawsuits so as to sow them; it gathers corrupt and slippery morals; with its laws it attacks the laws; it destroys law by law.

[Note: Thus manuscripts Rem., Tol., Pomp., and Vat.; elsewhere and in printed editions, “distinguishes.” Here *distringo* means “I destroy, overturn, overthrow,” as in Florus, book IV, ch. 1, “to destroy a city by fires,” and as the ninth chapter of Frontinus’ first book bears the title *On Destroying Enemies* in the same sense.]

Who does not see that it has never done, and never can do, anything right in what it has done? Do you wish to know how just it is? It considers itself wretched unless it has overthrown truth.

[Note: Thus manuscripts Rem., Tol., and Pomp.; elsewhere and in printed editions, *aestuans* (“seething”). Here the author attacks the wisdom of Gentile orators, placed in eloquence, by which they led hearers and judges to their own opinion, not through reason but through emotions. Rhetoricians taught that such emotions were often to be stirred up against reason and laws if advantage so required. Among many precepts of this kind, let us cite one from Cicero, book II, *On the Orator*, p. 70: “Nothing is greater in speaking than that the listener should favour the orator, and that he himself should be so moved as to be governed more by some impulse and agitation of mind than by judgment or deliberation. For people decide far more matters through hatred or love, desire or anger, pain or joy, hope or fear, error or some disturbance of mind, than through truth, prescription, any rule of law, a judicial formula, or laws.” See what is argued against this type of eloquence in the dialogue *On the Causes of Corrupt Eloquence*, no. 25, attributed by some to Seneca, by others to Quintilian, and by others to others; it is therefore printed among the works of various authors. Shortly afterward manuscript Urb. has *congerit* (“he heaps up”) for *colligit* (“he gathers”).]

But courage, which human beings share with savagery, places every right in force; whatever it has strength to do, it judges right. Therefore, with no reverence at all for divine or human religion, it ruthlessly destroys by fire and sword inhabitants, cities, and countryside together with all their possessions, fearing nothing because it trusts in a friendly death. Finally, what wisdom gathers by industry through laws, courage sometimes scatters in a single assault, with eyes shut.

[Note: Printed editions have *adeo quod*; manuscript Rem. has *ideo*; in Pomp. *quod* is lacking. On their basis, the reading *ideoque* (“and therefore”) was preferred. The passage in Lactantius, book VI, ch. 6, may shed light on the text: he reports that the Gentiles heaped the highest praises upon brave men who offered themselves to death for their country, overthrowing cities, destroying nations, caring for their country, extending its boundaries, and so forth; and in ch. 9: “The Roman people itself, through the Fetiales, by declaring wars and legally committing injustices, and by always desiring and seizing what belonged to others, acquired possession of the entire world.”]

[Note: In printed editions, “with shut eyes.” Both manuscripts and printed editions run this passage together in such a way that it cannot be understood at all: “with shut eyes she is thirdly rich in avarice.” We have corrected it as in the text: first, the verb “scatters” had plainly to be supplied for the sense to stand; then punctuation had to be placed, after which Zeno explains the third element proposed by Paul, concerning avarice, in the words: “Thirdly, avarice is rich,” etc. Thus it is conveniently understood that both eloquence and courage, which the author has thus far discussed, favour avarice.]

Thirdly, avarice is rich, and the former two strive with marvellous speed to magnify its wealth. The whole world serves it; every age is enslaved to it. Oh, wickedness! What darkness is this? It is in everyone, and is condemned by everyone as though it were not. It is accused, and yet cultivated; it murders, and is loved. Surely it is an invincible kind of calamity, to which courage will be enslaved once wisdom has been subjugated.

III. Do you now plainly see that the wisdom of this world is not justice—and indeed not even true wisdom? For it cannot be that one who is truly wise is not also just, or that one who is just is not likewise truly wise. A foolish person cannot be just, nor a wise person unjust, as reason itself teaches.

[Note: Lactantius, book V, ch. 17, has almost the same words, so much so that it appears Zeno profited from them and even copied some word for word: “Finally, to conclude the argument,” says Lactantius, “reason itself teaches that the same person cannot be just and foolish, wise and unjust. For one who is foolish does not know what is just and good, and therefore always sins. He is led captive, as it were, by vices and cannot resist at all, because he lacks the virtue which he does not know. But the just person abstains from every sin, which he cannot do otherwise than by possessing knowledge of right and wrong. But who can distinguish right from wrong unless he is wise? Thus it comes about that one who is foolish can never be just, nor one unjust be wise.” The Venetian edition has “good or evil” for “good and evil.”]

For one who is foolish does not know what good and evil are; nor can he know what to reject and what to retain. Therefore he always sins, which is contrary to justice. But the just person abstains from every sin. He does this because he possesses knowledge of evil and good, which surely belongs to the wise person. Hence it follows that one who is foolish can never be just, nor one who has been unjust wise. But whether the just person lacks wisdom or the wise person justice—what they supposed—he will certainly be neither wise nor just.

IV. I think the deceits of the world have been sufficiently exposed. Since all people practise them more skillfully than can be said, it is superfluous to dwell upon them. Let us now come to true justice, the source and mother of all virtues.

[Note: “Justice is the very source of virtue.” Lactantius, book V, ch. 5. A little later manuscripts Rem., Tol., and Zen. have *corrigit* (“corrects”) for *colligit* (“gathers”).]

Above all other virtues, it gathers and unfolds itself wholly toward the benefit of others, knowing what is principally owed to God; it claims nothing for itself and leaves nothing as its own, except that it faithfully performs His will without any boasting. It reaches out and is wholly diffused for the public good, yet desires rather to be felt than seen. It is utterly careful not to turn aside in any direction, not to find anything in itself for which it may reproach itself, and never to fail in a work once begun.

It breaks the yokes of captives by ransoming them; in caring for prisoners, gentle and wakeful concern knows the prison more fully; it shares sickness with the sick person; it does not permit abandoned corpses to remain unclothed and unburied. Neglecting its own need, it lavishly and secretly scatters seeds of mercy among the poor and miserable. It does not allow itself to be asked, nor to be repaid by the reciprocal wage of praise. It considers this a grievous loss, this a crime. For, leaving nothing to itself, with blessed desire it outruns avarice: avarice possesses human beings; justice possesses God.

[Note: “Yoke” is plainly taken for captivity, or for the instrument by which captives are bound, in analogy with the literal yoke by which oxen are joined and subjected to service. Cicero, *Philippics* I, ch. 2: “They had cast off the slavish yoke from their necks”; and Pliny, *Panegyric*, ch. 11: “They had shaken off the yoke.” Lactantius, book VI, ch. 12, expounds almost the same works of mercy and justice which Zeno here enumerates more concisely.]

[Note: Manuscript Pomp. has *patitur* (“suffers”), but that word is repeated a little later.]

[Note: The Verona edition had *pietates largitur: furtim semina spargit* (“he bestows acts of mercy: secretly he scatters seeds”); the Venetian edition, *pietatis largitur: furtum*, etc.; manuscripts Rem., Tol., and Pomp., *pietatis largiter furtim semina spargit* (“he lavishly, secretly scatters seeds of mercy”). We have followed this reading, inserting *et* (“and”) between the adverbs *largiter* and *furtim*, without which the expression seems too harsh and foreign to Zeno’s style. Scribes could easily have passed over the conjunction because of the final letters *er* of *largiter*. Alms are aptly called seeds of mercy; similarly, in tractate 10, book I, no. 5, the author calls them “pious seeds.”]

Receive further how eagerly, with what love and devotion, justice hastens toward its appointed seat and crown. If anyone summons it to judgment in order to take away its tunic, it willingly yields him its cloak as well. It is cursed and blesses; it is beaten and gives thanks; it is slaughtered and does not resist; moreover, it prays to God for its assailants. Its one chief concern and greatest caution is that it owe nothing to the world, that it suffer none of these things deservedly.

Those who either have not read the divine writings, or have considered what they read vain, because of their low and unpolished style—though they say, “Unless you believe, you shall not understand” (Isa. 7:9, according to the Septuagint)—think justice foolish and mock it as vain, because, though it can enjoy the goods of the world, it neglects them and voluntarily makes itself unhappy. They do not believe that, by keeping God’s commandments, trampling secular pleasures under such duties, and becoming victorious and free from the bonds of the flesh, it will enjoy the inestimable blessedness of promised immortality.

[Note: Lactantius, book V, ch. 1: “This is the chief reason why Holy Scripture has no credit among the wise, learned, and rulers of this age: the prophets spoke in common and simple language, as to the people. Therefore they are despised by those who wish to hear or read nothing unless it is polished and eloquent.”

Likewise Cyril of Alexandria, book VII *Against Julian*, states this Gentile objection: the Gentiles despised the sacred books because of their low and unpolished language, as St. Zeno calls it, preferring their own authors, who used a more polished and copious style. “But perhaps someone will say: Holy Scripture contains a vulgar, common, and worn-out manner of speech; Greek writings, however, are pleasing and additionally abound in elegance and grace of expression.” Thus Cyril, p. 232, Leipzig edition of 1696. Hence Amelius the Platonist, in Cyril himself, p. 283, calls St. John a barbarian in the same sense. See Jerome, preface *On Ecclesiastical Writers*, for what other Gentiles spewed forth against the same authors of sacred books; see also Ambrose, epistle 8, which refutes the same charge against sacred writers.]

V. But what is it to us what they say? As our distinguished man says: “The Lord knows the thoughts of the wise, that they are foolish” (Ps. 93:11). Let them leave us our folly; let them keep their wisdom for themselves. Yet I see that almost all Christians are followers of that wisdom, who think perfect justice consists in protecting one’s own property and not seeking another’s, while neglecting the command of true wisdom, contained in these words: “If you wish to be perfect, go, sell all that you have; give to the poor; take up your cross; and come, follow me” (Matt. 19:21).

[Note: Printed editions insert “our Psalmist,” which is not found in manuscripts Rem., Pomp., and Zen. A little earlier manuscript Pomp. has *quod illi* (“what they”) for *quid illi* (“what do they”).]

I do not know what anyone can advance against this. But one thing I know: there is none among us who does not labour at every moment to have more than he had. In striving for this, he surely plays the part of avarice, which is justice’s enemy. Hence the granaries of a few are full of grain, while the bellies of the many are empty. Hence prices, more grievous to peoples than scarcity, are set by measures. Hence fraud, perjury, robberies, lawsuits, and wars. Profit is daily sought through the groans of others; confiscation is called industry; and the pursuit of another’s property is pressed, under the pretext of protecting and managing one’s own, by the most artful arguments, so that a person who is undefended or innocent loses by law what he possesses. This is worse than every violence, because what is taken by force can sometimes be recovered; what is taken by legal circumventions cannot.

[Note: “Are” has been restored from the manuscripts and the Venetian edition. Other editions have “is empty.” In the following clause manuscript Tol. has “by measures.”]

[Note: In the Verona edition, incorrectly, “prescription,” whereas the discussion concerns proscription or the public confiscation of goods.]

[Note: “To lose by laws” means the same as what was said in no. 2 concerning the stratagems of eloquence: “With its laws it attacks the laws; it destroys law by law.”]

Let whoever wishes glory in this justice; yet let him know that he is more wretched than the wretched person who grows rich from others’ misery. Can anyone consider just the person who prefers the advantage of his household estate to mercy; who, while human beings suffer hunger and nakedness, feeds moths, weevils, and worms; who, with unhappy tenacity, withholds what he has not only from others but even from himself?

VI. “But,” you say, “it is just that I preserve what is mine and seek nothing that belongs to another.” The Gentiles too have been accustomed to say this. But how unjust it is in God’s sight we shall presently see. First of all, excellent Christian, I wish to know what things are yours, when among those who fear God all things are common, as it is written: “The multitude of those who believed acted with one heart and soul” (Acts 4:32). There was no distinction among them, nor did they regard any of the goods they possessed as their own; rather, all things were common to them—as day, sun, night, rain, and the condition of being born and dying, which divine justice has bestowed equally upon the human race without any distinction of persons.

[Note: St. Zeno said these things in order to indicate the equality which Lactantius discusses at greater length in book V, chs. 14–15, where he proves that all are equal by divine institution—not that none should be rich or none poor, but that among those who fear God and cultivate true justice wealth should be distributed with a certain equality, so that the rich freely supply what the poor need. “Thus,” he says, “they are rich not because they have riches, but because they use them for works of justice; and those who seem poor are nevertheless rich in this, that they neither lack nor covet anything.” St. Zeno devotes the remaining part of this tractate to urging this equality, as he attacks the hardness of the rich toward the poor and commends liberality.]

Since this is so, without doubt the one who alone possesses what can benefit the welfare of many is no different from a tyrant. What of the fact that, while a poor person dies daily under oppression, hunger, cold, and wrong, you cultivate gold as your friend; guard silver; hold costly clothing and proud, superfluous ornaments sacred as an idol; adorn yourself moment by moment, rich in public, richer in private? Do you not understand that the person who can help one dying in want by such great resources, but does not help, seems himself to kill that person? Oh, how many souls’ murders hang upon the trinkets of adorned matrons! If you release a single ornament into money and distribute it among individual needs, you will learn from their relief how much misery that ornament costs.

[Note: *Quod* (“the fact that”) is absent from manuscript Pomp. Lower down, manuscripts Rem. and Tol. have *inimicum tibi excolis* (“you cultivate an enemy for yourself”) for *amicum tibi excolis* (“you cultivate a friend for yourself”). Then manuscript Vat. has *homini inopi morienti* (“to a needy dying person”) for *homini inopia morienti* (“to a person dying in want”); manuscript Urb. has *contimoratae matronae* [uncertain: perhaps “timidly adorned matrons”] for *ornatae matronae* (“adorned matrons”).]

VII. “I have children,” he says, “whom I ought not to strip naked.”

[Note: After *debeo* (“I ought”) manuscript Rem. has a blank line and a half, then *ista haec* for *ista est*; manuscript Tol. has *ista et infidelitatis est*. “The excuse of unbelief” here means what was said in no. 6: “The Gentiles too have been accustomed to say this.”]

This is the excuse of unbelief, which the Holy Spirit refutes through the prophet in these words: “I was young, and I have grown old; yet I have never seen the just person abandoned, nor his offspring begging bread” (Ps. 36:25). And again: “The rich have lacked and suffered hunger, but those who seek the Lord shall lack no good thing” (Ps. 33:11). This is very easy to prove by example.

We remember it recorded in the books of Kingdoms (3 Kings 17): in a time of famine, when people everywhere were dying, the memorable widow, when Elijah asked for food, did not divide but gave him all the last sustenance of herself and her children; she preferred to die with her children rather than fail justice. For so illustrious a deed she received from God food unfailing, which appetite could not diminish. It increased by being diminished: the store of the vessels remained always undiminished though full; and whatever long-continued necessity had taken from them in expenditure, renewed abundance restored.

[Note: “Of Kingdoms” for “of Kings” is also found in Hilary, *Prologue to the Psalms*, p. 4; Ambrose, book I *On Abel*, ch. 2; *Apology of David*, ch. 1; sermon 21 on Psalm 118, no. 20; and other ancient Fathers. Manuscript Urb. has *feriebatur* (“was struck”) for *moriebatur* (“was dying”).]

[Note: Manuscript Urb. has *nequisset* for *nequiret* (“could not”).]

Therefore, if you desire to be a good, provident, useful father, like Abraham you must love God more than your children, so that you may deserve to have them whole, safe, and blessed. It is foolish to wish to provide the substance of life for those to whom you have given neither birth nor breathed souls, and for whom you cannot secure salvation. Therefore, even late, restrain that sacrilegious utterance; mindful of human frailty, you do not know what may happen in the very matter of which we speak. Lay aside the deception of a vain excuse. You season avarice with the sin of ingratitude. The power to provide for future welfare belongs to God alone.

[Note: In a marginal correction in manuscript Pomp.: “Ungrateful.”]

## TRACTATE IV. On Chastity

[Note: **Tractate IV.**—The Venetian edition reads here: “On the praises of chastity and the detestable fruit of unchastity.” We have retained the title of the manuscripts and other editions: “On Chastity.”]

I. He who cultivates chastity most readily recognizes how great its nobility is [Note: [Col. 0288D] The printed editions have “recognizes”; for it is.] For it is a virtue so great that it is honorable even to its enemies. [Note: [Col. 0288D] The enemies of chastity here called such are especially the Gentiles, who, both through the shameful worship of unchaste gods and goddesses and through equally shameful spectacles, repeatedly noted by our Author, openly waged war upon chastity. We may pass over the Julian and Papian law, which, directed against celibacy and widowhood—whether enacted for increasing the treasury or promoting fertility—nevertheless in fact endeavored to cut off the two chief branches of chastity. To this St. Ambrose alludes in *On Widowhood*, ch. 14, no. 84: “Those,” he says, “who venerate the adulteries and disgraceful deeds of their gods, established penalties for celibacy and widowhood, so that, as rivals of crimes, they might punish the pursuits of virtues: ostensibly seeking fertility, but actually aiming to abolish the purpose of chastity.” Yet how greatly chastity was held in honor even among the pagans may be learned [Col. 0289B] from the worship which they rendered, not so much to chastity universally understood as to virginity and to virgins. Pliny, book II, ch. 7, indicates that Chastity was worshipped among the goddesses by the Romans; and Festus testifies that her statue stood in the Cattle Market. St. Ambrose, *On Virgins*, ch. 3, no. 13: “Certainly even among the Gentiles virginity is customarily held venerable amid altars and hearths.” Diana, as he himself observes in book III of *On Virgins*, ch. 2, no. 6, Minerva, and especially Vesta, were proclaimed virgins. We learn from Lactantius, *Institutes*, book I, ch. 21, that the Romans celebrated solemn rites in honor of the chastity preserved by the sacred Vestals; and, in ch. 22, Varro reports that Fauna’s chastity was especially praised, so much so that, because of the renown of her chastity, “women sacrifice to her in secret,” he says, “and call her the Good Goddess.” As for the honor accorded to Vestals because of their virginity, and their privileges and rewards, read Justus Lipsius, *Syntagma on the Vestals*, ch. 11. There also, in ch. 15, you will find not merely inscriptions set up to them commending their chastity, but [Col. 0289C] statues likewise erected because of their outstanding chastity. Hence Athanasius too, in his *Apology to Constantius*, no. 33, speaking of Christian virgins, says: “When the pagans see these, they admire them as they do the temple of Vesta.” Similarly St. John Chrysostom, in the treatise *That Canonical Women Ought Not to Cohabit with Men*, vol. I of the new edition, p. 249, testifies that “the Gentiles confess virginity to be a thing above nature and not human, and therefore we were objects of the highest admiration to them all.” Finally, the esteem of the unchaste themselves for chastity is suggested by those words of Zeno, no. 2: “She hates chastity, and yet wishes to seem what that is.”]

She confirms the foundations of the whole [Col. 0289A] human race; she gives to all affections their proper names; [Note: [Col. 0289C] The proper designations of affections are derived from chastity, as when one speaks of “chaste fidelity,” and so forth.] she guards the sacred rights of parents, spouses, and children. Conspicuous in either sex, admirable at every age, unquestioned in every condition, devoted to herself alone, always conscious of doing well, subject to absolutely nothing, she fears one thing only: lest she be anything more than what she is called. [Note: [Col. 0289C] The text read: “lest she be any longer than she is called”; but because this does not yield a sufficiently clear sense, we have written *quae* (“what”) for *quam* (“than”). If one maintains that *ne* cannot occur in desirable matters with verbs of fearing, unless the manuscripts of Cicero—for example, *Letters to Friends*, book VI, letter 1—Terence, and others are all also faulty, whose texts are generally corrected in printed editions, then the same suspicion of error applies here, and *ne non* should be read; or *quam* should be restored in place of *quae*.] Finally, in solitude—which those who are afraid call an opportunity—she fears herself as though she were a judge; [Note: [Col. 0289D] The Reims manuscript has “love and before”; the other codices and editions, “from those who fear.” Moreover, he used *arbiter* for judge or observer; Latin writers not infrequently employ this noun in both senses.] and she reveres every secret place more than a public one. She hates the deadly enticements of the hostile flesh; and whatever pleasure or gift the world may offer, she utterly rejects it, reckoning that she possesses everything if she is pure. She desires no one shamefully, nor [Col. 0290A] likewise makes herself desirable to anyone. In her own condition she remains everywhere and at all times, consulting honor more than advantage.

Do you wish to know how great her blessedness is? If she loves you, whoever possesses her loves her; and he who does not possess her loves her. Therefore, if her glory often exults among the Gentiles—although there [Note: [Col. 0289D] What St. Ambrose wrote concerning virginity cultivated by certain pagans illuminates this passage, where the subject is chastity understood universally, glorious even among them. Thus, in *On Virginity*, ch. 3, no. 13, speaking of the Gentiles, he says: “Among whom there is no piety of merits, no integrity of mind; yet among them virginity of the flesh is praised.” Zeno’s statement that chastity was not fruitful among the Gentiles is explained by Ambrose’s reason: among the Gentiles there was no piety of merits; by “piety” he means faith joined with love of God, without which, just as it is impossible [Col. 0290B] to please God, so no merit for eternal life can exist. Lactantius discusses this piety, understood as Christian faith, at length in *Institutes*, book V, ch. 14. Zeno’s further statement that chastity was not true among the pagans is explained by Ambrose’s reason that there was no integrity of mind among them. For though some fostered chastity in body, many of them were nevertheless unchaste in mind; some of their virgins were openly chaste only, while secretly serving unchastity. Hence we read that not a few Vestals were caught in guilt and punished with severe penalties. Lipsius collects several testimonies of this kind in *Syntagma on the Vestals*, ch. 13. Add that, according to Ambrose in the cited work, no. 13, some Vestals were forced into the profession of virginity, others induced by rewards: “There they are recalled from marriage by rewards . . . there violence is used so that they may be taken.” Chastity compelled by force or lured by rewards, rather than chosen willingly, is plainly far from true chastity. Accordingly Ambrose, letter 18 to Valentinian, says: “Virginity is not that which is bought for a price, nor possessed through zeal for virtue.” Moreover, in book I of *On Virgins*, ch. 3, no. 45, he observes that the virginity of Vestals was customarily prescribed by age: they were to remain virgins for a fixed number of years; afterward they were permitted—even instructed—to abandon virginity and marry. “They themselves teach their virgins that they ought not, and cannot, persevere, who have assigned an end to virginity.” Shortly before he had said: “What is this chastity, not of morals but of years, prescribed not by perpetuity but by age?” Finally, because the Gentiles lacked faith in God and hope for future things, concerning which St. Zeno has spoken sufficiently in the preceding treatise, just as true justice could not exist among them, so neither could any true virtue—as Lactantius proves at length in book VI, chs. 5 and 9—and consequently no true chastity, especially if they cultivated it not from love of virtue but from a certain earthly pleasure or pride. Augustine proved that this pride ruled among the virtues of the Gentiles, produced not by divine grace but natural power. [Col. 0290D] See *On Marriage and Concupiscence*, book I, ch. 3, and *Against Julian*, book IV, ch. 3. Hence Athanasius rightly wrote of virginity in the *Apology to Constantius*, no. 33: “It is certainly established that nowhere is this venerable and heavenly profession of chastity cultivated except among us Christians alone.” Therefore unbelief—which, together with pride, avarice, and other vices, prevailed among the Gentiles even in cultivating chastity—is that unchaste plunderer mentioned by our bishop: by corrupting their chastity through some vice, whence he is called “unchaste,” and by plundering all its merit, he ensured that it could not be fruitful or true.] it cannot be fruitful or true, because it lies under an unchaste plunderer—how much [Note: [Col. 0290D] “More glorious” is a pleonasm, as also “more admirable” in Treatise 7, no. 2. Thus Plautus, *Menaechmi*, Prologue, v. 55, has “more sweetly”; Virgil, *Culex*, v. 78, “more blessed,” etc. Below, “sanctifier” occurs in Tertullian, *Against Praxeas*, ch. 2.] more glorious ought she to be in the Christian people, who serve her inviolable sanctifier, God? For if the Church is Christ’s bride because she is chaste, and is honored with the yoke of the heavenly marriage-bed because even after marriage she remains thereafter a perpetual virgin, we who are born from so great a union ought by every means [Note: [Col. 0290D] We have preferred *conniti* (“to strive”), from the Reims and Vatican manuscripts, [Col. 0291B] to *adniti*. The manuscripts have *prosapiae* (“lineage”), whereas the printed editions have *prosapiei*.] to strive to show the nobility of [Col. 0291A] our lineage, not merely by descent, but also by the faith of resemblance.

Yet, beloved brethren, I declare openly that this assertion shines forth in you without ambiguity: [Note: [Col. 0291B] The printed editions read *retinet*; the Reims manuscript, perhaps *renit?*; and the Pompignan and Vatican manuscripts have *renitet*, which we have adopted as more fitting to the sense. For St. Zeno here says that he declares or glories that this assertion—that we make ourselves like God through chastity—shines unmistakably in his hearers, since it was evident that they zealously cultivated chastity.] you show that you both have and possess God as Father when you do not merely love chastity, in which God dwells, but adorn it with splendid conduct. Great, therefore, is the glory of adorning that by which you yourself are adorned; of preserving that by which you yourself [Note: [Col. 0291B] The Pompignan and Zeno manuscripts and the Verona edition have “are preserved”; and shortly afterward, in place of “love for her,” five manuscripts have “and love.”] are preserved. Finally, your praise is matched to the praise of chastity: she bestows holiness on you, and you bestow love on her. Through her you attain Christ; indeed, through you she embraces Christ together with you. Through her you obtain from God the Father what you ask; indeed, through you she obtains that for which you carefully labor, lest, when she asks anything, she should blush.

Blessed is she when she [Note: [Col. 0291C] The Reims, Vatican, and Pompignan manuscripts have *adludit*; the Urbino manuscript, *alludet*. For *lapsus*, the Reims manuscript has *lapsis*, the Vatican *lapsos*.] plays among children; more blessed when she happily fears falls among adolescents; most blessed when she labors to extinguish the fires of the flesh in young people. In the elderly, indeed, she is to be honored, but not wondered at; for though victorious, she shares the palm of her triumph with the rigor of old age. [Note: [Col. 0291C] The Reims manuscript has *patitur*, which is unsatisfactory. *Partitur* (“shares”) is used because a portion of the victory and triumph is due to the rigor of old age, as the following reasoning indicates. We have adopted *rigore* from the Zeno manuscript in place of *vigore*, since rigor resulting from cold is proper to old age, and the struggle of desire is weakened in the elderly by stiffness of limbs, not by vigor, and ease in conquering results. A little later, for *pugna*, where the Reims, Vatican, and Urbino manuscripts incorrectly have *pugna. At ubi*, we judged it better to restore *fiunt* from the Reims codex in place of *sunt* in the editions or *sint* in the Vatican and Urbino manuscripts.] For the struggle of desire ceases [Col. 0292A] where, as illnesses become more frequent, by necessity itself even the limbs of the unchaste become chaste.

II. Come now: let us briefly make known the rage of her rival, [Note: [Col. 0291C] The Reims and Urbino manuscripts read: “let us make known from the comparison of names.” The Pompignan and Zeno manuscripts: “let us make known no less from comparison.” The Vatican manuscript: “from the exercise of names.” The printed editions with the Toulouse manuscript: “from the comparison of names”; this reading seemed more probable, for the words immediately following concerning Antichrist falsely assuming Christ’s name, and unchastity bearing the sound of chastity’s name, seem to refer to this; or “names” may mean chastity and unchastity, which become clearer by comparison. Perhaps someone might judge, with a few words transposed, that one should write: “Come now, let us briefly make known the rage of her rival, so that from the comparison of names it may most readily be recognized what is to be sought and what avoided.” We have written “recognized” instead of “known,” on the authority of four manuscripts.] so that it may most readily be recognized what ought to be sought and what avoided. Under the veil of Christ’s name, brethren, Antichrist likewise endeavors to represent himself as chaste, in order to deceive. He draws after himself the sound of chastity’s name; but his author shows what fruits he bears.

For she rages madly through the peoples and hurls the unstable minds of human beings into frenzy with the blazing goads of lusts, sparing neither sex, nor age, nor piety, nor herself; because one who seeks another’s shame first loses his own. Neither night nor day succeeds in purity for her; for she is always submerged beneath the storm of her muddy whirlpool, [Col. 0292B] while the ever-boiling foulness of lust is perpetrated either in deed [Note: [Col. 0291D] Here the Author uses *veritas* (“truth”) for the thing itself and the actual deed, a sense in which Lampridius, in the first edition and in many manuscripts cited by Salmasius, p. 183, in the life of Elagabalus, has *veritate vendere* (“to sell in actual fact”), and Arnobius, book V, has *in veritate promiserat* (“had promised in fact”). Similarly, he uses *imago* (“image”) for thought, as Lactantius writes, book VI, ch. 23: “The mind becomes adulterous if it has even painted for itself an image of pleasure.”] or in imagination. She gives or receives payments; she corrupts or is corrupted; she inspires love, only soon afterward to make hatred out of love. She begets unlawful heirs and, knowing the crime, excuses it under the name of filial duty. [Note: [Col. 0292B] Although “unlawful heirs” can generally mean bastards born from condemned intercourse, namely adultery or incest, since by law they could receive none of their father’s inheritance—whereas other illegitimate children received a sixth part and could even receive the entire inheritance if legitimized—yet St. Zeno here seems to speak of children who are allowed to enter unlawfully, that is, into an inheritance not their own. Such are those begotten from another man’s wife and permitted to receive another man’s inheritance as though born from his true wife rather than from adultery. The crime is said to be excused under the names of filial duty, that provision may conveniently be made both for the woman’s reputation and for the child’s standing and support. The Reims and Urbino manuscripts have “those being born” in place of “knowing”; the Venetian edition, “being born.” The latter reading is not displeasing, insofar as the unlawful heir, after birth, is permitted to enjoy the possessions of a man who is not his father, and this is excused under the names of filial duty.] She either kills her own children or [Col. 0293A] strips them of affection. [Note: [Col. 0292C] This passage is read variously in the codices. Most have *negat* (“denies”); the Zeno and Pompignan manuscripts, *necat* (“kills”). If this clause referred to the preceding sentence, *negat* would be preferable, signifying that unchaste persons, to avoid supporting children begotten from another man’s wife, deny that those children are their own. But it is not easy to see how the name of filial duty could apply to this excuse for a known crime. Therefore this statement seems to concern children truly their own, whom someone has received from his own wife or concubine, as opposed [Col. 0292D] to those sown in another’s wife, whom the bishop called unlawful heirs in the immediately preceding testimony. The reading *necat* is more suited to this sense. Those who used a wife, or maintained a concubine, not for begetting offspring but for unchastity and pleasure, formerly used to kill their children or, more mildly, expose them, as is clear from numerous testimonies. Minucius Felix, *Octavius*, no. 30: “I see you exposing children whom you have begotten to wild beasts and birds, or destroying them by a miserable kind of death, strangled.” There are those who, by drugs swallowed in the womb itself, extinguish the origin of the future human being and commit parricide before they give birth. Tertullian, *Apology*, ch. 9: “Those who kill the children born to them. And indeed there is a difference in the kind of killing: more cruelly, you take away the breath in water, or expose them to cold, hunger, and dogs.” Lactantius, book I, ch. 9: “Those who strangle children born from them or, if they are excessively kind, expose them.” See also book VI, ch. 20; Clement of Alexandria, *Paedagogue*, book III, chs. 3 and 4; and Ambrose, letter V, no. 12. St. Zeno seems to have censured this evil custom of the unchaste in this text, which is punctuated in two clauses: “either kills, or strips of affection.” We have preferred to write *affectu* (“of affection”) rather than *affectus*, to make the sense complete. It signifies that such unchaste persons either killed their own children, who could not enter another’s inheritance—whether in the womb or after birth—or stripped them of all affection and nourishment, exposing or at least neglecting them as though they were strangers rather than their own.] She considers absolutely nothing shameful either to suffer or to do, provided her endeavors [Note: [Col. 0293C] The neuter plural *conata* is used by approved authors. Cornelius Nepos, *Life of Dionysius*, ch. 8: “to accomplish undertakings”; Velleius Paterculus, book II, ch. 29: “having carried out undertakings.” Shortly afterward the Vatican manuscript has “with another’s stain.”] succeed in their outcome. Yet in her very fruit, in which she is accustomed to rejoice at the stain of another’s conquered shame, she is always miserable. Finally, after the deed is done, she hates both herself and him whom she has conquered.

She has often declared war upon peaceful nations; she has more than once overthrown powerful kingdoms; beneath shameful or cruel deeds she has triumphed over the marriage-beds of those whom she enslaved; she [Note: [Col. 0293C] There were men who prostituted themselves as male prostitutes to male lust, for the payment customarily given to female prostitutes. Salvian mentions them in book VII of *On the Governance [of God]*: “Men proclaimed themselves women in relation to themselves.” See Clement of Alexandria, *Paedagogue*, book III, and Justin, *Apology*. Their proper names were *cinaedi* and *exoleti*. Severus intended to prohibit them, and Philip carried it out, according to Lampridius in the *Life of Alexander Severus*. In the Justinian Code, book IX, title 9, law 31 of Constantius and Constans is entitled “On male Venus,” and concerns this matter; it is clear from it that people of this kind used women’s clothing.] has taught men, crazed by a mad feminine passion, to violate their own nature by unexpectedly prostituting themselves for a fee unknown even to women themselves; she has placed the wages of lust especially in the deaths of parents, children, husbands, and wives; she has sometimes destroyed the names of filial duty by monstrous intercourse, [Col. 0293B] pursuing the chaste indeed, but killing the unchaste only in a fitting manner. [Note: [Col. 0293D] Any incest among persons to whom filial duty is owed is opposed to filial duty. Since, properly speaking, “monstrous” denotes whatever is contrary to the laws and order of nature, intercourse apart from or against nature could be called monstrous by Zeno. Yet in no. 5 he says that the old men who shamefully lusted after Susanna were inflamed by one prodigy, although they did not wish to sin against nature. Perhaps he called this unchastity of old men a prodigy because so great a conspiracy and passion of love in old men seemed astonishing. Shortly afterward the Urbino manuscript has “merely incongruously” for “merely fittingly.”] She, I say, [Note: [Col. 0293D] St. Zeno used the same formula in Treatise 1, no. 4: “He seeks protections moment by moment.” In Treatise 53, book II, he said “at moments whenever you wish” for “at whatever time you wish.” [Col. 0294B] Therefore, in Zeno *per momenta* means the same as “through time” or “as opportunity permits.”] from time to time both gives birth to everything evil and has given birth to everything worse; for among idols [Note: [Col. 0294B] Venus, counted among the goddesses by the pagans, is reported to have been a prostitute by Arnobius, book IV, p. 143; Firmicus, *On the Error of Profane Religion*, p. 34; and others. There were other goddesses called Venuses, whom Arnobius, book VI, p. 207, calls goddesses of lust and pleasure. Moreover, unchastity was worshipped in other pagan gods, whose adulteries and sexual violations of males and females are known not merely to learned men but are also represented [Col. 0294C] in theaters. These are Lactantius’s words, *Institutes*, book I. See Clement of Alexandria in the *Exhortation*, Minucius Felix, and others who, writing against the Gentiles, exposed the wantonness of those whom they worshipped as gods.] she is a goddess, and among their worshippers [Note: [Col. 0294C] Unchastity acted as the servant of unchaste gods in many unchaste rites and games, celebrated at fixed times in worship of the unchastity of those same gods; they are things which it is tiresome and shameful even to indicate. Let one passage of Ambrose be heard, *On Virgins*, book I, ch. 4, no. 16: “What shall I say of the Phrygian rites, in which unchastity is a religious discipline—and would that it were only of the weaker sex? What of the orgies of Liber, where the mystery of religion is an incentive to lust? What manner of life, then, can priests have where the gods’ sexual violation is worshipped?” Indeed, the deeds performed in some rites were so foul to mention that Piso and Gabinius, while consuls, expelled certain gods from the Capitol—that is, from the assembly of gods—and overthrew their altars because exceedingly shameful acts were performed in their rites, with no other purpose than to restrain the faults of shameful and idle superstitions. Tertullian records this in the *Apology*, ch. 6. See also Augustine, *City of God*, book VI, ch. 9. Yet Tertullian likewise recalls that their statues and rites were repeatedly restored by force of the populace, *To the Nations*, book I, ch. 10; against this attempt the aforementioned Gabinius vigorously intervened.] she is their minister. She makes herself venerable in temples, cheerful in theaters, importunate in [Col. 0294A] public places, opportune in every secret place. Wanton, sparing neither tongues, nor eyes, nor ears, she jokes, hopes, courts favor, yields, grows jealous, raves, arms herself with entreaties, and arms herself with anger; likewise, she sometimes forcibly extorts what she could not obtain by blandishments.

She always delights in the varied exchange of lusts; she regrets, yet never reaches satiety by slippery gratification. [Note: [Col. 0294D] Here *utilitas* seems to mean use, as in Plautus, *Epidicus*, V.1.28, where we read “the use of the eyes”: “Do I obtain sufficient use of my eyes?” Unless one prefers to understand *utilitas* in Zeno as pleasure, which is the utility of acts of this kind.] She desires to do what she fears may be made public; [Note: [Col. 0294D] *Totum* (“the whole”) for “all things” occurs repeatedly in our Author. Treatise 7, book I, no. 4: “The modest prophet can do everything; he conceals himself from everything.” See Treatise 6, no. 8, and Treatise 10, no. 3. Similarly Spartianus, in *Severus*: “You were everything; you conquered everything.” I pass over other frequent instances in later authors. The Toulouse and Zeno manuscripts have *temptat* for *tentat*.] she attempts absolutely everything, in order to claim everything for herself. It is a new kind of monstrosity: she hates chastity, and yet wishes to seem what chastity is.

III. Meanwhile she cultivates herself with marvelous arts, and seeks in herself a face which she does not possess. She paints herself upon herself, and, by the varied cosmetic coloring of the skillful beautifier, [Col. 0294B] clothes her own face in others’ faces. She will become, not what nature bestowed, but what the temporary judgment of the mirror has dictated to her as its standard. Now she corrects, now erases the features she had loved; now she adds others, now produces new ones. A brazen hydra of forms, made by her own hands, always walks abroad, because she does not know how to blush under borrowed colors; [Col. 0295A] unknown to her household, her relatives, her husbands, and even herself—for that which is always certain can be neither known nor true. [Note: [Col. 0295B] Five manuscripts read: “not known to domestic affections, not to husbands.” If St. Augustine had read this entire description of Zeno, he would surely have included it in *On Christian Doctrine*, book IV, ch. 21, no. 49, among those examples of elevated style which he cites from Cyprian and Ambrose on the same subject.]

Moreover, she never loves God, whom she knows to be opposed to her works. She is indeed the devil’s slave, for she possesses his kingdom. For [Note: [Col. 0295B] The origin of very many gods and goddesses, if one consults even pagan writings themselves, flows from shameful lusts. “Jupiter,” says Athanasius in his *Oration against the Gentiles*, “committed not only sexual violations, but even enrolled among the gods the children whom he had begotten through them, using the appearance of divinity to conceal his depravity.” Among these are Bacchus, Hercules, the Dioscuri, Mercury, Perseus, and Sospita. Arnobius, book IV, extensively lists many others, children not only of Jupiter but of other gods, shamefully born and granted divine honors. Minucius Felix in the *Octavius*, Clement of Alexandria, Lactantius, Gregory Nazianzen, Firmicus, and others likewise discuss these matters [Col. 0295C] in works published against the superstition of the Gentiles.] she herself gave birth to gods; she herself introduced them into the world, through whom, or in whom, the devil is worshipped, and whose origin is displayed in their deeds. She herself made Jupiter, by countless, varied, and great crimes, “the greatest.” She [Note: [Col. 0295C] In the printed editions and the Pompignan manuscript the text was: “She herself shamefully conquered Hercules, worse than his stepmother, with the torches of lust.” In the Reims, Toulouse, and Urbino manuscripts: “She herself shamefully conquered Hercules, worse than his stepmother, in the not-false lusts”; the Vatican manuscript likewise has “worse.” This reading, though corrupted by scribal error, nevertheless furnished evidence of the genuine reading which we have inserted in the text. For from *deteriori non falis libidinum* one readily obtains *deterior in Omphalis libidine turpiter vicit*—“worse in Omphale’s lust, shamefully conquered”—with *f* for *ph*, frequent in manuscripts. This reading seemed preferable, not only because it agrees better with more and the oldest manuscripts, but because St. Zeno here seems to have intended Hercules’ passion for Omphale, which other Fathers, execrating the unchastity of pagan gods, also mention. See the Fathers cited in the preceding note. It thus also becomes clear why the bishop called unchastity worse than Hercules’ stepmother. The poets show how ill Juno, Hercules’ stepmother, treated him. But unchastity treated him far worse, since it subjected Hercules, captive to Omphale’s love, to a shameful slavery and even brought him to spin and turn the distaff, at Omphale’s command, with the hand by which he had subdued monsters—something Juno never imposed, utterly unworthy of Hercules. See Fulgentius, *Mythologies*, book II, ch. 5, p. 182; Lactantius, book I, ch. 9; Donatus, on Terence’s *Eunuch*, v. 7. We have no doubt that this is what St. Zeno had in view.] herself shamefully conquered Hercules, worse than his stepmother, in his passion for Omphale—a man whom the dreadful throng of monsters could not overcome. She herself exposed Venus, naked in every limb, [Col. 0296A] who was trying to cover herself with curved hands, [Note: [Col. 0295D] Thus from the Reims, Vatican, Pompignan, and Urbino manuscripts. The printed editions have “covering herself with joined hands”; the Toulouse codex likewise writes “to cover.” Then the Reims, Toulouse, and Urbino manuscripts have “after many things” for “after much.”] yet displaying the vice of her mind and body; after many adulteries, she prostituted her also to the spectacle of the entire world.

There is no need to go through every instance. Although these things were not worthy to be spoken, nevertheless they seemed necessary for expressing the force of unchastity, so that each person may know [Note: [Col. 0295D] Luxury pertains to idolatry: first, because unchastity is worshipped in pagan gods, whence Ambrose, *On Virgins*, book I, ch. 4, no. 16: “The sexual violation of the gods is worshipped”; and *On Widows*, ch. 14, no. 84: “They venerate the adulteries and disgraceful deeds of their gods.” Second, because shameful rites and games were instituted in honor of unchaste gods and goddesses, concerning which note 23 says enough. Third, because divine honors were granted to unchaste men and women on account of unchastity, so that people might have grounds for excusing their lusts by the example of the gods and even turning them into praise, since they could see that through them they imitated gods. Lactantius, book II, ch. 6, reports that for the same reason they worshipped avarice and desires, showing that they loved and imitated gods; Minucius sufficiently indicates the same in the *Octavius*, no. 31. See Chrysologus’s notable testimony on this subject, sermon 155. The manuscripts write *idolatriam* for *idololatriam*.] that luxury belongs to idolatry.
