She herself, I say, [Note: [Col. 0296B] It was at first doubtful whether St. Zeno here had in view the words in Treatise 15, no. 5, where he mentions those “who run about among tombs, who sacrifice banquets to the foul-smelling corpses of the dead, who through love of luxury,” and so forth. But upon closer consideration of the context of the present passage, since both before and after he speaks of the unchastity of gods set before human beings for worship and imitation, we believe that Zeno indicates that unchaste human beings—such as Jupiter, Venus, and others were said to have been—were for that reason counted among the gods by the Gentiles: their tombs were made into temples, burial mounds into altars, corpses into images, and so forth, so that by this religion they might favor unchastity and by a pleasing festival persuade the wicked that the crimes of wicked persons were both to be worshipped and imitated. Other Fathers too are recorded as having charged pagan worshippers of idols with a similar purpose, as may be found in the authors cited at note 27. Clement of Alexandria states unequivocally in the *Exhortation* that the first temples of idolatry were tombs of the dead: “Temples—for I shall not pass these over either—are indeed called temples by a splendid name; but they were tombs, that is, the tombs themselves were called temples,” etc. Prudentius, in book I *Against Symmachus*, alludes to this:

> And as many temples of gods as Rome had in the city,  
> one may count as many heroes.

[Col. 0296D] Cicero says nothing inconsistent with this when, in book I of *On Divination*, speaking of Capitoline Jupiter, he indicates that his Capitoline temple had been a tomb:

> He once sought his own tombs and temples.

Hence Nonius says: “By the authority of the ancients, a temple can also be called a tomb.” Read Arnobius, book VI *Against the Gentiles*, p. 193, where he proves that many temples are the burial places of dead bodies; Cyprian, at the beginning of *On the Vanity of Idols*; and Commodian, *Instructions* 2 and 20, who likewise report that divine honors were given to deceased human beings. The *parentalia*, later transformed into sacrifices, were libations, feasts, and other things of that kind celebrated annually in memory of the dead; sacrifices, however, concern divine worship. “Customs into sacred rites” seems to indicate a kind of worship by which the Gentiles turned unchaste customs and games into the worship of gods, concerning which note 23 says enough.] turned the tombs of the dead into temples, burial mounds into altars, corpses into images, funeral observances into sacrifices, customs into sacred rites. Thus, yes thus, she snatched the human race away from the worship of God, while by an enticing festival she persuades the wicked that the crimes of wicked persons are both to be worshipped and imitated.

[Col. 0297A] **47 IV.** Thus, contrary to God’s law and God’s justice, an unhappy, seemingly unrestricted liberty to wander outside the lawful marriage-bed into foreign lust is breathed into men; and so it also tears from modesty those women who, abandoned, compelled by passion or grief, if they do such things [Note: Four manuscripts: “commit them” (*gerant*).], think that they are either imitating or avenging themselves. Therefore the Lord says in his commandments: “Whoever dismisses his wife, except on account of adultery, makes her commit adultery.” What slippery husbands can answer here, I do not see: deceived by the unjust impunity of human laws [Note: This is not about men who sinned with another man’s wife; for such men were punished by human laws no less than the women themselves. “They punish adulteries by laws and inflict capital penalties upon those caught violating another’s marriage covenant by assault upon the marriage-bed”; thus Arnobius, *Against the Nations*, IV, p. 142. See Ammianus Marcellinus, XXVIII; Theodoret, Discourse 3 *Against the Greeks*; Cujacius, *Observations*, VI.11; Brissonius, on the Julian Law *On Adulteries*, p. 91; and Constantine’s Law 33 on that same Julian Law, where he calls persons of this kind sacrilegious violators of marriage.

Accordingly, this passage must be understood of men who, besides their wife, had relations with another woman—freeborn, a concubine, or a prostitute. Other Fathers confirm that civil laws imposed no penalty on them; like St. Zeno, they warn Christians not to suppose, because the law does not punish them short of adultery, that what is forbidden to wives is lawful for themselves. Lactantius, VI.23: “For, according to the rule of public law, only the woman who has another man is an adulteress; whereas the husband, even if he has several women, is free from the charge of adultery.” St. Augustine, *City of God*, XIV.18, states that no law of an earthly city punishes the shamefulness of prostitutes; and Jerome says, *Letter* 84 to Oceanus: “Although fornication and adultery are condemned, lust is everywhere permitted through brothels and female slaves.”

Among the Gentiles it seems to have been common to take several wives, since Tacitus observes with surprise, *On the Customs of the Germans*, 6: “Almost alone among barbarians, they are content with one wife each, with very few exceptions—men sought after for multiple marriages, not through lust but because of nobility.” Yet by “wives” he seems to mean secondary wives (*pellices*) or concubines, several of whom Romans did take. For among Romans themselves, taking more than one wife was formerly marked by the praetor with infamy, as Diocletian and Maximian attest, *Code*, II, *On Marriage*: “It is commonly evident that no one subject to Roman jurisdiction can have two wives, since such men are branded with infamy even in the praetor’s edict; a competent judge will not permit this matter to go unpunished.” See also Code XVIII, on the first Julian Law *On Adultery*.

The law that permitted concubines and prostitutes—called here and elsewhere by other Fathers—is the Julian Law *On Adulteries*, cited in Code IX.9, Laws 22 and 23. Ulpian himself noted its unfairness in the *Digest*, 48.5, Julian Law 13 *On Adulteries*, §3: “It seems grossly unfair that a husband should demand chastity from his wife which he himself does not show”; Seneca likewise insists upon this, *Letter* 94. St. Gregory Nazianzen seems to have touched on the cause of this unjust enactment in commenting on the evangelist’s words, “When Jesus had finished these sayings”: namely, he says, that men enacted it, and therefore it pursues and attacks women alone.], who, knowing true justice not even from their own will, willingly do what they do not wish to suffer. [Note: Manuscript Pomp.: *quia* for *qui*. “Profane lust” is described on the same principle as “foreign” lust shortly before: that is, lust sought outside the lawful marriage-bed. It is called theft because whatever is bestowed upon foreign women is taken away from one’s own wife. Hence shortly below: “each is bound to the other,” that is, the woman no less to the man than the man to the woman.

That husbands at that time held the mistaken opinion that, if they abstained from adultery with another man’s wife, whatever they did with unmarried women was permissible, Ambrose testifies, *On Abraham*, II.11.78: “Men believe that they sin lawfully if only they abstain from adultery; but they think that the use of prostitutes belongs, as it were, to the law of nature.” Augustine likewise indicates that a similar error prevailed in his time, though concerning concubines alone rather than prostitutes, *Sermon* 224.3: “Someone or other said: ‘She is not a prostitute whom I have; she is my concubine. Holy bishop, have you made my concubine a prostitute?’” And shortly afterward: “You say: ‘My female slave is my concubine. Do I go to another man’s wife? Do I go to a public prostitute? Is it not permitted to me?’” etc.

Something similar also prevailed in Salvian’s time. He left these words in *On the Government of God*, IV: “In comparison with the matters mentioned above, this is a kind of chastity: to be content with few wives and to restrain the reins of lust according to a fixed number of marriages. I said ‘marriage,’ because matters have reached such shamelessness that many men think their female slaves are wives; and would that, as they are regarded almost as spouses, they were at least kept as their only wives.” Caesarius likewise says similar things in Homily 16, warning that custom had become so strong that it was not even considered a sin. Men thought this was permitted to them but not to women. Human beings seem either to have introduced or confirmed this error through the impunity of civil laws. Hence St. Ambrose, like St. Zeno, warned Christians in *On Abraham*, I.4.25, that no one should flatter himself with human laws: “For every fornication,” he says, “is adultery, and what is not lawful for a woman is not lawful for a man.”], who, led away by the detestable theft of profane lust, no longer content with shameful hiding-places [Note: Shameful hiding-places were certain underground places in which prostitutes lived, which St. Ambrose, *Letter* 30 to Irenaeus, 1, calls *hypogea*: “It is luxurious to seek underground chambers . . . and therefore they seek shadowy inner rooms, either because in idleness they spend sluggish leisure beneath the earth, or finally because darkness and obscurity delight those more who think that their crimes may be covered up.”], sometimes—horror!—exhaust themselves in frenzied intercourse under the very eyes of matrons. Miserable men, they do not perceive that in such a matter, with God as judge, what is not lawful for wives is not lawful for husbands either. [Note: We have supplied “either” (*nec*) from manuscript Rem.; the printed editions have “such tablets” (*talibus tabulis*). Then we have corrected *Si igitur* (“if therefore”) to *Sic igitur* (“thus therefore”), so that the sense should not remain suspended.] As Paul the Apostle, prescribing for such persons, says: “The wife does not have authority over her own body, but the husband; likewise the husband does not have authority over his own body, but the wife” (1 Cor. 7:4).

Thus, because they are one flesh, one sacrament of the divine work; because the woman was made from her husband; because each is bound to the other; and because, consequently, by the law’s own line [Note: Among jurists, a “line” is the order of degrees of consanguinity or affinity by which persons are connected. But husband and wife, or father and mother, stand in the same line of connection under the laws themselves. Paulus, *Sentences Received*, IV, title 11: “In the first ascending degree of the line are included father and mother.”], they are joined as one, there is no doubt that whichever of the two has transgressed will be consumed by the everlasting torments of a dreadful punishment. [Note: Vatican and Toledo manuscripts: *absumpturum* (“will consume”); Remensis and Urbinas: *absumpturi* (“of one about to consume”).] Nor does it turn out with impunity for those who, without wives and freer in their love of sin, purchase for themselves uncertain and dishonourable wages of lust. [Note: The printed editions have *incestas* (“incestuous”); but manuscript Remensis has *incertas* (“uncertain”), rightly. For those are censured who, freed from wives, believed lawful not incestuous lusts indeed, but uncertain ones—those which they bought promiscuously from prostitutes for payment.] They do not perceive that whatever is outside marriage, though lawful in itself, is unhappy and unchaste; for, brothers, I do not think that anything beyond this is lawful to a Christian: he must be either continent or a husband.

**V.** I now come to examples, which are especially necessary for the matter; because what is done has more force than what is said, so that by one and the same presentation [Note: Manuscript Remensis has *suggestio*, but the marginal mark R indicates a doubtful passage. In other manuscripts and editions *suggestu* and *suggestus* are used for *suggestio*, that is, an addition or narration. Ulpian, *Digest*, I, *On the Jurisdiction of Magistrates*: “If the governor grants something upon their suggestion, or from names received from them.”] the evil of unchastity and the good of chastity may most easily be recognized.

Joseph, a Hebrew youth (Gen. 39), illustrious by birth, more illustrious in beauty, and most illustrious in uprightness of character, was younger in age among Jacob’s sons but greater in spirit. Through the impulse of his envious brothers [Col. 0299B] he was carried into Egypt and sold by them. The wife of his master began to love him more wickedly than his brothers had hated him. For when the woman burned to the marrow with the fire of insane desire, powerfully armed with arguments for her sacrilegious persuasion, she sought solitude and a secret place—the sort of place in which even unprovoked youth is often accustomed to become violent against unwilling women. [Note: Manuscript Remensis: *incitata* (“provoked”); shortly afterward, the same manuscript, as well as Urbinas and Zenonianus, has *derivari* (“to be diverted”) for *derivare*.]

But when, bursting into her intended attack, she found that neither caresses nor promises profited her, she laid hands upon him. Reversing the situation, she tried with all her strength to divert upon the youth, her own kindling fuel, the fire of his passion. He, however, in resisting, left behind the garment violently torn from him and fled naked from the pit of unchastity; yet clothed with the splendour of chastity, after his slanderous condemnation he was both freed by God and honoured. Finally, he was rightly made second in the kingdom, since he had already been a king distinguished by modesty.

**VI.** Susanna also—the pillar of matronly dignity, whose unadorned beauty was a fairer ornament of her beauty, a distinguished testimony to chastity—two elders, inflamed by one and the same monstrous passion, had begun, contrary to what was fitting, to desire unto death. [Note: *Matronatus* occurs in Apuleius, *Metamorphoses*, IV; *inaffectatus* (“unaffected,” “unpretentious”) in Quintilian XI.1 and Tertullian, *On the Pallium*, 4.] When they observed her enclosed by the wall of chastity—the true and eternal beauty indeed—in the solitude of a garden, where they remembered that Eve had been deceived by the author of her work, they took from that very circumstance their plan and began to try to ensnare her by deceit. Unless she yielded to guilt, they threatened her, as though she had been caught in adultery, with a great destruction. [Note: *Vera est* (“it is true”) is absent from manuscript Remensis, but present in Pomp., Urb., and others. Shortly afterward Remensis has “in solitude, where Eve”; Pomp. first wrote “into the solitude,” then “in the solitude, where Eve.” The same reading occurs in the Toledo, Vatican, and Zenonian codices; Urbinas has “in solitude, where Eve.” Hence the word *circumseptam* (“enclosed”) seems to have been inserted in the editions so that the words “by the wall of chastity” would not stand syntactically suspended. For this reason we retain it. Shortly afterward the editions read *culpae succumbat*; Remensis, *culpa succumbat*.]

But she—not Eve—though beset by the thought of a twofold fear, in which either her modesty must be slain or her soul, calling as witness only God, who knew her conscience, chose honourable death rather than a shameful life. She thought it better to be shown guilty before men than before God. [Note: The editions and several manuscripts have *praebere debere* (“ought to be shown”); we judge the final word excessively redundant and delete it on the authority of manuscript Pomp.] Meanwhile, those who had been lovers pressed their accusation against her; and while they craftily exaggerated their own crime, transferred to the simplicity of the entrapped woman, they thereby first condemned themselves.

Yet—horror!—their age is believed, their authority is believed; the adulterers exult, integrity is condemned. Now, now Susanna was being dragged, innocent, to punishment; now all the people swelled with rage for her blood; now even her own relatives, struck by the atrocity of this unprecedented event, groaning miserably with heads bowed, had abandoned every effort of defence. [Note: Urbinas and Pomp.: “had cast away” (*abjecerunt*).] She herself now hated delay in death, to abbreviate her shame—displeasing to all, yet pleasing to her conscience alone. [Note: *Compendium* signifies not so much economy as brevity; hence “a short route” in Pliny V.5 and “abbreviated methods of teaching” in Quintilian I.1. Thus Susanna is said to have hated delays in death for the sake of abridging shame, so that the shame which grievously distressed her might be shorter.]

Then suddenly God, who is never deceived by any cunning, was immediately present in the boy Daniel. He tore apart at once the whole scene of wickedness. [Note: The printed editions have *profictitium*; Remensis, Pomp., and Urbinas have *profectitium*, correctly. For *profectitium* means that which proceeds from elsewhere; thus the accusation laid upon Susanna proceeded from the elders’ slander. In the Toledo manuscript: “the crime, having come forth, is properly rendered, but the authors praise their own crime.” Vatican and Urbinas have similar readings. Remensis with Pomp. reads: “The external accusation is rendered proper, but the authors praise their own crime.” Shortly afterward Remensis has *impudicitiam renitentem* (“resisting unchastity”); Urbinas *enitentem*, for *impudicitia mentiente* (“with unchastity lying”). Likewise, four manuscripts have *thalamos* (“marriage-chambers”) for *thalamum* (“marriage-chamber”).] The accusation brought from outside was quickly exposed; the crime was returned upon its authors; and modesty was cleared through innocence. Thus victorious chastity brought Susanna—whom lying unchastity had dragged into public, now proved innocent and vindicated—back to her husband’s marriage-chamber amid immense triumph.

**VII.** But O how admirable you are, chastity! You do not wish to be praised otherwise than by being guarded, content with the sole adornment of a good conscience. You are happy in virgins, strong in widows, faithful in marriages, pure in priests, glorious in martyrs, bright in angels, and truly queen in all. [Note: We would prefer to read *conjugibus* (“spouses”) or the plural ablative *a conjugibus*; the form *conjugus* occurs in Pliny and others. The following sentence seems to mark the continence and celibacy of Christian priests even at that time.] You are never subject to the flesh, never subject to any law. You are born from the will, but by the good of purity you give birth to the will itself; for the will thereafter becomes your delight, when through it you gather daily thirtyfold, sixtyfold, and hundredfold fruit. You are rich in the poor, richer in the rich, and are perfected equally in all who are perfected. [Note: Both Zenonian manuscripts: *consummatis* (“in those made perfect”).] You are the honour of bodies, the treasure of souls, the foundation, summit, and fruit of all your coeval virtues. [Note: Some prefer to read *columen* (“pillar”), as above, §5, “pillar of matronly dignity.” After *nonnulla*, manuscript Remensis has *quoaequarum* for *coaequarum*. “A coeval part” occurs in Pliny VI.28.] You are the everlasting, indissoluble bond of your purpose. [Note: A “purpose” (*propositum*) is called the vow of virginity, as very often in Ambrose and other Fathers. See especially Augustine, *On the Good of Widowhood*, 9, and Leo the Great, *Letter* II to Rusticus of Narbonne, Question 15, where the purpose of virginity, even when combined with virgin dress, is distinguished from the consecration of virgins. Thus too, “to propose virginity” is the same as “to vow” in Augustine, *Sermon* 225.2.]

Through you lawful fasts are celebrated. [Note: During the time of fasting even married persons ought to observe continence, as several Fathers observed from Paul’s teaching. See Augustine, *Sermons* 208.1 and 209.3; Caesarius, Sermons 10 and 142 in the appendix to Augustine; and others. This discipline is known to have continued longer in the Church of Verona from Bishop Ratherius’s synodal letter to the priests of that church.] Through you prayers offered—before they are poured forth—are accepted. [Note: It may perhaps seem strange that prayers are said to be “presented” before they have been poured forth, since *allegare preces* is commonly taken in the same sense as “to pour forth prayers.” But here *allegare* properly means “to direct,” as Apuleius, *On the God of Socrates*, p. 61: “To whom, then, shall I direct prayers?” Thus prayers scarcely directed—that is, directed to God in the mind, or even when they begin—are immediately accepted through continence before they are poured forth.]

You are a sacrifice dear to God; you are the lawful temple of God, the sanctuary of modesty. [Note: Thus manuscript Urbinas. Toledo: “You yourself” (*tu te*); Remensis: “of you” (*tui*); printed editions with other manuscripts: “you” (*te*).] Corruption does not know how to enter into you. Through you the world is conquered, every desire is crushed, the devil is subdued, Antichrist is not feared, the Holy Spirit is brought in, Christ is glorified, God the almighty Father is propitiated. Finally, he shall happily reign in the world to come who arrives there with you. [Note: Manuscript Pomp. adds at the end: “Amen.”]

# TREATISE V. On Continence

**I.** If it seems harsh and difficult to anyone, brothers, that we speak boldly of a thing almost contrary to nature, [Note: **Treatise V.**—Virginity seemed almost contrary to nature—or, as St. John Chrysostom, cited above in Treatise IV, §3, says, beyond nature and not human. In this treatise St. Zeno chiefly undertook to commend it. How much effort he devoted to advancing this cause, and how successfully it turned out for him, may be inferred from the fact that at Verona, where perhaps he first established the faith within the walls and built a public church, as we have shown elsewhere, he also built a monastery for virgins and probably consecrated several other virgins living in private homes. We have said something about them in Dissertation III, chapter 1, §3.] let him now cease to be troubled, understanding that this is the greatest glory of Christian virtue: to tread nature itself underfoot.

But because virtue always casts pleasures into shadow, and nothing seems right to each person except what he loves—especially that which all peoples cultivate with one desire—there is no doubt that anyone who dissuades from marriage is either considered a public enemy or even judged insane. [Note: Whoever wishes to know the objections even of Christian people against those who commended virginity should consult Ambrose. Following in St. Zeno’s footsteps, when he spoke much in favour of virginity, he drew the hostility of very many upon himself, which he took pains to evade and restrain in more than one place. See especially *On Virginity*, chapter 5 and following. Among the several causes of hatred and envy which they mention, the principal one explains why, as Zeno relates, anyone dissuading from marriage was regarded as a public enemy. “I have heard some people say,” Ambrose says, chapter 7.37, “‘The world has perished, the human race has failed, marriages have been undermined.’” What our bishop adds—“or at least is judged insane”—refers either to the tenets of pagan philosophy, by which whatever Christian wisdom approved was called folly, as we saw in Treatise III, Note 2; or rather to the belief that it was madness to oppose marriage, which, he says, all peoples cultivate by universal consent, and to commend something which civil laws punished, as Note 3 to Treatise IV shows; which most people detested; and from which even parents sometimes tried to deter their daughters by threatening to withhold a dowry, as we infer from Ambrose, *On Virgins*, I.11.62.]

But I shall not fear whatever public hostility may say about me. For I do not condemn marriage, but set better things before marriage; indeed, Paul the Apostle himself urges this: “I say therefore to the unmarried and widows: it is good for them if they remain as I am. But if they cannot be continent, let them marry; for it is better to marry than to burn.” Elsewhere he says: “I say this by concession, not by command; but I wish all of you to be as I myself am” (1 Cor. 7:6–9). Therefore marriage is better because burning is worse. “All things are lawful, but not all things are beneficial.” Now, Christian, understand: choose what you will, a remedy or health. [Note: In the editions and some manuscripts, *te* (“you”) appears here; we have deleted it on the authority of manuscript Remensis.]

**II.** Finally, if it seems good, let us compare the difference between a virgin and a married woman. The married woman considers how she may please her husband; the virgin, how she may please God. The former adorns herself with foreign ornaments; [Note: Toledo, Vatican, and Urbinas manuscripts have *extraneis*; other codices and editions, *extrariis*. *Extrarium*, meaning foreign—originating and brought from another land—is found in Terence, *Phormio*, I.4.13; Suetonius, *Vespasian*, 5; and others. It is clear from this that women too obtained garments and ornaments from distant regions, a practice reproved in women not only by Clement of Alexandria, *Paedagogus*, II.10–11, with other Fathers, but also by Seneca, *Consolation to Albina*, 11, and *On Benefits*, VII.9.] the latter is far more adorned because she does not know how to be adorned from elsewhere. The former is fragrant with varied perfumes and scents; the latter, more delightful than any meadow, breathes joyfully up to heaven in the honour of her single flower. The former rejoices in children; the latter does not fear bereavement of children. The former is nourished by their blossoming caresses and daily delights in their growing maturity; the latter, sickened by the burden of nine months, does not carry its weight; amid an uncertain birth she does not groan over the safety of mother and child, nor is she tormented by the care of every moment of varied anxiety.

**III.** But someone will say: “Mary too was a virgin, married, and bore a child.” Let someone be such a one, and I yield. But she was a virgin after marriage, a virgin after conception, a virgin after bearing a son. [Note: This very concise testimony to Mary’s virginity, repeated in Book II, Treatise 8, is of great importance, since no Father older than Zeno has been found to use a formula so concise and now so famous. It seems to have been expressly said against certain persons who denied the Virgin Mary’s virginity. Around this same time St. Hilary, commenting on Matthew 1.3, notes that many irreligious persons, quite alien to spiritual teaching, had taken occasion from the words “before they came together,” etc., shamefully to hold opinions about Mary. Epiphanius also speaks of some such persons, *Heresies* 78.7, though he may have meant Helvidius and Jovinian, who lived in Zeno’s age. Yet in Zeno’s own time Eunomius, on the feast of Theophany, with Eudoxius the Arian bishop neither dissenting nor perhaps even without commanding it, publicly declared that Mary was known by Joseph after the birth of the divine Word, as Philostorgius relates in excerpts made by Photius, VI.2, under the year 361.]

Finally, if anything were better than virginity, the Son of God could have bestowed that rather upon his mother, whom he granted should shine with the honour of divine virginity. [Note: Pomp., Zen., Vatican manuscripts and the Venetian edition: *praestitit* (“granted”). For *divinae*, Pomp., Zen., Vatican, and Urbinas have *redivivae*; Venetian edition, *re divine*.] Therefore, remaining a virgin in the condition in which you were born, glory in it; and, subject to no law, preserve the flower of holy modesty, the treasure of faith. Be holy in body and spirit. Extinguish with love of Christ the fire of the flesh. I pass over the glory of the resurrection, which you already claim here, in which, as the Lord says, “They neither marry nor are given in marriage, but are as angels” (Matt. 22:30). [Note: Venetian edition: *nubent* (“marry”); and later *erunt* (“will be”) for “angels of God.”] You will gain a great benefit if, free, you live for God in pure morals and are not the slave of a man. [Note: “Women are subject to their husbands as to the Lord,” Eph. 5:22.]

**IV.** But you, widow, why do you desire second marriages when you see the Apostle restraining first ones? [Note: We have explained and defended more fully in Dissertation II, chapter 7, St. Zeno’s view of second marriages, consonant with the ancient Fathers and capable of being regarded as a mark of antiquity. Manuscript Toledo has *temptare* (“to test”) for *temperare* (“to restrain”).] These are his words: “The time is shortened. It remains that those who have wives should be as though they had none, for the form of this world is passing away” (1 Cor. 7:29, 31). But since this apostolic decree has been operative for nearly four hundred years, [Note: Thus all manuscripts and the first edition; only the Verona edition inserted “two hundred,” which passed into later editions. We have fully explained and rejected the rationale of this arbitrary emendation in Dissertation I, chapter 2, §1.] or more, in a time when human beings were more long-lived and Christians very rare, why should I now, when the world itself has become almost wholly Christian and human vitality has been worn down by the world’s aging, blunt the edge of truth with flattering words and fail fully to declare with what perfection of observance the worship of God ought to be kept? [Note: “World” may mean the whole Roman Empire, which was commonly called “the world,” as is clear from many witnesses, especially Firmicus, who expressly says so, and the ancient author of *On the Deaths of the Persecutors*, where “the world” frequently denotes the Roman Empire. Nepos, *Life of Atticus*, 25, speaking of Caesar and Antony: “Each wished to be leader not only of the city of Rome but of the world.” Virgil, *Eclogues* I.67: “Britons divided from the whole world.” Spartianus, *Hadrian*, p. 3: “Having obtained the empire . . . he devoted himself to maintaining peace throughout the world.” See Ovid, *Tristia*, I.4.69; Tacitus, *On the Customs of the Germans*, 1; Ambrose, *Letter* 17.5; Symmachus, *Relation* 9; and Zeno’s Treatise 10 of this Book I, §5. Hence Minucius, §12, did not hesitate to affirm that the Romans had spread throughout the whole world.]

For it is written especially in Solomon: “Even if children are multiplied, do not delight in them if the fear of the Lord is not with them; do not rejoice over their lives. For one who fears God is better than a thousand impious children” (Ecclus. 16:1–3). Since this is so, come then, widow: you often hurry to marry as does an innocent virgin. Answer one who asks you: have you lost a good husband or a bad one? If a bad one, and you desire marriage, you deserve to be afflicted by a worse. If a good one, preserve the seal of fidelity: he to whom you give testimony does not deserve to suffer injury.

Where is he for whom, when you mutually desired one another, the first day of marriage seemed slower than all the rest? Where are the festivals of precious virginity, sweet to both, its death? [Note: Venetian edition: *utriusque* (“of both”), and later *separante* for *superante*. Vatican has *occasio* for *occisio*; Remensis, *occiosio*.] Where is the love that, in a marriage equal and united, when one of the two surpasses the other, does not die? Are you not the woman who washed your husband’s laid-out body with tears, wiped it with kisses, veiled it at the cost of your hair, your cheeks torn, your breasts disfigured by bruising, covered more with filthy dust than with clothing? [Note: The custom of laying out corpses is indicated by Virgil, *Aeneid* VI: “Then they lay the mourned limbs upon a bier”; Servius comments: “Bodies were kept for eight days,” etc. Ovid, *Tristia* III, uses *depositum* (“laid down”) for *expositum* (“laid out”): “There will be no one to weep for me when I am laid out.” Pagans laid bodies in the entrance hall of a house, as may be inferred from Lucian, *On Mourning* (*περὶ πένθους*), Dio on the death of Livia, and Suetonius, *Augustus*, 100. Christian bodies also seem to have been laid out in churches. Jerome says of Paula’s body in her epitaph: “She was laid in the middle of the church of the Saviour’s cave.” That women there washed their husbands’ bodies with tears may be inferred from Treatise 16, §5, where the author finely recalls these actions done by women while priests performed the customary divine rites in order to commend the dead person’s soul to God; this must indeed have occurred in church. For *lavisti* (“you washed”), found in all manuscripts and the Venetian edition, the printed editions have *lavasti*. The statement that women covered a laid-out body with hair cut off at their own loss—repeated in Treatise 16, §5—describes a funeral custom common among Greeks and Romans. Women cut off their hair and cast it upon the corpse, as is clear from Homer, Herodian, Plutarch, and others cited by Everardus Feithius, *Homeric Antiquities*, I.13. The other things enumerated here and in Treatise 16 were likewise customary; it is therefore not surprising that women complying with custom rather than love could feign all of them.]

Are you not she who, now [Note: On *nunc* (“now”) used for a past time scarcely elapsed, see Treatise 2, Note 17. Below, the editions after Verona incorrectly have *elusis* for *clusis*. We have supplied “among relatives” from manuscript Pomp.; it signifies that wives, during their husbands’ funerals, often fell to the ground because their spirit failed, so that relatives present did not know for whom the funeral rites and tears were more due. Venetian edition has *morituro* (“the one about to die”) for *morienti* (“the dying one”).] rending heaven itself with your howls, cried that after such a husband you could not live for a moment? Now, your groans shut in by grief, often dead in spirit among your relatives, your limbs collapsing to the ground, you made the funeral rites uncertain: for whom should they offer more tears, the dead man or the dying woman? After this, if you wish to marry, you have lied in all those things.

What is this? Behold, you return again to the arts of seduction; you borrow from the cosmetic-box a colour you had condemned only a little before. Behold, you indulgently arrange your hair; you exchange the powder of mourning for perfumed powder; you confine your tears in stibium; [Note: *Stibium*, mentioned by Pliny, XXXIII.6.34, is a kind of mineral—called “black powder” by Tertullian, *On Women’s Dress*, and “alabaster” by others. Its Greek name derives from *στίβω* or *στείβω*, “I tighten,” because it has an astringent power. Women used it in colouring the face and polishing—or, as Tertullian says in *On Women’s Adornment*, lengthening—the eyes. See Georgius Agricola, *On the Nature of Fossils*, X.11. St. Zeno rightly declares that women’s tears are enclosed in stibium, with which the eyes are cleansed. Commodianus similarly reproaches widows for using stibium, *Instructions* 59.7.] you bind with adornment the neck which you had vowed to the noose; [Note: This refers to the imprecations by which widows in grief often pray for death and hanging for themselves.] from the mirror you seek oracles concerning how conveniently you may ensnare a suitor. [Note: Here *petitor* means one who seeks a widow as wife.] Whatever you do, you will no longer be a virgin; yet I know one thing: whoever changes both appearance and character for another’s sake differs little from a monstrosity.

**V.** But you say: “The heat of tender age compels me.” I believe you. Look: you have married. To say nothing of the frailty of humanity and of other misfortunes, suppose that on the next day some necessity carries off your husband and keeps him exiled far from you for ten years or more, as often happens. What will you do? Will you keep faith for his return, or seek elsewhere a remedy for your passion? If you promise faithfulness, you undoubtedly deceive, since the declaration of your impatience already binds you. [Note: Manuscript Pomp.: *polliceare* (“you promise”). Near the end of the section we write *quale libet* (“whatever it may be”) for *quale velit* (“whatever it may wish”); perhaps *libet* was written and became *velit*. *Quale libet* means “whatever sort it may be.” Cicero, *On the Nature of the Gods*, II.37.]

But if you are going to seek a remedy, there is no doubt that this alone is it: restrain your flames by contemplating the sword of marriage. Believe me: desire has no place where patience rules, where one lives soberly, where death is feared. Therefore transfer this fidelity and this fear—what is truer and more just—to God; and whatever it may be, that fire will suddenly be extinguished.

VI. But I linger over matters that are almost sound, as though the offenses that are truly to be execrated had already been corrected.

[Note: Second marriages are called “almost sound” in comparison with third, fourth, and further marriages, which seemed accursed to the ancients; on this see more in Dissertation II, chapter 7.]

I am ashamed to say, among a serious people, old women are often seen newly married, whose marriages are almost more numerous than their birthdays.

[Note: The Pompeian manuscript corrects “marriages” in the margin. A little later the Reims manuscript has *plus* for *plures*.] They are invited not to marry but to sleep; they are nearer the grave than the marriage-bed. They themselves perish and, by their detestable example, compel young girls also to perish.

[Note: “They perish” is said not of an actual fault, but of the loss of continence incurred by widows who marry repeatedly; thus they compel virgin girls by their example to perish, that is, to lose their virginity.]

[Col. 0306B] What son could love such women? What husband? They confuse the claims of blood, erase the deserts of husbands, flatter the living, sigh after the dead, and now hate old, now new, sons and husbands alike. On the other hand, let them themselves consider what it means that, in unions so solemn, it often happens that they have neither children nor husbands.

[Note: Toledo manuscript: “what they are,” for “what it is,” in “in unions so solemn.” A little later the Reims manuscript has *contigit* for *contingit*; and shortly afterward, with the Venetian edition, *fiunt una* for *sunt una*.]

The case is the same with husbands, to whom it is superfluous to say anything, since, if wife and husband are one flesh, there is no doubt that what one hears belongs to both.

What am I to do? Where am I to turn? I do not know what I should preach to the Gentiles in exhortations concerning the worship of God, which is divine and true. Shall I commend the blessedness of virginity? But they have their own virgins; and, even if they are not happy, they nevertheless have them. 58

[Note: Tertullian mentions not only Vestals but also other Gentile virgins in *Exhortation to Chastity*, chapter 13: “I have known virgins of Vesta and Juno at a town of Achaea, and of Apollo at Delphi, and of Minerva and Diana in certain places.” He repeats similar remarks in *To His Wife*, book I, chapter 6. Pausanias, book III, chapter 16, mentions virgins who were priestesses of Hilaria and Phoebe and were called Leucippides. Symmachus, prefect of the City, mentions Vestals still flourishing in his time, in his memorial addressed to Valentinian, Theodosius, and Arcadius, no. 11; so too Saint Ambrose, *On Virginity*, book I, chapter 4, and Letter 18, no. 11.]

But if I urge them toward the glorious struggle and palm of widowhood, perhaps they will mock us because our holy virgins and widows labor for the great reward of immortality, whereas theirs labor without recompense. Yet this alone is true—the point in which we surpass them—that Christian women marry more often because of their holiness. Add, concerning the Gentiles, a thing that cannot be said without great pain or groaning.

[Note: Marriages of Christian women with pagan men have always been rejected in the Church, especially because of the danger touched on here by Zeno. Tertullian’s entire second book *To His Wife* aims to persuade his wife, should she after his death find it extremely difficult to abstain from a second marriage, at least to beware of marrying a Gentile. There he presses arguments quite similar to those which our author expresses more concisely, but no less forcefully and elegantly. See Ambrose, *On Abraham*, book I, chapter 9, no. 84, and Letter 19 to Vigilius, whom, when he sought instruction as bishop of Trent, Ambrose first warned to see that no believing woman should be joined in marriage with an unbeliever. See more in Dissertation II, chapter 7.]

VII. For what voice, what rebuke, could suitably convict women who endow their disgrace with sacrilege, assign the members of Christ to the slaves of demons, open God’s temple to the profane, strip even the shrines themselves bare, mingle sacred things, rejoice in darkness after losing the light, and possess temples rather than homes?

[Note: This whole period seems to envisage the celebration of marriage with an unbeliever. As the members of Christ—that is, the woman’s body—are assigned to the slaves of demons—that is, pagan husbands—and the temple of God is opened to profane persons, Zeno understands the Christian woman herself. Cyprian likewise called her members a temple of God in his treatise *On the Dress of Virgins*. Hence Saint Zeno himself, book II, tract 42, using Paul’s celebrated expression, calls baptized persons “temples of God,” whom, while they were Gentiles, he had called shrines of idolatry: “Whom you knew as a shrine of idolatry, rejoice to know as a temple of God.” Thus we have no doubt that “shrines,” by a certain gradation, refer to the same thing. But what Zeno meant by “sacred things mingled” is unknown, unless perhaps he refers to rites performed, according to pagan custom, on the first day of marriage after idols brought by the pagan husband had been placed in the newly married woman’s chamber; in this way the house might be said to have been changed into a temple. Perhaps private houses could also be called temples because pagan homes contained idols honored with divine worship. For, as Tertullian says, *To His Wife*, book II, chapter 6: “The handmaid of God dwells with alien Lares, and among them, amid every honor paid to demons and every royal festival, at the beginning of the year and at the beginning of the month, she will be disturbed by the scent of incense and will go forth from a door garlanded with laurel and lit with lamps.” To these profane rites of her husband, the Christian woman ought to oppose others belonging to her own religion: namely, sacred prayers to God and perhaps also reception of the Eucharist, which Christians brought home and kept there, as will appear from Note 29. More probably, however, Paul’s words in 2 Corinthians 6:14 are intended here, words which most Fathers interpret as the Apostle’s prohibition of marriages with unbelievers: “Do not be yoked together with unbelievers. For what participation has righteousness with iniquity? Or what fellowship has light with darkness? What agreement has Christ with Belial? Or what portion has a believer with an unbeliever? What concord has the temple of God with idols? For you are the temple of the living God.”]

[Col. 0308A] Such women are rightly slaughtered: ungrateful for Christ’s benefits, they voluntarily return to the death from which they had escaped. Since the devil always lies in wait for those who do not seek him, consider what he does when he is invited. All entrances for doing harm are opened to him; without battle, without any labor, they offer him victory. For he will not attempt to bring under his dominion those who have desired to be his slave.

Finally, Christian believer, the things done in the house—and even in the temples themselves—cannot occur without you, 59 because you are an unhappy wife if you do not know what happens in your home; and certainly more unhappy if you do know.

VIII. Let us suppose, as often happens, that a day appointed for observance by two different religions falls at the same time: you must go to church, he to the temples.

[Note: From this it may be inferred that in Zeno’s age the buildings of idols were properly called *templa*, “temples,” while Christian sacred buildings were properly called *ecclesiae*, “churches”; the latter were not called temples, nor the former churches. I first find Christian churches called temples in Ambrose, Letter 20, no. 2, as Gothofredus observed in his notes on the title *On Pagans*, near the end, p. 253. One older testimony from Saint Hilary is nevertheless available, in Psalm 126, no. 3, where he says: “Our custom has been to call gatherings of churches, or those then of the Temple which the enclosure of buildings shuts in for the hidden worship of the sacraments, either the house of God or a temple.” These words may seem to signify that, even in Hilary’s time, when he wrote this commentary on the Psalms near the end of his life, shortly before A.D. 367, the usage had become customary by which ecclesiastical buildings were called either houses of God or temples. Yet someone might judge that an error underlies this passage, and that *vel templum* (“or a temple”) is a gloss that has crept from the margin into the text. Even if this does not please, the full text, if considered, will show that this is not its sense. It is written there: “Our custom has been to call gatherings of churches, or those then of the Temple, which the enclosure of buildings shuts in for the hidden worship of the sacraments, either the house of God, or a temple.” In particular, one should note in the first clause the particle *tum* (“then”), prefixed to the word *templi* (“of the Temple”). The discussion there concerns the building of Solomon’s Temple, the subject of that Psalm, and “or those then of the Temple” refers to that single building. If, with the Zenonian manuscripts to be mentioned in the Appendix—for that Hilary tract will be given there—you think *tum* should be omitted, no difficulty remains. For, intending to encompass all buildings of either Old or New Testament, Hilary could have understood by “churches” Christian buildings, which he notes were called houses of God; while by “temple” he meant Solomon’s building, which, as in our own time, is customarily called by the single name “temple,” not “church.” Thus in Hilary’s age that one alone, among all buildings dedicated to the true God, was customarily called a temple. Hence Saint Zeno, who never calls Christian sacred buildings temples, clearly designates Solomon’s building by that name in Sermon 14, no. 1. Anyone therefore who transfers this usage in Hilary to Christian assemblies is gravely mistaken. It is well known how much the early Christians shrank from applying the designation “temple” to their own congregations. They saw that the magnificent edifices of idols, to which carnal people paid the greatest reverence, were called temples. They therefore said such structures were necessary for persons of that sort, not for themselves, who bore the living temple of God within themselves, as they often repeated from the Apostle Paul. And just as during the heat of persecutions not a few declared that they had no temples—on which see Note 6 to Tract 14—so later they gave this name only to the buildings of idols, or also to Solomon’s structure, which was necessary to the carnal people of the Jews and was extolled as supremely magnificent because of the costliness of its construction and materials. Moreover, when Christians named their own assemblies, they called them *ecclesiae*, “churches,” to indicate rather the faithful themselves who gathered than the place in which they gathered; or, if they intended the place itself, they called it a house of prayer or, with Zeno in Tract 14, no. 1, a place of prayer. These matters had to be stated at greater length, not merely to elucidate the passage under notice, but also to explain other points that will prove useful or necessary for understanding others.]

By what manner will each of you arrange his own sacrifice? 60 At what expense? With what vessels? Or with what ministers? But if these things are done separately, it is of no use: for in going out from one place and returning to one place, they become one, if not by confusion, then by error. What of the fact that his sacrifice is public and yours secret?

[Note: He calls it “secret,” because, under the discipline of secrecy, the sacrifice—that is, the mystery of the Eucharist—had to be carefully concealed not only from pagans but even from catechumens.]

His may be handled freely by anyone; yours cannot be seen without sacrilege even by Christians themselves who are not consecrated.

[Note: The printed editions read *consecrati*; we have corrected this from the Pompeian manuscript and two Zenonian manuscripts. Those who had received baptism were called “consecrated.” Thus the “not consecrated” are catechumens, who were also called “not initiated” by another formula. Under the aforementioned discipline of secrecy, it was so carefully guarded that they should not set eyes upon the Eucharistic sacrament that Satyrus, brother of Saint Ambrose, still a catechumen, when in danger in a shipwreck begged initiated persons to give him the Eucharist, received it wrapped in a cloth, lest he cast curious eyes upon the mysteries. This is recorded by Ambrose, *On the Death of Satyrus*, book I, no. 43. Tillemont, Note 6 on article 7, “On the Persecution of Valerian,” title IV, observing that Zeno calls these “not consecrated” persons Christians, judges that baptized Christians, not catechumens, are meant here, since catechumens, unless—as he interprets—they were consecrated into the clergy, were not allowed to see the sacrifice; for in the West a veil was hung to prevent laypeople from looking upon the sacred mysteries. So he says. But that “sacrifice” here means the sacrament of the Eucharist, not the sacrifice of Masses—which misled Tillemont—will be clear from the following note. Moreover, that catechumens too were called “consecrated” appears from some witnesses; among them see Paschasinus of Lilybaeum, Letter to Leo, chapter 3, where, in referring to catechumens, he uses this name twice. We do not deny that those initiated by baptism were generally called Christians, and Augustine accordingly contrasts catechumens with them in Tractate 2 on John, chapter 3, no. 4: “Catechumens do not know what Christians receive.” But catechumens too were sometimes called Christians, especially in Zeno’s age, because they believed in Christ. This is evident from the Theodosian Code, book XVI, title 7, law 2 of Theodosius the Elder, A.D. 383, and from other examples in which Constantine and Valentinian the Younger, although catechumens, are nevertheless called Christian emperors. This point was especially relevant to Zeno, who calls all believers Christians insofar as they are contrasted with unbelievers; catechumens were certainly included in that number. That only these, and not baptized persons, were forbidden to behold the Eucharistic sacrament is evident even from the fact that baptized persons received it openly in church and also brought it home, in order to communicate themselves with it when necessary; this could not be done without seeing it.]

Finally, detestable is the condition of life in which a wife is not permitted to do what pleases her husband; in which you make it your rule that he himself must first have done whatever he permits you to do, because he allows you to do nothing except what he has determined. If it is not done, or if what has been done displeases him, then the whole house will roar with quarrels, God will be blasphemed, and perhaps, seizing your sacrifice itself, he will batter your breast with it and disfigure your face—rendering, at times, 61 even a benefit when he orders you not to come to church.

[Note: “Sacrifice” here plainly means the Eucharistic sacrament—as it also does in Tract 15, no. 5—which it was customary to bring home, not only in the first centuries of the Church when persecutions raged, but in Zeno’s own age, indeed even somewhat later, as is clear from Basil, Letter 289 to Caesarius, and Jerome, Letter 48 to Pammachius. It is worth quoting the words of an author contemporary with Basil: “Each of the laity also generally has communion in his own home, and communicates himself whenever he wishes.” Also memorable is what we learn from Ambrose, *On the Death of Satyrus*, book I, no. 43: Satyrus, then a catechumen, when in danger of shipwreck requested from those whom he knew to be initiated that divine sacrament of the faithful, not to cast curious eyes upon the mysteries, but to obtain help for his faith. He had it tied in a cloth and wrapped the cloth around his neck; then he leapt into the sea and escaped unharmed. From this it is clear that certain baptized companions of Satyrus had brought the Eucharist with them even on a sea voyage, so that this was known even to Satyrus, although he was a catechumen. Perhaps the added statement of Zeno, “he will batter your breast with your sacrifice,” may occasion difficulty. But apart from the possibility that the bread was rather thick and might inflict a blow, we shall infer from Tract 14, Note 18, that it was kept in a wooden container and brought home.]

But it is much worse if you please your husband; for you cannot please a sacrilegious man without sacrilege yourself. To state the matter briefly: upon returning from the temple, he will necessarily tell you, if you ask, what answers the gods gave him concerning the safety of you both or their own unanimity. If they are frightening, terror-stricken, perhaps while he is absent you will offer to them unlawful vows—something that many worse Eves, not disciples but teachers, have done even under believing husbands. For Eve was deceived; these women have voluntarily given themselves to the devil. But if the answers are peaceful and favorable, you will certainly rejoice, and, as an obedient wife in return for so great a message, if you do not initiate peace, you will not refuse it.

IX. What are you doing, unhappy woman? Why, madwoman, do you rejoice? This is not peace for you but war; not a kiss but poison.

[Note: Toledo manuscript: “That is not peace for you.”]

O monstrous wickedness! You embrace members still smoking from the burnt offering, and with your flesh wipe away the sweat—the vapor—of filthy altars; you jest, caress, and comply. If some solemn mystery has perhaps been received or brought back by a *fanaticus*, 62 you yourself receive it, put it away, and guard it.

[Note: The term is frequent in Cicero and other authors and usually means, figuratively, either a pyre or a tomb; properly, however, it denotes the very body which, before burial, was formerly customarily burned—the body itself, now burned. It is called *bustum*, says Festus, as though “well burned” (*bene ustum*). In this sense *bustum* here means a victim offered and burned to idols. For the same reason Ambrose similarly said, “smoke from the burnt offering,” in Letter 17 to Valentinian, no. 9, a passage worth quoting to confirm the meaning: “If today some pagan emperor—God forbid—were to erect an altar to images and compel Christians to gather there, to be present while sacrifices were made, so that ash and altar, the cinder from sacrilege, and smoke from the burnt offering might fill the breath and mouths of the faithful,” etc.]

[Note: The scholiast on Horace’s *Art of Poetry*, p. 638: “*Fanatici* are those driven by a frenzied spirit and afflicted with madness. They are so called metaphorically; properly, *fanaticus* derives from *fanum*, ‘temple,’ as *aridus* from *ara*, ‘altar,’ and denotes a class of priests who, aroused by a certain divine frenzy, as the Gentiles supposed, uttered prophetic answers from the temples of the gods.” Of these Juvenal says, *Satires* 4.123: “But as a priest, struck by your gadfly, Bellona, prophesies”; and Prudentius: “The panting temple-priest does not foam as he utters fates published in Sibylline books.” They are mentioned by Cicero, *For His House*, Arnobius, book I, p. 13, and many others. In the glosses *fanaticus* is rendered ἱερατικὸς ἱερόδουλος, “a priestly temple-servant.” Here, however, we understand anyone to be called *fanaticus* who, returning from temples, brought or reported something from them, especially one who repeated priestly responses—for which reason such persons were called *fanatici*—as was evidently the man of whom Saint Zeno speaks. Saint Augustine indeed calls *fanatici*, in Psalm 40, no. 1, p. 345, those pagans who answered one another, as though from an oracle, concerning the ruin of Christians.]

[Col. 0311A] Moreover, you take food from the same dish and, lapping with your lips, drain the remainder of the cup offered to you; you inaugurate, as it were, the first-fruits of a future draught, and willingly conceive through your husband the whole spirit of wickedness. Unhappy woman, more now remains in you than remained in the temple.

[Note: He does not condemn the mere eating of food with an unbelieving spouse, but eating food brought home by the husband from an idol-sacrifice, and other superstitious practices of this kind, customarily observed in food and drink on fixed days, in which a Christian woman could not participate without the stain of idolatry. See more on these matters in Tertullian’s work *On Idolatry*.]

But if you keep and restrain yourself, he will suppose that this is done not from love of divine worship but from desire for some other man, as an insult to himself; he will turn the virtue of chastity and self-restraint into an accusation. For what evil would a man not suspect or bring about, when he serves cruel gods—adulterous gods?

[Note: Tertullian observes in *To His Wife*, book II, chapter 5, that pagan husbands, if they saw Christian wives practicing restraint and concealing their rites, became suspicious that the women were practicing magic or plotting to prepare poison for them. Zeno mentions adulterous and cruel gods because a man who worships gods guilty of adultery and murder may readily suspect his wife of adulterous love or of plotting murder against himself.]

Therefore henceforth flee, virgin; flee, widow, marriages of this kind. No excuse at all is available to you. If you cannot remain continent, at least do not multiply your marriages, lest on the day of resurrection, among so many husbands, you be unable to recognize whose wife you were. Do not be sacrilegious; do not betray the law. Why marry a profane man when you can marry a Christian?

[Note: Here *fenerare* means “to multiply,” that is, to enter into several marriages. Similarly Ambrose, *On Duties*, book II, chapter 6, no. 40, used *fenerati proventus*, “increased returns,” for “multiplied returns.”]

63. TRACT VI. On Patience.

[Note: TRACT VI.—Casaubon calls this tract very weighty in his commentary on Spartian’s *Severus*, p. 122a. In the first Venetian edition it is entitled “On the Praises of Patience and the Evils of Impatience.” The beginning and end of this tract are inserted in the Life of Saint Zeno written by an ancient monk of the Zenonian monastery at Verona, published by Marquis Scipio Maffei among the documents appended to his *Diplomatic History*, published in 1727. From this Life we have adopted several not insignificant variant readings, which will be noted in their places.]

I. Although the blessed life is sought through diverse virtues, and humanity, burning with desire for it, sighs for it at every moment, yet all are carried by one and the same agreement, as it were, into a harbor of patience, without which nothing can be heard, understood, learned, or taught. For it alone is that to which absolutely everything looks; since there is no doubt that hope, faith, justice, humility, chastity, integrity, harmony, love, all arts and all virtues, and even the elements themselves, cannot endure without its training or restraint.

[Note: We corrected the text from the Life, since it had read *cupidinem*, “desire.” Pompeian manuscript: *cupiditate*, “with desire.”]

[Note: In the printed editions and manuscripts, *ejus, quod* (“of it, which”) occurs here; on the authority of the Life we have moved it to the phrase *sine ejus eruditione*, “without its training.”]

It is always mature, humble, careful, wise, provident, content with every necessity, tranquil amid every storm of disturbances.

[Note: The Life has *patientia matura*, “mature patience”; we do not know whether the writer of the Life inserted that term to make the sense easier, since it is certainly unnecessary.]

It does not know how to cloud its serenity with storms.

[Note: Pompeian manuscript corrects to *nobis turbulentare*; Zenonian manuscript and Venetian edition: *nobilis turbulentare*.]

It knows no repentance; it does not know what contention is; it either avoids or endures every injury.

[Note: Printed editions have *alteratio*, “alteration”; the manuscripts, the Life, and a marginal correction in the Veronese edition have *altercatio*, “contention,” a word which we have judged should be inserted in the text.]

It is uncertain whether it should be judged incapable of suffering, since, after suffering something, it is found as though it had suffered nothing. Finally, brothers, it is impossible to estimate the power of that virtue whose victory consists in being conquered. No force of place turns it aside; neither labor, hunger, nakedness, persecution, fear, danger, death, torments more grievous than death itself, power, ambition, nor prosperity. It remains always unmoved, strongly balanced by a lofty and divine moderation, calming all stirrings of the mind by gentle self-command; 64 and, so that it may overcome all things without great difficulty, it first overcomes itself.

[Note: Reims, Toledo, and Vatican manuscripts: *liberata*, “freed”; and, for *permotiones*, “stirrings,” the Pompeian manuscript has *promotiones*, “movements.”]

[Note: Here *non magnopere* is the same as *non magno opere*, as the Zenonian manuscript reads: “not with great effort,” that is, easily. Zeno uses it elsewhere in that sense, just as he uses *magnopere* for *magno opere*, “with great effort or industry,” in Tract 8, no. 2.]

II. Virtues could not be virtues, the enduring order of the elements could not endure, nor could the seasons travel in their customary, connected cycle into their appointed returns, unless patience, like a certain watchful mother, guarded the discipline and revolution of things.

[Note: Pompeian manuscript corrects *status*, “order.”]

The sun, although with wondrous swiftness it illumines the alternating bounds of the world, nevertheless never outruns its beloved and modest dawn. Indeed—and this is greater—it could not divide itself evenly into the twelve, not spaces but moments, of the hours, if impatience pressed its course.

[Note: Veronese edition and manuscripts: *aequabiliter se*; Venetian edition: *aequabili se*. Perhaps one should read simply *aequabiliter*, “evenly,” so that *partiri* is taken passively, as Cicero uses it in *On the Orator*, book III, chapter 30. Although among the ancients *dies*, “day,” taken broadly, comprised the space of twenty-four hours, taken strictly for the time from sunrise to sunset it contained only twelve equal hours. For it was ancient custom to divide days and nights, in summer as in winter, into twelve hours so equal that summer daytime hours were longer and winter daytime hours shorter; conversely, nighttime hours were shorter in summer and longer in winter. Yet equality was always maintained among the hours of the same day or night. See Censorinus, *On the Birthday*, chapter 18.]

Likewise the moon, which seems to some to wander in its monthly course, neither prematurely adds to nor subtracts from the regular fires of its appointed age. What else does this show than that it serves the moderation of its Maker through the most skillful discipline of distinguished patience? The sea too, when provoked by winds and enraged, though in reciprocal alternation its surges now strike heaven and now seek the earth, armed on every side with glassy mountains and raging in its whole body with violent masses of furious waves—nevertheless, at the pale return of its farthest billows, as though recognizing and avoiding violation of the earth’s right, it breaks against itself in marvelous patience and is restrained by the very waves by which it is driven.

This patience bestows both abundance and beauty upon sprouting meadows, golden harvests, winding vines, and half-pale olive trees, because it does not allow the fruit of each season, in raw and premature birth, to be hastened to the injury of another.

[Note: The Pompeian and Zenonian manuscripts read *patientia*, “patience”; the other codices and printed editions read *impatientia*, “impatience.” Either contrary ablative can suit the sense, if *impatientia* is referred to the verb *praecipitare*, “to hasten,” and *patientia* to *non sinit*, “does not permit.” Yet we have retained the reading of the more numerous and superior manuscripts. *Contumelia*, “injury,” is said not so much of words as of deeds; hence one reads not only “to utter an insult” but also “to commit an insult.” Here, therefore, “injury to another” means the harm which unripe fruits usually cause those who eat them, unless patience restrains them from eating.]

What of the beautiful exchanges and lettered communications of different birds? What of cranes in lofty flight through the air? What of the innumerable wedge-shaped formations of unlike fishes, ranked by age and each with their own leaders? Do they not, as they obey the invitation of the seasons, and in the splendid course of their customary oarsman either furrow the waters or divide the air, come patiently and depart patiently? 65

[Note: Veronese edition: *littoreaque*, “and shorely”; Venetian edition: *littorataque*, “and shore-marked.” Better, from the manuscripts, *litterataque*, “and lettered” (the Toledo and Urbino manuscripts, through a copyist’s error, have *litterat aeque*), for singing birds, while passing over, carry on certain lettered communications. In the manuscripts and Venetian edition *commertia* is written with *l*; and for *arduis volatibus*, “lofty flights,” the Reims manuscript has *arduus volatilibus*, while the Pompeian manuscript and Venetian edition have *arduis volatilibus*.]

[Note: *Gradatus* in Pliny, book XIII, chapter 4, means arranged in the form of steps. Certain fishes, therefore, like cranes, follow a leader and pass from one place to another in a wedge formation according to stages of age and the succession of seasons.]

III. Man alone is headlong; man alone is impatient. Daily he delights in wicked changeability, pursues variety, judges himself miserable if he is himself, and does not understand that it is akin to madness for the mind not to remain in its own condition.

[Note: We restored *animum*, “mind,” from the manuscripts and the Venetian edition. Somewhat later the Zenonian manuscript reads *factus improvidus*, “made improvident,” for *actus improvidus*, “improvidently driven.” Below, one might prefer *totus concitus* or *concitatus*, “wholly agitated,” to *totus concitans*; or perhaps “setting all things in motion,” taking *totum* to mean “everything,” as is frequent in this author.]

For what is impatience except a slippery mind, always assaulting itself by frequent and rapid agitations; a faithless spirit, imprudently driven even against itself, unstable, blind, incautious, inconstant, wholly rushing toward ruin; a thing without substance, a business without a person; quick to attempt everything, quick to disturb everything in a moment; mother of crimes, mistress of curiosity, sharpness of recklessness, author and likewise mistress of abominable evils? For from the very beginning of the world it broke forth, so that death might slaughter—and still slaughters—the salvation of humankind from its cradle.

Thus Adam, when he had still been placed in the citadel of paradise and possessed the sovereignty of the blessed world, most blessed indeed, lived happy and indestructible as long as he kept the commands of the royal decree. But when, by baleful consent, he borrowed impatience from the slippery seductiveness of the envious serpent and wickedly tasted the sweet fruit of the sacred tree, he found tears, pains and groans, acquired for himself thorns and thistles, and, distressed at last by sweat, left to his descendants the inheritance of undigested death, which soon produced murder.

[Note: Pompeian manuscript: “and the slippery serpent.” Lower down, four manuscripts and the Venetian edition read *mox ut peperit*, “as soon as it produced,” for *mox peperit*, “soon produced.”]

Indeed, there was no delay. Envious and impatient of his brother’s offering, Cain thirsts 66 for his brother’s destruction; and, with God looking on, he is a parricide in deed. Not even restrained by God’s voice does he check himself; rather, he presses on more and more, until the conceived crime is doubled by the shedding of blood. The emptied world marvels that it is made narrow by two persons. The elements marvel that a human being, made in God’s image and likeness, can be slaughtered—and by his brother. The untutored earth blushes, polluted by righteous blood. Cain alone, unhappy man, exults; and, because he lacks a human witness, thinks himself free of crime—though God saw him, conscience rebuked him, and his brother’s blood accused him.

[Note: Cain is more frequently called a *fratricide* by writers, as Baluze proves in no. 14 on Cyprian’s *On the Good of Patience*. But the term *parricide* has a broad range, as shown by Jerome in his dialogues against the Pelagians, where he calls a man a parricide if he can save someone from death but does not save him. That it is extended to killing a brother is clear from Ambrose, Letter 30, no. 2, and other Fathers, who similarly call Absalom or Cain parricides. Cicero too, *For Cluentius*, chapter 11, calls it “fraternal parricide.” Likewise Saint Zeno, Tract 7, no. 4, says of David: “He spares his parricidal sons.”]

[Note: “And” supplied from the Reims, Pompeian, Vatican, and Zenonian manuscripts and the Venetian edition.]

What of the impatient Sodomites? There, where men unlawfully violated men, divine fire will kindle the fires of monstrous lust; and a rain poured from heaven by the Lord, armed with flames and sulfur, destroyed with punitive storm the foul compact of an inward crime, by which men more wretched than those whom they subjugated, pursuing them with the infamous spear, ravaged the backs of their guests.

[Note: Perhaps someone would read “the impatience of the Sodomites.” But one may supply *meminerim*, “shall I mention,” which readily takes the genitive.]

[Note: The printed editions had *divinitus*, “divinely.”]

The Jews swell with public harangues; while they venerate the divine altars, they overthrow them; with varied slaughter they crush the prophets; in excessive passion they attempt to stone Moses (Exodus 14:10). Ever ungrateful toward the Lord, they fight against him by diverse schemes and desire to serve many gods and kings, though through impatience they could not serve the one God.

IV. But let the examples of impatience cited thus far be enough [Col. 0315B]; for it is not, I think, fitting deliberately to recall what one would wish restrained—especially since its nature is such that it never remains within its own bounds, but, wholly poured abroad into public view, flourishes by slanders, surges blindly in various ways here and there, and bursts forth; yet it is overcome if concealment obscures its notoriety. Let us now return to the virtue of patience, which produced for our forefathers everlasting glory and salvation through its illustrious virtue.  
[Note: The Pomp., Vat. manuscripts and the Venetian edition read *illustri* (“illustrious”). After *quia justus* (“because he was righteous”), the Vatican manuscript reads *quia illustris et justus* (“because he was illustrious and righteous”).]

Abel was therefore a martyr because he was righteous (Matt. XXIII.35); and he was righteous because he was patient. From him martyrs learned to suffer, gladly enduring what they do not deserve. When God announced that the deluge was imminent, by which all flesh would utterly be destroyed, Noah both believed and feared that it would come at any moment; and, in order that he and his own might be saved, he did not hastily knock together the ark which he had been commanded to make [Col. 0315C]. Nor did he seize upon so great a task as a presumptuous man or a madman; rather, he built it patiently, furnished it patiently, and patiently filled it with animals of diverse kinds.  
[Note: *Praesumptor* occurs in Tertullian, *On Repentance*, ch. 6; Ammianus Marcellinus XXVI; and Sedulius, no. 4. It denotes one who takes or snatches something before its time.]

He patiently waited for the command to enter and for the time to shut the door. He proved worthy to escape, because amid so great a terror of the world he did not hurry to escape.

V. I must now recall that wondrous trial of Abraham (Gen. XXII), which would have made him either sacrilegious if he disregarded God, or cruel if he killed his son, unless by a certain singular and truly divine patience he had balanced the matter between religion and fatherly affection—without refusing in hope to God that which he had received from God against hope (Rom. IV.18). Thus he disregards Isaac, his most beloved son [Col. 0316A], but a sweeter victim to God, in order to save him; he resolves to slaughter him, lest he slaughter him, confident that he cannot displease God by an act done at God’s command.

O unprecedented spectacle, truly worthy of God! In it it is difficult to decide whether priest or victim is the more patient. Neither the colour of the one striking nor of the one to be struck falters; no limbs quiver with trembling; their eyes are neither downcast nor fierce. No one pleads, no one trembles, no one excuses himself, no one is disturbed, lest it really be parricide.  
[Note: In the Pomp. manuscript the words “He carries before himself the wood upon which he is to be burned; he builds the altar” were lacking; but in the margin they are marked for insertion in the following period after the word *celebratur* (“is performed”). The words were inserted at this point in the printed editions, but wrongly, since the altar was constructed before the sword was drawn by the father. We have therefore followed the authority of the Rem. manuscript and restored the sentence to its proper place.]

He carries before himself the wood upon which he is to be burned; he builds the altar. The one draws the sword; the other offers his neck with one will and one devotion. Lest anything profane should occur, what is performed by the one is carried out carefully and patiently by the other. Beneath so great a dread—not, I would say, of humanity, but rather of nature itself—they are joyful. Affection yields to filial devotion alone; filial devotion yields to religion; religion favours them both. The sword, suspended without any obstacle, stands amazed that by a dreadful slaughter it has displayed itself as glory, not crime [Col. 0316B]. What is this? Behold: savagery becomes faith, and wickedness passes into a sacrament. The bloodless parricide returns, and he who was offered lives.

[Note: The Venetian edition reads: “Both, therefore, [are] an example of the glory of splendour.”]

Both are glory to one another; both an example of splendour; both an admirable testimony through the ages to the worship of God. Happy would the world have been, brothers, if all had become parricides in this manner.

VI. Jacob (Gen. XXVII), through patience, gained both the blessing and his brother.  
[Note: In the printed editions and most manuscripts, *lucratus est* (“gained”) is read; but the Rem. manuscript has *docuit* in place of *est*, and this is better. For Jacob through patience truly gained not his brother alone, but both the blessing and his brother.]

He gives place to anger, confident that he will return home. He commends himself to his father and departs gently and quietly, to prove that he both deserved, and did not ambitiously seek, what he deserved. And lest anyone obscure this patience under the name of timidity, the same disposition appears also in taking wives [Col. 0316C] (ibid. XXIX). He gladly accepts what comes; he waits through long periods; he gladly bears every command of his father-in-law. Had he been impatient when outwitted by deception, he would never afterward, in time that could not be restored, have served for Rachel.

Joseph likewise is found patient (ibid. XXXVII): patient when he is seized by his brothers from the pasture;  
[Note: The Rem., Tol., and Vet. manuscripts read *e pascua*; the others, *e pascuo*. *Pascuum* occurs in Columella III.14, while *pascuo* occurs in Tertullian, *Apology*, ch. 22.]

patient when he is lowered into the pit; patient when he is sold under the auction-spear;  
[Note: When something was sold by public auction, a spear was raised; concerning this practice see Junius Rabirius’s special dissertation on the origin of spears and auctions, in Graevius, vol. III, p. 19. Joseph is therefore said to have been “sold under the spear,” because he was disposed of at an auction to the highest bidder.]

patient in prison; more patient in royal power; most patient when he recognized his longed-for brothers.  
[Note: The Tol. manuscript reads *desideratus* (“longed for”).]

And when boasting cannot restrain itself, he restrained himself when placed in honour. Surely this is a heavenly patience, which neither hardship, nor prosperity, nor affection could move from its settled condition.

VII. Against Job (Job I–II), the devil—who is not said to be gentle—may be judged to have devised much when provoked, especially since he had received from God the power to strive, with whatever weapons and forces he could, to test the righteous man by the long-established cruelty of his malice [Col. 0317A]. Thus a new battle, almost beyond belief, is undertaken. The devil fights beyond all custom, but Job fights more powerfully by disregarding him (Job I). The devil destroys in one moment his great and exceedingly abundant estate; and with a most cruel blow, amid roofs and walls collapsing together, he hurriedly buries, in excessive cruelty, the flourishing company of his dear children before he kills them. Finally, having stripped Job himself of great riches, he clothes him with great ulcers, and moreover sends ravenous worms into them (ibid. II), so that, as the dying man was tortured, an added wound might end in the indwelling wound [Col. 0317B].

But Job, having defeated with calm expectation all the forces of the opposing side, became exceedingly stronger in himself. When all that war had destroyed was restored more richly, he did not lose the condition of his former prosperity by disregarding adversity; he transformed it.

Here I do not dare to mention the patience of the Lord,
