[Note: The Vatican manuscript reads *audebo* (“I shall dare”).]

lest God, reckoned among human beings, should suffer some injury; for it is not fitting praise  
[Note: The Pomp. manuscript reads *cum principatum* (“when it removes primacy”).]

that removes primacy by making equal. But since all those whom we have mentioned, and indeed all blessed people, are such by his gift, it is an insult to praise the Lord whose servant one is unable worthily to praise.

VIII. But how I wish, if I can, to celebrate you more in human conduct, patience, queen of all things! [Col. 0317C] For I know that you rest more gladly in your own habits, your own foundations [Col. 0318A], and your own counsels than in others’ modest words; nor do you place so great praise in multiplying virtues as in bringing them to completion.  
[Note: In the Life of Zeno, which we cited in annotation 1, *fruendis* (“enjoying”) is read.]

You ensure that virginity’s flower does not wither through any sickness or lapse of time. You are the most faithful harbour of widowhood, established amid the frequent storms of continually changing seasons.  
[Note: Thus the same Life reads, whereas elsewhere the text is: “You are the most faithful harbour of pitiable widowhood, established amid the frequent storms of continually changing seasons.” The reading of the Life seemed far more suitable.]

You guide those who submit their unbroken necks to the most holy yoke of marriage, whether toward equal exertion in labour or in love, with gentle reins like some skilled charioteer.  
[Note: The same Life adds *binos* (“in pairs”). Moreover, *subire jugo* with the dative is used, as in Ovid, *Letters from Pontus* IV.15: “to submit to a yoke in spirit.”]

[Note: Here the particle *vel* appears to be used copulatively, in the sense of *et* (“and”), as is demonstrated elsewhere among writers of the better periods—for example, *Aeneid* II.769 and Livy I.42.]

You taught friendship to will and not to will the same things. You are servitude’s sole and strongest consolation; you often bring forth freedom. You grant poverty this: that, while it bears everything, it possesses everything by being content with itself.

[Note: The Tol., Pomp., and Vat. manuscripts read: “You advanced the Prophets from Christ. You [advanced] the Apostles,” etc. The Zen. manuscript and the Life read: “You [advanced] Apostles for Christ,” etc.]

You advanced the Prophets; you bound the Apostles fast to Christ. You are both the daily mother and crown of martyrs.  
[Note: Concerning the interpretation of this passage, by which it is suggested that persecutions flourished in Zeno’s age, we said much in Dissertation I, ch. 2, §8, and shall touch upon some matters again in annotation 19 on Treatise XXVII, Book II.]

You are the wall of faith, the fruit of hope, the friend of charity.  
[Note: The Tol. and Vat. manuscripts read *anima* (“soul”).]

You gather together in a special manner the whole people and the divine virtues, like flowing hair into the knot of a single head, into one honour and beauty.  
[Note: *Specialiter* occurs in Apuleius, *On the World*, and in Columella III.9.]

Blessed, and eternally blessed, is the person who always has you within himself.  
[Note: The Life reads: “Blessed is he who has always had you in himself.”]

[Note: Several manuscript books and the Venetian edition close with “Amen.” The Rem. manuscript separately adds: “Of Saint Zeno, bishop.”]

## TREATISE VII. On Humility

[Note: TREATISE VII.—In the Verona edition and those following it, this treatise bears two prefixed titles: first, “First Sermon on Psalm CXXX”; second, “On Humility.” The latter title alone is found in the manuscripts and Venetian edition, as also in John the Presbyter of Verona and William Pastrengo. The former seems to have been added by the Veronese editors because they observed that some passages here were inserted from another treatise on Psalm CXXX [Col. 0318C], which they attributed to Zeno, but which we shall show in the preface to the Appendix to be the work of Hilary, excerpted from his Commentary on the Psalms. We do not doubt, however, that this single treatise entitled “On Humility” should be attributed to Zeno. There is no objection if three or four sayings of Hilary are read here, repeated partly in the same and partly in different words; this proves nothing except that Saint Zeno had seen Hilary’s sermon or commentary and transferred certain passages here, to be indicated shortly in their proper places—just as we have observed that he borrowed certain matters from Lactantius in Treatise III, “On Justice.” See more in Dissertation I, ch. 1, §2.]

I. The wise men of Greece, as they wished to appear—men more inquisitive than the rest—raised their hearts, in idle business, beyond what is lawful by insolent arguments.  
[Note: The Greek “wise men” named here are especially Greek philosophers, from whom the practice of philosophy passed to the Romans. Among the holy Fathers they had a bad reputation, because most heresies were thought to have arisen from philosophical doctrines. Among other works, read Tertullian’s *On Prescriptions*, whose seventh chapter is wholly devoted to demonstrating that philosophy is the origin of heresies. Some heretics are said to have emerged from Stoic, others from Pythagorean, others from Platonic, and most from Peripatetic schools. See Launoy, *On the Varied Fortune of Aristotle*, where you will find many patristic testimonies collected against Aristotelian doctrine in particular. Given the Fathers’ great hostility toward pagan philosophy, it is no wonder that Saint Zeno here and elsewhere attacks philosophers, especially since in his time the Arians were making very extensive misuse of philosophy, as we indicated in Dissertation II, ch. 2. Besides philosophers, our author seems also to touch upon poets—though poets and philosophers were formerly almost the same—when he mentions their poetry, that is, poetic fables. In discoursing concerning gods and goddesses, they more easily instilled the poisons of error into human minds when coated with the sweetness of verse.]

When they ascend into heaven with words; when they persuade men that God is what they wish him to be; when they pretend [Col. 0318C] to know the hidden things of nature; when they impose names upon the stars [Col. 0319A] and labours upon the sun; when they assign their errors to the lunar orbit; when they especially desire the poem of their own genius to be worshipped: thus they have ruined themselves and others. For, changing name and worship, as though stirred by dreams, they conveyed those scholastic calumnies concerning God even into the Church, so that there too, if anyone wishes to rave, God may not be worshipped by him but investigated.

[Note: The Arians are certainly indicated here. For those who, changing the name and guise of philosophy, transferred into the Church their schoolroom calumnies—that is, deceptions and subtleties born in philosophical schools—are indeed Arians. As Zeno stated in Treatise I, no. 2, and elsewhere, when faith was sought from their treatises, the result was that, if anyone chose to rave with them, God was not to be worshipped but investigated. A little later, in the words referring to the Church, “as though she were stirred by dreams,” the word *sit* (“she may be”) is absent from the Tol., Pomp., Sparav., Zenonian manuscripts and the Venetian edition, but wrongly.]

Let us hear what divine Scripture declares about the unbelievers who now do this. These are its words:

> Truth has diminished among the children of men. Each has spoken vanity to his neighbour; with deceitful lips they have spoken evil in their heart. May God destroy all deceitful lips and the boastful tongue—those who have said, “We shall magnify our tongue; our lips are our own; who is lord over us?” (Ps. XI.1 ff.)

[Note: The preposition *a* (“from”) is absent from the Pomp. manuscript and two Zen. manuscripts.]

II. Avoiding this pride of heart, the Prophet says to the Lord: “Lord, my heart has not been lifted up” (Ps. CXXX.1), though he knows it is written: “Man sees the face; God sees the heart” (1 Sam. XVI).  
[Note: Precisely the same interpretation appears in three manuscripts of Gaudentius, Sermon 11, p. 140, Padua edition of 1720, prepared by Paul Galeardus, canon of Brescia. See annotation 3 there.]

Will it not seem either insulting or superfluous to tell God what he knows? Far from it: he tells it, indeed, for us, whom he wishes to imitate what he does and proclaims. Therefore he says, “My heart has not been lifted up,” teaching that a contrite heart is the best sacrifice to God (Ps. L.29).  
[Note: In Hilary: “For a contrite heart is the best sacrifice to God. The heart must not be raised by prosperity, but, through the fear of God, must be restrained in humility within the bounds of gentleness.” This is the first and chief saying in which Zeno imitated Hilary, though it cannot be said to have been copied word for word. A little later in Zeno’s treatise, where the text reads *ipse nos pio*, the Pomp. manuscript has *ipse pio*; we have written *hortetur* rather than *hortatur* on the authority of the same manuscript.]

Therefore, brothers, it must not be lifted up by prosperity, but restrained by the fear of God, within the boundaries of gentleness, by the bridle of modesty, so that we may worthily deserve what Scripture says: “God is near to the contrite in heart, and he will save the humble in spirit” [Col. 0319C] (Ps. XXXIII.18). But hear also what the Lord himself urges upon us by his gracious promise: “Come,” he says, “you who labour and are burdened, and I will refresh you. Take my yoke upon you and learn from me, because I am gentle and humble in heart; and you shall find rest for your souls” (Matt. XI.28–29).

Our God, brothers, is humble [Col. 0320A] in heart; and that ineffable power of his wisdom and might lies hidden yet more wonderfully within the humanity he assumed, because he is so great and such as he is.  
[Note: In the *Bibliotheca Patrum*, and thence in Desiderius Heraldus’s notes on Arnobius, Book II, p. 113 [Col. 0320C], *vis* (“power”) is read in place of *ejus* (“his”). Had the manuscript supported that reading, we would have inserted it into the text.]

[Note: Many Fathers, before Nestorius’s heresy—and some even after it—said “to assume a man” for “to assume humanity.” We have sufficiently discussed this formula in Dissertation II, ch. 3.]

And does curious man lift up his heart and strive to comprehend the height of him whose humility he does not follow?

III. He continues and says: “Nor have my eyes been lifted up” (Ps. CXXX.1). The case of the eyes is worse, because exaltation of heart belongs to few, but the lifting up of the eyes to all. What John teaches his disciples concerning them is familiar to everyone: “Do not love the world, nor the things that are in the world. If anyone loves the world, the love of the Father is not in him; for all that is in the world is the desire of the flesh, the desire of the eyes, and worldly ambition” (1 John II.15–16).  
[Note: Against the manuscripts and other editions, the Padua edition reads *in visu* (“in sight”).]

For by these authors it is conceived, by these guides it is carried on, and by these servants it is fulfilled—whatever burns daily in the world with desire, ambition, and avarice [Col. 0320B]. Both, therefore, are vain: for exaltation of heart finds no fruit, while the pride of the eyes, carried from one thing to another, immediately loses through fleeting change whatever it has seen.

IV. “Then follows: ‘Neither have I walked in great things, nor in things too wonderful for me’” (Ps. CXXX.2).  
[Note: This is the second passage in which the author seems to have imitated Hilary, though mostly with different words and syntax. Hilary says: “Then follows: ‘Neither have I walked in great things, nor in things too wonderful for me.’ It is a matter of great danger if we walk in small matters and do not linger in wonderful things. The utterances of God are great; he himself is wonderful in the highest places. How, then, does the Prophet present as a good work of his own that he does not walk in great and wonderful things?”]

The utterances of God are great; he himself is wonderful in the highest places. If it would have been dangerous for the Prophet not to walk in these things, how does he further claim as a good work for himself his withdrawal from those things in which he ought to have walked?  
[Note: Context persuaded us to write *ambularet* (“he walked”) from the Tol. manuscript and the Padua edition, whereas all the other manuscripts and editions read *ambulet* (“he may walk”).]

The latter words, brothers, correspond to the former: he speaks of worldly matters. He says that he did not walk in great and wonderful things—not, of course, in God’s great things, but in those which people think great in this world. Yet when he added, “above me,” he showed that he was never lifted up when he had the power to be; for none are more easily puffed up than those whom the summit of unexpected honour exalts.

David, indeed, humble, lowly, and obscure, lay in his father’s house [Col. 0321A], always tending sheep, almost as a stranger, reckoned innocent among the innocent.  
[Note: Hilary expresses this third thought as follows: “For David, both prophet and king, was once humble and lowly, not even worthy of his father’s table; yet he pleased God. He was anointed king and inspired as a prophet. He does not grow insolent in kingship, is not stirred by hatred, loves his persecutor, honours his enemies’ deaths, and spares his incestuous and parricidal sons. The emperor is despised, the father injured, the prophet vexed: he does not pray for vengeance as prophet, does not exact retribution as father, does not pursue insult as emperor. Do you see how great is the change in both words and style in Zeno?”]

He pleased God, was anointed king, and inspired as a prophet. He did not grow insolent in kingship; he overshadowed no one with a prophet’s terror;  
[Note: This passage troubled Sparaverius, who would have preferred to read “surely no one with terror” and confessed that he could not grasp the meaning of *obumbrat* (“he overshadows”). But Zeno intended to express in other words what we cited from Hilary: “he does not pray for vengeance as prophet”; therefore the title “prophet” is by no means to be altered. *Obumbrat autem terrore* means “he surrounds with terror; he inspires terror.”]

he did not enforce his own injuries by royal power; he loved those who hated him; he spared his enemies;  
[Note: The Urb., Zen., and Pomp. manuscripts read *pepercit* (“he spared”). In the margin of the last, this was corrected to *parcit* (“he spares”), which is read in the other manuscripts and editions.]

he forgave his parricidal sons; and his persecutor—what is more, a king repeatedly delivered by God into his hands—he preferred always to fear rather than kill. By a grateful reversal of service, he hoped to please God by retaining God’s gift. A gentle king, a dutiful father, a modest prophet: he has power over everything, disregards everything, is not altered by the great and wonderful things of the world, and everywhere retains the gentle and humble shepherd.

V. He then added: “If I did not think humbly, but exalted my soul.” [Col. 0321B] Let us see whether perhaps the Prophet contradicts himself by exalting his soul when he boasts that he has not exalted his heart. He does not contradict himself, but shows that the soul’s elevation consists in overcoming higher things; for “he who exalts himself shall be humbled, and he who humbles himself shall be exalted” (Matt. XXIII.12). The soul’s depression is a heart lifted up; a restrained heart is the soul’s advancement.

Two men stand as witnesses to this, expounding the prophetic hymn by their actions: the Pharisee and the Tax Collector in God’s temple (Luke XVIII).  
[Note: “The prophetic hymn” denotes Psalm CXXX, discussed thus far.]

The Pharisee foolishly stretches toward heaven hands that have often, often been servants of murder and robbery. He shamelessly lifts up eyes by whose seduction the unhappy world is ruined. He thunders with a tongue that is never without the serpent’s poison;  
[Note: The Venetian edition and Pomp. manuscript read *caretque* (“and is without”), but wrongly. The statement does not refer to the Pharisee but to the tongue, which is said never to be without the serpent’s poison because the serpent’s tongue infused venom into Eve. If Zeno’s words are understood to refer to this—as indeed seems probable—then Sparaverius’s correction will be accepted: in the preceding sentence he judged that *infelix* (“unhappy”) should be substituted for *in flore* (“in bloom”), as though the holy bishop had regarded Eve’s fault, promoted by the eyes’ seduction, as the source from which the world’s unhappiness derived. Thus we have written it in the text, since *in flore* yields no satisfactory sense. The syntax of *caret*, moreover, is characteristic of Zeno; compare Treatise III, no. 2, *utraque cujus exaggerare opulentiam*, and Treatise IV, no. 5, *quavis versutia qui fallitur numquam*, etc.]

and, what is the greatest madness of all, he praises himself before God.

But the Tax Collector entreats God not limb by limb, but wholly, because in fear he is wholly humble.  
[Note: That is, he did not pray humbly for God’s favour merely by hands lifted to heaven, eyes, and tongue, as the Pharisee did while thinking proudly in his heart, but with his whole body and spirit.]

Confessing his sins, he repeatedly strikes his breast and in a manner modestly chastises with his hand his own heart, from which, according to the Lord’s saying (Matt. XV.19), every kind of sin proceeds;  
[Note: The relative *a quo* (“from which”) refers not to the Lord, but to the heart, although the latter is named afterward. The passage should therefore be construed thus: “Repeatedly striking his breast, he modestly chastises, as it were, with his hand his own heart, from which, according to the Lord’s saying, every kind of sin proceeds; and he asks,” etc. This unusual syntax, distinct from Hilary’s, clearly marks Zeno as author. A little later the Urb. manuscript reads *omnia* (“all things”) for *universa* (“the whole”).]

and he asks forgiveness of his sins by silence alone, not by voice. Hear what each obtained: he who had promised everything to himself departed empty; he who presumed nothing departed from the temple justified.

[Note: The Pomp. manuscript adds “Amen.” The Rem. manuscript further contains this closing: “The treatise of Saint Zeno on humility happily ends.”]

## TREATISE VIII. On Fear

[Note: TREATISE VIII.—Sayings from Hilary’s Commentary on the Psalms have been combined by Zeno in this treatise, but in a different order and in phrasing wholly Zenonian. How far this differs from Hilary’s style anyone may readily understand from the comparison of the sayings from Hilary which we shall set below.]

I. The term *fear*, beloved brothers, is indeed one, but with the addition of reason one fear is distinguished from another; for there are two kinds: one belonging to God, the other to nature. Natural fear is born in a human being; fear of God, however, is both learned and taught, because it consists not in trembling but in the rational principle of teaching. As it is written: “Come, children, listen to me; I will teach you the fear of God” (Ps. XXXIII.12).  
[Note: After citing the verse of the Psalm, Saint Hilary adds: “Fear, then, must be learned because it is taught; for it consists not in terror but in the rational principle of teaching.” From this Zeno drew the present statement and transferred it to another place.]

Natural fear, then, is not learned, but confronts us through the impulse of our own weakness;  
[Note: Hilary expresses the following two clauses separately in two places: first, “For we do not learn what is to be feared”; second, “It belongs to the fearful person to undergo what he would not wish to happen to himself.”]

for it is not an art to fear what you fear; and you fear what you do not want to happen to you.

Fear arises in diverse ways: when conscience seethes over some guilt; when an enemy’s threatening hand presses one’s safety with the sword; when a swollen serpent, ablaze with fiery scales and raised to strike a traveller on his road, confronts him;  
[Note: *Viantium* occurs in Solinus, ch. 42, and at the beginning of Apuleius’s *Florida*.]

when the savage rabies of a beast, eager for slaughter, attempts to load the fleeing person’s back with its nearby roar [Col. 0323A]; or when, the rudder lost, a groaning ship amid waves and winds battling one another gives birth to shipwreck. Of all these, the fear of conscience is the worse, because the things we have mentioned and others like them pass away together with their susceptibility to suffering; the fear of conscience is not erased.  
[Note: Arnobius, Book II, p. 62, wrote *passibilitate* (“susceptibility to suffering”).]

II. Now let us see how we should understand what the Prophet says: “Blessed are all who fear the Lord” (Ps. XII.1). If all who fear the Lord are blessed, then no one is unblessed; for there is no nation, no cattle, indeed no kind of living creature, that does not fear God.

[Note: Hilary says something similar, likewise in few words: “For if God is to be feared because many things have been burned by thunderbolts, struck down by thunder, or now fallen through an earthquake and now swallowed by an opening of the earth, then fear stirred by terror at such events contains no merit of faith.” Compare now Zeno’s and Hilary’s wording: who could fail wholly to distinguish the two, unless he has not merely no acquaintance with either Hilary’s or Zeno’s style, but lacks the ability to read and understand?]

When we are oppressed by crashing sounds and shaken hinges on every side; when the sky, roaring beyond its custom with terrifying din, resounds; when amid blind darkness gathered by heavy clouds, frequent flames flashing with curved fires instantly imitate the light of day that had been cut off;  
[Note: Three manuscripts write this inconsistently.]

when many things burn from lightning; when the earth either trembles or receives itself into its own chasm—there is no place here for blessedness, where what is feared arises not from devotion but necessity.

Therefore let us hear what Scripture says, whose admonition these words are: “And now, Israel, what does the Lord your God ask of you except that you fear the Lord your God, walk in all his ways [Col. 0324A], love him, keep his commandments with all your heart and with all your soul, and that it may be well with you?” (Deut. X.12–13).  
[Note: The Pomp. manuscript reads *ut bene* (“that it may be well”); shortly afterward it reads *nobis necessario necessarium* (“necessary for us by necessity”), likewise found in the Vatican manuscript.]

Do you see that this fear is necessary for us?  
[Note: What Saint Zeno here recalls in one period, Hilary states in two shorter ones: “For us, all fear of the Lord is in love, not in dread. The distinctive duty of our love is to obey admonitions, comply with ordinances, and trust promises.”]

It consists in the love of God; it brings itself forth by its own will; it builds its beauty through knowledge of the divine law; it boldly directs itself toward every kind of virtue;  
[Note: This is the reading of the manuscripts and editions we have seen. In the Padua edition alone, *pergit* (“proceeds”) was printed for *corrigit* (“directs”); on what authority is unknown. *Corrigo* sometimes means “to direct,” when something less straight or tending sideways is made straight. Thus Pliny, Book VII, ch. 20, uses it of straightening a finger; Seneca, in the satire on Claudius’s death, p. 23, of straightening curved things; and Augustus, in Macrobius, *Saturnalia* II.4, is reported to have answered jokingly a hunchbacked advocate who asked him to correct him should any wrong statement escape: “I can advise you, but I cannot straighten you.” Perhaps one might even read *corripit* (“it swiftly withdraws itself”) for *sese celeriter recipit*.]

it faithfully obeys every command; it lives innocently from its beginning; it cultivates righteousness; and it strives without end to fear, lest it fear anything besides the God whom it loves.

III. Finally, with the support of this fear Daniel (Dan. 14), unarmed, kills the dragon that terrified the peoples; cast to the lions, he dines in danger who is accustomed to fast outside danger. And Jonah, fearing the Lord, does not fear voluntarily to enter shipwreck (Jonah 1–2): when the whale opens its jaws, he is buried more miserably than he was cast down; yet he finds the shore toward which he was heading before he sees it—happier in a tomb than in a ship. At prayer the mountain trembles: trembling belongs to the mountain, not to the apostles. Peter is borne upon the sea-swell, not as a shipwrecked man but as a traveller (Matt. 14:29–30): the deep fears to engulf one who is not afraid; yet he does not entirely conceal his fear, lest he fail to believe that he walked upon the sea with his feet.

Against Thecla an exceedingly fierce accuser unsheathes the sword of his tongue; the public laws rage madly, with their own ministers, against themselves. Savagery is spurred into ferocity, yet is found gentler than men. Lest a spectacle so dreadful should seem to lack any element of humanity, sea-monsters too are let loose. The girl is stripped of every garment; she is clothed in fire. Amid so many instruments of death, while the spectator is afraid, she, secure, treads underfoot every kind of terror. Unharmed, as though she had conquered the world, she leaves the deadly enclosure—now no longer pitiable, but wonderful in its funereal circuit—bearing off the triumph over the defeated age, though all had believed that she would perish amid so many punishments.

[Note: Col. 0323D] Cardinal Baronius cites this passage in his *Annals*, under the year 47, no. 8, to show that the Acts of St Thecla now in circulation are the same as those read by St Zeno, and therefore differ from those which, as Tertullian recounts, a certain presbyter of Asia composed and published under Paul’s name, having himself been convicted and confessed the act; Gelasius also placed these among the apocrypha. But nothing is adduced that can persuade us that these differ from those; moreover, St Zeno’s authority (add also Ambrose’s, who among Western writers often mentions the same matter, especially *On Virgins*, book II, no. 30) is not wholly conclusive. For Fathers of that age, indeed even earlier ones, sometimes used apocryphal writings, as is clear among others from St Ignatius the Martyr and Papias of Hierapolis. The former, in his letter to the Smyrnaeans, no. 3, cites a passage from the Gospel according to the Hebrews; the latter, in the books *On the Interpretation of the Oracles of the Lord*, cited by Eusebius, book III, chapter 39, expounded a certain story from that same Gospel. As for Zeno, Baronius himself admits in the *Apparatus to the Annals*, no. 7, that he drew from apocryphal material the story of the midwife mentioned in Treatise VIII, Book II; we shall note more on it in its place.

We would rather observe this: even if, as Tertullian testifies in *On Baptism*, chapter 7, that Asian presbyter composed the aforementioned writing while John the Apostle was still alive, and was therefore removed from his rank by that apostle, it does not follow that everything there related about St Thecla is proved entirely fictitious, but only certain matters noted in that writing by Tertullian and Jerome. For it is not credible that the presbyter had reached such folly as to dare, toward the end of the first century in which he lived, or the beginning of the second, to invent wholesale the very famous martyrdom of Thecla, without fearing that someone might convict him of fabrication. Add that scarcely any martyr is mentioned so frequently and so anciently—especially in Greek churches—as St Thecla, as may be seen from the many witnesses cited by John Ernest Grabe, *Spicilegium of the Fathers of the First Century*, vol. I, notes on the Acts of Thecla.

Is it credible that so great a renown and cult of St Thecla should have existed in the Church from the earliest centuries if everything transmitted about her had been fabricated by that Asian presbyter, publicly condemned for this very reason by John the Apostle—a fabrication which such a solemn condemnation should have made known to all? Should we not rather recognize that Thecla’s person and martyrdom were not wholly fabricated, but that most things handed down about her are true; that the Asian presbyter made use of them in composing the writing concerning the career of Thecla and Paul; and that in it he inserted certain falsehoods which John the Apostle rejected?

Whatever the case, no Acts of St Thecla seem to have existed except those composed by the aforementioned presbyter. Of these alone, besides the Greek text, we possess a very ancient Latin translation, published by the aforementioned Grabe from a Bodleian manuscript. In this translation, indeed, as in the Greek text, are contained all the matters concerning the martyr cited by the Fathers—who nevertheless refrain from the rejected portions—except for a few which Zeno recounts differently, as will appear from the notes below. Yet these differences do not seem so great that one must therefore agree with Baronius that other Acts of St Thecla once existed. For antiquity would more readily have transmitted to posterity these Acts of the Asian presbyter as genuine rather than corrupt, and an interpretation of those rather than of the latter.

[Note: Col. 0325C] Savagery is said to be gentler than human beings, since Thecla is delivered to the beasts and exposed to them; yet one might see, by a certain transfusion of nature—as Ambrose admirably explains in the passage cited—men, having put on savagery, commanding cruelty to a beast, while the beast, kissing the virgin’s feet, teaches what human beings ought to do.

[Note: Col. 0325C] In the very ancient translation of the Acts of Thecla, in Grabe, vol. I, p. 125, after the martyr’s victory over the beasts has been described, these words are added: “Then they released many beasts against her. But she, stretching out her hands, prayed to the Lord; and when she had finished the prayer, she turned and saw a great pool full of water, in which were sea-beasts, to whom they intended to send Thecla.” Thecla is then said to have cast herself into that water in order to be baptized there, and the monsters did her no harm, because they were killed by a heavenly flash. These sea-monsters are called in the Greek Acts φῶκαι, *phōkai*, that is, seals or sea-dogs, which were swimming in the water. This is the first difference between Zeno’s account and the Acts; let others judge it.

[Note: Col. 0325D] Here *laciniis* means “garments,” as in Apuleius, *Metamorphoses*, book I: “I take off one of my two garments.”

[Note: Col. 0325D] If “she is clothed in fire” refers to the fire which the Acts say was kindled for Thecla before she was exposed to the beasts, St Zeno has passed over the order of the narrative. But if it indicates the fire which the Acts report was kindled in the ropes during the final contest with bulls, Zeno’s sequence is preserved; yet from the Acts that fire does not appear to have been so great that it could have covered Thecla. This is the second difference between Zeno’s narrative and the Acts.

[Note: Col. 0325D–0326C] That *cavea* means not only the enclosure in which birds or beasts are confined, and also the rows of steps or benches in a theatre or amphitheatre where hearers or spectators sat—whence frequent references to the first, second, and third *caveae*—but also the amphitheatre itself, or its lowest part, where St Thecla is said to have died when exposed to lions, we infer from this testimony of Zeno. Tertullian uses *cavea* for the arena in which gladiators fought, in *Apology*, chapter 15, and in *To the Nations*, chapter 10; and he mentions both kinds of *cavea* in *On Spectacles*, chapter 30. Salvian, in *On the Government of God*, book VI, evidently indicates that theatre and amphitheatre were customarily called by this name, distinguishing them from circus and stadium; he explicitly uses it for an amphitheatre. That Zeno is speaking of this is clear from his mention of the circuit of the *cavea*, which suits only an amphitheatre.

Nevertheless, the ancient author of the homily *On the Man Born Blind*, published in volume VIII of St John Chrysostom’s works, Appendix, p. 63, calls it a theatre: “What harm did it do the first martyr Thecla to contend naked in the theatre?” In the ancient version of the Acts, in the part where the Greek text is lacking, p. 108, amphitheatre, *cavea*, and arena are mentioned: “She was placed in the amphitheatre, in the enclosure where there was a most savage lioness, and entered the arena in the procession of the spectacle.” Cyprian of Antioch likewise calls it an amphitheatre, in the Cyprianic Appendix, p. 30.

O fear, necessary indeed! It does nothing but make people blessed: it fears by art, not by chance; by will, not by necessity; by religion, not by guilt. It fears God, not nature. Do you wish to know what its distinctive quality is? All fears destroy by increase those whom they seize; this one alone grows in order to make immortal the person whom it possesses.

## TREATISE IX. On Avarice. I

[Note: Col. 0326D] TREATISE IX.—This is the title in the manuscripts and editions, except the Venetian edition, where it reads: “On the detestable vice of avarice and covetousness.”

I. It is neither a singular nor a trivial crime, brothers, for a Christian especially to be bound in the chains of covetousness and, blinded by the deadly darkness of deep night, to be borne miserably downward into the depths. But because the whole world has caught fire from the blaze of this unquenchable plague, avarice is thought to have ceased to be a crime, because it leaves no one who can accuse himself. For everywhere men, in an insatiable madness, rush disgracefully into gain; nor can anyone at all be found who imposes upon it even for a moment the reins of justice.

It always seethes restlessly, rages, fights, snatches, gathers, and hoards: clinging to its own possessions, craving those of others, content neither with its own, nor with another’s, nor with the world itself. It possesses everything and always complains of poverty. Finally, it never attains its desires. The more it is increased, the more miserable it becomes: without leisure, without satiety. Through right and wrong alike, armed with many arts, ways, and stratagems, it riots about, despising its own salvation and that of others, fearing only that anyone may lack something to scrape away.

[Note: Col. 0326D] MS Remensis reads *fribulum*. Yet in Treatise X, no. 1, we read *frivolo* without any variant. In Isidore, book X, chapter 8, *fribolum* has an altogether peculiar sense, unsupported by any earlier author. In both passages of Zeno, however, it means light, empty, fragile, futile, and of no importance, as in Pliny, book VII, chapter 7, *frivola origo* (“a trifling origin”), and Suetonius, *Life of Nerva*, chapter 12, *frivolum auspicium* (“a trivial omen”).

Hence whole nations fall every moment under mutual wounds; shaken cities groan; devastated countryside cannot breathe again; the seas are more savage with pirates than by nature. Roads barred with swords grow fat on human blood. Heirs are astonished to hear wills read out naming unknown persons. The hand of a female friend, under the disguise of deceit, securely destroys innocent lives by a draught of poison. By a new madness of hatred, an unborn and unknown creature is buried before it is born—not now in its mother’s womb, but in a tomb: a creature that could experience neither a lawful death nor life.

[Note: Col. 0326D] The reading was *amica*; but it must be corrected to *amicae*, so that the phrase “a hand persuaded” may refer to a beloved woman.

[Note: Col. 0326D] Here *pecus* is taken to mean a fetus conceived in the mother’s womb, to which death is administered by some potion.

Therefore the Apostle rightly says: “Avarice is the root of all evils” (1 Tim. 6:10). For from this mother and teacher alike are born and openly practised all the evils we have mentioned, and many others besides—indeed, all the evils that continually well up from every side—though humanity hypocritically delights to condemn them. For it swallows the camel and strains out the gnat: it rejects drops of crimes, yet drinks down the fountain of avarice from which streams of crimes flow.

[Note: Col. 0327B] This is a proverb commonly used by the Fathers, as may be seen in Lucifer of Cagliari, *To Constantius*, book II, p. 209 of vol. IV of the Lyons edition of the *Library of the Fathers*; and in Jerome on Matthew 7, vol. VII of the Verona edition, p. 38, and on Matthew 23, p. 184.

II. No rights, laws, or honour opposes it; because whatever is bought or sold is not free. Not nobility: for through it avarice believes, cultivates, and finds for itself this name. Not holiness, not fortification: for nothing is so holy that it cannot be violated, nothing so fortified that money cannot storm it. Not kinship of blood, not friendship: because a person is loved or hated not for his own merit, but for the advantage of gold, silver, and wealth.

Hence it comes that we often see the sacred names of brothers more friendly to swords than to one another; that wealthy parents, having abolished the sanctity of their own name, allow their children, to the disgrace of both, to wander as beggars subject to street alms; that children, judging their parents’ lives to be a loss to themselves, violently lay hands upon nature itself and seize inheritances before their time, compelling their parents to live in misery and die possessed of means.

[Note: Col. 0327B–C] *Triviale* properly means what is done at crossroads or in some way pertains to crossroads. Hence Quintilian, book I, chapter 4, calls grammar a *trivial* discipline, because it was learned at crossroads. “Street alms” are so called because beggars especially sought alms at crowded crossroads; Apuleius, *Metamorphoses*, book I, p. 44, mentions alms distributed at crossroads. Here St Zeno notes the avarice of certain fathers who, rather than feed their children, forced them to beg for alms at crossroads.

[Note: Col. 0327C] MS Toletanus reads, “having invaded immaturely”; MS Urbanus, “having invaded nature itself.”

O wickedness! Wretched man, why do you take away what is your own? What would you do to a stranger, when you are miserly toward yourself? O evil more detestable than detestable! While they despoil, persecute, and deceive one another, they approve enemies, praise robbers, excuse thieves; and it never enters their minds that tomorrow is not in human power (Luke 11:20), nor even the present moment in which the matter is being transacted (James 4:14), because what is always turning may bring forth anything in a moment.

But blind though their eyes are open, they enlarge their barns (Luke 12:18), constrict the land, join woodlands to woodlands; and even if they possessed the whole world, they hate boundaries. They count it unlawful to have a neighbour.

[Note: Col. 0327C] MS Remensis reads, “their eyes upon their parents.”

[Note: Col. 0327C] The same manuscript reads “they constrict witnesses, press groves with groves.” “They press” is also found in the Toledo and Vatican manuscripts. We have written *terras* (“lands”) rather than *testes* (“witnesses”) on the authority of five manuscripts and the editions; *jungunt* (“they join”) rather than *urgent* (“they press”) from three manuscripts and the editions. The sense favoured this reading. Shortly afterward MS Urbanus reads *possiderent* rather than *possideant*.

They build estates, dig up tombs, and fear an omen though they do not fear death. Thus, thus slain, they commonly lie abandoned to dogs, birds, and wild beasts, scattered everywhere, lost on both sides, their bones half-eaten, stripped even of their own flesh. Behold a fate worthy of the avaricious person. He—he who possessed a large estate—does not possess even a small tomb. The noble Prophet rebukes such people in these words: “What did pride profit us? Or what did the pursuit of riches bring us? All these things passed away like a shadow” (Wisdom 5:8–9). And the Lord himself says: “What does it profit anyone to gain the world and suffer loss of his soul?” (Matt. 16:26).

[Note: Col. 0327C–0329B] MS Remensis reads: “They construct battles, despise tombs, and do not fear any death.” Likewise the Toledo and Vatican Basilica manuscripts have *praelia* (“battles”) for *praedia* (“estates”). If this were the genuine reading, it would concern avaricious persons who, wishing to extend the boundaries of their fields, try to usurp their neighbours’ lands; for this purpose they construct not estates but battles, which are often fought over usurped boundaries, and they “despise tombs,” that is, fear them less or scorn them (*de-* in compounds often has a diminishing force, as in *detumescere*, *detonare*, and so forth), and do not fear to undergo any death in these civil conflicts. The following words would also refer to this: “Thus, thus slain, they commonly lie exposed to dogs,” etc. That such events often occurred in civil or rural conflicts stirred up over field boundaries is clearly proved by the particular testimony of St Gregory of Nyssa, *First Sermon on Prayer*. While describing the effect of avarice, he says:

> “The farmer does not measure cultivation by necessary uses, but always directs his effort toward more. While extending his own fields more widely by usurping foreign boundaries, he opens a great entrance to sin against this pursuit and plan of life. Hence difficult disputes and lawsuits arise among persons once calm and composed, as those afflicted by the same disease of avarice raise mutual controversies concerning the boundaries of fields. Hence anger; hence an impulse to evil; hence attacks of some upon others, often beginning with bloodshed and slaughter.”

What could more clearly confirm the reading *praelia* in the sense described, found in three most ancient manuscripts? Add that it is not sufficiently clear how frequent killings would commonly have happened to diggers-up of tombs, whom the received reading mentions. Although Roman laws formerly punished them with death for this reason, their bodies are not said to have been handed over to beasts and birds by command of those same laws. Indeed, that penalty was formerly prescribed only for persons of lower condition in Law 11, title XII, book XLVII of the *Digest*; by Zeno’s time it had been abolished, death having been changed to a monetary fine by Law 2, title XVII, book IX of the Theodosian Code.

But since this Reims reading contains several expressions that seem remote from the characteristic purity of Zeno’s language, and since in the laws of Zeno’s century, title XVII, book IX of the cited Code, there frequently occurs condemnation of those who demolish tombs—“throw down,” Law 1; “cast down,” Law 2; “overturn,” Law 3; “destroy,” Law 4—which amount to the author’s *defodiunt* (“dig up”), we judged that the received reading, also found in the other manuscripts, should not be changed. The passage therefore concerns those who, from avarice, dug up tombs either to enlarge their fields—for tombs occupied part of the fields—or, as the cited laws of the Theodosian Code especially condemn, to sell tomb-columns, marble, and other materials useful for building, or to transfer them to their own use.

Concerning the *omen* added here, Heraldus, in his *Notes on Arnobius*, p. 100, judges that there is an error: “Without doubt,” he says, “it should read, ‘let those who do not fear death fear an omen’; that is, if those who do such things do not fear death, at least let them fear an omen. For when they dig up tombs, they make for themselves an omen of a detestable lot after death; and the very words of Zeno contain an omen, since from the digging-up of others’ tombs it happened that the bones and ashes of others were scattered. This was an omen of what was accustomed to happen to people of this kind, for whatever reason: that when killed, they should lack a grave.”

But since an omen derives from the superstition of idolatry, which the Fathers abhorred, we do not believe that the holy bishop intended to prescribe fear of such an omen, even in jest. Therefore we have retained “they fear an omen,” as it stands in all editions and manuscripts. Perhaps it hints at a certain excuse of such tomb-diggers: because of the proximity of tombs, they feared an omen of death, though in fact they feared no death at all. The repetition “thus, thus” is characteristic of Zeno, as may be seen in Treatise IV, no. 3, and elsewhere; it has been restored from the manuscripts, where “if thus” had been read.

III. Go now, insatiable man: compel even the elements themselves, by new arts, into the deadly profits of your detestable accumulation. Though your inner chambers gleam filled with the variegated forms of precious stones; though the earth groan under the weight of silver; though your whole house, blazing with gold, contend with the sun in its own flame; though the rank of honours drained by you cannot discover what it may bestow upon you—yet you must remember that death fears neither riches nor honours.

[Note: Col. 0329B] On the authority of MS Toletanus it seemed right to write *quid* (“what”) instead of *quod* (“which”); and, were the emendation not too free, we should also have written: “the ranks drained by you cannot find what they may bestow upon themselves.”

O blind mind of humankind! How variously, yet in one and the same way, it strives toward death: the poor person, when he unhappily seeks riches which he happily does not possess; the rich person, when he thinks he does not possess the riches which he does possess. In one case avarice strains; in another it rages; in both it grows; in both it does not cease. Yet in one instant a little earth both makes them equal and satisfies them—what gold, with all its ambition, cannot do.

[Note: Col. 0329B–D] MS Urbanus reads *patitur* (“suffers”).

MS Remensis reads *satiat in hormen, quia cum*; MS Pompensis and the Zenonian manuscript, *satiat in ormen quod cum*; finally, MSS Toletanus and Urbanus, *satiat in ormen, quam quod cum*. This agreement of the manuscripts in writing *in hormen* strongly suggests that editors have rejected a word not easily understood. It certainly seems superfluous. In Apuleius, *Metamorphoses*, book X, p. 592, occurs *hormum*, from Greek ὁρμή, meaning an onset or sudden impulse; he says *hormum canebat bellicosum*, “he sounded a martial onset,” for *classicum canebat*, “he sounded the trumpet-call.” Is *satiat in hormen* here likewise “satisfies at a rush,” or “in the twinkling of an eye,” as we commonly say? But in that case *in hormen* would mean the same as *uno momento* (“in one instant”), producing an entirely empty repetition.

It might more plausibly be written, with an easy change, *in eo omne*, so as to mean that in a single instant the tomb both makes poor and rich equal and satisfies them in every respect in which gold cannot. But a certain harshness alien to Zeno’s style prevents us from introducing this into the text. We shall offer one final conjecture. Perhaps, after *satiat*, a comma should be placed and one should write *enorme quod*, etc., referring to gold, and construe: “which gold, enormous—that is, of enormous quantity—cannot do with all its magnitude.” Likewise *inormi* for *enormi* is found in two manuscripts in Treatise LVII, Book II; and “enormity of profits” for great excess of profit occurs in Treatise X, no. 1. But let others, more fortunate than we, offer better conjectures.

IV. One person sets out his money like a hook in order to draw other people’s resources to himself. He does not cease to nourish it while it travels abroad, by deadly calculation, so as to seek not the sum lent, but the sum that days, months, and fingers, armed with numbers, have begotten for it.

[Note: Col. 0329D] The Venetian edition reads *humanum*; the other editions and manuscripts, *humum*. We have no doubt that *hamum* (“hook”) must be read, as the sense demands.

[Note: Col. 0329D] This expression properly belongs to money lent at interest: *fenus* is derived from “bearing,” as Varro testifies in book III of *On the Latin Language*, cited by Gellius, book VI, chapter 12. *Fenus* is said to come from *fetus*, offspring, and from a kind of bearing of money which produces and increases. Nonius, chapter I, confirms this and further observes that the Greeks call interest τόκος, *tokos*, from τίκτειν, “to beget” or “bear.”

[Note: Col. 0329D–0330B] Days are mentioned because it is characteristic of money lent at interest to begin producing from the first day on which the lender stipulated the contract, as St Basil, homily on Psalm 14, vol. I, p. 139, and St Ambrose, *On Tobit*, chapter 12, observed. See also the jurist Paulus, at the end of Law 40, *Digest*, “On Things Lent.” Hence in book XVIII of the Theodosian Code, “on the lustral contribution,” interest is called “an addition to money growing on individual days.”

[Note: Col. 0330B–C] Months seem to be mentioned because interest was formerly usually paid month by month. Thus Ambrose, *On Tobit*, chapter 12: “The Kalends come: the principal bears one per cent; each month comes: interest is generated.” Hence also the book in which paid or payable interest was recorded was customarily called a *Kalendarium*, because the day of the Kalends had been appointed for payment of monthly interest. Relevant here are Horace, *Epode* 2, “He seeks to place [money] at the Kalends,” and Ambrose, chapter III: “At the Kalends you will pay interest to the moneylender.”

[Note: Col. 0330C] Why fingers are mentioned is indicated by St Ambrose in the same work, *On Tobit*, no. 25: “The calculation of interest is repeatedly reckoned on both fingers.” The custom, evidently, was to use fingers in calculating how much one owed; hence the conventional phrase among Latin writers, “to calculate on one’s fingers.” This also relates to Lucian, *Gallus*, near the end: “Do you see this man too, wakeful with cares and reviewing the account of interest with twisted fingers?”

But often the moneylender himself, through his own industry, is stripped bare when fraud, poverty, flight, or death, arising from some mischance, has taken away his debtor. For it is natural to avarice to make a person more avaricious. Often it takes more away from the miser than it provides; and so it often happens that one justly loses even one’s own goods when one desires those of another.

[Note: Col. 0330C] MS Pompensis reads “it is natural,” with *res* (“thing”) added in the margin; MS Toletanus: “for avarice is natural, so that,” etc. Better in MS Urbanus: “for avarice is such by nature that,” etc.

[Note: Col. 0330C–D] *Ferre* (“to carry away”) for *auferre* occurs not infrequently among Latin writers. Virgil, *Eclogue* IX.51:

> “Time carries everything away, even the mind.”

Ovid, *Tristia*, book I, elegy 2:

> “What he gave, when he wishes, he himself will take away.”

Another blocks roads against travellers; he bars them from grass, from forests, from water. And though very many wealthy people possess idle abundance, he denies to human beings what he cannot deny to birds, serpents, and wild beasts. It is sheer madness to begrudge nature’s gifts.

[Note: Col. 0330D–0331D] *Copiis* (“abundance”) seems to be the reading. But if one reads *copiosis*, as is written in the manuscripts and editions, the wealthy are meant, as in Marcellinus, book XXVIII, chapter 4: “Some entice wealthy persons, free from occupation, to make wills according to their wishes.” “Wealthy persons free from occupation” seem to be those who possess idle riches; and the sense is that, although many wealthy persons use many possessions, and these possessions are idle, avarice nevertheless denies human beings—certainly those in need—what it cannot deny to birds, serpents, and beasts.

This relates, as appears, to the preceding statement: “Another blocks roads against travellers; he bars them from grass, forests, and water.” The target is those who, fearing that they may suffer some loss upon their estates or wishing to enlarge them, occupy roads open to all or close them with fences, with the result that no human being may touch the grass, enter forests, or even approach springs of water found on the estates—things which no one can prevent animals themselves from doing.

Another corners the entire market in necessities; he watches for the time to sell; he is smaller in measure and larger in price. He denies that he possesses what he is selling, so that he may be begged, so that he may slaughter. And would that the goods sold were at least unadulterated! Moreover, he groans if the year is barren, and still more if it is fertile: there because he sells little, here because he is not the only seller. Do you wish to know in how great darkness he is enveloped? He is angry with God if he is not always made rich by public misfortunes. Very well, very well: when someone seeks gold, he finds a sword.

V. Amid all this no one considers the condition of human frailty: no one considers an enemy, the treasury, a robber, a member of the household—who, through knowledge of a secret, is worse than all—or the impending flames of the day of judgment, through which we shall all pass naked. The only object of worship is that of which it is said: “The idols of the nations are silver and gold” (Ps. 113:4; Ps. 135:15), for which a man either is slaughtered or slaughters.

I should like to know what pleasure such madness affords, what it provides for its worshipper. It does not quench fever, dispel diseases, heal wounds, remove pains, or drive back death—except that it kills the healthy. Certainly it is neither eaten nor drunk; nor will it descend into hell with its plunderer. Its sole effect is to hurl unhappy eyes and an empty conscience into a dire craving for malignant glitter, in the hope of acquiring it, so that a man may not seem to have been killed for nothing.

[Note: Col. 0331D] “Into hell” in place of “into hellward” will be confirmed by examples from other ancient writers of recognized authority in note 7 on Treatise XVI, Book II.

VI. But, brothers, we have spoken not to the avaricious, but about the avaricious. Otherwise, if anyone here were such, we ought to have concluded by divine examples alone. But since faith and piety, the fitting expeller of avarice, remain and glory among you, you are all worthy not so much to possess gold and silver as to be gold and silver. For you are God’s living gold; you are Christ’s silver; you are the riches of the Holy Spirit. If you despise earthly metals, the treasure of your life is far beyond them.

That heavenly city built of gold is appointed for you. There is no delay for those wishing to enter: its twelve gates stand open; countless dwellings have been prepared; let no one be anxious about a home. It will be a notable mark of our certain glory if, by the blessedness of our number, we make the city of God too small. Therefore be secure. Nothing is ever lacking there; nothing is removed from its state or declines from it. Every good abounds everywhere and endures forever.

Certainly, first of all: no one is in need; no one envies; no one steals, snatches, proscribes, or slaughters; no one dies. All are happy, all unanimous, all immortal, all always equal. What belongs to one belongs to all; what belongs to all belongs to each. Do you wish to know what blessedness exists there? No one hides his own clothing, pearls, precious stones, gold, or silver; and yet no one fears theft.

[Note: Col. 0331D] MSS Remensis, Toletanus, Vaticanus, and Urbanus read: “no one does not fear the sword”; MS Pompensis reads: “no one does not fear the harbour,” though a later hand has deleted *non* (“not”). The Venetian edition reads: “no one does not fear theft.” The received reading seemed more consistent with the sense.

## TREATISE X. On Avarice II

[Note: Col. 0331D–0332D] TREATISE X.—The Venetian edition gives this title: “On the insatiability of avarice, on women’s excessive adornment, and on contempt for husbands.” We have demonstrated more fully in Dissertation I, chapter 2, §7, that this treatise was written by the author after the year 378.

I. Avarice, though it is easily condemned by everyone, would that it could as easily not be loved. For it is an ingenious and pleasant evil, ever hostile to all humankind. It implants in those without riches the desire to possess them; from those who possess them it takes away satiety. Thus it hurls all alike into madness by one tempest, so that you cannot tell where it is greater.

[Note: Col. 0332D] MSS Pompensis and Urbanus read “by human beings.”

[Note: Col. 0332D] MS Pompensis inserts *non* (“not”) in a later hand.

It is like a fire devouring dry fuel: unless the fuel comes to an end, the fire does not end. People of moderate means cultivate it by fraud, the rich by unrestrained power, judges by favouritism, eloquent persons by a hired and double tongue, kings by pride, merchants by cunning, the poor by empty desire, worshippers of God by feigned hatred, but whole peoples and nations by the sword.

[Note: Col. 0332D] The Venetian and Verona editions, with most manuscripts, read *in potentia*; MS Urbanus, *potentia*. But the Padua edition rightly has *impotentia*, “unrestrained power,” as in Velleius, book II, chapter 29; likewise Cornelius Nepos, *Lysander*, no. 1, uses *impotens* for “all-powerful.”

Throughout the whole world it rages madly, aflame with new and varied arts: never quiet, not by day, not by night, not in war, not in peace; never satisfied; made more miserable by the enormity of its gains. It is a new kind of calamity: it only grows and does not know how to grow old.

Neither filial devotion breaks it, nor the sweetness of children, nor marital affection, nor dear siblinghood, nor the law of friendship, nor a tender orphan, nor hard widowhood, nor pitiable poverty, nor contemplation of God. For behold: with every one of these, insofar as it can, it either flatters or harms by various arts, provided only that they possess something for it to take away. Whom indeed does it spare, when it hastens at every moment—even for a trivial and shameful profit—to die?

[Note: Col. 0332D] Here are indicated either gladiators, who for gain expose themselves to death, or those who, for the same reason, entrust themselves to the sea at risk of their lives.

II. Why then, wretched man, consumed by the empty desire for gold and silver bullion, are you tormented by vain concern? Why do you heap up great piles of talents? Why do you guard, with sleepless but futile anxiety, things that will remain here—allowing yourself no share of them? Moreover, you complain of poverty, though you do not know what you possess. Whatever you may do, you will carry none of these things with you to the realms below; for what belongs to nature can be transferred from place to place, but cannot be taken away from it. Finally, gold and silver, extracted from the earth’s depths with immense labour, must again be entrusted to the earth to be concealed: for possessing them is a false joy, while displaying them is a very certain danger. But there is no need to proceed through each detail: all its evils may be known from one example, as the Prophet says: “The idols of the nations are silver and gold” (Ps. CXIII [114], 4). Hence it is clear that one who loves gold and silver not only worships gods, but imitates their customs and deeds; and the proof of this is easy. Meanwhile, let us consider those things which are ours.

[Col. 0334A] III. Gold and silver, Christian, if the truth must be spoken, you execrate in idols alone, not in your own inner chambers. For there also, in countless gold and silver pieces of smoothly struck coinage, as though in temples, you likewise recognize the faces and emblems of rulers. The only difference is that in your house they are small, whereas in a temple they are larger: if you spend them, they are money; if you keep them, they are idols.

A handmaid of Christ, you reject the false idol; believe me, you worship it in yourself, since you do not lay aside its adornment and image. You go forth to the Church of God, your whole body gilded with elaborate workmanship, burdened with the accursed metal, delicate in every part, yet strong beneath necklaces. Finally, because of the very stiffness of your finery, you do not bend in prayer; you do not raise your hands; you disdain to prostrate the breast swollen with necklaces. Certainly, you bend your neck—not through devotion, but through weight. When will you make confession (*exomologesis*), you who are more anxious for adornment than for salvation? What, moreover, do you think you can obtain from God, when you entreat him by means of that through which he is angered? At last open the eyes of your heart: you will find that you are insulting rather than praying. Finally, brothers, she who does not fear Christ cannot fear her husband.

IV. From this it follows that spouses, resisting the most holy yoke of marriage and striving each on their own behalf—namely through excessive affection—seek one another’s inheritance; that parents hate children and children their parents; that friendship plays more upon the face than dwells in the heart; that the whole human race delights in its own ruin and its own calamities, valuing the soul more cheaply than money. From this it follows that justice, honour, piety, fidelity, and truth perish; that God himself suffers insult at every moment, since his commands are despised, and worship and love of the world are preferred to him. For anyone whose heart has been filled by the pestilential flame of implacable greed readily admits every sacrilegious act, crime, disgrace, and outrage.

V. But these things are not addressed to you, brothers, whose generosity is known in every province, whose pious seeds are scattered, as it were, through the members of the whole world. Through you many have been redeemed, many freed from deadly edicts, many stripped of harsh conditions give thanks. Your houses stand open to every stranger; under your care neither living nor dead has ever long been seen unclothed. Now our poor do not know how to ask for food. Now widows and the needy make wills. I could say more in praise of this your blessedness, were you not my own people. Yet one thing, out of joy, I cannot keep silent: by lending to the poor, you transfer all the resources subdued from greed into your estate without envy. For what can be richer than a person of whom God declares himself the debtor? He is blessed for ages of ages.

**TRACT XI. On Greed III.**

I. Rightly, brothers, as you have heard, God hates greed. For it is a deep-seated passion, blind desire, a mad storm, endless rapacity, unresting anxiety, never attaining its own wishes because it does not know how to be satisfied. It breaks faith, neglects charity, denies justice, recognizes no affection, despises divine laws, evades human laws by crafty arguments, and would seize the whole world if it could. Do you wish to know what kind of calamity it is? Indeed, it is more cruel toward the person who has loved it; but the one who conquers it shall have eternal life.

**TRACT XII. On Spirit and Body.**

I. If anyone, through a zeal either to know or to attack the sacred law of nature’s birth—the book of Moses—has repeatedly read it over, perhaps, such being the character of minds delighted daily by the crafty disputes they see, he may raise against us a slanderous question from the Apostle’s saying: “The first man was from the clay of the earth; the second from heaven” (1 Cor. 15:47). For there is no doubt that only one man was made by God from the clay of the earth, and that from his side a woman was drawn forth as a marital consolation (Gen. 2); from them the entire human race descended. But the heavenly man, in Genesis, is neither mentioned nor shown to have been made or born.

To this is added the very inversion of the order: for it is incongruous and absurd that the second should be immortal and the mortal one first, since immortality admits no order of time within itself, whereas mortality does; or, if the first is heavenly, what need was there for the earthly one also to be made?

That Gospel saying may be assailed by similar reasoning; for it is written: “No one has ascended into heaven except he who descended from heaven, the Son of Man, who was in heaven” (John 3:13). How could the Son of Man, or the son of what man, be born in heaven so as to descend from heaven, when both the possession and the nature of humanity are far removed from heaven? Come now, reader, awaken your understanding and you will find the truth. He who was in heaven descended from heaven; he who descended is himself also the one who ascended into heaven—the Son of Man who was in heaven (Eph. 4:9–10), Son of Man by designation, not by nature. For the Lord did not assume flesh twice; rather, it was fitting that he should thus be proclaimed, because before he was made that which he had willed himself to become, he had announced it abundantly both by figures and by oracles.

Therefore, “Son of God” pertains to his ineffable origin; “son of man,” to the mystery. I shall endeavour to unlock the secret of this mystery by clear reasoning, as with a key, so that anyone may most readily recognize both God’s providence, the power of the union of flesh and soul, and where the human being’s highest good has been established.

II. After God, brothers, had by marvellous skill completed this world—as a kind of house for the future human race—furnished and distinguished in many ways with elements, resources, living creatures, foods, and many great and varied utilities, so that no complaint might arise for its inhabitant, then he himself made for himself an image that could feel and understand, in his own image and likeness (Gen. 1:2): taking clay from the earth, he formed the human being and breathed into him the soul by which we live, from the very fountain of his own spirit. From *humus*, “earth,” he gave him the name *homo*, “human being,” I suppose—as the thing itself teaches—so that by contemplation of both maker and material he might always fear and venerate his own craftsman.

After this he subjected to him all the good things of the world (Gen. 2); and because he had already been made wise, equipped with senses for choosing death or life, and instructed by the commandment, he entrusted him to his own will. But that envious accuser—who received the name “serpent” because he creeps gradually—burning with detestable envy, and unable to prevail by himself, deceitfully assuming another form, persuaded the woman to transgress God’s command and thus miserably slew him. Thereafter, overwhelmed by an inherited condition, the whole human race perished alike. There was no place for any consolation: the living human being, as still now, was consumed by toil, groaning, impiety, pain, sickness, and misery. The devouring earth forever destroyed the body and that most flourishing form of the dead; and hell, with the everlasting punishment of an eternal and implacable prison, afflicted the soul banished into bearable darkness. Neither those above nor those below spared the image of God: for death had claimed the whole dominion for itself.

III. When these things had long remained so, the most skilful craftsman of all things, the Son of God—whose wisdom has no end and whose strength no measure—descended from heaven in love for his image. He illumines the dwelling of the virgin’s womb, and there encloses God in a human being. He also takes on human form and a mortal condition. He teaches that justice gains immortality; by deeds he fulfils his commands. Finally, he accepted death, so that, having conquered it, he might rise again and, for the human being by means of the human being whom he bore, bring both the hope of conquering death and admission to the rewards of immortality. Thus it came about that, just as through one man’s condemnation condemnation came upon all human beings, so through one man’s justification the justification of eternal life might extend to all human beings (Rom. 5:18). Do you now see clearly that in the assumption of humanity there was providence, in the Passion mystery, and in the Resurrection the highest good?

IV. Here, first of all, we must know that the human constitution is composed of two different and opposing things, joined together in a discordant harmony, with the soul enclosed within the outlines of the body. Hence two lives also have been granted us by God. One is that by which, unknowingly, we are brought forth by nature under a law shared with beasts; this is bodily life and therefore brief. The other is the life of the soul, which we ourselves acquire in this life through faith from the living stream of the sacred font: noble and eternal. For the soul which conquers the world by recognizing and observing true religion and true justice must necessarily enjoy, as the immortal reward of its labour, immortal blessedness.

Hence within the human being a hidden war rages at every moment, as each part strives to subdue the other, according to the Apostle’s words: “The flesh desires against the spirit, and the spirit against the flesh; these two are opposed to one another” (Gal. 5:17).

Notes

[Col. 0332D] The reading seems to be “of gold and silver metal.” In the Venetian edition and the Pompignan manuscript, *metallo* is incorrectly printed. A little later we have written *strues congeris* (“you heap up piles”) from the Remigian manuscript. In the other manuscripts and editions, *struis congeries*. Then, in place of *cassa* (“futile”), the Urbinate manuscript has *cassas*, and the Vatican manuscript *cassatur*.

[Col. 0333B] *Magnopere* (“with great labour”) in place of *magno opere*, *labore*, etc.; see Treatise VI, note 9.

[Col. 0333B] The printed editions read: *est illa, cum interim, quam nostra sunt, videmus*. To restore a fairer sense, we altered the punctuation, deleted *cum* on the authority of the Remigian and Pompignan manuscripts, and wrote *quae* for *quam* from the Venetian edition; for the sense seems to require *videamus* (“let us see”) rather than *videmus* (“we see”). Once the proof, described as easy, has been omitted, the transition is made to the things that are ours. The Remigian manuscript has *et illa* for *est illa*. Perhaps it would be better to write after *est*: “But meanwhile let us consider those things,” etc.

[Col. 0333B] The Pompignan and Urbinate manuscripts express this sentence differently: “What, Christian, if the truth must be spoken, you abhor in images, you worship in your own inner chambers.” Nor is *quoque* lacking in Zeno or in the Venetian edition.

[Col. 0333B] Gold and silver coins, serving as currency to be spent for daily needs, bore engraved images of rulers—that is, emperors. Hence Zeno adds: if you spend them, they are money.

[Col. 0333C] The images engraved on coins were not actual idols, as Cardinal Baronius mistakenly understood this passage in his notes on the second edition of the Martyrology for 12 April. Rather, Zeno calls the coins themselves “images,” because they displayed portraits of emperors and other customary coin-devices. If they are not spent, as coinage ordinarily is, but kept, as avarice causes them to be, they are rightly called idols, on the basis of Psalm CXXXIII: “The idols of the nations are silver and gold,” etc. Thus Zeno in some manner convicts the avaricious of idolatry. On the same reasoning, in Treatise III, section 6, he called costly garments and proud ornaments an idol, because some regard them as sacrosanct.

[Col. 0333C–0334B] Testimonies of many authors make clear that the luxury of ancient garments chiefly shone in gold, partly woven in and partly sewn on. The ancient author of the book *On the Good of Chastity*, in the appendix to Cyprian (our edition, vol. IV, col. 826), mentions sewn-on gold. Spartianus calls a cloak “sprinkled with gold” in his *Alexander Severus*, when he relates that this emperor, wishing to restrain extravagance in the use of gold, ordered that royal ladies alone should be content with a single gold-sprinkled cloak and a *cyclas* containing no more than six ounces of gold. Garments also glittered with sewn-on golden bands or strips, which our countrymen call *galloni*; these are called gilded *paragaudae* in Law XI, *On woollen garments*. From this we learn that there were also silken *paragaudae* woven with gold. That several such *paragaudae* were used is clear from Vopiscus, who mentions garments called *dilores* and *trilores*, that is, adorned with two, three, and so forth bands or strips. The Alexandrian Chronicle mentions golden stripes by which garments were distinguished. Besides the gold shining in garments, gold also glittered from the neck and on the arms, as we shall say in the following note and in note 16. Sandals and slippers too were adorned with gold, so much so that Pliny, book XXXIII, chapter 3, and Valerius Maximus, book IX, chapter 4, observed golden nails fastened beneath slippers. Hence we understand how Saint Zeno could call a woman’s whole body gilded.

[Col. 0334B] The printed editions wrongly read *mollibus* (“soft things”) for *monilibus* (“necklaces”). Properly, *monile* signifies an ornament for the neck, as is clear from Virgil, *Aeneid* I.658, and Ovid, *Metamorphoses* X.264. More broadly, however, Jerome says in his commentary on Isaiah 3:17 that *monilia* can in one word signify all ornaments. Zeno indicates the weight especially of gold and jewels, by which women, though burdened—as Ambrose says, *On Naboth*, book I, chapter 5, section 23; Gaudentius, Treatise 23, p. 161; and Jerome in his letter to Laeta—were nonetheless strong enough to bear them, though found delicate in other respects. Hence the author of *On the Good of Chastity* (our *Patrology*, vol. IV, col. 826, appendix to Cyprian) says: “Women, delicate in everything, are stronger than men for the burdens of vices”—he is speaking of gems and the rest of women’s adornment.

[Col. 0334C–0334D] *Rigor* means the immobile state of a body. Here, however, we infer that the stiffness caused by the gold with which women were burdened was particularly conspicuous from Lampridius, who says of Severus: “Even in a linen tunic—that is, an undergarment of linen—he thought gold the madness of fools when stiffness was added to roughness.” Linen undergarments were striped with purple or gold. Purple stripes made them rough; hence Severus himself refused to use purple on linen undergarments, customarily giving this reason: “If they are of linen in order to have nothing rough, what need is there of purple?” Golden stripes, moreover, made them additionally rigid; therefore he judged those mad who, not content with the roughness of purple, also used gold, so that stiffness might be added to roughness. Virgil, *Aeneid* I.649, is relevant:

> A robe stiff with figures and gold.

From this it is sufficiently inferred that stiffness is especially characteristic of gold. Hence the author of *On the Good of Chastity*, in the passage just cited, after condemning gold woven into garments, asks: “What are rigid metals doing amid the delicate threads of the warp?” Ambrose, *On Virgins*, book I, chapter 9, seems beautifully to depict the stiffness of women attributed by Zeno to gold when he observes that they walk like the litters of processions.

[Col. 0334D] Note the ancient custom of raising the hands in prayer, as priests now do during the solemnities of Mass. See Tertullian, *On Prayer*. From Ambrose, *On Naboth*, book I, chapter 5, section 25, we likewise learn that hands laden with gold could not easily be raised.

[Col. 0334D–0335B] These words sufficiently suggest the astonishing weight of gold hanging from women’s necks. Ambrose agrees, *On Penance*, book II, chapter 9, section 88: “You see women burdening their ears with pearls and bending their necks, which they would do better to bend to Christ than to gold.” Read Clement of Alexandria, *Paedagogue*, book II, chapter 12, and Commodian, *Instructions* 60.

[Col. 0335B] This word is written in Latin letters in the manuscripts. Since it has been naturalized in popular Latin speech, it ought to have been written in Latin, not Greek, as it appears in the printed editions. More concerning this word, which signifies repentance and confession of sins, will be discussed in note 40 to Treatise XIV, book II, where the holy bishop again mentions *exomologesis*.

[Col. 0335B] *Per* is absent from the Pompignan manuscript.

[Col. 0335B–0335D] Petronius Arbiter, chapter 124, calls such people inheritance-hunters (*heredipetae*). Not only the holy Fathers but even pagans condemned this type of person. Cicero, *On Duties*, book III, says: “Even genuine inheritances do not seem honourable to me if they are sought by deceitful flatteries of service, not by truth but by pretence.” Ambrose likewise inveighs against those who seek inheritances by hunting for them, *On Duties*, book III, chapter 9, section 58. The method by which spouses, especially from spouses, commonly sought inheritances in Zeno’s age may be inferred from Ammianus Marcellinus, book XXVIII, chapter 4: “A wife, as the old proverb says, by hammering the same anvil day and night compels her husband to make a will; and the husband urgently presses his wife to do the same. Legal experts—that is, those who suggest the form of a will—are enlisted on both sides, one in the bedroom and the other, his rival, in the dining-room, to deal with opposing claims. Along with them are engaged rival interpreters of the entrails of victims: the former lavishly promising prefectures and the burial of wealthy matrons, the latter intimating that preparations needed for the approaching funerals of men must be made.” Thus each spouse sought an inheritance from the other by calling both legal experts to argue contrary cases and haruspices, interpreters of entrails, to bring each hope that the other spouse would die sooner. Jerome indicates another device in his letter to Furia: “Marriage contracts are now written for you, so that later you may be compelled to make a will. The husband’s illness will be feigned; and what he wishes to make you die from, he himself, intending to live, will bring about.” Lucian, in the *Dialogues of the Dead*, in other words, and Quintilian, Declamation 325, suggest another way in which people sought inheritances: one showed the other a will in which he had appointed him heir, in order to remind him that he ought plainly to do the same in return.

[Col. 0335D] The Remigian manuscript and Venetian edition read *intuemur* (“we behold”); the Pompignan and Vatican manuscripts, *laetantur* (“they rejoice”); the Urbinate, *laetentur* (“may they rejoice”); the Toledan, *lactantur* (“they are suckled”). The reading of the Veronese edition pleased us, although the reading of the Remigian manuscript and Venetian edition is not displeasing.
