[Col. 0335D] Those captured by barbarians after the battle of Hadrianople in 378 seem to be indicated here; see Ambrose, *On Duties*, book II, section 70. More on this is discussed in Dissertation I, chapter 2, section 8.

[Col. 0336B–0336D] “Deadly edicts” are commonly called edicts commanding that death be inflicted. Thus Saint Gaudentius, Sermon XVII, p. 194, calls Diocletian’s edicts, by which persecution of Christians was decreed, the deadly edicts of an unjust king. In the same sense Saint Cyprian, Letter 52 to Antonianus and Letter 56 to the Thibaritans (our edition, vol. IV, col. 349), mentions deadly edicts issued against Christians. See also Macrobius the Donatist in the appendix to Optatus, p. 308, Dupin edition. Ambrose calls it a deadly decree, vol. I, p. 232, Benedictine edition. Salmasius therefore, in his notes on Capitolinus, *Life of Antoninus Pius*, p. 64, thinks that Zeno, as a contemporary of pagan persecutions, speaks of edicts ordering Christians to sacrifice to the gods. But since Saint Zeno flourished under Christian emperors in the fourth century, as we have shown in Dissertation I, chapters 2 and 3, it is established that other deadly edicts are meant here. Lucifer of Cagliari, in *On Dying for the Son of God*, p. 246, vol. 4 of the *Bibliotheca Patrum*, calls them deadly edicts; but he does not mention that they had been issued, rather he in some way urges Constantius, who favoured the Arians, to issue them so that sound faith might display greater courage: “Add fiercer executioners, more savage avengers, who may attack with the sword, crucify, burn with fire, or tear our entrails and limbs with any unheard-of kind of punishment, God’s devoted soldiers resisting your deadly edicts . . . .” Yet although in the period of the Arians some persecutions against Catholics occurred, in which some met death, others were punished with exile, and still others were harassed by various penalties—as we have shown more fully in the dissertation cited—nevertheless we believe from the entire context that Zeno had in view not deadly edicts issued in those persecutions, which Catholics could not evade by any gifts, but other edicts issued somewhere against the captives just mentioned. Ambrose indeed, *On Duties*, book II, section 70, counts rescuing people from death among works of generosity; he speaks of captives among barbarians, some of whom, unless ransomed, were subjected to death. See section 137 of the same book II of *On Duties*.

[Col. 0336D] We supplied *duris* (“harsh”) from the Toledan, Pompignan, Vatican, Urbinate, and Zeno manuscripts and the Venetian edition. The harsh condition appears to mean the grievous labours by which those captives were oppressed. In this sense the author of Treatise 57 says that the Hebrews were afflicted in Egypt by King Pharaoh with harsh conditions, that is, grievous labours. Likewise slavery is called a condition because slaves were bought into slavery on the harsh condition of labouring. Hence Arnobius, book III, speaks of imposing the condition of slavery. This explains Tertullian, *On Idolatry*, chapter 12: “I was conditional,” that is, I was bound to specified tasks by the condition of slavery.

[Col. 0336D–0337B] It has always been regarded as a religious duty to wrap the bodies of the dead in some garment, lest they be buried naked. Ecclesiasticus XXXVIII: “My son, shed tears for the dead . . . cover his body.” For this same rite, celebrated also among the pagans, see Lactantius, book II, chapter 4; Apuleius, *Florida*, book I; Arnobius, book V; Juvenal, Satire III; and others. Among Christians the following of Prudentius is commonly understood to refer to it, revealing both the customary kind and colour of the garment:

> It is customary to spread forth linen garments,
> shining with bright whiteness.

Read Jerome, *Life of Saint Paul the First Hermit*.

[Col. 0337B] Marchese Scipione Maffei, *Verona Illustrata*, vol. I, book VIII, p. 408, octavo, citing this passage in praise of Veronese generosity, thinks that the reading should be *avaritia subacta* (“greed subdued”).

TRACTATUS XI.—The Venetian edition bears the heading: “On the Evils of Greed.” This treatise may perhaps seem too brief, so that it should be called a fragment of a treatise rather than a treatise. But since the discourse appears complete enough from its beginning and end, and since the brevity of some of Zeno’s treatises is otherwise established, we dare affirm nothing.

[Col. 0337C] If the discourses against greed listed above are not indicated by this word, then it surely alludes to the preceding reading from sacred Scripture, in which greed hateful to God had been impressed upon the hearers.

[Col. 0337C] The phrase “sacred law” indicates sacred Scripture, which some pagans are known to have attacked. Patricius Junius, in his notes on Saint Clement’s First Epistle to the Corinthians, section 47, aptly observed that the word “Gospel” was sometimes used so as to include not only the Gospels properly so called but also other books of the New Testament. Thus Saint Clement in the passage cited calls Paul’s First Epistle to the Corinthians “Gospel”; similarly Saint Gregory of Nyssa, writing to Theophilus of Alexandria against Apollinaris, calls a passage from the Epistle of John by the same name. Cotelerius confirms this from book I, chapter 5 of the *Apostolic Constitutions*, and from Origen’s preface to his commentary on John and his commentary on Matthew 21:45. Likewise, it is evident from John 10:34 that not merely Moses’ Pentateuch but the entire Old Testament is called “law”: the passage of Psalm LXXXI, “Is it not written in your law, I said, you are gods?”, is called law; and in John 15:25, “The word written in their law, They hated me without cause,” comes from Psalm XXXIV:19. Paul likewise, citing Isaiah, says: “It is written in the law” (1 Cor. 14:21). Zeno’s testimony further teaches us that the whole Scripture, not so much of the Old as of the New Testament, was called sacred law, since some pagans whom he censures here were striving with equal effort to attack not only the Old but also the New Testament. Similarly, in Treatise III of the present book, section 2, the author, about to cite two Pauline testimonies from the New Testament, calls it sacred law: “Nor shall I cease to prove this from the testimonies of sacred law, whose words are these”; and he immediately adds two apostolic testimonies. If one asks whom Zeno may have meant among pagans devoting their efforts to attacking books of both Testaments, besides Celsus, Porphyry, and Julian—whom Jerome, in the preface to *On Ecclesiastical Writers* and in *On the Best Method of Translating*, chapter 3, recalls as having sharpened their pens against sacred Scriptures—Lactantius, *Divine Institutions*, book V, chapter 3, names a pagan instigator of persecution who wrote two pamphlets against Christians. In them, he says, the man attempted to prove the falsity of sacred Scripture as though it contradicted itself. He set out certain passages that seemed mutually contradictory, enumerating matters so numerous and so intimate that at times he seemed to belong to the same school. From *On the Deaths of the Persecutors*, chapter 16, we learn that this instigator was Hierocles, who urged Diocletian to raise persecution against Christians. Whether Saint Zeno censured one of these or another person from whom the objection between texts of Genesis and Paul was also excerpted and resolved by the author cannot be determined.

[Col. 0338C–0338D] “The book of nature’s birth” means the book of Genesis, of which Moses was author. If the term “nature” is referred not to “law” but to the “book of birth,” Saint Zeno surely meant that he spoke of the part of Genesis in which the origin of nature is described—the part to which the discussion of the creation of the first human being belongs. Philastrius, chapter 108, cites the same book of Genesis by a title not greatly different from Zeno’s: “In the book of the creation of the world, that is, in Genesis”; and again, chapter 79: “In the book of Genesis, that is, of the creation of the world.” The manuscripts write *Moysei* for *Moysis*.

[Col. 0338D] Some printed editions and manuscripts read *replicavit*. Cicero, in his speech for Sulla, chapter 9, and elsewhere, uses *replico* in the sense of reading and turning over.

[Col. 0338D] The Venetian edition reads *dubiumque non*; the other editions and some codices, *dubium quoque*. We judged *cum* (“since”) more suitable to the sense than *quoque* or *-que*.

[Col. 0338D] Some codices read *excussum*.

[Col. 0339C] The reader addressed here is to be understood as the person discussed at the beginning of the treatise, namely one who had repeatedly read over the sacred books.

[Col. 0339C] The Venetian edition reads *quid si fieri*.

[Col. 0339C] The Veronese edition and the Toledan and Zeno manuscripts read *publicatur*; the Urbinate, *praedicatur*. We corrected it from the Remigian and Pompignan manuscripts and the Venetian edition.

[Col. 0339C] Here *sacramentum* plainly signifies the incarnation of the Word. See Treatise II, note 54.

[Col. 0339C] We added *et* from the manuscripts and the Venetian edition.

[Col. 0339C] The Remigian, Toledan, and Pompignan manuscripts read *non multipliciter*, incorrectly.

[Col. 0339C–0339D] In composing this treatise Saint Zeno appears to have had Lactantius before his eyes; he sometimes transferred several thoughts from the books of the *Institutions* into this work in virtually the same words—unless, through long reading, Lactantius’s thoughts had become fixed in Zeno’s mind and escaped him without his noticing while he wrote this treatise. We thought it worthwhile carefully to indicate in the notes each place that displays some imitation. The principal passage is this one now under consideration. Lactantius, *Institutions*, book II, chapter 10, writes: “Then God himself made for himself an image that could feel and understand; that is, he formed the human being from the clay of the earth according to the form of his own image, than which nothing can be more perfect. But the image that can feel—that is, which feels (for *sensibile* is then taken both for what feels and for what is felt)—and understand is the soul, not the body.” Saint Zeno will discuss this more fully and brilliantly in book II, Treatise 19.

[Col. 0339D–0340C] We supplied “from the very fountain of his own spirit” from the manuscripts and the Venetian edition. The author did not thereby believe that the soul was a portion of the divine nature cut off, as it were, from God. Elsewhere he plainly teaches that it is infused and created by God, and shortly afterward calls it God’s image. But because Scripture says that God breathed it in, he affirmed that it was infused from the very fountain of the divine spirit. Lactantius similarly writes, *Institutions*, book II, chapter 12, section 3: “For, when he had formed the body, he breathed into it a soul from the life-giving fountain of his spirit.” There can be no doubt that Zeno drew from this source. Lactantius himself, who vigorously and expressly maintained the creation of the soul in many places, wrote somewhat harshly in book VII, chapter 5: “God clothed and wrapped his own spirit in an earthly body.”

[Col. 0340C–0340D] This etymology derives from Lactantius, who says, *Institutions*, book II, chapter 10, section 3: “He was called *homo* because he was made from *humus*”; and again, *On the Wrath of God*, chapter 10, section 43: “The body of man was made from earth, whence he received the name *homo*.” Ambrose, *On Duties*, book III, chapter 3, section 16, and Isidore, *Origins*, book II, chapter 1, support this etymology. Vossius defends it against Quintilian in *Etymologicum*, V, *homo*, as does Coelius Rhodiginus, *Ancient Readings*, book II, chapter 10. See also Andreas Masius, preface to his commentary on the book of Joshua, p. 4. This same etymology is approved in the ancient treatise *On Lazarus*, which, though published among the Zenonian works, we have relegated to the appendix and shall probably show in the preface to be attributable to Potamius, a Catholic bishop.

[Col. 0340D] Lactantius expresses a similar thought somewhat differently, *Institutions*, book II, chapter 12, section 17: “That accuser, envying the works of God, directed all his deceits and cunning toward deceiving the human being.” The word *criminator* seems indeed to have been drawn by Zeno from this. A little later, the Pompignan manuscript has *accipit* for *accepit*.

[Col. 0340D] This is an outstanding testimony to the tradition of original sin, a sin contracted by hereditary condition and the cause of all the punishments of this life; it also required the eternal punishment of hell, unless the Son of God redeemed us.

[Col. 0340D] The Pompignan manuscript reads *religatam*.

[Col. 0341C] See Dissertation II, chapter 3, concerning this formula.

[Col. 0341C] Here too Saint Zeno, from Lactantius, *Institutions*, book VI, chapter 10, section 1, has assimilated some things into his own substance and style, sometimes in the same words. Speaking of the incarnation of the Word, Lactantius says that it descended to earth in the form of a human being and in a mortal condition, so that, after performing the office of teacher, it might be handed over into the hands of the ungodly and undergo death, in order that, after death too had been conquered by power, it might rise again and bring to the human being whom it had assumed and borne both hope of conquering death and admission to the rewards of immortality. In Zeno’s text, for *postremo suscepit mortem* (“finally, he accepted death”), the Pompignan manuscript writes *postremam suscipit mortem* (“he accepts the final death”).

[Col. 0341C] The Toledan, Pompignan, and Zeno manuscripts and the Venetian edition read *unius hominis* (“of one human being”).

[Col. 0341C–0341D] Lactantius states this briefly in *Institutions*, book II, chapter 12, section 7: “Therefore the human being was made from different and opposing things . . . which he ordained should struggle against one another in the human being, so that if the soul, which comes from God, should prevail, it might be immortal and dwell in perpetual light; but if the body should conquer the soul and bring it under its rule, it might be in darkness and death.” From the earlier words the holy bishop took two or three; the thought of the rest supplies the subject of the remainder of the treatise, which he expounded at length and most eloquently in his own style.

[Col. 0341D] The Veronese edition wrongly read *et quia est* (“and because it is”) for *quae est* (“which is”). We corrected it from the Venetian edition and the Pompignan manuscript.

[Col. 0341D] In the Veronese edition, after *ipsi* (“ourselves”), the following words were added contrary to the evidence of the first edition and the manuscripts: “with God moving and helping.” More concerning this addition and the correct understanding of the passage, see Dissertation II, chapter 5.

V. From this point, the whole flesh, overflowing with delights, wreathed in the various gifts of the seasons, promises, displays, presents, and bestows manifold and deep riches; it puts forward its own appearance. Its face, ever uncertain through the accommodating mirror into whatever forms may please it, it changes daily with exotic colors: pampered by the toil of the palate, bright with bathing, smeared with perfumes, varied in its dress, entirely distinguished by necklaces, made pleasant by the splendor of banquets, drenched with wine [Col. 0342B], crowned with gems or flowers, wanton in the festivity of eyes and amusements, blind in avarice, stirred by lust, proud upon the downy tomb of a delicately swelling and yielding, resilient bed.

[Note: [Col. 0341D] “Yielding” (*restabile*) is said of that which readily gives way. Caelius Aurelianus, *Tand.* 4, 1, 6: “For you, things readily yielding.” Salmasius reads *restatilis thori* (“of a yielding bed”) in Zeno in the *Historia Augusta*, p. 193, and explains it thus: feather beds commonly do this, especially those filled with the finest and most delicate down: when pressed by sitting, they sink down and, as it were, swell back. This elegant passage of Zeno is cited by Lindenbrog in his observations on Ammianus Marcellinus, book XVI, p. 48.]

It flings itself playfully through groves, fountains, meadows, Baiae, cities, and country places; surrounded by every pleasure, inviting both sexes, every soul, every age, to desire itself by this formula:

[Note: [Col. 0342C] Baiae was a most delightful town of Campania, exceedingly suited, by reason of its warm waters, both to pleasure and to the restoration of health. Consequently any places delightful and abounding in luxuries came to be called “Baiae,” as here by Zeno. Similarly Cicero, *Pro Caelio*, ch. 16: “What woman had not always some openly appointed lover, to whose garden, house, or Baiae all pleasures might freely resort as of right?” From this passage of Cicero Hotman inferred that the Romans had in their gardens pleasant pools, supplied through aqueducts, in which they swam for relaxation, and called these too “Baiae.” Indeed, from Tibullus it appears that all warm waters were called Baiae; for thus he writes, book III, 5, 3:

> By the most sacred waters of Baiae;

[Col. 0342D] and Martial, book X, epigram 13:

> And couches should not surround dining rooms with but a single Baiae.]

[Note: [Col. 0342D] Among Latin writers of good standing, *carmen* (“song,” “formula”) is found used of certain solemn formulas expressed in fixed words, pronounced by jurists, praetors, Salii, fetial priests, and others. Livy, book II, ch. 24, calls the solemn formulas of treaties and oaths a *carmen*; and in ch. 26 he calls a capital sentence a *carmen*, as do Cicero, *Pro Rabirio*, ch. 4, and Pliny, *Panegyricus of Trajan*, chs. 63 and 92, who calls the prayer at the elections a *carmen*. This festive and well-known formula, therefore, taken from the Book of Wisdom, could suitably be called a *carmen* in Latin by St. Zeno.]

“The span of our life is short and wearisome, and there is no refreshment at a human being’s end; nor is anyone known to have returned from the lower world. For we were born from nothing, and after this we shall be as though we had not been; and there is no return from our end, because it is sealed, and no one returns” (Wisdom 2:1 ff.).

[Note: [Col. 0342D] The Venetian edition reads *nostri*, masculine; but *finis* (“end”) is also found as feminine [Col. 0343D] in Cicero and others.]

And below: “Come, therefore, let us enjoy the good things that exist [Col. 0343A], and make use of creation quickly, as in youth. Let us fill ourselves with precious wine and perfumes, and let not the flower of the season pass us by. Let us crown ourselves with roses before they wither. Let no meadow escape our luxury. Everywhere let us leave signs of gladness, for this is our portion and this our lot” (vv. 6 ff.).

[Note: [Col. 0343D] The Reims manuscript reads “as youth”; the Pompignan manuscript, “as with youth.”]

VI. On the other side, the spirit, like a most experienced general, foretells the flight of all these things: that one must stand most promptly under arms, keep watch diligently, fortify the camp on every side, defend the royal standards bravely and steadfastly; bear heat, cold, hunger, thirst, and every danger with equanimity; trample the world underfoot by renunciation; and regard death itself—followed by everlasting blessedness—not so much as death as the prize of victory. In plain discourse it preaches thus through John: “Do not love the world, nor the things that are in the world. If anyone loves the world, the love of the Father is not in him; because all that is in the world is the desire of the flesh, the desire of the eyes, and worldly ambition, which is not from the Father but from the desire of the world. And the world will pass away, and its desire. But whoever does the will of God remains forever, just as God remains forever” (1 John 2:15 ff.).

VII. But someone says: If this is so, why is the spirit especially defeated within itself? First, because humankind assents more readily to pleasure than to virtue, and consequently loves delights more than labor. Added to this is the fact that it finds the goods of the flesh without seeking them; and it prefers greater—or even lesser—present goods [Col. 0343C] to immense but delayed goods. But the goods of the spirit are not merely invisible, delayed, and hidden: they are also placed upon so steep a height that no one can reach them except with the utmost difficulty, great labors, and dangers. Add that the former moves upon its native soil; the latter is a stranger. The former, without any consideration of merits, lavishly heaps its gifts indiscriminately upon anyone, especially the undeserving, so as to gather crowds to itself; the latter never rewards anyone unless he first, as a conqueror, passes beyond the claims of death. This causes present things to be preferred to future things, evils to goods, fragile things to solid, false things to true, earthly things to heavenly, temporal things to everlasting—whether through fear or unbelief.

[Col. 0344A] VIII. O blind human mind! Why are you deceived by the fleeting charm of present bodily things? Why do you compel the better to be subjected to the worse?

[Note: [Col. 0343D] The Urbino manuscript reads *subjicere* (“to subject”). A little later, in place of *pecuinam*, the Venetian edition has *pecudem* (“a beast”). But the former reading must be retained with the manuscripts, for it refers to the mind, which Zeno addresses. *Pecuinus* occurs in Apuleius, *Metamorphoses*, book VIII, near the end.]

For when you know what is written, “All flesh is grass, and all its glory is like the flower of grass” (Isaiah 40:6), if you take care of it, you acknowledge yourself to be beastlike. Do you love its strength? Any pain breaks and subdues it. Its beauty?

[Note: [Col. 0343D] Thus we have corrected the text from the manuscripts, since the printed editions add after *pulchritudinem* (“beauty”), *ejus? et commutabilis* (“its? and changeable”).]

It is a slight and changeable thing, most easily destroyed by a single fever or by any injury whatever. Look: its stewards or governors, the eyes, are extinguished by some blow and sink away. Is it not a living corpse?

[Note: [Col. 0343D] The printed editions wrongly read *unum*; and shortly afterward, “all [the bones] by emaciation,” transposed in the editions, we have restored from the manuscripts.]

Look: a wasting lung, eaten away by rich phlegm, lays bare in loathsome emaciation all the bones of the body which bears it.

[Note: [Col. 0343D] Tertullian, *On the Spectacles*, final chapter, uses *sputamentum* for “phlegm.”]

Will not that stripped-of-flesh, touchable shadow in some sense become abhorrent even to itself?

[Note: [Col. 0344D] Just as *concarnatus* from *concarno* is read in the same Tertullian, *On the Flesh of Christ*, ch. 20, and *decarno* occurs in Apicius 7.9 and Vegetius, *On Veterinary Medicine* 2.27, so Zeno could write *excarnata* (“stripped of flesh”) from *excarno* in Latin.]

It would take too long to go through each detail. Look: some fatal illness throws the whole mechanism upon a bed. Look: the storm of death presses in from every side. Does not she who was the mistress of pleasures immediately become the prey of diseases? At last death claims the fallen remains for itself, soon to bring upon them the punishments of Gehenna.

[Note: [Col. 0344D] The Urbino manuscript reads *paratura*, “about to prepare.”]

Then that fleshly mime comes to an end; and all those ornaments, now offering no aid to the bloodless body, do not heal it—except that they are snatched away from one still living by falsely mourning people.

[Note: [Col. 0344D] Since everything in mimes was fictitious and simulated, the term *mimus* (“mime”) is metaphorically applied to other things having more appearance and pretense than truth. Suetonius, *Caligula*, ch. 45, calls a sham and false triumph a *mimus*. Augustus himself, when near death, in the same Suetonius, ch. 99, and likewise Seneca, *Letters* 81, called the course of human life a *mimus*.]

IX. Therefore, brothers, as true Christians, “like guests and strangers, abstain from fleshly desires, which wage war against the soul” (1 Peter 2:11). Nor let your resolve be broken because you do not know its hidden nature and form. If you despise it because you do not see it, you may similarly despise God, who is invisible [Col. 0344C]; for whoever does not love its likeness follows necessarily in hating the truth.

[Note: [Col. 0344D] He calls the soul the likeness of God, which Scripture teaches was created in God’s image.]

Thus fools prefer the body to the soul, an idol to God. But we who have put off Adam have put on Christ (Ephesians 4:22); we who, under God’s instruction, have learned what the force, outcome, and recompense of the flesh are, and what those of the soul are (Galatians 3:27); we who do not fail to know that in the victory of the flesh both are destroyed, while in the victory of the soul both are saved—let us pursue the better things, at least with the same zeal with which we pursue evils. No one has any excuse, especially since our affair has been entrusted to the will, as the Prophet says: “Before a human being are good and evil, death and life; what he chooses shall be given him” (Ecclesiasticus 15:18). Hence there is no doubt that our will grants victory to whichever side it joins; and that in its resurrection it will either enjoy an everlasting reward or be punished with a corresponding penalty.

[Note: [Col. 0344D] The editions read *justitiam* (“righteousness”); from the manuscripts we have substituted *victoriam* (“victory”). But because the author says that the penalty will be paid and the reward enjoyed in the resurrection [Col. 0345B], beware of supposing that St. Zeno agreed with those who, in great error, referred both matters to the day of judgment. For here the discourse concerns only the body, and the soul is said to pay the penalty or receive the reward in the body at the resurrection, because before then it will not experience in the body the penalty or reward due to the body. On Zeno’s Catholic opinion concerning this doctrine we have written more fully in Dissertation II, ch. 10.]

99. TRACTATE XIII. On circumcision.

[Note: [Col. 0345B] TRACTATE XIII.—The Venetian edition gives this title: “On the twofold circumcision, namely the carnal, which consists in cutting off the foreskin, and the spiritual, which is through baptism.” [Col. 0345C] In the margin of the Reims manuscript appears this note: “On the octave of the Lord: the bishop’s ninth lesson.” This codex was for the use of the Church of Verona; and on the octave of Christ’s Nativity this sermon was recited by the bishop himself during the sacred offices. From this may be learned the antiquity, at least in some churches, of the special reading assigned ninth place; we think, however, that it was read only at vigils of the more celebrated feasts, and on Sundays after the psalms sung during the night watches. Concerning such Sunday vigils, this instruction occurs in the ancient order of the Churches of Cambrai and Arras, published from the papers of Pithou in the appendix to the code of canons of the Roman Church: “Let the lessons be read distinctly with all decorum, and the responses be chanted; but let the ninth lesson be from the homilies of the Fathers, on the Gospel.” The whole homily upon the Gospel is to be read by the deacon, priest, or bishop—as, at Verona at least on this night, was done—unless the arrival of dawn [Col. 0345D] should postpone it. It is therefore not surprising that Zeno’s treatise on Circumcision, which is not very short, should have been taken to be read in full in this church, since it was permissible to break it off at dawn.]

I. Most carefully, dearest brothers, it seems that an account ought to be given of circumcision, of which the most blessed Paul made mention not only in the present reading but also in several places, so that the Christian may know the truth and the Jew his error.

[Note: [Col. 0345D] This tractate had been preceded by a reading; the reading seems to have been taken from some epistle of Paul in which circumcision is treated at length, especially from the Epistle to the Romans or to the Galatians.]

For the Jew often boasts with loud outcries that this is the nobility of his race, this the power of the heavenly sacrament, this the lawful mother of eternal life, this the perpetual companion of the kingdom to come, and that without it no one can at all attain the knowledge of God. Therefore I think that first of all we must define what circumcision is [Col. 0345B], so that only then may it rightly be recognized what sort of thing it is. Circumcision, brothers, is a circular scar made by the knife, at the cost of a rounded wound.

[Note: [Col. 0345D] *Circulata* is used passively from *circulo*, from which Cicero, *On Famous Orators*, ch. 54, used *circulantem*, and Apuleius, *Florida*, book II, *circulaverat*. Seneca, *Letters* 88, used *circulatus* in an active sense.]

If the Jew considers this a glory, then, to say nothing of other examples, greater is the glory of one who, in honor of his goddess—

[Note: [Col. 0345D] The priests of Cybele—also called the Idaean goddess and Mother of the Gods—were called Galli, after the river Gallus in Phrygia, according to Festus, under “Galli,” and Herodian, book I, ch. 11. Their chief was called the Archigallus, as Tertullian reports, *Apology*, ch. 25. In honor of their goddess they cut off their genitals: “Men, counterfeiting their own nature and no longer enduring to remain males, transformed themselves into women, believing that they would thereby do what was most pleasing and honorable to the Mother of the Gods”; thus Athanasius, *Against the Gentiles*, no. 26, p. 24. Bardesanes, a celebrated Syrian writer in the reign of Marcus Aurelius, says in his dialogue *On Fate*, addressed to Antoninus, preserved in Eusebius, *Preparation for the Gospel*, book VI, ch. 8: “In Syria and Osroene there are also Galli, and in Phrygia many are emasculated for the Mother of the Gods.” Ovid, *Ibis*:

> In frenzy you will cut yourself, and those whom the Cytherean mother  
> Urges to Phrygian rites with their vile members.

[Col. 0346C] The same is reported by Pliny, book II, ch. 49; Juvenal, *Satires* VI, near the middle; St. Justin, *Apology* I, commonly called the Second; Herodian, in the cited passage; Prudentius, *On the Crowns*, hymn 10; and Augustine, *City of God*, book VII, ch. 10.]

—indeed, an ugly old woman and a lover—

[Note: [Col. 0346C] We have supplied this from the manuscripts and the Venetian edition.]

[Note: [Col. 0346C] Zeno calls Cybele a lover because, inflamed with love and maddened by longing for the most beautiful youth Attis, she went mad, as Diodorus writes, book IV, ch. 5. See Catullus in his poem on Berecynthia and Attis.]

—offered in more shameful rites not a small piece of skin from that member, but the member itself, cut off at the root [Col. 0346A].

[Note: [Col. 0346C] The Venetian edition reads *ministeriis*, “rites” or “services.”]

The reason, plainly, is that after the sacrament a Jew can sin through this part, whereas the other thereafter can no longer sin through this part.

II. It follows that he must declare whether he maintains this circumcision to be carnal or spiritual. If spiritual, why does he glory in flesh? If carnal, it cannot benefit the soul, because “flesh and blood cannot possess the kingdom of God” (1 Corinthians 15:50). Furthermore, circumcision conflicts with the Sabbath, which the public proclamation declares must not be violated by any work at all.

[Note: [Col. 0346C] A person who circumcised a boy on that day under the compulsion of the command was not truly guilty of violating the Sabbath. But St. Zeno understands a certain material violation, as the schools speak, not a formal one; for circumcision in itself is reckoned among servile works, which would truly violate the Sabbath unless necessity compelled it. For this reason the ancient author of the *Questions and Answers* attributed to St. Justin, question 27, though showing that circumcision was permitted on the Sabbath day, nevertheless acknowledges that circumcision is of such a kind as to involve violation of the Sabbath. St. Zeno likewise affirms the same thing: not because circumcision truly conflicts with the Sabbath, since it tends to God’s honor and is done by reason of necessity and divine command, but because in itself—especially according to the Jewish notion, by which they imagine the Sabbath to be violated by any manual work—it belongs to its violation. *Praeconat*, found below, derives from *praeco* (“herald”) and means to proclaim aloud, as heralds do. Laws were promulgated through heralds. An “open law” is one which commanded rest from every work on the Sabbath and was promulgated with solemn ceremony, as we learn from Exodus 31.]

For it often happens that a son is born to him on the Sabbath, and that on the eighth day—that is, when the Sabbath returns—unless he circumcises him according to the law, the infant’s soul will perish from his people. Here, dearest brothers [Col. 0346B], let him choose what he wishes: let him circumcise or defer it. If he circumcises, he violates the Sabbath; if he does not circumcise, then, with the destruction of an innocent soul, he has rendered void the ordinances of the appointed circumcision.

[Note: [Col. 0346D] The Reims manuscript reads *vacavit*, “rendered void.”]

For God granted the privilege of circumcision to the eighth day alone, not to the seventh and not to the ninth; and consequently it is necessary [Col. 0347A] that both be void if one of the two can be invalidated.

III. What then? Was not righteous Abel found without this wound (Genesis 4)?

[Note: [Col. 0347B] *Est* is absent from the editions; it has been supplied from the Reims, Zeno, and Pompignan manuscripts.]

What then? Is Enoch not recorded as having been translated whole by God (Genesis 5)? What then? Was not uncircumcised Noah, while the flood raged, appointed by divine providence heir and father to the human race (Genesis 6, 7, 8)? What then? Was not that supreme priest Melchizedek, most acceptable to God, ignorant of this scar (Genesis 14)? What then? Was not the people of Nineveh delivered by God’s mercy while retaining their foreskin (Jonah 3)? God would surely have commanded all these to be circumcised if he had foreseen that circumcision of the flesh was necessary for the salvation of those whom he loved. Certainly he would have done so to Adam himself beforehand.

[Col. 0347B] IV. But perhaps someone may say: “Then was Abraham a sinner, that he was circumcised? Or was he righteous, and ought not to have been circumcised?” Abraham, brothers, was both a righteous man and yet necessarily circumcised.

[Note: [Col. 0347B] *Necessario* is missing in the Vatican manuscript.]

For what does Scripture say? “Abraham believed God, and it was reckoned to him as righteousness” (Romans 4:3). Does it say, “Abraham was circumcised, and it was reckoned to him as righteousness”? Therefore, since Abraham was justified whole, like Enoch and the others, and was circumcised afterward—

[Note: [Col. 0347B] *Abraham* is not read in the Vatican, Zeno, and Pompignan manuscripts.]

—it is clear that circumcision was not necessary for Abraham, but was provided as a designation [Col. 0348A] of the Jewish people, who were to be carnal.

[Note: [Col. 0347B] St. Zeno seems to have held that circumcision was given to the Jews merely as a sign by which they might be distinguished from other peoples, not that they received righteousness from it or that original sin was removed by it; likewise St. Justin Martyr, who in his *Dialogue with Trypho*, p. 243, wrote: “Abraham received circumcision as a sign, not for righteousness”; and at p. 366: “This circumcision of yours was given as a sign, not as a work necessary for the accomplishment of righteousness.” Augustine and other Fathers thought otherwise, teaching that original sin was removed in circumcision; see more in Estius, on the *Sentences*, book IV, distinction 1. But it is one thing that righteousness was formerly bestowed by God upon Jews in circumcision, another that they attained righteousness by the power of circumcision. The first is most true, and is not denied by Zeno or Justin. The second is false, since it is the settled opinion of Catholics that the sacraments of the old and new law do not differ merely in this, that their ceremonies and outward rites differ. The Council of Trent, Session VII, canon 11, condemned that view because of the word “merely”; rather, as Eugenius IV had explained somewhat earlier in the decree given to the Armenians, the old sacraments did not cause grace but only foreshadowed the grace to be given through Christ’s passion, whereas ours both contain grace and confer it on worthy recipients. Augustine indeed says, *Expositions on Psalm 73*, no. 2: “If we distinguish the two Testaments, Old and New, the sacraments are not the same . . . because some sacraments give salvation, others promise the Savior.” The sacraments of the New Testament give salvation; those of the Old Testament promised the Savior. See also book XIX, *Against Faustus*, chs. 13–14, where he calls those Old Testament sacraments prophetic announcements, since by them the Savior was only promised, not grace produced, except through faith by which the Savior, proclaimed beforehand in those sacraments, was believed to be yet to come—as the same holy doctor shows more fully. This one thing, therefore, is what St. Zeno, after Justin Martyr, denied to circumcision: that it should of itself produce true righteousness; this belongs only to the sacraments of the new law. Hence we know that our author departed in no respect [Col. 0348B] from the Catholic and sound understanding of the other Fathers.]

Finally, it bestowed nothing upon him, because he pleased God before, not after, he was circumcised; and he received the reward not of circumcision but of the promise earned in uncircumcision (*acrobystia*).

[Note: [Col. 0348B] The editions read *in hac robusta merita*; the Pompignan manuscript, *in ac robusti, ac meritae*; the Reims and Vatican manuscripts, *in hac robustia meritae*; *robustia* is likewise read in the Zeno manuscript. Without doubt one must read *in acrobustia meritae*. For *acrobustia*, or *acrobystia*, is the Greek noun frequently used by Paul the Apostle, ἀκροβυστία, rendered in Latin as *praeputium* (“foreskin”), and like some other Greek words could be expressed in Latin letters. Thus the best sense emerges: Abraham received the reward, not of circumcision, but of the promise earned in *acrobystia*, that is, while uncircumcised; namely, since the faith by which he believed God while still in the foreskin was reckoned to him as righteousness. The passage of Paul in view is Romans 4:9–10: “Abraham’s faith was reckoned as righteousness. How then was it reckoned? In circumcision or in uncircumcision? Not in circumcision, but in uncircumcision.” In both places, as always elsewhere, ἀκροβυστία occurs in the Greek text of Paul.]

It is therefore evident that Abraham bore in himself the type of a twofold people: by the mark of circumcision he represented the Jew; by the righteousness of faith, the Christian.

[Note: [Col. 0348C] Here also *credulitas* means “faith”; see note 6 on Tractate I.]

V. Add that this circumcision does not so much fail to promise salvation as point out the place and source of sin.

[Note: [Col. 0348C] From the Vatican and Urbino manuscripts we have added *non*, since this particle is joined by Zeno in section 6 with the same verb and in the same sense: “God not only does not promise salvation to circumcised persons of this kind,” etc. For the sense of this passage, see note 13.]

[Note: [Col. 0348C] On what is to be thought of this claim that Adam’s sin is attributed to fleshly pleasure enjoyed contrary to the prohibition, and from what source this opinion arose, we have written more fully in Dissertation II, ch. 4.]

For Adam, when he plucked the forbidden fruit with this member [Col. 0348B], thereby introduced into the human race the law of death.

[Note: [Col. 0348D] In the Verona edition, contrary to the authority of the manuscripts, the words were transposed thus: “When he plucks the forbidden fruit with this member.” Likewise, the Paduan edition, which alone reads *decerpsit* (“plucked”) with the Zeno manuscript.]

Therefore God necessarily gave this sign to a people given to lust, so that, when it marked the place of the maternal guilt, it might also know that other sins must be avoided. “By your own mouth, Christian, you have defeated yourself,” he says. “Therefore I too maintain that I possess eternal life, because I recognize that God has especially provided for me a cure for death.”

[Note: [Col. 0348D] *Cura* is here used for “cure” or “medicine,” as is clearly evident from what follows. It is similarly used by Grattius, *Cynegetica*, v. 366; Celsus, *On Medicine*, ch. 10; Petronius Arbiter, fragments, p. 668 of the new edition; and Claudian, *On the Gothic War*, v. 120. The editions read *annexam curam* (“an attached cure”). The Pompignan, Toledo, Vatican, and Zeno manuscripts read *anxiam* instead of *adnexam*. Both are absent from the ancient Reims codex, which has *cura praestita* in the ablative, but incorrectly. It has been aptly noted by Sparaverius that “death” may mean sin or condemnation.]

The Jew would rightly say this, brothers, if this cure could benefit both sexes.

[Note: [Col. 0349C] Justin Martyr likewise presses this argument against circumcision in his *Dialogue against Trypho*, p. 32: “Moreover, since the female sex cannot receive carnal circumcision, it is sufficiently evident that circumcision was given as a sign, not as a work of righteousness. For God gave to women also whatever belongs to righteousness and virtue.” Cyprian says the same more briefly, *Testimonies*, book I, ch. 8. There one may also observe that the same examples of Adam, Abel, Enoch, Noah, and Melchizedek are gathered together as Zeno expounds them here more fully; we have observed the same in Justin in the passage cited, and in Tertullian, *Against the Jews*, ch. 2 and following. There can therefore be no doubt that these were customary arguments among the ancient Fathers, by which, as Cyprian says, the first, carnal circumcision was shown to have been set aside.]

For, since a more serious matter remains, he acknowledges that he will perish unless he seeks the truth.

[Note: [Col. 0349D] Sparaverius preferred to write *remedium* (“remedy”), saying, “For I do not see what truth could mean in this place.” But neither he nor we dare to correct against the manuscripts; perhaps the author took “truth” to mean the true medicine, distinct from circumcision, which truly cures both sexes.]

For if it cures Adam, it certainly cannot cure Eve, in whom lies the whole sum of transgression, by this remedy.

[Note: [Col. 0349D] The printed editions had *in quo*, referring it to Adam; and someone likewise noted in the margin of the Pompignan manuscript that *in quo* should be corrected. Certainly the whole sum of sin is more truly found in Adam than in Eve, since original sin flowed to posterity especially from him as its head. But we have printed *in qua* not only by the authority of the Reims and Pompignan manuscripts, but especially because, from the context, the sentence seems more fittingly referred to Eve. “The sum of transgression” may be said to be in her insofar as she persuaded Adam to sin, and nevertheless the remedy of circumcision does her no good. The holy bishop called Eve the representative of all women, to whom circumcision was not given, just as he named Adam for all men.]

What then? I see that it benefits not even the man himself, because the cutting around of this mark is subject to the power of the heart. Unless the heart has been cleansed by the spiritual sacrament of true circumcision, the human being in question will perish forever. For the flesh can suffer loss, but cannot rule the mind. The mind itself, by the command of its royal power, compels the body subject to it to perform the servile offices required by the desires of its will; and if it is vicious, each person may commit as many crimes as he has members [Col. 0349B].

VI. Finally, Scripture marks out the Jews in this manner, beginning with their ears: “I called to them,” it says, “and they did not hear; they will call to me, and there will be none to hear them.” Likewise it says of the hands: “For your hands are defiled with blood, and your fingers with sins. Your lips have spoken iniquity, and your tongue devises injustice” (Isaiah 59:3). And again, concerning the other members: “Their throat is an open tomb; with their tongues they have dealt deceitfully; the poison of asps is beneath their lips; their mouth is full of cursing and bitterness; their feet are swift to shed blood; destruction and misery are in their ways, and they have not known the way of peace; there is no fear of God before their eyes” (Psalm 13 [23] ff.).

[Note: [Col. 0350C] The Zeno and Pompignan manuscripts, with the Venetian edition, read *amaritudinis* (“of bitterness”). Then, in place of *contritio* (“destruction”), the Urbino manuscript reads *contentio* (“strife”).]

And concerning circumcision itself, in symbolic language it says: “They inquired, and they proclaimed by their rods; they were led astray by a spirit of prostitution and prostituted themselves from their God” (Hosea 4:12).

[Note: [Col. 0350C] “In symbols” is written to indicate that circumcision is denoted in Hosea by the figurative expression which the text presents; for ancient writers often use *symbolum* for an obscure and metaphorical sign, as may be seen in Basilius Faber, *Thesaurus Eruditionis*, under “Symbolum.” Likewise Gellius, book VI, ch. 11, used *symbolice* for “figuratively.”]

Recognize, then, Jew, even if late, the wretched and obliterable distinction of your error [Col. 0350A], and tell us whether you observe circumcision or the law.

[Note: [Col. 0350C] The Vatican manuscript reads *miserrimum*, “most wretched.” Shortly afterward, in place of *et dic* (“and say”), the Reims, Vatican, and Pompignan manuscripts read *edic*, “declare.”]

If circumcision, the law is unnecessary for you, because righteous Abraham, who lived by faith, won God’s favor by faith, not by law. If the law, despise that circumcision of yours, which we see set aside by the law, as Jeremiah says: “Thus says the Lord to the men of Judah and to all who dwell in Jerusalem: Renew among yourselves renewal, and do not sow among thorns. Circumcise the foreskin of your hearts, lest my wrath go out like fire and burn, with none to quench it” (Jeremiah 4:3–4).

[Note: [Col. 0350C] Thus restored from the manuscripts and the Venetian edition.]

You see, therefore, brothers, that God not only does not promise salvation to persons circumcised in this way, but also threatens the punishment of unquenchable fire unless they are lawfully circumcised in heart [Col. 0350B].

[Note: [Col. 0350C] The Urbino manuscript reads “See.” Shortly afterward the Zeno manuscript has *quia* (“because”) for *quod* (“that”) [Col. 0350D].]

But Moses himself, whose disciples they often claim to be, speaks to Israel in the same spirit, saying: “In the last days God will circumcise your heart and the heart of your seed, to love the Lord your God” (Deuteronomy 30:6).

VII. From this I shall now speak to you again. Pharisee, answer: where do you hold the heart to be situated? If it is in the region of the breast, why do you measure the lower parts by a shameful wound? If, as indeed you rightly suppose, it is in the lower parts, you undoubtedly surpass all the sacrilegious, since, rejecting the saying of Moses, you presume that by this offensive offering of the body you can please God.

[Note: [Col. 0350D] Zeno says “you measure the lower regions” for “you circumcise the foreskin situated in the lower part.” A little later he calls this same foreskin an offensive contribution of the body, offered to God in the place of a tribute. A manuscript of Toledo has *existimas* (“you suppose”) for *aestimas* (“you judge”); but in Zeno you will often find *aestimo* used for *existimo*.]

“It has now been fulfilled in me,” he says, “through Joshua son of Nun, at the Lord’s command, the second circumcision which Moses had foretold. For it is written: ‘And God said to Joshua: Make for yourself very sharp stone knives; and sit down, and circumcise the children of Israel a second time’” (Josh. 5:2).

[Note: [Col. 0350D] The Verona edition read *abscinde* (“cut off”); the Venetian edition, *abscides* (“you shall cut off”); the Pomp. and Zen. manuscripts, *abscide et circumcide* (“cut off and circumcise”). But from the Rem. codex it seemed preferable to write *adside* (“sit down”), since this reading agrees with the text of the Septuagint interpreters, from whom these words were translated into Latin. Lactantius also, who similarly cites this text, *Divine Institutes* IV.17, has *et sede* (“and sit down”). Cyprian likewise, *Testimonies* I.8, has *et adsidens circumcide* (“and, sitting down, circumcise”).]

[Col. 0350C] Let us therefore see now, dearest brethren, what kind of circumcision that second circumcision performed by Joshua son of Nun with those stone knives was: whether he circumcised the heart or the foreskin. For if, according to them, we too understand this carnally, both prophets will be liable to accusation: either Moses is deceitful, if circumcision is circumcised again, so that it either does the same thing again or loses what it does not possess; or else Joshua son of Nun is a parricide, if he cuts men’s hearts with knives.

[Note: [Col. 0350D] All interpreters now acknowledge that in this passage of Scripture only one circumcision was commanded and carried out for the Jews, after they came from the wilderness into the promised land; for it is established from what follows in the same chapter of Joshua, verses 6 and 7, that the Hebrews did not practise circumcision in the wilderness. Why it was nevertheless said, “circumcise a second time,” although the commanded circumcision was the first, is very conveniently explained by Andreas Masius in his commentary on this passage, which, reader, you may consult. In any event, Zeno’s interpretation referred this second circumcision to circumcision of the heart, not because he thought they had already undergone a first circumcision, but because the customary opinion of the ancient Fathers—especially Justin, Cyprian, and Lactantius, whom we have no doubt Zeno followed—held that in that circumcision, which truly was the first, a second, circumcision of the heart had been prefigured. Indeed St Jerome, in his commentary on Galatians, chapter 3, p. 424, vol. VII of the Verona edition, though he admits that the Hebrews had previously remained uncircumcised in the wilderness, nevertheless plainly affirms that the circumcision commanded “a second time” concerned the spiritual circumcision of the heart. Finally, for forty years no one was circumcised in the wilderness: they lived entirely without mingling with another people. As soon as the people crossed the bank of the Jordan and the Jewish multitude poured into the land of Palestine, circumcision provided against the error which would arise from intercourse with the nations. But the statement that the people were circumcised a second time under Jesus their leader signifies both that circumcision, reasonably practised in Egypt, had ceased in the wilderness, and that believers were to be cleansed by the Lord Jesus Christ through spiritual circumcision.]

VIII. But far be it from us, brethren, to charge spiritual men with any error, especially since the prophecy has now arrived at the truth of what it said. For Joshua son of Nun bore the image of Christ, who is known to be the true saviour of all both in deeds and in name. For since he himself was also called the Rock (1 Cor. 10:4), he rightly made stone knives. Hence too, not without reason, he gave Simon—upon whom he built the Church—the name Peter (Mark 3:16), that is, he appointed apostles and all disciples as men shaped by his teaching and sharpened by the file of the Holy Spirit.

[Note: [Col. 0352C] The Rem. manuscript reads, “shaped by the Holy Spirit”; the Toledo and Zen. manuscripts, with the Venetian edition, “shaped, [by the] Holy Spirit.”]

As their tongues utter saving admonitions, like certain spiritual knives, he cuts away, among peoples who believe, according to Moses’ saying (Deut. 30:6), not the foreskin of the flesh to man’s harm, but the foreskin of the wicked heart for man’s increase.

IX. But perhaps someone may still ask why he too received the seal in the flesh, if it was not necessary for him. Brethren, receive the explanation of this question. Therefore, he who had come to give life to man had necessarily, through being man, to fulfil every ordinance of the Law, lest he be thought a phantom. For he could not have been either the end of the Law or the true Christ if he had omitted anything which another person might have supplied for the salvation of humankind.

[Note: [Col. 0352C] The Venetian edition reads *oportuisset* (“ought to have been supplied”).]

Furthermore, it was proclaimed that he would be David’s son according to the flesh. Unless he corresponded to the paternal seal of his race, he would neither have been David’s son, nor could Christ have come except as the son of David. He was therefore circumcised because he had been promised to the Jews; he was born with a foreskin because he was to benefit uncircumcised nations forever.

X. We have spoken of the first, fleshly circumcision, which belongs to the Jews. Now let us briefly set forth the second, spiritual circumcision, which is ours. It possesses such power that it began from a woman, a thing impossible for the former circumcision.

[Note: [Col. 0352C] Namely, from the Blessed Virgin, his mother, who cuts away every vice of the heart, as the author explains below. It was customary for the Fathers to attribute the beginning of salvation to the Blessed Virgin, just as they recognize that the beginning of perdition proceeded from Eve. See, among others, Irenaeus, III.33 and V.19, and Tertullian, *On the Flesh of Christ*, 17.]

Finally, the care of circumcision begins with the woman who had first sinned. And because the devil, entering by persuasion through the ear, wounded and killed Eve, Christ, entering Mary through the ear, cuts away every vice of the heart; and, while being born from the Virgin, heals the woman’s wound.

[Note: [Col. 0352C] The Verona edition has *suasionem* (“persuasion”); but the reading of the Pomp. and Zen. manuscripts and of the Venetian edition was judged better.]

Receive the sign of salvation: integrity followed corruption, and virginity followed childbirth. Adam likewise is circumcised by the Lord’s cross; and because, through the woman who alone had touched the deadly tree, both sexes had received death, conversely the whole human race was made alive through the man suspended on the tree. And lest the beginning should seem not to have been restored wholly to its original state, the first man is consummated on the cross; and when he has happily fallen asleep, likewise from his side, struck by the lance, not a rib is torn away, but through water and blood—the spiritual body of the spiritual woman, that is, baptism and martyrdom, is poured forth—so that Adam might lawfully be renewed through Christ, and Eve through the Church.

[Note: [Col. 0352C] That martyrdom supplies the place of baptism when someone cannot obtain water-baptism, and that the one baptism is signified by water and the other by blood flowing from Christ’s side, may be confirmed by this testimony. Other Fathers likewise attest it. It is fitting to quote one passage from Tertullian, *On Baptism*, 16: “Indeed, we also have a second washing, namely that of blood, of which the Lord said: ‘I have a baptism with which to be baptized,’ although he had already been baptized. For he came through water and blood, as John wrote, that he might be baptized with water and glorified with blood; and consequently might make us, called by water, chosen by blood. He sent forth these two baptisms from the wound of his pierced side, so that those who believed in his blood might be washed with water, and those washed with water might also drink his blood. This is the baptism which represents a washing not received and restores one lost.”]

[Col. 0352C] 107 XI. By this mystery, brethren, both men and women are circumcised. We are enrolled not by the seal of the Holy Spirit, but by its sign.

[Note: [Col. 0352D] *Signaculum* (“seal”) is said of bodily circumcision. Though the common Latin translator of Paul may call it a *signum* (“sign”), because it truly marks the body, yet insofar as it concerns the spirit it is called a seal of righteousness. In the language of the Fathers, moreover, a spiritual sign is nothing but that which affects and marks the soul. For this reason the sacraments of the new Law are called signs: they not only signify grace but also produce it. Those of the Old Testament, however, which merely signified grace, when referred to a spiritual sense, are found to be called only seals. St Cyprian, *Testimonies* I.8, takes “seal” of fleshly circumcision and “sign” of spiritual circumcision, just as St Zeno does. That seal does not profit women, but all are marked with the Lord’s sign. Similarly Minucius Felix, ch. 35, calls the former a bodily mark, but the latter a sign of innocence and modesty, by which, he says, Christians are readily recognized, as St Zeno said that they are reckoned by the same sign. Perhaps here, however, by the name “sign” he means baptism; see the following note.]

By this circumcision we lose nothing, but find ourselves growing through heavenly increase. We do not shed blood in a barren observance, but retain the blood of modesty, which we often eagerly pour out when, in persecution, by dying for the Lord’s name, we lay waste the devil. Finally, we cut off what we ought not to have, which we recognize was superadded to humanity by the enemy, as the Lord says: “The kingdom of heaven is like a man who sowed good seed in his field; but while men slept, his enemy came and sowed tares among the wheat” (Matt. 13:24–25).

[Note: [Col. 0353C] “What we ought not to have” here chiefly means original sin, which is cut off by the sign of the Holy Spirit—that is, by baptism—and therefore the heart is circumcised. Hence Cyprian defends, in Epistle LIX, that baptism is spiritual circumcision. That original guilt is chiefly being discussed here is further confirmed by the subsequent mention of “the contagion of dreadful seed,” which surely denotes sin propagated through generation, from which we are said to be cleansed by that sign, or spiritual circumcision. See note 40.]

We necessarily tear these tares out by the roots through circumcision, so that, cleansed from the contagion of dreadful seed, we may remain whole in the fertility of the Father’s seed. This circumcision, I say, is not excluded from granting salvation to human beings by day, night, hour, sex, age, condition, place, or race; rather, it is always found glorious in all persons.

[Note: [Col. 0353D] The editions and most manuscripts read “in granting salvation to man.” We corrected this from the very ancient Rem. manuscript. A little later the Vatican manuscript has *gloria* (“glory”) for *gloriosa* (“glorious”).]

In short, the first circumcision cuts the flesh; the second cuts the vices of the soul. The former uses iron, this one spirit; the former cuts a part, this one the whole person; the former only the male sex, this one both sexes; the former the foreskin of a little patch of skin, this one the foreskin of all worldly desire. The former is tied to the eighth day; to this belong all seasons, days, hours, and every moment.

[Note: [Col. 0353D] Baptism is plainly being discussed here, and thus it is confirmed that it was above called the sign of the Holy Spirit. For what other spiritual circumcision, benefiting men, women, and children alike and capable of being administered on any day, can there be but baptism? In Cyprian’s time a certain African named Fidus held that no one ought to be baptized except on the eighth day, in order that the law prescribed for circumcision might be observed. But St Cyprian refuted this error in a council; he discusses it at length in Epistle LIX.]

The former cannot help even a dying infant before or after the eighth day; this one, from the very cradle of infancy to the final departure of every age, grants its saving gift to both sexes. The former delights in blood; this one in grace. The former in an image; this one in truth. The former in loss; this one in gain. The former acts as a captive under the Law; this one grants all people in Christ the freedom of good faith.

Therefore you who have been circumcised with a circumcision not made by hand, in the stripping away not of flesh but through the circumcision of our Lord Jesus Christ, labour lest your wholeness be mutilated; lest the spiritual foreskin of rising sins, and nakedness wrongly resumed—as in Adam and Eve—condemn you again; lest the new person appear to possess anything of the Jew or of the Gentile.

[Note: [Col. 0354B] The Rem. manuscript reads *videantur* (“may appear”).]

For both are fleshly; both are without fruit. Hence there is no doubt that neither foreskin nor circumcision is anything, but only the observance of God’s will is necessary for those who live faithfully.

[Note: [Col. 0354B] The editions and some manuscripts have *solum* (“only”); the reading of the Rem. manuscript was judged preferable. The Rem. manuscript, together with Pomp. and the Venetian edition, adds “Amen” at the end.]

109 **TRACT XIV. On the Spiritual Building of the House of God.**

[Note: [Col. 0354C] **TRACT XIV.**—This tract appears to have been delivered at the dedication of a church built at Verona, as we have observed more fully in Dissertation I, ch. 2, §4. The manuscripts bear this title: “On the Building of the House of God by Solomon”; and John, priest of Verona, in his manuscript *Imperial History*, as well as William Pastrengo and Peter de Natalibus drawing from him, calls this tract, marked with the same title, a most beautiful exposition. The common title was preferred because Zeno’s discourse, beginning from the occasion of the church’s construction, so turns toward urging the spiritual building of God’s house that anyone can see this alone was Zeno’s purpose.]

I. I would, dearest brethren, employ a kind of triumphal discourse and multiply praises for the sacred height of this new work. Yet, although it is excellent to praise what belongs to God, this is not the chief thing, since it may be shared with Gentiles or Jews. For they too, if permitted or if they wish, may perhaps build synagogues more elegantly and erect more splendid Capitols. Yet in all these works, by sound judgment, the builders can please more than the priests.

[Note: [Col. 0354C] Since “if permitted” and “if they wish” are used disjunctively, it is unnecessary to understand both of Jews and Gentiles alike, as though both had been forbidden at the time when St Zeno delivered this tract—the former to build synagogues, the latter to erect Capitols. No laws against the Hebrews forbidding them to build new synagogues are found before Theodosius the Younger; indeed, from the laws which forbid it one may plainly infer that nothing of the sort had previously been prohibited. On this see Dissertation I, ch. 2. Therefore the reference “if permitted” should be understood solely of Gentile temples. Although under Julian the Apostate all authority had been restored to them which the emperors Constantine and Constantius had removed, by a law that temples of idols should not be opened, much less new ones erected, nevertheless under Jovian, Julian’s successor, we have no doubt that the Gentiles were deprived at least of permission to build new temples. Under Valentinian alone, however, the practice of their religion was allowed them; hence it is unsurprising if Zeno indicates that idol-temples, at least those openly accessible in the countryside, still stood: *Tract* V, Book I, no. 8, where he speaks of an unbelieving man going to temples of idols; and *Tract* XV, no. 5, where he discusses rural temples of pagans.]

[Note: [Col. 0355B] A *Capitolium*, that is, “the council-chamber of the gods,” as Tertullian explains in *Apology* 6, is often used for an idol-shrine or temple. Eumenius, in his panegyric, calls Apollo’s temple and the Capitol at Autun shrines “by far the most beautiful of all in that city.” The Synod of Elvira, canon 59, prohibits a Christian from ascending to the idol of the Capitol in order to sacrifice. See Cyprian, *On the Lapsed*, and Lactantius, I.12 and 21, and III.17, where he cites a passage from Cicero.]

What is more, throughout the whole Church of God there is either no part, or a very rare part, of a place of prayer that can even now be compared in any degree with temples of idolatry collapsing into ruin of whatever kind.

[Note: [Col. 0355C] Christian churches were customarily called “places of prayer,” whence the name *oratory* gradually became common; likewise, near the end of this tract, this place is called “of sacred prayer.” Nevertheless, St Zeno more than once calls it a church; while in the course of this discourse he argues from Paul the Apostle that only Christians themselves should be called a temple. See note 26 on Tract V. From this it is further understood how small and plain the buildings of Christian churches generally were at that time, so that none or few could be compared not only with Gentile temples but even with their surviving ruins. Since only under Constantine were Christians first permitted publicly to open churches, at the outset they either converted private houses to ecclesiastical use or, if they built places of prayer, must be thought to have constructed sacred buildings with rough, as they say, workmanship, providing sufficiently for the present need of church assemblies rather than competing in magnificence with costly temples of idols.]

[Note: [Col. 0355D] The ruin of idolaters’ buildings mentioned here cannot mean the destruction imposed by emperors through laws ordering idol-temples to be demolished, since that occurred later than can be referred to Zeno’s time. It means rather the ruin which those buildings threatened through any accident or through decay by age. The sense is that Christian places of prayer were so small that they could not be compared not only with standing idol-temples, but even with any crumbling ones—for this is how we think “sinking into themselves through any ruin” should be explained, that is, collapsing.]

For we have received that Solomon’s temple was built with splendid workmanship, and was wrought so elaborately that an observer did not know what especially to admire in it—its size, workmanship, ornamentation, or material. Thus all things combined into a single beauty, so that that perishable magnificence might be thought the fitting house of God. If this were so, it would always be found unequal in splendour to the things mentioned.

[Col. 0355B] II. But God declares that such worldly things, without a lawful and devout worshipper, are neither sufficient nor necessary for his honour, saying: “Heaven is my throne, and earth the footstool of my feet. What house will you build for me? Or what place is there for my rest? For my hand made all these things” (Isa. 66:1–2). In the Gospel too he says: “Jerusalem, Jerusalem, you who kill the prophets and stone those sent to you, how often I wished to gather your children as a hen gathers her chicks under her wings, and you were unwilling! Behold, your house shall be left to you” (Matt. 23:37–38). And again: “Not one stone shall be left upon another in the temple which shall not be thrown down” (Matt. 24:2; Mark 13:2; Luke 21:5).

Thus he rejects that temple, so immense, so remarkable, so rich, because within it there was no true temple. For this arrangement of walls is a human assembly-place; but the faithful people are the temple of God, as the Apostle says: “You are the temple of God, and the Spirit of God dwells in you” (2 Cor. 6:16).

[Note: [Col. 0355D] From this it is clear that *conciliabulum* means a place in which sacred assemblies were held, just as Livy, VII.5, speaks of holding *conciliabula* (“assemblies”). The author of *On the Deaths of the Persecutors*, ch. 15, plainly calls the very walls of churches *conventicula* (“meeting-places”), as does Arnobius near the end of Book IV. Compare Prudentius, *Apotheosis* V.778. Thus when the ancient Fathers denied that Christians had temples, they did not deny that they had definite places in which to hold sacred gatherings—for in the same works in which they denied possessing temples they expressly state that they held sacred assemblies on stated days, as is clear from Justin’s *Apology*, etc. Rather, they did not consider such places of meeting to be temples which God needed, as the idols of the Gentiles did, but merely locations suitable for gathering people together. Therefore St Zeno aptly calls them *conciliabula*, not temples. When he says that in the Jerusalem temple there was no true temple, perhaps he alludes to Revelation 21:22, where John, speaking of the new Jerusalem—which Ezekiel likewise foretold when he envisioned the construction of a new temple—says: “I saw no temple in it.”]

[Note: [Col. 0356C] As we have just indicated, it was customary for the ancient Fathers to declare that the living God had no need of temples built from material, but that the Christian people and the Church of believers itself are his living temple. See among others Lactantius, *Institutes* I.10 and IV.15; the author of *On the Deaths of the Persecutors*, ch. 15; Minucius Felix; Arnobius; and others. St Zeno surely intended this living temple when he says shortly afterwards: “With like devotion both priest and temple turn to God,” that is, the living Church of the faithful, which together with its priests offered praises and sacrifice to God.]

And this is true. For as temples resembling senseless idols suit idols, so living temples are necessary for the living God. In these alone the construction of God’s priests is both proper and enduring; by it we surpass Jews, Gentiles, and all others. But the glory is incomparable and truly worthy of God when, in one agreement and one faith, each commending the other, both priest and temple turn to God with like devotion.

Therefore rejoice, brethren, and recognize your own building in this new edifice, which you too, by the blessed size of your number, have made narrow. For precisely from the fact that this place does not contain us, it is understood that your faith contains God. Therefore, lest anyone perhaps inquire of me concerning the work, I shall briefly indicate it.

[Note: [Col. 0356C] Not only plain, as we saw in note 4, but also narrow were Christian churches generally at the beginning of the fourth century. Because of the small number of faithful who had embraced the catholic faith under persecutions, there was no need for very large basilicas; only as the number of believers gradually increased after peace was restored to the Church did it become necessary to build new and larger churches. This is clear from Athanasius, who in his *Apology to Constantius* states that the churches of Alexandria, the chief city of all Egypt, remained extremely narrow until the year 356. Since these could not hold the faithful, increasing day by day, a larger new church had been built; and, at the people’s request, it became necessary for them to assemble there on Easter Day before permission had been obtained from the emperor. See no. 14, p. 303. We know that something similar occurred at Verona. Indeed, here the multitude of believers had evidently grown so large that even the new church, said to have been sufficiently spacious and capacious in itself, was made narrow by the crowd alone. We think such an immense number of Christians should chiefly be attributed to the labours of St Zeno, so that the verse of the Anonymous Pipinian is true of him: “He led Verona to baptism.”]

[Note: [Col. 0357B] The Pomp. manuscript reads *vos* (“you”).]

III. In the foundations of the whole structure, there is not, as in the Jewish temple, a great many stones, but one great, illustrious, precious, and beautiful stone, which alone supports the whole mass of the square tower (Eph. 2:20). It is served not by an innumerably varied host of most strong columns, because seven alone suffice for it. No bronze sea is attached, because within it is the living sea of its own perennial fountain—not one that makes shipwrecked persons, but one that brings shipwrecked persons to sweet life. There is no gold and no silver, because it reckons its entire treasure in its martyrs. It does not seek light from windows, because the eternal sun remains within it.

[Note: [Col. 0357B] Casaubon reads *quadraturis* (“squared constructions”), citing this testimony in *Exercitations* 15 on Baronius’s *Annals*, no. 13, p. 360. The term occurs in Hyginus, *On Boundaries*, and Vopiscus, *Life of Firmus*. Zeno would be indicating squared stones, used in very strong buildings, from Isaiah 9:10; Ezekiel 40:42; Judith 1:2; Hermas, Book I, Vision 3; and elsewhere. Thus the first stone formerly laid in the foundations of churches was square in shape, as may be understood from an ancient inscription at Narbonne in Gruter, p. 1058: Rusticus, bishop and contemporary of Leo the Great, who built a new basilica at Narbonne, is said to have placed a square stone in the foundation. This custom also prevailed among Romans in constructing temples of the gods, as we learn from Livy, VI.5, who reports that the famous Capitoline temple at Rome, a temple of all the gods, was founded upon squared stone. But we did not wish needlessly to alter anything contrary to the authority of the manuscripts and editions, especially since the spiritual building of the Church, of which this passage speaks, is repeatedly called a tower by Zeno: first in no. 4, where he mentions the completed tower, and again in no. 5; and with a similar sense it is called a sacred citadel at the beginning. The square form is also mystically celebrated: it is attributed to the new city Jerusalem in Revelation 21:16 and Ezekiel 1. Towers likewise occur frequently in Scripture and in Hermas, Book III, ch. 19; there is no need to note more. See Jerome on Isaiah 9:10, where he interprets a tower as a temple.]

[Note: [Col. 0357C] The Pomp. manuscript corrects this to *varietatis* (“of variety”). If correction were permitted at discretion, we would rather read *innumerabili varietate* (“with innumerable variety”). The relative pronoun *cui* and what follows refer not to the cornerstone but to the mass, or Church.]

[Note: [Col. 0357D] Are the seven sacraments indicated here, by which Christ supports his Church as by columns? Or the seven gifts of the Holy Spirit, of which Isaiah speaks in ch. 11, v. 2? Or seven virtues? Or the ranks of seven orders? Ambrose discusses the number seven symbolically at greater length, Epistle XLIV, and before him Cyprian, *To Fortunatus, On the Praise of Martyrdom*, ch. 11, whose testimony Jerome cites in Epistle L to Pammachius.]

[Note: [Col. 0357D] This sea, which brings the shipwrecked to life, is undoubtedly the baptismal washing. Those who were baptized were formerly immersed in the sacred waters as though shipwrecked, as is well known from other sources. *Suavem* (“sweet”) is absent from the Rem. manuscript; the Toledo manuscript has *suam vere* (“its own truly”) in its place.]

It has three inestimable members of one fullness, one sanctuary, and twelve gates always open, which a projecting beam in the form of the letter Tau protects from hostile assault.

[Note: [Col. 0358B] It is not easy to affirm what these three members of the spiritual Church are. It seems more reasonable that the three parts of the Church are meant, commonly called Militant, Triumphant, and Purifying, from which the fullness of the whole Church is constituted. Other but less probable explanations are available, which there is no time to give. Let each person judge for himself. In fact, however, the three members of one fullness which St Zeno transfers allegorically from the material to the spiritual Church appear to be three sections of churches, separated by two intervening rows of columns, which nevertheless constitute one church. If it can be shown that the new Veronese church was built in this form, like other ancient churches, it is credible that the bishop used the example of the present building.]

[Note: [Col. 0358B] A *secretarium* was a small chamber adjoining a church, where sacred vessels and vestments were stored. Yet Mabillon observes, in his commentary on the Roman orders, vol. I of *Museum Italicum*, p. 22, §3, that the term is sometimes used for the sanctuary or presbytery itself. Among Romans, a *secretarium* was a place in which the Senate assembled; hence Christians frequently called places *secretaria* where bishops met, as is clear from many councils and their acts. This could be understood both of presbyteries and of the chambers mentioned. Perhaps here it means the part of the temple called the oracle in 1 Kings [3 Kings] 6, and there was only one sanctuary in the Jerusalem temple.]

[Note: [Col. 0358C] This word signifies the cross and refers to Ezekiel’s prophecy, 48:31, where those whose foreheads had been marked with the letter Tau are commanded to be saved from destruction. That this letter Tau bore the image of the cross was the customary opinion of the ancient Fathers. See Tertullian, *Against Marcion* III.22, and Jerome, *On Ezekiel* III, ch. 9, v. 4, where he also attests that crosses were constructed in the likeness of the letter Tau. Pamelius, in note 174 on the cited passage of Tertullian, records that in ancient manuscript missals, as they are called, at the beginning of the canon which starts with the letter Tau, he had seen an image of the Crucified painted there, with the letter Tau itself serving as the cross. Furthermore, a cross projected above the twelve gates of the church in the place of the cherubim which, in Ezekiel 41:25, are said to be carved upon the temple doors.]

113 O thing truly wonderful! It is built every day and dedicated every day; at every moment it is adorned with unfading flowers and with diverse gems, stones, and pearls. And because it is a living work, it has no roof except heaven.

IV. I shall add, moreover, what daily wages and what provision are distributed. To all alike one bread with wood is given,[^c0037-1] water with wine,[^c0037-2] salt, fire and oil, a new garment, and one denarius,[^c0037-3] which he who receives willingly, and does not despise when received, but perseveres in labor to the very end, will, when the tower is completed, dwell therein and possess immeasurable riches.
