[^c0037-1]: [Col. 0358D] The Eucharist is undoubtedly meant here, which was given to the faithful to be carried home, as is demonstrated by another testimony of Zeno, Tractate V, no. 8; see note 29 there. If anyone among us asks why it is said to have been given “with wood,” we shall first observe that perhaps *cum lino* (“with linen”) should be read, not on account of the linen of women, who, when about to communicate, received the Eucharist in cloths, while men alone received it with bare [Col. 0359A] hands—a matter discussed at length by Fr. Edmond Martène, *De Antiquis Ecclesiae Ritibus*, book I, part I, ch. 4, art. 10, no. 8—not, I say, on account of women’s linen (for St. Zeno, speaking generally, includes a rite common both to women and men), but because of the linen wrapping or pouch in which both men and women carried the Eucharist home.

Cardinal Bona, *Rerum Liturgicarum*, book I, ch. 25, §12, mentions pouches and cloths in which offerings were received. Yet the acts of St. Birinus, in Surius under 3 December, suggest that the Eucharist was likewise distributed in small cloths: they report that Pope Honorius gave him a covering upon which he kept the body of Christ, and in which, wrapped and suspended about his neck, he always carried the Lord’s body with him. Similarly St. Adalbert, bishop of Prague, as his life inserted in the fifth Benedictine century relates, no. 37, after once offering the sacrifice, ordered whatever remained from his own communion and that of the baptized to be collected, and, wrapped in a very clean cloth, kept it for himself.

Closer to Zeno’s time is what St. Ambrose reports, *On the Death of Satyrus*, book I, no. 43: namely, that Satyrus, still a catechumen and in danger of shipwreck, requested the Eucharist from Christians travelling with him; he had it tied in an *orarium* and wrapped the *orarium* around his neck. An *orarium* was a linen cloth or handkerchief, as may be seen from many passages in Du Cange. The Greeks, moreover, kept the Eucharist in churches in a pouch which they hung on the walls, as we learn from various documents cited in book III of the work entitled *The Perpetual Faith of the Church concerning the Eucharist*.

But these matters expressly concern the Eucharist carried on journeys or kept in churches; whether in the same way the Eucharist was given to every Christian returning home, no one states [Col. 0359C] with certainty. Elsewhere no manuscripts and no editions have *cum lino*. We therefore judged that *cum ligno* (“with wood”) should be retained. This suggests that the Eucharist, enclosed in a wooden box, was given to the faithful so that they might carry it home more carefully, lest any fragment should fall.

This makes easier sense of what St. Zeno affirms in Tractate V, no. 8, concerning a Gentile husband joined to a Christian wife: “Perhaps, seizing your sacrifice, he will strike your breast and disfigure your face.” For blows and violence of that kind well suit wooden cases in which the sacrifice—that is, the Eucharist—was stored, so that they could bruise the breast and disfigure the face. Cyprian perhaps refers to this when, in the book *On the Lapsed*, he mentions a woman who attempted unworthily to open her box, in which was the sacrament of the Lord, but was deterred by fire bursting forth from it, so that she did not dare touch it.

Nor is it surprising that so humble a material as wood was used for receiving the Eucharist. St. Jerome, Epistle 4 to Rusticus of Augustodunum, relates that the body of Christ was distributed by Exsuperius of Toulouse in a wicker basket. John the bishop and Epiphanius the presbyter attest the use of such baskets in distributing the Eucharist in their memorandum sent to Pope Hormisdas, tome V of the Councils, p. 655 of the Venetian edition, when they recall baskets—certainly woven of twigs and wicker, as is clear from Palladius and Isidore—full of the sacrament of the Eucharist, distributed to all at Thessalonica. Even in the time of Gregory XI the Eucharist was kept at Rome in a basket, according to the ceremonial of Peter Amelius, chs. 51 and 131. Certain Greeks even now, according to Furer in his *Itinerary*, p. 74, receive eucharistic bread from a basket.

Although among the ancients a *cophinus* was a measure which, according to Pollux, book IV, ch. 23, no. 168, measured liquids rather than dry goods—he adduces a notable passage of an ancient poet in confirmation—yet in the later period, according to the Glosses, it was taken to mean a basket woven from bent rods, as Isidore, XX.9, says. The Trullan Synod, canon 101, mentions vessels, not so much of gold as of other material, in which the Eucharist was received; and it is credible that the rich used caskets of precious material and the poor ones of cheap material. This testimony therefore shows that wooden boxes were in use in Zeno’s time.

[^c0037-2]: [Col. 0360A] These words express the cup’s draught. Mabillon shows, in his commentary on the Roman Order, tome I of the *Museum Italicum*, §9, p. 61, that its use continued in the Roman Church itself until the beginning of the twelfth century. “Water with wine,” rather than “wine with water,” seems to have been said for elegance, so as to correspond with the preceding “bread with wood”; therefore nothing may be inferred from this that water used in the sacrifice was thought to be taken in a greater, or nearly equal, proportion to the wine. Justin, in the Second Apology, wrote “wine and water.”

Since the ancient Fathers readily used such expressions because of the discipline of secrecy, their testimonies of this sort must not therefore be seized by heterodox persons, who chatter that Christ’s presence in the Eucharist was unknown to the ancients—a point sufficiently established by other testimonies. Beyond others, Zeno’s genius took remarkable delight in such expressions, since he frequently dealt in allegories of this kind, as is evident from his other tractates. It should further be noted that perhaps water and wine are here mentioned together to indicate baptism and the cup, of which even children scarcely baptized partook; see note VII on Tractate 32, book II.

[^c0037-3]: [Col. 0360B] Salt, fire, oil, and the new garment pertain to baptism. Fire indicates the bright lights of the neophytes, which St. Ambrose testifies were formerly used in baptism, *On the Fall of a Virgin*, ch. 5. Perhaps Zeno also indicates by “fire” that fire by which the water used in baptism was customarily tempered, [Col. 0360C] as we shall show from Tractate 35, book II, note 3. The new garment is the white clothing, which Marcellinus likewise calls a *tunica* in the *Chronicle* under the year 419. It is called new because it was fresh and not worn down by use; see note 12 on Tractate VIII, book II.

[Col. 0360C] The denarius contributed in the Church here, and placed by Zeno among the baptismal ceremonies, unquestionably pertains to baptism. It has been possible to find this singular testimony in our author alone; but he mentions the same denarius twice elsewhere, so that no doubt can arise. In Tractate 35, book II, he says: “Now the attendant at the bath stands girded, ready to provide what is needed for anointing and drying, and also a golden denarius marked by the union of three coins”; he is speaking to those about to be baptized. Again, in Tractate 42, to neophytes concerning divine providence, he says: “Lest he seem to love one more or another less, he gives to all one birth, one milk, one wage, one dignity of the Holy Spirit”; where *wage* plainly stands for *denarius*.

Was an actual denarius given to neophytes in baptism? Fr. Edmond Martène, *De Antiquis Ecclesiae Ritibus*, part I, book I, ch. 1, art. 18, published two orders of baptism: one, no. VI, from the Sacramentary book of the monastery of Gellone; another, no. 8, from a manuscript codex of St. Remigius written before the year 1000. In both, ten *silicae* are said to have been given to neophytes together with the white garments. Another Roman Order, VII, published by Mabillon, tome II of the *Museum Italicum*, p. 83, writes ten shekels; but we do not doubt that *ten silicae*, or *siliquae*, should be read, as indeed is written in Roman Order I, p. 7 of the same *Museum*. That *silicae* were a kind of denarius is clear from Gregory the Great, book IX, epistle XIV, and from the Charter of Full Security in Brissonius, *On Formulae*, book VI, in which places golden *siliquae* are repeatedly named. See also St. Isidore, *Origins*, book XVI, ch. 24.

These testimonies are indeed too late to be extended to Zeno’s time. Yet, [Col. 0361B] since it is sufficiently credible that this ceremony was not newly devised in those middle ages but derived from an ancient rite and preserved in those churches, it may perhaps have originated from the rite indicated here by Zeno and flourishing in the Church of Verona, or from some other similar rite. Nor should it cause difficulty that Zeno gives this denarius a mystical interpretation; [Col. 0361C] for every sacred ceremony always conveys something mystical, as is clear from the ecclesiastical formulae by which the white garment, salt, and so forth are given to the baptized. Indeed, since denarius, coin, or wage is constantly mentioned in Zeno’s tractates, it appears that some denarius—which mystically signified something, like salt and the white garment—was really given; its meaning we shall examine more diligently elsewhere, when a more suitable occasion arises. For when everything which Zeno mentions here was really given to the baptized, can we persuade ourselves that the denarius alone was not given?

V. It must also necessarily be recalled what is done in the temple. The priest calls; faith opens the door; simplicity brings in; understanding invites; truth persuades; fear keeps watch; discipline restrains; self-control curbs itself. Faith stands in the narrow place; chastity in the secret place; innocence in the first place; justice in the middle; patience at the end. Peace gathers; charity binds; watchfulness guards; righteousness distributes; piety ministers; purity entreats; the Spirit petitions; hope promises; wisdom, mistress of the house, bestows gifts.

Rejoice, elders: you are the supports of this work.[^c0037-4] Rejoice, young people: you are better than adamantine stones. Rejoice, children: sweet and priceless pearls of the sacred tower. [Col. 0361B] Rejoice, blessed marriages: you fashion gems for adornment better than you yourselves are.[^c0037-5] Rejoice, widows: by the foursquare character of your virtue you cleave in union to the cornerstone. Rejoice, virgins: by the honor of your bloom you adorn all this celebration. Rejoice, rich people,[^c0037-6] made truly rich by frequent and righteous distinctions; for this enduring praise of the divine work is due to the advancement of your heavenly dignity. Rejoice, poor in spirit: through you and in you the house of God is greater; for you are equal to all and surpass all the measurements[^c0037-7] by the circumference of your body. Finally, holy rich persons are few; you are more numerous.

[^c0037-4]: [Col. 0361C] In the Verona edition the printers, passing by a leap from the words “you are” to similar words in another sentence, had omitted an entire line. We supplied it from the manuscripts and Venetian edition. Only the Urbinas manuscript has *fundamenta* (“foundations”) for *firmamenta* (“supports”).

[^c0037-5]: [Col. 0361C] Children are called better gems, whom Christian spouses fashion like gems when they bring them up piously. They are called better than the spouses themselves because, in childhood while they are being educated, they are usually both virginal and innocent.

[^c0037-6]: [Col. 0361D] The new church had evidently been built through the benefactions of rich persons. Moreover, *promotio* (“advancement”), a word Zeno uses shortly afterward, occurs in Asconius Pedianus and Lampridius.

[^c0037-7]: [Col. 0361D] In the editions and some manuscripts, *praedaturas*, but incorrectly; we corrected it from the Remigian manuscript. A *pedatura* is a space bounded by a fixed number of feet, and also measurement by feet itself. See Goes’s index and Frontinus, *On Colonies*, pp. 333, 338, and 358.

VI. These, most beloved brothers, are your gifts of grace; these are the virtues by which spiritual Jerusalem is equipped, by which this new place of sacred prayer and its people are daily prepared through the providence of Christ, our God and Lord. This is our glorious labor; this the glory of all priests; this the mystery pleasing to God, this the beloved work, this living work: it is carried out bodily, but advanced spiritually. May God the almighty Father grant that, as we give him thanks in this earthly dwelling, so in the heavenly kingdoms we may render fuller thanks together with all the saints.[^c0037-8]

[^c0037-8]: [Col. 0361D] The Urbinas and Pompignan manuscripts and the Venetian edition add: “Amen.”

117. TRACTATE XV.[^c0037-9] On the Threefold Kind of Sacrifices.

[^c0037-9]: [Col. 0361D] **TRACTATE XV.**—In most manuscripts no title is prefixed to this tractate, but only, “Another tractate begins.” We transcribed the title from the Zenonian manuscript alone and the Venetian edition; [Col. 0362B] in the other editions this additional inscription is also appended: “On Psalm XLIX.” This tractate appears to have been delivered principally to neophytes, both from the words in no. 2, “Learn, newly made Christian,” and from those near the end, “Therefore, my sweetest flowers.” From these we also infer that this tractate was delivered at Eastertide, when Zeno delivered several other sermons to neophytes, to be printed in the following book. We placed it in this first book because it is much longer than the others and discusses the kind of sacrifices more fully, which suits the tractates of the first book.

[Col. 0362B]

I. In every matter, beloved brothers, unless one first knows its person and its rationale, one cannot know its truth. For this is what has made, and still makes, the Jew and the Christian worse than the Jew[^c0037-10] fail to believe that the Son of God is God. I should like them to be present for a little while and lend an ear to the reading[^c0037-11] [Col. 0363A] so that they may tell us who this God is who says: “Hear, my people, and I will speak; Israel, and I will testify to you: for I am God, your God” (Psalm XLIX). And below: “Mine is the world and its fullness. Shall I eat the flesh of bulls, or drink the blood of goats? Sacrifice to God a sacrifice of praise, and pay your vows to the Most High. And call upon me in the day of your distress, and I shall deliver you, and you shall glorify me” (Psalm XLIX.12 ff.).

If the Father speaks, brothers, who is this one to whom he grants so much? Who is he whom he calls the Most High, when he himself is the only one above whom there is no other higher? But if the Father’s words, granting every honor, are the words of the Son, you must recognize by what chains the mind of unbelievers is bound in darkness.

[^c0037-10]: [Col. 0362C] The Christians worse than the Jew, whom he censures here, are the Arians; for they, like the Jews but with a much graver crime, denied that the Son of God is God.

[^c0037-11]: [Col. 0362C] It may perhaps seem surprising to someone that psalms are said to be read, although it is certain that they were sung in church. Yet Zeno alone does not report that psalms were read, both here and in Tractate XXVII, book II, where in no. 1 he mentions a psalm read; other Fathers do so also. Among them Ambrose, Zeno’s contemporary, more than once took occasion for preaching from the reading of a psalm. Thus, for example, in *On Duties*, book I, ch. 3, no. 13: “You heard read today: ‘Be angry, and do not sin,’” etc.; and in Epistle XXII, recounting a sermon delivered at the discovery of the bodies of the holy martyrs Gervasius and Protasius, after stating at the beginning that he first felt inadequate to speak, he adds in no. 3: “But when the series of the holy Scriptures began to be read, the Holy Spirit, who spoke through the prophets, granted that we might produce something worthy of so great an assembly. . . .” In no. 4 he mentions Psalm XVIII, recited by chance reading; then, “another psalm was read,” he says in no. 7, “and it was Psalm CXII.”

Thus in that century, when no fixed reading of Scripture seems yet to have been established—hence Gregory of Tours, *History of the Franks*, book IV, ch. 16: “Whatever each person first opened in the book, he would read that also at Masses”—and Augustine relates something similar concerning the singing of psalms, *Sermon* 352, no. 1—not only were psalms sung, as we do not doubt, but other psalms were also read before the sermon, whether at the bishop’s order or by chance reading. Sometimes even the people repeated them, as is especially clear from Athanasius’s *Apology for His Flight*, near the end, where it is written: “Sitting in his seat, he ordered the deacon to read the psalm, and the people to respond: ‘For his mercy endures forever.’” If anyone wishes to hold that at this time also the custom had been introduced which in Augustine’s age was already flourishing in Africa, as the equally devout and learned Cardinal Thomasius confirms by many testimonies in the preface to the Psalms, p. 19—namely, that the reader should chant the psalms section by section and the people sing them in response—we shall not object; for this is enough to explain Zeno’s passage.

[Col. 0363D] The Zenonian and Pompignan manuscripts read: “in the day of **your** distress,” as indeed is read below in no. 3.

II. “Sacrifice to God a sacrifice of praise.” First of all, newly made Christian, learn that there are three kinds of sacrifices, lest you be led astray by some error. One is detestable, another rejected, the third pure. The Gentiles’ sacrifice is detestable; that of the Jews rejected; that of the Christian people pure.

Accordingly, as execrable as the Gentiles’ sacrifice is, so empty it is.[^c0037-12] For in their vanity they worship vain fabrications, fashioned by the measured tooth of the mother-file, at the expense of gold and silver, into every kind of form, face, sex, and age. What madness, then, is this—to procure sacrifice for things that do not know it, to bring light to the blind, to burn incense for things that do not breathe, to address prayers to the deaf; to seek protection from those whom a thief does not fear to rob?

God rightly grows angry with them, saying: “Do not walk after foreign gods to serve them, and do not worship them, lest you provoke me by the works of your hands and I destroy you” (Jeremiah XXV.6). And what these works of human hands are, the Holy Spirit declares in Psalm XCV: “All the gods of the Gentiles are demons, but the Lord made the heavens.” And in Deuteronomy (XXXII.17): “They sacrificed to demons and not to God.” And lest anyone should think sacrilege would go unpunished, Scripture again says in the same place: “Whoever sacrifices to gods shall be rooted out, except to the Lord alone” (Exodus XXII.20). This divine sentence awaits the Gentiles unless they are converted:[^c0037-13] they do not themselves know that they have either God or lawful sacrifice.

[^c0037-12]: [Col. 0363D] The editions and some manuscripts read *inane* (“empty”). We adopted this substantive form on the authority of the Toledo, Pompignan, and Zenonian codices.

[^c0037-13]: [Col. 0363D] We followed the reading of the oldest Remigian manuscript, although elsewhere *Gentes* is read; for *maneo* is correctly construed with the dative no less than with the accusative. Vergil, *Aeneid* I.257: “The unshaken fates of your people await you”; and Velleius, I.4.2: “The guardianship of ancestral rites remained to others.”

III. Now recognize also the sacrifices of the Jews rejected by God, who says to them in the book of Isaiah: “What is the multitude of your sacrifices to me? I am full of the burnt offerings of rams and the fat of lambs. I do not desire the blood of bulls and goats; for who has required these things from your hands?” (Isaiah I.11–12). Through another prophet also the Holy Spirit cries out and says: “Gird yourselves and lament, priests; mourn, all you who serve the altar, for offering and sacrifice have been taken away from the house [Col. 0364C] of your Lord”[^c0037-14] (Joel I.13). Much might be said; but it is quite idle to linger over things which now no longer exist at all.[^c0037-15]

[^c0037-14]: [Col. 0364C] The Toledo and Pompignan manuscripts read: “of **God**.”

[^c0037-15]: [Col. 0364D] That is, because the temple at Jerusalem has been destroyed; and once it was destroyed, the Jews were no longer permitted to sacrifice. Zeno again treats this matter in Tractate LX and following, book II.

IV. We shall, however, necessarily bring forward one example which both demonstrates the Jews’ sacrifice to be hateful and proves the Christian sacrifice acceptable and pleasing to God. In the prophet Malachi: “I have no pleasure in you, says the Lord, and I do not accept sacrifice from your hands; for from the rising of the sun to its setting my name is glorified among the Gentiles, and in every place incense is offered to my name, and a pure sacrifice; for my name is great among the Gentiles, says the Lord” (Malachi I.10).

“Sacrifice to God a sacrifice of praise” (Psalm XLIX.14). “Sacrifice,” he says, “to God,[^c0037-16] not to demons; a sacrifice of praise, not of reproach; and pay your vows to the Most High.” He renders all honor back to the Father, from whom are all things. And in saying, “Call upon me in your distress, and I shall deliver you,” he shows that he has carried out all things by himself. “And you shall glorify me”: this saying, brothers, you must not take in such a way that he declares the praise of his work to be due to himself alone. For in the Gospel he says: “If I do not do the works of my Father, do not believe me; but if you are unwilling to believe me, believe the works, and know that the Father is in me and I in him” (John X.37–38). It is spoken with the single significance of majesty and the undivided affection of filial love, because the praise of the Son belongs to the Father, and the praise of the Father to both.

[^c0037-16]: [Col. 0364D] The editions and some manuscripts have *et non* (“and not”); we rejected *et*, unknown to three codices.

V. Now it is fitting that we know the distinctive character of our sacrifice, which is easily known by contrast. For if a bodily sacrifice suits bodily gods, then a spiritual sacrifice is necessarily required for the spiritual God: one brought forth not from a pouch but from the heart; one compared not with foul-smelling cattle,[^c0037-17] but with the sweetest dispositions; one offered not with bloodstained hands but with pure thoughts; one not [Col. 0365A] slaughtered in order to perish, but, like Isaac, sacrificed in order to live. The apostle Paul exhorts us in these words: “Present your bodies as a living sacrifice,[^c0037-18] holy, pleasing to God” (Romans XII.1). For this is pleasing to the Lord when a pure mind has sacrificed itself to the Lord;[^c0037-19] but all other things will be of no benefit if the worshipper’s mind is not pure, as Solomon cries in Ecclesiasticus: “The Most High does not approve the gifts of the wicked” (Ecclesiasticus XXXIV.23).

[^c0037-17]: [Col. 0364D] The Venetian edition reads *brumosis*; the Verona edition, *bramosis*; but incorrectly. We have supplied *bromosis* from the manuscripts, although *brumosus* is also used interchangeably by authors. *Bromosus*, or *brumosus*, means “having a heavy, unpleasant smell,” from the Greek **βρῶμος**, “a strong smell,” and **βρωμώδης**, “fetid.” That this sense is intended is clear from Rufinus, *Lives of the Fathers*, book III, no. 39: “And when the water stank with a foul odor, he did not permit them to change it for other water.” Caelius Aurelianus, *On Chronic Diseases*, book III, ch. 2: “The corruption of things received, passing with sharpness into a foul-smelling or smoky condition,” etc. Hence we think a passage of St. Gaudentius, *Sermon* II, p. 44, should be corrected. It has been published thus: “But the reason why he established that the sacraments of his body and blood should be offered in the form of bread and wine is twofold: first, so that the spotless Lamb of God might give to a cleansed people a pure victim to be celebrated without burning, without blood, without *brodium*, that is, meat broth,” etc. In the word *brodio*, Ferrarius and Menagius thought they had detected the origin of the similar Italian word. But since all the manuscripts of Gaudentius cited by the editor’s note consistently write *sine bromo* (“without stench”), there was no reason this correction should not have been inserted into the text. For *bromus* means a strong odor or stench; Rufinus uses the word in his translation of the *Recognitions*, book II, no. 2: “Nor can I endure the stench and unpleasantness of the sea.” Thus we would read from the three codices cited by Cotelerius, p. 505. Much better, the word *brodium*, for which no example can be found in all antiquity, should be excluded from the text, as should likewise the words “that is, meat broth,” which are also absent from the manuscripts.

[^c0037-18]: [Col. 0365B] The Pompignan manuscript reads: “a **living** sacrifice.”

[^c0037-19]: [Col. 0365B] Thus in the Padua edition; the others, with the manuscripts, read: “but all the rest.”

VI. Here, Christians, ask whether your sacrifice can be acceptable—you who know every little clod, pebble, and twig of neighboring estates, yet do not know that in your own lands the shrines everywhere stand smoking; shrines which you carefully preserve by skilfully pretending not to notice them. The proof is not far away: every day you litigate lest anyone deprive you of the rights of your temples. Not only those who are such as these displease God, but also those who run about among tombs; who offer meals to the dead at stinking corpses; who, through love of luxury and drink, suddenly procure martyrs for themselves in disgraceful places, with bottles and cups; who observe days; who turn auspicious days into Egyptian days; who seek omens and, by violently cutting open the bellies of animals, seek their own safety; who embitter the yoke of marriage and, trampling affection underfoot, entrust the management of their household to substituted persons, so as to cloak the thefts of a most shameful advantage—not from love of fidelity, but of lust; who violently subject to themselves women employed in public service, thereby showing themselves more contemptible than those women are; who swell with anger, rage in lawsuits, and breed calumnies; who despoil the poor, widows, and orphans; who, neglecting the religion of God, corrupt the divine sacraments by calling others away with profane tales.

[Note: The manuscripts of Tolentino and Zeno read *glebas* (“clods”).]

[Note: These words plainly belong to the fourth century, as we observed in the first dissertation, chapter 2. Because of imperial laws, the continued attendance at shrines in rural districts for the old sacrifices was tolerated; hence worshippers of idols began also to be called *Pagani*, “country people” or “pagans.” Other Fathers of the same age teach that this was permitted only through the serious fault of owners who were Christians. It is enough to cite St Gaudentius of Brescia, bishop of a neighboring city and Zeno’s contemporary, so that no one, imagining this custom foreign to the fourth century, may argue from it that St Zeno was much earlier. Gaudentius likewise says, Sermon 13, p. 160: “Do you suppose that the lukewarm and negligent Christian loves God, who permits idols to be worshipped on his estates, who allows a shrine to demons and an altar of the devil to stand as an insult to God?”]

[Note: This passage does not concern the legal rights of temples situated in cities, since such temples and their rights did not belong to private persons, to whom Zeno here plainly addresses himself. Rather, it concerns the rights of rural temples, which stood upon private estates and under private ownership. “Rights of temples” is found used for revenues owed to temples in Ambrose, Letter XVIII to Valentinian, no. 19: “And certainly many years ago the rights of temples were abolished throughout the world.” There he signifies the revenues or public expenditures assigned to temple use. Constantine first removed them, as appears from Libanius’ Oration for the Temples, p. 473, ed. Gothofredus; Julian the Apostate restored them; and Gratian completely abolished them, as is clear from Law 20 of Honorius, *On Pagans*, Theodosian Code, and from the context of Ambrose’s letter itself. See also Theodosian Code X.1.8, *On the Right of the Treasury*. Here, however, Zeno understands temple-right differently: namely, as the right of private owners over temples or shrines constructed upon their own estates, in which, as is clear from what precedes, pagans performed sacrifices.

Law 12 of the Theodosian Code, title *On Pagans*, sheds light upon this right. In it Theodosius the Great prohibits even all private idolatrous sacrifices and orders offenders to be punished by forfeiture of the house or estate itself, which is to be assigned to the treasury, if they are discovered to have sacrificed there—provided, he says in §3, “it is proved that those places were in the legal possession of the incense-burners.” There plainly appears the right of the incense-burning owners. Section 4 follows: “But if anyone attempts to perform such a kind of sacrifice in public temples or shrines, or in another person’s houses or lands, and it is established that he acted without the owner’s knowledge, he shall be compelled to pay a fine of twenty-five pounds of gold; but an owner conniving at this crime shall incur the same punishment as the sacrificer.” The words “without the owner’s knowledge” sufficiently indicate the owners’ right. It seems possible to infer from Zeno that this right was daily litigated in its defense, perhaps because certain persons had dared to sacrifice in those temples without first seeking permission from the owners. At any rate, since owners litigated so scrupulously over the temple-right and were unwilling to demolish these shrines, though they could have done so, while others repeatedly visited them to sacrifice without having sought or obtained leave, the owners are said to preserve the shrines by dissimulation—that is, through lawsuits. We readily understand how great a fault that dissimulation was for the owners, since they could both prohibit sacrifices by virtue of their right and prevent them by demolishing the shrines.]

[Note: “Among tombs,” that is, in cemeteries, where graves of the dead had been placed and distributed throughout the countryside. That the other practices mentioned here, especially meals, were also carried out there is clear from Augustine, Letter XXIX. See the following note and note 18.]

[Note: The reading was *prandiis* (“meals”), but wrongly. What is meant here are *parentalia*, funerary observances; since these were a kind of sacrifice, their use by Christians is rightly condemned. St Gaudentius carefully warned neophytes especially to avoid them, Sermon IV, p. 57; the author of Sermon 190, p. 318 of the Appendix to Augustine, no. 2, repeats the same warning. Law 19 of the Theodosian Code, title *On Pagans*, says: “It shall not be permitted … to hold banquets in places of mourning.” Gothofredus takes the phrase *funestioribus locis* (“places of mourning”) to refer to temples; but from this testimony of Zeno we learn that it must be understood of burial-places or cemeteries.]

[Note: In former times Christians customarily celebrated sacred rites in cemeteries, both because of persecutions and out of reverence for the martyrs resting there. Hence there were edicts of Valerian and other emperors forbidding them to visit cemeteries; those caught in that religious observance were punished by death. When peace was restored to the churches, great crowds of Christians gathered at these cemeteries, and on martyrs’ feast days meals were distributed to the poor, called *agapae*, “love-feasts.” In time, as charity grew cold, this pious institution declined into gluttony and sexual immorality.

In order that self-indulgent and lustful Christians might excuse their feasts and debaucheries under some respectable name, and defend the occasion of their licence under the name of piety and religion, they proclaimed that the dead whom they visited in cemeteries or tombs, and honored with meals as though they were *agapae*, were martyrs. St Zeno exposes and refutes that excuse here. Bishops were rightly indignant that *agapae*, originally introduced under the name of charity even on the martyrs’ own feast days—a practice which indeed could not be condemned, and for which Pammachius, who about the year 397 provided a banquet for the poor at his wife’s funeral, is praised by St Paulinus in the letter addressed to him—had gradually been diverted into luxury and drunkenness.

On this matter Ambrose should be heard, *On Elijah and Fasting*, 17.62, where he rebukes those who bring cups to martyrs’ graves and drink there until evening, believing that otherwise they cannot be heard: “O the folly of men, who think drunkenness a sacrifice, who suppose that drunkenness pleases those who learned to endure suffering by fasting!” Augustine teaches substantially the same in *Against Faustus*, XX.21. In *Confessions* VI.2, as also in Letter XXIX and especially Letter XXII, he praises the bishops of Italy who had diligently—and successfully—worked to eliminate this corrupted custom from their churches. No one will deny that St Zeno was among them.]

[Note: The received reading was *Aegyptio corde candidis*, “with an Egyptian heart, [making] white [days],” which yields no satisfactory sense. Sparaverius thought that *Aegyptiaco die candidis* should be read. We judged that the text should be written as above. This reading gives an excellent sense and differs from the editions and manuscripts only by the separation of one syllable and the substitution of *s* for *r*; indeed, it occurs repeatedly and clearly in the Tolentino manuscript.

In an ancient calendar published with notes by Lambecius and written under Emperor Constantius in Zeno’s age, as also in two other very similar calendars published by Muratori, *Rerum Italicarum*, II.II, Egyptian days are frequently mentioned: two such days are marked in every month except January, which displays three. Lambecius frankly acknowledged that the meaning of these days was not yet sufficiently clear to him. From Ambrose and Augustine, however, we learn that they were days superstitiously and vainly considered unlucky and unsuitable for beginning undertakings. Ambrose, Letter XXIII.4: “Many are accustomed to avoid the following days, or Egyptian days.” Just as the days immediately following the Kalends, Nones, or Ides were held unlucky by the Romans, according to Gellius, IV.17, so too were the Egyptian days. Augustine says of them in his Commentary on Galatians, no. 35: “Our congregations are full of people who take from astrologers the times for conducting affairs. They often do not hesitate to warn us that nothing should be begun—whether buildings or any works of that sort—on the days which they call Egyptian.”

Thus in an old parchment manuscript which Lindembrog mentions as being in his possession, in his observations on Ammianus Marcellinus XXVIII, p. 184, the Egyptian days listed in order bore this heading: “Here begin the Egyptian days, on which you ought not to begin any work.” Days of this type appear to have been marked in popular calendars, called *ephemerides* by the Latins, so that, when something needed doing, one might consult the calendar and easily learn whether the day was favorable for action or not. Augustine, observing people who kept Egyptian days in the passage cited, said that they steered their shipwrecked lives by an *ephemeris*; similarly Ammianus Marcellinus, XXVIII, p. 400, speaks of an *ephemeris* “scrupulously consulted,” and earlier Juvenal, *Satires* VI: “You see worn-out calendars, and the hour is taken from a book.”

Why days thought unlucky were called Egyptian may be inferred from Zeno’s text: Romans called them Egyptian in order to mean “black,” and accordingly contrasted them with white days. Both Latin and Greek authors sometimes use “Egyptian” for “black”; see Basil Faber, *Thesaurus Eruditionis*. Thus human superstition had grown so strong that people made unlucky, or Egyptian, days out of white—that is, fortunate—ones. Yet we do not wish to conceal that the name may have derived from the Egyptians, whom Marinus, in the *Life of Proclus*, suggests were authors of observations of this sort, when he writes: “He observed the days regarded among the Egyptians as ἀποφράδες, unlucky.” Augustine, in the passage cited, seems to attribute the practice to the Chaldaeans, calling them days marked by astrologers and Chaldaeans. But Augustine may have called astrologers “Chaldaeans,” since the populace applied the name of the Chaldaeans not to a people but to an art, as we gather from Cicero, *On Divination* I.1, and from the title *On Sorcerers and Astrologers* in the Theodosian Code. When the discoverers of practices are sought, it is customary for different persons to assign them to different peoples, as many have observed. See note 18 on Book V of the *Recognitions*, p. 545, ed. Cotelerius.]

[Note: We restore *suam* (“their own”) from the manuscripts and the Venetian edition. The subject here is diviners who foretold future events by examining the entrails of animals.]

[Note: The Urbino manuscript reads *subditis*. But *subdititius*—a word found also in Cicero, Third Oration against Verres, no. 27, and in Plautus, *Pseudolus* II.4.62—means “substituted” or “supposititious.” Here Zeno seems to indicate people who entrusted care and management of their property to outsiders instead of household servants, allegedly so that those persons might manage the estate more effectively, but really so that they might shamefully use these substituted persons—whether maidservants or freedwomen—and conceal adulteries under the pretense of domestic business. We observed in Treatise IV, note 34, that “thefts” can mean adulteries. We also noted in the same treatise, note 24, that *utilitas* may mean “use,” so that *voluptatis* (“pleasure”), preferred by Sparaverius, should not be written. The editions and several manuscripts read: “not from love of fidelity, but of lust”; but we retain the syntax of the Reims manuscript.]

[Note: *Publicanae* properly were women appointed to collect public taxes, just as *publicani* were those who contracted for and administered the same public revenues. This is thought to be the sense of Cicero, Third Oration against Verres, no. 34: “He did not wish to give the woman tax-collector too much profit from the tithes.” Yet this passage of Zeno plainly shows that *publicanae* could also mean “public women,” so that any women exposed to the public—whether for collecting taxes, earning money by their bodies, or for another reason—were called *publicanae*. In this sense the holy bishop, Treatise I.4, called the Catholic faith itself *publicana*, because it had been openly exposed through the Arians and subjected to the mockery of the profane, that is, of pagans. Nevertheless, the women whom the author says here were subjected by force do not appear to be public prostitutes, with whom no force would be necessary, but entirely different women who, while performing some public duty, were violently oppressed by immoral men. The words “they show themselves more contemptible than those women are” nevertheless indicate that these women were held in contempt.]

[Note: Cyprian also three times applies the name *secta* (“religious body,” “way”) to Christian religion: Letter XXII, “modest through fear of our sect”; *On the Good of Patience*, shortly after the beginning, “the sect of our faith is guided”; and in the preface to the *Books of Testimonies*, “to the religious discipline of our sect.” Tertullian likewise says “God’s sect” in *Apology* 39, “the Christian sect” in 40, and in 46, “Unbelief is offended by the good of this sect.” See also *To the Nations* I.10. Prudentius, *Romanus*, v. 125, has “Christ’s sect.” The use of *secta* to signify communities following an erroneous religion is later.]

[Note: The Pompone manuscript and Venetian edition read *vocantes* (“calling”). Here Zeno perhaps censures those who drew Christians away to profane tales—that is, theatrical comedies. The unanimous judgment of the Fathers was that the sacraments of Christian religion, by which Christians had especially bound themselves in baptism when renouncing the devil’s pomps and spectacles, were most shamefully defiled by such conduct. For just as *sacramentum* among the Romans means an oath, so the Fathers used it for the solemn profession by which those about to enlist in Christ’s army pledged their faith. Tertullian, *To the Martyrs*, 3: “We were called to the warfare of the living God already when we answered to the words of the sacrament”—that is, at baptism, as he himself explains in *On Spectacles*, 3. Jerome, Letter to Heliodorus: “Remember the day of your enlistment, when, buried with Christ in baptism, you swore to the words of the sacrament.”]

Now let each person consider how he receives or offers the sacrifice. For as it is sacrilegious to offer it unworthily, so it is deadly to eat it unworthily, Scripture saying in Leviticus: “Everyone who is clean shall eat the flesh. But the person who eats of the flesh of the sacrifice of well-being, which belongs to the Lord, while his uncleanness is upon him, that person shall perish from his people” [Leviticus 7:19–20].

[Note: We gladly emend *sacrilegum* (“sacrilegious”) from the Tolentino and Pompone manuscripts, since it excellently accords with the adjective *mortiferum* (“deadly”) in the following clause. The editions and several manuscripts read *sacrilegium* (“sacrilege”). This plainly refutes an observation of Matthieu Larroque, who, concerning this treatise of Zeno—formerly entitled *On Psalm 49*—wrote as follows in his *Histoire de l’Eucharistie*, Amsterdam, 1671, p. 187: “Zeno of Verona, having laid down that there were three kinds of sacrifices—that of the Gentiles, that of the Jews, and that of Christians—understands the sacrifice of the last sort as that of which Malachi speaks, and explains it as a sacrifice of praise and a spiritual sacrifice of ourselves: ‘Sacrifice to God,’ he says, ‘a sacrifice of praise, and present your bodies as a living sacrifice, pleasing to God.’”

How erroneous this is appears not only because, in establishing his point, Larroque cites as Zeno’s own words two distinct testimonies of Scripture—Malachi and Paul—which Zeno had above cited separately, and combines them into one; and likewise interprets them as though only a sacrifice of praise were affirmed and every other sacrifice excluded, although neither Scripture nor Zeno’s words says this. It is especially clear from the present passage. For since the holy bishop is expressly speaking here of a sacrifice which people receive and eat, the author undoubtedly knew another sacrifice distinct from the sacrifice of praise; and it is manifest that he means here the sacrament of the Eucharistic bread, which it is sacrilegious to offer unworthily and deadly to eat unworthily. We have shown by clear testimony, in note 29 on Treatise V, that the author elsewhere calls this Eucharistic sacrament a sacrifice. It is also apparent there that this sacrament was held in such high regard that even Christians not yet consecrated—that is, catechumens—could not see it. See note 28 in the same place. Who could maintain that the sacrifice of praise is intended here, upon which one’s eyes should be fixed? But enough on refuting claims that display the weakness of the cause which the opponent sought to defend. We only observe that the same empty argument is also pressed by another heterodox writer, Johann Heinrich Ott, in *Examen perpetuum in Annales Card. Baronii*, Century 3, §7, p. 204.]

These things, brothers, are to be avoided by us; and likewise those things which are good, pure, simple, devout, and holy are to be embraced, as you do, so that people, seeing your good works, may glorify your Father who is in heaven. Therefore, my beloved flowers, procure such sacrifices as the Holy Spirit may gladly offer, the Father approve, and the Son—who is our teacher—glory in when approved, through him who is blessed for ages of ages.

[Note: “My flowers,” as we observed in note 1, means the neophytes. Hence there is no need to supply “brothers,” as Sparaverius thinks. The author affirms in Book II, Treatise LIII, that these persons were made neophytes from the *Competentes* and were transformed into flowers.]

[Note: The Urbino manuscript reads *glorificet*, “may glorify.”]

125. TREATISE XVI. On the Resurrection.

[Note: TREATISE XVI.—Gaspar Barthius devoted himself to elucidating this entire treatise in three passages of his *Adversaria*: XLIII.10; XLII.5 and 15. Whatever we have gained from him will be frankly attributed to him in the notes. The Venetian edition gives this title: “That there will be a resurrection of bodies, and on the immortality of the soul.”

Among the ancient Fathers, even after Zeno’s age, it was common to establish the doctrine of resurrection in sermons, since the whole hope of the future and therefore the chief foundation of Christian life itself rest upon it. The reason why it was so strongly and repeatedly inculcated was that, in that age when pagans were intermingled with Christians, not only Christians but also many pagans attended when bishops addressed the people, as is clear from note 2 on Treatise III. How implausible the doctrine of resurrection appeared to pagans is well known from what happened to the apostle Paul when he discoursed on the matter at Athens. Arnobius, addressing pagans, says, II, p. 51: “Do you dare to laugh at us because we speak of the resurrection of the dead?”

Yet St Zeno does not seem to have composed this treatise expressly against pagans, since he always addresses Christians and hints that some among them were wavering. This may have arisen because some Christians had been led into doubt by conversations with pagans with whom they were closely acquainted; or because in these regions there were some people, if not Seleucians, Hermians, or Proclanites, whom Philastrius and Augustine mention, at least Marcionites, whom Justin in the *Dialogue with Trypho* records as denying the resurrection of the flesh. That Marcionites still flourished in the fourth century is testified by Pacian of Barcelona, *To Sympronianus the Novatian, On the Catholic Name*, p. 306, vol. IV of the Lyons edition of the *Bibliotheca Patrum*. We infer from Theodoret that many of them existed also in the following century, for he reports that ten thousand Marcionites were baptized by him: Letters LXXXI to the consular Tamo and CXLV to the Cypriot Monks. John Philoponus, of a much later age, published a book against the doctrine of resurrection, mentioned by Photius, codex 21; Theodosius is said to have written against that book, codex 22. Others also, even after the Council of Chalcedon, attempted to overthrow the same doctrine. Thus it is no wonder that bishops frequently preached on the resurrection in order to restore such people to sound judgment, as St Ambrose did in these regions after Zeno, and others elsewhere.

Epiphanius, Zeno’s contemporary, states that there were many Marcionites in Italy in his time, *Heresy* 42: “The heresy of Marcion still exists even now in Rome and Italy.” This may be confirmed by a somewhat earlier constitution of Constantine the Great, which Eusebius reports in *Life of Constantine* III.64. It is scarcely credible, however, that our author was attacking Priscillianists, who did not believe in the resurrection and whose remnants still existed in Spain in the age of St Leo the Great, according to Letter XV.7.]

I. Whoever denies the resurrection condemns his very self to death. For why should one deserve to behold the blessedness of the time to come, when you see him, through sacrilegious unbelief, detracting from God’s power? But they do this from love of their crimes, so that they may think the things they do secretly will go unpunished. For if they perceived that the course of events was already drawing near to the day of judgment, without doubt they would both hate the present and believe—and fear—the future. For no one is so devoid even of a taste for this world’s wisdom that he dares say that souls perish together with bodies, or heavenly things are consumed with earthly things; especially when that wisest man says that this is death: when the soul is held shut up with the body as in a prison; but that is true life: when the same soul, freed from the prison’s confinement, returns to the place from which it came. If, then, he who did not know Christ thought this, why should the Christian doubt, who hears, hopes for, and anticipates from Christ the resurrection to come and laid up for him?

[Note: The editions read *suammet ipse*; the Reims and Tolentino manuscripts, *suam semetipse*. We correct from the Pompone manuscript, where *sequemet* stands in place of *et semet*.]

[Note: It was customary among Fathers not merely of the Middle Ages but also of antiquity to announce the day of judgment as near, as everyone knows. The Urbino manuscript reads: “For if they perceived that the course was already undoubtedly drawing near to the bright day, they would [hate] the present …” A little later, *tam* (“so”) is absent in the Vatican manuscript after *ab illis*, or after *ab istius*.]

[Note: He means Plato, who, Cicero says in *On Friendship*, was judged by Apollo’s oracle to be the wisest man. Many Fathers cited him for his eloquent teaching on the soul’s immortality: see Tertullian, *On the Resurrection of the Flesh*, 3; Lactantius, VII.9; Athanasius, *Oration against the Pagans*; Augustine, Sermons 240, 241, and 242. Plato establishes the immortality of souls in many places, especially in the *Phaedo* and in Book X of the *Republic*, where the views indicated here by Zeno occur. They are also read in Cicero, partly in the *Dream of Scipio*, partly in *On Old Age*, and in *On Friendship*. But that Cicero took them from Plato and sometimes rendered them into Latin in the very same words is expressly testified by Macrobius, *Commentary on the Dream of Scipio* II, p. 82, in addition to Lactantius, *Divine Institutes* I.5.

Lactantius, VII.8, moreover, quotes the following from Plato, from which St Zeno perhaps drew: “Because no origin can be found on earth for a soul capable of receiving and containing such great things, since it has nothing derived from an earthly compound mixed with it. What in a human being is weighty and dissoluble must necessarily be dissolved into the earth; but what is subtle and lofty is indivisible and, released from the dwelling of the body as from a prison, flies back to heaven and to its own nature.” These are, in brief, Plato’s views, which he himself explains broadly and copiously. Plato should be read in the *Phaedo*, p. 53; the *Meno*, p. 415; and *Republic* X, p. 757.]

[Note: Let us give a comparable Platonic sentiment as found in Cicero’s *Dream of Scipio*, where he says of excellent men who, upon leaving this life, were thought dead: “Indeed, they live, who have escaped from the chains of their bodies as from a prison,” etc. Lactantius derived similar sayings from the same source, VII.9.]

[Note: The Pompone codex reads *devenerit*, “has arrived.”]

[Note: *Vidit* (“saw”) was read in the editions and several manuscripts. The reading of the Pompone manuscript seemed better. Then *praesumit* means *antesumit*, or, as Barthius explains it, “tastes beforehand.” St Zeno refers to Paul, 1 Corinthians 15, where faith in the resurrection is confirmed from Christ’s resurrection.]

II. Therefore, I think it must first of all be proved that our souls are not dissolved in that first death together with the remains of their bodies, nor together with the ruin of this fleshly dwelling; but that, according to the character of their deeds, some are banished to places of punishment and others cherished in peaceful abodes. Then at last it may be believed that what is manifestly not utterly extinguished will rise again.

[Note: We would not have anyone suppose here that the author was among those who thought that the souls of the righteous rest still in Abraham’s bosom in a literal sense and would not enjoy the blessedness of paradise and the vision of God before the day of final judgment. We have established his Catholic view at length in Dissertation II, chapter 10, where we explain this passage also from other passages.]

Even pagans, who do not believe these things, nevertheless run to tombs with an ill-omened libation, and assert that the dead, whom they recognize in the stillness of silent night, sometimes demand food from them. Thus they establish the reality of what they reject.

[Note: On pagan libations made at the graves of the dead, see Cardinal Noris, *On the Pisan Cenotaphs*, Dissertation III.5. Cicero presses this same argument for establishing immortality in *On Friendship*: “The authority of the ancients, or of our own forefathers, who gave such religious rites to the dead, has great weight with me; for surely they would not have done so if they had thought that nothing concerned the dead.” Other Fathers also pressed this argument against pagans: Tertullian, *On the Resurrection of the Flesh*, 1, and *On the Testimony of the Soul*, 4; Epiphanius in the *Anchoratus*; and others. St Zeno himself touched on this custom, still current in his own age, in the preceding treatise; see note 17 there.]

[Note: The preposition *a* is absent in the Reims manuscript, perhaps better, to avoid repetition of the same preposition; for *a se* occurs later in the sentence. Shortly afterward the Pompone manuscript has *inquietae et* in place of *in quiete*, but wrongly.]

Philosophers have said various things about the soul; yet they establish its immortality and refute by plain argument the folly of Epicurus, Dicaearchus, and Democritus.

[Note: Not Plato alone, but Zeno, Pherecydes, and Pythagoras also taught that the soul is immortal, as Lactantius relates in VIII.7, where he mentions Pherecydes and Zeno of Citium, and in chapter 8, where he mentions Pythagoras. Cicero, *Tusculan Disputations* I.16, reports that Pherecydes of Syros was the first to declare that human souls are everlasting. Lactantius, VII.8, reports that he was Pythagoras’ teacher; hence there is no doubt that both held the same view concerning the soul’s immortality. As for the philosopher Zeno and the Stoics who derived their origin from him, Tertullian’s statement in *On the Soul* 54 is certain: “The Stoics place the souls of the wise in dwellings above.” What the holy bishop means in saying that these philosophers spoke variously concerning the soul is explained by a notable passage of Tertullian in the same work and chapter: “With Plato wise souls are raised into the ether, with Arius into the air, with the Stoics beneath the moon.” There is no need to speak of the Pythagoreans’ opinion, since it is exceedingly well known. We pass over many other matters that could be gathered for this purpose, since what we have thus far selected is sufficient for understanding Zeno’s meaning. The Urbino and Vatican manuscripts read *disserunt* for *dixerunt*.]

[Note: Lactantius, VII.7, says: “Against this view”—that is, the immortality of souls—“Dicaearchus argued first, then Democritus, and finally Epicurus.” Of Dicaearchus Cicero says, *Tusculan Disputations* I: “Dicaearchus argued against this immortality; for he wrote three books called *Lesbiaca*, because the dialogue is held at Mytilene, in which he seeks to prove that souls are mortal.” He maintained that the soul was absolutely nothing but a single and simple body, so constituted that it lived and sensed through a natural tempering. Democritus held much the same view, according to the same authority: “He made the soul out of light and round particles by some fortuitous concurrence; for with him there was nothing which a swarm of atoms had not produced.” Finally Epicurus, following the same tracks, is so represented both by Diogenes Laertius, *Life of Epicurus* X.128, 139, and by Aulus Gellius, *Attic Nights* II.8.]

[Note: From what has been said, St Zeno seems to have had Lactantius’ discourse before him, since he imitated Lactantius elsewhere and here teaches the same things in different words. This is clearer from the testimony now under consideration. Lactantius, after mentioning in VI.3 a certain twofold path known from Pythagoras, as Ausonius reports in the *Monosyllables*—one path to happiness and the other to misery, both bounded by the one duration of life—adds words with which Zeno fully agrees: “The poets perhaps did better in wishing this twofold path to be in the underworld.” In chapter 4, after indicating the life of the good which leads, in the poets’ language, to the Elysian fields, he quotes these verses from Virgil, *Aeneid* VI.542:

> But on the left hand the wicked  
> suffer punishment, and he sends them to impious Tartarus.

In VII.20 and 21 he transcribes other pertinent verses from the same poet. Augustine, Sermon 241, quotes two verses of Virgil to the same effect.]

But poets do better, who place a twofold path in the underworld: one for the impious, leading to Tartarus; another for the pious, leading to Elysium. They add with still greater force that there the dead are recognized not so much by their appearances as by their deeds, and necessarily receive according to what they bear in their actions from their earthly stewardship—rightly saying:

> Each of us suffers his own spirits of the dead.  
> (*Aeneid* VI.743)

[Note: The editions, with the Tolentino and Zeno manuscripts, read *alteram* (“another”). On the words “bear in their actions,” Barthius notes in *Adversaria* XLII.5: “The philosophizing poets say that evidence of deeds remains in the shades of the dead themselves, and that from it they are judged in the underworld. Rhadamanthus in Claudian’s *Against Rufinus*:

> Why, madman, do you deny what is manifest? Behold:  
> branded stains disfigure your breast, and the image of your vices has become ingrained.

Zeno also took the word *administratio* (“stewardship”) from pagan philosophy when speaking of it, for they said that every human being had been placed in his own sphere as a kind of administrator by the supreme Lord. Persius, *Satires* 3.” Thus far Barthius.]

[Note: Lactantius does not cite this verse; from this we infer that Zeno was familiar with Virgil himself. Virgil is said to have called *manes* the guardian spirits (*Genii*) whom Plato taught, as Apuleius reports in *On the God of Socrates*, to attend each person as companions and witnesses of life. With them present, as Servius notes on this passage, after death we are either assigned to a better life or condemned to a worse one. Thus in whatever way he did so, Virgil acknowledged the immortality of the soul. The Urbino manuscript reads *patitur* for *patimur*. Barthius observed that lower down *suspicio* means a tentative opinion or weak knowledge, from Cyril’s Glossary; we discussed this more fully in note 4 on Treatise 2 of Book II.]

III. But we, brothers, whom not ingenious conjecture but God the teacher has instructed—by proving in himself, for our sake, what he taught—are able not so much to say as to demonstrate by visible facts that the souls of the dead live. Finally, wandering and unclean spirits of either human sex break into the bodily dwellings of the living by the deceitful snare of flatteries or by violence, and seek a ruinous hiding-place for themselves in their captives.

> [Note: The Veronese edition and the Urbino, Pomp., and Zen. manuscripts read *perniciosum* (“ruinous”).]

> [Note: In this passage the Veronese editors used a freer hand, adding some things at their own discretion, removing others, and even transferring certain matters from one place to another; these we have restored from the manuscripts and the Venetian edition. Here, however, they had written: “spirits under the pretext of souls of either sex,” etc.; this addition does not appear in the manuscripts or in the edition mentioned. Cyprian, *On the Vanity of Idols*, p. 450, calls these spirits, described by Zeno as wandering and unclean, “insincere and wandering”; likewise, in his letter to Donatus, p. 3, he calls them “unclean and erratic.” Lactantius, Book II, ch. 14, calls them “contaminated and ruined spirits wandering through all lands”; Prudentius, in his poem on St. Vincent, calls them wandering, unruly, and filthy. The Tolentino and Vatican manuscripts read *blanditia ex captione* (“flattery arising from entrapment”) instead of *blanditiarum captione* (“the snare of flatteries”).]

But when they have come onto the field of divine combat and begin to be struck by the weapon of the sacred Name,

> [Note: The same edition reads *tunc vexatum certari misereris*. Barthius recognized this passage as corrupt and attempted to emend it. We have supplied it from the manuscripts and the Venetian edition. In only a few manuscripts *miseris* is read for *misereris*, but wrongly. On the authority of the manuscripts, we have deleted *enim*, inserted in the printed editions after the word *discoloratur*. From the Urbino and Zen. manuscripts we have corrected *horrores*, for which Barthius had advised reading *horroris*.]

then, when you recognize one person, you pity another struggling. Their color changes from moment to moment; nature strips away their own form; the circles of their eyes are driven madly into distorted terrors; their teeth, terrible with foaming masses between bluish lips, grind; all their limbs everywhere quiver with twisted trembling; they groan and weep; they fear the announced day of judgment and lament that they are being driven out. They confess their sex; they confess the time and place of their assault; they confess their own name and their departure—or they make plain by evident signs who they are—so that we often recognize them as those whom we remember to have died recently, especially by some violence, while engaged in idolatry.

> [Note: The words “they confess their sex” had been removed by the Veronese editors. Zeno says “sex,” evidently because the souls confessed themselves to be those of human beings of either sex; see note 20. The Reims manuscript reads *confitetur et egressum* (“he confesses, and [his] departure”) instead of *confiterentur aggressurae tempus* (“they confess the time of the attack”), but wrongly, since departure is immediately added. *Aggressura* occurs in Ulpian, Book III, §4, *On the Syllanian and Claudian Decree of the Senate*. Elsewhere the author uses the same word twice, as will be clear from the index of words. We have also supplied both *nomen* (“name”) and the conjunction from the Venetian edition. The edition had written this in order to suggest that the demons’ confession was feigned.]

> [Note: In the Veronese edition: “that we recognize them to be those named, whom,” etc., contrary to the manuscripts and the Venetian edition. Lactantius too, *Divine Institutes*, V.21, reports that demons sometimes disclosed their own names: “When questioned who they are, when they came, and how they slipped into a human being, they confess.” Other Fathers state the matter more explicitly, recounting that those demons asserted that they were Jupiter, Mercury, Saturn, or some other of those whom the Gentiles worshipped as gods; on this subject one may read Minucius Felix, *Octavius*, ch. 27, and Sulpicius Severus, *Dialogues*, 3. But that they confessed themselves to be the souls of the impious and of murderers, no one, so far as we have been able to discover, intimates besides Zeno. We find only that some held the souls of wicked persons and of those who had perished by violent death to linger and wander for some time around their bodies and tombs; see Porphyry, *On Abstinence*, II, p. 89, a view also favored by Macrobius, *Commentary on the Dream of Scipio*, I.13. But setting aside this little pagan fable, we have defended at greater length, in Dissertation II, ch. 8, the singular account of the possessed persons mentioned by Zeno, lest it offend anyone—as it indeed seems to have offended the Veronese editors, who judged it needed correction in places.]

Now answer me, you who maintain that nothing of a human being remains after death: how did that dead person whom you recognized speak through another? But you say: “The demons fabricate these things.” The proof is all the stronger because even deceivers bear testimony to the truth.

> [Note: In place of the words copied both from the manuscripts and from the Venetian edition, the Veronese edition and those following it substituted: “you maintain: on what argument do demons rely if the souls of the dead do not live? But you say,” etc. The manuscripts of Pomp., two Zen., and the Venetian edition read *Hoc daemones* instead of *Haec daemones*. This objection is answered in the editions and manuscripts thus: “O better proof!”—an exclamation that plainly seems foolish. Barthius’s emendation seemed sufficiently secure to be inserted into the text.]

Why should they fabricate names when their confession in other respects is true? Or why should they rely on an argument which benefits more toward fear of God the people whom they desire to destroy, while bringing no advantage to themselves? Certainly they might rightly be thought to do this if, under the pretext of another’s name, they had been able to retain possession of those whom they invaded. But when, by divine adjuration, on the spiritual rack, they unwillingly declare who they are and depart against their will, beyond doubt they are what they confess themselves, each one, to be.

> [Note: Everything placed in the text after the word “truth” up to “Receive also” was cut out by the Veronese editors; only the final sentence was transferred, with some alterations, to an unsuitable place, as we observed in note 21. We have printed the reading of the manuscripts and Venetian edition. The Reims, Urbino, and Vatican manuscripts, together with the Venetian edition, read *capiunt* (“they seize”) for *cupiunt* (“they desire”), but incorrectly, since the subject is demons, who seek to gain human souls. Moreover, other Fathers too advance this argument, used by the author to urge belief in the demons’ confession delivered against themselves. Tertullian, *Apology*, ch. 23: “Believe those who speak truth about themselves, since you believe them when they lie. No one lies to his own disgrace, but rather for honor. Faith is more appropriately placed in those confessing against themselves than in those denying for themselves.” Likewise Minucius, *Octavius*, ch. 27: “Saturn himself, and Serapis, and Jupiter, and whatever demons you worship, conquered by pain, declare what they are; nor indeed do they lie to their own disgrace, especially while some of you are present. Believe their own testimony, when these demons confess the truth about themselves.”]

IV. Receive also other examples, and indeed more certain ones. First, in the book of the words of Samuel, that eminent priest, already marked out by the law of death, when King Saul desired him, presented not only his own presence without ambiguity but also answered questions (1 Kings 28); and, though dead, he prophesied more freely than he had been accustomed to do while alive. Thus one may well exclaim: “This man has rather departed than died.”

> [Note: Nowhere have we found the first Book of Kings designated by this title; rather, it is the first book of Samuel.]

> [Note: Although some Fathers, with Jerome, *Against Jovinian*, I, deny the priesthood to Samuel, he is nonetheless called a priest by Lucifer of Cagliari, *On Not Sparing Those Who Sin against God*, p. 227, vol. IV of the *Library of the Fathers*; and in the *Apostolic Constitutions*, VIII.1, he is called ἀρχιερεύς, “high priest,” and in ch. 5, ἱερεύς, “priest”; similarly by others, to whom St. Zeno joined himself. The expression here, “marked out by the law of death,” appears to be African usage. Tertullian, *Testimony of the Soul*, ch. 4, says “the marking-off of life” (*vitae dispunctionem*).]

> [Note: A great question is debated among the Fathers concerning Samuel: whether Saul truly saw the soul of Samuel himself. Those adopting the negative view include Tertullian, *On the Soul*, ch. 57; the author of the *Questions* among Justin’s works, question 52; St. Pionius, no. 14 of the exhortation incorporated into his acts; Eustathius of Antioch, in the dissertation against Origen published by Allatius; St. Jerome on Ezekiel 13; the author of the *Questions on the Old and New Testaments* attributed to Augustine, question 27; and, under Augustine’s name, the author of *On the Wonders of Holy Scripture*, II.11. Most ancient and modern writers, however, uphold the affirmative view with our Zeno: Josephus, *Antiquities*, VI.15; St. Methodius, bishop and martyr, in Photius, codex 234; St. Justin, *Dialogue with Trypho*, p. 72; Origen on 1 Kings 28; St. Basil, Letter VIII to Eustathius; St. Ambrose on Luke 1; and others. St. Augustine discusses both sides more fully in *Questions to Simplicianus*, question 3, and *Questions to Dulcitius*, question 6; but in *On Care for the Dead* he inclines toward Zeno’s view, which Ecclesiasticus 46:23 also seems to support.]

In the Gospel as well, Peter and the sons of Zebedee, standing with the Lord, see Moses and Elijah shining in glory (Matt. 17). Since, on account of the then obstacle of the flesh, they could not see them, they see them by the freedom of the spirit; thus they understand that what in this world is seen to perish for a time rests unharmed, laid up in the treasury of nature.

> [Note: The Reims and Vatican codices have *praeter tunc impedimento*; the Pomp. and Urbino manuscripts likewise have *impedimento*.]

> [Note: “Treasury of nature” here means the tomb, in which the bodies of the dead are kept for resurrection; for *thesaurus* properly signifies a compartment in which something is deposited for safekeeping. See Basilius Faber, *Treasury of Learning*, vol. II, p. 983. We may add Barthius’s observation from Book II, ch. 15: “Most beautifully, by ‘the treasury of nature,’ he understands the whole universe, τὸ πᾶν, because all things that perish are deposited in it as in a true storehouse and, though changed in form, return to life; since the destruction of one thing is the life of another, and the life of one is the destruction of another, and thus there is a kind of circle of succeeding things. This is what he says below: ‘All things live by their deaths’; Victorinus teaches this elegantly and extensively in *Against the Arians*, IV. … Sacred Scripture often alludes to this treasury when it says that those who die in the Lord are gathered into it and to their fathers. … No less learnedly, below, our Zeno calls it ‘the secret place of nature.’”]

Likewise, in hell that most grasping rich man, whom an immense chaos separates from the happiness of the poor man (Luke 16), while begging amid his fires for refreshment, recognizes too late that Lazarus is the true rich man. Though dead, he wishes to be touched even by one finger of those hands to which, while living, he had refused alms. Without reason he now hates what he had formerly loved; he finds happier what he had hated. He groans that, with his known resources, he cannot provide any remedy for his present punishment; for a single point of rest, he is immediately ready, if permitted, to offer all things. At least he desires provision to be made for his surviving brothers. He earnestly entreats father Abraham that some messenger may go to make them certain of so great a matter. But Abraham answered him: “They have Moses and the prophets; if they do not believe them, neither will they believe one sent from here” (Luke 16:29, 31), plainly showing that truth is not in bodily eyes but rests in the faith of believers.

> [Note: The Volterra manuscript reads *cernit* (“he sees”). From the same codex, and also from the Vatican and Urbino manuscripts, we write *tota, si liceat* (“all things, if permitted”) instead of *tota scilicet*. Moreover, *tota* is used for *omnia*, “all things,” just as *totum* is used in the same sense; see Treatise IV, note 25. So Virgil, *Aeneid* I.189: *Tota armenta sequuntur* (“all the herds follow”); Juvenal X.237: *bona tota* (“all goods”); Caesar too, *Civil War* I.1, says *totis ripis* (“along the whole banks”); Apuleius, *Metamorphoses* 6, *toti dii* (“all the gods”), etc. A little later we restored *saltem* (“at least”) from the manuscripts in place of *salutem* (“salvation”), which was wrongly read in the editions.]

V. And the Lord, confirming these examples, said to one of the thieves who believed in him, as they hung to right and left with him upon the cross: “Amen, amen, I say to you: today you shall be with me in paradise” (Luke 23:43). Therefore, if a human being who has died perishes forever, then the Lord lied when he promised paradise to one who would thereafter have no existence. Moreover, the human being himself whom the Lord assumed perishes if Jesus did not rise. But if he rose, he gave a pattern to the human race, because God tasted the rights of death for humanity in order that humanity might receive from God the right of immortality which it had lost.

> [Note: The sequence of the sentence suggested correcting *cum eo* (“with him”), found both in the manuscripts and editions, to *cum eo de* (“with him from”). We restored *amen* from the Reims and Pomp. manuscripts.]

For this reason the most blessed Paul says: “We do not wish you, brothers, to be ignorant concerning those who sleep, lest you grieve as the rest do who have no hope. For if we believe that Jesus died and rose, so also God will bring with him those who have fallen asleep in Jesus” (1 Thess. 4:12–13). God also speaks through Ezekiel the prophet, saying: “Behold, I open your tombs and lead you out from your tombs and bring you into the land of Israel; I will put my spirit in you, and you shall live” (Ezek. 37:12 ff.).

VI. Since these things are so, Christian, why do you not believe in the future resurrection? Why do you so stubbornly mourn those who pass from the decay of this world into better things? Alas for such wickedness! Here a mother, her garment torn, her hair and cheeks lacerated, her whole breast bruised by repeated blows, raves madly around the corpse of the one she has lost in pagan vanity. Nor does she recall the mother of the Maccabees, who, armed with hope in the things to come, while Antiochus raged, willingly, I will not say bore, seven sons at once—or rather herself happily put them to death by her exhortations—trusting devoutly that she had borne her sons for God, not for the world (1 Macc. 7).

> [Note: The editions and several manuscripts read *de hujusmodi* (“concerning things of this kind”). We preferred the reading of the Tolentino, Vatican, and Urbino codices, *de hujus mundi labe* (“from the decay of this world”). Then, in place of *migrantes* (“those departing”), which the editions have along with several manuscripts, the Reims codex reads *migrantis*, the Tolentino *migraturus*, and the Urbino *migratus*. But the discussion concerns the living, who mourn dying or dead persons, as is clear from the following examples of mothers and wives.]

> [Note: The editions, along with some manuscripts, read *saevienti* (“raging”). We corrected this from the Reims and Pomp. manuscripts and the Venetian edition.]

Here a wife declares that she cannot endure the desolation caused by her lost husband; she laments the cold side of her improperly widened bed; with resentful cries she composes an accusation against God. She sometimes interrupts, with profane howls, the very sacred rites by which the dead are customarily commended by God’s priests. Defiling her whole appearance with hideous filth, she embraces the corpse after its final death-cry; with repeated kisses she warms its chilled lips; she bathes the whole body with showers of tears, covering it at the expense of her hair. By piteous addresses she kindles into still fuller weeping even people whom the cause does not affect, being so much more ostentatious in grief as she is richer—indeed, miserable after a moment, and, would that it were only once, about to marry from excessive grief.

> [Note: Zeno uses *invidiosis vocibus*, “resentful words,” for “lamenting words,” and *concinnere invidiam*, “to concoct an accusation,” for lamenting, because complaints and reproaches make the object of complaint hated and envied. Likewise, Quintilian says that a mother mourning her son’s death brings reproach upon the gods, *Declamations* VIII.14. Silius Italicus, VI: “She went, bearing reproach against heaven and the gods.” Seneca, *Hercules on Oeta*: “Though weary, let your arms be loosened for lamentation, that by grieving you may bring reproach upon the gods.” And St. Zeno, Treatise XV, Book II, no. 1: “When this report was received, the servant of God tore his garments, not in order to bring reproach upon God, but …”]

> [Note: This is notable evidence of the ancient custom of offering sacrifice for the dead. Similar passages occur in Cyprian, Letter LXVI; Tertullian, *On Monogamy*, ch. 10; *On the Soldier’s Crown*, ch. 3; *Exhortation to Chastity*, ch. 11; and others. The Veronese edition, with two Zen. manuscripts, shortly afterwards reads *terraque illuvie* (“with earthly filth”) for *tetraque illuvie* (“with hideous filth”), apparently through an error of printer or copyist.]

> [Note: This formula was famous among the Romans in funeral observance. When someone had breathed out the soul, the corpse was called aloud repeatedly, as Servius notes on Virgil, *Aeneid* VI.218: “Some [bring] warm water,” etc. “Bodies,” he says, “were kept for eight days, washed while still warm, and washed after the final calling.” Lucan II.22: “Bodies lie not yet called aloud.” Apuleius, *Metamorphoses* I: “You are already mourned and called aloud”; and II: “Behold, the dead man, now finally mourned and called aloud, was proceeding.” Thus *conclamatum* in Zeno means the final calling, as likewise in Terence, *Eunuch* II.3.56: “Stop now; it is called aloud.”]

> [Note: The Reims manuscript reads *quam* (“than”).]

> [Note: He says “only once” because some women married twice, three times, or even more often. We have noted that Zeno, like most ancient Fathers, was hostile to second marriages and argued much more severely against repeatedly renewed marriages in Treatise V and, more fully, Dissertation II, ch. 7, where we believe that we defended his opinion at length. A little later Barthius thinks *mimico dolore* (“theatrical grief”) should be read instead of *nimio dolore* (“excessive grief”); for all authors use *mimicum* of what is feigned and, by empty display, falsifies reality. But the author may have said *nimio* ironically; and, since the manuscripts provide no support, we judged that nothing should be changed.]

Here—here—I see no way in which anyone can excuse herself. For someone is at hand to say: “If there is a resurrection, why do you mourn?
