If you do it from love for your husband, why do you marry afterward?” It is an accursed thing, brothers, neither to preserve affection for one’s spouse nor faithfulness to God. This rebuke awaits men also.

VII. Therefore a Christian must not doubt at all that the dead will be raised into their former state, and that, on the appointed day, they will be brought forth before God’s presence from that secret place of nature such as each was received according to his own condition. For the Apostle says: “We must all be made manifest before the judgment-seat of Christ, that each may receive the deserts of his body according to what he has done, whether good or evil” (2 Cor. 6:10).

> [Note: He calls the tomb “the secret place of nature,” just as above he called it “the treasury of nature.” See note 29.]

For, brothers, it is easier to reform what has existed than to establish what did not previously exist. If what did not exist now exists, much more can what existed exist again. For it is the very practice of that most mighty craftsman, the creator of all things, to affirm the possibility of things deemed impossible, and, from what is not, to make what is; to create nature beyond nature; to have nothing whatever difficult; and that the only thing lacking to him is that which he does not will to be. For it is God’s proper characteristic to accomplish what cannot be believed.

> [Note: Thus from the Pomp. manuscript, which agrees wonderfully with *institui* (“to establish”); elsewhere *reformare* (“to reform”) was read.]

> [Note: This does not mean that God makes possible things which are truly impossible, but that things apparently and supposedly impossible to human beings are possible to him—such as restoring the dead to life. In this sense Zeno says shortly afterward: “For it is God’s proper characteristic to accomplish what cannot be believed.” Marius Victorinus explains this more plainly in *On the Creation of the World*, I: “Always believe that God can do whatever is thought impossible to be done.” Arnobius likewise, Book II: “What is impossible for us to do is possible for him and wholly ready for accomplishment”; and he gives the reason: “Shall we infer from our distinctions what can or cannot be done?” He does not suggest that God can truly do what is in fact impossible; rather, he reproves only the belief that things impossible for us to do are impossible for God, and the desire to measure by human reasoning what is or is not impossible for God. Accordingly, the old proverb mentioned by Synesius, Letter 11, must be understood in the same sense: “All things are possible to God, even impossibilities.” Augustine grants this to Plato in Sermon 242, no. 7. The Urbino manuscript reads *impossibilium possibilitate se adserere*, “to establish himself by the possibility of impossibilities,” that is, to display his own power, instead of *impossibilium possibilitatem adserere*; this reading comes to the same thing and is by no means displeasing.]

> [Note: To “create beyond nature” is to create beyond all the powers of nature, since no natural powers can bring something out of nothing. It may also mean “outside nature,” namely that the things created have no pre-existent nature from which they are made as from material; for things created from nothing previously were nothing.]

VIII. Therefore not human beings only, but almost all things live through their deaths. I shall touch upon a few among many, so that in a few examples I may undoubtedly explain the proof of all.

> [Note: Very nearly the same comparisons are pressed by many ancient Fathers for establishing or explaining the resurrection: Tertullian, *On the Resurrection*, chs. 12–13, and *Apology*, ch. 48; Minucius Felix, *Octavius*, no. 5; Theophilus, *To Autolycus*, II; Ambrose, *Hexaemeron*, V.22–23, and *On Faith in the Resurrection*, II.53; and others.]

Falling stars slip from heaven and, behind them, with a long train of whitening flames, are led down to their settings with the solemnity of a funeral torch, as though with certain funeral rites. If you seek them through the regions from which they were torn away, you will recognize that, by the law of renewed light, they have risen again into their places. The sun is born every day and dies on the very day on which it is born; yet it is not terrified by the fate of its approaching end, so as to slow its course, lengthen its hours and moments, or remain, if only a little longer, alive in its day. But always faithful and always fearless, it hastens to the tomb of its kindred night, knowing that in that very tomb it possesses what makes it live. Indeed, its rising is taken away if its setting is taken away.

> [Note: Apuleius, *Metamorphoses* VIII, has *repigratur impetus*, “the impulse is checked,” that is, relaxed; and I, *repigrato fetu*. The Urbino manuscript reads *currus* (“chariot”) for *cursus* (“course”); below, the Tolentino manuscript reads *cognitae* (“known”) for *cognatae* (“kindred”), while the Urbino manuscript has *sciens* (“knowing”) for *scius* (“aware”).]

> [Note: The Reims, Tolentino, Pomp., Vatican, and Urbino manuscripts read *auferatur* (“is taken away”); the editions, with the Zen. manuscript, have *aufertur*.]

The moon also, which truly portrays in itself all the features of human existence, first appears, in the tender blood-red stage of its birth, as though from a cradle in a doubtful horn. Then, increasing little by little, now a girl, now a maiden, advancing with the growth of daily age, it runs through the worldly courses in the winding paths of its playful course. But when, mature, it has completed its silvery globe in the narrow circuits, matching in its labors its brother, the light-bearing charioteer ablaze with golden fire, it gradually declines into old age. At last, consumed by final old age, it comes alive again through its own death and, with the customary monthly shoot of fire kindled, again takes a beginning from its end.

> [Note: We here add Barthius’s note from Book XLIII, ch. 10: “What has the moon to do with human reason? One should read *nationis*, from birth, or *sationis*, from the succession of human stock.” But *ratio* may be understood as method or order of nature.]

> [Note: Another observation of the same Baronius should be added. “Blood-red tenderness” denotes the earliest time after birth. Thus the *sanguinolenti* in the Code are newborn children. Emperor Constantine, *On Fathers Who Destroy Their Children*, II: “If anyone, because of extreme poverty and lack of food, destroys a son or daughter while blood-red [that is, newborn] …”; likewise in the inscription concerning abandoned infants, Law 8 of the Justinian Code.]

> [Note: Some manuscripts and the editions read *angustis* (“narrow”). We preferred the reading of the Reims codex. The Urbino manuscript has *angusti circuli* (“a narrow circle”).]

IX. Likewise, that precious bird the phoenix plainly teaches us the laws of resurrection. It receives the nobility of its race not from parents and does not pass it on to children. It is both sexes to itself, all affection to itself, its own race, its own end, its own beginning. It is born not from intercourse and nourished not by another’s service. It dies neither unwillingly nor unknowingly; but when the ripe time of death has come, it most gladly burns itself by sacred fires summoned by itself. Its nest is its tomb; ashes are its nurses; its ash is the seed of a body to be propagated; death is its birthday. Finally, after a moment it exults in its festive tomb—not a shadow but reality, not an image but a phoenix; not another, yet another inasmuch as better, nevertheless the very same former one. Blush, Christian conscience; from so many and such great things, recognize how you too, again the same as you are, will be made better.

> [Note: Some critics may perhaps be angry with Zeno because he presents the fable of the phoenix so prominently. But let them remember that sacred writers frequently employed the phoenix to explain various mysteries: virgin birth, the resurrection both of the Lord and of ourselves, and sometimes moral conduct. Some, too, have used it to establish false doctrines; see Augustine, *On the Soul and Its Origin*, IV.20. As a symbol of resurrection, the phoenix is found engraved even upon the tombs of ancient Christians; it is incredible how many Greek and Latin Fathers bear witness to it. Besides Job 29:18, where some maintain that the phoenix is mentioned by a particular pointing of the Hebrew text and others confirm this from the Septuagint, and besides the ambiguous reading of the same translators in Psalm 91:13, there are well-known passages in St. Clement, Pope, *Letter to the Corinthians*, 25; Tertullian; Origen; Eusebius; Lactantius; Cyril of Jerusalem; Gregory Nazianzen; Epiphanius; Jerome; Ambrose; and others too numerous even to list. Moreover, many pagan authors also related it as true history: Herodotus, Dio, Ovid, Tacitus, Plutarch, Pliny, Solinus, Aristides, Claudian, and others. Since the Christian Fathers had to contend against the Gentiles, who can accuse them if they took from the phoenix—a history considered certain among the Gentiles—an example by which to confirm their purpose? Grotius, though heterodox, was moved by this consideration to acknowledge that the Fathers were sufficiently cleared of the censure of certain critics. Thus he writes in the letter to Bignon, cited and praised by Joachinus Joannes Maderus in his preface to St. Clement’s Letter to the Corinthians: “That the matter concerning the phoenix was believed by learned persons in that age, and that Clement uses this argument not to prove τῶν νεκρῶν ἀνάστασιν, ‘the resurrection of the dead,’ but to show from a believed fact that it is not among τῶν ἀδυνάτων, ‘impossibilities.’”]

> [Note: The Pomp., Urbino, and two Zen. manuscripts read *accepit* (“receives”). The phoenix itself is said to be both sexes to itself because it is both father and mother to itself; it is all affection to itself because it is said to be unique, with no other of its species that it could love.]

> [Note: The “invited sacred fires” are the fires which poets say the phoenix draws to itself from the sun when, now about to die, it has settled upon its nest. Barthius, however, doubts whether *initiatis* (“consecrated”) should not better be read: “For,” he says in Book XLII, ch. 10, “our Zeno grants it no origin except from itself”; yet no manuscript reads so.]

> [Note: Both manuscripts and editions read: “how again you too might be the same and better,” etc. Barthius, in the passage cited, proposed a most felicitous correction: “The final words, which concern Christians, are not free from blemish but must be more sharply restored. For the words ‘how again you too might be the same,’ bear an appearance of truth in their reading but have been very badly corrupted; for nothing is more certain than that Zeno wrote … ‘again the same, who you are, you shall be better.’ Only thus will the comparison between the restoration of Christians and of the phoenix be fitting in its several respects. The same body in both will be restored: to the phoenix after fire; to the Christian human being after every dissolution. Yet it will be the same in such a way that, while it is by no means another, it is nevertheless better than what was the same. This is the certain restoration; and thus he has just said of the phoenix most clearly: ‘Not another, yet another inasmuch as better, nevertheless the very same former one.’”]

X. Furthermore, the seed of every kind of grain, placed in the earth, dies; yet that which is within it comes alive again. It does not take death into its marrow, but, breathing out its generative power into a shoot of its own, its old bodily surface wiped away—indeed, transferred into the rights of a better nature—it raises aloft toward heaven its blessed head, crowned with green locks, as though emerging from the underworld, destined to maintain the glory of perpetuity by abundant fruit. Paul confirms this when he says: “Fool, what you sow is not made alive unless it has died” (1 Cor. 16:36). And he adds: “So also is the resurrection of the dead: it is sown into corruption; it rises into incorruption. It is sown in humility; it rises in glory. It is sown in weakness; it rises in power. It is sown a natural body; it rises a spiritual body” (ibid., 42 ff.). Enough, I think, has made the truth of the resurrection clear to everyone.

> [Note: In the editions, through repetition and apparently an error of printers or copyists, *in infirmitatem* (“in weakness”) appeared twice.]

XI. But it is necessary to discuss what distinction there is in it between the unjust and the just, lest the generality of the term bring the glory of Christian blessedness into comparison with evils. There are therefore two forms of rising. The first is that of the saints: summoned by the royal signal of the first trumpet, they will receive that kingdom of blessedness with immense triumph under Christ, the eternal King. The second consigns the impious, together with sinners and all unbelieving nations, to everlasting punishment. For the Holy Spirit says in the Psalms: “Therefore the impious do not rise in judgment, nor sinners in the council of the righteous; for the Lord knows the way of the righteous, and the path of the impious shall perish” (Ps. 1:5–6).

> [Note: A *tessera* was any sign given especially to soldiers, by which, as by a symbol, they recognized one another. Thus Silius Italicus, XV.478: “The watchword gives a silent signal.” Here it is understood as the signal that will be given, with the trumpet sounding, on the day of final judgment.]

> [Note: In distinguishing the impious from sinners, he has in view the distinction in the Psalm quoted below; we shall discuss it more fully in Treatise XXI, Book II, and Dissertation II, ch. 10.]

XII. It follows that we ought to know in what condition this our human being, who is making his way toward heaven, will reign, lest he perhaps perish with the flesh through a vain hope, if he be captivated by something fleeting and fleshly, of which the Apostle says: “Flesh and blood cannot possess the kingdom of God” (1 Cor. 15:50).

[Note: Here he seems to be alluding to those who promised themselves pleasures of the flesh in another life and, led by this vain hope, perished. Barthius, book XLIII, chapter 10, conjectures that one should read *vana specie* (“by a vain appearance”), or *vana spes* (“vain hope”): “if he has been captured by an appearance,” etc.]

But, on the other hand, I seem to hear someone crying out: “If this is the condition of the flesh, what then is it that we believe in the Church: the forgiveness of sins and the resurrection of the flesh?”

[Note: The Reims manuscript reads *remissa peccatorum et resurrectio carnis* (“the forgiveness of sins and the resurrection of the flesh”). *Remissa*, *remissae*, in place of *remissio, -onis*, occurs frequently in Tertullian and Cyprian. See Cyprian’s Epistle VI to Magnus and Epistle IX to Januarius, as well as Optatus, book I. But the Vatican and Zeno manuscripts have *remissionem*. Zeno nevertheless again uses *remissam* in Treatise L, book II.]

Easily, brethren, this apparent conflict is reconciled, and the character of the future state is disclosed, if faith is kept unblemished. I shall therefore explain the matter briefly. All flesh, so long as it is agitated by the shameful allurements of this world and by deathly darkness, is assuredly bestial flesh and exists under a wretched, frail, and detestable condition.

[Note: “Bestial flesh”: flesh belonging to beasts. Similarly Apuleius, *Metamorphoses*, book VIII: “bestial bones.”]

[Note: *Jus* here means state or condition, as in Cicero, *On the Agrarian Law* III.2: “Estates are certainly under the best legal condition when they are in the best condition.” “Free women are under a better legal condition than slave women.” And *Against Verres* II, §27: “The allies are under such a legal condition that they are not even permitted to lament their misfortunes.”]

138 But when, through the pure faith of one who believes, it has been put to death in the saving baptism, it rises anew from the sacred flood of the Father’s font: now pure, now free, now estranged from the manner of life of this world, now superior to death, now breathing after heavenly things; now, I do not say, scorning the toys of the age, but—so as to be more honorable—scorning itself; now seeking truth rather than an image, now desiring spiritual things rather than its own things. Of it Paul says: “Not all flesh is the same flesh: one is the flesh of human beings, another of beasts, another the flesh of birds, another of fishes. And there are heavenly bodies and earthly bodies” (1 Cor. 15:39–40).

[Note: The Reims and Urbino manuscripts read “believing by thin faith”; other manuscripts read “of one believing by pure faith,” and the printed editions have the same. Perhaps, however, *vera* (“true”) should be read for *mera* (“pure”), or *sacra* (“sacred”) for *macra* (“thin”), or something similar. Yet we retained the reading of the greater number of manuscripts in the text. This reading means nothing other than that baptism is beneficial through faith—namely, that faith which, as the author teaches elsewhere, can act only through charity; this we have seen at greater length in Dissertation II, chapter 6. Moreover, in baptism the flesh of the old human being is said to be put to death, in order that the new one may rise in Christ; more on this follows.]

[Note: The Toledo and Vatican manuscripts read: “another is that of a beast.”]

Thus, having first been made fruitful by the implanted seed of immortality—of which the wisest Poet also gave foreknowledge when he said:

> “For within them is a fiery power and a heavenly origin  
>  in their seeds”—

that is, by the conception of the Holy Spirit, so that, when the time of its dissolution and lawful restoration has come, corresponding by right to its own seed, it may deserve to receive what we believe.

The matter is not uncertain. For just as that prince of iniquity, by his own seed and through envy, transformed the first-created parents from angels into human beings, so the Lord will raise all who believe in him, through the seed of the Holy Spirit, from the dead and once more glorious into angels (Matt. 23:30).

[Note: Barthius, book XLII, chapter 10, thinks that there is an allusion here to the opinion of certain persons who taught that human beings, when angels had fallen, were appointed in their place. But Zeno’s words do not appear to bear this meaning. He speaks of the fall of the first parents, whom the devil through envy drew into guilt. And just as he undoubtedly called them angels in that state of innocence in which, endowed with the gifts of immortality and grace, they were approaching angelic glory—of whom the Psalmist said, “You made him a little lower than the angels” (hence, in Treatise XXVII, book II, at the end, he similarly said that a martyr had been transformed from a human being into an angel)—so he called them human beings as mortals and sinners, the condition into which they had most miserably passed through guilt. The sense, therefore, is this: the devil, the prince of iniquity, stirred by envy, by his own seed—that which he sowed through temptation—led or turned the first-created persons, that is, the first parents, from innocent and immortal angels into sinful and mortal human beings. For *derivare*, figuratively, means to lead elsewhere or turn aside. Thus Cicero, *Against Verres* III, §56, says “to divert his answer elsewhere,” and in book IV of the same work, §20, “to divert blame onto someone.” From these remarks you will readily understand what follows. The word *protoplasti*, meaning “those first created,” is also used by Tertullian in *Exhortation to Chastity*, chapter 2, and is commonly taken by other Fathers to mean the first parents. Prudentius says *primo plastos* (“first fashioned”) in the *Hymn of Every Hour*, verse 17. The Toledo manuscript has *sursum* for *rursus* (“again”); the Urbino manuscript, however, has *sursus in angelos* (“upward into angels”).]

139 XIII. Let us still produce one evident example for this one point, although something merely probable cannot possess force equal to truth.

[Note: We preferred the manuscript reading; the printed editions have *proponamus* (“let us set forth”).]

The wild olive is unfortunate and bitter in its own nature; but when it has been cut back, with necessary foresight, by the hand of a most skilled farmer and craftsman, it is made pregnant with the nobility of an alien seed and is nourished by that very thing which it nourishes, until, taken up into the adopted richness of the guest-graft—indeed, itself made richness—and adorned throughout its branches, rising again, by advancement to the honor of new foliage, it is no longer a wild olive but an olive; although it is a wild olive, it nevertheless marvels that it is, in a certain manner, no longer itself a wild olive.

[Note: The printed editions, with most manuscripts, read: “transformed into acceptance, in honor by the advancement of new foliage.” Barthius judged that this should be corrected to: “transformed into acceptance, by the dishonorable advancement of new foliage.” But the very ancient Reims manuscript supplied what seemed the fairer reading, deleting only the first particle *in*, which is likewise absent from the Vatican and Urbino manuscripts, and changing *honore* to *honorem*. Moreover, Lampridius in *Antoninus Diadumenianus*, chapter 2, and Julius Firmicus, *On the Positions of the Fixed Stars* 3.7 and 5, etc., use the term *promotio* (“advancement”). From the same Reims manuscript we have written *resurgescentibus* (“rising again”) for *resurgentibus* (“rising”).]

[Note: Vatican manuscript: “that it is now no longer.” Then the Urbino manuscript: “in some manner, even itself.”]

Therefore, if a human being can cause a tree to become what it was not, while preserving what it was, how much more can God raise a human being into that which he was before he sinned in paradise?

[Note: The unusual syntax must be construed thus: “raise into that which he was before he sinned in paradise,” that is, raise into immortal life.]

The most blessed Paul also subtly expressed this principle of seeds, saying: “He who sows according to the flesh will reap destruction from his flesh; but he who sows in the Spirit will reap eternal life from the Spirit” (Gal. 6:8).

[Note: The Reims manuscript has “in destruction”; but “in the Spirit” is lacking in this manuscript. The Verona edition omitted “from the Spirit.” We supplied it from most manuscripts and from the Venetian edition. A little later, for “teaching this,” the Toledo manuscript has “teaching himself this”; the Urbino manuscript, “also teaching this.”]

But the Lord, plainly teaching this, said to the disciples: “The kingdom of heaven is like a man who sowed good seed in his field; but while people slept, his enemy came and sowed tares over the wheat” (Matt. 13:24–25).

XIV. But perhaps someone may still say: “If the flesh perishes, by what means is the one who rises recognized?” Flesh, brethren, is as it were a mirror, made pregnant by the fullness of the beholder, which bears in its functions not so much its own image as the image of him to whom it belongs.

[Note: The Pompignan manuscripts have *gravatum* (“weighed down”). Cicero called the earth “made pregnant with seeds,” *On the Nature of the Gods*, book II, §32.]

[Note: That is, the spirit united to the body and using the flesh. He calls flesh the image of the spirit because the various movements and affections of the mind often shine forth in the body, as is clear from what follows. Tertullian says the same splendidly in *On the Resurrection*, chapter 15: “Let the soul ponder something; the countenance supplies the indication; the face is the mirror of all intentions.” See more in Pliny, book II, chapter 37; and read also, if you please, Nazarius and Pacatus in their Panegyrics, and Jerome in his letter to Furia. The Toledo, Vatican, and Urbino manuscripts have *quaerit* (“seeks”) for *gerit* (“bears”).]

For it produces as many expressions as the inner person has made sad or cheerful movements of his own. Paul teaches us this principle: “Now,” he says, “we see through a mirror in an enigma, but then face to face” (1 Cor. 13:12).

Therefore there is no doubt that in our bodies, 140 while they are sown under the law of death, not the substance, not the image, but only that which is useless is broken apart, that which is worn away is changed, as it is written: “For this corruptible thing must put on incorruption, and this mortal thing must put on immortality” (1 Cor. 15:53). For otherwise that robe of immortality is not received unless first this fleshly spoil, the pleasant poison of the soul, is returned, in accordance with God’s sentence, to the place from which it was taken. For God says to Adam: “Cursed shall the earth be in all your works; in the groaning of sorrow you shall eat from it all the days of your life. It shall bring forth thorns and thistles for you, and you shall eat the food of the field. In the sweat of your face you shall eat your bread, until you return to the earth” (Gen. 3:17 ff.).

[Note: The Lord too is said to speak “in the person of a human being,” that is, as a human being. Christ did not wish in those words to act or present himself as God, but as a human being. In this sense the ancients often called something a *persona*, as when they spoke of “the person of a father, brother, ruler, friend,” etc., meaning “as a father, brother, ruler, friend,” etc. We have touched upon some points concerning this expression of Zeno in Dissertation II, chapter 3. The same formula is found in Saint Hilary, *On Psalm LIV*, p. 118, and *On Psalm CXXXVIII*, p. 565; Saint Ambrose, *On Faith* II.8.61, IV.6.69, and V.10.124. Similarly Phoebadius, in his book *Against the Arians*, p. 303, volume IV of the *Library of the Fathers*, attributes a saying of Solomon to “the person of wisdom,” because wisdom speaks in it as though it itself were wisdom. Therefore “the person of a human being” here is not to be understood in the sense in which, with Nestorius, a human person is attributed to Christ, but in the sense in which human actions and passions befitted him as a true human being.]

And the Lord, speaking in the person of the human being whom he had assumed, says: “My soul is sorrowful even unto death” (Matt. 26:38). This saying is not so much that of one who fears as of one who rejoices and teaches. Certainly he could not fear anything—he who raised the dead, who had authority to lay down his life and to take it up again (John 10:18). Rather, he taught that while one lives in this world, one is always in tribulation, and the righteous person is always under punishment. But when death, which is thought fearful, is tasted, then the promised blessedness is bestowed upon him in the blessed dwellings of glory that endures forever, and it will thereafter experience none of the world’s miseries. Thus holy David says: “Return, my soul, to your rest, because the Lord has dealt kindly with me; because he has delivered my soul from death, my eyes from tears, my feet from falling. I shall please the Lord in the land of the living” (Ps. 114:7 ff.).

This blessedness awaits us; this gift is in store. Let us therefore live in such a way that, adorned with good works, we too may deserve to please God the Father, with the Lord Christ helping us, who is blessed unto ages of ages.

141 BOOK TWO OF THE TREATISES OF SAINT ZENO, BISHOP OF VERONA.

## TREATISE I. On Genesis.—Against the Arians.

[Note: TREATISE I.—The manuscripts have: “Begins, On Genesis.” This title, retained in the printed editions, did not need to be changed by us. Throughout this treatise Zeno defends the divinity of the eternal Word against the Arians, as also in the two immediately following treatises, which bear the same title in the manuscripts.]

I. People of fleshly mind, most beloved brethren, take offense—not from a desire to know truth, but to frustrate it—whenever the Son of God, who is the greatest glory of the Father, is proclaimed by Catholics to be equal to the Father.

[Note: *Denique* is not always a particle marking the last member of an enumeration, so as to mean “finally”; sometimes it is placed after a single member, as here by Zeno, or even when nothing has preceded, as he uses it in Treatise VI of this book, where he begins an enumeration. Then it means approximately, “to put it briefly”; see Schultinger’s notes on Quintilian’s *Declamation* I, p. 15. Examples occur in Nepos XII.1, Florus I.16, Justin, Papinian, and others cited by Freinsheim in his edition of Florus.]

For this reason, despising the foundations of the Law, they hasten by a crafty disputation—passing over God proceeding from God—to the common human titles of Father and Son, which can be reached by arguments. Nor do they understand that, at the beginning of the sacred poem, God, compared with God both in his divinity and in his name, excludes all conjectures of human thought. For he says: “Let us make humankind in our image and likeness”; he does not say, “Make [them] in your image,” but says, “Let us make [them] in our image” (Gen. 1:26), lest the Son, who was to put on human nature, appear to suffer any injury.

[Note: By “Law” Zeno means Sacred Scripture, as we observed in Treatise XII, book I, note 1.]

[Note: The book of Genesis is called a sacred poem, although it is historical. Similarly, the book of Isaiah is called “the poem of Isaiah” in Treatises 23 and 26, and “the divine poem” in the same Isaiah. Sparaverius has more on this use of *carmen*. Below, we have written *dicat* (“he says”) from the Toledo, Urbino, Pompignan, and Zeno manuscripts, in place of *dicit* (“he says”) found in the printed editions and other manuscripts.]

[Note: Did Saint Zeno intend here to criticize Tertullian’s interpretation, according to which humankind was made in Christ’s image? Tertullian writes thus in *Against Marcion* V.8: “The Father, looking upon Christ his Word, who was to come: ‘Let us make,’ he says, ‘humankind,’ etc.” And in *On the Resurrection of the Flesh*, chapter 6: “And God made humankind—that which he fashioned, indeed; he made it in the image of God, namely, of Christ.” Although this interpretation did no injury to the Son for Tertullian, who rightly held the Son’s divinity, it nevertheless involved no slight danger that the Arians might turn it toward diminishing or denying the Son’s divinity, as though he could not be equal to the Father if the Father were not reported to have said: “Let us make in our image, in which we are equal,” but “Make in your image,” which the human being, once made, would presumably bear.]

Do you see, most beloved brethren, that here no one expressly commands another, and that no one is idle in the work? O holy equality, most worthy of the indivisible deity alone! One human being is fashioned in the image and likeness of two; yet in that human being it is not discovered what belongs to either one.

[Note: *Exserte* occurs explicitly in Tertullian, *To His Wife* I.1: “The Apostle does not advise but expressly commands,” that is, openly and distinctly. Apuleius, *Metamorphoses* I, has *exserte clamitans*, “crying out plainly.”]

[Note: We preferred the reading of the very many manuscripts and printed editions, which also occurs in Treatise VI, book II. Some manuscripts have *aequabilitas* (“uniformity”). Below the Reims manuscript writes *dealitatis* for *deitatis* (“deity”); we find this noun in use in Zeno’s century both in Hilary’s book *On the Synods* and in Lucifer of Cagliari, book I *For Athanasius*, p. 198.]

[Note: The word “two” is absent from the Pompignan manuscript, as though the two things in whose image one human being is said to have been fashioned were image and likeness. But they are undoubtedly the Father and Son, of whom Genesis says “in our [image],” and whose image and likeness the one human being exhibits in such a way that it cannot at all be distinguished in him what is the Father’s and what the Son’s. From this a not weak argument against the Arians is drawn.]

If, therefore, sacred equality cannot be distinguished in a work external to itself, how can God be inferior to himself in another? For whatever you subtract from one of the two, who resemble each other indiscriminately in all things, you do not know from which one you have subtracted it.

[Note: *Similo* is found likewise in Martial, book II, epigram 35, and in Marcellus Empiricus, chapter 8. But in Martial some read *simulo*, and Burmann, in Quintilian VII.10 and Ovid, *Metamorphoses* III.158, maintains that *similare* and *assimilare* cannot correctly be said in Latin. Yet this word now seems sufficiently vindicated by the authority of Zeno’s manuscripts, which plainly write *similantibus*, derived from *similo*. When Zeno affirms that the Father and Son resemble one another in all things, how remote he is from the Semi-Arian view, which called the Son’s substance “similar” to God’s, is clear from the entire context. He said *similantes* in order to maintain the comparison which he had made from the human being created in the likeness of Father and Son; by adding “in all things” he plainly shows that he admits the most perfect possible likeness, such as exists among those of one and the same substance. That the Father and Son are indeed so, he most expressly affirms in many passages of Dissertation I, cited in chapter 2, §2.]

[Note: In the printed editions, “I do not know”; we followed the manuscript reading.]

143 II. “But he to whom the command is given,” you say, “is inferior.”

[Note: The Vatican and Zeno manuscripts read *inquit* (“he says”). This is the famous objection of the Arians, to which Zeno gives two replies; both may be found among other Fathers. Some acknowledged a command of the Father to the Son, yet held that it caused no prejudice to their equality; see Irenaeus III.8; Tertullian, *Against Praxeas*, chapter 12; Origen, volume II on John, p. 61, ed. Huet; Basil, *On the Holy Spirit* I.16; Cyril, *Thesaurus* I.29, p. 225; Athanasius, *On the Decrees of the Nicene Synod*, on Psalm 33, “He commanded, and they were created”; Marius Victorinus, *On the Creation of Things* I; and finally Hilary, *On the Trinity* IV.16. In all these passages there is explicit mention both of the Father commanding and the Son carrying out the command. Zeno briefly explains correctly how this does not offend the Son: to perform great things—namely, to create the world, which assuredly belongs only to almighty God—is no less than to speak, that is, command, that the world be created. Yet, lest anyone should infer from this first answer that the Son is the Father’s minister and inferior with prejudice to equality, Zeno adds another answer, which he plainly indicates he prefers to the former: namely, that the Son himself, insofar as he is the Father’s Word, is the Father’s very command by which all things were commanded to come into being; he is also that power by which all things were created by the Father through the Son. Hence in Treatise IV, book II: “Whatever the Father commanded to be made, the Son, as the power of God and wisdom of God, completed all by his marvelous work together with the spoken word.” Likewise, other Fathers either did not approve at all the formulas of commanding and obeying, or approved them only insofar as the Father’s command and mandate itself is recognized to be the Son, while the execution of creating and making indicates the Father’s power in the Son. Read Athanasius, *Oration III against the Arians*; Cyril, *On John* I.5; Hilary IV.27 ff.; and Augustine, who in *The Literal Meaning of Genesis* II.6 criticizes the expression “command,” but nevertheless in *Tractate XXI on John* and in *Against an Arian Sermon*, chapter 3, shows that the Father’s command itself is the Father’s Son. With what brevity and force Zeno embraces all this! See what will be noted on the same point in the following Treatise IV, note 6, where he again mentions the Father’s command and the Son’s execution, while confirming their equality by striking testimony and argument.]

What then? It is proved from this very point that he is not inferior, because he is the executor of the Father’s heart, from which he proceeded. For it is no less to do great things than to speak.

[Note: We do not know on what authority the Verona editors wrote *excultor*. But *exsecutor*, which is found in the manuscripts and Venetian edition, indicates that the Son was he through whom all things that the Father willed were created; this will be discussed more fully in Treatise IV, where we shall note more. Observe also the syntax, which must be construed thus: “because he is the executor of the Father’s heart, from which he proceeded.” That the Son is said to have proceeded from the Father’s heart refers to Psalm 44:1: “My heart has uttered a good Word.” Certain ancient Fathers interpreted this as spoken by the Father concerning the Son. Thus Tertullian, *Against Praxeas*, chapter 8: “From that Father, proceeding, the Son was made: firstborn, as begotten before all things; only-begotten, as alone begotten properly from God, from the womb of his heart itself, according to that to which his Father also bears witness: ‘My heart has uttered,’ etc.” This testimony is frequently cited in the same sense among the Fathers who opposed the Arians, as Augustine notes in his exposition of Psalm 44, §4. Perhaps Psalm 109:3 also belongs here: “From the womb, before the morning star, I begot you.” Augustine yields the explanation of these words in *Against Maximinus* I.7 and II.18. What this generation of the Son from the Father’s heart is like we have taught more fully in Dissertation II, chapter 1, §3 ff.]

Moreover, what has been said by the Father, or can be said, does not exist without the Son, because the Son is the Word; and what has been done by the Son, or can be done, does not exist without the Father’s gracious will, because the Son does not exist without the Father. He himself says: “If I do not do the works of my Father, do not believe me. But if you are unwilling to believe me, believe the works, and know that the Father is in me and I in him” (John 10:37–38).

It is therefore established that he is equal, because each contains the other together with the Holy Spirit.

[Note: Thus the manuscripts and the Venetian edition read. But since the old edition had written *q.*, the Padua edition wrote *qui* (“who”).]

## TREATISE II. On Genesis.

Unless one conquers the enemy by whom one is attacked, one will never be able to enjoy one’s goods securely. For there are many who try to assert that in the beginning there was chaos—that is, an unformed and disordered mass of latent nature, remaining by itself within itself as a heap of its own magnitude—and that afterward God separated this mass and from it at once constructed and adorned the world.

[Note: TREATISE II.—Among heretics some posited matter as coeternal with and uncreated by God: Hermogenes, whom not only Tertullian refutes in the surviving books against him, but also Theophilus of Antioch in Eusebius IV.24, and Maximus in Eusebius V.27. The Manichaeans likewise adopted the same error, according to Jerome, on Ephesians 1, verse 4. Philastrius, *Heresies* LV, and Augustine, deriving it from him, *Heresies* 59, testify that the Seleucians and Hermians were implicated in the same heresy. Procopius, in his *Commentary on Genesis*, mentions other authors of the same error, who distorted the opening words of Genesis in support of it. We do not venture to affirm whether Saint Bishop Zeno intended to strike at these. Rather, we think that he here means the poets and philosophers of the Gentiles, who had taught the same error long before. At the beginning of this treatise Saint Zeno appears to imitate Lactantius, *Institutes* II.8, from whom he expressed several things in almost the same words, as we shall shortly see. Lactantius explicitly calls them pagan poets and philosophers. He says first concerning the poets: “Nor should poets be heard, who say that there was chaos in the beginning, that is, a confusion of things and elements; and that afterward God separated the whole mass, and, after individual things had been separated from the confused heap and ordered, constructed and adorned the world at once.” From this it is clear that Zeno profited somewhat in writing his first period. Ovid, *Metamorphoses* I, and certain Greek poets clearly taught the same things. Lactantius further cites from the philosophers a notable testimony of Marcus Tullius, in which this view is explicitly set forth; it is a fragment of the book *On the Nature of the Gods*, which either reached us mutilated or has completely perished. There Cicero seems to have described not his own but another philosopher’s opinion, since elsewhere he expressed the correct judgment concerning the creation of the world. See Theodoret, *On Heresies* V.6, and Saint Basil, *Homily I on the Hexaemeron*.]

Thus, if, as they wish, God did not make the matter which he used, but it is eternal as he is, then there are two principles, and indeed mutually opposed ones. Therefore we must necessarily inquire which of the two is stronger: that which has perception, or that which lacks perception.

[Note: The Toledo manuscript has *manente* (“remaining”). The same manuscript has “the Lord” for “God,” and *diremsisse* for *diremisse* (“separated”).]

[Note: *Ergo* (“therefore”) is absent from the Pompignan, Zeno, and Spire manuscripts. Why these two principles are called opposed will be stated in the following note.]

[Note: Here too some things seem to have been taken from Lactantius. Thus he says, *Institutes* II.8, by a different kind of argument, but one which comes to almost the same point: “Therefore either God came from matter, or matter from God. Which of these is truer is easy to understand: for of these two, one has perception, the other lacks perception.” For that reason Saint Zeno called the two principles opposed. “The power to make something cannot exist except in that which feels, knows, thinks, and moves”; our author especially uses these final words.]

But who doubts that that is stronger which feels, which knows, which thinks, which moves, which is moved, which by marvelous providence caused chaos itself not to be chaos, which separated its members, arranged them by reason, adorned them with colors, bounded them by measure, and commanded them to serve through functions and effects suited to them?

[Note: Perhaps someone will think that one should read “which moves, which is not moved,” lest contrary things seem to be said of the same subject. Similarly, the soul is said, from Plato, in Ambrose, Epistle 34, §1, to be that which moves itself and is not moved by another. But Zeno most fittingly says “moves and is moved” without contradiction, referring to the philosophers’ opinion clearly expounded by Cicero in the *Dream of Scipio*. There, seeking to prove God to be the principle of all things, Cicero holds him to be that which moves itself, because it is never abandoned by itself and never even ceases to move; indeed, he is the source and principle of motion for all other things that move. Thus “moves” refers to others, while “is moved” refers to itself. See Cicero’s passage, from which you will find other points brought by Zeno here into a brief summary to establish God as the principle of all things.]

That which grows old is not a principle; nor that which is an alien work made; nor that which is not established in its own power; nor that which is taken away from its own substance; nor that which changes; nor that which is moved by an alien impulse; nor that which can never perceive what it is, what it was, or what it will be.

God alone, therefore, is the principle: he gave himself his own beginning from himself. He alone is before all things and after all things, because all things enclosed in his hand are what they are from him. He alone is conscious of himself—how great and what kind he is. He alone is perfect, because nothing can be added to or subtracted from him. He alone is almighty, because he established the universe from nothing, governs it by power, and guards it by majesty. He alone is unchangeable and always equal to himself, because he admits no age within himself. He alone is everlasting, because he is Lord of immortality.

[Note: Lactantius splendidly says, *Institutes* I.7: “But because it cannot be that what exists did not at some time begin to be, it follows that, since nothing existed before him, he himself was brought forth before all things from himself; and therefore by Apollo he is called αὐτοφυής (*self-grown*), by the Sibyl αὐτογενής (*self-generated*), ἀγέννητος (*unbegotten*), and ἀποίητος (*unmade*) . . . God made himself.” This formula is frequent among the Fathers; Cyril mentions it from Orpheus in *Against Julian* I: “One is begotten from himself.” And Jerome, on Ephesians 3: “God, who always is, has no beginning from elsewhere and is himself his own origin.” Read others in Petavius, *On the Trinity* V.5.14. Although this expression is in no way proper—for no one is both giver and gift to himself, as Hilary observed, book II, §7—it may nevertheless rightly be understood so that “he gave himself his own beginning” means the same as “he received the communication of his substance from no other principle.”]

This is our God, who unfolded himself into God. This is the Father who, while his own state remained whole, poured back his whole self into the Son, lest he take anything away from himself.

[Note: Here Zeno intimates the generation of the Son from the Father, concerning which he speaks more openly in what follows.]

[Note: The author wished to make this point lest someone perhaps suppose that the Father’s substance was changed through the generation of the Son. For the Arians reproached Catholics who confessed the Father’s and Son’s substance to be the same, arguing that the Son was a portion of the divine substance separated from the Father by generation. See Hilary, *On the Trinity* IV.4.]

[Note: *Reciprocavit se* (“poured himself back”) is most aptly used to explain Zeno’s meaning: something is called reciprocal when, having gone out from somewhere, it flows back to the place from which it went out. Thus the Father is said to have poured himself back into the Son because he communicated his entire self to the Son in such a way that he nevertheless retained his entire self, as though, while communicating all, he had received all back. The author expressed this in another formula, Treatise II, book I, §9: “From the Fatherly fountain you are wholly poured forth into the Son; yet when you are wholly poured forth, you do not depart.”]

Finally, one rejoices in the other, shining forth in one original coeternity through the fullness of the Holy Spirit.

[Note: Here Saint Zeno undoubtedly indicates the procession of the Holy Spirit, which shines in the mutual love of Father and Son. Hence in Treatise II, book I, §9, speaking of charity, he said: “You rejoice in the Holy Spirit.”]

Just as—if it is worthy to say it—two seas, lying back into themselves and connected by a strait that brings their alternate tides into one, though distinct in their own identity, places, and names, nevertheless possess one power of their threefold deep vapor, one substance, one nature of flowing; nor can the incomprehensible and common abundance of the wave be divided, while each flows copiously into the other, belonging to both and withheld from neither. For they would suffer loss of abundance and grace if that were taken away by which, in one and the same tide, each is adorned from the other.

[Note: Such and other similar comparisons transferred from earthly things to explain divine things, though Hilary warned that they are unequal, *On the Trinity* I.19 and IV.2, he nevertheless did not doubt to be useful in accommodating the weakness of our minds.]

[Note: The Reims, Toledo, Vatican, and Urbino manuscripts have *saporis* (“flavor”). Then the Toledo manuscript has *fluenti* for *fluendi* (“of flowing”).]

[Note: Almost every manuscript presents different readings in this passage. Some have “the greatness of the wave, and to be divided, while each passes into the other”; others, “the greatness of the wave and to be divided, passing into each other”; others, “the greatness of the wave to be divided, and yet each passing into the other”; finally others, “the greatness of the wave to be divided, and with each into the other,” etc. We judged that this last reading should be preferred, with the conjunction *et* deleted as superfluous.]

### TREATISE III. On Genesis, or on the eternal generation of the Son of God

[Note: [Col. 0392C] TREATISE III.—This first title occurs in all the manuscripts except the Zenonian, which, together with the printed editions, prefers the other. Moreover, an excellent marginal notice, written in capital letters and appended to this treatise in the Reims manuscript, reads as follows: “To be read to the brethren in the chamber on the Nativity of the Lord, after the entrance of the deacons and before the pontiff.” It seems worth observing here that it was the duty of the deacons to enter to the pontiff, or bishop, whenever he was to proceed from the chamber to the sacred offices. For whenever the chamber is mentioned in other marginal notices of this kind, the deacons are always said either to have entered in order to receive the pontiff or to have gone out from the chamber with him. These deacons appear to have been those who, several at once and clothed in sacred vestments, customarily ministered in solemn rite to the bishop as he celebrated the sacred rites, as we learn from several Ordines published by Martene, vol. I, *De Antiquis Ecclesiae Ritibus*, pp. 568, 573, 613, Paris edition.]

[Col. 0392B]

The Beginning, [Note: [Col. 0392C] Christ himself plainly affirmed that he is the Beginning in John 8:25. For when the Jews asked, “Who are you?” he answered, “The Beginning, who also speak to you.” The sense in which Christ, the Son of God, is the Beginning is explained by Theophilus of Antioch, *To Autolycus*, book II, where, discussing the divine Word, he says: “This is called the Beginning because it has primacy and dominion over all things made through it.” Although the Father may also be called Beginning for the same reason, the term is applied in a particular manner to the Son, insofar as the Son is that Word through whom all things were made, as is stated in Sacred Scripture with a certain special propriety. On this see Dissertation II, chapter 1, §§4–5.

Indeed, among the ancients it is a customary and widespread view that the term “beginning,” occurring in Genesis 1:1, signifies the same divine Word. Some even asserted that the Hebrew manuscripts read, “In the Son God made heaven and earth,” instead of “In the beginning”; Jerome reports this at the opening of his *Hebrew Questions* and cites Tertullian, *Against Praxeas*, as authority. Tertullian certainly uses this argument in chapter 5 of that work to establish the distinction of the divine persons against the error which anticipated Sabellianism; but he speaks not in his own name, but rather according to the view of others: “They do indeed say that Genesis begins thus in Hebrew: ‘In the beginning he made for himself a Son.’” Yet this error is easily refuted by those skilled in the Hebrew language.

Other Fathers, however, although they did not suppose that the Hebrew read thus, indicated that the Son should nevertheless be understood there under the name “Beginning.” Origen is explicit, *Homily 1 on Genesis*: after saying that the Son is the beginning of all things, he says, “Therefore in this Beginning, that is, in his Word, God made heaven and earth.” This interpretation is supported by Clement of Alexandria, *Stromata*, book VI, p. 644; Hilary, *On Psalm 2*; Ambrose, *Hexameron*, book I, chapter 2; Augustine, *On Genesis according to the Letter*, book I, chapter 5; *Confessions*, book XI, chapter 9, and especially book XII, chapters 19, 20, and 28. There Augustine consistently interprets “in the beginning” as “in the Word,” “in the Son,” “in Wisdom”; thus God created all things in the Son because he created all things in Wisdom—the Wisdom that is the artificer of all things, as Proverbs 8 calls it.

Those who called the Beginning *sophia* (σοφία, “Wisdom”) in Greek, as Methodius does in Photius, Codex 235, and also *sophia* in Latin, as Tertullian does in *Against Hermogenes*, chapter 20, differ not at all from this view. Hence Proclus, *Oration* 2, p. 102, calls the Son, who is said to be the Father’s Wisdom, the *authentēs dēmiourgos* (αὐθέντην δημιουργόν), the principal artificer. But however this may be, that Zeno speaks of the Son as the Beginning of all things, through whom and in whom all things were established, is evident from Treatise 5 of this book, where, repeating almost word for word what is said here, he adds several remarks concerning the creation of the world.], beloved brethren, is certainly our Lord [Col. 0393A] 148 [Note: [Col. 0393C] The printed editions read *incontanter*, though this does not occur in the manuscripts. Yet *incuntanter* and *incontanter* are found written interchangeably. *Incuntanter* occurs in Lactantius, book VI, chapter 12; *incontanter* in Apuleius, book XI, shortly after the beginning. Similarly, *cuntari* and *contari* occur.

Now just as *contor* or *cuntor* means not so much “to delay” or “to procrastinate” as “to raise a question” or “to hold the mind in suspense” (hence Apuleius says, *Metamorphoses* 8, “She investigates, being doubtful [*contabunda*], that is, undecided and suspended”; “He speaks hesitantly [*cuntabundus*]”; Tacitus, *Annals* I.7, and Apuleius, *Metamorphoses* 7, use it in the same sense: “No delay, nor hesitation [*contario*], or, as others read, *cuntatio*.” There he distinguishes hesitation from delay and understands it as suspense of mind or questioning. Similarly Paulinus, poem 23 on St Felix, line 416, uses *Paridae cuntamine mentis* in the same sense), so *incuntanter*, or *incontanter*, in Zeno must likewise be understood as “without question,” “without controversy,” “without doubt,” rather than “without delay,” as may appear at first sight—unless “delay” is understood as a suspension of mind. Thus perhaps Paulinus of Périgueux said *incuntante fide*, “with faith that does not doubt,” book V, line 132.] Christ, whom before all ages the Father held in the unfathomable secret of his sacred mind, known to himself alone in consciousness, with affection for the Son indeed, but [Note: [Col. 0393D] The Pompignan manuscript reads: “the sacred secrets of the mind.” A secret is called *insuspicabile*, “beyond conjecture,” because it cannot be penetrated or known even through inferences. For in Zeno, Treatise 16, book I, section 3, no less than in Cyril’s Glossary, *suspicio* is a slight opinion and uncertain knowledge; and in Arnobius *suspicabile* is that which we attain by uncertain knowledge and conjecture. Hence he called medicine an art of conjecture, wavering upon estimates based on inferences, book I, p. 28. The old translator of Ecclesiasticus uses *insuspicabilis* in the same sense in chapters 11:5 and 25:9.] without disclosure. [Note: [Col. 0393D] He says, “without disclosure,” because when the Father eternally begot the Son, he did not reveal him, hidden in the profound secret of his sacred mind, nor manifest him outwardly. This began to occur through creation, when all things were made through him, John 1; and through the incarnation, when he dwelt among human beings, Baruch 3:38. On these matters see further Dissertation II, chapter 1, §3. Likewise Chrysologus, Sermon 67, at the end: “The Son of God always remained in the secret place of God the Father.”]

Therefore that ineffable and incomprehensible [Col. 0394A] Wisdom brings forth Wisdom; Omnipotence brings forth Omnipotence. [Note: [Col. 0394A] These are customary formulations among the Fathers, expressing the complete equality of the divine Word with the Father against the Arians, who heard them most unwillingly and made them a ground of accusation. “There are many,” says Hilary of such people, *On the Trinity*, book III, section 8, “wise in the world, whose wisdom is foolishness with God, who, when they hear that God has been born from God, the true from the true, the perfect from the perfect, one from one, object as though we were preaching impossibilities.”

Similar expressions occur in the creed of the Synod of Antioch, reported by Hilary in *On the Synods*, section 29: “God from God, whole from whole, one from one, perfect from perfect”; and also in the ancient author of the *Treatise on Orthodox Faith against the Arians*, apparently Gregory of Baetica, vol. II, Appendix to Ambrose, p. 347a. “Only from only” is particularly apt for refuting those who interpreted John 17:3—where Christ addresses the Father, “And this is eternal life, that they may know you, the only true God, and Jesus Christ whom you have sent”—as though Christ affirmed that the Father alone is God. The Fathers explain Christ’s statement concerning the Father as the only true God not as excluding himself from divinity, but as removing those who are not true by nature, as Athanasius says, *Against the Arians*, book IV; or, as Ambrose says, *On Faith*, book V, chapter 1, section 20, lest he seem to speak of two gods. Thus Zeno likewise affirms “only from only”; unless perhaps he says “only from only” in the sense of “one from one,” in order, as Hilary explains, *On the Synods*, section 33, to exclude the sufferings of human childbirth and conception.

Why he is said to be “whole from whole,” as Hilary also says, *On the Trinity*, book III, section 4, and book VI, section 10, is sufficiently explained by what Zeno adds: “Possessing all that belongs to the Father, diminishing nothing of the Father.” Or, as Hilary explains in the latter passage: “The whole fullness of divinity is in the Son, so that nothing of it is lacking to the Father.” Zeno is no less explicit in Treatise 6, section 4: “The Father is whole; the Son possesses the whole. What belongs to both is one thing; what one possesses belongs to each.” See Phoebadius, *Against the Arians*, p. 302e, book IV of the *Bibliotheca Patrum*, Lyons edition, who explains at length the formula “perfect from perfect,” and ibid., g, and p. 303g.] God is born from God: the Only-begotten from the Unbegotten, the Only from the Only, the Whole from the Whole, the True from the True, the Perfect from the Perfect—possessing all that belongs to the Father and diminishing nothing of the Father. [Note: [Col. 0394C] We have explained at length in Dissertation II, chapter 1, §6, what birth is under discussion here and the authentic meaning of this passage, which others have not properly grasped. [Col. 0394D] For the present, it is enough to indicate that Zeno is not speaking of that birth of Christ by which he was born from the Virgin, but of that by which he proceeded eternally from the Father—not, indeed, of that inconjecturable birth, as the author calls it, by which the Father held the Son in the depth of his sacred mind without disclosure, but of that birth by which the only-begotten Son came forth from the mouth of the same Father so that the nature of things, which did not exist, might be fashioned, as the same author says in the following treatise. That is, when the Father established the decree to create the world; this decree itself, as we have seen from the testimony of many Fathers in the passage cited, is called the Word.

Thus the Son was begotten by the Father before he was born in the issuing of the decree; this must be understood as a priority of reason, as the schools speak, not of time. For the begotten Son is conceived in the Father before the decree to create the world is conceived—a decree pronounced in the same Son as the Father’s Word.] He proceeds into birth, [Col. 0395A] he who was [Note: [Col. 0395A] Hilary also said, “He was with him before he was born,” *On Matthew*, chapter 31, section 3. The Arians used the contrary formula: “He was not before he was born.” Attacking this in *On the Trinity*, book XII, Hilary did not wish either that the Son was with the Father before he was born, or that he was not, section 31. Otherwise they might twist the former formula, which Hilary himself had used in those commentaries in a Catholic sense, into a perverse meaning—as though a time could be conceived in which the Son, not yet born, had existed with the Father as if in a root; this would have greatly favored the Arians. For Father and Son have existed together from eternity in such a way that the Son was never without the Father, nor was the Father ever at any time without the Son. The distinctive sense of this Zenonian testimony has been indicated in the preceding note, and is more fully explained and established in the cited Dissertation II, chapter 1, §6.] before he was born, equal to the Father in all things; because the Father [Note: [Col. 0395B] The expression *in ipsum* for *in ipso* (“into him” for “in him”) is occasionally attested by examples from other authors, which will be given more suitably in note 5 on Treatise 15, book II. Here it appears to have been used for force of expression, so that the meaning is that, in begetting the Son, the Father in some manner poured himself into him through the communication of the same substance. Thus in begetting the Son he is said to have begotten another self from himself, because he begot God from God, only from only, whole from whole, perfect from perfect, and so forth, as Zeno said shortly above.] begot another self into him from himself, namely from that unbegotten substance of his, in which, remaining blessed forever, he brought forth a Son possessing all things equal [Note: [Col. 0395B] Latin writers regularly use *procreare* in the sense of “beget.” Not a few Fathers observed that it is employed in the same sense in the sacred writings to explain the generation of the divine Word in Proverbs 8:22, translated thus from Greek: “The Lord created me,” ἔκτισέ με; many held this to have been spoken of the divine Son. The meaning, therefore, is: the Father begot a Son possessing things equal to all that he himself possesses. Here *paria* (“equal things”) is used in the same sense in which the Son is called equal to the Father. Thus the Son is said to possess things equal to all that the Father possesses, just as shortly before he was said to be equal in all things.] to all that he has—he who is God, blessed unto ages of ages.

### TREATISE IV. On Genesis, or on the eternal generation of the Son of God

[Note: [Col. 0395C] TREATISE IV.—This title occurs in all the manuscripts except the Zenonian, in which, together with the printed editions, the other title is read.]

[Col. 0396A]

As Sacred Scripture testifies, before all things there existed, remaining, [Note: [Col. 0395C] Thus in the Reims, Toledo, Vatican, Urbino, Vatican Basilica manuscripts and in the Venetian edition. Other, more recent manuscripts—the Zenonian, Pompignan, and Spanish—write *aeternaliter* (“eternally”) in place of *et idem alter* (“and the same, another”). This reading is less attractive, both because the word is not easily found in Latin except among writers of a much later age, and because it appears redundant: “there was, remaining before all things” sufficiently expresses this point. Especially since the author’s purpose is to indicate not that, if one may so speak, aspect of eternity conceived as before the creation of the world, but that priority of reason, as the scholastics call it, by which God, existing first in himself, is conceived before he eternally decreed anything concerning the nature of things to be created. To explain this view it was enough to state that God existed before all things and to explain who he was; there was no need to mention eternal duration, which is usually related to the beginning of created things.

Add the authority of the very oldest manuscripts, which wholly favors our reading. Moreover, it is much more credible that copyists who did not understand the sense wrote the single word *aeternaliter* from *et idem alter* than that *et idem alter* was written from *aeternaliter*. The Verona edition, supported by no manuscript, made a third reading by taking something from each: *et idem aeternaliter* (“and the same eternally”).

As for the author’s meaning, he seems to have said, “one and the same, another God from himself into himself,” in order to assert against the Arians that the Father and Son are two distinct persons and yet one God. When he mentions “one” and “another,” he surely implies a distinction of persons. Yet he sufficiently indicates that they are one God, not only when he says that this God is one and that this same one is at the same time another—which cannot otherwise be understood unless the two persons have one nature—but much more when this one and same other is said to be God from himself into himself: namely, one begotten from the same one God into that same God. This he explains more clearly in the following treatise: “The Father rejoices in another self, whom he begot from himself.” Therefore this other self, whom the Father begot from himself, is the one and same other God from himself into himself mentioned here.

Perhaps the words in the preceding Treatise 2 refer to this: “God alone, therefore, is the Beginning, who gave a Beginning to himself from himself.” They may indicate not merely that God is self-existent, as the schools say, receiving his origin from no external principle, but also that God the Father begot the Son from his own substance—a Son no less the Beginning than the Father. This is a splendid confession of the Son’s divinity against the Arians: it shows that the divine Word is equal to the Father and was begotten secretly before the ages, indeed before—by priority of reason—the decree to create the world was made. This birth is not impeded by the other birth attributed by St Zeno, with other Fathers, to the same Son: through the decree of creation he was in a certain way begotten again and then, in creation itself, came visibly forth, as they say. St Zeno speaks more fully of this birth in the second period and at the beginning of the following treatise; see also Dissertation II, chapter 1. From this it is understood that the Sacred Scripture said to testify, “There was one, remaining before all things,” and so forth, is perhaps John 1, Ecclesiasticus 1:1, or something similar.] one and the same, another God from himself into himself, 151 [Note: [Col. 0396C] The Son is certainly indicated here, whom, as he plainly says in Treatise 3, “before all ages the Father held in the unfathomable secret of his sacred mind, in a consciousness known to himself alone, with filial affection indeed, but without disclosure.” Especially noteworthy are the words “in a consciousness known to himself alone,” corresponding to those in the following treatise, section 1, “veiled in I know not what consciousness of his own,” and to similar words in Treatise 8, book II, section 1. This constant repetition of similar expressions, entirely consistent with the phrase written here, “alone conscious of his own secret,” openly indicates that the discourse here concerns the Son, who, veiled by the Father in the secret or depth of his heart, was known in a consciousness known only to himself before any decree was made concerning the creation of a world in which he would be manifested.

Nor shall we omit another observation: here the very generation of the Son is called “secret” (as will become clear from note 17 on the following treatise), because the Fathers teach that it is ineffable for human beings and known to God alone; see note 8. Other Fathers also speak in expressions very similar to Zeno’s. Ambrose, *On Faith*, book I, section 64: “For me it is impossible to know the secret of the generation.” Prudentius, reproving the Arians in the *Apotheosis*: “They proceed further, investigating what begetting itself is … even to the secret.” Peter Chrysologus, Sermon 61: “That he was born must be confessed; how he was born must be kept silent, because what is secret cannot be known.” Indeed, other Fathers so teach that God alone is conscious of this secret that they affirm that even angels do not fully know the generation of the divine Word. Gregory Nazianzen, *Oration on the Son* I: “But how he was begotten, I would not grant even the angels, much less you, to understand.” St Ambrose, *On Faith*, book I, section 64, adds to the words just cited: “The mind fails; the voice is silent—not mine only, but above the powers of angels, above angels, above Cherubim, above Seraphim, above every understanding.” Before them all, Irenaeus, book II, chapter 48: “No one knows his generation, which is beyond description … neither angels nor archangels, nor principalities nor powers, except the Father who begot and the Son who was begotten.” Thus you see Zeno’s position fully vindicated. Since it is clear from this that “secret” means the eternal generation of the Son, the reading discussed in note 2—“one and the same, another,” and so forth—is powerfully confirmed, where we showed that Zeno mentions the Father and Son distinctly.] alone conscious of his own secret. [Col. 0397A] From whose mouth, [Note: [Col. 0397B] The divine Word, which, according to the author’s view set out thus far, was begotten eternally by the Father from himself into himself—a birth all Catholics confess—came forth from the mouth of God as the only-begotten Son so that the nature of things, which did not exist, might be formed. This is readily understood if, besides that proper and hidden birth of the same Word, we admit, following the language of certain Fathers, another and less proper birth, intended for outward manifestation. Such is the case when God decreed to create the world. Since he decreed this in the Word and it was to be carried out through the Word—as has been demonstrated in Dissertation II, chapter 1—it could rightly be called, in a certain way, another procession of the divine Word, coming forth outwardly at the appointed time. For in the former birth the Son was, and remains, hidden in the depth of the Father’s sacred mind, utterly beyond conjecture and comprehension for every creature; nor would he ever have come outwardly had no decree for the world’s creation been issued.

This decree, eternally spoken by the Father in the Word, is itself said by Zeno to be the Word born by a new sort of generation. Likewise, in the following treatise he says: “In order that he might arrange the order of things conceived, that ineffable power and incomprehensible Wisdom belches forth the Word from the region of the heart; Omnipotence brings forth itself; God is born from God,” and so forth. On this see further Dissertation II, chapter 1, where the interpretation briefly indicated here is fully established and explained. If anyone is further troubled by the expression “from the mouth,” occurring here, let him consult Treatise 5, note 5.] the only-begotten Son came forth, so that the nature of things, which did not exist, might be formed; from then on, as the noble indweller of his heart, he was necessarily made visible, [Note: [Col. 0397C] This passage is strikingly mutilated and corrupted in the Verona edition and those following it, which read only: “made visible, because he was about to visit the human race,” and so forth. Since the editors of Verona did not grasp the author’s genuine meaning, they seem to have written this from fear of offense at the complete wording. All the manuscripts and the Venetian edition, however, read as we have printed it. The sense is sufficiently clear from what precedes.

The adverb “necessarily” need not be deleted. Once the decree already mentioned had been issued, it was altogether necessary that the Son, in whom we said the decree was made, should become visible. This was so in two ways: first, in creation itself, when all things were made through him; then in the incarnation, which was included in that decree. For not creation alone, but the whole order of “things conceived,” as Zeno says in Treatise 5, section 1, and therefore the incarnation as well, was decreed; the present statement, “he was about to visit the human race,” refers to this.

Observe carefully that St Zeno does not here call the external processions of the Word—by which either the world was created through the Word or the Word assumed human nature—the birth by which the only-begotten Son came forth from the Father’s mouth [Col. 0398A] and God was born from God, as though this birth had happened to the divine Word in the creation and incarnation of things, and thus in time. Rather, he calls the decree itself, eternally issued in the Word, a certain procession of the Word, in the sense explained more fully in the cited Dissertation II, chapter 1. [Col. 0398B] Everyone understands how far this is from the impiety of the Arians, who held that the Son was the first creature of God the Father, created at the beginning of time so that the Father might employ him as an instrument in the creation of the remaining things.] because he himself was about to make the earthly world and visit the human race, though otherwise equal to the Father in all things. For whatever the Father commanded to be made, [Note: [Col. 0398B] For how the fact that the Father is said to have commanded the Son does not impair their equality, see Treatise 1, book II, note 11.] the Son, as the power of God and the wisdom of God, completed all these things by his wondrous work together with his utterance. [Note: [Col. 0398B] “Together with” is supplied from the manuscripts and the Venetian edition. The same expression occurs in the following treatise, where it was not omitted by the Verona editors: “The work is completed by the Son together with the utterance.” The utterance by which the work of creation was completed is surely that command expressed in Sacred Scripture by the word *fiat*, “Let there be.” Though spoken outwardly, it is attributed to the divine Word—not because this spoken word is the Son of God, for Zeno calls him the power of God and the wisdom of God, but because he is the Word of God of whom Scripture testifies, on account of his power and wisdom: “All things were made through him, and without him nothing was made.”]

They [Note: [Col. 0398B] These are the Arians, whom the author therefore censures because, attempting through subtle disputations to investigate and explain the inscrutable generation of the Son, they fell into various errors through vain opinions. Other Fathers likewise customarily reproved this curious investigation of so great a mystery in the same sense; see Petavius, vol. II, *On the Trinity*, book V, chapter 6, sections 2–3. Indeed, the pagan Ammianus Marcellinus, alluding to this, near the end of book XXI, accuses the emperor Constantius himself of the same inquisitiveness. In investigating the Christian religion—that is, in promoting Arian disputations—he stirred up many dissensions and, as they spread more widely, nourished them by contention over words. Ammianus thereby indicates those formulas of faith published from Arian zeal with varying words and meanings; we have said not a little concerning them in Dissertation II, chapter 2, and in Treatise 1, book I.] attempt to violate this by vain conjectures of inquisitiveness; [Note: [Col. 0398C] Toledo manuscript: “various.”] now, miserable men, they understand that inquisitiveness makes one culpable, not learned. [Note: [Col. 0398C] Inquisitiveness makes one guilty because it exposes one to the danger of error and very often also leads one into errors. Hence the common saying among the Fathers, which we shall cite from Ambrose, *On Faith*, book I, section 65: “It is not permitted to scrutinize the higher mysteries. It is permitted to know that he was born; it is not permitted to examine how he was born. I may not deny the former; to investigate the latter is fearful.”]

154 ### TREATISE V. On Faith, or On the eternal generation of the Son of God

[Note: [Col. 0398D] TREATISE V.—This too is the first title in every manuscript without exception, with this one difference: in most it reads “Treatise of Faith,” in others “On Faith.” This, therefore, is the second of the two treatises *On Faith* mentioned by John of Verona, Pastrengo, and Peter de Natalibus, concerning whom we have spoken sufficiently in note 1 on Treatise 1, book I. The other title appears in all the printed editions and has therefore been retained, because it declares the subject of the treatise more expressly. The first period corresponds closely with the first period of Treatise 3; the notes placed there should be consulted here.]

I. The Beginning, brethren, is our Lord Christ, whom before all ages the Father, still God in himself in both respects, in the undivided fullness of the blessed eternity of the Spirit, veiled in some manner within his own consciousness, embraced with affection as the Son, yet without distinction. But, in order to establish the sequence of things, that ineffable power and incomprehensible wisdom (Ps. 44:1) brings forth a word from the region of the heart and propagates itself by omnipotence. God is born from God, possessing the whole of the Father and taking nothing away from the Father. The one shines back in the other; their glory is an honour held in common: for what belongs to the Son belongs to the Father, and what belongs to the Father belongs to both. The Father rejoices in himself in the other whom he begot from himself. But it is madness to speculate how he was begotten who proceeded forth; for the Son tempers himself on account of the nature of created things, lest the limited capacity of this world should be unable to bear the Lord of unveiled majesty.

> [Note: Col. 0398D] Others read *inconstanter* (“inconstantly”). Derive the meaning from note 3 on Tractate 3.

> [Note: Cols. 0398D–0399B] This passage causes considerable difficulty. The reading was *utrumque* (“both”), which at first seemed capable of being referred to the Father and the Son and to contain a formula similar to that of the preceding tractate, “one and the same other,” on which see note 2 there. But since no satisfactory sense subsequently emerged by which it could be understood in that way, we finally judged that *vel utcumque* (“in whatsoever manner”) should be read. This reading indicates that the Father was most completely God in himself in every possible way together with the Son, even while he embraced the same Son, veiled in his consciousness, in the undivided fullness of the Spirit. Or, rather, read *utrinque* (“in both respects”), so as to signify that the Father was one God in himself both from his own person and from that of the Son, since the Son is God in no other than the Father. We have inserted this reading into the text as much the more satisfactory one. If others suggest a better reading, we shall gladly receive it.  
>
