> “Without distinction,” which follows shortly, means the same as “in the undivided fullness of the Spirit”: not that Father and Son were one and the same person, which was Sabellius’ heresy (for in Zeno both Father and Son exist, and the Father loves the Son with genuine affection), but that Father and Son have always existed as one and the same God. Finally, what he says, “he embraced without distinction,” is expressed and explained differently in Tractate 3: “he embraced without a veil”; on this see Dissertation 2, chapter 1, §3.

> [Note: Col. 0399B] On this testimony, which Petavius rather harshly criticized in *On the Trinity*, book 1, chapter 5, no. 7, without properly grasping it, we have discussed enough in note 4 on Tractate 4, and more extensively in Dissertation 2, chapter 1, through several sections.

> [Note: Cols. 0399B–0399C] Here he says “from the region of the heart,” whereas in Tractate 4 he said “from the mouth.” The author has different Scriptural testimonies in view in the different passages. When he says “from the mouth,” he had in view Ecclesiasticus 24:5: “I came forth from the mouth of the Most High.” You will find that statement, spoken of Wisdom, commonly attributed by the Fathers to the divine Word, who is the Father’s Wisdom. But when it is said here, “from the region of the heart,” Psalm 44:1 is in view: “My heart has poured forth a good word.” Augustine observed in his exposition of that psalm that these words too were understood and explained of the divine Word, especially by the ancient Fathers.  
>
> Nor are these things inconsistent. Just as a word is first conceived in the heart and then manifested through the mouth, so the decree of the divine heart concerning the creation of the world, eternally first conceived and uttered in the Word, attributes to that Word a certain eternal generation, which we explained in note 4 on Tractate 4. Yet it did not come forth perfectly outwardly until the very word *let there be* flowed, so to speak, from the mouth of God; by its power all things were created through the Word.

> [Note: Col. 0399D] Manuscript of Pomposa: *repropagat* (“propagates again”).

> [Note: Col. 0399D] Manuscript of Reims: *Domino* (“from the Lord”).

> [Note: Col. 0399D] In the Verona edition and the Toledo manuscript: *retinet* (“is retained”).

> [Note: Col. 0399D] “What belongs to the Father belongs to both” was absent from the Venice edition; it is read in the manuscripts and the remaining editions.

> [Note: Cols. 0399D–0400B] Here he attacks not those who believe in the generation of the divine Word, but those who, investigating the manner of that generation, attempt to violate it with empty speculations, as he writes in Tractate 4. This concerns Arian disputations. Further, just as in Tractate 4 he censures those who inquire not only into that generation in which the Son of God lay hidden in the Father’s consciousness, but also into that in which he came forth from the Father’s mouth for the creation of the world, so here too he charges with madness those who wish to speculate in either respect. Thus, in Zeno’s phrase, “how he was begotten who proceeded forth,” the word “proceeded” signifies the Son’s procession from the Father. Chrysologus likewise says in Sermon 57 on the Creed: “The Son proceeded from the Father.”  
>
> But “was begotten” appears to indicate the generation of the same Son in the decree of creation. Since this generation is eternal and, as we have shown in Dissertation 2, chapter 1, §5, one with that other generation which we conceive as prior, the author knows it to surpass the human mind and therefore considers it folly to speculate about this also. For although this second, so to speak, generation of the Son came forth outwardly in creation, nevertheless, since the Son moderated himself in that external manifestation, as Zeno immediately adds, it is utter madness to speculate upon this eternal generation and in some manner measure it by the external manifestation.

> [Note: Cols. 0400B–0401D] We have now corrected this from the manuscripts of Reims, Toledo, and the Vatican, since elsewhere the text reads *aeternae* (“eternal”). Divine majesty, or divinity—for in Zeno “majesty” expresses divinity; see note 1 on Tractate 9, book 2—is called *exserta*, that is, uncovered and openly displayed, to signify that, if shown unveiled, it cannot be endured by human beings. To obtain this sense syntactically, observe that the particle *ne* (“lest”) refers to *possit* (“may be able”), not to *sustinere* (“bear”): “lest the limited capacity of this world may be unable to bear the Lord of unveiled majesty.” Cicero similarly writes in *For Milo*, chapter 1: “Lest we may not even be able to be unafraid without some fear,” where *ne* must be referred not to “be afraid” but to “may be able.”  
>
> As for the sense of the word “tempers,” Tertullian writes in *Against Praxeas*, chapter 14: “He presented the Father as invisible because of the fullness of majesty, but the Son as visible because of the measure of derivation.” He confirms this by the example of the sun and its ray: the Father, like the sun, could not be seen, but the Son, like a ray, could be seen because of this moderation. Petavius brings a serious accusation against Tertullian on this account in *On the Trinity*, book 1, chapter 5, as though he made the Son far inferior to the Father. Yet, while much could be adduced from Tertullian’s other books in his defense, it presently seems sufficient that by “moderation” he meant nothing other than that the Son made himself visible to human beings, not in his own divine substance, which he knew human beings incapable of seeing, but—as he says in the same chapter 14—“in a mirror, in an enigma, in a vision, in a dream, and in an imaginary form.” This does no injury to the Son’s divinity, by which Tertullian confesses him equal to the Father.  
>
> Read Tertullian’s *Against Marcion*, book 2, chapter 27, where he writes these remarkable words, most useful for understanding Zeno: “God could not enter into intercourse with human beings unless he had assumed human senses and affections, through which he might temper, by humility, the force of his majesty—certainly intolerable to human limitation.” Other Fathers taught similar things, not only before the Nicene Synod but also afterward. See especially the author of the work *On the Orthodox Faith against the Arians*, volume 2 of the Ambrosian Appendix, p. 354.  
>
> It seems, indeed, to have been a settled opinion among nearly all Fathers before Augustine that, in many visions which befell the ancient patriarchs, the Son offered himself to them to be seen; Petavius carefully recounts their testimonies in *On the Trinity*, book 8, chapter 2, from no. 3 onward. If any taught the contrary, the Synod of Sirmium in 351 judged them liable to anathema against Photinus. But since Arians sometimes attempted deceit in this matter, proclaiming that the visible Son was unlike in nature to the invisible Father—as they said in Augustine, Sermon 7, no. 4: “The Son was seen by the patriarchs; the Father was not seen. The invisible and the visible are of different natures,” and so forth—Augustine considered that another course should be adopted in explaining the visions of the Old Testament. He judged it more probable that they should be attributed to angels, as may be seen in books 2 and 3 of *On the Trinity*.  
>
> Nevertheless, many followed the interpretation of the ancient Fathers even after Augustine, including St Leo, Epistle 27; Cassian, *On the Incarnation*, book 4, chapter 9; St Isidore, *On the Nativity of the Lord*, chapter 1; and others. Indeed, Augustine himself in several places agreed that God had been seen by the ancient patriarchs, though with a caution in which he does not differ at all from the ancient Fathers: in *Against Maximinus*, book 2, chapter 26, no. 12, he says that divinity appeared to mortal eyes “not through its own substance, in which it is invisible and unchangeable, but through a creature subject to it, whenever it willed.” What he calls “through a subject creature” here is the same as what others called “in a mirror,” “in an enigma,” or, as Hilary observes in *On the Trinity*, book 12, nos. 45–46, now in human guise, now in the appearance of fire, and the like.  
>
> Augustine plainly admits in Epistle 147, no. 20, that God offered himself to Moses in the form in which he appeared to him. On Moses’ words, “Show me yourself,” he comments: “What then? Was it not he himself? If it were not he himself, Moses would not say to him, ‘Show me yourself,’ but, ‘Show me God.’ … He himself, then, was in that form in which he had wished to appear; but he himself did not appear in his proper nature, which Moses wished to see.” Moreover, although Augustine teaches elsewhere that angels presented themselves to the patriarchs, he at the same time teaches that God himself presented himself to them, because God himself spoke in the angels. Thus, in *Against Maximinus*, book 2, no. 11, he says concerning the bush in which Moses’ famous vision occurred: “Scripture itself declares that an angel appeared there. … But who could doubt that God was in the angel?” Athanasius had taught the same before Augustine, *Oration 4 against the Arians*, p. 467; see also Jerome on Galatians chapter 3 and Gregory the Great in the preface to his Commentary on Job, chapter 2.  
>
> Since, therefore, with so great a consensus—however one may finally prefer to explain it—God appeared to the ancient Fathers, why those Fathers taught that the Son rather than the Father or the Holy Spirit made himself visible, though the Father no less than the Son could be seen “in a mirror, in an enigma,” is clearly explained by Petavius in the passage cited. From this, meanwhile, we believe it evident in what sense St Zeno should be understood.

When the Father commands that the world be made, the work is completed by the Son together with the word. But how great or of what kind it ought to be made, no one commands, no one asks; for it could not be without injury to the Father if such a necessity belonged to him who, abiding in the Father’s bosom, had not learned the perfection of his will but possessed it.

> [Note: Col. 0401D] The thought is similar in Tractate 4; see note 7.

> [Note: Cols. 0401D–0402B] A distinguished passage of St Athanasius, *Oration 2 against the Arians*, no. 31, p. 439, sheds light on this testimony. Seeking to show against the Arians that the Word of God was not made for our sake—as they wished, so that all things might thereafter be made through him as an intermediary creature—Athanasius says, p. 432, that although all things were made through him and nothing could be made without him, God did not employ him as a minister; he neither commanded him nor asked him a question, as though the Son did not know what the Father wished, since the Son is the same as the Father and knows all things in him.  
>
> Having cited Genesis, “Let there be light,” and Psalm 38: “He spoke, and they were made; he commanded, and they were created,” he says: “He said it, I say, not so that, as commonly happens among human beings, some minister might hear, and, once he had learned the speaker’s will, hasten to perform the work; for this belongs to created things. … Therefore Holy Scripture does not say that he heard or answered, ‘How and what sort of things do you wish made?’ It says only, ‘God said, Let there be,’ and then adds, ‘and it was so.’” A little later: “When the Word himself acts and creates, there is no question or answer, for the Father is in him and the Word in the Father. For the work to be done, it was enough to will it; thus the word ‘he said’ is, for our sake, an indication of the divine will, while the words ‘and it was so’ signify that the work was done through the Word and Wisdom, in which Wisdom the will of the Father also exists.” Thus St Zeno likewise says that the Father’s will was fully known to the Son, since he was the same in the Father; so that no one asked and no one commanded. See what Zeno says on this matter in Tractate 1, book 2, notes 12 and 13.

II. Therefore, when the world had been completed, man is fashioned last from the clay of the earth by the finger and hand of God. A moving image, wholly ignorant of itself, is fashioned; and, in order that it may be the image of God, God breathes into it a living soul. It likewise received a spirit which it does not know; it does not see it entering, nor can it prevent it from departing. And does anyone suppose that he can know God’s secret, when he does not know the hidden mystery of his own body? Therefore, brethren, let us fear, love, and honour the God whom we have found, for whose sake we were made and born. Let those who do not have him with them indeed seek him.

> [Note: Col. 0402C] Man is called an image insofar as, through the soul mentioned immediately below, he is the image of God. He is called an image ignorant of itself because he receives a spirit which he does not know. More will be said concerning this image of God in the human soul in Tractate 19.

> [Note: Col. 0402C] The words “of God” are absent from the manuscript of Pomposa.

> [Note: Col. 0402C] Thus the manuscripts of Reims, Toledo, Urban, and Zeno; this adverb is familiar to Zeno. The Pomposa codex reads *Adae quod* [an incomplete reading]; the printed editions have “Adam.”

> [Note: Col. 0402C] The “secret” here is plainly the divine Word, or the generation of the divine Word, concerning which see more in Tractate 4, note 3. The argument is forceful enough to restrain the rash curiosity of the Arians in investigating the generation of that Word. For if the image of God which man bears within himself is unknown to him, of how great arrogance are those convicted who presume that they can know the image of the Father’s Word, which lies hidden in the Father’s secret?

## 158. TRACTATE VI

### On the text: “When he shall have delivered up the kingdom to God and the Father” (1 Cor. 15:24)

> [Note: Cols. 0402C–0402D] TRACTATE VI.—In the Verona edition and subsequent editions, in addition to this title another inscription is appended to this tractate: “Sermon on the First Epistle of Blessed Paul to the Corinthians.” We have placed this tractate here because, since it defends the generation of the divine Word, it should not be separated from those which concern the same subject.

I. When divine Scripture speaks of the Son of God, it does not contradict itself; rather, it distinguishes with necessary moderation between God and the man whom he assumed. For if it always proclaimed him pure God, there would be no place for passion and resurrection, and Christ would have bestowed nothing upon the world. If it proclaimed him man only—as some think—having taken his beginning from the virgin’s womb, what hope of future blessedness would there be for the believer, when it is written: “Cursed is the man who puts his hope in man” (Jer. 17:5)?

> [Note: Col. 0402D] This was the error of the Gnostics, Saturnians, Basilideans, and other heretics of that kind: they called Christ pure God, who assumed only the appearance of a man.

> [Note: Cols. 0402D–0403B] The opposite error was maintained by eleven sects of heterodox persons named by Theodoret in *Against Heresies*, book 2: namely, Ebionites, Nazarenes, Cerinthians, Artemon, Theodotus, Melchizedekians, Elcesaites, Paul of Samosata, Sabellius, Marcellus, and Photinians. To these should be added two more: the Carpocratians, from Irenaeus, book 1, chapter 24, and Beryllus, from Eusebius, book 6, chapter 21. The Photinians, the latest of them all and condemned even by the Arians, seem to be indicated here by Zeno’s expression “as some think,” referring, as some judge, to his own time.

Therefore, where it signifies pure God, Scripture says in Genesis: “And God made man in the image and likeness of God” (Gen. 1:27); and in the Psalms: “But God, our king before the ages, worked salvation in the midst of the earth” (Ps. 73:12); and elsewhere: “Your throne, O God, is prepared from then; you are from everlasting” (Ps. 92:2). Where it speaks of the God-man, it continues thus: “Say to the daughter of Zion: Behold, your king comes to you, just, holy, and saving, meek, sitting upon a colt, the foal of an ass” (Zech. 9:9; Isa. 62:11); and again: “Lift up your gates, O princes, and be lifted up, eternal gates, and the king of glory shall enter” (Ps. 23:7); and again the Magi say: “Where is he who has been born king of the Jews?” (Matt. 2:2).

> [Note: Col. 0403B] On this formula see sufficiently Dissertation 2, chapter 3. In the following text, *sanctus* (“holy”) is absent from the Toledo, Pomposa, and Zeno manuscripts.

II. This, brethren, is he whose coming was foretold through the prophets: he who according to the flesh was born in time; who is exalted in the heights and humble on earth; the begetter of the ages, the son of a virgin, immortal in himself, yet destined to die as man. He tastes death in order to conquer death; he penetrates hell in order to bring the dead back from there alive. He is the only-begotten, coming forth from the Father before the origin of things; the firstborn from the dead (Col. 1:18), as the Apostle says, after the death of many peoples. He is the one to whose name power in heaven and on earth has been given by his God, he himself saying: “I have glorified you on earth; I have completed the work which you gave me to do. And now glorify me, you, with yourself, with the glory which I had with you before the world was made” (John 17:4; Matt. 11:27). Rising again, he says: “All things have been handed over to me by my Father” (Luke 10:22). He who came down from heaven pure ascended into heaven made flesh. He, I say, is the one of whom Paul says: “He who receives the kingdom reigns and will hand it over to God and the Father,” and so forth (1 Cor. 1:24).

> [Note: Cols. 0403B–0403C] Manuscript of Pomposa: *nuntiatus* (“announced”).

> [Note: Col. 0403B] Manuscript of Reims: “in man,” a reading which suggests that the divine Word, immortal in himself, underwent death from human nature. A little later the printed editions have *gestat* (“bears”) instead of *gustat* (“tastes”), contrary to the manuscripts.

> [Note: Col. 0403C] Thus other Fathers also believed, against the opinion of heretics, that Christ truly descended into hell.

> [Note: Col. 0403C] In the margin of the Verona edition: “to the man.”

> [Note: Col. 0403C] The author seems to have slipped in memory, since these words were spoken before the Passion.

> [Note: Col. 0403C] *Carno, carnis*, from which *carnatus* (“made flesh”), is quite an ancient word, as the many compounds from it show, such as *concarno*, *excarno*, *decarno*, *incarno*, and so forth. Caelius Aurelianus likewise said, 1.4.95, “to show a body made flesh.”

III. Why, Christian, do you take offense here and form judgments concerning the mysteries of the divine gracious dispensation from your own nature? If you think less highly of the Son because the kingdom is delivered to the Father, the injury to the Father is greater if he is ever without a kingdom. Moreover, we pray daily that the Father’s kingdom may come (Matt. 6:10), and we hope for the Son’s kingdom also (2 Pet. 1:11). Thus the governance of the present time is vacant if both cease; and the world and its entire substance are finished if divine sovereignty ceases even for a single moment. But if, as reason itself declares, this diversity of kingdom can in no way cease from the giver of the law, it is assigned, when all things have been ordered, to the man assumed by God and to his righteous ones—not to God, not to the everlasting ruler—especially since the Gospel says: “The Lord God will give him the throne of David his father, and he will reign over the house of Jacob for ages, and there will be no end of his kingdom” (Luke 1:32).

> [Note: Cols. 0403C–0403D] What Zeno calls *provisio* (“provision”) is to be understood as the incarnation of the divine Word; the Greek Fathers call it *οἰκονομία*, while Latin writers call it *dispensatio* (“dispensation”), and sometimes, in Greek fashion, *oeconomia*. Cicero used *provisio* in Latin in *Tusculan Disputations* 3.14. Since the holy bishop has so far argued against those who called Christ either pure God, with the Gnostics and other ancient heretics, or pure man, with the Photinians, he now introduces, from Paul’s last testimony, the Arian objection. That they used it to maintain that the Son was subject to and less than the Father is evident from Athanasius, Hilary, and other Fathers, who likewise endeavoured to explain that testimony against the Arians.

> [Note: Cols. 0403C–0405C] Sparaverius judged this entire text very corrupt and mutilated. He preferred to read *vastitas* (“emptiness”) instead of *varietas* (“diversity”), as though the author’s point were to show that the kingdom of Father and Son is one and undivided. In the remainder he thought that dots indicating lacunae should be inserted in places; but without manuscripts these cannot and should not be supplied at will. Although we were permitted to consult several manuscript books, they contributed nothing toward restoring this passage; this should not surprise us, since all may flow from the same ancient source.  
>
> We shall attempt to explain the obscure sentence just as though nothing were corrupt or defective. The attempt may perhaps seem not implausible if attention is given to what precedes and follows. The holy bishop raises a question concerning 1 Corinthians 15:24, where the kingdom received by the Son is said to be delivered to the Father. Having first raised the difficulty against the Son’s divinity—as though, if he is to deliver the kingdom to the Father, he will at some time be without a kingdom—and immediately dissolved it, because a grave injury would thereby also accrue to the Father if he were for some time without a kingdom before receiving it from the Son, he adds that we pray for the coming of the Father’s kingdom and also await the Son’s kingdom. This confirms that the Father’s and Son’s kingdom are the same.  
>
> Yet these statements do not as yet explain Paul’s text and instead occasion a new difficulty. For if the Father’s and Son’s kingdom is to come, does the governance of the present time—that is, of this world—stand vacant, so that it is ruled neither by the Father nor by the Son? He rejects this as absurd, because the consequence would be that the world and its whole substance would perish if divine sovereignty ceased for even a moment. Therefore God is shown to reign not so much in the future kingdom we await as in the present kingdom.  
>
> This twofold kingdom, not only different in itself but succeeding one another, is called by the author “this diversity of kingdom.” It cannot in any way cease from the giver of the law, that is, from God, who set the law for each of these kingdoms and in whom both kingdoms, though diverse to us, are one and constant. This diversity is therefore assigned not to God, the eternal ruler, but to the man assumed by God—that is, to the Redeemer—and to his righteous ones, who are shortly called his servants, when all things have been ordered, or by the very ordering of things established by the law of the creator. In the temporal kingdom, of which alone Paul speaks, as the author observes, Christ the assumed man must reign with his servants, whom he will join to himself until the end of the world, as the whole passage—or Paul’s context in verse 25—testifies. Then, when this first temporal kingdom has ended or been completed, and the powers of hell have been subdued and death itself conquered on the day of judgment, when no one further can enter Christ’s kingdom, Christ will hand over to the Father the now completed kingdom of his servants, from whom they will receive an everlasting kingdom.  
>
> But Christ, who as the Son of God abides in the Father’s eternity, never at any time received or laid aside the kingdom, and will reign perpetually in them. This is expressed by the two testimonies from the Gospel and Solomon. Thus Paul’s meaning is made clear, and the apparent contradiction between him and those testimonies disappears: Paul must be understood to speak of Christ’s temporal kingdom, while they speak of the eternal kingdom which will succeed the former after it has been completed at judgment.

Solomon similarly says in Wisdom, when speaking of his servants: “And though they suffered torments before men, their hope is full of immortality; and, though afflicted in few things, in many things they shall be well ordered, because God tested them and found them worthy of himself. Like gold in a furnace he tested them, and received them as burnt offerings; and in the time of their visitation there will be regard for them. They shall judge nations and rule peoples, and their Lord shall reign forever” (Wis. 3:4 ff.).

> [Note: Col. 0405C] The Pomposa manuscript and the Venice edition read *fuerint* (“have been”) and *immortalitatis* (“of immortality”) instead of *immortalitate* (“with immortality”). Then the Venice edition has *et quasi holocaustomata* (“and as burnt offerings”) and *tanquam holocaustomata* (“as burnt offerings”). We have supplied the particle *et* (“and”) from this edition and from the Pomposa and Zeno manuscripts.

What is this? If he reigns forever, Paul was mistaken; if he is to deliver up the kingdom, these writers speak falsely. Far be it! There is no error here, no diversity. For Paul spoke of the temporal kingdom of the assumed man, in which he will come and judge the living and the dead (2 Tim. 4:1), as the whole passage testifies. It proclaims that Christ must reign with his saints until, when every principality and power and might and dominion have been abolished, all his enemies are put under his feet and death, the enemy, is destroyed (1 Cor. 15:24 ff.). But these writers refer to the principal power, in whose eternity the Son, abiding forever, never at any time received the kingdom from the Father nor laid it aside; for he always reigned with him, according to John—*kata* (κατά) John—when he himself says: “My kingdom is not of this world” (John 18:36). Paul expressed this more plainly, saying: “For you must know this: that every fornicator, or impure person, or fraudster—which is the service of idols—has no inheritance in the kingdom of God and of Christ” (Eph. 5:5), showing that the kingdom of Father and Son is one.

> [Note: Cols. 0405C–0405D] The text read *vocatis* (“called”). We have corrected it from 1 Corinthians 15:24, from which these words are taken: “When he shall have abolished every principality and power and might,” that is, the principality of hell and so forth, having completely subdued it; see note 13.

> [Note: Col. 0405D] That is, Luke and Solomon, whose testimonies he had just cited as apparently contrary to Paul. See note 13.

> [Note: Col. 0405D] The Pomposa, Vatican, Urban, and Zeno manuscripts read thus; the printed editions together with other manuscripts have *accipit* (“receives”).

> [Note: Cols. 0405D–0406C] In the Verona edition, *kata* was written in Greek letters, contrary to the manuscripts and the first edition. Likewise, *cata*, when the Evangelists are cited, is very frequently rendered in Latin letters by Latin writers in manuscripts, as Baluzius attests regarding Cyprian manuscripts; it is also found so written in printed editions. See the three books of *Testimonies* in many places, and the author of the catalogue of heretics placed after Tertullian’s book *On Prescription*, where the doctrine of heretics is said to have been called *cata Proclum*, *cata Aeschinem*, after the likeness of the Gospels. In Jerome, however, *kata Loukan* (κατὰ Λουκᾶν, “according to Luke”) is printed in Greek letters in book 3 on chapter 6 of the Epistle to the Ephesians, p. 678, Verona edition. But Sirmond printed *cata Galla patricia* in Latin letters in the decree of Stephen II concerning the Roman hospice, volume 2 of the Gallican Councils, p. 38; similarly, the nun of Heidenheim wrote *illorum cata normam* in Latin in the *Hodoeporicon* of St Willibald, in Canisius, volume 4 of *Antiquae Lectiones*, p. 512, Ingolstadt edition.

> [Note: Col. 0406C] Manuscript of Pomposa: *habent* (“have”).

IV. Therefore he rightly delivers the kingdom to the Father who said in his teachings that a kingdom cannot stand divided (Luke 11:17–18). Hence, brethren, we must not think that the Father will receive what he did not have, or that the Son, by delivering what he has, will lose it. For the Father has what he will receive, and the Son does not lack what he will give. The Father possesses all; the Son possesses all. What belongs to both belongs to one; what one possesses belongs to each, as the Lord himself says: “All things whatsoever the Father has are mine” (John 16:15); and again: “Father, all mine are yours, and all yours are mine” (John 17:20). For the Father is in the Son and the Son abides in the Father, to whom he is subject by affection, not by condition; by love, not by necessity; by dignity, through whom the Father is always honoured. Finally, he says: “I and the Father are one” (John 10:30).

> [Note: Col. 0406C] As in Tractate 4, book 1, no. 3, St Zeno wrote, “the Lord says in the precepts,” so here, “in the teachings.” The Gospels are sometimes cited by such expressions. St Leo similarly says in Sermon 9 on Lent, chapter 1: “For the Lord said in his exhortations.”

> [Note: Col. 0406C] The printed editions wrongly read *non habeat* (“does not have”); we have corrected it from the Pomposa, Speyer, and Zeno manuscripts.

> [Note: Cols. 0406C–0406D] He adds, “not by condition,” that is, not by servitude—for *conditio* has this meaning in Zeno; see note 23 on Tractate 10, book 1—which produces necessity, but by love and affection. He has the creation of the world in view: for all things were made through him. Although the Father is said to have commanded and the Son to have carried out the work, the love in both was nevertheless one. It commanded in the Father and obeyed in the Son, as he aptly observes in Tractate 2, book 1, no. 9. See more on these matters in Tractate 1, book 2, notes 12 and 13, and in Tractate 5, note 13, where St Zeno treats the same argument, lest anyone suppose the Son inferior to the Father from the creation of the world, which is attributed to the Son. He immediately calls this subjection of the Son, proceeding from love rather than servile necessity, religious rather than diminishing, because nothing is thereby detracted from the Son’s equality and dignity.

Thus the Son is subject to the Father by a religious, not a diminishing, subjection, as I have said. With him there is one possession of the original and everlasting kingdom, one substance of coeternity and omnipotence, one equality, one power of august majesty, and one dignity preserved in a single light. For if you take anything from the Son, it will amount to injury of the Father, whose whole being he possesses. Nor is there anything in him that is inferior, because, like the Father, he can possess neither more nor less. For one is poured into the fullness of the other, so that God may be all in all: the blessed Father in the Son, the Son in the Father, with the Holy Spirit. Amen.

> [Note: Col. 0406D] Manuscript of Pomposa: *aequabilitas* (“evenness” or “equality”). Likewise, in Tractate 1, book 2, some manuscripts write *aequabilitas*, although elsewhere *aequalitas* (“equality”) is read.

> [Note: Col. 0406D] Some manuscripts and printed editions read *unito* (“united”); the first edition reads *unico* (“single”), which seemed more consistent with the sense.

> [Note: Col. 0407B] Thus the Pomposa manuscript; the others read *injuria* (“injury”). Whatever is taken from the Son pertains to injury of the Father, whether because the Father is proclaimed to have a degenerate Son—as Hilary frequently implies and Augustine proves at length in Sermon 139, no. 5, and Ambrose in *On Faith*, book 1, chapter 6—or because he is said at some time to have been without Word and Wisdom, so that he had to receive them from elsewhere. Athanasius demonstrates this in *Oration 2 against the Arians*.

## 163. TRACTATE VII

### On the Nativity of the Lord. I

> [Note: Cols. 0407B–0407C] TRACTATE VII.—In the printed editions and in the Urban manuscript: “First sermon on the Nativity of Christ”; the other manuscripts read “On the Nativity of the Lord.” The following tractate is entitled, both in the editions and in the manuscripts, “On the Nativity of Christ.” Christian Daumius inserted this tractate and the two following, with the emendations of Gaspar Barthius, among the homilies of the Fathers, as Fabricius records in *Bibliotheca Latina*, vol. 3, p. 421, and vol. 12, p. 797 of the *Bibliotheca Graeca*. We have not yet been able to see that exceedingly rare edition of the homilies.

I. Although there are several sects that strive to invent an affront to Christ, yet three are in some sense principal; of these, two pretend to be worshippers of him whom they desire to corrupt. [Note: [Col. 0407C] Venetian edition: “worshippers” (*cultores*).] [Note: [Col. 0407C] Above, in note 3 on the preceding tractate, we listed more than ten heads of heresy relevant here, insofar as they maintained that Christ was merely a man and had his beginning from Mary’s womb. Insofar as the same Christ is said to have become God because of righteousness, this was indeed the celebrated error of Nestorius, but one already preached long before by Paul of Samosata and Photinus, with this difference: Nestorius, as Garnerius notes in Dissertation 7, *On the Origin and Growth of the Pelagian Heresy*, ch. 7, taught that Christ the man was assumed by the Divine Word from his mother’s womb onward, not through merits but through divine grace; whereas Paul of Samosata and Photinus said that the same Christ was born a man and advanced into God through the merit of his virtues—what Zeno calls “righteousness.” See the third anathema of the booklet bearing Rufinus’ name [Col. 0407D], published at the same time by Norisius and Garnerius. Origen seems to have anticipated this error, *On First Principles*, II.6: “By the merit of its virtues,” he says, “the soul of Christ becomes one with the Word of God.” It is easy to understand that our author intended to strike at the Photinians, whom other Fathers of Zeno’s age also frequently refute.] One, finally—that is, in a few words [Note: [Col. 0407D] “Finally” here means “in a few words”; other writers have used the same particle in this sense. See note 2 on Tractate I, book II.]—asserts that Jesus Christ took his beginning from the womb of the Virgin Mary, and that thereafter he became God because of righteousness, rather than being born God. [Note: [Col. 0407D] This is the heresy of the Arians. Although they proclaimed Christ to be the Son of God, they declared him to have been begotten not eternally but in time; hence their familiar saying: “There was a time when he was not.” See Athanasius, *On the Decrees of Nicaea*, §18; Hilary, *On the Trinity*, IV and VI, where he cites Arius’ own letter, in which the same formula is repeatedly pressed. Nor should one be surprised that here the Son could be called God and yet be denied to be coeternal and equal with the Father: for the Arians acknowledged him as God improperly, not properly, as is known from Hilary, *Fragments*, §26, and elsewhere. Since the editors of the Veronese edition contend that Zeno lived in the third century, they ascribe the same error to Origen. Yet he expressly rebukes it in the fragment cited by Athanasius, *On the Decrees of Nicaea*, §27: “Let him understand,” says Origen, “who dares to say, ‘There was once when the Son was not.’” This does prove that certain others taught this error at that time, which Origen rebuked. Dionysius of Alexandria likewise, Origen’s disciple, while attacking the Sabellians in his letter to Euphranor and Ammonius—the fragment is supplied in Athanasius’ *Letter on the Opinion of Dionysius*, §4—said: “For, since it is a thing made, it was not before it was made.” On that account he was denounced to Dionysius of Rome and rebuked by him; in an apology he cleared himself, adducing many points by which he rejects the error later taken up by the Arians. Thus, when they appealed to his authority on their own behalf, Athanasius, in the place mentioned, §9, excellently vindicates his predecessor’s meaning and vigorously wrests his authority from the hands of his enemies. Therefore, although some persons at Alexandria may once have taught the error censured by Origen, it is clear that St. Zeno wished to strike not at those people, who had no bearing on us, but at the Arians, who had also disseminated that formula in these regions.] Another, more restrained in expression but more venomously harmful, does indeed call the Son of God “God,” but denies that he was begotten from the Father in the everlasting continuity of divine dignity; and says that there was a time when he was not. [Col. 0408A] The third is truly blind Judaism: though it reads everywhere in its Law—as it is accustomed to say—that two persons, the Father and the Son, are designated, it still insists that God has no Son. [Note: [Col. 0408C] “The Law,” from the Hebrew language, was thus the name given to the whole Old Testament; see note 1 on Tractate 12, book I. The passages of the Old Testament indicated here are those from which Zeno shortly cites three.] The examples and reasoning which we shall set forth will, in one stroke, sever every sinew of the whole argument of all these people.

Accordingly, the Christian people must necessarily know that our Lord Jesus Christ has two births, lest they endure any error: one by which he was born, the other by which he was born anew. But as the first is spiritual and without a mother, so the second is bodily and without a father. The latter is wondrous; the former beyond telling, as the prophet says: “Who shall declare his generation?” (Isa. 53:8). [Note: [Col. 0408D] The Pomp. manuscript and the two Zen. manuscripts add *autem* (“but”). The birth of the Divine Word is called beyond telling not with respect to the fact itself, which is known through faith, rather than unknown—as some Arians falsely claimed—but with respect to the manner of his birth, as Victorinus and Phoebadius explain at greater length.] Let us learn why it is beyond telling from the Father himself as he speaks. The Lord himself teaches us: “My heart has uttered a good Word,” and so forth (Ps. 44:2). [Note: [Col. 0408D] The same manuscripts, together with the Vatican manuscript and Venetian edition, read: “My heart has uttered,” he says, etc.] And Solomon says to this effect: “I came forth from the mouth of the Most High before every creature” (Ecclesiasticus 24:5).

II. Since these things are so, O cunning humanity, recognize it at last, and put the reins of silence upon your intemperate tongue. [Note: [Col. 0408D] The reading of the two Zen. manuscripts was preferred, whereas elsewhere *intemperati* was read.] [Note: [Col. 0408D] Although *frenum* (“rein”) is not found in the singular except as neuter, in the plural it also admits a masculine declension, as in Virgil, *Georgics* III; Livy, XXXIV.2; Valerius Maximus; and others.] It is a kind of madness to wish to speculate about the secret of the invisible and incomprehensible One, and to scrutinize the inward things of him whose outward things one cannot even conjecture. [Note: [Col. 0409B] The Pomp. codex adds “of God.” Shortly below, “the secret” refers especially to the generation of the Divine Word, concerning which the author very frequently warns that a human being must not inquire rashly. See Tractate 4, note 3.] For God is “I am who I am” (Exod. 3:14); but whatever man thinks he has defined is not God. [Note: [Col. 0409B] It is a familiar and frequent maxim among the Fathers that whatever is said about God is not truly God. For human beings, as Fulgentius perceptively observes in his book against the sermon of Fastidius, ch. 5, “being devoted to bodily senses, cannot think even of God except bodily. While such persons roll their souls in the mud of the flesh, burdened by created images and the weight of vanity, the more they occupy themselves with the thought of things which present corporeal mass to bodily eyes, the less able are they to rise to an understanding of deity.” Thus Marius Victorinus, *Against Arius*, IV, rightly observed that, when we affirmatively ascribe to God things suitable to him—such as being, living, and understanding—he is still not those things which we say, because he is above all things. He adds: “Therefore he is called *anyparktos*, *anousios*, *anous*, and *azōos*—without existence, without substance, without intelligence, without life—not through *sterēsis*, that is, privation, but through transcendence. For all things which words name come after him; hence he is not *on* [being], but rather *proon* [before being].” On this point John of Damascus, I.4, taught that it is more fitting to predicate something of God in such a way that all things are removed from him, since he is none of the things that are, but is rather above them. Hence most Fathers and philosophers have held that one who wishes to define God should employ negative rather than affirmative formulas; for, as Augustine writes on Psalm 84, “We say more easily what he is not than what he is.”]

For hear, brothers, what the Apostle John proclaims in the Gospel: “In the beginning was the Word, and the Word was with God, and the Word was God. He was in the beginning with God” (John 1:1). Wonderful grace, beloved brothers, of manifest truth: though it can be distinguished, it cannot be external to itself. For if the Word is in God, and God is the Word, and that in which it is is what he is who is within it, there are two persons and two names, [Note: [Col. 0409C] This is a splendid confession against the Patripassians, or—as they were later called by Latin writers—the Sabellians, who imagined one person of the Father distinguished only by a twofold designation. The Catholic Fathers, however, confess the Father and the Son to be two persons distinguished by two names. The ancient author of the tractate *On the Orthodox Faith*, p. 346 of the Appendix to Ambrose, uses *vocabulum* for “name,” where he provides an outstanding testimony in the same sense as Zeno; likewise ch. 6, p. 352. Again, in an ancient formula of faith written for the instruction of those to be baptized, published by Fr. Martene, I, *On Ancient Church Rites*, ch. 1, art. 12, p. 163: “Except for the names which indicate the proper characteristics of the persons, whatever is said of one person may most fittingly be understood of all three.”] but one substance of original eternity and deity. The Lord himself says: “I and the Father are one” (John 10:30). He certainly did not say this so as to merge two into one and confuse them, but to teach us that the two possess one omnipotence of deity and power. It follows, and he says: “All things were made through him, and without him nothing was made” (John 1:3).

III. Let us now see, excellent Christian, how you force time in between the Father and the Son. [Note: [Col. 0409D] We have emended this from the Pomp., Vatican, and two Zen. manuscripts, whereas others write *infulciat*. The discourse here is addressed to Arians—called “excellent Christians” ironically—who wished the Divine Word begotten of the Father to have been begotten in time; for they proclaimed that there had been a time when he was not. *Infulcire* is used in the sense of “to impose” also by Seneca, *Letters* 114, and Suetonius, *Life of Tiberius* 53.] If one owes one’s existence to time rather than to oneself, then one is dependent upon the other; and beyond doubt, as you wish it, nature is greater than God. But since Christ made nature from nothing, and time comes from nature, it is sufficiently absurd to place the work before its maker; and they differ in this respect alone, that they alone know themselves. Finally, in Isaiah the Lord God of hosts says to the Son: “Egypt has labored, and the merchandise of the Ethiopians; [Note: [Col. 0410B] The Tol. manuscript reads “and Saba.”] men of lofty stature from Saba shall pass over to you, and shall be your servants; they shall follow you bound in fetters, and shall worship you, [Note: [Col. 0410B] The preposition “in” was added from the Tol., Pomp., and both Zen. codices and the Venetian edition. Other Latin Fathers also read it this way: Lactantius, *Institutions* IV.13; Hilary, *On the Trinity* IV.38; Ambrose, *On Faith* I.3. This reading derives from the Septuagint, from which the Latins drew. Other manuscripts and the Veronese edition write “pray to you” without *in*, as does the author of *On the Orthodox Faith*, ch. 6, p. 353 in the Appendix to Ambrose. There is no small variation in interpreting this testimony, as comparison of the authors’ passages shows. Yet they agree in referring this testimony, as our Zeno does, to Christ. See Jerome’s commentary on this passage, etc. Both Zen. manuscripts read *praedicabuntur* [“they shall be proclaimed”] for *precabuntur* [“they shall pray”].] and shall pray in you, because God is in you, and there is no other God besides you” (Isa. 45:14).

Jeremiah also speaks in the same Spirit, saying: [Note: [Col. 0410C] In the Veronese edition Baruch is substituted in place of Jeremiah, since this passage is truly taken from the Book of Baruch. But we have restored “Jeremiah” from all manuscripts and the Venetian edition. Even if this reading could not be defended, it should nevertheless have remained in the text, while the author’s lapse should have been identified in the notes. Thus Busaeus, in his edition of Peter of Blois, Letter 141, printed “Zechariah,” who is cited in place of Jeremiah; and Billius, while editing Gregory Nazianzen, noted—but left untouched—the error by which, in his address to Julian, Gregory cited Solomon in place of Job. For the same reason, the passage in the Roman edition of Cassian, *Conferences* 7.12, where Job is praised in place of Solomon, should not have been corrected; nor Canon 13 of the Council of Seville, where printed texts have Isaiah although, as Baluze notes, the ancient codices read Jeremiah. Corrections of this sort may provide the true citation, but they do not represent the mind of the authors, who plainly lapsed in memory. By the same lapse Marius Mercator, p. 28 of Baluze’s edition, cited John the Evangelist in place of Paul; and Gregory, in his Oration on Love for the Poor, named Micah for Amos and Amos for Micah. If, from Zeno’s words so far, the passage would not have been subject to editorial correction even if it contained a grave error, much less can the editors’ license be approved in a citation that can be defended and justified by sufficiently respectable reasons. For among the ancient Fathers there grew up the custom of taking Baruch—who was Jeremiah’s amanuensis, as is indicated in Jeremiah 36:4 and 45:1—for Jeremiah, to such an extent that they considered Baruch’s little book a secretary’s work to be attributed to its master. Moreover, in the Septuagint edition Baruch’s work is joined to Jeremiah’s book, as Jerome observed in the prologue to his commentary on Jeremiah. Therefore many who cite the sacred books of the Old Testament from the Septuagint considered Baruch’s book and Jeremiah’s book to be one and the same. For these reasons Cyprian calls Baruch Jeremiah, *On the Lord’s Prayer*, p. 416; Clement of Alexandria, *The Instructor*, pp. 129–130; St. Hilary, *On the Trinity* IV.42 and on Psalm 68, §19; the author of *On the Orthodox Faith*, ch. 7, in the Appendix to Ambrose; Julius Firmicus, *On the Error of Profane Religions*, ch. 29; Ambrose, *On Cain and Abel* I.9 and *On Faith* I.28; and many others.] “This is our God, and no other God shall be reckoned beside him; he discovered the way of understanding and revealed it to Jacob his servant and to Israel his beloved. After this he was seen upon earth and conversed with human beings” (Baruch 3:36–38). In what form, let us learn as the Holy Spirit speaks: [Note: [Col. 0411C] This passage is not to be found in either Jeremiah or Baruch—the latter of which, as we saw in note 18, was attributed to Jeremiah. Yet it is found in the Greek Jeremiah of the Septuagint; accordingly Epiphanius cites it in Greek under Jeremiah’s name, *Heresies* LIV.4. It is likewise given in Latin, in the same words, by Tertullian, *Against the Jews*, final chapter; *Against Marcion* III.7; and *On the Flesh of Christ* 15; by Cyprian, *Against the Jews* 10; Lactantius, *Institutions* IV.13; Ambrose, *On the Instruction of Virgins* 16 and Letter 46.7; and others. All of them, together with Zeno, refer this testimony to the incarnation of the Word. On this interpretation, see Jerome’s comments on this place.] “And he is man; and who shall know him?” (Jer. 17:9, from the Septuagint). If this is so, then Isaiah has disclosed in these words how he could be recognized: “Hear then, house of David: Is it too little for you to contend with human beings, that God should offer battle? Therefore God will give you a sign: behold, a virgin shall conceive in her womb and bear a son, and his name shall be called Emmanuel. He shall eat butter and honey before the child knows good or evil.” [Note: [Col. 0411D] The Pomp., Vatican, and both Zen. manuscripts read “you shall call.” Shortly afterward, “child” is absent from the Pomp. manuscript.] He also made the sign plain elsewhere through the designation of his forerunner [*prodromus*]: [Note: [Col. 0411D] *Prodromus*, “forerunner,” namely St. John the Baptist, of whom the following words speak, is Latin; so Cicero, *Letters to Atticus* I.12: “The Pompeian forerunners report to me”; and Pliny, *Natural History* II.47 calls the north winds which precede the rising of the Dog Star by eight days *prodromi*. Below, *dilucidavit* [“made clear”] is defended as Latin usage from the author of *Rhetoric for Herennius* III.4, who wrote *causa rei dilucidandae*, “for the purpose of clarifying the matter.”] “Behold, I send my angel before your face, who shall prepare your way.” Who is this angel, brothers, but John the Baptist? His preparation is: “A voice crying in the wilderness: Prepare the way of the Lord; make straight the paths of our God.”

IV. Let us now see what follows. At the same time two kinswomen conceive: one contrary to hope, the other by a word. The former marvels that she has what she does not understand; the latter rejoices because she understands. [Note: [Col. 0412C] Thus the Rem. and Tol. manuscripts; the rest, together with the editions, read “knows.” Then *maiestate* means deity, or divine power; see note 1 on Tractate IX, book II.] Elizabeth’s barren womb happily swells with fruitfulness; Mary’s with divine majesty. The one bears the herald; the other, the judge. Rejoice, women, and acknowledge the exaltation of your sex. The ancient fault has been erased: behold, through you we are joined to heaven. For an old woman bore an angel, and a virgin bore God.

This is our God, who, setting aside his dignity for a time but not his power, out of love for humankind, whose form he was to assume, and becoming a creature, was called angel, man, child, bridegroom, giant, crucified, buried, and firstborn from the dead. [Note: [Col. 0412C] Christ is signified by these names in passages of the Old and New Testaments. It is enough to indicate the principal ones: “Angel of great counsel” (Isa. 9:6), according to the Septuagint; “man” and “child” very frequently; “bridegroom” and “giant” (Ps. 18:6); “crucified” and “buried” throughout the New Testament; “firstborn from the dead” (Col. 1:18).] This is he, I say, who is all things in all things, because through him and in him are all things.

Nor should the worldly and truly childish disputation of thoughtless people trouble you, brothers: [Note: [Col. 0412C] Those struck at here are sufficiently discussed in note 3 on Tractate 6 of this book.] they suffer this just error because they do not understand Christ as man made from God, but as God made from man. Yet if they thought spiritually, they would proclaim precisely in him what they judge to be weakest. For God would not truly be perfect if there were something which, though wishing to be it, he could not be. Finally, do you wish to know the truth briefly? He became what he was not; yet he did not cease to be what he had been.

## TRACTATE VIII. On the Nativity of the Lord, II

[Col. 0412B] I. The true knowledge of the unfathomable mystery and venerable majesty is this: that none but God knows God, and that nothing further should be required of him than that a person know his will, without which one can neither lawfully serve him nor please him. [Note: [Col. 0412D] An “unfathomable mystery” is one which may not be investigated even through conjectures; see note 4 on Tractate III, book II. The Arians are attacked, for they strove to penetrate God’s hidden things by argument.] But to wish to form vain speculations about the ordered plan of the provident God concerning God is not the act of a worshipper but of a madman. [Note: [Col. 0412D] Sparaverius preferred to write *procedentis* (“proceeding”), since the following discussion concerns the generation of the Divine Word. A similar statement appears in Tractate 5: “But it is madness to speculate how he who proceeded was generated.” Yet no manuscripts support this emendation, and Zeno could elsewhere call the inner ordering of the provident God his *dispositus* (“arrangement”).] [Note: [Col. 0412D] *Dispositus* for *dispositio* is found in Tacitus, *Histories* II.5.2. Shortly afterward, the Rem. manuscript reads *utrum patiatur* (“which one suffers”) for *uter patietur* (“which one will suffer”).] Especially if, as contentious people think, God is subject to arrangement: for if for a moment you remove the names “Father” and “Son,” you cannot know which suffers injury—except that both suffer, because the one name of both is “God.” Therefore, unlearned or negligent Christian, learn that there are two births of our Lord Jesus Christ, lest you be deceived by some error: one which you are not permitted to investigate, and another concerning which you are lawfully permitted, if you can, to be instructed. The first birth of our Lord remains in the awareness of the Father and the Son alone, and has nothing intervening or cognizant, [Note: [Col. 0412D] The Tol., Vatican, and Urb. manuscripts suitably correct *qui* (“who”) to *quod* (“because”), since elsewhere *qui* was read without a substantive noun to which it could refer. Unless perhaps something has fallen out, for example, “except him who,” in which case the Holy Spirit would be indicated, who proceeds in one accord from Father and Son. Yet St. Zeno does not customarily mention the Holy Spirit in this formula, by which he indicates a procession proper to the Son from the Father’s mouth. In Tractates III and IV, while firmly teaching that the Son’s generation is known to the Father alone, he seems to have had the same point in view here, looking forward to Matthew 11:27: “No one knows the Son except the Father.” These words, however, do not exclude the Holy Spirit, as both Fathers and interpreters demonstrate.] because it proceeded from the affection of the Father’s mouth in one accord. The second birth, however, is bodily; and as it has been foretold by frequent oracles, so we find it fulfilled.

II. For the Son of God, God, when the appointed time came, concealing his majesty for a while, [Note: [Col. 0413B] See note 11 on Tractate 5, book I.] departed from his heavenly seat and marked out a camp for himself in the temple of the predestined virgin; [Note: [Col. 0413B] The Venetian edition reads “from the eternal”; the Rem. manuscript, “from the ethereal”; the Tol., Pomp., and Zen. manuscripts read *aetherea* without *ab*. Shortly afterward, the Tol., Pomp., and Zen. manuscripts and Sparaverius, along with the Venetian edition, write “into the temple.”] [Note: [Col. 0413B] Festus says that camps are “marked out” (*metari*) because they are laid out by boundary marks (*metae*): that is, a site suitable for a camp is selected when this is done by setting or aligning such marks. Hence Curtius, III.8: “He had ordered his men to mark out their camp in that very place.” In Virgil, *Georgics* II.274, Servius interprets *metari* as “to choose.” Likewise in Lucan IV.382 *metator* means one who prepares lodgings; and in Cicero, *Philippics* II.5, *metator castrorum* means one who designates and prepares the place for a camp. Vegetius, II.7: “Scouts who go ahead select a place for the camp”; and Nonius Marcellus: “*Metari* means to prepare, whence also *metatores*.” Thus the holy bishop says metaphorically that the Divine Word marked out a camp for himself in the Virgin’s womb: that is, he prepared and arranged a dwelling for himself there. Likewise, in the following tractate he uses *metatura* for the preparation of lodging. The Tol. manuscript reads *castramentatur* (“he encamps”) for *castra metatur* (“he marks out a camp”).] into which he is secretly poured, about to be born as a human being; and there, while preserving what he was, he plans to become what he was not. [Note: [Col. 0413C] We have discussed this formula extensively in Dissertation II, ch. 3.] Thus mingled with human flesh, he fashions himself as an infant. Mary’s womb rises proudly, not through the gift of marriage, but through faith; by the Word, not by seed.

She knows none of the weariness of ten months, [Note: [Col. 0413D] Here there is a clear allusion to Virgil, *Eclogues* IV.61: “Ten long months of weariness had borne down the mother.” We have no doubt that Zeno’s phrase derives from this, as does a similar one in St. Ambrose, Sermon 15 on Psalm 118, §16, where he speaks of a mother carrying the burden of a holy child through the long weariness of ten months. Although some would take the poet’s words to mean lunar months, so as to reduce them to approximately nine solar months, we think they should be understood as solar months, since several writers taught that the lawful term of childbirth extended not only to the ninth but also to the tenth month. Wisdom 7:2: “In the time of ten months I was compacted in blood.” Aulus Gellius, *Attic Nights* III.16: “There is a widespread opinion, now received as certain . . . that a human being is born rarely in the seventh month, never in the eighth, and often in the tenth.” He cites many ancient Greek and Latin authorities for the tenth month. This was so firmly believed among the Romans that, by enacted law, they ordered children born in the tenth month after their father’s death to be considered legitimate. In *Digest*, “Gallus,” on freed persons and posthumous children, and in the final law of the *Code* on posthumous heirs, one reads: “If a son or daughter has been born within the period of ten months after the death of the father, they shall be heirs.” Gellius cites the judgment of the Decemvirs, and also Hadrian’s decree extending the matter even to the eleventh month; other writers agree with him and Hippocrates. Martin Schurig, *Embryologia, Medical History*, IV.2, §§1 and 9, discusses this matter at length and clearly, citing the testimony of many writers for the tenth month. Among sacred writers, besides Zeno, one might cite Ambrose, *On Faith* I.1.72; Jerome, *Against Helvidius*, §2; Chrysologus, Sermons 5 and 6 on the Creed; and others.] since she conceived within herself the Creator of the world. She gives birth not in pain but in joy. A marvelous thing: rejoicing, she brings forth an infant older than the antiquity of all nature. [Note: [Col. 0414C] “Brings forth” (*exponit*) is here explained in an entirely special sense as “gives birth.” Perhaps Zeno used the nautical term metaphorically: sailors are said to *exponere* those whom, after reaching port, they put ashore or carry out from the ship, as is clear from Nepos II.8, Horace, *Satires* V.20, and Caesar, *Civil War* I.31. Thus a mother, after completing the course of months in which she carried her son in her womb, could be said at last to “put him forth” when she gives birth.]

Meanwhile the inexperienced new mother does not groan. [Note: [Col. 0414C] *Foeta* has a broader range than *gravida*: *gravidae* are only those who carry a fetus in the womb, but *foetae* are those who have recently brought forth a fetus, according to Censorinus, *On the Birthday*, ch. 11; see Vossius, *Institutes of Oratory* V, p. 278. Varro, *On Agriculture*, calls such women *puerperae*, and Cerda observes on Virgil, *Aeneid* VIII.630 that pregnant animals are never called *foeta*; although this is true in Virgil, it is not so in all other authors, as Basilius Faber observes in his *Thesaurus*. Our author calls the Virgin, Christ’s mother, an inexperienced new mother after giving birth, to signify that she had never previously borne a child: for *rudis* denotes whatever is new, recent, and unpracticed. First-time mothers normally suffer greater pain than others. Thus Mary’s privilege is here extolled: though an inexperienced new mother, she does not groan.] The infant, entering not the world—as is usual—when born, does not spontaneously inaugurate the beginnings of creeping life with preceding tears. [Note: [Col. 0414D] Thus we have corrected the text from the Tol., Zen., and Sp. manuscripts; the reading accords better with the repetition that follows. Others write: “The world, not as is usual, etc.”] His mother was not exhausted by the weight of so great a birth, lying pale with all her limbs relaxed and her womb spent. The mother’s Son was not tainted by any uncleanness of his own; for in truth he could have nothing unclean about him, since he had come to cleanse the sins, filth, and stains of the human race. Finally, no discharges—which are dangerous when delayed—followed the child to the harm of the mother’s organs. [Note: [Col. 0414D] The Pomp., Tol., Zen., and Sp. manuscripts read: “No injuries from the maternal womb accompanied him”; likewise *damno* in the Vatican manuscript.] No customary fomentations were applied to the inexperienced new mother; for, brothers, she could not need them, she who had deserved to receive into her womb the Son, the Savior of all souls.

O great mystery! Mary, an uncorrupted virgin, conceived; after conceiving, a virgin gave birth; after giving birth, she remained a virgin. [Note: [Col. 0414D] It may perhaps seem remarkable that the holy author proclaims and establishes Mary’s virginity in such explicit words. Certainly this is a precise confession against some error of his age. At about the same time, we read St. Ambrose of Milan, *On the Instruction of Virgins*, from ch. 5 onward, and St. Gaudentius of Brescia, Tractate 9, p. 100, contending for the same doctrine against certain people who believed Mary a virgin in Christ’s conception, but denied that she remained a virgin either in giving birth or afterward. Ambrose plainly identifies a certain bishop, whom some believe to have been Bonosus, whose case the Synod of Capua referred to neighboring bishops. See note 5 on Tractate 5, book I, where the same doctrine is clearly emphasized.] [Note: [Col. 0415B] At this point the Veronese editors made a major mutilation, from “of the incredulous midwife” through “she departed healed.” We have restored the text from the manuscripts and the first edition, from which Baronius quoted this whole passage in §§6–7 of the *Apparatus to the Ecclesiastical Annals*, and others from him. The story seems to have offended the editors, who thought it better to cut it away than retain it. But even if the story should be judged unacceptable, it would have been enough to note that in an annotation, leaving the author’s text untouched. To say something in defense of Zeno concerning the matter itself: it was customary among the ancients to have virgins examined by midwives to establish whether or not they were such. See Cyprian, Letter 62; Ambrose, Letter 5.10 to Syagrius; Augustine, *City of God* III.18. The same is reported of Mary, Christ’s mother, by certain persons cited in Clement of Alexandria, *Stromata* VII, p. 889: “Some say that, after she had given birth, she was examined by a midwife and found to be a virgin.” This story originated in the book *On St. Mary and the Midwife*, listed among apocrypha in the Gelasian Decree. Something similar is found in the *Protoevangelium of James*, in Fabricius, *Codex Apocryphus*, p. 517, §19; but there, §20, not the midwife but Salome—who is said to have entered Mary’s dwelling together with the midwife—is assigned both the test of virginity by touch and the punishment and healing of her hand. In the *Gospel of the Infancy*, translated from Arabic into Latin by Henry Sike, p. 170 of the *Codex Apocryphus*, no testing by the midwife is mentioned, but only healing. Jerome, among others, rejects this tale as derived from apocryphal writings, saying against Helvidius: “No midwife, no fussing of women, intervenes there. Mary herself wrapped the infant; she herself was both mother and midwife. For she herself laid him in the manger; she herself wrapped him in swaddling clothes” (Luke 2:4); hence the inventions of the apocryphal books are refuted. Read Suidas under *Iēsous*, who recounts at length the same midwife story, as it had been differently written by a late Hebrew author. Matthew Bossus of Verona refutes this little tale, such as it is related in Suidas, in Letter 79, book I, to Polycletus the Physician. A manuscript in the Vatican contains it separately from the works of Suidas, exactly like the manuscript which Kuster attests, in his notes on Suidas, to exist in the Royal Library at Paris, no. 3437, containing the same account separately. In Bossus’ day this fabulous narrative had been translated into Latin by Laurus Quirinus, a Cretan Venetian patrician, and presented to King René by Marcellus; it circulated abroad, giving Bossus occasion to refute it. But to return to Zeno: it is clear that this ancient Father imbibed the story from some apocryphal source, as is well known to have happened not infrequently to other ancient writers—even older ones. See note 14 on Tractate 8, book I.]

The hand of an unbelieving midwife, testing Mary after she had given birth, catches fire; Mary is found, as testimony, to possess the same virginity. But when the hand touches the infant, that devouring flame is immediately quenched. Thus the inquisitive midwife, happily healed, afterward marveling at the woman as virgin and marveling at the infant as God, leapt with great joy: she came to heal, and departed healed. [Note: [Col. 0416B] The Venetian edition and the Pomp. manuscript read *enixa*; but *enixam*, read by the other editions and manuscripts, better accords with the sense, since the discussion concerns the midwife who wished to test with her own hand whether Mary, having given birth—that is, having been relieved by delivery—was a virgin or not. Later, the Rem., Tol., Vatican, and Urb. manuscripts read “the same” for “her own.”] Thus Christ caused himself to be born as a man in the manner in which a human being cannot be born. Finally, his whole body shone with its own light and cast no shadow; [Note: [Col. 0416C] The Rem. manuscript reads “answering.”] lowly in flesh, yet exalted in the majesty of omnipotent power. He truly deigned to put on flesh for this reason: that, when the day of judgment comes, no one may excuse himself on account of the flesh.

## TREATISE IX. [Col. 0415B] On the Nativity of the Lord and [Note: [Col. 0416C] TREATISE IX.—This title appears in the manuscripts; in the editions, however, only “On the Nativity of Christ.” Here Zeno uses *Majesty* for Divinity or divine power; hence shortly below: “The womb swells with majesty, not with seed,” that is, by divine, not human power; and later: “proving the flesh by weaknesses and the Majesty by powers.” Likewise, it is clear from the testimonies collected by Theodoret at the end of Dialogue III against the Theopaschites, and frequently from Hilary—whose passages Fr. Coustant discusses in the preface, no. 148—as well as from Ambrose, *On the Faith*, II, no. 56, etc., that the term *power* is understood by very many Greek and Latin Fathers to mean Christ’s Divinity.] Majesty.

### I.

In accordance with what God had promised through His prophets—that at the fitting, ripe time He would send His Son as Savior to the human race—having meanwhile laid aside the rank of His divinity, though not His power, He came forth from heaven. [Note: [Col. 0416D] The ancient translator of Jeremiah, cited by Cyprian, *Testimonies*, I, ch. 3, and Lactantius, *Divine Institutes*, IV, ch. 11, reads *metaturam*, though in another sense. Here it is understood of the lodging which the Son of God provided for Himself in Mary’s womb (on this meaning see note 7 on the preceding treatise); and the word *guest*, immediately added, plainly confirms this. This lodging is called foretold because the ancient Scriptures had announced that God would be conceived by that Virgin whom He had chosen for His mother. In the praised treatise, the sentence “In the temple of the predestined Virgin He marks out quarters for Himself” has a similar sense. MS Urb.: “sent forth from heaven, about to mark out quarters.”] As a modest guest, about to mark out the foretold lodging within the sanctuary of the virginal temple, He enters; and there He determines what He wishes to be.

Indeed, what He had long before ordained to accomplish, He secretly assumes. [Note: [Col. 0416D] We shall discuss this more fully, though covertly, in note 2 on Treatise 29.] For He gladly rests in the most flourishing dwelling-place of chastity, and in the womb of the holy Virgin prepares for Himself the body in which, by His own judgment, He is to be born. Adapted to humanity, God is enclosed in the covering of flesh; and He borrows from time a human life, He who bestows eternity upon [Note: [Col. 0416D] MS Pomp.: “upon the times.”] time.

A wondrous thing: Mary conceives Him whom she gives birth to; the womb swells with Majesty, not with seed; and the Virgin contains Him whom the world and the world’s [Note: [Col. 0416D] Editions: “greatness.”] fullness cannot contain. [Col. 0416B] Meanwhile, the limbs advance their Creator, and the work clothes its craftsman in its own form. Mary gives birth not [Col. 0417A] in pain but in joy. The Son is born without a father, [Note: [Col. 0417C] He does not say that Christ was wholly of His mother, in order to signify that He was conceived by divine power. On this ground Hilary also, *On the Trinity*, IX, no. 7, said that Christ was born “from Himself,” since by His own force and power He took upon Himself that which was alien to Him. This is rightly explained from the same author’s Book II, no. 26: although there he speaks of the Holy Spirit coming upon Mary, he nevertheless teaches similar things clearly concerning the Son in Book X, no. 15.] not wholly of His mother; owing to Himself what He is as conceived, granting to His mother what He is as born. She is especially amazed that such a Son has come to her—a Son who, though born from her, would not have been believed to be [such], unless [Note: [Col. 0417C] *Unless because* does not please Sparaverius, who would prefer *since*, and *remained* in place of *remains*. *Because* is absent from MSS Pomp., Tol., and Zen.; we have written *remains* in place of *remained* from MS Vat., since this reading appears more suitable.] she, as she was an uncorrupted Virgin after conception, likewise remains such after childbirth.

### II.

O new order! Compelled by love for His own image, God becomes an infant and cries; He permits Himself to be bound in swaddling clothes, though He had come to discharge the debts of the whole [Note: [Col. 0417C] We supplied *world*, absent from the Venetian and Veronese editions, from the manuscripts. In the Paduan edition, since something similar was evidently thought necessary, *of the world* was inserted by conjecture. Shortly above, MS Tol. has *to be bound* for *bound*.] world. He is laid in a manger in a stable, declaring Himself to be the shepherd and food of the peoples. He subjects Himself to the stages of life, though His eternity admits no age within itself. [Note: [Col. 0417D] Zeno frequently uses *the whole* for *all things*. See note 25 on Treatise 4, Book I.] All this against His own awareness: He suffers as a frail human being, so that immortality may be granted to the human being consumed under the law of death.

For this is God’s power: while preserving what it is, it can become what it is not. This is our God, the Son coeternal with the eternal God. He is both man and God, because He stood as mediator between the Father and humankind, proving the flesh by weaknesses and the Majesty by powers. He is our sun, the true sun, who from the fullness of His brightness kindles the resplendent fires of the world—the kindred brightness of the stars and gleaming poles. He is the One who once set and rose again, never to undergo sunset again. He, I say, whom a crown of twelve rays—that is, the twelve Apostles—surrounds; whom, throughout the circuit of the whole world, not four mute living creatures but the four Gospels bear about by their saving proclamations. Concerning the force of His robe and chariot, the prophet bears witness in these words: “God will come as fire, and His chariots as a storm, to repay vengeance in wrath” [Col. 0417C]. [Note: [Col. 0417D] MS Pomp. and the Venetian edition add “Amen.” The Remiremont manuscript adds: “Here ends the Treatise of Saint Zeno on the Nativity of Christ and Majesty.”]

## TREATISE X. On [Note: [Col. 0417D] TREATISE X.—Here the treatise was reprinted by Lippomano, vol. II of *Lives of the Saints*.] Abraham I

[Col. 0418A]

### I.

Beloved brethren, the acts of the ancient Law testify what a gift of divine mercy Abraham received. His wife Sarah, not inferior [Note: [Col. 0417D] The manuscript reading here is utterly corrupt; they read: “After the courses of a long life had passed, devout—or a son he would produce—she received by the outpouring of childbirth. But He had taken from both,” etc. We retain the reading of the editions, which gives a meaning consistent with Scripture. The reference is to Genesis 21:6, where Sarah, after bearing a son, is reported to have said: “God has made laughter for me,” etc. The first Venetian edition differs from the others only in two points: first, it has *he would produce* for *she produced*; then it writes *received* for *she has received.*] [to him], after the courses of a long life had passed, perceived, in the outcome of childbirth, what kind of son she had borne.

But because age had taken from both of them all hope of offspring, they obtained a substitute [Note: [Col. 0418C] Sparaverius rightly observed that a son is called *succidaneus* (“substitute”) when he succeeds in the place of one whom Abraham’s age, while it was still vigorous, had not given him. Likewise substitute victims, Gellius testifies, *Attic Nights*, IV, ch. 6, were so called because, if the first victims had not propitiated the deity, other victims, led after them, were slain. Festus may also be compared. Shortly below, MS Rem. reads: “Thus he deserved, by faithfulness, he extracted of belief,” where a scribal error and omission are manifest. MSS Pomp., Tol., Vat., Urb., Zen., and Sp.: “Thus he deserved by faithfulness, that,” etc. Tol., Vat., Urb. have *belief* for *belief [as subject]*; likewise incorrectly.] pledge. Thus faith obtained what time had taken away; [Note: [Col. 0418D] *Credulitas* means faith granted to God revealing, without rational proofs or arguments, as is clear from note 6 on Treatise 1, Book I.] trust wrested away what nature had denied.

Our patriarch Abraham, [Note: [Col. 0418D] Here too a scribal omission can plainly be seen in MS Rem.: “is tested by God, anxious,” etc.] tested by God, received in old age his only son, yet a son causing the father no anxiety. His age was turning, in years [Note: [Col. 0418D] MSS Tol. and Vat. have *pressing*. *Boundary* for *boundary [accusative]* occurs in MSS Pomp. and Spar. Choose whichever you wish; each yields a sound meaning.] declining, toward the boundary of its setting; the time for rearing him was brief, [Col. 0418B] and death was already near to old age.

Behold the first devotion: gladly to receive what is offered, and to rejoice in the burden of care undertaken in most sorrowful old age. For Sarah too laughed as she received, in old age, the gift of youth; whence the child received his name, [Note: [Col. 0418D] The name Isaac means “laughter” in Hebrew; hence Sarah testified that in bearing him God had made laughter for her.] who afterward proved Abraham’s mind holy before God.

### II.

That only son of the anxious old man, still a little child, to whom especial affection and compassion were due, is demanded as a victim. If, through [Note: [Col. 0418D] MS Rem.: “through human frailty.”] human frailty, some bodily illness had arisen in him, or a human death had happened, the father could scarcely have survived his misfortunes, had he died in his tender years. This child, [Note: [Col. 0418D] The same manuscript reads: “this child, on whose life paternal affection and mother hang depended”; MSS Tol., Vat., and Urb. have the same.] upon whose life paternal and maternal affection depended, is demanded by a divine voice as a victim, for the testing of Abraham’s faith.

“I wish,” God said, “that a sacrifice be offered to Me, Abraham, by your hands on the mountain, from your son. This victim pleases Me; with this blood you will appease Me; he is due to My sacred rites. [Note: [Col. 0418D] The manuscripts and editions read *whence*; in the margin of Codex Rem., however, an ancient correction has *this one*, which clearly had to be inserted into the text. Later, MS Vat. has *I shall see* for *I command.*] This one I now command to be sacrificed.”

Most devoted Abraham does not darken his brow; grief does not persuade the father to tears. Rather, he exults and rejoices. He does not fear that parricide will be charged against him, but is the more eager to obey devotion; he rejoiced that God had commanded this. [Note: [Col. 0419C] Through bad punctuation and a clear error, several manuscripts and the editions had: “A victim was promptly prepared from his son. Finally,” etc. MSS Tol. and Urb.: “Prepare promptly a victim from your son”; Vat.: the same; but all wrongly. Yet from all these readings we have composed the reading of the text, which offers a more equitable meaning.] He prepares a victim from his son; [Col. 0419A] finally, he hastens to fulfill the sacrifice, lest delay produce sin. [Note: [Col. 0419C] MS Vat. suggested this reading as better suited to the sense, since elsewhere the text was read, punctuated after *sin*: “he is immediately prepared for the necessary sacraments.” Though this could be understood of the sacrifice, the printed reading presents Zeno’s manner and clarity more vividly. MS Rem. likewise has *they are prepared*; the Venetian edition changes *n* to *r*, giving *he would be prepared*. Among Christian authors, *sacramentum* is commonly used for “mystery,” as many have already observed. Thus what Zeno here calls a *sacrament*, he shortly afterward calls a *mystery*: “When every mystery and sacrifice had been arranged.” Similarly, in Treatise 12, no. 3, he calls the mystery of the number three a sacrament of number, and does so frequently elsewhere.
