Here we understand *mystery* as something that signifies something mystically; certainly everything Abraham did in the offering of his son contained a mystical meaning. Jerome similarly called the gifts offered to the newborn Christ by the Magi “sacraments,” that is, mysteries, in his commentary on Matthew 2:11. And on Matthew 27:27, speaking of what happened to Christ from the soldiers in the praetorium, after warning that all these things should be understood mystically, he adds: “Whatever these men did, although they did it with another intention, they handed down to us who believe sacraments—that is, things to be interpreted mystically”; and he then continues with that mystical interpretation.] He is immediately made ready for the mysteries required; they ascend the mountain.

When every mystery and sacrifice had been arranged, the son is led forth rejoicing, by a rejoicing father, to be struck by the father’s right hand. Before he came to the mountain, when he asked his father where the victim was that he intended to prepare and sacrifice, his father—secure in faith concerning his offspring, of whom he did not doubt—revealed to his son that the Lord had demanded [Note: [Col. 0420C] MS Pomp.: “God.”] him, and showed what he himself had promised the Lord.

The boy rejoiced in his faithful father, himself yet more faithful. He did not refuse the death which God, who had given him life, commanded. The father rejoices that his son too rejoices; and with joy he binds the hands of his only pledge, hands which the boy offers all the more willingly to be bound. He binds his feet also, lest, at the approach of death, the excited victim kick out. For the excellent father, secure in his son, feared lest pain be permitted any power over his death.

### III.

O, [Note: [Col. 0420C] Sparaverius thinks it should be read: “O secure devotion of a father!”] brethren, secure devotion! O father pursuing the spirit, but despising body and death! O man who remembered himself to be so completely the Lord’s servant that he did not know himself to be a father! What is a father? Behold, beneath his eyes lies his son bound fast in chains. Where are the tears? Where the grief that is accustomed to dwell in human feelings? In such a calamity of his son, he rejoices and exults; [Col. 0419C] and triumphs that he has deserved the Lord’s favor.

He has already received [Col. 0420A] the rewards he deserves; [Note: [Col. 0420C] The editions and a few manuscripts read: “for divine.”] for the trials of divine testing are presented. He draws the sword and raises his armed right hand; but the voice of Him who had demanded [Note: [Col. 0420C] “That victim” in MSS Pomp., Zen., and Urb.] the victim opposes him. “Look behind you,” God said; “and before you look, spare him.”

Behold also the chief merit: to have deserved divine mercy in the midst of adversity. For [Note: [Col. 0420C] *And* added from Codex Pomp.] Abraham, looking behind him, found a victim which he might sacrifice innocently. With the sword by which he was already preparing to strike his son, he slew the ram. From son to lamb he transferred his right hand, still always rejoicing and exulting. His expression did not change when the victim was exchanged. He offered the ram with as great joy as he had offered his son; for where faith was, grief was not. In that sacrifice God alone felt grief, because He provided another victim. [Col. 0420B] Thus Abraham, with his son, was tested by God in such a way that, without asking, he deserved mercy.

### IV.

Let us consider, beloved brethren, the hidden things of the Law, and bring forward a deeper understanding. Abraham was not under the Law, yet he alone fulfilled the Law; and he who was bound by no legal right [Note: [Col. 0420C] This distinction between the twofold right—of the Law and of God—should be noted. The law’s right means written law; because it had not yet been given, Abraham was not bound by it. Divine right, however, means the natural law, insofar as it commands obedience above all things to God who gives commands; and Abraham is said especially to have kept this law. MS Vat. has after *kept*: “and he whose offering,” etc. *Offering* is used here actively and signifies Abraham’s action and sacrifice; and the son himself, requested as a victim, is said to have rejoiced in this very virtue of his father.] especially kept every divine right—an offering at which he too rejoiced who was being prepared as the victim.

A ram was caught in [Note: [Col. 0420D] We retain the reading of MSS Tol., Urb., and the first edition, since it accords better with the testimony of Genesis, where at ch. 22, v. 13, Abraham is said to have found a ram among the thorns. The reading of MS Rem., *verbe* for *vepre* (“in a thorn-bush”), also supports it—unless perhaps *verbes* are a kind of vervain resembling thorn-bushes; for *verbena* signifies not so much a shrub as all branches collectively, as may be seen in Basilius Faber, *Thesaurus antiquitatum*, p. 1133. But we have been unable to find *verbes* anywhere. The Veronese edition and some manuscripts instead have *eruo*, a species of legume particularly suitable as fodder for cattle, as Pliny, *Natural History*, XVIII, ch. 15, and Columella, *On Agriculture*, VI, ch. 2, relate. This is irrelevant to our matter.] a thorn-bush, entangled in thorns, its head held fast. This is the one sacrificed to God instead of Isaac. Abraham offered this one; he was commanded to sacrifice this one.

## TREATISE XI. On Abraham II. (The beginning is missing.)

[Col. 0420C]

### I.

For virginity is not urged by a command, [Col. 0421A] [Note: [Col. 0421B] We have preferred to write *by a command* from MSS Tol. and Pomp., in place of the reading *commanded* in the others. For virginity could not be called commanded: no command to preserve it was ever given in the Old Testament, or indeed even in the New, according to Paul, 1 Corinthians 7: “Concerning virgins I have no command of the Lord.” Therefore it may fittingly be said that virginity was urged by no command, as follows conveniently from the reading adopted. [Col. 0421C] But perhaps *commanded virginity* means virginity “previously undertaken,” and perhaps the statement refers to Mary’s virginity—of which the author may have spoken in the missing portion—which God preferred to marital continence; nevertheless, though He decreed that the Word should be born from a Virgin, He did not reject marital continence, which He rewarded in Abraham and Sarah. Shortly afterward we preferred to write “the son Isaac formerly” in place of “the son Isaac indeed,” especially since *indeed* is immediately repeated. Likewise, it would please us to write *meaning* in place of *utterance*, if manuscripts supported it or if the received text did not differ greatly.] nor is continence, once relinquished, rejected. As a witness to this, beloved, we have the holy author Abraham, who formerly had his son Isaac. The term is simple indeed, but its expression manifold.

For this Isaac, beloved, despaired of by his parents but received at God’s promise, is conceived amid the flowering of age already spent and of generative organs. [Note: [Col. 0421C] All manuscripts and editions have *flore* (“flowering”); Sparaverius would prefer *fluore* (“flow”), since he thinks it unbelievable that the holy bishop wished to reckon an exhausted age and dry generative organs among the privileges of those in their prime. But perhaps he attributes flowering to the old man because of the divine miracle through which Abraham, though old, begot a son as if he were a youth in his prime. Others might perhaps prefer *languore* (“languor”), or something similar. Yet nothing ought to be altered without evident necessity. We subsequently wrote *is conceived* in place of *is consumed*, as the sense requires.] He deserved to be begotten not so much from his parents as by divine [Note: [Col. 0421D] The editions and manuscripts read *precept*. But since the divine promise recalled by Paul at Galatians 4:23 is plainly in view here—where Isaac is said to have been received by Abraham from his free wife through the promise made to Abraham by God at Genesis 17:19—it seems that *promise* should be written in place of *precept*. Yet just as *I command* is sometimes used for “to admonish,” “to teach,” and “to indicate,” so perhaps *precept* may here be understood as God’s promise, insofar as Abraham was forewarned by it concerning future offspring, and was moreover given in it the command by which God ordered every male to be circumcised. Therefore, since no manifest error is present in this passage, we have changed nothing. Add that Isaac is called below “the offspring of divine ordinance,” where *ordinance* stands for what is here called *precept.*] precept; and, in the final course of life, the son opened Sarah’s womb [Note: [Col. 0422A] The first word read *aperto* (“having opened”). Since this could not stand by itself and *son* was governed by no verb, we first thought of reading *to open* or *he opened* with “mother” as object: for when Isaac was born, Sarah’s womb was opened and she began to be called a mother, whereas venerable old age had already bestowed upon her the honor of grandmother. In no. 2 likewise, these two terms, mother and grandmother, are contrasted: “Her age declared her a grandmother; childbirth adorned her as a mother.” But this emendation seemed too free. Therefore, retaining the first word, which can be understood without difficulty insofar as Sarah’s womb was opened by the first utterance which she pronounced in bearing Isaac—“The Lord has made laughter for me”—we judged only that *aperto* should be changed to *aperuit*, so that there would be a verb governing *son*. Shortly above we corrected *from the inner parts*, the manuscript and printed reading, with Sparaverius, to *in the final stages*. Below, however, MSS Pomp. and Zen. wrongly write *reverentia* for *reverentiam*.] with his first utterance, though modest old age had already bestowed on her the honor due to a grandmother.

Thus, beloved, born amid the [Note: [Col. 0422B] The editions and manuscripts read “in the birth of hope.” Suspecting an obvious error, Sparaverius would prefer “at the hoped-for birth.” But we judged that “in the despair of birth,” or better, “in the despair concerning birth,” should be written, since in everything Zeno says afterward this offspring, and therefore its birth itself, is described not as hoped for but as despaired of: “Nor could she hope for offspring”; and below, “He was judged happier because of despair.” Likewise, “despaired-of fertility,” etc. Hence, after rejecting not so much Sparaverius’s correction as the received reading *sperationis* (“of hope”)—especially since we have thus far been unable to find *speratio* in established Latin authors—“despair concerning birth” should not be judged an excessively rash insertion.] despair of birth and wonder, in the first rudiments of infancy he is offered, an innocent martyr, to God who commands and requires him: an immaculate offering, and no unprepared victim. [Note: [Col. 0422C] We wrote “and no unprepared victim” in place of the reading “and no unprepared victim [masculine],” since not only Latin syntax and construction but Zeno’s own style appear to require that *immaculate* and *unprepared* correspond.] As a witness of divine fear, he is demanded by the Lord for faith and led by his parent; yet he is an offering not of blood but of salvation. To this glory, therefore, the abundance of delayed childbirth and fertility despaired of are brought forth.

### II.

Abraham’s wife, unacquainted with pregnancy—her old age having chilled her womb, so that she could neither hope for offspring nor trust herself able to bear one—undertook the duties of a mother, though she no longer knew the offices [Note: [Col. 0422C] The editions and several manuscripts read “marital offices”; but the reading of MSS Basilica Vaticana, Urb., and Pomp. is more pleasing. In Zeno’s manner of writing, “a wife’s offices” corresponds to the words “a mother’s duties” in the preceding clause. Sparaverius would prefer “had forsaken womanly functions” to “did not know a wife’s offices,” since Genesis 18:11 relates that Sarah’s womanly functions had ceased. But at v. 12 it also relates that, when told she would conceive a son, Sarah said: “After I have grown old, and my lord is old, shall I devote myself to pleasure?” This sufficiently indicates that, because of their age, Abraham and Sarah had long discontinued marital intercourse; Zeno appears to speak of that when he says that Sarah no longer knew a wife’s offices. Similarly, in Treatise 7 of this book, no. 2, he uses “marital office” in the same sense.] of a wife. The child is brought forth at the very time when vital heat was leaving the generative organs.

Truly wondrous, beloved, and not to be hoped for by ages yet to come, is this offspring of divine ordinance [Note: [Col. 0422D] We have adopted Sparaverius’s emendation, which changes nothing in the sense but renders the passage more polished and Zenonian. The reading was *formed*. Shortly above, we judged it necessary to write “not to be hoped for by ages yet to come” in place of “and to be hoped for,” because offspring such as Isaac’s in old age exceeds every hope, and wonder arises over a matter for which there is no hope, not over something which one may hope for again. Isaac is called the offspring of divine ordinance because, as was said above, he deserved to be begotten by divine precept.] formed. [Col. 0423A] Age already spent is recalled to its beginning; fertility is equipped out of barrenness, so that what was written through the Prophet might be fulfilled: [Note: [Col. 0423C] MSS Vat. and Basilica Vaticana have: “Rejoice, barren woman, who did not bear.” Codices Tol. and Zen. likewise have *did not bear*. The Tolentan manuscripts have “you forsake” for “forsaken.”] “Rejoice, barren woman, who did not bear; break forth and cry aloud, you who do not travail; for many are the children of the forsaken woman” (Isaiah 54:1).

For behold, beloved, in Sarah, when age had drawn tight her sinews, the moisture of blood was failing, the veins were drying up, and the skin was hard with the internal organs; when a misshapen, sallow pallor had nearly destroyed the human appearance of her face, and no movement in her limbs remained for pleasure—nothing remained in the substance of her body; yet nothing was denied to the child in the womb. Her age declared her a grandmother, but childbirth adorned her as a mother. While affection wavered beneath an uncertain designation, [Note: [Col. 0423C] MS Rem.: “affection wavered”; MSS Vat., Urb., and Basilica Vaticana: “to nourish affection.”] and while the womb brought forth a son, old age wished for a grandson.

Thus, when Isaac was born, contrary to expectation through a conflict of time and nature, an angel bestowed his name, in order that joy might confirm what the frailty of age had despaired of. A new affection toward their son grew in the parents: he was thought more certain because of promise, sweeter because of delay, happier because of despair. Only in number and already first in the solidity of their love, he occupied the whole breast of maternal affection. Reared with hasty care, he was to provide God with a victim and his parents with a loving parricide [Note: [Col. 0423C] MSS Rem. and Urb.: “pleasing.”].

### III.

Behold, beloved, as the Apostle says, Abraham leads his son, born against hope, to the altar in order to sacrifice him at the Lord’s command (Romans 4:18); nor is a sword lacking for the service, so that the father might be priest at once. The son likewise has a similar assurance, arising from the divine will. [Col. 0424A] When he did not see the victim [Note: [Col. 0423C] MS Rem. has *pervidet* (“he clearly sees”); the Venetian edition and MS Pomp., *praevidet* (“he foresees”); the other manuscripts with the Veronese edition, except MS Basilica Vaticana, have *providet* (“he provides”), while that manuscript has *provideret*. Since Genesis 22:7 is indicated, where Isaac, secure and not seeing the victim for the burnt offering, asked his father for it, we judged that one should write “he does not see,” or rather “he did not see.” Shortly afterward MSS Rem., Urb., Zen., Basilica Vaticana, and the Venetian edition have *chosen* for [Col. 0423D] *chosen [masculine].*] in whose place he himself had been chosen, he asked for it.

But his still tender hands are handed over to bonds; and, lest anything be lacking in the victim, a binding restrains his foot, lest the excited offering prove displeasing. Therefore, beloved, let the detestable suspicion of impiety cease here. Abraham set the Lord before his son, and the priest before the father; nor did he consider himself loving unless he had proved himself faithful.

Finally, beloved, he is armed, undaunted, for the ministry of sacrifice. [Note: [Col. 0423D] MSS Tol., Basilica Vaticana, and Pomp. have “the beloved one is balanced,” a reading also found in MSS Urb., Zen., and the Venetian edition.] His mind examines the stroke of the wound with confidence, but his hand with still greater confidence; the sword, raised [Note: [Col. 0423D] MSS Rem. and Vat. have “the sword examines for the sacrificed one.” MSS Basilica Vaticana, Urb., Pomp., and Zen. have “the sword examines for sacrificing.” Thus Tol. has *libratur* twice, while Rem. and Vat. have *rimatur* twice. We suitably retained the received reading: in the first place *rimatur* (“examines”), where the investigation of the mind is being discussed; in the second, where the sword is meant, *libratur* (“is poised”), which better suits a sword. Only the editions had *in* written for *ad*.] for the sacrifice, is poised. Nor does approaching death sadden the boy, lest fear disclose a weak faith.

By this steadfastness of the one sacrificing and the one to be sacrificed, he deserved to be released, when he laid aside human fear from himself. So far as faith was concerned, the father fulfilled what had been promised; the Lord, having tested his purpose, forbade the parricide.

IV. Therefore, in reference to his person, Christ’s birth is called modest—that is, venerable—but the more secret chamber of a virginal womb bore a body fashioned by the art of the divine Word, a body that was to waste away within itself.

[Note: “Modest” (*verecunda*) is understood in the sense of “venerable,” as Sparaverius proves from Valesius’s notes on Ammianus Marcellinus, book XIV, chapter 6, where three passages of the same Ammianus are brought forward to the same effect. Indeed, *verecundia* is used for reverence and obedience in Livy I.1.3 and Pliny VII.30.]

[Note: We have printed *formatum* (“fashioned”) instead of *formata* (“fashioned,” feminine), following the manuscript of the Vatican Basilica, so that it may refer to Christ’s body; otherwise it is not apparent what the womb bore of the body wasting away within itself.]

But the impious designs of the Jews blazed forth against the most certain Lord, begotten by heavenly offspring—that is, by heavenly power, not by seed. They led Christ to be raised upon the cross, silent as though liable to punishment and grieving only for their blindness, just as Isaac, not destined to perish, was led to the altar by wicked men.

[Note: Sparaverius rightly wished for ancient books by which he might restore the exceedingly disordered and corrupted passages of this treatise. Here, where a striking corruption appears, although we have used more manuscripts than he did, and sufficiently ancient ones, we have nevertheless achieved nothing. From the manuscripts of Reims, Toledo, and the Vatican we could derive only *semina* (“seeds”) in place of *non semine* (“not by seed”), and *conscientia* (“conscience”) in place of *consilia* (“plans”), which latter reading likewise occurs in the manuscripts of the Vatican Basilica and Urbino; but both are erroneous, as is clear from the context. The Vatican Basilica manuscript has *femina* (“woman”) in place of *non semine*, and there, together with the Vatican and Toledo manuscripts, *coelesti prole* (“by heavenly offspring”) without the preposition *in*, though with little or no support. What then? Let it suffice to have exposed the sore; let others, more fortunate, supply the remedy. Meanwhile, for the passage to yield some sense, it seems it must be constructed thus: “But the impious designs of the Jews blazed forth against the most certain Lord, begotten by heavenly offspring, that is, heavenly power, not seed.” For *proles* (“offspring”) in the sense of the generative power itself may commonly be inferred from Arnobius, book VII. This is certainly the author’s meaning; perhaps it would be preferable to write: “But against one begotten by heavenly offspring, not seed, the impious designs blazed forth against the most certain Lord,” or “against heavenly offspring begotten not by seed—or from a woman—but most certain,” etc.]

But because eternity does not know how to die, the Lord revived after the tomb; and among the Jews there remained only the odium of their condemned intention, because they were unwilling to acknowledge the Lord and believed that he was to be punished merely by their own judgment—he whom it had been wicked even belatedly to worship.

[Note: The printed editions had *aut Dominus post sepulcrum* (“or the Lord after the tomb”); likewise the manuscripts, except for that of the Vatican Basilica, which omits the word *Dominus*. Here Sparaverius supplies “does not know how to die,” signifying that Christ, neither as eternal God nor as a human being united to God—though he was indeed born in order to die—could be so overcome by death as to lie dead long after the tomb. Hence, victorious over death and immortal, on the third day he returned to life. But since the particle *sed quia* (“but because”) still hangs without completion, requiring some answering verb, we have written *revixit* (“revived”) in place of *aut* (“or”), as both the matter and the sense demand, and as expresses and properly completes Zeno’s thought. Moreover, among the Jews there is said to have remained only the odium of their condemned will, because they are guilty of that faithless intention by which, though in vain, they attempted out of malice to inflict eternal death upon him; nor did they gain anything even from his resurrection.]

[Note: Vatican manuscript: *qui Dominum*. Shortly afterward it appears that *crucifixione* (“by crucifixion”) should be written in place of *cogitatione* (“by thought”); for the Jews believed Christ was to be punished not by thought alone, but by crucifixion—unless the author used “by thought alone” to mean “by opinion alone”: that Christ was guilty not in fact, nor through proofs—of which the Jews brought none convincing before Pilate—but solely in their own minds, and was believed to be justly punished by crucifixion, according to Isaiah 53:4: “We considered him as though leprous and struck by God and humbled.”]

At the cruelty of this monstrous deed, the dreadful aspect of the elements was changed, and nature revealed God’s injury before the Jewish people understood it. Thus from the author of light began the horror of their frenzy. The death-dealing crowd girds itself, and the point of swords is turned against the Invisible One hanging there. Yet, as I have said, the cruelty of their crime did not obtain its intended result; because, just as in Isaac one thing is offered and another sacrificed, so also in Christ’s passion that which had sinned through Adam is set free through Christ.

[Note: Sparaverius understands Judas, whom the Acts of the Apostles call the leader of those who arrested Jesus, chapter I, verse 16. The Toledo and Vatican Basilica manuscripts have: “From the author,” a reading perhaps better if it is referred to Christ and some things in what follows are altered so as to explain that the Jews exercised their fury against Christ. The ensuing words belong to this: “The death-dealing crowd girds itself,” etc.; otherwise they would stand out of place. But Judas cannot be mentioned here, since the things described immediately followed Christ’s crucifixion, whereas Judas had long before died hanging by a noose. Perhaps, since Zeno indicated in the preceding period the signs of nature accompanying the Lord’s crucifixion, “From the author of light began,” etc., it should be written so that the first and chief sign may be the darkening of the sun, which is the author of light. But since the manuscripts offer no support, it is enough to identify the passage as corrupt, shapeless, or mutilated.]

[Note: The text read *connectitur* (“is joined”). The sense will approve the emendation. Christ is called the Invisible One hanging—namely, from the cross—because his divinity was invisible to the Jews, since they did not believe it was in him. In place of *gladiorum* (“of swords”), *labiorum* (“of lips”) seems to be required, since the Jews used not swords but their tongues in assaulting Christ already fastened to the cross.]

[Note: Reims manuscript: *credulitas* (“credulity”).]

---

## TREATISE XII. On Abraham. III.

[Column 0425B]

I. Abraham, in order to become the father of many nations, did not learn righteousness here, but begot it. He had not been corrupted by intercourse with cities. He had no law, whose manner of life was itself a law. He hears from God the command of exile, that he should leave both his kindred and his land. Then Abraham, looking with his eyes, saw three; he ran, worshipped with his face to the ground, and offered a victim. “Refresh yourselves,” he says, “under this great tree” (Gen. 18:4). He mixes fine flour; he cuts up a calf. After this, a son is promised him from lawful marriage, from faith rather than from age. Sarah conceives; she carries, without labor, the burden of a womb though she could not walk about. She learns that she is a mother when she ceases. Her withered breasts show an abundance of milk, and a sturdier boy is nourished from her fasting age. Nothing is difficult for faith, which possesses as much as it believes.

[Note: TREATISE XII.—The author here calls faith “righteousness,” which, as he likewise says in Treatise 1, Book I, §3, “did not learn to believe but presumed”; and which the Apostle in Romans 4 calls “the righteousness of faith,” because, as he says, Abraham’s faith “was reckoned to him for righteousness.” Ambrose notes on this in *On Abraham*, book I, chapter 3, §21: “Therefore it was reckoned to him for righteousness, because he did not seek a reason but believed with the most ready faith.” And St. Zeno says in Treatise 2, Book I, §2: “Abraham believed God, and it was reckoned to him for righteousness; he was righteous because faithful, for the righteous lives by faith; faithful because he believed God.”]

[Note: Abraham is said to have begotten righteousness, or faith, either because through such faith he himself became—as Paul says in the cited passage—the father of all believers, since he first conceived faith, which in some manner was derived from him to all believers; hence at the end of this treatise: “Through faith we have become sons of Abraham” (on which see Note 34 on Treatise 1, Book I); or, more probably, in the sense in which the author stated in the same Treatise 1, Book I, §1, that faith is not lent by another to teach it, but arises from the will. Thus Abraham is signified not to have learned faith from human beings by arguments but to have begotten it from his own will, by which he yielded to divine authority without arguments. This certainly accords with the faith which the holy bishop frequently commends in this same patriarch. See Note 6 on the cited treatise.]

[Note: We have supplied, from the manuscripts, “He had no law.” Moreover, the conduct of one who had no law is said to have been a law because, without a written law—which he did not possess—he himself, as is evident from his conduct, that is, his habitual life and morals, was a law to himself, as Paul says of the Gentiles.]

[Note: The manuscripts of Pomp., Toledo, and Zeno have *concepit* (“conceived”); and later, in place of *inambulare* (“to walk about”), which those manuscripts have, the printed editions read *jam ambulare* (“now to walk”). Arnobius, book III, p. 106, likewise calls the burden of the womb an “inward weight.”]

II. Thus Isaac, the only son, hope of peoples and nations, origin of so many kings, clung to his dear father’s embraces. He had bound up in himself his father’s affection: because he was only, because late-born, because promised, because he alone, the only hope, was to repair all the losses of former barrenness. A reason was found for Abraham’s faith to serve more stoutly in temptation. The limbs of his beloved son, which he had been accustomed to press with kisses, he is commanded, armed with a sword, to kill. What could affection do? The command cannot be delayed. “You were better off, mother, when you were barren; the boy is born for the sword.” No one mourns such a fate except the mother who bore him. No one bewails this living funeral procession; no one beforehand wets with tears the service due to an innocent man, lest the father seem to have hesitated if he wept. With a devoted, stern countenance he leads the boy to the altar; he raises the sword between them. The breast of faith was in service; his face did not grow pale, his hand did not tremble. The boy asks where the victim is. The victim then appears, so that tender age might not thus be struck down; therefore the father could not strike, because the Lord did not demand human blood. The devout executioner draws the sword. It was the father’s act that raised it; it was God’s that spared. Neither he who was struck feared, nor he who struck was alarmed. The Lord’s sacrifice is not abandoned but changed. He preserved his son better by not sparing him; for faith alone walks safely among swords, is friendly among hungry beasts, is cool in fires—faith alone is to be preferred. Through it, we who have become sons of Abraham by faith are to believe that we shall arrive in his bosom.

[Note: We have written *regum* (“kings”) in place of *rerum* (“things”), since several kings trace their descent from Isaac; this better accords with the sense.]

[Note: *Praestiteras* means “you were in a better condition” and “you stood in a more excellent state.” Similar is Cicero, *To Atticus* XIV.9: “It is a thousand times better to die than to suffer these things.”]

[Note: This concerns the lamentations which, customarily accompanying the pomp of funerals, were considered a dutiful observance of the living toward the dead. An image of this practice is described in Book I, Treatise 5, §4, and Treatise 16, §6. Zeno calls them “living funerals,” since Isaac, while alive, was to be accompanied as a man delivered over to death on his way to punishment. Shortly afterward the preposition *ante* is absent from the Toledo manuscript.]

[Note: Sparaverius would prefer *sicco* or *soluto vultu*, “with a dry” or “untroubled countenance,” and rightly so; perhaps *siccato*, “with dried countenance,” would be better. But *sic stricto*, or rather *districto vultu*, seems to have been written in the sense of a stern, not relaxed or fearless, countenance, to express what is added shortly afterward: “His face does not grow pale.” The text then read *reprimit gladium*, “he restrains the sword.” But since *reprimit* applies to one resisting, it does not suit Abraham; therefore we corrected it with a slight alteration to *exprimit*, “he raises.” For *exprimo* in the sense of “raise” or “lift up,” see Caesar, *Gallic War* VII.22: “to the height to which the daily mound had raised our towers,” etc. See also Vitruvius VIII.7.]

[Note: Earlier in this book, Treatise 6, §5, speaking of this same sacrifice of Abraham, Zeno says: “The sword, suspended midway without any hindrance, is astonished”; it is called “midway” between father and son.]

[Note: The Verona edition notes in the margin *quem*, a reading unsupported by any manuscript but proposed because the meaning of the passage under the common text was considered uncertain; that text is also transmitted in the manuscripts: *quae mox ita ne percuteret, tenera aetas ostendit*. The emendation *quem* would please if that alone healed the passage and if “tender age,” that is Isaac, had truly been the one who showed the victim. But the son, as the author himself indicates in the preceding treatise, did not see this victim; and it encountered Abraham’s eyes without anyone pointing it out, God alone so arranging, as Genesis 22:13 testifies. Therefore, since another correction is necessary, we retained *quae* and, following Sparaverius, corrected two other words with the slightest alteration. Though not attested by any manuscript, we inserted them into the text, since otherwise the truth of the narrative does not stand. Thus the sense is: “That victim then encountered—or came before—Abraham, so that tender age, that is Isaac, might not thus be struck.” The words which follow also cause Sparaverius difficulty: “therefore the father could not strike, because the Lord,” etc. He accordingly thought *quo* should be written in place of *quod*, so that the sense would be that the victim appeared of itself in order that Abraham, as father—that is, without parricide—might be unable to strike. But that interpretation is too harsh. We have retained *quo*, and take *posset* in the sense of *liceret*: the father was not permitted to strike because the Lord did not demand human blood.]

[Note: The Pomp. and Zeno manuscripts read *deambulabat* (“walked about”).]

[Note: After the words “faith alone,” the Verona editors inserted “adorned with works, as Abraham’s was.” We have said enough concerning this addition in Dissertation 2, chapter 6.]

[Note: The manuscripts of Reims, Vatican, and Urbino read *nobis* (“to us”), wrongly. The Venetian edition reads *nos* (“we”) here, as other manuscripts do, and repeats *nos* before *credamus* (“let us believe”), as in the Toledo, Vatican, and Urbino manuscripts.]

---

## TREATISE XIII. On Jacob’s Dream.

[Column 0428A]

I. Truly, dearest brothers, the heart of him who knows the dream and hidden matters of this man does not sleep (Gen. 28); for prophecy always speaks by changing figures, but one reality is found in all of them. Thus Jacob bears the image of Christ; and so does the stone itself which he is known to have placed at his head (Acts 4:11), since Christ is the head of the man (Eph. 2:20), and is at times called a stone. The ladder, moreover, signifies the two Testaments, which, interwoven with evangelical commands, have been accustomed to raise believing people who do the will of God to heaven, as it were by certain steps of obedience.

[Note: TREATISE XIII.—“His” means Jacob’s. Hence it is clear either that the reading of that chapter of Genesis in which Jacob’s dream is described preceded this discourse, or that the sermon is headless, so that some mention of Jacob came before. The former is more pleasing, however, since a sufficiently appropriate beginning seems to be set before this treatise.]

[Note: Thus from the Pomp. manuscript, which is more satisfactory than *quia*, found elsewhere.]

John in the Apocalypse called this ladder a two-edged sword with one hilt, which he described as proceeding from the Lord’s mouth (Rev. 1:16). For the sword is the Holy Spirit, having one hilt—that is, one substance, power, divinity, majesty, and will of Father and Son—bearing witness by its two edges, that is, carrying the two Testaments. By their royal commands the believing and devoted are saved, while the unbelieving and deserters are punished. Isaiah saw it in the form of tongs (Isa. 6:6), with which, he prophesied, a coal taken by one of the Seraphim from God’s altar was brought to fuse polluted lips.

[Note: The Venetian edition has *captulo*; the others, *capulo*; but the manuscripts have *capitulo*, which we would have retained if it could be shown by any example to have been used in the same sense as *capulum*. Here it is utterly clear that *capulum*, the sword’s hilt, is meant. Nowhere else have we found *capitulum* in the same sense. We therefore retained *capulo*, and also below retained *capulum* with the printed editions, where the manuscripts have *capitulum*. We believe the error belongs to an ancient copyist from whom the others derived, who, supposing *capulo* and *capulum* to be written in abbreviation, expanded them as *capitulo* and *capitulum*.]

[Note: From most manuscripts: *descripsit* (“described”); printed editions: *describit* (“describes”).]

[Note: Reims manuscript: *contestantes*. But *contestans* is preferable, since it refers to the sword, which by its central hilt bears witness through two edges, that is, brings forward one testimony concerning Christ.]

For we should understand the two polluted lips as the two peoples, Jews and Gentiles. Since they had been defiled by the crimes of their former life—the one by blaspheming and persecuting Christ, the other by asserting gods and worshipping abominable inventions—they are known, by the touch of the coal, to have been fused into one people through confession of Christ’s name. For fusion signifies both purity and unity: the coal is the word of God, the altar is the law, and the tongs are the two Testaments, which believers hold, while they cut unbelievers.

[Note: Reims and Toledo manuscripts, and the Venetian edition: *designabat* (“signified”).]

II. David also called this a reed-pen, saying: “My tongue is the pen of a swiftly writing scribe” (Ps. 44:2). The pen is split, brothers, and bears two points arranged in the narrowness of a single tip, making one letter by both; if you remove one, its use thereafter is empty. Therefore the Testaments are rightly two, which likewise with two points form one letter: that is, by the two ordinances of the sacred law they write one Christ, the Son of God, in spiritual harmony. They cannot be useful without one another; for as the New gives faith to the Old, so the Old bears testimony to the New, as it is written: “Once has the Lord spoken, and these two things have we heard” (Ps. 61:12).

[Note: “Which cannot be useful without one another,” that is, neither of the Testaments can be useful without the other.]

The Lord himself also expresses this principle in the Gospel, saying to Peter: “Cast the hook into the sea; take the first fish that comes up, and, opening its mouth, you will find two denarii; give them for me and for yourself” (Matt. 17:23). We must understand the first fish rising from the dead as Christ, from whose mouth were brought forth two denarii—that is, the two Testaments—which benefited the two peoples, to the salvation with the Lord’s glory and Peter’s blessedness, since upon him he built the Church. The sea unquestionably signifies the world. The hook signifies preaching, because, just as a hook cast into the sea signifies the fish’s death, so evangelical preaching sent through the world bears witness to the Lord’s death and coming, as it is written to the Corinthians: “You will proclaim the Lord’s death until he comes” (1 Cor. 2). “You will open the fish’s mouth,” that is, a mystery: you will explain to those who do not understand the things I have spoken in parables. Finally, elsewhere he says this more plainly to all the disciples: “Go therefore and teach all nations, baptizing them in the name of the Father and of the Son and of the Holy Spirit, teaching them to observe all things whatsoever I have commanded you” (Matt. 28:19–20). “You will give for me and for yourself,” that is: you will preach my cross, and you too will likewise rejoice in the honor of your own cross.

[Note: In the Vulgate, following the Greek, one reads: “you will find a stater.” A stater is said to contain two didrachmas, as Jerome explains on this passage, p. 756, vol. VII of the Verona edition. Indeed, a didrachma was due from each person, as is clear from Matthew 17:23; hence a stater containing two didrachmas had to be found, so that payment might be made both for Christ and for Peter. But a didrachma was valued at two denarii, while a stater at four, as may be inferred from Hilary’s Commentary on this passage of Matthew, §§12–13. Accordingly, a stater weighing two didrachmas, or four drachmas, ought to have been reckoned at four denarii. Why, then, did St. Zeno render the stater mentioned in the Greek Scripture at this point of Matthew as two denarii rather than four, or at least—as it might have pleased him to adhere to the allegory of the double number—as two didrachmas? If this Gospel testimony were to be understood of the tribute paid to Caesar, as several interpreters thought, then, since only one denarius was paid by each person—as Grotius observed on Matthew 22:19, and therefore whenever the Gospel speaks of Caesar’s tribute it always mentions one denarius—St. Zeno could rightly have written “two denarii,” signifying the tribute to be paid for Christ and Peter. But many learned persons have already shown that this passage in Matthew concerns not a tax paid to the Romans but a tribute contributed to the sanctuary, commanded in Exodus 30:12 and 2 Chronicles 24:5. That temple tribute is called in Hebrew half a shekel; the shekel is equivalent to the stater. Thus the common translator rendered what is called *siclus* in Hebrew sometimes “shekel,” sometimes “stater,” interchangeably. Symmachus likewise, at Joshua 7:21, wrote Greek *στατήρ* (*statēr*, “stater”) for the Hebrew *sicul*, and Aquila usually did the same, as may be seen from the Hexapla, as did the Syriac and Arabic versions. Hence St. Jerome, Book I on Ezekiel chapter 4, affirms that the shekel is not so much a stater as, like a stater, it contains four drachmas or denarii: “The shekel, that is, the stater, contains four drachmas.” Among these matters one passage of Sedulius seems to approach Zeno’s present interpretation. For in Book III, verse 316, expounding the same testimony of Matthew, he used a single didrachma in place of a stater—that is, two denarii:

> He commands the hook to bear the carrier of a golden didrachma.

Accordingly, he seems to have followed an interpretation wholly similar to Zeno’s. We observe, however, that the Seventy Interpreters in many places of the Old Testament rendered a shekel as a didrachma, and half a shekel as half a didrachma or a drachma. See Genesis 24:22; 23:15; Exodus 30:13; Joshua 7:21, etc. Sedulius and Zeno, then, may seem to have followed this authority of the Seventy Interpreters when they used “didrachma” or “two denarii” for the stater, which is valued as a shekel. It is not our task to seek the rationale for defending this interpretation, or to examine whether the Seventy Interpreters and Sedulius with them had in view a golden stater valued at two Attic drachmas, according to Pollux, book IV, chapter 31, §173—especially since Cicero, in *Pro Flacco*, reports that the temple tribute was customarily paid by the Jews in gold. But if they cannot be defended from error, because by no reasoning can either the shekel or the stater be reduced to a didrachma, we can still sufficiently vindicate Zeno, who renders not two drachmas but two denarii: he may have used “two denarii” not strictly for two drachmas but broadly for two didrachmas, since *denarius* is not infrequently used by other writers for any kind of coin. Further, in Matthew’s text, according to the author’s interpretation, the Pomp. and Vatican manuscripts read “and for you” in place of “and you.” Shortly before, the words “take and” are absent in the Pomp., Toledo, and Zeno manuscripts.]

[Note: Pomp., Vatican manuscripts, and the Venetian edition: *annuntiatis* (“you proclaim”).]

[Note: Here also, as we have noted elsewhere, *sacramentum* is used for *mysterium*, namely for something having a mystical interpretation. Thus Christ’s command to open the fish’s mouth is understood as a mystery, or mystical figure, of apostolic preaching, by which what Christ had spoken in parables was to be explained to those who did not understand.]

[Note: The ancient Fathers, especially African ones, often used *tingere* (“to dip”) for “to baptize.”]

III. Therefore we learn from David’s saying what material this ladder was made of, upon which the Lord rested: “Your rod and your staff, they have comforted me” (Ps. 22:4). The rod and staff are certainly the two Testaments. They are compared to wooden material either because, through their use, the enduring and entire will of the testator remains inscribed, or because, converging as it were crosswise into one faith, they announced that the Son of God ought to be crucified. They confirm him as most rightly placed upon the ladder, because the history of the whole Scripture was fulfilled both on his account and through him as its author. Finally, he says to the disciples: “Every scribe instructed in the kingdom of heaven is like a householder bringing forth from his treasures things new and old” (Matt. 13:52). The scribe, brothers, is the preacher; the householder is Christ; his treasures are the Father’s substance and will of undiminished divinity; the new and old things are the two Testaments. You see that these too are rightly and without ambiguity clothed by the Lord in the figure of two denarii, for this reason: in his treasures he intended the two denarii to signify the two Testaments in their newness and antiquity.

[Note: Wooden testamentary tablets are also mentioned by Ulpian, Digest book XXXVII, title 11, *On Possession of an Inheritance according to the Tablets*, law 1, and seem to be the same as the waxed tablets famous elsewhere. For wills were generally written upon the wax with which wooden tablets were covered, so that the stylus might readily make furrows in it while writing.]

[Note: We would read *debuisse* (“ought to have”) in place of *habuisse* (“to have had”). Was *habuisse* ever used for *debuisse*? Similarly, in the following treatise, §13, the Reims manuscript has *habere* for *debere*, but hitherto no other ancient example of this kind has been found. We corrected *nuntiabant* (“they announced”) for *nuntiabat* from the Pomp., Vatican, and Sp. manuscripts. The sense required that *confirmant* (“they confirm”) be emended in place of *confirmat*.]

[Note: Pomp. manuscript: *patrisfamilias* (“of a householder”).]

[Note: The Reims manuscript writes *indeptae* in the text; but in the margin, in an ancient hand, *indept., adept., consecut.* (“unattained, attained, obtained”). This marginal notation passed into the text of the Venetian edition as follows: “of undiminished divinity, having attained, acquired, obtained the Father’s substance,” etc.]

The Lord recalls that these two denarii were given by the Samaritan to the innkeeper for the man who had suffered attack from robbers (Luke 10:35). This parable, removing doubt, disclosed the mystery of the ladder to those who contemplate it spiritually. The man who suffered attack is known to be Adam; the robbers, the devil; Eve, concupiscence; the Samaritan, the Lord, of whom the Jews said: “This man is a Samaritan and has a demon” (John 8:48). The innkeeper is the teacher of the law. Having received the two denarii, that is, the saving instructions of the two Testaments, he treats with the daily medicines of preaching, in the inn—that is, in the Church, into which God’s sheep enter—the man who had suffered attack through the robbery of the devil, his angels, and this world, and who had been received by the venerable mystery.

[Note: *Aggressuram* again in Treatise 16, Book I. See Note 19.]

[Note: Reims, Toledo, Zeno, and Pomp. manuscripts together with the Venetian edition read *sacramentorum* (“of mysteries”), but wrongly. For throughout the preceding symbols, the number two is said to signify the two Testaments; moreover, saving instructions are most plainly contained in the two Testaments, Old and New.]

IV. As for his statement that angels were ascending and descending, some think that those ascending are angels of light and those descending angels of darkness. But I observe, dearest brothers, that this is quite absurd and unsuitable: for neither do the fallen angels descend, since after their sin they are known never to have been received into heaven; nor do those of light ascend, since they have never remained on earth but always in heaven. Therefore I think that “angels” are rightly called human beings, to whom the Lord says through the Holy Spirit: “I said, You are gods, and all sons of the Most High; but you shall die like men” (Ps. 81:6–7). We also remember that it was said of John the Baptist: “Behold, I send my angel before your face, who will prepare your way” (Mal. 3; Luke 7:27; Mark 1:2; Matt. 11:10). Thus it is clear that, in the manner of prophecy, righteous and unrighteous people are generally called angels. But examples show us who are ascending and descending. Those descending are persons who, having renounced the world, return again to the world. Of them the Lord says: “No one who looks back and puts his hand to the plow is fit for the kingdom of God” (Luke 9:62). And again: “Remember Lot’s wife” (Luke 17:32). The Apostle likewise says: “How can you return again to the weak and needy elements?” (Gal. 4:9). But those ascending are the righteous, who by upright conduct are borne heavenward each day in the glory of their spiritual journey, through the steps of obedience to divine commands; the Apostle Paul exhorts and directs them, saying: “If you have risen with Christ, seek the things above, where Christ sits at the right hand of God” (Col. 3:1).

[Note: The Pomp., Zeno, and Sp. manuscripts have *adscendunt* (“ascend”); and below, in place of *adscendunt*, the same manuscripts read *descendunt* (“descend”), in an entirely contrary sense.]

[Note: The printed editions read *supponens* (“putting under”); the manuscripts suggested the emendation *superponens* (“putting upon”).]

We may also, brothers, understand this statement as referring to ministers and angels, whom we find performed service for the Lord while he was on earth, when he himself said: “Amen, amen, I say to you, you shall see heaven opened, and the angels of God ascending and descending upon the Son of Man” (John 1:52). And so it occurred, as the Evangelist says: “Then the devil left him, and behold, angels came and ministered to him” (Matt. 4:11). Hence there is no doubt that angels of light and righteous human beings have one path to the summit of the air.

[Note: Pomp., Zeno, and Sp. manuscripts have only one *amen*.]

V. Therefore all these things, joined together, are brought into the unity of one result, because all things, though known to be double, nevertheless spring from one root. The Testaments are two, but the testator is one. The reed used for writing is divided, but the pen is one. The shears are drawn out into two blades, but their bite is one. The sword bears two edges, but they are sides of one body. The denarii are two, but they are stamped with one coinage.

[Note: *Combinata*, that is, “joined together,” as the Greco-Latin glosses explain. This word may be found in Diomedes, and *combinans* in Sidonius Apollinaris, book IX, letter VIII.]

[Note: Reeds for writing were made chiefly from Egyptian reeds or canes, as Pliny teaches, book XVI, chapter 37: “Reeds serve for paper, especially the Egyptian ones, by a certain kinship with papyrus.” Persius speaks more plainly of canes, *Satires* III.11:

> Into the hands come sheets and the knotted reed;  
> then one asks what thick moisture hangs from the pen.

]

[Note: *Moneta* was properly among the Romans a surname of Juno, bestowed from *monendo* (“warning”), as mythologists explain. From this it was transferred to coinage, either because coins were struck in Juno’s temple on the Capitol, as some suppose, or rather because coins remind us both of their maker and of their value. Basilius Faber inferred from this passage of Zeno that the marks stamped upon coins are *moneta*, so that “two denarii stamped with one coinage” means nothing other than two denarii struck with the same signs and marks. This can be confirmed from Prudentius, who similarly used *numisma* for the figure impressed on coins:

> Behold, Caesar recognizes his own—
The coinage stamped upon the coins. Yet since St. Zeno here has in view the single stater mentioned in Matthew, as is clear from note 10, he more probably meant one coin equivalent to two denarii—that is, two didrachmas—at which value a single stater was assessed, as will be evident from the same note. Lampridius, in *Alexander Severus*, p. 127, mentions “double, triple, quadruple forms,” etc., indicating coins which, according to Salmasius’s interpretation, p. 218, were worth two, three, or four gold pieces. Therefore this currency of which Zeno speaks was in some manner of a double denomination, namely one valued at two denarii or didrachmas, as you will learn from the note cited.

Stamped with one coinage. And a ladder has two sidepieces [Note: [Col. 0433D] Vitruvius too, book IX, chapter 2, called the ladder’s sidepieces *scapi*; these are the two beams supporting its rungs. Casaubon inferred this from the present Zenonian testimony in his commentary on Trebellius Pollio, p. 210. There he errs only in citing, through a lapse of memory, Sermon 3 on Abraham rather than the sermon on Jacob’s Dream. *Scaphos* is written in the Pomp. and Zen. manuscripts, and below *scaphorum* is likewise read in those codices, and also in Rem. and the Venetian edition, but wrongly; for, according to Vitruvius, *scaphus* is the hollow of a vessel or of another object, which does not fit the present sense.], and many rungs; but its ascent is one. Its rungs, moreover, beloved brethren, if you wish to know what they are called, listen: conversion, hearing, understanding, belief, fear, wisdom, sobriety, gentleness, self-control, chastity, piety, charity, faith, truth, humility, grace, honourableness, modesty, patience, perseverance, consummation. The names of the sidepieces are the two Testaments [Col. 0433B]. The ladder itself is properly called the cross, because through it the Lord Jesus Christ [Note: [Col. 0434B] The Venetian edition reads *ministeria*, “ministries,” and below writes *conducens* for *concludens*, wrongly. All the mysteries are understood to have been accomplished and brought to completion on the cross insofar as there everything that had been prefigured and foretold concerning Christ was fulfilled.], accomplishing and bringing together all the mysteries, restored them to the Father and to Adam, and opened the way to heaven for all who follow him.

## TREATISE XIV

[Note: [Col. 0434B] TREATISE XIV.—This treatise is cited four times by Ratherius, bishop of Verona, and is reliably attributed to St. Zeno as his predecessor, as note 32 will show. The Venetian edition prefixes this title: “On Judah, the patriarch son of Jacob, and Tamar.” In the inscription of the Urbinas manuscript are read: “Third Sunday in Lent, readings 1, 2, and 3; Treatise on Judah, ch. XIII” [Col. 0434C]—that is, Treatise 13 of Book I in the order of the treatises in that codex. The letter C means “chapter”; for the two books of treatises are there divided into as many chapters as they contain treatises. Three readings were taken from this treatise and recited in the liturgical offices on the third Sunday of Lent, at least in the Church of Verona.] On Judah.

[Col. 0434A]

### I

Judah had three sons: Er, [Note: [Col. 0434C] We restore from the manuscript readings and the Venetian edition “Aunan, Selon,” in place of what was written, “Onan, Shelah.” Zeno’s spelling derives from the Septuagint interpreters, who rendered the second son of Judah, called *Onam* in Hebrew, as Αὐνάν, *Aunan*. Cotelerius rightly observed that the same word should be restored in Philo’s work *That God Is Immutable*, shortly after the beginning, where Ἂνναν has been corruptly printed; see no. 17 on the Epistle of Barnabas the Apostle.] Aunan, and Selon (Gen. 38). To his elder son he gave in marriage a woman whose name was Tamar. Since that son behaved wickedly before the Lord’s face, Scripture testifies that he was slain by God. Judah commands the second to go in to [Note: [Col. 0434C] Rem. manuscript: “his father’s,” wrongly.] his brother’s wife and raise up offspring for his brother; but he went in and spilled his seed upon the ground. Since this too seemed wicked to God, he condemned him to the same death. He excused the union of the third son with his daughter-in-law on account of his age, [Note: [Col. 0434C] Thus from the Vatican and Urbinas manuscripts, supported by the reading *deterritur* in the Toledo codex, with *s* changed to *r*. The printed editions, with several manuscripts, read *deterretur*.] being afraid that he too might die likewise; and he ordered the woman to remain a widow in her father’s house and await a marriageable age.

When matters stood thus [Col. 0434B], his wife died. After he had been consoled, he went to shear his sheep; and when [Note: [Col. 0434D] This is absent from the Rem. manuscript.] this was reported to Tamar, who saw that [Note: [Col. 0434D] Thus the manuscripts and Venetian edition, for “Shelah.”] Selon was mature and nevertheless had not married her, she put off her widow’s garment [Note: [Col. 0434D] Here *exponit* means “puts off” or “lays aside,” as Genesis 38:14 speaks of garments of widowhood being put off. Plautus and Terence use *apponere* in the same sense: the former, *Poenulus* 4.2.35, “lay down the burden,” and the latter, *Heautontimorumenos* 1.1.36, “lay down the rakes,” that is, “put them down.” Later writers more often said *exponere*: Cyprian, *On the Lapsed*, no. 28, “lay down a burden”; the bishops in Hilary’s interpretation of the pseudo-synod of Sardica, “lay down bishops”; Arnobius, “lay down vigour”; and others similarly in other cases.], put on summer garments [Note: [Col. 0434D] The Vulgate translator used *theristrum*, a term from the Greek σθέρος, meaning a woman’s summer garment, as Jerome teaches on Isaiah chapter 3, and Isidore after him, book XIX, chapter 25. See Pollux, book VII, chapter 3, and Tertullian, *On the Pallium*, chapter 5. St. Zeno rendered this foreign term in Latin.], adorned herself becomingly, and stationed herself in the place [Col. 0435A] through which Judah was to pass. But he, seeing the woman, thinks her a prostitute [Note: [Col. 0435C] The Vulgate translator calls her a prostitute.], though by veiling her face she displayed the integrity of her modesty. He addresses her, asks to go in to her, and promises that he will send her a kid. But she demands [Note: [Col. 0435C] Toledo, Pomp., and Vatican manuscripts: *promisso*, “of the promise.”] a pledge of the promise, being more content with it than with the reward. And she received from him his necklace, ring, and staff. [Note: [Col. 0435C] The printed editions and some manuscripts read *cumque*; we have corrected it from the Pomp. manuscript.] Then, when the transaction was completed, marked by conception—which true prostitutes find hateful and always avoid—she again took up her widow’s garment.

Meanwhile, according to the agreement, a kid is sent; the prostitute is sought, and the inhabitants report that none had ever been there. But in the course of time Tamar’s womb too advances. See, indeed, the wonderful mystery. She who had concealed her face does not conceal her belly. The pregnant widow is denounced as guilty of prostitution [Col. 0435B], without any effort by an accuser. Her father-in-law is angered, orders her brought out and burned. But she appears steadfastly, she who had undertaken in herself an affair not of unchastity but [Note: [Col. 0435C] Toledo manuscript: “she, fearing nothing, steadfastly”—wrongly, unless one reads, “she, fearing nothing,” etc.] an affair for future generations, and says that she owes her conception to the man whose necklace, ring, and staff she holds. [Note: [Col. 0435C] Pomp. and Zen. manuscripts: *futuris licet indicia*; Vatican and Rem.: *futuris licet initia*; Toledo: *futuris licet uncia*; the printed text: *futuri scilicet indicii*; and the margin of the Verona edition notes *judicii* in place of *indicii*. In Urbinas, *in se jam* is written for the same expression. This passage is remarkably corrupt. While its sense is clear—that Tamar, in this matter, had furthered the cause of the future offspring from which Christ was to arise, contrary to the custom of prostitutes, who hate conception and always avoid it, as Zeno himself observed shortly before—the genuine reading is not sufficiently certain. We retain *futuris*, “for those to come,” found in most manuscripts, and *in se jam* from Urbinas. Together these quite suitably signify that Tamar offered this excuse for her charge: she had not furthered an affair of unchastity for herself, as prostitutes do, but had furthered in herself an affair for those to come, or posterity. For this Judah confessed her more righteous than himself (Gen. 38:26). We think that the words *scilicet initia* entered the text from a marginal gloss—by which, as often happens in codices, someone explained what kind of matter Tamar had advanced: namely, the beginnings of posterity, which were lacking. The Rem. manuscript has *procuraret* for *procuraverat*.] Once this was known, Judah not only restrained himself from her; he moreover declared her righteous.

### II

Judah, so far as can be understood, was in part a type of the prophets, and in part of the patriarchs and fathers, who, because of God’s righteousness, counted all human beings as sons [Note: [Col. 0436C] Pomp. manuscript: “sons of God.”]. Thus the firstborn son Er represents the first-born people: that is, the [Note: [Col. 0436C] This word is written in Latin, not Greek, in the manuscripts; the Rem. manuscript and Venetian edition instead have *henithei*. The word occurs in Servius on *Aeneid* VIII.314: “According to Hesiod’s *Theogony*, it should be known that first gods were born, then demigods, then heroes.” Then Martianus Capella, 2.40: “Demigods and heroes.” Arnobius, *Against the Nations*, book II, p. 97, attests that these demigods, or semi-gods—which is the same thing—were human beings with enormous and huge bodies; they are those called giants in Scripture, especially in Genesis 6:4, from which St. Zeno has brought this description [Col. 0436D] here. Mythologists explain at greater length that many Gentile gods originated from these.] demigods (*hemithei*): all-powerful persons and kings who, fighting one another with the savagery of strength and the frenzy of lust, had corrupted the whole world; who in addition decreed temples for themselves as homes, erected altars to their own name, and did not know that they would have tombs; who promised heaven to themselves, though the earth itself, if it could, would blush for their deeds; and finally asserted that they were gods in opposition to God. [Note: [Col. 0436D] Rem. manuscript: *quia sane*, for which one should better read *qui a sanae*, etc. Toledo manuscript: *sane mentis*.] Persons of sound mind judged them unworthy even of the name of human beings. For these reasons they were not only destroyed by God, but also consigned to everlasting penal punishment.

### III

Aunan, the second brother, is the Jewish people, who are commanded to raise up seed for their brother—not, of course, that seed which rightly seemed condemned by God, but to awaken the remaining nations, which the poisons of the dispersed idolatry of which we have spoken had corrupted, [Note: [Col. 0436D] Rem. manuscript: “may bring together.”] to the worship of God by examples of good life and devout exhortations from the sacred law. [Note: [Col. 0436D] The same codex reads “religion,” wrongly.] But he spilled his seed on the ground. Seed signifies not the seed of bodily generation [Col. 0436B], but that of the heart. For the seed of the heart is the word of God, as the Lord says in Luke [Note: [Col. 0436D] See note 18 on Treatise VI of Book II; Rem. manuscript: *cata Lucanum*, “according to Luke.”] (and this is the parable): “The seed is the word of God. . . . Those beside the way are those who hear the word; and the devil comes and takes the word from their heart, lest, by believing, they should be saved” (Luke 8:11–12). But earth signifies both a human being and an idol, [Note: [Col. 0436D] The same manuscript: “and an idol.”] because God fashioned the human being from earth, and a human being fashioned an idol from earth. He therefore spilled his seed upon the earth: that is, he neglected God’s commandments and lavished them upon idols. For this reason he likewise received from God the present sentence of condemnation, [Note: [Col. 0436D] The word *praesentem*, “present,” is absent in the same manuscript.] because, just as one who, being human, makes himself out to be God is detestable, so one who worships a god whom he himself has devised is still more detestable.

### IV

Selon, [Note: [Col. 0436D] The printed editions had “Shelah.” See note 2.] the younger third brother of those mentioned before, portrayed the image of the new people coming [Col. 0436C] from the Gentiles [Note: [Col. 0436D] Rem. manuscript: “coming.” Toledo, Pomp., Zen., Vatican, Urbinas, Sp., and Venetian edition: *veniens*, “coming.” We preferred the reading of the Verona and Padua editions, since the participle *veniens* refers not to Selon, who was of the same generation as his brothers [Col. 0437C], but to the new people who were passing largely from the Gentiles to the Christian faith.]. Tamar represented the Church. She was rightly not married to him [Col. 0437A], because, when Christ came, reborn in the bosom through the spiritual water of baptism, he would become the Church’s son, not her husband.

Judah loses his wife (Gen. 28:12): that is, faith in the synagogue dies. [Note: [Col. 0437C] Urbinas manuscript: “the son dies.”] And when it says that he “was consoled,” this is understood to mean that he was consoled by the hope [Note: [Col. 0437C] Rem. manuscript: “hope.”] of the coming Christ, who not only gave consolation to the prophets desolated by the synagogue’s fall, but is also accustomed to refresh us all when placed in any distress. He goes to shear his sheep: that is, he demands the fruits of good works from righteous people. When Tamar heard this, while she was in her father’s house—that is, in temples and the disreputable places of every kind of spectacle [Note: [Col. 0437C] This is the testimony cited four times by Ratherius. In his *History of the Eucharist*, published in French at Amsterdam in 1671, p. 393, Matthaeus Larrogue cites from Ratherius this same testimony much more extensively than it occurs in Zeno; he therefore intimates that something is missing here in the printed editions. Yet all the manuscripts contain nothing beyond what is found in the editions, in agreement with the Remensis manuscript itself, which is older than Ratherius. That heterodox writer moreover erred in citing Zeno’s testimony, taking as Zeno’s words what Ratherius himself authored. Ratherius cites only this one statement as Zeno’s: “The devil is the father of all who live corruptly.” This is evident from comparing and reconciling the four passages of Ratherius; they all emphasize only this one point from Zeno [Col. 0437D], which is indeed contained in the present treatise. First, part I of *On Contempt for the Canons*, p. 352, vol. I of the most recent edition of Acherius’s *Spicilegium*: “Here I shall avail myself of the authority of blessed Zeno, in the sermon which, in his usual most eloquent manner, he delivered on Judah the patriarch and Tamar his daughter-in-law, saying: ‘The devil is the father of all who live corruptly.’” Again, a little later on the same page: “He who is shown to be the devil’s son by living corruptly, as holy Zeno affirms.” Again, at the end of Sermon I on Lent, p. 391: “But, on the contrary, blessed Zeno says that the devil is the father of all who live corruptly.” Finally, in the Synodal Letter to the Priests, p. 377, col. 2: “And since our particular teacher and guardian, namely blessed Zeno, says in the sermon which he most elegantly composed on Judah, son of Jacob, and Tamar his daughter-in-law, that the devil [Col. 0438C] is the father of all who live corruptly.” From all these passages it is clear that Ratherius praises as Zeno’s only this repeatedly quoted statement. But the words Ratherius himself added after Zeno’s words in the first passage—“And for this reason he does not eat the venerable flesh of the Lord nor drink his blood,” etc.—Matthaeus Larrogue, failing altogether to notice the distinction, quoted in one continuous text as though they were Zeno’s. This will be obvious to a reader who examines everything more carefully. It is also clear that Jo. Henricus Ottius was misled by the same error when, in his examination against Baronius’s *Annals*, century 3, under the year 260, §7, p. 204, he cites from Ratherius as Zenonian precisely the words belonging to Ratherius’s addition. Yet it is sufficiently shown from the same author’s letter to Patricius, vol. I of the *Spicilegium*, p. 376, that those heterodox writers vainly claim Ratherius’s support, even in those words, for excluding Christ’s presence from the sacrament of the Eucharist; there he confirms Christ’s presence by the most certain testimony. But these matters must be discussed more fully in the edition of Ratherius.]—for the devil is designated as the father of all who live corruptly, as the Lord rebuked the Jews: “You are of your father the devil, and you wish to do the desires of your father” [John IX, 19]—she put off the garment of widowhood: that is, she cast away the foul rites of a foul religion. She put on summer garments.

The summer garment, brethren, is both clean and fitted, so that in it one may readily perform work and endure the heat of summer—that is, temptation—which unquestionably is *credulitas*, simple faith [Note: [Col. 0438D] *Credulitas*, that is, simple faith, which seeks no rational arguments, as Zeno very often understands it; see note 6 on Treatise I of Book I.]; for whoever possesses this must necessarily live with freedom and purity. Therefore, lest she be recognized, she necessarily darkens her face with a veil, because Christ, the defender of her modesty, had not yet come. She is not recognized by her father-in-law, for the prophets had been sent to the Jews, not to the Gentiles. He rightly thinks her a prostitute [Note: [Col. 0438D] Rem. manuscript: “through a prostitute.”], because she served the people of gods [Note: [Col. 0438D] The same codex: “the Jewish people.”]. He desires to lie with her because the Gentiles were going to believe prophecies more readily than the Jews, as the Lord says: [Note: [Col. 0438D] Pomp. and Zen. manuscripts: “Amen, amen, I say to you.” The same codices and the Venetian edition have *praecedunt*, “go before,” in place of *praecedent*. From the manuscripts we have written “into the kingdom” rather than the printed “in the kingdom.”] “Amen, I say to you [Col. 0438A], tax collectors and prostitutes will go before you into the kingdom of God” (Matt. 21:31).

He promises her a kid: that is, he shows what the sinner’s reward for sin is. She avoided receiving it, because the person who received the pledge of the Trinity is to be counted among the sheep in the time to come, not among the goats. [Note: [Col. 0438D] Toledo manuscript: “received.”] Finally, she is described as having demanded and received the necklace, ring, and staff. To what does this symbolism apply? The necklace, beloved brethren, is the law, which by saving admonitions, diverse virtues, and the diverse charism of all believers is accustomed to adorn not necks but hearts. The staff, by means of wood, proclaimed the sacrament of the Lord’s passion, as the clear example found in the book of Psalms declares: “Your rod and your staff, they comforted me. You prepared a table before me against those who trouble me [Col. 0438B]. You anointed my head with oil, and your cup which intoxicates me—how excellent!” (Ps. 22:4–5 [23:4–5]).

Surely, brethren, the cup signifies the blood, the table the body, the oil the gift of the Holy Spirit, and the rod with the staff the cross, upon which God deigned to hang for the sake of humanity, in order to transform into God the human being whom he had assumed. The ring also is the seal of faith, which is Christ. Impressed and sealed by the radiance of his majesty, by living sincerely we bear, through the Holy Spirit, the image which we hold, for the protection of our salvation. [Note: [Col. 0438D] In the Verona edition: “When he lies with her, it signifies the sacrament of holy communion.” We have restored the whole passage from the manuscripts and the Venetian edition. Only the Venetian edition has *significat*, “signifies,” in place of *significabat*, “signified.”] His lying with her signified the sacrament of the holy communion of believers. Tamar conceived in her womb; the Church conceived in her heart: Tamar by seed, the Church by the word. A kid is sent to her, certainly as a sign of temptation; for the one who follows righteousness must necessarily be tested [Col. 0439A]. [Note: [Col. 0439C] Toledo manuscript: “may be tested.”] Finally, when the prostitute was sought, she was not found, because one reborn through water and the Holy Spirit ceases to be what one was and begins to be what one was not.

It follows that she again took up the garment of widowhood, certainly not in order to do what she had done, but in order to mourn that she had done what she had done. Otherwise, even one who is righteous cannot be saved unless, making *exomologesis*—confession and repentance—and extinguishing present sins, that person also repels future ones. [Note: [Col. 0439C] In the text of the Remensis manuscript, through an omission and with error: “which the righteous man commanded, unless he extinguish,” etc. Below, however, it was corrected in an old but second hand, as in the remaining manuscripts and editions. *Exomologesin* is written in Latin letters in all codices, not in Greek as the Verona edition and later editions print. The term means confession and repentance for sins. That it signifies repentance is clear from Irenaeus, who frequently uses it; see book I, chapter 9, and book III, chapter 4. Eusebius quotes the latter testimony in Greek in book IV, chapter 11; Rufinus rendered it in Latin by writing *poenitens*, “repenting,” where the ancient translation of Irenaeus has *exomologesin faciens*. Tertullian uses the word in the same sense in *On Repentance*, chapter 9: “Exomologesis,” he says, “is the discipline of prostrating and humbling oneself.” There he also takes the name for confession, which is indeed a part of repentance, writing: “That act of repentance which is more commonly expressed and used by the Greek term is *exomologesis*, by which we confess our sin to the Lord—not as if he were ignorant, but because satisfaction is arranged through confession; repentance arises from confession,” etc. St. Cyprian often uses the same word, now to mean repentance and now confession made to God before his priests. Thus in *On the Lapsed*, no. 28, p. 382 (col. 488 of our edition): “Confessing sorrowfully and simply before the priests of God, they make *exomologesis* of their crimes; they lay down the burden of their soul,” etc. He again writes “they make *exomologesis* of their crimes” in the same sense in Epistle 55 to Cornelius; in the Laetiensis codex, Baluzio observes in note 60, an old hand wrote above *exomologesin*: “that is, confession.” In the same work, *On the Lapsed*, no. 31, p. 384 (col. 490 of our edition), he introduces Daniel “making *exomologesis* and saying,” and immediately recites the confession of sins described in Daniel chapter 9 [Col. 0440C]. Pacian of Barcelona, Epistle 1 against the Novatians, and Salvian in the preface to *On the Governance of God*, use the term in both or either sense. St. Zeno uses it again in Treatise 10 of Book I, no. 3. In both places he most certainly means repentance, and also confession of sins insofar as that was chiefly included among the works of repentance or *exomologesis*.]

Tamar is accused of having conceived by prostitution. [Note: [Col. 0440C] Toledo manuscript: “conceived.” A little below, Pomp. manuscript has “elders” in place of “senior men.”] And the Church, as though an adulteress against the law, is accused by the Jewish elders because she broke the Sabbath and rejected their traditions. Tamar brought forth the necklace, ring, and staff, and freed herself by the sacrament of the number [Note: [Col. 0440C] Urbinas manuscript: “by the sacred number.” It is customary for Zeno to call symbols of the Holy Trinity or of another sacred reality *sacramenta*, “sacraments” or “mysteries.” Likewise, in Treatise 71 he calls the number of the three youths the sacrament of the Trinity, and says that they were fortified by the sacrament of that number. Treatise 76. See note 12 on Treatise 10 of Book II.] from the impending punishment. The Church, by truth itself, in the name of the Father and the Son and the Holy Spirit [Col. 0439B], not only extinguishes the devil’s present fires but will also overcome the conflagrations of judgment on the future day. Tamar departed justified; the Church, glorified by the increase of the true number, [Note: [Col. 0440C] Three manuscripts: “your.”] and by faith, will remain with Christ through eternal ages, through our Lord and Saviour Jesus Christ, who is blessed with the Father and the Holy Spirit before the ages, and in the ages, and unto all ages of ages. Amen.

## TREATISE XV

[Note: [Col. 0440C] TREATISE XV.—In the Urbinas manuscript the following heading is read: “Treatise on Job. Reading of blessed Zeno, bishop of this see.” [Col. 0440D] This treatise, however, is considered uncertain by Lippomanus, vol. II, *Lives of the Saints*, part II.] On Job.

### I

Beloved brethren, the narrative of sacred history has been handed down for us to read for this purpose: that we may imitate, if possible, at least to some extent the conduct of our forebears, if we cannot imitate their virtues. For they lived with such uprightness [Col. 0440A] that it is a part of blessedness to know what they did. [Note: [Col. 0440D] Pomp. manuscript: “our,” wrongly.] Thus Job was a righteous and truthful man, separated from every desire of this world, pure in conduct and purer in mind; so circumspect and blameless that he was commended by God’s own testimony (Job 1:8). Therefore, not undeservedly, being blessed, he enjoyed a blessed life. He had a most splendid house, abundant wealth, and also a great number of children—of both sexes, which is welcome to parents—and they loved one another (ibid. 1:3). For their number he offered daily sacrifices to God (ibid. 1:4–5). He was so fortified by a wall of purity and faith that the devil did not dare attack him unless he received authority from God (ibid. 1:12). Consider now, brethren, how fiercely he raged when provoked—he who is intolerable even when he flatters.

Thus a battle renowned in report is joined. [Note: [Col. 0440D] *Famigerabile* is likewise found in Apuleius, *Metamorphoses* I, p. 67, and II, p. 271. It has the same meaning as *famigeratus* in Apuleius, *Florida* II, and in Mela 2.7: that is, illustrious and known by reputation.
