Hence Plautus uses *famigeratio* for renown in *Trinummus* 3.2.6.] On one side the devil thunders dreadfully with all his weapons, summons his servants as auxiliaries, sounds a terrifying trumpet, inflames the hearts of robbers with a Furies’ torch [Note: [Col. 0440D] Pomp. and Zen. manuscripts and the Venetian edition: “and of robbers.”], and with repeated assaults everywhere attacks the entire wealth of the man of God. In one moment he destroys everything by sudden robbery, fire, and sword (vv. 15 ff.). On the other side Job, made strong by the deep root of faith, is struck by so many mournful messengers but is not moved; he only blesses God, and by despising his possessions preserves them.

But when the devil sees that he has achieved nothing by attacks so great, he pours the whole frenzy of his impiety upon Job’s children. For while, according to their customary practice, they were feasting harmoniously together in one house, suddenly its four corners were shaken with all force, and, as walls and roofs collapsed into a confused heap [Col. 0441A], he buries that most holy company of brothers before he slaughters them. [Note: [Col. 0440D] The preposition *in* with the accusative is sometimes joined by ancient writers to a construction that, by common rules, would require the ablative. Plautus, *Bacchides* 1.3.53: “Has it come into your mind?” where one ordinarily says “in your mind.” Cicero similarly wrote in *On the Manilian Law*, chapter 12, *in praedonum potestatem fuisse*, “to have been in the power of pirates,” rather than *in potestate*. Aulus Gellius excellently defends this reading, book I, chapter 7, where he also cites another passage of Plautus, *Amphitruo* 1.1.25: *Numero in mihi mentem fuit*. “*In mentem*,” says Gellius, “not *in mente*, as is customary”; and for euphony he notes many other expressions of the same kind. Thus St. Zeno wrote quite properly and in good Latin *in molem*, “into a mass,” for *in mole* or *inter molem*, “in/among a heap.” *In* is also read as used for *inter*, though more commonly with the ablative, yet sometimes with the accusative, as perhaps in Livy I.35: *Centum in Patres legit*, “he enrolled a hundred among the senators,” though this may be understood otherwise, namely as expressing purpose: that they should be among the senators. A little below, we have inserted the substantive “ruin” into the words “and devised such a ruin,” from the Toledo and Vatican manuscripts; the latter writes “piety” for “impiety.”]

He devised so ruinous a work of impiety that, in that crowd of one funeral, a father’s grief was inadequate for his bereavement: he does not know whom to lament first, whom to find before another, for whom first to perform the due rites of cruel burial. [Note: [Col. 0441C] *Justa* denotes the rites rendered to the dead, so called because they are rightly bestowed upon those who have deserved well of us. Livy calls them *justa funebria*, funeral rites, I.2; Cicero, near the end of book II of *On the Laws*, *justa funerum*. Hence the Latin expressions *justa facere* and *justa solvere*, “perform funeral rites.” Cicero, *For Flaccus*: “The funeral rites of Catiline were performed”; and in *For Rabirius*, in wording very similar to Zeno’s: “He had not yet performed the due rites for his father’s funeral.” See Pliny, book II, final chapter; Curtius IV.12.2; and book II, *On Not Summoning to Court*. The Venetian edition with the Toledo and Urbinas manuscripts reads *justitiam habebat*, “he had justice,” as does the Pomp. codex, though it is corrected there to *justa*.]

Upon receiving this news, God’s servant tore his garments, not to create resentment against God [Note: [Col. 0441D] Zeno used the phrase “to devise resentment” in Book I, Treatise 16. See note 34 there.], but so that, unencumbered, he might fight against the enemy. Finally, in his lost possessions he despised the rich man; in his lost children he disregarded the father; and in the suffering of his own body, the righteous man. For, struck by the enemy’s plague from the summit of his head to the lowest nails of his feet, he was not marked out by many separate ulcers, but became wholly one wound. [Note: [Col. 0441D] The printed editions read *distinctum*, but the manuscripts have *distinctus*, used in the same way as Cicero, *Verrines* IV.27, “cups distinguished by gold and gems,” meaning varied by gems distributed and set apart. The meaning is not that Job was afflicted with numerous but separate sores, leaving some healthy part, but that his whole body had become one wound. For this reason we would more readily have inserted “was made” shortly below from the marginal note in the Verona edition in place of what elsewhere is read, “was made for him”; but the Urbinas manuscript’s reading *effectus*, “made,” seemed preferable. “Numerous ulcers” means many and frequent ulcers, as Fulgentius, *Mythologies* I, uses “a multitude of lights” for a multitude of lights. St. Bishop Zeno uses “abundant fruit” in the same sense in Book I, Treatise 16, no. 10.]

Yet in all these things he speaks no wicked word against God [Col. 0441B]. He does not yield to his wife when she urges what is unlawful; he does not give way to friends who insult him. Rather, victorious over cruelty and impiety, he sits on a foul dungheap teeming with worms, as though he had suffered nothing, content only with the fear of God. O happy man! By wondrous patience he won God’s favour, conquered the devil, recovered health, and did not lose his possessions and children [Note: [Col. 0442C] “His” is absent from the Zen. manuscript.], but exchanged them.

II. Job, so far as can be understood, most beloved brethren, bore the image of Christ.

[Note: [Col. 0442C] Finally, here he openly indicates this in brief, as we observed in note 4 on tractate 7 of this book. The manuscripts of Toledo, Pompeii, and the Vatican write *indicat* (“indicates”) for *inducat* (“introduces”). A little later the same codices have *Adest vera* (“the true one is present”) for *At est vera* (“but the true one is”).]

For the comparison introduces the truth. Job was called just by God. Christ himself is Justice, from whose fountain all who are blessed drink; for behold, it was said of him: “For you the sun of justice shall rise” (Mal. IV, 2). Job was called truthful. But the Lord is true Truth, who says in the Gospel: “I am the way and the truth” [Col. 0442A]. Job was rich. And who is richer than the Lord? All rich men are his servants; the whole world and all nature are his, as most blessed David says: “The earth is the Lord’s and its fullness, the world and all who dwell in it” (Ps. XXII, 1).

The devil tempted Job three times. Likewise, as the Evangelist reports (Matt. IV; Luke IV), he attempted to tempt the Lord three times. Job lost the possessions which he had. And the Lord, for love of us, disregarded his heavenly goods and made himself poor, in order to make us rich. The raging devil killed Job’s sons. And the mad Pharisaic people killed the Lord’s sons, the prophets. Job was stained with sores. And the Lord, by assuming flesh, was defiled with the filth of the sins of the whole human race.

[Note: [Col. 0442C] *Obsoletare*, an obsolete word, means “to defile,” “to pollute.” Thus Tertullian, *Against the Gnostics*, ch. 6: “Those who had soiled the wedding garment.” Hence Zeno’s *obsoletatus* means “defiled with filth.”]

Job’s own wife urges him to sin. And [Col. 0442B] the synagogue presses the Lord to follow the corruption of the elders. Job’s friends are reported to have mocked him. And the Lord’s own priests, his own worshippers, mocked him. Job sits on a dung-heap full of worms. The Lord also moved about in a true dung-heap—that is, in the mire of this world—among men bubbling over with diverse crimes and lusts, who are true worms. Job recovered both health and property. But the Lord, rising again, bestowed not health alone but immortality on those who believe in him, and recovered dominion over all nature, as he himself testified when he said: “All things have been handed over to me by my Father” (Matt. XI, 27; Luke X, 2).

Job begot replacement sons.

[Note: [Col. 0442C–D] Those are called substitutes (*vicarii*) who perform another’s part; and not only those who undertake a business at the command of someone whose duty it was to carry it out, and whose person they represent—this is the sense now commonly prevailing—but also those who voluntarily undertake something on another’s behalf. Thus Cicero, *Against Verres* IV, §37, says that Scipio promised, though present, to act as a substitute for the duty; and Seneca writes to Helvia of a woman “who gave herself as a substitute for her husband.” Or they are those who succeed in another’s place after his death, even if they perform the role of the deceased only in a broad sense. By this reasoning, those who are installed in the same see after Saint Peter the Apostle are often called Peter’s substitutes, although they possess no less authority than he once did; and in Otto’s diploma in Ughelli, vol. V, p. 746, Hilderic, bishop of Verona, is called the Substitute of Saint Zeno. Therefore it is clear from what has been said why the sons whom Job received from God after the death of the former sons, to take their place, are called substitutes.]

The Lord also, after the prophets, begot holy sons, the Apostles [Col. 0443A].

[Note: [Col. 0442D–0443C] This seems to refer to Ps. XLIV, 17: “In place of your fathers, sons have been born to you; you shall appoint them rulers over all the earth,” which the holy Fathers frequently interpret of the Apostles. Among commentators on Scripture, there is a much-debated question whether, in that verse of the Psalm, the pronouns “your” and “to you” refer to the king or to the queen. Certainly, since in Hebrew they are masculine, it appears that the speech is directed to the king, the bridegroom; nevertheless, as some learned critics demonstrate at length, they can also be extended to the queen, the bride, as most Fathers do. It is clear that Saint Zeno, more in accordance with the Hebrew, referred these words to the mystical bridegroom, Christ the Lord. Irenaeus, Cyril, Didymus, and other Fathers press this interpretation; and it is indeed the more fitting sense: that Christ was prophetically told, “In place of your fathers according to the flesh”—that is, Abraham, Isaac, Jacob, and the others from whom you sprang—“sons have been born to you,” or, from the Hebrew, “sons shall be born to you,” namely the Apostles, “whom you shall appoint rulers over all the earth.”]

Job, blessed, rested in peace. But the Lord remains blessed for ever: before the ages, from the ages, and unto all ages of ages.

[Note: [Col. 0443C] The manuscripts of Pompeii and the Venetian edition add “Amen” at the end.]

203. TRACTATE XVI. On Susanna.

[Note: [Col. 0443C–D] TRACTATE XVI.—You will find this tractate in Lippomano, vol. II, *Lives of the Saints*, p. 21. This same tractate, but interpolated and frequently variant, was formerly inserted among the Augustinian sermons as Sermon CCXLII *On the Season*; afterwards it was relegated to the Appendix, first as Sermon LXIX and later as Sermon LX in the edition of the Benedictine Fathers of the Congregation of Saint Maur. They judged it to be the work of an unknown and unlearned author—an author who indeed took material from Zeno, but added much of his own and altered it, as the same Benedictines repeatedly observed in the Additions prefixed to Augustine’s sermons in vol. V. Of a similar kind is Sermon LXI of the same Augustinian Appendix, which is Sermon LIII of Saint Peter Chrysologus, but, as the same Fathers observe, is frequently interpolated, or enlarged with many additional passages, as happened to the Zeno text. Nevertheless, several variant readings will be supplied from that same Appendix where the same periods are reproduced in almost the same words.]

Whenever, in this perverse age, manifold snares are laid against praiseworthy men,

[Note: [Col. 0443D] In the Appendix to Augustine: “or diverse occasions of calumny may arise.”]

and factious accusations arise in various kinds of calumny, what a pestilent man may devise, or what the devil may contrive, the righteous man does not fear, because God is with him.

[Note: [Col. 0443D–0444B] In the same Appendix: “the righteous man will not fear, because Christ is with him.” After this, more than sixteen lines are inserted, discussing Zechariah and Daniel. Then follows what concerns Susanna; yet from this point onward scarcely one line can be found without additions or omissions, and these by no means slight, as anyone comparing the texts will see.]

Thus Susanna, an illustrious Hebrew woman, taught women by the example of her chastity, the true glory of purity. Susanna stood in judgment, crushed by the lies of ruinous false witnesses, yet content with the good secrets of her conscience [Col. 0443B]: not so much an accused woman about to receive sentence, as a woman consecrated to God, courageously about to die for chastity’s sake. And she whom the perverse judgment of those judging had cast down was raised up by the illustrious integrity of her conscience.

[Note: [Col. 0444B] The manuscripts of Reims and the Vatican read *quamquam dicata* (“although consecrated”); the Vatican also has *quamquam indicata* (“although accused”).]

Therefore the conscience of chastity is sufficient; God is its witness. Chastity did not look to what the false witnesses might say, or how deceived judges might condemn her, nor indeed to how the devil might defame her—he who could not overthrow the foundations of modesty. The body proceeding to execution was not adulterous, a body in which the final lust of old men had flamed up; rather, it was a body which [Col. 0444A] the devil had defamed, virtue had protected, and uninjured modesty adorned.

[Note: [Col. 0444B] The same manuscript of Reims and the Venetian edition read *infirmaverat* (“had weakened”); the Appendix to Augustine has *inflammaverat* (“had inflamed”).]

Then the Holy Spirit entered into the holy boy Daniel and said, while she was being led to punishment: “Return to judgment, for these men have borne false witness against her” (Dan. XIII, 49).

[Note: [Col. 0444B–C] In note 5 on the preceding tractate we showed, by many examples from the ancients, that the preposition *in* was joined with an accusative in the sense in which grammatical rules would require an ablative. From this testimony it is clear that it could sometimes be joined with an ablative where an accusative would be required. Similar are Arnobius, II, p. 43: “Who introduced the true religion into the world”; and I: “Things which have proceeded from him in us.” Nor are ancient examples lacking. Phaedrus, V.1.15: “He dares to come in my sight.” Manilius, V.384: “When you come into the region of your form, Capricorn.” These testimonies vindicate another passage of Zeno, tractate 9, book I, §5: “he shall descend in hell.”]

The people are astonished that one condemned should be called back from punishment for a renewed trial. Terror seizes the false witnesses. The devil trembles because his own inventions are uncovered. The angels rejoice because oppressed truth is at last defended on earth. The husband triumphs because he has found his wife chaste. The whole household rejoices because reputation finds in her nothing to strike. The devil is tormented because he has accomplished none of his will [Col. 0444B]: for he neither committed the adultery which he was spreading abroad as having been done, nor found the murder which he was procuring.

[Note: [Col. 0444C] The manuscripts of Toledo, the Vatican, and Urbino have *et* (“and”) in place of *nec* (“nor”), with an entirely contrary sense; but it would then have to be referred to the murder of the elders, who were punished with death in Susanna’s place: namely, that they found the death which they had procured for Susanna.]

[Note: [Col. 0444C] The Venetian edition reads *invenerit* (“he found”); the Appendix to Augustine has *impleverit* (“he fulfilled”).]

205. TRACTATE XVII. On Jonah the Prophet.

[Note: [Col. 0444D] TRACTATE XVII.—This tractate too is found in Lippomano, vol. II, *Lives of the Saints*, p. 24. At its beginning Saint Zeno borrowed a few things from Hilary’s commentary on Psalm CXXIX; but these are expressed in a different order and in almost entirely different words, with some additions and changes, as comparison shows. We have relegated to the Appendix the mentioned commentary of Hilary, which had formerly been inserted among Zeno’s sermons.]

I. It is the devout confession of human reverence to know this about God: what is lawful to know.

[Note: [Col. 0444D–0445B] Here those are rebuked who try to investigate, beyond what God willed us to know, matters which exceed the power of human understanding; and the matters especially indicated here are those pertaining to natural philosophy. Most ancient Fathers, like Saint Zeno, reproved its study as wholly vain and fruitless, and attempted to call men’s minds away from it. They almost extol Socrates for this reason: when, as Lactantius says, *Institutions* III.20, “the minds of very learned men wandered astray in blind disputation and tried to explain the measurements of the sun, moon, and other stars with arguments more talkative than certain, and even dared to encompass the whole extent of the world”—which were branches of natural philosophy—Socrates first drew the mind away from these unlearned pursuits, and so forth. Cicero had long before counted this same point to Socrates’ credit in *Tusculan Disputations* V and *Academic Questions* I. See Minucius Felix, *Dialogue*, §13 (vol. III of this edition); Lactantius, *Institutions* III, chs. 3–5; Cyril of Alexandria, V *Against Julian*; Hilary on Ps. CXXIX, §1; and, omitting others, Jerome, *Apology against Rufinus* II, somewhat after the middle. There Jerome praises another saying of Socrates, recommended by Minucius and Lactantius: when censuring as foolish those who investigate heavenly and unknown matters—as Xenophon reports, *Memorabilia* I, p. 710, and IV, p. 815, and Gellius IV.4—he used to declare: “What is above us is nothing to us.” The same Fathers refer this saying to the study of heavenly bodies, that is, to natural philosophy.]

For just as his testimonies are to be examined with a simple [Col. 0445A] heart, so his secrets are not to be investigated with curiosity. For who knows the causes and natures of this heaven and of the higher heavens?

[Note: [Col. 0445B–C] Here “causes” means the principles of things, of which natural things consist. Knowledge of them was considered so difficult that Virgil wrote in the same sense, *Georgics* II.496: “Happy is he who has been able to know the causes of things.” Hence, in the controversy over what and how many principles or causes of things there were, most philosophers set forth many mutually contradictory theories, too numerous even to enumerate. See the extensive accounts in Clement of Alexandria, *Paedagogue* I; Lactantius, *Institutions* II and III; Arnobius II; and Seneca, Letter LXVI. But since Zeno distinguishes “natures” from “causes,” or principles, of which the heavens consist, he seems by “nature” to mean the force attributed to the heavens by some. Hilary expresses a similar thought in Ps. LXVIII, §29, calling the earth overshadowed by the natures above, that is, of the heavens.]

[Note: [Col. 0445C] Many ancient examples show that “heaven” means not so much the heavenly bodies—the stars and planets, which Saint Zeno calls the higher heavens—as this earthly globe encircled by air, and is used as a name for this heaven. The ancients often used *caelum* for the air we breathe and the region we inhabit. See Basil Faber’s *Thesaurus Eruditionis*, p. 380. Zeno drew this wording from Hilary, who similarly wrote on Ps. CXXIX: “Who knows the causes and natures of this heaven and of the higher one and of the rest?”]

Who can falsely claim that he can explain the material emptiness of this air, as some suppose [Col. 0446A]?

[Note: [Col. 0445C–D] Hilary attributes this to popular opinion in his commentary on the same Ps. CXXIX, §1: “Who will measure this fullness of air, empty to us as we suppose—that is, as is commonly believed?” Saint Zeno’s “material emptiness of the air,” or Saint Hilary’s “fullness of empty air,” means the whole magnitude of the world, which the ancients believed filled in this lower earthly region with air and in the higher regions with ether. They long ridiculed the effort of those who claimed to be able to measure it, even among pagans themselves, as Pliny, II.1 and 23, and Quintilian, *Institutes* II.17, attest. Further, although air and ether seem to be empty and void bodies, they are nevertheless truly bodies and occupy and fill these spaces; rightly, therefore, Zeno calls them a “material emptiness.”]

Who will presume that he knows whether the earth is carried by the water or whether the water is contained in the bosom of the earth?

[Note: [Col. 0445D–0446C] The earth is carried by the water if the earth is in the water like an island set in waters, as the Stoics, according to Laertius, ch. 201, taught. On the other hand, water is contained in the bosom of the earth if it is enclosed and surrounded by the boundaries of the earth. This kind of difficulty, which may now appear resolved after discovery of the New World, was especially powerful among the ancients, to whom America was unknown. It was then uncertain how far the Ocean extended, and therefore whether water occupied the greater part all around, with the earth established in it like an island. Thus Saint Clement, Pope, in First Corinthians, §20, called the Ocean impassable to men; and Hilary, on Ps. LXVIII, §29, says: “The sea … by the barrier of its deep and boundless expanse exceeds the capacity of human thought, so that by following perception we cannot grasp either what lies beyond it or what lies within it.” Ambrose in the *Hexaemeron* asks: “Who then knows how far that great sea, untried by navigators and unattempted by sailors, extends?” Jerome agrees in ch. 4 of the letter to the Ephesians, V.7: “The sea is immense, and its extent known to God alone.” Therefore Irenaeus, II.4, judged it impossible to determine whether anything lay beyond the Ocean sea.

Hence the opinion of antipodes was almost rejected by the ancients, since they supposed that beyond—or beneath—the land known to them there was nothing but water. Or, if they believed it possible that solid land might be found elsewhere, they conceived it to be separated from us by such a breadth of ocean that Augustine, *City of God* XVI.9, declared it most absurd to say that people could have sailed and arrived from this side to that through the immensity of the Ocean. Those ancients who hinted that antipodes existed called them inhabitants, because of the same vast intervening sea, of another world or globe. Thus Pope Clement, in the cited letter, §20, after the words “the Ocean impassable to men,” adds, “and the worlds beyond it”; Origen, *On First Principles* II.3, observes that this means the Antichthones, or, as they are commonly called, the Antipodes. Pliny, VI.22, Mela, I.9, and Hipparchus, cited by Mela, III.7, call the other terrestrial world inhabited by the Antichthones. From these it is clear that the “other world” mentioned by Pope Zachary in his letter, and said to bear other human beings beneath the earth, was truly this other globe of the Antipodes, whatever some have recently thought. To return therefore to the matter at hand: since the ancients were so uncertain concerning the bounds of the sea, they were equally in great doubt whether, as Zeno says, the earth is borne by water or water ought rather to be said to be contained in the bosom of the earth.]

Who knows the airy spirits, who the shapes of the winds, who, amid sea-swells, the increases of rivers [Col. 0447A], and finally who will boast that he has discovered the workmanship of the Lord and God’s plan?

[Note: [Col. 0446C–D] We do not believe that “airy spirits” here means demons, of whom some Fathers taught that many dwell in the air; Petavius collects their testimonies in *On Angels* III.4. More attractive is Sparaverius’s opinion: that a light breeze is called “spirit,” and that, by setting against it “wind,” that is, a stronger blast, Zeno indicates an important unresolved physical question—the question, of which this passage is indeed speaking, why the air at one time breathes gently and at another is carried with great force. Moreover, what Saint Zeno here and there calls “forms of winds,” Hilary, from whom we have observed that he borrowed several things, calls “blasts of winds”; and Arnobius, II, includes among difficult questions the source and nature of wind.]

[Note: [Col. 0446D–0447C] Does this refer to what Pliny says of the rise and fall of certain streams or springs, *Natural History* II.97? “At Gades, the spring nearest the temple of Hercules, enclosed like a well, sometimes increases and decreases together with the Ocean, but at other times the two do so at opposite seasons. Another spring in the same place corresponds to the seasons of the Ocean.” Varenius, *Geography* I.17, proposition 17, also mentions springs of this kind which, even today, increase and diminish in the same manner. Nor should the fact that our writer uses the word “river” trouble anyone: for in Latin *flumen* could be said also of spring water which flows continuously, as many ancient examples listed in Latin dictionaries prove.]

[Note: [Col. 0447C] Among ecclesiastical writers, “the Lord’s workmanship” signifies the creation of the world. Thus Lactantius entitled his book addressed to Demetrianus concerning the creation of the world *On the Workmanship of God*, as Jerome likewise calls it in *On Illustrious Men*.]

For the Apostle says: “O the depth of the riches of the wisdom and knowledge of God! How unutterable are his judgments, and how unsearchable his ways! For who has known the mind of the Lord?” (Rom. II, 33–34).

[Note: [Col. 0447C–D] When Saint Zeno cites this same testimony in tractate 1, book I, §5, he writes *inexquisita* (“unsearchable”) in place of *inenarrabilia* (“unutterable”). The reason for this variant seems to arise from the Hilary exemplar which, as we have recalled, Zeno used. For he probably had before his eyes Hilary’s exposition of Ps. CXXIX, in the same exemplar as the Hilary tractate once printed among Zeno’s works, which we have now restored to Hilary and transferred to the Appendix. There likewise *inenarrabilia* is read, although in Hilary’s manuscripts another reading occurs in this and in several other words of the same testimony, as we shall note in the Appendix. Similarly, tractate 1 has “For who has known the thought of God?” in place of what is read here, no less than in the Hilary tractate: “For who has known the mind of God?”]

For the Prophet does not say, while boiling over in inquiry into these matters: “Out of the depths I cried to you, O Lord” (Ps. CXXIX, 1). Rather, he cries from the depths—that is, from the inmost heart. He cries from the depths, hemmed in as he was, sorrowful and sad, by human calamities; and he cries not with his voice but with his heart, not with an outcry but with faith, which he knows God gladly hears.

Thus Peter likewise, crying from the deep, obtained from the Lord that he might both walk across and escape the slippery hollows of the deep sea and the yielding surface of the liquid waters, beneath human footsteps, where the trembling traveler was being swallowed up [Col. 0447B] (Matt. XIV, 30–31). Paul also cries from the depths, overwhelmed by blessed afflictions: when, for the Lord’s name, he suffers robbers on journeys and robbers in cities; when he is beaten three times with rods by the Jews and drenched in three shipwrecks; when, in the furious tempest of a mad people, he is happily hailed with showers of stones; when, after remaining in the depths of the sea by day [Col. 0448A] and by night, he cries to God and is cast out unharmed from there (II Cor. II).

[Note: [Col. 0447D–0448C] In Latin dictionaries *grandinat* is used impersonally on the authority of Seneca, *Natural Questions* IV.4. But from this testimony of Zeno we learn that *grandinor* was also conjugated passively: had Basil Faber noticed this—he inserted many other things into his celebrated *Thesaurus Eruditionis* on Zeno’s sole authority—we do not doubt that he would have included this word as well. The ancient glosses have *grandinatus*, which they translate passively as χαλασθείς, “having been pelted with hail.”]

II. Jonah the prophet likewise was sent by God to the Ninevites, to announce that destruction threatened their city (Jonah I), for they were weighed down by immense burdens of sins. But he turned aside by another route and boarded a ship bound for Tarsus. Suddenly the sea roars, violently assailed by the blast of contending [Col. 0447C] winds; and, with the gray rolling masses of its troubled gulf, like steep mountains, crushing the foam-covered mouths of resisting shores, it threatens shipwreck at every moment.

[Note: [Col. 0448C] Notice the unusual syntax, which must be construed backward as follows: “And, crushing the foam-covered mouths of shores resisting the gray rolling masses of the steep mountains of the troubled gulf, it threatens shipwreck,” and so forth.]

The multiplying storms rage; the ropes hiss terribly; the yards groan as the sails give way; and the battered prow finds no passage anywhere [Col. 0448A]. The sailors tremble and hasten in vain to lighten the ship of its burdens by throwing cargo overboard, though it was weighed down by the weight of the prophet. Then Jonah, whom that favorable calm alone sought,

[Note: [Col. 0448C] The manuscripts of Toledo and Pompeii, and two Zeno manuscripts, have *exspectabat* (“awaited”), which is also given in the marginal note of the Verona edition.]

is chosen by lot as a castaway—rather, he is transferred from a wooden vessel to a life-giving ship. When he is cast into the deep and received into the lodging of a beastly abyss, he keeps watch in the whale, though he had slept in the ship.

[Note: [Col. 0448C–D] Not only poets but also prose authors used *altum*, “the deep,” for the sea: thus Cicero, *On Ends* IV, §23, “to emerge from the deep,” and *On Invention* II, §32, “a storm on the deep.”]

A marvelous thing! After shipwreck, after a swimming tomb, safe on the third day he enlightens the Ninevites, about to bring salvation to the believing city by dreadful oracles.

[Note: [Col. 0448D] Just as *credulitas* is used by Zeno and other Fathers in the good sense of faith—not faith as the fault of credulity, but faith as a virtue—as we showed in note 6 on tractate 7, book I, so *credulus* is here used in a good sense.]

III. So far as may be understood, brethren, the ship is a type of the synagogue. By its pilot we understand the priestly body [Col. 0448B];

[Note: [Col. 0448D] In Plautus, *Rudens* IV.3.75, the *proreta* is distinguished from the ship’s helmsman: he is the man who sits at the prow to guide it: “If you are the prow-pilot of that ship, I shall be the helmsman.” See Turnebus, *Adversaria* XXVIII.32.]

by the sailors, the scribes and Pharisees; by the casting out of cargo, the rejection of the prophets and all the saints, whom the synagogue had cast out and the Jews slaughtered in unworthy killings, to the ruin of their own salvation. The diverse raging winds are the kings—

[Note: [Col. 0448D] The “kings” here are the emperors Vespasian and Titus, as well as Hadrian and Antoninus Pius, whom we understand to have been hostile to the Jews.]

—who, with the mournful blare of trumpets and the terrible crash of arms, while storms of war pressed from every side, miserably dispersed Judaea throughout the whole world.

Jonah sleeping in the ship bore the image of the Lord’s mystery. For the ship’s wood signified the cross, and sleep the Passion. The sea, moreover, is this swelling world. Its waves are the Jewish peoples and the Gentiles, who raged vainly against God. The lot gave Jonah over to be cast down; prophecy foretold that the Lord would suffer: both willingly—Jonah by compulsion, the Lord by mercy [Col. 0448C]. There is no doubt that the whale is hell. For as Jonah was three days and three nights in the whale’s belly and, vomited out, came to the city of Nineveh,

[Note: [Col. 0448D] Thus, from the manuscript of Pompeii, with a Greek genitive: *Ninives*. The other codices have *Ninive*. It may also be written *Ninivi*, as it was corrected in a later hand in the same manuscript of Pompeii.]

so the Lord, rising from hell on the following day, came to the city of Jerusalem [Col. 0449A] before ascending to heaven.

But Nineveh bears the image of the Church, in which our people from the Gentiles were already then dwelling. It was not without reason called by God a great city, for it was to come about that, with the peoples of all nations believing in Christ, the whole world should be rendered to God as one city. Finally, saving deeds confirm the comparison, and these remain in us as well.

When destruction was announced to the Ninevites, brethren, they believe and fear; and

[Note: [Col. 0449B] The Venetian edition reads *quantum*, “by as much as.”]

the more they know that the Lord is not deceitful, the more earnestly they trust in his mercy. Immediately condemning the practices of their former life, they do not, in order to redeem salvation, run in their accustomed way to stupid idols; they do not kindle baleful fires upon stinking altars, burn incense, or pour out unmixed wine. Nor do they consult the fibers of a still-breathing liver, snatched from cattle by unforeseen [Col. 0449B] death.

[Note: [Col. 0449B–C] The manuscript of Pompeii reads *inspectata*, “examined”; but the common reading, found in the other manuscripts, is truer, since the discourse concerns animals and victims slaughtered alive without warning. Haruspices inspected their entrails or fibers while still breathing—that is, still agitated by vital motion—and predicted the future from them. The custom of haruspices consulting breathing fibers and entrails is also gathered from Virgil’s familiar line, *Aeneid* IV.64: “She consults the breathing entrails”; and from Seneca’s *Oedipus*: “Father, what is this? The entrails do not tremble, stirred by a light motion as is their wont; rather they shake whole hands, and fresh blood springs forth.” In the discipline of the haruspices this was the standard formula for offering sacrificial entrails: *Exta porriciunto*, “Let the entrails be presented,” as Veranius attests in Macrobius, *Saturnalia* III.2. Indeed, we have found the verb *porricere* joined only with *exta* in Plautus, *Pseudolus* I.3.32, and Virgil, *Aeneid* V.775. Properly, the entrails were called *porrecta* when they were sacrificed to the gods immediately after the victim, still breathing, had been slaughtered. From this came the elegant proverb *inter caesa et porrecta*, “between the slaughtered and the presented,” in Cicero, *Letters to Atticus* V.18, meaning that there is no, or scarcely any, interval of time—as there was none between the slaughtered victims and the presentation of their entrails to the gods. Hence Arnobius, I, p. 91, says that the Gentiles offered half-raw and faintly animate entrails. That the still-breathing liver in particular was inspected among all animal entrails in Zeno’s age may also be inferred from Ammianus Marcellinus, XXII, at the beginning.]

Nor do they seek, through the various flights of birds and empty conjectures, the condition of their feather-light salvation;

[Note: [Col. 0449C–D] Casaubon, p. 164, on the passage of Lampridius where Severus is said to have been a great ὀρνεοσκόπος, “bird-observer,” derives the Greek word’s explanation from this passage of Zeno: “Zeno of Verona elegantly expresses ὀρνεοσκόπος by this circumlocution: ‘who through various …’” Our author calls salvation “feather-light” on account of its lightness, and refers to the practice of haruspices, who inferred the future from the wings of birds flying past in an uncertain course, whether light or—as Ammianus Marcellinus notes, XXI, shortly after the beginning—otherwise.]

but seek the saving remedy from their own heart, and offer their spirit, contrite in all humility, as an eager sacrifice. Thus, by lawfully practicing repentance, they made God propitious to themselves. This is what we too have done,

[Note: [Col. 0449D] The manuscript of Pompeii and two Zeno manuscripts read: “and have done.”]

and ought often to do, in order that we may deserve to escape both the temptations of the present time and the punishments of the future judgment through Christ our Lord.

[Note: [Col. 0449D] We added *poenas*, “punishments,” on the authority of a Zeno manuscript. The two Zeno manuscripts, as well as those of Toledo, Pompeii, the Vatican, and Urbino, then have: “Through Jesus Christ our Lord.”]

211. TRACTATE XVIII. On the Feast of Saint Arcadius, whose feast falls on the day before the Ides of January, in the city of Caesarea in Mauretania.

[Note: [Col. 0449D–0451B] TRACTATE XVIII.—This title is read in the manuscripts of Reims and Pompeii, while the printed editions and the Zeno manuscript have only: “On Saint Arcadius the Martyr.” The Urbino manuscript has the same title as the two cited codices, except that through a scribal leap it wrongly gives *Idus* for *pridie Idus*, “the day before the Ides,” and omits mention of Mauretania. The Vatican manuscript reads: “Tractate XXXIX of Saint Arcadius, born in the city of Caesarea”; and the Toledo manuscript somewhat differently: “On the birth-feast of Saint Arcadius the martyr, born in the city of Caesarea.”

Peter Calo, a thirteenth-century writer of the Order of Preachers, included this tractate, which has been regarded as a source concerning Saint Arcadius, in the manuscript *Collections* cited by Henschenius, vol. II, April 12, pp. 74 and 76. Lippomano also published it, vol. I, *Lives of the Saints*, p. 262; likewise Surius and Bollandus, vol. I, January 12. Peter de Natalibus, together with Guglielmo Pastrengo, refers to Zeno’s writings in the unpublished history of the emperors by John of Verona, calls this tractate an epistle, and makes Arcadius a martyr contemporary with Zeno. But this is erroneous, since it follows from the long-established opinion that Zeno lived in the time of Gallienus, an opinion which we have extensively refuted in Dissertation I.

Bollandus published the Acts of this martyr in the cited place, and Ruinart reproduced them in the *Sincere Acts*, p. 466. Comparing the Acts with the present tractate, Bollandus found the two so consistent and similar that either the Acts seem to have been composed from the sermon or the sermon sketched from the Acts, as he says in the preface to those Acts, p. 722, §4. We prefer that the Acts were composed from Zeno’s tractate. For Zeno testifies that he is committing this martyr’s deeds to annals, as though they had not previously been written; he surely would not have said this had he himself drawn upon previously written Acts. Besides, the style of the Acts is often more polished, and it is unlikely that Zeno would have made an obscure text out of a more polished one. Indeed, in excerpts from other authors whom he imitated, he is consistently found to have used equal or even greater clarity.

Add that the Acts say Arcadius suffered in Achaia, which cannot be read in the genuine Acts, not only because it conflicts with the authority of Zeno’s manuscripts, but also because all who mention the place of his martyrdom, agreeing with Zeno’s manuscripts, give Mauretania, not Achaia: Usuard, Caesarea in Mauretania; Galesinius, Mauretania. Moreover, Bede in the common text, Ado, Notker, and other Latin authors mention this martyr, but no Greek author does; this would not have happened if he had suffered martyrdom in Achaia. Indeed, Bollandus proves in the cited preface, §2, and confirms in the Appendix, p. 1109, that Saint Arcadius was venerated in Spain, to which crossing from Mauretania is easy. Ruinart offers a sufficiently probable conjecture by which it becomes credible that the name Achaia was inserted into the Acts by a foreign hand.

In correcting this tractate, besides the seven Zeno manuscripts, we shall use Bollandus’s edition, which he testifies that he collated with an old manuscript of Saint Mary of Ripatoria and with other manuscripts. Gaspar Barthius illustrates this tractate in places in *Adversaria* XLVI.7; if we take anything from him, the author will be cited in the notes themselves. Finally, in the same notes we shall sometimes use, to explain the text, the aid of authors edited by Bollandus and Ruinart, since we are persuaded that these were copied from Zeno’s tractate in almost the same words.]

[Col. 0450B] I. While we commit to the annals the triumphs worthy of celebration of the blessed martyr Arcadius, Christian zeal is always stirred toward the contest for immortal praise. [Note: [Col. 0451B] The word “annals” is absent from the Vatican and Toledo manuscripts, both of which lack very many readings found in other manuscripts and required by the sense. Bollandus, however, reads: “We commit for recording in the annals of faith the deeds, sublime in the honour of a heavenly triumph.” We fear that this reading, differing so extensively from the other reliable Zenonian manuscripts, arose from the freer hand of a copyist who occasionally endeavoured to convey Zeno’s sense rather than his words; this will also be confirmed by what follows, when we present variant readings from Zeno’s treatise as found in Bollandus. We think that Bollandus used manuscripts not of Zeno but of the kind commonly called lectionaries—such indeed as those which Ruinart saw in the Colbert Library and that of the Feuillants of Paris, [Col. 0451C] where he observed this same treatise inserted without any author’s name. How freely copyists sometimes acted in these is well known. Therefore, unless necessity compels us, we shall not depart from Zeno’s manuscripts. From the manuscripts of St. Basil’s, the Vatican, Pomp., and Zen. we have corrected *in agonem* (“to the contest”), since others write *in agone* (“in the contest”). The same manuscripts have *immortalitatis* (“of immortality”) instead of *immortalis* (“immortal”).]

There will be a twofold exchange arising from religious devotion when the people are kindled toward the heavenly reward and the martyr’s merits are not passed over in silence. [Note: [Col. 0451C] In Bollandus it is made twofold.] But who can fittingly describe, in speech worthy of it, the palm-bearing, trophy-won crown of an illustrious martyrdom, [Note: [Col. 0451C] Likewise, “by so many trophies.”] when there appear in one body as many martyrdoms as there are members? [Note: [Col. 0451C] The Venetian edition and Bollandus suggest *cum* (“when”) for *dum* (“while”). In the Basilica Vaticana manuscript, *dum . . . videntur* appears. Bollandus adds: “when in the spiritual arena victory shines forth manifoldly by the abundance of its own number; when in one,” etc. Perhaps in the Zenonian manuscripts that clause was omitted through a copyist’s leap, as we have found to have happened elsewhere. Yet the unanimous agreement of all the manuscripts prevented us from inserting those words into the text, since the sentence otherwise stands very well.] The ancient deserter, champion of inveterate hatred, had armed his attendants against the Lord’s people, [Note: [Col. 0451C] “The ancient deserter of inveterate hatred,” Bollandus.] and was harassing the whole household of the Lord with the ravaging violence of savage cruelty. [Note: [Col. 0451C] Bollandus likewise reads *Christi impastae*. But the Urbinas manuscript has *Domini in partem* (“of the Lord into a part”).] He had declared war against God in man, [Note: [Col. 0451D] The Pomp., Zen., and Venetian-edition manuscripts read “against the man of God.” The Basilica Vaticana manuscript reads “in the man of God.”] and throughout the whole world had rebuilt the funeral pyre, complicit in wickedness, at the burial-place (*bustum*) of an ill-omened superstition. [Note: [Col. 0451D] What *bustum* means we explained more fully in Treatise 5, Book I, note 31.] [Note: [Col. 0451D] Thus in Bollandus; the reading of the Basilica Vaticana and Pomp. manuscripts, *refunere cerat rogum*—in the margin of the Pomp. manuscript, *resumere cera trugum*—does not differ greatly. The Venetian edition with the Zen. manuscript reads *refundere cerat rogum*. In other manuscripts and editions the reading was: “throughout the whole world he had rebuilt the pyre.”]

Public wickedness overflowed through the roofs of the highest houses, and there was no place in which sacrilege was not committed in the name of religion. [Col. 0451B] Christ’s people were compelled to take part in vain superstitions, and, in worship of the accursed rite, either to pour out impious libations, [Note: [Col. 0451D] Just as *castus* (“chaste”) is taken for “whole” and “holy,” as Basilius Faber demonstrates at length in the *Thesaurus Eruditionis*, s.v. *Castus*, no. 2, so *incestus* may be used for “impious” and “wicked,” and *inceste* for “impiously” and “wickedly.” Livy, I.45, said: “You are preparing to sacrifice to Diana *inceste*,” that is, improperly and contrary to the laws, as is inferred from what follows. Barthius, in the cited passage, confirms this explanation by the authority of Virgil and Statius. Bollandus writes *incesta*. Then, in the Basilica Vaticana manuscript, *ornatus* stands for *ornatas*.] or to lead victims adorned with garlands, [Col. 0452A] or to kindle heavy incense with its vapours, or, amid smoky fires and pale fat, [Note: [Col. 0452B] The Reims, Toledo, Vatican, Urbinas, and Basilica Vaticana manuscripts read *pallentia ruinis funesto*; the Venetian edition, *pallenti ruinis*; the Pomp. manuscript, *pallentia ruina*, corrected by a later hand to *pallenti arvina*, a reading retained in other editions. If one prefers to read *pallentia*, it must be referred to the incense, or to “heavy with vapours,” or to “pale amid smoky fires.” But then what is to be understood by *ruina* or *ruinis*? Moreover, the sequence requires the present phrase to depend upon *prolitare* (“to offer sacrifice”), and to signify that sacrifice was made to the gods with the ominous blood of victims amid fires made smoky by pale *arvina*—that is, hard fatty tissue between skin and flesh, which others explain as bacon, as Servius notes on verse 627 of *Aeneid* VII. [Col. 0452C] *Prolito* is the same as *perlito*, found in authors and having the sense of sacrificing, as does *lito*; it is found construed with the ablative, as in Apuleius, *Metamorphoses* VIII: “I shall offer sacrifice with blood.” In the Acts of the holy martyr this period is given thus, retaining the word *arvina*: “Christ’s people were compelled to take part in vain superstitions, and either to pour out impious libations in worship of the accursed rite, or to lead victims adorned with garlands and wreaths, or to kindle fragrant incense, and amid smoky fires and the vapours of fat to chant in the manner of bacchants, so that God might be driven out from Christian minds by these celebrated performances of sacrifices.”] to offer sacrifice with ominous blood, so that, through the celebrated administration of this rite, [Note: [Col. 0452C] The Venetian edition reads “administration of the mystery,” wrongly.] God might be expelled from Christian minds. [Note: [Col. 0452C] In Bollandus: “God might [be expelled] from Christian minds.” The Pomp. and Zen. manuscripts read *possit* (“may be able”), while other sources read *Christi panis mentibus possit* (“the bread of Christ may [be expelled] from minds”). We have corrected from both readings, since “bread” used for the Eucharist did not seem suitable here. [Col. 0452D]]

II. But while the war of a harsh struggle was being waged and the household of the Lord was tested under heaven’s gaze, [Note: [Col. 0452D] The Bollandus manuscript reads “is challenged.”] the most blessed martyr Arcadius, struck by horror at this unexpected sacrilege, [Note: [Col. 0452D] In the same source, “of the messenger”; and “shocked” for “struck.”] delayed the contest for a little while, now due for his crown. [Note: [Col. 0452D] The Pomp. manuscripts and Bollandus record another reading, namely “given over.” Barthius here remarks: “When Aeneas in Virgil, Book XII, says, ‘These sacred rites now owe Turnus to me,’ he bears in his breast the favourable omen of a glorious victory in anticipation, as though certain that Turnus could not resist him, if only he might gain an encounter with him. Zeno says the same: ‘Now due for the crown.’ Horace: ‘We and our possessions are owed to death.’” A little later the Pomp. manuscript has *quoque* for *quosque*; Toledo, Vatican, Urbinas, and Basilica Vaticana better read *quaque*.]

For when he learned that the city was being disturbed by the deadly assembly and that every individual was being dragged to that fatal spectacle, he despised all his possessions, cut away the roots binding him to the world, and, concealing himself, entrusted himself to the shelter of withdrawal. [Note: [Col. 0452D] A manuscript in Bollandus reads, “showing himself a true Christian in purpose.” The Pomp. manuscript has *recedendo* (“retreating”) for *secedendo* (“withdrawing”).] In this he fulfilled both aspects of Christian duty: he might not seem too far from the battle [Col. 0452B] and, by withdrawing, might be encouraged by the example of the evangelical command (Matt. 10:23).

Behold: into his lodging, as upon hostile plunder, burst headlong the band of marauding [Col. 0453A] attendants. [Note: [Col. 0453B] In Bollandus: “hoping by hasty occupation [to seize] the servant of God,” etc. A little later, the Vatican, Urbinas, Zen., and Basilica Vaticana manuscripts read “the blessed martyr’s kinsman” for “the blessed kinsman of the martyr.” *Beatus* (“blessed”) is likewise found in the Pomp. manuscript and Venetian edition.] They hastened in hope of catching the servant of God; but the blessed kinsman of the martyr, who happened to be staying in his dwelling, repeatedly cried out that he was absent. This man, however, when he confessed, the servants of a criminal purpose seized for an accursed custody; [Note: [Col. 0453C] Three manuscripts read *mancipe*. A *manceps* means a tax farmer and, generally, the purchaser and contractor for any undertaking. But here it seems to mean an executioner or attendant, and may suitably be taken from the verb *mancipo*, deriving from *manu capere*, “to seize by the hand.” Thus Solinus, ch. 20, says of Gangavia: “It is difficult to *mancipari*,” that is, “to be seized by hand.” In a not greatly different sense St Cyprian, Epistle 69, calls the leader of murderers a *manceps*, as the context makes clear; and in exactly this sense Lucifer of Cagliari, *Apology II for St Athanasius*, calls the Emperor the *manceps* of robbers. More aptly for our purpose, Prudentius in his poem on St Vincent the martyr calls the prison keeper a *manceps*: “Then the very *manceps* of the prison and keeper of the chains.” A little later, the Acts read “with strict custodial surveillance” for “with strict surveillance,” and report that the governor ordered Arcadius’s kinsman, captured by the attendants, to be held in custody until he disclosed the place [Col. 0453D] to which Arcadius had fled.] the cruelest governor ordered him, when presented to him, to be held under strict guard.

As a testimony to his future glory, blessed Arcadius had in some manner reserved a pledge of his destined martyrdom: [Note: [Col. 0453D] These matters are explained more plainly in the Acts, which relate that Arcadius, when he learned that his kinsman had been captured and detained because of him, immediately abandoned his hiding-place, since he wished neither to conceal Christ’s confession longer nor to leave his kinsman afflicted on his account.] in it he would abandon neither Christ nor his kinsman. At once the blessed martyr did not allow himself to remain hidden; [Note: [Col. 0453D] Thus Bollandus: “the most blessed martyr.” Moreover, the Reims, Basilica Vaticana, Pomp., Zen., and Toledo manuscripts, together with the Venetian edition, read “the martyr to hide himself” for “the martyr hid himself.” Five manuscripts read *judiciis* (“judgments”), and the Venetian edition *judicii moram* (“delay of judgment”), for *judici moram* (“delay to the judge”).] voluntarily presenting himself to the judge, he excused his delay by the grounds of a voluntary self-offering. [Note: [Col. 0453D] Bollandus: “by the grounds of voluntary self-offering.”]

When the governor of the province promised pardon for his former flight on the condition that, even late, he would join himself to accursed superstitions, [Col. 0453B] [Note: [Col. 0453D] Bollandus likewise reads “would join himself.”] the most holy martyr burst out against him in these words:

“What, most empty-headed of all judges? Do you suppose that the household of God can be terrified either by the incongruous interest of this light, or by the sudden losses of a too-hasty death, when we know that it is written in apostolic faith: ‘For to me, to live is Christ, and to die is gain’? Devise torments more grievous than any you can; kindle yourself with the greater goads of madness. [Note: [Col. 0454B] We have written *accende* (“kindle yourself”) more suitably from Bollandus and the Acts than *accendam* (“I shall kindle”), which manuscripts and editions have, since martyrs ought not to stir tyrants’ wrath, whereas tyrants rather incite themselves to anger because of the constancy of martyrs. Then, for “however great a mass of tortures you employ,” the Urbinas, Vatican, and Pomp. manuscripts read “by whatever mass you employ tortures”; the Basilica Vaticana manuscript, “however great a mass you employ with tortures.”] However great the mass of tortures you employ, [Note: [Col. 0454C] Bollandus and the Acts read: “you will not be able to separate us from God.” The Vatican and Basilica Vaticana manuscripts, as well as the Venetian edition, likewise read *separare* (“separate”).] you cannot thereby overcome us.”

III. At once the judge, stirred by the gall of viperous venom, ordered the executioners to rage against the martyr’s limbs by a punishment [Note: [Col. 0454C] “By a new and unusual punishment,” in the Zenonian treatise as found in Surius. In the Acts, “new and unheard-of.”] not customary, and by no usual law applied to the accused. The claws grew powerless; [Note: [Col. 0454C] The editions read “The claws ceased,” and the same occurs in several more recent manuscripts. But most and older ones—namely Reims, Toledo, Vatican, Urbinas, and Basilica Vaticana—read “The claws became powerless.” We have corrected *Viluerunt* from Bollandus and the Acts.] the blows of the lead-weighted scourges seemed useless; the despised rack stood idle; frequent showers of clubs were disregarded in view of a greater punishment. A new and astonishing torture was devised, by which he thought he would conquer God in a man.

[Note: [Col. 0454C] Not only in the Acts but also in Zeno’s treatise as found in Bollandus and Surius—the form preserved in ancient lectionaries—some passages apparently excerpted from the Acts are inserted, which are absent from all Zeno manuscripts. They are these: “He orders the most holy martyr to be handed over to men conscious of his rage, to whom he gives no command except that the martyr’s spirit must not pass to heaven by too swift a departure. ‘Let him await his death,’ he says, ‘and, stretched out limb by limb, see himself alive as a corpse through the tearing of his own body. Let them be cut,’ etc.” There the treatise of Zeno and the Acts differ only slightly.]

“Let the hands be cut off at the joints,” he said, “the feet from the legs. Let him behold himself a living corpse.”

To him blessed Arcadius said: “O madman among men! Your madness has cheated you: there still remained in the Lord’s victim something which you might offer. You did not know to order the tongue cut off—the tongue which is ordinarily the first to confess the Lord in the struggle of martyrdom.”

At last blessed Arcadius was led to the place desired in his righteous prayers, and, gazing at heaven, stood secure while God looked on. He had extended his neck for the coming blows; he had bared his throat for the approaching swords; he had thought to satisfy the judge’s deadly madness with the lot of a swift death. But suddenly he was ordered to stretch out his hand and, stripped naked, to be thrown face down upon the turf and bare the extremities of his feet. [Note: [Col. 0454D] Four manuscripts read: “to stretch out [his limbs] and, truly naked, upon the turf,” etc.] [Note: [Col. 0454D] One manuscript in Bollandus reads: “stretch out the foot, give the hand. Behold,” etc.]

See how, amid the very torments, he was not permitted to be idle, but fashioned the counterpart of prayer through the executioner’s tortures. The mad striker raised his axe and, marking out the line of the wound with his eyes, repeatedly brandished the deadly stroke. The martyr’s hands remained fixed by the glue of his fearless confession; nor did his projecting fingers tremble at the destruction of their approaching death. Such was the constancy in the martyr’s devotion that he came ready in every part of his body for glory.

IV. Accordingly, as soon as the executioner saw the body devoted to wounds, [Note: [Col. 0454D] In Surius, “the body devoted, that is, destined, to wounds.” Below, *securis* (“axe”) is absent in most manuscripts; Bollandus reads “by the blow of an axe.”] at once the falling axe-stroke severed the connected sinews and, shattering the frame, broke all the body’s joints. [Col. 0455A] The severed hands sprang away, and, as the stupor of the veins came a little to itself, a rushing stream of blood again poured forth. [Note: [Col. 0455C] Bollandus reads: “and, as the veins came a little to themselves again from the returning fear, the fugitive stupor [passed], and a rushing flood of gore again poured forth streams of blood. Then,” etc. Barthius judges with some probability that the text should be corrected thus: “The veins’ stupor comes a little to itself, and again a rushing stream of blood [flows] into the mouth, or mouths.”]

Then, with knees and calves stretched out, the boundary of his feet was cut away from the natural union by the sword of the savage robber, and the martyr’s body was bereft of the service of its feet. Let those who can number torments number the martyrdoms; and in one body, to the extent that the devil was publicly shown raging, so let the Lord be acknowledged to have triumphed. Yet amid these things the martyr’s spirit endured, and, preserved alive by the multitude of delays, remained living while a portion of his body was already buried. [Note: [Col. 0455C] Bollandus adds: “He is delayed, held back in the light, though the tomb is already filled with his limbs. O worthy,” etc.]

O end worthy of such a glorious departure! About to ascend to heaven’s height, he sends ahead the encumbrances of his body and himself goes before the funeral rites of his own burial. [Note: [Col. 0455C] We have added *sui* (“his own”) from Bollandus. A little later, we restored “To what can this confession be compared?” from the Reims, Basilica Vaticana, and Pomp. manuscripts and the Venetian edition, since *est* is absent from the others.] To what can this confession be compared? It must be joined to the number of the Maccabees; it must be equated with Eleazar in purpose, [Col. 0455B] compared with him in resolve. The most blessed martyr Arcadius still lingers in this world, and already is enrolled as a martyr in heaven. [Note: [Col. 0455C] Bollandus adds this at the end: “That the name of the Lord may be blessed, who reigns for ages of ages. Amen.”]

217

## TREATISE XIX

On that passage of [Note: [Col. 0455C] TREATISE XIX.—This treatise and the following one, with a few additions and certain alterations, are entirely the same. Both are entitled “On Genesis” in the manuscripts and the Verona edition. But since the four treatises on Genesis which discuss the eternal generation of the divine Word have been placed at the beginning of this book among those which argue on the same subject, [Col. 0455D] whereas we have transferred here those which merely interpret a particular passage of Scripture, we have considered the title should be altered somewhat.] Genesis: “Let us make man in our image and likeness.”

Nothing, beloved brethren, is before all things so necessary and fitting for a person who fears God as to know himself. For it is a kind of madness for a person to investigate the reason of nature’s hidden mystery when he cannot account for his own life. [Note: [Col. 0455D] In the Venetian edition the word *eum* (“for a person”) is lacking. Further, these words, “who cannot account for his own life,” are absent from that edition and from the Toledo, Vatican, Zen., and Pomp. manuscripts, though they occur in other codices and also in the following treatise. Here the inquisitive are being censured; concerning them see Treatise 16, no. 2.] For nature’s substance cannot by any means be comprehended by human opinions, [Col. 0456A] since no one knows it except the one who made it.

Therefore, as particularly concerns our purpose, let us consider what God means when he says: “Let us make man in our image and likeness.” And God, it says, “made man in the image and likeness of God” (Gen. 1:26–27); and elsewhere he says: “I am who I am, and I do not change” (Mal. 3:6). This being so, how does man bear God’s image? His countenance is subject to every alteration; it changes at every moment through exertion, age, illness, anger, joy, and sorrow, and assumes as many faces as there are movements of the mind. There is absolutely no day on which it seems continuously like itself.

[Note: [Col. 0455D] These words and those that follow may appear to have been directed against Audius, or Audaeus, who, as we learn from Epiphanius, *Heresy* 70, abused the testimony of Genesis in order to show that God’s image lies not in the soul but in the body; Philastrius likewise mentions this heresy, *Heresy* 97. More probably, however, Zeno should be thought to have attacked those whom St Hilary, contemporary with Zeno, refutes in his commentary on Psalm 129. We have shown in Treatise 17, Book II, that our author saw this commentary and elsewhere borrowed certain things from it. St Athanasius also seems to attack these same people in *Oration against the Gentiles*, no. 34, and Marius Victorinus in Book I *Against Arius*, who presses and defends the same argument and the same interpretation of the Genesis passage as Zeno. Whether all these oppose the view of certain ancient Fathers who locate God’s image in the body—men Petavius clearly enumerates in Book II, chapter 2, of *On the Work of the Six Days*—let others decide. It is enough for us that Zeno agrees with the greater number of Fathers who derive God’s image from the soul; these may be read there in Petavius.]

Since this is otherwise impossible, then do we not have God’s image? We certainly do, and it is manifest precisely because it is not known to us who bear it. [Col. 0456B] For the image of the incomprehensible God must necessarily be invisible. Finally, it is not subject to bodily eyes. Neither when it enters our body nor when it leaves the body can it be perceived by anyone; and it has such power that, though enclosed by the barrier of its dwelling, it nevertheless illuminates whatever it wishes at every moment.

Therefore we must not understand this fleshly dwelling to be the image of God, but rather the spiritual image of the heavenly man, which the Lord, from the gracious fountain of his fullness, grants to those renewed by an ethereal birth and believing in him, through our Lord Jesus Christ. [Note: [Col. 0456C] It is common among the Fathers to say that we bear God’s image only because through the grace of the Holy Spirit, sealed in the sacraments and especially in baptism, we express the image of the Son, who is the true image of God the Father. See further patristic testimonies in the cited Petavius, vol. II, Book VI, chapter 5, no. 10 ff.] [Note: [Col. 0456C] Here he clearly alludes to the baptized, whom elsewhere he calls an “ethereal race,” clothed in an ethereal garment; and he evidently believed that the grace poured in through the Holy Spirit at baptism expresses God’s image. Epiphanius, *Heresy* 70, no. 3, and *Ancoratus* 55, thinks that God’s image must not be located in baptism, indeed in nothing known to us; he maintains that Church tradition establishes only that man was made in God’s image, while no thing or part in man may be specified as the site of that image. Yet other Fathers did not hesitate to explain God’s image; and among them not a few place it in sanctifying grace, infused through the sacraments and especially baptism. Those who, with the apostle Paul at Colossians 3:10, locate this image of God in the inner and new person, renewed in the sacraments and through grace according to the image of God who created him, do not differ much from them. See what the author argues in the same sense near the end of the following treatise. Philastrius, *Heresies* 134 and 147, should also be read. [Col. 0456D]]

219

## TREATISE XX

[Note: [Col. 0457C] TREATISE XX.—In all manuscripts this treatise is the thirtieth and last of Book II, and the last of all those having Zeno as author; for writings by others are immediately added, written in the very ancient Reims manuscript in another script and by another hand, and transferred by us to the Appendix. In that same Reims manuscript, and also in the Toledo, Vatican, and Urbinas manuscripts, this title occurs: “On Genesis, by the author above”; and at the end are written: “Here ends the treatise on Genesis, by the author above,” where the words “by the author above” pertain to the attribution of the treatise’s author to St Zeno, whose name is explicitly recorded in the title or conclusion of other preceding treatises. In the Pomp. manuscript, however, Zeno’s name is expressly given in this treatise, though it is elsewhere omitted: “St Zeno of Verona on Genesis,” so that no one can doubt its author.]

On the same passage of Genesis. With a few additions and certain alterations, this contains what is in the preceding treatise.

[Col. 0457A]

Nothing, beloved brethren, is before all things so necessary and fitting for a person born as to know himself. For it is a kind of madness for a person to investigate the reason of nature’s hidden mystery when he cannot account for his own life; nor can the elements be more beautifully or truly established by human words than they were made, or appear, by God.

Therefore, as concerns us, let us consider what God means when he says: “Let us make man in our image and likeness.” And God, it says, “made man in the image and likeness of God” (Gen. 1:26); and elsewhere he says: “I [Col. 0457B] am who I am, and I do not change” (Mal. 3:6). This being so, how does man bear God’s image? His countenance, subject to every alteration, changes at every moment through exertion, age, illness, joy, and sorrow: now deformed by emaciation, now by enormous fatness; so uncertain that the same one cannot be found in two persons throughout the whole world.

Since these things do not occur in God, then do we not have God’s [Note: [Col. 0457C] The Reims, Toledo, Vatican, and Urbinas manuscripts read “therefore, God’s.”] image? Far from it, brethren. We certainly have it, and it is manifest precisely because it is not known to us who bear it. [Note: [Col. 0457C] Two Toledo and Vatican codices read “known in the body: for incomprehensible,” etc.] For the image of the incomprehensible God must necessarily be invisible. Finally, it is not subject to mortal eyes; for neither when it enters the body nor when it leaves the body can it be seen by anyone. [Col. 0458A] And it has such power that, though enclosed by the barrier of its dwelling, it nevertheless illuminates whatever it wishes at every moment.

Therefore we must not understand this fleshly garment to be the image of God, but rather the spiritual image of the heavenly man, which he grants us from the gracious fountain of his fullness. Paul plainly disclosed this principle when he said: “As we have borne the image of him who is of the dust, let us bear also the image of him who is from heaven.” Those who bear this image in holiness, like all the apostles and all the righteous, will bear not only the image but God himself also, as it is written: “You are God’s temple, and the Spirit of God dwells in you” (1 Cor. 15:49).

## TREATISE XXI

On [Note: [Col. 0457C] TREATISE XXI.—In this treatise St Zeno had before his eyes Hilary’s commentary on Psalm 1 and took certain passages from it for imitation, sometimes expressing one idea in different words, at other times in nearly the same words, as the notes below will establish. Nevertheless, the style of the present treatise plainly reveals Zeno; moreover, it is rightly entitled “On Psalm One Hundred” from the words, “Therefore, in the present psalm, when the Prophet says: ‘I will sing to you of mercy and judgment,’” which are drawn from Psalm 100. Thus it differs from Hilary’s treatise, which clearly concerns Psalm 1. This is the author’s only treatise on the Psalms—for the two titled “On Psalm 41” in the Zenonian manuscripts are properly invitations to the fountains, not interpretations of that psalm, as we shall note in their place in Treatises 35 and 36—and it seems to have been delivered on the occasion of Psalm 100’s recitation in the sacred offices, a psalm on which Hilary did not write a commentary. The other five treatises on psalms circulated under Zeno’s name [Col. 0458C] have been restored to Hilary as their author and transferred to the Appendix, for reasons proposed partly in Dissertation I, chapter 1, §2, and partly in the preface to that Appendix. Meanwhile, observe the title of the present Zenonian treatise as it occurs in the manuscripts: “Here begins the treatise on Psalm One Hundred,” exactly the formula prefixed to other genuinely Zenonian treatises, such as “Here begins the treatise on Isaiah,” “Here begins the treatise on Daniel,” and so forth. The five Hilary treatises, however, are all inscribed by another formula: “Interpretation of Psalm 126,” “On Psalm 127,” etc., as will be evident to anyone comparing the table of manuscripts supplied after the monuments.] Psalm One Hundred.

[Col. 0458B] I. Those negligent in the observance of sacred law are often entangled in serious error, either because they do not understand sayings according to their contexts or because they do not investigate the meanings of what is said. [Note: [Col. 0458C] Hilary expressed Zeno’s opening statements more briefly in these words, no. 16: “The Lord’s saying troubles the negligence of hearers and the uncritical readiness of readers. For when he says, ‘Whoever believes in me shall not be judged,’ he exempts believers from judgment; and when he adds, ‘But whoever does not believe has already been judged,’ he does not admit unbelievers to judgment.”]

Therefore, in the present psalm, when the Prophet says, “I will sing to you of mercy and judgment, O Lord” (Ps. 100:1), how does the Lord say in the Gospel: “Whoever believes in me shall not be judged; but whoever does not believe has already been judged” (John 3:18)? By saying this he exempts believers from judgment and does not admit unbelievers to judgment. But if both groups are exempt from judgment, [Col. 0458D] how will recompense be rendered to each person according to his deed? For the righteous person would seem to labour without purpose unless the unjust person receives according to his deeds what he has done. [Note: [Col. 0458D] Having raised another difficulty from a different Gospel testimony, Hilary proceeds in other words as follows, which Zeno plainly imitates here: “And this indeed will seem so to negligent hearers and uncritical readers. But the force of the words itself contains the precise meaning and understanding of the saying. Then, in almost the same words as Zeno, no. 17: ‘Whoever believes,’ he says, ‘shall not be judged.’ For why is it necessary to judge the believer? Judgment arises from ambiguous matters; and when ambiguity is removed, judicial examination is not required. Hence unbelievers also need not be judged, because no uncertainty remains that they are unbelievers.” From this Hilary reading we corrected *judicari* (“to be judged”), where Zeno had *judicare* (“to judge”). Moreover, we defended Zeno’s view on this matter—by which he seems with Hilary to exempt some people from the judgment of the last day—in Dissertation 2, chapter 9.]

Therefore it must not be understood as the uninstructed suppose. Rather, the force and rationale of the Lord’s saying are explained by the very precision of its words: “Whoever believes in me,” he says, “shall not be judged” (John 3:18). Rightly so: for what need is there to judge the believer? Judgment arises from ambiguous matters; once ambiguity is removed, no judicial examination is required. Hence unbelievers also need not be judged, because they have already been condemned by their own unbelief. For who carries away from this life either a crown or a punishment for himself?

David expressed this principle in the first psalm in these words: “The wicked shall not rise in judgment, nor sinners in the council of the righteous” (Ps. 1:5). [Note: [Col. 0459B] The Reims manuscript reads “second.” If the first psalm were cited as the second, the matter would lack neither precedent nor rationale: similarly, in the Vulgate translation of Acts 13, the psalm now second is called the first; and in certain Greek manuscripts of Acts it is likewise called first, though others call it second. Petilianus also calls it the first, in Augustine, Book II, no. 202; moreover, some teach that the first and second psalms, once joined in one sequence, were regarded as a single psalm. These may be read in Hilary on Psalm 2 and in the notes thereon. But no reason or example suggests how the first psalm could have been designated second by Zeno; therefore, despite the antiquity of the codex, we abandoned its reading in favour of the other manuscripts, which likewise read “in the first psalm.” [Col. 0459C]]

By a graduated distinction according to merits, as though in a few verdicts, he designated in very few words the judgment of the whole human race. [Note: [Col. 0459C] *Elogium* is used variously, and not only in a good but sometimes also in a bad sense. Here it means a sentence of condemnation, as in the ancient author of the treatise *On the Orthodox Faith against the Arians*, included in the Appendix to St Ambrose and cited by St Augustine under the name of Gregory of the East, believed to be Gregory of Baetica, Zeno’s contemporary. Thus he says, p. 348: “Those who are bound by the *elogium* of Arian taint,” that is, by the sentence issued against Arians. Ammianus Marcellinus, Book XIV, p. 17, Lindembrog edition: “He ordered the leaders of the Athenian order to be put to death under one *elogium*.” P. 47: “It was established that we were all to be punished with death under one *elogium*”; and Book XIX, p. 164: “He was ordered to be tortured by the emperor’s *elogium*.” We omit other frequent examples from the same author. Perhaps this also pertains to the *elogium* called by Victor of Tunnuna, *On Penance*, ch. 6, Appendix to Ambrose: “The *elogium* of condemnation was immediately erased by the tears of those confessing”; and by the author of the treatise *On the Martyrdom of Isaiah*, which we shall give in the Appendix, “the *elogium* of future condemnation”—unless in these testimonies there is indicated perhaps not so much the sentence of condemnation as the ground which supplied the cause for the sentence, and which was sometimes expressed in rendering sentences. Thus in the very ancient translation of the *Acts of St Thecla*, edited by Johann Ernst Grabe, vol. I of the *Spicilegium*, p. 108, these words occur, indicating the reason for which she had been condemned: “For her *eulogium*—perhaps *eclogium* had formerly been written, as some maintain it should be, instead of *elogium*—was written: ‘Sacrilegious.’” Digest, Book XLVIII, title 3, law 6, is entitled *On elogia*, and by that name means a capital judgment in which the proceedings against the accused and the cause of condemnation are described; and law 11: “Let him send him back with the *elogium* to the one governing the province.” Likewise, in documents of disinheritance, the stated ground for disinheriting is called an *elogium* by authors. See Petronius Arbiter, ch. 53; Quintilian, *Institutions* VII.4 and *Declamation* 2, no. 15; and Apuleius, *Apology*. Thus Zeno calls the deeds of righteous and wicked persons—by which they supplied the grounds for eternal reward and punishment—an *elogium*. [Col. 0459D]]

For as great as the difference is between the wicked person and the sinner, so great is the difference between the sinner and the righteous person. Finally, he himself leaves no judgment for the wicked, because they are already prejudged by their own impiety; nor did he consider sinners, who are to be judged, worthy of the counsel of the righteous, who shall not be judged. [Note: [Col. 0460B] After much that St Zeno transposed, Hilary gives this passage in these words, no. 18: “He did not leave judgment to the wicked, because they have already been judged; but he denied sinners the counsel of the righteous, because they are to be judged. For impiety makes the former prejudged; sin holds the latter for judgment.” [Col. 0460C]]

## II

Now we must know—since the righteous are destined for everlasting life, the ungodly for eternal punishment, and no further examination awaits them—who those are for whom judgment has been prepared; and from whom ought we to learn this, if not from the Lord himself, who continues his saying thus: “And this is the judgment: that light came into this world, and men loved darkness rather than light” (John 3:19)?

> [Note: Here certain passages from Hilary, no. 17, should be recalled, which St Zeno expressed more clearly in almost different words: “But, when judgment has been removed from believers and unbelievers, the Lord added the cause of judgment and those responsible, upon whom judgment must necessarily be passed. For there are some between the ungodly and the godly, who are intermediate, mingled from both groups, yet properly belonging to neither, because they consist in this very respect of both: they are not to be counted among believers, because some unbelief has been introduced into them; nor are they to be reckoned among unbelief, because they possess something also of faith.”]

He plainly identified wavering and unstable Christians, who are intermediate between the godly and the ungodly,

> [Note: Among writers of this age, *medius*, “intermediate,” was said of one who was neither wholly good nor evil. Besides the passage of Hilary just cited in note 8, Flavius Vopiscus says in *Carus*: “Let us come to Carus, an intermediate man, to be placed among good rather than bad emperors.” Ammianus Marcellinus, book XIV, p. 24, ed. Lindenbrog, similarly calls the emperor Constantius an intermediate ruler.
