Tacitus, though earlier in date, says of Galba, *Histories* I.49: “His own character was intermediate, more free from vices than endowed with virtues.” Zeno calls such Christians “ambiguous”; Hermas, book III, chapter 21, calls them “doubtful.”]

holding no side fully, since they do not cease to hold both. They are not believers, because they have some unbelief mingled in them. They are not unbelievers, because they have an appearance of faith: in profession they serve God, in deeds the world. They wish to know the Law; they do not wish to keep its commandments. They venerate the saving sign, and yet do not withdraw from the mysteries of demons.

> [Note: Thus read the manuscripts of Reims, Pomp., Zen., and Spar. The others, together with the printed editions, have “ministries.”]

> [Note: Hilary, no. 17, continues, partly in the same and partly in another order: “For the fear of God keeps many within the Church; yet the enticements of the world draw these same persons toward secular vices. They pray because they are afraid; they sin because they wish to; they call themselves Christians because the hope of eternity is good; they act as pagans because present things are pleasant. They do not remain ungodly, because God’s name is held in honour by them; they are not godly, because they pursue things alien to godliness.”]

For fear of God keeps many within the Church; yet worldly pleasure draws them to itself. They do not remain ungodly, because God’s name is held in honour by them. They are not godly, because by depraved conduct they wrong the Father who ought to be revered. They pray because they fear; they sin because they wish. Thus guilt is not acquitted where judgment is demanded between two mutually opposed parties in comparison of love; for unless ambiguity has been examined, it cannot rightly deserve a sentence.

> [Note: The Toledo manuscript reads: “a judgment of parties opposed to itself.” Then the Urbino manuscript has *discursa*, “run through,” for *discussa*, “examined.”]

And who are these persons whom ambiguity has reserved for judgment?

> [Note: Three manuscripts and the Venetian edition add “its own.” A little later, in the Apostle’s text, the Pomp. manuscript writes “never” in place of “not as,” and the Toledo manuscript “God” for “Lord.”]

Certainly those of whom the Apostle also speaks: those who, though they knew God, did not honour him as Lord, nor give him thanks; but their thoughts were led away by vain reasonings, and their heart was covered in darkness

> [Note: We have added *est*, “is/was,” from the Pomp., Urb., and Zen. manuscripts.]

(Romans 1:21), so that they loved darkness rather than light, the creature rather than the Creator.

## III

Accordingly, there must be three judgments. One is that of the righteous, who not only, as has been said, will not be judged,

> [Note: We have supplied the words “but will judge this world” from the manuscripts and the Venetian edition.]

but will judge this world, as the Apostle says: “Do you not know that the saints will judge this world?” (1 Corinthians 6:2). Another is that of the ungodly, who are not to be judged because they have already been judged, but are to perish, as Scripture says: “The way of the ungodly shall perish” (Psalm 1:6). The third is that of sinners, whose hidden deeds of crooked and double-minded life must necessarily be examined. The Apostle treats of both: “For those,” he says, “who have sinned without the Law

> [Note: The Toledo, Pomp., and Urb. manuscripts read “have sinned.”]

will perish without the Law. But those who have sinned under the Law will be judged by the Law” (Romans 2:12).

Do you see, brethren, how great the difference is between one condemned and one to be judged? Even human society, unjust though it is, maintains this form of judgment. No householder judges his servant when that servant brings him honourable gains from faithful service, but honours him as a son. But another servant, whom he discovers mixing poisons, in adultery, in murder,

> [Note: The reading was “in false wrongdoing”; we have corrected it on the authority of three manuscripts and the first edition.]

in fraud, or in criminal conduct, he at once assigns to the executioner—not to be heard, but to be tortured with the fitting penalties. A third servant also, whom he observes to be deceitful, excusing his thefts by plausible calculations, he reserves for examination, so that, after the losses have been weighed and the property preserved, sentence may lawfully be pronounced against him according to the debt in which he is found to stand.

Thus a crown will be given to the righteous; pardon to sinners who are either excused or corrected; and eternal punishment to the ungodly. Through the Lord Jesus Christ, who is blessed with the Holy Spirit unto the eternal ages of ages.

> [Note: The Pomp. manuscript reads, “through our Lord Jesus,” etc. The words “with the Holy Spirit” are absent from the Toledo manuscript. The Venetian edition has “with”; the Urb. and Pomp. manuscripts add “Amen” at the end.]

# TREATISE XXII. On Isaiah I

## I

“Hear, O heaven, and give ear, O earth, for the Lord has spoken: I have begotten and exalted sons, but they have despised me” (Isaiah 1:2).

> [Note: TREATISE XXII.—The Reims and Toledo codices read “I have rejoiced.” Lactantius employs this testimony from Isaiah in *Divine Institutes* IV.11, with the same purpose as St Zeno: to show that Christ assumed flesh in order to transfer to the Gentiles the holy religion of God that had been rejected by the Jewish people.]

The opening of this book declares the great offence of the Jewish nation and displays the wrath of divine indignation. It exhorts other persons, so that the word of God may rather be heard by them:

> [Note: The manuscripts and Venetian edition have “exhorts us”; but wrongly, since the phrase refers to other persons. At the end of the present section, no. 1, the Urbino manuscript has “despised” for “may have despised.”]

for it is no small offence that, while the divine discourse has always been delivered among them, it now seems to be directed to others. Hence the rejection of the Jews is the election of other persons; for when others are told that they ought to hear the word of God, Israel is thereby found reprobate; and when the prophet cries, “Hear, O heaven and earth,” he signifies that they have scorned to hear.

## II

“Hear,” he says, “O heaven, and give ear, O earth.”

> [Note: In the manuscripts this passage is various and exceedingly corrupted. First, the words “Concerning heaven and earth” are absent from the Pomp., Toledo, and Vatican-Basil manuscripts, though they occur elsewhere and in the editions. Then the Reims manuscript writes “only” for “having testified.” However one reads it, the sense is difficult to extract. We have retained the text as it appears in the editions and several manuscripts. Sparaverius thinks that one should write: “That the prophet testified concerning heaven and earth, as though he were complaining of some matter”; that is, the prophet summoned heaven and earth as witnesses concerning the complaints which he poured out, not upon them, but upon ungrateful children. This conjecture is indeed confirmed by what follows in the subsequent treatises: in Treatise 24 he says, “He summons heaven and earth as witnesses”; in Treatise 25, “He resolved to mark them out with heaven and earth as witnesses”; and finally in Treatise 26, “He summons heaven and earth as witnesses of his injury.” Yet the meaning of this passage seems altogether different. Since St Zeno is about to interpret the prophet’s words, and thinks that the names heaven and earth should not be understood literally of earth and heaven, but, as he immediately explains, of the Apostles and the Gentiles, he here prepares the way for such an interpretation by implying that the literal sense concerning heaven and earth cannot be accepted: there is no reason why the prophet should complain literally concerning heaven and earth, as though heaven or earth had never heard, and so forth. Therefore this testimony should rightly have been expressed as a question, in order to indicate the rejection of the literal interpretation. If it were permissible, with no manuscript authority, to alter the text, then, with some interrogative particle or word understood immediately at the beginning—for example, “Is it credible?”—we should write: “Is it credible that the prophet testified concerning heaven and earth, or complained as though about some matter, when he says, ‘Hear, O heaven and earth,’ as though heaven had never …?” We have printed *dicit*, “he says,” for *dicitur*, “it is said,” on the authority of five manuscripts.]

Did the prophet testify concerning heaven and earth as though he were complaining of some matter? Or, when he says, “Hear, O heaven and earth,” is it as though heaven had never heard, or earth, when heaven obeys God’s command

> [Note: Four manuscripts—Reims, Pomp., Zen., and Vatican-Basil—read: “and heaven obeys God’s command.” This final verb, *obsecundetur*, is also in the Vatican manuscript.]

and earth does not deny heaven its rains and its crops? But because this prophecy was to be fulfilled in the last times, at the coming of the Lord and Saviour, whom the Jewish peoples would not hear, but whom the Apostles and people from the Gentiles would hear, he therefore says: “Hear, O heaven and earth.”

He affirms by the clear testimony of truth that the Apostles are heavens. For thus he says: “And I shall behold the heavens, the works of your fingers” (Psalm 8:5). Here he plainly does not speak of these heavens, which he had always seen, but of the Apostles, whom he desired to see. Again: “His power has covered the heavens” (Habakkuk 3:3), because the Holy Spirit overshadowed and covered the Apostles in order to perform wonders. And again: “The heavens,” he says, “declare the glory of God” (Psalm 18:2). Here too he does not say that the heavens speak—heavens which no one has heard speaking—but asserts that the Apostles do, by whose preaching the Lord’s glory has been proclaimed throughout all the regions of the earth.

The frequent assertion of the prophets has shown that “earth” means human beings: “Make a joyful noise,” he says, “all the earth.” And elsewhere: “Hear, O earth, from my mouth” (Psalm 65:2).

> [Note: The word “human beings” is absent from the Toledo manuscript.]

By this term he undoubtedly includes Gentile human beings, in whom earthly works still remained. This therefore is what he says: “Hear, O heaven and earth”: since the Jews would not hear, Christ the Lord would be heard by the Apostles and the Gentiles.

## III

“I have begotten and exalted sons,” he says. This is the Lord’s voice, because even then, through the prophet, he rebuked the unbelieving Jews and announced beforehand things that would come to pass before they occurred. For it belongs properly to God to know what is past and to know what is to come.

“I have begotten and exalted sons,” he says. By their boundless unbelief the Jews earned great hatred from our Lord, because

> [Note: We have written “because” in place of “which” from the Pomp. manuscript. Perhaps *quoniam*, “because,” should also be read instead of *quo* or *quod*. The Urbino manuscript has “from fear” for “from love.”]

as great as the favour of his love had been, so great would be the vengeance for their offence. For it is certain that great punishment is exacted from a son after he has sinned, when his father loved him with abundant affection; and as much tenderness as a loving father showed his beloved son, so much vengeance does he demand when wronged. For when a beloved son has not returned due reciprocity to his father, he receives a fitting sentence when disowned. For how great a crime it is cannot be expressed: not to have loved God as Father, when it is a sin not to have loved a human being.

> [Note: Sidonius uses this adverb in book VII, letter II, and elsewhere. A little later the Urbino manuscript has “loving father” for “beloved father,” and “Lord” for “God” in the Pomp. manuscript.]

Hence unhappy and wretched are the Jews, who rejected God the Father by whom they were begotten, forgetful of so great an honour and ignorant of so great a dignity. For what is more blessed than that God should deem human beings worthy of paternal regard, and that such exalted majesty should hold human lowliness dear or beloved? “I have begotten sons,” he says. How sweet that the Lord should say this of human beings; how shameful to have injured such a Father! “I have begotten and exalted sons.”

Certainly the Lord begot the sons of Israel: he chose Abraham, from whom they were to be born (Genesis 12; Exodus 17). He begot them in Egypt, where, though few people had entered, an innumerable multitude came forth; and he led them into the wilderness with a strong hand and uplifted arm (Psalm 135:12). Israel was exalted when darkness and gloom surrounded all Egypt for three days (Exodus 10:22). Israel was exalted when, amid so many and such great torments of the Egyptians, it alone neither feared nor felt anything. What of the fact that he led them through the midst of the sea by a dry passage? (Exodus 14).

> [Note: Here the reading of both editions and manuscripts is various and corrupt. The editions read: “What of those for whom daily manna from heaven in the wilderness, and drink of water from a rock; which, made sweet from bitter through wood, we Gentiles, having excluded bitterness through the wood of the cross, were to drink?” Besides the fact that *nos ex amara dulcis effecta*, “we made sweet from bitter,” should be read in place of *quae*, “which,” and that *Gentilitas*, “the Gentile world,” appears to have been wrongly placed for *ex origine Gentiles*, “Gentiles by origin,” the chief difficulty is that the miracle in which bitter water was changed into sweet, Exodus 16, is not stated of the water that Moses drew from the rock with his rod, but of water found at Marah which the Jews could not drink because of its bitterness; Moses made it sweet by casting wood, or a rod, into it. Most manuscripts provide no remedy, but rather introduce new difficulties. In the Toledo manuscript the words “and water” are absent; in Pomp. and Zen. only the conjunction is lacking. Reims has: “What, for whom daily [food] from heaven in the wilderness, drink from a rock and, through wood, bitter made sweet, which the wood of the cross, etc.” Vatican has: “from a rock, who through wood bitter made sweet, which the wood of the cross [its] bitterness, etc.” Finally the Vatican-Basil codex has: “What, for whom daily [food] from heaven in the wilderness, drink from a rock, because through wood bitter water made sweet, which by the wood of the cross, bitterness having been excluded from Gentilehood, we were to drink.” Since this reading removes the chief difficulty arising from the miracle of bitter water, it seemed preferable. Adding *manna* from some editions and manuscripts, writing *et*, “and,” for *q* or *que*, and *Gentilitatis*, “of Gentilehood,” for *Gentilitate*, and finally retaining from the editions “which through the wood,” we inserted it in the text. The meaning is: “What of those for whom daily manna fell from heaven in the wilderness, drink flowed from a rock, and bitter water was made sweet through wood?”]

What of those for whom daily manna came from heaven in the wilderness (Exodus 16), drink from the rock (Exodus 17), and bitter water was made sweet through wood? This water we were to drink through the wood of the cross, after the bitterness of Gentile life had been removed (Exodus 16:17).

The sons of Israel were exalted when Israel came safely from Horeb to the Jordan (Deuteronomy 1).

> [Note: The Pomp. and Zen. manuscripts read “came safely through the Jordan to Horeb” (the Reims manuscript lacks *through* and likewise reads “to Horeb”); but wrongly, for Israel journeyed from Horeb to the Jordan, as the sacred writings make clear. The Vatican manuscript has “to Choreb” for “from Horeb”; but Choreb and Horeb signify the same mountain, the words differing only by aspiration. The Venetian edition has “they came” instead of “he came,” though the phrase seems to refer to the sons of Israel. Yet besides the fact that “safe” would also have needed to be written in the plural, “he came” may aptly refer to Israel.]

What of God’s daily conversations? (Exodus, chapter 14).

> [Note: The Pomp. manuscript has “God’s conversation” for “God’s conversations”; and the Toledo, Urbino, and Vatican manuscripts read “escaped” for “they escaped.”]

“But they despised me”: for they led him to the cross, through which cross they escaped Pharaoh; but “the daughter of Zion shall again be left” (Isaiah 1:8).

*Some material seems to be missing.*

# TREATISE XXIII. On Isaiah II

> [Note: TREATISE XXIII.—We here append four further treatises, though shorter ones, since they refer to the same passage of Isaiah discussed in the preceding treatise: “Hear, O heaven, and give ear, O earth,” etc. They appear to have been delivered during Passiontide, when the text indicated here was read in the sacred offices to reproach Jewish unbelief. It is clear that Zeno delivered these treatises on the occasion of the sacred reading; and since the sacred offices at that season required a longer time, the holy bishop seems to have chosen to offer a brief and suitable reflection upon Isaiah’s reading, completing the treatises in a few words so as not entirely to withhold pastoral instruction from the people. We shall say more fully about this in the prefatory admonition to Treatise 30.]

As the utterance of most blessed Isaiah indicates, God is angry with the Jewish people

> [Note: Concerning the word *carmen*, “utterance/song,” which occurs at the beginning of the proposition and is understood as an oracle, a fixed solemn formula, or even a prophetic writing, we have said enough in note 26 to Treatise 12 and note 49 to Treatise 1, book I.]

and refutes them with public rebuke, lest perhaps they repent.

> [Note: Here the author appears to refer to Isaiah 6:9–10: “Go and say to this people: Hear indeed, but do not understand; see the vision, but do not know. Blind the heart of this people, make their ears heavy, and shut their eyes, lest perhaps they see with their eyes, hear with their ears, understand with their heart, turn, and I heal them.”]

For to a person who thinks in human terms,

> [Note: What is meant by “to one thinking in human terms, to be *nundinari* is worse than to be punished” is explained in the following treatise: “Among the wise and honourable, it is more grievous to be confounded by some public stigma than to die.” Similar words occur in Treatise 25: “Among unbelievers, death is considered a shortening of future punishment; and what is not publicly disgraced is regarded almost as though it had not been done.” Thus *nundinari* means to be confounded or publicly defamed by some stigma. This meaning seems to have arisen because the Romans had established market-days, *nundinae*, so that country people might assemble not so much for buying and selling as for bringing accusations—by the Hortensian law, market-days were made judicial days from non-judicial days for the convenience of country people, as Macrobius testifies, *Saturnalia* I, p. 9—if they had any criminal complaint against someone which, occupied with other concerns on other days, they could not readily raise and pursue. Everyone understands how much disgrace for defendants attended that kind of proceeding because of the crowds at the markets. This disgrace especially affected those burdened with debt. If these persons had been convicted or confessed before the praetor, and had not paid within the thirty days called “lawful,” they were summoned again before the praetor; under Law III of the Twelve Tables, they were held bound in stocks or fetters for sixty days, during which they could settle with their creditor. During those days they were brought before the praetor in the Comitium on three successive market-days, and the sum for which they had been adjudged liable was proclaimed. On the third market-day they paid the penalty with their lives or were sold abroad beyond the Tiber, according to Gellius, book XX, chapter 10. This, then, was the disgrace contained in the word *nundinari*, subsequently extended to every public stigma; hence St Zeno shortly before called it “public rebuke.” That *nundinor* could be used passively is suggested by an example from Capitolinus, *Gordian* 24, where *nundinatus*, “sold,” is passive. Firmicus too, book VI, chapter 31, wrote *nundinare* actively. In the Urbino and Zen. manuscripts “is absent” is lacking from the words “is worse than.”]

to be publicly disgraced is worse than to be punished. Thus he calls them sons, that disinheritance may be feared; exalted, that their ruin may be a terror; despisers, that they may know that they bring upon themselves the punishment of penalty. Flee this example resolutely, brethren; and at the same time rejoice that by the blows dealt to others you learn God’s discipline through our Lord Jesus Christ.

> [Note: The words “God’s voice” are absent from the Pomp. manuscript; the Vatican and Urbino manuscripts write “God.” The word “our” is absent from the same Vatican and Urbino manuscripts.]

# TREATISE XXIV. On Isaiah III

> [Note: TREATISE XXIV.—In the Spar. manuscripts this and the following treatise are entitled “On the Jews, a treatise on Isaiah.” The Venetian edition gives this same title not only to these but also to the fifth treatise on Isaiah and to others to be noted in their proper places, together with the Zen. manuscript. In the remaining manuscript books it is called “On Isaiah.” The Verona edition preserved both titles. We have written “On Isaiah,” because in the manuscripts some of these treatises are entitled “on Isaiah,” others “of Isaiah,” and others “into Isaiah”; and this last reading pleased us more, lest these treatises appear to have been delivered about Isaiah’s person, like the preceding ones about Abraham, Jacob, and so forth, whereas they are upon Isaiah’s text. It is enough to have noted this once.]

A violent disturbance, brethren, occurs when the person who complains of an injury done to him is able most easily to avenge himself. But because among the wise and honourable it is more grievous to be confounded by some public stigma than to die, God rebukes the Jewish people—corrupted by the overflowing heat of luxury—with public reproach.

> [Note: The Pomp. manuscript reads “surpassing”; the Reims codex has “the heat of luxury” before the corruption.]

He summons heaven and earth as witnesses (Isaiah 1:2), in order to magnify the crime; he calls them sons, that disinheritance may be feared; exalted, that ruin may be feared; his despisers, to show them ungodly. Unhappy is the guilt, brethren, in which no kind of excuse finds a place.

> [Note: *Qualiscumque*, “of whatever kind,” is absent from the Vatican manuscript.]

Certainly detestable is the son whom a loving father—whom a father—condemns unwillingly.

# TREATISE XXV. On Isaiah IV

Human speech fails before the ungodliness of the Jewish people, whose stubbornness of heart surpassed God’s patience with its impatience. For it is no slight crime on his part

> [Note: TREATISE XXV.—Why the word “his” was excluded by the Verona edition and subsequent editions, although it occurs in all the manuscripts we were able to see and also in the Venetian edition, is unknown—unless it was considered superfluous. Yet it gives the sentence a clearer and more certain meaning.]

when he complains concerning that person whom he could immediately punish. But because,

> [Note: See note 4 to Treatise 23 on this matter.]

among unbelievers, death is considered a shortening of future punishment, and what is not publicly disgraced is regarded almost as though it had not been done, he resolved to mark them out with heaven and earth as witnesses, so that they might be subject to fitting judgment for an inexcusable crime. Finally, the matter was fulfilled in the Lord’s Passion: heaven lost daylight in the middle of the day, and earth lost its firmness in a mighty tremor.

> [Note: The particle “in” is absent from four manuscripts.]

> [Note: The Pomp. manuscript repeats here: “lost its firmness.”]

From this one may judge what is reserved for those on whose account nature endured the punishment of a funeral lament.

# TREATISE XXVI. On Isaiah V

The text of the divine prophetic utterance shows that the Jewish people wholly abandoned the safeguard of their salvation.

> [Note: TREATISE XXVI.—In the margin of the Pomp. codex, “corrected: *amisisse*, ‘to have abandoned.’” Concerning the word *carmen*, by which the book of Isaiah is indicated, see note 2 to Treatise 23.]

In this matter, venerable brethren, it is not severity that condemns them before all, but compassion. For no one can confer good upon one whom the most patient and merciful Father has disowned—indeed, one convicted not by accusation but by proof. Finally, he summons heaven and earth as witnesses of his injury (Isaiah 1:2): earth, upon which all things are done; heaven, beneath which they are done. He calls them sons to magnify the crime; exalted, to show them ungrateful. He sets an ox and an ass before them, that, if they recover their senses, they may be tormented more grievously by the comparison than by punishment (Isaiah 1:3).

> [Note: Zeno refers to what follows in Isaiah 1:3: “The ox knows its owner, and the ass its master’s manger; but Israel has not known me.” Some Fathers taught that the ox and ass signify the Gentiles allegorically. See, among others, St Gaudentius, sermon X, p. 123.]

# TREATISE XXVII. On Isaiah VI

> [Note: TREATISE XXVII.—The Venetian edition read: “On Psalm 79,” and this treatise was indeed delivered on the occasion of the reading of Psalm 79, as is clear from the first period. In that psalm, verses 9 and following offer the comparison of the vine explained in this treatise: “You transplanted a vine from Egypt,” etc. Hence the Verona edition and those following added to the title “On Psalm 79” this other title, “Comparison of the Vine,” perhaps from the Zenonian manuscript, which has this title alone. Yet we judged preferable the title found in all manuscripts except the Zenonian, “On Isaiah”; for the prophet Isaiah presses the comparison of the vine more strongly toward Zeno’s purpose. Accordingly, the next treatise, which likewise treats this comparison of the vine, bears the same title both in manuscripts and editions.]

## I

The fact that the prophet sought the flourishing in due time of a new vine in place of the old vine, which had been planted by the Lord in Egypt,

> [Note: Psalm 79:9 relates that the Jews, like a vine, were transplanted from Egypt’s barren land to the fertile soil of Palestine, signifying that they were transferred from Egyptian captivity to Palestine. But St Zeno, looking here to the title of that psalm, “For those who shall be changed,” understands it of the new Church, gathered from the Gentiles in place of the Jews, which yielded more abundant fruit to God the planter. Thus Zeno calls the Jewish people the old vine, planted in Egypt—that is, in altogether barren soil—of which Isaiah complains under the image of an unfruitful vine in chapter 5. The young vine is the Church of Christians gathered from the Gentiles, to whom, after the Jews were abandoned because of wickedness, the Gospel and faith passed.]

is declared by the very inscription of the psalm’s title that was read.

> [Note: Thus the psalms were also read, not merely sung; see more fully note 3 to Treatise 15, book I. Below, the word “Lord’s,” absent from the Pomp. manuscript, is read as “God’s” in the Toledo and Zen. manuscripts.]

For it runs thus: “Unto the end, for those who shall be changed” (Psalm 79:1). The Jewish people, indeed, who were called the Lord’s first vine, flourished, but unhappily: when its blossom was scattered, it could bear no fruit (Isaiah 5:4, 6). Instead of fruit it produced thorns; instead of grapes, wild grapes. Abhorring the misfortune of that thing, the Lord planted for himself another vine—that is, our people—according to his own will; into it all prophetic fruit flowed.

> [Note: Unless an error of transcription lies in the noun, the construction seems decidedly more satisfactory if it is referred to the pronoun *cujus*, “whose,” as follows: “The Lord, abhorring the misfortune of that thing, etc.”]

Most blessed cultivators, forgive me, your rustic, if our lack of skill should detract in any respect from your expertise in giving an account of the vine.

## II

Therefore, as you often remember very well, a cutting is cut to a prescribed measure,

> [Note: A *surculus* is a leafy part of a branch cut from a living tree to be planted in the ground. Hence Cicero, *On the Orator* II.69: “Give me from that tree some cuttings to plant.” The cuttings had to have a fixed measure, as is clear from Palladius, book III, no. 9, where he sets a measure of one cubit for the cutting which he calls a *sarmentum*.]

and a shoot is placed in a pit,

> [Note: When cuttings were planted, according to Columella, book III, no. 4, a nursery-vineyard (*vitiarium*) was made. A *vitiarium* was a nursery for vines, as Palladius explains, book III, no. 10. The little branches arising from cuttings were called young shoots (*novelli palmites*) or *malleoli*, according to Columella, book III, no. 6. Cut from the original cuttings so as to retain none of the old cutting, they were transferred from the nursery-vineyard into the fields and placed in a pit (*scrobs*). A *scrobs* was a hole prepared in the earth to receive vine shoots. See Columella IV.4, VII.5, and XI.2. These matters, and those that follow, had to be explained more carefully for understanding the terms used by Zeno and the process that he briefly describes.]

so that, once it has taken life there, the generative sap may nourish it while its substance always remains with it. A supporting stake is necessarily joined to it, under whose protection it may raise itself up. But when it has grown into a mature vine and reached the crossbar,

> [Note: In vineyards, the *jugum*, “yoke/crossbar,” is a transverse pole to which vines are tied when they have grown to a specified height; after superfluous growth has been cut away, they are not allowed to extend further. See Pliny XVII.21–22 and Columella IV.17, who in no. 19 defines the height and placement of the crossbar.]

all its luxuriant locks are pruned with the vine-dresser’s sickle,

> [Note: We have added *falce*, “with a sickle,” from the Reims, Toledo, Urbino, Zen., and Pomp. manuscripts and the Venetian edition; in place of this word the Vatican manuscript wrongly has *facile*, “easily.” Columella, book IV, no. 25, describes the pruning-sickle. We have corrected *tunduntur*, “are beaten,” found in both manuscripts and editions, to *tondentur*, “are pruned”; for it is the function of a sickle to prune, not beat. Likewise, a little later in no. 3, we have written *tondentur*, where all manuscripts and editions give the name of the sickle. Copyists easily confused *tondere*, “to prune,” and *tundere*, “to beat.” Thus, for example, in manuscripts of Vegetius’ *Veterinary Art*, *tondeo* is frequently written for *tundo*, as Giovanni Battista Morgagni observed in Epistle IV, §4, appended to the agricultural writers, and Matthaeus Gesner in the index to those same writers. Vatican: *tunsa*, “beaten.”]

the clean material is carried to lofts,

> [Note: A *tabulatum* is said by Columella, book XII, no. 50, to be a raised storehouse resembling a granary. Dry materials—grain, hay, leaves, straw, and the like—were stored in it; see likewise book I, no. 6.]

and it is tied with knots, lest it be separated by any force from the wood by which it is borne, or by whose support or guidance it is induced to extend further toward abundant fruit.

> [Note: The subject here is the vine, not the material cut from vines. The vine was tied with knots to the supporting stakes mentioned shortly before. For more, see the cited Columella, book IV, no. 26, where he discusses the care of supporting and training the vine.]

Then, weeping ceremonially, it gently bedews with its rain and promises streams of must conceived by its fruitful tears. Immediately, when its eyes are opened, radiant leaves emerge; beneath them the following fruits, hanging down and commending themselves, smile. The heat of the sun, rain, and winds advance them by testing them and bring them to maturity.

> [Note: Agricultural writers call the buds of vines “eyes” and also “gems.” See Columella III.18 and IV.24. We have written *adridunt*, “smile,” from most manuscripts, especially Reims, in place of *arrident*. The form *rido, ridis* is as good Latin as *rideo*; hence Lucretius, book I, verse 22: “It smiles with diffused light.”]

But when the time of vintage has come, its beauty scattered, the grape is plucked everywhere and, laid beneath the workers’ feet in the wine-press, is trodden.

> [Note: A *torcular*, “wine-press,” was not a single implement, as many have believed, but a place appointed for receiving grapes, containing several implements and vessels used for expressing must. See Cato, *On Agriculture*, chapter 12. In the wine-press was a treading-floor, mentioned by Palladius, book I, chapter 18, where grapes were trodden under the workers’ feet.]

It is pressed by the press and powerfully squeezed between two boards until all its sweetness is extracted from the marrow.

> [Note: According to Cato in the passage cited, the wine-press also contained a press-beam. Hence Cyprian, Letter LXIII to Caecilius, mentions in the wine-press not only the treading underfoot, as he calls it, but also the pressure of the press; moreover he says: “In the wine-press there is water which is trodden by feet or expressed by the press.” Presses, Servius says on Virgil, *Georgics* II.242, are beams by which grapes already trodden are pressed. Varro similarly, *On Agriculture* I.54: “When the grapes have been trodden, their husks with the skins are to be placed beneath the press.” Cato, chapter 17, supplies the shape of this press; and from it one understands why St Zeno shortly afterwards mentions the weight of the press: the whole force of pressing depended upon the beam’s weight, and the press was not then shaped as it is in our times. Below, the Reims, Pomp., and Zen. manuscripts and the Venetian edition have *veterescendo*, “by growing old,” for *veterascendo*.]

Thus the precious liquid is both drunk by those who trod it and carried into the householder’s wine-cellars, so that it may become better by ageing.

### III.

So far as our limited capacity can spiritually discern, the vine-shoot measured to the proper length signifies the candidate, examined by the lawful number of scrutinies.

> [Note: The lawful number of examinations, which St. Zeno here calls “legitimate,” is those seven scrutinies by which candidates were tested before they were admitted to baptism. See Martene, *De Antiquis Ecclesiae Ritibus*, part I, book I, chapter 11, article 11. MS Zen. has *examinatur* (“is examined”) for *examinatus* (“having been examined”).]

By the pit we ought to understand the sacred font, which truly receives dead persons in the sacrament and, once inspired by heavenly water, makes them alive. The supporting piece of wood by which it is stretched or carried is the sign of the Lord’s cross, without which a Christian cannot at all live or attain immortality. Its being carried up onto platforms indicates the height of the heavenly way and life.

It is bound with ties when, renouncing the world, a person is spiritually bound by the sacred interrogations through the pledge that has been made.

> [Note: Those pledges, by which persons about to be baptized professed, in answer to the priest’s questions, that they renounced the world, were always regarded not as a mere ceremony but as a solemn sacrament—that is, an oath—as is clear from this testimony of Zeno and of other Fathers. From this one may infer that the form of this sacrament, consisting of the priest’s questions and the candidates’ answers, had already been established at that time, as is customary even in our own day; this can also easily be demonstrated from Cyril’s *Catecheses*.]

Its luxuriant locks are cut back by the pruning-hook: that is, every sin whatsoever is cut away by baptism and by the power of the Holy Spirit. The vine, cleansed of its material burden, happily weeps; from the washed person there flow yet more happily the heavenly, divine streams of teaching, their eyes burst open—that is, spiritually opened.

> [Note: MSS Vat. and Urb. insert “spiritually heavenly.”]

The sequence of fruit commends itself through the leaves that precede it.

> [Note: For *sequela* (“sequence”), see Scaevola, *Digest*, law 93, *On Discharges*; Tertullian, *On Patience*, chapter 5; Lactantius, *Divine Institutes*, book VII, chapter 5; and *On the Workmanship of God*, chapter 4.]

Likewise, the Christian, obediently following the divine admonitions that go before—wherein lies the fruit of eternal life—is at once defended and nourished. He comes to the yoke when, having first bestowed all his possessions on the poor, carrying his own cross, and having completed all righteousness, he follows Christ more unencumbered.

> [Note: *Praerogo* is used in the sense of “I contribute beforehand” or “I expend beforehand,” as is clear from the Code, book X, title III, law 40, where one reads: “Whatever expenses the city shall have advanced for these persons.” See also Ulpian, *Digest* 19.2.19 §6.]

By the force of storm, sun, and rain it is driven to maturity; and the righteous person is brought to the crown through frequent, great, and varied trials. But when the time of the vintage comes—that is, the days of persecution—grapes are snatched away everywhere: that is, violent hands are rashly laid upon all the saints. They are carried to the winepress—that is, led to the place of punishment. There they are trampled by the workers: that is, amid the utmost contempt they are mocked and slaughtered by persecutors.

> [Note: If St. Zeno intended here to indicate some persecution of his own time as well as earlier ones, he may have meant that stirred up against Catholics under Constantius, patron of the Arians. Lucifer of Cagliari writes of it in *That One Must Die for the Son of God*, volume IV of the *Bibliotheca Patrum*, p. 242: “You have slaughtered very many at Alexandria; you have torn some to pieces throughout the whole world; you have scattered those who resisted you in various places; yet all of them—though you are utterly unwilling to hear it—are martyrs. We believe that all those most blessed persons slain by your sword are in paradise,” etc.  
>
> Hilary, looking to this same matter at the beginning of his book against that emperor, p. 561, says: “Let the shepherds cry out, because the hired servants have fled. Let us lay down our lives for the sheep, because thieves have entered and the raging lion prowls around. Let us go out to martyrdom at these words, because the angel of Satan has transformed himself into an angel of light,” etc. See Dissertation 1, chapter 2, §8, where, besides several others, we have set forth for consideration that notable persecution which Valens stirred up more bitterly and pursued longer, and to which Zeno may especially have directed his attention here.  
>
> Hilary, speaking quite similarly, in Psalm 118, letter 15, no. 3, p. 371, volume I, Verona edition, has handed down the following concerning martyrs as though they were present: “For the Lord knows that there are many of such unwise love that, when they see their children persisting in the glory of martyrdom, they beg them to yield to the times and entreat them to change their resolve; they exercise toward them the affection of an impious piety. Thus an aged mother and an old father display to their son, in the very contest of martyrdom, their pitiable gray hairs, reproaching the harshness of his resolve; thus too a wife is present, accompanied by her children, and begs him rather to live for her and for them; thus brothers and sisters plead with the flattering familiarity of their names; and the soul itself, long since captivated by the enticements of life, steals in with certain silent counsels so as to bend the resolution toward compliance. Therefore at such a time the Lord commanded us to hate father, mother, wife, children, brothers, sisters, and even our own life.” If anyone wishes to apply these words specifically to martyrs of earlier times, he will be still less able to doubt that St. Zeno at the same time speaks here and elsewhere of earlier martyrs.  
>
> Shortly afterward MS Pompeianus reads “persons” for “all.”]

Their juice is dried out under the final weight of the press and between its two boards.

> [Note: This is the reading of the manuscripts and editions. Unless it contains a scribal error and one should read *exprimitur* (“is pressed out”), as shortly afterward *exigitur* (“is exacted”) and a little earlier *exigatur* occur, *exsicco* (“I dry out”) is plainly to be understood metaphorically for “I press out,” just as Horace, *Odes* I.31, used *exsiccet* for “shall drain”: “Let the merchant drain the wines from his little cellars.”]

Likewise, on the day of judgment, Christ exacts, according to the tablets of the law, vengeance for the blood of the confessors down to the last farthing. The treaders drink from that same must; and persecutors, often coming to believe in Christ, taste—and some even drink—the precious cup which shortly before they had poured out by trampling. The must is stored in the householder’s cellar so that it may become more precious by transfusion; and the martyr is received into the hidden dwelling of the Lord, so that, there transformed from a human being into an angel, he may glory in the blessedness of eternal life.

> [Note: Above: “that it may become better by aging”; here, however, *transfretatione* (“by sea-crossing”) was mistakenly written and printed in place of *veterascendo* (“by aging”), since there is no place for sea-crossing when must is transferred into a wine-cellar. Perhaps someone will suppose that Zeno meant the Raetian wine of the district of Verona, famous enough from Pliny, book IV, chapter 6, and many writers, which was stored in wine-cellars and was at that time considered so valuable that it was sent by sea to distant regions. But this is not attractive either, since the author seems to speak of wine made more precious in the wine-cellar itself. We therefore judged that *transfusione* (“by transfusion”) should be restored: wine repeatedly racked in wine-cellars becomes purer and more precious. Accordingly, in the allegorical explanation immediately following, the martyr is said in similar language to be transfused from a human being into an angel.]  
>
> [Note: MS Pompeianus adds “Amen.” In MS Remensis: “Here ends St. Zeno’s treatise on Isaiah.”]

## 236. TREATISE XXVIII. On Isaiah VII

As the sound of the reading indicates, brothers, the Jewish people is indeed reproved for impiety, but the Christian is likewise warned not to become such a person (Isaiah, chapter V). Thus, that the latter may fear more, the former is terrorized; the former is beaten so that the latter may advance. It is a concise form of happiness to learn from another’s danger what one ought to avoid. Therefore, brothers, in such a matter eloquence is not to be displayed, but care; receive this in a few words.

Whoever wishes to escape the wrath of God, who threatens generally, must serve him blamelessly.

> [Note: TREATISE XXVIII.—This treatise is rightly placed after the preceding one, since it concerns the same passage of Isaiah in which the vineyard is mentioned. Sparaverius, however, in his final note on the preceding treatise, thought that the discussion of the aforesaid vineyard, mentioned a little later in this treatise, was the preceding treatise itself, once entitled *On Psalm 79*, in which the praised vineyard is discussed more fully. But we think it beyond doubt that the author refers to the reading from the Book of Isaiah indicated at the beginning of the treatise, which furnished the occasion for this discourse. Shortly afterward MS Pompeianus has *peragere* (“to carry through”) for *peragrare* (“to traverse”).]

The discussion of the aforesaid vineyard, most beloved brothers, has boundaries extending far and wide, which the weight of the pressing sacraments does not allow us to traverse in an adequate discourse. Yet, lest the solemnity entirely cease, taste something of its discourse in a few words.

The first vineyard of God was the synagogue, mean with the woody tresses of its wandering branches; when it spread itself everywhere with wanton foliage through luxurious and profane places, it bore thorns instead of fruit and a wild grape instead of grapes.

> [Note: MSS Tol. and Vat. read *lasciva pars se*. MS Urb. has *diffudit* for *diffundit*. The Venetian edition has *labruscas* for *labruscam*. Below, MS Urb. has *correptus* for *commotus*.]

Moved by the indignity of this, the Lord deserted it and planted for himself another according to his will—the mother Church. Cultivating her with priestly offices and making her fruitful with a devout draught, he taught her, suspended from the blessed wood, to produce a most abundant vintage.

> [Note: MS Remensis: “and, by a devout draught of fruitfulness, suspended upon the blessed wood.” MS Pompeianus and the Venetian edition likewise have *suspensa* (“suspended”).]

Hence it is that today, from your number, new vines brought to the yoke, bubbling with the sweet flow of gushing must, have filled the Lord’s wine-cellar with common joy.

> [Note: These are the neophytes. Therefore the weight and solemnity of the pressing sacraments, which Zeno shortly before said prevented him from giving a fuller discussion, are undoubtedly the Paschal festivals, at which Zeno customarily delivered a brief discourse to neophytes, as will appear from what follows. The new vines brought to the yoke are those who have passed from catechumens to the grace of baptism. The allegory is aptly understood of them: boiling with the sweet flow of bubbling must, they filled with common joy the Lord’s wine-cellar—that is, the Church, into which they entered through baptism. Thus also the words “from your number,” from which such new vines are said to have been brought to the yoke, indicate all the catechumens, to whom the author repeatedly promises that the same thing will happen as their faith grows: namely, that they too will someday be brought to the yoke, or baptized. It is therefore clear that this treatise was delivered both to neophytes and to catechumens.]

May God the almighty Father grant that this may happen to you also, as your faith grows, through the Lord Jesus Christ, who is blessed with the Holy Spirit unto ages of ages.

## TREATISE XXIX. On Isaiah VIII, or On Christ’s Coming into the World

> [Note: TREATISE XXIX.—The first title occurs in the manuscripts, except for Zen., which has “On Christ”; the second is found in the editions. We therefore could omit neither. On the authority of the manuscripts it is placed after the treatises on Isaiah. We believe this was done because this discourse is mutilated, so that it should be regarded as a fragment of a treatise rather than a treatise. Perhaps, if the complete treatise had reached us, something from Isaiah would have appeared here, no less than in the preceding treatises.]

Christ entered the world secretly, lest the devil, wise in his own eyes, should perceive him. He who had deceived humankind by counsel is conquered by counsel, so that, just as the human being had not recognized the devil in paradise, so the devil in the world might not easily recognize Christ.

> [Note: This is the well-known saying of St. Ignatius the martyr, *Letter to the Ephesians*, no. 19: “The virginity of Mary and her childbirth were hidden from the ruler of this world.” We have no doubt that St. Zeno refers to this, since other Fathers also repeat the same saying from Ignatius. See Origen, *Homily VI on Luke*; Jerome, on Matthew chapter I; Basil, *Homily 25 on Christ’s Nativity*; Ambrose, *On Luke*, book II, no. 3; and Jobius the Monk, in Photius, codex 222.]  
>
> [Note: MSS Remensis and Pompeianus read “into paradise,” a reading which, if genuine, would be of the same kind as those discussed in note 5 on Treatise 15, book II.]

The remainder is lacking.

## 238. PREFACE TO THE FOLLOWING TREATISES

There remain several brief treatises which, though marked with various titles, all nevertheless belong to the same Paschal season and generally contain mention of baptism being conferred or having been conferred at that time; for this reason we have judged that they should all be presented together. If any treatises described above seem to concern the same Paschal rites because they contain some address to the newly baptized, we have not thought them to be transferred here: either because they are much longer and mention baptism only incidentally, or because we judged that they should not be detached from their proper title—for example, “On Isaiah”—under which other, non-Paschal treatises occur.

You may perhaps first marvel, reader, at the brevity of those which we now set forth, and then also at the resemblance of some of them. These two difficulties so disturbed some persons that, being ignorant what these writings were and whose they were, they thought that doubt should be cast upon all the Zenonian treatises among which they are interspersed. Yet we have clearly established in Dissertation I, chapter 3, chiefly from the most ancient Rheims manuscript, that these, if any, certainly have Zeno as their author. Indeed, they are for the most part so full of many testimonies from both profane antiquity and sacred rites, and from various doctrines, that they yield to none, or to few, of the longer treatises found also among other Fathers, as will become clear from the reading itself and the notes appended.

Three observations sufficiently explain their brevity. First, the Paschal rites to which these treatises belong did not permit a longer discourse, as Zeno himself remarked in Treatise 28: “The discussion of the aforesaid vineyard, most beloved brothers, has boundaries extending far and wide, which the weight of the pressing sacraments does not allow us to traverse in an adequate discourse. Yet, lest the solemnity entirely cease, taste something of its discourse in a few words.” Likewise, in Treatises 56 and 58: “Time does not permit, brothers, the truth to be rendered to the image.”

Second, these should not properly be considered treatises, but rather certain ecclesiastical prefaces, or addresses given to those about to be baptized or to neophytes. Indeed, some are entitled “Prefaces” or “Invitations” in the very manuscripts. They are, as it were, certain solemn formulas, such as are now prescribed in the Pontifical or Ritual for bishops to use in sacred ceremonies. Accordingly, several Zenonian pieces passed into fixed formulas which, as we have shown from the Rheims manuscript in the preface, our bishops used on certain stated days.

Finally, Plato noted in the *Menexenus* that great orators were accustomed to prepare several preambles or openings for speeches, to use as occasion required. Cicero, *Letters to Atticus* XVI.3, mentions a volume of preambles from which he used to choose whenever he undertook a *syngramma* (a written composition). See also *Letters to Friends* IX.8, to Paetus. More than sixty-five of these survive among the works of Demosthenes; they are extremely brief. Jerome Wolf observed, in his address to the reader, p. 130, that Demosthenes used them as occasion presented itself. Why should one not believe that St. Zeno, most devoted to rhetorical and oratorical training, did something similar: preparing several such prefaces for the Paschal feasts, to employ as circumstance and business required?

Perhaps in this sense certain treatises of this sort are called *Prefaces* in the manuscripts. Thus St. Peter Chrysologus calls Sermon XL, on the Good Shepherd, a preface in the course of the discourse itself; he similarly calls Sermon LXXXVII a preface, apparently using *preface* in the sense of an opening. We have clearly shown in note 1 there that Treatise 77, book II, is an opening. But this is enough on brevity, which may be observed in a not very dissimilar manner in several treatises of other Fathers, for example Peter Chrysologus and St. Leo.

The resemblance among some of them, such that two or three of the treatises to be set forth repeat the same thoughts, indeed sometimes exactly the same number of words, should, if it troubles anyone, be evidence that St. Zeno wrote several forms of a single treatise or address—either because the first or even second did not satisfy him, or because, being required to speak each year upon the same subject when the same feasts and readings from Exodus, Daniel, and so forth recurred (from which he could in no way depart because of the ecclesiastical discipline that had appointed those readings as symbols of baptism and so forth), he was compelled to say or even write the same things extemporaneously, with some additions or changes lest the same things be repeated altogether.

We shall also add Sparaverius’s observation from note 4 on Treatise 26: “He repeats these things so often that a man of such great talent may seem to have suffered from a lack of arguments. But a man distinguished in learning and piety preferred that his reputation should decline rather than that the seed of his words should be suppressed in the Church. He did not utter these things daily, but yearly, or at fixed seasons of the year, or perhaps after longer intervals, so that repetition of something done previously would not have been unwelcome to hearers who could neither know nor remember it. In this confidence it is credible that he withdrew time to be spent in more fruitful worship of God from inventing new arguments and from the elaborate embellishment of words, for which—if there had been need—he was not unequal.”

Moreover, in St. Leo one may find several letters which, with a few additions or changes, repeat not merely the same thoughts but also the same words in a similar manner. Likewise, among his sermons are some from which much has been transferred word for word into letters, as you will learn from the notes placed in the margins of the sermons and letters in the latest edition. See certain other matters discussed on this same subject in Dissertation I, chapter 2, §2.

Finally—and this is especially relevant to the defense against several objections which could be raised, and which we proposed to consider in the general preface—one must distinguish between discourses collected and published by their authors and those which others published after the authors’ deaths, gathered from their papers. When authors published their own writings, they published only what was polished, refined, and complete; therefore one does not usually read in them anything repeated, gaping, or mutilated, as can be seen in the treatises of St. Gaudentius, which he delivered to Benivolus in the same century as our author. But when others made a collection, then, according to the merit and esteem in which authors were held by the collectors, everything whatever that they found could be gathered from their papers—even repetitions, mutilated pieces, and rough drafts—which the authors, had they been present, would have judged should be rejected or completed.

Zeno’s fame and the reverence shown him by all, however, seem to have been so great that the collector considered it a religious obligation to discard nothing found among his papers. Thus he judged that many repeated, mutilated, and wholly unfinished treatises should be inserted in the collection.

Now, to say something concerning the order of these treatises relating to the Paschal rites: first will be placed the Invitations to the Font together with two treatises on Psalm 41, which, since they concern the same matter, will bear the same title. Then will come seven treatises to the neophytes after baptism; then nine treatises on Easter Day; finally, fifteen treatises on Exodus and nine on Daniel at Easter. All of these splendidly present the image of the Paschal feast or of baptism from the readings from Exodus or Daniel solemnly recited during sacred rites. In publishing these treatises or addresses, we have not always followed the manuscript titles, since they are not consistent even in those treatises which contain nearly the same words, much less the same thoughts. The titles of the editions seemed more suitable, as will be clear from the notes on those titles.

## TREATISE XXX. Invitation to the Font I

> [Note: TREATISE XXX.—Besides this title, which occurs both in the manuscripts and in the editions, the Rheims codex has in its margin the following rubric: “To be recited by the bishop from the ambo to the children at the first delivery of the creed.” To understand this rubric, one must know that the creed was delivered by the bishop to chosen catechumens when they had been judged fit to receive baptism. It is not possible to establish universally on what day this was prescribed: some delivered it on Palm Sunday, others on the Wednesday after the fourth Sunday of Lent, still others on other days before Easter, as Father Martene observes, book I, chapter 1, article 11 and following. Some also delivered it once, others twice, and others three times, as he likewise notes. From this marginal rubric, which mentions the first delivery of the creed, it is entirely clear that at Verona it was delivered more than once.  
>
> The words of Ambrose, *Letter 20 to Marcellina*, imply that a bishop delivered some discourse before the handing over of the creed: “On the following day—it was Palm Sunday—after the readings and the discourse, when the catechumens had been dismissed, I was delivering the creed to certain candidates in the baptisteries of the basilica.” From the rubric cited, we learn that the bishops of Verona recited this treatise from the ambo before delivering the creed.]

Rejoice, brothers, in Christ; and, hastening with every desire, receive the heavenly gifts. Already the healing warmth of the everlasting font invites you. Already our mother adopts you in order to bear you—but not under the law by which your mothers bore you, mothers who themselves groaned with the pain of childbirth and brought you into this world crying, filthy, bound in filthy cloths, and enslaved to this world. Rather, joyful, rejoicing, heavenly, free from every sin, she will happily nourish you at the sweetly fragrant rails of the sacred altar, not in foul cradles, through our Lord Jesus Christ.

> [Note: Mother Church adopts those to be baptized in order to bear them, because she receives them as her own, admits and instructs them among the catechumens, and finally bears them when she begets them for Christ through the sacrament of baptism.]  
>
> [Note: Perhaps someone would read: “rejoicing, heavenly, free from every sin”—such as those truly become who receive baptism—so that there may be a contrast with the same number of adjectives set forth before: “crying, filthy, bound in filthy cloths, enslaved to this world.” But perhaps, just as “joyful,” so also “heavenly” and “free” refer to Mother Church: joyful because she brings forth rejoicing persons, heavenly and free because she brings into the world persons freed from every sin, certainly through baptism, whom she will nourish not in fetid cradles but at the sweetly fragrant rails of the sacred altar.]  
>
> [Note: One must read the active *enutritura* (“about to nourish”) rather than *enutrita* (“nourished”), which stood in the manuscripts and editions. For just as a mother nourishes her children in cradles after bearing them, so the Church is indicated as accustomed to nourish, by the sacrament of the sacred altar, the new children whom she begets through baptism. It is established that neophytes of old received the Eucharist immediately after baptism. It is also noteworthy that, at this time as well, the sacred altar in the church of Verona was enclosed by rails, lest the people, rushing tumultuously toward the altar, disturb the priest as he performed the sacred rites.]

## TREATISE XXXI. Invitation to the Font II

Enter, brothers, more swiftly than speech itself, through the ethereal gates. Do not suppose that those who immerse you in the generative channel of the eternal deep perform here any grace according to persons. Be born by your own judgment, knowing that whoever has believed more will make himself nobler. Therefore cast off steadfastly and faithfully this old human being of yours with his own foul garments; all of you are new, all candidates in white, all soon to come forth rich in the gift of the Holy Spirit.

> [Note: TREATISE XXXI.—Some manuscripts and editions had “into the ethereal [gates].” It seemed proper to delete from other manuscripts the word *ad* (“to”), which accords less well with the verb “enter.” Zeno appears to call the gates of the baptistery “ethereal,” because through them access is opened in baptism to the ethereal life, as he speaks elsewhere. Edmund Martene shows that the baptistery was generally a place separate from the church, *De Antiquis Ecclesiae Ritibus*, part I, book I, chapter 1, article 2. From this testimony it may reasonably be inferred that the baptistery of the church of Verona was such in Zeno’s time, since Zeno appears to address those about to be baptized within the church itself and nevertheless commands them to enter the ethereal gates—surely those of the baptistery—unless one prefers to think that this treatise was given outside the church or at its doors.]  
>
> [Note: All manuscripts with the editions read *ullam* (“any”), except the Patavine edition, where *vilem* (“base”) was substituted; but neither is satisfactory. Sparaverius preferred *capientes aquam* (“receiving water”) for *condentes ullam*, but that emendation is too free and departs too far from the manuscript text. We would rather write *conditi* (“being immersed”) for *condentes* (“immersing”), since similarly active forms with passive meaning occur in Treatise 35, and *undam* (“water”) for *ullam*: this would mean that Zeno exhorts the faithful, when they are immersed in the channel of the generative font, not to think that the water of that font works grace here—that is, in this sacrament—according to persons or with partiality, since in the following treatises he teaches that the sacrament regards neither lineage, age, nor sex. See Treatise 33 and especially Treatise 42: “Lest they appear to love anyone more or less, God’s providence grants to all one birth, one milk, one payment, one dignity of the Holy Spirit.”  
>
> In the present treatise, however, Zeno seems to imply, in order to exclude partiality, that greater grace can arise from merits alone, as we shall observe in the following note. The same thought may be reconciled with the received reading *ullam* if one construes it thus: “Do not suppose that those who immerse you—that is, those who immerse you in the generative channel of the eternal deep, or baptize you—perform here any grace according to persons.”]  
>
> [Note: The author says that the person who has believed more will be nobler, in order to suggest that the attainment of greater grace, if greater merits are present in someone, depends upon merits alone. Hence the words in Treatise 33: “As much as anyone has believed, so much blessedness will he also have.”]  
>
> [Note: The editions had “with foul garments,” but the codices add “their own,” a reading consistent with Paul’s words at Colossians 3:9, where the person about to take Christ’s name is commanded to put off the old human being with his deeds. Zeno’s allegory points to this.]  
>
> [Note: Neophytes are called *candidati* (“those clothed in white”) because they put on white garments as a sign of innocence; for the antiquity of this rite see Edmund Martene, *De Antiquis Ecclesiae Ritibus*, part I, book I, chapter 1, article 15, no. 5. Since neophytes received white garments not before but after baptism, the words “all new, all candidates in white,” and so forth, plainly refer to their imminent future coming forth, not to the present time.]

## 243. TREATISE XXXII. Invitation to the Font III

> [Note: TREATISE XXXII.—In the manuscripts: “Invitation of the font of the one mentioned above,” that is, of Zeno mentioned earlier. This same treatise is recited in the *Life of Zeno*, written about the twelfth century and published by Scipio Maffei among the shorter works appended to his *History of Diplomatic Matters*, p. 320. From this document we shall provide variant readings in the following notes, marked by the syllable *Vit.* The treatise appears there much longer, but its author compiled it from two treatises of Zeno: this entire one and a portion of Treatise 48, as we have noted in the Preface to the Documents. This will become still clearer from Treatise 48 itself, where the relevant words are marked.]

Come now, why do you stand still, brothers—you whom the generative wave conceived through faith, and now bears through the sacraments? Hasten as quickly as possible to the Things Desired.

> [Note: The *Life* reads “you whom [he conceived] through faith.” But the manuscript reading is better: it presents Zenonian syntax and omits the superfluous and harsh-sounding *vos* (“you”). At the end of MS Pompeianus is found the same *Life*, written by a Zenonian monk; there too *vos* is omitted. Shortly afterward the *Life* has *concipit* (“conceives”) for *concepit* (“conceived”).]  
>
> [Note: This word refers to the sacred mysteries of the liturgy. Thus, in the Greek-Latin Glossary, *Desiderata* is explained as *λειτουργία τελετή*, that is, “the completion of the liturgy or public sacred ministry,” because those instructed according to the discipline of the sacred liturgy sought this completion with the greatest desire. Among pagans, the *epoptai* mentioned by Tertullian at the beginning of *Against the Valentinians* were instructed by priests through an entire five years before initiation, in order by this means to intensify their desire. Similarly, catechumens among Christians were tested for a long time so that, as Gregory the Great says, *Letters* VII.34, “the longer the festival awaited by them, the more they ought to prepare themselves and sustain it with fervent desire.”  
>
> Thus *Desiderata* (“the Things Desired”) means baptism and any other sacrament, but especially, by antonomasia, the Eucharist. Casaubon observed, *Exercise 16 on Baronius’s Annals*, no. 45, p. 501, that the Fathers used the language of desiring particularly and frequently for this sacrament. Here, since the holy bishop addresses persons whom he says are not only conceived through faith but are already being born through the sacraments—that is, through baptism—it is plain that the *Desiderata* to which he urges them to hasten as swiftly as possible is nothing other than the sacred Eucharist, to which they were admitted scarcely after being baptized, as we noted in note 4 on Treatise 30.  
>
> Tertullian’s words in *To His Wife* II.6 are relevant: “From whose hand will she desire?” Just as *desiderabit* (“she will desire”) there means “she will receive the Eucharist,” so Zeno could use *Desiderata* for reception of the Eucharist. How especially great was the desire for the Eucharist is learned from the author of the books *On the Sacraments*, included among Ambrose’s works, book IV, chapter 2, no. 7: “You came, then, desiring the altar … you came desiring the altar, that you might receive the sacrament.” Why the Eucharist was called *Desiderata* rather than by its proper name must be referred to the discipline of secrecy, by which the holy Fathers took care not expressly to name Christ’s body and blood, especially when speaking to persons not yet initiated.]  
>
> [Note: In the Antiphonary published by Cardinal Thomasius, p. 66, the following is recorded concerning the singing of a hymn after the rite of baptism: “When baptism has been completed, the verse follows:
>
> *Hear the voices of the hymn,*  
> *You also who are worthy,*  
> *On this blessed night* …”]

“Come down to the fonts,” etc.] Behold, the solemn hymn is already being sung; behold, the voice of infants and sweet crying is heard; behold, a most illustrious throng issues from one womb of her who gives birth. It is a new thing: that each person should rightly be born by the Spirit. Run eagerly to the mother, who does not then labor, even if she cannot count those whom she bears. Enter, therefore; enter, happy ones, all of you who are at once to become nursing children.

[Note: We have corrected, following Vit. and the manuscript Sp., “the voice of infants and sweet crying,” where the printed edition and other manuscripts read “soon the sweet crying of infants.” A little later Vit. reads “of her who is in labor” for “of her who gives birth,” and “is reborn” for “is born.”]

## TRACTATE XXXIII

[Note: TRACTATE XXXIII.—The manuscripts wrongly entitle this “To the Neophytes,” although it is, like the others, an Invitation to the Font, delivered to persons not yet baptized. We have therefore preferred here the title of the printed editions.]

### Invitation to the Font IV

Why do you stand still, diverse in origin, age, sex, and condition, though you are shortly to become one? Hasten together to the sweet womb of the font of the ever-virgin Mother; and there ennoble yourselves, knowing by faith that each shall possess as much blessedness as he has believed. O admirable and truly divine, most holy condescension! In it she who gives birth does not groan; he who is reborn does not know how to weep. This renewal, this resurrection, this eternal life—this is the mother of all, who afterward makes us, gathered together from every people and nation, into one body.

[Note: Manuscript Urbin.: “Why do you stand?”]

[Note: The Venetian edition reads *nobilitari*, “to be ennobled,” wrongly. But *nobilitate* is here a verb in the imperative, not a noun.]

[Note: After the words “as much as he has believed,” the Verona editors added “and wrought,” contrary to the testimony of all manuscripts and of the first edition. For more on this see Dissertation 2, chapter 6, where we have elsewhere sufficiently defended Zeno’s teaching on this doctrine.]

## TRACTATE XXXIV

[Note: This tractate is entitled “On Baptism” in the manuscripts. But lest we disturb the sequence of invitations, we have retained the title of the editions, to which the tractate indeed corresponds.]

### Invitation to the Font V

Exult, brethren, whom your own faith brings to birth; you who, fleeing the snares, guilt, wounds, and death of this world, have implored the aid of the Father’s majesty. Hasten to the pool of the holy font, not with the speed of your feet but of your mind. Steadfastly immerse yourselves, so that, with your state of salvation preserved, you may conquer by the happy death of your old man.

[Note: Learn from this that Zeno employed baptism by immersion; further testimonies concerning this rite will appear below.]

[Note: Here reference is made to Paul’s passage at Colossians 3:9, where the “old man” is understood as the man according to sinful Adam, in whom we all died; when that man is killed through baptism, we begin the heavenly life.]

## TRACTATE XXXV

[Note: TRACTATE XXXV.—This tractate and the following one are entitled “On Psalm XLI” in the manuscripts Rem., Tol., Vat., and Urbin. There is also extant in the Appendix to vol. VI of St. Augustine, p. 287 (our edition, vol. VI, col. 1203), a sermon to Neophytes by a very ancient author on that psalm. The allusion is to the words of that same psalm: “As the deer longs for springs of water”; these words were sung not only formerly, as we learn from certain ancient orders in Martene, part IV, chapter 24, but are sung even today on Holy Saturday when the blessing of baptismal water begins.

It should further be noted that this tractate is entitled “On the forty-first Psalm” in the index of the Reims manuscript, whereas the other tractate which follows is entitled “Tractate on the fortieth Psalm”; the Vatican Basilica manuscript places the latter title at the head of this very tractate. Hence John of Verona, in manuscript *History of the Empire*, book I, and William Pastrengo, drawing from him, list among Zeno’s sermons tractates on Psalm XL and Psalm XLI. Yet it is evident that both these tractates, though delivered on the occasion of Psalm XLI, are invitations to the font; indeed, Tractate 37, which repeats Tractate 36 that follows in almost identical words, is entitled “Invitation to the Font” in all manuscripts. Therefore, continuing the sequence of invitations, we have retained this title, which alone is found in the manuscripts Pomp. and Zen. and in all the printed editions.

Finally, the Reims manuscript attaches to the present tractate this marginal rubric, from which it appears that it passed into a formula used by our bishops when they were about to administer baptism at Pentecost. For we read in that ancient manuscript: “To be recited by the bishop to children before baptism at Pentecost.”]

### Invitation to the Font VI

Hurry, hurry, brethren who are soon to be well washed. Living water, tempered by the Holy Spirit and the sweetest fire, already invites you with its gentle murmur. The attendant of the bath, girded for service, awaits you, ready to provide what is needed for anointing and drying, and also a golden denarius stamped with the union of a threefold coinage. Rejoice, therefore. You will indeed go down naked into the font, but you will soon rise from it as candidates clothed in a heavenly garment; and whoever does not stain it shall possess the kingdoms of heaven: through the Lord Jesus Christ.

[Note: Without doubt one must read *luendi*, “to be washed,” since the address is to brethren to be washed by baptism. The manuscripts Rem., Tol., and Vat. wrongly read *locuturi*, “about to speak,” which had also been written in the Pompeian manuscript in the first hand.]

[Note: From this passage we learn that the water in the baptistery was warmed somewhat, lest those immersed in it—especially children—should suffer any harm from the cold; we do not recall observing this elsewhere. For the purpose indicated, we suppose that the water was tempered with a most sweet, that is, gentle, fire. It is scarcely conceivable that Zeno applied fire to the water with the intention held by certain ancient heretics, who, on the basis of Luke 3:16, “But you shall be baptized in the Holy Spirit and fire,” supposed that water in baptism was insufficient unless fire were added to it, so that scarcely had anyone descended into the font when fire appeared. This may be inferred from the ancient author of the book *On Rebaptism*, in the Appendix to Cyprian, p. 643 (our edition, vol. III, col. 1183).

What, moreover, was that gentle murmur—or, as it is called in the following tractate, sweet murmur—by which those to be baptized were sufficiently invited? It cannot be understood of bubbling, which deters rather than invites and does not involve a moderate warmth. It must rather be understood of some flowing of the baptismal water, so that it could be called “living water,” or, as in the following tractate, a stream and an overflowing river. This continual flow of water, especially in great cities, was introduced by the large multitude of candidates for baptism, lest all should be immersed in the same water, which would have caused nausea to some. Hence also the proper designation “font,” from which ever-new water flowed. Certain monuments suggest that water carried through channels flowed continuously into the baptistery as needed. In the *Life of St. Avitus of Vienne*, chapter 5, a baptistery with an aqueduct is mentioned; and Ennodius, Epigram 145, speaking of the font of St. Stephen, mentions water flowing through columns. The *Liber Pontificalis* relates that silver stags pouring water into the baptistery’s font were made by Innocent I and Sixtus III.]

[Note: This testimony of Zeno is cited by Laurentius Pignorius in his commentary *On Slaves*, p. 38 of the second Paduan edition, to explain from it the office of the bath-attendant. A *balneator* was a slave who was in charge of baths and served their needs; see further Ursinus in the Appendix to Ciacconius, *On the Triclinium*, p. 159; Gronovius, vol. IX, p. 641; Salmasius on Lampridius, *Commodus*, chapter 7; and others, who almost all cite this exceptionally clear testimony of Zeno. Apuleius mentions the same rite in nearly the same words in *Metamorphoses*, book I, p. 49, although he does not use the name *balneator*: “Straightway I hand him over to the bath, providing in advance what is needed for anointing and drying; I laboriously scrub away the enormous filth.” The utensils of the bath are indicated: namely, the oil-flask, the toothed strigil, and the linen cloths with which the ancients dried themselves.

In this tractate, moreover, the term *balneator* seems metaphorically to signify the bishop, who alone baptized; for baptismal washing is very probably here envisaged under the image of a bath. The sacred anointing of baptism, which the author mentions, partly preceded and partly followed it. The former was that by which Latins anointed the breast and between the shoulders, while Greeks anointed the whole body; see Martene, part I, book I, chapter 1, article 13, no. 10. The latter followed, being repeated on the crown of the head before the white garment, apart from that which was immediately added when the baptized person was at once confirmed with holy chrism; see the authors cited by Martene in the place mentioned, article 15, nos. 2 and 11.

Yet perhaps another washing is meant, by which in some places the feet, and sometimes the head, of candidates for baptism or neophytes were washed before baptism, and in others after it; for this rite read the author mentioned above, article 13, no. 1, and article 15, no. 8. But since the washing that preceded baptism took place some days before it, and perhaps was in use even where the other post-baptismal washing was not observed, whereas Zeno here speaks of a washing which, if distinct from baptism, was nevertheless performed on the same day, there can be little doubt that he indicates here the washing which an ancient author of the books *On the Sacraments*, among Ambrose’s works, expressly says was performed after baptism and before the presentation of the white garment by the bishop with garments tucked up, book III, chapter 1: “You came up from the font. What followed? … the chief priest, I say, with his garments tucked up, washed your feet.” Ambrose agrees with this in *On the Mysteries*, chapter 6. If the author of *On the Sacraments* testifies that this custom was foreign to the Roman Church, that does not prevent its having been practiced at Verona by Zeno; and churches besides the Milanese followed the same rite, as is evident from the Gothic and Old Gallican Missals, where there are formulas to be said when the feet of neophytes are washed.]
