[Note: We discussed this type of denarius at length in note 21 on Tractate 14, book I, where from other Zenonian testimonies, which call the same denarius a *stipendium*, “payment,” we conjectured not implausibly that an actual denarius was given at baptism. But mention here of a golden denarius creates difficulty. For it is altogether incredible, in view of the bishop’s scarcity and poverty, sufficiently treated elsewhere, that in so great a number of baptizands he should liberally have given a golden denarius to each. Since holy Zeno frequently uses allegories, the denarius evidently must here be understood allegorically; the phrase “stamped with the union of a threefold coinage” likewise indicates this, for it cannot be understood of a real golden denarius.

Accordingly, some may perhaps understand the Eucharist, which Ernulf, bishop of Rochester, records in his letter to Lambert as given in the form of a coin, *Spicilegium* of d’Achery, vol. III, p. 471 of the latest edition, or “in the manner of a denarius,” as Honorius says, book I of *The Jewel of the Soul*, chapter 66. Perhaps the Eucharist displayed three circles corresponding to the union of a threefold coinage. But besides the fact that these testimonies are of a much later age, St. Zeno in Tractate 14 speaks of the denarius in such a way as sufficiently to distinguish it from the Eucharistic bread; see notes 18 and 19 there.

Perhaps grace is better understood, which was most generously bestowed through the threefold sacrament of baptism, confirmation, and Eucharist, all conferred on the same day. But whatever may be understood of the mystical interpretation, one may still say that some denarius was given together with baptism, though it was golden and stamped with the union of a threefold coinage only in its mystical meaning. These remarks are offered as mere conjecture, not as an assertion. Let others devise better explanations; if they offer anything more probable, we shall receive it with open arms.]

[Note: Manuscript Rem. reads *demergetis*, “you will immerse”; the others, together with the editions, read *demergitis*, “you immerse.” Both are wrong, and one must read *demergemini*, “you will be immersed.” For one who baptizes another by immersion is said to immerse the candidate, while here the candidate is said to be immersed. It is universally known that those about to receive baptism were naked when immersed in the font.]

[Note: It is clear from what follows—“whoever does not stain it”—that the garment of innocence and grace is indicated here, without, however, excluding the white garment placed upon the baptized, which represented innocence and grace. Zeno is accustomed to have in view at once both the thing and its mystical meaning, so that he says some things applicable both to the thing itself and to mystical speech, and others which can be referred only to the mystical significance of the thing; this is especially frequent in these tractates.]

## TRACTATE XXXVI

[Note: TRACTATE XXXVI.—On this title see our observations in note 1 to the preceding tractate. In the margin of the Reims manuscript this too is added: “To be recited by the bishop to children before baptism.”]

### Invitation to the Font VII

Come now, brethren, whom the desired heat of blessed thirst inflames, whom the sweet murmur of the nectar-like stream invites: hasten without delay to the milky water of the generative font. Drink deeply and bravely while it is permitted; subjected to the waves of the overflowing river, fill your vessels with all your energy and all your devotion, so that water may always suffice you. Know this before all else: you may neither pour this out nor draw it again.

[Note: In the editions and some manuscripts: “hasten together; and without delay.” But other codices write *convolate incunctanter*, “hasten without delay,” as one phrase and without the conjunction *and*. We should have inserted the conjunction more willingly before “while it is permitted,” or before “of the overflowing,” had any manuscripts supported it.]

[Note: What is taught here and in what follows—that one may not draw baptismal water again—plainly indicates the Catholic doctrine that baptism cannot be conferred a second time. Other Fathers expressed the same point in other formulas. At the end the Pompeian codex adds “Amen.”]

## TRACTATE XXXVII

[Note: TRACTATE XXXVII.—The manuscripts bear a double title: “Tractate for Easter,” or “Invitation to the Font.” See note 1 on Tractate 35.]

### Invitation to the Font VIII

With very few additions and certain changes, this contains what appears in the preceding tractate.

Come now, brethren, whom the desired heat of blessed thirst inflames: with the longing and swiftness of a deer, hasten to the milky water of the generative font. Drink bravely, so that water may always suffice you, knowing chiefly this: that it is permitted neither to pour it out nor to draw it again.

[Note: “Of a deer,” he says, looking to the words of Psalm XLI: “As the deer longs for springs of water,” etc.]

[Note: The Reims manuscript adds: “Here ends St. Zeno’s Easter tractate.”]

## TRACTATE XXXVIII

[Note: TRACTATE XXXVIII.—Here and in the following tractate we have retained the title of the Verona edition; in the manuscripts, however, it is “Tractate after baptism has been conferred.” That Zeno delivered this tractate on Easter Day itself is evident from its opening period. This marginal rubric is also found in the Reims codex: “To be recited by the bishop at Easter to children after baptism.”]

### To the Neophytes after Baptism I

After the most devout and chaste fasts of sacred expiation have been completed; after the sweet vigils of the most brilliant night, with its own sun; after your souls, through the life-giving washing of the milky font, have sprung forth into hope of immortality—you who were diverse in age and diverse in nation have suddenly emerged as brothers born of the same womb, suddenly as only-begotten infants. I exhort you to celebrate the feast of so great a birth with joyful banqueting; but not with that banquet in which the chest, burdened by the rivalry of various dishes striving for supremacy through the seductive flavor of highly seasoned foods, is often oppressed by undigested and sour vomitings; in which the worldly sweetness of your new wine is spoiled by the fetid vapor of yesterday’s wine. Rather, celebrate with a heavenly meal: honorable, pure, healthful, and perpetual. Receive it hungering, so that you may always be full and happy.

The master of the household lavishly supplies you, from his provisions and his table, with precious bread and wine. The three unanimous youths are first to bring legumes, sprinkling them with the salt of wisdom that their flavor may be pleasing. Christ pours in oil. Moses quickly procured the firstborn and mature lamb. Abraham faithfully provides a fattened and seasoned calf. Isaac innocently carries the oil and the wood. Jacob patiently presents varied flocks. Joseph, advanced in rank, apportions grain to all by measure. Indeed, if anyone should desire anything, Noah, keeper of the ark, will not refuse him anything. Peter the fisherman abundantly sets before you fresh sea-fish with a remarkable sardine. Tobias the traveler carefully prepares and roasts the entrails of a river fish. John, the keeper of camels, devoutly running ahead, brought honey and locusts from the forest. Paul, the inviter, admonishes that one who does not eat should not reproach one who eats. David, the royal shepherd, at every moment supplies everyone with silvery milk and cheese. Zacchaeus without delay distributes fourfold farewell-gifts. God and our Lord Jesus Christ, the Son of God, distributes sweets, as he says who was first fed at this meal before us—namely David, whose words to God are these: “How sweet are your words to my palate, more than honey and the honeycomb to my mouth!” (Ps. 118:103).

Brethren, whoever gladly believes these things will find still more abundant foods; if he is diligent with them, he will always satisfy both himself and others with every good thing: through our Lord Jesus Christ.

[Note: Here the completion of the Lenten fast is plainly indicated. It may perhaps be called “chaste” because even married persons practiced continence during the Lenten fast; for another substantial testimony of Zeno on this, see note 53 on Tractate IV, book I. Three codices read *contemplata*, “contemplated,” for *completa*, “completed.”]

[Note: Zeno calls it “most brilliant”; St. Gaudentius, Sermon V, p. 60, calls it “the most splendid night of vigils.” This sufficiently shows that Christians were accustomed to kindle a very great number of candles and lamps during the vigil of the Easter feast. St. Gregory Nazianzen, Oration II, *On Easter*, explicitly mentions the same custom, and something similar is found in the preface of the *Exsultet*, still sung today at the blessing of the candle. Although Constantine the Great was not yet a catechumen but was devoted to Christ, he ordered, to give a splendid proof of his piety toward him, that candles and lamps be lit in such abundance not only in church but throughout the whole city that, as Eusebius relates in book IV, chapter 22, of his *Life of Constantine*, “that mystic vigil was made more splendid than any day, however splendid.” Ammianus Marcellinus, book XIV, records that in his age the custom flourished at Rome of lighting lamps throughout the city every night for public convenience: “the brightness of lights burning through the night is accustomed to imitate the radiance of day.” But either this practice did not exist, at least in that city, in Constantine’s age, or he ordered the celebration of Easter night to be heightened by more lights, so that it might become brighter than the brightest day.

The splendor of this night in the churches came not so much from the lamps or candles of the churches themselves as from the candles of the neophytes. These, lit along with the church lamps in great numbers—for very many persons were baptized together at that time—marvelously increased the brilliance of the sacred place. For these candles of neophytes, see Ambrose, *On the Fall of a Virgin*, chapter 5, to omit other writers cited by Martene, part I, book I, chapter 1, article 15, nos. 9 and 10. Of the vigils held on this night we say only that they are so ancient that Jerome, on Matthew 25:6, taught that they were handed down by the apostles; there too he testifies that this rite arose from a similar Jewish practice. Epiphanius likewise, *Heresies* LXX, §10, attributes it to the Apostolic Constitution, from which a similar ordinance among the Clementines, book V, chapter 19, appears to have been taken; there these same Easter vigils are expressly commanded.]

[Note: In Tractate 33 the holy bishop addressed those whom he was to baptize at Verona as diverse in origin, age, sex, and condition. Here he adds diversity of nation, which seemed worth noting, in order that it may appear that persons came even from distant lands to this city to be baptized—unless perhaps this is to be understood of persons of other nations who had come to dwell at Verona or happened to be staying there for another reason.]

[Note: Augustine, Sermon CCXXVIII, no. 1: “Those who a little while ago were called *competentes* are now called infants. … They are called infants because they have now been born to Christ, whereas before they had been born to the world.” This formula derives from 1 Peter 2:2: “Like newborn infants.” Augustine also has several sermons entitled “On Easter Day, to the Infants.” See Clement of Alexandria, *Paedagogue*, book I, chapter 4, where he defends this infancy of neophytes, as it was called even then, against pagan criticisms.]

[Note: Manuscript Rem.: “to celebrate the joyful feast with a banquet.” The banquet here denotes the Eucharist, which was given to the Neophytes after the night vigils on Easter Day itself. Tertullian also calls it by this name in book II *To His Wife*, as do Optatus, book V, Ambrose, book I, *On Abel and Cain*, and others. The author shortly afterward calls it a meal in the same sense. In the Appendix to Cyprian, p. 268 of the Venetian edition (our edition, vol. IV, col. 926), something similar is explained under the name of supper by various symbols of foods, all referring to and signifying the same thing.]

[Note: Thus from manuscript Rem.; the other codices and the editions have *nutrimentorum*, “of foods,” except manuscript Pomp., where the first hand wrote *intrimentorum*, but a later hand wrongly substituted *nutrimentorum*. *Intrimentum* is a kind of very tasty seasoning, as may be understood from Apuleius, *Metamorphoses*, book X: “He softened stews seasoned with most savory *intrimenta* in their juicy steam.”]

[Note: The frequent intemperance of profane feasts, generally followed by vomiting, is noted here. Shortly afterward, before the words “of your new wine,” three manuscripts wrongly add “not new wine.”]

[Note: The master of the household here seems to be called Melchizedek, who is said in Genesis 14:18 to have brought forth bread and wine. He was a figure of Christ instituting the Eucharist under both kinds, which was in fact formerly given to Neophytes under both kinds.]

[Note: In manuscript Rem. it is *aginam*, but this was written through a copyist’s error. For *agina*, with a single *n*, is the upper part of a balance upon which equilibrium turns, or the scales. But *agninum* means whatever belongs to lambs, as in Horace, *Epistles*, book I, 15.35, *omasi agnini*, “lamb tripe”; and in Plautus, *Aulularia* II.5.4, *agnina* alone means lamb flesh. The passage intended is Exodus 12, where a lamb is commanded to be eaten at Passover. Zeno repeatedly teaches in the tractates on Exodus, which follow, that this lamb had to be firstborn; all know that the lamb was a symbol of Christ and of the Eucharist.]

[Note: Pignorius thinks that *praemotus* should be corrected to *promotus*, “advanced,” and *praerogat*, “apportions.” For stewards were called *prorogatores*, “distributors,” as he demonstrates by many examples.]

[Note: Noah is called *arcarius*, “keeper of the ark,” as its maker and overseer. The Romans called *arcarii* stewards who presided over the administration either of the state or of a household, and who, as supervisors of the store-room, chest, or cellar, managed the distribution of necessary things. Noah is wittily said not to be about to deny anything if something should be wanted at the banquet, as though he could bring out from the ark, in accordance with need or desire, any kind of animal that had been stored there. The Venetian and Verona editions, together with most manuscripts, read *negavit*, “did not deny,” for *negabit*, “will not deny”; we corrected this from manuscript Tol. and the Paduan edition.]

[Note: In Pliny, book VIII, chapter 27 and book XXX, chapter 7, *interanea* means the inner parts, that is, entrails or viscera.]

[Note: A *camelarius*, according to Digest, last law, §10, *On Public Services and Burdens*, is one who has charge of camels and cares for them. John is perhaps called a *camelarius* here because he wore a garment of camel hair; Matthew 3:4.]

[Note: The Venetian edition reads *devoret*, “devour,” but wrongly; the reference is to Paul’s passage at Romans 14:3: “Let not him who does not eat judge him who eats.”]

[Note: *Apophoreta* are the little gifts given after a formal meal which may be carried home. Hence Ambrose, *Exhortation to Virginity*, no. 7: “Those invited to a great banquet are accustomed to take *apophoreta* home with them.” Thus, to signify that nothing is lacking from this banquet, St. Zeno records that Zacchaeus finally brings to it fourfold—that is, most abundant—*apophoreta*. The word *expungit*, “he distributes,” must here be understood as “he distributes the farewell-gifts among the diners,” as another similar passage from Tractate 53 plainly suggests, where he is expressly said to *expungere munera*, “distribute gifts”; see note 2 there, where we establish this meaning.]

[Note: On the authority of the Vatican manuscript we inserted the word *dulcia*, “sweets,” which was plainly missing. Thus it is suitably understood that Jesus Christ, the Son of God, at the end of the banquet distributes sweets—*dulcia*, a word customarily used substantively for sweet things, as may be shown from Lampridius, *Life of Heliogabalus*, chapter 27—as he says, or calls them, who was fed at this meal before us, namely David, whose words to God are: “How sweet are [your words] to my palate,” etc.]

[Note: In Hilary too, on Psalm CXVIII, letter 13, p. 355, in the text of the psalm itself which is prefixed, the same reading occurs: “More than honey and the honeycomb to my mouth.” Although the words “and the honeycomb” are absent from the explanation of letter 13 itself, p. 359, no. 11, Hilary’s explanation of letter 17 plainly indicates that he read “and the honeycomb,” in these words, p. 388, no. 5: “The word of God plucks bitterness from the heart, which delights the mouth beyond honey and the honeycomb.”]

[Note: Manuscript Vat. adds: “who reigns with you for ages of ages.”]

## TRACTATE XXXIX

[Note: TRACTATE XXXIX.—Most manuscripts begin “On Baptism”; John of Verona and his copyists Pastrengo and Peter de Natalibus agree with them, listing two tractates on Baptism. One Zenonian manuscript, with the first edition, entitles it “After baptism has been conferred.” We have retained the title of the Verona edition, lest we interrupt the sequence of tractates to the Neophytes by changing the title; this is to be understood also of what follows.]

### To the Neophytes after Baptism II
Rightly does the most holy David say: “Blessed are those whose iniquities are forgiven and whose sins are covered” (Ps. XXXI.1). For, brothers, one who remains in the first birth cannot be blessed: he whom the blazing torch of seething offenses scorches at every moment; who carries with him the stench of his own prison; who feels the executioner before he sees him; who dreads the name of the judge; who, wherever a whisper arises, thinks that he is being sought, thinks that he has been found; for whom there is no advance toward security, even should it happen that he lacks an accuser or a witness privy to his deeds, since he cannot lack himself—because conscience, more violent than every torturer, never abandons its sinner.

[Note: [Col. 0486C] The reading was *fex* (“dregs”). Sparaverius’s emendation has been preferred; see him, if you wish.]

In this guilt, brothers, you have been until now. But you have been courageously examined; and, that you might receive pardon, you kept watch well on your own behalf, and you were heard most favorably.

[Note: [Col. 0486C–D] The examination of catechumens, performed in the scrutinies, is noted here. For more on it see Martene, *De Antiquis Ecclesiae Ritibus*, part 1, book I, chapter 1, article 11.]

A new kind of judgment: in it the accused person is condemned if he excuses his crime, and acquitted if he confesses it.

[Note: [Col. 0486D–0487C] The confession of sins preceding baptism is indicated here. On this more fully, see Treatises 40 and 41. Tertullian, *On Baptism*, chapter 20: “Those about to enter baptism ought to pray with frequent prayers, fastings, kneelings, and vigils, and with confession of all their former offenses.” The ancient author of the sermon on Psalm XLI addressed to the Neophytes, in the Appendix to vol. VI of the works of St Augustine, p. 287 (in our edition, vol. VI, col. 1203), agrees. Speaking of the same persons and of what they were like during Lent before baptism, he says: “Throughout the whole Lent they devoted themselves to prayer and fasting; they slept in sackcloth and ashes, seeking the life to come by confession of their sins.” From this we think it may be inferred that their manner of confession was not such that, by the necessity of baptism, they had to confess everything, [Col. 0487B] but rather that, setting forth their former life in the scrutinies, they might inquire what they ought to abandon, what to follow, and what rule of life they ought to adopt, so that they might truly put on the Christian person.

A contemporary author, St Ambrose, seems to remember this rite when, in book VI on Luke, chapter 3, he says: “Therefore God is justified in baptism, in which there is confession and forgiveness of sins.” So too St Gregory Nazianzen, in his discourse on the holy washing, addressing one to be baptized: “Do not disdain to disclose your sin, knowing how John baptized, so that by present confession you may escape the future”; by these words a new form of confession is proposed. Eusebius, *History*, book V, chapter 17, recounting an occasion on which many were converted to the Christian religion, says of them: “Confessing their sins, they received Christ’s baptism.” We omit other examples and testimonies of this kind that might be offered.]

O great power, great wisdom, [Col. 0487A] great mercy of our Judge! Sinners of every kind hasten to be punished by him, that they may be able to live blessedly.

[Note: [Col. 0487C–D] Penance is indicated, imposed upon adults seeking baptism before they received it, as is clear from the testimonies cited in the preceding note. Other witnesses are discussed at length by Fr. Martene, book I, chapter 1, article 10, no. 10. We judge that the purpose of imposing this penance was not only that those seeking baptism might make some satisfaction for their sins and at the same time show whether they truly detested their former life and sought baptism, but also that flesh nourished in vices, subdued by this mortification, might become accustomed to serve the spirit.

Some trace the institution of this penance to Peter’s command, as we learn from Herivaeus of Rheims’s letter to Witton of Rouen, chapter 6. There he reports that Clovis remained for several days with St Remigius before baptism, in order first to be washed by tears of penance according to the apostolic command, as Blessed Peter, prince of the apostles, said: “Repent, and let every one of you be baptized.” Certainly penance of this kind is commanded to be imposed and undertaken before baptism in the so-called Apostolic Constitutions, book VII, chapter 32, and in many other canonical decrees. This discipline remained so vigorous for many centuries that the author of the *Sermon on the Dedication of a Church*, believed by some to be St Caesarius, no. 5, did not hesitate to declare one who despises such penance guilty of no slight sin.]

For the merciful sword descends into the sinner’s inward parts, and with one and the same stroke—while the substance of the body remains unharmed—it kills the old person, creates a new one, and buries him in the element of the sacred pool. And although the nature of all waters is such that, when they have received living persons into their depth, they cast them out dead, our water receives the dead and casts them out living: from animals made true human beings, from human beings destined to pass into angels, if the advancing course of their life does not alter their infancy.

[Note: [Col. 0487D] The manuscripts of Rheims and the Vatican read *receperit*, “has received.”]

[Note: [Col. 0487D–0488B] That is, if they do not change into malice and sin the baptismal innocence or grace by which, according to 1 Peter II.2, they are called newborn infants. The Pompignan manuscript adds at the end: “Amen.”]

## 255. TREATISE XL

[Note: [Col. 0488B] TREATISE XL.—Thus the Verona edition; the manuscripts bear the title “On Baptism.” The Venetian edition, with the Zenonian manuscript: “After baptism has been conferred.”]

To the Neophytes after Baptism, III.

[Col. 0487B] Let us rejoice, brothers, in Christ; and with hymns, lyres, timbrels, and songs let us render thanks to the everlasting conqueror, who, fulfilling his promises, has sent us truly golden keys by a merciful ordinance, as they say.

[Note: [Col. 0488B–C] Strictly speaking, a *sanctio* is a law with a penalty attached. Justinian, *Institutes*, book II.1: “Therefore we call sanctions those parts of laws by which we establish penalties against those who act contrary to the laws.” That this was also the proper designation among earlier writers may be inferred from this passage of Zeno: by inserting a parenthesis, as they say, and calling the ordinance of the keys “merciful” according to ordinary usage, he notes a formula widespread in his time.

Although the ordinance of the keys included some penalty, by which not only those who had sinned after baptism but also those approaching baptism with their own sins were subjected to penance, as we showed in note 5 on the preceding treatise, yet, since this penalty was extremely light in comparison with the gravity of the crimes and was exacted not as punishment but rather for the person’s benefit, Zeno rightly called it what it was commonly called: the merciful ordinance of the keys.]

Not indeed those keys which, by a baneful favor, admit crimes; which spare the body but cannot free the soul; which, while passing sins over by concealing them, [Col. 0488A] do not take them away but shut them in; which dismiss the guilty person exactly as they found him; which, in the same case, can be of no benefit to their very bestower. But ours absolve in a mass whatever they find, and permit nothing to remain over; they open every innermost chamber of hearts, carefully expel every crime, and then carefully shut it again, lest anything, however trifling, of what has been expelled should return there.

[Note: [Col. 0488C–D] Some manuscripts read *subsicivi*; others think that *succisivi* or *subcisivi* should be read. Notice here the power of the keys in baptism: when they absolve in a mass whatever they find, nothing residual or remaining is left, whether as to guilt or penalty. Furthermore, after all crimes have once been erased, they allow none of them to revive. This is plainly indicated by the words: “They carefully expel every crime, and then carefully shut it again, lest anything, however trifling, of what has been expelled should return there.” A little later the Toledo and Vatican manuscripts read *peccatorum* (“of sinners”) for *pector[u]m* (“of hearts”); the Toledo manuscript with the Venetian edition reads *accludunt* (“shut in”) for *occludunt* (“shut”).]

A marvelous principle, a marvelous blessedness! While the accused person remains safe, the guilt is punished in the accused person; and, while his state remains whole, that by reason of which the human being was destined to die dies within him.

[Note: [Col. 0488D] The reading was *in eo* (“in him”), but the Toledo, Vatican, Urbino, Pompignan, Spanish, and Zenonian codices write *in reo* (“in the accused”), and all manuscripts and printed editions have the same reading in the following treatise, where this same meaning is expressed in precisely the same words.]

Hence [256] our confession has no need of tortures: without the sweat of a torturer, the accused spontaneously confesses his crimes in order that he may become innocent.

[Note: [Col. 0488D] The subject here is the confession made by catechumens before baptism, since this treatise was delivered to Neophytes recently baptized, as is clear from its title and conclusion. On this confession we have said enough in note 4 on the preceding treatise.]

Precious is the pardon, brothers, which grants both forgiveness [Col. 0488B] and healing. But if a person spares a poisoner, a murderer, an adulterer, an incestuous person, or a sacrilegious person, without curing his mind, I do not see what benefit he has conferred upon him.

O profound providence of our Deliverer! O singular excellence! O sweet sentence! O necessary condemnation! A human being is slain in order that he may live. The striker and the striker’s sword are not seen; the wound of the one struck [Col. 0489A] does not gape, blood does not flow, and his color does not grow pale. He is the same person, and yet he is not the same. The dwelling indeed appears old, but its inhabitant is new, showing by diverse virtues to unbelievers, through a change of conduct, the nobility of his birth.

[Note: [Col. 0488D–0489B] Understand: the striker is not seen, nor is the striker’s sword seen. The Pompignan manuscript writes, without a conjunction, “the wound of the struck does not gape”; but perhaps the following treatise should be read: “The striker is not seen, the striker’s sword is not perceived, the wound of the struck does not gape.”]

[Note: [Col. 0489B] The new inhabitant is Christ through grace, by which he dwells in the baptized. Hence it is clear to whom the relative *cuius*, which follows, refers: “whose ordinance,” etc.]

Keep his ordinance, while the whole course of your life remains ever in its infancy; and carefully guard against ever recalling the memory of your former first human being.

[Note: [Col. 0489B–C] “The first human being,” that is, sinful Adam, was once yours—that is, the baptized persons’—because before baptism the Neophytes were sinners as Adam was and bore the person of the old human being, in Paul’s phrase. They put this off in order to put on Christ, the new human being, in baptism. Zeno exhorts them to remember this and not to return from grace to sin. See Ephesians IV.22, 24, and Colossians III.9.]

## 257. TREATISE XLI

[Note: [Col. 0489C–0490C] The manuscripts entitle it: “Treatise to the Neophytes, on another day of Easter”; the Venetian edition, with the Zenonian manuscript: “To the Neophytes.” The Rheims manuscript also has this marginal note: “To be read by a subdeacon from the ambo while the bishop sits in the assembly with the brethren.”

We learn from Gregory, book IV, letter 44, that readings were at times recited by subdeacons. That readings were delivered from an ambo is known from several witnesses cited by Martene, vol. IV, *De Antiquis Ecclesiae Ritibus*, chapter V, no. 11. The gathering here mentioned is called by other writers “the gathering of the brethren.” It seems sufficiently indicated by Caesarius of Arles, Homily II, that this gathering was a place distinct from the church, where sacred readings were customarily held: “I see that you faithfully hasten to the gathering of the brethren, or to the church, in order to hear the divine readings”; and shortly afterward: “He comes to the church or to the gathering of the brethren.”

Some have indeed taken *or* as conjunctive, as though the gathering of the brethren and the church were synonymous. But, apart from the fact that this repeated formula with the disjunctive particle does not seem to allow that interpretation, it is clear that the gathering of the brethren was a place separate from the church, called by others the Chapter, from Roman Order IX, published by Mabillon in vol. II of the *Museum Italicum*, p. 10. Its opening reads: “After the first hour has been celebrated in the gathering of the brethren, which among some is called the Chapter, etc.” That the Chapter was a place distinct from the church, where, after Prime and before Mass, the clergy especially assembled to hear readings, is plainly gathered from the ancient order of the Churches of Cambrai and Arras, published from Pithou’s papers:

“And as soon as the sun has risen, the signal for Prime shall be sounded, where all the clergy shall assemble. Then they shall leave the church in silence and sit in the Chapter, where the weekly minister shall read the sacred lesson. There the prelates are to address the reading itself and the conduct of the clergy; and afterward follow the matters pertaining to Mass.”

That, at least in ancient times, laypeople also could gather there, besides the clergy, to hear the sacred reading is clear from Caesarius’s testimony. Furthermore, that there was an ambo in the gathering or Chapter from which sacred books were read is evident from the marginal note on the present treatise.

Nor should the marginal note on Treatise 45 trouble anyone. It says that certain things were done in the gathering which, according to other orders, were customarily done in the choir before or after the nocturnal prayers of Vigils—what we call Matins—such as the offering of peace mentioned in several documents cited by Martene, vol. IV, *De Antiquis Ecclesiae Ritibus*, chapter 25, no. 5, and the antiphon “Christ has risen,” etc.; on this account the gathering of the brethren might seem to mean the choir itself, where the clergy indeed assemble. This marginal note, I say, should not trouble anyone. Since the rite explained by that note appears to be a particular rite of the Church of Verona, and specifically of Easter Day, and is not of the same kind as the rite celebrated before or after nocturnal prayers in the documents reported by Martene, there is no need to transfer the name “gathering” to an alien meaning which cannot be confirmed by other documents. See what we shall say on that note in its proper place.]

To the Neophytes after Baptism, IV. Here, with a few additions and certain changes, are contained matters presented partly in Treatise XXXIX and partly in Treatise XL.

[Col. 0489B] Rejoice, brothers, in Christ, and diligently, courageously, and [Col. 0490A] faithfully guard the royal benefit of the pardon you have received. For every bond incurred by all your deeds has been removed; rejoice in security: you now owe nothing to the world.

[Note: [Col. 0490C–D] This opening sentence is repeated in the following treatise with a different reading: “And diligently, courageously, and faithfully guard the royal benefit of the pardon you have received; for your bond has been removed.” In both places the Rheims manuscript reads *ablatus* (“removed”); the Toledo manuscript reads *sublatus* (“taken away”). Here *contractus* means sins, from which we incurred a twofold debt of guilt and penalty. Since both debts have been remitted in baptism, every bond is rightly called removed—or *albatus*, “whitened,” that is, erased. It seems to be called *contractus* because the Apostle, Colossians II.14, calls it a handwritten bond: “Blotting out the handwriting of the decree that was against us, he removed it from the midst, fastening it to the cross.” Here there is also mention of the removed and whitened, or erased, bond.]

[Note: [Col. 0490D] The Toledo and Pompignan manuscripts: “Until now you have indeed been under great guilt.” Treatise 39, from which this sentence is almost taken: “In this guilt, brothers, you have been until now.” See what we noted there.]

You have until now been an image of guilt; but you have been courageously examined, and, that you might receive pardon, you kept watch well for your own selves, and you were heard most favorably.

[Note: [Col. 0490D] *Ipsis* (“selves”) has been added from five manuscripts. The Vatican codex has: “well for your own good selves.”]

It is a new kind of judgment in which the accused person, if he excuses his crime, is condemned; if he confesses, he is acquitted. Great is the principle, great the power, great the mercy of our Judge, by whom sinners of every kind hasten to be punished, that they may be able to live blessedly.

[Note: [Col. 0490D] Here begin the passages repeated from Treatise 40 in almost exactly the same words.]

A marvelous principle—indeed, a marvelous mystery! While the accused person is safe, the guilt is punished in the accused person; and, while his state remains whole, that by reason of which the human being was destined to die dies within him. Hence our confession has no need of tortures, because, without the sweat of a fierce torturer, the accused person spontaneously [Col. 0490B] confesses his crimes in order that he may become innocent.

[Note: [Col. 0490D] Three manuscripts—the Rheims, Vatican, and Pompignan—read *quod* (“because”), while others incorrectly give *quae*. The same wording occurs in the preceding treatise.]

It is a precious thing, brothers, which confers both honor and reward. O profound providence of [Col. 0491A] our Deliverer! O singular excellence! O sweet sentence! O necessary condemnation! Within himself the human being is slain in order that he may live: the striker is not seen, the striker’s sword is not perceived, the wound of the struck does not gape, the blood of one expiring does not flow, the body does not throb, and his color does not grow pale. He is the same person, yet he is not the same. The dwelling indeed appears old; but the new inhabitant rejoices in a change of conduct and will prove, by diverse virtues, to unbelievers the nobility of his birth.

## 259. TREATISE XLII

[Note: [Col. 0491B] TREATISE XLII.—In the manuscripts it is entitled “Easter Treatise,” except for the Zenonian manuscript, which, with the Venetian edition, has “After baptism has been conferred.” A fragment of this treatise is quoted near its end in the *Life of St Zeno* written by a Zenonian monk. From it we shall likewise provide variants, distinguished by the letters Vit.]

To the Neophytes after Baptism, V.

Greetings today, brothers born in Christ. Diligently, courageously, and [Col. 0491B] faithfully guard the royal benefit of the pardon you have received; for every bond you incurred has been removed. Rejoice in security: you now owe nothing to the world.

[Note: [Col. 0491C] See note 2 on the preceding treatise.]

See: no weight, no clanking of worldly chains is upon your necks. Your hands are hindered by no fetters, your feet burdened by no shackles. No terror disturbs you, no stains darken you. You who feared one privy to your deeds do not fear conscience: for your old human being has been happily condemned so that he might be acquitted; buried in the wave of the sacred pool, so that, brought to life in the nest of the tomb, [Col. 0492A] he might taste the rights of resurrection.

O great providence of our God!

[Note: [Col. 0491C] Here begins the fragment mentioned in note 1, inserted by the author of the *Life of St Zeno*, p. 326 of the *Historia diplomatica*, at the end of which the following was appended by Marquis Maffei. The monk, however, omitted some lines not relevant to his purpose.]

O pure love of a good mother! Receiving persons of different stock, sex, age, and condition, she kills them out of hatred for their crimes, as a stepmother; she preserves them with affection, as a mother. Nor does she restore the slain to life until she has extinguished every poison of the old state. In order that she may bear no adulterate offspring, and may not appear to love one more or another less, she bestows upon all one birth, one milk, one [260] wage, one dignity of the Holy Spirit.

[Note: [Col. 0491C] The Vatican manuscript reads *adulterium* (“adultery”); but we have seen, in note 42 on Treatise 1, book I, that reputable authors and Zeno use *adulterum* in the sense of *adulterinum*, “adulterate.”]

[Note: [Col. 0491C–0492C] It may perhaps seem surprising that Zeno names one milk here and elsewhere, but not honey, although it is certain that in the Western Church honey was given to the newly baptized no less than milk, as several witnesses cited by Martene, vol. I, chapter 15, no. 16, plainly prove. Yet St Jerome likewise names milk, but not honey, in his commentary on Isaiah LV, vol. IV, p. 644 of the Verona edition, although in his *Dialogue against the Luciferians*, no. 8, vol. II, p. 180, he mentions both milk and honey, saying: “Many other things observed in the churches through tradition have assumed for themselves the authority of written law; for example, dipping the head three times in the washing, then, after emerging, tasting the union of milk and honey as a sign of infancy.”

Observe, however, the words “the union of milk and honey,” from which it is clear that the Neophytes received not milk and honey separately, but honey mixed with milk. Thus Tertullian twice calls it “the sharing of milk and honey,” in *On the Soldier’s Crown*, chapter 3, and *Against Marcion*, book I, chapter 14. Hence liturgical books also contain a single blessing of honey and milk and likewise a single formula for giving honey and milk. It was therefore easy to call it “one milk,” not because milk alone was given, but because it is the more usual food of infants.

Moreover, although this rite was employed by pagans, who fed newborn children with honey and milk, as learned writers have noted from several ancient authors—as may be seen in Cotelerius, note 51 on chapter 6 of the Epistle of Barnabas—it should not, as some think, be referred to pagan origin, but to the Old Testament, where the land of promise is often described as flowing with milk and honey. “Beginning their journey toward it,” says John the Deacon in his letter to Senarius, vol. I of the *Museum Italicum*, p. 75, “the baptized are nourished with milk and honey like little children.”

Yet we fear that in this passage of Zeno “milk” should be understood as Christ’s blood, on which we have spoken more fully in note 7 on Treatise 32, or as the doctrine of faith itself, which we see understood under the name of milk in the Epistle of Barnabas, no. 8. For all the baptized alike were nourished by this food.]

[Note: [Col. 0492C] On this wage, apparently elsewhere called the denarius, we have discussed much in note 5 on Treatise 35, which should certainly be read together with our remarks in note 21 on Treatise 14, book II, where we proposed consideration of this same text.]

How beautiful, brothers, and how salutary it is to admire one whom shortly before you considered ridiculous; to desire to imitate the virtue of one whose corruption you had cursed; to be astonished that one whom you had always abhorred as greedy pours out all his goods everywhere upon the poor and needy; finally, to rejoice that one whom you knew to be a shrine of idolatry [Col. 0492B] is a temple of God.

[Note: [Col. 0492C] The *Life* adds “that,” etc.; by the same reasoning this particle ought to have been placed before the pronoun *cuius*, which the author of the Life omits together with its clause. Thus he writes by omission: “How beautiful it is, brothers, that one whom you had known to be greedy,” etc.]

Therefore he is always blessed who remembers that he has been reborn; more blessed is one who does not remember what he was before he was reborn; most blessed is one who does not alter his infancy as time advances.

[Note: [Col. 0492C–D] The printed editions read: “who does not remember that he was before he was reborn,” and this concerns those who received baptism in infancy or do not remember it. The author calls these more blessed because before baptism they committed no personal evil. The *Life*: “Who does not remember being what he was before he was reborn.” The Rheims, Urbino, Pompignan, and Vatican Basilica manuscripts, together with the same *Life* at the end of the Pompignan codex, read: “Who does not remember, before he was born, what he was.” From these readings it seemed best to write: “who does not remember what he was before he was reborn.”]

[Note: [Col. 0492D] See note 5 on Treatise 39.]

## 261. TREATISE XLIII

[Note: [Col. 0492D–0494B] TREATISE XLIII.—The first title is found in the Verona edition (in the Zenonian codex, only “To the Neophytes”); the alternative title, “On the Twelve Signs,” with the addition “To the Neophytes,” appears in the remaining manuscripts and in the Venetian edition. Since it was customary among pagan mathematicians—for astrologers were then so called—to cast nativities by means of the signs of the Zodiac, as we learn from Philastrius, heresy CXX, entitled “On the Signs of the Zodiac and Human Birth,” St Zeno in this treatise transferred that custom from profane observation to sacred use.

Further, in the margin of the Rheims manuscript: “To be read from the ambo at St Stephen’s at the Martyrs on Easter Monday, before the bishop begins to celebrate the sealing of the Holy Spirit.” This is perhaps the most ancient testimony to this rite, in which the sacrament of confirmation, called “sealing,” was conferred by the bishop on Easter Monday.

From many other documents diligently collected by Fr. Edmund Martene, part I of *De Antiquis Ecclesiae Ritibus*, chapter 2, article 1, nos. 2 and 3, it is established that formerly bishops, when they baptized—and they generally baptized amid the very solemnities of Easter Day, beginning with the vigil of Holy Saturday—always administered confirmation and the Eucharist as well as baptism to the Neophytes at once on the same day. Why, then, is confirmation here postponed to the second day of Easter? Yet this document, belonging approximately to the eighth century, is not so late that we need say the discipline had changed at that time; rather, it is clear from several other witnesses cited there by Martene that it continued into later centuries.

Light is shed upon this difficulty by the acts of St Ulrich, bishop of Augsburg, chapter 4. He is said to have had the custom of confirming, on the Monday after Easter, the multitude of people assembling at St Afra’s. This was perhaps done not because the bishop did not confirm at Easter those whom he himself had baptized then, but in order to provide for persons baptized in the countryside. For, after several baptisteries had been established, priests were permitted to administer baptism at Easter; but since priests could not confirm, nor could infants immediately be sent into the city to be confirmed by the bishop on the same day, provision seems to have been made that, as soon as possible, they might receive both sacraments: each person was to bring to the city on Monday the children baptized at the Easter feast. We suppose that in St Ulrich’s time, and similarly at Verona at least by the eighth century, the custom had become established that, solely for their benefit, confirmation was administered by bishops in a fixed church with solemn ceremony on that day.

Moreover, just as at Augsburg the church assigned to this function was St Afra’s, so at Verona it was St Stephen’s at the Martyrs. It is clear from the manuscript *Carpsum* of Stephen the priest, preserved in the library of the Chapter of Verona, that a station was still held at that church on Easter Monday around the tenth century. Prescribing the rites of the Church of Verona for individual days, it notes the station at St Stephen’s on that same Monday. This Church of St Stephen is very ancient, and it is known to have existed already in the time of Theodoric, king of the Goths, from the Anonymous Valesianus. It was called “at the Martyrs” because the bodies of forty martyrs rest there. The Anonymous Pipinianus speaks splendidly of them in the *Rhythm on the Praises of Verona*, p. 180 of Marquis Maffei’s *Historia diplomatica*: “On the eastern side you have first the proto-martyr Stephen, Florentius, Vindemialis, and Bishop Maurus; Mama, Andronicus, and Probus, with the forty martyrs.”

John, a priest of Verona, mentions them in the manuscript *Imperial History*, book I, p. 130. We thought it fitting to publish here a fragment of it copied from the manuscript by Hieronymus Tartarotius and kindly communicated to us. This John, an early fourteenth-century writer, when writing about the Virgin Placidia, who departed to the Lord on 11 October and whose body “was buried in the church of St Stephen in the castle . . .,” adds:

“This church was formerly the cathedral church of Verona, in which lie the bodies of the forty holy martyrs who suffered under Diocletian in that same city . . . . There also lie the bodies of the holy bishops of that city: Simplicius, Petronius, Innocentius, Senator, Felix, Gaudentius, Probus, Andronicus, Salvinus, Mama, Maurus, John, Alexander, Moderatus, and many others.”

An ancient inscription concerning these martyrs also remains in the same church. They are distinct from the Forty Martyrs of Sebaste, as is also known from the different days assigned to the feasts of each group. At the beginning of the present treatise, those whom the author calls “heavenly peoples” are said in Treatise 35 to be clothed in heavenly raiment. See what we noted there.]

To the Neophytes after Baptism, IV. On the Twelve Signs.

I. Heavenly peoples, rejoice: new pledges in [Col. 0493A] Christ, preserve with unceasing diligence the brightness of your flourishing spiritual birth of today, lest you stain it in any way; for he does not know how to repeat what he bestows.

[Note: [Col. 0494B] The Urbino manuscript reads: “does not know how to preserve.” Notice here also a new testimony implying that baptism cannot be repeated. In place of the nominative, Christ is understood, whom Zeno mentioned shortly before.]

Behold: boys, adolescents, young adults, old people of both sexes—you who were guilty, and were unclean by your worldly birth, are now, freed from every guilt, clean infants. And, wonderfully and delightfully, in one instant you have suddenly become contemporaries, though of different ages.

[Note: [Col. 0494B–C] The stages of life are listed here. For more on them see Censorinus, *On the Birthday*, chapter 13. From Varro, cited there, you will learn that youth is placed after adolescence between the ages of thirty and forty; hence persons of settled age whom we ordinarily call men or adults are found called *iuvenes*, “young men.” Observe also that elderly persons of both sexes were baptized, because in Zeno’s age, after peace had been restored to the Church, many pagans came into the Church, including those who had spent their lives in idolatry even into old age.]

[Note: [Col. 0494C] The Rheims and Pompignan manuscripts incorrectly read: “worldly against birth, every …”; the Toledo and Urbino manuscripts: “worldly against birth, every …”]

But I know your curiosity well from your former-life practice; and that will no longer be permitted you.

[Note: [Col. 0494C] The author calls “curiosity” the practice by which those not yet baptized, while they lived among pagans the life of the old human being, used to ask mathematicians for a horoscope. Foreseeing that in this new birth they might seek something similar, he warns them that it is not lawful for them to seek a nativity from astrologers. Yet, transforming a profane observance into a sacred one, he begins to describe allegorically a spiritual natal chart from the same zodiacal signs by which mathematicians customarily cast horoscopes. Three manuscripts read *usurpati* for *usurpatione*.]

Perhaps you will ask us also under what nativity, and under what sign, your one mother has borne you all—so diverse, so numerous, so unlike—in one single birth. I shall indulge you as little children and disclose, with all brevity, the secrets of the sacred horoscope.

[Note: [Col. 0494C–D] A horoscope here is that point in time at which someone is born, as in Persius, *Satires* VI.18; Manilius, book III, verse 189, calls it the rising pivot. In two manuscripts *Oroscopi* is written without aspiration.]

263 II. Therefore, brothers, such is your *genesis*—your birth-chart. [Note: [Col. 0494D] The author begins with Aries in composing a mystical nativity for the newly baptized, both because the year began with this sign—not only the civil year but also the ecclesiastical year, which, as we shall see in note 2 on Tractate 45, took its beginning from Easter falling within the sign of Aries, the time when the newly baptized were reborn through baptism into a new life—and because astrologers followed the same order in casting nativities. This may be inferred from Augustine, *Heresies* 70, concerning the Priscillianists: “For,” he says (p. 22, vol. VIII), “they place Aries at the head, Taurus at the neck, Gemini at the shoulders, Cancer at the breast, and, proceeding through the remaining signs by name, reach the soles of the feet, which they assign to Pisces,” the sign astrologers name last.] The first to receive you—who rejects no one believing in him—was not a Ram but the Lamb. He clothed your nakedness in the snowy brightness of his fleece; with kindly indulgence he poured his blessed milk into your lips as they opened in infant crying. [Note: [Col. 0494D] On the milk given to the baptized—a rite apparently indicated here—see note 7 on Tractate 32 and note 5 on Tractate 42. Here, however, the “blessed milk” seems to mean Christ’s blood, offered to those to be baptized as to infants. The Reims manuscript incorrectly reads “with blessed milk to mouths opening in crying,” etc. The Vatican manuscript likewise reads *lacte*, “milk.” Later, the Reims, Pomp., Vatican, Urban, Zenonian manuscripts and the Venetian edition have *infundit*, “pours,” instead of *infudit*, “poured.”]

The same one, not a Bull puffed up in the neck, grim in brow, or threatening in horn, but the best, gentle, winning, and mild Calf, admonishes you: seeking omens in no undertaking, submit without malice to his yoke; tame the soil of your flesh and make it fruitful, so that you may bring a glad harvest of divine seed into the heavenly granaries. [Note: [Col. 0495C] It is plain to all that Christ is frequently called a lamb in Scripture; that he is also called a calf is attested by the Epistle of St. Barnabas, no. 8, which St. Jerome cites for this purpose at Ezekiel 43:19. Below, the Reims and Pomp. manuscripts have *idolatria* for *idololatria*, “idolatry,” a frequent manuscript form, as Baluzius has already observed.]

And Gemini follows, that is, the two Testaments proclaiming salvation, exhorting you above all to flee idolatry, sexual immorality, and greed, which is an incurable cancer. But our Lion—as Genesis declares, “he is a lion’s whelp” (Gen. 49:9)—is he whose devout mysteries we celebrate. He lay down and slept in order to conquer death; he awoke in order to bestow upon us the gift of immortality through his blessed resurrection.

The Virgin fittingly follows him, heralding the Balance, so that we might know that equity and justice were brought to earth by the Son of God, who, having become incarnate, came forth from a virgin. [Note: [Col. 0495C] The Reims and Zenonian manuscripts read “through the Son of God.” Note: “came forth from a Virgin” for “was born of a Virgin.”] Whoever holds fast to and faithfully administers this equity and justice will tread with unharmed foot—not merely the Scorpion, but, as the Lord says in the Gospel, every kind of serpent.

264 Nor will such a person ever fear the devil himself, who is truly the most fierce Archer, armed with varied and fiery arrows and continually assailing the hearts of the whole human race. Therefore the Apostle Paul says: “Put on the armor of God, that you may be able to stand against the wickednesses of the devil, taking up the shield of faith, through which you will be able to extinguish all his evil arrows, which are full of fire” (Eph. 6:11). [Note: [Col. 0495C] This adjective, together with the following one, is referred to Sagittarius by a rare syntactical construction, though not foreign to Zeno.]

For he sometimes sends against the unfortunate a Capricorn, hideous in appearance, who bubbles forth through a horn at the livid lips of the emaciated one, with foaming veins, and rages miserably through every limb of his captive in quivering ruin. [Note: [Col. 0495C] The Pomp. manuscript, with others and the editions, originally had this reading, but it was corrected to *Iis*; that is unsatisfactory, for the subject is the devil. Then, instead of “hideous and through the horn of the more slender one,” the Toledo and Zenonian manuscripts read “hideous through the horn of the more slender one.” The Urban manuscript reads: “hideous, who leaps forth by a horn.”] He makes some mad, some raging, some murderers, some adulterers, some sacrilegious persons, and others blind through greed. It would take too long to go through each case. He possesses varied and innumerable arts of doing harm; but our Aquarius, flowing with the saving stream, is accustomed to destroy all these without much difficulty. [Note: [Col. 0495D] The Verona edition, with several manuscripts, has *omne*, incorrectly. On *non magno pere* for *non magno opere*, “without great effort,” that is, easily, see note 9 on Tractate 6, book I.] Two Fish necessarily follow him in one sign: that is, two peoples, Jews and Gentiles, living by the water of baptism and marked with the one sign into the one people of Christ.

## TRACTATE XLIV

[Note: [Col. 0495D] TRACTATE XLIV.—The first title occurs in the Verona edition. In the Zenonian manuscript and Venetian edition: “To the Newly Baptized”; in the other manuscripts, however, the second title. Just as St. Zeno, explaining the comparison of the vineyard in Tractate 27, set before the reader, briefly but quite clearly, the ancient method of preparing wine, so now, intending to present the newly baptized with the comparison of wheat, he displays no less carefully, in few words, the ancient method of making bread. Seneca, *Letters* 90, is commonly cited on this subject, but our Zeno explains it much more clearly. The occasion of this comparison was perhaps given by the Apostle Paul’s allegory concerning the paschal unleavened bread (1 Cor. 5:7), a reading still used in the Easter season. Other Fathers speaking of the newly baptized likewise employ this comparison of bread, calling them breads after Paul. See, among others, Augustine, Sermons 227 and 229, where he develops and explains the same allegory at length.] To the Newly Baptized after Baptism VII.

[Col. 0496B]

### On the Lord’s Day: the comparison of wheat

I. Let us rejoice, brothers, in Christ; enriched by the return of so great a yield, let us offer praise and thanks to God the almighty Father. He has changed tares, darnel, burdock, and thorns into glad grain. Purified by careful cultivation and happily crushed under the devout weight of the millstone, they were sifted in due order, all bran cast away, and gleamed with marvelous brightness as white flour. [Note: [Col. 0496C] Here *cretus* derives not from *cresco*, whence *cretus* would mean “created” or “begotten,” but from *cerno*, “to sift.” Pliny, book 33, no. 26, p. 260, vol. II: “It is sifted through a fine sieve”; and book 18, no. 19, p. 14: “it is further sifted through a flour-sieve.” Thus things are called *ordinabiliter creta*, “sifted in due order,” because they have been sifted successively. In a similar sense Palladius, book 12, ch. 22, speaks of “well-sifted ashes.”] It was mixed and thoroughly kneaded without any corrupting leaven. [Note: [Col. 0496C] The Reims manuscript and Venetian edition read *consparsa*, and indeed Tertullian, *Against Marcion*, book IV, ch. 24, similarly has some witnesses reading *consparsionum* for *conspersionum*. But *conspersa*, the more usual spelling, is preferred. This passage is excellently illuminated by Cato, *On Agriculture*, ch. 74: “Put the flour into the mortar; add water gradually, and knead it well,” where *subigere*, “to knead,” means to handle, work, and mix.]

Salt was put into it; it was softened with lamp-oil; and, prepared with the appropriate services, it was made into unleavened loaves. [Note: [Col. 0496D] The editions and several manuscripts have *germinali*, but three others—the Reims, Toledo, and Urban manuscripts—read *gremiali*. Two authors of the same period, Quintus Octavius Horatianus, ch. 9, and Theodorus Priscianus, book I, ch. 3, who likewise have “lap-oil,” almost persuaded us to retain this reading; Fabricius, however, shows in his *Latin Library* that they should be regarded as one and the same author. Yet *cremiale* should be read. The letter *g* is often written for *c* in manuscripts; accordingly, in Columella, book XII, ch. 19, manuscripts read *gremia* where *cremia* was correctly printed; similarly Nerius, *Analecta*, no. 11, observed that *cremiales arbores* should be read in Ulpian, book XXIV, Digest, title 3, law concerning dissolved marriage, §10, where the Florentine Pandects write *gremiales arbores*. *Cremium* and *cremiale* are named from burning, because they can readily be burned. In the passage cited, Columella calls *cremia* thin, dry pieces of wood which catch fire easily: “We shall kindle the oven with a light fire and very thin wood, which country people call *cremia*.” Hence also the meaning of Psalm 101:4 in the Vulgate: “My bones dried up like *cremium*”; Jerome gives the same meaning in his commentary on Hosea 10. Likewise, *cremiales arbores* in the Pandects are trees that ignite readily. Thus *cremiale oil* should similarly be read in the writers mentioned, and it denotes, as in Zeno, the ordinary oil used in lamps. Finally, it should be observed that, besides salt, the already mixed and kneaded mass of flour was customarily sprinkled with oil in order to make bread. We do not think this applies to every bread, but to a particular bread which the author here transfers to the newly baptized, signifying the oil with which they were customarily anointed either before or after baptism, especially in chrism; Augustine, Sermon 227, calls it oil.]

These are the loaves you see, fragrant with excellent baking: baked not in an oven but in a font; not by human fire but by divine fire. No breeze corrupted them; no bitter smoke infected them; no cold crushed them; 266 and—what is more—they rose without leaven. [Note: [Col. 0497B] The author seems to have in view Paul’s words at 1 Corinthians 5:7, where he calls those first Christians unleavened loaves: having, as he says, purged out the old leaven of malice and wickedness, they were raised from the font as pure unleavened bread by a new mixture without any leaven, by which the whole dough is corrupted.] Certainly, they are not common, sooty loaves; not stale, burnt, underbaked, or moldy. Their color is milky; their taste is milky. [Note: [Col. 0497B] One might think *cacabacei* should be read, since manuscripts of Tertullian, *Against Hermogenes*, ch. 41, write *cacabaceus*. But Papias, under “Bread,” has *cacabacius*: “Likewise hot *cacabacius* bread dries; cold bread, however, being much less dry, thins only in part.” In Tertullian *cacabaceus* expresses the force of disturbed, turbulent motion observed in boiling cauldrons: “a motion not turbulent or *cacabaceus*—that is, like a cauldron or pot boiling on all sides, as he himself had said shortly before—but composed and moderated.” It cannot be understood how this sense could suit loaves. Another interpretation corresponding to the word in Zeno’s period must therefore be sought. John Filesacus, *Selecta*, book I, chs. 3 and 14, derives it from κακαβίζειν, the cry of partridges, so as to mean “chattering” and “trifling.” But though that may suit people, the author calls not people but breads *cacabacii*, and there is no reason to think he spoke in that sense. The derivation from *cacabi*, “cauldrons,” is obvious. Varro, *On the Latin Language*, book IV, ch. 27, says that cauldrons were kitchen vessels; Columella, book XII, chs. 41 and 46, distinguishes two kinds, earthenware and bronze. Casaubon, in his commentary on Lampridius’s *Heliogabalus*, p. 150, and, following him, Bulenger, *On Banquets*, book IV, ch. 18, infer from this single passage of Zeno that there were bakers’ cauldrons in which bakers cooked loaves. Such loaves, they say, were called *cacabacii* because they retained a bad flavor from water heated in the cauldron. But this explanation too is unsatisfactory: it is not clear how bakers used cauldrons in baking bread so that an allegedly bad flavor would be passed into the bread itself to its detriment. Papias mentions *clibanicium* bread, baked in an earthen vessel, and says that it is very dry; thus it may seem identical with what he shortly before called *cacabacius*, while an earthen vessel is a type of cauldron. Yet a passage of St. Paulinus of Nola, *Letter* 33, no. 9, p. 201, Verona edition, sheds light on this word: “When you behold the buildings which, spotless, still shine in honor of your work, darkened by the trifles of my folly and—if I may use a word worthy of my verses—*cacabata*, while many laugh. …” Here Paulinus uses *cacabata* as a popular adjective to signify something more than merely “darkened.” Rosweyde explains it in his notes, p. 906, as “blackened.” Thus at Pelagius, *Lives of the Fathers*, booklet XV, *cacabata* pots are pots blackened with soot. Consequently *cacabacii* loaves are common and cheap loaves, made from flour neither very choice nor well sifted, and therefore dark. Zeno contrasts them with milky-colored loaves, and with those which bakers offer for sale marked with a fixed shape and definite stamp. Finally, these *cacabacii* loaves seem to be those called “dirty” and “Sardinian” in Valentinian’s law *On the Civic Grain Supply and the Ranks of Bread*, where “clean” loaves are placed in contrast; perhaps they are also the common bread to which Seneca, *Letter* 119, opposes white bread made from the choicest flour.]

[Col. 0498A]

II. But perhaps, because some appear smaller in form, if anyone thinks otherwise of the baker, it makes no difference to me, brothers. Although I am poor, I nevertheless protect my honor and know my good faith. [Note: [Col. 0498B] At first sight these words create very great difficulty, since it is not immediately understood how some of the newly baptized could seem smaller in form and thus give rise to suspicion of theft against the baker—that is, Bishop Zeno—who professes himself poor, a suspicion from which he thinks he must clear himself here. But since other tractates establish that very many children, adolescents, young people, and old people of both sexes and every condition were baptized, and that they generally passed from paganism to Christianity, we began to suspect that some children or young adolescents of pagans, admitted to baptism, could allegorically be thought smaller in form because, on account of their very tender age, they did not seem the kind of persons sufficiently capable, instructed, or free to seek baptism. Hence a certain suspicion of theft fell upon the bishop, as if, eager for gain, he had taken very many children—smaller than was proper, that is, not yet their own masters, unable to decide upon adopting religion, or insufficiently instructed and tested—away from their parents’ sides. This could not be done without theft, since children may not be taken from their parents unless, being their own masters, they desire to embrace Christian faith and leave their fathers. Zeno clears himself of this suspicion only by the test and examination of those whom he presents to the hearers for testing; he does not doubt that all will be found *tripondes*—that is, as we shall explain, sufficiently instructed, free, and equal to all the rest, with age posing no obstacle. Perhaps he also speaks of adults, who were thought not to be admitted immediately unless they had been thoroughly tested and instructed; the haste of some in admitting them was criticized. See Martène, vol. I, *On Ancient Ecclesiastical Rites*, ch. 1, art. 8, no. 5 and following. The defense against this criticism is the same.]

Let the workers who are with me speak, if they know anything. [Note: [Col. 0498D] The workers cooperating with Zeno in instructing, testing, and initiating catechumens—whom he calls as witnesses if they know anything against him concerning the newly baptized—are undoubtedly priests and deacons. It is therefore clear that Zeno already had a clergy.] I rejoice in profit, I openly admit it, but without consciousness of theft. Finally, you too retain the ancient weight; you have the balance-beam; make the weighing as you wish; weigh each one: you will find none to have less. [Note: [Col. 0498D] Since this passage allegorically concerns the weight of bakers’ bread, which must also have been fixed in ancient times, *agina* should rightly be written, with Casaubon on Lampridius, p. 150, instead of *edignam*, found in three manuscripts, or *haeginam*, found in other manuscripts and editions. Festus says that an *agina* is the part of a balance on which weights are moved beneath the standard weight. Hence Tertullian, *Against Hermogenes*, ch. 41, says: “He was borne with the balanced force of the middle *agina*, neither leaning nor rushing headlong to either side.” *Exagium* is the same as *examen*, a weighing by means of a balance. Greek-Latin Glossary: “Εξάγιον: weighing.” Likewise Cassian, *Conference* 1, ch. 22, calls *exagium* the test by which coins are examined to determine whether they have the proper weight. The term occurs in Theodosius’s Novella *On the Price of the Solidus*, and in an ancient inscription in Gruter, p. 647, no. 6: “They shall sell livestock under the standard weight.” Thus St. Zeno means that the newly baptized about whom there was doubt should likewise be called to examination, and he has no doubt that, if weighed, all will be found equal and fit. This is what the words mean: “You will find none”—the Pomp. and Vatican reading, judged preferable to the others’ “none [feminine]”—“to have less than the others,” namely, less than what is required for receiving baptism and found in the other newly baptized.]

267 All are *tripondes*, marked with one pound of the sacred coinage, who serve the table. [Note: [Col. 0499B] Casaubon, commenting on the same passage in Lampridius, notes that the word *tripondes* is unique in Zeno and reads *omnes*, “all,” very well instead of *homines*, “people,” since mention of persons does not suit the allegory of bread, whereas all loaves may properly be called *tripondes*. But he thought that *tripondes* and *omnes* refer not to loaves or newly baptized persons, but to the author’s tractates: Zeno, he says, signifies that he maintained intact in all his sermons the faith received concerning the most holy Trinity. This is mistaken, since the tractate consistently concerns loaves, not sermons; consequently the loaves discussed hitherto, that is, the newly baptized, are called *tripondes*. In all of them St. Zeno promises that the same faith, instruction, and disposition required for baptism will be found under the standard weight—that is, examination. To say something further about the word itself: *tripondium* is the weight of a triple established measure—for example, three pounds or asses (see *Institutes*, “On Instituting Heirs,” § “If there are several”)—just as a *dupondius* or *dipondius* was a coin of two weights. Thus *tripondes* are loaves weighing three fixed weights, for example, pounds. The loaves distributed to the people through imperial largesse under Aurelian weighed two pounds each, as may be inferred from Zosimus. Their weight was later increased, partly by Aurelian himself and partly by others, up to three pounds, as Salmasius notes in Vopiscus, p. 373. Did Zeno call three-pound loaves *tripondes*? Yet because he calls the loaves of which he speaks—loaves sold by bakers for public use, marked with a certain stamp—“marked with one pound,” he sufficiently suggests that bakers’ bread at that time weighed one pound. Nothing prevents loaves from having weighed half as much, as did the six loaves or rolls mentioned in Valentinian’s law, *Code of Theodosius, On the Civic Grain Supply and the Ranks of Bread*, which together consisted of thirty-six ounces. That half-pound weight, however, seems to have belonged only to children’s bread. Cassian, *Conference* 11, ch. 19, calls the given loaves *paxamatia*—then the name of a small loaf—and says: “It is most certain that the little loaves scarcely have the weight of one pound.” This must be understood to mean that not each *paxamatium*, but the two together, scarcely weighed one pound, as the context shows. Thus small loaves could conveniently weigh half a pound and larger ones one pound. But why did the author call them *tripondes* if they were marked with one pound rather than three? This can only be understood if we consider that Zeno regularly introduces, wherever possible, three and one into all allegories he applies to the newly baptized. Thus in Tractate 35 he likewise mentions a gold coin marked by the union of a triple coinage. This either refers to faith in God, one and triune—a faith in which no one was admitted to baptism unless well instructed and steadfast—or it concerns baptism itself, which is bestowed in the confession and name of that same Unity and Trinity. Finally, when the author here says “marked with one pound,” at the end of Tractate 43 he said “marked with one sign.”]

[Note: [Col. 0500A] These final words seem intended to indicate that all the newly baptized are loaves not *cacabacei*, that is, common loaves, but the choicest kind, such as are made by bakers for table use with a fixed size and definite weight, as we have conjectured more fully in note 6. Otherwise these words would not cohere with the foregoing sense, and the meaning would be mutilated, lacking something needed for a satisfactory conclusion. Perhaps a full stop should precede these words: “who serve the table”; these are the sacred ministers of Zeno serving at the altar, while the rest is missing.]

## TRACTATE XLV

[Note: [Col. 0500B] TRACTATE XLV.—In the manuscripts: “A Tractate for the Lord’s Day Begins.” The Venetian edition: “On the Lord’s Day.” John of Verona and those who excerpted him, William Pastrengo and Peter de Natalibus, list two tractates “On the Lord’s Day,” since, as we have seen, the preceding tractate has the same title in the manuscripts. The Verona edition: “On Easter.” Since this tractate was delivered at Easter and concerns Easter Sunday itself, the title we have placed at its head was constructed. In the Reims manuscript there is this long marginal note: “To be recited in the assembly by the deacon on Easter Day itself before the bishop, after he has descended from his chamber with the deacons and taken his seat, with apples handed out according to custom and peace bestowed, the bishop saying: ‘Christ has risen’; the others: ‘And he has shone.’” Thus it stands there. This distinctive and important Easter-Day rite of the Veronese Church, confirmed by no other example, did not belong to the public sacred offices held in the church choir, but took place in the assembly—that is, as we saw in note 1 on Tractate 41, in the chapter meeting—to which it is clear from many sources that the bishop repeatedly descended with the clergy before proceeding into the church for the sacred offices. We nevertheless read of the custom of handing out apples after Mass on another day in a very ancient ritual published for the use of the Church of Reims, mentioned by Fr. Martène, vol. IV, *On Ancient Ecclesiastical Rites*, ch. 33, no. 8. It has this rubric before the blessing of apples on the feast day of Saints James and Christopher: “After the Mass of the said day, the priest, coming out in albs and stole, blesses the new apples; and after the blessing, the cleric distributes them to those present.” The blessing follows, etc. Likewise at Rome, in the Greek church of St. Athanasius on Epiphany, oranges blessed by the Greek bishop presiding over that church are still handed out to those present according to an ancient rite. Something similar was done at Verona on Easter Day itself about the eighth century, as may be inferred from this marginal note. When the bishop gave the peace, he seems to have said, “Christ has risen,” and those receiving the peace are reported to have answered, “And he has shone,” that is, “and he has shone upon us”—words proper to Easter Day and well known in ancient orders as well. See also note 1 on Tractate 41.] On Easter Sunday I.

[Col. 0500A]

The heir of the ages, running and returning in swift course, revolving upon itself in solemn movement, bringing forth from its end its own beginning and from its setting innumerable births, the everlasting day has shone forth. [Note: [Col. 0500D] The editions have *paterno*; the Reims, Toledo, and Vatican manuscripts have *paternici*, and this was also originally written in the Pomp. manuscript, though corrected by a later hand to *paterni*. From *paternici*, however, we judge that *pernici*, “swift,” must be restored with the Urban manuscript. The subject is the course of the Easter Day, which the author calls swift in its annual orbit in Tractate 51. He calls the day of the paschal resurrection “heir of the ages” because, returning in a perpetual orbit, it represents the image of eternal ages. Only the Verona edition had *revertens*, “returning,” for *recurrens*, “running back.” In four manuscripts and the Venetian edition we found *rotatus in sese*, “revolving upon itself,” with *se* written twice. The same day is also called a beginning, specifically the beginning of the year, as will be clear from the following tractates. “Easter is truly the beginning of the year,” says Ambrose, *On the Mysteries*, ch. 2: “the beginning of the first month, the new renewal of shoots, and, when the dark night of winter has been dispersed, the restored delight of early spring.” These words explain what St. Zeno immediately adds when he places Easter Day at the beginning of spring. You will find the same in Ambrose, *Hexaemeron*, book I, ch. 4, with which St. Gaudentius agrees in Tractate 1, p. 24. He traces the origin of this matter to the ancient rite of the Hebrews, among whom Nisan, corresponding to March, was by God’s command the first of months; nevertheless, Christians were not prohibited from sometimes transferring Easter to April for the special reason that the same bishop considers there. On whatever day of March or April Easter fell, it was always regarded as the beginning of the ecclesiastical year, although popular custom, agreeing with the Roman practice, began the year in March.]

When the sadness of folded winter has been dispelled, and the new west wind, Favonius, breathes gently, meadows everywhere in bud breathe sweetly, spread abroad in one birth with diverse flowers differing in kind, color, and fragrance. A new summer exults, 270 yet rich, happily threshing the ears of grain into varied heaps; ripe-with-must autumn will fittingly follow, so that the delight of wine may necessarily be joined to the grace of bread. [Note: [Col. 0501C] This passage was corrupted in the editions, which read: “the palm happily beating the ear.” The manuscripts supplied the correction, indicating that ears of grain are beaten during summer into various heaps or piles, since the ears are threshed at that time on the threshing-floor and the grains gathered into various heaps are carried into granaries. Likewise, from six manuscripts and the Venetian edition, we have printed *prosequetur*, “will follow,” rather than *consequitur*, since the future following of autumn does not suit the time of summer.]

Who would not recognize these things as fitted to heavenly mysteries? For sluggish, foul, and sad winter belongs to those who serve idolatry, are fettered by worldly pleasures, give themselves to lust and gluttony, and are far removed—*moliti*, that is, assigned by God to eternal death—because they have loved the work of darkness. [Note: [Col. 0501D] Three manuscripts have *inoliti*. But *moliti* is preferable, since *molio* occurs no less than *molior*. Thus Nonius, II.543, cites Lucilius’s passive use of *molior*; hence here *longe moliti* means “assigned far away,” as St. Zeno himself explains.]

We must understand the holy spring as the font. From its rich channel, with Favonius not as wind but as the Holy Spirit bringing forth life, our most radiant and sweet children are poured out: blessed flowers of the Church, breathing a divine fragrance in faith, differing in charism but united in one birth. [Note: [Col. 0501D] The gifts of grace in baptism differ to the extent that those being baptized differ in disposition. “For the more a person has believed, the more noble he will make himself,” says the holy bishop in Tractate 31.
