In Tractate 33, exhorting catechumens to increase faith, he gives this reason: “For as much as anyone has believed, so much blessedness shall he have.”]

Summer, moreover, is the faithful people, angelic and pure. [Note: [Col. 0502B] We have written *angelicus*, “angelic,” instead of *angelus*, so that all the terms may be epithets of “people,” since the discourse concerns the newly baptized, whom the author elsewhere declares in some manner changed into angels through baptism and calls ethereal.] Cleansed of the chaff of sins, steadfastly and courageously maintaining openly the pledge they made, they desire to bring themselves as precious grain into the divine granaries. Though they abound through their own font, they nevertheless continually burn with the ardor of righteous action. [Note: [Col. 0502B] *Limpidatus* means “purified, cleansed,” from *limpidus*; Vegetius uses the verb, book II, 18.1, and likewise II.27.4, *elimpido*. A little later *uberet* is taken in a neuter sense for “be fruitful, abound,” as Columella also uses it, book V, ch. 9, no. 11: “For the olive does not continually bear abundantly every second year,” that is, it is not fruitful. The newly baptized, however, are fruitful and fertile from the grace received in the holy font.]

Autumn also is the place of martyrdom, where it is not the vine’s blood but the digger’s blood that is shed, so that the vintage of precious death may obtain blessed life. [Note: [Col. 0502C] Zeno not infrequently mentions martyrs; how this can belong to his era, since he lived in the fourth century, see note 20 on Tractate 27 and especially Dissertation I, ch. 2, §8. You may perhaps ask why the blood said to be shed is not that of the vine but of the diggers. This applies especially to fourth-century martyrs, since bishops and ecclesiastics were generally the diggers and cultivators of the sacred vineyard; these, above all, we read were attacked in that century. This does not wholly fit earlier centuries, when both clerical and lay Christians were everywhere slaughtered by pagans. Nor should anyone suppose that Christ is meant by “vine,” because he said of himself, “I am the true vine,” and that the diggers are all Christ’s cultivators. If the author had intended the Gospel allegory, they should have been called not diggers but branches, and the Father should have been called the digger or farmer, since John 15 says: “I am the vine; you are the branches. I am the true vine, and my Father is the farmer.”]

The day pertains to the mystery of the resurrection of our Lord Jesus Christ, who is all things in all things; who is truly eternal and day without night. The twelve hours serve him in the Apostles; the twelve months, in the Prophets; the four saving seasons of the Gospels proclaim him. [Note: [Col. 0502D] The four seasons here are the four seasons of the year mentioned above, which the author takes as symbols of the four Gospels.] To him respond not yearly but daily fruits, singing a hymn to God among believing peoples, who are propagated through every seed of immortality unto the ages. Walking in the light of this day, let us exult in faith and rejoice in good conduct, so that we may deserve to attain everlasting life; through the Lord Jesus Christ.

## TRACTATE XLVI

[Note: [Col. 0502D] TRACTATE XLVI.—In the manuscripts: “Tractate of Easter”; in the editions with the Zenonian manuscript: “On Easter II.” This tractate and the next contain similar material and sometimes employ the same words, so that each may be corrected, explained, and understood from the other.] On Easter II.

[Note: [Col. 0502D] The Venetian edition has *intestabili*; the other printed books, *instabili*. Four manuscripts read *instabilis cursus*, “an unsteady course”; two others separately, *in stabili cursu*, “in a steady course,” which is preferable with Sparaverius, especially since at the beginning of the following tractate a “steady runner” is read in the same sense. The Reims manuscript incorrectly writes “by multiform grace” here, but correctly writes “with multiform grace” in the following tractate, as the other manuscripts and editions prefer in both places. The Reims, Vatican, and Urban manuscripts have *per temporum*, but incorrectly, unless perhaps the accusative *ambages*, “windings,” is missing, as it occurs in the following tractate.]

In a steady course, adorned with manifold grace, the saving day arrives along the solemn track of the seasons. It is its own successor and its own predecessor, ever young in its long age; parent of the year and offspring of the year, it goes before and follows the endless seasons and ages. It gives birth to its own beginning from its end, and yet does not depart from the cradle of its birth. [Note: [Col. 0503B] Easter Day is called the parent of the year because the year begins from it; we have said enough on this in note 2 on the preceding tractate.]

Certainly it bears the image of the Lord’s mystery: in its setting it celebrates his Passion, and in its returning dawn his Resurrection, through which it promises us the gift of future blessedness. It will also grant this to our candidates, whom the blessed sunset now invites, so that, plunged in the milky depth of the sacred ocean, they may rise from it new with the new day and, together with us, attain the glory of immortality. [Note: [Col. 0503C] On the *competentes*, “candidates,” see what will be said in Tractate 50, note 5. In the following tractate the same thought is expressed thus: “Rising from there new with the new day,” etc.]

273. TRACT XLVII. [Col. 0503B] On [Note: [Col. 0503C] TRACT XLVII.—In the manuscripts and the Venetian edition, “Easter Preface”; in the Veronese edition, “On Easter VII.” It resembles the preceding tract and therefore the notes made there are to be repeated here. In a marginal note in the Rheims manuscript these words occur: “To be recited on the Thursday of Easter, in the assembly of the brethren before the bishop, before the station.” We have said enough on the assembly in note 1 on Tract 41. A *station*, moreover, is so called from standing, because the people, standing before God, offered prayers. Although it was once used for the fast itself (as is apparent from Hermas, Book III, Similitude 4, on which see Cotelerius’s note 56), because stations were held on each day of fasting, nevertheless any solemn prayer held by the people standing in a prescribed procession from one church, or oratory, to another, or even at some altar, began in time to be called a station. It is in this sense that *station* is used in the marginal note, [Col. 0503D] since on the Easter days, when there was no fasting, these and other stations were designated for the following tracts in the Rheims manuscript. St Gregory of Tours mentions these Easter supplications in his book *On the Lives of the Fathers*, chapter 6; and certain rubrics of their rite are found in the ancient Orders, or Ordinaries, of some churches. In our Veronese Church, moreover, the same stations were held on the second, third, fourth, and fifth weekdays within the octave of Easter, as is clear from this and other marginal notes attached to the Rheims manuscript, to be reported in their places below; we have set their catalogue before the reader, arranged in the sequence of weekdays, in the general preface. Whether stations were held on the other days of the same week cannot be established from these notes; yet they may nevertheless have been held, so that there was no need to mention them in the cited manuscript, because before those stations either nothing, or some other reading from elsewhere, was recited. Indeed, in the *Carpsus*, the ritual book [Col. 0504B] of the Veronese Church, written before the middle of the twelfth century by Stephen, priest and cantor, as we have shown more fully in Dissertation 3, chapter 2, §1, stations are assigned to particular churches on every day of Easter week. We think their catalogue should be appended here, especially since some, chiefly Veronese readers, will be very pleased to learn the names of the churches [Col. 0504C] at which the stations indicated in the Rheims manuscript were held.

Monday: Station at St Stephen’s. Tuesday: Station at the Holy Apostles and St Lawrence’s. Wednesday: Station at SS Peter and John’s. Thursday: Station at St Firmus’s. Friday: Station at St Mary Organum and St Vitalis’s. Saturday: Station at SS Zeno and Proculus’s. On the Sunday of the octave of Easter: Station at St Anastasia’s.] Easter III.

The saving day arrives: a steadfast runner, endowed with manifold grace, swiftly retracing with nimble feet, through the windings of times, its own tracks in its solemn course. [Note: [Col. 0504C] Urbinate manuscript: “through the course of time.” Then *his own* instead of *its own* is read in the Vatican, Rheims, and Pompeian manuscripts; and “the day of the Saviour” instead of “the saving day” in the same Vatican manuscript.] It is its own successor and likewise its own predecessor; ever new in its long-lived age; parent of the year and offspring of the year; it goes before the times which follow it, and scatters the infinite ages. It begets for itself a beginning from its end. This too it will today bestow upon our catechumens preparing for baptism, [Col. 0504A] who are now invited by the blessed setting, so that, plunged in the milky depth of the sacred ocean, rising thence new with the new day, radiant with their own light, they may, keeping their course through the airy path, reach with us the time of promise unto immortality, where one rises for ever.

TRACT XLVIII. On [Note: [Col. 0504C] TRACT XLVIII.—“Easter tract” in the manuscripts; but “Sermon III on Easter” in the Veronese edition. From the middle to the end it resembles Tract 46, as will be evident upon comparison.] Easter IV.

[Note: [Col. 0504D] These words are drawn from the commonly related accounts of the phoenix, an animal which the Fathers often mention as a symbol of resurrection and Easter, as does St Zeno in Book I, Tract 16, no. 9.] Living by its death, nourished in the nest of its tomb, the great day arrives, traversing the countless boundaries of time in its perpetual chariot, along one and the same circuit; unfolding months into seasons, seasons into years, and years into ages. [Note: [Col. 0504D] In Tract 49 mention is made of the “chariot of eternity.” Although the Pompeian manuscript has *course*, the addition of the word *charioteer* suggests that *chariot* should be retained. Here, however, the Venetian edition has *course* for *chariot*; and in Tract 50 all manuscripts and editions prefer, in similar writing, “not in an idle course.” Either may most fairly be written and understood.] Without pause it grows old, yet [Col. 0504B] does not depart from its natal cradle. Surely it bears the image of the Lord’s mystery: for in its setting it celebrates the Passion, and in its returning rising the Resurrection, through which it promises us also the resurrection of future blessedness.

275. TRACT XLIX. On [Note: [Col. 0504D] TRACT XLIX.—Thus in the editions; but in the manuscripts: “Likewise on Easter Day.” This tract also, like the others that follow, contains some similar material, often expressed in the same words; it is enough to have noted this once.] Easter V.

The charioteer of the eternal chariot, retracing its solemn tracks by circling its smooth turning-post, the saving day arrives. [Note: [Col. 0504D] Pompeian manuscript: “course.” In the Toledo manuscript, *earthly* is written in place of *smooth*, perhaps *terrestrial*.] It is its own successor and likewise its own predecessor; ever new in its long-lived age; parent of the year and offspring of the year. [Note: [Col. 0505A] Vatican manuscript: “goes before.” Shortly after, *seeds* for *ages* in the Pompeian manuscript.] It goes before the times which follow it; and, in order to scatter ages for gathering, it begets for itself a beginning from its end. This is the day on which, likewise—but once only—the Maker of humankind, our God and Lord, died for love of his human creature and rose again, assuredly never to repeat his setting. This, I say, is the day on which the deadly darkness was broken apart; on which death was subdued; on which the underworld was compelled to restore alive the people whom it had received [Note: [Col. 0505A] Urbinate manuscript: “had taken up.”] as dead. May God the almighty Father grant that we may celebrate it always and everywhere with our brethren, increasing in faith, number, and love. [Col. 0506A]

TRACT L. On [Note: [Col. 0505B] TRACT L.—“Easter Preface,” or “Likewise a Preface,” in most manuscripts and the Venetian edition; but “On Easter V” in the other editions. The Rheims manuscript adds this marginal note: “To be recited on the third day of Easter, in the assembly of the brethren before the bishop, before the station.” See note 1 on Tract 47.] Easter VI.

Not in an idle course, perpetuating by the returning circuits of the world’s work its allotted tasks, [Note: [Col. 0505B] The Rheims and Vatican manuscripts have *of perpetuity*; the Toledo manuscript and Venetian edition, *perpetuated*. But we preferred *perpetuating*, from other manuscripts and editions, by which it is signified that the Easter day arrives which, through the recurrent windings of the world’s work, reaps its tasks in perpetual going and returning. In Book I, Tract 16, no. 8: “its course reaps the worldly tasks by winding circuits”; the author writes similarly while discussing the moon. See Tract 52, where the same allegory occurs in other words. Shortly after, the Pompeian manuscript reads *gift* for *gifts*.] ever born, new in its setting, rolling back from itself into itself through its own tracks, the saving day arrives, bountiful in every kind of gift to every office of the Lord’s mystery. For it grants reward to pious priests, increase of advancement to ministers who follow them, [Note: [Col. 0505B] St Zeno here briefly indicates the principal sacred offices performed at Verona on Easter day itself—although it began with the vigils of Holy Saturday—in the fourth century. Learned readers will immediately understand the value of this testimony, especially from what is said concerning the advancement, or ordination, of ministers and the care, or reconciliation, of penitents on this day.

With respect to the advancement of ministers, this testimony, so far as we remember and have read, is not only the oldest of all, but the only one in which Easter day is mentioned as a day upon which ordination was performed according to established rite. There is indeed Leo’s Letter 11, alternatively 81, to Dioscorus of Alexandria. In it, the lawful time for sacred ordinations is fixed as after the Saturday of the night which dawns into the first day of the week; and since those who prepared the old editions of Leo believed that this day was Easter itself, they thought the following title should be added to, or retained for, this letter: “On the ordination of a priest or deacon, to be celebrated on Holy Saturday, that is, the Lord’s Day.” [Col. 0505D]

But the most recent editor of St Leo’s works, Dissertation 3, no. 5, and in notes on the same Letter XI, shows not only that this opinion cannot be inferred from Leo’s text, since it speaks there of every Sunday and not of Easter, the principal day; but also, considering other evidence—both Gelasius’s Letter IX to the bishops established throughout Bruttium and Lucania, chapter 11, where, after all the presently lawful times for ordinations have been mentioned, Holy Saturday alone, on which ordinations may even now lawfully be held, is omitted; and the Roman synod under Pope Zachary, A.D. 743, chapter 2; the Council of Limoges under Benedict, A.D. 1034; the Council of Clermont under Urban II, A.D. 1095; and so forth, where there is complete silence concerning ordinations on that Saturday while the other lawful days are enumerated—he declares in general that ordination blessings were never celebrated at Easter. He confirms this even from the fact that the whole solemnity was devoted to the regeneration of catechumens.

Mabillon himself agrees with this view, *Museum Italicum*, vol. II, p. 104. If these things had been stated concerning the rite of the Roman Church alone, they could easily be granted, since no Roman record exists of the discipline now at issue. But since the discipline of all churches is being determined, how false this is is proved by this one testimony of Zeno. For it openly speaks both of Easter day and of the advancement of ministers, which was customarily held on that chief day according to a certain rite. Indeed, the present custom by which bishops may perform lawful ordinations on Holy Saturday ought to have been believed to flow from ancient discipline, rather than to have been newly invented; but it could be confirmed by no surviving ancient document except this one, which we submit from St Zeno for consideration.

Let us add another record which, if it does not indicate the principal rite of this discipline, as is inferred from Zeno, at least confirms the practice by which ordinations were demonstrably held lawfully even on Easter day. This record is supplied [Col. 0506C] by the codex of the Priory of St Gabriel, a fragment of which is quoted in the manuscript *History of the Monastery of Fécamp* in Martène, vol. II, p. 666, *On Ancient Ecclesiastical Rites*: “In the days of Maurilius the archbishop, two bishops of France came to Fécamp for the Easter feast, namely Letzelinus of Paris and Fulco of Amiens, sent on an embassy to William . . . and on that most sacred day of the Resurrection the aforesaid bishop Letzelinus, with the consent and at the request of the abbot of Fécamp, publicly celebrated Masses and, within the sacred solemnities of the Masses, ordained some of the monks priests.”

This testimony concerns times much too late to contribute anything to Zeno’s age; nevertheless, it has some relevance to refuting the view we oppose here and demonstrating the continuance of the rite which we trace from Zeno’s age. Further, in Zeno’s text the word *ministers* should be noted: by it the author indicates all ranks of clergy which follow the priesthood—for *priests* here, as also in Book I, Tract XVI, no. 6, means presbyters, [Col. 0506D] although among the ancients the title *priest* generally denotes a bishop. By affirming that an increase of advancement was granted them on this day, he indicates that they were promoted from one lower rank to another higher one; and thereby plainly implies that there was a diversity of ranks among those promoted. If you consider these words to have been addressed to the clergy of Verona, you will readily infer that at this same period several grades of clergy were present in this city among the workers mentioned by Zeno in Tract 44. On the care of penitents, see the following note.] the fruit of immortality to the faithful, [Note: [Col. 0506D] The reconciliation of penitents does not seem formerly to have taken place either on Easter day itself or on Holy Saturday, but on Thursday in the Lord’s Supper, as is clear from the Gelasian Sacramentary and all the Orders and writers. Was Verona’s discipline, at least at that time, exceptional? Just as in the Church of Milan [Col. 0507B] in Ambrose’s age penitents were reconciled on Friday in the Preparation, according to his Letter XX to Marcellina, no. 26; and the same obtained much later in Spain and in some Gallican churches, as Martène proves, vol. II, *On Ancient Ecclesiastical Rites*, Book I, chapter 6, article 5, no. 10. But perhaps Zeno calls it the care of penitents by which they were perfectly restored to Christ, because they were admitted to the sacred synaxis only on Easter day itself.] care to penitents, [Col. 0507A] the way of light to catechumens, [Note: [Col. 0507B] He here notes two grades of those preparing for baptism: catechumens and *competentes* (“candidates”). Although in the later age all persons to be baptized were divided into three or even four grades, as may be seen in Du Cange, formerly they were divided only into the two grades mentioned here by St Zeno, as is clear from Origen, *Against Celsus*, Book III; St Isidore, *On the Divine Offices*, Book II; Hrabanus, *On the Institution of Clerics*, Book I; and Leidrad of Lyons, *On the Sacrament of Baptism*, chapter 1.

The difference between the two was this: catechumens, so called from hearing catecheses—and therefore frequently called *hearers* by the Latin Fathers, including Tertullian, *On Penance*; Cyprian, Letters XIII and 24; and others—were instructed in the word of God so that, as St Zeno says, they might know the way of light. *Competentes*, however, were those already sufficiently instructed in the way of salvation who earnestly sought baptism together. “For what else are the *competentes*,” Augustine says, Sermon CCXVI, no. 1, “but those who seek together?” After the scrutinies had been completed, they were baptized especially in the Easter vigils, receiving forgiveness of all sins.] and forgiveness of all sins to the candidates. [Note: [Col. 0507D] The Rheims manuscript reads *forgiven*, incorrectly; for the accusative case of this noun is apparent from the context, and “forgiveness of sins” is similarly written in Book I, Tract XVI, no. 12. See note 53 there, where we showed that *forgiveness* is used by others in place of *remission*.] Thus he leads all, gathered into the one grace of Christ’s body, to the heavenly kingdoms, through our Lord and Saviour Jesus Christ, who is blessed unto ages of ages. [Note: [Col. 0507D] The Toledo codex adds “Amen.”]

278. TRACT LI. On [Note: [Col. 0507D] TRACT LI.—Thus in the Veronese edition. In the manuscripts and Venetian edition: “Easter Preface.” The Rheims codex, however, has this marginal note: “On Easter, on the fourth weekday of Easter, to be recited in the assembly of the brethren before the bishop, before the station.”] Easter VII.

The great day arrives, circling the swift course of the perpetual year through the increase of its twice-sixfold change, [Note: [Col. 0507D] We have written *twice-sixfold* as one word, as in the manuscripts, although the editions prefer it separately. So other manuscripts and editions of other authors often write the same word together. The twice-sixfold change concerns the twelve months through which the annual orbit is completed and Easter day returns. St Zeno’s lively ingenuity is evident in these words: he calls the yearly orbit, through which Easter day completes its course, one and the same—not itself, but itself—by antithesis. Not very unlike this expression is that in Book I, Tract 16, no. 8, when he speaks of the phoenix being reborn immediately after its setting: “Finally,” he says, “in the tomb there rejoices at the feast, not a shadow but reality; not an image but the phoenix; not another, but—although another, yet a better one—the former self.” [Col. 0508C]] one and the same orbit, not itself, but itself—ever new to itself in its setting. What is passing follows; what is to come goes before. [Note: [Col. 0508C] “It arrives. It follows what . . .” in the Vatican manuscript.] In all things it is new, yet in all things it is old. It is changed in every point, not in nature but in number. It becomes [Col. 0507B] the son of the hours, though it is the father of all ages.

This is the day, brethren, on which the whole world was redeemed by our Lord; on which, made new by heavenly seed, [Note: [Col. 0508C] That is, the Christian people was made alive. In the Urbinate codex, both “that is, our people” and “that is, the Christian people” are perhaps glosses which entered the text from the margin, where someone had written them.] that is, our people was given life. This, I say, is the day which shows us an example of resurrection. Certainly, by its condition we are more blessed than it: for it dies in order always to live; but the faithful person, rising after the setting of the second birth, is never overtaken by the horror of darkness. [Col. 0508A]

279. TRACT LII. On [Note: [Col. 0508C] TRACT LII.—In the manuscripts, “A Preface Begins,” or “Likewise a Preface”; in the Venetian edition with the Zeno manuscript, “Easter Preface”; in the Veronese and other editions, “On Easter: Sermon VII.” The Rheims manuscript has this marginal note: “On the second weekday of Easter, to be recited in the assembly of the brethren before the bishop, before the station.”] Easter VIII.

Bent in a beautiful circle, the sacred day is borne through the allotted tasks of the world’s work in the four-horsed chariot of the seasons, [Note: [Col. 0508C] *Quadriga* is ablative and is used for the four seasons of the year.] rich in the twelvefold changes of months with its perpetual chariot, content with no stopping-place, because its course is immortality. Yet whether it runs forward or returns is uncertain, since its past remains in order that it may return. A wondrous principle indeed! By wearing away it renews the varied spaces of innumerable ages; yet its orbit is always one. It admonishes us, brethren, to celebrate in unity and concord the saving mysteries of the Lord’s Passion and Resurrection; through our Lord and Saviour Jesus Christ. [Col. 0508B] [Note: [Col. 0508C] “Amen” in the Pompeian and Urbinate codices.]

TRACT LIII. On [Note: [Col. 0508C] TRACT LIII.—Venetian edition: “Easter Preface.” The Zeno manuscript adds: “for those to be baptized.” Veronese edition: “Sermon IX on Easter for those to be baptized.” Finally, the other manuscripts: “Easter Tract.”] Easter IX.

The splendid day, beloved brethren, the father of the ages, is present, rich in every kind of fruitful offspring; from its abundant bosom, at whatever moments it wills, it distributes the gifts of the four seasons. [Note: [Col. 0508D] *Expungere* is used for *distribute*, as in Tract 38, “he distributes the *apophoreta*,” that is, small gifts to be carried home. See note 16 there. Thus in the Greek-Latin Glossaries, Greek *diairetēs*, “distributor,” is rendered *expunctor*, as though to divide or distribute and to distribute were the same, as is the Greek verb *dihairéō* (διαιρέω).]

Finally, for our candidates [Col. 0509A] the winter of sins ends today; with the oil prepared they will rejoice. [Note: [Col. 0508D] *Finally* is customary in Zeno for “in a few words,” as may be seen from the index; this meaning is defended in note 4 on Tract 7 of this book. In the editions and manuscripts the punctuation was wrong: “Finally, for our candidates winter ends today. They will rejoice in the oil of sins.” What oil of sins could bring joy to the candidates? The error is obvious. The Pompeian manuscript had *sins*, and a second hand corrected it to *sinners*; but this does not entirely remove the difficulty. We therefore judged that different punctuation must be used. [Col. 0509B]

By the oil, moreover, the ancients understand the sacred chrism. Optatus says in Book VII against Parmenian: “They call oil that liquid which is prepared in Christ’s name, and after it has been prepared it is called chrism.” Since Zeno attributes the fruit of gladness to this oil, it seems that the oil is meant with which, as Cyprian says in Letter 70, the baptized are anointed—namely, when the neophytes were confirmed on Easter day. The author calls oil the gift of the Holy Spirit in Book II, Tract 14; Augustine speaks explicitly about it in Sermon CCXXVII, which he delivered to the baptized on Easter day. Yet we would not deny that the anointing with chrism, counted among the rites of baptism, may be meant.] Today the smiling spring will render them into diverse flowers by diverse charisma, [Note: [Col. 0509C] The Pompeian manuscript and Venetian edition have *will render* without the particle *is*, which is likewise absent in the Toledo and Zeno codices. But *is going to render* must plainly be read, since it refers to the neuter *spring*, which is going to render, that is, change, the candidates into diverse flowers—such as the sweet-smelling neophytes are customarily called. Indeed, Zeno calls them “my sweetest flowers” at the end of Book I, Tract 15, no. 5. These flowers are diverse through diverse charisma, namely through different preparation and faith, concerning which distinction Zeno has said enough in Tracts 31 and 33.] when, washed in the health-giving water, they begin to eat the new bread and rejoice in the harvest of clear summer. [Note: [Col. 0509C] This bread is the Eucharist given to the neophytes under the appearance of bread; likewise, the word *mustum* (“new wine”) signifies the same Eucharist, which they received under the appearance of wine. Although St Zeno frequently uses such allegories in other matters, he uses them more frequently in indicating mysteries and sacraments, which, by the discipline of secrecy, were guarded against being openly explained in their proper terms. On this subject Emmanuel Schelstrate discusses much, and eloquently, in his separate treatise *On the Discipline of Secrecy*, chapter 4, sole article, §5, where he also considers this passage of Zeno, whom he calls a most ancient and learned author.] Nor will the autumnal new wine delay them; filled and intoxicated by it, they will happily glow with the heat of the Holy Spirit. May God the almighty Father grant that they may never grow cold. [Note: [Col. 0509D] The Toledo and Vatican manuscripts, with the Venetian edition, read “in all things.” The same edition, with the Pompeian manuscript, adds “Amen” at the end.]

281. TRACT LIV. On [Note: [Col. 0509D] TRACT LIV.—The Vatican, Toledo, Urbinate, and Pompeian manuscripts, and the Rheims index: “Tract for Easter Day, by the aforesaid,” that is, St Zeno, who had been named in the conclusions of the preceding tracts. This tract agrees with several immediately following, which are entitled “On Exodus” in the same manuscripts. Therefore this same title has rightly been prefixed to this tract also in the editions. We have retained both the manuscript and printed titles in this first tract because it was delivered at the Easter feast on the occasion of the reading from Exodus concerning the crossing of the Red Sea, which was a symbol of Easter and baptism; for this reason that reading was customarily read and explained at Easter time. [Col. 0510C] The same consideration applies to the tracts which follow.] Exodus I. On Easter Day.

As the divine reading testifies, in Egypt the people of God, Israel, was most harshly oppressed by Pharaoh and his people beneath the enormous yoke of captivity (Exodus 1). [Note: [Col. 0510C] The editions, with a few manuscripts: “enslaved.”] God commands this people to depart, under the leadership, namely, of Moses and Aaron (Exod. 12:31). A pillar of cloud showed the way by day, and the same pillar of fire by night (Exod. 13:21–22). The sea is split; and the astonished water is fixed solid, heaped up in steep banks on right and left (Exod. 14:21–22). God’s people sails with its feet. A marvellous thing! Though barbarians press them violently, neither horseman nor ship can follow their route. Miriam beats the timbrel with the women (Exod. 15:20); a hymn is sung; God’s people [Col. 0510A] is set free; and, when the waters close again, the way is destroyed together with the pursuer (Exod. 14:28).

So far as spiritual understanding permits, Egypt is this world; Pharaoh with his people is the devil and every spirit of wickedness; Israel is the Christian people, commanded to depart so as to hasten toward the things to come. Moses and Aaron, by what they were, represented the priesthood; by their number, they represented the mystery of the two Testaments. [Note: [Col. 0510C] Sparaverius thinks that the following should be read by correction and addition: “Moses and Aaron, by what they were—the priesthood—and by their number . . .” But there is no need, since St Zeno’s meaning is to indicate that Moses and Aaron, by what they were—for they were priests, Psalm 98:6—represented the priesthood; and by their number represented the two Testaments, which Zeno customarily asserted were signified by all binary numbers, as is clear from Book II, Tract 13.] The pillar showing the way is Christ the Lord. Its twofold appearance, of cloud and fire, signifies two judgments: one of water, which has occurred; the other of fire, which [Note: [Col. 0510C] The judgment by fire is indicated, by which at the end of the world all things will be burned, according to 2 Peter 3:7: “The heavens and earth are reserved for fire unto the day of judgment and destruction of ungodly people.” John likewise signified this in Revelation 20:9 and following.] is to come.

We ought to understand the sea as the sacred font, [Note: [Col. 0510C] That the crossing of the Red Sea was a type of baptism, as we noted in note 1, is explicitly taught along with Zeno by the holy Fathers. It is enough to name Cyril of Jerusalem, who says in Catechesis 1 to the newly enlightened: “That tyrant”—that is, Pharaoh—“pursued the people of old as far as the sea; but the shameless prince of wickedness, the devil, pursued you as far as the saving waters. He was drowned in the sea; this one is suffocated in the water of salvation.” [Col. 0510D]] in which, by the same waters through which God’s servants are delivered, those who do not flee but bear sins are destroyed. Miriam, who [Col. 0510B] beats the timbrel with the women, was a type of the Church. She, with all the churches to which she has given birth, sings a hymn and beats the true timbrel of the breast, [Note: [Col. 0510D] The Toledo and Vatican manuscripts read “of the sinner,” but “of the breast” is correct.] leading the Christian people not into the wilderness but to heaven.

TRACT LV. On [Note: [Col. 0510D] TRACT LV.—In the Rheims manuscript, “Likewise a tract,” without another title. All the other manuscripts and editions: “On Exodus.” This marginal rubric is found in the Rheims manuscript: “On Easter, to be recited before the bishop in the chamber, after the entrance of the deacons, on Easter day itself.”] Exodus II.

The one who receives the sacred law spiritually, brethren, is the one nourished by its fruit. [Note: [Col. 0510D] Sparaverius thinks *rejoices* should be read, a correction not far from the Toledo manuscript, which reads *having rejoiced*. But *lactatur* may be said for *is fed*.] For when Jews think carnally [Col. 0511A] and seek in flocks of cattle a lamb of twofold nature entrusted to them—a lamb which cannot be found—they thus lose the true lamb, Christ, whom they had found. [Note: [Col. 0511C] The author calls the lamb’s nature twofold because it consists of the two species of goats and sheep, as will be clear from the following tracts.] [Note: [Col. 0511C] The words *lamb* and *Christ* are absent from the Rheims manuscript. In the Toledo manuscript, *Christ* is absent.] For they did not understand that the human flesh, burdened with its sins, was represented by the goats; the Spirit of majesty, by the sheep. When these two were united in Christ, they made the legitimate lamb.

This is the lamb, brethren, of whom the Law says: “It is the Lord’s Passover” (Exod. 12:11, 27). [Note: [Col. 0511C] The Venetian edition has “the Law said it had to sacrifice” in place of “the Law says”; the Veronese edition, “to rejoice”; the Zeno and Sp. manuscripts, “rejoice”—but none yields a satisfactory sense. The other codices have “the Law says,” where *Law*, as often, is used for the books of Moses and here indicates the book of Exodus, in which the text “It is the Lord’s Passover” is indeed read. Nor should one be disturbed that the Vulgate’s interpretation of the passage is “Phase, that is, the Lord’s passing-over”; for *pascha*, *phase*, and “passing-over” are the same. In Jerome’s words on Isaiah 31, p. 423, vol. IV: “It is clear that Pascha, that is, the Lord’s phase, does not signify passion, but passing-over.” Hence the same Zenoian interpretation appears in Tertullian, *Against the Jews*, chapter 11, and especially in Gaudentius, Sermon 2, p. 40.] The apostle Paul also says: “Christ, our Passover, has been sacrificed” (1 Cor. 5:7). Why he deigned to be sacrificed John the Baptist first proclaimed in these words: “Behold the Lamb of God; behold him who takes away [Note: [Col. 0511D] Thus the Rheims and Toledo manuscripts. It was also so in the Pompeian manuscript, but it was corrected to *sin*, as it is also read in the editions.] the sins of the world” (John 1:29).

Therefore he is called first-born, because he alone knows the antiquity of the Father. [Note: [Col. 0511D] In Tract 62 of this book, where similar material is repeated, the author says: “First-born, because before him none exists except the Father, and he is first.”] He is mature, because after him there is none. [Note: [Col. 0511B] Sparaverius would prefer *only*, rightly. But in the cited Tract 62 *mature* is repeated for another reason, because he is eternal. On the authority of the very ancient Rheims manuscript, we have written “there is not any” instead of what is written elsewhere, “there is none.”] He is eternal, because he was slain and was found alive. He is without stain of sin, because he alone is pure. He is saving, because through him we conquer death. He is male, because he is God’s power. This, I say, is the perfect lamb, because in him the great priest, enclosed in his own victim by a holy mystery, has today made God of the man whom he offered in sacrifice. [Note: [Col. 0511D] Namely, he sacrificed him, since Christ offered himself as man to God the Father through the death of the cross, in order in some manner to make man God.]

TRACT LVI. On [Note: [Col. 0511D] TRACT LVI.—The Rheims, Toledo, Vatican, and Urbinate manuscripts: “The continuation of Exodus”; the Pompeian and Zeno manuscripts: “Likewise on Exodus”; the editions: “On Exodus.” This tract resembles Tract 58, and each should be compared with the other in order to be understood more easily; for in some places where they differ, one is explained by the other.] Exodus III.

Time does not allow us, brethren, to render truth to the image. [Note: [Col. 0512C] To “render truth to the image” is the same as to explain what the image or figure truly signifies. Zeno indicates that he is prevented by the short time remaining amid so many Easter offices from explaining what was represented in the figure when the Jews were once freed from Egypt. The Pompeian manuscript reads *of the image*; the Venetian edition, *truth*; neither is satisfactory.] Yet, Jew, why do you rejoice in the records [Col. 0512A] of your crime? [Note: [Col. 0512C] The author calls the Exodus history itself “the records of the Jews’ crime,” since it makes clear that they were guilty of various offences, whether in captivity, while being delivered, or afterwards, as he sufficiently explains below. Zeno declares that the Jews brought forward the Exodus story in commendation of their own name and rejoiced in it wrongly, because it rebounds upon them with no less disgrace than glory: if the divine benefits bestowed on them are evident, their harsh and criminal deeds, by which they responded badly to divine benefits, are also exposed.] You served long in Egypt, [Note: [Col. 0512C] Zeno affirms that the Jews remained in captivity for a long time not by the lot of a foreigner but, as Tract 58 says, “not by necessity but by desert,” namely because of their crimes.] not by the lot of an alien, but by desert. You were rescued thence; you did not escape by your own strength. The pillar of cloud led you by day, that it might show you blind (Exod. 13); [Note: [Col. 0512D] Rheims manuscript: “might guard.”] the pillar of fire by night, that it might warn you of burning. The angel going before advanced your camp, so that you might be proved ungrateful even to God present (Exod. 14). You walked on foot through the sea, that you might suffer shipwreck on land (Exod. 17). Indeed, you drank water from the rock in the wilderness and tasted manna from heaven (Exod. 16) for this purpose: that when afterwards you had fallen into want, you might be more sharply tormented by the memory of former blessings.

TRACT LVII. On [Note: [Col. 0512D] TRACT LVII.—Manuscripts: “The second section of Exodus begins”; editions: “On Exodus.” This tract was delivered after the reading from Exodus, as is evident from its opening period.] Exodus IV.

[Col. 0512B]

Wonderful, dearest brethren, is the narrative of sacred history which has thus been read.

**[Note: [Col. 0512D] Manuscripts Tol., Pomp., Vat., Urb. read *dilectissimi* (“most beloved”). This is lacking in manuscript Vat. and indeed seems superfluous. Manuscript Tol. subsequently has *praelecta* (“read aloud beforehand”) for *perlecta* (“read through”).]** When the people of Israel, crushed beneath the enormous yoke of captivity,

**[Note: [Col. 0512D] Two manuscripts, Rem. and Tol., read *in ormi*; manuscript Pomp., *mortis*; the other manuscripts and editions, *in ortu*, except the Urbinate codex, which exhibits the genuine reading adopted in the text. A little later the same manuscript Urb. has *prehensus* for *depressus*, and manuscript Pomp. reads merely *Moyses*, in place of *duce Moyse*.]** were being destroyed in Egypt by King Pharaoh under harsh conditions (Exodus, ch. 1), they were commanded, through God’s compassion and under the leadership of Moses, to depart (ch. 12). For them, not the circuit of the sun by day, but a pillar of cloud; not the white moon, but a pillar of fire by night, opened an unknown way. When they came between the two elements, there they feared the immediate issue of death (ch. 14).

**[Note: [Col. 0512D] The Venetian edition reads *praesentatae* for *praesentariae*.]** For on this side they were pressed by the hostile swords of the pursuing Egyptians; on that, they were pressed in by the great barrier of the sea.

**[Note: [Col. 0512D–0513B] So that the word *premebatur* (“was pressed”), which recurs in this same clause, need not be repeated, Sparaverius would prefer it to be understood here, or *terrebatur* (“was terrified”) to be read. A little later, manuscripts Rem. and Tol. have *clausui* for *clausus*, and codex Vat. has *clausui objicere* for *clausus obice*.]**

Indeed, they had no ships, no means of crossing the water. Yet suddenly, by divine providence, the sea is divided: the waters, checked on right and left in icy astonishment, are raised into glassy walls, awaiting the passage of God’s people, so that they may be a causeway for those passing through and a sea for those pursuing.

**[Note: [Col. 0513B–C] Manuscript Pomp. reads *transeuntibus* (“for those passing through”); if this is to be read, as is quite probable, something is lacking here and should be supplied thus: “so that there may be a causeway for those passing through, a sea for those pursuing.” We have used *agger* (“causeway”), since the waves suspended on either side are called *aggeres* in Treatise 59.]** Ungrateful Israel is led into a path in which it can fear neither swords nor waves. A wonderful thing! In the middle of the deep he rejoices, dry and dusty, who sees around him his triumph perish happily in shipwreck. The Jew proclaims these things, brethren, and yet, madman that he is, still does not believe God, who is blessed for ages of ages. Amen.

## TREATISE LVIII. On Exodus V.

**[Note: TREATISE LVIII.—Manuscripts Sp., Zen. add “against the Jews.” That discourses were sometimes delivered by the Fathers against Jews even in a later age is clear, to omit other witnesses, from Possidius’s catalogue, where two treatises of St Augustine against the Jews are mentioned which have perished through the injuries of time. Nor should this surprise anyone. After peace had been restored to the Church and public churches had been opened, the practice was introduced that not only the faithful and catechumens, but also heretics, Gentiles, and Jews should attend episcopal sermons. Hence canon 84 of the Fourth Council of Carthage decrees that a bishop must forbid no one—Gentile, heretic, or Jew—from entering the church and hearing the word of God, up to the Mass of the Catechumens. By “Mass of the Catechumens” is meant the dismissal by which catechumens were sent away after the divine word. From this practice, as the Council of Valencia, canon 1, testifies, some were brought to faith: “For,” it says, “we plainly know that, after hearing the preaching of bishops, some have been drawn to the faith.” We wished to point this out not because we believe that Zeno truly delivered these treatises against Jews who were actually present, but so that it may appear how weak is the argument of those who use these treatises to place Zeno in earlier centuries, as though bishops of a later age had not publicly spoken against Jews in churches. Rather, it is evident that Zeno recited these treatises on the occasion of the Paschal readings, in which God’s benefits toward the Jews are discussed, in order, after reproaching their fault of ingratitude, to indicate that true worship of God had been transferred to Christians, to whom indeed all things happen that are signified in the figures of the Old Testament. This treatise, with a few additions and alterations, contains the same material as Treatise 56. See therefore what we noted there.]**

Time does not permit the image to be restored to its truth. Yet, Jew, why do you rejoice in the designation of your crime?

**[Note: Treatise 56 reads: “the memorials of your crime.”]** You served in Egypt for a long time, not by necessity but by desert (Exodus, ch. 1). You were rescued from there (ch. 15): you did not escape by your own strength. A pillar of cloud led you by day, to show that you were blind; a pillar of fire by night, to signify that you would burn (ch. 13). An angel goes before your camp, lest you make any excuse for your crime. You walk through the sea (ch. 14): the wave fleeing to right and left bears witness to your swift feet, ready to shed blood (Psalm 13).

Finally, you are received into the wilderness (Exodus, ch. 17), where you recognize that you have now arrived. There, indeed, you drank water from the rock and tasted manna from heaven (ch. 16), so that, wretched man, you might know what you had been going to lose.

**[Note: The Remensis manuscript concludes: “The treatise of St Zeno on Exodus ends.”]**

## TREATISE LIX. On Exodus VI.

**[Note: TREATISE LIX.—The Venetian edition, with manuscript Zen., entitles this and the following eight treatises “On the Jews”; the remaining manuscripts, “On Exodus.” The Veronese edition prefixed both titles; it is enough to have noted this once.]**

The very things from which Jews consider themselves blessed show them to be unhappy. For I think it more advantageous for a miserable person to remain in his condition than for one who is blessed to fall into the uttermost miseries.

**[Note: Manuscript Urb. reads *esse* (“to be”) more suitably. To avoid ambiguity, understand “for a miserable person”; the meaning is that it is far better for a miserable person to remain in his state than for one blessed and prosperous to be cast down into the final miseries.]**

For they proclaim that their fathers destroyed the Egyptian people by fleeing from them (Exodus, ch. 14);

**[Note: The Veronese edition and several manuscripts read *praedicat* (“proclaims”); we corrected this from five manuscripts and the Venetian edition, since the Jews are understood in place of a nominative subject.]** that God presided over their ancestors and went before their journey. They do not understand that from that point he had removed them from his face and cast them behind his back together with their future descendants:

> The Red Sea also, split in the middle into two shores, and with embankments drawn up on the right and left in close array, its waters remaining intact, suspended nature—dried out in the deep, resisting itself against itself—in astonishment: an earthly road shone between the waves.

This, surely, did not foretell the merit of a heavenly people, but the destruction of their future dispersion throughout the whole world.

**[Note: Sparaverius, judging this text corrupt, thought it should be corrected, though he admitted that he could not restore it without ancient books. He proposed: “The Red Sea also, split in the middle into two shores, and with embankments drawn up on right and left, its waves massed in battle-line, the pathway of the deep dried by the clear water, nature—astonished and pressing against itself—hung suspended.” We had several manuscripts, but nowhere did anything of that sort emerge. From the punctuation we have adopted, we think that the passage need not seem so corrupt that it cannot be understood.]**

Therefore he led them thence into the wilderness (Exodus, ch. 15), and instructed them to heal the wounds of their detestable mind by providing milk and honey (ch. 16). For upon the weak and languid he sprinkled the tenderness of manna; they were not fit or worthy to enjoy the lasting solidity of heavenly bread. The rock gushed forth for them into a spring (ch. 17), so that, after their cisterns had been ruined, they might later drink, as they deserved, muddy water, the Lord saying: “They have forsaken me, the fountain of living water, and have dug for themselves broken cisterns, which cannot hold water” (Jeremiah 2:13).

**[Note: Manuscript Rem. has *senaculis* for *lacunis*, wrongly; a *senaculum* is a place in which the senate meets. Perhaps *coenaculis*, from *coenum*, “mud.” Here, however, the hollows mentioned in Jeremiah 2:13 are indicated. In Zeno’s interpretation they are called ruined reservoirs; in the Vulgate, “broken cisterns,” that is, exhausted cisterns incapable of holding water.]**

Finally, what do these unhappy people hope from the image, whose truth they have not deserved to know—our Lord Jesus Christ?

**[Note: Manuscripts Vat., Pomp., Urb., and the Venetian edition read *per Dominum* (“through the Lord”), but wrongly; for *Dominum* refers to the truth which Zeno says the Jews have not deserved to know.]**

## TREATISE LX. On Exodus VII.

**[Note: TREATISE LX.—Manuscripts Rem., Tol., Urb., Pomp.: “The following material of Exodus”; Vat.: “The treatise on the sequence of Exodus begins”; manuscript Zen. and the Venetian edition: “On the Jews.” The Veronese editors prefixed both headings.]**

I do not see how a Pharisee can celebrate the lawful Passover, since that lofty and famous temple lies buried in its own dust, levelled with the plains by a pitiable devastation. The priestly seat of pestilence (Psalm 1:1) has rightly been destroyed by the sacrilege of its worshippers.

**[Note: Manuscripts Rem., Vat., and Pomp. read *sacrilego jure* (“by sacrilegious law”).]** The emptied horn no longer breathes out ointments. The prophets testify that its feast days have been turned into mourning (Amos 5:21), and its songs into lamentation (Amos 5:23; 5:22; Isaiah 1:14). We have received that bulls, rams, goats, and lambs have often been rejected by the Lord (Jeremiah 6:20).

**[Note: This reading is from manuscripts Rem., Tol., Pomp., Vat., and Urb.; elsewhere *acceperunt* (“they received”) was read.]**

What more is there? No one, brethren, can celebrate any mystery whose sacrifice you perceive has been condemned by divine judgment, through our Lord Jesus Christ, who is blessed with the Father and the Holy Spirit for all ages of ages.

**[Note: Manuscripts Tol., Vat., Urb., Pomp., and Zen. add: “with the Holy Spirit.”]**

## TREATISE LXI. On Exodus VIII.

**[Note: TREATISE LXI.—Manuscripts: “Begins on Exodus”; Venetian edition: “On the Jews,” added in another hand in manuscript Pomp. With a few additions and alterations, this treatise contains the same material as Treatise 60, given above, and Treatise 62, which follows.]**

The Jew maintains that he observes the lawful Passover; yet nothing remains to him of the ancient sacrament except a story woven with empty sighs. Indeed, that royal temple lies levelled with the plains. Its altars, overturned by the hand together with their sacrifices, have vanished, scattered into dust. The priestly seat of pestilence has been destroyed by its very name (Psalm 1:1).

**[Note: On the authority of manuscripts Tol. and Vat., we have removed the word “God,” which was read after “altars.” Subsequently manuscript Urb. has *delata* (“carried away”) for *deleta* (“destroyed”); but this same thought, repeated almost in the same words in the preceding treatise, has *deleta*.]**

The saving lamb (Exodus 12:5), which is designated as being from sheep and goats, cannot be found among the flocks.

**[Note: Exodus 12:5, according to the Vulgate interpreter, gives this command concerning the Paschal lamb: “Your lamb shall be without blemish, a male of the first year; according to this rite you shall take also a kid.” In this rendering lamb and kid are considered distinct, not one animal sharing the nature of lamb and kid, as Zeno’s text presents it. Yet St Gaudentius agrees with Zeno. In Sermon IV, p. 53, after citing the precept of Exodus, he observes: “From this the Jews ought to have noticed that the law of God must be understood spiritually, because they read that the lamb to be sacrificed was to be taken from lambs and kids; whereas it is contradictory that, if it is a lamb, it should be from lambs and likewise from kids.” This observation, however, is alien to the Hebrew truth and flowed from some interpretation, which Gaudentius himself there gives: “You shall take from lambs and kids.” He likewise cites the whole of Exodus 12:5 in Sermon III, p. 48: “The lamb shall be perfect, male, one year old for you; you shall take from lambs and kids.” Ambrose has precisely the same translation and reading in *On Abraham*, book I, ch. 5, no. 40, and in Epistle 23 to the bishops of Aemilia, no. 19.

This translation, although it appears fully to agree with the Hebrew text, nevertheless does not completely convey the force of the Hebrew expression and gave occasion for the argument used by Zeno and Gaudentius. Since the command is conveyed by the force of the translation that the lamb to be sacrificed at Passover is to be taken from lambs and kids, that lamb was believed to have to share the nature of lambs and kids. Yet the logic of the Hebrew expression does not signify this. The animal commanded in the first part of the verse is called in Hebrew by a word which, although it sometimes means a lamb—as in Jeremiah 50:17, “flocks of sheep”—at other times indicates the offspring of goats, as in Deuteronomy 14:14, “flocks of goats.” Thus the word by itself properly means not a lamb, but an animal of either species, whether from sheep or goats. It is used in this sense in Exodus 12:5; moreover, in the second clause of that verse the Hebrew particle prefixed to “goats” is to be taken not as “and” but as “or,” as it often is elsewhere. Thus the verse should be understood: “An animal, or offspring of wool-bearing animals—for this is what the word for livestock means, concerning which see note 4 on Treatise 65—shall be perfect, male, one year old for you; and you shall take it from sheep or from goats.” Thus a slight difference in the Latin translation led Zeno and Gaudentius into an erroneous explanation.]**

Its feast days and songs, according to the word of God, have advanced into weeping and mourning (Amos 5:23). That proud city is enslaved. Yet it kills countless flocks of sheep, which it consumes in bitterness. Who does not understand, brethren, that this is not Passover, but the bromosus banquet of a bloody robber?

**[Note: Thus read manuscripts Rem. and Pomp. Filesacus, *Selecta*, book I, p. 241, interprets this *bromosum convivium* as a meal consisting of the flesh of birds or lambs, perhaps because βρῶμι in Hesychius signifies βρῶσις, “food.” But we explained the meaning of this word, used elsewhere by Zeno, in note 10 on Treatise 15, book I. There also we showed that a passage of St Gaudentius, Sermon 2, must be restored: asserting that our Paschal Lamb should be taken “without *bromus*” (not “without broth,” as the received reading has it), he sufficiently indicates that the Jews’ Paschal meal was accompanied by *bromus*, which Zeno here calls *bromosus*.]**

**[Note: Manuscripts Tol., Vat., Urb., Pomp., Zen., and the Venetian edition append this conclusion: “through our Lord Jesus Christ.” The word *our*, however, is absent from manuscript Tol.]**

## TREATISE LXII. On Exodus IX.

**[Note: TREATISE LXII.—Manuscript Zen. and the Venetian edition: “On the Jews”; the other codices: “Begins on Exodus.” With a few additions and changes, the same matters are repeated here as in the second and two preceding treatises; therefore the notes on those should be consulted.]**

The Pharisees maintain that they perform the lawful Passover. Yet along with the supreme temple, as it was thought, they lost the high priesthood; they have been deprived of the horn of royal anointing. Circumcision, the testimony of an impure mind, threatens them with an imminent punishment by the infliction of the mark that denotes it. Every kind of livestock, along with its sacrifice, is rejected. Their fasts, feast days, and every solemn observance are an abomination before God (Amos 5:21; Isaiah 1:14; Jeremiah 6:20; Isaiah 58:5; Zechariah 7:5).

Since these things are so, by whom, how, and from where is Passover celebrated?

**[Note: The same manuscript has *sunt* (“are”) here; a little later manuscript Rem. has *Addo* for *Adde*.]**

Add that, through their own fault, they have lost the lawful lamb which they had found, which Scripture designated as from sheep and goats (Exodus 12:5): from goats, certainly, on account of the garment of sinful flesh; from sheep, on account of the spirit of majesty.

**[Note: See note 3 on the preceding treatise. A different, though not very dissimilar, allegorical interpretation may be found in St Gaudentius in the passage cited there.]**

He is called firstborn because, apart from the Father, none is first before him. Mature, because eternal. Perfect, because he is the power of God and the wisdom of God. Immaculate, because he alone has no sin. Saving, because he changed death into life: for our sake he was slain, and lives; buried, and rose again; reckoned a man, and found to be God, glorious for ages of ages.

**[Note: The printed editions and manuscript Zen. read: “apart from the Father, with whom he is also coeternal in divinity with the Holy Spirit, none is first before him,” etc. But the words placed between the two commas are absent from the remaining manuscripts and appear only to have been added in a later hand in the margin of manuscript Pomp.; thence they were intruded into the text of St Zeno. Indeed, in Treatise 55, where the same thought recurs, no mention is made of the Holy Spirit: “He is therefore called firstborn because he alone is conscious of the Father’s antiquity.” Nor does this detract in any way from the eternity of the Holy Spirit, whom St Zeno elsewhere plainly declares coeternal with the Father and Son. See, among other places, Treatise XIII, book II, no. 1.]**

## TREATISE LXIII. On Exodus X.

**[Note: TREATISE LXIII.—Manuscripts: “The following material of Exodus,” except Zen., which, like the Venetian edition, has “On the Jews.” It should also be noted that this treatise is marked by no number in any manuscript; accordingly its heading is missing from the prefixed table in the Remensis manuscript, though in the body it appears without a number between Treatises 46 and 47 of book I.]**

If Jews glory in the memory of an emptied image, how much more should the Christian glory, in whom there is not a figure but truth? Recognize and prove this alike from the realities themselves. Jews proclaim that their ancestors, crushed beneath the heavy yoke of Pharaoh and his army, were freed from Egypt (Exodus 14).

**[Note: Manuscripts Tol. and Vat. read *praedicabant* (“proclaimed”).]** From the fury of the devil and the violent host of idols, not only our ancestors but the whole Christian offspring is continually delivered, at every moment, from the true Egypt—that is, from this world. Moses provided leadership for them; Christ the Lord is our leader. For them a pillar of cloud and fire showed the way; for us the most brilliant oracles of the Old and New Testaments have disclosed the way and the true Christ the Lord, who says:

**[Note: The particle *et* (“and”) is absent from manuscript Pomp.]** “I am the way and the truth” (John 14:6).

Their fugitive people crossed the Red Sea on dry foot, while the cliffs of waters stood astonished on the right and left (Exodus 14:21). But our sea, receiving those who come voluntarily, happily makes them shipwrecked; and, destroying every sin, it submerges them in the birth-giving wave, so that, made heavenly, they no longer know how to desire the earth.

**[Note: Although the relative *quos* (“whom”) is absent from the manuscripts, it is retained, as all printed editions have it, since the sense appears to require it.]**

Finally, after the sea they came to the wilderness; after baptism we come to paradise.

**[Note: Here the author calls not heaven but the Church “paradise,” into which we enter through baptism. The word *paradise*, common among Greeks and deriving from a Hebrew word for an orchard or garden, has the same proper meaning, as can be seen in Xenophon’s *Oeconomicus* and *Hellenica*, book IV, ch. 4. Transferred from Greek to Latin, the word retained the same proper meaning, as appears from Firmilian’s Epistle 75 among those of Cyprian and from the Vulgate in Song of Songs 4:13, and elsewhere. Hence that exceedingly pleasant garden in which the first parents were placed by God is properly called paradise. But just as, allegorically, that heavenly region abounding in delights, which the blessed shall possess eternally, is called paradise, so by a similar allegory St Zeno could call the Church paradise, which certain Fathers observed to be signified in Scripture by the name of the enclosed garden. In this sense he very aptly contrasts it with the wilderness.]**

Manna was sprinkled upon them when they were hungry (Exodus 15); but we cannot hunger forever, since we carry with us the provision of heavenly bread.

**[Note: We preferred *sempiternum*, “forever,” an adverb also used by Plautus, *Aulularia* II.1.16, to the senseless *sempiternam* found in the printed editions and manuscripts. Does this refer to the ancient practice of always carrying the Eucharistic bread with one, even home—a practice sufficiently discussed in Treatise 5, book I, note 29?]**

For them, when thirsty, the rock flowed out as drink (ibid., 17:6);

**[Note: Manuscript Pomp. reads *at* for *ad*.]** whoever drinks at Christ’s fountain does not know how to thirst forever. In the desert they were offered the sweetness of milk and honey; but to us there shall be granted in God’s kingdom what is greater: the blessedness of eternal life, sweeter than honey and whiter than milk.

## TREATISE LXIV. On Exodus XI.

**[Note: TREATISE LXIV.—The titles of this treatise in both manuscripts and editions are exactly the same as those of the preceding treatise.]**

Why does the empty Pharisee swell with pride, whom the shadow of the past delights for a moment?

**[Note: Manuscript Vat. reads *momentis*. Later, manuscripts Rem., Tol., Vat., and Urb. read *delectatur* (“is delighted”) for *delectat* (“delights”); we would gladly have printed this if *qui* (“who”) rather than *quem* (“whom”) had been read.]** He exults because he grew in Egypt; yet in his native soil he diminished. Because he was released from the bonds of captivity; yet even now he is bound by the customs of barbarous madness. God gave him leadership; the same God afterward cast him away from his face. He gained a kingdom, in order that after royal dignity he might serve the Roman Empire with greater disgrace.

**[Note: Manuscript Rem. reads “forever Roman”; manuscripts Vat., Tol., Urb., “forever to the Roman”; Venetian edition, “forever to the Roman Empire”; the other manuscripts and editions have the text printed above.]**

Would you know how great his holiness is? The sea could support him united; the earth cannot carry him dispersed.

## TREATISE LXV. On Exodus XII.

**[Note: TREATISE LXV.—Manuscripts: “Likewise, on the Day of Passover”; manuscript Zen.: “To the Jews”; Venetian edition: “On the Jews”; Veronese edition: both “On Exodus” and “On the Jews.” We retain “On Exodus,” since it agrees with the preceding titles headed “On Exodus,” and the sequence of headings should not seem to be altered for this one instance.]**

How long, Jew, will you fail to dispel the darkness of your dull heart

**[Note: Nonius, II.75: *brutus* means dull and obtuse. The ancient scholiast on Horace, who uses the word in Book I, Ode 34, verse 9, notes: “The *bruti* are called heavy and slow”; hence Isidore, Book X, under B: “*Brutus* is, as it were, *obrutus* (‘buried over’), because he lacks understanding; for he is without reason and prudence.”]** and to recognize, by proving them, the oracles of the sacred law now fulfilled in Christ? Yet if, according to your own understanding, you wish to celebrate a lawful Passover, you must seek the lamb (Exodus 12:5), as it was commanded: one formed from the discordant natures of lambs and kids, which your own ancestors did not find among the wool-bearing flocks.

**[Note: See note 3 on Treatise 61.]**

And would that you might find it. For you are worthy of such a sacrifice, since you suppose your salvation to lie in the entrails of an uncertain animal.

**[Note: “Uncertain animal”: the author calls the lamb uncertain because, as sharing the nature of lambs and kids, it is found nowhere among wool-bearing animals. Read the note just cited. “Among wool-bearing animals,” I say; for the word used here is *pecus*, not *pecudis*. *Pecus pecudis* signifies every animal that feeds on terrestrial pasture; but *pecus pecoris* chiefly signifies animals that bear wool, as Basilius Faber establishes in the *Thesaurus eruditionis*, under *Pecus*. Compare Treatise 61: “among the flocks.”]**

That you kill many indiscriminately is due to your gluttony. That you do so in different places is due to vanity.

**[Note: The Venetian edition wrongly reads *vagaris* (“you wander”) for *vanitatis* (“vanity”).]** That you eat them with bitterness is due to unhappiness. I pass over the fact that the sacrifice which he who commanded it now rejects is a memorial of the ungrateful, not a remedy.

**[Note: For the benefit of younger readers, this syntax should be construed thus: “I pass over the fact that the sacrifice which he himself who commanded it rejects as being done is a memorial, not a remedy, of the ungrateful.”]**

This alone I say: fulfill the law in its other requirements also, as it is written: “Gird your loins. Put sandals on your feet. Take a staff in your hand” (ibid., ch. 11). Set out for the wilderness, if you wish to imitate your ancestors.

**[Note: Manuscript Tol. reads *mores*, “customs,” for *majores*, “ancestors.” Manuscript Rem. adds this conclusion: “The treatise of St Zeno on the Day of Passover ends happily.”]**

## TREATISE LXVI. On Exodus XIII.

**[Note: TREATISE LXVI.—Manuscript: “Begins Exodus.” Only codex Zen., with the Venetian edition, has “On the Jews.” The Veronese edition uses both titles. It contains material similar to Treatise 60.]**

Christian, learn briefly why Jews cannot celebrate the lawful Passover. Solomon’s temple, overthrown by hostile devastation, lies buried with its ruin: where do they sacrifice? They no longer have priests to sacrifice for their salvation. Bulls, goats, rams, and lambs are abhorrent to the Lord: from where do they sacrifice? They have forsaken God and overthrown his altars: to whom do they sacrifice?

**[Note: Sparaverius thinks this sentence too, like the others, should be phrased as a question; then he would write *quis* (“who”) for *qui* (“who”), and *sacrificet* (“may sacrifice”) for *sacrificent* (“may sacrifice”).]**

Yet they retain this one thing as their own: that, in order to increase their base lust more and more, they constantly wash themselves in still baser baths, ever ungrateful to God.

**[Note: The use among Hebrews of water for washing themselves and their possessions was both very ancient and very frequent, as is evident from Exodus 29:4 and 30:19; Leviticus 16; Deuteronomy 21:6; and other passages. St Mark the Evangelist recalls many Jewish baptisms in ch. 7:3–4: “For the Pharisees and all Jews, unless they wash their hands frequently, do not eat, holding the traditions of the elders. And when they come from the market, unless they baptize themselves, they do not eat. And there are many other things handed down to them to observe: baptisms of cups and pots and bronze vessels and beds.” St Basil mentions baptism employed by Jews for purification from sins in his homily *On Baptism*. Maimonides, *Hilcoth Issure*, ch. 13, nos. 1, 4, and 5, offers very full testimony concerning baptism by which proselytes were washed—namely, anyone, whether from the Gentiles or Christians, who wished to be admitted among Hebrews.

Here, however, since St Zeno mentions those baptisms whose frequency increases lust more and more, he appears rather to indicate baths, common among Hebrews as also among Gentiles. That these contributed greatly to lust is evident from Jerome, Epistle 79 to Salvina, no. 7, where he warned her to beware lest the heat of baths inflame the young woman’s fresh blood. Tertullian, *On Prayer*, ch. 17, testifies that Hebrews were accustomed daily to wash all their limbs. See also Gaudentius, Sermon IX, p. 108. There was also a Jewish sect of persons called in the Greek formula for renouncing the Jewish religion, published from a royal manuscript by Cotelerius in his observations on book I of the *Recognitions* of St Clement, §53, Ἡμεροβαπτίσται—that is, “daily baptizers”—who taught, as is there reported, that no one could be saved unless he washed daily.]**

## TREATISE LXVII. On Exodus XIV.

**[Note: TREATISE LXVII.—All manuscripts: “On the Day of Passover”; Zen., with the Venetian edition: “On the Jews.” In the Veronese edition there are two headings: “On Exodus XIV” and “On the Jews.” So as not to disrupt the sequence, we retain the title “On Exodus,” since it contains almost the same matters as the other treatises marked by this heading, sometimes repeated here in the very same words.]**

Learn briefly that Jews are not only unable to celebrate the lawful Passover, but retain absolutely nothing of divine religion. Solomon’s temple, on which they relied, has fallen.

**[Note: This was corrected from manuscripts Rem., Vat., Pomp., Urb., Zen., and the Venetian edition; the remaining manuscripts and editions read *excipit*.]** They themselves overthrew God’s altars. The law and the prophets were until John. Mourning is appointed for their priests. Sacrifice is taken away. The anointing oil ceases. Circumcision is emptied. The Sabbath is reproved. New moons and feast days are held in hatred (Isaiah 1:13). Romans possess their kingdom.

**[Note: Here *denotare* means to accuse, rebuke, or mark with some reproach, as it often does in Tertullian: *On the Pallium*, ch. 1, “to criticize attire”; ch. 2, “why do you criticize people?”; and *On Prayer*, ch. 2, “we criticize those who have forgotten the Father.” The Sabbaths are reproved by God in Isaiah 1:13.]**

Nothing, I think, remains to them as their own, except that, having neglected the saving Lamb, they ungratefully eat contemptible lambs with bitterness—bitter men.

**[Note: Manuscript Pomp. originally read “bitter men” with others, but was corrected in another hand to “bitter things,” wrongly. At the end manuscript Rem. reads: “The treatise of St Zeno on the Day of Passover ends”; manuscript Pomp. has similar wording.]**

## TREATISE LXVIII. On Exodus XV.

**[Note: TREATISE LXVIII.—Manuscripts Rem., Tol., Vat., Urb.: “Treatise on Passover”; Pomp.: “On Passover”; Zen.: “On Passover and the Jews”; Venetian edition: “On the Jews”; Veronese edition: “On Exodus XV; On the Jews.”]**
The Jews cannot celebrate the lawful Passover: you who are skilled in the Law, recognize this from God Himself speaking. Their synagogue is called “a den of robbers” [Matt. 21:13; Luke 19:46; Jer. 7:11]; their priestly chair, “pestilence” [Ps. 1:1]; their sacrifice, “a slaughter of dogs” [Isa. 66:3; see Deut. 23:18]; their fasts, “hatred” [Isa. 58:5; Zech. 7:5]; their people, “a brood of vipers” [Matt. 3:7; 12:34]. After this, I cannot judge what men can presume—men who place their salvation in the death of cattle—when God, after they had departed from Egypt, where they performed an imaginary Passover, says: “I am full of the burnt-offerings of rams and the fat of lambs: for who has required these things from your hands?” [Exod. 12; Isa. 1:11–12]. Certainly, brethren, He without hesitation took away the Passover from those whose very means of performing the Passover He rejected. Yet they worship an image. Indeed, one who falsely worships an image does not worship even the image itself, since he does not love its truth. Certainly, this alone do these innocents appropriately perform: they slaughter lambs everywhere, like ravening wolves.

[Note: Col. 0522D. “Imaginary Passover.” Livy, book III, chapter 41: “imaginary poverty”; Seneca, Letter 20.]

[Note: Col. 0522D. Tolentinate and Vatican manuscripts: *occiderunt*, “they killed.”]

## TREATISE LXIX. On Daniel at Easter I

[Note: Col. 0522D. TREATISE LXIX.—The title prefixed in the manuscripts to this treatise and the last, as well as the text of several treatises that mention baptism bestowed at Easter, sufficiently show that all these treatises on Daniel were delivered during the Paschal season, on the occasion of the readings from Daniel that were also recited at that time during the sacred Easter offices. This first treatise on Daniel is entitled in the Rheims, Tolentino, Vatican, and Urbino manuscripts, “A Treatise on Daniel at Easter.” In the Pompeian manuscript: “A Treatise on Daniel at Easter, by the aforementioned—that is, Saint Zeno.” In the Zenonian manuscript and the Venetian edition: “On the Three Children.” Finally, in the Veronese edition: “On Daniel VIII: On the Three Children.”]

Awake, Christian; shake off every numbness of worldly sleep, open the ears of your heart, and learn courage from the children. But take care not to think false what happened to them in the fire. Reason bears witness to its truth. He who now baptizes those who believe in Him with the Holy Spirit and fire was then also present in the number of His Trinity.

[Note: Col. 0522D–0523B. The author affirms that the three children bore the figure of the Trinity, and that the event occurred sacramentally—that is, figuratively. He mentions this mystery of the Trinity because of the number of the three children in Treatises 71, 73, and 74; see note 3 on Treatise 71.]

Finally, recognize that the matter was enacted as a sacrament. Cast into the furnace [Dan. 3], when they were plunged into the flames, the blaze was immediately tempered by invisible dew; death, recoiling, changed its office; the burners were burned; the flame caressed those who had been burned as they sang a hymn; God was blessed by all creation. In the three, one mind, one courage, one triumphant joy exults. Life is improved by punishment. The king would not have begrudged the children if he had not ordered them to burn.

[Note: Col. 0523B. Vatican and Pompeian manuscripts: *jussi*, “ordered,” for *missi*, “sent/cast.”]

[Note: Col. 0523B. Tolentinate manuscripts: *sibilo roris*, “by the hissing of dew,” for *invisibili rore*, “by invisible dew.”]

[Note: Col. 0523B. *Meliorare proprietatem*: “to improve an estate,” Digest XIII, §5, *On usufruct and its mode*.]

## TREATISE LXX. On Daniel II

[Note: Col. 0523B–0523D. TREATISE LXX.—Tolentinate, Vatican, and Urbino manuscripts: “Treatise on Daniel.” Pompeian manuscript and Venetian edition: “On Daniel.” Zenonian manuscript: “On the Three Children.” Both titles are prefixed in the Veronese edition. Although it is titled no. XI, “Treatise on Daniel,” in the table of the first book of the Rheims manuscript, it lacks a title in the body of the text. In the margin occurs this rubric: “To be recited to the brethren on the feast of the holy brothers Firmus and Rusticus.”

These martyrs, who consecrated Verona by their blood under the emperors Diocletian and Maximian, and whose bodies, once removed elsewhere, were restored to the same city under King Liutprand through the care of Saint Anno, bishop, together with the sacred remains of four other martyrs, were always held in such great honor among the Veronese that not only were many churches dedicated to God in their memory, both in the city and throughout the diocese, and their names inserted in public litanies and in the prayers printed at the end of the Roman Order from the capitulary manuscript edited by Francesco Bianchini; but special mention of them was also made in the Canon of the Mass. They were honored with a special office, with proper antiphons and responsories, as is evident from the manuscript liturgical books of the Church of Verona. Three Masses in their memory were celebrated, described in a twelfth-century manuscript Missal: the first, on the eleventh day before the Kalends of June, p. 111, titled: “Translation of Saints Firmus and Rusticus, Primus and Marcus, Apollinaris and Lazarus”; the second, on the sixth day before the Ides of August, p. 129: “Vigil of Firmus and Rusticus”; the third, on the very day of their martyrdom, namely the fifth day before the Ides of August, on the same page: “Of Saints Firmus and Rusticus.” Since the Church of Verona honored these martyrs with such solemnity, it is not surprising that this sermon of Saint Zeno was recited to the brethren amid the sacred ceremonies on their feast day. This also very strongly confirms that the Rheims manuscript belonged to that same Church.]

In a certain sense, beloved brethren, it is part of martyrdom that martyrs did not shrink from punishment. For as much as the mournful sight of manifold cruelty draws one back from the crown, so much does noble and perfect faith gather its own desires around whatever suffering was before them. Thus the three children, in that sacred contest, set God before their eyes, not the flames [Dan. 3]; the future reward, not the punishment. And so, triumphant amid the black billows of the surging fire, they taught the barbarian king, all threats, and punishment itself that flames are not stronger than holy men, through the Lord Jesus, who is blessed for ages of ages.

[Note: Col. 0523D–0524B. Venetian and Veronese editions, with several manuscripts: *crudelitas*, “cruelty.” We have corrected this from the Paduan edition and the Tolentinate, Pompeian, and Zenonian manuscripts. Shortly afterward the Tolentinate and Vatican manuscripts have *recta*, “upright,” for *perfecta*, “perfect.”]

[Note: Col. 0524B. Sparaverius prefers to read *fuerint*, “were.” Then the Urbino manuscript has *pia*, “pious,” for *sua*, “their own”; and the Pompeian manuscript writes in the margin *amputat*, “cuts away,” for *complicat*, “gathers together.”]

[Note: Col. 0524B. Tolentinate, Vatican, and Rheims manuscripts: *futuri*, “future”; later the same manuscripts and the Zenonian manuscript: *caeteros*, “the rest,” for *tetros*, “dark.” The Rheims and Pompeian manuscripts read *barbarorum*, “of barbarians,” for *barbarum*, “barbarian,” though the Pompeian manuscript corrects this to *barbarum*.]

## TREATISE LXXI. On Daniel III
