[Note: Col. 0524B. TREATISE LXXI.—The manuscripts begin “Treatise on Daniel,” except the Zenonian manuscript, which has “On the Three Children,” as does the Venetian edition.]

He who believes without fear in the martyrdom of the three children can himself also attain martyrdom. For such was the force of their contest that even the fire itself recoiled from it. For, at the barbarian king’s command—his excessive cruelty being directed against the three children—the fire of the furnace was furnished with fuel sevenfold beyond its usual measure [Dan. 3]. I believe that, through the mystery of the Trinity, the spiritual number also corresponds. Finally, the grace of baptism was not lacking to them in the dew-sprinkled furnace. O wondrous fire! O spectacle truly worthy of God! Those who hear are afraid; those who kindled the fire burn; those who were burned come forth from the furnace sanctified and unharmed, through our Lord Jesus Christ.

[Note: Col. 0524C. They are also called martyrs who, subjected to torments, did not die. Hence Commodian, *Instructions* 48: “There are many martyrdoms in which no blood is shed.” Well known are the headings of Letters VIII and X of Saint Cyprian, “To Martyrs and Confessors,” in which those not killed in their torments are nevertheless called martyrs. For, as Cyprian himself adds in Letter 37, neither their courage nor their honor is less, so that they too should not be gathered among the blessed martyrs. Nor does our Zeno say otherwise in the preceding treatise: “In a certain sense, it is part of martyrdom that martyrs did not shrink from punishment.” The Pompeian manuscript and Venetian edition wrongly write *martyrum*, “of martyrs,” for *martyrium*, “martyrdom”; but the Pompeian manuscript has the latter corrected by a later hand.]

[Note: Col. 0524C–0524D. It is customary for Zeno to detect in Scripture, from the number two, three, seven, and so forth, a sacrament—that is, some mystery and figure. For the number two see many examples in Treatise 13, Book II; for seven, see the example in Treatise 14, Book I, note 12; for three, see here the number of the three children, called “the sacrament of number” in Treatise 76. Similarly, in Treatise 14, Book II, he called the three things brought forth by Tamar—the necklace, ring, and staff—a “sacrament of number.” Rheims manuscript and Venetian edition: *spiritalis quoque numerus*, “the spiritual number also”; Urbino manuscript: *specialis quoque numerus*, “the special number also”; Vatican manuscript: *Trinitatis quoque numerus*, “the number of the Trinity also.”]

[Note: Col. 0524D. Tolentinate manuscript: *inrotati*; perhaps *inrorati*, “bedewed,” should be read, as in Columella 9.14, *inroratis floribus*, “flowers sprinkled with dew.” Zeno, however, states in Treatise 69 that the furnace-fire was tempered by invisible dew.]

## TREATISE LXXII. On Daniel IV

[Note: Col. 0524D–0525D. TREATISE LXXII.—The titles in both manuscripts and editions are the same as those noted for the preceding treatise. The Rheims manuscript adds in the margin: “To be recited before the bishop on the first Saturday of the first month, before the procession.” For the ancients, the first month was March.

Since the writer of the marginal notes here uses “procession,” rather than, as elsewhere, “station,” he indicates some such procession as the sixth Roman Order, published by Mabillon, records as customarily held from the assembly of brethren, or chapter—for we observe from other annotations that the Veronese clergy met in such a place—to the church. After the assembly of brethren in the chapter, mentioned at the beginning of that Order, a procession was made to the church for the bishop to celebrate Mass. Thus the Order is titled: “Order of the procession, whenever the bishop wishes to celebrate Mass on feast days”; it begins: “After the first hour has been celebrated, in the assembly of the brethren, which among some is called the chapter,” and then gives the order of procession.

In the manuscript *Carpsus* of our Church of Verona, frequent mention is made of a procession in which the clergy proceeded from the sacristy to the church, or from the choir to some altar, and so on. Therefore this treatise of Saint Zeno was read before the bishop in the assembly of brethren—that is, in the sacristy or choir—on the first Saturday of the first month, before a procession was held either to the church or to some altar.]

A great punishment is sometimes followed by still greater glory, especially in divine matters, in which the blessed, with earnest devotion, preserve their religion rather than their safety. Therefore, when I hear that the three children were burned [Dan. 3], I first shudder violently; but then I would desire to share their lot, when I learn that amid the flames they sang a dewy hymn to God without fear [ibid., ch. 4]. So great are the strength and power of faith that it compels even the elements themselves to serve its worshippers against their own nature. Therefore, brethren, do not let the contemplation of a most dreadful event terrify you: no punishment is now to be feared, when the life that survives those who kindle the fire mocks the flames.

[Note: Col. 0525D. Since the Song of the Three Children is not found in the Hebrew text of Daniel, it is rejected both by Jews and by certain heterodox persons. Yet from this it is sufficiently evident that Saint Zeno, together with other Fathers and the Catholic Church, received it as canonical. The manuscripts and the Venetian and Veronese editions read *rosculentos*, “dewy”; but *rorulentos*, “bedewed,” should be written, as corrected in the Paduan edition, as is evident from Treatise 69.]

[Note: Col. 0525D. Urbino manuscript: *insultat*, “mocks.”]

## TREATISE LXXIII. On Daniel V

[Note: Col. 0525D. TREATISE LXXIII.—Manuscripts: “Treatise on Daniel.” Zenonian manuscript with Venetian edition: “On the Three Children.” The Veronese edition gives both titles.]

A wondrous and delightful contest, beloved brethren, between fire and faith, sacred history has handed down to us [Dan. 3]. For two discordant things came together in one harmony through devotion to the Lord: in the three children faith did not fear punishment; when they were cast into the furnace, the blazing fire yielded, once it perceived that they possessed one and the same strength. Thus the fire burned the burners, not the burned. O admirable order! O inestimable glory of God! Through the mystery of the Trinity, the nature of so powerful an element was subdued. Those who were thought to be extinguished by fire shine forth more blessed because they were burned.

[Note: Col. 0526C. Here *detulit* is understood as “yielded” or “reverenced.”]

[Note: Col. 0526C. See note 3 on Treatise 71.]

## TREATISE LXXIV. On Daniel VI

[Note: Col. 0526C. TREATISE LXXIV.—The titles are the same as in the preceding treatise.]

Receive with a believing heart, Christian, a wondrous deed renowned by every example of virtue. The three Hebrew children—greater than old men in constancy, stronger than youths in courage, equal to one another, fortified by the mystery of the Trinity, firm in the one faith of unity, equal in their equality, glorious in the victory of their suffering—were ordered by the barbarian king to be burned because they had disdained to worship his statue. When they were cast into the burning furnace, the fire eagerly and reverently received them. The caressing flames lick those covered with dew. A wondrous thing! Within is shade; without is fire. Within a hymn is sung; without a howl is heard. O great power of God! The burners were consumed by the fire; and those who were burned, surviving their own fire, come triumphantly from the furnace, through the gift of our Lord Jesus Christ.

[Note: Col. 0526C. Rheims manuscript: *Hebraeis*, “Hebrews.” Tolentinate manuscript: *verum*, “but,” for *vere*, “truly”; and below, *solida*, “solid,” for *solidi*, “firm.”]

[Note: Col. 0526C. Tolentinate manuscript: *roscidos*, “dewy”; *roscidus* is indeed written more frequently. But the other manuscripts have *rosidos*, and likewise *rosida mella*, “dewy honey,” in manuscripts of Virgil, *Eclogues* VIII.37; and *rosidum solum*, “dewy ground,” Columella 5.6. *Roscidus* or *rosidus* is the same as *roridus*, *rorulentus*: “sprinkled with dew.”]

[Note: Col. 0526C. Pompeian manuscript: *incendio Dei*, “by the fire of God.” In the Rheims manuscript the scribe omitted the intervening words by a jump from one occurrence of *incendio*, “fire,” to the other similar occurrence.]

## TREATISE LXXV. On Daniel VII

[Note: Col. 0526C–0526D. TREATISE LXXV.—In most manuscripts: “Invitation of the Font.” Zenonian manuscript and Venetian edition: “On the Three Children”; retaining this title, the Veronese edition added “On Daniel.” We have retained only this title, as required by the sequence of the other treatises and by the sense.]

Rejoice, Christian, and fear God strongly, if you wish not to fear the devil’s fires. Behold: the children, fortified by the mystery, three in number but one in strength, are not harmed by the panting flames and the roaring furnace. Though burned, they sing a hymn; by the persistence of their faith they confound the barbarian king. They are avenged upon those who burned them. They see God. Death passes into life; fear into glory. Thus who would not wish to burn?

[Note: Col. 0526D. See note 3 on Treatise 71.]

[Note: Col. 0526D. The Rheims and Pompeian manuscripts and the Venetian edition add: “Amen.” The Rheims manuscript further reads: “Here ends the Treatise on Daniel of Saint Zeno.”]

## TREATISE LXXVI. On Daniel VIII

[Note: Col. 0526D. TREATISE LXXVI.—The title is the same as in Treatise 73.]

The three venerable Hebrews, fortified by the mystery of number, tender in age but strong in the firmness of faith, made glorious by the very punishment that supported them, disdained, out of love for divine religion, to worship the king’s image, as men who had disdained the king himself. Inflamed with rage, he ordered the furnace to be fired seven times more than usual. And lest anything be lacking to his raging savagery, the fire, armed with pitch and tow, is urged on; amid its boiling globes even heaven itself reddens with flames not its own. The innocent are hurled into it; and there they find Him for whose sake they are hurled in. Finally, they are received not by flame but by dew—not by punishment but by God’s gracious favor. O blessed punishment, which victorious preservation is followed by immortality and a crown!

[Note: Col. 0526D. The text read *citatur*, “is summoned”; we supplied *incitatur*, “is urged on,” from the Pompeian manuscript, in which it is unclear why or by what hand it was nearly erased.]

[Note: Col. 0526D–0527A. Printed books had *rore Dei, dignitate, non poena*, “by God’s dew, by dignity, not punishment.” But since the manuscript books have *dignatione*, “gracious favor,” for *dignitate*, a change of punctuation yields the best sense.]

## TREATISE LXXVII. On Daniel IX

[Note: Col. 0527A–0527C. TREATISE LXXVII.—The edition bore the title “For the Truth of the Faith,” which we found in one recent Zenonian manuscript. The others have “Treatise on Daniel at Easter,” and we therefore judged that it should be placed in the series of treatises on Daniel. It seemed proper to place it last, since the author recalls that he had already delivered other treatises on the fire of the three children.

We judge that it is wrongly titled “On Daniel,” since it is not a treatise dealing with Daniel, but rather the opening of a longer treatise in which he promises to speak not of Daniel, Jonah, the three children, human deeds, or merits, but of our Lord. Perhaps it was one of those openings that we observed, in the Admonition before Treatise 30, to have been prepared even by great orators, with the body of the speech then supplied extemporaneously. This may explain why the remainder of the speech, delivered extemporaneously and not written down, is missing.

But because the discourse itself is absent—which appears to have concerned Christ’s eternal generation, for Zeno undertakes to dispute against the Arian heresy—and because every manuscript except one entitles it “On Daniel,” and because that title is cited by John, Mansionary of Verona, William of Pastrengo, and Peter de Natalibus, who cite two treatises “On Daniel at Easter,” namely Treatise 69 and the present one, which are marked with that title in the manuscripts, we judged that this title should not now be abandoned.]

My discourse to you today, dearest brethren, is not about human deeds or merits; Daniel is not introduced, fearless amid the savage jaws of roaring lions, satisfied with a heavenly meal [Dan. 14]; nor Jonah, safer within the belly of a fish amid the raging storms and mad waves of the troubled sea than a ship within its hull [Jonah 1–2]; nor the three children, avenged upon those who burned them by the fire in which they were thought to burn. Rather, it is about our Lord, whom outsiders—if indeed it may be said—venerate while His own people attack Him.

[Note: Col. 0527C. The author seems here to indicate that he had already delivered Treatise 16, Book II, “On Susanna,” which does indeed concern human deeds or merits.]

[Note: Col. 0527C. He dealt briefly with this in Treatise 8, Book I, no. 3.]

[Note: Col. 0527C. See Treatise 17, Book II, entitled “On Jonah.”]

[Note: Col. 0527C. *Alveo*, “within its hull,” is absent from the Tolentinate manuscript.]

[Note: Col. 0527C–0528C. The outsiders who venerated our Lord Jesus Christ while He was attacked by His own—that is, by the Arians—if they may be said to have venerated Him, since they did not worship Him with true Christian worship, are certainly pagans. Perhaps the author principally means those Gentiles who, amid so many disputes between Arians and Christians, in some measure approved the Christians who defended Christ’s divinity by simple faith and tradition, while opposing the artifices and violence by which the Arians upheld their heresy.

Let Ammianus Marcellinus, a famous pagan writer of this period, be heard, book XXI, chapter 16: “Confusing the Christian religion, which is absolute and simple, with old wives’ superstition, Constantius, patron of the Arians, aroused very many dissensions by investigating it with greater subtlety than he used to settle it. These, spreading more widely, he fostered by verbal contention, so that, as crowds of bishops travelled back and forth in public vehicles to the synods, as they call them, while he tried to bend every rite to his own decision, he cut the sinews of the public transport service.”

Themistius attempted by another method to restrain the Arians, who under Valens had launched a most bitter persecution against Catholics. In the speech to that same emperor entitled *Prosphoneticus* (“Address of Greeting”), while he endeavored to show that divine matters lie beyond the power of human reasoning, he honored the divine generation of the Word in another way, just as Catholics did, who with Zeno condemned Arian curiosity. By this means the same pagan philosopher obtained from Valens more moderate treatment of Christians, as Socrates, book IV, chapter 32, and Sozomen, book VI, chapter 36, relate. That speech of Themistius to Valens still survives.]

I come armed with none of the arguments which they gladly employ—those who construct falsehoods against truth—but with many heavenly testimonies, clear and pure, so that the learned may approve, the less instructed may strengthen themselves, the untrained may learn, and those themselves who strive to blaspheme may, for the good of their salvation, at last, if possible, come to their senses.

[Note: Col. 0528C. He promises that he will use no arguments of the sort by which the Arians delighted to investigate Christ’s divine generation too curiously, a habit of the Arians which Saint Zeno elsewhere frequently rebukes. See, among other passages, the entirety of Treatise 1, Book I. Vatican manuscript: *armatur*, “is armed,” for *armatus*, “armed”; either may be read, provided it is referred not to Zeno’s person but to the discourse, which comes forth armed with no arguments.]

[Note: Col. 0528C. Saint Zeno, therefore, intended in this treatise to argue extensively against the Arians. From this it is also established that there were some Arians in Verona, for whose salvation he sought to provide by preaching.]

[Note: Col. 0528C. The Rheims manuscript reads: “Here ends the Treatise on Daniel at Easter.”]

# FIRST APPENDIX TO THE WORKS OF SAINT ZENO, BISHOP, CONTAINING:

1. Two treatises and one letter of Potamius;
2. Saint Hilary’s exposition of five Psalms;
3. Four treatises of Saint Basil of Caesarea.

[Col. 0527]

[Col. 0527]

## EDITOR’S NOTICE

[Col. 0527D] We ought not to reprint here this threefold series of short works, since the first lies entire in volume VIII and the second in volume IX of our *Patrology*, while the third is more properly reserved for placement among the works of Saint Basil. Thus, considering on the one hand the interests of readers and on the other the unity of our series, we shall incur no expense of paper for a superfluous reprinting. We shall copy absolutely nothing except certain observations prefixed at this place in their edition by the Ballerini brothers. As for the works themselves which make up this appendix, we refer the reader to volumes VIII and IX of our Library, where the treatises of Potamius and Hilary mentioned here may be read; concerning Saint Basil, we ask him to await the edition of that Father’s works.

Yet, lest by acting thus we seem to contradict ourselves—for in the second volume of Saint Hilary’s works we have reprinted several letters previously published elsewhere—it should be noted that these letters were not cited, so to speak, for their own sake, as though they had been wrongly attributed to Hilary by some persons. Rather, they form an integral part of the historical work composed by Saint Hilary, and could not be detached from the arguments of the holy bishop, with which they are interwoven, without inconvenience to the reader. Thus we have more than sufficiently escaped the charge alike of inconsistency and incompetence. Since occasion presents itself, however, we give notice that in similar circumstances we shall act so as to avoid both an excessively scrupulous and an excessively free manner of proceeding. M.

[Col. 0529]

# FIRST OBSERVATIONS OF THE BALLERINI BROTHERS, PREFIXED TO THE APPENDIX OF ZENO’S WORKS

[Col. 0529B] I. Those eleven treatises—namely, two by Potamius, five by Hilary, and four by Basil—which were appended to the Zenonian works in the Rheims manuscript by a different hand, but copied at the end of other codices by other scribes in the same order and in the same hand, and which, being taken by editors as Zenonian, were mixed in and published among the Zenonian works (the chief cause or occasion of all the controversies), we now, aided by the manuscripts and instructed by certain indications, separate from the others and relegate to the first Appendix. On this subject, let what we discussed more extensively in the preface to the first dissertation suffice. We must now inquire and determine to which authors they should be assigned, since this is not evident from the cited codices.

There can be no doubt that the five treatises on the Psalms are the work of Saint Hilary, the contemporary bishop of Poitiers, since not only does their style openly recall Hilary, but they are also found word for word among Hilary’s works. Moreover, not only Hincmar in his book *On Predestination*, chapter 25, but Jerome as well, in Letter XXXIV to Marcella, §§3 and 5, cites as Hilary’s certain statements found in these treatises. We may also set aside the fact that, in the exposition of Psalm 127, §11, interpretations of earlier Psalms are cited, clearly indicating a Hilarian commentary on other Psalms, of which there is nothing in Zeno’s codices.

[Col. 0529D] II. Further, no one who compares the Greek Basilian works on the same subjects can doubt that the four treatises *On Envy and Jealousy*, *On Give Heed to Yourself*, *On Fasting*, and *On the Rich Miser* were translated from Saint Basil into Latin, the first two complete and the latter two mutilated. This translation is ancient and appears to have been produced in Zeno’s age. It does not altogether correspond word for word with the Greek text, but was rendered with freer judgment.

Saint Augustine mentions this translation, which we firmly believe to be the same one, of the treatise *On Fasting*, long circulated throughout the world, in book I *Against Julian*, §18, and book I of the *Unfinished Work*, §52. When he found that it did not wholly adhere to the Greek exemplar, he declares there that he undertook a new translation: “Although I found it translated, nevertheless, for the sake of a more careful fidelity to truth, I preferred to translate word for word from the Greek.”

If anyone asks us who the translator was, we judge him to have been Rufinus, presbyter of Aquileia. For Rufinus himself makes sufficiently clear in his *History*, book II, chapter 9, that he rendered several of Basil’s homilies into Latin. Moreover, the character of the style and the freedom of translation apparent in these versions agree well with Rufinus’s other works. These considerations are probable. But to demonstration is added Rufinus’s own preface, which Father Jean Garnier, a Benedictine, published in the most recent edition of Basil’s works, volume II, p. 713, from two manuscripts, the Royal and the Colbertine. This preface was placed before eight treatises of Basil translated into Latin by Rufinus. In it Rufinus plainly states:

> “Long ago, my dearest son Apronianus, you had asked me to translate some things into Latin for you. I did this in part while I was in Rome, and I have now added somewhat more. Therefore I have translated these eight short homiletic books of blessed Basil.”

Now among the eight treatises following this preface are found three of those circulated among the Zenonian works: *On Envy and Jealousy*, there Homily IV, p. 726; *On Give Heed to Yourself*, Homily II, p. 717; and *On the Rich Miser*, Homily III, p. 723. The fourth, *On Fasting*, absent there, is the one cited by Augustine in the passages mentioned and displays the same freedom of translation and style; no one can doubt that it was rendered by the same translator.

[Col. 0530D] This also resolves the question raised by the Benedictine editor in the general preface to volume II, §61: namely, whether Rufinus translated eight or ten sermons of Basil. Two statements of Rufinus himself provide grounds for doubt: first, the preface just cited, where he sent Apronianus eight homilies translated by himself; secondly, book II, chapter 9 of his *History*, where he declares that he rendered almost ten of them into Latin:

> “There are also splendid monuments of the genius of both Basil and Gregory Nazianzen, in the treatises which they delivered extemporaneously in churches; from these we rendered almost ten short discourses of each into Latin.”

From this latter passage Tillemont, vol. IX, p. 501, concludes that Rufinus translated ten homilies of Basil into Latin. Father Garnier, considering the word *ferme* (“almost”), supposes that Rufinus translated no more than eight speeches, since he sent Apronianus no more than that number. But if to those eight is added the homily *On Fasting*, noted by Augustine and found in our codices, it is plain that at least nine were translated by Rufinus. Perhaps he rendered just that number into Latin, which agrees wonderfully with the phrase “almost ten.”

III. It remains to investigate the author of the two short treatises inserted in our codices among the Hilarian and Basilian works. Their Latin and syntax are indeed very obscure and involved, and differ greatly from Zeno’s. Thus Gaspar Barthius, apparently looking at these treatises, wrote that some sermons mixed among the Zenonian works are much more recent than any of the other body of homilies, as though their author belonged to a much later age in which barbarous Latin was written.

Yet one passage, omitted in the Veronese edition and its derivatives but restored by us from the Venetian edition and all the manuscripts, seemed to reveal an ancient and definite author. For the treatise *On Lazarus* reads: “Come, come, Photamius, servant of the living God: if you have any power, tell something at length about the Lord’s tears.” It is evident that the author, turning an awkward apostrophe upon himself, speaks with himself and urges himself to discuss the Lord’s tears more fully. Therefore *Photamius* is his name; restoring suitably the name of Greek origin with a P—for P and Ph are sometimes written interchangeably in ancient monuments, as scholars know—the author of these treatises appears to be Potamius, that bishop Potamius, whose letter to Saint Athanasius is found among the documents published by Acherius.

Certainly the style is plainly the same. To make this still clearer, we judged that the letter should be appended to the treatises; and thus, for the first time, you will have together and restored to their proper author all the works of that Potamius which have come down to us. But who this Potamius was is not clear. His style is so very obscure that not even Mercury could interpret it anywhere; this led the new editor of Acherius’s *Spicilegium* to suspect that he was Greek, that he had written in Greek, and that he was translated into Latin by some interpreter of a later age.

For in the chronological index of volume III, speaking of Potamius’s aforementioned letter, written shortly after the middle of the fourth century, he says: “It appears to be translated from Greek, but has come down to us strewn with the foulest errors.” And in the note on the same letter, p. 299, he again speaks of a translation and wonders why Acherius published so obscure and corrupt a version of the letter.

This view could not be refuted so long as only one letter was under consideration, for writings of this sort translated from Greek into Latin are readily found. But from the treatises—which we find rendered into Latin only from more celebrated writers—we infer that the author was perhaps Greek by origin but bishop of some Latin city. Being compelled to write in the language of the city over which he presided, he used a difficult style, just as other authors of Greek origin who wrote in Latin generally fall short of the purity and felicity natural to the Roman tongue.

Nevertheless, this Potamius is altogether different from the bishop of Lisbon of the same name and period, to whom Phoebadius plainly refers the letter written at Sirmium and found among Hilary’s *Fragments*—see p. 301, volume IV of the *Library of the Fathers*. Potamius of Lisbon, once a defender of the Nicene faith, was corrupted by Constantius and went over to the Arians. Our Potamius, however—the author of the letter we shall append—wrote to Athanasius as an advocate of the Catholic faith not merely after the Council of Sirmium but even after the Council of Rimini, if the manuscript heading is to be trusted. He must therefore be judged bishop of another, uncertain but Latin, city.

[Note: Col. 0531D. Compare the French Preface to Potamius, volume VIII of our Library, col. 1411, from line 3.]

311. IV. As for the remaining treatises which, as we mentioned in the general preface, are copied at the end in the two Urbinate and Vatican manuscripts, there is no reason for us to trouble ourselves over them. For in those same codices each is certainly assigned to its own proper author; they were not ascribed to Gaudentius, Vigilius, Jerome, or Zeno, nor indeed could they have been so ascribed. One treatise, *On the Sign of the Holy Cross* [Col. 0532C], which in two manuscripts—the Tolentinate and Vatican Basilian—immediately follows the works translated by Rufinus without any author’s name, but in the Pompeian codex was copied continuously after the final treatise of Basil, appears to have something distinctive warranting its being placed in the Appendix with the rest. For it appears to be attributed to Zeno no less than the others; hence the Tolentinate manuscript appends this conclusion at its end: “Here end the treatises of St. Zeno,” etc. But since it has neither been attached to Zeno in the printed editions nor found in all the Zenonian codices, we judged that it should not be printed under his name. It will be sufficient here merely to state what it is and whose work it is.

Although in all the codices it is copied continuously, in the form of the other treatises and of continuous prose, it is in fact a hymn in catalectic iambic dimeter verses, beginning *Cultor Dei momento* (“Worshipper of God, at a moment”), and consisting of eight stanzas. Having discovered this, we diligently investigated the author, lest what had happily occurred in the other cases should fail in this one; and after much searching we finally discovered that the hymn is a fragment of a longer hymn by Prudentius—namely, hymn 6 of the book *Καθημερινῶν* (*Daily Hymns*). In Prudentius this hymn is entitled *Before Sleep* and consists of thirty-nine stanzas. Of these, only the final seven, which speak of the Cross, are found in our hymn; for the eighth supplies a sort of conclusion to hymns. We found the same hymn also in George Cassander’s *Ecclesiastical Hymns*, p. 217 [Col. 0533A] of the Paris edition of 1616, which he printed from a codex containing an old collection of hymns. It is therefore clear that the hymn had long since been excerpted from Prudentius, and could thus have been introduced into the Zenonian codices.

We here transcribe one concluding stanza of the hymn, which we have found neither in Prudentius nor in Cassander, at least not in any hymn:

> Let praise be to the highest Father,  
> Whom no one has ever seen;  
> To Christ, the Father’s Word,  
> And to the gracious Spirit. Amen.

[Col. 0533]

[TRACTATES.]

TWO TREATISES OF BISHOP POTAMIUS, TO WHICH IS ADDED A LETTER TO ATHANASIUS. (C)

TREATISE I. ON LAZARUS.

[Col. 0533B]

“Brethren, amid great astonishment and a great miracle, I am tossed by downward-driving waves, now this way, now that, through uncertain anxieties in the hollow recess of a whirling eddy,” etc.

For the rest, see *Patrologia*, vol. VIII, cols. 1411–1415.

TREATISE II. ON THE MARTYRDOM OF THE PROPHET ISAIAH.

“When Isaiah preached Christ, or when he announced to the Israelite people the sentence of their future condemnation, the barbarous savagery of blasphemers, stirred by cruel ferocity,” etc.

For the rest, see the same place, cols. 1415–1416.

LETTER TO ATHANASIUS, ASSAILED BY THE ARIANS, AFTER THEY SUBSCRIBED AT THE COUNCIL OF RIMINI.

[Col. 0533C]

Potamius to his most glorious and blessed lord brother Athanasius, bishop.

“The pit of so great a prison heaps together the raw filth of a condemnable workshop,” etc.

For the rest, see the same place, cols. 1416–1418.

TREATISES OF ST. HILARY, BISHOP, ON PSALMS 126–130. (C)

TREATISE ON PSALM 126.

I. “Unless the Lord builds the house, those who build it labor in vain. Unless the Lord guards the city, those who guard it keep watch in vain. It is in vain for you to rise early.” Many maintain that holy Solomon, intent upon building the city and the temple, [Col. 0533D] etc.

You may read the remainder in our *Patrologia*, vol. IX, cols. 694–703.

TREATISE ON PSALM 127.

I. Whenever Scripture speaks of the fear of the Lord, [Col. 0534A] it must be observed that it is never left alone, as though sufficient for us to bring faith to completion; rather, much is added to it and set before it, etc.

You will find the remainder in the same place, cols. 704–710.

TREATISE ON PSALM 128.

“They have often attacked me from my youth—let Israel now say—they have often attacked me from my youth. Yet they have not prevailed against me . . . . And those who passed by did not say: ‘The blessing be upon you; we bless you in the name of the Lord.’”

I. We are instructed by prophetic utterances toward the endurance of present sufferings, etc.

For the rest, see the same place, cols. 711–718.

TREATISE ON PSALM 129.

[Col. 0534B]

I. Among the many splendid things which the Apostle writes to the Romans, after speaking about the faith of the Gentiles and the unbelief of the Jews, and after treating at length of the judgments of God, he says, etc.

For the rest, see the same place, cols. 718–725.

TREATISE ON PSALM 130.

I. This is a short psalm, to be explained more by division than by exposition; it teaches us humility and gentleness, etc.

For the remainder, see the same place, cols. 725–727.

FOUR TREATISES OF ST. BASIL OF CAESAREA, TRANSLATED BY RUFINUS.

TREATISE I. ON JEALOUSY AND ENVY.

[Col. 0534C]

I. God is good and grants good things even to the undeserving; the devil is evil and teaches human beings also the wickedness which he himself once conceived, etc.

TREATISE II. ON “GIVE HEED TO YOURSELF.”

I. God, who created us, granted us the use of speech so that through the service of words we might disclose to one another the hidden counsels of our hearts, etc.

TREATISE III. ON FASTING.

I. “Sound the trumpet at the beginning of the month, on the day of your solemn festival,” the prophet commanded the people of Israel, etc.

TREATISE IV. ON THE RICH MAN WHO WAS GREEDY.

I. There are two kinds of temptations. Either tribulation afflicts [Col. 0534D] the human heart, and, like gold in a furnace, etc.

As we have already observed, we reserve those four treatises for placement among the works of St. Basil.

[Col. 0533]

NOTICE CONCERNING SPARAVERIUS’S NOTES.

Francis Sparaverius, a nobleman of Verona, exceptionally well versed in Latin and Greek authors and an outstanding cultivator of refined letters and learning—of whom Scipio Maffei has reported more fully in Part II of *Verona Illustrata*—after producing several learned works with the highest praise, in his later years planned a new edition of St. Zeno, for which he prepared many annotations. But death overtook him in 1697, leaving the work unfinished.

Following the order of the Veronese edition, he carried his commentary as far as the middle of the sermon *On the Building of the House of God* [Col. 0535A]. After this, thirteen further sermons remain in that edition without any commentary. Yet certain annotations, in which he directs the reader to observations on those final sermons too, indicate that he had prepared such a commentary, even if it was not copied out, or at least had conceived it in his mind. In these annotations he energetically and learnedly attempted both to correct several more corrupt passages and explain certain more difficult statements. Having used one manuscript, which he also seems to have received only later, he frequently wished for others by which he might restore the sound reading.

He plainly recognized some treatises as spurious. Yet, because he had not yet uncovered the prevalent prejudice concerning Gallienus’s age, he sometimes hesitated to judge certain interpolated treatises foreign to Zeno [Col. 0535B], and sometimes thought that a genuine sermon of Zeno, incompatible with that age, should be denied to him. Thus it is not certain whether he would have changed his judgment had time remained to complete the edition and to reflect longer upon it.

Although this work is unfinished and, as it were, composed extemporaneously and without premeditation—whence its author entitled it an *αὐτοσχεδίασμα* (*an improvised composition*)—and is the premature offspring of a most celebrated man, we nevertheless judged that it should not be omitted from our edition because of the many excellent things it contains. Thus neither the expectation of very many persons to whom it is known and desired, nor the praise due to that man who has deserved well of this edition, should be disappointed.

Two points in particular should finally be noted. First, we shall give these observations in the sequence of the new edition, changing the author’s order, because this seemed necessary for readers’ convenience when, in reading Zeno’s treatises, they may wish to consult Sparaverius’s observations. Secondly, wherever you find a reading indicated by him differing from ours, it is the reading of the Veronese edition; you may find it mentioned by us in its proper place in the annotations [Col. 0536B].

[Col. 0535]

FRANCIS SPARAVERIUS’S IMPROVISED NOTES ON THE SERMONS OF BLESSED ZENO OF VERONA.

ON TREATISE I, BOOK I, ON FAITH.

P. 4. “It is not born from another source, but through the inspiration of the Holy Spirit, preceding by his will, and through his aid,” etc. The manuscript reads: “It is not borrowed from another, but is born by his will.” Moreover, if, etc. St. Paul, *Romans*, chapter 10, number [Note: [Col. 0535D] For the author, “number” is the same as “verse.”] 17: “Faith comes from hearing, and hearing through the word of God.” Cyril of Jerusalem, *Catecheses*, Prologue, fol. 6: “One must hear about the living God; one must hear about judgment; one must hear about Christ; one must hear about the resurrection; and much besides,” etc. Compare the argument from the same chapter of Romans, number 14.

P. 4. “Unless faith, preceded by the exhortation of the law and girded with every devotion, embraces it,” etc. He does not deny the necessity of teaching (*didaskalia*), nor abolish hearing; rather, he requires the inspiration and assistance of the Holy Spirit. Clement of Alexandria, *Stromata*, Book II, p. 364, called faith a grace because it “causes the simple person to ascend from things not demonstrated to the universal, which is neither with matter, nor matter, nor under matter”: that is, to rise from indemonstrable things to the incomprehensible, which is neither with matter, nor matter, nor under matter. But for this is required a divinely anticipated opinion: a *prolēpsis*, or preconception, by which one judges sound the opinion one has formed about matters to be believed and shows oneself compliant toward the teacher. For it is not enough to hear; one must hear instruction and freely embrace it. Clement of Alexandria: “Faith is a voluntary anticipation.” Nor did Epicurus judge badly when he said, as quoted by the same author: “No one can either inquire, doubt, form an opinion, or refute, without a preconception.” The same is found in Laertius, p. 274.

P. 5. “Otherwise that countless multitude, happier in its simplicity,” etc. He calls the Christian throng happy in its simplicity—good with the true simplicity praised by Martial. For this reason Christians were represented among the pagans as dull and foolish, as Arnobius indicates among others, Book II, 45: because, being unlearned, they readily assented. But Jesus, rejoicing in the Spirit, gives thanks to the Father in Matthew, chapter 11, number 25, because he has hidden the mysteries from the wise and understanding and revealed them to little ones; that is, as St. Paul interprets it in 1 Corinthians, chapter 14, number 20, little ones in malice but mature in virtue. Tertullian, Book VI *Against Marcion*, chapter 25: “He held the wise and prudent guilty, because from works so many and so great they did not seek the intelligible God, or philosophized wrongly about him, and supplied their intellectual gifts to heretics.”

P. 6. “For through it the will of God is made known to the peoples,” [Col. 0536C] etc. That is: it is taught, made known. Aelius Spartianus, near the end of *Verus*: “This indeed is contrary to what has been made known by very many authors concerning regret for the adoption.” Ammianus Marcellinus, Book XXVIII, chapter 3: “[They] made known to our generals the alarms of neighboring peoples”; and the phrase occurs repeatedly in the *Theodosian Code*.

Same place. “Now stern, now gentle, it displays reward and sword,” etc. St. Paul, Romans, chapter 4, number 15: “For the law produces wrath,” that is, it punishes those who transgress it. But I think the following words corrupt: “bestowing upon each one what he has chosen, so that he may lawfully fulfill what he performs”; nor am I able to provide even subsidiary assistance.

P. 7. “The law always flows from its original book; but faith clings firmly to its own single purpose,” etc. Anyone who has read Plutarch’s *Solon*, Livy, and Dionysius in their histories will know that laws were recorded on *axones* among the Athenians and on tablets among the Romans in antiquity. But in later times, when the annual edicts of the praetors were drawn from the whiteboard into permanent law by the jurist Julian under the authority of Emperor Hadrian, they were entered in books, as is clear from the first law *On Those Marked with Infamy*. He therefore says that they remain perpetually the same, which is true until they are repealed. Their book he calls “original” (*genitalis*), that is, the original or archetype from which their authority might be established. Faith, by contrast, rests on nothing other than itself; and if it alone totters and is not restored, it perishes.

Same place. “The law can only address human conscience; it cannot see,” etc. It can teach what ought to be done or believed; it cannot see what a person believes, nor know his faith.

Same place. “The law is both learned and taught in parts,” etc. Namely, the divisible law, which, as he adds, is neither understood nor held as a whole. Faith, however, is indivisible. Tertullian, *On the Veiling of Virgins*, chapter 1: “The rule of faith is absolutely one, alone immovable and irreformable.”

Same place. “Add that it is sought by all, yet fulfilled by none,” etc. I read: “and fulfilled by none.” They wish it to be observed more than they themselves wish to observe it.

Same place. “Add that it is an index of God’s will, not of God’s origin or nature,” etc. God himself promulgated the law, and St. Paul for that reason called it holy in Romans, chapter 7, number 12; nevertheless, in chapter 8, number 2, he called it the law of sin and death, and set it against faith, which he called the law of the Spirit of life in Christ. He continues at number 11: “But if the Spirit of him who raised Jesus from the dead dwells in you, he who raised Christ from the dead will also give life to your mortal bodies through his Spirit dwelling in you.” Justin Martyr, *First Apology*, 58: “That we came into existence in the beginning was not our doing; likewise, that, by making a choice, we pursue things pleasing to him comes about through the rational powers granted by him, as he himself persuades us and leads us to faith.” I believe Zeno referred to this when he said “God’s origin or nature.”

P. 8. “If we should call it a discussion of faith,” etc. By this argument he seems to mean that faith cannot be treated by discussion, since it rests in correct judgment and, as Clement of Alexandria says, *Stromata*, Book II, p. 362, is “the foundation of prudent choice”; nor can faith be reconciled with disputation because demonstrations are lacking. The same author says: “He therefore who has believed the divine Scriptures, having firm judgment—a demonstration that cannot be contradicted—receives the voice of God who gave the Scriptures.” To this purpose Ambrose used to say: “Remove arguments where faith is sought. Let dialectic now fall silent even in its own schools: fishermen are believed, not dialecticians.” So too Augustine: “Do not understand in order that you may believe, but believe in order that you may understand: understanding is the reward of faith.” Yet faith requires knowledge. Theodoret, Discourse 1, *On the Cure [of Greek Afflictions]*, p. 479: “Faith indeed requires knowledge, just as knowledge requires faith; for faith could not arise without knowledge, nor knowledge without faith.” Nor does it less require discussion. Clement of Alexandria, *Stromata*, Book I, p. 286: “Just as we say that one can be faithful even without letters, so we confess that one who has not learned cannot understand what is said in faith.”

P. 8. “Moreover, I see, as the names of those who assert [these things] indicate—if you remove them, perhaps no …,” namely, the heretics, who tear apart Christ’s body, the Church, with impious sects.

P. 9. “There were many treatises,” etc. “Treatises” are disputations by which they promoted their opinions; for by effort and favor they sought persons whom they might persuade and by whom they might seduce true Christians. Tertullian, *On the Resurrection of the Flesh*, chapter 5: “Thus the heretics also challenge us to employ rhetoric, just as they do to employ philosophy.”

Same place. “What ought to be chosen cannot be known,” etc. Understand this of a catechumen or candidate for initiation; otherwise it would be paradoxical. For there is one true faith, from which one may neither fall away nor depart, and which he below calls that noble and ancient faith which, by believing God upon God’s word, won approval, and which did not learn to believe but presumed.

P. 11. “And which did not learn to believe but presumed”: compare the notes on this same sermon above, p. 2, on the words “unless faith, preceded by the exhortation of the law.” There were persons inspired by God who, becoming Christians on the occasion itself, spontaneously offered themselves to death by confession, with no prior instruction or professed intention. Yet it must not be denied that some cause preceded, which, with God moving them, impressed an opinion upon them; from its preconception they learned to believe. Zeno must therefore be understood here in a broad sense.

Same place. “Lest faith perish,” he says, “when it is either wrongly believed or wrongly taught,” etc. Tertullian’s judgment was the same; both derive it from the Apostle, Titus chapter 3, number 9. In *On the Prescription against Heretics*, chapter 14: “Faith is established in a rule; to know nothing against the rule is to know everything.” He then continues: “But while they do hold and believe, they nevertheless say that inquiry is necessary so that they may defend [the faith]; before they defend it, they deny what they confess—namely, that they have not yet believed while they inquire.”

Same place. “Now I wish to know whether faith consists in teaching, in credulity, or in both,” etc. Cyril of Jerusalem, *Catechesis* 5, makes faith, indivisible by nature, at its first level a dogmatic “assent of the soul”; at the second and higher level, it is that which takes place “by grace from Christ.” He warns us that in order to obtain the latter faith and grace, we should imbibe the former from the sap of the Catholic Church, not be led about by various questions and curious conversations, but strengthen ourselves through the comparison of Holy Scriptures.

Same place. “But if it consists of both, the faith of the patriarchs is half-measured, and consequently to them,” etc. *Semensa* means imperfect, as though defrauded of half a measure. To measure is to supply by measure; to measure out with a smaller measure is to falsify the measure. Caesar, *Gallic War*, Book VII, chapter 71: “He began to distribute grain sparingly and little by little”—that is, sparingly and restrictively, as circumstances and the dearness of grain required. Cyprian, Letter 76, near the end, says similarly and in the same sense: “Did they indeed receive the Lord’s grace, but in a briefer and lesser measure?” This is “half-measured grace.” Our author’s entire point is that just as Abraham and the other patriarchs were justified by faith without teaching, but by inspiration (*epipnoia*) alone, so he wishes every Christian, precisely as a Christian, to be constituted by no other assistance than the Spirit that comes upon him. But what then becomes of the Lord’s words, “Go, teaching,” Matthew 28:19? What becomes [Col. 0538C] of Paul in Romans 11:17: “Faith comes from hearing”? But, as may be seen, he does not disapprove teaching that has been instilled simply and purely by a true Christian; rather, he disapproves teaching disguised by empty talk, swollen with circumlocutions devised for display, touching upon the chief matters only superficially. See St. Paul, 1 Timothy, chapter 6, number 4, and Clement of Alexandria, *Stromata*, Book I, not far from its beginning. For if they had believed simply and had not burdened their minds with imperceptible matters, Saturnilus would not have devised doctrines so absurd and monstrous, nor Basilides, nor Carpocrates, nor Valentinus, nor so many others. What drew Origen into error? What drew Arius? Nothing but superfluous inquiry in faith, by which, in the pursuit of wisdom, they destroyed wisdom. To this must be referred our author’s words quoted a little above: “For what always has an uncertain standing will be neither proper nor firm, since one person’s choice is another’s rejection; or, if all must altogether be embraced,” etc. Moreover, it creates obscurity that he uses “law” now for a commandment of the Old Testament, now for the teaching of Christian faith; this is rough and confused. For if, as he himself approves, we are no longer under law but under grace, what need is there to debate concerning the law that commands, which is useless to the Christian? If you observe this distinction in its proper place and time, the matter will proceed more easily in this treatise.

P. 14. “When two Christians contend, what is not transferred from one of them is called perfidy; when transferred, faith,” etc. That is, when it is not transferred into their minds, into assent—when it is not believed. Livy calls this “being brought over to an opinion,” Book XLIV, chapter 40; Cicero, Book IV of *On Ends*, at the beginning: “If you attain this, you may bring me wholly over to your side.”

Same place. “O how presumptuously,” etc. Claudius Salmasius notes on Aelius Spartianus, chapter 2, that *praesumptio* sometimes means confidence about a nearly certain matter, a certain trust and undoubted hope of something necessarily to occur, as here. Zeno therefore exclaims: “O faith, badly presumed!” The word “badly” must be understood: faith, which should previously have been held undoubted, must give place to a novel tradition.

P. 15. “Perhaps someone considers himself more faithful in this matter”: read *lege* (“read”) from the manuscript.

Same place. “For the matter has come to such a pass that our faith is sought through an injury to God,” etc. An anonymous writer quoted by Eusebius, *Ecclesiastical History*, Book V, final chapter, says concerning the heretics things which I gladly transfer here to illuminate Zeno: “They have boldly adulterated the Holy Scriptures, rejected the rule of the primitive faith, and, ignorant of Christ himself, contend not over what the sacred Scriptures teach, but over what sort of figure of syllogisms may confirm their impiety.”

P. 16. “Why do you constrain law by law?” etc. Here understand “law” as ecclesiastical doctrine.

Same place. “But if you know the faith of the Spirit,” etc. Cyril of Jerusalem, *Catechesis* 5: “This faith, then, which is bestowed according to grace by the Spirit, is not merely dogmatic, but also effective beyond human powers.” For there are divisions of gifts, ministries, and workings, from one and the same Spirit, who distributes separately to each as he wills. See Paul, 1 Corinthians, chapter 12.

Same place. “The whale-boat,” etc. Metaphorically he calls the whale which swallowed Jonah and bore him alive through the seas a “whale-boat.”

Same place. “The course of the sun and moon from the west,” etc. He refers to the history in Joshua, chapter 10, numbers 12 and 13.

Same place. “If hard things happen, show that you possess faith like a grain of mustard seed,” etc. Rather, hope; but hope is not without faith. Our author, in the following sermon: “If faith is not present, how will hope itself arise?” Clement of Alexandria, *Paedagogue*, Book I, chapter 6: “Hope is truly the blood of faith, in which it is contained as faith is in the soul. When hope expires, the vital faculty is dissolved, just as if blood had flowed out.”

P. 17. “Here I do not dare answer you,” etc., because it is not for a human being to know the divine nature. Clement of Alexandria, *Stromata*, Book V, p. 582: “Inquiry is neither by form nor by sight; but the grace of knowledge comes from God himself through the Son.” Yet this is not perfect even now. For, as Aurelius Augustine says, *On the Trinity*, Book V, we understand God as far as we can: namely, as good without quality, great without quantity, creator without need, present without position, containing without habit, wholly everywhere without place, eternal without time, changing all things without any change in himself, and impassible. “Whoever thinks of God thus, even if he cannot yet discover what God is, nevertheless piously takes care, so far as he can, not to think of him anything that he is not.” We know not what he is, but what he is not, as Clement says in the same place.

Same place. “For their suspicion deceived many.” The manuscript adds: “and the suspicion of them held their minds in vanity.”

P. 18. “Nor should they pay attention to myths and genealogies,” etc. 1 Timothy, chapter 1, number 5. On this passage Theodoret says: “They rehearsed genealogies derived from Abraham and David, investigating whether the Lord had been born from them according to the flesh.”

Same place. “Whoever in some way denies God by human reasonings,” etc. The manuscript reads more closely and more solidly: “Whoever asserts God in some way denies God. For defense,” etc.

ON TREATISE II, BOOK I: ON FAITH, HOPE, AND CHARITY.

P. 19. “If you deny charity to these, both will be useless” [Col. 0540A]. The manuscript: “If you deny charity to these, both will cease.”

Same place. “Take away hope and all things are destroyed,” etc. Cyril of Jerusalem, *Catechesis* 5, and Theodoret, *Discourse I on the Cure [of Greek Afflictions]*, applied this same argument to faith; but our author applies it much more aptly to hope. Reader, it is for you to compare them.

Same place. “A boy [is entrusted] to a schoolmaster,” etc. A *litterator* is one who teaches the first elements, reading and writing. Lampridius, in *Alexander Severus*, chapter 3, calls them teachers of early childhood, in contrast to *litterati*; I make the familiar point from Salmasius’s notes on Tertullian, *On the Pallium*, final chapter, and Vossius, *On the Grammatical Art*, Book I, chapter 1.

Same place. “The sailor entrusted himself to the deep gulf,” etc. Here *gurges* means “sea,” following the example of other writers. Propertius, Book I, Elegy XVII, v. 14:

> Ah, may whoever first prepared ships and sails perish,  
> and made his way upon the unwilling deep.

The same poet, Book III, Elegy VII, v. 25:

> His life laid down in the deep,  
> let cheap sand cover Paetus by your own choice.

P. 19. “Although it is placed in the future, it is nevertheless rightly subject to faith,” etc. He had in mind St. Paul, Romans, chapter 8, number 25: “But if we hope for what we do not see, we await it through patience.” Hope is always directed toward the future. Seneca, speaking of Hope, says in Letter 101: “No one ought to promise himself anything from the future.” Achilles Tatius, *Leucippe and Clitophon*, Book IV, p. 221: “I rejoiced in the hope of what was to come.” Maximus of Tyre, Discourse XXXVII: “Hopes impel persons to labor at things which can neither be accomplished nor have an end.” Moreover, I would read *iuri subiecta* (“subject to law/right”), so that the syntax may proceed. For since the sufferings of this world are not worthy to be compared with the future glory, as St. Paul says somewhere, hope in that future must be established through faith; otherwise [Col. 0540C] it too must necessarily collapse.

Same place. “And it must be guarded by every kind of virtue,” etc.: seek what and what kinds from St. Paul, Romans, chapter 12, from number 7 onward.

P. 20. “The beauty or wall of the Church,” etc. I would rather read “or tower.”

Same place. “But against hope is what is impossible,” etc. The manuscript reads: “But against hope is that which is impossible and is not seen; yet it becomes possible and an object of hope when, without doubt, [one trusts] God’s word,” etc.

Same place. “That we may rightly hope for things belonging to another,” etc. The faith which we receive from God is ours; what we await by faith is not ours, but must be sought through virtues and uprightness of life. He therefore called “another’s” what God must determine. “The kingdom of heaven suffers violence, and the violent seize it,” Matthew, chapter 11, number 12. This is not by contentious prayers, but through constancy in upright living and most humble, devout, unceasing petitions. Since by these the seeds of former sins are uprooted and stains removed [Col. 0540D], violence is said to be done—to us and to heaven—as Clement of Alexandria suggests, *Stromata*, Book V, p. 553.

Same place. “For no one entrusts property to a debtor,” etc. He gives the reason for the preceding statement. For no one, if he seizes a person who is in his debt, will overwhelm him, at his own risk, with a greater debt; nor will a king give the prize to a deserter, but to the victor, or to one who bravely maintains each of his duties to the best of his ability.

P. 21. “To him who has, it shall be given,” etc. Matthew, chapter 12, number 12, and chapter 25, number 29, and elsewhere in the other Evangelists.

Same place. “Escaping through this, Noah found no one with whom he could compare the flood,” etc. For he alone believed God’s true threats and obeyed his commands, and was saved through faith; so that after the flood, with every person killed except his companions in the ark, he had no one with whom to converse concerning the immensity of the waters.

[Col. 0541A] P. 21. “This made the Red Sea a glassy land for Moses,” etc. In the sixth sermon above, *On Exodus*—now Treatise 50, Book II—he meant something else: namely, that Moses did not walk upon the surface of the waters, but that when the sea was divided, gaping open, and as though banked up on either side, a path was made through the depths of the sea so that the Jews might escape. I think it should read: “The Red Sea, too, split into twin shores, and with banks raised right and left, its waters massed in ranks, the pathway of the deep was dried by clear water.”

Same place. “Paralytics are re-formed,” etc. Paralysis is a loss of motion and activity. But to be deprived of motion or activity, and to recover motion or the capacity for activity, does not seem properly called “to be re-formed.” For in respect of health and disease, it is a quality, and such things are called affections in the categories, since they can readily be changed; but forms do not change except by a change of the whole body, when what it previously was is destroyed. Nevertheless Trebellius Pollio speaks in the same sense in his compilation on the Thirty Tyrants, twice concerning Lollianus and once concerning Odenathus: “He had now restored the East to its former condition, but had completely restored every part of the whole world.”

Same place. “With his own funeral rites,” etc. Either I am mistaken, or Zeno wrote *exuviis* (“spoils,” “cast-off coverings”). For *exuviae* are not merely things stripped off, but things which, having been put on, can be stripped off. Perhaps he had in mind Tertullian’s *Apology*, chapter 21, who called them “the spoils of the tomb,” or, as Rigaltius preferred, “of the buried man.” Yet, however this may be, I think it more tolerable that he should have said *exuviis* than *exsequiis* (“funeral rites”).

P. 22. “Yet without this, neither will profit.” The manuscript: “Without this, neither will stand.”

Same place. “Faith belongs to few; charity to all,” etc. What does this mean? Must not charity be united to Christian faith, so that it is of no avail for salvation unless it proceeds through faith? Certainly St. Paul, 1 Corinthians, chapter 13, placed charity above faith and hope. And it must be admitted that charity is more difficult, because it imparts not only affection, but also substance and resources, the deprivation of which is thought a greater sacrifice. The reading should therefore rather be: “Faith belongs to all; charity to few.”

Same place. “Hope and faith have their time,” etc. Faith is superfluous in the future life, when things appear plainly; likewise hope, once the things hoped for have been obtained, is abolished. But when the soul has been freed from the body, it is not troubled by disturbances, and then charity has greater strength. Theodoret, on St. Paul’s First Epistle to the Corinthians, number 13.

Same place. “And the more it is increased among those who love one another, the more is mutually owed,” etc. Not only is charity not diminished after death; even in this life, if one may say so, it continually grows. That is, if you are provoked by fuller services, you too should increase the degrees of your affection; for one makes a reciprocal exchange of charity who responds on equal terms. This seems to be his meaning; nevertheless, observe that it conflicts with what he says a little below: “Not according to time, because it is not variable.”

Same place. “According to person,” etc. Read “from person,” just as “from rank” and “from sex”: that is, there is no respect of persons or distinction.

Same place. “This preserves farms, cities, and peoples in ordered peace,” etc. I read: “in ordered peace.”

P. 23. “It abolishes laws.” To abolish laws is to impair the force of laws, to neglect and despise them. Below, concerning circumcision: “If he circumcises, he violates the Sabbath. If he does not circumcise, he has abolished the laws of the appointed circumcision by the destruction of an innocent soul.” So Tertullian, *On the Soul*, chapter 46: “The Telmessians abolish no dreams,” that is, they do not scorn or despise them. He expresses the Apostle’s words in 1 Corinthians, chapter 13, numbers 5 and 7: “Charity does not seek its own; it bears all things, endures all things.” Tertullian gives the reason, *On Patience*, chapter 12: “Charity does not seek even its own interests, if it offers its own things in order to benefit another.”

Same place. “It restrains the forums,” etc.—that is, forums otherwise noisy and contentious. Cicero, *Brutus*, 280: “Thucydides did not treat this forensic, contentious, judicial kind [of eloquence].” Propertius, Book IV, Elegy 1:

> And he forbids mad words to resound in the forum.

Seneca, *Hercules Furens*, v. 172:

> Here, selling the raging quarrels  
> of the noisy forum, that shameless man  
> lets out anger and words.

Same place. “It crosses the sea, circles the city, supplies the commerce necessary to nations,” etc. I fear that Zeno said these things more for rhetorical display, to support his discourse, than because he thought they were actually so. For attempting sea crossings, testing dangers, exposing oneself to shipwreck, and entering upon hazards to life were not, in Horace’s view, undertaken out of charity for others, but from the desire of possession and because man was

> Unable to endure poverty.

Likewise Ovid, *Metamorphoses*, Book I, v. 131, attributes the daring to give sails to the winds to the criminal love of possession. From this, however, Zeno perhaps inferred that, when control of things had become shared through commercial exchange, charity could be exercised; but this is remote from the subject.

Likewise. Its office is that it sets before us from books the virtues of the ancients, etc. It is most certain that, through historians, events performed in ages long past are set before our eyes as if present; and that from the books of philosophers and other writers one derives disciplines, sciences, and manners. Books indeed have been called dead teachers, because they readily admit those who turn their pages and do not, by putting them to shame, interrupt them two or more times. Since their use is an instrument of learning, Pliny the Elder aptly said that no book is so bad that it cannot be useful in some respect. We ought therefore to be especially indebted and grateful to those who have wished their labours, thoughts, and discoveries to be shared with us. Granted that they chiefly spread their sails for their own glory; yet, since that glory was to be hoped for from the favour and benefit of readers, so that by these means they might obtain what they desired in full measure, they must for this reason also be said to have laboured for the advantage of posterity. For, on the contrary, there are so many envious and ill-disposed persons who do not publish their discoveries but, by defrauding others of their benefit, prefer that they perish with themselves rather than enrich the knowledge of others.

Likewise. “Tossed by the rage of a bold wolf”: in the manuscript, “devoured”; wrongly.

Page 24. “Long ago it would have discovered, destruction, unless it,” etc. Delete the comma before *interitus* [“destruction”], and interpret it as *interiissent* [“they would have perished”]. For this is what he means by this periphrasis.

Likewise. “Kindly charity had bound [them] with the faithful offspring of a perpetual marriage.” The elements serve one another and return into themselves by reciprocal movement. Hence Empedocles, in Sextus Empiricus, *Against the Mathematicians*, book VIII, counted friendship and strife among the elements as necessary concomitants, since they reconcile one to another and again dissolve them. Seneca, *Natural Questions*, book III, chapter 10: “All the elements have alternating returns: whatever perishes in one passes into another.” Consult him. Thus our author properly speaks of “the faithful offspring of a perpetual marriage.”

Likewise. “It is learned from the law, but born in minds,” etc. Ambrose, on Psalm CXVIII: “He truly loves who preserves the commandments without sadness and without fear, from voluntary zeal rather than under compulsion.” Aristotle says that habit differs from affection because habit is more lasting and permanent, whereas affection is easily moved and changed. But virtue, when it passes into a habit, is a certain *teleiōsis* [completion, perfection]; and, as St Paul says of charity, *oudenpote ekpiptei*, “it never fails.” He says that it is born in minds because, as Augustine says somewhere, charity feeds the hungry, but pride also feeds them; charity clothes the naked, but pride also clothes them; charity fasts, but pride also fasts—or, to speak more mildly, it is obedience to a commandment, not charity or mercy, that ought to do everything.

[Col. 0543A]

Likewise. “And therefore, since it works wrath, it is rightly subject to law,” etc. “Wrath” means punishment and penal correction in Paul, Romans chapter XIII, no. 5. Thus, for Zeno, “to work wrath” is to bring upon oneself the penalty deserved by transgressing the law.

Likewise. “It is a certain stern form of love,” etc. To correct is indeed a form of love, and belongs to one who is well-disposed (*eunoōn*), as Clement of Alexandria says, *Paedagogue*, book I, chapter 8. For one who threatens openly shows that he wishes to do no harm and does not wish to carry out the things he threatens: “But, having struck them with fear, he checks the rush toward sins, and manifests his love for humankind, while still delaying, and making clear what they will suffer if they remain sinners.” By instilling fear, moreover, he restrains the onset of sins and displays his benevolence toward human beings, still postponing punishment and showing what they will suffer if they continue in sin.

Page 25. “Because it presumes that it alone can preserve what it commands,” etc. With a slight alteration I read *cum praecipit* [“when it commands”], so that the reading, if not certain, may at least be probable.

Likewise. “What we observe by another’s right,” etc. For charity is owed to one’s neighbour by divine command.

Likewise. “But when, at the invitation of that devotion, we begin to be inhabited by the same,” etc. That is: when, invited by God through the fervour of charity, we begin to be inhabited [by him]. Charity is a right will, kindled by a certain fire of the Holy Spirit, from whom it comes and to whom it is referred, as Prosper of Aquitaine has it, *On the Contemplative Life*, chapter 13. John Cassian, in the *Conferences*, defines devotion as the fervour of a good will.

Likewise. “What is his becomes for our parts,” etc. I read: *fit pro partibus nostrum* [“becomes for our parts / on our behalf”].

Likewise. “Lest by admonition something be taken away from piety,” etc. Punctuate: “lest, by admonition, something be taken away from piety.” For to love one’s neighbour is to love oneself, and to hate him is the same as hating oneself.

Likewise. “We should endure reverence for the truth,” etc., of the archetype: for man is in the image of God. Below: “and by most worthily venerating the image of God, let us declare what we owe to truth itself,” that is, to the archetype.

Likewise. “We should endure reverence for truth; in it, when the matter has been dismissed by condition,” etc. Read and punctuate: “of truth, and in it the matter,” etc.

Page 26. “If the countenance of some illustrious king, though [but] of a man, anyone …”: punctuate: “If the countenance of some illustrious king—though of a man—anyone …”

Likewise. “Whom alone does he revere, whatever is feared even in kings themselves among the virtues of nature?” I judge that one should read: “whom he not only reveres, whatever [is eminent] among the virtues of nature, but even kings themselves,” etc. He rises from the lesser to the greater. If the image of a king, who is a man, exacts such reverence, how much more that of God, who is above the foremost things of nature and above kings, who are inferior to nature in their powers. By “virtues of nature” he means whatever stands out in nature: namely heaven, earth, stars, and heavenly bodies. Diogenes Laërtius, in his account of Zeno: *Aretē de toi hē men tis koinōs panti teleiōsis*—“Virtue, in one sense, is generally the perfection of each thing.” Plato, *Laws*, book V, 851: *to nyn dē legomenon phaulotētos te kai aretēs chōras*—“what has just been said about the wretchedness and excellence of a country.” These things, however, revere God as Creator, and it is certain that they obey his command.

Likewise. “Lest the rule of truth be violated under the sound of the name,” etc. That is, lest one transgress against truth and become liable for falsehood. “Lest one incur [liability] against the rule of truth.” Jurists call a stipulation “incurred” (*commissa*) when an agreement is not observed, so that it is necessary either to render under the stipulation the interest at stake, or the sum included in the stipulation as its equivalent; as in Law 14, *Si pact.*, Code of Justinian, *On Pacts*. What in Law 9, *Si quis cautioni non obt.* is “the stipulation is not incurred,” is rendered in Greek *ouk eneketai*, “he is not bound”—that is, the promisor cannot be sued before a judge, because he has not committed an act contrary to what was promised in the stipulation. Under the title *Bem. rat. hab.* the Latin reads “the stipulation is incurred”; the Greek has *bebaioutai hē eperōtēsis*, “the stipulation is confirmed,” that is, suit may be brought upon it because the agreement has been violated. Thus “to incur a penalty” is, by one’s act, to become liable to penalty; when a penalty is not incurred, one is not subject to its force. The Greeks translate *bebaioutai hē poinē*, “the penalty is confirmed,” for “the penalty is incurred” in the cited Law 9, §1, *Si qui caut. non obtemp.*: that is, a fault has been committed which entails the penalty. For one becomes liable to punishment who transgresses a command. In Law 2 of the Theodosian Code, *On Provincial Administrators*, book XII, occurs: “lest he incur the law of the offence committed,” that is, lest he fall under the penalty which the law has imposed upon persons committing such an act. Therefore Turnebus, *Adversaria*, book XXVIII, chapter 46, aptly taught that an offence requiring expiation is called *commissum piaculum* when that has been perpetrated for which an expiatory offering must be made.

Page 27. “Therefore naked, because his will is shamefulness,” etc. For it belongs to an impudent person to uncover the shameful parts which decency has wished covered. Most wittily, though in another sense, in the dispute of Hadrian with Epictetus, when the latter asks why Venus is painted naked, the reply is:

> Venus is painted naked, and the Loves are painted naked;  
> Those whom naked Venus pleases, she ought to send away naked.

Likewise. “Because a sword is always joined to unlawful passions,” etc.: violence and frenzy.

Likewise. “Here Joseph demands to be violent toward a woman, whom, even while she strips him, he does not find immodest,” etc. These words are distorted and do not have a regular syntactical construction; without manuscripts it is hardly easy for me to recover it. I shall state what I judge better: “Here Joseph—the indeclinable form standing for *Josephum* [Joseph, accusative]—is assailed by a woman’s violence; even while she strips him, she does not find him immodest.”

Likewise. “Here he conquered the Synagogue, when he grants her his own weapons,” etc. I think this refers to the story told in Numbers chapter XXV, and then to that recounted in Judges chapters XX and XXI.

Likewise. “And he flatters worse than he rages,” etc. When someone has compliant love, he is held by jealousy and servitude to his beloved; he squanders his estate in order to satisfy his lust—indeed, he neglects himself and his reputation. But without reciprocal love, what agonies of heart, what torments of spirit, what alienation from oneself, what madness! Zeno, however, concludes that the flatteries of love are worse, because, if it is illegitimate, the offence against God is kindled, an offence to be avoided above all else.

Likewise. “Even in its own fruit it hates itself,” etc. The fruit of love is reciprocal love, in which no one hates himself and of which no one repents; see Ficino’s most beautiful discussion in *On the Banquet*, oration II, chapter 8, and oration V, chapter 9. But after enjoyment of the beloved object, repentance comes. Petronius Afranius:

> In intercourse the pleasure is foul and brief,  
> And one is weary of Venus as soon as she is accomplished.

Aristaenetus, book I, letter 21: *elpizomenos ho gamos, hēdys eucharis, kai lian euktaios; gegone, periephronēthē*—“Expected intercourse is sweet, pleasing, and greatly desired; once it has happened, contempt follows.” Therefore it would be better to read, “in the very enjoyment of itself,” that is, in the enjoyment and pleasure itself. Ancient scholia on Terence, *Heautontimorumenos*, act I, scene 1, in Vossius: properly speaking, *frui* is to take delight from use; from *fruor* come *fruiscor* and *fruniscor*.

Page 28. “It captivates and deceives human minds, and thus began to be called desire,” etc. He sought a paronomasia in the words *capio* [I take/capture] and *cupio* [I desire].

Likewise. “With the ever number-bearing delight of alternation,” etc. Without doubt this word *numeriferum* is extraordinary. What does it mean? Must we understand it because *numerus* is sometimes used for a body, or for a principal part of a body, as in Sallust, *Catiline*, 19, “C. Manlius sends envoys from his own number,” and in Horace, *Epistles* II, 27, “We are a number”—namely, something bringing with it either all or the principal part of the stars? It would have been clearer to say *numeroso* [abundant, manifold], as Pliny says *varietas numerosa*, *Natural History* IX, chapter 17, namely, a manifold change. Martianus Capella, book IX, said *astriferum* [star-bearing]:

> Nor do the cares of the star-bearing chamber trouble you.

Likewise. “You, briefly shortened for a little while,” etc. *Breviatum* means diminished; *breviare* is to make smaller. Quintilian, book I, chapter 9: “First to paraphrase verse, then to interpret it with changed words, then more boldly to render it by paraphrase, in which one may both shorten certain things and embellish them, while preserving the poet’s meaning.” In the New Testament, Matthew chapter XXIV, no. 22, and Mark chapter XIII, no. 20, the Vulgate translator has *breviabuntur dies illi*, “those days shall be shortened”; in Greek, *kolobōthēsontai*. This suits diminution more than mutilation, as grammarians teach.

Likewise. “You possess the soul of the heavenly people,” etc. As if he said: “You restore to earth the qualities of paradise’s fellowship, insofar as you adorn peace,” etc.

Page 29. “You make the martyrs glorious by their confession,” etc. In this short section he speaks of charity toward God, which is otherwise called piety; the preceding words concern charity toward one’s neighbour. He took it from St Paul, Romans chapter VIII, who calls it charity, as does St Matthew, chapter XXIV: “Iniquity shall abound, and the charity of many shall grow cold.” Soon he returns to charity toward neighbour, in his usual way confusing different things, though not different in name.

Likewise. “You are rightly called God, because [you are] of the Trinity,” etc. Clement of Alexandria, *Stromata* IV: *agapē toinyn kai ho Theos eirētai, agathos ōn*—“Charity therefore is also called God, since he is good.”

## IN TREATISE VII, BOOK I: ON HUMILITY

Page 70. In the manuscript the title is simply “On Humility.” We know that the title “on Psalm CXXX” was added by the author himself, for while interpreting Psalm CXXX he declares that he had treated humility under another heading: “But since in many other places we have treated somewhat of humility.”

Likewise. “With idle business,” etc.: while they spend leisure in empty business. It is most elegantly said, as if he had said what people commonly express as being wholly occupied in doing nothing. Attilius, in Pliny the Younger, *To Minucius Fundanus*, letter I, thought it preferable to be idle than, while busy, to do nothing: in the same vein.

Likewise. “When they ascend to heaven in words,” etc.; that is, when they speak about divine matters and profess that they are able to speak of them. Recall the notes at folio …

Page 71. “For, with the name changed, and worship as though it were ready to dreams, they transmitted those scholastic calumnies all the way to God and the Church,” etc. This passage troubled me; nevertheless I thought one should read *permota sit somniis* [“as though it had been moved by dreams”]: that is, they transmitted those scholastic calumnies to the Church, as though it had been moved, or ought to have been moved, by their dreams; thus they should be explained as an apposition for the sake of the sentence’s illustration. Let anyone who can suggest something better. The manuscript reads *quasi promota somniis*. A Greek idiom.

Likewise. “Scholastic calumnies,” etc.: scholastic frustrations, deceptions, errors, from *calvor*, “I deceive, frustrate”; as Charisius and Priscian teach.

Likewise. “God ought not to be worshipped by them, but sought,” etc. Whoever allows himself to be led about by their various opinions will establish nothing fixed, nor know anything clearly. On their differing views see Plutarch, *Opinions of the Philosophers*, book I, chapter 7.

Likewise. “He points it out, but to us,” etc. “When servants of God conceal their good works, they preserve them for themselves; when they publish them, they make them useful to others,” says Pope St Gregory somewhere.
