Page 72. “Exaltation of heart belongs to few; lifting up of the eyes, to all,” etc. Magnanimity is a natural virtue, but it is not given to all, nor cultivated by all. The power of the eyes is indiscriminately common to everyone; nature therefore placed them in the lofty part of the body, so that their use might be more ready. By them we either breathe pride, or direct love like darts, or look upon what ought not to be known, and the like, from which the Prophet declares himself free.

Page 75. “The Prophet’s terror would overshadow no one,” etc. These things are very obscure to me, nor can my understanding provide light. I thought perhaps one might read *neminem profecto terrore* [“certainly no one by terror”], but I cannot discover what to supply for *tō obumbret* [“that it may overshadow”]; otherwise it is alien and unsuitable here.

Likewise. “By whose enticement the world is in bloom,” etc. The eyes act as go-betweens by conveying forms to the soul, from which affection is born. For, as affection is born in the seats of the senses when they perceive, so it is born in the soul when it understands, as Nemesius teaches, chapter 7, *On the Imaginative Faculty*. What if one read, “the world is wretched,” alluding to Eve’s sight of the apple, by which she brought death upon the human race? Genesis chapter III, no. 5: *kai eiden hē gynē hoti areston tois ophthalmois*—“and the woman saw that it was pleasing to the eyes.”

Page 74. “He prays to God not limb by limb, but wholly,” etc.; not by bodily gesture, but by humble consciousness of himself: not stretching out his hands, not lifting up his eyes, not raising his voice, as the author says that the Pharisee did—freely indeed, and in accordance with his own bent, attributing to him things which he had not drawn from the sacred text.

## IN TREATISE XIII, BOOK I: ON CIRCUMCISION

[Col. 0546B]

Page 99. “This power of the heavenly sacrament,” etc. Here *sacramentum* means mystery. Nemesianus and the others writing to Cyprian, among his letters no. 78: “For while you do not cease in your treatises to unveil hidden mysteries, thus we …”

Likewise. “Circumcision is a scar, made by the knife in the loss of a round wound,” etc.; that is, a cutting-away around the sexual organ made with a knife. It is a distinctive manner of expression in our author. The *damnum* [loss] is the cutting-away itself. Varro, *On the Latin Language*, book IV: “Loss is from taking away, when less has been remade than its cost.” Paulus the jurist, in book III *On Threatened Damage*: “Loss and condemnation come from taking away and, as it were, diminution of property.” What those writers understood of patrimony or merchandise, our author extended, by no unusual metaphor, to any matter. Juvenal, *Satires* XII, 34:

> Imitating Castor, who makes himself  
> A eunuch, wishing to escape the loss  
> Of his testicles.

In the Theodosian Code, book VII, title XIII, constitution 5, the emperors say: “If anyone is found to have avoided military service, let him have escaped the loss of his body by the amputation of his fingers” (for that reason they are called *poltroni* in Italian, as though “with thumbs cut off”). He calls circumcision itself a “round wound,” which the Greeks call *peritomē*, because it surrounds and removes the foreskin. “A circular scar” and “a round wound” may appear tautological. But he found it expedient to say this, lest we think that medicine had repaired the wound and restored those parts whose mutilation itself displayed the nation’s mark, by which they were distinguished from foreigners. Therefore the circular scar had to remain, corresponding to the kind of wound there had been.

Likewise. “Greater is that [injury] of him who, in honour of his goddess, an ugly and wanton old woman,” etc. He touches on the story of Attis and Cybele, concerning whom see Pausanias, *Achaica*, and Arnobius, book V.

Page 100. “He fights against the Sabbath, which he proclaims must not be violated by any work at all,” etc. *Praeconat* is a coined verb, like Seneca’s *apologavit*, “he made a defence,” and Pliny the Younger’s *proaemiatur*, “he makes a preface”: it means he declares, proclaims loudly, threatens, or makes known. Plautus, *Asinaria*, prologue:

> Now do you, herald, make the whole audience listen.

For the function of a herald was to make what was said more clearly heard. Clement of Alexandria, *Stromata*, book I, 277; Theognis 883:

> *Mēde liēn kērykos an ous eche makra boōntos.*  
> Do not lend your ear too much to a herald crying loudly far and wide.

Therefore the edicts of magistrates also used to be announced through a herald; hence the oracle:

> *Eudaimon ptoliethron henos kērykos akouein.*  
> Happy is the city which hears the voice of one herald.

Plutarch cites it in the *Banquet of the Seven Sages*. Moreover, the Hebrews were commanded to rest from every work on the Sabbath under the most severe penalty of death: Exodus XXXI, 14.

[Col. 0547A]

Likewise. “He has emptied the rights of circumcision,” etc.: he has undermined them. Cyprian, *Testimonies against the Jews*, I, chapter 16: “That the old sacrifice might be made void and the new celebrated.” Likewise, in letter LXXVI, he joins “empty” and “void.”

Page 102. “Add that this circumcision promises not so much salvation as it points out the place and source of the crime,” etc. As if he said that sin was born in Adam from the woman’s enticement, and was to be restrained in Abraham and his offspring by mutilation of the member through which a man’s desire for women is consummated. Philo the Jew, *On Circumcision*: *Epeidē gar ta nikētēria pheretai tōn en hēdonais philtrōn hē andros pros gynaika synousia, to hypēretoun tais toiautais homiliais organon akrōtēriazein edoxe*—“For since a man’s intercourse with a woman carries off the prize among all the enticements of pleasures, it seemed right to mutilate the organ serving such intercourse.” The rest of what is in Philo our author subsequently sets out as well.

Likewise. “For Adam plucked the forbidden apple with this member.” Manuscript: “For Adam, when he plucked the forbidden apple, [did so] with this member.”

Likewise. “Because I recognize that a special care against death has been provided for me by God,” etc. Here *cura* means a remedy or medicine. Cicero, *Tusculan Disputations* III, near the beginning: “Bodies can be cured; there is no medicine for minds, though this properly ought to be called treatment.” Cornelius Celsus uses it in the same way; but our author likes to speak thus, as others have approved. See Claudius Salmasius on Julius Capitolinus, p. 245. “Death,” that is, sin and damnation. Cyprian, *On Works and Alms*: “Almsgiving frees from death.” Philo the Jew, *Allegories*, book I, near the end, speaks of two deaths: one by which the soul is separated from the body, the other which he calls the death of the soul, namely when there is *aretēs phthora kai kakias analēpsis*, “corruption of virtue and the assumption of vice.”

Page 103. “That he would perish unless he sought truth again,” etc. I do not see what “truth” is doing in this place. I should seek a remedy from the manuscripts, if I could hope for one. By conjecture I cannot help a passage that, in my judgment, is corrupt.

Likewise. “Because the circumscription of this mark is subject to the power of the heart,” etc. In order to be proved circumcised, the heart must ward off sins and flee the wicked affections of the mind. Therefore the fleshly circumcision of the foreskin is worthless unless inward and spiritual circumcision is added—as he teaches more plainly below from Jeremiah chapter IV.

Page 104. “Through this injurious tribute of the body,” etc. The foreskin, as though offered in tribute. See Law *ager.*, *On the Meaning of Words*, etc.

Page 105. “Either Moses is deceptive, if circumcision is circumcised again in order to do this same thing,” etc. The force is that of an enthymeme. Either Moses, Deuteronomy chapter XXX, no. 6, wrongly announced that circumcision must be performed in the heart, not on the *verpa* [penis]; or Joshua sinned, because he carried out circumcision on the *verpa*, not in the heart: Joshua chapter V. For, he says, either Joshua circumcised those already circumcised a second time and could remove a part of the member omitted in the first circumcision—which is impossible—or, in accordance with Moses’ meaning, he circumcised hearts and thus became a murderer; for to strike the heart with a scalpel, whether of iron, stone, or any material whatsoever, even with a light stylus, is to inflict immediate death. Thus he argues that bodily circumcision can have place in neither way. The most eloquent Father, moreover, adapts this most ingeniously to his own meaning by comparing the effects of spiritual and bodily circumcision. Not that Joshua circumcised the circumcised, but because the Hebrews had been in the wilderness for forty years and very many had omitted this rite through either negligence or impiety, it had to be restored, so that the command might be fulfilled in all the uncircumcised, not in persons previously circumcised. He was pleased, however, to invent certain things, in order to pass by a most pleasant step from Jesus son of Nun to Jesus Christ, and to show the latter as the fulfiller of the true circumcision, which the former had foreshown under a sign.

Likewise. “With tongues singing,” etc. It occurs to me that one might write *cientibus* or *concientibus*, etc. Virgil, *Aeneid* VI, 165:

> To summon men with bronze.

Page 106. “And lest the first man, completed on the cross, should seem not to have been restored wholly to his original state,” etc. He means: lest the human race should be thought not to have been restored perfectly to the life from which it had fallen through Adam. Christ expiated Adam’s guilt by the wood, and, offering himself as a propitiation to God, left life upon the wood. “Not wholly”: not perfectly, not fully. “Restored to its original state,” that is, to life.

Likewise. “Of the spiritual woman,” etc. What if we read “of the spiritual Church”?

Page 107. “We are marked not with the seal, but with the sign, of the Holy Spirit,” etc. Minucius Felix, chapter 35, uses the same expression: “Thus, finally, we are readily recognized not by a bodily mark, but by the sign of innocence and modesty.” *Signaculum* and *notaculum* are the same. Both mean circumcision. Tertullian, *Apology*, chapter 21: “Nor do we deal with the bodily seal itself, nor with sharing a name with the Jews.” *Sphragis* means “seal,” *sēmeion* “sign.” Yet St Paul used *sphragida* for *sēmeion* in 1 Corinthians IX, no. 2: *hē gar sphragis tēs emēs apostolēs hymeis este en Kyriō*—“For you are the seal of my apostleship in the Lord.” That is, you demonstrate and provide testimony that I, as an apostle, have won you for Christ. Again, in 2 Timothy chapter II, no. 19, the Christian’s seal is called hope of the resurrection. This is, for our author and Minucius, a sign, not a seal—that is, observance of God’s will. They mean the seal to remain in the body, the sign in the mind and soul.

## IN TREATISE XIV, BOOK I: ON THE SPIRITUAL BUILDING OF THE HOUSE OF GOD

Page 109. In the manuscript it is entitled “On the Building of the House of God by Solomon.” It is known that in antiquity Christians not only did not profess temples, but considered the name alien to their own institution. Arnobius, *Against the Nations*, book VI, p. 191, while criticizing the use of temples, shows that Christians disapproved of them, lest they seem to participate in Jewish superstition or Gentile impiety, since the latter had confined their worship to corners of walls assigned to God. Christians did indeed assemble in certain houses, and sometimes in crypts, where they might hide from the danger posed by persecuting tyrants. But as their number increased and God advanced their cause, it became necessary to enlarge the number of houses, so that they could receive the multitude of newcomers and perform God’s service according to discipline, even in the very city where this occurred. Eusebius testifies to this, *Ecclesiastical History* VIII, chapters 1 and 2. He calls these places *oikous* [houses], not *naous* [temples] or *ta hiera* [sanctuaries], so that the customary designation of churches might remain; they were also called “houses of God,” because they were set apart for obedience to God and the observance of discipline. For the faithful came and assembled there, as Pliny the Younger testifies in his letter on Christians, book X, to Trajan, “to chant responsively among themselves a hymn to Christ as to a god, and bind themselves by an oath—not to some crime, but not to commit thefts, robberies, or adulteries, not to break faith, not to deny a deposit,” etc. Hence came the name *ecclesia* from the Greek word denoting a “gathering of a crowd.” Clement of Alexandria, book VII: *Ou gar nyn ton topon alla to athroisma tōn eklektōn ekklēsian kalō*—“For I call not the place, but the assembly of the elect, the Church.” Nor was anyone regarded as a temple otherwise than if he lived according to God’s commandments. Aratus the Deacon, book II, *On Demetrius the Statuary*:

> For we are temples, if our crimes depart.

Likewise with our Zeno in this treatise and in the sermon on Psalm CXXXVI, whether the latter is his or another’s.

Likewise. “To employ a kind of triumphal style,” etc. Just as triumphal equipment and triumphal ornaments ought to correspond to the eminent title of triumph, so triumphal oratory ought to be worthy of the glory of one who triumphs: that is, ornate, elevated, jewelled, and expressed in embellished words. For, Quintilian says, it matters greatly what is the nature of the thing we set forth.

Likewise. “To redouble with praises the sacred citadel of a new work,” etc. It is clear that he speaks of the place in which the church assembled, perhaps newly chosen and adapted to this use. This is proved by what he says below: “Recognize your own building from this newly built structure, whose capacity you too, by your fortunate number, have made narrow.” For if one house did not suffice because of the increase of believers, they selected others, so that there were different members of one body, joined together with one another. Eusebius, in the passage already cited: *Hōn dē heneka mēdamōs eti tois palaiois oikodomēmasin arkoumenoi, eureias eis platos ana pasas tas poleis ek themeliōn anistōn ekklēsias*—“For this reason, no longer content with the old buildings, they erected spacious churches from the foundations in every city.” See Valesius’s notes on chapter 11, book VII, of the same history.

Likewise. “Builders can please more than priests,” etc. This concerns the temple at Ephesus and the Capitol, in which worship unacceptable to the true God was professed, although the magnificence of the builders, the elegance of the construction, and the arrangement of the work displayed such supreme skill as to win the craftsmen admiration.

Page 110. “Which can [find] any place, with the temples of idolatry collapsing upon themselves,” etc. A monstrous reading. You will make it smoother by adding the negative particle *non*: “which cannot.” What does he mean? “Will there not be found, or will it be difficult to find, even a very small place in which a dwelling may be made for God, over which the danger of collapse does not hang?” The temples of idols collapse or may collapse. Solomon’s own temple, though already approved by God and constructed with such solid and perfect workmanship, exists no longer. God declared that heaven is his throne and earth his footstool, Isaiah LXVI. “What then?” he says. “I shall give a temple stronger, more stable, and more pleasing to God: a faithful people, over whom collapse does not threaten except by their own will.” The Apostle supports this, 1 Corinthians chapter III, no. 16. In accordance with his meaning Theodoret, on Isaiah chapter LXVI, no. 2, interprets the true house of God and holy temple as: *ton kata tas Theou entolas politeuomenon, ton dediota kai tremonta tēn tou Theou prostagmatōn parabasin, ton praō tropō kai tapeinō phronēmati chrōmenon*—“one who lives according to God’s commandments, fears and dreads transgression of the divine commands, and has gentle manners and a humble mind.”

Likewise. “But if it is so among the things mentioned,” etc. Another argument against material temples. If expenditure added weight to religion, Christian material churches, in which a religion superior to the others was professed, would have been inferior in worship to Solomon’s temple, the Ephesian temple, and the Roman temple.

Page 111. “Recognize your building from this newly built structure,” etc. Namely, the spiritual building from the material one, which he calls new.

Likewise. “Therefore, lest anyone perhaps demand from me the work,” etc., namely, of this spiritual building.

Likewise. “One beautiful stone,” etc.: Christ. Peter the Apostle, First Epistle, chapter II, no. 4: “Coming to him, a living stone, rejected indeed by men but chosen and honoured by God, you yourselves also, as living stones, are built up.”

Page 112. “Seven alone suffice for him,” etc.: namely, the virtues, which are seven in number.

Likewise. “No bronze sea is attached,” etc. There was one in Solomon’s temple, 3 Kings chapter VII, no. 23. But in the Church there is the font of baptism.

Likewise. “His three members of inestimable fullness are one,” etc.: the Holy Trinity, one God alone. He called the persons “members”; I do not know whether Augustine speaks more precisely and truly, *On the Trinity*, book VI: “In the highest Trinity, one is as great as three together; nor are two more than one thing; and they are infinite in themselves. Thus each is in each, and all are in each, and each is in all, and all are in all, and all are one.”

Likewise. The rest is wanting; for this is the last treatise, and Sparaverius of Verona, following the order of the edition, was interrupted by death while preparing his annotations.

## IN TREATISE XV, BOOK I: ON THE THREEFOLD KIND OF SACRIFICES

Page 117. “Unless someone first knows the person and the rationale,” etc. *Ratio* is the mind and marrow of a matter, as Cassiodorus explains in his *Rhetoric*. Understand, moreover, “person” and “rationale” disjunctively. Quintilian, book V, chapter 8: “There is no question that is not either in the matter or in the person.” That is: where knowledge of the person is necessary, it must be acquired; where the matter or rationale is concerned, that must be investigated; where both are concerned, the inquiry must be combined. Aristotle, *Rhetoric*, book II, chapter 18: *Ta te gar amphisbētoumena zēteitai pōs echei, kai peri hōn bouleuontai*—“For matters in dispute are investigated as to how they stand, and deliberation concerns the matters about which men deliberate.” In this discourse, therefore, he combines an investigation of the divine person and of the rationale of sacrifices, in order both to conclude that Christ is God and to persuade that Christian sacrifice alone is acceptable to God.

Page 117. “You are a Christian worse than a Jew,” etc. Such were Ebion, Carpocrates, Prodicus, and their followers; on them see Theodoret, *Heretical Fables*, book I, chapters 5 and 6, and book II, chapter 1.

Page 118. “How great is the travail of the mind of unbelievers, bound in chains of darkness,” etc. Those who, assailed by the force of the Scriptures, neither yield to truth nor can defend the contrary position they have adopted.

Likewise. “Fashioned by the restrained tooth of the mother-file, to the loss of gold and silver,” etc. I punctuate: “to the loss of gold and silver, fashioned by the restrained tooth of the mother-file.” “To the loss of gold and silver” means objects which, though they could have been converted to a better use, were converted into empty images and foundations of impiety. He calls the file the mother of these gods, because she furnished the material for their birth, more powerful than the Great Mother [Cybele] for Attis. Arnobius, book VI, p. 200, says: “scraped down by files.” For the restrained tooth of a file, as our author says, can do nothing but remove filings by scraping.

Likewise. “Now the sacrifices of the Jews also rejected by God.” The manuscript reading “rejected by God” is more elegant.

Page 119. “What is offered not from a sack, but from the heart,” etc. What living victims come from a sack? One might speak of flour or loaves, whose use in sacrifice is established. A sack or little bag is properly for receiving loaves, flour, and grain. See Aristophanes, *Lysistrata* 909, and Bisset’s scholium there.

Likewise. “With stinking cattle,” etc. Read *bromosis*, from the Greek *brōmeō*, “to stink,” thus “foul-smelling” or “malodorous”; in Isidore’s glossary one also finds the word for “unclean.” There is a difference between *brōmeō* and *bromeō*, concerning which see below.

Page 120. “But on your estates smoking shrines everywhere, not ours,” etc. Temples and altars were everywhere situated in fields and on farmers’ estates through superstition, as though all prosperity would thereby accrue to their owners from nearby deities. In chapter 58 of the Code of Canons of the African Church, the Fathers lament that temples of idols remain: *en pollois topois parathalassiois, kai diaphthorois ktēsesin, kai en tois agrois, kai apokekrymmenois topois*—“in many coastal places, on various estates, in fields, and in hidden and secluded places.” In a suppliant petition they decree that the Emperor should be asked to have them demolished; and the same is attested by Theodosian Code XVI, *On Pagan Sacrifices*: “If there are any temples in the fields, let them be demolished without crowd or disturbance.” Moreover, by saying “but on your estates smoking shrines everywhere,” he indicates that people everywhere burned incense at will, whether on their own land or another’s. A most explicit proof appears in book XII of the Theodosian Code, *On Pagans*, etc., or Law 16, title X, where one also reads that they “smoked with vapour,” a synonym for “smoking shrines everywhere.” Horace, book III, ode 18:

> The ancient altar with much
It smokes with its odor. Arnobius, Book VII: “What difference does it make from what source the smoke is produced upon the sacred altars, or from what kind of mistletoe the clouds of incense rise steaming?” Zeno therefore laments that those who had taken the name of Christ permitted not only temples to remain standing on their estates, but impious rites to be performed in them, although by demolishing them they could prevent the condemned superstition; indeed, they even pride themselves on their possession and ownership of them, when they assert before a judge their right in the temples in order to protect them from occupiers.

Page 121. “But also those who run about among tombs, who sacrifice to corpses with fetid banquets,” etc. The ancients customarily held meals at monuments on a fixed day, most often on the annual anniversary; [Col. 0551B] they called these *nekyssia* [funeral observances] or *perideipna* [meals around the tomb]. Inscriptions in Gruter, folio 237, no. 5, from a Ravenna marble, teach this: “On this condition, that every year they bring roses to his monument and feast there”; and another in Spon, p. 292, from a Neapolitan marble, mentions a right in a monument together with a dining-room.

The same practice seems to have been carried on by Christians through the contagion of pagan superstitions, which they had retained also in many other rites, since it was not so easy to cut off at one stroke a vigorous popular custom. They were less at fault when they venerated Christ’s martyrs, who had suffered death for steadfast faith in him, as “divine and God-beloved men,” rather than as dead human beings. But that they did not refrain even from arranging certain love-feasts and banquets in cemeteries in memory of relatives is clear both because Zeno still attempts to extirpate this superstition and because Cyprian, in Letter LXVIII, reproaches a certain Martial, who professed himself a Christian, [Col. 0551C] for having long frequented the shameful, filthy banquets and associations of the Gentiles, for having placed his sons in the same association at profane tombs, and buried them there. Who can doubt that those thus buried were subjected to the rites of pagans? For banquets appointed after the manner of unbelievers for the faithful dead seemed impious—banquets which true Christians, while living, too ought to have avoided.

Incidentally, I observe that Prudentius, in his hymn for the funerals of the dead, long after Zeno’s time, asserts that Christians sprinkled monuments with garlands, flowers, and liquid offerings; Theodoret, *Therapeutics*, Book VIII, p. 599, who lived about his time, denies this. Did the former speak as a poet? Or was discipline stricter among Eastern Christians? As for the word *foeterosis* [fetid], which seems excessively foul, in the sermon on Jonah below one reads: “They do not kindle funereal fires upon fetid altars”; and in the third invitation to the font (now Tractate 30) he called the cradles “fetid,” which reading I have restored here also, although the earlier word is again found in the commonly printed fourth invitation to the font (now Tractate 31). Tertullian, in *Apology*, chapter 14, called them “decaying animals,” [Col. 0551D] with an equal pollution.

In the same place. “They suddenly produced martyrs for themselves,” etc. It is known from Canon 83 of the African Church that people were accustomed to build, through fields and along roads, altars as though in memory of martyrs, though no body of any such martyr, nor even any portion of one, was found there. The canon calls the dreams and fabricated revelations of those who everywhere established such shrines supposedly pious and fitting to the martyrs’ honor. Zeno therefore condemns those who, from love of luxury and drinking amid jars and cups in infamous places, suddenly produced martyrs for themselves, while professing the Christian name yet retaining pagan rites. It was characteristic of pagans, at such solemnities, to drench themselves in drink and amuse themselves with ridiculous and obscene songs, as is known from Libanius’ discourse published by Allatius.

True Christians rejected luxury and this intemperance in eating; they offered sacrifices for the martyrs, as Cyprian testifies in Letter XXXIV was done in his age. [Col. 0552A] Theodoret describes such sacrifices for us at the end of Book VIII of the *Therapeutics*, in this Latin sense: “The martyrs’ solemnities are observed; and in place of that ancient pomp and shameful obscenity of things and words, modest festivals are celebrated, displaying not drunkenness, jokes, and laughter, but divine songs, the hearing of sacred discourses, and prayers adorned with laudable tears.”

Page 122. “Who make offerings with white animals on an Egyptian day,” etc. The passage is corrupt. I would read: “who, on an Egyptian day, make offerings with white animals.” An “Egyptian day” occurs frequently in Herwart’s old Roman calendar. Others have noted that it was unlucky; I am therefore persuaded that people made offerings with white animals in order to avert its ominous influence. Horace, in the *Epodes*:

> And you who worship with white oxen.

Arnobius, Book II, §91: “Formerly, on Mount Alban, no bulls except snow-white ones were permitted to be sacrificed because of their whiteness.” Moreover, *facere* [to make] is proper language for sacrifices. Cato, *On Agriculture*, chapter 139: “That you may have right, if you make atonement with a pig.” [Col. 0552B] Columella, Book II, chapter 22: “Unless you have first made an offering with a puppy.” So too the Greeks: Theocritus, *Idyll* 28, near the end, *rexō portin erōti*—“I shall make [an offering of] a heifer to Love.” At the Council of Auxerre, Canon 1, it is forbidden that, on the Kalends of January, “a little cow or a little stag be made,” as Fronto Ducaeus reads it; see him on that council. To “make a little cow or little stag” means to sacrifice a little cow or little stag.

Page 123. “And they seek the health of their cattle, their bellies violently slit,” etc. Read from the manuscripts: “And they seek their own health in the violently slit bellies of cattle.”

In the same place. “That they may conceal the thefts of a most shameful profit”: I read, “of a most shameful pleasure.” He refers to husbands who are madly in love with slave women or freedwomen, to whom they entrust household business so that intercourse may be easier, or so that its sexual pretext may be less shameful; by the frequent necessary sharing of business concerns, they conceal the secret of their pleasurable affair.

In the same place. “Those publican women,” etc.: public, common women. Papias: “*Publicus*, *publicanus*, as *rusticus*, *rusticanus*.” [Col. 0552C] He calls them *publicanae*, as though they held under contract the shameful tax-revenue of the people. See the jurist Gaius in Law 13, *On Tax-Farmers*. Moreover, I do not see what the phrase *to vi* [“by force”] means here; for against such women no force other than silver or gold ought to have been used.

Page 124. “Therefore, my sweetest flowers,” etc. I do not doubt that everyone sees that “my brothers” should be read. The error perhaps arose from abbreviated writing in a manuscript.

## IN TRACTATE I, BOOK II, ON GENESIS

Page 141. “At the beginning of the sacred poem,” etc. Ovid, *Remedies for Love*, 252, contrasts a *carmen sacrum* [sacred chant] with an infamous or magical chant, just as, in the Theodosian Code, Book XVI, title X, chapter 7, “dire chants” are contrasted with chaste prayers. The word had a very broad use: it was assigned not only to poetic verses, but also to things pronounced in a fixed verbal formula, as in prayers and dedications. Evidence occurs in Livy, Book XXXIX, chapter 15; in Pliny the Younger’s *Panegyric* [Col. 0552D], chapter 63; and in Seneca’s *Consolation to Marcia*, chapter 13:

> While he was holding the doorpost beside the cushion and dedicating the Capitol, news was brought of his son’s death. Pretending not to have heard it, he pronounced the solemn words of the pontifical chant, while no groan interrupted his prayer.

Likewise in imprecations. Livy, Book X, chapter 28: “He was compelled to swear a certain dire chant composed for the execration of his own head, family, and stock.” And that prophets “sang” predicted events is known from the same author, Book I, chapter 55. The name *carmen* was used in all these instances because, as I infer from Festus under *occentassit*, the utterances were pronounced loudly and with a certain chant, so that they could be heard from a distance. Hence in Pliny, Book XXVIII, chapter 2, “the incantations of chants”; and in the Twelve Tables, “one who enchanted away crops” and “one who chanted an evil chant”—for this reason, I suppose.

But from these examples I cannot see how *carmen* applies to the sacred books. I am not unaware that *carmen* can also mean unmetrical discourse, not formally [Col. 0553A] composed. Cicero, *On the Laws*, Book II, 202: “For as boys we learned the Twelve Tables as a necessary chant.” Livy, Book I, chapter 25: “The treaty, pronounced in many words in a long chant, it is not worthwhile to report.” Pliny, *Panegyric*, chapter 3: “And he is considered more acceptable who brings to the shrines of the gods a pure and chaste mind than one who brings a premeditated chant.” Zeno, perhaps indulging his expansive genius and eloquence, sought novelty and rarity in that term by allusion; for this reason he used it also in Sermon V on Isaiah and elsewhere.

Page 142. “He does not say, ‘Make according to your [image],’ but says, ‘Let us make according to our [image],’” etc. Tertullian has similar remarks in *Against Praxeas*, chapter 12, from whom our author seems to have taken them.

In the same place. “One man is fashioned according to the image and likeness of two, yet nothing is found in him that belongs to either,” etc. From this passage he infers that there are two who command and two who act: the work is brought into likeness with its makers, not into the likeness of either one separately, whom one might say was made; therefore those two are the same.

[Col. 0553B] In the same place. “Whom you will have deprived, I do not know.” More correctly, the manuscript reads: “Whom you will have deprived, you do not know.”

Page 143. “But he to whom the command is given is, you say, inferior,” etc. Whatever the Father does through the Son, he does not do through a servile instrument but through natural power and substance, says John of Damascus, *On the Orthodox Faith*, Book II, chapter 4. Tertullian, in the passage just cited from *Against Praxeas*: “For with whom was he making man, and to whom was he making him similar? With the Son indeed, who was to put on man; and with the Spirit, who was to sanctify man. He spoke as though with ministers and arbiters, from the unity of the Trinity.”

In the same place. “He is the cultivator of the Father’s heart,” etc. Origen, *On John*, tome I, §42, interprets the heart of God as “his intellectual and purposive power concerning all things”; and the *Logos* as that which manifests the things in that heart—his power surpassing understanding and ordering all things according to their nature. He infers that no one could be conceived more fitting to reveal the Father’s counsels than the Savior. [Col. 0553C] This accords most suitably with Zeno’s intention. But the manuscript reads “executor,” not “cultivator.”

## IN TRACTATE II, BOOK II, ON GENESIS

Page 144. “Unless one conquers the enemy by whom he is attacked, he can never be secure in his goods,” etc. Hence the saying: “Peace comes from war.” Vegetius, before Book III: “Let him who desires peace prepare war; no one dares attack one whom he understands will be superior if he fights.” Saint Augustine, *On the Words of the Lord*: “Peace is not sought in order that war may be practiced; war is waged in order that peace may be acquired.”

In the same place. “That Chaos existed in the beginning, that is, an unformed and disordered mass of hidden matter,” etc. What Chaos is, I have said elsewhere. Here he speaks in the common sense; otherwise, he himself speaks more correctly, according to the proper meaning of the word, in the sermon on the Resurrection: “Likewise in Hell, that most grasping rich man, whom an immense Chaos separated from the happiness of the poor man.” [Col. 0553D] Philo called this the abyss and Tartarus in *On the Creation of the World*. Lucian, *On Astrology*.

Page 145. “Therefore, if, as they wish, God did not make the matter which he used, but it is eternal as he is, there are then two principles, and indeed opposing ones,” etc. He concludes that, between two principles, one must be more ancient, and the other must not depend on it. “For what is principal,” says Tertullian, *Against Hermogenes*, chapter 4, “unless that which is above all things? Unless that which is before all things? And from which are all things?” Aristotle, *Physics*, Book I, chapter 6, no. 2: “The principles must neither derive from one another nor from other things, but all things must derive from them”—a most harmonious statement. He has similar words in *Metaphysics*, Book V, chapter 1.

In the same place. The manuscript lacks *ergo* [therefore], and reads: “There are two principles.”

In the same place. “Whence it is not a principle,” etc. That is: [Col. 0554A] it is so far from being stronger that it cannot even be believed to be a principle. Thus Martial, Epigram XV, Book I:

> How can a hungry lion spare captured prey?

That is, “How can it?”

In the same place. “Whence that which grows old is not a principle,” etc. For a principle is ungenerated and incorruptible, and incapable of change either from lesser to greater or from greater to worse. For growing old is the worst of changes, close to corruption, and, as Solon is reported to have said, “the winter of life.” Prudentius, in his funeral hymn:

> Because all created things must  
> At last grow feeble and old,  
> And things joined together be dissolved.

Page 146. “This is our God, who differentiated himself into God,” etc. A most obscure manner of speaking has shadowed forth a most obscure matter. For God alone knows the manner of Christ’s generation; no one else understands it. [Col. 0554B] Below, Tractate 3, Book II: “He who was before he was born proceeds into birth, equal to the Father in all things, because the Father begot in him another self from himself, namely from that unbegotten substance of his.” Likewise, Tractate 5 of the same book: “To suppose how he who proceeded was generated is madness.” Likewise, Tractate 1, Book II: “What? That he is thereby proved not inferior, because he who proceeded from there is the cultivator of the Father’s heart.” It pleased them to call the eternal generation of Jesus Christ a “procession.” Thus Cyril of Alexandria, *On the Holy Creed*, VI, 42, called the generation of the Word “an ineffable and inexpressible procession.”

Page 147. “And yet, passing from each into the other.” More correctly the manuscript reads: “and passing from each into each.”

## IN TRACTATE III, BOOK II, ON GENESIS

Page 148. “Christ is without hesitation,” etc. That is, without wavering, without doubt; for delay—that is, hesitation—arises from wavering and [Col. 0554C] doubt. Cicero, *Against Catiline*, Oration II, folio 124: “When he hesitated, when he delayed, I asked what he doubted.” Another reading is *incontanter* [without delay], but the former is correct and is retained by the manuscript.

In the same place. “By a secret beyond suspicion,” etc. Not discoverable even by investigation through suspicion. Papias: “Suspicions are certain indications and traces.” Again: “Suspicion arises, as it were, from certain conjectures.” *Insuspicabile* is that which cannot be reached even by conjecture: that is, neither by demonstrations nor by conjectures.

In the same place. “He embraced the Son not without affection, but without revelation,” etc. For that the Father loves the Son is declared in several Gospel passages: John 3:35; likewise John 5:20: “For the Father loves the Son and has shown him all things.” Elsewhere: “This is my beloved Son.” But because he sent his Son not from the beginning, but at the fitting time—that is, when the fullness of time had come, as Saint Paul says in Galatians 4:4—or, as our author says below in Sermon IV, made himself visible when he was about to visit humankind, [Col. 0554D] he therefore said “without revelation”: that is, unknown to the world, not revealed.

Page 149. “He proceeds into birth,” etc. I have spoken of this in the note on page 139.

Page 150. “From that unbegotten substance of his,” etc. When Thales was asked what was the most ancient of all things, he is said to have replied: “God, for he is ungenerated.” For he lacks generation, beginning, and end, since he is infinite. God is not said to have been born, but to have taken flesh; and, insofar as the man assumed by God was born of the Virgin Mary, she was called *Theotokos* [God-bearer] at the Council of Ephesus. This does not mean that the nature of the Word and his divinity took their beginning from the holy Virgin, but that the sacred body, complete with a rational soul, was derived from her and united hypostatically with the Word of God; according to the flesh, he is said to have been born. Thus Cyril wrote to Nestorius, and the Synod subscribed to this opinion in its first session.

In the same place. “In which, remaining blessed forever, [Col. 0555A] he begot a Son possessing equally all that he possesses,” etc. Here too no trace whatever of a sound meaning appears. To say nothing further, I conjecture that it may be read thus: “He provided equal things for all who possess the Son.” The words at the end of the fifth preceding sermon have led me to restore the earlier wording: “Indeed, let those who do not have him with them seek him.” For he often uses the same words and sense in similar places, so that one passage illuminates another. To seek God is to devote oneself wholly to him in fear and obedience; but to possess God is when God truly dwells in our habitation and when faith, hope, purity, and fear are in us—as Clement of Alexandria reports that the Apostle Barnabas wrote, *Stromata*, Book II, p. 411. Moreover, instead of “begot equal things,” I restore “provided equal things,” referring to that blessedness in which God was said shortly before to remain forever. For it is granted to the faithful and upright that they too may become children of God. Saint Paul, Romans 8:14: “For all who are led by the Spirit of God, these are children of God.”

## IN TRACTATE IV, BOOK II, ON GENESIS

[Col. 0555B]

In the same place. “Remaining one eternally from himself”: thus in the manuscript. “Thereupon he was necessarily made visible, because he himself was about to make the world and visit humankind.” Thus in the manuscript.

## IN TRACTATE V, BOOK II, ON FAITH

Page 154. In the manuscript it is entitled “On Faith.”

In the same place. “Of undivided perpetuity,” etc. A little later he will say “without distinction,” which has the same meaning—that is, inseparably. Sermon III: “Without revelation.” Sermon IV: “Thereupon made visible.” Sermon V: “Incomprehensible wisdom from the region of the heart brings forth the Word; omnipotence propagates itself.”

Page 155. “For the Son tempers himself for the sake of the nature of things, lest the limited capacity of this world be unable to bear the Lord of eternal majesty,” etc. He [Col. 0555C] emptied himself, lest the world collapse, unaccustomed to the summit of divine majesty. “For no one shall see God and live.” Tertullian, *Against Praxeas*, chapter 14: “God was seen according to human capacity, not according to the fullness of divinity.”

## IN TRACTATE VI, BOOK II, ON WHAT IS WRITTEN, ETC.

Page 158. “If [Christ were] only a man, as some suppose, from the womb of the Virgin,” etc. Such was Carpocrates; see Theodoret, *Compendium of Heretical Fables*, Book I, chapter 5. But Christ is true God and true man. Cyril of Alexandria, in the Letter to the Egyptian Monks, folio 15:

> The Word of God therefore took hold of the seed of Abraham and shared in blood and flesh, making the body from a woman his own, so that, existing not merely as God but now also having become man like us because of the union, he might be understood as such. Thus Emmanuel is confessedly composed of two realities, divinity and humanity. Yet there is one Lord Jesus Christ, one true Son, both God and [Col. 0555D] man; not a man made divine like those who become partakers of the divine nature by grace, but rather true God, who appeared for our sake in human form.

The Word of God, therefore, took the seed of Abraham and, forming for himself a body from a woman, became a participant in flesh and blood. Thus he is not only God, but because of the union of the natures is also understood to be a man like us. For Emmanuel certainly consists of two realities, namely divinity and humanity; there is one Lord Jesus Christ, one true Son, at once God and man—not a man deified, like those who by grace are made partakers of the divine nature, but the true God who appeared in human form for our sake.

Bishop Vitalian, from the sermon on faith among the materials before the Council of Ephesus: “If anyone divides our Lord and Savior into two, calls one the Word, the Son of God, but calls the other the assumed man, and does not confess one and the same person, let him be anathema.”

In the same place. “He bears death in order to conquer death.” I do not know why [Col. 0556A] they rejected the manuscript reading, “He tastes death.”

Page 159. “Of pious providence,” etc. That is, of the providence of the divine economy. Someone in Suidas makes three grades of divine providence: “according to economy, according to good pleasure, according to concession.” Here we must say that Zeno understood the providence that is “according to economy,” which Tertullian called the “mystery of the economy” in *Against Praxeas*, chapter 2: namely, that which disposes unity in Trinity, directing the three—the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit. Yet they are three not in state but in rank; not in substance but in form; not in power but in aspect, etc. Aemilius Portus either did not understand or did not express what divine providence “according to economy” meant in Suidas.

In the same place. “But if, as reason itself declares, this diversity of kingdom can by no means cease,” etc. What, pray, is this “diversity,” when his whole purpose is to show the one and indivisible kingdom of Father and Son? What if one reads *vastitas* [vastness]? At least it will better fit the sense. Pliny, chapter 7, [Col. 0556B] had called God’s service manifold, though in an atheistic and impious sense. It is difficult to judge soundly in the writings of others without an autograph, or at least a copy; for whatever one may conjecture will generally depart from the author’s conception, which could have been expressed in different words even if one attains his thought.

In the same place. “By the giver of the law, to the man assumed by God, it is assigned to his just things when matters have been arranged, not to God, not to the eternal ruler, especially since the Gospel says thus,” etc. As all this hangs together poorly, so I believe it is full of gaps and cannot be supplied without the guidance of manuscripts. I understand the entire passage in this form; if someone conjectures better, I shall agree: “This vastness of kingdom can by no means cease . . .; the ordering of things is assigned by the giver of the law to the man assumed by God”—that is, Christ—“and to his righteous [ones].” For so I read, not “when matters have been arranged” . . . “not to God, not to the eternal ruler,” etc.

Page 161. “Or will the Son, in handing over what he does not possess, lose it,” etc. “What he possesses” must be read, as the sense itself [Col. 0556C] requires; and I later found that it was so written in the manuscript.

## IN TRACTATE VII, BOOK II, ON THE NATIVITY OF THE LORD. I

Page 163. “Another, harming more modestly but more sharply, indeed calls the Son of God God, but denies that he was begotten from the Father by the perpetuity of noble origin,” etc. The reference here to the Arian heresy can undoubtedly persuade us that this sermon was not written by Zeno (see Dissertation I, chapters 2 and 3). For since he lived under Gallienus, while Arius disseminated his doctrine under Constantine, it is certain that what had not yet occurred in the writer’s time could not here have been denounced as past.

I would not deny that Justinian’s letter to Mennas expressly suggests that Arius drank Origen’s poisons when he devised grades in the holy and consubstantial Trinity; nor that Epiphanius and Jerome call Origen the father of Arians, Anomoeans, and Manichaeans. From this [Col. 0556D] the Veronese editor inferred that the doctrines condemned by Zeno were not Arius’ doctrines, because Arius came later, but Arian doctrines already in Origen, who had preceded him. But although I do not deny that Arius constructed his doctrine from Origen’s teaching, no one can say that Origen and Arius held the same views.

Certainly Origen believed that the Son was a portion of the Father’s substance and coeternal with the Father, as Socrates shows, *Ecclesiastical History*, Book VII, chapter 6; and Huet agrees in *Origeniana*, Book II, chapter 2, question 2, no. 24. Arius, by contrast, held: “The Word of God was not always; rather, he came to be from things that were not; therefore there was once when he was not.” So Gelasius of Cyzicus, Book II, chapter 3; Socrates, Book I, chapter 5; and Hermias Sozomen, Book I, chapter 15: “The Word of God was not from eternity, but arose from nothing; consequently there was at some time when he was not.” These are precisely the claims made by the writer of this sermon—claims incommunicable to Origen.

Moreover Sozomen says of this doctrine of Arius that matters previously unexamined were “called into question”; [Col. 0557A] and Gelasius states more plainly in the cited Book II, chapter 2: “He began to advance certain strange doctrines concerning faith in Christ, which no one in earlier times had ever investigated or introduced.” Therefore the opinion of those who directed the Veronese edition falls to the ground, when they thought that this sermon could have been ascribed to Zeno because errors disseminated by Arius had existed before Arius was born; this is proved false by the authority of writers and comparison of the facts.

## IN TRACTATE VIII, BOOK II, ON THE NATIVITY OF THE LORD. II

Page 168. “Of a secret beyond suspicion,” etc. See the notes on page 142.

In the same place. “True knowledge is to know God except as God,” etc. I shall speak of this in the sermon on Jonah, page 194. For it belongs to human moderation to remain within the orbit of one’s own knowledge.

[Col. 0557B] In the same place. “And nothing further is to be sought from him than that one should know his will,” etc. Lactantius Firmianus, *Divine Institutes*, Book II, chapter 5, writes piously and elegantly to this effect: “It is sufficient for a human being, for complete and perfect wisdom, if he understands that God exists; and the force and sum of that understanding is that he reverence and honor the common Father of humankind,” etc. Connect the notes above on Tractate 3, Book II.

In the same place. “But with vain reasonings concerning the provident God from God,” etc. If one reads *providentis* [provident], it must be understood of the divine economy, by which the things belonging to the constitution of the Trinity stand. If one reads *procedentis* [proceeding], it will seem more suitable to the sermon’s title. Let the reader decide. Above, from Cyril, I noted that the generation of the Word is called “an ineffable and inexpressible procession.”

In the same place. “To will what has been ordained,” etc.: to wish to grasp what has been ordained by divine decrees.

In the same place. “As contentious persons think,” etc. Namely philosophers, who, by investigating a matter on both sides, [Col. 0557C] contend and dispute; if this is done beyond measure, let them hear Publilius Syrus, in Aulus Gellius, Book XVII, chapter 14:

> By excessive disputation truth is lost.

Page 169. “May be subject to disposition,” etc.: that is, to fate, which they impiously believed to stand above God. Homer, *Odyssey*, Book III, verse 236:

> Not even the gods themselves  
> Can ward [death] off even from a beloved man, whenever  
> The destructive Fate of grievous death has seized him at last.

And Homer frequently says the same elsewhere. Seneca, tragedy *Oedipus*, verse 989:

> It is not permitted even to God to overturn  
> Things which run bound in their own chain of causes.

[Col. 0557D] Hence Cyniscus, in Lucian’s *Jupiter Confuted*, mocks Jupiter’s own powerlessness because he must depend on fate. “Disposition” is called fate because, according to the sounder view, it is divine ordering and providence. Seneca, *Natural Questions*, Book V, chapter 18: “That disposer of the world, God, who provides and orders all things by governing them with his decrees.” On fate see Hierocles and Lipsius in the little golden book *On Constancy*.

In the same place. “For if, for a little while, the names of Father and Son are set aside,” etc. Suppose you do not consider fatherhood and sonship, in which one passes, by an injury, into the other. See the materials collected under the title of the Digest of the jurists, *On Injuries*.

In the same place. “In the temple of the Virgin predestined for himself” (manuscript: *templum*), “he marks out lodging for himself,” etc. *Castra* [camp/lodging] is used figuratively for a seat or dwelling. More correctly he speaks in the following sermon, folio 165: “Having left heaven, the chaste guest slips into the lodging previously marked out—the foretold sanctuary of the virginal temple.” [Col. 0558A] “Predestined” means chosen beforehand, the dwelling foretold for him. *Metatum*, *metatio*, and *metatura* mean the same thing. Tertullian, *On the Pallium*, chapter 2: “Our lodging is wholly changeable,” that is, our dwelling, that in which we remain in this world. The Greeks translate and explain the title of Justinian’s Code *On Lodgings* as “concerning lodgings, that is, quarters.” In Isidore’s glossary, *metatores* are “preparers of lodgings.” Pacatus, *Panegyric*, chapter 6: “Or if that divine spirit, about to enter a body, first marks out a worthy lodging,” that is, prepares it. In Book XV of the Theodosian Code, *On Lodgings*: “No one who enjoys possession of his own house, protected by military service, shall attempt to harass another’s house; but let him be content with his own, or at least receive in his own house him who thinks that lodging in another’s is to be claimed for himself.” A *metator*, therefore, prepares a lodging; *metatum*, *metatio*, and *metatura* are the lodging itself; and in the Theodosian Code, also the burden itself of receiving guests.

In the same place. “About to be begotten into man,” etc.: “about to be generated as man.”

[Col. 0558B] In the same place. “And there, while preserving what he was, he plans to become what he was not,” etc. While preserving divinity, he plans to become man. Cyril of Alexandria, to Nestorius, in the letter beginning *Kataphlyarousi men hōs akouō*, folio 165: “He came forth as a man from a woman, not casting away his being God or his birth from God the Father; rather, even in the assumption of flesh, he remained what he was.” That is: he came forth as a man from a woman without abandoning either his divinity or his birth from the Father; in the very assumption of flesh he remained what he had been.

Page 170. “Entering the world, not cast forth as an infant usually is, he voluntarily inaugurates his creeping life with tears that precede it,” etc. Pliny, Book VII, preface, complains that nature casts a human being naked upon the bare ground on the day of birth, immediately to wailing and weeping, and that no other animal among so many is subject to tears, and those from the very beginning of life. Zeno had this in view when he wrote.

[Col. 0558C] Page 171. “Finally, the purgations, which are dangerous because of their delay,” etc. That is, difficult purgations, in Hippocrates’ terminology, in *On Airs, Waters, and Places*: “not beneficial,” for which he prescribes remedies in Book I, *On Diseases of Women*, p. 603. They call easy purgations “beneficial,” when they proceed well and according to nature’s prescription; so Erotianus interprets *chrēstōs* as “well.” See Bartholomaeus Eustathius in Erotianus’ Lexicon, under *kalōs* [well].

In the same place. “No injuries of the maternal womb attended the child,” etc. The manuscript reads: “No injury of the maternal womb attended the child.”

In the same place. “After the birth she remained a virgin; the incredulous midwife, who had rashly tested her, was found to bear witness to that same virginity. Her hand was burned, but when it touched the infant, that devouring flame was immediately quenched; and so that inquisitive midwife, after long marveling at the woman as virgin and at the infant as God, exulting with immense joy, came to heal and departed healed. Thus Christ caused himself to be born as man,” etc. Thus in the manuscript.

[Col. 0558D] Page 172. “Thus Christ caused himself to be born as man,” etc. Above he had said that in the first generation the Son proceeded by a single concord from the affection of the Father’s mouth. Here he speaks of the second: by equal concord the Son subjected himself to humanity. This is what “he caused himself to be born as man” means. But he adds that he was born in such a way as no human being can be born: no one with the mother’s virginity unviolated; no one without a woman in labor’s pain; no one without cries and tears; no one without the wrappings of uncleanness; and so forth.

## IN TRACTATE IX, BOOK II, ON THE NATIVITY AND MAJESTY OF THE LORD

In the same place. “Having left heaven, the lodging foretold,” etc. Consult the notes on the preceding sermon.

Page 173. “He prepares for himself a body, being about to be born by his own judgment,” etc. That is, by his own decree and will, in language consonant with the sacred books. John 5:27: “The Father gave the Son authority also to exercise judgment”—that is, to act according to his own determination.

In the same place. “He who was born from himself would not be believed, unless, because as she was an incorrupt virgin after conception, she remains such also after birth,” etc. “Unless because” has been inserted and is forced in against the proper sense. Whatever the author wrote, for the present I judge the reading should be: “He would not be believed, since, as she was an incorrupt virgin after conception, she remained such also,” etc.

Page 174. “Because he stood in the middle between the Father and humankind,” etc. John Chrysostom explains this more fully in his sermon on Christ’s Ascension:

> God was angry with us, while we turned away from the loving Lord. Christ, placing himself in the middle, brought both natures into friendship and himself endured the punishment from the Father that hung over us.

## IN TRACTATE X, BOOK II, ON ABRAHAM. I

[Col. 0559B]

In the same place. “His wife Sarah, no less [than he], after the courses of a long life had passed, learned, through the outpouring of childbirth, what kind of son she had borne. But because age had taken from them both the hope of offspring, a substitute pledge,” etc. The manuscript has: “His wife Sarah, no less [than he], after the courses of a long life had passed, a pious son would bring forth, she would receive by the outpouring of childbirth. But [age] had taken hope of offspring from them both,” etc. The passage is corrupt.

In the same place. “A substitute pledge,” etc.: as something succeeding what was not granted, but was granted when vigorous age had passed. He alludes to substitute victims. Aulus Gellius, Book IV, chapter 6: “Victims are called substitute victims because, if the first victims had not secured favorable omens, other victims were led out and slaughtered after them.”

In the same place. “Faith deserved what time had taken away.” The manuscript’s “By the merit of faith, what time had taken away” is incorrect.

Page 175. “He was turning toward the boundary of his setting.” The manuscript reads better: “at the boundary of his setting.”

[Col. 0559C] In the same place. “Behold the first devotion,” etc. Devotion is not merely worship, but also recognition of an obligation toward a superior or benefactor, as though one submitted and consecrated one’s vows to him. Seneca, *On Benefits*, Book III, chapter 5: “Hear the words of petitioners: everyone has said that remembrance will always live in his mind; everyone has professed himself surrendered and devoted.” Nemesianus, *Cynegetics*, 82:

> And leaders faithful in war, and battle-lines  
> With many a soldier, whose brave minds devotion inspires.

In the same place. “That only son of the anxious old man.” Read from the manuscript: “anxious.”

Page 176. “He is immediately prepared with the necessary sacraments,” etc. He alludes to the etymology of *sacramentum*, which they derive from *sacer* or *sacrum*, so that whatever pertains to the sacred is a sacrament. To sacrifice a victim to God is to perform a sacred act; for this instruments were required—fire, wood, a sword—which Zeno calls *sacramenta* [sacred implements], and shortly afterward *mysteria* [mysteries].

[Col. 0559D] In the same place. “The father, secure concerning the faithfulness of his offspring, [speaks] to his son.” Punctuate with the manuscript: “The father [speaks] to the son, concerning whom he had no doubt,” etc.

In the same place. “He also binds the feet, lest the victim, excited at the approach of death, kick,” etc. In the next sermon below: “And lest anything be lacking from the victim, he tightens the foot with a binding, lest the excited victim be displeasing.” The Vulgate version of Genesis 22:9 has: “and when he had bound Isaac his son.” From this it remains uncertain whether he bound him by the hands or feet; but the Greek reads, “and having bound together the feet of Isaac his son.” Philo also recognizes this reading in his commentary *That God Is Immutable*, and Zeno expressed it. Suidas: “Having bound together the feet: having tied the feet.” For then they believed the sacrifice acceptable, and the victim fit, says Servius on *Georgics* II.395, when the animal consecrated for sacrifice was found patient. Pliny, Book VIII, chapter 45: “It has been observed that the gods are not appeased by a limping victim, one belonging to another, or one dragging itself away from the altars.”

[Col. 0560A] **Same place.** “O brethren, secure devotion!” etc. Read: “O secure devotion of the father!”

**Same place.** “For the trials of testing are prolonged,” etc. That is, God still proceeds to test Abraham, allowing the sword to be drawn by him and the blow, with his hand raised, almost to fall upon his son’s neck, so that amid such great agitations of mind—which Zeno calls *casus* (“circumstances” or “events”)—his faith and piety toward God might be more clearly manifest. He could indeed have proved enough from Abraham’s having led his son up the mountain without hesitation, and offered his only son readily; but he wished the trials of testing to be extended, and permitted the sword to be drawn and the blow poised, so that, at the last extremity, when the father’s constancy had been tested, he himself might intervene.

**Same place.** “But you of him.” Read: *voice*.

Page 177. “In that sacrifice God alone grieved,” etc. This is said *katachrēstikōs*, by an improper or extended use of language: grief is attributed to God; and with still greater licence, if Zeno seemed to have intended it so, loss is ascribed to God. But he spoke *tō idiōtismō*, in ordinary popular language. Those grieve who lose something; hence he says that God grieved because, when the present human victim had been released, he had, if one may say so, to substitute another victim, a ram from his own possession, in order that the sacred rite might be completed.

## In Treatise XI, Book II, On Abraham II

Page 178. “For commanded virginity is not provoked. But neither,” etc. In this exceedingly difficult passage I would not venture to pronounce freely. In my judgment, therefore, either the work is *akephalon* (“headless,” lacking its beginning), or an unnoticed gap lies concealed, or sections torn from elsewhere have been transferred to a less suitable place. I leave their disentangling to more fortunate minds.

**Same place.** “In the flower of a bygone age and of generative genital power she is consumed,” etc. What if one reads *fluore*, “by wasting away” or “decline”? Thus, in Vergil, *Aeneid* II.169:

> From that time onward they began to waste away and slip backward, etc.

Certainly it is not credible that he intended to treat barren old age and dried-up genitals as a prerogative of those in bloom.

Page 179. “And from the innermost courses of life,” etc. [Col. 0560C] This passage is as corrupt as it is elegant and richly expressive, and can scarcely be healed without the guidance of better manuscripts. The received reading is here both incomplete and senseless. I would read, nearer to the author’s meaning: “and in the last stages of life a son opened Sarah’s womb, to which reverent old age had already accorded the dignity of grandmother.”

**Same place.** “Under this birth, therefore, dearest brethren, of hope,” etc. In this clause I point out the wound, but cannot supply the remedy; let better Aesculapii provide it. What if one reads *sperata*, “hoped-for”?

**Same place.** “An immaculate victim,” etc.: without stain and fault.

**Same place.** “Nor an unready victim,” etc.: ready, not resisting.

**Same place.** “The duties of a wife,” etc. Does he mean the wifely functions which spouses render in producing children—functions interrupted in Sarah by age? But then the reading should have been not “she did not know,” but “she had omitted.” Or should one read “womanly functions,” such as menstrual flow, required [Col. 0560D] for the formation and nourishment of the foetus? I prefer this; for to deprive Sarah of “wifely functions,” which consist in the mutual sharing of affection, counsel, and duties, and not merely in intercourse and sexual union, is to inflict a manifest injury upon her. Certainly, in the sacred books, Genesis 18:11 reads: “And womanly functions had ceased to come to Sarah,” etc.

**Same place.** “A truly wondrous offspring of the divine ordering, dearest brethren, formed and to be hoped for in ages yet to come; completed age is recalled to its beginning.” I read and punctuate: “A truly wondrous offspring of divine ordering is formed, dearest brethren, and one to be hoped for in ages yet to come: completed age is recalled to its beginning,” etc. For in Isaac there is a type of Christ, through whose birth the human race was to be redeemed in later ages. Clement of Alexandria, *Stromata* II, p. 367:

> “He allegorically chose Isaac for himself as a consecrated sacrificial victim, to be for us a type of the saving dispensation.”

“Isaac, as a consecrated victim, [Col. 0561A] he chose for himself allegorically, as a type of the saving dispensation”; and this is what Zeno intended.

Page 180. “Completed age is recalled to its beginning,” etc. End and beginning, old age and youth, are set in contrast. Here the beginning is youth; “completed age” is old age.

**Same place.** “Nothing had settled in the substance of the body,” etc. That is, no bodily moisture had settled in the body. An abundance of moisture makes the body fuller and more corpulent; thinness makes it leaner and emaciated. Tertullian, *On the Chameleon*: “Indeed, the body has no moisture, as is very evident in the stronger creatures; for the chameleon is so emaciated and devoid of juice that it is said to live on air.” *Substance* is that by which each thing is what it is. Suidas:

> “*Ousia* [substance]: philosophical usage knows that the name *ousia* is derived from the verb ‘to be,’ calling the thing that actually is ‘substance.’”

That is, it must be the body itself. Isidore, *Origins*: “A body subsists, and therefore it is substance.”

Lucretius, Book I, sang:

> “For nothing can touch or be touched unless it is a body.”

Spiritual substances [Col. 0561B], just as they do not possess body, are likewise not properly to be denied a body by this expression. The term *substantia* came late into Latin, and even then only with difficulty; yet by Zeno’s age it had already gained currency. Thus, when he wrote, “nothing had settled in the substance of the body,” it is as if he had said, “nothing had settled in the body of the body.” Martial, Book VII, *Spectacles*:

> “And nowhere in all that body was there body.”

We call persons of this kind shadows and pumice-stones, or as dry as pumice-stones, as in Plautus’ *Aulularia*, Act II, scene iv, line 18.

**Same place.** “The angel bestowed the name Isaac, that he might establish joy,” etc. In the sacred books it is not said that the name was bestowed by an angel, but by the father. Philo the Jew, Clement of Alexandria, and others interpret the name as “laughter,” because Sarah smiled when God said that she would bear a child beyond hope of conception, since age had decreed otherwise. Josephus, chapter 23, *On Antiquities*.

**Same place.** “Nourished by accelerated upbringing,” etc. Quintilian uses *educationem natura praeveniente* in the same sense in the preface to Book VI: “accelerated maturity hastens more quickly to perish.” This is what Philo had said in his book *On Abraham*, p. 377:

> “Already he displayed the virtues of a more perfect age,” etc.

Upbringing (*educatio*, *paideia*) is not merely the method of instruction itself, but the completion of education, *teleiōsis*. Cassiodorus, *Variae*, Book IX, letter 23: “He reared children equal in balanced character and truly brothers in their shared morals; their infancy, nurtured in worthy arts, and their youth, too, he exercised in arms—forming their minds by letters, their limbs by gymnasia; and whatever divine favour granted in that man, you may see transmitted to his descendants in entire perfection.”

**Same place.** “As the Apostle says, born contrary to hope,” etc. Romans 4:18: “Who beyond hope believed in hope” (*hos par’ elpida ep’ elpidi episteusen*): contrary to hope insofar as nature was concerned, but in hope because he believed God’s promise.

Page 181. “When he looked for the victim, in whose place he had been chosen,” etc.: he who anxiously made himself the substitute for the victim, as though it said: while he sought the victim, he sought himself. [Col. 0561D]

**Same place.** “Therefore a modest birth is truly referred to the person of Christ,” etc. I had not doubted that the reading should be “a venerable birth”; for it was not fitting that one should be ashamed or abashed where there was no disgrace in conception and birth—indeed, where the hope of redemption was fulfilled. Yet Valesius approves the received reading from this very passage in his notes on Ammianus, Book XIV, chapter 6; and compare Book XXI, chapter 16: “unlike that Marcus, a modest prince”; and Book XXX, chapter 8, on Artaxerxes: “His moderation of character made him so tolerable and modest.” I therefore leave the choice to the reader.

**Same place.** “But the more secret chamber of the virgin womb,” etc.: a womb untouched by a man. For although Isaac is a type of Christ, the difference between their conceptions is very great: Isaac proceeded naturally; Christ, supernaturally and divinely.

**Same place.** “But the more secret chamber of the virgin womb, formed by the art of the divine Word, bore within itself the womb of a decaying body,” etc. This passage too belongs among those which call for the assistance of manuscripts and the care of a more discerning mind. It is certain that the point is to show that, by God’s will—not from blood, nor from the will of flesh or man, but by the Word rather than seed, as our author says elsewhere—the Son, coeternal with the Father and of immortal and incorruptible nature, descended into the womb of an earthly woman subject to human decay, in order to assume flesh from her, becoming God and man together for human salvation: possessing flesh without seed from a human being, and spirit with seed from God, as Tertullian says in *On the Flesh of Christ*, chapter 18.

But the sentence is defective. For “formed by the art of the divine Word” cannot properly be referred to the virginal chamber, which was not formed in a special manner but specially sanctified; nor can one discover what “the womb of a decaying body” bore within itself unless something is supplied. But what? Beware of understanding the decaying body to be Christ’s; for his body was subject neither to decay nor to corruption, as Psalm 15:10 says: “Nor wilt thou give thy Holy One to see corruption.” Perhaps something is missing and the sentence is incomplete; but it would be useless to guess without manuscripts. What if one reads, “the body of the divine Word, formed by art”? That is, Christ’s body. It may perhaps be tolerated; but I am not yet satisfied.

Page 182. “The most certain Lord, not begotten from seed,” etc. That *certissimum* (“most certain”) seems to me most suspect.

**Same place.** “But because eternity does not know how to die,” etc. I restore this entire passage by conjecture: “But because eternity does not know how to die, nor did the Lord remain among the Jews after the tomb”—with *does not know how to die* repeated *apo koinou*—“there remained only the reproach of their condemned will, because they were unwilling to acknowledge the Lord, when it would have been wicked even to worship him too late.”

He concludes most elegantly: God, as immortal, could not suffer death; as man united to God, after voluntary death he could not remain dead long. The Jews were therefore guilty because they vainly desired wholly to remove him whom they denied to be Christ and whom, from his deeds, they ought to have worshipped. I do not see what “they believed that *ta* and only thought were punished” means, nor what relevance it has; therefore I reject those words as perhaps badly inserted by someone. The gloss “only the reproach of condemned will” is inept.

**Same place.** “By the author, therefore,” etc.: by Judas, whom Acts 1:16 calls “the guide of those who seized Jesus” (*hodēgon tois syllabousin Iēsoun*).

## In Treatise XII, Book II, On Abraham III

Page 184. “This man did not learn righteousness, but begot it,” etc. He was not taught by another, but himself followed the order of nature. Tertullian, *Against the Jews*, chapter 2: “Whence was Abraham reckoned a friend of God, if not from the equity and justice of the natural law?” He “begot righteousness” because he believed God; for this reason he received the sign of circumcision, “a seal of the righteousness of faith which he had in uncircumcision,” that he might be father of all who believe through uncircumcision, so that righteousness might be reckoned to them; and father of circumcision, [Col. 0562D] not only of those who are of the circumcision, but also of those who follow the footsteps of the faith which our father Abraham had in uncircumcision, as Saint Paul teaches in Romans 4.

**Same place.** “The access of cities had not corrupted him, whose manner of life was law,” etc. More fully in the manuscript: “the access of cities had not corrupted him; he did not have a law, whose manner of life was law,” etc.

Page 184. “Refresh yourselves,” he says, “under this great tree,” etc. For in ancient times people dwelt beneath trees. The *Etymologicum* and Suidas, under *dendryazein* (“to dwell among trees”), state that, with some artifice added to their covering, they kept off rain and the injuries of the weather, especially under oaks, whose fruit also nourished them. Juvenal, *Satires* VI:

> “While her husband belched acorns.”

And again:

> “When the mountain wife spread her woodland bed  
> With leaves.”

And Abraham’s tree was specifically an oak. Genesis 18: “By the oak of Mamre.”

[Col. 0563A] **Same place.** “An occasion was found in which Abraham’s faith might wage a stronger warfare through temptation.” The statement found in the *Lesser Genesis* is apocryphal: Mastipha, chief of the demons, addresses God in these words: “If Abraham loves you, let him sacrifice his son” (*Ei agapa se Abraam, thyetō ton huion autou*). It is borrowed from Job 1:9 and following.

**Same place.** “Thus, devoted, with a drawn expression, he leads the boy to the altar; he checks the sword halfway; the breast of faith was in warfare,” etc. In place of “with a drawn expression,” which I think is worthless here, I would restore “with a dry expression,” that is, free of tears. For tears appear upon the face and, settling there, run down from it. Vergil, *Aeneid* I.469, of Aeneas:

> “Sighing deeply, he moistens his face with a copious stream.”

Silius Italicus, Book II, likewise calls faces wet with sweat, not in an unusual manner of speaking. Vergil again, *Aeneid* IX.251:

> “And he drenched his face and cheeks with tears.”

And Seneca, *Hercules*, line 1228:

> “This face, hardened by misfortunes,  
> Knows not how to weep.”

“One may also read ‘with an untroubled expression.’”

**Same place.** “He leads the boy to the altar; he checks the sword halfway; the breast of faith was in warfare,” etc. If Abraham’s mind is to be shown undisturbed, “he checks the sword” does not fit, since it indicates the action of one resisting rather than willing; moreover, I cannot see what “a halfway sword” means. In order for the sense to stand, I should think the whole passage ought to read: “Thus, devoted, with a dry expression, he leads the boy to the altar; he seizes the sword, for the breast of faith was in warfare. His face did not grow pale; his hand did not tremble. The boy asks where the victim is, which soon, lest tender age be struck, he found—so that the father might not be able to strike.”

The alteration is very slight. Following the Vulgate, in place of *medium* (“halfway”), which cannot suit Abraham’s sword, I restore *namque* (“for”), a connective particle supporting the following clause, which otherwise gapes. It follows: “which soon, so that he might not strike.” The Verona editor, uncertain of this reading, placed *quem* (“whom”) in the margin, whether as a variant or an emendation, though he showed no correlative for that relative pronoun. “So that he might strike” presupposes a quality of action, yet none is stated; I therefore judged that adverb should be deleted. The text reads, “tender age showed”; but it is far from the truth that Isaac showed the victim, since, bound and blindfolded, he could not point to what was behind both himself and his father. Rather, the father himself found it. Genesis 22:13: “Abraham raised his eyes and saw behind him a ram caught by its horns among the thorns; taking it, he offered it as a burnt offering in place of his son.” Therefore I restore *offendit* (“found”): that victim, namely, lest tender age—that is, Isaac—should be struck, the father found, so that he might sacrifice, and not the father—that is, without parricide.

## In Treatise XIII, Book II, On Jacob’s Dream

Page 180. “Testifying,” etc. He himself seems to interpret it as meaning “bearing the two testaments”; but “bearing” seems superfluous and inserted contrary to reason. Simpler would be: “testifying to the two ranks,” that is, to the two testaments—that is, bearing witness and by his testimony approving both testaments.

**Same place.** “Isaiah saw this in the form of tongs, by which one of the Seraphim from God’s altar was to fuse his unclean lips,” etc. The passage is Isaiah 6 according to the edition of the Septuagint, which he always follows. Yet in it there is nothing about fusing; it reads only, “he touched my mouth” (*hēpsato tou stomatos mou*), as also in the Vulgate. But the author delights in playing upon the word which he used in the phrase “they are known to have been fused into one people by confession of Christ’s name,” so that he could conclude: fusion signifies both purity and unity.

Page 189. “Which are therefore compared to the material of wood, whether because in their use the continual and entire will of the testator remains,” etc. Tryphoninus, in the title *On Possession of Goods Contrary to a Will*, chapter 19: “Possession of goods was granted to children contrary to the wood,” that is, contrary to a testament written on wooden tablets. Isidore, Book IV, chapter 24: “The tablets of a testament are so called,” etc., “because before paper and parchment were used, not only testaments but also communications by letter were written upon smoothed tablets.” Whoever desires fuller information should consult Cujas, *Observations*, Book II, chapter 14.

**Same place.** “He announced the Son of God.” Correct from the manuscript: “they announced.”

**Same place.** “Because neither do the fugitives descend,” etc. Better in the manuscript: “Because neither do the fugitives ascend, who after sin are known never to have been received into heaven; nor do those of light descend, because they never remained on earth but always in heaven.”

**Same place.** “Amen, amen, I say to you,” etc. The manuscript has only one *Amen*.
