Page 191. “All these things therefore combined,” etc. The gloss explains *combinare* by *zeugnyein*, “to join, couple,” properly of two things; and this is what our author intended by the very word *combinata*, as though he said that the two testaments, joined together, bring forth one fruit.

[Col. 0564B] **Same place.** “Conversion, hearing, understanding,” etc. The rungs of this ladder to heaven deserve to be known and preserved, especially by those whom the dew of heavenly teaching has now nourished; for these are the summits of virtues, and in them the whole teaching of Christ is contained. Conversion, hearing, and understanding belong especially to neophytes, or rather to those tending toward faith. Conversion is an inclination away from another sect toward the Christian faith. Cyprian, speaking of himself to Donatus: “How, I used to say, is so great a conversion possible, that what has been hardened either by the innate condition of natural material or by long-established habit through the antiquity of age should suddenly and swiftly be put off?” Hearing leads to the reception of mysteries. Saint Paul, Romans 10:17: “Faith comes from hearing, and hearing through the word of Christ.” Cyril of Jerusalem, in his preface: “Let your feet hasten to hear the catechetical instructions” (*hoi podes sou eis tas katēchēseis speudetōsan*). Finally, understanding is a right will adapting itself to Christian wisdom. “Understanding,” says Synesius in *Dio*, “is a name coupled with intelligible things”; so that, if the end is to behold heaven, it is not enough not to bend toward the ground, but after the intermediate station of sight one must turn to things above.

**Same place.** “Perseverance is completion,” etc. This refers to Christ’s saying in Matthew 24:13: “But whoever endures to the end, that person shall be saved” (*Ho de hypomeinas eis telos, houtos sōthēsetai*). It is not enough to persevere; one must also attain completion (*teleiein*).

## In Treatise XIV, Book II, On Judah

Page 193. “Having been comforted,” etc.: after the customary rites of mourning. For mourning ceased at the prescribed time, and all joyful acts and customary duties were performed; and nature also brings about what Seneca says in Letter 63: even grief that is guarded slips away, and the sharper it is, the sooner it ceases.

**Same place.** “She put on summer clothing,” etc. Both the Greek and Latin versions have *theristron*, which Hesychius interprets as “a fine woven cloth, a summer garment” (*lepton hyphasma, therinon himation*): a thin textile or veil, summer dress. Saint Jerome, in the *Hebrew Traditions*, says that it is a kind of Arabian garment with which women of that province are veiled.

**Same place.** “By veiling her face, she displayed the integrity of modesty,” etc. Tertullian, *On the Veiling of Virgins*, chapter 3: “The matter was left to choice, so that each woman might wish either to be covered or to prostitute herself.” Nonnus of Panopolis, *Dionysiaca* XLII.351, calls women who veil their faces *aidomenai*, “modest women.” For, as Tertullian repeats in the same work, chapter 14, “the desire not to hide oneself is not modest,” although the very appearance of concealment may otherwise sharpen desire more strongly; for those devotees of Venus:

> “The more they gaze upon women,  
> The more they desire a covered face.”

Nonnus, same passage.

**Same place.** “Marked by conception, which true prostitutes hate.” Aristaenetus, Book I, letter 19:

> “It was not expedient that she should become pregnant, lest childbearing make her less valued by her lovers, as the flower of her prime was prematurely lost in the labours of childbirth.”

Procopius, *Secret History*, folio 76, on Theodora while still an actress:

> “It happened that she conceived by one of her lovers; discovering the misfortune late and out of season, she tried everything, as she was accustomed, to procure an abortion.”

**Same place.** “According to the agreement,” etc. Festus says that *condictum* is what has been stated jointly. Papias more simply: *condicere*, “to arrange, announce, decree”; and in our author’s sense, “according to decrees and agreements,” or “according to what had been settled.” Plautus, *Curculio*, scene I, verse 5:

> “Whether it is midnight or early evening,  
> If an appointed day of truce with an enemy intervenes, still one must go.”

[Col. 0565B] **Same place.** “A pregnant widow, without the labour of an accuser,” etc. For her pregnant and swollen belly itself indicated that she was guilty of intercourse. Aristotle, *Rhetoric* I.15, puts the matter thus:

> “There would be no need of witnesses if it were sufficient to perceive the matter from the arguments.”

For what is manifest is manifest to everyone and admits no proof. Quintilian, Book V, chapter 12: “To argue in matters that are obvious is as foolish as to bring mortal light to the brightest sun.”

Page 194. “Judah, as can be understood from the part of the Prophets and the part of the Patriarchs, was a type of the fathers who, because of God’s justice, counted all human beings as sons,” etc. The patriarchs were Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob; Clement of Alexandria, *Stromata* I, p. 284, recognizes these three alone as forefathers. Judah was not a patriarch but next in rank to the patriarchs and their offspring; he possessed in himself the knowledge handed down from his ancestors concerning the divine promises by which their descendants would become a great nation. Neither was he a prophet, although he may be believed to have perceived that, by God’s justice, all human beings and all nations would be blessed in Abraham and his seed, and that a New Testament would come by which the Mosaic covenant would be abolished through faith in Christ. Jeremiah finally uttered that prophecy in chapter 31.

This is what the author means when he says that Judah was a type partly of the Prophets and partly of the Patriarchs: namely, insofar as he recognized that Abraham’s seed, and his own, was to be reckoned not only among the Jewish people but among the other nations through faith; Genesis 18:18; 22:18; and 26:4. Thus he proceeds to make an ingenious and subtle argument concerning Er, Onan, and Shelah as representing the Gentile, Jewish, and Christian peoples. On the justice of God, see the notes on Treatise 3, Book I.

**Same place.** “Therefore Er, the firstborn son, is the people, that is, the demigods.” The demigods are said to have existed more than 1,300 years before Judah. Therefore they could not be compared to Judah’s firstborn [Col. 0565D] son, since they were before him. But, having adopted his figure, he accommodates the narrative to it, preserving the elegance of expression rather than historical accuracy. In the manuscript: “Therefore Er, the firstborn son—the firstborn is the people—that is, the demigods”; and I approve this.

Page 195. “But Shelah, the younger third brother of those mentioned, coming from the Gentiles,” etc. The manuscript reading is preferable: “coming from the Gentiles.”

Page 196. “They go before you in the Kingdom of God.” More elegantly in the manuscript: “into the kingdom.”

**Same place.** “When he came together with her, it signifies the sacrament of holy communion.” Manuscript: “When he came together in her, he signified the sacrament of the holy communion of believers.”

Page 188. *Amen.* It is absent in the manuscript.

## In Treatise XV, Book II, On Job

Page 199. “That it may be part of happiness to know what they have done,” etc. Theophylact Simocatta called history “a delight to hearing and a school for the soul” (*akoē hēdysma, tē de psychē paideutērion*). Agathias gives the reason in the preface to his *History*: history “gently and quietly lodges virtues in souls” (*lanthanei tais psychais hērema tas aretas enoikizousa*). Examples instruct us; imitation guides us more than nature or precepts.

**Same place.** “Into a confused mass, as walls and roofs collapsed,” etc. *In ruta, caesa*: “demolished things, cut-down things.” Things *ruta*, according to Nonius, are things torn down; things *caesa*, according to Palladius, Book I, chapter 9, are things crushed. Festus includes both meanings: *ruta caesa* are things which a seller of property has cut down and collected by demolition for his own use. This I judge the truer explanation, though Ulpian, in Book XVII, section 6, *On Actions Arising from Purchases*, says that *ruta* are things dug out, such as sand, clay, and the like, while *caesa* are felled trees and charcoal. But it is customary for different matters to be gathered under one term as time goes on.

Page 200. “He buries before he slaughters, and having devised such a destruction of impiety,” etc. With a very slight change I read: “He slaughters. Having devised such,” etc. Thus the words sound more pleasantly to the ear.

**Same place.** “With populous ulcers,” etc.: spreading [Col. 0566B] and creeping so extensively that the wound became, in part, the whole body.

**Same place.** “He was not distinguished by populous ulcers, but his whole body became one wound,” etc. The correction of the Verona editor does not please me; he wished to read, “he was not distinguished, but his whole body became one wound.” I would read: “It was not distinct”—understanding “the wound”—“but his whole body became one wound.”

## In Treatise XVII, Book II, On the Prophet Jonah

Page 205. “Secrets are not to be investigated with curiosity,” etc. “For they are most foolish who prejudge divine things from human ones,” says Tertullian, Book II *Against Marcion*, chapter 6. Agathias, Book II, folio 67, Regius edition, says that to investigate heavenly things is “a matter so blessed, inaccessible, surpassing human capacities, and admirable for the very reason that it is unknown” (*pragma houtō makariotēn te kai anephikton kai meizon ē kat’ anthrōpous kai monō tō agnoeisthai thaumazomenon*).

Page 206. “That he can explain the corporeal emptiness of this air, as some think,” etc. There is matter in air, and therefore it has body. In Sextus Empiricus, *Against the Mathematicians* VIII.367, philosophers who held that the elements were earth, water, air, and fire are said to have regarded the elements as corporeal. Air certainly has body, since it is capable of rarity and density. But because it cannot be seen or touched on account of its rarity, and because, as Philo says in *On Dreams*, it “yields to and surrounds bodies” (*eikei te kai antiperistamenos tois sōmasi*), it has the appearance of emptiness—so that, in the same way, wherever dense bodies are absent, the air is called empty. Martial, *Spectacles*, epigram 11:

> “Let the hunter seize his prey in the empty air.”

But Pliny, Book II, chapter 38, calls it not wholly empty but like emptiness, for the reasons already mentioned. Nor can that which is the instrument of life, respiration, sight, hearing, and the other senses be empty; without its use, even for a brief time, a human being must perish, as Hippocrates teaches in his book *On Winds*.

[Col. 0566D] **Same place.** “Who would presume to know whether the earth is borne by water, or water held in the earth’s bosom?” The Stoics held that earth and sea form one globe and have a common centre. Diogenes Laertius, in the account of Zeno, p. 201:

> “The earth lies in the middle, occupying the position of a centre; after it is spherical water, having the same centre as the earth.”

Strabo, Book II, p. 112:

> “Let the earth, together with the sea, be assumed to be spherical, having one and the same surface in its seas.”

Therefore hold this as certain: the earth together with the sea is a globe, and it has the same surface with the seas. Philo the Jew, *On the Creation of the World*, says that earth and water are held together “as though by a bond” (*hōs an hypo desmou*), so that water not only surrounds the earth but penetrates and underlies it. Pliny, Book II, chapter 65, states most elegantly:

> “Nature, the artificer, must be believed to have so formed them [Col. 0567A] that, since dry and arid earth could not exist by itself and without moisture, and water, in turn, could not stand unless supported by earth, they are joined in mutual embrace: the earth opening its recesses, while the water permeates it throughout, within, without, and above, running through veins and bonds.”

Since this sufficiently establishes the unity of the terrestrial and aqueous globe, it is more probable that water is contained in the bosom of earth, as Pliny thinks—and, according to Casaubon’s notes on Strabo, pp. 5–6, Ptolemy thought—than that the earth is like an island surrounded by sea, as Cicero held in *On the Republic*, cited by Macrobius, *Commentary* II.5, or that “the earth is in water,” as the Stoics held in the passage from Laertius cited above. For water is wandering and fluid, whereas earth is solid and stable; it is more consistent with nature that the former be held by the latter than conversely. Aristotle too seems to have indicated this when he says in *Meteorology* II.2:

> “Flow tends toward what is most hollow, and the sea occupies such a place in the earth.”

Let it be permitted, however, to reason briefly on this matter. At the world’s birth, the earth was surrounded and oppressed by waters; Genesis 1:9–10. God willed water to be separated from earth, and it was so: at his command the earth emerged, which Scripture calls dry land. The words of Psalm 32:7—“Gathering the waters of the sea as in a skin-bag”—indicate that in the earth he hollowed out very deep channels in which the seas might be placed. Therefore the waters are in the earth as in a skin-bag, or, if you prefer, in a vessel.

The Conimbricenses also hold that channels and cavities were made in the earth as receptacles for water: *Physics* IV.5, question 3, article 2; and *On the Heavens* II.14, question 3, article 2. They cite also John Damascene, Allatius in the notes to Eustathius, folio 6 and folio 46, and Gerard John Vossius, *On Idolatry* II.67. Nor is there lacking an argument: if water were not supported by earth, the sea could have no depth; but nautical experience testifies that it does have depths, within its own limits and quantities—excepting places around the Flemish islands and some others in the Pacific Ocean. Therefore the sea clings to the earth and is supported by it. Natural reason, I hope, will settle the question of these matters.

[Col. 0567C] **Same place.** “Who [would know] airy breaths, who the shapes of winds,” etc. I think he understands *spiritus* as “breeze” or a gentle breath, when it descends in a mild and tranquil movement, as in Catullus’ wedding song:

> “As a flower … which breezes caress.”

And Ovid, *Metamorphoses* I.107:

> “And the gentle Zephyrs, with warming breezes, caressed [the world].”

Understand such a breeze in the Greek epigram, *Anthology* VII.117:

> “Would that I were a wind, and that you, stepping forth at dawn,  
> Might bare your breast and receive me as I blow.”

But he calls them winds when they blow more violently and when a more plentiful matter supplies greater and more lasting force. Achilles Tatius, on Aratus, p. 158:

> “Others wish to distinguish wind from breeze: wind, they say, is flowing air, whereas a breeze is an exhalation from the earth.”

You may see this distinction in the author of *On the World*. I think Aristotle, *Meteorology* II.4, distinguishes by the same reasoning between breath, which he calls *pneuma*, and wind, which he calls *anemos*. Yet, as we have seen, the terms are confused.

Page 207. “Who [would know] the increases of rivers amid the marine tides,” etc. Up to now, so far as I remember, I have neither seen nor read in books anything on rivers increased or diminished by the rising or recession of the sea. There is some discussion of one spring at Gades and another at Bordeaux, whose causes we must admit are unknown to us—unless we say, with Socrates in the *Phaedo*, that there are many cavities beneath the earth through which waters meet and break into one another, and that they enter these springs more readily than others. Yet the difficulty is not removed: why should they do so in these rather than in all?

Page 208. “Beating against the foaming mouths of resistant shores with the grey billows of an anxious whirlpool of precipitous mountains,” etc. No one will fail to see that these words are corrupt. Until knowledge of a better text is supplied, I would read: “The provoked sea roars; it stirs up whirlpools with the grey billows of precipitous mountains and the foam of resisting shores,” etc. For *gurges* means “wave.” Vergil, *Aeneid* III.564:

> “We are lifted toward heaven on the curved wave.”

Thus “precipitous mountains” are the waves themselves, as though broken off from a greater mountain and tossed by the winds. Vergil again, *Aeneid* I.109:

> “A steep mountain of water follows in a mass.”

They seemed like portions of mountains, grey with whitening foam. Apollonius Rhodius, *Argonautica* II.571:

> “High upon the shore  
> The white froth of the roaring wave spread forth.”

That is, “upon the highest shore the white down of the broken wave foams.” Sea-foam itself is already corrupt in the text. Moreover, Apollonius himself, in the same Book II, line 583, calls these swollen tides and waves of the sea “equals of a sheer cliff” (*apotmētēi skopiēi ison*). Achilles Tatius, *Eros* II: “Of the waves, some resembled mountains, others chasms” (*eōike de tōn kymatōn, ta men oresin, ta de chasmasin*).

**Same place.** “That good weather alone sought,” etc. Apuleius speaks similarly in Book I of *The Golden Ass*: “But those were good and faithful doors.” Shortly afterward: “And I remembered that good Meroe had spared my throat not from pity, but had reserved me for torture out of cruelty.” “That good weather” is ironic: they awaited what they desired, not what suited Zeno’s genius; it sought what we have retained as the better reading.

**Same place.** “From wooden [vessel] to life-giving ship,” etc. He calls the whale a “life-giving ship,” which shortly afterward he calls a beastly gulf.

## In Treatise XIX, Book II, On the Passage of Genesis, etc.

Page 217. “Nothing is so necessary and fitting for a person who fears God as to know himself,” etc. The well-known saying is “Know thyself” (*gnōthi seauton*), which some take as an exhortation to moderation and others to confidence. Our author exhorts humanity, in order to show how great a thing a human being is, to recognize itself from the image of God which it bears—an image which a person has been made worthy to bear insofar as he has not damaged it by his actions, or, more damnably, erased it. The purpose is that he may despise the enticements of the world and restore to his Creator his own image: pure, unimpaired, and worthy of the heavenly dwelling.

Pag. 218. The soul has such power that, although it is confined within the enclosure of its dwelling, nevertheless at every moment it illumines whatever it wills, etc. Cicero, *Cato the Elder* [Col. 0568D], 195: “I believe that the immortal gods have scattered souls among human bodies, so that there might be persons to watch over the earth and, contemplating the order of heavenly things, imitate it in their manner and steadfastness of life.” Philo the Jew expresses this more elegantly and plainly, *On the Creation of the World*, 15:

> “Cutting open all the broad highways, it travels through land and sea, investigating the things that belong to each nature; and again, lifted up as though winged, having contemplated the air and its affections, it is borne higher toward the upper ether,” etc.

It opens for itself every route through land and sea, to investigate the nature of each. Again, soaring aloft and contemplating the air and its conditions, it is carried further upward to the highest ether, and so forth. If you compare this with Maximus of Tyre at the end of his sixth dissertation, you will find similar thoughts expressed with no less elegance.

Likewise. Therefore we ought not to understand this fleshly dwelling to be the image of God, but the spiritual image of the heavenly man, which the Lord [forms] in those who believe in him, etc. This was also Origen’s view [Col. 0569A]: he held that God’s image is represented in us not by bodily shape nor by disposition of mind, but by actions. He draws this from the Apostle: first, 1 Corinthians 15:49, where he says, “Just as we have borne the image of the earthly man, so let us also bear the image of the heavenly man”; then Colossians 3:10, where, giving precepts for right living, he exhorts us to become “according to the image of him who created [us].” You will find Origen’s opinion, overlooked by Huet, among Theodoret’s *Questions on Genesis*, Question 20. And this is what Zeno says here: “the spiritual [image] of the heavenly man,” therefore not that of the earthly man. He develops this more explicitly at the end of Sermon IV on Genesis (now Tract XX, Book II), adding: “Paul has plainly disclosed the reason, saying: ‘Just as we have borne the image of him who is from the clay, let us bear the image of him who is from heaven.’” For God, as Theodoret says in his commentary on Colossians 3:10 [Col. 0569B], and Augustine somewhere also, created man in purity and therefore in his own likeness; but through sin man crushed the image. That he might be able to renew it, Christ came, forgiving sins by grace.

Interpretation of this mystery has varied. For our author elsewhere seems to refer it to the soul—in this very sermon, and in IV, now XX—and elsewhere, in Sermon III, now Tract V, Book II, to that which God was to assume in man, when he says: “Lest the Son, who was to put on man, should seem to suffer any injury.” Tertullian held this view as well. Theodoret differs. But we are acting as philologists, not theologians.

## In Tract XX, Book II, on the Same Passage of Genesis

Pag. 219. So changeable that the same [appearance] cannot be found in two persons throughout the whole world, etc. He imitated Pliny, Book VII, chapter 1, in which the supreme power of nature shines forth—or rather the power of the supreme God—who supplies diverse forms in countless persons, and infinite varieties; something which, as Pliny says, art cannot accomplish in a few cases by striving after it. But, for greater clarity, the passage should be punctuated thus: “Through sadness; now made ugly by emaciation, now by excessive fatness: so changeable,” etc.

## In Tract XXI, Book II, on Psalm 100

Pag. 220. He asks elegantly, devoutly, and for the benefit of the people entrusted to him, how mercy and judgment can coexist in God, since the one belongs to one who is indulgent and gracious, the other to one exasperated and provoked by human wrongs. To resolve this, he distinguishes three kinds of people: one, the impious, concerning whom he says that judgment has already been executed; another, the truly pious, in whom judgment has no place; and a third, those who are pious only in name but otherwise dishonor God. He concludes that judgment and mercy can have a place only in these latter.

Likewise. “When they do not understand words as light,” etc. If you read “not for words,” the sense will be clearer and more fitting.

Pag. 223. “Yet from the ministries of demons,” etc. In the manuscript: “from the mysteries.”

[Col. 0569D] Likewise. “For the fear of God restrains many in the Church.” There is fear of God, and there is fear of ecclesiastical punishments. The fear of God is the sole discipline of Christianity; it is not distinct from love. For to have true understanding is to fear God: Psalm 110:9. Our author, below, on Psalm 127—now in the Appendix, where we deny that it belongs to Hilary—says: “For us, all fear of the Lord is in love, not in dread; and this is the proper duty of our love toward him: to obey his admonitions, submit to his ordinances, and trust in his promises.” Clement of Alexandria, *Stromata*, Book II, derives love from fear, because fear is the beginning of love: by increasing, it becomes faith, and then love. Sophocles, *Ajax*, 1104:

> “For whoever possesses fear, and shame along with it,  
> Know that such a person can be kept safe.”

I do not know, therefore, why he wishes to diminish the standing of one who is restrained in the Church by fear of God. But there was also fear of ecclesiastical punishments, for sinners were subject to inquiry and formal denunciation. See Canons 61 and 71 of Basil the Great in the *Epitome of Canons* of Harmenopulus, Book V, title III; perhaps this is what Zeno meant.

Likewise. “One class [is] that of the righteous, who, as has been said, will not merely not be judged.” Supply from the manuscript: “They will not be judged, but will themselves judge this world, as the Apostle says,” etc.

Pag. 224. “In a false evil deed.” In the manuscript, distinguish: “in falsehood, in evil-doing.”

Likewise. “But the other, whom poisons are wearing down in adultery,” etc. Distinguish: “But the other, whom poisons are wearing down, in adultery, in homicide,” etc.

Likewise. “Thus for the righteous there will be a crown; for sinners, if excused or corrected, pardon.” Theodoret, on Isaiah 64:5: “God’s mercy is not devoid of judgment, nor is judgment devoid of mercy; therefore he joined the bestowal of mercy to those who wait and do righteousness.”

## In Tract XXII, Book II, on Isaiah 1

Pag. 225. “That the Prophet had called heaven and earth to witness, as though he were complaining about some matter,” etc. A question mark is absent from the manuscript, and it seems to have no place here. “Had called to witness” means “had summoned as witnesses.” Heaven and earth, however, are summoned as witnesses not against themselves but against ungrateful children and the faithlessness of the Jews. Therefore this passage seems to need correction: “that the prophet had called heaven and earth to witness.” I proceed to emend it according to my judgment: “Or when he says, ‘Hear, O heaven and earth,’ as though heaven or earth had ever failed to hear, when both heaven and earth obey God’s command: when heaven does not withhold rain, nor earth its crops.” Thus the period will be fuller and more conclusive.

[Col. 0570C] Likewise. “Or when it is said.” Manuscript: “Or when he says.”

Pag. 226. “That he made a passage through the middle of the sea,” etc. Put a comma after “the middle of the sea”; that is, he made a land passage through the midst of the sea.

Pag. 227. “Through which they escaped Pharaoh,” etc. In Philo the Jew’s work *That the Worse Is Apt to Attack the Better*, Pharaoh is “a dissipator and destroyer of good opinions.” Theodoret likewise, on 1 Corinthians 10, calls him “an image of the devil.” From these passages one can very easily interpret what Zeno means by these words.

## In Tract XXIII, Book II, on Isaiah 2

Pag. 228. “And lest he perhaps repent, he rebukes him publicly,” etc. Does he rebuke him lest he repent? (See annotation 3 on this Tract XXIII, Book II.) Nonsense: rather, “unless perhaps he repents.” From section 16 onward he shows them, in his kindness, the way of salvation. The reading should be *nisi forte poeniteat*, “unless perhaps he repents.” He adds “perhaps” with reference to the outcome, because, always hardened toward worse things, they deserved no result of the threats through repentance—threats which Isaiah, chapter 1, denounces against them in those words of God.

Likewise. “For one whose thinking is human, to be publicly disgraced is worse than to be punished,” etc. In the following sermon he explains “one whose thinking is human” as being much the same as being among the wise and honorable. In that same subsequent sermon, “to be publicly disgraced” corresponds to “to be marked by shame.” Zeno drew *nundinari* from the ancient practice of the Twelve Tables: an accuser lacking testimony would, on three market-days, complain with abuse before the defendant’s door about the defendant. This was called *vagulari*, “to cry out publicly,” and *vagulatio*, “public clamoring.” See Festus under “Portum” and “Vagulatio.”

## In Tract XXIV, Book II, on Isaiah 3

Pag. 229. “It is a vehement disturbance, brothers, when one who can very easily avenge himself complains of an injury done to him,” etc. This maxim pleased him so much that he repeats it below, in Sermon 4 [Col. 0571A]: “For it is no slight offense when the complaint comes from one who can immediately punish him.” Rather, that is a mild disturbance when one pursues with words and threats what could be carried out by punishment. Ammianus Marcellinus, Book XIX, at the end, says of Lauricius, who, when the Isaurians were in revolt and advancing no just demands, corrected most matters by threats rather than harshness: he could have acted by force and arms, but hoped to correct by words what had been done. Divine threats likewise aimed at persuading people to reform; nor does he cease to invite them in section 17: “Learn to do good; though your sins be as scarlet, I will make them white as wool.”

Likewise. “Among honorable persons it is more grievous to be marked by some disgrace than to die,” etc. That is, disgrace is worse than death. Claudian, *On the Gildonic War*, 451:

> “Is it not better to die than to endure shame in life?”

## In Tract XXV, Book II, on Isaiah 4

Pag. 230. “And here it is entitled ‘On the Jews’” in the manuscript.

Likewise. “But because among unbelievers death is thought to be a shortening of future punishment,” etc. Horace expresses their view, *Epistles*, Book I, XVI, final verse:

> “Death is the final boundary of things.”

And Seneca, *Troades*, 397:

> “After death there is nothing; death itself is nothing,  
> The furthest goal of swift course.”

But judgment remains after death, from which either glory or eternal punishment follows.

Likewise. “And almost as though it had not been done,” etc. Here it means “as though not to be done”: the perfect participle is used for the future.

Likewise. “And finally the matter was fulfilled in the Lord’s Passion,” etc. Isaiah had called heaven and earth to witness; but at midday the former lost its daylight, and the latter, shaken by an earthquake, lost its firmness. Both bore witness: the announced punishment had made the Jews guilty, when they committed the most execrable and detestable of sins in Christ’s death.

Likewise. “Heaven lost [the light] at midday.” Manuscript: “Heaven [lost it] in the midst of the day.”

[Col. 0571C] Likewise. “From this one may judge what has been reserved for them,” etc. He concludes from the preceding proposition that death does not end all punishments.

## In Tract XXVI, Book II, on Isaiah 5

Likewise. “That the Jewish people abandoned the defense of its salvation,” etc. Though warned by Isaiah’s divine threat, it did not desist from impiety, and chose willingly to remain guilty rather than strive for salvation.

Likewise. “In this, venerable brothers, it is not severity that condemns him in the eyes of all, but compassion,” etc.—as though he were saying: he deserves mercy rather than reproach. For it is human to pity one’s neighbor, whether ruined or perishing through voluntary self-destruction.

Likewise. “For one cannot deserve well of anyone whom the most patient and merciful Father has disowned,” etc. Here the sentence breaks off, and I cannot see to what these words are to be referred or what they mean. Therefore I judge that something is missing.

[Col. 0571D] Pag. 231. “He calls them sons in order to magnify the crime,” etc. He repeats these things so often that this man of great talent may seem to have suffered from a lack of arguments. But, distinguished in learning and piety, he preferred for his own reputation to decline rather than suppress in the Church the seed of his words. He did not utter these things every day, but yearly, or at fixed times of the year, or perhaps at longer intervals; thus the repetition would not have been unwelcome to his hearers, who could neither know nor remember what had been said on an earlier occasion. With this confidence, it is believable that he withheld time—which should be spent in more fruitful worship of God—from inventing new arguments and from elaborate verbal ornament, of which, had there been need, he was not lacking.

## In Tract XXVII, Book II, on Isaiah 6

Likewise. “That the Prophet, on behalf of the old vine,” etc. From the Psalm’s title he argues that what Asaph sought in the old Jewish vine was fulfilled in the time of the new Christian vine. It would be impious and utterly frivolous to despise and reject the titles of the Psalms, preserved through Ezra, themselves prophetic, and translated into Greek by the seventy elders under divine inspiration. See Theodoret’s preface to the Psalms.

Likewise. “Which was first called the Lord’s vine,” etc. Besides the authority of this Psalm, Isaiah 5:7 calls the house of Israel “the vine of the Lord of hosts”; God himself declares through Jeremiah 2:21 that he planted a fruitful vine, wholly true; and Hosea 10, at its beginning, calls Israel a luxuriant vine, in which fruit is abundant.

Likewise. “Instead of fruit it produced thorns, instead of grapes wild grapes,” etc. Isaiah 5:2: “I expected it to produce grapes, but it produced wild grapes.” In the Greek text is *akanthas*, “thorns.” Our author follows both readings. For the wild vine does not bring its fruit to maturity, but produces it only as far as flowering; Dioscorides, Book V, chapter 2. Therefore he said, “It did indeed flower, but unhappily: when the flower had been scattered, it could bear no fruit.” He added “thorns,” to which, Theodoret says, there is an allusion to the crown with which they encircled the Lord’s head.

[Col. 0572B] Pag. 232. “He planted another for himself—that is, for our people—according to his will,” etc. Isaiah, in the said chapter 5:6–7:

> “And I will abandon my vineyard; it shall not be pruned nor dug, and thorns shall come up upon it as upon uncultivated ground; and I shall command the clouds not to rain upon it. For the vineyard of the Lord Sabaoth is the house of Israel, and the man of Judah is a beloved new planting.”

The Vulgate differs. Origen, on Matthew 21:33, observes that Christ uttered threats not against the vineyard but against the tenants, understanding the vineyard to be the kingdom of God or the mysteries of God’s kingdom. Since these had been held carelessly and fraudulently by the former tenants, they were leased to more faithful and diligent cultivators, namely Christians. Zeno adheres to the words and meaning of the Psalm and Isaiah as he renders them from the Greek. Moreover, the words “that is, for our people” seem to be a gloss inserted by someone other than the author.

Likewise. “Most blessed cultivators, forgive,” etc. Horace, *Epodes* 2, called the farmer blessed; see there for the reasons. Our author, imitating him, said “most blessed.” Philostratus, in the *Heroicus*, admires the farmer’s blessedness even among vineyards: “How varied is the beauty of your estate, and how cheerfully the clusters have burst forth!”

Likewise. “The measurement, once observed, is reckoned for the shoot,” etc.—for the vine-cutting (*malleolus*); consult Columella, Book III, chapter 19, concerning its measurement.

Likewise. “The generative moisture, animated there, is nourished while the substance always remains,” etc. I read: “with the substance of the generative moisture always remaining.” For it is not the generative moisture that is animated, but the cutting is animated by the generative moisture—that is, by the substance of the earth. Lucretius, Book II:

> “When mother earth has received drops of moisture,  
> Pregnant, she bears shining crops and flourishing trees.”

Cicero, *On the Nature of the Gods*, Book II: “Earth, impregnated with seeds, brings forth everything and sends it out from herself; embracing plants, she nourishes and enlarges them, and she herself in turn is nourished by the natures above and outside her.”

Likewise. “Pure growth is set upon the platforms,” etc. Farmers usually pollard trees where this seems expedient. Nature assists the cut part by supplying new shoots; once these have grown after a year, they partly cut them off and partly leave them. Selecting each year in the same place, they make a broad bench in the tree, called a *tabulatum*, a platform; and, as it were, a spreading base from which the stronger retained branches support the vine’s new tendrils in hope of a future crop. Columella, Book V, chapter 6: “Then, when they begin to grow, the trees must be shaped with the pruning-hook and platforms established; for by this name farmers designate the projecting branches and trunks, which they either restrain more closely with the knife or allow to extend farther, so that the vines may spread more widely.” Pliny, Book XVII, chapter 23: “The platforms of elms are spread from a height of eight feet in hills and dry fields, from twelve feet in level and damp ground.” Through these benches or platforms selected shoots are arranged; he calls them “pure growth,” for *materia* means young shoots intended for future yield. Columella, Book III, chapter 10: “Very vigorous shoots are found either at the head of the vine or on the stock near the roots.” The same author, Book V, chapter 5: “The method of pruning is the same as for yoked vines; it differs only in this, that in place of longer shoots four or five buds are left.” He calls it “pure” because not every shoot is to be retained; rather, the more fruitful are to be selected with skill. In the same work, 180: “Then, when the vine’s growth requires it, the vine-dresser follows and removes the superfluous shoots, while allowing the fruitful shoots to remain.” The same, in the following chapter, 188: “The remaining procedure of pruning is this: all old shoots from which the previous year’s crop hung are cut away; the new ones, after the tendrils and secondary shoots that have arisen from them are trimmed all around, are left.” Pliny, Book XVII, chapter 22: “Whatever is taken from the growth is added to the fruit.”

Pag. 233. “It is drawn out farther by invitation,” etc.—as though, by the extension and spreading of the shoots, it were invited to more extensive fertility.

Likewise. “Its beauty scattered,” etc. For it is not simply gathered, like other fruits, in order to be preserved; rather, what is gathered for making wine is gathered in order to be trodden and crushed.

Likewise. “And it is pressed hard by two boards,” etc. For the press by itself would squeeze only a small amount. Servius, on *Georgics* II, 242, teaches that presses are beams by which grapes already trodden are pressed. Understand that in the winepress there is an upper and a lower board. The lower is the lower part of the press itself, consisting of joined and planked timbers, upon which the grapes are first trodden and squeezed out. By another board placed above, formed of loosened and separated planks so that it may be lowered and raised, the stubborn juice is forced out, lest anything remain. Pliny, Book XVIII, chapter 31, says of presses: “The spacious ones press better.” Presses must therefore be assisted by boards, since work is completed more quickly when a larger quantity of material is enclosed.

Likewise. “That it may be squeezed out to the marrow,” etc. The marrow is the innermost part. “To suck out from the marrow” is to press out everything. Thus juice is squeezed out from the grape skins to the very last, so that not the least remains.

Likewise. “And for the master of the household’s wine-cellars,” etc. The manuscript’s reading, “of the master of the household,” is better.

Likewise. “That by aging it may become better,” etc. Wine is commended by long aging. Pindar, *Olympian* IX, antistrophe 2:

> “Praise old wine indeed, but the flowers of newer hymns.”

Cicero, *Laelius*, 223: “Those wines which endure age ought to be the most pleasant.” Concerning wines that withstand age, and how much aging they can bear, consult Athenaeus, *Deipnosophists*, Book I, chapter 21.

Pag. 234. “Luxuriant locks are beaten with the pruning-hook,” etc. The editor at Verona rightly suspected that *tondentur*, “are clipped,” should be read, so that both proper diction and sense may be preserved. Vines are not to be beaten, nor cut with a blunt pruning-hook; Columella, Book IV, chapter 24: “Lest the vine, torn and roughened, rot from moisture and the wounds fail to heal.”

Likewise. “It comes to the yoke.” A yoked vine is one led crosswise over various supports. Varro, *On Agriculture*, Book I, chapter 8: “The upright things by which the vine stands are called supports; those which are yoked crosswise are called yokes.” One yoke is simple, another four-sided and roof-shaped. Pliny, Book XVII, chapter 21: “With shoots spread upon the ground, or with the vine raised by itself, or with a support without a yoke, or trained on a simple yoke, or roof-trained on a fourfold yoke.” The same author, in the same book, next chapter: “Some cut back the following year, but only in the fourth bring it to the yoke.” A yoked vine has the shape of a cross. Therefore he says: “It comes to the yoke when, having distributed all its property in advance, it bears its cross for the poor.” Such comparisons pleased the ancient Fathers, as may be seen in Justin Martyr, *Apology* II, folio 90, and Tertullian, *Apologeticus*, chapter 16.

Likewise. “Having distributed all its property in advance,” etc. *Erogare* means to distribute, to bestow liberally. Pliny, *Panegyric*, 75: “You seem to need to be asked whether you have calculated the revenues of the empire sufficiently, or whether the prince’s frugality has such strength that it alone can suffice for so many expenditures, so many distributions.” Therefore *praeerogata*, “distributed in advance,” should be read, not *praerogata*, as in the Verona edition. Christians at that time—for persecution was always threatening—used to sell their goods and distribute the proceeds to churches for the use of poor believers, or themselves bestow them on persons of their own choice. They did this not only so that, free from worldly cares, they might go more readily to martyrdom, but also to obey Christ’s command. Mark 10:21: “We should sell all things and give to the poor, so that we might have treasure in heaven and follow him more eagerly.” Pontius, *On Cyprian*: “Having sold his possessions to support the need of the poor, and distributing the price of entire estates, he joined two good things at once: he despised worldly ambition, than which nothing is more destructive, and fulfilled mercy, which God preferred even to his sacrifices.”

Likewise. “All righteousness having been fulfilled,” etc.—that is, when everything belonging to divine righteousness has been accomplished. What divine righteousness is, gather from the notes below, at folio 337, now Tract III, Book I. Cyprian uses the same coloring, Epistle LXXVII: “That peace may already have preceded from you in the fulfillment of his martyrdom”—that is, that whatever was required for confessing Christ may have been completed.

Pag. 235. “Likewise, on the day of judgment, vengeance for the blood of confessors is exacted by Christ to the last farthing,” etc. Here the comparison goes too far and breaks down. No fault could be imagined in those who press the must such as could be exacted from those who shed innocent Christian blood. The former devoted themselves to collecting must and completing their service; the latter, to spilling blood and destroying discipline. The former are owed payment; the latter punishment.

## In Tract XXVIII, Book II, on Isaiah 7

Pag. 236. “It is a concise form of happiness to learn from another’s danger what you ought to avoid,” etc. Publilius Syrus, to this very effect:

> “It is good to observe what must be avoided in another’s misfortune.  
> From another’s fault a wise person corrects his own.”

Likewise. “Whoever wishes to escape the wrath of God, generally threatened, must serve him blamelessly,” etc. For the aim of the divine law is to cut away vices and recall wandering minds to the way of reason. Hierocles, *Commentary on the Pythagorean Verses*, 18: “God punishes as wicked those whom voluntary impulses of the will have led away [from the right], and who seem to have forgotten the right reason that is within them, in accordance with the law that forbids evil.” For the reason why, consult Clement of Alexandria, *Stromata*, Book IV, 536.

Likewise. “The weight of pressing sacraments does not permit,” etc. As many mysteries as there are in the Christian faith, so many are called sacraments by ancient writers; and Christian profession itself is called the sacrament of the Christian religion by Septimius Florens [Tertullian], *Against Marcion*, Book IV, chapter 2. I think that the sacraments named by our author mean the Eucharistic supper, which Cyprian called “the sacrament of the Lord’s sacrifice,” Epistle LXIII. Certainly, apart from this, there can be no other urgent sacrament: the rest may be deferred, but this has its appointed time and cannot be postponed if it is to be performed with proper dignity and merit. It may also be understood of the immersion of catechumens, since that too, once prescribed, was not to be postponed.

Likewise. “The vine of God,” etc. Compare the sermon formerly on Psalm 79, now Tract 27, Book II, and what I noted there. For this sermon seems to have been delivered not long after that sermon, since it speaks of “the discussion of the vine mentioned,” which occurs nowhere but in that sermon on Psalm 79.

## In Tract XXX, Book II, Invitation to the Font I

Pag. 240. “Now our mother adopts us in order to bear us, but not under that law,” etc. To bear is greater than to adopt. Bearing is the work of nature; adoption belongs to law and imitates nature. He means that adoption through baptism is not merely adoption into sonship, but a true birth by which we become true children of God; indeed, a birth not like that of a woman, but such as grace divinely infused by the mystery accomplishes in a human being and claims for God.

Pag. 241. “Happily nourished by the railings of the altar,” etc. The altar was apparently enclosed by railings, so that the crowd’s disorderly approach might not disturb the priest’s offerings or diminish reverence for sacred things. Eusebius, *Ecclesiastical History*, Book X, chapter 4, from the panegyric oration on the rebuilding of churches, 381: “Finally, he placed the holy of holies—that is, the altar—in the middle; and, in order that these sanctuaries might be inaccessible to the multitude, he secured them with wooden railings.” The author of the *Life of Basil I the Macedonian*, chapters 55–56: “And the railings that separate the sanctuary from the outer part [of the church].”

## In Tract XXXI, Book II, Invitation to the Font II

Likewise. “Enter, brothers, the heavenly gates,” etc. Manuscript: “the heavenly gates,” with the preposition omitted; I retain this.

Likewise. “In the generative channel of the eternal flood, depositing [something], do not suppose that grace here operates for persons,” etc. What is this *condentes*, “depositing”? It is plainly unsuitable; one ought rather to say *condendi*, “of depositing,” if the sense allowed it. This reading long perplexed me, nor did any nail-biting help me discover what to substitute according to the author’s manner. What if we read *capientes undam*, “receiving the water,” metaphorically, as he often does? Thus the text should read: “receiving the water in the generative channel of the eternal flood, do not suppose that grace operates for persons,” etc.

Likewise. “Do not suppose that grace here operates for persons,” etc. The following fourth invitation explains this: those who differ in origin, age, sex, and condition will soon become one; and in Sermon I to the newly baptized: “From this, you who had differed in age and differed in nation suddenly emerged as full brothers, suddenly as newborn infants.”

Likewise. “Be born by your own judgment,” etc.—that is, by your own choice and faith, with steadfast purpose.

Likewise. “This old man of yours,” etc. Tertullian, *On the Resurrection of the Flesh*, chapter 47: “For by a likeness we die in baptism, but by reality we rise again in the flesh.” Extracts from Theodotus, published after Clement of Alexandria, folio 800: “Baptism is called the death and end of the old [man].”

[Col. 0575D] Pag. 242. “With foul-smelling rags,” etc. See the notes above, on page 115.

## In Tract XXXII, Book II, Invitation to the Font III

Pag. 243. “Hasten as quickly as possible to the things desired,” etc.—namely, the sacraments of baptism. Faith has already drawn you; catechesis has strengthened you; the destined generative water has conceived; water will bring forth through the sacrament. Strive therefore toward the birth, so that you may together become infants at the breast.

Pag. 244. “Behold, soon the sweet crying of infants is heard.” Correct from the manuscript: “Behold, the voice of infants and sweet crying is heard.”

Likewise. “Who then does not labor,” etc. She who receives children, however numerous they are, indicates the Church seeking the salvation in Christ of all persons, etc.

## In Tract XXXIII, Book II, Invitation to the Font IV

Likewise. “Soon to become one,” etc. See the end, and explain this from those words: “This is the mother of all, who gathers us united from every tribe and nation and afterwards makes us one body.” Add St. Paul, 1 Corinthians 12:12.

Likewise. “Because according as each person has believed and acted,” etc. In the manuscript the words “and acted” are absent.

Pag. 245. “This is the mother of all,” etc.—the Church. Above, Invitation III: “Run eagerly to the mother, who then does not labor if she cannot count some together [with the rest].”

## In Tract XXXIV, Book II, Invitation to the Font V

Likewise. “Whom its own faith gives birth to,” etc. For through faith a person comes to baptism, believing that in this way he or she will please God and that God will be a rewarder; through this the person is reborn and becomes a new birth.

Likewise. “Fleeing the snares of this world,” etc. For baptism not only cuts away past sins but also, as Theodoret says, *Compendium of Heretical Fables*, Book V, chapter 18, makes people participants in the Lord’s death and resurrection, bestows the gifts of the Holy Spirit, and makes them heirs of God and co-heirs with Christ. See Cyril of Jerusalem, *Mystagogical Catechesis* 2, folio 233.

## In Tract XXXV, Book II, Invitation to the Font VI

Pag. 246. “Tempered by most sweet fire, it already awaits you with gentle murmur,” etc. He alludes to baths, customary and luxurious among the ancients, some boiling, some hot, some warm, some cold, according to circumstance and taste. That epigrammatist cited by Salmasius on Lampridius, folio 113, detests boiling baths, as does Antiphanes in Athenaeus, Book I, chapter 14; and Cornelius Celsus, Book I, chapter 3, forbids persons wearied by exertion to use them. By these baths they induced perspiration, as distinct from dry sweating—so called by Celsus, Book III, chapter 23—which was sought in the Laconicum. Plutarch, in his treatise *On the Preservation of Health*, forbids cold baths after exercise. Vitruvius, Book V, chapter 10, expressly distinguishes hot baths from warm ones. Thus warm baths, tempered by most sweet fire, which would relieve and soothe rather than weaken, were more pleasing.

[Col. 0576C] Pag. 247. “What is needed for anointing, what for cleansing,” etc. Homer, *Iliad*, Book X, 577:

> “And when they had bathed and anointed themselves with rich oil.”

Cornelius Celsus, Book I, chapter 3: “When they have rested a little, they should enter and descend into the bath; then be anointed with much oil and gently rubbed.”

## In Tract XXXVI, Book II, Invitation to the Font VII

Pag. 248. “Run together to the milky water of the generative font,” etc. He alludes to the new birth, by which one regenerated in baptism sucks the water of the font as the milk of the nursing Church, not by the mouth but through immersion and washing. In this and similar expressions he is plainly playing figuratively: the water was not to be drunk, vessels were not to be filled, and bodily burning thirst was not to be quenched; rather, the sacrament was to be imbibed, the inward temple prepared for the divine Spirit, and the ardor of divine love awakened and increased, not extinguished. Yet the ready abundance of an eloquent man sometimes seems to have produced expressions not precisely conformed to the rule, in order to gain grace and make a pleasing ornament for attentive minds. In the manuscript it is read as one phrase: “Run together constantly, and drink bravely,” which sounds more elegant.

Pag. 249. “Knowing this before all else: that it is permitted neither to pour it out nor to draw it again,” etc. Understand this as “without repentance,” an interpretation which he himself gave above, in the sixth Invitation: “Whoever has not defiled it shall possess the heavenly kingdoms.” In another sense, it is “not drawn again” because this sacred immersion is not repeated.

## In Tract XXXVII, Book II, Invitation to the Font VIII

Likewise. “With the desire and swiftness of a deer,” etc. The allusion to Psalm 41 is evident: “As the deer longs for streams of water.” It is apt if, as Theodoret teaches us on that Psalm, deer acquire most violent thirst when they have devoured hunting wild beasts, so that they necessarily seek water intensely. This will indeed fit the person who, made filthy by the squalor of sins and having infected the soul with poisonous corruption and the serpent, when touched by heavenly power hastens to the font of baptism: that the person may be freed from the devil’s captivity, obtain remission of sins, regenerate the soul, receive the holy and indelible seal, and, reconciled to the heavenly kingdom, deserve to receive God’s adoption—such as Cyril of Jerusalem describes in his Prologue.

## In Tract XXXVIII, Book II, to the Newly Baptized I

Pag. 250. “After the most devout rites of sacred expiation have been completed,” etc. Before baptism the catechumens prepared themselves by fasting. In the Extracts from Theodotus, folio 801A: “For this reason there are fasts, supplications, prayers, and kneelings.” Tertullian, *On Baptism*, chapter 10: “Those about to enter baptism ought to pray with frequent prayers, fasts, kneelings, and vigils, and also with confession of all their former sins.” Hence the first Saturday after Easter, when the Lenten fast and the exercise of repentance had been completed, was appointed for baptism. Cyril of Jerusalem, in the Prologue to the Catecheses: “You have a sufficiently long interval: you have repentance for forty days.” Tertullian, in the same work, chapter 9: “Easter provides the more solemn day for baptism.” See Laodicean Canons 45 and 46. On confession before baptism, see the same Cyril, Catechesis 3.18.

Likewise. “After the sun of the radiant night,” etc. Christ, the Sun of righteousness, kept vigil, illuminating [them] by the splendor of his divinity. For they kept vigil, as the already cited Tertullian confirms, and spent the night-watch devoutly in prayer, as may be inferred from the Council of Elvira, canon 35.

Likewise. “After the life-giving washing of the milky font,” etc. He calls it “milky” as appropriate to the new birth, nourishment that will lead to immortality.

Likewise. “From this, you who had differed in age,” etc. St. Paul, 1 Corinthians 12:12.

Pag. 251. “He celebrates with a joyful banquet,” etc. Justin Martyr gives the rite, *Apology* II, 92; Tertullian before him, *Against Marcion*, Book IV, chapter 34, 558C; and Jobius in Photius, 595.43. For the necessity of joy and the rejoicing of salvation lead to this, as Tertullian says at the end of *On Baptism*.

Likewise. “By the charm of provisions,” that is, by the variety of foods sought by gluttons.

Likewise. A breast oppressed is often violently distressed by raw and sour vomitings, etc. The breast is oppressed when foods overcome the body and are not overcome by the body, as Hippocrates says, *On the Regions in Man*. Cyprian, Letter 64: “Even now they hanker after dinners and banquets, the surfeit of which, while the rawness still survived, they recently kept belching up day after day.” He says “is violently distressed” because the vomitings were induced. Seneca, *Consolation to Helvia*, ch. 9: “They vomit in order to eat; they eat in order to vomit, and they do not deign to digest the banquets they gather from the whole world.” Suetonius, *Vitellius*, ch. 13: “For breakfasts, lunches, dinners, and revels he was easily sufficient for all, owing to his habitual vomiting” [Col. 0577D].

Likewise. “In which is the sweetness of your new wine.” In the manuscript: “in which is not the sweetness of your new wine,” etc.

Likewise. “Receive it hungrily,” etc. Soberly, not to the point of satiety.

Likewise. “The master of the household,” etc.: Christ, who communicates his body and blood by wine and bread.

Likewise. “The three boys, unanimous, [ate] legumes,” etc.: Hananiah, Mishael, and Azariah. See Daniel, ch. I.

Likewise. “Christ pours in the oil,” etc. For they used to be stripped and anointed from hair to feet with *exorcistic* oil (*oleum eporkistō*, ἐπορκιστῷ), that is, exorcised oil; thereafter they were led to the washing of baptism. Cyril of Jerusalem teaches and explains the rite, *Mystagogical Catechesis* II, 231–232.

## In Treatise XXXIX, Book II, To the Newly Baptized II

Page 253. “Remaining in the first birth,” etc. He calls the first birth that which he had from his mother, and the second that which he had from the sacred Font [Col. 0578A]. When Christ said in John ch. III, “Unless you are reborn of water and Spirit,” he indicated a second birth.

Likewise. “A burning dreg consumes at every moment,” etc. I should rather read “torch” (*fax*). Thus Cyprian, speaking of himself in *To Donatus*: “After, through the Spirit breathed in from heaven, a second birth had restored me into a new man”; and then he adds: “Yielding assent to my clinging vices, and through despair of better things, I favoured my evils as though they were my own and native possessions.” The same letter, *To Donatus*. Seneca, *Controversies* I.8: “That passion rules us which first entered the mind. Luxury, avarice, idleness, injustice, and fear are not unlearned; and every day all these things are reproved or punished: so tenacious are we even of vices.”

Likewise. “Conscience never abandons its sinner.” Seneca, Letter XLIII: “A good conscience summons a crowd; a bad one is anxious and troubled even in solitude.”

Likewise. “But you have been tested bravely,” etc., a phrase drawn [Col. 0578B] from soldiers, who were called “brave” and were bound to act bravely as their duty required. Trebellius Pollio, *Claudius*, ch. 9: “Those who survived acting bravely.” Ammianus Marcellinus XVII.6: “That he was afterwards consul, was present, and acted bravely is established.” Themistius, Oration 9: “The Roman language and the constitution of the state have legislated that soldiers receive their appellations from courage alone.” Christians, moreover, are said to serve as soldiers. Tertullian, *To the Martyrs*, ch. 3: “We have been called to the warfare of the living God.” By “tested bravely” he means that they have performed their military probation manfully and without blame.

Likewise. “A new kind of judgment,” etc.: that is, what Tertullian elsewhere said in a different sense—“a confession of the name, not an examination of the crime.” A person is acquitted if he admits that he is impious, that he is guilty; he must not excuse what he ought to abhor and renounce.

Page 254. “They hasten to be punished,” etc. The harmless punishment of baptism. He alludes to the fact that through baptism the old man dies [Col. 0578C]; hence he proceeds to the sword, killing, and burial in the flood of the sacred element.

## In Treatise XL, To the Newly Baptized III

Page 255. “By a pious ordinance, as they say, he sent truly golden keys,” etc. That phrase, “as they say,” is commonly used of a popular saying, as it were a proverb; but I have been unable to find it among collectors of proverbs, so that it may conveniently be removed. We already know that “golden” things are whatever are highly valued, and Martial touches on this in connection with the poems of Pythagoras. So too the keys of which Zeno speaks here are undoubtedly of whatever price and esteem one may name, since by them the gate of heaven is opened. For through them the ministers of the Church are given authority to bind and loose souls: both those sinning after baptism and repenting, and those coming up to baptism from an impious sect and giving their name to Christ. Thus they may rightly be called nothing less than golden, since they can achieve so much as to claim us for God—provided, however, that we are willing to remain in his commandments and deserve the fruit of Christ’s blood.

[Col. 0578D] Likewise. “Not those which, by a malicious favour, conceal crimes,” etc.: those which hide the guilty person so that he may be withdrawn from punishment; this he calls a malicious favour.

Likewise. “They absolve ours in heaps,” etc.: from any mass whatever of sins. Above, on Psalm LXXIX, now Treatise XXVII: “All sins whatsoever are entirely cut away by baptism through the power of the Holy Spirit.”

Likewise. “Nor do they allow anything to remain over,” that is, they leave nothing unpardoned, nothing excluded: all offences are erased by the grace of this sacrament. A *subsecivum* is whatever remains at the end of a measuring-rod, so called from the cutting line, says Frontinus, *On the Quality of Land* 49. Surveyors used to divide fields into quadrilateral centuries; whatever lay outside the square and extended beyond the end of the measuring-rod they called *subsecivum*. A *century* is a field of two hundred *iugera*, which among the ancients was allotted with one hundred men, and received its name from this, says Siculus Flaccus, *On the Conditions of Land* [Col. 0579A]. Agennius, on Frontinus: “Those things are called *subseciva* which could not be assigned; that is, when centuriated land has been divided into cultivated plots which were to form centuries, but a century could not be completed, they call it *subsecivum*. The author of the division sometimes reserved these for himself, sometimes granted them to certain persons, sometimes to the state, or to private persons; some sold these *subseciva*,” etc. See the same Agennius, fols. 57–58, to learn most fully about *subseciva*. These points suffice for grasping Zeno’s meaning: by this custom he wished to indicate that through the power of baptism nothing is excepted.

Likewise. “With the accused person saved, the guilt in him is punished.” The manuscript has: “the guilt in the accused person is punished.”

Page 256. “Hence our confession has no need of tortures,” etc., for it was made voluntarily. Matthew ch. III, v. 6; Mark ch. I, v. 5; Acts ch. XIX, v. 18. Cyril of Jerusalem, *Catechesis* 3: “First they displayed the wounds; then he applied the remedies” [Col. 0579B]. He speaks of John baptizing.

Likewise. “But he who spares the poisoner, murderer, adulterer,” etc., unless he has healed his mind, etc. Seneca, Letter 95, after the middle: “Tranquillity does not befall those who have not attained a fixed and unchangeable judgment; the rest continually fall and are restored, and fluctuate by turns between what they have abandoned and what they seek.” In the new birth, it was incumbent upon the Christian to be reborn with the habits of the preceding day changed. For a new profession, provided it was not counterfeit, was a death of crimes and a life of virtues—as Cyprian of Carthage says elegantly and in a godly manner (*theothen*, θεόθεν) in his most elegant letter; these words of his also bear upon this matter: “Only let the breast thirst and lie open: in the measure in which we bring a capacity for faith, we draw in the overflowing grace.”

## In Treatise XLII, To the Newly Baptized V

Page 259. “For all your bond has been removed” [Col. 0579C], etc. This is to be referred to the year of Jubilee—not because that custom and Mosaic law held a place among Christians, but because he illustrates by analogy how great the difference was between impious pagan superstition and the religious security of Christianity. Concerning the Jubilee, it is known from the sacred books and from Josephus, *Antiquities* III.10, that every fiftieth year all obligations were equalized, interest remitted, and slaves emancipated. What had been ordained concerning bodily things Zeno applies to spiritual matters, in order to say that the bonds of the world, of pleasures, and of the devil are loosed, broken, and snapped through baptism; and that the newly baptized person is established in the confidence of conscience, by which he may strive toward the life of salvation, if he remains steadfast in faith, hope, charity, and constancy in God’s commandments.

Likewise. “Let no terror agitate you,” etc.: be steadfast in faith and hope.

Likewise. “Lest it bear anything adulterous,” etc. I read: “anything spurious” (*adulterinum*).

## In Treatise XLIII, To the Newly Baptized VI

[Col. 0579D] Page 262. “But I know your curiosity well,” etc. He calls them curious concerning how infants of the same age may be said to be reborn when the practice of their old life still lies under their instruction; and henceforth they employ this curiosity. As he deters them from it, so he elegantly investigates the horoscopes of their new birth, ingeniously and suitably to his purpose.

Page 264. “But all these, flowing with the saving whole, not very greatly,” etc. Read, as in the manuscript, “stream” (*amne*).

## In Treatise XLIV, Book II, To the Newly Baptized VII

Page 265. “Which has been adulterated by no leaven,” etc. Drawn from Christ’s saying in Matthew ch. XVI: “Beware of the leaven of the Pharisees,” which Origen interprets as the doctrine of the Pharisees, of which Jesus does not wish his disciples to eat, having prepared for them a better, fresh, and spiritual dough. Theodoret, on First Corinthians ch. V, v. 6, says that the Apostle called “old leaven” “that which was before baptism” [Col. 0580A], which the baptized had to unlearn and replace with unleavened bread, as the Jews ate at Passover, Christ—who is their true Passover—having now been sacrificed for Christians.

Likewise. “It has been made smooth with generative oil,” etc. Tertullian, *On Baptism*, ch. 7: “Thereupon, emerging from the washing, we are anointed with blessed unction.” Cyril of Jerusalem, already cited, says that they were first anointed before baptism; but see Pamelius on the passage of Tertullian.

Likewise. “Tempered with fitting services,” etc., which he describes in Sermon I, 235.

Page 266. “Certainly they are not *cacabacii*,” etc. Tertullian, *Against Hermogenes*, ch. 41: “If it is of equal weight, it is no longer turbulent or *cacabacius*, but composed and tempered.” *Turbulentus* seems to be opposed to “composed” and “calm”; *cacabacius*, to “boiling” and “foaming,” so that *turbulentus* denotes liquid stirred in a pot by the bubbling heat of fire. *Cacabacius* seems to mean bubbling even after the motion of boiling has subsided, so that it cannot be borne when applied to the lips. Our author appears to have meant that the loaves should not be so hot with heat as to repel lips and teeth, not so stale as to break the teeth, not so burned as to be coals rather than bread, not raw so that they are still dough, nor mouldy so as to provoke nausea. Yet loaves were baked in an oven; porridge was cooked in a pot. Julius Paulus, Digest XXXIII, *On Bequests of Household Furnishings*, law XVIII, §3; thus Zeno seems to have spoken less correctly when he said that loaves were *cacabacii*. But (see Note 6, on p. 266) he seems to have loved the word more than precision [Col. 0580B].

Likewise. “But perhaps because some seem smaller in form,” etc. What is this? Does he persist in the metaphor of unleavened loaves? Yet below he will say that all are three-pounders without distinction. Or does he mean bodily form and stature? But this does not fall under the proposed subject of new birth and is remote from the point. These matters are obscure to me.

Page 267. “Finally, you too retain the old weight; you have a *haedina*,” etc. Isaac Casaubon, on Aelius Lampridius, p. 150, very rightly observes that *aginam* should be read in place of *haedinam*. This reading is confirmed by Tertullian in the passage just cited from *Against Hermogenes*: “Inclining and rushing headlong toward neither side, they were borne along with the balanced force of the middle *agina*, as they say.” On *agina*, see Festus.

Likewise. “Make an *exagium*,” etc. Inscription VI, fol. 647: “Reason has taught, persuasion by utility, that, the custom of bargaining by fingers being removed, livestock should rather be sold by weight under an *exagium* than handed over by clasping fingers, so that, with the animal weighed, the seller may benefit under public observation when the reliability of the weight has been proved, and both buyer and seller may know how much the flesh of the slaughtered animal weighs.” In Theodosius’s Novella XV: “Concerning weights also, that fraud may be utterly removed, *exagia* are issued by us.” An *exagium*, therefore, is a weighing. Glosses: ἐξάγιον, “weighing”; ἐξαγιάζω, “I examine, weigh.”

Likewise. “Weigh them singly: you will find none to have less,” etc. Less than what? The sense itself demands that something denoting quantity be absent; for I do not think that the “none” substituted by others can have any place [Col. 0580D].

Page 268. “They are three-pounders,” etc. That is, they have been increased and endowed with the weight of threefold power: baptized in the name of the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit, they have not only cast off their former sins, but, made sons of God and co-heirs with Christ, share in his death, his resurrection, and the gifts of the Holy Spirit. Moreover, *dupondium* and *tripondium* in writers mean “two pounds” and “three pounds,” with the word appropriate to the matter in question understood. Thus Varro, *On the Latin Language* IV, near the end, says that *dupondium* is named from two weights, thereby indicating that it denotes neither a species nor bodies, but the weight of anything whatever. These names are therefore applied broadly; and in the glosses *dupondium* is called δινούμμιον, although *nummus* may mean any kind of money. Emperor Justinian, in the preface to the *Digest*, forbids those applying themselves to civil law in their first year thereafter to be called *dupondii*, as though they were delayed by a frivolous and contemptuous nickname [Col. 0581A]; rather, he would have them encouraged by the dignity of the name and the honour of their studies, to which he granted an honourable title from his own name. We should therefore certainly believe that by *dupondium* he understood drachmas of the most worthless value, in which sense, among others, Seneca, Letter XVIII, wished him to be “filled for a *dupondius*” who could be satisfied by the cheapest and most worthless food. Conversely, in other glosses it is taken for two or three gold coins; see Salmasius on Lampridius. It is also elsewhere adapted to books, indeed to golden ones, as Gronovius, *On the Sestertius* I.7, whom I offer as a witness, maintains. Our author spoke of the sacrament of baptism as of a matter of greater weight: one baptized, having drawn upon the power of the divine Trinity, has obtained a weight of whatever price and dignity. Casaubon, however, in the cited passage on Lampridius, p. 150, observed that one should read, “All are three-pounders,” not “They are three-pounders,” and the sense requires it.

Likewise. “Those who serve at the table,” etc. I do not understand to what end these words are said; so far as I am concerned, they may be absent.

## In Treatise XLV, Book II, On the Lord’s Day of Passover I

[Col. 0581B]

Page 269. In the manuscript it is without a title and is entitled Sermon XXXIII, Book I.

Likewise. “Heir of the ages,” etc. He called the day heir of the ages because it is continually reborn from age to age, and thus shares the common condition of the ages. Accordingly, Neoptolemus in Sophocles’ *Philoctetes* 1322, despairing of escape from evils, declares that this will happen to him:

> Ὡς ἂν αὐτὸς ἥλιος  
> Ταύτῃ μὲν αἴρῃ, τῇ δὲ δ᾽ ἂν δύνῃ πάλιν.

“So long as this very sun rises here and, in turn, sets there.”

Likewise. “In its paternal course,” etc., because day is the son of the sun. Pindar, *Olympian* [Ode] B, antistrophe 2, called day “the child of Helios”: ἀμέραν παῖδα Ἁλίου.

Likewise. “Turned upon itself like a turning-post.” The manuscript has “upon itself” (*in sese*).

Likewise. “Bringing forth for itself a beginning from its end,” etc. This is what he says a little later: “bringing forth infinite birthdays,” that is, infinite births from its setting; and what in the following sermon [Col. 0581C] he says: “the same, its own successor and likewise its own predecessor”; and what in Sermon 5: “It bears for itself a beginning from its end”; and in the seventh: “What passes away follows; what is to come precedes.” By these and other elegant formulae of expression elsewhere, one may infer from an example how great a store of language he possessed. In Athenaeus X.19 is the following riddle:

> Εἰσὶ κασίγνηται διτταί, ὧν ἡ μία τίκτει  
> Τὴν ἑτέραν· αὐτὴ δὲ τεκοῦσα πάλιν γ᾽ ὑπὸ ταύτης τεκνοῦται.

“There are two sisters, of whom one bears the other; and the one that has borne is in turn borne by the other.” It means day and night.

Page 270. “But the rich man, happily striking the ear of grain with his palm into diverse heaps of wheat,” etc. I cannot extricate myself from this without a better guide. Perhaps one may read: “Where the rich man, into diverse heaps of grain, happily strikes the stalks and the ear with his palm,” that is, threshes; or perhaps something is missing. In the manuscript: “Happily striking the ear with his palm,” which he will suitably continue, etc.

Likewise. “Far-ground for the throat,” that is, they are for eternal death from God, because it is a work of darkness, etc. In the manuscript: “Far-ingrained for the throat,” that is, they are therefore for eternal death, because it is a work of darkness [Col. 0581D].

## In Treatise XLVI, Book II, On Passover II

Page 272. “With unsteady course, redeemed by manifold grace, the saving day comes by the solemn track of times,” etc. Read separately: “with steady course,” so that it corresponds to “solemn track,” that is, fixed and established: “redeemed by manifold grace,” etc. This reading is confirmed by Sermon 8 (now the following treatise) and is thus found in the manuscript.

Likewise. “Parent of the year and offspring of the year, it precedes,” etc. Distinguish and punctuate: “offspring, it precedes and follows,” etc. It is called parent of the year because the beginning of the old ecclesiastical year was reckoned from Passover, and Passover was called the New Year, as Joseph Scaliger teaches, besides the authority of our author, *On the Emendation of Chronology* I, fol. 6. Why it is called the offspring of the year will be known to anyone who has read Cleobulus’s riddle of the year in Laertius.

[Col. 0582A] Likewise. “Then, newly born, and with the newly born day,” etc. The day is newly born for one who, now reborn through the saving washing, begins a new life; and he himself is newly born, like a young plant. Cyril of Jerusalem, *Catechesis* I: “Before this you were a catechumen; now indeed you shall be called a believer. You are transplanted henceforth into the spiritual olive trees,” etc. Therefore Saint Paul calls them νεόφυτοι, “newly planted,” in First Timothy ch. III, v. 6; and our author himself addresses the newly baptized seven times below after baptism, as young shoots planted in the Church.

## In Treatise XLVIII, Book II, On Passover IV

Page 274. “Living by its death,” etc. Because it can set and return, as Catullus said.

Likewise. “Without pause it grows into old age, yet does not depart from its birth-cradle,” etc. Times are said to grow old, though they are renewed from day to day. He says “without pause” because time secretly flees and flies. Ovid, *Metamorphoses* XV.183:

> Thus times flee alike and alike follow,  
> And are always new: for what was before is left behind,  
> And what had not been comes to be; every moment is renewed.

## In Treatise L, Book II, On Passover VI

Page 277. “For the catechumens seeking the way of light,” etc., that is, seeking it together. The manuscript punctuates: “For the catechumens, the way of light; for those seeking, remission of all sins,” which I embrace and approve. Below, Sermon VIII (now above, Treatise XLVII): “This too he is about to grant today to our seekers,” etc.

## In Treatise LII, Book II, On Passover VII

Page 279. “The sacred day, having bent,” etc.: of Passover.

Likewise. “But whether it runs or runs back is uncertain; its past remains so that it may return,” etc. Cicero, *On Old Age* 192, says the opposite: “Hours indeed pass away, and days, and months, and years; nor does past time ever return.” We must therefore believe that Zeno means the name, as though he said that the festival of Passover so remains as to return again, although completed in previous years. Thus Tibullus calls Messalla’s birthday “anniversary day,” as though it were that very day of his actual birth, I.7.

Likewise. “A truly wonderful principle: by wearing away the spaces of innumerable ages with diverse measure, it renews them; yet its orbit is always one,” etc. Aristotle, *Physics* VI.11.4, teaches: “It is impossible that anything which is always one and the same should either come to be or perish,” as in the motion of heaven. Zeno means that it is wonderful that times are worn down and consumed by the manifold recurrence of ages, while their orbit nevertheless always remains the same. “Diverse” means manifold, as in the preceding sermon he said “one and the same, yet not itself, but itself.” Moreover, “it renews spaces” means times; for time was called the space of the motion of the world, as Plato and Zeno of Citium held, according to Laertius and Alcinous.

## In Treatise LIV, Book II, On Exodus I

[Col. 0582D] Page 281. “Moses and Aaron through that by which they were,” etc. I read: “Moses and Aaron, through the priesthood which they possessed, and through their number,” etc.

## In Treatise LV, Book II, On Exodus II

Page 282. “This is he who is nourished by its fruit,” etc. I prefer “rejoices” (*laetatur*): below, “of whom it is the Lord’s Passover to rejoice.” Those who thought themselves correct in emending it to “offers sacrifice” (*litare*) were mistaken. Tertullian, *On the Crown*, ch. 3: “With the same immunity, from the day of Passover until Pentecost we rejoice.” Celerinus, among Cyprian’s letters, no. 20: “For his deeds I weep in the joy of Passover day and night.”

Likewise. “And in flocks of livestock, a lamb endowed with a twofold nature, which cannot be found,” etc. He draws an argument from absurdity, as though a lamb-kid ought to have been used for the Jewish Passover, like a goat-stag, which does not exist. The Greek of Exodus ch. XII, v. 3 has: λαβέτωσαν ἕκαστος πρόβατον κατ᾽ οἰκίαν, “let each take a sheep according to the household”; then, v. 5: πρόβατον τέλειον ἄρσεν, ἐνιαύσιον, ἀπὸ τῶν ἀρνῶν καὶ τῶν ἐρίφων λήψεσθε, “you shall take a perfect male sheep, one year old, from lambs and kids.” The translator rendered *pecus*, “livestock,” too loosely.
