Cyprian is better, *Testimonies* II.15: “Let each take for himself a sheep without blemish, perfect, male, one year old; you shall take it from lambs and kids.” The Vulgate has “you shall take a lamb,” then at v. 5, “you shall also take a kid,” so as to remove the ambiguity; for a sheep cannot be the common mother of lambs and kids. Theodoret, *Questions on Exodus* 24: “He therefore commands them to take not only yearling lambs from sheep, but also kids from goats.” They could therefore use either a lamb or a kid indiscriminately, so that, if one kind was not available, the other would not be excluded. The Italian translator expressed this by saying, *prenda un agnello, od un capretto*—“let him take a lamb or a kid”—and this is the “lamb of twofold nature in flocks of livestock.” Yet a kid is not well expressed by calling it a lamb of another nature; the statement is not merely obscure but improper. He uses *bifariam* adjectivally for “twofold,” as Apuleius also does in his book *On Rational Philosophy* [Col. 0583B].

Likewise. “This is the lamb, brothers, of whom it is the Lord’s Passover to rejoice,” etc. The manuscript reads *laetare*, but diphthongs never have a place in it. Jews celebrate Passover by the slaughter of the true lamb; Christians rejoice together in the typological lamb and recall the memory of their redemption. Origen, *On John* X.160, calls that the true Passover which “is accomplished in Spirit and truth by those who worship God in Spirit and truth.” But what the flourishing addresses of our most eloquent author in his sermons on Passover do not suggest for celebrating with joy the true Passover! In them he sets forth the fruit of redemption received, stirs the affections so that we may recognize the worth of the gift, and, while making us recognize it, floods us with the joy of salvation obtained.

Page 283. “This one is mature, because after him there is none,” etc. The Greek text has ἐντέλειον, which may be translated “perfect” or “mature,” and I would not reject that. But the qualities here enumerated are not those of the lamb, but of Christ; for the lamb, as lamb, need not be first-born, cannot be eternal, is not immaculate from sin—since sin does not apply to a brute animal—nor are the other qualities he adds proper to any but Christ. Hence I think one should read “this one is unique” (*hic unicus*), a word agreeing with what follows, “because after him there is none,” and tending toward “only-begotten” and “first-born,” titles by which Christ is adorned by John ch. I, v. 14 and ch. III, v. 16, and by the Apostle, Colossians ch. I, v. 18. The reading “this one is unique” is all the more confirmed because he speaks of the perfect lamb below, in the final place.

Likewise. “He rendered to God the man whom he sacrificed,” etc. Suetonius, *Otho*, ch. 8: “For he offered the victims sacrificed to his deified father,” in the same sense.

## In Treatise LV, Book III, On Exodus III

[Col. 0583D]

Page 284. “You served long, not by the lot of a stranger, but by desert.” What? Were strangers given over to serve natives? On the contrary, they should be valued and defended by inhabitants. Plato, *Laws* V: “For the stranger, being bereft of companions and kinsfolk, is more deserving of pity among human beings and gods.” This applies especially to the Hebrews, who, by Joseph’s merit, could expect both the patronage of the Egyptian king and protection in the place they had acquired through Joseph: they were subjects, not slaves. But friendly intercourse among different peoples is rare; for just as these retain toward those, so those toward these, a difference of feelings amid a diversity of customs, so that inhabitants, as the more powerful party, are prone to oppress them. Add Herodotus, *Euterpe*, ch. 160.

Likewise. “A column of fire by night, that it might warn [them] of a coming burning,” etc. I thought this referred to the conflagration that occurred in the destruction of the Temple, narrated by Josephus, *On the Capture* VII, from ch. 22. But the author himself declares otherwise below, Sermon V (now above, Treatise LIV): he professes to understand it of the eternal fire to be inflicted on the Jews by Christ’s sentence, when he says: “Because it bears the double image of cloud and fire, it signifies two judgments: one of water, which has occurred; the other of fire, which is to come” [Col. 0584A].

## In Treatise LVII, Book II, On Exodus IV

Likewise. “Depressed under the yoke at the beginning of captivity,” etc. Below, Sermon V (now Treatise LIV): “As the divine reading testifies, in Egypt Israel, the people of God, was most harshly oppressed under a mighty yoke by Pharaoh and his people.” Zeno means that the Jewish people had formerly dwelt in Egypt without resentment, owing to their long cohabitation and the grateful memory of Joseph; then the Egyptians, moved by suspicion of their prosperity or by envy, determined to oppress them. Zeno calls that decree the beginning of the captivity of the people of Israel, and hence calls the people captive.

Page 285. “Then, shut in by the great barrier of the sea, he was oppressed,” etc. The word “was oppressed,” used in the preceding period, may suitably be deleted lest the repetition of the word become unpleasant; the sense will otherwise stand, with the same verb understood in common. What if one substituted “he was terrified”? I should prefer this, and think no word more suitable.

Likewise. “Dusty in the midst,” etc. That is, dry, devoid of the moisture of waters.

Likewise. “Because around itself,” etc. I read: “with around itself” (*cum circa se*).

Likewise. “His triumph,” etc. The conquered enemy, by metonymy.

## In Treatise LVIII, Book II, On Exodus V

Likewise. The manuscript adds “to the Jews.”

Page 286. “In Egypt you served long, not from necessity but from desert,” etc. Not because, as a foreigner, you were hated—not by the chance of a stranger, as he says above—nor because you differed in religion; but because you had ruined your own religion, you deserved punishment. I infer an indication that they sinned by idolatry in Egypt from Theodoret, *Questions on Exodus* 40 [Col. 0584C].

Likewise. “The wave, fleeing back upon itself to right and left, testifies to your swift feet for shedding blood,” etc. Do not suppose he charges them with the fact that so many enemies fell and that they shed their blood in gaining the promised land, for they acted by God’s command. Rather, he means the blood of Christ, which they were going to shed, driven by the fury of such great injustice.

## In Treatise LIX, Book II, On Exodus VI

Likewise. “I think it more fitting for one who remains wretched in his own condition than for one happy to be hurled down into the uttermost miseries,” etc. Euripides, *Bellerophon*, in Stobaeus, Sermon XCVII:

> “But he who is continually unfortunate to the end gains this advantage:  
> for one always accustomed to misfortune does not know, when deprived of prosperity, that he is badly off.  
> Thus it is best never to have experienced good things;  
> For this thought clings fast:  
> ‘What a man I once was, and I too perhaps was once fortunate!’”

From Hugo Grotius’s translation: “But he who is miserable continually to the end of life [Col. 0584D] surpasses others in this: accustomed to misfortune, he does not feel himself deprived of good things. It is so much safer never to have known better things. For that always clings fast: ‘Ah, what and how great a man I was, once acquainted with prosperous fates!’” Verses of similar sentiment occur in the same author’s *Trojan Women*, v. 634, and *Iphigenia among the Taurians*, v. 1021.

Page 287. “Also the Red Sea, cleft in the middle into two shores, and, with banks drawn up to right and left, waves massed in battle-array, its liquid preserved, the dried path of the deep, pressing against itself in opposition, nature stood suspended in astonishment,” etc. No one can fail to see that this passage is full of errors; I do not claim that I can heal them without manuscripts. Yet it was necessary to venture something, leaving the matter afresh to better minds. Thus I read: “Also the Red Sea, cleft in the middle into two shores, and, with banks drawn up to right and left, waves massed in battle-array, with its water clear, the path of the dried deep stood suspended in astonishment, pressing against itself in opposition.”

[Col. 0585A] Likewise. “Which indeed [was] not the merit of the heavenly people,” etc. The manuscript reads “merits.”

## In Treatise LXI, Book II, On Exodus VIII

Page 289. “The saving lamb, which is designated from sheep and kids, cannot be found among livestock,” etc. I cannot pass over the author’s opinion, who seems to have thought that an animal partaking of the nature of sheep and kid had to be used in the Hebrew Passover. I have noted above, in Sermon 2 on Exodus, p. 282, that he erred in this (see our Note 4 on Treatise 61). That this is not believed there to be a joke, but a consistent opinion, is shown not only by what is said here but by what he says below in Sermon XII (now Treatise LXV): “You must seek a lamb from lambs and kids, of discordant nature, which your own ancestors did not find among flocks of livestock.”

Page 290. “They profited into lamentation and mourning,” etc. Add from the manuscript: “They profited.”

Likewise. “But the noisy banquet of the bloody robber,” etc. Read *bromosum*, from Greek βρόμεω, “I make a noise, roar”; from this Bacchus was called Bromius. The author of the *Etymologicum*: “Bromius [is named] from *bromos*, for when Semele was struck by lightning,” etc. [Col. 0585B].

## In Treatise LXVI, Book II, On Exodus XIII

Page 295. “They no longer have priests who sacrifice for their salvation,” etc. Read, in agreement with the rest: “They no longer have priests: who will sacrifice for their salvation?”

Likewise. “In order that they may increase their vile lust more and more, at every moment they baptize themselves in still viler baths,” etc. Strabo, XVI, testifies that this custom also existed among the Assyrians: “Bathing is customary,” which may be referred to cleanliness. Ovid, *Amores* V.7, at the end, has been understood by some to refer also to pleasures and incentives to lust. Artemidorus II.66 called it “a road to food” (ὁδὸν ἐπὶ τροφήν), because, as he inferred, they did not eat before bathing, and then took food, even before dinner. But Suidas reads “a road to pleasures” (ἐπὶ τρυφήν), which Rigault also thought correct. Another writer in the same Suidas, under λουτρά, says, “baths are used with pleasure and for benefit,” etc. Jerome warns Salvina to beware lest the heat of baths kindle a new heat of youth. Certainly Athenaeus, I.19, also teaches that bathing relieves fatigue [Col. 0585C].

## In Treatise LXX, Book II, On Daniel II

Page 298. “In a certain manner it is part of martyrdom, dearly beloved brothers, that the martyrs did not shrink from punishment,” etc. Tertullian, *Scorpiace*, ch. 8, on these same three boys: “O martyrdom, perfected even without suffering! They suffered enough, they were burned enough—those whom God therefore protected, lest they should seem to have falsified his power.”

Likewise. “For manifold cruelty,” read from the manuscript: “a mournful spectacle of manifold cruelty.”

Likewise. “And whatever torment confronted them, it gathers up its own vows”; one should evidently read *fuerit*, that is, they desired the contest all the more ardently the more cruel it seemed that which they had to confront [Col. 0585D]. I think *fuerint* was a typographical error for the *fuerit* he wrote.

## In Treatise LXXIV, Book II, On Daniel VI

Page 301. In the manuscript, except for the first, all are entitled “On the Three Boys.”

Page 302. “The caressing flames lick with dewy [tongues].” Below, Sermon VII, now Treatise LXXVI: “They are received not by flame but by God’s dew.”

## In Treatise LXXV, Book II, On Daniel VII

Likewise. “They are not harmed by panting flames and a roaring furnace,” etc. *Anhelantibus* means gaping, craving, seeking. At the beginning of Cicero’s First *Catilinarian*, Catiline is “panting after crime” (*scelus anhelantem*) in his mad audacity. Ammianus Marcellinus XXVI, fol. 449: “Like a kinsman of the emperor, he was panting after higher things”: he strove to attain the higher things which he had conceived in his mind. Fire seems borne along by such an appetite in order to gnaw away and seize surrounding things [Col. 0586A]. Ovid, *Metamorphoses* IX.172:

> Greedy flames swallow up my vitals.

Related are Solomon’s words in Proverbs ch. XXX, v. 16, concerning fire, which never says, “Enough.” He adds “roaring furnace,” that is, a furnace with crackling flame. Virgil, *Georgics* I.85:

> And to burn the light stubble with crackling flames.

## In Treatise LXXVI, Book II, On Daniel VIII

Page 303. “Made glorious by the aid of punishment,” etc. That is, the very punishment they were to suffer became refreshment for them.

Likewise. “He ordered the furnace to be kindled,” etc.: a furnace. Virgil, *Aeneid* III.579:

> And Etna, heaped huge above, breathes forth flame from its burst furnaces.

On this Servius comments: “He called furnaces *camini*, using a Greek term.” Isidore, XIX.6: “A *caminus* is a furnace, and is a Greek derivative from καῦμα, that is, ‘heat.’”

[Col. 0586B] Likewise. “With seething globes,” etc. Virgil, *Georgics* I.472:

> We have seen Etna, billowing from burst furnaces,  
> Roll globes of flame and molten rocks.

Pindar, *Pythian* Ode 1, strophe 2, said that from Etna’s caverns were belched forth “the purest [perhaps: most fluid, ὑγροτάτας] springs and rivers of fire” (πυρὸς ἁγνότατας [perhaps ὑγροτάτας] παγὰς ποταμούς τε).

Likewise. “The heaven itself too grows red with fires not its own,” etc. Varro, *On the Latin Language*, book VI, 78: “It is called *aurora* before sunrise because the air then becomes golden-red (*aurescit*) from the sun’s fire.” For air and heaven have the same meaning. Pliny, book II, chapter 38: “The ancients also called this ‘heaven,’ which they otherwise called air. For, owing to its rarity, the air easily receives every sort of impression: in the sun it has a clear light; in the moon, a fainter one; in the stars, an uncertain one; in cloudy weather, a disturbed one by day; by night it wholly lacks light; in the rainbow it displays coloured circles.” Thus in a great conflagration it too seems to catch fire and take redness from the fire, whereas the flame itself rather diffuses its force and colour into the air, just as the force and power of the sun alters qualities in the air, as Cleomedes teaches in book II of his *Πυλικῆς θεωρίας* (“theory”; title uncertain in the supplied text).

## IN TRACTATE LXXVII, BOOK II, ON DANIEL IX

Page 304. “Nor were the three youths, thought to be burning in that fire, delivered from their own burners.” A different punctuation occurs in the manuscript: “Thought to be burning in that fire, from their own burners,” etc.

Likewise. “But concerning our Lord, whom—shocking impiety!—they worship,” etc. Since the subject of this passage is unknown to me, I cannot guess for what purpose he introduced these words. It is indeed established that there were several heretics in Zeno’s time; but the brevity of the discourse does not allow us to know whom he intended.

Likewise. “Armed with no arguments,” etc.—that is, philosophical and demonstrative arguments, which ought to be absent from a Christian, since faith is a firm conviction, as Cicero says in *The Orator’s Partitions*, 21, and requires no demonstration. Cyril: “What is accepted by faith ought not to be subjected to curious inquiry; for what is tested by examination, how is it still believed?” On this subject, more fully above.

**N.B.** In the notes which follow from this point through column 600, corresponding to the text printed in the two preceding volumes of the *Patrologia*, we have prefixed, in parentheses, the pagination of those volumes. Let the reader who wishes consult them.

## ON THE TREATISE ON LAZARUS, RELEGATED TO THE APPENDIX

Page 313. (*Our edition of the Patrologia*, vol. VIII, col. 1411). “In the hollow recess of a whirlpool,” etc. I think *voraginis* (“of a gulf”) should be read.

Likewise (ibid.). “Here intimate with God.” The manuscript reads: “Here intimate with God, as is reported, according to the testimony of the Gospel, when, in John, [a person] of forty years …”

Likewise (ibid.). “When he had weighed the losses of the flesh by the gesture of a forty-year-old will,” etc. What “the gesture of a forty-year-old will” means, I do not understand; perhaps no one else does either. It suggests that one might read *quadragenariae vitae gestu*, “by the condition of a forty-year life,” since below he calls Lazarus a young man; and this is not incongruous as an indication of an age of forty years and settled maturity. To “carry on life” is to bear the burden of flesh, whose smallest particles are continually passing away, while others from without take their place, as Alfenus says in Digest 5.1.76; and that is to make up for the flesh’s losses.

Likewise (ibid.). “For already, beneath its hurrying setting,” etc. Seneca, *Hercules Furens*, v. 178:

> Life hastens  
> With rapid course.

Before him Anacreon, in the ode beginning, “Upon tender myrtles”:

> For life rolls onward  
> Like the wheel of a chariot.

> For swiftly indeed runs our age.

Likewise (ibid.). “What was owed to earthly limbs,” etc.—to man from the earth; indeed, rather to the earth than to man.

Likewise (ibid.). “So that, according to the book of Genesis, for us ourselves,” etc. Thus, according to Scripture and as is common to us, mud supplied both the cause and the material from which we were made.

Likewise (ibid.). “The finest fluid of mud,” etc. In my judgment *optimus* (“finest”) is superfluous. He called it “the fluid of mud,” that is, pliable mud of the kind required for modelling.

Likewise (ibid.). “Christ judging far otherwise,” etc. Rather, *censente*, “Christ judging,” since he did not wish dead Lazarus to be death’s slave, whom he was about to recall to life. Thus I think it should be read.

Likewise (ibid., col. 1412). “When he ceases to be what he was, a form or a fiction,” etc. He had the form of a man, but without spirit he was not a man: he was a form, a fiction, a mockery of humanity and of human pride.

Likewise (ibid.). “Heavy masses of darkness,” etc.—dense and thick darkness.

Likewise (ibid.). “Cut off, they are reborn through the alternation of increase and decrease,” etc. Tertullian, *On the Pallium*, chapter 2: “Day and night turn into one another.” But the last day is said not to return. Propertius, book II, elegy XV:

> For us, when once the brief light has set,  
> One everlasting night must be slept;

as Catullus sings, not poetically but truthfully, in poem 5, line 5.

Page 314 (ibid.). “With the hanging gape of the jaws,” etc. *Rictus* means not merely the mouth and opening, but the lips which cover the jaws; therefore by “the gape of the jaws” he means the lips. Pomponius, *Prestibula*, in Nonius: “Who is this, and why does he stand here displaying his mouth?—when I observe his lips.” Lucilius, *Satires*, book III, in the same author: “We raise our cheeks and use our mouths.” Ovid, *Metamorphoses*, book XIV:

> I shall behold jaws dripping with human blood.

The distinction which Theodore Gaza makes in Aristotle between *mandibulae* and *maxillae* is rejected by Julius Caesar Scaliger in *On the History of Animals*, book I, section 95. Hippocrates, *Prognostics*: “It is also fatal when the lips become relaxed, cold, and exceedingly pale.” At times the author offends through affectation; when corrupt writing is added to this, obscurity necessarily results.

Likewise (ibid.). “With the teeth knocked out in his mouth,” etc. If the text is free from error, it is scarcely credible that his teeth should have fallen out after lying dead for four days. If we read *interclusis dentibus*, “with his teeth shut together,” it may seem more fitting.

Likewise (ibid.). “Worn away by earthly defilement,” etc.—by earthly filth and dirt; hence he elegantly adds, “the rotten clod was decaying.”

Likewise (ibid.). “The connecting courses of the sinews,” etc. Since the sinews are joined together and, as it were, connected one to another by their courses, beginning from the brain or spinal marrow—as Hippocrates and Galen determine, whose view I find preferred to Aristotle’s, who wished them to originate from the heart, direct observation itself standing against him.

Likewise (ibid.). “With the body’s quality,” etc.—a circumlocution for the body itself.

Likewise (ibid.). “Unhappy burial would condemn him to miserable corruption.” Arnobius, book IV, with equal elegance: “And to be consumed into final decay by the wasting away of dissolving entrails.”

Likewise (ibid.). “With limbs drawn together,” etc. What Ovid said of the Isthmus in *Fasti*, book VI, 495,

> It is constricted in narrow space,

our author said of dead Lazarus, because dead limbs, having lost their life-giving juice, become smaller and more contracted.

Likewise (ibid.). “Between the lean and countable ribs,” etc.—emaciated ribs, stripped of flesh and therefore more prominent, so that they could be counted more plainly.

Likewise (ibid.). “Now a foul bilge,” etc.—the basin of the body.

Likewise (ibid.). “By the very ground of the corpse,” etc. He refers to what preceded: that is, to the earth itself more than to the man. For he wishes man to be earth, soil, ground, mud.

Likewise (ibid.). “Alas! when could it not?” etc. That is: would it have been surprising? How could it not? *Quando* is used for *quomodo*, “how.”

Likewise (ibid.). “Alas, how could a corpse, for four days and four nights, not breathe forth through the lungs’ passages foul-smelling streams of bilges—from mouth, bile, and phlegm—from its corrupt limbs?” etc. [The syntax of the quoted lemma is corrupt.] The physician Moschion, in the final chapter of the third book of Plutarch’s *Table Talk*, said: “Putrefaction is a melting and a kind of flowing of flesh which has decayed and changed into fluid.” Plutarch himself repeats this in his treatise entitled *Whether Water or Fire Is More Useful*; hence he rightly said “streams.” By “bilges,” moreover, he means the sources from which flow the streams of corrupt and inimical humours. For as the gall-bladder draws in bitter bile and expels it—and this is more liable to corruption in a living person, how much more in a dead one—so too phlegm, a cold and moist excretion, more easily decays in what has decayed, namely where that little Plautine “salt of the soul” is absent. But what did he say about the mouth? Was it because foul odours issue from its throat?

Likewise (ibid.). “When even the rose itself, with the fragrant leaf of modesty and beauty,” etc. The praises of the rose are found in Anacreon and Achilles Tatius, who make it an object of envy to all flowers. But flowers newly discovered in this age may rightly raise a controversy regarding the judgment of the ancients.

Likewise (ibid.). “Plucked from the rose-garden by the sickle of the thumb,” etc. He metaphorically called the hand itself “the sickle of the thumb,” for one plucks with thumb and forefinger brought together. Martial, book X, epigram 93:

> A rose delights when it is gathered by the first thumb.

Likewise (ibid.). “It grows pale, sad in withering death,” etc. Not only the rose, but whatever is beautiful in appearance easily vanishes. In Plato’s epigram in Diogenes Laertius, concerning an apple:

> Consider how short-lived beauty is.

Apuleius translates in the *Apology*:

> See how beauty perishes in a brief time.

Catullus, in the wedding-song, or poem LXIII, most aptly and elegantly:

> As a flower is born hidden in fenced gardens,  
> Unknown to cattle, bruised by no plough,  
> Which breezes caress, the sun strengthens, rain brings forth—  
> Many boys, many girls desire it.  
> The same flower, when plucked and withered by a tender nail,  
> No boys, no girls desire.

Anyone comparing them may observe the clear allusion of “plucked by the sickle of the thumb, it grows pale in withering death” to:

> When plucked and withered by a tender nail.

Likewise (ibid.). “So that it lacks the colour of a flower.” The manuscript adds: “So that it lacks both the flower’s colour and its scent.”

Likewise (ibid.). “Water itself, if drawn from a river,” etc. How this happens the author himself says: because it contracts mud. For water and air are intermediate elements and undergo mixture, as Aristotle teaches toward the end of book II, chapter 3, of *Generation and Corruption*. Aristotle himself gives the reason for this putrefaction in *Meteorology*, book IV, chapter 1: the greater its own inherent heat and cold, the more these exceed the powers present in the surrounding air. Hence also the sea, when divided into portions, quickly putrefies; but whole and entire it does not at all, nor do the remaining portions of water.

Likewise (ibid.). “The liquid carries off mud.” The manuscript has “covers over.”

Likewise (ibid.). The manuscript reads: “Therefore no one ought to wonder if the man whom the spirit of wisdom, seasoned with salt, had preserved in fragrant air, and whose body the soul had governed from heaven’s sweetness with nectarean vitality and honey-sweet excellence of balsam, should, through the separation of the departing spirit, become a clayey mass, ill-disposed, a sluggish and perishable clod,” etc.

Likewise (ibid.). “And had governed it with honey-sweet excellence of balsam, lest through the separation of the departing spirit it should become a clayey mass,” etc. He says: a rose torn from its rose-garden becomes torpid; water separated from its own body putrefies. What wonder if a man stinks after losing his spirit? In demonstrating this, where the meaning is wholly clear, he should undoubtedly be believed not to have written “lest it should become, through the separation of the departing [spirit],” etc., since this destroys the construction adopted; but to have written *cum*, “when,” instead of *ne*, “lest,” or something similar, which was easy for a copyist to corrupt from an abbreviated writing. Moreover, those epithets “nectarean” and “honey-sweet” are too lowly; perhaps he wrote something more suitable to this elegant discourse.

Likewise (ibid.). “The falling line of the dead,” etc. These words might be omitted; I believe they were heedlessly inserted by another, for they disfigure rather than embellish the discourse.

Likewise (ibid., col. 1413). “Hence it is that through the distance of things,” etc. What if one reads “through the discordance of things”? For things which have been compacted into one cannot be distant from one another. Their dissolution is described below most elegantly.

Likewise (ibid.). “Who [is] the body’s *floriarum*,” etc. This is a new word, hitherto uncorrupted.

Likewise (ibid.). “With livid cheek,” etc.—with a livid face showing pallor, sallow. Silius Italicus, book XIII, v. 559:

> Pale Death, everywhere opening its black mouth.

Euripides, *Electra*, 319: “But my father’s blood is still blackly decaying in the house.” Virgil, *Aeneid*, book III, 622: “And he feeds on black blood.” From this passage and Euripides it is clear that Servius’s interpretation is not to be accepted there.

Likewise (ibid.). “And instead of the voice of the corpse, the foul stench of black bile, dead [and] fetid, is drawn in,” etc. I punctuate: “And instead of the voice of the corpse, the foul stench of black bile is drawn in,” deleting the word *mortui*, “dead,” which is superfluous in sense and construction. He means that what is perceived from the corpse is a foul smell: the “voice” which the corpse gives forth is the stench from black bile, that is, dead and corrupt bile.

Page 315 (ibid.). “Who had assigned places to these four parts,” etc. That is, who kept these qualities in balance: he had not assigned them a place, but restrained and checked them in their proper place.

Likewise (ibid.). “With the whip holding sway,” etc. Reason goes before; he metaphorically calls it a whip, because it ought to govern and restrain motions after the manner of a charioteer, as Pythagoras calls it at the end of the *Golden Verses*, and Plato in the *Phaedrus*. A whip is the charioteer’s proper implement. Euripides, *Rhesus*, 766: “The goads upon the horses’ yokes,” etc.; and whips were applied to the yokes of horses. Suidas: “Goads and the horses’ whips.” Euripides, *Iphigenia at Aulis*, 220. Moreover, Plutarch too calls reason “the divine guide of life” in his poem *On Listening*.

Likewise (ibid.). “This Lazarus, then, whose limbs had wasted away through the blue veins with a wandering livid tightening,” etc. Here I must be silent and refrain even from conjectures: so blind am I that I see nothing; and in the manuscript these words are most corrupt.

Likewise (ibid.). “Covered by a monstrous weight, the heavy balance of the everlasting door had thrust him down after his fall,” etc. I think one may read: “covered by the monstrous weight of a stone, the heavy balance had thrust him beneath an everlasting door.” He calls the door everlasting because it was never to be opened for him. He preferred the singular *valva* for plural doors. By “heavy balance” he means what poets call inexorable Fate, *Atropos*, “the unturning one”: “all things that are past are unalterable,” as the author of *On the World*, chapter 7, says. Apuleius translates: “Atropos, the fate of time past, which not even God will make undone”; but he has not rendered the Greek words, which mean: “For what has passed cannot be turned back or restored.” If we prefer *lapsis*, as in the printed texts, we shall say that it was used archaically for *lapidis*, “of stone,” a usage supported by Ennius, book XV of the *Annals*:

> Many fall in death, by sword and by stone.

Likewise (ibid.). “Drunk with abundant tears,” etc. This is said metaphorically: as if they had been abstaining from food and drink and were dry, they were wetted and drenched by the abundance of tears.

Likewise (ibid.). “And Hebrew utterances,” etc.—in Hebrew speech and language, which was natural and customary to them. The manuscript has “and Hebrew utterances, Greekifying,” which I do not understand.

Likewise (ibid.). “They purified, mingled in the Saviour’s praises,” etc. Zeno is always hostile to the Hebrews and never omits an opportunity to prick them; hence one might believe that he meant Hebrew words otherwise hateful to Christ, purified by his praises. What if, instead of *expiabant*, “they purified,” one reads *complicabant*, “they intertwined,” which would not be alien to the author’s manner? But whichever sense one follows, I advise deleting the preposition *in*, thus: “mingled with the Saviour’s praises.” The manuscript punctuates: “Hebrew utterances, mingled with broken sobs into one, they purified in the Saviour’s praises.”

Page 316 (ibid., col. 1414). “He is said to have wept.” The manuscript reads: “He is said to have wept. Come, come, Photamius, servant of the living God, if you have any power, tell us at least something about the Lord’s tears. God wept, stirred by the tears of mortals.”

Likewise (ibid.). “The devil, by his own malice, caused the guilty to be discovered. Alas, frail breath from heaven, you were leaving the body which you had governed amid falling limbs; but neither Father nor Son ever despised you: Christ himself became mortal for his own death. At these tears,” etc. These words are omitted in the printed edition.

Likewise (ibid.). “But that he might temper the sisters’ weeping.” What he says below, “he counter-sounded weeping with weeping,” means in unison. Aristides Quintilianus, book I, *On Music*: “Unison sounds are those which have a different power of voice but retain equal pitch.” Whatever *recontrabat* may be, I would rather amend it to *econtrabat*, formed from *econtra*, “in return.”

Likewise (ibid., col. 1415). “And himself as an example of virtues,” etc. I punctuate: “And, as an example of virtues, he himself who had been …” so that they might learn Christ’s power. The passage is otherwise read in the manuscript: “And, as an example of virtues, he himself, dead and still bound at the feet, as Christ had commanded, loosed himself with his own hands. What, I ask you,” etc.

Page 317 (ibid.). “The attack is directed against the parents,” etc. Cicero, *Against Verres*, book VII, joins *parents* and kinsfolk. Formerly *parentes* meant father, mother, and those in the place of parents. Gaius, in Digest 50.16, *On the Meaning of Words*, says that later, in a subsequent age, all who were connected in any way were called so. Julius Capitolinus, *Gordian III*, chapter 23: “He married the daughter of Misitheus, whom, because of his eloquence, he thought worthy of relationship with himself.” Flavius Vopiscus, *Aurelian*, chapter 31: “Certain kinsman of Zenobia, Achilleus, preparing to seize power.” The same, *Tacitus*, chapter 10: “Cornelius Tacitus, whom he called his relative.” “The attack is directed against the parents,” that is, against Mary and Martha, his sisters, as I agree with Casaubon in his note on Capitolinus’s *Marcus*.

## ON THE MARTYRDOM OF THE PROPHET ISAIAH, RELEGATED TO THE APPENDIX

Likewise (ibid.). It is certain that Isaiah’s martyrdom is not found in Holy Scripture, but, disseminated from an apocryphal work, it is mentioned by many. Let Justin Martyr, in the *Dialogue with Trypho*, 349; Tertullian, *Scorpiace*, chapter 8; and Origen, both in his *Commentary on Matthew*, 225, and in his reply to Africanus, 232, stand for all. Whether it was true or false I do not investigate. Huet reports, in his note on the former passage of Origen, that among the Hebrews it is held as certain.

Likewise (ibid., col. 1415). “When Isaiah foretold Christ, or when [he uttered] the sentence of future condemnation,” etc. The cause is uncertain, nor is there any certainty among other authors. Some, in Origen’s first homily on Isaiah, believed that he was sawn apart as one who transgressed the law.

Page 318 (ibid.). “By violent punishment he split him in two, as though into bifurcated lumps,” etc. An *offa* is a piece of flesh in the form of a rounded mass; hence Martial calls it curved, in his final book, epigram 221. It was then called *penita* when joined with a tail; for *penis* anciently meant “tail.” See Festus under *Penis* and *penita offa*; Arnobius, book VII, 230: “A *penita offa* is when part of an internal organ is cut off together with the tail of a beast.” Isidore, *Etymologies*, book XX, chapter 2. I do not know whence he got the notion that *offa* properly means a fragment of teeth. Or was the jaw, by some resemblance, in that later age called *offa* and *offula*? Our author used the term for a part torn from the body, and for any severed portion of flesh.

Likewise (ibid.). “Or the very blade, with the shrieking stroke of a cruel cord across the ribs, might furrow the innocent man through a field,” etc. I follow the opinion of Octavius Ferrari, “the blessed man,” who in *Select Studies*, book I, chapter 6, teaches that *fidiculae* were sinews or cords by which the limbs of a martyr or crucified person were bound extremely tightly, so that the swelling part might be torn more cruelly. Hence the metaphor of the field and furrowing. For claws cut the limbs apart, and as they ran along the ribs they made a shrieking sound by striking against the bones. In any case, the distorted syntax cries out that the text is corrupt.

Likewise (ibid.). “But in so great a miracle of the heavenly wrestling-ground, no one, as I suppose, at the spectacle rebounding, will be able thus to behold him who tries to count the deeds,” etc. I perceive that this is corrupt and perhaps should be reconstructed thus: “But in so great a miracle of the heavenly wrestling-ground, no one, as I suppose, with the spectacle resisting, will thus be able to behold,” etc. Some spectacles are pleasant, to which we gladly direct our sight; others are unpleasant and inhuman, which we abhor even in thought and from which we turn our eyes. Such is the case in Sophocles’ *Oedipus Tyrannus*, 1305:

> … such as might move even an enemy to pity.

For, as Polybius says somewhere, 721: “No one delights in lingering over things contrary to nature.” A spectacle, then, is said to resist when it repels the viewer, as happened—though for a different reason—in Aeschylus’ tragedy *Eumenides*: when the chorus entered onto the stage, “it so struck the people with terror that the little children fainted and pregnant women miscarried,” as the author of Aeschylus’ life relates.

Likewise (ibid.). “He will be able thus to behold him,” etc.; the manuscript has “he will be able thus to behold himself.”

Likewise (ibid.). “Observe the new solemnity of sufferings within the old discipline,” etc. From the old dignity, observe how great is the dignity of Christian suffering because of Christ’s martyrdom. Tertullian, *Scorpiace*, chapter 8, concerning those before Christ: “As soon as God began to be worshipped, religion acquired envy; he who had pleased God is slain.” Then concerning Christians: “Certainly those who were moved by the Spirit of God were directed by him himself toward martyrdom.” Finally he concludes: “Such commandments and examples from the beginning show faith to be indebted to martyrdom.”

Likewise (ibid., col. 1416). “When, in the head—that is, in the centre of gathered sensation,” etc. He calls the head the centre, that is, the centre of all sensation; for in the head every motion and sensation takes its beginning, which the subject limbs execute in obedience. As the heart is the workshop of vital spirits, so the animal spirits reside in the brain, where also lies the seat of all the senses. Pliny, book II, chapter 37: “There they have the citadel of the senses; thither the whole force of the veins tends from the heart; there it ends; there is the loftiest summit; there is the governance of the mind.”

Likewise (ibid.). “And with reciprocal grinding he might trace furrows with his teeth, he was slipping,” etc. These limbs collide with one another and produce something discordant—whether through the author’s fault or that of copyists, I do not know. Once he has completed the teeth-grinding, he proceeds to begin on the crop of hair and the stripped scalp, which is out of order.

Likewise (ibid.). “He plunged the Hebrew letters of the head into the pot-sherd of the crown,” etc. It is more well known than needs saying that the priestly office was one thing and the prophetic office another. That the high priests, among the ornaments of priestly dress, also had on their head, upon the mitre, the name of God inscribed upon a gold plate, is known from Exodus, chapter XXVIII, beginning at verse 36. But this was neither permanent in the high priest, nor on the skin, nor common to a prophet. What, then, these words of Zeno mean—of Potamius, not Zeno, as is clear from our Admonition—it is better to confess that I do not understand than to invent notions of another’s devising which, far from clarifying, would rather obscure an already most obscure sentence.

Likewise (ibid.). “The anxious cutter, by the effort of his fitting, had fixed,” etc. That he might keep to the middle of the spine and the saw might not deviate to either side—a concern requiring careful attention amid so great an articulation of bones—he calls it, in his own manner, “the effort of fitting.” The manuscript has *nissus est*, which means “by effort” (*nixu*).

Likewise (ibid.). “The streams of a crimson fountain, with the channels of the veins loosened,” etc.—with the ducts laid open and exposed, blood would fall, no longer in drops that could be wiped away with a finger, but in a rush and flood that would overwhelm the entire body. Moreover, the punctuation should be corrected: two points have no place after “he poured down rain,” but a comma should replace them, thus: “he poured down rain, so that the roofs [were covered] by the flood.”

Likewise (ibid.). “Lest the profane man should [tear] the veins with his thumb in little-worm fashion,” etc. The manuscript has *profanatus*, “having profaned.”

Likewise (ibid.). “He would neither tremble nor wonder what that was by which the conquered man was forced to blush,” etc. Perhaps one should read: “He would neither terrify nor wonder, whatever it might be, by which the conquered man was forced to blush.” That is, he did not accuse the deed or reproach the author of his murder. For what would he reproach, if the deed itself ought to have forced him to shame, or if he had perpetrated things so undeserved and so atrocious upon the prophet? He calls him conquered who had contrived the prophet’s murder, when he saw him undaunted and, though near death, a despiser of death. Eusebius, *Ecclesiastical History*, book V, chapter 1: “For they were not restrained by shame at having been conquered by the martyrs, because they possessed no human reasoning.” They are distressed when they cannot accomplish what they strain to achieve, and are therefore conquered. Achilles Tatius, book VI, 407: “Behold a new contest: one woman contends against every torture and conquers all.” That is, she persists in her resolve and is not moved, however much she is worn away and mangled by your torments.

Likewise (ibid.). “So that, covered by the flood,” etc. The manuscript has: “So that, covered by the flood of blood, the pattern of veins might not tremble, and he might wonder what that was by which the conquered man was forced to blush.”

Likewise (ibid.). “For the inner organs were laid bare,” etc. Thus far in this discourse we have proceeded through circumlocutions and perhaps added conjectures alien to the author’s mind, since we could not do otherwise in so tangled and confused a labyrinth. Yet, having progressed thus far somehow or other, we have decided to pause for a little while; for to linger fruitlessly over certain things is neither praiseworthy nor worth the labour. First, we must confess our ignorance of the *castidicus* young man of whom he speaks [the term is uncertain]. Since Isaiah was already an old man, eighty and beyond—for he is said to have lived that long—he does not deserve the name “young man.” We may understand “latticed transactions” to mean the intestines, which are folded back upon themselves in winding coils and bends, as Aristotle says; but what has this to do with the rest? What is the sound of a striking trumpet? Nor is any assistance to be obtained from the acts of this martyrdom. In place of Belial, it is certain that Manasseh son of Hezekiah is meant, under whom, as St Jerome says, Isaiah perished sawn in two. But when he calls him “prodigal of genealogy,” we remain uncertain whether he meant to disparage his offspring and successor—which Matthew chapter I refutes: “Manasseh begot Amon”—or something else that I cannot even conceive.

Page 319 (ibid.). “A bloody man and prodigal of genealogy.” My mind still longs to attempt these matters. Nothing concerning profligacy is imputed to Manasseh either in the sacred writings or in Josephus. Therefore this text is suspect. It is not credible that Zeno, furnished with knowledge of events and steeped in sacred reading, wished to ascribe to him an undeserved fault. I would therefore judge that *cruoris prodigus*, “prodigal of blood,” should rather be read in place of *cruentus et prodigus*, “bloody and prodigal.” Josephus supports this: in *Antiquities*, book X, chapter 4, he says under this king: “Jerusalem overflowed with blood.” Moreover, for the reasons already stated, I do not see why he should have called him “prodigal of genealogy.” Thus we shall say that the text does not proceed correctly; and if the matter were left to my judgment, I would write *genethliacus* in place of *genealogiae*. For the title *genethliaci* properly fits those whom he rightly attributes as Manasseh’s dependants, from 2 Kings [4 Kings], chapter XXI, verse 6. Aulus Gellius, at the beginning of book XIV, calls *genethliaci* those who profess to be able to foretell future events from the movement and position of the stars. But Manilius, book I, folio 2, from verse 30, puts it more closely and properly:

> First by their art they perceived fates dependent on the wandering stars:  
> On what day each person would be born, what life he would have,  
> Under what laws of fortune each hour would hold power.

They inquire into a person’s birth-chart and hour of birth in order to adapt their predictions to the course of that person’s life.

Likewise (ibid.). “An astrologer (*mathematicus*), chief of catabolici, diviners, and pythonic practitioners,” etc. The manuscript reads *phitidicorum* for *fatidicorum*, a monstrous reading. In its proper meaning, a *mathematicus* is one who knows the disciplines and who, being occupied with them, seems to have attained the object he desired with the praise and renown of his name, as Cicero says near the beginning of book I of *On the Orator*. But common usage meant something else: those who ought to have been called Chaldeans by their pagan name began to be called *mathematici*, as Aulus Gellius, book I, chapter 9, says—namely, those who subject human fates to the power of the stars. Sextus Empiricus, book V: “The Chaldeans, adorning genealogy with more imposing names, call themselves mathematicians and astrologers.” Hence magicians, enchanters, mathematicians, and astrologers are held equivalent in canon 36 of the Synod of Laodicea.

Likewise (ibid.). “Chief of catabolici, diviners, and pythonic practitioners.” Tertullian, *On the Soul*, chapter 28, at the end: “We know also that magic is permitted to explore hidden matters through catabolic, attendant, and pythonic spirits.” From Tertullian’s cited passage we are certain of the word *catabolici*, about which we formerly doubted; but we do not have an interpretation of it to our satisfaction. For Turnebus’s explanation in his *Adversaria* does not please us at all, although it appears approved by Leo Allatius in his work *On Engastrimyths*, chapter 4; consult him, and there his discussion of pythonic practitioners.

Likewise (ibid.). “Within the breastplate of the sacred breast, the assembly of faith, of preaching,” etc. From these words Isaiah seems to have been dissected as though they were seeking future things from his entrails, which contradicts the reasons touched upon at the beginning of the discourse. It would be useless to remind one that “sacred breast” here stands for the heart in which the mind resides, and “breastplate” for the bones which nature placed around the chest and vital organs.

Likewise (ibid.). “He sought the council-chamber of the civic preaching of letters,” etc. I read *litterariam curiam*, “the literary council-chamber,” as though they hoped to see written upon his heart what he had preached or would preach. For the council-chamber is the temple of mind and deliberation, as Cicero calls it in *For Milo*.

Likewise (ibid.). “And what that might be,” etc. I read “and such that might be.”

Likewise (ibid.). “He was forced to blush.” The manuscript has “he wondered.”

Likewise (ibid.). “With others’ teeth,” etc.—[read] “with a saw.”

Likewise (ibid.). “The sawyers lying back and hanging,” etc. For they ought to have stood bent and stooping, that they might draw and redraw the saw upon the lower parts.

Likewise (ibid.). “Who condemned the figures of the nations together with their persecutor,” etc. Justin Martyr, *Dialogue with Trypho*: “If your teachers understood them, believe me, they would have recognized those things written concerning Isaiah’s slaughter—Isaiah whom you cut apart with a wooden saw. This also is a mystery: Christ will cut your race in two, counting some worthy, those who believe in him, together with the holy patriarchs and prophets, worthy of the eternal kingdom; but sending the others, unbelievers together with the nations, to condemnation.”

## ON THE INTERPRETATION OF PSALM CXXVI, RELEGATED TO THE APPENDIX

Page 322 (*our Patrologia*, vol. IX, col. 692). It is contrary to Zeno’s manner to concern himself with histories and to investigate superstitiously the times at which those events occurred which are prefigured in the sacred books. For he has always particularly endeavoured to lead the people where, under Christ the chief Shepherd, he might impress Christian teaching upon the minds of the faithful, leaving nothing to be sought from him in carrying out his assigned ministry. In this work likewise he uses long digressions beyond his usual practice, and, in applying prophecy alone, directs himself to a certain external inquiry which contributes nothing to the spirit and everything to empty curiosity. Otherwise accustomed to probe his hearers’ minds with keen discourse, he is more *didactic* (*didaskalikos*) than *exegetical* (*exēgētikos*); moreover, the exegesis itself is enthusiastic and incoherent. For example: what is the point of the long digression (*parekbasis*) on the house of God? He should rather have laboured to show that divine favour is required—according to the prophet’s purpose—for every kind of house, spiritual and bodily, animate and inanimate. Even if the prophet perhaps set before himself the Temple at Jerusalem, the text might more fruitfully be applied simply to any house and city, indeed to every human undertaking, in which, unless the Lord assists, a person can accomplish nothing. Nor is it sufficiently established that a Christian full of God’s virtues and teachings, like a house built upon these foundations by the Lord, ought not to be guarded by his own care; since Christ commands even his chosen apostles to watch and pray lest temptation deceive them, and St Paul says in Romans, chapter XI, verse 22: “See therefore the goodness and severity of God: severity indeed toward those who fell, but goodness toward you, if you continue in goodness; otherwise you too will be cut off.” Therefore effort must come from our side, so that we may uphold what God has bestowed upon us. Human nature’s weakness is indeed extreme; but divine grace is present for one resisting temptations, as the same Apostle teaches in 2 Corinthians, chapter XII, verse 8. I pass over the rest, for since these words are found verbatim in Hilary of Poitiers, I believe justice required that they be left to him and that Zeno’s conscience not be burdened with another’s labour. That they are Hilary’s is further indicated by the fact that he is said to have copied Origen’s work on the Psalms; if one considers the matter correctly, this is wholly an Origenian method of interpretation, as is clear by comparison with what remains of Origen’s commentaries on Sacred Scripture.

## ON THE INTERPRETATION OF PSALM CXXVII, RELEGATED TO THE APPENDIX
Page 330 (Vol. IX of our edition, col. 703). The discourse on Psalm 127 is found in the same words in the *Syntagma* of the works of Hilary of Poitiers; but, just as we did not hesitate to restore the preceding one to him, neither have we ventured altogether to deprive our author of this one. For it has a Zenonian flavour, and that elegant majesty by which Isaac Casaubon, a man of most penetrating judgment, thought him pre-eminent among the Latin Fathers. Moreover, the author is consistent with himself in this discourse, just as he wanders in the other; hence one may very readily recognize the offspring of a different genius. Yet in the treatise on Fear (now Treatise VIII, Book I) you find the same thoughts, the same fragments of expression, the same conceptions of mind—indeed, more tersely and compactly expressed—so that you may recognize that he composed that one earlier and this one later, and that both are the work of the same mind [Col. 0595B] (see our Dissertation I, ch. 1, §2, and the notes on Treatise 8, Book I).

In the same place (ibid.). “That it is never left solitary,” etc. The fear of the Lord is obedience to the commandments, and it is also called holy in Psalm 18, v. 10. When it is stirred by faith, instructed by commandments, imbued with piety, and strengthened by the will, it produces wisdom. Since, therefore, it is born with this fellowship of virtues, it cannot be called solitary.

In the same place (ibid., col. 704). “What was spoken through Solomon in Proverbs,” etc., ch. 2, no. 3, which the Scholia of the Seventy Interpreters attribute to Hilary; yet I am not persuaded by their authority. Certainly, this discourse agrees so closely with the discourse on Fear that its thoughts are indeed Zeno’s, while its diction and composition are not dissimilar, so that scarcely any room remains for doubt.

Page 331 (ibid.). “Of one who fears undergoing what he would not wish to happen to himself,” etc. Below, in the discourse on Fear: “But you fear what you would not wish to happen to yourself.” Aristotle, *Ethics*, Book III, ch. 9: “We plainly fear fearful things; and these are, to put it simply, evils.” The entire passage should be read from the manuscript: “But so far as concerns the common trembling of human weakness, it belongs to one who fears to undergo what he would not wish to happen to himself. There arises and is stirred within us concerning guilt,” etc.

In the same place (ibid.). “Therefore this fear is not taught,” etc. Below, in the discourse on Fear (now Treatise VIII, Book I): “The fear of God is both learned and taught, because it consists not in trembling but in the principle of instruction; as it is written: ‘Come, children, hear me; I will teach you the fear of God.’” It follows: “But it arises from the weakness of nature”; the manuscript reads, “but from the nature of weakness.”

In the same place (ibid., col. 705). “But if someone should fear and yet not spare”: read from the manuscript, “and yet not obey.”

Page 332 (ibid.). “Now there are many ways of the Lord,” etc. Origen, in his ninth volume on John, teaches that there are very many ways of removing sin: some are plainly visible to the multitude, while others become known only to those who, enlightened by divine [Col. 0595D] wisdom, can recognize them. Among these he includes scourges, evil spirits, most grievous diseases, and most burdensome infirmities. In a word, this is the cross which Christ commands one who wishes to come after him to take up; as Clement of Alexandria says in *Stromata*, Book VII, it is taken up not from necessity, fear, or hope, but from a free resolve of mind. He calls it the royal way, trodden by the royal race: “This very way is called royal, which the royal race travels.”

In the same place (ibid.). “Teaching us all.” The manuscript punctuates better: “teaching us, all who have believed in Christ, to be one,” etc.

In the same place (ibid., col. 706). “The labours of fruits to be eaten,” etc.; in Greek: “You shall eat the labours of your fruits.” The Greek scholiasts note: “They called not the yield ‘fruit,’ but the part of the hands.” Symmachus, cited by Theodoret, has: “eating the labour of your hands,” to which they add: “Thus it is plain that the Seventy also called not the yield ‘fruits,’ but the part of the hands.” Yet our writer displays the sharpness of his intellect even in this difficult interpretation of the Psalm. Fruit is the reward of labour, not labour the reward of fruits. But what we work for God is spiritual; thus to “eat the labours of fruits” is to obtain a reward from the fruit of goodness, chastity, mercy, patience, and tranquillity—fruits by which our soul must be nourished in this bodily life, so that it may enjoy eternal goods.

Page 333 (ibid., col. 707). “That from the mercy of God [there may be] peaceful and useful,” etc.: the governing verb is lacking; restore from the manuscript: “That through the mercy of God there may be supplied peaceful and useful,” etc.

In the same place (ibid.). “But even if these had been perfect goods, they are nevertheless not heavenly goods,” etc. In Psalm 126, no. 3, children are called the inheritance of the Lord; but this inheritance is not always pleasant or welcome, since it is neither perpetual—indeed, it is rare—that children are a joy to their parents. There is a proverbial expression: “The children of heroic men are calamities,” to which Euripides’ *Oenomaus*, in Stobaeus, Title 76, corresponds: “Born of evil character, [they are] a most hateful plague.” Moreover, he did not call children perfect goods, taking his example from Abraham, who remained childless into decrepit old age although he was acceptable and pleasing to God; and from Isaac’s sons, who disturbed their father’s affections by fraternal discord although he too enjoyed divine favour. Nor does he allow them to be called heavenly goods, since they are denied to saints, common among sinners, and not to be hoped for by virgins, whose unmarried condition is proclaimed happier.

In the same place (ibid.). “Whose wife, long barren, was twice seized,” etc. Once in Egypt, Genesis ch. 12; again at Gerar in Palestine by Abimelech, Genesis ch. 20.

In the same place (ibid.). “And, mourning the funeral of one still alive through the parricidal lie of his brothers.” He means Joseph, whom his father mourned as dead after he had been sold by his brothers, Genesis ch. 37.

Page 335 (ibid., col. 709). “But there is no doubt that this is the dwelling-place of our soul,” etc. Justin Martyr, *Dialogue with Trypho*: “The mystery and hidden meaning of the lamb which God commanded to be sacrificed at Passover was a type and figure of Christ. Those who believe in him sprinkle their houses—that is, themselves—with his blood, according to the measure of their faith in him.””

In the same place (ibid.). “Unless they are engaged in the service of good works,” etc.: the word *good* is absent from the manuscript.

In the same place (ibid.). “As it were, of the choicest labours”: the manuscript has *opimorum*, “richest” or “most abundant.”

In the same place (ibid.). “It is planted in this earth of our body”: the manuscript has *plantantur*, “they are planted,” and this, I think, is correct.

Page 336 (ibid.). “Standing by; and because,” etc. The manuscript’s reading is: “standing by like olive plants around the circuit of our table, because this is the blessedness of those who fear [God].” The prophet [Col. 0596D] adds: “Behold, thus shall [the man] be blessed,” etc.

In the same place (ibid., col. 710). “We have frequently spoken of Jerusalem and Zion in the preceding Psalms,” etc. From this you may argue that he published discourses on other Psalms and that they have perished. Others take it as an argument for Hilary: since he wrote on the preceding Psalms, and in them something may be read concerning Jerusalem and Zion, this discourse too, they say, must be attributed to Hilary. But the subject of Zion and Jerusalem could have been common to all, as we see everywhere. It is established that Zeno lived centuries before Hilary. Therefore, since very many and the principal matters in this discourse are found borrowed from the discourse on Fear, which bears our author’s name, either that discourse too must be rejected from him, or, just as that must be assigned to Zeno, so must this; or else Hilary must be said to have stolen from Zeno. In so great an uncertainty I conclude, with Origen concerning Paul’s Epistle to the Hebrews: “If anyone holds the same account as Zeno, let him be approved for this as well. For the ancients did not without reason hand it down as Zeno’s. But who wrote the discourse, God knows the truth.”

## ON THE INTERPRETATION OF PSALM 128, RELEGATED TO THE APPENDIX

Page 337 (ibid., col. 711). “The virtue of a religious man is not idle, nor does it require a quiet life,” etc. They wrongly attempt to correct this to “a life is not idle.” The marginal notes in the Veronese edition are for the most part erroneous, and, while attempting correction, they grievously corrupt the text. The reading must be *virtue*, as is indicated by the author’s statement a little below: “but these are often hostile even from the very beginnings of life.” Had he said *life* earlier, he would not have repeated *life*. It is further confirmed below by: “Yet struggle is not sufficient for the crown,” etc. It is as though this contest must be carried through by virtue that is steadfast, enduring, and continuous—which belongs to virtue, not to life. For the more our enemy sees us rebelling against him, the more eagerly he strives to overcome us; for he neglects to assail those whom he perceives himself to possess by peaceful [Col. 0597B] right, to use the words and thought of Gregory the Great, Homily 2.

Page 338 (ibid., col. 712). “First to become enslaved through the plundering of his substance,” etc. I read *desaeviturus*, “first to rage violently against.”

In the same place (ibid.). “And no one accomplishes it of himself who does anything through the onset of a turbulent will,” etc. *Non sibi efficit* is a novel form of expression for *non a se efficit*, “does not accomplish it by himself.” Aristotle expresses something similar to Zeno’s meaning in *Ethics*, Book II, ch. 4: “We are not called good or bad according to passions, just as we are called so according to habits of virtues or vices, because we are said to be moved according to passions, but according to virtues and vices not to be moved, but to be disposed.”

In the same place (ibid.). “Or we are urged by an incitement to nourish bodily pleasures,” etc. Clement of Alexandria, *Paedagogue*, Book III, ch. 7, sets pleasure in opposition to the honourable. For if everyone is allowed to eat anything, drink anything, and indulge freely in sexual intercourse at will, an impious pursuit of riches and contempt for divine commandments will arise; thereby we shall be excluded from the inheritance of God’s kingdom. To secure this result, our enemy offers the enticement of pleasures, which is the most powerful of all.

In the same place (ibid.). “But rather, in these persons, the intervention of a detestable service is foul and pitiable, because they are vessels of the devil,” etc. Titus, in Philostratus’ *Life of Apollonius*, Book VI, ch. 14, refused crowns offered after the Jews had been conquered and Jerusalem taken, because he said that he himself had not accomplished such deeds, but had merely lent his hands to the wrath of God when it manifested itself. In the same manner Clement of Alexandria, *Stromata*, Book VII, calls the devil in our sins a *synergos* (“co-worker”) rather than an *energos* (“agent”); what this means he explains in the final commentary on the entire work of the *Stromata*, saying: “*Synergos* signifies service and working jointly with another.” Such a subordinate minister is called a *ferialis minister* in Law VI, *On the Custody of Accused Persons*, in the Theodosian Code, Book IX, title 3.

[Col. 0597D] Page 339 (ibid., col. 713). “They have often attacked me from my youth,” etc. The manuscript reads differently: “They have often attacked me from my youth—let Israel now say: What should he say?” Then, as though taught and imbued with the example of the prophet’s confession, Israel himself now speaks.

In the same place (ibid.). “Because it is necessary to repeat what is both long continued and never attained,” etc. Appius Claudius in Livy, Book V, ch. 6: “It was of the highest importance for military discipline that our soldier become accustomed, if the matter were slower, to endure weariness and await an outcome, however late the hope; and, if the war was not completed in summer, to spend the winter under arms.” Augustine depicts our adversary of this kind in *On the Singular Life of Clerics*: “For so long the devil hides the dormant fire without any flames, until, joining two torches, he sets both ablaze at once; and for so long he refrains from applying the weapons of his cruelty, until, like an experienced hunter, he binds with the cords of a snare that which he intends to kill.”

[Col. 0598A] In the same place (ibid.). “And hence the constancy of the assault upon us is due to the fact that the strength of those assailing us is not overpowering,” etc. For the reason why he attacks continually is that he does not conquer; and from this his weakness is demonstrated.

In the same place (ibid.). “It is the custom of those who do not prevail in long and continuous battles to approach from the rear a victorious army advancing in firm ranks,” etc. Vegetius, Book III, ch. 9: “If he recognizes that his adversary is stronger, he avoids an open engagement; for forces fewer in number and inferior in strength, falling unexpectedly upon the enemy and laying ambushes, have often won victory under good commanders.”

In the same place (ibid.). “Thus sinners also vainly tempt faithful men,” etc. The manuscript has “tempt,” and this is correct; it refers to what was said above: “In every injury, therefore, which we suffer, one party’s is the deed, another’s the instigation.”

In the same place (ibid.). “They were fashioning: for this has the force of an indefinite tense,” etc. He is mistaken. It has the force not of an indefinite but of an imperfect tense; *chronos aoristos* (“indefinite time”) is one thing, *chronos paratatikos* (“imperfect or durative time”) another. Hesychius defines *paratatikos* as “extended,” as it were, prolonged in an unfinished action. Thus Pliny, in the preface to his *Natural History*, testifies that Apelles and Polyclitus inscribed *faciebat* (“was making”) upon their works, as though their art were always only begun and unfinished, so that against the variety of judgments the artist might retain recourse to pardon, as if intending to correct whatever was lacking. Diomedes, Book I, ch. 4: “The imperfect past, that is, past but not completed: when we affirm that time has, as it were, passed, yet we have only begun and have not completed; hence some have called it the inceptive tense.”

Page 340 (ibid., col. 714). “And, as though [making] a long rope, always extending these things interwoven,” etc. The manuscript reads: “And, as a rope, in its manner, extending continually in length [things] interwoven,” etc., fol. 141.

In the same place (ibid.). “Moses *arcuit* to the Lord”: the manuscript has *arguit*, “argued” or “reasoned.”

Page 341 (ibid., col. 715). “Conforming the body of our humility to the glory of his body.” Correct from the manuscript: “the body of our humanity.”

In the same place (ibid.). “For the hatred of all unbelievers against the faithful is special,” etc. Thus Tertullian, *Apology*, ch. 1, reproaches the Gentiles because they condemned Christians, convicted of no crime, through hatred alone; for Aristotle, *Rhetoric*, Book II, ch. 4, states that hatred arising from a preconceived opinion may occur against classes.

In the same place (ibid.). “Returning to their earthly and original elements,” etc. Prudentius, *On the Funeral Rites of the Dead*:

> If perhaps an earthly will  
> Savours of clay and seeks what is heavy,  
> The mind also, conquered by the weight,  
> Follows its limbs downward.

In the same place (ibid.). “Feeling shame for their iniquity at the time of judgment”: in the manuscript, *suae* (“their”) is absent, more elegantly.

In the same place (ibid.). “Having lost the transformation of resurrection,” etc. I think that, in writing this, he had before his eyes St Paul’s passage in Philippians ch. 3, v. 21: “From whom we also await a Saviour, the Lord Jesus Christ, who will transform the body of our humiliation so that it may be conformed to the body of his glory.” Hence: “From whom we also await our Saviour, the Lord Jesus [Col. 0598D] Christ, who will reform the body of our humility, making it conformable to the body of his glory.”

Page 342 (ibid., col. 716). “Human bodies are either firm or [fall] through unbelief,” etc.; the manuscript reads: “Human bodies are either firm through faith or destined to fall through unbelief.”

In the same place (ibid.). “For conscience reaps more than it bears,” etc. Read *gestat*, “bears,” so that the sense may stand; and so the manuscript reads. Moreover, although this Commentary on Psalm 129 is found in Hilary in almost exactly the same words, I nevertheless would not dare [Note: [Col. 0598D] See the General Preface, no. 2, and especially the introduction to the first dissertation at its end.] to take it from Zeno, since it is said to be attributed to him in an old manuscript. By the interdict *uti possidetis*, as jurists say, our author must prevail. Certainly it shares much with Zeno, unless we say that Hilary adapted it for his own use and added some things, especially from the middle onward, where it seems to depart from Zeno. [Col. 0599A] But the following discourse on Psalm 129, in my judgment, differs in such an economy, rationale, and manner of expression that I believe I can attest, without fraudulent intent, that it is not Zeno’s.

## ON THE INTERPRETATION OF PSALM 130, RELEGATED TO THE APPENDIX

Page 350 (ibid., col. 725). Concerning the later discourse [Note: [Col. 0599A] See the introduction to Dissertation I at the end, and ch. 1, §2 of that dissertation, together with the Preface to the Appendix.] on Psalm 130, which is found in Hilary and in which virtually all the arguments and stylistic colours found in [Col. 0600A] the earlier discourse occur, it must be concluded either that it is rightly Zeno’s, in keeping with his habit of repeatedly returning to matters already treated in one discourse, or that it has been patched together out of the earlier one. Certainly it is not to be attributed to Hilary, since its structure is Zeno’s, its thought is his, and its manner of expression is his, except insofar as it is either more compressed or arranged somewhat differently. Hence it is also clear that those who ascribed the discourses on Psalms 127 and 128 to Hilary incurred the charge of plagiarism, although an evil hand intervened, corrupted the text in order to embellish it, and mixed flat wine with wine. There remain no observations on this discourse which have not been noted on the earlier one. I therefore add nothing.

Page 351 (ibid., col. 726). “But with the heart, from which according to the Gospel.” The manuscript has: “But the heart, from which,” etc.

# SECOND APPENDIX, COMPRISING TWO BOOKS ON THE DISCOURSES AND MARTYRDOM OF SAINT ZENO, WITH TWO DISSERTATIONS APPENDED TO THEM, BY FRANCESCO BONACCHI

[Col. 0599]

[Col. 0599]

## [ON THE DISCOURSES AND MARTYRDOM OF ST ZENO]

# BOOK ONE: ON THE DISCOURSES OF SAINT ZENO, BISHOP OF VERONA

## CHAPTER I. Reasons for doubting whether St Zeno is the author of the discourses bearing his name

[Col. 0599B]

Scholars differ in their judgment concerning the discourses attributed to St Zeno. Some, especially more recent writers, believe that St Zeno wrote none of them; the works published under his name, they say, are a collection of discourses having several authors. Others judge more correctly that Zeno published the discourses in question, with certain exceptions. Yet they are chiefly led to doubt their authorship for the following reasons: namely, that these discourses were entirely unknown in antiquity; that a number of them occur in other authors—for example, the discourses on the Psalms, which are read in almost exactly the same words in the commentaries of St Hilary; and that the discourses on “Take heed to yourself” and on Envy and Jealousy appear, both from their style and their general argument, to be by St Basil. But the greatest weight added to these doubts comes from chronological conjecture. For St Zeno is said to have undergone martyrdom in 360, under the emperor Gallienus; yet the author of these discourses is clearly far removed from Gallienus’ time, since in the discourse on Continence, citing St Paul’s First Epistle to the Corinthians, he reckons almost four hundred years from the writing of that epistle, which is believed to have been sent to the Corinthians in the fifty-seventh year of Christ. Again, in certain [Col. 0599D] discourses he refutes the errors of Arius, whose impious doctrines were condemned by decree of the Council of Nicaea in A.D. 325, during Arius’s lifetime, and committed to the flames by the order of Emperor Constantine. We shall examine these reasons, and any others there may be, and, God willing, demonstrate what judgment should be made in this question. First, however, we shall show that the author of these discourses was not unknown to the ancients; then we shall examine with the greatest care the opinions of more recent scholars.

## CHAPTER II. The discourses of St Zeno known in antiquity

Raphael Bagatta and Baptista Perettus testify in their preface to the same discourses, printed at Verona in 1586, that the discourses of St Zeno existed among the Veronese in an ancient manuscript codex made of parchment. They further say that they were found in a very ancient book of the bishopric of Verona by the orator Guarino, and that they are mentioned in the ancient lessons of the Office of St Zeno. But long before Guarino, the same discourses were seen by Ratherius, bishop of Verona, who, according to Ughelli, governed the Church of Verona in 929. In fact, he mentions these discourses in his own works (brought out of obscurity by D’Achery and included in the second volume of the *Spicilegium*). First, while dealing with contempt for the canons, he writes:

> Here I shall use the authority of blessed Zeno in the discourse which, as was his custom, he composed most eloquently on the patriarch Judah and Tamar his daughter-in-law, saying: “The devil is the father of all who live corruptly.”

D’Achery notes in the margin that this passage is not found in the printed discourses. In the Paris edition of the *Bibliotheca Patrum* of 1624, it appears in these words: “The devil is designated the father of all who live corruptly.” And in the manuscript of St Zeno’s discourses preserved in the archive of the Most Reverend Canons of this distinguished Cathedral Church of Pistoia: “For the devil is designated the father of all who live corruptly.” Ratherius cites the same passage in his *Synodica*: “And since our own special Doctor and guardian, namely blessed Zeno, says in the discourse which he composed most elegantly on Judah son of Jacob and Tamar his daughter-in-law, that the devil is the father of all who live corruptly.”

Nor were these discourses of St Zeno known only to the Veronese. In the monastery of St Remigius at Rheims, as Ruinart testifies in the *Acts of St Arcadius the Martyr*, there is a manuscript codex which Hincmar, bishop of Rheims, granted to that monastery in the ninth century. It contains the treatises of St Zeno, bishop of Verona, divided into two books, precisely the same as those published in the *Bibliotheca Patrum*. The monks of St Maur testify to this also in the Paris edition of St Hilary’s works of 1693, in their notice before Psalm 126.

There is also preserved in the archive of the Most Reverend Canons of this Cathedral the aforementioned parchment manuscript codex, in which appear the treatises of St Zeno, bishop of Verona, likewise arranged in two books. They are the same discourses as those read in the *Bibliotheca [Col. 0601B] Patrum*, though in another order—the order in which Bagatta and Perettus say, in the same preface, that they arranged them. At the end of this Pistoian manuscript two discourses are inserted: one by St Gaudentius, bishop of Brescia, which is not found in the Veronese manuscript; the other by St Vigilius, bishop, on the holy martyrs Sisinnius, Alexander, and Martyrius. The titles in this Pistoian manuscript do not agree with those prefixed to the printed discourses. From some of them it may be inferred that the Veronese customarily read St Zeno’s discourses in the Divine Office. Thus, the discourse on Genesis which stands first among the printed works is seventh in the manuscript order, and bears this title: “Treatise on Genesis. On Sexagesima. Lesson I: seek the second below, on the fifth folio.” The same may be observed elsewhere. Thus, the discourse on Genesis which is second among those published is twenty-seventh in the manuscript order, and concludes in the customary manner: “But you, O Lord, have mercy upon us.” The discourse on Job, which is fifteenth in the manuscript, begins: “Treatise on Job. A lesson of the blessed Zeno, bishop of this see.” Thus in ancient times the churches were accustomed to read the letters of Polycarp and of certain disciples of the apostles, the book of Hermas, and others. In the second manuscript book, moreover, the end of several discourses reads: “The treatise of St Zeno on humility ends happily”; and so in the others. Therefore, the publication of these discourses is not to be credited to Guarino alone, since they were customarily read publicly in choir at Verona, cited by other authors, and found in other libraries. Peter de Natalibus mentions them in his *Catalogue of Saints* (Book I, ch. 43) and enumerates several; so too Paul, bishop of Semproniensis, and other more recent authors. But enough has been said of these matters. Let us now examine more carefully the judgment of those scholars who deny that St Zeno authored these discourses.

## CHAPTER III. The judgment of Sixtus of Siena concerning the discourses of St Zeno considered

Sixtus of Siena infers that the discourses attributed to the holy bishop were collected from various authors who flourished nearly two hundred years after St Zeno, because some discourses on the Psalms among them were transcribed from St Hilary’s commentaries without even a word changed. He also argues this because the discourse on “Take heed to yourself” and the discourse on Envy and Jealousy are by St Basil. Owing likewise to diversity of style in the remaining discourses, he suspects diverse authors, especially because, in the discourse on Continence, the author asserts that more than four hundred years had elapsed since Christ’s birth. It must therefore be said that Sixtus of Siena’s enumeration of the aforesaid discourses concerned with the exposition of Holy Scripture is rather inaccurate, perhaps because he employed the work of others in compiling his collection. For Sixtus reads only five discourses written on Genesis, to which he adds the discourses on Abraham, Jacob’s dream, Judah, and Tamar. Yet nine are printed: four on Genesis, three on Abraham, one on Jacob’s dream, and one on Judah. Sixtus counts five on Exodus, whereas fifteen are found in the said edition. He has seven on the Psalms, whereas nine are printed. It must also be noted, with Perettus and Bagatta, that Sixtus erred in saying that the discourse on Psalm 79 and the discourse on Psalm 100 are found in St Hilary; this is false. Nor is the treatise or discourse on Psalm 49, which is among St Zeno’s works, read in Hilary’s works. Five discourses, however, are found both in St Zeno and in St Hilary: namely, on Psalm 126, without the prologue; and on Psalms 127, [Col. 0602C] 128, 129, and 130. Nor is the first discourse on Psalm 30, on humility, found among Hilary’s discourses, as the Fathers of the Congregation of St Maur also note in the aforementioned 1693 edition of Hilary’s works. Sixtus counts four on Isaiah; seven appear in the printed edition if the discourse on the Martyrdom of Isaiah is included. He assigns three to Daniel; nine appear in the said edition.

These points having been observed, it must be admitted that the aforesaid five discourses on the Psalms are read in St Hilary, and that the aforementioned Fathers of the Congregation of St Maur prove St Hilary to be their author.
