It must also be admitted that among Basil’s works are found not only the two discourses noted by Sixtus—the discourse on “Take heed to yourself” and the discourse on Envy and Jealousy—but also the discourse on the Gospel according to Luke concerning the twofold kind of temptations, and the discourse on Fasting. Yet despite these facts Sixtus of Siena wrongly concludes that the discourses circulated under St Zeno’s name are a collection from various authors, who lived nearly two hundred years after Zeno. For the discourses in question number one hundred and four, whereas those found in Hilary and Basil number nine. Why, therefore, should not the remaining ninety-five be attributed to St Zeno? What is more common in the works of the ancient Fathers than to find among the writings of one holy Father compositions of other Fathers, and even of heretical authors? This is plainly evident in the books of Tertullian, Origen, Sts Cyprian, Ambrose, Jerome, and John Chrysostom, as Bellarmine and others who treat of ecclesiastical writers show. But if, because of only those nine discourses found in other authors, St Zeno’s discourses were to be doubted, then the works of many holy Fathers—whose authorship no one doubts—would likewise have to be doubted. It also seems necessary to consider that, if Zeno’s works had been collected from various authors, then, just as those nine discourses are found among other authors’ works, the rest would likewise be read under other authors. There is no reason to believe that the names and works of every author from whom the aforesaid discourses are thought to have been copied have entirely disappeared. Therefore, if only those nine are found in Hilary and Basil, the remainder must be said to be Zeno’s work; unknown authors should not lightly be imagined when we possess so many ancient monuments inscribed with St Zeno’s name, of which we spoke above in Chapter 2. Had Sixtus of Siena seen these, he would not so readily have asserted that St Zeno’s work was a collection of discourses from diverse authors.

## CHAPTER IV. On the more than four hundred years that slipped into the discourse on Continence

As for the discourse on Continence, where the author adduces a testimony from St Paul’s First Epistle to the Corinthians in these words: “The time is shortened; it remains that those who have wives should be as though they had none, for the form of this world passes away,” he adds: [Col. 0603C] “But since this apostolic injunction has been operative for almost four hundred years, or more.” (For the author does not say, as Sixtus of Siena has it, that four hundred years had passed from Christ’s birth; rather, he says that four hundred years and more had elapsed from the writing of the First Epistle to the Corinthians.) It therefore appears certain, as Sixtus observes, that this discourse cannot fit the time of Gallienus, under whom St Zeno is traditionally said to have suffered martyrdom. But Cardinal Baronius removed this difficulty in his notes on the Roman Martyrology for 12 April; it is not burdensome to quote his words here:

> With respect to St Zeno the martyr, those seem certainly to us to be mistaken who, maintaining that there was but one Zeno, wish him to have lived in Ambrose’s time. They rely chiefly on the reason that the author, in his discourse on chastity (otherwise, on continence), counts from the time when the Apostle Paul wrote his First Epistle to the Corinthians almost four hundred years, as he says, and more. Certainly, if anyone counts four hundred years from A.D. 57, in which year we have demonstrated in the *Annals* that Paul wrote that epistle, the author must have written in A.D. 457—sixty years after the death of Ambrose, who, as Marcellinus has in his Chronicle, died in A.D. 397. Thus, since this numerical statement cannot be fitted, as they wish, even to Ambrose’s time, no one, I think, can rightly deny that it is corrupt. But there is in addition the fact that, while the author in the same discourse inveighs very vehemently against women who marry Gentiles, he very plainly shows that temples of idols were then open and that sacrifices were customarily offered. The author thereby openly signifies that that age was wholly different from the age of Ambrose. For it is established that sacrifices had long before been forbidden and temples ordered closed, not only by Constantine, as Eusebius says in his *Life of Constantine*, Book II, chs. 42–43, but also by Constantius, as Ammonius, Book XIX, and others testify. At that time the Romans could not even obtain permission to erect a single altar of Victory, as Ambrose writes at length to Valentinian and argues against Symmachus. Therefore, since, from the foregoing, that reading of four hundred years cannot stand on any grounds—and still less when the fifty-seven years preceding the writing of Paul’s epistle are added—it was rightly and properly restored in a more recent edition as two hundred years. For, counting two hundred years and more, as the old reading has it, from A.D. 257, when, as we have said, that epistle to the Corinthians was written, to the time of Gallienus, who began to rule in A.D. 255 and under whom Zeno is said to have suffered, produces the restored number. Again, in the second discourse on avarice, when the author says that the emblem of idolatry was customarily struck upon coins, and clearly refers to the same idols that were worshipped in the temple, he plainly demonstrates that the author flourished long before the age of Christian emperors. For Sozomen, Book I, ch. 8, testifies that Constantine the Great ordered the sign of the Cross to be impressed on coinage. The coins of Constantine himself and of the succeeding emperors which remain demonstrate this much more clearly. Further, when the author in the discourse on the spiritual building of God’s house fully demonstrates that at that time no church, or very few, had been built which might be compared with the temples of idols, he plainly signifies that he flourished before Constantine’s time. It is certain that, through Constantine’s works, most magnificent basilicas were built in both West—especially at Rome—and East, at Jerusalem, Antioch, Constantinople, and elsewhere.

Combefis ventures only very lightly to weaken these observations of the most eminent Baronius. In discussing St Zeno in his judgment of the authors reviewed in the first volume of his *Bibliotheca Concionatoria*, he offers nothing against them other than these words: “So that there is no need to resort to the arguments Baronius uses to defend the new Martyrology’s dating of Zeno under Gallienus.” Had he touched them even with the tips of his lips, he would by no means have said that Baronius laboured in vain to uphold the chronology of the new Martyrology—as though the new Martyrology needed fabricated arguments to sustain its authority.

## CHAPTER V. Tillemont’s errors in refuting Baronius
Tillemont indeed employs a rather sharper pen against Baronius (Note 6, vol. IV, on the persecution of Valerian), as though Baronius had gathered trivialities in a useless effort to maintain that Saint Zeno was the author of the sermons under discussion. Certainly Baronius himself admits that among the sermons commonly attributed to Saint Zeno there are some of which that holy bishop was not the author, especially [Col. 0605A] those directed against the Arians, which we shall discuss below (ch. 7). Yet, as we have seen, a few sermons by other persons having been mixed among the sermons of Saint Zeno is no reason why the remaining sermons should not be ascribed to Saint Zeno.

Tillemont is therefore mistaken, first in asserting that Baronius made no mention in his *Annals* either of Saint Zeno or of his sermons. For before the first year of Christ, he lists a certain sermon of Saint Zeno on the Nativity, which he calls the sixth, whereas in the Paris edition in the *Library of the Fathers* of 1624 it is the second; there he notes that what is said about the unbelieving midwife was taken from apocryphal writings. Yet in the aforementioned edition nothing is read concerning this midwife. In this Pistoian manuscript, however, the material concerning the midwife noted by Baronius is found. Perhaps Peretti and Bagatta used an older [Col. 0605B] and more correct autograph manuscript when publishing the works of Saint Zeno.

Likewise, under the year of Christ 47, Baronius confirms from Saint Zeno’s sermon *On Fear* that Saint Thecla was condemned both to beasts and to fire. And under the year 589, he recounts the miracle which then occurred when the River Adige overflowed and rose to the windows of the church of Saint Zeno, martyr and bishop: although the doors stood open, the waters did not enter the church. The reason Baronius did not treat Saint Zeno expressly in the *Annals* was not, as Tillemont supposes, that he had established nothing certain about him, but that it was not his purpose to pursue the affairs of individual churches, as Baronius himself states under the year of Christ 75.

Tillemont is also mistaken when he says that in ancient times only clerics were permitted [Col. 0605C] to see the sacrifice of the Mass, and not other Christians. What could be more absurd from a man versed in ecclesiastical history, when it is clearer than daylight that only the excommunicated, catechumens, and penitents were forbidden to attend the sacrifice of the Mass? As for his addition concerning a curtain spread out so that laypeople were prevented from seeing the sacrifice of the Mass, this was customary not in the Western Church, as he falsely supposes, but in the Eastern Church. For in the Western Church, and especially at Rome, sacred rites were celebrated without any curtains, contrary to the custom of the Valentinians, whose rites were performed in concealment. Thus Baronius, under the year of Christ 145:

> “We think this also happened at Rome, where Valentinus remained for a long time: the sacred rites themselves were by no means [Col. 0605D] covered during their celebration by drawn curtains, as is customary in the East; rather, with everything open, they were made bright and visible everywhere, not only by daylight but also by lit lamps. For truth is ashamed of nothing except concealment. Therefore, lest sacrifices hidden beneath spread curtains should seem similar to their rites, the Roman Church deliberately wished her mysteries to be open and accessible to all.”

Tillemont employs these contrivances in order to evade one of Baronius’s observations—and indeed a most apt one—by which he demonstrates that an error has crept in regarding the number of years. For from the fact that the author of the sermon *On Continence* inveighs against women who marry Gentiles, and says that at that time [Col. 0606A] the temples of idols stood open and victims were customarily sacrificed, Baronius manifestly concludes that this time cannot possibly agree with the four hundred years specified in the same sermon. How could the error have been demonstrated more clearly than from the very context of the sermon?

But so that it may appear still more plainly that Tillemont is talking nonsense rather than criticizing Baronius, let us cite the words of the same sermon:

> “What then? His sacrifice—that of the Gentile husband—is public; yours—that of the Christian wife—is secret. His may freely be handled by anyone; yours may not even be seen being consecrated by Christians without sacrilege.”

These words plainly must be understood not of a difference in worship, as Tillemont thinks, but of freedom to exercise worship. For Saint Zeno here [Col. 0606B] deals with the impediment which comes to a wife from marriage with a Gentile regarding the exercise and freedom of religion. He therefore first considers the case in which it happens that festivals are celebrated both in the church and in the pagan shrine on the same day. Thus, before the quoted words:

> “Let us suppose, then, as often happens, that one and the same day arrives on which you must go to church and he to the temples.”

Then he adds another impediment: Gentile worship is exercised freely and publicly, whereas Christian worship is exercised secretly and contrary to the emperors’ commands. He therefore says that Christians were not permitted to see the sacrifice being consecrated without being guilty of sacrilege—“without sacrilege,” I say, because those who attended Christian sacred rites, even though Christians, were punished as sacrilegious persons and despisers of the gods:

> “Yours may not even be seen being consecrated by Christians without sacrilege.” [Col. 0606C]

Why, then, does Tillemont distort these words and invent sacrilege on the part of Christians if, while attending Mass, they see the consecration? Certainly, if the author of the sermon *On Continence* had lived four hundred years or more after the composition of First Corinthians—which, according to Baronius, as we saw (ch. 4), was written in the fifty-seventh year of Christ—he would necessarily have lived in the time of the emperors Marcian or Leo, when Saint Leo was pope in the Roman see, in the year 457. But at that time he certainly would not have said that sacrifices were publicly offered to idols and Christian rites performed secretly, since Tillemont himself (*History of the Emperors*, vol. IV, art. 54) recounts that, long before the time of Constantine the Great, the temples of idols had been closed and the public worship of the Christian religion [Col. 0606D] had spread. Yet it is remarkable how boldly he says that the arguments adduced by Baronius can easily be disposed of.

Tillemont attacks only one observation of Baronius, and that very lightly. Of the rest—which we have set forth above in Baronius’s own words—he says not a word: namely, that in the sermon *On Avarice* the author of the sermons says that idols worshipped in the temple were customarily stamped on coins; and that in the sermon *On the Spiritual Building of God’s House* the same author affirms that at that time no Christian church, or very rarely one, had been built which could be compared with the edifices of idols. What does Tillemont object to these points, that he may refute Baronius so easily?

There are other signs of antiquity in the preface to the works [Col. 0607A] of Saint Zeno which ought not to be passed over as Tillemont passes them over. For the reader’s convenience, we transcribe them here from that same preface. It is an indication of a most ancient author that he frequently addressed the Jews; invited catechumens to the sacred font; reproved Greeks then converted to the faith of Christ because, even in the Church of God, they introduced certain vain notions about God from their vain philosophy—as is shown in the first sermon on Psalm 130 (this sermon is not found in Hilary). The same is shown when, in the sermon *On the Spiritual Building of God’s House*, the author demonstrates that Christian churches had not yet been built at that time and that the new people was small in number.

Further, in Sermon IV to the Neophytes, when he mentions those who distribute all their possessions to the poor, because they are the temple [Col. 0607B] of God, though they had formerly been temples of idolatry. The same thing may also be seen in Sermon V to the Neophytes, where he exhorts them to flee idolatry and no longer to seek auguries. What then? Does this not plainly appear from the first sermon *On Easter* and the sermon *On Patience*? In one, he interprets autumn as signifying the martyrs of his own time; in the other, he calls patience the daily crown of martyrs. Blessed Thecla, disciple of the apostle Saint Paul and the first female martyr, is cited in the sermon *On Fear* as an example of the fear of the Lord. In the sermon *On the Resurrection*, he mentions certain persons who died in idolatry in his own time; and he rebukes certain Christians for not believing in the resurrection of bodies. Moreover, the life of Saint Arcadius, crowned by martyrdom [Col. 0607C] in Mauretania, was written by him in his own time, as Peter Equilinus testifies. By these and very many other such considerations, the author of these sermons is shown to be most ancient.

## CHAPTER VI. On the diversity of style observed by Sixtus of Siena and other modern writers in the sermons of Saint Zeno.

The diversity of style in the sermons of Saint Zeno—apart from those which are found in other authors—is certainly not so great that the distinctive character of the same holy bishop cannot be recognized in them. Even if the same sermons had been written in differing styles, it must be held as certain that a different author cannot be inferred merely from diversity of style. This is indeed the exception most frequently used by heterodox writers to discredit [Col. 0607D] the genuine works of the holy Fathers.

Here it may be permitted to cite the judgment of the Pistoian evangelist Marcellinus, of the family of Saint Francis called the Observant [Franciscans], a man illustrious indeed for learning, but especially for holiness and apostolic zeal in preaching, whom Possevino mentions in his *Apparatus*. He published not only the treatise *On the Conversion of a Sinner to God* and the lectures on Tobit noted by Possevino, but also annotations on the Book of Judges and lectures on the Song of Songs. There, when discussing Saint Basil’s commentaries on the prophet [Col. 0608A] Isaiah against Erasmus, he argued as follows on diversity of style in the vernacular, which we have rendered into Latin (Lecture 21):

> He—speaking of Erasmus—undertook to translate Basil’s commentaries on Isaiah from Greek into Latin . . . and says that their style is not Basil’s, but that of someone called by the same name, or of another person who published them under Saint Basil’s name. For since their phraseology and texture of words are very different from those employed by Basil, it cannot be that these commentaries were written by so eloquent a theologian. Thus it happens that the reader of little discernment no longer trusts those commentaries, does not use them, and values them little. What I affirm concerning Basil must be said likewise concerning Augustine in various places, Jerome, and others. . . . Diversity of style does not indicate a different author, since the same author uses one style in some books and another in others, as is plainly evident from Augustine, who uses one style in the books *On the City of God* and another in the Psalms. Erasmus himself will not deny that different modes are employed in one and the same book [Col. 0608B], as Augustine does in his treatment of the Psalms; for, as Erasmus himself affirms elsewhere, he uses one method at the beginning and another at the end. I say another method, not merely because here he is briefer and there longer, but because here and there he proceeds in different ways. For it is one thing to set out opinions summarily, as notes, and another to explain them more fully in the manner of a homily. . . . Therefore, since at the beginning of the Psalms Augustine writes in a style of notes, so to speak, but at the end—where Erasmus admits it—extends his discourse at greater length, as is done in homilies, is Augustine himself therefore to be called a different author in the same book? Why linger over a matter so evident? Does not the precept of Basil the Great, in the prologue to *On the True and Pious Faith*, require that a teacher vary his style according to the time, place, and hearers to whom he speaks [Col. 0608C] or writes? Are not these Basil’s own words?
>
> “For just as the man about to enter battle and the man wishing to cultivate a field will not take the same implements in hand—for one set of instruments is suitable to those who, in the peaceful calm, procure what they need for sustenance, while another array of arms belongs to those who equip themselves in war against hostile forces—so likewise the person who exhorts in sacred teaching will by no means use the same kind of speech as the one who rebukes opponents in debate. For one kind of speech is used in refutation, another in exhortation.” . . .
>
> He therefore concludes—for the sake of brevity the whole need not be copied here—that style ought to be adapted as seems expedient. This being so, Erasmus’s argument proves little—indeed, nothing—when he says: “This does not smell of the style of this or that person; therefore we are far from recognizing it as his offspring.”

These remarks on diversity of style in the sermons of Saint Zeno are sufficient. [Col. 0608D] For, as we said at the outset, in all his sermons, except those which we excluded, Saint Zeno employs his own characteristic style and phraseology, as is evident to anyone who examines them.

## CHAPTER VII. The sermons of Saint Zeno in which he treats against Arius’s errors suit the times of Saint Zeno himself.

Baronius notes (*Notes on the Martyrology*, the day before the Ides of April) that the fifth sermon of Book III—which in the printed Paris edition is the first among the sermons [Col. 0609A] *On the Nativity of Christ*—contains an excellent refutation and overthrow of the Arian heresy:

> “Where he deals with those heretics who said that the Son of God was God, but not coeternal with the Father, and that there was a time when he was not. No one acquainted with the events of those times can fail to know that such monstrous utterances and opinions had never been heard before the emergence of Arius’s heresy.”

Thus Baronius himself, from which it seems necessarily to follow that the aforesaid sermon is wholly incompatible with Saint Zeno’s time. Yet, to state frankly what I think, I believe that Baronius’s memory failed him here. To recognize this, one must note that Saint Zeno makes no mention of Arius, whether in the last-mentioned sermon or elsewhere. But concerning Arius’s error he says:

> “Another, more restrained in speech but more mordantly harmful, says indeed that the Son of God is God, but that he was not begotten from a share in nobility through eternal generation, and that there was a time when he was not.”

Baronius says that this error was unheard of before Arius. Yet Baronius himself acknowledges in his *Annals* the same error long before Arius and before Saint Zeno: namely, in the year of Christ 229, when a certain Beryllus, bishop of Bostra in Arabia, rashly dared to assert that our Savior and Lord Jesus Christ did not exist before his transition into human flesh by a distinct circumscription of substance of his own, and did not possess divinity of his own from himself, but that the Father’s divinity alone existed in him. Thus Eusebius, Book VI, chapter 26, cited by Baronius under the aforementioned year.

[Col. 0609C] Saint Jerome mentions this Beryllus and his heresy in the book *On Ecclesiastical Writers*, and Augustine in the book *Definitions of the Orthodox Faith*, chapter 3. That this is the same heresy as Arius’s is evident from Athanasius, who reports Arius’s opinion in these words (*On the Synods*, in the *Defense of the Decree against the Arian Heresy*):

> “The Son did not exist before he was begotten,”

and from this they wished to reason that he did not exist even before assuming the nature of flesh. This is the same as what we read in Saint Zeno: “There was a time when he was not.”

Nor should one say that Beryllus’s heresy, which scarcely arose before it immediately perished, could not have become known. For Beryllus himself was brought back to the Catholic position by Origen in a synod held against him in Arabia. Moreover, Saint Zeno, either Syrian by origin or having arrived in Syria and preached there—as is stated in an old manuscript at the beginning of Saint Zeno’s works, [Col. 0609D] printed in the aforementioned Paris edition:

> “I cannot recount the many great works of this saint, the wonders which God displayed through him as he came from Syria as far as Italy”—

had knowledge of Eastern affairs. In the West, moreover, this heresy is known to have been widespread from the fact that Pope Dionysius, who governed Peter’s chair in the year of Christ 261, while Saint Zeno was still alive, in the case of Dionysius of Alexandria, who had been accused before the Roman pontiff as seeming to admit a division in the divine Persons, not only acquitted Dionysius of Alexandria after clearing him of false accusations and condemned the Sabellian heresy in a council convened at Rome, but also, in published treatises, refuted the contrary opinion of Arius long before Arius, as Athanasius testifies [Col. 0610A] (*On the Opinion of Dionysius against the Arians*):

> “Moreover, from the volumes of Dionysius, bishop of Rome, written against those who maintain that the Son of God is a work or creature, it is clearly shown that the heresy of the Arians, rebels against Christ, was not then for the first time, but had long ago been condemned by all.”

Thus Athanasius in Baronius, under the year of Christ 263. Since, therefore, Arius’s error had appeared even in Saint Zeno’s time, what is surprising if he treated against it in his sermons? The sermons in which Arian errors are refuted do not, therefore, differ from Saint Zeno’s age, nor is there any need to invent a later, second Zeno as their author. On the two Zenones, however, below in Chapter XI.

## CHAPTER VIII. On the judgment of the Most Eminent Bellarmine concerning the sermons of Saint Zeno.

[Col. 0610B] Bellarmine (*On Ecclesiastical Writers*, year 260) gave a most fair judgment on Saint Zeno’s sermons. He openly says that the sermons on “Attend to Yourself,” on the Gospel of Luke, on fasting, and on envy and jealousy are by Saint Basil; and that the sermons on the Psalms, if not all of them, are for the most part found in Saint Hilary. In the other sermons he rightly observes Zeno to be concise and obscure, and in some of them to repeat the same things very frequently. He says nothing about correcting the number of years in the sermon *On Continence*, since he had weighed Baronius’s most wise observations and deferred to his judgment. Nor does he say anything about Arius’s error. Nor, following the manner of Sixtus of Siena, does he infer from the things he observes in these same sermons that all of them must be entirely taken away from Saint Zeno.

[Col. 0610C] He candidly admits that what troubles his mind is that no mention of Saint Zeno’s sermons appears among the ancients. Yet he did not see the things reported above (ch. 2), from which it is plainly known that Saint Zeno’s sermons were not unknown to the ancients. The fact that Eusebius and Jerome did not mention them does not entail that they should not be attributed to Saint Zeno, because both Jerome and Eusebius, as Bellarmine himself observes concerning Athenagoras, passed over other authors. “That Saint Jerome omitted this writer is not so remarkable, since it is sufficiently certain that Jerome’s catalogue was drawn from Eusebius’s history, as regards those writers who preceded Eusebius.” Thus Bellarmine.

[Col. 0610D] Perhaps Eusebius deliberately passed over Saint Zeno lest he point out that Arius’s errors had been reproved so long beforehand in his works. Jerome likewise, and Bellarmine under the year 260—when Saint Zeno is said to have suffered martyrdom—say nothing of Aurelius, the companion and fellow-lodger of Saint Pontius, of whom Oudin writes in the supplement to *On Ecclesiastical Writers*. It should therefore not be surprising that Saint Zeno was omitted by Jerome and Eusebius.

But we must readily admit Bellarmine’s observation that some sermons of Saint Zeno are so short that they scarcely deserve to be called sermons. Yet these shorter pieces are entitled “preface” in this Pistoian manuscript. Thus the sixth sermon, which in the printed editions is the fifth *On Easter*, bears the title: “Here begins the Preface.” And the sixteenth sermon [Col. 0611A], which in print is the sixth *On Easter*: “Here begins the Easter Preface.” And the twenty-sixth sermon, which in print is the seventh *On Easter*: “Here begins the Preface.” And the forty-fourth, which in print is the eighth: “Easter Preface.”

Since it is established from the ancient Gallican liturgy in Martène (vol. V, p. 86, Paris edition, 1717) that before the readings from the Prophets and Apostles a preface was customarily read to exhort the people to attend the sacred rites with fitting devotion, perhaps Saint Zeno composed or delivered these prefaces for that or a similar use. This may reasonably be inferred because these short sermons discuss the mysteries celebrated on that day. For in the printed texts certain short sermons also bear the titles “Invitation of the Font” or “Invitation to the Font,” in which he addresses [Col. 0611B] catechumens about to be baptized.

Other pieces may likewise be beginnings of sermons which Saint Zeno did not write down, but which his disciples recorded while he was speaking and did not afterwards complete, leaving them unfinished. Thus some sermons contain the same things as others, because, I think, several people were recording sermons, and, retaining the sense, expressed it in different words.

## CHAPTER IX. Philip Labbe’s dissertation on Saint Zeno examined.

Philip Labbe, in treating of Saint Zeno, has relied on the works of others, and on sources not very trustworthy, in composing this dissertation. For not everything he collects against Saint Zeno’s sermons agrees with the authors whom he cites. [Col. 0611C] He first asserts that the sermons under discussion are falsely attributed to Saint Zeno, and thinks that many support his position, whom he lists. “Of Catholic authors,” he says, “Sixtus of Siena, Baronius, Molanus, Possevino, Bellarmine, Miraeus, and their apes Cocus and Rivetus, together with similar critical innovators, are of this opinion; so that Raphael Bagatta and Baptista Peretti may seem to have lost their oil and their labor before competent judges, since they wished, against the most learned censure of Sixtus of Siena, to vindicate all—or at least all of them—for Zeno, bishop of Verona, who suffered martyrdom under Gallienus.”

But he is mistaken in adducing Baronius for himself, as Tillemont himself observes (vol. IV, note 6, on the persecution of Valerian). For Baronius denies only that certain sermons among those whose author is called Saint Zeno should be ascribed to him; he recognizes the rest as properly Saint Zeno’s [Col. 0611D] and cites passages from some of them in the *Annals*, as noted above (ch. 5). Nor does he think that Bagatta and Peretti lost their oil and labor, since he commends them in his notes (the day before the Ides of April) to the Roman Martyrology. You may find several additional points learnedly noted upon this same subject in the preface to the works of Saint Zeno—namely that of Bagatta and Peretti—which were recently published by order and through the diligence of the most illustrious and reverend Augustine Valerio, most eminent cardinal and bishop of Verona. We approve it as a work admirably executed with much care, although in certain matters—as we have said—concerning the genuineness of some sermons, we do not agree with it equally.

[Col. 0612A] I have not seen Molanus. Possevino, in volume III of the *Sacred Apparatus*, under the letter Z and the entry “Saint Zeno,” repeats word for word the judgment of Sixtus of Siena. He adds this of his own:

> “Moreover, since in volume II of the second edition of the *Library of the Holy Fathers* there are, under the same title, works of Saint Zeno, bishop and martyr of Verona, and eminent teacher, on several passages of Scripture and subjects of divine doctrine; and since they were also published at Verona in 1588 . . .”

By this he seems rather to affirm than deny that the sermons are Saint Zeno’s. We have already seen (ch. 8) what Bellarmine criticizes in these sermons; since he refers the reader to Baronius’s censure, he seems to favor Saint Zeno. Miraeus, in the *Supplement to Ecclesiastical Writers*, chapter 25, says:

> “Saint Zeno, bishop of Verona, suffered martyrdom under the emperor Gallienus; Gregory the Great mentions him in the *Dialogues*, Book III, chapter 19. Various sermons were published under his name [Col. 0612B], first at Venice in 1508 and afterward in a more corrected edition at Verona in 1586. Sixtus of Siena, Molanus, Bellarmine, and others note that no few of these were transcribed from Basil, Hilary, and later authors. Besides these, Baronius may be consulted in his notes on the Martyrology.”

Miraeus therefore does not deprive Saint Zeno of all the sermons, but only of those found in other authors—especially since he agrees with Baronius, who, with a few exceptions, admits Saint Zeno as the author of the remaining sermons.

Labbe is also mistaken about the number of the sermons, which he counts as ninety. There are, however, one hundred and four. What he brings forward concerning the sermons of Saint Basil and Hilary has been discussed above (ch. 3, ch. 6, ch. 7), as has the matter of diversity of style. Nothing need be added concerning the sermons against the Arians to what we have said above.

[Col. 0612C] Yet Labbe does not appear to have pronounced his own opinion concerning Saint Zeno’s sermons. For first he advises consulting Baronius; then he cites the judgment of John Maria in the expurgatory index, whose words are these:

> “John Maria, however, seems to wish to affirm nothing in the expurgatory index. Nevertheless,” he says, “although the arguments opposing the attribution of the sermons to Saint Zeno are not strong conjectures, Baronius believes that some are not his, especially those in which the Arian heresy is refuted. He professes to possess many arguments and most excellent conjectures to prove this.”

John Maria nevertheless appears to agree with Baronius, since he openly says that the conjectures against Saint Zeno’s sermons are not weighty: “although the arguments opposing the attribution of the sermons to Saint Zeno are not strong conjectures.”

[Col. 0612D] Finally, as regards Peretti and Bagatta, Labbe seems to affirm that both attributed to Saint Zeno every sermon bearing Saint Zeno’s name:

> “So that Raphael Bagatta and Baptista Peretti may seem to have lost their oil and their labor before competent judges, since they wished, against the most learned censure of Sixtus of Siena, to vindicate all—or at least all of them—for Zeno, bishop of Verona, who suffered martyrdom under Gallienus.”

To establish what Bagatta and Peretti intended to maintain concerning these sermons, we shall transcribe their words from the preface cited above:

> “But whereas three or four sermons are found among these which some think cannot be ascribed to Saint Zeno—namely, that entitled *On the Precept, Attend to Yourself*; the sermon *On the Gospel according to Luke, On the Threefold Kind of [Col. 0613A] Temptations*; the sermon *On Envy and Jealousy*; and the sermon *On Fasting*, which are found written in Greek among Saint Basil’s homilies—although arguments are not lacking by which it would be possible to prove that these sermons also belong to our Saint Zeno, since he converted very many people to Christ in Greece by preaching, with the greatest zeal and through most arduous labors, long before Saint Basil, yet we do not wish to be contentious in this matter.
>
> “As to what the author of the *Sacred Library* writes—namely, that seven sermons on the Psalms, which he enumerates, were copied from Saint Hilary’s commentaries—we say that he erred as to their number. For the sermons on Psalm 79 and Psalm 100 are not found in Saint Hilary’s commentaries. As to the other five: since two sermons on Psalm 130 are read among these sermons, and the second is similar to the first in certain [Col. 0613B] expressions and almost the same opinions, while the first is not found in Saint Hilary’s commentaries, we say that the second too was repeated by Saint Zeno in some manner according to his custom and therefore belongs to him. But it was inserted into Saint Hilary’s commentaries by someone else, just as we see sermons and little works by not insignificant authors having crept into the works of Jerome, Augustine, and some of the holy Fathers. Whether the other four were inserted into the same commentaries in the same way is for others to judge.”

If, therefore, they do not refuse to abide by the judgment of others, and do not wish to be contentious about those sermons concerning which there is doubt, Bagatta and Peretti’s intent was not to prove that all sermons must be attributed to Saint Zeno.

## CHAPTER X. On Dupin and Combefis.

[Col. 0613C]

Dupin, according to his custom, judges very rashly concerning Saint Zeno in this controversy over the sermons. Yet he has nothing which he does not borrow from others. For what he received from Baronius concerning Arius’s errors in the fifth sermon *On the Nativity* is shown above in Chapter VII, by Baronius’s own testimony, to be erroneous: Arius’s errors were condemned even before Saint Zeno and, still more, before Arius himself. We have said in Chapter III that the sermons found in Saints Basil and Hilary, as Dupin himself notes from Sixtus of Siena and Bellarmine, do no harm to the remaining sermons of Saint Zeno. In Chapter IV we acknowledged that the error in the number of years in the sermon *On Continence* [Col. 0613D] must be corrected with Baronius. The same must be said concerning Combefis, since he too brings forward nothing not already treated above. It remains to be considered whether another Saint Zeno really existed, whose work the disputed sermons could be.

## CHAPTER XI. There is one Saint Zeno, bishop of Verona.

Baronius himself believed that there had been two Zenons, as may be seen in his annotations on the Roman Martyrology for 3 May. There, while treating of St Juvenal, bishop of Narni, he cites the Church of Verona as an example, because it had had two Zenons, in order to make it seem probable that two Juvenals had likewise occupied the see of Narni. Yet in the notes to the same Martyrology for 12 April, while treating of St Zeno’s martyrdom, he retracts this view. Since, as we have learned, the Church of Verona does not acknowledge two Zenons, we willingly abandon our former opinion. Tillemont noticed this, but Ughelli did not, nor did Papebroch, who cite Baronius in support of the assertion that there were two Zenons.

It is indeed difficult to maintain—as Dupin and others do, contrary to the history and tradition of the Church of Verona—that the letter of St Ambrose alone admits two Zenons, or removes from consideration the earlier one in the time of Gallienus. For Baronius, who had seen St Ambrose’s letter and had thought its authority could settle the dispute concerning St Zeno’s sermons, withdrew from the opinion of two Zenons when he learned that the Church of Verona received only one Zeno.

The words of St Ambrose are these (Book VI, chapter 46): “But you”—he writes to Syagrius, bishop of Verona—“thought that this case was to be judged by yourself alone, without the counsel of any brother; although before the trial you had already formed a prejudgment, thinking that the girl of Zeno, of holy memory, who had been approved by his judgment and sanctified by his blessing, after so many years, without an author of accusation, without an accuser, without a formal presenter of the charge, ought to be brought into danger of conviction.”

Nothing further concerning Zeno is added in this whole letter, nor in the following letter to the same Syagrius, bishop of Verona. In these words, as is evident, St Ambrose does not call Zeno a bishop, as Tillemont asserts; although from the fact that Indicia was approved and sanctified by a blessing one may infer that Zeno was a bishop—if “blessing” is understood as formal consecration, a point which I leave to others’ judgment. But this is certain: Ambrose neither calls this Zeno a Veronese nor calls him Syagrius’s predecessor.

Accordingly, from these very words of St Ambrose the manifest error of Ughelli (*Italia Sacra*, vol. V, on the bishops of Verona), Papebroch (*Acta Sanctorum*, 12 April, chapter 1, no. 2), Labbe, and Combefis appears. They make Syagrius Zeno’s successor through a mistaken understanding of St Ambrose’s authority, as is clear from the words quoted above. Indeed, if the letter is carefully considered, the opposite rather seems to be meant. For the Zeno whom Ambrose names could be considered bishop of Verona only if the virgin Indicia, approved by Zeno and sanctified by his blessing, had been subject to that same Zeno at Verona.

But that Indicia was not a Veronese is demonstrated by the clearest inferences from the same letter of St Ambrose. First, Ambrose reproves Syagrius because he subjected the virgin Indicia to examination without a prior investigation: “But you thought that this case was to be judged by yourself alone, without the counsel of another brother.” If Indicia had been a Veronese, he would have had no need of counsel, since she would have been known to him as his subject. Therefore, if Ambrose reproves him in this way, he does so because Indicia was not subject to the bishop of Verona; this is made still clearer by the words, “you thought she was to be judged by yourself alone.” This cannot mean that Veronese priests, who had no judicial authority—the whole of which in the diocese of Verona belonged to Syagrius—were to be associated with him in the trial, but rather other bishops. For Indicia lived in several places, as we shall see below. If Syagrius had judged her to be his own subject, what other colleague would he have needed to employ in judging? Did Ambrose mean to reproach Syagrius for incompetence, as though he needed an assessor? Syagrius was highly learned, as Ughelli testifies.

It must therefore be said that, although the alleged fornication was said to have been committed at Verona, the virgin believed to have been defiled was not a Veronese; and for that reason her bishop ought to have been consulted, so that information might be obtained regarding Indicia and her character. From this one may also infer that Indicia was not a Milanese, since St Ambrose himself sought information about her from others: “Especially since this judgment of ours proceeded after being shared with our brethren and fellow-bishops.” That those from whom he sought counsel were bishops he himself says at the end of the letter: “On the day appointed for the hearing, they withdrew from the assembly of bishops.”

As for what Ambrose adds about Zeno’s blessing and approval, if Indicia had been approved and sanctified at Verona, Ambrose would certainly not have passed this over in silence. Therefore he seems to have offered Syagrius this external information in defense of the accused virgin. He says only that Indicia was at Verona when her pregnancy was suspected and her alleged fornication presumed:

> “But when the child had been born and exposed, or killed—while men were more intent on rancour than proof—the matter was spread abroad through everyone’s ears, and the freedom of calumny was strangled. If she gave birth, then she was at Verona. She was frequently seen by virgins and women, always held in honour. She was seen by priests because of reverence for her chastity and because she was a pattern of gravity. How, then, could she conceal a crime which would betray her even by its appearance? How did she hide her womb? How, while giving birth, did she suppress her voice? But pain does not permit this.”

But when Ambrose investigates Indicia’s manner of life more deeply, he does not call Veronese witnesses; instead, he calls his own sister, affirming in the same place that Indicia had lived at Rome: “That she lived at Rome in our house while we were absent, and gave herself to no familiarity with men.” He brings forward another witness, whom he calls his daughter—perhaps because she was a Milanese and therefore subject to him: “I also questioned our daughter in the paternal household.” It must be supposed that Indicia had remained at Rome for a long time, for a stay of brief duration could not suffice to discern the habits of one’s life. And it may be inferred that she made this stay at Rome before St Ambrose’s episcopate from his saying “while we were absent.” For if Indicia had been at Rome during his episcopate, it would seem superfluous for him to have mentioned his own absence.

In order to inspect Indicia’s entire life, he seeks testimony from her nurse as well: “We also questioned the nurse, a woman of free condition, to whom both a station not at all degraded by servile subjection gave freedom to speak the truth, and whose trustworthiness and age supported the truth, while the office of nurse supplied knowledge of the secret.” Since, then, St Ambrose establishes Indicia’s innocence through witnesses to her life and conduct who were not Veronese, it must certainly be said that she was not Veronese. Ambrose would wrongly have introduced foreign witnesses to whom Indicia’s habits could not have been known. But if Indicia was not a Veronese, neither is Zeno, praised by Ambrose as the one who consecrated her to God by his blessing, to be considered Veronese; nor should the sermons of St Zeno, bishop of Verona, be ascribed to him.

For this reason Godfrey, in his *Life of St Ambrose*, Book IX, chapter 8, without any basis or authority, called this Indicia a Veronese. Tillemont acted more cautiously, for he did not dare to assert that she was Veronese. I think she should perhaps rather be called a Carthaginian. For, since Ambrose’s testimony establishes that she was in his household at Rome, and Paulinus, the writer of Ambrose’s Life, says that two other virgins cultivated virginity together with Ambrose’s sister, Baronius very plausibly conjectures in his *Life of Ambrose* that Indicia was among them: “Other virgins also joined her, among whom was Indicia.”

Paulinus himself testifies that one of these women was living at Carthage in old age when he wrote; thus it seems by no means remote from the truth to regard her as Carthaginian. These are Paulinus’s words:

> “Afterward, when he had grown up and was living in the city of Rome with his widowed mother and his sister, who had already professed virginity, accompanied by another virgin—the sister of that virgin, Candida, herself also of the same profession, now lives at Carthage, already an old woman.”

I confess, however, that from the quoted words it is not sufficiently clear whether Candida or her sister is said to have been at Carthage. But since Paulinus affirms that they were sisters, it seems safer to regard their homeland as common to both. Nor am I moved away from this opinion by the fact that Indicia had a sister married at Verona, since she could have had a third sister, and marriages between outsiders are not uncommon; nor by Ambrose’s additional statement that Indicia lived at Rome in his household while he was absent: “That she lived at Rome in our house while we were absent.” For Ambrose should be understood to have indicated his absence so that Indicia might not appear to have cultivated virtue and chastity because of Ambrose’s presence. It should not be believed, however, that when Ambrose was still a young man at Rome, Indicia did not live in his house even while he was present, since Paulinus’s testimony establishes that other virgins were then with Marcellina, Ambrose’s sister.

Dupin and Tillemont fall into an even graver error when, entirely by conjecture, they deny that Zeno lived in the time of Gallienus. For this is made certain not only by Veronese history and tradition, but by the old manuscript reported by Mabillon in his *Analecta*, in which St Zeno, bishop of Verona, is placed eighth, as all also affirm. But the eighth bishop of Verona cannot in any way be assigned to the times of St Ambrose. Ughelli, who counts a second Zeno among the bishops of Verona, places him eighteenth; yet he rests on no authority except Ambrose, from whom, as we have shown, this cannot be asserted, and Baronius, who abandoned his own opinion. Papebroch was therefore mistaken in considering the succession of the first eleven bishops of Verona uncertain, since it is proved certain by Mabillon’s manuscript. There is, then, only one St Zeno, the eighth bishop of Verona, who governed that Church around the time of Gallienus.

## CHAPTER XII. No one other than St Zeno should be assigned the sermons in question.

Since, then, for so many centuries—as was shown above (chapter 2)—both outsiders and Veronese have ascribed the praised sermons, inscribed with St Zeno’s name, to that holy bishop, I do not see why they should be assigned to other, more recent persons whose names are unknown, apart from those whom we have listed above (chapter 3). This is especially so since those matters which seemed wholly inconsistent with the times of St Zeno have been removed, and diversity of style presents no obstacle (chapters 4, 5, and 7).

Who, then, can deny that St Zeno’s name ought to be affixed to these sermons, and that they should be considered the genuine offspring of the holy Zeno? I am indeed astonished that Dupin so readily numbered John Nesteutes, or the Faster, among ecclesiastical writers and ascribed to him certain works utterly unknown to the ancients—although we shall show at the end, in the notes on Dupin, on what slight grounds Dupin was led. I am likewise astonished that Tillemont and others, especially heterodox writers, deprive St Chrysostom of homilies in order to assign them to this John, whom they themselves admit to have been a man of only slight learning. Yet they show themselves so hostile to St Zeno that they report only what may seem to detract from his sermons. They pass over so much—as we saw above in dealing with Dupin and Tillemont—which demonstrates St Zeno himself to be the author of these sermons.

Let us therefore beware of them as unjust judges and poor assessors of matters, who rashly pronounce their judgment while either not examining or concealing the truth, and with such confidence as though they were delivering oracles and answers from a tripod by divine inspiration. With a stronger claim of truth, then, let us disregard their cavils. For how can trust be placed in those who craftily deny the truth and most shamelessly reject it? Let us therefore dismiss those who have thought contrary to us, and acknowledge that St Zeno was the author of the sermons of which we have treated.

# BOOK II. ON THE MARTYRDOM OF ST ZENO, BISHOP OF VERONA

[Col. 0617]

## CHAPTER I. St Zeno’s martyrdom is proved from ancient monuments of the Church of Verona.

[Col. 0617B]

[Col. 0617C] At Verona, in the monastery of St Zeno, there survives in an old manuscript a certain rhythmic account of the city of Verona. Anyone may see part of it both prefixed to the works of St Zeno published at Verona and in the Library of the Fathers; in it St Zeno is adorned with the title of martyr:

> Zeno, the eighth pastor and confessor,  
> An illustrious martyr.

The most distinguished Ludovico Antonio Muratori, in his celebrated work *On the Writers of Italian Affairs* (vol. II, part 2), judges this account to have been composed in 790. He prints it entire from Mabillon (*Analecta*, vol. VIII, Paris edition, 1675, p. 375), who copied it from the autograph manuscript of Lobbes and says that it was placed there by Ratherius, bishop of Verona, during the reign of Pippin, Charlemagne’s son, in the year which Muratori judges to have been 970.

Philip Ferrarius of the Order of Servants likewise, in his *Catalogue of the Saints of Italy* for 12 April, cites from the ancient Office of St Zeno part of a hymn in which St Zeno too is called martyr:

> He was a martyr of the Most High and a priest,  
> Traversing the unrestrained peoples of the sea.  
> Then God saw fit to send him  
> To the city of Verona.  
>
> There, having won many people for God,  
> He instructed them by words and strengthened them by deeds.  
> At last, suffering death for God,  
> He lives for ever.

The hymn survives complete among the works of the holy Zeno printed at Verona; it begins, “Of the holy bishop.” Ferrarius also notes the following concerning St Zeno’s Life: “Although the kind of martyrdom by which St Zeno died is unknown, it should nevertheless not be doubted that he was a martyr, since Pope St Gregory, in Book III, chapter 19 of the *Dialogues*, calls him a martyr, and the Church of Verona has always venerated him as a martyr. There is added, what is greater, the authority of the Roman Martyrology—to omit the many writers who speak of St Zeno as a martyr, among them Paul the Deacon, Book XVIII of the *Deeds of the Romans* under Maurice.”

Peretti and Bagatta also testify, in the abridgment of St Zeno’s Life attached to his works in the Library of the Fathers, that St Zeno was a martyr from the readings formerly read in his Office. Joseph Dondori of the Capuchin Order confirms this (*Pietà di Pistoia*, part 2, *Life of St Zeno*); he saw these readings both in the lectionary of the Church of Pistoia, now lost, and in that of Verona. To this man’s diligence we owe many ancient monuments of our city, which he sought out with careful industry and made public.

This distinguished author further observes that three feasts of St Zeno are celebrated at Verona: the more solemn feast of his Ordination, 6 December, on which, he says, no mention is made of St Zeno’s martyrdom at Verona; that of his Martyrdom, 12 April; and that of his Translation, 21 May. The latter feast alone is celebrated; the feasts of Ordination and Martyrdom are observed also at Pistoia. It is therefore established that in antiquity St Zeno was regarded at Verona as a martyr. Cardinal Valerius, bishop of Verona, also testifies in the dedicatory letter of St Zeno’s Works to Sixtus V, Supreme Pontiff, that he has been adorned with this title by perpetual and continuous tradition. The objections brought against this Veronese tradition will be refuted below, in chapter 6.

## CHAPTER II. The monuments of the Church of Pistoia demonstrate that St Zeno was a martyr.

The reason why the cathedral church of Pistoia, which had previously venerated St Martin, bishop, as its titular saint, adopted St Zeno as patron and changed its title can be conjectured rather than demonstrated. In Joseph Dondori (*Pietà di Pistoia*, part 1, “On the Cathedral Church”) there is an account suggesting that, after the miracle of the Adige, which stopped with its waters at the doors of the Church of St Zeno at Verona and did not flow inside, the people of Pistoia began to venerate this holy bishop; and that, in the course of time, after choosing him as patron, they adorned their cathedral church with the title of his name.

That this change of title was very ancient in the Church of Pistoia may be recognized from a martyrology and calendar found in an old manuscript codex in the archive of the chapter of that cathedral, together with the book of canonical life issued by command of Emperor Louis the Pious at the council of bishops held at Aachen in 816, as is stated at the beginning of that book. Baronius, however, places this council in 817. In this calendar mention is made of St Zeno the martyr as patron of this church, as we shall see below.

Likewise, in another manuscript entitled *Order of the Divine Offices according to the Custom of the Church of Pistoia*, whose antiquity may be inferred from the rubric concerning the public reconciliation by the bishop of penitents on Thursday in the Lord’s Supper, the following is written for 6 December concerning the feast of St Zeno: “On the feast of St Zeno, our patron, our Church celebrates more devoutly and carefully than on other feasts.”

That the Church of Pistoia venerated St Zeno as a martyr in ancient times is established by these same manuscripts. For in the aforesaid manuscript calendar, on 21 April, the day on which St Zeno’s natal feast was celebrated, one reads: “The deposition of St Zeno, our patron, martyr of Verona.” Yet on 6 December the same calendar reads: “The nativity of St Zeno, our patron.”

In the other manuscript mentioned above, entitled *Order of the Divine Offices according to the Custom of the Church of Pistoia*, on 6 December at Lauds and at Vespers, the hymn “Of the Holy Bishop” is noted, part of which we have quoted above (chapter 1), and in which St Zeno’s martyrdom is commemorated. The entire Office, however, is for a confessor-bishop. But on the April feast, the antiphons at Lauds are marked as those of martyrs in Paschal time, namely: “Your saints, O Lord.” For the *Benedictus*, the antiphon is “Acceptable,” which is proper to St Zeno, or “Everlasting light,” which belongs to martyrs. At Prime, the antiphon is “In the heavenly kingdoms,” likewise from the common of martyrs in Paschal time. At Vespers, the antiphon is “Your saints, O Lord,” from the common of martyrs in Paschal time. In the other antiphons and responsories drawn from the history of St Zeno, which are not given in full, perhaps the martyrdom of this holy bishop is commemorated. But since I have not seen the old Office, I do not dare affirm this.

There is another manuscript in the same archive concerning the Divine Offices of the Church of Pistoia, more recent than the one just mentioned. For in this latter manuscript the order of the Office for the feast of St Francis appears, while in the former only the Offices of more ancient saints are arranged; and in my judgment it was written in the tenth century. This later manuscript notes an Office only for the feast of St Zeno in December. It mentions his martyrdom only at Vespers and Lauds, where it indicates the hymn “Of the Holy Bishop,” in which St Zeno’s martyrdom is commemorated (see chapter 1); the rest of the Office and the Mass are for a confessor-bishop. For on this feast St Zeno’s Ordination is celebrated.

In another manuscript likewise preserved in the same archive, entitled *Book of Hymns and Calendar of the Church of Pistoia*, the following appears: “6 December: St Zeno, bishop.” But in April there is nothing concerning St Zeno. In the above-mentioned manuscript martyrology from the same archive, which, as may be inferred from the saints listed, was written in the tenth century, the entry for 6 December is: “On the same day, the natal feast of St Zeno, bishop and confessor.” On 20 April nothing appears in the text concerning the feast of St Zeno. Yet in the margin, in different ink and a much more recent hand, is written: “Likewise, on the same day, the deposition of St Zeno, bishop, and . . . our patron”; after the word “and” a symbol is inserted signifying “confessor.” But the letter where the symbol occurs seems to have been erased—probably, I think, an *M*, formerly reading “martyr,” because the narrow space did not allow the whole word *confessor* to be written. I would say that the symbol was added by someone who considered St Zeno a confessor.

The same may be observed in another tenth-century manuscript martyrology existing at Pistoia in the public library of the venerable House of Wisdom. It reads:

> “On the day before the Ides of April . . . and confessor. On the same day, St Zeno, bishop, who amid the storms of persecution wonderfully governed the Church of Verona . . . of Valerian and . . . and in the time of the emperors Gallienus converted a multitude of pa . . . gans to the faith; nevertheless, his deposition is celebrated at Pistoia on 20 April. And his solemn feast is on 6 December, as is there stated.”

The words “and confessor” have been added in a different script and ink, as have “of Valerian and.” After the name “Gallienus,” something has been erased over a space just large enough to contain the words *martyrio coronatus est*, “he was crowned with martyrdom.” In their place, in the same different hand, are written “of the emperors, and a multitude of pa . . .”; the remainder is in the margin in the same hand. That the words *martyrio coronatus est* were erased is clearly apparent both from the erased space and from the superadded word “confessor.”

This error crept in because the more solemn feast of St Zeno was held at Verona on 6 December and is still observed at Pistoia; this is the day of his Ordination, and the Office is read for a confessor-bishop, especially at Verona, where, as Dondori observes (loc. cit., chapter 1), no mention whatever is made of St Zeno’s martyrdom. At Pistoia, however, as we observed above, St Zeno’s martyrdom was commemorated in the hymn “Of the Holy Bishop,” and is still commemorated in the Prayer and in the Lessons of the second Nocturn.

But I believe this correction was made by someone ignorant of the Offices of the Church of Pistoia. His ignorance is evident from the words “of Valerian and . . .” and from the added words, “And in the time of the emperors Gallienus he converted a multitude of pagans to the faith,” which do not at all cohere with what precedes. For there is plainly no reason why the same feast should be celebrated twice a year in the same church. Therefore the April feast must be different from the December feast: namely, the latter is that of Ordination, the former that of the natal day; nor should they be distinguished merely by a more or less solemn rite. Hence he wrongly noted, “His solemn feast is on 6 December,” and so forth.

This error passed from the manuscript into certain printed martyrologies, as may be seen in the public and extensive library built at Pistoia at the expense of the Most Eminent Cardinal Fabroni. There is preserved there a martyrology printed at Florence through the work of Francesco de Bonaccursiis in 1486, which says of St Zeno:

> “On the day before the Ides of April . . . Likewise St Zeno, bishop and confessor of Verona, who for three years under Valerian and Gallienus, illustrious in faith and conspicuous in holiness, preached Christ’s faith most fervently to his people and converted a great multitude of pagans to the faith of Christ. Nevertheless, his feast is celebrated on 6 December.”

But in December the same martyrology reads: “6 December, at Verona, St Zeno, bishop and confessor of the same city, a man of every holiness.” Here nothing is said of the feast of Ordination, and it is quite plainly evident that the feasts of Ordination and Deposition, or martyrdom, are confused—feasts which are correctly distinguished in the Roman Martyrology and others. Although, therefore, confusion is found in ancient monuments of this Church of Pistoia concerning the Office of St Zeno in the rite of martyr and confessor, it is nonetheless evident that he was always considered a martyr. Thus the uninterrupted tradition concerning St Zeno’s martyrdom is most clearly demonstrated, and it continues even in our own times.

## CHAPTER III. St Zeno’s martyrdom is proved by external authorities.

St Gregory the Great, Book III of the *Dialogues*, chapter 19, in recounting the miracle of the River Adige, calls St Zeno a martyr:

> “Near the city of Verona, the River Adige, rising in flood, came to the church of blessed Zeno, martyr and bishop. Although the doors of that church were open, the water did not enter it.”

Paul the Deacon too, in *The Deeds of the Lombards*, Book III, chapter 23, calls him a martyr while treating of the miracle of the Adige:

> “The roads were destroyed, the ways ruined, and the River Adige then rose so high that around the basilica of blessed Zeno the martyr, which stands outside the walls of the city of Verona, the water reached the upper windows; although blessed Pope Gregory wrote that the water did not enter the same basilica.”

The Modenese manuscript, as Muratori notes (*Rerum Italicarum*, vol. I, p. 447), adds to the word “martyr,” “and confessor.” Rabanus, cited by Papebroch, has the following concerning St Zeno: “On the same day, in the city of Verona, the Passion of St Zeno, martyr.” But on 8 December: “In the city of Verona, the natal feast of St Zeno, martyr.” Rabanus wrote during the reign of Louis the Pious. Notker likewise calls St Zeno a martyr on 12 April and 6 December. The Church of Freising too venerates St Zeno as bishop and martyr, as the same Papebroch affirms (*Acta Sanctorum*, April, 12th day, chapter 2, no. 3).

Bede likewise, in his Martyrology, writes for 12 April: “At the city of Verona, the Passion of St Zeno, martyr”; and for 6 December: “In the city of Verona, the natal feast of St Zeno, martyr, concerning whom blessed Gregory relates in the book of the *Dialogues*.” Usuard, too, in his Martyrology for 12 April says: “On the same day, St Zeno, bishop, who amid the storms of persecution wonderfully governed the Church of Verona and, in the time of Gallienus, was crowned with martyrdom.”

Note here Usuard’s words, which are the very same as the words of the manuscript martyrology preserved here at Pistoia in the library of the venerable House of Wisdom, of which we spoke in chapter 2 when we dealt with the correction—or rather corruption—of that manuscript. This confirms our opinion: namely, that the words “he was crowned with martyrdom” were deleted in that manuscript. Wandelbert, in his metrical Martyrology for 6 December, sang thus (in D’Achery, *Spicilegium*, vol. V):

> Zeno also possesses this day  
> With the united honour of martyrdom.

Likewise Peter Galesinius writes in his notes for 12 April: “St Zeno, bishop and martyr, as is established from the testimony of St Gregory and from every martyrology; and this is shown more fully in the book recently published concerning the holy bishops of Verona. On this very day his Martyrdom is celebrated; on 6 December, his Ordination; on 21 May, his Translation at Verona. His Life, written by Coronatus the notary, survives at Lobbes. Read Surius besides.”

Constantius Felicius, in his calendar, has the following in the vernacular for 12 April, which we render into Latin: “Zeno, bishop of Verona, martyr under the emperor Gallienus.” And on 6 December: “Zeno, bishop of Verona, very celebrated for miracles, flourished in the time of the emperor Gallienus; he had freed the emperor’s daughter from a demon.”

Therefore De Aste must be read cautiously. In his *Disputations on the Roman Martyrology* for 12 April he adduces Felicius and Galesinius as persons who called St Zeno a confessor rather than a martyr. One must consequently fear that he is mistaken in citing other authors as well, just as he is mistaken in these. For it is false when he says: “Likewise Vuitford, Bellinus, Galesinius, and Felicius, all proclaiming with one voice, call St Zeno bishop and confessor.” That this departs from the truth may be recognized from the Galesinius and Felicius passages just quoted.

## CHAPTER IV. The authority of the Roman Martyrology assigns the title of martyr to St Zeno.

All those whom we have listed above testify to St Zeno’s martyrdom before the Roman Martyrology was corrected by Pope Gregory XIII. The same Martyrology agrees with them, and correctly distinguishes the feast of St Zeno’s martyrdom from that of his Ordination. For on 12 April it says concerning St Zeno’s martyrdom: “At Verona, the Passion of St Zeno, bishop, who amid the storms of persecution governed that Church with admirable constancy and, in the time of Gallienus, was crowned with martyrdom.” On 6 December: “At Verona, the Ordination of St Zeno, bishop.”

The authority of this Martyrology ought to suffice for fair-minded judges. For no one is unaware that the Roman Church, head and teacher of the others, has always employed the greatest diligence in investigating the acts of martyrs and in protecting them from the errors of unlearned persons and heretics. Although the Roman Church has always exercised this diligence, it took still more exact care in correcting the Martyrology, as Gregory himself testifies in the brief prefixed to it: namely, that the Roman Martyrology, “in some places corrupted by the negligence of copyists and printers, had been corrected by learned men according to the truth of history, which comprises a variety of events, persons, places, and times, with older and more accurate manuscripts also being used.”

We shall show, in refuting contrary objections below (chapter 7), that those who try to maintain from the authority of the old Roman Martyrology that St Zeno was not a martyr but a confessor are mistaken. It is indeed astonishing that some persons who wish to be numbered among Catholics speak so carelessly against the Roman Martyrology, showing that in their view it possesses no authority at all.

## CHAPTER V. What trust is due to the Life of St Zeno written by a certain Coronatus, notary, in which St Zeno is called a confessor.

We must now answer the objections. First we must deal with a certain Coronatus, notary, who, in describing St Zeno’s Life in a crude style, writes the following concerning his death: “When it pleased the will of God, he was received in peace.” Thus Ughelli (*Italia Sacra*, vol. V, “On the Bishops of Verona,” no. 8, *Life of St Zeno*).

The Fathers of the Congregation of St Maur also mention this Coronatus in the prefatory notice to Psalm 126 in their edition of the Works of St Hilary. They say that a commentary on the Life of St Zeno is preserved at the beginning of the works of that holy bishop in the Library of St Remigius, bearing this title: “Sermon of the venerable Coronatus, notary, on the life of St Zeno, bishop and confessor.” In this sermon Zeno is proclaimed as sanctified from his mother’s womb. Concerning his death it says: “Not long afterward he was received in peace.”

Ughelli copied this little work word for word from an Aedine codex of the Abbey of St Saviour of Monte Amiata, and it contains nothing at all about the sanctification of St Zeno in his mother’s womb. Its words concerning his death also differ, as may be seen in Ughelli at the passage cited above, where one reads: “When it pleased [God’s] will, he was received in peace.” In the codex of St Remigius: “Not long afterward he was received in peace.”

Another difference in these two codices should also be noted. In the Reims codex, St Zeno is said to have been ordained bishop of the Veronese; of this Ordination the codex of the Abbey of St Saviour of Monte Amiata, as printed by Ughelli, makes no mention. Moreover, the Life of St Zeno said to have been written by Coronatus and printed by Ughelli differs from that read in Papebroch (vol. II, 12 April). Tillemont therefore considers Coronatus’s work to possess no authority, a judgment made more certain by the difference noted in the two manuscripts. Thus Combefis should not be trusted too much when he says that the manuscript codices of St Zeno’s Life written by Coronatus are not dissimilar; for, as we shall see below, he is not sufficiently reliable in citing authorities.

Tillemont believes that this same work of Coronatus was written after the translation of St Zeno’s body, which took place in 805, in the time of King Pippin. But it is certain that this notary Coronatus did not live in St Zeno’s own age, for he relates the miracle of the Adige, which certainly occurred in the time of St Gregory the Great, more than three hundred years after St Zeno. Therefore the reliability of this manuscript is uncertain, and it should not be preferred to the many ancient and certain monuments reported above. Rather, anyone of understanding must reject it as doubtful.

## CHAPTER VI. Panvinio is explained: in Book IV of the *Antiquities of Verona* he says that the Church of Verona did not formerly venerate St Zeno as a martyr, and that Aloysius Lippomanus was the first to order the Office of St Zeno as that of a martyr-bishop.

[Col. 0624C]

Panvinius of Verona is highly praised by Dupin, Tillemont, and others who oppose St. Zeno’s martyrdom. We have undertaken here to explain his authority as received from Ughelli:

> “But since, as I suppose, the manner of his martyrdom was not established, the Church of Verona, from the beginning down to our own age, made an annual commemoration of him as of a confessor-bishop. Aloysius Lippomano, bishop of Verona, was the first, having been persuaded in our time by the testimonies which I have cited above, to institute in the Church of Verona a solemn commemoration of him as of a martyr-bishop.”

[Col. 0624D] De Aste testifies that Cardinal Valerio asserted the same in his book *On the Bishops of Verona*, folio 15. But Cardinal Valerio, in the dedication of St. Zeno’s works addressed to Sixtus V, calls St. Zeno a martyr; and in the same book on the holy bishops of Verona, as is apparent from Peter Galesinus, whom we cited above (chap. 3), he affirms the same. Panvinius himself also maintains that St. Zeno was a martyr, although he held the opinion that the Church of Verona had formerly celebrated the Office of St. Zeno as that of a confessor-bishop.

Dupin and Tillemont did not observe this from Panvinius’s words, but only that which favored their own opinion: namely, the alleged tradition of the Church of Verona [Col. 0625A] concerning the title “Confessor.” In this they depart from that faith which, if it be lacking, leaves the whole truth of history unsteady. Yet this question is easily resolved upon inspection of the manuscript evidence. For from the records of the Churches of Verona and Pistoia cited above (chaps. 1 and 2), and especially from those which one must believe the Church of Pistoia borrowed from that of Verona, it is clear that St. Zeno’s martyrdom is commemorated in the Lessons, Hymn, and Antiphons.

It is indeed true that the remaining Office for St. Zeno’s feasts was arranged from the common Office of confessor-bishops. Thus the rite for a martyr and that for a confessor are plainly combined in the Office of St. Zeno. This may perhaps have been because, since the solemn feast of St. Zeno was celebrated both among the Veronese and among the Pistoiese on the sixth day before the Ides of December—the day of his ordination—[Col. 0625B] early simplicity adapted only one Office to the two feasts. Thus the memory of St. Zeno’s martyrdom was preserved solely in the Lessons, Hymn, Antiphons, and perhaps in the Prayer, which even in our present Office does not appear to have been altered, since it bears many marks of antiquity.

Therefore this is what Lippomano must be said to have done: he removed this confusion in the Office; retaining the rite of a confessor-bishop for the feast-day of the Ordination, he assigned the rite of the entire Office of a martyr-bishop to the natal feast of St. Zeno, on the day before the Ides of April. It is certain, moreover, that before Lippomano the feast of the Ordination, on the sixth day before the Ides of December, used to be celebrated more solemnly at Verona; but after Lippomano the more solemn feast at Verona was also customarily celebrated in our own times on the day of the Nativity, or martyrdom, [Col. 0625C] the day before the Ides of April. I should judge that Lippomano prescribed this so that St. Zeno’s martyrdom might be commemorated with greater solemnity.

But it cannot in any way be said that Lippomano was the first to institute the commemoration of St. Zeno’s martyrdom, since that contradicts every ancient record. Lippomano, therefore, did not first establish the celebration of the martyrdom; rather, he distinguished the Offices that had been combined, assigning the Office of a Confessor to the Ordination and that of a Martyr to St. Zeno’s Nativity.

## CHAPTER VII. On Usuard’s Martyrology as corrected by Molanus, the ancient Roman Martyrology, and other Martyrologies

In his annotations on Usuard’s Martyrology, on the day before the Ides of April, where St. Zeno is concerned, Molanus removed [Col. 0625D] these words of Usuard: “And in the time of Gallienus he was crowned by martyrdom.” He gives the reason for this correction in these words:

> “Concerning Zeno, I removed Usuard’s words, ‘and in the time of Gallienus he was crowned by martyrdom.’ It is established from the Roman Martyrology, the Office of the Church of Milan on the eighth day of December, and elsewhere, that he is honored as a confessor. There also survives at Lobbes the account by the venerable Coronatus, most Christian notary, concerning the life of St. Zeno, bishop and confessor. Nevertheless, in book three of the *Dialogues*, chapter 19, Gregory preferred twice to call him a martyr rather than a confessor, because amid the storms of persecution he bore many things courageously; for the same reason he elsewhere calls Juvenal a martyr as well.”

We have already spoken of the account of Coronatus the notary (chap. 5). As for the Office of the Church of Milan, [Col. 0626A] there is nothing to be said: on the eighth day of December the feast of St. Zeno’s ordination is celebrated as that of a confessor-bishop, not only at Milan, but also at Verona, Pistoia, and Pisa. Thus the feast of the Chair of St. Peter, both Roman and Antiochene, is celebrated without any mention of martyrdom.

Yet in the Ambrosian Missal published by order of Frederick Cardinal Borromeo, Archbishop of Milan, the eighth day of December contains the feast of the Conception of the Blessed Virgin Mary, with a commemoration of St. Zeno; and in the prayers St. Zeno is called martyr and bishop. Nor is it surprising, as Tillemont affirms, that in the Ambrosian Missal of 1560 no commemoration is made of martyrdom, since even at Verona—as we noted above from Dondorius (chap. 1)—there is complete silence concerning St. Zeno’s martyrdom on the feast of his ordination. [Col. 0626B]

We must now speak of the Roman Martyrology. The question, however, is not about the corrected Roman Martyrology, in which St. Zeno is adorned with the title of martyr, but about the ancient Roman Martyrology as Combefis thought it to be. He failed to notice Molanus’s error, although Molanus himself, after publishing Usuard’s Martyrology, recognized it. For in his letter to the reader, before Usuard’s Martyrology, Molanus admits that he had used Bellini of Padua’s Martyrology as the Roman Martyrology, and that he had seen no other Roman Martyrology:

> “There exist,” he says, “other Martyrologies of the Roman Church, which I have not seen.”

But when he had seen the Roman Martyrology published in Baronius’s time, he corrected his notes on Usuard and adapted them to the Roman Martyrology; yet, overtaken by death, he could not publish them. [Col. 0626C] Baronius so testifies in the prolegomena to the Roman Martyrology, before his notes, chapter nine:

> “Very many ancient manuscript copies of the Roman Martyrology escaped Molanus; from them he could have understood more certainly what the genuine Roman Martyrology itself was and what sort of work it was. His error is indeed tolerable and worthy of pardon, since, living so far away, he was ignorant of matters which those residing in Rome have obtained only with great labor, sleepless diligence, and utmost industry. I was, moreover, not a little pleased when, just as the printer was most opportunely preparing for a second edition, I learned from the letters of the most reverend Lord Henry Gravius, theologian of Louvain, that this conjecture and suspicion of mine was by no means empty or groundless. For he writes to me that the most reverend Lord Molanus, after receiving the recently published Roman Martyrology, thoroughly revised and enlarged the notes which he had long before written on Usuard, and adjusted and adapted them to that Martyrology; but, being carried off by untimely death, he was unable to do more.” [Col. 0626D]

So writes Baronius.
