It should also be observed that Molanus himself, in his little work *On Martyrologies*, affirms that the Roman Church had been accustomed to use an enlarged Martyrology of Usuard, in which St. Zeno is said to have been crowned by martyrdom in the time of Gallienus. The Roman Martyrology, therefore—which, in Molanus’s own judgment, is the same as Usuard’s enlarged Martyrology—confirms that St. Zeno was a martyr. But Bellini’s Martyrology, which Molanus saw, calls St. Zeno a confessor on the sixth day before the Ides of December, [Col. 0627A] that is, on the day when the feast of his ordination is celebrated. On the day before the Ides of April, however, Bellini makes no mention whatsoever of St. Zeno.

Therefore it is not surprising that Bellini considered St. Zeno a confessor on the day when his commemoration was celebrated by the Office of confessors. The same is done in this diocese of Pistoia, where St. Zeno is honored as a martyr even to the present day. Yet on the sixth day before the Ides of December he is annually designated in the calendar by the title of confessor, in order to indicate the rite by which his feast is celebrated, although in the prayer and the lessons of the second nocturn the memory of his martyrdom is recalled:

> Eighth of December: Ordination of St. Zeno, bishop and confessor, patron and titular of the cathedral church.  
> Twelfth of April: St. Zeno, bishop and martyr.  
> (*Calendar of Pistoia.*)

The same should also be noted [Col. 0627B] in the edict issued in this year 1732 by the most illustrious and reverend Lord Columbino Bassi, our bishop of Pistoia and Prato, concerning the transfer of certain feasts. There the feast of the Immaculate Conception of the Blessed Virgin Mary is transferred because it coincides with the feast of St. Zeno’s ordination; and in that place St. Zeno is called by the title of confessor:

> “The Office of the Conception of the Blessed Virgin Mary, double of the second class, is to be recited on the eighth day of December; this day is most solemn for us because of the feast of the Ordination of St. Zeno, bishop and confessor, patron and titular of the cathedral church, double of the first class.”

The same is to be said of the manuscript Martyrology discussed above (chap. 2), for on the eighth day of December St. Zeno is there called bishop and confessor. Indeed, the corrected Roman Martyrology itself, on the same day of St. Zeno’s ordination, does not call him a martyr; it reads: [Col. 0627C] “At Verona, the ordination of St. Zeno, bishop.” The ancient calendars of the Church of Pistoia listed above agree with this. For in the first one we cited, on the sixth day before the Ides of December, one reads: “The nativity of St. Zeno, our patron,” although in the same calendar, on the twelfth day before the Kalends of May, St. Zeno is distinguished by the title of martyr. In another manuscript cited, on the sixth day before the Ides of December: “St. Zeno, bishop.”

Therefore, if St. Zeno is called a confessor in other Martyrologies also on the sixth day before the Ides of December, this must be said to have been done because on that day St. Zeno’s feast is celebrated by the rite of confessors. Since that feast was more celebrated than the others, the authors of Martyrologies took the title “confessor” from it; Felicius likewise retained this in his calendar. For when he had called St. Zeno a martyr on the day before the Ides of April, he called him merely bishop on the sixth day before the Ides of December. [Col. 0627D] There is therefore no reason why we should take from St. Zeno the palm of martyrdom, even though in some Martyrologies St. Zeno is simply named.

## CHAPTER VIII. The objections brought by certain authors, especially Dupin and Tillemont, against the authority of St. Gregory are weighed

Dupin and Tillemont attempt to diminish the authority of St. Gregory (*Sixth Century*, vol. IV, on St. Gregory, cited place), accusing him of excessive credulity; and Tillemont adds that St. Gregory bestowed the title of martyr upon others contrary to historical truth. But these latter-day writers have drawn these streams of calumny from the sources of heretics.

How rashly they accuse St. Gregory of frivolity is evident from the instruction which that most holy pontiff gave Augustine, Archbishop of Canterbury, concerning the rendering of cult to someone as a martyr, when he granted Augustine relics of St. Sixtus the martyr (*Letters*, book II, indiction 7):

> “We have done what you asked, so that the people who are said to venerate, in a certain place, the body of St. Sixtus the martyr—which does not seem either genuine or truly holy to your Fraternity—may receive sure benefits from a most holy and fully approved martyr, and ought not to venerate what is uncertain. Yet it seems to me that, if the body believed by the people to be that of a certain martyr is not made illustrious by any miracles, and if none of the older people can be found who admit that they heard of his passion from their parents, the relics which you requested must be deposited separately, so that the place where the aforesaid body lies may be closed off in every way, and the people may not be permitted to forsake what is certain and venerate what is uncertain.” [Col. 0628B]

Is this to be regarded as credulity, when, before the title of martyr is bestowed upon anyone, it disregards popular report and requires either miracles or a verified tradition of the ancients? Should we believe that St. Gregory did not himself practice, in granting the cult of a martyr, what he prescribed to others?

What do these modern writers possess by which to charge St. Gregory with error in giving St. Zeno the title of martyr? The account of Coronatus the notary? An apocryphal little work by an uncertain author, worthy of no credence, as they themselves admit and as we have proved above (chap. 5)? A contrary tradition of the Church of Verona? A manifest error of Panvinius, as the ancient records establish (chap. 6)? The authority of the ancient Roman Martyrology? Molanus’s imprudent mistake, in which he used Bellini’s Martyrology in place of the Roman one (chap. 7)? [Col. 0628C]

Are these the arguments by which they demonstrate that St. Gregory should not be believed? His authority agrees both with the tradition of the Church of Verona and with that of this Church of Pistoia, and with the more ancient manuscripts (chaps. 1, 2).

Perhaps they will say that the response of St. Gregory just cited concerns not merely the title of martyr, but the granting of cult to doubtful relics of a holy martyr; nor is it in doubt whether St. Zeno deserves the crown of sanctity, but only whether he is to be regarded merely as a confessor or also as a martyr. Yet if the holy pontiff was so prudent and cautious in permitting the cult of a doubtful relic, ought he to have been so careless as to call Zeno a martyr for the first time, when, if Zeno had not been a martyr, all Verona would have venerated him as a confessor? [Col. 0628D]

Let St. Zeno, then, rejoice that he has so great a patron and defender of his glorious martyrdom: one who employed such counsel and such prudence before considering saints worthy of the cult of martyrdom. Nor should these modern writers, with so blind an onslaught of their sharp pens, tear apart the authority of so great a pontiff. Why do they adduce, without any discrimination, only those things which are so easily shown to be uncertain and false against St. Gregory’s established credibility? Why have they neglected to consider the matters arranged in this treatise, many of which they could have seen in Baronius and the other authors whom we have cited? [Col. 0629A]

They should therefore refrain from calumnies, and should not blame Bede or others if, perhaps guided by St. Gregory’s authority, they called St. Zeno a martyr. Is not Verona a famous city of Italy, whose holy patron Gregory, the supreme pontiff—himself an Italian Roman, thoroughly versed in Italian affairs both through events in Italy and through the administration of the Roman pontificate—could easily have known?

And why do they doubt concerning Paul the Deacon, who calls St. Zeno a martyr? On what ground do they suppose that he affirmed this under the influence of St. Gregory’s authority? For Paul, an Aquileian by birth and secretary to Desiderius, king of the Lombards, knew exceptionally well the city of Verona, situated not very far from Pavia. Could he have been ignorant of the cult with which all Verona honored its patron? [Col. 0629B] Let these remarks suffice in defense of St. Gregory’s authority, since in book III of the *Dialogues*, chapter 19, he declares St. Zeno to be a martyr. But the matter which Tillemont very rashly affirms—namely, that St. Gregory called other saints martyrs contrary to historical truth—must be treated separately.

## CHAPTER IX. How lightly Dupin and Tillemont assert that St. Zeno was not a martyr but a confessor

Since, therefore, we have overthrown the objections raised against St. Zeno’s martyrdom, the assurance of Dupin, Tillemont, and certain modern writers seems truly worthy of astonishment. Disdaining antiquity, they always rush headlong into new opinions. To make this plainly evident, we here set forth their statements translated from French into Latin.

“Common opinion,” says Dupin, “is that there was a certain Zeno, bishop of Verona, who suffered martyrdom under the empire of Gallienus. Certain sermons are also attributed to him by Guarino, printed at Venice and Verona in 1508 and 1586, which were afterwards inserted in the Library of the Fathers. But the works of this author, whom antiquity wholly ignored, are rejected. And it is questioned whether there was a bishop of this name at Verona who died a martyr under Gallienus’s empire.” [Col. 0629C]

To prove this, he adduces nothing but St. Ambrose’s letter written to Syagrius (book I, chapter 11), in which he says that mention is made of a certain Zeno, falsely described as Syagrius’s predecessor. He also adduces Molanus’s correction and Panvinius’s opinion concerning the tradition of the Church of Verona, matters of which we have spoken above (book II, chaps. 6, 7).

But how shamefully he errs in denying that St. Zeno was bishop of Verona in Gallienus’s time is plain from Mabillon’s manuscript cited above (book II, chap. 1), which places Zeno eighth in the list of the bishops of Verona. The eighth bishop of Verona can fit no time except that of Gallienus.

Tillemont also (*Ecclesiastical Memoirs*, vol. IV, on the Persecution of Valerian, note 5) values so highly the arguments we have rejected above that he thinks this question cannot be resolved in any other way than by believing that St. Zeno did not live in Gallienus’s time:

> “The easiest way to extricate ourselves from all these difficulties is honestly to acknowledge that we have no evidence that St. Zeno lived in Gallienus’s time.” [Col. 0630A]

He mentions the Missal of Milan, published in 1560, in which St. Zeno’s feast is observed by the rite of a confessor. But he should have observed that it is the feast of the Ordination, not of the martyrdom; even at Verona no mention of martyrdom is made in that feast (book II, chap. 7).

He proves that St. Zeno was a confessor by the authority of Coronatus the notary:

> “The sole history that we have of this saint, which is said to have been written after St. Gregory and before the ninth century, says that he rested in peace and recounts nothing that he suffered for the faith.”

He later rejects that history because it says that St. Zeno lived in Gallienus’s time:

> “However this life, composed by a certain Coronatus the notary, may stand, it abounds in so many errors that it should be regarded as of no authority.” [Col. 0630B]

We omit other matters that we have discussed above. From these things, however, it is clear how rashly they disdain the more ancient authors and records, and impose upon us their path to truth while advancing only uncertain and false arguments. For how can anyone give credence to what is brought forward by an uncertain writer of no authority, and scorn what the Roman Martyrology itself, Bede, Paul the Deacon, and other most distinguished authors attest? Their works, spread everywhere, would not have escaped just censure if any error had crept into them.

But these modern writers, who falsely suppose themselves wiser than all the ancients and who receive or reject the same authorities at will, criticize ancient writers with excessive ease. Yet to depart from their judgment, especially in matters pertaining to ancient history, unless they are convicted of a most manifest error, is not sufficiently safe; indeed, I should judge that it is not far removed from danger. [Col. 0630C]

## CHAPTER X. The remaining points reported by Papebroch on the day before the Ides of April, by which St. Zeno is maintained to be a confessor, are examined

Several matters are found in Papebroch which we have fittingly treated above. We spoke of Bellini and Molanus in chapter 7, and likewise of the tradition of the Church of Verona in chapter 6. We shall here discuss the remaining matters, so that we may examine everything we know.

It should therefore not seem surprising that in the Ambrosian Church, and in its Missals of 1522 and 1560, as also in the Breviary, St. Zeno is called a confessor, since [Col. 0630D] that Church observes only the feast of St. Zeno’s Ordination. This is celebrated for a confessor-bishop, both in the Church of Verona and in that of Pistoia, where, as we observed (chap. 7), even to the present time the same feast is marked in the Calendar under the title “Confessor-Bishop,” to indicate the rite.

But now the Ambrosian Church itself, as may be seen in the aforesaid Missal of 1692, honors St. Zeno as a martyr on the day before the Ides of December. This is no slight argument for confirming the truth of St. Zeno’s martyrdom. For that Church, so scrupulous in observing its own rites, corrected its ancient Missals in this way; and it certainly would not have done so unless it had been certain that St. Zeno was crowned by martyrdom.

If, however, we read St. Zeno called a confessor rather than a martyr in certain Martyrologies and Missals because the feast of his Ordination was being celebrated, then he could easily have been called St. Zeno the Confessor in the charter of Louis the Pious, because his principal feast, namely that of the Ordination, was more solemnly celebrated at Verona, and men scarcely knew from generation to generation that the feast of his martyrdom was celebrated. [Col. 0631A]

This becomes more probable because in antiquity no feast of saints was celebrated during Lent, as may be inferred from the canon of the Council of Toledo held in 656 (in Martène, vol. V, p. 63):

> “Nothing concerning the solemnities of saints, as has been prescribed by regular antiquity, should be celebrated.”

A manuscript of this cathedral Church of Pistoia agrees with this canon, and from it the antiquity of our Church is confirmed. For concerning the feast of St. Zeno’s martyrdom in April, it says:

> “If the feast of Blessed Zeno falls on any day of Lent, or on the day of the Resurrection, or on the following Monday or Tuesday, in that year we do nothing concerning him. But if it falls on Wednesday, or on any subsequent day of that Paschal week, or on the very day of the Octave of the Resurrection, then only the Prayer is said for him, with its Antiphon.”  
> (*Order of the Offices of the Church of Pistoia*, title “On the Deposition of St. Zeno,” chap. 2.)

For this reason I think that, in another manuscript Calendar discussed above, the feast of St. Zeno was assigned in this Church of Pistoia to the twelfth day before the Kalends of May, lest it occur and be impeded so frequently during Lent or at the Paschal solemnity. [Col. 0631B]

Since, therefore, the feast of St. Zeno’s martyrdom on the day before the Ides often either was omitted during Lent or at the Paschal solemnities, or was only commemorated, knowledge of it was either nonexistent or so obscure that, especially among laypeople, he was called a confessor rather than a martyr because of the more solemn feast of his Ordination.

As for the relics of St. Zeno the Confessor which are venerated outside the city of Verona, I say that there were several St. Zenos who were confessors, as is evident from the Martyrologies, and that these are not relics of St. Zeno of Verona, except for that one which Hermannus Contractus says was translated to Ulm in 1038 by Walter the German, bishop of Verona (Ughelli, vol. V, *Italia Sacra*, “On the Bishops of Verona”).

Accordingly, Papebroch acted most wisely in choosing to refrain from giving his own judgment because he had not discovered every record concerning St. Zeno’s martyrdom. We leave everything to the judgment of wiser men. It is enough to have shown what we have found written concerning St. Zeno. Thus far he.

## CHAPTER XI. A brief epilogue gathers together the matters set forth above concerning St. Zeno’s martyrdom

[Col. 0632A]

The continuous tradition of the Church of Verona, as also of this distinguished cathedral Church of Pistoia, demonstrates that St. Zeno was a martyr. Although in celebrating St. Zeno’s feasts the rite of martyr and confessor has been combined, these two Churches, which venerate and honor St. Zeno as their patron, have nevertheless always remembered his martyrdom.

This tradition, confirmed by the authority of St. Gregory as early as the year 595, is also established in subsequent centuries by the testimony of most celebrated authors and by most ancient records. It is confirmed first by the testimony of the Venerable Bede, who flourished about the year 731; it is confirmed by the testimony [Col. 0632B] of Paul the Deacon, who flourished after 774; and it is confirmed by the testimony of Wandelbert, who flourished in or about the year 855.

The rhymed account discussed above (chap. 1), which, as Muratori thinks, was composed about the year 790 and deposited by Ratherius, bishop of Verona, in the monastery of Lobbes in 970, confirms that St. Zeno was a martyr. The Martyrology in the Library of the pious House of Wisdom at Pistoia, although corrupted, attributes the name of martyr to St. Zeno toward the close of the eleventh century. Other manuscripts extant at Pistoia—namely, a Calendar and the Order of the Divine Office of this cathedral Church from subsequent centuries—also confer on the same holy bishop the cult of martyr.

Galesinus and Felicius do not oppose these witnesses, nor does the Roman Martyrology before its correction by Gregory XIII. The latter wrote in 1578, and the former in 1556. Finally, the Roman Martyrology corrected in 1584 removed every ground for doubt and declared St. Zeno a martyr. Thus there is no need to accept De Aste’s correction, who, failing to recognize Molanus’s error in the corrected Roman Martyrology, wanted it to read:

> “Let this controversy, so involved, be presently removed; by the intervening judgment of sounder men, let it be declared after the manner of Molanus: At Verona, St. Zeno, bishop, who governed that Church amid the storms of persecution and, after suffering much, ended his life.” [Col. 0632C]

But if in some Martyrologies St. Zeno is called only a confessor, this is recorded either on the sixth day before the Ides of December, when the feast of his ordination is celebrated for a confessor-bishop, or is found added on the day before the Ides of April through the ignorance of some persons. Not fully understanding the feasts of the Ordination and the Martyrdom, they borrowed the title “Confessor” from the more solemn feast of the Ordination and bestowed it also on the feast of the Martyrdom.

[Col. 0631]

# TWO DISSERTATIONS ADDED AS AN APPENDIX TO THE TWO PRECEDING BOOKS ON THE SERMONS AND MARTYRDOM OF ST. ZENO, BY FRANCESCO BONACCHI

# FIRST DISSERTATION, OR THE CHRONOLOGY OF ST. ZENO, BISHOP OF VERONA

[Col. 0631]

## CHAPTER ONE

### § I. The occasion and purpose of writing again

Nearly two years after the publication of my studies on the Sermons and [Col. 0632D] Martyrdom of St. Zeno, I obtained a copy of the book by the most distinguished men Pietro and Girolamo Ballerini, priests of Verona, printed at Verona in 1739. It is indeed an outstanding and painstaking work. By collecting older manuscripts from every quarter and supplying most appropriate and learned annotations, it has restored the Sermons of St. Zeno to their proper polish—and to that degree of splendor which they had never attained in other editions—and vindicated them for their author, rightly and deservedly.

I was filled with the greatest pleasure when, fixing not so much my eyes as my mind upon the work, I considered its excellently arranged order of subjects, the polished elegance of its Latin style, and its perfected learning of every kind, and rejoiced that I could not admire it enough. But when I saw that by so many distinguished arguments and records St. Zeno’s sermons were being assigned to him, I did not regret that my own slight efforts in maintaining those same sermons as the genuine offspring of that holy Father had been outweighed by so abundant a wealth of learning. [Col. 0633B]

Yet I found myself at a standstill when I discovered that these most distinguished men held, in establishing the chronology of this same St. Zeno, an opinion different from the old common view to which I had assented, and supported their position with arguments of no slight weight. Therefore, lest I should abandon my own opinion without judgment or persist rashly in it, I judged that those matters which created difficulties should be examined more carefully. With what outcome, however, I willingly and sincerely leave to the reader’s judgment.

I cannot at all approve Tillemont’s plan of changing the chronology of St. Zeno in order to extricate himself from various doubts. In attempting to establish it in Gallienus’s time, he acts like an astronomer who invents systems for himself at will in order to reconcile the movements of the planets. But historians, in narrating the deeds of the ancients, must rest upon ancient records; if these are lacking, they must leave the matters in their obscurity. [Col. 0633C]

With this intention, therefore, I have resolved to discuss the time when St. Zeno held the episcopate of the Church of Verona—not so as to persist in my opinion with a stubbornly fixed mind, but to test whether it may be possible to bring diverse and mutually opposed arguments into harmony with truth. See chapter 9, “On the Martyrdom of St. Zeno,” book II.

### § II. The first argument for placing St. Zeno’s chronology after the Arian period

The argument presses hard: namely, that certain sermons of St. Zeno attack the errors of Arius, so that one might judge Zeno to be later than Arius, or suppose that those sermons are not the product of Zeno. The most eminent Baronius held the latter; the most distinguished Ballerini the former. We refuted Baronius’s arguments in book I, chapter 7, *On the Sermons of St. Zeno*. We must now discuss those matters which the most learned men have treated and annotated most fully in the latest Veronese edition (First Dissertation, chap. 2, § 2).

It will therefore be worthwhile to recount the principal errors of Arius and investigate their origin; then to compare the statements of St. Zeno advanced against those errors, so that, by placing the opposing views side by side, we may distinguish them with clearer discrimination.

### § III. The principal errors of Arius

St. Alexander, patriarch of Alexandria, who was the first to attack Arius’s impiety and struck him with an anathema together with his author, enumerates Arius’s errors in a letter to Alexander, bishop of Constantinople:

> “They assert that there was once a time when the Son of God did not exist; that he subsequently came into being when he had not existed before; and that when he was made, he was such as any human being is. For they say that God made all things out of nothing, and in this assertion they include the Son of God. Accordingly, they add that by nature he can change and is capable of virtue and vice. Thus, having posited that he was made out of nothing—for they affirm that no one is Son of God by nature, nor that anyone has any prerogative above the other sons, nor anyone joined to him in any proper relation—they say that, although mutable by nature, because through particular diligence and zeal in the rightly ordered formation of his life and morals he did not turn aside to vices, God chose him.”  
> (Reported by Theodoret, *Ecclesiastical History*, chap. 4.) [Col. 0634B]

### § IV. From whom Arius drew the errors just listed

Arius did not devise these impious blasphemies against the Son of God, but received them from earlier heretics, as the same St. Alexander testifies:

> “For since you yourselves are taught by God and are not ignorant both of the teaching of Ebion and Artemas, which not long ago began to assail the Church’s true piety, and of the destructive doctrine of Paul of Samosata, bishop of Antioch, who was cast out by the council of all bishops everywhere and indeed by the judgment of the Church: Lucian, who became his successor, remained excluded from the Church for many years, that is, for as long as three bishops successively governed that Church. These men now brought forth into the light, who assert that the Son of God arose from nothing and who are like hidden shoots springing from the souls of those earlier men, have drained the dregs of those heretics’ impiety: I mean Arius, Achillas, and the rest of the mob adhering to them.”  
> (*In the same letter.*)

St. Athanasius agrees:

> “It seems to me that they either craftily feign ignorance, as though they did not know that, even before the Council of Nicaea, this abominable heresy existed, at the time when Artemas was laying its foundations.”  
> (*On the Synods of Ariminum and Seleucia.*) [Col. 0634C]

### § V. Ebion’s errors concerning the divinity of the Son

St. Alexander names Ebion not as the first, but as a principal enemy of the Son’s divinity. Ebion himself renewed and propagated the already collapsed heresy of Cerinthus, a disciple of Simon Magus and a contemporary of the apostles. (Tillemont, vol. 2, preliminary note on the Cerinthians; Theodoret, book II, *Against Heresies*, chap. 3.)

For Cerinthus said, like the Hebrews, that Jesus was born naturally from a man and a woman, namely Joseph and Mary; but that he had surpassed others in temperance, righteousness, and other virtues; that Christ descended upon him from heaven in the form of a dove; that then he disclosed the God who had been unknown and performed the miracles recorded in Scripture; but that at the time of the Passion Christ departed, while Jesus underwent suffering.

In the same manner Ebion, while granting that the Son had his entire beginning from Mary, produces not a man from God but a god from a human being. He says that the Virgin did not receive in the flesh the Word, God who in the beginning was with God and existed beforehand; rather, that she generated flesh through the Word, because he says that in the Word there was not the nature of the only-begotten God existing beforehand, but merely an uttered sound of the voice. [Col. 0635A]

Theodoret also reports Ebion’s error:

> “He said that the Lord Jesus Christ was born from Joseph and Mary; that he was indeed a human being, but excelled all others in virtue and in the innocence and integrity of his life.”

Carpocrates, whom we place after Ebion, likewise embraced the error of Cerinthus and Ebion, to use Augustine’s words (*On Heresies*, chap. 7):

> “He too is reported to have believed that Jesus was merely a human being, born of both sexes, but to have received such a soul as knew the things above and announced them.”

### § VI. On Artemas, or Artemon
Artemas did not himself revive Ebion’s heresy; rather, Theodotion [Col. 0635B] recalled it from the dead. Yet Artemas is better known than Theodotion: although the latter was its author or restorer, the former propagated it (Eusebius, *History*, V.28). Accordingly, Saint Alexander, passing over Theodotion, names Artemas as the defender of this heresy, as does Augustine. Thus, the heresy belonged to a certain Artemon, but, when it had declined, it was restored by Paul. Nevertheless, in Heresy XXXIII Augustine acknowledges Theodotion as the author of this error: “The Theodotians, founded by a certain Theodotion, maintain that Christ was merely a man.” Theodoret places Artemon first and reports his error thus: “Artemon said that the Lord Jesus Christ was merely a man, born of a virgin, but surpassing the prophets in power.” Then comes Theodotus, of whom he says briefly: “Theodotus of Byzantium, a leather-worker, held the same opinion as Artemon.” These two heretics [Col. 0635C] were either contemporaries or near contemporaries, about the year of Christ 200. Pope Victor also condemned by anathema their errors, which had been publicly disseminated even at Rome, together with their authors Theodotion and Artemas.

## § VII.—On Paul of Samosata

We have already related what Saint Augustine and Theodoret said in summary concerning Cerinthus, Ebion, Theodotion, and Artemas. Now, in treating of Paul of Samosata, we shall perceive more distinctly the impious doctrines of the heretics just mentioned—doctrines renewed by Samosata, examined by Saint Dionysius of Alexandria against him, and debated and condemned in the councils of Antioch.

Thus Dionysius, writing against ten questions of Paul of Samosata, states the latter’s opinion concerning Christ the Lord before the first question as follows:

> “You say that there are two hypostases and two persons, of the one and only Christ; and two Christs and two Sons: one, the Son of God by nature, who was before the ages; and another Christ and Son of David homonymously so called, who was not before, but came to be in time and received the name of Son according to God’s good pleasure.”

(*Letter to Paul of Samosata*, reported by Labbe, *Collection of Councils*, in the First Council of Antioch, p. 850, Paris edition.)

Thus Samosata confused the persons in God, asserting one God, as Dionysius reproaches him: “The Church, you say, does not speak of two Gods, nor has she received such a tradition.” He confused the Father with the Son, whom, as Dionysius had reported above, he called the Son of God by nature.

[Col. 0636A] Concerning the fifth question: “By saying that the Father is unbegotten, Samosata means to teach that Christ is recent and a creature.” He also boasted that Christ did not exist before Mary: “But you say that he was not before Mary.” Thus Saint Dionysius testifies, before the first question, concerning Samosata’s own opinion.

Paul himself openly asserts that Christ was a mere man:

> “For we see Christ going to his Passion and saying, ‘Now my soul is troubled.’ Come then: is this the nature of God?”

Again he presses this objection against Dionysius:

> “Of whom do you wish us to confess that it is written, ‘My soul is sorrowful unto death’? Is not he whose soul is sorrowful a man by nature?”

In the same way, throughout all his other questions he repeats this error. Yet Paul also confesses [Col. 0636B] that Christ was born of a virgin: “It is written in the Gospel that the child grew and was strengthened,” as though saying: “Jesus grew, having been born of the Holy Spirit and of the Virgin Mary.”

Here he adheres to Ebion’s error, for Ebion too—as we reported above from Hilary—acknowledges Jesus as born of a virgin. In this he differs from Cerinthus and Carpocrates, who held that Christ was born naturally from man and woman, namely Joseph and Mary, and from both sexes. Yet Theodoret reports that Ebion himself also taught that Christ was born from Joseph and Mary (*Book II of Heretical Fables*, on the Ebionites). He distinguishes, however, two Ebionite sects, differing only in this: one wished Christ to have been born from both sexes, the other from a virgin. Eusebius likewise affirms this (*Ecclesiastical History*, [Col. 0636C] III.3).

Although Samosata called Christ a man, he nevertheless wished him to have been assumed into God because of his exceptional virtue. Dionysius therefore says against him: “You see into what absurdities you cast yourself when you say that the man was assumed by God the Word.” And above: “It is absurd to say that the man Christ pleased God more than all men, so that God might dwell in him.” Thus he acknowledged Christ to be God, not by nature but by participation.

For this reason the same Saint Dionysius warns against Paul’s saying that Christ was born of the Holy Spirit and Mary:

> “When Samosata craftily says, ‘of the Holy Spirit and Mary,’ he wishes to deceive, so that, just as it is written, ‘they were born not of blood, but of God,’ so he may say this of the One born of the God-bearer.”

And “by saying that the Father is unbegotten, he says it [Col. 0636D] in order to teach that Christ is recent and a creature.”

Against these errors of Paul of Samosata, the Fathers of the First Council of Antioch wrote to Paul:

> “We have known, confess, and proclaim, both in the Old and New Testament, this begotten Son—the only-begotten, the image of the invisible God, the firstborn of every creature, the Wisdom and Word and Power of God—as the Son of God, God from God, before the ages, not by foreknowledge but by substance and hypostasis. But whoever says that the Son of God was not before the foundation of the world, and says that to believe and confess that he is God is nothing other than to proclaim two Gods—whoever proclaims that the Son of God is not God, we judge to be alien from the Rule of the Church; and all the Catholic Churches agree with us.”  
> (*Letter of the Six Bishops concerning Samosata*, in Labbe.)

Having noted these matters concerning the errors of Paul of Samosata, we may ask why Saint Alexander, Patriarch, omitted Cerinthus, Carpocrates, and Theodotion and mentioned only Ebion and Artemas. The reason was both the agreement of Ebion and Artemas with Paul of Samosata in error, and the disagreement of Cerinthus and Carpocrates with Ebion and Artemas: the latter asserted that Christ was born of a virgin, whereas the former said that he was born from Joseph and Mary. As for Theodotion, the fact that the holy Patriarch apparently makes no mention of him was prompted not by a difference of errors but by the fact that Artemas made Theodotion’s errors more prominent.

## § VIII.—The errors of Arius enumerated by Saint Alexander the Patriarch conform to the errors of Ebion, Artemas, and Paul of Samosata

First, Saint Alexander rebukes the Arians: “They asserted that there was once a time when the Son of God did not exist.” Ebion granted the entire beginning of the Son to come from Mary. Artemon said that the Lord Jesus Christ was merely a man born of a virgin. Paul of Samosata said that Christ, the Son of David, “was not before, but came to be in time,” and repeatedly called him a man, as we have noted.

Second: “For they say that God made all things out of nothing,” and under this proposition they include even the Son of God. Although this error follows from the preceding propositions, it is not explicitly found in the heretics mentioned above. Thus the Arians themselves unfolded the teaching of those same heretics.

[Col. 0637C] Third: “They further add, consequently, that he is mutable by nature and capable of virtue and vice.” For they maintain that he possessed no prerogative by nature, nor anything beyond the rest of the sons—for they affirm that no one is the Son of God by nature, nor anyone united with him by any property—but that, though mutable by nature and not turning aside to vices because of his singular diligence and zeal in the proper formation of his life and morals, God chose him.

That Christ is mutable by nature follows from the false proposition by which Ebion and Artemas wished him to be merely a man. Saint Alexander therefore aptly says: “They further add, consequently.” Samosata, however, openly asserted this error: “How then do you say that he who grew and was strengthened existed before the ages?” Saint [Col. 0637D] Dionysius likewise draws this absurd conclusion against Samosata, answering the objection in which he had opposed the Gospel text, “My soul is sorrowful unto death,” and adding: “Otherwise Samosata will also understand the Holy Spirit to be passible.”

Ebion taught, as appears from the cited text of Saint Hilary, that Christ was not the Son of the eternal Father by nature but was assumed to the dignity of Son because of his exceptional virtues: “Ebion brings forth God from man, not from God.” Theodoret also testifies to Ebion’s error, reporting: “He was indeed a man, but he surpassed others in virtue and in the innocence and integrity of his life.” And Saint Augustine says that Jesus “received such a soul as knew heavenly things and proclaimed them.” Artemas held the same view: “[He was] superior to the prophets in power.”

More clearly, Samosata, following the error of Ebion and Artemas, expounds their opinion:

> “You say that there are two Sons: one, the Son of God by nature, who was before the ages; and another, Christ and Son of David homonymously so called, who was not before but came to be in time and received the name of Son according to God’s good pleasure.”

Thus Dionysius speaks against Paul; and below:

> “For you say that the Word was before Mary, but Christ was not before Mary; and that Mary did not bear the Word—for she is not older than the Word—but bore Christ, who thereafter was honored as Son of God.”

He manifestly asserts that Christ is a creature and not Son of God by nature: “By saying that the Father is unbegotten, he says it in order to teach that Christ is recent and a creature.” Thus Dionysius of Alexandria exposes Paul’s deception.

[Col. 0638B] The Ballerini brothers ascribe the same errors, on Theodoret’s authority, to other heretics. They say that this contrary error was held by eleven heterodox sects named by Theodoret in Book XI *Against Heresies*: namely, the Ebionites, Nazarenes, Cerinthians, Artemon, Theodotus, Melchizedekians, Elcesaites, Paul of Samosata, Sabellius, Marcellus, and Photinians. Two others must be added: the Carpocratians, from Irenaeus, Book I, chapter 24; and Beryllus, from Eusebius, Book VI, chapter 11.

Yet this must not be understood as though these founders of heresies agreed in every respect. For the Nazarenes, Augustine testifies, confessed Christ as the Son of God: “Although the Nazarenes confess that Christ is the Son of God, they nevertheless observe all things of the old law.” Therefore, when Epiphanius says that the Nazarenes had much in common with Ebion, this must be understood regarding the observance of legal prescriptions, since the Ebionites too observed the law. “The Ebionites also call Christ merely a man. They observe the carnal commandments of the law—namely, circumcision of the flesh and the rest—from the works of which we have been set free by the New Testament” (Saint Augustine, *On Heresies*, chapter 10, §7).

Thus the Nazarenes and Ebionites disagreed concerning Christ’s divinity: the latter acknowledged Christ as merely a man, the former as the Son of God. We have also noted that Cerinthus and Carpocrates did not agree with Ebion in this, since Ebion asserted that Christ was born of a virgin, whereas they said he was born from Joseph and Mary, from both sexes. There can be no doubt that Photinus revived the errors of Ebion and Paul of Samosata. The same note by the Ballerini brothers maintains that he was condemned about the middle of the fourth century at the Council of Sardica and, together with his followers, by the Arians themselves at their conventicle at Sirmium; and that Saint Zeno attacked his followers:

> “The Photinians, latest of all, whom the Arians themselves condemned, seem to be indicated by Zeno in this place, especially from the formula, as some think.”

Yet Saint Zeno, writing in the time of Gallienus, could also have assailed older heretics. The words of the holy bishop concern only those who asserted that Christ was a mere man:

> “If, as some think, he took his beginning merely as a man from the womb of the Virgin, what hope of future blessedness remains for the believer, when it is written: ‘Cursed is the man who places his hope in man’?”

He especially has in view those who confessed him to be born of a virgin, such as Ebion, Artemas, and [Col. 0639A] Paul of Samosata—not Cerinthus, Carpocrates, and others who blasphemed by saying that Christ was born from Joseph and Mary and from both sexes. We shall demonstrate below that the error which held Christ to be a mere man born of a virgin was spreading and widely disseminated in the Church in the age of Gallienus. For the present, it is enough to note that Saint Alexander, Patriarch of Alexandria, in the letter cited, enumerated Ebion, Artemas, and Samosata before Gallienus and in Gallienus’s own age, since they prepared the way more closely in their error for the Arian heresy.

## § IX.—Arius’s inconsistency and variability concerning his errors

When Saint Alexander had been raised to the Alexandrian see, Arius, resenting that he had been passed over, wasted away with envy. Since he could say nothing against Alexander’s unblemished morals, he dared to whet his tooth against his teaching. For when Saint Alexander confessed the Son equal to the Father in honor and of the same essence, Arius began foolishly to call the Son a creature and a thing made, to say that there was a time when he was not, and uttered matters still more impious—things surely worthy to be consigned to oblivion and eternal silence. Thus says Gregory of Caesarea.

Although Arius had begun, while the most glorious martyr Saint Peter, Patriarch of Alexandria, was still living, to spew forth his poison and had for that reason been deposed by him, nevertheless at that time—as Christianus Lupus puts it—being only a deacon, he could not yet preach or teach the people publicly. But in Alexander’s time, now a priest and entrusted with the duty of preaching the Word, he began openly in sermons to disparage Alexander’s apostolic doctrine and to set against it, like warmed-over cabbage, the errors of Ebion, Artemas, and Paul.

Accordingly, condemned by Saint Alexander and expelled from the Church, he did not dare openly to teach and defend the heresies of Ebion and Artemas, which he had propagated and which Pope Victor of Rome had condemned, or those of Paul of Samosata, who had dared to restore them and whom so great a multitude of bishops had overthrown in the Council of Antioch. Proceeding more cautiously, he sought to cloak those same doctrines and devise them under another appearance.

In the first place, he moderated those blasphemies which he had initially scattered—namely, that Christ did not exist before Mary; that there was a time when the Son did not exist; and that he was mutable and created by God—so that he confessed the Son to have existed before times and ages as full God, the only-begotten, immutable. Peddling his impious teaching as Catholic doctrine, he professed to teach that the Son was not unbegotten like the Father, nor a part of the Unbegotten. In this he criticized Catholics, as though those who asserted the Son’s equality with the Father and sameness of substance made the Son unbegotten and taught that he was a part of the Father’s substance.

Yet retaining his impiety, he taught in the same place that the Son was created from no underlying subject—that is, from nothing—by the will and counsel of the Father; and that, before he was begotten, he did not exist, understanding “creation” under the word “generation.” We shall understand all this more clearly from Arius’s own letter to Eusebius, bishop of Nicomedia:

> “But this is our belief and judgment, both what we have taught and teach: that the Son is neither unbegotten nor in any way a part of the Unbegotten, nor derived from any underlying subject; but by the will and counsel of the Father he existed before times and before ages, full God, only-begotten, immutable. Before he was begotten or created or determined or founded, he did not exist; for he was not unbegotten. We are persecuted because we say that the Son has a beginning, whereas God the Father is without beginning; and because we say that he is from nothing. We have said this because he is neither a part of God nor derived from any underlying subject. For this reason they persecute us.”  
> (Extant in Theodoret, *Ecclesiastical History*, chapter 4.)

Eusebius [Col. 0640B] of Nicomedia himself, the strongest champion of Arius and of the Arian heresy, expressed the same matter more closely, but with greater deception:

> “For we have neither heard nor learned nor believed, my lord Paulinus, that there are two unbegottens, or that one has been divided into two, or that it has undergone any bodily affection. Rather, we believe in one unbegotten, and one truly begotten from him, though not from his substance: one wholly devoid of the nature and essence of the Unbegotten.”  
> (*Letter to Paulinus*)

The Catholic Church confesses one Unbegotten, so that Eusebius appears to condemn Menander’s error, who called the Lord Jesus Christ unbegotten. Ebion also called him unbegotten, as Theodoret reports: “He said that there was one unbegotten, as we also do, and he declared him to be the maker of the world.” This is the same cunning which Saint Dionysius of Alexandria noted in Samosata: “By saying that the Father is unbegotten, he says it to teach that Christ is recent [Col. 0640C] and a creature.”

He calls God indivisible and incorporeal in order to insinuate that Catholics, in maintaining the Son’s consubstantiality with the Father, admit division in God. The Praxeans likewise falsely reproached Catholics in their zeal for religion, as appears from Tertullian. How number can be posited without division will be shown in the discussions that follow.

Eusebius therefore denies consubstantiality: “One unbegotten, and one truly begotten from him, though not from his substance; one wholly devoid of the nature and essence of the Unbegotten.” He passes over in silence the other errors which Arius openly asserts as following from his denial of consubstantiality—namely, that the Son did not exist before he was begotten or created, and that he was brought forth from nothing—in order, so far as he can, to hide the poison of the doctrine.

Augustine noted this variability of Arius and his followers concerning their errors:

> “I hear that you have now corrected yourselves. Or is it perhaps false that they at one time said that the Father was once without the Son, as though eternal light had been without the brightness it generated?”

And in the books *On the Trinity*: “If the Son is Son, he is begotten; if begotten, there was a time when the Son was not.” The later Arians had abandoned that opinion. That this variation began with Arius himself is clear from what we have related above in this same paragraph from Theodoret.

## § X.—The distinctive formulas of Arius and the Arians in explaining their errors

The distinctive words employed by Arius and his followers in expressing their own errors, or reviving ancient ones, seem deserving of careful review, so that, by comparing the statements of Saint Zeno, it may be seen more clearly whether the holy bishop spoke against Arius or against the more ancient heretics.

Arius therefore began, according to Saint Athanasius (*First Oration against the Arians*), to rage against Saint Alexander’s Catholic doctrine:

> “God was not always Father; the Son was not always [Son]. For, since all things are from nothing, the Son of God too emerged from nothing. And since all things are created, he too must be considered something created and a work. And since all things previously did not exist but subsequently came into being, there was certainly a time when the Word was not. And because he was not before he was made, he had a beginning of existence. For he came into being when God wished to create him.”

Further below [Col. 0641B] Athanasius says:

> “They further add that he does not exist naturally in the Father and is not the Word proper to his substance, nor the proper Wisdom in which he created this world; but that there is in the Father another proper and peculiar Word and likewise another proper Wisdom, in which Wisdom he made this Word. Thus the Lord Christ himself is called Word in relation to rational beings who use words.”

Athanasius continues to enumerate Arius’s errors:

> “Again he says that God created us not for his sake, but him for our sake. For, he says, God was alone and the Word was not with him. Then, when he wished to create us, he also created him, and, after he was begotten, called him Word. For the Word is not the Father’s proper and natural offspring, but himself too came to be by grace.”

They further maintain that Christ is not God’s natural and true power, but that, just as caterpillars are called the powers of almighty God, so he too is called the Father’s omnipotence. Among other things Arius also added that the Son does not know the Father exactly, nor even fully know his own substance.

Finally, the whole dispute between Catholics and Arians was reduced to the one issue of asserting or denying the Son’s consubstantiality with the Father. To establish this fact, it will suffice to cite the creed put forward by Valens, Ursacius, and other associates at the Synod of Rimini:

> “We believe in one only and true God, the Father almighty, creator and maker of all things; and in the only-begotten Son of God, existing before all ages and beginnings and before every time that can be conceived, and begotten impassibly from God before every comprehensible substance: God from God, only from the only Father, like the Father who begot him—whose generation, according to the Scriptures, no one knows except the Father who begot him. But the term ‘substance,’ because it was used by the Fathers more simply, is unknown to the people, and gives offence because it is not contained in the Scriptures; it has therefore been resolved that it be removed, and that henceforth no mention of substance be made concerning God.”  
> (Reported by Saint Athanasius, *On the Councils of Ariminum and Seleucia*.)

The Ballerini brothers maintain that Saint Zeno was bishop of the Church of Verona in this period, extending his episcopate from A.D. 356 to 380. Whatever the case, the age of Bishop Zeno must beyond doubt be placed approximately between 356 and 380. The chronological system concerning this period will be considered below.

## § XI.—The chronology of the errors reviewed thus far, down to Gallienus

Leaving aside those heretics who agreed less closely among themselves in their errors, the dates of Ebion, Artemas, and Paul of Samosata must be established; and inquiry must be made whether any held their errors between Artemas and Samosata. For Saint Alexander the Patriarch testifies, as we have seen, that these three heretics spread the same error before Gallienus or in Gallienus’s time, and preceded Arius and the Arians in undermining the divinity of the Son.

This brief chronological inquiry is highly useful for establishing the date of Saint Zeno, since we see that his statements attack these errors. Tillemont therefore places Ebion in the first declining century, about A.D. 82 (*vol.* II, preliminary note on the Nazarenes and Ebionites, and in the chronological table, A.D. 82; compare A.D. 74). Baronius places him in A.D. 74. Ebion spread his errors not only in Asia but also at Rome.

Artemas restored Ebion’s errors; but it was not he first, rather Theodotus or Theodotion of Byzantium, with whom Artemas allied himself, who made the heresy more famous. They were condemned by Pope Victor about A.D. 196. Tillemont conjectures that Theodotion died before A.D. 219. Artemas, perhaps surviving Theodotion, seems to have been acknowledged as the author of the heresy.

Although this error was condemned by Pope Victor, it must be said not to have been immediately extinguished, for it is also noted in Tertullian:

> “God is both Father and Judge; yet he is not therefore always Father and always Judge because he is always God. For he could not be Father before the Son, nor Judge before sin. But there was a time when neither sin nor the Son existed, when there was neither that which would make God Judge nor that which would make him Father and Lord.”

Tertullian wrote this about A.D. 216. Beryllus, bishop of Bostra in Arabia, was likewise accused of the same error about A.D. 229. He dared to assert, as Eusebius relates (*History*, VI.33), “that our Lord and Savior did not subsist in a distinct personal existence before he lived among men, nor possess any divinity proper to himself, but only the Father’s divinity dwelling within him.” Since many bishops held examinations and disputations against him on this matter, Origen too was summoned with the others. At first he conversed familiarly with Beryllus in order to discover what the man’s opinion was; but, after clearly learning what he said, he refuted his error and, having convinced him by arguments and demonstrations, as it were taking him by the hand, led him back to the way of truth.

Origen, who was still alive before A.D. 256, likewise refuted this error: “Let him understand who dares to say: ‘There was once when the Son was not.’” From these words the most learned Ballerini brothers rightly infer: “Hence it is indeed proved that certain others taught at that time the error which Origen rebuked.”

Saint Dionysius, Patriarch of Alexandria, who is said to have died in A.D. 266, came nearer to Gallienus’s time. As the same very learned Ballerini brothers note, in his letter to Euphranor, of which a fragment is supplied in Athanasius’s *Letter on the Opinion of Dionysius*, no. 4, he attacks the Sabellians, saying: “Since it is a thing made, it was not before it was made.” For this reason he was denounced to Dionysius of Rome and rebuked by him; in his defense he cleared himself by an apology, in which he brought together many points rejecting that error which the Arians subsequently adopted. Therefore, when they appealed to his authority in their own support, Athanasius, in the place mentioned, no. 9, admirably vindicated his predecessor’s opinion and newly snatched that authority from the hands of his enemies. In the same period Paul of Samosata dared to bring to light the errors which he had drawn from Ebion and Artemas; against him, as we have seen, Saint Dionysius also wrote.

Thus we find that Ebion’s heresy, arising while the first century was still declining, was restored by Artemon near the end of the second century and the beginning of the third; that it continued to spread in the Church throughout the third century down to Gallienus’s time and even after Gallienus; and that it was widely disseminated not only in Alexandria but also in Italy and Rome. Arius adopted it to the great detriment of the Catholic Church, so that after the passage of so many centuries it still diffuses its destructive power through new Arians.

## § XII.—Texts of Saint Zeno thought to be directed against the errors of Arius

Having set down those preliminary matters that seemed relevant to the present subject, we must now approach more closely the knot of the question, examining the texts of Saint Zeno that are cited against Arius. The Ballerini brothers adduce these, and we transcribe them here in their own words:

> “In order that the force of these principal expressions and words may become more evident, it will be highly useful to set forth under certain headings what the Arians thought on the one hand, and what the Author wrote in opposition on the other, so that even those not fully learned in these matters may recognize that the Author is deliberately arguing against the Arians. These heretics, speaking of the Son of God, used such formulas, according to Athanasius in *On the Decrees of Nicaea*, no. 18, p. 215: ‘From non-existent things’; ‘He was not before he was begotten’; ‘There was once when he was not.’ By these they signified that the divine Word had been created from non-existent things—that is, from nothing, like other creatures—and did not exist before he was begotten; whence it followed that there was once when he was not. To oppose these, our Author, together with Catholics, first taught in Tractate III, Book II, that God the Father ‘begot another self, that is, God the Son, from himself, from his unbegotten substance; and, remaining blessed for ever in that substance, brought forth a Son possessing all things equally with himself.’ And in Tractate II, Book II: ‘The Father gave his whole self back in the Son.’ By these statements he openly declared that the divine Word was begotten not from nothing or non-existent things, but from the Father’s own substance. Then, to demolish the other formula, ‘He was not before he was born,’ or the equivalent formula, ‘There was once when he was not,’ by which the Arians denied eternity to the divine Son, he repeatedly insists upon coeternity: in Tractate II, Book II, ‘one original coeternity’; in Tractate VI, Book II, no. 4, ‘with whom there is one possession of the original and perpetual kingdom, one substance of coeternity and omnipotence, one equality, one power of august majesty.’ To this belong also those words in Tractate LV, where he confesses the Son alone to know the Father’s antiquity, that is, to be coeternal with the Father; and, to omit other passages, in Tractate VII he most clearly notes the heresy which, more modestly but more corrosively harmful, says indeed that the Son of God is God, but not begotten from the Father in the perpetuity of nobility, and that there was a time when he was not. These words especially influenced Baronius, since they strike directly at the Arian heresy: for no one before Arius taught similar things; no one before this time noted and refuted such a heresy so expressly; indeed, no one could have noted and refuted it.”  

These are the words of the Ballerini brothers. But before treating of these and other passages of Saint Zeno cited by them, the following must be prefaced.

## § XIII.—Knowledge of the mystery of the most Holy Trinity flourished from the Church’s very beginning, especially in its third century

The highly esteemed Petavius, adducing the testimonies of Athanasius and Basil, clearly shows that in the Church’s earliest centuries many holy and learned Fathers existed who both held the sound and orthodox doctrine of the Trinity and transmitted it to those among whom they lived through teaching, and to posterity through writing. Thomasinus does the same. From these authorities we shall select some statements of the holy Fathers to furnish the title of this paragraph, especially those which the Fathers of the third century set forth.

Leaving aside, therefore, what is found in the book entitled *The Shepherd*; in the writings of Saint Clement of Rome, Ignatius the martyr, Aristides of Athens, and Polycarp the martyr, who are counted in the first century; and in the statements of Justin the Philosopher and martyr, Irenaeus, Athenagoras, and Theophilus of Antioch, who belong to the second century—and which may be seen in Petavius himself—we shall bring forward more explicit monuments of those holy Fathers who, in the decline of the second century or during the third, spoke of the mystery of the most Holy Trinity, since they touch more closely upon the period of this discussion.

Petavius presents statements concerning the most Holy Trinity from Hippolytus the Martyr, who flourished about A.D. 222:

> “The same Hippolytus gave much clearer testimonies, in his treatises against Beron and Helix, preserved in Athanasius, to the Son’s perfect and true divinity and to his person as distinct from the Father. In them he carefully distinguishes the two natures in Christ and demonstrates that the divine nature is precisely the same as that in the Father. For he says that ‘the Word of God was changed in no respect by putting on flesh, and that in no respect in which he is the same as the Father did he become the same as the flesh because of the emptying; but that, as he was without flesh, so he remained beyond every circumscription.’ Again, ‘he says that the infinite and uncircumscribed God is at the same time man, and that he is understood to possess the substance of each perfectly complete.’”

What could be a clearer proclamation of Christ’s supreme and absolute divinity? For Hippolytus declares him to be infinite God, immense, immutable, and altogether the same as the Father in respect of nature; and, being the Father’s Son, he is therefore truly distinct from him. Finally, “the divinity,” he says, according to Anastasius’s translation, “as it was before the incarnation, is also after the incarnation by nature infinite, incomprehensible, impassible, incomparable—or rather unchangeable—immutable, unconvertible, powerful in itself, and, to say all in one word, subsisting, substantial Goodness of infinite power alone.” Could anyone, even in this century, have explained more clearly, expressly, or significantly the Son’s divinity and the distinction of the Persons than that ancient writer did before the Nicene assembly had articulated clear knowledge on the matter?

Petavius refers readers seeking Clement of Alexandria’s statements on the Trinity—written, he acknowledges, without suspicion of error—to Book I of *On the Trinity*. We shall cite Thomasinus, who demonstrates that Clement is wholly free from any suspicion of error. See, says Thomasinus (vol. III, *Dogmatic Theology*, treatise 2, chapter 44, no. 1), how Clement establishes Christ’s eternity before time:

> “Certainly no human being or god existed before this world; but we existed before the foundation of the world, because we were destined to exist and were begotten in God himself. We are rational creatures of God’s Word, through whom we are ancient, because in the beginning was the Word. But because the Word had an origin from on high, the divine beginning of all things, he both was and is. And because he has now received the name, long sanctified and worthy of power, Christ, he is called by me a new song. This Word, therefore, is Christ; and he was in God, both so that we might exist from of old and because he was the cause through which we rightly see. But now this same Word has appeared to human beings, he who alone is both God and man.”

See how immediately Clement says that Christ, before assuming flesh, was that very God who is—that is, Being itself—and that he was in “the One who is,” namely, the Father:

> “The Savior, who existed before, appeared recently; he appeared who is in him who is: ὁ ἐν τῷ ὄντι ὤν, ‘he who is in the One who is,’ because the Word that was with God appeared as teacher, through whom all things were made.”

And below:

> “The Word, the Lord, who is truly God most manifest, equal to the Lord of all, because he was his Son, and the Word was in God.”

He teaches most openly that the Word is God and, as Son, equal to the Father.

From the first book of *The Instructor*, see how he joins together the three divine hypostases, distinguishes them from all other beings, and then associates with them the whole intellectual nature, the Church:

> “O mystical wonder! One indeed is the Father of all; one also is the Word of all; and one is the Holy Spirit, who is everywhere the same. But there is one mother alone, a virgin; and I delight to call her the Church.”

[Col. 0646A] After Clement of Alexandria, we shall place Origen, the disciple beneath his master, following the same Thomassin; yet perhaps below we shall have to allege contrary evidence concerning him, since Origen is often found differing from himself and sometimes contradicting himself, so that St. Jerome truly said of him: “At times even great Homer nods.” Thomassin drew the testimonies of Origen which we set forth below from St. Athanasius. “If,” says Origen, “there is any image of the invisible God, that image too will be invisible; indeed, I should venture to add this also: since He is the likeness of the Father, it cannot be that there was a time when He was not. For when did God, who according to John the Evangelist is called light, lack the radiance of His Majesty, so that anyone should dare to assign a beginning to the Son, as though He had not previously existed? And when was that ineffable, unnameable, and inexpressible image, form, and reason of the Father’s substance—which knows the Father—not?” Let whoever dares to say, “There was when the Son was not,” consider that he is saying precisely this: “There was when Wisdom was not, when Reason was not, when Life was not.” And immediately in the same place.

Elsewhere the same Origen says: “But it is neither lawful nor, in view of our weakness, free from danger, so far as lies in us, to strip the Father of His Only-Begotten, the Word ever existing with Him; likewise, to strip Him of the Wisdom in which He rejoiced. For it would follow that He had not always rejoiced.” Behold, we show that a judgment of this kind has been handed down from Fathers to Fathers, as it were from hand to hand. But you are new Jews and disciples of Caiaphas: show us who the fathers and elders of your words are, when you cannot cite even one of the wise or learned as your author.

[Col. 0646C] We add Theognostus from Athanasius, since you see him named together with Origen in the library of Photius. “Learn therefore now,” says Athanasius, “you Arians, rebels against Christ, that Theognostus, an eloquent man, did not shrink from the term ‘substance.’ For, writing on faith in the *Hypotyposes*, he spoke thus: ‘The substance of the Son does not consist of something external or of alien things, nor is He produced from non-existent things; but He has been begotten from the substance of the Father, as a beam from light or vapour from water. For vapour is not the same thing as water, nor is a beam the same thing as the sun; nevertheless, neither is alien to these things, so that you may call Him an outflow of the Father’s substance—yet in such a way that the Father’s substance suffers no division. For just as the sun is not diminished by the rays flowing forth from itself, so neither does the substance of the Father suffer diminution when it begets the Son, His own image.’”

[Col. 0646D] Finally, we cite Gregory of Neocaesarea, who in his Confession of Faith says thus: “One God, Father of the living Word, of subsisting Wisdom, and of His power and eternal image: the perfect Begetter of the Perfect; Father of the Only-Begotten Son; one Lord, alone from the Alone, God from God, and true Son of the true Father.” Then: “And one Holy Spirit,” he says, “having His substance from God,” etc. “The perfect image of the Perfect Son, the life which is the cause of the living, the holy fountain, holiness bestowing sanctification.” At last he concludes: “A perfect Trinity.”

[Col. 0647A] These matters seem sufficient to demonstrate that the faith in the most holy Trinity and the Incarnation was known and manifest, especially in the third century of the Church. Whoever desires more will find it in Petavius and Thomassin. Yet let us now observe how highly the monuments of these most holy Fathers whom we have cited ought to be valued for overthrowing the errors of Arius and the Arians. Are Hippolytus the Martyr, Clement of Alexandria, Origen, Theognostus, and Gregory of Neocaesarea, then, to be reckoned later than Arius and the Arians? Why then is our Zeno later than Arius?

§ XIV.—The opinions of St. Zeno by which the holy Father himself is believed to oppose the Arians are considered.

We must now proceed to examine the opinions of St. Zeno. The first is cited from the third tract, or sermon, of the second book: “God the Father begot from Himself another Himself, and God the Son, from that unbegotten substance in which, remaining blessed forever, He produced the Son as possessing all things equally with Himself.” Since this entire sermon is short, we shall transcribe it here; for not all who read this work of ours will have access to the sermons of St. Zeno.

[Col. 0647B] “The beginning, beloved brethren, is assuredly our Lord Christ, whom before all ages the Father embraced in the unfathomable secret of His mind, in a consciousness beyond surmise and known to Himself alone, as the Son—not without affection, but without disclosure. Therefore that ineffable and incomprehensible Wisdom begets Wisdom; Omnipotence begets Omnipotence. God is born from God; the Only-Begotten from the Unbegotten; the Perfect from the Perfect: possessing the whole Father, taking nothing away from the Father. He proceeds into birth, He who before being born existed in the Father, equal in all things; for the Father begot in Him another Himself from Himself, from that His unbegotten substance, in which, remaining blessed forever, He produced the Son as possessing all things equally with Himself—He who is God, blessed unto ages of ages.”

In this sermon St. Zeno attacks no error, but explains the divinity of the Son to the people. How, then, can it even lightly be suspected that he is contradicting the Arians? Here, in order to oppose the Arians, our author first taught with the Catholics, etc. Does not our author speak consistently with St. Hippolytus, who says that the Word is the same as the Father? St. Zeno, however, says that the Father “begot in Him another Himself from Himself, namely from that His unbegotten substance.”

[Col. 0647D] And does he not agree with St. Clement of Alexandria, who says, “The Beginning of all things both was and is the Word”? St. Zeno at the opening of the sermon says: “The beginning, beloved brethren, is assuredly Christ our Lord.” Again, St. Clement says of the Son: “For He was in God, who is in Him who is, and the Word was in God.” St. Zeno likewise says: “God is born from God, who before being born existed in the Father, equal in all things.” Finally Gregory the Wonderworker, who died in the time of Gallienus, speaks thus of the Father and Son: “The perfect Begetter of the Perfect, Father of the Only-Begotten Son; one Lord, alone from the Alone, God from God.” St. Zeno echoes him not merely in the same sense but almost in the same words: “God is born from God; the Only-Begotten from the Unbegotten; the Alone from the Alone; the Whole from the Whole; the True from the True; the Perfect from the Perfect.”

[Col. 0648A] Therefore, since neither Hippolytus the Martyr, nor Clement of Alexandria, nor Gregory the Wonderworker—who all preceded Arius by so many years—acted against the Arians, neither may St. Zeno be said to have acted against them.

But if something must be conceded, namely that St. Zeno in the sermon praised above refuted some error, it can only be in these words: “He proceeds into birth, He who before being born existed in the Father, equal in all things.” By these words no error is attacked except that of Ebion, Artemas, and Paul of Samosata, who long before Arius asserted that Christ the Lord did not exist before Mary. For the third birth of the Word, even by way of analogy, which the most learned Ballerini brothers devise, does not seem to be approvable, since St. Zeno most explicitly acknowledges only two births of Christ; but of this below. Origen too attacks the same error: “Since He is the likeness of the Father, it cannot be that there was when He was not. Let whoever dares to say, ‘There was when He was not,’ consider within himself.” Therefore no reason can be drawn from the words of this tract of St. Zeno by which it may be proved that he attacked the errors of Arius or the Arians.

As regards the second tract, the Ballerini brothers cite from it these words: “The Father turned His whole self back into the Son”; by which, as they infer, he openly declared that the divine Word was begotten not from nothing, or from non-existent things, but from the Father’s own substance.

[Col. 0648C] Certainly it must be admitted that not only from the words of this sermon is the Son consubstantial with the Father, but that this is most clearly inferred from many other statements of St. Zeno. But what follows from this regarding the Arians, when many most holy Fathers, before Arius, writing in the first, second, and third centuries of the Church, openly taught it? Indeed Theognostus, before Arius, as Athanasius testifies, asserted more plainly than St. Zeno that the Son was produced not from non-existent things but from the substance of the Father.

In their note on this second sermon, the same Ballerini brothers maintain that St. Zeno is acting against Hermogenes and other heretics who posited matter as coeternal and uncreated with God; or rather, as they suppose, that St. Zeno refers here to the poets and pagan philosophers who had long taught the same error. To me, however, it seems that the contemporary heresy of Sabellius is being assailed here.

[Col. 0648D] For Sabellius embraced Hermogenes’ error concerning unbegotten matter. This conjecture is supported by the fact that in this same sermon St. Zeno admirably expresses the distinction of the divine Persons: “This is our God, who arranged Himself into God. This is the Father who, His own state remaining intact, turned His whole self back into the Son, lest He take anything away from Himself. Finally, One rejoices in the Other, retaining, with the fullness of the Holy Spirit, one original coeternity.” He explains this by the same most fitting analogy, as you may see in the same sermon. All these things are excellently directed against Sabellius.

To say that St. Zeno imitated Lactantius in treating these matters is a matter of conjecture. It must first be proved that Zeno was later than Lactantius. But if St. Zeno wrote before Lactantius, as we shall show with God’s help, Lactantius must be called Zeno’s imitator.

[Col. 0649A] Nor should the note of those most learned annotators be accepted. On St. Zeno’s words, “This is the Father who, His own state remaining intact, turned His whole self back into the Son, lest He take anything away from Himself,” they maintain that St. Zeno is attacking the Arians, lest someone perhaps think that the Father’s substance was changed by the generation of the Son. For the Arians reproached Catholics who confessed the same substance of Father and Son, arguing that on this account the Son was a particle of the divine substance separated from the Father through generation.

Yet the most ancient martyr Justin expressed the same view more plainly in the *Dialogue with Trypho*: that this power is God’s and is called God by the Prophet, not as sunlight is counted as distinct merely in name, but as something numerically other; nevertheless, not by severance, as though the Father’s substance were cut, just as other things divided and cut are not the same as they were before the cutting. He offers this example: fire from which many fires are kindled, without any change in that fire from which the many have been kindled.

[Col. 0649B] What could be expressed more clearly against the Arians? Tertullian likewise, discussing the three Persons against Praxeas, says: “The discussions to follow will show how those proceeding [from the Father] admit number without division.” Add what we reported in § XIII from Athanasius concerning Theognostus: “Neither does the Father’s substance suffer diminution when it begets the Son, His own image.” Are Justin, Tertullian, and Theognostus then later than Arius? Away with it! Nor, therefore, is Zeno.

From these things it is clearly recognized that the division of the divine substance inferred from the distinction of Persons in the most holy Trinity was not an objection made against Catholics by the Arians alone, but was common to Jews, Patripassians, Sabellians, and Samosatenians, or Paulianists.

[Col. 0649C] The same must be said of the word “coeternity,” often insisted upon by St. Zeno in Tract II, Book II, and Tract VI, Book II, no. 4, in order to reject the formula, “He was not before He was known,” or the equivalent formula, “There was once when He was not.” For it is established that not Arians alone denied eternity to the Son by these formulas, but especially Ebion, Artemas, and Paul of Samosata. Thus St. Dionysius of Alexandria also repeatedly insists on the very term “coeternity” against Samosata himself:

“There is therefore one Christ, who is the coeternal Word in the Father, one Person of Him, invisible God and made visible. For God appeared in the flesh, born of a woman—He who had been begotten from God the Father from the womb before the morning star, as the Word brought forth from the Father’s heart; and the simple Word, without parts, became flesh according to the Scriptures, not divided into flesh and Word as though the Word dwelt in a man; for this is an evasion of generation” (*Letter to Paul of Samosata*).

Samosata himself objects to St. Dionysius (Question 5): “How then do you say that He who grew and was strengthened existed before the ages, and was together with the unbegotten Father, without beginning and coeternal?” Dionysius replies: “The mind cannot comprehend the generation of Christ from the Father from eternity.”

[Col. 0650A] You see that the hinge of the controversy is the eternity of the Son in the error of Ebion, Artemas, and Paul of Samosata, who held the same view. Likewise, although the six bishops in their letter to the same Samosata do not use the term “coeternity,” the same sense is present in these words: “We believe that this Son, who is always with the Father, fulfilled the Father’s will in the creation of the universe” (found in Labbe, with the preface, vol. I of the *Councils*, p. 845).

If you recall what is contained in § XIII, you will certainly understand that knowledge of the Son’s coeternity with the Father is so ancient that it was manifest among Christians from the very beginning of the Church. For whoever professes one God in three distinct Persons must also confess the Son as coeternal with the Father.

[Col. 0650B] § XV. The seventh tract of the second book, in which St. Zeno chiefly deals with heretics, is weighed in particular consideration.

Above we considered other tracts, or sermons, of St. Zeno; in them he does not openly argue against heretics. But in this one he expressly says that he is disputing against heretics. The examples and argument which we shall pursue cut, with one blow, all the sinews of the whole argument advanced by them. At the beginning, therefore, he proposes to treat especially against three sects hostile to Christ’s divinity, for he begins thus:

“Although there are many sects which strive to fabricate an affront to Christ, yet there are, in a certain way, three principal ones, two of which pretend to be worshippers of Him whom they desire to corrupt. One, finally, asserts that Jesus Christ took His beginning from the womb of the Virgin Mary, and that thereafter He became God by reason of righteousness, not by birth. Another, more restrained but more biting in its harm, indeed calls the Son of God ‘God,’ but says that He was not begotten from the Father in the perpetuity of nobility, and that there was a time when He was not. The third is truly blind Judaism: although it reads everywhere in its law, as it is accustomed to say, that two Persons, Father and Son, are indicated, still to this day it maintains that God has no Son.”

We must now see what these sects indicated by St. Zeno are.
