[Col. 0650C] The distinguished Ballerini brothers note that St. Zeno meant the Photinians in the first of the sects listed. You will readily understand that they hold our author intended to strike at the Photinians, whom Fathers of Zeno’s age elsewhere commonly refute. But since Photinus did not teach the same error here indicated by St. Zeno, it must be said that he is not being attacked here. “One, finally, asserts that Jesus Christ took His beginning from the womb of the Virgin Mary, and that thereafter He became God by reason of righteousness, not by birth.” So says St. Zeno. But Photinus said not that Christ began to exist from the Virgin Mary’s womb, but when the Holy Spirit was seen above Him.

Since, however, St. Zeno should rather be said to have attacked the Photinians, they offer this argument: “Insofar as He is said to have become God by righteousness, this was indeed Nestorius’s famous error; but it had long before been taught by Paul of Samosata and Photinus, with this distinction: Nestorius, as Garnerius notes in Dissertation 7, *On the Origin and Growth of the Pelagian Heresy*, chapter 7, taught that Christ the man was assumed by the divine Word from His mother’s womb onward, not through merits but by divine grace; whereas Paul of Samosata said that the same Christ was born a man and advanced into God through the merit of virtues”—what Zeno calls “righteousness.”

[Col. 0651A] But let us grant that Photinus held the same opinion as Samosata: if the same error had long before been preached by Paul of Samosata, why should St. Zeno be thought to attack the later Photinus rather than the earlier Samosata? Why should we not say that St. Zeno argues against the error of Paul of Samosata, who at least during Gallienus’s reign propagated his impious doctrine? Yet he himself was not the author of that heresy, which, as we have seen, Cerinthus, Ebion, Carpocrates, and Artemas had disseminated much earlier. For they taught not only that Christ took His beginning from Mary’s womb, but that through the merit of His virtue He excelled others and became God. Thus even in the time of Gallienus St. Zeno could have argued against the same error, and there is no need to resort to the Photinians.

In the second place, the holy bishop of Verona sets forth this heresy: “Another, more restrained but more biting in its harm, indeed calls the Son of God ‘God,’ but says that He was not begotten from the Father in the perpetuity of nobility, and that there was a time when He was not.”

[Col. 0651B] The Ballerini brothers note that this is the heresy of the Arians. Although the Arians proclaimed Christ to be the Son of God, they represented Him as begotten not from eternity but in time; hence their customary utterance: “There was a time when He was not.” See Athanasius, *On the Decrees of Nicaea*, no. 18; and Hilary, *On the Trinity*, Books IV and VI, where he cites Arius’s own letter, in which the same formula is repeated.

Nor should you wonder that here the Son could be called God and nevertheless be denied to be coeternal and equal with the Father. For the Arians acknowledged Him as God improperly, not properly, as is known from fragment 26 of Hilary and from elsewhere. It must indeed be admitted that this was one of Arius’s errors; Arius, however, was not its author, according to the most learned annotators themselves. Defending Origen against Perettus and Bagatta, they prove from Athanasius, by citing Origen’s own words, that Origen reproved the same error: “Let him understand who dares to say, ‘There was once when the Son was not’”—which we have also noted above, and have cited other texts of Origen.

[Col. 0651C] They therefore admit that the cited opinions of Origen prove that some others in that time—Origen’s time—taught this error which Origen reproved. Since Origen refutes this error in more than one place, and with deliberate and weighty arguments, it is established that it was prevalent even in Origen’s time. Consequently St. Zeno could have overthrown it long before the Arians. Recall what we related above concerning Tertullian, Beryllus, and Dionysius of Alexandria, who defends himself against the same charge before St. Dionysius, Roman Pontiff: “We are accused as though we said that the Son was one among the number of created things and in no way consubstantial with His Father. The charge made against me—that I denied Christ to be consubstantial with God—is false.” And from what we have presented concerning Paul of Samosata, you will understand that it is abundantly evident that this error had spread both before and during the time of Gallienus. Therefore it is no wonder that the holy bishop delivered a sermon against it to the people in that same age; hence there is no need on this account to relegate him to the fourth century.

[Col. 0652A] Indeed, if there is room for conjecture, I think that St. Zeno had in view his contemporary Dionysius of Alexandria. For, having noted three heresies at the beginning of the sermon, he afterwards, under the third number, turns his words to a Christian: “Let us now see, excellent Christian, how you insert time between the Father and the Son.” He attacks this with a powerful argument:

“For if they do not owe to time the fact that one is subject to the other, then undoubtedly, as you wish, nature is greater than God. But since Christ made nature from nothing, and time is from nature, it is quite absurd to place the work before its own craftsman; and herein lies the only distinction: they alone know themselves.”

The most learned annotators wish these words to be directed to the Arians, and say that “excellent Christians” is spoken ironically. But there is nothing in the text that savours of irony; consequently, they should be taken as spoken seriously. Observe above with what ardour he speaks when he attacks heretics: “Since these things are so, O cunning humanity, recognize yourself at last, even late; and put the reins of silence on your intemperate tongue. It is a kind of madness to desire to speculate upon the secret of the invisible and incomprehensible” (Note 14 on the same sermon, on Tract 7, no. 2).

[Col. 0652C] “The third is truly blind Judaism,” says St. Zeno, “which, although it reads everywhere in its law, as it is accustomed to say, that two Persons, Father and Son, are indicated, still to this day maintains that God has no Son.” This must certainly be taken as said against the Sabellians, whose heresy was then widespread. St. Basil also called that heresy Judaism: “Judaism is Sabellianism imported into evangelical preaching. For one who says that one thing is called by several names—Father, Son, and Holy Spirit—and expounds one hypostasis of the three, what else does he do? Does he not deny the eternal existence of the Only-Begotten which preceded the ages? Does he not likewise deny that His coming to humankind occurred through a certain dispensation, His descent into hell, His resurrection, and His judgment? Does he not further deny the distinctive operations of the Spirit?”

Novatian too observes this error among heretics: “For this insult of heretics will recoil even upon God the Father Himself, if God the Father could not beget the Son as God.” Yet he says this not against the later Sabellians themselves but against the Praxeans.

[Col. 0652D] The Ballerini brothers themselves support my opinion, for they note that this sermon excellently argues against the Patripassians and Sabellians: “This is a splendid confession against the Patripassians, or—as they were later called by the Latins—the Sabellians, who imagined one Person of the Father distinguished only by a double name. Catholics, however, confess the Father and Son as two Persons, distinguished by two names.”

[Col. 0653A] When these matters are carefully weighed, it is evident that no argument can be drawn for placing St. Zeno after Arius in the fourth century. For the matters in his sermons that seemed to have been said against Arius or the Arians ought properly to be placed around the time of Gallienus, because the errors which the holy bishop either alludes to or refutes were then especially vigorous. The Ballerini brothers do not concede this. Rather, they affirm that these same errors would have been unknown to St. Zeno if his age is placed in the third century. Let us therefore untie this knot of their argument.

§ XVI. Knowledge of the heresies mentioned by St. Zeno was common around the time of Gallienus.

Concerning the cited statement of Origen, which we have already mentioned above—“Let him understand who dares to say, ‘There was once when the Son was not’”—the Ballerini brothers concede, in their notes on the seventh tract of St. Zeno’s second book, that certain others taught this error in that time.

[Col. 0653B] Yet in chapter 1, § 2 of their first dissertation, they seem to suppose that only one or two persons were defenders of this error: “There was also, at that time, some other person who taught what the Arians afterwards taught.” They also cite St. Dionysius of Alexandria: “In Egypt, indeed, there was St. Dionysius of Alexandria, a disciple of Origen, who—not in order to pave the way for the Arians, but in order to oppose the Sabellian heresy then raging in Libya and neighbouring nations—carelessly employed that expression.”

Then, after recounting Dionysius’s accusation before Pope Dionysius, the latter’s rebuke, and Dionysius of Alexandria’s defense, they continue: “From this history, therefore, it is established that in the third century this formula was used by some persons only in Egypt—whence it is read in only a few monuments concerning the Alexandrian Church—and that they used it with the intention of refuting the Sabellian heresy in a Catholic sense, not of introducing and defending a new one. When Dionysius of Alexandria was warned that the formula was displeasing, he so expressly confirmed Catholic doctrine in his *Apology* that among the ancients no one can be found who rejected Arius’s error more vigorously and clearly than Dionysius.”

[Col. 0653C] Who, then, could suppose that our sole author in these western regions often and vehemently argued in public against this man, or another person of the same kind and place, as someone upholding Arian errors? Would one not rather understand that this writer openly attacks the Arians of the fourth century, raging everywhere and especially in these parts of Italy under Auxentius’s leadership—particularly since he attacks deliberately and repeatedly not that formula alone which was reproved in St. Dionysius of Alexandria, but several other expressions never heard from anyone before Arius?

The Ballerini brothers would have the heresy of Beryllus and the verbal lapse of Dionysius of Alexandria treated as a domestic matter conducted within enclosed walls and kept hidden. But the history of those times does not permit this. Let us hear what Eusebius testifies concerning Beryllus (*History*, Book V, chapter 23):

[Col. 0654A] “At that time Beryllus, mentioned above, bishop of Bostra in Arabia, was perverting the ecclesiastical rule and attempted to introduce certain new doctrines alien to the Catholic faith. He rashly dared to assert that our Lord and Saviour, before He lived among humankind, did not subsist with a distinct personal existence, nor have any divinity of His own residing in Him, but only the Father’s divinity. Since very many bishops held inquiries and disputations against him on this matter, Origen, summoned with the others, first conversed with him privately in order to ascertain the man’s opinion. But after he had clearly learned what Beryllus was saying, he exposed his error; and by arguments and demonstrations, having convicted the man and, as it were, taken him by the hand, he led him to the way of truth and restored him to his former sound opinion. Even today there remain published records both of Beryllus and of the synod assembled on his account, containing the disputations held in his church and everything that was then done.”

You see here that very many bishops held inquiries concerning Beryllus’s error; that a synod was held; and that disputations and published records existed. If Eusebius saw them about a hundred years later, St. Zeno could have seen them in the time of Gallienus. That both the holy bishop and other bishops, priests, and certain faithful persons zealous for the purity of faith saw them and that they became known in the Church is evident from the fact that our holy Doctor publicly argued against the same error.

[Col. 0654C] St. Athanasius (*On the Opinions of Dionysius*) recounts the affair concerning Dionysius of Alexandria as follows: “When Bishop Dionysius had learned of the Pentapolitans, he wrote this letter, as I have said, to Ammonius and Euphranor against Sabellius’s heresy, prompted by zeal for religion. Some from the Church, orthodox in opinion but unaware of the reason why he had written thus, went up to Rome and accused him there before Dionysius, the Roman bishop of the same name. When he learned the facts, the Alexandrian composed a work simultaneously against the followers of Sabellius’s sect and against the doctrines of Arius, for which Arius was expelled from the Church. In it he teaches that the heresy of Sabellius and the blasphemies of those who say that God’s Word is a work or creature are equal but opposite heresies. He asked the Roman bishop to send him the proceedings; having received them, he issued a work entitled *Refutation and Defense*, in which he rebukes the impious activity of Christ’s rebels and shows how they raised this slander against him.”

[Col. 0654D] Since the Pentapolitans had been infected by Sabellius’s heresy, St. Dionysius of Alexandria sent a letter to Ammonius and Euphranor to restore them to the faith; from this letter the disagreement arose, as Athanasius himself testifies: “Whence suspicion arose. Since some things were read in the same letter that were not consonant with purity of faith, some from the Church went up to Rome and accused him there before Dionysius, bishop of the same name.”

The letters to Ammonius and Euphranor therefore did not lie hidden in private archives, but became known to the Alexandrian Church. For certain persons from that Church—namely from the clergy of that Church, and, as it is reasonable to believe, appointed by that clergy, since their own bishop was being accused before the Supreme Pontiff—went up to Rome and accused him there. Could a public accusation, brought by the Alexandrian Church against its own bishop to Rome before the Supreme Pontiff, have been concealed from all Italy?

[Col. 0655A] Must it not be said that notice of so great a matter, dealing as it did with Christ’s divinity, was spread abroad also among all the Churches of the world? For there was a very great controversy regarding Dionysius and very great disturbances were stirred up, as Thomassin aptly observes. Here it must be seriously considered how great a storm was raised against Dionysius because one or two letters seemed to depart somewhat from the most constant and ancient doctrine of all the Churches in professing the divinity of the Son. “For unless that faith of the Churches had been most constant and most ancient, Dionysius would not have been driven to the need to clear himself, would not have been accused before Dionysius, bishop of the Roman Church, and would not have been compelled to clear himself by letters.” Thus Thomassin, whom Dionysius of Alexandria himself supports in his *Apology* to Dionysius, Roman Pontiff: “But these and similar things written by me they pretend not to see, as though half-blind; and with disorderly little opinions, like stones thrown from afar, they try to stone me.”

[Col. 0655B] What wonder, then, if the bishop of Verona, St. Zeno, publicly reproved the error for which Dionysius was accused—especially since, as we have noted, his very manner of rebuke supports this conclusion? This also demonstrates the affair’s most manifest and public notoriety: Dionysius not only defended himself against that charge in several letters. “If consideration of the time and person drew him to write such things, he afterwards also wrote other letters in which he cleared himself of suspicion.” But he issued two volumes. The first was against Sabellius’s heresy and at the same time against those who charged him with holding an unsound view of Christ’s divinity: “When he learned the facts, the Alexandrian composed a work simultaneously against the followers of Sabellius’s sect and against the doctrines of Arius …”—Athanasius calls them “Arius’s doctrines,” although Dionysius wrote so many years before Arius.

[Col. 0655C] He wrote the second to the Roman Pontiff in self-defense: “He asked the Roman bishop to send him the proceedings; having received them, he issued a work entitled *Refutation and Defense*.” Pope Dionysius himself, according to the same Athanasius, whose words I have cited, also published commentaries. From the volumes written against those who asserted that the Son was a work or creature, it is plainly shown that the heresy of Arians, rebels against Christ, was not then condemned for the first time, but had long before been condemned by all. “By all,” he says: thus he says that the condemned heresy was known to all, for it could not have been condemned by all unless it had also been known to all.

Dionysius of Alexandria had an interest in making his writings public for his own defense not only in the Alexandrian Church but also at Rome, in Italy, and throughout the whole Church, in order to repel the disgrace inflicted upon him. It was likewise the duty of Dionysius of Rome to show that the error had been condemned throughout the whole Church.

[Col. 0656A] Therefore it must be granted to the Ballerini brothers that St. Dionysius of Alexandria used the formula, “Since He is a thing made, He was not before He was made,” with the intention of refuting the Sabellian heresy in a Catholic sense. Yet from this it by no means follows that this error was less known and therefore should not have been rebuked, even if it had occurred only as a lapse of Dionysius of Alexandria. On the contrary, it was especially to be publicly reproved for this reason: lest the authority and sanctity of Dionysius of Alexandria, as though with the hand of a midwife, give the error being spread great weight and opportunity.

For this reason, dealing more gently with him, he warns him thus: “Let us now see, excellent Christian, how you insert time between the Father and the Son. For if they do not owe to time the fact that one is subject to the other, then undoubtedly, as you wish, nature is greater than God. But since Christ made nature from nothing, and time is from nature, it is quite absurd to place the work before its own craftsman; and herein lies the only distinction: they alone know themselves” (St. Zeno, Sermon VII, Book II).

[Col. 0656B] It pleased me to repeat St. Zeno’s words, for they themselves demonstrate that he addresses Dionysius of Alexandria, although absent, in the rhetorical manner. They breathe charity, express the highest esteem for the man, and, in brief but vigorous force, refute an error most fittingly suited to Dionysius’s time.

But it must not be conceded that this formula is found only in Dionysius of Alexandria, or in a few writers of the third century in Egypt alone, and only in a small number of monuments concerning the Alexandrian Church, as the Ballerini brothers suppose (Dissertation I, ch. 1, §2). [Col. 0656C] Rather, it must be held certain that this heresy was spread throughout the whole Church around the time of Dionysius of Alexandria—indeed, around the beginning of the third century. To make this plain, we must recall what was set forth above concerning the age of this heresy: namely, that Ebion’s error was widespread not only in Asia before the beginning of the second century, but also at Rome, and was increasingly disseminated, with Theodotion and Artemas condemned by Pope Victor around A.D. 196.

After the error had been struck down, it is found still to have crept through the Church, not only in the East but also in the West, though with some moderation, as heretics are accustomed to do in order to evade the Church’s censure. Artemon, indeed, said that Christ the Lord was merely a man born of the Virgin, superior to the prophets. [Col. 0656D] Once the heresy had been condemned, the heterodox no longer asserted so openly that Christ had not existed before Mary; rather, they maintained that there had been a time when he was not, and that there was no proper divinity in him, but only that of the Father. We find that Tertullian adopted their opinion in the words already cited, at the beginning of the century:

> Both the Father is God and the Judge is God; nevertheless, the Father and the Judge are not therefore eternal, because God is eternal. For he could not be Father before the Son, nor Judge before sin. But there was a time when neither sin nor the Son existed—those things which made God Judge and Father.

After Tertullian’s death, Beryllus of Bostra—commended by Eusebius for his distinguished doctrine—asserted the same error around A.D. 230. That it was still spreading about the [Col. 0657A] middle of that same third century, in Italy and at Rome, is plainly evident from the fact that Novatian, a Roman presbyter, still a Catholic under Pope St. Fabian, argued against the same error:

> Therefore, since he is begotten of the Father, he is always in the Father. And I say “always” in such a way as to prove him not unbegotten, but begotten . . . But because he is before all time, he must be said always to have been in the Father. For time cannot be assigned to him who is before time. He is always in the Father, lest the Father should not always be Father.

Origen also argued against the same error, although he was not consistent in his sound doctrine concerning the mystery of the Holy Trinity:

> Since he is the likeness of the Father, it cannot be that there was a time when he was not.

Accordingly, Beryllus’s heresy cannot be called momentary, [Col. 0657B] nor wholly unknown to the West and perhaps known only to Zeno. From the evidence adduced, it is shown to have resounded throughout the universal Church, known and publicly manifest, to Tertullian, Novatian, and Dionysius, bishop of Rome—the Latin Fathers; to Origen, Theognostus, and Dionysius of Alexandria—the Greek Fathers; to Paul of Samosata himself, a heretic; and throughout the whole third century.

To complete this paragraph, let us cite the text of Dionysius of Alexandria from Athanasius (*On the Decrees of the Nicene Synod*):

> There was never a time when God was not Father; Christ was always Word, Wisdom, and Power. For God did not first fail to beget these and then later beget them; nor is the Son from himself, but he has his being from the Father. Now, because he is the radiance of Eternal [Col. 0657C] Light, he too is in every respect eternal. For since the Light always exists, it is certain that its radiance always exists as well; for light is understood to be light precisely by shining. It cannot be that light should not shine . . . I have mentioned the Holy Spirit, but in such a way that I joined with it whence he came and through whom: but they do not know that the Father cannot be separated from the Son, that under the name of Father the primary source of their conjunction is contained, and that the Son is not removed from the Father as from a dwelling-place, since the title “Father” indicates this communion; and that the Holy Spirit is in the hands of the Father and the Son, yet is separated neither from him who sends nor from him who bears. How, then, could it be that, when I use these names, I should be suspected of thinking that they are separable and divisible? In this manner, therefore, we extend the indivisible Unity into the Trinity, and bring the Trinity, which cannot be diminished, to completion in Unity . . . And yet we are accused of saying that the Son is one among the number of created things and in no way consubstantial with his Father.

St. Dionysius adduces other matters as well; but these suffice to confirm what we have proposed. How highly they should be valued, let the reader understand for himself.

## § XVII. Whether St. Zeno attacked other formulas attributed to the Arians

We have demonstrated that the three heresies attacked by St. Zeno had been disseminated long before Arius arose, and that the holy Doctor could also have refuted them in the third century. [Col. 0658A] Yet the Ballerini brothers insist, saying:

> He attacks not only that formula which was reproved in St. Dionysius of Alexandria, but several other expressions, deliberately and repeatedly, which had never been heard from anyone before Arius.

They proceed to prove, by the authority of Socrates, Sozomen, Rufinus, and Hilary, that these expressions were unheard of before Arius. But from what we have brought forward, it is more than sufficiently clear that the formulas considered hitherto had been heard before Arius; likewise, that Zeno was not the only one to argue against them, and that they were not unknown in the West. Let us consider the other formulas which they adduce, so that it may be evident whether St. Zeno delivered his sermons against formulas unheard of before Arius, and whether he attacked them deliberately and repeatedly.

The Arians, say the Ballerini brothers, denied the equality of the Son with the [Col. 0658B] Father and declared the Son inferior to the Father. In Treatises III and IV of Book II, the author forcefully calls the Son “equal” to the Father “in all things,” and in Treatise VI, no. 4, he insists upon “the one equality of both.” He establishes this in expressions so explicit, and repeats it so often in other terms, that he seems to indicate that he professes these things not accidentally, but deliberately, against an error already prevailing. Thus, in Treatise I of Book II, he distinctly affirms that Catholics proclaim “the Son of God, God,” equal to the Father—an affirmation which belongs only to the fourth century in opposition to Arius’s heresy. Further, the author did not merely assert this equality; in several cases he wished to establish and confirm it in entire treatises, rejecting objections raised only by the Arians. See Treatises I and VI, Book II.

Before St. Zeno, all the Fathers who wrote on Christ’s divinity defended the equality of the Son with the [Col. 0658C] Father. For all the earlier heresies which denied that Christ was God and claimed that he was a man attacked that equality. Accordingly, long before Gallienus’s time, St. Hippolytus the Martyr asserted Christ’s equality with the Father in the words we have cited, in which he says most explicitly that the Word is identical with the Father. Clement of Alexandria also, cited above, says:

> The Divine Word, who truly is most manifest God, is equal to the Lord of all.

Nevertheless, there was a more pressing need to defend the equality of the Son with the Father in the age when St. Zeno perhaps governed the Church of Verona, because Origen had argued against that very equality in his book *Against Celsus*:

> The Son of God, the Word, is the immediate maker of the world, as though he fashioned the world with his own hand. But the Father of the Word, precisely because he commanded his Son and Word to make the world, is the primary craftsman.

This particular error was refuted by St. Zeno in the first sermon indicated by the Ballerini brothers:

> “But he to whom a command is given,” you say, “is inferior.” What then? It is not proved thereby that he is inferior, because he is the executor of the Father’s heart, from which he proceeded; for it is no lesser thing to do great things than to speak them. And although it is said by the Father—or may be said—that the Word is the Son, he is not without the Son; and what was done by the Son—or may be done—is not without the Father’s gracious will, because the Son is not without the Father.

Likewise, in the fifth sermon:

> When the Father commands that the world be made, the work is accomplished together with the word by the [Col. 0659A] Son. Yet no one commands how great or what kind it should be; no one asks. For there could be no injury to the Father if the Son needed such instruction—he who, abiding in the Father’s bosom, had not learned the perfection of his will but possessed it.

With such majesty of speech and such force of reasoning the holy bishop attacks the heterodox.

St. Jerome, however, asserts that Origen spoke more openly against the equality of the Son with the Father, testifying that Origen wrote:

> God the Father is incomprehensible light; Christ, by comparison with the Father, is a very small radiance, though to us he appears great because of our weakness.

He gives the example of two statues: one large and one small—the former filling the world and in a manner invisible because of its size, the latter falling beneath the eyes—and compares the Father to the former and the Son to the latter. In the same letter St. Jerome reports the same error of Origen concerning the Person of the Holy Spirit:

> The Holy Spirit is third in rank and honor after the Father and the Son . . . Again, the Son’s Power is greater than that of the Holy Spirit; and consequently the power of the Holy Spirit himself is greater than that of all other things called holy.

Thus St. Zeno did not lack, even in Gallienus’s time, an available occasion vigorously to treat in his sermons of the equality not only of the Son with the Father, but also of the Holy Spirit with the Father and the Son. Therefore he concludes his first sermon thus:

> It is established, therefore, that he is equal, since he lives reciprocally with the Holy Spirit.

[Col. 0659C] The First Council of Antioch likewise reproved the same error in Paul of Samosata: namely, that in producing the world the Son fulfilled the Father’s will, and that the Father commanded him to do this. The Fathers of that council exclude inequality:

> He works as Word and God together, through whom the Father made all things—not as through an instrument, nor as through knowledge not existing of itself.

Dionysius of Alexandria speaks in the same sense when, against Samosatenus, he explains these words of Jeremiah, “I was like an innocent lamb led to sacrifice,” as spoken in the Person of Christ:

> I, that is, Christ, who am always a Person equal to the Father, coeternal with the Lord Spirit, with no dissimilarity of substance, etc.

It is therefore established that this error concerning the inequality [Col. 0659D] of the Son in relation to the Father prevailed in the third century, under Gallienus, so that the need of the time pressed him to argue against it. For the Arians were not the only ones to speak against the equality of the Son with the Father. But perhaps someone may claim that Origen’s writings were falsified by the Arians. Is he perhaps unaware of Origen’s turbulent genius, like a sea not always calmed by tranquil truth, but frequently boiling with the waves of varied opinions and dashing upon the rocks of falsehood? Jerome shows by compelling reasoning that this alleged corruption of Origen’s writings is an empty fiction:

> Was Origen alone found whose writings were simultaneously falsified throughout the whole world, and was all truth, as though at Mithridates’ letters, erased in a single day from his volumes? If one book was corrupted, could not all his works, which he published at different places and times, have been corrupted together?

They think that they discern another formula proper to the Arians in the sermons of St. Zeno. Since the author vehemently insists upon “one substance,” as other Fathers of the same age, deliberately fighting against the Arians, insisted upon it; although he never employs the word *consubstantial*, he nevertheless shows sufficiently that he is fighting against that heresy.

I had thought that St. Zeno, bishop of Verona, would be exempt from this argument, for the very reason suggested by the Ballerini brothers: “although he never employs the word *consubstantial*.” But in my judgment, even if St. Zeno had employed the word *consubstantial* repeatedly, I should still hold certainly that he is not to be removed from the third century. [Col. 0660B] I am led to this belief because the word *consubstantial* was in use among the Fathers and doctors of the Church long before the Council of Nicaea.

Eusebius of Caesarea himself, an enemy of the word *consubstantial*, testifies to this, as quoted by Athanasius (*Letter to the Bishops in Africa*):

> Meanwhile, they strangely complain that they have been condemned through terms not customary in Scripture, though piously coined; while they themselves, like outsiders sprung from the earth, speak otherwise. The bishops, however, did not devise these terms themselves, but received them as attested by the Fathers and inserted them in their writings. For the ancient bishops, nearly one hundred and thirty years ago, both those who exercised the episcopate at Rome and those in our own city, accused those who called the Son [Col. 0660C] a creature or denied that he was consubstantial with the Father.

Eusebius, bishop of Caesarea, was not ignorant of this. Though he had first supported the Arian party, he afterwards subscribed to the decrees of the Nicene Council and affirmed the same in letters to his own people. These are his words:

> We know that certain learned and illustrious bishops and other writers of old, when speaking of the divinity of the Father and the Son, used the term *consubstantiality*.

St. Dionysius of Alexandria, a contemporary of Gallienus, used this word as received from the Fathers against Samosatenus:

> You call him who was Lord by nature and the Father’s Word—through whom he likewise made all things, and through whom the holy Fathers called him *homoousios*, “consubstantial with the Father”—forsaken.

That the use of this term was older than Dionysius is proved by the most learned Christian Lupus, who, having cited several texts of St. Irenaeus and Tertullian, concludes:

> Therefore these expressions—“consubstantial,” “consubstantial Power,” and “of the same substance”—belong neither to Dionysius of Rome or Alexandria in their opposition to Paul of Samosata, nor to Tertullian, nor likewise to St. Irenaeus, but to the Apostles themselves. For not only both Dionysii and Tertullian, but St. Irenaeus himself, the disciple of St. Polycarp, uses them as terms common in the Church, and therefore apostolic. Tertullian received them from the Latin Church, Irenaeus from the Greek Church. Hence they are most ancient in both.  
> (*Dissertation appended to his work on the terms Substance, Essence, and Person*, ch. 4, question 2, new Venetian edition, 1724.)

[Col. 0661A] Very well indeed. For that most wise man knew the Church’s practice of handing down the Apostles’ Creed to catechumens. Did they perhaps hand down bare letters? Did they not also explain the mysteries contained in it? Hence, everywhere and always, the Son’s divinity and consubstantiality with the Father were transmitted and so deeply impressed upon the hearts of believers that the orthodox judged this confession of faith worthy of defense against heretics with such courage and constancy—in exile, torture, blood, and death itself.

Petavius, Lupus, and Thomassinus acknowledge that this faith in the divinity of the Word was widespread, common, and public in the Church because such great controversies were stirred up concerning Dionysius of Alexandria. Hear Lupus:

> That term, then beautiful and glorious—namely, *consubstantial*—was so not only in the Roman Church, [Col. 0661B] and therefore in the whole Latin Church, but also throughout the Pentapolis and the whole Egyptian diocese. The renown of this term was the basis for accusing and correcting the Patriarch. Fourth, we learn that Dionysius the Patriarch also acknowledged that denial of the term was a crime. Accordingly, he disavowed that denial, and wrote back that he had said nothing else concerning that term except that it was not expressed in the sacred Scriptures. Without doubt this statement made him suspect, gave rise to the accusation, and led him, in defending himself, to declare that not merely the thing signified but the term itself was entirely approved by him.

These matters concern Gallienus’s time. Why then, even if St. Zeno had used the expression “one substance” not twice or three times but a hundred times, and even the word “consubstantial,” should it be judged that he preached against the Arians, when [Col. 0661C] in the third century, amid the resounding accusations against Dionysius of Alexandria and the raging heresy of Paul of Samosata, he had so great an occasion to insist upon that very term? The argument would have some force, though not a sound one, if St. Zeno had mentioned the word *homoousios*, or *consubstantial*, only once—for he and the earlier Fathers used only the expression “of one substance.” But since nothing of the kind can be found in him even in shadow, I do not see why he should be forced down from his own age, namely the third century.

The same must be said of the absurdity which the Arians charged upon Catholics. To abolish this one substance, the Arians objected that something had been taken away from the Father’s substance in order that the Son might be begotten, and thus [Col. 0661D] they declared that Catholics must admit a diminished and imperfect Father. Yet faith in one God in three distinct persons—that is, the confession of one divine substance in three persons distinct from one another—has always flourished in the Church. It has been customary for heretics to press this calumny against Catholics: that by distinguishing the persons they divide and diminish the divine substance, and admit several gods. The Fathers of the First Council of Antioch observed this against Samosatenus:

> Whoever denies that the Son of God existed before the foundation of the world, and says that he believes and confesses God, does nothing other than proclaim two gods. [Col. 0662A] We judge him who proclaims that the Son of God is not God to be alien from the ecclesiastical rule.

St. Justin Martyr, one of the most ancient Fathers, argues against this calumny no less clearly than St. Zeno. Hear him again:

> That Power of God—he speaks of God the Word—is called God by the Prophet, not in such a way as the light of the sun is counted by name alone, but as something numerically other; yet not by severance, as though the Father’s substance were cut off, for things divided and cut off are not the same as they were before the cutting.  
> (*Dialogue with Trypho*)

See what I said in §§13 and 14.

## § XVIII. St. Zeno nowhere mentions formulas proper to the Arians

[Col. 0662B] We trust that it has been demonstrated, concerning the Arian formulas considered thus far, that St. Zeno did not at all argue against the Arians in his sermons. Now we also lay down as certain that the holy bishop did not even lightly touch upon a single formula proper to the Arians. To establish this, one must recall what we showed above: namely, that Arius and his followers, after Arius’s expulsion from the Church, in some measure altered their errors and presented them clothed in other forms.

He especially corrected that error received from Beryllus or Samosatenus which St. Alexander, Patriarch, first charged against Arius: “They assert that there was once a time when the Son of God did not exist.” In his letter to Eusebius of Nicomedia, Arius admits that the Son was begotten before times and had existed as full God before times and before ages. St. Zeno refuted Arius’s first [Col. 0662C] error in these words:

> Let us now see, excellent Christian, how you insert time between the Father and the Son. For if they do not owe to time their being subject one to the other, then certainly, as you wish, nature is greater than God. But since Christ made nature from nothing, and time belongs to nature, it is sufficiently absurd to prefer a work to its Craftsman.

The argument proceeds excellently against the first error, because the insertion of time between Father and Son would entail that nature is greater than God: “Certainly, as you wish, nature is greater than God.” For Christ made nature from nothing: “Since Christ made nature from nothing.” But time is something natural: “And time belongs to nature.” Therefore, if time was created before Christ God, the work is preferred to its Craftsman.

[Col. 0662D] But the argument has no force against Arius’s revised error, namely that Christ existed before times and before ages as full God, because in revising his error Arius places time after the Creator, and it cannot be inferred: “It is sufficiently absurd to prefer a work to its Craftsman.” Therefore Zeno’s reasoning is directed against the first error, which Arius borrowed from earlier heretics. Accordingly, St. Zeno must be said to have made the argument either against Samosatenus, his contemporary, or against Dionysius of Alexandria’s imprudent slip of expression—not against Arius, who had retreated from his former error and taught a new one, and whom the holy Doctor’s argument does not refute.

[Col. 0663A] But this must especially be noted: St. Zeno sets forth as certain that Christ made the nature of things from nothing: “Since Christ made nature from nothing.” Arius, however, said that Christ was from nothing: “When we say that he—Christ—consists from nothing.” Thus Arius. St. Zeno does not attack this error by a single word. Therefore it was not known to him, since, when it was precisely the error that needed to be refuted, he passed over the argument particularly suited to establish his case. Therefore he wrote before that error.

As to the remaining formulas proper to the Arians which we have enumerated, St. Zeno maintains profound silence. These are the Arian formulas:

> God was not always Father; the Son was not always . . . Since all things were created, he too—the Son—must be regarded as something created and a work . . . [Col. 0663B] The Son does not exist naturally in the Father, nor is he the proper Word of the Father’s substance, nor the proper Wisdom through which he created the world; rather, there is in the Father another proper and peculiar Word, and likewise another proper Wisdom, through which Wisdom he made the Word itself. Thus the Lord Christ himself is called Word only in relation to rational beings which use words . . . God created not us for his sake—the Son’s—but him for our sake . . . When he wished to create us, then he also created him; and, after he had been created, he called him Word. But he too came to be by grace . . . Christ is not the natural and true power of God, but, just as caterpillars and locusts are called the powers of almighty God, so he too is called the Father’s omnipotence . . . The Son does not know the Father exactly, nor does he even know his own substance.

[Col. 0663C] These are the assertions that Socrates, Book I, chapter 6, called Arius’s novel and unheard-of assertions; and Sozomen, Book I, chapter 15, says that Arius dared to preach in the Church what no one had ever said. Before both of them, Rufinus, *History*, Book X, chapter 1, says:

> Arius began to put forward certain perverse opinions concerning the faith of Christ, opinions which had never previously come into question.

Hence Hilary calls Arianism a “new heresy” in Book VII of *On the Trinity*, no. 3; a “novel heresy,” no. 6; and, in Book I *To Constantius*, no. 5, “a recent plague, newly invented after almost four hundred years”—that is, a heresy which no one taught or defended before Arius. Against these things St. Zeno does not so much as utter a sound. We have seen that our author attacked other formulas, or errors, which Arius drew from Samosatenus, Artemas, and Ebion, as well as statements made by Dionysius of Alexandria because he put them forward incautiously: “Since a thing was made, it did not exist before it was made.” [Col. 0663D] These things, as has been shown above, were widespread and condemned by the Church, and do not at all indicate Arius’s time, but Gallienus’s. Therefore St. Zeno cannot on any ground be removed from the age of that emperor; indeed, since he makes no mention of Arius’s distinctive errors, he must be said to have lived much earlier.

It is certainly clear from the fact that St. Zeno wrote in the third century that Petavius, of whom we shall speak below, thinks he finds in some of St. Zeno’s sermons a certain affinity of wording with Arius’s principal error:

> When the Father wished to create us, he then also created him—the Son.

[Col. 0664A] For if St. Zeno had composed his sermons after Arius, he would surely have expressed his own thought more cautiously and could not have been brought under suspicion of Arianism, as we find happened even to other pre-Nicene Fathers.

It is also plainly concluded that our Zeno did not have Arius’s impious doctrines before his eyes, because the first heresy which he mentions in Treatise VII of Book II is this:

> Finally, one [heresy] asserts that Jesus Christ took his beginning from the womb of the Virgin Mary, and that thereafter he was made God because of righteousness, not born God.

This is the error of Paul of Samosata. It indicates an error contrary to Arius’s. [Col. 0664B] Arius, for his part, proclaims that Christ was made God by grace:

> When he wished to create us, then he also created him, and after he was created he called him Word; but he too came to be by grace.

Arius, I say, declares that he became God by grace. The error attacked by St. Zeno asserts that he was made God not by grace but by merit, because of righteousness.

How far St. Zeno, bishop of Verona, was from attacking the impiety of Arius and the Arians is plainly demonstrated by this manifest observation: Arius or the Arians are never named in the holy Doctor’s Treatises; not a word is found concerning the Council of Nicaea; no mention is made of Constantine or Constantius.

Yet the Ballerini brothers place St. Zeno in those times when the Arians themselves had anathematized the original errors of their impious teacher which had been received from ancient heretics. Thus at the Arian synod held at Antioch after Constantine’s death, in A.D. 341, a formula of faith was issued which condemns those who assert:

> [Col. 0664C] That there is or was a time, moment, or age before the Son was begotten; or if anyone says that the Son is a creature like one of created things.

Likewise, in the formula promulgated by Narcissus of Cilicia and three other bishops, those are struck with anathema who say that the Son is from non-existent things, or from another hypostasis and not from God, or that there was once a time when he did not yet exist. The same occurred at the Arian Synod of Sirmium in A.D. 351.

When, I say, the Ballerini brothers place St. Zeno’s age after all these events, is it credible that St. Zeno would have wished to argue against ancient heresies condemned by the Arians themselves and omit the recent ones? Or that he should have said absolutely nothing concerning the celebrated controversy over the word *homoousion*, “consubstantial,” which was both defended and attacked with such fervor by Catholics and Arians at precisely the time when those learned men place St. Zeno over the Church of Verona? [Col. 0664D] We shall discuss this when the question of the Arian formulas returns. Therefore, since St. Zeno left the distinctive Arian formulas untouched, it is most plainly established that he is not to be regarded as later than Arius.

## § XIX. Holy Fathers later than Arius expressly state the distinctive formulas of Arius and the Arians in their works

Let us select several statements of holy Fathers who wrote after Arius, so that in them we may indicate the distinctive Arian formulas. The first of the Arian formulas enumerated above is: “God was not always Father; the Son was not always.” Against this error St. Alexander, Patriarch of Alexandria, who first condemned that heresy, cried out in a sermon [Col. 0665A] to the people:

> God always; Son always; Father and Son together. The Son exists perpetually with the unbegotten God, always begotten from the Unbegotten; neither in thought nor in any moment does God precede the Son. God always; Son always; the Son from God himself always.

Theodoret likewise appends this addition to the synodal letters of the Council of Sardica:

> We confess that neither was the Father ever without the Son, nor the Son ever without the Father, nor can that be which is Word without Spirit. For it is most absurd to say that the Father was at some time not Father; and the Father can neither be named nor exist without the Son, as the Son himself testifies.

[Col. 0665B] The second heresy of Arius is: “Since all things are from nothing, the Son of God also emerged from nothing.” Athanasius recounts this formula in the aforementioned first Oration against the Arians, as also the rest which we cited from him. St. Hilary also mentions it:

> Many argue that he is not truly God by divinity, nor does he subsist from the property of the Father’s majesty and nature, but that he has been constituted from a substance different from God and from the eternal substance, chosen into adoption as Son after the manner of creatures from nothing, which have no prior origin.

And in Book II of *On the Trinity*, no. 4:

> Like certain preachers of the present time, who bring forth the Form, Wisdom, and Power of God from nothing and from time.

St. Gregory Nazianzen (*Oration* 49) speaks of those who imagine the Son of God to be mutable and changeable, as one not constituted from the Father’s substance:

> [Col. 0665C] And who have always taught that he has a beginning from time, an origin from nothing, and a name from another.

Lucifer of Cagliari, in Book I of his *Apology for St. Athanasius*, says that this is the Catholic faith which says that God does not have a true Son; which says that there was a time when he was not; which says that he was made from nothing. Thus he speaks against Emperor Constantius.

The third Arian formula is:

> They also add this: that he does not exist naturally in the Father, nor is he the proper Word of the Father’s substance, nor the proper Wisdom through which he created this world; but there is in the Father another proper and peculiar Word, and likewise another proper Wisdom, through which Wisdom he made that Word; and hence the Lord Christ himself is called Word only in relation to rational beings that use words.

So says St. Athanasius (*Third Oration against the Arians*, cited above), [Col. 0665D] and likewise in *On the Opinion of Dionysius*:

> To their other evils they have added this opinion also, drawn from a dunghill: that the Word is not the Father’s own and proper Word, but that there is another Word in God; and that our Lord is foreign to the Father’s substance, is called Word only imaginatively, and is not naturally the true Son of God, but has obtained this name by adoption, as a creature.

The fourth formula of Arius, from the same Athanasius, is:

> Again, he says that God created not us for his sake, but him for ours: “For God,” he says, “was alone, and the Word was not with him. Then, when he wished to create us, he also created this one, [Col. 0666A] and after he was created called him Word.”

St. Hilary, second historical fragment, no. 26:

> They handed down such doctrines as Arius’s: that God the Father begot the Son for the purpose of establishing the world and, by his power, made him from nothing into a new and other substance, a new and other God. They are profane toward the Father in thinking that something like himself could be generated from nothing; blasphemous toward Christ in stripping him of the Father’s infinite generative nature.

In Book XII of *On the Trinity*, no. 43, Hilary says:

> Or perhaps you wish what is created for works to be understood thus: that it was created on account of works; that is, that Christ was created as the cause of making works, so that he might remain merely the servant and maker of the world, and not be born Lord of glory.

[Col. 0666B] St. Gregory Nazianzen also, in *Oration* 46, recalls this fourth and the following fifth formula:

> The Son too is to be believed in the manner in which it was said to the people through Isaiah: “I have begotten sons and exalted them”; and elsewhere: “You are gods, and all are called sons of the Most High.” He is likewise to be considered firstborn as Israel also was called by God his firstborn son, and indeed “firstborn of all creation,” as though he were firstborn in the order of things made, from whom they assign a certain sequence to the creation of the world’s things.

The fifth formula: “For the Word is not the Father’s proper and natural offspring, but he too came to be by grace.” St. Hilary expresses the same in Book IV of *On the Trinity*, no. 3:

> For the heretics say that Christ is not from God—that is, that the Son was not born from the Father, nor is God by nature, but by appointment; [Col. 0666C] namely, that his sonship is adoption in name, because, just as there are many sons of God, he too is a son; then, that his divinity is a bestowed dignity, because, just as there are many gods, he too is God. Yet in him there is a more generous favor both of adoption and designation: he is adopted before the rest, is himself a Son greater than the other adopted sons, and is created more excellent than all natures, surpassing the other creatures themselves. Some of them also, while confessing God’s omnipotence, say that he was created in God’s likeness and from nothing, as God, that eternal Creator, established all other things after his own image: namely, that the Word was commanded to subsist from non-being, God being able to select from nothing a likeness of himself.

[Col. 0666D] These things may suffice to indicate that the holy Fathers who wrote after Arius stated and refuted Arius’s distinctive heresies—something which cannot be found in St. Zeno’s sermons.

## § XX. No argument for establishing the date of the holy Fathers can be drawn from the fact that later heresies are either hinted at or refuted in their works
I certainly do not deny that, from what St. Zeno says in his treatises, one may plainly perceive the truth opposed to every error of Arius. For since he most explicitly confesses that the Son is of the same substance as the Father, and equal and coeternal with the Father himself, it follows that he asserts the Father always to have been Father; that the Son was not created from nothing; that he did not have a beginning even before all creatures, as the Arians raved; [Col. 0667A] that there is not one Word in the Father distinct from Christ the Lord; and, still less, that the Word was made for our sake, or that he comprehends the Father’s essence by his own knowledge. These things are undoubtedly shown, from the teaching of this same St. Zeno, to depart from the faith. Yet, since it has been shown above that the mystery of the Holy Trinity was known from the very beginning of the Church, there is surely nothing surprising if, in explaining it, opposing errors, even later ones, are touched upon.

A practice received from the fathers has always prevailed in the Church, and still prevails: newly arisen errors are refuted by the teaching of the Old and New Testaments and of the holy Fathers. This too is practiced at the present time in refuting the impious doctrines of more recent heretics. Are, then, the canonical Scriptures, all the more ancient holy Fathers, [Col. 0667B] and the Doctors of the Church later than Calvin, Luther, and Jansen? Who would dare even to suspect this?

Certainly, at the Council of Ephesus, to cite a principal example, held in the year of Christ 431, testimonies were produced—as is clear from the acts of that council—and the opinions of Basil, who died in A.D. 378; Ambrose, in A.D. 397; Gregory Nazianzen, in A.D. 389; and Gregory of Nyssa, in A.D. 394, were cited, I say, to overthrow Nestorius’s errors; indeed, so too were those of St. Cyprian, who had died 170 years, and Athanasius, who had died nearly sixty years, before that same Ephesian council. Yet no one dared to assert that these holy Fathers were later than the Council of Ephesus, although they had condemned later heresies in advance. But I should like to produce [Col. 0667C] a text of St. Athanasius in which, nearly seventy years beforehand, he so precisely refutes the error later raised by Eutyches that he seems to have had it before his eyes:

> When did these things appear? Indeed, what hell belched them forth: that one should say that the body born of Mary is consubstantial with the divinity of the Word; or that the Word was changed into flesh, bones, ribs, sinews, and altogether into a body, and degenerated from his own nature? Who heard this in the Church or among Christians: that God the Word became a body by appearance, not in reality? Or who was so impious as either to say in words or to think in mind that the very Godhead, by which he is consubstantial with the Father, was circumcised and made imperfect from perfect? And that the body which hung upon the cross was not a human body, but Wisdom itself, the maker of all things?  
> (*Letter to Epictetus, bishop of Corinth* [Col. 0667D]).

What could be more explicit for disproving Eutyches’s heresy, by which he taught that in Christ there was only one nature, not two—namely, divine and human—but that these two natures, after their union, had been confused and blended? Yet Eutyches dreamed these ravings so long after Athanasius, while this same holy Doctor refutes them with such ardor.

The following circumstance also confirms this point: when the word *consubstantial* (*homoousios*) was explained at the Council of Nicaea itself, held in 325, Eutyches’s heresy was condemned in the very explanation of the word—a heresy proscribed 126 years later at the Council of Chalcedon. This is proved by the testimony of Eusebius of Caesarea [Col. 0668A] in the letter which he addressed to the clergy of his church:

> Likewise, it was examined and proved that the statement that the Son is consubstantial with the Father must not be understood in a bodily manner, nor as having anything resembling mortal living creatures. For it cannot consist either in a division of substance or in a change of the Father’s essence and power. For the unbegotten nature of the Father is altogether foreign to all such things. It means nothing else than that the Son of God has no likeness to the remaining creatures, but is altogether like the one Father who begot him, and is begotten from no substance and essence other than that of the Father.

The same letter states that Constantine the Great understood the Word to be consubstantial:

> *Consubstantial* cannot be understood in terms of bodily affections, nor can the Son of God consist from the Father by division or, so to speak, diminution. For it cannot happen that a nature devoid of matter, apprehended by intellect alone, and free from body, should receive in itself any bodily affection [Col. 0668B].

You see how precisely Eutyches’s error is set out and overthrown—the error which imagined that Christ’s flesh had passed into the divinity. For it cannot happen that a nature devoid of matter, apprehended by intellect alone, and free from body, should receive in itself any bodily affection. And that other assertion of Eutyches, “that Christ, as God, suffered,” is most explicitly refuted: “It cannot consist either through division of substance, diminution, or change of the Father’s essence and power.”

Thus, in explaining the term *consubstantial*, which must be understood of Christ’s divinity alone, since he has the same substance as the Father, two natures in Christ are most explicitly acknowledged, namely divine and human, against the impious doctrine of Eutyches. For Eutyches, confusing them after the union, admitted in Christ only one confused nature, both divine and human. Therefore, no inference can be drawn from St. Zeno’s teachings adduced against Arian errors that he was later than Arius. To do so would be equivalent to placing Athanasius and the Council of Nicaea after the Council of Chalcedon. Therefore what we undertook to prove stands: no argument for establishing the age of the holy Fathers can be drawn from their teaching by which later heresies are overthrown.

## § XXI. The “Treatises on the Faith” mentioned by St. Zeno in the first book, in the first Sermon on Faith, are not to be understood as Arian formularies

At the words of St. Zeno in the first Sermon on Faith, “It follows that we must know whether we ought to maintain a treatise of faith, or the faith of a treatise,” the most learned Ballerini brothers note:

> Here St. Zeno does not mean the Nicene treatise, but those composed by the Arians after Nicaea, which shortly afterward he calls “many treatises,” because they were issued both in pseudo-synods and separately by certain bishops.

Thus, in notes 15, 16, 29, and 32, and especially in note 33, they maintain that the treatises mentioned by St. Zeno are formularies concerning the faith composed by the Arians. They think this observation confirmed by the following: “These statements of St. Zeno agree well with the history of those times”—that is, the period in which the Arian heresy was widespread—“so much so that nothing similar can be adduced from earlier centuries, in which some suppose that he lived, to which they correspond equally.” They make the same assertion in chapter 1 of their second Dissertation. For there were then many formularies of faith, issued both by various Arian and Semi-Arian synods and by certain bishops in defense of their own sect. These, then, are the “many treatises, many faiths, indeed novel ones, nourished by the toil and favor of controversy,” which St. Zeno mentions in Treatise I, no. 3, book I.

Yet there is no necessity to understand the treatises named by St. Zeno as Arian formularies. To make this clear, one should observe [Col. 0669B] that, although the same Ballerini brothers learnedly note that Expositions of Faith, or formularies of faith, issued by bishops deliberating in a council, are customarily called “treatises on faith,” or even simply “treatises,” still the name “treatise” is not so proper to these formularies or expositions of faith that it cannot signify any other discussion conducted outside a council: namely, a sermon addressed to the people, or apologetic treatises for or against the faith. This is proved by St. Zeno’s own sermons, all of which are entitled “Treatises.” Therefore, as those distinguished men themselves observe further on, St. Zeno understood by the name “treatises” not simple formularies of faith, but fuller expositions of the faith, in which each person endeavored to establish his own view of faith by arguments and reasons, as is clear from the context [Col. 0669C].

In this sense Tertullian also calls *retractatus* the disputations of the Valentinians, Marcionites, and other heretics against the faith:

> The same subjects are debated among heretics and philosophers; the same *retractatus* are entangled.

Again, speaking specifically of heretics, he says:

> But when, for the sake of deceiving, they pretend that they are still seeking, they introduce their treatises to us by instilling anxiety.

Tertullian deals not only with heretical disputations concerning the faith, but also with Catholic ones:

> I come, then, to that article which our own people also put forward in order to open an inquiry, and heretics press in order to introduce scrupulosity.

Likewise, in this Sermon on Faith, St. Zeno understands by the name “treatises” every sort of discussion in which faith is treated, whether Catholic or heretical. This may be perceived especially from his own words in no. 2:

> For disputation, just as it cultivates faith, so, if it is crafty, uproots faith; because faith is surely not present where faith is being sought.

And below:

> There have been many treatises, many faiths—indeed, novel ones—nourished by the toil and favor of controversy.

But after the middle of the same sermon he adds concerning Catholic disputations about faith:

> But I do not say this in order to render the benefit of teaching unwelcome, but so that everyone may know that faith is one thing and a treatise another, and that faith cannot be given, born, or destroyed through a treatise.

It should also be noted that many similar statements occur both in Tertullian and in this Sermon of St. Zeno; it will not be tedious to compare them here.

Tertullian says:

> This is the subject-matter of worldly wisdom, the rash interpreter of the Divine Nature and Economy.

He attacks Valentinus, adding:

> Hence the aeons, certain forms, and Valentinus’s trinity of man.

St. Zeno (*the aforementioned Sermon*, no. 3):

> But if, what is worse, inflamed by a worldly love of display under the sound of law and faith, you presume, by arguments, to be able to compel, examine, measure, and distinguish the inestimable and incomprehensible perpetuity of the divinity of the God born from God and of the Holy Spirit, by that very right whereby he exists from himself.

The words “inflamed by a worldly love of display” and “to compel, examine, measure, and discuss by arguments” [Col. 0670B] censure the philosophy of the Gentiles, as Tertullian does: “This is the subject-matter of worldly wisdom, the rash interpreter of the Divine Nature.” But in St. Zeno’s other words, “of the God born from God and of the Holy Spirit,” etc., the Valentinians seem to be censured, who so shamefully raved concerning the origin of God—if the expression may be pardoned—in their aeons. For at the end of the sermon our author also cites the text of the Apostle Paul in which the holy Apostle censures genealogies and fables.

Tertullian (*ibid.*, ch. 10):

> But if, because such great things have also been instituted by others, we must therefore believe only insofar as we can discover, we shall always seek and never wholly believe. Where will be the end of seeking? Where the resting-place of believing?

St. Zeno:

> Moreover, I see, as the names of their assertions indicate—if you remove these, perhaps there is no contest at all—that there have been many treatises, many faiths, and indeed novel ones, nourished by the toil and favor of controversy. Since truth can scarcely be found among them, I think they were put up for sale so that they might not suffer from a shortage of people. Yet from all these it cannot arise, nor be grasped, what ought to be chosen; for that which always remains uncertain can be neither distinctive nor firm, since the choice of one is the rejection of another.

Thus, even in Tertullian’s time there were many Treatises on Faith: “such great things have also been instituted by others.” St. Zeno agrees: “There have been many treatises, many faiths, and indeed novel ones.” Both also complain of uncertainty. Tertullian: “We shall always seek and never wholly believe. Where will be the end of seeking? Where the resting-place of believing?” St. Zeno: [Col. 0670D] “That which always remains uncertain can be neither distinctive nor firm, since the choice of one is the rejection of another.”

Tertullian (*ibid.*, ch. 11):

> But if I have believed what I ought to have believed and yet think that something else must again be sought, I surely hope that something else is to be found. I could not hope for this unless I had either not believed, though I seemed to have believed. Thus, abandoning my faith, I prove a denier. Let me say it once for all: no one believes unless he has either not possessed or has lost [faith].

St. Zeno states it more concisely, but with equal force:

> Faith surely is not present where faith is sought.

Tertullian:

> But when they say that even one who holds the faith, as they suppose, must nevertheless seek in order to defend it, they deny before defending what they believe, confessing that they have not yet believed while they are seeking.

St. Zeno:

> Let this pernicious invention of its treatise tell me: what benefit does the contest bring? “Lest faith perish,” it says, “when it is wrongly believed or taught.” We shall shortly see what is evil in this reasoning.

And in no. 6 he says:

> In a certain way, whoever asserts God denies God; for a defense is supplied only for the weak, nor can one revere him whom one thinks has been assessed by one’s own ingenuity.

Tertullian:

> Finally, it is better to be ignorant, lest you know what you ought not, because you know what you ought. “Your faith,” he says, “has saved you,” not exercise in the Scriptures. Faith is set in a rule. You have the law and salvation from observing the law; but exercise consists in curiosity, having glory only from zeal for expertise. Let curiosity yield to faith; let glory yield to salvation. Certainly, let them either not clamor against the rule, or be silent. To know nothing further is to know everything.

St. Zeno:

> I think it most manifest that the simple person is better than the excessively clever; for the simple person simply believes all God’s words, while the clever person, made foolish by excessive wisdom, confounds himself in vain investigations.

See how many uniform thoughts are contained under different phrasing; anyone may note other similar ones. Meanwhile, I am convinced—and I trust others will be convinced—that from these treatises or disputations concerning faith one can in no way infer times later than Arius and his followers. For in Tertullian’s age these many treatises, both Catholic and heretical, [Col. 0671C] were circulated, and he himself argues at length against them. The passages cited, moreover, are general statements against curiosity in handling matters of faith and can be applied in any age.

But why should I speak only of Tertullian, as though he alone had argued about this subject? Did not Fathers earlier than he, in the second century, also compose longer discussions? St. Irenaeus certainly prefaces his five books *Against Heresies* by saying that he wrote them for this reason:

> For some, rejecting the truth, introduce discourses and various genealogies, which, as the Apostle says, furnish questions rather than the edification of God which is in faith; and by a specious plausibility craftily constructed, they seduce the minds of the inexperienced, dragging them captive by corrupting the Divine oracles [Col. 0671D] and by badly expounding what has been rightly said, and overthrow many under the pretext of knowledge.

In the same sense St. Zeno says (*Sermon* I, no. 4, book I):

> Therefore, since it does not lie within human possibility to see the secrets of faith, nowhere, brother, does your curiosity profit; nowhere does your contest profit. For the man whom you consider most faithful even in your own studies is unfaithful, and the man whom you suppose unfaithful is faithful. Perhaps someone thinks himself more faithful if he speaks cleverly, whereas he is more truly faithful who, in his preaching, has not extended the point of his mind beyond what is permitted. For matters have come to such a pass that our faith is sought by injury to God.... Since these things are so, why do you strain law by law? Why do you abandon faith under the image of faith? Why do you attempt to exhaust the very Fountain of Divinity by philosophical arguments? If you desire to display knowledge of the law, clear away the clouds of the readings. Teach that it is not contrary to itself; teach that everything which it sings must be believed. But if you approve one part of it and disapprove another, how do you seek faith through that by which you make faith itself guilty of unbelief?

You see here that St. Zeno censures those who deceive believers by craftiness: “The man whom you consider most faithful even in your own studies is unfaithful.” St. Irenaeus also censures them: “For some, rejecting the truth, introduce discourses and various genealogies, and by a specious plausibility craftily constructed seduce the minds of the inexperienced.” St. Zeno commends those who pursue simplicity in explaining the Scriptures, and censures those who contradict faith by corrupting the Scriptures:

> He is more truly faithful who, in sacred preaching, has not extended the point of his mind beyond what is permitted. For matters have come to such a pass that our faith is sought by injury to God.... Since these things are so, why do you strain law by law? Why do you abandon faith under the image of faith? ... If you desire to display knowledge of the law, clear away the clouds of the readings. Teach that it is not contrary to itself.... But if you approve one part of it and disapprove another, how do you seek faith through that by which you make faith itself guilty of unbelief? [Col. 0672B]

What is it to seek faith by injury to God; to strain law by law; to abandon faith under the image of faith; to approve one part of the law and disapprove another; to make faith guilty of unbelief—unless it is to oppose Catholic truth by corrupting and wrongly adducing texts of Scripture? St. Irenaeus rebukes this, not with equal elegance of expression but in plainer language: “Dragging them captive by corrupting the Divine oracles and by badly expounding what has been rightly said.” St. Zeno detests philosophical subtleties: “Why do you attempt to exhaust the very Fountain of Divinity by philosophical arguments?” St. Irenaeus detests them too: “They introduce discourses and various genealogies, which, as the Apostle says, furnish questions rather than...” St. Zeno complains of an affectation of knowledge: “If you desire to display knowledge of the law.” St. Irenaeus says the same: “They overthrow many under the pretext of knowledge.”

Of the statements of St. Zeno cited thus far, who would think that they bear the stamp of Arian times? Nor should it be said that those which we are about to cite, even though noted as especially definite, refer to Arian times [Col. 0672D]. For the sense of St. Zeno’s words does not permit his statement that “novel faiths,” or treatises, were offered for sale to be explained as referring to the gifts bestowed by Constantius on those who supported the Arians. His words are:

> Since truth can scarcely be found among them, I think they were put up for sale so that they might not suffer from a shortage of people.

The obvious sense is that, lest there should be a shortage of people for disputations or treatises concerning faith—which St. Zeno calls novel because they are contrary to the Catholic faith—they were displayed in the marketplace in order to be sold to curious purchasers.

Likewise, what ground is there for explaining these words of St. Zeno—

> O how undefended is that faith which, from moment to moment, seeks the patronage of kings, judges, rich men, and, sometimes, what is worse, of nations!

—as referring to the patronage sought for their own sect from the emperors Constantius and Valens by the Arians? For it is established that after the first century of the Church defenses of Christians were presented to emperors and to the Roman Senate: by St. Quadratus, bishop of Athens, and Aristides, the Christian philosopher, to Emperor Hadrian; by St. Justin Martyr, first to Antoninus Pius and then to Emperors Marcus Aurelius and Lucius Verus, as well as to the Roman Senate; by Melito, bishop of Sardis in Asia, to Marcus Aurelius; and by others, namely Apollinaris, bishop of Hierapolis, Miltiades the theologian, and others. To imagine that those called “kings” are Christians is an invented interpretation, unsupported by any, even slight, conjecture [Col. 0673B].

The proper sense of the cited words is that Treatises on Faith borrow their force and operation from kings, judges, and rich men, and, more urgently still, from Gentile philosophy itself and the fables of poets. That this was done in the listed Christian apologies is undisputed. For Justin Martyr himself, according to Eusebius (*Ecclesiastical History*, IV.18), confirmed his defense for Christians, where he treated the Christian faith, “not only from our writings, that is, the Divine writings, but also from those of the Gentiles.” This interpretation of St. Zeno’s words accords with their context, since in this same section he is treating doctrine, not violence inflicted on Catholics by emperors, prefects, or judges:

> Now I wish to know: does faith consist in teaching, or in belief, or in both? But if in both, the faith of the patriarchs is half faith; and consequently books must be assigned to them for determining our constitution, so that they may be perfect. O how miserable is the faith which words compose! O how weak, whose limbs are daily scattered by various arguments! O how undefended, which seeks the patronage of kings, etc. [Col. 0673C]

You see doctrine, books, words, and arguments mentioned here—not arms or soldiers—as one sees in the testimonies of the holy Fathers cited in the note: St. Ambrose:

> Set now before your eyes the Arians intent on worldly pursuits, who seek fellowship with royal power in order to attack the truth of the Church with military arms.

St. Hilary:

> Let them not thereafter presume and usurp, and imagine that they know the agreement of the clergy, and break and harass innocent people with various afflictions, threats, violence, and terrors.

But if we examine St. Zeno’s meaning closely, his words cannot, without manifest distortion, be understood of the protection granted by Arian emperors to Arius’s followers. For those emperors attacked the faith; and Ambrose and Hilary complain of this in the passages praised above. St. Zeno, however, speaks of patronage to be secured from emperors, as the words indicate: “they seek, from moment to moment, patronage.” This is what St. Quadratus, St. Justin, and the other writers of apologies sought from emperors and the Senate: that persecution should cease and that persecuting judges, governors, and officials should be commanded to leave Christians free.

The distinguished Ballerini brothers think that they can also infer the time when this Treatise of St. Zeno was written (note 38):

> If this seems probable to anyone, then this first Treatise would have been composed after the fourth day before the Kalends of April in the year 364, when Valens began to reign.

So they say. But since we have seen their interpretation to be foreign to the text, their chronological conjecture falls away.

If, however, conjecture may be indulged, it must with better right be said that this treatise was written before A.D. 254, in which year Origen is believed to have died, or after Origen’s death. Let us consider the grounds of this conjecture.

The first reason is that this Treatise seems rather to have been a letter than a sermon addressed to the people. The very learned Ballerini brothers themselves note this:

> One thing prevented us from numbering this among the first Zenonian Treatises: it appears to be rather a letter delivered to some person whom he calls “brother,” than a treatise addressed to the people. For he addresses him continually, and by many arguments endeavors to deter and remove him from writing such treatises, which were full of danger [Col. 0674B].

Moreover, Peter Calo of the Order of Preachers, who lived at the beginning of the fourteenth century, in manuscript collections held by Henschenius, vol.
