II for April, p. 76, while enumerating the works of St. Zeno which he says he saw “in a manuscript of the Monastery of St. Zeno at Verona,” affirms that he read there not only “eighty treatises” but also “letters.” Among the works of St. Zeno, no treatise is more fittingly called a letter than this one.

If, therefore, this Treatise should be called a letter—which is not remote from probability—I say that this letter was sent by St. Zeno to Origen after A.D. 232, when Origen, while living at Alexandria, was assailed by such great vexations because of the errors with which his writings abounded, especially that work entitled *Peri Archōn*, or *On First Principles*. In that book he borrowed much from pagan philosophers and, being filled with many errors, is censured by St. Jerome. But if anyone should think that the letter was written after Origen’s death, it must be said that it was sent to some follower of Origen. For everything which the holy Doctor heaps up against these treatises seems most aptly directed against the book *Peri Archōn*. This is confirmed by a second reason.

Namely, throughout this same treatise or letter St. Zeno nowhere mentions heretics by name, nor attacks them anywhere. Therefore, in the brother whom he addresses he seems rather to censure excessive curiosity and over-subtlety in matters of faith, and the following of philosophical reason in explaining them. This is clear from the passages of St. Zeno cited above, and is even more evident from the whole context of this Treatise [Col. 0674D]. For the holy Doctor’s whole purpose is to show that faith is not acquired like other disciplines. Thus, at the beginning, in these words, he calls it inward:

> The greatest happiness of Christian fidelity is to know the nature of faith, which is such and so great that it is not lent to any person by another, but is born from his will.

By the word “will” he does not exclude grace—as the celebrated Ballerini brothers aptly observe (note 3, Treatise 1). When St. Zeno said this, he had only one thing in mind: not to exclude grace, which was not then under discussion and which he sufficiently clearly establishes both shortly afterward and elsewhere, but to refute those who tried to set forth faith by arguments and treatises, as though faith were implanted in hearts by such industry. The gloss forced into St. Zeno’s text against the manuscript evidence, “It is born to a human being not from another, but from his will, through the prevenient inspiration and assistance of the Holy Spirit,” they rightly erased.

St. Zeno therefore affirms that faith is inward; it is not learned, but conceived through God’s illumination and revelation. Hence he continues:

> But if, as some think, it depends on the mouth of a teacher, it surely perishes when that teacher either ceases or teaches otherwise [Col. 0675B].

The principal aim of the holy Doctor, therefore, is to show that faith is not possessed by human art, or by the learning and expertise of educated people, since the human mind is liable to error and the teacher may teach otherwise. He does not, indeed, reject teaching:

> But I do not say this in order to render the benefit of teaching unwelcome, but so that everyone may know that faith is one thing and a treatise another.

For he openly teaches that faith is above nature:

> Therefore, since it does not lie within human possibility to see the secrets of faith.

Yet, always adhering to his argument, he excellently censures the fault of treatises or disputations concerning faith whenever one indulges too much in philosophical argumentation and human reasoning. He prescribes to the brother whom he addresses the proper manner of treating faith. See the same Treatise near the end, nos. 5 and 6. Since all this agrees with the treatises written by the authors mentioned above in the second and third centuries of the Church, there is no reason to assign this Sermon of St. Zeno to formularies of faith issued by the Arians. Rather, it seems preferable to acknowledge that it was written in Origen’s time, or transmitted to Origen himself, who, through excessive devotion to philosophy, sprinkled his works with so many errors. It could also have been written after Origen’s death to someone devoted to Origenian teaching, for that person’s instruction.

A third and final reason is added: no circumstance is found in this Treatise of St. Zeno—or in the others, as will become clear in those we shall produce—that must necessarily be fitted to Arian times.

The most diligent Veronese annotators, indeed, think that they find such circumstances, and incontrovertible ones at that (note 33, the same Treatise II, book I):

> In order that what is there stated concerning the vague and uncertain condition of Arian faith may be understood, and that it may at the same time be clearly confirmed that these statements of St. Zeno agree well with the history of this period, so that nothing similar can be adduced from earlier centuries, in which some suppose that he lived, to which they correspond equally, we think that several notable passages of the Fathers which wonderfully agree with the present matter should be cited.

They then cite two texts of St. Athanasius and one of St. Hilary. In the cited text of St. Athanasius, the decrees and assemblies of the Arians are mentioned:

> Yet they are not content with their own decrees.... They also assemble and pretend to determine concerning the faith.

The Council of Nicaea and an Arian pseudo-synod are mentioned in the second text of the same Athanasius:

> Disputing against the Nicene Synod, they too held many synods.

And in Hilary’s text the Nicene Synod is mentioned, together with anathemas issued in synods:

> For we are mutually conscious that, after the synod of the Nicene assembly, nothing else is done but faith being written.... We decree monstrous faiths concerning God; we repent of decrees; having repented, we defend them; having defended them, we anathematize them.

Certainly, no one will read matters of this kind in St. Zeno’s Treatise even in a dream. There is nothing about Arius, whom he nowhere names even implicitly in his Treatises; nothing about the Council of Nicaea; nothing about Arian synods; nothing about anathemas [Col. 0676B]. By what conjecture, then, can anyone show St. Zeno’s sermons to conform to Arian times? The difference in manner of writing between St. Zeno’s sermons and the cited texts of Athanasius and Hilary is quite evident—something anyone can see even with dimmed eyes.

The very perceptive Veronese annotators themselves acknowledge (note 36, on the same Treatise I, book I) that St. Zeno did not understand by the name “treatises” formularies or creeds of faith, but fuller expositions of faith in which each person attempts to establish his view of faith by arguments and reasons, as is clear from the context. These Treatises on Faith, or disputations, were in use from the age of the nascent Church. Why, then, should St. Zeno’s statements be restricted to Arian formularies alone, when no circumstances of Arian times can be found in them? I say that this cannot be done without open violence to the text.

For that circumstance concerning the multitude of formularies of faith and their mutual opposition reveals nothing whatever about Arius’s followers, since, in the opinion of the Ballerini brothers themselves, St. Zeno is not speaking of shorter formularies in the manner of a creed—such as Arian formularies were—but of fuller expositions of faith. Ecclesiastical history records that the multitude of such treatises concerning faith was indeed greater among Gnostics and Valentinians. We therefore judge that we have shown more than sufficiently that there is no necessity to relegate St. Zeno’s statements to Arian times. Rather, since they agree especially well with Origen’s time, sounder judgment would affirm that this first Treatise on Faith was directed to Origen [Col. 0676D]. Nothing in this Treatise conflicts with that conclusion; indeed, from what has been said, it is easy to suppose that all things agree with it remarkably.

There are indeed many other passages, both in this and in St. Zeno’s remaining Treatises, which the distinguished annotators draw toward the Arians; and they themselves fabricate for the second book of these Treatises the title *Against the Arians*. Yet in all this an attentive reader will discover quite exceptional learning, but in the interpretations concerning Arius’s errors and period, preference rather than St. Zeno’s genuine meaning.

## § XXII. St. Zeno’s teaching, charged by Petavius with seeming to smell of Arianism, is explained, defended, and demonstrated to be sound and Catholic.

The greatest weight accrues to what we have argued thus far from the fact that, so far is St. Zeno from having opposed the errors of Arius of which we have spoken, that Petavius charges him with those very errors. For Petavius, having mistranslated several ante-Nicene Fathers, when he comes to Zeno, bishop of Verona—whom he suggests flourished after the Nicene Synod, and whom he elsewhere cites as bearing witness against the Arians—does not hesitate, on account of several expressions of the same kind, to bring him, together with Marius Victorinus, a writer of the same century, under suspicion of the same error. Petavius accordingly ranks St. Zeno among those ante-Nicene Fathers who thought the Father superior to the Word in age, dignity, and power [Col. 0677B], on the basis of certain passages cited from that same holy Father. It will suffice to adduce one, from Book II, Tractate V:

> “The beginning, brethren, is unquestionably our Lord Christ, whom, before all ages, the Father—God, still embracing both within Himself in the undivided fullness of the Spirit of blessed eternity—held, veiled by some consciousness of His own, with a filial affection indeed, yet without distinction. But, in order to establish the ordering of the things He had devised, that ineffable Power and incomprehensible Wisdom brings forth the Word from the region of the heart; Omnipotence propagates itself; God is born from God, possessing all that belongs to the Father and detracting nothing from the Father,” etc.

Thus St. Zeno. Petavius then adds concerning this passage:

> “Here Zeno shows that the Word of God, from all eternity, remained and lay hidden in the bosom and essence of the Father, as though undistinguished and attached [Col. 0677C]; but afterwards, when He wished to fashion the universe which He had planned, he says that the Father propagated and begot that same Word from Himself. And this is the first of the two births which he expounds in the following discourses” (now Tractates VII and VIII).

Yet it is clear that the following statement of the same holy Doctor—which is praised as especially important in the said Dissertation II, chapter 1, §2—casts no light upon the passage cited:

> “Let us now see, most excellent Christian, how you thrust time in between the Father and the Son.”

For it must be recalled what we observed above, in the ninth paragraph, concerning Arius’s errors: namely, that Arius at first, together with Ebion, Artemas, and Paul of Samosata, maintained that Christ did not exist before Mary, and that there was a time when He was not. But afterwards, when St. Alexander, Patriarch of Alexandria, expelled him from the Church [Col. 0677D], he corrected this error, asserting that the Son existed before times and before ages as the complete God, the only-begotten, immutable; and that before He was begotten, created, or predetermined, He was not—for He was not unbegotten.

Therefore St. Zeno’s words, “Let us now see, most excellent Christian, how you thrust time in between the Father and the Son,” exclude only time between the Father and the Son. This was the first error, drawn by Arius from earlier heretics and spread abroad by him. They do not, however, exclude the error corrected by Arius; for by that correction Arius himself excluded time between Father and Son, affirming that the Son existed as complete God before times and before ages.

It is this Arian sense which Petavius detects in St. Zeno’s words cited above: namely, that “the Word of God, from all eternity, remained and lay hidden in the bosom and essence of the Father, as though undistinguished and attached . . . but afterwards, when He wished to fashion the universe which He had planned, He propagated and begot Him from Himself.” These words exclude time between Father and Son, I say, but not an earlier and a later. Since, in Arius’s view, the Father begot the Son before all created time, St. Zeno’s statement does not seem opposed to him: namely, that the Son, veiled and hidden in God the Father, then came forth from the Father’s heart when He wished to create all things. Petavius explains it thus, citing these words of St. Zeno:

> “From whose mouth, in order that the nature of things, which did not exist, might be fashioned, there came forth the noble inmate of His heart, thereafter made visible because He was to visit the human race.” [Col. 0678B]

For this reason, the same ambiguity remains in St. Zeno’s meaning, and the same conjecture of error.

Yet let suspicion of such an Arian plague be far—far indeed—from our St. Zeno. His teaching on the Most Holy Trinity, and especially on the divinity of the Son, is entirely sound. I do not see from what source his Catholic mind can be more clearly established than from his own words. Let, then, the statements of Zeno be produced in which he so plainly sets forth the truth of the Son’s coeternity, equality with the Father, identity of substance, and distinction in Person.

What could be clearer regarding coeternity?

> “This is our God, the coeternal Son of the eternal God” (St. Zeno, Book II, Tractate IX, §2).

If He is the coeternal Son, then the Father is not earlier and the Son later; rather, the Son exists wholly together with the Father in eternity, one with the Father in substance and distinct from Him in Person.

Concerning the coeternity not only of the Son but also of the Holy Spirit with the Father:

> “This is our God, who unfolded Himself into God. This is the Father who, while His own condition remained whole, returned all of Himself into the Son, lest He detract anything from Himself. Finally, one rejoices in the other, shining forth with the fullness of the Holy Spirit in one original coeternity.”

And, speaking of the Son and explaining why He is called firstborn before every other creature, he likewise confirms His coeternity with the Father:

> “He is therefore called the First-begotten because He alone is conscious of the Father’s antiquity.”

If conscious of it, then coeternal; for one who is conscious knows at the same time. By the very same knowledge as the Father, He knows His own antiquity—or rather, eternity.

[Col. 0678D] He also most expressly professes the coeternity of the Son together with unity of substance and equality with the Father:

> “With whom”—that is, with the Son and the Father—“there is one possession of an original and perpetual kingdom, one substance of coeternity and omnipotence, one equality, one power of august majesty.”

Nor can anything clearer be conceived concerning the distinction of the Person of the Son from the Person of the Father within unity of substance and coeternity than the statement which follows:

> “For if the Word is in God, and God is the Word, and that which is in Him is what He is who is in it: there are two Persons, two names; but there is one substance of original eternity and Deity. The Lord Himself says: ‘I and the Father are one’; which He plainly did not say in order to confuse two by reducing them to one [Col. 0679A], but in order to teach us that the two possess one omnipotence of Deity and Power.”  
> (St. Zeno, cited Book II, Tractate VII, no. 2.)

He acknowledges two Persons, Father and Son, in the one substance of original eternity and Deity. Thus St. Zeno professes original eternity both in the distinction of Persons and in unity of substance.

But what ought especially to be adduced for discerning St. Zeno’s sound doctrine concerning the Most Holy Trinity is what he sets forth in the first tractate of that same second book concerning the equality of Father, Son, and Holy Spirit. We transcribe it in full. Let the reader recognize that even in the earliest times of the Church a perfect knowledge of the mystery of the Most Holy Trinity flourished.

> “Men of carnal mind, most beloved brethren, take offense—not through zeal to know the truth, but to frustrate it—whenever God the Son of God, who is the Father’s greatest glory, is proclaimed by Catholics to be equal to the Father. Thus it is that, despising the foundations of the Law, by crafty disputation they pass over the God proceeding from God and hasten to the common human names of Father and Son, which can be reached by arguments. Nor do they understand that, at the beginning of the sacred song, God, described as God from God both by His Deity and by His name, excludes every conjecture of human understanding, when He says: ‘Let us make man in our image and likeness.’ He does not say, ‘Make [him] in your [image],’ but says, ‘Let us make [him] in our [image],’ lest the Son, who was to put on man, seem to suffer any indignity.
>
> “Do you see, most beloved brethren, that here no one expressly commands another in the work, and no one is idle? O holy equality, and indivisible Deity most worthy of itself alone! One man is fashioned in the image and likeness of two, yet it cannot be discovered in what respect he belongs to either one. If, therefore, sacred equality cannot be distinguished in an external work, how can God be inferior in another?
>
> “For whatever you take away from one of two who in all things resemble one another without distinction, you do not know from which you have taken it away. [Col. 0679C]
>
> “But, you say, the one who is commanded is inferior. What if he is thereby shown not to be inferior, because he is the executor of what proceeds from the Father’s heart? For it is no less to do great things than to speak them. Moreover, neither what is said by the Father can be said nor what is done by the Son can be done without the Father’s gracious will; for the Son is not without the Father, He Himself saying . . . ‘If I do not do the works of my Father, do not believe me; but if you are unwilling to believe me, believe the works, and know that the Father is in me and I in him’ . . . It is therefore evident that He is equal, since They mutually contain one another in the Holy Spirit.” [Col. 0679D]

By so great a weight of reasoning and authority of Scripture Zeno demonstrates equality in the Father and Son. From this demonstrated equality necessarily arise coeternity, unity of substance, and distinction of Persons. For no one is equal to himself, but to another.

Having thus explained St. Zeno’s mind concerning the mystery of the Most Holy Trinity and the Son’s divinity, we must now examine those texts from which this holy Doctor’s teaching is suspected of savoring of Arius. We cited one above; but for the sake of greater clarity it seems appropriate to set it forth here again:

> “The beginning, brethren, is unquestionably our Lord Christ, whom, before all ages, the Father—God, somehow still embracing within Himself, in the undivided fullness of the Spirit of blessed eternity, Him who was veiled by some consciousness of His own, with a filial affection indeed but without distinction—held. But, in order to establish the ordering of the things He had devised, that ineffable Power and incomprehensible substance brings forth the Word from the region of the heart. Omnipotence propagates itself. God is born from God, possessing all that belongs to the Father and detracting nothing from the Father,” etc.
>
> “But it is madness to speculate how He who proceeded was begotten. For the Son tempers Himself on account of the nature of things, lest the limited capacity of this world be unable to sustain the Lord of eternal Majesty. When the Father commands the world to be made, the work is completed by the Son together with the command.” [Col. 0680B]

The second text noted by Petavius is this:

> “The Father, before all ages, embraced Him”—the Son—“in the unfathomable mystery of His mind, in a consciousness unsuspected and known to Himself alone, with a filial affection indeed but without disclosure. Therefore ineffable and incomprehensible Wisdom propagates Wisdom; Omnipotence, Omnipotence. God is born from God; the Only-begotten from the Unbegotten; the only One from the only One; the whole from the whole; the true from the true; the perfect from the perfect. Possessing all that belongs to the Father and detracting nothing from the Father, He proceeds into birth—He who existed in the Father before He was born.”

To these words Petavius adds:

> “He therefore signifies that the Son existed in the Father before He was begotten by the Father; but generation and birth occurred when He wished to create all things, as he declares in the second discourse: [Col. 0680C] ‘From whose mouth, in order that the nature of things which did not exist might be fashioned, the Only-begotten Son came forth, the noble inmate of His heart, thereafter made visible because He was to visit the human race,’ etc.”

Petavius therefore admits that St. Zeno recognized two births in Christ the Lord. He thinks that the holy Doctor assigned the first not to eternity, but to the time when God wished to create all things; and thus that the Son, from all eternity, remained in the bosom and essence of the Father as though undistinguished and attached—that is, undistinguished from the Father’s Person and without a proper hypostasis before the creation of things.

But St. Zeno—as the distinguished Ballerini most aptly reply—asserts that the first birth of the Word is eternal, as is strikingly shown by his own statement. Behold the holy Doctor’s words:

> “Therefore the Christian people must necessarily know that there are two births of our Lord Jesus Christ, lest they suffer any error: one by which He was born, the other by which He was reborn. But as the first is spiritual and without a mother, so the second is carnal and without a father: this one is wonderful, that one inexpressible, as the Prophet says: ‘Who shall declare His generation?’ But let us learn why it is inexpressible, the Father speaking. The Lord Himself teaches us: ‘My heart has poured forth a good Word,’ etc.; and in Solomon He speaks thus far, saying: ‘I came forth from the mouth of the Most High before every creature.’”

St. Zeno continues in the same tractate, discussing this same first generation or birth:

> “Admirable grace, most dear brethren, of manifest truth: though it can be distinguished, it cannot be external to itself. For if the Word is in God and God is the Word, and that which is in Him is what He is who is in it: there are two Persons, two names, but one substance of original eternity and Deity, the Lord Himself saying, ‘I and the Father are one.’ He plainly did not say this so as to confuse two by reducing them to one, but to teach us that the two possess one omnipotence of Deity and Power.” [Col. 0681A]

The holy Doctor also treats these two births in Tractate VIII, no. 1:

> “Therefore, untrained or negligent Christian, learn that there are two births of the Lord Jesus Christ, lest you be deceived by any error: one which you are not permitted to investigate, and another concerning which, if you can, you are lawfully permitted to be instructed. The first birth of our Lord remains in the consciousness of the Father and Son alone, and has nothing interposed or cognizant between them; it proceeded from the affection of fatherhood by one consent. But we find that the second, the carnal birth made manifest, was thus fulfilled.” [Col. 0681B]

St. Zeno therefore professes two Persons in this first birth: “For if the Word is in God . . . there are two Persons, two names.” And he most plainly asserts that these two Persons are of one substance of original eternity: “But there is one substance of original eternity and Deity.” He declares outright that they are not confused, for he immediately continues: “The Lord Himself saying, ‘I and the Father are one’; which He plainly did not say so as to confuse two by reducing them to one, but to teach us that the two possess one omnipotence of Deity and Power.”

What could be said more clearly to express the eternal unity of the divine substance and the distinction of Persons? For coeternity is distinctly expressed when he says: “There is one substance of original eternity and Deity.” These statements of St. Zeno therefore utterly exclude Petavius’s interpretation, by which he maintains that the holy bishop of Verona asserted that “the Word of God, from all eternity, remained in the bosom and essence of the Father as though undistinguished”—in Person—“and attached; but afterwards, when He wished to fashion the universe which He had planned, He propagated and begot Him from Himself.”

For what the same holy Doctor manifestly teaches would not be absolutely true: “He plainly did not say this so as to confuse two by reducing them to one.” Indeed, if before the Father actually wished to fashion the universe He had planned, the Son—although from all eternity remaining in the bosom and essence of the Father as though undistinguished in Person and attached—were understood to have remained there, then the two would surely have been confused by being reduced to one, at least before the Father wished to fashion the universe He had planned. Nothing could be more discordant with Zeno’s teaching.

Nor does that other statement of St. Zeno concerning the same first birth of Christ the Lord permit Petavius’s interpretation:

> “The first birth of our Lord remains in the consciousness of the Father and Son alone, and has nothing interposed or cognizant between them; it proceeded from the affection of the Father’s mouth by one consent.”

If the first birth of our Lord has nothing interposed, then neither an earlier nor a later can intervene. It is therefore eternal. But why dwell upon St. Zeno’s so clear teaching concerning the eternal generation of the Son? For what he declared in the most explicit terms in Tractate IX, no. 2, needs no explanation:

> “O new mode! God, compelled by love for His image, cries as an infant. For this is the power of God: that, while preserving what He is, He can become what He is not. This is our God, the coeternal Son of the eternal God.” [Col. 0682A]

St. Zeno himself therefore explains what he meant in the texts objected by Petavius, when he says that the Father embraced the Son, “veiled by some consciousness of His own, in the undivided fullness of the Spirit, without distinction.” And in Book II, Tractate III:

> “Whom, before all ages, the Father embraced in the unfathomable mystery of His mind, in a consciousness unsuspected and known to Himself alone, with a filial affection indeed but without disclosure.”

Certainly he means nothing other than that the distinction between the eternal birth of the Word and the temporal incarnation of that same Son of God is this: he calls the latter wonderful and declares the former unfathomable by various circumlocutions. “There are,” he says, “two births of our Lord Jesus Christ . . . one which you are not permitted to investigate, and another concerning which, if you can, you are lawfully permitted to be instructed.”

He continues in almost the same words as in the objected texts: “The first birth of our Lord remains in the consciousness of the Father and Son alone”; hence he earlier called it unfathomable: “veiled by some consciousness of His own”—that is, the Father’s. “It remains in the consciousness of the Father and Son alone”: this amounts to the same thing, expressing the depth and incomprehensibility of the mystery. Yet he does not exclude the Son from knowledge of this generation, since both are conscious of it: the Father and the Son, as he himself says, in that it “remains in the consciousness of the Father and Son alone.” [Col. 0682C]

The phrase, “has nothing interposed,” signifies the same as the other words, “in the undivided fullness of the Spirit.” Since the Son is one substance with the Father, the words “fullness of the Spirit” express the divine essence or substance. In the same sense we must understand “veiled by some consciousness of His own”: namely, that the generation of the Word is imperceptible. What follows—“without distinction,” “has nothing interposed”—expresses unity of essence. These matters are especially directed against Valentinus’s Aeons, by which that impious heresiarch so perversely attempted to confuse the eternal generation of the Word.

In the same sense, in Book II, Tractate VII, treating of the two births of Christ, St. Zeno calls the eternal generation of the Word inexpressible and the temporal one wonderful:

> “This one is wonderful”—namely, the temporal—“that one inexpressible,” the Prophet saying: “Who shall declare His generation?”

He calls it inexpressible because the divine heart poured forth the good Word and the eternal Word came forth from the mouth of the Most High; that is, as he says elsewhere, because the generation of the Word remains in the consciousness of the Father and Son alone, “veiled by His own consciousness.” Therefore he more vehemently attacks those who investigate the Divine Majesty:

> “It is a kind of madness to wish to speculate about an invisible and incomprehensible secret, and to examine the inner things of Him whose outer things one cannot even conjecture.”

So in the same Tractate VII, where there is more on this same subject. Elsewhere:

> “It is not the part of one who worships, but of one who is mad, to wish by vain arguments to speculate on what the provident God has ordained concerning God.” [Col. 0683A]

These passages and others in Tractate VIII, no. 1, concern the same eternal generation of the Word. When, therefore, St. Zeno says that the Word is veiled in the bosom or consciousness of the Father, he expresses nothing other than the incomprehensible and hidden generation of the eternal Word. That the Word is distinct from the Father in Person is most manifest in the statements of St. Zeno cited above. To say that the Word, undistinguished and without distinction, lies hidden in the Father’s bosom is the same as professing one substance in Father and Son and the incomprehensible generation of that Word.

The remaining words, however, create a greater difficulty:

> “But, in order to establish the ordering of the things He had devised, that ineffable Power and incomprehensible Wisdom brings forth the Word from the region of the heart. Omnipotence propagates itself; God is born from God, possessing all that belongs to the Father and detracting nothing from the Father,” etc.
>
> “But it is madness to speculate how He who proceeded was begotten. For the Son tempers Himself on account of the nature of things, lest the limited capacity of this world be unable to sustain the Lord of eternal Majesty. When the Father commands the world to be made, the work is completed by the Son together with the command.” [Col. 0683B]

And in Book II, Tractate III:

> “Therefore ineffable and incomprehensible Wisdom propagates Wisdom; Omnipotence, Omnipotence. God is born from God; the Only-begotten from the Unbegotten; the only One from the only One; the whole from the whole; the true from the true; the perfect from the perfect; possessing all that belongs to the Father and detracting nothing from the Father, He proceeds into birth—He who existed before He was born.”

Finally, in Tractate IV of the same second book:

> “From whose mouth, in order that the nature of things which did not exist might be fashioned, there proceeds the Only-begotten, the Son, the noble inmate of His heart, thereafter made visible because He was to visit the human race.” [Col. 0683C]

These statements of St. Zeno, I say, signify nothing other than that the production of the eternal Word proceeds not only from knowledge of the divine essence and of the divine Persons, but also from knowledge of creatures, both as to essence and as to existence, and likewise from knowledge of possible things; and of all these there is one knowledge in the Father. God the Father would not have spoken Himself wholly and perfectly if there were anything less in the Word than in Himself, as St. Augustine teaches (St. Augustine, *On the Trinity*, Book XV, chapter 14).

The following words of St. Zeno express this most clearly (Zeno, Book II, Tractate V):

> “But, in order to establish the ordering of the things He had devised, that ineffable Power and incomprehensible Wisdom brings forth the Word from the region of the heart. Omnipotence propagates itself; God is born from God, possessing all that belongs to the Father and detracting nothing from the Father,” etc.
>
> “But it is madness to speculate how He who proceeded was begotten. For the Son tempers Himself on account of the nature of things, lest the limited capacity of this world be unable to sustain the Lord of eternal Majesty.”

He said, “the ordering of the things He had devised,” in order to signify the Father’s eternal knowledge; then he adds, “Omnipotence propagates itself,” in order to signify the future creation of things outside the divine essence. For divine Omnipotence works by creating outside itself the things of this world. He immediately says that the Word is produced by this knowledge of the things devised for the establishment of order: “That ineffable Power and incomprehensible Wisdom brings forth the Word from the region of the heart.” He adds, “possessing all that belongs to the Father and detracting nothing from the Father,” in order to signify that the generation of the divine Word proceeded from the Father’s complete and perfect knowledge alike of the divine substance and divine Persons and of all creatures, both in their nature and their existence.

In the same sense he says elsewhere (Book II, Tractate IV):

> “As sacred Scripture testifies, He existed before all things, remaining one and the same, another [note the eternal distinction of the Persons of Father and Son], God from Himself into Himself, alone conscious of His secret; from whose mouth, in order that the nature of things which did not exist might be fashioned, the Only-begotten Son, the noble inmate of His heart, came forth, thereafter necessarily made visible because He Himself was to make the world of earth and visit the human race—otherwise equal to the Father in all things.” [Col. 0684B]

The words “God from Himself into Himself” deserve notice; they signify the procession of the Word from knowledge of the divine essence. Then there are the others: “From whose mouth, in order that the nature of things which did not exist might be fashioned, the Only-begotten Son came forth,” etc. These likewise signify the procession of the same Word from divine knowledge of creatures, by one act of the divine mind—not when they were created, but from eternity. For he asserts that the nature of things did not yet exist and that creation was future: “in order that the nature of things which did not exist might be fashioned”; “He Himself was to make the world of earth.” All this is concluded by the words: “otherwise equal to the Father in all things.” If equal in all things, then equal also in eternity.

He calls this generation ineffable:

> “But it is madness to speculate how He who proceeded was begotten.”

And to establish the hidden mystery of this ineffable generation, he adds:

> “For the Son tempers Himself on account of the nature of things, lest the limited capacity of this world be unable to sustain the Lord of eternal Majesty.”

At the same time he forestalls the objection that one might ascend from these creatures to knowledge of God. For although the Word proceeds from the divine intellect’s knowledge of created things, nevertheless, since they are finite, the Word in creating them does not exert His full power—as we speak according to our capacity—but “the Son tempers Himself on account of the nature of things,” that is, their finite nature. Thus we cannot attain the eternal generation of the divine Word by knowledge of these things.

Therefore, when St. Zeno says elsewhere, “He proceeds into birth who existed before He was born” (Tractate III, Book II, Note 7 on these same words), this birth must be understood not of the eternal generation of the Son, as the Veronese annotators explain, but of the second birth, or incarnation. Otherwise we are compelled to admit a third birth of the divine Word contrary to the holy Doctor’s meaning, as was demonstrated above. I judge that that scholastic distinction must be rejected—namely, that St. Zeno understood the Son to have been begotten by the Father before He decreed to create this universe, not by priority of time but by priority of reason—as entirely unsuited to Zeno’s age. Although in that discourse the holy Doctor principally treats the eternal generation of the Word, nothing prevents him from incidentally inserting those few words concerning the Incarnation, by which he distinguishes eternal generation from temporal birth. By this genuine meaning of St. Zeno’s words, all ambiguity and the imagined suspicion of an Arian plague are utterly excluded. [Col. 0685A]

Nevertheless, Petavius must be granted that in the last-reported statements St. Zeno did not speak distinctly enough against Arius’s error: namely, that the Word alone was created by the Father before all ages, and that the Word Himself created all other things. The learned Ballerini themselves will admit this, though throughout almost the whole first chapter of their second dissertation they strive with such zeal, learning, and doctrine to vindicate St. Zeno from that error.

Yet Petavius should not be followed, since, without investigating the matter, he seems to agree with those who make St. Zeno later than the Nicene Council. For it is plainly evident from this that he wrote long before that Council: he did not argue so distinctly against Arius’s own error because it was unknown to him and had not yet been invented. Had he written his discourses after Arius, how clearly would he have overturned Arius’s impious errors—he who assailed and defeated with such force and eloquence other errors adopted by Arius and circulated before him.

This is indeed the proper argument for defending St. Zeno’s Catholic teaching. For what we have argued so far shows that no error peculiar to Arius was attacked by St. Zeno. Indeed, as happens with other ante-Nicene Fathers, certain things are found in his sermons which, on the surface of their wording, may seem to favor Arius; but when compared with his other statements, they are recognized to contain the Catholic teaching. This is likewise to show utterly overturned the opinion of those who, from errors of Arius mentioned and refuted by St. Zeno—as they falsely maintain—strive in a vain attempt to remove that holy Doctor from the third century and assign him to the fourth. [Col. 0685C]

# CHAPTER II. THE MOST LEARNED BALLERINI DRAW FURTHER ARGUMENTS FROM ST. ZENO’S SERMONS TO ESTABLISH HIS DATE IN THE FOURTH CENTURY. WE HAVE CONSIDERED THE MORE IMPORTANT ONES CONCERNING ARIAN ERRORS IN THE FIRST CHAPTER; OTHERS REMAIN, WHICH WE SHALL WEIGH IN THE BALANCE IN THE FOLLOWING PARAGRAPHS.

[Col. 0685D]

## § I. St. Zeno Does Not Treat of Other Heresies Which Arose in the Fourth Century.

The distinguished Ballerini assert (*Dissertation* I, chapter 2, §3) that St. Zeno wished by his sermons to uproot certain heresies which, during the course of the fourth century, were springing up like poisonous weeds in the field of the Church:

> “First, in Book I, Tractate 1, no. 5, besides those who spread errors concerning the Son of God, he also rebukes”—as they think—“those who sinned by subtler reasoning regarding the divinity of the Holy Spirit. ‘Inflamed,’ he says, ‘by the sound of the Law and by the love of worldly display, you presume that by arguments you can compel, examine, measure, and distinguish the immeasurable eternity of the divinity of God born from God and of the Holy Spirit, by that very right whereby He exists from Himself.’”
>
> “And against those who prejudiced the equality of the Holy Spirit, in Book II, Tractate 13, no. 1, he issued that celebrated profession: ‘The Holy Spirit . . . possessing one substance, power, deity, majesty, and will with the Father and Son.’ But among the earlier heretics, there is not one who diminished and disparaged the Holy Spirit together with the Son, as the author’s text has it. Only the later Arians—or rather Semi-Arians—introduced that error.”

They confirm this by the authority of Sozomen (*Ecclesiastical History*, Book VI, chapter 23):

> “Both”—that is, the Anomoeans, or strict Arians, and the Semi-Arians—“maintained that the Holy Spirit was a minister, third in rank and honor, and similar in substance.”

In the quoted words of St. Zeno, Book I, Tractate I, no. 5 [Col. 0686B], I read nothing concerning the Holy Spirit intended to assail the error of those who said that the Holy Spirit was a minister, third in rank and honor, and unlike the Father and Son in substance. The holy Doctor rebukes those who presume to investigate by philosophical arguments the divinity of the Son and Holy Spirit:

> “Inflamed by the love of worldly display, you presume that by arguments you can compel, examine, measure, and distinguish the immeasurable eternity of the divinity of God born from God and of the Holy Spirit, by that very right whereby He exists from Himself.”

The words, “by that very right whereby He exists from Himself,” do not admit the distinction of Persons; nor do the relations among the Persons express the divine nature, which exists of itself. The Person of the Son, however, proceeds from the Father, and the Person of the Holy Spirit from the Father and the Son. Therefore St. Zeno rebukes investigators into the divine essence and Majesty; he does not treat of the equality of Father, Son, and Holy Spirit which the Semi-Arians attacked.

This is the aim of St. Zeno’s tractate, and its whole purpose is to show that matters of faith are not to be investigated by human reasoning. This is plainly evident to anyone reading the tractate, especially in the following words in no. 5:

> “Why do you bind the Law with the Law? Why, under the appearance of faith, do you lay aside faith? Why do you try to drain the very fountain of Divinity by philosophical arguments?”

In the other words quoted above, from Book II, Tractate XIII, no. 1, St. Zeno does not profess a creed or argue against heresies; rather, he explains the mystery of Jacob’s dream. This is, indeed, the title of the discourse: “On Jacob’s Dream.” St. Zeno says of it:

> “Jacob bears the image of Christ, and so also does the stone which he is known to have placed at his head, because Christ, the head of man, is sometimes called a stone. The ladder signifies the two Testaments; by these, believing persons, following the precepts woven into the Gospel and doing God’s will, are accustomed to be raised to heaven as if by certain steps of observance.
>
> “In the Apocalypse John called this a two-edged sword with one hilt, which he described as proceeding from the Lord’s mouth. For the sword is the Holy Spirit, having one hilt—that is, one substance, power, deity, majesty, and will—with the Father and Son; bearing two edges—that is, the two Testaments—by whose royal commands the faithful and devout are preserved, while unbelievers and deserters are punished.” [Col. 0687A]

The words “one substance, power, deity, majesty, and will with the Father and Son” explain the likeness of the sword. Hence St. Zeno first said: “For the sword is the Holy Spirit, having one hilt, that is, one substance,” etc. On this occasion he also hands down sound and Catholic teaching concerning the Holy Spirit. For even before the Semi-Arians, the divinity of the Holy Spirit and His equality with the Father and Son were known.

It is therefore no wonder that St. Zeno, while explaining Jacob’s dream, wrote the foregoing concerning the divinity of the Holy Spirit. Although these matters oppose the Semi-Arians, they do not make St. Zeno either contemporary with or later than the Semi-Arians. Read the statements of the holy Fathers which Petavius collects against errors concerning the Holy Spirit advanced by later heretics, *Theological Dogmas*, Treatise II, Book VII, chapter 8.

Yet the Arians were not the only ones to spread errors against the Holy Spirit. Petavius shows that Origen was the first to speak against the equality of the Holy Spirit with the Father and the Son (On the Trinity, book I, ch. 14; *Theological Dogmatics*, Treatise II, no. 8). He also decisively refutes the evasion of certain defenders of Origen—that his writings had been corrupted by the Arians. We cited above Origen’s text in which he argues against the Holy Spirit (ch. 1, §18, Epistle 41, in Petavius, no. 13). St Basil observes that the writings of St Dionysius of Alexandria were likewise tainted by the stain of this same error concerning the person of the Holy Spirit. Therefore, even if St Zeno had expressly treated against those attacking the divinity of the Holy Spirit, that would provide no reason to conclude that he had the Semi-Arians in view, since both Origen and St Dionysius are found infected with this error already in the third century. [Col. 0687C]

We showed above (ch. 1, §25) that our holy Doctor does not rebuke the Photinians in the words of Treatise VII, book II: “One, finally, maintains that Jesus Christ took his beginning from the womb of the Virgin Mary, and that thereafter he became God on account of righteousness—not that he was born God.” There we also considered the third note, in which the same distinguished annotators cite a text of Origen proving that this error was current already in the third century (Ballerini, on Treatise VII, book II, note 3; Origen, book VIII): “By the merit of its virtues, Christ’s soul is made one with the Word of God.” Thus Origen, cited there.

Nor do those words in Treatise VI of the same eighth book—namely, “if he took his beginning from the womb of the Virgin merely as a man, as some suppose, what hope,” etc.—designate the Photinians. For that conjecture is drawn from the words “as some suppose,” as though they indicated this error to be present, just as the Arian error was; this is what the same annotators observed. “The Photinians, the latest of all, whom the Arians themselves condemned, seem to be indicated here by St Zeno”—especially on the basis of the formula, “as some suppose”—but this proves nothing. For in that same highly learned third note they themselves observe that the same error had been disseminated by several earlier heretics. Who would dare, among so many heretics, to distinguish the Photinians alone? Especially since St Zeno could also have said, in the literal mathematical sense of time, “as some suppose,” regarding the times of Origen, Sabellius, and Paul of Samosata, who wrote in the third century. See what we have said in ch. 1, §15. [Col. 0687D–0688A]

There is likewise no basis whatever for asserting that St Zeno refuted Audius, or Audaeus, from whom the heresy of the Anthropomorphites sprang. In the cited Treatise XIX and in Treatise XX of book II, he expounds the words of Genesis: “Let us make man in our image and likeness.” He maintains that this image does not consist in the body:

> Therefore we must not understand this fleshly dwelling to be the image of God, but rather the spiritual image of the heavenly man, which the Lord, renewing in himself those who believe by a heavenly birth, graciously bestows from the devout fountain of his fullness.

He identifies no defender of the opposite error and rebukes no one. If, however, we wish to suppose that the holy Doctor silently censured some error, he may have had in view the opinions of Tertullian, who located the image of God in the human body, believing man to have been created in the image of Christ: “That clay was already clothed with the image of Christ” (Tertullian, *On the Resurrection of the Flesh*, ch. 6). The same is noted in St Irenaeus, as though he had placed the image of God in the body. See Petavius, *Theological Dogmatics*, Treatise III, *On the Work of God*, book II, ch. 2, no. 3. [Col. 0688A–B]

The same must be said of the formulas which the most illustrious Ballerini brothers call categorical; namely, in Treatise V, book I, where St Zeno writes:

> But someone will say: “Mary too was a virgin, and yet she married and bore a child.” Let such a woman be produced, if there is one; but Mary was a virgin after marriage, a virgin after conception, a virgin after bearing a Son.

And in Treatise II, book II:

> Mary, an uncorrupted virgin, conceived; after conception she, a virgin, gave birth; after childbirth she remained a virgin.

In these formulas the same annotators read that Mary is called a virgin before childbirth, in childbirth, and after childbirth. In the first text, St Zeno refutes an objection not of heretics but of those who marry. In the second, as is his custom, he describes in sufficiently eloquent and rhetorical fashion the Virgin’s unique childbirth, and makes no mention of any error by which Mary’s virginity was called into question. Whether one can maintain that such formulas are nowhere found before the virginity of Blessed Mary was attacked in the fourth century—when we do not possess all the works of the holy Fathers published in the first, second, and third centuries—we leave others to decide.

But this must be held certain: Mary’s virginity was impugned already in the first century by Cerinthus and Carpocrates, and by other heretics who maintained that Christ the Lord had been born from both sexes. In the third century, moreover, Tertullian held an erroneous view concerning Mary’s virginity after childbirth:

> “The Virgin indeed bore Christ, being to marry once after childbirth, so that through a virgin mother and a mother of one husband both titles of holiness might be fulfilled in Christ’s register.”

Origen too testifies that in his time Mary’s virginity was attacked, and he rebukes the error:

> “For someone broke forth into such madness that he asserted Mary had been repudiated by the Savior because, after his birth, she had been joined to Joseph.”

Helvidius cited Tertullian’s testimony to attack Mary’s virginity; St Jerome replies to him:

> “He summons Tertullian as a witness and puts forward words of Victorinus, bishop of Poitiers. As for Tertullian, I say no more than that he was not a man of the Church. … But we waste our time on trifles, and, leaving the fountain of truth, pursue the rivulets of opinion. Can I not bring before you the whole succession of ancient writers—Ignatius, Polycarp, Irenaeus, Justin Martyr, and many other apostolic and eloquent men—who, holding these same views against Ebion and Theodotus of Byzantium, composed volumes full of wisdom?”

St Zeno, therefore, is not alone in defending Mary’s virginity, since Jerome adduces so many Fathers from the earliest centuries of the Church, before Zeno himself, as defenders of Mary’s virginity. Nor was Mary’s virginity exposed to the impious calumnies of heretics only in the fourth century. Hence the reason advanced proves nothing for supposing that St Zeno wished to refute Eunomius, who publicly asserted that Mary was known by Joseph after the birth of the divine Word. For on the same reasoning Zeno cannot be excluded from the third century, unless we choose to assign to the fourth century Ignatius the martyr, Polycarp, Irenaeus likewise a martyr, and the other apostolic and eloquent men who, holding these same views against Ebion, Theodotus of Byzantium, and Valentinus, composed many volumes full of wisdom. [Col. 0688B–0689B]

## § II. Treatise XIV of Book I, delivered on the occasion of the new church built at Verona by St Zeno, does not point to the fourth century.

During the first three centuries of the Church, Christians held their sacred assemblies in certain private places, which they called churches; yet they were not permitted to erect new public buildings for that purpose. Only through the emperor Constantine, who professed the name of Christ, was permission first granted in the fourth century to build public churches. Consequently, it would be erroneous to say that an author discussing so distinctly a new public church lived before that century. Thus the Ballerini brothers.

Yet ecclesiastical history plainly contradicts this categorical assertion: namely, that Christians possessed no public churches before Constantine.

For Eusebius testifies that in the third century Christians had erected public and more spacious churches (*Ecclesiastical History*, book VIII, ch. 1):

> Likewise, you might have seen the highest honor, reverence, and goodwill shown to the leaders of each church by everyone, both private persons and provincial governors. Who could number the innumerable multitude of people continually flocking to the Christian faith, or the number of churches in each city, as they built spacious churches from their very foundations? And these things, increasing in the course of time and advancing daily toward greater and better things, no envy could wear down, no malice of the devil could bewitch, nor could human snares ever prevent them, so long as the right hand of almighty God sheltered and guarded his people as worthy of such protection.

These are Eusebius’s words concerning the state of the Church before Diocletian’s persecution; and they are confirmed by Diocletian’s own edict, commanding the churches of Christians to be demolished. Therefore several public churches, indeed large ones, had been built by Christians before Constantine, who came after Diocletian. [Col. 0689C–0690A]

Tillemont places the construction of public churches among Christians at an earlier date, being led by the authority of Origen, who mentions churches burned down. Tillemont argues by various conjectures that this happened in the persecution of Maximinus (Tillemont, Treatise 3, *Ecclesiastical Monuments*, on the persecution of Maximinus, art. 6). He also proves that Christians were permitted to build churches in the time of the emperor Alexander. For Emperor Alexander planned to build a temple to Christ; and, according to Lampridius, he granted Christians a certain public site which tavern-keepers claimed should be adjudged to them, saying that it was better that God should be worshipped there in whatever manner than that it should be given to tavern-keepers. Cardinal Bona rightly judges that Christians built a church there.

It is also clear from St John Chrysostom that Christians had public churches in the age of the Apostles. He says that the church at Antioch was founded by the Apostles themselves and, for that reason, calls it the mother of all churches; though repeatedly destroyed, it was always rebuilt. St Augustine likewise testifies that the chapel of St Stephen, visible in his own day, had been built there from apostolic times. And the most eminent Bona proves from very ancient records that the Church of St Peter in Chains at Rome was consecrated by St Peter himself. Eusebius also reports, from a certain Gaius, that churches had been built at the places where the Apostles St Peter and St Paul suffered martyrdom. [Col. 0690A–B]

Before Decius’s persecution, according to St Gregory of Nyssa, Christians everywhere had raised temples and demolished and overthrown the shrines of idols (*Life of St Gregory Thaumaturgus*):

> When the preaching of the divine Word had already been spread into every region, and all alike—both those dwelling in the city and those living in the neighboring countryside—had been brought over to the pious faith of the doctrine, the altars and shrines containing images there having been overthrown … and when all everywhere were zealously building churches for prayer in the name of Christ, a certain rage and envy seized him who then held the Roman imperial power.

Tillemont gathers these things, but appears to advance not a few of them hesitantly. As to what he reports from Cardinal Bona, he says that he has no leisure to submit it to examination and determine what should be thought of it. Concerning the memorials which Eusebius, on Gaius’s authority, says were erected where Saints Peter and Paul suffered martyrdom, Tillemont considers it probable that Christians designated those places for holding assemblies. He accepts the authority of Gregory of Nyssa, who testifies that Christians everywhere erected churches in honor of Christ, subject to the restriction that it be understood literally. [Col. 0690C–D]

He dissents, however, from Baronius, who, on the authority of the so-called *Pontifical of Damasus*, maintains that Pope Callixtus built a church in Rome across the Tiber in honor of the most blessed Virgin Mary. Tillemont objects that so great a matter cannot be established on conjectures alone and on testimony of such slight weight as the *Pontifical of Damasus*, a book in which many false and uncertain statements are found. First, in the *Pontifical of Damasus* published by Bolland, where the lives of the popes are arranged down to Felix IV, these matters are nowhere found.

Leaving aside, therefore, Tillemont’s doubts—which he piles up against Cardinal Bona, Eusebius, and Gregory of Nyssa without adducing any ground for those doubts—let us consider more carefully the objections he raises against the church built by Callixtus across the Tiber at Rome.

Tillemont’s opinion concerning the purported *Pontifical of Damasus* and its authority varies. Honoratus of St Mary, a Discalced Carmelite who rendered distinguished service to critical scholarship, observes this. Whenever Tillemont needs the authority of the *Pontifical* to establish his own opinions, he commends it; whenever it conflicts with him, he dismisses it. Thus the author just cited writes:

> Tillemont, needing this Index in order to establish the date of the Apostles’ death, mentions it with praise. But when it differs from his opinion concerning the year of the Apostles’ departure—which Tillemont places in 66 and Bucherius in 65—then, he adds, it matters little what this Index reports; for it is wholly in error down to Atherus. … Baronius seeks to establish, on the authority of this Damasian *Pontifical*, that Pope Callixtus caused a church to be built across the Tiber for the Blessed Virgin. But Tillemont, fearing this might damage his opinion that the Virgin Mary rested at Ephesus—against which a church consecrated to the Mother of God, bearing her name alone at that early time, would be no slight monument—says that a matter so great should not be supported by the testimony of this calendar, an authority as slight as that of the *Pontifical of Damasus*.

The *Pontifical* book has not been so despised by great men renowned in the learned world—Blanchini and Schelstrate, to omit the ancients, and even not a few heterodox writers, among whom Blondel deservedly must be numbered. But with respect to the church of St Mary across the Tiber at Rome, built by Pope Callixtus in the reign of the emperor Alexander, every historical conjecture confirms this account of the *Pontifical*.

That emperor granted Christians complete freedom in the exercise of religion, as Tillemont himself admits. According to Lampridius, Emperor Alexander granted the Christians a site across the Tiber so that worship of God might be conducted there. Certainly this site could serve no purpose except the erection of a public church. If Christians had wished to worship God in private assemblies, then, as Baronius rightly observes, numerous private places could not have been lacking to them for this purpose. They therefore asked that a site be granted them to build a public church, and especially to raise there a church to the Virgin Mother of God, where a fountain of oil had miraculously flowed forth to signify her childbirth. They could not have made a cemetery on that site, since the prescription of the Twelve Tables forbade the burial of the dead within Rome. [Col. 0691A–D]

Thus it is established from what we have discussed so far that Christians had public and numerous churches from the apostolic age and the Church’s second century, but especially in the third, during the reigns of Alexander and the Philips. Therefore, the fact that St Zeno delivered a sermon upon the occasion of a newly built church does not in the least require us to place him in the fourth century, since ecclesiastical history records many church constructions in the age in which he governed the Church of Verona. [Col. 0692A]

The Ballerini brothers bring together much material, and with very great learning, against Baronius, Peretti, and Bagatta, to demonstrate that the church built at Verona in St Zeno’s time was public (*Dissertation* I, ch. 2, §§4–5). We have already demonstrated that churches throughout the Church were public and numerous. But this was not merely after Constantine gave Christians permission to build churches, as they maintain; it was especially so even in the third century. Hence the public church of which St Zeno speaks cannot establish that this sermon of the holy bishop was delivered in the fourth century. [Col. 0692A–B]

Arguing against Baronius, the same illustrious men chiefly press this argument: Baronius gathered from St Zeno’s words—“In the whole Church of God, there is either no member, or a very rare one, of a place of prayer that can in any degree be compared with the buildings of idolatry collapsing into themselves in whatever ruin”—that St Zeno, the author of this sermon, flourished before Constantine’s times, since through that emperor’s efforts especially magnificent basilicas were erected at Rome. This, they continue, would be very well argued if the author had asserted only that no place of prayer could be compared with the buildings of idols; yet he adds “or a very rare one.” Hence he sufficiently indicates that some church somewhere was not inferior to the most magnificent temples of idols.

But what must be especially noted here—and they themselves observe it—is that the words “the buildings of idolatry collapsing into themselves in whatever ruin” establish a comparison between Christian churches and temples of idols, not intact, but destroyed by ruins. Thus the churches were not comparable, not merely with standing temples of idols, but not even with ruined ones. In this sense, who would not say that we are seeking a knot in a reed if we reproach Baronius for rightly and deservedly considering these words applicable to the times before Constantine? For if Zeno had written after Constantine’s time, would he not on this occasion have celebrated Constantine’s piety, by which he adorned the fallen Christian religion with so many most spacious churches? And how could the holy bishop of Verona, without incurring the charge of envy, have maintained that after Constantine had enlarged the religion, Christian churches were not comparable even with ruined temples of idols? Nor should Peretti and Bagatta be called mistaken for having inferred from St Zeno’s statement that at that time no churches had yet been built for Christians—meaning, of course, conspicuous buildings—by the same reasoning by which St Zeno affirmed that in his age churches could not be compared even with ruined temples of idols. [Col. 0692B–0693A]

The Ballerini brothers further observe that St Zeno’s words, “the buildings of idolatry collapsing into themselves in whatever ruin,” are not to be understood of the destruction inflicted by imperial laws when they commanded the temples of idols to be destroyed (*note* 5). I willingly agree with that note. But I think it foreign to St Zeno’s meaning to understand them as referring to a destruction with which those buildings threatened themselves through any accident or the ravages of age. Rather, that destruction seems to be indicated in the time of the emperor Philip, when Christians were permitted with impunity to destroy temples of idols, as we stated above from St Gregory of Nyssa.

It is therefore not surprising that Christian women coming to church were rebuked by St Zeno because they walked resplendent with gold—“their whole body covered in gold”—or that pagans, if by *viri docti* [learned men] the pagans themselves are to be understood, as the Ballerini brothers explain, attended St Zeno’s sermons; nor that catechumens in great numbers, of every class, age, sex, condition, and even nation, were washed in holy baptism while the Church enjoyed profound peace. Such conjectures do not point to the fourth century. For even during the persecution of Valerian and Gallienus, the body of St Cyprian, bishop of Carthage, who suffered martyrdom, was committed to burial with great honor and in a solemn public procession (Spondanus, under the year 261, no. 11, §4). [Col. 0693A–B]

The most learned men draw another argument to prove that the fourth century is indicated in this same sermon from other words of St Zeno. It is worth reproducing it in their own words:

> After St Zeno had said that it was not especially praiseworthy to multiply praises over the construction of a new church, since this could be common to pagans or Jews, he gives the reason for this latter statement: “For they too, if permitted, or perhaps if they wished, might build more elegant synagogues or raise more elegant capitolia.”

They observe that *capitolia* is written for “temples,” and then continue:

> Now note the two alternatives placed disjunctively: “if permitted,” or “if they wished.” The first cannot apply to Jews, since the Jewish sect is reported not to have been forbidden by any law … until Theodosius, in the law concerning Jews of the year 393; and only in the year 421, law 22 of the same title, was provision made that thereafter they should build no new synagogues … as is also recorded to have been confirmed in the year 423, laws 25 and 27. Therefore the second alternative, “if they wished,” concerns the Jews; but the first, “if permitted,” plainly concerns the pagans, who were clearly not allowed in the author’s age to build temples. This can belong only to the fourth century, since, under Christian emperors, temples of idols were either closed before Julian or, after Julian, tolerated in such a way that new ones nevertheless were not permitted to be constructed.

This is indeed an acute and fitting argument if it were established that St Zeno wrote in the fourth century. But since what has been considered from the beginning until now establishes that St Zeno cannot be removed from the third century, we should rather say that the phrase “if permitted” refers to the Jews, and the other phrase, “if they wished,” to the pagans, who were free in the third century to build temples. Jews, however, were never permitted to build synagogues without imperial authorization, since they lived as aliens and foreigners upon another’s soil. Indeed, Josephus testifies (*Jewish Antiquities*, book XIV, ch. 17) that in Asia Jews were at times forbidden by provincial governors and magistrates even to practise their own rites; and that they were allowed to do so by decree of the emperors—namely, by Caesar after the victory recovered from Pompey, and by Mark Antony and P. Dolabella. The other matters advanced by the Ballerini brothers in those two paragraphs, namely the fourth and fifth, we shall treat in a more suitable place. [Col. 0693C–0694A]

My fellow-countryman, Don Cajetanus Cennius, beneficiary priest of the most holy Vatican basilica, agrees with the most learned Ballerini brothers. Yet, eagerly pressing forward his opinion with considerable confidence, he thinks those who affirm that public churches of Christians existed before Constantine were deceived by impostors and still inexperienced in ecclesiastical affairs. Let him consider whom he attacks: namely, the most eminent Baronius and Bona, and Tillemont, whom he values so highly. Above all, he attacks Bencini and Thomassinus in a thoroughly vain attempt.

Yet, fearing the arguments of the distinguished Bencini and the decisive texts of Eusebius which Bencini adduces, he admits that public churches were erected before Constantine in the East but denies it in the West. Let us examine his reasoning. First, the eminent Bencini cites Gallienus’s edict, addressed to Pope Dionysius and other bishops, ordering throughout the whole world that Christian religious places be restored. The assertion of the *Book of the Popes* in the Life of Dionysius is confirmed by this: “He, Dionysius, assigned churches, cemeteries, and parishes to the presbyters, and instituted dioceses.” Bencini therefore rightly concludes: “By Gallienus’s indulgence Dionysius rather restored, apportioned, and reformed to their former condition all the churches of Christians plundered in the Decian persecution.”

What does Cennius say to this? Will he restrict a permission granted “throughout the whole world” to the East alone? Bencini himself next adduces from Vopiscus Valerian’s address to the senate concerning the opening of the Sibylline books: “I marvel, Conscript Fathers, that you have so long hesitated about opening the Sibylline books, as though you were deliberating in a church of Christians, not in a temple of all the gods.” Bencini adds: “He opposes the church of Christians to the temple of the Gentiles, and thus [shows] that Christians possessed and regarded it as a religious place, so that every activity not sacred was prohibited there. Therefore Christians had churches, that is, sacred buildings for carrying out the mysteries of religion.”

Who, being prudent, would deny that Valerian’s words concerning a church of Christians are to be understood of the church at Rome? Therefore churches existed also in the West. Bencini adds the rescript of Emperor Alexander for the Christians against the tavern-keepers, of which we spoke above and which we proved can only be understood of a church to be built at Rome; and also the text of Eusebius cited above, which it is a distortion to understand as referring only to churches erected in the East.

Cennius thinks he easily disposes of these matters by saying: “They do nothing to advance my different view of Christian affairs before Constantine; for I regard the churches throughout the West as like the *tituli* of the city—that is, private houses of believers assigned to the church, hidden from pagans or idolaters, for holding synaxes and assemblies.” Let him add: in the time of persecutions. A ready argument indeed: let him consider it as he pleases. But what prudent person would allow himself to be deceived by an opinion contrary to all ancient monuments and devised at will? For he falsely asserts: “Certainly no witness is adduced for churches in the West.” Its falsity is evident from the evidence just supplied. And as for the claim that no church consecration is recorded as having been solemnly performed before Constantine—what follows from that? It is a wholly empty argument. Could public churches not have been built without solemn consecration? How many public churches even in these times have not been consecrated? [Col. 0694B–0695B]

## § III. What St Zeno states in Treatise X of Book I concerning the gifts of the Veronese, by which, he says, many were redeemed, does not point to persons captured by barbarians after the battle of Hadrianople.

The distinguished Ballerini brothers cite St Zeno’s text (*Dissertation* I, ch. 2, §7) and, comparing it with two texts of St Ambrose, judge from their supposed correspondence that St Zeno refers to the redemption of captives after the Roman disaster at Hadrianople. We must therefore first consider the correspondence of these texts and transcribe the texts themselves, so that their correspondence may be examined.

They report St Zeno’s text as follows:

> At the end of Treatise X, book I, the author, St Zeno, commending the generosity of his hearers, says: “But this does not apply to you, brethren, whose generosity is known in all provinces, whose pious seed is scattered, as it were, through the members of the whole world. Through you many have been redeemed; many have been freed from deadly edicts; many, stripped of harsh conditions, give thanks.”

They cite two texts of St Ambrose as follows:

> Here two testimonies of St Ambrose from book II of *On Duties* must be quoted, which certainly speak of this redemption; and from them it will appear how great the misery of the captives was, and how closely their author agrees with ours.

First, St Ambrose, ch. 15, no. 70:

> “It is also the height of generosity to ransom captives, to snatch people from the hands of enemies, to rescue them from death—and especially women from disgrace—to restore children to parents, parents to children, and citizens to their country. These things are all too well known from the devastation of Illyricum and Thrace. How many captives were everywhere for sale throughout the whole world! If you summoned them back, they could not fill the number of one province.”

For, he continues in no. 71:

> “The barbarians showed no humanity inclined to mercy, except what avarice had preserved for ransom.”

The other testimony, ch. 28, no. 136, of the same book II, is given in these words:

> “We have sometimes incurred reproach because we broke up the sacred vessels in order to ransom captives. … But who is so hard, cruel, and iron-hearted as to disapprove of a man’s being redeemed from death, or a woman from the defilements of barbarians, which are more grievous than death? Or of young girls, boys, or infants [being redeemed] from the contagion of idols, by which they were defiled through fear of death?”

“Have you noticed,” the Ballerini brothers continue, “the phrase, ‘captives throughout the whole world’ … whom the redeemer would rescue from death? What agrees more closely with our author’s words?” Therefore, to return at last to the main point of the argument: since our author, praising the extraordinary generosity of his hearers shown in ransoming captives, has in view the redemption of the same captives about whom Ambrose wrote—the only event through which it could become true that this kind of generosity “was known in all provinces” and that its “pious seed was scattered, as it were, through the members of the whole world,” as the same author declares—it is clearly established that Treatise X of book II was delivered after the year 378, when the barbarians carried off such a multitude of captives, partly from the Roman soldiers already defeated and partly from so many subdued Roman provinces. [Col. 0695B–0696B]

St Zeno says that many were redeemed: “many redeemed.” Yet he does not call them captives, as St Ambrose does: “to ransom captives, to snatch [them] from the hands of enemies; how many captives were everywhere for sale.” The word *redeemed* does not necessarily include the captivity of those redeemed. Christians who, by paying a price to the authorities, were freed from being compelled to renounce the faith and worship idols were also said to be redeemed; and this is St Zeno’s genuine meaning. For when he had said “many redeemed,” to make clear that he was speaking not of persons captured by enemies but of Christians forced into idolatry by imperial edicts, he immediately continues: “many freed from deadly edicts.” He does not say that they were freed from captivity, but from deadly edicts by which persecution was proclaimed against Christians, on the condition that, unless they renounced Christ, they would suffer confiscation of property, exile, tortures, and death. St Zeno calls harsh these conditions by which Christians were bound under the edicts, and those freed from them through the assistance of the Veronese professed themselves to have received the greatest benefit: “Many, stripped of harsh conditions, give thanks.” [Col. 0696B–C]

Lest, however, we seem to interpret St Zeno’s text arbitrarily, we should recall the twelfth canon of the first synod of St Peter, bishop of Alexandria. By it, unbelievers who bought themselves free from persecution with money are declared free of all guilt; and this is confirmed by the example of St Paul the Apostle, who, at Thessalonica, permitted his persecutions—as Christianus Lupus explains (Lupus, vol. I, preliminary dissertation after ch. 16)—to be redeemed by Jason and other citizens through money, and thus freed himself from the necessity either of apostatizing or dying.

Whoever wishes to know that this liberation was expressed by the term *redemption* should read Tertullian, who uses this same term again and again in his book *On Flight*. He who asks whether persecution should be fled must necessarily look ahead to the further question whether, if it is not to be fled, it ought at least to be redeemed. Thus Tertullian begins to treat the matter, condemning flight during persecution as contrary to the mind of the Gospel, and at the same time condemning redemption from persecution—the Tertullian who, after abandoning the Church, went over to Montanus. In that passage he repeatedly stresses the term *redemption*.

The diligent reader should consult Christianus Lupus and will find that this practice of redeeming oneself was very common before Tertullian:

> “I believe it was ancient,” Lupus argues forcefully against Baronius. “Certainly, if it had been new, Tertullian would have attacked it with his very familiar argument from novelty.”

Nor did only one or two people seek by this aid to remove themselves from the fury of persecution; Tertullian shows that whole churches endeavoured by this redemption to provide for their own immunity: “It is finally too little if one or another person is thus rescued: entire churches collectively imposed a tribute upon themselves” (*ibid.*, ch. 12). And this was done not only to escape torture and death, but also so that they might be permitted to perform divine worship. The cited interpreter of the canons infers this from Tertullian:

> “From these things we learn that there were two reasons for such redemptions: not only to avoid persecution, but also to obtain freedom for the synaxes [religious assemblies].”

It is therefore foreign to St Zeno’s meaning to interpret his statement that people were redeemed as meaning that he intended Christians captured by the Goths in the disaster at Hadrianople, rather than believers freed by the generosity of the Veronese from deadly edicts. [Col. 0696C–0697B]

Nor should St Zeno’s text be said to agree with the cited statements of Ambrose, since the words “freed from deadly edicts,” found in St Zeno’s sermon, do not denote persons captured by enemies, as Ambrose expresses it—“to snatch [them] from the hands of enemies”—but Christians delivered from persecution.

[Col. 0697C] This difference, however, especially deserves notice. For St. Ambrose, who wrote after the disaster at Hadrianople, expressly names it: “These things are only too well known from the devastation of Illyricum and Thrace.” But St. Zeno does not mention it even in a dream; rather, in the words “freed from deadly edicts,” a circumstance is expressed that cannot at all suit persons captured by the Goths. For they were oppressed by no edict, but, having been reduced to captivity by arms and force, were redeemed by agreement and money.
