Moreover, it is especially clear that St. Ambrose wrote at times different from St. Zeno’s, since in the second statement of St. Ambrose cited above these words are omitted after *redimeremus* (“we might ransom”), with punctuation placed there: “That which could displease the Arians—not so much that the deed itself might displease them, as that there might be something [Col. 0697D] in us for them to reproach.”

For who, even if endowed with the sharpest and most lynx-like sight, could perceive in the individual sermons of St. Zeno any mention of the Arians? It is truly remarkable that, in all the works of the Fathers written in the age of Arius and the Arians, many things are found expressly marking the Arian times, whereas in St. Zeno’s sermons not even the slightest trace of this matter can be seen. Is this not evident proof that he wrote long before Arius? There is therefore no agreement between the statements of St. Zeno and Ambrose which the most learned Ballerini so greatly magnify: “You have noticed . . . captives throughout the whole world . . . whom whoever should ransom . . . would withdraw from death . . .” For St. Zeno says that they were “freed from deadly edicts.”

[Col. 0698A] § IV. Baronius rightly infers from the tenth sermon of the first book, in the final Veronese edition, that St. Zeno flourished long before the age of Christian emperors, because there St. Zeno says that the emblem of idolatry, and the same idols worshipped in temples, were customarily struck on coins.

These are the holy Doctor’s words:

> “Christian, if the truth must be spoken, you abhor gold and silver in images only, not in your own inner chambers; for there also, in countless pieces of gold and silver, as though in little temples, struck in smooth coinage, you recognize that the faces and emblems of kings are likewise contained. And there is no difference except that in your house they are small, while in the temple they are larger. If you spend them, they are money; if you keep them, they are images.”  
> (Book I, Treatise 10, no. 3)

The most learned Ballerini criticize Baronius, [Col. 0698B] observing on the word *simulacra* (“images”):

> “The images were not actual idols sculpted on coins, as Cardinal Baronius wrongly understands this passage in his notes on the second edition of the Martyrology, under 12 April; rather, Zeno calls the coins themselves ‘images,’ since they displayed the faces of emperors and other marks customarily engraved upon coins.”

Who does not see that the holy Doctor speaks of the same engraved images that were worshipped in temples? “There is no difference except that in your house they are small, while in the temple they are larger.” For when he says, “And there also, in countless pieces of gold and silver, as though in little temples, struck in smooth coinage, you recognize that the faces and emblems of kings are likewise contained; and there is no difference except that in your house they are small, while in the temple they are larger,” he plainly signifies that the same [Col. 0698C] emblems and likenesses of kings that were larger in temples above the altars were engraved upon coins.

This statement of our holy bishop confirms the point: namely, that pagan emperors customarily represented their own faces on coins under the image of their gods—as in an ancient coin on which Serapis is seen portrayed in the likeness of Hadrian—and that this was a very ancient practice, as Spondanus attests from Baronius (*Spondanus, under the year 362, § 6*):

> “Indeed, the very images of the gentile emperors struck on coins were worshipped in temples, since, once enrolled among the gods, they were regarded by the pagans as gods, with altars, statues, and temples erected in their honor.”

There is therefore no reason to be angry with Baronius, who, grasping St. Zeno’s genuine meaning, rightly and deservedly infers from it that St. Zeno flourished long [Col. 0698D] before the age of Christian emperors. Other words of St. Zeno—“if you spend them, they are money; if you keep them, they are images”—indicate that Christians were permitted to use money struck with marks of idolatry for spending, that is, solely for the purpose of ordinary human commerce. But one who kept the money misused it and, looking not to its use but to the thing itself, seemed to pursue with a certain attachment and reverence the idols contained upon the coins.

§ V. St. Zeno, Treatise XLV of the second book, does not indicate the fourth century.

And these are St. Zeno’s words: “Autumn also is the place of martyrdom, in which not the vine, but the digger’s blood [Col. 0699A] is shed” (Note 8 on the same treatise). The Ballerini gentlemen wish this to imply the fourth century. Thus they write: “It pertains especially to the martyrs of the fourth century, since bishops and ecclesiastics were almost entirely the diggers and cultivators of the sacred vineyard, and we read that they were chiefly attacked in that century; this does not altogether fit the earlier centuries, when both clerics and lay Christians were everywhere slaughtered by the pagans.”

But Eusebius testifies that it does fit the earlier centuries (*History*, Book VI, ch. 21): namely, that the Emperor Maximinus, having stirred up persecution against Christians, ordered only the heads of the Churches to be put to death as authors of the Gospel teaching. Then the two supreme pontiffs Pontian and Anterus died as martyrs within less than two months. It is also clear from the letter of St. Cyprian and from St. [Col. 0699B] Zeno that, in the age of the Emperor Valerian, punishment was directed chiefly by edict against bishops, presbyters, and deacons. Thus Pope Sixtus, St. Lawrence the deacon, St. Cyprian himself, and other bishops are recorded to have been crowned with martyrdom in the same year.

Accordingly, one must say that St. Zeno designated these holy bishops by the name “digger”; nor, solely on the supposition that St. Zeno wrote in the fourth century, should one resort to bishops who suffered martyrdom in the Arian persecution of the fourth century. For nowhere in ecclesiastical history is it read that, in the fourth century, persecution raged chiefly against bishops by a promulgated edict. Nor does any testimony of the holy Fathers cited by the Ballerini gentlemen indicate this even slightly. If those testimonies are compared with the words of St. Zeno, anyone at first glance will see that a different century is indicated, because in those testimonies the Arians, the Council of Nicaea, and the Emperor Valens are mentioned by their proper names—something wholly foreign to Zeno, as has often been noted above.

§ VI. The number of four hundred years in the fifth treatise of the first book of St. Zeno, *On Continence*, is an anachronism introduced into the manuscript through the fault of copyists, and sufficiently carefully corrected by Baronius, Peretto, and Bagatta.

This indication of four hundred years, found in St. Zeno’s treatise *On Continence*, is perhaps the chief argument that those who deny that this same holy bishop flourished under Gallienus can use to remove [Col. 0699D] his date from the third century. The distinguished Ballerini, together with Tillemont, make much of the same point (*Dissertation I*, ch. 2, § 1). In order to proceed with complete clarity in examining it, we shall transcribe their words.

Thus, the indication of approximately four hundred years, reckoned from Paul’s Epistle delivered to the Corinthians down to the author’s age in Treatise V of Book I, is clear proof that he wrote in the fourth century. For this is what is found there:

> “But since this apostolic decree has been effective for almost four hundred years, or even more—when men were more vigorous and Christians very rare—why, therefore, now that almost the entire world itself is Christian, and human vigor, worn away as the world grows old, has become blunted, should I dull the edge of truth with flattering words?” [Col. 0700A]

This chronological indication is plainly and distinctly given both in all the manuscripts and in the first Venetian edition. Only in the later Veronese edition, from which the others derive, did the editors Peretto and Bagatta allege an error in the numerals and alter them on their own initiative, moved by the sole preconception that the author had lived in the third century.

They say:

> “To the objection that the sermon *On Continence* is not by St. Zeno the martyr because its author is there read to be four hundred years and more removed from the publication of St. Paul’s teaching . . . we reply that the text, as it is corrupt in many places—as often happens with numbers—is corrupted there as well.”

Considering this manner of correction, unsupported by any manuscript and indeed employed against the evidence of the manuscripts—which, moreover, express the number not by the numerical letters *CCCC* but by the word *quadringentas* (“four hundred”)—Tillemont says, in Note 6 on the persecution of Valerian, that it is sufficiently certain and safe for someone readily to withdraw and extricate himself from the gravest difficulties.

Therefore St. Zeno’s text must be judged uncorrupted in this place; and the indication of four hundred years will consequently compel us to admit that the same holy Doctor was writing in the fifth century. For since, according to Baronius’s chronology, the First Epistle to the Corinthians was written in A.D. 57, St. Zeno therefore delivered this sermon in the year 457. I should not at all believe that this would please the most learned Ballerini, who contend most fiercely for the fourth century; nor, as can readily be shown, do the other matters read in that treatise agree sufficiently with that period.

Since, therefore, the reading “four hundred years” contradicts the text of the sermon itself, as Baronius very well observed, an anachronism and an error concerning the number of years are plainly discerned to have entered St. Zeno’s text.

To support their position, the eminent Ballerini maintain that the text is uncorrupted and that the number of four hundred years was not corrupted. But they adopt the following method in order to bring St. Zeno back to the fourth century: they say that it was customary among writers before, contemporary with, and subsequent to Zeno not to take account of an excess of fifty years. To establish their assertion, they produce several examples, which we shall examine here.

[Col. 0700D] Arnobius, who flourished under Diocletian—that is, at the beginning of the fourth century, according to Jerome—does he not introduce the following pagan speaker in Book II, p. 44, addressing Christians: “Four hundred years ago, your religion did not exist . . .”? In the Formula of Faith which the pseudo-synod of Antioch wrote in 345 and which Athanasius recites in his book *On the Synods*, the following is said concerning the Paulianists:

> “Christ Himself, and the Son of God, became such from the time when He assumed our flesh from the Virgin—not four complete hundred years ago.”

Eusebius of Caesarea, a writer of the same century who died in 340, speaks thus in Book II *Against Marcellus of Ancyra*, ch. 1:

> “First, it is paradoxical that this Word should have begun from four hundred complete years ago . . .” [Col. 0701A]

The pseudo-synod of Sardica, in its decree in Hilary, fragment 3, no. 1, vol. II, p. 648 of the Veronese edition—vol. X, col. 659 in our edition—rebukes the same Marcellus of Ancyra, among other things, because:

> “he says . . . that the Lord received the beginning . . . of His reign four hundred years ago . . .”

This pseudo-synod was held in 347.

The testimony of Arnobius adduced by the Ballerini gentlemen contains an excess of about ninety years; that of the pseudo-synod of Antioch, unless the phrase “not complete” is taken to mean the last incomplete year, fifty-four years; that of Eusebius *Against Marcellus*, sixty and more; and that of the pseudo-synod of Sardica expresses an excess of fifty-three years. How, then, can a chronological rule be established from calculations of years so diverse, as the Ballerini wish—namely, that writers of the fourth century did not attend to an excess of fifty years? The very texts adduced wholly oppose this entirely new rule. The text of the pseudo-synod of Antioch opposes it, for the words “not complete” indicate that account is taken even of years counted above tens or hundreds. Eusebius’s text indicates the same by the words “four hundred complete.”

But that this was not customary among fourth-century writers is evident. For Arnobius, in Book I *Against the Nations*, when defining the beginning of the Christian religion, states plainly:

> “It is, indeed, about three hundred years, less or somewhat more, since we began to be Christians and to be reckoned in the world of lands.”

From this text Sevvechius, Note 106 on Arnobius’s second book, proves that there is an anachronism in the cited number of four hundred years. There is no need to say that the passage is corrupt because Arnobius wrote in Book I that it was three hundred years, more or less, since Christians had begun to exist and be reckoned in the world. It is easy to see that, in that objection of the pagan, when he says “four hundred,” there has been a serious error in the numerical notation.

As to the pseudo-synod of Antioch, I say that the error of Marcellus is indicated, for immediately after the reported words, “not complete four hundred years ago,” it adds:

> “For from that time they wish Christ to have obtained the beginning of His reign and to have the end of His reign after the consummation and judgment. Such are the disciples of Marcellus and Scotinus.”

Eusebius likewise attacks the error of Marcellus, and the pseudo-synod of [Col. 0701D] Sardica rebukes it. I certainly do not see why the error of one heretic and his followers can be alleged to prove an established practice among all fourth-century writers, who think against that very error. Since they reject the whole error, they must be judged also to reject its chronological date. Eusebius certainly must be said to have disapproved it if we review what he writes about Christ’s birth. See Spondanus, *Apparatus to Baronius’s Annals*, no. 31.

The Ballerini gentlemen heap up other testimonies of the Fathers: namely, St. Philastrius, bishop of Brescia, who was contemporary with St. Ambrose and wrote before 391. In all editions prior to the Hamburg edition prepared by Johann Fabricius, he gives the following in chapter 3:

> “And from the Lord until now, four hundred and ninety years, more.”

But Philastrius, Fabricius immediately adds in the note appended below, indicates in chapter 83 that he wrote before A.D. 391, and he attended the Council of Aquileia in 387. Latinus Latinius therefore judged that the number was plainly corrupt and ought to be restored thus, a judgment with which other learned men agree. Accordingly, in the text of the Hamburg edition he corrected it as follows:

> “And from the Lord until now, three hundred and eighty years, more . . .”

Nevertheless, these things depend upon the unobserved custom of that age in marking years. Indeed, Philastrius is read to have used the same notation not in this one chapter only, but also in chapter 106, p. 206, where it is written:

> “That which is found contrary, if any so think, we know that not more than four hundred years have now passed since the Lord came, and completed . . .” [Col. 0702B]

Here Fabricius thinks that *minus* (“less”) should be read: “we know that approximately four hundred years have now passed . . .,” since, if the holy bishop had wished to signify this, he would not have added, “and completed.”

Fabricius is wrongly accused of correcting St. Philastrius’s texts at his own discretion. For the alleged custom is asserted, not proved; and who would dare criticize him for correcting manifestly corrupt texts from one uncorrupted text, as Fabricius does? For if St. Philastrius himself testifies that he wrote before A.D. 391, who does not see that the number of four hundred years in the other texts is corrupt? The words of those same corrupt texts expose the fault. For the words “more or less” and “and completed” indicate, as we have already noted, that the years are not described in a careless fashion, but approximately. Yet who would take this “approximately” to mean an excess of ninety or even fifty years? For after he had first said “more or less,” he then corrects it by saying “and completed”—as if someone were to say, “four hundred years, more or less—indeed, completed.” Since St. Philastrius affirms that he wrote before A.D. 391, how could he afterward assert that four hundred years had been completed?

The text, therefore, is corrupt; or the holy writer himself erred in calculating years. Christian Lupus rebukes him as not especially exact in chronology, when treating the origin of the Meletian schism: “He mingles events, diverse times, truth with falsehood.” Thus the same Lupus speaks of St. Philastrius. Baronius, moreover, judges the manuscript corrupted with regard to the number of four hundred years.

They also cite in the same dissertation a text of Tertullian. [Col. 0702D] Tertullian, in *Against the Nations*, Book I, written at the beginning of the third century, claims approximately three hundred years—rather than two hundred—for the Christian religion, ch. 7:

> “Thus our age is not yet three hundred years . . .”

One should write “two hundred and fifty,” on the evidence of the following testimony, rather than what stands in the editions, “three hundred,” with *c* changed into *l*. And in chapter 9:

> “As we have said above, our age is not yet three hundred years . . .”

But why should the text of chapter 9, where “three hundred years” is read, not rather be corrected from chapter 7, where two hundred and fifty are counted, since the text of chapter 7 agrees better with the truth? Is an uncorrupted text to be corrected from a corrupt text? Or is error to be preferred to truth? For the phrase “as we have said above” adds nothing if two hundred and fifty years are to be read instead of three hundred [Col. 0703A] years. The exaggerated claim that ancient writers took no account of an interval of fifty years therefore has no standing.

That Tertullian, moreover, held the true epoch of Christian years is clear from the fact that, counting the years—as our St. Zeno did—he states one hundred and sixty years from the time when the first epistle of the blessed Paul was written. If fifty-seven years are added, when that epistle itself was sent, he indicates the year 217, in which Tertullian himself was writing.

In the remaining chronological indications that are cited, namely that of St. Peter Chrysologus, who flourished about the middle of the fifth century, in Sermon 145, *On the Birth of Christ*, at the end, he counts “about five hundred years” from Christ’s birth. The assertion of St. Hilary in Book I *To Constantius*, which the Ballerini gentlemen likewise cite, agrees with this statement of St. Peter Chrysologus. It must indeed be conceded that, when centuries are counted in round numbers, no attention is paid to an intermediate number of years; this is still done now when we speak of the sixth, tenth, or twelfth century. Thus we are said to live in the eighteenth century, although we have not yet reached the middle of that century.

But this designation of centuries does nothing for the purpose at hand, because St. Zeno in this sermon does not count centuries, but years from the writing of the first epistle of the blessed Paul to the Corinthians, as he himself indicates by the words “approximately, or even more,” which are not used when complete centuries are meant. Accordingly, he must not be explained by the same method as those who indicate centuries.

[Col. 0703C] It is certainly difficult to establish a firm epoch from a single anachronism—for such things are very frequently found in older books—an epoch whose support requires the invention of an entirely new conjecture, one that has occurred to no critic until now and cannot be proved by any reasoning: namely, that an excess of fifty years should be counted as nothing in the writings of the ancients. This is surely divination, if chronological difficulties are to be dissolved by such a rule.

Why, then, has there been such great controversy among learned men concerning St. Irenaeus’s opinion about the age of Jesus Christ? The question is parallel, for the epoch of the Christian religion begins from the years of Jesus Christ. He is attributed with having thought that Christ the Lord was not taken from this life until after His fiftieth year. Why, in his defense, bring forward the claim that his books were corrupt? Irenaeus would certainly have used less license if he had prolonged the life of Jesus Christ by merely twenty years than other ancient writers did, who, according to this new conjecture, set forth the Christian era in their calculations of years as exceeding it by fifty, ninety, and more years.

Nor would Petavius have called incurable the passage of St. Epiphanius in which he placed the martyrdom of St. Justin under Hadrian, although St. Justin died as a martyr about thirty years later under Antoninus. For this conjecture could have remedied it, by which not so much an excess as a deficiency of years can be supplied. Yet it is certain that Justin did not use it, since in his *First Apology*, without any excess or deficiency, [Col. 0704A] he gave the true year of the Christian era:

> “Lest anyone, unreasonably and for the overthrow of what we have taught, say that we assert that Christ was born under Cyrenius one hundred and fifty years ago, and taught what He taught later under Pontius Pilate,” etc.

And the anachronism is demonstrated from St. Epiphanius’s own words. Who, then, will deny that, by this sole rule of cutting away an excess of years in anachronisms, all chronology is utterly ruined, overturned, and thrown into confusion?

I admit that for many centuries of the Church years were recorded by the sequence of consuls. But this is the true method for counting the years of Christ, as Augustine teaches:

> “Through Olympiads and the names of consuls, many matters are often investigated by us; and ignorance of the consulship in which the Lord was born and in which He suffered compelled many to err.”

Having therefore obtained the true Christian epoch from those same consular registers, Augustine, in his letter to Hesychius, gave the true number of years from the birth of Christ the Lord down to his own time:

> “From the birth of the Lord about 420 years are counted today; but from His resurrection or ascension, 390 years.”

The holy Fathers were therefore not forced, when years were arranged by the succession of consuls, to use some round number containing an excess not of one, two, or ten, but of fifty or even ninety years. Indeed, according to Augustine, if an error was found in the number of years, it must be said to have arisen from ignorance of the consular records: “Ignorance of the consulship in which the Lord was born and in which He suffered compelled many to err.” This is especially to be noted: Augustine does not invoke this supposed custom to reconcile ancient anachronisms, but says that genuine errors “compelled [them] to err.” Who, moreover, ought better to have recognized this custom, if it then prevailed: Augustine, their near contemporary or contemporary, or more recent writers of our age, separated from them by so many centuries, who invent these things to defend their own chronologies?

[Col. 0704C] But lest we wander too far from our aim, we must return to the number of four hundred years which we read in the treatise of the holy Zeno *On Continence*. Although we held it certain, as the Ballerini gentlemen assert, that an excess of fifty years need not be counted in ancient writers, it is nevertheless so certain that this indication of four hundred years in the same treatise of the holy Zeno contains an anachronism that—even if we generously conceded that it cannot be inferred from this indication that the holy bishop flourished in the fifth century, namely in the year 457, which results from adding four hundred years, as stated in the cited sermon, to the year 57 of Christ, when the First Epistle to the Corinthians was written—yet the date of St. Zeno’s episcopate could in no way be fixed between the years 356 and 380, as those same distinguished men strive to establish.

This is proved by the inescapable argument that the text of the same sermon can be fitted not only to neither the ecclesiastical ordering of the fifth century, but not even to that of the fourth century—especially if we consider only the period from 356 to 380.

Seeking in the same treatise to dissuade a Christian woman from marriage [Col. 0705A] with a pagan man, the holy bishop sets before her in very clear terms the disadvantages that arise from such a marriage concerning the exercise of religion. Among other things he says:

> “What of this: his sacrifice is public, and yours secret? His may be handled freely by anyone; yours cannot even be seen without sacrilege by Christians themselves not consecrated.”

Thus in the final Veronese edition; but the Pistoian manuscript has *sacrificio* (“sacrifice”) in place of *sacrilegio* (“sacrilege”): “Yours cannot even be consecrated by Christians themselves without sacrifice.” In the *Library of the Fathers*: “Yours can even be seen without sacrilege by Christians themselves not consecrated.”

The words, “His sacrifice is public, and yours secret. His may be handled freely by anyone; yours cannot even be consecrated by Christians themselves without sacrilege”—for the reasons set forth below, this is the reading I prefer with [Col. 0705B] the editions—cannot possibly fit the stated period, namely from the year 356 to 380. For in 356, when Constantius, son of Constantine the Great, was emperor, temples of idols had been closed and sacrifices prohibited by a law enacted by Constantius himself. The temples were not reopened nor sacrifices to idols permitted until Julian the Apostate came to power after Constantius in 361.

Yet although Julian endeavored to restore worship to idols, during the very brief course of his reign—or tyranny—he never prohibited Christian sacrifices. Thereafter, under Jovian as emperor, and under Valens and Valentinian, then Gratian and Valentinian the Younger, and finally Theodosius until the year 390 and beyond, although pagan superstition was still permitted, it is beyond doubt from ecclesiastical history that Christian churches were frequented openly and publicly and that sacrifices were freely performed there in the Christian manner.

Throughout that whole time, therefore—from 356 to 380 and beyond—Christian sacrifices were public and could be freely performed, not secret. Thus St. Zeno was not writing in this period, for he says, on the contrary, that pagan sacrifices were public and could be freely handled by anyone, whereas Christian sacrifices were secret. St. Zeno’s date must therefore be placed in the third century, when pagan sacrifices were public and Christian ones secret, as Baronius, Peretto, and Bagatta place it. They correct that indication of four hundred years not arbitrarily, not on their own initiative, nor without support from any manuscript or against the evidence of manuscripts, but from the very context of this treatise—as the most careful Ballerini themselves correct other things in these same treatises of St. Zeno.

[Col. 0705D] This is also the chief reason why the reading found in the editions should be preferred to that which the same editors give in the final Veronese edition: the former, but not the latter, accords most fully with the sense demanded by St. Zeno’s treatise itself. For the holy Doctor, in order to deter a Christian woman from marriage with a pagan man, compares the worship of the Christian religion with that of idols:

> “His sacrifice is public, yours secret; his may be handled freely by anyone; yours cannot even be consecrated by Christians themselves without sacrilege.”

Here is an antithesis containing two mutually opposed parts of the sentence. The first: “His sacrifice is public, yours secret.” Here the solemn and widespread worship of idols is most plainly expressed. In contrast stand the words, “yours secret,” which plainly signify a Christian religion prohibited and liable to dangers and penalties imposed by tyrants. We have already seen that the sense of these words cannot be accommodated to either the fifth or the fourth century.

The second part of the sentence, or antithesis: “His may be handled freely by anyone.” Here freedom publicly to sacrifice to idols is plainly stated. “Yours cannot even be consecrated by Christians themselves without sacrilege”: by these words no one can rightly deny that freedom of religion was taken away from Christians; and thus the opposition demanded by the force and ornament of the sentence is entirely evident in this reading.

But in the manner in which the Ballerini gentlemen read and explain it, St. Zeno’s meaning does not stand and the force and ornament of the antithesis are removed. For they wish the words “yours secret” to signify the Church’s discipline of concealing the most holy Eucharist not only from pagans but also from catechumens. They call it secret because, under the discipline of the *arcane* (*disciplina arcani*), the sacrifice or mystery of the Eucharist had to be carefully concealed not merely from pagans but from catechumens themselves. And they correct the word *consecrari* (“to be consecrated”) as follows:

> “The editions read *consecrati*; we corrected it from the Pompian manuscript and two Zenonian manuscripts, namely *consecratis*. Those who had received baptism, moreover, were called *consecrati*.”

Thus those “not consecrated” are catechumens, who by another formula were called “not initiated.” Under the aforesaid discipline of the arcane, it was prescribed concerning them that they should not cast their eyes upon the Sacrament of the Eucharist.

[Col. 0706C] If catechumens were to be understood by “not consecrated,” St. Zeno’s words would contribute nothing to the intended argument, and there would be no antithesis in them. For even if catechumens were excluded from seeing the sacrifice, the sacrifice would nonetheless have been public and could have been freely performed by Christians. Therefore the holy Doctor would wrongly have said: “His sacrifice is public, yours secret; his may be handled freely by anyone; yours can even be seen without sacrilege by Christians themselves not consecrated.”

For the concealment of the most holy Eucharist from catechumens and their dismissal from the church at the time of sacrifice neither made Christian sacrifice secret nor deprived Christians of liberty to sacrifice. Therefore, for the meaning of the aforementioned words to stand, *consecrari* must be read in place of *consecratis*, and the words must be understood concerning the liberty, taken away from Christians by tyrants, of performing sacred ministries. This is required by the context of the sermon itself; it suits neither the circumstances of the fourth nor of the fifth century, but necessarily indicates the condition of the third century, when Christ’s faithful, as sacrilegious persons and contemners of the gods, were punished by imperial edicts if they performed sacred rites or attended them.

Nothing is more common in ancient manuscripts than, through the carelessness of copyists, for one letter to be written in place of another, so that for *consecrari* [Col. 0707A] they wrote *consecrati*. The Ballerini themselves adopted precisely such a correction of a single letter, despite the opposition of both printed editions and manuscripts, in publishing these sermons: thus, in note 24 on the second tractate of Book I: “*Urbem* for *Orbem* has been wrongly written in the manuscripts and editions through an easy alteration of one letter. The sense has persuaded us of the correction.” They likewise prefer the reading of the editions to that of the manuscripts in note 4 on Tractate XIII of Book II:

> The Venetian edition has *captulo*, the others *capulo*, whereas the manuscripts have *capitulo*; we should have retained the latter if it could have been shown by any example that it had been used in the same sense as *capulum*. But here *capulum*, that is, “the hilt of a sword,” is most plainly meant. Nowhere else do we find *capitulum* signifying the same thing. We therefore retained *capulo*, as we also retained *capulum* below, [Col. 0707B] with the editions, where the manuscripts have *capitulum*. And we believe this is to be attributed to an ancient copyist, from whom the others derived: thinking that the words *capulo* and *capulum* were written in abbreviation, he wrote them out as *capitulo* and *capitulum*.

Those most diligent annotators have even sometimes been compelled to add an entire word, as in Tractate III of Book I, note 13:

> In the editions: *clausis*. Moreover, in both manuscripts and editions this passage is presented as one continuous sentence, so that it cannot be understood at all; for it is written thus: “With eyes shut, avarice is rich a third time.” We corrected it as in the text, where the verb *dispergit* [“scatters”] plainly had to be supplied for the sense to stand; and a full stop had then to be inserted, after which the third part of the proposition advanced by Paul, concerning avarice, is expounded by Zeno in the words: “Avarice is rich a third time,” etc. Thus [Col. 0707C] it is conveniently understood as referring to eloquence and to the fortitude of those making use of avarice, of which he had hitherto been speaking.

Throughout the most learned notes on the Tractates of St Zeno composed by the Ballerini, one may see corrections of this kind, beyond the readings of both editions and manuscripts, supported by such reasons as: “that the sense may stand”; “lest the sense remain suspended”; “the context has persuaded us”; “the meaning has persuaded us”; “as the meaning requires”; “more fitting to the meaning.” Since, therefore, the reading of the editions in this passage also accords better with the context, it must be retained in preference to the other readings; and the text should be read:

> “His may be handled freely by anyone; yours, however, may not even be consecrated by Christians themselves without appearing sacrilegious.”

The meaning is that Christians attending sacred rites were punished as sacrilegious in contravention of the imperial edicts, as we have already [Col. 0707D] explained against Tillemont.

From this genuine restoration of the text an anachronism plainly emerges concerning the words preceding those quoted here: “But since this apostolic decree has been operative for almost four hundred years or more.” Since in the year of Christ 475 it could not be asserted either that from 360 to 380 Christian sacrifices had been secret and forbidden while those of idols were public and free, one must undoubtedly read *two hundred* instead of *four hundred*, as Baronius most aptly corrects this text. Nor does the fact that all manuscripts give *four hundred* obstruct this correction; for we believe this too must be attributed to the ancient copyist from whom the others derived. Hence the most wise warning of the distinguished Fr. Honoratus of St Mary:

> No greater deference is to be given to a large number of similar [Col. 0708A] manuscripts, since all may perhaps have descended from the same corrupt exemplar, from which they have also acquired the same blemishes.

Indeed, understanding and the argument of the discourse’s context may serve to distinguish the author’s words from those of the copyist. The most celebrated critics have followed this rule—namely Étienne Baluze, Nicolas Rigault, and others. Baluze, on the word *Absinthia* in his notes on Salvian, writes:

> We corrected this passage by our own authority, although both the editions and the manuscripts opposed us. For in both places the constant reading is: “What advantage does abstinence bring to the stomach if,” etc. But this error crept in through the fault of copyists. Salvian intended to contrast wormwood with sweet things, just as silence with clamor and an antidote with poison. Salvian himself confirms our conjecture.

From this one may meanwhile infer that Nicolas Rigault’s observation is entirely true; in his preface to Tertullian he noted that utterly false readings are maintained even on the authority of ancient books. “For,” he says, “there are books corrected in the most corrupt fashion, and there is no hope whatever of recovering the truth unless we find copies so ancient that they are older than all the antiquity of the correctors.” And elsewhere Baluze says:

> Thus we corrected by conjecture, where previously *injuriae* was read; for just as he contrasts the softness of pleasure with hardships, so he contrasts long delights with injuries. Otherwise the word *injuriae* makes no good sense here.

We have adduced these examples, which are decisive, since in St Zeno’s text the antithetical opposition can be found in no other sense than that in which we have explained his words; nor can any stronger reason be given for correcting the text in this way than the meaning supplied by the context itself. [Col. 0708C]

There remains to be considered, in this fifth tractate of Book I of St Zeno, the argument constructed from these words:

> “But since this apostolic decree has been operative for nearly four hundred years”—one must read *two hundred* by correction—“or more, when men too were more vigorous and Christians very few, why, now that the Christian world itself is almost wholly Christian, and the vigor of human beings has been worn away as the world grows old, should I blunt the edge of truth with flattering words?” etc.

They employ the words “now that the Christian world itself is almost wholly Christian” in order to contend that the fourth century is indicated; the Ballerini cite Marcellinus’s authority to confirm their view, stating in Book XXI, chapter 2, that even the soldiers of the Roman Empire were Christians. They add the text of Zonaras, supplying it with these words:

> Hence Julian, when acclaimed Augustus in Gaul, “in order to attract all men to his support without hindrance, pretended adherence to Christian worship; for he feared,” says Zonaras, Book XIII, no. 11, [Col. 0708D] “the soldiers, whom he knew to be almost universally Christians.”

They then attempt to explain Tertullian, whom they perceive to be against them: Tertullian testifies that in his own time all Roman cities were filled with Christians. They maintain that he speaks rhetorically. His words are these:

> “We are outsiders, and we have filled everything belonging to you: cities, islands, forts, towns, market-centres, the very camps, tribes, decuries, the palace, the senate, the forum. We have left you only your temples.” (*Apology*, ch. 37)

Let us grant that this was said rhetorically and with a certain exaggeration. Yet who [Col. 0709A] would suppose that Tertullian, in defending Christians before pagans, would have uttered such things if Christians themselves had been so very few in number? He would have made his *Apology* wholly ridiculous. Therefore, in Tertullian’s time, if Christians had not filled cities, islands, forts, towns, and so forth in such a manner that there was no room for pagans, they were nevertheless so numerous that they might in some sense seem to fill them. Accordingly, just as Tertullian’s expression cannot at all be assigned to the fourth century, neither should St Zeno’s text, in which we read that almost the entire world was already Christian, be drawn into the fourth century. The same must be said of the other statements of Eusebius adduced by the Ballerini.

But, indeed, in order that St Zeno’s meaning may stand more firmly, let us consider with particular care Gallienus’s edict. Eusebius reports it:

> “We order that the indulgence of our benefaction be extended throughout the whole world, so that all [pagans] may withdraw from religious places.”

The emperor orders that religious places be restored to Christians throughout the whole world. Christians, therefore, were spread throughout the whole world in the third century. Shall we say that Gallienus also spoke rhetorically in this edict? It is also clear that from Trajan’s time the faithful of Christ had grown to such a number that magistrates were unable to put them to death. The abundant fruit with which Christ’s faith spread in that same third century is also demonstrated by the fact that Gregory Thaumaturgus, dying in the Lord, could glory that he left only fifteen unbelievers—there had been just as many believers when he assumed the episcopal see of Neocaesarea. Gregory of Nyssa testifies to this:

> “The mystery of Christians increased, and through those who were always added to the word, the Church, rising to greatness, was propagated into a multitude everywhere throughout the earth.” (*Vol.* III, *Life of Gregory Thaumaturgus*)

Indeed, Cyprian himself, the most holy martyr, crowned with martyrdom under the emperor Gallienus, writes to Antonianus concerning the peace granted to the lapsed:

> “These letters were sent throughout the whole world and conveyed to the knowledge of all the Churches and all the brethren.”

It is therefore established from all that we have considered from the beginning until now that no argument can be deduced from St Zeno’s texts which would compel anyone to place his epoch in the fourth century. With God’s help, let us proceed shortly to other arguments drawn from external sources. [Col. 0709D]

## CHAPTER III

### § I. It cannot be proved from St Ambrose’s letter to Syagrius, bishop of Verona, that St Zeno lived in the fourth century.

The Ballerini assert that the context of Ambrose’s letter itself plainly proves that Syagrius, to whom Ambrose wrote on the occasion of the virgin Indicia, was then bishop of Verona; and that the entire letter shows Indicia the virgin, subjected by Syagrius to examination against the rule of law, to have been under Syagrius’s jurisdiction. Yet I have alleged several arguments in Book I, chapter 11, of my work on the sermons of St Zeno to demonstrate that Indicia was not Veronese. It is plainly apparent from the context of the letter itself that St Ambrose calls neither the man named Zeno nor anyone else “Veronese” or “bishop.” I demonstrated in the cited place, by the clearest inferences drawn from the text of that same letter, that Indicia was not subject to Syagrius except on account of the crime of which this virgin was accused, though falsely.

To make this still clearer, it should be observed that Ambrose’s reply to Syagrius concerns an unlawful trial instituted at Verona by Syagrius against Indicia:

> “But you, without the counsel of any brother, thought that this judgment ought to be judged by yourself alone; and yet before the trial you had already prejudged the case, since you judged that a maiden approved by the judgment of Zeno of holy memory and sanctified by his blessing [Col. 0710B] should, after so many years, be brought into danger of accusation without the originator of the charge, without an accuser, without a formal declaration of the denunciation.”

The accusation was a slanderous charge, wickedly fabricated by frivolous persons, heretics as they themselves would have it, and disreputable people.

Now the Church’s discipline of judicial proceedings, established also in Ambrose’s time by the fifth and sixteenth Nicene canons and confirmed by canons XIII and XIV of the Council of Sardica, was such that no bishop might judge, detain, excommunicate, or ordain a parishioner belonging to another diocese. For although, in times of persecution and under the compulsion of necessity, a bishop had been permitted to exercise jurisdiction in another diocese or over someone subject to another bishop, this custom was abolished by the Nicene canons mentioned; as Christianus Lupus rightly observes against Socrates:

> Secondly, it is false—thus Lupus, vol. I, in the scholium on canon 2 of the Council of Constantinople—that the migration of bishops to foreign Churches, or their intervention in foreign Churches with regard to trials, ordinations, or any administration whatsoever, was forbidden in order to exclude an ancient practice formerly tolerated because of pagan persecutions. Pagan persecutions had long since ceased; and the Nicene Synod had already abolished, by the fourth and sixth canons, the practice tolerated from necessity under those persecutions, which was confirmed and renewed by the third canon of Sardica.

By canon XIV of that council, only an appeal to the metropolitan is permitted to one who complains that he has been unjustly excommunicated by his ordinary bishop:

> He who is expelled shall have the power to take refuge with the bishop of the metropolis of the same province. Meanwhile, while the appeal is being heard, the ordinary’s sentence remains in force, until a judgment has lawfully been rendered at second instance. But before every matter has been carefully and faithfully examined, one who does not have communion ought not to claim communion for himself before the case has been heard.

Lupus notes that all this was renewed by the second canon of the Council of Constantinople held in the year of Christ 581. [Col. 0710D]

Since this discipline was in force in Ambrose’s age too, how could Ambrose have been angry with Syagrius—“But you, without the counsel of another brother, thought that this judgment ought to be judged by yourself alone”—if Indicia had been subject to Syagrius? Syagrius could indeed exercise judgment even upon one not subject to him because of the alleged crime committed at Verona. But Ambrose reproves him for conducting the trial without the counsel of another brother—modestly indicating himself. For, although on account of the alleged fornication Indicia fell under Syagrius’s jurisdiction, she was nevertheless a foreigner; hence, in order that he might know her life and character, Syagrius ought to have sought counsel, above all from Ambrose himself, to whom Indicia was known. No other explanation of this rebuke can be given. For if the virgin had been Veronese, falsely believed to have committed fornication, and known to Syagrius himself, why would information about her have had to be sought from others? That St Ambrose is speaking of this knowledge is evident from the words of the letter itself, since he provides Syagrius with such knowledge by alleging Zeno’s blessing and sanctification on Indicia’s behalf, and by proving her blameless conduct from texts—not from Veronese sources, but foreign ones, as I showed more fully in the same eleventh chapter. [Col. 0711B] Indicia, therefore, was not Veronese.

The eminent Ballerini themselves adduce Ambrose’s text, by which, they say, it is more evidently established that Indicia was Veronese. “What if,” they ask, “from the very things narrated in Ambrose’s letter we should more brilliantly confirm that the virgin Indicia was Veronese? For Maximus, the husband of her sister, after beginning litigation against Indicia concerning certain property . . . and when he was greatly distressed . . . because the virgin had withdrawn from the society of his kindred upon the estate, he ordered—by inserting a wall, in the same house of course—that the dwelling-places of his wife and of the virgin should be separated, and that the fellowship of sisterhood between the sisters should be divided. . . . This is an evident argument that half of the house belonged to Indicia; for if she had come to Verona from another city, Maximus, because of his hostile and adverse feeling toward her, could have expelled her from the house and city and sent her back to her native country.” Thus those distinguished men argue from St Ambrose’s own text.

But if we submit the same text to examination, we shall readily discover that Maximus did not litigate with Indicia concerning certain property, and that the house was not one and the same house divided by Indicia’s relative Maximus with a wall inserted. Let us produce Ambrose’s complete text:

> “I am surprised, brother,” Ambrose says to Syagrius, “that you so earnestly defend Maximus as not having been an accuser, but as having grieved with a parent’s sorrow over the resentment caused by a rumor that had spread; when he could not deny, as one who had already set a quarrel in motion, that he was an enemy and adversary litigant against the sacred virgin, that he had initiated proceedings, and that, by inserting a wall, he had separated the dwelling-places of his wife and the virgin, divided the fellowship of sisterhood between the sisters, and other things besides—alas!—and that the virgin had withdrawn from the society of his kindred upon the estate.”

Ambrose proves Maximus’s hostility from the quarrel already begun, and from the fellowship between the sisters having been divided by a wall inserted, and their dwellings separated. If a civil suit concerning property had been in question, Ambrose could not have proved hostility from litigation having been begun. For to pursue one’s legal right by a civil action does not at all indicate an inimical disposition or hatred. But Ambrose demonstrates Maximus to be an enemy because the virgin Indicia, steadfast in her purpose, shunned secular gatherings, conversations, and amusements; and because, so that she might devote herself to God, she had even withdrawn from association with her kindred on the estate, and perhaps, as Ambrose seems to suggest in adding “and other things besides—alas!,” from Maximus’s license. Therefore Maximus, burning with hatred against Indicia, fabricated a calumny; and its supporters were those offended by the continence of the virgin Indicia and her avoidance of secular society. For Ambrose says:

> “For we have long seen here, and have learned that there too are those who complain of this fabricated calumny, and who, they say, being offended, supported Maximus because that virgin does not go about houses, nor greet and court their matrons.”

There is here no mention of family property. Therefore, if we examine Ambrose’s words in their proper sense, the truth of the occurrence emerges most plainly from the words themselves. [Col. 0712B] Indicia, who had been at Rome and elsewhere for a long time, as is evident from the text of this letter and from what we have considered elsewhere, came to Verona in order to live with her sister. With Maximus’s consent, she rented a house adjoining Maximus’s house, with an opening made in the wall, so that, having access to her sister, she might live freely with her; she did not wish to be distracted by the company of others in the house of her relative, and for this reason she did not wish to be in the country with Maximus either.

Offended by the virgin Indicia’s continence, Maximus first quarrelled, apparently over Indicia’s free access from her own house to his wife’s house; then, after initiating a legal action—an occasion for which may have been afforded by Maximus’s consent to the opening of the wall—he blocked the entrance with a wall, and forbade his wife to go to her sister Indicia, perhaps with his own wife herself bearing this grievously. Finally, he fabricated against Indicia the slanderous charge of fornication. These things arise in their obvious sense from what is read in Ambrose.

Moreover, to say that there was a dispute concerning certain property and that one house was divided by Maximus is mere divination. For if it is objected that there would have been no need of litigation to block the entrance with a wall if there had been two houses, since Maximus could have done this by his own decision: what if he perhaps attempted it, and, owing to resistance from his own people and from Indicia’s household—which seems to have given rise to the quarrel mentioned by Ambrose—he found it necessary to resort to legal proceedings? But if these things are not accepted, it must be said that they are less to be accepted than those proposals which are put forward without any supporting testimony from the text. To speak of a suit arising from a quarrel already begun, and of Indicia’s access to the wife alone being forbidden by a wall inserted, when no mention of family property has been made, indicates not a civil trial but one concerning a crime. For Maximus, who charged Indicia with the crime of fornication, could also have suggested to the judge a fear of theft in order that permission might be granted to block the entrance after consent had already been given. [Col. 0712D]

But why seek a knot in a rush? Let Indicia have been Veronese. What follows from that? Does it follow that Zeno, who blessed and sanctified her, was a bishop? Nothing could be further from the truth. The blessing and sanctification bestowed upon Indicia by Zeno was not her solemn consecration as a virgin. To make this evident, Ambrose’s words must be observed:

> “A maiden approved by the judgment of Zeno of holy memory, and sanctified by his blessing, after so many years . . . you judged should be brought into danger of accusation.”

Notice the word “maiden” (*puellam*). Maidens were not consecrated, but women of mature and more advanced age, after virginity had been proved for forty years, according to the constitution of St Leo the Great. See Christianus Lupus, on Tertullian’s *On Prescription*, scholium on chapter 3, under the word “if a virgin,” question 6. In question 2 also, from Letter 2 of Innocent I to St Victricius, archbishop of Rouen, chapters 12 and 13, he distinguishes virgins: some who deserved to be veiled, and others who, though not yet covered by the sacred veil, nevertheless promised always to remain in the virginal purpose. These were maidens who had not attained more advanced age, as in the same letter, chapters 1 and 2: “A maiden who has not yet been veiled but has resolved to remain thus.” Since, therefore, Indicia was a maiden when she was blessed by Zeno, no conclusion can be drawn from this blessing—distinguished from the solemn consecration which a bishop must perform—that the Zeno named by Ambrose was a bishop.

Indeed, even if this blessing by Zeno were understood as a solemn consecration, it could not be inferred from this that Zeno was a bishop. For although in the Latin Church only a bishop could ordinarily consecrate sacred virgins by his ordinary authority, a presbyter could also consecrate them by delegation from the bishop. This is clear from the Third Council of Carthage, chapter 36, held about the year of Christ 398—that is, shortly after the Ballerini wish St Zeno to have died:

> “A presbyter shall not consecrate virgins without consulting the bishop; but he shall never make chrism.”

See Lupus again, question 5. The conjecture concerning the episcopate of the Zeno who blessed Indicia therefore disappears, since Ambrose calls him neither bishop, nor can his episcopate be inferred from his blessing of Indicia. Hence every suspicion is removed that this Zeno was the same person as the holy bishop of Verona, as Dupin and Tillemont asserted without any reason, daring, in sheer conjecture, to affirm that a Zeno, bishop of Verona, did not exist in the time of Gallienus. [Col. 0713C]

### § II. The ancient order of the bishops of Verona does not prove that St Zeno lived in the fourth century; rather, it confirms that he lived in the third century.

The Ballerini, most expert in ancient matters, cite a sufficiently ancient Rhythm by which they think the age of St Zeno is fixed in the fourth century (*Dissertation* I, ch. 3, § 3). Receive the Rhythm, attentive reader:

> First Euprepius preached at Verona, bishop;  
> Second, Dimidrianus; third, Simplicius;  
> Fourth, Proclus the confessor, an outstanding shepherd;  
> Fifth was Saturninus, and sixth Lucilius;  
> Seventh was Gricinus, teacher and bishop;  
> Eighth, shepherd and confessor, Zeno the illustrious martyr.

Thus far the Ballerini; but the following lines, which immediately follow, must also be added:

> Who by preaching brought Verona back to baptism.  
> He healed the daughter of Gallienus from an evil spirit;  
> He brought back from the sea the oxen, together with . . . turning [away].

The Ballerini note that in this penultimate verse *Gallieni* is to be read from the Lobbes manuscript written in the hand of Ratherius himself, bishop of Verona. In it one reads plainly “the daughter of Gallienus,” not “of Gallus,” as Mabillon had printed, nor “of Caesar Gallienus,” as we wrote from two later manuscripts—namely the Zenonian and the Pompian manuscript—in the passage cited (*Dissertation* III, ch. 1, § 54). They believe that this Rhythm was drawn from the diptychs of the Church of Verona and judge it to be of the highest value. They further warn:

> Nor should it be objected that certain falsehoods have crept into later catalogues, so as to diminish on that account even the order of the bishops. For the names of the bishops alone, arranged in order, could have been taken from the diptychs, in which nothing besides their names was read. Accordingly, this series is to be considered sufficiently secure and true. But as regards historical deeds or chronological notices, since these had to be taken from elsewhere, they could, according to the nature of the monuments from which they were derived, be either true or fabulous when inserted among the order of bishops; and often certain things have been introduced from the opinion of the common people, too readily assenting to fables, which scholars have demonstrated to be utterly false.

They wish this warning especially to prevent anyone from thinking that faith must be given to all the statements of the Pippinian Anonymous apart from the order of bishops, since what he inserted concerning the daughter of the emperor Gallienus is false, as we shall show in the following paragraph. [Col. 0714C] Thus they wish attention to be paid in the cited Rhythm only to the order and succession of the bishops of Verona, maintaining that the statements concerning Gallienus’s daughter are false.

I too once judged the antiquity of this Rhythm most worthy of respect when treating of a single Zeno, bishop of Verona, and on the authority of the Rhythm asserted against Papebroch the certain succession of the first eight bishops of Verona. Yet truth requires me candidly to confess that this distinguished man reproved me for error in this matter not without cause. This will become evident from what I now undertake to discuss.

The most learned Ballerini make three assertions concerning this Rhythm. First, they say that it was compiled from the diptychs of the Church of Verona. Secondly, that it contains the genuine succession and order of the first eight bishops. [Col. 0714D] Thirdly, that what is said in it concerning the daughter of the emperor Gallienus is false. Let us weigh each point.

That this Rhythm was drawn from the diptychs of the Church of Verona is proved by no monument, ancient or modern; for no diptychs of the Church of Verona survive. The only conjecture offered is that, according to ancient discipline, it was customary in both East and West to write the bishops of each city in order in diptychs and to recite all the saints during the solemnities of Mass after the second *Memento*. There is no need to call into question whether this was so; it suffices merely to indicate how slight is the basis on which it is asserted that this Rhythm derives from the diptychs of the Church of Verona. If these diptychs survived, it could then be discovered by comparing them with the Rhythm whether the latter had been derived from them. But since they do not survive, anyone may invent at will the source from which this Rhythm was obtained.

A not insignificant argument that it was not derived from them is the discrepancy between the ancient monuments of the Church of Verona and this Rhythm. For in this Rhythm Dimidrianus is called the second bishop of Verona, Simplicius the third, and Gricinus the seventh. But on the stone tablet visible near the door of the Church of St Proculus, this succession of the first bishops is read:

> “In this most ancient church, the shrine of many holy men: Euprepius, disciple of Peter the Apostle, first bishop of this city; Gricinus, second; Agapius, third; Proculus, fourth; and the martyrs Cosmas and Damian,” etc.

This stone was indeed placed in that church in 1502, but all older monuments agree with it. An ancient parchment agrees (*Ancient Monuments of the Holy Bishops of Verona*, collected by Bagatta and Peretti, Venice, 1576):

> “These are the bodies of the saints buried in the Church of St Proculus. First, in the lower altar of the same church lies the body of St Proculus, bishop of Verona, and he was the fourth bishop. . . . In another altar at the right side of the aforesaid altar lies the body of St Agabius, bishop, and he was the third bishop of Verona. In another altar on the left side of the aforesaid altar lie the bodies of Saints Euprepius and Gricinus. Euprepius indeed was the first bishop of Verona, sent and consecrated by the blessed Peter the Apostle, and likewise Gricinus was the second bishop of Verona.”

The inscription on the altar erected to St Agabius agrees: “To Agabius, who succeeded third in the episcopate.” The inscription on the altar of Saints Euprepius and Gricinus in the Church of St Proculus agrees: “To Euprepius, first bishop of Verona from the year of Christ 72, and to Gricinus, companion and associate in his labors, this place restored.” Thus two different orders of the bishops of Verona are found. Which, then, is to be said to derive from the diptychs: the one read in the Rhythm, or the one in the ancient monuments? Or should the Pippinian Anonymous, as the Ballerini call the author of the Rhythm, be thought to have drawn it from diptychs which he perhaps never saw? Or rather the Church, where the same monuments are publicly displayed, in which, so long as the custom of reading the names inscribed in the diptychs continued, they were read daily? Does the Rhythm surpass the other monuments in antiquity and therefore also in truth because it is older? What if a manifest error is found in it, even one shared by the other monuments? The Ballerini themselves think that the Rhythm contains errors:

> “Lest anyone should think that faith must be given to all the statements of the Pippinian Anonymous apart from the order of the bishops, since what he inserted concerning the daughter of Caesar Gallienus is false.”

Who would believe that the later monuments were invented only when they were inscribed on stones and parchments? Must we not, by every right, judge that they were derived from other, more ancient sources? He would surely be the laughingstock of all who, without any support from antiquity, presented as ancient things which he himself invented by his own resources. [Col. 0716A]

But I shall state openly what I think. I do not believe that either the succession of the bishops of Verona which is read in the Rhythm, or that which is read in the ancient monuments, was drawn from the diptychs of the Church of Verona. I am led to this belief because in both the Rhythm and the Veronese monuments a manifest error is found concerning the dates of the bishops. In both, St Proculus is called the fourth bishop of Verona, and in both he is said to have lived before the emperor Gallienus: in both places he is called the fourth bishop, and St Zeno the eighth, whom they most plainly affirm to have held the episcopate of Verona in Gallienus’s time:

> “He healed the daughter of Gallienus from an evil spirit.”

So says the Rhythm. In an ancient Psalter of the Church of the Holy Apostles, it is noted that St Proculus lived in the year 236:

> “In the year of the Lord 236 lived St Proculus, fourth bishop of Verona, brother of St Tusca the virgin, teacher of St Teuteria the virgin.”

And in the martyrology of the Cathedral Church of Verona, on 23 March, one reads:

> “On the same day, St Proculus, bishop of Verona, who in the time of Maximinus followed the most blessed martyrs Firmus and Rusticus, wishing to be crowned with martyrdom together with them; but he was driven out by the guards and rested in peace.”

The same appears in other manuscripts. But the time when St Proculus presided over the Church of Verona is established from certain monuments, as the distinguished Ballerini demonstrate in the aforementioned *Dissertation* I, ch. 3, § 3:

> “St Proculus,” say the same authors, “was alive at the beginning of the fourth century, when Saints Firmus and Rusticus were led to Verona under the emperor Maximian and soon afterwards crowned with martyrdom, as is plainly evident from their ancient acts, published by Marquis Maffei at the end of his diplomatic history, p. 303. In certain manuscript copies of the acts, Maximinus is indeed read in place of Maximian; therefore some have thought that Proculus’s lifetime should be assigned to Maximinus’s reign. But since it is evident from the acts that the emperor was then at Milan, whereas Maximinus was never in that city—for scarcely having entered Italy, he met his death during the siege of Aquileia, as our Fr Peter of Padua of the Order of Friars Minor Conventual rightly proved in Ughelli, vol. V of *Italia Sacra*, p. 685—and since it is clear from many examples that the two names Maximian and Maximinus are written indiscriminately in codices and easily confused, the reading *Maximian* in the other manuscripts appears preferable, indeed genuine. This reading was found in the ancient manuscripts seen and cited by the Bollandist associates under 24 March in the case of St Proculus. Therefore St Proculus and Saints Firmus and Rusticus are rightly assigned in all ancient martyrologies, including the Roman, to the persecution of Diocletian and Maximian, which began to rage in the year 303.”

Therefore, they conclude, the fourth bishop of Verona flourished at the beginning of the fourth century. [Col. 0716D]

Their treatment of St Proculus’s date is indeed excellent; but the conclusion cannot be drawn: “Therefore the fourth bishop of Verona flourished at the beginning of the fourth century.” For the reason why St Proculus was placed fourth in the succession of the bishops of Verona is that all the monuments of the Church of Verona and the Rhythm itself report that he flourished in the time of Maximinus and before the time of Gallienus; hence they state both the year and the emperor: “St Proculus lived in the year of the Lord 236,” thus in the ancient Psalter cited above; and in the martyrology of the Cathedral Church: “On the same day, St Proculus, bishop of Verona, who in the time of Maximinus followed the most blessed martyrs,” etc. Accordingly, this error caused those who undertook to compile the succession of the first bishops of Verona to place St Proculus fourth bishop, so that he might accord with the time of Maximinus. Thus it is plainly discerned that the succession itself was compiled not from ancient diptychs but from various monuments.

The Ballerini gentlemen do indeed attempt to remove this error from the same Rhythm by restoring the genuine reading from the Lobbes manuscript: “He healed Gallienus’ daughter from an evil spirit” [Col. 0717B]. In this verse Mabillon had read *Galli* instead of *Gallieni*. Their reasoning is that the poem does not read “of Gallienus Caesar,” as in other manuscripts, but merely “of Gallienus”; from this observation they suppose that the name Gallienus denotes not the emperor, but another Gallienus living in the fourth century, whose daughter Saint Zeno freed from demonic possession. This restored reading also removes the sole difficulty which we thought present in the Pipinian Anonymous, namely the appearance that it had absorbed the story concerning the emperor Gallienus. It may therefore seem to confirm what we conjectured in Dissertation I, chapter 3, §4: that the man whose daughter Saint Zeno healed of a demon was indeed some Gallienus, who was transformed by some writers into the emperor.

I too regard the reading of the older Lobbes manuscript as genuine and preferable to the others [Col. 0717C], chiefly because the verse “He healed Gallienus’ daughter from an evil spirit” has the same metrical count as the other verses, as is evident on inspection. But if either *Galli* or “Gallienus Caesar’s” is read, it does not have the same count. Yet I by no means agree that, merely because *Gallieni* is read without the addition *Caesaris*, another Gallienus, distinct from the emperor, must be imagined. Gallienus is frequently named without the appended title Caesar or emperor, and no person other than the emperor Gallienus can be understood.

We have a ready example in the cited text of the martyrology of the Church of Verona: “On the same day, Saint Proculus, Bishop of Verona, who in the time of Maximinus followed the most blessed martyrs,” etc.; and the name Maximinus is not supplemented by *Caesaris*. Must another Maximinus therefore be sought [Col. 0717D]? The same is found in the Martyrology of the Order of Preachers: “On the day before the Ides of April: On the same day, Saint Zeno the Bishop, who amid the storms of persecutions wonderfully governed the city of Verona, and in the time of Gallienus was crowned with martyrdom.” *GALLIENI* is written without *CAESARIS*. Indeed Usuard, in his Martyrology for the day before the Ides of April, has: “On the same day, Saint Zeno the Bishop … and in the time of Gallienus was crowned with martyrdom.” And in the Roman Martyrology published in 1584 by command of Gregory XIII, under 12 April: “At Verona, the passion of Saint Zeno, Bishop, who amid the storms of persecution governed that Church with remarkable constancy and in the time of Gallienus was crowned with martyrdom.” There the name *GALLIENI* appears without his being called either Caesar or emperor [Col. 0718A], as anyone may observe frequently in other manuscripts and editions.

Therefore no argument follows from the fact that in this Rhythm the name Gallienus appears without the added word *Caesar*; nor can anyone deny that this Gallienus is Caesar. It is consequently superfluous to invent another Gallienus in the fourth century, since it is clear that in this Rhythm a title of dignity was not added to Gallienus’ name, so that the verse would retain the same metrical count as the others. For the other manuscripts, in which the name Caesar has been added, have destroyed the Rhythm’s metre:

> “He healed Gallienus’ daughter from an evil spirit.”

Thus the Lobbes manuscript, and rightly so.

> “He healed the daughter of Gallienus Caesar from an evil spirit.”

Thus the Rimini manuscript, in which the same metrical count is not retained.

That the author of the Rhythm kept the number of syllables before his eyes is clear from the preceding verse [Col. 0718B]:

> “Who by preaching brought Verona back to baptism,  
> He healed Gallienus’ daughter from an evil spirit.”

For in the first verse he wrote not *baptismum* but *baptismium*, and for no other reason than that the verses might have the same count. Thus in this Rhythm too the name Gallienus must be understood as Gallienus Caesar. It follows that this Rhythm shares the error found in other ancient manuscripts, namely that Saint Proculus was Bishop of Verona under the emperor Maximinus, whereas he in fact flourished under Maximian. Led by this error, the authors of the ancient monuments listed Saint Proculus fourth among the bishops of Verona. Yet that he was later than Saint Zeno is shown by the Rhythm itself and by the other monuments, because both the Rhythm and the manuscripts place Saint Zeno [Col. 0718C] in the time of Gallienus. Ughelli therefore rightly and deservedly, on the authority of Peter of Padua—whom the Ballerini gentlemen themselves commend—makes Saint Proculus later than Zeno.

But even if it were established that the succession of the bishops of Verona had been taken from the most ancient diptychs of that Church itself, no one could thereby assert that those same diptychs preserve an unaltered order of bishops. This is proved by the very examples adduced by the Ballerini gentlemen: namely, the Mozarabic Missal. To make this truth evident, we transcribe here its text from the title called “Of All Who Make the Offering,” where it reads:

> “Making commemoration of the most blessed Apostles and Martyrs: the glorious Holy Virgin Mary; Zachariah; John; the Infants; Peter; Paul; John; James; Andrew; Philip; Thomas; Bartholomew; Matthew; James; Simon and Jude; Matthias; Mark and Luke.”

Observe the words “John, the Infants.” If the time of their death is considered, John the Baptist was killed long before the Innocents were slain. If the time of birth is meant, it is uncertain. Observe also that, as to the order of the Apostles, Paul, the last of the Apostles, is named in second place after Peter—not for chronological or hierarchical reasons, but because it has always been the custom of the Roman Church, as Le Brun observes, never to separate the Apostles Peter and Paul. Nor is the order of the remainder that set out in Luke’s Gospel preserved; it is also read differently in Matthew 10:1 and Mark 3:16 [Col. 0719A].

After the names of the Apostles, the Mozarabic text continues:

> “Likewise, for the spirits of those at rest: Hilary, Athanasius, Martin, Ambrose, Augustine, Fulgentius, Leander, Isidore, David, Julian, likewise Julian.”

Here Hilary, Athanasius, Martin, Ambrose, and Augustine are listed. They occupied episcopal sees in different churches, both in East and West, and none was bishop of a Spanish church. Hence it seems that no order was observed here; rather, these holy bishops must be said to have been entered in the diptychs solely out of devotion.

There then follow, in the same Mozarabic text, Leander and Isidore, bishops of Seville. Isidore succeeded Leander; but Leander assumed the episcopate in the year 584, according to the chronology of our *Cenni*. Was he himself the first Bishop of Seville? Not one of his predecessors is named. Sabinus certainly, who signed the Council of Elvira at the beginning of the fourth century, was Bishop of Seville, yet is not listed in these diptychs; nor is any other bishop who held the Church of Seville after Sabinus and before Leander. Before Leander, Sallustius occupied the see of Seville; around the year 519, with John of Elche, he was appointed Apostolic Vicar by Pope Hormisdas [Col. 0719B]. Thus no order of bishops is considered here.

After Isidore, David is placed. He signed the Fourth Council of Toledo through his vicar, the priest Marcus; Saint Isidore presided over that council, and David was Bishop of Auria. Thus the succession of the Bishops of Seville is not respected here either [Col. 0719C]; indeed, it is interrupted. For after David, Bishop of Auria, Julian of Seville is named; he governed the Church of Seville about the year 681, while others who governed it between Isidore and Julian are omitted. Another Julian, of Toledo, follows Julian of Seville. These observations on the Mozarabic Missal may suffice: from them it plainly appears that no order was preserved in listing the bishops’ names.

As to the Roman Order, which the very celebrated Francesco Bianchini published from a manuscript of the Chapter of Verona in the Prolegomena to Anastasius, Treatise 3, p. 51, it reads as follows:

> “Hear us, O Christ … life to our bishop N., chosen by God, threefold. Saint Firmus.”  
> Response: “Assist him.”  
> “Saint Proculus.”  
> Response: “Assist him.”  
> “Saint Zeno.”  
> “Assist him.”  
> “Hear us, O Christ, for our lord N., our most serene Augustus and emperor, crowned by God; great and peace-giving: life and victory, threefold. Saint Paul.”  
> Response: “Assist him.”  
> “Hear us, O Christ: health and life to our Lady the Empress. Holy Mary.”  
> Response: “Assist her.”

And Saint Proculus is certainly invoked before Saint Zeno; but this is for the reason given above, namely that all ancient Veronese monuments, through error, placed Saint Proculus under the reign of Maximinus. This must also be noted in the other monuments cited by the Ballerini gentlemen [Col. 0719D].

Nor in the Ambrosian Church is order seen to be observed in the Canon of the Mass, either before or after the consecration. In the first *Memento*:

> “And also of your blessed Apostles and Martyrs Peter and Paul, Andrew, James, John, Thomas, James, Philip, Bartholomew, Matthew, Simon and Thaddaeus; Sixtus, Lawrence, Hippolytus, Vincent, Cornelius, Cyprian, Clement, Chrysogonus, John and Paul, Cosmas and Damian, Apollinaris, Vitalis, Nazarius and Celsus, Protasius and Gervasius, Victor, Nabor, Felix and Calimerius.”

After the consecration:

> “Deign also to grant us fellowship with your Saints, Apostles, and Martyrs: John, James, Stephen, Andrew, Barnabas, Peter, Marcellinus, Agnes, Cecilia, Felicity, Perpetua, Anastasia, Agatha, Euphemia, Lucy, Justina, Sabina, Thecla, Pelagia, and Catherine,” etc.

Here you see Saint Hippolytus, who died a martyr under the emperor Alexander around the year 229, named after Pope and martyr Saint Sixtus and the martyr Saint Lawrence, who suffered death for the Faith in the time of Gallienus, around the year 260 [Col. 0720B]. Vincent, who was martyred under Diocletian, is placed before Cornelius, under Gallus, and Cyprian, who were crowned with martyrdom in Gallienus’ age. Clement, who lived under Trajan at the beginning of the second century, is placed after Cornelius and Cyprian. John and Paul, martyred under Julian the Apostate, are placed before Cosmas and Damian, martyrs under the emperor Diocletian. Finally, not to detain the reader longer in demonstrating a matter obvious in itself, after the consecration in the same Ambrosian Missal Thecla, disciple of Saint Paul, is named after other holy women martyrs who died in the second, third, and fourth centuries [Col. 0720C].

The diligent reader will observe the same thing for himself in the Canon of the Roman Missal. Therefore it is beyond doubt that order is by no means considered, nor can it be considered, in such diptychs. For in recording the saints’ names, either the time at which they were placed in the Canon or in the Litany is observed—as is clear from the recent addition made by Pope Benedict XIV, who placed Saint Joseph after John the Baptist in the Litany—or some other prerogative of the saint. Thus martyrs are placed before pontiffs, pontiffs before confessors, and virgins, though later in time, are assigned their place. Moreover, in such diptychs holy bishops were customarily listed separately from the rest; and heretical or schismatic bishops were forbidden to be entered among them [Col. 0720D].

What basis, then, can arise from such diptychs for establishing the date of any saint, especially Saint Zeno, when it is in no way proved that the succession of the first eight Bishops of Verona was taken from the diptychs of that Church, and no diptychs of this kind are any longer found? Since it has been established that Saint Proculus was listed fourth among the Bishops of Verona through error; since no reason exists to prove that the Rhythm of the Pipinian Anonymous was compiled from the diptychs of the Church of Verona; and since, even if the order of bishops were derived from the same diptychs, it would not present their dates and succession in an ordered form—the argument advanced by the Ballerini gentlemen collapses.
