[Col. 0721A] “Therefore the fourth Bishop of Verona, Saint Proculus, flourished at the beginning of the fourth century.” Since Saint Zeno is counted eighth among the Bishops of Verona, they conclude from this that he presided over the Church of Verona after the middle of the fourth century. But although it cannot be doubted that Saint Proculus flourished at the beginning of the fourth century, it is false, for the reasons shown above, that Saint Proculus was the fourth Bishop of Verona. Saint Proculus therefore lived at the beginning of the fourth century, but not before Saint Zeno, who held the see of Verona in Gallienus’ age, after the middle of the third century, as we shall also show below. Nor should Proculus be called the fourth Bishop of Verona; rather, with Ughelli, he should be called the ninth, successor of Saint Zeno, who was the eighth.

[Col. 0721B] In this same Rhythm we read that the sixth Bishop of Verona was Lucilius. The Ballerini gentlemen maintain that he was Lucillus, who subscribed to the Council of Sardica in the year 347. Yet they themselves, with the integrity that distinguishes them, note in this especially Zenonian edition that in the acts of the same Council of Sardica the subscriber is found as Lucius, as likewise in the synodal letter to Pope Julius. I consider it certain that this Lucius is the same person whom Saint Athanasius, in both the First and the Second Apology to Constantius, calls Lucillus. Although he called himself Lucius, he was perhaps popularly called Lucillus as a diminutive because of his small stature, as the Ballerini gentlemen aptly note.

An example is provided by a letter, subscribed in his own hand by Saint Antoninus, Bishop of Florence, which is kept with special veneration among the relics in the episcopal oratory at Pistoia [Col. 0721C]. In it he subscribed himself *Antonius*, not *Antoninus*, by which name he is commonly called. I therefore admit that Lucillus subscribed to the Council of Sardica in 347, and I do not agree with Ughelli, who says that Lucidus rather than Lucillus subscribed to that council.

Nevertheless, I hold it certain that this Lucillus was not the sixth Bishop of Verona. For in the Rhythm *Lucilius* is read in place of *Lucidius*, not *Lucillus* in place of *Lucius*. That Lucius should have been called Lucillus occurs frequently in other names by a sort of diminutive formation; but to write *Lucidus* for Lucius or Lucillus is no diminutive, expressing either the person’s stature or the affection of the speaker, but an altogether different name. That *Lucilius* should be read for *Lucidius* may have arisen through the fault of a copyist. Perhaps an ancient character had lost, through wear, the body of its *d* and retained only the stroke of an *l*, with the result that an *l* was written for a *d*, and *Lucilius* for *Lucidius* [Col. 0721D].

Among the ancient Bishops of Verona, Lucidius and Lucillus are found; Lucilius, however, never. This Lucidius, distinguished for holiness, is venerated at Verona. The ancient monuments concerning the holy Bishops of Verona state of him:

> “The body of Saint Lucidius, Bishop of Verona, rests in the Church of Saint Stephen,”

as follows from an ancient parchment tablet in the sacristy of Saint Stephen, from Francesco Corna, and from the table of saints for 26 April, mentioned above. The Roman Martyrology also commemorates the same Lucidius on 26 April. Therefore no argument can be drawn from the cited Rhythm for placing Saint Zeno’s date in the fourth century, since Saint Proculus, who governed the Church of Verona at the beginning of the fourth century, was placed fourth among the Bishops of Verona through error, as was shown above. And Lucilius, who is counted the sixth bishop, should truly be called Lucidius and is another person than Saint Lucillus, who attended the Council of Sardica; for Lucilius is never found among the Bishops of Verona, but Lucidius is [Col. 0722A]. It must now be considered whether what is related in this same Rhythm concerning Gallienus’ daughter is in fact false.

### § III. What should be thought of the narrative of Coronatus the Notary, or the Life of Saint Zeno written by Coronatus the Notary

The Ballerini gentlemen count Coronatus the Notary’s narrative of Saint Zeno among fables, chiefly for these reasons (Dissertation I, chapter 3, §3). First, the remarkable event in which Gallienus’ only daughter is said to have been freed from a demon when Zeno was summoned to the emperor by messengers ought to have been so notable and solemn that it is wholly incredible that for roughly five centuries no one committed anything about it to writing, and that Coronatus the Notary should have been the first to mention it in the seventh or eighth century.

Next, in number 5, the monastery in which Saint Zeno lived with many others, likewise called Zeno, is represented as a public institution at Verona. This is altogether incredible of the first three centuries, when Christians, hiding because of persecution, displayed no public buildings. Further, when Zeno, requested by the emperor to heal his daughter tormented by a demon, went with him and expelled the demon, he is said to have received from Gallienus the imperial crown which the emperor Gallienus himself wore on his head, and immediately distributed it to the poor [Col. 0722C]; although Roman emperors did not use an ornament of that kind before Aurelian. Again, who could plausibly maintain that a pagan emperor granted Zeno permission to destroy all the idols and build churches in Christ’s name, and that this happened when he returned to Verona? Thus, although not even one public Christian church existed elsewhere, several were constructed at Verona by Zeno at the emperor’s command, as is reported in number 7. But let us omit many other matters which might be considered; for these are more than sufficient, in the judgment of competent judges, to demonstrate that this narrative is a fabrication.

We too rejected this narrative of Coronatus as uncertain and doubtful, chiefly because of the differences found in different manuscripts. I possess another manuscript, written in a comparatively recent hand but, as is reasonable to believe, copied from older manuscripts. It was given to me by an abbess, a nun of the Pistoian convent of Saint John the Baptist; the reader may inspect a copy of it at the end of this paragraph. It differs in many respects from the manuscript which the Ballerini gentlemen print among the monuments concerning Saint Zeno, p. CXLVII.

Among other things, this Pistoian manuscript has the following, which are not read in the text published by those distinguished men in the latest Veronese edition:

> “In the days of the emperor Gallienus, who, in the succession of Caesars, was appointed twenty-seventh in their catalogue, at which time also Dionysius, a most reverend man and the twenty-sixth from the blessed Apostle Peter, presided over the Roman Church, the deeds of Blessed Zeno shone forth in the province of Italy, in the city of Verona.”

The following words are absent:

> “Although there are many persons in our monastery bearing the name which you mention.”

These occur in number 4 of the printed version. In number 5, the printed text reads:

> “When the holy Bishop of God was travelling, he arrived before the soldiers who had been sent.”

But the manuscript reads:

> “The holy bishop also, travelling with swift progress, arrived before the soldiers who had been sent.”

The manuscript ends with the account of the miracle by which Gallienus’ daughter was freed from a demon. I think this was because the nuns devoted to the Rule of Saint Francis celebrated only the feast of Saint Zeno without an octave, as is still done today; they therefore procured for themselves only those readings needed for the office on the feast day, omitting the rest, which were read on the days of the octave and in which the matters occurring after the deliverance of Gallienus’ daughter are set out in the manuscript [Col. 0723B].

Although I have believed, and still believe, this same narrative uncertain and doubtful, I shall not hesitate, upon better consideration, to state more openly what I think of it. The title *Notary* added to Coronatus seems to indicate that the Life of Saint Zeno was written by a notary who recorded Acts of the Martyrs during the age of persecutions, and who was contemporary with Saint Zeno. But I think that this Life is entitled “A Sermon of the Venerable Coronatus,” etc., because it was reduced to readings for the Divine Office, since it accorded with the tradition of the Church of Verona.

It therefore does not seem far from probable that in ancient times some fragment of this Life written by Coronatus the Notary, but not the whole work which he composed, was discovered. Hence, in order to continue the same Life, some material was inserted by different persons. This is suggested by the diversity of the manuscripts. Since churches which celebrated Saint Zeno’s feast saw an incomplete Life of Saint Zeno and only a few things written by Coronatus the Notary, each took care to supply what was missing in different words; not one person but several undertook the task separately. Yet all retained the things read in the little papers, or remnants, of Coronatus’ writings [Col. 0723C], perhaps adding something that is not visible in all manuscripts: for example, that Saint Zeno was sanctified from his mother’s womb, that he was ordained Bishop of Verona, and the like. They amplified other matters: namely, that all idols in Verona were destroyed, that several churches were built, and that Saint Zeno died in peace—something which I noted is expressed in different words in the manuscripts.

We see the same thing to have occurred in hymns, especially in the hymn *Praesulis Sancti*, in which the printed monuments published by the Ballerini gentlemen, p. 168, read:

> “He was a great priest of the Most High.”

Ferrarius, however, reads from other manuscripts:

> “He was a martyr of the Most High, and a priest.”

For the words were changed according to the various solemnities of Saint Zeno: on the feast of his Ordination they sang, “He was a great priest of the Most High”; on the feast of his Nativity, “He was a martyr of the Most High.” Thus in the readings too they considered it a religious duty to commemorate Saint Zeno’s martyrdom on the feast of his Ordination; hence they read that he died in peace, while leaving untouched expressions equivalent to martyrdom, as in the same hymn *Praesulis Sancti*:

> “At last, by suffering death for God, he lives forever.”

But in the Pistoian manuscript just mentioned, it reads:

> “At last, by suffering death in God, he lives forever.”

If these things do not please anyone, it is nevertheless certain that they rest on the same authority, tradition, and other conjectures which we have set out. But the invention of a fourth-century Gallienus different from the emperor Gallienus is supported by no argument, as will be clear both from the matters considered from the beginning to this point and from those which we shall presently add [Col. 0724B].

First: it cannot be asserted that the remarkable event in which Gallienus’ only daughter was wonderfully freed from a demon, after Zeno had been summoned to the emperor by messengers, was not transmitted in writing by anyone. What if Saint Zeno’s Acts perished in the persecution of Diocletian? Can we produce an inventory of the acts of the Church of Verona and of its more ancient monuments in which we see that nothing on this matter was recorded? Was not almost all Verona consumed by fire? Therefore one must not say that events which have not reached us in writing were never committed to writing.

Moreover, that the confused ancient writings which we have about Saint Zeno were derived from it is demonstrated by the fact that the works published under Coronatus the Notary’s name read: “We unfold the virtues of so great a man.” On these words the Ballerini gentlemen note: “Beware lest from this word *volvimus* [‘we unfold’] you suppose that something had been written before Coronatus about Zeno’s deeds, from which he drew what he committed to writing.” They offer nothing to establish this warning. Indeed, the Pistoian manuscript to be produced below plainly shows that the materials which we now possess were taken from older manuscripts:

> “Therefore, although we are unequal to those who wrote such things, and wholly unable to express what they accomplished, since the composition of words cannot equal the subject matter, nevertheless let us recount what we have been able to learn concerning the virtues of Blessed Zeno, whether from writings or hymns.”

What credit is to be given to this manuscript will become clear from the notes below [Col. 0724C]. It is not implausible that these accounts were compiled from the remaining little papers concerning the Life of Saint Zeno by Coronatus the Notary, Saint Zeno’s contemporary. Though they are read in different words in different manuscripts, they agree in substance. From this it is inferred that all who narrated Saint Zeno’s miracles had before them one written work, though mutilated and worn, to which they conformed. Thus the things written about Saint Zeno, especially those concerning Gallienus’ daughter, do not rest upon a single popular tradition. This is enough concerning the first conjecture by which the Ballerini gentlemen attack the narrative.

The second argument is certainly more pressing. It censures the following words in Coronatus’ narrative:

> “Tell us whether you have seen Zeno the bishop, whom we seek by the emperor’s command.”

Thus the soldiers address Saint Zeno. To them he replies:

> “Although there are many persons in our monastery with the name which you mention, nevertheless say what you have been sent for.”

But in the frequently cited Pistoian manuscript these words are absent. It reads:

> “Tell us whether you have seen Zeno the bishop, whom we seek by the king’s command.”  
> He replied: “Say what you have been sent for.”

They therefore seem to have been added by someone else for the reason given above: so that, from the worn and mutilated papers of Coronatus the Notary, the narrative might be continued sufficiently for the readings in Saint Zeno’s office—not only for the feast day, but for the entire octave. That this was done in other passages of the narrative also appears from the differing manuscripts [Col. 0725A].

Tillemont, especially, attaches such importance to the third conjecture raised by the Ballerini gentlemen that he thinks it alone demolishes the entire narrative of Gallienus’ imperial daughter being freed from a demon. For this reason they either judge, with Mabillon, that *Gallus*, not *Gallienus*, should be read in the ancient Rhythm—though the very diligent Veronese editors prove from the Lobbes manuscript that *Gallienus* is the true reading—or they invent a Gallienus other than the emperor Gallienus.

The conjecture is drawn from the fact that, when Gallienus’ daughter had been freed from the demon, Gallienus gave the holy bishop a golden crown which the emperor Gallienus himself wore upon his head. They maintain that Roman emperors did not use an ornament of this kind before Aurelian. But how far they are from the truth is apparent from several ancient coins. Augustus is seen in the image on a coin with his head encircled by a radiate crown. Trajan likewise appears so adorned on two coins; Valerian, Gallienus’ father, on one; and Gallienus himself on three. Hardouin displays these coins after the second volume of Pliny the Elder edited by him [Col. 0725C]. In the collection of gold coins of Roman emperors made by Jacques de Bie, moreover, Pupienus in plate 40; Philip the father and Philip the son in plates 41 and 42; Hostilian in plate 42; Aemilian in plate 43; and Valerian and Gallienus in plate 44, are seen distinguished by the same radiate crown.

Furthermore, while ancient foundations were being excavated in the Barberini buildings at Rome, a coin was discovered, as the Roman literary journal for the year 1677, p. 173, reports, engraved with three portraits: those of the emperors Valerian and Gallienus, and of the younger Valerian. Gallienus is distinguished there by a radiate crown [Col. 0725D]. Greater caution is therefore needed in matters of antiquity. We have not examined every ancient monument; very many have perished. Ancient manuscripts which are more truthful are sometimes rashly despised, as occurs in this narrative of Coronatus. For the very point by which it was thought to be weakened is seen to confirm it more strongly: from Gallienus’ gift of a crown to Saint Zeno it plainly appears that not everything contained in it should be counted among fables, especially what is written concerning Gallienus’ daughter.

Nor is the truth of Gallienus’ daughter’s deliverance impaired by the point made by the same very learned Ballerini gentlemen in historical matters (Note 10, in *Monum.*, p. 148): namely, that in Coronatus’ narrative she is three times called Gallienus’ “only daughter,” although, besides a daughter, he had two sons as well, as they themselves show from an inscription in Gruter, p. 275. For since Gallienus had only one daughter, which is expressed by the word *unica* [“only”], this must be excused as part of the barbarous diction with which the whole narrative abounds [Col. 0726A].

Finally, as to the apparent improbability that a pagan emperor granted Zeno permission to destroy all idols and build churches in Christ’s name: it must be admitted that this was exaggeratedly stated, not by Coronatus but by his compilers. For it is otherwise established that Gallienus publicly decreed that places of Christian worship should be restored to Christians. Hence it does not seem inconsistent with probability that he also permitted Saint Zeno to build the church concerning which, as we have seen above, the holy bishop spoke. These matters, however, are not found in every manuscript; they are absent from the manuscript of the Abbey of Saint Saviour on Monte Amiata, which Ughelli reports [Col. 0726B].

The following, then, appears to be the proper judgment regarding this narrative of Coronatus the Notary. The prologue was added by various persons, as the divergence itself among the numerous manuscripts suggests. From Coronatus’ ancient materials only two miracles survived the injuries of time: the miracle of the man drowned in the Adige while being carried in a cart and freed by Saint Zeno; and the deliverance of the daughter of the emperor Gallienus. Yet these miracles are not narrated in Coronatus’ own words, except perhaps for certain words found in the same manuscript. This seems to have occurred because Coronatus’ words, with their letters interpolated and corrupted, did not convey a complete sense. Other material was added to continue the narrative, and some things which do not seem acceptable are precisely those which are not found in every exemplar, as anyone may infer from a comparison of the manuscripts [Col. 0726C]. This may also be observed in the present manuscript, which we faithfully reproduce, if it is compared with the text published by the Ballerini gentlemen. Nothing, however, should be said to be more certain in the same narrative than that Gallienus gave a crown to Saint Zeno, as is established by various coins.

## I. Pistoian Manuscript of the Monastery of Saint John the Baptist

On the solemnity of Saint Zeno, Bishop and Confessor. At Vespers, Antiphon: “The Lord Jesus Christ,” with the remainder from Lauds; at the end of Lauds.

[D.]: all.

Chapter: “Behold, a great priest.”

### HYMN

> Of holy Zeno, the bishop,  
> We offer a hymn to Christ—  
> He who shunned the world,  
> Having purchased Christ’s reward.
>
> In youth he kept  
> The commandments of God,  
> And continually distributed  
> Generous alms to the poor.
>
> He practised the art of fishing,  
> Following orthodox doctrine;  
> He plunged his hand into the deep  
> And caught the grace of Christ.
>
> Like the Apostle Peter,  
> Having obtained worthy merits,  
> Father of the Pistoian people,  
> Confessor, jewel of bishops.
>
> By frequent fasts also  
> He drove away the vices of the flesh;  
> Often, by teaching the people,  
> He destroyed the idols of the world.
>
> A great physician,  
> Healing infirm bodies,  
> He often freed souls  
> Possessed by the devil.
>
> Filled with such great grace,  
> He died into Christ’s rest,  
> And always shows to us  
> Very great wonders.
>
> Therefore let us, the people, beseech  
> The Confessor of the Most High,  
> That he may obtain for us  
> Peace and forgiveness. Amen.

℣. Pray for us, Blessed Zeno.  
℟. That we may be made worthy of Christ’s promises.

At the *Magnificat*, Antiphon: “When Zeno greatly flourished in the honour of the pontificate, possessing many merits, he healed by God’s power the daughter of Gallienus Caesar from destructive plague.” Psalm: *Magnificat* [Col. 0727B].

At Matins, Invitatory:

> Let us adore the King of Confessors, who granted to his Saint Zeno the reward and glory of the heavenly kingdom.

Psalm: “Come, let us rejoice.”

In the First Nocturn, Antiphon:

> Blessed Zeno was sanctified from his mother’s womb and blessed from the cradle.

Psalm: “Blessed is the man who …”

Antiphon:

> By continual growth in uprightness and knowledge he deserved to attain such a point that, through his most holy life, he became a shepherd among peoples.

Psalm: “Why do the nations rage …”

Antiphon:

> By continual fasts and frequent prayers he asked the Lord to open for him an entrance for preaching among the peoples.

Psalm: “O Lord, why are they multiplied …” [Col. 0727C]

℣. Blessed Zeno was sanctified from his mother’s womb.  
℟. And blessed from the cradle.

On the feast of Saint Zeno, Bishop and Confessor. Lesson I.

Long ago it was the praiseworthy custom of men most skilled in learning to seek out, by diligent investigation, the lives of the saints, and carefully and intelligently to commit their sequence, through the service of the pen, to the memory of posterity. Thus, through zeal for their teaching, they might attain imitation of such men in the world and someday enjoy their fellowship in the glory of eternal life. For the mind of the wise earnestly seeks out the lives of the saints as a man, thirsty and scorched by the sun’s heat, eagerly desires flowing springs; or as one longs to hear most welcome news from a distant land; or, indeed, as someone reared on luxurious food, placed upon a long journey, being hungry longs to reach the familiar satisfaction of his stomach [Col. 0727D].

℟. This is the holy bishop Zeno, whom the Lord adorned with the twofold virtue of holiness and wisdom. His splendid miracles shone in the world, and in heaven he attained the fellowship of angels.

℣. This is he who performed great miracles before God, and the whole earth was filled with his teaching.

℟. His … etc.

Lesson II.

Therefore, although we are unequal to those who wrote such things [Col. 0728A], and wholly incapable of expressing what they accomplished—since verbal composition cannot match the substance of the matter—let us nevertheless recount what we have been able to learn concerning the virtues of Blessed Zeno, whether from writings or from hymns.

℟. Blessed Zeno was sanctified from his mother’s womb and blessed from the cradle; through this he deserved to attain such a point that, through his most holy life, he became a shepherd among peoples.

℣. The report of his manner of life went out into all the earth, and his holiness shone forth brightly.

℟. That he became a shepherd, etc.

Lesson III.

In the days of the Emperor Gallienus, who, in the succession of the Caesars, was entered as the twenty-seventh in their catalogue, at which same time Dionysius, a man most reverend, was the twenty-sixth from the blessed Apostle Peter to preside over the Roman Church, the deeds of Blessed Zeno shone forth in the province of Italy, in the city of Verona. Since we are not equal to explaining fully the virtues which this man performed in his conduct and miracles, we nevertheless endeavour to recount truthfully some of them, insofar as we are able to attain to them.

R\. In a more secluded part of the oratory, through continual fasts and frequent prayers, he asked the Lord to deign to open for him an entrance for preaching among the people. V\. He was devoted day and night to converting the souls of men to love of the Bishop. That, etc.

In the second Nocturn. Ant. He was so gracious in speech, and gentle in bearing, that God was praised in him by all who came to him. — Ps. *When I call.* — Ant. [Col. 0728C] While engaged in fishing in the river, he saw a certain man seated in a cart, plunging headlong with it into the stream. Ps. *My words.* Ant. The man of God, raising his hand on high, made the sign of the holy Cross, saying: “Get behind me, Satan; do not destroy the man whom God created.” Ps. *O Lord, our Lord.* V\. The priest of God, Zeno, sat upon a stone. R\. And, following the lessons of the apostolic art, he fished in the river.

### Lesson IV

Accordingly, he was sanctified from his mother’s womb and blessed from the cradle, so that there seemed to be repeated in him, by divine declaration, what was said to Jeremiah: “Before I formed you in the womb, I knew you; and before you came forth from the belly, I sanctified you.” Finally, by unceasing growth in uprightness and knowledge, [Col. 0728D] he deserved to attain such a degree that, through a most holy life, he might become a shepherd among the people. Let all peoples therefore hear who desire to know his miracles: for the sound of his manner of life went forth into all the earth, and holiness shone brightly. R\. He was so gracious in speech, and gentle in disposition and bearing, that God was praised in him by all who came to him. V\. He was so eager that those hastening to him immediately, abandoning idols, believed in the Lord Jesus Christ. That God.

### Lesson V

For he sat in a monastery in a more secluded part of the town of Verona and, through continual fasts and frequent prayers, asked the Lord to deign to open for him an entrance [Col. 0729A] for honey-sweet preaching among the people. Thus he was devoted day and night to converting the souls of men to the love of Christ. Truly, the Holy Spirit was his teacher, the illuminator of pure minds, as Truth itself says: “For it is not you who speak, but the Spirit of your Father who speaks in you.” He was indeed so gracious in speech and gentle in bearing that God was rightly praised in him by all who came to him. He was so eager, and so lively in the splendid brilliance of eloquence, that those hastening to him immediately, abandoning idols and the depravity of paganism, believed in the Lord Jesus Christ. R\. While engaged in fishing in the river Adige, he raised his eyes and saw a man seated in a cart, with oxen yoked to it, plunging into the stream. V\. For he was being borne along with such [Col. 0729B] speed that it was shown to all that this had been accomplished by the craft of the ancient enemy. With the oxen.

### Lesson VI

At the same time, near the city of Verona, when that same man had left the monastery and was engaged in fishing in the river Adige, he raised his eyes and saw, opposite him, a certain man seated in a cart, with oxen yoked to it, plunging headlong into the stream. For he was carried along with such miserable speed that all who plainly beheld it were given to understand that this had been brought about by the devil’s artifice. Therefore, when the holy man, fixing his gaze, perceived this from afar, he recognized that the man’s frenzied ruin was the work of the devil. Meanwhile, then, the man of God, raising his hand on high, made the sign of the holy cross and repeatedly said: [Col. 0729C] “Get behind me, Satan; do not destroy the man whom God created.”

R\. When the devil saw this sign, he vanished like smoke carried away by the wind; and, as he fell with force from a high cliff amid cries and an accursed shrieking, he said: V\. “And if you do not permit me here to gain the souls of men by my possession, yet I am prepared persistently to go about thwarting you in the native districts situated round about.” And if, etc.

In the third Nocturn. Ant. Blessed Zeno said: “The Lord does not permit you to do anything against His servant.” Ps. *Lord, who?* — Ant. The unhappy father and the whole royal household were afflicted with grief because the girl was being violently choked. Ps. *O Lord, in thy strength.* Ant. The priest of God, Zeno, sat upon a stone and, following the lessons of the apostolic art, [Col. 0729D] fished in the river. Ps. *The Lord’s.* V\. When the demon saw this sign, he vanished like smoke. R\. Amid cries and accursed shrieking.

### Lesson VII

When these things had been done, he departed with detestable howling and shouting. Hastening on, the demon swiftly entered the palace of Caesar Gallienus and, seizing his daughter, who at that time was her parents’ only child, began cruelly to torment her. The unhappy father, therefore, together with the whole royal household, was plunged into sorrow, tormented and afflicted by great grief, because the girl was being violently choked. While she was seized by cruel torment, the demon began to cry through the mouth of the little daughter of the king, [Col. 0730A] saying: “I shall not go forth from this body unless Bishop Zeno comes; and I shall depart only when compelled by his command.” As soon as this was made known to King Gallienus, he sent officers and began with anxious intent to search for a means of finding the holy man. R\. Hastening on, the demon entered the palace of Caesar Gallienus and, seizing his daughter, began to torment her so cruelly. V\. The unhappy father and the whole royal household were afflicted by anguish and grief. And seizing, etc.

### Lesson VIII

By the king’s command, soldiers proceeded to the man of God. He was sitting upon a stone near the monastery and, practising the lessons of the apostolic art, was fishing in the river as usual. [Col. 0730B] When the soldiers arrived, because he was unknown to them, they began anxiously to question the holy man of God, saying: “Who are you, man of God? Tell us whether you have seen Bishop Zeno, whom we are seeking by the king’s command.” But he answered: “Tell me why you were sent. For although I am but a very little servant, I am nevertheless called Zeno of Christ.” Then the soldiers conferred with one another, saying among themselves: “Why do we talk at length? Let us tell this man why we have been sent.” Then, plainly informing the blessed priest, they said: “The king asks you to come to him, because he wishes to see your face.” “Why does the king wish to see my face—he who does not cease to be, by manifest proofs, an enemy of all Christians?” But they replied: [Col. 0730C] “For the king entreats you to restore his daughter to health; she is being tormented with dreadful cruelty by a demon, and she is his only child.” But he said to them: “The Lord Jesus Christ is almighty. Go,” he said; “I shall follow you shortly. For it is fitting that the wonders of God be made manifest to all more clearly than light.” Having said this, the soldiers retraced the way by which they had come. R\. When Christ’s confessor entered the palace and made the sign of the cross, the demon immediately began to cry, saying: “You, Zeno, drive me out. I cannot remain because of your holiness.” V\. “And if I depart from here, I go to Verona, and there you will find me.” I cannot remain because of your holiness. V\. Glory be to the Father. I.

### Lesson IX

But Blessed Zeno the priest arose, lest the city set upon a mountain should remain hidden any longer; [Col. 0730D] he prayed and went to the palace, where the king was tormented and mournfully afflicted for his daughter. The holy bishop, travelling swiftly, arrived before the soldiers who had been sent. When Christ’s confessor entered the palace and made the sign of the Cross, the demon immediately began to cry through the little girl’s mouth, saying: “Behold, you, Zeno, have come to drive me out, and I cannot remain because of your holiness.” On hearing this, the priest took the girl’s hand and said: “In the name of our Lord Jesus Christ, I command you: come out of her, demon.” But the demon began to cry in a public and terrible voice, saying: “Even if I am driven out from you here, I shall go to Verona, and there you will find me [Col. 0731A] and those in whom I dwell, standing in the street and waiting for you.” Thus the priest of Christ immediately restored the king’s daughter from every delusion of demonic assault.

At Lauds and the Hours. Ant.

The Lord Jesus Christ is almighty; for it is fitting that the wonders of God be made manifest to all. Ps. *The Lord reigns*, with the remainder from Lauds. Ant. Blessed Zeno the priest arose, prayed, and went to the palace, where the king was afflicted for his daughter. Ant. When Christ’s confessor entered the palace and made the sign of the cross, the demon cried through the girl’s mouth, saying: “You, Zeno, have come to drive me out, and I cannot remain because of your holiness.” Ant. Taking the girl’s hand, Blessed Zeno said: “In the name of the Lord Jesus Christ, [Col. 0731B] I command you: come out of her, demon.” Ant. For the priest of Christ restored the king’s daughter whole from every delusion of demonic assault. Chapter.

“Behold the great priest, who in his days pleased God and was found just; and in the time of wrath he became reconciliation.”

### HYMN

The venerable feast of the holy bishop Zeno,
who followed the Lord,
returns; by his blessed end
he made this day sacred for us.

He was a great priest of the Most High,
preaching well to nations beyond the seas;
from there God saw fit to send him
to the city of Verona.

There he won many people for God,
instructed them by his words, confirmed them by his deeds,
and at last, suffering death in God,
he lives for ever.

Now he shines brightly for ever through his merits,
renowned and manifest to the whole world,
he who, while living in the body,
strove to please God alone.

O shepherd radiant with everlasting triumph,
hear your little servants who pray to you;
ask for a reward for the righteous
and pardon for those fallen through sin;

so that, by God’s great mercy,
filling the tenth order of heaven,
we may behold His worship
through every age of the world. Amen.

V\. Pray for us, Blessed Zeno. R\. That we may be made worthy, etc.

At *Benedictus*. Ant. Blessed Zeno distributed among the poor the crown he had received from the king, saying: “If the Lord accomplishes lofty things, let perpetual praises and glory be rendered to Him.” Ps. *Blessed*.

[Col. 0731D] Prayer. O God, who gladdenest us by the yearly solemnity of the blessed confession of thy holy priest and confessor Zeno, grant, we beseech thee, that, strengthened by thy power, we may overcome the crafty assault of the enemy and, through his intercession, deserve to attain eternal joys. Through, etc. At Terce, chapter: “Behold the priest.”

R\. Short. From his mother’s womb Blessed Zeno was sanctified. V\. And from the cradle blessed. V\. Glory be to the Father. From his mother’s womb. V\. When he saw this sign. R\. Amid cries.

At Sext. Chapter. “None was found like him who kept the law of the Most High; therefore the Lord made him increase among his people by an oath.”

R\. Short. When the demon saw this sign, he vanished like [Col. 0732A] smoke. V\. Amid cries and accursed shrieking. He vanished. V\. Glory be to the Father. When he saw this sign. V\. The priest of God. R\. And the apostolic art.

At None, chapter. “To exercise the priesthood, to have praise in His name, and to offer Him worthy incense for a sweet-smelling savour.”

R\. Short. The priest of God, Zeno, sat upon a stone. V\. And, following the lessons of the apostolic art, he fished in the river. He sat. V\. Glory be to the Father. The priest.

V\. He led the righteous man. R\. And showed him.

At second Vespers. Ant. The Lord Jesus, with the remainder. Ps. *The Lord said*, at the end of the psalm: “Remember.” Chapter: “Behold the priest.” Hymn: *Of Saint Zeno*. Verse: Pray for us. R\. That we may be made worthy, etc. At *Magnificat*. Ant. Holy confessor [Col. 0732B] Zeno, shepherd of the Lord’s flock, we beseech you: intercede for us, that we may deserve to be with you in heaven. Ps. *Magnificat*. Prayer as above.

Praise be to God the Father.

### Notes on the cited Pistoian manuscript

1. First, the conformity of this Pistoian manuscript with the older Veronese manuscripts should be noted. For the antiphons at Vespers and Lauds are the same as those which the Ballerini brothers report from Veronese manuscripts among the documents on pp. CLXIV and CLXV. Likewise, excepting very few items, the responsories for the lessons, as also the prayer, “O God, who [makest] this present day,” etc., are entirely the same as on p. CLXII; and the hymns *Praesulis Sancti* and *Sancti Zenonis praesuli* are on pp. [Col. 0732C] CLXVIII and CLXIX. From this it is clear that this Pistoian manuscript, although written in a recent hand, was copied from the most ancient Veronese manuscripts.

2. Let the diligent reader note the longer preface, and its difference in several respects from that read in the latest Veronese edition; this sufficiently indicates that it is not by Coronatus the Notary.

3. This is, I think, an error of the copyist; for in numbering the supreme pontiffs, Dionysius is correctly counted as the twenty-sixth from Blessed Peter. But the Emperor Gallienus is numbered forty-third in the sequence of Roman Caesars by Johann Ludwig Gottfried in his *Anthologia cosmica*, book I, in the list of western emperors.

4. After this, this Pistoian manuscript agrees completely in substance with that published by the Ballerini brothers on p. CXLVII, though not in wording. Yet much is read in both in the same words, which supports our conjecture: namely, that certain leaves, containing the Life of Saint Zeno written by Coronatus the Notary, were found with their characters worn and corroded; that they were supplemented and continued in different words by different persons, with some additions not found in every manuscript; and that what could be read in those corrupted leaves was retained—the same material that is read in this manuscript.

5. These words are said not of a Confessor but of a Martyr. Therefore this prayer appears to have been adapted for the feast of Ordination, whereas at the feast of Martyrdom perhaps the following was read: “O God, who gladdenest us by the yearly solemnity of the blessed confession of thy holy priest and [Col. 0733A] martyr Zeno,” etc. But at the feast of Ordination, after the word *martyr* had been removed, *confessor* was substituted in its place, while the remaining words, “blessed confession,” were left unchanged—words which suit only a martyr, not a confessor. We leave the reader to note the rest from comparison with the edition published by the Ballerini brothers; for we have presented this Pistoian manuscript with such fidelity that we have even left intact the copyist’s errors.

## CHAPTER IV. WE TRUST THAT THE MATTERS WHICH APPEARED TO MAKE AGAINST MAINTAINING THE THIRD-CENTURY DATE OF SAINT ZENO HAVE NOW BEEN REMOVED; WE NOW UNDERTAKE TO CONFIRM THAT SAME DATE BY VARIOUS REASONS.

### § I. It is shown that the date of Saint Zeno, bishop of Verona and martyr, must be assigned to the third century from what has been observed, and also remains to be observed, concerning his sermons.

We have discussed many matters bearing on this question, which it does not seem useless briefly to review here. For they serve not only to remove the objections, but also contribute greatly to establishing the date of Saint Zeno. Yet, to spare the reader weariness, it will suffice to indicate the places where these matters have been treated more fully above. The principal argument, by which it is demonstrated most evidently that Saint Zeno flourished in the third century, is this: no trace, however slight, can be found in his sermons to indicate the fourth century. Nowhere does he name Arius, even in passing. We have shown in chapter 1, §§ 11–17, that the errors against the faith which he either hints at or refutes preceded Arius. Nor have we found that Saint Zeno indicated in his writings the distinctive formulas of the Arians’ errors (§§ 18–19), although the holy Fathers subsequent to Arius frequently mentioned them (§§ 19–21). So far is it from being the case that Saint Zeno wrote against Arius that Petavius criticized certain expressions in his sermons—wrongly—as smelling of Arianism. For if this holy doctor had written after Arius in the fourth century, it must be supposed that he would have removed from himself every suspicion of agreeing in sentiment with Arius. In § 22 he makes no mention of the heresies that arose in the fourth century; see chapter 2, § 1. What he says about a public church being built, or about the faithful of Verona being redeemed from deadly edicts through benefactions, is shown in §§ 2–3 to fit the third century as well. [Col. 0733D] Moreover, it is established that Saint Zeno expressly indicates the third century because he says that the sign of idolatry was customarily struck on coins, and because the same idols were worshipped in the temple (§ 4). We have shown in § 6 that the anachronism of four hundred years, found in the sermon on Continence, entered through a copyist’s error. Further, it is an empty invention to imagine another Zeno in the time of Saint Ambrose, as is clear from the material brought forward in chapter 3.

There are further matters in Saint Zeno’s sermons indicating an antiquity earlier than the fourth century. What he asserts concerning the unbelieving midwife—whose hand, burned while she sought to inspect the unimpaired purity of the Virgin Mother of God, is said to have been healed by the Child Jesus—is nowhere read in the Fathers of the fourth century. Yet Clement of Alexandria mentions the matter; by the end of the second century it was rejected as apocryphal, as the same Ballerini brothers note from Jerome (*Book II, Tract VIII*, note 17).

In the fifth tract of the first book, the words, “What of the fact that His sacrifice is public, yours secret? His may be handled freely by anyone; yours cannot even be consecrated by Christians themselves without appearing sacrilegious,” have been shown above, chapter 2, § 6, to be utterly incompatible with the fourth century.

There is also what Saint Zeno says in the sermon on circumcision concerning the sin of the first parents: “For when Adam plucked the renowned apple with this member, he thereby introduced into the human race the law of death. Therefore God necessarily gave this sign to a lustful people, so that, while it denounces the place of the maternal fault, it might also teach them that other crimes are to be avoided.” That is, Adam sinned not by eating the forbidden apple, but by having intercourse with Eve without waiting for God’s command. Although Zeno reported this opinion not as his own but as that of others—as the Ballerini brothers rightly establish, citing other passages of the holy doctor in which the true and common teaching on original sin is expressed (*Dissertation II*, chapter 4)—it is nevertheless so ancient that traces of it are read in Clement of Alexandria alone among the other holy Fathers. By the fourth century, however, it was so obsolete [Col. 0734C] that not even a word about it is found in writers of that age.

Likewise, what Saint Zeno says in tract V of book I about second and third marriages agrees remarkably with what Saint Irenaeus, Clement of Alexandria, Origen, Tertullian, and other most ancient Fathers declared on that subject. See chapter seven of the second dissertation, and there the matters which the Ballerini brothers discuss with great learning.

But in tract, or sermon, XXVII of book II, no. 3, Saint Zeno compares the persecution of the Church to vintage-time and says: “But when the time of the vintage comes—that is, the day of persecution—the grapes are seized everywhere; that is, violent hands are rashly laid upon all the saints. They are taken to the winepress—that is, to the place of punishment. There they are trampled by the workers; that is, amid the greatest insults, they are mocked and slain by the persecutors,” etc. These words indicate a present persecution, or one frequent and readily encountered. The Ballerini brothers indeed attempt to assign these words to the persecution of Constantius against Catholics, but no supporting text assists them; and the passages which they produce from other Fathers of the same age expressly identify the time of Constantius, something which cannot at all be observed in Saint Zeno’s words. More explicitly, in the sermon on the praises of Patience, extolling it, he says: “You have advanced the prophets; you have bound the apostles to Christ. You are each day the mother and crown of martyrs” (book I, tract VI, no. 8). Speaking of prophets and apostles, he uses the past tense; but concerning martyrs, the present. Likewise, in sermon 13 of book I, no. 11, comparing martyrdom with circumcision: “We do not shed blood in a barren ceremony, but retain the blood of modesty, which we often pour out ambitiously when, stirring up the devil, we lay waste for the Lord’s name” (*Tract VII*, no. 1). And in the following sermon, on Humility, when writing against philosophers under the name of Greeks, he refers to idolatry as present. To understand Arians under the name “philosophers,” as the Veronese annotators explain (notes 2 and 3 on the same passage), seems alien to Saint Zeno’s meaning; for he censures unbelievers strictly speaking: “What unbelievers now do.” Under the name of unbelievers he signifies not Arians, who were washed in the lustral waters of baptism, but pagans. See also tract 15, no. 2. There are many further points of this kind to be observed in the sermons of Saint Zeno, which I am now weary of investigating.

### § II. The constant and continuous tradition demonstrates that Saint Zeno flourished in the time of Gallienus.

All the ancient records of the Church of Verona bear witness to this tradition: namely, that Saint Zeno held the episcopal see of that Church in the age of the Emperor Gallienus. The reader may see them in the book entitled *Ancient Documents of the Holy Bishops of Verona*, published by Raphael Bagatta and Baptista Peretto and printed at Venice in 1576; and in the final Veronese edition of Saint Zeno’s sermons by the Ballerini brothers, after the third Dissertation. The records of this Church of Pistoia also bear witness. So too do calendars and nearly all the more celebrated martyrologies—above all, and of greatest importance among them, the Roman Martyrology. All authors, down to the sixteenth century, held the same view. This opinion was so deeply fixed in their minds that they would rather assert that the sermons were not Saint Zeno’s, on the ground that they seemed unable to fit the times of Gallienus, than be compelled to remove Saint Zeno’s date from the age of that Gallienus. The eminent Ballerini brothers observe this concerning Sixtus of Siena and Labbe. Yet the strength and foundations of this tradition must be thoroughly examined.

The first person to have laid the foundations of this tradition, as the Ballerini brothers think, is believed to have been Coronatus the Notary, author of the Life of Saint Zeno. “One Coronatus the Notary, a writer of the seventh or eighth century, laid the foundation for this tradition—or rather prejudice—from which others afterward proclaimed an antiquity honourable not only to Zeno but also to the Church of Verona” (*First Dissertation*, chapter 2, § 2; chapter 3, § 3). They accumulate further points to discredit Coronatus’s narrative, which we have discussed above. Yet let us now proceed more indulgently. If Saint Zeno died in the fourth century, namely around the year 380 (as the Ballerini brothers suppose, though the considerations examined above show that this must not be granted), while Coronatus wrote his life in the seventh century—let us grant the year 650, that is, 270 years after Saint Zeno’s death—then Coronatus must have spread this supposed prejudice so successfully that it was embraced by everyone, not only the common people but also the clergy, who divided Coronatus’s narrative into antiphons, lessons, responsories, verses, and hymns, and used these in the Divine Offices. One must therefore suppose that Verona had so completely forgotten its patron, whom it had always honoured and revered with such devotion, that in so short a time—270 years—it retained no memory whatever of Zeno’s age. Who, if prudent, could bring himself to think this? Therefore, in the seventh century there remained a memory of the time in which Saint Zeno had lived. Accordingly, if Saint Zeno had lived in the fourth century, it would not have been in the time of Gallienus, but around the year 380, when Gratian, Valentinian, and Theodosius were emperors. How could Coronatus have deceived the Church of Verona so thoroughly that it would assent to so manifest a lie and sing it at its most solemn observance in the church itself? Are we to judge our ancient fathers so shameless? Coronatus, therefore, recounted Saint Zeno’s age according to the tradition of the Church of Verona, not that of the populace.

But you will say: other things reported concerning Zeno in the ancient Offices of the Church of Verona have the flavour of fable. What are these things? Certainly nothing else seems improbable except this: that Saint Zeno was sanctified in his mother’s womb, as though he were another Baptist, if those words are to be understood in that way: “He was sanctified from his mother’s womb and blessed from the cradle, so that there seemed to be repeated in him, by divine declaration, what was said to Jeremiah: ‘Before I formed you in the womb, I knew you; and before you came forth from the belly I sanctified you’” (Lesson IV of the Office of Saint Zeno; see above, manuscript of the Nuns of Saint John the Baptist [Col. 0736C] at Pistoia). In the Life by Coronatus the Notary, as printed among the documents by the Ballerini brothers, this is read differently: “And because the Lord Himself said to those who do good: ‘Before I formed you in the womb, I knew you; and before you came forth from the belly I sanctified you.’ For he was blessed from the cradle and sanctified from the womb.” But we ought not to be preoccupied with hostility toward the ancients and immediately accept the sense which these words convey at first sight; rather, we must ask what the ancient writers themselves intended to express in these words. For the words, “He was sanctified from his mother’s womb and blessed from the cradle,” or, in the Pistoian manuscript’s aforesaid Life, “For he was blessed from the cradle and sanctified from the womb,” do not properly signify sanctification in the womb and before birth, but after birth. “Sanctified from his mother’s womb, and blessed from the cradle.” The proper meaning therefore appears to be that Saint Zeno, immediately upon his birth, was baptized as an infant. It is clear that this did not occur indiscriminately in those earliest times of the Church; for very many persons were converted from idolatry to the faith as adults. Thus, it seemed fitting to commend in Saint Zeno a kind of special distinction: that he was judged to have been born of Christian parents. The words which follow in the manuscript confirm this true meaning: “Finally, by unceasing growth in uprightness and knowledge, he deserved to attain such a degree that through a most holy life he might become a shepherd among the people.” Likewise in the Life: “And he deserved to attain such a degree that by a holy life he might deserve to be a shepherd among the people; and therefore, because his sound went forth into all the earth and holiness shone forth.” These words indicate that Zeno was raised to the see of Verona because, born of Christian parents, he had lived a most holy life continuously, devoted to sacred studies. That Coronatus or others applied Jeremiah’s text to the baptism of the infant Zeno must be said to have been done encomiastically; for we see Jeremiah’s text introduced with a certain caution in the Pistoian manuscript: “So that there seemed to be repeated in him, by divine declaration, what was said to Jeremiah,” etc. Therefore, nothing incongruous or fabulous concerning Saint Zeno is found in the Offices of the Church of Verona that could impair this tradition. See what we have said above concerning Gallienus’s daughter, freed from a demon by Saint Zeno.

[Col. 0737B] But indeed, to assert that the claim that Saint Zeno governed the Church of Verona in the time of the Emperor Gallienus flowed from the single narrative of Coronatus the Notary—and that the Church of Verona and so many others received this tradition from him—is not sufficiently safe. What if Coronatus the Notary borrowed from the Offices of the Church of Verona what he assembled in his history? I mean this to be said on the Ballerini brothers’ own view, since they believe Coronatus the Notary wrote in the seventh or eighth century. For, once this date of Coronatus the Notary is established, since it cannot be doubted that Offices for Saint Zeno were celebrated in the Church of Verona before the seventh and eighth centuries, it must be said that Coronatus received from the Offices of the Church of Verona, rather than that the Church of Verona received from Coronatus. For the presumption arising from greater antiquity recommends this. Even if in the fourth and fifth centuries ecclesiastical Offices were perhaps not arranged in the same manner as the ancient manuscripts show them arranged after the tenth century, it is evident that the changed form of the Offices does no harm to the histories of saints read in the Church from the earliest centuries.

It is further established that there were anciently other records in the Church of Verona besides the narrative of Coronatus the Notary. For the eminent Ballerini brothers themselves observe that a miracle performed by Saint Zeno is lacking in Coronatus’s narrative: namely, that a dead man swept away by the river was restored to life . . . . . The anonymous writer of Pipino bears witness to this miracle, although Coronatus omitted it, as we have restored the passage from two manuscripts. The anonymous writer of Pipino, later than Coronatus the Notary, whom the Ballerini brothers prove most convincingly from the context itself to have written at the end of the eighth century, or at least at the beginning of the ninth, commemorated in his *Rhythmus* this miracle omitted by Coronatus, in these words: “He raised to life one taken dead from the river.” He did not, therefore, receive it from Coronatus, but elsewhere. From where? From popular tradition? Could he not also have had it from other, older records? Therefore, to suppose without any reason that he obtained it from the crossroads of the populace is a prejudice of those who rate ancient writings too low, since it is very difficult to adopt the view that the people of Verona preserved absolutely no older information concerning Zeno. There is mention of this miracle, and of the second lesson of the second Nocturn now read in the Office of Saint Zeno: “But because the priests of the Gentiles cried out against him [Zeno] on this account, the holy man confirmed his teaching by a miracle. For he called from afar the corpse of a man which happened then to be rolling in the river and restored him to life, to the amazement of all. By this miracle, almost the entire city, casting aside the images of the gods, received the faith of Christ.” More is read here than in the anonymous writer of Pipino. Since Coronatus does not report it either, it must be said to have arisen from other, older manuscripts. Therefore, the accounts concerning Saint Zeno do not derive from Coronatus the Notary alone, but either from the tradition of the Church of Verona or from earlier records. For this reason, the liberation of the daughter of the Emperor [Col. 0738B] Gallienus from the demon should not be relegated among fables, nor should Saint Zeno’s date in the time of Gallienus be rejected as false, since nothing can be criticized in these historical deeds which appears deserving of disapproval.

But the following point must be said to have the greatest weight in this matter. Let us compare the tradition of the Church of Verona for vindicating Saint Zeno’s sermons with the same Veronese Church’s tradition concerning the age of its holy bishop. The Ballerini brothers rightly and deservedly rely on the former tradition (*Dissertation I*, § 1) to demonstrate that Saint Zeno was the author of the sermons: they cite a Rheims manuscript older than the ninth century; the testimony of Ratherius, bishop of Verona, writing in the tenth century, who praises Saint Zeno’s sermons in three places; the testimony of a certain anonymous monk of a Veronese monastery, who testifies that he has read Saint Zeno’s sermons; and John, a priest and resident cleric of the Church of Verona, confirms the same. They also cite other authors of the fourteenth and fifteenth centuries: Peter Calo of the Order of Preachers, William Poetrengus, Peter de Natalibus, and Flavio Biondo; see *Dissertation I*, chapter 3, § 1. Add to these all the manuscripts in which Saint Zeno’s name is inscribed not only in the title, but repeatedly either at the beginning or the end of the sermons. We observed the same in this Pistoian capitular manuscript.

No fewer, nor less authoritative, arguments support the tradition assigning Saint Zeno’s age to the era of the Emperor Gallienus. First, there is the Rheims manuscript, into which the Life of Saint Zeno by Coronatus the Notary is inserted. In the part especially treating of Gallienus’s daughter freed from demonic possession, this Life—defended against the introduced marks of falsity—must be regarded as genuine. The Ballerini brothers think it was written in the seventh or eighth century. There is also the unknown writer whom the same Ballerini brothers say that they learned from Bartholomew Campagnola, chancellor of the Chapter, had been found in a ninth-century manuscript of the Chapter of Verona; they print his writing among the documents on p. 151. There is the monk whom those same authors call the Zenonian monk, who is said in the Life of Saint Zeno here to have lived around the end of the fourth century, and whom they conjecture to have used some older record. Consequently, perhaps one could not rightly blame someone [Col. 0739A] for saying that the assertion of those who claim that this Zenonian monk derived from the narrative of Coronatus the Notary—perhaps a narrative he never saw—what he committed to writing about Saint Zeno, ought itself to be regarded as a prejudice. Likewise, the anonymous writer of Pipino, writing toward the end of the ninth century, whose *Rhythmus*, written in the hand of Ratherius, bishop of Verona, survives at Lobbes, must be understood to mean the Emperor Gallienus in this verse: “He healed Gallienus’s daughter from an evil spirit . . .”

As noted above, all the manuscripts prove that St. Zeno lived under the emperor Gallienus, as may be seen in the offices for St. Zeno printed among the documents by the Ballerini brothers, p. CLXIV and following. These accord with the Pistoian manuscript mentioned above at the end of § 3, ch. 3. These manuscripts of the Church of Verona and of other churches [Col. 0739B] which received the same offices from the Veronese are so many irrefragable arguments proving the tradition of that same Church of Verona; nor should what was recited in the Divine Offices be said to have arisen from popular rumour. [Col. 0740A] The martyrologies likewise confirm the same thing, both those of Verona and those written or published elsewhere. See what Perettus and Bagatta report in *Ancient Documents concerning the Holy Bishops of Verona*, p. 12 and following. See what I have reported in Book II, on the Martyrdom of St. Zeno, chs. 1, 2, 4, 7, and 11.

There is no need here to collect authors who support this tradition, since all who wrote before Dupin and Tillemont place the period of St. Zeno under the emperor Gallienus. Who, then, if he has sound judgment, would dare approve the opinion of Dupin and Tillemont, since they have dared, as we showed above, to assail with vain labour a tradition confirmed over so many centuries, by false and empty suspicions? If, therefore, the tradition concerning the sermons [Col. 0740B] of St. Zeno, unsupported by such great attestations, is to be accepted as constant and true—as I gladly accept it—then I do not see why the tradition concerning St. Zeno’s age, during Gallienus’ reign, should be rejected.

## SECOND DISSERTATION. EXAMINATION AND JUDGMENT OF THE REASONS WHICH THE BALLERINI BROTHERS OFFER FOR AND AGAINST THE MARTYRDOM OF ST. ZENO.

[Col. 0739]

[Col. 0739B] I should certainly seem to act without judgment and rashly if I dared to pronounce judgment concerning the martyrdom of St. Zeno. The most learned Ballerini brothers, so deeply engaged in the study of St. Zeno’s affairs, refrained from making such a judgment after weighing the reasons on both sides. What could I presume to affirm, so unequal as I am to men endowed with the greatest powers, talent, learning, and the accomplishments of humane letters? Yet [Col. 0739C] the thought occurs to me that these eminent men did not withhold their assent from either opinion because they were deterred by the difficulty of the question, but readily left the outcome of the question to their readers. We refer everything to the judgment of readers, which will not be difficult to render. I do not doubt that I may undertake this without the charge of rashness. For these candid and wise men know Cicero’s warning: that the authority of those who profess to teach often hinders those who wish to learn; for they cease to exercise their own judgment, and regard as settled whatever they see judged by one whom they approve (*On the Nature of the Gods*). They know St. Ambrose’s saying: “Diligence opens for itself the gate of truth” (*On Luke*, prologue). Accordingly, with particular care selecting everything on either side—both what is advanced by those who prove that St. Zeno was [Col. 0739D] a martyr and what is alleged against it by those who deny that he was a martyr—they lay out the case so that its truth may readily be discerned by anyone. The case having thus been set forth, judgment must be given by weighing not so much the force of authority as that of reason. With God’s help, I undertake to do this to the best of my ability.

### § 1. Whether St. Ambrose may be called as a witness against St. Zeno’s martyrdom.

Those who maintain that St. Zeno was a confessor, not a martyr, magnify the authority of St. Ambrose. They assert that in his letter to Syagrius—whom they take to be Zeno’s successor—Ambrose calls this same Zeno, whom they claim to have been Zeno’s peer, not a martyr but a bishop “of holy memory.” From this they first infer: “Thus it plainly appears that Ambrose knew nothing of his martyrdom; and if Ambrose learned nothing of it, it is highly probable that Zeno ended his life not by martyrdom but by a natural death in peace, unless Ambrose’s testimony is overthrown by evidence of equal age and authority” (in Ballerini, Dissertation III, ch. 2, § 2). Yet it is easy to demonstrate that those who assert this so confidently offend very seriously [Col. 0740C] against the principal rule of sound criticism. The rule of criticism requires us to beware, above all, of attaching to an author’s words meanings which the words themselves do not express, or adapting those words to our own opinions.

St. Ambrose mentions a certain Zeno in his letter to Syagrius in these words: “But you thought that this judgment ought to be judged by you alone, without the counsel of another brother; yet before passing judgment, you had already made a prejudgment, when you considered that the young woman, approved by the judgment of Zeno of holy memory and sanctified by his blessing, ought, after so many years, to be brought into danger of accusation without an author of the charge, without an accuser, without one who formally avowed the denunciation” (St. Ambrose, Book VI, ch. 46). I appeal to the reader’s judgment whether from these words alone it may be inferred [Col. 0740D] that this Zeno was bishop of Verona and Syagrius’ predecessor; and whether, because Ambrose did not call this Zeno a martyr but “of holy memory,” anyone can prudently conjecture that St. Zeno, bishop of Verona, was not a martyr. Indeed, no other mention of Zeno occurs in the cited letter. I have treated this matter in Book I of the Sermons of St. Zeno, ch. 11, and in the appended dissertation, ch. 3, § 1.

### § II. Examination of the objections raised to diminish the authority of St. Gregory the Great, who calls St. Zeno a martyr.

Compared with this testimony of Ambrose, the authority available for the martyrdom of St. Zeno from St. Gregory the Great is much too late, they say. For Gregory, who lived two centuries later, when recounting the miracle of the Adige (*Athisis*) and calling Zeno a martyr, may have suffered a lapse of memory and believed him to be called a martyr, whereas John, from whom he had learned the miracle, had described him simply as a bishop and confessor—unless, perhaps, it is thought more probable that John himself erred in the title. Thus argue against St. Gregory the Great, who calls St. Zeno a martyr, those who regard the Veronese bishop as a confessor (in Ballerini, Dissertation III, ch. 2, § 2). Let us now examine whether they proceed according to the standard of sound criticism.

When the Holy Fathers of the Church are in question, critical scholars—even Dupin and Tillemont themselves—prescribe [Col. 0741B] that Catholics must receive with the highest veneration the authority of approved ancient writers, and must not depart from it except for the most compelling reasons.

Is it a compelling reason to oppose the uncertain text of St. Ambrose to the explicit text of St. Gregory? Ambrose names Zeno, but calls him neither bishop, nor Veronese, nor Syagrius’ predecessor. Even if it were granted—though it is not—that St. Ambrose named Zeno of Verona, and named him incidentally, what necessity was there for him to call him a martyr? Nor does Ambrose call Zeno a bishop. Why, then, do they maintain that he was a bishop and a Veronese? If they refuse to regard Zeno as a martyr because Ambrose does not call him a martyr, then by the same reasoning they are compelled to admit that he was neither bishop nor Veronese. See above, ch. 3, § 1.

Is this their most compelling reason? “For Gregory, who lived two centuries later, when recounting the miracle of the Adige and calling him a martyr, may have suffered a lapse of memory and believed that he was called a martyr, whereas John, from whom he had learned the miracle, had described him simply as a bishop and confessor—unless perhaps it is more probable that John himself erred in this title.” If it were otherwise certainly established that St. Zeno was a confessor and not a martyr, then I should readily judge it plausible to suppose that St. Gregory had suffered a lapse of memory. But since this is not established from the uncertain text of St. Ambrose that has been cited, the invention of a lapse of memory is so far from being a compelling reason that no one will rightly deny that it must be regarded as calumny. [Col. 0741D]

Perhaps those opposed to St. Zeno’s martyrdom will consider it a most compelling reason that errors of this kind in St. Gregory are not without precedent. For, as Molanus observed in the second edition of Usuard, St. Juvenal, bishop of Narni, whose feast is marked on 5 May in the Roman Martyrology, is called a martyr by St. Gregory, Book IV, ch. 12, though he was merely a confessor. We offer another example from what was formerly Epistle 73, Book IX, now Epistle 62, Book VI, where the same pontiff calls St. Leucius, bishop of Brindisi, “most blessed martyr.” Yet in the martyrology mentioned above, and likewise in a manuscript calendar of the Casanatensian Library, written at the beginning of the ninth century and formerly belonging to a certain Beneventan monastery, he is called, on 11 January, [Col. 0742A] bishop and confessor; and, indeed, he is still venerated in his own Church of Brindisi as a confessor. This reason surely presses very hard: St. Gregory erred in calling St. Juvenal, bishop of Narni, and St. Leucius, bishop of Brindisi, martyrs; therefore he erred in calling St. Zeno a martyr; therefore he erred in everything.

Particular errors do not prove that Gregory erred in other matters. But he did not err in calling St. Juvenal, bishop of Narni, a martyr, as we showed in the dissertation after the two books on the Sermons and Martyrdom of St. Zeno; nor is he proved to have erred concerning St. Leucius, bishop of Brindisi. The Ballerini brothers themselves admit that in other editions he is called Leontius, not Leucius. It is true that editions after the Roman edition call him Leontius, not Leucius. But since his body is said to rest at Brindisi, and the city of Brindisi never recognized that the body of any St. Leontius rested there, whereas it once had that of St. Leucius, its bishop, before it was transferred to Benevento, the reading of the earlier editions of Gregory appears preferable; together with five manuscripts cited in the Benedictine edition, they read “Leucius.” [Col. 0742B]

Yet the context of the letter itself makes it sufficiently clear that St. Gregory wrote “Leontius,” not “Leucius.” For if he had been speaking of the relics of St. Leucius the bishop, Gregory would have called him a bishop, and bishop of Brindisi. The holy pontiff merely states that the body of a holy martyr rests in the church of Brindisi: “Because the body of that most blessed martyr is known to be in the church at Brindisi, to which he discharges the duty of visitation.” Earlier, moreover, he indicates that the church of the monastery over which Abbot Opportunus presided—the abbot who sought the sacred relics—was adorned with that saint’s name: “The holy relics of that same martyr, which, as he asserts, had been stolen from the church dedicated to his name.” Therefore, had he been speaking of St. Leucius, who was bishop of the Church of Brindisi, he would surely have indicated this as well. Or shall we say that Gregory also suffered a lapse of memory in this matter, heaping calumnies upon him?

But the assertion that the Church of Brindisi “never recognized that the body of any St. Leontius rested there” is gratuitous. It may be asserted that no memory of him now survives in that Church. But who would dare, against St. Gregory’s authority, to mutter that the body of this St. Leontius did not rest at Brindisi in the sixth century? How many bodies of saints have existed in many churches, though their memory has disappeared through wars, fires, and devastations? Those responsible for the Roman edition testify that they used a multitude of very ancient copies. Therefore the reasons adduced are not compelling, and one ought not depart from St. Gregory’s assertion concerning St. Zeno’s martyrdom.

The assertion of Notary Coronatus, who wrote St. Zeno’s life, carries less weight; for even those who oppose St. Zeno’s martyrdom admit that it is filled with many improbabilities. Who would dare compare an improbable writing with the authority of St. Gregory? But whoever dared would, as everyone sees, wrong the holy pontiff under the pretext of reverence. [Col. 0743A] On this life written by Coronatus, see above, First Dissertation, ch. 3, § 3.

They add, moreover: “In a very ancient manuscript of Reims … where the miracle of the Adige is narrated, the very words of St. Gregory appear inserted … and there, where St. Gregory writes, ‘to show the merit of the martyr,’ the text instead reads, ‘to show the merit of the confessor.’ Hence arises a suspicion that whatever Veronese inserted that addition in the manuscript, formerly Veronese but now at Reims, corrected ‘martyr’ to ‘confessor’ in Gregory’s words and thought that the holy pontiff had erred, since St. Zeno was held at Verona to be a confessor, not a martyr. For the same reason the Zenonian monk, when mentioning Gregory and quoting his words, omitted the word ‘martyr’ and substituted ‘saint,’ writing: ‘to show the merit of the saint’; or, as is read in the manuscript Brescian lectionary mentioned by our Maffei in his preface to the Zenonian Monk, p. 317 of *Historia diplomatica*: ‘to show the merit of the confessor.’ Unless, perhaps, this manuscript Brescian lectionary contains Coronatus’s life itself, copied from a similar Reims exemplar—as indeed another manuscript lectionary of the Church of Trent contains it, with the same addition and Gregory’s formula placed before the words.”

In the manuscript of Coronatus reported by Ughelli, the words of St. Gregory concerning the swelling of the Adige are not inserted, as they are in the Reims manuscript and in the manuscript lectionaries of Brescia and Trent. This diversity confirms our conjecture that Notary Coronatus’s Life [Col. 0743C] of St. Zeno did not reach posterity intact; rather, after the pages had been gnawed away by age, a few remnants remained, which were later continued by different persons in different words. This is evident here, where Gregory’s words are inserted in the Reims, Brescian, and Tridentine manuscripts, though they are not inserted in other manuscripts.

The alleged reason for the correction—that “there is a suspicion that whatever Veronese inserted that addition … corrected ‘martyr’ to ‘confessor’ in Gregory’s words and thought the holy pontiff mistaken, because St. Zeno was held at Verona to be a confessor, not a martyr”—is, I say, unsupported by any sign of a probable circumstance and seems borrowed or contrived. A more probable explanation is available, and the Ballerini brothers themselves supply it in their notice to the documents, no. 2: namely, [Col. 0743D] that Coronatus’s small work, in which he wrote the Life of St. Zeno, was included in a lectionary; this they also testify concerning the Zenonian Monk’s writing: “In the sacred offices, the writing of the Zenonian Monk almost took the place of the Life of Coronatus.”

These offices, arranged for the Feast of the Ordination of St. Zeno as bishop, concerned a confessor-pontiff. For in ancient times the feast of St. Zeno’s martyrdom was rarely celebrated, as is clear from the canon of the Council of Toledo of 656 and from the manuscript of the Chapter of Pistoia, which you may see transcribed in Book II, on the Martyrdom of St. Zeno, ch. 10. On 8 December, however, the Mass for St. Zeno is read in the Sacramentary of Gregory the Great as for a confessor-pontiff: “You who prepared an eternal crown in heaven for the blessed episcopate of Zeno”—thus in the secret prayer of the same Mass; and: “O God, who made him such a bishop for your Church.” These plainly commemorate Zeno’s ordination.

Thus, in the first prayer, Gregory himself, who had twice called St. Zeno a martyr and was not ignorant of the custom of the Church of Verona, calls him a confessor: “Today, as we celebrate in devotion the venerable day of your blessed confessor Zeno, may we complete …” These prayers are the same as those recited in the third Mass for the Church of Verona, or the monastery of St. Zeno, and on the day of St. Zeno’s ordination, as the Ballerini brothers note. Therefore, just as Zeno is called a confessor in the Mass and in the Office, so also in martyrologies and lectionaries—not because they did not consider him a martyr, just as they did not consider him a confessor, but because St. Gregory regarded him as a martyr. Rather, they adapted the prayers and readings [Col. 0744B] to the rite of the office. More on this may be seen in the cited Book II.

It should not be omitted that in the Zenonian Monk’s writing the correction was made in this manner: instead of St. Gregory’s words, “to show the merit of the martyr,” it reads, “to show the merit of the saint.” The reason, it should be believed, is that the corrector thought it sufficient, in order that no word might detract from the rite of a confessor, merely to suppress the word “martyr,” without adding the word “confessor.” Otherwise, knowing that Zeno truly was a martyr, he did not wish to call him a confessor. Perhaps for this reason the words found in Coronatus’s little work—“Not long after, he was received in peace”—were inserted in place of the omitted mention of St. Zeno’s martyrdom. For different readings appear in other manuscripts, as we noted in the same Book II, ch. 5, on St. Zeno’s martyrdom.

This variation is most clearly read also in an ancient manuscript lectionary discovered in the episcopal archive of Pistoia by the most learned Fr. Zacharias, S.J., and expressed in these words: “And while, with God’s help, he was doing this, when it pleased God’s will, not long afterward he was received in peace.” The readings were arranged for 8 December, on which the Feast of Ordination is celebrated. Perettus, Bagatta, and our Dondorius—eyewitnesses—also testify that in the readings arranged for the feast of St. Zeno’s martyrdom, which are known to have been drawn from Coronatus’s work, mention of martyrdom is made both at Verona and at Pistoia. See what we have presented in Book II, ch. 1, on St. Zeno’s martyrdom. [Col. 0744D]

The corrections in question, therefore, did not arise from an opinion that anyone believed St. Gregory to have erred in assigning St. Zeno the title of martyr. They arose because these writings were used in readings arranged for the Office of St. Zeno’s Ordination. For this reason, too, in the hymn *Praesulis Sancti* (“Of the Holy Bishop”), the first verse of the second strophe is read differently: “He was a great priest of the Most High” (*Magnus Excelsi fuerat sacerdos*); elsewhere: “He was a martyr of the Most High, and a priest” (*Martyr Excelsi fuit, et Sacerdos*). That is, “great” is used for the Feast of Ordination and “martyr” for the feast of his birth, or martyrdom, since it is otherwise clear from the third strophe that he was a martyr: “At last, suffering death for God, he lives for ever.” These words were not so easily altered, although in the manuscript of Pistoia quoted above a change is visible even in them: “At last, suffering death in God, he lives for ever” (*In Deo tandem patiendo mortem, vivit in aevum*) in place of “for God” (*pro Deo*). Such care did they take that the word “martyr” or any mention of martyrdom should not be introduced into the Office of a bishop’s Ordination.

### § III. On other writers after St. Gregory who affirm that St. Zeno was a martyr.

Those who think otherwise suppose that what often happens in warfare also happened in this literary controversy concerning St. Zeno’s martyrdom: when the commander is killed, the whole army is scattered and falls into the plundering hands of the enemy. Once the authority of St. Gregory the Great has been overthrown, they openly proclaim that the multitude of other writers adhering to St. Zeno’s martyrdom has been struck down at a single blow.
