[Col. 0745B] “If from these things it is probable that St. Gregory, when he called Zeno a martyr, failed through an error concerning one name, the testimonies of Paul the Deacon, John the Deacon, Rabanus Maurus, and Notker are of no use; for it is plain that, just as they derived the miracle of the Adige which they mention from St. Gregory’s *Dialogues*, so also they derived the title of martyr which they attach to Zeno. By the same reasoning, the other later writers—Wandelbert, Usuard, or rather the addition to Usuard, and the authors of Ado, and others customarily cited—also fall, since it is sufficiently credible that they derived their account either from St. Gregory or from other followers of Gregory” (in Ballerini, Dissertation III, ch. 2, § 2).

But St. Gregory’s assertion concerning St. Zeno’s martyrdom still stands entire; and therefore the authority of the remaining writers does not at all waver under so great a leader. But on what grounds do they proclaim so confidently that all writers after St. Gregory derived their accounts either from Gregory or from other followers of Gregory? Did Paul the Deacon, as we observed elsewhere, living so near Verona, have no other work before him while composing his history than St. Gregory’s *Dialogues*? Sigebert testifies that Paul himself, by Charlemagne’s command, arranged the readings of the saints for the feasts of the whole year. Therefore he saw authors other than Gregory, and the institutions of the Church of Verona were known to him. Hence, if Gregory had erred in calling St. Zeno a martyr contrary to the tradition of the Church of Verona, Paul would rather have corrected that error, or at least passed it over in silence, than praised Gregory as the authority for his own assertion. If, therefore, he praised him, he knew that what St. Gregory [Col. 0745D] asserted was true, even in his own time, as the eighth century was drawing to its close.

Did Wandelbert, Usuard, Ado, though far distant from Verona, or the authors of the additions to Usuard and of Ado, study Gregory alone? On what grounds can this be made plausible? Indeed, since all published martyrologies of the more celebrated authors agree in calling St. Zeno a martyr, who can bring himself to believe that not one of them detected Gregory’s error—especially when, as is supposed, the custom of the Church of Verona opposed it by celebrating St. Zeno’s feast with the rite of a confessor rather than of a martyr? This must especially be said of those who added St. Zeno’s name as a martyr to the martyrologies of Usuard and Ado. [Col. 0746A] It is certain that they possessed a clear knowledge of the holy bishop which Usuard and Ado did not possess. Therefore, if they added St. Zeno’s name as a martyr in those martyrologies, it ought not in the least to be doubted that in the times of these authors St. Zeno was considered a martyr.

The manuscripts cited do not contradict these authors’ assertion. Not the Vatican manuscript of 1806, in whose calendar St. Zeno the martyr is expressly mentioned in April. That in the first prayer for the Mass in December he is called a confessor happened because the feast then celebrated was that of his Ordination, not of his Martyrdom, which was omitted when it fell during Lent or Easter. Nor does the Veronese manuscript of the Monastery of the Holy Spirit cause difficulty: likewise in April it commemorates St. Zeno as a martyr, although on the day of his Translation and Ordination it calls him a confessor, for the reason given above.

This should not seem unusual in the ecclesiastical office. At the Nativity of St. John the Baptist, at the chair of St. Peter—both Roman and Antiochene—and at the feast of St. John the Evangelist, their feasts are likewise celebrated without commemoration of martyrdom, although the memory of martyrdom is recalled at the Decollation of St. John the Baptist and at the feasts of St. Peter and St. John before the Latin Gate. Most noteworthy, however, is the Ballerini brothers’ testimony in their notice to the documents: namely, that the Mass arranged for the Feast of St. Zeno’s Ordination was read also on the other feasts, that of his Martyrdom and that of his Translation. This Mass is also placed on 8 December [Col. 0746C] under the title “Dedication of St. Zeno,” and in that missal no other Masses for St. Zeno are found anywhere else. Since this day, 8 December—the sixth day before the Ides of December—is the first of the three days dedicated to St. Zeno, for the missal begins with Advent, this same Mass was read on the other days as well. Thus it is not surprising that the title “martyr” is not found in the prayers copied there, since they were composed for the Feast of Ordination. On the other feasts, a change of one word—from “confessor” to “martyr”—was easy, without needing a separate rubric to note it.

### § IV. On the tradition and ancient manuscripts of the Churches of Verona and Pistoia celebrating the feasts of St. Zeno.

[Col. 0746D] The Ballerini brothers admit, among the arguments they bring against St. Zeno’s martyrdom, that at Eastertide, namely in April, when the commemoration of St. Zeno’s martyrdom is celebrated, the antiphons and Gospel are specified from the Common of Martyrs. It cannot indeed be denied that the antiphons indicated for the Eastertide Mass of St. Zeno in the *Carpsus*—the so-called ancient martyrology or ritual of the Church of Verona—and likewise the Gospel of the same season copied in two other codices, are such as are customarily said of martyrs during that season. The same is observable in manuscript codices of this Church of Pistoia, which we have already displayed in the book on St. Zeno’s martyrdom, ch. 2; it is also so in the Vespers and Lauds, which are indicated from the Common of Martyrs at Eastertide. [Col. 0747A] This demonstrates Panvinio’s error in asserting that, before Lippomano, the Church of Verona venerated St. Zeno in the ecclesiastical offices with the cult of a confessor. For it is clear from the matters cited above that, before Lippomano, the Churches of Verona and Pistoia celebrated St. Zeno’s feast in April with the rite of a martyr. But on this matter see what we have said in the aforesaid second book, ch. 6.

Those who think otherwise attempt to evade this tradition by supposing that in ancient times, during Eastertide, those antiphons and Gospels were common to martyrs and confessors. They strive to prove this by the following conjecture: “For indeed, in the ancient books of Masses published by the Venerable Cardinal Tommasi, the rubric ‘In the Common of One Martyr or Confessor’ is found appended both in the Antiphonary for the Office of Eastertide, p. 281, and in the Lectionary, p. 80, and in the Capitular of Gospels, p. 217. The same is also noted in the Responsorial and Antiphonary for the Office of Eastertide, p. 314, and for the Common Office, p. 361. Thus the argument drawn from antiphons and Gospels of this kind cannot be employed to establish the cult of a martyr rather than a confessor.

“But the evidence of cult which we can certainly derive from Masses lies in the prayers or in the gradual responsory, if it bears the saint’s proper name. For where the title of martyr or confessor is added to the proper name, one may safely judge whether he was held to be a confessor or a martyr. Yet all the prayers which may be read in the six manuscript books of the Church of Verona, and indeed in all the Masses of St. Zeno to be described below, invariably give him the single title of confessor-pontiff, not martyr. And the gradual responsory following the Epistle, designated in the *Carpsus* itself, calls the same saint by no other title: ‘Holy confessor Zeno,’ etc. Who, then, would wish from antiphons and the Gospel—which are found to have been formerly common to martyr or confessor—to argue for establishing martyrdom against the express testimony of the prayers? Indeed, from this one may rather confirm that the antiphons and Gospel of St. Zeno’s Easter Mass, now regarded as proper to martyrs, were formerly also common to confessors; especially since the same *Carpsus* and other ritual books prescribe the whole Easter office of St. Zeno to be recited for a confessor-pontiff. They certainly would not have done this if the Easter Mass, which had to accord with the office, had been designated as proper to a martyr.”

[Col. 0747D] It is entirely new and unheard of in the Church to employ the same rite of office—for martyrs and confessors alike—in celebrating a martyr’s feast or the day of a confessor’s death; indeed, I would call it an invention. For the rubric of the ancient missals published by Tommasi—“In the Common of One Martyr or Confessor”—must not be understood in the sense in which the title “confessor” is received in our own time. Nowadays, confessors are called those who, living piously and religiously, endowed with singular holiness, fell asleep in the Lord. In ancient times, however, confessors were those who publicly professed the faith before a governor or amid tortures, although they had not consummated martyrdom by blood and death. The rubric must therefore be understood of these.

This is especially so because the terms “confessor” and “martyr” seem formerly to have been synonymous, as in the Gothic Missal published by the same Most Eminent Tommasi. There, in the collect for SS. Ferreolus and Ferruccio, it reads: “O God, for whose love your most devout confessors and martyrs Ferreolus and Ferruccio attest by their blood and confirm by their death; who, while they willingly devote to you the gift of life received from you, etc.” And in the Sacramentary of St. Gregory, St. Donatus, martyr and bishop of Arezzo, is distinguished by the title of confessor: “Of your holy confessor and bishop Donatus.” Sollerius also notes, in his observation on Usuard’s text for 7 August, that this same St. Donatus, though universally known in the martyrologies as a martyr, is called only a confessor in certain Hieronymian copies. The same should be observed concerning Pope St. Marcellus on 16 January. In the missal published at Rome by Tommasi, he is called confessor and pontiff: “Of St. Marcellus, confessor and pontiff.” Yet in Gregory’s Sacramentary he is called martyr: “Of your blessed martyr and pontiff Marcellus.” Likewise St. Felix, priest of Nola and martyr, is inscribed with the title of confessor on 14 January: “The feast of St. Felix, confessor.”

Therefore no distinction is to be made in the rubric cited from Tommasi, since the names martyr and confessor were anciently understood in the same sense, and even one who consummated martyrdom by death is given the name confessor. From this it is plainly clear [Col. 0748C] how slight a basis there is for imagining, from the rubric’s words “In the Common of One Martyr or Confessor,” that antiphons and Gospels now used during Eastertide solely for martyrs were formerly common to martyrs and confessors alike, in the sense in which the title “confessor” is now understood.

But, to deal more indulgently with the matter, if some distinction between the names confessor and martyr must be admitted in that rubric, only this distinction can be admitted: namely, that the same office arranged for martyrs was common to those who are called confessors in the strict sense—that is, those who publicly professed the faith and were tortured, but were not subjected to a bloody death. These are also venerated in the same Office of Martyrs at present and are true martyrs: St. Marcellus, St. John, St. Silverius, and SS. Martin and Pontian, all pontiffs. They differ from other martyrs only in the eighth responsory at Matins. For martyrs who died in torments, the responsory is appointed: “This is truly a martyr, who shed his blood for Christ’s name,” etc. For those named above, the responsory is: “Lord, you have gone before him.” See the Roman Breviary, Common of One Martyr.

Nor does the observation offered for distinguishing a martyr from a confessor contribute anything: “But the evidence of cult which we can certainly derive from Masses lies in the prayers or the gradual responsory, if it bears the saint’s proper name; for there [Col. 0749A] the title of martyr or confessor, added to the proper name, permits one safely to judge whether he was considered a confessor or martyr.” For the names of many saints who were martyrs are commemorated in the prayers of Mass without the title of martyr, as may be seen in the Sacramentary of St. Gregory: on 12 June, at the feast of Saints Basilides, Cyrinus, Nabor, and Nazarius; on 29 November, at the feast of Saints Felix and Adauctus; on 11 September, at the feast of Saints Protus and Hyacinthus; on 14 October, at the feast of St. Callistus, pope; and in the missals published by Tommasi, on 28 August, at the feast of St. Hermas—or Hermes—and on 7 October, at the feast of SS. Marcellus and Apuleius, etc.

In the gradual after the Epistle, especially in ancient books of Mass, one scarcely finds—as in the Mass of St. Zeno—the proper name of the saint whose feast is celebrated. At the feast of St. Martin, bishop, on 11 November, his name appears in the gradual without the addition “confessor.” Therefore saints must be distinguished as martyrs or confessors not from the prayers or the gradual responsory, but from other evidence. And below we shall show that St. Zeno’s martyrdom is established from other evidence.

But in the matter under discussion there is a different reason. It certainly cannot be denied that St. Zeno is called a confessor in the prayers and in the gradual after the Epistle. But this is at the Feast of Ordination, at which a Mass of a confessor-pontiff is recited; we shall discuss this later as well. Accordingly, since several feast days are celebrated for St. Zeno, no argument should be drawn from the one Feast of Ordination concerning the other feasts; nor should it be inferred from it that he himself was a confessor and not a martyr. Still less should it be inferred that, during Eastertide, both martyr-pontiffs and confessor-pontiffs were honoured with the same antiphons and Gospel. Since, therefore, even those who think otherwise admit that it cannot be doubted that in the ancient codices of the Churches of Verona and Pistoia, on 12 April, a Mass and Office of One Martyr are appointed for St. Zeno’s feast, nothing can be more certain than that these same churches venerated this bishop as a martyr.

If, however, some confusion of Offices crept into these churches, it arose because, once the proper Office for the Feast of St. Zeno’s Ordination had been composed, they used it also on the other feasts, namely those of his Martyrdom and Translation. [Col. 0749D] Yet the Church of Verona, notwithstanding this confusion of Office, always recited at Prime on the April feast—as Baptista Perettus proves from ancient martyrologies in his Scholia on the Life of St. Zeno—“On the day before the Ides of April: On the same day, St. Zeno, bishop, who wonderfully governed the city of Verona amid the storms of persecutions and was crowned with martyrdom in the time of Gallienus”; and the Church of Pistoia used, at Vespers, Lauds, and the Hours, antiphons from the Common of One Martyr. Lippomano removed this confusion of Offices. That he did so rightly and deservedly is clear both from what has already been adduced and from what will be brought forward.

Above all, this must be observed: in the very Office composed for the Feast of the Ordination [Col. 0750A] there are certain things that can be understood only of a martyr. In the first Mass among the documents published by the Ballerini brothers (p. CLVIII), two prayers are placed before the Epistle; and in the second one it reads:

> O God, who gladden us by the annual solemnity of the blessed confession of thy priest and confessor, St. Zeno, grant, we beseech thee, etc.

This Mass, composed for the day of Ordination, was also recited on the other feasts of St. Zeno. The same Mass was read on other days as well, as appears in the admonition to document no. 5 and in note 2 on the same Mass. The Church of Verona appears to have used this prayer in the Offices of each feast of St. Zeno, from a Capitular manuscript and another manuscript of the nuns of St. Mary in Campo Marzio. The same prayer is also found in the Pistoian manuscript mentioned above [Col. 0750B].

Accordingly, in this prayer those words, “by the annual solemnity of the blessed confession,” cannot be understood of a mere confessor, for they express a confession signifying a public confession of the faith. Therefore, since the Church of Verona is said to have used the same prayer at every feast of St. Zeno, it ought to have used it with some alteration. For the words “by the annual solemnity of the blessed confession” could not be adapted to the Feast of the Translation or of the Ordination. It is thus probable that the word *Confessionis* (“of confession”) was customarily changed to *Ordinationis* (“of ordination”) or *Translationis* (“of translation”), as the feast required. This is still done in commemorations, or suffrages, of the saints after Lauds and Vespers: in the prayer of St. Zeno the words “that, as we rejoice in his solemnity” are changed to “that, as we rejoice in his [Col. 0750C] commemoration,” although no rubric prescribes it. We must say that this was done, even though it is not noted in the old ritual books.

For this reason, both the name “Confessor” must be understood as referring to a martyr, as we have shown above, and the accompanying words advise the same conclusion: “by the annual solemnity of the blessed confession.” Or one must suppose that the very name “Confessor” was changed to “Martyr.” Whatever may be said of this alteration, the words “of the blessed confession” properly belong to a martyr, not to a mere confessor.

In the second Mass, the prayer after Communion reads:

> Grant, we beseech thee, almighty God, that we who [celebrate] the venerable translation of thy glorious confessor Zeno, etc.

The added word “glorious” does not suit a mere confessor. Among those things called common and pertaining to the Masses of St. Zeno, the Introit for Mass is “The Lord established for him”—for a martyr-bishop, as likewise apparently for a martyr who is not a bishop in the Common. In these materials the Gospel for martyrs in Paschal time is noted. Hence it is established that in April the Mass of St. Zeno was customarily celebrated as that of a martyr-bishop. Other elements that are read in the Mass for a confessor-bishop are intermingled, according to the differing feasts of St. Zeno.

In the verse of the second Nocturn, another verse from the Common of a Martyr is noted:

> Thou hast set, O Lord, upon his head.

The second hymn begins:

> O God of thy soldiers,

as a hymn for one martyr.

The second strophe of the fifth hymn, beginning “Great [servant] of the Most High,” is elsewhere read, “Martyr of the Most High,” according to the testimony of Perettus [Col. 0751A] and Bagatta, in ancient monuments concerning the holy bishops of Verona, and in Ferrarius’s Life of St. Zeno. It was evidently changed according to the feast: “Great” on the Feast of Ordination, “Martyr” on the Feast of Martyrdom. Yet in that same strophe remembrance of martyrdom is expressly made:

> At last, by suffering death for God,  
> He lives for ever.

These words did not admit of such an easy alteration.

The formula of blessing on the Feast of St. Zeno runs thus:

> May almighty God and Lord grant you an abundance of blessing, who has taken blessed Zeno to himself through the power of confession. Amen.

The words “through the power of confession” express martyrdom. For in a similar manner, in Thomasius, on the eighteenth day before the Kalends of February, St. Felix’s martyrdom is indicated [Col. 0751B] in the prayer: “May the recounted confession of St. Felix, O Lord, bestow upon us, etc.,” he “who, persevering in the confession of thy name, deserved to be honoured.” And on the feast-day of the holy martyrs Processus and Martinianus, the sixth day before the Nones of July, the Sacramentary of St. Gregory reads: “O God, who surround and protect us by the glorious confessions of thy saints Processus and Martinianus,” without any further mention of martyrdom.

## § V. By What Rite Other Churches Celebrated the Feasts of St. Zeno

The most learned Ballerini brothers prove that the cult of St. Zeno was widely diffused both in Italy and beyond it. At Milan, Padua, Pisa, in the dioceses of Como, Trent, Treviso, Aquileia, and many others [Col. 0751C], the Feast of St. Zeno’s Ordination is observed on the sixth day before the Ides of December, according to the rite of a confessor-bishop. But in the diocese of Brescia six churches, which celebrate the feast on the day before the Ides of April, venerate St. Zeno according to the rite of a martyr; and in the city of Brescia itself one church, which formerly kept the feast on the sixth day before the Ides of December according to the rite of a confessor, now observes St. Zeno’s natal feast on the day before the Ides of April according to the rite of a martyr. There is one church in the diocese of Treviso which on the same day recites the Office of a confessor-bishop.

But throughout the entire Congregation of Monte Cassino, as appears in the Calendar compiled for that Congregation, on the eighth day of December there is a commemoration of St. Zeno, bishop and martyr. The Church of Freising, which began to venerate St. Zeno from the year 730 onward, commemorates St. Zeno’s feast-day according to the rite of a martyr-bishop. [Col. 0751D] Likewise the monastery of St. Zeno at Halle accords him that rite on the day before the Ides of April, and the cult of a confessor-bishop on the sixth day before the Ides of December.

Thus this custom is evident both in Verona and in the other churches: they celebrate the Feast of St. Zeno’s Ordination on the sixth day before the Ides of December according to the rite of a confessor-bishop; on the day before the Ides of April, according to the rite of a martyr—except for one church in the diocese of Treviso. To celebrate the Feast of Ordination as that of a confessor-bishop is not only in conformity with the usage of the Church of Verona, but also with the common rite of the Roman Church. Therefore Sixtus V, in his Brief of 26 November 1588, on the reports of the most eminent Cardinals of the Congregation of Rites—to whom the matter had been entrusted by that Pope—ordered that on the day [Col. 0752A] of St. Zeno’s Ordination the feast should be celebrated as that of a confessor-bishop, and on the other two feasts, namely the Natal Feast and the Translation, as that of a martyr-bishop.

> Since, by command of Sixtus V, the proper Office of St. Zeno was most diligently revised according to the form of the said Roman Breviary by the Congregation of the most illustrious Cardinals appointed over ecclesiastical rites and ceremonies, and by certain men outstanding in learning and piety, chosen for this purpose by the authority of that same Supreme Pontiff; and since they had first been fully informed concerning the use and title of the Office, as it had been celebrated in the church and its diocese at various times before and after the reform, and had also examined—so that nothing might be lacking for this information—certain reasons sent to them from Verona by others; judging that the Office ought not to be made for a martyr but only for a confessor, and rejecting those reasons as ill-founded, it was confirmed by His Holiness, with a command directed to all secular and regular clergy of either sex in the diocese of Verona—namely, to those who recite the Divine Office according to the rite of the Roman Breviary—that they must devoutly recite it at its proper time. This is set forth at length in the Apostolic Brief dated 26 November 1587, printed with the said Office in the following year, 1588. In that Office a proper provision was made for each of the three feasts mentioned above: on the first, the Office is that of a confessor-bishop; on the other two, that of a martyr-bishop, as is read in the said Office.

## § VI. Concerning Other Documents and Ancient Manuscripts

[Col. 0752C] The very ancient monument of the Anonymous Pipinian calls St. Zeno “the eighth shepherd” and “the illustrious martyr Zeno, confessor”; William Pastrengo also supports this. Those who seek to strip St. Zeno of the martyr’s crown say that these men merely followed St. Gregory (Ballerini, cited Dissertation 3, ch. 2, § 2). But St. Gregory was neither deceived nor forgetful in calling St. Zeno a martyr, as has been shown above. Therefore the authority both of the Anonymous Pipinian and of Pastrengo stands in support of St. Zeno’s martyrdom. They say that these writers followed St. Gregory, but do not prove it.

Nor do they shrink from adding this:

> Indeed, since the Anonymous Pipinian calls St. Zeno both martyr and confessor, it is apparent even from this that he did not know whether St. Zeno was a martyr [Col. 0752D] or a confessor; wishing, lest he err, to satisfy both appellations then current, he therefore adopted the title “martyr” from St. Gregory, yet did not think the name “confessor,” derived from the ancient tradition of his church and established by so many testimonies, should be omitted. For the same reason, one might suppose that in the Medoetian manuscript of Paul the Deacon, *Rerum Italicarum*, VI.1, p. 447, and in one of the two documents objected to, both names are similarly joined.

Very cleverly indeed—but altogether superficially! These are inventions of men who leave no stone unturned to give their opinion a false colouring. Were they present when the Anonymous Pipinian wrote these things, so that he disclosed to them the secret of his mind? If such crafty contrivances are admitted, what monument, however solid and certain, can remain safe? They ought rather to study antiquity, and they will find in other ancient codices the words “confessor” and “martyr” joined together, as we gave an example above in the case of the holy martyrs Ferreolus and Ferrucio.

They should also know that, in ancient times, when feasts of mere confessors were scarcely celebrated, the title “confessor” was sometimes understood to mean a bishop. This appears in the Gothic Missal published by Thomasius, where the heading reads: “Mass of One Confessor.” But in the first prayer it is written: “of thy holy confessor and bishop”; in the Secret: “of thy holy confessor”; and in two other prayers: “confessor and bishop.” In the heading and the Secret prayer, the name “confessor” has the same force as “confessor and bishop” in the others. [Col. 0753B] Likewise in the Missal of the Franks, published by the same most eminent Thomasius, St. Hilary is designated by the title “confessor”: “St. Hilary thy confessor,” in both the prayer and the petitions; but in the prayer over the offerings he is called “confessor and bishop.” Therefore the Anonymous Pipinian, who calls St. Zeno confessor and martyr, must be thought to have meant bishop and martyr. The same applies to the Medoetian manuscript and elsewhere where this inscription is found.

They are no less mistaken concerning a charter written in 769 in the village of Campellione in the diocese of Milan, published by the illustrious Marquis Maffei—who deserved exceedingly well of the republic of letters—among the documents he used in elucidating the history of Verona, part I, p. 375. In it the Basilica is described as belonging to “the most blessed Zeno, confessor of Christ.” Who does not see [Col. 0753C] that the words “confessor of Christ” cannot be said of a mere confessor?

Why, moreover, do they still bring up the inscription erected in the time of Andrew, Patriarch of Aquileia—that is, in the ninth century—in the church of St. Gregory, now commonly called St. Helena, and still visible there as a monument of its dedication? Among the relics of saints contained there, it lists: “St. Vigilius, confessor; St. Proculus, confessor; St. Zeno, confessor.” Baptista Perettus, however, clearly demonstrates in his Scholia on the Life of St. Zeno the manifest error of that inscription.

In the authentic instrument of the first consecration of the Church of St. Gregory Martyr near the Cathedral, also called St. Helena, discussed above in chapter 7 and preserved in the archive of the most reverend chapter of the lord canons, the following is read:

> Maxentius, Patriarch of Aquileia, consecrated the church built by Pacificus, archdeacon of the Church of Verona, in honour of the blessed martyrs George and Zeno and of other venerable saints, on the sixteenth day before the Kalends of October; and with his own hand he placed the relics of the aforesaid saints in the altar-receptacle of the same church. In the reign of Lord Charles in Italy, in the forty-first year of his piety, in the fifth indiction. Rotaldus, bishop of Verona, was present at this consecration.

This is taken from the memorandum of Alexander Canobio, who assures me that he faithfully transcribed it from the said instrument. Lord Charles died on 28 January, in the year of Christ 814, according to Carlo Sigonio, *Histories of the Kingdom of Italy*, book IV . . . . . Someone perhaps will not be lacking [Col. 0754A] to object that St. Zeno was not a martyr-bishop, since the stone set in the wall of the aforesaid Church of St. Gregory, also called St. Helena, bears an inscription stating that at the reconsecration of that church, on 1 December 1140, among the other relics placed in the recess of the high altar were also placed relics of St. Zeno the Confessor . . . . . The answer will be that these relics are the very same as those formerly deposited there at the first consecration by Patriarch Maxentius under the title of St. Zeno Martyr, as was said shortly above. Therefore no reason allows one to depart from the truth of St. Zeno’s martyrdom because of whatever is said on that stone contrary to the evidence of the instrument of the first consecration and the truth of history. They confuse the first consecration, celebrated on the sixteenth day before the Kalends of October at the beginning of the ninth century [Col. 0754B], with the second, on 1 December 1140. The manifest error evident in the inscription shows the value to be assigned to this inscription placed at the second consecration: it calls St. Vigilius, bishop of Trent, a confessor, whereas he died unquestionably as a martyr.

Nor are they afraid to cite Notary Coronatus, who asserts that St. Zeno “rested in peace”—Coronatus, I say, whom they formerly rejected as wholly teeming with fables, but now commend and whose authority they invoke. But we have already observed above that Coronatus’s account was divided into lessons for the Office of St. Zeno’s Ordination. Therefore it is not implausible for someone to suppose that the mention of martyrdom was removed for that feast. This is suggested by the variant reading found in different manuscripts, as we noted in the book on St. Zeno’s martyrdom, chapter 5; similar alterations in the same Office, noted above, suggest it as well.

Indeed, John, priest and mansionary of the Church of Verona, likewise asserts in his manuscript imperial history concerning St. Zeno: “He rested in Christ.” But immediately beforehand he writes: “After many sufferings he rested in Christ.” Perhaps, in the lessons for the Feast of Ordination, the words expressing martyrdom were removed, leaving only: “He rested,” or “he was received into peace”—just as if someone had deleted the words “after many sufferings” from the text of the recently cited priest John and left “he rested in Christ.” Nor are these words inappropriate in commemorating a martyr’s feast, as in the Roman Martyrology of 1584, on the nineteenth day before the Kalends of February, where [Col. 0754D] St. Felix is said to have “rested in peace, renowned for miracles.” That the mention of martyrdom was removed from the Feast of Ordination is established by the testimony of Perettus and Bagatta together with our Dondoro, who state that they saw it in the lessons anciently read at Verona and Pistoia on 12 April, the feast of St. Zeno’s martyrdom.

As regards the statutes of the city of Verona, in which the cult of Zeno is discussed and which Perettus reports in his Scholia on the Life of St. Zeno, St. Zeno is called in them neither martyr nor confessor, but patron and protector of the city. Elsewhere, perhaps, St. Zeno is written with the added title “confessor.” But in the ancient codices, as we have seen above, it is certain that the name “confessor” signifies a martyr. If it is found somewhere in a later age, it must be said to have been derived from the older books [Col. 0755A]. For the makers of statutes did not consult ecclesiastical rubrics when framing laws, but the *Code* and the *Digest*.

I should like to give another example, plainly demonstrating that martyrs are called confessors. Perettus supplies it. St. Paulinus, for instance, several times calls St. Felix of Nola confessor and several times martyr:

> The Creator himself, God our light, willed to adorn  
> The birthday of his friend Felix with so great a healing,  
> That by an openly bestowed gift he might show forth  
> The sublime merit of the confessor—not so as to add honour  
> By this work to the martyr, on whom long ago he bestowed  
> Palms bearing noble titles in his blessed name.

In the same way St. Paulinus now honours St. Felix with the title of confessor, now with that of martyr, in the hexameter Life of the same St. Felix. St. Augustine himself calls the same St. Felix now confessor, now martyr, in *On Care for the Dead*, chapter 1:

> What she desired in maternal and pious affection was accomplished: namely, that he should be laid in the basilica of the most blessed Felix the confessor.

And in chapter 4:

> Therefore, when the faithful mother of a deceased faithful son desired that his body be placed in the basilica of a martyr, she believed, of course, that his soul might be assisted by the merits of the martyr.

Augustine is speaking of the same basilica of St. Felix.

If, however, St. Zeno is numbered among confessors in the litanies and Canon of the Mass, this must be thought to have occurred because the procession took place on the day of Ordination (as it still does today in this Pistoian church), so that the litanies and Canon of the Mass might agree with the Office. [Col. 0755C] Moreover, it is proper to believe that St. Zeno was placed after the confessor-bishops in the Canon because he was added later; for St. Proculus is also read after Saints Hilary, Martin, Augustine, Gregory, and Jerome, although he preceded them in age. But if the litanies were recited at another time and on another occasion, what follows from that? They used litanies already arranged for the Feast of Ordination.

In the common commemorations, or suffrages of saints, if St. Zeno is called confessor, it is already clear from the examples so often adduced that, in ancient usage, martyrs too were called confessors. For in the pontifical blessing on the Feast of St. Zeno, where he is especially designated confessor, these words are read:

> May almighty God and Lord grant us an abundance of blessing, who has taken blessed Zeno to himself through the power of confession.

[Col. 0755D] These words, “through the power of confession,” signify a martyr, not a mere confessor.

The remaining arguments are these: that neither Ratherius, who cites St. Zeno in his works, indeed with honourable titles, nor manuscript treatises, among which the very ancient Rheims manuscript served this church itself among its sacred Offices, nor calendars, whether ours or foreign, many of which Father Henschenius saw, chapter 1, no. 3, p. 70, call him a martyr but distinguish him solely by the title of confessor. These, I say, display an abuse of negative argument in this dispute, and are not weighty enough to deserve a direct reply, since St. Zeno’s martyrdom is demonstrated by so many other documents, as we shall shortly see. As for [Col. 0756A] the calendars, recall what we have said and what we also discussed in the book on St. Zeno’s martyrdom, chapter 10. But it is superfluous to inquire whether it be probable that St. Zeno underwent martyrdom under the emperors Gratian, Valentinian the Younger, and Theodosius, since we have already established above St. Zeno’s epoch in the age of the emperor Gallienus.

Having examined all these objections raised against St. Zeno’s martyrdom, this should not be passed over: after the Ballerini brothers had published the book of St. Zeno’s sermons, the editors themselves found a sermon of St. Petronius, bishop of Verona, in which St. Zeno is called confessor in these words:

> The heightened loftiness of this shrine proves it; while it holds within its bosom the most holy confessor, the fragrance of his sweetness is dispersed far and wide.

The title of the sermon is: “Sermon of St. Petronius, Bishop of Verona, on the Feast of St. Zeno.” The most distinguished ornament of the republic of letters, Marquis Scipio Maffei, published this sermon, saying among other things:

> The codex is of little antiquity, but was copied from another which must have been of much greater age.

Since, therefore, this manuscript derives from an older codex, and since there are examples of older manuscripts concerning St. Zeno’s martyrdom having been corrupted by a second hand—as we showed in two martyrologies of the cathedral chapter of Pistoia and the library of the venerable House of Wisdom in that same city, in the book on St. Zeno’s Martyrdom, chapter 2—it is uncertain whether the word “confessor” is truly read in the autograph sermon of St. Petronius. For the epithet “most holy” [Col. 0756C] seems rather proper to a martyr than to a confessor. Yet, if we take the name “confession” to mean martyrdom—as it is beyond doubt that it did in ancient times—it is perfectly clear that it in no way prejudices the martyrdom of St. Zeno. The prudent reader may judge from the following paragraph how much weight such arguments possess.

## § VII. Manuscript Authors and Documents Asserting the Martyrdom of St. Zeno

In treating of St. Zeno’s martyrdom in book II, chapters 1, 2, 3, and 4, we have assembled many materials which the learned reader may inspect there: the uncorrupted testimony of St. Gregory; that of Paul the Deacon, Rabanus, Notker, Bede, Usuard, Wandalbert, and other later writers, who by common assent declare St. Zeno a martyr. Nor are many others lacking who agree with them: John the Deacon in the *Life of Gregory*, 35; Ado, in his additions for 8 December; William Pastrengo of Verona, who wrote in the fourteenth century in his book *On Origins*:

> Zeno, bishop of Verona, is held illustrious in the time of the emperor Gallienus, and suffers martyrdom.

So Pastrengo. Sixtus of Siena, in the *Bibliotheca*, book IV: “Zeno, bishop and martyr of Verona, 604.” Hermannus Contractus, in the *Chronicle of the Six Ages of the World*: “There suffered [under Gallienus] at Rome Pope Fabian . . . and at Verona Bishop Zeno.” Bernardino Corio, also in his Milanese History, speaking of the emperor Gallienus, says that St. Zeno, bishop of Verona, was crowned with martyrdom. Vincent of Beauvais asserts the same in his *Historical Mirror*, book II, chapter 83. Marianus Scotus places St. Zeno’s martyrdom in the year of Christ 369. The objections raised against the authority of so many men have been rejected above.

Very many manuscripts and ancient documents also confirm St. Zeno as a martyr. We transcribed in chapter 2 of the book on St. Zeno’s Martyrdom those found in the Church of Pistoia. Yet on p. 69 an error crept into the citation of the words of a certain catalogue:

> The deposition of St. Zeno, our patron, martyr of Verona.

I read it thus because the ancient characters, considerably worn by age, presented that appearance at first sight. But when the archive of the most illustrious Canons was examined by the Reverend Father Francesco Antonio Zaccaria, S.J., a man of consummate learning and most expert in antiquities, whose keen eye misses nothing, and the manuscript was inspected with closer care, it was discovered that it should be read, as you see here: “our [patron]. Victor, martyr.” For after the words “our patron” there is a full stop; the other words are to be read separately from what precedes: “of Victor, martyr.” I am not ashamed to acknowledge my errors.

The very ancient manuscript of the Anonymous Pipinian, written at the end of the eighth century or at least at the beginning of the ninth, as the Ballerini brothers very rightly conjecture, sings of St. Zeno as a martyr in its *Rhythm*:

> The eighth shepherd and confessor, Zeno, illustrious martyr.

An authentic instrument executed in the time of Charles, king of Italy—who, according to Sigonio, book IV of the *History of the Kingdom of Italy*, died in 814—on the occasion of the first consecration [Col. 0757C] of the Church of Saints Gregory and Zeno, now called St. Helena at Verona, the words of which we have quoted above, adorns St. Zeno with the title of martyr.

In a privilege granted by Berengar to the monastery of St. Zeno in 901, St. Zeno is twice called confessor and once martyr, in accordance with the ancient practice of calling martyrs confessors as well.

In another privilege granted to the same monastery by Emperor Henry in 1055, St. Zeno is twice called martyr.

The Church of Freising, which received the cult of St. Zeno from St. Corbinian, first bishop of that church, whose death occurred in 730, always acknowledged him as a martyr.

A ninth-century calendar prefixed to the Sacramentary of St. Gregory [Col. 0757D], in the Vatican Library in 1806, calls St. Zeno a martyr on 12 April.

To this must be added the manuscripts of the Churches of Verona and Pistoia, of which we spoke above.

There follow other printed and manuscript martyrologies and calendars: the Cassinese calendar, published in vol. VII of *Rerum Italicarum*, p. 936, in which, in April, Zeno is said to have “been crowned with martyrdom”; John, priest of Verona, in his manuscript imperial history, writes: “After many sufferings St. Zeno rested in Christ, on the second day before the Ides of April”; and a charter written in 769 in the village of Campellione in the diocese of Milan calls St. Zeno “the most blessed confessor of Christ.” St. Zeno is also called martyr in an ancient parchment manuscript martyrology of Verona Cathedral; likewise in a most ancient martyrology of the Brothers of the Order of Preachers, preserved in the place called the repository of the Brothers of St. Anastasia; likewise in an ancient parchment manuscript martyrology of the nuns of the Church of St. Mary Magdalene in Campo Marzio of the Order of Friars Minor; likewise in the martyrology of the nuns of St. Lucy at Verona of the Order of St. Benedict, as Perettus reports in his Scholia. In the martyrology of the Order of Preachers revised after the Council of Trent, it is said:

> On the day before the Ides of April, the same day: St. Zeno, bishop, who wonderfully governed the city of Verona amid the storms of persecutions and was crowned with martyrdom in the time of Gallienus.

In nearly the same words Perettus reports another martyrology entitled *Viola of the Saints*, and another martyrology at St. Mark’s in the city of Rome.

Perettus also testifies that he saw certain fragments collected by Panvinio that mention St. Zeno’s martyrdom. I shall quote his words from chapter 5 of the Life of St. Zeno:

> In certain fragments of Brother Onofrio Panvinio of Verona, a most diligent chronicler and investigator of antiquities, which we saw on 4 February 1574 in the possession of his brother Paolo, mention is made that St. Zeno, bishop of Verona, was bound, repeatedly captured, and beaten. A corresponding event is said to have happened to him when he went to preach in the overseas regions of Asia, especially in Syria. For he was seized by a priest of false and lying gods, together with his followers; he was bound and beaten, then cruelly dragged over rough places. His hands and feet were bound, he was cruelly beaten, and, half alive and dying, was abandoned by them. But immediately after their departure, by divine power he was preserved from death, freed from his bonds, and miraculously restored to his former condition. Afterwards, when he delivered the son of that impious and cruel idolatrous priest from the demon that most cruelly tormented him because of the cruelty used by the father against the person of St. Zeno, the fame of these two miracles at once spread through those regions. A great multitude of sick persons therefore flocked to him so that through him they might obtain the benefit of health; and by divine power he restored them to their former health. There he bore great fruit, destroying idols and confirming his teaching by miracles, especially by driving out demons [Col. 0758D] from human bodies and from places dedicated to idols.

These fragments agree with what is read in the hymn of the holy bishop:

> He was a great priest of the Most High,  
> Penetrating the unbridled peoples beyond the sea;  
> From there God ordained  
> To send him to the city of Verona.

The very ancient manuscript of the Anonymous Pipinian agrees as well:

> I cannot recount the many works of this saint  
> And the wonders which God showed through him  
> As he came from Syria all the way to Italy.

Many churches venerate St. Zeno as a martyr. In the diocese of Padua, among other churches, there is one at Mount Silicis, called that of St. Thomas the Apostle and St. Zeno, Confessor of Christ. In the diocese of Brescia, where St. Zeno’s cult was extremely ancient, fifteen churches dedicated to St. Zeno are counted: nine observe the Feast of Ordination on 8 December with the Office of a confessor-bishop, while the rest observe it on the day before the Ides of April with the Office of a martyr. At the monastery at Halle in the diocese of Salzburg, St. Zeno is likewise venerated with the Office of a martyr both on the April feast and on the day of his Translation. Throughout the whole Congregation of Monte Cassino we learned from the Calendar prefixed to the *Monastic Psalter of the Order of St. Benedict of the Cassinese Congregation of St. Justina of Padua*, published at Venice in 1606, that the memorial of this saint, Zeno, was kept. It reads under 8 December:

> The Conception of the Blessed Virgin Mary, greater double; and a commemoration of Zeno, bishop and martyr.

These things suffice, leaving aside other evidence that might be adduced and that we have mentioned in this Dissertation; for they seem sufficient to prove St. Zeno’s martyrdom.

For what do those who deny St. Zeno’s martyrdom offer against these things? A forced and uncertain text of St. Ambrose; a begged-for and implausible lapse of memory attributed to St. Gregory; an unwise credulity attributed to illustrious authors. They offer several manuscripts which call St. Zeno confessor on the Feast of his Ordination, precisely when the feast ought to be celebrated with the Office of a confessor-bishop. But how shamelessly they assert: “Neither calendars, whether ours or foreign . . . call him a martyr, but distinguish him solely by the title of confessor”! From the manuscripts, martyrologies, and calendars just cited, this is plainly disproved. They also offer the stone inscription in the Church of St. George at Verona, now St. Helena, in which a manifest error is detected and falsehood demonstrated.

They have one church of St. Zeno at Ruvico in the diocese of Treviso, which, on the day before the Ides of April, when the feast of martyrdom is celebrated, commemorates St. Zeno with the Office of a confessor-bishop. They also have another inscription in the Church of Monte Aureo in the diocese of Verona, hitherto unpublished, carefully transcribed long ago by Father Giuseppe Bianchini and published by the Ballerini brothers, in which St. Zeno is written “Confessor.” Who, even with eyes closed, would not recognize the error of the Church of St. Zeno at Ruvico [Col. 0760B] and of these two inscriptions, set against so many documents and traditions of very many other churches? What weight have these things, that they could nullify the others? And who would not laugh at that fiction, emerging only from a mind hardened in its own opinion: namely, that antiphons and Gospels for martyrs in Paschal time are also common to a confessor-bishop?

## JUDGMENT
Saint Zeno’s martyrdom, established on the authority of Saint Gregory the Great, cannot be called into doubt when it is supported by the tradition of the Church of Verona and of other Churches, and by the unanimous agreement of the more celebrated authors and of ancient codices and manuscripts, plainly expressed in their writings. The title “Confessor” [Col. 0760B] assigned to Saint Zeno at the feast of his Ordination, and the office of a Confessor Bishop celebrated on the same feast-day, are in accordance with ecclesiastical rite. Nor can the one church in the diocese of Treviso which, on the day before the Ides of April, celebrates the feast of a Confessor Bishop when Saint Zeno’s martyrdom is commemorated, be an argument, against so many other Churches which on that same day celebrate the feast of a Martyr Bishop, for counting Saint Zeno among Confessors rather than Martyrs. For the distinction between Saint Zeno’s feasts is evident: all the other Churches celebrate Saint Zeno’s Ordination on the sixth day before the Ides of December with the office of a Confessor Bishop; but on the day before the Ides of April they commemorate his martyrdom with the office of a Martyr Bishop. Therefore, if in any Martyrology Saint Zeno is called a Confessor on that same April feast [Col. 0760C], it is clear that this was done in error, contrary to the judgment of so many distinguished authors, the most ancient testimony of old codices, and the tradition of the Church of Verona and of other Churches. Accordingly, since the Supreme Pontiff Sixtus V, after an exact examination of this cause, delivered his judgment in his Brief dated 26 November 1588, commanding that Saint Zeno’s Ordination be celebrated with the office of a Confessor Bishop, but the feasts of his Martyrdom and Translation with the office of a Martyr Bishop, everyone ought to embrace this judgment and venerate Saint Zeno as a true martyr, henceforth abstaining from all dispute. Praise be to God, to the Virgin Mother of God, and to Saint Zeno, Martyr and Bishop of Verona. Amen.

## A.D. 370–374. SAINT OPTATUS, BISHOP OF MILEVIS

## PROLEGOMENA

[Col. 0759]

### 1. PREFACE

*(By Louis Ellies du Pin.)*

[Col. 0759C] This Preface will have three parts. The first concerns the Life [Col. 0759D] of Optatus; the second, his books; the third, a new edition of them [Col. 0760C] and of other monuments concerning the Donatists [Col. 0760D].

## I.—ON THE LIFE OF OPTATUS

[Col. 0761A]

Optatus: an African and bishop of Milevis. When he wrote. How long he lived. How highly honored his memory was. How his name entered the Roman Martyrology.—The first point may be disposed of briefly: for scarcely anything else is known to us concerning Optatus except that he was African, as Jerome testifies, and bishop of Milevis. The time at which he flourished is inferred from his work. For in Book I, §13, he says that sixty years and more before, the storm of persecution had spread throughout all Africa. The persecution of Diocletian, of which he unquestionably speaks here, began in February of the common era 303 and ceased in the West in 305. From this it follows that Optatus wrote after 365, and about 370. [Col. 0761B] In Book IV of the same work he calls Photinus “a heretic of the present time,” words which seem to indicate that Photinus was still alive when he wrote. But Photinus died in 376, as Jerome’s *Chronicle* teaches. To this is added Jerome’s testimony that Optatus wrote under the emperors Valentinian and Valens, and therefore between 372, when Valentinian was elected emperor on the day following the leap-day, and 375, when the same emperor, struck by apoplexy, died on the fifteenth day before the Kalends of September at the fortress of Brigetio, as Idatius testifies.

There is one point which can scarcely be reconciled with this chronology: namely, the name of Siricius, which occurs after Damasus in the list of Roman bishops drawn up by Optatus in Book II, §3. Since Siricius was not [Col. 0761C] elevated to the Roman see before 384—some years after the death of Valentinian and Valens, and eighty years after the persecution of Diocletian—Optatus could not, about 370 while Valentinian was alive, enumerate Siricius among the Roman bishops and write that he was his colleague, and that the whole world, through him and the exchange of letters of communion, agreed with him in a single fellowship of communion. But this difficulty is easily resolved if we say—as must necessarily be assumed—that Siricius’ name was added after the work had been completed, either by another person or, more probably, by Optatus himself.

The reason for assigning this addition to Optatus rather than another is that, at the beginning of the following section, the writer, setting forth the succession of those who, on Donatus’ side, claimed to be Roman bishops, speaks of Macrobius as present and alive when [Col. 0761D] he wrote: “Behold,” he says, “there are present there, at Rome, the memorials of the two apostles. Say whether he could enter among these or offer there, where the memorials of the saints are known to be. It remains, therefore, that your associate Macrobius admit that he sits there where Encolpius once sat,” and so forth. Who would not understand from this that Macrobius, Encolpius’ successor in the succession of Roman bishops on Donatus’ side, was still alive when Optatus wrote this? Yet at the end of this chapter two are listed after Macrobius. Thus Claudianus seems to have succeeded Lucianus, Lucianus Macrobius, Macrobius Encolpius, Encolpius Bonifacius, and Bonifacius Victor. It is therefore evident that the names of Claudianus and Lucianus were added after the work had been written. But [Col. 0762A] these additions appear to have been made by the author rather than by another—certainly not by a later copyist, to whom the names of those obscure bishops, concerning whom history is utterly silent, could not have been known.

Accordingly, about the year 370, under Valentinian and Valens, while Damasus occupied the see at Rome, Optatus composed his six books against Parmenianus. But he lived until the pontificate of Siricius and the reign of Theodosius, at which time he revised his books and perhaps composed those additions contained in Book VII, of which we shall presently speak. In what year he died is uncertain. Yet his memory was always held in honor among Christians because of his distinguished defense of the Church. Augustine calls him “a bishop of the Catholic communion, of venerable memory,” and does not hesitate to compare his testimony with Ambrose’s. From the beginning of the sixth century after Christ, the name “Saint” is found bestowed upon him by Fulgentius, bishop of Ruspe, a man of outstanding holiness and learning, who joins the authority of Saint Optatus to the testimonies of Saint Ambrose and Saint Augustine.

In the Roman Martyrology, under 4 June, Baronius entered among the saints Optatus of Milevis, [Col. 0762B] whose name is found in no other Martyrology except in the catalogue of Peter de Natalibus. Peter thought that Optatus, bishop of Auxerre, whose feast is celebrated on 31 August, was the same person as Optatus of Milevis, and believed that his commemoration was made on that day. Recognizing this error, Baronius restored the Optatus of Auxerre to 31 August; but, considering it a matter of conscience wholly to erase our Optatus—whom Peter de Natalibus had assigned a place among the saints—from the Martyrology, he transferred him to 4 June, for what reason I do not know, unless perhaps because the person who had preceded Baronius in the new edition of the Roman Martyrology had entered Caecilius, a priest of Carthage, among the saints on the preceding day. For both the year and day of Optatus’ death are wholly uncertain, and nowhere in the world is any church or altar consecrated to God found under his invocation.

## II.—ON THE BOOKS OF OPTATUS

The occasion of Optatus’ work. Who Parmenianus was, whom Optatus refutes. Parmenianus’ work.—Optatus’ work, though small in bulk, offers us much more ample matter for discussion. The author himself explains its occasion in Book I, §1: “The Donatists everywhere rang out with abusive cries against the Catholics. Many Catholics had often desired that a debate should be held by some defenders of the parties, in order to bring out the truth. But the Donatists, distrustful of their cause and fleeing the Catholics, prevented access, barred entry, avoided a meeting, and refused a conference. But Parmenianus, their bishop, not content to assail the Catholics with words which vanish into the winds, set forth the thoughts of his mind in writing. Seizing this opportunity, Optatus, compelled by truth, undertook to answer his writings, so that in this way there might, as it were, be a conference between persons absent.”

That Parmenianus, whose work Optatus refutes, succeeded Donatus about 350 [Col. 0763A] in the see which Majorinus had established at Carthage against Caecilianus. That Parmenianus was not African is clear from Optatus’ testimony: twice he calls him a foreigner, once in Book I, §5, and again in Book III, §3. Moreover, he testifies that Parmenianus was among those whom the Donatists, roaming over seas and lands, had made their proselytes and ordained at Carthage. The work of Parmenianus to which Optatus replies differs from the letter of the same Parmenianus to the Donatist Tichonius, against which Augustine wrote three books. In that letter Parmenianus criticized what Tichonius, a Donatist, had written concerning the Church contrary to his sect’s doctrines. In the treatise refuted by Optatus, however, he attacked the Catholic Church. The division, method, and subject of the two works differ, although the same insults against the Catholic Church were read in both.

Division of Optatus’ work. Whether Optatus’ seventh book is genuine. Grounds for doubt. What judgment should be made of it.—Optatus divides his whole reply to Parmenianus’ treatise into six books, the contents of which he gives in Book I, §7. Jerome likewise enumerates six books of Optatus, and no more. A seventh book has now been added; formerly, following learned men, I considered it spurious and by another author. Three considerations chiefly moved me to this opinion. First, the silence of Optatus himself and of Jerome. Even if it were said that Optatus, having first intended to write only six books, added a seventh afterwards, it can scarcely be believed or maintained concerning Jerome that, if the seventh book had been joined to the others in his time, he would have omitted it in his *Catalogue*. The second and principal reason which influenced me was that the crime of *traditio*—the surrender of sacred books—which Optatus in Book I calls the worst of crimes, compares to idolatry, and teaches is punishable by the loss of eternal life, is greatly minimized in this book. Its author, accumulating from every direction rather weak arguments and examples wholly irrelevant to the matter, endeavors and labors to excuse the *traditores* from the charge. Thirdly, some difference of style between this book and the others seemed to me to suggest that another was its author.

Such was my view before I had consulted Optatus’ manuscript codices. But after I learned that everything tending to minimize the crime of *traditio* is absent from the manuscripts which I had the opportunity to see, I realized that the chief battering-ram directed against this book had been taken from me. Then, when I saw that a portion of this seventh book had been appended to the end of Book III—though, because of similarity of subject, it belongs there, it is nevertheless referred to the seventh book in all manuscripts—I was led, after more careful consideration, to the opinion that the part of Optatus’ work called Book VII is not really a book distinct from the others, but additions composed by Optatus himself after the work was completed and attached to certain books.

Indeed, since the Donatists might object to what he had said in Book I about their *traditores*, whom he nevertheless wished to regard as brothers—“If our fathers are *traditores*, why do you call us brothers? Why do you invite us to your communion?”—Optatus judged that he ought to meet this difficulty by explaining why and for what reason he invited the Donatists to his communion even though they were sons of *traditores*. This he does in §§1, 2, and 3, and these passages consequently belong to Book I. What is said in §§4 and 5 about dying flies that spoil the sweetness of ointment, and about Jannes and Mambres, belongs to the end of Book II, or rather to Book IV, where similar reproaches are refuted. What follows about Macarius has no connection with what precedes, but is undoubtedly an addition to Book III. Thus what is called Optatus’ seventh book is nothing other than a threefold addition to three books of Optatus; consequently, there were in reality no more than six books, nor should more be counted.

It is likely that, in the old codices of Optatus which Jerome had before him, these additions were placed at the end without the heading “Book VII”; hence he mentioned only six books of Optatus. Finally, the dissimilarity of style which had also troubled me appeared chiefly in the spurious addition minimizing the gravity of *traditio*; moreover, readers will see that Optatus’ style is not altogether even. From this, it is sufficiently clear what should be thought of Optatus’ seventh book.

Usefulness of Optatus’ books.—The subject of the work shows how useful Optatus’ books are. He vigorously defends the Catholic Church against sectarians; writings of this kind are equally useful in every age. For controversies concerning the Church must not be judged in the same way as private questions concerning some particular doctrine. The latter remain current and debated so long as the sects endure which either attack a Catholic doctrine or teach some error; once such sects have disappeared, they are effaced by oblivion, and, when a heresy has been extinguished, books attacking it are not so useful. But since all heresies and schisms have this in common, that they attack the Church from which they have departed, writings in which the Church has been defended against some particular opponents are equally valid against all; they oppose all heretics, whatever they may be, and will be judged equally useful to Catholics as long as heretics or schismatics exist.

How many and how great matters concerning the Church’s doctrine and discipline are contained in Optatus’ books.—But apart from what concerns the defense of the Church and the Donatist schism, scarcely any ancient monument can be found—not merely of the same size, but even a far more extensive work—that contains so many and such important matters concerning Christian doctrine and discipline so explicitly. Optatus testifies that all Christians possess one and the same faith and one and the same creed, from which heretics have deserted. He explains the principal articles of faith briefly, clearly, and altogether orthodoxly. He shows that there is one holy Catholic Church spread throughout the whole world, and that no other can exist, nor can it be confined within the narrow limits of any one region. He declares that it consists of bishops, priests, deacons, and the body of the faithful. He affirms that bishops hold the first priesthood, priests the second, and deacons the third; by this he sufficiently shows that bishops stand above priests, just as priests stand above deacons. He acknowledges the Roman Church as mother of the others and the center of unity, on account of Peter, who was head of the apostles.

He teaches that human beings are weak and imperfect by their own nature, and need God’s grace in order to become perfect; that sin is innate in all of us, and baptism necessary in order that we may obtain its remission. “Nevertheless,” he says, “it belongs to the human being to will what is good and to run in what he has willed, although it is not given to him to bring it to completion, so that, after the course which a human being ought to complete, something may remain for God, that He may assist the one who falls short.” By these words he seems to attribute rather more to the powers of our free will than is proper. He says that “no human being is free from sin during this life, and that the sacrament of baptism, once conferred in the name of the Trinity, must not be repeated.” Yet he seems to hold as certain that the washing of those baptized among heretics is invalid, because it requires faith in the minister; but because he assumes that faith in the recipient is necessary, as may be seen in Book V, §8, he does not doubt that the baptism of those baptized in faith by schismatics or evil ministers ought to be held valid. He thinks that those once immersed in John’s baptism before the institution of Christ’s baptism were not washed again. He commends exorcism as a rite preceding baptism. He mentions chrism as a holy thing, and also the anointing customarily performed in baptism.

He sets forth his mind concerning the real presence of Christ’s Body and Blood in the Eucharist, and the adoration due to it, in words so clear that nothing more explicit could be desired. He observes many ceremonies pertaining to the celebration of the Eucharist, which he designates by the name of sacrifice. From what he says, it is evident that in his time sacrifice was offered for the whole Church; that the Lord’s Prayer was customarily recited in it; that the sacred rites were celebrated upon a decorated wooden altar, covered with linen for greater reverence; and that golden and silver chalices and ornaments were used. He says that the Church has its own judges; that crimes are punished; and that those who confess to having committed grave sins, or are convicted of them, are subjected to penance.

He praises virginity, but does not wish anyone to be bound to preserve it except those who have bound themselves by a vow. He observes that in his time virgins who consecrated themselves to God solemnly pronounced that vow, and that veils were placed upon their heads as a sign of the vow they had made. He sufficiently testifies to the reverence in which relics of the saints were held in his time when he speaks of the tomb of the blessed Peter and Paul; when he censures Lucilla’s act, who was said to kiss the bone of a pseudo-martyr, or at least of a martyr not yet vindicated; and when in Book III he speaks of those whom the Donatists [Col. 0766A] venerated as martyrs. He indicates that preaching the divine word was a duty proper to bishops, and that it was the solemn custom for every discourse in the Church to begin with God’s name and end with the name of the same God.

From the saying of Purpurius of Limata, reported by Optatus himself in Book I—“Let him come out here as though a hand were laid upon him for the episcopate and his head were freed from penance”—it may be inferred that persons once subjected to public penance were forbidden to advance to orders. It also follows that episcopal ordination is performed by the laying on of hands. But what Caecilianus says in the same place—that, if Felix had contributed nothing against him, he should be ordained as if still a deacon—gives room for the suspicion that in that period a deacon was ordained bishop without prior laying on of hands as priest. From the same Optatus it is certain that Christians had several basilicas; indeed, Book I, §4 testifies that Rome already had more than forty when Victor, sent there by the Donatists, was made bishop. These and many other matters of the same kind will present themselves as most worthy of notice to careful readers of Optatus’ books.

On Optatus’ style.—As for his style, it is grand, forceful, and compact, though less elegant and polished. He presses fiercely those whom he attacks; he sets before the eyes, as it were, the events he narrates; he explains passages ingeniously; he expresses his thought with the utmost subtlety and acuteness; and he uses words and expressions especially fitted to signify what he wishes to state. He constructs lively and delightful narratives. Whoever wishes for an example should read the description of bird-catching which closes Book VI; nothing more elegant or more apt could be devised. In a word, no one versed in these matters will deny that the author of this work possessed great learning and outstanding talent.

On the allegorical exposition of Scripture followed by Optatus.—One thing may be blamed in him: that allegorical sense according to which he expounds very many testimonies of Holy Scripture. A defect tolerable in a preacher seems scarcely pardonable in a polemical author defending religion against heretics, in controversies with whom arguments ought to be firm and indisputable. But Optatus dealt with adversaries who proceeded in the same way and abused testimonies of Scripture in order to calumniate the Church and praise their own sect. The testimonies cited by Parmenianus in this work may be seen; he twists them into a meaning wholly alien to their true sense. Having noted this, it remains to explain what we have done in this edition of Optatus.

## III.—ON THIS NEW EDITION OF OPTATUS’ BOOKS AND OTHER MONUMENTS CONCERNING THE DONATISTS

What we have done.—Our labor has been chiefly occupied with four things: correcting the text; preparing new notes or publishing others’ observations [Col. 0767A]; adding ancient monuments relating to the history of the Donatists; and briefly composing a history of this schism from its origin to its end.

Optatus’ text hitherto extremely corrupt. List of earlier editions. Manuscript codices used by us.—Hitherto Optatus’ text has been extremely corrupt. It was first printed at Mainz in 1549 through the care of Johannes Cochlaeus. Balduin, who prepared a new edition of this work at Paris in 1563 with the assistance of a collation of a manuscript supplied to him by Espensaeus, a Parisian theologian of some distinction, states that there were more errors than verses in that edition. This edition contained only the first six books; but shortly afterward they added the seventh, printed in smaller type. In 1569, however, the same editor issued a more corrected edition at Paris, using two manuscripts, one owed to Jean de Tillet, bishop of Meaux, the other to Maceraeus, a Parisian theologian. With their help he restored many passages; yet he admits in his Preface that many errors and many lacunae still remained. The Commelinian edition was produced in 1599 from that edition.

In the following century, Albaspinaeus, bishop of Orléans—who was almost the first among our countrymen seriously to devote himself to elucidating the discipline of the ancient Church—undertook a new edition of Optatus’ books, which appeared at Paris immediately after his death in 1631. Yet so far was the text from having been improved in this edition that, on the contrary, it abounds in countless typographical errors, against which the editor’s negligence made little provision. In the same year Meric Casaubon published the seven books of Optatus in London; but in correcting this author he used no manuscript codex, and changed many passages from conjecture alone, whether rightly or wrongly.

The most learned Rigalt, after publishing Tertullian, Minucius, and Cyprian, had resolved to add Optatus also. One may suppose that, being most skilled in textual criticism and well versed in antiquity and the knowledge of manuscript codices, he would have removed many errors of great importance and restored Optatus’ text entire. But he died before undertaking the work. Finally, Prior presided over a new edition of Optatus’ books, published at Paris at the expense of the bookseller Jean Dupuis. In his notice to the reader he admits that Optatus’ text is extremely corrupt. Yet not only did he do nothing whatever to make it appear more correct; by his negligence he also allowed new *sphalmata*—errors—to creep into the text. “What,” he says, “can one do where there is the greatest scarcity of manuscripts of better [Col. 0767D] quality?” Nothing indeed, if matters stood so. But though manuscript codices of Optatus are very rare, they are not altogether nonexistent; and had he applied even a little diligence, it could scarcely have happened that he would not have encountered one or two codices of Optatus.

I, whether more fortunate or more careful than Prior, found five manuscript codices of Optatus. By their help nearly innumerable errors have been removed, and the text has almost everywhere been restored entire. The first, and most ancient, is the codex of Saint-Theodoric at Rheims, at least seven hundred years old. The second, not indeed of the same antiquity but of the highest quality, is the manuscript codex of Saint-Germain-des-Prés, certainly very correct. The third, formerly belonging to Maceraeus, the Parisian theologian, was supplied to me by Philippe Sylvius, doctor of the Sacred Faculty of Paris, into whose hands it had come. It is written in a later hand and is very faulty. The fourth is the manuscript codex of Saint-Paul of Cormery near Tours, now entered in the Colbert Library under number 1951. This codex is more than six hundred years old and of the highest quality. Would that all of Optatus’ books were still preserved in it; but, regrettably, the leaves containing the first five books and the beginning of the sixth have been lost.

Besides these, this manuscript codex contains monuments relating to the history of the ancient Donatists, which are found in no other manuscript codex. One point should be noted concerning these codices: the codex of Philippe Sylvius appears to have been copied from that of Saint-Theodoric, and the Saint-Germain codex from the Cormery codex. With the aid of these codices it can scarcely be stated how many passages we have restored: we corrected corrupt readings, restored displaced passages to their proper places, supplied omissions, and cut out interpolations. In a word, Optatus’ text appears entire and corrected, restored to its native splendor. We have scarcely indulged conjecture at all except where supported by manuscript codices. We have set down the variant readings separately from the notes at the foot of each page; from them one may see how many and what great errors and faults have been removed by us, and how many obscure passages, and passages wholly devoid of sense, have received light. Such is our work concerning the correction of the text. Its elucidation is also greatly assisted by its division into articles or paragraphs, with brief arguments set in the margin—something never before done in Optatus’ books.

As regards the notes, we have composed afresh only a few—brief and necessary ones—and placed them at the foot of each page after the variant readings, together with the notes of Albaspinaeus, Meric Casaubon, Barthius, and an unknown writer. We have added Balduin’s observations and Albaspinaeus’ appendices entire to Optatus’ books, but cleansed of the countless typographical errors that had crept into the editions of Albaspinaeus and Prior. We should not have omitted Prior’s notes if anything of any value had been found in them that had not been observed by others; but whoever possesses the annotations of the others would seek these in vain.

Monuments appended by Optatus himself to his books.—The notes of various writers are followed by ancient monuments relating to the history of the Donatists, arranged chronologically and corrected from manuscript codices and better editions.

It is not new to attach monuments of this sort to Optatus’ books. Optatus himself had done the same: in order to establish the truth of what he had written concerning Donatist history, he had appended at the end of his books the acts themselves and the documentary records. This he testifies in Book I, [Col. 0769A] §13, where, speaking of the Council of Cirta, he cites as evidence the writings of Nundinarius the deacon and the ancient parchments of the acts of this council, which, he says, “we shall be able to produce for those who doubt; for we have added the full account of these matters in the final part of these little books in order to establish the truth.” Likewise, speaking in the same book, §20, of the letter of Majorinus’ ordainers against Caecilianus, he says that he has it among the other acts for later use. In the same place, §26, he also testifies that he had transcribed the volume of the acts of Eunomius and Olympius in the final parts of his work. In the following section the acts of Felix’s vindication are likewise mentioned by him; it is not likely that he omitted them from his collection of records.

From these acts, perhaps, which Saint Optatus had appended to the end of his work, were derived the records of the vindication of Caecilianus and Felix of Aptunga held in the manuscript codex of Saint-Paul of Cormery, together with the collection of various letters of Emperor Constantine concerning the Donatists. These monuments were appended to Optatus’ books in the editions of Albaspinaeus and Prior, together with the Conference of Carthage, although Masson had first published them separately in 1589, and Pithou afterwards.

Following their example, in our edition we have presented all the ancient monuments relating to the history of the Donatists: namely, the acts of councils and episcopal conferences, bishops’ letters, imperial edicts and letters, and proconsular proceedings.

[Col. 0769C] First among these stands the edict against Christians issued by Diocletian and Maximian, whose text we give from Lactantius and Eusebius. Although it does not concern the Donatists, because it later gave occasion to the schism and the chronology of the Donatist sect is reckoned from it, we judged that it should be placed at the head of the records relating to Donatist history.

There follow the acts of African martyrs, which concern the charge of *traditio* imputed by the Donatists to the Catholics. These are followed by the records of the vindication of Felix and Caecilianus, which, though later, explain the events that occurred during the persecution. In these we followed the edition of the most distinguished Baluze, who inserted these acts in Book II of his *Miscellanea* after collating them with the Thouane manuscript codex, now in the Colbert Library, [Col. 0770A] and we have also appended his notes. After this are read certain monuments relating to the beginning of the Donatist schism. Then follow Constantine’s letters concerning the case of Caecilianus and the Donatists, together with the decrees issued on the matter under his rule.

The Donatists cast nothing more frequently in the Catholics’ teeth than what they had suffered under Leontius, Ursatius, and Macarius. Relevant to this is the sermon of a certain Donatist, now first published by us from a manuscript codex in the library of the most illustrious and reverend bishop of Châlons, approximately five hundred years old but the work of a very ancient writer.
