This is followed by the Passion of Marculus, a Donatist priest, also mentioned by Optatus. It had already been published in Volume IV of Mabillon’s *Analecta*, but now appears more correctly after collation with the Corbie codex. This codex also supplied us with the complete Passion of the Donatists Maximian and Isaac, only part of which Mabillon had published there. Then, down to the Conference of Carthage, come the ecclesiastical and civil laws enacted against the Donatists. To the civil laws taken from the Theodosian Code, we have appended the commentary of the most learned Jacques Godefroy.

The acts of the Conference of Carthage, corrected through the care and industry of the most distinguished and learned Baluze, are inserted in their proper place according to his edition. We have prepared new notes, especially concerning the sees of the African bishops present at the conference. Baluze had already observed much about them, but after him the learned Father Thierry Ruinart treated the matter more carefully in his notes to the *Notitia of the African Bishops under Huneric*. From these we have, to conceal nothing, borrowed almost everything that we have said concerning those sees. In order to exhaust the subject, we have composed a sacred geography, or account of the provinces and bishoprics of Africa. It is followed by a geographical map drawn by a most skilled geographer, in which the division of the African provinces and the position of the principal episcopal sees are set before the eyes.

Finally, after this Preface we have prefixed to the entire work a history of the Donatist schism, in which events are set forth, not in an elaborate or ornate manner, but accurately and chronologically, each assigned to its proper time.

## 7. TESTIMONIES OF THE ANCIENTS CONCERNING OPTATUS AND HIS BOOKS

### Saint Jerome, in *On Illustrious Men*, chapter 121

[Col. 0769C]

[Col. 0769D] Optatus, an African and bishop of Milevis, wrote on the Catholic side under the emperors Valentinian and Valens six books against the calumny of the Donatist party, in which he maintains that the charge of the Donatists is falsely turned against us.

### Saint Augustine, Book II of *On Christian Doctrine*, chapter 40, no. 61

[Col. 0770C]

[Col. 0770D] Do we not see how richly Cyprian, most pleasing teacher and most blessed martyr, departed from Egypt laden with gold, silver, and clothing; how richly Lactantius, Victorinus, Optatus, and Hilary did likewise—to say nothing of those still living?

### The same, Book I against the Letter of Parmenianus, chapter 13, no. 5

[Col. 0771A]

Let those who wish read what Optatus, bishop of Milevis, of the Catholic communion and venerable memory, recounts, and by what documents he establishes so many facts: whether concerning Lucilla, then a very wealthy and highly factional woman, whom Saint Caecilianus, while still a deacon, had offended in enforcing the Church’s discipline; or concerning the other associates of her faction—whether thieves of the Church’s silver, or persons aggrieved that they had not attained the episcopate and who, resenting Caecilianus’ preference over them, persecuted him by every intrigue within their power; or concerning the Numidian bishops whom this faction had summoned for Caecilianus’ destruction, so that, after he was deposed, another might be ordained for them. These matters are found in Optatus’ first book.

### The same, in *On the Unity of the Church*, chapter 19, no. 50

[Col. 0771B]

Nor do we say that we ought to be believed merely because Optatus of Milevis or Ambrose of Milan has commended the very Church which we hold.

### The same, in the *Short Account of the Conference*, chapter 20, no. 38
But, repulsed on this point, the Donatist bishops, as though they were about to produce something of the greatest force, demanded that Optatus be read—something they had also demanded earlier—by which, they said, they would prove that Caecilian had been condemned by the emperor. … They pressed much more insistently for Optatus to be read. … Optatus was read, as the Donatists read the passage where he says: “At the same time Donatus requested permission to return and to proceed to Carthage; then Philumenus, his advocate, represented to the emperor that, for the sake of peace, Caecilian should be kept at Brescia”; and this was done. … Since in these words of Optatus no condemnation whatsoever of Caecilian could be found—as they had promised they would demonstrate—the judicial examiner ordered the entire page to be read, so that from the preceding and following words the intention of the writer might be known. And the official record was read: “Caecilian was pronounced innocent by the judgments of all the aforesaid persons.” While this was being read, the Donatists said that they had not requested that passage to be read, angrily reacting against those who could not restrain their laughter when they heard how plainly a page had been produced against the Donatists themselves. See concerning the same matter chapters 375, 477, and following, down to 484, of the third day of the Conference of Carthage; and afterwards chapter 532 and following, down to 539; and the letter of the Council of Zerta in St Augustine, Letter 141, no. 9.

**8. St Fulgentius, Book II to Monimus, chapter 13.**

The holy bishop of Milevis, moreover, testifies in the sixth book against Parmenian that Paul went beyond obligation in his counsel concerning virgins, in these words: “Virginity is a matter of will, not of necessity”; and the rest found below, Book VI, §4, p. 94, and chapter 15. For there is no departure from truth in this supererogation of the Apostle, whether what St Ambrose, St Augustine, or St Optatus thought is also held by us without injury to the truth of the faith.

**Honorius of Autun, in the Book on Ecclesiastical Writers, chapter III.**

Optatus, an African and bishop of Milevis, wrote under Valens against the calumny of the Donatist party.

**Roman Martyrology, 4 June.**

[Col. 0772C] At Milevis in Numidia, St Optatus, bishop, distinguished for learning and holiness.

[Col. 0771]

# 1. HISTORY OF THE DONATISTS

[Col. 0771C] **The origin of the Christian religion in Africa. Persecutions of Christians. The persecution of Diocletian. The surrender of sacred books.**—Africa did not receive the Christian religion from the beginning, from the Apostles themselves [Note: [Col. 0771D] **Africa did not receive it from the beginning, from the Apostles themselves.** Petilian, in the letter refuted by St Augustine in *On the Unity of the Church*, chapter 15, speaks thus concerning the origin of the Christian religion in Africa: “Of us African Christians it was said: ‘Those who were last shall be first.’ For the Gospel came to Africa later; and therefore nowhere in the Apostolic writings is Africa said to have believed.” In replying, Augustine does not contend that the Africans received the Gospel from the Apostles themselves and from the beginning, but only that certain barbarian nations believed even later than Africa. Hence it is certain that Africa was not last in the order of believing. Tertullian likewise, in *On Prescription against Heretics*, acknowledges that the African Churches were not apostolic—that is, that they had not been founded either by Apostles or by apostolic men who had persevered with the Apostles. Salvian, on the contrary, seems to hold in Book VII of *On Providence* that the Church of Carthage was established by the Apostles. But less credit is due to him, as an outsider and later writer, than to other Africans who were earlier.] but, as is probable, after a century had already elapsed, from the Romans [Note: [Col. 0772D] **From the Romans, as is probable.** St Augustine, in Letter formerly 162, now 43, speaking of the Roman Church: “From which,” he says, “the Gospel came even to Africa.” Innocent I, in his letter to Decentius of Gubbio, says that it is manifest that no one established churches throughout all Italy, Gaul, Spain, Africa, Sicily, and the islands lying between, except those whom the venerable Apostle Peter or his successors appointed as priests. And St Gregory, Book VII, Letter 32, to Dominic, bishop of Carthage: “Knowing besides,” he says, “from what source the priesthood took its beginning in the African regions, you act commendably in that, by loving the Apostolic See, you return with prudent remembrance to the origin of your office.”]; it received the first seeds of the Gospel. Gradually cultivated, they soon produced a great harvest. Although at times the fury of persecutions cut down part of it, it received increase from the very tortures and slaughterings, so that Tertullian could truly say to the pagans concerning the Christians in Africa: “We become more numerous whenever you reap us. The blood of Christians is seed.”

[Col. 0773A] Yet no storm more savage was ever raised against Christians in Africa than that under the emperors Diocletian and Maximian, after the edicts against Christians had been published throughout the world at the beginning of the year 303. Then Anulinus in the proconsular province, and Florus in Numidia, waged war upon the Christian name. Optatus describes it thus, Book III, §8:

> All know what their ingenious cruelty accomplished. The war declared against Christians raged; in the temples of demons the Devil triumphed; the altars smoked with unclean vapours; and, because people could not be brought to sacrilege, they were compelled everywhere to offer incense. Every place became a temple for crime. Old men almost at the point of death were defiled; unwitting childhood was polluted; little children were carried by their mothers to wickedness; parents were compelled to commit bloodless parricides. Some were compelled to overthrow the temples of the living God; others to deny Christ; others to burn the divine laws; others to offer incense.

And the same author, Book I, §13:

> The storm of this persecution, spreading throughout all Africa, made some martyrs and others confessors; it brought down some to a ruinous death and left those in hiding unharmed. Why should I mention the laity, who at that time held no rank in the Church? Why the many ministers? Why the deacons established in the third rank, or the presbyters in the second priesthood? Even some bishops—the very chief persons and leaders of all—at that time, in order to purchase the briefest delays of this uncertain life at the cost of eternal life, wickedly surrendered the instruments of the divine law.

[Col. 0773B] This was the particular evil of the Diocletianic persecution: Christians were compelled to surrender sacred books to be burned. For crafty men thought that the Christian religion could above all be erased from human minds by removing the books in which Christian teaching was contained. Therefore the edict of Diocletian and Maximian particularly provided that the sacred codices should be consumed by flames. To ensure its execution, governors and magistrates in every locality were commanded to wrest the divine books from the hands of bishops and presbyters, as is related in the Acts of Felix, bishop of Tubyzaca.

Obeying this edict, local magistrates ordered readers, presbyters, and bishops to appear before them and demanded the Scriptures from them. Those refusing to surrender them were tortured and thrown into prison; those persisting in their resolution were sent to the proconsul or another higher magistrate and put to death. Officials and soldiers ranged through the houses of Christians, searched the more hidden parts of their dwellings, and carried away not only sacred books but sacred vessels of gold and silver—chalices, lamps, and other furnishings—wherever they found them. They did not even spare garments set aside for the poor. Finally, as commonly happens in such circumstances, utterly depraved men plundered every valuable object, whether sacred or profane.

[Col. 0773D] Ancient records appended to the books of Optatus demonstrate that the madness of the persecutors raged especially in Africa. Yet, more grievously, they also show that many Christians—not only laypeople but clergy and even bishops themselves—through fear of torture and death surrendered both sacred codices and other sacred vessels or implements. These were commonly called *traditores*, “surrenderers.” Others, on the contrary, burning with excessive zeal, openly professed—even when no one was investigating—that they possessed sacred codices which they would not surrender, and thus exposed themselves to death. How much wiser, and at the same time more devout, were those who preserved the sacred codices concealed by their silence, provided that, when seized and questioned, they neither surrendered them nor declared that they would surrender them.

**What Mensurius of Carthage thought about surrendering sacred books. What Secundus of Tigisis, primate of Numidia, thought.**—Among these was Mensurius, bishop of Carthage. Following the teaching of his predecessor Cyprian, he disapproved of persons who, without having been arrested, offered themselves to persecution and voluntarily declared that they possessed Scriptures which they would not surrender, although nobody had asked them this; he forbade them to be honoured as martyrs. He himself testified in a letter to Secundus that he had removed and preserved the sacred codices so that they might not be discovered by the persecutors, and had left in their place in the basilica writings of heretics. When the persecutors found and carried these away, nothing further was demanded.

[Col. 0774B] For although certain persons of the Carthaginian council later alleged to the proconsul that those sent to remove and burn Christian Scriptures had been deceived, because they found only certain things that did not concern them, while the Scriptures themselves were kept in the bishop’s house and should be brought out and burned, the proconsul would not agree to this. Thus, by Mensurius’s prudence, the principal codices of the sacred books were preserved at Carthage.

Secundus of Tigisis, primate of Numidia, boasted in words of glory and deceived those ignorant of what had happened; but, devoid of courage, he was ridiculed by those to whom his actions were known. For he sent Mensurius a letter in which he said:

> “A centurion and a *beneficiarius* had been sent to me by the curator and council, demanding divine codices for burning. I replied: ‘I am a Christian and a bishop, not a surrenderer.’ When they wished to receive from me some *ecbola* [probably ‘documents’] or anything whatever, I did not give them this either, following the example of Eleazar the Maccabee, who would not even pretend to eat swine’s flesh, lest he offer others an example of apostasy.”

But Purpurius, bishop of Limata—a man of brazen effrontery—checked Secundus’s boastfulness with the following reproach. When Secundus accused him of homicide, Purpurius mocked him in these words:

> “What did you do, you who were detained by the curator and council to surrender the Scriptures? How did you get free from them, unless you gave, or ordered something to be given? For they would not simply let you go.”

[Col. 0774D] This insult suppressed Secundus’s boldness. From accuser he became accused; fearing for himself as conscious of surrender, he remitted the whole affair to God’s judgment at the counsel of Secundus the younger, his brother’s son. He allowed his fellow bishops—plainly convicted of surrender by their own confession—to remain immune from every penalty, lest he himself too should be prosecuted as guilty of the same crime.

**Sacred codices surrendered by Paul of Cirta and Silvanus.**—[Col. 0775A] Paul was bishop of Cirta, the city which was the civil metropolis of the province of Numidia. On the fourteenth day before the Kalends of June, Munatius Felix, perpetual priest and curator of the colony of Cirta, came to him. He summoned the bishop to produce the books of the law and anything else he possessed. Paul answered that the Scriptures were with the readers, but that whatever he himself had he was ready to give. Again ordered to point out the readers or send to them, he replied that they were known to the clerks Edesius and Junius.

Then Paul and his clergy surrendered to the searchers chalices, lamps, garments for the poor, and the entire equipment of the Church, as well as one codex. Afterwards the magistrates went to the houses of the readers, who, offering little resistance, surrendered the sacred codices. Silvanus in particular, then a subdeacon, voluntarily produced a lamp and a silver *capitulata* [an uncertain type of vessel or ornament] which had been concealed, saying that he had found them behind a chest.

**Christians seized in the city of Abitina and cast into prison. Caecilian’s and Mensurius’s plan for cautiously visiting the martyrs.**—While the persecution was still raging, on the day before the Ides of February in the year 304, in the city of Abitina, Saturnus the presbyter, with his four children—Saturninus the younger and Felix, readers; Mary, a consecrated virgin; and the child Hilarion—and likewise Dativus, Felix, Ampelius, and many others, both men and women, celebrating the Lord’s sacraments, were seized by the magistrates of the colony. They were brought together to Carthage and, after their glorious confession, thrown into prison.

[Col. 0775C] To meet and visit them, Christians—as is natural to suppose—rushed together imprudently and in crowds; this stirred up hostility and exposed more persons to death. Mensurius, seeing this, instructed Caecilian, the archdeacon, to keep that unconsidered crowd away from the prison doors, lest a disturbance arise and hostility be provoked. Hence Caecilian’s opponents later seized an occasion to slander him, inventing that he had stationed armed men with thongs and whips before the prison doors and had violently driven away from entry and access everyone bringing food and drink to the martyrs. This calumny is wholly at odds with probability and appears to have no other origin than the fact that, following Cyprian’s advice, he recommended that Christians should come cautiously, not in crowds—Cyprian’s words in Letter V—nor in a throng attached to one another, to sustain and visit the confessors; and that this should be done with moderation, by presbyters going there in turns, so that due regard might be paid to circumstances, peace preserved, and the people provided for.

**What was established regarding the case of Felix of Aptunga.**—The Donatists also defamed Felix, bishop of Aptunga, who, as we shall presently say, ordained Caecilian, with the charge of surrender. But testimony received after an inquiry was held in 314 by the proconsul Aelianus at the command of Emperor Constantine established that Felix was free from that charge.

[Col. 0775D] Caecilian, who had been duumvir of the colony of Aptunga, testified that, when the edict ordering the destruction of churches and burning of Christian books was published, he was at Zama when the edict arrived. Certain Christians came to ask whether the sacred command had reached him. He answered, “Not yet”; but he had seen copies of it, and at both Zama and Furni basilicas and Scriptures were being destroyed. He therefore told them to produce whatever Scriptures they possessed. He then sent them to Felix’s house, while he himself went with Galatius to the place where Christian prayers were customarily made. There a chair and letters of greeting were removed, and all the doors burned. When he sent public officials to the house of Felix the bishop, they reported that Felix was absent. Thus this testimony established that Felix surrendered nothing.

Ingentius, however, later a decurion of Ziqua, was hostile to Felix because Felix had excommunicated Maurus, bishop of Utica, Ingentius’s friend and guest, for having purchased a bishopric. Ingentius approached Caecilian and, ostensibly in Felix’s name, asked him to certify in writing that sacred codices had been burned during his duumvirate. When Caecilian refused him, he employed as mediator Augentius, Caecilian’s friend and colleague in the aedileship. At his request Caecilian wrote a letter to Felix, testifying that in the year of his duumvirate, in Galatius’s presence, certain letters of greeting had been removed from the basilica.

[Col. 0776B] Ingentius added to this letter that Felix had said: “Take the key, and take the books on the chair and the codices on the stone; but see that the officials do not take the oil and wheat.” When Caecilian replied: “Do you not know that where Scriptures are found, the house itself is destroyed?”, Felix allegedly said: “What then shall we do?” Caecilian allegedly answered: “Let one of your people take them into the courtyard where you hold prayers and put them there; then I shall come with the officials and remove them.” Ingentius added that Felix followed this counsel and ordered sacred codices to be placed in the courtyard; that Caecilian came there with officials and removed everything in accordance with the sacred command.

At the trial Caecilian maintained that all this had been added to his letter and convicted Ingentius of forgery. Suspended in fear of the impending tortures, Ingentius confessed that he had added these things to the letter in revenge for his guest Maurus, in order to brand Felix with the stigma of surrender.

**Names of the bishops at the Council of Cirta.**—When the persecution concerning the surrender of codices had somewhat relaxed, in the year 305 of the common era, on the third day before the Nones of March [Note: [Col. 0776D] **In the year 303, on the third day before the Nones of March.** On this date see annotation 62 in Book I of Optatus.], ten or eleven bishops of Numidia assembled at Cirta in the house of Urbanus Donatus to ordain a bishop in that city in place of Paul of Cirta.

[Col. 0776D] Secundus of Tigisis held the first place among them by right of seniority. With him sat Donatus of Mascula, Victor of Rusicade, Marinus of the Waters of Thibilis, Donatus of Calama, Purpurius of Limata, Victor of Garba, Felix of Rotarium, Nabor of Centuriones, and Secundus the younger, son of the brother of Secundus of Tigisis. Menalius, bishop of an uncertain Numidian see, had also come to Cirta; but fearing that his own citizens might prove that he had offered incense, he pretended an eye ailment and hesitated to come forward to sit with his colleagues.

**Several are accused of surrender by Secundus. Purpurius, accused of homicide, replies fiercely. All are acquitted, their case being reserved to God.**—In the council Secundus proposed that, before they ordained a bishop, those present should prove themselves—that is, clear themselves of accusations or suspicions of crimes. He then asked Donatus of Mascula whether he had surrendered anything. Donatus neither frankly confessed the deed nor entirely denied it, but answered that Florus had demanded that he offer incense, and that nothing had been handed over into his hands. He added: “Since God has forgiven me, preserve me also for God.” Thus he sought pardon for a crime as though committed.

[Col. 0777A] Secundus replied: “What then are we to do about the martyrs, since they did not surrender and were therefore crowned?” Donatus again said: “Send me to God, and there I shall give account.” Secundus then ordered him to withdraw to the other side and stand as an accused person.

He next addressed Marinus of the Waters of Thibilis: “It is said that you too surrendered.” Marinus replied that he had given Paul documents, but that his own codices were safe. Secundus also ordered him to withdraw to the other side. Donatus of Calama, similarly questioned, answered that he had given up medical books; having given this answer, he stood in the middle. Victor of Rusicade, accused by Secundus of surrendering four Gospels, openly and without evasion confessed the charge: “Valentinian was curator; he compelled me to send them. Forgive me this offence, and God forgives me.” Upon this answer, he too was immediately ordered to stand with the accused.

[Col. 0777C] Secundus then accused Purpurius of Limata not of surrender but of homicide, addressing him thus: “It is said that at Mileum you killed two sons of your sister.” This fierce and shameless man turned the accusation back upon his accuser:

> “Do you think that I am frightened by you, as the others are? What did you do, you who were detained by the curator and council to surrender the Scriptures? How did you get free from them, unless you gave, or ordered something to be given? For they would not simply let you go.”

Then he burst out into threats: “I have killed, and I kill those who act against me”—O bestial savagery!—“therefore do not provoke me to say more. You know that I spare no one.” At once all the accused standing together began to murmur against Secundus.

Secundus the younger, the son of his brother, seeing this, addressed his uncle thus: “Do you hear what he says against you? He is ready to withdraw and create a schism—not he alone, but all whom you accuse. I know that they will abandon you and pronounce judgment against you, and you will remain alone as a heretic. Therefore, what concern is it to you what anyone has done? He must render account to God.”

[Col. 0777D] Secundus of Tigisis, fearing this, consulted Victor of Garba, Felix of Rotarium, and Nabor of Centuriones—the three remaining judges—who adopted the opinion of Secundus the younger and judged that such a case should be reserved to God. He pronounced the acquittal of the accused and ordered them to sit down. Then all said, “Thanks be to God,” and they sat down.

**Ordination of Silvanus. The dissent of the deacon Nundinarius from Silvanus.**—[Col. 0778A] This was the first part of the synod. The second was the election and ordination of a bishop in place of the deceased. Silvanus, mentioned above—the man who, under Bishop Paul, had voluntarily surrendered a lamp and a silver *capitulata*—was proposed for ordination in Paul’s place. Then the people cried out: “He is a surrenderer; let another be made bishop. We want our fellow citizen pure and upright.”

The clergy and respected citizens protested against this election. But rough arena-workers and other men from the lowest rabble, hired for pay, shut the respected citizens inside the courtyard of the martyrs. Muto, an arena-worker, raised up Silvanus and proclaimed him bishop; Secundus and the other bishops who had come to Cirta ordained him. Afterwards, in the bishops’ presence, Silvanus ordained Victor, a presbyter. To become a presbyter, Victor gave Silvanus twenty *folles*, which, laid before the bishops’ chair, they divided among themselves.

[Col. 0778B] Nundinarius, Silvanus’s deacon, disclosed all these things in anger against his bishop, who had removed him from office. This led Purpurius of Limata and another bishop of the same faction named Fortis to write to Silvanus and the people of Cirta that Nundinarius’s embittered mind ought by every means to be placated, lest he make public what he knew. When this was not done, Silvanus produced documents and witnesses concerning these matters before Zenophilus the proconsul, as the official records relate.

**Origin of the schism. Lucilla’s quarrels with Caecilian.**—However poorly Secundus of Tigisis and Mensurius of Carthage agreed, no schism broke out between them while Mensurius lived. But after his death, the same bishops who had attended the Council of Cirta divided first the Church of Carthage and afterwards all Africa into two parts by ordaining Majorinus, whom they set up against Caecilian, already ordained. The origin and causes of this division cannot be described more accurately or elegantly than in Optatus’s own words:

> No one is unaware that this schism arose at Carthage after Caecilian’s ordination, through Lucilla, a certain factious woman. Before the peace was shaken by the storms of persecution, while the Church was still tranquil, she was unable to endure the correction of the archdeacon Caecilian. Before receiving spiritual food and drink, she was said to kiss the mouth of some martyr—if indeed he was a martyr. And because she preferred, to the cup of salvation, the mouth of some dead man, even if a martyr, yet not as yet vindicated, she was rebuked and departed in anger and disgrace. Suddenly the storm of persecution arose, meeting her in her anger and grief, so that she might not yield to discipline.

**4. Mensurius, summoned before the curia, entrusts the Church’s ornaments to Botrus and Celestius.**—[Col. 0778D] At the same time, a certain deacon Felix, so called because of some notorious letter written at that time concerning the tyrant-emperor, is said to have hidden with Bishop Mensurius out of fear of danger. When Mensurius publicly denied that Felix was in his custody, a report was sent, and a rescript came ordering that, if Mensurius did not surrender the deacon Felix, he should be sent to the imperial court.

He was suffering no slight embarrassment. The Church possessed very many ornaments of gold and silver, which he could neither bury in the ground nor carry with him. He entrusted them as if to trustworthy elders, making a memorandum which, it is said, he gave to a certain old woman, on the condition that, if he did not return, when peace had been restored to Christians the old woman should give them to whomever she found seated in the episcopal chair. He set out and pleaded his case; he was ordered to return, but could not reach Carthage.

**Ordination of Caecilian as bishop of Carthage, and the causes and origin of the schism.**—The storm of persecution was over and ended. By God’s command, and through the indulgence granted by Maxentius, liberty was restored to Christians. Botrus and Celestius, wishing, it is said, to be ordained at Carthage, worked to ensure that only neighbouring bishops should be sought to conduct the ordination at Carthage, while the Numidians were absent.

[Col. 0779B] Then Caecilian was chosen by the vote of all the people, and Felix of Aptunga laid hands upon him and ordained him bishop. Botrus and Celestius were disappointed in their expectation. The inventory of gold and silver was handed over to Caecilian as he sat in office, as Mensurius had directed, witnesses being present. The aforementioned elders were summoned; they had swallowed up, in the throat of avarice, the plunder entrusted to them. When compelled to restore it, they withdrew from communion.

No less did the office-seekers withdraw, since they too had failed to obtain ordination; nor did Lucilla, who had long been unable to endure discipline, wish to join in communion. Powerful and factious, she stood with all her followers. Thus, when these three causes and parties came together, malice achieved its effect. Therefore the anger of an affronted woman gave birth to the schism at that time; ambition nourished it, and avarice strengthened it. From these three parties charges were fabricated against Caecilian, so that his ordination might be called invalid.

**At what time the beginning of the schism should be placed.**—These events occurred after the persecution had ended and liberty had been restored to Christians in Africa by the indulgence of Maxentius; consequently, after he had gained possession of Africa. This did not happen until after the death of Maximian Herculius, who was removed from life in the year 310, and after Alexander—who at that time was acting in Africa as praetorian prefect and supporting Galerius’s party—had been defeated and killed by Rufius Volusianus and Zenas, whom Maxentius had sent into Africa with troops, as Zosimus and Aurelius Victor testify.

[Col. 0779D] Therefore this indulgence could not have been sent by Maxentius into Africa, nor liberty restored by him to Christians, before the year 311, in which Eusebius testifies that the persecution ended in the western regions.

**A visitor assigned to the Church of Carthage by Secundus’s clergy.**—Before Caecilian was ordained, Secundus had already sent clergy to Carthage. Although they refused to approach the clergy of Carthage, they were received by Lucilla and appointed a visitor, if Augustine is to be believed when he relates this in Sermon XLVI, *On Pastors*, chapter 15. At this time the Church of Carthage was also disturbed by Donatus of Cellae Nigrae (“Black Huts”), who, according to the same witness, was convicted on the third day of the Conference in the Roman council of having made a schism at Carthage while Caecilian was still a deacon.

**Council of seventy Numidians at Carthage; accusation of Caecilian.**—[Col. 0780A] Secundus and the bishops of Numidia, summoned to Carthage for the ordination of a bishop, found Caecilian already ordained. They resented not having been awaited, especially Secundus the primate, who thought it proper that a chief should be ordained by a chief—that is, a primate by a primate. But the clergy and people of Carthage, who had long disliked Secundus and the Numidians, refused to receive them. They were welcomed instead by those hostile to Caecilian: Lucilla and her supporters; the elders to whom the sacred ornaments had been entrusted; and Botrus and Celestius, indignant that they themselves had not been ordained.

There were, according to Augustine, about seventy bishops of Numidia, including all those who had attended the Council of Cirta: namely, the *traditores* and murderers, together with Silvanus of Cirta and Donatus of Cellae Nigrae, the principal instigator of the dissension. None entered the basilica in which Christians assembled; rather, they held their conventicle in a private house. Caecilian was summoned by them. Confident of his innocence, he sent them this response: “If there is anything to be proved against me, let an accuser come forward and prove it.”

[Col. 0780B] “At that time,” says Optatus, “nothing could be fabricated against him by so many enemies; but he was deemed worthy of defamation concerning his ordainer, whom they falsely called a surrenderer.” Caecilian again sent word that, if Felix had conferred nothing upon him—as they supposed—they should ordain Caecilian as though he were still a deacon. Then Purpurius, relying upon his habitual malice, spoke as though Caecilian were also his sister’s son: “Let him come out here as though hands were to be laid on him for the episcopate, and let his head be shaken in penance.” When these matters became known, the whole Church retained Caecilian, lest he hand himself over to brigands.

**Condemnation of Caecilian.**—Accordingly, they condemned Caecilian in his absence: because, though summoned, he would not appear; because he had been ordained by *traditores*; and because he was said to have forbidden food to be brought to martyrs kept in custody. Having pronounced against him and his ordainers a sentence of deposition and excommunication, they unlawfully ordained in his place Majorinus—who had been a reader while Caecilian was archdeacon; a member of Lucilla’s household, elected through her support, and corrupted by her money, for it was later discovered that she had given the bishops four hundred *folles* for this purpose.

[Col. 0780D] Thus altar was set up against altar; from this came the beginning of schism and dissension.

**Letter of the synod against Caecilian. Division of Africa. Caecilian remains in communion with the whole world.**—After pronouncing their judgment, they sent letters in the name of the council, as was customary, to the African Churches. According to Optatus, they were drafted at the dictation of Tivore. In them they slandered Caecilian’s ordainers as guilty of surrender, declared Caecilian’s ordination invalid, and warned all to abstain from communion with him and acknowledge Majorinus as the legitimate bishop.

Many Africans believed the letters issued against Caecilian by this numerous council. Hence not only the Church of Carthage but the whole African Church was divided into two parts: some defended Caecilian’s innocence and retained communion with him; others stood on Majorinus’s side and withdrew from communion with Caecilian.

[Col. 0781A] But since Caecilian’s opponents did not at that time dare to refer this case to the Churches across the sea, Caecilian remained in communion with the Churches of the whole world. Majorinus, on the other hand, had no one outside Africa who communicated with him or regarded him as bishop of Carthage. Letters of communion were sent to Caecilian by all the overseas Churches, but not to Majorinus.

**5. Constantine recognizes Caecilian as the legitimate bishop.**—[Col. 0781B] Moreover, after defeating Maxentius in 312 and adding Italy and Africa to his empire, Emperor Constantine entrusted to Caecilian, as legitimate bishop of Carthage, the distribution of funds which he granted from the treasury for the support of the ministers of the Catholic Church in the provinces of Africa, Numidia, and the two Mauretaniae. In his letter to Caecilian he sharply censures the schismatics as men of disordered mind, seeking by wicked and adulterous deceit to corrupt the people of the most holy and Catholic Church.

He says that he had directed Anulinus, proconsul, and the patrician vicar of the prefects to take care of the matter; and he writes to Caecilian that, if any such persons should persist in this madness, he should approach the aforementioned judges without hesitation and report it to them, so that they might punish the guilty persons as he had ordered in their presence.

Caecilian’s adversaries submit memorials against him to the proconsul. They ask the emperor to appoint judges for them. — The same emperor, writing to Anulinus concerning the exemption of clerics in Africa, exempted from public duties only those who served the most holy religion in the Catholic Church over which Caecilian presided. Upon receiving these letters, Anulinus summoned Caecilian and the clerics of the Church of Carthage; after reading the imperial instruction to them, he exhorted them, now that unity had been achieved by the agreement of all, to enjoy the exemption granted them and henceforth to devote themselves without hindrance to divine matters.

A few days later, however, certain adversaries of Caecilian, joined by a crowd of people, approached the proconsul and presented two memorials: one, sealed in parchment, bore this heading: “Memorial of the Catholic Church concerning the crimes of Caecilian, submitted by the party of Majorinus”; the other, without a seal, was attached to the same parchment. They asked him to send these memorials to the imperial court. Anulinus himself reports the matter thus in a report addressed to the emperor, delivered at Carthage on the seventeenth day before the Kalends of May, when Constantine Augustus was consul for the third time—this consulship falling in A.D. 313. Anulinus sent the memorials presented to him, together with his report, to the emperor, so that he might fully investigate everything. Meanwhile, he left Caecilian in his office.

The unsigned memorial attached to the parchment was none other than that in which they requested that judges be assigned them from Gaul. Optatus records it in these terms:

> “We ask you, Constantine, best of emperors, since you are of a just stock, whose father, among the other emperors, did not carry out persecution, and Gaul is free from this crime. For in Africa there are disputes between us and the other bishops; we request that your Piety command judges to be assigned us from Gaul.”

Given by Lucianus, Dignus, Nasutius, Capito, Fidentius, and the other bishops of Donatus’s party—or rather Majorinus’s, as we have observed in this place.

Constantine appoints three Gallic bishops as judges, to decide the case at Rome together with Miltiades, bishop of Rome. — Emperor Constantine, upon receiving in Gaul, where he was then staying, the report of the proconsul Anulinus and the memorials attached to it, was deeply distressed—as he himself says in his letter to Miltiades—that, in those provinces which divine Providence had surrendered to his devotion by voluntary submission, and in which the population was exceedingly numerous, the people were being divided, as it were, into two parties and drawn toward worse things, while bishops disagreed among themselves.

Therefore, to put an end to the dissension, Constantine appointed three bishops from Gaul as judges: Maternus of Cologne, Reticius of Autun, and Marinus of Arles. They were to hear the matter at Rome together with Miltiades, bishop of Rome. At the same time he ordered Anulinus to command Caecilian, with ten bishops of his party, and Caecilian’s adversaries in equal number, to sail to Rome by the sixth day before the Nones of October, so that their case might there be argued before an episcopal tribunal.

And so that the appointed judges might have the fullest possible knowledge of the matter, he sent each of them copies of the memorials transmitted by Anulinus, together with letters exhorting them to examine this case most carefully and to judge according to the rule of justice. His letter to Miltiades survives. In it he wills that Miltiades himself be a judge in this case together with Reticius, Maternus, and Marinus, his colleagues.

They are sent to Rome from both parties. The Roman council under Miltiades. Caecilian is declared innocent; sentence is pronounced against Donatus. — In accordance with the emperor’s command, Anulinus ordered Caecilian and his adversaries to send ten men from each side to Rome. When both parties promised to comply with this order, he informed the emperor accordingly.

Thus Caecilian, together with ten bishops of his party and an equal number from among his adversaries—whose standard-bearer was Donatus of Casae—came to Rome. The three Gallic bishops appointed by Constantine as judges also arrived there. They, together with Miltiades and fifteen Italian bishops, whose names and sees Optatus records in Book I, §23, assembled in Fausta’s house in the Lateran—that is, in the portion of the Lateran palace assigned to the Empress Fausta—on the sixth day before the Nones of October, a Friday, in the year 313, when Constantine was consul for the third time and Licinius for the second.

As these nineteen bishops sat in judgment, the case of Caecilian and Donatus began to be heard. The proceedings lasted three days, with notaries present to draw up the record. On the first day Caecilian and his accusers appeared before the judges. The persons of the accusers were considered, and certain of them, whose lives were stained with blemishes, were excluded from bringing the action in accordance with the laws. The others were asked to produce witnesses and proofs against Caecilian. They could bring forward nothing against him; they alleged only that Caecilian had been accused by the entire people of Carthage.

But the judges considered that no account should be taken of an accusation resting merely on disorderly shouts, without documentary attestation or credible witnesses. They required them to produce definite accusers and witnesses, who had come with them from Africa and who, though present, were said to have been withdrawn by Donatus because they had testified that they possessed nothing to say against Caecilian. Donatus promised to produce them; and so Caecilian’s case remained pending.

Donatus of Casae, however, was accused and convicted of having caused a schism at Carthage while Caecilian was still archdeacon. He confessed that he had rebaptized and had imposed hands upon lapsed bishops. On the second day certain persons submitted a new memorial of accusation against Caecilian. The inquiry was consequently resumed, yet still nothing whatever could be proved against Caecilian.

On the same day, it appears, the council of seventy bishops who had condemned Caecilian was discussed; their authority was advanced as especially weighty. Much was said against them: that Caecilian’s enemies had been traditores, ambitious men, dependent upon Lucilla and corrupted by her money, and other charges of that sort. Against Caecilian it was alleged that he had been ordained by Felix of Aptunga, who was accused of having committed *traditio* [surrender of sacred books or objects].

These were numerous and exceedingly intricate questions. The fathers of the Roman council judged that they should abstain from them and wished to pronounce judgment only concerning Caecilian and Donatus. Donatus again promised that on the following day he would produce competent witnesses to Caecilian’s crimes; but, unable to abide by his promise, he refused to appear further for judgment. Accordingly, on the third day Caecilian was unanimously declared innocent, and communion with him was maintained. Conversely, individual sentences were pronounced against Donatus, convicted by his own confession.

Nothing, however, was pronounced against the other bishops who had condemned Caecilian, nor was any of them expelled from the Church’s communion. Rather, all bishops of Majorinus’s party were given the option of retaining their offices, should they wish to return to unity, even if they had been ordained outside the Church by Majorinus. Thus, wherever there were two bishops—one ordained by Caecilian and the other by Majorinus—the one ordained first was to be confirmed; another people was to be assigned to the other bishop for governance. We have collected these matters from Optatus, Book I, §24, Augustine, Letter XLIII, and the Breviculus of the proceedings, day 3.

After these matters had been completed, Miltiades and the remaining bishops sent to Emperor Constantine all that had been done in the council, together with the council’s acts. They also declared verbally that their judgment had been rendered in accordance with the equity of the facts, and that those who had attempted to stir up accusations against Caecilian were rather themselves liable to blame.

[Col. 0784A]

What was done in Africa after the Roman synod. — After this judgment, I think, occurred what Optatus narrates in Book I, §26, in these words:

> “At the same time this same Donatus asked that he be permitted to return, provided that he did not approach Carthage. Then Filuminus, his supporter, proposed to the emperor that, for the good of peace, Caecilian should be kept at Brescia; and this was done. Then two bishops, Eunomius and Olympius, were sent to Africa. They came and remained near Carthage for forty days, in order to declare where the Catholic Church was. The seditious party of Donatus did not permit this to be done. Daily disturbances took place through party zeal. The final ruling of the same bishops, Eunomius and Olympius, is read as follows: ‘They declared that that Church was Catholic which was spread throughout the whole world, and that the judgment already rendered by nineteen bishops could not be annulled.’ Thus they communicated with Caecilian’s clergy and returned. We possess volumes of records concerning these matters; whoever wishes may read them in the final sections. While this was occurring, Donatus himself returned first, of his own accord, to Carthage. When he heard this, Caecilian hastened to his own people. In this manner the factions were renewed once more.”

New disturbances of the Donatist faction against Caecilian. — Thus the adherents of the Donatist faction, persisting in their obstinacy, began to stir up further disturbances throughout Africa. Some of them even dared to approach the emperor and accuse Caecilian anew. When the emperor replied that they were asserting this in vain, since the matter had been decided at the city of Rome by suitable and thoroughly approved men, bishops, they answered insistently and stubbornly that their entire case had not been heard; rather, the same bishops had shut themselves up in some place and judged as seemed fitting to them.

Their new complaints to the emperor. Proceedings before Aelianus, proconsul of Africa, concerning the innocence of Felix of Aptunga. — Moved by this, Emperor Constantine, in order finally to put an end to the dissensions, ordered that the case of Felix of Aptunga be examined in a public court in Africa, and convened at the city of Arles a council much more numerous than the former one, so that Caecilian’s whole case might again be brought under examination.

Accordingly, he wrote to Verus, or Verinus, vicar of Africa, ordering a public inquiry into the life of Felix of Aptunga and into the charge of *traditio* of which he was accused. But since Verus was prevented by ill health, Aelianus the proconsul conducted the investigation in the vicar’s place. He ordered Alf[i]us Caecilianus—who had been curator of the municipality of Autumnita during the time of persecution—to be summoned, together with Ingentius the clerk, Claudius, Saturninus, Calidius, Gratianus, Superius the *stationarius*, Solon the public slave, and other witnesses necessary to the inquiry.

The municipal records were read; Saturninus and the younger Calidius, the curators, Superius the *stationarius*, and Caecilianus the duumvir were questioned; Ingentius was subjected to examination. After hearing them all, the proconsul pronounced this judgment:

> “It is manifest that the reverend bishop Felix is free from the burning of the divine documents, since no one has been able to prove against him that he surrendered or burned the most holy Scriptures. For the examination of all the persons named above has shown that no divine Scriptures were either found, corrupted, or burned. The acts contain the fact that the reverend bishop Felix was neither present at that time, nor lent his consent, nor ordered anything of the sort to be done.”

Ingentius, on the contrary, having been convicted of adding certain matters to the letter of Alf[i]us Caecilianus by which the crime of *traditio* was imputed to Felix, was thrown into prison and detained there until Constantine, in the following year, wrote to Probianus, Aelianus’s successor as proconsul, ordering him to send Ingentius to the imperial court.

Those proceedings were completed under the consulship of Aelianus Volusianus and Annianus, on the fifteenth day before the Kalends of March—that is, on 15 February 314—four months after the Roman synod.

> [Note: [Col. 0785D] On 15 February 314. Augustine teaches this in his book *To the Donatists after the Conference*. Yet in the proceedings it is said that Caecilianus the duumvir was heard on the fourteenth day before the Kalends of September, under the consulship of Volusianus and Annianus. To reconcile these statements, Valesius thinks that the inquiry began in February and was completed in August. But it is scarcely credible that an investigation which Augustine calls “a most careful examination” should have been interrupted, or left pending before the judge, for so long—especially since, according to Optatus, the emperor had ordered that an inquiry into the life of Felix of Aptunga should be made after public business had been set aside, evidently wishing this judgment to precede that at Arles [Col. 0786D]. It is more probable that the proceedings contain an error, particularly since Licinius is joined with Constantine in them as a partner in the empire; Licinius waged war against Constantine near the end of this year and was defeated in the battle of Cibalae, fought on 8 October.]

Constantine’s letters convening the Council of Arles. — In the same year, in the month of August, the Council of Arles was held. Constantine had written to Aelafius—

> [Note: [Col. 0786D] Aelafius. In the manuscript codex the reading is *Aelafio*, but no remembrance of such a person occurs among ancient writers; by contrast, the name Ablavius is distinguished. Ablavius could have been vicar of Africa at that time. Baluzius considers that Aelianus should be read instead of Aelafius; this Aelianus was then proconsul of Africa, as appears from the proceedings mentioned above, and this is not inconsistent with probability.]

—or, as others read, Ablavius, or rather Aelianus, proconsul of Africa. He ordered him to have Caecilian, with other bishops whom Caecilian himself should choose, as well as certain others from the provinces of Byzacena, Tripolitana, Numidia, and the Mauritanias, and also some of his adversaries, conveyed by public transport through Africa and Mauritania and thence to Spain, so that they might arrive at Arles by the day of the Kalends of August.

The emperor had also given letters to the bishops whom he wished to attend the council, commanding them, upon receiving public transport, to assemble in the city of Arles by the Kalends of August. He had determined that bishops should be present there from diverse and almost innumerable places, so that the already adjudicated case of Caecilian and the Donatists might be decided after the parties had again been heard.

Eusebius has preserved a copy of this letter, written to Chrestus of Syracuse; it is reasonable to believe that similar copies were sent to the other bishops. In the letter directed to Chrestus, Constantine authorizes him to take with him two persons of the second rank—that is, in my view, presbyters, deacons, or other clerics—and three servants as companions on his journey. That the same concession was granted to the other bishops also is evident from the fact that many presbyters, deacons, and other clerics were present at the council together with the bishops and subscribed its acts.

Names and number of the bishops of the Council of Arles. [Col. 0785D] — Writers dispute the number of bishops at the Council of Arles. Ado writes that there were six hundred, but he is a writer of very slight authority in this matter. Baronius conjectured that there were two hundred from a corrupt passage of Augustine, Book I *Against Parmenianus*, ch. 5. There, after mention of the Roman judgment under Miltiades, whom the Donatists accused of *traditio*, the following words appeared after the sentence pronounced by him:

> “Men are so utterly mad that they think two hundred judges, before whom they were defeated, ought to be set aside in favour of defeated litigants.”

Baronius supposed that what is here said of two hundred judges referred to the Council of Arles, although the passage concerns the Roman council, which undoubtedly had only nineteen bishops. But in Augustine’s genuine text there is nothing about two hundred judges. Rather, as restored from an old Vatican codex in the latest edition of Augustine’s works, the reading should be:

> “Men are so utterly mad that they think defeated litigants are to be believed against the judges before whom they were defeated.”

That this is the genuine reading of the passage is clear. For all manuscript codices omit the final words, “ought to be set aside,” which the Louvain editors added to produce some sense. And since the word *contra* [“against”] may perhaps have been represented by a copyist through a double *c*, or *cc*, later copyists produced the number “two hundred.” Thus Baronius’s conjecture collapses entirely, and the number of bishops at the Council of Arles must be determined from elsewhere.

Constantine, in his letter to Chrestus, says that he had ordered a great many bishops from diverse and almost innumerable places to gather in Arles by the Kalends of August. These words seem to imply that the council was very numerous. Yet first, it is agreed by all that only bishops from the western regions subject to Constantine were summoned; and among the thirty-three whose names occur in the subscriptions are bishops from every western region—Italy, Apulia, Dalmatia, Gaul, Britain, Sardinia, Sicily, Spain, and Africa. Nothing prevents bishops from so many different regions from being called persons gathered from diverse and almost innumerable places.

Further, whether all the bishops summoned by Constantine were present is uncertain. There are only two documents from which the number and names of bishops who assembled at this council may be gathered: namely, the heading of the council’s own letter and the council’s subscriptions. The heading has more certain authority, for the subscriptions vary and are considerably disordered and corrupt. Yet in both the number of bishops is equal, not exceeding thirty-three, and the names are almost the same; each document elucidates and corrects the other.

In the heading, Marinus of Arles occurs first; then Acratius, more correctly Agraetius of Trier in the subscriptions; Theodorus of Aquileia; Natalis, presbyter of the city of the Ursolenses, perhaps Urgel; Proterius, bishop of Capua; Vocius of Lyons; Verus of Vienne; Probatianus, or Probatius, presbyter of Tarragona; Caecilian of Carthage; Faustinus, presbyter from the city of the Arausicani; Surgentius, bishop of the city of Pocofeltis, perhaps the village of Bilta in Africa; Gregorius of Portus; Reticius of Autun; Ambitausus, or Imbetausus, of Reims; Termatius, presbyter from the city of the Basti; Merocles of Milan; Pardus of Arpi; Adelfius from the colony of the Londoners; Hibernius, perhaps Eborius of York; Fortunatus, bishop of Caesarea in Mauretania; Aristasius, perhaps Anastasius of Benevento; Lampadius of Utica; Vitalis of Verecunda in Proconsular Africa; Maternus of Cologne; Liberius of Mérida; another Gregorius, whose name and place do not survive in the subscriptions; Crescens, perhaps identical with Chrestus of Syracuse; Avitianus of Rouen; Daphnus of Vaison; Orientalis of Bordeaux; Quintasius of Cagliari; Victor of Utica; and Epictetus of Centumcellae.

Valesius, considering all these to be bishops’ names, concluded that thirty-three bishops attended the Synod of Arles. But since the subscriptions establish that four of these thirty-three were presbyters—namely Natalis, Probatius, Faustinus, and Termatius—there remain only twenty-nine bishops. To these must be added, from the subscriptions, Oresius of Marseille, Mamertinus of Elusa, Restitutus of London, Faustus of Tuburbo, and Victor from the city of Legisvolumum, or Legesis, in Numidia, whose names are omitted from the heading of the synodical letter. The total number of bishops therefore rises to thirty-four.

To them must be added fifteen presbyters, twenty-five deacons, six exorcists, and two readers, whose names occur in the subscriptions. This is what may be said concerning the number of fathers who attended the Council of Arles.

President of the council. Decrees of the Council of Arles. — Marinus of Arles presided over the assembly; his name is read first in the heading of the synodical letter. The other two judges who had sat at the earlier judgment, Maternus and Agraetius, were present. Sylvester, who had succeeded Miltiades as Roman pontiff, could not leave the city at all; he therefore sent the presbyters Claudianus and Vitus as legates to discharge his functions, with two deacons.

Moreover, although bishops gathered at this council from all the western regions, the greater part of them came from Gaul, for sixteen Gallic bishops are counted in the subscriptions. The bishops, therefore, having assembled in the city of Arles on the Kalends of August, in A.D. 314, during the second consulship of Volusianus and the consulship of Annianus, examined Caecilian’s case anew.

The accused was present, and the accusers were present. Concerning them the council says in its synodical letter:

> “We endured men of unbridled minds, grievous and destructive to our law and tradition—men whom both the present authority of our God and the tradition and rule of truth so reject that in them no ground for speaking remained, no method of accusation, nor any suitable proof.”

Caecilian was therefore declared innocent of their calumnies. They themselves, however—these are the words of the council’s synodical letter—“judged by God and Mother Church, who knows and approves her own,” were either condemned or rejected: the chief accusers and authors of the schism, namely, were condemned; the rest were excluded from communion until they returned to the Catholic Church. In that event, Donatist clerics were permitted to remain in their rank.

With regard to bishops, the same rule was laid down as before at the Roman council: where only one bishop of Majorinus’s party existed, he was to remain there; but where there was one bishop in Caecilian’s communion and another in Majorinus’s, the one ordained first was to be confirmed. Another people was to be entrusted to the other bishop for governance, or he was to remain in the same church, retaining the honour and dignity of a bishop, and upon his colleague’s death was to succeed to his place.

For this reason the council, in its synodical letter, indicates that it had treated the schismatics more mildly. It writes to Sylvester:

> “Would that, most beloved brother, you had thought it worthwhile to be present at so great a spectacle. We certainly believe that a severer sentence would have been pronounced against them, and that, had you joined with us in judging, our assembly would have rejoiced with greater gladness.”

Canons of the Council of Arles. — Once the judgment in the case for which the bishops had been summoned to Arles had been completed, they thought that they should not deal only with the matters for which they had been invited. In addition, in order to provide for their churches, they decreed laws to be observed in their provinces. They accordingly composed twenty-two canons and sent them to Pope Sylvester, so that through the one who presided over the first and chief Church of the world they might become known to the other churches.

Canons of the council against the *traditores* and concerning the baptism of heretics. — Of these canons, two especially concern the present case. The thirteenth provides that those who are said to have surrendered the holy Scriptures, sacred vessels, or the names of their brethren are to be removed from the clerical order. But because many, opposing ecclesiastical rule, think that they should be admitted to prosecute accusations through bribed witnesses, it is decreed that they are not to be admitted unless they establish from public records that the crime of *traditio* was committed by those whom they accuse.

The ordination of persons ordained by *traditores*, however, is declared not invalid, nor is anything declared detrimental to those ordained. Both points concern Caecilian’s case. The first does so because the crime of *traditio*, which his adversaries charged against Felix of Aptunga, Mensurius, and other Catholic bishops, they could not prove from public records; they alleged only popular rumour or witnesses corrupted with money to defame them. The second does so because they attacked Caecilian’s ordination above all, on the ground that he had been ordained by Felix of Aptunga, accused of *traditio*, and by other bishops who were *traditores*. This argument had no force once the ordination of a *traditor* was not invalid.

The other canon that concerns the Africans is the eighth, concerning the baptism of heretics. Its wording is:

> “Concerning the Africans, because they employ their own rule in rebaptizing: it has seemed good that, if anyone comes to the Church from heresy, he should be questioned concerning the creed; and if it is found that he was baptized in the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit, hands alone should be laid upon him, so that he may receive the Holy Spirit. But if, when questioned, he does not answer this Trinity, he is to be baptized.”

By this canon, the African practice of rebaptizing those who came to the Church was restricted to those heretics only who did not acknowledge the Trinity and consequently had not been baptized in the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit—that is, in that faith of the Trinity. For the council does not say that they should be questioned concerning the baptismal formula, but concerning faith: “Question him concerning the creed . . . But if, when questioned, he does not answer this Trinity, let him be baptized.”

Optatus’s teaching concerning the baptism of heretics seems consistent with this definition. In Book I, §10, he acknowledges that all which Parmenianus had said concerning a defective and invalid baptism relates to the baptism of those heretics who falsified the creed and thought wrongly concerning the Trinity. In Book V, §§3, 4, and 8, he requires the same faith in the Trinity in the recipient. Finally, in the same place, he reproves the Donatists because, after a person questioned in baptism had answered the faith of the Trinity, they required another *credo* after the one *credo*. Whatever the case may be, the canon of Arles under discussion was not composed specifically against Majorinus’s party, but concerned the African rule of rebaptizing those baptized by heretics when they came to the Church; this council moderated that rule by the canon.

[Col. 0789C]

Synodical letter of the Council of Arles. — Before departing, the bishops who had assembled at Arles wrote a synodical letter to Sylvester, informing him of what they had done and at the same time transmitting to him the canons they had composed, so that through him they might become known to the other churches. They also wrote to the emperor and requested permission to depart.

Meanwhile, certain persons from Majorinus’s party approached Constantine, appealing to his judgment.

> [Note: [Col. 0789D] Appealing to his judgment. Some think that this Donatist appeal to the emperor was lodged after the judgment of Miltiades and the Roman council. But whenever Augustine speaks of the Roman and Arles judgments, he says that the Donatists complained to the emperor concerning the first judgment and appealed from the second to the emperor himself. The emperor himself, in his letter to Aelafius, reporting what the Donatists had said to him concerning the Roman judgment, says that they replied: “Their entire case had not been heard there; rather, a few bishops had shut themselves up in some place and judged as seemed fitting to them.” But the same Constantine, in a letter to the bishops—which scarcely anyone can doubt was addressed to the fathers of the Synod of Arles—says that they appealed to his judgment and denounces this appeal in the words: “O mad audacity of fury!” and so forth. Optatus reports these words as uttered after the judgment of the Roman synod. But since he makes no mention of the Council of Arles, it is not surprising if he referred to the Roman synod words that pertain to the judgment at Arles.]

At first Constantine denounced their appeal, bursting out in these words: “O mad audacity of fury! They have lodged an appeal, as is customary in the cases of pagans.” He was indignant, of course, that they would not abide by the bishops’ judgment, but appealed to secular courts and demanded his own judgment.

He therefore wrote to the bishops of the Council of Arles, sharply censuring the obstinacy of these men, praising the council’s judgment, and asking the bishops to show the patience exemplified by Christ, while still giving the schismatics the choice of what they preferred. If the bishops observed them persisting in their course, they were to return at once to their own sees.

Finally, in the same letter, he informed them that he had sent his officers to Arles to bring the obstinate persons to the imperial court, and had given letters to the vicar of Africa ordering him to send immediately to the court all whom he found afflicted with the same madness, so that at last an end might be imposed upon the disturbances and dissension.

### The Donatists’ Appeal to the Emperor. Caecilian and His Opponents Summoned

Upon receiving this news, many on Donatus’s side, fearing the emperor’s anger, returned to concord with Caecilian. Those who proved more obstinate were brought before the imperial court. There [Col. 0790B], partly in person and partly through the influence of supporters whom they had at court, they did not cease petitioning the emperor to render judgment between the parties himself. Constantine at first rejected this; but at last, overcome by the Donatists’ repeated applications, he yielded and, in order to silence them altogether, resolved to pronounce judgment on Caecilian’s innocence.

At first he had decided to summon Caecilian from Africa; but, changing his mind at the request of the Donatist bishops, he ordered the bishops of Donatus’s party who were at court to return to Africa, so that the entire case which they had against Caecilian might there be heard and concluded by friends or judges whom he should appoint. But shortly afterward it occurred to the emperor that, if the investigation of this case were held in Africa, certain turbulent persons from the Donatist faction might disturb the judgment [Col. 0790C], so that it would not be rendered according to truth; or that, if the matter were rightly judged, they, being of such obstinate temper, would refuse to acquiesce in the judgment. Changing his plan, he resolved instead that Caecilian and his opponents should be summoned to the imperial court, so that he himself might render judgment between them.

Accordingly, he wrote both to Caecilian and to the bishops opposed to him, ordering them to come to him at Rome, where he was staying in August of the year 315, as is clear from the Theodosian Code. There survives his letter to the bishops opposed to Caecilian. After explaining the reason for his altered plan, he promises them that, if, with Caecilian present, they should be able to prove even one of the charges on which they accused him, this would have the same force before him as if all the accusations they had brought against him [Col. 0790D] had been proved.

At the same time he seems to have written to Probianus, proconsul of Africa:

> **[Note: Col. 0790D. At the same time he seems to have written to Probianus, proconsul of Africa.]** Some hold that this letter was written in the preceding year, before the Council of Arles. But it is more likely that Ingentius was not summoned [Col. 0791C] by Constantine until Constantine himself resolved to judge the case. For, if he had been summoned for the judgment at Arles, Constantine would have ordered Probianus to send him to Arles, not to the imperial court.  
>   
> That Probianus was proconsul of Africa in 315 is shown by Law 1, *On the Grain Supply*, in the Theodosian Code, addressed to Proclinianus—Probianus is to be read, as in Law 3, *On Appeals*—which was issued at Rome in that same year, 315. Probianus had certainly already succeeded Aelianus, who was proconsul of Africa in 314. It could indeed have happened that Probianus succeeded him in 314, after the judgment on Felix’s innocence had been held; and some seek to prove this from Law 1, *On the Claudian Senatorial Decree*, in the Theodosian Code, issued on the Kalends of April in 314, addressed to Probus, to whom also Law 3 of the Justinian Code, *On Fugitive Slaves*, is directed. But there is nothing to prove that this Probus was proconsul of Africa or that he was the same person as Probianus.

He instructed him to send Ingentius, a decurion of Ziqua, 9 who had been convicted before Aelianus, proconsul and Probianus’s predecessor, of having forged Felix’s letter [Col. 0791A], and who had therefore been cast into prison by Aelianus’s order, to the imperial court under suitable escort, “so that, in the hearing and presence of those who are now acting and who do not cease day after day to present petitions, it may appear and be made known that they have vainly sought to create prejudice against Bishop Caecilian and to rise violently against him. For thus it will come about that, abandoning—as they ought—contentions of this kind, the people may serve their own religion with due reverence and without any dissension.”

On the appointed day Caecilian, for some reason unknown to me, did not appear at Rome as he had been ordered. Then his opponents, who had returned to the imperial court, petitioned the emperor to pronounce sentence against Caecilian as one in contempt. [Col. 0791B] But the emperor granted a postponement and ordered them to follow him to Milan. Thereupon some, distressed that Constantine had refused to condemn Caecilian in his absence, and suspecting that he favored Caecilian and was hostile to themselves, began to withdraw by flight. When the prudent emperor learned this, he ordered that the rest, kept under guard by officials, should be brought to Milan.

Those who had secretly withdrawn from the imperial court, when they reached Africa, stirred up new disturbances there. Their leader and standard-bearer was that savage man Menalius, mentioned above, who, persisting in his old madness, was ready to provoke sedition, had not Domitius Celsus, vicar of Africa, suppressed the tumult which they were preparing. When Constantine was informed of this matter by Celsus, he wrote to him that he should make it publicly known to Caecilian [Col. 0791C] and his opponents that he would shortly come to Africa and there, after careful investigation, render judgment between the parties [Col. 0792A], and punish the seditious and irreligious.

With this intention he allowed the Donatist bishops Lucianus, Capito, Fidentius, and Nasutius, together with the presbyter Mammarius—who had come to Gaul by the emperor’s command in order to accuse Caecilian—to return to their homes. He ordered the praetorian prefects to provide them with a travel warrant and grain allowance as far as the port of Arles, from which they might sail to Africa. The prefects notified Celsus, vicar of Africa, of this in letters issued on the fourth day before the Kalends of May, 316.

> **[Note: Col. 0791D. In letters issued on the fourth day before the Kalends of May, 316.]** Celsus was vicar of Africa at the beginning of 316, as Law 1 of the Theodosian Code, *On the Office of Judges*, issued at Trier on the third day before the Ides of January, in the consulship of Sabinus and Rufinus—which fell in 316—shows. Baronius thought that the letter under discussion was issued after the Council of Arles; but he was mistaken, since that council was not held before the Kalends of August. This letter, however, was issued on the third day before the Kalends of May; and thus it cannot have been issued to bishops of Donatus’s party departing from the Council of Arles.

### The Emperor’s Judgment in Favor of Caecilian

At last Constantine abandoned his plan of crossing into Africa and resolved to judge Caecilian’s case. When Caecilian and his opponents had come to Milan, [Col. 0792B] where Constantine was staying in November 316, the emperor examined the case, excluding all arbitrators. Having heard the allegations of both parties and investigated and examined the entire controversy with the utmost care, since none of the charges brought against Caecilian could be proved by his accusers, he pronounced Caecilian innocent and them utterly calumnious. He sent a rescript concerning this decision to Eumalius, vicar of Africa, dated the fourth day before the Ides of November, in the consulship of Sabinus and Rufinus, in 316.

### On Donatus of Carthage

Meanwhile Majorinus died, and in his place Donatus was ordained at Carthage by the bishops of his communion. This was not the Donatus, so often mentioned already, bishop of Casae Nigrae, but another man of the same name, who arrogated to himself leadership [Col. 0792C] among his followers and from whom the Donatists received their name.

> **[Note: Col. 0791D. Not the Donatus, so often mentioned already, bishop of Casae Nigrae, but another of the same name, from whom the Donatists received their name.]** St. Augustine at one time believed that Donatus of Carthage was the same man as the one who, with others, presented a petition to the emperor requesting that overseas judges be appointed against Caecilian [Col. 0792C]. But later he judged it more probable that this act had been done not by him but by another Donatus of the same schism—one who was not the Donatist bishop of Carthage, but was from Casae Nigrae, and who nevertheless first committed that impious schism itself at Carthage, as Augustine himself says in Book I, chapter 21, of the *Retractations*.  
>   
> At the Conference of Carthage, when the Catholics alleged that Donatus of Carthage had been condemned at the Roman synod under Miltiades, the Donatists maintained—as Augustine relates in the *Short Account of the Conference*, day 3—that it was not the Carthaginian but the bishop from Casae who had appeared at the judgment of Miltiades; and the Catholics conceded this. Optatus also seems, in Book III, to suppose that Donatus from Casae Nigrae and Donatus of Carthage were one and the same, when he adduces the supplicatory petition presented to Constantine, allegedly by bishops of Donatus’s party, in order to prove that Donatus of Carthage had always wished to be called the leader of this faction [Col. 0792D]. But Augustine, mentioning that supplicatory petition, speaks, as we have noted, of Majorinus’s party, not Donatus’s party.  
>   
> Albaspinaeus does indeed distinguish two Donatuses, but suspects that each was bishop of Carthage, and thinks that the bishop from Casae was transferred to the Carthaginian see after Majorinus’s death, and was succeeded by another Donatus, “the Great,” predecessor of Parmenian. But Optatus recognizes only one bishop between Parmenian and Majorinus, as we have observed. It might more plausibly be said that Donatus from Casae Nigrae was transferred to the see of Carthage, was simply called “of Carthage,” and held that see for a long time. Yet, since it was established between the disputing parties at the Conference of Carthage that the Carthaginian was distinct from the bishop from Casae, there is now no reason to doubt the matter—especially since [Col. 0793D] the transfer of bishops was not customary in the West, nor was it ever alleged against Donatus that he had been transferred by intrigue [Col. 0794D] from the see of Casae to that of Carthage.

He was skilled in humane letters [Col. 0793A], eloquent, learned, commendable for integrity of character and self-restraint; but his spirit was so proud that he thought no man comparable with himself. He treated the bishops of his party as slaves, and despised all mortals, even emperors and magistrates appointed by them. He acquired such authority among his followers that all revered him intensely, swore by him, and in popular speech did not say “the bishop,” but “Donatus of Carthage.”

He divided all Africa into two parts, one of which he wished to be called his own party. Thus, when persons came to Carthage from the several provinces of Africa, he did not ask the customary human questions about rain, peace, or the year’s produce; rather, these were his words to every visitor [Col. 0793B]: “What is being done among you concerning my party?” Consequently, not only were members of his communion commonly called Donatists, but they themselves declared in judicial proceedings and public records that they belonged to Donatus’s party.

When this was reproached to them at the Conference of Carthage, although they repudiated the name, they nevertheless spoke so magnificently of Donatus as their author 10 through the mouth of Petilian:

> “But Donatus, a man of holy memory and martyrial glory, namely our predecessor”—note these words, by which he is called the predecessor not merely of a single bishop of Carthage but of all the bishops of this party—“we rightly and deservedly venerate as the ornament of the Church of this city in his own place.”

Nor did he merely use his authority and various devices to spread the schism throughout Africa; he also undertook to defend it in writings.
