In Jerome’s time there were many of his small works concerning his heresy, and a book *On the Holy Spirit*, which Jerome testifies was consistent with Arian doctrine. Speaking of the same writings, St. Augustine observes that Donatus also held an uncatholic opinion concerning the Trinity: although he affirmed that the Son was of the same substance, he nevertheless believed the Son inferior to the Father and the Holy Spirit inferior to the Son.

“But,” says Augustine, “the multitude of Donatists did not devote attention to this error of his concerning the Trinity, nor is anyone readily found among them who knows that he held this opinion.” Augustine nevertheless testifies elsewhere, in Letter 185 to Count Boniface, that some shared Donatus’s view; but almost all professed that they believed concerning the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit exactly what the Catholic Church believes. Although some of them, wishing to win over the Goths when they saw that the Goths had power, said that they believed what the Goths believed. “But,” Augustine says, “they are convicted by the authority of their ancestors, because Donatus himself, whose party they boast of belonging to, is not said to have believed thus.” Perhaps for this reason Epiphanius and Theodoret attribute the Arian error to the Donatists.

Yet there was no controversy with them concerning doctrines of faith, but only concerning communion itself, the Church, and the authority of the sacraments administered in it. On this last point [Col. 0794A] Donatus had subscribed a letter whose purpose was to establish the belief that the baptism of Christ existed only in his communion. Augustine wrote a book against it, which no longer survives, though the subject of it is reported in Book I, chapter 21, of the *Retractations*.

### Constantine’s Laws against the Donatists

As the number and fury of the Donatists grew, Emperor Constantine enacted a most severe law against them, ordering that their basilicas and the places in which they assembled be taken from them and confiscated to the treasury. But this severity not only did not restrain their insolence; it even inflamed it. So far were they from being brought back to the bosom of the Catholic Church that, on the contrary, they raged against it more fiercely and wantonly.

When Constantine learned this, he wrote a very prudent and gentle letter to all bishops and to the people of the Catholic Church throughout Africa [Col. 0794B]. In it he says that he had tried, as faith demanded, as far as prudence was able, and insofar as purity permitted, by every act of humanity and moderation, to ensure that the peace of the most holy brotherhood, established through concord, might be preserved. But since, because of the obstinacy of some, he had not been able to obtain this, counsels must be governed in such a way that, until the heavenly remedy took effect, those things which most wicked men attempted and did should be borne patiently, and no injury should be repaid in return, their vengeance being reserved for God.

If this were observed, he hoped that, through the grace of the supreme God, when their institutions or dispositions had weakened, the disturbances would soon cease among those who presented themselves as standard-bearers of a most miserable contention. But those whom severity had not restrained could not be subdued by the gentleness and mildness [Col. 0794C] of the excellent prince. Rather, taking greater boldness from his indulgence, they harassed Catholics more grievously each day.

At this time the Circumcellions seem to have arisen: rustic and savage men, so called because they roamed about the *cellae*, harassing and plundering Catholics at the behest of Donatist bishops, so that they even killed some of them. Constantine’s words in the letter just cited seem to concern them: “Since our faith ought to trust that whatever it suffers from the fury of men of this kind will be effective before God for the grace of martyrdom.”

### Proceedings before Zenophilus

Among the Donatist leaders was Silvanus, bishop of Constantine, who, as we have said, had been ordained by the first authors of the schism [Col. 0794D], though as a deacon he had been stained by the charge of having been a *traditor*—one who surrendered sacred books or vessels. He had as his deacon Nundinarius, who knew all the secrets of this sect. When Silvanus excommunicated him and refused to be reconciled with him, Nundinarius publicly revealed everything—above all, that Silvanus had been a *traditor*, and that money had been given by Lucilla in order that Majorinus might be ordained bishop.

Since these two matters were of great importance and greatly damaged the Donatists’ cause—for it followed that they were guilty of the crime of which they accused the Church, and that Majorinus’s ordination was demonstrably defective—the Catholics demanded that proof of them be made by public records and before a judge [Col. 0795A]. The matter was entrusted to Zenophilus, consular governor of Numidia, and the proceedings were held on the Ides of December in the sixth consulship of Constantine Maximus Augustus and the consulship of Constantine the Younger, Noble Caesar: that is, the year of Christ 320.

The proceedings of Munatius Felix, curator of Cirta, were produced, dated the fourteenth day before the Kalends of June, in the eighth consulship of Diocletian and seventh of Maximian. From them it was established that Silvanus had voluntarily surrendered a silver lamp and a silver *capitulata*. Letters of Purpurius of Limata, Fortis, and another bishop, written on Nundinarius’s behalf, were read; from these it was understood how much they feared that Nundinarius would reveal what he knew.

Witnesses were produced who affirmed that Silvanus had been proclaimed bishop by the *Arenarii* against the will of the leading and honorable men of the people of Cirta, and afterward ordained; and that he had then been publicly accused of being a *traditor*. They added that money had been given to Silvanus and bishops by Victor in order that he might be ordained presbyter; and that casks of vinegar had been removed from the temple of Serapis by Bishops Silvanus and Purpurius, together with the presbyters Dontius and Superius and the deacon Lucian.

Witnesses were also heard concerning money given by Lucilla to Numidian bishops in order that Majorinus might be ordained bishop. We possess the greater part of these proceedings, but Zenophilus’s judgment is lacking. Yet it is certain that Silvanus was declared a *traditor*. For he was immediately driven into exile, not because, as Cresconius alleged, he refused to communicate with the persecuting Ursatius and Zenophilus, but, as Augustine asserts in Book III, chapter 30, against this Donatist:

> “Because, though he had been a *traditor*, he also chose to remain a heretic, so that he might hold a false honor in Donatus’s party, which he could hold in the Catholic Church not at all, once the public proceedings of his manifest surrender had been disclosed by judicial judgment.” [Col. 0795C]

It is also clear from this that at that time Count Ursatius opposed himself to the Donatists’ fury in Africa and acted in support of the Catholics against them. Hence the Donatists denounced him as the first cause of the storm stirred up against themselves.

### The Donatists’ Petition to Constantine, Which He Granted

Since Ursatius would not permit the Donatists to rage and was compelling them into the Catholic Church, in 321 they presented a petition to Emperor Constantine asking that he allow them to act freely and not compel them against their will into Caecilian’s communion. They added that they would by no means communicate with “that rascal of a bishop”—meaning Caecilian, whom they called the emperor’s bishop because he had pronounced him innocent and regarded him as the lawful bishop of Carthage. They declared themselves ready rather to suffer whatever he might wish to do to them. [Col. 0795D]

In this petition they also asked the emperor to recall Silvanus and his colleagues from exile. At this the most merciful emperor not only 11 did not flare up, as he might justly have done, but, on the contrary, in his customary kindness granted them all that they requested. In a rescript to Valerius, or Verinus, vicar of Africa, he ordered that they should be allowed to act freely and that their fury should be left to God the avenger; at the same time he permitted those driven into exile to return home. This rescript was issued on 5 May 330.

### The Donatists’ Harassment of Catholics. Constantine’s Laws in Favor of Catholics

This excessive gentleness of the emperor caused members of the Donatist faction to assault Catholics more freely, especially in Numidia, where Donatus’s party was more numerous and powerful. Among other acts, they forcibly seized the basilica which the emperor had ordered built in the city of Constantine, the metropolis of Numidia—formerly called Cirta—and, though repeatedly warned by Catholic bishops and by judges under the emperor’s orders, refused to restore it.

They even incited the decurions and leading men of the cities by malicious insinuations to summon readers, subdeacons, and the other clergy of the Catholic Church to the decurionate and the duties of public offices. Therefore the bishops of the Catholic Church throughout Numidia were compelled to write to the emperor [Col. 0796B] and implore his help. Since they knew that the emperor’s disposition inclined toward gentleness and patience, they requested no vengeance against their enemies; nor did they ask that the basilica be restored to them by force and imperial authority. Instead, they requested that another site from the imperial estate be granted to them, so that they might build a new church there.

After inveighing at length against the Donatist faction and warmly praising the patience of the Catholic bishops, the emperor granted what they requested. He immediately wrote to the *rationalis*, ordering him to transfer to the Catholic Church ownership of a site belonging to the treasury and to erect a basilica there at the treasury’s expense. He also ordered the consular governor to assist the bishops in constructing this church. He ruled that readers of the Catholic Church, subdeacons, and the remaining clergy were not to be compelled to public duties and the decurionate; and he ordered that those summoned to such duties at Donatist instigation should be released from them.

That law survives in the Theodosian Code, Law 7, *On Bishops*, addressed to Valentinus, consular governor of Numidia, in almost the same words as those reported in Constantine’s letter to the Numidian bishops:

> “Readers of the divine writings, subdeacons, and the remaining clergy who have been summoned to the municipal council through the injury of heretics shall be released; and henceforth, in the manner of the East, they shall by no means be summoned to municipal councils, but shall enjoy the fullest exemption.”

This law, like the letter, was issued at Serdica on the Nones of February. The names of the consuls, which are not appended in the letter, are found in the law: namely, Gallicanus and Symmachus, whose consulship fell in [Col. 0796D] 330. Therefore, with a recent writer of exact learning, we assign that letter of Constantine and the entire affair of the Constantinian basilica to this year, rather than to 317 or 318, when Henry Valesius supposed these things had occurred.

### Donatist Doctrines

When the Donatists understood that the Churches throughout the world adhered to Caecilian’s communion and were alien to their own, they went so far in rashness as to say that the Catholic Church had remained only in their own party and had been extinguished in the other parts of the world, as though by contagion of communion. Persisting more obstinately in the ancient African opinion that baptism and the other sacraments were invalid outside the true Church [Col. 0797A], they ordered all who came to them, having been baptized in Churches which they considered adulterous, to be baptized again.

They detested the sacrifices and all the sacred rites of Catholics as impure; they trampled underfoot the Eucharist consecrated by Catholics as a profane object; they judged the preparation of chrism, sacred anointing, ordinations, and all other sacraments invalid. They scraped down or burned altars as polluted by the impure sacrifices of Catholics; broke chalices; washed the walls and floors of churches with water; held that the priesthoods of bishops and the vows of virgins made among Catholics had no force; and, finally, utterly abhorred communion with Catholics.

These and their other doctrines followed from that false persuasion that the Church [Col. 0797B] had perished throughout the whole world, and from the old teaching of African bishops that nothing valid or effective could be done outside the Church. They said that the Church had perished because it had recognized Caecilian—ordained by Felix of Aptunga, accused of *traditio*—and other manifest *traditores*, as they alleged, as bishops, and had not expelled them from its communion.

They believed, namely, that the true Church ought to consist only of men outwardly holy and righteous. They admitted indeed that bad persons were mingled with good persons in the Church, but only if they were hidden, not public and manifest. This had indeed been the discipline of the early Church: communion was denied to those who communicated with idolaters and other sinners guilty of crimes who had been expelled from the Church. Thus, at the beginning of the schism, when Caecilian had been condemned by a council of seventy bishops [Col. 0797C], some of those who refused communion with him could be excused.

But when subsequent judgments pronounced him innocent, none but the obstinate could avoid communion with him, particularly since he had been condemned by judges to whom this judgment did not belong. And after all Churches outside Africa communicated with him, to assert that the Catholic Church had consequently perished was the height of madness.

Those who first acted against the Donatists concentrated on clearing Caecilian and Felix, his ordainer, of the charges brought against them, and thus on showing that they rightly maintained communion with them; while, conversely, their opponents were themselves *traditores* or sons of *traditores*. But as time passed [Col. 0797D], defenders of the Church applied themselves to proving that it was impossible for the Catholic Church to have perished from the whole world and remained only in Donatus’s party—that is, among a few Africans. Once this was proved, it was already evident that baptism and the other sacraments conferred by Catholics were valid and effective.

But Augustine, and in some measure Optatus before him, further endeavored to show that baptism would be valid even if conferred by schismatics or heretics. Consequently the Donatists sinned on two counts when they rebaptized persons baptized by Catholics: first, because they rejected the baptism of the true Church; second, because they repeated legitimate baptism, by whomever it had been conferred.

### A Donatist Council against Repeated Baptism

Nor was every Donatist unanimous about repeating baptism. For Tychonius the Donatist wrote, as Augustine reports in Letter 93 to Vincentius the Rogatist, section 43, that a council of 270 bishops of the Donatist communion had been held at Carthage. In that council, after seventy-five days, all earlier matters having been set aside, a considered decision was reached and decreed: that *traditores*, guilty of an enormous crime, should, if unwilling to be baptized, be admitted to communion as whole and unimpaired persons. He further wrote that Deuterius, bishop of Macriana and of the same communion, had mingled a gathered people of *traditores* with the Church; that Deuterius had made unity with the *traditores* according to the decrees of that council; and that Donatus had continually communicated with Deuterius after this act—12 and not only with Deuterius, but with all the bishops of the Moors [Col. 0798B], who for forty years, until the persecution carried out through Macarius, communicated with *traditores* without baptism.

No trace of this council is found elsewhere. It seems not to have been held before 330, and not at the beginning of the schism. First, the great number of bishops in this council proves that the Donatist faction had then become established and widely extended in Africa. Second, Tychonius’s words show this: when writing, he observed that many of those through whom these facts could be shown to be most certain and obvious—that is, eyewitnesses—were still alive. Tychonius flourished about 380; and so this must have happened many years after the beginning of the schism.

Third, because he indicates that Donatus, bishop of Carthage, was then living [Col. 0798C]. For, after saying that Deuterius had made unity with the *traditores* according to the decrees of this council, he adds that Donatus continually communicated with the same Deuterius after this act. Therefore that council was held about 330, in the time of Donatus of Carthage, under whom the Donatist faction especially flourished.

Augustine maintains that Tychonius’s testimony concerning that council is true because Parmenian, replying against him, did not refute these points as false; and because Tychonius states that, when he wrote, many were alive through whom these facts could be shown to be most certain and obvious. Nevertheless Donatus himself and other Donatists, disregarding this council’s authority, presumed to rebaptize those baptized by Catholics.

### Donatist Bishops in the City of Rome

[Col. 0798D] At the same time, or even some years earlier, the Donatists, so that they might appear to have a party in Rome, first secretly sent from Africa visiting bishops to govern a few wandering persons and especially African foreigners then residing at Rome. The first of them was Victor, bishop of Garba in Numidia, who does not seem to be different from the Victor who attended the Council of Cirta.

When he came to Rome, he was, as Optatus says, “a son without a father, a novice without a leader, a disciple without a teacher, a follower without one going before him, an inhabitant without a house, a guest without lodging, a shepherd without a flock, a bishop without a people.” For the few persons who had no place in which to gather among the forty-odd basilicas then existing at Rome could not be called a flock or a people. Therefore they enclosed with wickerwork a certain cave outside the city, where they held their assembly. Hence at Rome they were called the Mountaineers, or the Campites, or the Rock-Dwellers.

He was succeeded by Boniface, bishop of Ballita, likewise of Numidia, also sent from Africa to Rome. These are the two of whom Augustine says, in *On the One Baptism against Petilian*, that the Donatists first secretly sent visiting and foreign bishops from among the Africans of their party to distant places. Since they were bishops of other sees in Africa and had not been ordained under the title of the Roman see, they could not be called Roman bishops, but only visitors, as the ancients liked to speak.

Afterward they ordained, for the little populace deceived in Rome, bishops as though their own. The first among these was Encolpius, of whom nothing is known. [Col. 0799B] He was succeeded by Macrobius, who had first been a presbyter of the Catholic Church in Africa and had written a book *To Confessors and Virgins*. It was a moral work, but one of very necessary teaching, especially well furnished with highly apt maxims for preserving chastity. Later, having departed from the Catholic Church, he was a secret Donatist bishop in Rome, as we learn from Gennadius.

This Macrobius was still alive and held his seat at Rome when Optatus first wrote, that is, about 370. He was succeeded by Lucianus Claudianus, who was living at Rome after 380, as we learn from the letter of the bishops of Italy to Emperors Gratian and Valentinian. Writing to them concerning the Donatists and Claudianus, they say:

> “Your Clemency ordered that a man named Restitutus should state his case before bishops in Africa. He ought to have submitted, but he fled from the necessity of pleading his case by the same cruel and insolent band. Again in Africa, at God’s prompting, you commanded that the sacrilegious rebaptizers be expelled; but Claudianus was ordained by the expelled persons and is sent to disturb the city of Rome as though he were a bishop. Contrary to the precepts of divine Scripture and to the laws of the Gospel, he says that all bishops, whether of former times or the present, were devoid of the mysteries and, to repeat his own word, pagans. Your Serenity ordered him, once expelled from Rome, to return to his own homeland. But, despising the judgments, though he has indeed often been restrained, he still remains, frequently soliciting poorer people with money and not fearing to rebaptize those whom he has bought off. He deprives them rather of what they had received than gives what manifestly cannot be conferred twice.” [Col. 0799D]

In response to their report, Gratian wrote to Aquilinus, vicar of the city, concerning this Claudianus:

> “Claudianus too, summoned by those who, against the divine precepts, restore the corruptions of religion—by those, I say, whom we ordered expelled—is said, as though he had undertaken too small a crime had he remained in Africa, to have established himself in Rome. And this false teacher endeavors either to profane with a perverse mystery those who are still uninitiated, or, by a greater crime, to corrupt afresh those already initiated. For repetition does not add to the discipline of the most holy religion, but overthrows it. We, pursuing Claudianus with a punishment unlike that which he deserved, ordered him merely to return to his homeland, having thus far set severity aside; [Col. 0800A] but he is said even now to remain, soliciting the ignorant and demanding a wholly empty reward, while destroying the souls of bodies redeemed.”

Who succeeded Claudianus is uncertain. But Felix attended the Conference of Carthage and called himself bishop of the city of Rome. He subscribed the Donatist authorization, as is recorded in the proceedings of the Conference, day 1, chapter 149. When his name had been read aloud and he himself came forward, Aurelius, bishop of the Catholic Church at Carthage, protested:

> “Granted that he calls himself bishop of the city of Rome, why is prejudice being caused to the absent man—namely Innocent, the true bishop of Rome?”

Felix was probably Roman, for Petilian immediately says: “No one is ignorant of what reason brought him here. All Roman nobility is here, as you yourselves also know.” Thus the same tempest and the same necessity—namely, the disaster of the city of Rome, which Alaric captured on the ninth day before the Kalends of September, 410 [Col. 0800B]—brought him there. With this Felix the succession of the pseudo-bishops of Donatus’s party at Rome seems to have failed.

The Donatists sent bishops not only to Rome, but also to Spain, where, as Augustine testifies, they sent a fictitious bishop to the household of a single woman. They omitted nothing in their journeys over sea and land to add proselytes to their sect. Yet their sect remained confined to Africa, where for some time it was very numerous; and to a few Mountaineers at Rome, and to the household or estate of one Spanish woman.

Donatists Invited to Unity by Various Means. — After Constantine’s death, Africa fell to Constans. There, when the Donatist faction raised fresh disturbances, efforts were made by order of the emperor—at the time at Caecilian’s urging, with the approval of Count Leontius, under the leadership of Ursatius, and with Marcellinus then serving as tribune—to bring the Donatists back to Catholic unity. They were offered the retention of their ecclesiastical rank if they wished to be united with the Catholic Church. They were enticed toward salvation by rewards and various inducements; but since their spirit remained rigid and unyielding in schism, and since they daily devised new measures against the Catholic Church, they were restrained with the aid of secular authority. Leontius and Ursatius dealt harshly with certain of the more turbulent among them; several basilicas which they had seized were taken from them, which could not be accomplished without force. Some were thrown into prison, others proscribed and sent into exile. Although these penalties were deserved by their offenses, they nevertheless seized upon them as an occasion to calumniate the Catholics as persecutors and enemies of Christians, cruelly raging against the innocent. These matters and others may be seen in the discourse of a certain Donatist, which we now publish for the first time. Gregory succeeded Ursatius and Leontius, who are recorded as the first to suppress the Donatists by force of arms. Donatus addressed to Gregory a letter so insulting that he called him “the stain of the senate” and “the disgrace of prefects,” and assailed him with other insults of this kind.

Gratus, Successor of Caecilian. Paul and Macarius Sent to Africa; and the Cause of the Circumcellions’ Fury. — When Caecilian of Carthage died before the year 347, [Col. 0801A] Gratus succeeded him. He was present among the Catholic bishops at the Council of Sardica in that year. Donatus of Carthage was still alive at that time; the opponents of Athanasius wrote to him from the pseudo-Sardican synod. The Donatists later displayed that letter in order to prove that they had at some time been in communion with the Eastern Churches.

During the episcopate of this Gratus of Carthage, and perhaps at his request, the emperor Constans sent Paul and Macarius into Africa in 348—not primarily to establish unity, but to distribute alms from the public treasury to the poor. When they came to Donatus and explained the reason for which they had been sent, he was inflamed with his customary madness and, according to Optatus, burst out with the words: “What has the emperor to do with the Church?” From the fountain of his frivolity [Col. 0801B] he poured forth many curses.

“The emperor,” says the same author, “had sent ornaments for the houses of God; he had sent alms for the poor—nothing for Donatus.” Why, then, did he rage? Why was he angry? Why did he reject what had been sent? When those who had been dispatched said that they were going through each province and would give to all who wished to receive, he said that he had sent letters beforehand everywhere, forbidding the distribution anywhere to the poor of what had been brought.

Nevertheless, Paul and Macarius travelled through the provinces, scattering alms among the people and exhorting all to unity. When they arrived at the Numidian city of Bagaï, another Donatus, bishop of that city, wishing to set an obstacle and impediment against unity before them, sent heralds through the neighboring places and throughout all the markets, and stirred up against them a great crowd of frenzied persons [Col. 0801C] called Circumcellions. They were, Augustine says, a rustic class of men of notorious audacity, committing monstrous crimes not only against others but, with the same insane ferocity, not even sparing themselves. They considered it glorious and nearly equivalent to martyrdom to procure death for themselves by precipices, fire, or water.

Donatus called them *agonistici*, “combatants,” as though they were contending for truth and justice, although they plundered others’ property contrary to every law, human and divine, and raged savagely against others. Even before the arrival of Paul and Macarius, this class of men wandered through the districts under the leadership of Axido and Fasir, whom those same madmen called “leaders of the saints.” No one was permitted to be secure, as Optatus relates the matter (book III, §4). In their own estates, promissory notes for debts had lost their force [Col. 0801D]; at that time no creditor had freedom to demand payment. All were intimidated by the letters of those who boasted that they were leaders of the saints; and if anyone delayed in complying with their commands, a mad multitude suddenly rushed upon him. Terror went before them, and creditors were surrounded by dangers, so that those who ought to have been petitioned for repayment of what was due them were driven by fear of death humbly to make entreaties. Each person hastened to forfeit even very large debts; escaping their outrages was counted gain.

Even journeys could not be entirely safe, because masters, thrown down from their vehicles before their slaves, ran servilely while the slaves sat in the masters’ places. At their judgment and command the condition of masters and slaves was reversed. Therefore, when odium was then incurred by the bishops of that party, they are said to have written to Taurinus, then count, that men of this sort could not be corrected within the Church, and directed that they should receive discipline from the aforesaid count.

Taurinus, in response to their letter, ordered armed soldiers to go through the markets where Circumcellion fury was accustomed to range. At Octava many were killed and many mutilated; their bodies could, even to the present day, be counted by the whitened altars or tables. When some of their number began to be buried in basilicas, Clarus, a presbyter at Subbula, was compelled by his bishop to make the burial an unburial. Hence it was handed down that an order had been given for what was done, since not even burial in the house of God had been permitted to them.

Their multitude afterward recovered its strength. Thus Donatus of Bagaï found the means to bring a frenzied crowd against Macarius [Col. 0802B]. From this very class came those who, through desire for false martyrdom, hired persons to strike them down to their own ruin; and likewise those who cast their worthless lives from the summits of high mountains, throwing themselves headlong. See from what sort of population Bishop Donatus had formed troops for himself.

Terrified by this danger, those who carried the treasures to distribute among the poor found, in so great a necessity, the expedient of requesting armed soldiers from Count Silvester—not that they might inflict violence upon anyone, but that they might prevent the violence arranged by the above-mentioned Bishop Donatus. For this reason soldiers appeared under arms. Now consider to whom whatever followed ought or can be attributed. They had there an innumerable crowd of summoned persons, and it is certain that an adequate supply of provisions had been prepared. They had made public granaries, as it were, out of the basilica [Col. 0802C], awaiting people upon whom they might exercise their rage and do whatever their madness dictated, had not the presence of armed troops stood in the way.

For when surveyors were sent ahead of the soldiers who were to come, as is customary, they were not suitably received in accordance with the Apostle’s command: “Render honor to whom honor is due; revenue to whom revenue; tribute to whom tribute; owe no one anything.” Those sent, with their horses, were beaten by men whose names Parmenian was fanning with the bellows of hatred. They themselves became the teachers of the wrong done to them; by the injuries they had first inflicted, they taught what they themselves might suffer. The soldiers returned to their units after being harassed, and what two or three had suffered grieved them all. Everyone was stirred; not even their commanders could restrain the angry soldiers.

Thus occurred that through which odium was cast upon unity: namely, the Circumcellions’ audacity was forcibly suppressed. Indeed, some were killed, including Marculus and Donatus of Bagaï, Maximianus and Isaac. The Donatists celebrated their memory as that of martyrs and composed acts of their passion, which we have published at the end of this work. Most of the schismatic bishops, together with their clergy, fled in fear; some died; those who were more resolute were captured and banished to distant places. Donatus of Carthage seems to have been among these; hence, at the Conference of Carthage, Petilian calls him a man of martyrlike glory. These events occurred especially in Numidia, for the proconsular province was free from these disturbances.

These were the times and deeds called Macarian [Col. 0803A], from which the Donatists manufactured charges against the Catholics. And yet, says Optatus, “nothing of all this was done at the wish of the Catholics, nothing by their counsel, nothing with their knowledge, nothing by their action; but everything occurred amid the bitter grief of God, who wept, and in vengeance for the water”—that is, the sacred washing—which they were again administering contrary to the prohibition.

By this means, however, unity was secured and peace restored in Africa. Gratus, bishop of Carthage, gives thanks to God for this benefit, in the name of all the Catholic bishops of Africa, at the Council of Carthage of 349, in these words:

> Thanks be to almighty God and to Christ Jesus, who put an end to evil schisms and looked upon his Church, so as to raise into her bosom all her scattered members; who commanded the most religious Emperor Constans to carry out the desire for unity and to send the servants of the holy work, the servants of God, Paul and Macarius.

Two Canons against the Donatists. — At the same council two canons concerning the Donatists were enacted. One established that rebaptisms were unlawful in the case of persons who, when questioned, had confessed the Trinity according to the faith of the Gospel and the teaching of the Apostles and had afterward been immersed in water. The other forbade the veneration as martyrs of persons who had thrown themselves headlong, or procured death for themselves in some other way, or deserved to be killed.

Calumny against Macarius concerning the Placement of an Image on the Altar. — About this time, the event occurred which Optatus relates: the Donatists spread among the populace the rumor that Paul and Macarius were coming to take part in the sacrifice, and that, when the altars had been solemnly prepared, they would bring forward an image and place it first upon the altar, after which the sacrifice would be offered. When this rumor reached people’s ears, their minds were struck, and every tongue was set in motion with these words: “Whoever tastes therefrom tastes of something sacred.” This would have been rightly said if truth corresponding to such a report had followed.

But when the aforesaid men arrived, nothing of the kind appeared. The eyes of Christians saw nothing at which to shudder; sight confirmed none of the things by which hearing had been disturbed. Purity was seen, and the customary solemn observance was perceived. They saw that in the divine sacrifices nothing had been changed, added, or taken away. The peace commended by God pleased those who were willing; therefore no one should blame any who passed from the fellowship of the Donatists to peace. Those disturbed by an adverse report were confirmed by simple and pure truth.

Driven from this calumny, the Donatists resorted to another, saying that Macarius ought not to have been admitted by the bishops to communion, much less allowed to address the people in church, since this appeared to belong only to bishops. Optatus replies that Macarius communicated with the bishops as a layman, not as a bishop; that he did indeed address the people in church, but for the purpose of introducing some matter, not of expounding—that is, preaching—which belongs to bishops. Nor did he greet the people, as bishops do, in God’s name at the beginning of prayer [Col. 0804A], nor perform any priestly office.

How Long the Peace of the African Church Lasted. Donatus’ Death in Exile. Parmenian, Donatus’ Successor. — The unity and peace of the African Church, brought about by Macarius, endured for almost fourteen years under Constans and Constantius. At that time Vitellius the African appears to have composed a book on the theme that the servants of God are hated by the world. In it he attacked Catholics as persecutors and represented his own party as servants of God suffering persecution unjustly. He also wrote another work in which he renewed against the Catholics the old calumny concerning the crime of “handing over” (*traditio*).

It is inferred from Optatus that Donatus of Carthage ended his life in exile before Julian’s accession. For, in book III, §3, Optatus says that in Donatus was fulfilled what the Prophet had said about the prince of Tyre: that he would die in a land not his own; and that it was known to all that this happened to Donatus. Parmenian succeeded Donatus after 350, perhaps in 355, the year in which Jerome mentions him in the *Chronicle*. He is the man refuted by Optatus and already discussed at sufficient length in the preface to this work. Meanwhile, Gratus was succeeded in the Catholic see by Restitutus, who attended the Council of Rimini in 359; and Restitutus by Genethlius, who lived until 390.

State of the African Church after Unity Had Been Restored. — Optatus rightly describes the state of the African Church after unity was restored, in book II, §15:

> When one peace united the African peoples, the Eastern peoples, and the other peoples across the sea, and unity itself, with all its members restored, knit together the body of the Church, the devil grieved—he who is always tormented by the peace of brethren. At that time, under a Christian emperor, abandoned among idols as though shut up, he lay in the temples. At this same time, the leaders and chiefs of the Donatists had withdrawn into deserved exile. There were no schisms in the Church, nor were pagans permitted to practice sacrileges. Peace pleasing to God dwelt among all Christian peoples; the devil mourned in the temples, the Donatists in foreign regions.

Freedom Restored to the Donatists by Julian. — But after Constantius died on 3 November 361, the Donatists presented a petition to the Emperor Julian, requesting the restoration of the basilicas of which they complained that they had been deprived, and the recovery of their former freedom. The petition was offered in the name of Rogatianus, Pontius, Cassianus, and other bishops and clergy of the party of Donatus. In it, they flattered Julian servilely, not shrinking from declaring that justice alone had access to him.

The apostate emperor readily granted their request, since he desired to destroy the Christian religion by every artifice, foreseeing that great harm to the African Church would result. He therefore ordered those whom he understood would return in fury to disturb the peace to return according to their desire. Repealing the measures enacted against the Donatists, he granted them every freedom—or rather license—to devise whatever they wished. Thus the Donatists’ freedom was restored by the same proclamation by which the temples of idols were ordered opened.

The returning bishops, among whom Parmenian, bishop of Carthage, is counted, presented their petitions and the emperor’s rescript to the magistrates. Armed with this authority, they shrank from no act against the Catholics. Optatus describes their deeds at that time as follows (book II, §17):

> At almost the same moment at which the devil is released from his prisons, your fury returns into Africa. And are you not ashamed that, at one and the same time, you share common joys with the enemy? You came rabid; you came enraged; tearing the limbs of the Church; subtle in seductions, monstrous in slaughter, provoking the children of peace to war. You made many exiles from their homes when, coming with a hired band, you seized basilicas. Many from your number committed bloody massacres in many places—too many to name individually—and atrocities so grave that reports concerning such deeds were sent to the judges of that time.

At that time the Donatists committed innumerable crimes and sacrileges, described at length by Optatus in the same book and also in book VI, where they may be read.

Laws of the Emperors against the Donatists. — Julian, who was killed on 26 June 363, was succeeded by Jovian. Jovian died quickly and could make no determinations concerning matters pertaining to the African Church. But Valentinian the Elder restrained the Donatists by severe laws. One still survives, issued at Trier on 20 February 373, declaring a bishop who repeats baptism unworthy of the priesthood.

At the same time Count Romanus, who commanded the forces in Africa until 373, did not permit the schismatics freely to do what they wished. The Donatists count him among their persecutors at the Conference of Carthage. After this, Gratian enacted a severe law against them on 17 October 377.

Donatists Divided into Many Sects. — Around this time the sect of Donatus was divided into many parts. Leaving aside the disagreement between Tichonius and Parmenian concerning the Church and rebaptism, several factions arose among the Donatists in Mauretania and Numidia, which Augustine writes were not widely known: the Urbanenses in a corner of Numidia, and the Claudianists, who later returned to favor with Primian, Parmenian’s successor. But Augustine mentions the Rogatists and Maximianists more frequently, and their history is better known.

The Rogatist Schism. — The founder of the Rogatists was Rogatus, a Moorish bishop, perhaps bishop of Cartenna. They were consequently scattered through Mauretania Caesariensis and few in number. The cause of their separation from the other Donatists is uncertain. They were gentler than the rest and made no use of bands of Circumcellions. Yet Rogatus is recorded as having fought with most bitter persistence, even in litigation, concerning certain unspecified affairs of his own people. They boasted that, when Christ came for judgment, he would find faith only among them; thus they were no less hateful to the Donatists than to Catholics.

Therefore, since the remaining body of Donatists took this faction very badly, it stirred up secular rulers against them. At that time, while Valentinian and Valens were emperors, Firmus the Moor—the son of Nubel, king of Mauretania—had secretly killed his brother Zamma. Because of this, he was hostile toward the Count of Africa, Romanus by name, to whom Zamma had been dear; fearing condemnation and death, he rebelled against imperial authority and seized the kingdom of Mauretania.

The Donatists used this opportunity to harass Rogatus and his followers in Mauretania Caesariensis most savagely and cruelly through the barbarian king. The Rogatists consequently called them Firmians, just as Donatists customarily called Catholics Macarians. They left nothing undone to compel them to return to their fold or to satisfy their cruelty by vengeance. This persecution lasted until Theodosius the Elder, sent by Valentinian into Africa with an army against Firmus, defeated the rebel against the empire in several battles and compelled him to end his life by hanging. Rogatus survived Firmus and remained in schism.

At that time the Caesarean bishop of the Rogatists made an agreement with the tyrant Firmus for the safety of his own people, opened the gates to him, and delivered not merely the Catholics but the entire city to devastation. After Rogatus’ death, Vincentius succeeded him both in his see and in the schism. There was also another Vincentius Victor of the same sect, disciple and admirer of the first Vincentius. Although he had returned to Catholic unity, he had not so completely laid aside his former veneration for Vincentius that he did not boast that Vincentius had appeared to him and aided him in composing the work on the soul and its origin which he published against Augustine.

The Maximianist Schism. Primian Condemns Maximian. Council of Carthage against Primian. [Col. 0806C] Council of Cabarsussa against Primian. — No disagreement among the Donatists was greater or more celebrated than that between the Primianists and the Maximianists. This schism began shortly after 391, when Primian was ordained bishop of Carthage, in the party of Donatus, in place of Parmenian; at roughly the same time Aurelius succeeded Genethlius among the Catholics.

Soon after his ordination, Primian resolved to condemn Maximian, a deacon of his church said to have been related to Donatus, whose pride he believed had injured him. With Maximian he condemned three other deacons—Rogatian, Donatus, and Salgamius—and in fact pronounced sentence against the absent Maximian.

Maximian, relying on the resources of a wealthy woman, just as Majorinus of old had relied on Lucilla’s influence, resisted Primian. Having attached to himself part of the people of Carthage and certain elders, he sent letters and envoys in their name to the whole body of bishops, begging them to come to Carthage. Maximian himself approached neighboring bishops, laid his innocence before them, stirred hostility toward Primian, and afterward accused him before them.

When these bishops, forty-three in number, came to Carthage, Primian refused to meet them. Hiring a crowd and securing officials, he blockaded the doors of the basilicas and prevented the bishops who had come against him from entering them and carrying out the customary proceedings. Summoned once, twice, and three times to their council, he refused to attend, and harshly mistreated those whom the council had sent.

The bishops then did not dare to pronounce final judgment upon him in his absence. Instead, Augustine says (*Against Cresconius*, IV.6), they provided by a kind of preliminary judgment that, if Primian trusted his case, an opportunity would remain for him to answer and clear himself at the next, more numerous council. This council was held shortly afterward at Cabarsussa in Byzacena. It was more numerous than the first and, if Augustine is to be believed, comprised one hundred bishops, although the subscription to the letter of this council preserves only fifty-three names.

At this council a definitive sentence was pronounced against Primian in these terms:

> We, all the priests of God, the Holy Spirit being present, have decreed this same Primian to be perpetually condemned from the priestly body: first, because he appointed other bishops over living bishops; because he mixed incestuous persons with the communion of the saints; because he attempted to compel presbyters to enter into conspiracy; because he had the presbyter Fortunatus cast into a sewer when he had brought baptismal aid to the sick; because he denied communion to the presbyter Demetrius in order to compel him to disown his son; because the same presbyter was rebuked for having received bishops as guests; because the aforesaid Primian sent a crowd to tear down Christians’ houses; because bishops together with clergy were besieged and afterward stoned by his retainers; because elders were beaten in the basilica because they resented the admission of Claudianists to communion; because he judged innocent clergy to be deserving of condemnation; because he refused to present himself for a hearing before us, having closed off even the entrance of the basilicas to us by crowd and official force; because he insultingly rejected envoys sent from us to him; because he seized many places, first by force and afterward by judicial authority; besides his other unlawful acts, which for the dignity of our style we have passed over in silence—lest, through contact with him, the Church of God be stained either by contagion or by some crime.

> It has indeed pleased us and the Holy Spirit that a period be reserved for the slow to convert, on condition that any fellow priests or clergy, forgetful of their salvation, who have not withdrawn from communion with the condemned Primian from the day of his condemnation—that is, from the eighth day before the Kalends of July [24 June]—until the sixteenth day before the Kalends of January [17 December], shall be bound by this sentence. Laypeople likewise, unless they separate themselves from his association from the aforesaid day of his condemnation until the coming Easter Day, cannot be restored to the Church except through penance, if indeed they remember.

From this we learn that the council was held on 24 June 393, since the Council of Bagaï, in which its acts were rescinded, bears the consuls of 394. After Primian’s deposition, the same bishops designated Maximian bishop of Carthage in his place. Shortly afterward he was ordained by twelve bishops against Primian, just as Majorinus had formerly been ordained against Caecilian.

Council of Bagaï against Maximian and His Followers. Persecution of the Maximianists by the Primianists. — To defend himself against their efforts, Primian did not hesitate to summon a larger council and to have Maximian’s case tried there. It was held at Bagaï in Numidia on 24 April 394. Three hundred and ten bishops were present. There Maximian was not only acquitted but condemned, together with his ordainers and the clergy of the Church of Carthage who had attended his ordination.

Those who had followed Maximian’s party were given time until 25 December. If they returned within it, no penalty was imposed upon them; if they neglected to do so, sentence was imposed, so that after the appointed day they could be admitted only through penance and, consequently, after losing their offices. Emeritus, bishop of Caesarea, was the author of this sentence, which we have reproduced almost in full from various passages of St Augustine among the ancient documents. When it was read out to be decreed by the council, all acclaimed it with the greatest delight: some rejoicing that it was so eloquent, others that it had so conspicuously mocked their schismatics.

After it had been published by the unanimous consent of all, they immediately began with great zeal to persecute those condemned. Turning against Maximian’s basilica, which they called not a basilica but a cave, they had their excited mob demolish it. Nor was Primian content with this: he drove Maximian from his own house, through an agent commissioned for the purpose, so that it might be converted into an ecclesiastical exorcistery; the official delegate from Carthage supported him.

Frightened by these beginnings, many Maximianists returned to their former associates before the end of the period of delay and were received by them as cleansed and innocent. Others, however, remained obstinately fixed in their purpose and could not be induced to return to Primian. The matter was therefore brought before proconsuls who, though appointed by Christian emperors, were nevertheless pagans. Before them the Bagaï decree was produced and laws against heretics were cited, by which they were ordered to be expelled from basilicas. Orders were secured for execution of these measures, and the assistance of government offices and cities was requested, so that those condemned at the Council of Bagaï, who frequented their own separate meeting places, might be expelled from the places and basilicas which they had not seized but had held in continuous possession with the communities adhering to them.

Some yielded easily to these vexations and suffered little. But those who attempted resistance were grievously afflicted; those unable to prevail by force were defeated and expelled, and others were ordained in their place.

Proceedings of the Primianists against Salvius of Membresa, Felicianus of Musti, and Praetextatus of Assuras. [Col. 0808D] — Particular violence was directed against Maximian’s ordainers, who had been expressly condemned at the Council of Bagaï, especially against Salvius, bishop of Membresa. In his place, in that same year 394, Restitutus had been ordained by the Primianists.

The case was brought before the proconsul Herodes. Nummasius, advocate of Restitutus, requested that the Church of Membresa be handed over to Primian’s communion, alleging that Salvius, one of Maximian’s ordainers, had been condemned by decree of the plenary Council of Bagaï and therefore, as a heretic, ought to yield to Restitutus all places which he held as bishop, or at least return to Primian. The proconsul judged accordingly.

They also accused Felicianus of Musti and Praetextatus of Assuras, likewise among Maximian’s ordainers, before the same proconsul. Titianus conducted the case against the former on 2 March 395 and alleged against him the same matters that Nummasius had alleged against Salvius. Proconsul Herodes, who had already pronounced sentence against Salvius and Praetextatus, condemned Felicianus too, ordering that, once the Maximianists had been expelled, the churches should be delivered to Primianist bishops.

Nevertheless, Felicianus and Praetextatus retained their churches, although Rogatus had been ordained by the Primianists as bishop of Assuras. After Rogatus later turned Catholic, the Donatist army—that is, the band of Circumcellions—cut off his tongue and hands. In vain did the Primianists appeal in the following year to Proconsul Theodorus and to the magistrates. Felicianus and Praetextatus remained in their sees until, overcome by misfortunes, they returned to communion with Primian.

Salvius of Membresa, however, was again summoned before Proconsul Serenus and defended his case in court—perhaps, Augustine says, in the confidence that he knew his opponents could not employ before a judge the laws promulgated against heretics without equally entangling themselves in them.

Before Proconsul Serenus, however, either influence prevailed more strongly, or perhaps the Council of Bagaï, which was also read there against the same Salvius, prevailed more strongly. For the proconsul delivered this ruling:

> A dispute of bishops must be heard by bishops according to the law. The bishops have judged. Therefore either return to the body of the old fellowship under satisfaction, or, as you have it written, offer your back to persecutors.

When Salvius refused to comply with the proconsul’s advice, the proconsul ordered him expelled from his church. Because Salvius attempted to retain his see through confidence in the people of Membresa who favored him, the neighboring inhabitants of Abitina were directed to execute the judgment rendered against him.

They seized Salvius and not only drove him from his church, but made him the object of a miserable public spectacle. Having captured the old man, Augustine relates (*Against Cresconius*, IV), they tied dead dogs around his neck and danced with him as long as they pleased. It was an inhuman deed, comparable to that of the Etruscan kings, who bound dead bodies to the living—indeed, all the more foul because dead dogs are more loathsome than dead human beings. Thus, had the old man and bishop Salvius been required to choose between the two punishments, he would by far have preferred to be fastened to human corpses rather than dance with dogs’ carcasses.

Meanwhile Salvius could be deprived of his church and his see and suffer all these things, yet he would not return to Primian’s communion. He dealt in this way with his followers, exalted the justice for which he said he suffered such things, persuaded them that he was holy because he had suffered, and that his opponents were most unjust because they had inflicted these things. Consequently his party built him another basilica at Membresa. While seated there, he suffered new harassment from his opponent Restitutus; he contended with him in court, amid noise and dispute, concerning chapels and small estates. Thus the party of Primian litigated against Maximian and those condemned with him at the Council of Bagaï before four or more proconsuls, through advocates.

Gildo’s Tyranny. — After Theodosius died on 16 January 395, Count Gildo, master of both branches of military service in Africa since 386, seized tyranny after a few months and took possession of all Africa. With this barbarous pagan man, Optatus, bishop of Thamugadi in Numidia, had great influence among other Donatists. He was called a “Gildonian satellite” because he belonged to Gildo’s retinue.

This savage man, not unlike Gildo, was burdensome not only to Catholics but to everyone. Customarily proceeding attended by a military escort, he oppressed widows, ruined orphans through their property, tore wives from their husbands, compelled masters to sell their possessions, and shared the price of what was sold with the sellers. In a word, he ranged against all by force, plunder [Col. 0810B], and fraud.

Yet, such as he was, his own party held him in such esteem that they not only did not dare condemn him but did not even dare admonish him. Amid the groans of all Africa, they did not refuse the kiss of peace; they placed the Eucharist in his hands and received it from him in return. Finally, after he had died in prison because he had belonged to Gildo’s retinue, they celebrated Optatus’ birthday every year with great solemnity as though he were a martyr.

The Primianists used his assistance to harass the Maximianists and Rogatists severely and compel most of them to return to Primian. As stated above, the citizens of Assuras and Musti had until then defended their bishops, Felicianus and Praetextatus, against Primianist attacks. Optatus threatened them with the gravest destruction unless they abandoned the defense of their bishops [Col. 0810C] and compelled them to return to Primian’s communion. Fearing Optatus’ soldiers, the citizens obeyed.

Felicianus and Praetextatus, unable otherwise to retain their sees, yielded. A large assembly of bishops was held, attended by Primian together with Optatus the Gildonian. There the two bishops were received with their rank preserved and their sees retained. They were accepted by the Primianists, and all who had been baptized by them during the schism were received without rebaptism.

Optatus also harassed the Rogatists considerably, but he raged especially against the Catholics and again stirred the Circumcellions against them. The Catholics suffered innumerable evils at their hands. For they no longer ranged about armed only with clubs, as formerly, but, equipped with weapons and missiles of every sort, openly employed violence [Col. 0810D], invaded and plundered basilicas, killed or cruelly mistreated bishops and clergy, and openly and publicly practiced brigandage.

### Honorius’s Law against Invaders of Churches

To suppress these disturbances, after Gildo had already been removed (he, attacked by his brother Mascezel and abandoned by his own men, ended his life by hanging at the beginning of the year 398), the Emperor Honorius issued a law on 25 April 398. By it he ordered that those who, rushing into Catholic churches, committed any outrage against priests, ministers, worship, or the sacred place should be apprehended and, once convicted, punished capitally. He further decreed that all should be free to prosecute, as a public crime, grievous injuries inflicted upon priests or ministers. But if a violent multitude protected itself by arms or by the difficulty of the terrain [Col. 0811A], he instructed the judges to request from the Count of Africa the protection of an armed force, lest those guilty of such crimes escape.

### Decrees of Councils concerning Donatists to Be Promoted to the Clergy or Retained in It

Meanwhile the Catholics left nothing untried in inviting the Donatists to concord. It has already been noted that, at the beginning of the schism, bishops and clerics returning to the Church from Donatus’s party were received with their ranks. But as their number and obstinacy increased, subsequent councils had decreed that no Donatist should be received into the Church with his rank, but only among the laity.

At the Council of Hippo in 393 it was proposed that those be exempted from this rule who were known either not to have rebaptized, or who wished to pass with their congregations into Catholic communion [Col. 0811B]. But it was decided that this exception should not be confirmed until the overseas Church had been consulted about it. Again, at the Council of Carthage in 397, it was ordered that Siricius, Bishop of Rome, and Simplicianus of Milan be consulted as to whether children baptized by Donatists, upon returning to the Church of God with a salutary intention, could be promoted to the ministry of the sacred altar. The bishops of Rome and Milan replied to the question put to them that this was forbidden.

Nevertheless, the African bishops, compelled by a shortage of clerics and by the needs of their churches—which were so deserted that many churches did not possess even a deacon, however unlettered—decreed that children baptized among the Donatists before reaching the use of reason, who afterwards, having recognized the truth, came to the Church of God and were received by the laying on of hands, could be promoted to the clergy [Col. 0811C]. And in order that this decree might be acceptable to the overseas bishops, they sent a solemn embassy, from the Council of Carthage held in June 401, to Anastasius of Rome and Venerius of Milan.

They also added the proposal previously made: that certain Donatist clerics who wished to transfer with their ranks and congregations might be received. But they did not dare to press this point. They judged, however, that every effort should be made concerning the promotion to the clergy of those baptized as infants among the Donatists, so that the overseas bishops might assent to the wish of the Africans. What Anastasius replied to this is not certainly clear. For at the Council of Carthage held in the same year, in September [Col. 0811D], this alone is recorded from his letter: that, with the concern and sincerity of paternal and brotherly charity, he exhorted the African bishops by no means to overlook the injuries of heretics and schismatics, by which they grievously harassed the African Church.

It is nevertheless probable that he permitted children baptized among the Donatists to be promoted to orders; for on this point the Africans ask nothing further of the Apostolic See. But concerning the other matter, the reception of Donatists with their ranks, they decreed that letters should be sent to their brethren and fellow-bishops, especially to the Apostolic See over which Anastasius presided, so that he might know that Africa had a great need, for the peace and benefit of the Church, that among the Donatists, whatever clerics, upon correcting their purpose, wished to pass to Catholic unity, should—according to the will and judgment of each Catholic bishop governing the Church in that place—be received in their ranks, if this seemed conducive to Christian peace [Col. 0812A].

They added that this had been done in earlier times of the same division; nor did they request or decree that the decision of the council held in the overseas regions on this subject should be dissolved. Rather, it was to remain in force with respect to those from whose return no great gain of souls would accrue—that is, that these should not be received in their ranks in accordance with the decree of the overseas council; but those through whom provision was made for Catholic unity should be excepted.

In the same African council the Catholic bishops decreed [Col. 0812B] that letters should be given to the African judges, asking them, by their judicial authority and diligence in the Christian faith, to investigate what had occurred in every place where the Maximianists, who had made a schism from them, had occupied basilicas; and, for the sake of firm knowledge necessary to all, to cause this to be entered in the public records.

Then it also pleased the bishops to send from their own number envoys to the bishops and peoples of the Donatists, to preach that peace and unity without which Christian salvation cannot be obtained. Through them all might learn how completely the Donatists had nothing to say against the Catholic Church; and it might become manifest to all through municipal records what they themselves had done concerning the Maximianists: after condemning them by the authority of their plenary council of eighteen [bishops], they received them again in their ranks, and accepted the baptism which those condemned and excluded persons had administered [Col. 0812C]. Thus it might be known with what foolish heart they resisted peace with the Church spread throughout the whole world, when they did such things for Donatus’s party and yet said that they were not polluted, for the sake of peace, by communion with those whom they had thus received; while they contended that we—that is, the Catholic Church established even in the farthest parts of the earth—were defiled by communion with persons whom, while accusing them, they had then been unable to prove guilty.

With the utmost vigilance, the Catholic bishops labored by their own devices to call the Donatists back from schism and bring them into the Church.

### The Writings and Activities of Saint Augustine against the Donatists: The Alphabetical Psalm

But it is now time to speak of the writings and contests of Saint Augustine against the Donatists, by which they were broken, weakened, and at last conquered. When in 391 he had been promoted to the rank of presbyter in the Church of Hippo, he composed an alphabetical psalm, adapted to the understanding of the less educated people, so that the Donatist cause might reach the awareness of the humblest populace and of persons wholly unlearned, and might adhere to their memory as far as possible. In it he set forth, in lowly and plain speech, the history of the entire schism and a brief refutation of it. In the *Retractations* he places this little work after the other work, *On Faith and the Creed*, which he composed at the Council of Hippo in 393 [Col. 0812D].

### Book against Donatus’s Letter

He also testifies, in Book I, chapter 21 of the *Retractations*, that he wrote, while still a presbyter, a book against the letter of Donatus, who was the second bishop of Donatus’s party after Majorinus. [Col. 0813A] In this letter Donatus sought to establish the belief that Christ’s baptism existed only in his own communion.

### Letter to Maximinus

There also survives a letter of his, written while he was still a presbyter (no. 23), to Maximinus, the Donatist bishop of the town of Siniti. Maximinus was said to have rebaptized a Catholic of the Church of Mutugenna and made him his deacon. Augustine urges him either to admit the deed and defend it in his letter with whatever proofs he could, or, if he denied it and considered that one ought not to be rebaptized, to profess this openly and return to the Church. Finally, he invites him either to a conference or to a written reply, so that the concord of the Church might be established.

This bishop later, after a journey overseas, embraced Catholic peace and remained in the same see, as we learn from Augustine’s Letter 105 [Col. 0813B]. But after Augustine became a bishop, he did not cease to assail the Donatists by writings, letters, sermons, and conferences.

### Proculeianus Invited by Augustine to a Conference

At the beginning of his episcopate, Augustine invited by letter to a conference Proculeianus, the now elderly Donatist bishop at Hippo and therefore his own opponent. Proculeianus at first pretended that he did not refuse a conference, provided that ten serious and honorable men from each side should be present. But changing his mind, he asked why Augustine had not gone to Constantine, where they themselves were more numerous, or why he ought not to go to Milevis, where they were soon to hold a council—thus indicating that he was no match for Augustine.

In other letters addressed also to Eusebius, a Donatist bishop, Augustine reproached this same Proculeianus [Col. 0813C] because he had received a young man who was accustomed to beat his mother and had threatened that, once he had crossed over to Donatus’s party, he would kill her; and because he had rebaptized one reeking with his mother’s blood. Again Augustine invites Proculeianus to a discussion and offers that, if he considers himself unequal to the task, he may summon the aid of whichever colleague he wishes:

> “Although,” he says, “I do not sufficiently understand what this man, who says that he has been a bishop for so many years, fears in me, a novice, that prevents him from being willing to confer with me. If it is learning in the liberal arts, which perhaps he either has not learned or has learned less thoroughly, what does this have to do with the question which must be discussed either from the holy Scriptures or from ecclesiastical or public documents? In these he has been engaged for so many years, and therefore ought to be more skilled than I. Finally, here is my brother and colleague Samfucius, of the Church of Turris, who has learned none of the things which this man is said to fear. Let him be present; let him deal with him.”

He sent a third letter on this subject to the same Eusebius to whom the preceding one had been sent. In it he admonishes Proculeianus, now warned about the mother beaten by this young man, to exclude him from communion. He adds that a certain subdeacon of the Spanish Church, named Primus, had been removed from the clergy because he was prevented from making undisciplined approaches to consecrated women; angered by discipline, he had transferred to the Donatists and had been rebaptized by them. Two consecrated women, his fellow-settlers, from an estate of Catholic Christians—either carried away by him or following him of their own accord—had likewise been rebaptized [Col. 0814A], and were now associating with bands of Circumcellions among wandering bands of women. Augustine wished this too to become known to Proculeianus through Eusebius, so that he might remove from his communion a man who had chosen it for no other reason than that he had lost his clerical standing in the Catholic Church through disobedience and depraved conduct.

Finally, Augustine says that he observes the rule that whoever among the Donatists has been degraded for disciplinary reasons and wishes to transfer to the Catholic Church is received in the humiliation of penitence—a condition which they themselves perhaps would have imposed upon him had he wished to remain among them. Augustine’s letters containing these matters are now nos. 33, 34, and 35.

### Saint Augustine’s Conferences with Donatists

There were subsequently conferences held by the holy Doctor with Donatists: one, in 397 or the following year, at Tubursicum, with Fortunius, the Donatist bishop of that city, and other Donatists. On this, consult Saint Augustine’s Letters 43 and 44. Another conference was conducted by letters with another bishop of that sect, named Honoratus, and with Clarentius, likewise a bishop. The same would have been done with Crispinus of Calama, celebrated among his people for age and reputation, had he not prevented it. Augustine also exhorted his kinsman Severinus, in the letter now numbered 52, to abandon the Donatist schism [Col. 0814B].

### Book against Donatus’s Party; Books against Parmenian’s Letter; Books on Baptism

At about the same time Augustine wrote two books entitled *Against Donatus’s Party*. In the first he had said that he did not approve of schismatics being forcibly constrained to communion by the violence of any secular power. “And indeed,” he says, “at that time I did not approve of it, because I had not yet experienced either how much evil their impunity would dare, or how much the careful application of discipline could contribute to changing them for the better.” This work, composed by Augustine about 398 or 399, is still sought in vain.

To the year 400 should be assigned his books against Parmenian’s letter to Tychonius. In them he treats and resolves the celebrated question whether, within unity and the communion of the same sacraments, evil persons contaminate the good. In the same work he promises to treat baptism more fully, and immediately fulfilled that promise by publishing seven books *On Baptism* [Col. 0814C].

### Book against What Centurius Brought from the Donatists

At about the same time, a certain layman named Centurius brought to the Church certain Donatist dictations or writings against Catholics, arranged in a few passages as if they were testimonies thought to support their cause. Augustine answered them very briefly in a little book bearing this title: *Against What Centurius Brought from the Donatists*. This small work does not survive [Col. 0814D].

### 19. Books against Petilian

We have spoken elsewhere of Petilian, Donatist bishop of the Constantinians. When he had written one letter against Catholics to Donatist presbyters and deacons, the Catholics of that city presented a portion of it to Saint Augustine, in the presence of Fortunatus, the Catholic bishop of the same place, and Alypius of Tagaste. Augustine immediately undertook to refute this fragment of the letter, completing it in his first book.

Afterwards, when he had obtained the whole of Petilian’s letter, he wrote his second book against it, while Anastasius was Bishop of Rome—or at least before he had learned of Anastasius’s death, which occurred on 27 April 402 [Col. 0815A]. In it he reproduces every word of Petilian and appends his own answer to it. But what he had written against part of the letter first reached Petilian, who attempted a response; Augustine opposed to that response a third book.

### Book on the Unity of the Church

Before that reply was published, he seems to have composed the letter to Catholics which is commonly called the *Book on the Unity of the Church*. At its beginning he mentions the first two books against Petilian, but not the third.

### Books against Cresconius

A certain Donatist grammarian, Cresconius, having found Augustine’s first book against Petilian, thought that it required an answer and sent his response to Augustine. Augustine replied to this work in four books. In three of them he dealt with all that the entire response demanded. But seeing that every point which Cresconius had written could be answered from the case of the Maximianists alone—those whom the Donatists had condemned as their own schismatics, afterwards receiving some of them again in their ranks, and whose baptism administered outside their communion they did not repeat—he added a fourth book, in which he demonstrated this as carefully and clearly as he could [Col. 0815B].

When he wrote these four books, the Emperor Honorius had already enacted laws against the Donatists. Augustine himself says this concerning the work in Book II of the *Retractations*, from which we understand that it was written after 406, since the laws of Honorius of which he speaks were issued in 405.

### Books of Proofs and Testimonies against the Donatists

“After this,” says Augustine in the same place, “so that they might reach the Donatists, I took care to compile, against their error and for Catholic truth, the necessary documents, whether from ecclesiastical records, public records, or canonical Scriptures; and I first sent to them the same materials I had promised, so that they might themselves request them if possible. When these had come into the hands of certain of them, someone arose who wrote against them without giving his name, confessing himself to be a Donatist as though that were his name. In answering him, I wrote another book. I joined the documents which I had promised, and wished the two to be one work; and I published it in such a manner that it might be read upon the walls of the basilica which had formerly belonged to the Donatists. Its title is *Proofs and Testimonies against the Donatists*” [Col. 0815C].

He wished the title of the other book mentioned above to be *Against Some Unknown Donatist*.

### Admonition of the Donatists concerning the Maximianists

To these two books, which are now missing, was added a third, likewise lost, entitled *Admonition of the Donatists concerning the Maximianists*. It was a very brief pamphlet, so that by the ease of copying it might reach the hands of many and, by its very brevity, be more readily committed to memory [Col. 0815D].

### Book on the One Baptism

Some time later, but before the Conference of Carthage, a certain friend received from an unknown Donatist presbyter Petilian’s book *On the One Baptism* and brought it to Augustine, earnestly asking him to answer it. Augustine granted his request, and wished the book in which he replied to bear the same title, *On the One Baptism*. This book survives [Col. 0816A].

There does not survive another large book against the Donatists, in which he demonstrated that their impious and most arrogant error against the Catholic Church was utterly overthrown by the case of the Maximianists alone.

### Catholics Invite the Donatists to a Conference

While Augustine was privately undertaking these measures against the Donatists, the African bishops were working to bring the Donatists by every means to a conference, believing that schismatics could neither be reconciled nor defeated by any other way. Thus, at the general council of the bishops of Africa, held at Carthage on 25 August 403, it was decreed that the Donatists should be summoned by a solemn instrument to a conference to be held between bishops selected from either side [Col. 0816B].

At the same time they requested and obtained from Septiminius permission both to meet the Donatists and to investigate the records in the case of the Maximianists. The Donatists, according to their custom, refused the conference. Augustine then wrote a letter to the lay members of that sect, so that from this refusal by their bishops they might at last learn to regard the justice of their cause with suspicion.

### Donatists Angered by This Summons; Envoys Sent by Catholics to the Emperor

But the more gently and urgently the Donatists were invited to peace, the more fiercely and cruelly they began to rage against the Catholics. Crispinus, bishop of Calama, a man of great authority among his own people, may serve as evidence: he so persecuted Possidius, the Catholic bishop of that city, that Possidius could scarcely secure his safety by flight [Col. 0816C].

For these and other crimes Crispinus was summoned to trial and accused as a heretic. When he saw that a fine of ten pounds of gold had been imposed upon him under the provision of the Theodosian law of 392, he pleaded his cause for three days before the proconsul and attempted to free himself from the charge of heresy. But Possidius proved in a public disputation that the sentence delivered under that designation had been just and lawful. Yet, although the fine was remitted at Possidius’s request, Crispinus appealed to the emperor, who imposed the same fine upon him and the other Donatists.

While these events were occurring, Circumcellions so atrociously attacked Maximinus of Bagai, who had reclaimed a basilica under the laws, and Servus, bishop of Tubursicuburi, who sought another basilica, as well as other bishops, clerics, and laypeople [Col. 0816D], that the fathers of the Council of Carthage held in 404 judged, on 26 June, that Theasius and Evodius should be sent as envoys to the emperor.
