They were to explain to him how monstrous were the acts perpetrated by the Donatists against Catholics, and request that he provide for the Church’s protection and confirm and order to be enforced against the Donatists the law of Theodosius promulgated against heretical ordainers or ordained persons, and also against possessors of places in which their congregation was found.

Likewise, they requested that another law, which deprived heretics of the right to receive or leave anything by donations or wills, should be renewed; yet so that those wishing, out of regard for unity and peace, to reform themselves might have access to inheritance, if anything should accrue to persons still in heresy through gift or inheritance [Col. 0817A]. Excepted, however, were those who, having been challenged by litigation, thought they ought to cross over to Catholicism; for it was credible that such persons had preferred Catholic unity from greed for earthly advantage rather than from fear of heavenly judgment.

To this public embassy and to the council’s letters to the emperor were added the complaints of private persons who had suffered injury from the Donatists.

### The Edict on Unity Issued by Honorius; Unity Established at Carthage

Moved by these events, Honorius issued a most severe edict against the Donatists, or Rebaptizers, on the day before the Ides of February, in the consulship of Stilicho II and Anthemius—that is, in 405. Four laws in the Theodosian Code, all issued on this same day, form parts of this edict. It was called the Edict of Unity because through it heretics and schismatics were commanded, under twenty very severe penalties, to return to the Catholic Church [Col. 0817B].

It was sent to Hadrianus, Praetorian Prefect of Italy, and specifically on 5 March to the Proconsul of Africa, to be promulgated and executed there. By force of this edict unity was quickly achieved at Carthage, though it could be obtained more slowly in the other provinces of Africa. At the Council of Carthage held on 23 August of the same year, it was decreed that, since unity had been established only at Carthage, letters should also be given to the judges, ordering them to devote effort to unity in other provinces and cities. Thanksgivings on behalf of all Africa, for the exclusion of the Donatists from the Church of Carthage, were to be sent to the imperial court with the bishops’ letters. Two clerics were again sent to court to give thanks and request the exclusion of the Donatists throughout Africa [Col. 0817C].

### Maximinus, a Donatist of Siniti, Requests a Conference

On 30 January 406, Maximinus, bishop of Siniti, and several other Donatists requested a hearing in a public session at Ravenna before the Praetorian Prefect, in which they might argue their cause with the Catholics. What was decided is uncertain; certainly nothing came of it. Upon returning to Africa, Maximinus joined the Catholic Church.

### Decree concerning Donatist Bishops and Bishoprics

In 407, at the Council of Carthage in June, it was decreed that congregations converted from the Donatists which had bishops might retain them without consulting the council. But congregations which had had a bishop, and after his death did not wish to have a bishop of their own but to belong to the diocese of some bishop, were not to be denied this either [Col. 0817D].

Concerning the bishops themselves, this was decreed: those who had come to Catholicism before the emperor’s law on Unity had been issued were to retain their congregations and churches. But those who had come to the Church only after that edict had been promulgated were wholly deprived of their churches, which, together with all things belonging to them, were assigned to the Catholic bishops of those places.

### Honorius’s Laws against the Donatists

In the same year Honorius issued a law granting heretics and schismatics returning to the Church immunity from all penalties they had incurred under the laws.

In 408, after Stilicho had been put to death on 23 August, new disturbances were stirred up by the Donatists, as though his death had released them from the laws. To give their audacity some pretext, they invented an indulgence granted by Honorius. But laws issued by the emperor against them in that year and the following immediately dispersed this fiction [Col. 0818A].

While governors were intent on rigorously enforcing these laws, Augustine attempted to avert the penalty of blood from factious schismatics. Yet such are the shifting laws of rulers that about the middle of 409 Honorius granted heretics permission to practice their superstition. But in the same year, at the demand of the fathers of the Council of Carthage, who had sent an embassy of five bishops to the imperial court, he revoked that liberty and issued against them a most severe law, dated 25 August 410, to Heraclianus, Count of Africa. By it, having wholly removed the rescript under cover of which persons devoted to heretical superstition had insinuated themselves for their rites, he decreed that they should be punished by proscription and death if they should thereafter dare, in the detestable rashness of their crime, to assemble publicly [Col. 0818B].

### Edicts Summoning Bishops to a Conference

At last, since a conference had been requested by both sides and was urgently demanded by the Catholics, who had sent envoys to the Emperor Honorius for this purpose, an edict was issued by him. It was a decree given at Ravenna on the day before the Ides of October, under the consulship of Varane—that is, in 410—commanding Donatist and Catholic bishops to assemble in the city of Carthage within four months, so that the case might be committed for discussion to priests selected from either side [Col. 0818C].

If Donatist bishops did not assemble within the prescribed time, they were to be declared contumacious after a threefold edict of summons. When this was completed, if those summoned should disdain to appear, the people were to yield, with their churches, since they would recognize that their teachers had been defeated in silence; and they were to know that the true commands of Catholic law must be obeyed.

For this disputation the emperor wished Flavius Marcellinus, a notary, to sit as judge in the first place. He granted him full power to assemble and summon bishops, to institute and regulate the proceedings, and to determine the entire affair. Armed with this edict, Marcellinus issued an order admonishing all bishops throughout Africa, both Catholic and Donatist, to come to Carthage for holding the council within the period prescribed by law—that is, within the four months ending on the Kalends of June [Col. 0818D]. He also commanded all magistrates throughout Africa to meet with the bishops and notify them that they must come to Carthage within four months.

Moreover, to render the Donatists readier for the conference, he ordered that churches and places which they were shown to have previously held should be restored to those who answered that they would be present before him. He added that, if he were suspect to the Donatists, he would not refuse to have another judge, chosen by them, of the Donatist party and faith, whether of higher or equal rank, sit with him. Finally, he declared that whichever sentence should be rendered, whether for the Donatists or for the Catholics, the Donatist bishops would suffer no inconvenience; rather, free and exempt from every injury, they would return to their own homes [Col. 0819A].

### Instructions of Bishops to the Colleagues Who Were to Hold the Conference

In accordance with that order, Donatist bishops hastened to Carthage from all the African provinces. Having assembled there, on the fifteenth day before the Kalends of June, they informed Marcellinus by letter that they had arrived in the city in order to enter the conference. The Catholic bishops too, when they had arrived, gave Marcellinus a letter testifying that the conference was welcome to them. They agreed that those to whom they had delegated the task of conducting their case should sign their pleadings and argue in the name of all.

With the unanimous consent of all their bishops, they offered the Donatists this condition [Col. 0819B]: if their opponents could show that the Church had perished and remained only in Donatus’s party, the Catholics would have no place among them in episcopal office or honor. But if, conversely, the Donatists were defeated and wished to return to unity, the Catholics granted them that they should not lose the honor of the episcopate. Thus, where there were two bishops, the Catholic bishop, joined to his colleague in honor, should both sit in a more distinguished place, like a visiting bishop beside his colleague; and thereafter, anticipating one another in honor, should occupy first place in different basilicas in turn. When one of them died, then one bishop at a time should succeed in each place according to the former custom.

Or, if Christian peoples perhaps preferred individual bishops and could not endure, in this unprecedented situation, the partnership of two, both Catholics and Donatists should withdraw from office [Col. 0819C], and, once the cause of schism had been condemned and each church established in peaceful unity, bishops should be appointed in the several places from among those who, unity having been achieved, were found individually in the individual churches.

### Proceedings of the Conference

On the Kalends of June 411, the bishops of both parties assembled in the secretarium, or praetorium, of the Gargilian Baths at Carthage. After the emperor’s edict, Marcellinus’s order, and the letters of the Catholic and Donatist bishops had been read, the twenty-one Donatists chose no judge other than Marcellinus, though they made some quibbles concerning elapsed time. The bishops present and those who had subscribed to the mandates were then counted: 286 Catholics and 279 Donatists were found.

Seven were selected from each side to conduct the case in the name of all [Col. 0819D]. What was said was taken down and checked by notaries from both sides, after which the official staff prepared the record. When this had been done, the hearing was adjourned to 3 June. On that day only the selected advocates from each side, together with an equal number of advisers, four keepers of documents, and the notaries, came to the place of conference. Since the proceedings had not yet been transcribed, after a brief altercation the conference was postponed until the sixth day before the Ides of June.

On that day the case was argued between the parties with great contention of mind and voice. There is no need here to report what was said and alleged by either side, since it can be abundantly recovered from the acts of the conference itself and from Saint Augustine’s brief summary, mentioned by us at the end of this work. For the present I shall say only this: after a sharp and prolonged conference, the judge rendered judgment in favor of the Catholics against the Donatists and again prohibited Donatist conventicles [Col. 0820A]. He ordered that the churches which he had wished to be restored to the Donatists by a provisional decree should be handed over to the Catholics.

He nevertheless permitted the Donatist bishops to return to their homes, so that, while remaining there, they might either return to the one true Church or satisfy the laws. Finally, he decreed that the places in which bands of Circumcellions met should be seized by the fisc. Augustine composed a summary of this conference and, after it, wrote a book to the Donatists, lest they should any longer be led astray by their bishops.

### Honorius’s Law against the Donatists after the Conference

When the emperor had received the record of all that had been done in the conference and the sentence rendered by the judge, in the following year, on the third day before the Kalends of February, he issued a law imposing various monetary fines, according to each person’s condition, upon Donatists who refused to join the Catholic Church. He ordered their bishops and clerics expelled from Africa and sent into exile, and assigned to Catholic churches whatever had been bestowed upon their churches [Col. 0820B].

### The Donatists’ Enraged Fury

By this law many Donatists were corrected and returned to Catholicism; but some, made more bitter by it, became more mad than before. In the diocese of Hippo they murdered the Catholic presbyter Restitutus, whom they had caught in an ambush; and they mutilated the presbyter Innocentius, dragging him from his house, gouging out his eye, and cutting off his finger.

Marcellinus, the tribune charged with executing this case, conducted a moderate examination of the accused. He extracted confessions of their crimes not by tearing hooks or burning flames, but by beatings with rods [Col. 0820C]. The accused ought, according to the severity of the laws, to have been punished so as to suffer what they had done. But Augustine, who approved of no cruel penalties and especially not capital punishment, wrote with the utmost urgency to Marcellinus, the proconsul Donatus, and Apringius, asking that the penalty of death—and indeed even mutilation of limbs—be remitted.

He did, however, ask Marcellinus to make public and display to the people the records by which the Donatists’ crimes were proven, so that shame and disgrace might turn people away from persons committing such crimes against other people. The other bishops likewise interceded with the judges for the accused, that they should not suffer capital punishment [Col. 0820D]. Yet this gentleness of the Catholics could not moderate the Donatists’ fury. Augustine recounts that Macrobius, one of their bishops, surrounded by troops of depraved persons of both sexes, went about here and there and forcibly opened basilicas for himself.

### The Donatists’ Slanders against Marcellinus

In order to invalidate the judgment rendered against them by Marcellinus, they alleged that he had been bribed and had favored the Catholics, with whom he was in communion, and that he had pronounced his decision in their favor—but wrongly and at night. They further maintained that Marcellinus had not allowed the Donatists to present everything on behalf of their party, and complained that violence had been done them because, during the conference, they had been shut up in the record-room of the Baths of Gargilius. [Col. 0821A]

The Catholics rightly mocked these evasions of petty litigants. For they said that the judge had been corrupted by gold gratuitously and without a witness; whereas, if anything were to be alleged against him, they ought to have done so before the opening of the disputation. Not only had they not done this, but when he offered them the choice of another judge to sit with him, they replied that they wanted no second judge; and they had repeatedly praised this very man at length. As regards the proceedings, he had given each person, with a water-clock assigned to him, leave to speak whatever and as much as he wished.

Nor could the Catholics complain any more than the Donatists of violence having been done them because they had been enclosed in the Baths of Gargilius—if there was any ground for complaint—since both parties were there alike. But how could a place be regarded as a prison [Col. 0821B] where the judge himself was present, and in which they were not detained, but from which they were dismissed whenever they wished? The allegation that the decision had been given at night was a cavilling quibble of Petilianus, the forensic declaimer; for nothing prevents a judge, if the case requires it, from sitting longer even into the night.

Nevertheless, this audacity and obstinacy of the Donatists in slandering grew to such a degree that the African Fathers jointly considered what remedy should be applied at the Synod of Cirta, or Zerta, held in the year after the conference. In the name of that synod Augustine wrote the letter to the Donatists formerly numbered 152, now 141, in which he refutes this kind of calumny. It was dated on the eighteenth day before the Kalends of July [14 June].

### Death of Marcellinus. Confirmation of Marcellinus’s Judgment

But the Donatists, not content with defaming Marcellinus’s reputation by their slanders, also sought his life. [Col. 0821C] By representing him as a partisan of Heraclianus, they brought it about that, although innocent, he was put to death as one overwhelmed by the odium of tyranny: on 13 September 413, by order of Count Marinus, who had defeated Heraclianus in Africa, he was beheaded.

From this they began to take occasion to proclaim that the judgment rendered by Marcellinus was void. When Honorius learned this, he enacted a very severe law against them on 22 June 414; and by another law, issued 30 August 415, he decreed that the proceedings conducted against the Donatists by Marcellinus—whom he calls “a man of distinguished memory”—and entered in the public records, should possess perpetual validity.

Nor did the Donatists fare better in their importunate appeal to Count Boniface. He rejected the calumnies of these most mendacious men and preferred Augustine’s counsels, [Col. 0821D] as prescribed for him in that outstanding book, or letter, *On the Correction of the Donatists*.

### Augustine’s Proceedings with Emeritus

In the year 418, on 1 May, the Fathers of the universal Council of Carthage framed decrees to extirpate the remnants of the Donatist sect. In the following September, while Augustine was staying at Julia Caesarea with some colleagues, he happened to encounter Emeritus, bishop of that city from the party of Donatus, who had been one of the representatives at the conference. Augustine brought him to the church and wished to debate with him. But Emeritus did not dare even to utter or open his lips, and patiently listened to Augustine’s discourse against his own party.

A little before this Augustine had written a book against this Emeritus, [Col. 0822A] entitled *To Emeritus, Bishop of the Donatists, after the Conference*, in which he briefly summarized the matters by which they are defeated, or shown to have been defeated. That book has perished; but his book *On the Proceedings with Emeritus* survives, as does the sermon delivered to the people of the Church of Caesarea in Emeritus’s presence.

### 22. Council of the Donatists

At about the same time a gathering of the Donatists was held, at which Petilianus attended with more than thirty other bishops. They devised a plan for resisting the edicts by which they were so greatly oppressed. They appeared more ready to commit themselves to their former fires—indeed, they actually did so, in the hope of obtaining among their followers the title of martyrs—than to be deported to islands.

At the same assembly they enacted the following: that those who had communicated with the Catholics, [Col. 0822B] if they were only bishops or presbyters and had neither offered sacrifice nor preached to the people, should obtain pardon and be restored to their offices.

### The Donatist Schism Weakened

Meanwhile Dulcitius, tribune and notary, the executor in Africa of the imperial commands against the Donatists, rigorously exacted the penalties laid down against them by the laws. He declared the Donatists incapable of making wills, imposed the prescribed fines, adjudged their basilicas and property to the Catholic Church, and sent bishops and clerics into exile on islands and in distant provinces.

Through his vigilance, therefore, many at that time returned to the Church; and the Donatist sect, which had previously flourished in Africa, was utterly broken and weakened. Yet some persisted obstinately in their stubbornness. Some killed themselves by various kinds of death, in their customary manner, [Col. 0822C] lest their basilicas be handed over to the Catholics, and so that they might be considered martyrs. Some attacked Catholics and put many of them to death, while, on the other hand, Catholic bishops diligently sought to avert the penalty of death from the Donatists’ heads.

### On Gaudentius of Thamugadi

Since Gaudentius of Thamugadi, one of the seven Donatist representatives at the conference, was the leader and incendiary of evils of this kind, Dulcitius wrote to him. He exhorted him to Catholic unity and dissuaded him from the conflagration by which he threatened to consume himself and his followers together with the church itself. He added that, if they considered themselves righteous, they should rather flee according to the command of the Lord Christ than burn themselves in impious fires.

Gaudentius replied [Col. 0822D] in two letters: one short letter, because, as was said, the bearer was in haste; the other lengthy, as though offering a fuller and more careful reply. Dulcitius, considering both to be letters of Gaudentius, sent them to Augustine for refutation; at the same time he consulted him by letter as to what answer ought to be given to these heretics. Augustine refuted both letters of Gaudentius in one book. When it came into Gaudentius’s hands, he wrote in reply what seemed good to him; but Augustine disregarded his answer and judged it unworthy of refutation. In answer, however, to Dulcitius’s request, Augustine stated that their madness ought not to hinder efforts toward achieving unity and carrying the Emperor’s laws into effect.

### Law of Theodosius the Younger against the Donatists

[Col. 0823A] The same laws were renewed by Theodosius the Younger in a law issued on 30 May 428. But shortly thereafter the Donatist sect was protected from the emperors’ laws by the invasion of the Vandals. The Vandals also appear to have favored some among them who pretended not to be opponents of the Arians. Nevertheless, most of them underwent the same fate as the Catholics and lived a miserable life beneath the Arian yoke. Certainly Fastidiosus, an Arian bishop whose words are cited by Fulgentius, persecutes Donatists no less than Catholics.

### Remnants of the Donatists down to the Sixth Century

Yet remnants of this schism, though weakened and worn down, survived in Africa for a very long time, as is clear from Gregory the Great’s letters to the Africans. From them we learn that there were still quite a number of Donatists in Africa, [Col. 0823B] and that their number had increased at this very time, although they were restrained by Gennadius the Exarch. They had brought more persons into their sect and rebaptized them; they had even driven some Catholic bishops from their churches.

To remedy this evil, Gregory ordered a synod to be assembled. Dominicus, [Col. 0824A] bishop of Carthage, held it, applying every effort to purge the African Church of this stain. Rescripts were then sent against them by the Emperor Maurice; but the African bishops complained that they were not being put into execution. Gregory informed the emperor of this matter by letters sent from the Africans and requested that severe measures be taken against them. He himself wrote to the African bishops that Donatist bishops who came over to the Church were to be received on the condition that access to the primacy should not be open to them.

Thus this schism endured in Africa for more than three hundred years. It arose at an unhappy time and under an unhappy omen; under Constantine it could not be extinguished either by ecclesiastical or civil judgments; suppressed under the Emperor Constans, it revived for a time under Julian [Col. 0824B] and occupied a large part of Africa for many years. At length it was diminished by writings, disputations, and imperial laws, and reduced to a few persons, whose unhappy heirs lurked in certain corners of Africa down to the sixth or seventh century.

[Col. 0823]

## 23. SACRED GEOGRAPHY OF AFRICA, OR AN ACCOUNT OF ALL THE EPISCOPAL SEES OF THE AFRICAN CHURCH, EXTRACTED FROM THE CONFERENCE OF CARTHAGE, THE LIST OF THE BISHOPS OF AFRICA UNDER HUNERIC, THE COUNCIL OF CARTHAGE UNDER CYPRIAN, OTHER AFRICAN AND GENERAL COUNCILS, AND SACRED AND PROFANE MONUMENTS

### Description of Africa

[Col. 0823C] We read that the name “Africa” was formerly, and is now, used in three senses.

First, it denotes the third part of the world, separated from Asia by the isthmus or the mouths of the Nile, and surrounded on every side by sea. This territorial expanse includes not only the provinces washed by the Mediterranean—namely, Mauretania, the province of Zeugitana, whose capital is Carthage, Libya, and Egypt—but also the interior regions, scarcely known to the ancients, designated by the name Ethiopia.

The second sense of “Africa” is not so extensive. According to it, not only is Ethiopia separated from Africa, but Africa itself constitutes a distinct diocese, as they say, separate from Egypt and extending from the Atlantic Ocean to the innermost gulf of the Greater Syrtis. It includes the provinces of Mauretania, Numidia, Tripolitana, and Zeugitana. [Col. 0823D]

The last of these provinces, the proconsular province, is properly called Africa. This is the third and most restricted sense of the term.

Africa in this intermediate sense is washed on the west and north by the sea along the oblique expanse of its coasts. Its western side extends in length from Mount Atlas to Cape Cotes, near the strait, for 1,500 Roman miles. From there, on the northern side, from the mouths of the Strait of Hercules to Cape Mercury, according to [Col. 0824C] Pliny, there are 1,110 Roman miles; according to Antonine’s *Itinerary*, 1,431. But if the coast alone is disregarded—that is, its bays and windings—and only the heavens are considered—that is, if a straight line is drawn from Cotes to Cape Mercury—the distance is 1,030 Roman miles.

From Cape Mercury to the inner shore of the Lesser Syrtis, facing east, Polybius, Pliny, and Antonine give 300 Roman miles; our calculations do not differ greatly from this. The region between the two Syrtes, turning northward, is given by Pliny as 250 Roman miles, by Antonine as 380 Roman miles, and by us as 350 Roman miles. The Greater Syrtis, if Pliny is to be believed, has a circumference of 625 Roman miles, an entrance of 315, and a circuit of 450. According to our measurement, its entrance is no more than 250 Roman miles. From the headland to the innermost part of the gulf [Col. 0824D] there are 210 Roman miles. There are the Altars of the Philaeni, the outermost boundary of Africa.

To the south Africa adjoins the mountains and interior Libya, and is broader or narrower according as the land projects more or less into the sea. All this may be seen on the geographical map.

### Division of Africa

Africa is divided by Pliny into two Mauretanias—Tingitana and Caesariensis—Numidia, and Zeugitana, which is Africa properly so called [Col. 0825A] and is distributed into two parts, one called Byzacena and the other Tripolitana.

In the ancient *Notice of Africa*, said to have been composed in the time of the Emperor Constantius, Africa is described and divided thus:

> Going toward the south, you will find the land of Mauretania, whose inhabitants are barbarians in their way of life and customs, though subject to the Romans . . . After Mauretania comes the province of Numidia . . . Next to this province appears the African region, rich in every respect.

In Ptolemy and Pomponius Mela, Africa too is divided into only three parts: Mauretania, Numidia, and Africa taken in the strict sense, under which Byzacena and Tripolitana are included.

This also was the most ancient division of the African Church, as St Cyprian, a witness beyond all exception, attests [Col. 0825B] in Letter 48 of the Oxford edition, to Cornelius, where he describes the boundaries and divisions of the African Church as follows:

> But because our province extends widely, it includes Numidia and the two adjoining Mauretanias.

At the Council of Carthage on the repetition of baptism, held under the same Cyprian, when twenty-four bishops, most of them from the province of Africa, Numidia, and Mauretania, had assembled together at Carthage, it is clear that already then the churches of these provinces formed one body of churches and were divided into four ecclesiastical provinces.

Nothing, or very little, seems to have been changed in this division of Africa in the time of the Emperor Constantine. For in his letter to Caecilianus of Carthage, quoted by Eusebius, *Ecclesiastical History*, book X, chapter 6, he likewise enumerates four African provinces in these words:

> Since it has pleased us that, throughout all the provinces of Africa, Numidia, and both Mauretanias . . .

Nevertheless, in the same emperor’s letter to Ablavius concerning the Council of Arles, he adds Tripolitana as a province and speaks of the Numidias in the plural. He directs Ablavius to send Caecilianus, with some whom he himself selects, and also one person each, with certain of their associates whom they judge fit to choose, from the provinces of Byzacena, Tripolitana, the Numidias, and the Mauretanias, to Arles. Here Tripolitana seems already to be established as a province of Africa distinct from the other four.

Although the Numidias are mentioned here and elsewhere in the plural, one should not therefore suppose that there were two provinces of Numidia, whether civil or ecclesiastical. For the two Numidias always formed one province, which had only one metropolitan city and one primate, as is clear from the Council of Milevis of 402. It decreed that the archive of Numidia should be both at the first see and in the metropolis—that is, at Constantine. [Col. 0825D] Here, then, there is one metropolis and one primate for all Numidia.

And lest anyone say that this concerns only one Numidia: at the Council of Carthage of 397, Crescentianus is called bishop of the first see of the Numidias; in Greek, *prōtēs kathedras tōn duo Noumidiōn*—“of the first chair of the two Numidias.” St Augustine, in Letter 59 to Victorinus, treating of the dispute between two bishops over the primacy of Numidia, assumes that all bishops of Numidia obeyed one primate.

Some think that Mauretania Sitifensis, which was subsequently detached from Numidia and constituted a distinct province, was the second of the two Numidias. But at the Council of Carthage of 416 the two Numidias are expressly distinguished from the Mauretanias of Sitifensis and Caesariensis. [Col. 0826A]

Around the time of the Emperor Theodosius, Africa was divided into six provinces, which are enumerated by Sextus Rufus and in the *Notice of the Empire*: Africa in the strict sense, or the proconsular province; Numidia; Byzacium; Tripolis; Mauretania Sitifensis; and Mauretania Caesariensis. Tingitana, however, was detached from Africa and assigned to Spain.

The ecclesiastical *politeia*—that is, constitution or polity—assumed the same provincial division and form, as is known from councils gathered from all the African provinces, in which these six provinces are enumerated.

Some believe that the province of Sitifensis did not obtain a distinct place among the ecclesiastical provinces of Africa, and possess a primate, before 419; they infer this from Canon 17 of the Council of Carthage in that year. But they are greatly mistaken. For at the Council of Carthage in 397, delegates of Mauretania Sitifensis are recorded as having come to Carthage for the council in the name of their province and submitted all their requests. This was permitted only to provinces that had first sees, as is clear from Canon 18 of the African Code.

In Augustine’s Letter to Victorinus, now numbered 59 and written in 401, it is explicitly stated not merely that there were two Mauretanias, but that each had its own primate:

> I read in the same circular letter that it was also written to the Mauretanias, which provinces we know to have primates. [Col. 0826B]

In 402 Nicetius of Sitifis, who attended the Council of Milevis, is called bishop of the first see of Mauretania Sitifensis. In 403 Lucianus and Macrianus, bishops of the province of Sitifensis, served as delegates at the Council of Carthage. In 407 the bishops of Sitifensis are separately enumerated as belonging to a province distinct from the others. In 411, at the Conference of Carthage, the six provinces are separately enumerated, including Sitifensis:

> All are present from all the African provinces, namely from the proconsular province, the province of Byzacena, Numidia, the Mauretanias of Sitifensis and Caesariensis, and the province of Tripolitana.

And chapter 72 of the first day of the Conference of Carthage says:

> If there is doubt about the number, let the provincials go to the Moors; let them go to the Numidians; let them go to the Byzacenes; let them also go to the Tripolitanians; let them go [Col. 0826C] to those of the Proconsular Province.

In 418 delegates from this province were chosen to remain at Carthage. Finally, at the beginning of the Council of 419, delegates were present in the council in the name of the Sitifensians before Canon 17 had been drawn up. Nothing, therefore, could be more absurd than to pretend that it was only then, in this council, that Mauretania Sitifensis, distinct from Caesariensis, was constituted an ecclesiastical province.

As for Canon 17 of the Council of Carthage of 419, in the code of canons of the African Church it reads as follows:

> It was resolved that Mauretania Sitifensis, as it requested, should be permitted to have as its primate the primate of the province of Numidia, from whose body it is separated, with the consent of all the primates of the African provinces and all the bishops, on account of the distance.

Read in this way, the canon would deprive the province of Sitifensis of its own primate and subject it to the primate of Numidia—something that no one will say was requested by the delegates of the province of Sitifensis or decreed by the synod.

But the canon is read differently in two manuscripts, to this effect:

> Concerning the primacy of Mauretania Sitifensis. When the bishops of Mauretania Sitifensis requested a primate of their own, the whole council of Numidian bishops, with the consent of all the primates and all the bishops of the African provinces, permitted it to have a primate because of the novelty of the long journey. This was done with the counsel of the Church of Carthage. [Col. 0827A]

Ferrandus reads this canon in the same way, explaining its decree thus in his *Epitome of the Canons*, chapter 82:

> That Mauretania Sitifensis should have a primate of its own.

But this canon must be understood not as though the province of Sitifensis then first acquired a primate, since the contrary is plainly established by what has been said, but in the sense that this right was then confirmed to it by a conciliar decree, with the consent of the bishops of Numidia, who had hitherto objected.

For this reason, perhaps, the letter of the Council of Cabarsussa, held by the Donatists in 393, mentions only one Mauretania:

> To the most holy brethren and colleagues established throughout Africa, that is, the Proconsular province, Numidia, Mauretania, Byzacena, and Tripolis.

But, as we have already observed, delegates of Mauretania Sitifensis attended the Catholic Council of 397 and subsequent councils as delegates of an African province distinct from [Col. 0827B] the others and possessing its own primate.

Although Tingitana was assigned to Spain and was no longer counted among the provinces of Africa, its bishops were nevertheless counted in these councils among the bishops of Mauretania Caesariensis. This is clear from the *Notice of the Bishops of Africa under Huneric*, in which bishops of the province of Tingitana are listed under Mauretania Caesariensis. It is therefore likely that the Tingitanian churches always belonged to Africa. Hence, in Siricius’s letter to Himerius of Tarragona, only five Spanish provinces are enumerated: Tarraconensis, Carthaginensis, Baetica, Lusitania, [and] Gallaecia; no mention is made of Tingitana.

Finally, when the Emperor Justinian recovered Africa in the year 534 of the common era, he restored this region to its former condition by his constitution, found in the Code of Justinian, book 1, title 27, and divided it into six dioceses: Tingitana, Carthage, Byzacium, Tripolis, Numidia, and Mauretania, to which he added Sardinia. [Col. 0827C–D]

### On the Primates of Africa

Each province in Africa had its own primate. But unlike other regions of the world, where ecclesiastical metropolitan authority was attached to metropolitan cities, there the entire authority of a metropolitan bishop was assigned to the senior bishop of the province—except for the see of Carthage, which was not only the fixed metropolis of the proconsular province but also the head of all western Africa.

Accordingly, they were commonly called not metropolitans but primates, [Col. 0828A] as they are very frequently called in African councils; the title “metropolis” was reserved for civil metropolitan cities. Thus we find that the primates were not always bishops of the same see, but of different sees.

Accordingly, the metropolitan of Numidia was:

- In Cyprian’s time, Novatus of Thamugadi, as is clear from Cyprian’s council.
- In 305, Secundus of Tigisis, according to Optatus.
- In 393, Megalius of Calama, according to Augustine.
- In 397, Crescentianus, bishop of another see, according to the Council of Carthage.
- In 401 and 402, Xantippus of Tagosa, according to Augustine.
- In 411, Silvanus of Summa, according to the Conference of Carthage.
- In 418, Valentinus of Vaia.
- In 484, Felix of Bercerita, according to the catalogue of Catholic bishops of Africa under Huneric.

Likewise, the primate of the province of Byzacena was Polycarpus of Hadrumetum in Cyprian’s time; around the time of the Conference of Carthage, Mizonius of Zella; in 417, Latomius of Tenita; in 418, Donatianus of Telepte; and in Huneric’s time, the bishop of Nobasinna.

The primate of Mauretania Caesariensis at the Conference of Carthage was Martinus of Tabora; in the catalogue of African bishops under Huneric, Glorinus of Junca. The primate of Mauretania Sitifensis in 402 was Nicetius, bishop of the civil metropolis; but Novatus, bishop of the same see, had no prerogative at the conference, and in 408 acted as delegate for his province. He was therefore not president of the council or primate. But in Huneric’s time the primate was Ruffinus of Tamallum. [Col. 0828B]

From these facts it is abundantly clear that primatial or metropolitan right in Africa was not attached to the civil metropolis, but to the seniority of the bishop; thus the ecclesiastical metropolis was the see of the senior bishop.

Augustine testifies to the same point quite plainly when, in Letter 149, now 38, he asks Profuturus who succeeded Megalius of Calama in the primacy:

> We wish to know the successor to his primacy.

And in Letter 261, now 299—if indeed this letter is Augustine’s, since many learned persons call it into question—he writes to Celestine that the episcopate in the province of Caesariensis had been left to Priscus, but on the condition that access to the primacy should not be open to him as it was to others:

> Let Priscus, bishop of the province of Caesariensis, cry out: either access to the primacy ought to have been open to me, as to the others, or the episcopate ought not to have remained to me. [Col. 0828C]

From this it follows more clearly than light that the primacy was open to all African bishops and was not attached to a civil metropolis. For the bishop of Caesariensis, who was bishop of the civil metropolis, is not deprived of ecclesiastical metropolitan right; rather, access to the exercise of metropolitan right is closed to him.

In Letter 217, now 59, Augustine excuses himself for not having attended the Council of Numidia to which Victorinus had summoned him, because the aged Xantippus of Tagosa—or, more correctly, Tagora—claimed the primacy for himself, and therefore also the right of convening the council. If metropolitan rights had been attached to the city, no dispute over the primacy could have arisen between bishops, since it would have been evident which city was the metropolis of Numidia.

That the dispute concerned solely the seniority of the bishop, rather than the dignity of the city, is made clear by the decree of the Council of Milevis of 402, at which Xantippus himself was present and exercised the right of primacy, as can be seen in Canon 53 of the council commonly called African. This decree, chapter 56, is as follows:

> It was resolved that all who are henceforth ordained by bishops throughout the African provinces should receive from their ordainers letters written in their own hand, containing the consulship and the day, so that no dispute may arise concerning who is later or earlier. [Col. 0829A]

From this it is evident that all rank among African bishops was derived from the seniority of their episcopate, and in no way from the size or dignity of the city.

The same is specifically clear concerning Numidia from Canon 53, which decrees that the register and archive of Numidia shall be at the first see and in the metropolis—that is, Constantine. Here is an explicit distinction between the civil and ecclesiastical metropolis.

Therefore the author of the *Life of St Fulgentius*, chapter 29, testifies that, at the Council of Junca, Fulgentius was preferred to Quodvultdeus in the dispute over the primacy, but afterward yielded his right to him. Having related this, the author adds:

> Where now are those whose desire to rise above others makes them domineer, who set themselves even above their superiors, claiming privileges not due to them? Behold, blessed Fulgentius was unwilling to defend even the primacy which he had deserved. [Col. 0829B]

Among African bishops in Fulgentius’s time, then, the primacy belonged to those earlier in episcopal seniority and was attached to no see. Finally, Victor of Tunnuna reports in his chronicle that, after the death of Boethius the Byzacene, Primasius of Hadrumetum consented to the condemnation of the Three Chapters in order that he might enjoy the right of primacy.

This custom persisted in Africa down to the time of Gregory the Great. For in book I, Letter 75, to the bishops of Numidia, he decrees:

> That their custom concerning the appointment of primates and other matters remain unchanged, except in the case of those who have come from the Donatists to the episcopate. Even if the order of clerics assigns them to that same position, he utterly forbids their advancement to the dignity of primacy.

Accordingly, in Gregory’s time the primacy among Africans was not attached to sees, but was enjoyed without distinction by all bishops who were senior in rank, except those who had been heretics, whom Gregory wished excluded from this right—just as Priscus had formerly been excluded from it, according to Augustine’s testimony. [Col. 0829C]

Even in the proconsular province, the senior bishop was held in highest honor, although he was preceded by the bishop of Carthage, primate of all Africa. Thus at the second Council of Carthage Victor of Abdera, and at the third a bishop named Victor of Pupiana, are preferred to all others except the bishop of Carthage. Concerning this Victor, Epigonius says in chapter 54 of the Code of Canons of the African Church:

> Victor, our praiseworthy brother and colleague, a father by age and most senior by his very promotion, wishes this general petition to be made effective for all.

In a word: in Africa honor, dignity, and even the rights and privileges of bishops were assigned to the seniority of episcopal ordination, not to the dignity of the church over which they presided. This is clear from what has been said, and especially from Augustine’s Letter 59, in which he complains that he, who had not long been a bishop, was named third [Col. 0830A] and set above others who were his seniors:

> This is quite injurious to others and brings odium upon me.

And this is clearly confirmed by Canon 56 of the African Council cited above.

### Prerogatives of the Bishop of Carthage

The bishop of Carthage, however, must always be excepted from this rule. He was primate and exarch of all Africa, or, so to speak, patriarch. Long before Cyprian himself, Agrippinus enjoyed this right; Cyprian indicates that Agrippinus had been president of the other bishops:

> This, indeed, he determined together with the other bishops who at that time governed the Church of God in the province of Africa and Numidia.

The great privileges and rights of this see also appear in Cyprian’s letters. Thus in Letter 45 he calls all Africa his province:

> Because our province extends widely, it includes Numidia and the two Mauretanias adjoining it. [Col. 0830B]

Hence he was consulted from every province of Africa and replied as one possessing preeminent authority, as may be seen in Letters 59, 61, 70, 71, 73, and especially 65.

After this period, the dignity of the bishop of Carthage was not diminished. This is clear from all African councils, which met at his direction and over which he presided, though he might be younger than the others. He was the author and head of all that was done. If letters were to be written by the councils, he dictated them and signed them in the name of all. Appeals were made to his council from all African provinces and synods. He watched over the observance of ecclesiastical rules throughout all Africa and over the preservation of the faith undefiled. He announced the day of Easter to all Africans, as is clear from Canon 51 of the African Code. In a word, he bore the care and solicitude of all the African churches.

Accordingly, Bishop Aurelius says in Canon 55 of the African Code that he bears the care of many churches and of persons to be ordained . . . and afterward, that by God’s gracious favor he bears the solicitude of all the churches. Therefore he is there permitted, wherever he wished and from whatever place the assembly had been summoned, to ordain a bishop in accordance with the need of each church.

Hence he was obliged to visit all the provinces of Africa, as may be inferred from Canon 52 of the Code of Canons of the African Church, containing the Council of Carthage of 397. There Honoratus and Urbanus, delegates of the province of Mauretania [Col. 0830C] Sitifensis, say that it had been decided at the Council of Hippo that the provinces should each be visited at the time of the council, and they ask Aurelius to deign to visit the province of Mauretania either that year or another. Aurelius replied:

> We made no determination concerning the province of Mauretania because it lies on the borders of Africa and is close to barbarian territory. But may God grant that, though we make no promise beyond our means, we may be able to come to your province. For you must consider, brothers, that the Tripolitan and Arzugitan brothers could have demanded this for themselves also, if circumstances allowed.

Perhaps the following question may occur to someone: whether it was better and more fitting for metropolitan dignity to be attached to seniority rather than to a city. Here it seems proper for me to explain my opinion. I hold, therefore, subject to the judgment of others, that it is far better for metropolitan dignity to be attached to a city than to seniority in the priesthood. For when it is attached to a particular see, a person capable of sustaining this dignity is chosen for it. But where it is indiscriminately conferred upon everyone by right of seniority, it can come to less suitable persons. Moreover, old age is less fit for bearing labors and lacks the vigor of mind and body especially required in a metropolitan.

Therefore Gregory very wisely writes in book I, Letter 72, to Gennadius, patrician and exarch of Africa, that he should admonish the Council of Catholics not to make a person primate merely by order of place while disregarding the merits of life:

> For before God it is not a more distinguished rank, but the conduct of a better life, that is approved. [Col. 0831A]

He further directs that the primate should reside not indiscriminately, as the custom was, in rural towns, but in one city according to their election. Yet in Letter 75 to the Africans he allows their custom—which is known to introduce nothing contrary to the Catholic faith—to remain unchanged, whether in appointing primates and so forth.

However this may be, the bishop of Carthage enjoyed a prerogative not only of honor but also of dignity and authority throughout all the African provinces; and in particular he was primate of the proconsular province, which was reckoned first among the others.

This province is bounded in the midst of the African provinces by the African Sea on the east and north. On the west it is divided from Numidia by a line drawn from the mouths of the River Rubricatus to Mustis, where it reaches the River Bagrada; thence it is drawn back westward to Naraggara, and from there to Ammaedara, where it again reaches and crosses the River Bagrada as far as the Numidian town of Capsa to the south. On the east and south it is separated from Byzacena by a line drawn from Uzita to the River Bagrada. It has three promontories: Candidum; that of Apollo, opposite Sardinia; and that of Mercury, opposite Sicily. Projecting far into the sea, these form two gulfs. [Col. 0831B–C]

NUMIDIA, formerly the kingdom of the Numidians, famous for the name of Masinissa, was called by the Greeks the land of Metagonitis. The Numidians, or Nomads, were so called because they changed their pastures, carrying about their *mapalia*—that is, their houses—on wagons. On the east it adjoins the proconsular province, from which it is separated by the line described above. On the north it is washed by the sea. On the west it is bounded by a line drawn from the mouths of the River Ampsaga southward to the town of Maximianum. On the south it has interior Libya. The civil metropolis of this province is the colony of Cirta, which was called, and is still called, Constantine. [Col. 0831D]

BYZACENA is the name given to a province, a region of extraordinary fertility. On the east it has the River Triton; on the west, Numidia, along the line explained above; on the south, Inner Libya. Its principal city is Hadrumetum.

The province of TRIPOLITANIA extends from the River Triton and the Lesser Syrtis to the altar of the Philaeni. It is washed by the sea on the north; bounded on the west by the River Triton; and on the south by the Libyan deserts.

[Col. 0832A] MAURETANIA SITIFENSIS has on the east the line drawn from the mouths of the River Ampsaga southward as far as the town of Maximianum.

To the west of Sitifensis lies CAESARIENSIS, which is separated from Tingitana by the River Malva; and from Sitifensis by a line drawn from the western promontory of the Numidian gulf, where the city of Vabar is situated, obliquely eastward as far as the town of Tubunas, to the River Uzar near Zaratha. The capital of Sitifensis is the city of Sitifis; that of Caesariensis, Julia Caesarea.

The boundaries of MAURETANIA TINGITANA are: on the east, the River Malva; on the west, the Atlantic Ocean; on the north, the Strait of Hercules and the Mediterranean Sea; and on the south, the Atlas Mountains. Tingis is the principal city of this province.

[Col. 0832B] The multitude of bishoprics in Africa.—This whole region, both before it submitted to Roman rule and afterward, had almost countless inhabitants. It contained cities, towns, municipalities, forts, and villages, in great number, both of indigenous people and settlers; and it was exceedingly rich both in the fertility of its soil and abundance of crops, and in commercial trade. Hence there was so great a multitude of Christians in these places, to govern whom very many bishops were appointed—indeed, far more numerous and closely distributed than in any other parts of the Christian world. For elsewhere bishops were customarily appointed only in large cities, not in villages, rural settlements, or small towns, as was ordained by Canon 57 of the Council of Laodicea and Canon 7 of Sardica. But this rule did not obtain in Africa, [Col. 0832C] where bishops are recorded as having been ordained not merely in great cities, but in every town, and sometimes even in villages and forts. The rivalry of Catholics and Donatists increased this multitude of episcopal sees, which had arisen from the earliest beginnings of the African churches.

Certainly, when at the Conference of Carthage, on the first day, chapter 181, Alypius, bishop of the Catholic Church, observed that some Donatist bishops had been ordained in villages and estates, rather than in cities, the Donatist Petilianus retorted the same charge against the Catholics, saying: “So you too have many scattered throughout all the countryside.” At this conference it was frequently alleged by both sides that bishops had newly been appointed in many places by either party, so as to outnumber their opponents. Augustine himself, [Col. 0832D] judging his diocese to be too extensive, arranged for a bishop to be ordained in the fort of Fussala, which was forty miles from Hippo Regius, as he teaches in Letter 261.

But lest disturbances and dissensions arise from this, the Second Council of Carthage decreed in Canon 5 that dioceses which had never had bishops should not have them; and that a diocese which had once had one should have its own . . . . . And if, with the passage of time and the growth of the faith, the people of God should increase and desire to have their own ruler, then, with the consent of the person in whose authority the diocese was constituted, they should have a bishop. This law does not forbid the establishment of a new bishopric as the number of believers increases, but forbids its establishment except with the consent and will of the bishop to whose diocese [Col. 0833A] the place belonged which is being raised to the dignity of an episcopal see.

At the Council of Carthage of the year 497, Canon 53 of the African Code, Epigonius complained:

> Although it has been decreed at many councils by the assembly of bishops that communities retained within dioceses by bishops, which have never had bishops, should receive their own episcopal rulers only with the consent of the bishop by whom they are held, nevertheless certain persons, having acquired a kind of lordship, shrink from communion with their brethren; or at least, when they have become corrupt, they claim for themselves dominion as though from some tyrannical citadel. Swollen and foolish, they raise their necks against the bishop, either gathering a people to themselves by insults, or seeking by malicious persuasion and unlawful favor to install the same persons as rulers for themselves. We recognize, brother Aurelius, reverently, this notable desire of your mind, [Col. 0833B] since you have often checked these abuses by taking no notice of such petitioners. But because of their evil designs and their perverse, persistent schemes, I say that a community which has always been subject within a diocese and has never had its own bishop ought not to receive a ruler. Therefore, if this proposal which I have set forth pleases the whole most holy assembly, let it be confirmed.

Bishop Aurelius said:

> I do not oppose the proposal of our brother and fellow-priest. But I profess that I have done, and will do, this with regard to those, certainly, who remain in concord not merely with the Church of Carthage but with the whole fellowship of bishops. For there are very many who conspire with their own communities, whom they deceive, as has been said, tickling their ears, flattering them in order to lead them astray—men of corrupt life, or at least puffed up and separated from this [Col. 0833C] fellowship. They think that they must devote themselves to their own people, and sometimes, when summoned to a council, refuse to come, perhaps fearing that their misdeeds may be exposed. I say, if it pleases you, that in their case not only should the dioceses not be preserved for them, but that every effort should be made, even through public authority, to expel them from the very church that has wrongly favored them and to remove them from their principal seats. For it is right that one who adheres to all the brethren and to the whole council should possess not only his own see in unimpaired right, but also his dioceses. But those who think their own communities sufficient for themselves, despising fraternal charity, should lose not only their dioceses, but, as I have said, should also be deprived by public authority of their own churches, as rebels.

Bishops Honoratus and Urbanus said:

> The supreme prudence of your holiness has found agreement in the minds of each and all; and [Col. 0833D] I think that what you have deigned to set forth should be confirmed by the response of all.

All the bishops said: “It is approved, it is approved.”

And again, in Canon 56 of the same council:

Bishops Honoratus and Urbanus said:

> We have heard the decree that dioceses should not be deemed entitled to receive bishops except by consent of him under whose authority they had been constituted. But in our province, when bishops have perhaps been ordained in a diocese with the permission of the bishop under whose authority they had been constituted, they claim the dioceses also for themselves. This must be corrected by the judgment of your charity and forbidden for the future.

Bishop Epigonius said:

> What was fitting has been preserved for each bishop: that no portion should be taken from the mass of dioceses to have its own bishop unless he himself had given consent to its separation. [Col. 0834A] It is enough, if he has granted it, that the particular diocese thus permitted should have only its own bishop; it should not claim the remaining dioceses for itself, because, taken alone out of a bundle of many, it alone has deserved to receive the honor of the episcopate.

Bishop Aurelius said:

> I do not doubt that it pleases the charity of you all that one who has been ordained in a diocese with the permission of the bishop who held the mother church should retain only that same community in which he was ordained. Therefore, since I judge that everything has been discussed, if all these things agree with your mind, confirm them all by your word.

All the bishops said: “All these things please us, and we have confirmed them by our subscription.” And they subscribed.

Aurelius, bishop of the Church of Carthage, said: “I consent to this decree and, having read it aloud, have subscribed.” The other bishops likewise subscribed.

[Col. 0834B] From what has been said, two conclusions follow. First, in Africa bishops were appointed not only in great cities, but in all towns, indeed even in villages and forts. Second, new bishoprics were readily established in different places as the number of believers grew, provided that the bishop to whose diocese the place belonged gave consent. Hence the great multitude of bishops in Africa.

At the beginning of the second century, Agrippinus, bishop of Carthage, held a council at Carthage of very many bishops from Africa and Numidia, as Cyprian testifies in Letters 71, to Quintus, and 73, to Jubaianus. He does not state their number. But Saint Augustine, in his work *On the One Baptism against Petilianus*, suggests that there were seventy, in these words: “For what he adds concerning Agrippinus, bishop of Carthage, concerning [Col. 0834C] the illustrious martyr Cyprian, concerning Cyprian’s seventy predecessors, because they did this and ordered it to be done.”

Under Donatus, Cyprian’s predecessor, Privatus of Lambaesis was condemned at a council of ninety bishops, as Cyprian testifies in Letter 59. Under Cyprian three large councils concerning the baptism of heretics were held. Seventy bishops attended two of them, as the Letter to Jubaianus testifies; and eighty-seven are recorded as having attended the third, besides whom it is very likely that many more were absent.

But there are two records from which the number of African bishops can be determined with certainty. The first is the Conference of Carthage, in which the Catholics thus enumerate their number: two hundred and sixty-six bishops signed the mandate; twenty were present; one hundred and twenty-eight [Col. 0834D] are said to have been absent; and sixty-four churches besides were vacant. From these figures arises a total of four hundred and seventy episcopal sees in Africa. The second is the register of African bishops under Huneric, which counts four hundred and sixty-six bishops; if eight Sardinian bishops are subtracted, all the remainder belong to Africa.

After Africa was recovered by Emperor Justinian, Reparatus held a general council of Africa, at which 217 bishops were present. This is evidence that, out of that enormous number of bishoprics, many still survived at this time. At the Lateran Council under Martin, sixty-nine bishops of the Proconsular province subscribed the synodal letter of the Fathers of that province; [Col. 0835A] and forty-six bishops subscribed the synodal letter of the Byzacenes.

But after the Romans had been driven out of Africa by the Saracens, the condition of the African Church was most lamentable, and it had very few bishops. Thus, in the time of Gregory VII, it scarcely had three bishops, as may be inferred from his letters, especially Book III, Letter 19, written in 1076, where he says that it had reached his ears that Africa, “which is said to be a part of the world, and which even in ancient times, while Christianity flourished there, was governed by a very great number of bishops, has come into such danger that, for the ordination of a bishop, it does not have three bishops.” In the same place he says that he had recently laid hands on someone, so that he might be a second bishop; and when they requested a third so that others might be ordained by them, he writes in Letter 20, to the clergy and people of Hippo, and Letter 21, [Col. 0835B] to Azir, king of Mauretania, that Servandus, a presbyter sent to him from Africa at their request, had been consecrated bishop.

But to return to those happier times of the African Church: from ancient records we have extracted the names of six hundred and ninety bishoprics in Africa: namely, 136 in the Proconsular province, 155 in Numidia, 135 in Byzacena, 135 collectively in Mauretania Caesariensis and Tingitana, 46 in Sitifensis, 5 in Tripolitana, and 78 of uncertain province, making a total of 690. Yet, just as I cannot affirm that all Africa’s episcopal sees are included here, so neither would I venture to assert that all these places were episcopal sees simultaneously at one and the same time. But there is none among them that did not at some time have a bishop, as [Col. 0835C] may be gathered from ecclesiastical records.

Although the province of most episcopal sees has been discovered, the number whose definite location could be assigned on the geographical map is much smaller. For the author of the map, however shrewd and experienced in these matters, was able to establish the certain position of only 257 episcopal places. Of these, 52 are in Proconsularis, 71 in Numidia, 51 in Byzacena, 51 in Mauretania Caesariensis, 46 in Sitifensis; while five episcopal cities of Tripolitana are known. So that the reader may immediately understand which sees have been located on the map, those have an asterisk prefixed, lest he labor in vain by seeking those which have no place on the map.

Moreover, we have found a much larger number of bishoprics assigned to the individual provinces than those who wrote on this subject before us; and the author of the map has discovered and marked the sites of many more. We have removed many errors, separated bishoprics improperly combined into one, assigned one proper place under its true name to the same see repeatedly listed under different names, removed fictitious names, and corrected corrupt or wrongly written names. How much we have accomplished in these matters will be understood by anyone willing to compare our register with that of Charles of Saint Paul. I would not wish to detract anything from that man’s learning and labor; yet I would venture to affirm that his register and map contain more than two hundred errors into which we have not fallen. Nor for that reason [Col. 0836A] do we dare affirm that our work is complete in every respect and free from error. We know how prone and easy it is to err in these matters, even for very learned men highly experienced in subjects of this kind.

An example is the error of the most learned Holstenius in this inquiry, who counts *Vicus-nigratem* among the bishoprics of Africa: “Vicus,” he says, “Nigras in the territory of Vaga; bishop of Vici-nigratis, in Gennadius, *On Illustrious Writers*, chapter 73.” But the text here reads—and ought to read: “Asclepius, bishop of a not large village in the territory of Vaga (or Baia).” If any manuscript codices, as he observes, read otherwise, no one can fail to see that they are corrupt. For who has ever heard such a name as *Vicus-nigras*? There was indeed in Africa a see of the Greater Nigrenses; but *Vicus-nigras* is a monstrosity and fabrication. Likewise *Duedemsai* has been written in place of *a Senemsalis*, as Baluze happily restored it; *Felicianentensis* for *Feliciani Utinensis*; *Vivensis* for *Vinensis*; and many other errors whose recital would be lengthy.

But before presenting an account of the individual bishoprics, we have judged it worthwhile to preface a few remarks on the fortunes and location of the city of Carthage, and likewise on its Church and bishops.

History of the city of Carthage.—CARTHAGE, number 1 in the register of the Proconsular province, the renowned city called Καρχηδών (*Karchēdōn*) by the Greeks, is described by Solinus the Polyhistor as the second glory of the world after Rome. All agree that it was founded by Tyrians; but writers differ, as Appian observes, concerning the founders’ names and the time of its foundation. Philistus, cited by Eusebius, Stephanus in *On Cities*, and Appian write that it was founded by Zorus and Carchedon. Romans and Carthaginians attribute it to Dido, a woman who departed from Tyre. Others think that Carthage was not founded at a single time.

They hold that its earlier settlement was Βύρσα (*Byrsa*), which in their language was called *Busra*, that is, “citadel.” For that is what the word means among Phoenicians and Hebrews, who shared one language; in Hebrew, what we now pronounce *Botsra*. The later city, however, was called Carthage from the likewise Phoenician term *Kartha-Chadtha*, meaning Νεάπολις (*Neapolis*), or “New City,” to distinguish it from the old city, which in their own language was called Καδμεῖα (*Kadmeia*).

There is also remarkable diversity among writers about the time of its foundation. Eusebius, in his *Chronicle*, reports three opinions concerning its date. The first is that of Philistus, [Col. 0836D] who places it at Eusebius’s year-number 808—that is, twenty-seven years before the foundation of Troy according to Eusebius himself. At year 971, the same Eusebius says that Carthage was founded 143 years after the Trojan War. Finally, at year 1167 he notes that some thought Carthage founded in this era; this is the opinion of Trogus Pompeius, who says that Carthage was founded seventy-three years before the first Olympiad, which coincides with this year.

But Dido’s arrival may be calculated from Phoenician annals. For from the beginning of the reign of Iromus, king of the Tyrians—in whose eleventh year, according to the sacred Scriptures, Solomon’s Temple was built—to the seventh year of Pygmalion, when Dido fled to Libya, there elapsed 138 years. Now Pygmalion’s seventh year coincides with year 3821 of the Julian period; this fell in Eusebius’s year 1124, 290 years after the foundation of Troy, and 127 years after the foundations of Solomon’s Temple were laid. This is the more probable [Col. 0837A] date of Carthage’s foundation. Josephus is not far from it, for he says that Carthage was founded by the Tyrians 143 years after Solomon’s Temple.

This city, Rome’s rival, stood for 848 years, until it was utterly destroyed and burned by Scipio under the consulship of Cornelius Lentulus and Lucius Mummius, in the 608th year from the foundation of Rome and the 4568th of the Julian period. It lay desolate and ruined for twenty-two years. But in the twenty-third year of its desolation, when Quintus Caecilius Metellus Balearicus and Titus Quintus Flaminius were consuls at Rome, a Roman colony was led thither on the initiative of Gaius Sempronius Gracchus, tribune of the plebs. Thus a town was restored on that site and called Junonia, though under unhappy auspices and with no success of fortune.

But in the 102nd year after its destruction, when Gaius Julius Caesar, consul for the fifth time, was slain in the senate house at Rome, a larger body of colonists was sent there at Caesar’s own initiative. Under more favorable auspices its walls were rebuilt, the city was more extensively adorned with buildings and made more populous, and its former name of Carthage was restored, in the 810th year from Rome’s foundation, coinciding with the first year of the 184th Olympiad. From this restoration its prosperity again grew so greatly that in the centuries immediately following it surpassed the other cities of Africa in size, splendor, and wealth; and it was the head not only of the Proconsular province but of all Africa. Indeed, it even competed with Alexandria of Egypt and Antioch of [Col. 0837C] Syria for first place among all cities of the Roman Empire.

Let us hear Salvian, in Book VII of *On the Government of God*, discussing with his customary eloquence the dignity and power of this city at that time:

> I am content with one city alone, the chief and, as it were, mother of all the cities there [in Africa]: namely, that city always rival to the Roman strongholds—formerly in arms and courage, afterward in splendor and dignity. I mean Carthage, the greatest adversary of the city of Rome and, as it were, Rome within the African world. It possessed within itself all the institutions by which public affairs are administered or governed throughout the world. There were all the instruments of public offices; there the schools of liberal arts; there the workshops of philosophers; in short, every gymnasium of languages and manners. There also were military resources and the magistrates directing military service; there was proconsular rank; there the daily judge and ruler—proconsul in title, but consul in power. There, finally, were all the administrators of affairs and dignities differing among themselves both in rank and title, governors, so to speak, of all streets and crossroads, ruling almost all the places of the city and the members of the populace.

But when the Vandals under Genseric invaded Africa, Carthage was taken and occupied on 19 October 439. It remained under the power of Vandal kings for forty-five years; after this, when Africa was recovered by Belisarius in 534, the city of Carthage was restored to imperial rule. Finally, after it had stood for about 172 years, it came into the power of the Saracens and, almost wholly demolished, fell utterly to ruin; its fortune passed to the neighboring city of Tunis. This disaster occurred under the emperor Constantine Pogonatus, in the commonly reckoned year 585.

As to the site of Carthage, Polybius describes it thus in Book I:

> The city of Carthage slopes toward a certain gulf and approaches the form of a peninsula, being surrounded for the greater part of its extent by sea on one side and a lake on the other. The isthmus by which it is joined to Africa is twenty-five stades broad. It lies on the side of this space that inclines toward the sea. Utica is at a short distance from the city; on the other side, beside the lake, is Tunis. When the mercenaries brought their camp up to these two places and cut off the Carthaginians from the rest of the country, they threatened Carthage itself, and by approaching the walls now by day, now by night, threw everything inside into the utmost terror and confusion.

[Col. 0838B] The same Polybius, shortly afterward, speaking of the general Hamilcar, says:

> The neck which joins Carthage to Africa has, at the very junction, difficult and steep earthen hills; and the roads by which passage into the country lies open are skillfully fortified in them. At that time Matho—for he was the commander of the enemy—guarded with garrisons all strategically useful places in those hills. Moreover, since the River Macar in certain places likewise hinders the passage of those going from the city into the country and, because of the abundance of water, can for the most part not be crossed by ford, Matho guarded with great diligence the one bridge laid across that river, a town having also been built by it. Thus it happened that they could not lead not only an army but not even individual persons into the country, if they sought to escape the enemy by crossing. Seeing this, Hamilcar, etc.

The same Polybius, in the same book, setting out the causes and beginnings of this war, says of the town of Tunis, near Carthage:

> The mercenaries, inflamed by anger against the Carthaginians, advanced in hostility against the city and encamped at Tunis, fifteen Roman miles from it. They numbered more than twenty thousand. Then at last the Carthaginians saw their error before their eyes, when belated repentance helped them nothing.

And shortly afterward he reports that the general Gisco was sent from the city of Carthage with money to appease these enraged soldiers, and arrived at Tunis by sea. The Greek words, among others, run thus:

> Ὁ Γέσκων παραγενόμενος κατὰ θάλατταν μετὰ τῶν χρημάτων, καὶ προσπλεύσας πρὸς τὸν Τύνητα, τὸ μὲν πρῶτον λαμβάνων τοὺς ἡγεμόνας etc.

> “Gisco, having come by sea with the money and having sailed up to Tunis, at first taking the commanders . . .”

These words seem to indicate that Tunis could be reached and approached by sea. I leave the judgment to the reader. And again, in Book XIV, the same author says: “Tunis is about 120 stades from Carthage. The place is secure both by its works and by its natural situation, as we have already shown, and can be seen from almost every part of Carthage.”

Livy, incorporating this same passage of Polybius into his history, writes:

> Scipio, leading an army now laden with the spoils of many cities, having sent captives and other booty to the old camp at Utica, and now directing his attention toward Carthage, occupied TUNIS, abandoned by its guards in flight. It is nearly twelve Roman miles from Carthage, a place secure both by fortifications and its natural situation; from Carthage it could be seen, and it itself afforded a view both toward the city and toward the sea surrounding the city.

*Decade* III, Book X.

[Col. 0839A] Strabo, the most ancient of the geographers whose writings have reached us, describes the site of Carthage thus:

> CARTHAGE lies upon a peninsula, enclosed by a wall with a circumference of 360 stades. Its neck, extending from sea to sea, occupies a length of sixty stades; there the Carthaginians had their elephant stables, and the place is very spacious. In the middle of the city was a citadel called Byrsa, a fairly steep eminence, inhabited all around; at its summit was a temple of Aesculapius, which Hasdrubal’s wife burned together with herself when the city was taken. Below the citadel lie the harbors, and the Cothon, a small round island surrounded by a channel, on both sides of which are shipyards arranged in a circle. Dido founded this city after departing from Tyre and bringing settlers there. And this Phoenician colony prospered exceedingly, etc.

And shortly afterward:

> By means of these resources the Carthaginians made their city a rival of Rome and fought three very great wars against the Romans. You may judge the Carthaginians’ power most fully from their last war, in which they were conquered by Scipio Aemilianus and their city was razed to the ground. At the beginning of that war they possessed three hundred cities in Africa and had seven hundred thousand inhabitants in the city. When besieged and compelled to contemplate surrender, they handed over two hundred thousand suits of heavy armor and three thousand catapult-engines, so that war might no longer be waged against them. But when they resolved again to wage war, they immediately began to manufacture weapons. Every day 140 shields were completed and brought into the arsenal, together with 300 swords, 500 spears, and 1,000 missiles to be shot from catapults; for making the ropes of these engines, female slaves supplied their hair. [Col. 0839C] They still had twelve ships left from the fiftieth year after the treaties concluded in the Second War. Then, though they had taken refuge in the citadel, they built 120 decked ships in two months; and, when the mouth of the Cothon was occupied by a guard, they dug another outlet, from which their fleet suddenly emerged. For they still had old timber readily available and a multitude of workmen, maintained at public expense, intent upon the work. Yet Carthage, great as it was, was taken and destroyed.

A little before the passage already cited, the same Strabo writes of Utica, neighboring Carthage:

> Utica is second to Carthage both in size and dignity; when Carthage was destroyed, it was the capital of the region (μητρόπολις, “mother-city”) and the Roman base of operations (ὁρμητήριον) for conducting affairs in Africa. It lies in the same gulf as Carthage, by the other of the promontories which form the gulf. [Col. 0839D] Of these, the one near Utica is called Apollonium and the other Hormaeum. The cities themselves are so situated that one may be seen from the other. Near Utica flows the River Bagradas.

Appian of Alexandria, translated by the most learned Sigismund Gelenius, says in his book *On the Punic Wars*:

> Carthage lay in the innermost part of a great gulf, resembling a peninsula. For a neck twenty-five stades broad separated it from the mainland. From that neck a certain oblong tongue of land, half a stade broad, stretched westward between lagoon and sea, fortified on every side by cliffs and by a single wall. Toward the south and the mainland, where Byrsa also stood on the neck, there was a triple wall, thirty cubits high, not including battlements and towers. The towers stood all around at intervals of two plethra, founded on bases thirty feet deep, each with four stories. The walls reached to the second story. They were vaulted and capacious; in their lowest part were stabled three hundred elephants, together with storehouses for fodder. Above were stables for four thousand horses, with stores of barley; likewise quarters for twenty thousand infantrymen and four thousand cavalrymen. So great a military establishment had its ordinary accommodation in the walls alone. [Col. 0840A] The angle where this wall bent toward the harbors beyond the aforesaid tongue was alone weak and low, having been neglected from the beginning.

> The harbors were so arranged that vessels could pass from one into the other, and from the open sea there was one common entrance, seventy feet wide, closed with iron chains. The first harbor was for merchants, and in it were many shops of various kinds for the use of sailors.
