In the middle of the inner harbor was an island which, like the harbor itself, had continuous great quays filled with shipyards, capable of receiving 220 ships. Above them were chambers in which the equipment of triremes was stored. Each shipyard had two Ionic columns on its façade, so that, to those looking around, both harbor and island presented the appearance of a colonnade. On the island also was the admiral’s headquarters, from which the trumpeter customarily sounded the signal for the fleet, the herald made proclamations, and the admiral kept watch. The island stood opposite the harbor mouth and extended over a considerable distance, so that the admiral could see from afar everything occurring on the open sea; but approaching mariners could not see the recesses of the harbors. Indeed, even merchants entering their own harbor did not immediately see the shipyards. [Col. 0840B] For they were enclosed by a double wall, and a gate conveyed merchants from the first harbor into the city without their passing through the shipyards.

Such was the appearance of Carthage at that time. Thus far Appian’s words; combined with the testimony of Polybius, Livy, and Strabo, they provide an exact representation of Carthage’s site. Although not even the ruins of Carthage now remain, that peninsula is still called by sailors the Promontory of Carthage.

Bishops of Carthage.—The first of the bishops of Carthage whose memory has reached us is AGRIPPINUS. Cyprian mentions him in the letter now numbered 71, to Quintus. Maintaining there that the baptism of heretics is invalid, Cyprian thus commends Agrippinus’s decree on that subject:

> Agrippinus, a man of blessed memory, together with his fellow bishops who at that time governed the Church of the Lord in the provinces of Africa and Numidia, decreed this and established it after a weighed examination of their common counsel.

And in Letter 73, to Jubaianus, he says:

> Among us, however, it is not a new or sudden matter that we judge those coming to the Church from heretics to need baptism. For many years and a long period have already passed since, under Agrippinus, a man of blessed memory, very many bishops assembled together and decreed this.

Cyprian wrote these things in 254, when already a long period and many years had elapsed since Agrippinus’s decree. Accordingly, Agrippinus seems to have occupied the see of Carthage not in the third century, as is commonly thought, but near the end of the second century of the Church. [Col. 0841A] Certainly Tertullian, discussing the baptism of heretics in *On Baptism*, which he composed about the year 200, seems to have referred to Agrippinus’s decree when he says: “With regard to heretics, moreover, let each properly reconsider what is to be observed. For it has been promulgated for us.” By the words “it has been promulgated for us,” I have no doubt that Agrippinus’s decree is indicated.

After him, some place Cyrus, whose memory occurs in the Roman Martyrology on the day before the Ides of July, and on whose feast Possidius says that Saint Augustine delivered a sermon. But in neither place is he said to have been bishop of Carthage.

That DONATUS was Cyprian’s predecessor is certain from Cyprian himself, in the letter formerly numbered 55, now 59, to Cornelius, bishop of Rome, where he relates:

> Privatus, an old heretic, was condemned many years ago in the colony of Lambaesis for many grave offenses by the judgment of ninety bishops; and he was most severely censured in the letters of our predecessors, as you also know, Fabian and Donatus.

Here Cyprian calls Donatus his predecessor in the same rank in which Fabian was Cornelius’s predecessor; and therefore, as no one was between Fabian and Cornelius in the Roman see, so no one was between Donatus and Cyprian in the see of Carthage.

Cyprian therefore succeeded him in the year 248. He suffered martyrdom on the eighteenth day before the Kalends of August, under the consuls Tuscus and Bassus, in the commonly reckoned year 258, as is recorded in the fasti of Idatius.

LUCIANUS succeeded Cyprian. Optatus mentions him in Book I, section 19, where he lists Caecilian’s predecessors in the see of Carthage as follows: “The altar was in its place, on which the peaceful bishops of former times offered: Cyprian, Lucianus, etc.” [Col. 0841C] In the Saint-Germain manuscript, the name Carpophorus is read between Cyprian and Lucianus; whether this crept in through the copyist’s error or fell out of other manuscripts is uncertain.

After Lucianus no one occurs except MENSURIUS, of whom Optatus speaks in Book I. He held the see at Carthage during Diocletian’s persecution. Finally, he was summoned by Maxentius because he had concealed the deacon Felix, who was said to have written a notorious letter against the tyrant. As he was returning to Carthage after pleading his case, he died on the journey in 311.

In his place CAECILIANUS, the archdeacon, was chosen and ordained by Felix of Aptunga. Against him [Col. 0841D] MAJORINUS, a servant of Lucilla who had been a lector during Caecilian’s diaconate, was improperly ordained by Numidians. From this came the schism of which DONATUS, who succeeded Majorinus about 316, was the standard-bearer.

GRATUS succeeded Caecilianus before 347. He attended the Council of Sardica while Donatus was still alive. Donatus was exiled under Constans and died in exile; about 355 he had PARMENIANUS as successor.

On the other hand, RESTITUTUS succeeded Gratus as bishop; he attended the Council of Rimini in 359. GENETHLIUS succeeded Restitutus and lived until the year 390.

When he died near the end of that year, AURELIUS succeeded him, who at about the same time had as rival PRIMIANUS, [Col. 0842A] Parmenianus’s successor. With him the succession of Donatist bishops of Carthage seems to have failed.

CAPREOLUS succeeded Aurelius about 425. According to Liberatus, *Breviary*, chapter 5, he sent his deacon Besula to the Council of Ephesus.

QUODVULTDEUS was substituted for Capreolus. Under him Genseric invaded Carthage in 439, in the consulship of Theodosius XVII and Festus; and, as Victor of Vita relates, he placed Quodvultdeus and the clergy aboard leaky ships. Yet, through a favorable voyage, they reached Naples.

When he died in exile, DEOGRATIAS was, at the request of the Emperor Valentinian, ordained bishop of Carthage after “the long silence of desolation,” as Victor of Vita says, in the consulship of Aetius and Studius—that is, on the eighth day before the Kalends of November in the commonly reckoned year [Col. 0842B] 454. He presided over the Church of Carthage for three years in most difficult times; and after his death the Church of Carthage was without a pastor for twenty-four years. Near the end of his reign, Genseric ordered the Church of Carthage closed, Victor of Vita says, after presbyters and ministers had been scattered and dispersed among various places of exile, because there was no bishop.

Genseric having died on 25 January 477, his son and successor Huneric, during the reign of the emperor Zeno and at the request of Placidia, widow of Olybrius, granted permission for the Church of Carthage to ordain whomever it wished as bishop. Thus **EUGENIUS** was then ordained bishop of Carthage, late in 480 or at the beginning of 481. Distinguished by excellent writings and a splendid confession [Col. 0842C], he was driven into exile with the other bishops of Africa in 484. He was recalled from it by King Guntabund, Genseric’s successor, who granted the Catholics at Carthage the cemetery of the holy martyr Agileus. In the tenth year of his reign, this same king opened the Catholic churches and, at the request of the bishop of Carthage, recalled all God’s priests from exile, as Victor of Tours testifies in his *Chronicle*. Under this king, whatever some may say, Eugenius lived in peace; and only under Thrasamund, about the year 495, was he again sent into exile in Gaul. There, at Viancium in the territory of Albi, he is said to have ended his life about the year 505, on 6 September [VIII Ides of September].

After Eugenius had been expelled by Thrasamund, Anastasius the Librarian testifies that the see of Carthage stood vacant for twenty-seven years [Col. 0842D]—that is, throughout the entire reign of Thrasamund, who ruled for twenty-seven years and some months. Hilderic immediately restored liberty to the Catholic Church and gave the Church of Carthage its own bishop, **BONIFACE**, ordering him to be ordained in the church of St. Agileus in 523, at the request of the whole city of Carthage.

When he died about 534, **REPARATUS** was elevated to the bishopric of the Church of Carthage, at the end of that year or the beginning of the next. At that time Justinian recovered Africa through the patrician Belisarius. Immediately after his ordination, once the episcopal see of Carthage had been restored, Reparatus convened in the Basilica of Faustus a general council of all Africa, at which 217 bishops are said to have assembled [Col. 0843A]. The canons of the ancient councils were read there, and many decrees were issued to restore ecclesiastical discipline. Two embassies were sent from this synod: one to the Roman pontiff and the other to the Emperor Justinian. The emperor was asked that Catholic bishops and other sacred ministers should recover the property of churches which the barbarians had seized. By the other embassy the African bishops informed the Roman pontiff that peace had been restored to the churches, and sought his judgment concerning the reception into the Church of Arian presbyters who returned after renouncing their heresy, as well as concerning certain other matters of ecclesiastical discipline. The envoys were Caius and Peter, together with Liberatus, deacon of the Church of Carthage. They arrived after the death of John II [Col. 0843B] and were received by his successor Agapetus. There survive the synodal letter of this council to Pope John, Agapetus’s reply to the primates—namely Reparatus of Carthage, Florentius of Numidia, and Pontianus of Byzacena—and also separate special letters of the same pope to Reparatus.

Because of his defense of the Three Chapters, Reparatus was summoned to the imperial city in 552, deposed, and banished by Justinian to Euchaita. In exile he had as a faithful companion Liberatus, archdeacon of Carthage, author of the *Breviary*, which, after his bishop’s death in exile, he composed upon returning to his homeland in 564.

When Reparatus was deposed in 552, **PRIMOSUS**, Reparatus’s *apocrisiarius* [envoy] before the Emperor Justinian, was appointed in his place. He attended the Fifth General Council through a representative and died before Reparatus, in 562.

[Col. 0843C] Thus far extends the succession of African bishops; since it has been interrupted, it may not be continued. Only occasional mention is made of certain men: **DOMINICUS**, who held the see of Carthage in the time of Gregory the Great, about 590; **FORTUNIUS**, in the time of Pope Theodore, about 640; **VICTOR**, his successor, who flourished under Martin I in 650; and finally **CYRIACUS**, in the time of Gregory VII in the eleventh century. So much, then, concerning the Church of Carthage and its bishops. We must now enumerate the remaining sees, arranged by provinces.

## Proconsular Province

In it, besides **CARTHAGE**, of which more than enough has just been said, are the following bishoprics.

**ABBIRITA MAJOR**, or Abaritanus: *Notitia*, no. 2; *Collatio Carthaginensis*, day 1, ch. 133, note 172.

**ABBIRITA MINOR**: *Collatio Carthaginensis*, day 1, ch. 215, notes 172 and 454.

**ABIDENSIS**: *Collatio Carthaginensis*, day 1, ch. 126, note 100. It may, however, belong to Byzacena, where Ptolemy places Abidus.

**ABITINENSIS**: *Collatio Carthaginensis*, day 1, ch. 211, note 390.

**ABORENSIS**: *Collatio Carthaginensis*, day 1, ch. 133, note 178.

**ABSASALLENSIS**: Dominicus, bishop of the holy Church of Absasalla, subscribes to the synodal letter of the fathers of the Proconsular Province at the Lateran Council under Martin.

**ABZERITENSIS**, or Abzeritanus, or Abderitanus [Col. 0844A]: *Collatio Carthaginensis*, day 1, ch. 128, note 133. Ptolemy places Abdera here.

**ADVOCATENSIS**: *Collatio Carthaginensis*, day 1, ch. 206, note 407.

**AGENSIS**: Fortis, bishop of the holy Church of Agensis, subscribes last to the synodal letter of the fathers of the Proconsular Province at the Lateran Council under Martin. At the Council of Carthage under Cyprian, no. 65: Quintus of Aggia.

**ALTIBURITANUS**, or Altuburitanus: *Notitia*, no. 44; *Collatio Carthaginensis*, day 1, ch. 128, note 131.

**APTUGNITANUS**, Aptungitanus, or Autumnitanus: *Collatio Carthaginensis*, day 1, ch. 128, note 116.

**ARADITANUS**: *Notitia*, no. 13. Aemilianus, bishop of the people of Aradita, attended the Council of Carthage under Boniface in 525.

[Col. 0844B] **ASSURITANUS**: *Notitia*, no. 19; *Collatio Carthaginensis*, day 1, ch. 120, note 21.

**AUSANENSIS**: *Notitia*, no. 47.

**BENCENNENSIS**, perhaps Beneventensis or Benentensis: *Notitia*, no. 9; *Collatio Carthaginensis*, day 1, ch. 128, note 114. Among the subscriptions of the African bishops at the First Council of Arles is found Anastasius of the city of Beneventum.

**BONUSTENSIS**: *Notitia*, no. 31; *Collatio Carthaginensis*, day 1, ch. 133, note 164.

**BOSETENSIS**, or Busitanus: *Collatio Carthaginensis*, day 1, ch. 126, note 88.

**BULLENSIS**: *Notitia*, no. 34.

**BULLENSIUM REGIORUM**: *Notitia*, no. 50; *Collatio Carthaginensis*, day 1, ch. 135, note 233. Ptolemy too mentions two Bullas, one of which he calls Bullamensa [Col. 0844C], the other Bulla Regia.

**BULNENSIS**: Victor, bishop of the holy Church of Bulna, subscribes to the synodal letter of the fathers of the Proconsular Province at the Lateran Council under Martin.

**BURITANUS**: *Collatio Carthaginensis*, day 1, ch. 133, note 167.

**CAECIRITANUS**: Quobulus, bishop of the Church of Caecirita, subscribes to the synodal letter of the fathers of the Proconsular Province at the Lateran Council under Martin.

**CANIOPITANORUM**, perhaps Canapii: *Collatio Carthaginensis*, day 1, ch. 133, note 203. Ptolemy places Canopisium between Tabarca and Utica.

**CARPITANUS**: *Notitia*, no. 29; *Collatio Carthaginensis*, day 1, ch. 126, note 75.

**CEFALENSIS**: *Collatio Carthaginensis*, day 1, ch. 133, note 181.

**CELLENSIS**: *Notitia*, no. 45; *Collatio Carthaginensis*, day 1, ch. 126, note 73.

[Col. 0844D] **CESSITANUS**, or Cicsitanus, or Cissitanus: *Notitia*, no. 27; *Collatio Carthaginensis*, day 1, ch. 206, note 418.

**CILIBIENSIS**, or Elibiensis: *Collatio Carthaginensis*, day 1, ch. 206, note 410.

**CLYPEENSIS**: *Notitia*, no. 38; *Collatio Carthaginensis*, day 1, ch. 133, note 166. Today Quippia or Cupia, called Aclibia by the Arabs.

**CUBDENSIS**: *Collatio Carthaginensis*, day 1, ch. 133, note 189.

**CULUSITANUS**: *Notitia*, no. 33; *Collatio Carthaginensis*, day 1, ch. 138, note 263. It seems to be the same as Culcitanensis. Peter, bishop of the holy Church of Culcita, subscribes to the synodal letter of the fathers of the Proconsular Province at the Lateran Council under Martin.

[Col. 0845A] **CURUBITANUS**: *Notitia*, no. 36; *Collatio Carthaginensis*, day 1, ch. 198, note 366.

**DRUSILIANENSIS**: *Collatio Carthaginensis*, day 1, ch. 121, note 49.

**EGUGENSIS**: Florentius, bishop of the holy Church of Eguga, subscribes to the synodal letter of the fathers of the Proconsular Province at the Lateran Council under Martin.

**ELEFANTARIENSIS**: The Peutinger Tables place Elefantaria in the Proconsular Province, not far from Utica, distinct from Elefantaria in Mauretania Caesariensis. The Ravenna Anonymous also lists two Elefantarias.

**FURNITANUS**: *Collatio Carthaginensis*, day 1, ch. 198, note 367.

**GISIPENSIS MAJOR**: *Notitia*, no. 24; *Collatio Carthaginensis*, day 1, ch. 133, note 231.

**GIUTRAMBACARIENSIS**: Benenatus, bishop of the holy Church of Giutrambacaria, subscribes to the synodal letter of the fathers of the Proconsular Province [Col. 0845B] at the Lateran Council under Martin.

**GUNELENSIS**, or Gunelmensis: *Notitia*, no. 6.

**HILTENSIS**: *Collatio Carthaginensis*, day 1, ch. 133, note 230.

**HIPPONIENSIS DYARRHYTORUM**: *Notitia*, no. 5; *Collatio Carthaginensis*, day 1, ch. 132, note 161.

**HORTENSIS**: Donatus, bishop of the holy Church of Hortum, subscribes to the synodal letter of the fathers of the Proconsular Province at the Lateran Council under Martin.

**LABDENSIS**: *Notitia*, no. 18; *Collatio Carthaginensis*, day 1, ch. 198, note 358.

**OF THE SWEET LAKE**: *Collatio Carthaginensis*, day 1, ch. 187, note 305.

**LARENSIS**: *Collatio Carthaginensis*, day 1, ch. 131, note 158.

**LIBERTINENSIS**: *Collatio Carthaginensis*, day 1, ch. 116, note 17.

[Col. 0845C] **MATTIANENSIS**: Marcellus, bishop of Mattiana, subscribes in the synodal letter of the fathers of the Proconsular Province at the Lateran Council under Martin.

**MAXULITANUS**: *Notitia*, no. 30; *Collatio Carthaginensis*, day 1, ch. 188, note 324.

**MEGLAPOLITANUS**: *Notitia*, no. 39; *Collatio Carthaginensis*, day 1, ch. 133, note 216.

**MELZITANUS**, or Melditanus: *Collatio Carthaginensis*, day 1, ch. 121, note 35.

**MEMBLOSITANUS**, or Membrositanus: *Notitia*, no. 8; *Collatio Carthaginensis*, day 1, ch. 133, notes 205 and 225.

**MEMBRESSITANUS**: *Collatio Carthaginensis*, day 1, ch. 133, note 205.

**MIGIRPENSIS**: *Notitia*, no. 23; *Collatio Carthaginensis*, day 1, ch. 126, note 108.

[Col. 0845D] **MISSUENSIS**: *Notitia*, no. 17. Antoninus in the *Itinerary* and the Ravenna Anonymous mention Missua; Pliny and the Peutinger Tables call it Misua; Ptolemy, Nisua. Procopius, *Vandalic War*, book II, calls Missua the harbor of the Carthaginians. Servus Dei, bishop of Missua, attended the Council of Carthage under Boniface in 525.

**MULLITANUS**: *Notitia*, no. 15; *Collatio Carthaginensis*, day 1, ch. 133, note 168.

**MUSTITANUS**: *Collatio Carthaginensis*, day 1, ch. 121, note 53.

**MUZUENSIS**: *Notitia*, no. 49; *Collatio Carthaginensis*, day 1, ch. 128, note 112.

**NARAGGARITANUS**: *Notitia*, no. 48; *Collatio Carthaginensis*, day 1, ch. 208, note 430.

[Col. 0846A] **NEAPOLITANUS**: *Notitia*, no. 35; *Collatio Carthaginensis*, day 1, ch. 126, note 76. The Arabs today call it Nabel.

**NUMNULITANUS**: *Collatio Carthaginensis*, day 1, ch. 126, note 98.

**OFITANUS**: Fortunius, bishop of the holy Church of Ofita, subscribes to the synodal letter of the fathers of the Proconsular Province at the Lateran Council under Martin.

**PARIENSIS**: Felix, bishop of the holy Church of Paria, subscribes to the synodal letter of the fathers of the Proconsular Province at the Lateran Council under Martin.

**PERTUSENSIS**: Martialis, bishop of Pertusa, was condemned at the Council of Bagai. Pertusa is listed in the Peutinger Tables among the towns of the Proconsular Province.

**PIENSIS**: *Notitia*, no. 4. Perhaps it should be read **PICENSIS**, for Picus is mentioned in the Peutinger Tables [Col. 0846B]. Polybius mentions a place called Prion. Felix, bishop of Paria, subscribes to the synodal letter of the fathers of the Proconsular Province; whether anything there belongs to these Pienses is uncertain.

**PISITENSIS**: *Collatio Carthaginensis*, day 1, ch. 133, note 183.

**PUPPIANENSIS**: *Notitia*, no. 12. Victor the Elder of Puppiana attended the Council of Carthage under Aurelius in 397; and Gaudiosus, bishop of Ruppiana, the Council of Carthage under Boniface in 525. Boniface, bishop of the holy Church of Puppiana, subscribed to the synodal letter of the fathers of the Proconsular Province at the Lateran Council under Martin.

**PUPPITANUS**: *Notitia*, no. 11; *Collatio Carthaginensis*, day 1, ch. 126, note 77.

**RUCUMENSIS**: In the Proconsular Province. Lucianus of Rucuma attended the Council of Carthage [Col. 0846C] under Cyprian; and Maximus, bishop of the holy Church of Rucuma, subscribes to the synodal letter of the fathers of the Proconsular Province at the Lateran Council under Martin.

**SAIENSIS**, or Suensis: *Collatio Carthaginensis*, day 1, ch. 128, note 111.

**SICILITANUS**: *Collatio Carthaginensis*, day 1, ch. 143, note 272.

**SEMINENSIS**, or Siminensis, or Simminensis: *Notitia*, no. 49. The bishop of Seminensis subscribed to the synodal letter of the fathers of the Proconsular Province at the Lateran Council under Martin; and Junianus, bishop of Siminensis, subscribed at the Council of Carthage under Boniface in 525. In the Ravenna Anonymous, Suminina is read.

**OF SENEMSALIS**: *Collatio Carthaginensis*, day 1, ch. 201, note 393.

[Col. 0846D] **OF SICCENNI**, perhaps Sinitensis or Sinicensis: *Collatio Carthaginensis*, day 1, ch. 133, note 186.

**SICCENSIS**: *Collatio Carthaginensis*, day 1, ch. 139, note 265.

**SICILIBENSIS**: *Collatio Carthaginensis*, day 1, ch. 198, note 348.

**SILEMSILENSIS**: *Collatio Carthaginensis*, day 1, ch. 201, note 396.

**SIMIDICCENSIS**: *Collatio Carthaginensis*, day 1, ch. 135, note 256.

**SIMITTENSIS**: *Notitia*, no. 37; *Collatio Carthaginensis*, day 1, ch. 126, note 65.

**SINNUARITENSIS**, or Sinnuarensis, or Sinnarensis: *Collatio Carthaginensis*, day 1, ch. 133, note 185.

**SUCCUBENSIS**: Lucianus, bishop of the holy Church of Succuba, subscribes to the synodal letter of the fathers of the Proconsular Province at the Lateran Council under Martin. Perhaps Vindicius of Sacubasa, who attended the Council of Carthage [Col. 0847A] under Gratus in 348, was also bishop of this see.

**TABORENSIS**: *Collatio Carthaginensis*, day 1, ch. 126, note 70.

**TABRACENSIS**: *Collatio Carthaginensis*, day 1, ch. 126, note 63. Today it is the Genoese town of Tabarca.

**TABUCENSIS**: Paulus, bishop of the holy Church of Tabuca, subscribes to the synodal letter of the fathers of the Proconsular Province at the Lateran Council under Martin.

**TACAPITANUS**: *Notitia*, no. 5; *Collatio Carthaginensis*, day 1, ch. 133, note 227.

**TACIANA-MONTENSIS**: At the Council of Carthage in 525 Ruffinus, bishop of Tacia Montana, subscribes; at the Council of Cabarsussus, Cresconius of Tatiana; and in the synodal letter of the fathers of the Proconsular Province, Probus of Tatia Montana.

**TADUENSIS**: Cyprianus, bishop of the holy Church of Tadua, subscribes to the synodal letter of the fathers of the Proconsular Province [Col. 0847B] at the Lateran Council under Martin.

**TAGARATENSIS**: *Notitia*, no. 43; *Collatio Carthaginensis*, day 1, ch. 128, note 151.

**TAGORENSIS**: *Collatio Carthaginensis*, day 1, chs. 133 and 143, notes 201 and 275.

**TAURACINENSIS**: Clarissimus, bishop of the holy Church of Tauracina, subscribes to the synodal letter of the fathers of the Proconsular Province at the Lateran Council under Martin.

**TELENSIS**, for Zellensis: *Notitia*, no. 14; *Collatio Carthaginensis*, day 1, ch. 135, note 260.

**TENNONENSIS**: *Notitia*, no. 21. Optatus, bishop of Tonnona, subscribed to the Council of Carthage under Boniface in 525 [Col. 0847C]. Victor of Tunnuna, author of the *Chronicle*, is celebrated. Therefore *Turonensis* has intruded for *Tunnonensis* on pp. XXV and XXXI.

**THEODALENSIS**, or Theudalensis, and corruptly Eudalensis: *Notitia*, no. 53; *Collatio Carthaginensis*, day 1, ch. 126, note 107.

**TIBURICENSIS**: Valerius, bishop of the holy Church of Tiburica, subscribes to the synodal letter of the fathers of the Proconsular Province at the Lateran Council under Martin.

**TIBURNICENSIS**: Crescens, bishop of the Church of Tiburnica, subscribes to the synodal letter of the fathers of the Proconsular Province.

**TIGIMMENSIS**: *Collatio Carthaginensis*, day 1, ch. 133, note 184.

**TIJUCENSIS**, perhaps Tyzicensis: *Collatio Carthaginensis*, day 1, ch. 126, note 105.

[Col. 0847D] **TIMIDENSIS**: *Notitia*, no. 40. The feast of the martyrs of Timida is celebrated in the ancient Carthaginian calendar on 22 May [XI Kalends of June]. This city was called Timida Regia; Augustine praises its bishop, Faustus the Confessor, in *On Baptism against the Donatists*, book VII, ch. 22. He was present at the Council of Carthage under Cyprian. Restitutus, bishop of Timida Regia, subscribed to the Council of Carthage under Boniface. Among the bishops of the Proconsular Province at the Lateran Council under Martin, Felix, bishop of the Church of Timida, subscribed.

**TINNISENSIS**: *Notitia*, no. 32.

**TISILITANUS**: *Collatio Carthaginensis*, day 1, ch. 121, note 50.

[Col. 0848A] Peutinger places Tichilla in the Proconsular Province.

**TITULITANUS**: *Notitia*, no. 51; *Collatio Carthaginensis*, day 1, ch. 126, note 95.

**TIZZICENSIS**: Vitalis, bishop of the holy Church of Tizzica, subscribes to the synodal letter of the fathers of the Proconsular Province at the Lateran Council under Martin.

**TRISIPENSIS**, or Trisipellensis: *Collatio Carthaginensis*, day 1, ch. 128, note 113.

**TUBURBITA MAJOR**: *Collatio Carthaginensis*, day 1, chs. 133 and 135, notes 170 and 259. Among the bishops of Africa at the First Council of Arles, Faustus, bishop of the city of Tuburbita, subscribes. Germanus, bishop of the holy Church of “Ciumtuturbo,” subscribes to the synodal letter of the fathers of the Proconsular Province at the Lateran Council under Martin. I have no doubt that he was bishop of this city [Col. 0848B]. The text read *Civ. m. Tuturbo*, that is, “of the greater city of Tuburbita”; through a copyist’s error this became *Ciumtuturbo*.

**TUBURBITA MINOR**: *Notitia*, no. 52; *Collatio Carthaginensis*, day 1, ch. 133, note 170.

**TUBURSICUBURENSIS**: *Collatio Carthaginensis*, day 1, ch. 121, note 43.

**TUCABORENSIS**: *Collatio Carthaginensis*, day 1, ch. 208, note 426.

**TUGGENSIS**, or of the municipality of Togia: *Collatio Carthaginensis*, day 1, ch. 187, note 318.

**TULANENSIS**: *Notitia*, no. 54.

**TUNEIENSIS**: *Collatio Carthaginensis*, day 1, ch. 128, note 110.

**TURENSIS**: *Collatio Carthaginensis*, day 1, ch. 121, note 54.

**TURUDENSIS**, perhaps Turusensis: *Collatio Carthaginensis*, day 1, ch. 126, note 99.

[Col. 0848C] **TURUSITANUS**: *Collatio Carthaginensis*, day 1, ch. 133, note 187.

**VALLITANUS**: *Collatio Carthaginensis*, day 1, ch. 135, note 249.

**UCRENSIS**, or Verensis: *Notitia*, no. 26; *Collatio Carthaginensis*, day 1, ch. 208, note 428. At the First Council of Arles, Vitalis, bishop of the city of the Verenses, subscribes.

**UCULENSIS**: *Collatio Carthaginensis*, day 1, ch. 128, note 130.

**VILLA MAGNA**: *Collatio Carthaginensis*, day 1, ch. 133, note 173.

**VILTENSIS**, or Biltensis: *Collatio Carthaginensis*, day 1, ch. 208, note 431. Among the African bishops in the subscriptions to the First Council of Arles appears Surgentius, bishop of the city of Poco-feltis; perhaps it should be read *Vico-Beltis*.

**VINENSIS**: *Collatio Carthaginensis*, day 1, ch. 128, note 132.

[Col. 0848D] Vina is mentioned as a city in the *Itinerary* of Antoninus; in Peutinger, Vina is a village; in the Ravenna Anonymous, Benda.

**VISICENSIS**: *Collatio Carthaginensis*, day 1, ch. 126, note 69.

**VOLITANUS**: *Notitia*, no. 28; *Collatio Carthaginensis*, day 1, ch. 128, note 146.

**URCITANUS**, or of Uci Major: *Notitia*, no. 20; *Collatio Carthaginensis*, day 1, ch. 134, note 220.

**URUGITANUS**, perhaps Uracitanus or Urcitanus: *Notitia*, no. 20; *Collatio Carthaginensis*, day 1, ch. 187, note 315.

**UTICENSIS**: *Notitia*, no. 22; *Collatio Carthaginensis*, day 1, ch. 128, note 128. Among the bishops who subscribed to the First Council of Arles appears Victor, bishop of the city of Utica.

[Col. 0849A] **UTINENSIS**: *Collatio Carthaginensis*, day 1, chs. 128 and 133, notes 135 and 169. In the subscriptions to the First Council of Arles occurs the name of Lampadius, bishop of the city of Utina.

**UTINISENSIS**, or Tinnisensis: *Notitia*, no. 32; *Collatio Carthaginensis*, day 1, ch. 126, note 106.

**UTMENSIS**, or Utimmirensis: *Notitia*, no. 10; *Collatio Carthaginensis*, day 1, ch. 126, notes 66 and 104.

**UVAZENSIS**, or Uvaziensis: *Collatio Carthaginensis*, day 1, ch. 126, note 94.

**UZALENSIS**: *Notitia*, no. 7; *Collatio Carthaginensis*, ch. 204, note 404. Council of Carthage under Boniface; Augustine, *City of God*, book XXII, ch. 8.

**UTZIPPARITANORUM**: *Notitia*, no. 46; *Collatio Carthaginensis*, day 1, ch. 131, note 157. The Peutinger Tables have Uzippira [Col. 0849B].

**UZITENSIS**, or of Uci Minor: *Notitia*, no. 25; *Collatio Carthaginensis*, day 1, ch. 134, note 220. According to Hirtius, Uzita lies six miles from Leptis.

**ZARNENSIS**, or Zamensis: Vitalis, bishop of the holy Church of Zarna, subscribes to the synodal letter of the fathers of the Proconsular Province at the Lateran Council under Martin. Among the cities of the Proconsular Province, the Peutinger Tables read Zama Regia.

**ZEMTENSIS**: *Collatio Carthaginensis*, day 1, ch. 133, note 188.

**ZICENSIS**, perhaps Ziggensis: *Notitia*, no. 41; *Collatio Carthaginensis*, day 1, ch. 198, note 356.

**ZURENSIS**: *Collatio Carthaginensis*, day 1, ch. 133, note 179.

**CULLITANUS**: In Numidia there is the municipality of Cullu, mentioned in Antoninus’s *Itinerary* and in the Peutinger Tables, today Collo. Victor and Fidentius, mentioned in chapters 126 and 201 of the Carthaginian Conference, should more properly be called bishops of this place than of the city of Cululita in Byzacena; thus note 87 must be corrected.

**DIANENSIS**: *Collatio Carthaginensis*, day 1, ch. 198, note 352. Diana appears in Antoninus’s *Itinerary*.

**FORMENSIS**: *Notitia*, no. 108.

**FOSSALENSIS**, or rather Fussalensis: *Notitia*, no. 21. Fussala was a fortified place only forty miles from Hippo Regius and was detached from its diocese in the time of St. Augustine, as Letter 209 shows. In the same place Augustine relates miracles performed through the merits of St. Stephen, *City of God*, book XXII, ch. 8.

**GARBENSIS**: *Notitia*, no. 102; *Collatio Carthaginensis*, day 1, ch. 209, note 441.

**LAMBESITANUS**: Lamesa, or Lambesa, appears in Ptolemy and Antoninus. It is a city of Numidia, and its bishop Januarius subscribes to the Council of Carthage under Cyprian. Cyprian, Letter 55, mentions the condemnation in the colony of Lambesa of the heretic Privatus. Two bishops of Lambesa appear at the Council of Carthage under Cyprian, one at no. 6, the other at no. 75.

**LAMBIENSIS**, or Lambesitanus: *Collatio Carthaginensis*, day 1, ch. 201, note 375.

**LEGENSIS**: *Notitia*, no. 85; *Collatio Carthaginensis*, day 1, ch. 187, note 39. At the First Council of Arles Victor, bishop of the city of Legis in the province of Numidia, subscribes. Perhaps he is the Legensis.

## Province of Byzacena
*ABARADRENSIS,* *Notitia*, no. 23.  
ABIDENSIS. In the province of Byzacena according to Ptolemy.  
*ACOLITANEUS,* or Acolitanus, *Notitia*, no. 59. Quinctus, bishop of this Church, subscribed to the letter of the Fathers of Byzacena at the Lateran council under Martin.  
[Col. 0855B] *ADRUMETINUS,* Carthaginian Conference, day 1, ch. 126, note 67.  
AFUFENIENSIS, *Notitia*, no. 2.  
*AGGARITANUS,* *Notitia*, no. 108; Carthaginian Conference, day 1, ch. 126, note 91.  
AGGERITANUS, or Aggaritanus, *Notitia*, no. 29; Carthaginian Conference, day 1, ch. 126, note 91.  
*AMUDARSENSIS,* *Notitia*, no. 1; Carthaginian Conference, day 1, ch. 126, note 93.  
37 ANCUSENSIS, *Notitia*, no. 5; Carthaginian Conference, day 1, ch. 126, note 101.  
AQUAE-ALBENSIS, *Notitia*, no. 52; Carthaginian Conference, day 1, ch. 197, note 335.  
*AQUENSIUM REGIORUM,* *Notitia*, no. 86; Carthaginian Conference, day 1, ch. 126, note 74.  
AQUIABENSIS, *Notitia*, no. 26.  
[Col. 0855C] *ARSURITANUS,* *Notitia*, no. 67. Perhaps the bishop of the same place was Boniface, “bishop of the holy Church of Sasurita,” who subscribed to the letter of the Fathers of Byzacena at the Lateran council under Martin.  
*AUTENTENSIS,* *Notitia*, no. 104. Optatus, bishop of the holy Church of Autentum, subscribed to the letter of the bishops of the province of Byzacena at the Lateran council under Martin.  
*AUZAGERENSIS,* *Notitia*, no. 96; Carthaginian Conference, day 1, ch. 208, note 424.  
BAHANNENSIS, or Boanensis, or Banensis, *Notitia*, no. 73; Carthaginian Conference, day 1, ch. 126, note 80.  
BENNEFENSIS, or Benefensis, *Notitia*, no. 4; Carthaginian Conference, day 1, ch. 133, note 193.  
BIZACIENSIS. Ptolemy and Procopius mention the town of Bizacium in the province called Byzacena.  
[Col. 0855D] BULELIANENSIS, *Notitia*, no. 16. Perhaps the bishop of this see was Quodvultdeus, bishop of the people of Bulla, who subscribed to the Council of Carthage under Boniface in the year 525. Pliny, book V, ch. 5, mentions Bulula.  
CABARSUSSENSIS, Carthaginian Conference, day 1, ch. 208, note 438.

*RUSADITANUS,* *Notitia*, no. 69. Rusadir was a celebrated colony among the ancients. Ptolemy, Pliny, Antoninus, and Pomponius Mela mention it, but as belonging to the province of Tingitana, where the promontory of Russadir lies. But the place at issue here is rather Rusazus, a colony of Augustus, which Pliny, Ptolemy, and Antoninus list in Mauretania Caesariensis.  
*RUSGUNIENSIS,* *Notitia*, no. 64. The colony of Rusguniae is mentioned in Antoninus’s *Itinerary*, in Pliny, and in
