[Col. 0871]

**45. NOTICE CONCERNING THE GEOGRAPHICAL MAP**

[Col. 0871A] Gerardus Mercator depicted Africa—so called by the Romans in the strict sense—and Mauretania on two geographical maps drawn from Ptolemy. Abraham Ortelius compiled another map of the same regions from various authors. Yet neither work can give sufficient assistance to readers of civil and ecclesiastical history; this has become clear to all who have made even the slightest trial of the matter. Nicolas Sanson, most distinguished geographer to the Most Christian King, Father Philippe Briet of the Society of Jesus, and any others who have described the Roman Empire, have necessarily also touched upon this part of Africa, since it was included within that empire. Pierre Du Val also published a small map useful for explaining Caesar’s African War. But works of this kind, though perhaps they may appear sufficient to some for elucidating civil history, are by no means adequate for ecclesiastical history.

The first, so far as I know, to undertake the presentation of the ancient condition of the African Church on a geographical map was Father Charles of Saint-Paul, bishop-designate of Avranches. It was an arduous work; and although he made many errors in it, nevertheless everyone will acknowledge that by that work he rendered excellent service to the Christian commonwealth.

The difficulty of that work is exceedingly great and arises from many sources. First, there was the immense number of bishoprics, which were far more numerous in Africa than in any other province of the Christian world. Episcopal sees were established not only in cities, as in other regions of the world, but also in villages, forts, hamlets, and estates, so that more than six hundred episcopal sees are counted in Africa. Consequently, both because of their number and because the places in which they were situated are obscure, only the positions of the more notable sees, and not all of them, can be set out on a map. Thus, in what is called the placing of cities, anyone who wishes no episcopal see to be absent from his map must necessarily make many mistakes.

[Col. 0871C] Secondly, effort had to be devoted to ensuring the correct spelling of the names of episcopal sees, most of which have been distorted in many ways. Indeed, the variation in readings of these names is such that it is scarcely possible to know with certainty which reading ought especially to be followed. I think this variation arose partly from the nature of the matter itself and partly from the ignorance or recklessness of copyists. It arose from the matter itself because Pliny asserts that the names of African peoples and towns are unpronounceable except in African languages—a point rightly observed by Father Thierry Ruinart, a learned and equally diligent writer. Hence it was easy for different Romans to pronounce and write these names differently. As for copyists, it was very easy for them to err in writing so many proper names.

Certainly, whatever the source of this confusion, it is plainly great. Yet I do not see by what method it can be remedied: how corrupted names can be corrected, uncertain ones confirmed, and, among numerous and different forms of a name, which ought especially to be selected and whose reading may be supported. I know that Nicolas Sanson supplied many useful and promising suggestions for this purpose; but what rule can be laid down concerning matters liable to so many kinds of error, unless someone possesses a perfect knowledge of the Punic and African languages, by whose aid much could doubtless be restored? But in our ignorance of both languages and the great scarcity of authors, I do not sufficiently know what can rightly be done, or how it can be decided which spelling is faulty and which correct. In any case, this variation has afforded writers many opportunities for error: some have divided one city into several; others, perhaps through excessive ingenuity, have fused many into one. No one fails to see how disgracefully both errors distort geography.

[Col. 0872A] Thirdly, the greater part of the bishoprics are designated not by the proper name of the city, which is generally a substantive, but by an adjective and derivative. By what means that proper or substantive name, if it is not otherwise known, may be elicited from the adjective, let more learned men determine. For the most part such names are quite incapable of analogy, since nearly all of them have the flavor of gross barbarism, like the names occurring everywhere in Aethicus, the Peutinger Table, and the Anonymous Geographer of Ravenna. Even if they were capable of analogy, it is nevertheless certain that the rules of strict analogy have not been observed in them.

Charles of Saint-Paul, however, necessarily had to express most of these names, **46**, in substantive form. Those whose intention is merely to compile catalogues of bishoprics clearly need not do this. But those who wish to place these bishoprics on geographical maps are obliged to do so. It may rightly be doubted whether Father Charles of Saint-Paul carried this out sufficiently correctly: for he believes that the bishopric of Agensis is derived from the city Aga, although elsewhere a bishop is found called *Agensis*, or “from Aggia”; and he thinks the bishopric of Coviensis so called from the town Covium, whereas learned men judge it to be derived from the municipium Coba mentioned by the Ravenna Geographer. Holstenius also appears to me at times to have erred in the same way. Some names, moreover, are found among ancient authors in substantive form; others seem scarcely capable of being rendered as substantives.

Fourthly, some bishoprics are assigned by ecclesiastical authors to one or another province, though their principal towns, from which they take their names, appear to be assigned by other authors to another province. Examples are the bishoprics of Milevitanus, Idicrensis, and Cuiculitanus, which the *Ecclesiastical Notitia* assigns to the province of Numidia, although Antoninus assigns Mileum, Idicra, and Cuiculum to Mauretania. The same Antoninus assigns to Numidia Tabarca, Simitthu, Bulla Regia, Sicca Veneria, Altiburus, Ammædara, and other cities, which the *Notitia* transfers to Proconsular Africa. Thus one or the other must be mistaken; or at least the ecclesiastical provinces do not correspond everywhere and in every respect to the civil provinces—a question I leave to scholars to examine.

[Col. 0872C] Father Charles of Saint-Paul had to overcome these and other difficulties; therefore it is less surprising that he unwittingly struck upon so many rocks. Nicolas Sanson complains—and rightly—that he omitted very many bishoprics, duplicated or triplicated some, misspelled about three hundred names, and placed at most one hundred and seventy-two bishoprics on the map, whereas the location of three hundred could have been established. Of these one hundred and seventy-two bishoprics, he criticizes five or six, more or less, as having their proper place on the geographical map, all the rest as wrongly placed, along with other errors of the same sort. He then suggests many things useful for restoring the work, declaring that he too had expended no ordinary effort in examining these matters.

It is indeed regrettable, and especially unwelcome to me, that so great a man, so deserving in geographical studies, did not publish this work, which would have been extremely useful. But perhaps a day will come when the learned son of that learned father will rescue his father’s remains from moths and publish them for the public good.

[Col. 0873A] Meanwhile many learned men labored long and much to elucidate these same matters: Lucas Holstenius; Father Jean Garnier of the Society of Jesus; the most eminent and learned Cardinal Henry Noris; Étienne Baluze; and others, if any. Yet the diligence of all of them in this field was surpassed by Father Thierry Ruinart, a Benedictine monk. He published continuous and abundant notes on the *Notitia of Africa*; by collating manuscripts with one another, carefully reading ecclesiastical authors and all others who had written on the subject, correcting corrupt names, and undertaking other works of this kind for the public benefit, he seemed to have left future authors absolutely nothing in this field to attempt, much less to accomplish.

But behold, last in arrival, though not least in importance, comes the most illustrious and learned Monsieur Du Pin, doctor of the Sacred Faculty of Paris and royal professor. While preparing a new edition of Saint Optatus of Milevis and resolving to gather into one body everything relevant to the history of the Donatists, he determined to spare no labor whatever. He therefore resolved to turn this millstone himself and was not deterred by the labor of others. Since the ancient *Notitia* which the aforementioned Father Thierry Ruinart had undertaken to elucidate seemed defective and mutilated, Du Pin did not hesitate to publish another, more ample one, and, after so great a harvest of others, to make a gleaning—nor indeed without result, as I myself have found, such as no one else had even hoped for.

[Col. 0873B] Since he wished to leave nothing unattempted for a more complete edition of this exceptional work, it also seemed good to him to append a geographical map to his *Notitia*, setting before the eyes the condition of the African Church in that age, as far as that could be accomplished. He entrusted this task to me, who was certainly willing and did not refuse. I gladly accepted it, judging that I would do well if I relieved a man so deserving of the republic of letters, and then occupied with more serious concerns, of a labor useful indeed but thankless. It appeared honorable to me to contribute my share alongside so many learned men who had written on the subject, and above all delightful to draw the once most flourishing African Church out of darkness and display it as though restored to life.

Moreover, the most learned geographer Nicolas Sanson, who seemed to have promised an undertaking of this kind, was, I suppose, forestalled by death and could not come to it. If any assistance could now be hoped for, it lay in the single map of Charles of Saint-Paul, which, however, as we have said above, was marred by many errors. Therefore I undertook to produce a new map of Africa, believing that I could avoid the rocks upon which the aforementioned Father had struck, since I had long before been warned of them.

**47.** This was my reason for undertaking the work. But while I wished to assist others, I unwittingly imposed upon myself a very heavy burden, one that I would prove unequal to bearing. Conscious that I had read certain authors who had written historically or geographically about these regions, and trusting in my geographical extracts, which I had arranged for the purpose of making maps if ever there should be need, I thought that the principal part of the work had already been accomplished. Poorly cautious man that I was, to have anticipated so easily in my mind the execution of an undertaking nearly desperate! Yet much remained for me to read, and I did not know whether it would lessen the difficulty or perhaps even increase it.

[Col. 0873D] But the aforementioned most illustrious Monsieur Du Pin encouraged me. I trusted that he would be everything to me in this matter, since he had diligently collected everything written by Garnier, Noris, Baluze, Hardouin, and Ruinart, and would generously share with me his own notes as well. In a word, he gave me courage and stirred me to dare whatever this labor might require. Such, then, was the rationale of my undertaking.

I thought that every difficulty involved in determining the number of bishoprics, establishing the spelling of names, and assigning each bishopric to its own province ought to be referred to the learned men named above—especially to the man who had prompted me to undertake the work. For me, a layman in these matters, it would have been a scruple to move this stone; I was content with what such great men had written on the subject. I had no intention of exhausting their repositories or of cackling among the resonant swans.

But because their books contained little concerning the description of Africa, the arrangement of its provinces, the exact location of cities and other places, and matters of that sort, I thought it my responsibility to carry this out. Thus I first drew Africa accurately and in accordance with new observations; distributed the ecclesiastical provinces precisely; restored to their proper places episcopal sees that had not been suitably arranged on Charles of Saint-Paul’s map; supplied those omitted; and expended all the knowledge and skill available to me, so that this map might appear as corrected and accurate as possible.

[Col. 0874A] To accomplish this, I diligently collected whatever could be found in the geographers Pomponius Mela, Strabo, Pliny, and Ptolemy; in the itineraries and the Ravenna Geographer; likewise in the historians Polybius, Sallust, Hirtius, Livy, Ammianus, and Procopius; anything in the Arabs Abulfeda and the Nubian Geographer; and whatever might occur in more recent writers—John Leo, Sanuto, and Marmol. I recognized that the authors mentioned above had generally done the same, for they too had put their sickle into both harvests. From these materials I compiled this map, such as it is.

Yet lest anyone should regard everything contained in it as certain and beyond doubt, I wish to warn the reader of one or two points.

First, the positions of those cities washed by the sea, or connected with one another by lines, are certain, since they are better known from land and sea itineraries. Of the rest, some I have located from Ptolemy, some from historians; for the position of some, learned men have supplied me with information drawn from ecclesiastical historians—information not certain in every respect, but erroneous in few cases. Here certainty, if it is permissible to speak so, has its limits, beyond which scholars agree that there is scarcely anything other than conjecture.

[Col. 0874C] I judged it better to place certain cities by conjecture alone, although perhaps not in their proper location, than to omit them altogether, believing that the truth might thereby be more easily elicited. For scarcely anything certain in these matters can be established without autopsy, that is, personal inspection. The diversity of names is so great and so varied that a person who does not use the aid of his eyes can easily go astray. I am certainly fully persuaded that geographical maps, however poor they may be, nevertheless prepare the way to truth when better ones are unavailable. I shall count myself fortunate if this map, such as it is, can provide learned men with even a little assistance.

Secondly, I have displayed on this map not only cities certainly episcopal, but also inserted others, some of which perhaps are episcopal as well. My reason for inserting them was that they served the conjectures of learned men. In obscure matters, every smallest trace or indication of truth is valuable. I would have added more had the limited space of the sheet allowed it; therefore the names of peoples too are omitted here, not as altogether useless, but as less serviceable.

[Col. 0874D] Thirdly, wherever the proper or substantive names of cities could not be drawn from the pure source of the ancients, they have been taken from Father Charles of Saint-Paul or from Holstenius, and appear to have been formed, so far as possible, by analogy.

Fourthly, it would have been the duty of a diligent man to report any variant readings occurring in printed or manuscript copies, so that everyone might be free to form his own judgment; and Monsieur Du Pin carried this out at length. But because our geographical map could not accommodate such variation unless it became one-and-a-half times, or even twice, as large, one reading had to be selected from among the different readings. We selected that which we understood had found more approval among learned men than the others.

[Col. 0875A] Fifthly, since the appearance of regions frequently changes, at least with respect to the boundaries of empires, **48** the number of provinces, and the names of cities, peoples, and rivers—and since every notable alteration requires its own map representing the condition of that time—this map properly concerns the end of the fourth and the beginning of the fifth century, when the Donatist heresy was raging far and wide in Africa and that region was divided into six or seven provinces. Yet it can also serve for a slightly later period, when Vandal fury and persecution against Catholics prevailed.

Sixthly, although the part of Italy represented on the map, together with the adjacent islands, is useless for depicting the scene of the Conference of Carthage, which ought to be the special concern of this map, I nevertheless judged that I would act suitably by setting the city of Rome before the readers’ eyes, and the aforementioned islands contained in the *Notitia of the African Church*, as that church shortly afterward groaned beneath the Vandal yoke. We have not, however, marked episcopal sees in the Balearic and Pityusic Islands, since they are unknown to us; perhaps they had their see now here, now there, and were therefore called bishops of the whole region.

[Col. 0875B] Seventhly, we have marked civil metropolises with larger or initial letters, but not ecclesiastical metropolises, since I have learned that none of the latter had a fixed status apart from Carthage; the others were seats of senior bishops.

Eighthly, towns marked with an asterisk on the geographical map are those in which councils were held. You will find here the names of all of them except New Caesarea, Macriana, and Juncus, whose locations it was not possible to ascertain.

Moreover, I learned the position of the city of Bagai, which had eluded not a few learned men, from the Nubian Geography; and I seem to have seen traces of the city of Cabarsus in modern Susa. Let whoever wishes agree; I dare affirm nothing.

[Col. 0876A] I would also gladly have added certain cities, had it been possible: Tonona; Vita, whether city or small district; Casas Negras; and others of that kind, on account of Victor of Tonona, another Victor of Vita, Donatus of Casas Negras, and other famous men of this sort. Certainly every geographer must regret omitting places so celebrated. Yet I judged this preferable to casting the dice concerning them. Charles of Saint-Paul indeed gave a place to the city of Vita on his map, but by what authority or conjectures, I confess, I do not know.

Ninthly, you will find in the *Notitia* the modern names of certain ancient places. I refrained from anxiously searching for others, for this was extremely difficult—indeed, not to say impossible—since the present condition of those regions is little known. Moreover, it is not safe to employ more recent names in place of ancient ones. An example is a learned and diligent writer who, whenever he wished to name a Caesarean bishop in Mauretania, designated him an Algerian bishop. This is not likely.

[Col. 0875]

**LITERARY NOTICE**

(From Schönemann, vol. I, p. 343.)

### § I. Life of St. Optatus

An African, bishop of Milevis in Numidia, he wrote under the emperors Valentinian and Valens between 372 and 375. [Note: [Col. 0875D] Thus Jerome in the *Lives*.] Dupin plausibly maintains that he lived until the reign of Theodosius and of Siricius, who occupied the Roman episcopal see in the year 384. Nothing further concerning either his life or his death is known.

### § II. Writings

He wrote six books *On the Schism of the Donatists against Parmenian*, whose date Dupin has correctly estimated. For there is no need to extend their date to the time of Siricius, mentioned in Book II, §3: a view approved by Dupin rules this out, namely, that the author revised his work a second time and added, as supplements, the materials now appearing under the title of Book VII.

### § III. Editions

Johann Cochlaeus first brought Optatus out from the obscurity in which he had long lain in 1549, but conferred upon him no further benefit of light. Yet scarcely any ecclesiastical writer was more in need of generous assistance, whether owing to his own character or to the condition in which he then stood. He found no great number of patrons down to the present age, but two men, the equals of many, who earned everlasting merit in relation to him and every branch of ecclesiastical learning: François Balduin and Louis Ellies Dupin. For neither the edition of Albaspinaeus, published after his death in 1631, nor that of Meric Casaubon, issued in London in the same year, was of great service. Rigault’s edition met with no success. Through these two authors, however, two families of editions of Optatus steadily prevailed. Balduin’s, originating in the two editions of 1563 and 1569, endured to the end of the seventeenth century. Dupin’s, from 1700 onward, flourished in several reprints and recently in the editions of Galland and Oberthür. Let us examine the witnesses one by one.

### SIXTEENTH CENTURY, 1549–1600

#### 1549

At St. Victor near Mainz, from the press of the printer Franz Behem, folio. *Six Books of Optatus of Milevis, Formerly Bishop, on the Schism of the Donatists against Parmenian the Donatist, against whom St. Augustine also later published three books.* From the Cusan Library near Trier, together with the six books of Dr. Conrad Bruni, jurist, *On Heretics in General*, and his other shorter works, printed under a separate title in 1550. The title by which Optatus is distinguished from the remainder of the work is that given above.

The editor is Johann Cochlaeus, canon of Wrocław and friend of Bruni. His letter—to Arnold, abbot of the monastery of the Premonstratensian Order at Tongerlo—explains the copy from which he printed Optatus. It had been sent to him from the Hospital of St. Nicholas near Kues through Christopher, prior and brother of the Carthusian house at Trier. It had been written from some ancient codex, corruptly, by an unlearned copyist—such, he adds, as the literate servants of monasteries formerly were—and afterward copied anew by another hand much more corruptly still.

Moreover, while he was laboring over the publication of other books, he had received it only on the condition that he faithfully return it within three months. [Note: [Col. 0877D] He adds this in the notice to the reader found at the end of the book.] Hence nobody can be very surprised that, being excluded both from leisure itself and by other occupations, and lacking the assistance of another copy, he produced an Optatus only little cleansed of errors. He hopes and wishes that it will be completed and restored in every respect through both the resources of the very well-stocked library at Tongerlo and the genius of the abbot himself.

Cochlaeus disclosed examples of the corrections in the dedication mentioned above; the greater part concern letters and syllables wrongly joined or separated. Jerome’s testimonies are prefixed in the title itself; then, on the reverse of the title-page, those of Augustine against Parmenian; and poems of Gerhard Lorich of Hadamar in praise and commendation of Optatus. After the dedicatory letter follows a *Compendium of Summaries*, extracted from Optatus’s books and arranged in chapters; then a brief refutation of the Donatists from the words of St. Augustine on Psalm 85, and so forth; a concise comparison of the Donatists with the schismatics of that age; and finally an index of noteworthy matters. Nor did Cochlaeus neglect to prefix summaries to the individual books.

#### 1563

Paris, … octavo. *Seven Books of Optatus of Milevis to Parmenian, on the Schism of the Donatists.* Although Balduin declares that in this edition he can present our author corrected in six hundred places, most of them owing to a manuscript copy supplied for his use by Claude d’Espence, Parisian theologian, he nevertheless rightly warns that no much smaller number of passages remains under serious suspicion of corruption and can scarcely—indeed, hardly at all—be properly healed without the help of an ancient book. He therefore judged it better to make use of what was at hand than to allow Optatus to be reprinted in the same squalor by which he had previously been wholly defiled.

For some time he had hoped that a second aid for correction would be added from the codex of Jean du Tillet, bishop of Saint-Brieuc. But what could not then be accomplished, he bids readers await perhaps from a second edition. The editor prefixed a letter to Jean Lentallier, bishop of Aix-la-Chapelle, in which he discussed Optatus and these books of his very well; in addition, an extremely lengthy preface by Jean Lucan (Calvin), embracing much on every branch of ecclesiastical affairs together with a sharp attack on Calvin, which he removed in the second edition.

But whether Balduin already added the seventh book to this first edition, I have been unable to discover from any sufficiently certain evidence. [Note: [Col. 0877D] Dupin—and, following him, Fabricius in the Mansi edition of the *Bibliotheca Mediae et Infimae Latinitatis*, vol. V, p. 170—says that Book VII is printed in smaller type; [Col. 0878D] the second edition does not so present it, but prints it in the same kind of type as the remaining books. If one wishes, therefore, Dupin’s words may be referred to the first edition.] This first edition of Balduin is so rare that I do not remember having seen it mentioned even in catalogues of the best-stocked libraries.

#### 1569

Paris, at Claude Frémy’s, Rue Saint-Jacques, under the sign of St. Martin, octavo. *A Selection from African Ecclesiastical History; or, the Seven Books of Optatus of Milevis to Parmenian, on the Schism of the Donatists; and the Three Books of Victor of Utica on the Vandal Persecution in Africa, with Annotations from the Ecclesiastical-Historical Commentaries of François Balduin, Jurist.*

Balduin had presented Optatus in the earlier edition as corrected in at least six hundred places; he now states that this second recension brings him forth with not many fewer errors removed. It rests upon two manuscript copies, one owed to Jean du Tillet, bishop of Meaux, and the other to Macer, Parisian theologian. Yet he judges that he is still far from being able to say that the text has at last been wholly restored. “Indeed,” he says, “I have caused marks of lacunae to indicate that several passages remain mutilated even now.” The Tillet manuscript supplied several missing pages of Book VII, and other manuscripts supplied the final portion lacking in that copy.

Balduin’s annotations on each book of Optatus concern ecclesiastical history alone, a subject in which he was wonderfully skilled. To provide at once a fuller account of the history of the Donatists and ample satisfaction in respect of Optatus, he added a newly revised complete exposition of the debate concerning the Church held at the Conference of Carthage with the Donatists in the presence of Augustine, some years after Optatus’s death. He had published it separately in earlier years under the title *History of the Carthaginian Conference*. He removed items seeming less relevant, as well as passages written with greater heat against Calvin and Beza, and composed prolegomena to Victor in a similar manner. Hence he gave the volume the title *A Selection from African Ecclesiastical History*.

For no other reason than to avoid the odium incurred by more vehement invective and excessive harshness toward Calvin, he ordered the long discourse prefixed to the earlier edition to be kept away from this one, saying that it was more than sufficient for it to have been published once in its own time. He substituted another brief address to readers in its place. He dedicated the book to Caspar Barchin, jurist and judge of criminal cases at Milan.

Paris, at Michel Sonnius’s, under the Basel shield, Rue Saint-Jacques, octavo. Exactly the same as the preceding edition, differing only in the names of the booksellers.

#### 1599

[Col. 0878D] From the Commelin Bookshop, octavo. *Six Books of Optatus on the Schism of the Donatists against Parmenian, much more corrected than before. Added is the Conference of Carthage between Catholics and Donatists under the Emperor Honorius.*

This is Balduin’s first recension; accordingly, the dedicatory letter to the bishop of Aix-la-Chapelle is again printed. Book VII is also included, although absent from the title. Therefore, we seem not without grounds for conjecture in suspecting that this book was likewise appended to Balduin’s first edition. But do not expect the Conference of Carthage promised by the title. Rather, there is only a constitution of the emperors Honorius and Arcadius against the Donatists, issued at Ravenna in the consulship of Constantius and Constans, transcribed from the Theodosian Code, Book XVI, title 4, “Concerning Those Who Contend about Religion”; yet this is not indicated.

### SEVENTEENTH CENTURY, 1613

Leiden, from the press of Joannes Patius, octavo. *Seven Books of Optatus of Africa, Bishop of Milevis in Numidia, on the Schism of the Donatists against Parmenian, much more corrected than before and more fully illustrated by a booklet of emendations and notes.*

A reprint of the edition of 1599, that is, of Balduin’s first recension; the preface appears shorter in some places. The notes prefixed to the text consist for the most part of variant readings from Balduin’s second recension and certain corrections by Caspar Barthius. Every reader is rightly offended by this: although all the readings of Balduin’s second recension are praised without exception, the inferior first recension was nevertheless sent to press.

#### 1618

Cologne, at the expense of Anton Hierat, folio. *The Seventh Book of Optatus of Milevis on the Schism of the Donatists against Parmenian*, in the *Great Library of the Fathers*, vol. IV, p. 269.

#### 1631

Paris, at Claude Sonnius’s, Rue Saint-Jacques, under the Basel Shield and Golden Compasses, folio. *The Works of St. Optatus of Milevis, with Observations and Notes of the Reverend Gabriel Albaspinaeus, Bishop of Orléans. Added are two books by the same author, Observations on the Ancient Rites of the Church; Notes on the Council of Elvira and certain other ancient canons; and on several books of Tertullian.*
Viewing this edition, one would not know whom to blame more: the impudence of the booksellers, or the ignorance of the man who prepared it. The letter placed at the beginning of the book to Cardinal de Richelieu seems to show that he was Charles Paulin, of the Society of Jesus. For, apart from Albaspinaeus’s Observations—which had already appeared separately, and which, though useful enough in themselves, contribute less to Optatus, a defect for which Meric Casaubon also censures them—all the rest has been patched together with an ineptitude beyond expression. The text is indeed that of Baldwin’s second recension; immediately after it come Albaspinaeus’s notes on each of Optatus’s books, briefly explaining the meaning; then Baldwin’s annotations on each book; then the latter’s History of the Conference of Carthage, under the title *An Outline of African History*, a title which Baldwin had formerly prefixed to the whole volume containing Optatus and Victor, but which has here been transferred without sense. Next come those futile “emendations and notes” of an unknown author from the Leiden edition; since they say nothing beyond the difference of Baldwin’s second recension from the first, reproduced by the Batavian edition, they have here—where the second recension itself has been printed—been inserted with truly astonishing stupidity.

There follows an appendix from P. Pithoeus’s library:

> At the end: “Here end the seven books of O[ptatus], E[piscopal?], and the Acts of the Purging of Caecilian the Bishop and of Felix, his ordainer, together with the letters of the Emperor Constantine, thanks be to God.” Thus did the very ancient, though incomplete, copy of the books of Optatus of Milevis read, from which I first copied this appendix to them. By C. P. P., 1664.

This appendix contains those acts and proceedings often mentioned by Optatus, which Optatus himself had taken care to have attached to his books; then fragments from the History of the Passion of Saints Dativus, Saturninus, and others. Next appear the Acts of the Conference of Carthage, etc., as published at Paris by P. Masson in 1588, reproduced exactly, though compared and corrected by Pithoeus from a manuscript codex. Yet now, scarcely credibly, Baldwin’s History of the Conference of Carthage from the first edition is again included. Albaspinaeus’s Observations close the procession. Optatus’s text is preceded by Albaspinaeus’s Life and Observations on the principal points in the history of the Donatists and of Optatus. It remains to add that Dupin notes this work to swarm with innumerable typographical errors. Thus, we think enough has now been said to form a sounder judgment of this edition, which has perhaps been valued too highly because of the remarkable apparatus it undoubtedly offers.

London, printed by John Legat, octavo. *The Seven Books of Optatus of Milevis concerning the Schism of the Donatists against Parmenian the Donatist. Notes and Emendations on Them by Meric Casaubon, son of Isaac, Canon of Canterbury.*

Retaining the text of Baldwin’s second recension, Casaubon presented in his notes whatever he thought ought to be changed, elucidating briefly but excellently, by acute observation, passages that seemed corrupt or obscure. His emendations are indeed supported solely by ingenuity and the sharpness of conjecture, without the agreement of manuscripts. His preface is occupied with remarks on the Leiden and Paris editions and on Albaspinaeus’s Observations.

1644.

Paris, at the expense of Giles Morel, folio. *The Seven Books of Saint Optatus of Milevis on the Schism of the Donatists against Parmenian, with the commentaries and revisions of Francis Baldwin, distinguished man*; in the *Great Library of the Fathers*, vol. IV, col. 325.

1676.

Paris, the widow of John Dupuis, folio. *The Works of Optatus, Bishop of Milevis, with the complete observations and notes of Gabriel Albaspinaeus, Francis Baldwin, Caspar Barthius, Meric Casaubon, etc., edited and prefaced by Philip Priorius.* There are added the minor works of Facundus, Bishop of Hermiane, with annotations by Jacques Sirmond; also added are Gabriel Albaspinaeus’s ecclesiastical observations, together with his other works. *Catalogue of the Royal Library*, vol. I, p. 371.

1677.

Lyon, at the Anissons’, folio. *Saint Optatus of Milevis, on the Schism of the Donatists against Parmenian*, in the *Great Library of the Fathers*, vol. IV, fol. 341; with an addition to Book III, fol. 369.

1679.

[Col. 0881A]

Paris, at the expense of Antoine Dezallier, in the Rue Saint-Jacques, at the Golden Crown. *The Works of Saint Optatus, Bishop of Milevis, with the complete observations and notes of G. Albaspinaeus, Bishop of A[lais?], Francis Baldwin, jurist, Caspar Barthius, Meric Casaubon, etc. Philip Priorius added annotations and prefaces.* There are added the twelve books of Facundus, Bishop of Hermiane, *On the Three Chapters of the Council of Chalcedon*, with annotations by Jacques Sirmond, S.J., and Facundus’s minor works. To this edition also have been added Gabriel Albaspinaeus’s ecclesiastical observations, together with his other works.

The title has sufficiently set forth the merits of this edition; therefore a few words will suffice. The text is that of Baldwin’s first recension; or rather, the Leiden edition has been reproduced [Col. 0881B], except that the notes of the individual commentators have, for some convenience to the reader, been placed immediately after the text—those of Priorius separately first, then those of the others. Baldwin’s History of the Conference of Carthage is presented according to the first exemplar, published separately in 1566 and dedicated to John Tilius, Bishop of Meaux. Albaspinaeus’s ecclesiastical observations have been relegated to a place after Facundus.

Moreover, this edition, like the preceding Parisian and the Leiden edition, is owed solely to booksellers looking to their own profit; and Philip Priorius was only afterward consulted about some collation for the form of the work just described. Indeed, they added Facundus for no other reason than that Optatus, published in this format, might appear a work of adequate size. These are Priorius’s own words in his notice to the reader. Meric Casaubon aptly says in the preface to the London edition: “The matter has now come to this: books are valued not by use, but by bulk and weight; they are, of course, the better the larger they are.” The outward appearance of this edition is very elegant and neat. Yet Priorius too is said not to have safeguarded the new edition against printers’ errors.

1700.

Paris, at André Pralard’s, folio. *The Seven Books of Saint Optatus the African, Bishop of Milevis, on the Schism of the Donatists, compared with manuscript codices and old editions and corrected in innumerable places; to which have been added a history of the Donatists together with ancient documents relating to it, and an episcopal geography of Africa: the work and study of Louis Ellies du Pin.* *Catalogue of the Royal Library*, vol. I, [Col. 0881D] p. 371. This excellent edition itself is not at hand; see, however, the following Antwerp edition.

EIGHTEENTH CENTURY, 1701.

Amsterdam, folio. Dupin’s edition reprinted.

1702.

Antwerp, at G. Gallet’s, chief printer to the Huguetans. *The Seven Books of Saint Optatus the African, Bishop of Milevis, on the Schism of the Donatists: compared with manuscript codices and old editions and corrected in innumerable places. To which have been added a History of the Donatists, together with ancient documents relating to it, and an Episcopal Geography of Africa: the work and study of Monsieur Louis Ellies du Pin* (of the Sacred Faculty of Paris and Royal Professor of Philosophy), [Col. 0882A] *with his own notes and those of Gabriel Albaspinaeus, Meric Casaubon, Caspar Barthius, and others, placed beneath the individual pages in this edition.*

This reprint of Dupin is superior to the Paris edition at least in this respect: the notes of Albaspinaeus, Meric Casaubon, Caspar Barthius, and selected notes of that unknown writer—notes which the Paris edition, together with the more extensive observations of Baldwin and Albaspinaeus, had relegated to the end—are presented immediately beneath each page after Dupin’s own remarks. Dupin had five manuscripts available for restoring the text; “with their help,” he says, “it is scarcely possible to say how many passages we have restored: we corrected corrupt passages, returned displaced passages to their proper places, supplied omissions, removed interpolations; in a word, Optatus’s text, restored to its native [Col. 0882B] splendor, comes forth complete and corrected.”

The variant readings are conveniently entered separately from the notes at the foot of each page. The text has also, with good judgment, been divided into articles and paragraphs, with brief summaries placed in the margin. The editor added a few short notes of his own; then he included the writings of earlier editors—both those directly concerned with elucidating the text and the fuller commentaries of Baldwin and Albaspinaeus on ecclesiastical matters generally—purged of the innumerable typographical errors which had crept into the books of Albaspinaeus and Priorius. Priorius’s notes were omitted because they all seemed useless. The notes of various writers are followed by ancient documents concerning the history of the Donatists, added both by Optatus himself [Col. 0882C] and by previous editions, enlarged in this new edition and furnished with the commentaries of various learned men who had elucidated them either separately or in other works. Baldwin’s History of the Conference of Carthage was not omitted.

Furthermore, Dupin added observations on the sees of the African bishops who attended the Conference of Carthage, collected chiefly from Baluze and Ruinart. Finally, he composed a sacred geography—that is, an account of the provinces and bishoprics of Africa—and adorned it with a geographical map. Before the whole work, after the preface, he placed a history of the Donatist schism, written in the most exact chronological order. Full indexes conclude the work.

1769.

[Col. 0882D] Venice, from the press of Giovanni Battista Albrizzi, folio; in Saint Andrew Gallandi’s *Library of the Ancient Fathers*, vol. V, part I, pp. 461–675. *The Seven Books of Saint Optatus, Bishop of Milevis, on the Schism of the Donatists, compared with manuscript codices and old editions and corrected in innumerable places, by the work and study of Monsieur Louis Ellies Dupin. Ancient documents relating to the History of the Donatists are added, many of which are mentioned by Optatus himself.*

From Dupin’s notes Gallandi chiefly selected those which contributed to establishing the variations of the text, and here and there interwove several of his own notes prepared for the same purpose. He prefaced it with an account of Optatus in the *Prolegomena*, chapter XVIII, p. 29 ff.

1790–91.

[Col. 0883A]

Würzburg, at the Stahelian bookshop, octavo. Two volumes. *The Seven Books of Saint Optatus the African, Bishop of Milevis, on the Schism of the Donatists, and other ancient Documents relevant to this subject.* Dr. Francis Oberthür arranged their republication.

We searched in vain for the first volume of this edition among the local booksellers; only the second could be inspected. From it we learned that the former contains Optatus’s text and the documents concerning it; this latter contains selected Variant Readings and Annotations elucidating Optatus’s text, as well as Annotations on certain other ancient materials concerning the Donatist cause, selected from the resources provided by Dupin’s edition. He prefixed two very lengthy travel letters: one to the first volume, addressed to Professor Henckenius of Helmstedt; the other to the second, addressed to Professor Baenichius of Würzburg. In them, while you willingly allow yourself to be led through various regions of our Germany by a man of extraordinary candor and most delicate sensibility, you easily forget where you are supposed to arrive. A work by the celebrated author, published in these same years in three volumes, also belongs to this latest edition of Optatus: *The Biblical Idea of the Church of God*.

Translations. Only one French translation exists: that of Viel, based on Baldwin’s first edition. It was made in Paris in 1564 and printed by Frédéric Morel in octavo, under this title: *The History of the Schism, Blasphemies, Errors, Sacrileges, Homicides, Incests, and Other Impieties of the Donatians, written in Latin by Optatus, Bishop of Milevis, rendered into French and purged of many faults, also enlarged by the supplying of certain deficiencies and explanations of difficult passages, by Pierre Viel.* It was reprinted there by Robert Foust, octavo.

Manuscripts.

1. The manuscript of the Cusan Library near Trier, used by Cochlaeus. It is covered with errors of every kind.

2, 3, 4. Baldwin’s three manuscripts: one, used in the first edition, he had received from Espencaeus, theologian of Paris; another he owed to John Tilius, Bishop of Meaux and editor of Lucifer; the third to Maceraeus, theologian of Paris.

5. The manuscript of Saint-Theodoric near Rheims, estimated by Dupin to be about seven hundred years old.

6. The manuscript of Saint-Germain-des-Prés: not indeed of the same antiquity, but of the highest authority and more correct than the rest. It is Dupin’s second manuscript.

7. The manuscript of Saint-Paul of Cormery near Tours, which, when Dupin consulted it, was in the Colbert Library, no. 1951. It was six hundred years old and of the highest authority, but the first five books, together with the beginning of the sixth, had perished. It contained documents relating to the history of the ancient Donatists which at that time had not yet been found in any other manuscript codex. It is Dupin’s fourth manuscript.

8. The manuscript of Philip Sylvius, then doctor of the Sacred Faculty of Paris. It is Dupin’s third, but the same manuscript which Baldwin had already used while it was in Maceraeus’s possession; written in a later hand and very corrupt.

From these eight—or rather seven—manuscripts, you see that those employed by Dupin were superior to the others. He also observes that the Sylvius manuscript appears to have been copied from the manuscript of Saint-Theodoric, and the Saint-Germain manuscript from the Cormery manuscript. Yet, although he names five manuscripts [Col. 0884C], he lists no more than four.

## MANUSCRIPTS

[Col. 0883C]

In the Variant Readings which we have added at the foot of every page of Optatus’s books, the following signs are used:

Manuscript codex of Saint-Theodoric: ms. S. Th.

[Col. 0884] Manuscript codex of Saint-Germain-des-Prés: ms. S. G.

Manuscript codex of Philip Sylvius: ms. P. S.

Manuscript codex of Saint-Paul of Cormery, now the Colbert manuscript: ms. C.

[Col. 0883]

# 1. SAINT OPTATUS THE AFRICAN, BISHOP OF MILEVIS

[Note: In the manuscript of Saint-Theodoric, “Optatus of Milibis”; in the manuscript of Philip Sylvius, “Optatus of Milivis.” The title “bishop” is not read in the manuscripts except at the end of the work.]

[Note: Bishop of Milevis. This was a city of Numidia, called *Mileum* by Antoninus; *Milevis* by Augustine and Victor of Vita; *Mileu* in the Peutinger Tables; and *Mileum* in the Council of Carthage on rebaptizing heretics held under Cyprian. Optatus himself likewise calls it so below. Charles of Saint-Paul wrongly distinguishes Mileum from Milevus or Milevis; for there is no other town of this name in Numidia, and in manuscripts of Augustine’s letter to Eusebius, now letter 34, *Mileum* is found for *Milevis*. From *Mileo* or *Mileu* came *Milevum*, and thence *Milevis*. Two councils were held in this city, one in 402 and the other in 416, which are called Milevitan Councils. It lay about thirty miles from Cirta, the metropolis of Numidia, toward Sitifis. It is now commonly called Mela, a town in the Algerian kingdom. DU PIN.]

## ON THE SCHISM OF THE DONATISTS AGAINST PARMENIAN

[Note: In the manuscripts of Saint-Theodoric and Philip Sylvius: “Seven books.” Nothing is added in the title of the manuscripts; but at the end of the Saint-Theodoric manuscript occurs: “Here ends the book of Bishop Optatus, seven books in number, addressed to Parmenian, author of the schismatics.”]

(C, S)

## BOOK ONE

This first book contains an account of who were the *traditores* in the persecution, the causes of the schism, and where and by whom the schism was made.

[Note: This heading, which contains the subject of this book, is found in the manuscripts of Saint-Theodoric and Philip Sylvius.]

### I. The good of peace

All of us Christians, most illustrious brothers—

[Note: Brothers. We have spoken of Christian brotherhood in our observations, and there taught that the ancients placed much mystery and religious significance in it: namely, because all Christian intercourse consisted in this affinity and kinship. For they had put on and acquired, in the waters of baptism as though in the womb of the Church, a new person and a new nature; and by this they were joined to Christ and to all believers by a true, real kinship. They could not bear witness to this more strongly than by that appellation. Optatus therefore teaches that, through the birth shared by orthodox believers and schismatics, they were born and made brothers of the orthodox, though bad brothers, because they were insufficiently obedient to Mother Church, who had borne them. Moreover, it follows from this kinship that baptism received among schismatics has the power to produce Christians, since that kinship is contracted through it—a point the Donatists denied. ALBASP.]

—are commended to almighty God by one faith.

[Note: “One faith commends [us].” Does Optatus mean that we are pleasing and acceptable to God through a concordant and unanimous profession of the same faith? Or that faith is what commends us as Christians—namely, that, however many Christians we are and however much God recognizes us as Christians, we all obtain that standing by the one faith? Optatus himself seems to explain “one faith” thus in Book V: “One faith”—he says—“in this place, one faith is distinguished from the errors of heretics and from their various faith.” Nor does *commend* seem to be understood differently, or at any rate very differently, in many ancient passages where they speak of the Catholic Church. *Conference of Carthage*, Commelin edition, p. 6: “Following this authority of heavenly teaching, the Apostles commend the Church as bearing fruit and growing throughout the whole world,” etc. So too in the same Conference, p. 68. Augustine, *Brief Account of the Conference*, day 3, ch. 4: “Thus showing the divine testimonies to agree, both those by which the Church was commended as containing an admixture of evil persons,” etc.; “and those testimonies by which it was commended as not containing an admixture of evil persons,” etc. There *commend* means “is recognized” or “is described.” Augustine, in the same place, also says: “Since the Donatists had commended one Church by the testimony of the Scriptures,” that is, had proved that it was unique. But in these examples there is no dative of person, as there is in Optatus. Therefore I affirm nothing. MERIC CASAUBON.]

A part of this faith is to believe that the Son of God—

[Note: In the manuscripts of Saint-Germain-des-Prés and Philip Sylvius, “the Lord.” The sense is the same.]

—is to come as judge of the world;

[Note: “World” (*saeculum*) in writers of this kind means the world and whatever is lived in this life. Thus below in this book are the words of the Emperor Constantine: “You seek from me judgment in the world, whereas I await Christ’s judgment.” BARTHIUS.]

he who long ago came—

[Note: Thus in ms. S. G., better than in the other editions and manuscripts, which read “had come.”]

—and, in his humanity, was born through the Virgin Mary—

[Note: Thus in all the manuscripts. The editions read less well.]

—suffered, died, and—

[Note: Buried. Two matters are to be understood in this word: Christ’s burial and his descent to the underworld, which he does not mention because he is briefly touching upon these mysteries. Yet in writers of that age and province, such as Saint Augustine and Capreolus, reference to that descent is frequent. ALBASP.]

—was buried, rose again—

[Note: Thus in ms. S. G.]

—and, before he ascended into heaven—

[Note: In ms. S. G.: “before he ascended heaven.”]

—from which he had descended—left victorious peace, through the Apostles, to all Christians.

[Note: The editions read, “to all us Christians,” and so does ms. S. Th.; but in mss. S. G. and Philip Sylvius the word “us” is absent and superfluous.]

[Note: Peace. He uses this word frequently. It is therefore not irrelevant to note that visible and invisible Christian communion, and the unity and incorporation of the Church with Christ and, through Christ, with God, are understood through peace. ALBASP.]

[Note: We have followed here the authority of the Saint-Germain manuscript. In ms. S. Th., and also in the Sylvian manuscript, there is: “he left *storiam* peace through the Apostles.” It is difficult to guess what *storiam* means; perhaps it has been written for *consolatoriam* (“consoling”), or for *statoriam* (“steadfast”), that is, firm and enduring peace. Let others devise other, more plausible suggestions; for us, it is sufficient to indicate the reading of these codices. The editions read *suam* (“his own”), but wrongly; for Optatus immediately says that this peace belongs both to God and to believers.]

Lest he should seem to have left it to the Apostles alone, he therefore said: “What I say to one of you, I say to all” (Mark 13:37). Then he said: “My peace I give to you; my peace I leave to you” (John 14:27). Therefore peace was given to all Christians—

[Note: The editions read “Thus therefore”; ms. S. Th. reads “If therefore”; mss. S. G. and P. S. have nothing but “Therefore,” and that is better.]

—which is plainly God’s possession, since he says “my”—

[Note: Thus in all the manuscripts. The editions have “when,” but less well.]

—but when he says, “I give to you,” he wished it to be not only his own—

[Note: “Not only his own.” God’s peace ought to be among all who are brothers; it was given and left by Christ, so that it may be observed and honored among all who wish to be joined with him. ALBASP.]

—but also the possession of all who believe in him.

### II. Peace disturbed by schismatics

If that peace, as it was given, had remained whole and inviolate, and had not been disturbed by the authors of the schism—

[Note: “And had not been disturbed by the authors of the schism.” It was certainly not then being disturbed by the actual authors of the schism, who had long since ceased to exist; nor is that Optatus’s meaning. Here, then, understand *turbaretur* (“was disturbed”) as “had been disturbed,” just as later *posset* may mean “could have,” *haberetis* “you had had,” and so forth. Conversely, *potuissent* stands for *possent*, *remansisset* for *remaneret*, and six hundred other expressions of that kind. Optatus is not alone in speaking so: Arnobius, Zeno of Verona, Lucifer of Cagliari, and others do likewise. Even among writers of a better age, Terence and Virgil himself occasionally do so, and Cicero very often, as grammarians have observed. Hardly anyone, however, does so more frequently than our author. Having been warned of it once by us, the reader will observe it thereafter. MERIC CASAUBON.]

[Note: Authors of the schism: its leaders and standard-bearers. For he speaks both of those who had created the schism and of their successors. DU PIN.]

[Note: In ms. S. G., “of schisms”; in the others, “of the schism.”]

there would today be no dissension between us and our brothers;

[Note: In ms. S. G.: “and between.”]

nor would they cause those inconsolable tears of God, to which the prophet Isaiah bears witness (ch. 22:4);

[Note: “Nor would they cause those inconsolable tears of God, to which the prophet Isaiah bears witness.” He alludes to the words of Isaiah 22:4: “Depart from me; I will weep bitterly. Do not press upon me to comfort me over the devastation of the daughter of my people.” “They would cause tears to God” must not be understood of the tears of the authors of the schism, but of God’s own grief for the Church devastated by them, as Optatus himself explains at the beginning of Book III: “God indicates those tears of his which you have caused, which, he testifies, can be dried by no consolation, when he speaks to you through the prophet Isaiah, saying: ‘Leave me; I will weep bitterly; no one will be able to comfort me in the destruction of the daughter of my race.’” DU PIN.]

[Note: “Nor would they cause those inconsolable tears of God, which Isaiah bears witness to.” This refers to the words of Isaiah, ch. 22, v. 4: “Leave me; I will weep bitterly. No one will be able to comfort me in the destruction of the daughter of my race.” Thus it was formerly read. Optatus quotes and discusses the whole passage at length in Book III, not far from the beginning. The Paris editors therefore erred in following earlier editions that refer the reader to Isaiah chapter 32. MERIC CASAUBON.]

nor would they incur the name and deeds of false prophets—

[Note: The word “prophet” is absent from the editions but appears in all manuscripts.]

[Note: False prophets: pseudo-prophets, teachers of falsehood. Nor should they be called or recognized by their deeds as false teachers. DU PIN.]

[Note: “Name and deeds.” Your bishops would not be false, nor would their name be named in vain at the altar. By “name” one must understand episcopal honor and dignity; by “deeds,” their offices and functions. ALBASP.]

[Note: “They would incur the name and deeds of false prophets.” The learned and brilliantly gifted young man Caspar Barthius advises that one should read “false brothers,” not “false prophets,” from Saint Paul’s words in 2 Corinthians 11:27, *κινδύνοις ἐν θαλάσσῃ, κινδύνοις ἐν ψευδαδέλφοις*—“dangers at sea, dangers among false brothers”—to which Optatus, evidently, alludes. But see concerning false prophets in Book III. Moreover, he uses *incurrere* with the accusative also on the next page: “he deservedly incurs the yoke of slavery,” and in Book VI. UNKNOWN AUTHOR.]

nor would they build a ruinous and whitewashed wall.

[Note: Whitewashed. The Church is compared to a building, and bishops are said to build; this alludes either to the whitewashed tombs of those killed in Macarius’s time, whom the Donatists celebrated as martyrs. ALBASP.]

[Note: There are monstrosities here, and things more monstrous than monstrosities, which Albaspinaeus adduces in order to distort and obscure a passage clear and plain in itself. “The Church,” he says, “is compared to a building, and bishops are said to build; this alludes either to the whitewashed tombs of those who were killed in Macarius’s time and were celebrated by the Donatists as martyrs.” But his notes contain many things of this kind, so that no one should be surprised at this. As for the words, if anyone doubts, Optatus alludes to Ezekiel 13, where much is said against the whitewashed wall, as it was formerly read. Optatus himself quotes the entire passage and treats it at length in Book III, about the middle of the book. MERIC CASAUBON.]
would build a whitewashed wall. [Note: [Col. 0887D] “Nor would they build a crumbling, whitewashed wall.” He alludes to the words of the prophet Ezekiel, chapter XIII, speaking of the false prophets: “They deceive my people, saying, ‘Peace,’ when there is no peace.” He adds: “And he himself built a wall, while they coated it with mud,” so that when a storm came upon it, it was quickly thrown down. Optatus compares the leaders of the Donatists to prophets of this sort: their association was not a solid and enduring building like the Church of Christ, but merely a collapsing wall, though outwardly whitewashed. DU PIN.]

[Note: [Col. 0888B] “Nor would they overthrow minds that were less shrewd, but merely simple.” In these words, as Barth also thinks, there is neither sense nor life. “I,” he says, “shall restore both by a fine correction: read, ‘nor by threats would they overthrow shrewd minds, but only simple ones.’ Since everyone can still recognize all these arts today, I think it necessary that no one should fail to assent to the truth.” So he. But since the word *tantum* (“only”) is absent from the second edition of Franciscus Balduinus, it seems one should read: “Nor would they overthrow minds less shrewd and simple.” UNCERTAIN.]

nor would they overthrow minds less shrewd, but merely [Note: [Col. 0887A] Thus in all manuscripts; it can stand and be explained thus: “nor would they overthrow minds less cautious, and merely simple,” that is, those who are less prudent and less cautious because of excessive simplicity. Therefore nothing appears to need alteration.] simple ones; nor would they, by wrongly laying a hand upon [Note: [Col. 0888B] “Nor by wrongly laying upon all captives the hand of overthrow,” etc. Though this is a small point, it should nevertheless be noted that one must read “upon all heads,” not for the reason offered by Albaspinaeus—that in Book II he said the same thing: “You stretched out your hand and spread deadly veils over every head,” etc. If that reasoning were valid, since he later also mentions captives and captivity in the same matter, nothing here would need changing. But since it is certain that he alludes to the following words of the Prophet, [Col. 0888C] “over every head,” there is no doubt that Optatus intended the same here as well. What veils he means—those which here and elsewhere he repeatedly calls “veils of overthrow”—he himself explains in Book II: “Woe to those making a veil,” that is, “by laying a hand upon every age,” etc. No one should refer this to sackcloth, with which the heads of public penitents are ordered to be covered in the Council of Agde, distinction 50, canon 63; concerning it also in the preceding canon: “Penitents, at the time when they ask for penance, are to receive from the priest the laying on of hands and sackcloth upon the head, as has certainly been established,” etc. Jerome also bears witness, in Letter XXX, that “Fabiola, clothed in sackcloth, stood in the rank of penitents,” etc., to omit others. What follows, “nor would they curse God,” he himself explains at greater length about the middle of Book IV, if anyone should hesitate here. M. CASAUB.]

all heads [Note: [Col. 0888C] “Upon all heads [they laid] a hand.” “Upon all heads” must be read, I think, as is clear from Book II: “You stretched out your hand over every head.” By these words he teaches that the Donatists imposed penance upon bishops, [Col. 0888D] presbyters, the remaining clergy, believers, children, and all whom they could deceive and overthrow. ALBASP.] [Note: [Col. 0888A] In the manuscript S. Th., “captives,” but wrongly. Other manuscripts have “heads,” and this is certainly the correct reading.] —veils [Note: [Col. 0888D] “Of overthrow.” Whoever formerly imposed solemn penance upon an innocent person overthrew him, because he made an accused person out of a believer. Moreover, he deprived him of communion in Christ’s body; those deprived of it were regarded as dead and as lacking the true enjoyment of life. ALBASP.] [Note: [Col. 0888D] “Veils.” The laying on of hands in penance is, as it were, a kind of overshadowing: when bishops extended their hand over penitents, they overshadowed them, so to speak; therefore he calls that laying on of hands a veil. ALBASP.] of overthrow—would stretch forth. [Note: [Col. 0888D] “They would stretch out veils of overthrow.” He continues to allude to the subsequent words of Ezekiel, in the same chapter, verse 18, where the Hebrew and the Septuagint read: “Woe to those who sew cushions under every elbow of the hand, and who make veils over the head of every age in order to overthrow souls.” [Col. 0889B] Thus the Donatists, by laying hands—which bears the appearance of a veil—upon believers of every kind, that is, by imposing penance upon bishops, presbyters, the other clergy, believers, children, and all whom they could deceive and overthrow, overthrew their souls, stripping them of their innocence and their ranks both before God and before men. Optatus expounds his meaning thus in Book II: “God grieves over these deeds of yours in the prophet Ezekiel, when he says: ‘Woe to those making a veil,’ that is, laying a hand upon every age in order to overthrow souls. You found children; you wounded them with penance, lest some should be capable of ordination: acknowledge that you have overthrown souls. You found long-standing believers; you made them penitents: acknowledge that you have overthrown souls. You found deacons, presbyters, bishops; you made them laymen: acknowledge that you have overthrown souls.” DU PIN.] [Note: [Col. 0888A] In manuscript Ph. S IV, “veil”; and so it has also been corrected, by an old and perhaps the same hand, in manuscript S. Th.] [Col. 0889A]

[Note: [Col. 0889B] “Nor would they curse God.” Whoever formerly rebaptized a believer, or imposed the hands of penance upon a faithful and innocent person, cursed God; for in both [Col. 0889C] sacraments exorcisms were formerly performed, by which Satan was rebuked and commanded to depart and make room for the true God. Therefore the Donatists, in the penance which they imposed upon the innocent and in rebaptism, cursed God, because they exorcized a believer in whom God dwelt and burdened him with curses as though he were Satan. Thus in nearly all Augustine’s books the Donatists are charged with blowing away God, Christ, or finally the Holy Spirit—that is, with frightening and driving them away by exorcisms and exsufflations. For in former times Christians blew out demons with breath and spittle. Tertullian, *To His Wife*, Book II: “or you spit out something unclean with your breath.” ALBASP.¹]

nor would they curse God [Note: [Col. 0889C] “Nor would they curse God.” This also occurs in that passage of Ezekiel: “And you have profaned me among my people,” etc. To profane, or render profane, is to assail with curses, to dishonour. DU PIN.]; nor would they rebaptize believers; nor would we grieve over the overthrown or slain souls of innocent persons [Note: [Col. 0889A] In manuscript P. S., “innocent persons.”], whom God first grieved over through the prophet Ezekiel, saying: [Note: [Col. 0889C] “Woe to those making a veil,” etc. Thus they read it then at Ezekiel XIII.18. If you consult the present Vulgate, [Col. 0889D] you will see that it differs greatly. This is not surprising, for they rarely agree. There is a greater agreement—though not in this particular passage, yet in very many others—with the Greek of the ancients, as one may generally observe in writings of the same or even greater antiquity. For example, Optatus shortly cites Isaiah: “You who fear the name of the Lord, hear the name of the Lord. Those who hate you, abominate you, and refuse to be called our brothers—yet say to them, ‘You are our brothers.’” Earlier editions wrongly refer this to Isaiah LIX; it is Isaiah LXVI.5. There the Vulgate has an altogether different sense: “Hear the word of the Lord, you who tremble at his word. Your brothers who hate you and cast you out because of my name said, ‘Let the Lord be glorified, and we shall see your joy,’” etc. But the Greeks read: “Hear the words of the Lord, you who tremble at his word; say, ‘Our brothers,’ to those who hate you [Col. 0890B] and abominate you,” etc.; you see that they agree throughout. For the words in Optatus, “and refuse to be called our brothers,” are Optatus’s own, since when he has brought forward testimonies from Scripture he customarily inserts something by way of supplementation, to make his citation clearer, often to make passages otherwise insufficiently apposite seem suited to his purpose. Hence also the word “yet”: “yet say to them,” etc. The remainder is word for word from the Greek, except that “hear the name of the Lord” occurs instead of “hear the word of the Lord,” which I think has crept in. Augustine also uses this same testimony against the Donatists after the Conference, in the final chapter. Tertullian likewise cites it from the same translation as Optatus, *Against Marcion*, Book IV, chapter 16. See also the First Conference of Carthage, p. 64, from which it will clearly appear what Optatus added of his own. By this example the reader may, if worthwhile, examine other similar passages, compare them also with the Hebrew truth, and thereby investigate the causes of variation—which will succeed in many cases. In this great and most blessed light of learning, we have preferred to leave these matters to the reader, except where something occurs worthy of a defender, rather than dwell upon things [Col. 0890C] that most people disdain as obvious to anyone; and because they are numerous, they would extend and diffuse these brief notes of ours beyond the purpose intended. M. CASAUB.]

“Woe to those who make [Note: [Col. 0890C] “Woe to those who make.” Thus the entire passage stands in the Septuagint, Ezekiel XIII.18–19: “Woe to the women who sew cushions beneath every elbow of the hand, and make coverings upon every head of every age in order to pervert souls. The souls of my people were perverted, and they preserved souls for themselves. And they profaned me among my people for a handful of barley and pieces of bread, to kill souls which ought not to die and to preserve souls which ought not to live, while you utter vain utterances to a people listening.” “Woe to those who sew pillows beneath every elbow of the hand, and make head-coverings beneath every head of every age to ensnare souls; and when they ensnared the souls of my people, they kept their souls alive. K. says are veils with which women covered their faces. The Greek word *epibolaia* generally means a garment or covering. But “covering of a bed” in Galen—the source followed by our translator—was read “veil” in Optatus’s time. DU PIN.]

a veil over every head and over every age, in order to overthrow souls. the name of the Lord [Note: [Col. 0890A] In manuscript S. [Col. 0892A] IV. Why He Undertakes to Refute Parmenian’s Book

All of them indeed make a loud clamour in every place with their abusive voices—though I shall answer some matters as occasion arises [Note: [Col. 0891B] In manuscript S. G., these words are inserted parenthetically and are absent from the other manuscripts, but they do not appear foreign or extraneous.]; [Note: [Col. 0891D] “But we scarcely find even one with whom by letters,” etc. That is, “with whom we can speak.” This is a familiar phrase of the jurists: Book XI, §4; Book VI, §11, *Digest*, *On Judgments*, where they use *revocant domum* for “can recall home,” *fungitur* for “can perform,” and similar expressions occurring very frequently in the laws. The same jurists use *possum facere* (“I can do”) for *debeo* (“I ought to do”), which is related to this usage and was noted by our late friend C. Ritterhusius on Paul’s *Sentences*, Book IV. Pliny, Valerian, Book IV, chapter 6, on the gourd: “Its dry rinds can effectively heal burns.” The same author, chapter 36: “It can cure cancers with honey and, when drunk in wine, alleviate pains in the side,” chapter 40. Sometimes the usage is more absolute. The same author, chapter 48 of that book: “Fresh pods upset the stomach and loosen the bowels; the dried ones can do the opposite.” BARTH.]

but we scarcely find even one with [Note: [Col. 0891B] Absent from manuscript S. [Note: [Col. 0892C] “And because they refuse,” etc. The episcopal college is nothing other than the whole order and fellowship of bishops, extending as widely as it does. Thus in Sidonius Apollinaris, “the crowd of the college” means the number of bishops, Letter I, Book VI; and those whom he calls “provincial colleagues,” Letter V, Book VII, he calls “provincial priests,” Letter XXV, Book VI—meaning whatever bishops were in the same province. And because [Note: [Col. 0892C] “The episcopal college.” The ecclesiastical and episcopal society, communion, fellowship, and brotherhood. windily and nakedly [Note: [Col. 0891B] Thus in the manuscripts. Since truth compels us to answer his assertions, there will be, in some fashion, a conference between us though absent. In this way the wishes of certain people will also be satisfied. For many have often [Note: [Col. 0892B] All manuscript codices attest this word, which is absent from printed editions.] desired that, to bring out [Note: [Col. 0892B] Manuscripts S. T. and P. G., after these words is added: “I now ask.”].

V. The Character of the Contents of Parmenian’s Book

For I understand, you do not deny, and every intelligent person plainly sees, that you treated these matters at such length for no other reason than to assail the Catholic Church shamefully in your treatises. But, as can be understood, the mind holds one thing and speech sounds another. In short, I see that you have not said everything against the Catholic [Note: [Col. 0893B] Thus in the manuscripts. In printed editions, most wrongly and contrary to Optatus’s meaning, the negative particle is absent.] [Note: [Col. 0893B] In manuscript S. G., “faith” is added, but wrongly, for the subject is the [Col. 0893C] Church, not faith.] Church; rather, though you are not Catholic, you have said much in support of the Catholic Church, so that we have not needed to answer your treatises—except insofar as, being ill-informed, you spoke about what you had not seen [Note: [Col. 0893C] “What you had not seen.” Either because these events had occurred long before Parmenian, or because he was a foreigner and thus had not seen them. ALBASP.] [Note: [Col. 0893C] In manuscript S. G., “you may have seen.”] but had heard falsely; although in the epistle of the apostle Peter [Note: [Col. 0893C] “Although we have read in Peter’s epistle: ‘Do not…’” Rather, in James, if I am not greatly mistaken, chapter IV, verse 11. CASAUB.] [Note: [Col. 0893D] “In Peter’s epistle.” There is nothing similar in Peter’s epistle, but in James, chapter IV, verse 11, where it reads: “Do not speak evil of one another, brothers. Moreover, elsewhere in your treatises some things have been said for us [Col. 0894A] and against you: for example, the comparison of the Flood and circumcision; some things both [Note: [Col. 0893D] “For you and for us.” The baptism of the Donatists was approved by the orthodox; hence whatever was said in praise of baptism seemed said for both parties. Ibid. “In the Trinity of baptism.” The order of the words, which otherwise may seem somewhat obscure, is this: “we who defend the unity of baptism in the Trinity,” that is, baptism [Col. 0895B] administered in the name of the Trinity. Yet someone might not unreasonably suspect that Optatus here means by “the Trinity of baptism” those three immersions which the so-called Apostolic Canons, canon 50, call “three baptisms,” *tria baptismata*, and that one should understand or restore “its” or “of baptism” after “in the Trinity of baptism,” thus: “we who defend its unity, or the unity of baptism, in the Trinity of baptism.” Nevertheless I prefer the former interpretation, since others also speak this way, “to baptize in the Trinity,” for “in the name of the Trinity.” Optatus himself, Book V, says “the baptism of Christians completed by the Trinity,” and in the same book, “No one had yet been immersed in the Trinity,” and often thereafter. M. CASAUB.]

you cunningly inserted your own party, so that, as though because it is permitted once, it may be permitted to you [Note: [Col. 0895D] “So that, as though because it is permitted once, it may be permitted to you.” The Donatists did indeed maintain that baptism was to be conferred once, but they denied that baptism among Catholics was true baptism, declaring that only baptism administered by their own people was valid and effective. VI. The Arguments of Parmenian’s Books

You, brother Parmenian, have indeed discussed many matters. But I see that I must not answer in the same order in which each item was set forth by [Col. 0896A] you. For in the first place you gave comparisons and praises of baptism; and except for your mistreatment of Christ’s flesh, you said the rest well. That you spoke these matters more in our favour will be shown in its place. In the second place, after excluding heretics, you said that there is one Church, but you refused to acknowledge where it is. In the third place you accused traitors without naming any definite persons [Note: [Col. 0896C] “Without definite persons.” Without witnesses or records; or, you accuse no orthodox person by a particular name or a formal proceeding of the crime of betrayal, but condemn them all under this charge. ALBASP.] or names. Fourth, the workers of unity were torn to pieces by you [Note: [Col. 0896C] “Workers of unity.” Paul and Macarius, who, by command of the Emperor Constans, brought about unity in Africa—that is, who wished to lead the Donatists into the Catholic Church. ALBASP.]. Fifth, to omit smaller matters [Note: [Col. 0896B] In manuscript S. G., “to pass over minor matters”; the sense is the same.], you spoke [Note: [Col. 0896C] “On the oil and sacrifice of the sinner.” In these two things nearly the whole force and activity of the priesthood consists; by oil are understood nearly all sacraments in which [Col. 0896D] holy oil is used. ALBASP.] of the oil and sacrifice of the sinner.

VII. Division of This Work and Arguments of Its Individual Books

But it seems to me that first the cities, persons, and names of traitors and schismatics must be identified [Note: [Col. 0896D] “The cities must be identified.” It must be stated in what city they handed over the sacred codices, so that from that city’s public records it could be made evident and read which persons, in the time of Diocletian or Maxentius, were guilty of this crime. ALBASP.], so that those things which you have said concerning them [Col. 0896B] may recognize their true authors and certain culprits. Next I must say what the one Church is, or where it is, because besides the one there is no other. Third, that no soldiers were requested by us, and that what is said to have been committed by the workers of unity does not concern us [Note: [Col. 0896D] “By the workers of unity.” The Donatists continually complained about Paul and Macarius, as may be seen in St Augustine; but Augustine and Optatus denied that anything done contrary to Christian charity in that expedition pertained to the Church. ALBASP.]. Fourth, who the sinner is whose sacrifice God rejects, and whose [Note: [Col. 0896D] “Oil to be avoided.” The oil of heretics or sinners must be avoided and despised, because God does not pour his grace into that anointing. ALBASP.] oil [Col. 0897A] is to be avoided. Fifth, concerning baptism. [Note: [Col. 0897C] “Sixth, concerning rash matters.” These are treated in Book VI. ALBASP.] Sixth, concerning your rash presumptions and errors.

VIII. Parmenian ought not to have called Christ’s flesh either sinful or submerged in water.---But before I say anything about the individual matters, I shall briefly show how wrongly you have treated the flesh of Christ. For you said that “that flesh was sinful,” that it was submerged by the flood of the Jordan, and cleansed of every defilement.

[Note: “That flesh was sinful.” Parmenian had uttered this blasphemy concerning Christ’s own flesh, not concerning His mystical body. ALBASP.]

You would rightly have said this if Christ’s flesh, baptized for all, were sufficient so that no one should be baptized for himself. If that were so, the whole human race would have been there: everything born bodily would have been there.

[Note: In MS S. G., “human.”]

There would be no difference between believers and each Gentile, because flesh is in all; and since there is no one who does not have flesh, if, as you said, Christ’s flesh was submerged in the flood of the Jordan, all flesh would obtain this benefit.

[Note: “As you said, Christ’s flesh.” Read *si ut*, “if, as,” as two words in place of *sicut*; for the sense requires it, whereas no meaning at all can otherwise be extracted from the received reading. “If,” he says, “as you indeed maintain and interpret it, Christ’s flesh—that is, all sinful flesh,” etc. As for “there is no one not” for “there is no one,” although harsh, I would nevertheless not dare amend it, because I have observed something not unlike it elsewhere. M. CASAUB.]

[Note: Thus in MS S. G. In the printed editions and MS S. T., *sicut*, but this accords less well with the writer’s meaning.]

For Christ’s flesh in Christ is one thing; each person’s flesh in himself is another. What did you mean by calling Christ’s flesh sinful? Would that you had said, “the flesh of human beings in Christ’s flesh”; even then you would not have spoken plausibly, because each believer is baptized in the name of Christ, not in Christ’s flesh, which belonged especially to Him.
