[Note: Thus in all MSS. The printed editions have *dixeris*, “you would have said.”]

[Note: In MSS S. G. and P. S., “can be baptized.”]

[Col. 0898A] I add that His flesh, conceived of the Holy Spirit, could not be immersed among others for the remission of sins, since it appeared to have committed no sin.

[Note: In MS S. G., “add.”]

[Note: “Could not be immersed for the remission of sins.” He uses *remissam peccatorum* for *remissionem peccatorum*, “remission of sins,” as elsewhere; Cyprian likewise uses it in *On the Benefit of Patience*: “The Lord is baptized by a servant; though about to grant remission of sins, He Himself does not disdain to wash His body in the laver of regeneration.” Likewise, Book III, Epistle 14: “But whoever blasphemes against the Holy Spirit has no remission, but is guilty of an eternal sin.” Similar usages occur in other authors. Nor is *offensa*, “offence,” otherwise commonly used for *offensio*. UNCERTAIN.]

[Note: “Which appeared to have committed no sin.” Optatus may seem to some to have spoken less cautiously—indeed, less piously—if they fail to notice the force of this expression, not unknown indeed, but less customary among the ancients. “Which appeared to have committed no sin” means “which had committed no sin.” Thus Lampridius, in *Alexander Severus*: “He ordered thieves never to appear in any cities for trial.” If you seek more examples, consult Casaubon on the words of Capitolinus, “he appeared to have exceeded eight feet by a finger,” p. 399. The Apostle speaks similarly, as I note in passing, 1 Cor. 11:6: “If anyone appears to be contentious.” Again in the following chapter: “the members which appear,” etc.; likewise Christ, Luke 8:18, “what he appears to have,” etc.; and finally the writer to the Hebrews, 4:1, “lest any one of you should seem,” etc. Since nearly every page supplies examples of this usage in our author, one warning is enough. But in Book II: “Why do you wish the Holy Spirit to appear false?” etc. Even if this can be tolerated in Optatus, I think nevertheless that he wrote *videre*, “to appear.” M. CASAUB.]

[Note: “Which appeared to have committed no sin,” that is, “which had committed no sin.” See M. Casaubon’s note on this passage. DU PIN.]

You further said that it was submerged in the flood of the Jordan. You used that word quite thoughtlessly. It properly belonged only to Pharaoh and his people, who, weighed down by the burden of their sins like lead, were so sunk that they remained there. But when Christ’s flesh descended into and ascended from the Jordan, you ought not to have called it submerged; for His flesh is found holier than the Jordan itself, so that by its descent it cleansed the water rather than itself being cleansed.

[Note: In MS S. G., “submerged in the flood.”]

[Note: In MSS S. T. and P. S., “by the Jordan itself.”]

[Note: In MS S. G., “purer.”]

[Note: In MS S. G., these words refer to Christ, not to His flesh, and read: “so that by His descent He cleansed the water itself rather than Himself being cleansed.”]

IX. Parmenian unnecessarily mentioned heretics.---I also cannot pass over what I perceive you did with subtlety: in order to influence or deceive your hearers’ minds, after your description of circumcision and the flood, and after your praise of baptism, you wished in a sense to revive heretics—dead along with their errors and now buried in oblivion—though throughout the provinces of Africa not only their vices but even their names seemed unknown.

[Note: In MS S. G., “already dead with their errors”; the particle *iam*, “already,” is omitted in the latter member.]

Marcion, Praxeas, Sabellius, Valentinus, and the rest, down to the Cataphrygians, were overcome in their own times by Victorinus of Petavium, by Zephyrinus the Roman, by Tertullian of Carthage, and by other champions of the Catholic Church.

[Note: We restore these words to their proper place.]

[Note: “Victorinus.” The bishop of Pictavium, who was crowned by martyrdom under Diocletian and, according to St Jerome, wrote much—of which we do not possess even a page. ALBASP.

Ibid. “Victorinus of Pictavium, and Zephyrinus the Roman.” This is a manner of speaking long observed by many. Thus Victor of Vita, in Book I of *The Vandal Persecution*: “The Roman captives mourned his departure so that they thought themselves more truly delivered into barbarian hands when he went on to heaven.” That he is speaking of captives together with Romans may be learned from the preceding context. Below, Optatus says, “after he was ordained, he was cleansed in the city,” that is, at Rome; and elsewhere similarly refers to “the Roman city.” M. CASAUB.]

[Note: In MSS S. T. and P. S., *Pectaviensi*; in MS S. G., *Pictaviensi*. St Jerome calls him Pictaviensis or Pitabiensis in several places. In the heading of this commentary by Victorinus he is called Pictabiensis, as also in the old catalogue of apocryphal books of Pope Gelasius, in the martyrologies of Usuard and Ado, and in other ancient monuments. Pitabium, Petabium, or Petavium was a town of Noricum, mentioned by Tacitus, *Histories* III; in the cosmography of Aethicus; in the Antonine Itinerary; in Ammianus Marcellinus, *Histories* XIV; and in Ptolemy, II.15. Victorinus was bishop of this city, not of the Pictones in Gaul, as the learned Launoy demonstrates at length in his *Dissertation on Victorinus, Bishop and Martyr*. There he emends this passage of Optatus conjecturally, observes also that the editions of Optatus are corrupt, and expresses the wish for a more correct edition.]

[Col. 0899A]

[Note: “Zephyrinus the Roman.” He was pontiff of the city of Rome; for among ancient writers *Roman* is used for inhabitants of Rome, as at the First Council of Arles. ALBASP.]

[Note: Thus in MSS S. G. and P. S. In MS S. T. and the printed editions, *Zepherino*; but he is commonly called Zephyrinus.]

[Note: “The Roman.” Bishop of the city of Rome. A notable expression. DU PIN.]

[Note: “Tertullian.” He counted Tertullian among the defenders and champions of Catholic history, and not without reason; for no author ever more fiercely exacted vengeance upon heretics and pursued them than this writer. ALBASP.]

Why do you wage war with the dead, which does not concern the affair of our own time? But because, as a schismatic today, you have no sin which you can prove against Catholics, you wished to mention so many heretics with their errors merely to enlarge the length of your writing.

[Note: “Why do you wage war with the dead?” *Ut quid* means “why?” Thus immediately below: “Why were those men mentioned by you?” And in Book II: “Why do you violate such a promise?” and in Book III: “Why was this done to you?” St Jerome, *Life of Hilarion*: “‘Why,’ he answered, ‘should I enter one who had my colleague?’” The highly polished writer Martial uses the expression, Book VII, Epigram 33: “Why do you set [something] before the gifts of our Lord and God?” and elsewhere. UNCERTAIN.]

[Note: In MS S. G., “who do not concern the affair of our own time.”]

[Note: The printed editions and MSS S. T. and P. S. read: “but because today you have something of schism [which you can prove against Catholics, you do not have.”] The reading of the manuscript is undoubtedly preferable.]

X. The distinction between heretics and schismatics.---Now there is another question: why were those men mentioned by you, among whom there are no sacraments, whereas these sacraments appear common to us and you?

[Note: “Among whom there are no sacraments.” From this and many other passages, so far as I can judge, Optatus did not think heretics able to baptize; whatever the case may be, he draws a great distinction between heretics and schismatics. ALBASP.

Ibid. “Among whom there are no sacraments,” etc. This was also the opinion in Africa of many Catholics from the time of Cyprian onward, as Balduin shows in more than one place: those baptized by heretics should be rebaptized. Therefore, when later in this very book he points out that Donatus’ confession that he had rebaptized was foreign to the Church, Balduin judges that this was pronounced not in Africa but at Rome, where the contrary opinion always prevailed. This is true, since it forms part of the judgment delivered by the Roman Melchiades against Donatus. Yet nothing prevents the same judgment also having been pronounced in Africa by African Catholics. For those words concern not the rebaptism of heretics, but that of schismatics, which African Catholics condemned no less than Catholics overseas. For the distinction observed by the ancient Church in rebaptizing or not rebaptizing heretics, consult the ancient canons and Augustine’s *On Baptism*. M. CASAUB.]

Health does not require medicine; virtue, secure in itself, seeks no external aids; truth does not need arguments. It is the sick person’s part to seek remedies, the idle and weak person’s part to procure help, and the liar’s part to hunt for arguments.

[Note: “Health does not require medicine,” etc. By these comparisons Optatus seeks to show that Parmenian distrusted his own cause, since he wandered from his subject and attacked heretics when his quarrel was with Catholics. DU PIN.]

Meanwhile you said that the Church’s endowments cannot exist among heretics; and you spoke rightly. For we know that the individual churches of heretics are prostitutes, lacking the lawful sacraments and the right of honourable marriage in themselves, whom Christ rejects as not belonging to Him, since He is bridegroom of one Church.

[Note: “Endowments.” By endowments he means the Church’s properties—such as authority, the chair, the ring, the font, and the like—which were assigned to her by Christ as dowry-gifts. ALBASP.]

[Note: “Lawful sacraments.” Since the Church is Christ’s bride, the ancients explain much about her through the legal principles and laws of marriage. Thus Optatus says here that heretics cannot lawfully and by the force of marriage employ the sacraments as orthodox Christians did, because they were not joined to Christ in the dignity of marriage. ALBASP.]

[Note: “The right of honourable marriage.” The marital right exercised by the Church is that by which she confers all the sacraments and, by the authority of legitimate marriage, distributes and grants to whom she wishes the dowry-gifts she received from Christ. Heretics cannot exercise this right, because they lack these dowry-gifts; and although through baptism they have been joined to Christ, by their subsequent heresy they have lost the right of legitimate marriage. ALBASP.]

[Note: “Whom Christ rejects as not necessary.” That is, as strangers and unknown persons. Thus in Book III: “Impute it to those who divided the people of God and made unnecessary basilicas,” that is, new and foreign ones, having nothing in common with the genuine and lawful; “who erected altar against altar,” etc. For those called *necessarii* in law, consult the jurists; yet more truly, he alludes to the passage of the prophet Isaiah, which he later adduces in Book III: “Therefore, because you ascended into superfluous temples,” etc. They seem properly to have used the term of temples. Thus Victor of Vita, after relating that the Vandals had destroyed the shrines of pagan deities, passes to the devastation of Christians: “And, to speak of the necessary places, the greater basilica, where the bodies of the holy martyrs,” etc. M. CASAUB.

Ibid. “Not necessary.” Only one is joined with Christ and is His bride; therefore the rest are adulteresses and are not necessary. ALBASP.]

[Note: “Not necessary”: strangers, foreigners. DU PIN.]

As He Himself declares in the Song of Songs (Song 6): when He praises one, He condemns the others, because apart from the one which is the true Catholic Church, the others are thought to exist among heretics, but do not exist. As He indicates, as we said above, in the Song of Songs: His dove is one, the same one is the chosen bride, the enclosed garden, and the sealed fountain (Song 4). Thus none of the heretics possesses the keys which Peter alone received, nor the ring by which the fountain is said to be sealed, nor is any one of them a person to whom that garden belongs, in which God plants little trees.

[Note: “Which Peter alone received.” In many places he teaches that the keys were given to Peter alone, from which it follows that all who do not commune with Peter, his chair, and his successor must be regarded as schismatics. ALBASP.]

[Col. 0901A]

[Note: “Which Peter alone received”—namely, in the name of the Church, whose person he represented. DU PIN.]

[Note: “Ring.” What writers of that antiquity understand by the ring is not sufficiently clear. Tertullian, in *On Modesty*, seems to use it not for baptism but for absolution: “the ring, again, the seal of the washing”; for he speaks of a sinner returning to the Church who was not to be rebaptized, unless he means that by absolution the grace of baptism and union with Christ are recovered. Our author likewise, when he says that the fountain is sealed with a ring, seems to designate something other than baptism. Clement uses it in the same sense in Book II, chapter 4 of the *Constitutions*: “when the ancient garment, ring, and shoes have been restored to him.” ALBASP.

Ibid. “Nor the ring by which the fountain is said,” etc. Here Albaspinaeus impales himself on the question of what the ancients understood by the ring, greatly anxious. Though unable to extricate himself, he produces here, and again in Book II where he investigates the ring with equal anxiety and equal success, several passages of Tertullian that mention a ring, as though they would shed no little light upon Optatus. In both places he goes utterly astray. “What writers of that antiquity understand by the ring,” he says, “is not sufficiently clear. Tertullian, *On Modesty*, does not use it for baptism,” etc. First I should like him to explain which ring of the ancients he means, concerning which matters are not sufficiently clear; what passages of those ancients concerning one and the same ring create the difficulty. Tertullian speaks of a ring, and Optatus speaks of a ring. But Optatus, while discussing the Church’s endowments and the ring which, though not read in Song 4:12, is nevertheless understood by Optatus because a sealed fountain is read there, includes and enumerates that ring among the Church’s endowments. On what basis, or what he understood by the sealed fountain whose ring he mentions, he does not explain.

Yet since two uses of rings in rites of baptism were formerly current among the ancients, as scholars have observed—one by which it was customary at certain times to seal fonts or baptisteries, the other by which those to be baptized sealed their profession of faith, later entered in public records—it is likely that by the sealed fountain Optatus alludes to that ancient custom of sealing the baptistery, and that his mention of the ring must likewise be referred to the same custom. Yet I dare affirm nothing. Tertullian’s mention of the ring in *On Modesty* arises from the parable of the prodigal son narrated in Luke 15. Catholics interpreted that parable as promising forgiveness before God and restoration to their former state of grace for those who truly repent. Tertullian, defending the contrary position, ridicules and rejects their interpretation. In the same place he also mentions the robe and the fatted calf, which belong to the same parable; he attacks the interpretations of them received from others and invents and adduces others himself. Tertullian and Optatus therefore do not speak of the same ring; thus it is unsurprising if they do not say the same things.

Nevertheless, each interpretation of the rings which Tertullian gives seems also to concern those solemn baptismal rites. In the former interpretation, which Tertullian rejects, the ring is explained as “the seal of the washing”; in the latter, it is described by Tertullian as that by which those questioned sealed the covenant of their faith. Let Albaspinaeus read this, whoever cares to know with how much skill and judgment he was engaged in reading the ancients. He represents Tertullian and Optatus as though they spoke of the same ring. He confuses Tertullian’s different interpretations of the same parable. In the former interpretation he ascribes to the ring the explanation given for the robe or former garment. Since he not only failed to grasp, but could not even suspect, either understanding of the ring in the twofold interpretation of that parable, he himself invents others—false, ridiculous, and foolish—so as to surpass all credibility. At times he interprets it as absolution, at times as the Holy Spirit, and finally as confirmation. How unfairly things are arranged: those who are most unlearned are always the most audacious! For who otherwise would believe that a grave man of such rank in the Church would have so poorly consulted his own reputation?

But I gladly agree with Balduin, a most learned man, that this entire teaching of Optatus concerning the Church’s endowments or ornaments is both jejune and obscure. It is jejune indeed, because it rests wholly upon such weak foundations; obscure because it is here incomplete and, so far as I know, has not been handed down by any ancient author besides Optatus himself, from whom we might borrow light for Optatus’ less complete and lucid passages. I also agree with Balduin that he wished to set forth certain marks and badges by which the Church might be recognized. He makes five such marks, three of which—the font, the ring, and the angel—belong to baptism. He bases the font and ring on Song 4:12, and the angel, of whom we shall speak further below, on the angel of the pool of Bethesda. For they believed both that an angel took part in the waters of the sacred washing and that that pool was a figure of baptism, as we shall show more fully later.

Yet Optatus himself, in Book II, distinguishes these endowments from the very members and entrails, as he calls them, of the Church; he maintains that these consist in the sacraments and names, or Persons, of the Trinity—namely, true recognition of the Trinity—not in ornaments. He thus distinguishes these endowments from sacraments, although most of them pertain to baptism. Further, if he wished to establish marks and indications by which the adorned Church might be known, why mention the angel? Even if we grant that it is present in performing the mysteries of the saving water, no one would call it so present that it can be seen. I say these things at some length lest anyone, in these subtle quibbles over which our author here fruitlessly torments himself with such exertion, suppose that he will extract great mysteries from them. When examined, they prove more trifling than subtle. For that reason alone, I think, more serious and learned men have abstained from them. M. CASAUB.]

[Note: “Nor the ring by which the fountain is said to be sealed.” By the fountain he seems to understand faith; by the ring, the creed or baptism, which, as Tertullian says in *On Repentance*, is the sealing of faith. Hence among the ancients baptism is often called a seal. Optatus himself, Book II: “For the font also is acknowledged to be one of the endowments; from it heretics cannot either drink themselves or give drink to others, because, not possessing the unbroken seal—that is, the Catholic creed—they cannot open access to the true fountain.” And below in this book: “You rightly withdrew the ring from those who are not permitted to open the fountain”; that is, you rightly removed from heretics the power of sealing by sacred baptism. DU PIN.]

[Note: “Nor is any one of them.” Correct Latin would require, “nor may any one of them be.” Optatus perhaps wrote *esset*, “was,” instead of *sit*, “may be,” by his customary interchange; later, after the case of *aliquis* was changed, an infinitive resulted. Or, if we retain *aliquem*, Optatus must have written *esse necesse*, one of the two words having been omitted on account of the similarity in writing—a very easy slip, commonly found in manuscripts, as we shall note later. What if ancient scribes sought abbreviations of such syllables or even whole words, so that *esset* might stand for *necesse esset*, “it was necessary”? I recall observing that printers sometimes retained this too. Yet I rather think that the text, whatever it is, comes from Optatus himself; nor is it out of keeping with that age. What especially moves me is that similar solecisms—or, if you prefer, anacolutha—with the preceding particle *ut* occur in more than one place in our author. M. CASAUB.]

[Col. 0903A]

[Note: In MS S. G., “nor with any one,” incorrectly.]

[Note: “Garden.” The Church, unless I am mistaken. ALBASP.]

Concerning these heretics, although it does not pertain to the present case, you have spoken at length; enough and more than enough. But I wonder why you thought fit to join even yourselves to them, though you are admittedly schismatics, when you denied the Church’s endowments both to heretics themselves and to yourselves as schismatics. For among other things you said that schismatics are cut off from the vine like branches, destined for punishments and reserved for the fires of Gehenna like dry wood.

[Note: “While [you deny] the Church’s endowments.” When you join schismatics to heretics, you deny the Church’s endowments to yourselves, who are admittedly schismatics. ALBASP.]

[Note: “From the vine.” Optatus does not seem to agree with this. ALBASP.]

[Note: In MS S. G., “destined.”]

But I see that you still do not know that the schism at Carthage was caused by your leaders. Investigate the origin of these events, and you will discover that you have uttered this judgment against yourselves when you associated heretics with schismatics. For Caecilian did not depart from Majorinus, your grandfather; rather, Majorinus departed from Caecilian. Nor did Caecilian depart from the chair of Peter or Cyprian, but Majorinus, in whose chair you sit—a chair which had no origin before Majorinus himself.

[Note: “Caecilian.” He succeeded Mensurius; under him and on his account the schism arose. ALBASP.]

[Note: “Departed from Majorinus.” Caecilian was first ordained bishop; Majorinus was ordained against him and withdrew from his communion. DU PIN.

Ibid. “Departed.” Caecilian was ordained after Mensurius by the lawful and ordinary way. After his ordination, Majorinus was ordained through the faction of that woman; therefore Majorinus departed and withdrew from Caecilian, not Caecilian from Majorinus. For he is considered to depart who makes a schism and who, while another occupies the place, seeks to seize his position and see. ALBASP.]

[Note: “Your grandfather.” These statements seem inconsistent with what we said in the third observation concerning Donatus of Casae Nigrae, for whom no place remains in the see of Carthage if Parmenian had Majorinus as his grandfather; for it is established that Donatus was ordained at Carthage after the death of the great Donatus. But ancient writers explain episcopal successions and ordinations in no other way than the generations and relationships of mortal persons; they speak of them as they would of a family and household. For a bishop ordained to the see of a dead bishop was called the son and offspring of him in whose place he was appointed; the succession of ordinations was reckoned in these terms of kinship. ALBASP.]

[Note: “Majorinus, your grandfather”—that is, the predecessor of Donatus, who after Majorinus seized the Carthaginian chair. Augustine, *Retractations* II.17: “In the three books,” he says, “against the Epistle of Parmenian, bishop of the Donatists at Carthage and successor of Donatus.” Augustine likewise, Book II *Against the Epistle of Parmenian*, names Majorinus, Donatus, and Parmenian as three successive figures without an intermediary. What some infer from St Augustine’s sermon *On Peace and Charity*, delivered before the conference—that Gaius and Lucius were bishops of Carthage between Donatus and Parmenian—is futile. Augustine’s words are: “I will not leave Donatus; I will not leave some Gaius or Lucius and Parmenian—thousands of names, thousands of divisions.” From this one can infer only that Gaius and Lucius were among the principal bishops of the Donatists; that they presided over the Donatist Church at Carthage does not follow soundly. DU PIN.]

[Note: “Majorinus.” A member of the household of Lucilla the Spaniard; he had been a reader under Caecilian and was ordained against Caecilian, erecting altar against altar in the city of Carthage. ALBASP.]

[Note: “Nor did Caecilian depart from the chair of Peter.” I want you to know, reader, that Albaspinaeus draws many things from this and similar passages into the cause of religion, and repeatedly inserts material from Cardinals Baronius and Perron; we deliberately pass over all of it. We do so both because this would be a more lengthy labour and foreign to our purpose, and because we saw that he introduced nothing new which had not already been twisted and retwisted back and forth to the point of disgust, and which is now thoroughly worn-out and hackneyed in the many writings on that subject. M. CASAUB.]

[Note: “From the chair of Peter.” There is only one chair in the Church, received by Peter from Christ and communicated by him to each bishop, and now daily communicated through the pontiffs who are considered to be, and are, one and the same flesh and person with him. This is the doctrine of the ancients. He therefore rightly calls the chair of Carthage the chair of Peter, because Peter begot it, as Tertullian says. ALBASP.]

[Note: “Or Cyprian.” He mentions Cyprian because no one had occupied this chair with greater glory or reputation for holiness, or perhaps because the Donatists did not dispute his see and chair. ALBASP.]

[Note: “From the chair of Peter or Cyprian.” The same arguments may be read in Cyprian’s *On the Unity of the Church* and Epistle 43. The episcopal chair or see is the supreme authority for governing the people by priestly power; this authority is one, and each holds a share of it in its entirety. Whoever does not obey his legitimately established and ordained bishop, but departs from him and regards either himself or another as bishop, is rightly said to depart from the chair of his own bishop and from Peter’s chair—that is, from the Apostolic See—with which that bishop is united in communion. DU PIN.]

[Note: “In whose chair you sit.” He was a schismatic bishop of Carthage. ALBASP.

Ibid. “In whose chair you sit.” To use *sedere*, “sit,” for *insidere*, “sit upon,” is customary in this author, as Vincentius uses *suadere*. Yet this is a sacerdotal expression of our author: “Cyprian, whose chair you occupy.” BARTH.]

[Note: “Origin.” Parmenian’s chair had no origin because it succeeded Majorinus, and Majorinus had succeeded no one. Caecilian held the place and chair of Mensurius. Thus Majorinus’ chair had no origin: it was adulterous, false, new, without a father, begotten and introduced through schism. ALBASP.]

[Note: In MS S. G., “does not have.”]

[Note: “Had no origin.” Majorinus succeeded no one. Caecilian held Mensurius’ place and chair; after Mensurius’ death he had been lawfully appointed in his place. Majorinus had no predecessor. DU PIN.]

And since these events are most plainly established, and it is clearly apparent that you are heirs of traitors and schismatics, I greatly wonder, brother Parmenian, that, being a schismatic, you wished to join schismatics with heretics. Or if this is your view and pleases you, add together those things which you said shortly before.

[Note: “Against those [things].” Something seems lacking in this sentence; but the sense is: If it pleases you to join schismatics with heretics, I wonder that you said anything against heretics, because the same must be said about schismatics and about Donatists, who are schismatics. ALBASP.

Ibid. “Against those things said by you a little before.” Here *contra* has the same force as if he had said “conversely,” “again,” or “then indeed,” repeating the word “I wonder” from the beginning. Yet since later follows, “you turned the sword of judgment against yourself, while thinking that you attacked others,” one may not wrongly restore: “Against those things said a little before, you said.” The error arose from the same source as many others elsewhere: namely, from the fact that the second *dixisti*, “you said,” immediately follows. Although even that *dixisti* will not be needed if you understand “are” or “make.” But this is a minor matter. Still, it had to be noted so that no one might, with Albaspinaeus, suppose anything lacking here. M. CASAUB.]

[Col. 0905A]

[Note: The printed editions most corruptly read “against those things,” and MSS S. T. and P. S. no better, “with those things.” We owe this restoration to the Saint-Germain manuscript.]

[Note: “Add together those things.” After this restoration, no difficulty remains in this passage, which had tortured commentators to an extraordinary degree. See what follows from your own principles against you, if there is no distinction between heretics and schismatics. DU PIN.]

For you said that it cannot happen that one defiled by false baptism should wash another, that the unclean should cleanse, the deceiver raise up, the lost set free, the guilty grant pardon, or the condemned absolve. All these statements could apply only to heretics who have falsified the creed: one saying there are two gods, although God is one; another maintaining that the Father is to be known in the person of the Son; another taking flesh away from the Son of God, through whom the world was reconciled to God; and others of that kind, known to be alien from Catholic sacraments.

[Note: In the printed editions and MSS S. T. and P. S., “in false baptism.”]

[Note: Omitted in MS S. G.]

[Note: Thus in all MSS. The printed editions incorrectly have *poterunt*, “will be able.”]

[Note: “Only to heretics.” He does not mean that heretics cannot baptize, but only those heretics who did not baptize in the name of the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit and who thought wrongly concerning the three Persons. ALBASP.]

[Note: Thus in MS S. G. MSS S. T., P. S., and the printed editions have *quia non omnino*, “because not entirely.”]

[Note: In MS S. G., “said.”]

[Note: “One saying there are two gods.” Cerdon and Marcion. DU PIN.]

[Note: “Another maintains that the Father is to be known in the person of the Son.” MSS S. T. and P. S. have “into the person”; MS S. G. has “to be known.”]

[Note: “Another taking flesh away.” Valentinus and the other Docetists. DU PIN.]

[Note: “Alien from Catholic sacraments”: from the creed and the articles of faith. ALBASP.]

Therefore repent that you joined schismatics also to such people. For you turned the sword of judgment against yourself while thinking that you were attacking others; and you did not consider how great is the difference between schismatics and heretics. This is why you do not know what the holy Church is, and thus you have confused everything.

[Col. 0906A] XI. Marks of the Catholic Church and of schism.---[Note: [Col. 0905D] “The Catholic Church is made by a simple and true understanding, to understand.” For the sentence to make sense, either *to understand* must be deleted—which would certainly be better—or it must be joined to the preceding *makes*: “makes [one] understand,” that is, declares or indicates. For *to understand* is often superfluous; thus, shortly below, “you are understood to be ignorant” means simply “you are ignorant”; and in Book II you will notice once and again [Col. 0906B] that it is used in such a way that the sense loses nothing if it is removed. Moreover, *understanding* and *intelligence* are used, as we commonly speak, for sense or interpretation; this is a customary usage among ecclesiastical writers. Presently, however, whoever is troubled by the indicative *they depart*, used for the subjunctive—which would have been regular—[Col. 0906C] should read *let him depart* and *they may abandon*, not, as here, *that they may abandon*. Yet I take a different view. M. CASAUB.]

What makes the Church Catholic is a simple and true understanding of the Law, a unique and most true sacrament, and unity of minds. [Note: [Col. 0906B] In the printed editions: “to understand”; and in MSS S. T. and P. S. But “of the Law,” found in MS S. G., is more pleasing: namely, that the marks of the Catholic Church are sincere faith, consisting in a genuine understanding of the one and most true sacrament—that is, the Creed—and unity of minds.]

[Note: [Col. 0906C] *Sacrament*: one Creed; one rule of faith. ALBASP.]

[Note: [Col. 0906C] *Unity of minds*: an inward communion of souls; the same judgment, the same will. ALBASP.]

But schism is produced when the bond of peace has been scattered and judgments have been divided; it is nourished by envy and strengthened by rivalry and quarrels. Thus, when the Catholic mother has been abandoned, impious children, in going outside and separating themselves—as you have done—from the root of mother Church, severed by the sickles of envy, depart in rebellious wandering. And they can neither devise nor do anything new or different except what they long ago learned from their own mother. [Note: [Col. 0906C] “Schism is produced when the bond of peace has been scattered.” Varro most elegantly used *coagulum*, “coagulating agent” or “bond,” for a connection, in fragments of his Satires, concerning wine:

> This bond holds feasts together.

And Publilius Syrus, in the Mimes:

> The one bond of friendship is trust.

INCERT.

Ibid. “When the bond of peace has been scattered.” He most elegantly said *coagulum* for a connecting bond. Publilius Syrus:

> The one bond of friendship is trust.

Varro, concerning wine:

> This bond holds feasts together.

[Col. 0906D] See more below in the commentary on these matters. Virgil has “a bond of treachery” at the end of Book I. BARTH.]

[Note: [Col. 0906D] “They learned [it] from their own mother”: from the true Church, from which, having withdrawn, they cannot think otherwise concerning the faith or celebrate the sacraments otherwise than mother Church does. ALBASP.]

[Note: [Col. 0906D] “They learned [it] from their own mother”: namely, the Church which had formerly been their mother. DU PIN.]

XII. Again, concerning the distinction between heretics and schismatics.---But heretics, exiles from truth and deserters of the sound and most true Creed, corrupted by impious opinions from the bosom of the holy [Col. 0906B] Church, despising the fact that they had been well born, wished to be born from themselves, so as to deceive the ignorant and unlearned. [Note: [Col. 0906D] “Deserters of the Creed”: overthrowing and abandoning the rule of faith, as Tertullian says in *On Prescription*. ALBASP.]

[Note: [Col. 0906B] MS S. G.: “true.”]

[Note: [Col. 0906D] “That they had been well born”: they had been born in the Church. ALBASP.]

[Note: [Col. 0906D] “They wished to be born from themselves”: they set up a new head, as John of Jerusalem says to Epiphanius; they established a new Church and a chair not begotten or descended from anyone. This is “to be born from themselves”: they either abandoned the origin they had possessed [Col. 0907B] and set up a new Church. ALBASP.---Optatus imitates Tiberius’s saying about Curtius Rufus, born of obscure parents, who obtained the praetorship through the emperor’s favor; Tiberius concealed the disgrace of his birth in these words: “Curtius Rufus seems to me to have been born from himself.” See Tacitus, *Annals*, Book XI, ch. 21. CLERICUS.]

And those who had long been nourished upon life-giving food vomited deadly poisons, through the corrupting effect of bad digestion, in the ruin of wretched persons by impious disputations. [Note: [Col. 0907B] “And those who had long been fed upon such foods.” Read: “had long been fed upon life-giving foods.” Certainly, with Barthius, I would not venture to adopt the reading “long ago upon wholesome [foods].” Yet I subsequently learned, after examining Fr. Balduin, that the better manuscript contains the restoration I proposed. INCERT.

[Col. 0907C] Ibid. “And those who had long been fed upon life-giving [foods],” etc. Since he does not state what sort of foods they had formerly been, I would venture to adopt “long ago upon wholesome [foods]” instead of “upon such [foods]”; and any child could see that *ruin* must be substituted for *in the ruin*. BARTH.]

[Note: [Col. 0907C] “In the ruin of wretched persons”: wrongly written; and any child can see that “and ruin” must be substituted. INCERT.

Ibid. “In the ruin of wretched persons by impious disputations,” etc. Note L says wrongly that “and ruin” must be substituted, and that any child can see it. Usage would indeed demand this; but these writers favor a different construction, and nothing at all should be emended. Thus Salvian somewhere says “to place in the exercise of mercy.” Our author, Book V: “See what Christ has promised in the salvation of the human race.” The same author shortly afterward: “When he baptized many in repentance and forgiveness of sins,” etc. You may find many such expressions. Likewise Victor of Utica says: “To rage in churches and basilicas,” etc.; “to cast out into maritime regions,” etc.; “to throw into chains,” etc.; “to exile into regions of the desert,” etc.; “to drive into distant and remote lands,” etc. Luci­fer of Cagliari: [Col. 0907D] “to send into a furnace of fire.” But this is less surprising in him, [Col. 0907D] since everywhere he writes in a wholly barbarous manner. M. CASAUB.]

You see, therefore, brother Parmenianus, that heretics, far indeed from the house of truth, alone possess various and false baptisms. [Note: [Col. 0907D] “Far indeed from the house of truth”: *satis*, “indeed,” has the force of “exceedingly.” Arnobius, Book V: “What seemed so wicked that a father should not mingle with his daughter in marital union?” So also frequently St Augustine, Jerome, Rufinus, and others. INCERT.]

[Note: [Col. 0907D] “Various and false”: because, entertaining false views of the Trinity, as he says above, they were regarded as deserters of the Creed. ALBASP.]

[Note: [Col. 0907B] MS S. G.: “and various,” perhaps “vain and false.”]

A polluted person cannot wash with them; an unclean person cannot cleanse; one who trips others up cannot raise them; one who is lost cannot set free; one under accusation cannot grant pardon; one condemned cannot absolve. You did well to close the garden against heretics; well to restore the keys to Peter; well to take away from them the power of cultivating, lest those whom it is clear are strangers to the little garden and paradise of God should cultivate little trees. [Note: [Col. 0907D] “The keys to Peter”: that is, there is one Chair, and it is recognized through communion with the supreme pontiff. ALBASP.]

[Note: [Col. 0907D] “The power of cultivating”: feeding believers in the faith through sacrifices and sacraments. ALBASP.]

You did well to take away the ring from those who are not permitted to open the fountain. [Note: [Col. 0908B] For “are not permitted,” perhaps someone may prefer “were not permitted.” Our author rashly says, Book II, “Not possessing the intact seal, they cannot open the true fountain”; and it should be known that Optatus makes remarkable use of particles of this kind. Yet, although our author repeats this type of construction, I would not choose to imitate it, since it is more native to the Hebrews than to our Latin writers. For the ring, see also p. 10, v. 7: he means the ring by which heads of households sealed what they wished kept safe and secure. Plautus, Cicero, Martial, and others speak of this ancient practice. See, among others, Lipsius on Tacitus, *Annals* 11. Add also the passage [Col. 0908C] aptly supplied by Barthius from the medieval author Venantius Fortunatus, Book XI, *Life of Blessed Martin*:

> The author, redeeming the entire world with the treasure of his body,  
> Had one jewel, which sufficed for every vessel.

INCERT.]

[Note: [Col. 0908C] “You did well to take away the ring from those who are not permitted to open the fountain.” This alludes to *Song of Songs* 4:12: “A garden enclosed is my sister, my bride; a fountain sealed.” Heretics do not have the ring by which they may open the seal of the true faith and, once opened, seal it again. DU PIN.]

But these things cannot be denied to you schismatics, although you are not in the Catholic Church, because you have received from us true sacraments held in common. Therefore, since all these things are rightly denied to heretics, why did you think it right to wish to deny them also to yourselves, whom it is manifest are schismatics? For you go outside. So far as lies in us, we wished heretics alone to be condemned; so far as lies in you, you wished to strike even yourselves together with them by a single sentence. [Note: [Col. 0907B] Thus in MSS S. T. and S. G. The printed editions have “so far as lies in you,” and join these words to the preceding “you go outside”; but the latter part of the sentence [Col. 0908B] confirms our emendation, “so far as lies in you.”]

[Note: [Col. 0908C] “We wished heretics alone to be condemned.” From a fuller manuscript Fr. Balduin restored in the second edition: “you wished to strike [them] by a single sentence.” Excellent. INCERT.]

[Note: [Col. 0908B] Thus in MS S. G.; the others have “I wished.” The sense is the same.]

XIII. That the founders of the Donatists were *traditores*.---But now, in order to return to the intended order of the individual matters, first hear who the *traditores* were, and learn more fully who were the authors of the schism. It is established that two evils, and very grievous ones, were committed in Africa: one in the surrender [of sacred books], the other in schism. Yet both evils seem to have been committed at one and the same time and by the same authors. You must therefore, brother Parmenianus, learn what you are understood to be ignorant of. For about sixty years ago, and a little more, a storm of persecution spread throughout all Africa; it made some martyrs, others confessors, struck some down into a dreadful death, and left those in hiding unharmed. [Note: [Col. 0908C] “One in surrender”: during the persecution of Maxentius, many in Africa surrendered sacred books; among these, Mensurius, Felix, and Caecilian were falsely and undeservedly accused by the Donatists. ALBASP.]

[Note: [Col. 0908B] MS S. G.: “long and secure,” evidently through a copyist’s error.]

[Note: [Col. 0908D] “Storm”: a persecution which makes martyrs and confessors, as Tertullian says. ALBASP.]

[Note: [Col. 0908D] “About sixty years ago, and a little more, a storm of persecution spread throughout all Africa.” He speaks of the Diocletianic persecution, which began in February 303 and ended in the West in 305. From this you may infer that Optatus wrote these things around 370. DU PIN.]

[Note: [Col. 0908D] “It made some martyrs”: namely, those who underwent death. DU PIN.]

[Note: [Col. 0908D] “Others confessors”: those who steadfastly confessed and incurred no guilt of idolatry, but were not therefore killed. DU PIN.]

[Note: [Col. 0908D] “It struck some down into a death of doom”: some, overcome by tortures, denied Christ. ALBASP.]

[Col. 0909A] [Note: [Col. 0909A] Thus in MS S. G. The others read: “a death of doom struck down into death.”]

[Note: [Col. 0909A] “It struck some down into a death of doom”: those who, overcome by torture, either denied Christ, burned incense to idols, or surrendered the instruments of divine law. These can truly be called dead and struck down by a death of doom. DU PIN.]

[Note: [Col. 0909A] “It left those in hiding unharmed”: namely, those who avoided danger by flight or concealment. DU PIN.]

Why should I mention the laypeople, who at that time were supported by no rank in the Church? Why the many ministers? Why deacons, established in the third priesthood? Why presbyters, established in the second priesthood? Why some bishops, the very summits and chiefs of all, who in those times impiously surrendered the instruments of divine law in order to exchange the eternal life they stood to lose for the very brief delay of this uncertain light? [Col. 0910A] [Note: [Col. 0910A] Absent from MS S. G.]

[Note: [Col. 0909A] “Why the many ministers? Why deacons in the third [priesthood],” etc. This is novel and unusual, and especially worthy of our notice: Optatus here includes even deacons within sacred priesthood. Certainly, anyone who has even glanced at ancient writers cannot be ignorant that among the ancients *priest* was commonly applied to presbyters and bishops, and *priests* to bishops; and that *priesthood* was not infrequently used for the episcopate. Hence Augustine somewhere calls a council “of seventy priests”; and in Victor of Utica, *On the Vandal Persecution*, Book III, Huneric’s edict speaks of “a council of so many priests.” Anyone who fails to observe that in Victor alone, on almost every page, *priest* means bishop and *priesthood* episcopate, makes a disgraceful blunder. Conversely, *bishop* was sometimes used by the ancients for presbyter, although this has been more rarely observed by scholars. Hence the old formula of speech arose for distinction: a priest of the first order was sometimes called a bishop, while a priest of the second order or rank was what is commonly called a presbyter. The most learned Savaro discusses this formula of speech in several places in his notes on Sidonius Apollinaris.

But it is strange that, although that most learned man confirms his opinion concerning the twofold priesthood by, among other things, this testimony of Optatus, and praises Optatus’s words concerning the third grade of priesthood here, he nevertheless remains silent about it, as though deliberately passing it over lest it inconvenience the view he wished to uphold. Yet against the ancient canons, which expressly decree that deacons are ordained for ministry, not for priesthood, and that the only orders of priesthood are the two, presbyterate and episcopate; and against the usage received from the ancients, no one or two passages such as this of Optatus, in which *priesthood* is taken more broadly, should trouble us. But in canon law it is not uncommon for the designation *priesthood* to be extended to all those in the orders commonly called sacred, and in this way it includes subdeacons too. Thus, Distinction 31, canon 14: “The tradition of the Eastern Churches differs from that of this Holy Roman Church. For their priests, deacons, and subdeacons contract marriage, whereas in this Church, or in the Western Churches, no priest, from subdeacon up to bishop, has permission to marry.” [Col. 0909D] See also the canon “of all priests,” etc., and “let the impious blush,” etc. Indeed, you may find that all clerics without exception are sometimes included under this designation. Thus Victor of Utica, Book III: “If a conference was desired, why [was there] the plundering of others’ property, not only of priests but also of laypeople?” He contrasts priests with laypeople while meaning clerics.

But Optatus here speaks quite differently: in explicit terms he excludes all the remaining ranks, whom he calls collectively “ministers,” from priesthood; and no less explicitly he establishes the order of deacons as the third rank of priesthood. I therefore say that the fact that most ancient writers—Cyprian, Augustine, and others—when listing ecclesiastical ranks either mention only bishops, presbyters, and deacons, omitting all the others entirely, or, as Optatus does here, comprehend the rest, as lesser orders, under the general designation of ministers, ministries, or *hypēretai* (“attendants”), pertains to and should be referred to the dignity of deacons. [Col. 0910A] Perhaps they sometimes mention the others as well; I do not deny it. Yet they more often omit them when naming bishops, presbyters, and deacons. Indeed, Dionysius, *On Ecclesiastical Hierarchy*, ch. 5, and Jerome on Isaiah, ch. 19, name and enumerate these three in such a fashion that they appear not so much to omit the others as not to recognize them.

To answer this, a man of great name in the controversy becomes more tortured himself—whether he tortures them is uncertain. He invents that Dionysius is listing not ecclesiastical orders but hierarchies; and that Jerome, in the stated passage, is himself listing not ranks of clerics but ranks of Christians, and making that enumeration serve his purpose. But, without saying anything about the matter itself or bringing him into conflict with Thomas Aquinas and Peter Lombard, who plainly maintain the opposite—in fact Aquinas relies on this very Dionysius, *Supplement*, question 37, response to objection 2—besides Dionysius and Jerome, others speak in the same manner, to whom that learned man’s response cannot possibly be applied. Among them is our author himself, near the end of Book II: “Since there are in the Church four kinds of heads: bishops, presbyters, deacons, and believers,” etc.

Meanwhile, that which Bellarmine proves—that deacons too shared with bishops and presbyters in the governance of the Church, and were held in honor as superiors while the remaining clerics merely ministered—will make clear to you how much greater in former times the dignity and authority of this order was than it later became. Nor was it without reason that, when no account at all was taken of the other orders, or they were included under the general designation of ministers, as we have said, deacons alone, as participants in the same dignity, [Col. 0910C] were joined with priests, that is, bishops and presbyters. To the evidence advanced by Bellarmine I add the notable passage of Eusebius—or rather Constantine—in the letter to Eusebius, *Life* II, where you may see deacons associated with and numbered among the bishops and presbyters who stood around, as joined to them in the same lot and condition. Augustine too, in Letter 148 to Valerius, when discussing the merit and preeminence of the priestly office, joins deacons to bishops and presbyters as being of the same or a not dissimilar condition. And Jerome, where he maintains that they are inferior to presbyters in priesthood, acknowledges, though indignant, that at least in Rome they are superior in income and dignity. From this also you may infer why it was so often necessary for canons and censures against them to bring into order those who grew proud, exalted themselves above presbyters, and were sometimes even insolent and abusive toward bishops—as Cyprian says of one—and to restrain their arrogance. But I fear I have said too much on these matters. [Col. 0910D] Yet, however slight these points may appear at first sight, once observed they will be found of great use in reading the ancients. It is shameful to say how foully even very great men sometimes err through ignorance of such seemingly trivial matters. Quite recently this very passage of Optatus was rendered in a work of admirable learning and unequalled excellence in such a way that nothing more unworthy of it, or more alien to Optatus’s mind, could be imagined. MER. CASAUB.]

[Note: Ibid. “Ministers”: lesser clerics. ALBASP.]

[Note: [Col. 0910D] “Deacons in the third [rank]”: bishops occupy the first place in ecclesiastical communion, presbyters the second, and finally deacons the third. ALBASP.]

[Note: [Col. 0910D] “Established in the third priesthood”: here Optatus uses the name *priesthood* generally for the right and power of carrying out some ecclesiastical office; in this sense deacons may rightly be said to occupy the third order in priesthood. DU PIN.]

[Note: [Col. 0911B] “Established in the second priesthood”: there are only two grades of priesthood, episcopate and presbyterate. For deacons do not receive priestly power and consecration, as the fathers of the Council of Carthage say; nor, at their consecration, was the hand laid upon them by all the clerics. When a deacon is ordained, the bishop alone who blesses him lays his hand upon his head, because he is consecrated not for priesthood but for ministry. ALBASP.]

[Note: [Col. 0911B] “The very summits and chiefs of all, some bishops”: from this one may sufficiently understand how great was then the bishops’ superiority, *hyperochē*, above presbyters. DU PIN.]

[Note: [Col. 0911A] MS S. G.: “of that time.”]

Among these were Donatus of Mascula, Victor of Rusiccada, Marinus from the waters of Thibilis, Donatus of Calama, and Purpurius of Limata, a murderer. [Note: [Col. 0911B] “Donatus of Mascula”: Mascula was a city of Numidia according to Antoninus and Augustine. In Cyprian’s Council of Carthage: “the famous confessor from Mascula.” In the *Register of African Bishops*: Marculitanus. In the Carthaginian Conference: Masculitanus. At the Council of Carthage in 525 Donatus of Mascula subscribed. Victor of Vita, Book I, no. 15, mentions the *archinimus* of Mascula. DU PIN.]

[Note: [Col. 0911C] “Of Rusiccada”: Rusiccada was a maritime Numidian city mentioned by Pliny. Antoninus’s itinerary mentions Rusiccada not far from the Hippo Regius. The anonymous Ravenna geographer also lists it among the cities of Numidia. It is now Estora in the Tunisian kingdom. In the register of African bishops there is, among the Numidian bishops, a bishop of Russiniaca. DU PIN.]

[Note: [Col. 0911C] “From the waters of Thibilis”: an inland place where the city of Thibilis stood, according to Antoninus, not far from Cirta. A bishop of Thibilis appears among the bishops in the register of African bishops. At the Carthaginian Conference there was also a bishop of Thibilis, distinct from one of Thisilis. Augustine mentions the waters of Thibilis in Book XXII of *The City of God*, ch. 8, recounting a miracle that occurred at the memorial shrine of St Stephen near the waters of Thibilis under Proculus, [Col. 0911D] bishop of that place. The anonymous Ravenna geographer has Tibili. Thibilis and the waters of Thibilis do not appear to be separate towns, although they are separately placed on the Peutinger Tables. DU PIN.]

[Note: [Col. 0911D] “Of Calama”: Calama was a town of Africa Proconsularis according to some, but rather of Numidia, since a bishop of Calama is found among the Numidian bishops in the register. Augustine often mentions this city and Megalius, bishop of Calama and primate of Numidia. Possidius, his successor as bishop of Calama, attended the Carthaginian Conference and wrote Augustine’s life. In the register published by Goar, Carolus a Sancto Paulo, and Beveridge, composed under Leo the Wise near the end of the ninth century, Calama is listed first among the towns of Numidia. DU PIN.]

[Note: [Col. 0911D] “Purpurius of Limata, a murderer”: Balduin’s second edition reads “of Limata.” Correctly, for Limata was an African city according to St Augustine, who also mentions a bishop of Limata. INCERT.]

[Note: [Col. 0912B] “Of Limata”: Augustine also mentions a bishop of Limata; perhaps he is the same as the Lamiggizian bishop in the register. DU PIN.]

[Note: [Col. 0911A] MS S. G.: “of Liniata.” In the acts of the Council of Cirta in Augustine, Book III *Against Cresconius*, ch. 26, Limata is named as this bishop’s see; but the Corbie manuscript also reads [Col. 0912A] Liniata, as do some manuscripts of Augustine’s Letter 34.]

When questioned about his sister’s sons, whom he was said to have killed in prison at Mileum, he confessed, saying: “I killed them; and I kill—not them alone, but anyone whatsoever who acts against me.” And Menalius, lest his fellow citizens should prove that he had burned incense, pretended to have pain in his eyes and was afraid to appear before the assembly of his own people. [Note: [Col. 0912B] “Menalius”: Menalius feigned an eye complaint when he returned after being intercepted by soldiers, lest he should be ashamed in the church and in the assembly of his people, and have to confess that he had burned incense and complied with the emperor’s edict. ALBASP.]

[Note: [Col. 0912B] “To burn incense”: to honor false gods with incense. Thus also in Book II, he says that, during persecution, certain bishops, through cowardice falling away from confession of God’s name, had burned incense. BARTHIUS.]

[Note: [Col. 0912B] “He was afraid to appear before the assembly of his own people.” Read *assembly*, as Fr. Balduin’s second edition expressly does. INCERT.]

XIV. Acts of the Council of Cirta.---After the persecution, these men, and the others whom we shall shortly show to have been your leaders, sat down at the city of Cirta—because the basilicas had not yet been restored—in the house of Urbanus Carisius, on the third day before the Ides of May, as the records of Nundinarius, then a deacon, testify, and as the antiquity of the parchments bears witness; we shall be able to produce them for those who doubt. We have appended the full text of these matters in the final part of these books, in order to establish the facts. [Note: [Col. 0912B] “After the persecution”: of Maxentius. ALBASP.]

[Note: [Col. 0912B] “After the persecution.” Augustine likewise says, [Col. 0912C] in Book III *Against Cresconius*, ch. 26, that the Diocletianic persecution, especially that concerning the surrender of sacred books, had by then subsided in Africa. Augustine speaks specifically of it as “after the persecution for surrendering books.” At the Carthaginian Conference the Donatists maintained that it was then a time of persecution and that therefore a council could not have been assembled; they attempted to prove this from the acts of the martyrs. But upon closer examination it later became known that the Council of Cirta had occurred thirteen months after those acts. DU PIN.]

[Note: [Col. 0912C] “At Cirta”: in order to ordain a bishop in that city. ALBASP.]

[Note: [Col. 0912A] MS S. Th.: “around Cirta.”]

[Note: [Col. 0912C] “Basilicas”: bishops were ordained in basilicas; but because these had not yet been restored, they assembled in a private house. Augustine, *Breviculus after the Conference*, ch. 17. ALBASP.]

[Note: [Col. 0912A] MS S. G.: “in the house.”]

[Note: [Col. 0912A] MS S. T.: “Garisius.”]

[Note: [Col. 0912C] “Urbanus Carisius”: in the acts reported by Augustine, Urbanus Donatus. DU PIN.]

[Note: [Col. 0912D] “On the third day before the Ides of May.” The acts of the Council of Cirta in Augustine, Book III *Against Cresconius*, ch. 27, are headed: “Diocletian, consul for the eighth time, and Maximian, consul for the seventh time; fourth day before the Nones of March.” But Augustine observes in the *Breviculus of the Conference* that this consular date is corrupt. When, at the Conference, the Donatists maintained from the acts of the martyrs that persecution had not yet ended under the consuls in whose term the Council of Cirta was said to have been held, the Catholics replied that nearly a year had followed the martyrdom of those whose acts were produced before the consulship and day of the Council of Cirta. The response of the calculating office was that only one month intervened; but it was afterward discovered that the office had erred. For Augustine says: “The acts of the martyrs, by which the time of persecution was shown, were drawn up [Col. 0913A] under Diocletian for the ninth time and Maximian for the eighth time, on the day before the Ides of February. But the episcopal acts of the decree of Cirta were drawn up after their consulship, on the third day before the Nones of March; and consequently more than eleven, namely thirteen, months are found to intervene. The Catholics had previously replied, in calculating less carefully, that [Col. 0913B] there were eleven [months]; but the office, in erring and replying that only a month intervened, assumed the same consulship and failed to notice ‘after the consulship,’ when another year was already under way.”

This, therefore, is the true date of the Council of Cirta: after the consulship of Diocletian for the ninth time and Maximian for the eighth time, that is, in the year 305, on the third day before the Nones of March. The month was always settled at the Conference, for the acts of the martyrs were dated the day before the Ides of February, and the office said that only a month intervened between the martyrs’ passion and the council’s day. Augustine says that thirteen months intervened. Therefore it was agreed that the council was held in March, not May; otherwise either three or fifteen months would have intervened between the martyrs’ passion and the council’s day. Thus Optatus’s passage must be corrected, and “the third day before the Ides of May” must be read as “the third day before the Nones of March.” DU PIN.]

[Col. 0913A] [Note: [Col. 0913B] NUNDINARIUS. Much concerning this Nundinarius is found in the acts of the exculpation of Caecilian and Felix. ALBASP.]

[Note: [Col. 0913A] Absent from MSS S. G.]

When Secundus of Tigisis questioned them, these bishops confessed that they had surrendered [the sacred books]. [Note: [Col. 0913C] “When Secundus questioned [them]”: he was then primate of Numidia. Augustine in the same place calls him “bishop of the first chair,” and in Book I *Against Parmenianus*, ch. 3, says that they came with their primate Secundus of Tigisis. Note, however, that in Africa the primacy was not attached to fixed places or persons; rather, in each province except Carthaginian Africa, the senior bishops held this dignity, as appears from ch. 13 of the *Breviculus*. ALBASP.]

[Note: [Col. 0913C] “Secundus of Tigisis”: bishop of Tigisis in Numidia, who then exercised the office of metropolitan among the Numidian bishops because he was senior. There were two African cities of this name: one in Numidia, mentioned by Procopius, *Vandalic War*, Book II, and this Secundus was its bishop; the other in Mauretania Caesariensis. Both occur in the register of African bishops. DU PIN.]

[Note: [Col. 0913C] “They confessed that they had surrendered [them]”: see the acts themselves below. DU PIN.]

And when Secundus himself was reproached by Purpurius because he too had long been with the [Col. 0914A] stationarii, had not fled, but had been dismissed—being dismissed not without cause, unless because he had surrendered [the books]—[Note: [Col. 0913C] “With the stationarii”: with soldiers stationed at a post. ALBASP.]

[Note: [Col. 0913A] MS S. G.: “stationarius.”]

[Note: [Col. 0913D] “Now all the heretics began to murmur.” Whom does Optatus mean by “heretics”? Augustine discusses at length, *Against Cresconius*, Book II, how the Donatists—or Donatians, as Cresconius preferred—could be called and designated heretics on this account. In his book *On Heresies* he likewise teaches that they turned schism into heresy, and he rarely calls them anything but heretics. I am also persuaded that people of old used *heretic* indiscriminately for *schismatic*; and even today, in Constantine’s letters, you may read “heretics or schismatics,” as though the terms were equivalent, concerning Donatists. Grant, moreover, that those who assembled at this council did become authors of schism at a later council—on the occasion indeed of this council, but being all, or at least most, the same men—yet who could believe that Optatus, while relating the events that preceded the schism, spoke of them as though already known and convicted heretics? Optatus, who had just argued this point and strongly censured Parmenianus for rashly mixing schismatics with heretics; Optatus, who himself held that they must be mutually distinguished by a great difference, and not merely held it but carefully taught the distinction. Consider only these words: “I wonder what led you to think that you should join even yourselves to heretics, when it is established that you are schismatics,” etc. Soon again: “I greatly wonder at you, brother Parmenianus, that though you are a schismatic, you wished to join schismatics with heretics,” etc.; and again: “I wished heretics alone to be condemned; so far as lies in you, you wished to strike yourselves too with them by a single sentence,” etc.

I do not doubt that Optatus wrote, “Now all those men began to murmur,” [*iam omnes ei coeperunt murmurare*], not “Now all the heretics began to murmur.” He immediately inserts their words, so that no one may be surprised at what happened here. It is well known, even to those not yet washed in air, that persons pressed so hard either by words or by the facts themselves that they cannot escape, or at least cannot easily extricate themselves, are said to have “water sticking to them” [*aqua haerere*]. Although the dative is not expressed, it must nevertheless be supplied; and those who explain the phrase as “he sticks in water” are mistaken. This is abundantly confirmed by a single example from Cicero, whose words in Letter VII, Book II, to his brother Quintus are: [Col. 0914C] “What had been said on the Ides and the following day—that action would be taken concerning the Campanian land—was not done. In this matter water sticks to me.” Since Optatus wrote briefly and perhaps people then commonly spoke “it sticks to him,” whereas earlier they had said more fully, “water sticks to him,” an unskilled copyist, to whom the water here stuck because he did not understand that Optatus was employing their own expression and did not recall the old word, made one word, *heretics*, out of the two words *haeret ei*, “it sticks to him.” This reading is so impossible here that this one little word overturns the whole preceding discussion of heretics and schismatics. Whoever considers that discussion will not doubt at all the necessity of this correction. M. CASAUB.]

[Note: Ibid. “Heretics.” Optatus calls these bishops heretics because shortly afterward they made a schism. Augustine calls them by the same name; and in the acts of that council: “You are ready to make a schism; because they are going to dismiss you and pronounce sentence against you, you will remain the sole heretic.” In Book III *Against Cresconius*, schismatics are treated as heretics, and before secular judges they are addressed by this name: “Advocates were equipped for those trials and stirred up as against heretics.” Or he calls them heretics because, in Parmenianus’s view, schismatics were heretics.

ALBASP.] All had now risen. [Note: [Col. 0913A] We owe this emendation to the manuscript of St. Gall. In the other manuscripts [Col. 0914A] and in the printed editions, *haeretici* (“heretics”) appears, wholly wrongly; this has tormented critics.] [Note: [Col. 0914D] *Erecti* (“risen”). As soon as they were accused, they rose and went over to the other side, as is clear from the proceedings. DU PIN.] They had begun to murmur. Fearing their temper, Secundus took counsel from Secundus the younger, the son of his brother, that [Note: [Col. 0914D] *Talem causam Deo servaret* (“he should reserve such a case for God”). When formerly they did not wish to judge some case or offence, they referred and remitted the matter to God. Cyprian does so in several places where he discusses the penance of the lapsed; and Augustine, *Against Cresconius*, book III, chapter 28, says that he had left all those matters to divine judgment. ALBASP.] he should reserve such a case for God. [Note: [Col. 0914D] *Talem causam Deo servaret.* He should leave it to God’s judgment. DU PIN.] Those who remained were consulted [Note: [Col. 0914D] *Those who remained.* Twelve bishops were present at that council, as is clear in the *Breviculus*, chapter 17, [Col. 0915C] six of whom were accused. The rest were consulted; they replied that, for the sake of peace, this case should be reserved for God, and that those accused would have God as judge and would render an account to him. ALBASP.] [Note: [Col. 0915C] *Those who remained were consulted.* In chapter 17 of the *Breviculus of the Conference*, eleven or twelve bishops are said to have assembled for this council. From Optatus’s account it is clear that there were only eleven, of whom six were accused. Secundus of Tigisis, the president, could not pronounce judgment. Secundus the younger, his brother’s son, had already disclosed his own opinion. Thus only three remained to be consulted; Secundus followed their judgment, and so six bishops were absolved by five. DU PIN.]—that is, Victor of Garba [Note: [Col. 0915B] In manuscripts S. T. and P. S., *Gardensis*; but later, in book II, *Garbensis*. In manuscript S. G., *Gabrensis*. In the printed editions, *Garbiensis*. In Augustine, at the Conference of Carthage, and in the *Notice of the Bishops of Africa*, *Garbensis*.], Felix of Rotaria [Note: [Col. 0915B] In manuscripts S. T. and P. S., *a Ratorio*. In Augustine, *Rotaria*.], and Nabor of Centuriones [Note: [Col. 0915B] So also at the Conference of Carthage: Januarius, bishop of Centuriones. In the manuscripts of the *Notice of Africa*, *Centurianensis*, wrongly.]. They said that such a case ought to be reserved for the Lord [Note: [Col. 0916B] In manuscript S. G., “ought to be reserved for God.”]; and Secundus said, [Note: [Col. 0915C] *Sit down, all of you.* From the proceedings of Caecilian’s vindication, from the *Breviculus*, and from *Against Cresconius*, book III, it is clear that, when Secundus questioned them, these bishops rose and crossed over to another place; once absolved, they returned to their seats after these words, which [Col. 0915D] seem to possess some force and form of absolution, together with the subsequent words: “and they sat down and answered, ‘Thanks be to God.’” ALBASP.

*Ibid. Sit down, all of you.* To what Balduin observes here, I add a passage from the Conference of Carthage, Conference I. When the examiner Marcellinus wished the parties or advocates to sit down, the Donatists answered and excused themselves among other things thus: “This is expedient and necessary for us: when the case is being pleaded, when it is first opened, it is fitting that each person who has undertaken the test of debate should stand, so that the persons themselves may also be identified.” M. CASAUB.] “Sit down, all of you.” [Note: [Col. 0915D] *Sit down, all of you.* As judges. Let each take his own place. DU PIN.] 16 Then all said, “Thanks be to God,” and sat down. You have, therefore, brother Parmenianus, those who were manifestly traitors.

XV. The schism arose from the ordination of Majorinus.—Then, not long afterward [Note: [Col. 0915D] *Not long afterward.* Yet several years must have intervened. For Maxentius, after whose indulgence Caecilian’s ordination was performed, as is said below, did not gain possession of Africa until the year 311, after defeating [Col. 0916C] Alexander, who was exercising tyranny in that region. Alexander was not defeated until after the death of Herculius, which occurred in 310, according to Zosimus. DU PIN.], [Note: [Col. 0916C] *The very same men.* Together with Silvanus, who had been ordained bishop of Cirta in that council. ALBASP.] the very same men—so numerous and so notable—traitors who had travelled to Carthage, burners of incense [Note: [Col. 0916B] That is, those who had burned incense to idols. So in all manuscripts. In the printed editions, by what a mistake, *conjurati* (“conspirators”).], murderers, ordained Majorinus after Caecilian’s ordination (whose chair you occupy), thus making a schism. And since it has been shown that those guilty of handing over the Scriptures were your leaders, it follows that the same men were the authors [Note: [Col. 0916B] In manuscript S. G.: “and authors.”] of the schism. In order that this may be clear and evident to all, it must be shown from what root the branches of error have extended down to the present day [Col. 0915B], and from what spring this little stream of malignant liquid, creeping secretly, has flowed down to our own times. It must be stated whence, where, and by whom this second evil is known to have arisen; what causes converged; what persons were at work; who were the authors of this evil; who nourished it; by whom judgments between the parties were requested from the Emperor; who sat as [Col. 0916A] judges; where [Note: [Col. 0916C] The council was held: at Rome, under Melchiades. ALBASP.] the council was held; and what judgments were pronounced. The issue is division; and in Africa, as in the other provinces, there was one Church before it was divided by the ordainers of Majorinus, [Note: [Col. 0916C] *Whose hereditary chair you occupy.* Bishops are not merely heirs of their predecessors but also their sons; therefore he had such a chair as his predecessors had possessed. ALBASP.] whose hereditary chair you occupy. It must be considered who [Note: [Col. 0916C] *In the root.* It must be considered who remained in the chair in communion with the whole world, with which the other chairs have fellowship, and which communicates with the Roman chair, the root through which peace and Christian unity are nourished throughout the world. ALBASP.] remained in the root with the whole world; who went outside; who sat in another chair that had not existed before; who set up altar against altar; who performed an ordination while the other ordained bishop remained; who lies under the sentence of the Apostle John, who said that many Antichrists would go out: “They were not of us,” he says, “for if they had been of us, they would have remained with us” (1 John 2:19). Therefore, he who refused to remain one with his brethren, having followed heretics, went outside like an Antichrist.

[Col. 0916B] XVI. Lucilla’s quarrel with Caecilian.—That this occurred at Carthage after Caecilian’s ordination, no one fails to know [Note: [Col. 0916B] In manuscripts S. T. and P. S., “no one who does not know.” In manuscript S. G., “who does not know?”]: namely, through Lucilla, some unknown factional woman. Before the peace, shaken by the storms of persecution, while the Church was still tranquil, because she could not bear [Note: [Col. 0916C] *Rebuke.* Deacons moved about through the Church in order to keep the faithful to their duty, supervise them, and correct those who did anything contrary to Church discipline. [Col. 0916D] ALBASP.] the rebuke of Caecilian the archdeacon [Note: [Col. 0916B] In manuscript S. T.: “because Lucilla could not bear it.”]: [Note: [Col. 0916D] *She was said, before spiritual food and drink, to kiss, if indeed it was a martyr’s, [the relic].* This was the religious practice of that time. Paula and Eustochium, writing to Marcella among Jerome’s letters: “We venerate everywhere the tombs of martyrs, and, setting the holy ashes before our eyes, if permitted, we even touch them with our lips.” Here Optatus calls “martyr” one who had been declared, by the common judgment of the devout, to that highest rank. BARTII.

*Ibid. She was said, before spiritual food and drink, etc.* Besides Balsamon, cited by Balduin, see also Damascene. In Balsamon one may rightly wonder that he remembers this bone as though it were the chief practice of that sect and as though its superstition consisted principally in this. Unless, indeed, it is more remarkable that most Greeks make no mention at all of the Donatists, as if they had not even heard of them. Concerning the “vindicated martyr” that follows, I entirely agree with Baronius, who interprets it in the *Martyrology* as one neither received nor approved, rather than, as others do, one marked out by holiness—though I do not know how well. For not all martyrs, even those who suffered death and torments for the faith, were marked out by holiness, since among them there were sometimes criminals, schismatics, and heretics (as Baronius shows there at greater length), whom, I suppose, the Church did not regard as blessed or marked out by holiness. But Optatus’s hesitation and doubt here about the martyr are not without reason, since there had long been discovered quite a few people whose sole occupation and craft of life was to carry about relics even of false martyrs [Col. 0917C] and sell them to the more simple-minded. I call Augustine as witness, *On the Work of Monks*, chapter 28: “Some sell limbs of martyrs—if, indeed, they are martyrs; others make much of their fringes and phylacteries; others [make much] of their parents or relatives,” etc.; “and all ask, all demand, either the expenses of a profitable poverty or the price of a feigned holiness.” M. CASAUB.] she was said, before spiritual food and drink, to kiss the mouth of some martyr—[Col. 0917A] if indeed it was a martyr—[Note: [Col. 0917C] *She was said to kiss.* That is, to kiss reverently. Shortly before receiving the Eucharist, Christians formerly greeted one another with mutual kisses in order to make peace; and the priest, in the name of the whole Church, reverently kissed any relics of martyrs that lay in the altar. That woman imitated this rite with certain private relics that she carried, making peace and communion with them before approaching the Eucharist; but because that martyr had not been vindicated and approved by the Church, Caecilian rebuked her. ALBASP.]—to kiss [Note: [Col. 0917C] *To kiss.* To kiss reverently. DU PIN.] it. And because she placed [Note: [Col. 0917C] *Placed before.* She kissed and touched it before the cup. ALBASP.] before 17 the cup of salvation the mouth [Note: [Col. 0917D] *Of some unknown dead man.* Whose martyrdom was not established. ALBASP.] of some unknown dead man, even if he were a martyr, but [Note: [Col. 0917D] *Not yet vindicated.* Not yet entered by the Church in the number of martyrs; not yet enrolled in the canon and diptychs. ALBASP.

*Ibid. A vindicated martyr.* Optatus calls one so designated by the common judgment of the devout to that highest dignity, enrolled among the denizens of heaven.

INCERT.] not yet vindicated [Note: [Col. 0917D] *Not yet vindicated.* Not yet included by the Church among the number of martyrs. DU PIN.], she was rebuked and departed in anger and shame. While she was angry and being instructed, [Note: [Col. 0917D] *Lest she submit to discipline.* Lest she be criticized and chastised by the bishop, because she not only acted contrary to Church discipline by holding communion with a martyr of uncertain status, not yet approved by the Church, but also infected the other faithful with that same communion. For, just as in sacred things they admitted fellowship with none except the holy and faithful, so in those same sacred rites they did not wish communion to be held with the relics of martyrs whom the Church did not recognize, lest the faithful be infected by that communion. [Col. 0918B] ALBASP.] lest she submit to discipline [Note: [Col. 0918B] *Lest she submit to discipline.* Lest she therefore be punished by the bishop. DU PIN.], the storm of persecution suddenly arose [Note: [Col. 0917B] In the manuscripts, *innata* (“inborn”); but *enata* (“arisen”) is better.].

XVII. Mensurius, summoned before the municipal council, entrusts the Church’s ornaments to Botrus and Celestius.— [Note: [Col. 0918B] *At the same time.* Under Maxentius. ALBASP.] At the same time a certain deacon Felix, because of [Note: [Col. 0917B] In manuscripts S. T. and S. G., *per* (“through”); but *propter* (“because of”) should be read.] some famous writing against the tyrant-emperor [Note: [Col. 0918B] *Against the tyrant.* Maxentius. Felix had written that famous pamphlet against him while Alexander, bitterly hostile to Maxentius, held Africa. After Alexander’s death, Maxentius wished to take vengeance on Felix.
