Zosimus testifies that Maxentius raged especially against Alexander’s supporters. [Col. 0918C] DU PIN.], was summoned [Note: [Col. 0917B] In manuscripts S. T. and S. G., *epistolarius*, as if that deacon were called “letter-carrier” because of the famous letter; but *appellatus* (“summoned”), that is, summoned before the [Col. 0918B] municipal council, as the following words show, is much more correct.] and, fearing danger, is said to have hidden with Bishop Mensurius. [Note: [Col. 0918C] *He is said to have hidden.* People fled to bishops’ houses as to an altar; it was not lawful to violate them, even during persecutions. ALBASP.] When Mensurius publicly refused to surrender him upon demand, a report was sent; a rescript came ordering that, unless Mensurius handed over the deacon Felix, he should be sent to the imperial court. [Note: [Col. 0918C] *He was suffering no slight pressure from being summoned.* Soldiers had summoned Mensurius to send the deacon Felix to the emperor. Here *conventus* is used adjectivally, as in several places in Augustine, in canon 12 of the First Council of Carthage, and canon 28 of the Third Council: *modeste conventus* (“moderately summoned”), as in the Council of Cologne; it is not a substantive meaning “assemblies of Africa,” as some interpret it. ALBASP.] He was suffering no slight pressure from this summons. For the Church possessed very many ornaments of gold and silver, which he could neither bury in the ground nor take with him. These [Note: [Col. 0918B] This wholly necessary word has been supplied from manuscript S. G.] he entrusted, as though to faithful persons, to elders, [Note: [Col. 0918C] *He entrusted them to elders, as though to faithful persons.* Formerly there were lay elders, entirely secular persons; and there were others, likewise laymen, who nevertheless might in some measure also be called ecclesiastical persons, much as those now commonly called guardians of temples or churches among us. The former were commonly called elders of places or towns; the latter, elders of the Church or ecclesiastical elders. [Col. 0918D] But the most learned Christopher Justel, who has deserved so much in this field, collected much concerning these persons in his commentary on the canons of the African Church; anyone wishing to know more should consult him, for he deserves that all should reap the fruit of his diligence and learning. M. CASAUB.

*Ibid. He entrusted them to elders.* Besides ecclesiastical persons and clerics, certain elders from the people, of approved life, administered the Church’s property; this passage must be understood of them. In the proceedings: “Call in the fellow clerics and the ecclesiastical elders of the people.” Likewise: “to the clerics and elders of Cirta”; likewise: “you elders cried out.”

ALBASP.] having drawn up an inventory memorandum, [Note: [Col. 0918D] *Inventory memorandum.* He calls it a brief document, as he says later, in which all the Church’s possessions were listed, so that the depositor might testify that he had entrusted the goods to the recipient’s keeping, and the latter that he had received them. BARTH.] which he is said to have given to a certain old woman, on the condition that, if he himself did not return after peace had been restored to Christians, the old woman should give it [Note: [Col. 0918B] In manuscript S. G., “return it.”] to whomever she found sitting in the episcopal chair. He departed and pleaded his case; he was ordered to return, but could not reach Carthage.

XVIII. Caecilian’s ordination as bishop of Carthage, and the cause and origin of the schism.—The storm [Col. 0919A] of persecution had passed and was ended. [Note: [Col. 0919B] *Had passed and was ended.* It had first subsided in 305, but soon flared up again; peace was not fully restored until Maxentius gained control of Africa [Col. 0919C] in 311. DU PIN.] At God’s command, Maxentius sent an act of indulgence, [Note: [Col. 0919C] *Maxentius sending an indulgence.* Although cruel and savage, he nevertheless seemed to favour Christians. DU PIN.] and liberty was restored to Christians. Botrus and Celestius [Note: [Col. 0919B] Thus in manuscript S. G. Augustine also calls him so in the alphabetic Psalm against the Donatists: “Botrus and Celestius were bitter enemies of Caecilian—ungodly, thieves, proud men—of whom it would take long to speak.” On the authority of this passage I have restored *Celestius* for *Celesius*, which appears in manuscripts S. Th. and Ph. and in the printed editions.] are said to have desired ordination at Carthage; they arranged that, [Note: [Col. 0919C] *With the Numidians absent.* The Donatists objected to Caecilian that, since he was primate, he had not been ordained by the nearest primate. Augustine replied in the *Breviculus* that the bishop of the Roman Church was not ordained by some metropolitan but by the bishop of Ostia. ALBASP.] with the Numidians absent, [Note: [Col. 0919C] *With the Numidians absent.* The Donatists objected that Caecilian, as primate, had not been ordained by a metropolitan. Optatus observes that Botrus and Celestius themselves, aspirants to the episcopate who later broke with Caecilian, had instigated the ordination to be performed in the Numidians’ absence. Augustine replied that it was not necessary for a primate to be ordained by a metropolitan, citing the Roman bishop, who was ordained by the bishop of Ostia. DU PIN.] only neighbouring bishops should be invited to celebrate the ordination at Carthage. Then Caecilian was chosen by the vote [Note: [Col. 0919C] *Of the whole people.* Elections were made by the people and [Col. 0919D] clergy, and the agreement of all was required; this was later abolished. ALBASP.] of the whole people; and, with Felix of Autumnum laying hands upon him, [Note: [Col. 0919B] Thus in all manuscripts and in the proceedings of Felix’s vindication.] [Note: [Col. 0919D] *Of Autumnum.* Thus in all manuscripts and in the proceedings of Felix’s vindication. In Augustine everywhere, *Aptugnensis*; in the printed editions of Optatus, *Aptungitanus*. From this passage it is inferred that this town was near Carthage and in the proconsular province. I am surprised that so prominent a town of that time is not mentioned in the *Notice of the Bishops of Africa*, nor elsewhere. DU PIN.] he was ordained bishop. Botrus and Celestius [Note: [Col. 0919B] Thus in manuscript S. G.; in the others, *Celesius*.] were disappointed of their hope. An inventory memorandum [Note: [Col. 0920B] In manuscript S. G., “Then the inventory memorandum.”] of the gold and silver was handed to Caecilian as he sat, 18 just as Mensurius had directed, witnesses being present. The above-mentioned elders were summoned, who had swallowed up the prize entrusted to them in the jaws of greed. When they were compelled to restore it, [Note: [Col. 0919D] *They withdrew their foot from communion.* They withdrew from communion with Caecilian. ALBASP.

*Ibid. They withdrew their foot from communion.* Better is the reading already printed long ago: *subduxerunt communioni pedem* (“they withdrew their foot from communion”). He immediately repeats the same thing in other words: “The aspirants also, no less … and Lucilla, refused to join in communion.” M. CASAUB.] they withdrew their foot from communion [Col. 0919B] [Note: [Col. 0920B] In more recent editions, *plebem* (“the people”) is wrongly read; by far the larger part of the people remained with Caecilian.]. No less did the aspirants, who likewise failed to be ordained; and Lucilla also, who had long before been unable [Note: [Col. 0919D] *She could not bear it.* She feared that she would be rebuked more sharply by the same man, now [Col. 0920B] bishop, since he had rebuked her when he was a deacon. ALBASP.] to bear discipline. This influential and factional woman, with all her household [Note: [Col. 0920B] *With all her household.* She had a large and extensive household, and withdrew the whole of it, together with friends, clients, and slaves, from Caecilian’s communion. [Col. 0920C] ALBASP.], refused to join in communion. Thus, when these three causes and persons had come together, malice achieved its effect.

XIX. The unlawful ordination of Majorinus against Caecilian by the bishops of Numidia.—Thus at that time the anger of an embarrassed woman gave birth to the schism, ambition [Note: [Col. 0920B] In manuscript S. G., *ambitio* (“ambition”).] nourished it, and greed strengthened it. From these three persons charges were fabricated against Caecilian, so that blame might be cast upon him. [Note: [Col. 0920C] *To Secundus of Tigisis.* Because he was primate of Numidia, which borders the province of Carthage. ALBASP.] A message was sent to Secundus of Tigisis [Note: [Col. 0920B] In manuscript S. G., “it was written.”] that he should come to Carthage. All the above-mentioned traitors set out, [Note: [Col. 0920C] *The above-mentioned traitors.* Those twelve who had ordained Silvanus at the council of Cirta. ALBASP.] [Note: [Col. 0920C] *The above-mentioned traitors.* Bishops who had attended the council of Cirta, with the addition of Silvanus, who had been ordained bishop of Cirta at that council. Optatus seems to acknowledge no others than these. Yet in the proceedings of this conventicle they were said to number about seventy, as may be read in the *Breviculus of the Conference of Carthage*, chapter 14, no. 26. DU PIN.], and were received as guests [Note: [Col. 0920C] *Received as guests.* Bishops formerly summoned to ordain a bishop in place of one deceased received hospitality from clerics and lay elders; but Secundus, contrary to Church discipline, was received with his Numidians by the angry Lucilla, the ambitious Botrus [Col. 0920D] and Celesius, and the greedy elders who withheld the Church’s deposit. Optatus notes this in order to show that Majorinus’s election began contrary to Church order. ALBASP.] by the greedy, [Note: [Col. 0920D] *Received as guests by the greedy,* etc.: by the angry Lucilla, the aspiring Botrus and Celestius, and those greedy, thieving elders. DU PIN.] the ambitious, and the angry—not by the Catholics, at whose request Caecilian had been ordained. Meanwhile, none of the persons just mentioned came to the basilica, [Note: [Col. 0920D] *To the basilica.* In former times elections and ordinations of bishops were held in churches, as may be inferred from what I have said above concerning the election of Silvanus, bishop of Cirta. But Majorinus’s election, being illegal, was not held in the principal basilica. ALBASP.] where the whole civic population was gathered with Caecilian [Note: [Col. 0920B] Thus in manuscript S. G. In the others and the printed editions: “the whole city had been gathered in an assembly.”]. Then Caecilian sent this message: [Col. 0920B] [Note: [Col. 0920B] Absent in manuscript S. G.] “If there is anything that can be proved against me, let an accuser come forward and prove it.” At that time, despite so many enemies, nothing could be fabricated against him; but his ordainer [Note: [Col. 0920D] *His ordainer:* Felix of Aptunga. ALBASP.], whom they falsely called a traitor, was made [Note: [Col. 0920D] *He deserved to be defamed.* That is: when they could fabricate nothing against Caecilian, they accused Felix, his ordainer, of handing over the Scriptures and of idolatry, so as by this means to invalidate Caecilian’s ordination as performed by an idolater. But the fathers of the First Council of Arles answered this argument in canon 13: “For if such persons are discovered to have ordained any, and the standing of those whom they ordained remains valid, their ordination shall remain valid.” ALBASP.] the object of defamation. [Note: [Col. 0921A] *Concerning his ordainer, because he was falsely called a traitor by them, he was made the object of defamation.* They had nothing that they could fabricate against Caecilian, but alleged that Felix, his ordainer, had incurred the charge of handing over the Scriptures, in order thereby to invalidate Felix’s ordination as one performed by a man who had lost his rank through the crime of handing over the Scriptures. DU PIN.] Again Caecilian sent word that, if Felix, as they supposed, had conferred [Note: [Col. 0921B] *Had conferred nothing.* Augustine teaches in the *Breviculus* that Caecilian said this in jest and mockery, and recounts the story in these words: “If those who ordained me are traitors, ordain me.” ALBASP.] nothing upon him, [Note: [Col. 0921B] *If Felix, as they supposed, had conferred nothing upon him.* For the sake of peace Caecilian offers the Numidians this condition. DU PIN.] they should themselves ordain Caecilian as though he were still a deacon. [Note: [Col. 0921B] *As though still a deacon.* He had been made bishop from a deacon. DU PIN.] Then Purpurius, trusting in his habitual malice [Note: [Col. 0921B] *Habitual malice.* Because he had killed his sister’s sons. ALBASP.], as though Caecilian too were the son of his sister, said: “ [Note: [Col. 0921B] *Let him come out here.* Purpurius threatens Caecilian with death, and declares that he will lay violent hands upon him—not for the episcopate, [Col. 0921C] but to kill him. ALBASP.] Let him come out here, [Note: [Col. 0921C] *As though hands might be laid on him for the episcopate,* etc. Since Caecilian had again offered to be ordained, whether seriously or ironically, as Augustine understands it, Purpurius, relying on his accustomed malice and turning secret schemes in his mind, said: “Come, let Caecilian approach so that hands may be laid upon him for the episcopate”—that is, for admission to the episcopate. In truth, however, he intended that when Caecilian had approached and placed himself in their hands, they should “shake his head for penance,” that is, compel him to undergo the penance of the lapsed, or *hypoptōsis* (ὑπόπτωσις). Once this had been performed, anyone who was a cleric immediately lost his rank, *ipso facto*, as they say; and anyone not yet a cleric was, under the ancient canons, deprived of every hope and possibility of obtaining that office in future. Augustine, Letter 50, to Boniface: “The rule established in the Church, that no one after the penance for some crime should receive clerical office, return to clerical office, or remain in clerical office, was made not because forgiveness was despaired of, but because of the strictness of discipline,” etc. But, not to go too far afield, Optatus himself says explicitly in book II: “You found boys and wounded them with penance, lest any might be ordained.” Now “to wound with penance,” or, which amounts to the same thing, “to shake someone’s head,” is a familiar and elegant *phrāsis* (φράσις) of Optatus, as elsewhere: “to vindicate holiness against pride,” book III; “they were part of the seasoning of poverty of spirit,” book VII; and, in the same book, “made foolish by dissension.” I omit countless similar passages. Thus Sidonius Apollinaris, book IX, letter IX: “to pursue pride through distinctions of dress.” Cyprian especially likes this usage, as can be shown from innumerable passages. We shall be content with one example, from *On the Vanity of Idols*, near the end: “And so, when Christ, in accordance with what had previously been foretold by the prophets, by the command of word and voice drove demons out of men, restored paralytics, cleansed lepers,” etc., “the Jews, who believed him a mere man because of the humility of his flesh and body, regarded him as a magician because of his freedom.” In some editions which I have used, *diligentia* (“diligence”) is most wrongly printed instead of *de licentia potestatis* (“because of the licence of power”). M. CASAUB.] as though hands might be laid [Note: [Col. 0921A] In manuscript S. G.: “as though in order that hands might be laid.”] 19 upon him for the episcopate, and [Note: [Col. 0922A] *His head may be shaken for penance.* Caecilian was regarded as guilty of handing over the Scriptures and, for this reason, liable to penance; therefore Purpurius says that his head must be shaken for penance. ALBASP.] his head shaken [Col. 0922A] for penance [Note: [Col. 0922B] *For penance.* For sins for which he ought to perform penance. ALBASP.] [Note: [Col. 0922B] *His head may be shaken for penance.* Let hands be laid on him for penance; let him be subjected to public penance and thus be expelled from the clergy and reduced to lay status. For this was the established rule, as Augustine says in Letter 50, now 185, no. 45: “That no one after the penance for some crime should receive clerical office, return to clerical office, or remain in clerical office.” DU PIN.].” Once these things were learned, [Note: [Col. 0922B] *The whole Church.* The whole city. ALBASP.] the whole Church held Caecilian back [Note: [Col. 0921A] In manuscript S. G.: “held him.”], so that he should not hand himself over to brigands. [Note: [Col. 0922B] *Brigands.* Murderers: “Every banditry outside a forest is murder,” Tertullian, *On Modesty*. ALBASP.] At that time either the accused man ought to have been expelled from his seat [Note: [Col. 0922B] *Either the accused man should be expelled.* Before ordaining another, they ought to have expelled Caecilian; for two bishops were not to be ordained in the same place. ALBASP.] [Note: [Col. 0922A] These words were added from manuscripts S. T. and P. S.] [Note: [Col. 0922A] In manuscript S. G.: “ought.”] or the innocent man ought to have been admitted to communion. [Note: [Col. 0922B] *Admitted to communion.* They acknowledged him neither as accused nor as brother. ALBASP.] The Church was crowded with people; [Note: [Col. 0922C] *The Church was crowded.* The entire multitude was in the basilica with Caecilian. ALBASP.] the episcopal chair was occupied; [Note: [Col. 0922C] *Chair, Church, altar.* These three were the marks of a lawful ordination. For one who occupied the church in which the people usually gathered, sat in the chair in which bishops of that place had formerly sat, and offered at the altar at which his predecessors had offered, was considered duly ordained. Therefore, in order to show that Majorinus was not duly ordained, Optatus reports that he lacked all these things. ALBASP.] the altar stood in its proper place, [Note: [Col. 0922C] *The altar in its proper place.* In the place known to God and the predecessors—that is, in the place of the predecessors—because God had received many offerings there and the people had made many there; consequently it ought not to have been moved. He says “its proper place” because a bishop’s altar ought to be in the basilica which is the centre of communion, where the people are assembled with and by the bishop. For that was formerly the place of the altar: the place which God regarded, which the people recognized, and in which offerings and prayers were made in the name of the whole Church. The other [Col. 0922D] altars are, as it were, permitted as aids to communion. Moreover, when someone was formerly ordained bishop, he immediately proceeded to perform the sacred rites and give the peace; he sat in the episcopal chair, addressed the people, then offered at the same altar at which his predecessors had offered, and held communion there with them and with the people, beneath which altar they lay. With reference to this rite Optatus says that Majorinus was not ordained in the principal church, with the people present and acclaiming; did not sit in the episcopal chair; nor finally hold communion with Saint Cyprian, Lucian, and the other bishops who had presided over the Church of Carthage and who still belonged to the communion of Carthage. Had he been lawfully ordained, all this ought to have been done by him. ALBASP.] at which the peaceful bishops of former times [Col. 0923A] had offered—Cyprian, Lucian [Note: [Col. 0923B] In manuscript S. G., Carpophorus is placed third between Cyprian and Lucian.] and the rest. [Note: [Col. 0923B] *Thus he went outside.* Thus the schism was made by Majorinus. ALBASP.] Thus they went outside, and [Note: [Col. 0923B] *Altar against altar.* Another body of Christ was enacted and another communion formed, because Majorinus did not communicate with Cyprian, to whom the body and communion of the whole people adhered. ALBASP.] altar was set up against altar; an unlawful ordination [Note: [Col. 0923B] In manuscript S. G., “unlawful.”] was performed; and Majorinus—[Note: [Col. 0923B] *Who had been a reader in Caecilian’s diaconate.* That is, while Caecilian was still archdeacon, during his archidiaconate. Otherwise, we are not unaware that *diaconium*, or *diakonikon* (διακονικόν), may refer to the most sacred place of the Church, from which a canon of the Council of Laodicea—“that servants must not have a place in the *diakonikon*” (ὅτι οὐ δεῖ ὑπηρέτας ἔχειν χώραν ἐν τῷ διακονικῷ)—excludes ministers; [Col. 0923C] Balsamon interprets *hypēretas* (ὑπηρέτας) as subdeacons, whereas the Council of Agde, canon 66, interprets it as ordained ministers. M. CASAUB.] who had been a reader [Note: [Col. 0923C] *In Caecilian’s diaconate.* All lower clerics were arranged beneath deacons, deacons beneath presbyters, and presbyters beneath bishops, as though in ranks. And just as no presbyter was appointed without a deacon, so no deacon was appointed without lower clerics, because the duty of all of them could not properly be performed without the work and service of the others. Optatus notes that Majorinus was promoted from reading to the episcopate in order to show that his ordination was less rightful and orderly; for order required that presbyters or deacons be ordained before readers, if suitable men were found. ALBASP.] in Caecilian’s diaconate [Note: [Col. 0923C] *Who had been a reader in Caecilian’s diaconate.* Who had been a reader while Caecilian was archdeacon. DU PIN.], a member of Lucilla’s household—was ordained bishop by the traitors, [Note: [Col. 0923C] *She herself casting her vote.* As though giving a vote, because [Col. 0923D] she had corrupted votes with money. ALBASP.] with Lucilla herself supporting him [Note: [Col. 0923D] *She herself supporting him.* The bishops having been corrupted with money; for it is established in the proceedings before Zenophilus that she gave four hundred *folles*. DU PIN.], who at the council of Numidia [Note: [Col. 0923D] *Of Numidia:* the council of Cirta. ALBASP.] (as we said above) confessed their crimes to one another and [Note: [Col. 0923D] *Indulgence.* Secundus, guilty of handing over the Scriptures, absolved others guilty of idolatry and was absolved by them. ALBASP.] granted one another indulgence. It is therefore plain that those ordainers who handed over the Scriptures went out from the Church, and Majorinus who was ordained. [Note: [Col. 0923D] *The ordainers.* One who ordains another while the lawful bishop remains does no less to divide the Church than the person ordained. ALBASP.]

XX. Letters of the bishops of Numidia against Felix, Caecilian’s ordainer.—Meanwhile, from the fountain of their own crimes, which had overflowed among them in streams of many shameful acts, they thought that one charge of handing over the Scriptures ought to be diverted [Col. 0923B] onto Caecilian’s ordainer:

[Col. 0924A] [Note: [Col. 0923D]

*Foreseeing that rumour.* Lest they should be accused by Caecilian of handing over the Scriptures, they wrote letters to all bishops and neighbours, making Felix guilty of the same crime. Their purpose was that they should not be regarded as traitors; for one and the same thing is not readily believed of two persons at the same time, and the breath of the earlier rumour always prevails. ALBASP.]

Ibid. “Foreseeing that report [spoke of] two similar things at one [time].” [Col. 0924B] Read: “that report could not speak of two different things simultaneously and at the same time.” Instead of *different*, the copyist had written *dras* in abbreviation; this was later omitted because of its resemblance to the preceding *two*, or *dras* was turned into *two*. The sense can properly stand without it. Comparable in wording is book VII: “The same workman cannot at the same time do two incompatible and contrary things,” as here: “two different things.” M. CASAUBON.]

Foreseeing that report could not speak of two similar things at the same time, they tried to malign another’s life in order to consign their own crimes to silence. [Note: [Col. 0924B] They tried to malign another’s life: namely, that of Caecilian, his colleagues, and Felix of Aptunga. “They accused Caecilian,” says Augustine, *Post Collationem*, book I, ch. 22, [Col. 0924C] “of having been ordained by traditors, and of having, while he was a deacon, forbidden food to be brought to martyrs held in custody.” Certain colleagues of Caecilian were named, whom public records alleged to be traditors; yet those records were not read. Among them were Novellus of Thysdrus and Faustinus of Tuburbo, and especially Felix of Aptunga, who was accused more bitterly, so that he was called the marketplace of every evil. These matters were contained in the acts of this council, read at the Conference of Carthage, as Augustine states in the *Breviculus of the Conference*, ch. 14, no. 26. These were the contents of the Numidian bishops’ letters, composed at the prompting of envy, which Optatus had reproduced at the end of his work. DU PIN.]

Though they themselves could be accused by the innocent, they endeavoured to accuse the innocent, sending everywhere letters composed at the prompting of envy, [Note: [Col. 0924C] *At the prompting of envy*: below, “with full envy.” ALBASP.] which we have among the other records later on. [Note: [Col. 0924C] “We have among the other records later on.” Perhaps better: “in the later part.” Above in this book, p. 16: “For we have appended the full account of these matters in the final part of these documents, in order to complete the proof.” And below: “Concerning these matters we have volumes of records; [Col. 0924D] if anyone wishes, let him read them in the final sections.” UNCERTAIN.]

While still at Carthage, they sent their letters ahead of themselves, [Note: [Col. 0924D] “They sent their letters ahead of themselves.” He puts this most elegantly, as though they sent them before their own arrival; just as Claudian speaks of a rumour of war preceding the emperor and of a laurel wreath preceding him. BARTH.] [Note: [Col. 0924D] “They sent their letters ahead of themselves.” Before they came to the churches, they had sent there a letter written by the council. DU PIN.] so that, by false rumours spread among the peoples, they might plant a lie in everyone’s ears. And while falsehoods concerning one man were being proclaimed, [Note: [Col. 0924D] “Concerning one man”: Caecilian or Felix. ALBASP.] the entirely genuine crimes of the persons mentioned above lay hidden in silence.

Often people are ashamed of crime; but at that time there was no one before whom they could be ashamed, because, apart from a few Catholics, [Note: [Col. 0924D] “A few Catholics”: apart from the laypeople who had been present at this ordination. ALBASP.] all had sinned, [Note: [Col. 0924D] “They had sinned”: they had been traditors. ALBASP.] and an outrage committed among many was, as it were, an image of innocence. [Note: [Col. 0924D] “Or because it was an image.” Something seems either lacking or superfluous. For the period must be understood thus: “An outrage committed among many was an image of innocence.” By this he means that it was an image of innocence that none of those bishops was accused, or could be accused, because all had sinned. ALBASP.] [Note: [Col. 0924B] Thus in manuscript S. G. In manuscripts S. T. P. S. and the printed editions: *quod* (“because”); but the sense requires correction to *quasi* (“as it were”).]

[Col. 0925A] [Note: [Col. 0925B] “It was little”: a new period. ALBASP.] It was no small crime of surrendering the Scriptures, proved to have been committed by Donatus of Masculae and the other persons mentioned above; they also joined to the surrender an enormous crime of schism. [Note: [Col. 0925B] Thus in all manuscripts. The printed editions wrongly have *parvum* rather than *parum*.] [Note: [Col. 0925B] “Also enormous”: these words are not to be separated from what precedes, but belong to its sense. ALBASP.]

## XXI. How grave is the evil of schism, of which the Donatists are guilty

You see then, brother Parmenian, that these two crimes, so evil and so grave—surrendering the Scriptures and schism—belong to your leaders. Recognise, even late, that you have fallen upon your own people while attacking others; and, since it is established that your predecessors committed this second outrage, you too strive to follow in their criminal footsteps, so that what those earlier men did under the title of schism, [Note: [Col. 0925C] “Under the title of schism”: in the charge of schism; in book VII, however, “in this title,” that is, in this cause. Augustine, *Against Cresconius*, book II, ch. 10: “Discord does not possess under the title of peace.” Likewise: “What reason is there why the title should not be laid aside, so that peace may be laid aside?” ALBASP.] [Col. 0926B] [Note: [Col. 0926B] In manuscript S. T.: *in titulos*.] [Note: [Col. 0925C] “Under the title of schism”: in producing schism, at the beginning of their separation, at the outset of schism. DU PIN.] you appear long ago to have done and to be doing now.

They broke peace in their time; you destroy unity. [Note: [Col. 0925C] “You destroy unity”: Macarius wished to bring about unity and to compel the Donatist people, by arms and imperial authority, into the Catholic Church; the Donatists impeded that union. ALBASP.] Of your parents and of yourselves one may rightly say: “If a blind man leads a blind man, both fall into a pit” (Matt. 15:14). [Note: [Col. 0926B] In manuscript S. G.: “each falls into a pit.”]

[Note: [Col. 0925C] “Mad envy had blinded the eyes of your fathers, and emulation deprived yours of sight.” *Orbatio* (“bereavement,” “loss”) is said of eyes as it is of children; for these are very often compared with the former. Ausonius, *Parentalia*:

> You mourned your son, lost after three decades,  
> Wounded, and deprived of one light.

[Col. 0925D] Lipsius cited Quintilian’s passage from book VI, preface, in his *Epistolae Quaestiones*. Euripides, *Andromache*: “This child was the one remaining eye of my life.” Alcimus Ecdicius Avitus, book III, on the lost son, Luke 15:

> And the joyful gathering celebrates its solemn feast,  
> Because offspring, restored to its own, rises as if from some death,  
> And new lights return to the bereaved father.

Paulinus, *On the Death of Celsus*: “Celsus, love and longing, and the light of your own.” Ruricius uses the expression in the same sense in his letters. BARTH.]

Mad envy had blinded the eyes of your fathers; emulation has deprived yours of sight. You cannot possibly deny that schism is the supreme evil. Yet you have fearlessly imitated Dathan, Abiram, and Korah, your ruined masters; nor have you wished to set before your eyes that this evil was both forbidden by God’s words and, once committed, severely punished.

Moreover, the difference between offences is shown either by pardon or by punishment. Among the other commandments, divine injunction also forbade these three: “You shall not kill”; “you shall not go after foreign gods”; and, in the chief summary of the commandments, “you shall not make schism.” [Note: [Col. 0925D] “In the chief summary of the commandments.” Those who make schism and divide the Church appear to introduce several gods; and when they withdraw from the communion of the Church, they necessarily withdraw from God, with whom the Church is united [Col. 0926B] and joined together through Christ. The author in the same place: “They had in some sense declared war on God, as though there were another God who would receive another sacrifice.” ALBASP.]

[Note: [Col. 0925D] “And in the chief summary of the commandments: You shall not make schism.” These words, “You shall not make schism,” ought not to have been printed in different type as though they were the very words of Scripture quoted by Optatus. They neither exist now nor ever existed in any Greek or Latin version. Optatus himself suggests this when he says “in the chief summary of the commandments,” plainly referring to the Apostle’s words at Rom. 13:9: “For ‘You shall not commit adultery,’ etc., ‘and if there is any other commandment,’ it is summed up in this saying: ‘You shall love your neighbour as yourself.’”

What is now rendered “is summed up” was formerly read, at least by some, “is recapitulated,” as also in Eph. 1:10. Citing that passage, Tertullian, *Against Marcion*, book V, ch. 17, uses *recapitulate* in the sense of “make present again,” though elsewhere he renders it “bring back to the head,” and in another place “gather together to the beginning.” It is well known that schism is properly and chiefly reckoned among sins committed against one’s neighbour. “Among sins against one’s neighbour, the sin of schism seems to be greatest, because it is against the spiritual good of the multitude”: Aquinas, *Summa Theologiae*, II–II, question 39, article 2, reply to objection 3, etc. Thus “in the chief summary of the commandments” here means in the summary or recapitulation of the commandments.

Nevertheless, Albaspinaeus’s interpretation is not displeasing, referring it to the first commandment, since Optatus shortly afterward says: “God, to whom schism is displeasing, could not willingly behold this; they had in some sense declared war on God, as though there were another God,” etc. Both interpretations may be true if we say that Optatus had in view Christ’s words in [Col. 0926D] Matt. 22:37–38. M. CASAUBON.]

[Note: [Col. 0926D] “Let us consider these three.” He teaches that God punished schism more severely than homicide or idolatry. ALBASP.]

Let us consider these three: what ought to have been punished, and what deserved to be remitted. Parricide is the principal crime; yet Cain is not struck down by God as a guilty man, and when killed he is moreover avenged (Gen. 4). In the city of Nineveh there were one hundred and twenty thousand sacrilegious people who seemed to follow foreign gods; after God’s anger and the message of the prophet Jonah, a brief fast and prayer deserved pardon (Jonah 3). [Note: [Col. 0926D] “In the city of Nineveh there were one hundred and twenty thousand people,” etc. This error is not peculiar to Optatus. The very polished ecclesiastical writer Sulpicius, *Sacred History*, book I, says of Nineveh: “That city, formerly founded by Asshur son of Shem, was the capital of the Assyrian kingdom; it then nourished a dense population, one hundred and twenty thousand men, and, as is usual in a great people, abounded in vices.” Yet Scripture does not say that there were so many persons in the city altogether, but that there were so many who could not distinguish their right hand from their left. This surely cannot be understood except of very young children, unless one has recourse to allegorical interpretations. See Jerome and the glosses; see also Drusius. M. CASAUBON.] [Note: [Col. 0927B] In manuscript S. G.: “After a brief fast had been observed, they deserved pardon.”]

Let us see whether those who first dared to divide the people of God obtained anything like this. Over so many thousands of the children of Israel, from whose necks divine providence had cast off the yoke of slavery, it had set one holy priest, Aaron (Num. 16). But when his ministers, coveting a priesthood not owed to them, unlawfully invaded it after leading astray a portion of the people, imitating the rite of sacred observances, they placed before the deceived people two hundred and some additional ministers, doomed to perish with them, holding censers. [Note: [Col. 0927B] Omitted in manuscript S. G.]

God, to whom schism is displeasing, could not willingly behold this. They had in some sense declared war on God, as though there were another God who would receive another sacrifice. Therefore God was angry with great wrath because his commandments had been disregarded, [Note: [Col. 0927B] Thus in manuscripts S. T. and P. S., from which the word *his* has been supplied; it was absent from the printed editions. The copyist of codex S. G. seems to have explained the words on his own initiative, substituting “because schism had been made.”] and what he had not done against sacrilegious persons and the parricide, [Col. 0927B] he did against schismatics.

The ranks of ministers and the sacrilegious multitude stood there, their sacrifices forbidden and themselves immediately destined to perish. Time for repentance was denied and withdrawn, because this was not the kind of offence that deserved pardon. Hunger was commanded upon the earth: immediately it opened its jaws upon the dividers of the people, [Note: [Col. 0927B] In manuscript S. G.: “upon the death of the divider of the people,” less well.] and with greedy mouth [Note: [Col. 0927B] In manuscript S. G.: “gaping.”] [Col. 0928A] swallowed the despisers of God’s commandments.

[Note: [Col. 0927C] Below: “within the space of a moment, to swallow,” etc. He said *transglutire* for *deglutire* (“swallow down”). Thus Cyprian—or Tertullian?—in the poem *Genesis*, verses 31 and 57, uses *transvena* for *advena* (“a newcomer”). UNCERTAIN.]

[Note: [Col. 0927C] “Within the space of a moment,” etc. Optatus here employs, with elegance, the style called *asyndeton* to express the speed of the event, as though he imitated Caesar’s “I came, I saw, I conquered.” Indeed, many things testify to his uncommon elegance and no less to his talent, especially when he narrates or describes something. Would that his learning had equalled it. For, when he argues, he is commonly deficient; but I do not wish to speak more harshly of a holy man, especially since this was the misfortune of the times rather than of the man. M. CASAUBON.]

Within the space of a moment, the earth opened to swallow the aforesaid persons, seized them, and closed again. And lest they should seem to receive the benefit of a swift death, since they were unworthy to live, they were not even permitted to die: suddenly shut in a Tartarean prison, they were buried before they were dead.

And do you wonder that something of this kind has been done harshly to you, who either make or cultivate schism, [Note: [Col. 0927B] In manuscript S. G.: “who, under the usurped name of Church, either make schism or gather [people].”] when you see what the first teachers of schism deserved to suffer? [Note: [Col. 0927B] In manuscript S. G.: “your primitive masters.”] [Note: [Col. 0927D] “Or because such vengeance now ceases.” Tertullian, *On Patience*: “[God delays] in order to take patience from himself; for many do not believe in the Lord for this reason, because they do not know that he has been angry with the world for so long.” ALBASP.]

Or, because such vengeance now ceases, do you claim innocence for yourself and yours? In every matter God has established a pattern by examples, so that he may have something to charge against those who imitate them: he restrained the first sins by a present punishment as an example; the second he will reserve for judgement. [Note: [Col. 0927D] “So that he may have something to charge against those who imitate the first sins.” The *and* is not idle here but has great and elegant force. “So that,” he says, “he may rightly have something to charge against them, and so render inexcusable whomever continue to imitate the first sinners, whom God punished so exemplarily.” What follows in the same sentence—“the present punishment restrained [them] as an example; he will reserve the second for judgement”—cannot yield any satisfactory sense. I think anyone will readily agree with me that, by a slight and almost insignificant alteration of letters, it should be corrected: “When the present punishment has gone before as an example, he will reserve the second for judgement,” or “the second will be reserved for judgement.” When, he says, a present punishment—that is, one exacted in this world publicly and in everyone’s sight—has gone before as an example, it is no wonder if God does not exact similar punishments from all schismatics, since he has reserved for universal judgement the second and every subsequent punishment owed on that account to sinners. These words may also be understood more broadly of sinners of every kind. M. CASAUBON.]

[Note: [Col. 0927B] This passage has seemed extremely difficult to some and has been variously tortured by various persons. Yet its meaning is easy and plain, if only it is punctuated as we have done, as is observed in manuscript S. T.; that is, if “the first sins” is referred not to the participle “those who imitate,” but to what follows. Then there is no further obscurity in the latter member: “As an example, present punishment restrained the first sins; he will reserve the second for judgement.” The passage stands in manuscripts S. T. and P. S. as it lies here, except that after *imputet* (“he may charge”) the conjunction *and* is added: “he may charge, and [against] those who imitate”—which appears superfluous. But the copyist of codex S. G., not understanding the passage, corrupted and interpolated it thus: “In every matter God established a pattern of examples, so that he might have something to charge against those who imitate: setting forth the first commandments as an example, present punishment restrained [them]; he will reserve the second for judgement.”]

What will you say to this, you who nourish schism under the usurped name of Church and secretly, [Note: [Col. 0928B] In manuscript S. G.: *stulte*, “foolishly.”] [Col. 0928B] and defend it shamelessly?

## XXII. Letters of the bishops of Donatus’s party to Emperor Constantine, requesting judges

But because I hear that certain persons of your association possess some documents, through a zeal for litigation, [Note: [Col. 0928B] In manuscript S. G.: *litigantes*, “litigants,” but incorrectly.] [Note: [Col. 0928D] “To possess documents”: imperial mandates, acts of councils, letters of Mensurius, and similar things mentioned in the Conference. ALBASP.] it must be asked which documents deserve credit, which agree with reason, and which accord with truth. [Note: [Col. 0928D] “Which accord with truth.” Barth uses *confabulari* in the sense of “agree.”]

[Note: [Col. 0928D] “Which accord with truth.” I have not observed this word elsewhere in that sense. I judge it spurious, and would substitute *confibulentur* (“are joined together”). Tertullian uses this more than once, indeed with the preceding word “harmony” or “harmonise,” as here. In *On the Trinity*—whether that work be the offspring of Tertullian or of Novatian—speaking of Christ: “For if he came to humanity in order to be mediator between God and human beings, he had to be with humanity, and the Word had to become flesh, so that [Col. 0929B] he might join together in himself the harmony of earthly and heavenly things, binding in himself the pledges of both parts,” etc. Again, at the end of the immediately following chapter, *concordia* and *confibulatio* are joined together. M. CASAUBON.]

[Note: [Col. 0928C] In the manuscripts: *confabulent*. In the printed editions: *confabulentur*. Most suitably for the sense: *confibulent*, meaning “harmonise” or “be connected.” *Fibulare* is used in this sense by Columella.]

If you have any documents, yours may perhaps appear tainted with lies. Our documents are proved by the conflicts of the cases, the disputes of the parties, the outcomes of the judgements, and Constantine’s letters. For when you say of us, “What have Christians to do with kings?” or “What have bishops to do with the palace?” [Note: [Col. 0929B] “With the palace.” They did not use these words at the beginning of the schism. For when they did not submit to the Council of Arles and to the supreme pontiff, after all those judgements they sought help from the palace. ALBASP.] if it is a disgrace to know kings, you are wholly covered with odium. [Note: [Col. 0929B] “If it is known”: if it is a fault. ALBASP.] [Note: [Col. 0929A] Omitted in manuscript S. G.]

For your predecessors—Lucianus, Dignus, Nasutius, Capito, Fidentius, and the rest—addressed the emperor Constantine, still ignorant of these matters, with these petitions, a copy of which is written below: “We beseech you, most excellent Emperor Constantine, [Note: [Col. 0929B] “We beseech you,” etc. This is the unsigned petition which they handed to Anulinus together with the indictment of Caecilian, asking that it be sent by him to the imperial court, as is clear from Anulinus’s report in Augustine, *Letter* 88. DU PIN.] since you are of a righteous stock, [Note: [Col. 0929B] “Of a righteous stock”: his father in Gaul and Britain had not persecuted Christians. ALBASP.] whose father, among the other emperors, [Col. 0930A] did not conduct persecution, and Gaul is free from this crime; [Note: [Col. 0929C] “From this crime”: from the cruelty which the other emperors exercised against Christians. ALBASP.] [Note: [Col. 0929A] In manuscripts S. T. and P. S.: *ob* rather than *ab*.] for in Africa disputes exist between us and the other bishops. We request that your piety command judges to be given to us from Gaul.” [Note: [Col. 0929C] “That [judges] be [given] from Gaul.” Yet of nineteen judges only three were from Gaul; the others were chosen and added by the supreme pontiff, to whom the emperor had lawfully entrusted the hearing of the case. ALBASP.] [Note: [Col. 0929C] “From Gaul”: because Constantine was then in Gaul. DU PIN.]

Given by Lucianus, Dignus, Nasutius, Capito, Fidentius, and the other bishops of Donatus’s party. [Note: [Col. 0929C] “And the others of Donatus’s party.” Therefore the schism received its name from Donatus of Casae Nigrae; whence it follows that Donatus of Carthage did not give this sect its name, since his ordination is assigned by the most eminent Cardinal Baronius to the year 331. ALBASP.] [Note: [Col. 0929C] “Donatus’s party.” Read: “Majorinus’s party”; for in Anulinus’s report it reads: “The petition of the Catholic Church concerning Caecilian’s crimes, handed over by Majorinus’s party.” Augustine too, whenever he speaks of this petition, says that it was presented by Majorinus’s party. But because the party that was first called Majorinus’s was, in Optatus’s time, called Donatus’s party, he substituted the better-known name for the old one. Further, that petition was presented at the beginning of 313; for Anulinus’s report was issued at Carthage on 15 April, in Constantine Augustus’s third consulship, which falls in A.D. 313. It is likely that the petitions had been presented not long before. Perhaps it was even written, “on behalf of Donatus’s party,” because Donatus of Casae Nigrae was already their standard-bearer and Caecilian’s chief accuser, as appears from the proceedings of the Roman council. DU PIN.]

## XXIII. Constantine’s response: judges appointed by him to meet at Rome

[Note: [Col. 0929D] “After these had been read.” Those bishops had not presented their petition directly, but had given it to Anullinus, proconsul of Africa, to be sent onward. ALBASP.]

After these had been read, Constantine replied with full indignation. [Note: [Col. 0930B] “With full indignation”: he was astonished that bishops sought judges from laypersons. ALBASP.] [Note: [Col. 0930A] In manuscript S. G.: “petition” in place of “indignation.”] [Note: [Col. 0930B] “Constantine replied with full indignation.” These are words from Constantine’s letter to the bishops of the Council of Arles, and therefore are not inserted by Optatus in their proper place. DU PIN.]

In that reply he also exposed their petitions, saying: “You seek judgement from me, who am in the world, [Note: [Col. 0930B] “You seek [judgement] from me in the world.” This response deserves notice: the emperor wished to show that bishops’ disputes ought rather to be judged by bishops themselves, who bear Christ’s office, than by laypersons. ALBASP.] [Note: [Col. 0930B] “In the world”: from me, who am not of the communion and body of bishops. ALBASP.] [Note: [Col. 0930A] In place of this word, manuscript S. G. has “bishops.”] [Note: [Col. 0930B] “Judgement”: “judges,” for they had not asked the emperor to hear their controversy himself, but to appoint judges. ALBASP.] when I myself await Christ’s judgement.” [Note: [Col. 0930B] “When I myself”: I ought rather to be judged by you. ALBASP.]

[Note: [Col. 0930C] “And yet judges were appointed.” Namely, three from Gaul: Maternus, Marinus, and Rheticius; for the other fifteen were selected and added by Melchiades. Moreover, there survives Constantine’s letter to Melchiades concerning this case, whose heading reads: “To Melchiades, bishop of Rome, and Marcus, greetings.” Interpreters have enough trouble explaining these words, for it is not easy to guess why he placed that Marcus with the supreme pontiff, or who and what sort of person Marcus was.

Nothing in this matter seems more probable than the conjecture of the most eminent Cardinal du Perron, who suspected that one should read *καὶ ἱεραρχῷ*—that is, “to Melchiades, Roman hierarch.” The other suggestions are either empty or trifling: for example, the claim that the emperor wrote to the deacon Marcus along with Melchiades, lest superiors stand out without inferiors and so that the variety of ranks in ecclesiastical communion might appear. Yet, when he issued letters concerning the same case and business to Xystus of Syracuse and to other bishops of Gaul, Spain, and Africa, he mentioned deacons so that the variety of ranks might not pass without greeting. Or must it be said that Xystus was punished together with his deacon lest the higher ranks stand out in martyrdom without the lower, and that Caesars hostile to the Christian name observed this hierarchy of grades in punishments and tortures?

Nor are the words of St Cyprian to Pope Cornelius more relevant, because the letter from which they are taken was a letter of greeting, belonging to the class called “peace-bearing” and “communicatory” letters—as are the letters of St Paul—by which communion was cultivated among those absent and far apart. Therefore it is no wonder that such letters mention persons of every rank, or that St Cyprian or St Paul mentioned deacons when they wrote communicatory letters to churches or bishops. ALBASP.]

[Note: [Col. 0930D] “And yet judges were appointed.” Albaspinaeus here takes an untimely occasion to digress on the heading of Constantine’s letter to Melchiades. For, while contributing nothing new himself, he falsely attributes to Cardinal du Perron the old conjecture of Baronius, correcting *καὶ Μαρκῷ* to *ἱεραρχῷ*, which learned men had long ago rejected. Du Perron was so ashamed of it—as is clear from his latest writing to the king of England—that he thought anything should be devised rather than that the Baronian conjecture should even be deemed worthy of mention. M. CASAUBON.]

Yet judges were appointed: Maternus from the city of Agrippina, [Col. 0931A] Rheticius [Note: [Col. 0931A] Thus in manuscript S. G. Manuscripts S. T. and P. S. read *Reticus*.] from the city of Augustodunum, and Marinus of Arles. These three Gauls came to the city of Rome, together with fifteen other Italians. [Note: [Col. 0931B] “And fifteen other [Italians]”: whom Melchiades had summoned. ALBASP.]

They met in Fausta’s house in the Lateran, [Note: [Col. 0931B] “In Fausta’s house in the Lateran.” Constantine’s letter to Ablavius says that they shut themselves up in a certain place. ALBASP.] [Note: [Col. 0931A] In the manuscripts: “in the Laterani.”] [Note: [Col. 0931B] “In Fausta’s house in the Lateran”: namely, that part of the Lateran palace assigned as the dwelling of the empress Fausta. DU PIN.] in the consulship of Constantine for the fourth time [Note: [Col. 0931C] “Constantine for the fourth time and Licinius for the third, consuls.” Baronius and Balduin judge that this is the correct reading, but Augustine records: “Constantine for the third time and Licinius for the second, consuls.” ALBASP.] and Licinius for the third time, on the sixth day before the Nones of October, [Note: [Col. 0931C] “Constantine for the fourth time.” We have altered nothing in the text, since it is so written in the manuscripts; but Augustine, *Post Collationem*, book I, ch. 33, says: “Melchiades judged in the consulship of Constantine for the third time and Licinius for the second, on the sixth day before the Nones of October.” It is certain that one must read “Constantine in his third consulship,” for his fourth consulship fell in 315, after the Roman and Arles councils. [Note: [Col. 0931C] “On Friday.” In former times the days of the week were not divided by the days of Jupiter, Venus, and the Sun, but by ferias. The sixth feria was Friday—that is, for Christians a day of mourning and station, on which they stood in church from early morning until the third hour. [Col. 0931D] I therefore do not know how they could have judged this case on a Friday. ALBASP.]

## XXIV. The Roman council’s decision in Caecilian’s favour

With these nineteen bishops seated, the case of Donatus [Note: [Col. 0931D] “The case of Donatus.” Thus Donatus of Casae Nigrae was already [Col. 0932B] the leading accuser of Caecilian. DU PIN.] and Caecilian was brought forward. [Note: [Col. 0932B] “Brought forward”: debated and examined. ALBASP.] [Note: [Col. 0932B] “Brought forward.” The case was heard over three days, for it is established from the heading 323 of the Conference of Carthage and from the *Breviculus of the Conference*, day 13, ch. 17, that there were three hearings. Each pronounced this judgement against Donatus: [Note: [Col. 0932B] “Each”: either those bishops who had met in Fausta’s house, or those who had come with Caecilian or Donatus. ALBASP.] [Note: [Col. 0932B] “Against Donatus”: Donatus of Casae Nigrae. ALBASP.] [Note: [Col. 0932B] “These judgements were pronounced.” In councils, the judgements of all bishops were not merely counted, but each was entered in the records and reported in the very words in which it had been given, as may be seen in certain councils and in the Council of Carthage held under St Cyprian. Optatus therefore meant that Donatus had been condemned by the individual judgements of all those bishops, and that none of them had failed to establish this judgement against him in the same terms. ALBASP.]

“Because he confessed that he had rebaptised, [Note: [Col. 0932B] “Because he confessed.” It is probable that Caecilian used a formal charge and accused Donatus before Melchiades [Col. 0932C] of rebaptising. ALBASP.] [Note: [Col. 0932C] “Of rebaptising”: namely, persons baptised by orthodox Christians after the schism; those washed before the schism were not rebaptised by the Donatists. ALBASP.] [Note: [Col. 0932A] In manuscripts S. T. and Ph. S.: *rebaptizare*, “to rebaptise.”] [Note: [Col. 0932C] “Because he confessed that he had rebaptised”: namely, persons baptised by Catholics. DU PIN.] and had laid hands upon lapsed bishops—”

[Note: [Col. 0932C] “Lapsed bishops”: those who had handed over sacred books to be burned or had offered incense. In antiquity, *lapsi* (“the lapsed”) did not mean persons who had committed homicide or any other sin, however grave, but only those who had sacrificed to idols or in some manner abandoned the faith. ALBASP.]

[Note: [Col. 0932C] “And had laid hands upon lapsed bishops,” etc. Albaspinaeus is extensive in his observations, assembling many passages of Optatus as so many arguments to prove that this laying on of hands—of which Optatus speaks here—should be understood not as reordination of bishops who defected to the Donatists, as Balduin and some other learned men explained it, but as the *cheirothesia* (laying on of hands) for penitents. Certainly, in most places where Optatus mentions hands laid on by Donatists, no one will, I think, deny that he means penitents; the very words sufficiently establish it. Yet, since it is probable—however much Albaspinaeus denies it—that some persons had already then been reordained by them, nothing prevents these words from being understood of such persons. Nevertheless, the words of Pope Leo, distinction 50, canon 67, strongly persuade me that this should rather be understood of the *cheirothesia* of penitents: “It is contrary to ecclesiastical ordinance that those consecrated in presbyteral rank or in the grade of the diaconate should, for some crime of their own, receive through the laying on of hands a remedy of repentance.”

M. CASAUBON.]

[Note: [Col. 0932D] “Had laid hands.” We have shown in the observations that these words must be explained as the laying on of hands for penance, not as reordination.]

ALBASP.] that they had imposed hands on fallen bishops. [Note: [Col. 0933A] *That they had imposed hands on fallen bishops.* That is, they had imposed hands for penance upon those bishops whom they accused of being traditores—a practice contrary to ecclesiastical custom, as St. Leo has it in the letter now numbered 2 to Rusticus of Narbonne, replying in these words: “It is contrary to ecclesiastical custom that those who have been consecrated in priestly rank or in the office of deacon should, for any fault of their own, receive through imposition of hands a remedy of penance.” This doubtless descends from apostolic tradition. What St. Leo affirms here concerning presbyters and deacons is much more clearly established concerning bishops. Some understand this of episcopal imposition of hands, or reordination; but Optatus nowhere accuses the Donatists of having ordained Catholic bishops a second time. Indeed, it is evident from him that hands were imposed for penance upon fallen bishops by those who stood on Donatus’s side. Yet it is not likely that they subsequently made bishops of those whom they had driven into penance. Indeed, as we have just observed, Purpurius of Limata wished to impose hands on Caecilian for this purpose: that his head might be shaken in penance—that is, that he might be cast down not merely from every rank, but even from every hope [Col. 0933C] of receiving the episcopate. But what need is there to hunt out Optatus’s meaning, when he himself explains it expressly in Book II, §25, where, speaking of the imposition of hands employed by the Donatists, he says: “It is known and proved to many that, in the time of persecution, certain bishops, having fallen away from confessing God’s name through inertia, offered incense; yet none of those who escaped either imposed hands on the fallen or commanded them to bend the knee. And today, after unity, you do what no one did after the offering of incense.” The Donatists therefore sinned: first, against ecclesiastical law and custom, which forbade the imposition of hands for penance upon fallen bishops; secondly, against justice, by imposing hands for penance upon innocent Catholic bishops—not, however, by reordaining bishops who had been driven into penance. DU PIN.]; [Col. 0933A] a thing alien to the Church.

[Note: [Col. 0933C] *Witnesses produced by Donatus.* In Constantine’s letters each party was permitted to bring from Africa to Rome ten witnesses necessary to its case. ALBASP.]

The witnesses produced by Donatus confessed that they had nothing to say against Caecilian. >

That he is not accused according to his profession.* Does he mean that they had failed to do what they had professed they would do—namely, accuse Caecilian—and had abandoned the role of accusers which they had undertaken? >

Yet I do not deny that these words can be explained otherwise, and that “I judge that Caecilian must be retained in unimpaired status in his own communion” can mean that Caecilian, together with all who communicate with him, must be retained in Catholic communion. ### XXV. Donatus’s appeal from the Roman judgment, and Constantine’s response to it

It is sufficient, therefore, that Donatus was struck down by so many judgments, and Caecilian cleared by so great a tribunal. Yet Donatus [Note: [Col. 0934C] *That an appeal should be made from the bishops.* He did not wish to say “from Melchiades,” lest he injure the authority of the supreme pontiff. ALBASP.] thought that an appeal should be made [Note: [Col. 0934D] *That an appeal should be made.* Strictly speaking, he did not appeal from the Roman judges, but complained of their judgment, as Augustine often observes. ### XXVI. What was done in Africa after the Roman synod

[Note: [Col. 0935B] *At the same time the same Donatus requested permission to return.* [Col. 0935C] Balduin thought that here should follow the history of the Council of Arles and Constantine’s investigation or judgment at Milan. But I agree rather with Baronius, who judges that these matters belong after Felix’s acquittal, not before; and this may, if necessary, be confirmed by fresh arguments. Yet whether anything at all is missing, and whether all that is lacking in Optatus on this matter was not omitted by Optatus himself, I think Balduin had reason to doubt. For, even if I grant what Baronius especially presses—that an event famous throughout the world could not have been unknown to Optatus—I nevertheless think it could have happened that the matters he omitted were not so fully established for him, and so forth; and that he lacked the records of what he was to report, as likewise of everything else which preceded. Moreover, since almost everything pronounced afterward by the Council of Arles or Constantine depended upon the credibility and truth of the proceedings for the acquittal of Felix, Caecilian’s ordainer, before Aelianus, proconsul of Africa, it mattered little for Africans to learn what had been discovered and pronounced [Col. 0935D] so far away, once they were certain of the truth of matters done at home, that is, in Africa. The African proceedings sufficed for this purpose. M. CASAUB.]

S. read: “that it might be granted to him, when returning to Carthage,” which lacks sense. Hence it is clear that Caecilian was detained at Brescia only because Donatus had been ordered not to approach Carthage. [Note: [Col. 0936D] *In this manner the factions were again renewed*, etc. He means that the conflict broke out anew, again inflamed by fresh partisan zeal. *Renovellare*, “to renew,” means “to restore,” and is derived from vines. From the answers of all, nothing was found in the life of Bishop Felix on account of which he could not have ordained [Note: [Col. 0938C] *To tarnish the life of Bishop Felix.* *Sordidare* means “to make filthy,” as Sidonius Apollinaris often uses it. *Limpidare* occurs in Caelius Aurelianus and Pliny Valerianus with the opposite meaning. G. reads: “which the life of Bishop Felix could not [Col. 0938B] have ordained.” From these readings the passage can easily be restored as we have restored it. The matter concerned Caecilian’s ordination: the Donatists alleged it void because of the crime of handing over sacred books committed by Felix. The alleged crime was found false, and therefore there was nothing in his life on account of which he could not have ordained Caecilian.] [Caecilian].

There is a volume of proceedings [Note: [Col. 0938B] MSS S. T. and P. S. have *volumina*, “volumes,” but the following reads *in quo*, “in which,” not *in quibus*, “in which [plural]”; hence *volumen*, singular, should be read.] containing the names of those present in the case of Claudius Saturianus, curator; Caecilianus, magistrate; Superius, stationarius; Ingentius, clerk; and Solon, public official [Note: [Col. 0938C] *Solon, public official.* He is called a public slave in Constantine’s letter. DU PIN.] of that time. After their answers, this portion of the judgment was pronounced by the aforesaid proconsul:

G., in agreement with the proceedings for Felix’s acquittal in the Cormaric manuscript. MSS S. T. and P. S. have *prodiderit*, “betrayed.”]

[Note: [Col. 0938D]  
*For the examination of all those named above clearly establishes that no writings*, etc. Francis Balduin varies here also: “for the examination of all above clearly establishes that no writings . . .” Barth corrects: “for the hand of all the interrogations has testified.” “But,” he says, “this is the proconsular judgment.” By Hercules, he has not done badly; but it may also seem possible to read: “for it is clear from all the interrogated persons,” etc.; or perhaps Optatus wrote: “for it is clear from the testimony of all the interrogated persons,” etc. We often complain that one or two words have dropped out through copyists’ carelessness in reading authors. INCERT.

*Ibid. For the examination of all*, etc. “Examination” must here be understood as the whole proceeding, including the answers. For it is not, properly and strictly, the examination of the judge or investigator, but the answers of witnesses or accused persons, that make the matter clear. Thus, a little before, this judgment of the proconsul is said to have followed the answers of those examined. Relevant is Tertullian, *On the Resurrection of the Flesh*, ch. 48, who interpreted the Greek ἐπερώτημα in 1 Peter 3 as *responsio*, “answer,” in these words: “For the soul is sanctified not by washing but by an answer”; as was long ago observed by a learned interpreter. M. CASAUB.]

For the examination of all those named above clearly establishes [Note: [Col. 0938B] Thus MS S. G. and the proceedings, correctly. Less well, MSS S. T. and P. S. have *interrogantium*, “of those questioning.”] that no divine writings had been either found, corrupted, or burned. [Col. 0938B] The proceedings contain the fact that [Col. 0939A] Felix, the reverend bishop, was neither present at that time, nor [Note: [Col. 0939B] *Nor accommodated his conscience.* He neither ordered that letter to be written nor gave his consent for books to be taken from the shrines of the martyrs. ALBASP.] gave his consent, nor ordered anything of the sort to be done. Therefore, when the slander had been driven away [Note: [Col. 0939B] MS S. G. has *repulsa*, “driven back.”] and wiped out, he withdrew from that judgment with great praise.

For a long time the truth had seemed to lie hidden amid uncertain opinion and the mists exhaled by spite and envy. But now every document mentioned, [Note: [Col. 0939B] *But now every document mentioned*, etc. From this too one may infer how little reliance should always be placed either on the soundness of the manuscript codices upon which Balduin based this second edition [Col. 0939C] or on Balduin’s own judgment. Since the principal editions of Optatus formerly read *revelata est*, “was disclosed,” Balduin congratulates himself that he was the first to restore *renovata*, “renewed,” from his manuscript copy; he imagined that no one would doubt the truth of the correction. Yet any intelligent reader will readily observe how mutilated and incomplete the preceding period hangs because of this correction, and how difficult it is to draw anything sound or clear from it. By contrast, if one retains the earlier reading and restores *ea jam* for *etiam*—“but now that whole document mentioned,” etc. (errors of this kind are among the easiest in all writing)—then everything will cohere excellently, so that nothing can be clearer or plainer. M. CASAUB.] was disclosed by the volumes of proceedings [Note: [Col. 0939C] *Disclosed by the letters mentioned or read.* Fr. Balduin, from a manuscript, has “renewed.” INCERT.] and by the letters mentioned or read. [Note: [Col. 0939B] MS P. S. has *renovata*, “renewed,” not well.]

### XXVIII. Conclusion of this first book

You see, brother Parmenian, that the accusation of being traditores, falsely brought against Catholics, [Note: [Col. 0939C] *Was invented in vain.* It would scarcely be worth noting that *inventum* here means *invectum*, “brought against,” unless all the editions I have seen made the same error in this very word. But for the following Latin to be coherent and appropriate, a new period must begin at *mutans*, “changing,” and what follows must be connected suitably as it is here, not as in other editions. Although, if I maintained that *mutans* was here used for *mutantem*, no one who had observed similar solecisms in more than one place in the earlier writer Lucifer of Cagliari—not to mention others—would be greatly surprised. Granted this, everyone sees how much better the following sentence begins after *clausisti*, “you closed.” Victor too, though not much better, in Book 2: “He burned a vigorous and very learned man in a fire, thinking that by instilling fear through such an example he would crush the rest”; and in Book 3: “In a throng and funeral procession of young men, old men, boys, and also girls, wherever they could and however they could, they spread abroad everywhere, going round towns, villages, and individual cities.” M. CASAUB.] was invented in vain: you changed the persons and transferred the guilt. You closed your eyes so that you would not recognize your own forefathers as guilty; you opened them in order to join innocent persons, undeserving of accusation, to the charge. [Col. 0940A] Everything according to expediency, nothing according to truth. Thus the blessed Apostle Paul may have said also of you: “But certain persons have turned aside into empty talk, desiring to be teachers of the law, without understanding either what they say or the things concerning which they make confident assertions” (1 Tim. 1:6).

A little earlier we showed that your forefathers were traditores and schismatics; and you are their heir. [Note: [Col. 0939B] MS S. T. adds *fuisse*, “were.”]

[Note: [Col. 0940B]  
*And you were unwilling to spare traditores.* You are heir of traditores; hence I wonder all the more why you are unwilling to spare Catholics, whom you call traditores. ALBASP.

*Ibid. And you were unwilling to spare traditores.* Since a few words earlier Optatus complains that Parmenian has changed persons and transferred accusations, I think that, in order to complete the thought, we must read a double *nos*, “us,” for the double *nec*, “nor”: “us schismatics, us traditores,” etc. He used *parere* in the sense of “to represent as having begotten” or “to declare born,” as in the great poet in these verses:

> Who would strew the ground with flowering grasses  
> [Col. 0940C] . . . ?

Here *spargeret*, “would strew,” means “would sing that it had been strewn.” And again:

> Then he surrounds the Phaethon’s daughters with the moss of bitter bark  
> and raises tall alders from the ground, etc.

There *circumdat*, “surrounds,” and *erigit*, “raises,” mean “sings that they had been surrounded and raised,” as Servius observed. So Leviticus 13: “the priest shall make unclean and shall make clean”; and Jeremiah 1:10: “Behold, I have set you today over nations and kingdoms, to pluck up and to destroy,” etc. Also Hebrews 7:3: ἀπάτωρ, ἀμήτωρ, ἀγενεαλόγητος, “without father, without mother, without genealogy.” The Syriac interpreter: “whose father and mother are not written in the descent or genealogy,” as though ἀγενεαλόγητος had been added merely as an explanation of the preceding words. Thus those are said by Aristotle to γὲννᾷν τὸν οὐρανὸν, “beget the heaven,” who wrote that heaven was begotten or created; as was observed by my late parent in his note on Persius, “if any [Col. 0940D] Procnes,” etc. The following may be added to make this conjecture more plausible: as is sufficiently clear from what precedes, Parmenian undertook to accuse Optatus’s ancestors, not to excuse his own. Since no controversy had hitherto arisen even about their legitimate descent, he thought his own forefathers did not require this defense; and he assumed that whatever was vehemently said against traditores in general, without definite persons or names, related to Optatus’s ancestors or predecessors—as our author here testifies. But a learned and acute man, who perhaps visited me at Canterbury because of our friendship when these pages were being printed in London, conjectured that *parcere*, “to spare,” should be read for *parere*, “to obey” or “to produce”; thus no other correction is needed. Although I cannot yet wholly agree with him, I admit that his conjecture pleased me so greatly that I would not deprive the reader of it. M. CASAUB.]

And you were unwilling to spare either schismatics or traditores. [Note: [Col. 0939B] We restore this from MS S. G.; it is the genuine reading, although MSS S. T. and P. The others have *quia*, “because.”] we remain both in the root and, throughout the whole world, are with all. [Note: [Col. 0940B] Here, as usual, the manuscripts conclude: “The first book ends.”]

## BOOK TWO

[Note: [Col. 0941B] In MS S. T. the chapter headings of Book Two begin here. MS S. G. has: “Summary of the second book.”]

In this second little book it is declared what the one true Catholic Church is, where it is and among whom it abides; that the five endowments of the Church are found more truly in the Catholic Church than in the party which the schismatics wished to make for themselves; that they impiously shaved the heads of priests with the razor of penance; that they committed murders; and that they either gave to dogs or threw away those things which had been provided for the salvation of believers.

[Note: [Col. 0941B] After the summary the manuscripts read: “Book Two begins.”]

[Col. 0941]

[Col. 0941A] I. What the Catholic Church is, where it is, and that it is spread throughout the whole world. — Since it has also been shown who the *traditores* were, and since the origin of the schism has been so displayed that it may almost seem to have been seen with the eyes; and since we have shown how heresy differs from schism: it is now the next thing to demonstrate [Note: [Col. 0942B] In MS S. G.: “is now immediately at hand.”] (what we promised to discuss secondly) what is the one Church which Christ calls his dove and bride. ALBASP.] whose holiness is gathered from the sacraments, not weighed by the pride of persons.
