They said that all others were infected, corrupted, and impure through the crime of the *traditio*, because they had communion with *traditores*. DU PIN.] Therefore Christ calls this one Church his dove and beloved bride. It cannot exist among all heretics and schismatics. It remains, then, that it exists in one place.

[Note: [Col. 0941C] **You, brother Parmenian, said that it was among you alone, etc.** I read it as a question: “Did you say?” that is, “Did you endure to say it? Have you reached such madness as to say it?” Unless perhaps “therefore, so that,” etc., should be read otherwise. What follows likewise, down to “from them therefore, so that,” is far more graceful and emphatic when the question is continued through several periods. For it makes the speech more forceful, as the argument here requires it to be. You will therefore read: “So then, can it exist among you in a portion of Africa, in a corner of a small region, but not among us in another part of Africa? Will it not exist in Spain, Gaul, Italy, where you are not?” etc. If anyone prefers to take it sarcastically without a question, I do not object, although I approve the former interpretation more. M. CASAUB.]

You, brother Parmenian, said that it was among you alone—unless perhaps because you strive arrogantly to claim a special holiness for yourselves—[Col. 0941B] so that the Church may be where you wish it to be, and may not be where you do not wish it to be. [Col. 0942A] So then, can it exist among you in a portion of Africa, in a corner of a small region, and not exist among us in another part of Africa? Will it not exist in Spain, Gaul, and Italy, where you are not? If you wish it to exist only among yourselves, will it not exist in the three Pannonias, Dacia, Moesia, Thrace, Achaia, Macedonia, and throughout all Greece, where you are not? So that it may exist among you, will it not exist in Pontus, Galatia, Cappadocia, Pamphylia, Phrygia, Cilicia, the three Syrias, the two Armenias, all Egypt, and Mesopotamia, where you are not? And through so many innumerable islands and the remaining provinces, which can scarcely be counted, where you are not—will it not exist?

[Note: [Col. 0941D] **Where, then, is the proper force of the name “Catholic”?** How can the Church be Catholic if you drive it out of all those provinces and confine it within such very narrow boundaries? ALBASP.]

Where, then, will be the proper force of the name “Catholic,” since it is called [Col. 0942B] Catholic because it is [Note: [Col. 0941D]

**“Since it is called Catholic because it is rational,” etc.** Nothing could be said more contrary to Optatus’s meaning—not to mention the matter itself—than what Balduin here adduces: namely, that Optatus calls the Church “rational” because it is perceived not so much by the eyes as by reason, that is, grasped by mind and understanding. Wherever that interpretation may have force, it certainly cannot have a place here. Not to mention that *rationabilis* and *rationalis* are different words, though this interpretation recklessly confuses them. Moreover, who does not see that Optatus’s argument is drawn here from the force of the word itself and the etymology of the name *Catholic*? Yet among all grammarians and scholars of languages, was there ever anyone who thought that it was called Catholic because it was rational and spread everywhere?

As regards “rational,” I do not deny that in an ancient glossary *katholikous* (καθολικούς) is translated *rationales*, “rational,” and translated very well. Yet those who know who are called *rationales* or *Catholici* in law and among certain ancient writers, and who know the ancient usage of both names, will concede that this has absolutely nothing to do with the present passage. Whether this was, however, the cause of Optatus’s error, I would not readily say. But I confidently maintain that he plainly believed that “Catholic” was called, as it were, “rational and spread everywhere.” Such was the great, indeed the thoroughly Catholic, ignorance of Greek that even men otherwise very learned frequently fell into similar errors.

We could demonstrate this by the most certain arguments if we thought there were anyone acquainted with reading the ancients who could doubt it. To avoid seeking proofs far away, who would not be equally astonished at that derivation of the name *Catholic*—“obedience of all,” or “one everywhere”—which Pacian nevertheless expressly affirms? Let anyone who does not believe me hear Pacian himself, *Letter I to Sempronianus*: “Finally, if an account must be given of the term *Catholic*, and it must be rendered from Greek in a Latin interpretation: *Catholic* is called ‘one everywhere,’ or, as the more learned suppose, ‘the obedience of all,’ namely, to God’s commands. Hence the Apostle: ‘If you are obedient in all things,’ etc.” Shortly afterward: “But if ‘Catholic’ is ‘one everywhere,’ as those above suppose,” etc. Yet Pacian is one who yields neither in antiquity—he was even earlier by several years—nor in learning to Optatus.

Come then: at the Conference of Carthage, when nearly all the African bishops had assembled and the most learned men among them all had been selected to undertake the case on behalf of the rest, what finally did they determine concerning the name *Catholic*? That *Catholic* comes from *Catholon*, and that *Catholon* means “according to the whole.” I confess that this is closer to the individual words: for it is true that *to katholou* (τὸ καθόλου), whence *katholikos* (καθολικός), comes from *kata* (κατά) and *holon* (ὅλον). Yet it is not much closer to the force and true meaning which the words have together than the derivation offered by Optatus. Augustine likewise repeatedly introduces and defends this derivation in *Against the Letters of Petilian*, Book II, chapter 38.

Nor is it doubtful that the notion of “rational” arose from certain traces of *kata* (κατά) and *logos* (λόγος), which they thought flowed out in the word *katholikos* (καθολικός); perhaps they imagined that something in the final syllable should be traced to *cheō* (χέω), “to pour forth,” whence they saw in it the sense “spread abroad.” It seems more likely to me that Optatus here joins and confuses two different etymologies—or rather the dreams and delusions, not to say ravings, of different persons.

It is not surprising, however, that these fancies pleased Optatus and readily commended themselves to him. For since heresy and schism are opposed to the Catholic Church—heresy being properly constituted by error and schism by separation, as Jerome and Augustine long ago distinguished them (to which also belong the statements above)—the Catholic Church is made to understand by a simple and true understanding, etc., while heretics are exiles from truth, corrupted by impious opinions, etc. Thus, by this double property of the name *Catholic*, it is defended alike from heresy and schism: from the error of heresy, because it is *rationabilis*, that is, consonant with reason and truth—a sense in which you will often find *rationabile* among ecclesiastical writers; and from schismatic separation and that proud confinement of the Church to one corner—which Optatus had just charged against the Donatists—because it is spread everywhere.

I have said so much for this reason: that no room may later remain for new conjectures. For I see that learned men have troubled this passage of Optatus in various ways, now by emendations, now by interpretations. At one time *nationalis* indeed seemed plausible even to us; but we rightly rejected it. If anything must be changed, it would much sooner be proper to write *rationabiliter ubique*, “rationally everywhere,” in place of *rationabilis et ubique*, “rational and everywhere.” Not only Optatus in his final book, but also Cyprian—or whoever wrote *On the Singularity of Clerics* among Cyprian’s works—Augustine, Salvian, Victor of Utica, and others have used that expression. But absolutely nothing should be changed. M. CASAUB.

**Ibid. “Rational.”** It seems that the meaning of this word *rationabilis* is: “holding and professing the same rule of faith everywhere.” ALBASP.]

rational [Note: [Col. 0942B] Some conjecture that the reading is not *nationalis*, “national,” but “spread everywhere.”] and spread everywhere [Col. 0943A] [Note: [Col. 0944B] **“Rational and spread everywhere.”** Optatus here plays upon two etymologies of the word *Catholic*. One is from *apo tou kata logon* (ἀπὸ τοῦ κατὰ λόγον), “from that which is according to reason”; the other from *kata* (κατά) and *holon* (ὅλον), “according to the whole.” From the first root perhaps the imperial fiscal administrators were called *katholikoi* (καθολικοί), and *rationales*, “rational officials.” There is an entirely similar play upon the name *Catholic* in a letter of Dionysius of Alexandria reported by Eusebius, *Ecclesiastical History* VII.10. Speaking of a certain Macrianus, an enemy of Christians, he mocks him thus: “He who at first was said to be over the emperor’s general accounts [*katholou logoi*, καθόλου λόγοι], conceived nothing reasonable [*eulogon*, εὔλογον] and nothing catholic [*katholikon*, καθολικόν].” Valesius translated it: “He who at first, when he was called *katholikos*, that is, the emperor’s rational official, entertained nothing consonant with reason, nothing catholic or public.” DU PIN.]? G.: *terminos*, “boundaries.”] When the whole earth was promised by God the Father to the Savior, there is nothing in any part of the world which seems excluded from his possession. G.: “could have.”] say that the Holy Spirit exhorted you alone. **Ibid. “Outside the law.”** Outside the law of Christ. ALBASP.]

Can pagans, who are outside the law [Note: [Col. 0945B] In MS S. G.: “outside the laws.”] [Note: [Col. 0945C] **Pagans outside the law.** Those who have not become participants in the divine law. DU PIN.] sing to God or praise the Lord’s name—or can the Church alone [Note: [Col. 0945C] **The Church which is within the law.** “Law” means covenant, and those outside the law are those excluded from the covenant. Thus, at the Conference of Carthage, 371 and 373, testimonies or proofs are called *legalia*, “legal,” even when they are produced from the New Testament. Cyprian likewise at one point speaks of “the law of the Gospel.” Ignorance of this expression led the very learned Balduin into a great error. For when Optatus says in Book I: “For this is our voice, we who defend unity in the baptism of the Trinity—not on behalf of you, who boldly repeat baptism in the image of those two [persons], and do what is contrary to the laws”; Balduin, taking this to mean the laws of emperors, labors greatly to discover which imperial laws Optatus could have meant.

Yet the following lines themselves—“although you yourselves do not deny that what has once been commanded to be done ought not to be repeated”—and that oft-repeated and thoroughly familiar saying, “he who has once been washed has no need of being washed again,” with which the martyrs of those times especially used to arm themselves against the force and insistence of heretics wishing to rebaptize, and which Optatus himself treats at length in Book V, ought to have recalled to his mind that Optatus had regard to these things and alluded to “once” in this phrase. Therefore, “what is contrary to the laws” means what is contrary to the Scriptures and Gospel precepts. He explains “once” in the same way in Book V: “Of this washing he said: ‘He who has once been washed has no need of being washed again.’ By saying ‘once,’ he prohibited its being done again.” You may also find, in the same Book V, that Optatus properly and specifically calls them “the laws of baptism,” which he also repeatedly calls precepts.

See, reader, how much depends upon words, even the smallest ones, being rightly weighed and understood. In the judgment of every sound-minded person, it depends so much that those who neglect and despise such matters—as many today do, who alone seem wise to themselves—must necessarily despise the very best ancient writers; or, if they read them, profit from their reading no more than if they had never seen them. M. CASAUB.] [Col. 0946A] the Church that is within the law? If you say that it exists only among yourselves, you defraud the ears of God. If you alone give praise, the whole world—from the rising of the sun to its setting—will be silent. You have closed the mouths of all Christian nations; you have imposed silence upon all peoples who wish to praise God continually. **Through the exchange of *formatae*.** Those absent communicated through *formatae*, concerning which letters Bernardinus Ferrarius wrote. Therefore, for communion to stand, and for all parts of Christ’s body to communicate with one another, [Col. 0950B] all bishops annually—or even more often—sent letters of communion to the pontiff, in order that they might cultivate for the people entrusted to them communion with Christ. St Augustine, *Against Cresconius*, Book III, chapter 34: “This is especially credible from the fact that no Eastern Catholic would ever write to the bishop of Carthage while passing over the bishop of Rome; yet there, at least, your bishop ought to have been written, whom you customarily send from Africa to Rome with a few of your number.”

Such correspondence could take place between other bishops: the bishop of Carthage could send a *formata* and write to the bishop of Caesarea. But he could not do so while passing over the bishop of Rome; that is, he ought first to learn from the bishop of Rome who was the legitimate bishop of Caesarea, and only then write to him. Further, bishops did not need to write mutual letters to one another in order for communion between them to be celebrated; for since all communicated with the supreme pontiff, through that communion they all communicated with one another. ALBASP.

**Ibid. Through the exchange of *formatae*.** After so many learned men who have treated this subject at length, there is no reason for us to say anything here. The matter is well known, and we have no intention here of copying others. M. CASAUB.]

#### IV. Donatist Pseudo-Bishops and Conventicles in the City of Rome

Here he uses *memoria* for the relics of St Peter, which Macrobius did not dare to approach or communicate with because he was a schismatic. In former times all bishops held communion with their predecessors, because they were regarded as one and the same person and body with them; and because the body of Christ consists not only of members who are seen, but also of those who have departed in peace. Therefore, in order that communion might be complete and might appear joined to the first bishop who had sat in that see, they held communion with all deceased bishops. This was done in many ways: by celebrating Mass over their relics, by kissing them, or by reciting their names from the diptychs during the sacred rites. Thus, in order to show **[Col. 0951C]** that Macrobius was not the lawful bishop of the Roman Church and accordingly did not communicate with Peter, Optatus says that he had not approached Peter’s relics. ALBASP.] as a schismatic, acting contrary to the Apostle, who says:

[Note: **[Col. 0951C]** *“Communicating in the memorials of the saints,” etc.* Rom. 12:13, where some ancient witnesses read *μνείαις* (“memorials”) for *χρείαις* (“needs”). Balduin noted this at this passage, and Lucas of Bruges says more in his notes on the New Testament. Albaspinaeus thinks that wherever he finds *memoriae*, it must mean “relics”; although some of the most ancient writers who mention that reading understood it as “remembrance,” and among others *memoriae* does not mean the same as relics. For memorials were erected; relics were deposited. What were erected were either churches or altars, in which, if they possessed genuine relics of saints, they customarily deposited and preserved them. Thus *memoriae* are usually churches, sometimes merely altars, which were often built separately and individually.

Albaspinaeus, however, makes so much of this reading, as expounded and explained by himself, that, although he does not dare altogether reject the reading accepted by all in the Vulgate—“sharing in the needs of the saints”—he nevertheless does not hesitate to pronounce the other reading, if received, more consonant with ancient discipline. So thoroughly did anything offend this man, formed as he was solely by antiquity, if he could not trace it back to ancient rites, whether genuine or fictitious in his own judgment. For my part, I would maintain that the old version is so consonant with ancient discipline that none could be more so. Hence it came about in former times that, whenever there was nothing from which the needs of the poor might be relieved, there was no scruple about melting down, breaking up, or selling even the holiest vessels consecrated to God, veils, or any other objects, in order somehow to satisfy this most holy commandment. The histories of those times testify that this was often done by ancient bishops of the Church, men of genuine and ancient piety; sometimes not without criticism, but always with greater praise.

But, lest the notes grow too large, henceforth **[Col. 0952A]** I shall omit Albaspinaeus altogether, except perhaps in a very few instances. I would also ask the reader not to blame me if I omit anything rather obscure before consulting Balduin, in whom I hope will be found whatever may be wanted in these notes. M. CASAUB.]

[Note: **[Col. 0952B]** *Sharing in the memorials of the saints.* Albaspinaeus explains this passage in Romans, with Hilary, Rufinus, and Ambrose, as concerning relics and memorials of saints, not their needs; this reading would be more consonant with ancient discipline. ALBASP.]

“Sharing in the memorials **[Col. 0952A]** of the saints” [Note: **[Col. 0952B]** *Sharing in the memorials of the saints.* The passage is Paul’s Epistle to the Romans, chapter 12, verse 13, where the reading is “sharing in the needs,” or necessities, *ταῖς χρείαις*, of the saints. *Foreigner.* Formerly one was counted a foreigner if one had not been born in the place in which one was ordained, even if one had lived there for many years. What is this, that all Africans and foreigners are known to have succeeded one another in that city? Does no trickery appear? No faction—the mother of schism?

[Note: **[Col. 0953D]** *Meanwhile, that Victor of Garba should be sent from here first.* The repeated *mitteretur* (“should be sent”) disturbs the order of the sentence and makes it intricate if read continuously through to the second *mitteretur*. Thus they fenced off a certain cave outside the city, **[Col. 0955A]** with lattices, [Note: **[Col. 0955C]** *They fenced it with steps, etc.* I do not sufficiently understand what “to fence with steps” means, unless it refers somehow to steps, perhaps by which one descended into the cave. On Virgil, *Aeneid* IV, “He set up a hundred altars,” Servius says: “Others call it a temple, not only because it can be closed, but because it is enclosed with stakes or spears or something of that sort, and with lines or straps or a similar thing, which has been consecrated by augury.” Thus Joseph Scaliger, a famous hero of immortal memory, emends the final words in Festus, p. 88, where previously the text read “and it was done.”

As for Optatus’s phrase *ipso tempore*, there was no need for Barth’s correction, who reads *ubi* for *tempore*. It means “at that” or “at this time.” Thus Optatus himself, book I: “a public official of that very time,” **[Col. 0955D]** that is, of the same time. So too Victor of Utica, book I: “which was done at that very time.” And a few pages later: “those who, gradually failing, are now at the same time the three survivors.” He meant those whom he names afterwards. Let the fair-minded reader pardon us if we sometimes pursue these trifles. It is not because they themselves are of such importance, but because the errors of others in such trifles have made them seem important. M. CASAUB.]

[Note: **[Col. 0955B]** Thus in the manuscript of St Gall, *cratibus* (“with lattices”), better than the *gradibus* (“with steps”) found in the manuscripts S. T. and P. S.; for no fence is made with steps, but with lattices.]

[Note: **[Col. 0955D]** *Where at that time they might have had a conventicle.* “What, or what kind of, is this ‘at that time’?” Barth asks, and reads *ubi* (“where”) for *tempore* (“at the time”). *Potuissent* is placed for *possent*, as usage of the Latin language indeed required; but Optatus follows a manner of speech which may be called change of tense in verbs, classed by the grammarian Diomedes among the forms of solecism, book II: “And lest they might have been able to return to better things, they themselves put upon themselves the shackles of schism.” Arnobius likewise, book I: “Finally, if dumb living creatures themselves might have been able to utter speech, if they might have been released into the ease of our languages; indeed, if trees, clods of earth, and stones, endowed with living perception, could produce the sound of a voice and form articulate words.” A most learned critic ought not to have troubled this passage by changing *potuissent* into *potissent*. Optatus likewise uses *potuissent* for *potuerint* on p. 73; elsewhere *facerent* for *fecissent*; *intraverat* for *intravisset*. All these, like his saying on p. 53, *loquimur* for *locuti sumus*, ought to be regarded as instances of the same kind, namely a change in the name of the tense. See also the notes above on book I. [Note: **[Col. 0956B]** *They were called Montenses.* Jerome, in his Chronicle under the year of Christ 356: “Donatus, from whom we have said above that the Donatists take their name, is expelled from Carthage. Augustine, in Letter 165 in the old enumeration, now 53, after listing, following Optatus’s example, the succession of Roman pontiffs, argues likewise: “In this succession no Donatist bishop is found. But they sent from Africa a man ordained irregularly, who, presiding over a few Africans in the city of Rome, propagated the name of Montenses or Cutzupitani.” For Cutzupitani or Cuzupitani, most wish to read Rupitani here; Augustine calls the Donatists Rupitani, as in *On the Unity of the Church*, chapter 3: “among the few Rupitani or Montenses at Rome.” But in the latest edition of Augustine’s works, on the authority of the manuscript of Fleury, *Cutzupitanis* has been restored. In the former passage, two Vatican manuscripts have *Cutrumpitarum*. Cotelerius thinks that one should conjecturally read *Scototopitarum*, from *σκότος*, “darkness,” and *τόπος*, “place.” Perhaps these passages of Augustine should be corrected from Jerome and *Campitae* read—a term which wonderfully agrees with Optatus, who says that they fenced off a certain cave outside the city with lattices: for from this they could equally have been called Campitae as Montenses. Yet Augustine, in *On Heresies*, chapter 69, speaking of the Donatists living at Rome, calls them only Montenses: “These heretics in the city of Rome are called Montenses; they usually send them a bishop from Africa, or their African bishops go from here to there, if perhaps they decide that he should be ordained there.” In Honorius’s law concerning heretics, in the Theodosian Code, book 43, they are likewise called Montenses. Therefore, since Claudianus appears to have succeeded Lucianus, Lucianus Macrobius, [and] Macrobius Encolpius, Encolpius Boniface, and Boniface Victor: if Victor were asked where he sat, he would show neither anyone there before himself nor any chair, unless he showed a pestilence. #### V. The Donatists, Authors of Division and Enemies of Peace

Why, then, do you struggle to arrogate to yourselves the keys of the kingdom of heaven [Note: **[Col. 0955B]** Thus in the manuscript of St Gall; absent from the others.]—you who [Note: **[Col. 0956D]** *Against the chair of Peter.* The Donatists fought against Peter’s chair because they said that the Church existed nowhere except among the Donatists. ALBASP.] in your presumption and audacity make sacrilegious war against Peter’s chair? You reject the blessedness by which he deserved to be praised who “did not walk in the counsel of the ungodly, did not stand in the way of sinners, and did not sit in the chair of pestilence” [Note: **[Col. 0956B]** In the manuscript of St Gall, “of pestilent persons.”] (Ps. 1:1).

Your ancestors entered into a counsel of impiety, that the Church might be divided. [Note: **[Col. 0956B]** Thus in all the manuscripts we have seen. In printed editions, “that they might divide the Church.”] They also entered [Note: **[Col. 0956B]** In printed editions, *iverunt* (“they went”), less well.] the way of sinners when they attempted to divide Christ, **[Col. 0957A]** whose garments even the Jews did not wish to tear. [Note: **[Col. 0957C]** In the manuscript of St Gall, “they tore.”] For the Apostle Paul cries aloud and says, “Has Christ been divided?” (1 Cor. 1).

Would that, once they had entered upon that evil way, they had returned to themselves [Note: **[Col. 0957C]** *They returned to themselves.* They returned to the Church. ALBASP.] upon recognizing their sin—that is, corrected what they had done wrongly—and recalled the peace which they had driven away. CASAUB.] for on a way one walks, not stands.

But because your parents refused to return, it is clear that they stood in the way of sinners. Fury had driven their steps onward; sluggish discord bound them fast. And lest they might return to better things, they themselves placed on themselves the shackles [Note: **[Col. 0957C]** In the manuscript of St Gall, “a limit.”] of schism, that they might stand stubbornly in their error and not be able to return to the peace they had abandoned. Nor did they listen to the Holy Spirit saying in Psalm 33:15, “Turn away from evil and do **[Col. 0957B]** good; seek peace and pursue it”; but they stood in the way of their sins.

They also sat in the chair of pestilence, which, as we said above, sends those whom it has deceived to [Note: **[Col. 0957C]** In the manuscripts S. T. and P. S., “into.”] death. And you, in cherishing your parents’ error and zealously defending it, chose to be heirs of crime, although even late you might have been children of peace. For it is written in the prophet Ezekiel: “Raise your voice against the son of a sinner, lest he follow in his father’s footsteps; for the soul of the father is mine, and the soul of the son is mine. The soul that sins shall alone be punished” (Ezek. 18:3, 19, 20).

If what your parents sinned had displeased you, they alone would have rendered account for their deed. T. and P. S. and the printed editions add “was.”]

What else is it to have one’s will in the law than reverently to learn the divine commandments and fulfill them with fear? In that law it is written in the Gospel: “Peace to people of good will on earth” (Luke 2:14); and elsewhere in the prophet Isaiah: “I will lay **[Col. 0958A]** foundations of peace in Zion” (Isa. 60:17); and elsewhere, in Psalm 84: “Let us see what the Lord will say, for he will speak peace to his people”; and elsewhere, in Psalm 75: “The Son of God came, and his place was made in peace”; and elsewhere, in Psalm 71: “Let the mountains receive peace for the people, and the hills righteousness”; and in the Gospel: “I give you my peace; I leave you my peace” (John 14:27); and Paul says, “He who sows peace shall also reap peace” (2 Cor. 9); and in all 36 of his epistles, “May peace abound in you.” [Note: **[Col. 0957C]** The manuscripts S. T., Ph. S., and printed editions add: “in the name **[Col. 0958C]** of the Father and of the Son and of the Holy Spirit.”] And in Psalm 33:15: “Seek peace, and you shall attain it.”

Peace, driven away, had departed from your parents. You ought to have sought it, as God commanded; [Note: **[Col. 0958C]** Thus in the manuscript of St Gall. In the manuscripts S. T. and P. S.: “if you sought it, as commanded by the Lord.” Incorrectly in printed editions: “you do not seek.”] yet you were unwilling even of yourselves to seek it [Note: **[Col. 0957D]** *Nor gladly accept it when offered.* Other editions read better here “nor accept it when offered”; perhaps, however, the word *non* should not rashly be inserted here. For who in so many **[Col. 0958B]** provinces in which you were born has heard of this? And if anyone has heard, who would not marvel at your error? Who would not condemn your crime? Therefore, since it is manifest and clearer than light itself that we are joined with countless peoples and so many provinces, you now see that you are situated in one part of one region and separated from the Church by your errors. In vain do you claim for yourselves alone the name of Church together with its endowments. These are more among us than among you; and they are so connected and indivisible that one is understood not to be separable from another. For they are enumerated by name, but are joined in one conception in the body, like the fingers on a hand, each of which we see distinct from the others by spaces between them. Hence one who holds one must necessarily hold them all, since none can be separated from its fellows. Add that we rightly possess not one alone, but all of them.

Behold, now the endowments cannot be among you. For you cannot claim the Spirit of God for yourselves alone, [Col. 0959B] nor confine what is understood but not seen. For thus it is written in the Gospel: “For [Col. 0960A] God is Spirit, and he breathes where he wills; you hear his voice, and [Note: [Col. 0959B] In MSS S, T, and P, “but.”] you do not know whence he comes or where he goes” (John 3). Allow God the [37] freedom to go where he wishes and to approach where he wishes: he can be heard but cannot be seen.

And yet, eager to accuse, you willingly chose to blaspheme, saying: “For what spirit can be in that Church, unless she bears children of Gehenna?” You spewed an insult from your own breast, and thought that a testimony from the Gospel should be added, where it is read: “Woe to you, hypocrites, who traverse seas and lands to make one proselyte; and when you have found him, you make him twice as much a son of Gehenna as yourselves” (Matt. 23:15).

[Note: [Col. 0960C] “If this insult had to be made,” etc. This whole passage is badly corrupted; yet its sense is not obscure, so that one need not labour excessively over the wording. Perhaps Optatus wrote: “If this insult had to be made, although it be made without cause, would that someone else from your party had said this; and yet I am greatly astonished that you said it falsely of another, when, if you consider your ordination, you may even blush.” Or: “And yet I am greatly astonished that you have said this.” I entirely remove, as a gloss, the phrase “although it be made without cause,” such glosses commonly creeping from the margin into the text itself. It has long been observed from the historian Vopiscus that *tamen* is sometimes used in the sense of *autem* (“but”). If anyone wishes to distinguish these things more subtly, reading “it is not permitted, and it is made without cause,” I permit him to do so, provided that I remain free to follow the reading I approve more. Optatus says this because Parmenian was a foreigner, a point which, though he does not state it expressly here, he charges against him elsewhere in explicit words. If we retain “although it be made without cause,” you may also interpret it thus: “Since, however, you are resolved to utter an insult, illicit in whatever way, would that,” etc. M. Casaubon.]
