## VIII. On the font, seal, and navel, marks of the Church.

[Note: [Col. 0961C] “For the font also.” Something seems to be missing here, since these words do not cohere with the rest. Albaspinaeus.]

For it is agreed that the font also is one of the endowments, from which heretics can neither drink themselves nor give drink to others; because, lacking the seal intact—that is, the [Col. 0961B] catholic creed—they cannot open access to the true font.

[Note: [Col. 0961D] “For since in the Song of Songs.” These words do not cohere with what precedes. This whole discussion of the endowments consisted chiefly of two parts. In the first, Optatus acknowledges the five endowments discussed by Parmenian, but maintains that they belong to the true Catholic Church; he refutes and unravels Parmenian’s erroneous statements concerning them. Afterwards he refuted Parmenian’s error concerning their number, since Parmenian counted six whereas Optatus maintained that there were only five. He was still occupied with the first part and was discussing the preceding proposition concerning the font; and behold, a new subject is treated here, a new argument introduced, without conclusion of what precedes or transition opening a way to the new argument. Therefore asterisks, signs of a gap, should have been placed here—not immediately, as Balduin wishes, before “it remains.” For after he showed and established that the navel ought not to be counted as a sixth endowment, as Parmenian had maintained, he rightly then concludes—since no other dispute over the number remained: “It now remains that the endowments appear to be five,” etc. M. Casaubon.]

For since it is written in the Song of Songs: “Your navel is like a turned bowl” [Note: [Col. 0961B] In MS S.G., “turned.”] (Song 7:2), [Note: [Col. 0962C] “The navel [is] the altar.” Parmenian made the navel a sixth endowment of the Church. Albaspinaeus.] you have attempted to assert that the navel is the altar. If the navel is a member of the body, [Col. 0962A] what is a member cannot be among the endowments. But if [Note: [Col. 0961B] In MS S.G., “And if.”] it is an ornament, it is not a part of the body.

## IX. The endowments of the Church are among the Catholics, not at all among the Donatists.

It now remains that the endowments appear to be five [Note: [Col. 0962C] “That the endowments appear to be five.” This was the conclusion of the discussion in which he had proved that the navel could not be an endowment of the Church. Du Pin.]. Since these endowments belong to the Catholic Church—which is in all the provinces mentioned above—they cannot be lacking among us here in Africa either.

Understand, though late, that you are impious children; that you are branches broken from the tree; that you are shoots cut from the vine; that you are a stream severed from the fountain. For a little stream cannot be its own source, [38] and [Note: [Col. 0962C] “It does not arise from itself.” That is, it does not arise from another known and visible fountain. See the note on Book I, where Optatus reproaches the Donatists for being born from themselves. Clericus.] does not arise from itself; nor can a tree be a severed branch, [Note: [Col. 0962B] In MSS S.T. and the editions, “to be cut from a branch,” but this is less in keeping with the writer’s meaning.] since the tree rejoices in being founded upon its roots, while a branch, if cut off, withers.

Do you now see, brother Parmenian? Do you now perceive? Do you now understand that [Col. 0962B] you have made your own arguments serve against you? For it has been proved that we know in the holy Catholic Church those among whom there are also [Note: [Col. 0962C] “The creed of the Trinity.” Does he here call the mystery a *symbolum* (“creed”), as “symbolic” and “mystical” are sometimes confused? Or rather, by synecdoche, or *κατ᾽ ἐξοχήν* (“pre-eminently”), does he call the Apostles’ Creed “the creed,” because the mystery of the Trinity is its chief article? I prefer to understand it simply as faith and profession, so that “the creed of the Trinity” is nothing other than what Victor of Utica, Book II, calls “the whole faith of the Trinity.” The reason is obvious: the creed is the summary of our faith. Thus the two are sometimes joined as synonyms. Augustine writes in *Retractations*, I.17, that as a presbyter he had composed a work “On Faith and the Creed”; and such a work by him is published, as others speak likewise. M. Casaubon.] the creed of the Trinity, [Note: [Col. 0962B] This whole passage is found in an entirely different form in MS S.G.: “when it has been proved that they are not in the holy Catholic Church, among whom there is not the creed of the Trinity”; but nothing should be altered.] and, [Note: [Col. 0962D] “And through the chair of Peter.” By the communion he had with St Peter and Siricius, he proves that the other endowments are among his party. That is: according to Optatus, whoever does not communicate with the supreme pontiff can possess no endowment of the Church. Albaspinaeus.] through Peter’s chair, which is ours, through that chair the other endowments also are among us.

Likewise the priesthood, which you seemed to [Col. 0963A] invalidate among us: in excusing [Note: [Col. 0963B] In MS P.S., “in carrying out.”] your error and envy, while you rebaptize after us [Note: [Col. 0963B] In MS S.G., “baptize.”] and do not do this after your associates have been exposed in sin. For you said that, if a priest is in sin, only the endowments can work.

Therefore, since we have explained what heresy is, what schism is, and what the holy Church is; and since the person of this holy Church is [Note: [Col. 0963C] “Its person is constituted.” That is, the Church is constituted in the person of the supreme pontiff, as in its head; and it is there where, and with those with whom, he communicates. Albaspinaeus.] constituted, and since this Church is Catholic, being spread throughout the whole world, of whose members we too are among others, and whose endowments are everywhere among her; moreover, in the first book we proved that the reproach of handing over the Scriptures does not concern us, and that this accusation too has been condemned by us.

## X. The true sacraments of the Church are among the Catholics.

Now I want you to answer me this: when you chose to speak only about the Church’s [Col. 0963B] endowments and were silent about her holy members and inward parts—which are undoubtedly in the sacraments and [Note: [Col. 0963C] “And in the names of the Trinity,” etc. Here, as in Tertullian, *On Baptism*, VII, “the names of the Trinity” means the number of divine names, that is, persons. Below, in Book III, our author uses “names of piety” for persons joined to one another by the bond of piety; and in Book V, “three names,” that is, three persons. I knowingly pass over what follows concerning the faith and profession of believers, since others have often expounded it. Moreover, that an angel intervenes in the waters is affirmed by Tertullian, *On Baptism*, chapters 5–6; but not only in waters, also in prayers, *On Prayer*, chapter 12, and in the rites of marriage, *To His Wife*, II, final chapter. On baptism Augustine too, *On the Creed for Catechumens*, after some remarks concerning profession, says: “See, beloved, that you bring this your profession into the court of angels; the names of those making profession are received into the book of life, not by any human being but by a higher heavenly power,” etc. This passage remarkably illustrates Optatus here. “Acts” is used here, as elsewhere “secrets,” “studies,” “spectacles,” and countless such terms, for the places themselves where acts, secrets, etc., occur. Thus a hundred times in the Conference of Carthage, “before the acts” and “in the acts,” that is, publicly, before the official staff or public notary, etc. Next, “the Trinity,” that is, the persons of the Trinity—Father, Son, and Holy Spirit—God, of course, concurring and acting together with the very faith and profession of those to be baptized, etc. M. Casaubon.] in the names of the Trinity [Note: [Col. 0963D] “In the sacraments and in the names of the Trinity.” In the sacrament of baptism, which is conferred with invocation of the Trinity. Du Pin.]? To these concur the faith of believers and their profession, which [Note: [Col. 0964C] “Which is completed before the records of angels.” Tertullian: “the angels report those who are sealed; the Father ratifies it,” *To His Wife*, II. Albaspinaeus.] is completed before the records of angels, [Note: [Col. 0964C] “Which is completed before the records of angels.” Tertullian, *On Baptism*, 5–6, affirms that an angel intervenes in the baptismal waters. Augustine, *On the Creed for Catechumens*, after some remarks concerning profession, says: “See, beloved, that you bring this your profession into the court of angels; the names of those making profession are received into the book of life.” How consonant these words are with Optatus’s saying! Du Pin.] where heavenly and spiritual seeds are mingled, so that by a holy seed a new character of those reborn may be brought forth; so that, when the Trinity agrees with faith, one who was born to the world may be reborn spiritually to God. Thus God becomes the Father of human beings; thus the Church becomes the holy mother.

I understand that you omitted all these things for this reason: lest in all of them [Col. 0964A] the principle of baptism should be recognized, in which no minister, being a human being, claims anything for himself—[Note: [Col. 0964C] “Which you do.” They said that baptism and its grace are conferred *ex opere operantis*, from the work of the one performing it. Albaspinaeus.] as you do. Therefore you chose to have recourse only to the endowments, which you tried in vain to claim for yourselves alone, denying them to Catholics as though held in the hand or [Note: [Col. 0964C] “Or shut up in water.” I do not know why water is mentioned here, unless perhaps it may remove the corruption hidden here—and so foul a corruption that it is astonishing it long escaped learned men. For instead of *aqua* (“water”), one must write with Optatus *arca* (“chest”), formerly written *arqua*, just as *arqus* for *arcus*, as Priscian testifies. We do not fail to know that Nonius Marcellus distinguishes them. But Priscian and others furnish many examples of that old spelling, some of which we retain even today, such as *quum*, *sequutus*, etc. Those who did not understand this, because baptism had shortly before been mentioned, changed it into “water.” Yet above we have: “Unless perhaps, claiming him for yourselves, you have him shut up in little chests”—understand, the angel. Nothing is more like an egg than these two expressions: to have something “shut in little chests” and “enclosed in a chest.” M. Casaubon.] enclosed in a chest. [Note: [Col. 0963B] Thus, excellently, in MS S.G. In MSS S.T. and P.S., [Col. 0964B] “water.”]

Since the matter concerns regeneration, [Note: [Col. 0964B] These words are omitted in MS S.G.] since it concerns renewing the human being, you named neither the believers’ faith nor their profession; [Note: [Col. 0964B] In MS S.G., “promise.”] while wishing to speak of endowments alone, you consigned to silence all these things without which that [39] spiritual birth cannot be renewed. And since endowments belong to the bride, not the bride to the endowments, you arranged the endowments as though they themselves appeared to generate, [Note: [Col. 0964D] “Not the inward parts.” The Fathers say that human beings are born and reborn in the baptistery as in a womb; hence he rightly calls the sacraments the Church’s inward parts. Albaspinaeus.] rather than the inward parts—which are understood to be situated more in the sacraments than in ornaments.

## XI. The Church is rightly called paradise, but corresponds to the whole world.

Nor do I pass over the fact that you called the Church paradise—by your mouth, but in our sense. This is undoubtedly true: in this garden God plants little trees. Yet you have denied God his riches, whose garden you confine within narrow limits while wrongly claiming everything for yourselves alone. God’s plantings are indeed various seeds through various precepts. The righteous, the continent, the merciful, and virgins are spiritual seeds; God plants the little trees of these things [Note: [Col. 0964D] “God plants into paradise.” *In paradisum* here and elsewhere is like Cicero’s *in potestatem*, Plautus’s *in mentem*, and others’ *in controversiam esse*, meaning “into power,” etc. I note this not because it is especially new [Col. 0965C] or unusual, but lest someone who notices it less carefully consider it suspect. M. Casaubon.] in paradise.

Grant God that his garden is spread far and wide. Why do you deny him the Christian peoples of the provinces of the East, [Col. 0965A] North, and West, and of all the innumerable islands? Against them you alone are few, rebels, and have no fellowship of communion with them.

## XII. From the prayer of the offering it is inferred that the Church is one and spread everywhere.

Here too your falsehood may justly be condemned, by which [Note: [Col. 0965C] “By which sacrifices are daily offered by you.” They lied when, during the sacred rites, they asked God to unite his Church, because they themselves divided it by their schism. Then they lied when in the prayers of the sacrifice they proclaimed her one, because they made her many. Albaspinaeus.] sacrifices are daily offered by you. For who doubts that, in the mystery of the sacraments, you cannot omit that prescribed formula? You say that you offer to God for the Church which is one. This very thing is part of your falsehood: you call one that which you have made two; and you say that you offer to God [Note: [Col. 0965C] Omitted in MSS S.T. and P.S. and in the editions.] for the one Church spread throughout the whole world.

What if God should say to each of you: “Why do you offer [Col. 0965B] for the whole, when you are not in the whole?” If we displease you, what has the city of [Note: [Col. 0965D] “The city of Antioch.” They did not accuse Arabs or Syrians of handing over the Scriptures; nevertheless, they rebaptized them no less than Africans. Albaspinaeus.] Antioch done to you? What has the province of Arabia? [Note: [Col. 0965D] “Whence we prove.” *Probamus* stands, *ἀντὶ τοῦ* (“instead of”), for “we can prove,” as in the Conference of Carthage II. When the notary asked when the records could be entered on slips and their publication completed, they replied: “Today we complete the slips.” The tribune, taking this up and explaining it, repeats: “Since the office has represented that it can complete the slips today,” etc. Further, *meminis* for *meministi* has not hitherto, so far as I know, been observed; perhaps *meministi* should be restored, although *meminens* is used by many. M. Casaubon.] From there we can prove that those coming from you were rebaptized.

## XIII. The praises of the Church mentioned by Parmenian belong to the Catholics.

In this one respect alone, brother Parmenian, we cannot be ungrateful to you: you wished to praise our Church—that is, the Catholic Church, which is contained throughout the whole world—although you are alien from it, in enumerating its endowments. In their number you erred greatly, and also in saying that she is a garden enclosed, a fountain sealed, and the one bride. We say this of what is ours; for you spoke of what belongs to another. Whatever you could say in praise of the Church, we [Note: [Col. 0965C] In MS S.G., “and we.”] say the same things first.

We too condemn the traditors along with you—[Col. 0965C] namely, those whom, if you remember, we showed [Note: [Col. 0966C] In MS S.G., “we showed in the first fashion/book.”] in the first book. And since we have communion with the whole world, with all provinces in communion with us, you have long wanted to compare two Churches, [Note: [Col. 0965D] “As though Africa alone possessed Christian peoples, in which.” Whenever Catholics reproached the Donatists on the basis of the distinctive meaning of the name “Catholic,” the latter replied that they were Christians; they openly declared that they cared less about possession of the first title than of the second, which they claimed as their own, although they would not allow the former to be denied them either, but asserted it only insofar as they were Christians. Optatus therefore says that Parmenian argued about two Churches in such a way that, while claiming the Christian name for his own party, he confined Christians to Africa, as though it alone—divided, that is, by them—contained a Church in which the Donatists had force and existed somewhere and in some number. M. Casaubon.] as though Africa alone possessed Christian peoples, [Col. 0966A] in which, through your fault, two parties seem to have been created. And while you forgot Christ saying that his bride is one, you did not say that there were two parties in Africa, but two Churches. Certainly there is one, which deserved to be indicated by Christ’s voice, when he said: “My dove is one; my bride is one.”

## XIV. The Catholics have done nothing cruelly.

And forgetting this saying, in order to arouse hostility against the Catholics, you spoke in these words: “For that cannot be called a Church [Note: [Col. 0966D] “By bloody bites.” This must be understood of Macarius’s expedition. Albaspinaeus.] which feeds upon bloody bites and is fattened by the blood and flesh of the saints.”

The Church has its definite members: bishops, presbyters, deacons, ministers, and the multitude of believers. Say to what class of persons in our Church this can be attributed which you wished to object. Name some minister specifically; [Col. 0966B] show some deacon by name; indicate that this was done by some presbyter; prove that bishops committed it; show that one of ours plotted against anyone. Which one of us persecuted anyone? Whom can you either say or prove was persecuted by us? [40]

[Note: [Col. 0966D] “But because unity displeases you.” Macarius had made unity, compelling some into the Church by prayers and exhortation and others by force. Therefore the Donatists said that unity had not been made without blood, and that the Church communicating with Macarius was cruel. Albaspinaeus.]

But because unity displeases you, if you think this a crime, accuse us of having communicated with the Thessalonians, Corinthians, Galatians, and the seven Churches which are in Asia. If it seems wicked to you, or [Note: [Col. 0966D] “You consider it guilt to communicate with the memorials of the apostles.” It is not easy to say why he mentions the relics of saints here, when he is not discussing relics but communion between Churches. He mentions relics because communion cannot be complete unless it is made among all its members, that is, between the living and the dead. Albaspinaeus.] if you count it guilt to have communicated with the memorials of the apostles and all the saints: we not only do not deny having done this, but even glory in it.

## XV. The Church’s peace and prosperity before it was disturbed by the Donatists.

But in order to show that your party, as I said, has fed upon bloody bites and been fattened by the blood [Col. 0966C] and flesh of Christians, your now-raging fury must be recalled from its beginning; your impiety must now be unfolded; your folly displayed. First, one must show your shameful joy and criminal rejoicing: [Note: [Col. 0966D] “That it befell you to receive freedom from your former error.” Plainly this is contrary to Optatus’s meaning, to the matter itself, and to the truth of the event, as the following words openly show. Earlier editions read: “that it was established that liberty had been made for you to your former error”; whence, with a slight change: “that liberty was made for you to your former errors.” If anyone prefers, “that it happened for you to return to the liberty of your former error,” which is closer to Balduin, the sense remains the same. If further anyone thinks that Optatus here uses “error” for exile, I would not strongly disagree, since he is speaking of Donatists recalled from exile. M. Casaubon.] that it happened for you to be granted the liberty of your former [Col. 0967A] error. [Note: [Col. 0967B] This passage has been corrected partly from conjecture and partly from manuscript authority. MSS S.T. and P.S. read: “that it was established that liberty had been made for you to the liberty of former error.” MS S.G. reads: “that it happened for you to return to the liberty of former error.” The author’s meaning is: first one must show with what joy, with what malicious delights, you were affected [Col. 0968B] because the Emperor Julian restored to you the freedom which Constantine had taken away.]

Review the times; examine the circumstances; consider the differing wishes and the different persons. Let the Emperor Constantine [Note: [Col. 0967C] “The Emperor Constantine.” What Optatus says about the peace of the African Church and the condition of the Donatists is more appropriate to the reign of Constans than Constantine’s; for under Constantine they were neither suppressed nor deprived of basilicas, but under Constans. Moreover Julian is reported as the immediate successor of this emperor. Nevertheless, because all manuscripts read “Constantine,” we judged that nothing should be altered. Du Pin.] the Christian return to mind: what service he rendered to God, what desires he held—that, after schisms had been removed and every dissension had died away, [Note: [Col. 0967D] “That under the whole heaven the holy mother Church might joyfully see her children in one.” This passage is wrongly suspected of corruption; the author speaks thus elsewhere more than once. Yet Barthius proposes: “might joyfully see in her bosom,” drawing support from Book VII: “When the Catholic Church ought to receive you in her pious bosom.” See also Book I. Anonymous.] under the whole heaven the holy mother Church might joyfully see her children in one. [Note: [Col. 0967D] “Might see … in one,” etc. In the margin is written: “elsewhere read, ‘into one.’” From this variation I suspect both readings must be removed and “might see in her bosom” written, supported by the words of Book VII: “When the Catholic Church ought to receive you in her pious bosom.” Barthius.]

He restored one communion: wives to husbands, children to parents, brothers to brothers. God testifies that he delights in these things, saying in Psalm 132: “Behold, how good and pleasant it is for brothers to dwell together in unity.” For when one peace united the African peoples, the Eastern peoples, and the other peoples beyond the sea, and unity itself, with all its members made present, bound together the body of the Church, [Col. 0967B] the devil grieved—he who is always tormented by the peace of brethren.

At that time, under a Christian emperor, abandoned in the idols as though imprisoned, he lay [Note: [Col. 0968B] In MS S.G. and some printed editions, “lay hidden.”] in the temples. At the same time the deserts of your leaders and princes had relegated [Note: [Col. 0968B] In the manuscripts, “bound.”] them. There had been no schisms in the Church, nor were pagans permitted to practise sacrileges. Peace pleasing to God dwelt among all Christian peoples; the devil mourned in the temples, [Note: [Col. 0967D] “You in foreign regions.” Because Constantine had punished them with exile. Albaspinaeus.] and you were in foreign regions.

## XVI. Julian’s edict in favour of the Donatists.

Then, as is known to us, another emperor followed, [Note: [Col. 0967D] “Another emperor.” Julian, who had granted basilicas to the Donatists. Albaspinaeus.] [Note: [Col. 0968C] “Another emperor.” Julian. The Donatists presented this emperor with a petition, asking that the basilicas which they complained had been taken from them be restored and that they might recover their former liberty. Optatus mentions this petition below in Book III, recalling the same requests as submitted by Cassianus, Rogatianus, Pontius, and the other bishops of Donatus’s party. Augustine also frequently mentions it and names the same authors. In it they praised the Emperor Julian, saying that justice alone had a place with him. See Augustine, Epistle formerly 166, now 105. These things occurred in the year 362.]

Conceiving hostile designs together with you, he changed from a servant of God into a minister of the enemy; by his edicts he showed himself to be an apostate [Note: [Col. 0968B] MS S.G. adds “everywhere.”]—the man whom you begged, by your petitions, that you might be allowed to return. If you deny having sent these petitions, we have read them. Nor did the man whom you petitioned create any difficulty: he ordered [Note: [Col. 0968B] MS S.G. adds “you.”] you to go according to his wish, since he understood that you would return with fury in order to disturb the peace. Blush, if any shame remains: by the same decree by which liberty was restored to you, the temples of idols were ordered opened.

## XVII. The fury and cruelty of the Donatists.

At almost the same moment that the devil was released from his prisons, your fury returned into Africa. And are you not ashamed to share [Col. 0968B] [41] common joys with the enemy at one and the same time? [Note: [Col. 0968C] “Common joys.” One member ought to rejoice or grieve with another; therefore, when the devil rejoiced, the Donatists rejoiced. Albaspinaeus.] You came raging; you came angry; you came tearing the Church’s members apart—subtle in seductions, savage in killings, provoking the children of peace to war. You made many exiles from their homes when you came with a hired band and seized basilicas. Many from your number, in very many places—which would take too long to name individually—[Note: [Col. 0968C]

“They committed bloody massacres,” etc. What novelty is this? Were, then, all crimes so atrocious in their execrable manner which were customarily reported to judges? Nor is it enough to show that a report was sent to judges [Col. 0968D] in order to demonstrate in us some itch for alteration, as the very learned man who not long ago appended little pages of notes to Optatus thought; for neither were we previously ignorant of this. But let him tell me, please, if this is mere itchiness: did Optatus join “atrocious” crimes to killings because these were reported to judges? There is indeed a kind of itch in censuring learned and careful men which believes this and does not consider that something else must follow, since ordinary killings, or even lesser crimes, are reported to judges, and there is no need to infer from this their unusual atrocity. Therefore I still think one should read: “a report was feared.” That is, before judges who feared to report to the palace—as our Optatus says elsewhere in relation to this very occurrence—such dreadful crimes committed by bishops bearing the Christian appearance, lest the whole religion suffer slander, since very many persons at the imperial court were most devoted to paganism. Barthius.

Ibid. “They committed bloody massacres.” An error has escaped notice in the final word; once removed, it will make the entire passage clear. It should read: “a report was feared by the judges.” I think no one would doubt that this is Optatus’s genuine reading. So Barthius. But I myself doubt not without reason, and say that no question of textual status should be raised here, since this is confirmed by another passage of the same author, Book I: “At the same time one Felix, a deacon, who is said to have been named in some notorious letter then composed concerning the tyrant-emperor, fearing danger is said to have hidden with Bishop Mensurius. When Mensurius publicly denied that he had been demanded, a report was sent: a rescript came ordering that, if Mensurius did not surrender the deacon Felix, he should be sent to the palace.” Therefore, reader, refrain from the itch to emend; from that passage borrow light for this obscure one. Anonymous.]
cruel massacres were perpetrated, and so atrocious that, concerning such deeds, a report was sent by the judges of that time to [Col. 0969A] him.

[Note: [Col. 0969B] This is how it should be read, as found in MS S. G.: not “to the judges,” as in MSS S. T. P. S. and the printed editions; for a report is sent by judges to the emperor, not to judges.]

[Note: [Col. 0969C] “A report was sent.” Official notices (*elogia*), letters, and reports concerning that slaughter were sent to the emperor. Some substitute “was feared,” but this makes no sense. ALBASP.]

But God’s judgment intervened and came to pass: that irreligious and sacrilegious emperor—the one who had long before ordered you to return—died, although at your instigation he had already sent, or was preparing to send, persecution against you.

## XVIII. The slaughter and crimes of the Donatists

At the places mentioned above, a massacre was perpetrated against Catholics. Recall, place by place, the course taken by your people. Were not Felix of Zabe and Januarius of Flumenpis among your number, along with the rest, who rushed with all speed to the fortress-town of Lemelle?

[Note: [Col. 0969B] Thus in MS S. G. In MSS S. Th. and Ph. S.: “Diabensis.” [Col. 0970B] The former reading must be retained; see our observation on this passage.]

[Note: [Col. 0969C] “Of Zabe.” In the Notice of Africa there is a bishop of Zabe in Numidia, and likewise a Numidian bishop of this name in the Conference of Carthage. But there is another Zabe in Sitifian territory, of which this Felix was bishop, as the proximity of the fortress-town of Lemelle shows. DU PIN.]

[Note: [Col. 0969C]

“Januarius Flamen Pistensis.” Correctly: a certain Januarius, bishop of Flamenpis. ALBASP.

Ibid. “Januarius Flamen Pistensis.” On the basis of a probable conjecture, a learned man in his notes on Optatus maintains that, instead of *Flamen Pistensis* or *Flumen Pistensis*, which others give, *Flumenpiscensis* should be restored from the Conference of Carthage. I do not disagree; amid such obscurity concerning these places—which fill both pages in the Carthaginian Conference—I judge it difficult to determine anything with certainty.

A little later: “against their importunity,” etc. I warn the less cautious not to take *importunitas* in its ordinary sense, but as Virgil, Cicero, and Terence—the finest authors of Latin—often use it: namely, for sheer savagery and the utmost extremity of wickedness. Yet I do not think that our author here imitates them so much as the phraseology of Scripture, in which Greek *atopoi* (“absurd,” “out of place”) properly means “criminal and impious.” See Luke XXIII.41 and 2 Thessalonians III.2, where the Vulgate has “wicked and troublesome men,” etc. Shall we likewise interpret “troublesome sins” in Book VII? Unless, however, he there calls sins “troublesome” because they were sown in a place and time not their own but another’s. For he speaks of tares, which the devil, by stealthy sowing in darkness, mingles with good crops. M. CASAUB.

Ibid. “Januarius Flamen Pistensis.” The mention of “Januarius Flamen” rightly troubled Barthius at this point; but he candidly confesses that he does not know how it might be emended for the better. In Balduin’s second edition: “Januarius Flamen Pistensis,” whence I should read *Flumenpiscensis*. The Conference of Carthage with the Donatists, first conducted by Papirius under public authority, mentions an African place called Flumenpis: Commelin’s edition, p. 195, names Restitutus, bishop of Flumenpis. Africa likewise has the episcopal see of the Flumenzeritani; see Victor of Utica, *On the Vandal Persecution*. INCERT.]

Januarius of Flumenpis.

[Note: [Col. 0970B] This should be read as in MSS S. T. and S. G., not “Flamen Piscensis” or “Flamen Pistensis,” as in the printed editions.]

[Note: [Col. 0970C] “Flumenpiscensis.” At the Conference of Carthage Victor, bishop of Flumenpis, is listed among the Donatist bishops. A bishop of the same name occurs in the Notice of Mauretania Sitifensis. DU PIN.]

[Note: [Col. 0970C] “Lemelle.” Also a town of Mauretania Sitifensis, mentioned in the Notice. DU PIN.]

There, when they saw that the basilica had been shut against their savagery, they ordered their companions who were present to climb onto the roofs, strip off the roofing, and hurl tiles. Their orders were carried out without delay. While Catholic deacons defended the altar, many were bloodied by tiles; two were killed: Primus, son of Januarius, and Donatus, son of Ninus. This occurred while your aforementioned fellow-bishops pressed on and stood by, so that the saying was undoubtedly spoken of you: “Their feet are swift to shed blood” (Ps. XIII.3).

[Note: [Col. 0970C] “Two were killed.” They are called Primus and Donatus in the Roman Martyrology under 9 February, on which day their commemoration is observed. DU PIN.]

Concerning this matter Primosus, the Catholic bishop of the aforesaid place, lodged a complaint in your council at the city of Theneste, and you heard his complaints with studied indifference.

[Note: [Col. 0970C] “Theneste.” Thenae was a city in the province of Byzacena, mentioned by Pliny and in Antonine’s *Itinerary*. DU PIN.]

See: you have done what you said—that the Church is not that which feeds upon bloody bites. Soldiers who are sent are one thing; bishops who are ordained another.

[Note: [Col. 0970C] “Soldiers who are sent are another thing.” There is a great difference between what you have done and what you allege against us. For even if Macarius brought about unity, and was asked by us to do so, still, if anything less than humane occurred in that expedition, we neither ordered nor did it. But your bishops, in Julian’s time, perpetrated many killings with their own hands. ALBASP.]

What you say against us maliciously was done by others, not by us; what you say ought not to have been done, you yourselves did. You also mentioned the most blessed Apostle Paul as saying that the Church ought to be without wrinkle and without stain. At your bishops’ command and in their presence, Catholic deacons were killed upon the altar; likewise at Carpi.

[Note: [Col. 0970D] “At Carpi.” Carpis, a city of proconsular Africa, is mentioned by Ptolemy, Book IV, chapter III. Pliny calls this city Carpi. Secundinus of Carpi attended the Council of Carthage under Cyprian. At the Carthaginian Conference two bishops of Carpi appear, one Catholic and one of Donatus’s party. Bishops of Carpi attended the Council of Carthage under Aurelius in 419 and, in the following century, the council under Boniface. The Notice of bishops of the proconsular province includes a bishop of Carpi. Finally, at the Lateran Council under Martin II, act 2, Bassus, bishop of the Church of Carpi, is mentioned. DU PIN.]

Do these not seem to you inexpiable stains?

[Note: [Col. 0971B] In MSS S. T. and P. S., not “are divided,” but incorrectly.]

In the cities of Mauretania, when you entered, the people were shattered; those who were to be born died in their mothers’ wombs. Does there not appear to you a wrinkle that cannot be stretched out or smoothed away by any acts of satisfaction? What like this has been committed by us? We await God as avenger. Yet you make Macarius odious; if he did anything harsh for unity, it may appear slight, whereas you, for dissension, committed such bitter, bloody, and hostile evils.

[Note: [Col. 0971B] In MS S. G.: “useless,” through a copyist’s error.]

Why should I mention Tipasa, a city of Caesarean Mauretania?

[Note: [Col. 0971C] “Tipasa.” A city of Caesarean Mauretania, as Optatus observes here. Ptolemy mentions it; it occurs in Antonine’s *Itinerary*. Pliny writes that it received Latin rights. The Notice of bishops of this province has a bishop of Tipasa. Victor of Vita, Book V, no. 6, praises the outstanding faith of this city’s inhabitants. DU PIN.]

To it Urbanus of Forma and Felix of Idicra, two torches inflamed by envy, ran from Numidia.

[Note: [Col. 0971C] “Of Forma.” Two episcopal sees of this name are listed in the Notice of Numidia. Justus, bishop of Forma, attended the Carthaginian Conference. DU PIN.]

[Note: [Col. 0971B] In MS S. T.: “Idierensis”; but later in the same manuscript: “Idicrensis.”]

[Note: [Col. 0971C] “Idicrensis.” A bishopric of Numidia in the Notice and in the Carthaginian Conference. DU PIN.]

[Note: [Col. 0971C] “Who, disturbing the minds of those settled in quiet and peace.” Either *perturbantes* (“disturbing”) stands for *perturbaverunt* (“they disturbed”), as a few pages later *militantes* and *destruentes* stand for “you waged war” and “you destroyed”; or it is nominative in place of the genitive, examples of which *antiptōseis* you will observe, in considerable number, even in the New Testament. See the learned interpreter on Mark XII.40 and 2 Corinthians IV.13, who teaches that this is sometimes done on the analogy of very elegant writers. The old translator has sometimes retained it too, as at Colossians III.16: “Let the word of Christ dwell in you abundantly in all wisdom, teaching and admonishing yourselves.”

At the beginning of the Council of Carthage of 419: Bishop Aurelius said: “After the appointed day of the council, as you remember, most blessed brethren, many matters were sought while awaiting our brethren”; correctly rendered by the Greek translator: *en tō anámenein hēmas tous adelphous hēmōn* (“while we were awaiting our brethren”). And shortly thereafter again: “confirming the same synod from our predecessors,” *apo tōn proēgēsamenōn hēmas tēn autēn synodon bebaiōsantōn* (“from those who had preceded us in confirming the same synod”). M. CASAUB.]

[Note: [Col. 0971B] In MS S. T. and the printed editions: “who also [disturbed] the minds of these persons in peace,” etc.]

They disturbed the minds of those who were quiet and at peace. With the assistance both of the favor and rage of certain officials, and while the governor Athenio was present with military standards, the Catholic congregation was driven out, bloodied, and expelled from its seats. Men were torn to pieces, matrons dragged away, infants killed, unborn children forced from the womb. See what kind of Church yours was, feeding upon bloody bites under the leadership of bishops.

After this you also added: “Let the greed of vultures consume as much as it wishes; yet the number of doves is greater.” Where is the common saying that a liar ought to have a memory as his guardian?

[Note: [Col. 0971C] In MS S. G.: “that memory ought to be the guardian of a liar.” [Col. 0972B] In MS S. T.: “to have memory [as] guardian is a liar.”]

You forgot what you had said a little earlier: that the Church is the one dove of Christ in the Song of Songs.

[Note: [Col. 0972B] In MS S. T.: “what.” In MS S. G.: “because.”]

[Note: [Col. 0972B] In MS S. T.: “Catholic,” through a copyist’s error.]

If the Church among you is one, the dove is one. What, then, did you mean when you said, “the number of doves is greater”?

## XIX. The Eucharist given by Donatists to dogs; the ampoule of chrism hurled down; and their other sacrileges

And what seems trivial to you: a monstrous crime was committed, when your aforesaid bishops violated every sacred thing.

[Note: [Col. 0971D] “They ordered the Eucharist…” The Donatists denied that the Eucharist was validly consecrated by the orthodox. ALBASP.]

They ordered the Eucharist to be poured out for dogs.

[Note: [Col. 0972B] In MS S. G.: “to pour out.”]

Nor was this without a sign of divine judgment: for the same dogs, inflamed with rabies, tore their own masters to pieces with avenging teeth—as though they were robbers, guilty of the holy body, strangers and enemies. They also threw the ampoule of chrism through a window in order to break it. Although its being thrown down aided its fall, an angelic hand was not lacking to carry the ampoule down by spiritual conveyance. Though cast down, it could not experience a fall; guarded by God, it came to rest unharmed among the rocks.

[Note: [Col. 0971D] “And these things could have not been done.” The *meiosis* should be observed: it means, “these things certainly would not have been done; they could not have been done,” as in the Theodosian Code and in Cassiodorus, *non iubemus* (“we do not order”) means “we forbid.” See on Lampridius, p. 356. Thus the *Apostolic Constitutions*, Book III, chapter 20: “We do not order a presbyter or deacon to be ordained”—that is, “we forbid anyone, whether presbyter,” etc. The Greek was not at hand when I wrote this; but I suppose the translator here also rendered word for word.

Yet one should know that the verb can often be superfluous where there is no place for *meiosis*. Thus near the end of this very book, *mereri possunt* means “they deserve”; *mori potuerunt*, “they died”; and *pati potuerunt*, “they suffered”; likewise *potuit geri*, “it was done.” I spare labor and paper lest I heap up further examples; but a diligent reader may observe many more instances of similar speech in this single author. Perhaps Mark VI.5 bears upon this too: *kai ouk ēdynato*—“and he was unable there to do any mighty work,” etc.—as also Genesis XIX.22, which the Vulgate renders literally: “because I shall not be able to do anything.” M. CASAUB.]

And these things could have not been done, if you had kept in mind Christ’s commands, who said: “Do not give what is holy to dogs, nor cast your pearls before swine, lest they trample them under their feet and turn and tear you to pieces” (Matt. VII.6). What like this could have been done by the workers of unity, for which you labor to bring empty odium against us Catholics?

[Note: [Col. 0972C] In MS S. G.: “you wished.”]

On their return, Urbanus of Forma and Felix of Idicra found mothers whom they had made women out of consecrated virgins.

[Note: [Col. 0972D] “They found mothers whom they had made out of consecrated women.” We may understand “mothers” as abbesses. For just as those who presided over monks were called fathers, as Augustine teaches in *On the Morals of the Catholic Church*, chapter 31, so women who presided over nuns were formerly called mothers. Jerome, writing to the fallen deacon Sabinianus: “It is the custom in Egyptian and Syrian monasteries that every virgin or widow who has vowed herself to the Lord and, renouncing the world, has trampled underfoot all worldly pleasures, offers her hair to the mothers of the monasteries to be cut; afterward she goes with her head not uncovered, according to the Apostle’s will, but bound up and veiled alike.” I copied this from an old manuscript which I recently obtained in this city.

The same Jerome, from the same manuscript, against Vigilantius near the end: “We call [them] mothers, sisters, and daughters; and we are not ashamed to cover our vices with names of devotion. What is a monk doing in the cells of women?” Further, this author habitually uses *invenire* (“find”) in this connection; a few pages later: “you found boys,” “you found old believers,” “you found deacons, presbyters,” etc. Why, nevertheless, would he here mention mothers, each of whom presided, rather than nuns living under their rule and discipline? Moreover, it is credible that there were then so many virgins consecrated to God, whether monasteries or hostels—Augustine, chapter 33 of *On the Morals of the Church*—that, if there were several mothers, this would follow. Therefore I judge it truer that “mother” should here be understood in the common sense, namely, a woman who has given birth; the statement will then indeed be sharper. But *fecerunt* (“they did”) should be replaced with *fecerant* (“they had done”), unless the very word *fecerant* is present. Formerly I read *mitratas* (“women wearing mitres”) for *matres*, but I do not approve it.

As for mitres and little mitres, the veils of holy virgins, the rite of cleansing by ashes and salted water, and whatever else relating to ancient rites belongs to our author here—as well as many observations about penitence throughout—these matters have long been occupied by learned men, and we deliberately pass them over. For we are not trying to fill pages or, proudly decked in the feathers of others, to display ourselves, as many now do. Rather, we have undertaken to elucidate whatever remains obscure in Optatus and, so far as we know, untouched by others. M. CASAUB.]

[Note: [Col. 0973B] Thus in MS S. G. Incorrectly in MS S. T. and the printed editions: “they did.”]

[Note: [Col. 0973D] “They found mothers whom they had made women out of consecrated women.” They found that those from whom they had stripped the veil of virginity had given birth, and that they had thus made women out of consecrated virgins. DU PIN.]

See what kind of bishops you conceal, brother Parmenian; and though you ought to have been ashamed for the sake of your own people, you accuse innocent Catholics.

[Note: [Col. 0973B] In MS S. G.: “what sort he is,” through a copyist’s slip.]

[Note: [Col. 0973B] Perhaps *zelas* (“you emulate”) rather than *celas* (“you conceal”).]

Meanwhile the aforementioned Felix, among his crimes and unspeakable deeds, did not hesitate wickedly to violate a girl whom he himself had invested with the *mitra*, and by whom he had shortly before been called father.

[Note: [Col. 0973D] “Mitre.” A kind of garment and covering used by women consecrated to God. ALBASP.]

[Note: [Col. 0973D] “Mitre.” On this term see what we shall say below in the notes on Book VI. DU PIN.]

[Note: [Col. 0973D] “He was called father.” Because, when she became a consecrated virgin, he had in a sense begotten her for God. ALBASP.]

And, as though he became holier by sinning, he hurried swiftly to Tysedis.

[Note: [Col. 0973B] Thus in MS S. G. In MSS S. T. and P. S.: “to the seat”; corruptly, in the printed editions, “thence.” Tysedis was a place of which Donatus was bishop. At the Carthaginian Conference there is a bishop of Tysedis in Numidia; Sallust mentions Tisidium in *The Jugurthine War*, chapter 62. In the Notice of African bishops: “Tididitanus” or “Tiditanus”; and in Leo’s Notice: “Titisis.”]

Thus he dared to strip Donatus, a seventy-year-old bishop and an innocent man, of episcopal name, office, and honor.

[Note: [Col. 0973D] “Donatus.” A certain bishop of the orthodox party. ALBASP.]

[Note: [Col. 0973D] “Name.” Name, office, and honor: these three were distinguished in a bishop. Some were deprived of office, while neither episcopal honor nor name was taken from them. Others again were stripped both of honor and office, while the name of bishop remained. Finally, when they were reduced to the lay state and deposed, they were punished by deprivation of all three. ALBASP.]

A schismatic came to a Catholic bishop; a guilty man to an innocent one; a sacrilegious man to God’s priest; an incestuous man to a chaste one; one no longer a bishop to a bishop. Yet he was secure because of your plan and conspiracy, armed with your laws and decrees.

[Note: [Col. 0974C] “By consent.” Better: “from the palace.” ALBASP.]

He laid hands upon the head of an innocent man—hands which sins had shortly before weighed down.

[Note: [Col. 0974C] “Hands which sins had shortly before made gross.” Fr. Balduin likewise reads “weighed down.” Barthius says that *crassare*, “to make gross,” is a word common in the later age, used by Sidonius Apollinaris and employed by Agroetius to embellish his treatise on orthography. There he says: “*Crassari* belongs to the body and fattening; *grassari* to the mind and cruelty.” See also Zeno, bishop of Verona. INCERT.]

[Note: [Col. 0974B] Thus in MS S. G. In MSS S. T. and P. S.: “had made gross.”]

And from that tongue he dared to pronounce a sentence—a tongue which no longer seemed even fit to undertake penance.

[Note: [Col. 0974C] “Which was now not even fit for penance.” This tongue dared to condemn Donatus, a bishop of seventy years, though after so many crimes it was not worthy to be admitted to penance, but ought to have been excluded from the Church forever. ALBASP.]

[Note: [Col. 0974B] Absent in MS S. G.]

See what kind of men you defend, brother Parmenian; see for what kind you said long ago that endowments accomplish their work.

[Note: [Col. 0974C] “For what kind.” See whose works—and, by the work of the worker, whose sacraments and sacramental grace—you wish to be conferred. ALBASP.]

## XX. Against Donatists who call themselves holy: no human being is free from sin and perfect

Even you yourselves, who wish to appear holy and innocent before people, tell us: whence comes this holiness which you so freely claim for yourselves? The Apostle John does not dare to profess it, for he says: “If we say that we have no sin, we deceive ourselves, and the truth is not in us” (1 John I.8). He who said this wisely reserved himself for God’s grace. For it belongs to the Christian person to will what is good and, in what he has willed well, to run; but it has not been given to a human being to bring it to completion. Thus, after the courses which a person ought to complete, something remains for God, who comes to the aid of one who fails; for he alone is perfection, and Christ, the Son of God, alone is perfect. All the rest of us are half-perfect.

[Note: [Col. 0974B] In MS S. G.: “You who are as though holy.”]

[Note: [Col. 0974D] “And in God, that which [he] wills well.” Even a blind man can see that one must write “and in him,” not “and in God”; for he says immediately: “Ours is the willing, ours is the running; God’s is the completing.” He plainly has in view the Apostle’s words: “Therefore it is not of the one who wills nor of the one who runs, but of God who shows mercy.” Those who do not notice the force of the Hebrew words and the very pleasing and elegant *paronomasia* which the Apostle then had in mind, and which occasioned these words, lose something; the first syllable of *tou* must also be attended to as part of the wordplay.

Optatus’s words should be understood aptly and in accordance with the Apostle’s meaning, lest he seem to contradict the same Apostle at Philippians II.12: “For God is…” If you wish, consult the most distinguished man—whom we count among the no small blessings of fortune as our close friend—in his highly praised work, Book IV, part two. M. CASAUB.]

[Note: [Col. 0974B] Thus in MS S. G. In MSS S. T. and P. S., and in the printed editions: “in God”; but contrary to the author’s meaning, who immediately says, “ours is the willing, ours is the running; God’s is the completing.”]

For ours is the willing, ours is the running; God’s is the completing. Hence the most blessed Apostle Paul says: “It depends neither on one who wills nor on one who runs, but on one who belongs to God’s grace” (Rom. IX.16). For perfect holiness has not been given by Christ our Savior, but promised. Thus he says: “You shall be holy, for I am holy” (Lev. XI.45). Therefore he alone is perfect and holy. He did not say, “You are holy,” but said, “You shall be holy.” Whence, then, do you arrogate perfect holiness to yourselves through pride? Unless it is so that it may appear that you deceive yourselves and that the truth is not in us. You refused to be in John’s school.

For when you lead some astray, you promise that you will grant forgiveness of sins. When you wish to forgive sins, you profess your own innocence; and you grant remission of sins as though you yourselves had no sin. This is not confidence, but deception; not truth, but falsehood. Indeed, within adjacent moments, while you lay hands on people and forgive sins, immediately afterward, turning to the altar, you cannot omit the Lord’s Prayer.

[Note: [Col. 0975D] “You lay hands [on them].” Formerly penitents were publicly absolved, even during the Mass. Tertullian, *On Modesty*: “[one] prostrating himself in the midst”; likewise, “you fill the rest also with fear.” ALBASP.]

[Note: [Col. 0975D] “Immediately afterward, turning to the altar.” When penitents had been absolved, bishops returned to the altar. ALBASP.]

[Note: [Col. 0975D] “The Lord’s Prayer.” Therefore absolution took place before the Lord’s Prayer and before communion. ALBASP.]

And certainly you say: “Our Father, who art in heaven, forgive us our debts and sins.” What are you called when you confess your own sins, if you are holy when you forgive another’s? In this way you too deceive yourselves, and the truth is not in you.

[Note: [Col. 0975C] In MS S. G.: “what are you habitually called?”]

But, as is evident, your nurse Pride dictates this to you. Christ attests to her in the Gospel: though he did not name you, he nevertheless displayed your character through a parable. For it is written: “Jesus spoke this parable concerning those who consider themselves holy and despise others” (Luke XVIII.9). The matter itself plainly shows that this was said of you, since you exalt yourselves as holy and openly, unmistakably despise us. “Two men,” he says, “went up into the temple to pray, one a Pharisee and the other a tax collector” (ibid. 10). The Pharisee was swollen, proud, puffed up—such as we see you to be—not with body humbled or neck bent, but with face raised and breast puffed out: “I thank you, God, because I have committed no sin.” That is to say to God: “I have nothing for you to forgive.” This is mad frenzy, pride deserving punishment and condemnation. God is ready to forgive, and the guilty person hastens to refuse pardon.

The humble tax collector, knowing himself to be human, prayed thus: “Be merciful to me, Lord, a sinner” (ibid. 14). Thus humility deserved to be justified; thus pride, in the Pharisee your teacher, descended from the temple condemned.

[Note: [Col. 0975C] This word has been added from MS S. G.]

Sins accompanied by humility were found better than innocence accompanied by pride. Moreover, although you do not lack the grave sins of betrayal and schism, you also congratulate yourselves for being proud.

[Note: [Col. 0975D] Thus in MS S. G. In MS S. T.: “and, moreover, you congratulate yourselves for being above yourselves”; *super vos* for *superbos*, “proud.”]

## XXI. The Donatists reproved for stripping bishops of rank and subjecting them to the labors of penance

Now that we have demonstrated your shameful joys and your frenzy has been shown in so many places, it remains to say something about your profound impiety. For who could recount everything that is done or has been done by you? It is clear that you arranged everything with a certain malice so that, in a single form of your action, you might fill up other forms as well: so that, while a presbyter or bishop was cast down, the people might thereby be captured.

[Note: [Col. 0975D] “While a bishop is cast down.” He is removed from his position. Tertullian, *On Exhortation*: “I remember men twice married cast down from their position.” They drove bishops from their sees, made them laypeople, and laid the hand of penance upon them—all this in order to turn the minds of believers away from the Church. ALBASP.]

How could a crowd of people remain firm when it saw its leader crushed by you? It is no different from the case in which, when a shepherd is slain by any misfortune, wolves ravage. You exorcised believers and washed walls for no reason, in order by this kind of wickedness to overthrow the minds of the simplest people.

[Note: [Col. 0976B] In MSS S. T. and P. S.: “when.”]

[Note: [Col. 0976B] MS S. G. adds “believers,” omitted in MSS S. T. and Ph. S.]

By your such schemes, the minds of some were slaughtered. Under a cloud of apparent simplicity, with the light of cunning obscured, you sent forth arrows from the quiver of your breast—your seductions beforehand—in order to strike down the wretched. Thus the Holy Spirit foretold concerning you through David the prophet in the Psalm: “For behold, sinners have bent the bow; they have prepared arrows in their quiver to shoot at the upright in heart in the dark of the moon” (Ps. X.3). What did your schemes leave undone? Innocent people were wounded, believers disarmed, priests stripped of the honor of their title.

[Note: [Col. 0976B] Thus in MS S. G. In MS S. T. and the printed editions: “shot with arrows.”]

O unheard-of impiety: to keep alive amid the torments of penance the man whom you have slain!

[Note: [Col. 0975D]

“The one whom you have slain, [you keep] amid penance.” Other editions read this: “O unheard-of impiety, which securely slays amid the torments of penance!” This fits what precedes reasonably well, but what follows seems rather to require the reading in this edition. M. CASAUB.

Ibid. “To keep alive amid penance and torments.” The bishops whom they had deposed and killed through deprivation of the episcopate they then enrolled among penitents. This was to keep alive, amid the torments of penance, those whom they had slain. ALBASP.]

[Note: [Col. 0976D] Thus in MS S. G. In MSS S. T. and P. S.: “to rage.”]

[Note: [Col. 0976D] “To keep alive amid the torments of penance the one whom you have slain.” To keep in the labors of penance a priest whom you have cast down from his rank. DU PIN.]

Compared with your deed, the savagery of robbers appears lighter.

[Note: [Col. 0976D]

“You commit a living murder.” You allow the bishops whom you killed and stripped of rank to drag out a miserable life among penitents. This is to commit a living murder. ALBASP.

Ibid. “But you commit a living murder.” He said this in place of: “you cause eminent men, stripped of goods and dignities, to live as a punishment, as though you had made them survive themselves.” Manilius, Book V:

> The living funeral of a maiden is snatched away without a funeral.

Goods and dignities are another life for human beings, another blood, as Accursius—the jurist barbarous in vocabulary but by no means in intellect—said. We wish you to see other examples of this kind in the miscellaneous observations of Joannes Meursius, a most excellent and learned man and our close friend. Of the same meaning is Ulysses’ verse to Penelope in Ovid:

> Your possessions tear apart our very entrails.

BARTH.]

You commit a living murder.

[Note: [Col. 0977C] “You commit a living murder.” You compel bishops whom you have killed with respect to civil life—that is, whom you have stripped of honor and rank—to drag out a miserable life among penitents. This is to commit a living murder. [Col. 0977D] DU PIN.]

A robber gives those he has cut down the relief of death. Those whom you were able to deceive were ensnared by poverty of understanding. For they had been made perfect—by God’s work, that is—when they were ordained in his name. But you, waging hostile war against God’s work and destroying the divine work with the levers of wickedness. Thus it is clear that the saying concerning you occurs in Psalm X: “What you have made perfect, they have destroyed” (Ps. X.4).

[Note: [Col. 0977B] Thus in MS S. G. In MSS S. T. and P. S.: “of warfare.”]

Your impiety made you proud; but justice, looking down from heaven, accuses you. While you act unjustly, human error praises you, so that the Holy Spirit said concerning you in Psalm IX: “For the sinner is praised in the desires of his soul, and he who has acted unjustly shall be blessed” (Ps. IX.24). What is more unjust than to exorcise the Holy Spirit, break altars, and throw the Eucharist to animals? And, so that your own people may lead you into error, they call you blessed in their praise, speak blessing upon you, swear by you, and are known already to treat your persons as God.

[Note: [Col. 0977D] “And so that your people may lead you into error, they call you blessed in praise and speak blessing upon you,” etc. “They speak blessing upon you,” that is, they utter your names in place of every good thing. Tibullus, Book II, elegy 1:

> But let each man speak well of Messalla over his cups;
>
> Let every word resound with the name of the absent man.

BARTH.]

[Note: [Col. 0978C]

“And they speak blessing upon you.” That is, they utter your names in place of every good omen. A learned man on this passage also produces the lines of Tibullus:

> But let each man speak well of Messalla over his cups;
>
> Let every word resound with the name of the absent man.

Perhaps that is true, but this seems insufficiently appropriate, unless I am mistaken. For it is one thing to remember friends, whether present or absent, while drinking and wish them well with the Plautine formula, “Well to me, well to you, well to us, well to you, and well also to our Stephanium”; it is another to utter someone’s name as an omen of good, and the person who does this rather wishes good to himself. I am not unaware that drinkers were also accustomed to invoke gods and goddesses, whom one may more plausibly suppose were named as a good omen; but that relates neither to this passage of Optatus nor to that of Tibullus.

You may also interpret *bene nominant* as meaning: whenever they name you, they call you blessed—just as Tertullian, in several short chapters addressed to martyrs, properly calls designated martyrs “the blessed” and “blessed women.” Augustine shows at length that Donatists commonly complain of persecution by Catholics and call themselves and their followers martyrs for the truth. M. CASAUB.]

[Note: [Col. 0978C] “They speak blessing upon you.” They pray well for you; they proclaim you holy and friends of God. DU PIN.]

[Note: [Col. 0978C]

“They swear by you.” These words should be referred to Donatus of Carthage, who tolerated people’s swearing by him. ALBASP.

Ibid. “They swear by you and are known to regard your persons as God.” See also Book III. Horace, *Odes*, Book IV, ode 5, addressed to Augustus:

> From this point, joyful, he returns to wine and at the second table
>
> he welcomes you as a god.

Likewise:

> And we set up altars to be sworn by in your name.

INCERT.]

## XXII. The impiety of Donatists who swore by their bishops

God is customarily named by people in an oath in order to test faith; but when people swear by you, silence is already kept among your followers regarding God and Christ.

[Note: [Col. 0977B] In MS S. G.: “is kept silent.”]

If divine religion has migrated from heaven to you because people swear by you, let none of you or your people fall ill. Do not die. Command the clouds; rain, if you can, so that people may swear more fully by you and be silent about God. For in earlier ages, in order that temples might be built and idols made, what more could the devil accomplish through your people? Nothing else than that people should be silent about God while, through error, they spoke only of the devil.

### XXIII. The Donatists Are Rebuked for Shaving the Heads of Priests Anointed by God

O sacrilege joined to impiety! [Note: [Col. 0977B] Thus in MS S. T.: that is, “sacrilege joined to impiety.” [Col. 0978B] For it is sacrilege to swear by a human being; it is impiety to be silent concerning God and not to hear his voice.] While you willingly hear people swearing by you, you do not admit to your ears the voice of God, who says in Psalm 104 [105], verse 15: “Do not touch my anointed ones, nor lay hands upon my prophets.” The books of Kings show that both kings and priests are anointed; and David says in Psalm 132 [133], verse 2: “Like the ointment upon the head, which runs down [Col. 0978B] upon Aaron’s beard.”

[Note: [Col. 0978D] “And yet you, against those same powers.” I wonder how this entered the improved edition, when the earlier reading was better: “and yet you, having exerted yourselves against with these same powers,” etc. M. Casaubon.]

46. And yet you have endeavoured, with the same powers by which those who fear God seek to fulfill his commands, to despise his precepts. Teach us where you were commanded to shave the heads of priests, [Note: [Col. 0978D] “To shave the heads of priests.” The heads of penitents were shaved and sprinkled with ashes; thus, when the Donatists imposed penance on priests, they shaved their heads. Albaspinaeus.] [Note: [Col. 0978D] “To shave the heads of priests.” The Donatists shaved [Col. 0979C] the heads of priests, as though to remove their priestly anointing. Du Pin.] whereas, on the contrary, so many examples have been set before us showing that this ought not to be done.

Before Saul sinned, he deserved to be anointed; after his anointing, he committed no slight offence. When God saw this, wishing to furnish an example that the oil must not be touched, he professed repentance. For the Lord is read to have said: “I repent that I anointed Saul king” (1 Kings 15:11); and surely God could have taken away the oil which he had bestowed. But, because he wished to teach that the oil must not be touched even in a sinner, he who had given it expressed repentance. Therefore, if God, in order to teach you, did not take away what he had given—because he did not wish to do so—who are you to take away what you did not give? You, who ought to have prepared your ears to hear, prepared a razor to commit wrongdoing. Though you could have been sons of God, you chose to be sons of men; and, in order to fasten a bite upon the honours belonging to others, you turned your teeth into arrows and weapons, and sharpened your tongues into swords. You fulfilled what is written of you in Psalm 56 [57]: “The sons of men: their teeth are weapons and arrows, and their tongue a sharp sword” (Ps. 56 [57]:4).

### XXIV. The Wrong Done by the Donatists to Every Class and Age of Human Beings through the Imposition of Hands for Penance

[Col. 0979B] Therefore you sharpened your tongues into swords, which you set in motion [Note: [Col. 0979C] “Unto deaths, not of bodies but of honours.” Because they stripped bishops of honour and office. Albaspinaeus.] for deaths—not deaths of bodies, but of honours. You slaughtered not limbs, [Note: [Col. 0979C]

“You slaughtered names.” You removed their dignity. Albaspinaeus.

Ibid. “You slaughtered not limbs, but names.” He uses *names* for dignities and honours. He immediately adds: “they bear the funerals of a dignity taken away”; and on p. 60, “the funerals of honours are by no means enough for your throat”; likewise, on p. 60, “with the sword of your tongue you slaughtered God’s bishops, shedding not the blood of the body but of honour,” etc. Anonymous.

Ibid. “But names.” We noted that *names* are used for dignities: “you slaughtered not limbs but names,” since he immediately says, “they bear the funeral of dignity taken away.” Ovid:

> Live for yourself, and cultivate great names from afar.

Barth.] but names. What advantage is it that the persons live, when they have been killed by you in honour? Albaspinaeus.] Their limbs are indeed sound, but they bear the funeral of their dignity, which has been taken away.

[Note: [Col. 0979D] “For you stretched out your hand.” You imposed penance upon everyone and made all ranks—bishops, presbyters, deacons, and laypeople—truly into laypersons. Albaspinaeus.]

For you stretched out your hand, and spread deadly coverings over every head. Albaspinaeus.] Although there are, as I said above, [Note: [Col. 0979D] “Four classes of heads.” If we believe those who grant equally to priests and laypeople the power of offering sacrifice, there will be only one class of heads.] four classes of heads in the Church—bishops, presbyters, deacons, and believers—you would spare not one of them. “Overthrew.” Whoever cuts a believer off from the law and body of Christ overthrows the standing of believers. Albaspinaeus.

You overthrew the souls of men. You found children and wounded them through penance, lest some might have been ordained. Acknowledge that you overthrew souls. ### XXV. Again against the Donatists, Who Stripped Innocent Priests of Dignity and Honour and Assigned Them to Penance

[Note: [Col. 0980D] “Your companion and fellow.” That is, those bishops whom you wounded with penance were your companions and brothers. If they had done anything, they were to be deposed, not punished by penance or subjected to this disgrace; for God’s oil must not be violated. Albaspinaeus.]

He who was formerly your companion and fellow is the one against whom you now have attempted to raise your hand. You ran together. Suppose that he sinned—though it is clear that it was not a sin. In your judgment he had fallen. If you have read the Apostle, consider to whom it belongs to stand and to whom it belongs to fall. If you are a servant, acknowledge your master and understand that the man who shortly before had been running with you had not fallen for you. [Col. 0980B] Why do you rush into another’s jurisdiction? Why, rash man, do you mount God’s tribunal? Though you yourself are accused, do you dare to pass sentence on another? You have read: “He who stands stands to his own lord, and he who falls falls to his own lord” (Rom. 14:4). And his lord is able to raise him up. Who are you, to judge another’s servant?

You ought to have learned from David, God’s servant, that you must not touch oil bestowed by God upon a priest. Samuel anointed David in such a way that what had long before been given to Saul was by no means 47 taken away (1 Kings 16). Finally, when, whether by God’s command or by the ordering of events, one cave enclosed them both, Saul, who had sinned, came into the power of the young David.

[Note: [Col. 0980D] “He sees, though not seeing,” etc. Read separately: “of a closed mouth.” But *os* denotes the whole face. Germanicus, concerning Astraea:

> And, descending late from the mountains of heaven,  
> With veiled face.

Barth.]

He is seen, though not seeing: because [Col. 0981A] from a greater light, as commonly happens, [Note: [Col. 0981C]

“In the darkness of a closed air,” etc. Franciscus Balduinus likewise recognized an evident error and read the words separately, *clausideris*; but Barth emends to *clausi oris*, “of a closed mouth.” *Os* denotes the whole face; Germanicus Caesar, in the constellation of Astraea:

> And, descending late from the lofty mountains,  
> With veiled face.

Anonymous.

Ibid. “In the darkness of a closed air,” etc. He says that Saul was seen by David but could not himself see David, though both were in the same cave, because Saul’s eyes were still darkened by the greater light. We commonly experience that those who suddenly pass from open places into enclosed and dark ones, abruptly exchanging bright light for a darker place, see absolutely nothing for some time; and conversely, those who suddenly emerge from thick darkness into open light and admit the full sun at once have their eyes dazzled for a time by the sudden brightness.

As to the wording, either *coming* must be supplied—“coming from greater light”—or *from greater light* means “because of greater light,” “in consequence of greater light,” namely, the greater light which had shortly before filled his eyes, etc. The reading *clausi aeris*, “of a closed air,” as it stands can be accepted; though if anyone prefers “of a closed cave,” “of an enclosure,” or something similar that comes to the same sense, I would not contend. Barth, says the learned man, emends to *clausi oris*. This too can be accepted; but not what he immediately adds, that *os* sometimes denotes the entire face. What relevance has that here? Certainly, if we accept *oris*, no one, I think, will doubt that it is to be understood of the mouth of the cave, as sometimes occurs in the Vulgate, and not of a human mouth. Nor should the reading of the first edition, *in caligine clausus*, “shut up in darkness,” be despised.

A little later: “he could turn war by a short course into slaughter”; other editions more fully: “he could turn war into slaughter.” Shortly afterwards: “you sharpen razors on the whetstone of envy”; where, on first sight, I did not doubt that *in corde livoris*, “in the heart of envy,” should be restored, but it now seems to me that the transmitted reading is both more elegant and more pointed. Shortly afterwards, “to drag blind and ignorant peoples into captivity”: since the meaning is as clear as though written by a ray of sunlight, what are we to say of those who sought a knot in a rush by preferring to interpret *caecos in captivitatem* from Apuleius as “blind into captivity,” that is, as wholly blinded, bereft of eyes or captured? M. Casaubon.]

in the gloom of the enclosed air he could not see the other beside him. Countless armies followed the old king; yet the king himself had come into another’s power. David held in his hands an opportunity for victory: he could have slaughtered his heedless and unsuspecting enemy without labour; without bloodshed and without a conflict involving many persons, he could have turned war by a short course into slaughter. [Note: [Col. 0981B] In three manuscripts, “to send slaughter,” but correctly emended in the printed editions.] His young men and the opportunity urged him on; the favourable moment summoned him to victory.

He had already begun to draw his sword; his armed hand was already moving toward the throats of his enemies. But he was restrained by a memory full of divine commands. He resisted both the urging of his young men and the opportunity, as though saying also this: “Victory, you provoke me without cause; opportunity, you invite me to triumphs in vain.” He wished to conquer his enemy; but it was prior to preserve the Lord’s divine commands. “Shall I indeed stretch out my hand against the Lord’s anointed?” (1 Kings 24:7). He restrained his hand together with the sword; and, because he feared the oil, he spared his enemy. And, in order [Col. 0981B] to complete his reverence, he avenged him when he was slain (2 Kings 1).

But you neither fear God nor acknowledge brothers. On the whetstone [Note: [Col. 0981C] In MS S. You hunger for the honours of innocent priests. Whence has such hunger arisen in your frenzy that [Col. 0982A] you have made your throats open graves? One funeral is enough for each grave, and it is closed; but the funerals of honours were by no means sufficient for your throat, and it still stands open while you seek persons to devour. Thus it was rightly said of you: “Their throat is an open grave” (Ps. 5:11). For you also presume to curse, although it is written: “Bless, and do not curse” (Rom. 12:14). Whoever does anything against your will, you threaten with terrors and hold out curses.

[Note: [Col. 0982B] Missing in MSS S. T. and P. S.]

And because some people can deserve more evil than good, whatever [Note: [Col. 0982C]

“God’s judgment.” I do not sufficiently understand what it means to “claim by curses whatever God’s judgment has done,” unless he means whatever God has allowed to happen against their will. Albaspinaeus.

Ibid. “Whatever God’s judgment,” etc. Because, he says, events commonly occur such that not all are prosperous: whatever adversity happens to any of our people, you immediately claim and assert it for your curses, as though it had happened through their force and efficacy. Albaspinaeus’s explanation has led me to think this is the interpretation, lest anyone consider very obscure and recondite what he himself admits he does not understand. M. Casaubon.]

God’s judgment or the deserving of sin has brought about, you visit with your bitter curses.
