Certainly it is not lawful to kill. Or do you think yourselves innocent because you have not used the sword?

[Note: [Col. 0982D]

“Let even a poisoner judge himself innocent,” etc. By *venenarius* he means a poison-worker and compounder of harmful drugs (*κακῶν τῶν φαρμάκων*). The term deserves notice. It is not used by this writer alone, but by other writers of standing as well: Tertullian, Julius Firmicus, and finally Suetonius. Anonymous.

Ibid. “A poisoner.” He means a poison-worker, a maker of harmful drugs (*κακῶν φαρμάκων conditorem*). Saxo Grammaticus, the most eloquent writer of the last age, called them *venenatores*, as will be shown below in these books. Barth.]

Let even a poisoner judge himself innocent, if homicide consists only in the sword. Let him not regard himself as guilty who has killed another by withholding food. Let him judge himself innocent who, by preventing breathing, has suffocated one who wished to live. There are many kinds of killing, but death has one name. When, with confidence in your curses, you declare a person dead, what 48 difference is there whether you strike with a sword or wound with your tongue? You are unquestionably a murderer if someone who was alive has died through you.

Whoever among you is such a man [Col. 0983A] vainly professes himself a Christian or a priest of God, since he does not take care to imitate God’s gentleness, [Note: [Col. 0983B] We supplied these words from MS S. G. The others have a gap here, which Balduinus had filled with the word *ignorant*, “does not know.”] although it is written in Solomon: “God did not make death, nor does he rejoice in the destruction of the living” (Wis. 1:13). I believe that you cannot have forgotten what you did in certain places, when you wished to kill those who preached God’s law—that is, the prophets—contrary to God’s command: “Do not lay hands upon my prophets” (Ps. 104 [105]:15).

With the sword of your tongue you slaughtered Deuterius, Parthenius, Donatus, [Note: [Col. 0983B] Missing in MS S. G.] and Getulicus, bishops of God, shedding not the blood of the body but that of honour. The men lived afterwards, but you killed God’s priests in their honours. It is well known and proven that, during the persecution, some bishops who had fallen away [Note: [Col. 0983B]

“Cowardice.” They had denied Christ under tortures. Albaspinaeus.

Ibid. “Having fallen away from confession of God’s name through cowardice,” etc. Here Optatus does not use *inertia* for the atrocity of the crime, than which, in the ordinary understanding, scarcely any is greater. Rather, he calls *inertia* fear of death and love of the world and of temporal security—qualities truly proper to the inactive and cowardly. Hence in the New Testament *δειλοί*, “the fearful, timid,” and *ἄπιστοι*, “the faithless,” are joined together and excluded from the heavenly inheritance with the rest of the mass of sinners (Rev. 21:8). For it is the mark of a great and noble spirit to be a Christian.

Perhaps this also bears upon the saying of the Hebrews: “No boor [fool, simpleton] fears sin; nor is any *idiōtēs* [Hebrew: ‘person of the land’] pious,” whence come the common headings of the Fathers. Hebrews 6:11–12 also contrasts the sluggish and indolent with those who persevere in faith to the end. Blessed Chrysostom did not hesitate to attribute Judas’s unspeakable betrayal solely to his *inertia* and *ῥαθυμία*, “negligence”: “so great an evil is negligence” (*τοσοῦτόν ἐστι ῥαθυμία κακόν*), as he elegantly concludes there, vol. V, p. 363. The same blessed Father extensively maintains and argues that “wickedness comes from negligence, and virtue from diligence” (*ὅτι ἐκ ῥαθυμίας ἡ κακία, καὶ ἀπὸ σπουδῆς ἡ ἀρετή*), vol. VI, p. 844, etc. Above, in Book I, on the same matter: “so that they might compare the briefest delays of this uncertain light with the loss of eternal life,” etc.

Thus what he had earlier attributed to love and pursuit of the present life, he here attributes to cowardice; just as Quintus Curtius joined together the indolent and those who regard long life as the sole good: “Yet not even the indolent dispose of their own destinies; while they regard long life as the only good, bitter death often overtakes them” (*Deeds of Alexander*, Book IX). Below, “those who escaped” means those who did not yield to temptation or persecution, those who stood firm. For St Cyprian commonly contrasts “those standing” with “the fallen.” M. Casaubon.]

from confessing the name of God through cowardice had offered incense; [Col. 0983B] yet none of those who [Note: [Col. 0983D] “Escaped.” Those who did not deny Christ. Albaspinaeus.] the oil which belongs to God also be struck.

By his own judgment God preserved what was his; yet you rushed everywhere into what belonged to another, destroying the well-being of all.

### XXVI. Matrons, Children, and Virgins Unjustly Assigned to Penance by the Donatists

Matrons, children, and virgins alike were compelled by you, with no sin intervening; [Col. 0984B] preserving innocence and chastity, they learned at your teaching to perform penance. Is there a lesser misfortune?

[Note: [Col. 0984C] “You crushed the sexes; you afflicted the ages.” Either, with other editions, read: “Is there a lesser misfortune, when you afflicted the sexes that had been crushed?”—read *cum contritas*, as above *compressit* is used for *cum praecessit*, “when he went before”—“you afflicted the ages? Truly,” etc. Or, if “is there a lesser misfortune?” belongs to what precedes, write here: “You afflicted the ages crushed by sex?” But what does “ages crushed by sex” mean? Perhaps *utriusque*, “of both,” must be supplied or restored: “you afflicted the ages crushed of both sexes.” *Ages*, whether understood alone or joined with *contritas*, is elegantly used for old persons or persons worn out by old age, just as one finds “the old age of buildings” and “the age of buildings” used interchangeably.

Yet he had already mentioned virgins and matrons in the preceding period. Does he therefore say here once more, “both sexes”? Or rather old men: “you afflicted crushed old men,” as a few pages above, “you found ancient believers,” etc.? I once conjectured *contritas saxo vexastis*, “you afflicted those crushed by a stone,” since a little earlier he had said that kneeling was customarily required of penitents among their punishments. Besides, what relevance do the following words of the Psalmist, cited by Optatus, have here if this crushing being discussed comes not from the cruelty of those whom our author attacks, but from the old age of the elderly? Unless, indeed, “you afflicted the crushed” means “you afflicted them so as to crush them.”

Reader, it will be for you to choose whichever you prefer. I wish Optatus had not been excessively fond of such subtleties, as so many examples in the world establish. But regarding this passage, the same learned and acute B. B., whom I have already mentioned above, corrected it thus: “they learned to perform it. Is there a lesser misfortune? You crushed the sexes; you afflicted the ages. Truly, concerning you,” etc.—so that it alludes to the preceding words: “Woe to those who make a covering over every age,” etc. This too greatly pleases me. M. Casaubon.]

You crushed the sexes; [Note: [Col. 0984B] Thus in MS S. G. MSS S. T. and P. S., and the printed editions, have: “you afflicted the ages crushed by sex,” less well, for sex and age are two distinct members.] you afflicted the ages. Truly it was said [Col. 0985A] concerning you in Psalm 13 [14]: “Destruction and misery are in their ways; and they have not known the way of peace; there is no fear of God before their eyes.”

You imposed penance upon peoples. [Note: [Col. 0985B] “For it was not performed.” No one requested it. Albaspinaeus.] It was not performed by anyone of their own accord, 49 but exacted by you; nor did you impose it for equal [Note: [Col. 0985B] In MS S. G., “full.”] periods of time. [Note: [Col. 0985B] “For equal periods.” Even if, according to you, all had committed one and the same offence, their penance was dissimilar: this is respect of persons, which among the ancients could be no graver sin, nor anything more blameworthy in a bishop. Tertullian, *On Modesty*, and the Constitutions of Clement. Albaspinaeus.] Rather, you did everything according to persons: one performed penance for a whole year, another for a month, another scarcely for an entire day, at your command.

[Note: [Col. 0985C] “If to consent to unity.” If it was a sin to bring it about that Macarius should make unity. Albaspinaeus.]

If, as you maintain, it is a sin to consent to unity, and if the guilt is alike, why is the penance for the same charge unequal? There is no doubt that the people of believers is called Israel; [Note: [Col. 0985C] “That the people of believers is called Israel,” etc. I wonder what could have induced those from whom Optatus drew to interpret Israel as “one who sees God with the mind.” I do not ask how true this is—for no one can be ignorant that it is utterly false—but I look for some occasion for the error, such as we recognize in “seeing God” or “a man seeing God,” noted by Augustine and others. Or perhaps because the Seventy sometimes rendered it by *καταμανθάνειν*, “to observe attentively,” and *προσνοεῖν*, “to direct one’s mind toward,” they derived from this a name which also signified mind?

But whatever the matter may be, since Jerome adduces this among other interpretations—mockingly, indeed, but still adduces it—and since those after Jerome who collected the Hebrew words of Scripture also give it, there is no reason to doubt the antiquity of this interpretation. Yet the judicious reader should further consider how “to see God with the mind” and “to bend and incline necks,” which Optatus here sets as contraries, are opposed. I am fully persuaded that Optatus wrote *recte* or *erecte*, “uprightly”; later, because that was less familiar, though more correct and less remote from the Hebrew, it was changed to *mente*, “with the mind.” Thus, just as in the parable of the Publican and Pharisee an upright face and an inclined neck are contrasted, here too are one who sees uprightly and one who bends his neck. Related and from the same root is Jerome’s interpretation of Israel as “upright of God,” or *εὐθύτατος Θεοῦ*, “most upright of God.”

Remigius also gives this in his explanations of Hebrew names, of which an old manuscript survives even today in our, however inadequate, Canterbury library—once, alas once, exceedingly well furnished, but long ago plundered by impious zealots accustomed to cloak their robberies and sacrileges with piety, and, as they say, divided as spoils among the very plunderers. Below, I once thought that *massam poenitentium facere*, “to make a mass of penitents,” ought to be corrected to *ferre*, “to bear,” but I no longer approve this. For *massa* was used not only of weight, as “a mass of gold” or “of silver,” and the like, but of every heap or series of things of the same kind. Hence in Gregory and others one very often finds several joined country houses, which the Greeks call *συνοικίαι*, called *massae*: that is, estates or landed properties. In the Code of the Canons of the African Church, p. 157, a *massa diaeceseon* is called what shortly afterward is a *fascis dioecesium*, “a bundle of dioceses”; the Greek translator renders it *συγκλησίαν* and *σῶμα τῶν παροικιῶν*, “an assembly” and “a body of parishes.” M. Casaubon.

Casaubon is mistaken when he says that only Jerome, in his book *On Names*, has “a mind seeing God”; for it is also found in Greek fragments, *νοῦς ὁρῶν Θεοῦ* or *Θεόν*, “a mind seeing God” or “seeing God.” The Hebrew word itself does not contain the meaning “mind,” but the interpreter supplies it because God can be perceived only by the mind. Le Clerc.]

and each individual congregation is a daughter of Israel—that is, [Col. 0986A] those who have seen God with the mind [Note: [Col. 0986D] “Who sees God.” The faithful prayed to God with erect neck; penitents, however, with face cast down to the ground. Thus he says that the Donatists compelled those who ought to look upon God to fix their eyes on the ground and gaze upon the earth. Albaspinaeus.] and believed in God. God laments over these congregations through Ezekiel the prophet, saying: “Woe to the daughters who sew cushions” (Ezek. 13)—that is, parts of the neck, to be placed beneath the elbow and hand. Certainly they are beneath your elbows and hands when you stretch coverings of penance over their heads, whether men’s or women’s. Your impiety and fury have been shown, and your pride demonstrated; your folly too had to be disclosed, but I shall show it in Book VI. [Note: [Col. 0986B] MS S. G. has “we shall show.” After these words MSS S. T. and P. S. have: “The Second Book ends.” MS S. G. has: “The Second Book of Saint Optatus ends.”]

## 50. BOOK THREE

[Note: [Col. 0987A] In MSS S. T. and P. S.: “The chapters of Book Three begin.”]

This third book contains four causes why unity was achieved with no little severity. First, because the schismatics made the basilicas unnecessary and introduced rebaptism. [Note: [Col. 0987A] These words are absent from MSS S. T. and P. S.] Second, because Donatus of Carthage called for unity to be effected. Third, because Donatus of Bagaïa [Note: [Col. 0987A] Thus in MS S. T.; MS S. G., “of Vagaïa”; MS P. S., “of Vaga.”] assembled circumcellions [Note: [Col. 0987A] MSS S. T. have *cercilliones*.] in order to hinder the workers of unity. Fourth, that none of the things for which some people think unity should be reproached happened apart from God’s will. [Note: [Col. 0987A] In MSS S. T. and P. S. Book Three begins with these words, but wrongly; they belong to the book’s summary, not its subject matter.]

[Col. 0987]

[Col. 0987A] ### I. The More Severe Measures Taken against the Donatists Were Taken at Their Own Provocation and Must Not Be Imputed to the Catholics

[Note: [Col. 0987B] “Enough, I think, in the second book.” Other editions begin this book thus: “Enough, I think, from those things for which some people believe unity should be reproached,” etc. Since these words have no connection at all, I have no doubt that they are spurious intrusions and were rightly removed by Balduinus. Therefore recent editors had no reason to contaminate Balduinus’s edition with such scraps gathered from here and there; from the same source comes the impure gloss at the close of the preceding book, “cushions, that is, members of the neck,” which they restored to Optatus’s text against Balduinus’s judgment.

But, so that the issue may be beyond controversy and we may silence contentious persons, the origin of the corruption must also be indicated. In Cochlaeus’s German edition, summaries are prefixed to every book except the first; they are nearly, I think, Optatus’s own, and are certainly ancient. The summary of this third book is composed as follows: “This third book contains four causes why unity was achieved with no little severity. First, because the schismatics made the basilicas [Col. 0987C] unnecessary. Second, because Donatus of Carthage called for unity to be effected. Third, because Donatus of Bagaïa assembled circumcellions in order to hinder the workers of unity. Fourth, that nothing happened without God’s will.” It ought to have been followed by: “From those things for which some people think unity should be reproached.” But this was wrongly attached to the beginning of the following book.

Nor should anyone be surprised, since a similar thing occurred in Book V of the same edition. For just as here part of the summary was wrongly joined to the opening of the following book, so there several lines from the beginning of the book were added to its summary, though they are lacking from their proper place. For that book begins: “In the question now under discussion,” etc.; all that precedes must be restored from the book’s summary. I also note that Fulgentius the African, plainly a devoted reader of Optatus, begins his second book addressed to Monimus with precisely the words by which Optatus begins here: “Enough, I think, most dear Monimus,” etc. M. Casaubon.]

Enough, I think, was said in the second little book concerning the Church, the bride of Christ, her endowments, and the inheritance of the Saviour. It follows first to expose the errors of the schismatics; then to show what cause there was for unity to be established; [Note: [Col. 0988A] MSS S. Ibid. “By the agents of unity.” He calls the ministers of unity *operarii*; you will see examples of this usage in what follows, and let us interpret the author from the author himself. At first there was no terror; no one had seen a rod; no one a guard; there were only exhortations, as we have said above. You all were afraid, fled, and trembled; [Col. 0990A] so that what is written in Psalm LII might truly be said of you: “They trembled” [Note: [Col. 0990B] In MS S. G., “there they feared with fear.”] “where there was no fear” (Ps. LII, 6). Therefore all the bishops fled with their clergy; some died; those who were stronger were captured and [Note: [Col. 0989D] *Banished.* The Donatist bishops. ALBASP.] banished to distant places.

## II. That these things were done to the Donatists in vindication of God and the Church

And yet none of all these things was done [Note: [Col. 0989D] *According to our wish.* These things were not done by decision of our council. ALBASP.] at our wish, none by our counsel, none with our knowledge, none by our action; but all were done amid the grief of God, who wept bitterly, and [Note: [Col. 0989D] *In vindication of the water.* God wished through Macarius to avenge what you do against His baptism. ALBASP.] in vindication of the water [Note: [Col. 0989D] *Vindication of the water:* namely, of the sacred washing administered by Catholics, which the Donatists held to be worthless and profane, rebaptizing those who came over to them from the Catholics. DU PIN.], [Note: [Col. 0989D–0990C] *Which you stirred again contrary to the prohibition.* In these words Optatus alludes at once to several passages of Holy Scripture: doubtless, and chiefly, to the Evangelist’s account in John, chapter V; but also to those words of the prophet Isaiah, which he cites shortly afterward, concerning the ancient pool, and which he has transferred to this matter. When he says “contrary to the prohibition,” it has the same force as what he earlier called “contrary to the laws,” in book I, referring to the words: “He who has been washed once has no need to be washed again,” as we explained there. Unless perhaps he speaks also of the same pool: as though it were unlawful for the angel to stir it more than once, or, after it had once been stirred by him, if not unlawful, nevertheless foolish and pointless for anyone to stir it again.

Moreover, that pool of Bethesda was considered by others also to be a figure of baptism; see Tertullian, *On Baptism*, chapters 5 and 6. What Optatus infers here from the fish seems to result from his taking *piscina* in its ancient sense, as Pliny calls it, for a fish-preserve, not for a mere κολυμβήθρα, “bathing-pool,” although that word too is used for an ἰχθυοτροφεῖον, “fish-pond”: whether a place of waters introduced and conducted in for use, for some other purpose, or for swimming—this latter being the later frequent and usual sense of the word. M. CASAUB.]

which you stirred again contrary to the prohibition: you transferred to yourselves the water of the ancient pool; but I do not know whether together with that [Note: [Col. 0990C] *Fish.* That is, with Christ: I do not know whether those whom you baptize are reborn as Christians. Tertullian: “But we little fishes, according to our Fish, ἰχθύς, Jesus Christ, are born in the waters.” But one should read “by invocation,” not “by immersion.” Tertullian. ALBASP.] fish, who is understood to be Christ, [Note: [Col. 0990C–0991B] *Who is read in the Patriarch Tobit’s reading.* Other editions give “of the Patriarchs” for “of the Patriarch.” They differ only in this. But it is not easy to guess what Optatus means by “the reading of the Patriarch” or “of the Patriarchs.” I think no such writing ever existed, nor, so far as I know, does one exist anywhere today. I remember once seeing in the Library of the Fathers a certain fictitious and pseudepigraphic Testament under the name of the twelve patriarchs. It did not seem worthy of being read, although I do not deny that something of the sort existed in ancient times. But since everything which Optatus here relates occurs in Tobit, why should he seek witnesses elsewhere? I am therefore fully persuaded that he cites none other than Tobit himself.

Everyone at all acquainted with the books of ancient writers will, I think, observe how recent is the division of Holy Scripture into chapters and verses, or little readings, which we all now use. Since the ancients indicated the desired passage not by numbers, as we commonly do, nor by divisions of Scripture itself—except in the Psalms—but in different ways, many by the subject matter itself, sometimes quoting words from the sacred context itself, I think there were also some who made certain quasi-chapters from principal and especially memorable words conveniently excerpted here and there, and in that way divided books into parts. Since, therefore, the most distinctive feature of this part of Tobit, which we today still separate as a chapter, seemed to be its mention of patriarchs, the name “Patriarch,” or “Patriarchs,” attached itself to the whole section or chapter. Thus, I think, Optatus—or a reader of Optatus, who perhaps had noted it in the margin of his book and it was later admitted into the text—means nothing else here than to indicate that title or section of Tobit which contains the account of the fish caught in the river Tigris, what we today would call the sixth chapter of Tobit.

What follows, “with the entrails of the same fish,” etc., should not be connected with what precedes as though the latter clause narrated something new about the same fish. Since it repeats exactly the same things as before, it would commit a manifest tautology. Rather, *ejusdem* means “of one and the same”; he repeats the matter in slightly altered words in order to make the reader linger and dwell for a while on a remarkable event. Therefore I approve beginning a new period here also, with a full stop after *videntis* (“the sightless man”). M. CASAUB.]

who is read in the section of the Patriarch Tobit [Note: [Col. 0990B] Thus we restore the text from MS S. G.; in the others and in printed editions, “of the Patriarchs.”] as caught in the river Tigris, [Col. 0991A] whose gall and liver Tobit took for the protection of the woman Sarah and for the restoration of sight to Tobit when he could not see: with the entrails of that same fish [Note: [Col. 0991A] Absent from MSS S. T. and P. S.] the demon Asmodeus [Note: [Col. 0991A] In MS S. G., “Nasmodeus.”] [Note: [Col. 0991C] *Asmodeus.* This is the name of the demon who had killed Sarah’s seven former husbands. In Sebastian Münster’s Hebrew text, chapter VI, verse 14: “I have also heard that Asmodeus, prince of demons, killed them; therefore I am greatly afraid that perhaps Asmodeus will kill me too.” DU PIN.] was driven from the maiden Sarah (who is understood to signify the Church), and blindness was expelled from Tobit (Tobit VI).

[Note: [Col. 0991C] *This fish, which in baptism through invocation,* etc. Fr. Baldwin’s second edition has “through invocation”; but why should we not follow Barth, who emends it to “through immersion” from book V? UNCERTAIN.]

This is the fish who, in baptism, is introduced into the waters of the font through invocation, so that the water which had been water might also be called a *piscina*, “fish-pool,” from the fish. The name of this fish, according to its Greek designation, contains in the individual letters of one word a multitude of holy names [Note: [Col. 0991C–D] *It contains a multitude of holy names.* For the individual characters of the word ΙΧΘΥΣ are the initial letters of the names of Christ: Ἰησοῦς Χριστὸς, Θεοῦ Υἱὸς, Σωτήρ—“Jesus Christ, Son of God, Saviour.” Tertullian alludes to the same thing at the beginning of *On Baptism*: “But we little fishes, after our Fish Jesus Christ, are born in the water, nor are we saved otherwise than by remaining in water.” Augustine also explains this mystery in *The City of God*, book XXVIII, chapter 23: “Of these five Greek words—Ἰησοῦς Χριστὸς, Θεοῦ Υἱὸς, Σωτήρ—which in Latin are JESUS CHRIST, SON OF GOD, SAVIOUR, if you join the first letters, you will have ἰχθύς, that is, ‘fish’; in this name Christ is understood mystically, because in the abyss of this mortality, as though in the depths of waters, He could remain alive—that is, without sin.” Thus the Africans were pleased to play upon this word. DU PIN.]: ἸΧΘΥΣ, which in Latin is JESUS CHRIST, SON OF GOD, SAVIOUR.

This pool, [Col. 0992A] which throughout every Catholic Church over the whole world overflows with saving waters for the life of humankind, you have transferred to your own will and dissolved the one baptism. From that baptism people [Note: [Col. 0991A] In MS S. G., “believers.”] were made walls for protection; and you made, as it were, [Note: [Col. 0991D] *Other walls.* Christians are temples of God; you make other temples. ALBASP.] other walls, erecting no good [Note: [Col. 0991A] In MSS S. T. and P. S., “no new”; in MS S. G. [Col. 0992A], “much good.” From both we restore “no good.”] building: you could not build unless you first destroyed. And [Note: [Col. 0992A] In MS S. G., “But.”] what sort of building can that be which [Note: [Col. 0991D] *Is built from ruin.* Tertullian: “For their work itself does not arise from their own proper building, but they undermine our structure of truth in order to build their own.” ALBASP.] is built from ruin?

Through Isaiah the prophet God grieves and weeps over this matter when He says that the daughter of His own race has been crushed (Isa. 22): [Note: [Col. 0991D–0992B] *God’s race is to have no race.* This is a statement of the most elegant wit, and one more penetratingly expressed and more appropriate to the matter itself than, I think, any other in all Optatus. BARTH.] God’s race is to have no race—He who exists from Himself and remains unto eternity [Note: [Col. 0992A] In MSS S. T. and P. S., “unto eternity”; in certain printed editions, incorrectly, “in eternity.”].

[Note: [Col. 0992B–0994C] *And the water is similar, which we do not read …* Optatus’s purpose here is to persuade us that the words of Isaiah the prophet, concerning God lamenting over the crushing of the daughter of His own race—he cites the whole passage at length later—refer to water. To achieve this, he derives the following argument from the prophet’s own words (I speak with Optatus, for the reader need not be informed what the Hebrew has here or elsewhere): the prophet represents God as lamenting over the daughter of His own race; but God’s race is to have no race. It followed that he should prove the same thing of water. Optatus certainly did not omit this, nor indeed could he altogether omit it. Yet what argument he used can scarcely, if at all, be detected from this edition.

For Baldwin—if indeed it was Baldwin—imitated bad surgeons here: since he could not heal a severely diseased passage, he nevertheless drew the skin over it in such a way that a superficial observer would suspect no internal wound. Earlier editions present the passage thus: “And the water is similar, which we do not read, in the injury done to which water,” etc. From this it is easy to restore what both the sense requires and the matter itself cries out was written by Optatus: “The water is similar, whose race we do not read; in the injury done to which water,” etc. The resemblance of *genus* (“race”) to the final syllables of the preceding word caused its omission, as often happens. Once it had been omitted, to produce some sense—or, if not sense, at least Latin—*quam* was substituted for *cujus*; afterward, since *non* appeared to hinder the sense, and some sense, however poor, seemed preferable to none, it too was displaced and expelled from its place.

As regards the matter itself, I do not know whether it is of any importance to mention that Thales the philosopher, according to Diogenes Laertius, made water the ἀρχὴ τῶν πάντων, “principle of all things”; or that Plutarch in *On Isis and Osiris* records that Homer also believed this, and affirms that both drew it from Egyptian philosophy. Ambrose also bears witness concerning Thales, alluding at the beginning of the *Hexaemeron*, apparently with ridicule, to that water from which all things arose: “Although he took his name from water, he nevertheless did not think it should be said that all things consisted of water, as Thales said.”

What concerns us and Optatus more is that there were once people who inferred from the creation narrative something such as Optatus appears here to imply: namely, that waters, because Scripture did not expressly mention their creation—as they inferred—existed before all things, indeed were eternal and coeternal with God. Regarding the first point, the ancient author circulated under the name of Junilius says in his *On Genesis*, Paris edition of 1556, fol. 41: “For it is not permissible to believe that the waters were made before all things [read *ante omnia*]. Although Scripture does not openly say here that the waters were created, along with the other things that were created, so that the mouths of those holding the contrary view might be stopped, it nevertheless openly indicates this when it suggests that they were illumined by God and arranged at His command, as the Psalm also says plainly,” etc.

Optatus seems to say the same in book VI: “O water, sweet water created by God, over which the Holy Spirit was borne before the birth of the world itself,” etc. But perhaps Optatus meant nothing there except what Tertullian says in book III of *On Baptism*. Among other notions he invents in praise of water, Tertullian celebrates it also because it was part of that chaos from which the ordered world afterward arose—not merely a part, but the most excellent part, and the only one complete and perfected. For earth, heaven, and all the rest were still unformed and uncultivated; but nothing was lacking from the waters whereby they might be more adorned or perfected: they remained in their first created state. So I understand Optatus when he says that the waters existed before the birth of the world itself: “world” here properly means κόσμος, the ordered and adorned world, which Tertullian calls the “structure of the world.” Before this structure of the world there was neither *mundus* nor κόσμος in the proper sense, but mere chaos, a rough and disordered mass, as the poet calls it. The waters, therefore, were before the world, though not uncreated.

There is rather more difficulty in this other passage of Optatus. For although he subtly establishes a comparison of God and water with regard to race or origin, yet, by mentioning God’s eternity, he seems, as the logic of his intended comparison requires, to present water as eternal or coeternal with Him. Augustine sufficiently indicates that there were once those who inferred this also from Moses’ own account. Since his words strongly confirm our correction, I shall cite them, *Confessions*, book XII, chapter 22: “Even if Genesis omitted that God made something which nevertheless neither sound faith nor assured understanding doubts that God made, no sober doctrine would therefore dare to say that these waters are coeternal with God because we have heard them mentioned in the book of Genesis but do not find where they were made. Why not also that unformed matter,” etc.

Eucherius, bishop of Lyons—following the text of the most ancient and earliest edition—says the same in his *Difficult Questions on Genesis*, question 3, but in words so express and apt that no clearer light need be borrowed from elsewhere for this passage of Optatus. Thus he writes in that most ancient edition, fol. 25: “Where do we read that waters were made by God? [τὸ: materially uncertain OCR.] I would also have the next part of the reading carefully observed. Although the text of divine reading does not plainly state that they were made at the beginning of creation, they nevertheless were made by God,” etc. What then if Optatus also wrote—though this would come to exactly the same thing—“which we do not read was made by God”?

There is no doubt, however, that whatever Optatus’s final words were, someone erased and struck them out because their meaning seemed too harsh. This often occurs in the writings of the ancients. But since Optatus is not treating the matter here deliberately, he must be excused if, δουλεύων ὑποθέσει, “serving his hypothesis,” he spoke with insufficient caution; just as we sometimes tolerate and excuse many things in even the best writers which otherwise would be unacceptable. For that he himself held the right view, since no one charged him with heterodoxy on this account—though Augustine, *On Heresies*, chapter 75, and others report and criticize those who maintained that waters were not created by God but coeternal with God—who can doubt at all?

Nor must every point in such comparisons be pressed too pedantically. For although when God is said to have no race or origin, He is understood to be eternal, it is sufficient for the comparison Optatus has undertaken if he proves that waters in some manner have no race or origin. This can be understood either in this way: just as Melchizedek is believed by many to have been a type of Christ, not because he was actually ἀπάτωρ and ἀμήτωρ, “without father and without mother,” as we said earlier, but because his lineage is not narrated; so waters may be said to have no race because Scripture does not expressly and by name mention their creation. Or it can be understood thus: waters are said to have no race because they were part of that first matter created from nothing, from which all other things were formed; as we were just discussing from Tertullian and from the other passage of Optatus. Whatever is created from nothing can rightly be called without race or origin.

I would also remind a reader not indifferent to the elegances of Latin style that in the immediately preceding words Optatus repeats *aquae* (“of the water”), where a pronoun might have sufficed—something for which Jerome somewhere, though unjustly, made an occasion to attack Rufinus. Optatus does this in his usual manner, and has for the practice an author and an exceedingly weighty defender: Marcus Tullius Cicero, easily the foremost among Latin writers in eloquence and every branch of humane learning. Thus a little earlier: “You dissolved the one baptism, from which baptism,” etc.; in book II: “Whom you asked in prayers that you might be able to return; which prayers,” etc.; and in the same book: “For pestilence sends men destroyed by diseases down to the underworld. That the underworld is known to have its gates, against which gates,” etc. He speaks so often in this way that he might seem to have deliberately cultivated it rather than merely imitated it.

I have made this observation here all the more willingly because, since it was necessary to supply something in this very passage, the reader might understand from the sequence of words and from the distinctive form of expression which Optatus favors that what was missing was very slight; and the observation may also add some weight to our conjecture. Yet I shall not conceal that in the first of all editions, Cochlaeus’s, this passage is written: “And the water is similar, which we have just read,” etc. Some perhaps will prefer to retain this, so that *legimus* (“we read”) refers not to the creation narrative but to the words of the prophet just cited. Whichever reading one adopts, the sense remains the same. Yet this seems harsher to me: that Optatus should have compared waters ἁπλῶς, “simply and absolutely,” with God, eternal and unbegotten. M. Casaubon. This passage has been restored from the manuscript.]

The water also is similar, [Col. 0993A] which we do not read to have been made [Note: [Col. 0993A] We have supplied this word from MS S. G.; it is absent from MSS S. T. and P. [Note: [Col. 0994D–0995B] *Finally, he does not say “in Zion.”* Optatus, intending to cite at length a passage from Isaiah the prophet against the Donatists, first proves through “the daughter of His own race” that water is meant by God; then, lest he seem to say nothing, he proceeds to show that the Zion proposed as the subject of this prophecy should be understood not of the physical mountain—as he himself calls it—the particular Zion which had once existed, but of the spiritual Zion which then existed: that is, the whole universal Church. The version used by Optatus was rendered from the Greek, whose translators rendered the Hebrew “oracle of the valley of vision” as τὸ ὅραμα τῆς φάραγγος Σιών, “the vision of the valley of Zion.”

Moreover, understand “were celebrated” to mean proceedings or judgments, as shortly afterward: “where no lawsuit was heard, nor any judicial proceeding celebrated by anyone,” etc.; and again in book VII: “No judgment was celebrated, but the effect of the sentences was carried out.” Unless perhaps Optatus wrote *sententia* (“decision”) instead of *sunt* (“were”); once contracted in an abbreviated script, it was later changed into *sunt*. For even below in this very book he uses *celebrare actionem*, “to conduct a proceeding,” so that you may not suppose the expression applies only to a judicial hearing. M. CASAUB.]

Finally, these things were conducted not in all Zion [Note: [Col. 0994A] In MS T. and printed editions, “he does not say in Zion”: less well.], but in one of its valleys [Col. 0995A]: not on that Mount Zion which a small stream separates from the walls of Jerusalem in Syrian Palestine, on whose summit is a not extensive plain, where there were synagogues [Note: [Col. 0995A] In the same MSS and printed editions, “there were seven synagogues.” We follow MS S. G.], in which the Jewish people assembling could have learned the law given through Moses [Note: [Col. 0996A] In MS S. T., “might rather learn.”]. Rather, it was where no lawsuit was heard, no judicial proceeding was conducted by anyone, and no sentence was delivered there by any judge, because it was a place of instruction, not of controversy after instruction. If anything had to be transacted, it was transacted within the walls of Jerusalem. Hence it is written [Col. 0996A] in Isaiah the prophet: “From Zion the law shall go forth, and the word of the Lord from Jerusalem” (Isa. II, 3). Therefore Isaiah does not see a valley on that Mount Zion, but on the holy mountain, which is the Church, which [Note: [Col. 0995B] *It has raised its head throughout the entire Roman world.* What Optatus means here by “the entire Roman world” is sufficiently indicated both by the immediately following phrase “under the whole heaven” and by the words which occur shortly afterward, “which is throughout the whole world.” Thus he calls the Roman world what we call the universal world, as in Lampridius, in the life of Alexander Severus, when the consulted diviners replied:

The dominion of heaven, earth, and sea awaits you. From this they understood that the Roman Empire itself was foretold to him; and Lampridius himself there calls him the ruler of the Roman Empire, and shortly afterwards the ruler of the human race. Yet no one should infer from this that the Gospel had already at that time penetrated to absolutely every nation, or that Optatus asserts of his own age what Augustine, somewhat later, expressly denies of his own in Letter 80, where he discusses excellently the last day of the world; any more than one should infer from the Apostle’s words, “as also in all the world” (*καθὼς καὶ ἐν παντὶ τῷ κόσμῳ*), at Colossians 1:6 and 23, “which has been proclaimed in all creation under heaven” (*τοῦ κηρυχθέντος ἐν πάσῃ τῇ κτίσει, τῇ ὑπὸ τὸν οὐρανὸν*), and similar passages, that the Gospel had already then been preached throughout the whole world, whether by the Apostles themselves (as Augustine testifies that some believed) or by others. For, strictly speaking, as everyone knows, the Romans were not even then masters of the entire known world. See also Tertullian, *Against the Jews*, ch. 7.

Elsewhere, however, “the Roman world” does not mean, as here, the whole world, but that which is properly set in opposition to barbarian lands, as “the blessed man” teaches in his note on Lampridius, p. 386. Thus our author, a page or two later: “things found in Lebanon,” that is, in the Roman Empire, “where there are priesthoods, chastity, and virginity—things not found among barbarian nations; and if they were, they could not be safe.” It is plain that the Roman Empire and barbarian nations, or Barbary, are here opposed, and that the entire world is comprised under these two divisions. But it is not equally plain how what Optatus says can be understood or excused: namely, that he encloses the Catholic Church, forgetful of himself, if we take him thus, within the Roman world, excluding the barbarians.

For it is certainly clear from Augustine’s refutation that there were people who restricted those promises concerning the Gospel’s propagation among the nations to the Roman world: “But the inland peoples”—he speaks of the barbarian Africans—“who are under no Roman power and in none of their communities are held by the Christian religion, certainly cannot in any way be said not to belong to God’s promise. For the Lord promised not Roman nations, but all nations, to Abraham’s seed, confirming it even by an oath. From this promise,” etc. If this was also Optatus’s opinion, then whenever he names the whole world, we must say that he means only the Roman world, but not conversely. Yet I would not readily concede that this was his view, whatever may be determined concerning one or two passages in him.

Then again, how is Optatus’s addition to be understood—that among barbarians there are no priesthoods, chastity, or virginity? That this is false of barbarians universally is as certain as anything can be. For what were the Brahmans, Gymnosophists, Druids, and other figures mentioned by ancient writers, but priests of various barbarian peoples? I say nothing of chastity and virginity, which can be refuted with equal ease. Later African writers, when they name barbarians, generally mean the Vandals, who at that time invaded Africa and threw everything into confusion by their most cruel devastation. The historians of that period repeatedly complain that they spared neither property nor persons: that consecrated virgins and all who lived continently were scattered everywhere by them (Possidius, *Life of Augustine*, ch. 28), and that women and virgins were violated and stripped naked contrary to the laws of nature (Victor of Utica, *On the Vandal Persecution*).

But Optatus, who lived so many years earlier, could not have meant them. And although they perhaps abused the Africans in Africa with the unrestrained and shameful license of conquerors, Salvian at length teaches in *On the Government of God*, Book VII, that otherwise they provided by their laws for chastity no less—and indeed far better—than did the Romans; throughout that book he praises remarkably their outstanding continence and chastity, and calls the barbarians chaste. It remains, then, that we must understand not merely peoples called barbarian in opposition to the Romans, but peoples truly and completely barbarous and savage, living more like beasts than human beings, without law or commonwealth—such as we commonly call *Sauvages*. Perhaps Augustine too means these in the letter already cited above: “For among us,” that is, in Africa, “there are innumerable barbarian peoples, among whom the Gospel has not yet been preached, as is evident from those who are brought captive from there,” etc.  
—M. Casaubon.

Throughout the Roman world, it raised its head under the whole heaven. On this mountain the Son of God rejoices that He has been established as king by God the Father [Note: [Col. 0996C] “He rejoices in the second Psalm,” etc. In earlier editions this read not “the second” but “the first”; and I greatly fear that the modern division of the Psalms deceived the most learned Balduinus, leading him to think it should be altered. Yet formerly the first and second Psalms were one and the same Psalm for many readers. That is, among those who, at Acts 13:33, read not, as today, “in the second Psalm,” but, as formerly attested by Jerome, Hilary, and other ancient writers, “in the first Psalm,” or simply “in the Psalm” (*ψαλμῷ*). See Erasmus on Acts, and Genebrard on the Psalms. Moreover, as Ambrose says somewhere, the Lord Himself rejoiced that David called Him Son. Hence also in Book V, *gratulation* is used for *thanks*: “that thanks may be returned to them for the humanity shown.” Besides, there is no doubt that other numerical errors have slipped into the citations of Scripture passages. But we considered it sufficient to warn the reader where there was some difficulty, and faithfully to reproduce the Balduinian edition. —M. Casaubon.], in the first Psalm [Note: [Col. 0996A] MS S. G. reads “testifies.”] [Note: [Col. 0996D] “In the first Psalm.” Formerly the first and second Psalms were one and the same Psalm for many who read Acts 13:33 not, as today, in the second Psalm, but, as formerly attested by Jerome, Hilary, and others, in the first Psalm. —Du Pin.], saying: “For he has established me as king over Zion, his holy mountain” (Ps. 2:6): certainly over the Church, of which he is king, bridegroom, and head.

Not on that mountain, where there are no gates which God loves [Col. 0997A], but on the mountain of the Church, which is so called spiritually. The innocent, the righteous, the merciful, the continent, and virgins enter the gates of this Church; these are the gates which the Holy Spirit mentions through David in Psalm 86, when he says: “Its foundations are upon the holy mountains; the Lord loves the gates of Zion.” Not those of the bodily mountain, where there are now no gates; after the victories of the Emperor Vespasian, scarcely even traces of the ancient ruins remain.

Therefore the Church is the spiritual Zion, in which Christ has been established as king by God the Father; it is throughout the whole world, in which there is one Catholic Church. For elsewhere too the most holy prophet David testifies that Zion is the Church, saying: “Praise your God, O Zion, who has strengthened the bars of your gates; he has blessed your children within you” (Ps. 147:1–2).

[Note: [Col. 0997C] “Through the individual provinces,” etc. By “the individual valleys of the mountain” Optatus undoubtedly means the individual provinces of the whole world; and perhaps he wrote *pro* (“for”) rather than *per* (“through”), unless someone prefers additionally to restore *pro* in place of *per*. For he continues in an explanation—or rather an application—of the Prophet’s words, which he is about to quote and claims apply to the Donatists. —M. Casaubon.]

We understand the individual valleys of the mountain to mean the individual provinces of the whole world [Note: [Col. 0997B] We have supplied this from MS S. G.; it is omitted in the other manuscripts and in the printed editions.]. And whereas Isaiah sees not the whole mountain but one valley only—that is, Africa alone—in which, although the fifty-five churches of God already existing were sufficient, your leaders wished to build others; in which alone [Note: [Col. 0997C] “The walls were thrown down in order that walls might be made.” The faithful were cast down and rebaptized in order that they might become faithful; in order that they might become Christians, they were made non-Christians. —Albaspinaeus.] the walls were cast down, and, in order that walls might be made, the water of the holy pool was diverted [Note: [Col. 0997B] MSS S. T. and P. S. read: “holy water and a pool.”], and by you novelty was instituted against antiquity, and human water was appointed against divine water [Note: [Col. 0997C] We have supplied this from MS S. G.; it is lacking in the other manuscripts and in the printed editions.].

God both questions and rebukes all this in the valley of Mount Zion, saying: “Why has this happened to you? Because you ascended to superfluous temples. [Col. 0998A] Every city is filled with those crying aloud; your wounded are not wounded by the sword, and your dead are not dead in battle. From the least to the greatest they are in error. All your leaders, wandering in the mountains, have turned to flight; and those who were captured are grievously bound, and your stronger men have been driven far away. Let me go; I shall weep bitterly. No one will be able to console me in the destruction of the daughter of my people. And the Elamites shall come up with quivers.”

(“Elamites” [Note: [Col. 0997C] “Elamites are called *chori castrorum* [military companies] in the Latin language.” It is useless for anyone to torment himself in order to hammer or extract from *Elamite* “military companies,” or anything similar. I would dare to extract water from pumice with less labour. But what it was that deceived those who first interpreted it thus—if it is permitted us to conjecture—I, though only as a diviner, judge as follows. In Song of Songs 7:1 it is read: “What will you see in the Shulammite but military companies?” In the margin is noted the variant reading *Sulamite*, which is the Greek and truer spelling, since it reproduces the original. Therefore, since Optatus had thought that the words “military companies” were an interpretation of the foreign word immediately preceding (unless someone more favorable to Optatus prefers to call it a gloss), he later slipped, because of the similarity of the words, and transferred to *Elamite*, by a greater error, what he had read—or wrongly believed he had read—about the word *Shulammite*: namely, that it signified “military company.” This is my conjecture, ready to accept anything more certain that someone may offer. —M. Casaubon.] are called “military companies” in the Latin language [Note: [Col. 0997D] “Elamites are called military companies in the Latin language.” He seems to allude to these words in Song of Songs 7:1—in Hebrew, ch. 6, the final verse—“What will you see in the Shulammite but military companies?” Yet I do not think with Casaubon that Optatus took *Shulammite* for *Elamite*; rather, he derived the name “Elamites” from the Hebrew words *Meliolath Mahanaim* [uncertain OCR/transliteration]. Perhaps he also derived the name “Elamites” from another Hebrew word, *Aialim*, which signifies an army or forces—Daniel 11:10 and elsewhere. —Du Pin.]); and he continued, saying: “Your inner chambers shall be brought forth [Note: [Col. 0998B] MS S. G. reads *proferentur* (“shall be brought forth”) in place of *deferentur* (“shall be carried away”).] publicly, and the secrets of the house of Israel shall be laid bare.”

This happened in Africa; and God indicated why all this [Note: [Col. 0998B] We have supplied this word from MS S. G.; in the others, “in Africa” occurs in its place through a copyist’s inadvertence.] occurred, when he charges it against you, saying: “Because you diverted the water of the ancient pool toward your city, and threw down the walls of Jerusalem [Col. 0998B] in order to make another fortification, and set water between the two fortifications, and would not look to the ancient pool, nor to him who created it from the beginning” (Isa. 22:1 ff.).

### III. The Pride of Donatus

You now see, brother Parmenianus, that everything rebounds upon you, since the cause of all these things was sown by your leaders. Next comes Donatus of Carthage, by whose *veneficium*—“poisoning” or malign influence—the affair of unity appears to have been stirred up.

> **Note [Col. 0998C]. “By whose veneficium.”**  
> “By whose audacity and shamelessness Macarius was induced to bring about unity.” —Albaspinaeus.  
>   
> “The business of unity appears to have been stirred up by whose *veneficium*, etc.” Perhaps *veneficium* stands for *beneficium* (“benefaction”): the learned man notes this in passing, but would that he had added how it could apply here. Is *beneficium* a middle term, capable of being taken in either a bad or a good sense, like *meritum* and *mereri* everywhere? Or is it used ironically (*eirōnikōs*) or sarcastically (*euthērōs*) for *maleficium*? Or does what follows explain it—“while he strives to seem great”—as though he meant, “while Donatus pleases himself, serves his own ambition, and spreads his sails”? If none of these explanations pleases, it remains, so far as I can see, that we should retain *veneficio*: here *veneficium* stands for abusive speech and unrestrained insolence. For we too commonly speak of “the poison of the tongue,” and in Sacred Scripture there is “the venom of the lips,” used passively. Optatus begins here, and continues at length afterward, to attribute this business of unity to Donatus’s abusive speech. Yet *veneficium* may also have been used by Optatus simply for “crime,” just as *veneficus* and Greek *pharmakeus* are not infrequently used for a criminal and a wicked person. —M. Casaubon.

> **Note [Col. 0998B].** In manuscript S. G., *beneficio* (“by whose benefaction”).

> **Note [Col. 0998D]. “Veneficio.”** Namely, by evil arts, pride, and envy. —Du Pin.

In this matter I shall show that his agents did nothing either at our wish or through their own malice, but because causes and persons provoked and impelled them—persons whom Donatus of Carthage, by his frivolity, established while striving to appear great.

> **Note [Col. 0998C].** This is supplied from manuscript S. G.

For who, except yourself—for you are a stranger, and false accounts may have been told you—does not know, or who can deny, a fact of which all Carthage is principally witness: that the Emperor Constans originally sent Paul and Macarius not to create unity, but with alms, so that poverty, relieved through each of the churches, might breathe again, be clothed, fed, and rejoice?

> **Note [Col. 0999C]. “Because you are a stranger.”** Because you were not born in Carthage, over which you preside. —Albaspinaeus.

> **Note [Col. 0999C]. “The Emperor Constans.”** The First Council of Carthage relates that this was done not under Constans but under Constantine: “that he might carry out the vow of unity to the most religious Emperor Constantine and send the ministers of the holy work, the servants of God Paul and Macarius.” —Albaspinaeus.

> **Note [Col. 0999B].** We have added this word from manuscript S. G.

When they came to Donatus, your father, and explained why they had come, he, inflamed by his usual fury, burst out in these words: “What has the emperor to do with the Church?”

> **Note [Col. 0999C]. “Your father.”** The man who begot you in that see, to which you succeeded. All bishops are called the sons of those whom they succeed or by whom they are ordained. —Albaspinaeus.

> **Note [Col. 0999C]. “What has the emperor to do with the Church?”** The Donatists were the first to appeal to Constantine; when they found him less favourable to their cause, they used these and similar words. —Albaspinaeus.

And, from the spring of his frivolity, he poured forth many insults—no less than he once did against Gregory, to whom he did not hesitate to write: “Gregory, stain of the senate, disgrace of the prefects,” and the like. The aforesaid Gregory replied to Donatus with episcopal patience.

Copies of these letters are everywhere recited by many mouths. Even then he was devising, contrary to the command of the Apostle Paul, to insult authorities and kings, for whom, if he had listened to the Apostle, he ought to have prayed every day. For the blessed Apostle Paul teaches thus: “Pray for kings and authorities, that we may lead a quiet and tranquil life with them” (1 Tim. 2:2).

> **Note [Col. 0999C]. “For the commonwealth is not in the Church.”** Those men who favour innovations exalt this saying extraordinarily. They suppose it means that emperors do not belong to the Church, but that the Church is subject to them; or that there can be a commonwealth without the Church, whereas the Church cannot exist without the commonwealth. Yet anyone attending to this passage will explain it very differently. Optatus wished to say that Roman emperors ought not to be reviled but prayed for according to the Apostle, because Christians led a quieter life with them than among other nations, where, because they were barbarous, Christians could not live so peacefully. Thus, “the commonwealth is not in the Church” means that the Church does not wage wars, enact laws, restrain peoples under laws, conduct civil affairs, and the like. But the Church is in the commonwealth: Christians live under the emperors’ laws, are protected, and lead a quiet life under them and through their protection. —Albaspinaeus.

For the commonwealth is not in the Church, but the Church is in the commonwealth—that is, in the Roman Empire. Christ calls it Lebanon in the Song of Songs when he says: “Come, my bride, discovered from Lebanon” (Song 4:8), that is, from the Roman Empire. There too are holy priesthoods, chastity, and virginity, which are not among barbarian nations; and, if they were, they could not be safe.

> **Note [Col. 1000C]. “Holy priesthoods.”** It is ambiguous whether he speaks of Christian or pagan priesthoods; I judge that it refers to Christian priesthoods. For some manuscripts read “holy priesthoods.” The sense, therefore, is that Christian priesthoods are exercised more safely under Roman emperors than among barbarian peoples, among whom the virginity and chastity of Christian virgins are never sufficiently secure; but among Romans they are secure, even though the Romans are not Christians, because their laws fostered innocence. —Albaspinaeus.

> **Note [Col. 1000C]. “Holy.”** That is, sacred and venerable, where priesthoods, chastity, and virginity are held in honour. This should be understood generally of priesthoods, chastity, and virginity, both pagan and Christian. —Du Pin.

> **Note [Col. 1000C]. “And if they existed, they could not be safe.”** Perhaps more correctly: “they could not be secure.” —Anonymous. Thus restored.

Paul rightly teaches that kings and authorities should be prayed for, even if the emperor in question were living as a pagan; how much more so if he were Christian, if he feared God, if he were devout, if he were merciful—as the fact itself proves. For he had sent ornaments for the houses of God; he had sent alms for the poor; nothing to Donatus. Why, then, did he rage? Why was he angry? Why did he reject what had been sent? And when those who had been sent said that they would go through every province and give to those willing to receive it, he said that he had sent letters beforehand everywhere, so that what had been brought might nowhere be distributed to the poor.

> **Note [Col. 0999B].** Manuscript S. G. reads: “how much more so if.”

> **Note [Col. 1000B].** Manuscript S. G. reads: “the Lord.”

> **Note [Col. 1000D]. “O to take thought for the wretched! O to provide, etc.”** If the word *fuerat* (“had been”) were absent, I would alter nothing. But as the words now stand, rather than remove anything, I would restore: “This is taking thought for the wretched! This is providing for, etc.” We know that *ho* is often written for *o*, and indeed, unless I am mistaken, it is printed so somewhere in this work. Hence it could easily happen that *ho* was written for *hoc*, and finally, with the aspiration omitted, *o* appeared in place of *hoc*. Shortly afterward, “with God” does not refer to the dwellings of the blessed—as though these too received schismatics such as that Donatus—but to the other world or age: that is, both are now dead and have finished their lives. A little later, I think it should be written: “what sort of man will he be, who through frivolity and fury laboured to hinder so many poor persons,” that is, as often, “so many,” though perhaps “giving” is intended. —M. Casaubon.

“O to take thought for the wretched! O to provide for the poor! O to assist sinners!” God cries out, saying: “I am he who made both poor and rich.” Not because he could not give to the poor as well, but because, if he gave to both, the sinner would not find a means of helping himself. For it is written: “As water extinguishes fire, so almsgiving extinguishes sin” (Ecclus. 3:33).

Certainly both are now before God: the man who wished to give and the man who prevented the gift. What if God should now say to Donatus: “Bishop, what do you say Constans was? If innocent, why were you unwilling to receive from an innocent man? If a sinner, why did you not permit him to give, for whose sake I made the poor?” Under this interrogation, what sort of man will he be? What did he labour, in frivolity and fury, to hinder for so many poor persons?

He believed that he held the primacy of Carthage. And since there is none above the emperor but God alone, who made the emperor, Donatus, by exalting himself above the emperor, had already, as it were, passed beyond the limits of humanity, so that he almost considered himself God rather than man, by not reverencing him who, after God, was feared by human beings.

Accordingly, through Ezekiel the Holy Spirit rebukes the prince of Tyre—that is, the prince of Carthage—when he speaks through the prophet in these words: “Son of man, speak against the prince of Tyre. Thus says the Lord God: Because your heart has been exalted, you have said, ‘I am God’” (Ezek. 28:2).

Isaiah first proves that Tyre is Carthage, where we read, “A vision concerning Tyre,” followed by: “Howl, ships of Carthage” (Isa. 23:1).

> **Note [Col. 1001B]. “Ships of Carthage.”** Thus the Septuagint: *Hololyxate ploia Karchēdonos* (“Howl, ships of Carthage”); in the Hebrew, “ships of Tarshish,” which the Vulgate renders “ships of the sea.” For, as Jerome observes, the word *Tarshish* generally denotes the sea or regions beyond the sea. But since Optatus had a translation prepared from the Greek Septuagint, he read: “Howl, ships of Carthage.” Saint Augustine also applies the same passage from Ezekiel concerning the Prince of Tyre to Donatus, *On the Unity of the Church*, ch. 16, no. 42. —Du Pin.

Then secular writings also attest that Tyre is Carthage. And if there is another city bearing this name, nothing seems to have happened there which is known to have occurred at Carthage.

> **Note [Col. 1001B].** Thus manuscript S. G. Manuscript S. T. reads: “that Carthage itself is.”

> **Note [Col. 1001B].** Manuscript S. T. and P. S. read *alia* (“another”) in place of *illa* (“there”).

“Speak,” God says, “against the prince of Tyre” (Ezek. 28:2). He does not say that one must speak against some secular king, nor against many persons, but against one: that is, against Donatus the bishop. For it would not have been proper for the prophet Ezekiel, whom I mentioned just above, to compare a bishop except with a prince—namely Donatus, who, as we have said, claimed the primacy of Carthage, exalted his heart, appeared to himself superior to human beings, and wished to have all his fellow bishops beneath him.

> **Note [Col. 1001C]. “Unless to compare him with the prince of bishops, etc.”** I correct: “unless to compare the bishop with the prince,” or “with a prince,” etc. —M. Casaubon. Thus restored.

> **Note [Col. 1001B].** We corrected this passage, which lay in error, by adding the word *principi* (“with the prince”), which seemed necessary although it is not found in the manuscripts. Manuscript S. T.: “unless I were to compare [him] with a bishop.” Manuscript S. G.: “unless to compare with a bishop.” In the latest edition: “unless to compare him with a bishop.” None of these expresses the author’s meaning, which we have recovered from what follows.

> **Note [Col. 1002B].** Manuscript S. T.: “he appeared superior to himself from human beings.” Manuscript S. G.: “he appeared superior to himself from all human beings.” Manuscript P. S.: “he appeared superior to human beings.” The sense is much clearer if the word *ab* (“from”) is deleted.

> **Note [Col. 1001C]. “And to have all his companions beneath him.”** He wanted all bishops to be subject to himself. —Albaspinaeus.

He was never willing to receive from their offerings.

> **Note [Col. 1001C]. “From whose offerings.”** They celebrated offerings of *eulogiae* in houses of piety in order to make some sharing of communion. Donatus therefore did not wish to share this communion and offering with the other bishops, but did something or other in secret. —Albaspinaeus.  
>   
> “From whose offerings, etc.” I read and punctuate this whole passage, which is somewhat obscure and plainly corrupt, as follows: “from whose offerings he never deigned to receive; in this matter faith and Christ God are involved; hence—or from that—many complaints,” etc. “In this matter” belongs to what precedes, though here it is very badly connected with frequent interruptions. He speaks similarly in Book V: “Now baptism must be discussed in this place, in which matter, etc.” So too in Book I: “Thus peace was granted to all Christians—a thing which is known to be God’s work,” etc. And in Book VI: “Your hands, with which before us you handled those same chalices. Yet you ordered that thing to be sold everywhere,” etc.  
>   
> By “offerings” I understand *eulogiae*, that is, blessed loaves, also called offerings, customarily sent back and forth among friends as a token of unity or unanimity. Paulinus speaks of this in his letter to Alypius among Augustine’s letters, and also in his letter to Augustine himself. The most learned cardinal treated this custom extensively, in many chapters, in his annals under the year 313; we are not so thankless or illiberal as to endure copying him. Let the reader consult him if this is still unfamiliar. That I should understand this as referring to the blessed loaf is urged not only by the matter itself but by the observed, almost customary mode of speech: here, “he deigned to receive”; similarly Paulinus to Severus, Letter 1, “deign to receive”; and in Augustine, “the condescension of receiving,” and Augustine himself, “the condescension of the recipient.” By such proper and customary expressions they describe their gift.  
>   
> Optatus’s addition that faith and Christ God are involved in this matter serves to intensify Donatus’s proud disdain. In proudly rejecting an offering consecrated in Christ’s name and customarily received in God’s name—under which name Paulinus also commends it to Severus, and in which, moreover, the solidity of the Trinity was contained, as Paulinus says—he seemed simultaneously to renounce both Christ and faith. Where, instead of *ejus* (“of it”), I write *hinc* or *inde* (“hence” or “from that”), I do not doubt that “Jesus”—since Sacred Scripture has taught us to say “Christ Jesus” no less than “Jesus Christ”—would appeal more to some because it comes nearer to the text. But we have followed the requirements of what follows. —M. Casaubon.

> **Note [Col. 1002C]. “Offerings.”** The *eulogiae* which bishops sent one another as signs both of peace and friendship. —Du Pin.

> **Note [Col. 1002D]. “In this matter faith is involved.”** God and the Christian law command a different manner of life and require one to value bishops’ offerings more highly. —Albaspinaeus.

> **Note [Col. 1002D]. “Faith is involved.”** That is, his conscience is witness, Christ is witness, and the complaints of many are witnesses. —Du Pin.

In this matter faith and Christ God are involved, together with the complaints of many, upon whom he inflicted this injury within that very fellowship: so that he alone did something or other in secret, and afterward joined with the others merely perfunctorily.

> **Note [Col. 1002D]. “Alone in secret.”** He did not communicate with the others. —Albaspinaeus.

> **Note [Col. 1002D]. “So that he alone did something or other.”** He alone celebrated the divine mysteries privately, not publicly with the other bishops, presbyters, and clerics. He avoided communion with them and mingled with them only superficially and in passing, as though occupied with something else. —Du Pin.

Now his heart was exalted, so that he seemed to himself no longer a human being but God. Finally, among the people he was rarely called “bishop”; rather, he was called “Donatus of Carthage.”

> **Note [Col. 1002D]. “He was rarely called bishop, but Donatus, etc.”** Optatus does not blame the fact that Donatus, bishop of Carthage, was called “Donatus of Carthage”—for Optatus himself speaks in this manner whenever he names bishops—but that, as though he were something greater, Donatus did not willingly hear himself called “bishop.” Shortly afterward: “therefore, although he did not dare,” etc. Other editions read more fully: “therefore, because although,” etc. —M. Casaubon.

And rightly he deserved to be called and rebuked as the prince of Tyre, that is, of Carthage, because he was first among the bishops as though he himself were more than the rest; and, while unwilling to possess anything human, he exalted his heart—not like the heart of a human being, but like the heart of God—while desiring to be something more than other people.

> **Note [Col. 1003B].** Manuscript S. G. reads *quani*.

> **Note [Col. 1003C]. “First among bishops.”** The bishop of the first see in Africa, but not thereby greater than the rest, since priesthood is one and the same in all. —Du Pin.

> **Note [Col. 1003B].** Manuscript S. T. reads “but.”

> **Note [Col. 1003B].** These words are absent from manuscript S. T. through a copyist’s error.

God continues, saying to him: “You said, ‘I am God’” (Ezek. 28:2). This is so because, although he did not use those words, he either did or allowed what fulfilled the effect of those words. He raised his heart so as to judge that no person was comparable to himself; and in the swelling of his mind he seemed to himself to be higher, because whatever is above human beings is already, as it were, God.

Then, although bishops ought to serve God, he demanded so much from his own bishops that all revered him with no less fear than God. This is what it means that he appeared to himself to be God.

> **Note [Col. 1003C]. “Bishops ought to serve God.”** Episcopal dignity was formerly very great. —Albaspinaeus.

> **Note [Col. 1003C]. “Then, although bishops ought to serve God, etc.”** All bishops are servants of God; none of them ought slavishly to obey another, and none among them should claim lordship over the others. —Du Pin.

> **Note [Col. 1003B].** Manuscript S. G. reads *famulatum* (“service”).

> **Note [Col. 1003B].** Manuscript S. T.: “he exacted bishops for himself.”

> **Note [Col. 1003B].** Manuscript S. G. reads *suspicerent* (“admired” or “revered”).

And whereas people customarily swear by God alone, he allowed people to swear by himself as though by God. If any person erred in this, he himself ought to have forbidden it; since he did not forbid it, he appeared to himself to be God.

Further, before his pride, all who believed in Christ were called Christians; but he dared to divide the people from God, so that those who followed him were called no longer Christians but Donatists.

> **Note [Col. 1003B].** Manuscript S. G. reads *vocentur* (“may be called”).

> **Note [Col. 1003C]. “And if at any time some persons came to him from an African province.”** “Macarius has exacted vengeance, if they had committed no offence—why are they said to have been killed? Barthius says: ‘Read throughout: But if at any time persons came to him from an African province: Macarius has exacted vengeance. If they had committed no offence, why are they said to have been killed? This is perfectly clear to anyone who examines the author’s meaning.’ These are his words. But he says nothing. For these things do not cohere at all, and there is a huge gap in this edition, namely of about twelve pages of this sort. See without fail the second edition of François Balduin, from which this lacuna must be supplied. These same words are also read below, near the end of this book, in a less appropriate place, and must be restored to their proper order, from the words ‘He did not ask that,’ etc., to the words ‘Phinehas exacted vengeance.’ All the intervening matter must be placed under these words: ‘And if at any time persons came to him from an African province, he did not ask what ordinary human custom always requires—to ask something about rain, peace, or the year’s yield—but these were his words to each person who came: “What is happening among you concerning my party?”’ Vengeance never follows unless its cause has preceded. Moses, as we have said, exacted vengeance; Elijah exacted vengeance; Phinehas exacted vengeance; Macarius exacted vengeance. If they had committed no offence, why are they said to have been killed? Macarius becomes guilty in that he alone, etc. This exceptionally disordered and distorted passage must necessarily be interpolated. See the notes below. —Anonymous. Thus restored.

> **Note [Col. 1004B].** Here in manuscript S. T. the following material has been moved from its place and transferred elsewhere; the words that follow are “MACARIUS EXTRACTED VENGEANCE,” etc., which occur below.

And if at any time persons came to him from some African province, he did not ask what ordinary human custom always requires—he did not inquire about rain, peace, or the year’s yield. Rather, these were his words to every person who came: “What is happening among you concerning my party?”

> **Note [Col. 1004B].** Manuscript S. G. adds: “so that he said.”

> **Note [Col. 1004B].** Manuscript S. G. reads: “it seems.”

As though he had already truly divided the people from God, he fearlessly called it his own party. Indeed, from his time until the present day, whenever some action concerning ecclesiastical affairs has been conducted in public courts, each person questioned has spoken in the official record so as to say that he belonged to the party of Donatus; they have been silent about Christ.

And why should I speak of the clerics, when petitions are read—mentioned by us in the first book—long ago sent to Constantine and subscribed, containing the names of bishops: “Presented by Capito, Nasucius, Dignus, and the other bishops of Donatus’s party.” They were certainly petitioning against bishops who, because they were not in Donatus’s party, remained in Christ’s catholic Church. Since, therefore, he was not a bishop among his fellow bishops and did not wish to be a human being among human beings, it is clear that he exalted his heart and appeared to himself to be God.

> **Note [Col. 1004B].** Manuscripts S. T. and P. S. read *subscribente* (“subscribing”).

> **Note [Col. 1004C]. “Donatus’s party.”** When bishops were formerly questioned and stood before judges, they professed themselves bishops of Christ and of the Church. In the *Life of Saint Cyprian*: “Are you he whom Christians call their pope?” The holy man of God replied: “I am.” But the Donatists answered that they were bishops of Donatus, not of Christ; Optatus charges this against them. —Albaspinaeus.

> **Note [Col. 1004C]. “For since even your ordainers, etc.”** This entire period, down to “here now what will they answer?” suffers from an evident lack of grammatical sequence (*anakolouthia*), though perhaps from Optatus himself. The matter and sense are nevertheless excellent as they stand; therefore the words should not be rashly disturbed. There is no need to explain that *preces* in these writers means a written petition, or, as we commonly say, a supplicatory memorial. But jurists—whom I should gladly consult here, if they were present—would better explain what it means to “submit petitions before judges.” In the meantime, I think this: they did not themselves, or through their own representatives—immediately, as people say—deliver their petitions; rather, they first had them subscribed and sealed before an official recorder in the provincial judges’ court, by whom they were entered into the public record. Unless my reasoning fails me, this is the “submission”; hence also the “acts of submission,” mentioned concerning this very matter both by Augustine against Petilian and by Honorius in an edict against the Donatists.  
>   
> What we find in other editions after *allegarent* (“they submitted”)—“to be added in the records of the bishops, of which it is written below”—I think arose from the mistake of those who supposed that Optatus, in the words “of which it is written below,” or as they read, “of whom it is written below,” was directing his reader to records once appended to these books, as he often does. But let them see to that. A little later, instead of *alio modo*, I write *aliquo modo* (“in some manner”). He says that, while they willingly professed themselves to be of Donatus’s party, they confessed, though not expressly, at least in some way, that they were not of Christ’s Church. Nor would it be displeasing if someone understood it thus: What will those answer in the approaching divine judgment who have confessed in this world, in another manner, etc.? —M. Casaubon.

For since even your ordainers—whose names, brother Parmenianus, you know well, and you are not ignorant where they were, whom or through whom they petitioned, and whom they asked to return, and who could have returned with you—and since we too learned, when they submitted before the African judges the same petition that they had presented, in which it is written: “Presented by bishops of Donatus’s party”—what answer will they now give at that approaching divine judgment, they who in this world have confessed in another manner that they are not of Christ’s Church? They willingly professed that they were of Donatus’s party, whereas it is written in the Gospel, Christ saying: “Whoever confesses me before human beings, I will confess him before my Father” (John 12:8). They confessed Donatus, not Christ.

> **Note [Col. 1005C].** Manuscript S. G. reads “what.”

> **Note [Col. 1005C].** Manuscript S. G. and P. S. read “we say.”

> **Note [Col. 1005C].** Manuscript S. T. reads “they presented.”

> **Note [Col. 1005D]. “The petition which they had presented.”** A supplicatory memorial asking that Parmenianus be ordained bishop for them. —Du Pin.

> **Note [Col. 1005C].** Manuscripts S. T. and P. S. read “so that before.”

> **Note [Col. 1005C].** Thus in manuscript S. G. In manuscripts S. T. and P. S., the marginal words “to be added in the records of the bishops, of which it is written below” have intruded into the running text; they plainly have the character of a note written in the margin.

And lest this proof, shown to concern his own person, should seem insignificant, there is added also that testimony with which the rebuke mentioned above was concluded: God said that he would not die on land, and everyone knows that it happened so.

> **Note [Col. 1005D]. “With which the rebuke mentioned above was concluded.”** The prophecy appears there in Ezekiel 28:9: “You shall die the death of the slain in the heart of the sea.” —Du Pin.

> **Note [Col. 1005D].** Manuscript S. G. reads “in his own land.”

He lived in the house of God and was in the heart of the sea. We everywhere read “sea” as meaning the world.
