Since he was not only beloved by some Christians, but was also, because of his knowledge of secular literature, in the heart of the sea—that is, in the affection of the age—he considered himself wise because of his learning.

> **Note [Col. 1005D].** Manuscript S. G. reads “of secular persons.”

But God emptied out this wisdom of his when he said: “Are you wiser than Daniel?” (Ezek. 28:3). And rightly his wisdom was humbled—he thought himself wiser than Daniel in rejecting a king’s gifts, when he was unwilling to receive what appeared to have been sent by a Christian emperor.

> **Note [Col. 1005D].** Manuscript S. G. reads “for which reason deservedly.” Printed editions: “deservedly and rightly.”

He appeared to himself either a new Daniel or one preferred in wisdom to Daniel. For Daniel himself, when King Belshazzar once compelled him to accept gifts—that is, a ring, a necklace, and the rest—is read to have said: “Let your gifts remain with you, O king” (Dan. 5:17). He answered wisely; he did not insult the king; he did not condemn what was offered, but deferred it. Donatus did otherwise: he uttered as many insults against Constans as he could, and rejected what had been sent by him for the poor.

But holy Daniel was found wise in not accepting the gifts offered on that day.

> **Note [Col. 1006C].** Manuscript S. G. reads: “sufficiently and truly wisely.”

For what was sought from him was still in heaven; and he would have been foolish to accept as though it were payment for an act which he did not yet have in his power. Therefore he did not wish to accept the gifts offered that day for the time being.

> **Note [Col. 1006C].** Manuscript S. G. reads “to seek.”

> **Note [Col. 1006C].** Omitted in manuscript S. G.

Finally, when God showed him what he should announce to the aforementioned king, he reported it to Belshazzar; and what he had seemed previously to reject, he afterward willingly accepted.

God therefore rightly rebukes Donatus, the prince of Tyre, saying: “Are you wiser than Daniel?” (Ezek. 28:3). But how far Donatus’s presumption is from the person of Daniel! What Belshazzar gave was not for the poor; what Constans, the Christian emperor, then sent, he sent on for the poor, not to Donatus.

Finally, he says: “The wise have not taught you their wisdom,” because you refused to learn from Solomon what he says: “Hide bread in the heart of the poor man, and he himself will pray for you” (Ecclus. 29:15).

> **Note [Col. 1006C].** Manuscript S. G. reads “then.”

Because he also refused to learn from Daniel himself the counsel which Daniel gave Nebuchadnezzar, concerning how one who had offended God might make satisfaction: “And you, O king,” he says, “hear my counsel, and let it please you: redeem your sins with alms, and your injustices with acts of mercy toward the poor” (Dan. 4:24).

> **Note [Col. 1006C].** Manuscript S. G. reads “into acts of mercy,” adding: “and God will be gracious concerning sin.”

Daniel urges a sinful and sacrilegious king to give alms. Donatus, who deserved rebuke, opposed the Christian Emperor Constans so that he should not be merciful. Therefore he is rebuked because the wise had not taught him their wisdom: whatever had been sent by the emperor, he did not allow to be distributed. Hence it is clear that Donatus was the source of evil causes.

> **Note [Col. 1006C].** After these words manuscript S. G. contains the following, though less suitably: “But when I consider you also, I fear that the second reading may remain for you. Therefore, whatever, etc.”

[Col. 1006C] IV. Account of what was done violently by the Donatists and against the Donatists.—Whatever harsh measures could have been taken in establishing unity, you see, brother Parmenianus, to whom they should be imputed. Do you say that soldiers were requested by us Catholics? [Note: [Col. 1006D] Absent in MS S. G.] If so, then did no one see an armed soldier at that time in the proconsular province? [Note: [Col. 1006D] “Paul and Macarius were coming, to *dispungere* the poor everywhere.” *Dispungerent* is equivalent to “they consoled”; a remarkable expression. INCERT.] Paul and Macarius were coming, [Note: [Col. 1006D] “To *dispungere* the poor everywhere.” This learned man says that *dispungerent* means “they consoled,” adding that it is a remarkable expression; but remarkable is his interpretation. Since *pungere* is not infrequently used for “to burn” or “to distress,” he supposes that *dispungere* means “to console.” But the learned man misses the point, because he did not understand—or at least did not consider—that the word derives from financial accounts, in which sense Tertullian frequently uses it with the same or a similar meaning to that used here by Optatus [Col. 1007B], as when he speaks of a life being *dispunctum*—settled or closed—with honour and service. What wonder, then, if the poor are said to have been *dispuncti*, when he had previously said that Constantine had sent alms by which they might be relieved, breathe again, be clothed, fed, and rejoice? Nor need we understand this as referring to their debts [Col. 1007C], though perhaps that too is true; it is more elegant to say that poverty itself, a most grievous—indeed by itself sufficient—burden, was settled. M. CASAUB.  
Ibid. *Dispungerent.* In *On the Soldier’s Crown*, where imperial largesse is discussed: “the laurel-crowned soldiers were *expungebantur*”—they were enrolled and marked. ALBASP.] to settle the accounts of the poor everywhere and to urge each person toward unity. [Col. 1007A] When they were approaching the city of Bagai, [Note: [Col. 1007B] In MSS S. T. and S. G., “Vagai.”] [Note: [Col. 1007C] “Were approaching the city”: likewise an African manner of speaking. INCERT.] then the other Donatus—as we said above—the bishop of that city, wishing to place an impediment and obstacle in the way of the aforementioned men who were coming for unity, sent heralds through neighbouring places and [Note: [Col. 1007C] “And through all the markets he sent [them], calling the Circumcellions Agonistici.” The passage should be punctuated thus: “He sent heralds through neighbouring places and through all the markets, calling together the Circumcellions, the Agonistici, to assemble at the aforesaid place,” etc., as in Cochlaeus. M. CASAUB.] through all the markets, summoning the Circumcellions [Note: [Col. 1007C] Circumcellions. They are frequently mentioned in connection with this schism. ALBASP.] as “Agonistici.” [Note: [Col. 1007C] Circumcellions. Augustine gives the etymology of this word while describing them in *Against Cresconius*, I.28: “For who does not know this class of men—restless in dreadful crimes, idle in useful labours, most cruel in the deaths of others, most contemptible in their own, wandering especially in the countryside and going round the rural huts for the sake of their subsistence? From this they received the name Circumcellions. They are famous almost throughout the whole world, the disgrace of African error.” DU PIN.] [Note: [Col. 1007D] Agonistici: because they fought against those who defended their own property. DU PIN.] He invited them to gather at the aforesaid place. At that time their assembly was called for—men whose madness had shortly before seemed impiously to have been stirred up by the bishops themselves. [Note: [Col. 1007D] Madness: because these Circumcellions perpetrated many monstrous and unheard-of acts, and many of them hurled themselves down in order to obtain the glory of martyrdom. M. CASAUB.] [Note: [Col. 1007B] MSS S. G. read *compressa*, “restrained,” but wrongly.]

For before unity, this kind of people wandered through every district. [Note: [Col. 1007D] “Before unity”: before Macarius compelled the Donatists to unity; Circumcellions had already existed from Constantine’s time. DU PIN.] Axido and Fasir [Note: [Col. 1007D] Axido and Fasir: so were the leaders of the Circumcellions called. DU PIN.] were called “leaders of the saints” by these madmen themselves. No one was permitted to remain safe on his own estates; written acknowledgements of debt lost their force; [Col. 1007B] at that time no creditor had liberty [Note: [Col. 1007B] MSS S. G. read *potestatem*, “power.”] to exact payment. Everyone was terrorized by letters from men who boasted of having been leaders of the saints; [Note: [Col. 1007B] Absent in MS S. G.] and if anyone delayed obeying their commands, suddenly [Col. 1008A] a mad mob swooped down, and, terror preceding it, creditors were surrounded by dangers, so that [Note: [Col. 1007B] Thus in MS S. G.] those who [Note: [Col. 1007D] “And those who ought to have been asked for what they had advanced,” etc. Either write *ut qui* in place of *et qui*, or understand the later *impellerentur* as standing for *impellebantur*. M. CASAUB.; thus restored from the MSS.] ought to have been petitioned for what they had advanced [Note: [Col. 1008B] MS S. T. reads *meruerant*, “had deserved.”] were, through fear of death, humbly compelled to make petitions. Each person hastened to lose even very large debts, and regarded it as profit to have escaped their injuries.

Even the roads could not be entirely safe, because masters were thrown down from their vehicles [Note: [Col. 1008B] Absent in MS S. G.] before their own towns and, while slaves sat in their masters’ places, ran like slaves. By their judgement and command, the condition of masters and slaves was reversed. Accordingly, when odium was then incurred by the bishops of your party, they are said to have written to Taurinus, then count, that such people could not be corrected in the Church; they ordered that they should receive discipline from the aforesaid count. Then Taurinus, in response to their letter, ordered armed soldiers [Col. 1008B] to go through the markets where the fury of the Circumcellions had usually ranged. In the place called Octava [Note: [Col. 1008B] MS S. G. reads *Octaviensi*.] [Note: [Col. 1008B] “The place Octava”: a town of Numidia. Among the bishops giving judgment at the Council of Carthage under Cyprian is Victor of Octava. In the list of bishops of Numidia there is a bishop of Octoba or Octava. DU PIN.] very many were killed [Note: [Col. 1008B] MSS S. T. and P. S. add “and.”], and many were mutilated. Their bodies could, even to this day, be counted [Note: [Col. 1008C] “By whitewashed altars”: that is, whitewashed tombs built in the form of altars. Sacred rites were formerly performed at martyrs’ monuments and memorials; so that this might conveniently be done, their monuments were raised in the form of altars. Thus the Donatists had erected altars and memorials for those Circumcellions—who had also died during Macarius’ expedition—from which the bodies of the slain could be counted. First Council of Carthage, canon 2: “or calls those who have cast themselves down in madness by the name of martyrs.” The Fifth Council: “It was likewise decreed that altars which are everywhere set up in fields or beside roads as memorials of martyrs …” Augustine, *Against Parmenianus*, III, near the end: “They dare to compare the temporal penalties of their schism with the sufferings of martyrs, so that the anniversaries of their punishments may be celebrated by a great gathering of madmen.” ALBASP.  
Ibid. “By whitewashed altars or tables,” etc. Seneca, *Letters* 86: “Lying in Scipio Africanus’ own villa, I write this to you, after paying reverence to his spirit and to an altar, which I suppose to be the tomb of so great a man,” etc. On *mensa*, Cicero, *On the Laws*, II, near the end: “He set a limit upon new tombs; for upon a mound of earth he did not wish anything to be set up except a column no more than three feet high, or a table, or a small altar,” etc. Related to this is the fact that the place where Cyprian suffered was commonly called Cyprian’s Table. Victor of Vita, *On the Persecution*, I, teaches us that this blessed martyr suffered in one place and was buried in another, and that his memory was venerated in both places. Augustine, *Sermons on Various Subjects* 113, teaches, however, that the former place was so designated from an altar, or table constructed there in the form of an altar. If Optatus truly and properly means “whitewashed” by these altars and tables, I think this arose from the religious veneration of those regarded as martyrs. For Plutarch also teaches, in the Roman [Questions], “Why do they wear white?” etc. [Col. 1009A], vol. X, pp. 82, 483, that white is particularly suited to the dead and to the pure, innocent souls of the departed. [Col. 1009A] But if *dealbatas* means simply white or bright, this may have been the natural colour of the earth or place where they were buried. [Col. 1009B] Everyone knows that the three hundred martyrs commemorated on 24 August were called the “white mass” from the lime-kiln in which they suffered and were consumed. Likewise, I would suppose that the innumerable martyrs who suffered under Dacian, governor of Spain, and whose commemoration is celebrated on 3 November in the Roman Calendar, were also called the “white mass” for no other reason than the natural whiteness of the place, soil, lime, or something else of that sort—though I know that others give another explanation of this title. M. CASAUB.] by means of whitewashed altars [Col. 1009A] or tables. [Note: [Col. 1009B] “By whitewashed altars or tables”: that is, whitewashed tombs constructed in the form of altars. Since the Donatists regarded the Circumcellions who had been killed as martyrs, they erected altars over their graves. For the early Christians were accustomed to erect altars over martyrs’ tombs and celebrate sacred rites there. Such altars were also called *mensae*, “tables.” A notable passage on this subject occurs in St Augustine’s sermon *On Various Subjects*, formerly no. 113, now no. 310, on the birthday of Cyprian the martyr: [Col. 1009C] “Finally,” he says, “as you know, all of you who know Carthage, a table was built to God in that same place, and yet it is called Cyprian’s Table—not because Cyprian ever ate there, but because he was sacrificed there, and by that very sacrifice prepared this table: not one at which he feeds or is fed, but one at which sacrifice is offered to God, to whom he too was offered.” That altars or tables of this kind were customarily built over martyrs’ tombs throughout fields and along roads, especially in Africa, is taught by the already cited canon of the Fifth Council of Carthage: “It was decreed that altars which are everywhere established in fields or beside roads as memorials of martyrs …” There are also other examples demonstrating that altars and tables could be spoken of over the graves of the dead. Ovid mentions sepulchral altars. Seneca, *Letter* 86: “Lying in Scipio Africanus’ own villa, I write this to you, after paying reverence to his spirit and to an altar which I suppose to be the tomb of so great a man.” Cicero, *On the Laws* II: “He set a limit upon new tombs; for upon a mound of earth [Col. 1009D] he did not wish anything to be set up except a column no more than three feet high, or a table, or a small altar.” The Donatists had whitewashed the altars and tables placed over the graves of those whom they regarded as their martyrs, so that they might be more recognizable and conspicuous, and distinguished from the others. DU PIN.] [Note: [Col. 1009A] Thus in all MSS; the printed editions incorrectly have “will be able.”]

When some of these began to be buried in basilicas, [Note: [Col. 1009D] “In basilicas”: he is speaking of Circumcellions killed by Taurinus, not by Macarius. To show that they were frenzied and insane, he says that the Donatist bishop of the place Subbula denied them burial in church. ALBASP.] the presbyter Clarus, at Subbula, was compelled by his bishop [61] to make the burial unburied—[Note: [Col. 1009D] “To make the burial unburied”: to expel those burials from the church. ALBASP.] [Note: [Col. 1009D] “To make the burial unburied”: to exhume or cast out a body already buried or about to be buried. This imitates Cicero, *First Philippic*, ch. 2, concerning Julius Caesar’s funeral: “When an endless evil spread through the city and flowed more widely day by day, the same men who made a pyre in the Forum had made that burial unburied.” See the commentators on this passage. CLERICUS.]

[Note: [Col. 1010B] “Whence it became known”: hence it was made known that the Donatists had denied even their own people burial in God’s house. ALBASP.  
Ibid. “Whence it became known that it had been ordered to be done which was done,” etc. The Donatists, he says, seized this occasion to malign the Catholics, as though they had been the instigators and authors of that slaughter and massacre of Circumcellions, because they afterwards did not permit those killed to be buried in basilicas—as though denying burial in church and depriving someone of life were the same thing. Balduin directs us to observe that burial in a temple or church was then prohibited. But if Optatus means that what was denied to these persons was denied by public law and custom, I do not see how the Donatists could have derived from it even the slightest argument that the Catholics had ordered their slaughter—though Optatus seems to suggest this and to give it as the ground of their suspicion and calumny. I know that several canons exist which forbid it, and perhaps also some imperial laws. Yet I suspect that in African churches this rule had force only to the extent that no one could be buried without the bishop’s permission. In my judgment, both Optatus here and Augustine, *On Care for the Dead*, indicate this fairly clearly. When Armogastes, in Victor of Vita, I, was dying and asked Felix to deem him worthy to be buried beneath a carob tree, Felix replied: “Far be that from you, venerable confessor; I shall bury you in one of the basilicas, with the triumph and honour that you deserve.” Roman laws—those still extant abundantly attest it—held it unlawful to bury anyone within the city walls, except for a few whom a special privilege exempted from the bond of the common law. Although this custom began to disappear soon after Constantine’s time and was eventually wholly abrogated by imperial laws, it nevertheless persisted much longer elsewhere, as in cities of Gaul and even in England. But this by the way. What Baronius, in the year of Christ 309, §4, infers from the book *On the Roman Pontiffs*—that the Roman Church had already received from Maxentius, son of Maximian, permission to bury the bodies of Christian martyrs within the city—does not seem probable to me until confirmed from another source, given the still recent law of Diocletian and Maximian which prohibited it both to Christians and to all others. M. CASAUB.]

Whence it became known that it had been ordered to be done which was done: [Note: [Col. 1010D] “Whence it became known that it had been ordered to be done which was done”: from this the Donatists seized an occasion to malign the Catholics as authors of the Circumcellions’ slaughter. DU PIN.] since burial in the house of God had not even been permitted. [Note: [Col. 1010D] “Since burial in the house of God had not even been permitted”: as if he said, “The Donatists altogether wrongly reproached the Catholics because one of their presbyters forbade Circumcellions to be buried in basilicas, since burial in God’s house is not customarily granted everywhere to everyone, much less to criminals who had deservedly been killed.” DU PIN.]

[Note: [Col. 1010D] “Their number afterwards grew strong”: from these madmen, to whom you denied burial, Donatus of Bagai subsequently recruited a crowd and soldiers against Macarius. ALBASP.] Afterwards their number grew strong. Thus Donatus of Bagai found a means of recruiting a frenzied [Col. 1010A] crowd against Macarius. From this very class came those who, in pursuit of a false martyrdom, hired assassins against themselves to bring about their own destruction. From it also came those who, casting their worthless lives from the summits of lofty mountains, threw themselves down headlong. Behold from what sort of number the other bishop Donatus had formed his cohorts. [Note: [Col. 1009A] MS G. reads *consortes*, “companions,” incorrectly.]

Frightened by this danger, those who were carrying treasuries [Note: [Col. 1010A] MS S. T. reads: “who were carrying near the treasures.”] to distribute to the poor found in such necessity the expedient of requesting armed soldiers from Count Silvester, [Col. 1011A] not in order to use violence against anyone, but in order to prevent the violence arranged by the aforementioned bishop Donatus. For this reason the soldiers appeared armed. Now consider to whom whatever followed should or can be ascribed.

There they had an innumerable crowd of persons summoned [Note: [Col. 1011B] MS S. G.: “There raged innumerable thousands of summoned people, for whom provisions also …”], and it is certain that an adequate supply of food had been prepared: the basilica was like public granaries. They waited for persons upon whom they might exercise their fury and do whatever their madness dictated, unless the presence of armed soldiers prevented them. For when, before the soldiers’ arrival, surveyors [Note: [Col. 1011C] *Metatores*: surveyors of camps. ALBASP.] [Note: [Col. 1011C] He calls *metatores* those sent ahead to designate lodging or places for tents for the soldiers who were coming. In civil law they are called *mensores*. In the commentary on Suidas, μετάτωρ is explained as ὁ προαποστελλόμενος ἄγγελος πρὸ τοῦ ἄρχοντος, “a messenger sent before a ruler to designate lodging.” Sidonius Apollinaris, VIII, alludes to this: “I sent a *metatorial* letter, as though with a Muse going before”; that is, says Sirmondus, a letter announcing his arrival, as though it would designate lodgings, καὶ καταγωγήν (“and lodging”)—for this was the duty of *metatores*. DU PIN.] were sent, as is customary, they were not suitably received in accordance with the Apostle’s command: “To whom honour, honour; to whom custom, custom; to whom tribute, tribute; owe no one anything” (Rom. XII.7). They were beaten—[Note: [Col. 1011B] We have adopted this word because the sense of the passage demands it. For it is clear from what follows that those assaulted were soldiers sent out by the commanders, not Circumcellions. MSS S. T. and P. S. rightly read *contusi sunt*, “they were beaten,” although these words have been displaced from their proper location. MS S. G. reads *pompati sunt*.] [Note: [Col. 1011C] “Those sent with their horses,” etc. Other editions: “Those who had been sent with their horses were beaten by those whose …” He says they were caught unawares because those few men sent ahead were separately attacked before the remainder, who followed at no great interval, could arrive and rescue them from danger. Those whom he here calls *contusi*, “beaten,” he shortly afterwards calls *vexati*, “maltreated,” which comes to the same thing. Learned men Aulus Gellius and Macrobius long ago observed that *vexare* is not a mild word for insult or injury, but is suitable to a grave and atrocious matter; their observation is especially useful in reading ecclesiastical writers. What follows—“whose names you have fanned with the fan of envy,” etc.—is explained by Optatus himself elsewhere: “Let us see why Moses ordered three thousand persons to be killed,” etc.; “Why did Macarius order two to be killed, whose names, as I said above, you fan every day with the fan of envy?” Thus the reference is not to hatred or injury directed at their names themselves, but to the use of their names to stir up envy in others: they kept putting forward, as innocent persons and martyrs, the names of those who had mistreated the advance surveyors before the arrival of the rest and were afterward killed by angry soldiers, and, as Optatus says, fanned them with the fan of envy. Optatus correctly adds shortly afterwards: “They themselves were the teachers of their own injury; and by injuries bestowed beforehand they taught what they might suffer.” *Praerogare iniuriam*, “to bestow injury beforehand,” is unusual. Zeno of Verona several times uses *praerogare* for *erogare*, “to dispense,” and *praerogatio* for a gift or benefit, exactly in the sense used by our author in the Conference of Carthage, p. 394: “Why is not repaid to us what we bestowed beforehand?” In the next sentence, “their ranks” means their units or fellow soldiers, as in Tertullian, *Apology*, ch. 37: “If we wished to act as open enemies rather than merely hidden avengers, would we lack strength in numbers and forces?” So also others use it; but this is commonplace. M. CASAUB. This passage has been restored by us.] those who had been sent with their horses [62] by those whose names you have fanned with the fan of envy. [Note: [Col. 1011B] MS S. G. reads *ventilatis*, “you fan.”] [Note: [Col. 1012C] “By those whose names you have fanned with the fan of envy”: namely, by Donatus’ troops, whose names Parmenianus kept advertising in order to stir up hostility against Catholics. Thus Optatus himself says elsewhere in the same sense: “Why did Macarius order two to be killed, whose names, as I said above, you fan with the fan of envy?” DU PIN.]

They themselves were the teachers of their own injury, [Note: [Col. 1011B] MS S. G. reads *invidiae*, “envy.”] [Note: [Col. 1012D] “They themselves were the teachers of their own injury”: they themselves gave the example and first led the way by maltreating the surveyor-soldiers. From them the injuries began. DU PIN.] and by injuries bestowed beforehand they taught what they might suffer. [Note: [Col. 1012B] MS S. T. reads *potuissent*, “could have.”] [Note: [Col. 1012B] MS S. G. reads *praecogitatis*, “premeditated.”] The maltreated soldiers returned to their ranks, and what two or three had suffered grieved them all. [Col. 1012A] All were stirred; not even their commanders were able to restrain the angry soldiers. Thus occurred the thing through which, you have recalled, odium was brought upon unity. [Note: [Col. 1012B] MS S. G. reads: “Thus occurred that which you recall was done in the odium of unity.”] These matters, and the rest, are yours and have their own causes and the persons liable for them, whom I have identified. We did not even see this; we heard it together with you. If hearing makes persons guilty, we count you as partners, because you likewise heard it. [Note: [Col. 1012B] Thus in MS S. G., better than the other MSS and printed editions, which read “we heard.”] If hearing is exempt from guilt in the act, then what was done by others, though you allege it against us, ought not to be imputed to us.

[Note: [Col. 1012D] “You set forth the complaint in order”: the passage should be divided thus: very many were injured under Leontius and Ursacius; some were killed under Paul and Macarius; and some persons, I know not who, were proscribed for a time by their successors. ALBASP.  
Ibid. “You set forth the complaint in order: under Leontius …” Whether we read *deponitis* or *disponitis* makes little difference. But it matters considerably if the words are divided differently. Read, therefore, as others have already observed: “You set forth the complaint in order: under Leontius and Ursacius very many were injured; under Paul and Macarius some were killed; by their successors, some persons—I know not who—were proscribed for a time.” M. CASAUB.]

You set forth the complaint in order: that under Leontius and Ursacius very many were injured; that under Paul and Macarius some were killed; that by their successors, some persons of theirs—I do not know who—were proscribed for a time. What is this to us? What does it concern the Catholic Church? [Note: [Col. 1012B] Absent in MS S. G.] Whatever you have alleged, you yourselves did. You refused gladly to receive the peace commended by God, judging the inheritance of schism dearer than the precepts set before you by the Saviour. [Note: [Col. 1012B] MS S. T. and printed editions read *praepositi*, “set over.”] You accused the workers of unity; disprove unity itself, if you can. For I suppose you do not deny that unity is the highest good. What concern is it of ours [Note: [Col. 1012B] MS S. G. reads *quid nos*, “what [are] we,” for *quid ad nos*, “what concern is it of ours.”] what sort of workers they were, provided it is evident that what was produced is good? [Col. 1013A] Wine, after all, is worked and pressed even by sinful labourers, and from it a sacrifice is offered to God. Oil too is made by unclean persons, by some who live wickedly and speak impurely; yet it is still simply dispensed in flavour, in light, and even in holy chrism. [Note: [Col. 1013B] MSS S. T. read “in holy chrism”; MS S. P., “in the sacrament of chrism.”] [Note: [Col. 1013B] “And yet it is simply dispensed in flavour, in light, and even in holy chrism.” Earlier editions read: “and yet the liquid in light, even in holy …” Since either reading can be accepted without loss of sense, while the words can be joined and varied in more than one way, I think it difficult to decide the true reading without manuscript support, and equally pointless to labour excessively over it. Since Optatus first mentioned wine and only its sacred use in the spiritual sacrifice of the Eucharist, I do not think he wished to touch on any use of oil outside sacred matters. But I do not know what sacred “flavour” oil has. Nor would I readily concede that *sapor* is metaphorical here, as though he meant “an odour of sweetness” (εἰς ὀσμὴν εὐωδίας), or something similar. The use of oil in illumination and chrism, and its ancient and varied functions, is well known; but usage was not always identical in every church. In Africa, Victor of Vita, II, mentions lamps and candles among the customary furnishings of churches. If one wished to be more subtle, “light” might mean baptism, which St Gregory Nazianzen rightly calls φῶς, “light,” in *On Holy Baptism*. Dionysius the Areopagite, Cyril of Jerusalem, and others explain its various rites. Yet I think otherwise. Nor does τὸ χρίσμα (“the chrism”) here properly mean the anointing called chrism κατ’ ἐξοχήν (“pre-eminently”)—concerning which Cyril has a separate chapter or catechesis in his Mystagogical Lectures—but sacramental anointing generally, whatever sacred anointing was formerly employed by the ancient Church. M. CASAUB.] [Note: [Col. 1013D] “It is simply dispensed in flavour, in light, and even in holy chrism”: people use it harmlessly in seasonings, lamps, and the mysteries themselves. DU PIN.]

V. The workers of unity are excused for having acted rather harshly.—You say that the workers of unity were wicked—perhaps by God’s will, who sometimes [Note: [Col. 1013B] MSS S. T. and P. S. read *numquam*, “never,” but wrongly.] approves even what he could have prevented. For some evils are done wickedly; some evils are done rightly. A robber does evil wickedly; a judge does evil rightly when he punishes what the robber has sinned. For this is God’s utterance: “You shall not kill” (Exod. XX.13); and this too is his utterance: [Note: [Col. 1013B] MS S. G. adds, “in the book of Leviticus.”] “If a man is found sleeping with a woman who has a husband, you shall kill both of them” (Deut. XXII.22). [Note: [Col. 1013B] The words “In the First Book of Kingdoms” are wrongly inserted here in MS S. T.; they do not occur in MSS S. G. and P. S. and wholly disrupt the sense.] [Note: [Col. 1013D] “In the First Book of Kingdoms, one God,” etc. I cannot sufficiently wonder at the patience of learned men who have endured retaining for so long a reading which, if I see correctly, is utterly absurd and deserves to be banished altogether. What meaning can be extracted—or even scented out—from the text as it now stands? If we remove that utterly unsuitable gloss, “in the Book of Kingdoms,” no obscurity or suspicion remains in the words. I admit that it is easier to remove it and drive it from its unjust position than to conjecture whence or upon what first occasion it crept in. This at least occurred to me: because Phinehas is mentioned immediately afterwards, and because the name Phinehas occurs more than once in First Kings, an inattentive reader perhaps confused Phinehas, son of Eleazar, with the other Phinehas associated with Eli, and put “First Kings,” rather than Numbers, in the margin. M. CASAUB. These words have been removed by us and do not occur in the MSS.]

One God, and two different utterances. Finally, when Phinehas, the priest’s son, found an adulterer with an adulteress, he raised his hand with the sword and stood uncertain between two utterances of God: from one side sounded to him, “You shall not kill”; from the other sounded, “You shall kill both.” If he struck, he would sin; [Col. 1014A] if he did not strike, he would do wrong. He chose the better evil, that he might strike; and perhaps there were those who wished to brand the avenger of this act as a murderer. But in order to show that certain evils are rightly done, God spoke, saying: “Phinehas has appeased my anger” (Num. XXV.11). The homicide pleased God because adultery had been punished.

What if God also now approved what you say that you suffered—you who refused to possess unity with the whole world and [Note: [Col. 1014C] “With the whole world and with the memorials of the Apostles.” Note this way of speaking: “with the whole world and with the memorials of the Apostles.” Communion was not considered complete by the ancients, even if one possessed it with the whole world, unless one had it “with the memorials of the Apostles,” that is, unless one communicated with blessed Peter. The completeness of Christian communion depends upon the communion which we have with St Peter and his successors; otherwise it cannot be pleasing to God. ALBASP.] with the memorials of the Apostles—which was pleasing to God? [Note: [Col. 1014B] MSS S. T. and P. S. read *placitae sunt*, “which were pleasing.”]

VI. Against the Donatists’ Pseudo-Martyrs.—Reluctantly I am compelled here also to mention those persons whom I would rather not mention, whom you place among the martyrs, and by whom people of your communion swear as though by their sole religion. [Note: [Col. 1014C] “By their sole religion”: as though there were no religious obligation in other matters, and one should not believe or take an oath except by such martyrs. ALBASP.] I should indeed like to pass them over in silence, but the cause of truth does not permit itself to be silenced. From their very names [Note: [Col. 1014D] “Names”: because the Donatists recited their names, as those of principal martyrs, during sacred rites and from the diptychs. ALBASP.] a rabid hostility barks thoughtlessly against unity; [Note: [Col. 1014B] We have added this epithet from MS S. G.] and some, rejecting unity, think that it ought to be accused or avoided because Marculus and Donatus [Note: [Col. 1014D] “Rejecting”: if some were killed by Macarius, such as Marculus and Donatus, unity, which makes martyrs, must be avoided. ALBASP.] are said to have been killed and to have died. [Note: [Col. 1014D] Marculus and Donatus. This Donatus is the Donatus of Bagai, as may be learned from Augustine, Homily II on John: “Behold, Marculus was hurled down from a rock; behold, Donatus of Bagai was cast into a well.” Catholics said that they had thrown themselves down; Augustine nevertheless acknowledges in *Against the Letter of Petilian*, II.20, that this was uncertain. In *Against Cresconius*, III.49, he thinks it more credible because that sort of punishment was unusual. The *Passion of Marculus*, written by a certain Donatian, was published in Mabillon’s *Analecta*, IV; it is prefaced as dated three or eight days before the Kalends of December. There Marculus is called only a presbyter, not a bishop. It is also related that, by order of Macarius, whom Constans had sent into Africa with Paul, he was first arrested on the estate of Vegesela, where he encountered Macarius with certain Donatian bishops; after being beaten with ropes together with his companions, he was taken through several towns of Numidia under the strictest military guard as far as the fortress of Nova Petra, and finally, four days later, hurled by a soldier from the summit of a rock. At the Conference of Carthage, ch. 187, Dativus, Donatist bishop of Nova Petra, says that he has no adversary—that is, no Catholic bishop—because “Lord Marculus is there, whose blood God will require on the day of judgement.” The names of Donatus and Marculus seem therefore to have been transferred among Catholic martyrs: Donatus to 1 March, where Usuard says he suffered at Carthage under the commander Ursacius and the tribune Marcellinus; Marculus to 26 November. For Usuard’s Martyrology says of him: “At Nicomedia [for Numidia], blessed Marculus, priest and martyr, who in the time of the tyrant Constans endured the greatest persecutions and at last was hurled down from a high rock.” The martyr’s name, the emperor, and the manner of death agree; the place-name too is not very different. Constans is called “tyrant” there, a charge which could have been cast upon that pious ruler only by Donatists. In the Roman Martyrology Marculus’ name is changed to Marcellus, Constans’ to Constantius, and it says that he was hurled from a rock by Arians instead of Macarians. Rabanus likewise lists Marculus among the martyrs. Without doubt this is no other than the Donatist of whom Optatus speaks here. DU PIN.]

As though absolutely no one could deserve to be killed in God’s punishment. [Col. 1015A] No one ought to have been harmed by the workers of unity; [Note: [Col. 1016C] No one: Macarius ought not to have harmed anyone; but neither ought unity to have been impeded by your people. ALBASP.] but neither ought the divine commands to have been despised by bishops, to whom it is commanded: “Seek peace, and you shall attain it” (Ps. XXXIII.15); and again: “How good and how pleasant it is for brothers to dwell together in unity” (Ps. CXXXII.1); and again: “Blessed are the peacemakers, for they shall be called children of God” (Matt. V.9). Those who neither wished gladly to hear this nor wished devoutly to do it—whatever they could suffer, if being killed is evil, they themselves are the cause of their own evil.

VII. Macarius is defended against the calumnies of the Donatists.—But Macarius seems to you to deserve accusation (as you say), since you judge that he could not have done this by the will of God. [Note: Thus in MS P. S. In MS S. G.: “if you judge that he did this without the will of God.” In MS S. T.: “if you judge that he could have done this without the will of God.” We have preferred the first reading as plainer and more explicit.] You have ancient culprits of this sort: [Col. 1015B] accuse first Moses himself, the lawgiver. When he came down from Mount Sinai, when the tablets of the Law had scarcely yet been set forth, [Note: MS S. G. reads “laid down.”] upon which was written, “You shall not kill,” he ordered three thousand men to be killed in a single moment. Put Macarius aside for a little; summon Phinehas, the priest’s son, whom I mentioned shortly before, first [Note: “Call him to judgment: if nevertheless you find,” etc. The second, more elegant edition of François Balduin has *inveneritis*, “you find.” Although theologians of that age, especially Africans, did not observe these tenses so exactly. Tertullian and Arnobius are particularly witnesses; so is our author, Book I: “For although he is outside, nevertheless you are from us.” UNCERTAIN.] to judgment (Num. 25), if indeed you can find any judge besides God. [Note: MS S. G. reads “another.”] For what you accuse in his person was praised by God, because it was done in zeal for God.

[Note: “Suppress meanwhile the utterances which envy dictates against Macarius,” etc. Other editions read: “to which the envy uttered against Macarius returns; and first return to another prophet,” etc. Perhaps: “to which the envy uttered against Macarius returns. First return,” etc.; or, if you prefer, “which envy dictates against Macarius. Return,” etc. Moreover, *primo* means “first” in the sense of “beforehand,” for it is repeated three times. But they are told to return because they will shortly return to Macarius, and haste was necessary. For he had previously said: “Put Macarius aside for a little,” etc. M. Casaubon. This passage has been restored by us.]

Suppress meanwhile the utterances which envy dictates against Macarius. Return first to the prophet Elijah, [Note: MS S. T. wrongly reads “another.”] who, at the brook Kishon, in obeying the will of God, [Note: MS S. G. reads “at one hour with the will of God.”] killed four hundred and fifty men. But perhaps you will say that those were killed deservedly, these undeservedly. [Note: These words are absent from MS S. G.] Vengeance never follows unless its cause has first preceded it. Moses took vengeance, as we have said; Elijah took vengeance; Phinehas took vengeance; and you do not wish Macarius to have taken vengeance. “Those who are said to have been killed had done nothing wrong.” Let Macarius be guilty in that he alone, without our knowledge but at your provocation, did this. Why is blame cast upon us, when the deeds are another’s? The cause lies in you: for it is said to have happened on account of you, who were outside—though even now you seem to be outside—not on account of us, who dwell within and have never departed from the root.

But since we have spoken in order of the persons mentioned above, let us see why Moses ordered three thousand men to be killed (Exod. 32); why Phinehas killed two (Num. 25); why Elijah killed four hundred and fifty (3 Kings 18); and why Macarius killed two, whose names, as I said above, you daily toss about with the fan of envy. It is clear that vengeance was taken upon those by whom God’s command had been despised. For “You shall not make for yourself a carved image” (Exod. 20) [Col. 1016B] is the voice of God; and “You shall not commit adultery” is the voice of the same God; “You shall not sacrifice to idols” (Ps. 33:15) was spoken by the same God; and “You shall not make a schism,” and “Seek peace and pursue it,” are commands of that same God.

In the time of Moses, the people of Israel worshipped the head of a calf, which sacrilegious fire had cast for them. Therefore three thousand men deserved to be killed, because the voice of God seemed to have been despised. Phinehas struck adulterers with a single blow and deserved to be praised by God, because he killed despisers of the divine commands. [Note: MS S. G. reads “precepts.”] And the four hundred and fifty whom Elijah is read to have killed were killed because, contrary to God’s command, inasmuch as they were false prophets, they had despised God’s precepts.

Those whose names you use to accuse Macarius are not far removed from false prophets; for God said that you would be false [Col. 1016C] prophets, as we shall prove in the next section. And because they refused to look toward peace, lest they should dwell as one with their brethren, they stubbornly opposed the commands and the will [Col. 1017A] of God. Therefore you see that similar things were done by Moses, Phinehas, Elijah, and Macarius, because the precepts of one God were vindicated by them all. [Note: Thus in MS S. G. MSS S. T. and P. S. read: “the acts of vengeance of one God proceeded.”]

But I see that at this point you distinguish the times, holding that one time existed before the Gospel and another after the Gospel. Here you can say that it is written that the sword, with which Peter had cut off the ear of the high priest’s servant, was now to be sheathed by Peter (Matt. 26). [Note: MS S. T. reads “which”; printed editions, “by which.”] Devout Peter might have killed that servant; but Christ had come to suffer, not to be defended. [Note: “But Christ had come to suffer.” The Donatists replied that the times must be distinguished, that after Christ’s coming no one should be injured, and that Peter’s sword must be sheathed as an example. Optatus answers in turn that Peter did indeed sheath the sword because Christ had to suffer, not be defended; but that this example is not to be extended beyond Christ’s Passion. Albaspinaeus.]

[Note: “And if Peter carried out his intention,” etc. Write: “and if Saint Peter carried out his intention, in Christ’s Passion [Col. 1017D] the servant would seem to be avenged, not the people liberated.” That is: if Peter had carried out what his zeal prompted him to do, namely to kill that servant, Christ could have seemed to suffer as one guilty of slaughter and homicide committed by his disciple, rather than as one innocent suffering for the guilty. M. Casaubon. This passage has been restored by us.]

And if Peter carried out his intention, in Christ’s Passion the servant would seem to be avenged, not the people liberated. [Note: MSS S. T. and P. S. read: “And Peter seems to carry out his intention in Christ’s Passion, and the servant to be avenged, not the people liberated.”]

VIII. Macarius cannot be called a persecutor, nor those punished by him martyrs, since they were enemies of peace.—For Macarius too did not draw the sword that Peter had sheathed in its scabbard. God proves this when he speaks [Col. 1017B] to the valley of Zion, saying: “Those wounded in you were not wounded by the sword” (Isa. 22:2); or prove that anyone at that time was struck by the sword. Then he says: “Those dead in you were not dead in war.” Therefore you must take care lest it be rash to call martyrs those who experienced no warfare of Christians. [Note: “The war of Christians”: the persecution by emperors. Albaspinaeus.]

For nothing of the kind was done or heard which is customarily said or done in the war of Christians—that war which is called persecution—which operated under two of the four beasts that Daniel saw rising from the sea (Dan. 7). The first was like [Note: “Of” is absent from MSS S. T. and P. S.] a lion: this was the persecution under Decius and Valerian. The second was like a bear: another persecution, which occurred under Diocletian and Maximian. At that time there were also impious [Col. 1018A] judges bringing war against the Christian name; among them, in the proconsular province, sixty years and more ago, [Note: MS S. G. reads “nearly seventy.”] was Anulinus, and in Numidia, Florus. Everyone knows what their contrived cruelty accomplished. The war proclaimed against Christians raged; in the temples of demons the devil triumphed; altars smoked with unclean vapours.

[Note: “And because.” “And those who,” is better. Albaspinaeus. “And those who could not come to sacrilegious rites were compelled everywhere to place incense”—that is, to burn it, offer incense, and thus become *thurificati*, “incense-offerers,” so celebrated in the accounts of that time. He means the sick or aged, and those confined to bed (*κλινηρεῖς*), whom a culpable cause kept at home. Hence Optatus elegantly concludes: every place was a temple for crime. [Col. 1018C] I therefore wonder that anyone could be so tasteless as to prefer the old reading, “a temple or a crime.” M. Casaubon.]

And those who could not come to sacrilegious rites [65] were compelled to place incense wherever they were. Every place was a temple for crime. [Note: “A temple for crime.” “Or a crime” is better, says Albaspinaeus. On the contrary, this is erroneous. A temple (*templum*) for Optatus is the shrine of an idolatrous people; above, Book II: “For the former, that temples might be built and idols made.” Likewise in that book and in Book VI. UNCERTAIN. MSS S. Th. and Ph. S. read: “In all places there was a temple or a crime.”]

Elderly persons near death were defiled; unknowing childhood was polluted; little children were carried by their mothers to wickedness; parents were compelled to commit bloodless parricides; [Note: MS S. T. reads “bloody,” but wholly wrongly.] some were compelled [Note: MSS S. T. and S. G. read “pressed.”] to destroy the temples of the living God; others to deny Christ; others to burn the divine laws; others to offer incense. You yourselves will not even be able to invent that Macarius did anything of this kind. [Col. 1018B]

Under the persecutor Florus, Christians were compelled to go to the temples of idols; under Macarius, the slothful were compelled to go to the basilica. [Note: “Under Macarius the slothful were compelled,” etc. Here he does not mean persons who attended churches and ecclesiastical gatherings too negligently, but schismatics and others who sinned not through negligence but by deliberate purpose—or rather a settled madness—avoiding and shunning Catholic assemblies as though impure and polluted, and placing in this no small part of their religion. Thus the Donatists themselves called Catholics “slothful.” Our author, Book VI: “and they accuse those sitting in the bosom of Mother Church as slothful and slow,” etc.; see also above on Book II: “those who through indolence had fallen away from confession of God had offered incense,” etc. M. Casaubon.]

Under Florus it was said that Christ should be denied and idols worshipped. [Note: “Christ should be denied and idols worshipped.” *Rogare* means “to worship.” Below in this book: “We read the divine testament together; we worship one God.” Likewise: “You call him a pagan who has worshipped God through his Son before the altar.” UNCERTAIN.] By contrast, under Macarius all were admonished to worship one God together in the Church.

Therefore, [Note: This passage down to the words “you wish them to be martyrs,” absent from all printed editions and omitted in MSS S. T. and P. S., has been supplied from MS S. G.; no one can doubt that it is genuine.] since you see that there was no war of Christians, and that God records some as dead without war when he says, “Those dead in you were not dead in war”; since those may doubtfully be martyrs who were not summoned either to sacrilegious rites, or to unclean incense-offerings, or to denial of God’s name; and since there is no passage to martyrdom except through confession: how do you call martyrs those who were not confessors? [Col. 1019A] Or which of them was compelled to deny Christ and confessed him?

If, then, there can be no martyrdom without confession of Christ’s name, and no one confessed; if what you say was done was done in vindication of God’s commands; and if you do not prove that anything was done by us—when God both said that what was done would happen thus, and his precepts were vindicated—consider whether it is not only empty but even superstitious to place among those who died without war persons who could die for God’s name by confessing Christ. Or, if you wish them to be martyrs, prove that they loved peace, in which the first foundations of martyrdom lie; or that they loved the unity pleasing to God; or that they had charity with their brethren. For we proved in the first book [Col. 1019B] that all Christians are brethren, and shall doubtless prove it in the fourth.

Those whom you say ought to be called [Note: MS S. T. reads: “whom you say ought to be called.”] martyrs refused to recognize brethren and had no charity. Nor should it be said in excuse that they refused communion with traditors, since it has been proved most plainly that they themselves were children of traditors. Therefore there is no excuse, because it is wholly clear that they had no charity, without which no martyrdom can either be named or exist; without which the greatest and most commanding virtue is without effect; without which the knowledge of all languages is of no value; without which even fellowship with angels is of no value. [Note: “Fellowship with angels.” He seems to explain the Apostle’s words, “even of angels,” as some fellowship and communion with them; and “to speak the languages of all nations” as receiving letters of communion from all nations and communicating with them. Albaspinaeus.]

For the Apostle Paul says: “If I have within me power to command mountains to move themselves from place to place, and speak the languages of all nations, even of angels, and deliver my body to flames, [Col. 1019C] but do not have charity within me, I am nothing; rather, I shall be a sounding bronze in a desert, so that the work of the voice perishes where no hearing meets it” (1 Cor. 13:1).

If so great a person, if blessed Paul, if the vessel of election, declares himself to be nothing, even with commanding power and fellowship with angels, unless he has charity: consider whether those who, as deserters from charity, could suffer something for that very desertion deserve to be called not martyrs, but something else. [Note: “Something else” is absent from the manuscripts but necessary.]

IX. Unity was to be secured in Africa.—The whole [Col. 1020A] world rejoices in Catholic unity, [Note: MS S. G. reads “of the Catholic [Church].”] except for the part of Africa in which a conflagration was kindled from a spark. You complain that the workers for unity committed I know not what acts. Italy does not complain of this, [Note: MS S. G. has “Gaul” in place of “Italy”; we have restored both.] nor Gaul, nor Spain, nor Pannonia, nor Galatia, nor Greece, nor Asia with all its provinces. For nothing there needed to be corrected; no tailor, so to speak, was sent there. [Note: MS S. G. wrongly reads “sower.”] But here in Africa, when the people had long remained in unity, the garment was sound; it was torn by the hostile hand of the enemy. As it were, pieces of cloth hung from the one origin of the garment; and branches growing from one root were divided from one another.

Why does one part put itself before another part? [Note: These words have been supplied from MS S. G. “Why one part puts itself before another.” The orthodox wished to communicate with the Donatists; the Donatists resisted and fled their communion, and therefore set themselves above them. Albaspinaeus.] Why does one patch raise itself above another patch, when it cannot prove itself better? For what if the despised [Col. 1020B] patch says: “Why do you raise yourself so high? Did we not grow equally? Were we not together in the hands of those making us? Were we not cleansed together at the fuller’s?” [Note: “In the sheep.” Better than “did we not,” says Albaspinaeus. “Did we not grow as equals?” A boy reading this should observe that *pares*, “equals,” must be read, not *pars*, “part.” The second edition of François Balduin reads: “in the sheep we grew as equals.” UNCERTAIN. Thus restored.]

“The enemy wished to cut us off from one another; the adversary wished to deform our beauty. In the garment we are still one, but we hang apart in different places.” For what has been torn is divided in part, not wholly, since it is rightly established [Note: These words are absent from MS S. G.] that ecclesiastical practice is one for us and for you; [Note: “Practice”: one discipline. Albaspinaeus.] and though human minds contend, the sacraments do not contend.

Finally, we too can say: “We believed alike, [Note: MS S. T. reads “we believe.”] and were marked with one seal; we were baptized no differently from you. We read the divine testament together; we worship one God; [Note: “We read the divine testament,” etc. It should be noted that for this writer *rogare* means “to worship,” while *negare* means “to deny,” a word which remains intact today in the highly conservative Latin of Spanish. Barth.] the Lord’s Prayer is one among us and among you.” [Note: “The Lord’s Prayer”: by prayer he understands the sacrifice of the Mass. Albaspinaeus.]

But, as stated above, when the part was torn [Col. 1020C] and the portions hung on either side, stitching was necessary. [Note: Thus in MS S. T. But MS S. G. reads: “but when the tearing, as stated above, had occurred.” The meaning is the same in each.] Yet the craftsman or worker in this task, wishing to restore the garment to its former appearance, pierces the neighbouring threads. Does the tailor displease you because, in healing the tear, he wounds? He should displease you more [Note: This word is absent from MSS S. T. and P. S.] who caused the tailor to be able to offend. The things which you say were done to you by the workers for unity either concern your forefathers, on whose account they were done, or proceed from the will of God. We, however, [Note: MS S. T. reads “nevertheless.”] are strangers to them.

[Col. 1021A] X. The harsh measures taken against the Donatists were taken by the will of God, who threatened them through Ezekiel against false prophets.—What if, though harsh, they nevertheless appear to have been done, as we have said, [Note: MS S. T. reads “as I said.”] by the will of God? For in the prophet Ezekiel we read of a whitewashed wall, against which God [Note: “Who threatened a storm,” etc. The term “accusations,” which Optatus repeatedly uses here as if from the prophet, has no trace either in the extracts he gives from him or in the whole chapter of Ezekiel as it is now read. Yet the Greeks translated the Hebrew—at least so it is read today—as *καὶ πεσεῖται καὶ συντελεσθήσεται μετ’ ἐλέγχων* (“and it shall fall and be brought to an end with rebukes”), from which perhaps Optatus, or rather the interpreter whom he followed, derived it. The remaining matters from the same chapter, despite their great variation, will become clearer if compared with the Greek. But we have already noted this more than once and need not continually repeat it. We have also noted that Optatus sometimes inserts some of his own words among the words of Scripture, as shortly: “They are not the things I say, concerning mud or a wall,” which he himself supplies, as it were. What follows—“consider to which party the word ‘lead astray’ applies”—must be understood thus: from this word alone infer to which party the whole remaining passage applies; otherwise he should have said “this word.” Again, a little earlier, where the text has “but from its foundations it again repaired itself,” I would prefer with other editions: “but from its foundations,” etc. M. Casaubon.] threatened storm, rain, [Note: “Stones, *petrovolos*”: that is, *petrobolos*, stone-casting. Elsewhere too, in this word and others, *v* is put in place of *b*: *Savinus* for *Sabinus*, *Thevestina civitas* for *Thebestina*, and perhaps above *veneficium* for *beneficium*. UNCERTAIN.] stone-casting stones, and accusations:

“There shall be false prophets who build a crumbling wall, saying, ‘Peace, peace’; and where is peace?” (Ezek. 13:10).

Remember how, long ago, the members of Mother Church were torn apart from one another by you. [Note: “The members of the Church were destroyed from one another.” Read *distracta*, “torn apart,” as in the second edition of François Balduin. UNCERTAIN. Thus restored. “The members of the Church were torn apart from one another.” Read preferably *distracta sunt*, “were torn apart from one another,” a phrase which we shall elucidate later in these books. Acute is the observation concerning false sheepfolds below: “whoever enters is outside,” and again, “the enclosed house protects,” etc. The conveniences of a house are these: to protect those enclosed, to keep rain from bodies, and by fortified walls to prevent robbers, wild animals, and thieves from breaking in. The latter are called wall-breakers as a customary insult in Aristophanes and Plautus. Therefore our conjecture is entirely correct that the sense here requires *defendere*, “to ward off,” rather than *diffundere*, “to shed.” Then a very learned man published our notes, corrected according to Balduin’s second edition, with Optatus for the printer’s benefit, while sometimes, as though grieving, he sprinkled us with critical vinegar. Having read in Martial that a certain kind of roof tile was said to shed rain, he concluded from that passage that our conjecture ought to be corrected. But this is irrelevant. Optatus speaks of the general very purpose of covering a house; Martial, as I said, speaks of a particular kind of tile designed to discharge collected rain at a certain point. Martial’s words, Book V:

> When the villa refused to bear the rains and dripping Jove,  
> And, unskilled, swam in winter waters,  
> A roof tile, able to discharge very many sudden storms,  
> Came as a gift sent by you.

But *defendere* means “to ward off.” See the commentator on Horace, Book I, Ode 17; Nonius, chapter 4; and our frequent notes on Claudian. Barth.]

For you could not mislead every household at once. Either the wife departed and the husband remained, or the parents were led astray and the children refused to follow; or the brother stood firm while his sister departed. [Col. 1021B] By your persuasions both bodies and the names of piety were divided, and you could not omit [67] what is lawful. [Note: “What is lawful.” When the Donatists went through households to corrupt the simple, they did not omit the customary form of greeting commonly used among Christians, saying, “Peace to this house”; therefore the Prophet’s passage applied to them. Albaspinaeus.]

Certainly you said, “Peace be with you,” while God says in reply, “Peace—and where is peace?” That is to say: Why do you greet someone with what you do not possess? Why do you name what you have destroyed? You offer a greeting of peace, though you do not love peace. [Note: These words, absent from the other manuscripts, have been supplied from MS S. G.]

“These,” he says, “build a crumbling wall.” God’s house is one. Those who, in going outside, wished to make a part, made a wall, not a house, [Col. 1022A] because there is not another God to inhabit another house. Therefore false prophets are said to have made a wall; and if a door is set in it, whoever enters it is outside. [Note: “Whoever enters is outside.” A keen and elegant saying concerning false sheepfolds. UNCERTAIN.]

Nor can one wall possess the cornerstone, which stone is Christ, receiving into himself two peoples, one from the Gentiles and the other from the Jews, and joining the two walls by the bond of peace. For as many advantages as a house possesses, so many disadvantages a wall has. [Note: “The enclosed house protects, sheds rain.” Barth’s correction, “wards off rain,” so that *defendere* means “to keep off,” is less necessary here. For Martial had spoken similarly before Optatus: “A roof tile able to discharge very many sudden storms came as a gift sent by you.” UNCERTAIN.]

An enclosed house protects, breaks the force of a storm, [Note: These words are absent from MS S. T.] sheds rain, and admits neither robber nor wild beast. [Note: MSS S. T. and P. S., as well as printed editions, read “or thief or beast”; but “thief” is superfluous, since he has already mentioned a robber.] So also the Catholic Church embraces all children of peace in her lap and bosom. By contrast, the crumbling wall that has been built neither supports the cornerstone nor has a door for any purpose nor protects what is enclosed. It is soaked by rain and battered by storms; [Col. 1022B] it cannot ward off a robber or prevent approaching savagery. [Note: MSS S. T. and Ph. S. read “a thief.”]

A wall comes from a house, [Note: MS S. G. reads: “A wall is a thing from a house.”] but is not a house; and your party is, as it were, a Church, but not Catholic. “And they whitewash it,” he says: that is, you judge yourselves alone to be holy. You complain that you suffered certain things without us; it follows that you alone suffered certain things. For the time of peace is one thing, the time of persecution another. If you regard it as persecution, say what the universal provinces suffered with you, [Col. 1023A] provinces in which the Catholic Church is established. But because it was vengeance, not persecution, the wall alone suffered—the wall against which God threatened storm, rain, stone-casting stones, and accusations.

For he spoke thus: “Why have you built ruin? Why have you whitewashed? Why have you plastered? This is against my will, says the Lord.” You dislike the times of some Leontius, Ursacius, Macarius, and the rest. Correct the will of God, if you can—of him who said: “I will rise up against the wall in my wrath, and will send an excessive storm and rain, floods, and stone-casting stones; and I will strike the crumbling wall, and its joints shall be dissolved” (Ezek. 13:13).

But lest any of you say, “If unity is good, why could it not endure despite having been achieved so often?”—it is because the matter itself was so ordered by God, [Col. 1023B] who threatened storm, rain, stones, and accusations; and these four things could not happen at one time. First there was a storm under Ursacius; [Note: The three phrases “under Ursacius,” “under Gregory,” and “under the workers for unity” occur only in MS S. G.] the wall was shaken but did not fall, [Note: Read, with the second edition of François Balduin: “so that the rain might have somewhere to work.” UNCERTAIN.] so that the rain might have somewhere to work. [Note: “So that the rain may have where it works.” I conjectured that it should read: “so that the rain might have somewhere to work,” and the second edition of F. Balduin confirmed the same text. [Col. 1023D] Barth. Thus restored.]

Rain followed under Gregory; [Note: The three phrases “under Ursacius,” “under Gregory,” and “under the workers for unity” occur only in MS S. G.] the wall was wetted but not soaked through, so that the stones might have somewhere to work. After the rain came stones under the workers for unity; [Note: The three phrases “under Ursacius,” “under Gregory,” and “under the workers for unity” occur only in MS S. G.] the wall was scattered, but from its foundations it repaired itself again. Three things have now been accomplished; accusations are due to you—but how and when, he knows, who was pleased to foretell these things concerning you.

XI. It Is Shown That the Donatists Are Seducers. — And lest anyone should doubt this interpretation, God added, saying: “What I say is not about mud, or brick, or a wall, but about false prophets who lead my people astray” [Col. 1023C]. This word, “lead astray”—see to which party it applies.

> “See to which party it applies.” This is indeed how it should be read, for *videre* (“to see”) was printed erroneously. — Uncertain note.

We were all together; when we were absent, you broke in.

> MS S. G.: “you burst forth.”

But, in order to have those whom you desired to possess [Col. 1024A], you could not do so except by seducing them; and what the words of your seduction are is known to all.

> MS S. G.: “and what are the words of your seduction.”

It is yours to say, “Look behind you”; it is yours to say, “Redeem your souls”; it is yours to say to faithful people and clerics, “Become Christians.”

> “Clerics, become Christians.” They rejected the baptism of the orthodox. — Albaspinaeus.

But when you say, “Look behind you,” you act contrary to the Gospel, where it is said: “No one who holds the handle of the plough and looks behind him will enter the kingdoms of heaven” (Luke 9:62). And do you wish to know what the one who looked behind him deserved, and what the one who looked before him deserved? Remember the fugitives from Sodom, Lot and his wife.

> MS S. G. adds: “Molassadon” [uncertain].

She, looking behind herself, was changed into a pillar of salt (Gen. 19); he, looking before himself, escaped. What then is this that you say, “Look behind you”?

And when you say, “Redeem your souls,” from where did you buy them, that you may sell them?

> “What unknown angel?” Certainly an evil one, that is, the devil, who is immediately said to have possessed souls not yet redeemed by Christ. Perhaps this refers to Christ, who redeemed us and is the Angel of the Covenant (Malachi 3); or to heretics who maintained that angels were creators of souls. Augustine teaches that there were such heretics when discussing the Selencians or Hermians, though I do not think that point relevant here. — M. Casaubon.

Who is that unknown angel [Col. 1024B] who holds a market in souls, which the devil possessed before his coming?

> MSS S. T. and P. S.: “Who is some unknown angel?” MS S. G.: “Who is that angel?” We have judged that both readings should be joined.

> “Holds a market in souls.” He elegantly calls it a sale; I recall Nazianzenus using the expression *πανήγυριν τοῦ βίου*, “a market-fair of life.” — Barthius.

Christ our Savior redeemed them with his own blood, as the Apostle says: “For you were bought at a great price.” For it is established that all were redeemed by the blood of Christ. Christ did not sell those whom he redeemed. Souls bought by Christ could not be sold.

> MS S. G.: “disposed of.”

Thus, as you wish, they could not again be redeemed by you. Or how can one soul have two masters? Or is there another redeemer, whom the prophets announced would come?

> MS S. G.: “Christ.”

To what other Mary did Gabriel again speak? What virgin bore a child again? Who performed new or second miracles? If there is none besides the one who redeemed the souls of all believers, what is this that you say: “Redeem your souls”?

And what sort of thing is it that you say even to Christian people and clerics [Col. 1024C], “Become Christians”? And, with a certain air of astonishment, you dare say to each person, “Gaius Seius, Gaia Seia”—

> MSS S. T. and P. S.: *admiraculo*, “with amazement.”

> Three manuscripts: “Gaiseius, Gaiaseia.”

> “Gaius Seius, Gaia Seia.” François Balduin printed the passage more fully: “Gaius Seius, or Gaia Seia, are you still a pagan man or a pagan woman?” The passage beginning here—“He did not ask that which ordinary human custom always asks, concerning rains, peace,” etc.—which occupies the following twelve continuous pages and ends with the words “Elijah took vengeance; Phinehas took vengeance,” is found in an unsuitable place and must be referred to page 58, line 22, as we have noted there. Once these matters have been transferred to their proper place, the discourse should then be continued as follows: “And, with a certain air of astonishment, you say to each person, ‘Gaius Seius, or Gaia Seia, are you still a pagan man or a pagan woman?’ Do you call a pagan one who has professed himself converted to God?” etc. — Uncertain note.

“Are you still a pagan man, or a pagan woman?”

> “Gaius Seius, Gaia Seia.” These are common names used generically for “this man” and “that woman.” Thus Tertullian in the *Apology* mentions the common saying about a Christian: “Gaius Seius is a good man.” Augustine reports a similar address by Donatists to Catholics, *On Baptism*, book II, chapter 7: “You would be a good man if you were not a traitor; look to your soul; become a Christian.” To this Optatus exclaims likewise: “O shameless madness, when a Christian is told, ‘Become a Christian’! What else is said than ‘Deny that you are a Christian’?” Or, as the later edition has it: “What else is taught than to deny oneself to be a Christian?” — Du Pin.

You call a pagan one who has professed himself converted to God [Col. 1025A]; you call a pagan one who has been baptized, whether by us or by you, not in our name or yours, but in the name of Christ.

> “For there are those baptized by you.” They called pagans not only those baptized by the orthodox, but also those who, after receiving baptism from the Donatists, passed into communion with the orthodox. — Albaspinaeus.

For there are people baptized by you who afterward passed into our communion.

> MS S. G.: “who did not at all depart from our communion, and whom you call pagans in order to seduce them.”

You call a pagan one who has prayed to God the Father through his Son before the altar.

> “Who prayed to God before the altar.” Catechumens did not pray before the altar, nor did they call God “Father”; this was permitted only to the faithful. — Albaspinaeus.

> These words are absent from MS S. G. MS S. T. has *horam* (“hour”) in place of *aram* (“altar”), an intrusion.

For whoever has believed has believed in the name of the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit; and you call him a pagan after his profession of faith. If any Christian should sin—which God forbid—

> MS S. T.: “If any Christian whatsoever should sin—which God forbid.”

—he may be called a sinner.

> “May be called a sinner.” Whoever sins after baptism may be called a sinner, but not a pagan. — Albaspinaeus.

He cannot become a pagan again. But you wish all these things to be of no consequence. Yet if the person whom you seduce agrees with you, one act of assent, the extending of your hand, and a few words already make him, for you, a Christian out of a Christian [Col. 1025B]; and the person who has done what you wish seems to you a Christian, not the person whom faith has brought.

> “The extending of your hand.” These words seem to concern absolution, and he is speaking of those baptized among the Donatists—unless one says that the words “if he agrees with you” refer to those baptized among the orthodox. — Albaspinaeus.

> “A few words.” Prayer followed the laying on of hands. — Albaspinaeus.

> “A Christian out of a Christian.” The ancients did not value a sinner, before he had been granted repentance, more highly than a heathen; they regarded him as not being a Christian. Tertullian, *On Modesty*: “A second repentance will receive you; from an adulterer you will again become a Christian.” Accordingly, these words may be referred both to penitents and to the rebaptized. — Albaspinaeus.

> Here book III ends in MS S. G.; what follows appears in book VII. In MSS S. T. and P. S., the following passage down to the words “But let us return to what was said a little earlier” occurs here and is repeated in book VII. Yet it belongs to this book and has the same subject as the preceding material with which it is connected, although it also appears in book VII in the Colbert manuscript.

XII. A Calumny Invented against Macarius. — And if assent to your seduction has been given somewhat slowly, you also lack none of those arguments by which you may, as it were, easily persuade even unwilling persons to do what you want [Col. 1026A].

> MS C., MS S. T. in book VII, and MS S. G.: “by which, as it were, easily.” MS S. T. here: “by which how easily”; printed editions: “by which easily.”

For you say that it was said from the mouths of those who had long since belonged to your association: that whoever tasted or received anything from the sacrifice of the approaching unity would seem to taste of a sacred thing.

> “The sacrifice of the approaching unity”: the sacrifice of the Eucharist celebrated by the presbyters of Macarius. — Albaspinaeus.

> MS C.: “the unity approaching.”

> “Of a sacred thing”: foods offered in the sacrifices of the gods. — Albaspinaeus.

We do not deny that these things were said by some who afterward, with complete confidence, did what they had previously frightened the people from doing.

> “Did.” That is, they attended Mass and received the Eucharist. — Albaspinaeus.

But one reason demanded these words; another led them to the deed.

> “Another reason.” This is explained afterward, namely, the matter of the image. — Albaspinaeus.

> MS S. G., MS S. T. in book VII, and MS P. S. read *exegit*, “demanded.” MS C. and MS S. T. here read *exigit*, “demands,” but *exegit* should be read.

For, in order that those who are reported to have said these things might say them, a false rumor had filled their ears and those of all the people.

> MSS S. G. and C.: *compleverat*, “had filled.” MSS S. T. and P. S.: *oppleverat*, “had filled up.”

For it was said at that time that Paul and Macarius would come and attend the sacrifice; that, when the altars had been solemnly prepared, they would bring forth an image and place it first upon the altar, and then the sacrifice would be offered.

> “The altars were solemnly prepared.” Observe how the altars were solemnly made ready when a sacrifice was to be celebrated. — Albaspinaeus.

> “They would bring forth an image.” Baronius also interprets this passage as referring to imperial standards (*labara*) in the *Annals*, though he adduces nothing beyond what Balduin gives in his notes. Anyone desiring fuller information on these matters, whether concerning the rite or the term—and information certainly as worthy of knowing as any—should consult Claudius Salmasius, the singular glory of his age, in his work on the writers of the *Augustan History*. There is also a whole chapter on the same topic in Charlemagne’s *Against Images*, book III, chapter 15, whose heading is: “Against those who say that, when imperial images and effigies sent into cities and provinces are met by peoples with candles and incense, they honor not the wax-covered panel, but the emperor,” etc. — M. Casaubon.

> MSS C., S. T. in book VII, and S. G. read “they would bring forth an image.” MS S. T. here and MS P. S. read “there.”

> “They would bring forth an image”: namely, an image of the emperor. Pagan emperors customarily sent their images or statues into provinces and cities, and the peoples received and venerated them religiously. Christian emperors abolished this practice. To inspire horror of the sacred rites celebrated by Catholics, the Donatists alleged that an effigy of the emperor Constans was customarily placed on their altars while the sacrifice was celebrated—nothing could have been conceived as more odious among Christians. — Du Pin.

> “Which they would first place upon the altar.” Others understand it as an image of God. — Albaspinaeus.

> MSS C., S. T. in book VII, and S. G. read “and thus.” MS S. T. here reads “there,” and MS P. S. “thus.”

When their ears received this report, their minds too were struck [Col. 1026B], and everyone’s tongue was moved to these words, so that all who heard it said:

> MS C.: “Whoever hears this would say.”

“Whoever tastes from it tastes of a sacred thing.”

> “Whoever tastes from it.” Whoever tasted of the Eucharist offered upon the altar on which that image had been placed. — Albaspinaeus.

And this was rightly said, if a corresponding truth had followed such a rumor. But when the aforesaid persons arrived, nothing of the kind was seen; nothing that Christian eyes could dread was seen from what false rumor had previously alleged; sight approved none of those things by which hearing had been disturbed [Col. 1027A].

> We have deleted the particle *et* (“and”), which appears in MSS S. T. and P. S. but not in MSS C. and S. G., because it is superfluous.

Purity was seen, and the customary solemn practice was seen in its usual rite.

> MS S. T. in book VII and MS P. S.: “was completed.”

They saw that in the divine sacrifices nothing had been changed, added, or taken away.

> “The customary rite”: the rite of Christians. — Albaspinaeus.

The peace commended by God was pleasing to those who desired it; therefore none of those who passed from your association to peace ought to be accused. Those who had been disturbed by a hostile opinion were strengthened by simple and pure truth.

> “Peace commended by God,” etc. He alludes to the Gospel words he already cited above: “peace on earth to people of good will” (Luke 2:14). Optatus expressed “people of good will” in the more Latin form *volentes*, “those willing,” rather than the Hebraic expression; he did not have that Hebraism in mind. Those who explain it otherwise are therefore mistaken. Yet the learned interpreter not only praises this reading of the ancients and of the Vulgate even today, but declares himself ready to adopt it in his commentaries. — Albaspinaeus.
