> “Was pleasing to those who desired it”: to those who loved it, desired it. In ancient usage *volens* may mean a friend, one who desires, or one who is well-disposed. Virgil: “to give laws to a willing people,” that is, to an obedient people; Sallust: “alike willing, alike friendly.” — Albaspinaeus.

> MSS C. and S. G.: “a hostile opinion.” MS S. T. here: “this hostile opinion”; in book VII, “of the hostile party,” as also in MS P. S.

Nor should it be said that sweet was made from bitter, or bitter from sweet. The bitterness which had been reported through falsehood remained and stayed within the bosom of opinion [Col. 1028A].

> MSS C., S. G., S. T., and P. S. in book VII read “remained and stayed.” MSS S. T. and P. S. here read either “the saying remained” or “the seduction remained.”

The truth perceived by the eyes, containing its own sweetness within itself, was separated from the boundaries of false opinion. Therefore neither was sweet made from bitter, nor bitter from sweet, because what was seen was both other and outside, and far removed from what had been heard.

> “Because what was seen was both other and outside,” etc. I do not think Optatus means anything else by these words than what he might have said more plainly and commonly: that what was seen was altogether different from what had been heard. If, however, anyone wishes to extract something subtler from “outside,” because he first said that truth possesses its own sweetness within itself, I do not forbid it.

> Much more important is this: although everyone hitherto has placed the end of book III at these words, I have discovered, by comparing editions—as Albaspinaeus also noted—that much more is missing. It is wholly absent from Balduin’s second and better edition. Whether he did so deliberately or by accident cannot be sufficiently determined from his words. He says that he deleted what had been rashly repeated in book VII from book III concerning the case of Macarius. This would indeed have been rightly done if he had deleted only as much as had been rashly repeated and already stood in its proper place, but had transferred what was redundant in an improper place and lacking in its proper place. But there was no reason why he should delete anything altogether, so that a substantial part of the material wrongly carried over from book III into book VII should appear nowhere, neither in book III nor in book VII; and I scarcely think, whatever the accident, that this was done knowingly and prudently by him. For if he rejected it as spurious, he ought at least to have warned the reader and stated the reasons for so severe a judgment. But what reasons could anyone offer for suspecting it of being spurious? None at all, so far as I know.

> The reason why the whole of book VII was once suspected was that Jerome, in the *Catalogue*, mentions only six books of Optatus. Optatus himself, moreover, in book I, where he sets out the subjects of the individual books, mentions no more than six. Yet Optatus himself explains at the beginning of book VII why he was compelled to write more than he originally intended; thus this argument has no force at all. As for Jerome’s mentioning only six, I too am persuaded that there were no more; and what we now call the seventh was merely an appendix to the sixth and final book. For at its beginning he himself immediately predicts that he will add only a little. Nevertheless, once this appendix or addition grew to a bulk equal to, indeed greater than, some of the earlier books, I believe this is why it acquired the name of a book itself.

> Yet even this is of no great importance, whether we call it a book or an appendix to a book, provided it is agreed to be by Optatus; and I think no one who has read Optatus attentively and compared both works carefully will doubt this. Especially since there was no motive why anyone should invent it and deceive, falsely not merely in name—which might easily happen—but in style and in an imitation of the language pursued with such care and skill—which was not equally easy. For as to the Donatists, whom we might not unreasonably suspect alone, there is nothing here from which they could profit or by which they could support their case; throughout the entire book there is nothing that could have proceeded from them. Who in his right mind would suspect them? And if not them, much less anyone else, to whom it mattered far less.

> Therefore, since even Balduin attributed book VII to Optatus, there was no reason to reject this little excerpt (*ἀποσπάσματιον*, “small extract”) from book III as rashly stitched onto book VII. It ought not, then, to have been omitted altogether. Yet, because we promised to present Balduin’s edition, we preferred to insert in our notes what that edition wrongly omitted. — M. Casaubon.

> Here book III ends in MSS S. T. and P. S. What followed in the printed editions—“But let us return to what was said a little earlier,” etc., ending with “you cannot condemn our judgment”—is found in book VII in all the manuscripts. Since, however, it concerns the subject of this third book and is, as it were, its appendix, it was added here in the printed editions. Yet it does not seem to belong to this book: for the author treats the case of Macarius differently from the preceding discussion and refutes a new Donatist argument, assuming Macarius—whom in book III he had defended—not to be innocent. Therefore, following the authority of the manuscripts, we have relegated this passage to book VII, which contains additions of this sort. Here, however, we have added the conclusion of this book, which stood severed from its proper place at the end of book IV in MSS S. G. and P. S.: “Therefore you see,” etc.

Therefore you see that you uttered reproach without cause, inventing at your pleasure what you wished in order to tear Macarius and Taurinus to pieces. You lost the appearance of wisdom when envy corrupted your understanding and closed to you the avenues of comprehension.

> MS S. G.: “hearing.”

> At the end of book III the manuscripts customarily have: “Book III ends”; and MS S. G. adds: “of Saint Optatus.”

## BOOK FOUR

In this fourth volume, by God’s judgment it is shown who are sinners at this time; that God is angry through the prophet Jeremiah with the Jews, not with Christians; and that the broken cisterns are idols, not Macarius or Taurinus, as Parmenian thought.

[Col. 1029]

### I. The Argument of This Book

It has been openly and clearly shown, brother Parmenian [Col. 1029A], that you vainly fabricated against us a calumny concerning the requested soldier.

> MS S. T.: “brother to us.”

> “The soldier.” In the third book he dealt with the unity brought about through Macarius. — Albaspinaeus.

Learn also that what you said about the oil and sacrifice of a sinner applies rather to you; for he ought not to be a sinner whom you choose to make one. We too can imitate your presumption and say that you are sinners.

> “Presumption.” The Donatists boasted that they were holy and made the efficacy of the sacraments depend upon their holiness. — Albaspinaeus.

But let presumption depart from both sides.

> This passage has been restored from MS S. G. MSS S. T. and P. S., and likewise the printed editions, quite wrongly read: “make [it depart] from both sides.”

Let none of us condemn the other by human judgment. It belongs to God to know who is guilty and to pronounce judgment.

> “It belongs to God to know the guilty party, to him to pronounce judgment.” Remove the typographical error and read, with François Balduin’s edition, *nosse rerum* (“to know matters” [reading uncertain]). — Uncertain note.

> MS S. G.: “it belongs to the judge to pronounce judgment.”

Let all human beings be silent; let God alone declare who is the sinner, whose sacrifice is a canine offering and whose oil causes fear in one who desires anointing.

> “Canine offering.” Shortly afterward: “as though he sacrificed a dog.” — Albaspinaeus. Optatus refers to the law found in Deuteronomy 23:18: “You shall not offer the price of a dog in the house of the Lord your God,” although it seems better understood of a male prostitute than of a dog. — Clericus.

> “Causes fear.” The oil of sinners instills fear, but God’s oil exultation. — Albaspinaeus.

> MS S. G.: “whose oil appears to be feared.”

### II. The Donatists Are Brothers of the Catholics

Parmenian, brother, acknowledge the most manifest truth of this matter [Col. 1029B]. If indeed you deign willingly to hear this name of brotherhood, so frequently uttered by me, make it burdensome to yourself; nevertheless, it is necessary for us, lest by keeping silent about the matter we seem guilty under the evidence of this name.

> MS S. G.: “so many proofs.”

For if you do not wish to be a brother, I begin to be impious if I keep silent about this name. For you are our brothers, and we are yours, as the prophet says: “Has not one God created you? Has not one Father begotten you?” (Mal. 2:10).

For you cannot fail to be brothers, since it was said to all: “You are gods, and all of you sons of the Most High” (Ps. 81:6). Both you and we received the one command in which it was said: “Call no one your father on earth, for one is your Father in heaven” (Matt. 23:9). Christ our Savior alone was born the Son of God; but both we and you have been made sons of God in one manner, as it is written in the Gospel [Col. 1029C]: “The Son of God came; to all who received him he gave power to become sons of God, to those who believe in his name” (John 1:2).

Both we have been made sons and are called sons; you have been made sons but are not called sons, because you refuse to be peacemakers and refuse to hear the Son of God himself saying: “Blessed are the peacemakers, because they shall be called sons of God” (Matt. 5:9).

> “Have been made and are called.” Schismatics have been made brothers, but are not called brothers, because they have been torn away from their mother’s breasts. — Albaspinaeus.

Christ, by coming, restored God and man to peace: “And he made both one, removing the middle barrier of the wall” (Eph. 2:13). You do not wish to have peace with us—that is, with your brothers. For you cannot fail to be brothers, whom the one mother, the Church, bore from the same sacramental womb, and whom God the Father received alike as adopted sons.

Therefore Christ, foreknowing this age, because you would today be at variance with us, gave such commands for prayer that unity might remain even in prayer [Col. 1030B], so that prayers might join those whose parties were destined to differ.

> “That unity might remain even in prayer.” Unity remains in the Lord’s Prayer because, when we say “Our Father,” we make mention of all those who have the same Father and communicate with them; therefore unity and brotherhood remain in that prayer. Then we pray for you, because when we say “Forgive us,” we understand all who derive their origin from the same Father and have been made Christians. — Albaspinaeus.

> “That prayers might join those whose parties were destined to differ.” The verb *discrepare* is here used in the active sense. — Uncertain note.

> MS S. G.: “the walls were destined to be divided.”

We pray for you because we wish to do so; and you pray for us even when you do not wish to do so. Or let each of you say: “My Father, who art in heaven, give me today my daily bread, and forgive me my sins as I forgive my debtor.” Therefore, if the commands that have been given cannot be changed, you see that we are not wholly separated from one another: we pray for you willingly, and you pray for us, though unwillingly. You see, brother Parmenian, that the bonds of holy brotherhood between us and you cannot be entirely broken.

> MSS S. T. and P. S., and the printed editions, read “holy twinship,” less well.

### III. That the Donatists Are Sinners

Now the sinner must be sought whose oil could be feared or whose sacrifice rejected.

> “Whose oil might be feared.” For Scripture says: “May the oil of the sinner not anoint my head.” — Albaspinaeus.

Let human suspicion cease, and let the presumption of either party be silent; let God alone declare who is the sinner. We read in Psalm 49, under the second *diapsalma* [Col. 1031A], that the Holy Spirit said: “But God said to the sinner” (Ps. 49:16). At this point the whole attention of the mind must be applied, and we must see who the sinner is.

> “In Psalm 49, etc.” What is *Selah* in Hebrew, the Greeks generally render *διάψαλμα* (*diapsalma*). Many believed it marked, as it were, the beginning of another sense, as Jerome testifies; Augustine on Psalm 4 and others likewise attest this. Hence it is sometimes used for a section of a psalm, even though the whole psalm contains no *Selah* or *diapsalma*. Learned men attest, however, that *diapsalma* is still found here in certain copies. Since another one had already occurred in verse 6—for it ought not be removed, since it is also in Hebrew—perhaps this is why Optatus says “here, under the second,” etc. — M. Casaubon.

If, after the words that have been read, “But God said to the sinner,” words of this sort followed, and he said: “You took up arms, marched forth from camp, stood against the enemy in battle array,” the soldier would need to fear, because he himself might appear to be the sinner.

> “If after what has been selected,” etc. For *electum*, Barthius prefers *delectum*, “chosen.” There is a difference between saying that a soldier is *deligi* (“selected”) and *eligi* (“elected”); the former is the customary word for this matter, whereas the latter is not casually found of soldiers. François Balduin printed: “if after what has been read.” — Uncertain note.

Or if he said: “You bought wares, traveled abroad, conducted trade, and for profit sold what you had bought,” the merchant would need to fear, because he himself might appear to be the sinner. Or if he said: “You built a ship, rigged it with ropes, equipped it with sails, and sought favorable winds for sailing,” the sailor would need to fear, because he himself might appear to be the sinner.

> “The sailor would need to fear.” Read *nautae*, “the sailor,” as the sense requires and as fidelity in the same book enjoins [wording uncertain]. For *naturae*, “nature,” has indeed been printed here monstrously. — Uncertain note.

Or if, after the words read, “But God said to the sinner” [Col. 1031B], these words followed: “Dissension and schism displeased you; you came into agreement with your brother and with the one Church which is throughout the whole world; you communicated with the seven churches and with the memorial-shrines of the apostles; you embraced unity”—if the ensuing passage contained this, we would need to fear, for we might be sinners.

> “You communicated with the seven churches”: with the Christians of Asia. — Albaspinaeus.

> “And with the memorial-shrines of the apostles”: with the relics of the blessed Peter and Paul; such communion is necessary for someone to be in Christian unity. — Albaspinaeus.

But when God says: “Why do you recite my statutes and take my covenant upon your lips? Yet you despised discipline and cast my words behind you. Sitting against your brother, you slandered him, and against the son of your mother you set a stumbling-block. You saw a thief and ran with him, and placed your portion with adulterers” (Ps. 49:16), all these things are said to you. Clear yourselves of them all, if you can.

### IV. The Donatists, Despisers of Discipline

For discipline has been despised by you [Col. 1032A]. Why do you recite the Covenant, you who do not serve the Covenant, in which the discipline that you refuse to keep is described? For you cannot say that you observe that against which you wage war.

> MSS S. T. and P. S.: “have observed.”

God says: “Seek peace, and pursue it” (Ps. 33:15); you rejected peace: is this not despising discipline?

> “You rejected peace,” etc. Earlier editions contain the fuller complete period: “In the Gospel we read: ‘Peace to people of good will on earth.’ You wish to have neither good will nor peace: is that not despising discipline? Likewise in the Psalm,” etc. There is no doubt that it belongs to Optatus, nor is it difficult to conjecture why it was omitted. — M. Casaubon.

> MS S. G.: “This surely is despising discipline?” The same reading continues thereafter.

In the Gospel we read: “Peace to people of good will on earth” (Luke 2:14); you wish to have neither good will nor peace: is this not despising discipline?

> “In the Gospel we read.” We add these words from the German edition—and rightly, unless I am mistaken. — Albaspinaeus. Likewise, in Psalm 132 it is read: “Behold how good and pleasant it is to dwell together as one.” You do not wish to dwell as one with your brothers: is this not despising discipline? Christ says in the Gospel: “He who has been washed once has no need to be washed again” (John 13:10); you wash again by rebaptizing: is this not despising discipline? God says: “Do not touch my anointed ones, nor lay hands upon my prophets” (Ps. 104:15); you stripped so many priests of God of their honors: is this not despising discipline?

> “You stripped them of their honors.” Without cause and without crime you depose bishops; this was no less a crime than compelling an innocent person to do penance, for in either case a person is deprived of the rank and place that he had in Christ’s body. Add from Saint Cyprian that the episcopate is a divine honor: “joined in fellowship of divine honor,” *Letter* 5, book IV. — Albaspinaeus.

Christ says: “By this I know that you are my disciples: if you love one another” (John 13:34). You hate us, who are surely your brothers; nor did you wish to imitate the apostles, by whom even Peter, though he denied, was loved. Is this not despising discipline? You expound God’s ordinances and take his Covenant upon your lips; you recite the Covenant and do not serve the Covenant, in which discipline is described. How do you say, “Seek peace,” when you do not have peace?

### V. The Donatists: Slanderers, Detractors, and Authors of Scandals

[Note: “You have been elected, who, sitting …” Read rather: “You have been read,” meaning, “It has been written concerning you,” or something similar. For *lectum* (“read”) is used for *scriptum* (“written”) when passages from sacred writers are cited; and *lectio*, pre-eminently, for any section or pericope of Holy Scripture (which Tertullian and others call a *capitulum*), is so frequent in these and similar books that nothing could be more common. It is well known and familiar what many explain as *mikra* in Nehemiah 8:8, or what Hebrew teachers commonly denote by that term. By the same reasoning, many have supposed that the Koran is so called. But Thomas Erpenius—at whose premature death Oriental learning suffered as great a loss as any branch of learning ever suffered at the death of one man—observed, in his notes on the history of Joseph the Patriarch, that the most learned Arabs disagree and derive it from another meaning, though of the same root. The most learned Salmasius, in his admirable work, *Exercises on Pliny*, not only approves this view but confirms it by Greek testimonies so decisively that the matter ought no longer to be disputed. But since I have happened here to mention that admirable work, I should be ungrateful unless, in this very place, I offered most heartfelt thanks to its author, a most gracious man and one highly deserving of the entire republic of letters, through whose kindness I have become possessed of so great a treasure.

But to return to Optatus: just as here *electi* stands for *lecti*, even in this excellent edition, so in earlier editions, through the same error, *electum* was printed for *lectum*. For where, a page or two earlier, Optatus says, “For if after it has been read,” the earlier and final Balduinian editions gave, “For if after it has been elected.” Because something follows concerning soldiers, some wished in that place to emend *electum* into *delectum* (“a levy”), and invent extraordinary notions about the enlistment of soldiers. We could very well have dispensed with their absurdities, if N. L. and the Parisian printers had permitted it.

Moreover, Optatus’s words, “You have been read, who, sitting, teach the people,” should not be understood as though this very wording had been written concerning them. In his usual manner, he supplements and interpolates the words of Scripture, adapting them to his purpose—as if saying: “You have been read, you who, sitting”—that is, whenever you teach the people; you preach, which you certainly do sitting, according to the custom of expositors—“you slander us,” etc. M. Casaubon.]

“You have been read, you who, sitting, teach the people,” [Note: “You have been read, you who, sitting, teach the people.” For, as Optatus has just said, the people in church do not have permission to sit. This was granted only to bishops, who taught the people, in African churches—as Augustine also teaches, besides Optatus, in Book 1 of the *Homilies*, Homily 26; Tractates 19 and 112 on John; the exposition of Psalm 147; and frequently elsewhere.

Nevertheless, a different custom prevailed in certain overseas churches, as we learn from the same Augustine, *On Instructing Beginners*, ch. 13. There he advises those who teach others sometimes to relieve them by offering seats, although, he says, “Undoubtedly it is better, where this can be done appropriately, that the hearer should listen sitting from the beginning; and in certain overseas churches it is far more expedient: not only do bishops speak to the people sitting, but seats are also provided for the people themselves.” Thus at least some overseas churches observed one custom, African churches another: in the former, not only did bishops sit when speaking, but the hearers did also; in the latter, by contrast, only the bishops sat when addressing the people, while the people listened standing.

Yet St Augustine, in the twenty-sixth homily cited above, testifies that, for the sake of those whose feet hurt or who suffered some bodily infirmity, he advised and in a way begged that, whenever either lengthy accounts of sufferings or certain longer readings were being read, those unable to stand should humbly and silently sit and listen attentively to what was read. Du Pin.]

and yet you slander us, who are surely your brothers. For, as I said above, one mother, the Church, bore us, and one God the Father received us; yet you set scandals against us, instructing each person:

[Note: “That they should not greet us.” In former times Christians greeted one another with a kiss at home, in the streets, and in church. Albaspinaeus.

Ibid. “That they should not greet us”: that they should not receive a mark of courtesy from us. There is no need to explain what *dignatio* once meant; among writers of the later age and of declining Latin it is commonly understood as kindness or affability. Thus the prince of ancient and genuine eloquence said: “He who surpasses princes in dignity seems the equal of the humblest in affability.” Sidonius Apollinaris expressed it thus: “Distinguished in dignity, common in condescension.” Book I, Letter 9; and Book III, Letter 7, to Pope or Bishop Fontelus: “Though you are great in reputation and greatest in rank, you are nevertheless to be praised no more for dignity than for gracious condescension.” Hence it is also used of every reciprocal service which we perform and offer as evidence of kindness. Symmachus, Book IX, Letter 63: “But although you have anticipated me in the order of duty and in gracious condescension, you will nevertheless in future by no means judge me remiss,” etc. St Augustine, *Confessions*, Book VI, ch. 2, concerning his mother: “When she had brought a basket containing the customary food offerings to be tasted and distributed, she set down no more than one small cup, tempered to suit her very temperate taste, from which she might receive a courtesy.” Others printed “from which she might receive indignation,” which I consider truer if it is read separately: *in dignationem*. In our author here, unless I am mistaken, it means a kiss, as he himself seems to explain a few lines later, where he states this again in more words. M. Casaubon.]

“that they should not greet us; that they should not receive a courtesy from us.”

[Note: “That they should receive a courtesy.” Among the ancients, *dignatio* means favour. Cyprian, Book I, Letter 6. When, therefore, they kissed someone, they called this giving favour and communion; and since orthodox believers were unwilling to have this with Donatists, the office of the kiss was refused. Albaspinaeus.]

[Note: “That they should receive a courtesy.” Here *dignatio* is an act of kindness. Symmachus, Book IX, Letter 63: “But although you have anticipated me in the order of duty and in gracious condescension,” etc. Du Pin.]

Consider the words of your pride; consider your discourses; consider your commands; review also your actions.

[Note: Here the manuscripts and printed editions contain these words: “You will find that he who asked feared your oil”; but they are out of place. They do not cohere with what precedes or follows, and with them omitted the course of the argument is excellent.]

There is not one of you who does not mingle insults against us into his own discourses;

[Note: “Discourses.” These are bishops’ sermons and expositions of the Gospel in church. Cyprian, Letter 46, Book IV: “Nor should he listen to bishops while they are expounding.” Albaspinaeus.

Ibid. “There is not one of you who does not mingle insults against us into his own discourses.” By “insults against us” he means the charges hurled against us which he ought to have brought forward. Anonymous.]

who does not begin one thing and expound another.

[Note: “Who does not begin one thing or expound another.” *Initiare* means “to begin.” Thus below: “ministries to be begun and ordered.” Anonymous.]

[Note: “Begins.” “Begins.” Albaspinaeus.]

You begin the Lord’s readings, but unfold your discourses into injuries against us.

[Note: “The Lord’s readings.” You begin with a Gospel reading, but soon, leaving it aside, pass to insults. Albaspinaeus.]

You bring forth the Gospel and revile an absent brother.

[Note: “You bring forth the Gospel.” The sense is: you bring forth the Gospel of peace and sow hatreds. Albaspinaeus.]

You pour hatred into the minds of your hearers, and commend enmities by teaching them.

[Note: “You instil hatreds into the minds of your hearers,” etc. I once thought that one should read: “You teach enmities by commending them.” Barthius thinks that the word *docetis* (“you teach”) has fallen out and must necessarily be restored thus: “You teach enmities by commending them; by teaching, you commend them.” Franciscus Balduinus printed: “You inflict hatreds upon the minds of your hearers; by teaching enmities, you commend them.” Anonymous.]

[Note: In manuscripts S. T. and P. S.: “you fasten in.”]

By saying all these things, you set scandals against us. Therefore it was said to each one of you: “Sitting, you slandered your brother, and set a scandal against the son of your mother.” While God rebukes the sinner and reproves the one sitting, it is clear that this was said especially to you,

[Note: “Not to the people, who in church …” I confess that this passage troubled me for some time. For if one were simply to infer from it that formerly the people, or laity, were not permitted to sit in church, many objections came to mind. At length an appropriate passage of Augustine occurred, which, I hope, will satisfy the reader as fully as it satisfied me and dispel every obscurity in Optatus.

Augustine, then, in *On Instructing Beginners*, ch. 13, where he recommends relieving the weariness of a hearer by offering a seat, immediately adds: “Although it is undoubtedly better, where this can be done appropriately, that the hearer should listen sitting from the beginning. And in certain overseas churches it is far more expedient: not only do bishops speak to the people sitting, but seats are also provided for the people themselves,” etc. Nothing need be added to so clear a light. Only let no one be perplexed that Augustine the African calls “overseas churches” whatever churches then existed in the West. Optatus, Book II, divides the peoples of the whole world into Africans, Easterners, and Overseas peoples. The most learned Justellus has collected more concerning the use of this word in his notes on the Canons of the African Church. M. Casaubon.]

not to the people, who do not have permission to sit in church.

[Note: “Permission to sit.” Bishops and presbyters had the right to sit in church, but not the congregation, who prayed standing or with bent knees. Hence in ancient writers the priesthood is called “the honour of sitting together.” Albaspinaeus.]

You see, then, that beyond doubt it must be charged against you when God says: “Sitting, you set scandals against the son of your mother.”

[Note: “I have already proved so many times that we have one mother,” etc. Read: “I have already proved so many times that we have one mother; nor can you deny it, you who set scandals against us,” etc. M. Casaubon. Thus restored.]

I have already proved so many times that we have one mother; nor can you deny it, you who set scandals against us, while some of you produce readings which they do not understand,

[Note: “Which they do not understand.” Passages of Scripture which they explain wrongly. Albaspinaeus.]

in order to take away even that which is commonly shared by all: namely, the office of greeting. For some of you yourselves deny the customary kisses even in a casual greeting.

[Note: “In a casual greeting.” In a civil greeting: you deny us not only Christian greeting but even civil greeting. Albaspinaeus.]

And many are taught not to say “Hail” to any of us.

[Note: “Not to say ‘Hail.’” They gave a kiss and kind words. Albaspinaeus.]

They think that this is commanded them from a reading which they have not understood, not knowing of whom the apostle said this: “Do not even eat with such persons”; “Do not say ‘Hail’ to him”; “for their speech spreads like a cancer” (1 Cor. 5:11; 2 John 10; 2 Tim. 2:17). He said this concerning heretics whose doctrine had in those times begun to be corrupt, who by the subtle seduction of words, like diseases creeping obscurely, corrupted the health of faith: such as Marcion, who, having become an apostate from being a bishop, introduced two Gods and two Christs;

[Note: “Two Christs.” Balduinus restored this passage. For how the Marcionites posited two Christs and two Gods, see I. C. Perronius on Augustine’s passage *Against Adimantus*. Albaspinaeus.]

such as Praxeas,

[Note: All manuscripts and printed editions here read “Ebion” for “Praxeas.” But Praxeas, not Ebion, was the author of the error that the Father suffered. Praxeas is also named by Optatus in Book I. In Book V, manuscripts S. T. and P. S. read “Praxeas” for “Ebion”: “among Praxeas the Patripassian, who utterly denies the Son and maintains that the Father suffered.” From these facts we restore “Praxeas” for “Ebion,” although in this passage we lack manuscript authority. Perhaps one or two lines have been omitted in these manuscripts, and the text should read: “such as Ebion, who said that Christ was merely a man; such as Praxeas, who argued that the Father suffered.”]

who argued that the Father, not the Son, suffered; and Valentinus, who attempted to deprive Christ of flesh. The speech of these men was one which had become a cancer for assaulting the members of faith.

[Note: In manuscript S. G.: “which had become a cancer.” In printed editions: “which had become a crab.”]

[Note: “Such is also the speech of the Corpian heretic,” etc. Tertullian, among others, teaches who the heretics were who denied that martyrdom should be undergone; he wrote *On the Value of Martyrdom* against the Gnostics, notorious under that designation. But why Optatus calls those heretics “Corpians” is not equally clear. Balduinus testifies that in a manuscript he found *Scorpiani*, not *Corpiani*.

If Optatus thus named several heretics together, I would suppose he wrote *Scorpiaci*—for Tertullian calls his book *Scorpiace*, written against the Gnostics, whom he himself interprets as scorpions—or that he formed *Copriani* from κόπρος or κοπρία, “dung,” since it is established that the Gnostics were also called Borborites because of the filthiness both of their morals and doctrine; or finally, that he wrote *Coddiani*, which ancient writers report was also their name. But since Optatus mentions “the Corpian heretic” as one particular person whose proper name this was, I would not assert anything rashly—unless perhaps a singular stands for a plural, or Optatus himself stumbled over an unfamiliar name.

Augustine says that some Gnostics derive from the Nicolaitans, and others from the heretic Carpocrates. But this has nothing to do with the Corpian whom we are investigating, to whom Optatus assigns the distinctive doctrine of denying martyrdom. He next speaks of Arius, who attempted to teach that the Son of God was made from no substances, that is, as if ἐκ τῶν οὐκ ὄντων, “from things that are not”; whence they were also called Exoucontians. M. Casaubon.]

Such also is the speech of the Scorpian heretic,

[Note: “Caepian.” From the Tilius manuscript one should read *Scaepian*: those whom Tertullian calls Gnostics because they denied that martyrdom ought to be undergone. Albaspinaeus.]

[Note: In manuscripts S. T. and P. S.: “Corpian.”]

[Note: “The Scorpian heretic.” In this place Optatus seems to have been misled by the title of Tertullian’s book against the heretics who disparaged martyrdom, which Tertullian entitled *Scorpiace*. Hence Optatus perhaps thought that the heretic whom he attacks was called Scorpian. Yet at the beginning of the book Tertullian calls the heretics “scorpions” and declares that he is attacking Gnostics, Valentinians, and other opponents of martyrdom, who swarmed during persecution—not any one individual heretic. He says that, to treat these little beasts, he is preparing with his pen a ready theriac. Therefore there was no Scorpian or Corpian heretic for Tertullian; rather, those heretics who opposed martyrdom were rightly called by him “scorpions.” Du Pin.]

who denied that there ought to be martyrdoms. Let such people keep their poisons to themselves, and let their account not even slightly disturb the simple minds of hearers. It is his speech, therefore, which must be avoided, lest it spread like a cancer.

This was also said of Arius, who attempted to teach that the Son of God was made from no substances, not born from God. Unless his doctrine had been scattered by the 318 bishops at the Council of Nicaea, it had entered the hearts of many like a cancer. This was said of Photinus, a heretic of the present time, who dared to say that the Son of God was only a human being, not God.

It could also have been said of you, because your speech has brought no slight cancer into the minds and ears of some. For your speech is what you direct toward the children of peace when you say: “You have perished; look after yourselves; your soul will perish. How long do you hold to them?”

[Note: “You hold to them.” That is, “How long do you remain among the orthodox?” Albaspinaeus.]

Thus you made penitents out of believers; thus you killed the honours of priests. Behold, your speech too spreads like a cancer today, so that greeting and shared fellowship are forbidden.

[Note: In manuscript S. G.: “assembly.”]

What could our speech do that is like this? By straightforward teaching we retain the children of peace; we do not seduce strangers, nor do we cast anyone out. It is therefore clear that you daily set scandals against us. It would take too long to run through all the ways in which you slander us and all the means by which you set scandals.

### VI. The Donatists Are Thieves, and Why

Again, when he says, “You saw a thief and ran with him,” what matter do you suppose this was said about? Was it about a garment removed, or something stolen from the fold of a garment?

[Note: In manuscript S. G.: “unviolated,” but incorrectly.]

Or about any things which, when taken away, bring profit or loss among people? Such thefts too are indeed forbidden. But in this reading God rebukes those thefts which have been committed against himself. Do you ask what thefts have been committed against God? They are found among you.

God’s possession is the multitude of believers, from which the thief, the devil, daily desires to steal something: he wishes to corrupt in some respect either the will or character of a Christian man or woman,

[Note: In manuscript S. G.: “who in any Christian man or woman.”]

and, if not to seize the whole person, at least to snatch something from the person. When you saw such a thief using force against us, you assisted him by your actions. For no one fails to know that every person who is born, though born of Christian parents, cannot be without an unclean spirit,

[Note: “Without the spirit of the world,” that is, without an unclean spirit. Albaspinaeus.]

[Note: In manuscript S. T.: “of the world,” less well.]

which must be driven out and separated from the person before the saving washing.

[Note: “Driven out from the person.” He speaks of exorcism. Albaspinaeus.]

[Note: “This is what exorcism accomplishes.” St Augustine, Letter 105 to the presbyter Sixtus: “What answer do they give to the fact that infants are exorcised and exsufflated? For this is undoubtedly done falsely if the devil does not rule over them.” Albaspinaeus.]

This is what exorcism accomplishes: through it the unclean spirit is expelled

[Note: In manuscript S. G.: “repelled.”]

and driven into desert places.

[Note: “Into desert places.” He alludes to the history of Tobit. Albaspinaeus.]

A house becomes empty in the breast of the believer; a house becomes clean.

[Note: “The house becomes empty.” By baptism the house was cleansed; by confirmation it was adorned. Finally Christ entered and dwelt in it in the Eucharist. Origen: “But this house does not immediately deserve to have Christ as its inhabitant unless its life and conduct are so holy and pure.” Albaspinaeus.]

God enters and dwells there. As the apostle says: “You are the temple of God, and God dwells in you” (1 Cor. 3:16). And although each person is filled with God, from whom

[Note: In manuscript S. G.: “whence.”]

the thief, the devil, strives to steal something, you exorcise a faithful person in rebaptizing him, and say to the God who dwells there: “Accursed one, go out!”

Thus is fulfilled what God said through the prophet Ezekiel: “They cursed me among my people for a handful of barley and a morsel of bread, so as to kill souls which ought not to die, while they announce vain seductions to my people” (Ezek. 11:19). Therefore God hears insults not due to him and leaves such a dwelling. The person who entered the church filled with God goes out an empty vessel.

[Note: “An empty vessel.” He possessed Christ when you rebaptized him; through exorcisms you drove him away. Therefore the rebaptized person comes out empty from the waters; for he no longer has Christ or the Holy Spirit. Albaspinaeus.]

The devil, who as a thief wished to steal something

[Note: Manuscript S. G. adds: “from the person.”]

and was assisted by your acts, sees that the whole has become his, though he had wished to take only a little. Therefore God said of you: “You saw a thief and ran with him” (Ps. 49:18). Finally, the Gospel says this: when God has left a person, an empty vessel remains; but the unclean spirit, wandering hungry through desert places, says, “My house is empty” (Matt. 12:43). That is to say: “The one who expelled me has himself been expelled. I shall return there and dwell.” And he brings with him seven others more savage, and he will dwell there; and that person’s latter state will be worse than his former state.

[Note: “That is: ‘You saw a thief,’ etc.” Read: “That is: ‘You saw a thief and ran with him’;” and, after a short interval, “and you set your portion with adulterers,” etc. For Optatus often proceeds through and pursues each individual word of testimonies—or, as he calls them, readings—merely inserting a space as an indication of transition and, as it were, a new subject. The omission of these intervals and the failure to observe them have cast much obscurity over many passages in editions of Optatus. Otherwise Optatus would have said, “It follows: ‘and with adulterers,’” etc. M. Casaubon.]

That is: “You saw a thief and ran with him, and set your portion with adulterers.” By adulterers he means heretics, and by adulterous women their churches, which Christ despises and rejects in the Song of Songs, as though he were saying:

[Note: “Why do you gather for me …?” Why do you make a church for me? Albaspinaeus.]

“Why do you gather persons for me who are unnecessary? One is my beloved, one is my bride, one is my dove” (Song 6:8)—that is, the Catholic Church. Although you could be within it, by rebaptizing you chose to have a portion among adulterers.

[Note: Manuscript S. G. adds: “heretics.”]

And since it has been most clearly demonstrated by divine testimony that you are sinners, this too has been shown: the supports that you brought forward have fought against you. For you had called in the Prophet as an aid,

[Note: Manuscripts S. T. and Ph. S.: “you had added.”]

in whom it is read: “The sacrifice of a sinner is like one who sacrifices a dog” (Isa. 66:3).

[Note: “Sacrifices a dog.” A dog was so contemptible an animal to the Hebrews that not even its price could be accepted in the temple. Du Pin.]

Now acknowledge, if any shame remains, that you are sinners—with grief.

[Note: Manuscript S. G.: “if any fear remains, acknowledge with shame.”]

### VII. In What Sense It Is Said: “May the Oil of the Sinner Not Anoint My Head”

Learn also whose voice this is: “May the oil of the sinner not make my head fat” (Ps. 140:5). For you did not understand whose voice it is: certainly Christ’s, who had not yet been anointed when he prayed that the oil of the sinner might not make his head fat.

[Note: In manuscripts S. T. and P. S.: “might not defile.”]

[Note: “Because the Prophet feared the oil of the sinner,” etc. Distinguish thus: “Not understanding this, you said: ‘Because David the Prophet feared the oil of the sinner.’ He who sang had long before been anointed as a boy by Samuel”—that is, the psalmist, ὁ ψαλμῳδός. There was no reason for him to be anointed again; therefore, etc. M. Casaubon. This passage has been restored by us.]

Not understanding this, you said: “Because David the Prophet feared the oil of the sinner.” He who sang had long before been anointed by Samuel;

[Note: Manuscript S. G.: “had been anointed by the servant of God while a boy.”]

there was no reason for him to be anointed again. Therefore it is the voice of Christ saying: “May the oil of the sinner not anoint my head.”

[Note: Thus in manuscripts S. T. and S. G., and so it should be read in accordance with the Septuagint version.]

These are prayers, not commands; desires, not precepts. For if it were a command, it would say: “The oil of the sinner shall not anoint my head.”

[Note: Manuscript S. T.: “may anoint”; manuscript S. G.: “make fat,” but incorrectly.]

It is therefore the voice of the Son of God, already then fearing to incur the oil of the sinner—that is, the oil of any human being—for no one is without sin except God alone.

[Note: Manuscript S. G.: “lest his man should incur the oil of the sinner.”]

[Note: Manuscript S. T.: “there is no one who is not a sinner.”]

Therefore his Son feared the oil of a human being, because it would have been shameful for God to be anointed by a human being.

[Note: “That God should be anointed by a human being.” Anointing is a form of communion, as appears in Dionysius, final chapter of *Ecclesiastical Hierarchy*. Whoever grants communion to another appears superior to him; hence formerly no one could confer a sacrament upon a bishop. Optatus therefore says that it would have been unworthy for Christ to be perfected through a human being. Albaspinaeus.]

Therefore he entreats the Father not to be anointed by a human being, but by the Lord Father himself.

[Note: Manuscript S. G.: “prays.”]

The Son asks; let us see whether the Father assented. The Holy Spirit indicates and makes this clear in Psalm 44, where he says to the Son himself: “The Lord your God will anoint you with the oil of gladness differently from your companions” (Ps. 44:8). The priests and kings of the Jews had been companions, each of whom was plainly anointed by human beings. But because the Son was to be anointed by the Father—God by God—the Spirit proclaimed what had been promised according to the Son’s request, and the Father fulfilled it in the Jordan.

When the Son of God, our Saviour, came to John, he was shown by these words: “Behold the Lamb of God; this is he who takes away the sins of the world” (John 1:30). He descended into the water, not because there was anything in God to cleanse, but because water had to precede the oil which was to come,

[Note: “The water had to …” Baptism was conferred before confirmation. Albaspinaeus.]

for beginning, ordering, and completing the mysteries of baptism.

[Note: Manuscript S. T.: “ministries”; and below, “ministry” for “mystery.”]

After he had been washed, while he was held in John’s hands, the order of the mystery followed. The Father fulfilled what the Son had requested and what the Holy Spirit had foretold. Heaven was opened as God the Father anointed him; immediately the spiritual oil descended in the form of a dove,

[Note: “Immediately the oil.” They were confirmed where they had been baptized. Albaspinaeus.]

settled upon his head, and poured him over with oil.

[Note: Manuscripts S. T. and P. S.: “poured him over”; manuscript S. G.: “poured the oil”; one should read “with oil.” Manuscript S. T. adds after this, “and it was arranged”; manuscript S. G., “and it was arranged.” We have omitted this as superfluous.]

Thus he began to be called Christ, when he was anointed by God the Father.

[Note: “Whence Christ began.” Baptism made children; confirmation made Christians; the Church made believers. Albaspinaeus.]

And lest the laying on of hands should seem to have been absent,

[Note: “The laying on of hands.” And lest the prayer by which that confirmation was accomplished should be lacking: not only the extension of the hand was called the laying on of hands, but also the prayers pronounced while the hand was applied. Albaspinaeus.]

[Note: Manuscripts S. T. and P. S.: “the hand laid upon.”]

the voice of God was heard from the cloud, saying: “This is my Son, with whom I am well pleased; listen to him” (Matt. 3:17).

This, therefore, is what has been read: “May the oil of the sinner not anoint my head.”

[Note: “Learn the rationale of truth, brother Parmenian,” etc. Other editions read: “because now it is the time to discover learning.” I write: “because now it is not the time,” or, “now is not the time for youthful learning.” Earlier—or late—he says, as if to say: “Better late than never.” M. Casaubon. This passage has been restored by us.]

Learn, brother Parmenian, the rationale of truth, even if late, since you have now found a time for learning.

[Note: Manuscripts S. T. and P. S.: “it is time to discover learning.”]

### VIII. Heretics Properly Are Children of Adulterers

[Note: “And that passage which you said was read in Solomon the Prophet: ‘the children of adulterers completed.’” This is an outstanding passage and, if any passage in Optatus deserves attention, this one does. The word *consummatos* (“completed”) plainly conflicts with the author’s meaning. Wisdom 3 has these words: Τέκνα δὲ μοιχῶν ἀτέλεστα ἔσται, καὶ ἐκ παρανόμου κοίτης σπέρμα ἀφανισθήσεται—“But the children of adulterers shall be incomplete, and seed from a lawless bed shall be destroyed.” Considering the latter part, some do not hesitate to correct it to “children of adulterers, or born in sleep.” But this correction may perhaps appear to others itself born in sleep. I had long suspected that one should read “children of adulterers uncompleted.” For thus reads the Vulgate Latin edition of Wisdom: “The children of adulterers shall be in completion” [elsewhere, “uninitiated” or “imperfect”], “and seed from an unlawful bed shall be exterminated.” Anonymous.]

And that passage which you said was read in Solomon the Prophet: “The children of adulterers shall be uncompleted,

[Note: “Uncompleted.” We have restored this from the manuscripts. The printed editions wrongly have “completed.” In the Greek of Wisdom: τέκνα δὲ μοιχῶν ἀτέλεστα ἔσται, “but the children of adulterers shall be uncompleted.” The Greek word ἀτέλεστα, like the Latin, can mean “uncompleted,” “imperfect,” or “profane and without sacrifice.” Du Pin.]

and their spurious shoots

[Note: “Shoots.” He calls them suckers and offspring of trees. Anonymous.]

[Note: “Shoots.” Thus the Latin translator in ch. 4, v. 3, misled by the ambiguity of the Greek word μοσχεύματα, which means calves as well as shoots or slips, as may be seen in Theophrastus and other writers on agriculture. Du Pin.]

cannot put down deep roots” (Wisdom 3:16; 4:3). This can be understood literally. If you make it figurative, you have excused actual adulterers.

[Note: “You have excused actual adulterers,” namely by drawing into a spiritual sense what was said concerning them. Du Pin.]

But grant that it was said figuratively: it was said concerning heretics, among whom are false marriages of sacraments,

[Note: “False marriages.” Through all the sacraments there is union (*synaxis*) with Christ. Dionysius, *Ecclesiastical Hierarchy*. Therefore he elegantly calls the sacraments of heretics “false marriages,” because they do not unite heretics with Christ. Albaspinaeus.]

[Note: Manuscript S. G.: “banquets.”]

and in whose choirs iniquity is found, where the seeds have been corrupted to the destruction of faith.

[Note: “Destruction of faith.” He says, as below, that separation cannot occur without destruction. Anonymous.]

While Valentinus maintained that the Son of God existed in a phantom, not in flesh, he corrupted both his own faith and that of his followers. The seed of their birth has been destroyed: those who did not believe that the Son of God was born in flesh from the Virgin Mary and suffered in flesh.

IX. Jeremiah’s prophecy concerning the people who forsook the living fountain and dug for themselves broken cisterns is to be understood of the Jews who followed idols, not of the water of baptism. — For you also recall that you have read in the prophet Jeremiah how heaven was appalled because the people of God committed two evils: they forsook the fountain of living water and dug for themselves broken cisterns that could not hold water (Jer. 2:13). You did indeed read it, but, as things stand, you refused to understand it, arranging everything, out of eagerness to accuse, as a reproach against Catholics, and striving hard to bend it much according to your own judgment. [Note: In MS S. T., “to direct.”]

[Note: If you think that everything said through the prophets, etc. This is indeed true and weighty in Optatus—would that he had thought it said of himself. M. Casaubon.]

For if you think that everything said through the prophets was said in such a way as to apply to our times, you have excused the Jews, of whom it is clear that these things were said: they abandoned the living God, the true God, the God who had bestowed benefits upon them; and they made for themselves idols—that is, broken cisterns—which cannot hold water.

[Note: And they made for themselves idols, that is, etc. This is a notable passage, but phrased in exceedingly obscure words through scribal corruption. Optatus alludes to Jeremiah, chapter 2, where the Lord God complains that the Jewish people abandoned him, the true fountain, and worshipped the idols of the nations as broken cisterns. Barthius therefore very felicitously conjectures that one should read: “rejoicing while they reject enduring springs in God for the sea.” He uses *enduring springs* for fountains, and “sea” for their foul cisterns. This sense agrees most aptly with what follows. But the second edition of Fr. Balduin reads: “therefore everlasting majesty overflows.” INCERTAIN.]

[Note: Therefore everlasting. At this point we have corrected much from the German edition. ALBASP. — Ibid.: “Therefore everlasting majesty overflows,” etc. They also report this reading of that edition, yet commend N. L. Barthius’s conjecture, who emends: “rejoicing while they reject enduring sea[s] in God,” whereas it was formerly read, “therefore everlasting, rejecting badly, they rejoice.” But I consider what is here vastly preferable, and I do not doubt that it was drawn from better manuscripts—provided only that, instead of *therefore*, one corrects it to *in God*, and punctuates thus: “In God everlasting majesty overflows, as in a fountain water abounds from veins flowing forth in abundance.” Shortly afterward he again uses “majesty”; and rightly, in my judgment, and emphatically (*ἐμφατικῶς*), he set a word denoting greatness and amplitude—such as *majesty*—against the emptiness and vanity of idols. M. Casaubon. This passage has been restored by us.]

In God everlasting majesty overflows, as in a fountain that abounds from veins flowing forth in abundance. [Note: This passage was restored from MS S. G. It was exceedingly corrupt in MSS S. T., P. S., and the printed editions, which read: “Therefore everlasting, rejecting badly, they rejoice; as in a fountain water abounds from veins [Col. 1042B] flowing forth in abundance.” Without the help of the codex, no one could have guessed what should be read.]

But idols, unless they are made, do not exist; and cisterns, unless they are dug, cannot have capacious hollows. A cistern cannot be hollowed out without skill and tools; nor can an idol be made without an artisan.

[Note: There is no natural power in idols, etc. This passage is most corrupt—indeed, so is the text down to the end of this book. Balduin’s supposedly best edition is not best, but more corrupted and defective than the earlier ones. We shall therefore transcribe this whole passage from the earlier editions and then explain what seems right to us. They read as follows: “In idols there is no natural power; but by human error power is added and applied, and idols are judged to possess power. The power of water, which was not born there, is reckoned to be in it. It is a cistern hollowed out by art, whose structure is defective, so that it neither has water nor can retain what it receives. So also the idol is nothing in itself, and while it is worshipped it is nothing.” This is what God said, etc.

Optatus’s purpose here is to establish that the prophet’s words about dug and broken cisterns are to be interpreted of idols. To achieve this, he proceeds through and weighs each of the prophet’s words in his customary manner. Having shown that God is the living water of which Jeremiah speaks in this place, he goes on to discuss how idols may first be called cisterns, and then broken and dug cisterns. As to the first point, he says: idols, unless they are made, do not exist; and a cistern, unless it is dug, cannot possess a capacious hollow. A cistern cannot be hollowed out without skill and tools; nor can an idol be made without skill. There is no natural power in idols, but by human error it is added and applied. The power of water, which was not born there, is judged to be in it. [Col. 1042D] Thus far the comparison between idol and cistern is straightforward.

He now compares an idol with a broken and dug cistern—using the prophet’s own words—which cannot retain water. “A cistern,” he says, “is hollowed out by art” (*detritus* here has the same meaning as *effossus*, “dug out”); then he joins the words, “they made for themselves dug-out and broken cisterns,” whose defective structure means that they neither have water nor can retain what they receive. So likewise the idol is nothing in itself, and while it is worshipped it is nothing. One might also read it thus, which agrees much better with the apodosis: “This is a broken cistern whose structure is defective, so that it neither has water”—to which corresponds, “the idol is nothing in itself”—“nor can retain what it has received”; and correspondingly concerning the idol, “while it is worshipped it is nothing.” Thus, I hope, we have not altogether unsuccessfully restored the corrupted passage concerning the broken cistern. M. Casaubon. This passage too has been restored by us.]

There is no natural power in idols, but it is added and applied through human error: in the idol there is thought to be a power which was not born there. This is a broken cistern whose structure is defective, [Note: In the manuscripts, “by art”; but the meaning of the passage shows that “this” must be read.] so that it neither has water of itself nor can retain what it has received. [Note: In MS S. G., “vexations”; in MS S. T., “there is vexation.” It should be corrected to “is defective.” We have also corrected several other matters here by collation of the manuscripts and conjecture.] So too the idol is nothing in itself; and while it is worshipped, it is nothing.

This is what God said: that his people committed two evils, because they forsook the fountain of living water and made for themselves dug-out and broken cisterns. For the Jewish people had abandoned the true water; they did not know the majesty of God; [Col. 1043A] and they had followed the defiled religion of idols. This is what grieves God; this is what he says caused heaven to be appalled. For through the prophet Isaiah there is the same grief of God, when in this matter he calls two elements to witness, saying: “Hear, O heaven, and give ear, O earth: I have begotten and exalted sons, but they have forsaken me” (Isa. 1:2).

Why, brother Parmenianus, did you say nothing concerning this passage? [Note: Omitted in MS S. G.] Was it because water is not named here? [Note: It is understood that, out of eagerness to accuse, etc. The passage seems suspicious to me—unless he means that Parmenianus had so manipulated the law through his tricks and clever arguments as to make it appear harsher toward Catholics and their cause, while seeming to favor himself beyond measure: for he brings forth from it only what at least apparently suited him, while maliciously and deceitfully suppressing everything that utterly condemned him and openly aided his opponents. M. Casaubon.]

For it is understood that, out of eagerness to accuse, you so handled [Note: In MS S. G., “felt out.”] the law that wherever you read “water” written, you gathered it by certain tricks into material for odium; and, with a kind of dragnet woven from malicious arguments, you drew to yourself everything that is good.

[Note: “And, with a kind of course woven from malicious arguments, you drew to yourself everything that is good.” Barthius rightly suspects *curriculo* (“course”) to be an error and corrects it as *ceu riticulo* (“as if with a little net”); that is indeed the truth. But he is mistaken, and it must altogether be read *everriculo* (“with a dragnet”). He draws the comparison from fishing—not, by Hercules, more truly: [Col. 1044B] “The Pythian prophetess who speaks from Phoebus’ tripod and laurel.” INCERTAIN. This passage has been corrected by us.]

[Note: In MSS S. T. and P. S., “with a course”; but “with a dragnet,” as in MS S. G., is much more correct.]

For what sort of interpretation of this chapter of Jeremiah is yours, when God cries out that he has been forsaken and that cisterns have been dug? He is angered for his own sake, not for a thing belonging to him (Jer. 2).

[Note: The water of baptism is a thing of God, not God. Here too the older editions give a fuller complete period. I see no reason why Optatus should not acknowledge it as genuine, or why we, once we have acknowledged it and defended it openly, should not restore it to him. It runs thus: “For the water of baptism is a thing of God, not God. And if you think that you have been abandoned when those who were baptized among us were among you, so that they rightly appeared to come to us as deserters from you.” Here the fourth book ought to end. The following periods: one belongs at the end of the third book, as was rightly restored in the recent Paris edition; the other belongs to the beginning of the following book, as we shall presently prove. M. Casaubon.]

For the water of baptism is a thing of God, not God; and if you think yourselves abandoned when those who were baptized among us were among you, they would rightly appear to have come to us as deserters from you.

It has therefore been proved that what you said about the oil and the sacrifice of the sinner was said not against us but against yourselves.

79. BOOK V

In this fifth little book it is shown that in baptism human beings minister, while God washes; that Christ gives what is received in baptism; that those rebaptized cannot possess the kingdom of God; and that they have lost the wedding garment.

[Col. 1043]

I. Parmenianus’s own premises entail that there is one baptism. — We have shown in the first book, by the clearest proofs, who the *traditores* were [Note: Who the *traditores* and authors of the schism were, etc. Other editions begin: “And now, who the *traditores* were,” etc. I would maintain at any wager that this is correct, and that those words were struck out without reason. They were deleted because it seemed absurd for the book to begin with them. But learned men did not see that the words in Book IV, “and the way of understanding was closed to you,” or rather, “they would appear to come to us as deserters from you,” were the final words of the book and closed it.

Optatus began Book V with these words: “It has therefore been proved that what you said, not against us,” etc. Otherwise the ensuing review and recapitulation (*ἀνακεφαλαίωσις*) of the preceding books would be defective: although it mentions the first, second, and third books, it makes no mention of the fourth except by these words, which we assign to the fifth. Compare also the beginnings of the individual books, as of the third: “Enough, I think, in the second little book concerning the Church,” etc.; likewise the others, in which, as in this fifth book, he begins from the subject of the immediately preceding book.

The cause of the error, if you ask, was, I think, this. Optatus wrote: “It has therefore been proved,” etc., “concerning the oil and the sacrifice of the sinner, in Book IV.” Someone copied “Book V” for “Book IV,” or “V” for “IV”; later this was taken for the title of the following book, whose heading, as often happens in manuscripts, may perhaps have been omitted. Therefore the beginning should be restored thus: “Book V. It has therefore been proved that you said, not against us, what was previously said”—or rather “by you,” as above more than once—unless “you said what was said by you” is too tasteless: “concerning the oil and the sacrifice of the sinner, in Book IV. And now, who the *traditores* and authors of the schism were, we showed in the first book by manifest proofs,” etc. M. Casaubon.]

—and the authors of the schism; and in the second we showed that the one true Catholic Church is among us. In the third, moreover, we proved that the harsh actions said to have occurred do not at all pertain to us, and we taught by divine judgment that you are rather the sinners.

[Note: In MSS S. T. and P. S., “harsh.”]

Now we must speak here concerning baptism. The whole question now under discussion rests upon this matter: your audacity violated baptism when you wished to repeat what Christ commanded to be done once only. [Note: In MS S. G., “to be repeated.”] Nor do you deny this, brother Parmenianus, since at the beginning of your treatise you said many things against yourselves and in our favor—things that belong to us. [Note: Thus in MS S. G.; in the others, “because.”]

For in your comparison concerning baptism, you recalled that the Flood occurred once, and that there was one circumcision for the Jewish people. Although you discussed these matters at the beginning of your discourse, [Note: MSS S. T. and P. S. add, wrongly, “badly”; the latest edition adds “at length.” Both appear superfluous.] in the course of your treatise you nevertheless forgot them [Note: Omitted in MS S. G.], introducing two waters and intending to speak of true and false water. [Note: Here the manuscripts insert the word “arguments,” which does not cohere with the course of the sentence.] You foolishly arranged the beginning of your discourse so as to build your case in advance [Note: “The beginning of your discourse you foolishly, etc.” Others read, “you arranged while foolishly assailing.” I know the reading here can be defended. Yet I think Optatus wrote, “you arranged while foolishly constructing beforehand.” Since, he says, you were going to introduce two waters in the course of your treatise, you unhappily laid the groundwork for your argument by setting down the foundation of a single circumcision, etc. M. Casaubon.] [Note: Thus in MS S. G.; in MS P. S., “assailing beforehand”; in MS P. S., “striking at.”]—by weakening, you establish [Note: In MS S. G., “establishing.”] the unity of holy baptism.

You wished to lay down Jewish circumcision as a kind of foundation: that Christian baptism had been prefigured in the circumcision of the Hebrews. [Note: You defended the Catholic Church while attacking it. By saying that baptism exists among us, even though false, you prove it true and lawful, because among the Jews there was only one circumcision. ALBASP.] You defended the Catholic Church while attacking it.

[Note: For in the course of your treatise, etc. The matter itself cries out that several lines here suffer from corruption. I think it should be written and punctuated thus: “For in the course of your treatise, you professed to empty one so that you might seem to fill another, apart from the baptisms of heretics. While you call one and another, although you tried to show them different, you cannot deny that there are two. While you strive to take away one of them, you have labored to make the second appear as though it were the first. Circumcision,” etc. M. Casaubon. This passage has been restored by us.]

For in the course of your treatise you professed to empty one, so that you might seem to fill another. Apart from the baptism of heretics, [Note: Thus in MS S. T.; in MS S. G. and the printed editions, “baptisms.”] when you call one “one” and another “another,” though you have tried to show them different, you cannot deny that there are two. And while you try to take one away, you have labored to make the second appear as though it were the first.

But circumcision was set forth beforehand as a figure before the coming of baptism. [Note: This particle is absent in MS S. T.] [Note: We supplied this from MS S. G.] You have argued that Christians possess two waters; therefore show also that the Jews have two circumcisions, one better and the other worse. If you seek this, you will not be able to find it. The offspring of Abraham, by which the Jews are reckoned, [Note: In MSS S. T. and P. S., through scribal error, “wisdom” instead of “offspring.”] boasts of being marked with this seal. Therefore reality must correspond to the image that was set forth beforehand.

For God, who wished to show that a unique reality [Note: A unique thing. That a figure pertains to something unique and incapable of repetition. ALBASP.] ought afterward to follow in the ensuing reality, did not choose for something to be removed from an ear or a finger; rather, that part of the body was chosen from which the *peritome* (*περιτομή*, circumcision), once removed, might make in them a saving sign [Note: Thus in MS S. G.; in MSS S. T. and P. S., *deperitomen*, with the first two letters omitted. Hence the printed editions quite wrongly have *deperire* or *deperiri*.] which cannot be made again. [Note: In MSS S. T. and P. S., “may make.”] [Note: In MS S. G., “and thus so that it cannot be done again.”]

[Note: For once it has been done it preserves salvation. “It preserves salvation” is demanded by the sense, but the words do not bear it. Perhaps: “it retains saving power”? But what is this? I think it should read: “it serves for salvation.” M. Casaubon.]

For, once done, it preserves salvation; if done again, it can bring destruction. So too Christian baptism, performed with the Trinity, confers grace; if repeated, it brings loss of life.

Why then, brother Parmenianus, did it please you to present a unique thing and, contrary to this, to compare two different baptisms—one true, the other false? For afterward you argued that there are two waters, claiming one as true for yourselves and wishing to attribute the other, as deceitful, to us. [Note: We supplied this word from MS S. G.]

After this you also made mention of the Deluge. It was indeed an image of baptism: the whole defiled world, with sinners submerged, was cleansed through the intervening washing and restored to its former appearance. [Note: In MS S. T., “in its former appearance.”] But since you were subsequently going to say that, outside the diseased fountains of heretics, there is also another water—that is, a deceitful water opposed to the true—why did you wish to mention the Deluge, which occurred once? [Note: In MSS S. T. and P. S., “occurs.”] If this is so, first show two arks, even if unlike, and two unlike doves carrying different branches in their beaks (Gen. 8), if you are to prove a true and a false water. [Note: True and false water: two baptisms, one false and the other true. ALBASP.]

Therefore the one true water is that which is constituted not by place, [Note: Not from the person: not from the holiness of the person, but from the force of the sacrament. ALBASP.] not by a person, but by the Trinity. And since you said that there is also deceitful water, learn this too: where you may find it—among Praxeas, [Note: The name Praxeas is found in MSS S. T. and P. S., but the preposition “among” is absent; in its place stands “or Flavian.” In MS S. G. the name Praxeas is absent, and “among Ebion” occurs. But this was Praxeas’s error, not Ebion’s.] the Patripassian, who entirely denies the Son and maintains that the Father suffered.

And since the Son of God is truth, as he himself testifies, saying, “I am the door, and the way, and the truth” [Col. 1047A] (John 14:6), therefore the Son of God is truth. Where he is not, there is falsehood; and since among the Patripassians [Note: In MS S. G., “Patripassian.”] there is no Son, there is no truth. [Note: MSS S. T. and P. S. read, “nor is there truth”; because this is harsher, we follow MS S. G., in which *nor* is absent.] And where truth is not, there is deceitful water.

Therefore, even if late, cease inventing accusations; and do not transfer to Catholics what was said against the Patripassians. Now, since it has been clearly shown that what you said concerning the Flood and circumcision could have been said by us and on your behalf as well, it follows to show how you spoke in praise of baptism in such a way that, in it, much was for us and for you, but something nevertheless against you.

[Note: It is for both parties that which is common to us and you. One could read: “which is common to us, and therefore also to you, because you are from us.” Yet I think Optatus wrote: “It is for both parties that which is common to us and to you. And therefore also to you, because you derive from us.” Above, Book I: “Why were those persons mentioned by you among whom the sacraments are absent, which seem common to us and to you?” Nowhere have scribes erred more frequently than where the same words were immediately repeated or doubled, as we have already observed several times. M. Casaubon.]

What is for both parties is that which is common to us and you; [Note: Absent in MSS S. T. and P. S.] and it is also yours because you derive from us. [Note: It is also yours because you received these things from us. ALBASP.] For among you and among us there is one ecclesiastical practice, [Note: One ecclesiastical discipline. ALBASP.] common readings, [Note: We expound the Scriptures in the same manner. ALBASP.] the same faith, [Note: The articles or rule of faith. ALBASP.] the very sacraments of faith, [Note: The same mysteries. Augustine distinguishes mysteries from sacraments: a mystery is what is conferred or signified; a sacrament is the visible thing through which a spiritual reality is given. ALBASP.] and the same mysteries.

You have rightly praised baptism. For who among the faithful does not know that unique baptism is the life of virtues, [Note: The life of virtues, because virtues cannot be perfected without grace. ALBASP.] the death of crimes, immortal birth, the acquisition of the heavenly kingdom, the harbor of innocence, and—the expression you also used—the shipwreck of sins? These benefits are granted to every believer [Note: This word was added from MS S. G.] not by the minister of the rite, [Note: The person of the minister contributes nothing. ALBASP.] but by the faith of the believer and by the Trinity.

II. In baptism the Trinity acts, not the person of the minister. — Next you ask what, in your praise of baptism, you said against yourselves. Listen; but first you must acknowledge what none of you can possibly deny. For you say that the Trinity is held to be of no account [Note: The Trinity contributes nothing in baptism. ALBASP.] where your presence was not involved. [Note: In MS S. G., “was.”]

[Note: If you disparage us: Why do you say that our persons prevent someone from being rightly baptized among us, when God, who can accomplish all things, is invoked in baptism? ALBASP.]

If you disparage us, at least revere the Lord, who is first in the Trinity, and who, together with the Son and the Holy Spirit, works and completes all things—even where no human person is present.

But you, brother Parmenianus, in your praise of the water, from the reading of Genesis, said that the waters first produced living souls. [Note: In praise of the water from the reading of Genesis, etc. Victor of Utica, Book II: “The Spirit of God was borne over the waters, as the Creator, holding creation together by the power of his might, so that, about to produce all living things from them, he himself supplied the rudimentary elements with the particular nourishment of fire; and already, as the mystery of baptism shone forth, the nature of the liquid received the power of sanctification, and brought forth the first animate bodies unto life.” M. Casaubon.] [Note: Living waters. Tertullian, *On Baptism*: “The first liquid brought forth what lived; nor should it seem strange in baptism if waters know how to give life.” ALBASP.]

Could they have generated them of their own accord? Was not the entire Trinity there too? Certainly God the Father was there, who deigned to command, who said: “Let the waters bring forth swimming creatures, flying creatures, etc.” (Gen. 1:20). If what was made had occurred without an agent, God would have said: “Bring forth, waters” (ibid., [Gen.] 2). Therefore the Son of God was there, working; the Holy Spirit was there, as we read: “And the Spirit of God was borne over the waters.”

[Note: I do not see how much. I do not see that a human person contributes anything there: the three suffice. ALBASP.]

I see no fourth thing there, nothing lacking from the three; and nevertheless what the Trinity worked was born. [Note: Omitted in MS S. G.] And you were not there. Or if the Trinity ought to be permitted to do nothing without you, call the fish back to their origin; now plunge the flying birds into the waves, if the Trinity ought to work nothing in your absence. [Note: In MS S. G., “ought to be permitted to the Trinity.”]

[Col. 1048B] **III. Baptism is not to be repeated.**—Therefore, when you have said both that there was but one Flood and that circumcision cannot be repeated, and when we have shown that the heavenly gift is conferred upon every believer by the Trinity, not by a human being, why have you thought fit to duplicate baptism—not after us, but after the Trinity? No slight controversy has arisen concerning its sacrament, and the question is raised whether, after the Trinity, it is lawful to do this again in that same Trinity. You say it is lawful; we say it is not lawful. Between your “it is lawful” and our “it is not lawful,” the souls of the peoples waver and row to and fro. Let no one believe you; let no one believe us: we are all contentious persons. Judges must be sought. If they are Christians, they cannot be provided from either side, because party spirit obstructs the truth. A judge must be sought from outside.

[Note: [Col. 1048C] In MS S. G., *enim* (“for”).]

[Note: [Col. 1048C] MSS S. T. and P. S. read *et quid* (“and why”).]

[Col. 1048C] If he is a pagan, he cannot know Christian secrets; if a Jew, he is an enemy of Christian baptism. Therefore no judgment on this matter can be found on earth; a judge must be sought from heaven.

[Note: [Col. 1048D] A pagan cannot know Christian secrets. “Mysteries”: Tertullian: “it follows that they are outsiders; but how can outsiders have knowledge?” ALBASP.]

[Col. 1049A] But why do we knock at heaven, when here in the Gospel we have [p. 82] a testament?

[Note: [Col. 1049C] Here the manuscripts insert the word *inquam* (“I say”), which we have removed as superfluous.]

For in this matter earthly things may rightly be compared with heavenly. It is like a man who has many children: as long as their father is present, he himself commands each of them; a testament is not yet necessary. So too Christ, while he was present on earth—although even now he is not absent—commanded the Apostles, according to the occasion, whatever was necessary. But just as an earthly father, when he feels himself at the threshold of death, fearing that after his death the brothers may quarrel when peace has been broken, summons witnesses and transfers his will from his dying breast to tablets which will endure for a long time; and if contention arises between the brothers, they do not go to the tomb but seek the testament: so he who rests in the tomb speaks silently from the tablets.

[Note: [Col. 1049D] “And he who rests in the tomb,” etc. Earlier editions: “and he who rests in the tomb speaks silently from the tablets, and the living one whose …”; write: “and he who rests silently in the tomb speaks from the tablets, living.” The one whose testament it is, etc. You will see in Balduin’s notes how St Augustine imitated this entire passage; he quotes the passage. Whereas Optatus here says, “He who rests silently in the tomb,” Augustine says, “He lies without sense in the monument,” etc. M. CASAUBON. — “He who rests in the tomb speaks silently from the tablets.” Most elegantly said of one buried whose testament or codicils, when a dispute has arisen, are consulted. ANONYMOUS.]

The living one, whose testament it is, is in heaven; therefore his will must be sought in the Gospel as though in a testament. For Christ had already foreseen, by foreknowledge, the things which you now do.

[Note: [Col. 1049C] Thus in all the manuscripts; editors, failing to understand it as referring to Christ, who by foreknowledge knew future things, substituted “present things.”]
