Thus, when he washed his disciples’ feet, the Son of God said to Peter: “What I am doing you do not know; but afterward you will know” (John 13:8). In saying, “Afterward you will know,” he designated these times. Therefore among the other headings of the Testament he established this heading concerning water. When he washed his disciples’ feet, while the others were silent, if Peter too had remained silent, he would merely have provided a pattern of humility and would have said nothing concerning the sacrament of baptism.

[Note: [Col. 1049D] A pattern of humility. If Peter had not spoken and refused to be washed, Christ would have said nothing about baptism. ALBASP.]

But when Peter refused and would not permit his feet to be washed, Christ denied him the kingdom unless he accepted the service. Yet when the kingdom of heaven was mentioned, though one part of his body was sought for service, he offered his whole body for washing.

[Col. 1049C] Now attend, all crowds and every Christian people: learn what is lawful. While Peter challenges, Christ teaches; let him who doubts learn.

[Note: [Col. 1049D] For this is Christ’s voice: “He who has been washed once,” etc. Optatus was not the first—perhaps misled more by the wording than by the matter—to use this passage thus. Long before, Tertullian, *On Baptism*, ch. 12, had used it in almost the same way, except that Tertullian, though it comes to the same thing, rendered it: “He who has washed once has no need again.” Other editions give the complete passage: “He who has been washed once has no further need of washing, because he is wholly clean”; and Victor of Utica cites it at the end of his book, except that he has *lavari* (“to be washed”), where this text has *lavandi* (“of washing”). M. CASAUBON.]

For this is Christ’s voice: “He who has been washed once has no need to be washed again, because he is wholly clean” (John 13:10). And he pronounced this concerning that washing which he had commanded to be celebrated in the Trinity—not concerning that of Jews or heretics, who, while they wash, defile; but concerning the holy water which flows forth from the springs of the three names. For the Lord himself commanded it, saying: “Go, baptize all nations in the name of the Father, and of the Son, and of the Holy Spirit” (Matt. 28:29). Concerning this washing he said: “He who has been washed once has no need to be washed again” (John 13:10).

[Col. 1050A] By saying “once,” he forbade its being done again; and he spoke of the thing, not of the person.

[Note: [Col. 1050D] Not of the person. He said that the water washes, not the person administering the water. ALBASP.]

[Note: [Col. 1050D] For if there were a distinction: if there were a difference among the persons who baptize. ALBASP.]

For if there were a distinction, he would say, “He who has been washed well once”; but because he did not add the word *well*, he indicates that whatever has been done in the Trinity is well done. For this reason we receive simply those who come to us from you.

[Col. 1050B] When he says, “He has no need to be washed again,” this is a general statement, not a particular one. For if these words were spoken to Peter, Christ would say: “Because you have been washed once, you have no need to be washed again” (John 13:10).

[Note: [Col. 1049C] MS S. G. has *dum* (“while”) for *cum* (“when”).]

[Note: [Col. 1049C] MS S. G. has “and if” for “if Peter.”]

[Note: [Col. 1049C–1050C] This passage must be read as it stands in MS S. G.; Optatus’s argument demonstrates it. In MSS S. T. and P. S. it is wrongly expressed in the third person.]

Therefore, whenever anyone baptized by you wishes to come over to us, we receive the person who comes with complete simplicity, under this teaching and example.

[Note: [Col. 1050C] Thus in MS S. G. MSS S. T. and P. S. have *magisterio exemplo*, omitting the conjunction, which is nevertheless necessary; editors, not supplying it, changed *magisterio* (“teaching”) into *magistri* (“of the master”).]

[Note: [Col. 1050D] *Tota simplicitate*, “with complete simplicity.” He says *tota* for *omni* (“all”), as elsewhere “the whole importunity,” “the whole holiness,” and “the whole security”; Jerome and Vopiscus do likewise, as Isaac Casaubon, that most excellent critic, notes. ANONYMOUS.]

Far be it from us ever to exorcise a believer sound in faith.

[Note: [Col. 1050C] These words occur in MS S. G., not in the others.]

Far be it from us to call one already washed back to the font. Far be it from us to sin against the Holy Spirit (Matt. 12).

[Note: [Col. 1050D] “Against the Holy Spirit”: by driving him out through exorcisms. ALBASP.]

For this offense forgiveness is denied both in the present age and in the age to come. Far be it from us to repeat what is once done, or duplicate what is one. For thus it is written, as the Apostle says: “One God, one Christ, one faith, [Col. 1050C] one baptism” (Eph. 4:5).

Finally, you who strive as though gladly to duplicate baptism: [p. 83] if you give a second baptism, give a second faith; if you give a second faith, give also a second Christ; if you give a second Christ, give a second God. You cannot deny that God is one, lest you fall into Marcion’s pits.

[Col. 1051A] Therefore God is one; from the one God there is one Christ. One who is rebaptized was already a Christian: how can he be called a Christian again?

[Note: [Col. 1051B] These words are absent from MS S. G.]

[Note: [Col. 1051C] “A Christian again”: How can one who has been born be born again? Through the first baptism he acquired a new nature; how can he lose it through the second baptism and acquire that same nature again? ALBASP.]

“One faith” here distinguishes the unique faith from the errors of heretics and from their various faiths.

[Note: [Col. 1051C] “One faith” in this place, etc. Write: “One faith.” Here faith alone is distinguished from the heretics’ errors and their varying faith. He proceeds through each item of the passage just cited: first one God, one Christ; then follows one faith. After treating this also, he adds: “Then follows one baptism, so that because what is one,” etc. M. CASAUBON.]

[Note: [Col. 1051C] “One faith” in this place. The sense is: since there is only one faith, heretics, who do not possess the true and right faith concerning the Trinity, cannot baptize, because faith is distinguished from their empty faith. ALBASP.]

It is also prescribed against you, who do again what has once been done, placing everything in personal endowments and nothing in the sacraments.

[Note: [Col. 1051C–1051D] “It is also prescribed against you”: this too militates against you, because, since there is one faith, you cannot and ought not give another in rebaptism. ALBASP.]

[Note: [Col. 1051D] “Placing everything in endowments”: placing the whole force of the sacraments in the holiness of the administrator. ALBASP.]

For the name of faith belongs to the believer, not to the minister.

[Note: [Col. 1051D] “The name of faith”: the person baptized ought to believe and ought to have faith. If he has and ought to have it, the faith required will not be that of the baptizer, but of the baptized. ALBASP.]

For whoever asks him, the one who has believed has believed God; and after that person’s one *credo*, “I believe,” you demand another *credo*.

[Note: [Col. 1051D] “Another *credo*”: at baptism people were questioned and professed that they believed in Christ and in God. Since this was so, another *credo* ought not to have been demanded, because there is only one *credo*, not two. ALBASP.]

Then follows one baptism; and because what is one is holy through being one, it is distinguished not only from the profane and sacrilegious baptisms of heretics, but also so that what is one may not be duplicated or what has once been done repeated.

[Note: [Col. 1051B] MSS S. T. and Ph. S. have *ut* (“as” or “because”).]

[Note: [Col. 1051D–1052C] Not only from heretics. That unity of faith excludes not only the baptism of heretics, which was not given in that faith and in the Trinity, but also forbids faith itself to be duplicated and another faith to be extorted from or imposed upon those rebaptized. ALBASP.]

**IV. God, not the minister, is the one who washes in baptism.**—In celebrating this sacrament of baptism, it is agreed that there are three elements, which neither you can increase, diminish, nor omit.

[Note: [Col. 1052C] There are three elements: three things concur. ALBASP.]

The first element is in the Trinity; the second in the believer; the third in the minister. But the individual elements are not to be weighed on an equal scale. For I see two as necessary, and one as, so to speak, necessary. The Trinity occupies the principal place, without which the action itself cannot be performed.

[Note: [Col. 1052C] The first is in the Trinity. Baptism must be performed in the name of Father, Son, and Holy Spirit. ALBASP.]

The faith of the believer follows it; then comes the person of the minister, who cannot possess similar authority.

[Col. 1052A] The first two remain always unchangeable and unmoved. For the Trinity is always itself; faith is one in each person; both always retain their power. But the person of the minister is understood not to be capable of equality with the first two elements, because it alone appears capable of change.

[Note: [Col. 1051C] MSS S. T. and P. S. read *ideo quod*, “for this reason, because.”]

[Note: [Col. 1052C] “It appears changeable.” The person baptizing does not make the sacrament’s grace endure; rather, the faith of the baptized does. ALBASP.]

You wish there to be a difference between us and you in respect of the same sort of person; and, judging yourselves holier, you do not hesitate to set your pride before the Trinity.

[Note: [Col. 1052C] “A difference in the same sort of person”: you wish there to be a great difference between a Donatist and an orthodox person baptizing. ALBASP.]

[Note: [Col. 1052C] “To put your pride before the Trinity”: because you wish baptism’s holiness and effect to arise from the holiness of its administrator, not from faith. ALBASP.]

Yet the person of the minister can change, whereas the Trinity cannot change. And whereas baptism ought to be sought by those receiving it, you present yourselves as those who ought to be sought.

[Note: [Col. 1052C–1052D] “And whereas baptism ought to be sought by recipients,” etc. He says that baptism is what ought to be sought by those receiving it, not the Trinity or faith, contrary to some exceedingly foolish interpreters, who fail to notice that in former usage *desiderare*, “to seek” or “request,” was proper to our sacraments, Baptism and Eucharist. On this point the blessed father has much in his *Exercises on Baronius*, exercise 16, section 45. M. CASAUBON.]

[Note: [Col. 1052D] “Baptism ought to be sought.” Those to be baptized should strive with all their strength to believe perfectly; but you wish them rather to seek baptism from non-sinners and to hope more in the holiness of the baptizer than in faith and the Trinity. ALBASP.]

Since you are among the ministers, show what place you hold in this mystery, and whether you can belong to the same body. Baptism has one name, and beneath that name lies its own proper body.

[Col. 1052B]

[Note: [Col. 1052D] “Its own proper body.” Baptism consists, as they say, of its form and matter, among which the person of the baptizer is not counted. Why, then, do you claim for yourselves its entire account and essence, locating it in your own person? ALBASP.]

That body has definite members.

[Note: [Col. 1052B] MS S. G. has “whose body.”]

[Note: [Col. 1052D] Definite members: definite parts. ALBASP.]

Nothing can be added to or taken away from them. If a minister is found among those members as one who must be chosen, the entire body belongs to the minister. But all these members of this body are always and at once present together and cannot be changed; ministers, however, change daily in places, times, and persons.

[Note: [Col. 1052B] MS S. G. has “to which” for “among which.”]

For there is not one person who baptizes always or everywhere. In this work there were others long ago; there are others now; there will be others later. Ministers can change; sacraments cannot change.

[Note: [Col. 1052D–1053D] Read: “For there is not one person who baptizes always and everywhere. In this work there were others long ago, there are others now, and there will be others later. Ministers can change; sacraments …” M. CASAUBON.]

Therefore, since you see that all who baptize are ministers, [Col. 1053A] not masters, [p. 84] and that sacraments are holy in themselves, not through human beings, why do you claim so much for yourselves? Why do you strive to exclude God from his own gifts? Grant to God the performance of what is his. For a gift that is divine cannot be given by a human being.

If you think otherwise, you seek to render empty the voices of the Prophets and God’s promises, by which it is proved that God washes, not a human being. The prophet David stands against you and says in Psalm 50 (v. 9): “You will wash me, and I shall be made whiter than snow”; likewise in the same Psalm: “God, wash me from my iniquity, and cleanse me from my sin” (v. 4).

[Note: [Col. 1053C] MSS S. T. and P. S. have Psalm 49.]

He said, “Wash me”; he did not say, “Choose someone through whom you may wash me.” And the prophet Isaiah says: “For the Lord will wash away the filth of the sons and daughters of Zion” (Isa. 4:4).

[Note: [Col. 1053C] MS S. G. has “God washed.”]

[Note: [Col. 1053C] MS S. T. has the singular, “filth.”]

In the third book we proved that Zion is the Church; [Col. 1053B] therefore God washes the sons and daughters of the Church.

[Note: [Col. 1053C] These words are added from MS S. G.; they are absent from the others and from the printed editions.]

He did not say: “Those who think themselves holy will wash them.”

[Note: [Col. 1053D] MSS S. T. and P. S. have “me.”]

Allow yourselves to be overcome even by the prophets, or at least acknowledge in this way that a human being does not wash, but God. As long as you say, “How does one who does not have what to give give it?” see that the Lord is the giver.

[Note: [Col. 1053D] “How does one who does not have what to give give it?” This argument occurs in the council of St Cyprian. ALBASP.]

[Note: [Col. 1053D] MSS S. T. and P. S. read: “He who does not have, what he ought when he gives.”]

[Note: [Col. 1053D] These words are added from MS S. G.]

See that God cleanses every person. For no one but God, who is the maker of the mind itself, can wash away the mind’s dirt and stains. Or, if you think that the washing is yours, tell us what the mind is like which is washed through the body, what form it has, or in what place in a human being it resides. This knowledge has been denied to human beings. How then do you suppose that you wash, when you do not know what the thing is that you wash?

It is God’s work to cleanse, not a human being’s. For through the prophet Isaiah he himself promised that he would wash, saying: “Though your sins be like scarlet, I will make them white as snow” (Isa. 1:18).

[Note: [Col. 1054C] MSS S. T. and P. S. read “the Lord’s” for “God’s.”]

[Col. 1053C] He said, “I will make white,” not, “I will cause to be made white.” If God promised this, why do you wish to render what you are not permitted to promise, render, or possess? Behold: in Isaiah God promised that he himself would make white those afflicted by sins, not through a human being.

[Note: [Col. 1054C] MS S. G. has: “Behold, now by himself he promised.”]

[Note: [Col. 1054C] MS S. G. reads *effaetos*; the text has *affectos*, “afflicted.”]

Return to the Gospel. See what Christ promised for the salvation of humankind. When the Samaritan woman refused him water, the Son of God then spoke in a way that refutes your presumptions: “The water which I give—whoever drinks it shall never thirst [Col. 1054A] for ever” (John 4:13). “The water which I give,” he said; he did not say, “which those who think themselves holy will give,” as you seem to yourselves; rather, he said that he himself would give it.

[Note: [Col. 1054C] MSS S. T. and P. S. read “as you seem to yourselves”; MS S. G. reads “as you now seem to yourselves.”]

Therefore he is the giver; what is given belongs to him. Why do you strive with every importunity to claim it for yourselves?

**V. John’s baptism: when and why Christ’s baptism was conferred after it.**—John the Baptist, who came as the Savior’s forerunner, strengthens this point. While he baptized many for repentance and remission of sins, he announced that the Son of God would come. His words were: “Behold, he is coming who will baptize you” (John 1:33). Yet we do not read that Christ rebaptized anyone after John. Therefore, when he said, “He who will baptize you,” Christ, upon coming after John at that time, baptized.

[Col. 1054B] It was promised for our times that he himself would give what is given today, according to his saying: “The water which I give—whoever drinks it shall never thirst for ever” (John 4:13). Indeed, when John’s disciples said to their master, “Behold, the one whom you baptized,” he did baptize, but through the hands of the Apostles, to whom he had given the laws of baptism. For elsewhere we read: “He himself baptized no one, but his disciples” (John 3:6).

In this matter we are all his disciples: we are to act as ministers, while he gives, who promised that he would give. Yet although John baptized countless thousands of people, while Christ was already present the servant was at work and the Lord was inactive, before he gave the form for baptizing.

[Note: [Col. 1053D–1054D] “While Christ was already present,” etc. Perhaps someone will think that *vacabat* (“was inactive/free”) ought to be substituted for *vocabat* (“was calling”), since it fits well here and is later repeatedly introduced and contrasted with *operari*, “to work”; and so, to show that the Son of God was inactive, while faith alone was at work, etc. Nevertheless the transmitted reading may be retained, since that too fits the sense and context; compare elsewhere: “To the one in whom faith is placed, he himself gives what is believed, not the person through whom faith is placed.” The same point seems to be repeated elsewhere in different words, even using *operari* in what follows: “While all act as ministers, the works are human, but the gifts are God’s.” M. CASAUBON.]

[Note: [Col. 1054D] These words are supplied from MS S. G.; they were omitted in the others.]

After no small interval, thousands of people had been baptized for repentance and remission [Col. 1054C] of sins.

[Note: [Col. 1054D] MSS S. T. and P. S. read *per acceptum* for *peractum*.]

But no one had been baptized in the Trinity; no one yet knew Christ; no one had heard that there was a Holy Spirit. But when the fullness of time came, at the appointed time the Son of God gave the laws of baptism and the way by which people might go to the kingdom of heaven. Then also he commanded, saying: “Go, teach all nations, baptizing them in the name of the Father and of the Son and of the Holy Spirit” (Matt. 28:19). From that day onward what was commanded had [p. 85] to be done. Before the time, he did not wish to correct what had been performed, lest he grant a licence for rebaptizing, although John’s baptism was one thing and Christ’s another.

[Col. 1055A] Before the law, he wished John’s baptism, though not complete, to count as complete for the time being.

[Note: [Col. 1055C] In MS S. T., “baptism” is joined to the preceding words and “John” is substituted for “John’s,” wrongly; for the question here is not John’s will but his baptism, which Christ wished to count as complete for a time.]

Yet he could not deny the kingdom of heaven to the aforementioned thousands of people because they had believed in God, even though they did not know the Son of God and the Holy Spirit. Hence the Son of God’s statement: “From the days of John until today the kingdom of God suffers violence, and those who use violence seize it” (Matt. 11:12).

[Note: [Col. 1055C] MS S. G. has “they possess it.”]

He said, “They use violence,” because John was still baptizing.

[Note: [Col. 1055C] These words are added from MS S. G.]

Thus there was one time before the commandments and another after the commandments. Those baptized after the commandments in the name of the Savior entered the kingdom under the laws; those before the commandments used force without law, but were not excluded.

[Note: [Col. 1055C] “Into the kingdom under the laws”: according to the prescribed form of Baptism. ALBASP.]

Therefore, before the commandments, John’s baptism, though incomplete, was judged complete by him whom no one judges.

[Col. 1055B] And as though a certain boundary of the command had been fixed between the earlier and subsequent periods, when some people at Ephesus were baptized with John’s baptism after the commandments, the most blessed Paul, seeing them, asked whether they had received the Holy Spirit (Acts 19:2). They told him that they did not know whether there was a Holy Spirit, and he told them that after John’s baptism they should receive the Holy Spirit. For they had been baptized as many had been baptized by John.

But those baptized before the law belonged to indulgence, because the one able to grant indulgence was present. They were not wholly guilty, since they had not been encompassed by the laws. But those who, after the law, are read to have been baptized at Ephesus with John’s baptism had erred in the sacrament after the laws, because [Col. 1055C] the Lord’s baptism had already been introduced and that of the servant excluded. Therefore, because after the divine commands they ought to go to the kingdom under the laws, not by violence, [Col. 1056A] Christ had already fixed the temporal boundary by saying: “From the days of John until today” (Matt. 11:12). After “today,” what had been permitted to happen was no longer permitted.

Therefore do not flatter yourselves with the saying of the Apostle Paul, who did not inquire after the person of the minister, but after the thing: it was the thing, not the person, that displeased him.

[Note: [Col. 1055C–1055D] “He did not inquire after the person of the minister.” Note the phrase *interrogare post aliquem*, “to inquire after someone,” and likewise on this page *insectari in aliquem*, “to attack someone.” Optatus sometimes uses redundant particles, as in Book V, *de foris* for *foris*, and elsewhere “to knock at heaven”; compare the phrase above, “to open toward the font.” ANONYMOUS.]

Accordingly, he commanded the Savior’s baptism, so that those who did not know might learn that they had received not it but something else. But what do you change?

[Note: [Col. 1055C] Thus MSS S. Th. and Ph. S.; MS S. G. has “what do you imitate?”]

If you have been able to change the thing, you will have acted rightly—provided that you have done something according to the law.

[Note: [Col. 1056C] MS S. G. has “you did.”]

Paul said: “With what baptism were you baptized?” (Acts 19:3). They replied, “John’s.” He persuaded them to receive Christ’s baptism. You do not say, “What did you receive?” but, “From whom did you receive it?” You attack human persons and wish to repeat what has been done once.

[Col. 1056B] Those baptized at Ephesus had believed in repentance and remission of sins.

[Note: [Col. 1055D] “They had believed in remission”: they had not believed in Father, Son, and Holy Spirit. ALBASP.]

They were rightly told to be baptized in the name of Father, Son, and Holy Spirit. But what do you change in people who have already said that they believe in the name of Father, Son, and Holy Spirit? Whether you ask the very same question or a different one, you must be convicted of sin: either you inquire about what was not commanded, or you wish to do what has already been done.

**VI. Reply to the claim: “How does one who does not have what to give give it?”**—I return now to your statement: “How does one who does not have what to give give it?” What is the source of this saying? From what reading can it be recited? It is a saying gathered from the street, not read from a book: “How does one who does not have what to give give it?”

[Note: [Col. 1056C] Thus in MS S. G. MSS S. T., P. S., and the printed editions have: “It is a saying from the street, not gathered from a book”; but the antithesis *collecta*, “gathered,” and *lecta*, “read,” has Optatus’s style.]

These words are not written in the Law.

[Note: [Col. 1056C] These words are supplied from MS S. G.; they do not occur in MSS S. T. and P. S.]

[Col. 1056C] For if, as you wish, a human being gives, God is inactive; and if God is inactive and [p. 86] everything to be given belongs to you, [Col. 1057A] let conversion be directed to you; let those whom you baptize be baptized in your name.

[Note: [Col. 1055D–1056D] “And if God is inactive, and among you is everything to be given,” etc. Reader, I ask you: could anything have been said more clearly by Optatus? Does not the matter itself cry out that he spoke properly about conversion to God? Yet there are those who refer it to some supposed turning of candidates for baptism—a practice which they do not prove, for turning east when about to profess faith pertains no more to those being baptized than to any others; and, even if they proved it, I should still deny that it applies here. Briefly, reader, I warn you that this word *conversio*, “conversion,” often occurs among ancient writers in three uses: concerning the conversion of Gentiles or heretics to God’s true worship or to true religion; concerning wicked and impious Christians converted to true piety, as in common modern usage; and concerning continent husbands, a use once no less common. The most learned Filesacus has collected many passages in his *Selecta*, though many more might be added. Notable is this passage of Salvian, *On the Governance of God*, Book V: “Just as those too are thought to have reflected somewhat on conversion and God who abstain from their own wives but do not abstain from seizing other people’s goods, etc. An entirely new kind of conversion: they do not do what is permitted, and they do what is forbidden. They refrain from intercourse and do not refrain from plunder, etc. What you do is perverse; this is not conversion but turning away,” etc. M. CASAUBON.]

[Note: [Col. 1056D] “Let conversion be directed to you.” He alludes to the rite and ceremony of baptism: after Satan had been breathed upon and renounced while facing west, candidates for baptism immediately turned east and solemnly professed their faith in God. Optatus therefore says that candidates for baptism ought to turn to you, rather than to God, because you wish baptism to work from the person of the baptizer, not from the faith which each professes. ALBASP.]

Be ashamed before the blessed Paul, who cries out and declares his own thanksgiving: “Were you baptized in my name?” (1 Cor. 1:3). He rejoices that he baptized only two persons and one household; but you strive to rebaptize whole peoples, and rejoice that you have sinned and continue to sin, saying: “What does one give who does not have what to give?” The one in whom faith is placed himself gives what is believed, not the person through whom faith is placed.

Finally, under John an innumerable multitude of people was baptized. Prove that John either received or possessed what he could give.

[Note: [Col. 1057C] “Prove that John possessed”: prove that John had remission of sins. ALBASP.]

Yet while he was acting as minister, God gave—God who does not cease by giving.

[Note: [Col. 1057C–1057D] “While he was acting as minister, God gave, who does not cease by giving.” This statement is plainly impious unless interpretation comes to its aid. To “cease by giving” means to cease to give. Thus he says “to cease by giving,” not because he recognizes any failure of power in the author, but of will. ANONYMOUS.]

And now, while all act as ministers, the works are human, but the gifts are God’s.

VII. The grace of baptism is God’s gift, not a human being’s, who is shown to be merely a worker. — Now how ridiculous is that which is always heard from you, as though it were to your credit: “This gift of baptism belongs to the giver, not to the recipient.” Would that you said this of God, who is the giver of this thing. But, absurdly, you say that you yourselves are the givers. If this is so, let both we and you each take hold of a pagan: you who call yourselves holy, ask the one you have taken whether he renounces the devil and believes in the Lord; and let him say, “I will not.” On the other hand, let us sinners—as you wish to call us—ask another pagan whether he renounces the devil and believes in God, and so forth; and let him say, “I renounce and believe,” and so forth. Then let you immerse the unwilling man, and us the willing one; and let it be said which of them can belong to the grace of God. Surely, without doubt, it is the one who believes, not the one for whose will, as you say, your holiness takes effect.

[Note: [Col. 1057C] In MSS S, T, and P.S., there is added here: “it follows.”]

[Note: [Col. 1057C] In MS S.G.: “has believed.”]

Recognize, even if late, that you are workers. Or, if the reality itself lies in the worker and not in the thing itself, let certain people claim this for themselves in their crafts. Since you provoke us thus, let us compare human crafts even with divine matters:

[Note: [Col. 1057D] In their crafts. Dyes, not people, change wool; thus water, not the person baptizing, changes the baptized person. ALBASP.]

When a costly dye is applied, nature is often transformed, while by the process of dyeing a white fleece becomes purple. Thus white wool passes into royal purple, just as a catechumen passes into a believer; certainly, when it begins to be what it was not, it ceases to be what it had been. Wool changes both its colour and its name; a human being also changes both name and mind. The results must be considered; the causes must be examined.

[Note: [Col. 1057D] “When a costly dye is applied,” etc. Radulphus Fornierius long ago observed that *confectione* (“by preparation/dyeing”), rather than *convectione*, should be read; *Rerum quotidianarum*, book II, chapter 6. Although this is not strictly proper usage—for wool is properly said to be *infici* (“dyed”), not *confici* (“made/prepared”), which is something else—yet that this is certainly Optatus’s reading is shown by its repetition shortly afterwards with only a few words intervening. I think the entire passage should be punctuated thus: “When a costly dye is applied, nature is often transformed, while by dyeing a white fleece becomes purple. Thus white wool passes into royal purple, just as a catechumen into a believer. Certainly when it begins,” etc. M. CASAUB. Thus restored from the MSS.]

[Note: [Col. 1058C] “While by conversion.” I do not know whether *commixtione* (“by mixing”) should be read. ALBASP. — In the same place: “While by *convectione* a white fleece becomes purple.” The worst possible reading, *ullus* in place of *vellus*, circulates, though this should be apparent even to a blind man. Barthius therefore reads *continctione* (“by dipping/dyeing”). *Contingere* is Lucretian; perhaps *confectione*. INCERT.]

[Note: [Col. 1057C] Thus in MSS S.T. and S.G.; wrongly in the editions: *convectione*.]

[Note: [Col. 1058D] “Thus white wool passes into royal purple.” Boethius: “Purple marks kings.” INCERT.]

[Note: [Col. 1058D] “Just as a catechumen.” An elegant comparison. ALBASP.]

[Note: [Col. 1058C] In MS S.T.: “unbeliever.”]

[Note: [Col. 1058D] Name. From pagan he becomes Christian. ALBASP.]

[Note: [Col. 1058D] And mind. Because he is reborn, both his mind and his nature are changed in the waters. ALBASP.]

You say that you have given what made the man a believer. If this is wholly yours, then let the craftsman who works purple say that he possesses the costly colour in his own hands, and does not procure the costly dyes, unknown to many, from the Ocean—dyes by which fleeces, once coloured, are advanced through their colour to a wondrous dignity. Let him produce purple by mere touch, without the admixture of the blood of a fish.

[Note: [Col. 1058D] Dyes from the Ocean: the blood of a fish caught in the Ocean. ALBASP.]

If, therefore, this workman cannot impart colour by touch alone, neither can the worker of baptism impart anything from himself without the Trinity.

[Note: [Col. 1058C] This word is absent from MS S.T., but is found in MS S.G.]

This is also the point now at issue. For the Saviour commanded in whose name the nations should be baptized; by whom they should be baptized, he made no distinction or exception. The Apostle did not say: “You do it; let others not do it.” Whoever baptizes in the name of the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit fulfils the work of the Apostles.

Finally, we read in the Gospel that John said: “Master, we saw someone casting out demons in your name, and we forbade him, because he does not follow with us.” Thus Christ said: “Do not forbid him; for whoever is not against you is for you” (Luke 9:37). For even they were commanded in such a way that the work was theirs, but the sanctification belonged to the Trinity; and they were not to immerse in their own name, but in the name of the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit. Therefore it is the Name that sanctifies, not the work.

[Note: [Col. 1058C] These words have been supplied from MS S.G.; they are absent from MSS S.T., P.S., and most editions.]

Understand, then, even if late, that you are workers, not masters. And if the Church is a vineyard, if human beings are the vines and the appointed cultivators, why do you rush into the master’s ownership? Why do you claim for yourselves what belongs to God? Why do you want the whole to be yours, where you cannot possess even a part?

For because of your arrogance, by which you swell against us, the most blessed Paul rebukes the Corinthians. Applying the circumstances of our own time to himself and Apollos, he says: “that none of you may be puffed up against another” (1 Cor. 4:6).

[Note: [Col. 1059C] In MSS S.T. and S.G.: “confirms.”]

To show that this entire sacrament of baptism belongs to God, so that the worker claims nothing for himself in it, he says: “I planted” (1 Cor. 3:6), that is, “I made a catechumen out of a pagan.” Apollos watered—that is, he baptized the catechumen. But God caused what had been planted and watered to grow.

[Note: [Col. 1059C] “I made a catechumen out of a pagan.” I instructed him. ALBASP.]

For anyone today who wishes to cultivate his vineyard hires a worker for an agreed wage. With bent back and sweating sides, the worker makes furrows in the earth in which to set selected shoots, and channels water over the trodden planting-holes. He can dig the hole and set the shoots; he can introduce water; but he cannot command that it take root. For it belongs to God alone to bring forth from the marrow of the vine-shoots roots that unite with the earth, and budding eyes that put forth the growth of leaves.

[Note: [Col. 1059C] In MS S.G.: “sweated out.”]

[Note: [Col. 1059C–1060D] “He can introduce water; he cannot command that it take root.” I do not sufficiently understand what these words—“command that it take root”—mean, or in what sense they concern the vineyard under discussion. Optatus’s intention, however, is clear enough: it does not lie within the power of the vineyard-tender that it should ripen or become tender—as Tertullian says generally of trees—and bear fruit; the whole matter depends on God. I think that the words “that it take root” are a gloss by some foolish person who did not grasp the elegance and proper force of the word *imperare* (“to command, direct”), and who, because water had just been mentioned, thought the passage should be supplied thus. For Optatus earlier used not dissimilar words when he called a reservoir worn away which neither has water nor can retain water received. Moreover, Vergil uses *imperare arvis*, “to direct/cultivate fields,” in *Georgics* I, and Seneca in the final chapter of *On Tranquillity of Mind*. For beginners, I shall quote Seneca’s passage, which excellently explains the force of a word not familiar to all: “Fertile fields must not be driven too hard; unceasing fertility will quickly exhaust them; so continual labour breaks the impulse of the mind.” Pliny uses the word properly of vines and vineyards, *Natural History* XVII.22: “It is rash to train a vine before it has attained the thickness of a thumb.” Columella likewise, *On Agriculture* IV.24: “After abundant fruit vines must be spared and therefore pruned narrowly; after scant fruit they must be worked hard.” One might also read: “he cannot direct the vineyard.” M. CASAUB.]

Finally, the blessed Apostle Paul, to restrain your presumption and arrogance, lest the worker of baptism should consider himself to possess mastery or claim for himself some share of so great a gift, declares that all belongs to God and says: “Neither the one who plants nor the one who waters is anything, but God alone, who brings to growth” (1 Cor. 3:7).

[Note: [Col. 1060D] “You are workers among others when the sun is entering,” etc. I write: “You are workers among others. When the sun enters”—that is, when the age is ended—etc. Matthew 20:8: *opsias de genomenēs* [ὀψίας δὲ γενομένης, “when evening came”], etc. What this has to do with the present passage seems to arise from a Hebrew idiom, which uses “come” or “enter” of the sun in the west, just as it uses “go out” of it in the east. M. CASAUB.]

You are workers among others when the sun is entering; that is, when the age is ended, on the day of recompense you may contend with us for the wage. Do not claim for yourselves the mastery of majesty.

For if it were so, let the servants who wait upon the Lord’s table also claim that gratitude for the hospitality shown should be returned to them by the invited guests. It is Christ’s voice that invites: “Come, blessed of my Father” (Matt. 25:34).

[Note: [Col. 1059C] MS S.G. adds the following words of Christ: “inherit the kingdom prepared for you from the foundation of the world.”]

The nations come to grace; he who deigned to invite provides the feast; the crowd of servants performs the ministry. Thanks ought to be rendered not to those who serve, but to him who feeds.

[Note: [Col. 1059C] In MS S.G.: “glory,” but less suitably; for Optatus is speaking of this present age. [Col. 1060C]]

You, though you are servants, shamelessly claim for yourselves complete mastery over the banquet; while the most blessed Paul humbly acknowledges himself and the others to be servants. Lest anyone should think that hope is to be placed in the Apostles or bishops alone, he says: “For what is Paul, or what is Apollos? Surely servants of him in whom you believed” (1 Cor. 3:4). Therefore, in all who serve there is not mastery, but ministry.

[Note: [Col. 1060C] In MS S.T.: “fellow-servants with us”; but “with us” is superfluous.]

You see, then, brother Parmenian, from the three kinds mentioned above, that the first, divided into three parts, is fixed, unconquered, and unchangeable; whereas the person of the ministering agent is temporary.

[Note: [Col. 1060C] In MS S.G.: “temporal.”]

VIII. On the faith of the recipient of baptism. — It remains now to say something about the merit of the believer, whose faith the Son of God placed before both his holiness and his majesty. For you cannot be holier than Christ. When that woman came to him whose daughter was dead and begged that she might be raised, he promised nothing concerning his own power; instead, he questioned another’s faith, so that, if the woman believed, the daughter would rise through the mother’s faith, whereas if she did not believe, the power of the Son of God would remain inactive and at rest.

[Note: [Col. 1060C] In MS S.G.: “through the mother’s faith.”]

The woman was questioned and answered that she believed what she requested could happen. She was ordered to go. Returning home, she found the girl alive whom she had left dead. She did not rush into kisses or hasten into embraces; rather, she returned to give thanks to the Saviour. And, in order that the Son of God might show that he himself had remained inactive and faith alone had acted, he said: “Go, woman, in peace; your faith has saved you” (Luke 8:48).

Where, then, is your assertion that it belongs to the giver, not the recipient? And what do you think of the centurion’s faith? When his servant was ill, he asked the Saviour to drive death away from him. Christ was already coming to the dying servant; but the centurion restrained him, confessing that his roof was unworthy for the Son of God to enter bodily, and asking him instead to send his power, by which the servant, death driven away, might return to life. The centurion’s courage was not praised, nor his wisdom, but his faith; and the servant was healed in that hour (Matt. 8:13). Certainly it belongs to the giver, not the recipient.

[Note: [Col. 1060D–1061D] “And the servant was healed in that hour; certainly it belongs to the giver,” etc. The same point is repeated shortly afterwards; yet anyone who examines carefully will see that in both places this conflicts with Optatus’s thought. It would therefore be better to say: “Certainly it does not belong to the giver, but to the recipient.” Someone may perhaps reply that Optatus was not so much disputing with the Donatists about these exact words as about the impious doctrine with which they uttered them. Thus nothing prevented him from using their words with a meaning other than theirs; for earlier, when he throws these words at them, he immediately adds: “Would that you said this of God, who is the giver of this thing; but, absurdly, you say that you yourselves are the givers.” Thus here Optatus is not attempting to prove against the Donatists that it belongs to the recipient, but that it belongs to the giver—not the one they intended, namely the minister or worker, but God himself. Nor does his attribution to faith prevent him from ascribing the matter to God as well, since whatever is obtained from God through faith in God may rightly be said to proceed wholly from God and to be credited to him alone. Although we do not deny that this can truly be said, I do not think this was Optatus’s intention when he explicitly says that God remained inactive, that faith alone acted, that he promised nothing of his own power, but questioned another’s faith. Is “certainly,” then, a sort of ironic concession—“Certainly it belongs to the giver,” etc.? Or is it interrogative: “Certainly? Does it belong to the giver, not the recipient?” M. CASAUB.]

There are many such cases in the Gospel concerning perfect faith, but three testimonies to faith must at least be set forth. What do you think of that woman who, concerning the secret matter peculiar to women, had suffered for twelve years and spent all her substance on physicians? When she saw such great miracles being performed by the Son of God, she entered the crowd. She saw the physician and saw the people. Pain compelled her to seek healing; modesty prevented her from disclosing her condition before men. Silent faith found a plan: “I shall stretch out my hand,” she said, “and touch the fringe of this garment, and I shall be healed” (Matt. 9:21; Luke 8:43).

[Note: [Col. 1061D] “Concerning the secret matter.” Tertullian calls the intimacies of marriage “secrets.” Such indecent matters were explained in this fashion if one encountered a catechumen. This example can apply to a catechumen who rejected faith; but from it one will not prove that the person baptizing contributes more than the sacrament. ALBASP.]

Unseen amid the crowds, she stretched out her hand, touched it, and was healed; nor did she dare reveal what she had not dared to request.

[Note: [Col. 1061C] We have supplied this word from MS S.G.]

But lest the fruit of faith should seem hidden from those who were unaware, the Saviour said: “Who touched me?” His disciples marvelled and said: “The crowds press upon you, and you say, ‘Who touched me?’” And Christ said: “Who, I say, touched me? I felt power go out from me” (ibid., 45). Thus the woman confessed that she had touched him and was healed.

Earlier, a mother petitioned for her daughter; the centurion made request for his servant. In this case neither did the woman ask nor Christ promise; rather, faith obtained as much as it presumed. Certainly it belongs to the giver, not the recipient.

[Note: [Col. 1061C] In MS S.G.: “as much as it presumed for itself.”]

[Note: [Col. 1061C] After these words MS S.G. contains several periods presenting a new argument against repeated baptism. I consider them to be Optatus’s, although they are not found in MSS S.T. and P.S.; but they seem to have been placed here out of order. We have therefore moved them to the end of the book, which they conclude admirably.]

IX. The comparison of Naaman the Syrian, inappropriately introduced by Parmenian. — But as for your wishing, brother Parmenian, to describe at length Naaman the Syrian as though he were some immature mass of very hard, newly developing wounds, merely to amplify your arguments, what does this have to do with the present case?

[Note: [Col. 1062C] In MS S.G.: “to apply,” less well.]

You would say this well, and could rightly employ a long discourse, if you found some catechumen of exceedingly rough habits, bearing a very hard disposition, who refused to receive the very gentle grace of saving water. You would properly demonstrate by your words the renewal of a human being; you would properly show that an inveterate, natural hardness can be changed and softened into infant flesh.

[Note: [Col. 1062C] He means exceedingly rough habits. INCERT.]

[Note: [Col. 1062C] Renewal: regeneration. ALBASP.]

[Note: [Col. 1062C] In MSS S.T. and P.S.: “into infant flesh.”]

But in this matter, which is now under discussion between the parties, why has such a reading been recalled by you?

[Note: [Col. 1062C–1062D] “In which one does not read that anyone had previously washed that leprous Syrian,” etc. Other editions read: “In which one does not read that anyone had washed that leprous Syrian previously mentioned, either by Elisha’s command,” etc. I write: “In which one does not read that anyone had washed that leprous Syrian previously mentioned, or that Elisha had commanded him,” etc. He seems to say the same thing again shortly afterwards. Yet we may defend him from the fault of tautology if, as his words more carefully considered suggest, we punctuate thus: “One does not altogether read that anyone had washed him, from which we might infer that he was washed again in order to be washed better. Nor is there such necessity in this inference that it would suffice for you if the former statement were read, unless the latter too were expressly stated: that he was washed again because the first washing had achieved nothing. Yet even if this itself were read, you would still not establish your case; for if it had happened, it would have happened not to distinguish persons, but waters, and in testimony to the future pre-eminence, above the rest, of the river Jordan.” M. CASAUB.]

In that passage one does not read that anyone had previously washed that leprous Syrian, whether by Elisha’s command or otherwise, so that he might deservedly be washed again and better (4 Kings [2 Kings] 5).

[Note: [Col. 1062C] Absent from MS S.G.]

Even if this had happened, you would still have nothing that you could rightly imitate.

[Note: [Col. 1062C] These words are absent from MS S.T.]

For one does not read that he had first washed in the rivers of Syria, or had been washed by anyone and gained no benefit. Even if this were read, it would pertain not to Elisha’s praise—for he did not wash him, but gave advice—but to the glory of the Jordan; namely, that the man received original grace in that river in which, later, under John, the sins of the people were to die through the confession of repentance.

[Note: [Col. 1062C] In MS S.G.: “to the grace of the Jordan itself.”]

[Note: [Col. 1062C] In MS S.G.: “through the profession of the people’s repentance, their sins were to die.”]

X. The parable of the wedding wrongly cited by Parmenian. — Finally, what sort of part of your discourse is that concerning the heavenly wedding-feast? By saying that the person who has deceived your gatekeepers and ministers has been cast from your fellowship and sent outside the communion of believers with disgrace, you have cut off hope of the future and placed everything in the present time.

If this is so, there is nothing for faith to hope for; nothing for the resurrection to bring into presence; nothing more to await in heaven; nothing for that heavenly King and householder, God, to recognize at his banquet, while he rejoices in the presence of many and grieves at the absence of some. And when he says that many are called but few chosen, there will be nothing for him to be angry about in one who does not have the wedding garment.

[Note: [Col. 1062D] The resurrection brings into presence the kingdom of God and blessedness. ALBASP.]

[Note: [Col. 1062C] This has been added from MS S.G.]

[Note: [Col. 1063B] In MS S.G.: “at the presence.”]

[Note: [Col. 1063B] In MS S.G.: “that.”]

[Note: [Col. 1063B–1064C] “Since the Son of God, Christ himself, is the bridegroom,” etc. Do not let this mislead you as though it supplied the reason for the preceding words. Optatus is not giving the reason for what precedes, but continues the same argument, incidentally adding a description and mystical identification of that garment—namely, Christ himself, etc. I think the text should be read thus: “There was nothing for him to be angry about in one who did not have the wedding garment, since the Son of God himself is both bridegroom, garment, and tunic, swimming in water—that is, baptized, as he interprets it immediately below, and as elsewhere he repeatedly calls them ‘born’—who clothes many and awaits countless others,” etc. So too, among others, Victor of Vita, *On the Vandal Persecution*, book III, says of a certain apostate Elpidophorus: “For he had formerly been baptized among us in the church of Faustus; the venerable deacon Macarius had received him from the basin of the font, brought forth [*generatum*].” I mention this all the more willingly because I would have his words compared with Optatus, since not only does there occur in him a twofold and fuller exposition of this parable of the wedding garment which follows shortly in Optatus, but he also mentions the *sabana* or linen cloths, by which it was formerly customary to gird and cover those newly baptized; these too seem relevant to the interpretation of the same parable. M. CASAUB. The passage has been restored by us.]

For the Son of God, Christ himself, is the bridegroom (Matt. 22), and the garment and tunic swimming in the water, which clothes many and awaits countless others, nor is exhausted by clothing them. But lest anyone say that I have rashly called the Son of God a garment, let him read the Apostle saying: “As many of you as have been baptized in the name of Christ have put on Christ” (Gal. 3:27).

[Note: [Col. 1063B] In MS S.G.: “have clothed yourselves.”]

O tunic, always one and unchangeable, which fittingly clothes every age and form: neither wrinkled upon infants, nor stretched upon the young, nor changed upon women!

[Note: [Col. 1064C] Countless. He elegantly calls Christ’s one tunic “one.” INCERT.]

[Note: [Col. 1064C] “It is wrinkled”: it is too loose. ALBASP.]

[Note: [Col. 1064C] “It is changed upon women”: it fits and can be adapted to women and men alike. ALBASP.]

That day will surely come when the heavenly wedding-feast begins to be celebrated. There those who have preserved the single baptism will recline in security. For whoever has consented to be rebaptized by you is not denied resurrection, because he believed in the resurrection of the flesh; indeed he will rise, but naked. Yet because he allowed you to strip him of the wedding garment, he will hear this voice of the householder:

[Note: [Col. 1064C] “Friend,” that is, “I acknowledge you,” etc. Nothing is more confused than these several lines as printed here and commonly printed; nor are they free from error. Write therefore, on my assurance: “Friend”—that is to say, “I acknowledge you,” and therefore I call you friend, of course—“because you had once renounced the devil and turned to me, and I had given you a wedding garment: why have you come thus, not having the wedding garment?” That is to say: “Why do you not have what I gave you?” For no one can be angry with someone for not having a thing that was never given. “You had received the wedding garment among those people, and alone you do not have it? Why have you come naked and mournful? Who stripped you of your garments? What deceitful jaws did you approach? What robbers did you encounter?” M. CASAUB. The passage has been restored by us.]

“Friend”—that is to say, “I recognize you: once you had renounced the devil and turned to me, and I had given you a wedding garment. Why have you come thus, not having what I gave you?” That is to say: “Why do you not have what I gave you?” For no one can be angry with a person for not possessing a thing that was not given. You had received the wedding garment among those people, and you alone do not have it? Why have you come naked and mournful? Who stripped you of your garments? What deceitful jaws did you approach? What robbers did you encounter?”

All who will come in such a condition will have no place at that banquet.

[Note: [Col. 1063B] MS S.G. adds: “by this example.”]

[Note: [Col. 1063B–1064B] Here the fifth book ends in all the manuscripts, with the subscription: “The fifth book ends.” What follows belongs to this book and appears to be its conclusion; we have added it from codex S.G., in which it stood above in a place not its own, as we observed.]

XI. Since the Donatists cannot rebaptize dead infants, why do they rebaptize the living? — And, to make a summary at last, I think even this should suffice, even if we had not stated so many proofs. In your absence, a thousand people were baptized, merely in word; of these, a hundred have died according to their lot. For a little while, hold your hands back from this crime. Let your holiness, as you call it, first raise the buried dead; let it correct the dead, if it can; and then return to the living. If you cannot raise the dead, why do you attempt to lay hands upon the living? Unless it be to fulfil what God spoke through the prophet Ezekiel, saying: “so that they might kill souls which ought not to die” (Ezek. 13:19).

90. BOOK SIX. In this sixth book it is shown that the bishops of Donatus’s party, contrary to the law, broke altars, rashly melted down and everywhere sold vessels of the Lord, washed things that ought not to have been washed, and exchanged head-coverings for girls—matters concerning which no Scripture is read.

[Col. 1063D] I. [Note: [Col. 1064D] [[Col. 1063D] This note appears at the foot of column 1064, but the callout letter (c) has not been printed in the text.] In MS S. G. there is added here: “may have been committed.”] The Donatists impiously and foolishly broke or scraped the altars. — As it seems to me [Note: [Col. 1063D] Thus in MS S. G., far better than in MSS S. T. and P. S. [Col. 1064D] and in the printed editions, “Indubitably, clearly.”], it has been clearly demonstrated what wicked things you committed in the divine sacraments. [Col. 1064D] Now we must show those things which you did cruelly and foolishly, and which you will in no way be able to deny.

For what is so sacrilegious as to break, scrape, or remove the altars of God—upon which you yourselves too once [Col. 1065A] offered? Upon them both [Note: [Col. 1065C] *The vows of the people.* The vows of the people were brought by the bishop and offered at the altar. ALBASP.] the vows of the people and [Note: [Col. 1065C] *The members of Christ.* Besides the body of Christ which is offered upon the altar, the faithful too, who are united and made one with that same body, are offered. ALBASP.] the members of Christ were borne; there almighty God was invoked; there the Holy Spirit was petitioned to descend; and there many received both [Note: [Col. 1065C] *The pledge of eternal salvation.* From Saint Paul: “He will also give life to your mortal bodies through his Spirit dwelling in you.” ALBASP.] the pledge of eternal salvation, the safeguard of faith, and [Note: [Col. 1065C] *The hope of resurrection.* The Spirit of God is preserved within us, by whose power our bodies will rise. To the Ephesians: “Having believed, you were sealed with the Holy Spirit of promise, who is the pledge of our inheritance.” Note the manner of expression in “received by many”: that is, many received the Holy Spirit through prayers made at the altar, as in a more solemn place, and where God wills to be entreated. ALBASP.] the hope of resurrection.

Those altars, I say, [Note: [Col. 1065C] *Upon which the gifts of brotherhood.* The passage is to be understood of the offerings of the faithful which were consecrated upon the altar. From this it is clear that all the faithful formerly brought offerings and that these were consecrated upon the altar. ALBASP.] upon which the Saviour commanded that no gifts of brotherhood should be laid [Note: [Col. 1065B] MSS S. T. and P. S. have “placed.”] unless they had been established in peace: “Lay down,” he says, “your gift before the altar, and first return and be reconciled with your brother, that the priest may offer for you” (Matt. 5:24). For what is an altar [Note: [Col. 1065D] *Except the seat of the body.* Because from those offerings the body of Christ was made. ALBASP.] except the seat of both the body and blood of Christ? All these things your fury either scraped away, broke, or removed.

Therefore, if this inexpiable crime proceeded upon any rationale, it ought to have been done in one manner. But, as I suppose, in one place abundance of timber commanded that they should break them [Note: [Col. 1065B] These words and those following, down to “commanded,” occur in MS S. G. and are absent from MS S. T.]; in other places scarcity of timber commanded that they should [Col. 1065B] scrape the altars; while in still others [Note: [Col. 1065D] *Shame.* Namely, lest they should appear to communicate with the Orthodox; and this for two reasons: first, because they would have approved the Orthodox consecration if they offered upon an altar consecrated by them; second, because one who offers upon an altar upon which bishops have offered appears to communicate with them, since the altar is the seat of offerings, the place where the offering ought to be made and to which God gives greater regard. ALBASP.] shame persuaded them to remove them [Note: [Col. 1065B] Thus in MS S. G. MSS S. T. and P. S. have “commanded.”]. Yet everywhere it is a crime, since you laid sacrilegious and impious hands upon so great a thing. [Note: [Col. 1065D] *So great a thing:* the altars. ALBASP.] 91 Why should I recount the hired mob of ruined men and the wine given as payment for their crime? [Note: [Col. 1065D] “That it might be drunk with an unclean work,” etc. Write, “with an unclean mouth,” on the authority of Fr. Balduin’s repeated edition. UNCERTAIN.] So that it might be drunk with a polluted mouth in sacrilegious draughts, hot water was made from fragments of the altars. [Note: [Col. 1066C] *Hot water was made from fragments of the altars.* On the ancient use of hot water, both mixed and unmixed, many authors have already said much. Yet since there are very learned men who interpret *calida* otherwise and maintain that the ancients customarily heated water either not at all, or only for the benefit of the sick or infirm, this passage deserves the reader’s attention; it alone may suffice to refute that opinion. M. CASAUB.] [Note: [Col. 1066C] *Hot water was made.* That it might be mixed with wine; for the use of hot water was common among the ancients. DU PIN.]

If, in the judgment of envy, we seemed defiled to you, what had God done to you, who was customarily [Col. 1066A] invoked there? What had Christ offended you, whose body and blood dwelt there [Note: [Col. 1066C] *At fixed intervals:* where the body of Christ was at some time reserved. ALBASP.] at fixed [Note: [Col. 1066B] MSS S. T. and P. S. have “the rest.”] times? [Note: [Col. 1066C] *What had we offended you?* The Donatists later returned the basilicas which they had received from Julian; he speaks of their altars. ALBASP.] What had you yourselves offended, that you should break those altars upon which, before us, you had offered for long periods of time, holily, as you suppose? While you impiously persecute [Note: [Col. 1066C] *Our hands:* our sacrifices and yours. ALBASP.] our hands in the place where Christ’s body dwelt, you struck your own hands as well.

In this manner you have imitated the Jews: they laid hands upon Christ [Note: [Col. 1066C] *On the cross.* The cross is the altar of the bloody sacrifice, whereas our altars are of the unbloody sacrifice; therefore he rightly argues from the cross to altars. ALBASP.] upon the cross; by you he was struck upon the altar. If you wished to assail Catholics there, you should at least have spared your own [Note: [Col. 1066C] *Former offerings.* Offerings made upon those altars in the time of Saint Cyprian belonged no less to the Donatists [Col. 1066D] than to the Orthodox. He seems to have referred to them when he said “former.” ALBASP.] former offerings there. You are now found proud [Note: [Col. 1066D] *Proud.* From Donatus’s pride the others could be called proud; but, unless I am mistaken, he calls them proud here because they boasted themselves pure, and while all presbyters during the sacred rites called themselves sinners and priests unworthy of so great a sacrifice, they professed themselves *Cathars*, “the Pure.” ALBASP.] where long ago you offered humbly; you gladly sin where you had been accustomed to pray for the sins of many.

By doing this, you gladly entered the number of sacrilegious priests, joined in the crimes of the profane men concerning whom the prophet Elijah lodges a complaint before [Col. 1066B] the Lord. [Note: [Col. 1066B] MS S. G. has: “Before God a complaint is lodged by the prophet Elijah.”] For he spoke these words concerning them, by which you too deserved to be accused by him among others: “Lord,” he says, “they have broken down thy altars” (3 Kings 11:10). By saying “thy,” he indicates that the thing is God’s wherever anything has been offered to God by anyone.

It would have sufficed for your madness that you tore apart the members of the Church, that you divided by your seductions the peoples of God, long ago established in unity. Amid all this, you ought at least to have spared the altars. [Note: [Col. 1066D] *Why vows?* Note the eminent praises and names of altars: the seat of Christ’s body; the ladder of prayers; the way of petitions; the ascent of supplications; the dwelling of Christ’s body; the place of invocation; Christ’s altar; Christ’s cross; the place of gifts; the bearer of Christ’s members; the descent and gate of the Holy Spirit. ALBASP. *Ibid., Why the vows and desires of human beings,* etc.: Fr. Balduin. UNCERTAIN.] Why [Col. 1067A] did you break the vows and [Note: [Col. 1067C] *Desires.* See whether the old glossary is relevant here: *desiderata*, λειτουργία, τελετή—“service, rite.” UNCERTAIN.] desires of human beings together with the altars themselves? For from there the people’s prayer used to ascend to the ears of God. Why did you cut down the path of prayers? And, lest supplication might have its customary ascent to God, did you labor with impious hand, as it were, to draw away the ladder?

And yet, though all of you have one [Note: [Col. 1067C] *Conspiracy.* Since all hold the same opinion on this subject, why did you determine so differently concerning altars? ALBASP.] conspiracy, in this charge you sinned differently through a similar error. [Note: [Col. 1067C] Thus read: “If it was enough to remove them, it was unlawful to break them. If it was necessary to break them, it was sinful to transfer them. It was sinful to scrape them,” from the second edition of Fr. Balduin. UNCERTAIN.] If it was enough to remove them, it was unlawful to break them; if it was necessary [Note: [Col. 1067B] Here begins MS Saint-Paul of Cormery, now Colbert Library no. 1951.] to break them, it was sinful to scrape them. [Note: [Col. 1067C] *It was sinful to scrape them.* Because the greater part remains, even if you scrape it; and when you offer upon it together with us, you communicate with us, and thus sin. ALBASP.] For if it was not lawful, as was agreed among you, it seems right that he broke them who did break them. [Note: [Col. 1067C] Write: “For if it was unlawful; if, as was agreed among you, it seems right,” etc. Here too Optatus seems to have admitted a certain tautology (ταυτολογία), which would be very easy to remove by a slight alteration. Yet it is sometimes better to tolerate certain things than to be excessively acute in the writings of others. In the next period I wonder how *majestatis* (“majesty”) entered this edition in place of the earlier *vetustatis* (“antiquity”). For far be it from us to believe Balduin so dull of perception that he failed to see that the whole point, one of no ordinary subtlety, depends on that single word. Although what we commonly call “our ancestors” was called “our ancients” by some, such as Varro in the satire entitled *The Burial of Menippus*, I do not think that anyone ever used *majesty* for antiquity or oldness, or that this occurred to those through whom *majestatis* came to be read here in place of *vetustatis*. M. CASAUB.] [Note: [Col. 1067B] Thus in the Colbert and S. G. MSS. Others have “who may have broken them.”]

Now he is guilty who, by scraping, preserved the greater part. What is this new and foolish wisdom—to seek newness [Note: [Col. 1067D] *In the inmost parts of majesty.* In the German edition: “of antiquity.” But the word *majesty* can be retained, and the sense is this: the altar is a divine thing; when you have scraped off its first skin, that which grows again is divine too, because the entire object is divine. Thus you seek newness in the inmost parts of a divine thing, but will not find it, [Col. 1068C] because it is wholly divine, including its inmost parts. ALBASP. Thus restored from the MSS. *Ibid., In the inmost parts of antiquity.* The same Balduin edition has “majesty.” UNCERTAIN.] in the inmost parts of antiquity [Note: [Col. 1067B] Thus in all MSS. Incorrectly, “majesty,” in the latest edition.]? And, as though a certain skin of the body had been removed, to seek, in the hidden body, another sort of skin. [Note: [Col. 1068C] *To seek newness in the inmost parts of antiquity.* Underlying Optatus’s words is this thought: What good does it do you, Donatists, to scrape altars, as though by scraping you could renew and alter them? The inmost parts—that is, the interior parts—of the altar are old; nevertheless you wish, by scraping off the exterior, to seek newness in them, as though, having removed the outer skin of a body, you sought another skin in its interior parts. DU PIN.]

A gift [Note: [Col. 1068C] The same edition does not recognize any of these words. UNCERTAIN. This passage has been restored by us.] [Note: [Col. 1067B] Thus in the Colbert and S. G. MSS. MSS S. T. and P. S., and certain printed editions, have “until.”] which, so far as it concerns itself, is entire in itself because it is one, [Note: [Col. 1068C] *Gift.* The consecration of an altar is one and indivisible. Hence, when you remove something from an altar, you may diminish the altar, but not alter it—that is, make a consecrated thing impure or an impure thing sacred. [Col. 1068D] DU PIN.] [Col. 1067B] may be diminished when something is taken from it, but cannot be altered. [Note: [Col. 1067B] Thus in the Colbert and S. G. MSS. Others have, “cannot be changed.”] You scraped off what seemed fit to you; but what you hate is still there.

What if you have conspired in this way, so that things touched by us in God’s name [Note: [Col. 1068D] *In the very ministry.* The same edition has “mystery.” UNCERTAIN.] in the very ministry might appear impure? Who among the faithful does not know that, in the celebration of the mysteries, [Col. 1068A] the very wood is covered with [Note: [Col. 1068D] *A linen cloth.* In former times altars were covered and adorned with consecrated and sanctified linens. ALBASP.] a linen cloth? During the sacraments the covering might be touched, not the wood; or, if coverings can be penetrated by touch, then the wood too is penetrated; if the wood can be penetrated, the earth too is penetrated. If the wood is scraped by you, then let the earth beneath be dug up: [Note: [Col. 1068D] *Make a deep pit.* Lucan too uses *scrobs*, “pit,” as feminine in Book VIII:

> “Trembling, he laid the noble body in a shallow pit.”

Elsewhere it is generally masculine. UNCERTAIN.] make a deep pit while, according to your own judgment, you seek purity. But take heed lest you come to hell and find there the schismatics Korah, Dathan, and Abiram—your masters, that is (Num. 15).

It is therefore established that you both broke and scraped the altars. Why then did your fury in this matter afterward seem, as it were, to languish? [Note: [Col. 1067C] Thus in the Colbert and S. G. MSS. MSS S. T. and P. S. have “suddenly.”] For we see [Note: [Col. 1068B] MS S. T. has “we saw.”] that afterward you changed your policy, and that altars were no longer broken or scraped [Note: [Col. 1068B] Thus in MSS C. and S. G. MSS S. T. and Ph. S. have “but scraped,” which does not cohere with what precedes.] by you, but only removed. If this was enough, the things formerly done by you themselves pronounce judgment upon you [Note: [Col. 1068B] Thus in the MSS. Printed editions have “you judge.”], since they ought in no way to have been done.

[Col. 1068B] II. The Donatists sacrilegiously broke and sold chalices. — Yet you doubled this monstrous crime when you broke even the chalices, bearers of Christ’s blood [Note: [Col. 1068B] Thus in MSS C. and S. G.; incorrectly *portitores* in MSS S. T. and P. S.], whose forms [Note: [Col. 1068D] *Forms:* parts. ALBASP.] you reduced to masses of metal, obtaining merchandise by wicked trafficking. [Note: [Col. 1068D] The second edition of Fr. Balduin has, “procuring merchandise by wicked trafficking.” UNCERTAIN.] [Note: [Col. 1068B] Thus in MSS C. and S. G. MSS S. T. and P. S. have “seeking payment by wicked trafficking.”] You were unwilling even to select buyers for that merchandise. [Note: [Col. 1068D] *Select.* You ought to have sold them to Christians, lest pagans should purchase them for filthy uses. ALBASP.] You were greedy in selling them [Note: [Col. 1068B] We have supplied these words from MSS C. and S. G.]; sacrilegious in selling them heedlessly. [Note: [Col. 1068C] MSS C. and S. G. have “you committed sacrilege.”] [Col. 1069A]

[Note: [Col. 1069C] *You even allowed your hands to be burned,* by which, etc. I conjectured: “You would even have allowed your hands to be expiated by the very fire in which the sacred vessels were melted,” etc. But earlier he had said: “While you impiously persecute our hands in the place where Christ’s body dwelt, you struck (*feritis*? or *feristis*, by contraction for *feriistis*?) your own also.” And below likewise: “The altars and vessels mentioned above had long been both in your hands and ours. If you defame our hands, why do you condemn yours there too?” Perhaps here also he means the same thing by *inconsiderate*, “heedlessly,” as he did shortly before by *passim*, “indiscriminately,” and as follows below: either, as Optatus himself means, that no buyer was selected and no distinction was made among buyers—pious or impious, pagan or Christian. M. CASAUB.]

You even allowed your hands to be burned, [Note: [Col. 1069C] *To have your hands burned.* The chalices were melted in which you offered and consecrated Christ’s blood. ALBASP.] [Note: [Col. 1069D] Hands are considered to be burned when the vessels which they handled are burned. In the same sense he earlier said: “While you impiously persecute our hands where Christ’s body dwelt, you struck your own hands as well.” Here too *to burn* is understood as *to strike* was there; and below likewise: “If you defame our hands, why do you condemn yours there too?” DU PIN.] with which you handled those same chalices before us. When you ordered that thing to be sold indiscriminately [Note: [Col. 1069B] The MSS have “yet”; the printed editions, “however.”], perhaps filthy women bought them for their own uses; pagans bought them, intending to make vessels in which they might burn incense for their idols. O unspeakable wickedness! O unheard-of crime! To take from God what you provide to idols; to withdraw from Christ what may serve sacrilege.

III. The Donatists’ excuse is refuted: that the altars and sacred vessels had been defiled by Catholics. — But I see that in this matter you falsely manufacture odium against us and wish to flee to the prophet Haggai, where it is written: “What the defiled person touches is defiled” (Hag. 2:14). When envy intervenes, it is easy for angry persons to hurl abuse; but whenever an accusation is brought, clear proof is necessary. [Col. 1069B] For which of us entered temples? Who saw sacrilegious rites?

[Note: [Col. 1069D] *People can be defiled by sacrilegious smoke,* etc. The earlier text has: “People can be defiled by fumes, smells, sacrilegious blood.” I think Optatus wrote: “People can be defiled by sacrilegious fumes,” or “by sacrilegious smells, by the blood of a sacrilegious sacrifice,” etc. M. CASAUB.] People can be defiled by fumes, smells, sacrileges, sacrifices, blood; but in this case who entered a temple? Who burned offerings to idols? Who was stained by impure fumes? Who saw the blood either of an unclean beast or of a human being shed? Whom do you prove to have given counsel for any crime? Convict even one bishop, if you can, of partnership [Note: [Col. 1069B] MSS C. and S. G. have “into partnership.”] in any crime.

You conjecture about some Primate, who was said to have been walking about at the same time. [Note: [Col. 1069C] All this, down to the words “as we said above,” has been supplied from MSS C. and S. G.; it is omitted in MSS [Col. 1070B] S. T. and P. S., as well as in the printed editions.] Suspicion is not an adequate accusation. Who accused him? Who convicted him? Where [Col. 1070A] 93 did he either blush or stand confounded? Keep your suspicions to yourselves.

Therefore, as we said above, we have shown that in this matter whatever harsh action could have been done, when that affair [Note: [Col. 1069D] *At its origin.* He speaks of the unity established through Macarius, which must be referred back to Donatus as to Arius. ALBASP.] is traced back to its origin, belongs to your leaders. Why then do you call Catholics defiled? Is it because we followed the will and command of God, loving peace, communicating with the whole world, [Note: [Col. 1070C] *Joined with the Easterners.* They regarded Africans, Spaniards, Gauls, and Italians as suspect because they had condemned Donatus and communicated with Caecilian. But they could invent nothing at all against the Easterners; therefore Optatus very frequently reproaches them with not communicating with the Easterners, against whom they had nothing to say. ALBASP.] joined with the Easterners? There Christ was born according to his human nature; there his holy footprints were impressed; there walked the feet worthy of adoration; there the Son of God himself performed so many and such great miracles; there so many apostles accompanied him; there is the sevenfold Church, from which you have been cut off—and not only do you not grieve, but in some measure rejoice.

Because we have loved unity pleasing to God, [Note: [Col. 1070C] The same edition has “we have loved.” UNCERTAIN.] [Col. 1070B] [Note: [Col. 1070C] MSS S. T. and P. S. have “we have.”] you call us defiled. [Note: [Col. 1070C] MSS S. T. and P. S. have the singular, “you call.”] Because we gave our assent to the Corinthians, Galatians, and Thessalonians [Note: [Col. 1070C] *We gave our assent.* Because we communicated with them; for there is no greater communion than through assent, as Saint Augustine says against the Donatists. ALBASP.] and joined in communion, you call us defiled. Because we do not read with you stolen readings, [Note: [Col. 1070C] *Stolen:* corrupted readings of Scripture; or he calls them stolen because, since they did not communicate with the Churches to which Saint Paul’s epistles were written, they seemed [Col. 1070D] to steal them. ALBASP.] you call us defiled. Or deny, if you can, that you read texts belonging to others. [Note: [Col. 1070D] *Belonging to others.* If you do not read stolen readings, prove that you do not read texts belonging to others when you read the sacred epistles. But you cannot prove this, because you do not communicate with the Churches to which those epistles were written. ALBASP.]

Why do you dare to read Epistles written to the Corinthians when you refused to communicate with the Corinthians? Why do you recite writings addressed to the Galatians and Thessalonians, when you are not in their communion? Since all this is plainly so, understand that you have been cut off from the holy Church and that we are not defiled. Where, then, is the help which you think the prophet Haggai can give you? [Col. 1071A]

[Note: [Col. 1071B] *Therefore your altars mentioned above.* Correct from the more complete Book I of Fr.
