[Note: [Col. 1072C] **Mitellas.** A *mitra* or *mitella* is generally a kind of band or fillet by which something is encircled. In Homer it is used for a military girdle, by which the loins and belly were bound. In Herodotus, Euripides, Moschus, and other Greek writers, μίτρα means a band wound around the head. In Latin *mitra* has the same meaning. Cicero, *For Rabirius Postumus*: “For the sake of luxury and pleasure, we often see not only Roman citizens and noble young men, and even some senators born in the highest rank, wearing a *mitella*, not in their gardens or suburban estates, but at Naples, a most famous town.” Latin poets—Virgil, Propertius, Juvenal, [Col. 1072D] and Claudian—mention mitres and mitellas with which especially women’s heads were encircled. As Servius observes on *Aeneid* IX, “mitres are for women what caps are for men.” Tertullian, in *On the Veiling of Virgins*: “It is Christ,” he says, “who commands both other men’s brides and married women to be veiled—certainly much more his own. But we warn you women who have entered marriage, of another kind of chastity: do not so outgrow the veil . . . For some, with mitres and woollen coverings, do not veil their heads, but bind them up; protected at the forehead, where the head properly is, they leave it bare. Others cover themselves moderately with little cloths, I suppose lest their heads be pressed, and, with these not let down as far as the ears, cover only to the brain.” From this passage of Tertullian it may be understood that mitres or mitellas were an ornament both of married women, as he calls them, and of virgins betrothed to God. From it one may also infer how the mitella was a sign of professed virginity: namely, because those mitres were not worn by every virgin. For most virgins in Africa were not veiled before marriage, as appears from this work of Tertullian; and, even if they were veiled, they did not have mitres like married women, as did those who had professed virginity. The mitre, therefore, was a sign of virginity. Observe also that already in Tertullian’s time these mitres were woollen. **DU PIN.**] and receive others. [Note: [Col. 1072B] In manuscripts S. ## V. Sacred Books and the Lord’s Furnishings Violently Taken from Catholics by the Donatists

[Note: [Col. 1076D] **Through secular judgments.** This must be referred to the times of Julian, who ordered basilicas and sacred codices to be restored to the Donatists. **ALBASP.**] Through secular judgments and public laws you thought that the instruments of the divine law [Note: [Col. 1076D] **“By the enforcement of officials, to be extorted by many,” etc.** What does it matter what they said, when they actually extorted it—a far graver matter—as Optatus teaches? “You ordered them to be taken away” fits neither the wording nor the sense. I write, “you deemed them fit to be seized,” that is, you seized them; for this verb, like *I think* and *I believe*, is often redundant in these writers. *Officia* means officials, as *ministeria* means ministers, and in countless similar cases. In what follows, “you extorted veils and the Lord’s furnishings,” I think *volumina* (“books”) should be written instead of *velamina* (“veils”), with Cochlaeus—although I do not deny that churches were customarily adorned and decorated with curtains, veils, or coverings. Those who think the use of such curtains was confined to baptismal solemnities, and that they were therefore white because that colour especially suited the purity of the baptized—an opinion apparently held by the most learned Vicecomes—may be refuted even by these testimonies of Paulinus and Victor. Paulinus expressly says, in a martyr’s birthday poem:

> Now golden thresholds are adorned with snowy veils.

Victor, describing what he himself calls the customary ornament of a church (where I interpret “customary” as not daily, but used only on more solemn occasions and seasons), does not expressly state the colour of the coverings; yet, in attributing shining whiteness equally to the coverings, candles, and lamps, he seems to me sufficiently to indicate their colour. I suspect that *pallas* has intruded in the following text in place of *pallia*. For *palla* in this sense, as far as I recall, is scarcely found in any ancient author whose antiquity is certain and unquestioned. As for the letters of Clement cited by collectors of decrees, in which *pallae* is mentioned more than once, everyone knows what authority learned persons assign them. But *pallia*, for any sacred covering, is not rare among the ancients. Among others, Victor of Vita writes of “covering-cloths,” book II, and explicitly of “altar-cloths” in book I of *The Vandal Persecution*. **M. CASAUB.**] were to be extorted by the enforcement of officials from many persons. [Note: [Col. 1076B] Thus in manuscripts C. and S. G. 97. ## VI. The Folly of the Donatists in Washing Walls Is Ridiculed

What sort of thing is this: in many places [Note: [Col. 1078C] **“You even wished to wash the walls,” etc.** Since he had earlier joined sprinkled ashes with salt water, perhaps here too *with ashes* should be restored or the text punctuated: “You even wished the walls to be washed, and ordered the enclosed spaces to be sprinkled with salt water and ashes.” It would also be acceptable, if one follows the learned conjecture, to write *aspergi* (“be sprinkled”) for *et spargi*. By “enclosed spaces” he means either spaces within the altar-railings, or, more generally, whatever is enclosed by walls—namely the pavement itself or the floor. Perhaps it was not paved at all, as most churches of that period were not particularly splendid, and thus it could not be washed like the walls. He later calls it “the place”: “What had the place done to you? What had the walls themselves done?” [Col. 1078D] **M. CASAUB.**] you even wished to wash the walls and ordered enclosed [Note: [Col. 1078D] **“And ordered the spaces to be sprinkled with salt [water] without cause.”** The second edition of Balduin reads this differently: “and ordered the enclosed spaces also to be sprinkled with salt water.” I would read, “and ordered the enclosed spaces to be thoroughly sprinkled with salt water.” **UNCERTAIN.** — **Here, ‘enclosed spaces.’** This appears to mean the space around the altar. **ALBASP.**] spaces to be sprinkled with salt [Note: [Col. 1078B] Thus in manuscripts C. and S. G.] water. [Note: [Col. 1078B] This word is absent in manuscript S. T.]

O water, sweet water created by God, [Note: [Col. 1078B] Thus in manuscripts S. T. and P. S. In the others, “sweet, which was created by God.”] over which the Holy Spirit moved before the world itself was born! O water, which, to make the world clean, washed the earth [Note: [Col. 1078B] In manuscripts C. and S. G., “the raging nation of lands.”]! O water which, under Moses, that you might lose your natural bitterness, [Note: [Col. 1078D] **O water sweetened by wood!** *Indulcare* is compounded from *edulcare*, “to sweeten,” according to Gnaeus Matius:

> It is fitting wisely to sweeten life  
> And govern bitter cares with one’s faculties.

**UNCERTAIN.**] sweetened by wood (Exod. 15), satisfied the hearts of so many peoples with most pleasant draughts! It remained for you, after such advancement, [Note: [Col. 1078D] **After advancement.** After so many things God accomplished through you. Tertullian, *On Baptism*, on how great a benefit it brings to the world. **ALBASP.**] to be grievously degraded.

[Note: [Col. 1078D] **“In you, by Moses’ presence, bitterness dies,” etc.** Does “Moses’ presence” here mean Moses’ time, or the time when Moses was alive? This seems harsh to me unless softened by some example elsewhere. Meanwhile, I think it should be written: “by Moses’ prayer bitterness died in you,” etc. The earlier corresponds to the later “today”: “and today, by schismatics, amid the multitude of Catholics, your sweetness is harassed.” On Moses’ prayer, see Exodus 15:25: “But he cried to the Lord, who showed him a piece of wood,” etc. *Moritur* means “has died,” as often—indeed, almost always. **M. CASAUB.**] By Moses’ presence bitterness dies in you, [Col. 1079A] and today, through schismatics amid the throng of Catholics, your sweetness is harassed. We suffer a like war; we await a like avenging God.

Tell me, brother Parmenian, what had the place done to you? What had the walls themselves done, that they should suffer these things from you? Was it because God was entreated there? Because Christ was praised there? Because the Holy Spirit was invoked there? Because, in your absence, the prophets and holy Gospels were read there? Because there the minds of brothers who had long been quarrelling had come into harmony? Because unity, pleasing to God, had found a house in which to dwell?

Tell us what you could have washed there. If we Catholics have trodden lane and street, why do you not cleanse everything? For the same baths have washed both you and us alike for the care of our bodies, [Note: [Col. 1079D] **“The same baths have washed both us and you alike,” etc.** On the use of baths among Christians too, see F. M.’s parent in Spartianus, p. 75. **M. CASAUB.**] [Note: [Col. 1079D] In manuscripts C. and S. G., “we have.”] and many of ours have frequently bathed before you. If you think everything must be purified after us, [Note: [Col. 1079D] **“If you think [things] must be purified after us.”** Write: “If you think [things] must be purified after us?” Thus the second edition of François Balduin. *Si* stands for *an*, as I recall having noted above. **UNCERTAIN.**] wash even the water, if you can. Or, if our footprints, as we said above, seem polluted to you, earth would have sufficed. Why did you wish to wash the walls too, upon which human footprints cannot be placed? We could not tread on the walls; we could only see them. If what sight touches must also be washed, why did you leave the rest unwashed? We see the roof; we see the sky as well. These cannot be washed by you. [Note: [Col. 1079D] **“By washing those things you have earned God’s favour.”** The word *si* must necessarily be prefixed. **UNCERTAIN.**] By washing those things you have earned God’s favour; by not washing these, you seem to have incurred an inexpiable sin.

[Note: [Col. 1079D] **“Therefore, although elsewhere you had been found seemingly careful.”** The passage is mutilated; supplement from the second edition of François Balduin: “Therefore, although elsewhere you wish to seem careful, elsewhere you have been found negligent.” **UNCERTAIN.**] Therefore, although elsewhere you were found seemingly careful—if nevertheless folly may be called carefulness, and your [Note: [Col. 1079D] In manuscripts C. and S. G., “can be called.”] [Note: [Col. 1079C] Thus in manuscripts C. and S. G. In the others, “may be called.”] vanity, to use its true name—unless perhaps by doing this you struck [Col. 1079C] ignorant peoples with fear, so that, because a [Note: [Col. 1079D] **Pillar.** Since you wash the walls, you wash Christians again. **ALBASP.**] pillar had been washed, their bodies should also be washed. If there is a purpose hidden in these actions, you have subtly deceived the wretched; if such a thing was done without purpose, your stupidity is plain. Those whom you have deceived know that you acted foolishly, and you yourselves will not be able to deny it.

[Col. 1080A] ## VII. The Donatists Also Raged against the Dead, Refusing Burial to Catholic Bodies

Why should I recount that impiety too, arising from your conspiracy, [Note: [Col. 1080C] **“Because you wished to invade basilicas for this purpose,” etc.** I write: “You wished to invade basilicas for this purpose: that you might claim cemeteries for yourselves alone, not allowing Catholic bodies to be buried, so that you might frighten”—or, as in others, “frighten”—“the living, mistreating,” etc. **M. CASAUB.** — **Here, “basilicas for this purpose.”** In many places there were two basilicas, namely a Donatist basilica and an Orthodox basilica; but, with Julian’s favour, the Donatists had seized the latter in order to deprive the Orthodox of burial. **ALBASP.**] because you wished to invade basilicas in order to claim [Note: [Col. 1080D] **For yourselves alone.** Burial in Christian cemeteries was a form of communion; therefore the Donatists claimed them for themselves alone. **ALBASP.**] cemeteries [Note: [Col. 1080D] **Cemeteries.** People were buried in basilicas or in cemeteries located beside basilicas. **ALBASP.**] for yourselves alone, not permitting Catholic bodies to be buried; so that you might frighten [Note: [Col. 1079C] In manuscript S. T., “they might frighten,” and later “you treated likewise.”] the living, [Note: [Col. 1080D] **You mistreat [them].** You deprive them of this communion. **ALBASP.**] you mistreat the dead as well, denying a place for burial. 98. If there was conflict among the living, let even another’s death restrain your hatreds. The man with whom you quarrelled a little while ago is now silent. Why do you insult a funeral? Why hinder burial? [Note: [Col. 1080C] Thus in manuscript C. In manuscripts S. T. and S. G., “why do you hinder a burial?”] Why do you quarrel with the dead? You have lost the fruit of malice. And if you do not wish bodies to rest together in one place, you still cannot separate souls placed together with God in one. [Note: [Col. 1080D] **In one.** Unity with Christ. **ALBASP.**]

VIII. An elegant and striking comparison of the Donatists with bird-catchers. [Col. 1080B]—Finally, it is impossible to recount in full everything that is done by you; yet let it be granted to you, [Note: In MS S. T.: “but let it be granted.”] who possess the mastery of this error. [Note: “Who possess the mastery of this error.” And who could now remain silent even about your own people? That is, about those, etc. This passage should be corrected and punctuated thus. Moreover, what follows likewise suffers from faulty punctuation. UNCERTAIN.] For who could remain silent even about your own people—those, namely, whom you have been able to seduce, whether by faction or by subtlety, so as to make them yours? Not only men, but women also: from sheep they have suddenly become foxes; from faithful persons, faithless; from patient persons, raging; from peaceable persons, contentious; from simple persons, deceivers; from modest persons, shameless; from gentle persons, fierce; from innocent persons, craftsmen of malice.

After they have fallen away to you, men or women alike, they resent that others remain where they were born. They invite those who stand firm to share their fall; if they knew that they had attained glory, they would quietly enjoy their own good fortune. But now, wishing to console themselves for their own ruin by their defections, they invite others to fall in the same manner; and they accuse those who sit in the bosom of Mother Church as sluggish and slow. [Col. 1080C] [Note: For they are not ashamed to speak in these words: “Cai Sei, Caia Seia, how long will you hold yourself back?” That is to say: After this, the second edition of Fr. Balduin inserts: “Now you must follow my error; now you must abandon the truth. ‘How long will you hold yourself back?’ means to say, ‘Imitate,’ etc.” UNCERTAIN.]

For they are not ashamed to speak in these words: “Cai Sei,” or “Caia Seia,” [Note: In the manuscripts: “Gaïseï,” or “Gaïaseïa.”] “how long will you hold yourself back?” That is to say: “Imitate my fall; imitate my shameful defections. How long will you be called faithful? Now abandon faith; now learn repentance.” [Col. 1081A] You are bird-catchers, and those men or women are birds. [Note: “You are bird-catchers.” The dead birds are to be understood as those whom they had rebaptized; those shut in cages, as those whom they had compelled to do penance. The sense, therefore, is this: when you send penitents through houses, this is a kind of bird-catching; for there are birds confined by which you wish to lure others. But when you display rebaptized persons in order to seduce our people by their example, these are dead birds which you use to capture other birds. ALBASP.]

But because there is not one single kind of bird-catcher: some employ a simple art and seek trees, deeply rooted and spread out over the face of the wood, where birds settle in natural branches by simple flight. There no deceits are counted, no contrived plans: there is one art alone, the skill of catching. [Note: “Because there is not one kind of bird-catcher: some are those who, by a simple art, settle upon natural branches in natural flight.” At the place where I have put an asterisk, the same edition is fuller and more copious in these words: “they seek trees rooted deep and spread over the face of the wood, where birds by simple flight,” etc. Correct, therefore, as far as possible, Bartholomew [Barthius] in correcting, who has: “they put a net upon natural branches for simple flight.” UNCERTAIN.] [Note: In MSS C and S. G.: “bird-catching.”]

You, however, I call like that bird-catcher who, after night has departed and before daylight comes, does not, like others, go to natural trees. Rather, carrying a tree himself, [Note: “He carries a tree.” Because they did not possess the true Church. ALBASP.] he binds together a future wood into a bundle; he constructs, with manifold deceit, a dry tree supported by no roots. Into it he grafts counterfeit branches, and, having long ago lost the foliage cut from its own limbs, it receives another’s leaves.

He carries other birds shut up in a cage; [Col. 1082A] [Note: “He carries [them] in a cage.” Penitents, because they did not communicate. ALBASP. In the same place: “He carries other birds shut up in a cage, and disembowelled.” Fr. Balduin’s second edition: “In a disembowelled cage.” From traces of the received reading, it seems one should write: “He carries other birds shut up in a cage; and blinded twice over.” Barthius emends: “In a cage and blinded as to sight.” UNCERTAIN.] [Note: “He carries other birds shut up in a cage, etc.” Write: “He carries other birds shut up in a cage, and other birds stuffed out to resemble living ones,” which is the reading of the first edition: *visceratas*, that is, stuffed and distended; its opposite is *evisceratas*, “disembowelled.” It is well known that birds and any rarer animals were accustomed to be preserved by extracting their entrails and the whole body, leaving only the skin, which was then filled out and distended with hay, bran, scraps, and trifles of every kind. It is also possible that *evisceratas* should be read. M. CASAUBON.]

Other birds, long since killed, are disembowelled and set upon deceptive branches in the likeness of living birds. [Note: “Long since killed.” By rebaptism. ALBASP.] Some lie hidden in cages; others appear to be alive upon the branches. A single cunning is joined with a twofold deceit; and so that the simplicity of living birds in flight may be deceived, [Note: Restored from a better exemplar by Fr. Balduin: “so that the simplicity of birds in flight may be deceived.” UNCERTAIN.] [Note: In MS S. G.: “of birds.”] those which are known to be dead seem to stretch out their necks with calls, while those hidden in their prison seem to sing from another’s throat. [Note: “They sing with another’s throat.” Because penitents in the Church could neither speak nor do anything. ALBASP.] Between one bird’s appearance and another’s voice, a single fraud does its work: captives capture the free, and dead birds kill the living.

Such are those whom you have wounded either by rebaptism or by penance; [Note: “Such are those whom you have [done this to] either by rebaptism, etc.” Whoever wishes to retain this may do so with my permission. Yet, since he speaks here of the lost and those seduced to their own destruction, and since in Book II, *On Penance*, he said “you wound” on this very matter, I am mistaken, or *sauciastis* (“you wounded”) is truer here than *sociastis* (“you joined”). Still, let each enjoy freedom of judgment. The first edition supports us, reading *sauciastis*, not *sociastis*. M. CASAUBON. Thus restored from the manuscripts.] lest they seem to have perished alone, they strive with great zeal and effort to make others, men or women, perish with them.

99. [Note: At one time I suspected that this Book—which was also omitted in Cochlaeus’s German edition—was not by Optatus, since Jerome writes that he composed only six books, and Optatus himself, in Book I, sets out the subject matter of only six books. But since this seventh Book was found in the three manuscript copies which I used, and its style and subject agree, I acknowledge it to be by Optatus; yet I say that it was written after the publication of the preceding six. Thus Fr. Balduin. UNCERTAIN.]

# BOOK SEVEN

[Note: “Book Seven.” For what is to be thought about this seventh Book, see what we have said in discussing the writings of Optatus. DU PIN.]

This final book maintains that the *Traditores*—those shown in the first little book by their names, places, and confessions—had not committed a grave sin when they sinned under necessity rather than willingly, and that, for the good of unity, even such persons could have been received into communion.

[Col. 1081]

## I. The Donatists are less culpable, and can more readily be admitted to communion, than their parents, who were guilty of surrendering the Scriptures.

After the *Traditores* had been exposed, the holy Church demonstrated, the slanders which you advanced repelled, and your sins—which deserved to be reproved by God—set forth in their order; after also the repetition of the sacraments [Note: MSS C and S. G.: “the surrender”; MS S. T.: “by reason”; MS P. S.: “by discourse.” We restore *iteratio*, “repetition,” by conjecture, because here Optatus reviews the arguments of the individual books, and in these words indicates the subject of Book V, which treats of the repetition of baptism.], your presumptions, [Col. 1083A] [Note: “Presumptions”: namely, because they said that the holiness of persons baptized and remitted sins, rather than the sacraments. ALBASP.] and your terrors had been exposed—our answers and statements should now have come to an end. But since, after the forest of hostility was cut down by the axes of truth, I see that your challenges, or those of your people, still sprout anew—challenges which I hear you make, [Note: Thus in MSS C and S. G.; MSS S. T. and P. S.: “which you are able to make.”] saying that you ought not to have been sought out for one communion, [Note: “For one communion.” The Donatists were compelled toward unity and said: “Why do you bring us by force into your communion, when, as you say, we are *Traditores* and sons of *Traditores*?” ALBASP.] [Note: MS S. T.: “ought not to have come.”] since you are known to be sons of *Traditores*—I shall make a brief reply to this.

Indeed, the Catholic Church was sufficient to itself, possessing innumerable peoples throughout all provinces; it was sufficient also in Africa, though among few people. But your separation did not please God, because the members of one body [Note: “Of one body”: the Church which was in Africa. ALB.] had been torn apart, and, contrary to God’s will, brothers were estranged from brothers.

Although a domestic judgment [Note: “Domestic judgment”: because they separated themselves from the Church; or because in the Council of Numidia they confessed themselves to be *Traditores*. ALBASP.] operated in your parents, so that those who ought to have been expelled for the surrender they had committed [Col. 1083B] [Note: MSS S. T. and P. S.: “for the guilt of surrender.”] voluntarily withdrew, no judgment was held; rather, the effect of a sentence took place. [Note: “No judgment.” No council was held to expel from the Church those who ordained Majorinus; rather, they withdrew from it of their own accord. ALBASP.] They should have been expelled after the surrender which they confessed against themselves in the Council of Numidia. But lest there should be hostility, [Note: Thus in MSS S. T. and P. S., better than the other manuscripts, which have “there would be hostilities,” unless the *est* found later in the other manuscripts should be read as “there would be.”] [Note: “Lest there should be hostility”: lest, when they had been expelled, ill will should arise against others because they had expelled so many bishops. DU PIN.] the severity of judgment was excused, [Note: “Severity of judging.” Secundus, who presided, did not dare to judge lest he should remain alone, as is related in Book I. ALBASP.] while your forefathers themselves voluntarily devised a plan concerning their guilt: they covered over their crime and departed as though proud, [Note: “As though proud”: as though condemning others and as though innocent; see Book VI, at “now found proud,” etc. ALBASP.] although they ought both to have grieved and to have been ashamed.

For if, at that time, they had made unity for the good of peace, [Note: MSS C and S. G.: “they ought to have made unity.” After these words the printed editions contain a certain inserted passage in which the crime of surrender is excused. I do not know from where it was drawn. It appears in none of the four manuscript codices which I have seen, nor in Balduin’s first edition; it does not agree with what precedes and follows, which cohere excellently when it is removed; it has none of Optatus’s style and is wholly contrary to his views and teaching. For these reasons we have omitted this passage here and relegated it to the appendix.] and if they had come voluntarily to the Catholic Church [Note: These two particles are absent from MS S. G.] [Note: Thus MSS S. T. and P. S.; MS S. G. has “might come” for “had come.”]—not like you, who are plainly known to have been brought in not without God’s will, [Note: Thus MSS S. T. and P. S.; MS S. G. has “helped,” incorrectly.] so that you might return from where you had wandered, although you still wander—if, as I have said, they had come voluntarily to the Catholic Church, because they were *Traditores*, perhaps our forefathers would have hesitated about receiving such persons. But we may rejoice that persons such as these did not survive into our own times.

Therefore the matter today is a new one, since we must deal with you, not with them. Although a hereditary stain may seem to have been transmitted from them to you, nevertheless, in this charge you cannot be held guilty together with your fathers, according to the judgment of God, who spoke through the prophet Ezekiel, saying: “The soul of the father is mine, and the soul of the son is mine; the soul that sins, it alone shall be punished” (Ezek. 18:4).

This matter had already been proved in ancient ages, at the very birth of the world: Adam’s offence did not attach to Seth, Adam’s son. [Note: “It did not attach to Seth, son of Adam,” etc. Augustine, *On Heresies*, ch. 19: “The Sethians took their name from Seth, Adam’s son. They honor him, indeed, but with fabulous and heretical vanity,” etc. Tertullian adds that they believed Christ to be none other than Seth. I omit what others say about them. As concerns Optatus’s words, I am no longer one who would pronounce anything severe upon a holy man. I shall say only this: I fear that these words escaped him imprudently and incautiously, and that they may scarcely withstand the rigor of a stricter examination. Therefore I gladly leave this province to others. M. CASAUBON.]

But lest anyone say that elsewhere the Lord is written to have said, “I will repay the evils of the fathers unto the fourth generation” (Exod. 20:5): beyond doubt both utterances are his, but they do not both address one people. [Col. 1084B] The first was through Moses [Note: MS S. T.: “to Moses.”] to one particular class of persons; the second, through Ezekiel, to another class of persons.

Since God knew that the Jews, before Pontius Pilate, would declare: “His blood be upon us and upon our children” (Matt. 27:25), God, by foreknowledge, saw that what they were going to say would be too little in proportion to the magnitude of their guilt; and so that the offence might be paid for by fitting punishments, he threatened the Jews themselves, saying that he would repay the evils of the fathers unto the fourth generation. Therefore this utterance applies specifically to the Jews alone. The other, however, applies to Christians: by it he has deigned to promise that he will not take vengeance upon children for anything sinned by fathers, nor upon fathers for anything that children may perhaps commit. [Note: Here another inserted passage appears in the printed editions, except Balduin’s first edition, to excuse the crime of surrender. It is to be rejected for the same reasons for which we rejected the earlier one: it is absent likewise from all the manuscripts, interrupts the course of the discourse, and is foreign to Optatus’s teaching.]

At the time of unity, your leaders who are proved to have done these things had already departed this life, leaving you, as it were, a hereditary stain. [Col. 1084C] [Note: Absent from MS S. G.] Yet God had previously washed this away from you by his providence, when he separated fathers and children, as we said above. Therefore, since to surrender is a sin, let your parents see what answer they will make at God’s judgment. Yet it cannot be your sin, because you belong to different times. [Note: MS S. G.: “who from”; MS S. T.: “because from.”]

## II. In God’s Church, good and evil people are found until the day of judgment, and the evil must be tolerated.

This is why we have long wished to receive you into our communion: [Note: “We wished to receive [you].” He answers the same objection: “If we are sons of *Traditores*, why do you wish to communicate with us?” ALBASP.] you did not sin at that time, but your leaders did. [Note: Here the printed editions, except Balduin’s edition, insert three lines which are absent from the manuscripts. They are given in the appendix together with other additions to this book.]

Nor should anyone, as if wholly holy, judge another, because it is written in the Gospel, Christ saying: “Do not judge, lest you be judged” (Matt. 7:1); especially since no one can be found wholly holy. For if there are persons who can have no sins, they lie in the Lord’s Prayer when they ask forgiveness without cause, saying to God the Father: “Forgive us our sins, as we also forgive our debtors” (Matt. 6:12; Luke 11:4). For the apostle John both discloses everyone’s consciences and unveils his own in these words: “If we say that we have no sin, we deceive ourselves, and the truth is not in us” (1 John 1:8). [Note: MSS C and S. G. have “designates”; but “unveils” is more suitable.] We have explained the reasoning of this statement more fully in Book IV.

But grant that some persons are perfect in complete holiness: they may not be without brethren, whom the Gospel precepts forbid us to reject. These precepts describe the field [Note: “Field.” The whole Conference of Carthage was concluded by this argument: he says, therefore, that one must live with sinners, because the Church is a field containing wheat and tares. ALBASP.] [Note: We restore this passage from MSS S. T. and P. S. In the other manuscripts and printed editions it is very corruptly read: “declaiming, [Col. 1086C] they are fortified by Scripture. Field.”]—the whole world—in which the Church is found, and Christ is the sower, who gives saving commands.

On the other hand, the evil man is the devil, who sows troublesome sins not in light but through darkness. In one field diverse seeds grow, just as the multitude of souls in the Church is not uniform. The field receives good or evil seeds; there is diversity of seeds, but there is one Creator of all souls, [Col. 1086A] one Lord of the field [Note: Thus MSS S. T. and P. S.; MSS C and S. G.: “one field of the Lord.”] in which there are evil tares. There are two authors of the seeds, but the field has one Lord: God himself, the Lord. The earth is his; the good seeds are his; and the rain is his.

Therefore we agreed to receive you, when you were brought in, into unity, because we are not permitted either to separate or to reject you, although sinners, born with us in one field and nourished by one rain—that is, by one baptism. Thus the apostles were not permitted to separate tares from wheat, because separation cannot be made without destruction: lest, while that which is unnecessary is pulled up, that which is necessary be trampled down.

Christ likewise commanded that, throughout the whole world, in his field—which is the one Church—his own seeds and alien seeds should grow. [Note: “And let his seeds grow, and alien [seeds] after their growth,” etc. There were those who, from these words of Optatus, coined some elegant—I would say new to me—word, *postcrementum*, and said that this is what he calls things which have grown afterward. But I do not inquire about the elegance of the word. Certainly it is not Optatus’s word; I know that he wrote: “and let his seeds grow and alien [seeds]. After their common growth, he will come,” etc. The word *crementum* (“growth”), if anyone doubts it, may be defended by capable patrons—Tertullian, Cyprian, and others, if necessary. M. CASAUBON. Restored from the manuscripts.] [Note: “After their growth”: he means those things which have grown afterward. UNCERTAIN.]

After the common growth will come the day of judgment, which is the harvest of souls. The Judge, the Son of God, will sit, and he knows what is his and what is another’s. It will be his to choose what he stores in the granary and what he hands over to fire; whom he assigns to unending torments, and to whom he presents the promised rewards.

Let us acknowledge that we are all human beings. Let no one arrogate to himself the power of divine judgment. For if any bishop claims the whole power for himself, [Note: “For if he claims the whole [power] for himself.” What, pray, will Christ separate and judge on the day of judgment, if a bishop wishes to separate all sinners from the Church? ALBASP.] let it be said what Christ will do at the judgment. It is enough for a person not to be guilty of his own sin, rather than to desire to be judge of another’s. Finally, it is our profession, for the good of peace, not to reject you. [Note: MSS C and S. G.: “not to reject the good of peace.” The printed editions here have: “Not only not to reject you, but also not to reject your parents—if unity had occurred in their time—for the good of peace”; but these words are absent from all manuscripts and from Balduin’s first edition, and appear to be interpolated.] For it is wicked for us bishops to do what the apostles did not do, who were not permitted either to separate the seeds or to pull the tares from the wheat.

## III. The Donatists can make use of the example of the apostle Peter, so that pardon may be granted them. [Col. 1086C]

But if the Catholic Church had hesitated to receive you, ought you not to have pursued the model of unity? Yet you were unwilling to put forward examples read in the Gospel, such as the passage concerning the person of the most blessed Peter, from which the pattern for preserving or establishing unity is set forth and recounted. [Note: “The pattern for preserving unity.” On this same pattern of unity, before Optatus, Cyprian excellently wrote in *On the Unity of the Church*: “In order to manifest unity, he established one chair, and by his authority arranged the origin of that same unity as beginning from one. Certainly the other apostles were what Peter was, endowed with an equal fellowship of honor and authority; but the beginning proceeds from unity, so that Christ’s Church may be shown to be one; and all are shepherds, but one flock is shown, which is fed by all the apostles in unanimous agreement,” etc. Pacian, Optatus’s contemporary, agrees excellently in Epistle III: “The Lord spoke to Peter, therefore to one, in order to found unity from one; immediately afterwards commanding the same thing to all in common.” UNCERTAIN.]

Certainly it is evil to do something contrary to a prohibition; but it is worse not to possess unity when you can. We see that Christ himself placed this unity above his own vengeance: he preferred that all his disciples should be one rather than avenge the offence committed against him. For, when he did not wish to be denied, he declared that he would deny before the Father the one who denied him. [Note: “When he did not wish to be denied, he promised,” that is, threatened. So in Lucifer of Cagliari, *For St. Athanasius*, Book I: “As the Lord threatens those who despise him,” and again, with a few words inserted, “if these things were threatened against Eli because of the sin of his sons,” etc. M. CASAUBON.] [Note: The printed editions add here: “before men. And yet he did not promise that he would not punish anyone who surrendered some Scripture; for it is more serious to deny him who spoke than to surrender the words which he spoke.” These words are plainly spurious.]

And although these things are written, [Note: MSS S. T. and P. S.: “but.”] [Note: Absent from MS S. G.] nevertheless, for the good of unity, the blessed Peter—who might have thought himself sufficiently fortunate if, after his denial, he obtained forgiveness alone [Note: MSS S. T. and P. S.: “deserved.”]—both deserved to be set above all the apostles and alone received the keys of the kingdom of heaven, to be shared with the others.

For the good of unity, we are given to understand that sins ought to be buried, because the most blessed apostle Paul says that charity can cover a multitude of sins: “Bear one another’s burdens” (Gal. 6:2), he says; and elsewhere he says: “Charity is long-suffering; charity is kind; charity does not envy; charity is not puffed up; it does not seek its own” (1 Cor. 13:4–5). And he spoke rightly. For he had seen all these things in the other apostles, who, for the good of unity, through charity did not wish to withdraw from communion with Peter—that is, with him who had denied Christ.

If love of innocence had been greater than the advantage of peace and unity, they would have said that they ought not to communicate with Peter, who had denied his master and the Lord, God’s Son. They could have refused communion with the most blessed Peter, as was said above; they could have recited against him Christ’s words, who had declared that he would deny before the Father the person who had denied him before men.

This pattern deserves careful attention. While I briefly recall it, may the blessedness of Saint Peter himself grant pardon if I seem to recall what is known and read to have happened. I hesitate to say that such great holiness sinned; but Peter himself proves the fact, for he grieved bitterly and wept abundantly. He would neither have grieved nor wept unless some offence had occurred.

The head of the apostles could indeed have governed himself in such a way as to incur nothing over which he would grieve. But many faults are seen under this one charge [Note: “Under one charge”: in one sin. ALBASP.] so that it might be shown that, for the good of unity, all things ought to be left to God. And I do not know whether this kind of sin could be of such great weight in another person as it was plainly in the blessed Peter.

For whoever, perhaps in some persecution, has denied the Son of God will seem, in comparison with the blessed Peter, to have sinned more lightly if he denied one whom he had not seen; if he denied one whom he had not recognized; if he denied one to whom he had promised nothing; if he denied only once. For in the blessed Peter this kind of sin was extended. First, when Christ asked them all who people said that he was, one said Elijah, another said a prophet. Then Christ is recorded as saying: “But who do you say that I am?” [Note: MSS S. T. and P. S.: “you, Peter, who do you say that I am?”] Peter said to him: “You are the Son of the living God” (Matt. 16:15–16). For this recognition he deserved to be praised by him: [Note: The printed editions add after this word: “because he had said this by the prompting of God the Father.”] “Behold, [Note: Thus MS S. T.; the others read “and.”] while the others did not recognize the Son of God, Peter alone recognized him.”

Then, on the day of the Passion, when Christ said: “Behold, I am taken, and you will all flee” (Matt. 26:32), while the others were silent, he alone promised that he would not depart. By foreknowledge the Son of God said: “Peter, before the cock crows, you will deny me three times” (ibid., 34). Another thing was added to the weight of the sin: namely, a promise which he would not fulfill.

After Christ had been led into Caiaphas’s house, to complete the measure of the offence, from so great a number no one but the blessed Peter was questioned. Questioned the first time, he denied; questioned again, he denied; the third time, he said that he did not know Christ at all. Then the cock crowed—not to distinguish the hours by its cry, but so that the blessed Peter might recognize that he had sinned. Finally, he grieved bitterly and wept abundantly.

Behold: as was said above, while the others did not recognize him, Peter alone recognized him; [Note: MSS S. T. and P. S. add “the Son.”] while the others made no promise, he alone promised; while the others did not deny even once, he alone denied three times. Yet, for the good of unity, he did not deserve to be separated from the number of the apostles.

Hence it is understood that everything was ordered by the providence of the Savior so that Peter himself might receive the keys. [Col. 1088C] The way of malice was blocked, lest the apostles should conceive in their minds a license to judge and should harshly despise him who had denied Christ. So many innocent persons stand by, and a sinner receives the keys, so that the matter of unity might be given its pattern. It was provided that a sinner should open to the innocent, lest the innocent should shut the door against sinners [Note: MSS S. T. and P. S.: “the sinner.”] and the unity which is necessary could not exist.

If you had recalled these things, while desiring communion, when would the Catholic Church have hesitated to receive you into her devout bosom, since it is certain that you are not *Traditores*, but sons of *Traditores*?

#### IV. The saying about dying flies applies to the Donatists, not to the Catholics

For some among you, wishing to make us appear contemptible to their people, introduce even into their discourses the saying of Solomon the prophet: “Dying flies spoil the sweetness of the oil” (Eccles. 10:1). And they call us “dying flies,” and call “oil” that liquid which is prepared in the name of Christ and which, once prepared, is called chrism. Before it is made, it is still oil in its simple natural state; it becomes sweet when it is prepared in the name of Christ.

[Note: In manuscripts S. T. and P. S., “oppose” is read.]

[Note: “Discourses.” *Tractare* is the work of bishops and means “to preach”; thus below on this page he calls someone a *tractator*, one who speaks for the purpose of explaining some matter, though not one who “discourses” in the episcopal sense. Thus, unless I am mistaken—for the book is not at hand—the most polished Sulpicius Severus calls Origen a *tractator* of all the bishops of Gaul. UNCERTAIN.]

[Note: In manuscripts C and S. G.: “and, as it were, dying flies.”]

[Note: “Oil.” Thus our heretics contemptuously call chrism “oil.” ALBASP.]

[Note: We restore this passage from manuscripts S. T. and P. S.; other manuscripts and printed editions incorrectly read “becomes” (*fiet*).]

Therefore there are three things named by Solomon the prophet: oil, sweetness, and dying flies which destroy the sweetness. These three things have their places in sequence: first comes oil; second, sweetness from its preparation; third, dying flies that destroy the sweetness.

Whoever among you is such a preacher, let him prove how he calls us dying flies. If you think that among yourselves there is a preparation which gives sweetness to the oil, then among you are the oil and the sweetness. Do we destroy your oil, so that you rightly call us dying flies? What belongs to you remains among you. And if someone passes from you to us, he is preserved by us just as he is dismissed by you. How, then, do you say that we are dying flies corrupting the sweetness of the oil, when after you we do nothing of the kind?

[Note: Thus he is preserved by us: he is not rebaptized. ALBASP.]

Or, if you say that we can corrupt the sweetness of the oil, then either we have some power and give sweetness to the oil; or, if—as you wish—we have no power, the oil remains such as it was by nature. How then do you say that we are dying flies corrupting the sweetness of the oil?

[Note: “Or we can.” If we give sweetness to the oil, we can do something, and thus we can baptize; if we give nothing, the oil among us does not become sweet. ALBASP.]

Therefore, before the oil is prepared by us, it is such as it was by nature; once prepared, it can receive sweetness from the name of Christ. How can we, by one act, both prepare and corrupt it?

[Col. 1089A]  
[Col. 1089B]  
[Col. 1089C]  
[Col. 1090A]

[Note: In manuscripts C and S. G., “in a single moment.”]

It follows that, if the oil is sweet in itself, what is done by human beings is pointless when it is prepared by a human being in Christ’s name. The same workman cannot simultaneously do two mutually repugnant and contrary things. If, in your absence, we prepare it, we do not corrupt it. If we corrupt it, who had prepared before us what we were to corrupt?

[Note: In manuscripts S. T. and P. S.: “we prepared it, and afterward corrupted it.”]

Therefore, lest the prophet’s saying be idle—if this is so—understand that you are the dying flies. For you have destroyed not what was born, but what had been prepared; for it is written that sweetness, not nature, can be corrupted. Oil is simple and has one proper name of its own; once prepared, it is called chrism, in which is a sweetness that softens the skin of the conscience, after the hardness of sins has been driven out; that renews the soul to gentleness; that prepares a dwelling for the Holy Spirit, so that, invited there and with harshness banished, he may graciously deign gladly to dwell there.

[Col. 1090B]

This is the sweetness of the oil which dying flies can corrupt. If we destroyed the oil prepared by you, you could rightly call us dying flies. But since we preserve what was anointed by you just as we received it, we cannot be dying flies. Yet you, driven by storms of envy, as though you fell into the oil, destroy in rebaptism the sweetness of that oil which was prepared in Christ’s name—the source from which dispositions were to be seasoned, and the light of the mind kindled unto saving and true understanding.

[Note: In manuscripts S. T. and P. S.: “unto saving parts.”]

You destroy the thing in which there were oil and sweetness. How could we corrupt a sweetness which before us had been prepared by no one? You deceived people, rebaptized them, and anointed them again. Alas! Not without your own death, you destroyed what had been prepared in Christ’s name, after the manner of flies, which, while perishing, destroy.

[Col. 1090C]

[Note: In manuscripts S. T. and P. S.: “destroying.”]

[Note: “Because death is sin,” etc. I distinguish the phrase “which, while perishing, destroy.” Because death is sin which has no forgiveness, it is written: “Because whoever shall sin,” etc. Perhaps the Greek *ὅτι* (“because”) has been repeated from the preceding verse, where: *amēn legō hymin hoti*, etc.

For Optatus more fully proves that the words concerning dying flies which destroy the sweetness of the oil apply to the Donatists, after he has already shown that they corrupt the sweetness of the oil by rebaptizing those rightly baptized. He further adds that they imitate flies in that they too do this while dying. Why are they dying and destined to die? Because the sin committed in rebaptizing has no forgiveness—that is, it is unforgivable. And no one doubts that any unforgivable sin is death. Yet this is no clearer than it would have been had he produced nothing to prove it.

Moreover, how could Optatus say that the sin of Donatists who rebaptize cannot be forgiven? Therefore, unless some more suitable interpretation of these words can be devised, I should think that all this ought to be deleted as spurious: “It is written that whoever sins against the Holy Spirit shall not be forgiven, neither in this age nor in the age to come.”

Thus the sense of Optatus’s words would be: those who rebaptize sin most grievously against the divine commands; but sin which has no forgiveness—that is, so long as, or insofar as, it has not been expiated and forgiven—is death. Therefore, “not without your own death,” etc. Nor is it surprising if a reader who understood the phrase “sin which has no forgiveness” to mean unforgivable and unpardonable sin (*asyn­gnōstō kai asyngnōrētō*) noted in the margin the scriptural passage relevant to it. And once noted in the margin, it is much less surprising that it was later received into the text itself.

As for these words of Holy Scripture, I plainly judge that they can have no place here. But Optatus himself will teach, in Book V, “Far be it that the Holy Spirit,” etc., that these words of Optatus have another sense and that his judgment was different from what we might prefer and gladly commend to the reader. See also, near the end, “For whoever,” etc., in the *Brief Confession of Faith against the Arians* by an uncertain author, recently published by V. Cl. M. CASAUB.]

For death is sin which has no forgiveness. It is written: “Whoever shall sin against the Holy Spirit shall not be forgiven, neither in this age nor in the age to come” (Matt. 12:32).

[Col. 1091A]

Therefore, since you falsely call us flies, hasten to undo all that is done by us, and say that we ought to be despised and scorned, while claiming holiness for yourselves alone, you put forward your own innocence so as to promise that you can forgive other people’s sins. You see, therefore, that the blessed Apostle Paul spoke not of us, as you contend, but of you: “People shall be lovers of themselves, greedy, boastful in themselves, proud, blasphemers, disobedient to parents, ungrateful, wicked; not keeping peace, without affection, slanderers, harsh, without kindness,” etc. (2 Tim. 3:2).

[Note: In manuscripts: “you see” in the singular.]

#### V. The Donatists, not the Catholics, are like Jannes and Mambres

For what kind of thing is this as well: that, at your own pleasure, you wished to impose upon us the person of Moses, against whom the Apostle Paul records that Jannes and Mambres stood? If this is so, what truth can be found among you which the Catholic Church seems to oppose, or what falsehood existing among us can you prove? Can you prove falsehood in our being in one communion with the whole world? Can you prove falsehood in our retaining and defending the true and only creed? Can you prove falsehood in the Chair of Peter and the keys of the kingdom of heaven granted by Christ, where our fellowship is?

[Col. 1091B]

[Note: “Can you prove falsehood in the very reading which you cited,” etc. These writings—or rather, however you may write or alter them—are such that not even Oedipus or Apollo himself could extract anything sound from them or restore them to integrity. A remedy must therefore be sought from afar for this passage, though it is certain and minimal: no change whatever is needed except in the punctuation. Let the reader know, then, that many preceding periods suffer, although not with the same obscurity, from the same fault of false punctuation as this passage; and we cannot restore this passage unless they have first been rightly arranged.

The whole passage must therefore be understood thus: “If this is so”—for here is the origin of the corruption continued through several sentences—“what truth can be found among you which the Catholic Church seems to oppose, or what falsehood existing among us can you prove? Our being in one communion with the whole world—can you prove that to be falsehood? Our retaining and defending the true and only creed—can you prove that to be falsehood? The Chair of Peter and the keys of the kingdom of heaven granted to Christians, where our fellowship is—can you prove that to be falsehood? In the very reading which you cited, consider among the persons themselves the order of events; observe who was first.” Certainly, etc. M. CASAUB.]

[Note: “The Chair of Peter.” From his communion with the bishop of Rome he infers that he cannot err or teach a false creed. ALBASP.]

In the very reading which you cited, consider among the persons themselves the order of events, and observe who was first. Certainly Jannes and Mambres are in the second place: they wished to fight against Moses and the truth by false arts; and Moses had gone before them, whose miracles they vainly attempted to assail.

[Col. 1092A]

[Note: In manuscripts S. T. and P. S.: “Aaron.”]

As Moses is first, so also the Catholic Church is first; as Jannes and Mambres stood against him in opposition, so you rebels wage war against the true Catholic Church.

[Note: In manuscripts S. T. and P. S.: “truth.”]

What, then, is the point of your wishing to exchange the names assigned to us and to yourselves, unless it was to make yourself equal to your associates?

[Note: “For there are some among you,” etc. At the words “while they still,” anyone may at once recognize that something is missing here. Yet attentive consideration of the whole passage to its end will make clear to a willing and diligent reader that whatever is missing cannot be much. Certainly there would be no loss of meaning or connection even if more were absent—namely all these words: “For there are some among you who, forgetful or ignorant of earlier times, [say of] those long ago,” and the period would then begin: “who [fell] from the Catholic Church,” or “those long ago who [fell] from the Catholic Church,” etc. For later he repeats the sense and subject of the preceding words, and it was not necessary to introduce them here.

I explain the sense thus—for let each person settle the wording as he himself prefers: “For there are some among you who, forgetful or ignorant of earlier times, now say of us things that apply to those who long ago fell from the Catholic Church and ordained Majorinus”—namely, those authors of schism and betrayal. Or what if you read: “For there are some among you who are forgetful—or ignorant—of earlier times, [regarding] those who long ago fell from the Catholic Church and ordained Majorinus”; namely, [they do not know them] to have been authors of schism and betrayal. Those, of course, were the authors of schism and betrayal.

“While they still,” etc. Certainly, whoever compares the earlier editions of Optatus with this better, second edition of Balduin will find this edition especially fertile in this book for gaps and omissions, whenever the same syllables, words, or even whole lines were immediately repeated. But if anyone can establish that nothing is lacking in the sense, let him exercise his ingenuity in restoring the words. M. CASAUB.]

There are indeed some among you who, forgetful or ignorant of past times, say against us things which concern those who long ago fell away from the Catholic Church and ordained Majorinus—those, namely, authors of schism and betrayal.

[Note: We have supplied from conjecture what is missing in the manuscripts, so that the discourse might not be gaping and defective.]

While they still preserved peace, before they destroyed the unity pleasing to God, they were rightly called the light of the world and the salt of the earth. While they taught peace, they were still called peaceable. Before they became puffed up, they were blessed for poverty of spirit and were part of the seasoning. They were blessed while gentle, and were part of the seasoning; blessed while righteous, and were part of the seasoning; blessed while peaceable, and were the whole seasoning.

[Col. 1092B]

[Note: “Before they were puffed-up schismatics.” Tertullian, *On Monogamy*: “when we are puffed up and exalted against the oil.” ALBASP.]

But after they gave the riches of error to their spirit and lungs, and made a schism, they were found harsh; they were less merciful when they impiously divided the members of the Church; pursuing injustice, they despised the kingdom of God; and by dividing the Church they refused to be peaceable. They themselves became salt that had lost its savor, from which nothing could be seasoned in a way pleasing to God for its sweetness.

And although this evil belongs to your leaders, some of your associates argue otherwise: they say that those who recognized the truth, even late, and, withdrawing from schism, recognized the Catholic Church as their mother and followed peace, were foolish. Some among you think these persons to have erred; they think that, as though made tasteless, they departed from wisdom.

[Col. 1093A]

Hence it is apparent that you all err in the same way in transferring names: you compared Jannes and Mambres to peaceful Catholics, and yourselves, schismatics, to Moses—which is alien from the truth. Some of your associates wished to judge the wise as foolish, saying that peaceable persons had become fools; and they refused to understand that their own forefathers had become tasteless through dissension.

[Note: Here the seventh book, and the whole work of Optatus, ends in the printed editions; what follows in the manuscripts has been transferred to the end of Book III. As regards the material concerning the Donatists’ accusation that Macarius had profaned Christian sacred things, beginning “And if through deception,” etc., and ending “what appeared to have been heard,” it is found in Book III, as also in Book VII in manuscripts S. T. and P. S.; and we have placed it above at the end of Book III. But what follows, since in all manuscripts it belongs to Book VII and nowhere to Book III, we judged should be placed here as an appendix to Book III added by Optatus in Book VII after he had completed his work.]

#### VI. In what way and why Macarius was admitted to communion

Now your envy comes down to that point: you say that after those actions Macarius ought not to have been admitted to communion, but rather avoided by Catholic bishops.

[Note: Before these words the manuscripts read: “But let us return to what was said a little earlier”; this seems superfluous and perhaps was added by copyists.]

[Col. 1093B]  
[Col. 1094A]

First, “communion” is one name, but its modes differ: it is one thing for bishop to communicate with bishop, another for a layman to communicate with a bishop.

[Note: Thus in manuscripts S. T. and P. S.; other manuscripts read “acts.”]

It would then have been serious if Macarius had done what he is said to have done of his own will. Those who do such things are punished for the deed by public judgments and Roman laws. For he is a murderer who, constrained by no necessity, command, or authority, but driven by frenzy, of his own will does what the laws forbid.

But Macarius did what he is said to have done at your provocation. He was neither a bishop nor engaged in episcopal office; he laid hands on no one and offered no sacrifice. Since, then, it is clear that he was outside the acts proper to bishops, no bishop appears to have been defiled by one who did not offer sacrifice with bishops.

It remains for you to say that he communicated with the people. It is agreed that he said something among the people, but for the purpose of explaining some matter, not of preaching in the way proper to bishops. For he spoke nakedly, insofar as he could say anything.

[Col. 1094B]

[Note: “Not, however, to preach, which belongs to bishops.” What then of presbyters—were they not accustomed to preach too? I see that many today believe that only bishops had the right to teach; but, unless I am mistaken, this is a great error.

We do not deny that in African churches it long prevailed that presbyters should not speak in the bishop’s presence—as Jerome says to Nepotian—or, as Possidius says in the *Life of Augustine*, should not preach or deliver discourses before a bishop. But I do not see why the learned men who conclude from this, among them Baronius, that presbyters were not permitted to preach in Africa, should think the conclusion necessary. Indeed, carefully considered, the words of Possidius and Jerome seem to suggest the contrary. Neither says simply and absolutely that presbyters were not accustomed to preach; they say that they were not accustomed to do so in the bishop’s presence.

Augustine also, in Epistle 77, when he thanks and rejoices to Aurelius for abolishing this custom, does not speak as though the faculty of preaching had then for the first time been granted to presbyters. Rather, he says that it had now become permitted for them to do what he himself did not disdain to hear the Lord speak through them while he was present.

Whatever this custom of African churches may have been—a custom abolished while Augustine was still alive—it was by no means a universal custom of the Catholic Church. This is clear even from Jerome, who says that it occurred only in certain churches; and Possidius is an excellent witness that Eastern churches followed another practice, and that African churches abolished this custom by imitation of them.

I find no ancient canons expressly establishing any such restriction. I pay no attention to their interpreters, who do not seem to me consistent with themselves on this subject. Balsamon, certainly, commenting on Canon 2 of the Synod of Constantinople, expressly determines that *tous hiereis mē einai didaskalous*—“priests are not teachers”; and on Canon 19 of the Synod in Trullo, that *hoti to didaskein ton laon monois enedothē tois episkopois*—“that teaching the people has been entrusted to bishops alone.” Yet in his commentary on the canons called Apostolic, and on Canon 58 of the Synod in Trullo—where, however, the Greek is lacking—he lays down the exact opposite. And does not Canon 1 of the Synod of Ancyra include *to homilein*, “to address/preach,” which Balsamon interprets as *didaskein*, “to teach,” among the proper duties of presbyters, to omit similar examples?

If in some places it occasionally happened that bishops, whether prompted by envy—as Jerome says somewhere—or impelled by some legitimate reason, imposed silence through their episcopal authority and power upon one presbyter or several together, one should not therefore rightly conclude that presbyters were formerly not permitted to preach. For what is permitted to a presbyter without the bishop’s permission, or contrary to his prohibition? By the same reasoning one could conclude that presbyters were not accustomed to baptize or administer the Eucharist. For when did Ignatius’s teaching to the Smyrnaeans not prevail: *mēdeis chōris episkopou*, etc.—“let no one [do anything] apart from the bishop”? He also adds: *ouk exón eti chōris tou episkopou oute baptizein, oute prospherein, oute thysian proskomizein, oute dochēn epitelein*, etc.—“apart from the bishop it is not permitted either to baptize, to offer, to present sacrifice, or to conduct an agape-feast,” etc. See also the so-called Apostolic Canons, chapter 39. Relying even on Ignatius, I would venture to assert that Balsamon’s interpretation is plainly contrary to the canon’s meaning. Tertullian likewise asks, in *On Baptism*, chapter 17, about the right to baptize, which properly belongs to the bishop alone, and those to whom it has been permitted by the bishop.

Certain learned men have believed, among them Bellarmine in *On the Church*, Book I, chapter 13, that deacons also undertook the duty of preaching. I fear that their opinion rests upon an insufficiently firm foundation. For if the matter is to be decided by examples, ancient history supplies examples even of persons far below deacons, wholly uninitiated into sacred orders, who addressed the people in the manner of preachers. And there is reason to doubt whether they correctly understood the words of Gregory which they cite.

Gregory says in Epistle 44, Book IV of the Roman edition: “It is unjust that those established in the order of deacons should be occupied with vocal modulation, when it would be fitting for them to devote themselves to the office of proclamation and the care of alms.” By “the office of proclamation” they think Gregory means the duty of delivering discourses or sermons. Jerome himself, Distinction 93, chapter 23, confirms that deacons were accustomed to preach, and in the same ancient canons *to kēryssein*, “to proclaim,” is sometimes assigned to them. But interpreters explain that the word has one force when attributed to deacons and another when attributed to priests. We agree with them, and contend that Jerome’s and Gregory’s words are to be understood of the same or a similar proclamation, not a priestly preaching. Gregory himself immediately identifies what he had called “the office of proclamation” with the office of reading the Gospel.

Otherwise, by the same reasoning we should conclude that readers also preached, since Isidore, Distinction 21, Canon 1, reports that they “proclaim to the people what they ought to follow.” Ambrose likewise judges that they can be called shepherds in his commentary on Ephesians 4, because, as he says, they feed the people who hear them by readings. For who, unless a fanatic driven by a passion for novelty, would deny that God’s word is no less proclaimed when it is read in church by anyone in its pure and simple form than when it is expounded from the pulpit according to a priest’s capacity?

Cyprian, however—which has much greater weight with me—even though he nowhere says that deacons were accustomed to preach, nevertheless says that they performed the duty of guiding and directing, by their counsels and the precepts of sacred Scripture, the desires of martyrs whom they visited in prison, and of instructing them most fully concerning the law of the Gospel. He seems to me to describe men not unworthy to have matters of the greatest importance entrusted to their prudence and wisdom. But enough, indeed more than enough, about these matters here.

What then does Optatus mean here by saying that *tractare*, “to deliver discourses,” belongs to bishops? Since Cyprian and others call bishops *tractantes*, I think nothing else can be inferred except that this duty, as the gravest of all, chiefly rested upon bishops as high priests and supreme governors of churches—here we speak of ecclesiastical matters—who generally surpassed the rest not less in learning and merit than in rank and authority. It was truly, as the poet says somewhere of Atlas’s burden, *achthos ouk euankalon*, “a burden not easy to bear.” At times it was improper for presbyters, while bishops were present, and disgraceful and shameful for bishops, that priests of lower rank should address and teach the people. This does not mean that the ancients believed preaching by presbyters, in bishops’ absence, to be contrary to law or custom, or outside or above the bounds of their office. M. CASAUB.]

[Note: The following through the words “deigned to separate the roles” are lacking in manuscript S. T. Whether they were lacking in manuscript P. S. is uncertain, for its final pages are torn from this point.]

[Note: “If pagan judges also are ministers of God’s will,” etc. Write: “if it is permitted [to say that] pagan judges are ministers of God’s will,” etc. But we warn the reader that several errors of this kind occurred in these few pages and have been corrected in the text itself. A little later, some might prefer “Macarius in his deed” or “Macarius in secular life” to “Macarius in his own [sphere]”; for afterward follows “judges in the Church.” But I judge that no alteration is required. M. CASAUB.]

By contrast, an episcopal discourse is recognized by all, clothed in holiness, namely by its double salutation. A bishop begins no address to the people unless he first greets the people in God’s name. Endings correspond to beginnings. Every discourse in the Church begins in the name of God and ends in the name of that same God.

[Col. 1095A]

[Note: “Recognized by all, clothed in holiness,” etc. Take care here not to understand *vestitus* as “vestment.” He is not speaking here of episcopal attire, but says that all—or any—present recognize and understand an episcopal discourse clothed in holiness by its double greeting. He used this metaphor because he had previously said of the layman, “he spoke nakedly.” Moreover, it seems that from this solemn custom of greeting arose the name *salutatorium* among Latin bishops, and *aspastikon* (“greeting-place”) among Greeks, for the place from which bishops formerly addressed the people, as the most illustrious Scaliger observed on Propertius 4. M. CASAUB.]

Which of you dares say that Macarius greeted the people in the manner of bishops? Therefore, since he neither greeted them before saying anything, nor dared greet them after he had spoken, nor laid hands on anyone, nor offered sacrifice to God in the episcopal rite, why do you say that the episcopal college could have been polluted, when you see that Macarius was outside every episcopal duty?

Your envy, having trodden on the footprint of truth at this point, seems to raise its head again. For you say that he ought not even to have communicated among the laity. Certainly, it is established—as the Apostle Paul proves—that he was a minister of God’s will. And what wonder, if even pagan judges deserved to be considered ministers of God’s will, the Apostle saying: “The judge does not bear the sword without cause” (Rom. 13:4). For he is a minister of God’s will. And Macarius too seemed to have been a judge in his own sphere. If he was not a judge in what he did, then under Roman laws he ought to have been punished by judges.

[Col. 1095B]  
[Col. 1096A]

Or if you say that not even in this way ought he to have communicated, nevertheless we do not see that one ought to have been avoided who did what Moses did. After twenty-three thousand men were killed, God did not avoid Moses with contempt, but invited him again to speak with him. Nor do we see that one should have been avoided who did what Phinehas did—Phinehas, whom I mentioned a little earlier, and who deserved to be praised by God himself for homicide. Nor does it seem to us that one should more especially have been avoided who did what the prophet Elijah did, when he killed so many false prophets; for we have already proved above that those too were false prophets.

#### VII. Even if Macarius had been guilty, he could not have been expelled from communion

But, leaving these examples aside, let us also say what you say: that Macarius was guilty. If he was, we were not permitted to exclude him while his accuser remained silent. For it is written that no one is to be condemned before his case has been heard. Tell us: who accused him and was not heard? Say that Macarius confessed guilt and that our judgment remained silent.

For we are judges, such as we are, in the Church—which you yourselves do not deny, although you insist that we ought to have been true judges.

[Col. 1096B]  
[Col. 1097A]

[Note: “For we are judges, such as we are,” etc. Since in the preceding words he had spoken of Macarius as subject to the bishops’ judgment, lest he seem to attribute too much authority over an imperial envoy to bishops, he now confines his absolute statement to ecclesiastical judgments and censures, whose force and authority extend to all Christians. He says “judges, such as we are,” because the word *judge* was no less proper among them to secular magistrates than “bishop” was to spiritual persons, although no one will deny that each term applies to each group in its own sphere. Moreover, see Augustine, *On the Work of Monks*, chapter 29, on how familiar and customary episcopal jurisdiction over laypersons and the Church’s hearing of cases were in Africa. M. CASAUB.]

[Note: “Although you insist that we ought to have been true judges.” This is a shameful error; correct it thus: “although you insist that we ought to have been stricter judges.” UNCERTAIN.]

For we cannot do what God did not do—God, who deigned in his judgment to separate the roles. He did not will the accuser and judge to be the same person. No one can, in one cause and at the same moment, bear two roles, so as to be both accuser and judge in the same proceeding. God did not do this even by omnipotence. To show us the form of judgment, he taught that an accused person ought not to be condemned without an accuser, and that the accuser must not be the person who is to be judge in that case.

[Note: “Finally, among the very beginnings of the ages,” etc. The Lyons, or Barthian, notes should be called notes on these words of the first book: “Thus the parties were again newly planted.” They say that *renovellare* means “to renew,” derived from vines. The author of Book VII similarly says: “while humanity’s birth was newly planted.” But in what sense, I ask, could Optatus call the first creation of the human race its restoration? The learned man was deceived by the prefix *re-*, which he did not notice is idle here, as in many other usages in which that age took excessive pleasure. Thus they used *repromittere* for simple *promittere*, “to promise,” and commonly called the land of promise the “land of re-promise.” Similarly *remittere* means “to send back,” *reddere*, “to give back,” and countless other such cases, examples of which are found even in better writers. Therefore there was no reason why the holy Father and most learned man Jerome should so sharply and severely attack his rival Rufinus because he used *refestinare* for simple *festinare*, “to hasten”—a most tawdry redundancy of expression, as Jerome judged, *perissologia*.

Thus *renovellare* is nothing other than *novellare*, that is, *phyteuein*, “to plant,” as we read in an ancient glossary; and *novelletum*, “a newly planted grove,” is *neophyton*. This, unless I am very much mistaken, suits the present passage far better than the sense “to restore.” M. CASAUB.]

Finally, at the very beginning of the ages, while the birth of humankind was newly planted, when brother Abel had been killed by Cain, we read: “And God called Cain and asked him where his brother was” (Gen. 4:9). He doubled his sin and, as though he could make God ignorant, said that he did not know. Yet when could the Lord fail to know anything, under whose eyes and gaze are all things that happen? And nevertheless God does not judge without an accuser; he asks what he certainly knew.

[Col. 1097B]

And you wish us to have excluded one whom we did not see doing evil and who had no accuser. I see what your envy whispers here. You say that we were not ignorant of what happened. We admit that we heard it, but it would have been a sin to condemn one whom no one dared accuse.

[Note: In manuscripts C and S. G.: incorrectly, “doing.”]

[Note: In manuscripts C and S. G.: “charge.”]

But if you say that the deed was not hidden from us, tell God why he asked, though he had seen the fratricide. We too ought not to do what God did not wish to do, for he did not wish to pronounce sentence except upon an accused person. Produce an accuser; otherwise the sentence could not be just unless the very person who was to judge also accused.

Therefore he said: “Behold, your brother’s blood cries out to me from the ground” (Gen. 4:10). Thus, since you cannot at all prove that Macarius was accused before any of us, you cannot condemn our judgment.

[Col. 1097C]

[Note: In manuscript S. T.: “Here ends the seventh book of Optatus, Catholic bishop, Book VII, addressed to Parmenianus, author of the schismatics.” In manuscript C: “Here ends the seventh book of Optatus.” In manuscript S. G.: “Here ends the seventh book of St. Optatus the bishop.”]

**N.B.** Up to this point, Book VII follows the manuscript codices and Balduin’s first edition. What follows is found in his second edition, from the manuscript of Tilianus, as he says, which we have not had an opportunity to see. But since it is absent from the four manuscripts we used, and seems alien to Optatus’s meaning and unlike his style, we removed it from the text as having been inserted without warrant into Optatus’s discourse. Yet, lest anything that seemed to pertain to Optatus should be lacking from our work, we judged that it ought to be transcribed here.

### The Charge of Handing Over Is Mitigated

After these words, p. 100, at the beginning: “For if they at that time, in the good of peace,” the following occurs:

> [Note: [Col. 1098C] “For if they at that time, in the good of peace,” etc. *They ought to have made*, that is, they would have done it, would have wished to do it; so in the Conference of Africa, p. 83: “That it may first be established concerning the number of the petitions, and how many my party have demanded, or how many they are about to demand,” says Bishop Petilian, “I first request of your Nobility that it may not be superfluous for your Highness to be obliged to render judgment concerning the number of each party.” From these words we may easily learn how much that age delighted in excessively redundant and superfluous expressions. For this is what he meant: “I request of your Nobility that your Highness judge concerning the number of each party.” In the same Conference, p. 2, *ought to be present* for *to be present*; and in the Canons of the African Church, ed. Cl. Justel, p. 45, *may deign to send persons who ought to convey* for *who may convey*. M. Casaubon.]

they ought to have made unity, they too ought not to have been excluded from the Church, in whom necessity had excused the will.

> [Note: [Col. 1098C] Necessity: because they had done it through fear of tortures. Albaspinaeus.]

For none of them had handed things over voluntarily, nor can this sin be equated with other offences.

> [Note: [Col. 1098C] “With other offences”: those committed voluntarily. Albaspinaeus.]

For whatever God did not wish to be done, he forbade by his own mouth, as when he said: “You shall not kill; you shall not commit adultery,” etc. (Exod. 20:13). He could likewise have forbidden this thing which your ancestors committed. But since one thing is what the mind does, another what the outcome brings about, whatever a human being can do by will deserved to be forbidden; whatever necessity does wrongly cannot be strongly accused. In short, will has punishment; necessity has pardon. A murderer, while no one compels him, can commit his crime and can refrain from it. An adulterer, while no external force drives him, can commit adultery and can refrain from it; and so likewise in other such matters, in which free choice exists. Therefore, acts that are forbidden are assigned to judgment when they are committed, not things called “prohibited” when they occur through some necessity.

> [Note: [Col. 1098C] “Prohibited”: he calls prohibited things which are not sins in themselves. Albaspinaeus.]

Perhaps he may readily deign to forgive what he was unwilling to forbid.

Accordingly, if the offence which could be alleged against your parents as though capital—if at that time they were exposed or summoned to trial—they could support themselves by more than one precedent.
