For it is recorded that in earlier times either the tablets of the Law were broken, or books were handed over, or cut up and burned, and no one was condemned.

If, as I said above, your parents had been exposed at that time, if they could have been accused, they would undoubtedly have said that they had done nothing more than Moses the lawgiver did. Although necessity and will do not resemble one another but conflict with one another, the case of your parents and of Moses was one under the same name of the Law. Your parents could say that they had done under necessity what Moses had previously done by will. When he was angry with the people, he did not consider that God had written with his own finger. And what is written in heaven is greater than what is written on earth; nor is what the finger of God made identical with what a pen, fashioned by a human hand, wrote. Moses carried what he had received through the cloud; your parents handed over what they had caused to be produced at their own expense.

> [Note: [Col. 1099D] “Having paid money”: what they had arranged to have written. Albaspinaeus.]

Your parents would rightly defend themselves by showing that it was not a capital crime if each of them, terrified by great fear, did what Moses had done in anger. We do not read that the Lord was angry with Moses, or avenged the tablets which he had written out with his own hand; Moses was neither called a sinner nor punished. Thus the Law proceeded from God as water flows down from a spring, or as fruits are gathered from a tree while its root remains intact: what is distributed does not perish if it remains safe in its source.

> [Note: [Col. 1099D] “Accordingly Moses after the tablets,” etc. I write: “Accordingly, Moses, after the tablets of the Law had been scattered and shattered, did not deserve to be condemned,” etc.; and shortly afterward, read *betrayed the Law* rather than *came forth*. M. Casaubon.]

Accordingly, after the tablets of the Law had been scattered and shattered, Moses did not deserve condemnation; afterward he was called back to Mount Sinai, ascended it, deserved again to speak with God, and received the Law renewed, as the title of the book written under the Greek name *Deuteronomos* [Deuteronomy] declares. Behold: in the Law, what had remained safe in its source did not perish.

But lest anyone think that Moses possessed such merit as to have a certain confidence before God because of his conversation with him, and that therefore God was not angry—and, if this were so, friendship ought always to demand its own merit and reward—why was vengeance afterward exacted upon him for offending? Was it not to show that the thing he had committed in anger was slight?

> [Note: [Col. 1099D] “The Law was sound in God,” etc. Thus we have corrected what was formerly read: “The Law was sound in God, and after it had been made by a human being together with stone tablets, the devotion owed by a human being,” etc. M. Casaubon.]

The Law was sound in God; and after it was broken by a human being together with the stone tablets, when the devotion owed by a human being was not rendered, Moses deserved that punishment—

> [Note: [Col. 1100D] “Or punishment”: other manuscripts may have *you could write*. Albaspinaeus.]

—that he should die midway on the journey and not enter the land of promise. Hence it is clear that what could be committed without punishment in this present example cannot be reckoned a great sin.

> [Note: [Col. 1100D] “What could [be done] in the example concerning the commandments,” etc. Perhaps someone would prefer *in the present or preceding example* to *in the commandments*. But I rather agree with those who understand “commandments” as the ten tablets containing commandments. M. Casaubon. Likewise: “In the commandments”: in the tablets which contained the commandments. Albaspinaeus.]

What if they also advanced the ensuing precedents, in which it is recorded that, although the renewed Law was kept in the ark, the people of Israel were defeated in battle? The Law which, by the people’s counsel, had been carried against the enemy in the ark, which could not be defended by the priests themselves and the other sons of Israel, was handed over to the enemy when it was not brought back. Those who had said that it should be carried fled in fear after the Law had been handed over, and are not afterward recorded to have suffered anything by way of punishment. If your parents had offered this argument, who could have excluded them from his communion?

> [Note: [Col. 1100D] “From his communion”: who would have wished to depose them? Albaspinaeus.]

What if your leaders had not kept silent about those further examples in which it is recorded that Baruch handed to the scribe Jehudi the book of the Law which he had received from the mouth of Jeremiah the prophet, and that the king’s officials ordered both Baruch, who had written it down, and Jeremiah, through whom God had spoken, to flee and hide? Jeremiah dictated; Baruch handed it over; both fled. The book was brought to King Jehoiakim. Since the king had a burning brazier before him because of the cold season and was unwilling to hear the book read aloud by Jehudi the scribe, he repeatedly cut it into small pieces and threw them upon the fire. Yet God was not angry either with Jeremiah, who had fled, or with Baruch, who, fleeing with him, had received it. Had God been angry with them, he would have spoken to another prophet. But he spoke not to another, but to Jeremiah himself. For it is thus written:

> “And the word of the Lord came to Jeremiah, after the king had burned the scroll of the book and the words which Baruch had written from the mouth of Jeremiah. God said to Jeremiah: Take another scroll and write all your words which had been written in the book which Jehoiakim king of Judah burned” (Jer. 36:27).

Behold: God was not angry; what had been burned did not perish; Baruch was not punished; Jeremiah was not despised by God. Hence it appears that in this matter there was never a grave fault which vengeance could never follow. If your parents had alleged these things, who could have withdrawn them from communion?

Accordingly, when God saw both that Moses had broken the tablets of the Law, that the ark had been left to enemies, and that, after Baruch handed it over, the book of the Law had been cut up and burned, he disclosed his providence and promised that henceforth he would write the Law neither on tablets nor in books, but in the inward person himself—that is, in the mind and heart of every believer—as he had written it in the heart of Noah, Abraham, Isaac, Jacob, and the other patriarchs, who, it is agreed, lived lawfully without the Law. The blessed apostle Paul also proves this point when he says: “Written not with ink, but with the Spirit of the living God; not on tablets of stone, but on tablets of fleshly hearts” (2 Cor. 3:3).

After the Law had been broken by Moses, abandoned to enemies by the children of Israel, and—when Baruch brought it to King Jehoiakim—cut up and burned before Christian times, God indicated through the Prophet where he would afterward write it better, saying:

> “For this is my covenant which I shall establish with the house of Israel and with the house of Judah; and after those days, says the Lord, giving my laws in their hearts, I shall write them in their minds” (Jer. 31:31).

He promised this long ago and fulfilled it quite recently in Christian times.

> [Note: [Col. 1101D] “Fulfilled it quite recently”: these words and those following seem to imply that what has been handed down to us without Scripture can suffice. Albaspinaeus.]

Therefore paper now occupies the second place, and parchment the second place. Since the Law has been written by God where it cannot be handed over, your parents, who already believed in the Trinity, though they handed over books, did not hand over their hearts or minds, in which God wrote his Law as he had promised to write it. Where, then, brother Parmenian, is what you said—that the Law had been utterly burned by the traditores? Behold: it was neither utterly burned nor entirely removed, since it remains in the hearts of believers and thousands of books are read everywhere.

> [Note: [Col. 1101D] “Whence it appears that you wished to accuse your parents,” etc. Unless other considerations also showed that Optatus sometimes speaks incautiously, I should judge this seventh book alien to him especially on this ground. For this entire argument is insufficiently sound unless softened by a favorable and charitable interpretation. M. Casaubon.]

Whence it appears that you wished, though through ignorance, to accuse your parents in vain. Therefore, if your parents came into the times of unity and gave such reasonable answers by so many examples, they too could not be excluded from communion—especially when you, who are known not to be traditores but sons of traditores, must be distinguished from them in both persons and names, as fathers and sons are distinguished. Where there is no common guilt between those persons, there cannot be one sentence.

> [Note: [Col. 1101D] “Although”: the sense is: even if your ancestors ought not to have been excluded from communion for these reasons, nevertheless, because they had sinned, they ought to have sought and requested it; but you ought to be invited freely to unity, because you have sinned in nothing. Albaspinaeus. Likewise: “Although, even if their unity should be effected,” etc. I write: “Although, even if their unity should be effected and they should come voluntarily to the Catholic Church,” etc. M. Casaubon.]

Although, even if their unity should be effected, they should come voluntarily to the Catholic Church. The rest is found in our edition (namely, the Dupin edition), p. 100.

After these words, p. 100, about the middle: “If anything perhaps be committed wrongly by the children,” the following occurs:

Since in Moses’ time the Law was repeated without anyone’s punishment, the ark of the Testament was voluntarily returned by enemies, and, at God’s command through Jeremiah, another scroll was written, why is it thought that among your ancestors alone there was a capital sin in a case in which no one was condemned through so many precedents? For if the Law was given in order that human beings might be instructed, not in order that the Law itself might be worshipped as if it were God, after the deed of your fathers the multitude of believers suffered no loss. Each of them lost his own codices under fear. For the Law which was necessary remains effective among the teachers of peoples and worshippers of God. Libraries are full of books; the Church lacks nothing; in every place the divine proclamation sounds everywhere; the mouths of readers are not silent; everyone’s hands are full of codices; those who desire instruction lack nothing. Yet the Law seems to have been written not so much for teaching as for future judgment, that the sinner may know what he can suffer if he has lived less than rightly.

Indeed, it is written and read that the Law was not given for the righteous (1 Tim. 1:9), because every righteous person is himself a law to himself (Rom. 2:14–15). And elsewhere the same blessed apostle Paul says that the Law does not make people righteous, but itself loves righteousness. In all producing things, their effects are always sought: the Law that produces is superfluous if the thing produced is available by a shorter way. Thus Abraham was not told, “Believe”; rather, he believed of his own accord. In him, without the Law, the effect of the Law was fulfilled. We do not read, “Abraham heard the Law and believed,” but: “Abraham believed God, and it was reckoned to him as righteousness” (Rom. 4:3). In the earliest times, too, Noah the patriarch did nothing in order to become righteous, yet he was chosen as righteous, and, after building the ark, sailed safely in the flood. It would take long to go through each person who was found righteous without the Law.

If your parents had said these things in their time, who could have excluded them from communion? What if they had said that one ought not pass over in silence what the Apostle says concerning those outside the Law: “The nations which do not know the Law do the things of the Law; for they have the Law written in their hearts.” For many are shown to have sinned under the Law, and many to have lived well without the Law. Law and human being are two things, but they cannot be equal. A human being was not made for the Law; the Law was given for human beings. I see nowhere any injury done to God, since the source of the Law remains with him. And after the Scripture is said to have been handed over by your parents, nothing is lacking: all the members of the Law are whole, safe, and read aloud. Nothing of the Law is diminished for those desiring either to teach or to be taught.

Or was it more necessary that a human being should be killed in order that some Scripture might not be handed over? Yet neither were human beings killed, nor are all the Scriptures lacking. The Law and God are not one and the same. If it was necessary to die for God—who can both raise the dead and give reward—the book not handed over can do neither of these two things.

> [Note: [Col. 1102D] “Necessity therefore obstructs its powers.” Write: “Necessity therefore expends,” etc.; that is, as is said shortly afterward, necessity has acted. It follows: “Why then are some negligent persons not condemned?” It is not far [from the text], etc. But a good many things of this kind followed, which, lest we should seem too fastidious, we corrected in the text itself. M. Casaubon.]

Necessity therefore expends its powers. We see negligence acting no less frequently than necessity has acted. For if parchments or books containing legitimate Scripture ought to be preserved wholly intact, why then are some negligent persons not condemned? It is not far from handing over to placing badly or carrying badly. One placed a book in a house, and that house was burned by fire: let the man who placed it negligently be condemned, if the person who, terrified, gave up a book demanded from him is to be condemned. Let those also be condemned who so negligently placed parchments or books that household little beasts—that is, mice—gnawed them so that they cannot be read. Let him too be condemned who placed a book in a house in such a way that, because of excessive rains, certain roofs leaked so much that everything was obliterated by damp and cannot be read. Let those also be condemned who, carrying books of the Law, rashly entrusted themselves to the rapacious waters of rivers and, wishing to save themselves, released the Scriptures from their hands into the water.

Therefore, if Scripture is one thing, and the person who could not preserve it is guilty: one handed it over to waters, another left it to gnawing beasts, another neglected it to be spoiled by dripping water, another human being, terrified by fear of death, gave it to another human being. If the offence committed by all is one, why is one selected for condemnation, when the guilt of the traditor is lighter than that of the negligent person? He who placed it before mice or left it under dripping water was negligent voluntarily; he who lost it in a river sinned through rashness; he who, through fear of death, handed something over gave it as one human being to another. It was intact with the giver and intact with the receiver. If the receiver hands it over to flames, the sin belongs more to the burner than to the person who handed it over. If your ancestors had said these things, when could we have excluded them from our communion?

If they had also wished to recall the times of King Antiochus, when all the Jews were compelled to give their books into the fire, and all Scripture was so handed over that not a single stroke of a letter remained in any book: no Jew was condemned at that time, nor was any sentence pronounced by God or by any angel against any Jew, because the sin belonged to the ruler who ordered and threatened, not to the people who handed things over with trembling and grief.

> [Note: [Col. 1103B] “That Antiochus, lest he should seem to have harmed the primitive people,” etc. Does he call *the primitive people* τοὺς ἀρχαίους, “the ancients,” or those whom sacred history at times calls “the firstborn”? The Vulgate interpreter elsewhere also uses *primitiva* for “firstborn.” But no one so sleepy or ignorant as not immediately to notice how many things Optatus here says, in a few words, without any fidelity to history, by a remarkable example of thoughtlessness. To pursue these matters at length would perhaps be neither our duty nor good manners. At least it seemed proper to warn the reader to note that at 2 Maccabees 8:23, the Latin Vulgate reads Ezra in place of Eleazar, which is in the Greek; and that it joins the following words differently than both the Greek texts and the logic of the matter require. Learned men have thought this did not begin yesterday or today, nor arise through the carelessness of more recent copyists, but that it had long been read in this way and was an error of the most ancient antiquity, so to speak. For there can be no doubt that this was the source and origin for our author’s many blunders, into which he runs within a few lines. M. Casaubon.]

That Antiochus, lest he should seem to have harmed the original people at all, God immediately provided that through one man, Ezra, who was also called a reader at that time, the whole Law should be dictated again exactly as it had previously stood. Thus the tyrant Antiochus could not reap the fruit of his malice: apart from seven brothers and one elder who refused to eat swine’s flesh, he killed no Jew, and the Law could not perish. So too your parents in their time were not killed, and the books of the Lord’s Law are read entire everywhere. If your parents, as I said above, spoke these things, who would not boldly receive them into his communion, when, as has been said, necessity had sinned, not will? In the times of unity, your leaders—[the rest as on p. 100 of our, that is, Dupin’s, edition].

After these words, on the same page, a little after the middle: “But your leaders,” the following occurs:

For when a sinner such as your ancestors were comes to the Church and explains the reason for his necessity, he must first be received,

> [Note: [Col. 1104C] “First received”: first, he is not to be excommunicated. Albaspinaeus.]

then sustained in the compassionate bosom of Mother Church while awaiting his repentance.

> [Note: [Col. 1104C] “Sustained”: his repentance must be awaited. Albaspinaeus.]

And not as though wholly holy—[the rest as in our, that is, Dupin’s, edition, p. 100].

## Annotations of Balduin

### Notice Concerning the Following Annotations

Although, after the restorations which we have made in the books of Optatus with the aid of manuscript codices, very many difficulties upon whose solution most learned men had labored have been entirely removed, and the remaining ones appear sufficiently and abundantly resolved by our annotations; nevertheless, since in the annotations of others there are not a few things that illuminate the history of the Donatists and the ancient discipline of the Church, and contain a remarkable variety of matters pertaining to sacred and secular learning, it seemed proper to add at the end the lengthy observations of Balduin and Albaspinaeus, as well as the shorter annotations of these men, of Meric Casaubon, and of others, marking beforehand the pages on which the individual passages to which they refer may be found.

## Prefaces of François Balduin to the First Edition of Optatus

### François Balduin to the Reverend Sir Jean Lentallier, Bishop of Saint-Omer, Greetings

When, in recent days, Irenaeus, in the form first published by Erasmus, was reprinted in this city, I regretted that the publisher had not been warned to publish alongside it that excellent Greek portion of Irenaeus which survives entire in the books of Epiphanius. Thus this most ancient writer of the Christian Church would have come into people’s hands in a much better form, although the remaining portion of the same kind would still be wanting.

But now, as at this time many people are turning their studies back to the reading and examination of religious and ecclesiastical antiquity—and, if many were wise, more would turn back to it—when there was also discussion of reprinting Optatus the African, who was formerly published in Germany in a most corrupt state, the publisher approached me. He suspected that I would gladly take from my civil studies of law whatever small amount of time I could give to these ecclesiastical writers. Yet he was in greater haste than would permit all the resources to be sought out that might restore Optatus to wholeness.

I therefore replied that this writer was certainly most worthy of a more careful recension, but that I could at that time contribute only the correction of six hundred passages in him. The greater part of these corrections I derived from a manuscript copy which the most learned Parisian theologian Claude d’Espence had at one time given me to use. Although I knew that scarcely fewer passages remained which lay under grave suspicion of corruption and could hardly—indeed, scarcely at all—be healed without the aid of an old book, and that I could therefore not give Optatus to the world in the best possible form, as I wished, I nevertheless did not decline meanwhile to have him published much better than he had been hitherto, rather than have the same text reprinted in the utterly polluted state in which it had formerly stood.

I had certainly hoped that a second aid toward correction would be supplied by the codex of Jean de Tillet, bishop of Saint-Brieuc, a most devoted student both of old books and of ecclesiastical antiquities. But what could not be provided now because of the absence of that most learned bishop may perhaps be provided in a later edition.

I can neither conceal nor wish to conceal that I am moved by a singular reverence toward the African teachers of the ancient Church. I perceive that they deserved most nobly of it and, when other Latin writers seemed, as it were, to fail, furnished it with reinforcements so faithfully and courageously. I recall that, some years ago, when I published Minucius and compared him with Tertullian, Cyprian, and Arnobius, I praised for this reason that fertile and blessed Africa. Just as it was always said in former times—so I wrote then—to produce something new, so it also produced the most learned and keenest defenders and champions of our religion. For from it also came enemies far from indolent.

The flames of the Donatist faction bear witness to the war which one Donatus of Numidia declared against the Church, and to the conflagration he kindled. What would have happened had that same land not sent forth, to extinguish those fires, either our Optatus, bishop of Milevis in Numidia, or Augustine himself a little later—those two lights of the Church, I say, and two thunderbolts of a most holy warfare against the enemies of piety? The Council of Milevis, at which Augustine too was present, was certainly a great bulwark of religion. But a little earlier the Church of Milevis had given the Catholic Church great assistance when, against the force and snares of the Donatists, it gave her its Optatus.

We read, indeed, that in those times there were many men in Africa called Optatus, otherwise very unlike one another. Augustine, for example, in his books against Parmenian, remembers both our Optatus and another man of that name who followed Donatus. And just as a certain Optatus is named among the bishops of the Donatists at their assembly at Bagai, so another Optatus, a defender of the good cause, is mentioned at the Catholic synod of Cirta together with Augustine himself. Augustine also wrote his book *On the Unity of the Trinity* against the Arian Felicianus to an Optatus, whom he calls his dearly beloved son.

Our man, then, was another Optatus, and much older. Nor did he have anything in common with that Optatus of Gildo, whom Augustine frequently mentions. I do not even think he was the same man whom Athanasius praises and says was his defender at the Synod of Tyre; for Athanasius says that he was an Egyptian bishop.

The period in which our Optatus flourished is clear, since he calls Siricius, bishop of Rome, his colleague. Jerome testifies that he wrote these books while Valens and Valentinian were emperors. He might have said, “under Theodosius.” But it matters greatly to know at what time someone wrote something, especially where ecclesiastical controversies are being investigated.

From Augustine we have learned that Parmenian, whom Optatus attacks, was successor not of that Donatus of Casae Nigrae who began to harass Caecilian, but of another no less mad Donatus of Carthage. That Donatus had succeeded Majorinus, whom the earlier Donatus had ordained bishop of Carthage in order to overthrow Caecilian. Augustine likewise indicates that Parmenian’s letter, to which Optatus replies, was written to Ticonius, a learned and eloquent man who otherwise did not seem sufficiently Donatist; Augustine afterward wrote three books against that letter of Parmenian.

Jerome says that our Optatus wrote six books. I know that a certain seventh circulates; but Optatus himself declares plainly enough that only six were written by him, where he also outlines rather elegantly the subject of each one. He promises to add certain proceedings, but I do not find this appendix. Augustine also summarized the principal chapters of the first book in his first book against Parmenian. “Let those who wish,” he says, “read what the bishop Optatus of Milevis, of venerable memory and of Catholic communion, relates, and by what evidence he establishes so many points: whether concerning Lucilla, the woman then richest and most factious, whom Saint Caecilian, still a deacon, had offended for the sake of ecclesiastical discipline; or concerning the other associates in her faction, thieves of ecclesiastical silver; or those who grieved that they had not attained the episcopate and persecuted Caecilian, who had been preferred to them, with whatever snares they could; or concerning the Numidian bishops whom that faction had summoned for Caecilian’s destruction, so that, once he was deposed, another might be ordained.”

These are his words. I have quoted them now all the more gladly because our Optatus is there called a man of Catholic communion. Therefore, although he seems to have adopted Cyprian’s view, and the view of those who at one time agreed with him, concerning the baptism of heretics—a view which Augustine afterward both condemned and showed ought to be condemned—he nevertheless remained in the Catholic Church, in which Cyprian also remained. For the ancients neither lightly nor readily—as now is most commonly done with excessive rashness, obstinacy, hostility, indeed, not to say slander—branded or stained anyone with the black and grave mark of heresy so as immediately to exclude him from communion with the Church.

I shall not say that Optatus always cites passages of Holy Scripture very aptly, or never bends or twists them. I shall rather admit that he very often uses them ineptly. The old saying applies: he speaks well, but does not prove well. Thus the proposition remains true even though a false proof is sometimes employed to establish it.

Nothing more vapid or foolish could have been said than Parmenian’s use, to reject the baptism of Catholics, of David’s words: “The oil of the sinner shall not anoint my head.” Nothing would have been easier than, by examining the passage and setting forth its true interpretation, to refute with ridicule the absurd foolishness of an unlearned trifler. Yet Optatus labors, as if Parmenian had said something relevant, and tortures himself in vain in order to hammer out some answer; and he gives one no less alien from David’s meaning. Let this indeed have been the wretched darkness of unhappy times; if more light has shone upon our age, let us congratulate it.

Meanwhile, those of sound judgment can recognize in this writer what we admire also in other African authors: a vehement, sharp, dense, and sinewy style, whether in speaking or arguing, especially when an attack must be made upon a person. This writer must certainly have possessed great authority from the outset because of his reputation for good and sincere faithfulness in narration, since even the Donatists whom he otherwise attacks most fiercely thought themselves victorious if they could at any time use his testimony.

Thus, concerning the fiction and fable they advanced that their Donatus had been acquitted and Caecilian condemned, they tried—though with calumny no less impudent than treacherous—to establish it by a crafty use of our Optatus’s words. “Accordingly,” Augustine says in his brief account of the conference with the Donatists, “as though they were about to produce something of the greatest force, they requested that Optatus be read, as they had requested before; and the passage of Optatus which the Donatists were putting forward was read. The question concerned its meaning. The Catholics, not so much astonished as laughing at the madness of their opponents, asked that Optatus be read entire, since he alone could refute the lies of the Donatists most openly.”

Thus that dispute was decided by the testimony of this one writer. He must, I repeat, have been a witness of great authority and dignity—a witness whom the Donatists, who otherwise dared anything, did not dare reject, although they felt themselves slaughtered by him. Indeed, they preferred to be convicted of calumny and falsehood rather than appear to place no trust in him.

I do not propose to explain at greater length how much benefit can come to the Church from these books of Optatus. I say only this: even if the sole thing present in them were the history of the rising and strengthening Donatist sect and faction, they were highly useful to the Christian commonwealth not only formerly, but still are. And indeed, if there is any history which above all others we ought to desire in this age to be read and known by many, this surely is the one. In it one might say both that the intemperance of our own time is almost portrayed and that the image of the conflicts by which our world is shaken is represented in living colors.

I do not wish now to pursue the comparison, because I could do so neither without hateful resentment nor even without the bitterest grief. Perhaps it is in the interest of the Christian name that the foul reproaches which this age witnesses should be buried in everlasting oblivion rather than transmitted to the memory of posterity. Yet, though they may now be suppressed, they somehow seem both to survive and to be read in the proceedings of the Donatists and in their whole terrible tragedy. From the spark or smoke of some ambitious contention, I know not whose, it blazed into flames which not only spread through all Africa and mingled it in a most deadly schism, but also involved the Christian world in a fire spreading farther for more than three hundred years. For we learn from the letters of Pope Gregory that it endured even in his time.

The rage of the Donatists had scarcely settled in Africa in any fashion when another flood of Arian Vandals poured in, of the kind described by Victor of Utica. I shall not be a prophet if I say what dangers hang over our own times, for they are already seen with our eyes and held in our hands. But you know what the ungrateful world still deserves.

Therefore I wished both to address you in this edition—for I recently heard your pious groans—and to dedicate to you this testimony of my regard. For I remember, and shall never forget, that recently, when, at your prompting, I had spoken on civil law in the new Belgian school, our conversation turned to the remembrance of ancient ecclesiastical history; and we found that you shared the same judgment as I concerning these letters and studies. This came about, surely, not so much through country, education, or common friendship as through a certain similar concern for the commonwealth. Farewell.

Paris, the Kalends of September.

### To Jean Lucanius. The Same [Author] to Calvin.

As the bookseller was now about to publish these books of Optatus, certain friends and intimates reminded me that I could not without reproach pass over [Col. 1108D] what I seemed incidentally to have promised in my second reply to you last year: namely, that I would at some other time say that the history of the trial in which Caecilian and Donatus contended cannot yield the conclusion which you—who seem not to recount so great a matter in the best faith—draw from it with such confidence, and which I too, having once followed an erring guide with a certain childish credulity, included in my commentaries on Constantine. Certainly, since a hidden error spreads and grows more widely, concealment that either nourishes or covers it is excessively treacherous—especially in ecclesiastical controversies.

Thus I remember that Peter the Martyr, a man both learned and diligent, because he had not been warned, was led by your same error to wish to state further from the history of which I speak [Col. 1109A] that rulers are the lawful judges of religion: because, he says, Constantine did not reject the Donatists’ appeal from Miltiades, bishop of Rome, by whom they had been condemned, but entrusted the matter to the bishop of Arles. I was at Strasbourg, in his house, when he was writing such things in his book on Judges. But Optatus was not present to dispel, by his testimony and authority, the clouds of false opinion, as it were brooding over that history.

And first, indeed, I know that many wonder how it happens that, although Optatus and Augustine, in recounting this history, nevertheless extol the prerogatives (*presbeia*) of the ancient Roman Church, you and yours now wish from that same history to diminish those prerogatives, or even overthrow them. They wonder too that, in recounting it, you were able to praise Augustine’s one-hundred-and-sixty-second letter, [Col. 1109B] which, while truthfully narrating what we are investigating, also adds concerning the Roman Church what you deny.

Yet that trial must have carried some great—if I may put it so—prejudice or presumption, since its records and their truth were subsequently so fiercely disputed. Optatus and Augustine worked especially hard to establish and defend it against the slanders of the Donatists. All the more intolerable, then, would it be if it were now corrupted again. Yet I shall be less surprised if someone errs in recounting it, since I remember that Augustine himself too, when publishing his commentaries of proofs and testimonies against the Donatists, committed a certain *mnēmonikon hamartēma*—an error of memory—which he confessed in his books of Retractations.

I shall state briefly what I believe truer, not in order to teach you—for who [Col. 1109C] could carry owls to Athens?—but to confess that from Optatus I have learned something in this matter which I could not learn in your school of “unhistoricalness” (*tēs anistorēsias*).

First, I think it clear that Caecilian was unjustly condemned in a certain synod at Carthage while absent, but did not appeal to Constantine. Rather, the Donatists, through one Anullinus, an impious man, took care that this case should be referred to Constantine, who shortly before had crushed Maxentius in Italy. Distrusting, I suppose, the judgment of the African bishops—which had been unjustly pronounced against an absent man rather than a contumacious one—they wished it to be confirmed by an imperial decision, which they trusted they could obtain no less easily.

But, sensing that this precedent, by which such jurisdiction was assigned to rulers, was odious and unusual in ecclesiastical cases, they shamelessly cavilled that Caecilian himself had done what they had done. And this is the single factual question between our Optatus and Parmenianus. But Optatus clearly proves that the Donatists did what they malignantly charged Caecilian with doing—that is, sought judges from Constantine—when he produces their petition submitted to Constantine.

At the same time he adds—which I ask you to observe with me in the second place—Constantine’s reply, as though out of a certain scruple recoiling from cognizance of this case, and refusing and rejecting it as far as he could: “You ask judgment from me in the secular sphere, when I myself await Christ’s judgment.” Therefore the excellent Emperor declares that this case belongs neither to [Col. 1110A] his court nor to his jurisdiction. He did the same again at the Synod of Nicaea, when bishops disputing among themselves offered him their memorials.

Therefore he remitted the case of Caecilian and Donatus to ecclesiastical judgment, over which Miltiades, bishop of Rome, lawfully presided. Yet you recount that he was judge only by the emperor’s commission. Shall we then say that he judged by delegated imperial authority, as the laws of that time spoke? You add that Constantine appointed judges not only from Italy and Gaul, but also from Spain. Why do you add Spain? For I do not recall any bishops other than those of Italy and Gaul. Although Augustine reports Parmenianus as saying that assistance was rendered to Caecilian through Hosius the Spaniard, he does not say that Hosius was his judge.

[Col. 1110B] There was no doubt concerning Miltiades, bishop of Rome. But the Donatists wished to have judges from Gaul. Optatus relates that three were appointed from Gaul, and fifteen from Italy, in addition to Miltiades, who was an African but bishop of Rome.

Now, in the third place, 114 note carefully that Optatus counts Marinus, bishop of Arles, among those Gauls, and indicates that he came to Rome in order to sit with Miltiades. This is chiefly what deceived you. I say so with your leave and goodwill, because I have been accustomed to speak freely and familiarly with you.

You contend that in this case the bishop of Arles was superior to the Roman bishop. First, this is unprecedented and unheard of. Certainly Cyprian the African, although by no means flattering Stephen, bishop of Rome, nevertheless says that Stephen had authority to censure and depose Marcian, bishop of Arles. Now a Frenchman seeks to prove that the bishop of Arles was judge of the Roman bishop himself. But let us hear the proof.

You say that Donatus, condemned by Miltiades, appealed, and that Constantine entrusted judgment of this appeal to the bishop of Arles, who sits as judge in order to pronounce, after the Roman pontiff, whatever may seem right. Is that really so? What remains but to place the bishop of Arles above the throne even of Constantine himself, who in ancient inscriptions is also called *pontifex maximus*?

Yet Optatus refutes you when he affirms that the bishop of Arles was present at the earlier judgment and sat with Miltiades. Likewise, he overturns your second fabrication when he relates that Constantine, being appealed to again, [Col. 1110D] himself rejected cognizance of this case; indeed, detesting this kind of frenzied appeal, he exclaimed: “O mad audacity of frenzy!” and so forth. For this is what is written in Constantine’s manuscript letter, in which this history is again narrated; and, to increase the abhorrence, it is added that this appeal appeared to have been interposed from the heavenly judgment to an earthly one.

Accordingly, chiefly from that letter I restored and corrected this passage of Optatus, which was otherwise corrupt and faulty. I recognized that the emendation of a learned and ingenious jurist must be rejected. Noticing that, in place of *a rabida*, some books read *orbita*, others *arbita*, he cleverly conjectured that these were traces of an ancient formula signifying: “You have rashly appealed from a matter [Col. 1111A] rightly adjudged.” But if we cannot say that Constantine then examined and judged this appeal, why should we ascribe to him the formula of a sentence by which he declared that the appeal had been unjustly made? Certainly, when he was at last afterwards compelled to judge, Augustine testifies that he used very different words.

Optatus indeed makes no mention of other judges being appointed again; nevertheless, you exult because, as you say, Constantine entrusted judgment of this appeal to the bishop of Arles. Is that really so? But this bishop of Arles had already been a judge with Miltiades. Does the same person appeal from himself? Or will the one who judged be judge again of the appeal? Why should I adduce our laws? Common sense itself refutes such a monstrosity.

But you cite Augustine as witness. [Col. 1111B] I accept him. What does he say? In that very letter which you praise, he says only that Constantine took care that the same case should be examined and determined at Arles, and that he gave—such are his words—“another judgment at Arles, of other bishops”; not because it was now necessary, but yielding to the perversity of the Donatists and desiring by every means to restrain such impudence.

From these words of Augustine I certainly understand that Constantine made an extraordinary concession to the Donatists’ importunity, which you would have considered part of ordinary law. Yet, when you hear that it was the judgment of other bishops, you ought to have inferred that it was not the judgment of the bishop of Arles.

What then? A synod of many bishops had assembled at Arles to judge many ecclesiastical cases. [Col. 1111C] Among them were also many who had earlier judged Donatus at Rome with Miltiades. Taking this opportunity, so that he might leave nothing undone to crush the Donatists’ obstinacy, Constantine did not refuse to let them be heard again in such a synod. Why are you surprised that Miltiades did not object to this? Indeed, why do you affirm that the bishop of Arles, who had already judged that case at Rome, was judge of the appeal? Why do you not rather recognize that such cognizance was left to other bishops, who had not formerly judged at Rome with Miltiades? For it is established that very many others came together at Arles “from diverse and innumerable places” (*ek diaphorōn kai amythētōn topōn*), as Constantine himself says in his letter to Chrestus, bishop of Syracuse, by which he summons him from Sicily to this assembly.

[Col. 1111D] For my own part, as you know, I have no private interest in whether the Roman bishop is greater than the bishop of Arles, or the bishop of Arles greater than the Roman, whether now or formerly. But no honorable man can calmly endure even secular histories to be polluted by fabricated falsehoods.

At least you ought to have read the records of that Synod of Arles, which I recently obtained. For in them you would have read the bishops’ letter to Sylvester, successor of Miltiades, who had meanwhile died. From it you would readily have understood how far they were from exalting themselves above the bishop of the City; indeed, how they deferred everything to him; and also how greatly they wished that he might have presided over them at Arles, had he been able to leave Rome at that time. Finally, you would have understood that they had not assembled for the sake of Donatus alone.

It is remarkable, moreover, that you did not add that, although Caecilian [Col. 1112A] was again acquitted by them, the Donatists nevertheless did not cease, since they would accept no judge but Constantine—so that Constantine, who up to that point had remitted this judgment from himself to bishops, finally undertook it. But you could not deny that this was an extraordinary example which, as our lawyers say, cannot be drawn into a precedent; nor should anyone be tolerated who therefore said that Constantine was superior to both bishops and councils in ecclesiastical causes. Indeed, he himself frankly declared that in such matters he was greatly their inferior; from the beginning he condemned this appeal; and if he was at last compelled to undertake the examination, he undertook it in such a way as afterwards to seek pardon from the holy bishops, as Augustine says.

[Col. 1112B] Nor would it have been new had he not refused to investigate at least the factual question underlying that case. For he could lawfully undertake the inquiry which he entrusted to the proconsul Aelianus. The question was whether Felix, who had ordained Caecilian, or Caecilian himself, had been a *traditor*, as they then spoke: that is, whether he had handed over the most holy copies of the sacred books to the agents and investigators of Diocletian, who had decreed that the Christians’ sacred writings should be destroyed. Whoever, in the end, is judge of that question, it detracts nothing from ecclesiastical jurisdiction.

Since I am not writing a history, but merely briefly indicating what you seemed not sufficiently to have observed in this history, I shall not linger over it now. For we shall inquire on another occasion, when you wish, concerning ecclesiastical appeals: whether what the Synod of Sardica decreed had also previously been decreed by Nicaea—which was once doubted in Africa and which you deny, while Athanasius affirms it—and what transmarine appeals were forbidden by the Council of Milevis. [Col. 1112C] Such questions are historical rather than contentious, and not foreign to civil law; just as one might say that, formerly, in civil cases there was an appeal from Africa to the praetorian prefect of Italy, but that our Justinian exempted Africa from this Italian praetorian prefecture and gave it a prefecture of its own, under whose administration were also Numidia 115 and Byzacium.

[Col. 1112D] I say Byzacium, which Pliny also counts among the regions of Africa and which Augustine indicates to have been polluted by the Donatists, mentioning the Donatists of Byzacium in his book *On the Unity of the Church*, as does Epiphanius—although in the latter that word is corrupt; just as one of your printers recently made Byzantium out of this Byzacium.

I had not intended to write more—indeed, not even so much—now to you, most learned sir; but you have recently deserved so well of me that I cannot fail to return some gratitude. Yet I can return no other at present than this: if, while rereading such histories, I happen to observe something else which it would concern you not to be ignorant of, I shall report it to you familiarly. Nor shall I go far.

Although I know that you have read the acts of the Council of Nicaea more than those of Arles, [Col. 1113A] I nevertheless wonder all the more that you write—even in your *Institutes*—that Athanasius presided at that council, and that on this account you again insult the bishop of Rome. You know that it is of no concern to me whether what you report is true or not. But all histories relate that Athanasius was then very young and only a deacon. What kind of council, then, do you construct for us, in which a young deacon sits before all bishops and archbishops and even presides over them? And why do you prefer him to his own bishop of Alexandria?

No less unprecedented is your statement in the same place that, by decree of that council, first place among the patriarchs was assigned to the bishop of Rome, but that his legates were relegated in the assembly to fourth place. It is also new for you to say that what the synod itself declares to have been “an ancient and customary practice” (*archaion ethos kai synēthes*) was decreed only by that synod.

[Col. 1113B] I pass over your not recounting in better faith that a decree concerning the marriage or celibacy of ministers was made there in accordance with Paphnutius’ opinion. But I cannot conceal what I ought not to be silent about. You know what I wrote long ago concerning Arius in my *Constantine*, and yet, while attacking another man’s little book, you did not blush shamelessly to attribute and impute to me I know not what defense of Arius’s impiety.

But, that you may perceive that you were then carried away by a kind of blind vertigo, reread what you also falsely attribute to me: that the Arians denied that *logos* in John means hypostasis or person. Who ever said this except you? Certainly, at Nicaea the bishop of Alexandria cited against the Arians that first chapter of John, when the question was not what *logos* meant, but what these words meant: “In the beginning” (*en archē*). Therefore it was not a mark of your exceedingly lofty learning to confuse ignorantly the doctrine of Paul of Samosata with that of Arius.

[Col. 1113C] But what is it that you do not mingle together when you choose? You do not hesitate, even in your *Institutes*, to write that Sabellius arose after Arius. So much are you a stranger and foreigner in the history in which you wish to appear preeminent. You will say that our Optatus is unlearned; yet he might at least teach you that Sabellius was much earlier than Arius, and that what you said of Sabellius you ought rather to have said of Photinus, whom he calls the heretic of his own time.

But come: these are merely chronological points, which you will say you despise because you are occupied with theology. It is not ours to admonish you about other matters. Yet I cannot suppress everything.

[Col. 1113D] I have often wondered why you deny that the Creed for which the Synod of Nicaea has thus far been so greatly praised, and which has in turn been so greatly praised because of it, is Nicene. You remember, I suppose, when in former years you dictated to one of your ministers and colleagues your defense of your honor against Peter Caroli, your former colleague, who accused you of Arianism; you remember, I say, what sort of confession you wished to be published. For you not only confess that you denied that this formula proceeded from the Synod of Nicaea, but also that you said it seemed rather a tautological song, fit only to be chanted.

There are here surely two great sins of great audacity and dangerous example. That this Creed is Nicene is as certain as that there was a Council of Nicaea. [Col. 1114A] Athanasius, Hilary, Epiphanius, Nazianzen, Basil, Theodoret, and Socrates are weighty witnesses, and they recite this formula from that council. Why you do not believe them, I do not know.

But to call a prattling and ridiculous chant that which religious antiquity judged to be a solemn and divine formula concerning so great a mystery—is it not blasphemy? You yourself would say so, if you were judging another.

So be it. There has already been published there, not without your privilege, I suppose, some compilation concerning the state of the Church, which your bookseller wonderfully extols, almost as though it were the flower of ecclesiastical history. Although it is otherwise stitched together from stale fables and trifles, it at least does this in good faith: it includes among the acts of the Council of Nicaea the formula I mentioned. Yet it mingles with it such a dregs of lies, drawn from I know not what cesspools, [Col. 1114B] that I cannot wonder enough that such a sewer has long failed to smell foul to you. If it came forth from elsewhere, I might perhaps wonder less, and it might perhaps do less harm. But because it has come from your side, and is believed to have appeared only on your authority, I both wonder and grieve that it is filled with such impure drivel.

What then? While examining matters pertaining to Optatus’s discussion of baptism, I was also astonished by the audacity of that compilation, which confidently declares it a manifest error of the Council of Nicaea to decree that Paulianists must be rebaptized. Yet Augustine, who otherwise fought most vigorously for the one baptism, says very differently: [Col. 1114C] “The Council of Nicaea decreed that the Paulianists are to be baptized in the Catholic Church. Hence it must be believed that they do not retain the rule of baptism which many heretics carried away with them and observed when they departed from the Catholic Church.”

Just as our Optatus has caused me to reflect more carefully on the history of the Donatists, so now, I do not know how, he also causes me to answer you again, most desired sir, and your accusations; and not wholly to disregard many matters which, though perhaps troublesome to you, nevertheless occur to me.

Once, compelled by an importunate and insulting slander of yours, I abruptly sent you a brief commentary, drawn from the laws and our civil law, concerning slanderers. I suppose you recognize that it was not without reason that in that commentary I made mention not only of you but also of the Donatists. But instead of satisfaction, you replied [Col. 1114D] that our response was a cold rhapsody.

I admit that something harsher and more vehement might have been said. But I saw that Optatus and Augustine had been content with such moderation in a similar case. Optatus says: “When envy intervenes, it is easy for angry people to hurl abuse; but whenever an accusation is pressed, clear proof is necessary.” Augustine, against Petilian: “He who makes an accusation without witness and without any evidence proves to be a reviling abuser rather than a truthful accuser.” And in another book against the same man: “Why do you shout before you prove? In the great expanse of speech, you are confined within the narrowest straits by one very brief word: ‘Prove it.’”

[Col. 1115A] I think this brief prescription sufficient to refute whatever you have uttered slanderously against me. And I do not know how it happens that, reading what was once answered to the Donatists, I seem to have something to answer you in precisely the same words. Thus I could easily have enlarged that commentary of mine, had I wished.

But let us dismiss these matters, which concern private actions and persons. For the commonwealth is little concerned with what is determined concerning me or you. Nor do I compare myself with Caecilian, or you with Donatus. I should be exceedingly foolish if I even entertained the thought, and intolerable.

But a far different and much greater cause, as it was formerly conducted, is now at issue; and in it there is a most important question of law. Augustine indeed writes in the *Retractations* that in his books against Parmenianus a great question is debated and resolved: whether, within unity and the common participation of the same sacraments, evil persons contaminate good persons. [Col. 1115B] But there was another question no less great: whether the sacraments depend upon the worthiness of the minister; whether baptism administered by unworthy persons is null; whether, on account of their unworthiness, Christ’s Church would cease to be Church if it employed them; and whether the Donatists could with any right contend that the Church was enclosed solely within their schismatic conventicles—though they had separated themselves from the rest of the body on the slightest, indeed almost nonexistent, occasion.

The dispute, therefore, is great and concerns the greatest of all matters; and I do not know whether the remedy for schism is not more difficult than that for heresy. Augustine wrote against Petilian *On the Unity of the Church*; Cyprian had written on it before him. For the treatise of Cyprian commonly entitled *On the Simplicity of Prelates*, I learned at Trent ought to be entitled *On the Unity of the Church*. I learned this from a manuscript found in Apulia by Antonio Agustín, jurist and bishop.

[Col. 1115C] But I do not think even the judgments or counsels of such arbiters will restore to us the unity (*henotēta*) we desire, unless God himself reconciles human minds; for the division lies in them rather than in the matters themselves. Africa had its *Catholicus*—that is, the agent of Caesar or the fisc, for so he was called—and he at one time attempted to reconcile even the Donatists with the Catholic Church. But he accomplished nothing. A suitable judge for the whole controversy is still sought.

[Col. 1115D] Yet so be it. I hope I shall do you a very welcome service when, in these disputes, I praise the rule and formula of judgment which our Optatus gives, having most elegantly transferred to ecclesiastical cases a certain example from civil law. Therefore, what he says concerning a will in Book V, I assure you greatly pleases me, although I grant you that the passage he cites from John’s Gospel is irrelevant to the proposed question concerning baptism.

But as regards the proposition, even if that alone were read in Optatus’s books, those who now have them in everyone’s hands would for that reason be blocks of wood. Nor do I doubt that Augustine, delighted by this transference from our law, alluded to that passage of Optatus when he wrote similar things concerning a will in Psalm 21 against the Donatists, who refused to acknowledge the Catholic Church spread throughout the whole world.

[Col. 1116A] But tell me, will you also grant that one may say here what the laws concerning a military will say: that it is enough if the intention is established in any manner whatever; that we cannot reject an oral declaration without writing if witnesses are not lacking; and, finally, that trusts (*fideicommissa*) have their own law? Why this? Because, when Augustine disputes with the Donatists concerning baptism, he contends that usage, consent, and the testimony of the Church rightly prove that certain commands, precepts, and institutions are apostolic, although they were not written by the apostles themselves.

See, I beg you, my friend, what so great a bishop—whom you too once attribute so much to—writes in Book IV of *On Baptism against the Donatists*, chapters 6 and 24; Book V, chapter 23; and Book I against Cresconius, chapter 33.

[Col. 1116B] But you recently wrote to me, I may say, a terrible letter and pressed upon me a controversy concerning unwritten traditions (*peri paradoseōn agraphōn*). Because I had not written about them, though the best bishops of the ancient Church had written about them, you assailed the matter so that, passing them by, you seemed to attack me alone.

Let this indeed be permitted you under your new law. But there is another wrong: that in this question you confuse everything so thoroughly that, while we now wonder what you mean, you almost prescribe silence—because you think that you too are permitted now to affirm and now to deny.

I do not have so much leisure as to turn over all your volumes, with which you could load many wagons; nor, if I did, should I greatly wish to abuse it so. But from those parts which I have sampled at various times, if my memory does not deceive me, you seem first to have written that you do not object to traditions of this kind which are demonstrated from the certain and perpetual consensus of the orthodox. You concede this to Pighius when you argue against him concerning free will.

Afterward, when you wrote on the Epistle to the Corinthians, you wrote that you did not deny [Col. 1116C] that some apostolic traditions had not been written down, but did not concede that they were parts of doctrine; rather, they concerned only order and polity—words by which, I suppose, you include rites and ceremonies as well.

Finally, when you declaimed against me, you seemed unwilling to acknowledge any traditions at all.

> By what knot am I to hold Proteus, who changes his face?

The Donatists, when they disputed concerning the charge of “tradition,” as they called it, were not so double-faced—gladly using your own word—as you are when you dispute concerning an entirely different kind of tradition. In each controversy the first question is one of fact.

[Col. 1116D] But what Augustine so often demanded from the Donatists in the “conference,” as it was called—that there should be some definite state of the case and a definite judgment—I demand first of all from you, and indeed by my own law. As for what remains, I shall supply it. But so long as you change and speak variously, and are not consistent with yourself, I say nothing.

Thus, when sacred writings are at issue, now you employ their so-called canon, now you reject it as uncertain and variable. I say nothing that is not found in your books. Thus you now praise, now trample underfoot, the ancient writers of the Church. Indeed, in your declamation against me you wrote that no certainty of Christian doctrine could be drawn from any of them.

Good God, what do I hear when I hear that? And what will they say if they now hear it said? What shall we say, when we praise that first Church which survived after the apostles had departed: it is not merely derided by others [Col. 1117A] as a crazed and superstitious old woman, or some foolish Fauna, or a masked Lamia; it is also accused almost as a workshop of falsehood, imposture, and fraud—although it is precisely the Church from which we have received the sacred writings, and by whose testimony we maintain them to be authenticated and common.

To what have we now come, if it is permitted to accuse it of malicious deceit? Indeed, where are you rushing if you make it guilty? And how will you stand if you have such an adversary?

When you hear this, perhaps you will again exclaim and repeat what you wrote in your declamation against me: that we set before men the phantom of antiquity, from which presently there gushes a monstrous heap of every error; for, as you say, if one asks what antiquity we mean, we shall put forward insipid trifles circulated under the name of Ignatius and men like him.

[Col. 1117B] Fair words, master. Although we do not possess the salt that is in you, you nevertheless know that we strongly shrink from insipidities, whether trifles or absurdities. You know that we have often condemned pseudepigraphic writings (*pseudepigrapha*); and, if you have read our own commentaries on the method of history, you do not fail to know how I hate fables.

But, to be brief, I shall answer you in the same situation, and in precisely the same words, most modestly, as you once answered Sadoleto when he called you an enemy of the ancient Church:

> Here I shall not demand that you deal truly and candidly with us—although this was a thing that a philosopher, much less a Christian, ought to offer of his own accord—but shall ask only that you do not descend to such an illiberal license of slander as will greatly injure your reputation among good and serious men, even if we ourselves are silent.

[Col. 1117C] You know this, my John; and if you persist in denying it, I shall make all understand that you knew it and craftily, knowingly dissembled it: namely, that we in good faith derive the memory of religious antiquity which we commend from the best and purest monuments.

I wonder what entered your mind when, contrary to your conscience, you attributed to me what you say concerning Ignatius. Certainly I recognize and revere certain fragments of his in the books of Eusebius and Theodoret. Will you reject those too? Recently, when a very learned man had cited something from them to you concerning the Eucharist, because it pressed you, you exclaimed that it was taken from the trifling letters that circulate under Ignatius’s name. But you are wrong, master. That statement is not found in them. It is found, however, and cited in the best books of Theodoret.

[Col. 1117D] Would that what Eusebius testifies Ignatius wrote concerning apostolic traditions still survived. We should have in that excellent testimony a great defense against your denials. But although many monuments of this kind have perished, you shall not sink the remnants that press you.

What then? I shall use your advice in order to accomplish what I desire. For now there comes to mind something that I once read in the same letter from which I repeated a few words a little earlier. You recently wrote, in order to mock my folly, that as a boy I had been able to recite that whole letter from memory. I do not remember that I was ever blessed with such a memory, or that I wished to use it so childishly. Yet, although through age I have become forgetful, it is well that not everything has slipped away.

[Col. 1118A] Thus I recall that, when in that letter you boasted that you attempted nothing except that the ancient face of the Church might someday be restored, you added these words:

> Set before your eyes, I pray, that ancient face of the Church, such as the monuments themselves show it to have existed among the Greeks in the age of Chrysostom and Basil, and among the Latins in the century of Cyprian, Ambrose, and Augustine.

So you spoke formerly. Because I thought that you said these things seriously, I therefore turned to those monuments, to which, as you see, I now add the books of Optatus. When in such mirrors I seemed somehow to see that face, I shuddered when afterwards I beheld it defiled and polluted. And just as Apelles, if he saw his Venus, or Protogenes his Ialysus, smeared with mud, would suffer great grief, so I did not doubt that those teachers of the ancient Church whom you praised, if they lived, could not behold such deformity without great pain.

[Col. 1118B] Nor did it fail to occur to me that the words which Scipio Africanus used might be said of those against whom he spoke. Praising that old verse,

> By ancient morals and by men the Roman state stands,

and lamenting the ruin of his commonwealth, he once said:

> Our age, having received the commonwealth like an excellent painting, though one fading with age, not only neglected to renew it in the same colors in which it had been, but did not even take care to preserve its form, or at least its outer lineaments, as it were. Of so great an evil [Col. 1118C] we must not only render an account, but must also plead our cause in some manner as defendants in a capital charge. For through our own vices, not by any chance, we retain the commonwealth in name but have long since lost it in reality.

So spoke that Roman. I thought that you, as a youth, bewailed in the same spirit the deformity, wrinkles, filth, and decay of the aging Church, and that at the same time you had taken up a paintbrush to restore its former appearance, rather than a sponge with which to erase even its outer lineaments.

For in the same letter, when you took offense at being accused by an adversary of despising the ancient Church, you exclaimed:

> Will you now call him an enemy of antiquity who, through zeal for ancient piety and holiness, dissatisfied with the present corruption of things, endeavors to correct for the better and restore to its former splendor what has been scattered and corrupted in the Church?

When I heard this as a boy, I confess that I leapt up and cried:

> Sweep the pavement; display the shining columns,  
> while the dry spider descends with all her web.

[Col. 1118D] But now that you have gained power, you display only your own—your own, my Calvin—new form; and, so that it alone may be seen, you erase and efface the old. You are angry with us because we cannot wholly forget sound antiquity, and because we recall you to that face of the Church which existed in the age of Basil, Chrysostom, Optatus, Ambrose, and Augustine, just as you once recalled us to it. Are you surprised if one whose better opinion of you has deceived him grieves that he has been deceived?

[Col. 1119A] Yet you deal even more dishonestly with me. For you nevertheless wish to persuade men that you are still animated by the same zeal for antiquity which you formerly professed, whereas I merely set forth an empty phantom. These are marvelous tricks. To expose them, you say, a lawful inquiry must be instituted. But you disturb that inquiry by raising tumult and hurling abuse.

> You fling forth puffed-up phrases and words a foot and a half long.

Thus, by mere noise you drive your opponent away. Yet, though you may frighten children, this is—using your own word—spitting, not speaking. Although nothing is further from my profession than quarrelling with you, nevertheless come: since you provoke me, allow a fair hearing to be granted on equal terms and in good faith. Though my weakness is by no means suited to a formal contest, I shall nevertheless make those who are willing understand that you stand farther removed from religious antiquity; and that you do not always reproduce in good faith whatever you recite from it, whether this be through negligence or design. I shall also make you understand that the man whom you falsely pretend to be pursuing some improper aim [Col. 1119B] seeks truth seriously, diligently, and religiously; that he is swayed by no party hatred; that, when he accuses one person’s fault, he does not excuse another’s; and that he is not frightened by your resounding rattles.

Let a hearing be granted, to the hope of which I am now in some measure called. I shall make you see, even unwillingly, that he—though you cry out that he is a nobody—nevertheless shuns the extremes that are faulty and seeks the middle course, so far as it is sound and right; that he wishes to avoid the error which Nazianzen said ignorant peasants made in trying to straighten a crooked tree, by failing to take sufficient care; and that he nevertheless wishes to preserve what this age has most rightly corrected. He would be exceedingly ungrateful if he did not acknowledge how great a light God has kindled in this age, and how splendidly many have deserved of religion [Col. 1119C]. But he would again be exceedingly blind if he did not see into what ruin others meanwhile rush. It is an old saying which Cicero relates was once wittily thrown at your pagan: “Does he limp?” Do not take it ill that I observe the same thing in your own advances.

As I allowed Cassander, to whom this task more properly belonged, to speak first on the subject about which you declaimed with utter lack of restraint in order to harass both him and me, so I have long been waiting to see what answer you will at last give to his reply. But again 118 I promise you: the good cause shall not lack an advocate if you continue to calumniate. At least grant me that I may deal with you civilly, since I see that the issue is one of fact rather than law—the sort I perceive in the matters about which you dispute with me. Thus, in this conjectural state of the case, I shall have only [Col. 1119D] to deal with proofs, witnesses, and the reliability of documents. I shall use none except the best and most authentic.

If you plead an objection of forgery, take care not to entangle yourself in that very charge—whether you recklessly assert that the names of the excellent witnesses cited are false, or say that they lie and wish, without any proof, to prosecute as guilty of *pseudomartyria* (false witness) persons whom you do not convict. Consider also whether, contrary to the rules of our law, you may later reject persons whom you have once approved, and approve again those whom you had rejected. This may indeed be permitted where their diverse and private opinions are at issue; but those are not now our concern. When, however, testimony is sought concerning some public fact: if the person giving that testimony knowingly deceives, a good man will not do so knowingly, and he will sin not through error [Col. 1120A] but through fraud. Consider what will follow if whenever you please you wish to deprive religious antiquity of credit.

Meanwhile, allow me to recall to your memory what Augustine once wrote against the Manichaeans: “The result will be a complete perversion of all literature, and the abolition of all books committed to memory, if what has been strengthened by the religious reverence of so many peoples and confirmed by the agreement of so many persons and ages is brought into such doubt that it cannot retain even the credibility and authority of ordinary history.”

I return to the case of the Donatists. See: the question is whether those baptized by heretics ought to be baptized again in the Church. You will answer, “They ought not.” Why so? Optatus and Augustine produce a certain passage from the Gospel of John concerning the one washing [Col. 1120B]; you will say that it is irrelevant. You do not allow the passage from the Acts of the Apostles which the Donatists adduced to be explained by drawing a distinction between Christ’s baptism and John’s baptism—the distinction used by Optatus and Augustine. Rejecting it, however, you prefer to interpret the word “baptism” in that passage of Acts singularly and innovatively as not signifying baptism. Yet in the end you return to Augustine on the one baptism and approve the ancient custom which he approves, though it had at one time been interrupted. Correctly. But by what argument? By what conjecture or reasoning do you refer that most ancient custom to the times of the Apostles? You are no longer free to object without contradicting yourself, especially since you disapprove the objection Cyprian made against Augustine.

If here you concede what you do not deny Augustine—although I shall not use this example except in a matter less doubtful—I have what I want: let the judges withdraw for deliberation. Where the fact is established, I have argued my case and spoken. Do not trouble me further. For I shall then accept whatever sound safeguards you wish: that no one abuse this precedent; that fraud and prejudice be not done to truth; that the truth of matters not be corrupted by errors in past acts; that consideration be given not only to what was done at Rome, but also to what ought to be done; and finally, that the distinction between fact and law not be rashly confused. Such safeguards are also in our books of law; never suppose that I wish to forget them.

Since it is permitted to take counsel—as the old jurists’ phrase is—and since by a certain right of ancient friendship [Col. 1120D] I may deal more freely with you, I shall conceal nothing. The dispute with the Donatists concerns the Church. You remember the marks by which you customarily teach that the Church is to be recognized. I beg you, my Censor: do these sufficiently identify and exclude the synagogues of the Donatists? Why do Optatus and Augustine allege marks entirely different? And what, indeed, do you think about those marks? When the question concerns the body, you say that the head must be inspected. Correct. Yet Augustine says that his controversy with the Donatists concerns not the head but the body, *On the Unity of the Church*, chapter 4. Therefore there is agreement about the head, and yet the controversy concerns the body. What else, do you think, did Optatus and Augustine say in order to establish this? And what do you determine concerning arguments of this kind? What, I say, do you judge when you hear them seeking to prove [Col. 1121A] that the possession of the Church is theirs by a certain perpetual succession—and, indeed, being content for its proof with the agreement and uninterrupted succession of at least the Roman bishops with whom they communicated, descending, as they say, from the Apostles; a succession whose series they enumerate from a catalogue?

Irenaeus, Tertullian, and others had previously done this with no dissimilar confidence. For, since that succession rested not upon some hereditary right of blood but upon ecclesiastical election and ordination, they did not doubt that a succession resting upon such a condition was a suitable witness to their apostolic doctrine, joined and continued with it. Christ spoke, as you know, of those who sit in Moses’ seat; the ancient Christians spoke of those who sit in Peter’s. I pass over what might now aptly and weightily be said concerning the status of either seat or the comparison of the chairs—especially by you, if you acted calmly. But I should gladly hear what you likewise decide concerning that law of Theodosius which Optatus heard proclaimed first, and which stands first in our legal books:

> “We desire all peoples whom the government of our clemency rules to practise that religion which the divine Apostle Peter delivered to the Romans, as the religion introduced by him himself and preserved to the present declares, and which it is evident that Pope Damasus follows,” etc. [Col. 1121B]

Here, I suppose, you will admit that the same succession is praised, although it is well known both what has been handed down concerning Liberius, whom Damasus succeeded—namely, that he was at one point nearly compelled into Arianism—and what Ammianus writes concerning Damasus’s elevation to this see: not without sweat and blood, not without force and arms, not without tumult and slaughter. Yet I suppose you will not here cry out what one of that order is reported later to have said: that more succeed Romulus in parricides than Peter in feeding sheep. For we are not now dealing with men’s vices, but with confession of religion and preservation of doctrine.

Come then: because the succession which they boast of is the sharpest battering-ram of our Optatus and of Augustine, who followed him, against the Donatists—and because the matter is important—I ask that I may hear your judgment on it. Indeed, you will say that you have already replied angrily. For in your declamation against me you imperiously ordered that the matter be repeated from your two books which you praised. It was not, you said, compatible with your dignity to say the same thing often. I shall do what you command, master.

In your *Institutes*, disputing against the Papists—whom you call so, unless you now prefer “Papans,” as from Rome we say “Romans”—who urge how highly Irenaeus, Tertullian, Origen, Augustine, and others valued this succession [Col. 1121D] (you do not name Optatus, because you had not yet read him), you preface that you will make good and studious men understand what this means. Then you ask your opponents why they do not cite Africa and all Asia. But because you say that you know their answer—that the Church had ceased there—why do you not rather ask this yourself of Irenaeus, who also lived in Asia, or of Tertullian, Optatus, and Augustine [Col. 1122A] 119, who lived in Africa at a time when churches still flourished there? Why, I say, do they instead cite and praise the succession of the Roman bishops and cling to that alone? Here I shall again await your answer.

At last, after a long digression, returning to the question at hand, you write that those holy doctors, because it was beyond controversy that nothing had been changed from the beginning down to that age in doctrine, whether at Rome or in other cities—for you added this in the French translation of your *Institutes*—took up what was sufficient to refute all new errors: namely, that their opponents were attacking a doctrine constantly retained from the Apostles themselves by unanimous agreement. But, my doctor, the opponents denied this very point: that it had been constantly retained and that nothing in it had been changed. That was the controversy which they raised. Our writers, however, adduce succession as proof; it not only included the condition that the same doctrine be retained and continued, but also proved that this condition had been fulfilled.

But I beg you, do you speak seriously when you seem to concede that down to Augustine’s age nothing, especially at Rome, had been changed in apostolic doctrine, and that the Roman bishops enumerated by Optatus or Augustine had been steadfast and faithful guardians of that doctrine?
