If you wrote this seriously and do not change your opinion, the matter is settled. But how I fear that you will not stand by the terms agreed! You wish, of course, to be granted what we are accustomed to allow in the Twelve Tables: that you may recover your stake if you regret some payment; as in Cicero’s *Hortensius* [Col. 1122C]. This is a hard condition if we are to deal with you. But you think anything is permitted you.

Thus, after you had commended to us both the doctrine and succession of the Roman bishops—at least down to Augustine’s age—you elsewhere, when it pleases you, accuse the same men of defection and corrupt religion. Thus you tear to pieces and savagely slaughter Siricius by name, whom Optatus praises last, when you attack celibacy. Yet, to say this in passing, I fear that in reporting what he wrote to the Spaniards concerning marriage you rashly attribute something to him. Among Ambrose’s letters there survives a letter of Siricius containing nothing of the sort; and you, who otherwise are by no means credulous, ought not so easily to have drawn from Gratian’s miscellany something which you would dishonourably ascribe to him [Col. 1122D].

But come now: say seriously and in good faith how long you think that succession of which we inquire endured, and when, or through whom, it was so interrupted that it wholly ceased. I have read the lives of the popes and the tragedies. But you see that what I ask of you, and to which you do not respond, is something else. For even if you interpret what Paul writes and predicts to the Thessalonians concerning the defection—which the ancients understood as concerning the Roman Empire—as an apostasy from the faith, and say that it happened long ago, you nevertheless do not say when it happened. When you say that, I shall consider it. But lest you suppose it enough to say anything whatever, know that you are not dealing with your foolish boys or servants.

Nor indeed need you torment yourself, as you do, to prove that succession is not genuine without doctrine. For I confess this freely, willingly, and at length; and where it is established that the doctrine is different, I agree with you that the right is different. Nor do I doubt the complete truth of what you say: that the tyranny of Caligula, Nero, Heliogabalus, and their like cannot be called the true constitution of the republic merely because they succeeded Brutus, Scipio, and Camillus. Nor, if you add that scorpions succeeded the Scipios, shall I object. And if you wish even to thunder and hurl lightning against such men—not successors but plunderers—I shall not merely join my voice to yours but shall, by my own complaint, increase with all the force of voice and lungs that I can the most just outcry. But nothing is achieved if there is only confused shouting and no definition of the thing at issue. Yet you define nothing so long as you do not specify the time from [Col. 1123A] which you hold that the succession in question defected.

In this question you habitually recall us to the example of the Jewish Church. But even there you do not define what you mean. You say that there were certain stages of defection in it. Correct. But when you begin to skim its history, you escape in such a way as to leave us in suspense. You say there were various changes in Judaea, until even the priests themselves polluted the temple of God with profane and abominable rites. But when did that happen, so that we may know from what time it was not lawful to communicate with them?

A little later in that same *Institutes*, you write that the prophets who were at Jerusalem or in Judaea, although conditions there were exceedingly corrupt, nevertheless did not hold separate assemblies of their own, but gathered with others in the temple because they were not compelled to engage in any superstitious worship; and that they acknowledged the Levitical priests, because, however unworthy of that honour, they had not yet been deposed. Yet on the very next page you recount that the prophets cried out that those assemblies were profane, assemblies to which it was no more permissible to assent than to deny God, and that they had necessarily to withdraw from participation in their gatherings, which was nothing other than an impious conspiracy against God [Col. 1123C]. Forgive my dullness if I still cannot perceive how the things you say cohere and agree. I am far from understanding sufficiently how you wish to determine from them the question concerning the Christian Church.

And although in your declamation against me you again say the same things on this subject, I still doubt what you mean. As for what you add concerning Jeroboam’s kingdom [Col. 1123D] and Israel’s apostasy, I confess it is clear; nor did you need to sweat in vain to explain it to me in so many words. But it has nothing to do with the Jewish Church. There, where the origin itself was defective, the question was not one of succession.

I call heaven and earth to witness that I deal with you religiously, so that, if you can, you may explain and free those whom you entangle in your evasions. This is no place for playing or mockery. Now, since in another passage you have again discussed the succession about which we inquire—the passage which you bid us hear—we shall hear you again, in the hope that perhaps your exposition may again shed some light upon Optatus and release us from great difficulty.

When you wrote against Charles V’s book against Augustine, you wrote that Irenaeus, who alleges the succession of which I spoke, properly opposed to charlatans spreading certain novel and impious doctrines the testimony and agreement of churches founded by the Apostles, which were therefore not rashly believed to be guardians of apostolic doctrine, whose memory was still fresh. Correct. But since I hold you to this, do not cleverly slip away. Rather, for your own sake, consider what answer you will give when someone presses you with such testimony and agreement. You certainly harassed me too angrily when a friend of mine happened to appear to attribute great weight to such testimony.

To say it in a word, do you know what I wish? I wish that you and everyone may resolve that the whole ancient Church, once founded by the Apostles, now be summoned as a capital defendant before your tribunal [Col. 1124B], and that inquiry be made what judgment at last should be rendered concerning it as a whole. Although I do not fail to know what your boldness is, nevertheless I think that, when you see such a host under such an accusation in your criminal consistory, you will be broken by a certain shame, like that ungrateful young man 120 long ago at Rome who accused his aged, white-haired father of treason before Tiberius. Terrified by the sight of his father staring sternly at him and by the sound of his chains, he immediately fled.

Proceed. You say that Augustine fought against the Donatists and not without reason opposed to them the succession and testimony of the Catholic Church, since they did not deny that the Church from which they had nevertheless defected had retained apostolic doctrine. But what will you say when Augustine relies on the same defence against the Manichaeans? Certainly they disputed about doctrine. It is strange indeed that you should think Augustine did not dispute about it [Col. 1124C] against the Donatists. If you said this of Optatus, who seems to have regarded them more as schismatics than as heretics, you might perhaps be heard more readily. But you know that Augustine calls them heretics a hundred times; and he would certainly have wronged them if they confessed what you report.

Indeed, if they confessed this, how could they deny either that baptism was legitimate or that the Church of the Catholics was the true Church? Did they wish, in order to condemn themselves, to confess that they were apostates, while shouting that their own Church alone was Christian and apostolic, and that the rest were apostate? I know that Cresconius the grammarian, their advocate, cleverly contended that although they were called schismatics, they could not be called heretics, and that Augustine, who accused them of heresy, had therefore branded them maliciously. But you know what Augustine replied to this trifler.

I pass over the fact that Epiphanius and Theodoret also charge them with Arian impiety. Jerome certainly says in the *Catalogue* that Donatus wrote a book on the Holy Spirit conforming to Arian doctrine. And Augustine, in *On Heresies*, writes that Donatus of Carthage did not hold the Catholic doctrine concerning the Trinity, although the multitude of Donatists did not notice this. And in Letter 163 he says that he had heard that the Arians, having separated from Catholic communion, tried to associate the Donatists with themselves in Africa. Nor do I doubt that most of them would readily do and say whatever distressed Catholics, since they did not even refuse to conspire [Col. 1125A] with Julian the Apostate.

For the present, let it suffice that their doctrine concerning baptism and the Church was impious and destructive. What should I say of the fact that Gaudentius, one of their bishops, dared publicly to say that the Catholic Church was a human fabrication? Augustine is witness in his second book against him. Did men who did not hesitate to vomit forth such things admit that that Church was guardian of apostolic doctrine?

But I return again to the succession at issue. For I perceive that nothing has yet been accomplished, because elsewhere you deny the very premise that had never been doubted, and by a new denial charge the ancients with falsehood, as though they had invented a false origin: you contend that the person whom they praise as author of the succession neither existed nor could have existed, because at Rome he had no see or chair. What sort of novelty is this? Our Optatus says to Parmenian: “You cannot deny that you know that at Rome the episcopal chair was first conferred on Peter.” What do you say? In your *Institutes*, although you deny that Peter was bishop there, or at least sat there as long as others relate, you nevertheless wrote that, because of the consensus of ancient writers, you did not contend against his having died there. But afterward, in your commentaries on Peter’s epistles, you denied even that.

“Indeed,” you say, “unless Peter flew across seas and lands in an instant, it is certain that he died far from Italy.” But how do you prove this certainty against the testimony of all antiquity? And where, then, do you think he died instead? At Babylon, because his first epistle is said to have been written from Babylon? What follows? “I do not approve,” you say, “the ancients’ opinion that Rome is meant in that passage; nor do I see why they thought so, except because they were already possessed by the error that Peter had been in Rome.” But concerning this “error,” as you call it—an error which could not exist in such a quasi-public fact—we shall consider at another time.

You have not yet proved what you desire: that he died at Babylon. “Indeed,” you say, “because in the second epistle he says that he is near death.” Yet you deny that the second epistle was written by Peter himself; nor did anyone ever say it was written in Babylon. Nor is someone who believes himself near death therefore to be said to have died immediately. Paul says to Timothy: “I am already being poured out, and the time of my departure is at hand.” Yet not even you would affirm that he died then. Certainly, if you said it was not clear in what year Peter came to Rome, died at Rome, or how long he lived there, perhaps I should not object. But to disdain the testimony and agreement of all antiquity—against which you had otherwise said that you did not wish to contend—and now affirm that Peter never came to Rome or died there: that is surely a paradoxical proposition which you will not persuade me to accept unless you persuade me that the whole ecclesiastical history is a stale fable and that all the most ancient and trustworthy ecclesiastical writers are both triflers and impostors [Col. 1125D].

What then? That Julius Caesar died at Rome is not transmitted on more numerous or better testimonies than that Peter died at Rome. Now, if someone cries out that he did not even die within the Roman world, he may invent, if he pleases, that he was buried among the Antipodes. Truly remarkable is the audacity—or should I say shamelessness?—of people determined to disagree with others. For what will they not say rather than refrain from contradicting others? But if it is enough to deny what is reported by the most certain and trustworthy records, what will become of us? What, I say, will become of all ecclesiastical history if its principles and, as it were, foundations—fortified by testimonies scarcely capable of greater certainty—are either fabulous or can be overthrown by the mere hiss of someone’s denial? Finally, what will a man not dare who dares this?

I know that many stale fables have been scattered like stains even over the very foundations of ecclesiastical history; I reject them and desire that they be erased [Col. 1126B]. But shall I therefore allow truth to be rashly erased together with falsehood? I know that there are certain uncertain matters about which one may doubt. But either what you deny here is certain, or I do not know what you call certain; and, as that Roman said, either the witnesses by whom it is proved are sufficient, or I do not know what is sufficient.

You write somewhere: “The ancients unanimously report that Simon Magus disputed with Peter at Rome.” You say that this is suspect to you; yet you do not openly dare to say what you think, namely, that Simon never came to Rome. Surely even the inscribed stones of the Tiber Island would refute such a denial of yours. Why do you dare more boldly deny that other matter, which is still more fully attested? Your followers most confidently deny that Judas was present at the Lord’s Supper or communicated there with the other Apostles, although Augustine, against the Donatists, holds it certain and assumes it as admitted. They are heard because they have some support from the ancients. But your denial concerning Peter is one of unheard-of audacity.

Who would not wonder that, when you wish, you sometimes so readily assent not merely to doubtful but even to false conjectures, while at other times you place no faith even in certain and clear proofs? Yet I should not say this unless, if I yielded to your denial 121, it were not only Optatus who was at stake, but you also pierced through, at Optatus’s side, the remarkable agreement of the ancient Church in this matter. If it lied here, I do not know in what matter it will deserve belief.

Certainly, I shall readily grant you that what Optatus adds—that Peter was called Cephas because he was head of the Apostles—is a ridiculous and childish error: it is the error of a man who thinks a Greek word is Syriac, and consequently fashions “head” from *petra* or *saxum* (“rock”) even more foolishly than if he had alleged what Festus wrote, that Rome was once called Cephalon [Col. 1126D]. You acted with restraint elsewhere when you denied that an interpretation which Gratian, in his rhapsody, ascribes to Anacletus could be Anacletus’s—an interpretation which no sane or sober person could suppose. But modestly admitting that our forefathers very often erred through ignorance of the Hebrew language is also a mark of candour.

I know that you can also point out in Optatus many passages of Holy Scripture either incorrectly cited or inappropriately explained. By all means, you may do this, so far as I am concerned. I shall never defend what I know to be faulty. And that you may henceforth be fairer to me, I openly profess—what I have often done elsewhere—that I not only do not defend the solecism which I mentioned, but most severely detest those who thrust upon the world other and graver solecisms of that kind, persons worthy not so much of a schoolmaster’s rod as of the whip and lash of the master of folly. At the same time I curse the authors of many wicked fables, invented and spread in order either to stain or to bury the entire good memory of that ancient Church; finally, I reject those who wish to abuse the title of sound and religious antiquity as a cosmetic for concealing the crimes of degenerate posterity.

But since under this pretext you further wish to erase the whole memory of antiquity, I say that those who do not resist these snares of yours are guilty either of shameful ignorance or wicked treachery, or of both [Col. 1127B]. Therefore I also wish the willing wrong-mindedness (*ethelokakia*, ἐθελοκακία) of those who yield to you so readily to be chastised. Against them, however, I shall now bring only that ancient saying:

> Hand over the standards to men, you cowardly Quirites.

And, to conclude what I have said about succession, I say again—and shall always declare openly—that I desire unworthy successors, who are deserters, traitors, and (to use an old term without saying anything harsher) *traditores*, to suffer the penalties they deserve. Yet you know who it is that wishes and hopes they may be such, so that, once they are cast down, he may immediately occupy the vacant place and found for himself a new kingdom with far greater arrogance; and who therefore would not wish others to come to their senses, perform their duty, and cleanse the Church’s defiled face. For while its foul squalor, hideous deformity, and mute corpse have alienated many peoples—whom you could easily draw to your side by your pleasant singing—its former and better form, its brightness, dignity, voice, and speech would recall them to itself and keep them in unity.

To return to Optatus, two questions remain that require your answer. What do you think of the Donatist schism and of their actions, which they themselves claimed were a religious and ecclesiastical reformation? And lest your private cause and inclination impede a candid confession, we ask that, when you must answer concerning them, you forget yourself for a little while and do not suppose that the matter concerns you.

You know what the condition of the Church was in the time of Optatus or Augustine. I ask whether you believe that the Donatists had no just reason for seceding from communion with that Church. I think you will say: none. Yet the things which you now chiefly accuse, flee from, and abolish had already then gained strength. You need not wait for me to enumerate them one by one. For, if you wish, you remember them.

The Donatists ought not privately to have established another baptism for themselves and their followers. I do not now speak of their rebaptism. I ask whether, when they first baptized someone from their flock who had not yet been baptized, according to their own manner rather than allowing him to be baptized in the Catholic Church, they acted rightly. I think you will deny that they acted rightly. Yet from Optatus himself you will learn that exorcism and chrism [anointing] were already used in baptism in that Catholic Church—practices which you judge so intolerable that for that reason you have established another form of baptism, and have fiercely assailed me, though I am neither the author of those practices nor have written anything concerning them, out of hatred for them.

Will you say that the Donatists acted rightly and religiously when they contemptuously trampled underfoot that chrism which you spit upon far more vehemently? Yet Optatus will tell you that God’s judgment against them was sealed even by a miracle. If you say that he lies, consider what proof you will use to convict him of falsehood. Nevertheless, in this matter the remarkable consensus of the ancient Church continually presses upon you.

Will you admit that the Donatists ought not, as your people do, to have overthrown altars? Yet you teach that Optatus’s assertion that Christ’s body had dwelt upon them is so unworthy and monstrous that you loudly proclaim it to be the very just cause why all altars should be overthrown.

Does it please you that the Donatists are said to have raised altar against altar? Yet this has always been held to be a most serious crime. Not only do Optatus and Augustine accuse the Donatists for it, as if in a fixed formula and in prescribed words, but Cyprian earlier accused the Novatians in exactly the same words. You know, I think, that by the word “altar” they meant the entire ministry of the Church; this is also sometimes denoted by the term “baptism.” Indeed, in Egypt the churches themselves were called *labra* [basins], if I am not mistaken in what I noticed a few days ago in Epiphanius.

Or did those who privately and separately set up these things—which Augustine calls among the Donatists not so much sacraments as execrations—these, I say, most deadly signs of dissension, lay the foundations of reformation rather than of deformity and confusion?

And what will you say about their having been restrained by a remarkable divine bridle: although otherwise they dared anything and would do whatever their hatred of Catholics prompted, they nevertheless did not dare, as Optatus relates, to alter the ceremonies or formulas received in the Church, even though they regarded these too as hostile to themselves? Is boldness now more religious because it is greater? Or wiser because it destroys everything?

Following the example of the Novatians, the Donatists wished to appear *Cathari* (“the Pure”); they even cleansed with water whatever had been touched by those from whom they had seceded, declaring it polluted. Was this a very pure purification? We know that in later centuries the Greeks in their schism behaved no less arrogantly and contemptuously toward the Latins. But when today you hear such execrations, which burst forth from the blaze of hatreds, do they seem religious to you?

Come now. When, within a short time, Donatus drew nearly all Africa to his side—not merely without the aid of the rulers, but rather despite their opposition—so that there were almost more Donatist than Catholic bishops there, ought he, exalted by such success and victory, and puffed up by glory and pride as by leaven, to have raised his crest in the way Optatus relates that he did in Book III? Perhaps you will be less surprised that this happened, since you know the character and swelling magnitude of human pride. Yet you ought also to remember that nothing is more alien from religion, both in reality and in appearance. [Col. 1129A]

What shall I say of that Donatus, the pseudo-bishop of Carthage, a rogue risen from the mire, who suddenly became not only some Regulus, daring what neither Hannibal nor Hasdrubal had ever dared there, but also a most insolent tyrant who did not hesitate contemptuously to scorn the Roman emperor? Indeed, he seemed to himself like a god. For Optatus likewise describes such an idol, which that people—otherwise cunning and acute—worshipped in a kind of brutish stupor.

There is much here which I would have you and others observe with me. But chiefly observe what and how great is the vanity of an empty windbag, drunk and intoxicated with blind admiration of himself, who nevertheless wished to be called and regarded as a restorer of Religion and of the Church. It is not without reason that I wish you to look upon this image, not of human weakness, but of madness. But it will be enough to point it out, as with a finger, by one word.

That fool had heard that foolish emperors had wished an oath to be framed by their own genius and majesty. He too arrogated this semblance of divinity to himself when he did not refuse to have his followers swear by his own name, as though it were some divinity. Priscillian, a more impure heresiarch in Gaul at the same time, desired the same thing. What do shameless hypocrites, who presume so much for themselves, not arrogate to themselves? But I ask you: are those who wish everyone to swear by their words any less insolent today?

I shall say nothing now concerning the martyrdoms and miracles of the Donatists. The former prove that they were fanatical people who, carried away by blind frenzy, hurled themselves headlong and brought death upon themselves by a kind of boastful display, as our Ulpian says. [Col. 1129C] And what else did the miracles which they vaunted signify, except that they too were great tricksters and impostors? Augustine in one place calls them “wonder-workers,” where he reports that they even boasted that, when Donatus prayed, God answered him from heaven. But I ask: do you not now also pity the bewitched multitude that is being deceived?

Finally, what shall I say of the robberies, sacrileges, and parricides of the Donatists? Most Donatists claimed to condemn these monstrous deeds of the Circumcellions, yet they employed them. You do not fail to know what is now taking place; for the sake of your honor I keep silent. For perhaps it would not even be permissible to bring before the public all the events that would furnish a new and astonishing history of one year. Let ancient things alone now be read.

I had read much about the Jewish Zealots of Jerusalem. But the retainers of the Donatist faction far surpassed them. They called themselves, as Optatus says, “leaders of the Saints,” while meanwhile they surpassed not only the savagery of all barbarians, robbers, assassins, and pirates, but also the ferocity of the devil himself—who, Augustine says, is the master of every cruelty. [Col. 1129D] See to what the tragedy of that African reformation immediately came. May our own age not see a similar intensification or catastrophe of its drama.

Yet if the evil hanging over us is fated, we resist in vain. For I know what those who admit no correction deserve, and I acknowledge the just judgment of God, pursuing them as it were with an armed hand, so that those who do not heed him speaking may feel him striking. But I leave prophecies to you.

I shall add one word about the Donatists, which it concerns you also to remember: such, I say, was their shamelessness that they loudly claimed to be suffering unjustly what they themselves did cruelly. I suppose they added this by way of mockery; it is the climax of bitter insult. Certainly, while clamoring about the cruelty either of the laws by which they were disciplined or of our bishops—who were their advocates rather than their accusers—they mocked both the mildness of those laws and the gentleness of those bishops.

But since neither our laws nor the replies of Optatus and Augustine satisfy you—you who have decreed, on your own authority, that heretics, whom you will indeed condemn for heresy, ought to be punished by death—this place would require me to discuss their lawful coercion with you at greater length. [Col. 1130B] Yet perhaps my other reply to you, which admonished you on this matter, has already satisfied you; therefore I shall not now trouble you longer.

Meanwhile, if you are a good man, you will not take it ill that one formerly familiar to you should deal with you freely and familiarly. He does this because you provoked him; yet, as you know, he is not pleading his own cause. For what private interest has he, even if you overthrow everything you attack? You will therefore all the more acknowledge that he acts generously and candidly. Nor, because he is a jurist and does not otherwise customarily cultivate the studies you pursue, will you take it amiss that he is not unfamiliar with sacred and ecclesiastical literature; indeed, that he is a student of both laws. Farewell.

## FRANCIS BALDUIN, JURIST: PREFACE TO THE READER

Prefixed to the second edition of Optatus.

[Col. 1130C]

The treatises of Optatus of Milevis and Victor of Utica belong to the ancient history of Africa. Nor shall I deny that, in reading them, one must also keep in view the geography of all Africa. Yet, just as I acknowledge that some light is shed upon these treatises by the description of Africa formerly supplied by Strabo, Mela, Pliny, and Ptolemy, so I say conversely that they in turn shed light upon that description itself, and upon its boundaries and cities.

I add that not only Orosius himself, in Book I, chapter 2, but also, lastly, our own Justinian, in Books I and II of the Code, *On the Office of the Praetorian Prefect of Africa*, when he appointed a new and particular praetorian prefect to govern Africa, which he had recovered from the Vandals, with his seat at Carthage, enumerates the seven provinces which he wished it to have and, as it were, the metropolitan cities of each.

Indeed, at the Council of Milevis only five had been enumerated. But Justinian adds first what he calls Zeugi; it is commonly printed incorrectly as Tingi. For Tingi belongs rather to Mauretania itself, which is therefore also called Tingitanian. Victor of Utica, like Pliny, often mentions the province of Zeugitana in Africa.

Justinian calls the second province of Africa simply Carthaginian, and notes that it had formerly been called Proconsular. Certainly Optatus and Victor regularly call it Proconsular, and it is often so named in the Code of Constitutions. Justinian likewise names the remaining African provinces that are named in the Milevitan Synod and scattered throughout these treatises of Optatus and Victor: Tripolitania, whose dux he wishes to reside at Leptis Magna; Byzacena, whose dux is to reside at Capsa and the other Leptis; Numidia, whose dux is at the city of Constantine; Mauretania, whose dux is at Caesarea; and finally the island of Sardinia, which he also orders to belong to the African diocese. For the Vandal tyrant of Africa had earlier occupied it together with Corsica, as Victor narrates in Book I. [Col. 1131A]

It was through ignorance of African geography that, when our Optatus is called Milevitan, some persons not only doubted where he came from but even invented that he was an islander. I had indeed pointed out that Donatus “of the Black Huts” was a Numidian; so I added that Optatus, Donatus’s opponent, should be understood as a Numidian bishop when he is called Milevitan. I had thought no educated person denied it.

And now I hear that some people still think—than which nothing more foolish could be imagined—that he was instead Melitan. For Quintinus of Autun, who in recent years taught what is called canon law in the school where I now teach civil law—a doctor of canons certainly not unlearned—when he was describing the island of Malta and wished to praise it, because he had at one time been educated there among the knights called Rhodians, wrote that the council called Milevitan had been Melitan, and that the city Milevis was somehow named from Malta.

I laughed when I read this, and it seemed to me as monstrous as if someone said that the Council of Sardica was Sardinian. Therefore I thought no one could approve it. But I was all the more astonished when I heard that our Quintinus had persuaded not only many of his own hearers, but also that Cologne compiler of councils, who likewise warns that the Milevitan Council was held on the island now called Malta. Is that so indeed? I have never come so near the African shore by sailing as Doctor Quintinus did while following the fleet of his knights. Yet I know he cannot prove his assertion unless he proves either that Numidia is on the island of Malta or that Malta is an island in Numidia.

I fear, too, that some clever fellow may here object to what Lucian wittily wrote: that, through the ignorance of a certain person, partly geographer and partly historian, he had suddenly been changed from a Greek into a Babylonian, and his native land had been torn away from the Hellespont and transferred, walls and towers included, into the middle of Mesopotamia. [Col. 1131D] But what would Optatus say, what would the Milevitan Fathers say, if they now heard that they were being transported from Milevis in Numidia to the island of Malta, as persons once condemned were sent to Sardinia?

Certainly, just as Optatus, when he calls a council “of Numidia,” understands a council at Cirta, so Augustine regularly calls the Milevitan Council the council of Numidia—for example, in Letters XLVII, XCII, XCIV, and XCV. And just as the Milevitan Fathers profess that they write to Pope Innocent from the council of Numidia, so Innocent says in his reply to them that he was written to from the Milevitan Council.

I once hesitated while looking for a place in Numidia whose name came nearer to “Milevitan” even than Malta did. At length I conveniently came upon Augustine’s Letter CLXVIII, in which he calls Milevis a town. Moreover, when in Cyprian’s Carthaginian synod, where the bishops of Numidia state their opinion about rebaptism, I read that a certain Pollianus “from Mileo” was listed and named among them, as it is printed in Cyprian’s books, I suspected some error and conjectured that it should rather be read “Pollianus of Milevis.” I consulted the other text of the acts of that council, likewise recited by Augustine in Book VI of *On Baptism*, and found there the very reading which I had divined ought to be written. And together with that Pollianus of Milevis, two other bishops of the same Numidia are named a little earlier in that council: Felix of Bagai and Crescens of Cirta. I think not even Quintinus doubts that Cirta is in Numidia.

If anyone doubts about Bagai, let him read the Donatist Council of Bagai in Augustine, Book III *Against Cresconius*, chapters 53 and 56, and recognize that “Milevitan” is formed from Milevis just as “Bagaian” is from Bagai. Nor should anyone be more astonished that we place Milevis or Bagai among the towns of Numidia than that Pliny, Book V, chapter 4, places Tuburbo or Curubis among the towns of Africa. Finally, it is well known that Pliny himself says that the names of African peoples and towns are especially unpronounceable except in their own languages. Anyone who has read the treatises of Optatus and Victor which we publish will say this all the more. [Col. 1132C]

I do not doubt that it can readily be proved to everyone that, in Possidius’s *Life of Augustine*, “Cittensian Church” is mistakenly read for “Cirtensian Church”; likewise in our Florentine Pandects mention is made of the *res publica Cirtensium* [commonwealth of the people of Cirta], whereas other books corruptly read “Cyrenensium,” in law IX, *On Ignorance of Law and Fact*. Who for that reason would tolerate Cirta’s being moved from Numidia into Cyrenaica? Quintinus himself, while explaining Zonaras on the Apostolic Canons, rightly mocks those who once fabricated Chalcedon out of Carchedon, that is, Carthage. Nor will he deny that the same rebuke is deserved by those who imagine that Byzacium, which is in Africa, is Byzantium in Thrace, and who have polluted even law books with such an error. Let him now judge whether the man who transforms Milevis into Malta deserves applause or laughter in a law lecture hall. [Col. 1132D]

I would not have said so much on this subject unless this ludicrous error could not be removed from Quintinus’s hearers in one word. Yet it has even less color than if someone said that the Milevitan Council was named from Melitene, that Armenian metropolis which our Justinian so greatly extols in Novel 31. For Sozomen, Book IV, chapter 24, mentions a Melitene synod; but I have nowhere read anyone mentioning any Melitan one. And what sense would the African Fathers have had, if, abandoning all their Africa—where they had far different matters to attend to—they had crossed by dangerous navigation through the midst of the Syrtes to that dry and narrow island, in order to deliberate there, as though shut up in a prison and separated from the entire world, concerning matters pertaining to the African Church, and in the middle of the sea to prohibit transmarine appeals—for the Milevitan Synod restrains these? Therefore I do not permit this injury to be done, by a ridiculous fiction, either to that most distinguished synod or to our Optatus.

To provide a successor for Optatus: Augustine, in Letter XXXIV to Paulinus, praises the most blessed Severus, as he calls him, his fellow pupil and bishop of the Milevitan Church, “well known,” he says, “to the brethren in that same city.” Augustine also mentions, in Book III *Against Petilian*, chapter 38, a certain Honorius of Milevis condemned in the African Church. Finally, he says that the Manichaean Faustus, an African by race, was a citizen of Milevis: “a man,” he says, “of acute intelligence and polished speech, but a most wicked slanderer of the Christian religion.” [Col. 1133A]

[Col. 1133B]

If I could not bear for our Optatus to be made Melitan instead of Milevitan, or an islander instead of a Numidian, I ought still less to bear his being confused with other Optati. I pass over the Donatist Optatus, whom I hear Augustine commemorating in the Council of Bagai, and the Catholic Optatus, whom Augustine commemorates at Cirta. More celebrated and notorious was Optatus Gildonianus, whom Augustine frequently mentions. But who would not indignantly object that some persons today do not distinguish the Gildonian from the Milevitan, when there was as much difference between them as between a most wicked leader of Donatists and a most holy bishop of the Catholic Church?

If anyone asks why the other is called Gildonianus, I shall answer with Augustine. In Book II *Against Petilian*, chapter 92, he writes that this Optatus was accused of belonging to Gildo’s retinue and suffered punishment, being put to death by a dreadful form of execution. So too our laws declare that they pursue not only Gildo the tyrant, who took up arms in Africa against Emperor Honorius, but also his retainers: Theodosian Code, law XIX, *On Punishments*; law XIX, *On Proscribed Goods*. Likewise, in law VII, *On Billeting*, the estates of Gildo, a public enemy, and of his retainers are said to have been confiscated; it is an Honorian law issued at Milan to Pompeianus, proconsul of Africa. [Col. 1133C]

Just as Claudian himself, in his most elegant verses, describes that Gildo as a tyrant and robber in Africa, so Augustine describes a certain Donatist Optatus, Gildo’s retainer, whom for this reason he generally calls Gildonianus. But although he sometimes does not add “Gildonianus” and calls him simply Optatus, he testifies that he was so wicked a rogue that even the Donatists themselves were ashamed of him.

Yet as vehemently as he properly detests such an Optatus, so vehemently does he praise our Optatus of Milevis. In Book I *Against Parmenian* he calls him both “of venerable memory” and “of Catholic communion.” In the book *After the Conference* he calls him a Catholic bishop; and in *On Unity*, chapter 16, he seems to compare him with Ambrose himself. Likewise later Fulgentius, in Book II to Monimus, judges that this our Optatus, whom he calls holy, was as faithful an interpreter of Paul as Ambrose or Augustine. Yet I would not have the reader impeded by this comparison from discerning how much difference there was, likewise with regard to literary learning. Augustine, in Book III *On Christian Doctrine*, chapter 40, seems to compare him with Cyprian, Lactantius, and Victorinus. [Col. 1134B]

Further, just as, where Optatus ends, I began from Augustine to relate what follows in the history of the African Church, so, where Augustine ends, it seemed proper to append what Victor of Utica then narrates.

> [Note: [Col. 1133C] Balduin errs here. For that Victor was not of Utica, but of Vite.]

But concerning Utica, as concerning Milevis, there is no need for me now to add anything. I omit also what I read in our Pandects, that Utica no less than Carthage possessed Italian law, final law, *On the Census*. Yet, so that this neighboring colleague from Utica may be more welcome to the Milevitan or Numidian, I shall say that the colony of Cirta in Numidia appears to have been founded from the Utican conventus [district]. For Pliny testifies that it was called the colony of the Sittiani, and Hirtius writes that Publius Sittius, a Roman knight, was from the Utican conventus. [Col. 1134C]

The remainder concerning Optatus and Victor should be sought in our annotations below. As for the long preface which I placed six years ago before the earlier edition of Optatus—not only concerning Optatus, but also on many other subjects of ecclesiastical affairs, which at that time I was compelled to discuss by the circumstances of that controversy into which I had been drawn, even against my will, and by the necessity of refuting certain points of my very fierce opponent—I did not wish to force that more vehement preface upon this edition. It is more than enough that it was published once in its own time.

Paris, the Ides of March, 1569.

[Col. 1133]

## ANNOTATIONS ON THE SEVEN BOOKS OF OPTATUS OF MILEVIS

From the Commentaries on Ecclesiastical Affairs of Francis Balduin, Jurist.

### ON BOOK ONE

[Col. 1133D]

Page 1. Jerome testifies in the *Catalogue* that Donatus of Carthage, bishop of the Donatists, wrote much relating to his heresy; and Gennadius writes that at the same time Vitellius the African was a most vigorous defender of his faction. So too Parmenianus, [Col. 1134D] who succeeded Donatus, armed his sect with many treatises. Meanwhile, however, I do not know how, the Catholics in Africa were almost mute; certainly they did not oppose their own writings to his. But finally, in Numidia, Optatus, bishop of Milevis, began to answer.

I once thought that these books of Optatus against Parmenian had been written against Parmenian’s letter to Tyconius, against which Augustine later wrote three books. But when I compared each item more closely, I readily observed that the kind of Parmenian writing which Optatus refutes and calls *tractatus* [treatises] was something else. Nevertheless, the dispute was always the same. For this was characteristic of the Donatists: they repeatedly sang the same refrain, just as Augustine writes that they often said, repeated, and pressed the same things over and over.

Further, since the Latin books of the ancients, especially Africans, have been contaminated by many scribal errors, I think scarcely any book was ever more depraved than this little work of Optatus. For the Donatists themselves corrupted it as soon as it was published; and, impudent as they were, they mangled and defiled it. The barbarous posterity of scribes nearly overwhelmed it with many blemishes. Thus it lay hidden for many centuries as though in a tomb. And when Cochlaeus’s German edition brought it to light, it contained more errors than lines.

In the earlier Paris edition, aided by a collation of a manuscript supplied to me by the theologian Espensaeus, I took pains to correct at least six hundred passages. This second edition will now correct not many fewer, supported by two manuscript or handwritten copies: one of which we owe to J. Tilius, bishop of Meaux, the other to Macer, theologian of Paris. Yet I am far from saying that Optatus has now at last been entirely restored to completeness. On the contrary, I have marked gaps to indicate that several passages still survive in mutilated form.

Further, it must be said once for all that Optatus used a version of Holy Scripture that was not wholly corrected—at least, one far different from that used in the same Africa by Tertullian, Cyprian, Arnobius, or Augustine. But I declare that I have by no means undertaken to correct it. If I can correct most passages in Optatus which a scribe corrupted long ago, I shall think that I have now performed my duty. Nor shall I now ostentatiously note and indicate what I have accomplished in this respect. Such display of petty critical points (*leptologēmata*) is tasteless; nor, as the saying goes, does it help to seek a little laurel wreath on a honey-cake.

See: shortly after the beginning of Book I, where the German edition first read *cum nequitiose* (“with wickedness”), and then the Paris edition *cum venenose* (“with poisonously”), I have now corrected and restored from a better copy *ne ventose* (“not puffedly”); and after the middle of that book, where it previously read *in talibus pasti fuerant cibis* (“they had been fed on such foods”), I have now corrected from the same copy *vitalibus pasti fuerant cibis* (“they had been fed on life-giving foods”); and shortly afterward, where it read *vos ipsos cum iis unam sententiam ferre* (“that you yourselves hold one opinion with them”), I restored *una sententia ferire* (“to strike with one judgment”); and a little before the end of Book I, where it previously read *revelata* (“revealed”), and earlier still *revelata*, I restored from the same copy *renovata* (“renewed”). There are six hundred corrections of this kind, and indeed more in the following books, in which the manuscript copy I used was more complete. [Col. 1135C]

Page 3. As to the subject itself, concerning which I would prefer to make some annotation, Optatus at the beginning shows why he calls his Donatist opponents “brothers,” although they did not wish to be so called by Catholics and indeed still refused the title at the Carthaginian Conference, as Augustine testifies in Book III *Against Gaudentius*. Augustine, in Book III *Against Parmenian*, chapter 2, confirms what Optatus says here.

I add that David too, in 1 Samuel 30, called the sons of Belial—wicked men who were nevertheless Jews—“brothers.” As for the passage from the prophet Isaiah which Optatus cites here, Augustine, treating the same matter, presses the same passage in more words and, as he is accustomed, amplifies this entire passage of Optatus in Psalm 32. Tertullian indicates in the *Apology* why Christians called one another brothers. The Church itself was also formerly called “the brotherhood,” as we have learned from Tertullian, Cyprian, Ambrose, and Jerome.

Page 4. In the second place Optatus indicates that the Donatists rejected every conference with the Catholics. Their pride and self-will (*καὶ αὐθάδεια*) were the same many years later. Augustine, in Letter CLXVI to the Donatists, says: “Your bishops, when approached by us, never wished to confer peaceably with us, as though fleeing from conversation with sinners.” Therefore, to cast down such arrogance, in Letter LXVIII he objects that not only did Paul confer with Epicureans, but Christ himself discussed the law with the devil. Finally, several years after Optatus’s death, by an edict and command of Emperor Honorius, the Donatists were drawn, even unwillingly, into the Carthaginian Conference with the Catholics. I have set forth the history of this elsewhere. [Col. 1136A]

Page 6. Optatus says that the Donatists’ repetition of baptism was contrary to laws. He seems to mean a law of the Emperor Valentinian, then reigning, enacted at the time this book was written. I would add another law of Valens and Gratian, issued seven years after the earlier one. Both were addressed to African magistrates, and both stand in Book XVI, title VI, of the Theodosian Code. Tribonian combined them into one when it was inserted into Justinian’s Code. But I fear that the later one was enacted after Optatus wrote these books. Still, it indicates that Constantine had earlier enacted a law on the same subject, which Optatus was much more likely to have read.

Certainly Augustine, in his books *On Baptism*, does not object imperial laws—because the Donatists loudly claimed that they, or Christians in matters of religion, were not bound by them—but the canon of the Council of Nicaea. Although he does not name Nicaea, he sufficiently indicates that he is speaking of it, as I have said elsewhere in my history of the Carthaginian Conference. But I am compelled to draw out again many things which I said in that commentary.

One point is distinctive and has not yet been annotated: Augustine, in Letter CLXVI, cites words of a certain law, which I judge to be Constantine’s and which I have read nowhere else, worthy of being cited here:

> “Consider,” Augustine says to the Donatists, “with what most manifest truth God himself spoke through the heart of the king, which is in God’s hand, in that very law which you say was issued against you. But, if you understand, it was issued for you. Consider what the Prince’s words contain: for if the religion of baptism is judged weak in those who have been first initiated because those from whom it is received are thought to be sinners, it will be necessary for the sacrament once bestowed to be renewed as often as the minister who conferred baptism is found unworthy; and our faith will depend not on the free choice of our will nor on the grace of the divine gift, but on the merits of priests and the character of clergy. Let your bishops hold a thousand councils; let them answer this one proposition,” etc.

Thus Augustine.

Further, it should be noted once for all that Optatus, shortly afterward in his dispute concerning the one baptism, seems more to defend the baptism of schismatics than of heretics. Having adopted such a distinction, he appears to follow a certain middle position, new and unusual, between that formerly followed by Cyprian and that later maintained by Augustine. Yet afterward Optatus, as though forgetting his own new distinction, argues generally concerning the one baptism, like Augustine.

It is remarkable that Optatus does not mention the Nicene decree in this matter, nor even employ the distinction which, from Augustine, one may elsewhere gather that the Nicene Fathers employed. But the narrow bounds of these annotations cannot contain a fuller explanation of that matter. I return to what Optatus says. [Col. 1136D]

Page 12. “For nearly sixty years and what exceeds them.” First I note that Optatus uses the expression “and what exceeds” three times. Augustine too, who had carefully read Optatus, used the same phrase when indicating the very time now under discussion, in Book VII *On Baptism*, chapter 7. Our jurists likewise use it: for example Paul says, “ten and what exceeds,” etc., in law 26, final section, *On Deposit*. They commonly say *plus minus* (“more or less”). Jerome says *eo amplius* (“and more besides”): thus in *Against Lucifer*, speaking of the Nicene Fathers, “three hundred and more bishops”; likewise in the epitaph for Nepotian, “twenty and more years.”

As for the time discussed by Optatus, Augustine himself likewise says in Book VII *On Baptism*: “When forty years and what exceeds had passed after Cyprian’s death, the handing over of the books occurred, from which they began to be called *traditores*.” Jerome indeed writes in the *Catalogue* that Cyprian suffered and died under the emperors Valerian and Gallienus, in the eighth persecution. But in Eusebius’s *Chronicle*, the year of his martyrdom is indicated more simply and clearly: it is said to have been the 260th year of Christ. Hence Augustine would seem to indicate that the handing over of the books took place about A.D. 300.

Augustine also indicates this in the *Breviculus* when he relates that the matter now in question occurred under the consulship of Diocletian IX and Maximian VIII. But in Book III *Against Cresconius*, chapter 7, he has Diocletian VIII and Maximian VII as consuls. The difference is not great. Eusebius, in Book VIII of his *Ecclesiastical History*, places the beginning of that persecution in the nineteenth year of Diocletian’s reign, which was Diocletian’s eighth consulship. The following year, when Diocletian was consul for the ninth time, was the final year of his reign. For in that year, on 21 April—the day on which Diocletian had first become emperor—he voluntarily abdicated at Nicomedia. It was A.D. 304.

Since Optatus reckons the sixtieth year from that time, it can now sufficiently be understood in what year he wrote these things. But since he adds “and what exceeds,” and later mentions his associate Damasus, I readily allow that these books may be said to have been written by Optatus in the year 370, the year in which Damasus began to preside over the Roman Church, shortly after Valentinian and Valens began to reign. Jerome too, in the *Catalogue*, testifies that these books were written by Optatus under their rule. Therefore, I think we must say that in the following book of the catalogue of Roman bishops the name of Siricius must be deleted. For he first succeeded Damasus in A.D. 386.

Let us now examine a little more carefully what Optatus says here about the storm of persecution in his own time. He describes it again in Book III, where he says that, under Diocletian and Maximian, sixty years and more before, impious judges had been appointed to wage war upon the Christian name, compel Christians to sacrifice and deny Christ, overthrow the temples of the living God, and burn the divine laws. Here he presses the point that certain bishops, as he says, had impiously handed over the records of the divine law. Eusebius, in Book VIII, describes the storm of that persecution at greater length. Of Africa alone he says that there was then an innumerable multitude of martyrs there. He also says that the baths of Maximian were built in the city of Carthage at that time, as Diocletian’s were at Rome. We have learned that many thousands of Christians, like men condemned to the mines, were employed in constructing them.

This was new and unprecedented in Diocletian’s edict against the Christians: war was declared upon their most sacred books, so that they were to be sought out everywhere and destroyed. Arnobius, who lived in Africa at that time, says in Book IV *Against the Nations*: “Why have our writings deserved to be committed to the flames?” But the impious petty lawyers then objected that, as Ulpian says in Book IV *On the Duties of a Proconsul*, books of disapproved reading must be destroyed; and, of course, Christian books were of disapproved reading. That tyrant Antiochus Epiphanes, who attempted to exterminate the Jews, had likewise declared war on the Mosaic books. Diocletian seems to have followed such an example in his edict; just as that Vandal and Arian tyrant seems to have followed Diocletian’s example when, in Africa some years after Augustine’s death, he ordered the books of Catholics also to be destroyed by fire, as Victor of Utica relates.

Eusebius does not reproduce Diocletian’s edict, but relates that one of the leading court officials, a Christian, when at Nicomedia, where Diocletian was residing, saw the impious edict publicly posted and proclaimed, dared publicly to tear it down, and did not refuse the penalties which he knew would be inflicted for such an act.

As to civil law, although Diocletian had earlier issued so many rescripts, I have not read that he wrote or answered anything in the year when he was wholly occupied in issuing his final edicts against Christians—except that I now recall that the subtle law *Si certis annis*, *Code on Agreements*, was issued under the consulship of Diocletian VIII and Maximian VII. Finally, it is worth noting that the Donatists, who boasted so loudly that they hated betrayers of the most sacred books, nevertheless, when they burned Catholic basilicas, sometimes threw the Lord’s own codices into those very flames. Augustine testifies to this in Letter 50.

Moreover, as regards the whole history which Optatus here touches upon: just as Augustine, in Book I *Against Parmenian*, chapter 3, commends it and instructs us, when the origin of Donatus’s schism is being investigated, to go back to Optatus, so, since Augustine himself everywhere elucidates what Optatus writes, the explanation must in turn be sought from Augustine. For what Optatus here relates first concerning the earliest *traditores* and the murderer Purpurius is also related by Augustine in Book III *Against Cresconius*, chapter 27, and in the book *Against Fulgentius the Donatist*. When he says that Menalus “burned incense,” this was a customary expression in those times, by which it was said that someone had burned incense to idols and sacrificed. Hence such persons were also called *sacrificati*, as in Cyprian.

Pages 13 and 14. What follows in Optatus concerning the Council of Cirta and the proceedings or writings of a certain Nundinarius, which Optatus says that he appended to the end of these books—I should regret their loss, if I did not know that they can be recovered from Augustine’s Book III *Against Cresconius*, and Letters 163 and 165, and *On Unity*, chapter 20, section 126, and the summary of the Conference, at the end. I also note in passing that what Optatus says here was spoken by Secundus of Tigisis—“Sit down, all of you”—appears to have been a kind of formula, a tacit declaration and sign of acquittal. Thus, just as defendants are said to stand, so sitting, usually the posture of judges, is to be understood also as the posture of those acquitted, who have ceased to be defendants.

Page 16. What Optatus relates concerning Lucilla, a woman no less factious than wealthy, is also explained by Augustine in Letter 162 and Book III *Against Cresconius*, chapter 28; and in *On Unity*, chapter 3, and Book II *Against Petilian*, final chapter, he adds that she was Spanish. Finally, she must have been very famous, since Jerome too, writing to Ctesiphon that many women had been, as it were, nurses of heresies, says: “Donatus in Africa was assisted by Lucilla’s wealth.” I omit Augustine’s testimony in Letter 162 that another woman, wholly similar to her, was the author of a certain schism among the Donatists.

In the same place. Rarer and more obscure is what Optatus here indicates: that this Lucilla was reproved in the Church because, before holy communion, she had kissed the mouth of a certain dead person. What this meant I can scarcely guess; but I recall that Balsamon, the interpreter of the Council of Carthage, chapter 61, writes that Donatus, author and leader of the Donatists, taught that no one could partake of the divine mysteries unless, holding his mouth in his hand, he first greeted it.

[Col. 1138D] Pages 17 and 18. What Optatus relates about the deacon Felix, accused because of a notorious letter written against the emperor-tyrant, might be referred to the laws concerning defamatory libels. But because I have explained those laws more fully elsewhere, I shall not repeat them now. By the emperor-tyrant I have no doubt that Maxentius is meant, whom nevertheless Optatus shortly afterward indicates had at one time been almost indulgent. The laws of Constantine, who overthrew him, testify that he was a severe avenger of defamatory libels. Indeed, immediately after Maxentius had been removed, when Constantine had received from Africa an accusatory petition against Caecilian—a notorious calumny, rather—he decreed that unsigned defamatory libels were to be rejected, and sent laws on this subject into Africa to Verinus and Aelianus, whom we shall shortly hear praised in the Donatist case. Those laws are also said to have been posted expressly in the city of Carthage. Laws I and II, *Theodosian Code, On Defamatory Libels*.

[Col. 1139A] I might also cite here the laws concerning harbourers, where Optatus relates what the tyrant threatened Mensurius with as though he were harbouring a fugitive. But I shall add only that Jerome records in his Chronicle that a presbyter at Sirmium was most unjustly killed because he refused to betray Octavian, a proconsul hiding with him, in the year of Christ 376—that is, in the time of our Optatus.

Pages 17 and 18. I pass over many traces of ecclesiastical antiquity occurring in this book of Optatus: for example, that it is written there that, in Africa in the time of Maxentius, churches had very many, as he calls them, ornaments of gold and silver. Similarly, in Book III he praises Emperor Constans, who, when he sent alms to the poor in Africa, at the same time sent ornaments to the houses of God, as he calls them. He means vessels, vestments, and offerings of that kind, consecrated for the service of God, as our Justinian says, *Institutes*, “Sacred Things,” *On the Division of Things*, and Law *Sancimus*, *Code, On Holy Churches*.

Thus Theodoret, Book III, chapter 12, relates that Emperor Constantius gave the Church of Antioch very many objects of this kind, so precious that shortly afterward Julian’s impious and sacrilegious quaestor, when seizing them to bring into the treasury, cried out in mockery and insult: “Behold the vessels with which the son of Mary is served.” Yet it is more remarkable that Optatus indicates that such things existed even in African churches at a time when the Church otherwise lay oppressed under impious tyrants. Augustine too, Book III *Against Cresconius*, chapter 29, indicates that, in the time of Diocletian and the persecution he stirred up, the Church of Cirta held by the Donatists had two gold chalices, six silver ones, and a silver lamp.

I add this now: after Emperor Leo, by a law, had prohibited private persons from making royal ornaments of gold and silver—Law I, *Code, No One May...*—a later Emperor Leo, Novel 81, interpreted that law so that everyone understood that private persons were not forbidden to make sacred vessels of gold.

[Col. 1139C] Lest anyone think that the presence of such objects in the Church’s treasuries was merely the result of ostentatious superstition, let him know that, when necessity and the pious cause of feeding the poor required it, they were readily sold. Ambrose demonstrates this at length in Book II *On Duties*, chapter 28, as does the ecclesiastical history concerning Cyril of Jerusalem and Bishop Acacius. Indeed, Justinian’s own law, the said Law *Sancimus*, does so.

Not so much to oblige grammarians as students of law, I also note in passing that Optatus calls a document a *commemoratorium*, which shortly afterward he calls a *breve*. It is a legal word and means a petition, bond, or handwritten instrument; Constantine likewise used it in his letter to Caecilian, in Eusebius, Book IV *Life of Constantine*. Thus, too, in a constitution of Emperor Valens—issued in Optatus’s time—we read that among the papers of a certain confiscated person a certain *breve* was found. Final Law, *Code, On the Law of the Treasury*; add Law I, *Code, On Public Receipts*, and Theodosian Code, Law 13, *On Remission of Debts*.

[Col. 1139D] In the same place. I return to the history and do not pass over what Optatus says here: that, when Maxentius sent an indulgence, liberty was restored to Christians. Thus Eusebius, Book VIII, chapter 14, writes that Maxentius, at the beginning of his rule—or tyranny—in Italy and Africa, pretended some sort of religious favour toward Christians and ordered by edict that their persecution be stopped. But I am surprised that Eusebius himself did not sufficiently observe that, some years afterward, what is said of Emperor Galerius occurred: that he finally issued in the East an edict of that sort, Constantine his colleague willingly joining in its subscription. The heading is corrupt where Constantius is written for Constantine; but Rufinus gives the correct subscription of that edict, which says that it was published when Emperor Galerius was consul for the eighth time.

Yet although Optatus indicates that Maxentius had shortly before appeared to grant some favour to Christians in Africa, it is established that he was a tyrant—impious and cruel—and that Africa was severely harassed by him. This brings to mind what Nazarius’s ancient panegyric says: Maxentius exhausted Africa, which he had resolved to destroy; and therefore, after he had been defeated and slain, his head was sent to Africa by Constantine, “to soothe it,” as the panegyrist says, so that he whom it had afflicted most grievously while alive might, mutilated, satisfy it. And I infer that the indulgence which Optatus says he sent to restore liberty to Christians was an empty show of clemency without substance, from the fact that the Donatists themselves, when they denied that Caecilian had been ordained, alleged that he could not have been, because during the persecution bishops had not been free to assemble, as Augustine reports in the *Summary*.

In the same place. There is no reason for us to linger over what Optatus next relates about Botrus and Celesius, if I note in passing that the narrative is greatly illuminated by Augustine, Book I *Against the Letter of Parmenian*, chapter 3. But what Optatus finally says—that at that time one altar had been set up against another in Africa—deserves fuller explanation. Augustine, Book II *Against Cresconius*, chapter 2, says that the elder Donatus of Casae Nigrae first set up altar against altar in the city of Carthage; then the other Donatus, namely the Carthaginian, greatly strengthened this heresy.

The same writer, in Letter 171, explaining what that meant, says that the Donatists ordained bishop against bishop and set up altar against altar. And in Letter 162 he writes that, because of their schism, they were stained by the dreadful crime of the “raised altar,” as he puts it. But it must be observed that Cyprian had written much earlier in Africa that the Novatians set up altar against altar when they raised, as it were, the banner of their schism and defection from the Church. He indeed amplifies the charge of that schism just as Optatus does here against the Donatists, and Augustine after him in Letter 162. Indeed, the Donatists themselves, because Optatus had objected to them the example and history of Dathan, Korah, and Abiram, in turn brought the same charge in their Council of Bagai against the Maximianists, who had in some manner withdrawn and separated from them, though they had not returned to the Catholic Church, as Augustine relates in Book III *Against Cresconius*, chapter 53.

Page 18. What follows in Optatus must not be omitted: “Caecilian was again instructed that, if Felix had done nothing against him, they should themselves still ordain Caecilian as deacon.” This seems to be the passage which the Donatists—dull and dry calumniators indeed, who were evidently hunting subtly through Optatus’s books for something to object against Catholics—raised at the Carthaginian Conference with a quibble no less ridiculous than calumnious. “They said,” Augustine writes in the *Summary*, “that Optatus had written that Caecilian said: ‘If those who ordained me are betrayers, let them come and ordain me.’” If this was said, it had to be said in order to ridicule those to whom he is reported to have given this instruction, because he was certain that his ordainers had not been betrayers. For he did not say, “because they are betrayers,” but “if they are betrayers,” so that their innocence remained to be proved where it could rightly be proved.

Page 22. No less absurd was what Optatus next relates: that the Donatists, excessively courtly and palatine themselves, spitefully reproached our people in Africa, who were least of all courtly: “What have Christians to do with kings? What have bishops to do with the palace?” Thus again, in Book III, he says that Donatus once cried out: “What has the emperor to do with the Church?” Augustine too, in Tractate 6 on John, says that a certain Donatist used to say: “What have I to do with the emperor?” Petilian himself shouted: “What have we to do with the kings of this world, whom Christianity has never experienced except as hostile?” Augustine reports and refutes this in Book II *Against Petilian*, chapter 92. Likewise, in the book *To the Donatists after the Conference*, he relates that Primianus the Donatist, who spitefully insulted Catholics, made this reproach: “They carry the sacred letters of many emperors; we carry the Gospels alone.” By *sacrae* he means official letters; and in that age letters of the sovereign were called *sacrae*, “sacred,” as also “divine.” Thus they are often called in the code of constitutions.

[Col. 1141A] I confess that it was more ecclesiastical, and more fitting for Christians—still more for bishops—to make use rather of letters truly sacred, that is, prophetic and apostolic letters, than of imperial, courtly, or palatine letters. And this saying, “What have bishops to do with the palace?” was generally the voice not of Parmenian but of the Church. In short, good bishops were drawn no less unwillingly to courts, leaving, as it were, their sheepfolds, than to military camps. Indeed, the Synod of Sardica, thundering against degenerate and ambitious bishops who had abandoned their post and forgotten their office by running continually there, orders that other bishops who are, in its words, “in the canal”—that is, on the public road, or in the cities situated along it; for the laws in the Theodosian Code use the word similarly—and who see someone of their order hurrying that way, should seriously ask him where and why he is going. If they understand that he is going voluntarily, they are not to communicate with him any more than with one who has abandoned the Church or with an enemy. I return to the point from which I have digressed.

In the same place. Finally, Optatus recounts the history of the trial granted by Emperor Constantine in the case being litigated between Caecilian and Donatus. It is a memorable history, and I therefore marvel all the more that Greek writers, who otherwise wrote so much about Constantine’s times, passed it over. Augustine, Book I *Against Parmenian*, instructs us to recover it from this first book of Optatus; and we shall shortly hear that the Donatists themselves recovered it from there in the Carthaginian Conference. Augustine himself also repeatedly stresses many points relevant to it. But, to confess candidly what I think, not even Optatus satisfies me in this matter; and I see that in both writers many portions of this history are confused and omitted.

Optatus leaps from Caecilian’s ordination to the Donatists’ petition presented to Constantine. Yet seven or eight years intervened, during which I should like to know what the Donatists did at home by their disturbances and harassment of Caecilian. For I readily suspect that they did not remain quiet. Indeed, I infer that they greatly increased and grew strong in the meantime from Augustine’s statement in Letter 48 that two hundred and seventy Donatist bishops assembled forty years before the Macarian times, of which I shall speak later. If they were already so numerous forty years before the Macarian times, it is clear that they were numerous as soon as Constantine succeeded his father. But I believe that the Donatists did not appeal to Galerius or Maxentius, who ruled Africa, because those tyrants would not have heard the Donatists and would have rejected them no less than Catholics. The question of Caecilian’s ordination was therefore first brought before Constantine once he had gained power by removing Maxentius. For although Optatus writes that Constantine was then still ignorant of these ecclesiastical matters, he had begun to favour religion and the Church; and another opportunity, which Optatus should also have mentioned, presented itself.

Page 22. Optatus simply relates that the Donatists’ petition was presented to Constantine. But it must be observed that this happened when Constantine, after Maxentius was killed and his severed head dispatched, sent to Anullinus, proconsul in Africa, his edict granting immunity to Caecilian and the Carthaginian clergy. By some chance this edict was confusedly inserted in Book X of Eusebius’s Greek *Ecclesiastical History*. Anullinus’s reply and rescript are preserved in Augustine’s Letter 68. At the same time, seizing this opportunity, Anullinus sent to Constantine the Donatists’ petitions accusing Caecilian’s ordination.

Optatus declares that he is publishing a copy of them. Yet he seems not to publish the whole or complete document, and he publishes it without date or consuls. Augustine, however, in Letter 68 writes that two Donatist petitions of this kind were transmitted through Anullinus to Constantine: one subscribed on parchment in this manner: “Petition of the Catholic Church, concerning Caecilian’s crimes, submitted by the party of Majorinus”; the other, unsealed and attached to the same parchment, dated the seventeenth day before the Kalends of May, at Carthage, in the third consulship of our Lord Constantine Augustus. The words which Optatus quotes appear to have belonged to this latter petition. He does not mention the former.

I wondered why the petition quoted by Optatus contains so general, confused, obscure, and unlimited a complaint from the Donatists: “There are disputes between us and the other bishops.” I wondered why these bishops are not named here, not even Caecilian, nor is it stated what the disputes concerned—though this was above all what had to be stated and explained. But I suspect that all this was expressed more clearly in the earlier petition, and perhaps it even related how Caecilian had already been condemned by seventy bishops. Certainly it is remarkable that the Donatists wished to reopen litigation and preferred to request new judges rather than seek enforcement of the matter already adjudicated.

Further, it must be observed that Constantine was not in Italy when he received these Donatist petitions, but on the furthest frontier of Gaul along the Rhine. I inferred this from an ancient panegyric, which I suspect to be Nazarius’s panegyric to Constantine. It says that Constantine, shortly after defeating Maxentius at Rome, proceeded with the same force by which he had returned into his own Gauls to the lower German frontier, and hastened from the Tiber to the Rhine, intending, as it says, to extend the empire from the Etruscan Albula to the German Elbe.

Furthermore, if this history is to be carefully traced, I observe that Constantine immediately sent copies of the letters and petitions received from Africa to those three bishops of Gaul who will subsequently be named, and ordered them on that account to go to Rome; and that he wrote on the same matter to Miltiades, bishop of Rome. The rescript to the bishops of Gaul is not extant. But that written to Miltiades survives. By some chance it was inserted into the miscellany of Book X of Eusebius’s history in a place wholly inappropriate; and Nicephorus, Book VII, chapter 43, reproduces it no less confusedly and out of order, like a man ignorant of its relevance and one who entangles history rather than explains it. It should rather have been inserted here, or reproduced by Optatus. But for the present it is enough to have indicated where it may be found.

Moreover, just as Constantine testifies in that rescript that he wrote, as I have said, to those Gallic bishops, so he also relates that he simultaneously ordered the defendant Caecilian to come to Rome with ten bishops to support him and an equal number of opposing accusers. I find nowhere else this command of Constantine sent into Africa, though it would be important to this history that it had not been lost. Cujas, on Law I, *Code, On Transport Warrants*, quotes these words from a certain, as he calls it, constitution of Constantine: “Cause several of those who dissent against Caecilian, having been granted public transport through Africa and Mauretania, to proceed thence by a short route to Spain; and likewise grant to each bishop an individual transport warrant.” Because I have not read this “constitution,” as it is called, elsewhere, I cannot say clearly what it was; but I readily suspect that it was sent to Anullinus and related to the matter now under discussion.

[Col. 1142D] Page 23. Now when Optatus relates that they assembled and that Caecilian’s case was heard at Rome on the sixth day before the Kalends of October, in the third consulship of Constantine and the third of Licinius—for that is how Optatus’s passage must be read, as I proved elsewhere from Augustine—and when I have indicated from another passage of Augustine that the Donatists’ petitions were filed in Africa on the seventeenth day before the Kalends of May, under the same consuls and in the same year, we must observe the great and almost incredible diligence and speed which can here be noted, such as the safety of the Church at that time demanded.

In the same place. Optatus names the three Gallic bishops who were judges in this case with Miltiades, bishop of Rome: Maternus of Cologne, Marinus of Arles, and Rheticius of Autun. Here I am compelled to note in passing that Eusebius’s Chronicle is either false or very corrupt where, in Jerome’s translation, it is written that Miltiades died and Sylvester succeeded him before Maxentius was killed. I am astonished that Augustine Steuchus himself, a most learned man and papal librarian, when disputing with Lorenzo Valla about the truth of the Constantine history, so confidently affirmed that Miltiades was killed by Maxentius or Maximinus. Optatus alone certainly demonstrates clearly enough how false this is.

Further, the compilers of the so-called *Centuries* of ecclesiastical history must have read this passage of Optatus with insufficient attention, when, in Century IV, chapter 10, they say uncertainly that this Maternus and Marinus appear to have been bishops in Gaul or Italy. But Calvin deceived himself, and many others, much more seriously by failing to observe that the bishop of Arles sat as judge with Miltiades of Rome in this case. He therefore imagines that afterward he was judge of the appeal itself—something which the law of judicial proceedings would by no means allow. Finally, Augustine repeatedly testifies that at the Council of Arles, where Caecilian’s and Donatus’s case was heard again, bishops other—other, I say—than those who had been at Rome were judges.

Nor does the memory of antiquity allow us to say that the bishop of Arles was ambitiously raised above the bishop of Rome by Constantine. Why does not Calvin rather invent this about the bishop of Syracuse, to whom, as I shall shortly say, Constantine wrote expressly, ordering him to take cognizance at the Council of Arles of the case already judged at Rome? Certainly, before Donatus’s time, Cyprian of Carthage recognized that a certain Marcian, bishop of Arles and a Novatian, ought to be corrected by Stephen, bishop of Rome. And many years after Constantine, when a certain Hilary of Arles in Gaul despised Pope Leo’s authority, Emperor Valentinian III testified by an issued law how intolerable that was. Ausonius, writing in Optatus’s time, called Arles “Gallic Rome,” wishing with the diminutive term gently to signify that Arles was, as it were, a little Rome—that is, a kind of Rome in Gaul. Yet he knew that it was only a colony, which could not rise above its metropolis.

[Col. 1143C] As for Rheticius of Autun, I think that both the dignity of that city—which, as the capital of the Aedui, was so dear to Constantine that it was also called Flavia—and the merit of the man led to Rheticius being chosen as judge with Miltiades. For we know that he was learned and was numbered among the ecclesiastical writers of his time. He had written against the Novatians, who closely resembled the Donatists; so it is remarkable if the Donatists wished to have him assigned to them as judge. Jerome says, in his Letter to Florentius, that he also wrote treatises on the Song of Songs in lofty style. Yet in his Letter to Marcellus, although admitting that he was eloquent, Jerome calls him an inept interpreter.

Moreover, as concerns the history relevant to this passage, Jerome adds that Rheticius was sent to Rome by Emperor Constantine under Bishop Sylvester because of the Montensians.
