He should have said Miltiades instead of Sylvester. By “Montensians” he means Donatists. But they were not yet so called when Rheticius came to Rome. Augustine, indeed, in Book I *Against Julian*, chapter 2, introducing a certain statement of Rheticius on baptism, says: “The ecclesiastical acts of his episcopate show us that Rheticius, bishop of Autun, was of great authority in the Church in his own time, when in the city of Rome, with Miltiades, bishop of the Apostolic See, presiding, he sat as judge with others, condemned Donatus, who was the first author of the Donatist schism, and acquitted Caecilian, bishop of the Church of Carthage.”

It also helps to elucidate this history that Augustine says here that Miltiades presided in this trial. The Donatists had requested that judges be given them only from Gaul. But Constantine already perceived that the bishop of Rome ought to take cognizance of the case. He appears to have chosen at his own discretion those fifteen Italian bishops as assessors. Yet the Donatists did not dare to protest or reject such a judgment, although they would have preferred something else. Among those Italians Optatus counts some who belonged to Gallia Togata and Cisalpine Gaul, as the Romans once called it, such as Merocles of Milan.

The Milanese Chronicles, therefore—even those otherwise considered highly reliable, such as the Bossian ones—are false in saying that Merocles died in the year of Christ 268. Optatus testifies that he sat as judge at Rome in 313. It follows also that everything transmitted there about a certain Eustorgius, said to have been made bishop of Milan in that very year 313, is fabulous. Among those Italian bishops Optatus counts Florianus “of Sinna.” I think that one should read “of Cesena,” a distinguished city near Ravenna, in that part of Italy formerly called Gallia Togata, like Milan. What Sinna is, I do not know.

Pages 23 and 24. Further, when Optatus relates that Donatus was condemned, we must remember that he was Donatus of Casae Nigrae, as Augustine indicates in the *Summary*, and that from accuser he became defendant, perhaps because Caecilian used a countercharge. Yet he did not wish to turn back upon his adversary the simple charge of betrayal—which he could have done by right—but employed a graver and more theological accusation. Optatus gives the formula of the judgment by which Donatus was first condemned and Caecilian acquitted by Miltiades and his colleagues.

It should further be added that Augustine, in Letter 162, also relates that Miltiades wisely and kindly made an offer to such Donatists as wished to recover their senses and return to the Church. Since I have explained this more fully in my history of the Carthaginian Conference, I now refer the reader there. But I shall point out that two articles of this judgment against Donatus deserve notice: it says that he rebaptized and imposed hands upon fallen bishops, and pronounces both actions foreign to the Church.

As to the first, it must be observed that this was declared at Rome, where even that ancient Council of Cyprian concerning the rebaptism of those baptized by heretics had always been rejected; and the Council of Nicaea afterward confirmed Miltiades’s judgment on this point, though with a certain distinction regarding the Paulianists, as has been said elsewhere. More obscure is the reason why Donatus was condemned because he had imposed hands upon fallen bishops, and why this too is called foreign to the Church.

There were formerly three kinds of imposition of hands. Hands were imposed upon the baptized. Augustine, however, says in Book III *On Baptism against the Donatists*, chapter 16: “The imposition of hands cannot be repeated, just as baptism cannot.” Secondly, hands were imposed upon fallen penitents, to whom peace was given after exomologesis, or public confession. Although African bishops long considered, as Augustine indicates, that such penance was not to be repeated any more than baptism, anyone who denied that peace should at least once be given and hands imposed upon fallen penitents would have been a Novatian; and I would readily say that Donatus was nearly a Novatian.

But no one would be condemned for that. Therefore, when he is condemned by Miltiades for imposing hands on fallen bishops and the act is said to be foreign to the Church, another kind of imposition of hands is meant: namely, the third kind, pertaining to the ordination of bishops. The ancients judged that this, no more than baptism, ought to be repeated or reiterated. Thus, if bishops who had fallen into heresy were afterward reconciled as penitents by the imposition of hands, they were not, if they remained in their rank, to be ordained again; consequently hands were not to be imposed upon them again for that purpose, since their former ordination sufficed. Optatus continues: “Caecilian was pronounced innocent by the judgments of all those named above,” and so forth.

These are the very words afterward recited at the Carthaginian Conference which so struck the Donatists—though they otherwise shamelessly invented many things about Caecilian’s condemnation—that, since they did not dare to diminish the weight of Optatus’s testimony, for Optatus was already then of the highest authority and credibility in Africa, they at last fell silent in astonishment. Augustine testifies to this in the *Brief Summary of the Conference*, at the end, though Optatus’s words are not quoted there in full. For the word *sententiis*, “judgments,” is absent.

Although the Donatists were therefore shameless enough, when inventing and lying that Caecilian had been condemned by Constantine, to try by quibbling to corrupt the words of Optatus, whose testimony they wished to use—as I shall shortly show—their impudence, great as it was, was not so great that they dared also to invent that he had been condemned at Rome. I was therefore all the more astonished when, in recent days, I heard that in France a certain Morel, otherwise a learned man and eminent in the new order of new ministers, had confidently and boastfully written this in his French book addressed to Viret and elegantly entitled *On Ecclesiastical Discipline*. In it, among many other assertions very far from all credibility and from the truth of ecclesiastical history, he is said especially to affirm and relate that Caecilian was not only condemned by the bishops Miltiades, Rheticius, and Marinus as judges, but was also forced to abdicate. Nothing could even be invented that would be more evidently false.

I return to Optatus. He says, page 24: “To this appeal Emperor Constantine replied thus: ‘O mad…,’” etc. [Col. 1145B] In the earlier edition I corrected this passage and also supplied its gap by adding, from an old copy, the missing words: *appellationem interposuerunt*, “they lodged an appeal.” Thus I proved that the conjecture of an otherwise learned and ingenious interpreter of the laws must be rejected: he had guessed, from a false suspicion concerning abbreviations, a new reading which does not stand. Since I have shown this sufficiently elsewhere, I shall repeat nothing now. I add only that Augustine says in Letter 162 that the Donatists had raging mouths against Caecilian; thus I am less surprised that Constantine accuses in them a rabid audacity of frenzy.

I also now recall a law of Emperor Valentinian concerning a certain Bishop Chronopius, who, after being condemned by a tribunal of seventy bishops, appealed to the urban prefect. Valentinian replies that the unlawful appeal must be restrained by a monetary penalty, to be distributed to the poor. Theodosian Code, Law 19, *Whose Appeals Are Not Received*.

Ibid. Optatus says, “At the same time,” etc. In this [Col. 1145C] edition I ordered a blank lacuna to be marked before these words, to indicate that something seems to me to be missing and required before them. For, when I consider more closely the whole history in question here, I find that these words cannot be connected with what immediately precedes. Rather, several years intervened, during which Caecilian’s case was again heard and decided at the Synod of Arles, and then again at Milan by Constantine himself. It is to the time of this Milanese judgment, at last, that what follows in Optatus—“at the same time,” etc.—must be referred.

I would therefore suspect that what Optatus had inserted concerning that judgment, as also concerning the Council of Arles, was deleted by the Donatists, who grossly corrupted Optatus’s books. But I again doubt whether Optatus, shut up as he was in a corner of Numidia, knew and wrote everything that he ought concerning this matter. For at the Conference of Carthage, when Optatus’s testimony concerning Caecilian’s acquittal was read against the Donatists, nothing was read about the judgment at Arles or at Milan; yet this would not have been omitted if it had been set forth by Optatus [Col. 1145D]. And it was pointless, in that conference, to inquire what Optatus had thought at this point, if he had plainly written shortly before that Caecilian had been acquitted by Constantine. Shall we say that the Donatists had already suppressed and deleted what Optatus wrote on that subject?

But, however this may be, what I said is missing here may be recovered from elsewhere. And just as Constantine, at the beginning, although he showed that he took it indignantly that judges in Caecilian’s case were requested from him, nevertheless appointed ecclesiastical judges, who were otherwise competent judges, as our lawyers say; so now, although he indignantly exclaims that the obstinacy of the appealing Donatists is a rabid frenzy, he nevertheless admits the appeal in some fashion, and refers its hearing to the Synod of Arles, where he orders other bishops to hear this case again. Augustine recounts and emphasizes this so often that it would be tedious to indicate the passages encountered everywhere.

I shall add, however, something less common but especially relevant here: in Book X of Eusebius’s *History* there survives the complete rescript of Constantine to Chrestus, bishop of Syracuse, whom he orders to proceed from Sicily with two others to that Synod of Arles, there to judge Caecilian’s case with his fellow bishops. He indeed directs that this be done before the Kalends of August; but in what year? Since Constantine’s rescript bears no consuls subscribed, it is difficult to guess. Yet I reasonably suspect that this occurred in the consulship of Volusianus and Annianus—that is, in the year immediately after the Roman judgment. In that same year, on the third day before the Kalends of November, I recall that at Trier he issued a law concerning the admission of appeals, *Codex Theodosianus*, I.1, *de appellationibus*.

Moreover, in that rescript to Chrestus Constantine not only does not openly charge the Donatists’ appeal with rabid fury, but does not even name the Donatists. Simply and calmly he states that those judged at Rome refuse to abide by the judgment, because they allege that, before the case had been sufficiently investigated, a few judges had precipitately delivered their verdict [Col. 1146B]. He therefore directs that, since he has ordered bishops to assemble in the city of Arles from various and innumerable, as he says, places, an end be imposed upon this controversy by a common judgment, after the case has been diligently examined and both sides heard.

It is regrettable that the proceedings of that Synod of Arles have been lost. I once obtained certain fragments of them, but they were very corrupt; nevertheless, from them I learned that Silvester presided over that synod after the death of Miltiades. In the common miscellany of councils certain decrees are recited of the Council of Arles, said to have been the first. But most of them appear spurious. Among them is proposed one which mentions the Arians; it is thus also cited by Gratian, *De consecratione*, distinction 4, and likewise by the Magdeburgian compilers of the *Centuries*. Yet the name “Arians” had not yet arisen when the first Synod of Arles, with which we are concerned, assembled. I therefore gladly hear that in ancient manuscript copies, as the latest edition of those councils testifies [Col. 1146C], that canon is less corrupt and reads “Africans” (*Afris*) in place of “Arians” (*Arianis*).

In that miscellany something is also read that bears upon Caecilian’s case: namely, that those convicted of having handed over the sacred Scriptures are to be deposed. But they must be convicted not by bare words, but by the authority of public records. Something is added concerning those who ordain them; but that this fragment is defective is evident even from the insertion of the clause, “as we have said.” Yet nothing further on that matter is read there. It is regrettable—and indeed very regrettable—that the memory of the ancient Church is now so mutilated and corrupted, and that those who nevertheless consume and devour so much from ecclesiastical revenues take no care for this, although those resources ought at least in some part to be spent upon restoring and preserving such monuments.

It is established that Caecilian was again acquitted at the Council of Arles and Donatus condemned; and that for this reason the Donatists again appealed to Constantine [Col. 1146D]. Certainly there was a greater reason than before for rejecting so importunate an appeal. But Constantine allowed himself to be persuaded to permit the matter to be heard and to investigate it himself. Augustine therefore says, in Epistle 162, that Constantine judged this case at Milan. But what did he decide?

This must be recovered from another passage of Augustine, namely Book III *Against Cresconius*, chapter 71, where a letter of Constantine himself is quoted, recounting that he had investigated the matter between the parties and, after episcopal judgments, found Caecilian innocent: “I have seen,” he says, “that Caecilian is endowed with every innocence, observing the duties required by his religion and serving it as was fitting.” But at what time was this judgment rendered? I searched for this long. It did not readily and immediately occur to me, because the torn limbs of this history are miserably scattered. At last I recalled that Augustine, in *Against the Donatists after the Conference*, chapter 33, writes that Constantine wrote concerning Caecilian’s vindication on the fourth day before the Ides of November, in the consulship of Sabinus and Rufinus [Col. 1147A]. Thus only in the fourth year after this case had first been brought from Africa before Constantine was it at last finally decided.

Pages 24 and 25. The passage that follows in Optatus may now suitably be added: “At the same time the same Donatus requested,” etc. This is the passage which the Donatists at the Conference of Carthage shamelessly attempted to twist through cavilling. Their futility deserves to be displayed. Augustine, in the *Breviculus* near the end, says:

“They requested that Optatus be read, from whom they said they would prove that Caecilian had been condemned by the emperor. Optatus was read at the Donatists’ request, where he says: ‘At the same time the same Donatus requested that he be permitted to return and to go to Carthage. Then Philomenus, his petitioner before the emperor, represented that Caecilian should be kept at Brescia for the sake of peace; and this was done.’ Since in these words of Optatus no condemnation whatever of Caecilian could be found, as they had promised they would demonstrate, the presiding examiner ordered the entire page to be read, so that the intention of the author might be known from the preceding and following words [Col. 1147B]. And it was read from the official record: ‘Caecilian is pronounced innocent by the judgments of all those mentioned above.’ When this was read, the Donatists said that they had not requested this to be read, angered with those who could not restrain their laughter when they heard what an openly adverse page they had produced against themselves. Then, when from the words which they themselves had read they alleged that Optatus had softened Constantine’s condemnation and had refused to state it expressly, they were required to read from elsewhere clear proof of what they said had been softened by him.”

This is Augustine. In him I corrected what appears to be a corrupt quotation from Optatus: for example, *suggestore*, “representative,” has been wrongly substituted for *suffragatore*, “petitioner.” The terms *suffragium* and *suffragator* are familiar to students of law in this sense.

Nor shall I hesitate to add another passage of Augustine, since Augustine himself did not hesitate repeatedly to recount this matter. In *To the Donatists after the Conference*, chapter 31, he says:

“They thought that Optatus, the Catholic bishop of the Church of Milevis, should be read, promising that they would thereby prove Caecilian condemned by the emperor. When this reading was read all the more against them, no one could contain his laughter. What they wished to be read in their own favor was ambiguous. Therefore, when the examiner very properly ordered the passage somewhat above to be read, so that those words might, if possible, be made clear from it, this was read—which they did not wish: namely, that Caecilian had been vindicated, not, as they had claimed, condemned, but retained at Brescia for the sake of peace. When they said that by those words Optatus had intended to soften Caecilian’s condemnation, they were told to read from elsewhere an evident condemnation of Caecilian, so that it might be shown that it had been softened by Optatus, who had written most plainly that Caecilian had been vindicated.”

For the third time Augustine says the same in Epistle 152: “They produced the book of Optatus, from which they might prove Caecilian condemned by the emperor. When that book was read against them and showed all the more that Caecilian had been vindicated, they were laughed at by all.”

I emphasize this event and history now because I otherwise passed it over in my description of the Conference of Carthage [Col. 1147D], where at that time I pursued only the other principal part, containing the larger question concerning the Church. But just as I have elsewhere shown, in that question also, that the Catholic and Donatist disputants were not always sufficiently keen dialecticians, so I am now compelled to admit that in the question of fact—that is, when it was asked whether Caecilian had been condemned or acquitted—they were by no means sharp in debate after Optatus had been read.

The question was whether Optatus had written that Caecilian was condemned by Constantine. To establish this, the Donatists produced the statement that he had written Caecilian to have been retained at Brescia for the sake of peace. The answer was easy, and manifold. First, Optatus could not have written this without writing something shortly before concerning the Milanese judgment. But let us grant that Optatus wrote the consequence, not the antecedent: were there not other writers and witnesses to the Milanese judgment? Pages 25. Then, when Optatus says that Caecilian was retained at Brescia “for the sake of peace,” he does not thereby signify that he had been condemned. Indeed, the phrase “for the sake of peace” signifies that there was an entirely different reason for his detention. Finally, however much he may say that Caecilian was retained, he nevertheless writes openly a little later on the same page that Caecilian hurried to Carthage to his people as soon as he heard that Donatus had returned to Carthage [Col. 1148A]. The Catholics ought to have raised this to refute the Donatists’ quibble.

It is strange, however, that while they pass over all these points, they exult because Optatus wrote that Caecilian had been acquitted by Miltiades. Yet the Donatists did not deny this; nor was the question about Miltiades’ judgment, but Constantine’s. Augustine says that the Donatists were greatly ridiculed here. But there is reason to fear what Catullus says: nothing is more foolish than foolish laughter. Certainly, one who writes that Caecilian was acquitted by Miltiades does not thereby write that he was acquitted by Constantine. I therefore wonder all the more that the Donatists fell silent when they were ridiculed here. I believe they were as stupid and foolish as they were not keen and sharp.

[Col. 1148B] Ibid. I return to Optatus. He says: “In this way the parties were again *renovellatae*.” I would prefer *renovatae*, “renewed.” He means that the dispute revived, again inflamed by the fresh zeal of the factions. But although what is immediately added—“it is established, however,” etc.—seems to hang together poorly, the matter rather required that Constantine’s law now finally be added: not only that very severe law against the Donatists which Augustine mentions elsewhere, but also another, most lenient one. For Augustine himself, in *Against the Donatists after the Conference*, chapter 33, writes that Constantine, in the second consulship of Crispus and Constantine, gave letters to Valerius the Vicar releasing the Donatists from exile and leaving and remitting them to God the avenger.

Crispus and Constantine, most noble Caesars, sons of Constantine himself, were consuls for the second time in the ninth year after Maxentius’s death. Therefore the Donatists troubled Emperor Constantine for at least eight years while they harassed Caecilian. And since I recall that the Synod of Nicaea met in the fourth year thereafter—at which, as I have elsewhere noted, Caecilian alone was present from Africa [Col. 1148C]—I observe that the tragedy of Donatus was interrupted in Africa when Arius arose in Egypt.

Augustine himself, in Epistle 152, says that Constantine gave letters to Verinus the Vicar, in which he severely denounces the Donatists, but nevertheless says that they are to be released from exile and abandoned to their own frenzy, because God had now begun to take vengeance upon them. In what year those letters were written I do not know. But it is noted in the consular fasti that, in the second year after Crispus and Constantine had been consuls for the second time, Verinus was prefect of the city and succeeded Valerius.

Pages 25 and 26. “Then Constantine [wrote] to Aelianus.” It should be observed that this happened after Caecilian was, as Optatus says, “vindicated in the city,” that is, shortly after he was first acquitted by the judgment of Miltiades, bishop of Rome. Therefore this “then” must be referred only to what immediately precedes concerning Caecilian’s first vindication and acquittal at Rome [Col. 1148D], not also to the later matters, which occurred much afterward.

Augustine, in Epistle 152, says that not long after Caecilian had first been vindicated by episcopal judgment, Felix’s case was examined by Aelianus, the proconsul. I infer that this happened in the fourth month after that vindication from Augustine’s statement in *Against the Donatists after the Conference*, chapter 33, that it occurred on the fifteenth day before the Kalends of March, in the consulship of Volusianus and Annianus. Therefore, although the Donatists had appealed from Miltiades’ judgment and the principal case against Caecilian was still pending at the Synod of Arles, Felix’s own case was meanwhile heard in Africa. Under civil law, it would scarcely have been permissible thus to conjoin and intermingle prejudicial judgments.

Again, there was remarkable forgetfulness or shamelessness among the Donatists, who at the Conference of Carthage invented and boasted that Constantine, after Aelianus had decided that case, had reconsidered the judgment which he had delivered for Caecilian against the Donatists. Yet he had not then investigated that matter, and only after several years first pronounced that judgment at Milan [Col. 1149A]; and not after a short interval, but long after Felix had been acquitted by Aelianus, as Augustine says in Epistle 152.

Just as Optatus here relates that Constantine ordered a public inquiry into Felix’s life, so Augustine, in Epistle 68, says that this case was investigated and concluded by public trial. Optatus also describes here the form and procedure of this public trial or public inquiry. It would not be difficult for an interpreter versed in the books of law and Roman affairs to accumulate much that is said concerning the ancient procedure of public trials; but I am now hastening elsewhere.

I say only that from Optatus’s passage one may correct the corruptly written letter of Constantine dealing with this same matter, as Augustine quotes it in two places. There *Centurio* is written for *Saturianus*; *Calibius* for *Callidius*; and *Solus servus publicus*, “Solus, a public slave,” for *Solon officialis publicus*, “Solon, a public official.” As for what Optatus says about the scribe Ingentius, Augustine in the same places—Epistle 68 and Book III *Against Cresconius*, chapter 70—calls him sometimes, as frequently elsewhere, corruptly “Vigentius,” sometimes correctly “Ingentius.” He says that Ingentius was a decurion of the city of Ziqua; and Optatus is certainly speaking of him when he says: “He hung under fear of the impending tortures.”

Page 26. For he was accused of forgery, because he was said to have drawn up false records against Felix and to have forged a certain letter of Caecilian, as Augustine testifies. Augustine also appears to speak of him when, in Epistle 152, he speaks of someone suspended on the rack and also tormented by claws, while Felix could not object to so diligent or severe an investigation. Augustine indicates in Epistle 68 and Book III *Against Cresconius*, chapter 70, that Ingentius was indeed suspended but not tortured, because he said that he was a decurion; and this agrees with the Theodosian law, *Omnes*, *Codex*, *de Decurionibus*. When he had confessed the crime, he was sent to Constantine’s court.

Augustine further indicates that Aelianus made some pronouncement concerning him when he acquitted Felix; Augustine also quotes Aelianus’s sentence in precisely the same words as Optatus. When Optatus here names a *superstationarius*, we should observe that *stationarii* were drawn from the *cohortales*, that is, officials of provincial governors—one might call them attendants—who were stationed at fixed locations throughout the provinces and reported to magistrates what was happening. Their office was therefore called base and mean in the law-books, where *stationarii* are frequently mentioned: *Codex*, VI, *de Dignitatibus*; I, *de Cohortalibus*; and *Codex Theodosianus*, I, *de Cursu publico*, and *Si quis in hoc*, *de Episcopis et Clericis*.

Moreover, our learned juristic interpreter Renardus quotes this entire passage of Optatus in Book IV of his *Variae*, chapter 11, in order to prove that in former times a public inquiry was held concerning an accused person. But anyone who referred these words of Optatus—“He hung under fear of impending tortures”—to Felix as the accused would be mistaken. On the contrary, Augustine testifies near the end of the *Breviculus of the Conference* that Felix was acquitted by Aelianus in absentia. I mention this in passing because I see even the most learned men deceived in this entire history [Col. 1149D]. Accordingly, so far as I could, I have now attempted to set in order what was confused, and to unravel and explain clearly what had been indiscriminately mingled, especially since I observed that writers of ecclesiastical history had otherwise not sufficiently expounded this whole matter, which is particularly worthy of remembrance. Many things of this kind in the history of the ancient Church have been unworthily corrupted.

## On Book Two

Page 29. While disputing concerning the Catholic Church, and at the beginning of this book enumerating several provinces of the Christian world, Optatus mentions three Pannonias, three Syrias, and two Armenias. For formerly a single province, otherwise too extensive, was often divided into two or three, and a separate governor assigned to each. Thus the jurist Macer, in Book III *On the Duties of an Assessor*, says that this was done in Germany and Moesia; and Papinian, in Law IX *On Petitions*, mentions provinces bearing the same name. Double Aquitaine is also mentioned in the Itinerary of Antoninus.

Moreover, when Optatus adds that the Catholic Church is *rationalis*, “reasonable” or “rational,” he seems to call rational that which is apprehended not so much by the eyes as by reason—that is, by mind and understanding. Page 30. I have said more concerning the title “Catholic” in my history of the Conference of Carthage. Optatus then proves that his Church is part of the Catholic Church because it agrees with the Roman Church; and that the Roman Church, from Peter onward, has preserved unity of doctrine through a continuous succession of bishops, and, as it were, the foundation and body of the apostolic building.

Page 31. Optatus enumerates the bishops of Rome just as Augustine, for the same purpose, compiles a similar catalogue in Epistle 165; and before Optatus Irenaeus and Origen had used a similar argument. But we must again be warned that the words, “Damasus [and] Siricius today,” appear not to be Optatus’s but to belong to some writer slightly later than he [Col. 1150B]. For it is established that Optatus wrote these books around the year 370. Siricius, however, was not made bishop before the year 383, as has been said above. It is established, on Jerome’s testimony, that Optatus wrote these books during Valentinian’s reign. But it is likewise established that Damasus still lived during Theodosius’s reign; and the Theodosian law itself, *On the Supreme Trinity and the Catholic Faith*, testifies to this.

Page 32. What Optatus says concerning the exchange of *formatae* means those letters of communion drawn up in a fixed form, which orthodox bishops sent to the bishop of Rome as tokens of their faith and symbols of unity. Augustine himself testifies in Epistle 163 that they were called *formatae*. And when disputing with the Donatist Fortunius, who boasted that his church was Catholic, Augustine asked whether he could send such letters of communion wherever he wished. For in this way the question could most easily be settled.

Page 31. Concerning the words read a little before in Optatus—that Peter, because he was head of the apostles, was called Cephas—I have elsewhere said that this is the solecism of a man imagining that the Syriac word meaning “rock” is the Greek *kephalē* (κεφαλή), meaning “head.” But I suspect that the words “whence he was also called Cephas” are an inept gloss rashly written in the margin and afterwards inserted into the text by copyists. Certainly, in Book VII Optatus simply says that Peter was head of the apostles and adds nothing further. Valentinian calls him the summit of the episcopal crown in his Novella *On the Ordination of Bishops*.

I pass over many similar things occurring here and there, to return to the notes on Optatus’s second book. Here I cannot conceal that it may seem very strange [Col. 1150C], Page 33, that Optatus twists Paul’s words to the Romans, “sharing in the memorials of the saints,” to the basilicas of the Roman Church. In the Greek text of Paul’s epistle stands *chreiais* (χρείαις), that is, “needs” or “necessities.” The Latins who translated *memoriis*, “memorials,” appear to have read *mneiais* (μνείαις). But it is remarkable that Optatus interprets this as referring to the shrines of martyrs, which were called *memoriae*, as one might say “memorial monuments.” Turrianus cites an ancient book of Eustratius of Constantinople that referred Paul’s passage to the remembrance of deceased Christians for whom prayer should be offered.

Page 34. Optatus shortly afterward indicates why the Donatists at Rome were called Montenses, “Mountaineers.” Thus Jerome in the *Chronicle* says that the followers of Donatus of Carthage were called Montenses by some because they began to have their first church at Rome on a hill. In *Against the Luciferians* he names the Montenses or Campates. I agree with Erasmus that he added *Campates* or *Campenses* by a certain allusion to the Montenses. But I shall never say, as Erasmus does, that they were called Montenses after Montanus; nor shall I agree with Epiphanius, who writes in his *Ancoratus* that the Novatianists at Rome are called *montēsioi* (μοντησίους). He speaks through a manifest error about the Novatianists what should have been said about the Donatists.

Augustine, in *On Unity*, chapter 3, calls these persons at Rome Montenses or Rupitani, “Rock-dwellers” [Col. 1151A]. I believe the latter was another mocking allusion. The same writer, speaking in Epistle 165 of a Donatist bishop, says: “Presiding over a few Africans in the city of Rome, he spread the designation Montenses or Cuzupitani.” I suspect that *Rupitani* should be read. I pass over the fact that I recall that in a law of Honorius also, *Codex Theodosianus*, XLIII, *de Haereticis*, the Donatists are likewise called Montenses.

I shall rather add what Augustine says in *On Heresies*: “These heretics are called Montenses in the city of Rome. From Africa they are accustomed to send them a bishop, or their African bishops go from here to Rome, if perhaps it is decided to ordain one there.” Optatus here enumerates and names some who were ordained there. When among them he mentions Macrobius, I am reminded that Gennadius wrote that he had learned from Optatus’s writings that Macrobius—who, while still a presbyter in the Church of God, had written a book addressed to confessors and virgins—was later a clandestine bishop of the Donatists in the city of Rome, or of the Montenses.

[Col. 1151B] Page 37. In this book of Optatus, before the words “for also the fountain,” I ordered a lacuna to be marked with asterisks, to indicate that much is missing; likewise on the following page before the words “It remains.” Let no one otherwise wonder that the discussion of the Church and its gifts and marks is both meager, abrupt, and incomplete.

What Optatus says shortly afterward—that the Donatists do not rebaptize after their associates have been detected in sin—a certain very learned man has foolishly noted as referring to the Maximianists. For the dissension between the Donatists Primian and Maximian occurred after Optatus’s time. It was the beginning of a new schism among these schismatics, since each party alleged its own council—the one the Council of Carthage, the other the Council of Bagai—yet neither detracted in any respect from the other’s baptism. Augustine repeatedly charges the Donatists with rebaptizing after Catholics. But Optatus could not charge them with what had not yet happened; he nevertheless saw something not unlike it, which he charges here.

Augustine fully sets out the history of the Maximianists in *On the Proceedings with Emeritus*, Book IV *Against Cresconius*, chapter 10, and Book III, chapters 53 and 56, as well as on Psalm 36, page 26. Optatus says that the Donatists do not omit in the mystery of the sacraments something lawful. He means the solemn formula of the canonical prayer, as it was also called, in which sacrifice is said to be offered for the one Church spread throughout the whole world [Col. 1151C]. So in Book III he says that they could not omit the lawful phrase, “Peace be with you.” And in Book IV he says that they also used in baptism the solemn formula of that ecclesiastical exorcism: “Accursed one, come out!”

Thus Cyprian writes that the Novatianists did not dare in baptism to omit the solemn stipulation, “Do you believe in the forgiveness of sins?” although they themselves did not believe in this forgiveness. Similarly Augustine indicates that the Pelagians in the baptism of infants used also the formula, “Do you renounce Satan?”, though they otherwise denied that infants were bound by any original sin. Indeed, Firmilian, writing to Cyprian, shows that even the devil himself, when baptizing through a possessed prophetess, observed the solemn and customary words. Finally, Augustine, in Book II *On the Gift of Perseverance*, chapter 13, disputing against the Pelagians, tacitly indicates that they repeated something from the Church’s Eucharistic formula which they objected to; but he interprets it in such a way as to turn it against them: “What is said in the sacraments of the faithful—that we should have our hearts lifted up to the Lord—is the Lord’s gift. After this declaration, those to whom it is spoken are reminded by the priest to give thanks to the Lord our God for this gift; and they answer that it is fitting and right.”

Pages 40 and 41. Moreover, what Optatus relates about Julian the Apostate, who favored the Donatists and was invoked and praised by them, is more fully explained by Augustine in Epistles 148 and 166, and Book II *Against Petilian*, chapters 83 and 92. Indeed, in Book XVI, title V, chapter 37 of the Theodosian Code, a constitution of Honorius mentions a certain rescript which the Donatists were said to have obtained from Julian [Col. 1152A].

Page 42. What Optatus shortly afterward relates concerning deacons killed at the altar resembles what Augustine narrates in Book III *Against Cresconius*, chapter 43. And concerning the Donatists’ boast, which Optatus indicates—that they called themselves doves and called Catholics vultures—I add what Augustine says in Book II *Against Petilian*, chapter 83: “In this way also, when a kite has been frightened and cannot seize the chicks, it calls itself a dove.” Finally, when Optatus adds that the Donatists wished to trample the Eucharist underfoot, Victor of Utica relates that something not unlike this occurred again in Africa in his own time. Thus we may understand that in this respect also those Arian Vandals may be compared with the Donatists. But this should be sought from Victor’s own books, which we have now taken care to publish with Optatus.

## On Book Three

Page 50. In the German edition this entire Book III [Col. 1152B] was so confused and disordered by transposed pages that never were the Sibyl’s leaves more mixed, when, as the poet says, they became the sport of rushing winds. In my earlier Paris edition, through the benefit of the copy I used, I restored several pages to their proper places. In this edition I have again restored to their proper order an equal number which still lay rashly confused and transposed; and I did this with the aid of the Tilius manuscript.

Certainly, while the transpositions of pages I have mentioned mixed everything up, scarcely a sentence of this book could be understood. Here we recognize the remarkable negligence or ignorance of copyists in former times: they seemed not so much to copy books as to tear them to pieces, like puppies tearing rags, as Plato says somewhere. I now hope, however, that this book has been restored so fully that the reader will immediately recognize the benefit of this edition.

As to the matter itself: here the case of the prefect Macarius is treated. Because of his capital punishments, the Donatists maliciously declaimed that the Church of our party was bloodthirsty, and called it no longer the Catholic Church but the Macarian Church, as Augustine writes in Epistle 161. Likewise, in Epistle 164 to the Donatist Emeritus: “You call us Macarians.” Finally, just as Catholics called the Donatists the party of Donatus, so the Donatists called Catholics the party of Macarius. Augustine is witness in Book II *Against Petilian*, chapter 39. Yet this recrimination or retaliation was unjust. For the Donatists themselves had called themselves the party of Donatus from the beginning, as Optatus proves here. Catholics had never said that they were the party of Macarius.

Moreover, just as Augustine always attempted to separate Caecilian’s own case—which, though good, was personal—from the case of the Church, so he did with Macarius’s case. Thus in Epistle 203, to the Donatist Maximinus: “Do not cast the Macarian times against me, and I shall not cast the cruelty of the Circumcellions against you. If this does not concern you, neither does that concern me.” Optatus’s argument is similar. I add only that there survives a law of Arcadius and Honorius, *Codex Theodosianus*, XXXI, *On Bishops and Clerics*, which appears relevant here, since it grants African judges armed official protection against those who violently attacked churches and oppressed their clerics [Col. 1152D].

Page 52. What Optatus says after the beginning of this book about the word *ichthys* (ἰχθύς, “fish”) was so corrupted in the German edition that it appeared to be some monstrous thing. For it was written there *Xort*. In my earlier Paris edition I corrected and restored it, and at the same time added in the margin the passage of Augustine which more fully explains the mystery which Optatus indicates lies beneath it. That passage of Augustine is Book XVIII *City of God*, chapter 23. Now, lest anyone think that this meaning, whatever it may be, was invented or fabricated by Optatus, I add that Tertullian himself had previously mentioned it in *On Baptism*.

Page 52. Optatus then misuses the words of Isaiah the prophet, chapter 22 [Col. 1153A], twisting against the Donatist faction in Africa words simply spoken either concerning Judah, called a valley, or concerning the city of Jerusalem, to which some mournful calamity and desolation are announced. I do not know what translation or interpretation of Isaiah Optatus used. But I cannot conceal that what he attaches is very far removed both from that prophet’s meaning and from his words. I also believe that there are certain copyists’ errors: for example, when, while citing Isaiah, he has “temples” for “roofs” and “rod” for “flight.” But I have not undertaken to correct everything which Optatus cites from Scripture out of order or repeats ineptly—a fault of both that age and that region.

Pages 53 and 54. What Optatus says concerning Mount Zion—on whose summit were seven synagogues, and on which, after the victories of Emperor Vespasian, scarcely, as he says, traces of its ancient ruins remain (for so I corrected it from the Tilius manuscript)—contains something that the student of history should note. Jerome himself, on Jeremiah, chapter 19, writes that the city of the Jews had collapsed into everlasting ashes, the ruins of which were to remain until the consummation of the age [Col. 1153B]. Certainly, after Vespasian’s time, when that city lay demolished and ruined for nearly fifty years, Emperor Hadrian restored it in such a way that he was understood not to restore the old city but to construct an entirely new one. He therefore changed even its name and wished it to be called Aelia Capitolina instead of Jerusalem. It is so called both by Ulpian, in the *Digest*, title *On Censuses*, and by the Nicene Fathers themselves in the canons of that synod. Besides, Tertullian too, in two places—in *Against the Jews* and Book III *Against Marcion*—exclaims: “Zion no longer exists.”

Page 56. There is no statement in Optatus that seems more unusual than the one which follows shortly afterwards: “For the Commonwealth is not in the Church, but the Church is in the Commonwealth,” that is, in the Roman Empire. Others would interpret this to mean that the Commonwealth may indeed exist without the Church, as the Roman Commonwealth once did; but that the Church cannot exist without the Commonwealth, nay, that it is a part of it, since it is, as it were, incorporated within its bosom. I know also that much may plausibly be said in general concerning the relation between Commonwealth and Church; but another matter is now at issue and under inquiry. I shall therefore say what is more relevant to this passage.

In the Jewish Church there were formerly customary prayers for the kingdom of David, within which the Church was understood to be enclosed. To this belong Psalms 118, 72, and 122. Subsequently, in the Christian Church there were customary prayers for the Roman Empire, for many reasons. For although in the first centuries that Empire was very hostile and inimical to the Church, Christians nevertheless believed that the Empire’s extent assisted the propagation of religion, as Ambrose observes on Psalm 46, Eusebius at the end of Book III of the *Demonstration of the Gospel*, and Prudentius in Book II against Symmachus.

Further, the ancient Christians interpreted Paul’s passage to the Thessalonians concerning the apostasy, and commonly spoke of Antichrist, in such a way as to profess that Antichrist, who would strike the Church more grievously, would not come before the ruin and dissolution of the Roman Empire; nor would the world perish sooner. Therefore they were accustomed to pray to God for the Roman Empire, in whose preservation they judged that the preservation of the Church was for that reason included.

Tertullian, whom Optatus the African read in Africa, speaks thus in his *Apology to the Romans*: “The Apostle expressly and plainly says, ‘Pray for kings and for rulers and powers, that all things may be peaceful.’ For the Empire is shaken together with you; and when its other members too are shaken, we also, although we are considered strangers to public disturbances, are found somewhere within the sphere of the disaster. There is also another and greater necessity for us to pray for the emperors, even for the whole condition of the Empire and Roman affairs: because we know that the greatest force hanging over the entire world, and the very closing of the age, threatening terrible calamities, is delayed by the continuance of the Roman Empire. Therefore we do not wish to experience it; and while we pray for its postponement, we favour Rome’s long duration.”

And again, shortly afterwards: “We pray for the emperors, for their ministers and the powers of the age, for the tranquillity of affairs, for delay of the end.” The same author, in his work addressed to Scapula, not only repeats, “We offer sacrifice for the emperor’s welfare,” but also professes that a Christian must wish the emperor safe, together with the whole Roman Empire; and adds: “So long as the age shall stand, so long indeed shall the Empire stand.” In the treatise *On the Resurrection of the Flesh*, he likewise interprets Paul’s passage to the Thessalonians so that, just as the end of the age shall not come before Antichrist is revealed, so Antichrist shall not come before the Roman Empire fails. Therefore he says that the Roman order prevents his coming.

Certainly Optatus did not see that great ruin of the Roman Empire which the barbarians inflicted, such as Augustine and also Jerome saw. Jerome, when he beheld the city captured by the Goths, wrote to Gerontius that Antichrist was drawing near. But Optatus saw that Constantine had transferred the seat of the Roman Empire so to the East that at the same time that Empire became a bulwark of the Christian Church, and in it was fulfilled that saying of Isaiah 132 concerning the Church: “And kings shall be your foster-fathers.” Optatus could aptly have thrown this in the teeth of Donatus when he rejected the alms of the emperor Constans.

Pages 56 and 57. Shortly afterwards Optatus twists Ezekiel, chapter 28, concerning Tyre, to apply to Donatus of Carthage; as Augustine also does in Book I of *On Unity*, chapter 14—although elsewhere, namely in Book XI of *The Literal Meaning of Genesis*, chapter 25, he refers the same passage to the Devil. But in truth Ezekiel’s prophecy concerning the destruction of Tyre is nothing other than that which Isaiah himself had earlier issued in chapter 23. Nor is it written in Isaiah, as Optatus says, “the ships of Carthage,” but “the ships of Tarshish.” By this word transmarine Cilicia is rather signified, although Augustine, on Psalm 47, prefers Carthage to be understood by it. Yet Carthage was not Tyre; rather, it was a colony of Tyre.

Page 57. Moreover, to what Optatus relates concerning Donatus’s pride and arrogance, one might add that the Donatists boasted that God had answered Donatus from heaven while he prayed, as Augustine says in Tractate 12 on John; and that an angel had appeared to commend his sect, as the same Augustine reports in Letter 165. Yet the ambition and arrogance which Optatus here charges against Donatus was common to almost all heretics who so desired. “All are puffed up,” as Tertullian says in *On Prescription*. Finally, just as Optatus reports that the Donatists swore by the name of Donatus, so Sulpicius Severus reports that the Priscillianists swore by the name of their own Priscillian.

There also seems to me, as I read here that Donatus arrogated to himself the primacy of Carthage, to be added what Jerome notes in his *Chronicle*: that this Donatus was at last expelled from Carthage in the year of Christ 360, that is, not many years before Optatus wrote these books.

Page 58. What follows shortly afterwards concerning the persecution stirred up by Diocletian sixty years before Optatus wrote this has been explained in Book I, where I also spoke of Anullinus, who is mentioned here as well. I shall add only what perhaps not everyone would otherwise understand: by the name of the Proconsular province, Africa is here meant. This usage is frequent also in the laws: Law XI, *Code* on annual military disbursements; final law, *Theodosian Code*, on recruits; Law XIII, *Theodosian Code*, on debts owed.

Optatus then relates much concerning the savagery of the Circumcellions. Pages 59–60. Augustine recounts, in various places, matters partly similar and partly even more atrocious concerning them, and carefully explains what those Donatist henchmen were like. For he saw more of their crimes than Optatus did. I shall only compare what I recall Augustine narrating in Letter 50 concerning the wrong done to creditors and masters: the Donatists seemed both to summon slaves to the cap—the symbol of emancipation—and to grant debtors, as it were, new account-books:

> “Who was not compelled to fear his own slave, if that slave had fled to the patronage of the Donatists? Who could demand payment from any debtor seeking their assistance and protection? The tablets of the worst slaves were broken, so that they might depart as free persons. Written acknowledgments of debt extorted from debtors were returned to them.”

Jurists understand what it means to return written acknowledgments of debt to debtors: they know that release arises from this; Book IV, *On Pacts*, Law I, final section, and Law III, *On Release from Legacies*.

The student of law and antiquity will also observe that Optatus says shortly afterwards that burial was not permitted in the house of God, that is, in a temple or church. So too a law issued in Gratian’s time denies that the shrine of apostles or martyrs was granted for human bodies: Law II, *Code*, on Sacred Churches. Page 61. Augustine nevertheless, in *On Care for the Dead*, praises those who wished to be buried in a church near the tombs of martyrs.

In the same place. Further, our readers will note that not long afterwards Optatus writes that surveyors of quarters (*metatores*), as commonly happened, were sent ahead of the soldiers who were to come. He calls them *metatores* and attributes to them what, in the code of constitutions, is said rather to have been the duty of *mensorēs*, measurers: Laws I and V, *Code*, on Quartering. In civil law, *metata* are the lodgings which provincials are required to provide for soldiers; and *metatores* are the very guests who are received: Law IX, *Code*, on Quartering. But Optatus calls by this name those who are sent ahead in order first to mark out those lodgings, as we would say. Thus also in Suidas’s commentaries: “A *metator* is a messenger sent beforehand before the ruler.” Sidonius Apollinaris alludes to this in Book VIII: “I sent a billet concerning quarters, as it were, with the Muse going ahead.”

Page 68. From the books of the jurists there has also been corrected and restored what Optatus, near the end of Book III, cites as a Donatist saying: “Gaius Seius, Gaia Seia,” and again near the end of Book VI. Earlier it had been corruptly printed in Germany as *Gaiasei*. Students of law know that Gaius, Seius, or Titius is commonly used to designate any person. Hence our own Tertullian, in the *Apology*, recalls the common saying concerning a Christian: “Gaius Seius is a good man.”

Moreover, Augustine, Book II of *On Baptism*, chapter 7, again elucidates this passage of Optatus. He reports that these were the Donatists’ words to Catholics: “A good man—if only you were not a traitor. Take counsel for your soul. Become a Christian.” Here Augustine, following Optatus, exclaims: “O shameless madness! When a Christian is told, ‘Become a Christian,’ what else is said but, ‘Deny that you are a Christian’?” This is how I read and correct Augustine’s passage.

Certainly the same Augustine, in Letter 169 to Eusebius, indicates that when a Catholic defected to the Donatists and wished to be rebaptized by them, he had to say, in order to merit this, that until then he had been a pagan. Augustine says that so great was the blood of martyrs shed in order that this utterance might not proceed from a Christian mouth. Finally, the same Augustine, Book IV against Cresconius, chapter 59, says that this puffed-up pride belongs to all who sever themselves from Christ’s unity: they boast that they alone are Christians and condemn the rest. Elsewhere it has been said concerning this Donatist boast, “The whole world apostatized; we alone remained,” and so forth.

Page 69. The final passage in this third book of Optatus deserving particular observation concerns some image, I know not what, which Macarius was said to be about to place upon the altar contrary to Christian rite before the sacrifice was offered. I suspect that hostile slanderers maliciously invented this about a profane image or statue of the emperor himself, by whom Macarius had been sent. We should therefore not be surprised if Optatus says Christians abhorred such an effigy placed upon an altar, since this was done contrary even to the emperors’ commands. For although rulers themselves in those times highly valued their own statues, they did not wish them to be idols.

The younger Theodosius says in one constitution: “Whenever our statues or images are set up, let a judge be present, without the ostentatious height of adoration.” Thus it is read in the *Theodosian Code*, Book XV, title V. In the *Justinian Code*, however, *fastidio* (“aversion”) is read in place of *fastigio* (“height”), Book I, title XXIV. But if Theodosius does not wish the adoration of his statue to be treated with aversion, he requires only civil honour, of the kind then signified by the proud and ambitious word “adoration.” At least in the *Theodosian Code* there is appended a clause of that constitution which must not be disregarded here: “Worship exceeding human dignity shall be reserved for the divine power above.”

I say only that it was formerly customary for emperors to send their statues or images into provinces to which they themselves did not otherwise travel, and that these images were customarily received by the peoples almost religiously. Thus the emperor Theodosius, Book I, *Code*, on Public Rejoicings or on Consuls: “If perchance we bring our sacred countenances before eager peoples, we command that they be received without excessive expense.” These images were commonly called *laurata*, “laureate images.” Hence, in the acts of the Second Council of Nicaea, where sacred images were discussed, we read: “Peoples go forth to meet with candles and incense the laureate images and icons sent to cities or regions, honouring not a board covered with wax, but the emperor.”

## On Book IV

Page 71. In this book Optatus chiefly aims to answer the Donatists, who, while maintaining that baptism administered by sinners, as they called them, was void, most foolishly objected that passage from Psalm 140: “The oil of the sinner shall not anoint my head.” I wish that Optatus’s reply had set against it a more suitable interpretation; yet I grant that such an interpretation can be drawn from Augustine, who commonly seems to supply what is lacking in Optatus.

For the Donatists seem, in twisting that verse of the Psalm so foolishly to this matter, to have followed the perverse example of that Council of Carthage over which Cyprian presided, and in which that verse had been cited to disapprove baptism administered by heretics. We should therefore be less surprised if Parmenian, following such an example, ridiculously objected this point, and if it was later tediously repeated by Petilian and Cresconius, the illustrious champions of the Donatists. But Augustine did well to demolish their futile absurdities with the true interpretation, seriously and decisively, in Book II against Petilian, chapter 103; Book III, chapter 33; and Book II against Cresconius, chapter 24.

[Col. 1156C] Moreover, no one should wonder if Optatus so readily thinks that baptism is at once signified wherever oil or anointing is mentioned. For by the word “baptism” sacred Scripture sometimes signifies the entire ministry of the Church; and likewise our forefathers later commonly signified this by the name “altar.” So by the words *chrism* or “oil” they frequently understood the whole of baptism, especially because Christians of old commonly applied that sacred anointing both before and after baptism.

Page 74. I cannot pass over what Optatus then says: that Marcion became an apostate from being a bishop. Yet Tertullian, in *On Prescription*, says not that he was a bishop but the son of a bishop, and that he was excommunicated by his father on account of sexual immorality. Elsewhere Epiphanius writes that Marcion lived as a solitary. There is, moreover, an intolerable textual error in the reading of Optatus: “Marcion introduced two Scriptures.” Therefore from the Tilius manuscript I corrected and restored “two Christs.” What follows concerning Ebion, who is said to have taught that the Father suffered—I should prefer that this had been said of Praxeas, whom Optatus also mentions in Book I. For Tertullian, in *On Prescription*, testifies that many years after Ebion, Praxeas—whom Augustine says lived in Africa—introduced the heresy which taught that the almighty Father, as he puts it, was Jesus Christ, crucified and having suffered.

In the same place. What Optatus next says concerning Valentinus, who wished to deprive Christ of flesh: although Tertullian 133 in his books against the Valentinians, while attacking their other monstrosities, passes over this more or less silently, yet in *On the Flesh of Christ* he plainly accuses Valentinus of having, as he says, invented a spiritual flesh for Christ, as though Christ had brought it from heaven and had been born through, rather than from, the Virgin.

Optatus shortly afterwards mentions a certain heretic Corpianus. Page 75. In the Tilius manuscript the reading is *Scorpianus*. I do not recall reading anything elsewhere about him. I know that some worthless fellows once insultingly called Cyprian in Africa *Coprianus*, as though one should say “a dung-man.” But no one could say that Cyprian was hostile to martyrdom, since he wrote an exhortation to martyrdom and was himself a martyr.

Certainly the heresy which Optatus indicates as belonging to Corpianus—the denial that there ought to be martyrdoms—we know to have been rarer than the other one which, under Montanus’s leadership, required martyrdom so absolutely that it maintained none but martyrs would be saved. Eusebius, Book VI, chapter 38, relates from Origen that there was once a heresy of the Elcesaites which mocked Christians who risked death for confessing Christ; but he reports that this heresy was extinguished as soon as it arose.

Of greater importance is what Optatus next writes: that this was formerly the formula of exorcism in the baptism of children: “In the same place, accursed one, go out!”—a formula which still remains. I recall that Peter Martyr once told me familiarly, and later wrote in his commentary on the First Book of Kings, that when he carefully weighed a passage of Cyprian, he had singularly discovered and observed the origin, hardly known to the public, of joining exorcism with baptism. For Cyprian, writing to Magnus in Book IV, says that unclean spirits sometimes deceive the servants of God, pretending when adjured that they are leaving, yet not leaving. Cyprian then adds: “But when they have come to the water, there the Devil is utterly unable to remain and departs altogether.”

From this Peter Martyr boasts that he infers that formerly possessed persons who could not be cured by exorcisms were baptized. Later generations, however, universally and indiscriminately joined exorcisms with baptism. He indeed admits that Optatus, like Augustine, strongly approved this. But he reproaches both and accuses them of error for that reason. I pass over his foolish citation of some eighth book of Optatus, which does not exist. I say only that Optatus was so near to Cyprian’s time that what he reports as having been commonly done in his own time may be understood also to have been done in Cyprian’s time; nor can Optatus be accused as the author of this custom and practice.

## On Book V

[Col. 1157C]

Pages 81 and 82. No passage in this book is more illustrious than that drawn from the books of jurists concerning a will, by whose evidence the testator’s intention is usually judged. By such an example Optatus proves that the dispute raised by the Donatists must likewise be settled from the documents of sacred Scripture. Augustine, who commonly imitates Optatus, seems to have used a similar argument. For on Psalm 21, addressing the Donatists, he says:

> “We are brothers: why do we litigate? The father did not die intestate; he made a will and so died. A dispute over the inheritance of the dead lasts until the will is brought forth in public; when it has been produced, all are silent, so that the tablets may be opened and read. The attentive judge hears; the advocates are silent; the heralds order silence; the whole people hang in expectation that the words of the dead may be read. He lies senseless in his tomb, and yet his words prevail. Christ sits in heaven, and his will is contradicted.”

The same Augustine, in *On the Five Heresies*, says: “The laws provide that the testator’s will be obeyed in everything. If anyone wishes to act contrary to the testator’s will, let him be deprived of the inheritance. I produce the will; I recite the testator’s words.”

I should be foolish if I now sought, with pretension and indeed pointlessly, to draw many things of that sort from our books of law concerning the trustworthiness, authority, and testimony of wills. It is more relevant here to observe that Augustine uses this prior example and comparison more cautiously than Optatus. Optatus uses it when he adduces from the New Testament John’s Scripture concerning the washing of feet, in order to prove that baptism must not be repeated. But Augustine, who saw that this was forced, prefers to use the comparison above when he wishes to prove from the Psalms and prophetic writings that Christ’s Church is catholic. This was another dispute with the Donatists. Thus also in *On the Unity of the Church* against Petilian: “There are the Lord’s books, to whose authority we both consent, believe, and submit. There let us seek the Church; there let us examine our case.”

But when he disputes against the Donatists concerning the one baptism and its non-repetition, he relies less upon Scripture than upon apostolic tradition, as though he then preferred the testimony of an unwritten rather than a written will: Book II of *On Baptism*, chapter 7; Book IV, chapter 6; and Book V, chapter 23. He did indeed at one time cite John’s passage on the washing of feet, Book III of *On Baptism*, chapter 14. But when Petilian turned it against our party, Augustine answered in such a way that he did not conceal that he was not pressing such an argument very strongly: Book II against Petilian, chapter 22. Therefore in *On the Unity of the Church*, chapter 19, he immediately passes from that passage to the Church’s usage and authority.

Yet John’s passage was considered, many years even after Augustine, so applicable in Africa to the one baptism that, when the tyranny of the Vandals raged and those seven brothers—whose martyrdom was no less noble than that of the Maccabean brothers of old—were pressed by Arians toward a second baptism, they opposed nothing more strongly. Victor of Utica is the witness, Book IV, *On the Vandal Persecution*: our forefathers, it seems, were stronger martyrs than subtle disputants.

Pages 83 and 84. Finally, I note that in this book Optatus answers opponents who contended that baptism administered by schismatics was null and must therefore be repeated, since those baptized by John were baptized again by the apostles, as Luke relates. Optatus answers that the example is unlike, because John’s baptism was other and different from Christ’s baptism; but the baptism of schismatics is conferred in the name of the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit, as Christ’s baptism is. Jerome’s distinction and answer in the dialogue against the Luciferians is not unlike it, nor Augustine’s in Book II against Petilian, chapter 37; Book III, chapter 56; and Book V of *On Baptism against the Donatists*, chapters 9, 10, and so forth.

## On Book VI

[Col. 1158C]

Page 90. Nothing in this book today offends many more than the great value which Optatus places upon altars. Peter Martyr, certainly, greatly reproves Optatus for this in his commentary on the First Book of Kings, chapter 23. Yet it is strange that he does not rather reproach Tertullian himself, who is earlier, and who in *On Repentance* speaks of “the altars of God” in the Church.

Moreover, what Optatus here relates concerning the incredible pride of the Donatists and their savage hatred of Catholics, I recall was imitated many centuries later in the East by the Greeklings in their schism. For Innocent III, chapter 6 on Baptism, Book III of the *Decretals*, repeats this account from his Lateran Council, which met at Rome in 1215: “Whenever Latin priests had celebrated upon Greek altars, the Greeks did not sacrifice upon them until they had washed them as though polluted. With rash daring they also presumed to rebaptize persons baptized by Latins.”

Pages 93 and 94. Another chief passage here concerns the *Sanctimoniales*, as they were called—women consecrated to sacred life—whom I learned from Arnobius and Jerome were also once called *Nonnae* in Africa and Egypt. Ambrose indeed, Book I *On Virgins*, says that women had been brought to Milan from the furthest regions beyond both parts of Mauretania, eager to be consecrated by Ambrose. The Donatists too had their virgin *Sanctimoniales*. When they heard Catholics display them as a certain glory of the Church, they exerted themselves vigorously to entice them to their own side, as Augustine indicates in Letter 169.

This, therefore, is what Optatus—who had said something on this subject also in Book II—so strongly laments here: that such Vestals had been solicited by the Donatists; and why he so forcefully drives away not merely their abductors, but also their suitors. Shortly before Optatus wrote this, the emperor Jovian had issued a most severe law pronouncing capital punishment upon those who dared not only to abduct, but also to solicit for marriage, most holy virgins: Law V, *Code*, on Sacred Churches. Sozomen, Book VI, chapter 3, testifies that Jovian issued this decree to restrain the incestuous wantonness which had spread impiously and shamelessly in Julian’s time. But no law could restrain the Donatists’ audacity and sexual licentiousness.

Pages 93 and 94. Moreover, I conveniently recall now that Fulgentius the African, who shone and flourished in the African Church more than a hundred years after Optatus’s death, in Book II addressed to his Monimus, cites from this sixth book of Optatus, where virgins are treated, Optatus’s interpretation of Paul’s statement concerning them to the Corinthians: that it is counsel rather than command. He compares this interpretation with another exposition by Augustine and Ambrose. Since Fulgentius quotes Optatus’s words entire, let the reader inspect the passage and compare it with our edition. This is of greater importance than what Optatus additionally emphasizes concerning the veils with which the heads of consecrated virgins were covered and, as it were, shrouded.

Pages 93, 94, and 95. He calls them *mitrellae*, as though one said “little mitres.” *Mitra* is a Syriac word; the Greeks call it διάδημα, “diadem”; the Latins, *vitta*, “band,” and it properly means a binding or fillet. But just as there were virginal fillets, so there were others for married women. For married matrons covered and adorned their heads differently from virgins. Hence Propertius:

> “Another fillet bound her received locks.”

134 Page 95. What Optatus says near the end concerning a woman who marries a second time—“she is not lifted high”—has been noted by others as apparently said from African rather than Latin custom. For among the Carthaginians, as among the Egyptians and Greeks, it was customary for brides to sit in a curule chair and be conveyed high in a carriage from their father’s home to their husband’s dwelling. By Roman custom, however, brides were rather led by the hand.

Pages 97 and 98. The elegant comparison which Optatus finally draws from bird-catchers seems also to have been repeated by Augustine in imitation of him, in the work addressed to Honoratus, *On the Advantage of Believing*, chapter 1. I now print a correction: in place of *vivarum volentium*, “of living willing [creatures],” I have restored from a better manuscript *avium volantium*, “of flying birds.”

I also recall that when Fornierius, a jurist of Orléans, recently visited me and conversation happened to turn to Optatus, he suggested that in what Optatus says shortly afterwards, “to sing with another’s throat,” *alieno*, “another’s,” properly means “feigned,” as in Horace, *malis ridentem alienis*, “smiling with borrowed cheeks,” that is, with feigned and simulated cheeks, and likewise in Homer. But I replied that in Optatus the birds are said, as it were, to sing from another’s throat because their song, though real, is mistakenly taken for the song of other birds which are otherwise artificial and mute. I added that Valerius Flaccus’s “wandering cheeks, and joys with another countenance” resembles Horace’s verse.

## On Book VII

Page 99. I once suspected that this book—which was also omitted in the German edition—was not by Optatus, since Jerome writes that he composed only six books, and Optatus himself, in Book I, sets forth the subject of only six books. But since this Book VII is found in the three manuscript copies which I used, and its style and subject matter agree, I acknowledge it to be Optatus’s; yet I say that it was written after the preceding six had been published.

It is fortunate that many missing pages were discovered in the Tilius manuscript, and that the final part, absent from that manuscript, existed in other copies. Yet I did not hesitate to remove and delete what had rashly been repeated here from the end of Book III concerning the affair of Macarius, and ineptly added and stitched onto the end of this Book VII. But I did not wish, nor ought I, to pass over the final appendix which I found in two manuscripts, though it was absent from the Tilius manuscript. I confess only that, in emending this final book, I was by no means satisfied with myself, nor was I able to be so because of the variation in the text.

But, to complete what more directly concerns the matter, what a fuller history of the Donatists requires, and what may abundantly satisfy Optatus in this respect, it seemed good now to add a complete account of the discussion concerning the Church held with the Donatists in the great Conference at Carthage, in Augustine’s presence, some years after Optatus’s death. For in that conference, as it was called, the case of Optatus himself and of his books was in some measure also handled, as may be understood from what I noted shortly before.

[Col. 1159]

# Observations of Gabriel Albaspinaeus, Bishop of Orléans, on Saint Optatus, Bishop of Milevis

## First Observation: On the Errors and Crimes of the Donatists

[Col. 1159D]

Of all African writers who wrote against heretics on behalf of the Church, none has so long lacked the light of interpretation as Optatus of Milevis. Although he received some illumination from the jurist François Baudouin, Baudouin explained rather matters pertaining to history, in which he was especially learned, than those matters concerning the discipline of the ancient Church which occur in this author. Thus we may rightly say that Optatus has still lacked an interpreter—something that investigators of antiquity and students of controversy ought not to have endured longer, since many traces of both are found in Optatus that are not noted in other authors. But before we come to elucidate them, a few preliminary observations must be made concerning the Donatists’ errors and crimes.

The first Donatist crime, from which the rest of their offences—by which Africa was oppressed for so long—took their origin, was this: that they set up altar against altar at Carthage. That is, they ordained Majorinus in the church in which Caecilian, who had been duly installed, held his seat. There were many makers of this impiety; but Lucilla, a Spanish woman, first stirred up the movement. Since she could not bear her enemy Caecilian in that see, she corrupted with money many bishops together with Secundus, Primate of Numidia; and persuaded them, after deposing Caecilian, to set over the Church of Carthage Majorinus, her own household reader. Soon certain ambitious men, Botrus and Silesius, who themselves sought that episcopate, lent their efforts and support to him. Finally, certain elders, who withheld the Church’s deposited furnishings, joined them, and drove into the same schism that part of the people which had been drawn away from Caecilian and was already wavering.

With these beginnings and authors the Donatists’ divisions first arose. But when in the meantime they realized that Majorinus’s ordination could not stand, because it had been performed without cause and without any pretext while another still occupied the see, they were compelled to attack Caecilian with new and false accusations and charge him with handing over the Scriptures and with idolatry. This was the second Donatist crime, and the second pretext, which they did not put forward until some time after Majorinus’s ordination. For when Secundus and Lucilla’s other bishops laid hands on him, no one ever accused Caecilian—not merely of the worship of idols or of handing over books, but even of the slightest offence.

But lest Majorinus’s ordination be annulled because it had been performed contrary to Church discipline, they invented all these slanders against Caecilian. And lest he should quickly clear himself of them and show them false, they made, or attempted to make, his predecessor Mensurius and Felix, who had ordained him, guilty of the same charge. First, so that Caecilian’s ordination might be condemned because in it he had communicated with an idolatrous bishop; second, so that his mission and communion might seem to descend from a bishop prohibited from sacred functions, and take its origin from a father devoted to idols.

Although these accusations, full of calumny, had been judged by Pope Melchiades, by the emperor Constantine, by the Council of Arles, by two bishops sent to Africa on this matter so that Melchiades’s sentence and decree might stand, by nearly the common voice and agreement of all Africa, by the inquiries of Aelianus, proconsul of Africa, into the matter, and finally by the communion of the universal Church, the Donatists nevertheless did not cease from their calumnies. They even added new accusations and grounds, and obstinately remained in their opinion and schism.

Therefore, to persuade everyone that the charges with which they burdened Caecilian were neither false nor that another had been wrongly substituted in his place, they first separated from all the African churches which had entered into fellowship with Caecilian. Afterwards, as the madness and frenzy of schism grew, they withdrew at last from the peace and communion of the universal Church—that is, from the whole human race that agreed with Caecilian. This is the origin and, as it were, the first spark of this schism, which set almost all Africa and the Church ablaze.

In this matter it must be observed that, if the things which the Donatists falsely alleged against Caecilian had been true, and if Mensurius and Caecilian had defiled themselves by the false worship of gods, the Donatists would have committed no offence against Church discipline and canons by refusing communion with Caecilian and the rest who communicated and associated with him. For it was unlawful, not merely to consecrate an idolatrous bishop, but even to have any association with a lapsed layperson. And although the Church at that time had condemned the Novatians because they did not communicate with the lapsed after they had been purified by long penance, it nevertheless did not admit those who had fallen away from the faith, even amid chains and tortures, except after lengthy and severe penance. For this reason the Donatists were not considered heretics because they did not associate with Caecilian, his party, and those agreeing with him, but because they persisted obstinately in their stance, and because, scorning the judgment of the supreme pontiff and council, by which Caecilian had been found innocent, they factiously and stubbornly maintained their schism.

But to return to their errors and crimes: after this divorce and withdrawal from the Church, they were, as it were, compelled by necessity to commit the crimes which follow. First, they declared that the sacrifices of Caecilian and of all who held communion with him were impure, void, and hateful to God; and therefore could produce neither any peace among orthodox believers nor any union and bond between Christ and the Church.

Then they denied that the Eucharist consecrated in the churches of the orthodox was duly consecrated, on the ground that neither their bishops nor their priests had been duly consecrated, or possessed any force or authority to consecrate. Accordingly, whenever they seized the churches of the orthodox, they shamelessly and without fear of religion trampled underfoot the Eucharist cast upon the ground [Col. 1162A]. They plainly would not have done this unless they had called into question the authority of those who consecrated it and taught that the Eucharist could not have been consecrated by the orthodox.

For the same reason they cast away the holy chrism, as though it had not been consecrated.

Their fourth error and offence was that they washed again those who had been baptized. Here several points must be observed. First, rebaptisms were not performed by Donatist principle, or according to their professed conviction; for they firmly maintained with the orthodox that there is only one baptism and that Christians are to be baptized only once.
