But, since they accused the orthodox of heresy and idolatry because they communicated with Caecilian, they judged them to possess no power or authority to baptize. Second, the repetition of baptism was not a distinctive and peculiar crime of that sect, nor an invention of the Donatists; it had been introduced in the age of St Cyprian, who left behind throughout all Africa such an opinion and reputation of himself that whatever he had taught was regarded as a rule of faith [Col. 1162B]. For this reason the Donatists, looking to the teaching of so great a man, who had taught that heretics must be rebaptized, rebaptized the followers of Caecilian and all who had been baptized in the Church after Caecilian’s ordination, just as a large part of Africa rejected the baptism of heretics. For St Augustine, writing against the Donatists, would not have replied everywhere with passages and arguments drawn from St Cyprian and from the council held in his time, unless the Donatists had maintained this error according to St Cyprian’s judgment rather than their own.

Their fifth error and offence concerned confirmation. For as they repeated baptism, so too they repeated confirmation. Although Optatus charges them with this offence in only one word—“you anointed again”—it is nevertheless certain that they also confirmed anew those whom they had rebaptized. In earlier times confirmation always followed baptism [Col. 1162C], and in those first centuries no one was washed in the sacred waters without immediately being completed and perfected by the bishop through chrism. Therefore, since they immersed the orthodox again as though they had not been baptized, they likewise confirmed them again as though they had not been confirmed; just as they ordained and consecrated anew, and as though for the first time, bishops or presbyters whom they baptized afresh.

Their sixth offence was that they regarded all who had been initiated and ordained in the Church as unordained. Thus they denied that any bishop or presbyter was to be found in the whole Church and throughout the whole world, except in the corner of Africa where their schism and faction flourished; and every bishop, presbyter, and deacon who came into their power they enrolled among the profane and the laity, without any regard for rank, consecration, or holy oil. In antiquity this was a most heinous crime.

The seventh was that they considered all the churches of East and West infected, polluted, and guilty [Col. 1162D], because they had held communion and fellowship with Caecilian and his successors. Thus, when they encountered persons from Arabia, they rebaptized them no less than Carthaginians, although they knew nothing of all that was alleged against Caecilian.

The eighth was that the visible Church of Jesus Christ neither exists nor ought to consist except of the innocent, harmless, and those untouched by any stain or blemish. Hence, separated from all others and from the whole Church, they boasted that they were *Cathari*, “pure,” and undefiled, just as the Novatians did.

The ninth offence was that they laid hands upon lapsed bishops and presbyters, as may be inferred from Melchiades’ judgment. But the difficulty is to determine what laying on of hands is meant; for very many episcopal functions and ministries were performed by laying on of hands—such as baptism, confirmation [Col. 1163A], ordination, penance, blessing, healings, and miracles. But because the matter is dense and difficult, and also important, it seems to me worthy of more careful elucidation. We shall therefore discuss it in another observation.

The tenth was that they deprived bishops of office without any just cause and reduced them to the laity. This was formerly especially contrary to ecclesiastical discipline. Although we read in very many historical records that bishops were removed from sacred office and reduced to lay communion, this was done only for just and grave reasons and atrocious crimes, such as idolatry. But to strip a bishop of his rank and the honour of his seat without cause was a huge crime. For this was to divest him of the dignity which granted him a place and share in Christ’s body more eminent than that of others; and therefore it wronged both him and the Church alike, and deprived the Church of this member. The same may be asserted concerning presbyters and deacons, whom the Donatists removed from ecclesiastical communion without cause or crime [Col. 1163B].

The eleventh wickedness, generated in their minds by the same false opinion and foundation, was that they compelled all orthodox persons, though innocent, to do penance. This was most contrary to the ancient ecclesiastical canons. For it was impious to cut off from Christ’s body any member other than one that was rotten and infected, and to reduce it to the state of penance. Although this public penance was of the greatest and unique benefit to those who had lost the first brightness and innocence of baptism, and afforded a supreme and immediate remedy against the stains of sin, it was hateful to the innocent; nor was it lawful to impose it except upon those charged with crimes. For penitents were formerly enrolled among those excluded before they entered upon penance, and were thus regarded as, as it were, handed over to Satan. Moreover, in the first grade they sought pardon with tears and bewailed the misery of their condition; then, in the second, they were instructed like catechumens [Col. 1163C] and persons ignorant and untrained in Christian matters; and finally, in the third, they were delivered from the devil’s power by exorcisms and cleansed from his assaults. This was especially abhorrent for those who were innocent.

It should further be noted that the Donatists imposed penance upon all these persons only at the beginning of the schism, when they first made their secession, and only upon those baptized before the schism. For they could not impose penance upon those baptized after the schism, since these, of course, were to be rebaptized. Thus Optatus’ statement that they relegated innocents among the accused and penitents is to be referred not to Optatus’ own time—when they rebaptized whomever they could attract and draw away—but to the beginning of the schism, when many who had been baptized before Caecilian’s ordination went over to them and, in their view, could be cleansed only by penance.

The twelfth offence was that by this public penance they punished innocent children, not yet capable of sin, merely because they had communicated with Caecilian [Col. 1163D]. Here one must grant that Optatus speaks of the earliest period in which the schism arose, and of children born before the schism whom the Donatists did not rebaptize. For those born after the schism could not, as I have said, be enrolled among penitents, because they were rebaptized. Yet they subjected untaught children, at an age unfit for sin, to penance—not, of course, in order to free them from sin, but in order permanently to bar them from ecclesiastical communion and holy orders. For formerly a penitent could not be admitted into the clergy. Further, this compelled the orthodox 136 to seek and obtain strangers, persons born elsewhere whose lives could not be known to them, and to install them in episcopal and presbyteral sees. This, we read, was forbidden in antiquity.

The thirteenth offence was that they burned the altars of the orthodox [Col. 1164A], broke the chalices, and washed the walls and floors of churches as though polluted by the sacrifices of the orthodox.

The fourteenth was that they dissolved the solemn vows of virgins and thrust them among the penitents, on the ground that vows professed among the lapsed or idolaters were not binding and invalid.

The fifteenth was that, in places forcibly occupied where they possessed churches, they denied the peace and honour of burial to Catholic citizens and inhabitants, because they regarded and proclaimed them as lapsed and infected with idolatry through communion with Caecilian. Since the dead were formerly deemed through burial to communicate with the living and to share, no less than the living, in prayers, sacrifice, and all the communions performed in the Church and in sacred rites, they denied them a place in the churches and cemeteries which they occupied [Col. 1164B], lest they should be compelled to communicate after death with the orthodox, with whom while alive they had refused even to take food.

## OBSERVATION II. How the Novatians and Donatists agreed or differed

It will not be without purpose to elucidate and examine more closely whether the Donatists agreed in any respect with the Novatians. For many modern writers seem to imply that these sects either rested upon the same foundation or at least agreed in many points. But, whatever they may scrape together from Eusebius, Epiphanius, and Theodoret in support of their opinion, they are greatly mistaken.

First, it is established that the Novatians denied penance for almost all crimes. The Donatists, on the contrary, not only granted it to idolaters and murderers, but even imposed it of their own accord upon those unwilling, or at least undeserving, and subjected as it were innocent persons to the laws of penance. Second, among the Novatians the remedy of penance was not open to laypeople, even those weeping and pleading against their offence [Col. 1164C]; but in this heresy bishops were compelled to penance, which was contrary to ecclesiastical discipline. Third, the Novatians had neither right nor power to forgive sins, because they thought that the Church lacked this authority. The Donatists, however, taught precisely the opposite, for they admitted to fellowship those who had completed penance and been cleansed. Fourth, the former abhorred second marriages, whereas the latter did not differ from the orthodox on this matter.

Nevertheless, it cannot be denied that certain features were similar between them, such as the name *Cathari*, by which each displayed its own purity—but for different reasons. For the Novatians claimed to be pure because they held no communion with the lapsed, whether penitents or persons who had completed penance. The Donatists, however, wished to seem and be called purer, not because they shrank from penitents, but because they wished to preserve their own Church free from contamination by Caecilian’s crime.

## OBSERVATION III. Certain obscurities in this history

[Col. 1164D]

In this history, although carefully described by Balduin and Baronius, many things are found which cannot easily be decided and explained. First, all report that there were two Donati, authors and contrivers of this schism: one from Casae Nigrae, the other a Carthaginian distinguished by the surname Magnus. Both are frequently mentioned by the authors, but, in my judgment, so confusedly and disorderly that it is not sufficiently certain which of the two was condemned by Melchiades at Rome, or which of them is denoted by these words: “that he confessed that he had rebaptized and had laid hands upon lapsed bishops, which is foreign to the Church.” These words occur in the sentence and judgment which we read was pronounced by Melchiades upon Donatus. The matter was always so uncertain that, at the Conference of Carthage, the Catholics thought that the judgment had been passed upon Donatus Magnus [Col. 1165A], and that he had been punished at Rome. But when the Donatists maintained that the matter must be understood of the other Donatus, not of Donatus Magnus, the Catholics immediately adopted the same view, as appears from St Augustine’s Summary of the Third Day: they contended that it was not the Carthaginian but the man of Casae who had appeared in Melchiades’ judgment, which the Catholics conceded. St Augustine himself also confesses that he was mistaken in this matter, in *Retractations*, book 1, chapter 21:

> Likewise, whereas I said that Donatus, whose letter I was refuting, had asked the Emperor to appoint overseas judges between himself and Caecilian, it is found more probable that not he, but another Donatus of the same schism, did this. That man, however, was not the Donatist bishop of Carthage, but was from Casae Nigrae; yet he was the first who made the wicked schism at Carthage.

Although these points are exceedingly clear and plain, so that no one would fail to think that Donatus of Casae was condemned at Rome, nevertheless the contrary is gathered no less plainly from Optatus [Col. 1165B]. For he writes that Donatus Magnus himself—the very man who possessed such great authority in that schism—presented a petition to Constantine and requested overseas judges. If Donatus Magnus complained before the emperor about Caecilian’s ordination, then undoubtedly Melchiades’ sentence must be explained as concerning him. For all admit that the very man who authored the petition was convicted by the pontiff’s condemnation at Rome.

Optatus’ words are as follows, p. 58:

> But immediately, as they came to each individual, these were the words: “What is being done among us concerning my party?” As though he had already truly divided the people from God, so that he boldly called it his own party. For from his time until the present, whenever any proceeding concerning ecclesiastical matters has been conducted in public courts, those questioned have spoken thus in the records: they said that they belonged to the party of Donatus; of Christ they said nothing. And what shall I say of the clergy, when we read the petitions mentioned in the first book, long ago sent to Constantine and subscribed, which contained the names of bishops, thus submitted by Capito, Nasutius, Dignus, and the other bishops of Donatus’ party? They were certainly petitioning against bishops who, since they were not in Donatus’ party, remained in Christ’s Catholic Church. And when a bishop was unwilling to be among his fellow bishops, nor indeed to be a man among men, it is clear that he exalted his heart and seemed to himself to be God.

No one doubts that these final words refer to Donatus Magnus. For such was the arrogance and pride of that man that he despised all his fellow bishops and thought it beneath him to associate with them in communion. Moreover, it is certain that these same words, “the party of Donatus,” and the rest, were spoken and framed by Optatus concerning the same man. If this is so, it plainly follows from Optatus’ history and judgment that Donatus Magnus first brought the matter before Constantine and appeared at Rome for judgment; yet this is refuted by other authors.

Second, there is doubt, and rightly so, whence and from whom the name and designation of this schism arose [Col. 1165D]. For although it is commonly reported to have taken its name from Donatus Magnus, the schism was called “the party of Donatus” before Donatus the Carthaginian—who is Donatus Magnus—was placed at the head of Carthage, or before any mention had been made of him. For Magnus was installed at Carthage; but only in the sixth year after the Council of Nicaea was the petition presented to Constantine—in which this schism is called “the party of Donatus”—twelve or thirteen years before that council.

Third, I am not sufficiently convinced that Donatus of Casae was not bishop of Carthage. For I do not at all agree with St Augustine, who reports that he was not bishop of Carthage but was from Casae Nigrae; several considerations from elsewhere combine to incline my judgment rather to believe that he was transferred from Casae Nigrae to Carthage and succeeded Majorinus. First, why was the schism in that petition called “the party of Donatus” if Majorinus was then bishop of Carthage [Col. 1166A]? For the controversy concerned the see of Carthage and Mensurius’ successor, not rebaptism. Therefore the designation ought rather to have been drawn from Majorinus than Donatus of Casae, if Majorinus had then occupied that see.

Second, as I have said, the dispute at Rome and before the emperor concerned the see; and yet when the petition was presented to the emperor; when the emperor referred it to Melchiades; when the case was tried before the pontiff; when it was judged at Rome; finally, in the formula of the judgment and appeal—neither at Rome nor at Arles nor anywhere else is mention made of anyone but Donatus alone. Would it not have been fitting, if Majorinus sat at Carthage and disputed the episcopate with Caecilian, that he should be named in the judgment and that some mention of him should occur either in the hearing or in the emperor’s rescript? But Donatus alone is mentioned—surely because Majorinus had died and another had been substituted in his see.

Fourth, Optatus testifies that Olympius and Eunomius crossed into Africa in order to depose Donatus and Caecilian from the episcopate [Col. 1166B] and substitute another in the place of each, so that, once the two had been removed, they might ordain one man (for this passage see the variant readings, p. 25). Yet all interpreters adopt the opinion that these two were Caecilian and Donatus of Casae Nigrae. From this evidence it becomes probable that Donatus of Casae then presided at Carthage and that Majorinus had already died. For how could they have placed a third person in the see of two men unless it be granted that the two occupied the same episcopate? Finally, how could the pope together with the emperor have extinguished a schism that had arisen at Carthage by removing Donatus, unless Donatus had been bishop of Carthage?

### Succession of orthodox bishops who presided at Carthage from Mensurius to the Conference

MENSURIUS. [Col. 1166C] CAECILIAN. RUFUS. GRATUS. GENETLIUS. AURELIUS.

### Succession of Donatist bishops who were at Carthage during the same period

MAJORINUS, first bishop of the Donatists. DONATUS THE OTHER, or DONATUS OF CASAE. DONATUS MAGNUS. PARMENIANUS. PRIMIANUS.

## OBSERVATION IV. Whether Melchiades was appointed judge by Constantine in the Donatist case

Pages 22 and 23. Opponents use this history of the Donatists and Constantine’s letter to Melchiades, and deduce arguments from them to diminish and violate the dignity of the Holy See. Among them Calvin says that it makes against its authority that Melchiades was appointed judge in this case by the emperor, and that he was charged with settling the controversy in Africa between Caecilian and the Donatists by imperial command, not by order and in virtue of his office. For, they say, it must be admitted that the pontiffs did not preside over the Church at that time, nor possess supreme power to judge ecclesiastical matters, if Melchiades took part in this judgment by delegated rather than inherent authority [Col. 1166D].

Peter du Moulin, now a standard-bearer of the Calvinists, adds in the book which he recently composed against Cardinal du Perron that associates were assigned to Melchiades in the same delegation and endowed by the emperor with authority equal to his. Nor, he says, did Melchiades complain of that association or that judges were appointed together with the supreme pontiff. From this he thinks there is sufficient argument for admitting that in those ancient times and in Constantine’s age all bishops enjoyed equal rank and honour, since the same jurisdiction and authority were shared among them.

Here is the answer to all this given by the illustrious Cardinal Baronius and du Perron: the emperor did indeed appoint and select three bishops as judges in that case, but not Melchiades. The whole controversy was referred to Melchiades, not by delegation, but because cognizance of ecclesiastical matters belonged to him. To prove this, they rely on the emperor’s own admission: when pressed by the Donatists, he openly declared that he could not be judge in a case concerning bishops. But if he did not possess the right and authority to judge bishops, much less did he possess the right to appoint and delegate judges in their case. They add that, besides those designated by the emperor, Melchiades selected fifteen bishops from Italy to attend this council [Col. 1167A]; he could not have associated them with himself for judging this dispute if he had taken cognizance of it not by his own right but by delegated authority.

Furthermore, although the Donatists requested that judges be given them from Gaul, which was free from the charge of idolatry, Constantine did not at all satisfy their petition. Instead, he referred the matter to the supreme pontiff and compelled them, against their will, to plead their case before him [Col. 1167B]. He would not have done this—especially since the whole of Italy was suspect to the Donatists under the accusation of having surrendered the Scriptures—unless it had then been firm and constant among all that it belonged to the pontiff to judge controversies arising in the Church. Cardinal du Perron has assembled further points in his book addressed to the king of Britain, chapter 46, which I omit for brevity.

## OBSERVATION V. On the laying on of hands in Melchiades’ judgment

Therefore, when Caecilian and Donatus had presented their disputes and controversies in the Roman council, and their case had been examined by Melchiades and the other bishops, it was decided by this judgment, p. 23:

> Since he confessed that he had rebaptized and had laid hands upon lapsed bishops, which is foreign to ecclesiastical discipline.

The earlier words of this sentence raise no difficulty at all. For long before these times St Cyprian taught that heretics should be rebaptized [Col. 1167C] and rebaptized them. But the latter words are obscure, and interpreters disagree greatly about them. For the ancient forms of laying on of hands were various, and nearly every episcopal task and office was performed by the laying on of hands and called by that very name: baptism, confirmation, exorcisms, absolution, ordination, penance, peace, prayers, supplications, healings, blessings, and the other things administered by bishops. It is therefore rightly doubted and asked what laying on of hands Melchiades meant.

If the matter is referred to interpreters, especially to Franciscus Balduinus, and if we choose to abide by his judgment concerning the reordination of bishops who deserted the Church and fled to Donatus’ party, we shall interpret this laying on of hands as reordination. For in his notes on this treatise he teaches that bishops who had defected and deserted were reordained by the Donatists, just as laypeople were rebaptized by them. Nearly all who have encountered or mentioned these words have followed this explanation. I, however, hope to demonstrate from this author himself and from many weighty arguments drawn from the discipline of the ancient Church that this laying on of hands must be understood as penance, which the Donatists imposed upon bishops who defected from the Church, so that they might be cleansed from the crime of surrendering the Scriptures and of idolatry [Col. 1167D].

The first argument, drawn from these words in the first book of Optatus, p. 3, is this:

> Nor should they, by wrongly laying hands upon every head, display the veils of overthrow, nor curse God, nor rebaptize the faithful.

Without doubt he alludes to this laying on of hands mentioned by Melchiades and complains that the Donatists overturned the condition of all the faithful—namely, by imposing penance upon bishops and rebaptizing laypeople. If this laying on of hands removed bishops from their rank and status, it must be referred to penance rather than reordination, because reordination does not overthrow but rather raises up. It calls laypeople to higher grades and places them among the clergy, who hold the foremost place in Christ’s body. Penance, by contrast, with the gravest injury casts down those established at the summit of communion. Even if they were restored and reordained, they could not be driven from their see and enrolled among laypeople without disgrace.

The words “nor curse God” must further be examined and considered; they seem strongly to favour our interpretation. If they are joined with the preceding words and mean that the Donatists cursed God in that laying on of hands, no one will interpret it as reordination, in which the Donatists could no more curse God than in the first ordination, in which they had not cursed God. But in penance imposed upon those who did not deserve it, God was cursed. For in the third grade penitents were cleansed and delivered from the devil’s power and persuasions by exorcisms and layings on of hands [Col. 1168B]. This could not be done without injury to the Holy Spirit, who dwelt in those same persons. Again, just as St Augustine teaches and reproves the Donatists in many places because in rebaptism they drove God away and burdened him with injuries and curses in exorcisms, so Optatus here reproves them because, in the exorcisms of penance which they imposed upon bishops, they treated God with the injuries and insults of exorcisms, which were frequently used in penance just as in baptism.

Page 44. The second argument is from these words in the second book:

> So that, while a presbyter or bishop is cast down, the people might thus be captured.

Their sense is that the Donatists relegated orthodox bishops or presbyters to penance, so that, when the people saw the leaders and guides of the orthodox dwelling and mourning among their penitents, they would form the worst opinion of the orthodox. This sense cannot agree with reordination, which could give the Donatists no occasion to think ill of the orthodox [Col. 1168C]. Moreover, the word “is cast down” should not be passed over; it is characteristic of penitents, as may be gathered from Tertullian and the Fourth Council of Toledo: to cast down the spirit in grief.

Pages 46 and 47. The third argument is from these words:

> The priests have been stripped of the honour of their name.

By this he reproaches the Donatists for depriving bishops of the honour of priesthood and of their seat. For *honour* in Tertullian, Cyprian, and St Augustine means priesthood or the episcopate. But if the bishops of the orthodox had been reordained by the Donatists, they would by no means be said to have been deprived of honour, nor would Optatus rebuke the Donatists for this reason; for reordination does not strip one of the honour of one’s name.

Ibid. The fifth argument is from these words:

> O unheard-of impiety: to preserve in the midst of penance and torments one whom you have slain!

By these words he teaches that the Donatists preserved amid penance and torments bishops whom they had stripped of the honour of name, rank, and episcopate. It follows that the bishops were relegated by them to penance [Col. 1168D], since they could not have been preserved by penance unless they had undergone it.

What it means to preserve one slain amid the torments of penance, and how it should be understood, is easy to state. A bishop stripped of the honour of priesthood and making satisfaction to God by penance is rightly called slain and preserved. By deposition he had lost his dignity and that share which he possessed in Christ’s body, while by penance he was preserved for greater torments. For what misery could be greater, or what cruelty more severe, than to cast a man down from the highest dignity among penitents and daily lay upon him, amid the reproaches, miseries, and torments of penance, the hand of exorcisms? Tertullian says: “Through evil one arrives at misery.”

Ibid. The sixth argument is from these words:

> You commit a living murder.

For whoever makes a bishop a penitent slays and preserves him: he slays him by deprivation of rank and grade [Col. 1169A], but preserves him by leaving him to drag out a wretched life among penitents.

Ibid. The seventh argument is from these words:

> Those whom you were able to deceive were beset by the poverty of their own judgment; for they had been set over others by the work of God, since they had been ordained in his name.

These words must be joined to those above and understood of the same bishops upon whom hands had been laid. They seem to mean: the bishops whom you made penitents, and from whom you took the life of rank and honour, had been ordained in the Lord’s name, and this ordination was a divine work which you broke apart with the crowbars of malice. Therefore the saying is rightly applied to you Donatists: “What God completed, they destroyed.” Since this is so, it is established that the Donatists did something to bishops which overthrew God’s work. This was done especially by the penance which they imposed upon bishops whom they could deceive and who went over to them, not by reordination. For in antiquity it was thought that some injury was done to God and to his sacrament and character if a bishop or presbyter was seen among penitents [Col. 1169B] (Augustine, *On Baptism*, book 1). If, therefore, the Donatists imposed penance upon lapsed bishops, it is likely that Melchiades’ judgment is to be understood of that laying on of hands, not of reordination, by which God’s work could not be overthrown.

Page 46. The eighth argument is from these words:

> Show where you were commanded to shave the heads of priests.

They refer to the same matter as the preceding words and must be understood of the same injury and insult with which they treated bishops. But shaving heads would have been no greater an injury in a second ordination than in the first. To shave a bishop and deliver God’s anointed to penance, however, was wholly disgraceful and forbidden by God.

Ibid. The ninth argument is from these words:

> Who are you, to take away what you did not give?

They receive this interpretation: God could have taken away his oil and sacrament from Saul but did not wish to do so, in order to teach you that his anointed must not be injured. But you take away what you did not give [Col. 1169C] and wrong God’s anointed, because you shave them and condemn them to penance. This interpretation cannot agree with reordination.

Ibid. The tenth argument is from these words:

> What good is it that men live, when their honours have been slain by you?

Optatus would not have said this if the Donatists had reordained the bishops whom they deceived, because through reordination they were no more stripped or slain than through ordination.

Pages 46 and 47. The eleventh argument is from these words:

> You stretched forth your hand over every head.

This stretching forth of the hand cannot be referred to reordination, as is clear from what follows:

> That is, by laying hands upon every age in order to overthrow souls. You found children and wounded them with penance, lest any might be ordained.

It must rather be referred to penance, by which the standing of clergy, and especially bishops, was overthrown. Further, it is likely that he speaks of the same laying on of hands for which the Donatists had been condemned by Melchiades. Or, if this is not granted, let the opponent explain, I ask, what that stretching forth of the hand was by which the Donatists shaved every head [Col. 1169D]. If he speaks of the same thing, it must be admitted that Melchiades’ judgment is to be understood of penance.

Ibid. The twelfth argument is from these words:

> You found deacons, presbyters, and bishops; you made them laypeople.

From these words it follows that the Donatists enrolled among laypeople those whom they found to be bishops in the places they occupied. If this is so, how can interpreters say that the Donatists used reordination and reordained the bishops whom they seized?

Ibid. The thirteenth argument is from these words:

> Your associate and companion had long been one to whom you have now attempted to lay hands.

Together with the words that follow, these establish that the Donatists wished to lay some form of hands upon orthodox bishops by which they judged and condemned them as guilty. This fits the laying on of hands of penance better than that of reordination.

[Col. 1170A] Page 48. The fourteenth argument is from these words:

> You slew with the sword of the tongue Deuterius, Parthenius, Donatus, and Getulus, bishops of God.

For they had slain them by penance.

Ibid. The fifteenth argument is from these words:

> It is well known and proved that, in the time of persecution, certain bishops, having fallen through weakness from confessing God’s name, offered incense; and yet none of those who escaped either laid hands upon the lapsed or commanded them to bend their knees.

Here and in Melchiades’ judgment the discourse concerns one and the same laying on of hands. For just as Optatus says that the Donatists laid hands upon lapsed bishops, so Melchiades condemns them for having laid hands upon lapsed bishops. But that laying on of hands pertains to penance, not to reordination, as may be gathered from the words, “or commanded them to bend their knees.” The kneelings of penitents were signs of humiliation and acts of *exomologesis* (confession), which bishops could not perform without shame and disgrace. But kneelings performed in receiving orders could bring disgrace upon no one [Col. 1170B]. For what is more consistent with discipline than that one to be ordained should bend the knee and kneel before those ordaining him? If this is so, Melchiades’ judgment requires no further debate as to its interpretation.

Ibid. The sixteenth argument is from these words:

> While the sin of a man is being struck.

For by the laying on of hands about which Melchiades and Optatus complain, the sin of those bishops whom the Donatists made penitents was struck. This cannot suit reordination, but suits penance, by which sins are struck and blotted out.

Ibid. The seventeenth argument is from these words:

> For what greater misfortune is there than that God’s priests should live and yet not be what they were?

For he presses the same error and attacks the same laying on of hands, which cannot be referred to reordination, since he says that through it bishops were no longer what they had been.

Pag. 72–73. The eighteenth point from these words of Book IV: “You were unwilling to imitate the apostles, by whom even Peter, though a denier, was loved” [Col. 1170C]. By these words he teaches that the Donatists, following the example of the apostles, who loved Peter after his fall and denial, ought to have loved the fallen bishops. This makes it more probable that the Donatists imposed penance upon bishops rather than conferred orders upon them. For those who are ordained or reordained are honored with a kiss among the rites of reordination and are received by their ordainers as brethren; whereas those doing penance are rejected as outsiders and as severed from the brotherhood. Finally, these words of Book VI, p. 98—“whom you have wounded either by rebaptism or by penance”—accord with the judgment of Miltiades and seem to explain it; what is there signified by the laying on of hands is here explained as the imposition of penance.

## OBSERVATION VI. In which the same explanation is confirmed from the grounds of ancient discipline.

Since Miltiades, supreme pontiff, in his encomium and in that judgment [Col. 1170D], declares that the laying on of hands employed by the Donatists against fallen bishops was wholly contrary to ecclesiastical discipline; and since we wish to establish and persuade others that this laying on of hands must be referred not to reordination but to penance, we need the clearest and most certain arguments and reasons to show from ancient and old discipline that penance was not imposed upon bishops, whatever crime they might have incurred; nor did the piety of that age permit them to be enrolled among the mourners.

First, at the very threshold of penance, penitents deplored their sins with tears. But it was unfitting for a bishop—who ought rather to lament the sins of others than his own—to be seen outside the thresholds of the Church among those weeping, wailing, and lying upon the ground, kissing the footsteps of passing people.

Second, at that same stage of penance, penitents were instructed together with catechumens [Col. 1171A], and were taught the first rudiments and elements of faith. For it was thought that they could not have sinned after baptism except through forgetfulness of the fear of God and of the precepts and teachings which they had received during their catechumenate. Thus, like catechumens, they were again taught and trained in the institutions of the Christian religion. Yet such instruction could not be repeated without some disparagement of episcopal dignity; and not only catechumens but also their teachers and instructors ought to have been taught in this way.

Third, throughout the whole time during which penitents remained in the third stage, they were purified by public and solemn exorcisms, just as infants still are today when washed in the sacred font. It was intolerable that a bishop should, before the eyes of the people, be delivered and freed as one oppressed by a certain tyranny and dominion of the devil; nor was this consistent with the dignity of the Christian religion. For the bishop is the chief and head of communion with Christ and union with God; through his piety and holiness the other members gain access [Col. 1171B] to that same union.

Fourth, bishops are called fathers of the people, priests of God, overseers of Christ, mediators between Christ and the people, ambassadors of Christians, offerers of vows, intercessors for prayers and offerings, and supplicants. By their labor and ministry demons were cast out of bodies; whereas sinners, by the power which bishops received from Christ, are again delivered to Satan. In short, since bishops are those into whom Christ transfers and deposits whatever he has granted and assigned to his Church, who would not shudder to see bishops themselves stripped and deprived of all the endowments and offices just mentioned? Indeed, to see them in a worse condition than they would have been before baptism: surrendered and handed over to the empire and power of the devil; treated as though subject to the penalty of excommunication; whereas formerly they were considered to hold the place of shepherds, now reckoned as a lost and dead sheep; whereas they had subjected the devil, now called his most worthless slaves; whereas they were counted among the first and living members of Christ [Col. 1171C], now made to bear the role of putrid flesh and an unburied corpse; whereas they were called the beloved and delight of almighty God, now cast out and excluded as though struck by the sentence of an anathema. Their discipline could neither endure nor tolerate so detestable a disgrace, nor hear of so unheard-of and intolerable a transformation.

Fifth, just as that ancient discipline admitted none of the penitents among the clergy, so it enrolled none of the higher clergy among penitents. For it was no less shameful and unworthy to see a penitent among the clergy than a cleric in penance, or a bishop with downcast and depressed countenance displaying and exhibiting the shame of a disgraceful life.

Sixth, the ancient councils of Ancyra, Neocaesarea, Arles, Elvira, and Nicaea prescribe a kind of penance for every layperson, and even for lesser clerics, who in time of persecution had either fallen into idolatry or, cast down from constancy, had in some degree withdrawn from the profession of faith. Those councils, I say, make no mention whatever of the penance of bishops [Col. 1171D] or presbyters; indeed, among the ancient Fathers not even a single passage on this matter is found. Hence I am easily persuaded to believe that bishops and presbyters were never punished by that public penance.

Seventh, Optatus maintains that the consecration of the holy oil and the character of bishops belong to God alone, not to bishops; and that for this reason they ought to be honored even when sinners. From this it follows that those times did not permit them to take their place among penitents, lest they fall into contempt.

Eighth, when the canons define the penalties to be imposed for sins, they establish excommunication for laypeople and deposition for priests for the same offense. For example, they remove a layperson from the assembly of the faithful for adultery; but if a priest is guilty of the same crime, they cast him down from his rank. Therefore, the force and effect which excommunication or public penance had upon laypeople, deposition had and exercised toward bishops [Col. 1172A]. Accordingly, in those earliest times, no other reparation for fault existed for presbyters or bishops than simple deposition.

Ninth, let us consider what Saint Cyprian says concerning the sin and punishment of Trophimus. Although Trophimus had fallen away from the faith, he did not perform public penance; nor does Cyprian make any mention of any public and solemn penance or satisfaction on his part. Rather, he was expelled and deprived of his rank and cast back among the laity. Yet in the time in which Cyprian lived, idolaters began to be admitted and received into penance—persons who in previous centuries had either been separated from the Church forever, or at least compelled, after undertaking punishment, to expiate their offense throughout their lives. From this it may be inferred that bishops were not compelled to undertake public penance.

The tenth reason is this: in the fifth or sixth century, councils decree that ecclesiastics should perform penance in secluded, remote, and private places, so that laypeople might be offended as little as possible if those by whom they ought themselves to be ruled and governed were seen to have been implicated in a graver crime [Col. 1172B]. Yet he does not come forth in public, lest the flock of believers suffer scandal from it; for a priest ought not to do public penance like a layperson.

To all these may be added the reasons and arguments commonly offered by the Fathers when they speak of bishops: when they say that no one may offer prayers or supplications for them; that if they fall, no one can raise or support them; that the guardians of the people themselves are not ordinarily guarded. By these words they judge plainly enough that bishops were not liable to penance, for which not only bishops but also laypeople offered prayers. Thus Tertullian, in his book *On Penance*, says: “to charge the brethren with embassies of supplication.”

Origen too is commonly reported to have said the following, which greatly supports our position: “If penance were imposed upon bishops, it would not be penance but an injury.”

Finally, if these reasons were not sufficiently understood, the eighth canon of the Council of Carthage, which is called the Fifth [Col. 1172C], would not allow them to be called into doubt. It expressly forbids the laying on of hands for penance upon presbyters or deacons, however grave a crime or offense they may have committed:

> It has likewise been confirmed that, whenever presbyters or deacons are convicted of some graver offense for which it is necessary that they be removed from ministry, hands shall not be laid upon them as upon penitents or as upon lay believers.

From these words it is clear that penance was never imposed upon bishops or presbyters, and that the laying on of hands mentioned by Miltiades is precisely the same laying on of hands discussed by that canon. For it is probable that the same canon was enacted by African Fathers against the Donatists and that the very error condemned by Miltiades in that judgment was corrected by them; especially since the council was held in Africa, where that error flourished. Further, by the words “it has been confirmed,” the Fathers of that council appear by their decree to confirm what had previously been devised and established by others against the Donatists, and to look back to the judgment of Miltiades [Col. 1172D] and, as it were, repeat it. For they knew that this offense of Donatus had been condemned at Rome, which they condemn again in this canon for the sake of discipline. Whatever the case may be, it is certain that almost all the canons of African councils were framed against the Donatists. Since this is so, and since we learn elsewhere from Miltiades that they laid hands upon bishops, who can doubt that this canon was directed against the Donatists?

To all this, as a final addition, may be joined the fourteenth canon of the letter of Siricius, who held the pontificate in the time of the Donatists:

> Let provision also be made that, just as no cleric is permitted to perform penance, so after penance and renunciation no layperson may ever be permitted to attain the honor of the clerical office.

## OBSERVATION VII. In which certain objections are resolved.

Against what we have maintained—that in the earliest centuries public penance was never pronounced upon the higher ecclesiastics [Col. 1173A], even if they had incurred almost inexpiable fraud and guilt, and that their discipline and institutions did not allow this to happen—the canons of Pope Felix may be opposed and urged, by which bishops who had consented to rebaptism are compelled to enter upon penance.

To this I reply that the times must be considered, and that discipline in the time of Felix displayed less harshness and severity than in the earliest centuries. Next, in those canons laypeople are indeed commanded and compelled to undergo all the stages of penance, in which the disgraceful laying on of hands and frequent exorcisms took place; but bishops and presbyters are condemned to another, as it were, kind of penance. By this arrangement Felix affirms a great distinction and separation between the two groups. To this may be added that Felix says nothing concerning the place and stages of bishops’ penance; for in that century it was customary for them to mourn and perform penance in monasteries, rather than publicly and before the eyes of the people.

These words of Saint Cyprian to Antonianus may also be objected [Col. 1173B]: “and by a penance of supplication confessing his former error”; as though Cyprian meant by them that Bishop Trophimus had performed penance because he had fallen away from Christ, and had not returned to the Church until he had completed it. Yet those words testify to nothing other than that Trophimus repented of his defection and deeply grieved that he had grievously and atrociously offended God. It is no different from Tertullian’s statement in *The Prescriptions* that Marcion “confessed repentance.” By this expression he does not mean that Marcion performed penance, but that by his actions he declared, through an exomologesis itself and a kind of detestation, that he greatly repented of the crime he had committed. Moreover, among the ancients, “to confess repentance” means to display outwardly the greatest grief for an offense committed.

Third, it may be objected that bishops and presbyters could formerly be excommunicated, and therefore could also be compelled to undertake public penance, since penance could inflict upon bishops no greater or more shameful disgrace and infamy, or bring upon the Church no greater reproach, than excommunication [Col. 1173C].

I answer that not many examples of the excommunication of bishops can be brought forward. If they were formerly excommunicated, this undoubtedly occurred because they had separated themselves from the Church and fallen into apostasy. Finally, if we wish to reason correctly, in all those places in which the excommunication and anathema of bishops are discussed, you will find that this anathema and excommunication signify nothing other than separation from ecclesiastical persons and a severance judged to have occurred only from ecclesiastical communion, not from the body of the laity—or, so to speak, from the entire body of the Church. Thus a bishop or presbyter is called excommunicated when he is separated, not from lay communion, but only from ecclesiastical communion.

Fourth, it may be said that the three sins of homicide, adultery, and idolatry could in those earliest centuries be erased only by public and perpetual penance, or by a very long interval of several years; and that on this account ecclesiastics either were never absolved from those sins or were subjected to the shame of public penance [Col. 1173D].

Against this I reply that the decree of ancient discipline applied only to laypeople. But bishops or presbyters, if they were found guilty of these three sins or of one of them, were deprived of their rank or reduced to the laity. Such reduction or deposition took the place and function of public penance.

Fifth, it may be proved that the sin of bishops is far graver and more detestable before God and men than that of laypeople, since bishops are set forth as an example of virtue to be imitated. Therefore, if the offenses of laypeople in those earliest centuries required the punishments of public penance, how much more should the faults of clerics have been punished by the same censure?

Saint Augustine and Optatus long ago answered this: the character of bishops is called God’s character, and cannot be violated in any way without sin. If it had not been implanted and impressed in bishops, they ought to have been struck with a punishment more severe than that of laypeople. But because they feared nothing so much as offending God and provoking his wrath, they refrained from imposing penance upon bishops [Col. 1174A].

Sixth, the first canon of the Council of Orange may be objected: “Penance must not be denied even to clerics who desire it.” This seems to establish that penance is to be imposed upon ecclesiastics no less than upon laypeople.

But, first, it may be answered that by the name “clerics” this canon means clerics of the minor orders; and in those earliest centuries that term expressly and for the most part denoted lesser ministers. Second, the canon does not mention public and solemn penance, which was imposed even upon unwilling persons, or at least without whose assistance no return to the Church was open; rather, it speaks of voluntary penance, which some pious persons, properly disposed toward religion, vowed in later centuries—namely, the fifth and sixth—that they would undertake. The following canons demonstrate this: the fifteenth of the Council of Agde, “Penance is not easily to be entrusted even to young persons”; the twenty-third of Epaone, “If anyone, having accepted and professed penance”; likewise the fourth, “those who have professed penance”; the ninth of Gerona, “being brought low, [let him receive] the blessing of penance, which we regard as viaticum” [Col. 1174B].

Finally, we may use this very canon to prove that in the earliest centuries neither bishops nor presbyters were customarily subjected to public penance. For in subsequent centuries, when discipline was said not to be so severe, it was necessary by an edict and a new canon to command that voluntary penance be granted to them.

## OBSERVATION VIII. Whether the Donatists reordained some persons.

Although, so far as I can attain by conjecture and perceive, the laying on of hands mentioned in the judgment of Miltiades must be understood not as the laying on of hands in reordination [Col. 1174C], but as the imposition of penance, nevertheless I will not deny or refuse to admit that the Donatists sometimes judged ecclesiastics who followed their sect to be ordained and consecrated anew. It will nevertheless be worthwhile to weigh and examine many points, so that we may know why they did this. For they did not employ that reordination at every time, nor did they confer it indiscriminately upon anyone whatsoever.

First, it must be observed that the sect lasted more than a hundred years: for from the election of Majorinus to the Conference of Carthage there are counted one hundred and six years or thereabouts. But in the first years—that is, in the tenth or twelfth year after that ordination—it is credible, for the reasons I shall set out, that bishops and presbyters who flocked to their camp could not have been reordained.

The first reason is that the Donatists had separated from the Church for no other reason than that they shunned and abhorred all the bishops of Africa as fallen and idolatrous. But if they had received and reordained any one of these, although a deserter [Col. 1174D], they would have implicated themselves in the very crime and fault by which they considered the Catholics to be tainted.

Second, since the Donatists considered baptism administered before the schism to be lawful and true, it is reasonable to suppose that at the same time they considered ordinations conferred and instituted before it not to be invalid. Hence, if any bishop had joined himself from the Church to their flock at the beginning of that emerging schism, he was not to be reordained.

Third, the Donatists could not reordain anyone unless he had first been regarded as deposed and cleansed from the crime of *traditio*. For in their judgment no Orthodox person was free from this offense. Yet in those earliest centuries one will not easily find an example of a bishop who, while guilty of some grave fault and for that reason expelled from his rank, was reordained. Much less will one find this among the Donatists [Col. 1175A], who wished to be called purer and holier, and who openly professed themselves defenders and champions of a stricter ecclesiastical discipline.

Fourth, it was altogether necessary that those bishops whom the interpreters assert were reordained by the Donatists should first be acquitted of the charge of idolatry before being reordained. For, according to their discipline and customs, as we have shown above, no communion or fellowship could exist among them with persons bound by that crime. They proposed two remedies for washing away the stain of *traditio*: penance and rebaptism.

As to rebaptism, bishops were not to be rebaptized in the first years of the schism, because all had been baptized before the schism; for neophytes were not admitted to the episcopate. Accordingly, in those very beginnings of the schism, the Donatists could not rebaptize bishops in order to cleanse them of the crime of *traditio*. Penance therefore remained, which they could indeed employ toward those bishops whom they ensnared by their artifices and deceits. But that ancient discipline never admitted to the episcopate anyone who had been seen among penitents, much less did the Donatists, who were called Cathars [Col. 1175B].

Therefore it is evident and plain to everyone that the Donatists could in no way have reordained bishops or presbyters in the first times of the schism. It consequently follows that the judgment of Miltiades, issued at the beginning of the schism, cannot be understood of reordination.

We must now deal with the later times of this schism. In these I readily grant that bishops were reordained by the Donatists; this can easily be proved from the passages which we shall cite later. Yet we must examine and consider how and on what conditions or grounds this was granted and permitted. When, therefore, in those later times following the beginning of the schism, some bishop or presbyter defected from the Orthodox to the Donatists, they did not compel him to penance as they had under Majorinus. Rather, they rebaptized him and placed him in the order of laypeople; from there, when he was judged worthy, he was restored to the clergy by a renewed ordination [Col. 1175C]. No one was ever reordained except after rebaptism had first intervened.

First, they had to be released and free from the crime with which the Donatists said the Orthodox were tainted. Second, there was no need of penance for cleansing them, since baptism possesses the force to remove every stain of sins. Third, rebaptism effaced the mark of deposition.

Add to these points that Saint Augustine’s third book *Against the Letters of Petilian* makes clear that the Donatists reordained no persons who had not been rebaptized among them. Many passages from the Conference show them using rebaptism before imposing the hands of reordination:

> “They rebaptized that man, a bishop of ninety years.”

> “He is the bishop who was rebaptized and made an *auditor*.”

> “He himself rebaptized after joining the party of Donatus; he was previously rebaptized, and so was ordained.”

> “That Vitalis was a Catholic deacon in the city of Silifis; having been rebaptized, he became a presbyter; he was expelled for adultery and afterward became a bishop.”

The conclusion, therefore, of this chapter is that the judgment of Miltiades [Col. 1175D] cannot be applied to reordination, since in this chapter we have shown that the Donatists could not have reordained those who became Donatists by abandoning the faith within the first years of the schism.

## OBSERVATION IX. Certain objections against the preceding observation are resolved.

Against our statement that, under Majorinus, the Donatists could not use reordination from the first years of the schism, these words of Saint Augustine may be objected, Book III *On Baptism against the Donatists*, chapter 16: “But the laying on of hands can be repeated, unlike baptism.” From Augustine’s words some think that they have established, in his view and judgment, that reordination is no more lawful than rebaptism.

But I answer, first, that this is the laying on of hands by which the gifts of the Holy Spirit were formerly imparted—such as the gift of tongues, prophecy, healings, and the like—as is evident from reading that chapter [Col. 1176A]; it is not the laying on of hands by which ordination was performed. Therefore these words have nothing to do with the matter.

Second, that passage plainly and clearly conflicts with their opinion. For if the sense of the words is correctly observed, Saint Augustine intended to say that this laying on of hands can be repeated, whereas baptism cannot. Nor does it matter that, on the basis of a correction and emendation in the latest edition, and of an old printing, some think it should be read otherwise and contend that the final particle should not be deleted. For the following words of the same chapter reject that emendation: “For what is it other than a prayer over a person?” By these words Saint Augustine asserts, and seems to think, that those layings on of hands by which the gifts of the Holy Spirit were conveyed, and of which he had spoken a little above, ought to be called nothing but the prayers of bishops, not sacraments; therefore they can be repeated. Baptism, however, is a sacrament and for that reason is not repeated. From the sense and argument of his statement it is clear that that particle [Col. 1176B] ought not to be retained, and that the words are to be understood otherwise than some suppose.

The thirty-eighth canon of the Council of Carthage, held in the time of the Donatists, may likewise be objected. By it, as by the two preceding canons, many things wrongly and rashly introduced by the Donatists are rescinded: “Let rebaptisms, reordinations, or translations of bishops not be permitted.” By these words that council appears to reject Donatist reordinations just as it rejects their rebaptisms. And this is so clear and evident that all Greek and Latin interpreters have approved this explanation.

But I say in response that the canon was enacted at the end of that schism and thus has no force for weakening what we have said. For we do not deny, but believe, that the Donatists reordained some persons; but this was toward the end of the schism, and persons whom they had again washed in the sacred font, not at the beginning of the schism and not without repeated baptism.

I add, moreover, that the canon does not seem to speak of the reordination of the same person, but forbids the further ordination through factions of another bishop after one bishop had been ordained in one city, as we shall show elsewhere [Col. 1176C]. But the first solution has more than sufficiently answered the canon.

Finally, it may be said that Saint Augustine made no mention of the penance which the Donatists imposed upon bishops, nor wrote against that error, although he pursued all the errors of the Donatists. Therefore it may seem likely either that the Donatists did not cast bishops down among the penitents, or that this was not contrary to the ancient discipline of the Church, or finally that the laying on of hands mentioned in the judgment of Miltiades belongs to reordination.

I answer that Saint Augustine does not speak of crimes other than those committed by the Donatists in his own time, nor ought he to have made mention of others. Therefore he could not deal with the penance which the earliest Donatists imposed upon bishops, because in his age it was no longer practiced, having become obsolete. For whoever became Donatists in the time of Saint Augustine, whether bishops or presbyters, were all immersed anew in water and thus freed from sins without penance. But if Saint Augustine had lived in the times of Donatus or Majorinus, many traces of that error would be found in his writings [Col. 1176D].

## OBSERVATION X. On the Council of Arles.

No lesser dispute concerns the Council of Arles. For opponents object that it contains no traces of the supreme authority which pontiffs claim today. Indeed, they say, the Donatists dared to appeal from Miltiades to the emperor; they sought other judges after the pontiff; and Constantine appointed other bishops to hear the same cause that had been judged by Miltiades [Col. 1177A]. Finally, they say, papal judgments at that time did not possess such authority and firmness that they could not be overturned by other bishops, since the bishops of Arles permitted themselves to be appointed judges concerning Miltiades himself and his judgment. They add that Sylvester neither complained of this injury, or that the dignity of the Holy See was harmed by this action, nor appointed legates to prevent the judgments of the supreme pontiff from being brought into doubt and examined at that council. Calvin and Peter du Moulin accumulate these and similar arguments; they must be answered.

First, their claim that the Donatists appealed from Miltiades to the emperor is not very well established, and no argument of any importance can be derived from it. For if there was any appeal, it did not have, nor could it have had, the force of a true appeal, since the supreme pontiff himself was represented by legates—Marinus of Arles, Maternus of Agrippina, Rethicius of Autun, Merocles of Milan, and Poterius of Capua—from whose sentence and judgment they assert the Donatists appealed. These men attended the Council of Arles [Col. 1177B], sat among the other bishops, and heard the Donatists’ controversy and appeal. For judicial procedure would not have allowed the same judges to decide both an appeal and the judgment first rendered at Rome, from which appeal had been taken.

I further reply that even if that appeal had been a true appeal, the authority of the Holy See would in no way be harmed or attacked by it. For even now we appeal from pope to pope. In the same way the Donatists could appeal from Miltiades to Sylvester, who presided through legates over the Council of Arles, and could again submit and refer to his judgment the suit which they had lost at Rome. Finally, the Council of Arles is called by our elders, as by Saint Augustine, a plenary and general council. Since the holy pontiff sat in it and presided by legates, no one ought to find it surprising if he allowed his judgment to be examined and his decision to be reviewed by the bishops and by himself [Col. 1177C].

They further object that the bishops whom the emperor appointed judges in that council were appointed not only to examine the judgment rendered at Rome, but also to judge Miltiades himself. But I do not discover how they prove this, or where they read that the Council of Arles judged Miltiades. For although the Donatists were distressed that Caecilian had been acquitted at Rome and complained of his acquittal, we nevertheless do not read that they fabricated or alleged anything whatsoever against Miltiades at that council.

Third, their assertion that the same cause was again judged and examined at Arles, and that the bishops of Arles judged the same cause which the Donatists had lost at Rome, is not sufficiently established. For although many grant it, if we examine the matter more closely and seek to draw an inference from the acts and canons of the council itself, an altogether different cause was brought before the Council of Arles from that which had been judged at Rome.

There were two matters in controversy between Caecilian and the Donatists: *traditio* and schism. Caecilian was accused and prosecuted on two charges. He was acquitted of the latter at Rome, but left Arles acquitted of the former. For the cause of schism was in no way examined or judged at Arles, but only that of *traditio* [Col. 1177D]. This may be proved by many reasons. No mention or canon concerning schism or the ordination of Majorinus appears in that council. But from the thirteenth canon it is clear that the question there was whether the crime and fault of the ordainer passed to the ordained person, and whether the laying on of hands by a guilty person rendered the entire ordination invalid. Why, indeed, would the Fathers of that council have decreed that ordination did not harm those ordained, provided that the standing of those ordained remained secure, unless the Donatists had raised precisely this question, and the cause turned upon whether an ordination celebrated by one guilty and suspected of idolatry should be held invalid?

Or whom, finally, could the fourteenth canon [Col. 1178A] have concerned, or against whom could it seem to have been enacted—the canon which deprives, until the end, of communion those who falsely accuse brethren—if not the Donatists, who falsely charged Felix and Caecilian with idolatry? From these points there is no doubt that the Donatists, leaving aside the cause of schism which had been decided at Rome, resorted to the second charge of *traditio* and brought no other action against Caecilian at Arles than that his ordination should be annulled because of the crime of his ordainer.

Moreover, no reason can be given why the Fathers of Arles made no mention of schism and passed such severe judgments upon those who falsely accused brethren, unless the only matter at issue in that council and question was whether Caecilian ought to be removed from episcopal dignity because of the crime of Felix. Further, this agrees remarkably with the history of this schism and of the Donatists, who complain in Saint Augustine that a few judges had rashly hurried the judgment at Rome without observing any order. For it seemed that judgment ought first to have been given whether someone’s ordination was corrupted and polluted by the crime of his ordainer, and whether Felix had been a *traditor*, before inquiry was made concerning schism. This seemed to be required by the order of the cause. For what need was there to investigate which of the ordinations of Majorinus and Caecilian was more consistent with ecclesiastical discipline, if Felix, accused of idolatry, had possessed no right or authority to lay on hands? Therefore the Donatists said that Felix’s offense ought first to have been investigated before judgment was rendered concerning schism and the ordination of the bishop of Carthage, lest they suffer prejudice against Caecilian’s ordination from that judgment [Col. 1178B].

Finally, among the subscriptions of this council the name of Caecilian is found and read. This must be taken as evidence that the crime and cause of Felix rather than of Caecilian was dealt with in that council. For Caecilian would not have sat and judged among the other bishops unless he had been free and clear of every suspicion of crime and schism. The remaining points adduced by the opponents are either not very strong or can be resolved from what we have said.

## OBSERVATION XI. On the day and consuls of the proconsular judgment by which Felix of Apungita was cleared.

I find that all who have written concerning the Donatist schism agree that the case of Felix, bishop of Apungita, who was accused of *traditio* by the Donatists, was heard and decided by Aelianus the proconsul only after the judgment of Miltiades against Donatus. But it is much more obscure whether the judgment of the same Proconsul Aelianus, by which Felix was acquitted of idolatry, was later in time than the Council of Arles. For although Felix in Africa and Caecilian at Arles departed innocent and uncondemned under the same consuls, namely Volusianus and Annianus, the day of Felix’s acquittal is not sufficiently established. Yet it seems of great importance to the history to investigate and determine exactly on what day the judgment of Aelianus was issued and delivered.

[Col. 1178D] In chapter thirty-three of his *Treatise after the Conference*, St Augustine teaches that this took place on the fifteenth day before the Kalends of March; Cardinals Baronius and Perronius followed this opinion. Yet in a manuscript booklet supporting the same opinion, and in the very acts of the proconsul Aelianus, by which he investigated Felix’s conduct, the day is entered as the thirteenth before the Kalends of September.

Between these two opinions—one supported by the authority of most weighty writers, the other apparently by the reliability of a most ancient codex—it would be rash to decide anything. Yet the latter seems more suited and congruent with this history and with the Council of Arles. For after Melchiades’ judgment, by which the cause of the schism was settled, and after the embassy of Eunomius and Olympius and the crossing into Africa, by which communion with the Catholic Church was exhibited and declared to the Carthaginians, nothing remained to be decided at the Council of Arles, nor was anything in dispute between Donatus and Caecilian, except whether the charge against Felix—who had ordained Caecilian and whom the Donatists accused of *traditio* (“handing over” [the sacred books])—had rendered his imposition of hands invalid. For this was brought into debate and examination at Arles: namely, whether, once the crime of the ordainer had been established, the whole ordination ought to be annulled. And although some think that at that council the Donatists raised a question not only about Felix’s ordination but also about the origin of the schism, nevertheless the principal question, as we have shown in the preceding and immediately prior observation, was whether an ordination performed by a bishop guilty of *traditio* was to be held null.

This being so, it becomes probable that Felix had not yet been acquitted by Aelianus of *traditio* and idolatry when the council was held. For with what face could the Donatists, at the Council of Arles, convened in September, have pursued an action to annul Caecilian’s ordination, whose sole foundation was Felix’s alleged crime, if Felix had been cleared of that very crime on the fifteenth before the Kalends of March? There was no need to convene a council at such great expense, and to assemble bishops from every part of Africa, Gaul, Spain, Sicily, and Italy, in order to discuss a single question whose whole rationale and force rested upon Felix’s crime, if Felix had already been acquitted and declared innocent by Aelianus’ judgment. Nor would there have been lacking African bishops present at the council to say that the legal question was being raised in vain, since the factual basis upon which the law rested had not been established—indeed, since the exact opposite appeared altogether from the records of Felix’s acquittal.

For this reason, I judge that the manuscript’s testimony should be followed, and that these two things should be thought to have occurred at the same time: Caecilian’s ordination was confirmed at the Council of Arles, and Felix was cleared of the charge by Aelianus in the same month, or thereabouts. Nor do St Augustine’s words move me. Though in all other matters I would gladly yield to his authority, yet in this history, as Franciscus Balduinus rightly observed, he is not fully satisfactory, and many things relevant to it are passed over in his writings.

Further, I readily persuade myself that St Augustine, in the heat of disputation, assigned a somewhat earlier date to Aelianus’ judgment. For, in order to refute the Donatist objection that Constantine had reversed, by a later decision, his judgment by which, after the Council of Arles at Milan, he had acquitted Caecilian upon hearing Ingentius, sent to him through Aelianus—for the purpose, I say, of refuting this—it was necessary for Augustine to show that in the same decision in which Felix was acquitted by Aelianus, Ingentius was ordered to proceed to the imperial court; and that the emperor did not acquit or clear Caecilian until he had learned, through Ingentius and Aelianus’ judgment, of Felix’s conduct and acquittal. Therefore he placed the date of that judgment somewhat earlier, in order to show that Ingentius had been seen and heard by the emperor long before he pronounced for Caecilian at Milan.

These are St Augustine’s words in Letter 152, in which he noted neither the day nor the month of the proconsular trial—though he ought to have noted it there, had he known it:

> For if anyone now carefully observes the sequence of consuls and days set out in the records, he will find that Caecilian was first cleared by an episcopal judgment; then, not long afterward, the case of Felix of Apunga was investigated by the proconsul Aelianus, where he was found innocent. In that case Ingentius was ordered to be sent to the imperial court; and much later the emperor himself heard and concluded the case between the parties. In that hearing he judged Caecilian innocent and the others slanderers. In this sequence of consuls and days it is sufficiently shown that they falsely and slanderously alleged that, after Ingentius had been sent to the imperial court, the emperor altered his judgment and condemned Caecilian, whom he had previously acquitted. Not only could they read nothing of the kind, while they read so much against themselves; but we also convict them more clearly through the sequence of consuls: Felix’s case was concluded by proconsular judgment, in which Ingentius was ordered to be sent to the imperial court; and not after a short interval, but much later, when the aforesaid emperor had heard the case between the parties, Caecilian was acquitted.

[Col. 1179]

## 201. ANCIENT MONUMENTS RELATING TO THE HISTORY OF THE DONATISTS, FROM THE RESTORATION OF THEIR FREEDOM BY JULIAN TO THE EXTINCTION OF THE SCHISM

### A.D. 362. I. RESCRIPT OF THE EMPEROR JULIAN IN FAVOR OF THE DONATISTS

(From Augustine, Book II against the Letter of Petilian, chapter 97.) (S)

[Col. 1179C]

[Col. 1179D] Moreover, in response to the petitions of Rogatianus, Pontius, Cassianus, and the other bishops, and also of the clergy, this is added as a further measure: that, after the removal of those measures wrongly taken against them without a rescript, all things shall be restored to their former condition.

In the petitionary memorial, whose author was Pontius, they told Julian that with him justice alone had a place.

## 202. A.D. 373. II. CONSTITUTION OF VALENTINIAN THE ELDER AGAINST REBAPTIZERS

(From the Theodosian Code, Book XVI, Title VI, “That holy baptism shall not be repeated,” Law I.) The Emperors Valentinian and Valens Augusti to Julianus, Proconsul of Africa.

[Note: Valentinian the Elder, residing at Trier in Gaul, undoubtedly also by the counsel of the Gallican bishops, or in response to a report sent to him from Africa, declares by this law, A.D. 373, that a priest—or bishop—who rebaptizes is unworthy of his priesthood or episcopate throughout Proconsular Africa; and he undoubtedly orders that he be deprived of it. I say throughout Proconsular Africa, because this law is addressed to its proconsul.

Hence the conjecture is not empty that this law concerns the Donatists, just as the following four laws concern them, and likewise two others—namely, Laws 5 and 38 above, “On Heretics.” Augustine testifies, in Letter 164, that it concerns the Donatists, who had very recently supported the usurper Firmus in Africa. Valentinian undoubtedly tolerated them, granting everyone the license of *ἐθελοθρησκεία* (*ethelothrēskeia*, “self-willed religion”), of which I spoke under the preceding law, “On Sorcerers”; only rebaptism was condemned among them, under the penalty of deprivation of priesthood. For Valentinian proceeds no further.

Balduinus thinks that Optatus of Milevis the African had this very law in mind near the beginning of Book V:

> “This is our voice, we who defend the unity of baptism in the Trinity, not yours, who boldly and contrary to the laws repeat baptism, in whose image are those two things—although you yourselves do not deny that what was once commanded to be done ought not to be repeated.”

In this he is greatly mistaken. For, as he himself correctly teaches elsewhere, it is certain that Optatus wrote before this year, 373. Indeed, as Optatus himself openly declares, he wrote in the sixtieth and following year after the Diocletian persecution—that is, about A.D. 367—as I show at length elsewhere.

It is true, however, that this law belongs among those which Valentinian issued against rebaptizers, of which Gratian also makes mention in the second law below, expressly (*ῥητῶς*) against the Donatists, as Augustine testifies in Letter 166 to the Donatists:

> “Valentinian succeeded him [Jovian]. Read what he commanded against you.”

Something has already been said on this under Law III above, “On Heretics.” Therefore Optatus’ passage must be understood of other laws of Valentinian—if any were issued against the Donatists before this one—and likewise of Constantine and Constantius, or rather Constans, mentioned in Law II below.

Two notable points occur in this law. First, it says, “contrary to the ordinances of all”; this is explained more fully under the second law immediately following. Secondly, it calls baptism “grace” and “divine grace,” just as “the grace of communion” is so called in Law V below, “On Apostates.” Gratian likewise, Letter 17:

> “For those who may be overtaken by danger, even when at the point of death, let not your vigilance be lacking; for those imploring divine grace, let not the Lord’s mercy be denied.”

This passage must altogether be compared with Law I above, “On Actors.” Among Greeks likewise, just as the Eucharist, so baptism was called *χάρις* (*charis*, “grace”). Concerning the Eucharist, Cyril frequently uses the expressions *τῆς θείας χάριτος μεταλαμβάνειν* (“to partake of divine grace”) and *προσιέναι πρὸς τὴν ἐπουράνιον χάριν* (“to approach the heavenly grace”); and Optatus, Book V, likewise concerning the Eucharist:

> “The nations come to grace; he who deigned to invite presents it; a company of servants performs the ministry.”

I pass over other instances. No less frequently is this said of baptism, which has many names, enumerated by Clement of Alexandria in Book I, Gregory Nazianzen in Oration 40, and Chrysostom more than once; one of these names is *χάρισμα* (*charisma*, “gift of grace”) or *χάρις* (*charis*, “grace”). In Cyril’s fourth *Mystagogical Catechesis*, *προσέρχεσθαι τῇ χάριτι* means “to approach baptism.”
