And they subscribed. Again: “Aurelius, bishop of the Church of Carthage, assented to this decree and subscribed after it had been read.” Likewise the other bishops subscribed.

## 215. A.D. 405. Eighteenth: Law of Honorius Concerning Those Who Rebaptize

From the Theodosian Code, Book XVI, title 5, “Concerning Heretics,” law 38. The emperors Arcadius, Honorius, and Theodosius, Augusti.

[Col. 1204B]

[Col. 1204C] Let no one recall to mind a Manichaean or a Donatist—those who especially, as we have learned, do not cease to rage.

> **Note: [Col. 1203D]** By this edict in A.D. 405, the Emperor Honorius suppresses the spirit, frenzy, error, and seditious assemblies of the Manichaeans and Donatists, confirming the earlier enactments against them and his own law recently issued, setting forth very severe penalties, and inviting all to unity.
>
> This is, namely, the edict of unity sent by the Emperor Honorius throughout Africa. He himself mentions it in law II below, “Concerning Religion,” in the immediately following month of this year: “We desire,” says Honorius, “that the edict which Our Clemency directed through the African regions be posted in various places, so that it may become known that the one and true Catholic faith, which right belief confesses, must be maintained.”
>
> The statement of the author of the consular records appended to Hydatius is also to be understood of this same edict: “Under Stilicho II and Anthemius, consuls, unity was made between Catholics and Donatists.” “Unity was made,” that is, the edict of unity, or Henoticon, was issued.
>
> The African Fathers also mention it three years later in the Tenth Council of Carthage, A.D. 407, canon 99 of the African Code: “the Edict of Unity,” namely. The following words also show this: “Let there be one Catholic worship; let there be one salvation; let the equal and mutually concordant holiness of the Trinity be sought.”
>
> The Greeks call edicts of this sort *henotika* (ἑνωτικά, “unifying edicts”). Victor of Tunnuna relates in his Chronicle that the Emperor Zeno later issued one of this kind: “The Emperor Anastasius, holding a synod of heretics, confirms Zeno’s Henoticon.” Theodore the Reader, Eclogue 2, says: “He secretly suggested to the emperor that he should persuade the bishop of Rome to subscribe to Zeno’s Henoticon.” The whole account is found also in Evagrius, Book III, chapter 14.
>
> Nor is the edict of Theodosius contained above in the law *Cunctos populos*, “Concerning the Catholic Faith,” of a different sort. Indeed, law III below, “That Holy Baptism Is Not to Be Repeated,” is likewise a part of this Honor ian Henoticon and should therefore be joined to it. Moreover, I count as part of this edict the law mentioned by Augustine in Letter 196; see the note on the said law III.
>
> On the same day, special commands for implementing this edict of unity were issued by Honorius to Hadrian, Praetorian Prefect; they are contained in laws IV and V below, under the title “That Holy Baptism Is Not to Be Repeated.” Shortly afterward, by a further special law addressed to the proconsul of Africa, he ordered that this edict be posted in various places; see law VII below, “Concerning Religion.”
>
> The occasion for this edict was supplied both by the African Fathers assembled in the preceding year, A.D. 404, and by the events that followed from the Donatist party. For, when the African Fathers saw the obstinate spirit and fury of the Donatists and Circumcellions, whom they had invited in A.D. 404 to a friendly religious conference—as is clear from canons 91 and 92 of the African Code, or the final and penultimate canons of the Eighth Council of Carthage held in the preceding year—they both commended the cause of unity by an embassy sent to the Emperor Honorius and requested that penalties be enacted against the Donatists, which laws IV and V establish. They also requested protection against the fury of the Donatists, as canon 93 sets forth most fully. Among other things, they say there that the Donatists, having rejected a peaceful conference, turned to savage violence, so that they ambushed many bishops and clerics, to say nothing of laypersons; seized some churches; and attempted to seize others. And immediately afterward: “The detestable band of Circumcellions by which they rage is known and has often been denounced by laws; it has also been condemned by frequent enactments of those most religious princes themselves, against whose fury we may obtain safeguards neither unprecedented nor foreign to the Holy Scriptures.”
>
> To these must be added the private complaints of bishops, including those of Maximianus, bishop of Bagai, carried to the Emperor Honorius at the same time. On these, see Augustine, Letters 48 and 50; *To Boniface*, pp. 220, 221, 68; Book III against Cresconius, chapter 43; Book III against Julian, chapter 1; and the *Brief Record of the Conference*, day 3, chapter 11.
>
> Honorius, having learned these things—as he himself declares in this edict, “those who especially, as we have learned, do not cease to rage”—therefore promulgated this edict to restrain the frenzy and error of the Donatists and suppress their seditions. Hence the penalties set forth in law IV below, “That Holy Baptism Is Not to Be Repeated,” confirming the numerous earlier enactments in this matter, which the African Fathers themselves also mention there, and his own law recently promulgated.
>
> The Manichaeans are joined to the Donatists in this law; yet they are not mentioned in either the Fathers’ or private complaints sent to Honorius which, as I have said, occasioned this edict. Nevertheless, I am led by no empty conjecture to think that this was obtained by Augustine, who, under the preceding consuls, held a disputation with the Manichaean Felix and converted him to the Catholic faith; see Augustine’s *Life*, chapter 16. See also Augustine, *Against a Manichaean*, Book II at the end; and the materials extracted from a certain manuscript by Nicolaus Faber and mentioned by Baronius under the year 404, no. 128.
>
> But Honorius himself indicates the reason at the beginning of the law: namely, that these two principal kinds of heretics then disturbed Africa. This is shown, besides the present law, by law 35 above; it will be shown by laws 40, 41, and 43 below under this title. See also my remarks on the said law 35.
>
> Further, by this law Honorius threatens the snares, that is, the penalties, established by a law recently promulgated by himself. By these words I understand the pecuniary penalty of ten pounds of gold promulgated by Theodosius, which had previously been established; for I have already shown that this is among the things meant by “the snares of the law.” He even threatens a more severe penalty if crowds should assemble.
>
> Certainly the African Fathers too, at the council held in the preceding year as I have said, decreed that their envoys should request of Honorius that the law of Theodosius—concerning ten pounds of gold imposed upon ordainers or ordained heretics and upon proprietors where their assembly was discovered—be confirmed henceforth in such a way as to apply against those against whom Catholics, provoked by their plots, lodged a formal complaint.
>
> The relevant passage of Augustine’s letter to Boniface, p. 219, explains this particularly well. More on this at the next law.  
> —Jacob Gothofredus.

Let there be one Catholic worship; let there be one salvation; let the equal holiness of the Trinity, harmonious within itself, be sought. But if anyone should dare to involve himself in prohibited and unlawful practices, let him not escape the snares of the countless former enactments or of the law recently issued by Our Clemency; and if crowds should perhaps gather, let him not doubt that the goads of a sharper disturbance of the peace are to be employed against those stirred up for sedition.

Given on the day before the Ides of February at Ravenna, under the consulship of Stilicho for the second time and Anthemius.

## 216. A.D. 405. Nineteenth: Another Law of the Same Emperor Concerning Those Who Rebaptize

From the Theodosian Code, Book XVI, title VI, “That Holy Baptism Is Not to Be Repeated,” law 3. The emperors Arcadius, Honorius, and Theodosius, Augusti.

[Col. 1205A]

> **Note: [Col. 1206C]** Three enactments of Honorius concerning rebaptizers follow. All are indeed enactments directed against the Donatists; several further enactments against the Donatists appear under the title “Concerning Heretics,” eleven in number. See our remarks on law 38 under that title. Nevertheless, this same law appears to apply generally also to other heretics who rebaptize.
>
> Since its meaning is brief and clear, and is closer to a pronouncement than to a law, inasmuch as it neither defines nor enacts anything—and therefore is also absent from the Code of Justinian—there remains only one thing for us to observe and note: it is not addressed to any magistrate, but is called an edict.
>
> This law is a part of that solemn Honor ian edict of unity, or Henoticon, issued throughout the African regions in A.D. 405 in response to the embassy of the African Fathers, discussed in the notes on the preceding laws. It is so likewise with law 38 above, “Concerning Heretics,” which should consequently be joined to it. I have spoken fully there concerning this Henoticon, or edict of unity. Honorius himself mentions it in law II below, “Concerning Religion,” in canon 99 of the African Code; and Hydatius mentions it under the very consuls appended to this law: by that edict all were admonished to unity; the Donatists were specifically condemned, as were the Manichaeans; their assemblies were prohibited; and the error of the rebaptizers was likewise condemned, with very severe penalties proposed against them if they did not return to unity.
>
> This will be shown not only by the present law and the note on law 38, but also by the two immediately following laws, 4 and 5, which are likewise to be joined to it as issued on the same day, though addressed to Hadrian, Praetorian Prefect. For laws addressed to magistrates were customarily issued at the same time in order that edicts displayed and published to the people might be carried out.
>
> Finally, a provision of the constitution mentioned by Augustine in Letter 166 may perhaps also have been part of this very edict of unity, or Henoticon. Baldwin wrongly ascribes it to Constantine in his Notes on Optatus, p. 82, and records some of its words:
>
> “Consider,” he addresses the Donatists, “with what most manifest truth God himself has said, through the heart of the king which is in the hand of God, in this very law which you say was issued against you, though, if you understand it, it was issued for you. Consider the words of the emperor. For if, in the case of persons initiated for the first time, the religion of baptism is judged weak because those from whom it is received are thought to be sinners, the sacrament once bestowed would have to be renewed as often as the minister administering baptism were found unworthy; and our faith would depend not upon the choice of our own will or the grace of the divine gift, but upon the merits and moral quality of priests and clerics. Your bishops hold a thousand councils: let them answer this one pronouncement,” etc.  
> —J. G.

We do not permit the wandering errors of those who rebaptize, etc.

Given on the day before the Ides of February at Ravenna, under the consulship of Stilicho for the second time and Anthemius.

## XX. Third Law of Honorius Concerning Those Who Rebaptize

From the Theodosian Code, Book XVI, title VI, “That Holy Baptism Is Not to Be Repeated,” law 4. The emperors Arcadius, Honorius, and Theodosius, Augusti, to Hadrian, Praetorian Prefect.

[Col. 1206A]

By the authority of this decree we have taken care to root out the enemies of the Catholic faith. Therefore, by a new constitution, we have judged that sect in particular must be cut off [Col. 1207A] which, in order not to be called a heresy, adopted the designation of schism. For those called Donatists are said to have advanced to such a degree of wickedness that, scorning the mysteries, they rashly repeat the most holy baptism with harmful presumption and defile with the contamination of a profane repetition persons once washed, as was handed down, by the gift of divinity. Thus it has happened that heresy has arisen from schism.

From this, a seductive error invites credulous minds to hope for a second pardon. For it is easy to persuade sinners that forgiveness once granted can be granted anew; and if it can be granted again in the same manner, we do not understand why it should be denied a third time. They also pollute slaves or persons subject to their own authority with the sacrilege of repeated baptism.

We therefore enact by this law that whoever hereafter is discovered to have rebaptized shall be brought before the judge presiding over the province, so that, punished by the confiscation of all property, he may undergo the penalty of poverty which shall affect him permanently. Yet the paternal property shall not be lost to their children if they dissent from the perversity of their father’s association, so that, if perhaps the violence of paternal depravity has entangled them too and they now prefer to return to the Catholic religion, they may not be denied the opportunity of acquiring those goods.

Furthermore, those places or estates which are hereafter established to have afforded concealment to deadly sacrileges shall be added to the resources of the fisc, provided that the master or mistress is proved either to have been present or to have given consent; such persons shall also be marked with infamy by judicial sentence. But if, without their knowledge, it is proved that a crime of this kind was committed in their house by their tenant or agent, then, with confiscation of the estates held in abeyance, the authors of the implicated crime shall be punished by lead-weighted scourges and shall receive exile, in which they shall remain throughout [Col. 1207C] their entire life.

And lest it perhaps be permissible for anyone to conceal in silence, within domestic walls, awareness of a sacrilegious act committed, those who may perhaps be compelled to be rebaptized shall have freedom to flee to the Catholic Church, [Col. 1208A] so that, under its protection and the protection of liberty granted to them, they may be defended against the authors of this crime and association; and, under this condition, they may be permitted to keep the faith which the others attempted to extort from unwilling persons belonging to the Lord.

Nor should defenders of Catholic doctrine be bound by law to commit the crime in the way that other persons who are under authority ought to be bound; and it is especially fitting that all persons, without any distinction of condition or rank, should be guardians of holiness poured down from heaven.

Let those who have not feared to repeat baptism as described above, or who by consenting have condemned themselves through participation in this association’s crime, know that they are forever denied not only the capacity to make a will but also the opportunity to acquire anything under the appearance of a gift or through contractual dealings, unless, by returning to [Col. 1208B] the true faith, they correct the error of a perverse mind through reformation of purpose.

The same penalty shall likewise bind those who have connived at the prohibited assemblies or ministries of the persons mentioned. Thus provincial governors who believe that such consent should be granted in contempt of this enactment shall know that they are to be fined twenty pounds of gold. Their staffs also shall be subjected to a like condemnation. The principal officials or defenders of cities who fail to carry out what we command, or during whose presence violence is inflicted upon the Catholic Church, shall know that they are liable to the same fine.

Given on the day before the Ides of February at Ravenna, under the consulship of Stilicho for the second time and Anthemius.

## XXI. Fourth Law of Honorius Concerning Those Who Rebaptize

From the Theodosian Code, Book XVI, title VI, “That Holy Baptism Is Not to Be Repeated,” law 5. The emperors Arcadius, Honorius, and Theodosius, Augusti, to Hadrian, Praetorian Prefect.

[Note: [Col. 1207D] This constitution of Honorius, sent to the Praetorian Prefect Adrian, against the rebaptism of the Donatists, and against their violence and deception in this respect, enacted in A.D. 405, has two parts. Both were indeed issued on the same day and with the same concluding formula as the Edict of Union, of which Law 3 above and Law 38 above concerning heretics are parts; consequently these two parts also ought to be appended to it. For, as I have already indicated concerning the said Law 3, the Edict of Union was throughout issued with the same conclusion and posted for the people in the African provinces: it was intended to bring and invite the Donatists to unity; while this constitution was intended to break their obstinacy and audacity and to cut off their opportunity for deception, as Law 5 says.

By this twofold means, namely the admonition of the edict and the severity of penalties, Honorius undertook at this time to deal with the Donatists. He issued a constitution to Adrian, Praetorian Prefect, expressly, as Law 5 states, directing him to ensure that the severity of this law was enforced through provincial governors, officials, and defenders; such is the purpose of the law. It is merely astonishing that the compilers of this Code have here torn this one constitution into two laws, and that in the latter the very same enactment is repeated in precisely the same words as had already been contained in the former.

Before I proceed to the arrangement of the constitution itself, two matters must be set forth beforehand. First, it must be maintained that this constitution, like that Edict of Union, was issued by Emperor Honorius in response to the embassy of the Council of Carthage held in the preceding year, 404, in the sixth consulship of Honorius Augustus and that of Aristaenetus, on 26 June. This is suggested by the chronology itself; and it is fully confirmed by the articles of that embassy, and by the requests which the envoys were charged to make of Emperor Honorius, as contained in the memorandum extant in chapter 63 of the Code of Canons of the African Church, as we shall later show [Col. 1209A].

Secondly, we must consider the grounds by which Honorius, in these laws, tries to pierce and confound the Donatists and their rebaptism; and, conversely, those by which he commends the Catholic faith and the lawful and unique use of baptism, and thus the arguments by which he establishes it. It is useful first of all to gather together the distinctive and various names for baptism employed here. He calls it: first, a mystery; second, a gift of divinity; third, pardon; fourth, holiness infused from heaven; fifth, divine grace—concerning this designation “grace,” I have already spoken on Law 1 above.

There follow the expressions by which Honorius everywhere declares his hatred of the Donatist sect and its rebaptism and makes it known by the very harshness of his words. He calls them enemies of the Catholic faith; says that by the authority of this decree he has provided for their extirpation; declares that this sect is especially to be cut off—not “forbidden,” as some restore the reading; attributes to them crime, rashness, and harmful perversity; says that those washed are defiled by the contagion of profane repetition; that they are polluted by the sacrilege of repeated baptism; imputes to them the savagery of depravity; and speaks of deadly sacrileges, a wicked deed, a perpetrated expiatory crime, error of a perverse mind, grace polluted under repeated baptism, and a perverse doctrine.

Now, what especially deserves notice for the history of the Donatists, and likewise for the distinction between heresy and schism, is this. He says that the Donatists preferred for their sect the name of schism, though in reality it was a heresy arising from schism when they introduced rebaptism. As to the distinction between heresy and schism, it is already sufficiently well known from familiar testimonies of the ancients, among them Cyprian, Augustine, and Balsamon. At least the true author of the *Dialogue*, or *Consultation*, or *Disputation* between Apollonius the Philosopher and Zacchaeus the Christian, Book 2, speaking of the Novatians, says:

> They were once with us, but were separated through a certain Novatus as their author. Yet they are not to be equated with heretics, because they differ not from the Catholic confession but from charity; and, rebelling against the mercy of God in the matter of mercy alone, they exclude from restoration those once caught in the snares of the enemy. They call themselves pure—*Cathari*, to use their own word—and hold assemblies outside the Church.

The case of the Donatists and their schism is parallel; on this see Optatus of Milevis. But, as this law says, heresy arose from schism, as commonly happens elsewhere. For it is known that at first the Donatists withdrew from the Catholic Church, and thus from the body, with no disagreement about religion or doctrine; but afterwards they added heresy and obstinacy to schism by introducing rebaptism, and superimposed hatred of Catholics. They progressed to such crimes that Augustine records in more than one passage—for example, in Letter 164 [Col. 1209D], where he says that by wicked perseverance they made the crime of schism into heresy.

218 Also noteworthy are Honorius’s arguments from theology against rebaptism, undoubtedly suggested by the bishops whom he consulted. Besides the general arguments also contained in other laws, this is thoroughly theological:

> Hence flattering error invites credulous minds to hope for a second pardon. For it is easy to persuade sinners that pardon once granted can be granted again; and if it can be granted a second time in that manner, we do not understand why it should be refused a third time.

Relevant here is Tertullian’s statement in his book *On Baptism*: “We undergo baptism once; sins are washed away once, because they ought not to be repeated.”

Before we deal with the measures adopted, and therefore with the just severity of Honorius in these laws for restraining rebaptism, we must see how far the Donatists’ crime, deed, or deception had proceeded in this matter. They selected houses, places, or estates that would provide concealment for their deadly sacrileges, with the consent—if not of the owners—at least of their tenants or stewards, whom they drew to their side. Thus, within domestic walls, they concealed in silence the knowledge of an expiatory deed perpetrated in secret. They also compelled their slaves against their will to undergo it, and finally often had officials in office who connived with them. These were the three deceits of the Rebaptizers.

Against these men, therefore, and their rashness—indeed, against every opportunity for deception, as Law 5 of this title says—Honorius opposes in these laws just severity and enactment, and thus seven means and remedies. His Law 40 above concerning the Manichaeans, Phrygians, and Priscillianists, issued two years later, is entirely similar.

First, he makes this a public accusation, when in both Laws 4 and 5 [Col. 1210B] he provides that those detected in rebaptizing are to be brought before the judge presiding over the province; and immediately adds that it is especially fitting that all persons, without any distinction of condition or rank, should be guardians of holiness infused from heaven. On public accusation of heresy, as also of apostasy, see the respective titles. Thus he in a sense incites the whole human race against them.

Second, he commands that Rebaptizers be fined in their property, which is to accrue to the fisc, unless they have children already orthodox, or children who seriously wish to become so.

Third, he orders that places in which rebaptism has occurred, with the owner’s knowledge and consent, be confiscated; indeed, that the owner be branded with infamy.

Fourth, he orders that knowing tenants and stewards be beaten with lead-weighted scourges and sent into perpetual exile.

Fifth, he provides that slaves and coloni whom their masters wish to compel into rebaptism should have open access to the Church for refuge and should thereby attain freedom, or, as he puts it, be protected by the safeguard of freedom conferred upon them. This may seem to have been added because of Crispinus, Donatist bishop of Calama, who had rebaptized certain coloni enticed by payment; Augustine discusses him in Letter 173 and *Against the Letters of Petilian*, chapter 88. Let this case meanwhile be added to the others in which slaves and coloni obtain freedom as a reward.

Sixth, he removes from rebaptizers—and from those who offer connivance to their assemblies or ministries while remaining in error—the right to make a will, to acquire anything by gift, or to enter into contracts. This was enacted at the request and embassy of the African Fathers; for thus they stated in the memorandum given to the envoys:

> It must also be requested that the law which denies to heretics the ability to receive or leave anything by gifts or wills be renewed by their piety to this extent: that it take away the right of leaving or receiving from those who, blinded by the frenzy of obstinacy, should wish to persist in the error of the Donatists. But for those who wish to correct themselves for the sake of unity and peace, the right of taking an inheritance should remain open without the prohibition of this law [Col. 1210D], if anything by gift or inheritance should come to them while they are still established in heretical error.

Here you see the same exception also: “Unless,” says Honorius, “the error of a perverse mind, by returning again to the faith, has been corrected through an amendment of purpose.” Therefore pardon is granted to those returning to the Catholic faith, both to themselves and to their children mentioned above. Thus Honorius believed that, after the most severe penalties had been proposed, the Donatists’ stubbornness could be broken by hope of pardon. Yet the African Fathers added a certain limitation, excepting those who, when sued, thought it best to pass over to the Catholic side; for in their case it is credible that they preferred Catholic unity not from fear of heavenly judgment but from greed for earthly advantage. This limitation, however, displeased Honorius in 407, in Law 41 above concerning heretics, which is most elegant and humane in this regard.

Finally, he imposes this responsibility on provincial governors, their officials [Col. 1211B], provincials, and defenders, and Honorius even threatens a fine against those who connive at this matter or do not ward off violence. This is customary, and is used in the twin, closely related law of Emperor Honorius himself—Law 40 above concerning heretics—likewise in the case of Manichaeans, Phrygians, and Priscillianists; as also in Laws 45 and 46 of the same title. Just as he directed these same persons to remove violence by Jews and Gentiles against those living peaceably, in Law 24 below concerning Pagans [Col. 1211C], so this was requested by the African Fathers. For thus they state in the memorandum:

> But we ask that protection be afforded without any concealment to Catholics of the municipal orders—and thus also to the leading citizens—in every city, and to every neighboring landowner in various places.

And immediately afterwards:

> For all these matters there is need of the protection of their authorities in all the provinces whatsoever.

These, namely, were the four classes of persons in the provinces who ought to provide protection for the oppressed, and who needed to be vigilant lest anything be committed contrary to the laws. On defenders, see the materials gathered in the *Paratitlon* under the title *On Defenders*; on leading citizens, see the *Paratitlon* on decurions.] [Col. 1208B]

[Col. 1208C] To prevent the secret assemblies of the Donatists from violating divine grace, polluted under repeated baptism, and to remove the opportunity for deception by the severity of this command, [Col. 1209A] we decree that the penalty shall follow other persons of this kind and that they shall experience the avenging censure of the law who [Col. 1210A] have transgressed against the Catholic religion by a perverse doctrine. We therefore command that, if anyone hereafter is detected in rebaptizing [Col. 1211A], he shall be brought before the judge who presides over the province, so that, punished by the public confiscation of all his property, he may pay the penalty of poverty, etc. Given on the day before the Ides of February at Ravenna, in the consulship of Stilicho and Anthemius.

## XXII. LAW OF HONORIUS CONCERNING THE POSTING THROUGH AFRICA OF THE EDICT OF UNITY

From the *Theodosian Code*, Book XVI, Title II, *On Religion*, Law 2. Emperors Arcadius, Honorius, and Theodosius Augusti, to Diotimus, Proconsul of Africa.

[Note: [Col. 1211C] The Edict of Unity, or *Henoticon* (ἑνωτικόν), was sent by Emperor Honorius into Africa against the Manichaeans and Donatists in that same year 405, in the preceding month of February. The consular records of Hydatius also attest this: “In the consulship of Stilicho II and Anthemius, unity was made between Catholics and Donatists.” Law 38 above concerning heretics and Law 4 above, *That Holy Baptism Shall Not Be Repeated*, are parts of this Edict of Union. It is mentioned again three years later in the tenth Council of Carthage in 407, Canon 99 of the African Code.

Accordingly, just as on the same day special commands from Honorius were sent to Hadrian, Praetorian Prefect of Italy—under whom Africa was placed—for execution of this Edict (contained in Laws 4 and 5, *That Holy Baptism Shall Not Be Repeated*), so one month later, namely in March, Honorius commanded by this special law to the Proconsul of Africa that this edict be posted throughout Africa, so that it might become known to all. The custom and method of posting edicts have been fully discussed elsewhere. For more on this *Henoticon* and other Henotica, see what I have said more fully on the said Law 38 above, *On Heretics*. J. G.]

We wish the edict which our clemency sent concerning Unity through the African regions to be posted in various places, so that it may become known to all that the one and true Catholic faith of almighty God—the faith which right belief confesses—must be maintained. Given on 5 March at Ravenna, in the second consulship of Stilicho and the consulship of Anthemius.

## 219 XXIII. DECREE OF THE COUNCIL HELD AT CARTHAGE, IN THE BASILICA OF THE SECOND DISTRICT, ON 23 AUGUST, IN THE SECOND CONSULSHIP OF STILICHO AND THE CONSULSHIP OF ANTHEMIUS, VIR CLARISSIMUS

Since unity has been achieved only at Carthage, letters are also to be given to the judges, directing them to ensure that efforts are made for unity in the other provinces and cities as well. Thanksgivings are to be sent from the Church of Carthage, on behalf of all Africa, to the imperial court, concerning the exclusion of the Donatists, together with letters from the bishops. The letter of Pope Innocent was read: bishops should not readily travel overseas, and this is confirmed by the judgments of the bishops themselves. For the giving of thanks and the exclusion of the Donatists, two clerics of the Church of Carthage are to be sent to the imperial court. (*Council of Africa*, canon 61; *Code of Canons of the African Church*, canon 94.)

## XXIV. LAW OF HONORIUS IMPOSING A FINE UPON THE DONATISTS

From the *Theodosian Code*, Book XVI, Title V, *On Heretics*, Law 39. Emperors Arcadius, Honorius, and Theodosius Augusti, to Diotimus, their own, greeting.

[Note: [Col. 1211D] The monetary fine of ten pounds of gold imposed by Theodosius the Great upon clerics and ministers of heretics [Col. 1212B] in 392, Law 21 above, is by this constitution of his son Honorius expressly extended to Donatist heretics—who nevertheless denied that they were heretics—wherever they may be, whether confessing or convicted. It is extended, I say; for this is what those words indicate: “we decree that they shall pay the penalty due without delay, the tenor of the law being preserved.” Thus I am surprised that Baronius, having recorded this law, nevertheless writes that a constitution of Honorius requiring payment of the monetary fine of ten pounds of gold is lacking.

Let us see the stages through which Honorius was brought to enact this law. First, in the preceding year, 404, the African Fathers decreed in their council, as Canon 93 of the African Code records, that it should likewise be requested:

> That they command the confirmation henceforth of the law promulgated by their father Theodosius of religious memory concerning ten pounds of gold against ordainers or ordained heretics, or also against landowners where their assembly is discovered, so that it may have force against those against whom Catholic inhabitants have lodged a formal complaint because of their plots; that at least through this fear those who neglect to amend and correct themselves from consideration of eternal punishment may withdraw from schismatic or heretical perversity.

Now let passages of Augustine relevant to this matter follow. First comes the passage from Letter 50 to Boniface, Count of Military Affairs, *On the Moderate Coercion of Heretics*, page 219:

> Before these laws, by which they are compelled to enter the holy banquet, had been sent into Africa, it seemed to some brothers, among whom I was one [Col. 1212D], although the madness of the Donatists raged everywhere, that the emperors should not be asked to command that heresy itself should not exist at all by establishing a penalty for those who wished to be in it. Rather, they should establish that they would not tolerate the furious violence of those who either preached the Catholic truth in speech or commended it by enactment.  
>   
> I thought that this could to some extent be achieved if they confirmed more expressly against the Donatists, who denied that they were heretics, the law of Theodosius of most pious memory, which he promulgated generally against all heretics, requiring that any of their bishops or clerics found anywhere be fined ten pounds of gold; so that not all should be struck by this fine, but only those in whose districts the Catholic Church suffered some acts of violence from their clerics, Circumcellions, or people. Thus, after the formal complaint of the Catholics who had suffered these things, the bishops or other ministers would be liable, under the responsibility of the municipal authorities, to pay the fine [Col. 1213A].  
>   
> For we thought that if they were frightened and dared do nothing of this sort, Catholic truth could be taught and held freely; no one would be compelled to it, but anyone wishing could follow it without fear, lest we have false and pretended Catholics. Although other brothers—either older men or men drawing upon examples from many cities and places [Col. 1213B], where we saw the Catholic Church firm and true, though established and strengthened there by such benefits of God when people had been compelled by the laws of earlier emperors to enter Catholic communion—held another view, we nevertheless prevailed that the matter I have stated should rather be requested from the emperors. It was decreed in our council, and envoys were sent to the imperial court.  
>   
> But the greater mercy of God, who knew that the fear of those laws and a certain medicinal discomfort were necessary for perverse or lukewarm minds, and for that hardness which cannot be corrected by words but can nevertheless be disciplined by a measure of severity, brought it about that our envoys could not obtain what they had undertaken to obtain. For certain most serious complaints of bishops from other places had already preceded us, bishops who had suffered many evils from them and had been driven from their sees. Above all, the dreadful and incredible murder of Maximian, bishop of the Catholic Church at Vaga, caused our embassy to have nothing left to do. For a law had already been promulgated [Col. 1213C] that the Donatist heresy of such monstrous cruelty—toward which it seemed more cruel to show indulgence than the heresy itself was in its rage—should not merely be forbidden to act violently, but should not be permitted to exist at all with impunity. Yet no capital punishment was imposed, in order to preserve Christian gentleness even toward the unworthy; rather, financial losses were prescribed, and exile was decreed for their bishops and ministers.

And shortly afterwards:

> Thus it came about that the religious and pious Emperor, when such cases had been reported to his knowledge, preferred by most pious laws wholly to correct the error of that impiety, and to bring back to Catholic unity through fear and coercion those who bore Christ’s signs against Christ, rather than merely to remove their freedom to rage and leave them free to err and perish. And now, when the laws themselves came into Africa, etc.

The same writer, Letter 68:

> Crispinus was judged a heretic; yet through Catholic gentleness he was not allowed to be struck with the penalty of ten pounds of gold established by the emperors against heretics. Nevertheless, he thought fit to appeal to the Emperor. What response was made to his appeal in this matter? Did not the earlier wickedness of your people and this appeal of his exact it? Yet even after that rescript, through the intercession of our bishops with the Emperor, he was not fined the same gold penalty.

From our council, moreover, 220 our bishops sent envoys to the imperial court to obtain that not all bishops and clerics of your party should be subject to the same condemnation of ten pounds of gold established against all heretics, but only those in whose places the Catholic Church suffered some violence from your people. But when the envoys came to Rome, the dreadful and quite recent wounds of the Catholic bishop of Vaga had already moved the Emperor to send SUCH LAWS as were indeed sent.

The same writer, Letter 169, to the Donatists:

> Yet when Crispinus, on account of this deed, was convicted as a heretic in a proconsular court, through the intercession of the same bishop Possidius he was not required to pay ten pounds of gold. Unthankful for this kindness and gentleness, he dared to appeal to the Catholic emperors. Thus he provoked much more importunately and violently this wrath of God against you, of which you complain.

The same writer, Book 3, *Against Cresconius*, chapter 47:

> Your bishop Crispinus was brought forward and, because he denied to the inquiring proconsul that he was [a heretic], was very easily CONVICTED as a heretic. Yet, through the intercession of Possidius, he was not compelled to pay the TEN POUNDS OF GOLD—the fine that the greater Emperor THEODOSIUS had established against all heretics. Not content with this most lenient judgment, by some plan which, it was said, displeased all the others, he thought fit to appeal to the sons of that same Theodosius [Col. 1214B]. A rescript was received by which the party of Donatus now knew that it belonged, together with the other heretics, to that monetary PENALTY.

And what follows immediately, where he calls them “the most recent laws.”

The same writer, *Against the Letters of Petilian*, Book VII, chapter 83:

> The Catholic Church itself, supported by Catholic emperors and armed crowds by land and sea, was fiercely and hostilely attacked by Optatus. This caused that law concerning ten pounds of gold to be pleaded against you for the first time before the Vicar Seranus; none of your party has yet paid it, and you accuse us of cruelty.

The same writer, Letter 173, to Crispinus himself:

> For we could proceed to make you pay ten pounds of gold according to the imperial commands. Or perhaps you do not have the means to repay what Rebaptizers have been ordered to give because you spend the fine in buying persons to rebaptize?

Possidius also, in the *Life of Augustine*, chapter 12:

> Crispinus, he says, was DECLARED a heretic by a written judgment in the proconsular court. For him a Catholic bishop interceded with the judge [Col. 1214C], that the gold fine not be exacted; and this favor was obtained for him. But when, ungrateful, he had appealed to the most pious Emperor, a response due to the report was issued by the Emperor, and a command followed that the Donatists are HERETICS in every place whatsoever, and that they must EVERYWHERE be held subject to the rights of all LAWS enacted against heretics. Consequently both the judge, because of his office, and Crispinus himself—who had by no means been compelled to pay—were commanded to pay ten pounds of gold into the rights of the fisc.

This last passage from Possidius nearly expresses the sense and words of this law itself. He says that the Donatists are heretics. The law itself has “heretics of Donatist superstition,” and Law 44 below, “Donatist heretics,” on which more shortly. He says, “in absolutely no place”; likewise the law itself says, “in whatever place.” He says that they “must everywhere be held subject to the rights of all laws enacted against heretics”; the law itself says, “the tenor of the law being preserved.” Finally, he says they were commanded, since they had not been required to pay, to pay ten pounds of gold into the rights of the fisc. In the law itself Honorius says: “We decree that they shall pay the penalty due without delay.”

Therefore there is now no doubt [Col. 1214D] that this is that law of Honorius imposing upon Donatist heretics the fine of ten pounds of gold: heretical Donatists, I say. By this single expression Honorius indicates the rationale of this law and why he extends to the Donatists the fine generally imposed by his father Theodosius the Great upon heretics: because they too are heretics. Augustine likewise indicates this in Letter 50 to Boniface and Possidius in chapter 12 of the *Life of Augustine*, in the passages cited above. For this reason the same Honorius also said “Donatist heretics” in Law 44 below, where see still more that I shall say; and in Law 41, “heretics, whether Donatists or Manichaeans”; and in Law 46, “lest the vanity of the Donatists or of the other heretics.”

Although, more precisely, this term “heretics” seems still to refer to the ministers, clerics, and bishops of the Donatists. This penalty was not imposed by this law upon all Donatists, nor were all Donatists fined—which happened only later, in Laws 52 and 54 below—and then by different penalties. Finally, the history of this affair is as follows: in the preceding year the African Fathers had decreed that Honorius be asked to impose that monetary fine [Col. 1215B] only upon violent Donatists and Circumcellions. But both Crispinus’s appeal and the wounds [Col. 1215C] of the bishop of Vaga induced Honorius to impose the monetary penalty on all confessing or convicted clerics and ministers of the Donatists. Yet in this same year, seven months after the embassy of the African Fathers and before this law, Honorius had imposed a much harsher penalty upon Donatists who rebaptized—namely, confiscation of property—as the said Laws 4 and 5, at the end, *That Holy Baptism Shall Not Be Repeated*, show. J. G.] [Col. 1212A]

[Col. 1212B] We decree that heretics of Donatist superstition, in whatever place, whether confessing or convicted, shall, with the tenor of the law preserved, pay the penalty due without delay. Given on 8 December at Ravenna, in the second consulship of Stilicho and the consulship of Anthemius.

## XXV. DECREE OF THE COUNCIL HELD AT CARTHAGE, IN THE BASILICA OF THE SECOND DISTRICT, ON THE IDES OF JUNE, IN THE SEVENTH CONSULSHIP OF HONORIUS AND THE SECOND CONSULSHIP OF THEODOSIUS AUGUSTUS

Concerning congregations or dioceses converted from the Donatists.

[Col. 1213A]

Those congregations which have been converted from the Donatists and [Col. 1214A] have had bishops ought, without doubt, to be allowed to have them without consulting the council. But congregations which have had a bishop and, upon his death, wish not to have a bishop of their own but to belong to the diocese of some bishop, are not to be denied this. It was also proposed that bishops who converted any congregations to Catholicism before the imperial law concerning unity was enacted ought themselves to retain them. But from the law of unity onward, all Catholic bishops ought to claim for themselves the churches of those places to which, under the heretics, the places had belonged—whether of heretics converted to Catholicism or not converted—the dioceses, and whatever church documents or property-rights may belong to them. Those who have appropriated anything after the law was enacted, when challenged, shall restore what was appropriated. (*Council of Africa*, canon 66; *Code of Canons of the African Church*, canon 99.)

## XXVI. OCCASION OF THE LAWS THAT FOLLOW

At the Council of Carthage of the following year, 407, on 16 June, Bishop Fortunatianus again undertook an embassy [Col. 1215B] against Pagans and heretics. At another council in the same year 407, held at Carthage on 13 October, Bishops Restitutus and Florentius undertook an embassy against Pagans and heretics, at the time when Severus and Macarius were killed; and because of their case Bishops Evodius, Theasius, and Victor were beaten.

The reason for the embassy may be learned from Augustine’s Letter 96 to Olympius, section 2: namely, that through a new edict of the Emperor the enemies of the Church might know that the laws sent, while Stilicho was alive, concerning the destruction of idols and the correction of heretics had been established by the will of the most pious Emperor [Col. 1216A]. They either deceitfully assert, or willingly suppose, that these measures were taken without his knowledge or against his will; and on this account they make the minds of the uninstructed most turbulent and dangerously and violently hostile to Catholics. This, then, was the occasion of the laws that follow.

## 221 A.D. 408. XXVII. LAWS OF HONORIUS RENEWING THE PENALTIES ENACTED AGAINST DONATISTS AND OTHER HERETICS

From the *Theodosian Code*, Book XVI, Title V, *On Heretics*, Law XLI. Emperors Arcadius, Honorius, and Theodosius Augusti, to Porphyry, Proconsul of Africa.

Although punishment is accustomed to purge crimes, we nevertheless wish to reform the perverse wills of men through the admonition of repentance. Therefore, whoever among the heretics—whether Donatists, Manichaeans, or adherents of any other perverse opinion and sect—having been joined to profane rites, receives by a simple confession the Catholic faith and merit, which we desire all men to observe, even though he has nourished an evil so inveterate by long and persistent reflection that he seems liable even to laws previously enacted: nevertheless, we judge that, as soon as he has confessed God in simple religion, he is to be absolved from every penalty.

[Note: [Col. 1215C] By this constitution of Honorius, a wholly humane and generous pardon is granted throughout Africa to repentant or converted heretics—Donatists, Manichaeans, and the like—just as in the same year by Law XL immediately above, in the words “otherwise,” pardon was granted only to the children of Manichaeans, not to the Manichaeans themselves; and just as it is granted to repentant and converted children of Donatists by Law 4 below, *That Holy Baptism Shall Not Be Repeated*.

Indeed, by this law pardon is granted to repentant or converted persons upon a simple confession, at whatever time it may finally be made, even if they are converted by a late confession at the very point when execution is to take place; even though they have nourished an inveterate evil through long and persistent reflection [Col. 1215D], even amidst dangers themselves and in miseries themselves, having invoked the help of religion. Honorius intends that it make no difference—though this seems to have been the chief point of doubt—whether they fell into heresy before or after he enacted laws against heretics and then converted. Conversion of heretics is never too late for avoiding the penalties prescribed for heretics. Thus, I say, Honorius speaks generally, both concerning the avoidance of penalties and concerning abolition, as he calls it. All this ought to be noted as something distinctive.

In contrast, as regards acquiring an accruing benefit, I see that the eighth Council of Carthage, held in 404 three years earlier, had approved some distinction of time, as is clear from Canon 93 of the African Code:

> But for those who wish to correct themselves for the sake of unity and peace, access to taking an inheritance should remain open without the prohibition of this law, if anything by gift or inheritance has come to them while they are still established in heretical error [Col. 1216B]; excepting, however, those who, when sued, should think that they must pass over to Catholicism, because in their case it is credible that they preferred Catholic unity not from fear of heavenly judgment but from greed for earthly advantage.

Certainly, although pardon was offered to repentant apostates, it was given only to apostates who were catechumens, not to those who, from among the faithful or *competentes*—that is, after receiving holy baptism—had fallen into apostasy. Their offense is not erased by repentance; such is the ruling of Law 4 below, *On Apostates*, which Cujas never understood in the *Paratitlon*.

Therefore Honorius wished heretics to be absolved by the support of just repentance, however late. Nor do I doubt that this was enacted by Honorius on the occasion of the tenth Council of Carthage, which was held in this same year, A.D. 407, nearly six months earlier; just as, at its request, he gave Law 34 above, *On Bishops*, which must be joined to this law, as has been proved there. This is my first indication of the matter.

A second indication is supplied by the canon of the council I have mentioned, where Canon 99 of the African Code contains, among other things, the following:

> Those congregations converted from the Donatists which had bishops ought, without doubt, to be allowed to have them without consulting the council. But congregations which had a bishop and, on his death, wished not to have their own bishop but to belong to the diocese of some bishop, should not be denied this. It was also proposed that bishops who converted any congregations to Catholicism before the imperial law concerning unity was enacted should themselves retain them. But from the law—[that is, after the law]—of unity onward, all Catholic bishops ought to claim for themselves the churches of the places to which, under the heretics, the places had belonged, whether of heretics converted to Catholicism or not converted; the dioceses, and whatever church documents or property-rights may belong to them. Those who have appropriated anything after the law was enacted shall, when challenged, restore what was appropriated.

You see that converted persons are also being discussed; you see that the times mingled here are distinguished: namely, conversion before the law concerning unity was enacted, and conversion after it was enacted. JACOB GOTHOFR.]

…so that, with respect to every liability—whether it was incurred before or is incurred afterwards, which [Col. 1217A] we do not wish—even if punishment appears to press most urgently upon the guilty, it shall suffice for abolition that they have condemned their error by their own judgment and embraced the name of almighty God, sought even amid dangers themselves. For in miseries the assistance of religion, when invoked, ought never to be lacking.

Therefore, just as we order the former laws which we have established for the destruction of sacrilegious minds to be enforced with every effect of execution, so we judge that those who prefer the confession, however late, of simple faith and religion are not bound by the laws enacted. We have enacted this so that all may know that profane human pursuits do not lack punishment, and that the support of the laws is also present for the advancement of right worship. Given on 15 November at Rome, in the seventh consulship of Honorius and the second consulship of Theodosius Augustus.

## XXVIII.

In the same place, Law XLIII. The same Augusti, to Curtius, Praetorian Prefect.

[Col. 1217B]

Everything decreed by the authority of general laws by us against Donatists—who are also called Montenses—Manichaeans, Priscillianists, or Gentiles [Col. 1218A], we decree not merely shall remain in force, but shall be carried into the fullest execution and effect. Thus even the buildings of these persons, or of the Caelicolae also—who hold assemblies of some new doctrine, I know not what—shall be assigned to the churches. The penalty prescribed by law shall bind as though convicted those who have confessed themselves Donatists or have avoided communion with Catholics under the pretext of a savage religion, even though they pretend to be Christians, etc. Given on 15 November at Rome, in the consulship of Bassus and Philippus.

## 222 XXIX.

In the same place, Law XLIV. The same Augusti, to Habe Donate, *[official title abbreviated: K. NB]*.

[Note: These laws, as also law XIX below concerning Pagans (which must be joined to them), confirm the constitutions previously issued by Honorius in A.D. 408, after the killing of Stilicho, against Donatists, Manichaeans, Priscillianists, and Gentiles; indeed, the same measures are extended to the Coelicolists, of whom I shall speak under their proper heading, concerning Jews and Coelicolists. They are confirmed, I say, through the Praetorian Prefecture of Italy, and specifically at Rome (as is shown by the mention of the Montenses, who certainly existed nowhere but at Rome). For the Donatists were called Montenses at Rome because they first had their church there upon a hill.

Optatus of Milevis, book 2: “They enclosed a certain cave outside the city with steps, where at that time they were able to hold an assembly; hence they were called Montenses.” Augustine, in his book On Heresies, addressed to Quodvultdeus: “These heretics are called Montenses in the city of Rome; they are accustomed to have a bishop sent to them from Africa.” He also mentions them in Epistle 165. Jerome, in his Chronicle under the year 356: “Some followers of Donatus are also called Montenses, because they first began to have their church on a hill at Rome.” And in Against Lucifer: “Marcionites, Valentinians, Montenses or Campates.” And in his letter to Marcellus: “When Reticius, bishop of Augustodunum, who formerly had been sent to Rome by the emperor Constantine [wrongly read ‘Constantinopolitan’] under bishop Sylvester on account of the affair of the Montenses.”

Augustine, Epistle 165, speaking of a certain Donatist bishop: “But, he says, they sent from Africa, by a side route, one ordained there, who, presiding over a few Africans in the city of Rome, propagated the designation of Montenses or Cuzupitans.” Here Balduin conjectured that *Rupitans* should be read instead of *Cuzupitans*. For Augustine likewise says in On the Unity of the Church, chapter 3: “For if the holy Scriptures designate the Church only in Africa, and among the few Rupitans or Montenses at Rome, and in the house or estate of one Spanish woman, then, whatever else may be produced from other documents, none but the Donatists possess the Church.” Clearly they were called Rupitans by an analogous allusion and mockery to that in Montenses and Campates. Thus the Donatists were called Montenses at Rome. Therefore Epiphanius is mistaken in saying that the Novatians at Rome were called Μοντεσίους, “Montesians.” Still more mistaken are those who suppose that the Montenses were so named from Montanus.

Now to the matter. Moreover, the subscription of law 43 above under this title, and of law 9 below concerning Pagans, proves that this law pertains to the city of Rome: “Given at Rome,” that is, issued and posted there. For at this time Honorius was residing at Ravenna (as not only the chronology of the Theodosian Code but also Zosimus teaches). Again, it applies expressly to Africa; for Donatus, to whom law 44 is addressed, was at this time proconsul of Africa, as law 19 above, concerning penalties, shows; likewise Augustine, Epistles 137 and 138.

The occasion for issuing these laws was this. Stilicho having been killed in this very year, scarcely three months earlier, the heretics and pagans immediately began to spread the claim that the laws sent forth against them, concerning the destruction of idols and correction of heretics, and specifically dispatched to Africa while Stilicho was alive, had not been established by the will of Honorius, but without his knowledge or against his will. Augustine states this expressly in Epistle 129 to Count Olympius, master of the offices, to whom the preceding law is addressed. They therefore considered the laws void and demanded that they should be rescinded along with Stilicho’s other acts. Indeed, taking this occasion, they rose up against Catholics and threatened them with violence. Catholics thereupon requested, both privately and publicly, that those laws be renewed and confirmed.

Thus the African Fathers sent an embassy to Honorius this year, on 13 October, against pagans and heretics; the bishops went privately to the imperial court. Augustine too, privately and for that purpose, gave Olympius the letter I have mentioned, which ought here to be printed entire were I not exceeding the bounds of these commentaries. From it, indeed, it is clear concerning the plots of Gentiles and heretics after Stilicho’s death, of which I have spoken; concerning private complaints and the journey to the court; concerning envoys to be sent from Africa and admitted to Honorius; and concerning the speed which was to be shown. Stirred by such grave complaints, and, as is credible, by the exertions of Olympius, Honorius promulgated these laws to confirm his earlier laws. “All things,” says Honorius, “which have been decreed by us under the authority of general laws, we decree not merely to remain in force, but to be carried into the fullest execution and effect.”

Nevertheless, I am of the opinion that these laws were not issued in response to the petition of the African Fathers—for Augustine testifies in the said Epistle 179 to Olympius that their envoys arrived too late to reach Honorius—but in response to the private complaints of Augustine himself and others. Those complaints reached Honorius in midwinter, as Augustine himself testifies, and arrived before the envoys. Augustine himself urgently pressed Olympius that the business be hastened with the most diligent insistence, that it be expedited upon whatever occasion first arose, and that it be postponed in no way; even before he saw the bishops who had travelled for that purpose, it should be accelerated as soon as possible by vigilance. Therefore law 46, at the beginning of the following year, was finally issued in response to the request of the African Fathers.

Accordingly, Honorius commands that the Donatist heretics be punished, and expressly in law 44, because at this time they themselves had threatened Catholics with violence and death, some bishops even having been killed throughout Africa, of which Donatus, to whom that law is addressed, was proconsul. Augustine, however, in a special letter to this very Donatus, proconsul of Africa—namely Epistle 127—earnestly requested that Donatists be restrained, not killed. Among other things, observe the following:

“Therefore, from fear of temporal judgments and laws, lest they incur the penalties of eternal judgment, we desire that they be corrected, not slain; nor do we wish discipline concerning them to be neglected, nor that they be subjected to the punishments which they deserve. Restrain their sins, then, in such a way that there may remain persons who can repent of having sinned. We therefore beseech you that, when you hear the causes of the Church, however grievously and wickedly you may learn that she has been assailed or afflicted by injuries, you forget that you possess the power to kill; do not forget our petition.”

And shortly afterward: “Meanwhile, let the Donatist heretics quickly learn through an edict of your Excellency that the laws issued against their error remain in force, laws which they now suppose and proclaim to be powerless, so that perhaps even in this way they may spare us to some extent. Moreover, you will greatly assist the fruitfulness of our labours and dangers if you do not take care that their utterly vain sect, full of impious arrogance, be so crushed by imperial laws that they may seem to themselves or their followers to suffer whatever troubles they endure for truth and justice; but, when this is requested of you, permit them to be convicted and instructed by the clearest proofs of established facts in the official records, whether of your Excellency or of lesser judges,” etc.

What concerns the Gentiles will be treated more particularly in the said law 19 below, concerning Pagans. Among other provisions, it is commanded that the buildings in which assemblies of heretics and others are held be claimed for the churches; the same is also enacted in law 59 below, concerning …; and in laws 54, 57, and 65 below under this title. But as Honorius ordered by the said law 19, which must be joined to this one, that buildings of temples be claimed for public use, so shortly afterward he ordered the same concerning the buildings of heretics.

Further, it should be noted that these enactments—indeed capital punishment—are expressly imposed by law 44 upon Donatist heretics, of whom mention has already been made, and upon Coelicolists. A more suitable place for speaking of them will occur under law 19 of the same Honorius below, concerning Jews, issued in the following year, 409. In any event, this provision concerning Donatist heretics must be read in conjunction with the present law. Honorius, extending to them the general law issued by his father Theodosius against heretics, wished by this wording to state the reason why he extended it to Donatists as well: because they too were heretics. Similar formulas therefore occur in other constitutions of Honorius, laws 39 and 41 above and law 46 below. They correspond entirely to what Augustine writes in Epistle 50 to Boniface, and Possidius in the Life of Augustine, chapter 12, whose words I cited under law 39; and again to Epistle 127, whose words I quoted a little above.

Therefore the learned Petit is mistaken in thinking that the term “heretics” must here be joined with “Jews,” as though the passage indicated that the Coelicolists were Jewish heretics. More on this under the said law 19 below, title concerning Jews and Coelicolists. —JACOB GOTHOFRIED.]

The unprecedented and unheard-of audacity of Donatist heretics and Jews has revealed itself in their desire to disturb the sacraments of the Catholic faith. Therefore, lest this pestilence and contagion spread and flow more widely abroad, we command that the punishment of just correction be inflicted upon those who attempt anything contrary or opposed to the Catholic sect. Given on the eighth day before the Kalends of December at Ravenna, in the consulship of Bassus and Philippus.

223. XXX.

IBID., LAW XLV. The same Augusti to Theodorus, Prefect of the Praetorium, for the second time.

[Note: Heretical assemblies are again prohibited by Honorius in A.D. 408. This duty of prohibiting such assemblies is imposed upon the defenders, curiales, and staffs of judges, as in his other laws, law 40 above and law 4 below, *That Holy Baptism …*, where see what I have said, and the following law 46. The places in which the assemblies have been held are ordered confiscated. Furthermore, heretics who maintain doctrines contrary to the Catholic faith—that is, teachers of heretics—are to be deported, with confiscation of their property.

Meanwhile observe the phrase, “one who differs from a priest of the Catholic Church,” that is, one who holds separate meetings from the bishop of the Catholic Church, rejecting the pursuit of unity, which is the mark of the Catholic Church and to which heretics had been invited three years earlier by law 35 above. There is no doubt that this law applies to the same Donatists, whose attacks made it necessary for Honorius to confront them with so many laws. Thus those are deemed heretics who disagree with priests of the Catholic Church and meet unlawfully; and so heretics are restored to communion with the priests of the Catholic Church. To this also pertain laws 2 and 3 above concerning the Catholic faith, law 62 below under this title, and the final law below concerning matters contrary to religion. And rightly so, since, as is said here, they are truly priests of the Catholic Church, and the subordinate rule here corresponds to the principal rule.

Likewise observe the three classes of persons—the defenders, curiales, and all staffs—upon whom this care was imposed, that they should proceed against heretics. Law 40 above also attests this, and the following law 46 will attest it. Finally, I am led by no slight conjecture to think that law 39 above concerning bishops and law 3 of the Code concerning episcopal hearings should be joined to this law. If so, the conclusion from these three interconnected laws is that Honorius took various measures jointly to ensure that due reverence be accorded to the judgment of Catholic bishops: first, whether one considers doctrine itself; second, their assemblies; third, judicial inquiry and hearing. —JACOB GOTHOFRIED.]

Let the watchfulness of the defenders, curiales, and all official staffs ensure that no one who differs from a priest of the Catholic Church has the opportunity to hold an unlawful assembly within any city or in any secluded part of its territory. We decree that the places themselves likewise be transferred to public ownership, with every excuse excluded; and that those who dare to dispute and maintain matters condemned by divine institution be proscribed and driven into exile. Given on the fifth day before the Kalends of December at Ravenna, in the consulship of Bassus and Philippus.

IN THE YEAR OF OUR LORD 409. XXXI.

IBID., LAW XLVI. The same Augusti to Theodorus, Prefect of the Praetorium, for the second time. After other matters.

[Note: The laws and penalties against Donatists, other heretics, Jews, and likewise Gentiles are confirmed again by this constitution of Honorius at the beginning of A.D. 409. A penalty is imposed upon judges: loss of rank, and indeed a still graver punishment for affront to the emperor; upon officials and curiales, the same penalty which he had previously established. This appears to me to be the constitution of Honorius—rather than laws 43 and 44—which was issued in response to the request and complaint of the African Fathers. The basis of this conjecture I have also stated under that law. For Augustine testifies in Epistle 129 to Count Olympius and master of the offices that private complaints reached the court and Honorius in midwinter, that is, at the end of the preceding year, 408—when laws 44 and 45 above were certainly issued—but that the complaints of the African Fathers followed only afterward, and then this law.

Yet they always had the same purpose: namely, that it should be clear that the laws previously issued against heretics and similar persons were not to be ascribed to Stilicho, and thus annulled upon his death—as the heretics and Gentiles alleged—but must remain in force. To this pertains the language of law 43: “All things which have been decreed by us under the authority of general laws, we decree not merely to remain in force, but to be carried into the fullest execution and effect.” Likewise to the same effect belong the words of this law: “Lest the Donatists, etc., suppose that the provisions of laws previously issued against them have grown lax, let all judges know that their commands must be obeyed with loyal devotion; and among their principal duties, they must not hesitate to execute whatever we have decreed against them.” —J. G.]

Lest the Donatists, or the vanity of the remaining heretics, or the error of others to whom the observance of Catholic communion cannot be commended—Jews and Gentiles, whom people commonly call Pagans—suppose that the provisions of laws previously issued against them have grown lax, let all judges know that those commands must be obeyed with loyal devotion; and, among their principal duties, let them not hesitate to execute whatever we have decreed against them.

If any judge, in a position of authority, should omit to enforce the present law, let him know that, having lost his rank, he will incur a more serious indignation of Our Clemency. His staff also, if it has failed in its own safety by neglecting to make the required report, shall, after punishment of its three principal officers, be subject to a fine of twenty pounds of gold. Likewise, if municipal councils and duumvirs, in their own cities or territories, conceal any such offence in favour of the guilty, let them know that they will incur the penalty of deportation and loss of their own property. Given on the seventeenth day before the Kalends of February at Ravenna, in the consulship of the Augusti Honorius for the seventh time and Theodosius for the third time.

IN THE YEAR OF OUR LORD 410. 224. XXXII.

IBID., LAW LI, BY WHICH HE ABROGATES THE EDICT BY WHICH LIBERTY HAD BEEN GRANTED TO HERETICS. The same Augusti to Heraclianus, Count of Africa.

[Note: By this constitution, at the end of August in A.D. 410, in the consulship of Varanes, the Emperor Honorius invalidates throughout Africa the *Oraculum*, that is, the edict, law, or rescript by which he had granted heretics authority publicly to practise their rites and to assemble or gather, imposing the penalties of proscription and death. This is, indeed, that very edict invalidated by the present law, which the African Fathers mention in that same year 410, two months and somewhat more earlier. Its words, as preserved in the Code of the African Church, are these:

“After the consulship of the most glorious emperors Honorius for the eighth time and Theodosius for the third time, Augusti, on the eighteenth day before the Kalends of July, at Carthage, in the basilica of the second district. In this council Florentius, Possidius, Praesidius, and Benenatus, bishops, undertook an embassy against the Donatists at the time when a law was issued allowing each person freely to choose the observance of Christianity.”

Balsamon understood these words incorrectly and connected them with the twelfth canon of Neocaesarea. But the meaning of the Fathers is that Honorius had shortly before issued a law by which heretics and Donatists had been allowed to practise their rites. This is the *Oraculum* which is at once mentioned and abrogated by this law. Indeed, scarcely two months later, in his Instructions to Marcellinus, tribune and notary, sent to the Carthaginian conference—a portion of which is law 3 below concerning Religion—Honorius himself mentions both laws, that one and this one together, and confirms the latter:

“Nor is the language of the heavenly *Oraculum* unknown to our conscience; the savage interpretation of the Donatists declares that its language can advance their error. Although it had invited their depraved minds more gently to correction, we nevertheless ordered it to be abolished even before [namely, by the present law], lest any occasion be furnished to superstitions. We now likewise decree, by similar authority, that the fraudulent intrusion be excluded; and we declare, and properly so, that we gladly remove things which had been established, lest anyone suppose that, with us as authors, he can offend against divine worship.”

So it is found in the Acts of the Carthaginian Conference, pp. 5, 256, and 260. Therefore, in law 3 below concerning Religion, itself also a portion of those Instructions which I have mentioned, the “novel intrusion”—for I shall show that it must there be read thus—mentioned there is this very *Oraculum*, invalidated both by the present law and by the aforesaid provisions.

Moreover, as the preceding passage from the African Code and the chronology itself show, this law seems to have been issued in response to the request of the African Fathers. Honorius had been more lenient toward heretics in the final months of the preceding year, 409, and the first months of this year, particularly toward Donatists, whose depraved minds he believed ought to be invited more gently to correction, as he himself says in the passage cited above. Indeed, he had been lenient toward pagans also; for Zosimus, book 5, p. 821, testifies that at the time I have mentioned the law by which enemies of the Catholic sect—that is, both heretics and pagans—had been barred from the military palace, and thus law 42 above, had been abrogated.

Baronius also conjectures the causes of both laws in Africa: namely, that the former law, which is here abrogated, was forced from Honorius by the necessity of affairs, lest otherwise the Donatists, angered by so many laws, should support the party of the usurper Attalus, who seemed about to attack Africa; but that, when the danger had ceased, Attalus having been deposed, it was repealed by this law at the request of the African Fathers. Besides the chronology itself, this is made highly probable by the name of Heraclianus, Count of Africa, to whom this law is addressed.

For this is that Heraclianus who adhered to Honorius’ cause and retained Africa under Honorius’ rule. Against him, at the end of the preceding year, the usurper Attalus sent Constantinus with an army into Africa, hoping to take possession of it. He thus inspired the emperor Honorius with such terror and fear—as Honorius himself in some measure reveals in law 1 above concerning frontier lands—that, should the African expedition succeed for Attalus, Honorius intended to abandon the empire and flee eastward. But Constantinus was soon killed with his followers by Heraclianus’ army. Heraclianus then began to defend Africa all the more vigorously; having assigned guards to the African shores and ports, he forbade grain to be shipped to Rome. Hence famine arose at Rome; soon afterward Alaric stripped Attalus of imperial power, as Zosimus, book 6, pp. 827–830, and Sozomen, book 9, chapter 8, relate. More concerning this Attalus may be found under the penultimate and final laws above concerning pardon for crimes; under law 1 above concerning frontier lands; law 2 above concerning guards of coasts and roads; and law 6 above concerning remission of debts.

This law was repeated in A.D. 416 in precisely the same words, though with some additions, in law 56, where I shall discuss it. In both laws, the penalty of death with which Honorius threatens heretics who hold unlawful assemblies should be noted. He adopted this policy after the frequent attempts, fraudulent petitions, and factions of heretics. Otherwise the penalty of death was not commonly enacted against heretics, except against certain detestable and execrable persons, especially in laws 9, 51, and 56 above; but more on this in the *Paratitla* and under law 28 of this title.

The learned man is certainly mistaken who says that this law imposes the penalties of proscription and death successively—namely, that heretics are first punished by proscription and then, if they disregard that penalty, by death. Both penalties are imposed here simultaneously by the words of the constitution. Honorius further intensifies the penalty against Donatists because, though invited by gentler edicts or even subjected to penalties, they daily increased and exercised their fury; hence strong fear seemed necessary. —J. G.]

With the *Oraculum* wholly removed, through which heretical superstitions had crept into the exercise of their rites, let all enemies of the holy law know that they shall be punished both by proscription and by death if they further attempt, in the execrable audacity of their crime, to assemble publicly. Given on the eighth day before the Kalends of September, in the consulship of Varanes, a man of clarissimus rank.

225. IN THE YEAR OF OUR LORD 411. ACTS OF THE CONFERENCE HELD AT CARTHAGE BY ORDER OF THE EMPEROR HONORIUS BETWEEN CATHOLICS AND DONATISTS, BEFORE MARCELLINUS, A MAN OF CLARISSIMUS RANK, TRIBUNE AND NOTARY, AFTER THE CONSULSHIP OF VARANES, A MAN OF CLARISSIMUS RANK.

[Col. 1223]

[Col. 1223A]

PREFACE TO THE WORK, BY P. MASSON.

The Acts of the Carthaginian Conference were held by command of the most merciful emperor Honorius, during the pontificate of Innocent I, in the year after the consulship of Varanes, when there was no consul in the West because of the extreme disorder of affairs, Rome having recently been captured by Alaric, king of the Goths. The mandate ordering this disputation to be held specifies a place and a day; but inquisitive persons will search in vain for a consul, since there was none.

The bishops of the Catholic Church had requested that a conference be held against Donatus’ party. This is acknowledged by seven of them who were selected: Aurelius, Alypius, Augustine, Vincentius, Fortunatus, Fortunatianus, and Possidius; and by an equal number of Donatists: Primianus, Petilianus, Emeritus, Montanus, Gaudentius, Adeodatus, and Protasius. Among the absent bishops of their own party, in order to deceive, the latter named Felix as though he were bishop of the city of Rome, although the Catholics testified that Innocent then occupied the see, as was true and as annals of the highest credibility record for the year 411 from the Virgin’s childbirth.

The disputation is divided into the first, second, and third hearings. The third was held on the sixth day before the Ides of June; on that day Marcellinus, the judicial examiner, pronounced his judgment, declaring, to use the words of the divine Augustine, that the Donatists had been refuted by the Catholics through the disclosure of every proof. Emeritus and certain obstinate Donatists later slanderously alleged that the judgment had been bought by the Catholic examiner and issued at night. Augustine refutes them with great acuteness. Indeed, Augustine deserves praise because he wrote a very brief epitome of the conference, which will be all the more useful because a large part of the third hearing, missing here, must necessarily be sought from it.

There the question is treated of Caecilianus and Mensurius, and of those who surrendered the sacred books and the furnishings of the Church, while Diocletian and Maximian were persecuting the Church with utmost severity. Before Augustine, Optatus of Milevis had also narrated this matter fully in his work On Heresies. Augustine had indeed disputed against the Donatists before the conference and published books on the baptism of infants; he likewise argued against the letters of Petilianus, a bishop formerly a forensic advocate, and almost crushed the grammarian Cresconius in debate.
