After the conference, in the consulship of Honorius for the twelfth time and Theodosius for the eighth, Augustine himself, as he states in his preface, showed sufficiently in a separate book entitled *On the Proceedings with Emeritus* what he did with Emeritus. Augustine states in the second book of his Retractions that Emeritus was one of the seven whom the Donatists had selected for defending their cause and who had laboured most zealously in that cause; Possidius also records this in his Life of Augustine after Emeritus’ death. Finally, Augustine composed two books against Gaudentius, bishop of Thamugadi, whom he demonstrates in the same book to have belonged to that number.

The supreme benefit of that judgment was this: although the Donatists appealed to the emperor, it was confirmed by Honorius. We have appended to this disputation the edict from the Theodosian Code. In obedience to it, the Donatist people immediately abandoned their bishops and returned to the Catholic Church; and from Optatus’ most ancient manuscript codex we have taken care to add certain questions necessary for understanding the conference.

Orosius, in book 7, testifies that the judicial examiner was prudent, diligent, and most eager for honourable studies. Not long after the capture of Rome, Augustine wrote to him the twenty books *On the City of God*, as their preface indicates. Jerome speaks, in book 3 Against the Pelagians, of Marcellinus’ death; it must have been violent, for Orosius calls his killer and assassin by name. Marcellus also deserves praise: this volume of the Acts of the Conference, extremely copious and diffuse, he separated and compiled with “measured brevity,” as he himself says, as may be seen from his letter to Severianus and Julianus.

We think no more need be said here, because Balduin, my teacher of civil law, who had possessed the acts only on loan in ancient parchment leaves from Tillus, bishop of Meaux, published an elegant commentary upon them.

[Col. 1224C]

226. PREFACE OF THE MOST DISTINGUISHED MAN BALUZE TO THE SAME CONFERENCE.

The extant Acts of the Carthaginian Conference between the Catholic and Donatist bishops are not complete, but an abridgment of those written before Marcellinus the notary. For, since they were very lengthy, as Augustine says in Epistle 50, and since there was consequently a danger that they might come into contempt, Severianus and Julianus asked Marcellus the *Memorialis*, who had attended the conference and shared with Marcellinus the labour of weighing the dispute, to remove the tedium of reading by the remedy of brevity.

For the Donatists, unable to obtain from the judicial examiner either that the conference should not be held or that the case itself should not be heard at all, “achieved this,” Augustine says, “by much speaking: that what was done should be difficult to read.” Therefore Marcellus the *Memorialis*, complying with the requests of his friends, cut away what was superfluous and arranged the acts in the form in which they are now read by us.

“They had indeed once been carefully transcribed, written out, and collated,” says Balduin, “but had been lost through the ravages of time and the negligence of posterity, until at last, in the year 1566, they came into the hands of Balduin himself through the kindness of the most distinguished man John Tillus, bishop of Meaux.” That they did not perish entirely, we owe, I think—whatever others may think to the contrary—to the most noble Church of Lyons, which preserved this illustrious monument of antiquity in its library. Evidence for this is also provided by the ancient inscription placed at the beginning of the old copy, similar to that found at the head of the Tertullian codex which Archbishop Agobard gave to the same Church. Thus one reads on the front of these Acts:

**A BOOK OFFERED AT THE ALTAR OF SAINT STEPHEN IN FULFILMENT OF THE VOW OF FULCHERIUS, CANON.**
Then Baldwin, who rightly believed that a great treasure had been placed in his hands, read and weighed these proceedings with care; and, while they were being published, he brought out a history of this conference. He might, had he wished, have published the proceedings in a more summary form. But he undoubtedly understood that the old manuscript contained many errors which he intended to remove, as well as many passages requiring explanation if any benefit was to be derived from them. He would indeed have rendered a most welcome service to the Louvain theologian who undertook to correct Augustine’s *Breviculus*. For that man testifies that, having wished to obtain these acts at great cost, and having ordered inquiries among the friends and heirs of the then-deceased Baldwin, he learned that they had disappeared he knew not where. They had passed into the ownership and possession of the most celebrated Angelo Vergezio, a Greek indeed, but most learned in Latin; from him Claude Mondin, Advocate of Paris, afterwards obtained them. Papirius Masson writes that they were preserved through Mondin’s good offices. Their first edition accordingly appeared at Paris in 1589, through the efforts of Masson himself; but, regrettably, it was so faulty that, besides the mistakes of the ancient copyist, many new ones were introduced by him. At length, in February 1594, this venerable manuscript, worth its weight in gold, came into the hands of the great Pierre Pithou. Mondin gave it to him in exchange for manuscripts of Henry III, King of the French. Pithou, having collated it with the old exemplar, produced an edition better than Masson’s; [Col. 1225D] yet not such that, after the laborious and learned watchfulness of that eminent man, very many more things did not still remain to be corrected.

We therefore, understanding both how important it was to have these proceedings sound and how much benefit would accrue to the Church if they appeared in a more corrected form, willingly undertook this labour. We shall receive a sufficiently ample reward, whatever the quality of our work, if this endeavour of ours pleases the Church and the community of learned persons. First, then, we compared the editions of these distinguished men with the very old exemplar which they had used, now believed to be in the exceedingly rich Colbert Library. It is to be valued exceedingly highly, since it has not hitherto been ascertained that another exists anywhere. Next, to the extent of our powers, we removed the errors of the ancient copyist, which are very numerous, [Col. 1226A] following either the judgement of very learned men who had incidentally endeavoured to remedy various passages of these proceedings, or our own conjectures when they seemed certain to us. For what Jacques Cujas notes in *Observations*, Book IV, chapter 31—that the old method of writing by abbreviations introduced many errors into the books of civil law—may be affirmed of these proceedings without any risk of censure.

Moreover, we employed the authority of ancient writers, especially of Saint Augustine, bishop of Hippo, to whom, more than to all others in this matter, the Church is indebted. It would have been tedious to readers and not especially useful, while very burdensome to us, to give an account of every alteration we introduced into the text. We therefore generally passed over those that were obvious in silence; [Col. 1226B] but gave the reasons for those which seemed to involve some difficulty or required elucidation. We may indeed truly affirm that this edition of ours is much better than all those which have appeared up to this day. Those who compare it with the editions of Masson and Pithou, from which the rest arose, will readily understand this. For anyone with so much leisure will certainly easily observe how many things Masson and Pithou omitted which we have restored from the old manuscript, and how many errors escaped their notice which we have, as we think, corrected with reasonable success.

It is regrettable that we could not supply every gap, especially where the matter concerned restoring the names of twenty bishops of the Catholic Church which have fallen out in the recitation of the subscriptions. [Col. 1226C] Since, moreover, a large part of the third hearing is missing, and must necessarily be sought in Saint Augustine’s *Breviculus*, as Papirius Masson noted long ago, we have appended to the proceedings a fragment from that *Breviculus*, namely from the point at which the proceedings fail. How important it is for the Christian commonwealth to possess these documents sound and complete is evident even from the fact that Augustine himself testifies, in Letter 58 and in the book *On the Proceedings with Emeritus*, that they were read annually in the African churches.

At the urging of certain persons, we also appended to this fragment the names of the bishops of both parties recited at the hearing of the first day, and, separately, the names of those elected by each party to undertake the conference. For the same reason we there published the sermons delivered by that same holy bishop [Augustine] [Col. 1226D] as the conference approached and after it, which Possidius mentions in his catalogue of Augustine’s works. We further added the constitutions issued by Emperor Honorius after this conference, which we judge to refer to matters transacted in the conference, and which, we observe, several learned men have likewise understood in that way.

It remains for us to say something concerning the year in which these acts occurred. This inquiry would certainly be useless, since it is established that the conference was held in the year following the consulship of Varanes, unless Jacques Sirmond—a man most learned and one whom we must never name without praise—had assigned it to the second year after the consulship of Varanes, that is, to the year 412. His principal argument is that it is established that the conference began [Col. 1227A] on the Kalends of June, whereas from the sermon which Saint Augustine delivered as the conference approached, it is inferred that the fast of Pentecost had taken place shortly before the conference; in that year it ended on the fourth day before the Kalends of June.

“Pray with us,” Augustine says, “to the Lord with the solemn fasts which we already render to God; let us render them also for the cause. For now we are solemnly fasting after Pentecost; and certainly we should be fasting even if this cause did not exist.”

It is indeed true that in the year 412 Pentecost Sunday fell on the fourth day before the Kalends of June. But it cannot truly be said that the Pentecost fast ended on that day, since there was never any fast before Pentecost. Therefore the true and genuine sense, as I judge, of Augustine’s words is this: the fasts which we call the Ember Days of Pentecost were being observed, [Col. 1227B] fasts which the ancient law of the Church commands to be solemnly celebrated after Pentecost; and Augustine delivered that sermon as the conference approached. This is highly noteworthy. For it manifestly follows that, in the year when the bishops assembled at Carthage to hold the conference, the Pentecost Ember fast must have occurred before the Kalends of June, since the conference began on that day.

But that could not have occurred in the year 412, since Pentecost Sunday then fell on the fourth day before the Kalends of June, as noted above. The data agree more correctly with the year 411: Easter fell on the seventh day before the Kalends of April, Pentecost on the day before the Ides of May, and the Pentecost Ember fast began on the seventeenth day before the Kalends and ended on the fourteenth day before the Kalends of June—that is, ten days [Col. 1227C] before the bishops entered upon the dispute. For that the Catholic bishops were at Carthage on that day is clear from the first conference, chapters 27 and 29, and from the second conference, chapter 50.

[Col. 1228A] Meanwhile, while the day of the Kalends of June was awaited, the Catholic bishops, as they had often done before, conferred among themselves concerning ways of restoring and preserving unity in the African Church. Then an event truly memorable and of good example occurred, which rightly ought to be related here, so that it may serve as a kind of guide for following the divine Spirit who appears throughout every page of that conference. Saint Augustine relates it in *On the Proceedings with Emeritus*—a witness beyond every objection—in these words:

“I shall tell your charity and recall a most sweet and delightful thing which, with the Lord’s help, we experienced. Before the conference itself, when some brethren among us were discussing this matter, because bishops ought to exist—or ought not to exist—for the peace of Christ, [Col. 1228B] we must confess to you that, as we looked about among all our brethren and fellow bishops, those willing to undertake this and offer this humility as a sacrifice to God did not readily occur to us. We said, as people commonly do: ‘This man can; that man cannot; this one agrees to it; that one will not endure it’—speaking more from our suspicions, since we could not at all see their hearts.

“But when it came to be openly proposed in the council of all, so numerous, of almost three hundred bishops, they all blazed forth in such a way that they were ready to lay aside the episcopate for Christ’s unity—not to lose it, but to entrust it more safely to God. Scarcely two were found there to whom this displeased: one, an aged old man, who even dared to state this more freely; the other signified his will by a silent expression. But after the brotherly rebuke of all overwhelmed [Col. 1228C] that old man as he spoke his opposition more freely, he changed his opinion; and the other man changed his expression as well.”

[Col. 1227]

**229. ACCOUNT OF THE AFORESAID BISHOPS WHO UNDERTOOK THE CONFERENCE AT CARTHAGE**

[Col. 1229B] Not all the bishops, Catholic and Donatist alike, who had come to Carthage undertook the Carthaginian conference, but only eighteen from each party: namely, seven advocates, the same number of advisers, and four custodians of the records. In the case of the Catholics there is no doubt, for the names of every one of them are recorded in the mandate of the Council of Carthage, reported in the acts of the first hearing, chapter 55, and are individually enumerated in the acts of the third hearing, chapter 2.

In the latter passage the names are also given of the seven bishops upon whom the defence of Donatus’s party lay; only four advisers are joined to them, while the others are mentioned neither there nor elsewhere. Primianus of Carthage names two custodians of the records from the Donatist side in the acts of the first hearing, chapter 132: Victor of Hippo Diarrhytus [Col. 1229C] and Marinianus of Oea; and two others, namely Veratianus and Victor, are named there also, chapter 223. That Veratianus was bishop of the Church of Carpita is established by chapter 126. But it is difficult to say of what see Victor was bishop, since several Donatist bishops of that name occur in the Carthaginian conference.

We must now set out briefly what has been handed down concerning each. We shall begin with the Catholics.

First among the Catholic advocates is Aurelius, bishop of Carthage, a very well-known man whom Augustine, *Retractations*, Book II, chapter 21, calls “the venerable old man.” He presided over very many councils at Carthage and elsewhere in Africa, and Prosper rightly calls him, in his poem *Against the Ungrateful*, “the leader of the African council, whose intellect was Augustine.” The memory of Alypius of Thagaste, Augustine’s closest friend from his earliest years, is no less illustrious. He was a native of Thagaste, from one of its leading municipal families. He came to Rome shortly before Augustine and went with him to Milan; following Augustine’s purpose, he withdrew with him to Cassiciacum, a catechumen with a catechumen. Baptized at Milan, he returned to Africa and was later advanced to the bishopric of Thagaste. He was distinguished for learning and piety, and closely associated with Jerome, Sixtus, and the other Italians. He attended several African councils and possessed great authority among the African bishops.

Nothing need be said about Augustine, the third advocate. Vincentius of Colusita—or rather Culusita—a bishop in the proconsular province, attended the Councils of Carthage in 416 and 419. He is thought to be the same man praised by Paulinus in the final chapter of the *Life of Ambrose*. The name of Fortunatus of Constantine also occurs in the superscription of the Council of Milevis of 416; there too appears the name of Fortunatianus, who was elected at that council as one of the judges of the proconsular province and is honourably mentioned by Augustine in *Against the Letters of Petilian*, Book I, chapter 1, and Book III, chapter 38, and also in *On the One Baptism against the Same Man*, chapter 16. There he is called the successor in the see of Constantine to Profuturus, who had died only a very few years earlier.

Possidius, bishop of Calama, was Augustine’s disciple, nourished by him on God’s word and a most determined enemy of the Donatists, by whom he was nearly killed, as Augustine recounts in Letter 166. He wrote Augustine’s *Life*, in which he testifies that, by God’s gift, he had lived for forty years in familiar and sweet fellowship without any bitter disagreement. This is what may be said concerning the Catholic advocates. The rest are scarcely known otherwise than from the present proceedings, from which we have gathered their episcopal sees—the only information about them that remains.

Of the Donatist advocates, four or five are distinguished. Primianus, successor around the year of Christ 390 to the Donatist Parmenianus in the see of Carthage, was immediately condemned by Felicianus and other bishops of his party and deposed at the Council of Cabarsussa in 393, Maximianus being substituted in his place; but shortly afterwards he was acquitted and restored at the Council of Bagaia, while Maximianus was deposed. Augustine mentions this matter repeatedly. Petilianus, before becoming a bishop, had been a legal advocate; from being a catechumen among the Catholics, he was forcibly ordained bishop of Constantine by the Donatists. His letters survive, against which Augustine wrote. After [Col. 1230D] the common conference Augustine met Emeritus in his own city of Caesarea and dealt with him in the presence of bishops of the same province and of the people of the Church of Caesarea; Augustine himself wrote up the proceedings of that conference, in which he had the upper hand. Emeritus had been the author of the sentence pronounced by the Council of Bagaia against Maximianus. A report had spread that he had become Catholic near the end of his life; but this report was false. Though Augustine had refuted him, he nevertheless never entered Catholic communion and died obstinately in schism. Gaudentius of Thamugadi likewise gained renown through Augustine’s writings, which refute two of his letters. Of the remaining Donatist bishops we have nothing apart from the names of their sees, which are clear from the proceedings of the conference.

[Col. 1231]

**230. PREFACE**  
[Note: [Col. 1231B] Observe here that this preface is only an index of the chapters of the Carthaginian Conference, a work of Marcellus Memorialis. As regards the acts themselves, [Col. 1232B] they are not an abridgement prepared by this author, as otherwise learned men have thought, but the actual acts of the public notaries, as is evident to the reader.]  
**OF MARCELLUS MEMORIALIS TO SEVERIANUS AND JULIANUS. (C)**

[Col. 1231A] Marcellus Memorialis to his most beloved brethren, Severianus and Julianus, worthy of reverence in Christ’s name.

I gladly embrace the command by which you lovingly and confidently in the Lord directed me to distinguish and gather, in an abridgement arranged by me, the members of the whole affair and the heads of the proceeding which the pleadings of the parties unfolded through the protracted conflicts of this volume of acts; and I perceive and confess that charity alone makes me adequate to this work. For, in every fulfilment of a delegated office, he has more effective strength who obeys commands out of love for those commanding than he who obeys out of confidence in himself.

And indeed, in this undertaking in which, according to the ability of each, labour was expended in the Church’s cause, I contributed such a portion of my service as my modest capacity could provide. Having been called by the distinguished man Marcellinus, tribune and notary—one in whom [Col. 1231B] uprightness is especially conspicuous—to share his responsibilities, not so much through my own merit as through the gracious judgement of him who thought me worthy, I shared with the judge the labour of weighing the dispute. Yet I did not shrink from performing this further task which you wished me particularly to undertake. For I find no less delight and glory in now discharging an obligation to my brethren in the same matter than I did then in giving counsel to the presiding official.

Accordingly, whatever was argued at length by the parties, and whatever was recorded on both sides among the pronouncements of the judge, I have enclosed in a diligent abridgement. I have also appended in order the numerical marks familiar to reckoners, [Col. 1232A] so that the attention of an inquirer, following the index of the abridgement, may, guided by the numbers, arrive without inconvenience and by a short route at whatever it wishes to find in the pages of the proceedings.

Perhaps we may seem to have misused our leisure in recalling superfluous matters to labour. We should indeed admit that we had acted superfluously if people were willing and able to undertake the labour of reading the entire series of volumes. But it is quite unfair for those to complain that this diligence is a kind of emptiness who, if unremitting diligence in reading through the pages of this dispute were required of them, confess that it is not diligence but a burden. Therefore, in my judgement, we have not performed a fruitless work in removing the weariness of reading by the remedy of brevity. Certainly, even if it cannot be established from the result of the undertaking and its usefulness [Col. 1232B] that this labour has not been vain, nevertheless what I have done here is not inappropriate, because in doing it I obeyed your commands. Now I ask that, in return for this service, you may deem it worthy to pray for me. Thus it will come about that what you do willingly will nevertheless count toward my reward.

May the omnipotence of the Trinity—that is, the omnipotence of our God—continually preserve, in perpetual mercy, your charity mindful of us: lords most worthy of love and brethren worthy of reverence in Christ’s name.

Here ends the letter of the chapter-headings.

[Col. 1231]

Submission of the Donatists again concerning the person [Col. 1240D] of the envoys. 61. The Catholics’ reply to these matters. 62. Again the Donatists’ contention concerning the person of the envoys to be examined. 63. Protest of the Donatists: that the Catholics are contriving delays because they do not wish to disclose the persons of the envoys. 64. An interlocution: that the Emperor did not wish any inquiry concerning these persons. 65. Again the Donatists’ contention concerning the envoys. 66. An interlocution: that the Donatists should say whether, among the Catholics present, they can recognize those whom they call envoys; or, if they are absent, whether they ought to be produced. 67. Submission of the Donatists, in which they say that the envoys must be produced. 68. Reply of the Catholics, in which they say that their standing has already once been affirmed by the Donatists. [Col. 1241A] 69. Again the Donatists contend for examination of the envoys. 70. An interlocution: that, with the contention concerning the persons of the envoys cast aside, they should proceed to the substance of the matter. 71. Again the Donatists contend concerning the person of the envoys. 72. Where the Catholics demand that the Donatists ought to state the cause of their own separation. 73. Again the Donatists’ contention concerning the envoys. 74. Where the Catholics reply that the Emperor ordered nothing concerning examination of the person of the envoys, but rather inquiry into the beginning of the error. 75. Submission of the Donatists: that the Catholic Church is rather among themselves; and again a contention concerning examination of the envoys. 76. Submission of the Catholics, demanding that the Donatists prove by testimonies their assertion that “Catholic” belongs to themselves. 77. An interlocution: that the names of the envoys are demanded superfluously; omitting these, they must now proceed to the statement of the matter. [Col. 1241B] 78. Again the Donatists’ contention concerning the envoys. 79. An interlocution similar to the preceding one. 80. Submission of the Catholics, declaring that they have come to the conference as the Emperor wished. 81. An interlocution: that the persons of the envoys were to be examined when the embassy had carried out its function. 82. Where the Catholics demand that the Donatists publish the cause of their own separation. 83. Again the Donatists demand that the envoys be disclosed to them. 236. 84. An interlocution in which the cognitor says that he cannot depart from the form of the law and that all must cease their inquiry into the envoys, while the case must be stated. 85. Submission of the Donatists concerning disclosure of what the Catholics sought from the Emperor, and through whom they sought it. 86. An interlocution: that the order was not to investigate [Col. 1241C] what the Catholics sought from the Emperor, but that, once both parties’ standings had been confirmed, the matter must be set forth. 87. Again the Donatists’ contention on this point. 88. The Catholics’ reply to these matters, in which they also protest that the Donatists wish to make the proceedings excessively long. 89. Submission of the Donatists, in which they say that delays are caused by the Catholics; demand disclosure of what they sought from the Emperor; and ask whether the Catholics wish to litigate under public law or under divine laws. 90. An interlocution: that the Catholics sought from the Emperor only a conference. 91. Interpellation of the Donatists, declaring that they themselves ought rather to be called Catholics. 92. An interlocution that those be called Catholics whom the Emperor wished to be so called. 93. Submission of the Donatists: that the Catholic name must be reserved for the one whom victory has declared Christian. 94. An interlocution agreeing to this, and observing the form of the preceding order. [Col. 1241D] 95. Where the Donatists wish the judge to pronounce this very point without prejudice to their position. 96. An interlocution: that the beginning of the case now be stated, if the Donatists wish to show that the Catholic name does not belong to their opponents. 97. Submission of the Donatists: that the Catholics, since they do not wish to satisfy what has been adjudged, should at least answer whether they assume the position of plaintiff. 98. The Catholics’ reply to these matters, and concerning the Church spread throughout the world. 99. Submission of the Donatists: that they have nothing to do with foreign churches; that the Catholic name must be reserved for the victor; and that the Catholics ought to declare whether they claim for themselves the standing of plaintiffs. 100. Submission of the Catholics: how African Christians have communion with the whole world. [Col. 1242A] 101. Likewise a submission of the Catholics: that the Church must be sought where the Bridegroom of the Church—that is, Christ—is acknowledged; and a clear exposition of the name “Catholic.” 102. Submission of the Donatists, in which they attempt to interpret the name “Catholic” otherwise and again endeavor to return to matters already disposed of concerning the names of the envoys. 103. An interlocution of the judge: that, leaving aside what has already been disposed of, the promised rationale of the Catholic name be demonstrated. 104. Contention of the Donatists that the Catholics be compelled to set forth their case. 105. Likewise, the Donatists’ request that the judge pronounce upon each individual point. 106. Likewise, where the Donatists demand that the Catholics declare whether they claim for themselves the role of plaintiffs or of respondents. 107. An interlocution confirming these matters. 108. Where the Catholics declare that they entered [Col. 1242B] this judgment in order to answer their opponents’ accusations and charges. 109. Submission of the Donatists, asking by whom the Catholics were summoned to judgment. 110. Submission of the Catholics: that they came together with the Donatists for the conference in order to refute their accusations; and declaring that these same Donatists requested a hearing before the imperial court. 111. An interlocution that the Donatists now state the charges which they customarily make against the Catholics. 112. Submission of the Donatists: that the judge pronounce whether what the Donatists themselves demand is right. 113. An interlocution pronouncing both that they made their demand rightly and that the Catholics replied rightly. 114. Submission of the Donatists, in which they attempt to make the Catholics plaintiffs. 115. An interlocution of the judge: whether the Catholics make any charge against the Donatists. [Col. 1242C] 116. Submission of the Catholics: that they make no charge, but wish to refute charges made against them; that the Donatists, however, have repeatedly made charges, as can be shown both by the tenor of their own mandate and by the words of Bishop Primianus. 117. An interlocution that the Donatists support with proofs the accusation of handing-over (*traditio*) which they had included in their mandate against the Catholics. 118. Request of the Donatists: that the judge first pronounce concerning their standing, and that the case then proceed. 119. The Catholics’ contention in reply. 120. An interlocution: that the plaintiff is the one who makes an accusation. 121. Request of the Donatists: that the Catholics show that the conference was requested by both parties. 122. The Catholics’ reply to these matters. 123. Interruption of the Donatists, by which they assume for themselves the Catholic name; and contention on both sides concerning the names of their fathers. 124. Where the Catholics offer proceedings held in the court of the Prefecture, by which they prove what was promised. [Col. 1242D] 125. Where the Donatists refer back to matters already disposed of, so that the proceedings may not be read, and desire a pronouncement concerning standing. 126. An interlocution: that the Catholics requested only a conference and that judgment must be made only on this matter. 127. Where the Donatists contend that the judge must first pronounce concerning their own request. 128. Submission of the Catholics: that the Donatists produce evidence, if they have it, by which their falsehood may be convicted; and where they introduce the proceedings of the Prefecture. 129. Where the Donatists return to matters already disposed of, so that the proceedings held before the Prefecture may not be read. 130. An interlocution which, setting aside everything else, pronounces that those proceedings must be read. 131. Submission of the Donatists concerning the standing of the plaintiffs and the judge’s required pronouncement. 132. An interlocution, in which he promises that everything they offer will be read in order. [Col. 1243A] 133. Interruption of the Donatists, that the proceedings not be read. 134. An interlocution: that the standing of the plaintiff can be made clear from the reading of the proceedings. 135. Contention of the Donatists that the cognitor pronounce upon their demands. 136. Request of the Catholics that the proceedings be read. 137. An interlocution: that the cognitor ought not to be compelled to pronounce, when a volume of evidence was offered by the other party. 138. Submission of the Donatists, in which, so that the proceedings may not be read, they pursue another point and demand that the cognitor pronounce concerning the party. 237. 139. An interlocution that those proceedings be read. 140. Where, by many submissions, the Donatists do not permit the proceedings to be read, and, resisting the judge’s many pronouncements, evade the standing of plaintiff. 141. Where the same proceedings begin to be read; and the Donatists, wishing [Col. 1243B] to interrupt, offer proconsular or vicariate proceedings, by which they show that the Catholics made very many accusations against them. 142. Protest of the Catholics concerning the Donatists’ disorderly interruptions. 143. Request of the Donatists: that the documents of each party be read according to chronological order. 144. The Catholics’ reply to these matters. 145. An interlocution: whether the proceedings which the Donatists desire to have read are earlier. 146. The Donatists’ reply to the questions. 147. An interlocution: that the older proceedings be read first. 148. Where the Catholics offer the proceedings that are earlier than all the rest. 149. Submission of the Donatists: that, in order that certain proceedings might not be read, the Catholics have returned to forensic procedures, although they chose to have everything [Col. 1243C] examined under divine laws. 150. An interlocution that the older proceedings be read. 151. Where the Donatists profess surprise that they are being drawn into the case. 152. Where the Catholics reply that they have offered the proceedings to be read in order, as the Donatists themselves requested. 153. Submission of the Donatists, in which they reply that they requested something other than what the Catholics offer, and challenge them either to dispute solely by divine testimonies or by public law. 154. An interlocution that the dates of the proceedings be compared by the officials. 155. Submission of the Catholics concerning when the case ought to be handled by divine laws and when by public laws. 156. An interlocution judging the Catholics’ submission acceptable. 157. Submission of the Donatists, in which they return to earlier matters, demanding that the mandate and embassy be made public. 158. An interlocution against the Donatists’ submission. [Col. 1243D] 159. Submission of the Donatists concerning the mandate assigned to the advocates present and another mandate imposed on the earlier envoys. 160. The Catholics’ reply to these matters: that the mandate imposed upon the envoys also contains other matters, which ought not to be investigated by the present proceedings. 161. Submission of the Donatists, in which they make this very assertion a charge: namely, that the Catholics said the envoys’ mandate should not be disclosed. 162. The Catholics’ reply to these matters, explaining the meaning of the preceding submission. 163. Submission of the Donatists similar to the preceding one. 164. An interlocution: that the Catholics’ mandate ought not to be examined; but that the Donatists should rather declare whether they wish accusations of handing-over (*traditio*) to be demonstrated, or the matter of faith and of the Church to be handled. [Col. 1244A] 165. Submission of the Donatists: that the role of plaintiff is mockingly imposed upon them. 166. An interlocution: that the plaintiff can be shown by the reading of the proceedings; and the Donatists reply that order must be observed in their reading. 167. An interlocution ordering the officials to compare with one another the dates of the proconsular or prefectorial proceedings. 168. Where the Catholics offer proceedings earlier than those. 169. Where the cognitor orders that, if the Donatists wish to read, the officials should rather read what is to be read. 170. Where the Catholics reply that the proceedings which they offer are earlier. 171. Where the cognitor asks the officials which proceedings are earlier. 172. Where the officials reply that the proceedings offered from the Donatists’ codex are older. 173. Where the Catholics reply that they are producing earlier proceedings. [Col. 1244B] 174. Where the cognitor orders the Donatists’ proceedings, as though older, to be read; and the officials read the petition given by the Catholics to the proconsul Septiminus. 175. Where the Donatists wish the Catholics to be plaintiffs. 176. Submission of the Catholics, requesting that the earlier proceedings instead be read—those conducted before Anulinus the proconsul, with the Donatists as litigants. 177. An interlocution ordering the Catholics to prove the charge of schism which they make against the Donatists. 178. The Catholics’ reply to these matters. 179. An interlocution ordering all things to be read in sequence. 180. While they contend concerning the name of plaintiff, the judge interjects that the plaintiff can be better identified when everything has been read. 181. Submission of the Donatists: that the Catholics choose whether they wish to proceed under public laws or divine laws. [Col. 1244C] 182. The cognitor’s interlocution in reply: that the proceedings be read in sequence, so that the plaintiff may be recognized. 183. Where the Donatists, so that the proceedings held before Anulinus the proconsul may not be read, attempt to introduce a procedural bar based on the passage of time. 184. Where, as the Donatists contend this, the judge interjects that the bar based on the passage of time must be set aside, since the parties deferred the examination to this day by common agreement. 185. Where the Donatists say that they introduced the time-bar because the Catholics wished to proceed in forensic fashion by producing written documents. 186. An interlocution that the Catholics reply to the charges. 187. The Catholics’ reply to these matters: that they will proceed according to the divine Scriptures if there is a departure from accusations against persons and from the reading of documents. 188. Submission of the Donatists, in which they say that the Catholics have made no definite choice between the two; nor are they plaintiffs, since they came to judgment upon being summoned, but rather the Catholics themselves ought to set forth the case. [Col. 1244D] 189. Where the Catholics say that one against whom an accusation is made does not stand in the position of plaintiff. 190. An interlocution approving the matters stated above. 191. Where the Donatists say that the Catholics have given no reply concerning the proposed condition of a forensic or divine mode of proceeding. 192. The Catholics’ reply to these matters. 193. Where the Donatists say that they are gradually being drawn into the case, and that their fathers instructed them to stand in the role of respondent. 194. An interlocution stating that the judge himself answered one proposal of the Donatists, while the Catholics answered another. 195. Where the Donatists say that the judge ought to defend the position of absentees, not of those present. [Col. 1245A] 196. An interlocution replying that he has pronounced what the Donatists wished. 197. Submission of the Catholics, replying also that they have chosen the law under which they will dispute, and that the judge has done nothing on their behalf, but only on behalf of their parties. 238. 198. Submission of the Donatists: that it was not within their power that they came to judgment. 199. Where the Catholics ask the Donatists whether they will withdraw from accusations against persons. 200. Submission of the Donatists, in which they say that they cannot answer this question of the Catholics, but that the Catholics ought to stand in the position of plaintiff. 201. Submission of the Catholics, by which they declare that they have answered the conditions proposed by the Donatists. 202. An interlocution approving that the Catholics have replied, and ordering the earlier proceedings to be read so that the plaintiff may be shown. 203. Submission in which the Donatists, denying that the Catholics have chosen one definite course, return to the procedural bar based on [Col. 1245B] the passage of time. 204. The Catholics’ reply: that the Donatists did not appear at the final hearing, though they subsequently gave a mandate. 205. The Donatists’ resulting contention. 206. Submission of the Catholics concerning the declaration of Bishop Primianus, where they offer it for reading, by which they prove that the Donatists are reopening matters already disposed of. 207. Reply of the Donatists why they return to matters already concluded. 208. Submission of the Catholics: that the Donatists are acting merely to delay, and that proceedings which disclose the plaintiff must be read. 209. Where the Donatists wish to plead a bar in order that the proceedings not be read. 210. An interlocution: that the Donatists wish to act contrary to their own agreement and that the proceedings must be read. 211. Defence of the Donatists why they do not wish to preserve their own agreement for the Catholics. 212. An interlocution ordering the proceedings to be read, while preserving intact for the Donatists whatever may properly belong to them in law. [Col. 1245C] 213. Where the Donatists say that the Catholics ought to preserve their agreements, since they promised to proceed by divine laws. 214. The Catholics’ reply to these matters: that they promised to pursue not the case of Caecilian, but the case of the Church, by divine laws. 215. An interlocution that proceedings by which the plaintiff may be shown be read. 216. Where, after the heading of a report is read, the Donatists ask why the heading was read; and the cognitor orders that neither heading be entered in the acts. 217. Where, as the stenographer reads, the Donatists ask from where the documents have been produced. 218. Where the Catholics say that, once the proceedings have been read, they ought to be required to establish the validity of the reading itself. 219. An interlocution ordering, before the reading, an answer as to from where the proceedings were produced. 220. Where the Catholics reply that these were produced from the archive of the proconsul, [Col. 1245D] and they are read in order. 221. Where, when the reading of the proceedings is interrupted, the Donatists ask whether the man now acting is Caecilian’s son. 222. The Catholics’ reply to these matters: that it is written that a Christian must not call any portion his own on earth; and that they place no hope in Caecilian if he was innocent, nor, if he was guilty, is the Church to be abandoned. 223. Where, as the cognitor interjects that everything must be read, the Donatists request that they be ordered to make their submission. 224. Where the Catholics say that the standing of the plaintiff can be discovered from the reading of the proceedings. 225. Submission of the Donatists: that Caecilian’s person need not be examined, since—even if he is found a most manifest offender—he cannot harm the Catholics. [Col. 1246A] 226. The Catholics’ reply: that they introduced Caecilian’s person because it has always been charged against the Catholic Church itself; if the Donatists now keep silent concerning it, there is no longer any reason why the separation should be maintained. 227. Where the Donatists ask whether those who are acting are Caecilian’s sons. 228. The Catholics’ reply to these matters. 229. Again the Donatists’ question concerning the same point. 230. The Catholics’ reply: that Caecilian was neither their father nor mother, but their brother; there they also declare that Christ is the beginning of their faith. 231. Again the Donatists ask whether Caecilian was their father. 232. The Catholics’ reply to these matters, and the ensuing contention. 233. An interlocution declaring that the Catholics have answered the questions. 234. Where the Donatists, swearing an oath, charge the judge with defending the Catholics sufficiently. [Col. 1246B] 235. Submission of the Catholics containing a repetition concerning the name of father and brother; there it is also said that Caecilian’s case does not at all belong to the Church, but that he is to be defended as an innocent brother. 236. Submission of the Donatists: that Caecilian was the root or head of the Catholics, and that, if Caecilian was guilty, it is necessary that the same guilt which was in the head should also infect his offspring. 237. Where the Catholics reply that Christ is their head. 238. Where Petilianus interrupts and asks who ordained Augustine. 239. Likewise, a question raised by the Donatists concerning the Apostle, of whom it was said: “I begot you through the Gospel.” 240. Protest of the Catholics concerning the tumult of the opposing party. 241. An interlocution ordering the Catholics to reply [Col. 1246C] to the question raised concerning the Apostle. 242. The Catholics’ reply to the questions, with scriptural testimonies: that God alone is Father unto salvation, while others are called fathers by reason of honor, not salvation. 243. Where the Donatists ask who is said to have ordained Augustine. 244. Submission of the Catholics: that inquiry into Augustine’s ordainer has no bearing at all on the case. 245. Where, as the Donatists press the issue of Augustine’s ordainer, the Catholics reply that they have not undertaken to defend Augustine’s case, whatever it may be. 246. An interlocution ordering Augustine to answer the questions concerning his ordainer. 247. Where Augustine, first placing the cause of the Church in safety, plainly answers concerning his own ordainer and challenges the Donatists to make whatever charges they think fit. 248. An interlocution ordering the Donatists to explain the relevance of what they ask, although the question of persons does not delay the case. [Col. 1246D] 249. Submission of the Donatists, in which they say that the Church is stained by the faults of priests; and they offer for reading a volume containing divine testimonies, against those matters which they found set down in the mandate read by the Catholics at the first hearing. 250. An interlocution stating that what is offered by the Donatists can then at last be read, if they wish the cognitor to withdraw from examination of public documents. 251. Where the Donatists request that what they offer be read meanwhile, and it is read by the officials. 252. An interlocution stating that this document ought never to have been composed by persons through whose mandate, once it had been made, the whole matter had passed on. 253. Where the Donatists assert that they wish, by legal testimonies, to refute the legal testimonies put forward by the Catholics in their mandate, and ask that their letter be heard. [Col. 1247A] 254. An interlocution granting that what was not correctly composed according to public law be read; and it enumerates this very concession, lest the judge appear to have omitted the law. 255. While the stenographer reads, the Donatists say that the sense of the letter is not correctly divided. 256. Where the Catholics allow the Donatists themselves to read, although the latter had previously refused to allow the Catholics to read. 257. An interlocution stating that it makes no difference who reads. 258. Where the letter which the Donatists sent to the judge is read by a Donatist bishop: a letter full of legal testimonies, which attempts, by apparently contrary testimonies, to exclude all those testimonies which the Catholics put in their mandate. 259. An interlocution which, after the whole letter has been read, declares that patience has been shown by the Catholics [Col. 1247B] and orders the Catholics to reply against its text. 260. Submission of the Donatists, requesting that their testimonies be rebutted by testimonies. 261. Where the Catholics reply against the Donatists’ letter. 262. Where the Donatists wish to interrupt, denying that the threshing-floor is named in the Scriptures. 263. Likewise, where the Donatists assert that the Gospel commanded that the mixture of hidden and non-evident offenders be tolerated. 264. Where the Catholics request that they not be denied the patience which they themselves showed while the Donatists’ letter was read. 265. Submission of the Catholics, in which, among other repetitions of earlier points, it is maintained that the Church is included under the name “world.” 266. The Donatists’ contention against this: that the Church is not denoted by the name “world.” [Col. 1247C] 267. Where the Catholics request that the Donatists be admonished to show patience, since a reply is made immediately to their letter, without any interval of delay having been requested—as they themselves asked that they might reply to the Catholics’ mandate. 268. Where the Donatists reply that the very person who makes a long submission is shouting them down. 269. Where the Catholics request that, if the Donatists wish to dispute each point separately, the letter be removed; otherwise they should show patience, or a reply should be made to the letter. 270. Where the Donatists say that they cannot show patience because the Catholics wish to interpret the law differently. 271. An interlocution stating that patience must be shown, since the entire tenor of the letter was heard patiently by the Catholics. 272. Submission of the Catholics, declaring that everything is written down so that, if anything is forgotten, it may be recalled from the records; and stating that, both in an unfavorable and a favorable sense, “world” is named in scriptural testimonies. [Col. 1247D] 273. An interlocution ordering it to be recorded that the Donatists are shouting them down. 274. Where the Donatists assert that the Church cannot be interpreted through “world,” since Christ himself expressly said that the world is the field, not the Church. 275. An interlocution asking the Donatists what that world is which is said to be saved. 276. The Donatists’ reply to these matters: that this world is called the human being. 277. An interlocution asking whether the Church consists of those same human beings. 278. The Donatists’ contention in reply. 279. Where the stenographers and notaries report that, their codices being filled, they must withdraw and others be substituted. 280. An interlocution ordering that this be done. 281. Submission of the Catholics, fully replying to the letter produced by the Donatists.

**THE PROCEEDINGS EXTEND ONLY TO THIS POINT. THE REST IS MISSING.**
[Col. 1248A] 282. Statement of the Donatists against the statement of the Catholics which they made in reply to the Letter. 283. Statement of the Catholics, in which they show that evil persons have been sown in the Church—something the Donatists denied could occur—and defend what the Donatists said they had asserted concerning two Churches. 284. An interlocution ordering that it be read from the record whether the Catholic advocates had spoken of two Churches. 285. Where the Donatists seek to interpret the Catholics as having held an opinion about two Churches, since it was not established that they had called them two Churches. 286. Statement of the Catholics defending what they had said about the Church of the present age and of the age to come. 287. Statement of the Donatists, where they say that the Catholics had also called the Church mortal, although immortality has been promised to the Church. [Col. 1248B] 288. Statement of the Catholics, where they maintain, on the basis of their aforesaid assertions, that immortality has been promised to that Church which now on earth consists of righteous mortals. 289. An interlocution saying that, in the judgment, he will state what he thinks concerning the question already dealt with, and ordering that the cause of the error be disclosed. 290. Statement of the Donatists requesting that, after examination has proceeded through the individual articles, a ruling be pronounced upon each; and where they say that their legal proofs have not been answered. 291. Reply of the Catholics to these points in accordance with what was stated above. 292. An interlocution of the judge saying that the laws forbid judgment to be delivered on only part of the case. 293. The Donatists’ contention in reply, which also insults the Catholics by calling them false priests. [Col. 1248C] 294. The Catholics’ protest, in which they answer that they disregard the insult. 295. Statement of the Donatists, which says to the judge: “If you are not Christ, why do you judge concerning priests?” It maintains that this judgment must be reserved for Christ, and asks the Catholics whether Christ commanded them to demand a human judge. 296. Reply of the Catholics: first, that the early Donatists, in an episcopal case, demanded human courts; and that they themselves do not suffer persecution but inflict it. 297. Where the Donatists say that the acts of the circumcellions do not at all concern the priests. 298. Statement of the Catholics: that, by gouging out eyes, the Donatists have surpassed the devil. 299. Where the Donatists say that the devil has been defended by the Catholics. 300. Statement of the Catholics: that the Maximianists are better than the Donatists, by whom they suffered persecution, if endured persecution makes men better. [Col. 1248D] 301. Statement of the Donatists, where it is said that the devil made matters worse because he did not take away Job’s eyes, the spectators of his wounds. 302. Statement of the Catholics, where the Donatists are said to have performed *consolarium* [reading/meaning uncertain], and to have burned copies of the Lord’s Scriptures. 303. Statement of the Donatists: that their churches are still full of bloodied bodies. 304. An interlocution asking whether this itself was the cause of the schism. 305. Reply of the Donatists to these points. 306. Where the Catholics say that the Maximianists could make this charge against the Donatists. 307. An interlocution similar to the preceding one. 308. Where the Catholics challenge the Donatists to acknowledge the cause of the old schism. 309. Where the Donatists say that traitors—that is, a bad tree—can be known from their deeds, that is, from their fruits. [Col. 1249A] 310. Reply of the Catholics to these points. 311. An interlocution asking when the bad tree came into existence. 312. Statement of the Donatists: that they have not been answered on all points and individually. 313. That the judge ought to pronounce judgment, and that hereditary sin passed from the fault of the first man to all. 314. An interlocution: that judgment must be delivered upon all matters together, lest the judge’s inclination be disclosed before the end of the case. 315. Statement of the Catholics requesting that the documents whose reading had begun be read through. 316. An interlocution ordering them to be read; and the reading of the report sent by the proconsul Anullinus to Emperor Constantine, recording that Majorinus, opposing Caecilian, had handed over to the proconsul documents concerning his accusations for transmission to the emperor. [Col. 1249B] 317. Where, after the reading, the Donatists request that their right to make an opposing reply be reserved. 318. Likewise, the reading of another report sent by the same proconsul to the same emperor, in which the proconsul signifies that he had caused Caecilian, with his ten clerics, and an equal number of his opponents, to proceed to the city, as the emperor had ordered. 319. Likewise, the reading of Constantine’s letter sent to Miltiades, bishop of Rome, by which jurisdiction between Caecilian and his opponents is delegated to him and to the other bishops. 320. Statement of the Catholics calling what had been read to the attention of the commissioner and requesting that the judgment of Miltiades in Caecilian’s case be read. 321. Reading of Miltiades’ judgment. 322. Where the Donatists wish something else against Miltiades’ judgment to be read. 323. Where the Catholics say that Miltiades’ entire judgment has not been completed, since proceedings were then conducted for three days and there are three records. [Col. 1249C] 324. An interlocution: when the Donatists wish to proceed against what has been read, they are told first to allow all matters to be read in order. 325. Where the Donatists insist on proceeding against what has been read. 326. Where the Catholics say that something still remains to be read, since Miltiades’ sentence has not been read. 327. Statement of the Donatists, in which they say that they returned from exile for the trial because the commissioner had sworn to them by edict. 328. Reply of the Catholics: that the Donatists had not been in exile. 329. Statement of the Donatists concerning the status of the plaintiff, rehearsing what had occurred and saying that the exoneration of Caecilian ought not to have been read, since he had not yet been accused by them. 330. An interlocution: that the documents offered by the Donatists must be read, so that, once everything has been read, the status of the plaintiff may be determined. [Col. 1249D] 331. Where the Catholics contend that the reading of their documents ought not to be interrupted at all, but that everything must be read in order. 332. Where the Donatists reply that the reading concerning Caecilian the Catholic could not be relevant. 333. An interlocution: while the Catholics contend for the continuation of the reading, the commissioner orders instead that the materials offered by the Donatists be read. 334. Statement of the Donatists setting forth the beginning of the case: what Mensurius, bishop of the Church of Carthage, did during the persecution in the time of unity, and how the cause of the schism arose. 335. An interlocution demanding proof, if the charge of handing over sacred books is imputed to Mensurius. 336. Statement of the Catholics: while preserving the issue of the Church, they request that the charge of handing over sacred books be proved against Mensurius. 337. Where a private letter is read, [Col. 1250A] sent by Mensurius to Bishop Secundus, in which he informs him what had been done concerning himself during the persecution. 338. Statement of the Catholics, seeking to have it recorded that private letters are being read whose authenticity is uncertain. 339. Likewise, another private letter is read, in which Secundus replies to Mensurius. 340. Where the Catholics request that it be specified who this Secundus was. 341. Where the Donatists specify who Secundus was. 342. Reading of the aforesaid reply, in which Secundus in turn informs Mensurius what had occurred concerning himself in Numidia at that time. 343. An interlocution ordering the Donatists, once their letters have been read, patiently to hear what the Catholics had begun to read. 344. Statement of the Donatists saying that something remains for them to read concerning Caecilian. 345. An interlocution ordering that what remains concerning Caecilian also be read. [Col. 1250B] 346. Statement of the Catholics affirming that they are willing patiently to allow it to be read. 347. Where the Donatists offer a decree composed by their fathers concerning Caecilian’s condemnation, and it is read by the judge’s order. 348. When the reading is concluded, the judge states that, if anything remains which ought to be read concerning Caecilian, it should be indicated. 349. Statement of the Donatists, promising that they possess documents also concerning the other persons. 350. An interlocution ordering that what had been offered by the Catholics be read through. 351. Statement of the Catholics placing on record that no public judicial proceedings were conducted against Mensurius, and that Caecilian, being absent, was condemned by them in a council without consul or date—men who are found, in another council, to have mutually forgiven one another the charges of handing over sacred books which they had confessed against each other. [Col. 1250C] 352. An interlocution requiring that this very material be read. 353. Where, after the beginning of the council has been read, the Donatists interrupt, denying that a consul and date are customarily appended to ecclesiastical decrees. 354. Reply of the Catholics to these points. 355. An interlocution similar to the preceding one. 356. Where the Catholics demand that it be investigated whether Donatus, whose name has just been read, was among Caecilian’s condemners. 357. An interlocution requiring this to be investigated, and likewise the names of each individual. 358. Where the Donatists declare that they have shown patience, requesting reciprocal treatment when they begin to reply. 359. An interlocution requiring, according to the Donatists’ request, a declaration of patience from the Catholics. 360. Where the Catholics declare that they will show patience. 361. Where, after a portion of the record has been read, the Donatists demand that the whole be read. 362. Reply of the Catholics to these points. [Col. 1250D] 363. Statement of the Catholics maintaining that they had read what was read so that Caecilian’s exoneration might stand. 364. An interlocution admonishing the Donatists to reply against what the Catholics had read, so that the remaining interrupted materials may be read. 365. Statement of the Donatists maintaining that they issued a decree without the consul’s subscription in accordance with ancestral custom. 366. An interlocution saying that the Catholics did not make any issue of this. 367. Statement of the Catholics: that the Donatists do this in order to draw out the time. 368. Where the Donatists say that, if no one doubts the judgments pronounced, Caecilian was lawfully condemned. 369. Statement of the Catholics maintaining that what was done concerning Caecilian can be shown if the interrupted materials are read. [Col. 1251A] 370. Where the Donatists demand of the Catholics whether they acknowledge as genuine the council by which Caecilian was condemned. 371. Reply of the Catholics: even if that council is genuine, it cannot prejudice Caecilian while absent—just as the council of the Maximianists condemning Primian did not prejudice Primian. 372. Statement of the Donatists: neither one case prejudices another case, nor one person another person. 373. An interlocution requiring the Catholics to answer concerning Caecilian, who was condemned by seventy persons. 374. Statement of the Catholics: they mentioned Primian’s condemnation because the Gospel rule is that opponents must be charged from their own deeds. 375. Statement of the Donatists, repeating from the beginning what Caecilian did, and promising that from the writings of Optatus, a Catholic bishop, they can show that Caecilian confessed that he had been ordained by traitors. [Col. 1251B] 376. Statement of the Catholics requesting that the interrupted materials be read; and where they say that the Donatists of that period themselves judged from their own council, since they wished to accuse before Emperor Constantine the Caecilian whom they had condemned. 377. An interlocution asking whether, after this council, the Donatists submitted to the emperor their accusation of Caecilian. 378. Where the Donatists ask whether Caecilian appealed from that judgment of bishops. 379. Statement of the Catholics, demolishing the Donatists’ council either way: whether it was held before they sent Caecilian’s charges to the emperor, or whether it was assembled afterward. 380. An interlocution requiring the Donatists to answer whether it was held before or after Caecilian’s accusation. 381. Reply of the Donatists to these points. 382. Statement of the Catholics requesting that the acts performed afterward be read, so that it may be shown that Caecilian was acquitted and his accusers condemned. [Col. 1251C] 383. Statement of the Donatists, seeking to demonstrate by reading that ancestral custom did not append a consul’s name to an ecclesiastical judgment. 384. Where the Catholics say that what the Donatists wish to read is irrelevant to the case. 385. An interlocution asking the Catholics whether they do not consider false that decree which lacks a consul. 386. Reply of the Catholics to these points. 387. An interlocution ordering that the materials first interrupted be read. 388. Where the Donatists charge as false that council in which Caecilian’s condemners mutually forgave their crimes, because, contrary to ecclesiastical and apostolic custom, a consul was appended to it. 389. Statement of the Catholics requesting that, with superfluities cut away, the acts by which Caecilian can be shown to have been acquitted be read. [Col. 1251D] 390. Where the Donatists maintain that a consul is not customarily appended to ecclesiastical councils, and demand that this be proved from the Lord’s writings. 391. Where the Catholics request that the acts of Caecilian’s exoneration be read. 392. Statement of the Donatists compelling the Catholics to relinquish that decree which they read against Caecilian’s condemners. 393. An interlocution saying that, of the two decrees, the one lacking the consul’s name may rather be suspect; and ordering that the interrupted materials be read through. 394. Statement of the Catholics maintaining that they make no defense of that decree, but nevertheless ought not to be compelled to relinquish the other decree. 395. Reply of the Donatists to these points. 396. An interlocution: the addition of a consul through greater diligence does not destroy the decree’s credibility. [Col. 1252A] 397. The Donatists’ contention in reply. 398. Statement of the Catholics: Caecilian’s exoneration must be read in the trial. 399. Where the Donatists say that the Catholics cannot refute what has been charged. 400. Reply of the Catholics: why no date or consul is appended in apostolic councils; and that the individual periods are found in the prophetic books to have been attested by their own indications. 401. An interlocution ordering that the interrupted acts be read. 402. An interlocution in which, when the Donatists request a judgment, he says that judgment cannot be delivered on part of the case. 403. Reading of the judgment of Miltiades and likewise of other bishops, by which Caecilian is shown to have been acquitted. 404. Statement of the Donatists, in which they persist, as above, in demanding that the Catholics be compelled to relinquish the decree which they produced against Caecilian’s condemners. 405. An interlocution requiring the Donatists to state whether they have anything to produce against the judgment of Miltiades that has been read. [Col. 1252B] 406. Likewise, an interlocution admonishing the Donatists, who are pursuing another matter, to answer the questions asked. 407. Reply of the Catholics against the Donatists’ demand that they relinquish the decree they had produced. 408. Where the Donatists argue that the decree read by the Catholics against Caecilian’s condemners is supported by no truth, because a council could not have been assembled during the time of persecution. 409. Similar reply of the Catholics: that a council could have been held during persecution; and this is demonstrated by legal proofs. 410. Statement of the Donatists similar to the preceding one. 411. Reply of the Catholics: that a council could have been held during persecution, since at that time even the people could assemble, though secretly. [Col. 1252C] 412. Statement of the Donatists: that the Catholics never suffered persecution and do not know how great is its force. 413. Reply of the Catholics, asking the Donatists whether they deny that Christian assemblies are customarily held in times of persecution. 414. An interlocution determining that the Catholics must prove whether they know of a council held in a time of persecution. 415. Reply of the Catholics: that the Apostles held the first council amid Jewish persecutions. 416. The Donatists’ contention in reply. 417. An interlocution requiring the Catholics to demonstrate this. 418. Where the Catholics read a passage from the Acts of the Apostles by which they wish to prove what was required of them concerning a council. 419. An interlocution indicating that the passage read by the Catholics did not prove what was asked. 420. Statement of the Catholics maintaining that bishops could assemble a council in time of persecution, since congregations of the people are found at that time, from which martyrs were made. [Col. 1252D] 421. An interlocution requiring this to be proved, and where other shorthand writers are substituted. 422. Statement of the Catholics requesting that the Donatists be asked whether they possess no acts of martyrs who acknowledge that they were in assemblies during persecution. 423. An interlocution admonishing the Donatists to answer the questions. 424. Reply of the Donatists: that no house of bishops could have accommodated a council. 425. Where the Catholics reply that a house could have sufficed for the twelve bishops who were then in the council. 426. An interlocution asking how great the number of bishops in that council was. [Col. 1253A] 427. Statement of the Catholics similar to the preceding one. 428. An interlocution confirming what the Catholics said. 429. Where the Catholics ask the Donatists whether they deny that assemblies are customarily held during persecution. 430. Statement of the Donatists saying that this decree, which the Catholics produced as enacted by twelve bishops, is false either because it was not made at that time, or because, with the emperor located in nearby regions, no one there would have dared assemble a council. 431. Where the Catholics say that a small number of bishops could easily have been assembled at that time. 432. Reply of the Donatists to these points. 433. Where the Catholics protest that their agents, whom they had sent to bring forward records concerning martyrs who admit that they were in an assembly, are not being permitted to go out. 434. Where the Donatists themselves offer acts of martyrs to be read. 435. An interlocution ordering the same to be read. 436. Where, in the reading of the acts, the Donatists demand a consul and date, so that the consul and date of the decree may also be compared with the consul or date of those acts. [Col. 1253B] 437. An interlocution investigating how much time elapsed between the decree and the acts. 438. Where, since the Catholics give a different statement concerning the interval of time, the clerk answers how much time had elapsed.

> [Note: [Col. 1253D] In the manuscript: *pronuntiantium Catholicis quantum interfuerit scripta respondeat*—without sense; correctly emended by Baluze from Augustine, *Breviculus Collationis*, day 3, line 17.]

439. Where the Donatists forbid from being removed from the record the matter concerning which the Catholics had given a different report about the interval of time. 440. Where the Catholics excuse this very point and permit it to remain in the record. 441. Where the Donatists accuse the Catholics of falsehood on this account. 442. Reply of the Catholics, maintaining that that decree cannot be called false unless the Donatists prove that assemblies were not customarily held during persecution. 443. Statement of the Donatists: that a council could not have been assembled at the time when martyrs hung upon the rack. [Col. 1253C] 444. An interlocution repeating the Catholics’ reply to these points. 445. Where the Catholics reply that even during persecution Christians showed such diligence that martyrs baptized in prison held assemblies of the people; and that this can be made clear by reading the acts. 446. An interlocution ordering the acts to be read. 447. Where the Donatists say that they themselves had recently offered for reading these very acts which the Catholics now produce. 448. Likewise, the reading of acts containing the passions of martyrs. 449. Likewise, the Catholics offer and have read other acts of martyrs, from which it is shown that assemblies of the people were then held. 450. An interlocution determining from the reading of the acts that assemblies of the people were held during persecution. [Col. 1253D] 451. Statement of the Donatists, maintaining that the Catholics ought to relinquish that decree because an episcopal council could not have been assembled then. 452. An interlocution determining that twelve bishops could then have gathered in one house, when assemblies of the people could be held publicly. 453. Statement of the Donatists, still arguing that the decree is false, examining its very determinations and words, and saying that Caecilian could have defended himself against his condemners by that decree if it were established that the decree had then been made. 454. An interlocution against the Donatists’ statement: twelve bishops could both have gathered then and easily remained hidden; but Caecilian was acquitted not by that decree of twelve bishops, but rather by the judgment of Miltiades. [Col. 1254A] 455. Where the Donatists again compel the Catholics to relinquish that decree. 456. Where the Catholics wish to offer other documents of the imperial judgment concerning Caecilian’s acquittal. 457. An interlocution ordering this very material to be read. 458. Where the Donatists demand that the judge rule upon the falsity of that decree. 459. An interlocution: the acts have made clear that a council could then have been held. 460. Statement of the Catholics: while the Donatists are silent, they offer for reading Constantine’s judgment concerning Caecilian’s acquittal. 461. Statement of the Donatists, maintaining that a council could not then have been held and that the Catholics must bear the loss of that decree. 462. An interlocution: a more strenuous inquiry into that decree would have been necessary if Caecilian’s acquittal rested upon it; but now the Donatists must either say or produce something against Miltiades’ judgment by which Caecilian’s acquittal may be overturned. [Col. 1254B] 463. Statement of the Donatists, promising that they will reply against Miltiades’ judgment, but maintaining that the credibility of that decree must be investigated. 464. An interlocution requiring that something against Miltiades’ judgment be put forward, and deciding that a council could have been held during persecution. 465. Statement of the Catholics: there was a necessary reason why the bishops should then assemble. 466. An interlocution requiring the Donatists to make some reply against Caecilian’s acquittal. 467. Statement of the Donatists: although assemblies of the people were then held, nevertheless a council of bishops could not have been convened then. 468. An interlocution requiring the Donatists to read something against Miltiades’ judgment. 469. Statement of the Donatists: their bishops could not condemn another man in a crime if they themselves were liable to it. [Col. 1254C] 470. Reply of the Catholics from the Lord’s Scriptures to these points. 471. An interlocution requiring that something be produced against Caecilian’s acquittal. 472. Statement of the Donatists: Caecilian ought to have been cleared in Africa, where he had been condemned; but Miltiades’ judgment on his behalf is invalid because Miltiades too was implicated in a similar crime. 473. Statement of the Catholics requiring proof of what the Donatists had said concerning Miltiades’ crime. 474. An interlocution ordering that the allegation against Miltiades be proved. 475. Statement of the Donatists, promising to prove by the reading of acts what was done concerning Miltiades’ name. 476. Where the Catholics request that decided cases concerning Miltiades’ name be produced. 477. Where the Donatists say that they will show from the writings of Optatus, a Catholic bishop, [Col. 1254D] that Caecilian was condemned at Brescia. 478. An interlocution: leaving aside Optatus’ testimony for the moment, the Donatists must instead produce first what they had promised concerning Miltiades’ name. 479. Where the Donatists wish Optatus’ testimony to be read. 480. An interlocution promising that Optatus’ testimony will be read if what had first been promised against Miltiades is read first. 481. Statement of the Catholics: the testimony of one Optatus ought not to be accepted against the weighty judgments of bishops. 482. Statement of the Donatists: what Optatus, a Catholic, said against the Catholics is altogether true. [Col. 1255A] 483. Statement of the Catholics: Optatus’ writings are not held to be canonical Scriptures. 484. Statement in which the Donatists demand that the Catholics either condemn Optatus or allow his testimony to be read, in which he says Caecilian was condemned at Brescia; and in which they remind the judge to keep the fairness he had promised. 485. An interlocution similar to the preceding one. 486. Statement of the Catholics: the Donatists ought to produce some judgment against Miltiades. 487. An interlocution similar to the preceding one. 488. Where the Donatists say that what they wish to have read concerning Optatus is not lengthy. 489. An interlocution determining that order must be maintained: first something against Miltiades, and afterwards as much as they wish concerning Optatus, is to be read. 490. Where the Donatists offer acts held in the city. 491. Where the same acts are read, recording that in the city of Rome certain others, together with a certain Straton, committed the handing over of ecclesiastical property. [Col. 1255B] 492. An interlocution: in such lengthy acts nothing has been said concerning Miltiades’ name. 493. Where the Donatists say that they have not yet completed all that they promised to read. 494. Statement of the Catholics, declaring that they have shown patience through the lengthy acts and that nothing has been produced from them against Miltiades; hence they ought to be allowed to read the judgment concerning Caecilian’s acquittal, including that of Emperor Constantine. 495. Statement of the Donatists, declaring that they read the handing over in the earlier acts and that they still have material to read. 496. An interlocution permitting other acts concerning Miltiades’ person to be read, while reserving for the Catholics the right to read whatever they wish afterward. 497. Here the Catholics wish it to be recorded that the Donatists did not specify where the earlier acts had been completed. 498. An interlocution confirming what the Catholics said. [Col. 1255C] 499. Likewise, other acts are read by the Donatists, in which, after Christians had been granted freedom to conduct their affairs, ecclesiastical property that had been handed over was recovered from Straton and the others whom Bishop Miltiades had sent for that business. 500. An interlocution: that even the second acts contain nothing concerning Miltiades’ guilt. 501. Where the Donatists maintain that this Straton was sent by Miltiades, as though a deacon, to reclaim ecclesiastical property, though he is found previously to have handed it over. 502. An interlocution requesting that this be demonstrated. 503. Where Straton’s name is read from the first acts. 504. An interlocution requesting clear proof whether Straton was called a deacon in the first acts. 505. Where the Donatists seek to infer from the fact that he was called an *instigator of superstition* in the same acts that a deacon was meant there. 506. Where the Catholics infer from the Donatists’ statement [Col. 1255D] that Straton the instigator of superstition could have been another person. 507. The Donatists’ contention against these points. 508.
