An interlocution saying that both sets of acts were made in the same period, and that Straton ought to have been marked in both with the same title of instigator. 509. Likewise, an interlocution requiring that a clear charge and manifest condemnation of Miltiades be produced. 510. Statement of the Donatists: that the same Straton first handed things over and afterward received Church property; nor does it prejudice the truth that he is there called an instigator of superstition, because the pagans did not wish to call him the devil. Thus Miltiades ought to be judged as defiled by association with Straton. 511. An interlocution: it must be proved that this same Straton was also sent by Miltiades at the time when he is said to have handed things over. [Col. 1256A] 512. Statement of the Donatists: Miltiades’ name is not included there because he was not yet bishop; but Miltiades was thereby defiled because he included the traitor Straton among his deacons. 513. An interlocution declaring that the parties must make the arguments appropriate to them. 514. Statement of the Catholics: there could then have been two Stratons, nor is it contrary to custom for two persons to bear one name; moreover, Miltiades cannot be guilty unless it is shown that he knew of Straton’s handing over. 515. An interlocution: nothing should be conducted among bishops by suspicions, and Constantine’s judgment must be read. 516. Reading of Constantine’s judgment, by which the emperor signifies that Caecilian was also cleared before him after the Council of Arles. 517. An interlocution reminding the Donatists to say whether they have anything to read against these matters. 518. Where the Donatists again say that Miltiades was defiled by association with Straton. [Col. 1256B] 519. An interlocution similar to the preceding one. 520. Where the Donatists say that the judgment reported to Constantine’s ears is false. 521. An interlocution: the emperor delivered judgment between the parties. 522. Where the Donatists request that this be read. 523. An interlocution signifying this very point also from the rescript of the emperor read above. 524. Where the Donatists wish it recorded that the emperor’s rescript contains neither date nor consul. 525. Where the Catholics reply that the date was read from the rescript and offer again to have it read. 526. Statement of the Donatists: though the date was read, the consul was not read. 527. Reply of the Catholics: if doubt remains concerning the rescript, the authority of the archives should be consulted. 528. An interlocution: an imperial rescript lacking consul and date cannot be called into doubt. [Col. 1256C] 529. Where the Donatists complain that the Catholics earlier produced an episcopal decree with a consul, but now have an emperor’s letter read without a consul. 530. Where the Catholics challenge the Donatists to say that the emperor’s letter is false. 531. Where the Donatists request that they be allowed to produce the reading concerning Optatus which had been reserved for them. 532. An interlocution: the Donatists must first answer whether the emperor’s letter is false, and only then may they read whatever they wish concerning Optatus. 533. Where the Donatists maintain that the rescript does not help Caecilian, because he is found afterward to have been condemned; and they wish this to be established by the reading from Optatus. 534. Where the Catholics protest that Optatus’ error does not harm them; nevertheless, they permit Optatus to be read. 535. Where a consul is subsequently found in the imperial letter. 536. Where the reading from Optatus is read. [Col. 1256D] 537. Since Caecilian’s condemnation is not found in Optatus, the Donatists maintain that Optatus spoke more guardedly in saying that Caecilian was detained at Brescia. 538. An interlocution: the Donatists, who said that Optatus expressed this more guardedly, must more clearly prove that Caecilian was condemned by the emperor. 539. Statement of the Donatists: that there was no other Donatus of Casae. 540. Reply of the Catholics: that Donatus of Casae is expressly named in the acts of Miltiades. 541. Where Petilianus, bishop of the Donatist party, declares that because of hoarseness he is unable to proceed. 542. Where the Catholics declare that they wished to deny Petilianus this excuse because Donatus of Casae had been clearly shown to him from the acts. 543. An interlocution: where seven stand present, complaint may be made concerning the inability of one. [Col. 1257A] 544. Statement of the Donatists: their predecessors gave Emperor Constantine a petition, and, moved by it, the emperor granted them leave to proceed; and it sets out there the case of Felix, bishop of Aptunga, who had ordained Caecilian. 545. An interlocution requiring that what belongs to the Donatists’ case be shown by the production of documents. 546. Reading of the petition which the Donatists gave Emperor Constantine at that time. 547. Statement of the Catholics, maintaining that the petition read by the Donatists supports their own side. 548. An interlocution confirming what the Catholics said and ordering Constantine’s rescript to be read. 549. Where Constantine’s letter sent to the vicar Verinus is read, granting the Donatists liberty to proceed. 550. Statement of the Catholics: Constantine’s letter supports them all the more, because no judgment was rendered concerning Caecilian, but the Donatists were yielded to their own frenzy. [Col. 1257B] 551. An interlocution confirming what the Catholics said. 552. Where the Donatists request that the judge pronounce upon the freedom of decision granted them by Constantine. 553. An interlocution pronouncing upon what was requested, and maintaining that Emperor Honorius has today ordered inquiry into Caecilian’s acquittal. 554. Statement of the Donatists, interpreting the matter to mean that Caecilian does not appear to have been cleared: because, when the case of Felix, his ordainer, was reconsidered, a certain Ingentius was ordered to be sent to the imperial court, and no action by Ingentius is found by which Felix is known to have been acquitted. 555. Statement of the Catholics, promising that by reading the report of the proconsul Aelianus they will show what was done concerning Felix’s acquittal. 556. Where the Donatists argue that Constantine’s letters should rather be read, by which Ingentius was ordered to be sent to the palace. 557. An interlocution ordering this instead to be read. [Col. 1257C] 558. Where these very letters are read. 559. Statement of the Catholics, saying that the report of Proconsul Aelianus must be read, in which Felix is shown to have been acquitted. 560. Reading of that report. 561. An interlocution requesting that, for fuller assurance, the acts themselves by which Felix was cleared also be read. 562. Where the Donatists argue that what should rather be read is whether Ingentius was sent or conducted any proceeding before the emperor. 563. Statement of the Catholics: the acts ought rather to be read, so that, just as Caecilian has been shown to have been acquitted, Felix too may be shown to have been cleared. 564. An interlocution ordering the acts to be read. [Col. 1258A] 565. Reading of the acts concerning Felix, who had ordained Caecilian. 566. An interlocution requiring the parties to state what pertains to their case. 567. Statement of the Donatists against the acts produced on Felix’s behalf. 568. An interlocution: acts confirmed by antiquity can be overturned only by the production of other acts. 569. Statement of the Catholics: what they have read suffices for the case; and if the person of Ingentius overturns Caecilian’s exoneration, the Donatists ought rather to do this—
To demonstrate. 570. An interlocutory ruling requiring that this be read aloud. 571. The Donatists’ submission, in which they say that Felix, being present, ought to have been cleared, and ask whether Ingentius made any response before the emperor on Felix’s behalf. 572. The Catholics’ submission, in which they say that, since everything has been read in due order, the investigating judge ought, [Col. 1258B] setting aside evasions, to deliver judgment. 573. An interlocutory ruling requiring that something be read against the records by which Felix was acquitted. 574. The Catholics’ submission: that it is a proof of greater innocence that Felix was cleared while absent. 575. The Donatists’ submission, in which all the points of the entire case dealt with in the preceding various submissions are recapitulated. 576. An interlocutory ruling that matters already decided and concluded ought not to be reopened, again requiring that something be read against Felix’s acquittal. 577. The Catholics’ submission, requesting that, since all matters have been examined and superfluous points are being repeated, judgment now be pronounced. 578. An interlocutory ruling that something is to be read against Felix’s acquittal. 579. The Donatists’ submission: that the judge ought to decide concerning the matters that have been produced. [Col. 1258C] 580. The Catholics’ submission (in which they request) that the remaining materials also be read aloud. 581. An interlocutory ruling that everything ought to be read aloud, so that judgment may be made upon everything. 582. A Donatist submission similar to the preceding one. 583. An interlocutory ruling similar to the preceding one. 584. The Donatists’ submission: that, at the discretion of the opposing party, whatever had been produced by their own side was falsified and destroyed. 585. An interlocutory ruling that, if nothing remains to be read, the parties ought to withdraw so that the full judgment may be written. 586. An interlocutory ruling summoning the parties for the judgment to be read aloud. 587. The judgment as read aloud, which, having embraced the whole case, determines, for the sake of Catholic unity, what ought to be observed.

*The Capitula of the Third Hearing end.*

[Col. 1257]

[ACTS OF THE CONFERENCE AT CARTHAGE.]

246 **IN THE YEAR OF OUR LORD 411. THE ACTS OF THE FIRST HEARING BEGIN.**

[Col. 1257D] 1. After the consulship of Varane, vir clarissimus, on the Kalends of June, at Carthage, in the *Secretarium* [Note: [Col. 1257D] *In Secretario*: that is, in the audience hall, in the praetorium where justice was publicly administered. Cyprian, bishop of Carthage, was brought forth at Carthage in the *Secretarium* before the proconsul Paternus, as is read in his Acts. The *Secretarium* of the praetorium is mentioned by Augustine, book III against Cresconius, chapter 56; and the *Secretarium* of the proconsul by Evodius of Uzalis, book II, *On the Miracles of St. Stephen*, chapter 5. This place was situated in the middle of the city of Carthage, [Col. 1258D] as Augustine teaches in the book written to the Donatists after the conference, chapter 25; in the same work, chapter 35, it is described as spacious, bright, and cool. BALUZIUS.] of the Gargilian Baths [Col. 1258D] [Note: [Col. 1258D] *Of the Gargilian Baths*: a description of these survives in book II of Pithoeus’s *Old Epigrams*. From the first and last letters of the epigram in which those baths are described, Sirmond rightly inferred that they were restored by Thrasamund, king of the Vandals. BALUZIUS.], with Sebastian, Maximian, and Peter, most devoted men, protectors domestici, present; with Ursus, [Col. 1259A] Petronius, and Libosus, *ducenarii*, in attendance; Boniface and Evasius, attendants of the illustrious and eminent authorities; Philetus, attendant of the illustrious staff of the seat [Note: [Col. 1259D] *Of the seat*: that is, of the proconsular seat.]; Exitiosus, assistant *cornicularius*; Possidius, Quodvultdeus, and Colonicus, assistants of the records office of our lord, the vir clarissimus and spectabilis proconsul; Navigius, assistant of the accounts office of our lord, the vir clarissimus and spectabilis vicar; Nampius, clerk of the office of the vir clarissimus legate of noble Carthage; Rufinianus, clerk of the vir clarissimus curator of exalted Carthage; and also Hilary and Praetextatus, recorders of our lord, the vir clarissimus and spectabilis proconsul; Fabius, recorder of our lord, the vir clarissimus and spectabilis vicar; and Romulus, recorder of the vir clarissimus legate of noble Carthage; with Januarius and Vitalis, notaries of the Catholic Church, and Victor and Cresconius, notaries of the Donatists, also recording—Ursus, *ducenarius* of the illustrious and [Col. 1259B] eminent authorities, said:

“Some time ago, Your Sublimity [Note: [Col. 1259D] *Your Sublimity*: he addresses Marcellinus the tribune.] in accordance with the imperial command sent both us and the others who have been assigned to duties, whether from the most sacred imperial staff or from the African offices, to the several provinces; and you also issued edicts throughout all Africa, requiring that all bishops, both Catholic and Donatist, should attend the conference within the fourth month. That period appears to be completed on this day. Since all are present—from every African province, namely the proconsular province, Byzacene province [Note: [Col. 1259D] *Byzacene*: in an old copy one reads *Byzc.* [Col. 1260D], whence Masson and Pithoeus made *Burcensi*, but wrongly. It should be read *Byzacena*, as Baluzius observed.], Numidia, the Mauretanias of Sitifis and Caesarea, and also the province of Tripolitania—if Your Nobility commands, let these venerable men be admitted, so that everything may proceed in its proper order.”

[Col. 1259C] 2. Flavius Marcellinus, vir clarissimus, tribune and notary, said: “Let the venerable men whom you report to be present be admitted.” And all the bishops of the party of Donatus entered; Aurelius, Alypius, Augustine, Vincentius, Fortunatus, Fortunatianus, and Possidius, bishops of the Catholic Church, entered as well, with their fellow bishops Novatus, Florentius, Maurentius, Boniface, Priscus, Serenianus, and Scyllacius, together with Deuterius, Leo, Asterius, and Restitutus, bishops likewise and custodians of the records.

3. Marcellinus, vir clarissimus, tribune and notary, said:

“I should indeed have wished that the holiness of this great multitude, enrolled under the religion of the one Christ God, might be separated by no dissension from itself. But since it is certain that God now wills to correct what the error of the ancient enemy introduced long ago, so that true [Col. 1259D] religion may no longer make a spectacle for the nations through its own conflict; although it is beyond my deserts that I should undertake this judgment, so that I seem to judge those by whom I ought rather to have been judged—yet, since it is certain that this case must be conducted before God as spectator and angels as witnesses, and that, under the examination of heavenly faith, if it is proved it brings reward, but if violated it brings judgment, so that at last truth may shine out more clearly through the discussions of the bishops now present—let the imperial enactment first be read, that all may understand in what manner and form the hearing is to be undertaken, although it is sufficiently clear that it has become known to all.”

Martialis, recorder, read:

4. “The Emperors Caesar Flavius Honorius and Theodosius, pious, fortunate, victorious, triumphant, and ever Augusti, to Flavius Marcellinus, greetings.

“Among the greatest concerns of our empire, reverence for the Catholic law is always either first or alone. For whether we labor in war or establish policy in peace, we pursue no other object than that the devoted people of our world may preserve the true worship of God; a worship which it had long been fitting to require even the Donatists to fulfill, by fear or by admonition, since they disfigure Africa—that is, the greatest part of our realm, faithfully serving in secular duties—by empty error and needless dissension.

“Yet we do not shrink from repeatedly restating those same things which the devout authority toward God of all preceding [Col. 1260B] emperors established, lest posterity may rightly impute to us that, in our times, something was perhaps brought forth to the injury of the Catholic law. Nor indeed is our conscience ignorant of the saying of the heavenly oracle which the cruel interpretation of the Donatists asserts can profit through their error; though it invited corrupted minds more gently to correction, we nevertheless previously ordered it abolished, lest any occasion be afforded to superstitions. Now likewise, by similar authority, we decree that the fraudulent intrusion be excluded; and we rightly declare that we willingly remove what had been established, lest anyone suppose that, with us as authors, he can sin against divine worship.

“And although there is one clear and manifest judgment of all: that the full truth of the Catholic law has been confirmed by the proper worship of humankind and by the sentence of heaven—yet, out of zeal for peace and concord, we willingly received the embassy of the venerable bishops. It requests that the Donatist 247 bishops be assembled in the gathering of a most renowned city, so that, after selected clergy chosen by each party have held discussions, manifest reason may refute superstition. We order this matter to be completed within four months, so that our clemency may more speedily recognize, as it desires, the converted dispositions of the peoples (Augustine, *Breviculus of the Conference*, day 1, chapter 1).

“But if, within the appointed period, the Donatist bishops deliberately avoid assembling, the periods prescribed for contumacious persons shall be concluded by a threefold summons through edict. Once these have elapsed and passed, if they disdain to appear when summoned, the people, together with the churches, shall yield—having recognized in the silence of their teachers that they have been defeated—and shall at last rejoice that they have been overcome, and shall know that they must obey, if not our commands, at least the true commands of the Catholic law.

“We desire you to sit as judge in the foremost place in that dispute (you fully remember whatever you previously received in your instructions). We desire you to bear every responsibility, whether in assembling the bishops or summoning them if they disdain to appear, so that by proven diligence you may carry out [Col. 1261A] both what was formerly commanded and what you know has now been established. Above all, you shall observe this: that what antiquity long ago ordained concerning the Catholic law, what the religious authority of our forebears established, and what our Serenity confirmed, you shall preserve whole and inviolate, after removing a novel fraudulent intrusion (in the *Theodosian Code*, “superstition”) [in the *Theodosian Code*: “We command that it be preserved”].

“And so that suitable support may not be lacking for your proceedings, our Serenity has instructed the spectabiles, the proconsul and the vicar, that if they desire to retain the standing of their own ranks, and if they desire their official staffs to avoid the most extreme penalties, they must arrange for more than sufficient necessary personnel to be assigned, both from their own offices and from the staffs of all judges. It will be your concern, if you learn that anything is being delayed by any artifice, to report it by sending accounts, [Col. 1261B] so that fitting correction may punish the negligent.

“Moreover, you must report to us everything which either a completed discussion, with the bishops assembled in one body, shall establish, or which a judgment issued concerning the contumacious shall establish if they perhaps withdraw; so that we may more speedily learn what our command has accomplished for confirming the Catholic faith.

“And in the divine hand. Farewell, Marcellinus, most dear to us. Given at Ravenna, on the day before the Ides of October, in the consulship of Varane, vir clarissimus. [The consular date has been added from the *Theodosian Code*.]”

5. Marcellinus, vir clarissimus, tribune and notary, said: “Let the venerable law which has been read be inserted into the present records. Since its determination has plainly appeared, let the text of my edicts now be read in order (Augustine, *Breviculus of the Conference*, day 1, chapter 2).”

Martialis, recorder, read:

“What our most merciful prince, our lord Honorius, has decreed for the confirmation of the Catholic faith is shown by the tenor of the preceding imperial letters. For, willingly accepting the embassy of the venerable bishops, he did not permit Africa—always devoted to his rule—to be disturbed and disfigured any longer by the variety of religions. Out of zeal for peace and faith, he willed that the dissensions of such great peoples, arising from ancient persuasion, should be calmed through the manifestation of truth; so that those whom he saw could not be calmed by imperial enactments repeatedly extended and drawn to a single confession of faith might be recalled through a hearing of the two parties.

“For he willed that all bishops of both the Catholic and Donatist parties should be assembled together, so that, once the more learned men have been selected on each side and the truth of the certain faith examined, manifest reason might convict superstition. [Col. 1261D] Thus whatever each person considers available in support of his own party may be brought into the open, and so, even if late, the light of true faith may shine forth.

“For the concordant request of both parties prompted this imperial decision. Just as the Catholics recently requested a conference, so there can be no doubt that the Donatist bishops, a very short time earlier, requested a conference before the court of the illustrious authorities. And [Col. 1262A] since the imperial clemency willingly granted assent and decreed that a universal council of both parties be held within Africa (it seems that “bishops” should be added), in accordance with their request, it willed that I should sit as judge in the foremost place in this dispute.

“Accordingly, by the tenor of this edict I admonish all bishops throughout Africa, both of the Catholic and the Donatist party, that they must not delay to assemble in the splendid city of Carthage for holding the council within the period prescribed by law—that is, within four months, which period will undoubtedly end on the day of the Kalends of June—lest the party which is found absent may appear to have judged [perhaps: “doubted”] the merit of its own faith.

“I likewise summon all curators, magistrates, and members of the municipal councils of all provinces, and also agents, procurators, or [Col. 1262B] elders of the several places, with the same admonition, under liability affecting their own reputation and rank and at the peril of their safety: they must hasten to summon the bishops of both parties in the cities and places where they reside, either under the preparation of official records or with documentary proof of any kind. If they cannot be found in the cities at that very time, they must be sought out even through the countryside, so that both the form of the imperial command and the tenor of this edict may be made known to them, and so that within these four months I may learn, through a report of the municipal councils, the intention of each party.

“I also wish the bishops of the Donatist party to know that, should any of them answer that he will be present, the church that is perhaps held by the Catholics under the imperial command shall first be handed over to him, with all its rights, immediately through the municipal officials [Note: [Col. 1261D] *The church shall first be handed over to him*, etc. Augustine writes, *Breviculus of the Conference*, day 1, chapter 2, that Marcellinus granted this to the Donatists without the emperor’s command. In that edict, he restored basilicas, without an imperial order, to those Donatists who promised to come, in order to invite them by this benefit also to participate in the conference. Marcellinus himself likewise confirms Augustine’s testimony in the edict issued against the Donatists after the conference: “Let them hasten, without any delay, to hand over to the Catholics the churches which, by my humanity and without an imperial command, are known to have been granted to them until the day of judgment.” BALUZIUS.].

“But if all or individual bishops, remaining in their own places, answer that they will be present, then the churches and those places which are shown to have belonged to them or to have been held by them shall be restored to their right and possession through the diligence of the aforesaid municipal councils, so that their former condition may first be restored and the discussion may begin.

“And since the most august prince has willed to entrust to me the weight of so great a matter, I also willingly declare that, should any hesitation arise concerning my person, I will not refuse to have another judge sit with me—one chosen by the Donatist party and faith itself, whether of higher or equal rank. But whether I take part in judging this matter with another or alone, I promise, by the wondrous mystery of the Trinity, by the sacrament of the Lord’s Incarnation, and by the safety of the above-mentioned emperors, that I shall judge only according to what the examined allegations of the parties [Col. 1262D] can demonstrate and what faith finds to be true.

“Nor could I omit this point: whether judgment is rendered for the Donatists or for the Catholics, the Donatist bishops shall suffer no annoyance in any respect, but shall return freely and unharmed by every kind of injury to their own places. [Col. 1263A] 248 I promise, by the dreadful Day of Judgment and by the sacraments mentioned above, that I shall do this.

“Moreover, let all who were sent to the several provinces know that henceforth they must in no way summon or molest anyone among the Donatists, nor impose upon them any inconvenience of the earlier enforcement, unless they prefer to be subject to punishment for contempt of this more recent command. All persons of the Donatist party shall be free to make complaint concerning extortions and plundering, should they know that any were perhaps committed by those who were sent; and, once the nature of the offenses has been proved, fitting punishment shall proceed against them.

“And in another hand: ‘Let it be posted.’”

6. Marcellinus, vir clarissimus, tribune and notary, said: “The text of this edict will also be received into the body of the proceedings. It is clear from it that I have expressly offered that, if it pleased you, another investigator chosen by your party should sit with me. If he is present, let him please enter.”

7. Bishop Petilianus said: “It is not fitting for us to choose a second investigator when we did not ask for the first.” And in another hand: “I have verified it.”

8. Marcellinus, vir clarissimus, tribune and notary, said: “The tenor of the august command has stated with the greatest clarity that it was not an investigator who was requested for the conference, but that, by its own choice, it delegated judgment to my humble person. I must serve this in every way, since it is also plain that Your Holiness has assembled for the purpose of satisfying the imperial enactments.”

9. Bishop Petilianus said: “Without prejudice to everything that belongs to us, both concerning the person and in the case, let those who have deserved to obtain these things set forth their request.” And in another hand: “I, Petilianus, bishop, have verified it.”

Marcellinus, vir clarissimus, tribune and notary, said: “Without prejudice and with all matters intact which are accorded by the laws, let the texts of the edicts be read in order, as I previously directed.”

10. Martialis, recorder, read:

“The magnitude of this matter, which is undertaken for the recognition of truth and religion, even if it were weighed in an examination as of little importance, ought nonetheless to be evaluated by the gravity and authority of the disputants themselves. For no one doubts how weighty is a cause that is to be discussed between persons of bishops. But since august condescension has entrusted to me the hearing of this dispute [Col. 1263D] and given me as judge to persons whom I know, in reverence for so great a name, to be my superiors, Out of concern for my trustworthiness, I made provision by resolving that my judgment should itself be judged.

“Therefore, by the authority of this purpose, I considered that all bishops of both parties should be admonished beforehand that not more than seven bishops of each party should hold the conference of reciprocal discussion among themselves, those whom the choice of their respective parties has appointed to the duty of disputation. For the imperial authority has ordered that a definite number be selected from the parties.

“Seven others also, bishops selected by the judgment of their respective parties, shall be present. Having first preserved moderation of silence throughout the whole conference, they shall understand that their sole purpose in attending is this: if any one of the seven disputants on either side wishes to confer with one of his own associates, he may withdraw with him to one side, and there, after patiently sharing the reasoning to be considered, may return to his own place. He must faithfully maintain the division of duty: one, for whom it is necessary, commits matters to be heard by silence; the other, whose task it is, confirms what has been undertaken by speaking.

“The Gargilian Baths shall be the most suitable place for the conference. On the day of the Kalends of June, only those bishops who have been designated are to assemble there. From this it is certainly clear that no gathering of the people at all should take place there, since not even all the bishops are permitted to assemble there. For since the patience required for discussion, which alone is friendly to silence, utterly recoils from every noisy throng of a crowd, it makes no difference whether it is impeded by a mass of people or by a crowd of bishops.

“Therefore, only the bishops mentioned shall assemble at the prescribed place and time. Yet all the remaining bishops of both parties, before the day appointed for examination, shall indicate by letters sent to my office that they will consider valid whatever their seven fellow bishops on either side shall do. To these letters all shall also append before me the testimony of their own subscriptions. For it is wholly equitable that the entire conference of those selected by all should be promised as binding by all.

“Therefore, no layperson or bishop beyond the number established may attempt, contrary to the prohibition, to enter that most tranquil place of the council. Rather, let them also admonish their congregations, by a pious exhortation to quietness and moderation, treating this beforehand in their own churches, so that all crowds may refrain from the place and day of the discussion, and so that they may prepare, by the religious instruction of patience, a people softened toward Christian peace.

“For not bishops alone, but also a rational people, agree with the aforementioned disputants in this decision: where the greater attention of minds is fixed upon the search for truth, nothing disturbed, nothing tumultuous, and finally nothing untimely ought in any way to raise an interruption. For in order that what benefits everyone’s salvation may afterward be made public, secrecy must first be afforded to those examining the truth. But my judgment must be proclaimed throughout in such a manner that, once it is released to public knowledge, it may be weighed with the whole people of splendid Carthage as judge.

“Thus the whole course of the completed debate will be disclosed to the eyes not only of this city but also of the entire province, so that both the pleadings of the disputing bishops and the successive course of my own proceedings may be unfolded in volumes arranged for public view. For this is the security of faith in a judge: that he does not fear being judged concerning himself.

“Therefore, lest any slanderous suspicion creep at all into the examination for eliciting truth, and lest any argument of either party cover with clouds the clear light which perfect faith in evident proofs will make plain to public minds, the following provision has also necessarily been made against the disguises of suspicion and contrivances of deception. Let all know that this must not only be observed but is also expedient: after I have first subscribed in every respect to my own statements, all the disputing bishops likewise, without any excuse whatsoever, shall subscribe to their own pleadings on the document. For the merit of faith requires that, against a person who perhaps seeks to evade the obligation of his assertions in bad faith and to deny what he said, the authority of his own testimony should stand firm, where victory benefits truth alone.

“Besides those who attend from the public offices to perform recording duties for my office, four ecclesiastical notaries from each party shall also attend in alternation. So that their trustworthiness may not waver through any ambiguity, four bishops, chosen from each party by the judgment of their fellow members, shall preside over them, and shall guard the same recorders and [Col. 1265B] notaries with vigilant and careful oversight. Leaving in turns with those recorders and notaries, they shall promptly ensure that what has been said is arranged in a clear written record, so that, while the aforementioned bishops are still engaged in the dispute, some part of the question already disposed of may be transferred into a manifest written instrument, and they may at once provide it, with the appended subscriptions of the seven bishops, for the speedy knowledge expected by the public.

“After the first day of the conference, the hearing shall be deferred until the following day, which shall be devoted to writing and subscribing the records; so that if anything remains from the previous conference, the examination may proceed to the third day. Thus an intervening day shall separate each successive period of discussion, during which the records that must promptly be subscribed may be written in the presence of the watchful custody of those mentioned, who shall understand their function to be limited to this: not to say anything, but to preserve what has been said.

“Until, after the questions have been brought to their conclusion, fully clarified truth untangles every ambiguity, the sheets successively written and subscribed shall be sealed with the impressions of my seal and of the eight custodians. The authority of this edict shall also be made known to the Maximianists, so that they may understand that they must refrain from that council which the religious command of the merciful emperors has appointed to distinguish [perhaps *discingui*, ‘be disentangled,’ as in the Third Hearing, chapter 149] and adjudicate every conflict between Catholics and Donatists. Nor can the fact that they flatter themselves with the Donatist name afford them any assistance, since they are said to have been condemned by the Donatists.

“If any person does not wish in any respect to observe what the tenor of this proclamation embraces—provisions carefully made against all the snares of manifold suspicion, faithfully established, and diligently ordered—he declares not only what he thinks of his cause but also what he intends to undertake. For the present, it is sufficient for the investigator, by the prerogative of justice in this admonition, to have made the people of Carthage witnesses for himself before all the bishops, whom he will shortly have as judges.

“It remains that, before the day of the council, the bishops of both parties, without the least delay, promise in letters sent to my office that they will fulfill the whole tenor of this arrangement. This point must especially be hastened: the letters by which they declare that they agree to all the provisions of this edict shall be marked only by the subscriptions of the primate bishops. For it is sufficient that the universal subscription, so to speak, of all the bishops should adhere to those letters by which they promise that they will regard as binding the entire order of the discussion conducted by the seven representatives.”

11. Marcellinus, vir clarissimus, tribune and notary, said: “This edict also shall be received into the body of the acts. But lest anything relevant to the full truth of the proceedings seem lacking, let the office review all matters which the parties have written or communicated to the courts in the meantime.”

12. Bishop Petilianus said: “Noble sir, you have performed your part, both by promising that you will be just to the parties and by making yourself public to the ears of the people. But because all these things are before the case, not about the case, we first request of your authority that the person who caused me to be summoned by edicts, called from my own seat, and troubled me to undergo the labor of travel, should set forth the petition which he made as he wished: why he desired my presence, so that I may know whether, or what, I ought to answer.” And in another hand: “I, Petilianus, bishop, have verified it.”

13. Marcellinus, vir clarissimus, tribune and notary, said: “These matters will more properly be dealt with in their place and order. Meanwhile, let the office proceed with what I have directed.”

14. Romulus, recorder, read:

“Copy of the Donatists’ notarial document. After the consulship of Varane, vir clarissimus, on the eighth day before the Kalends of June, to Flavius Marcellinus, vir clarissimus and spectabilis, tribune and notary: Januarius, Primianus, and the other bishops of sincere Christianity [Col. 1266C] and of Catholic truth.

“We make known to your Integrity that, having been summoned by your edict, we hastened from the different regions of Africa and entered Carthage on the fifteenth day before the Kalends of June. All whom Carthage contains are witnesses of our arrival, and your Integrity is not unaware of it. For the force of the oath imposed by your edict was so great that, except for those whom adverse bodily conditions keep in their seats or illness overtook on the road, neither the great age of the aged nor the toil of a long journey could prevent anyone.

“Although that edict alone was sufficient before the case, you also thought fit to issue a second one. Though many features of it concern us, it causes us particular and great anxiety because you have judged that we ourselves must attest your edict by our letters, although neither public practice nor the custom of judges permits this. We therefore earnestly urge your Integrity to preserve the good faith of the first edict and order us all to come before you, so that our number—concerning which our adversaries have often falsely claimed that we are few—may be established as quickly as possible, and so that, once everything which belongs to our party has been duly arranged, the discussion may follow.

“Otherwise your edicts may either seem to Your Integrity to conflict with one another, or something may prejudice us: since, although you have commanded all to come, you now appear to wish only a few to be present. For it is fitting and expedient that, while all are present, a few should speak on behalf of the common matter.

“We have retained with us an identical copy of this notarial document.”

And in another hand: “I, Januarianus, bishop, have subscribed.” And in another hand: “I, Primianus, bishop, have subscribed.”

[Col. 1267A] 15. Marcellinus, vir clarissimus, tribune and notary, said: “Let the letter of the other party likewise be read.”

16. Romulus, recorder, read:

“To the honorable and beloved son, Marcellinus, vir clarissimus and spectabilis, tribune and notary: Aurelius, Sylvanus, and all the Catholic bishops.—By the edict of Your Spectability, etc.” It survives in Augustine, vol. II, col. 487, Epistle 128 of our edition.

17. Marcellinus, [250] vir clarissimus and spectabilis, tribune and notary, said:

“Since I remember that, prompted by justice or faith, I once pledged that whatever I should transact with the bishops of either party I would transmit to public knowledge, there is reason for me to have the edicts read again. For since the text of the earlier proclamation contains in orderly form the matters by which the arranged hearing may follow an unobstructed course of judgment, [Col. 1267B] I had considered it necessary to require by edict from all bishops what each party thought concerning it. In reply to my office, partly through a notarial document and partly through a letter, they have communicated what they think concerning the conditions recently proposed.

“I therefore judged that the form of both the letter and the notarial document should be offered to public view, so that the knowledge of the whole people, considering both what the text of the earlier edict required and what was reported in the answer of each party, might clearly perceive the intent of the examiner.”

After this had been inserted, he had the same document read.

18. “To the honorable and beloved son, Marcellinus, vir clarissimus and spectabilis, tribune and notary: Aurelius, Silvanus, and all the Catholic bishops.—The notarial document or letter of our brothers has caused us great concern, etc.” It survives in St Augustine, vol. II, col. 490, Epistle 119 of our edition.

252 19. Marcellinus, vir clarissimus, tribune and notary, said:

“It has plainly appeared that the edict of my office prescribed that the business of the case should be conducted by the appointed number which they would accept by the will of all, since its reading showed that the most sacred law also so willed. Since it has been shown that the Catholic bishops assented to the tenor of the edict, let the bishops of the other party indicate whether they have likewise satisfied this requirement, or whether they now wish to satisfy it.”

20. Bishop Emeritus said:

“The case has, as I think, been set in motion, and the identity of the disputants has not yet been determined. For nothing else rests upon you, most true of judges, than to hold to truth. If we turn to the procedure of all cases, we must first address the time, the commission, the person, and the cause; only then must we proceed to the merits of the case.

“But if, passing over these matters, legal form and language must always be observed by us according to the forensic insignia and the pretension of that controversy which claims the tribunals for itself, then judge, exalted sir, in a Christian case. For God judges this cause; and, weighing both our merits and the sentence of the true judge in an even balance, he takes care that it does not incline.

“As regards the intention of the judge, we see in the edicts issued by your presence nothing rash, incongruous, or directed against anyone. But as regards our answers, since they are known to be superfluous before the case and before the merits of the principal business, neither our proposal nor their answer can prejudice me. For, preserving all things intact, now that we have crossed the threshold of judgment before the case, we can determine what the merits of the case are.”

And in another hand: “I, Emeritus, bishop, have verified it.”

21. Marcellinus, vir clarissimus, tribune and notary, said: “It is established that nothing in the case has at all been mutilated, since I ordered only those matters to be read which were previously written or transacted. Accordingly, since it has been commanded that a definite number be appointed by the parties, let Your Venerability indicate whether the edict has been obeyed, as I have stated above.”

22. Bishop Emeritus said: “Admonished indeed by the edicts of your Integrity, we shall preserve all the matters of the case whole and untouched. We state this case, if the time and day permit. For we know from both the edict of Your Spectability and the tenor of the sacred rescript that the case must be concluded within four months. If this is the day, let us proceed to the case. For we cannot dispute anything concerning the merits unless judgment has first been rendered concerning the day.” And in another hand: “I, Emeritus, bishop, have verified it.”

23. Marcellinus, vir clarissimus, tribune and notary, said: “From the second edict you were able to know the day, which appears to have been fixed as the day of the Kalends of June, since the report of the office has shown that this is today and the reading of the edict has demonstrated it. It remains to be stated whether your party has complied with the arrangement of the proceedings and the selection of persons. For amid a confused multitude there cannot be a definite person, since this is established even by law.”

24. Bishop Emeritus said: “Whether the deadline prescribed by the edict, or the form of the imperial command, has enclosed the day of the proceedings must be determined by the judgment of Your Nobility.” And in another hand: “I, Emeritus, bishop, have verified it.”

25. Marcellinus, vir clarissimus, tribune and notary, said: “The day has been fixed by the edict according to the form of the imperial judgment; and since there must be no further delay in these matters, it remains for you to comply with the heavenly enactments in the selection.”

26. Bishop Emeritus said: “The form of the command is such that the case must be argued within four months. If the edict of Your Sublimity has been established according to this form, it remains that, upon the office’s report, the case should be brought forward.” And in another hand: “I, Emeritus, bishop, have verified it.”

27. Marcellinus, vir clarissimus, tribune and notary, said: “Let the office answer what has been asked.” Nampius, clerk, said: “According to the day of Your Nobility’s edict, the fourth month was completed on the fourteenth day before the Kalends of June.”

28. Marcellinus, vir clarissimus, tribune and notary, said: “Since both parties had come to Carthage, there can be no doubt that they assented to this day. For no request for delay, nor any demand for a judicial ruling, appears to have been made on this point.”

29. Bishop Petilianus said: We came to this city on the fifteenth day before the Kalends of June, and we sealed our official notice; we made witness not merely, I will not say Carthage, but [Col. 1269A] Africa entire. Had we not been present, the opposing party would undoubtedly already have demanded that sentence be pronounced against us as contumacious, and that the time had now been fixed beyond which those who came later would not be permitted either to conduct any business or to reply. Therefore, if you, noble sir, always hold and govern the balanced scale of your judgment so suspended in the middle that it inclines toward no side, by that favor which you know has been granted you by imperial authority in the commission and command, so that you may pronounce sentence against the contumacious: now, by that judicial impulse, you ought to observe that those things which would plainly befall the opposing party, and direct your judgment against this party, which has failed, which was absent, which has taken pleasure in my labors, which has even mocked me in this respect: that this most holy choir, this heavenly senate, should for a long time behold the authority of your judgment, [Col. 1269B] should keep watch almost daily, and should not themselves perform without anxiety the things belonging to God and sacred things. I therefore ask you to pronounce judgment and issue a sentence—not, I say, one harsher than that which you could have pronounced against me, but that which the laws and the imperial command make known to you and prescribe. For it is not lawful that you who could pronounce judgment against us should now be able to refuse a sentence against my adversaries. And in another hand: I, Bishop Petilianus, have reviewed it.

30. Marcellinus, most illustrious man, tribune and notary, said: I do not believe that it escapes your holiness and learning that it was established by the imperial injunction that the party which had refused to appear at the appointed meeting under the threefold edict should incur the sentence due to contumacy. For the most clement emperor, having weighed the matter with moderation, established that, [Col. 1269C] if because of the length of the journey the parties could not come to the appointed place within the fourth month, a respite of two months should be granted. I appear to have observed this provision, lest a complaint by either party should arise. Therefore, concerning the time—an objection which belongs more to the forum than to bishops, and which indeed could not have prevailed even in a public court under the terms of the imperial command, since it is quite clear that both parties observed it—as I said above, please declare whether persons have been chosen who can conduct the business by the will of all.

31. Bishop Emeritus said: The judge’s statement is a preliminary ruling in the case: that forensic practice and the customary mode of litigation ought not to be observed among bishops; that the cunning devices of laws and legal controversy ought not to flourish [Col. 1269D] where the state of faith and the matter of all holiness are under discussion. We receive this, eminent sir, with chaste and rightly believing ears. But lest these things perhaps be brought forward again to our ruin, and a right be granted to our adversaries to fight anew, and this be asserted against us on the ground that this legal requirement has been preserved: you ought to assent to this form of law; establish this very point by judicial authority, that the rule of episcopal custom requires us to adhere to holiness, so that the case may be heard not through the tricks of law or the bonds of anyone’s eloquence, but through the New and Old Testament which God instituted and the Lord Christ consecrated. And in another hand: I, Bishop Emeritus, have reviewed it.

32. Marcellinus, most illustrious man, tribune and notary, said: [Col. 1270A] Lest anything seem to be done disorderly, since both the rule of truth itself contains this and the authority of the laws prescribes it, the number of the persons must first be designated. Only then will the matters belonging to the parties be more properly conducted through those who have been duly authorized, lest these matters seem insecure among uncertain persons.

33. Bishop Emeritus said: Since all who are to give a mandate seem to be present, and since the identity of those present rather than the statement of those absent ought to prevail, what can hinder the proceedings, once all matters have been settled which first proceed from the law and which customarily make the beginning of a case, so that then at last we may come to the selection of advocates according to the decision contained in the edict of your highness? And in another hand: I, Bishop Emeritus, [Col. 1270B] have reviewed it.

34. Marcellinus, most illustrious man, tribune and notary, said: A multitude could never possess a definite legal identity, since even in public proceedings and corporate bodies it is customary to observe that all business be conducted through persons duly arranged and authorized.

35. Bishop Emeritus said: I trust your good faith, exalted sir: that no rule of legal law is to be imposed on me where faith is at issue. And in another hand: I, Bishop Emeritus, have reviewed it.

36. Marcellinus, most illustrious man, tribune and notary, said: My ruling most plainly determined not that law ought to cease, but that forensic contention ought to cease. For things belonging to the parties [Col. 1270C] cannot be denied them. But if this is the agreement of both parties—that nothing be done under public law, but that everything be conducted according to ecclesiastical rules, that is, according to the testimonies of the New and Old Testament—let each party designate its representatives.

37. Bishop Petilianus said: An excellent moderator. And in another hand: I, Bishop Petilianus, have reviewed it.

38. Aurelius, bishop of the Catholic Church, said: Since, according to the edict of your nobility (N. T.), not all our colleagues are present—they having obeyed the edict—and since the will of all is contained in the mandate, order that this same mandate be received by the official staff and read aloud. And in another hand: I have reviewed it.

39. Bishop Emeritus said: If you so order, this is appropriate to the case through your integrity. And in another hand: I, Bishop Emeritus, have reviewed it.

40. Marcellinus, most illustrious man, tribune and notary, said: It is established that a different question has been raised: whether you wish to depart from public law and have everything conducted by divine laws; demonstrate this by your declarations.

41. Aurelius, bishop of the Catholic Church of Carthage, said: Your highness will find this very point when the mandate has been read aloud. And in another hand: I have reviewed it.

42. Marcellinus, most illustrious man, tribune and notary, said: This too is most plainly contained in the mandate: that, public-law controversy being set aside, everything be conducted by divine laws.

[Col. 1271A] 43. Aurelius, bishop of the Catholic Church of Carthage, said: The reading of the mandate will be able to inform your understanding. And in another hand: I have reviewed it.

44. Bishop Petilianus said: Whoever doubts what he ought to profess rejects God’s law. And in another hand: I, Bishop Petilianus, have reviewed it.

45. Marcellinus, most illustrious man, tribune and notary, said: I wished these matters to be confirmed by the parties’ reply; otherwise, since everything is now being conducted under the imperial command, by which legal rights have been established, it is certain that I cannot in any way depart from it.

46. Aurelius, bishop of the Catholic Church of Carthage, said: We do not reject God’s law when we submit this mandate to be read, in which our whole case can be set forth. Nor can we go beyond [Col. 1271B] the bounds of this mandate, which our fathers and brothers of the universal council of the Catholic Church, assembled here at Carthage, entrusted to us. And in another hand: I have reviewed it.

47. Bishop Emeritus said: This is a case concerning faith, which can be conducted by right even without a mandate. For God does not have eyes elsewhere, nor has he deserted heaven so as not to attend to his own cause. Why is inquiry being made about a mandate, or the obligation of a mandate, subscription, manner, and formulae? Why does a claim, as though concerning one who objects or one who has not given a judicial mandate, seek a decision in this case, when each individual carries his own cause and the business of his salvation, and the mandate of the others is superfluous, since the whole person of the Church is found in one? Let your integrity observe, noble sir—an integrity which we already recognize as shining in this seat with a certain brightness—that truth ought so to preside [Col. 1271C] that, if forensic debate and a conflict of legal claims are introduced, let them be proposed; but if that simple truth by which life is given, the world is reborn, and the world was delivered, is sought in this spiritual judgment by means of contention, then, exalted sir, I ask that they propose both and choose one of the two. For either they cannot omit the merits of law and the preliminary bars to actions; or, if the question is of those most sacred laws to which common reverence must be rendered—upon which, perhaps, we depend—then I shall with greater patience embrace and hold fast to them, and shall always adore and venerate, as it were, the high priesthood of the heavenly altar, so that for you, an unimpaired judge, according to the disposition of your mind and the order of your character, there may be a definite [Col. 1271D] basis for judgment, and your judgment may not waver—a judgment concerning which God and the people will pass judgment. And in another hand: I, Bishop Emeritus, have reviewed it.

48. Fortunatianus, bishop of the Catholic Church, said: The Catholic Church, which, as promised, is spread throughout the whole world, since it has always offered the opposing party a conference both concerning faith and concerning the charge which they criminally bring against us, will more easily establish its case by public records, the testimony of many persons, and the agreement of magistrates. But, so that the cause of the conference itself may be secure in every respect, a confused multitude does not make it so. Therefore let our brethren who are present choose from the opposing side certain leading men of their rank, to whom they may entrust the whole substance of the proceeding [Col. 1272A] and who may give assurance on behalf of the present records; so that, if they should fail in the assertion of this case, the reading of the records may show without delay, in the persons of those who undertook such business, that they have been defeated. And therefore, because there is no need to conduct the case with manifold delay, let them choose, according to the tenor of the proposed edict, persons who may undertake the business of the conference, so that truth—always proved to all—may be shown more clearly than light. For the reading of the mandate, if the opposing party permits it, will more easily show that it contains nothing of legal pleading or forensic evasion. And in another hand: I have reviewed it.

49. Marcellinus, most illustrious man, tribune and notary, said: It is certain that your statement agrees with the imperial command, which established that a definite [Col. 1272B] number should be chosen by each party. For whether the case concerns law or faith, definite persons must be present, so that whatever is done may possess unimpaired force.

50. Fortunatianus, bishop of the Catholic Church, said: Therefore may your eminence deign to hand over the received mandate to the official staff and order it read aloud, so that, instructed by its tenor, the opposing party may deign to answer all the objections, and so that it may also become clear that we do not wish to evade public law. And in another hand: I have reviewed it.

51. Marcellinus, most illustrious man, tribune and notary, said: Your holiness has plainly received the declaration for which it was waiting. Therefore let it now permit the mandate to be read, with the reservation that each party recognizes that I must observe the terms of the imperial command. Fortunatianus, bishop of the Catholic Church, said: If your eminence orders it, let it be read.

52. Marcellinus, most illustrious man, tribune and notary, said: Let everything offered by the parties be read aloud by the official staff, so that every ambiguity may be removed.

53. Bishop Petilianus said: Let him read, without prejudice to our position, preserving the point that this is forensic pleading, not legal procedure. For to employ a mandate and presume upon these formulae is not an ecclesiastical custom but a forensic game and contest, that exercise which often rests more upon arguments than upon any faith. Therefore may the judgment of your noble eminence repeatedly remain upon this point and declare whether they wish the case to be conducted by divine law and the dispute itself argued between the parties, [Col. 1272D] or whether they wish to employ public laws altogether. For I have much that bears upon both alternatives: so that, if he departs from the law, he may show that he is not a bishop; but if he holds to the law, then I ought to answer him as one who desires to be a Christian. And in another hand: I, Bishop Petilianus, have reviewed it.

54. Marcellinus, most illustrious man, tribune and notary, said: If this dispute were being handled solely among bishops with no judge of secular authority presiding, then it would indeed be within their discretion, and perhaps rightly so, to wish that nothing be handled under public law. But since those who selected me as judge are the lawgivers, it is certain that I cannot depart from the laws, although your holiness has most plainly received the declaration [Col. 1273A] of the party coming from the opposite side, in which it is recognized that the point expressed is the very one your statement requested. Therefore let the mandate be read by the official staff.

55. Bishop Petilianus said: Let him read. And in another hand: I, Bishop Petilianus, have reviewed it. Romulus, recorder, read aloud: “After the consulship of the most illustrious man Varanius, on the third day before the Kalends of June. Mandate made in the Church.” And while he was reading, Bishop Adeodatus said: “Let it be read without prejudice to our position.” Marcellinus, most illustrious man, tribune and notary, said: “I have repeatedly stated that everything is to be read with the parties’ responses intact.” Romulus, recorder, read aloud: “Mandate made in the Church of Carthage by the universal council of Catholic bishops: Aurelius, bishop of the Church of Carthage, and Silvanus, [Col. 1273B] primate of Numidia, presiding. Although the cause of the Catholic Church against all false accusations, etc.” See Augustine, vol. IX, cols. 822–827 of our edition.

56. Marcellinus, most illustrious man, tribune and notary, said: Since, from the reading of the mandate which will be attached to the present proceedings, it has become clear that divine testimonies rather than forensic bonds were produced, that the tenor of my edict was likewise observed in the selection of a number, and that the form of the imperial constitution was nevertheless preserved, therefore—since the order of justice requires it—let the subscriptions of all likewise be read aloud.

57. Romulus, recorder, read aloud: “I, Aurelius, bishop of the Catholic Church of Carthage, residing at Carthage, in the presence of Marcellinus, most illustrious tribune and notary, have received and subscribed this mandate.” Likewise, in another hand: “I, Silvanus, of the first see of the province of Numidia, residing at Carthage in the presence of Marcellinus, most illustrious tribune and notary, agreed to and subscribed the mandate made by us.” Likewise, in another hand: “I, Valentinus, bishop of the Church of Vaiana, [Note: [Col. 1273D] “Vaianensis,” or “Baianensis,” as it is written in an old book. Below, chapters 99, 115, and 135, it is always written “Vaiensis”; but we have restored “Vaianensis” everywhere, because the correction is certainly sound. For Felix, bishop of Baiana, attended the Council of Carthage under Gratus, and Beianus of Baiana was condemned in the year 394 at the Council of Bagaia. There was an intention to assign this see to Mauretania Caesariensis, because among the bishops of that province expelled by Huneric, king of the Vandals, I find Caecilius of Beliana. But the subscriptions of the Council of Cabarsussa oppose this view, where the name of Pancratius of Baliana is read. For since that synod was held one year before the Council of Bagaia, at which Beianus of Baiana the Donatist was condemned, this seems to prove that the Church of Baliana was different from that of Baiana; indeed, it is not likely that two Donatist bishops were established in one Church. BALUZE adds: In the same Council of Cabarsussa, besides Pancratius of Baliana, there is Donatus, bishop of Beliana; hence it is certain that Baliana and Beliana were two sees.] residing at Carthage, in the presence of Marcellinus, most illustrious tribune and notary, have given this mandate and subscribed it.” And the remaining subscriptions of those whose names are contained in the mandate.

58. Marcellinus, most illustrious man, tribune and notary, said: The proceedings shall also receive these subscriptions together with the mandate. And he added: Let the number of subscribers likewise be indicated. Martialis, recorder, said: There are two hundred and sixty-six.

59. Bishop Petilianus said: Where are those who gave the mandate? [Col. 1273D] And in another hand: I, Bishop Petilianus, have reviewed it.

[Col. 1274A] 60. Aurelius, bishop of the Catholic Church, said: This is necessary: let them choose seven of their own and go to the place where they are assembled in the church, and see them. And in another hand: I have reviewed it.

61. Bishop Petilianus said: This is a subtle device: to make the judge a witness. For they could also have added any clerics of lower rank to their names and pretended that such was the honor which they consider supreme among themselves, when this is precisely the matter in doubt. Therefore let the notaries come into court, and let them be individually recognized by us. For we fear devices often sought out at length, which they daily contrive to destroy our simplicity. This, therefore, is the first matter of which we took care to inform your highness through our official statement; nor have we ceased seeking confirmation of our own number first, which they always falsely report to imperial ears as small. For whatever is obtained against us is always obtained as though against a very few. And in another hand: I, Bishop Petilianus, have reviewed it.

62. Marcellinus, most illustrious man, tribune and notary, said: It is neither fitting for a priest to make an accusation of forgery nor credible that he could have committed it. But this is what I desire to know from your venerability: whether you can recognize all the bishops against whom your charge proceeds and whose subscriptions have also been read aloud.

63. Bishop Petilianus said: We can readily recognize, each of us, the adversaries of our own sees. Certainly, we have not alleged forgery; rather, what we wish to establish is a matter of the greatest diligence. And in another hand: I, Bishop Petilianus, have reviewed it.

64. Marcellinus, most illustrious man, tribune and notary, said: I judge this more favorably of your holiness: that what your holiness believed should be said in the statement is a matter of diligence rather than an accusation of any crime. But I ask whether there may be two bishops, one from each party, in every locality and city; for thus they can fully recognize one another.

65. Bishop Petilianus said: You have most wisely and providently foreseen everything, noble sir. For in my people—that is, in the city of Constantine—I have Fortunatus as an adversary. But in the midst of my diocese I now have—or rather, they themselves have—one appointed, named Delphinus [Note: [Col. 1274D] Delphinus. He had been sent into Numidia by his fellow bishops because of the needs of the Church, as Augustine states in his letter to Marcellinus, formerly 158, now 139. He is also mentioned below in chapter 215. He had been newly established as bishop, because of the needs of the Church, in some city near Constantine.]. Your excellence now sees from this [Col. 1274D] that two have been fictitiously established among one people, [Note: [Col. 1274D] *Imaginarie*: under a fictitious and supposititious title; thus Colluthus is called by Athanasius not a true but an “imaginary” bishop.] so as both to increase their number, while the number of peoples is not correspondingly the same as that of these persons. This is an argument of the greatest importance: they seem to surpass us by this means if two or three are established against one. For even among the people of my present most holy colleague and brother Adeodatus—that is, in the city of Milevis—the matter has been so arranged that he has one adversary there [Note: [Col. 1275D] An adversary: namely Severus, who, as is stated in chapter 215, had shortly before departed after being struck by illness. His letter to Augustine survives among the Augustinian letters as no. 109, as do two letters of Augustine to him, nos. 110 and 62, in the last edition. In the same edition, letter 34 calls him Augustine’s fellow student.], another in the city of Tucca [Note: [Col. 1276D] Another in the city of Tucca: Sabinus, mentioned in chapter 130, bishop of this city in Numidia. It had not long before been made episcopal.], which from antiquity belongs to this people and appears to have received a bishop only two years ago; while a third is in the place called Ceramussa. Therefore, although there is one bishop of the city of Milevis from our party, three appear to have been established by them, in order that their number might be increased or perhaps exceed the number belonging to truth. It must therefore be investigated [Col. 1275B] when their number was increased, what origin it had, whether novelty caused this or antiquity produced it, whether, so to speak, this defect of novelty was introduced against venerable antiquity. And in another hand: I, Bishop Petilianus, have reviewed it.

66. Fortunatianus, bishop of the Catholic Church, said: Your gracious understanding perceives with me, excellent judge, that the Church’s cause ought not to be conducted by much speaking. And while he was speaking: And in another hand: I have reviewed it.

67. Bishop Petilianus said: You have written more than I said. And in another hand: I, Bishop Petilianus, have reviewed it.

68. Fortunatianus, bishop of the Catholic Church, said: Yet the most grave man Petilianus, although a little earlier [Col. 1275C] he had declared that the Church’s cause must be established by the divine Scriptures and had determined that it must be examined by divine testimonies, is now shown by his statement to wander in various directions among the persons of those ordained. Therefore, lest we seem like him, your highness has received the tenor of the decree, and its reading has shown what the ordinances of the Fathers intended. It is fitting that those present, all delaying proceedings having been rejected and overthrown, now choose suitable men from their party who can render an account of the instituted case and state the agreement of all in these proceedings, so that, when truth has been brought to light, no one may be in doubt. For, once the persons have been confirmed, no party will dare to say that the sentence cannot or ought not to stand, since their agreement will have been set forth in the records. Therefore let them either show themselves confirmed by the subscriptions which we produce, or let each individually make his agreement known, so that the action concerning the Church may begin in its proper order. And in another hand: I have reviewed it.

69. Marcellinus, most illustrious man, tribune and notary, said: Concerning those improperly ordained whom the most holy man Petilianus has included, it is certain that I, who appear to have been appointed by imperial authority as judge for another matter, cannot take cognizance. It remains that, if your venerability believes the number of bishops assembled by the official staff within this [Col. 1276A] splendid Carthage to be true, it should now deign to declare this.

70. Bishop Petilianus said: The party standing opposite has not understood what I have argued. For, since the number of those giving the mandate is now at issue, it was especially a matter of my diligence to ask where those are who gave a mandate to the persons present to act. Next, what I argued before your tribunal, noble sir, is not without relevance. Therefore, since they have both renounced those things which they could have employed under forensic barriers and laws and have read a mandate which is not so much forensic as legal, I now recognize that I ought fittingly to answer them under divine law. But first, that the number of those who gave mandates may be established, and how many on my side have given mandates or will give them, I ask this first of your nobility: that your highness ought to pronounce judgment concerning the number of each party, so that it may not be superfluous. And in another hand: I, Bishop Petilianus, have reviewed it.

71. Marcellinus, most illustrious man, tribune and notary, said: To avoid a multitude, those about whose number there is doubt are said not to have come to this place, especially since it was sufficient for them to have delegated the whole business to those present. But if any doubt is raised on this point, let it be presented to the court.

72. Aurelius, bishop of the Catholic Church of Carthage, said: We avoid disorder; that is why they did not come. But the mandate which was read to your nobility is most firm. If there is doubt about the number, let provincials go to the Moors, to the Numidians, to the Byzacenes, and also to the Tripolitanians; let those of the proconsular province who are present from their number go [to them] and recognize our men who subscribed to this mandate. And in another hand: I have reviewed it.

73. Marcellinus, most illustrious man, tribune and notary, said: I will not permit a superfluous matter to be delayed by the parties’ prolonged wrangling; let them all come.

74. Aurelius, bishop of the Catholic Church, said: What need is there for crowds? Both we and our colleagues have long resided in the city. They too, as they say, have remained in the city not merely today but for several days. Let the subscriptions be read; and whoever’s name they doubt, [Col. 1276D] let that man himself come. And in another hand: I have reviewed it.

75. Marcellinus, most illustrious man, tribune and notary, said: Are they all in one place, or cannot this be clearly established?

76. Aurelius, bishop of the Catholic Church, said: We do not know what need there was for them to remain confined after they gave the mandate. And in another hand: I have reviewed it. Augustine, bishop of the Catholic Church, said: Let those whose names are doubted come themselves. And in another hand: I have reviewed it.

[Col. 1277A] 77. Bishop Emeritus said: The proceeding contradicts itself, and there is conflicting contention from one party. One argues that they ought to come; another says that he does not know whether they can be present. Let them agree among themselves in their opinions and declare, by their own private deliberation, what they prefer to choose. In view of your merits, we await whatever these men may say they think should be chosen. For we have not alleged an accusation of forgery, but we want this very fact to be approved by the court. Better is the assurance entered into the present proceedings, and confidence in truth is confirmed by the truth of the documents. For this concerns a matter regarding which someone may deny: “I gave no mandate; I was not present; I do not know.” These statements do not originate with me, but rather with those who fabricate such things. Let them hold their own consultation and determine everything by their own judgment, [Col. 1277B] so that if they wish to give a mandate now, just as we now present in the proceedings of your highness the persons giving mandates, they may readily do so. Let them remove falsehood from the midst. We grant them everything which could have been brought forward from the injunction, so that it may appear to the judgment of your highness, from their side and ours, what can constitute a mandate. And in another hand: I, Bishop Emeritus, have reviewed it.

78. Augustine, bishop of the Catholic Church, said: Care had to be taken that no disturbance should occur, and you provided for this wisely and beneficially. And since it must be feared that, should some disturbance arise, it may be attributed rather to us, while it remains uncertain to people from which party it originated, we think your nobility can decide nothing better or more peaceably than that, once [Col. 1277C] all the names have been read, whoever they doubt should come. And in another hand: I have reviewed it.

79. Marcellinus, most illustrious man, tribune and notary, said: You have received the declaration of the opposing party. Let the appropriate measures be carried out.

80. Bishop Emeritus said: The patience of your nobility and your inmost impartiality, which you display to all, have become evident to the eyes of everyone. I trust your judgment; I trust its testimony. The course of the sun is now almost completed, the whole day has passed, and still no disturbance has arisen, though so great a multitude of God’s priests stands here. For who, other than those whom the truth of the proceedings commanded to be present, has answered either by muttering among themselves or in stammering speech? In the silent stillness of their tongues they await the unimpaired and severe judgment of a truth-speaking judge; and, as he said, with necks almost bent down, hanging upon you with all their attention, they anxiously seek what you will judge concerning God’s cause. [Col. 1277D] No noise, no speech; indeed, continuous prayer to God and a private voice directed toward heaven. From where, then, could this public disturbance arise—from private and scurrilous conversations, by which those who readily make noise, or who by habitual daily quarrelling do not fear the dread of courts, might produce it? For this purpose, so many priests of God, so many bishops, desiring to hear the cause of their souls and the account of their faith, seek most shamefully to disrupt the proceeding by a superfluous disturbance and a kind of quarrel, unwilling to submit to the truth of judgment. And in another hand: I, Bishop Emeritus, have reviewed it.

81. Augustine, bishop of the Catholic Church, said: [Col. 1278A] Your nobility should see how little I answer to the many remarks of my brother. If they should be willing to answer us, perhaps the entire case will quickly be concluded. It must be feared that there is no disturbance from this crowd now present because no other multitude is here to which blame can be shifted. And in another hand: I have reviewed it.

82. Bishop Petilianus (perhaps Emeritus) said: You admit that they will come with disorder. For this disturbance has not arisen, nor will it arise, from our party. And in another hand: I, Bishop Emeritus, have reviewed it.

83. Augustine, bishop of the Catholic Church, said: I do not admit that they will come with disorder; but I fear that the multitude now present remains quiet only because there is no one upon whom it can cast blame if anything should happen turbulently [Col. 1278B] when both multitudes are present. We request that what has been said be done: whoever is doubted should be produced. And in another hand: I have reviewed it.

84. Bishop Adeodatus said: If disorder cannot be caused among a few, how can it be caused among many? And in another hand: I have reviewed it. Aurelius, bishop of the Catholic Church, said: Judge. And in another hand: I have reviewed it.

85. Marcellinus, most illustrious man, tribune and notary, said: A multitude of priests, considering on both sides the divine judgment, can indeed maintain silence even in any crowd; but it is certain, and cannot in any way be doubted, that a smaller number can more readily give assent through silence. Therefore, lest we linger over superfluities, if there is any doubt concerning the subscriptions, I shall immediately cause those whom your holiness believes neither to be present nor able to have subscribed [Col. 1278C] to come before the court, so that at last, once the persons of both parties have been confirmed according to the imperial command, we may proceed to the merits of the case.

86. Bishop Emeritus said: The conflicting opinions from one side ought to agree. Either they say their people are here, in which case they ought to be present; or, if they profess them absent, let your nobility consider what it ought to judge concerning absentees.
