Perhaps the same see whose bishop Victor of Vita, *On the Vandal Persecution*, I.11, says was Faustus, whom he calls bishop of Buronita. It appears to have been a town of the proconsular province.], in the presence of Marcellinus, *vir clarissimus*, tribune and notary, I dictated and subscribed the foregoing at Carthage.”

After he had read this, he said: “The Donatists have no one there.”

And it was read aloud:

“Candorius, bishop of the people of Mullita [Note: [Col. 1300D] Mullita. In the proconsular province, as the *Notitia* teaches. At the Council of Carthage in 525, Segetius, bishop of the people of Mullita, subscribed.], in the presence of Marcellinus, *vir clarissimus*, tribune and notary, I dictated and subscribed the foregoing [Col. 1300B] at Carthage.”

Marcellinus, bishop, said: “I recognize him.”

And it was read aloud:

“Isaac, bishop of the people of Utina [Note: [Col. 1300D] Utina. In the proconsular province, as observed above.], in the presence of Marcellinus, *vir clarissimus*, tribune and notary, I dictated and subscribed the foregoing at Carthage.”

Bishop Felicianus said: “I recognize him.”

And it was read aloud:

“I, the aforementioned, on behalf of Bishop Victor of Tuburbium Minus [Note: [Col. 1300D] Tuburbium Minus. There were two Tuburbia in Africa, Greater and Lesser. The Lesser is mentioned here and in chapter 203; the Greater in chapters 135 and 201. Both towns belonged to the proconsular province. Only one appears in the *Notitia*.], being present but unable to write, in the presence of Marcellinus, *vir clarissimus*, tribune and notary, subscribed that he had dictated the foregoing at Carthage.”

Bishop Maximinus said: “I recognize him.”

And it was read aloud:

“Felix, bishop of Tubia [Note: [Col. 1300D] Tubia. In Mauretania Sitifensis. For at the Council of Carthage in 397, Canon 48 of the African Code, the delegates of the province of Mauretania Sitifensis complained concerning Cresconius, bishop of Villaregia in the province of Numidia, that he had seized the Church of Tubia. The town was therefore in the Sitifensian province, near Numidia.], in the presence of Marcellinus, *vir clarissimus*, tribune and notary [Col. 1301A], I dictated and subscribed the foregoing.”

He said: “It is Catholic alone.”

And it was read aloud:

“Felix, bishop of Abbir Major [Note: [Col. 1301B] 172 Abbir Major. There were two African towns named Abbir: the greater one, mentioned here, and [Col. 1301C] the other, mentioned in chapter 215. Victor of Vita, *On the Vandal Persecution*, II.8, mentions Felix, bishop of Abbir, sent into exile; perhaps he is the same Felix called bishop of Abarita in the *Notitia* of the proconsular province. The same Victor, I.4, mentions the Abaritan province as distinct from the proconsular province: Genseric is there said to have reserved for himself the provinces of Byzacena, Abaritana, Gaetulia, and part of Numidia, while assigning Zeugitania, or the proconsular province, to his army. At the Council of Carthage in 419, Bishop Candidus of Abbir was one of the delegates of the proconsular province; in the subscriptions he is called Candidus of Germania, since this city was called Abbir Germaniciana. Hence Successus of Abbir-Germaniciana attended the Council of Carthage under Cyprian. Germaniciana was part of Numidia, as may be inferred from Augustine, who in Letter 251 testifies that the Germanicians were entrusted to his care. In the Anonymous Ravennate and in the Peutinger Tables, the city of Germani [Col. 1301D] is placed in Numidia near Theveste; and in the *Notitia* of Numidia, no. 28 is Florentius of Noba-Germani, and no. 97 Crescentianus of Germani. Therefore Abbir Germaniciana would be thought distinct from Abbir in the proconsular province, unless Candidus, bishop of Abbir and delegate of the proconsular province at the Council of Carthage in 419, were called bishop of Germania or of the Germanicians. Antoninus, in the *Itinerary*, seems to assign Germaniciana to Byzacena. To reconcile these facts, one must say that the region of Germaniciana belonged partly to the proconsular province, partly to Byzacena, and partly to Numidia, or was situated on the boundaries of those three provinces. This Felix, who had no opponent, was bishop of one of the two sees of Abbir; Annibonius, mentioned in chapter 215, belonged to the other.], in the presence of Marcellinus, *vir clarissimus*, tribune and notary, I dictated and subscribed the foregoing at Carthage.”

When it had been read, he said: “It is Catholic alone.”

And it was read aloud:

“Augendus, bishop of the people of Villa Magna [Note: [Col. 1301D] Villa Magna. Cyprian, bishop of Villa Magna, subscribed the synodical letter of the proconsular bishops [Col. 1302B] at the Lateran Council under Martin.], in the presence of Marcellinus, *vir clarissimus*, tribune and notary, I dictated and subscribed the foregoing at Carthage.”

When it had been read, he said: “It is Catholic only.”

Primianus, bishop of Carthage, said: “He is the one [269] who long ago crossed over to that party.”

And it was read aloud:

“Lucidus, bishop of the people of Marcelliana [Note: [Col. 1302B] Marcelliana. In Numidia, in whose *Notitia* occurs the bishop of Giru-Marcelli. Julianus of Marcelliana [Col. 1302C] or Marcellina attended the Council of Carthage under Cyprian. This see is distinct from Masclinianum in the province of Byzacena: Lucidus here observes that this Church is Catholic—that is, that there is no Donatist bishop there—whereas chapter 208 mentions Plurianus, bishop of Masclinianum, on the Donatist side.] and of Bazita, in the presence of Marcellinus, *vir clarissimus*, tribune and notary, I dictated and subscribed the foregoing at Carthage.”

When it had been read, he said: “It is Catholic [Col. 1301B] (Not a few words are missing here), and to Marcellinus, tribune and notary, I dictated and subscribed the foregoing at Carthage.”

When it had been read, he said: “Restitutus is on the other side [Note: [Col. 1302C] Restitutus. There were five Donatist bishops of this name at the Conference of Carthage: those of Drusiliana, Segermis, Flumenpiscum, Membressa, and Larita. The bishop of Drusiliana had Rufinus, a Catholic bishop, as his opponent; the bishop of Membressa had Gennadius; and the bishop of Segermis had Felix. It is uncertain which of the other two is meant here.].”

Bishop Restitutus said: “I recognize him.”

And it was read aloud:

“Aufidius, bishop of the people of Tignica [Note: [Col. 1302C] Tignica. The Peutinger Tables place Tignica near Theclata, a city of Numidia.], in the presence of Marcellinus, *vir clarissimus*, tribune and notary, I dictated and subscribed the foregoing at Carthage.”

When it had been read, he said: “I have Julianus on the other side.”

Bishop Julianus said: “I recognize him.”

And it was read aloud:

“Fortunatus, bishop of the people of Abensa [Note: [Col. 1302C] Abensa. It is uncertain to which province it belonged.], in the presence of Marcellinus, *vir clarissimus*, tribune and [Col. 1302A] notary, I dictated and subscribed the foregoing.”

When it had been read, he said: “I have unity.”

Bishop Optatus said: “We do not have a bishop; we have a presbyter.”

And it was read aloud:

“Trifolius, bishop of the people of Abora [Note: [Col. 1302C] Abora. In the proconsular province, as the synodical letter of the bishops of that province at the Lateran Council teaches; Felix, bishop [Col. 1302D] of the holy Church of Abora, subscribed it.], in the presence of Marcellinus, *vir clarissimus*, tribune and notary, I dictated and subscribed the foregoing at Carthage.”

When it had been read, he said: “If the name of the Donatists is heard there, he is stoned.”

And it was read aloud:

“I, the aforementioned, on behalf of Paulinus of Zura [Note: [Col. 1302D] Zura. In the same proconsular province; for the bishop of Abora subscribes on his behalf, as for a neighboring bishop unable to write. Victor of Vita, *On the Vandal Persecution*, II.9, records a woman saying that she was the daughter of the bishop of the former city of Zura.], being present but unable to write, in the presence of Marcellinus, *vir clarissimus*, tribune and notary, I dictated and subscribed the foregoing at Carthage.”

When it had been read, and the Catholic bishop Paulinus had come forward, he said: “It is Catholic.”

Habetdeus, deacon of Bishop Primianus, said: “Our presbyter is there. It is our diocese.”

And it was read aloud:

“Lucrus, bishop of the people of Greater Nigra [Col. 1302B] [Note: [Col. 1302D] Greater Nigra. It is uncertain to which province it belonged.], in the presence of Marcellinus, *vir clarissimus*, tribune and notary, I dictated and subscribed the foregoing at Carthage.”

When it had been read, he said: “There is unity.”

Habetdeus, deacon, said: “He has a presbyter.”

And it was read aloud:

“Fidentius, bishop of the people of Cefala [Note: [Col. 1302D] Cefala. In the proconsular province, as is clear from the letter of the bishops of that province to Paul of Constantinople at the Lateran Council under Martin.], in the presence of Marcellinus, *vir clarissimus*, tribune and notary, I dictated and subscribed the foregoing at Carthage.”

When it had been read, he said: “I have unity.”

Valentinianus, deacon of Bishop Primianus, said: “He has just departed from the body. He was called Fidentius.”

And it was read aloud:

“Cresconius, bishop of the people of Rusuca [Note: [Col. 1302D] Rusuca. In Mauretania Caesariensis is Rusubus, whose bishop is called Rusuburitan in the *Notitia*. Perhaps it is the same as the Rusuca mentioned here; or it may be Rusucibar, a town mentioned by Ptolemy, IV.3.], in the presence of Marcellinus, *vir clarissimus*, tribune and notary [Col. 1303A], I dictated and subscribed the foregoing at Carthage.”

When it had been read, [he] said: “I have unity.”

Habetdeus, deacon, said: “We have none.”

And it was read aloud:

“Ambibius, bishop of the people of Pisita [Note: [Col. 1303C] Pisita. Baluzius places this city on the border of the provinces of Byzacena and Tripolitania, because the Peutinger Tables place Pisida between Putea, a city of Byzacena, and Sabrata in Tripolitania. Norisius, however, assigns the city of Pisita to the proconsular province and says that it is mentioned in Book I, chapter 13, of *The Miracles of Saint Stephen*, attributed to Evodius of Uzalis. Certainly Felix, Ambibius’s opponent mentioned here, differs from the bishop of Putea mentioned in chapter 204. For the person discussed in the present chapter was not at Carthage, whereas the other was present.], in the presence of Marcellinus, *vir clarissimus*, tribune and notary, I dictated and subscribed the foregoing at Carthage.”

When it had been read, he said: “I have Felix on the opposing side.”

Valentinianus, deacon, said: “He is called Felix; he sent a letter of excuse on account of old age.”

And it was read aloud:

“Rogatianus, bishop of the people of Tigimma [Note: [Col. 1303C] Tigimma. In the proconsular province, as the letter of the bishops of that province to Paul of Constantinople, cited at the Lateran Council under Martin, teaches.], in the presence of Marcellinus, *vir clarissimus*, tribune and notary, I dictated and subscribed the foregoing at Carthage.”

When it had been read, he said: “Victorianus is on the other side against me.”

And when Bishop Victorianus came forward, [he] said: “I recognize him.”

And it was read aloud:

“Stephanus, bishop of the people of Sinnuara [Note: [Col. 1303C] Sinnuara. In the proconsular province, where the *Notitia* shows that there was a see called Sinnuara or Sinnara. At the Fifth Ecumenical Council Victor, bishop of the municipality of Sinna in the proconsular province, subscribed.], in the presence of Marcellinus, *vir clarissimus* [Col. 1303B], tribune and notary, I dictated and subscribed the foregoing at Carthage.”

When it had been read, he said: “There is unity there; there is a Church there.”

Habetdeus, deacon, said: “That is the diocese of Cyprianus of Siccenna [Note: [Col. 1303D] Of Siccenna. A town in the proconsular province, for the Sinnuarians are described as its neighbors. Perhaps it is the same place whose bishop Maximinus is mentioned by Augustine, *City of God*, XXII.8, as bishop of Sinitum or Sinicum.]. He is called Bishop Cyprianus, and he attends there at Sinnuara.”

And it was read aloud:

“Serotinus, bishop of the people of Turuzus [Note: [Col. 1303D] Turuzus. This Turuzus differs from Tuzurus, whose bishop Aptus is mentioned in chapter 187. It appears, however, to have belonged to the proconsular province.], in the presence of Marcellinus, *vir clarissimus*, tribune and notary, I dictated and subscribed the foregoing at Carthage.”

When it had been read, he said: “It has never had one, nor does it have one.”

Habetdeus, deacon, said: “The presbyter Cattus is there.”

Serotinus, bishop of the Catholic Church, said: “He is there, but superfluously.”

And it was read aloud:

“Majorinus, bishop of the people of Zemta [Note: [Col. 1303D] Zemta. In the proconsular province, as the repeatedly cited letter of the bishops of that province teaches.], in the presence of Marcellinus, *vir clarissimus*, tribune and notary, I dictated and subscribed the foregoing at Carthage.”

When it had been read, he said: “It is Catholic [Col. 1304A]; it has neither had one nor does it have one.”

And it was read aloud:

“Thomas, bishop of the people of Cubda [Note: [Col. 1303D] Cubda. In the same place, on the authority of the same document.], in the presence of Marcellinus, *vir clarissimus*, tribune and notary, I dictated and subscribed the foregoing at Carthage.”

When it had been read, he said: “We have nobody on the opposing side.”

And it was read aloud:

“Restitutus, bishop of the people of Muzuca [Note: [Col. 1303D] Muzuca. A bishop in the province of Byzacena, as the *Notitia* teaches.], in the presence of Marcellinus, *vir clarissimus*, tribune and notary, I dictated and subscribed the foregoing at Carthage.”

When it had been read, he said: “Idaxius is on the opposing side against us.”

And when Bishop Idaxius came forward, he said: “I recognize him.”

And it was read aloud:

“Antonius, bishop of the people of Mutugenna [Note: [Col. 1303D] Mutugenna. In the diocese of Hippo Regius there was a village called Mutugenna, where, in Augustine’s time, a Donatist presbyter named Donatus served, as is clear from Augustine, Letters 23 and 173; but this village had no bishop.], in the presence of Marcellinus, *vir clarissimus*, tribune and notary, I dictated and subscribed the foregoing at Carthage.”

When it had been read, [270] [he] said: “Splendonius is on the opposing side.”

When Bishop Splendonius came forward, [he] said: “I recognize [Col. 1304B] him.”

And it was read aloud:

“Privatianus, bishop of the people of Vegesela [Note: [Col. 1304C] Vegesela. There were two Vegeselas in Africa, for another bishop of Vegesela occurs in chapter 135. One was in Numidia, and its bishop Januarius subscribed at the Council of Carthage under Boniface, both for himself and for Januarius of Mascula. This is undoubtedly the Megesela which the *Itinerary* of Antoninus places near Mascula. Privatus, bishop of Vegesela, attended the Council of Carthage under Gratus; Augustine praises the people of Vigisila in Letter 64; and the Donatist Marculus, whose acts we reported above, is said to have suffered at Vegesela in Numidia. Baluzius places the other Vegesela in Byzacena, because Antoninus’s *Itinerary* locates Vegesela, or Vergesalla, among the cities of Byzacena. Yet the *Notitia* of Numidia contains two sees of approximately this name: no. 59, Veselitanus, and no. 80, Velesitanus. It is more probable, however, that this Vegesela, whose bishop is here called Fortunatianus, was a village or fortress in Byzacena, for Donatus, bishop of Cillium on the Donatist side, immediately contends that Vegesela is part of his diocese. That the bishop of Cillium belonged to the province of Byzacena is established by the *Notitia*, Antoninus’s *Itinerary*, and the letter of the bishops of Byzacena at the Lateran Council. This Donatus also appears as the opponent of Tertiolus, Catholic bishop of Cillium, above in chapter 128. He was therefore simultaneously the opponent of the bishops of Cillium and Vegesela, because this Vegesela belonged to the city of Cillium and consequently lay in Byzacena.], in the presence of Marcellinus, *vir clarissimus*, tribune and notary, I dictated and subscribed the foregoing at Carthage.”

When it had been read, he said: “Donatus of Cillium is on the opposing side against me.”

And when Bishop Donatus of Cillium came forward, he said: “I have deacons there; the neighboring community conducts affairs there; it is my diocese.”

Privatianus, bishop of the Catholic Church, said: “Where do they assemble?”

Bishop Donatus said: “Yet you have forbidden both the places and the memorial shrines of the martyrs. Did I not have Candidus as a presbyter from there?”

Privatianus, bishop of the Catholic Church, said: “And where was this being conducted?”

And it was read aloud:

“Aemilianus, bishop of the Church of Bennefa [Note: [Col. 1304D] Bennefa. In the province of Byzacena, as the *Notitia* teaches. The author of the *Life of Saint Fulgentius*, chapter 14, says that the monastery into which Fulgentius withdrew was for the most part adjacent to the shore of Bennefa. Guntasius of Bennefa subscribed at the Council of Cabarsussa.], in the presence of Marcellinus, *vir clarissimus*, tribune and notary, I dictated and subscribed the foregoing at Carthage.”

When it had been read, he said: [Col. 1305A] “I have no one on the opposing side.”

Valentinianus, deacon, said: “He was called Maximianus; today he departed from the body.”

Aemilianus, bishop of the Catholic Church, said: “I have held it for three years, from the time when I was ordained; I know of no one there.”

Valentinianus, deacon, said: “Let someone be sent, and let them see him.”

And it was read aloud:

“Litorius, bishop of the people of Suava [Note: [Col. 1305C] Suava. In Numidia, as the *Notitia*, no. 96, teaches.], in the presence of Marcellinus, *vir clarissimus*, tribune and notary, I dictated and subscribed the foregoing at Carthage.”

When it had been read, he said: “There is unity there; all is Catholic.”

Habetdeus, deacon of the Donatist party, said: “We have none.”

And it was read aloud:

“Benenatus, bishop of the people of Hospita [Note: [Col. 1305C] Hospita. Likewise in Numidia, according to the *Notitia*, no. 110.], in the presence of Marcellinus, *vir clarissimus*, tribune and notary, I dictated and subscribed the foregoing at Carthage.”

When it had been read, he said: “There is no other bishop in my place.”

Bishop Lucullus [Col. 1305B] said: “Persecution has always driven me into flight.”

And it was read aloud:

“Leontius, bishop of the people of Muserta [Note: [Col. 1305C] Muserta. It seems that Mutecita should be read, a see found in the province of Mauretania Caesariensis, as the *Notitia* teaches. Thus Cresconius, his opponent below in chapter 206, is called bishop of Mustita, through another error. For chapter 122 establishes that the Catholic bishop of the see of Mustita, Victorianus, had Felicianus, not Cresconius, as his opponent. But the name Mutecitanus could easily have been changed into Mustitanus.], in the presence of Marcellinus, *vir clarissimus*, tribune and notary, I dictated and subscribed the foregoing at Carthage.”

When it had been read, [he said: “I have no one on the opposing side.”]

Habetdeus, deacon of the Donatist party, said: “Cresconius has now been ordained against him.”

And it was read aloud:

“Silvanus, bishop of the people of Macriana [Note: [Col. 1305C] Macriana. Only two sees called Macriana occur in the *Notitia* of African bishops: one in Byzacena, no. 80, and the other in Mauretania Sitifensis, no. 23. Yet this Conference has three: Ferox, bishop of Greater Macriana, in [Col. 1305D] chapter 126; this Silvanus of Macriana; and Felix, bishop of Macriana, in chapter 215. But two Catholic bishops could have existed in one see, as happened when a Donatist bishop entered into the unity of the Church: his episcopal title and place were retained for him, as is clear from Ampelius and Primulus, bishops of Vaga, in chapter 176 of the Conference of Carthage. This Silvanus of Macriana attended the Council of Carthage in 403. Ferrandus the deacon cites the Council of Macriana in his *Summary of Canons*.], in the presence of Marcellinus, *vir clarissimus*, tribune and notary, I dictated and subscribed the foregoing at Carthage.”

When it had been read, he said: “It has no one; it is Catholic.”

And it was read aloud:

“Eunomius, bishop of the people of Marazana [Note: [Col. 1305D] Marazana. In the province of Byzacena, as the *Notitia* teaches. Felix of Marrazana is listed at the Council of Carthage under Cyprian. Antoninus calls it Marazania in the *Itinerary*.], in the presence of Marcellinus, *vir clarissimus*, tribune and notary, I dictated and subscribed the foregoing at Carthage.”

When it had been read, he said: “Habetdeus is on the opposing side against me.”

Bishop Habetdeus said: “My predecessor was ordained for the place of Marazana. After he had taken his seat, he was expelled.”

Eunomius, bishop of the Catholic Church, said: “He never [Col. 1306A] took his seat.”

Bishop Habetdeus said: “I too was not admitted; I lodged three miles away from the city.”

Eunomius, bishop of the Catholic Church, said: “There never were Donatists, nor are there, nor have they ever occupied the episcopal chair.”

Bishop Habetdeus said: “They have only recently been suppressed.”

And it was read aloud:

“Barbarus, bishop of the people of Hierpiniana [Note: [Col. 1305D] Hierpiniana, or Irpiniana, in Byzacena, as the same *Notitia*, no. 53, teaches.], in the presence of Marcellinus, *vir clarissimus*, tribune and notary, [I dictated and] subscribed the foregoing at Carthage.”

When it had been read, he said: “I have no opponent.”

Valentinianus, deacon, said: “There was said to be a bishop named Moecopius; he has departed from the body.”

And it was read aloud:

“Secundianus, bishop of the people of Hermiana [Note: [Col. 1306C] Hermiana. In the same place, from the same source. Facundus of Hermiana, bishop of this see, is famous. Benadus, bishop of Hermiana, subscribed the letter of the bishops of Byzacena at the Lateran Council under Martin. Procopius, *Vandal War*, I, mentions Hermione, a place in Byzacena.], in the presence of Marcellinus, *vir clarissimus*, tribune and notary, I dictated and subscribed the foregoing at Carthage.”

When it had been read, he said: “Bishop Maximianus is opposed to me [Col. 1306B].”

And when Bishop Maximianus came forward, he said: “I recognize him.”

And it was read aloud:

“Postumianus, bishop of the people of Tagora [Note: [Col. 1306C] Tagora. Two sees of Tagora are mentioned in the Conference: this Postumianus here, and Restitutus, also of Tagora, in chapter 143, who was a guardian of the documents. One of these was in Numidia, as may be inferred from the *Notitia*, where Tagurensis occurs, and from Antoninus’s *Itinerary*. Augustine, Letter 59, mentions Xanthippus of Tagosa, who disputed with Victorinus about the primacy of Numidia. Most suppose him to have been bishop of Tagora [Col. 1306D], but all manuscripts consistently read *Tagosensis*, and one reads *Tagonensis*. The other Tagora, or Tacora, seems from the Peutinger Tables to have been situated in the proconsular province.], in the presence of Marcellinus, *vir clarissimus*, tribune and notary, I dictated and subscribed the foregoing at Carthage.”

When it had been read, he said: “It belongs to Catholic unity.”

And it was read aloud:

“Barbarianus, bishop of the people of Creperula [Note: [Col. 1306D] Creperula, or Crepedula, in the province of Byzacena, as the *Notitia* and the synodical letter of the fathers of Byzacena show; in the latter occurs a bishop of Secrepedula. It was written S. E., that is, ‘of the Holy Church of Crepedula.’], in the presence of Marcellinus, *vir clarissimus*, tribune and notary, I dictated and subscribed the foregoing at Carthage.”

When it had been read, he said: “It is Catholic only.”

Valentinianus, deacon, said: “We have none.”

And it was read aloud:

“Felix, bishop of the Caniopitani [Note: [Col. 1306D] Caniopitani. Perhaps Canapium in the proconsular province, whose see’s name is read in the repeatedly cited letter of the bishops of that province. Redemptus, bishop of the holy Church of the municipality of Canapium—or Canapu, as the Beauvais manuscript has it—subscribed.] 271, in the presence of Marcellinus, *vir clarissimus*, tribune and notary, I dictated and subscribed the foregoing at Carthage.”

When it had been read, Valentinianus, deacon, said: [Col. 1306C] “We have a presbyter named Restitutus.”

And it was read aloud:

“Victor, bishop of the people of Tibaris [Note: [Col. 1306D] Tibaris. At the Council of Carthage under Cyprian, Vincentius of Tibaris subscribed.], in the presence of Marcellinus, *vir clarissimus*, tribune and notary, I dictated and subscribed the foregoing [Col. 1307A] at Carthage.”

When it had been read, he said: “Bishop Victorianus is on the other side against me.”

When Bishop Victorianus came forward, he said: “I recognize him.”

And it was read aloud:

“Gennadius, bishop of the people of Membressa [Note: [Col. 1307C] Membressa. Two Catholic bishops of Membressa occur here in this very chapter: Gennadius, whose opponent is Restitutus, called bishop of Membressa in chapter 198; and later Theasius, bishop of the people of Memblosa, who has no opponent. The *Notitia* contains one Membrositan bishop—or, as the Haller manuscript has it, Membresitan—in proconsular Africa. The Anonymous Ravennate appears to mention both towns: in Book III, no. 5, he mentions Membrisca among the cities of the proconsular province, and in the following number Membron. Likewise the Peutinger Tables contain Membrissa and Membrion. Membrissa was certainly a town of the proconsular province: Procopius, *Vandal War*, II, says it was 350 stadia from Carthage, and places it among cities belonging to the proconsular province. The letter of the bishops of the proconsular province includes Victor, bishop of the Church of Membressa. At the Council of Carthage under Cyprian, Lucius of Membresa delivered an opinion; and Paschasius of Membressa [Col. 1307D] attended the Carthaginian synod under Boniface. Membrosa likewise belongs to that province—called Memblosa here below, or Memlo or Membro in Antoninus’s *Itinerary*—although the Anonymous Ravennate counts Membron among the towns of Numidia. Restitutus, Gennadius’s opponent, is the man ordained in place of Salvius of Membressa during the heat of the Donatist schism, as Augustine recounts in Letter 108 and *Against Cresconius*, IV.48.], in the presence of Marcellinus, *vir clarissimus*, tribune and notary, I dictated and subscribed the foregoing at Carthage.”

When it had been read, he said: “Restitutus is on the other side against me.”

And when Bishop Restitutus came forward, he said: “I recognize him.”

And it was read aloud:

“Restitutus, bishop of the people of Simingita [Note: [Col. 1307D] Simingita. At the Council of Carthage in 525, Cresconius, bishop of the people of Simingita, subscribed; but the location of this see is not stated.], in the presence of Marcellinus, *vir clarissimus*, tribune and notary, I dictated and subscribed the foregoing at Carthage.”

When it had been read, [he said: “All is Catholic.” Habetdeus, deacon, said: “We have none.”]

And it was read aloud:

“Octavius, bishop of the people of Utimma [Note: [Col. 1307D] Utimma. We already have two or three bishops of approximately this name: in chapter 126, Timianus of Utma and, in the same chapter, Severus, bishop of the people of Utimara; and in chapters 128 and 133, Isaac, Catholic bishop [Col. 1308C] of Utina, and Felicianus, his opponent and bishop of the same see. Now a fourth occurs, Octavius, bishop of Utimma; yet the African *Notitia* has only one Utimmirensian bishop, in the proconsular province, no. 10. Here, however, the old editions of the Conference read ‘bishop of the people of Utinuna’; and in chapter 198 Bonifacius, Octavius’s opponent, is called bishop of Utunna.], in the presence of Marcellinus, *vir clarissimus*, tribune and notary, I dictated and subscribed the foregoing at Carthage.”

When it had been read, [Col. 1307B] he said: “Bonifacius is on the other side against me.”

When Bishop Bonifacius came forward, he said: “I recognize him.”

And it was read aloud:

“Victorinus, bishop of the people of Tabuda [Note: [Col. 1308C] Tabuda. In Numidia, as the *Notitia*, no. 42, teaches.], in the presence of Marcellinus, *vir clarissimus*, tribune and notary, I dictated and subscribed the foregoing at Carthage.”

When it had been read, he said: “Argutus is on the opposing side.”

When Bishop Argutus came forward, he said: “I recognize him.”

And it was read aloud:

“Maximinus, bishop of the people of Enera [Note: [Col. 1308C] Enera. It is uncertain to which province it belonged.], in the presence of Marcellinus, *vir clarissimus*, tribune and notary, I dictated and subscribed the foregoing at Carthage.”

When it had been read, he said: “It is Catholic; I have unity.”

Bishop Quodvultdeus said: “It has a bishop, but it has him wrongly.”

And it was read aloud:

“Reginus, bishop of the people of Tigillava [Note: [Col. 1308C] Tigillava, or Tigillaba, in Numidia, as the *Notitia*, no. 33, teaches.], in the presence of Marcellinus, *vir clarissimus*, tribune and notary [Col. 1308A], I dictated and subscribed the foregoing at Carthage.”

When it had been read, [he said: “Donatus is on the other side against me.”]

Bishop Flavianus [Note: [Col. 1308C] Bishop Flavianus: bishop of Pauzera, below, chapter 187.] said: “Donatus returned from a journey because of illness.”

And it was read aloud:

“I, the aforementioned, on behalf of Cresconius, bishop of Centenaria [Note: [Col. 1308C] Centenaria. In Numidia, as the *Notitia*, no. 39, teaches. The Anonymous Ravennate lists Centenariae. The Peutinger Tables have *Ad Centenarium*.], in the presence of Marcellinus, *vir clarissimus*, tribune and notary, dictated and subscribed the foregoing at Carthage, because he was prevented by illness; at his direction I subscribed at Carthage.”

When it had been read, [he said: “On the other side is …”]

Bishop Quodvultdeus said: “He too is badly off.”

And it was read aloud:

“Felix, bishop of the people of Iziria [Note: [Col. 1308C] Iziria. Baluzius thinks Hizirzada should be read, from the *Notitia* of Numidia, no. 55. Certainly there is no doubt that the same see is meant in both places.], in the presence of Marcellinus, *vir clarissimus*, tribune and notary, I dictated and subscribed the foregoing at Carthage.”

When it had been read, he said: “Saturus is on the opposing side against me [Note: [Col. 1308C] Saturus. Below, in chapter 198, he is called bishop of Byzacium. For that reason Baluzius thinks that the name of the Donatist who was Felix of Iziria’s opponent, and the name of the Catholic bishop of Byzacium, have been omitted here [Col. 1308D]. But perhaps chapter 198 contains an error, and ‘Izirian’ should be read instead of ‘Byzacian.’].”

When Bishop Saturus came forward, he said: “He was my presbyter.”

And it was read aloud:

“Felicianus, bishop of the people of Lesser Feradita [Col. 1308B] [Note: [Col. 1308D] Lesser Feradita. Greater Feradita occurs in the *Notitia* of the province of Byzacena. It is likely that Lesser Feradita was in the same province, for towns of the same name, one called Greater and the other Lesser, were usually near one another. This seems to be the same as Peradamium, also found in the *Notitia* of Byzacena, no. 31.], in the presence of Marcellinus, *vir clarissimus*, tribune and notary, I dictated and subscribed the foregoing at Carthage.”

When it had been read, he said: “It is Catholic.”

Valentinianus, deacon, said: “We have none.”

And it was read aloud:

“Romanus, bishop of the people of Megalopolis [Note: [Col. 1308D] Megalopolis. In the proconsular province, as its *Notitia*, no. 39, and the synodical letter of the bishops of that province at the Lateran Council show; that letter contains the name of Reparatus, bishop of the holy Church of Megalopolis.], in the presence of Marcellinus, *vir clarissimus*, tribune and notary, I dictated and subscribed the foregoing at Carthage.”

When it had been read, he said: “I have no one on the opposing side.”

Bishop Felix said: “We have a presbyter, Maximianus; he is present.”

And it was read aloud:

“Restitutus, bishop of the people of Cincarita [Note: [Col. 1308D] Cincarita, or Cincaritan, as it appears [Col. 1309C] below in chapter 188. Perhaps it is Circinita in the province of Byzacena, as the *Notitia* teaches. Polybius and Ptolemy mention the islands of Cercina. Antoninus’s *Itinerary* says that they lie between Africa and Sicily, 622 stadia from Tacapae. Shortly before his death Fulgentius withdrew there, as is narrated in his *Life*, chapter 29. The letter of the bishops of the proconsular province, cited at the Lateran Council, contains a city called Cicitita, which Norisius suspects is not distinct from Cincarita.], in the presence of Marcellinus, *vir clarissimus*, tribune and notary, I dictated and subscribed the foregoing at Carthage.”

When it had been read, he said: “Bishop Campanus is on the opposing side against me.”

When Bishop Campanus [Col. 1309A] came forward, he said: “I recognize him.”

And it was read aloud:

“Nados, bishop of the people of Sabrata [Note: [Col. 1309C] Sabrata. In the province of Tripolitania, as the *Notitia*, no. 2, teaches. At the Council of Carthage under Cyprian, Pompeius, bishop of Sabrata, is mentioned. Victor of Vita, *On the Vandal Persecution*, I.7, mentions Vincentius of Sabrata. Donatus of Sabrata attended the Council of Cabarsussa in 393 and was deposed at Bagai in the following year. But by this time he was dead. Sabrata is mentioned by Ptolemy, IV.3; Antoninus in the *Itinerary*; the Peutinger Tables; Pliny, V.4.
and others. Procopius calls it Sabatra, *On Buildings*, book VI.] I dictated and signed the foregoing at Carthage before Marcellinus, vir clarissimus, tribune and notary. 272 When this had been read aloud, he said: “I had an opponent; now I do not.” And it was read aloud.

Caltasius, bishop of the people of Matarita [Note: [Col. 1309D] **Matarita.** In the register of the province of Byzacena there are two sees with nearly this name: Mactarita, no. 25, and Mattarita, no. 50. In this Conference likewise there are two bishops of these sees: this Caltasius, Catholic bishop of the people of Matarita, who has no opponent; and, in chapter 202, Comparator, Donatist bishop of Mactar. Among the bishops who sat in Cyprian’s council concerning the rebaptizing of heretics, Marcus of Mactar is listed as bishop of the latter see, if the reading is as it stands in Cyprian; but of the former, if it is read Mattar, as it is in Augustine. Pliny, book V, chapter 4, mentions the town of Mattera. In Cassiodorus, *On Divine Institutions*, chapter 29, Victor, an African bishop of Martarita, is said to have purged Cassian’s *Conferences*; he may perhaps be the same man as the bishop of Mattarita.], dictated and signed the foregoing at Carthage before Marcellinus, vir clarissimus, tribune and notary. When this had been read aloud, he said: “There is unity.”

Habetdeus, deacon, said: “We had Rusticianus; he has now departed from the body.” And it was read aloud.

Octavianus, bishop of the people of Ucimajor [Note: [Col. 1309D] **Ucimajor.** Pliny, book V, chapter 4, names among the towns of Africa two Ucitanae, the greater and the lesser. [Col. 1310C] In the register of the proconsular province there are also two sees which may be fitted to these: namely, Urcitanus, no. 20, and Uzitensis, no. 25. Victor of Vita, book I, no. 3, of *The Vandal Persecution*, mentions Mansuetus, the martyr of Uricita. In this Conference Paul of Uzitta has already been listed in chapter 128, and now this Octavianus of Ucimajor.], dictated and signed the foregoing at Carthage before Marcellinus, vir clarissimus, tribune and notary. When this had been read aloud, he said: “I have unity.”

Salvianus, bishop [Note: [Col. 1310C] **Bishop Salvianus.** Of Leptis, in the province of Tripolitania.], said: “It belongs to the diocese of the aged Victorianus; it has the presbyter Januarius.” [Col. 1309B] And it was read aloud.

Safargius, bishop of the people of Lampua [Note: [Col. 1310C] **Lampua.** In the register of Numidia, no. 87, Lamfua. At the Council of Carthage under Boniface in A.D. 525, Pontius, bishop of the people of Lamfua, subscribed.], dictated and signed the foregoing at Carthage before Marcellinus, vir clarissimus, tribune and notary.

Valentinianus, deacon of Bishop Primianus, said: “It belongs to the aged Cartherus; but he is absent and suffers from his feet, and therefore could not come.” And it was read aloud.

Victorinus, bishop of the people of Tabuda, on behalf of my fellow bishop Gorgonius, who is detained by illness, of the people of Liberalia [Note: [Col. 1310C] **Liberalia.** Near Tabuda in Numidia.], at his own direction I signed at Carthage before Marcellinus, vir clarissimus, tribune and notary. When this had been read aloud, the same Gorgonius said: “The heretics have taken away my basilica; I am alone.”

Protasius, bishop, said: “We have Bishop Victor there.” And it was read aloud.

Fortunatus, bishop of the locality of Casa-Calana [Note: [Col. 1310C] **Casa-Calana.** In Numidia, as the register shows, no. 43. The city of Casae Calanae is mentioned in the register of Leo published by Goar.], dictated and signed the foregoing at Carthage before Marcellinus, vir clarissimus, tribune [Col. 1310A] and notary. When this had been read aloud, he said: “I am alone.”

Verissimus, bishop, said: “Victorinus is presbyter there.” And it was read aloud.

Theasius, bishop of the people of Memblosita [Note: [Col. 1310C] **Memblosita.** On this see, see what we said above, note 205, p. 271.], dictated and signed the foregoing at Carthage before Marcellinus, vir clarissimus, tribune and notary. When this had been read aloud, he said: “Only the unity of the Catholic Church is there.”

Salvianus, bishop, said: “At the time of the persecution, the bishop who was there yielded.” And it was read aloud.

Probantius, bishop of the people of Trofimiana [Note: [Col. 1310D] **Trofimiana**, or Trofiniana, as it appears in the register of the province of Byzacena, no. 35.], dictated and signed the foregoing at Carthage before Marcellinus, vir clarissimus, tribune and notary. When this had been read aloud, he said: “I am alone.”

Valentinianus, deacon, said: “He has a presbyter.” And it was read aloud.

Dulcitius, bishop of the people of Tacape [Note: [Col. 1310D] **Tacape.** In the province of Tripolitania, as the register shows, no. 5. This town, Tacapes, is mentioned by Ptolemy, book IV, chapter 3; Pliny, book V, chapter 4; Procopius, book VI of *On Buildings*; and in the Peutinger Tables. Moreover, this Dulcitius, bishop of the province of Tripolitania, is named in the acts of the Council of Carthage of A.D. 403. Gaius, bishop of the same city and legate of his province, subscribed to the Council of Carthage under Boniface in A.D. 525, although in the acts of that council he is called Gallus.], in the presence of Marcellinus, vir [Col. 1310B] clarissimus, tribune and notary, dictated and signed the foregoing at Carthage. When this had been read aloud, he said: “[I have another man opposed to me.]”

Valentinianus, deacon, said: “He is called Felix. He is here, but he is unwell.” It was again read aloud.

Catulinus, bishop of the people of Gitta [Note: [Col. 1310D] **Gitta.** It is uncertain to which province it belongs.], dictated and signed the foregoing before Marcellinus, vir clarissimus, tribune and notary. When this had been read aloud, he said: “There is unity.”

Valentinianus, deacon of Bishop Primianus, said: “We do not have [one].” And it was read aloud.

Villaticus, bishop of the people of Sinnipsa [Note: [Col. 1310D] **Sinnipsa.** It is uncertain to which province it belongs.], dictated and signed the foregoing at Carthage before Marcellinus, vir clarissimus, tribune and notary. When this had been read aloud, he said: “There is unity.” And it was read aloud.

Hilarianus, bishop of the people of Hilta [Note: [Col. 1310D] **Hilta.** In the proconsular province, as the synodical letter of the bishops of this province at the Lateran Council under Martin shows.], dictated and signed the foregoing [Col. 1311A] at Carthage before Marcellinus, vir clarissimus, tribune and notary. When this had been read aloud, he said: “I have no opponent.”

And when Bishop Victor came forward, he said: “I have only now been ordained there; he does not know me.”

Hilarianus, bishop of the Catholic Church, said: “He does not have [one].”

And Januarius, bishop of the Church of Greater Gisipa [Note: [Col. 1311C] **Greater Gisipa.** In the proconsular province, as the register shows, no. 24. Redemptus of Gisipa attended the Council of Carthage in A.D. 525 under Boniface; and Mellosus, bishop of the same see, subscribed to the letter of the bishops of the proconsular province at the Lateran Council under Martin.], dictated and signed the foregoing at Carthage before Marcellinus, vir clarissimus, tribune and notary. When this had been read aloud, he said: “We do not have [one].” And it was read aloud.

Severianus, bishop of Ceramuna [Note: [Col. 1311C] **Ceramuna.** Above, in the table of chapters, and shortly below, Ceramussa. It is clear from the dispute here reported between Adeodatus and Severianus that this place was near the city of Milevis and consequently in Numidia.], dictated and signed the foregoing at Carthage before Marcellinus, vir clarissimus, tribune and notary. When this had been read aloud, he said: “All of it is Catholic.”

Habetdeus, deacon of Bishop Primianus, said: “We have the aged Adeodatus.”

Severianus, bishop of the Catholic Church, said: “Let him produce him.”

Adeodatus, bishop, [Col. 1311B] said: “Ceramussa is within my Milevitan community.”

134. Severianus, bishop of the Catholic Church, said: “The whole place has been Catholic from the beginning; Donatists have never been there.” Adeodatus, bishop, said: “It is within my congregation. By violence he drove out from there all the clerics and presbyters.” Severianus, bishop of the Catholic Church, said: “He lies, God being witness.” Marcellinus, most distinguished man, tribune and notary, said: “May Your Holiness be pleased simply to state whether there is now a bishop in that congregation.” Adeodatus, bishop, said: “It is within my congregation; everything round about belongs to me. Indeed, all who were established in that place yielded through fear of me.” Severianus, bishop of the Catholic Church, said: “He lies.” And he read:

273 **135.** “I, Dominicus, bishop of the congregation of Bullensium Regiorum [Royal Bulla], in the presence of Marcellinus, most distinguished tribune and notary, have dictated and subscribed the foregoing at Carthage.”

[Note: **[Col. 1311C] Bullentium Regiorum.** There were two episcopal sees called Bullensis in the proconsular province: one simply called Bullensis in the *Notitia*, no. 34; the other, Bullensium Regiorum, there no. 50. This latter and more celebrated place is mentioned in the Itinerary of Antoninus, in Ptolemy, and on the Peutinger Tables. At the Council of Carthage under Genethlius, Epigonius, bishop of Bullensium Regiorum, is mentioned. In the synodical letter of the bishops of the proconsular province at the Lateran Council under Martin, Mellosus, bishop of Bulleriensis, subscribes, as does Victor of Bulnensis, perhaps Bullensis.]

When this had been read, he said: “On the other side I have Felix; but he is the only one who is in communion with him.” And when Felix the bishop approached, he said: “I recognize him.” And he read:

“I, Valentinus, bishop of Vaiana, on behalf of my fellow bishop Reginus of the Church of Vegesela, who is detained here at Carthage on account of illness, have subscribed in the presence of Marcellinus, most distinguished tribune and notary.”

[Note: **[Col. 1311D] Vegeselitanae.** In Numidia, since the bishop of Vaiana was likewise a Numidian. See the notes on chapters 99 and 133.]

When this had been read, Alypius, bishop of the Catholic Church, said: “He is ill.” Habetdeus, deacon, said: “Gavinus is present.” And he read:

“I, Reparatus, bishop of the congregation of Sufasara, in the presence of Marcellinus, most distinguished tribune and notary, have dictated and subscribed the foregoing at Carthage.”

[Note: **[Col. 1311D] Gavinus.** Augustine mentions Gabinus, a Donatist bishop who had passed into Catholic unity, in Book I against Gaudentius, chapters 12 and 13; perhaps he is not different from this man.]

[Note: **[Col. 1311D] Sufasaritanae.** In the *Notitia* of Mauretania Caesariensis there occur two bishops of Sufara, one at no. 3 and the other at no. 87; yet the former is called Susaritanus in the Haller manuscript. In the Itinerary of Antoninus, among the cities of Mauretania, Sufasar is mentioned; this city is called Sufasa by the anonymous Ravennate. In Leo’s *Notitia*, Sufara.]

When this had been read, he said: “He has none; he was there.” Habetdeus, deacon, said: “He has only lately departed.” And he read:

“I, Proculus, bishop of the congregation of the place called Serra, in the presence of Marcellinus, most distinguished tribune and notary, have dictated and subscribed the foregoing at Carthage.”

[Note: **[Col. 1312C] Serrensis.** In Mauretania Caesariensis, as is clear from the *Notitia*, no. 117, where it is called Sertensis. Although besides this man there occur in this conference two Donatist bishops called Zertensis, one Gaudentius in chapter 187, and the other, named Salustius, in chapter 201, the man mentioned here has no opponent. There was a Zerta in Numidia, where the Council of Zerta was held after the conference, whose letter to the Donatists is among Augustine’s Letters, no. 141. Another Zertensis, perhaps, is the Sertensis of Mauretania Caesariensis or Zemtensis; if so called, the seat of this Serrensis will be uncertain. Otherwise, the other Zertensis may be the same as the Zemtensis of the proconsular province, whose see-name is read in the letter of the bishops of that province at the Lateran Council under Martin.]

When this had been read, he said: “I possess the unity.” Valentinianus, deacon, said: “We do not have [anyone there].” And he read:

“I, Publicius, bishop of the congregation of Gratianopolis, in the presence of Marcellinus, most distinguished tribune and notary, have dictated and subscribed the foregoing at Carthage.”

[Note: **[Col. 1312D] Gratianopolitanae plebis.** In Mauretania Caesariensis, as the *Notitia* teaches, no. 81.]

When this had been read, he said: “On the other side there is Deuterius, alone and without a congregation.” Deuterius, bishop, said: “Because you also demolished houses and persecuted me.” And he read:

“I, Maximianus, bishop of the congregation of Sugabbara, in the presence of Marcellinus, most distinguished tribune and notary, have dictated and subscribed the foregoing at Carthage.”

[Note: **[Col. 1312D] Sugabbaritanae.** In the same province, according to the *Notitia*, no. 20. Ammianus Marcellinus, Book XXIX: “The municipality of Sugabbara lies on the slope of Mount Transcellensis.” Ptolemy, Book IV, chapter 2, has Zuchabari from the Palatine manuscript.]

When this had been read, he said: “On the other side I have Germanus.” And when Germanus the bishop approached, he said: “I recognize him.” And he read:

“I, Pompeianus, bishop of Sucarda, in the presence of Marcellinus, most distinguished tribune and notary, have dictated and subscribed the foregoing at Carthage.”

[Note: **[Col. 1312D] Sucardensis.** In the same province, according to the *Notitia*, no. 13.]

When this had been read, Alypius, bishop of the Catholic Church, said: “He is here, but ill.” And he read:

“I, Fortunatus, bishop of the congregation of Rusuccurium, in the presence of Marcellinus, most distinguished tribune and notary, have dictated and subscribed the foregoing at Carthage.”

[Note: **[Col. 1312D] Rusuccurritanae.** In the same province, according to the *Notitia*, no. 54. At the Council of Carthage in 419 occurs Nicellus, legate of Rusurrensis or Rusurrianensis in Mauretania Caesariensis; in Labbe’s edition he is called Ruscuriensis, and in the margin Rusuccurrensis or Rusocorensis. Moreover, Pliny, Book V, chapter 2, says that Rusucurium was honored with civic rank by Claudius. Antoninus in the Itinerary and the Peutinger Tables call it a colony. In Ptolemy, Book IV, chapter 2, it is called Rusuccore.]

When this had been read, he said: “On the other side I have Optatus.” And when Optatus the bishop approached, he said: “I recognize him.” And he read:

“I, Victor, bishop of the congregation of Bartimis, in the presence of Marcellinus, most distinguished tribune and notary, have dictated and subscribed the foregoing at Carthage.”

[Note: **[Col. 1313C] Bartimisiensis.** In the same province of Mauretania Caesariensis; in its *Notitia*, no. 45, Vardimissensis occurs.]

When this had been read, he said: “It is Catholic.” Habetdeus, deacon, said: “We have none.” And he read:

“I, Restitutianus, bishop of the congregation of Sululitta, in the presence of Marcellinus, most distinguished tribune and notary, have dictated and subscribed the foregoing at Carthage.”

[Note: **[Col. 1313C] Sululittanae.** Again, in chapter 201, mention is made of Hilarus, bishop of Sullita. Neither place is found in the *Notitia* of Africa, unless perhaps Sululittana is the same as Cululitana, which is nevertheless more probably Cullitana, mentioned above.]

When this had been read, he said: “The whole place is Catholic; we have everyone as Catholics.” Valentinianus, deacon, said: “We have none.” And he read:

“I, Helpidius, bishop of the congregation of Aquae, in the presence of Marcellinus, most distinguished tribune and notary, have dictated and subscribed the foregoing at Carthage.”

[Note: **[Col. 1313D] Aquensis.** In Mauretania Caesariensis, according to the *Notitia*, no. 24. Crescens, metropolitan of the city of Aquae, mentioned by Victor of Vita, Book I, no. 7, appears to have belonged to this see. Other bishops called Aquensis are mentioned in this conference, concerning whom in their proper place.]

When this had been read, he said: “On the other side I have Bishop Reparatus.” And when Reparatus the bishop approached, he said: “It is he; I recognize him.” And he read:

“I, Victor, bishop of the congregation of Maliana, in the presence of Marcellinus, most distinguished tribune and notary, have dictated and subscribed the foregoing at Carthage.”

[Note: **[Col. 1313D] Malianensis.** In the *Notitia* of Mauretania Caesariensis, no. 8, Melianensis occurs; Malianensis should be read. For Antoninus, in the Itinerary, has Malliana among the cities of Mauretania Caesariensis, between Sufasar and Tigavascastra. In Augustine’s Letter 236, to Deuterius, mention is made of a certain Victorinus, subdeacon of Malliana, from the Manichaean sect, and also of the city of Malliana.]

When this had been read, he said: “On the other side I have Nestorius.” And when Nestorius the bishop approached, he said: “I recognize him.” And he read:

“I, Restitutus, bishop, having been requested by Victor, bishop of Mammilla, have subscribed before Marcellinus, most distinguished tribune and notary, that he dictated the foregoing to me.”

[Note: **[Col. 1313D] Mammillensi.** In Mauretania Caesariensis, as its *Notitia* teaches, no. 78.]

When this had been read, he said: “On the other side is Serenianus.” And when Serenianus the bishop approached, he said: “I recognize him.” And he read:

“I, Victor, bishop of the congregation of Tabaïcara, in the presence of Marcellinus, most distinguished tribune and notary, have dictated and subscribed the foregoing at Carthage.”

[Note: **[Col. 1313D] Tabaïcariensis.** In the same province, according to the same document, no. 103, where Tabadcarensis is read.]

When this had been read, he said: “On the other side is Marcianus.” And when Marcianus the bishop approached, he said: “I recognize him.” And he read:

“I, Victor, bishop of the congregation of Timici, in the presence of Marcellinus, most distinguished tribune and notary, have dictated and subscribed the foregoing at Carthage.”

[Note: **[Col. 1314C] Timicitanae.** In the same province, there, no. 6. Pliny, Book V, chapter 2, mentions Timici among the cities. Ptolemy, Book IV, chapter 2, lists Timice with the other cities of Mauretania.]

When this had been read, he said: “On the other side I have Optatus.” And when Optatus approached, he said: “It is he.” And he read:

274 “I, Bonifacius, bishop of the congregation of Vallis, in the presence of Marcellinus, most distinguished tribune and notary, have dictated and subscribed the foregoing at Carthage.”

[Note: **[Col. 1314C] Vallitanae.** Optatus, Book II, mentions Bonifacius, Ballitanus, a Donatist bishop at Rome. The Itinerary of Antoninus and the Peutinger Tables place Vallis in the proconsular province. At the Council of Carthage in 525, under Bonifacius, Restitutus, bishop of the congregation of Vallis, subscribes.]

When this had been read, he said: “I have none.” Valentinianus, deacon, said: “He died seven years ago. He was called Restitutus.” And he read:

“I, [the person] mentioned above, on behalf of Limenianus, bishop of the congregation of Taprura, have subscribed before Marcellinus, most distinguished tribune and notary, that he, being present at Carthage, dictated [the foregoing].”

[Note: **[Col. 1314C] Taprurensis.** This place is called Taparura on the Peutinger Tables, Taphrura in Ptolemy, and Taphra by Pliny. Here the manuscript has Taprurensis; but in chapter 187 it is called Taprura. It lies in the province of Byzacena and on the Numidian frontier, as may be inferred from Ptolemy and the Peutinger Tables.]

When this had been read, he said: “It is Catholic.” Habetdeus, deacon, said: “We have no opponent.” And he read:

“I, Proculus, bishop of the congregation of Giutsis Salaria, in the presence of Marcellinus, most distinguished tribune and notary, have dictated and subscribed the foregoing at Carthage.”

[Note: **[Col. 1314D] Giutsitensis Salariae.** It is uncertain to which province it belonged.]

When this had been read, he said: “It is Catholic.” Habetdeus, deacon, said: “He has the presbyter Lillybius.” And he read:

“I, Auxilius, bishop of the congregation of Nurco, in the presence of Marcellinus, most distinguished tribune and notary, have dictated and subscribed the foregoing at Carthage.”

[Note: **[Col. 1314D] Nurconensis.** In Mauretania Caesariensis, as the *Notitia* teaches, no. 102, where it is called Murconensis. The following words make it clear that this place was in Mauretania Caesariensis.]

When this had been read, he said: “We possess the unity, as all the Caesareans know. Severinus is here; let him speak.” Severinus, bishop, said: “He never had it.” And he read:

“I, Mensurius, bishop of the congregation of Medefessa, in the presence of Marcellinus, most distinguished tribune and notary, have dictated and subscribed the foregoing at Carthage.”

[Note: **[Col. 1314D] Medefessitanae.** In the province of Byzacena, as is clear from the *Notitia*, no. 57, where a bishop of Menefessa is mentioned. Procopius, *On the Vandalic War*, Book II, chapter 23, mentions Menefeseos in Byzacium.]

When this had been read, [he said: “I have no one against me.”] Valentinianus, deacon, said: “He has only lately departed from the body.” And he read:

“I, Honorius, bishop, being at Carthage on behalf of my brother and fellow bishop Januarius, of the congregation of Casae Medianae, have dictated the foregoing in the presence of Marcellinus, most distinguished tribune and notary, and have subscribed on his behalf.”

[Note: **[Col. 1314D] Casarum Medianensium.** Casae Medianae in Numidia, as the *Notitia* teaches, no. 29.]

When this had been read, and Januarius the Catholic bishop approached, he said: “On the other side I have Aemilianus.” And he read:

“I, Adeodatus, bishop of the congregation of Simidicca, in the presence of Marcellinus, most distinguished tribune and notary, have dictated and subscribed the foregoing at Carthage.”

[Note: **[Col. 1315C] Simidiccensis.** In the proconsular province. At the Council of Carthage in 419, this Adeodatus is called Simidicus, bishop, both in the manuscript of the *Canons of the African Church* and in the manuscript of the *Ecclesiastical Canons* from Dionysius Exiguus; in Greek, Σιμηδικίτης (*Simēdikitēs*). In Labbe’s edition, however, he is wrongly called Simituensis or Sumitensis. He was one of the delegates of the proconsular province.]

When this had been read, he said: “It is Catholic.” Habetdeus, deacon, said: “We have none.” And he read:

“I, Restitutus, bishop, on behalf of my colleague Solemnius, of the congregation of Tigisis, have dictated and subscribed the foregoing at Carthage in the presence of Marcellinus, most distinguished tribune and notary.”

[Note: **[Col. 1315C] Tigisitanae.** That is, the one in Numidia, not the one in Mauretania Caesariensis; for Restitutus, bishop of Novasium in Numidia, subscribes on behalf of Solemnius. On the sees of Tigisis, consult note 65 in Book I of Optatus, p. 15.]

When this had been read, he said: “On the other side is Paschasius.” And when Paschasius approached, he said: “I recognize him.” And he read:

“I, Lampadius, bishop of the congregation of Tisedis, in the presence of Marcellinus, most distinguished tribune and notary, have dictated and subscribed at Carthage.”

[Note: **[Col. 1315C] Tiseditensis.** For Baluze it is the same as Tididitanus, which occurs in the *Notitia* of Numidia, no. 24; for Holstenius it is the same as Tifiltensis, which occurs in the *Notitia* of Mauretania Caesariensis, no. 15.]

When this had been read, he said: “On the other side [I have Donatus. And when Donatus approached, he said]: I recognize him.” And he read:

“I, Cyprianus, bishop of the congregation of Greater Tuburbo, in the presence of Marcellinus, most distinguished tribune and notary, have dictated and subscribed the foregoing at Carthage.”

[Note: **[Col. 1315C] Tuburbitanorum Majorum.** In the proconsular province; for, as we have observed, towns of the same name, one of which is called Greater and the other Lesser, are usually close to one another.]

When this had been read, he said: “On the other side is Rufinus.” And when Rufinus approached, he said: “I recognize him.” And he read:

“I, Donatianus, bishop of the congregation of Zella, in the presence of Marcellinus, most distinguished tribune and notary, have dictated and subscribed the foregoing at Carthage.”

[Note: **[Col. 1315D] Zellensis, or rather Telensis.** In the proconsular province, as the *Notitia* teaches, no. 14; for Natalicus, his opponent, is called bishop of Tela at the Council of Cabarsussus. The letters Z and T are often interchanged. Yet another bishop of Tela from Donatus’s party, Felix by name, occurs in chapter 207; hence Baluze infers that Zella differs from Tela. But it could be that there were two Donatist bishops of the same city, or that the later name is corrupt. For Natalicus, who is here called bishop of Zella and is Donatianus’s opponent, is certainly known from the Council of Cabarsussus to have been bishop of Tela. In the synodical letter of the bishops of the proconsular province at the Lateran Council, the name of Bonifacius, bishop of Tela, is read. Zella is nowhere else mentioned.]

When this had been read, he said: “On the other side I have Natalicus.” And when Natalicus the bishop approached, he said: “I recognize him.” [And he read.]

**136.** “I, Alypius, bishop of the Catholic Church of Thagaste, being at Carthage in the presence of Marcellinus, most distinguished tribune and notary, have received and subscribed this mandate.”

[Note: **[Col. 1315D] Tagastensis.** In Numidia, as the *Notitia* teaches, no. 118; a city well known from the names of Augustine and Alypius. In the Itinerary of Antoninus it is placed midway between Hippo Regius and Naraggara.]

When this had been read, he said: “Would that, just as Thagaste enjoys its ancient unity, we might likewise rejoice concerning the other places.”

**137.** Petilianus, bishop, said: “The unity of innocence and crime is evil. The two cannot be mingled together side by side.” And in another hand: “I, Petilianus, bishop, have acknowledged [this].” And he read.

**138.** “I, Augustine, bishop of the Church of Hippo Regius, being at Carthage in the presence of Marcellinus, most distinguished tribune and notary, have received and subscribed this mandate.”

[Note: **[Col. 1316C] Hipponiensium regiorum.** A most famous ancient trading-town on the Numidian coast, mentioned by Strabo, Ptolemy, Antoninus in the Itinerary, Silius Italicus, and other ancient writers, between Tabarca and Cirta. It is scarcely possible to say how greatly this city was ennobled by Augustine’s episcopate.]

When this had been read, and the bishop approached, he said: “I recognize him.” And he read:

“I, Vincentius, bishop of the Church of Culusi, being at Carthage in the presence of Marcellinus, most distinguished tribune and notary, have received and subscribed this mandate.”

[Note: **[Col. 1316C] Culusitanae.** In the proconsular province, as the *Notitia* teaches, no. 33. Vincentius, its bishop, was one of the advocates of whom we have already spoken in the preface to the Acts. Marcianus, bishop of the congregation of Culusi, attended the Council of Carthage under Bonifacius in 525. Peter, bishop of the Church of Culcita, subscribes to the synodical letter of the bishops of the proconsular province at the Lateran Council under Martin.]

When this had been read, he said: “It is Catholic.” Habetdeus, deacon, said: “He had [a following], but lately joined their communion.” And he read:

“I, Fortunatus, bishop of the Church of Constantine, being at Carthage in the presence of Marcellinus, most distinguished tribune and notary, have received and subscribed this mandate.”

[Note: **[Col. 1316D] Constantiniensis, or Cirtensis, in Numidia.** A celebrated city of Numidia, formerly the royal city of Massinissa and the civil metropolis of all Numidia, known to Mela, Strabo, Caesar, Livy, Pliny, and all other geographers. In Antoninus’s Itinerary Circa is read for Cirta; and in the *Notitia* of the bishops of Numidia, Cicensis is also read. It bears the name Constantina from Constantine the Great, and is still called by that name.]

When this had been read, he said: “On the other side I have Petilianus.”

**139.** Petilianus, bishop, said: “He is a persecutor of the Church in the very city in which I am bishop.” Aurelius, bishop of the Catholic Church of Carthage, said: “And a little while ago you hurled an insult and did not receive one back.” Fortunatus, bishop of the Catholic Church, said: “In that same city all the altars were smashed by heretics.” Petilianus, bishop, said: “Let the proceedings prove that you are a persecutor. In due course you will hear what you deserve.” And he read:

“I, Fortunatianus, bishop of the Church of Sicca, being at Carthage in the presence of Marcellinus, most distinguished tribune and notary, have received and subscribed this mandate.”

[Note: **[Col. 1316D] Siccensis.** In the proconsular province, where was the city Sicca Veneria, mentioned by Antoninus in the Itinerary. It is also mentioned by Procopius in Book II of the *Vandalic War*, Victor of Vita, Augustine, and the Peutinger Tables. Its bishop subscribed the letter of the bishops of the proconsular province at the Lateran Council under Martin; and Castus of Sicca was one of the bishops who delivered an opinion at the Council of Carthage under Cyprian.]

When this had been read, he said: “I know the unity of the Church of Sicca; I have heard of its bishop only in name.” And he read:

“I, Possidius, bishop of the Catholic Church of Calama, being at Carthage in the presence of Marcellinus, most distinguished tribune and notary, have received and subscribed this mandate.”

[Note: **[Col. 1317C] Calamensis.** In Numidia, as the *Notitia* teaches, no. 3. See what we said concerning it in note 51 to Book I of Optatus, p. 15. Possidius also, its bishop, was discussed in the Preface to these Acts.]

Petilianus, bishop, said: “Crispinus lately departed from the body.” And he read:

“I, Florentinus, bishop of the Catholic Church of Hippo Zarytus, being at Carthage, before Marcellinus, most distinguished tribune and notary, have dictated and subscribed the foregoing.”

When this had been read, he said: “On the other side is Victor.” Habetdeus, deacon, said: “He has been appointed guardian of the records.”

**140.** Petilianus, bishop, said: “Some time ago, among the advocates to whom a mandate was given, I noticed that the names of Fortunatianus and Fortunatus were retained. Now too I perceive that those same men are being read as mandators. What is this distinction? No one has ever given a mandate to himself.”

**141.** Marcellinus, most distinguished man, tribune and notary, said: “Let it be read whether the subscription of those who undertook to conduct the case is equal and alike.” And he read:

“I, Fortunatus, bishop of the Church of Constantine, being at Carthage in the presence of Marcellinus, most distinguished tribune and notary, have received and subscribed this mandate.”

Likewise he read:

“I, Fortunatianus, bishop of the Church of Sicca, being at Carthage in the presence of Marcellinus, most distinguished tribune and notary, have received and subscribed this mandate.”

When this had been read:

**142.** Marcellinus, most distinguished man, tribune and notary, said: “Your Holiness perceives from their subscriptions that they have declared that they accepted the mandate. Therefore let the remainder be read in order.” And he read:

“I, Serenianus, bishop of Midita, being at Carthage in the presence of Marcellinus, most distinguished tribune and notary, have dictated and subscribed the foregoing.”

[Note: **[Col. 1317C] Miditensis.** In the province of Byzacena, as the *Notitia* teaches, no. 6.]

When this had been read, Peregrinus, bishop of Sufetula, said: “I have a presbyter there, Victor. It is my diocese.” Victor, bishop, said: “I am present. Let it be put in writing whether Florentius himself recognizes properly the man whom he persecuted when innocent, whom he seized and gave into the custody of the officials to be killed, where I spent three years.”

[Note: **[Col. 1317C] Peregrinus, bishop of Sufetula.** In the same province, according to the same *Notitia*, no. 21. At the Council of Carthage under Cyprian, Privatus of Sufis delivered an opinion. Sufis is mentioned in Antoninus’s Itinerary; it is also mentioned by Victor of Vita and in the *Life of Fulgentius*. Augustine, Letter 50, praises the sixty martyrs of Suffectum, whose commemoration the Roman Martyrology observes on 13 August.]

**143.** Marcellinus, most distinguished man, tribune and notary, said: “These matters shall be dealt with in their proper order, when you think fit.” And he read:

“I, Novatus, bishop of the Church of Sitifis, being at Carthage in the presence of Marcellinus, most distinguished tribune and notary, have dictated and subscribed the foregoing.”

[Note: **[Col. 1317D] Sitifensis.** A well-known city, if only because it gave its name to the entire province, of which it was also the capital. Antoninus in the Itinerary, Ptolemy, and other ancient writers mention it. This Novatus, delegate of his province, attended the Council of Carthage in 419, and Augustine praises him in Letter 229, written near the end of Augustine’s life.]

When this had been read, he said: “On the other side I have Marcianus.” And when Marcianus the bishop approached, he said: “I recognize my persecutor.” And he read:

“I, Maurentius, bishop of the Church of Tubursicum, being at Carthage in the presence of Marcellinus, most distinguished tribune and notary, have dictated and subscribed the foregoing.”

[Note: **[Col. 1317D] Tubursicensis.** In Numidia, as the *Notitia* teaches, no. 22. Antoninus mentions this town in the Itinerary. It was near Thagaste, as is clear from Augustine’s Letter 163.]

When this had been read, he said: “On the other side I have Januarianus.” And when Januarianus approached, he said: “I recognize him.” And he read:

“I, Bonifacius, bishop of the Church of Cataqua, being at Carthage in the presence of Marcellinus, most distinguished tribune and notary, have dictated and subscribed the foregoing at Carthage.”

[Note: **[Col. 1317D] Cataquensis.** In its place the *Notitia* of Numidia, no. 68, reads Cethaquensusca, undoubtedly corruptly. For when Cethaquensis had been written, someone learned added in the margin *ca* for *ce*, teaching that Cataquensis should be read; an unskilled copyist, not understanding this, added *ca* at the end. This Bonifacius had succeeded Paulus in the episcopate, as may be seen in Augustine, Letter 96.]

When this had been read, he said: “On the other side Speratus is mine.” And when Speratus approached, he said: “I recognize him.” And he read:

“I, Squillacius, bishop of the Church of Scillium, being at Carthage in the presence of Marcellinus, most distinguished tribune and notary, have dictated and subscribed the foregoing.”

[Note: **[Col. 1318C] Scillitanae.** There is a see of Sillita in Numidia, concerning which see above at chapter 128; but this one seems to belong to the proconsular province. Indeed, in the letter of the bishops of that province at the Lateran Council, Parjator, bishop of the holy Church of Scillium, subscribes. I suspect that the Scillitan martyrs were named from this town rather than from the other.]

When this had been read, he said: “On the other side I have Donatus.” And when Donatus the bishop approached, he said: “I recognize him.” And he read:

“I, Priscus, bishop of the Church of Quiza, being at Carthage in the presence of Marcellinus, most distinguished tribune and notary, have dictated and subscribed the foregoing.”

[Note: **[Col. 1318D] Quidiensis.** In Mauretania Caesariensis, as the *Notitia* teaches, no. 2. Pliny, Book V, chapter 2, calls Quiza Xenitana a town of foreigners. Pomponius Mela, Book I, chapter 6, calls it a fortress; Antoninus, in the Itinerary, a municipality; and Ptolemy, Book IV, chapter 2, a colony.]

When this had been read, he said: “I have no Donatists. The man who was there with a few of his relatives converted with them.” Honoratus, bishop, said: “Our bishop of Quiza yielded under persecution. Our presbyters are there.” And he read:

“I, Deuterius, bishop of Caesarea, being at Carthage in the presence of Marcellinus, most distinguished tribune and notary, have dictated [and subscribed] the foregoing.”

[Note: **[Col. 1318D] Caesariensis.** Caesarea, the metropolis of Mauretania, formerly called Iol, the royal city of King Juba, was granted colonial status by the deified Claudius, who ordered veterans to be settled there, as Pliny states, Book V, chapter 2. Ptolemy, Book II, chapter 4, calls it Iol Caesarea; Antoninus, in the Itinerary, Caesarea Colony; and Pomponius Mela, Book I, chapter 6, says: “Iol, formerly obscure on the sea, is now illustrious because it was Juba’s royal city and is called Caesarea.” Solinus observes that the royal city of King Bocchus, later of Juba, was given by the indulgence of the Roman people. It is now thought to be the city of Algiers. Its Donatist bishop Emeritus was one of the seven advocates of Donatus’s party, and the Catholic Deuterius one of the guardians of the records for the Catholic party.]

When this had been read, Fortunatianus, bishop of the Catholic Church, said: “He is guardian of the records.” Valentinianus, deacon of Bishop Primianus, said: “Emeritus is there.” And when Emeritus approached, he said: “I recognize him.” And he read:

“I, Restitutus, bishop of Tagora, being at Carthage in the presence of Marcellinus, most distinguished tribune and notary, have dictated [and subscribed] the foregoing.”

[Note: **[Col. 1319D] Tagorensis.** Of that Tagora which is in the proconsular province, not the one in Numidia. See above, note 201. This Restitutus was one of the guardians of the documents for the Catholic party.]

When this had been read, Fortunatianus, bishop of the Catholic Church, said: “He too is a guardian of the records.” Valentinianus, deacon of Bishop Primianus, said: “We have none.” And he read:

“I, Leo, bishop of the municipality of Mopti, being at Carthage in the presence of Marcellinus, most distinguished tribune and notary, have dictated and subscribed the foregoing.”

[Note: **[Col. 1319D] Moptensis.** In Mauretania Sitifensis. Leo, delegate of this province, attended the Council of Carthage in 419. Some manuscripts have Moctensis. Mopti is listed as a municipality on the Peutinger Tables. It appears to be the same as Mozotensis, mentioned in the *Notitia* of the province of Sitifis, no. 33.]

When this had been read, he said: “I have Felix.” And when Felix approached, he said: “I recognize him.” And he read:

“I, Asterius, bishop of the congregation of Vicus, being at Carthage before Marcellinus, most distinguished tribune and notary, have dictated and subscribed the foregoing.”

[Note: **[Col. 1320D] Vicensis.** Perhaps Vicus Pacensis in Numidia, which is the last see in its *Notitia*. Januarius of Vicus Caesaris attended the Council of Carthage under Cyprian; and at the Council of Carthage under Bonifacius in 525, Florentianus is Vicopacatensis.]

When this had been read, he said: “On that very soil no other bishop is with me.” And when Urbanus the bishop approached, he said: “God sees that I do not know him.”

**144.** Marcellinus, most distinguished man, tribune and notary, said: “It is certainly sufficiently clear that I have already offered Your Holiness the opportunity to discuss everything while seated, with fitting respect; for I am not unaware that it is burdensome for me to remain seated while so many venerable men stand. Therefore, even now, with the multitude removed, be pleased to sit.”

**145.** Petilianus, bishop, said: “We give thanks to your honorable rank, noble sir, because your kindness is such and so great that you deign to grant this favor to men of high deserts, to most ancient priests, and to those flourishing with the palms of so many persecutions: that grave old age, adorned by its years and merits, may refresh itself by sitting, lest it appear to be wearied by standing too long, and lest this burden also weigh down the modest strength of old age. But since the Lord supplies strength and makes reverend old age itself stronger, we neither blush, nor fear, nor avoid gladly standing while you, noble sir, are seated. For even Christ our Lord did not avoid this when he deigned to stand before the governor; how much less do we refuse, when you, honorable, just, respectful, and kind, offer this favor—a favor which may most frequently be repaid to you by the Lord who rewards, with the worthiest recompenses. Yet this is expedient and necessary for us: when the case is pleaded, when it is first begun, the persons also should be established; and it is fitting that each should stand who happens to undergo the examination of the dispute.” And in another hand: “I, Petilianus, bishop, have acknowledged [this].”

**146.** Marcellinus, most distinguished man, tribune and notary, said: “Since Your Holiness declines what has been offered, this point must be dealt with: because, as your religious devotion wished, the presence of all who subscribed has been demonstrated, in accordance with the form of the heavenly oracle; mindful also of your undertaking, select suitable advocates for your own assertion, so that, while they debate, and with the confusion of the multitude excluded as was earlier resolved, all matters may be fully examined.”

**147.** Emeritus, bishop, said: “The matter is plain: the persons giving the mandate are present, and we also bring the mandate. But in order that the reliability of the proceedings may be confirmed by our own subscription as well, both the declaration shall be read and what was subscribed in the agreement shall be attached to the proceedings.” And in another hand: “I, Emeritus, bishop, have acknowledged [this].”

**148.** Marcellinus, most distinguished man, tribune and notary, said: “Let the mandate received by the office be read.” And when they had handed it over, Rufinianus, assistant clerk, read:

“After the consulship of Varanius, on the eighth day before the Kalends of June, at Carthage: Junuarianus, Primianus, Felix, Donatus, Candorius, Optatus, Donatianus, Antonianus, Victorianus, Fortis, and the rest, present, send greetings to our fellow bishops Primianus, Petilianus, Emeritus, Protasius, Montanus, Gaudentius, and Adeodatus, present.

“We entrust to you the cause of the Church of God, and make you our advocates against our betrayers and persecutors, who wished to harass us before the tribunal of Marcellinus, most distinguished and eminent tribune and notary, by their petition and the edict which was issued, so that you may answer their charges. Whatever you do for the standing of the holy Church, we declare by our subscription that we shall hold ratified. And in another hand: We pray that you may fare well in the Lord and remember us.”

When this had been read.

149. Marcellinus, most distinguished man, tribune and notary, said: “Let the subscriptions to this mandate likewise be read aloud.” Rufinianus the clerk read:

“I, Januarianus, bishop of the Casenses Nigrenses, have subscribed to this our mandate.”

[Note: *Casenses-Nigrenses.* In Numidia Donatus of Casae Nigrae, author of the schism, is well known. Januarianus was primate of the Numidian bishops of the Donatist party, as the index of Possidius in the Colbert manuscript and the heading of St. Augustine’s Letter LXVIII show.]

Likewise, in another hand: “I, Primianus, bishop of Carthage, have subscribed to this mandate.” [Col. 1320D]

Likewise, in another hand: “I, Felix, bishop of the city of Rome, have subscribed to this mandate.”

[Note: *Felix of the City of Rome:* that is, the pseudo-bishop of the Montenses, who were living at Rome.]

Likewise, in another hand: “I, Donatus, [Col. 1321A] bishop of Botriana, have subscribed to this mandate.”

[Note: *Botrianensis:* it is uncertain in which province this see lay.]

Likewise, in another hand: “I, Florianus, bishop of Putiza, have subscribed.”

[Note: *Putiziensis:* two sees named Putia occur in the Notitia: one in the province of Numidia, no. 17, the other in Byzacena, no. 18. This man was perhaps bishop of the Byzacene see. Another Donatist bishop of Putia, named Felix, is found.]

Likewise, in another hand: “I, Candorius, bishop of Aggerita, have subscribed.”

Likewise, in another hand: “I, Antonianus, bishop of Lamsorta, have subscribed.”

[Note: *Lamsortensis:* in Numidia, as the Notitia, no. 23, shows. Florentius, bishop of Lamsorta, subscribed to the Council of Carthage under Boniface in 525.]

When this had been read aloud:

150. Possidius, bishop of the Catholic Church, said: “Let us also ascertain their personal presence.” [And in another hand:] “I have verified it.”
