[Note: **[Col. 1343D] Lambiritensis, or Lambiritanus.** In Numidia, no. 19 in the list. The Anonymous of Ravenna includes Lambridi among the cities of Numidia; it also appears in the Peutinger Tables.]

When he came forward, he said the same: “I gave instructions and subscribed; and I declare that I have no *traditores*.”

Aurelius, bishop of the Catholic Church at Macomades, said: “That declaration is superfluous. There was a bishop there; he died recently. Another will be ordained there.”

Likewise he read: “Habetdeus, bishop of Aurusulia.”

[Note: **[Col. 1343D] Aurusulianensis.** At the Council of Cabarsussa [Col. 1344C], Secundianus, bishop of Aurisilia, is recorded as having been present. Without doubt he was Habetdeus’s predecessor. I should judge Aurusulia to have been in Numidia.]

When he came forward, he said the same: “I gave [Col. 1343C] instructions and subscribed.”

Likewise he read: “Burcaton, bishop of Gemellae.”

[Note: **[Col. 1344C] Gemellensis.** Littaeus of Gemellae was one of the bishops present at the Council of Carthage under [Col. 1344D] Cyprian. Gemellae is inferred from the Antonine Itinerary to have lain on the borders of Mauretania Sitifensis and Numidia: there it is placed midway between New Sparsa of Numidia and Sitifis itself, twenty-five Roman miles distant from the latter.]

When he came forward, he said the same: “I gave instructions and subscribed. I have no *traditor*, nor have I ever had one.”

Likewise he read: “Januarius, bishop of Betagbarita.”

[Note: **[Col. 1344D] Betagbaritanus.** It is uncertain in which province this place lay.]

When he came forward, he said the same: “I gave instructions and subscribed.”

Likewise he read: “Donatianus, bishop of Lamzella.”

[Note: **[Col. 1344D] Lamzellensis.** It is uncertain in which province this place lay.]

When he came forward, he said the same: “I gave instructions and subscribed. But I have no *traditor*, have never had one, and never shall have one.”

Aurelius, bishop of the Catholic Church at Macomades, said: “Our Bishop Rufus was there. At Lamzella, Gildo was laid in our basilica.”

[Note: **[Col. 1344D] Gildo.** Baluzius thinks this refers to the tyrant Gildo; but it is more likely that Aurelius is speaking of a certain deceased bishop of Lamzella bearing this name.]

“Let this be recorded while an election is awaited. In any event, in Christ’s name, a bishop will be ordained there.”

Likewise he read: “Celer, bishop of Capsa.” When he came forward, he said the same: “I gave instructions and subscribed.”

Likewise he read: “Cresconius, bishop of Musertum.” When he came forward, he said the same: “I gave instructions [and subscribed].”

Likewise he read: “Donatus, bishop of Tubursicum.” When he came forward, he said the same: “I gave instructions and subscribed.”

Likewise he read: “Quodvultdeus, bishop of Cessita.”

[Note: **[Col. 1344D] Cessitanus.** In the list of African bishops there are two bishops of Cissita, one in the proconsular province, no. 27, and the other in Mauretania Caesariensis, no. 107. Here too there are two Donatist bishops of this name: Felix here, and later, in ch. 208, Flavosus, bishop of Cissita.]

207. Bishop Petilianus said: “He died on the journey.” And in another hand: “I, Bishop Petilianus, have verified it.”

Fortunatianus, bishop of the Catholic Church, said: “Let it be shown how the man said to have died on the journey is found to have subscribed.” And in another hand: “I have verified it.”

Bishop Petilianus said: “It was not said of him; you are proceeding maliciously. Information was given about another man.” And in another hand: “I, Bishop Petilianus, have verified it.”

Fortunatianus, bishop of the Catholic Church, said: “About whom?”

Bishop Petilianus said: “The man who died on the road.” And in another hand: “As above.”

Alypius, bishop of the Catholic Church, said: “Let the names be read, so that he may recognize the same person.” And in another hand: “I have verified it.”

Fortunatianus, bishop of the Catholic Church, said: “If he died on the road, how did he subscribe?” And in another hand: “I have verified it.”

Aurelius, bishop of the Catholic Church at Carthage, said: “Did a cleric subscribe on behalf of a dead man?” And in another hand: “I have verified it.”

Alypius, bishop of the Catholic Church, said: “Let him choose for himself, so that I may show how he lies.” And in another hand: “I have verified it.”

Marcellinus, a man of clarissimus rank, tribune and notary, said: “Let it be shown how the man said to have died on the journey subscribed.”

[Col. 1344C] Alypius, bishop of the Catholic Church, said: “Let it be read whether a cleric subscribed in his own name or in the name of the deceased.” And in another hand: “I have verified it.”

Marcellinus, a man of clarissimus rank, tribune and notary, said: “Let it be read in whose name the man said to have died on the journey subscribed.”

And he read: “Quodvultdeus, bishop of Cessita: I subscribed while ill.”

Fortunatianus, bishop of the Catholic Church, said: “Your nobility observes that no cleric’s name subscribed in the deceased man’s name, but that, as though he were alive, the subscription was produced for the man dead to us, who, according to their declaration, is said to have died on the road.” [Col. 1345A] And in another hand: “I have verified it.”

Bishop Petilianus said: “What if this man too, who subscribed while ill, should die? As though not one man died today!” And in another hand: “I, Bishop Petilianus, have verified it.”

[Note: **[Col. 1345D] As though not one man died today.** Namely Maximinianus of Bennefa, above, chs. 133 and 198.]

Aurelius, bishop of the Catholic Church at Carthage, said: “But you said that he died on the journey.” And in another hand: “I have verified it.”

Alypius, bishop of the Catholic Church, said: “These detected matters are enough. Let the rest follow.” And in another hand: “I have verified it.”

Bishop Petilianus said: “You have detected nothing; you argue against the truth.” And in another hand: “I, Bishop Petilianus, have verified it.”

Alypius, bishop of the Catholic Church, said: “You said it.” And in another hand: “I have verified it.”

208. Marcellinus, a man of clarissimus rank, tribune and notary, said: “If what you assert is true, that he died on the journey [Col. 1345B], it is established that his subscription was read out most falsely. But if he himself subscribed, he could not have died on the journey.”

Bishop Petilianus said: “Is it not human to die? Do not even dying persons subscribe their wills?” And in another hand: “I, Bishop Petilianus, have verified it.”

Alypius, bishop of the Catholic Church, said: “It is human to die, but it is inhuman to deceive.” And in another hand: “I have verified it.”

Bishop Petilianus said: “This is not deception, because he could have died on the journey while returning. I have only now received the mandate. I say what moves me.” And in another hand: “I, Bishop Petilianus, have verified it.”

Fortunatianus, bishop of the Catholic Church, said: “Let the date of the mandate produced by the party be read, so that it may appear, concerning the name of the deceased, which party has launched into falsehood.” And in another hand: “I have verified it.”

Marcellinus, a man of [Col. 1345C] clarissimus rank, tribune and notary, said: “Let the office disclose the date of the mandate.”

The scribe Rufinianus said: “I shall read the date of the mandate as your sublimity has ordered.”

And he read: “After the consulship of the clarissimus man Varanius, on the eighth day before the Kalends of June, at Carthage.”

And as he read, Marcellinus, a man of clarissimus rank, tribune and notary, said: “Let the remainder be read.”

The scribe Rufinianus read: “Januarianus, Primianus, Felix, Donatus, Candorius, Optatus, Donatianus, Antonianus, Victorianus, Fortis, and the rest, to Primianus, Petilianus, Emeritus, Protasius, Montanus, Gaudentius, Adeodatus, our fellow bishops, present to those present, greetings.”

And as he read, Aurelius, bishop of the Catholic Church, said: “He himself subscribed long ago. A moment ago he said that a cleric subscribed; a moment ago, that a bishop did.” And as he said this: “And in another hand: I have verified it.”

[Col. 1345D] Marcellinus, a man of clarissimus rank, tribune and notary, said: “You observe that those present gave a mandate to those present for carrying out the business. How then did this man, who admits that he was present in this city and, together with the others, unquestionably gave instructions, die on the journey and subscribe the mandate in this city?”

Bishop Adeodatus said: “Eight days elapsed while the mandate [Col. 1346A] was being drawn up. The man who gave instructions, whose name is now at issue, when he began to fall ill, died on the road while returning home.” And in another hand: “I, Bishop Adeodatus, have verified it.”

Vincentius, bishop of the Catholic Church, said: “Let him say where he died.” And in another hand: “I have verified it.”

Bishop Adeodatus said: “I do not know the place.” And in another hand: “As above.”

Marcellinus, a man of clarissimus rank, tribune and notary, said: “Since the statement of your holiness, by which you testify that he was here and, while ill, died on his way home, is plausible, it is at least fitting that you show this: under the attestation of God, declare whether he was in this city.”

Fortunatianus, bishop of the Catholic Church, said: “If your sublimity orders it, let the statement of the clarissimus man Petilianus be read, so that from the reading all may learn how [Col. 1346B] it is now falsely said that, on returning from Carthage, he died on the journey, because his statement showed him otherwise.” And in another hand: “I have verified it.”

Marcellinus, a man of clarissimus rank, tribune and notary, said: “Let the requested statement be read.”

And while it was being read from the codex, Marcellinus, a man of clarissimus rank, tribune and notary, said: “It seems to me that nothing further need be asked on this point, except that, under divine attestation, it be plainly declared by a straightforward profession whether the man in question was present here.”

Bishop Emeritus said: “What if someone else put himself forward as that man?” And in another hand: “I, Bishop Emeritus, have verified it.”

Marcellinus, most illustrious man, tribune and notary, said: “God’s judgment upon deceivers will be complete in every respect, even without the administration of an oath. Therefore let the remaining names of those who subscribed be read out.” And he read:

Quodvultdeus, bishop of Volitanus. When he had come forward, he said: “I directed it and subscribed.”

Likewise he read: Donatus, bishop of Turre Rotunda.

> [Note: [Col. 1345D] Turre Rotunda. Ptolemy, book IV, chapter 2, places Robunda among the towns of Numidia; Baluzius conjectures that it may be identical with Turre Rotunda.]

When he had come forward, he said: “I directed it and subscribed.”

Likewise he read: Victorius, bishop of Selendetensis.

> [Note: [Col. 1345D] Selendetensis. Among the bishops attending the Council of Carthage in 525 is named Felicissimus, bishop of Sedela.]

Crescentianus, bishop, said: “He is here; he is ill.”

Likewise he read: Crescentianus, bishop of Ammedera. When he had come forward, he said: “I directed it and subscribed.”

Likewise he read: Felix, bishop of Bulla. When he had come forward, he said: “I directed it and subscribed.”

Likewise he read: Cresconius, bishop of Cibaliana.

> [Note: [Col. 1346D] Of Cibaliana. Donatus of Cibaliana attended the Council of Carthage under Cyprian. It is uncertain to which province he belonged. Perhaps he is identical with the bishop of Seberiana in Byzacena, concerning whom see the *Notitia*. Constantius, bishop of the Church of Cerbalitana, attended the Council of Carthage under Boniface; was he perhaps of the same see as these men?]

When he had come forward, he said: “I directed it and subscribed.”

Likewise he read: Jurata, bishop of Turre-Tamallum. When he had come forward, he said: “I directed [Col. 1346D] it and subscribed.”

Likewise he read: Liberalis, bishop of Milidiensis.

> [Note: [Col. 1346D] Milidiensis. It is uncertain to which province it belonged.]

When he had come forward, he said: “I directed it and subscribed.”

Likewise he read: Donatus, bishop of Auzagerensis.

> [Note: [Col. 1346D] Auzagerensis. In the province of Byzacena; *Notitia*, [Col. 1347C] no. 96.]

When he had come forward, he said: “I directed it and subscribed.”

Likewise he read: Victor, bishop of Villaregensis. When he had come forward, he said: “I directed it and subscribed.”

Likewise he read: Donatus, bishop of [Col. 1347A] Buzensis. When he had come forward, he said: “I directed it and subscribed.”

Likewise he read: Lucius, bishop of Tamallum. When he had come forward, he said: “I directed it and subscribed.”

Likewise he read: Quintus, bishop of Tagarala. When he had come forward, he said: “I directed it and subscribed.”

Likewise he read: Datianus, bishop of Telepte.

> [Note: [Col. 1347C] Teleptensis. Another Donatist bishop of Telepte, named Bellicius, occurs in chapters 121 and 198. Telepte was nevertheless not a double see; rather, they put forward two bishops of the same see.]

When he had come forward, he said: “I directed it and subscribed.”

Likewise he read: Megasius, bishop of Tucabor.

> [Note: [Col. 1347C] Tucaborensis. In the proconsular province. For Stephanus, bishop of Tuccabor, subscribed to the synodical letter of the bishops of that province at the Lateran Council. Fortunatus of Tucabor attended the Council of Carthage under Cyprian.]

When he had come forward, he said: “I directed it and subscribed.”

Likewise he read: Honoratus, bishop of Jommitensis.

> [Note: [Col. 1347C] Jommitensis, or rather Jonnitensis. In Mauretania Caesariensis. The Antonine Itinerary and Ptolemy record the municipium of Jonnium.]

When he had come forward, he said: “I directed it and subscribed.”

Likewise he read: Vitalis, bishop of Ucrensis.

> [Note: [Col. 1347C] Ucrensis. It seems that Verensis should be read: this place is in the proconsular province in the *Notitia*, no. 26; [Col. 1347D] it is called Veris in the Peutinger Tables and in the Ravenna Cosmography. Vitalis, bishop from the city of the Verenses, attended the Council of Carthage under Cyprian; and Quodvultdeus, bishop of Verensis, subscribed to the Council of Carthage of 419 under Aurelius.]

When he had come forward, he said: “I directed it and subscribed.”

Likewise he read: Plutianus, bishop of Mascliana.

> [Note: [Col. 1347D] Masclianensis. In Byzacena, as the *Notitia*, no. 9, shows. Numidicus, bishop of Misclianum, is mentioned at the Council of Carthage under Genethlius.]

When he had come forward, [Col. 1347B] he said: “I directed it and subscribed.”

Likewise he read: Faustinus, bishop of Naraggara.

> [Note: [Col. 1347D] Naraggaritanus. In the proconsular province, according to the *Notitia*, no. 48, where Maraggaritanus is incorrectly read. Naraggara is a city known to Ptolemy. It is mentioned after Tagaste in the Antonine Itinerary and in the Peutinger Tables. At the Council of Carthage under Boniface in 525, Victorinus, bishop of the people of Nagargara, is recorded as having subscribed. In the synodical letter of the bishops of the proconsular province at the Lateran Council [Col. 1348C] under Martin, Benenatus, bishop of the Church of Naraggara, subscribes.]

When he had come forward, he said: “I directed it and subscribed.”

Likewise he read: Felicianus, bishop of Vilta.

> [Note: [Col. 1348C] Viltensis. In the proconsular province, as is inferred from the synodical letter just cited, to which Theodorus, bishop of Billa, subscribed. At the Council of Carthage in 525 under Boniface, Restitutus, bishop of the people of Vilta, subscribed.]

When he had come forward, he said: “I directed it and subscribed.”

Likewise he read: Felix, bishop of Boncara.

> [Note: [Col. 1348C] Boncarensis. In Mauretania Caesariensis, where the *Notitia*, no. 62, has Voncariensis.]

When he had come forward, he said: “I directed it and subscribed.”

Likewise he read: Felix, bishop of Tela. When he had come forward, he said: “I directed it and subscribed.”

Likewise he read: Secundus, bishop of Ara. When he had come forward, he said: “I directed it and subscribed: I have no opponent among my people.”

Likewise he read: Julianus, bishop of Tignica. When he had come forward, he said: “I directed it and subscribed.”

Likewise he read: Splendonius, bishop of Mutugenna. When he had come forward, he [Col. 1347C] said: “I directed it and subscribed.”

Likewise he read: Serenianus, bishop of Mammilla. When he had come forward, he said: “I directed it and subscribed.”

Likewise he read: Salvianus, [Col. 1348A] bishop of Leptis. When he had come forward, he said: “I directed it and subscribed.”

Likewise he read: Reperatus, bishop of Vindensis.

> [Note: [Col. 1348C] Vindensis. The location of this place is uncertain.]

When he had come forward, he said: “I directed it and subscribed.”

Likewise he read: Leontius, bishop of Praesidium.

> [Note: [Col. 1348C] Praesidiensis. In Byzacena, *Notitia*, no. 76. Praesidium occurs more than once in the Peutinger Tables, but as an adjunct.]

When he had come forward, he said: “I directed it and subscribed.”

Likewise he read: Titianus, bishop of Sufetula. When he had come forward, he said: “I directed 288 and subscribed.”

Likewise he read: Nestorius, bishop of Maliana. When he had come forward, he said: “I directed it and subscribed.”

Likewise he read: Donatus, bishop of Ancusa. When he had come forward, he said: “I directed it and subscribed.”

Likewise he read: Flavosus, bishop of Cissita. When he had come forward, he said: “I directed it and subscribed.”

Likewise he read: Maximinus, bishop of Turreblanda.

> [Note: [Col. 1348C] Turreblandensis, or Turreblandinus. In Byzacena, as the *Notitia*, no. 98, and the synodical letter [Col. 1348D] of the bishops of that province at the Lateran Council under Martin show; Datianus, bishop of the Church of Turreblanda, subscribed to that letter.]

[Col. 1348B] When he had come forward, he said: “I directed it and subscribed.”

Likewise he read: Miggin, bishop of Vagalita.

> [Note: [Col. 1348D] Vagalitanus. In Mauretania Caesariensis, as the *Notitia*, no. 26, shows. Antoninus mentions Vagal among the towns of Mauretania in his Itinerary.]

When he had come forward, he said: “I directed it and subscribed.”

Likewise he read: Donatianus, bishop of Capsa.

> [Note: [Col. 1348D] Donatianus, bishop of Capsa. Besides this Donatianus, another Donatist bishop of Capsa, named Celer, is listed. There were two sees of this name in Africa: one in Byzacena under Hadrumetum; the other near Inner Libya, amid vast wildernesses. See both on the map.]

When he had come forward, he said: “I directed it and subscribed.”

Likewise he read: Marcianus, bishop of Cebarsussa.

> [Note: [Col. 1348D] Cebarsussonsis. Cabarsussensis should be read, as the acts of the Donatist council held in this place show. There is a town, Susa, in Byzacena. *Cabar*, in the Phoenician language, means “great.” Hence perhaps Cabarsusa.]

When he had come forward, he said: “Although I have no opponent, nevertheless I directed it and subscribed.”

Likewise he read: Restitutus, bishop of Larita. When he had come forward, he said: “I directed it and subscribed.”

Likewise he read: Victorianus, bishop of Aquae. When he had come forward, he said: “I directed it and subscribed.”

Asellicus, bishop of the Catholic Church of the municipium of Tusurita, said: “Under the testimony of almighty God and of Jesus Christ our Saviour, I declare that we set out from [Col. 1348C] Arzuges on the third day before the Kalends of May. He was a presbyter, not a bishop; he was ordained on the journey. Yet, by the party with which he has influence, he is there a bishop, having been discovered in [Col. 1349A] adultery. The investigation is still pending.”

Marcellinus, most illustrious man, tribune and notary, said: “It is enough that he was ordained bishop. Passing over this matter, let the office proceed through the remainder.” And he read:

Faustinus, bishop of Natia.

> [Note: [Col. 1349D] Nationensis. In the province of Byzacena, as the *Notitia*, no. 75, shows.]

When he had come forward, he said: “I have no opponent; I directed it and subscribed.”

Likewise he read: Marcianus, bishop of Eminentius . . . . .

> [Note: [Col. 1349D] Eminentius. Perhaps Eminentianensis. In Mauretania Sitifensis, *Notitia*, no. 14; and the text should subsequently be supplied: “Felix, bishop of Novasinna, said: He remained on the journey; I subscribed for him.” Baluzius considers that the passage should be restored thus.]

“Bishop . . . . . remained on the journey. I, Felix of Novasinna, subscribed for him.”

Alypius, bishop of the Catholic Church, said: “How did persons present give instructions to persons present?”

Felix, bishop of Novasinna, said: “He himself asked me on the journey, and I subscribed for him.”

**209.** Marcellinus, most illustrious man, tribune and notary, said: “Although this has been read and said—that persons present gave instructions to persons present—nevertheless, lest superfluous delay be wasted, let the office proceed through the remainder.” And he read:

Martialis, bishop of Idicra, said: “For Felix of Garba and Justus of Forma, who were detained on the journey because of illness, I subscribed for them.”

> [Note: [Col. 1349D] Garbensis. In Numidia, as the *Notitia*, no. 102, shows. Victor of Garba is mentioned in the acts of the Council of Cirta and in Optatus, book I, no. 14.]

> [Note: [Col. 1349D] Formensis. Likewise in Numidia, *Notitia*, no. 104. Optatus, book II, §18, mentions Urbanus of Forma.]

Marcellinus, most illustrious man, tribune and notary, said: “This too is evidently similar to the preceding matter.” And he added: “Let another be read.”

Marcianus, bishop of the Catholic Church, said: “Felix, bishop of Garba, has not left his house.”

And he read:

Gaudentius, bishop of Tigisis.

> [Note: [Col. 1349D] Tigisitanus. In Mauretania Caesariensis. For another bishop of Tigisis in Numidia had subscribed above, as we observed at chapter 135.]

Cresconius, bishop of Siga, said: “Our colleague Gaudentius, bishop of the place Tigisis, remained on the journey because of illness; I subscribed for him.”

> [Note: [Col. 1349D] Siguitanus. Siga was a colony in Mauretania Caesariensis, according to Ptolemy, book V, chapter 2, [Col. 1350D] and the Antonine Itinerary.]

**210.** Fortunatianus, bishop of the Catholic Church, [Col. 1349C] said: “Let it be attested in the acts of your high office that this is being done in order that their number of bishops may appear greater, although not even so can it be made equal to the Catholics.” In another hand: “I have verified it.”

Likewise he read: Donatus, bishop of Sucarda.

Marinianus, bishop, said: “He is in the city, but is ill.”

**211.** Marcellinus, most illustrious man, tribune and notary, said: “As I have ordered, the readings shall be entered consecutively in the record. Let the office then set out by calculation how many bishops of each party there are whose subscriptions have been read.”

**212.** Alypius, bishop of the Catholic Church, said: “There are still present our colleagues who have not affixed their subscriptions to the authorization. For they had been occupied by illness or necessity, or had arrived later. Order that these too, once identified, come forward.” In another hand: “I have verified it.”

**213.** Marcellinus, most illustrious man, tribune and notary, said: “Meanwhile let the office show the number of those who subscribed.”

Rufinianus, clerk, said: “Excepting the page which contains an error in the Donatists’ subscription, we find that it contains the names.”

Marcellinus, most illustrious man, tribune and notary, said: “How many names, then, does that page itself contain?”

Alypius, bishop of the Catholic Church, said: “Six, including those also counted as absent.”

And as he spoke—“In another hand: I have verified it”—Rufinianus, clerk, said: “Six; thus the total comes to two hundred and seventy-nine.”

**214.** Marcellinus, most illustrious man, tribune and notary, said: “Let it likewise be stated how many bishops of the other party have been read out.”

Rufinianus, clerk, said: “The bishops of the Catholic party, according to the subscription inserted in this brief, amount to two hundred and sixty-six, apart from those whom they say have not yet subscribed.”

**215.** Marcellinus, most illustrious man, tribune and notary, said: “Let them state without delay how many are those whom they affirm to have subscribed.”

Alypius, bishop of the Catholic Church, said: “Let them come forward and be identified. There are twenty.” In another hand: “I have verified it.”

Marcellinus, most illustrious man, tribune and notary, said: “Therefore, if they are present, each must show his presence.”

When Apronianus, bishop, had come forward, Marcellinus, most illustrious man, tribune and notary, said: “Of what city are you bishop?”

Apronianus, bishop of the Catholic Church, said: “Of Mazaca.”

> [Note: [Col. 1350D] Mazacensis. In Numidia, as the *Notitia*, no. 81, shows.]

Marcellinus, most illustrious [Col. 1350C] man, tribune and notary, said: “Do you agree to the authorization which you did not subscribe because of your absence?”

Apronianus, bishop of the Catholic Church of Mazaca, said: “I agree.”

Likewise, when Maximinus, bishop of Sufetula, came forward, Marcellinus, most illustrious man, tribune and notary, said: “Do you also agree to the authorization?”

He said: “I agree and authorize.”

Likewise, when Victor, bishop of Ajura, came forward, he said: “I authorize and agree.”

Likewise, when Felix, bishop of Ficus, 289 came forward, he said: “I authorize and agree.”

> [Note: [Col. 1350D] Ficense. In Mauretania Sitifensis, as the *Notitia*, no. 22, shows. The Peutinger Tables mention *ad Ficum*, a place located in the Antonine Itinerary between Satafa and Igilgili.]

Likewise, when Felix, bishop of Macriana, came forward, he said: “I authorize and agree.”

Likewise, when Lucius, bishop of Oliva, came forward, he said: “I authorize and agree.”

> [Note: [Col. 1350D] Olivensis. In Mauretania Sitifensis. For Oliva is located between Assava and Moptum in the Peutinger Table.]

Likewise, when Tertullianus, bishop of Hirena, came forward, he said: “I authorize and agree.”

> [Note: [Col. 1350D] Hirenensis. Listed in the *Notitia* of the province of Byzacena, no. 94, as bishop of Irensis; Theodorus, bishop of Hirinensis, also subscribed to the synodical letter of the Byzacenes at the Lateran Council under Martin.]

Likewise, when John, bishop of Gummita, came forward, he said: [Col. 1351A] “I authorize and agree.”

> [Note: [Col. 1350D] Gummitanus. Of the same province, as the *Notitia*, no. 89, shows. At the Council of Carthage in 525, Sabinianus, bishop of the people of Gummenarta, subscribed. Stephanus, bishop of the city of Gummasis, subscribed to the synodical letter of the Fathers of Byzacena at the Lateran Council under Martin. In the eleventh century, in the time of Leo IX, when only five bishops of the African Church survived because of the flood of barbarians, one of them was the bishop of Gummita, who sought the title and honour of primate, as appears from letters 3 and 4 of Leo IX.]

Likewise, when Ampelius of Vaga came forward, he said: “I authorize and agree.”

> [Note: [Col. 1351D] Vagensis. Libosus of Vaga attended the Council of Carthage under Cyprian; Crescens of Vaga attended the Council of Carthage under Gratus. Ptolemy and Pliny recognize two places called Vaga, one in Mauretania Caesariensis, the other in Numidia. I would suppose Ampelius to have been bishop of the latter. There were two bishops of this city when Ampelius, initially a Donatist, entered the Church.]

Likewise, when Primulus, bishop of Vaga, came forward, he said: “I authorize and agree.”

Alypius, bishop of the Catholic Church, said: “Severus was present for a long time, but has now departed because of illness.”

> [Note: [Col. 1352D] Severus. Catholic bishop of Milevis, to whom Augustine’s Letter 73 is addressed, and whose letter to Augustine is Letter 69.]

Likewise, when Reginus, bishop of Tigillaba, came forward, he said: “I authorize and agree.”

Alypius, bishop of the Catholic Church, said: “Bishop Delphinus is here, but is prevented by illness. Bishop Faustinianus of Rusiccada is also here in this city, but is unwell; and Felix of Serteita has pain in his foot.”

> [Note: [Col. 1352D] Delphinus. A bishop of Numidia, as is evident from chapter 65 and from St Augustine’s Letter 158.]

Likewise, when Victor, bishop of Abitina, came forward, he said: “I authorize and agree.”

Likewise, when Aeneas, bishop of Turbunica, came forward, he said: “I authorize and agree.”

> [Note: [Col. 1352D] Of Turbunica. In the proconsular province. For Crescens, by the grace of God bishop of the holy Church of Tiburnica, subscribed to the synodical letter of the Fathers of that province at the Lateran Council under Martin.]

Likewise, when Annibonius, bishop of Abbirita, came forward, [Col. 1351B] he said: “I authorize and agree.”

> [Note: [Col. 1352D] Abbiritanus. Namely, of the lesser Abbiritae on the borders of the proconsular province.]

Likewise, when Felix, bishop of Nova, came forward, he said: “I authorize and agree.”

> [Note: [Col. 1352D] Novensis, or Nobensis. There were two sees called Noba in Mauretania Caesariensis, as the *Notitia* shows: one no. 19, the other no. 93.]

Likewise, when Argyrius of Sitipa came forward, he said: “I authorize and agree.”

> [Note: [Col. 1352D] Sitipensis. It is uncertain to which province it belonged.]

**216.** Marcellinus, most illustrious man, tribune and notary, said: “Let the office state how many are these whose declaration has now been made.”

Nampius, clerk, said: “There are twenty.”

Marcellinus, most illustrious man, tribune and notary, said: “It has become evident that the authorizations of all the bishops of both parties are certain and that the persons stand by them firmly. Therefore, the rest, now departing, must grant privacy to those to whom they have entrusted the entire case.”

**217.** Alypius, bishop of the Catholic Church, said: “Let it be written that one hundred and twenty are absent, whom illness, age, or certainly necessity has detained.” And [Col. 1351C] in another hand: “I have verified it.”

Marcellinus, most illustrious man, tribune and notary, said: “It shall be written.”

Petilianus, bishop, said: “Let it be written that many more of ours are absent, including vacant sees, for which bishops must be ordained.” In another hand: “As above.”

Marcellinus, most illustrious man, tribune and notary, said: “The record shall retain this also.”

Fortunatianus, bishop of the Catholic Church of Sicca, said: “Since most holy Petilianus has spoken of vacant sees, we likewise state for this record that we have sixty-four vacant ones.”

Marcellinus, most illustrious man, tribune and notary, said: “This too adheres to the public records.” And he added: “Let the bishops elected by each party remain, and let the others depart.”

When they had departed:

**218.** Marcellinus, most illustrious man, tribune and notary, [Col. 1352A] said: “Let the office state whether only those are present who are known to have been elected by the parties in accordance with the imperial command.”

Rufinianus, clerk, said: “On behalf of the Catholic Church, there stand, according to the form of the edict, eighteen in all: seven advocates, seven counsellors, and four for the documents. Likewise on the side of Donatus there stand eighteen: seven advocates, seven counsellors, and four for the documents.”

**219.** Marcellinus, most illustrious man, tribune and notary, said: “Let the office state how much of the day now appears to have elapsed.”

Rufinianus, clerk, said: “Eleven hours of the day have passed.”

**220.** Marcellinus, most illustrious man, tribune and notary, said: “Since almost the whole of the day is known to have elapsed, let it be stated whether, by common consent, it is thought proper to defer the business.”

Both parties said: “It is proper, since this day now appears to be spent.”

**221.** Marcellinus, most illustrious man, tribune and notary, said: “Let each party designate the day to which this adjournment is to be deferred.”

Alypius, bishop of the Catholic Church, said: “As your high office prescribed by edict, after leaving tomorrow free for the copying of the documents, we shall attend on the day after tomorrow, if you command.” In another hand: “I have verified it.”

Adeodatus, bishop, said: “We too agree that the business be conducted on the day after tomorrow.” In another hand: “I, Adeodatus, have verified it.”

**222.** Marcellinus, most illustrious man, tribune and notary, said: “As the parties have agreed, the business shall be resumed after an intervening day. Both parties, however, must ensure that the appointed guards supervise the shorthand writers and the codices during the copying of the documents, so that everything may be faithfully transcribed; and they must appoint two further guards each—so that there may be four—as was ordered, for those who took the notes recently.”

**223.** Alypius, bishop of the Catholic Church, said: “Two others are present, as the office has already reported: namely, our brothers Leo and Asterius.” In another hand: “I have verified it.”

Primianus, bishop, said: “We likewise provide four guardians of the documents. We have already given two; we now substitute two more, namely Veratianus and Victor, our colleagues who are present.” In another hand: “I, Petilianus, bishop, have verified it.”

Marcellinus, most illustrious man, tribune and notary, said: “Even if they object, what was subsequently taken down shall, after the documents are now sealed, be copied tomorrow.” In another hand: “Let them be produced.” Likewise in another hand: “We, Hilarus and Martialis, shorthand writers, have produced them.”

The proceedings of the first hearing are concluded.

290

## THE PROCEEDINGS OF THE SECOND HEARING BEGIN

Flavius Marcellinus, most illustrious and distinguished man, tribune and notary, said: “All are aware that, when I posted the edict some time ago, I promised that whatever was transacted between the bishops of both parties would promptly come to public notice. I have therefore taken care to lay before your holiness the matters transacted in the meantime, so that you may judge with your own eyes a part of the conflict that has taken place.” In another hand: “Let it be posted.”

[Col. 1353B]

**1.** After the consulship of Varanius, on the third day before the Nones of June, in the secretarium of the Baths of Gargilius at Carthage, with Sebastianus, Maximianus, and Peter—most devoted men, protectors domesticus—present; with Ursus, Petronius, and Libosus, ducenarii; likewise Boniface and Evasius, attendants of the illustrious and eminent authorities; Philetus, attendant of the illustrious staff of the *comes*; Exitiosus, assistant of the *cornicularius*; Possidius, Quodvultdeus, and Colonicus, assistants of the records office of our lord, the most illustrious and distinguished proconsul; Navigius, assistant of the accounts office of our lord, the most illustrious and distinguished vicar; Nampius, clerk of the office of the most illustrious legate of noble Carthage; Rufinianus, clerk of the most illustrious curator of exalted Carthage; and with Hilarus and Praetextatus, shorthand writers of our lord, the most illustrious and distinguished proconsul, Fabius, shorthand writer of our lord, the most illustrious and distinguished vicar, and Romulus, shorthand writer of the most illustrious legate of noble Carthage, taking down the proceedings; with Januarius and Vitalis, notaries of the Catholic Church, and Victor and Cresconius, notaries of the Donatist Church, likewise taking down the proceedings:

Libosus, ducenarius of the illustrious authorities, said: “Since the Hearing has been adjourned to this day, and the bishops of both parties are present, if your high office commands, they shall be admitted.”

**2.** Flavius Marcellinus, most illustrious man, tribune and notary, said: “Let them come.”

And when Aurelius, Alypius, Augustine, Vincentius, Fortunatus, Fortunatianus, Possidius, Novatus, Florentius, Maurentius, Priscus, Serenianus, Boniface, Scillatius, Deuterius, Leo, Asterius, [Col. 1353D] and Restitutus, bishops of the Catholic Church, had entered; and when, from the other side, Primianus, Petilianus, Emeritus, Protasius, Montanus, Gaudentius, and Adeodatus, bishops of the party of Donatus, had entered, Marcellinus, most illustrious man, tribune and notary, said:

**3.** “It is entirely certain that I often made this offer at the preceding hearing; and now I request that you deign to sit.”

When the Catholic bishops had sat down, Petilianus, bishop, said: “We do not dare to do what was not done at the previous hearing.” In another hand: “I, Petilianus, bishop, have verified it.”

Marcellinus, most illustrious man, tribune and notary, said: “Although I recall that I made this offer also at the preceding hearing, I think it was not then done for the reason that, since many bishops had gathered, [Col. 1354A] there could be no room for sitting. Therefore, since I now see that a defined number of persons have assembled, I request that you now at least deign to sit.”

**4.** Petilianus, bishop, said: “We do not sit while our fathers are absent, especially since sitting together is forbidden by divine law, lest we should wish to sit with adversaries such as these.” In another hand: “I, Petilianus, bishop, have verified it.”

**5.** Marcellinus, most illustrious man, tribune and notary, said: “If your holiness has neglected to hear my request that it deign to sit, I cannot be prevented from conducting the hearing while standing.”

When the Catholic bishops had risen, and the judge’s seat had been removed by order of the same judge, our lord Marcellinus, most illustrious and distinguished man, tribune and notary, also stood.

[Col. 1354B]

**6.** Petilianus, bishop, said: “Let it be written that this is your wish, not ours.” In another hand: “I, Petilianus, bishop, have verified it.”

**7.** Marcellinus, most illustrious man, tribune and notary, said: “Since you are standing, it is fitting that I should have such a wish, one which pertains to reverence for such great bishops.”

Petilianus, bishop, said: “You will have acted honourably.” In another hand: “I, Petilianus, bishop, have verified it.”

**8.** Martialis, shorthand writer, said: “We have in hand the written submission which the bishops presented yesterday to your high office. If your high office commands, we shall read it.”

**9.** Marcellinus, most illustrious man, tribune and notary, [Col. 1354C] said: “Let it be read, lest anything appear concealed from the other party.”

**10.** Petilianus, bishop, said: “We affirm that we are bishops of the truth of Christ our Lord; and this has often been said in public acts. We also rightly and deservedly venerate Donatus of holy memory, a man of martyrial glory, our predecessor, as an ornament of the Church in this city.” In another hand: “I, Petilianus, bishop, have verified it.”

**11.** Possidius, bishop of the Catholic Church, said: “Bishops of truth must prove it, not boast of it.” In another hand: “I have verified it.”

**12.** Marcellinus, most illustrious man, tribune and notary, said: “The proceedings shall retain the submissions of both parties.” And he added: “Let that which was ordered be read.”

Martialis, shorthand writer, read:

“After the consulship of Varanius, on the fourth day before the Nones of June, before Flavius Marcellinus, most illustrious and distinguished man, tribune and notary, Primianus, Petilianus, Emeritus, Protasius, Montanus, Gaudentius, and Adeodatus, bishops and defenders of the Church of truth, state the following through a written submission:

“Yesterday, on the Kalends of June, your distinguished office deigned to hear us and our adversaries. Since, after almost the whole day had elapsed, you afforded the parties patience and deigned to hear certain matters which were the beginnings of the business, it is necessary, for the case, that the authorization which our adversaries submitted be brought to our knowledge. Since the sequence of the acts cannot be unfolded because of its length, lest we appear to come unprepared to the judgment, command that the authorization which our adversaries gave to be read be given to us today, the fourth day before the Nones of June, in copies, so that, instructed concerning the business laid upon us, we may be able to attend.”

In another hand: “I, Primianus, bishop, subscribed to this written submission on the fourth day before the Nones of June at Carthage.”

Flavius Marcellinus, most illustrious man, tribune and notary, said: “Since it is clear that matters requested for purposes of preparation ought to be granted, so that no impediments of delay may suspend the forthcoming hearing, the office shall hasten to deliver to you the authorization submitted by the Catholic bishops, copied under the supervision of the guards jointly appointed.” And when he had read it:

**13.** Marcellinus, most illustrious man, tribune and notary, [Col. 1355B] said: “Let the reading be entered in the acts.” And he added: “Since among the many conditions determined at the previous hearing, it is established that this one was deferred: that, just as I should subscribe to my interlocutory rulings, so each person should subscribe to his own submissions, 291 you must state what seems good to your holiness on this matter.”

**14.** Augustine, bishop of the Catholic Church, said: “We expressed our agreement to this in our written submission.” In another hand: “I have verified it.”

**15.** Marcellinus, most illustrious man, tribune and notary, said: “Let it be stated also what the will of the other party is.”

**16.** Petilianus, bishop, said: “We are greatly troubled that this is required of us, and that we are commanded to do something which custom has never been accustomed to include.” [Col. 1355C] In another hand: “I, Petilianus, bishop, have verified it.”

**17.** Fortunatianus, bishop of the Catholic Church, said: “Let it be attested that the opposing party has refused what was published by the edict of your high office.” In another hand: “I have verified it.”

**18.** Petilianus, bishop, said: “Let it be attested that you have still not restored most of the churches, nor rendered satisfaction for its earlier edict.” In another hand: “As above.”

**19.** Marcellinus, most illustrious man, tribune and notary, said: “Therefore, for the complete reliability of the proceedings, does your holiness rest content with the guards chosen by each party, who appear to have been assigned to the notaries and shorthand writers?”

**20.** Petilianus, bishop, said: “Let the proceedings first be given to us; then we shall reply.” In another hand: “I, Petilianus, bishop, have verified it.”

**21.** Alypius, bishop of the Catholic Church, said: “Then there is doubt either about the reliability of the office or about the reliability of the guards.” In another hand: “I have verified it.”

**22.** Marcellinus, most illustrious man, tribune and notary, said: “The reliability of the preceding proceedings clearly shows that your holiness also agreed to this.”

**23.** Petilianus, bishop, said: “Let us read and review them.” In another hand: “As above.”

**24.** Marcellinus, most illustrious man, tribune and notary, said: “Let the office read out both the guards chosen by each party and the point to which the hearing was deferred.”

[Col. 1356A]

**25.** Emeritus, bishop, said: “If you command, let the proceedings first be given to us; let us read them over, review our words and our adversaries’ submission. This has always been permitted by the laws. Such is the humane order of affairs.” In another hand: “I, Emeritus, bishop, have verified it.”

**26.** Fortunatus, bishop of the Catholic Church, said: “Although no one could have missed a recent proceeding, we nevertheless wish to be instructed by this concerning the judgment of your high office, so that it may be understood that, by some postponement, they now do not wish to come to the business of the case.” In another hand: “I have verified it.”

**27.** Marcellinus, most illustrious man, tribune and notary, said: “Let what I ordered be read, that I may know to what point the hearing was deferred.”

[Col. 1356B]

**28.** Emeritus, bishop, said: “If you command, it is appropriate that I speak to this.”

Marcellinus, most illustrious man, tribune and notary, said: “Proceed.”

Emeritus, bishop, said: “Human minds are indeed by their native quickness so ready that they easily grasp by sight or hearing everything brought to their notice. But let this perhaps be permitted to learned or educated men, according to the nature of the matter itself; I, however, profess myself less suited to this task. For who, noble sir, can retain or comprehend in his understanding a fleeting sound and an easy utterance as it passes almost at its very peak, when, for every examination and dispute, both words and meanings and the inner substance of the matter must be considered? Therefore, when a document is read and fleeting sounds are, as it were, scattered on the air, our minds cannot grasp and retain them. To whom, or where, has this been granted? If they enjoy this good fortune of intellect, let them not boast in the arrogance of their memory.

“But for me, nothing is appropriate except to repeat matters often and to be instructed by prolonged reading, so that I may [find] assurance of the truth; so that I may reread what I have said and attend to what my adversary has objected. You understand that this is the nature of proceedings: written records are accordingly arranged by letters for the sake of memory, lest memory alone, which cannot contain everything, deceived by forgetfulness, fail to know what it has done. For knowledge of writings and public records were not otherwise provided by provident wisdom than so that, from a reading which perhaps through silence, through a long interval, or through the continuance of the proceedings themselves may be less fully grasped and understood, and from reading and the very constant consideration of the matter, what has been debated before judgment may be recognized.

“You see therefore, noble sir, that our request is just, and that the case should not be examined in passing, but should be heard after the proceedings have been produced and put into our knowledge, and after all matters have been considered.” In another hand: “As above.”

29. Possidius, bishop of the Catholic Church, said: “It is written: ‘In much speaking you will not escape sin.’ Since we have this before our eyes, by God’s inspiration, we do not wish to seem wordy. Therefore, if it please you, let us come to the case, which may promptly be heard and decided, and dispense with delaying pleadings.” And when he had spoken: (And in another hand: “I have reviewed it.”) Marcellinus, most distinguished tribune and notary, said: “Let what I ordered be read.”

[Col. 1357A] 30. Emeritus, bishop, said: “As he has cited Scripture, it is written for us: ‘Hidden wisdom, an unseen treasure: what profit is there in either?’” And in another hand: “I, Emeritus, bishop, have reviewed it.”

31. Possidius, bishop of the Catholic Church, said: “Wisdom has never consisted in much speaking.” And in another hand: “I have reviewed it.”

32. Martialis, recorder, read from the codex. “Your Nobility said: ‘Since it is clear that almost the entire day has elapsed, let it be stated whether it pleases you, by common consent, that the business be postponed.’ Both parties said: ‘It pleases us, since this day now appears to have elapsed.’ Your Nobility said: ‘Let each party designate the day to which this adjournment is to be deferred.’ Alypius, bishop of the Catholic Church, said: [Col. 1357B] ‘As your Nobility prescribed by edict, omitting tomorrow for the drafting of the sheets, let us meet on the day after tomorrow, if you command.’ Adeodatus, bishop, said: ‘We too agree that the business be conducted on the day after tomorrow.’ Your Nobility said: ‘As has pleased the parties, the business shall be resumed on the day after tomorrow.’” And when he had read this, Marcellinus, most distinguished tribune and notary, said: “Your Holinesses see that you cannot depart from your own agreement. Therefore let the case be argued.”

33. Emeritus, bishop, said: “We are not so forgetful as to depart from our own position. Nor do I here blame negligence in the office or carelessness by the recorders, where I understand that, because of the length of the proceedings, it could by no means have been completed within the day. But if it has been done, and the whole matter has been completed, why are the acts which were done not brought to our knowledge? For when the matters which your Nobility ordered to be read have been examined by the office, it is necessary that, after receiving everything, I should consider and investigate on what grounds and in what ways I ought to reply. For I have learned that the confusion introduced into the case by their mandate is so great that I must both be instructed concerning what has gone before and recognize to whom I must reply concerning the present matters.” And in another hand: “I, Emeritus, have reviewed it.”

34. Marcellinus, most distinguished tribune and notary, said: “Although the declaration of your Holiness alone is sufficient, nevertheless it is beyond doubt that yesterday you both requested and received whatever you believed could suffice for your fullest instruction. Therefore [Col. 1357D] let us now come to the merits of the case.”

35. Petilianus, bishop, said: “Your Excellency observed the recorder read from the codices what was either promised or declared the day before yesterday. From this I recognize all the more that the acts have not yet been set out. But if they have been set out and are ready, let that same recorder answer. Produce the proceedings. Have them subscribed; we shall consider them and reply afterwards.” And in another hand: “I, Petilianus, bishop, have reviewed it.”

36. Marcellinus, most distinguished tribune and notary, said: “I recognize an effort at delay, and an indication of altered intention. For your Holiness could, in the previous hearing, have requested that the business be deferred until today because of the bulk of the proceedings. Added to this is the fact that yesterday you requested, through a notarial application, that those things which you believed sufficient for your fullest instruction [Col. 1358A] be published for you.”

37. Petilianus, bishop, said: “Let the recorders say whether they could set out in one day what appears to have been completed in one day.” And in another hand: “As above.”

38. Marcellinus, most distinguished tribune and notary, said: “Let the recorders state for the record whether all the proceedings could yesterday have been written out on sheets.” Martialis, recorder, said: “We still have part of them in the codices. Indeed, even those bishops who were assigned to us as custodians are not unaware of this.”

39. Petilianus, bishop, said: “Your Excellency has learned from the office’s reply that the proceedings have not yet been arranged into pages, and that there is nothing which either party may read and review, or even briefly commit to memory or recall. Therefore, since an honorable request is being made, let your Excellency deign to grant what we ask: that the proceedings be issued in the customary manner. Let us read them, so that we may be able to reply.” And in another hand: “I, Petilianus, bishop, have reviewed it.”

40. Alypius, bishop of the Catholic Church, said: “The length of the proceedings consists more in the number of bishops and the replies of both parties than in any substantial presentation of the case. Therefore the opposing party has no ground for complaint or for postponing the hearing today, especially since they themselves declared that the business was to be deferred until today.” And in another hand: “I have reviewed it.”

41. Marcellinus, most distinguished tribune and notary, [Col. 1358C] said: “So that it may again be manifest to the parties, let the declaration of the venerable men be read once more.” Petilianus, bishop, said: “From where will it be read?” And in another hand: “As above.” Montanus, bishop, said: “Let it be read to us from the sheet.” And in another hand: “As above.”

42. Marcellinus, most distinguished tribune and notary, said: “Do they therefore think that what is entered in the codices, when such great priests have been appointed as custodians, ought to be brought into some doubt?”

43. Petilianus, bishop, said: “We do not know shorthand signs; nor is it in the nature of such things, or of the letters themselves, so to speak, that anyone can read another person’s shorthand. We cannot read in the codices. Unless the proceedings have been issued on pages, I have nothing to consider and nothing to read.” And in another hand: “As above.” Marcellinus, [Col. 1358D] most distinguished tribune and notary, said: “As has been said, let the declaration of the venerable men be read again.”

44. Martialis, recorder, again read from the codex of shorthand: “Your Nobility said: ‘Since it is clear that almost the entire day has elapsed, let it be stated whether it pleases you, by common consent, that the business be postponed.’ Both parties said: ‘It pleases us, since this day now appears to have elapsed.’ Your Nobility said: ‘Let each party designate the day to which this adjournment is to be deferred.’ Alypius, bishop of the Catholic Church, said: ‘As your Nobility prescribed by edict, omitting tomorrow for the drafting of the sheets, let us meet on the day after tomorrow, if you command.’ Adeodatus, [Col. 1359A] bishop, said: ‘We too agree that the business be conducted on the day after tomorrow.’ Your Excellency said: ‘As has pleased the parties, the business shall be resumed on the day after tomorrow.’” And when he had read this, Petilianus, bishop, said: “From where did he read?”

45. Marcellinus, most distinguished tribune and notary, said: “I think it cannot have escaped your Holiness that the authority of the laws has determined what concerns this matter: one may not depart from one’s own agreements. Therefore, lest there be any suspicion of fraud on the part of the office’s recorders, this same agreement shall be reread from the tablets of the ecclesiastical notaries.”

46. Emeritus, bishop, said: “When we entered, your Nobility deigned to say that, if we assented to the edicts which had been published, we should attach [Col. 1359B] our subscriptions to our own pleadings. I do not see how I can comply with this. For I am held by the proposal of your Nobility, by which you promised me that I should place my subscription upon the proceedings and that all matters publicly conducted should be publicly displayed. But now I am compelled to proceed and am hurried into the business before I have become acquainted with the proceedings. What is this? I do not know what I should choose first; I do not recognize what purpose of your judicial decisions I am to follow. If a page must be subscribed, let the page be issued so that it may be subscribed. If this requirement is to be abandoned, your entire edict will be shaken; whatever you proposed for public knowledge will be destroyed. For you said that, through our subscription and your Excellency’s notation, all that was done ought to be brought before public knowledge. It is necessary, therefore, that what was done should first [Col. 1359C] be read, published, and recognized, so that, by the judgment of your Excellency, we may proceed to the remaining matters of the case.” And in another hand: “I, Emeritus, bishop, have reviewed it.”

47. Marcellinus, most distinguished tribune and notary, said: “As I have ordered, let the ecclesiastical notaries go through those matters read by the office’s recorders.”

48. Petilianus, bishop, said: “Keep to your proper measure, noble sir; keep to the justice so often promised. For when, the day before yesterday, our side had objected that the lawful day for the case already appeared to have passed, and that those who summoned us to judgment had forfeited their case, we were compelled to wish that, withdrawing from that position, we should appear to consent to the present time. Let no one be ungrateful to me in this respect, noble sir. For if I conceded an equal amount of time, preserving these conditions, provided that they did not repudiate their own stipulations, why is a short time not granted to me, so that the proceedings may be written out, subscribed by your Excellency, and so that I may see and read through what I ought to subscribe; so that I may recover and grasp my own meaning, and also the subtle cunning and refined ingenuity of our opponents; and so that, fully instructed, I may be able to answer their allegations? I consider this humane and just. Do not, noble sir, give this matter and this most just petition any cause for me to fall into anxiety. For you have promised yourself to be most just, and we must believe this, provided only [Col. 1360A] that just things are in no way denied us.” And in another hand: “I, Petilianus, bishop, have reviewed it.”

49. Marcellinus, most distinguished tribune and notary, said: “These requests ought more properly and justly to have been made at the preceding hearing, at which, by agreement of both parties, the examination was deferred to this day. Therefore let the ecclesiastical notaries read to what day the examination was deferred.” Petilianus, bishop, said: “Then we have been circumvented.” And in another hand: “As above.” Augustine, bishop of the Catholic Church, said: “It was not through us that what our brothers standing on the opposing side wish to impute to us has occurred.” And when he had spoken: (And in another hand: “I have reviewed it.”) Petilianus, bishop, said: “You are doing us an injustice.” And in another hand: “As above.”

50. Augustine, bishop of the Catholic Church, said: [Col. 1360B] “The edict of your Nobility provides that the fourth month is to conclude on the Kalends of June [1 June]. But we came earlier; and those who seem to make us odious on this account appointed the eighth day before the Kalends of June [25 May], although, certainly, if they had come before that day, they ought to have made their appointment before the day itself. Let the declaration of Primianus himself also be read: on what day he promised that he would appear. Then let this question be resolved, by which great hostility against us has already been stirred up among the people.” And in another hand: “I have reviewed it.”

51. Marcellinus, most distinguished tribune and notary, said: “It is clear that these matters were already determined in the preceding hearing, especially since the persons on both sides appear to have been established. Yet, if, when the case begins to be reconsidered, your Holiness thinks that these matters should be reread, [Col. 1360C] then they may more properly be reread; although it is superfluous that they should again be reconsidered after the confirmation of the persons. Therefore, as I have directed, let what was ordered be read by the ecclesiastical notaries.”

52. Emeritus, bishop, said: “Let it be written that we consented to that day on condition that they retained their own intention.” And in another hand: “As above.”

53. Marcellinus, most distinguished tribune and notary, said: “Let the tablets received from the ecclesiastical notaries be read.” And when, within a *sabanum*—that is, a linen wrapper—the parchment sheet, partly written for the party, and the codices containing the tablets, sealed alike, were presented before the judicial view, Marcellinus, most distinguished tribune and notary, said: “Let the custodians state whether they recognize the seals.” [Col. 1360D] Leo, bishop of the Catholic Church, said: “I recognize my seal.” Marinianus, bishop, said: “I recognize my seal.” Marcellinus, most distinguished tribune and notary, said: “Since it is clear that the impression of the seals has been recognized by both parties, let the notaries read what I ordered.”

54. Petilianus, bishop, said: “This is how wills, not proceedings, are opened.” And in another hand: “As above.”

55. Marcellinus, most distinguished tribune and notary, said: “What was done for the assurance of both parties, and by common consent, ought not to be criticized.” Petilianus, bishop, said: “I do not criticize the precaution; but I ask, according to the customary procedure, that the proceedings be lawfully produced so that they may be read and considered. [Col. 1361A] What necessity presses? Why is there haste?” And in another hand: “I, Petilianus, bishop, have reviewed it.”

56. Augustine, bishop of the Catholic Church, said: “Let this alone be clear: they wish to postpone the matter. We ask your Excellency to grant it. It is humane: they wish to consider, they wish to examine, they wish to come better prepared, lest, while they are unwilling to postpone, we make the proceedings longer and the very length of the proceedings impose greater delays upon us.” And in another hand: “I have reviewed it.”

57. Marcellinus, most distinguished tribune and notary, said: “It is clear that both parties agreed that the examination should be deferred until this day; but I see that this cannot avail today. Meanwhile, as I ordered, let the ecclesiastical notaries read to what day the examination was deferred.”

[Col. 1361B] 58. Petilianus, bishop, said: “Let it be written that this does not happen through any fault of ours, but solely because the notaries or recorders could not be ready.” And in another hand: “I, Petilianus, bishop, have reviewed it.”

59. Marcellinus, most distinguished tribune and notary, said: “Read.” Januarius, notary of the Church of Sitifis of the Donatist party, read from the codex. “Your Nobility said: ‘Let the office declare how much of the day appears now to have elapsed.’ Rufinianus, clerk of the most distinguished curator, said: ‘Eleven hours of the day have passed.’ Your Nobility said: ‘Since it is clear that almost the entire day has elapsed, let it be stated whether it pleases you, by common consent, that the business be postponed.’ Both parties said: ‘It pleases us, since this day appears to have elapsed.’ Your Nobility said: ‘Let each party designate the day to which this adjournment [Col. 1361C] is to be deferred.’ Alypius, bishop of the Catholic Church, said: ‘As your Nobility prescribed by edict, omitting tomorrow because of the drafting of the sheets, we shall meet on the day after tomorrow, if you command.’ Adeodatus, bishop, said: ‘We too agree that the business be conducted on the day after tomorrow.’ Your Excellency said: ‘As has pleased the parties, the business shall be resumed on the day after tomorrow.’” And when he had read this:

60. Marcellinus, most distinguished tribune and notary, said: “By the declaration of both parties it has been shown that the examination was deferred until this day, so that the business might be discussed today.”

61. Petilianus, bishop, said: “If the recorders have completed the proceedings, let the matter be conducted.” And in another hand: “As above.”

Marcellinus, most distinguished tribune and notary, [Col. 1361D] said: “Although it has been indicated by the clearest declarations to what day the hearing had been deferred, nevertheless, lest it appear that anything has been denied to the party seeking delay, the examination shall be deferred, provided that it declares to what day the hearing ought to be prolonged.”

Petilianus, bishop, said: “Let the recorders say when they will publish the proceedings.” And in another hand: “I, Petilianus, bishop, have reviewed it.” Marcellinus, most distinguished tribune and notary, said: “Let the recorders state without delay when they can complete writing out and publishing the proceedings on sheets.” Hilarus, recorder, said: “Since both parties have agreed, once they have subscribed their pleadings on the sheet, we shall then be able to state the day for publishing the proceedings.”

[Col. 1362A] Marcellinus, most distinguished tribune and notary, said: “Can the sheets today either be completed by the office or subscribed by both parties?” Hilarus, recorder, said: “Today we shall complete the sheets.”

Marcellinus, most distinguished tribune and notary, said: “Since the office has stated that it can complete the sheets today, let your Holiness declare whether it is prepared to subscribe today or tomorrow.”

62. Adeodatus, bishop, said: “When the sheet is presented to us, we shall subscribe.” And in another hand: “I, Adeodatus, bishop, have reviewed it.”

63. Marcellinus, most distinguished tribune and notary, said: “Let the office now declare, after the sheets have been subscribed, how many days’ delay can suffice, without any excuse, even for publication of the proceedings.”

[Col. 1362B] 64. Hilarus, recorder, said: “If they subscribe tomorrow or today, then, keeping watch day and night, we can publish the proceedings after the third day, provided that their notaries dictate to us from the subscribed sheet.” Marcellinus, most distinguished tribune and notary, said: “Let the office designate which day that is.” Rufinianus, clerk of the most distinguished curator, said: “Today is the third day before the Nones of June [3 June].” Marcellinus, most distinguished tribune and notary, said: “I ask on what day publication of the proceedings has been promised.” Hilarus, recorder, said: “We can publish the proceedings on the seventh day before the Ides of June [7 June].”

65. Marcellinus, most distinguished tribune and notary, said: “Although great uncertainty now arises for me from your declarations, nevertheless let each party state anew whether, with all evasions removed, the principal business is to be discussed on the sixth day before the Ides [Col. 1362C] of June [8 June].”

66. Augustine, bishop of the Catholic Church, said: “We are willing even today, and, if it could be done, we would wish it. Yet, because it was humane to grant our brothers what they seem to have requested not unjustly from us, we promise that, on the sixth day before the Ides of June [8 June], with the help of the Lord our God, we shall be present to conduct the principal business of the Church.” And in another hand: “I have reviewed it.” Marcellinus, most distinguished tribune and notary, said: “Let the other party also deign to state what its intention is.”

67. Emeritus, bishop, said: “There is no uncertainty regarding our declarations. But as regards the instruction which we demanded should be provided in the hearing, your Nobility observes that we requested what was just and lawful. We shall observe the appointed day, namely the sixth day before the Ides of June [8 June], if God commands; provided, however, that when we have received the proceedings, the most equitable judge grants us some time in which they may be considered.” And in another hand: “I, Emeritus, bishop, have reviewed it.” Marcellinus, most distinguished tribune and notary, said: “The proceedings will be handed to you in the morning hours of the seventh day before the Ides of June [7 June]. State whether you will deign to be present on the following day, that is, the sixth day before the Ides of June [8 June], in order that the principal business may be conducted.” Emeritus, bishop, said: “We shall be present for the hearing, if what your Nobility has determined takes effect.” And in another hand: “I, Emeritus, bishop, have reviewed it.”

68. Marcellinus, most distinguished tribune and notary, [Col. 1363A] said: “Mindful of the risk and of their own declaration, the recorders will hasten to publish the proceedings on the appointed day, in the morning hours, namely the seventh day before the Ides of June [7 June], provided that the notaries of neither party are absent in the dictation. Let each party know that it must make arrangements with the office for receipt of the proceedings at the hour likewise designated. It is, moreover, fitting for priests that, all evasions removed, no impediments of delay be contrived.”

69. Alypius, bishop of the Catholic Church, said: “In accordance with your Nobility’s command, once we have received the proceedings, we shall duly make arrangements concerning the subscription and the time.” And in another hand: “I have reviewed it.”

70. Emeritus, bishop, said: “When the proceedings have been presented to us, we shall comply with what has been adjudged.” And in another hand: “I, Emeritus, bishop, have reviewed it.”

[Col. 1363B] 71. Marcellinus, most distinguished tribune and notary, said: “The office will also hasten to publish for you, on that same day, the proceedings of this day, so that there may again be no ground for complaint.”

72. Alypius, bishop of the Catholic Church, said: “Many false claims were bandied about the day before yesterday. Lest the people be disturbed by such deception, we ask that it be made known by the edict of your Nobility that they themselves requested the postponement.” And in another hand: “I have reviewed it.”

73. Marcellinus, most distinguished tribune and notary, said: “It is not fitting that what the people say should trouble your Holiness. Nevertheless, as has been determined by my edict, the proceedings shall be posted.” And below:

“We, Hilarus and Martialis, recorders, have published [these proceedings] and have likewise corrected them as above.”

[Col. 1363C] Here end the Proceedings of the Second Hearing, in which the Donatists requested a postponement.

THE PROCEEDINGS OF THE THIRD HEARING BEGIN.

1. After the consulship of the most distinguished Varane, on the sixth day before the Ides of June [8 June], at Carthage, in the Secretariat of the Baths of Gargilius, in the presence of Sebastianus, Maximianus, and Petrus, most devoted men, protectors of the household troops; also in the presence of Vincentius and Taurillus, most devoted men, imperial agents (*agentes in rebus*); Ursus, Petronius, and Libosus, officers of two hundred of the illustrious authorities; Bonifacius and Evasius, attendants of the illustrious and eminent authorities; Philetus and Octavianus, attendants of the illustrious staff of the seat; Restitutus and Exitiosus, assistants to the chief clerk; Possidius, Quodvultdeus, and Colonicus, assistants to the record-keepers [Col. 1363D] of the office of our lord, the most distinguished and eminent proconsul; Navigius, assistant of the fiscal staff; Peregrinus, assistant to the sub-assistants of the office of our lord, the most distinguished and eminent vicar; Nampius, clerk of the office of the most distinguished legate of noble Carthage; Rufinianus, clerk of the most distinguished curator of exalted Carthage; with Hilarus and Praetextatus, recorders of our lord, the most distinguished and eminent proconsul, taking down the proceedings; Fabius, recorder of our lord, the most distinguished and eminent vicar; Romulus, recorder of the most distinguished legate of noble Carthage; and also Januarius and Vitalis, notaries of the Catholic Church, Victor and Cresconius, notaries of the Church of the Donatists, taking down the proceedings. Ursus, officer of two hundred of the illustrious authorities, said: “At the preceding hearing the bishops of the Donatist party requested, for the present day, a delay in the case for the publication of the proceedings, so that, having thereby [Col. 1364A] been instructed, they might answer in the hearing before your Excellency. Now both parties are at the doors; if you command, they shall be admitted.”

2. Flavius Marcellinus, most distinguished tribune and notary, said: “Let them come.” And the Catholic bishops Aurelius, Alypius, Augustine, Vincentius, Fortunatus, Fortunatianus, and Possidius entered, together with their fellow bishops Novatus, Florentius, Maurentius, Bonifacius, Priscus, Serenianus, and Scillatius, and likewise Deuterius, Leo, Asterius, and Restitutus, their fellow bishops and custodians of the proceedings. Likewise, on the other side, the Donatist bishops Primianus, Petilianus, Emeritus, Montanus, Gaudentius, and Adeodatus entered, together with their fellow bishops Peregrinus, Aptus, Clarentius, and Habetdeus.

3. Marcellinus, most distinguished tribune and notary, [Col. 1364B] said: “It is certain that the business was deferred for this reason: that, once the proceedings had been published by today, the principal action might be argued. Let the office state whether this has been done.” Martialis, recorder of our lord, the most distinguished and eminent proconsul, said: “It is clear that, in accordance with your Nobility’s command, the proceedings were published before the day to which our insignificance had declared [they would be published]. If your Nobility commands, we shall demonstrate this fully by the acknowledgments of both parties.”

4. Marcellinus, most distinguished tribune and notary, said: “Let them be read.” Martialis, recorder, read: “After the consulship of the most distinguished Varane, on the eighth day before the Ides of June [6 June], I, Fortunatianus, Catholic bishop of the city of Sicca, have written that I received together the proceedings of the two hearings, the first held on the Kalends [1 June] [Col. 1364C] and the other held on the third day before the Nones [3 June]; and that I received them from Martialis, recorder of the proconsular seat, who has been assigned to Flavius Marcellinus, most distinguished tribune and notary, on the eighth day before the Ides of June [6 June], at the fifth hour of the day, in the restored Catholic Church. And although the recorders had promised to publish the proceedings on the seventh day before the Ides of June [7 June], their diligence nevertheless hastened more effectively, so that the acts of the two hearings were delivered to us together before the promised day. Having received them, we promise, instructed at the place and time written above, to come to conduct the business on the day stated in the acts.” When he had read this, he said: “I shall read another, if your Nobility commands.”

5. Marcellinus, most distinguished tribune and notary, said: “Read.” Martialis, recorder, read: “After the consulship [Col. 1364D] of the most distinguished Varane, on the eighth day before the Ides of June [6 June], I, Montanus, bishop of the city of Zama Regia, have written to you, Hilarus and Praetextatus, recorders, that I received from you the proceedings of the two hearings, in which we contended with our betrayers and persecutors; the first held on the Kalends of June [1 June], and the other on the third day before the Nones of the same month [3 June]. You, recorders of the aforesaid proconsular seat, delivered them to us before our fathers and fellow bishops on the eighth day before the Ides of June [6 June], at the third hour of the day, in the Church of Theoprepia. Having received them at the place and time written above, we declare that we shall come, in full order, to conduct the business on the day expressed in the acts.”

[Col. 1365A] 6. Marcellinus, most distinguished tribune and notary, said: “The acknowledgments which have been read shall be attached to the present proceedings.” And he added: “Since it is clear that the proceedings were published before the appointed day, it remains for the principal business to be put forward.”

7. Augustine, bishop of the Catholic Church, said: “The principal business is that which we have long desired to be concluded. Therefore, if it is granted even late, let them prove the charges so often brought against the holy Catholic Church, spread throughout the whole world, which they desire to oppose from the adverse side and have never proved.” And when he had spoken: (And in another hand: “I have reviewed it.”)

8. Adeodatus, bishop, said: “Let them put it forward. Let us know what they are doing.” And in another hand: “I, Adeodatus, bishop, have reviewed it, appeal reserved.”

[Col. 1365B] 9. Vincentius, bishop of the Catholic Church, said: “You have not learned the proposition from their mandate.” And in another hand: “I have reviewed it.”

10. Possidius, bishop of the Catholic Church, said: “Let no one introduce snares of delay if we have any confidence in the defense of our case.” And when he had spoken: (And in another hand: “I have reviewed it.”)

11. Marcellinus, most distinguished tribune and notary, said: “If any allegation is made, let it be put forward.”

12. Alypius, bishop of the Catholic Church, said: “Let their mandate be read, and from it your Nobility will recognize their allegation.” And in another hand: “I have reviewed it.”

13. Marcellinus, most distinguished tribune and notary, said: “All delays having been removed, since it is clear that everything concerning the beginnings of the case was settled in the preceding [Col. 1365C] hearing, let the case be argued.”

14. Fortunatus, bishop of the Catholic Church, said: “The opposing party is shown to have alleged two things in its mandate: betrayal and persecution. If, therefore, they wish us to conduct the case of the Church, let it now and at once be concluded by your judgment. For it is wrong that the people should be led into error by suspense. If the Church which has been promised is to be recognized as spread throughout the whole world, let this be shown by the testimonies of Scripture. But if the opposing party, by its accustomed tricks and evasions, intends to prevent us from coming to the truth, let this be stated, so that it may become known to all.” And in another hand: “I have reviewed it.”

15. Marcellinus, most distinguished tribune and notary, said: “What answer is made to this?”

Emeritus, bishop, said: “I do not remember patience ever having been condemned in a hearing. On the contrary, it is always praiseworthy for the tongue, keeping its reserve, to answer accusations clearly, if it can. Therefore, since every action must have its beginning, and the beginnings of the entire business customarily derive from themselves, why do we entangle the proceedings of the past days and rub them raw again, as though they had not been completed, when the proposition of the present day ought to take and receive its own proper form? Therefore, if their proposition and our reply are submitted to judgment, the status of the persons must first be examined: who brought [Col. 1366A] the matter to judgment, who caused the summons, who approached the secular rulers, who sent envoys, who petitioned, who obtained a law, who requested the hearing. Thus, once we have been instructed concerning their allegations, we may be able to reply.” And in another hand: “I, Emeritus, bishop, have reviewed it, appeal reserved.”

16. Fortunatianus, bishop of the Catholic Church, said: “It is distrust in their case to wish to examine persons whom they seemed to have confirmed in the previous dispute. Therefore let us conduct the case of the Church, which, as promised, is spread throughout the whole world.” And in another hand: “I have reviewed it.”

17. Marcellinus, most distinguished tribune and notary, said: “Your Holiness, I think, has not carefully attended to the proposition. For different matters are known to have been asked.”
