18. Alypius, bishop of the Catholic Church, said: “Then, regarding what they asked, order the mandates of both parties to be read, and they will be instructed concerning what they desired.” And in another hand: “I have reviewed it.”

19. Marcellinus, most distinguished tribune and notary, said: “It has been asked through whom this conference was requested, and who demanded that the bishops standing on the other side be summoned to judgment. Therefore your Holiness must answer these questions.”

20. Augustine, bishop of the Catholic Church, said: “It belongs to your Excellence to consider whether you judge this relevant to the matter. The tenor of the imperial rescript shows that the holding of a conference was granted to the Catholic bishops or to delegates of the Catholic bishops. Both parties have come; here we are. God commanded us to be disputants and conferees rather than litigants; and this is what the most merciful emperor, fearing God and serving God, willed—nothing else. Your Excellency judged on the first day of our dispute that lawful persons were present and that the mandates had been confirmed. Let matters unnecessary to the case not be introduced. The Church which we maintain on the testimonies of the divine Scriptures is known to all: established, as it is written, upon the highest mountain, and all nations come to it. If anything can be said against this Church, let it now be said, and let no delays be introduced. If nothing can be said, let whoever cannot affirm, demonstrate, and prove his accusation to human beings yield to the truth. How long is this great expectation of the people to remain suspended? All are thinking about their souls, while we introduce dilatory objections so that we may never arrive at the end of knowing the truth.” And in another hand: “I have reviewed it.”

[Col. 1366D] 21. Marcellinus, most distinguished tribune and notary, said: “So that it may be seen in what manner the hearing has been delegated, let the form of the imperial command be read.”

22. Petilianus, bishop, said: “It is marked in these proceedings that they have called themselves Catholics without prejudice to our rights. Preserve this point for the debate.” And in another hand: “I, Petilianus, bishop, have reviewed it, appeal reserved.” Alypius, bishop of the Catholic Church, said: “Let what you ordered be read.” And in another hand: “I have reviewed it.” Petilianus, bishop, said: “For the true Catholic Church is with us: it suffers persecution; it does not inflict it.” And in another hand: “I, Petilianus, bishop, have reviewed it, with the effect of appeal reserved.” Possidius, bishop of the Catholic Church, said: “This must [Col. 1367A] be proved, not merely asserted.” And in another hand: “I have reviewed it.”

23. Marcellinus, most distinguished tribune and notary, said: “The dispute of both parties will establish this.” And he added: “Meanwhile, let the imperial enactment be read.”

24. Martialis, recorder, read: “The emperors Caesars Flavius Honorius and Theodosius, pious, fortunate, victorious, triumphant, ever Augusti, to Flavius Marcellinus, greetings.” And as he read:

25. Petilianus, bishop, said: “The Emperor wished me to be intimidated, not killed; not to suffer persecution, not to be dragged away, not to be despoiled.” And in another hand: “I, Petilianus, bishop, have reviewed it, with our appeal reserved.”

[Col. 1367B] 26. Alypius, bishop of the Catholic Church, said: “Indeed, more than that: you were not even intimidated.” And in another hand: “I have reviewed it.”

27. Petilianus, bishop, said: “You have praised the constancy of good faith and of the discipline of the true Catholic Church.” And in another hand: “I, Petilianus, bishop, have reviewed it, appeal reserved.”

28. Alypius, bishop of the Catholic Church, said: “As was said, you were not intimidated, nor were you afraid.” And in another hand: “I have reviewed it.”

29. Martialis, recorder, said. “Among the greatest concerns of our Empire, reverence for the Catholic law always holds either the first place or the only place. For we undertake neither the labours of war nor the counsels of peace for any other purpose than that the devoted people of our world may preserve the true worship of God; and that the Donatists—whom it had long since been fitting to bring into compliance by either fear or admonition—may likewise be compelled: those who disfigure Africa, that is, the greatest part of our realm, though it faithfully serves in secular duties, by vain error and superfluous dissension. Yet we do not tire of setting forth more often the same things which the devout authority of all former princes has decreed concerning God, lest posterity be able justly to charge us if, in our times, anything should perhaps arise to the injury of the Catholic law.

“Nor indeed is that saying of the heavenly oracle unknown to our conscience, which the baleful interpretation of the Donatists professes can serve their error. Although it invited corrupted minds more gently to correction, we nevertheless previously ordered it abolished, lest any opportunity be afforded to superstitions. Now also, by similar authority, we judge that fraudulent insinuation must be excluded; and we rightly declare that we gladly remove things which had been enacted, lest anyone suppose that, with us as authors, he may sin against divine worship.

“And although the judgment of all is one and manifest—that the full truth of the Catholic law is established by the right worship of humankind and by heavenly pronouncement—yet, out of zeal for peace and favour, we have gladly received the embassy of venerable men, the bishops. It requests that the Donatist bishops be assembled for a meeting in a most celebrated city, so that, bishops also having been chosen by each party, and discussions having been held, manifest reason may refute superstition. We order this matter to be completed within four months, so that it may more swiftly recognize, even by our clemency, the converted minds of the peoples, as it desires.

“But if the bishops of the Donatists should deliberately decline to meet within the allotted time, we will the summons by triple edict to be observed, such that the periods for summoning the contumacious are concluded at intervals of twenty days. When these have elapsed and passed, if those summoned should disdain to appear, let the people, together with the churches, yield—having learned from their teachers’ silence that those teachers are defeated—and at last rejoice that they themselves have been conquered, and know that obedience must be rendered, if not to our commands, at least to the true ordinances of the Catholic law.

“We desire that you preside as judge in the foremost place at this disputation—you fully remember whatever you may previously have received in your instructions—and we desire that you undertake every care, whether in assembling the bishops or in summoning them should they disdain to appear, so that with approved diligence you may carry out both what was previously commanded and what you now know to have been decreed. Above all, you shall observe this: that, fraudulent novelty having been removed, you preserve whole and inviolate those things concerning the Catholic law which ancient times formerly ordered, which the religious authority of our fathers established, or which our serenity has confirmed.

“Moreover, lest suitable resources for your proceedings be lacking, our Serenity has warned the illustrious proconsul and vicar that, if they wish to retain the standing of their own dignities and if their staffs wish to avoid the ultimate penalties, they must ensure that a sufficient number of necessary persons are assigned, both from their own offices and from the staffs of all judges. It shall then be your concern, if you learn that anything is being delayed by any contrivance, to report it by dispatches, so that suitable correction may punish the negligent. Further, you must report everything that either the disputation, once the bishops have been gathered together, shall establish and confirm, or that a sentence issued against the contumacious may establish if they should perhaps desist, so that we may more promptly learn what our injunction has accomplished toward confirming the Catholic faith.”

And in the imperial hand: “Farewell, Marcellinus, most dear to us. Given at Ravenna, on the day before the Ides of October.”

30. Petilianus, bishop, said. “They think that we must be called Donatists; whereas, if paternal names are to be reckoned, I too can call them—indeed, I openly and plainly designate them—Mensurists and Caecilianists, likewise our betrayers and persecutors.”

And in another hand: “I, Petilianus, bishop, have reviewed this without prejudice to our appeal.” [Col. 1368D]

31. Vincentius, bishop of the Catholic Church, said. “And do you reject even that which you embraced according to your wish in the judgment before the prefects?”

And in another hand: “I have reviewed it.”

32. Petilianus, bishop, said. “Nor do I now deny that Donatus, bishop of this city, was my leader and was of most blessed and holy memory, and that his merits flourished so greatly that even antiquity itself [attests] the glory of that age.”

And as he spoke: “And in another hand: I, Petilianus, bishop, have reviewed this, with the effect of the appeal reserved.”

33. Alypius, bishop of the Catholic Church, said. “Let them condemn the name of Donatus, and thereafter we shall not call them Donatists.”

And in another hand: “I have reviewed it.”

34. Petilianus, bishop, said. “Condemn the name of Mensurius and Caecilianus, and you shall not be called either a Mensurist or a Caecilianist.”

And in another hand: “I, Petilianus, bishop, have reviewed this without prejudice to our appeal.” [Col. 1369A]

35. Alypius, bishop of the Catholic Church, said. “For did I mention Mensurius?”

And in another hand: “I have reviewed it.”

36. Marcellinus, most illustrious man, tribune and notary, said. “All these matters shall be preserved for both parties.” And he added: “It has plainly appeared that, at the request of the bishops seeking a disputation, I was commissioned by the venerable emperor to conduct the hearing, so that the cause of the original error may be examined, now that it has been brought forward.”

37. Emeritus, bishop, said. “The rescript has been read. Let the petitions also be read, so that the case may be heard.”

And in another hand: “I, Emeritus, bishop, have reviewed it.” [Col. 1369B]

38. Marcellinus, most illustrious man, tribune and notary, said. “I suppose that it has not escaped your Holinesses’ knowledge that petitions are not customarily inserted in pragmatic rescripts. Nor is it established that they proceeded from the bishops who requested the conference, 297 as the text of that same enactment shows. Therefore, at last, let the business be set forth.”

39. Emeritus, bishop, said. “If your Excellency’s interlocutory ruling has established that petitions are not customarily inserted in a pragmatic rescript, let those whom they said were ambassadors show whether they went by the will of all, whether by a common mandate, so that, if the person cannot stand on the petitions, it may at least stand on the ambassadors.”

And in another hand: “I, Emeritus, bishop, have reviewed this without prejudice to my appeal.” [Col. 1369C]

40. Augustine, bishop of the Catholic Church, said. “Let your Nobility observe how much is being done in order that nothing may be done.”

And in another hand: “I have reviewed it.”

Montanus, bishop, said. “The case must be conducted in its complete order.”

And in another hand: “I, Montanus, bishop, have reviewed this, with the appeal reserved.”

41. Augustine, bishop of the Catholic Church, said. “They are present; both parties have assembled. This place is almost filled with bishops; the mandates have been read and confirmed. It is not denied by our party that the conference was requested, in order that at last, in that conference, they may either prove—or be shown unable to prove—the accusations which they are accustomed to bring, not against us, not against any one of us, but against the whole Christian world. This Christian world is both promised and fulfilled, not by human opinion, but by divine testimonies.

“What is this? Do they who wish to be called bishops of Christ still interpose some delaying evasion or other? The expectation is suspended—not, I say, of this city only, but of nearly the whole human race—which desires to hear something concerning the Church; and we are still debating forensic formulas and litigating most miserably. Let your Nobility now observe what is being done. At last, having cut away every petty delay, deign, with God’s help, to release us from this business.”

And in another hand: “I have reviewed it.” [Col. 1369D]

42. Marcellinus, most illustrious man, tribune and notary, said. “I do not doubt that, for every confirmation, the subscriptions of all, inserted and arranged in the mandate at the previous hearing, can suffice. Therefore, since the consent of all has been expressed, let superfluities be removed and the business at last be set forth.”

43. Emeritus, bishop, said. “Two things have been submitted to the court, from which one may in no way depart: one, that they have shown themselves to proceed in the judgment according to the imperial command; the other, according to the tenor of the mandate. Therefore, if the two are connected, this must be shown; but if they are separate and distinct, those who do not wish to submit both to proof in court must necessarily relinquish one of them. For the mandate must accord with the rescript, and the meaning of the mandates must be bound to the form of the imperial enactment.

“But if your Excellency understands that neither is the case—that we do not wish to act by delays, nor to suspend ourselves from the prosecution of the case, but, having first laid the established foundations, wish to decide the ecclesiastical business—why are delay laid to our charge, and why, as though we were quibblers fleeing from examination, do they complain that certain delays are being contrived by us? For, if they take notice, we rather say that it is incumbent—indeed necessary—upon those who make the proposal that, all delays being cut away, one come to the documents and the summit of the business; so that it may be shown from the opposing party who petitioned, how he petitioned, and what he petitioned for. Thus, when I have embraced the points in agreement both from the mandate and from the rescript, both those matters confirmed in the rescript and those advanced on their own petition may be approved by judicial proceedings.”

And in another hand: “I, Emeritus, bishop, have reviewed it.” [Col. 1370C]

44. Augustine, bishop of the Catholic Church, said. “It is your office, noble sir. If he has answered what we said, it is necessary for us to answer. But if your Excellency perceives that he has answered nothing to what we justly demand, but has added other superfluous delays to superfluous delays, judge as seems right.”

And in another hand: “I have reviewed it.”

45. Marcellinus, most illustrious man, tribune and notary, said. “It is established that the determinate course of this examination has been defined by imperial authority. For the sequence of the enactment just reread showed that, once bishops had been summoned and parties chosen, manifest reason should refute superstition, to use the words of the law itself. Therefore, may your Holinesses deign to show more clearly in which party superstition is found.” [Col. 1370D]

46. Petilianus, bishop, said. “Your Sublimity sees that they have great mistrust and great falsehood, if they are unwilling to disclose what we demand. For he who fears to publish his own petition first judges against his own conscience. Therefore we are not causing any delay; rather, they themselves cause delays, as your Sublimity sees.”

And as he spoke: “And in another hand: I, Petilianus, bishop, have reviewed this, with the ground of our appeal reserved.”

47. Vincentius, bishop of the Catholic Church, said. “Is what the judge has answered you not enough?”

And in another hand: “I have reviewed it.”

Petilianus, bishop, said. “Either let them read what we demand, or deny it.”

And in another hand: “I, Petilianus, bishop, have reviewed this, with our appeal reserved.” [Col. 1371A]

Fortunatianus, bishop of the Catholic Church, said. “What relevance has that which the opposing party has pursued, and not for certain delays?”

And as he spoke: “And in another hand: I have reviewed it.”

Petilianus, bishop of Donatus’s party, [said.] “Judge.”

And in another hand: “I, Petilianus, bishop, have reviewed this, with the effect of our appeal reserved.”

48. Marcellinus, most illustrious man, tribune and notary, said. “Your Holinesses must indicate more plainly what you demand.”

49. Emeritus, bishop, said. “In a lengthy document, the opposing party, at the preceding hearing, set forth something like the tenor of a mandate. If a true assertion supports this matter, they ought to publish and disclose in court that they follow precisely this; but they ought to relinquish the imperial rescript, for the promulgation of which they were unwilling to show either the tenor of the petitions or the mandate of the ambassadors. Therefore, because what we request in court is not irrelevant, we ask that they first either relinquish the rescript or surrender their mandate, so that we may be able to come to the case.”

And in another hand: “I, Emeritus, bishop, have reviewed this without prejudice to our appeal.” [Col. 1371B]

50. Augustine, bishop of the Catholic Church, said. “Let our mandate be read, and they will understand how it contains everything.”

And in another hand: “I have reviewed it.”

Petilianus, bishop of Donatus’s party, said. “Allow it; grant the judge the patience which he grants us.”

And in another hand: “I, Petilianus, bishop, have reviewed this without prejudice to our appeal.”

51. Marcellinus, most illustrious man, tribune and notary, said. “I perceive that nothing else was chiefly established by the imperial enactment except that, when the bishops had assembled and a disputation had been held, the cause of the original error should be discovered. He wished me to sit as judge at that disputation. Your Holinesses have received the pleading of the party appearing on the other side, in which it was plainly shown and promised that the Church dispersed throughout the whole world would be demonstrated by divine testimonies. Since you see from the series of the mandate and from the present declaration that it was stated that all things should be proved by examples and evidences from the law, I do not know what more you desire.

“For the most clement emperor was not shown 298 to have prescribed the form of the conference, but merely judged that a conference ought to take place. Therefore, since their declaration has made clear that, according to your desire, they profess to proceed by divine testimonies, I do not know what further you desire.” [Col. 1371D]

52. Petilianus, bishop, said. “It is most plainly understood that, through mistrust or perhaps at last through shame, they act thus in order not to publish their petition before all, because it is evident that they lied to the most clement emperor.”

And in another hand: “I, Petilianus, bishop, have reviewed this without prejudice to our appeal.”

53. Augustine, bishop of the Catholic Church, said. “The conference was requested by our ambassadors. The law itself, which was issued to your Nobility, contains this.”

And in another hand: “I have reviewed it.”

54. Petilianus, bishop, said. “We are not delaying proceedings.”

And in another hand: “[Petilianus, bishop,] have reviewed this, with our appeal reserved.” [Col. 1372A]

55. Augustine, bishop of the Catholic Church, said. “It was issued. We all acknowledge that we requested a conference because you were refusing it, so that at last, at least in this way, we might come to this place or this time for the sake of conference, disputation, and demonstration of the truth. It has happened. We have come, and you are unwilling that our coming should avail anything. We acknowledge that we requested a conference. The emperor expressed nothing other than that we had requested a conference, in his own words. Let the conference itself now take place.

“Let us see what is said against the Church dispersed throughout the whole world, which we demonstrate both to have been promised by divine testimonies and now to be so displayed that it strikes the eyes of the blind and breaks in upon the ears of the deaf. Our brothers are unwilling to come to the demonstration of this, so that that which cannot be hidden may be demonstrated. Let them state the accusations. Let us see by what accusations that which was promised to Abraham has perished: ‘In your seed all nations shall be blessed.’ Let us hear, learn, know, and follow what accusations could have erased this promise of God who swore it. But if there is nothing that can be said against it, either pronounce judgment or remove all delays, and let the business at last be concluded.”

And in another hand: “I have reviewed it.” [Col. 1372B]

56. Emeritus, bishop, said. “Truth is concealed by a great argument: that when only a little has been produced from the opposing party in response to our inquiry, the rest is kept silent. For he said that his ambassadors had gone, but he is unwilling to publish before the court either their names, their rank, or their mandate. Therefore he must either relinquish this claim, because he cannot prove it; or, if he is able to establish this by laws, the mandate of the ambassadors must be brought to the knowledge of the courts—who the ambassadors were, when they were sent, and what they conveyed.

“Your Excellency sees that we request nothing irrelevant, since it is their own case which prevents our coming to the inner matters of the business. For they have proposed, from the tenor of their mandate, that they must stand against us by certain allegations, I know not what. We too can overcome those very allegations by legal testimonies. Therefore it is prior that, once the beginning of the action has been set forth, he should be able to establish in court his own standing, whether as representative or as principal; only then should one descend to the merits of the case.”

And in another hand: “I, Emeritus, bishop, have reviewed this, with the appeal reserved.” [Col. 1372D]

57. Vincentius, bishop of the Catholic Church, said. “What else is it to abandon the case and seek persons, except to wish to escape? Why did you come?”

And in another hand: “I have reviewed it.”

Petilianus, bishop, said. “Every case begins from the persons.”

And in another hand: “I, Petilianus, bishop, have reviewed this, with the effect of our appeal reserved.”

Vincentius, bishop of the Catholic Church, said. “Did not your own forum prescribe to you that matters omitted cannot be taken up again?”

And in another hand: “I have reviewed it.”

58. Marcellinus, most illustrious man, tribune and notary, said. “The form of the heavenly enactment has shown that a conference was requested and that a conference was granted. Why the persons of the ambassadors should now be brought forward, I have not yet carefully understood.” [Col. 1373A]

59. Augustine, bishop of the Catholic Church, said. “If we denied that we had requested a conference, we would be convicted by the emperor’s testimony. We have the emperor as witness; we acknowledge that we requested it. We have come so that what both we requested and he granted may occur; and still I know not what doubts or delays are interposed.”

And in another hand: “I have reviewed it.”

60. Emeritus, bishop, said. “See: you have now acknowledged the party. Say when you requested it; say through whom you requested it.”

And in another hand: “I, Emeritus, bishop, have reviewed this, with our appeal reserved.”

61. Fortunatianus, bishop of the Catholic Church, said. “For demonstrating truth, inquiry into persons is unnecessary.”

And in another hand: “I have reviewed it.”

62. Montanus, bishop, said. “Since the opposing party appealed to the most clement emperor, it must produce both the mandate and the embassy, so that, when we have been able to examine these, we may know in the judgment of your Nobility what we can answer.”

And in another hand: “I, Montanus, bishop, have reviewed this, with the appeal reserved.”

Vincentius, bishop of the Catholic Church, said. “It is far enough removed from the case—and outside this case—to wish to take up again those matters which the tenor of this judgment did not at all seek in establishing the subject of its inquiry.”

And in another hand: “I have reviewed it.”

Montanus, bishop, said. “What I demand belongs to your action.”

And in another hand: “I, Montanus, bishop, have reviewed this, with the effect of the appeal reserved.”

Vincentius, bishop of the Catholic Church, said. “The judgment of the presiding judge is definitive. It ought to be shame enough that we have been delayed until this day, if we pass over that concerning which we ourselves are judging the case.”

And as he spoke: “And in another hand: I have reviewed it.”

Montanus, bishop, said. “What I demand belongs to your action. You established the foundation of the case; you appealed to the emperor. Therefore I must demand both the mandate and the embassy—the words which you used—so that, when all these matters have been examined by us in the judgment of your Nobility, I may then at last be able to answer what is suitable to our interest.”

And in another hand: “I, Montanus, bishop, have reviewed this, with the effect of the appeal reserved.”

Vincentius, bishop of the Catholic Church, said. “You cannot overcome your own declaration. Recognize from what you have departed. You cannot take up again what you omitted.”

And in another hand: “I have reviewed it.”

Augustine, bishop of the Catholic Church, said. “Why do you demand when I requested it, when you see when I came? Why do you ask whether I requested it, when the whole Catholic council, present in this city, gave the mandate, subscribed to the mandate, and, while you were present and urging it, acknowledged the subscriptions? Nothing here is being sought except delays, because nothing can be said against the universal Church commended by God’s testimonies.”

And in another hand: “I have reviewed it.” [Col. 1373D]

63. Montanus, bishop, said. “Let it be written that the opposing party is contriving delays, since it does not disclose what is demanded by our party. Therefore, if they wish that same delay to be removed, let them disclose what we demand: let them disclose the mandate and the embassy also; then afterwards we shall come to the merits of the case.”

And in another hand: “I, Montanus, bishop, have reviewed my pleadings, with the effect of the appeal reserved.” [Col. 1374A]

64. Marcellinus, most illustrious man, tribune and notary, said. “The most clement emperor did not wish this to be investigated. He ordered the cause of the disagreement and error to be investigated.”

65. Montanus, bishop, said. “But the most clement emperor himself published in his rescript that they had inserted an embassy. Therefore, since in his clemency he also wished to grant us this 299 permission to inquire into this in court, they must produce both the mandate and the embassy, so that we may know what perhaps they lied about in that same text; and only then, when all these things have been examined, may we know the standing of the persons—whether they can answer while retaining their honours in unimpaired order.”

And in another hand: “I, Montanus, bishop, have reviewed this, with the effect of the appeal reserved.”

Marcellinus, most illustrious man, tribune and notary, said. “The tenor of the universal council and of its subscriptions plainly shows that they consented to the embassy. Indeed, when the names of all those subscribing were read for complete confirmation, your Holiness said that this could not fully suffice you unless all also came, so that, being present, they might state by their own declarations whether they themselves had subscribed and given the mandate.”

Montanus, bishop, said. “I demand the persons of those who gave the mandate to the most clement emperor, not those who came today to this hearing. Therefore, illustrious sir, these men must disclose in the judgment of your Nobility the proceeding which they evade. Let them therefore now disclose the mandate and the embassy, so that, when these have been read, we may see who entrusted them with these things and be able to answer their objections.”

And in another hand: “I, Montanus, bishop, have reviewed this, with the effect of the appeal reserved.” [Col. 1374C]

66. Marcellinus, most illustrious man, tribune and notary, said. “If you know that those whom you say carried out the embassy are present, or have subscribed to the mandate now in the present proceedings, show this plainly. But if they are absent, they must come, so that the whole matter may be examined.”

67. Montanus, bishop, said. “Therefore, illustrious sir, the presence must be procured of those who flew across the seas to the most clement emperor. Their own persons, standing present, must show that something was entrusted to them by these men, so that I may understand from the mandate itself what they wished to contrive in their case, and then perhaps what they lied about against us in that embassy. For it is always the endeavour of adversaries to insinuate uncertain things about their opponents into the ears of the most sacred authorities.

“Therefore, how shall I prove that the episcopal status which they boast of is such that, with due reverence and in writing, they could make some representation to the emperor, unless I can read through and judge the embassy itself or the mandate entrusted to them?”

And in another hand: “I, Montanus, bishop, have reviewed this, with the effect of the appeal reserved.” [Col. 1374D]

68. Alypius, bishop of the Catholic Church, said. “Your Nobility considers with us that the same superfluous matters are being repeated. The standing of the advocates is sufficiently established by the authority of the present mandate. Now, superfluities having been removed, let us come to the business, whose foundation can admit no doubt, since our persons, to whom the universal council entrusted its mandate, so confirmed the disputation ordered by the emperor that even those cannot doubt in whose sight all those who gave the mandate came forward.”

And in another hand: “I have reviewed it.”

Possidius, bishop of the Catholic Church, said. “Who could deny, or can deny, that we requested a conference?”

And in another hand: “I have reviewed it.” [Col. 1375A]

69. Emeritus, bishop, said. “What did you request? Whom did you send? State the name: what did you command?”

And in another hand: “I, Emeritus, bishop, have reviewed this, with the effect of the appeal reserved.”

Possidius, bishop of the Catholic Church, said. “Speak about the case. You have heard the mandate. Let it be recited again and again, and answer, if you have anything to say. You linger over superfluities.”

And in another hand: “I have reviewed it.”

Petilianus, bishop, said. “I must ascertain whom you sent, what you commanded, and what you did. For you are not permitted secretly to make a representation which afterwards ought not to be made public.”

And in another hand: “I, Petilianus, bishop, have reviewed this without prejudice to our appeal.” [Col. 1375B]

70. Marcellinus, most illustrious man, tribune and notary, said. “I do not know on what ground the names of the ambassadors are demanded, since the imperial enactment has carefully shown, as I said above, only that a conference was requested and that a conference was granted. Therefore may your Holinesses now deign to come to the inner matters of the business, so that truth may shine forth.”

71. Montanus, bishop, said. “But the most clement emperor intended rather to instruct me what we should demand concerning our opponents, when indeed he publishes their embassy.”

And in another hand: “I, Montanus, bishop, have reviewed this, with the effect of the appeal reserved.” [Col. 1375C]

72. Fortunatianus, bishop of the Catholic Church, said. “Set forth the causes of your separation and dissension from the universal Church, which is spread throughout the whole world.”

And in another hand: “I have reviewed it.”

73. Montanus, bishop, said. “Let it be read at the relevant place, whether the most clement emperor did not publish their embassy. He wished me to dispute concerning this matter, concerning this case; he wished their embassy to be published in court. One must not depart from the ordinances of the most clement emperor; satisfaction must be rendered in this place to the most clement emperor, since he wished us to examine their embassy once it had been published in court.”

And in another hand: “I, Montanus, bishop, have reviewed this, with the effect of our appeal remaining.” [Col. 1375D]

74. Fortunatianus, bishop of the Catholic Church, said. “The most clement emperor did not decree this; rather, he deigned to establish for the parties that, bishops having been selected from both parties, the truth should at last be brought forward and shown concerning the long-standing error, for the salvation of peoples and souls.”

And in another hand: “I have reviewed it.”

Petilianus, bishop, said. “Read whether you requested this.”

And in another hand: “I, Petilianus, bishop, have reviewed this, with our appeal reserved.”

Fortunatianus, bishop of the Catholic Church, said. “But you linger over superfluities. We demonstrate the Catholic Church from the Law, the Prophets, the Gospels, the Psalms, from all divine testimonies. Against this you bring forward a mandate. Make it public. Let us bring forward the Gospel with you to demonstrate the Church.”

And in another hand: “I have reviewed it.” [Col. 1376A]

75. Petilianus, bishop, said. “Both our pure observance and your vices and crimes establish that the Catholic Church is in my possession. Every Church of God ought to be pure, holy, without spot or wrinkle. Therefore, in order that we may descend to the discussion of this matter and, at a suitable time, to the Lord’s testimonies, first—as is proper—do what I demand from you, if you are not distrustful; especially since the most just examiner of the case acts so that whatever is to be done may be made public to the people.

“It is therefore sufficiently clear that you lied to the most clement emperor, since you hesitate to produce what you said, what you did, what you commanded, what that ambassador undertook, what mandate he received, and what he accomplished. Let the people be aware of these things; let the whole province know that these records fully contain the disputed matters. Let them know most plainly that you distrust your own falsehood and contrive delays in the proceedings, so that, with your tricks and mists obstructing it, one may never arrive at the truth.”

And in another hand: “I, Petilianus, bishop, have reviewed this, with our appeal reserved.”

Vincentius, bishop of the Catholic Church, said. “How do you censure that which you do not know whether I requested?”

And in another hand: “I have reviewed it.”

Petilianus, bishop, said. “He has acknowledged that he requested it.”

And in another hand: “I, Petilianus, bishop, have reviewed this, with our appeal reserved.” [Col. 1376B]

76. Fortunatianus, bishop of the Catholic Church, said. “He has testified that the 300 Catholic Church is with himself. We wished that this should be established by testimonies while your Nobility presides. Let him publish what he promises, so that either our agreement may accede to its manifest truth, or he may allow the truth, clearer than light, to be shown; and, at last abandoning error, let him suitably yield to truth for the sake of salvation—he who thinks of conquering in error against salvation.”

And in another hand: “I have reviewed it.”

Petilianus, bishop, said. “That we may do these things, first do what we demand from you.”

And in another hand: “I, Petilianus, bishop, have reviewed this without prejudice to our appeal.”

Fortunatianus, bishop of the Catholic Church, said. “If the order of the proceedings requires it, we shall make it public.”

And in another hand: “I have reviewed it.” [Col. 1376C]

77. Marcellinus, most illustrious man, tribune and notary, said. “Since the imperial injunction has shown the form of the embassy, I do not know why the names of the ambassadors are demanded. Does your Holiness think that the invincible emperor said something contrary to reason? Since the persons appear to have been specified and confirmed for conducting the case, I have not yet been able carefully to understand why mention is now made of the embassy, or why the names of the ambassadors are demanded. Therefore, at last, superfluities having been removed, let the business be set forth.” [Col. 1376D]

78. Emeritus, bishop, said. “The mandate which was read in the recent proceeding appears to have been inserted in the records. But they have been unwilling to disclose what they instructed their ambassadors.”

And in another hand: “I, Emeritus, bishop, have reviewed this, with the effect of our appeal reserved.”

79. Marcellinus, most illustrious man, tribune and notary, said. “The imperial enactment just read plainly declared that a conference was requested, and it is established that it was granted. Since your Holinesses have agreed to assemble as one body from those selected by each party who could conduct the business, I ask you at last to deign to set forth, conduct, and explain the business.”

Emeritus, bishop, said. “Let him say precisely what your Excellency established in your interlocutory ruling.”

And in another hand: “I, Emeritus, bishop, have reviewed this, with our appeal reserved.” [Col. 1377A]

80. Augustine, bishop of the Catholic Church, said. “This is what we have long cried out for: that it be done. A conference was requested; a conference was granted; we both came for the sake of the conference. Let that at last occur which we acknowledge was requested and which the grant itself has declared was granted.”

And in another hand: “I have reviewed it.”

Emeritus, bishop, said. “He said it was requested. Through whom did he request it?”

And in another hand: “I, Emeritus, bishop, have reviewed this, with our appeal reserved.”

Possidius, bishop of the Catholic Church, said. “They are unwilling to put an end to superfluities.”

And in another hand: “I have reviewed it.”

Montanus, bishop, said. “You are contriving delays in the proceeding.”

And in another hand: “I, Montanus, bishop, have reviewed this, with the effect of the appeal reserved.” [Col. 1377B]

81. Marcellinus, most illustrious man, tribune and notary, said. “The persons of the ambassadors ought to have been demanded there where the embassy was carried out. But since the most clement emperor chose to be silent concerning the ambassadors’ names, I do not know why they are wanted here.”

Emeritus, bishop, said. “Let them themselves not be silent, if the emperor was silent.”

And in another hand: “I, Emeritus, bishop, have reviewed this, with our appeal reserved.” [Col. 1377C]

82. Fortunatianus, bishop of the Catholic Church, said. “Let them state, as we have already said, the cause of their separation and division from the Church promised throughout the whole world, established by the Law, shown clearer than light by the testimonies of the prophets, and carried down to this day with great firmness by the Gospel. Let delaying evasions depart, and let them at last recognize the charge of separation.”

And in another hand: “I have reviewed it.”

83. Montanus, bishop, said. “When you have produced what we demand, we shall not be lacking to our assertions.”

And in another hand: “I, Montanus, bishop, have reviewed my pleadings, with the effect of the appeal reserved.”

84. Marcellinus, most illustrious man, tribune and notary, said. “The tenor of the imperial enactment shows that an embassy was undertaken by the Catholics, in which it is established that a conference was requested; and the same most clement emperor wished me to sit as judge in that conference. Therefore, since I have been instructed to inquire nothing concerning the persons of the ambassadors, and since your Holiness better recognizes with me that I cannot exceed the form of the command, deign at last to set forth the business, so that it may appear that full satisfaction has been rendered in all respects both to truth itself and to the imperial command.”

85. Bishop Emeritus said: “You understand, illustrious sir, what is being conducted in secret, while they wish to wrap in mists a matter placed in the open and almost clearer than daylight itself. The imperial order judged, according to its own intent, that a conference should take place between the parties. We too [are present] in accordance with their petition, as they say—a petition which they now deny in court and which they refuse to substantiate.” And while he was speaking: “And in another hand: I, Bishop Emeritus, without prejudice to our appeal, have reviewed [this].” Bishop Augustine of the Catholic Church said: “We do not deny it.” And in another hand: “I have reviewed [this].” Bishop Emeritus said: “Though summoned from our provinces, we openly declare that we ought by no means to flee the contest which they promise to undertake, yet refuse to make public. Therefore, since nothing has been done concerning the matter, the case, or the parties, whereas the first question to be examined ought to be whether they petitioned, through whom they petitioned, or what they petitioned for, let Your Excellency observe why they keep this silent and why they do not publish it. If the petitions agree, they ought to be examined in court. If they will do neither, they ought to yield one of the two points. If they wish to hold us to consent under the earlier mandate, we do not deny that, in accordance with the imperial order, we ought to be present for the disputation. But if they wish to proceed under the present mandate, they ought also to acknowledge examination of that same matter and declare their concurrence in it. If they hesitate to set forth [their petition], so that we may be able to answer their propositions, let Your Eminence see that the reason why the case is not examined does not arise from our side. For since one must descend to the merits of the case by this *agoga*, as it were, and by this gateway, Your Eminence understands that they either deny, or keep silent, or disdain to answer our propositions; and, having observed these things, may you deem it fitting to judge.” And in another hand: “I, Bishop Emeritus, with the effect of our appeal reserved, have reviewed [this].”

> **Note:** [Col. 1377D] *Agoga*. Pliny, book XXXIII, chapter 4, speaking of methods of seeking gold, says that *agogae* are trenches dug on level ground into which gold flows. —Baluze.

86. Marcellinus, most distinguished man, tribune and notary, said: “The most clement emperor did not order me to investigate what they petitioned for or what they submitted. But why the conference was requested has been shown most plainly: namely, that manifest reason might refute superstition. There is no doubt that this can be done today, since I know that persons selected from each side have assembled. Therefore, as I have repeatedly declared, let the case now be set forth.”

87. Bishop Emeritus said: “Did they petition, or did they not? Let them state through whom, or for what, they petitioned.” And in another hand: “I, Bishop Emeritus, without prejudice to our appeal, have reviewed [this].”

88. Alypius, bishop of the Catholic Church, said: “The reading of the rescript is now sufficient. They have acknowledged what the most clement emperor wished to be debated between us. Let superfluities be removed; let us come to the case. For one must consider what the opposing party is doing: namely, just as in the former hearing it sought delay by alleging the length of the earlier proceedings, so today too it wishes to burden the records with superfluities, in order again to complain of the delay required for transcribing or publishing the proceedings.” And in another hand: “I have reviewed [this].” Bishop Montanus said: “You are weaving delays, when you do not produce what we demand from you.” And in another hand: “I, Bishop Montanus, have reviewed my statement, with the effect of my appeal reserved.”

89. Bishop Petilianus said: “At the very recent hearing and controversy, though [the matter] had been examined before the beginning of the case, it is evident that the delay did not arise through our fault or at our request, but through the humanity of your court, which you could not refuse; for the recorders, burdened by the length and prolixity of the controversy, stated this themselves in their declaration. Since those matters have been completed, and since he has mentioned them today, I wished therefore to repeat this. But that these same men are now weaving delays and raising mists in the present proceeding lest we come to their falsehoods is shown by their very silence. For even in silence they speak: they fear to produce what they lied about to the most clement emperor. If, therefore, they rely upon the purpose and regularity of a good petition, why do they hesitate to examine it? And since Your Authority recalls that it was debated in the former controversy whether they should proceed by public law or descend to debate under the authority of the divine law, and since they promised me this by their own consent, while Your Nobility reserved for itself that it ought not to be removed from the laws, it is your part, noble sir, to maintain what belongs to the laws; theirs is the obligation they promised, that they should make their case under divine law. If, therefore, proceedings before you are under public laws, since you have declared yourself presiding under those same laws, require what the laws provide. But if a legal disputation is brought forward, I ask you: you who here seek to debate, what have you petitioned for, what have you done, what have you said against me? If I find that he has spoken truth, I must undertake a debate concerning his law. But if I learn that you began with bad faith and falsehood, I must altogether avoid your person from afar. For what profit is there to me in instructing a liar? What profit is there to me in giving an account to one who contradicts and will contradict?” And in another hand: “I, Bishop Petilianus, have reviewed [this] without prejudice to our appeal.”

90. Marcellinus, most distinguished man, tribune and notary, said: “The imperial enactment, reread, has shown that the conference was requested by the Catholics alone.”

91. Bishop Petilianus said: “Let the records establish that we are Catholics.” And in another hand: “I, Bishop Petilianus, have reviewed [this].”

92. Marcellinus, most distinguished man, tribune and notary, said: “I must call them by the name by which the most clement emperor wished them to be called.”

93. Bishop Petilianus said: “Before the case is decided, that name is empty for them. There will be debate and contention between us even concerning the name itself. Only then shall he obtain this name who is found to be a Christian.” And in another hand: “I, Bishop Petilianus, have reviewed [this].”

94. Marcellinus, most distinguished man, tribune and notary, said: “It is certain that, after the contest has been held, those among whom truth has been found are to be called Catholics. But even in this matter I must follow the form of the imperial instruction, in which she deigned to call them Catholics.”

95. Bishop Petilianus said: “Your Excellency has deigned to make this declaration without prejudice to our position.” And in another hand: “I, Bishop Petilianus, have reviewed [this], with the effect of our appeal reserved.”

96. Marcellinus, most distinguished man, tribune and notary, said: “If Your Holiness maintains that they have falsely been designated by this name, may it at last deign to set forth the case, so that, concerning the name presumptuously assumed, should it be capable of proof, the opposing party may be refuted in every respect.”

97. Bishop Emeritus said: “The matter has been dealt with in great volumes, and they refused to answer, adhering through a certain preconception to the determination that they would not satisfy the judgments.” And while he was speaking: “And in another hand: I, Bishop Emeritus, without prejudice to the appeal, have reviewed [this].” Bishop Augustine of the Catholic Church said: “What judgments?” [Col. 1380B] And in another hand: “I have reviewed [this].” Bishop Emeritus said: “Or at least may they deign to grant this to the reverence and patience of the court: to answer whether they stand in the position of petitioner, whether they themselves set forth the case, whether they themselves summon us into court; so that, once even this is learned from their answer, we may be able to respond to their propositions.” And in another hand: “I, Bishop Emeritus, without prejudice to the appeal, have reviewed [this].” Marcellinus, most distinguished man, tribune and notary, said: “Let an answer be made to the accusations.”

98. Bishop Augustine of the Catholic Church said: “The Church—which you do not wish to hear of, and which you must hear of, because it is proclaimed by so many testimonies and divine utterances to be spread throughout the whole world, and whose communion we appear to hold—has been assailed by you with false accusations. Hence came your separation, which we lament. Today we wish to hear whether these accusations, by which you habitually attack the Church spread through the whole world as it was promised, are true. For if the accusations which you are accustomed to bring against that Church are true—if you can show that it is polluted, stained, overthrown, destroyed, and extinguished through I know not what crimes of ours—then it remains for us to ask whether it has remained among you, though you cry out that it has perished everywhere. But if it could not perish, it remains for you to acknowledge it and at long last end the dispute.” And in another hand: “I have reviewed [this].” Marcellinus, most distinguished man, tribune and notary, said: “You have received the statement of the opposing party; deign to answer it.”

99. Bishop Emeritus said: “I think it improper to wish to defend another’s case and to bring into the present proceeding something which, except shamefully, no one can examine in court without a mandate. For I could now assert and cry out that the whole world resists and opposes these men. You did not authorize me; my conscience is far removed from the outcome of this inquiry. I acknowledge the victor. Whoever, on just and lawful grounds, is proved to be a Christian, he is my Catholic; this name is assigned to him, and he ought to claim this rule for himself. Although Catholic itself, which now appears to be duly directed against us as though upon a certain frontispiece, on the prescription of the opposing party, ought to be neutral, and ought to be so established in the judgment that the victor receives this name. Your Excellency understands that nothing concerning foreigners, nothing concerning those far removed, can prejudice us while this case is being examined among Africans; but rather that this should be awaited: that whoever is defeated by a truthful inquiry should be seen to have been rejected by the world. Let those who come from the other side answer our propositions, and let them not delay to state what standing they bear, whether present or absent, so that we may be able to answer their claims.” And in another hand: “I, Bishop Emeritus, with the effect of our appeal reserved, have reviewed [this].” Marcellinus, most distinguished man, tribune and notary, said: “What is the response?” Bishop Augustine of the Catholic Church said: “That the parties were established on the first day of the trial, and also on the following day by your ruling.” And while he was speaking: “And in another hand: I have reviewed [this].” Marcellinus, most distinguished man, tribune and notary, said: “Something else was asked.”

100. Bishop Augustine of the Catholic Church said: “The form of your ruling has declared it. But since he says that he has no concern with foreign Christians, and that all which is being done is being done among Africans, this is the voice of African Catholic Christians: ‘We cleave in communion to the whole Christian world. We have chosen to retain that Church which we found in the Scriptures.’” And while he was speaking: “And in another hand: I have reviewed [this].” Bishop Emeritus said: “Thus you have always been accustomed to choose and change.” And in another hand: “I, Bishop Emeritus, without prejudice to the appeal, have reviewed [this].”

101. Bishop Augustine of the Catholic Church said: “We retain that Church which we found in those Scriptures in which we also came to know Christ. For our Scriptures, to whose authority both sides submit, commend Christ and the Church as a holy marriage: Christ as bridegroom, she as bride. Where we know him, there we ought also to find her. If, therefore, we had now arisen and were considering in Africa to which communion of Christians we ought to attach ourselves, without doubt we ought to hold to that which we found in the Scriptures, rejecting the accusing opinions of men and adhering to the divine utterances alone, which cannot lie. This is what African Christians have done; they are called Catholics and rightly are Catholics, their very communion attesting the name. For *catholon* means ‘according to the whole.’ But he who has been separated from the whole and defends a part cut off from the entirety must not appropriate this name for himself; rather, let him hold the truth with us.” And in another hand: “I have reviewed [this].”

102. Bishop Gaudentius said: “They think that the name ‘Catholic’ must be referred to provinces or peoples, whereas ‘Catholic’ is the name of that which is full of sacraments, perfect, and unstained—not [a designation] of peoples. For let him show that all peoples communicate with him, and he is a Catholic in fullness. But first let them show what they petitioned for and what they deserved.” And in another hand: “I, Bishop Gaudentius, without prejudice to our appeal, have reviewed [this].” Bishop Petilianus said: “Deign to determine whether or not they ought to produce what we requested, so that—” And while he was speaking: “And in another hand: I, Bishop Petilianus, have reviewed [this] without prejudice to our appeal.” Alypius, bishop of the Catholic Church, said: “Either make a ruling, or order us to comply with the requests.” And in another hand: “I have reviewed [this].”

103. Marcellinus, most distinguished man, tribune and notary, said: “We are returning to matters already dealt with.” And he added: “Let the claim to the name Catholic be demonstrated, and let it be shown whether the Church which the opposing party has thought fit to maintain can be shown to be the same Catholic Church among all peoples.”

104. Bishop Emeritus said: “If he sets forth [a claim], let him prove it.” And in another hand: “I, Bishop Emeritus, have reviewed [this].” Bishop Petilianus said: “Deign to pronounce upon the matters stated above.” And in another hand: “I, Bishop Petilianus, without prejudice to our appeal, have reviewed [this].” Bishop Emeritus said: “If he sets forth [a claim], let him prove it. For if he refuses to set one forth, how will he prove [anything]?” And in another hand: “I, Bishop Emeritus, with the effect of the appeal entered reserved, have reviewed [this].”

105. Bishop Petilianus said: “Rule on each point.” And in another hand: “I, Bishop Petilianus, have reviewed [this] without prejudice to our appeal.” Possidius, bishop of the Catholic Church, said: “Tell me what they requested.” And in another hand: “I have reviewed [this].” Bishop Petilianus said: “Your person owes us this.” And in another hand: “I, Bishop Petilianus, have reviewed [this] without prejudice to our appeal.”

106. Bishop Emeritus said: “We ask that there be no delay, so that the standing may be either that of claimant or respondent. Therefore, since the matter must be proved and is now to be examined in court, let them declare whether they claim or answer, so that, when I see their claim in court, I may be able to answer.” And in another hand: “I, Bishop Emeritus, without prejudice to our appeal, have reviewed [this].”

107. Marcellinus, most distinguished man, tribune and notary, said: “What is requested is just. Let Your Holiness deign to declare whether it appears to stand in court in the position of petitioner.”

108. Bishop Augustine of the Catholic Church said: “It belongs to Your Excellency to judge; we have entered [this proceeding] in order to refute their accusations. They are accustomed to accuse the Church which we hold of the crime of handing over [the Scriptures].” And in another hand: “I have reviewed [this].”

109. Bishop Emeritus said: “Who summoned me into court? At whose suggestion did the emperor desire the conference to occur?” And in another hand: “I, Bishop Emeritus, with the effect of the appeal reserved, have reviewed [this].”

110. Bishop Augustine of the Catholic Church said: “They are accustomed to bring against the Church which we hold accusations of handing over [the Scriptures], and to contend that it has been destroyed and extinguished by the sins of I know not whom.” And in another hand: “I have reviewed [this].” Bishop Emeritus said: “That was not what I asked of you. Satisfy the rulings.” And in another hand: “I, Bishop Emeritus, with the effect of the appeal reserved, have reviewed [this].” Bishop Augustine of the Catholic Church said: “And by these accusations they deceive the hearts of the simple, whose salvation concerns us. Moved by these things, we met with them so that they might confer with us and show whether they could prove against the Church at which they aim what they assert. Since they had refused this meeting of ours, when some of them recently came to the imperial court, they also stated in the prefectural records that they wished to be heard and to have the matter examined. As they embraced us, we thought that consent for their conference should at last be sought from the emperor, so that a conference might occur for this purpose: that they should either prove the accusations which they habitually make against the universal Church, so that truth might appear, or fail to prove them, so that truth might nevertheless appear. If they wish or are able to show these accusations, let them produce and demonstrate them. But if they cannot or will not, it now belongs to Your Excellency to judge the whole matter, as reason itself indicates.” And in another hand: “I have reviewed [this].”

111. Marcellinus, most distinguished man, tribune and notary, said: “You have received the statement of the opposing party. If you have any accusation to make, set it forth now, without further delay.”

112. Bishop Petilianus said: “Let Your Nobility first rule whether we rightly request what we request, or not; then at last we shall answer them point by point.” And in another hand: “I, Bishop Petilianus, have reviewed [this] without prejudice to our appeal.”

113. Marcellinus, most distinguished man, tribune and notary, said: “The text of your statement shows that you make your request rightly; and it has likewise been shown that the party standing opposite has rightly answered their statements. For it has been asserted that, by I know not what accusations, the Church which they hold is still alleged by you today to be assailed. If there are any such accusations, you must state them. But if there are none, you must deign to answer these matters.”

114. Bishop Emeritus said: “Is this how a case is conducted, this the form of judgment, this the way truth is investigated: that the identity of the party is kept silent? He says that I, on the authority of I know not whom, advance accusations against the Church and, as though by some rumor, destroy its honor and merit. Whatever he wishes, by whatever name he wishes, by whatever argument he can, he must assign a designation to this very case, so that, since he again summons [us], he may stand as petitioner. Whether I said it or not, whether I spoke truly or invented it—when I have learned this from his own proposition, when what he accuses me of has been established as true and as uttered by me—then at last I must answer their claims. Your Excellency therefore sees that, without one who summons, the status of respondent is superfluous, and that no one can be called a respondent unless there has first been a claimant. Therefore, if he stands in the position of claimant—that is, of what is called petitioner—let him institute the action to which I ought to answer. For they very often say that we employ needless delaying devices lest the case be reached. Therefore, since this is the hinge of the case, that he who summons another into court must institute an action and call for an answer, let Your Excellency observe that they must pursue [the question] whether, and what action, they institute against us, so that we may answer.” And in another hand: “I, Bishop Emeritus, with the effect of our appeal reserved, have reviewed [this].”

115. Marcellinus, most distinguished man, tribune and notary, said: “Let the Catholic party declare whether it believes that anything ought to be alleged against those standing on the other side.”

116. Bishop Augustine of the Catholic Church said: “We requested a conference in which to refute accusations, not one in which to make accusations to be refuted. For, when they cannot prove their accusations, what they are and what remains to them will be utterly plain, even without our saying so, and will be judged by Your Excellency. We have now entered [the proceedings] to refute their accusations, which they are accustomed to bring against the Church which we hold; their own mandate also contains this: ‘Against our traditores and persecutors.’ Moreover, Primian, if he deigns, our brother, when summoned concerning this very conference, once answered: ‘It is unworthy that the sons of martyrs and the offspring of traditores should assemble together.’ We undertook to refute these accusations; we requested this conference so that these accusations might be refuted. It has been granted. Let them either be proved or cleared away.” And in another hand: “I have reviewed [this].”

117. Marcellinus, most distinguished man, tribune and notary, said: “The tenor of the mandate declares that the party standing opposite consists of *traditores*. Yet, if the statement of the Catholic party is supported by truth, it is agreed that the conference was requested by both parties. Therefore, let Your Holiness now support by proofs what appears to be expressed in the mandate. For from their statements you have received that they especially allege certain things against you, and that they wish to refute those accusations.”

118. Bishop Petilianus said: “Deign to rule concerning the party. Then one may proceed to the case.” And in another hand: “I, Bishop Petilianus, have reviewed [this] without prejudice to our appeal.”

119. Alypius, bishop of the Catholic Church, said: “It is no longer our part to make any superfluous answer on this matter.” And in another hand: “I have reviewed [this].” Possidius, bishop of the Catholic Church, said: “Let Your Excellency’s earlier rulings be read, and let them recognize what they request.” And in another hand: “I have reviewed [this].”

120. Marcellinus, most distinguished man, tribune and notary, said: “If it is agreed that the conference was requested by both parties, it is agreed that he is the petitioner who makes an accusation.”

121. Bishop Emeritus said: “Let him show that the conference was requested in court by both parties.” And in another hand: “I, Bishop Emeritus, have reviewed [this].”

122. Alypius, bishop of the Catholic Church, said: “We shall show it.” And in another hand: “I have reviewed [this].” Marcellinus, most distinguished man, tribune and notary, said: “The Catholic party will have to show this.”

123. Bishop Adeodatus said: “Let it be written that we are Catholics.” And in another hand: “I, Bishop Adeodatus, have reviewed my statement with the effect of the appeal reserved.” Fortunatianus, bishop of the Catholic Church, said: “From Primian’s mandate, we show that you are Donatists.” And in another hand: “I have reviewed [this].” Bishop Adeodatus said: “Let it be written that you are Caecilianists.” And in another hand: “I, Bishop Adeodatus, have reviewed my statement, without prejudice to the appeal.”

124. Fortunatianus, bishop of the Catholic Church, said: “If you order it, we shall read the proceedings held before the prefectural court, where the opposing party so urgently demanded to be heard. And therefore, if you order it—” And in another hand: “I have reviewed [this].” Marcellinus, most distinguished man, tribune and notary, said: “Let the proceedings held before the illustrious authorities, received from the official bureau, be read.”

125. Bishop Petilianus said: “Preserve against these matters whatever safeguards are appropriate.” And in another hand: “I, Bishop Petilianus, have reviewed [this] without prejudice to our appeal.” Marcellinus, most distinguished man, tribune and notary, said: “They shall be preserved.” Bishop Petilianus said: “Rule concerning the party. Let it be disclosed what they petitioned for, what they represented to the most clement emperor, or what they lied about. Rule here whether I demand this superfluously or not. Then at last one may proceed to the case.” And in another hand: “I, Bishop Petilianus, have reviewed [this], with the merits of our appeal reserved.”

126. Marcellinus, most distinguished man, tribune and notary, said: “The heavenly utterance shows that the conference was requested by the dispatch of envoys, and the enactment has plainly ordered that it be held; and I was at the same time appointed to sit as its judge. Your Holiness understands better with me that I cannot in any respect go beyond the form of this instruction.”

127. Bishop Petilianus said: “You ought firmly to rule, noble sir, whether those materials kept secretly and suppressed out of the shame of liars ought to be produced; or at least, if we request them superfluously, rule this.” And in another hand: “I, Bishop Petilianus, have reviewed [this] without prejudice to our appeal.”

128. Fortunatianus, bishop of the Catholic Church, said: “If there is anything which the opposing party can produce against us, where it alleges that we have lied, let it now produce it, lest, by bringing superfluous accusations against us, it continue to deceive the people for whose welfare we wish to provide. Therefore, if Your Nobility orders it, let the proceedings held before the prefectural office be read.” And in another hand: “I have reviewed [this].”

129. Bishop Petilianus said: “Let all things be read in their proper order. Let what we request be read first.” And in another hand: “I, Bishop Petilianus, have reviewed [this] without prejudice to our appeal.” Bishop Emeritus said: “This is what we wished to be brought to light in court: whether they informed the imperial ears that we had appeared before the prefectural court voluntarily, or that we had sought the contest. For if you had said these things, I could refute you in court by the authority of the official digest. But if you had not said them, let them understand that the appointed judge ought in every matter to refer himself to the emperor’s cognizance. Therefore, since we prove most plainly that these men have been unable to show either what they say they communicated to the emperor’s ears, or whether they went, or when they went, or with what mandate they went, may Your Authority deign itself to judge this: so that, if they think they can prove in court that our status is that of petitioners from the drawing up of the records held before the most illustrious authorities, you may deign to judge when this has been established by the reading of the proceedings.” And in another hand: “I, Bishop Emeritus, without prejudice to our appeal, have reviewed [this].”

130. Marcellinus, most distinguished man, tribune and notary, said: “It is quite clear that one ought not return to matters from which it is agreed that a transition has been made. Therefore, that the standing of the petitioner may be plainly shown, let the proceedings of the illustrious authorities be reread.”

131. Bishop Petilianus said: “This is a mist being raised. For we shall show at the outset, in the proper place, that they themselves are petitioners, when you deign to rule upon the matters which we have long requested and continue to request.” And in another hand: “I, Bishop Petilianus, have reviewed [this] without prejudice to our appeal.”

132. Marcellinus, most distinguished man, tribune and notary, said: “Let also those things which Your Holiness offers be reread in order.” And he added: “For the present, allow what has been requested to be read by the official bureau.”

133. Bishop Petilianus said: “Rule, and I permit it to be read.” And in another hand: “I, Bishop Petilianus, have reviewed [this], with the merits of our appeal reserved.”

134. Marcellinus, most distinguished man, tribune and notary, said: “The standing of the petitioner can then be openly shown when this has been proved by the clearest records.”

135. Bishop Petilianus said: “Rule whether I have rightly or wrongly requested what I have so long demanded. For our matter is with the people. You too wished to have an account with the people, since you wished your judgment to be judged.” And in another hand: “I, Bishop Petilianus, have reviewed [this] without prejudice to our appeal.”

136. Alypius, bishop of the Catholic Church, said: “Let the proceedings be read.” And in another hand: “I have reviewed [this].”

137. Marcellinus, most distinguished man, tribune and notary, said: “Your Holiness asks me to make a ruling while necessary records are being produced by the other side as evidence. Therefore, let Your Holiness permit this to be done. Then at last I shall consider whether a ruling ought to be made on this part of the case.”

138. Bishop Petilianus said: “He shows one thing when I request another. The public record itself preserves this, and I shall no longer be silent or defer, noble sir, [the fact] that you yourself promised the people in frequent edicts that whatever you should hear between the disputing parties, you would in turn publish by subsequent edicts. Consider this yourself; it concerns your reputation whether you ought so easily to compel me to debate the merits of the case when my adversary has denied me the very thing which I earnestly request to be disclosed. Consider it yourself; judge it as you wish. Yet I ask Your Excellency to provide what you think at this point. It is advantageous to me: I do not wish to be marked out by the people as one who passed over this issue and passed over the very place where I see that a falsehood, which ought to be published, is being hidden secretly. Therefore you, noble sir, who hold an intermediate position here, take up that pure and innocent constancy and do not hesitate to pronounce what is lawful. For it is not right that, when I have not been satisfied, I should be compelled to descend into the depths of the case. I indeed have great confidence concerning it; but I ought not to pass over what I request.” And in another hand: “I, Bishop Petilianus, have reviewed [this], with the merits of our appeal reserved.”

139. Marcellinus, most distinguished man, tribune and notary, said: “So that what ought to be judged may be more carefully considered, permit the proceedings to be read.”

140. Bishop Petilianus said: “This is not the order of the proceedings: that these should be read first.” And in another hand: “I, Bishop Petilianus, have reviewed [this], with our appeal reserved.” Marcellinus, most distinguished man, tribune and notary, said: “Nothing ought to be denied to the parties.” Bishop Adeodatus said: “If nothing is to be denied to the parties, then what we demanded must at last be granted to us. Let them produce the embassy. For this embassy could not have been framed in bare words. It was written down; let the documents be shown and made public. Let us see whether these things fabricated against us are true or false.” And in another hand: “I, Bishop Adeodatus, have reviewed my statement with the appeal reserved.” Marcellinus, most distinguished man, tribune and notary, said: “I have already ruled and decided that I cannot go beyond the form of the imperial oracle. For in my court it is not established that the identities of the envoys ought to be examined. Therefore let the proceedings be reread, so that it may be shown more clearly who stands in the position of petitioner.” Bishop Adeodatus said: “The emperor did not order that the proceedings of the illustrious authorities be produced in court; yet the opposing party is granted permission to produce them. They produce what they wish; we are not permitted to obtain what we request.” And in another hand: “I, Bishop Adeodatus, have reviewed my statement with the appeal reserved.” Marcellinus, most distinguished man, tribune and notary, said: “And whatever proceedings Your Holiness has offered, or promises to produce, must likewise be reread.” Bishop Adeodatus said: “Whatever is necessary to the case ought not to be denied.” And in another hand: “I, Bishop Adeodatus, have reviewed my statement with the appeal reserved.” Marcellinus, most distinguished man, tribune and notary, said: “Permit, then, that what the party standing opposite says is necessary to its own case be read by the official bureau.” Bishop Adeodatus said: “I cannot permit them to examine in court whatever they wish unless they first produce in court what I demanded concerning themselves.” And in another hand: “I, Bishop Adeodatus, have reviewed my statement with the appeal reserved.” Bishop Augustine of the Catholic Church said: “We received these materials from the archives. If there is anything which you too could have obtained, and you request that it be read, and we oppose it, count us unjust and return like for like.” And in another hand: “I have reviewed [this].” Marcellinus, most distinguished man, tribune and notary, said: “You cast suspicion upon the proceedings by refusing to permit these materials, although it is also lawful for you to publish everything you have submitted. Therefore let what has been offered at last be read.” Bishop Petilianus said: “Let the records contain that Your Authority has refused to rule on what we request. We can say nothing further, especially when I see that Your Authority wishes one thing while I demand another. Rule that I am requesting superfluously what I request; let there be something for me to maintain, something for the people to know. Then at last I shall descend to the matters necessary to the case.” And in another hand: “I, Bishop Petilianus, have reviewed my statement with the appeal unimpaired.” Marcellinus, most distinguished man, tribune and notary, said: “I cannot judge what has not yet been proved.” Bishop Petilianus said: “Rule whether I rightly request that what they secretly represented to the emperor ought to be produced.” And in another hand: “I, Bishop Petilianus, have reviewed this statement of mine with the appeal unimpaired.” Marcellinus, most distinguished man, tribune and notary, said: “That nothing was secretly represented to the emperor has been shown by the form of the enactment sent to all judges and also, in its reading, to my own humble office. Therefore, when I learn from the reading of the proceedings what I ought to judge, I shall undoubtedly judge.”

[Col. 1388B] **141.** Martialis, recorder, read aloud: “Copy of the proceedings held at Ravenna on the third day before the Kalends of February, in the consulship of our lords Arcadius, perpetual Augustus, and Probus, consul for the fourth time, 305.” And while he was reading, Bishop Petilian said: “If you so order, your Sublimity should observe in opposition to this that our requests have not yet been satisfied: namely, that their own pleading should establish that they are the petitioners and that they must set forth the charges which they thought ought to be made.” And in another hand: “I, Petilian, bishop, have reviewed my prosecution, my appeal remaining unimpaired.” Marcellinus, most illustrious man, tribune and notary, said: “Now, from the reading of the proceedings, it will be shown plainly and openly who stands here as petitioner.” Petilian the bishop said: “There are proceedings completed much earlier, before the distinguished men, the proconsuls.” And while he was speaking: “And in another hand [Col. 1388C]: I, Petilian, have reviewed it.” Possidius, bishop of the Catholic Church, said: “He fears his own pleadings; therefore he does not permit the proceedings to be read.” And while he was speaking: “And in another hand: I have reviewed it.” Petilian the bishop said: “There are proceedings held in the proconsular court, and also proceedings held before the vicariate prefecture, which show that they made very many charges against us. There are also other documents which they sought long before from the most merciful emperor, lying to him, that is, through persons appearing and petitioning—namely Theasius and Euvodius—those very men whom they always have as their forerunners and agents, ambassadors of their madness, to demand bloodshed, demand proscriptions, inspire fear, bring dangers upon us, and kill people throughout different provinces. Therefore order all these things to be read first [Col. 1388D]. Then you will find them to be the petitioners.” And in another hand: “I, Petilian, bishop, have reviewed my prosecution, my appeal remaining unimpaired.”

> [Note: Col. 1387D. “Long before”: in 403, when an embassy against the Donatists was decreed at the Council of Carthage.]

> [Note: Col. 1387D. “Theasius and Euvodius”: at the said council they were given a memorandum, extant in the Code of Canons of the African Church, canon 93.]

**142.** Possidius, bishop of the Catholic Church, said: “Let their impatience and tumultuous conduct be attested by these proceedings, through the ruling of your Nobility. For they greatly fear the case, the merits of which they wholly refuse to address. Let not everything which our side has said so extensively in its pleadings concerning the promises and manifestations of God’s Church be fruitless. Why do they evade the issue? Why do they search out I know not what legal technicalities? Let your Nobility now [Col. 1389A] deign to pronounce the character of their defence.” And in another hand: “I have reviewed it.”

**143.** Petilian the bishop said: “Let everything be read in its proper order, from the beginning. Then you will find the petitioner.” And in another hand: “I, Petilian, bishop, have reviewed my prosecution, my appeal remaining unimpaired.”
