**144.** Augustine, bishop of the Catholic Church, said: “If everything is to be read from the beginning, order read from the point at which they sent the case concerning Caecilian’s alleged crimes to the emperor Constantine.” And in another hand: “I have reviewed it.” Fortunatianus, bishop of the Catholic Church, said: “Since you wished mention to be made of the earlier proceedings.” And while he was speaking: “And in another hand: I have reviewed it.”

**145.** Marcellinus, most illustrious man, tribune and notary, said: “Are these proceedings which your Holiness requests to be read [Col. 1389B] later than, or earlier than, the proceedings produced by the Catholic party?”

**146.** Petilian the bishop said: “Indeed, there is no Catholic party except that which has won the crown in this contest. Therefore we desire that those documents be read which they themselves earlier presented and requested in the proconsular court and before the vicariate prefecture.” And in another hand: “I, Petilian, bishop, have reviewed my prosecution, my appeal remaining unimpaired.” Possidius, bishop of the Catholic Church, said: “If you had confidence in your case, you would come to its merits.” And in another hand: “I have reviewed it.”

**147.** Marcellinus, most illustrious man, tribune and notary, said: “Without prejudice, I call them Catholics, following the designation of the most merciful emperor. Therefore, if it pleases you, let the earlier proceedings be read by the official staff.”

[Col. 1389C] **148.** Possidius, bishop of the Catholic Church, said: “We offer the most ancient documents, which we request the official staff to receive. Let your Nobility order them to be read.”

**149.** Petilian the bishop said: “If this is the instruction given to your authority, and if they have not departed from what they long ago promised—namely, that they ought to proceed according to law—restore to us that first charge, of which we seem in some manner to have suffered the loss under the pretext of this exception. Therefore, if they adhere to the law, your Excellency sees that they can by no means make mention of these documents which they produce. And now, again and again, I demand that they declare what they choose: whether they proceed against me by a forensic action, or contend in a legal dispute. [Col. 1389D]” And in another hand: “I, Petilian, bishop, have reviewed my prosecution, my appeal remaining unimpaired.”

**150.** Marcellinus, most illustrious man, tribune and notary, said: “Let the official staff receive what is offered by both parties and compare the dates, so that those documents found to be earlier may be read.”

**151.** Petilian the bishop said: “We are being gradually led into the case.” And in another hand: “I, Petilian, bishop, have reviewed my prosecution, my appeal remaining unimpaired.”

**152.** Possidius, bishop of the Catholic Church, said: “We offer what you requested. Do not regret having requested it. You wished ancient proceedings to be read. We have these in hand; let your Nobility order what we offer to be read.” And in another hand: “I have reviewed it.”

[Col. 1390A] **153.** Petilian the bishop said: “The proceedings are still fresh in which I requested that they produce the matters concerning which they lied to the emperor, and read what they alleged; yet, against this, they want, amid such mists, to reread the proceedings held before the prefectural court—documents earlier than those I produced long ago. Therefore, noble sir, if the course of the case is as it appears to have been framed from the beginning, let them either abandon these public documents and come to a legal dispute; or, if they wish to use these materials, let them abandon the law of God.” And in another hand: “I, Petilian, bishop, have reviewed my prosecution, my appeal remaining unimpaired.”

**154.** Marcellinus, most illustrious man, tribune and notary, said: “Let the official staff carefully inspect the proconsular proceedings and those held before the illustrious authorities, so that [Col. 1390B] the earlier ones may be read first.”

**155.** Augustine, bishop of the Catholic Church, said: “Let your Sublimity attend briefly to what the opposing party has just pursued. We show, by the testimony of our communion itself, that we maintain the Catholic Church—the Church which, if they permit it, we undertake to prove not by human rumours or wandering opinions, but as declared by divine utterances. But they themselves, who proceed in this fashion, compel us to offer for reading in this conference laws, proceedings, or whatever is produced from the archives. For if, with all documents of this sort set aside, they were unwilling to consider the Church except in the Scriptures, we would desire nothing, wish for nothing else. They allege the crimes of *traditio*—the handing over [of sacred books]. Either they do not prove those crimes of *traditio* by archives, and say nothing; [Col. 1390C] or they prove them, and thereby compel us in turn to proceed by archives. Thus your Excellency sees that the issues must be distinguished: when we are compelled to proceed by public laws, and when we wish and desire the question of the Church to be decided only by divine utterances.” And in another hand: “I have reviewed it.” Petilian the bishop said: “Let him state what he has chosen. For they cannot hold both positions.” And in another hand: “I, Petilian, bishop, have reviewed my prosecution, my appeal remaining unimpaired.”

**156.** Marcellinus, most illustrious man, tribune and notary, said: “It is sufficiently clear that the opposing party’s pleading was entirely explicit: it appears to show that, if the charge of *traditio* is alleged—a charge which certainly cannot be proved by divine laws, but must be more carefully ascertained by the reliability of the proceedings—then all matters must be conducted by public proceedings. But if the case of faith begins to be argued, then recourse will be had to matters to be demonstrated by examples from the Old and New Testament. Therefore, if your Holiness wishes its petition and the opposing party’s prosecution to be strengthened by their declarations, show clearly whether you desire the charge of *traditio*, which cannot be proved at all except by certain most evident documents, to be tried in court, or whether you desire only the case of faith to be investigated and settled before my tribunal [Col. 1390D].”

**157.** Emeritus the bishop said: “I am not ashamed repeatedly to restate what belongs to the case. Indeed, at the very outset of the matter we requested that they demonstrate, clearer than daylight, the instruction given to their envoys, lest, when these matters were sent to trial, they perhaps refuse it. For they can say: ‘We gave other instructions; we did not decide the same things; nor did we agree that these should be requested by an imperial order.’ As they now do.” And while he was speaking: “And in another hand: I, Emeritus, bishop, have reviewed it, my appeal remaining unimpaired.”

**158.** Marcellinus, most illustrious man, tribune and notary, said: “It is established that these instructions were given by the subscriptions of all.”

**159.** Emeritus the bishop said: “Since there are two matters, there ought to be two mandates. The mandate which was read in the present matter has been inserted in the proceedings; but the mandate which appears to have been delivered to the envoys has in no way been read. We must therefore consider whether that too appears to have been drafted beforehand by the same persons, to be laid before the imperial ears [Col. 1391B]; so that, when both mandates have been read in court, you may judge whether they had one and the same intention.” And in another hand: “I, Emeritus, bishop, have reviewed it, the effect of my appeal being preserved.”

**160.** Augustine, bishop of the Catholic Church, said: “We have already cried this out so many times. They demand that the mandate imposed upon the bishops’ envoys be read to them by the bishops. This is to seek extraneous matters irrelevant to the case. The mandate imposed upon us for holding this conference with them—that has been read; let that suffice them. For what if certain instructions were given to the envoys which do not concern this case but which we do not wish them to know? It is sufficient that the emperor declared by his own testimony [Col. 1391C] that we requested the conference. It was granted; we have come to it; let it at last be conducted, and let human ears be open to the truth.” And in another hand: “I have reviewed it.”

**161.** Adeodatus the bishop said: “You have admitted what you formerly kept silent. You have shown that you gave many instructions against us which we should not readily know. Therefore your Sublimity may observe what we must infer from his pleading: what that mandate contains, the mandate against us which we should not readily be allowed to know.” And in another hand: “I, Adeodatus, bishop, have reviewed my prosecution, my appeal remaining unimpaired.”

**162.** Augustine, bishop of the Catholic Church, said: “I did not say this. You either did not notice, or pretend not to have heard, what I said. Listen: we shall say it more plainly, lest perhaps through my fault you did not understand what, in seeking brevity, [Col. 1391D] I stated somewhat obscurely and you could not grasp. It is known to all that the Church has many affairs—its own, and those of private persons entrusted to its care—and that many matters may concern the bishops’ intercession. The secrets of others’ business and cases are entrusted to us, in which our intervention is often sought and for which help is asked from the Church. These must not be disclosed, lest we be found betrayers. It is enough for you that the most merciful emperor himself testifies that I requested a conference in your case. Seek nothing further, if you do not seek other people’s affairs. For your business, what was read from the emperor’s law itself [Col. 1392A], confirmed by our mandate and subscriptions, is sufficient.” And in another hand: “I have reviewed it.”

**163.** Adeodatus the bishop said: “Different affairs cannot be ordered in one mandate. But if perhaps it is established that you gave the same instructions against us also against other provinces, you do well not to disclose them. Therefore do not put yourself forward publicly. Since you wish to pursue me first, you keep this in reserve for other provinces. You have shown what you did; you have shown what you conceal. I have hold of your lie; I have hold of your falsehood.” And in another hand: “I, Adeodatus, bishop, have reviewed it, my appeal remaining unimpaired.”

**164.** Marcellinus, most illustrious man, tribune and notary, said: “If your Holiness deigns carefully to observe his pleading, the venerable man has stated not that he gave instructions [Col. 1392B] against you, but that, in his own pleading, he indicated matters that do not pertain to you. He has confessed only one thing plainly: that he requested the conference in every way and that it was granted. Therefore, lest we seem to exceed the terms of the imperial command, I see that no mention ought to be made of that mandate. Accordingly, may your Holiness deign to answer what was asked: whether you wish the charge of *traditio*, which can be shown by public archives, to be tried in court, or whether you wish only the case of the Church and faith to be investigated.”

**165.** Petilian the bishop said: “We are artfully mocked: although they are the petitioners, and have always disturbed and troubled our peace, we are placed in the role of petitioners, though we have always been, and are, possessors of the peace and Church [Col. 1392C] of God. I therefore ask your Nobility to preserve this order. Let them show what they have done; there you will find the petitioners.” And in another hand: “I, Petilian, bishop, have reviewed it, my appeal remaining unimpaired.”

**166.** Marcellinus, most illustrious man, tribune and notary, said: “If your Holiness had allowed, or had permitted, the proceedings to be read, it could long ago have been shown who stood in the petitioner’s role. Therefore, even now, as I have ordered, let the earlier proceedings be read.” Petilian the bishop said: “Preserve the order of the proceedings.” And in another hand: “I, Petilian, bishop, have reviewed my prosecution, my appeal remaining unimpaired.”

**167.** Marcellinus, most illustrious man, tribune and notary, said: “Let the dates be read of the proceedings offered by the parties—that is, the proconsular proceedings and those of the most illustrious tribunal [Col. 1392D].”

**168.** Possidius, bishop of the Catholic Church, said: “We offer earlier documents, which will support our arguments.” And in another hand: “I have reviewed it.” Bishop Montanus said: “If you order it, I shall read from the codex.” And in another hand: “I, Montanus, bishop, have reviewed my prosecution, my appeal remaining unimpaired.”

**169.** Marcellinus, most illustrious man, tribune and notary, said: “As I have decided, let it be read by the official staff.” Navigius, assistant of the *numerarii*, read: “After the consulship of our lord Theodosius Augustus [the text is defective], at Carthage, on the Ides of September.” And while he was reading—

> [Note: Col. 1391D. It should be read: “in the consulship of our lords Theodosius, perpetual Augustus, and Rumoridus, most distinguished man,” as below; the year is 403.]

[Col. 1393A] **170.** Alypius, bishop of the Catholic Church, said: “We produce earlier documents.” And in another hand: “I have reviewed it.” Marcellinus, most illustrious man, tribune and notary, said: “Meanwhile, permit these earlier proceedings, held before the tribunal of the illustrious authorities, to be reread.” Navigius, assistant of the *numerarii*, read: “In the sixth consulship of our lord Arcadius Augustus and the consulship of Probus, most distinguished man” (A.D. 406). And while he was reading—

**171.** Marcellinus, most illustrious man, tribune and notary, said: “Let the earlier documents be produced by the official staff.”

**172.** Rufinianus, clerk of the most illustrious curator, said: “The earlier ones are those contained in the codex produced [by the Donatists].”

**173.** Alypius, bishop of the Catholic Church, said: “See, we produce earlier documents.” And in another hand: “I have reviewed it.” [Col. 1393B] Rufinianus, clerk of the most illustrious curator, said: “For, as we have reported, these contain the consulship of Theodosius Augustus and Rumoridus, most distinguished man; the others contain the sixth consulship of our lord Arcadius and the consulship of Probus, most distinguished man.”

**174.** Marcellinus, most illustrious man, tribune and notary, said: “Let the earlier documents be read.” Navigius, assistant of the *numerarii* in the office of the most illustrious and distinguished vicar, read:

“We petition your Equity, Septiminus, most distinguished man, most exalted proconsul. The Catholic Church endures many things from the heretics of the Donatist party contrary to divine and human laws. If we wished to request that these be prohibited and removed by either earlier or more recent imperial commands, they would by no means dare complain of our actions, knowing that, although no such law supported them, they nevertheless arranged for their own schismatics, the Maximianists, to be driven and expelled from their places and seats by judicial orders. Yet, consulting peacefully for their salvation and for our own reputation, because of the charity by which we are Christians, we wish gently to admonish them not to neglect, by reflection and recognition, their error; or, if they think they possess some truth, to defend it not by the frenzied violence of the Circumcellions against public peace, but by a calm rendering of reason. Therefore we petition your Sublimity that, when we wish to admonish them about this through magistrates, whether in cities or in the territories belonging to them, you order the proceedings to be made available to us and that they be formally summoned upon our allegation [Col. 1393D]. Having obtained this, we shall give abundant thanks to your Excellency before God.

“Given by all the Catholic bishops from the Council of Carthage (A.D. 403), in the consulship of our lord Theodosius Augustus and Rumoridus, most distinguished man, at Carthage, on the Ides of September.”

Septiminus, most distinguished man, proconsul, said: “In every place, bishops of the venerable law are granted the authority to have proceedings drawn up for the peace of the empire; with the further limitation prescribed by this order, that they understand that, when the teachers of an erring people make a salutary request, they must furnish the grounds of their own persuasion, so that, when the issues have been set out publicly, the friendly moderation of the law may be maintained and superstition overthrown.” After this was read—

[Col. 1394A] **175.** Petilian the bishop said: “The petitioner is the one who petitions—or what else is he to be called?” And in another hand: “I, Petilian, bishop, have reviewed my prosecution, my appeal remaining unimpaired.”

**176.** Augustine, bishop of the Catholic Church, said: “We requested these things, but after your earlier accusations and charges. For we produce the most ancient proceedings, in which your predecessors at that time came before Anulinus the proconsul, offered him documents in which they said the crimes of our predecessors were written down, and asked him to send those documents to the emperor Constantine. We offer them and ask your Nobility to order that they be received by the official staff and read in sequence.” And in another hand: “I have reviewed it.”

[Col. 1394B] **177.** Marcellinus, most illustrious man, tribune and notary, said: “The petition presented by you plainly shows that the charge of schism and heresy was made; it is for you to prove it.”

**178.** Possidius, bishop of the Catholic Church, said: “Everything will be proved, if you deign to order the documents we have produced both to be received and read by the official staff.” And in another hand: “I have reviewed it.”

**179.** Marcellinus, *vir clarissimus*, tribune and notary, said: “Let all be read in sequence.”

**180.** Emeritus the bishop said: “Therefore he is in the petitioner’s role.” And in another hand: “I, Emeritus, bishop, have reviewed it.” Possidius, bishop of the Catholic Church, said: “When the documents have been read, the petitioner will more easily be found.” And in another hand: “I have reviewed it.” Marcellinus, most illustrious man [Col. 1394C], tribune and notary, said: “Although from these proceedings they appear to stand in the role of petitioners, nevertheless it will be better and more clearly established when everything has been read.”

**181.** Petilian the bishop said: “If we return to a forensic contest, it is established that they have abandoned the law of God. Therefore let them answer again and again what I have demanded: whether they proceed by public laws or by contest under the law of God. Let them choose one of the two. For they cannot maintain both.” And in another hand: “I, Petilian, bishop, have reviewed it, my appeal remaining unimpaired.”

**182.** Marcellinus, most illustrious man, tribune and notary, said: “There is no doubt that these documents which your Holiness has produced for rereading, because they were made in the court of the distinguished proconsul, pertain to forensic dispute. Therefore, as I have directed, permit also those documents to be read, so that [Col. 1394D] it may be shown more carefully who stands in the petitioner’s role.”

**183.** Petilian the bishop said: “I enter a plea in bar against this. If it is a forensic action, noble sir, you have been directed to hear the case of this time. If the matter is conducted simply and according to ecclesiastical custom, I shall assent to what is produced under divine law, whether by me or by the opposing party. But if they wish to read aged and ancient little documents, I have valid pleas in bar on my side: I invoke that period by whose objection I have meanwhile secured a postponement. The case has incurred lapse; it cannot be heard again.” And in another hand: “I, Petilian, bishop, have reviewed it, my appeal remaining unimpaired.” Augustine, bishop of the Catholic Church, said: “They allege charges of *traditio* [Col. 1395A].” And in another hand: “I have reviewed it.” Petilian the bishop said: “That belongs to the case.” And in another hand: “I, Petilian, bishop, have reviewed it, my appeal remaining unimpaired.” Augustine, bishop of the Catholic Church, said: “Return the courtesy: you were heard when you made your plea, while we endured it. They customarily allege against the Church which we maintain the crimes of *traditio*.” And in another hand: “I have reviewed it.” Petilian, bishop of the Donatist party, said: “Does he proceed legally, or in forensic fashion?” And in another hand: “I, Petilian, bishop, have reviewed it.” Possidius, bishop of the Catholic Church, said: “You were the first to produce documents.” And in another hand: “I have reviewed it.” Petilian the bishop said: “Give me the date. Let the official staff calculate from the dates whether the case may be argued today, if we descend to forensic actions.” And in another hand: “I, Petilian, bishop, have reviewed it, my appeal remaining unimpaired.”

[Col. 1395B] **184.** Marcellinus, most illustrious man, tribune and notary, said: “Your Holiness too ought to judge on this point. For it is established that the hearing was postponed by the agreement of both parties. Why do you now think a plea in bar based on time should unnecessarily be raised, when it is clear that it was excluded by the parties’ agreement? Therefore it is manifest that the matters relevant to the case must now be conducted.”

**185.** Petilian the bishop said: “Because they themselves turned to forensic matters, I requested forensic procedure. Let me receive an answer to what I ask. Does he proceed according to forensic custom or ecclesiastical custom?” And in another hand: “I, Petilian, bishop, have reviewed it, my appeal remaining unimpaired.”

**186.** Marcellinus, most illustrious man, tribune and notary [Col. 1395C], said: “Let an answer be made to the charges.” Augustine, bishop of the Catholic Church, said: “If they permit us: they customarily allege against the Church which we maintain—as all know whose minds they habitually trouble by their accusations, and as they have declared even in the terms of their own mandate—the Church, I say, which we maintain, charges of *traditio*.” And in another hand: “I have reviewed it.” Petilian, bishop of the Donatist party, said: “Let them declare themselves on the questions asked. We asked for a declaration, not for a contest.” And in another hand: “I, Petilian, bishop, have reviewed it, my appeal remaining unimpaired.”

**187.** Augustine, bishop of the Catholic Church, said: “If they abandon these accusations, we shall produce nothing from public documents. But if they persist in the same accusation, we demonstrate through public documents that this case was settled long ago, although they have not ceased from making charges of this sort [Col. 1395D]. Therefore we requested this conference now, not in order that we might take up again for settlement that case of *traditio* which they alleged against Caecilian and his colleagues, but in order to show that it was settled long ago; so that peoples who do not know this and are still stirred by their accusations may at last learn in which Church to seek the way of Christian salvation. Therefore, if inquiry is made which Church it is, how extensive it is, and what its character is, divine testimonies alone suffice to demonstrate it. If they appeal to human beings, if they bring charges against human beings, although the case of the Church must be distinguished from the case of human beings, and the hope of the Church must not be placed in human beings—if they are good, nor, if they are evil, should the Church of God be judged to have perished—yet we undertake their case too, as that of our brothers. If they can be shown to us to be guilty, we anathematize them today; nevertheless, because of them, we do not abandon or forsake the Church promised and manifested by God [Col. 1396A]. Let them therefore choose what they wish. Let them bring no charges against people, and the documents will cease. Divine authority alone will speak; Scripture alone, to which we both submit, will be brought forward publicly.” And in another hand: “I have reviewed it.” Marcellinus, most illustrious man, tribune and notary, said: “What is their reply to this?”

**188.** Emeritus, bishop of the Donatist party, said: “I cannot reply to a lengthy speech. Nevertheless, as I can, I shall address summarily the matters superfluously brought into court: although they will not even clarify by rereading the requests proposed by our side, so as neither to wish to be petitioners nor to say that they stand as respondents; and although they have brought a prosecution against our side, so that, if they observe the order of forensic rule, I may not omit in my inward reflections the point concerning the conditional day; but if they prefer to struggle in court according to legal procedure, we must answer them from the divine Scriptures. First, however, what we demand in court is this: since they waver in court concerning the allegation of their mandates—for though they read one thing, they deny another, and yet say that they had previously sent envoys to the imperial ears—and since it would in turn follow that the reply of the proceedings would clearly show whether we were disturbers or were disturbed into coming to court, they refuse to answer these many propositions and cast themselves upon I know not what argument [Col. 1396C]. I ask you, noble sir, let them take a position; let them say under what order and by what kind of action they stand in court. For we, who have been brought to this dispute, cannot stand in the petitioner’s role. They must make their propositions, so that our party may be able to answer their propositions.” And in another hand: “I, Emeritus, bishop, have reviewed it, my appeal remaining unimpaired.”

**189.** Augustine, bishop of the Catholic Church, said: “If those who defend the charges made stand in the petitioner’s role, it is for your Nobility to pronounce.” And in another hand: “I have reviewed it.”

**190.** Marcellinus, most illustrious man, tribune and notary, said: “It is also established by the pleading of the venerable man Petilian that the Catholic party [Col. 1396D]—a name which I have made clear in many rulings that I use without prejudice—should plainly show whether it wished to proceed under public law or rather by divine testimonies. But an answer has again been given to the questions, and has shown most clearly that, if charges are not brought, public documents must be set aside, since it is certain that they cannot otherwise be proved except by the attestation of public proceedings; but if the case of the Church were to be considered, only legal testimonies would be produced. Let it be stated more clearly which of these is preferred.”

**191.** Petilian the bishop said: “There are two matters which, above all else, we have begun to press from the beginning of this day. One is that they should read what they represented to the most merciful emperor; the other is whether they wish to maintain a dispute under divine law [Col. 1397A] or under public laws. I have received no clear answer on either.” And in another hand: “I, Petilian, bishop, have reviewed it, my appeal remaining unimpaired.”

**192.** Possidius, bishop of the Catholic Church, said: “The preceding proceedings testify that everything has been answered.” And in another hand: “I have reviewed it.”

**193.** Petilian the bishop said: “Therefore your Sublimity sees that we are gradually being led into the inner matters of the case; your Excellency and keenness of mind see that I have received a response more through the rulings of your Nobility than through the answers of my opponents. Let something therefore be decided more explicitly; let it be more plainly established, so that I may know what I ought to answer. For, as your Nobility recalls, I too have received instructions from my party to answer charges, not to make some charge myself. I do not stand in the petitioner’s role, but in the role of one who will answer. Those who repeatedly bring us into accusation and odium before the emperor’s ears and before the whole people gathered, as they claim, on their side—calling us heretics and likewise schismatics—let them prove this; I refute it; I shall answer this matter, provided that they turn to legal procedure and seek the answers and judgments of the law itself. But if they mix both together, let this be specified more clearly. Let me know the kind of action; let no one reproach me in public, let no one judge me a weak defender of a good cause, let no one judge me evasive, nor judge my opponent deceitful and lawless, one to whom everything is permitted; so that, when just and plain matters are demanded of them, they may be pleased delicately to cast whatever mists and darkness they wish [Col. 1397C], in order that no approach may be made to the hinge of truth.” And in another hand: “I, Petilian, bishop, have reviewed it, my appeal remaining unimpaired.”

**194.** Marcellinus, most illustrious man, tribune and notary, said: “There are two things which your Holiness believed should be requested: first, that the mandate in which the envoys were selected by the party standing opposite should be reread; second, that they should demonstrate most plainly whether they were departing from divine laws.” Petilian the bishop said: “Let them answer both briefly.” And in another hand: “I, Petilian, bishop, have reviewed it.” Marcellinus, most illustrious man, tribune and notary, said: “I myself answered one matter, because it concerned me. For I could not doubt concerning those envoys whose mission the most merciful emperor had confirmed, lest anything seem to be revived to his injury [Col. 1397D]. But the other matter is established by their pleadings to have been settled: they plainly showed that they wish to depart from public law on the condition that you remain silent concerning the crimes of persons. Therefore, since the sole remaining issue is clearly to show who stands in the petitioner’s role, and since the proceedings produced by your party have been read, permit those also which the opposing party offers to be read by the official staff.”

**195.** Petilian the bishop said: “Whose proceedings are those which have been read from my party? If those standing opposite were absent, noble sir, you would have been permitted to defend the side of absent persons with a judge’s mind. But they are now present. Let them themselves answer me, let them themselves declare, let them not delay in answering both matters which I have proposed.” And in another hand: “I, Petilian, bishop, have reviewed it.” Possidius, bishop of the Catholic Church, said: “You do not even permit us to answer.” Petilian the bishop said: “It is yours to pronounce what is to be heard; it is for those who stand against me in the petitioner’s role to conduct the case.” And while he was speaking: “And in another hand: I, Petilian, bishop, have reviewed it.”

**196.** Marcellinus, most illustrious man, tribune and notary, said: “He has ruled that all these matters may be carefully recognized from the reading of the proceedings.” Petilian the bishop said: “Let them themselves speak; let them themselves declare.” And in another hand: “I, Petilian, bishop, have reviewed it, my appeal remaining unimpaired [Col. 1398B].”

**197.** Augustine, bishop of the Catholic Church, said: “We have already stated on what basis we should rather proceed: that is, whether by public documents or divine testimonies. It lies within your power. For if you cease from charges against human beings, we too shall cease from public documents and shall establish only the case of the Church by divine testimonies. But if you do not desist from charges against human beings, we must both demand public documents from you and produce public documents against you. When we set this before the judicial investigator, because it had not been removed from his mind by your numerous and superfluous pleadings, he himself was already giving you this answer on our behalf—not acting the part of our side, but his own, since we have already put it before him and deeply impressed upon his mind what we say [Col. 1398C].” And in another hand: “I have reviewed it.”

**198.** Adeodatus the bishop said: “It is not in our power to determine the order in which we should proceed, since even our coming was not in our power.” And in another hand: “I, Adeodatus, bishop, have reviewed it, my appeal remaining unimpaired.”

**199.** Augustine, bishop of the Catholic Church, said: “Then answer the questions. Do you withdraw from the charges of *traditio*? Let them answer our brief question. Do you abandon the accusations which you habitually make against Caecilian and his colleagues, or do you persist in the same accusation?” And in another hand: “I have reviewed it.” Marcellinus, most illustrious man, tribune and notary, said: “Answer the questions.”

[Col. 1398D] **200. Bishop Emeritus said:** “He says that his request is brief; our reply ought to be brief. Every proceeding is customarily undertaken by two persons: the petitioner and, on the other side, the respondent. Since this case follows its proper order and calls for a contest, why is it that, before the beginning of the business, a kind of choice is proposed to me by the opposing party, so that I should say whether I reject the accusations brought against Caecilian and remain silent about those same charges which I had alleged, or whether I can substantiate in court the allegations made?

“Most eminent judge, remember, as you customarily do, what the order of speaking is. For no one says to an opponent standing before him: ‘Choose whether you accuse me or not.’ No one says: ‘Are you going to bring an accusation, or will you bring nothing against me in court?’ Thus imposing a kind of mute silence upon your accusations, you would be said to have come from regions so far away vainly and without reason. Yet I stand here for this purpose: if he himself says that he made those statements which he either indignantly bears, or has subscribed in his petition for the imperial ears, then at last I shall choose and reply whether I wish, fortified by the legal confirmation of his accusations according to the tenor of his prosecution, to proceed against those charges, or to withdraw myself from this action.

“Your Excellence sees that I cannot reply when he has spoken vaguely, when he has proposed nothing of such a kind as requires my answer. For I say that he must state whether he stands as petitioner or respondent. He says to me: ‘If you abandon Caecilian’s case, then I am petitioner; but if you do not pass it over, I must answer the matters which appear to have been alleged.’ If you fear Caecilian’s case and fear that something may be alleged against you, you must yourself propose and institute the action in court. Bring me forward and place me in public. Say that I have commended to the public record some crime of yours which you brought to the imperial ears.

“But when I demand from you all the more what you have heard, what you allege that I said, what you declare that I represented to the courts, why do you fear—why do you shrink from—establishing this action in court? Doubtless you consider this: that, if you assume the role of petitioner and send those matters into court, you may be compelled in court to prove what was received, said, or published by someone.

“Consider, noble sir, the condition in which this case stands: I, who am attacked, ask that their petition be produced in court, and with every request at my disposal I continually entreat them that we may not be prevented by delaying tactics from coming to the heart of the matter. Therefore, the fact that nothing has yet been done in the case is not on our side. For, had they wished to establish their role in court, we would necessarily have had to answer the charges immediately.” And in another hand: “I, Bishop Emeritus, have reviewed this, reservation of appeal preserved.”

**201. Augustine, bishop of the Catholic Church, said:** “What a brief reply! How much is said when nothing can be found to say! I replied briefly to your requests. You wished to learn from me whether I would proceed by divine legal testimonies or by public records. I replied: if you withdraw from accusations which can be demonstrated only by public records, I withdraw from the public records and shall establish by divine testimonies alone the case of the Church which I defend. But if you do not wish to withdraw from those accusations, neither shall I withdraw from the documents by which I show that you bring false accusations either against us or against the Church itself which we hold.” And in another hand: “I have reviewed it.”

**202. Marcellinus, most illustrious tribune and notary, said:** “This is plainly a complete answer. But which party stands in the position of petitioner cannot at all be known except from the reading of the records. Since, as I have determined, the records offered by your side are established to have been presented, let them at last be read through.”

**203. Bishop Petilian said:** “No one chooses both of two alternatives. Therefore, when I proposed that he choose one, he clearly claimed both for himself. I do not fear; I do not refuse, if this can be maintained. First preserve for me the time limits prescribed by law; let a day be fixed. Let the staff answer that it was found that the day for the case had elapsed. Judge from this; from this you ought to render a decision. For you would have rendered judgment against me if I had perhaps failed to appear.” And in another hand: “I, Bishop Petilian, have reviewed this, reservation of appeal preserved.”

**204. Augustine, bishop of the Catholic Church, said:** “If they arrived on the fifteenth day in order to appear on the fourteenth, why did they present themselves on the eighth day before the Kalends?” And in another hand: “I have reviewed it.”

**205. Bishop Petilian said:** “You did not disturb me; I knew that you had defaulted. I entered the court unnecessarily, though I ought not to have entered after the day on which the matter had lapsed.” And in another hand: “I, Bishop Petilian, have reviewed this, appeal unimpaired.”

**206. Augustine, bishop of the Catholic Church, said:** “Why did Primian promise that he would be present on the Kalends?” And in another hand: “I have reviewed it.”

Alypius, bishop of the Catholic Church, said: “Order this to be read. Although these matters have been settled, although the opposing side throws up these mists in order to deceive the peoples, we nevertheless ask this also: order it to be read, so that they may at least recognize how shamelessly they repeat matters already disposed of.” And in another hand: “I have reviewed it.”

**207. Bishop Petilian said:** “Since you refuse to designate one of the two, while holding both, you make me repeat the same things.” And in another hand: “I, Bishop Petilian, have reviewed this, appeal unimpaired.”

[Col. 1400C] **208. Fortunatius, bishop of the Catholic Church, said:** “They know that they have nothing in the case of the Church. Therefore they proceed by delays. Accordingly, since those matters have already been settled, order the earlier records to be read, so that it may be known who is the petitioner.” And in another hand: “I have reviewed it.”

**209. Bishop Petilian said:** “If you wish to employ public laws, I enter an objection that you not read them.” And in another hand: “I, Bishop Petilian, have reviewed this, appeal unimpaired.”

**210. Marcellinus, most illustrious tribune and notary, said:** “You wish to act contrary to your own agreements, which is prohibited by law. For it is established by the agreement of the parties that the hearing was first postponed, so that the matter might be handled on another day, whether the third day or at least after publication of the records. Therefore, in order that it may be more carefully made clear who stands in the place of petitioner, let the records be read.”

[Col. 1400D] **211. Bishop Petilian said:** “I would preserve the agreement, if they too preserved it.” And in another hand: “I, Bishop Petilian, have reviewed this, appeal unimpaired.”

**212. Marcellinus, most illustrious tribune and notary, said:** “Let the records be read.”

Bishop Adeodatus said: “Against these matters, preserve what is proper.” And in another hand: “I, Bishop Adeodatus, have reviewed this, appeal unimpaired.”

Marcellinus, most illustrious tribune and notary, said: “Whatever may be consistent with reason and equity shall be preserved.”

**213. Bishop Adeodatus said:** “For if the agreement must be preserved, and we are to be held to our agreement, they too must keep faith with us in their agreement, by which they promised to proceed according to divine laws.” And in another hand: “I, Bishop Adeodatus, have reviewed this, appeal unimpaired.”

[Col. 1401A] **214. Augustine, bishop of the Catholic Church, said:** “But the case of the Church, not the case of Caecilian and his colleagues, against whom you bring charges. Behold, we promise—and promise as often as it is demanded of us, and offer it even when it is not demanded—that we establish, teach, and demonstrate the case of the Church by divine testimonies alone; but the case of Caecilian or of any persons whatever [we address] only by those documents through which such matters are customarily either demonstrated or cleared.” And in another hand: “I have reviewed it.”

**215. Marcellinus, most illustrious tribune and notary, said:** “These things have been said repeatedly. Therefore, since it is established that the role of petitioner must first be examined, let the records be read.”

Martialis, recorder, read: “The report of Anolinus, proconsul, begins, in which he shows that the Donatists referred Caecilian’s case to the Emperor Constantine.”

And while he was reading:

**216. Bishop Montanus said:** “Why is this heading being read?” And in another hand: “I, Bishop Montanus, have reviewed this, reservation of appeal preserved.”

Marcellinus, most illustrious tribune and notary, said: “Neither heading shall be inserted in the records.”

Martialis, recorder, read: “To our Augusti, Anolinus, most illustrious man, proconsul of Africa. Having received and reverently honored the heavenly writings of Your Majesty concerning Caecilian and those acting under him, who are called clerics, my devoted service took care to enter them in the records of my humble office.”

And while he was reading:

**217. Bishop Petilian said:** “From where does he produce this—from the public archive or from his own [papers]?” And in another hand: “I, Bishop Petilian, have reviewed it.”

**218. Augustine, bishop of the Catholic Church, said:** “Let him read, and then let him require of us proof of the validity of this reading.” And in another hand: “I have reviewed it.”

**219. Marcellinus, most illustrious tribune and notary, said:** “Before the reading, clearly show from where you produce it.”

**220. Augustine, bishop of the Catholic Church, said:** “If they doubt this, let the archives of the proconsul be consulted.” And in another hand: “I have reviewed it.”

Marcellinus, most illustrious tribune and notary, said: “Since you have said that the matters being read are contained in the public archives, the staff, as it began, must read everything through.”

Martialis, recorder, read from the earlier records: “And she likewise urged them that, unity having been established by the agreement of all, they might appear to have been freed by every [indeed, wholly] favor [indulgence] of Your Majesty, and might devote themselves to Catholic guardianship, the reverence due to the sanctity of the law, and divine things. But after a few days certain persons appeared, having gathered with themselves a multitude of people, who thought Caecilian ought to be opposed. They offered to my authority a packet sealed in leather and an unsigned petition, and urgently requested that I send them to the sacred and venerable imperial court of Your Divinity. While Caecilian remained in his position, my humble office took care to send them, together with the appended records of those same persons, so that Your Majesty might be able to take cognizance of everything.

“I sent two petitions: one, sealed in leather, as follows: ‘Petition of the Catholic Church concerning the crimes of Caecilian, delivered by the party of Majorinus’; likewise another unsealed petition, attached to the same leather covering. Given at Carthage, on the seventeenth day before the Kalends of May, in the third consulship of our Lord Constantine Augustus.”

When this had been read:

[Col. 1402A] **221. Bishop Petilian said:** “Who is this person who is acting? Is he Caecilian’s son or not?” And in another hand: “I, Bishop Petilian, have reviewed this, reservation of appeal preserved.”

**222. Augustine, bishop of the Catholic Church, said:** “We have heard together, read together, and preach together to the peoples: ‘Call no one your father on earth.’ Why do you ask me whether I am Caecilian’s son? If Caecilian was innocent, let him rejoice in his innocence, with me rejoicing with him—not placing my hope in his innocence. But if he was guilty, as perhaps the case when examined will establish, whether in this way or another, the Church which I hold endured him, so that I might not depart from the Lord’s comparisons: as chaff on the threshing floor, as goats in the same pastures, as bad fish in the same nets. Yet because of the bad, we ought neither to abandon the Lord’s threshing floor nor, in the wicked passion of schism, break apart the Lord’s nets and leap into the sea before the time of the shore.” And in another hand: “I have reviewed it.”

**223. Marcellinus, most illustrious tribune and notary, said:** “Let everything be read through as was ordered.”

Bishop Emeritus said: “Order us to proceed.” And in another hand: “I, Bishop Emeritus, have reviewed it.”

Marcellinus, *vir clarissimus*, tribune and notary, said: “Proceed.”

Bishop Emeritus said: “The document which the opposing party produced having been read—”

And while he said, “And in another hand: I, Bishop Emeritus, have reviewed it”:

**224. Fortunatianus, bishop of the Catholic Church, said:** “Who can be the petitioner may be discovered from these records.” And in another hand: “I have reviewed it.”

[Col. 1402C] **225. Bishop Emeritus said:** “The document which the opposing party produced having been read, my colleague, in a just prosecution, declared that the person who defends Caecilian’s case in court ought to have the designation imposed upon him. But constrained by these knots, the opposing side attempts, as though on slippery ground, to flee and escape; introducing two persons and two actions into the courts.

“For he says: ‘If Caecilian’s person can be destroyed by the charges brought, it will do no harm to the Church, since, when one man’s person has been destroyed, it appears to stand in the faith.’ What need, then, most eminent sir, is there to put Caecilian’s case before the court, if it harms them in no way and does nothing against them? Or why is it defended or accused in court? For since he says that Caecilian’s guilt does not harm him and cannot attach any cloud or stain to the Church, you see that Caecilian’s name has been brought into court superfluously. For by this quasi-peremptory objection he appears to have excused himself: if Caecilian is guilty, he seems alien to the Church; if innocent, he seems, as it were, cleansed and freed from the charges alleged, and to have stood rightly in his Church.

“Judge, most eminent sir, that they ought to hold to one position. If they defend Caecilian’s case, let them take pride in themselves and prosecute those matters which are produced in court against Caecilian as truth. But if they say that what Caecilian did can do them no harm whatever, what need is there to put Caecilian’s case before the court, when it cannot harm them even if he is found in court to be most clearly guilty?” And in another hand: “I, Bishop Emeritus, have reviewed this, reservation of appeal preserved.”

Marcellinus, most illustrious tribune and notary, said: “Let the opposing party explain what is being asked.”

[Col. 1403A] **226. Augustine, bishop of the Catholic Church, said:** “They customarily allege Caecilian’s case, or that of his colleagues, against the Catholic Church itself—or, to speak without dispute, against the Church which we hold. Therefore, as I see, they wish to gain a great shortcut. If they do not allege this case against the Church which we hold, let them say what they allege against it. If nothing, why are we separated? If something besides Caecilian’s case, let them put that forward; let them show it.” And in another hand: “I have reviewed it.”

**227. Bishop Petilian said:** “Who are you? Are you Caecilian’s son or not? Does Caecilian’s crime bind you or not, if he was guilty?”

And while he said, “And in another hand: I, Bishop Petilian, have reviewed this, appeal unimpaired”:

**228. Augustine, bishop of the Catholic Church, said:** “I am in the Church in which Caecilian was.” And in another hand: “I have reviewed it.”

**229. Bishop Petilian said:** “From where did you begin? Whom do you have as father? Otherwise, if you condemn your father, you acknowledge yourself to be a heretic, since you wish to have neither origin nor father.” And in another hand: “I, Bishop Petilian, have reviewed this, appeal unimpaired.”

**230. Augustine, bishop of the Catholic Church, said:** “We are in the Church in which Caecilian held the episcopate and died. We recite his name at the altar; we share in his commemoration as the commemoration of a brother, not as that of a father or mother. But you ask me from where my communion takes its beginning.

“The Lord Christ himself establishes the beginning of my communion, saying: ‘It was necessary that Christ should suffer and rise from the dead on the third day, and that repentance and remission of sins should be preached in his name among all nations, beginning from Jerusalem.’ This preaching began from Jerusalem; from that most illustrious beginning it spread abroad, spreading the Church which we hold. First through nearby places, then through remote places, it came even into Africa. We open our eyes to this Church; in divine utterances and testimonies we find it, just as we find the Lord Christ himself and our Redeemer. No man’s crimes and no man’s slanders shall separate me from that God as Father and from this Church as Mother.” And in another hand: “I have reviewed it.”

**231. Bishop Petilian said:** “Is Caecilian your father or mother, as you said?” And in another hand: “I, Bishop Petilian, have reviewed this, appeal unimpaired.”

**232. Augustine, bishop of the Catholic Church, said:** “You have already heard that he was a brother.” And in another hand: “I have reviewed it.”

Bishop Petilian said: “A brother is not one who begets children.” And in another hand: “I, Bishop Petilian, have reviewed this, appeal unimpaired.”

[Col. 1403D] **233. Marcellinus, most illustrious tribune and notary, said:** “By a most explicit prosecution he has declared that Caecilian is neither his father nor his mother.”

Augustine, bishop of the Catholic Church, said: “Caecilian is not my father. If he is good, he is my good brother; if he is bad, he is my bad brother. Yet, because of the sacraments, he is a brother, whether good or bad.” And in another hand: “I have reviewed it.”

Marcellinus, most illustrious tribune and notary, said: “That it may be more carefully demonstrated that Caecilian was neither his father nor his mother, let his earlier prosecution be reread.”

[Col. 1404A] **234. Bishop Petilian said:** “You defend them sufficiently, by God.” And in another hand: “I, Bishop Petilian, have reviewed this, appeal unimpaired.”

**235. Augustine, bishop of the Catholic Church, said:** “Behold, I say—and I say it as often as they wish—Caecilian is not my father, because I hear my Lord saying: ‘Call no one your father on earth: one is your Father, God.’ I call Caecilian a brother: a good brother if he is good; a bad brother if he is bad, since by reason of the sacraments we share he is my brother.

“But if you wish to hear my judgment concerning him, I believe him innocent; I think he was attacked by false accusations—but I think this as a man judging about a man, not as one believing something certain. If you allege Caecilian’s crimes against the Church, I stand and defend him as a brother, showing that they do not belong to the Church or to its case and do not prejudice it. Thus I show that you allege nothing against the Catholic Church, even if the charges against Caecilian are perhaps true—which you will by no means be able to demonstrate.

“But if you cannot demonstrate even that they are true, you see, even by your own judgment, where you have remained and what, after casting away the passionate spirit of error, you ought finally to choose: that you may hold the truth with us and, with error condemned, embrace charity with us.” And in another hand: “I have reviewed it.”

**236. Bishop Petilian said:** “These are those same ambiguities with which he has proceeded from the beginning of today’s session; yet he has never professed at any point that he holds one alternative, although he embraces both in a great grasp, fearing either to relinquish or to maintain either one. Let him at last say more plainly whether they regard Caecilian as father, from whom this offspring has been derived. For no thing can be born without its begetter, begin without its head, or grow without its root.

“Your Nobility sees, therefore, that he has repeatedly professed himself to have no origin. If, then, he has no origin, he is all the more a heretic: he has no father, and by his own judgment has condemned the father he had. Therefore, let him agree that, if his father is shown to have been guilty, the crimes bind him; but if innocent, he must necessarily be the son of an innocent man. And conversely, he must necessarily be the son of a guilty man if he is shown to have been guilty.” And in another hand: “I, Bishop Petilian, have reviewed this, appeal unimpaired.”

[Col. 1404D] **237. Augustine, bishop of the Catholic Church, said:** “I have a head, but it is Christ.”

Marcellinus, most illustrious tribune and notary, said: “Let it be more carefully demonstrated whether you say that Caecilian is your father or mother, as has been asked.”

Augustine, bishop of the Catholic Church, said: “I have a head, but it is Christ, whose Apostle I hear.”

And while he said, “And in another hand: I have reviewed it”:

**238. Bishop Petilian said:** “Who ordained you to be a bishop?” And in another hand: “I, Bishop Petilian, have reviewed it, the effect of appeal preserved.”

**239. Bishop Montanus said:** “And what of the Apostle Paul’s statement: ‘Even if you have ten thousand pedagogues in Christ, you do not have many fathers. For in Christ Jesus I begot you through the Gospel’?”

**240. And when they were shouting, Alypius, bishop of the Catholic Church, said:** “Let the disturbance be entered into the record.” And in another hand: “I have reviewed it.”

**241. Marcellinus, most illustrious tribune and notary, said:** “Answer what has been asked.”

**242. Augustine, bishop of the Catholic Church, said:** “I have a head, but it is Christ, whose Apostle I hear saying: ‘All things are yours, but you are Christ’s, and Christ is God’s.’ Indeed, where the Apostle called himself a father, lest we should suppose that the basis of that fatherhood was human frailty, he added: ‘Through the Gospel I begot you.’ Thus the seed, and the source of my seed, is derived from the Gospel.

“For the sake of honor, we call fathers those who have preceded us either in time or in merits. It is another matter when we ask whom we have as father for faith, whom we have as father for eternal salvation, whom we have as father for retaining the Church and receiving God’s promises. For this is a matter of honor: daily we say ‘Father’ to old men. Daily also we say ‘Brother’ to certain persons who are not with us in one Church or established in the same sacraments. Lot even said to the Sodomites, ‘Brothers,’ certainly to soften their violence, not because he acknowledged brotherhood or a shared inheritance, as it were.

“Therefore remove these matters. Let us distinguish the titles owed to human beings for honor from the title we seek for salvation. For eternal salvation, with the Apostle’s permission—or rather at the Apostle’s command—I say that the Apostle is not my father, since he tells me: ‘I planted, Apollos watered, but God gave the increase. Therefore neither he who plants is anything nor he who waters, but God who gives the increase.’

“Of this the Lord said: ‘Do not call anyone your father on earth.’ He certainly knew that the Apostle would say, ‘Through the Gospel I begot you.’ For the Apostle would not have been opposed to the Lord when the Lord said, ‘Do not call anyone your father on earth,’ by saying, ‘Though you have many fathers, through the Gospel I begot you.’ But because the Lord distinguished for what purpose he appointed a father for us, and for what honor we could receive the Apostle as father, the Apostle spoke thus, so that his speech would not contradict the Lord’s truth.

“Whatever fathers I acknowledge on earth, I acknowledge for the sake of honor. I recognize no father of my salvation except God, of whom the Lord said to me, ‘Do not call anyone your father on earth’; and [God] to whom we daily say, ‘Our Father who art in heaven.’” And in another hand: “I have reviewed it.”

[Col. 1405D] **243. Bishop Petilian said:** “Let the one who ordained him be named. Let him say who ordained him.” And in another hand: “I, Bishop Petilian, have reviewed this, appeal unimpaired.”

Marcellinus, most illustrious tribune and notary, said: “His ordainer is being sought. Let it be more clearly indicated who ordained him.”

Possidius, bishop of the Catholic Church, said: “Whom?”

[Col. 1406A] **244. Fortunatianus, bishop of the Catholic Church, said:** “We do not sufficiently see what the ordainer of any bishop has to do with the case of the truth. It is taught by divine testimonies that God is Father.” And in another hand: “I have reviewed it.”

Bishop Petilian said: “Let the person who ordained him, as he is called, state it.” And in another hand: “I, Bishop Petilian, have reviewed this, appeal unimpaired.”

Alypius, bishop of the Catholic Church, said: “Whom did he ordain? Many of us stand here; many have undertaken the defense of the case according to the tenor of the mandate. Let the opposing party explain whose ordainer he seeks, or whom he seeks, so that we may see whether it is fitting to answer these questions.” And in another hand: “I have reviewed it.”

**245. Bishop Adeodatus said:** “Augustine said these things. Let him say who ordained him.” And in another hand: “I, Bishop Adeodatus, have reviewed this, reservation of appeal preserved.”

Possidius, bishop of the Catholic Church, said: “We have not undertaken to defend Augustine’s case alone, whatever kind of case he has.”

And while he said, “And in another hand: I have reviewed it”:

Bishop Adeodatus said: “This is evidence of a desperate case: when we ask for one thing, other things are answered; because they cannot answer the allegations, they seek other things by which to weave mists. Therefore let Augustine say who ordained him.” And in another hand: “I, Bishop Adeodatus, have reviewed this, reservation of appeal preserved.”

Augustine, bishop of the Catholic Church, said: “I see that superfluous matters are being sought.”

And while he said, “And in another hand: I have reviewed it”:

**246. Marcellinus, most illustrious tribune and notary, said:** “Deign to answer the questions.”

**247. Augustine, bishop of the Catholic Church, said:** “I see that superfluous matters are being sought by our brothers standing on the opposing side. Yet I do not refuse an answer even to these superfluous matters, provided that the case of the Church—to which nothing can be answered—may be placed upon its most secure foundation.

“I, whose ordainer you seek, am a Christian man, a believer, Catholic—as I speak with God as witness. Hence we still debate who is worthy to be called by that name. I defend that Church; I affirm it with whatever voice I possess—the Church in which, whatever I may be, that Church is. I see where you are aiming: you pursue human slanders; and what you customarily throw out and say is not unfamiliar to our ears or hearts.

“Megalius, primate of the Catholic Church of Numidia, ordained me, at the time when he was able to ordain me. Behold, I have answered. Proceed; bring forth what you have prepared. There too you will appear slanderous. Behold, I have named my ordainer. Now bring forward your slanders.” And in another hand: “I have reviewed it.”

[Col. 1406D] **248. Marcellinus, most illustrious tribune and notary, said:** “You have received the prosecution. Therefore deign to answer as is fitting, although these matters concerning persons ought not to delay the investigation.”

**249. Bishop Emeritus said:** “If there is no proceeding concerning persons, why do they make mention of Caecilian in court? Either they rightly fear what they seek to excuse in him; or, if the superfluous action brought against Caecilian frees their character and purges their life, they ought to prove this very point by legal testimonies.

“For we say, on the basis of many legal documents, that the faults of priests, shameful conduct, and wicked manner of life always bring a stain or wrinkle upon the Church. For why does the Apostle say, ‘Having neither spot nor wrinkle’? And again: ‘A bishop must be blameless’? The divine law is also set forth by many documents, through which the blameless life of a pastor ought to be demonstrated by heavenly testimonies.

“But lest I create weariness in the hearing through the length of my prosecution, or perhaps pass over matters pertinent to the case, since we have in our hands a collection drawn from every direction, uniform in its divine authorities, let Your Power order read against their mandate—which they said was composed according to law—that same body [of material], so that, after the presentation of our prosecution and the reading of the petition or letters which we request to be examined in court, we may deal specifically with all matters belonging to our side.” And in another hand: “I, Bishop Emeritus, have reviewed this, reservation of appeal preserved.”

[Col. 1407B] **250. Marcellinus, most illustrious tribune and notary, said:** “I had wished first to establish, by the reading of the records, that it might be shown most clearly who stood in the position of petitioner. But if you wish me to depart from that point, clearly show that the matters you offer ought to be read.”

**251. Bishop Montanus said:** “Meanwhile, order them read, and we shall answer.” And in another hand: “I, Bishop Montanus, have reviewed my prosecution, reservation of appeal preserved.”

Marcellinus, most illustrious tribune and notary, said: “Let them be read.”

Romulus, recorder, read: “To Flavius Marcellinus, most illustrious and distinguished tribune and notary: Januarianus and the other bishops of the Catholic truth, which suffers persecution and does not inflict it. Because in the proceedings before Your Nobility we entrusted the defense to our brothers and colleagues—”

And while he was reading:

[Col. 1407C] **252. Marcellinus, most illustrious tribune and notary, said:** “So far as is shown by the opening of this letter which is produced, I see that another mandate has now again been submitted. For after confirmation of the persons, all matters belonging to the parties ought to have been made known to the court in your name, since after a mandate had once been given by them, the business is established to have passed on.”

**253. Bishop Emeritus said:** “They said that they had set out every legal matter in their mandate. We establish these same legal matters by legal writings. Nothing is outside the mandate. Indeed, we ask this in order that Your Excellence may grant a hearing.” And in another hand: “I, Bishop Emeritus, have reviewed this, reservation of appeal preserved.”

Marcellinus, most illustrious tribune and notary, said: “I did not forbid these matters to be produced; but it would have been more proper for them to be produced in your name, by those who stand here.”

Bishop Emeritus said: “Since the action belongs to us, it makes no difference with regard to the document of mandate whether it is produced in our person or by those who commissioned us, provided that you order this very document to be read.” And in another hand: “I, Bishop Emeritus, have reviewed this, reservation of appeal preserved.”

**254. Marcellinus, most illustrious tribune and notary, said:** “Let them be read. For I seem to have made this observation lest I omit anything that was required by law.”

Romulus, recorder, read: “It is a great indication of a just judge that he has granted [something] to one party—”

And while he was reading:

[Col. 1408A] **255. Bishop Emeritus said:** “He does not read; he does not distinguish the sense.” And in another hand: “I, Bishop Emeritus, have reviewed it.”

**256. Augustine, bishop of the Catholic Church, said:** “Let them themselves read. Let us grant them what they were unwilling to grant us.”

Marcellinus, most illustrious tribune and notary, said: “Let the ecclesiastical notaries read these matters through, so that what the venerable men have offered may be more clearly indicated.”

Possidius, bishop of the Catholic Church, said: “Let it be entered in writing that they requested that the records which they produce be read by their own notaries.” And in another hand: “I have reviewed it.”

Marcellinus, most illustrious tribune and notary, said: “It makes no difference by whom they are read.”

Bishop Petilian said: “The reliability of the staff is not in doubt, but its pronunciation.” And in another hand: “I, Bishop Petilian, have reviewed it.”

[Col. 1408B] **257. Marcellinus, most illustrious tribune and notary, said:** “This objection is superfluous. Therefore, in order that everything may be more carefully understood, let that which has been offered be read by the ecclesiastical notaries.”

Alypius, bishop of the Catholic Church, said: “Let it be read, since we grant what they were unwilling to grant us.”

Bishop Habetdeus said: “I shall read.”

Marcellinus, most illustrious tribune and notary, said: “Read.”

258. Bishop Habetdeus said: “To Flavius Marcellinus, most illustrious and distinguished tribune and notary, Januarianus and the other bishops of the Catholic truth—which suffers persecution, not inflicts it. Since, in the proceedings before your nobility, we have entrusted our defence to our brethren and colleagues, it is the mark of a great and just judge to grant to one party what he does not deny to the other, lest he seem to favour one party and oppress the other. This, in accordance with your prudence, it is fitting that you should both foresee from afar and, still more fittingly, guard against more remotely—especially since by edicts you invite the peoples to judge concerning the balance of your hearing.

“Accordingly, when our adversaries—our traditors and persecutors—were submitting into the proceedings the carefully composed volume of their petition, long conceived and set forth, you willingly heard it, without prejudice to us. We earnestly request that you grant the same to this letter of ours. Not because their warped and perverse doctrine alarms us, but lest it be burdensome for our defenders to contend against their lengthy book and their pleadings, when neither an entire day suffices for the case, nor voice or strength for the defence, so that book may contend with book and defence with defence. Therefore we ask that you order this letter of ours to be received and entered, and then deign to hear the case.

“For our adversaries, after running through testimonies in which the Church is everywhere spread abroad to its own praise, first instruct their defenders to accomplish this against us, who defend the Church’s purity: namely, to assert that the same Church is foretold as having good and bad persons mingled together within it until the end of the age. Against this we demonstrate more fully that the Church of the Lord is proclaimed in the divine Scriptures as holy and unstained everywhere.

“Through Isaiah: ‘Arise, Zion; put on your strength, Jerusalem, holy city: the uncircumcised and unclean shall no longer pass through you’ (Isa. 52).

“And again: ‘Say to the daughter of Zion: Behold, your Saviour shall come to you, having his reward and his work before his face; and he shall call them a holy people, redeemed by the Lord. But you shall be called the city desired, and not forsaken’ (Isa. 62).

“And again: ‘Strengthen feeble hands, and strengthen weak knees. You who are faint-hearted, do not fear. Our Lord will repay judgment; he himself shall come and save us. Then the eyes of the blind shall be opened, and the ears of the deaf shall hear; the tongue of the dumb shall be made plain, and the lame shall leap like a stag, because water has burst forth in the desert and a spring in the thirsty land’ (Isa. 35).

“And he added: ‘There shall be a clean way there, and it shall be called holy; no unclean person shall pass through it, nor shall there be an unclean way there. Nor shall there be a lion there, nor shall any evil beast ascend upon it, nor be found there; but the redeemed and chosen shall walk there.’

“Of this Church it is written in the Song of Songs, in the person of the Lord: ‘You are altogether beautiful, my sister, and there is no reproach in you’ (Song 4). This the Apostle Paul demonstrated most plainly, saying: ‘Christ loved the Church and gave himself for her, that he might sanctify her, cleansing her by the washing of water in the word, and joining her to himself as a glorious Church, not having spot or wrinkle or anything of the kind, but holy and unstained’ (Eph. 5). And again: ‘For I have betrothed you to one husband, to present you as a holy virgin to Christ’ (2 Cor. 11).

“Despising and rejecting, therefore, so many and such great testimonies concerning the purity of the Church, which was promised through the Spirit, they improperly affirm, from the comparison of the tares, that evil persons will remain in it among the good. Yet the Lord himself interpreted that comparison to his Apostles, saying: ‘He who sows the good seed is the Son of Man. The field is this world; the good seed are the children of the kingdom; the tares are the children of the evil one; the enemy who sows them is the devil; the harvest is the consummation of the age; and the reapers are angels’ (Matt. 13). And so forth.

“‘The field,’ he says, ‘is the world.’ Therefore it is not the Church but the world in which good and bad alike are reserved until the harvest—that is, until the divine judgment. For what has been interpreted by the Lord cannot indeed be corrupted. If the Apostles, companions of the Lord himself, had learned that tares—that is, sons of the devil—sprouting within the Church were to be left in communion with the saints, they would never have expelled Simon, Erastus, Philetus, Alexander, Demas, Hermogenes, and others like them from the thresholds of the Church. Indeed, if this were so, the whole proclamation of the divine Scriptures would be void, by which the polluted are commanded to be separated from the midst of the saints through the diligence of the priests. For the Lord says through Moses: ‘It shall be an everlasting ordinance throughout your generations, to distinguish between holy and profane, between clean and unclean’ (Lev. 10). Elsewhere the Spirit rebukes the neglect of this duty in the persons of the priests, saying: ‘Her priests rejected my law; they profaned my holy things; they did not distinguish between clean and unclean, and did not separate between holy and polluted’ (Ezek. 22).

“To this parable the adversaries also add that chaff ought to remain together with wheat in the Church. Jeremiah refutes this, saying: ‘What has chaff to do with wheat?’ And the Apostle Paul: ‘What share has faith with the unbeliever, or what fellowship has light with darkness?’ (1 Cor. 6). And Solomon: ‘If a wolf ever has fellowship with a lamb, so does a sinner with a righteous man’ (Ecclus. 13).

“They also maintain that good and bad fish are held and drawn together in one net until the shore—that is, righteous and unrighteous persons until the end of the age—without observing that this was said of hidden offenders. For when the net is cast into the sea, what it contains is unknown to fishermen—that is, to priests—until, when it has been drawn to shore, the good or bad are disclosed for sorting. Thus also those who are hidden, established in the Church, and unknown to priests, are exposed at the divine judgment and, like bad fish, are separated from the fellowship of the saints. So the Lord speaks figuratively in the Gospel concerning a hidden offender who had deceived the priests by stealth: ‘When the king entered to see those reclining, he saw there a man not wearing a wedding garment, and said to him: Friend, how did you come in here? But he was silent. And the king said to his servants: Bind him hand and foot, and cast him into the outer darkness; there shall be weeping and gnashing of teeth’ (Matt. 12).

“Accordingly, on this reasoning they have said in vain that the good should not be abandoned because of the bad by a sacrilegious separation, but that the bad should be tolerated because of the good by a pious unity. For the Lord shows elsewhere, in his indignation, that he is disturbed by this profane intermixture and provokes the greatest separation: ‘Because the whole house of Israel has become an intermixture to me—all bronze, silver, iron, tin, and lead mixed together in the midst of a burning furnace—therefore,’ he says, ‘thus says the Lord: Because you have all become one intermixture, therefore I will gather you into the midst of Jerusalem. As bronze, silver, iron, tin, and lead are gathered into the midst of a furnace to blow upon them with fire so that they may be melted, so I shall gather you in my wrath; I shall burn you and blow upon you with the blast of the fire of my wrath, and you shall be melted in its midst; and you shall know that I am the Lord, who poured out my wrath upon you’ (Ezek. 22).

“Against these and similar passages by which the Church of God is defended from contamination by the mingling of unclean persons, it is clear with what conscience the adversaries defend their errors and refuse to distinguish evil persons from the communion of the good. They proceed most openly to blaspheme, asserting that the Church cannot be stained by the sins even of manifestly evil persons; and they cite the examples of the prophets, who, although they rebuked such persons for their sins, nevertheless did not separate themselves bodily from them. Yet we show that that time was quite different, when persons were permitted to repeat baptism as often as they sinned.

“Nevertheless, even so, the same prophets are found to have abstained from communion with evil persons. Thus the prophet [uncertain: ‘Sophonias’ may be an OCR corruption] was sent to Jeroboam, who was established in schism, and was commanded to accept neither bread nor water; having been deceived and having violated the command, he was killed by a lion. Elijah also and Elisha never communicated with or consented to the schismatic altars of Samaria, but for the most part lived in solitude. Hosea too is shown not to have participated in the mysteries of those whose sacrifices he detests and condemns, saying: ‘Their sacrifices are like bread of mourning. Everyone who touches them shall be defiled’ (Hos. 9). Finally, how could Amos have mingled in Samaria’s mysteries, when the false prophet thus stirred up the king’s hostility against him: ‘Amos is gathering a conspiracy against you in the midst of the house of Israel. The land cannot bear his words’; and for this reason he was even expelled (Amos 7).

“Moreover, in Jerusalem itself, how could the prophets participate in the sacrifices of sinful men which they themselves, filled with the divine Spirit, condemned? Isaiah says: ‘What is the multitude of your sacrifices to me? says the Lord. I am full. I do not desire the burnt offerings of rams, nor the fat of lambs, nor the blood of bulls and goats; do not come thus into my presence. For who has required these things from your hands? You shall no longer tread my court. If you bring fine flour, it is vain. Incense is an abomination to me. I cannot endure your new moons, sabbaths, and great day. My soul hates your fasts, holidays, and feast days. For you have become a great burden to me. I will no longer spare your sins. When you stretch out your hands, I shall turn my eyes away from you; and if you multiply prayers, I shall not hear you. For your hands are full of blood’ (Isa. 1).

“And again: ‘The criminal who sacrifices me a calf is as one who kills a dog; and he who offers fine flour, as one who offers swine’s blood; and he who offers incense in memorial, as a blasphemer’ (Isa. 66). Haggai also utterly abominates not merely sacrifices but the sinful people themselves, saying: ‘So is this people, and so is this nation; and if anyone approaches there, he shall be defiled’ (Hag. 2). And Malachi: ‘You, O priests, who profane my name, have said: “How have we profaned your name?” By placing polluted breads upon my altar; and you have said: “How have we polluted them?” In saying: “The table of the Lord is blessed,” while you have made void what was placed upon it’ (Mal. 1).

“And so you will find in all the Prophets that, if they had communicated with those whom they condemned with such mighty voices, they would have incurred the charge of transgression. Their being among them, therefore, was a matter of dwelling, not of communion.

“They next take for themselves, in defence of their crime, the authority of the example of Judas the traitor. They say that he was both chosen by the Lord despite being foreknown, and tolerated despite being known. Yet Christ the Lord certainly admitted Judas into the number of the Apostles without prejudice to his own foreknowledge; and he tolerated him as known to himself, not to men, for the same reason by which he seems today to endure hidden persons. For it is written: ‘What is hidden belongs to me; what is manifest belongs to you and your children’ (Deut. 29). In the Psalms: ‘Will not God inquire into these things? For he himself knows the secrets of the heart’ (Ps. 43). In Kings: ‘Man sees the face, but God sees the heart’ (1 Sam. 16). And in the Apocalypse: ‘And all the Churches shall know that I am the searcher of reins and heart’ (Rev. 17).
