“Finally, when the Lord was reclining with his disciples and said, ‘One of you will betray me’ (Matt. 26), and Judas himself replied, ‘Is it I, Lord?’ and heard from the Lord, ‘You have said it’ (Mark 14), he immediately saw that he had been exposed and departed in confusion; but afterwards he came with the very crowd to betray the Lord. Let the enemies of the Lord’s truth, who in their accustomed way labour to defend the most manifest offenders, then go with their patron Judas.

“Again, in defence of their polluted intermixture, they object the words of the Apostle, by which he says: ‘Whether by pretext or by truth, I will have mercy, because they are children of fornication, because their mother has committed fornication; she who bore them has disgraced them’ (Phil. 1). And in Isaiah: ‘As a garment sprinkled with blood shall not be clean, so neither shall you be clean, because you have destroyed my land and killed my people. You shall not remain for everlasting time, evil seed. Prepare your children to be slain for the sins of their father, lest they rise again’ (Isa. 14). And in the Third Book of Kings: ‘And Solomon removed Abiathar from the priesthood of the Lord, so that the word of the Lord which he spoke concerning the house of Eli in Shiloh might be fulfilled’ (3 Kings 2).

“Further, what they say—that Christ’s baptism is defended just as the Catholic Church herself is defended everywhere, and exists among all persons—is summarily excluded by the decrees of our most blessed martyr-fathers. How carelessly, moreover—forgetting themselves—the enemies of truth contend that baptism administered among thieves, robbers, and any outsiders ought to be accepted, adducing for this matter the wholly unsuitable testimony of the Apostle: ‘Who hold the truth of God in unrighteousness’ (Rom. 1). In this place they have wished to defend theft with a thievish testimony. For the Apostle, speaking of Gentiles and rebuking unbelievers, said: ‘For the wrath of God shall be revealed from heaven against all impiety and unrighteousness of those who hold the truth of God in unrighteousness, because what may be known of God is manifest to them; for God has manifested it to them. For his invisible things, from the foundation of the world, are perceived through the things that have been made; likewise his everlasting power and divinity, so that they are without excuse. For although they knew God, they did not honour him as God or give thanks, but became vain in their thoughts, and their foolish heart was darkened. Claiming to be wise, they became foolish; and they changed the glory of the incorruptible God into the likeness of an image of corruptible man, birds, four-footed creatures, and serpents. Therefore God gave them over, in the desires of their heart, to uncleanness’ (Rom. 1).

“According to this interpretation, therefore, they profess that they also receive the defiled mysteries of the Gentiles. They have followed their error by piling up the most obvious blasphemies, saying that those who reject the baptism of heretics are capable of rejecting Christ, whom demons confessed. In this they not only insult the decrees of the holy martyrs, but are readier to mingle in communion with demons because they confessed Christ.

“But when, with subtle brevity, they said that one baptized outside must be received, not so that what is lacking may be present, but so that what is present may be useful, they show that they have entrapped themselves in both respects. For all these points, as has been said above, are nullified by the judgments of the holy martyrs. How can it be, if there is one Church and Christ is undivided, that a person outside may obtain baptism?

“Then, regarding what they say is objected to them by us—‘Lay hands hastily on no one, nor share in the sins of others’ (1 Tim. 5)—they answer as though men ought to be separated from evil persons in conduct rather than in body. Against this we prove, through very many legal testimonies, that persons ought to be separated from evil people not only in conduct but also bodily. In Numbers: ‘Depart from the tents of these most stubborn men, and touch nothing belonging to them, lest you too perish together with them in all their sins’ (Num. 16). Again, Isaiah: ‘Depart, go out from there, and touch no unclean thing; depart from the midst of those who bear the vessels of the Lord’ (Isa. 52). Again, the Apostle: ‘For you are the temple of the living God. For he himself says: “I shall dwell in them and walk in them, and I shall be their God, and they shall be my people. Therefore depart from their midst and be separated, and touch no unclean thing; and I shall receive you, and I shall be a father to you, and you shall be sons and daughters to me,” says the Lord Almighty’ (2 Cor. 6).

“What, moreover, is this: although we charge them with persecutions and monstrous cruelties by which they and their forefathers have, for one hundred years or more without interruption, afflicted and harassed us and our fathers, they are not ashamed to advance this defence—that certain Maximianists among our people inflicted persecutions? Yet it is certainly one thing to have sought, by civil means, to recover usurped ecclesiastical property and the property of the poor, while compelling no unwilling person to join our communion; and quite another to perpetrate every cruelty with open frenzy throughout the whole Christian people. For who does not know that these our traditors and persecutors, from the very beginning of their condemned betrayal, have through fabricated petitions supplicated all the rulers of this age for our death, and have constrained persons into their communion, contrary to God’s commands, by threats and proscriptions?

“For, not to mention how much Christian blood was shed through Leontius, Ursatius, Macarius, Paul, Taurinus, Romanus, and the other agents whom they obtained from the rulers of the age for the slaughter of the saints—when very many venerable priests were killed, others relegated into exile, Christianity widely harassed, consecrated virginity violated, the rich proscribed, the poor despoiled, basilicas taken away, and fugitive priests driven into flight—no one is unaware how much they have perpetrated in our own time. They have forced exile upon bishops, driven fleeing Christians over precipices, oppressed peoples, plundered clergy, seized basilicas, and inflicted beatings upon those unwilling to consent. Finally, in the single town of Bagaï alone, much Christian blood was shed on their account; and even so, not satisfied, they continue even to the present day and are content not to cease.

“Since it would be superfluous to append from the divine Scriptures testimonies against such extremely bitter charges of their monstrous cruelty, by which these crimes are forbidden, when they are not permitted even by secular laws, let it suffice that we have answered their error and washed away by divine testimonies what they have answered superfluously.”

And in another hand: “May the Lord preserve you safe, as we desire. I have read it.”

259. Marcellinus, most illustrious tribune and notary, said: “What has been read shall be attached to the present proceedings.” And he added: “And since patience has been shown in this matter, let those things which were offered earlier be read; and let the opposing party be compelled to answer all these matters.”

260. Bishop Emeritus said: “First let them refute testimonies with testimonies. Then we must proceed to those matters which your Highness shall judge.” And in another hand: “I, Emeritus, bishop, have reviewed it, saving my right of appeal.”

261. Augustine, bishop of the Catholic Church, said: “Allow us, exalted sir, not to linger longer over superfluities in the cause of the Church. Would that our brethren standing on the opposing side had produced this letter before all those delaying speeches of theirs, so that by now we might have dealt with something concerning the Church, on which the case turns.

“Your nobility has observed, then, that this letter contains two kinds of matters or objections to which we must reply: one concerning the divine Scriptures and the utterances of the holy Law; the other concerning human accusations, which I do not know who thought should be advanced more maliciously than truthfully. With the Lord’s help, we shall answer these two matters briefly, lest we repay such lengthiness with a lengthy speech.

“The question is whether the Church was foretold as destined to have evil persons mingled within it until the end, or rather to contain only good persons, all holy and unstained, in this age and at this very time, until the final end of the age. Both sets of testimonies are divine; and surely they ought not, nor indeed can they, be contradictory if they find an interpreter. I did not say that the Church is a threshing-floor. None of us did; rather, the Gospel speaks where it is written that he will come who bears the winnowing-fan in his hand and will cleanse his threshing-floor, gathering the grain into the barn.”

And while he was speaking—“And in another hand: ‘I have reviewed it’”—

262. Bishop Emeritus said: “He does not read ‘threshing-floor.’” And in another hand: “I, Bishop Emeritus, have reviewed it.”

Augustine, bishop of the Catholic Church, said: “John said: ‘He will cleanse his threshing-floor and gather the grain into the barn’ (Matt. 3:12; Luke 3:17).” And while he was speaking—“And in another hand: ‘I have reviewed it’”—Marcellinus, most illustrious tribune and notary, said: “Let what he requests be read again.”

263. Bishop Petilianus—or rather Emeritus—said: “The Evangelist said this about hidden offenders, not manifest ones, whom you want mingled with you.” And in another hand: “I, Bishop Petilianus, have reviewed it.”

264. Augustine, bishop of the Catholic Church, said: “Let our presentation be taken as a response to their letter. He began to read: no noise was made by us, no disturbance, no interruption. Let him permit me to finish what I began to say, and then let him answer. Why is not repaid to us what we granted beforehand? Your nobility observed our patience while so long a letter was being read.”

And while he was speaking—“And in another hand: ‘I have reviewed it’”—Bishop Emeritus said: “He burdens us when he calls himself patient; and he ought not to render judgment about himself, when another is judging him.” And in another hand: “I, Bishop Emeritus, have reviewed it.”

265. Augustine, bishop of the Catholic Church, said: “Oh, if you too were patient until I finish what I am pursuing! Therefore, as I had begun to say, the testimonies concerning tares and wheat which they attempted to interpret are divine. Yet regarding the nets they have at some point admitted that the Church will contain bad persons as well as good; but they said that such persons are unknown to priests and therefore do not prejudice the good because they are unknown.

“I, however, could show by arguments proportionate to my very limited ability that the truer interpretation is that the Church has both good and bad persons, namely tares and wheat; and that the world itself is called by the name of the Church, since the Lord himself says: ‘Not that he should judge the world, but that the world might be saved through him’ (John 3), whereas we know that the Lord saves none but the Church.” And in another hand: “I have reviewed it.”

266. Bishop Emeritus said: “‘The world did not know you.’ Therefore the Church did not acknowledge God, if the world is the Church. And again he said: ‘That the whole world may become guilty before God’ (1 John 5). And again he said: ‘If you were of the world, the world would love what was its own; but now, because you are not of the world, therefore the world hates and persecutes you’ (John 15). And again: ‘They are of the world, and the world obeys them’ (1 John 4). And again: ‘If anyone loves the world, the love of the Father is not in him’ (ibid., 2).” And in another hand: “I, Bishop Emeritus, have reviewed it, saving my right of appeal.”

267. Augustine, bishop of the Catholic Church, said: “We too could say all these things and resolve them as apparently contrary to what was first proposed. Thus they interrupt with this clamour without cause, since we might have done the same to their letter so that it could not be read. Let them listen patiently. Let them be admonished by your Highness to do what they ought voluntarily to have done. Let them listen patiently. The matter which we are handling is not trivial. Today, with God’s help, we have undertaken to answer their lengthy letter. Nor do we ask that it be given to us for consideration, that we may answer afterward, as they did with our petition. Let them grant us some patience, for the sake of your welfare.” And in another hand: “I have reviewed it.”

Marcellinus, most illustrious tribune and notary, said: “What is requested is just. It is certainly proper that patience be afforded to this presentation.”

268. Bishop Emeritus said: “He himself obstructs himself by making a long presentation.” And in another hand: “I, Bishop Emeritus, have reviewed it.”

269. Alypius, bishop of the Catholic Church, said: “If they wish to answer, let the letter be removed and let each of us answer separately. Otherwise, let them permit the response.”

270. Bishop Adeodatus said: “We can grant patience.” And while he was speaking—“And in another hand: ‘I, Bishop Adeodatus, have reviewed it’”—Augustine, bishop of the Catholic Church, said: “When the letter was being read, we regarded it as if they themselves were presenting it. We afforded their presentation silence. I do not wish to call it patience, because they make that a ground of accusation. Let them likewise afford us silence.” And in another hand: “I have reviewed it.”

Bishop Adeodatus said: “We can grant patience, indeed we grant it if what the opposing party maintains has the most solid reasoning. But when the law is interpreted otherwise than it is, who can bear it, who can endure in silence a prejudicial assertion being made?” And in another hand: “I, Bishop Adeodatus, have reviewed it.”

Vincentius, bishop of the Catholic Church, said: “Keep for yourself what you may criticize if anything is contradicted.” And in another hand: “I have reviewed it.”

271. Marcellinus, *vir clarissimus*, tribune and notary, said: “Let the promised patience be afforded.”

Bishop Montanus said: “When everything is retained in the mind, how can we fail to answer point by point?” And in another hand: “I, Bishop Montanus, have reviewed it.”

Marcellinus, most illustrious tribune and notary, said: “It is agreed that the tenor of the entire letter has been heard patiently. It follows that you should deign to hear patiently the answers to its individual points.”

272. Augustine, bishop of the Catholic Church, said: “For that reason those matters were written down, and these are being recorded. If memory fails on any point, I too may ask for the letter to be read to me; and they may likewise ask for it to be read to them from the codices. Let them grant silence. Let us accomplish something.

“Therefore, as I had begun to say, prompted by them we find in the Scriptures the name ‘world’ used in a bad sense and in a good sense. The name ‘world’ in a bad sense, as they themselves said: ‘And the world did not know him’ (John 1); and, ‘If anyone loves the world, the love of the Father is not in him’ (1 John 2), and so forth. But the name ‘world’ in a good sense: ‘That the world may believe that you have sent me’ (John 17). For believing is not characteristic of evil persons. The name ‘world’ in a good sense: ‘He did not come to judge the world, but that the world might be saved through him’ (John 3). Only the Church in the world will be saved.

“Since, then, ‘world’ is used both in a good and in a bad sense, why this quarrel over the Scriptures? If it lacks an interpreter, apply the light of understanding. See in the bad sense the world as all lovers of temporal things throughout all nations; see in the good sense the world as all believers who bear the hope of eternal life throughout all nations. ‘God was in Christ,’ he says, ‘reconciling the world to himself’ (2 Cor. 5). Let those who speak judge whether that world which is detested, of which it was said that the love of Christ is not in one who loves the world, can be reconciled to God.

“Let your nobility, therefore, listen patiently. I see that Holy Scripture has prefigured the Church as containing good and bad persons intermixed, as they themselves have now admitted concerning the nets.”

And while he was speaking and there was clamour, Alypius, bishop of the Catholic Church, said: “Let it be written down that they are making a disturbance.”

273. Marcellinus, most illustrious tribune and notary, said: “Let the proceedings record that they are making a disturbance.”

Alypius, bishop of the Catholic Church, said: “Where is the patience promised, and what reciprocity is being rendered? Do they not show how they disagree?” And in another hand: “I have reviewed it.”

274. Bishop Petilianus said: “What the world is and what the Church is has been defined most clearly by the very Author and Maker of the world, through whom all things were made and without whom nothing was made. For the Lord himself said: ‘The field is the world’ (Matt. 13). He could have said: ‘The world is the Church.’ Who, then, among men dares to define what the world is, when the Lord himself, its maker and craftsman, has already deigned to define it?” And in another hand: “I, Bishop Petilianus, have reviewed it.”

275. Marcellinus, most illustrious tribune and notary, said: “Show clearly what the world is which is said to be saved.”

276. Bishop Petilianus said: “Man is called ‘world’ where it says ‘reconciling the world to himself’; for God wished to reconcile to himself not beasts but men.” And in another hand: “I, Bishop Petilianus, have reviewed it.”

277. Marcellinus, most illustrious tribune and notary, said: “Do you say that the Church can consist of all those who are designated by the name ‘world,’ as will later be made clear, or do you deny it?”

278. Bishop Emeritus said: “You are drawing us away from a manifest prescription. Christ the Lord says in the Gospel: ‘The field is the world.’” And while he was speaking—“And in another hand: ‘I, Bishop Emeritus, have reviewed it’”—Marcellinus, most illustrious tribune and notary, said: “Permit them, then, to answer all that the text of the letter contains, and afterward I shall judge everything most fully.”

279. Hilarus, recorder, said: “Since the parties have been proceeding from dawn, and we have filled two codices, if your Excellency commands it, let other recorders be substituted for us, so that we may go out to compare the texts, guards having been assigned to us.”

Vitalis, notary of the Catholic Church, said: “I too submit what the recorder standing beside your nobility has proposed.”

280. Marcellinus, most illustrious tribune and notary, said: “As was also done at the previous hearing, let those who state that they have filled their tablets go out with guards, and let others be substituted in their place.”

And while this was being done:

281. Augustine, bishop of the Catholic Church, said: “The world, then, is understood in human beings—for it could not appear otherwise even to us. We are surely not so foolish as to say that beasts and any irrational animals belong to the salvation promised by Christ. We state precisely this: ‘The world lies in the evil one’: these are human beings. ‘That the world may believe that you sent me’: these are human beings. ‘Reconciling the world to himself’: these are human beings; and likewise the other things said in a bad sense—those human beings, those human beings.

“For throughout the whole world both kinds are present, the bad mingled with the good. Thus the Church also, which they have admitted is signified by the name of nets and contains bad persons—though they said that sinners are concealed—is now shown to contain good and bad persons. The question is whether, as regards concealment and non-concealment, it has belonged to the piety of good persons also to tolerate known evil persons lest they abandon the good, or whether, because evil persons appeared in the Church, they wished to abandon the whole body. That is the question. This is what we prove.

“For we say that ecclesiastical discipline must certainly not be neglected, and that wherever evil persons are exposed, they must be restrained in order that they may be corrected—not only by the word of correction, but also by excommunications and degradations—so that they may seek a humble place of salvation in the Church. This is done as a remedy for them, not out of hatred, but from concern for their brethren’s salvation; as the Apostle himself states most clearly in a certain passage: ‘If anyone does not obey our word by this letter, mark that person, and do not associate with him.’

**Note.** Since what followed has dropped out in the collection of the *Acts*, it may, if desired, be sought in St Augustine’s third book of the *Brief Account of the Conference with the Donatists*. See vol. IX, chapter 9 of this third book, col. 652, no. 16, beginning with the words: “When, therefore, the Catholics demanded their patience,” etc.

## Judgment of the Cognitor
Flavius Marcellinus, most illustrious man, tribune and notary, said:

I should indeed wish—and this is what I now desire with the entire intention of my prayers—that, just as great joy has arisen from the demonstration of truth and the eventual exposure of error, so great rejoicing might arise from the conversion from ancient superstition and from a judgment changed for the better. For who can doubt that there is great joy when an unexpected cure comes to a long-established sickness, and that restored health creates in such cases a greater cause for exultation than health continuously retained? But since the obstinacy of ruined minds, which the bonds of an equally perverse persuasion had bound, either feigns not to return to the way of salvation that has been shown, or—what is worse—fears to do so out of shamelessness, the sentence of the laws must now be brought forth and enforced, so that those whom milder remedies do not recall to sound health, after the truth has been plainly disclosed face to face, may be restored by a sharper application of cure.

For to whom would reason itself, as the appended sequence of proceedings demonstrates, and as the examples contained in the divine writings also attest, not clearly show that no one can in any way become liable for the guilt of another’s crime, even if that crime could be proved; and that the condition of the universal Church ought not to be overthrown by the accusation against Caecilian, against whom nothing blameworthy could be established; nor that the judgment pronounced against him by those who separated themselves from the body of the Church could have availed to prejudice him—just as the condemnation pronounced in recent times by the Maximianists against Primian in his absence did not avail to harm him? And for whom, for the purpose of correction, would the proof, established by so many judgments, that Donatus was the author of the schism, the acquittal and vindication of Caecilian, the final judgment of Constantine of triumphant memory—in which both Caecilian’s innocence and the calumnious accusation of Donatus and his associates are set forth more plainly—and likewise the vindication of Felix of Aptunga, Caecilian’s ordainer, demonstrated by the records of the proconsular judgment, not be sufficient in every respect?

Accordingly, if these matters, so clear and manifest, cannot cure an inveterate disease, the discharge of a festering wound must be restrained, so that, with freedom cut off, it may begin to harm only itself, since this is what it chooses. For by these means it will eventually wish to be healed. Let falsehood, now uncovered, therefore bow its neck to declared truth.

Accordingly, by the authority of this edict I admonish all men of rank, the owners of estates, agents, lessees both of the imperial domain and of private possessions, and the elders of all places, that, mindful of the laws, their rank, their property valuation, and their own safety, they should strive to prohibit Donatist assemblies in every city and place; and that they should hasten, without any delay, to hand over to the Catholics the churches which it is established that, by my indulgence and without an imperial command, had been granted to them until the day of judgment—unless they prefer to be entangled in the snares of so many enactments. If, indeed, they should choose to agree to Catholic unity, it is sufficiently certain that those churches belong to them.

But especially, and with greater diligence, now that unity has been demonstrated in every way and superstition convicted, they must be driven away from the pursuit of their own wrongdoing. Those, however, who after the prohibitions of the laws mingle themselves with their gatherings must unquestionably understand that they can no longer avoid the punishment prescribed by imperial decision: especially those who, after having recognized the reverence due to Catholic law, have plainly returned to their profane assemblies and communion. I had delayed preventing this earlier only out of consideration for patience and some hope of correction.

Let it suffice, then, that enemies of the Christian faith have hitherto insulted the laws, particularly since their persons are certainly known. What need is there for them to be subjected to the bonds of so many enactments, when no amendment has followed? Let the Donatists know, however, that the decision of the Catholic bishops remains in force even after truth’s victory: once the conferences have been completed—which public knowledge remembers were previously offered to them, and which it is now certainly beyond doubt are again being offered—they may know that they can be received.

It is certain that the authority of the preceding edict is to be maintained in all respects. Therefore every bishop of Donatus’s communion must return to his own locality without any disturbance or molestation, so that, once established in his own place, he may either return to the one true Church or may not delay, through evasion, to give full satisfaction to the laws.

Those who know that they have bands of Circumcellions on their estates should know that, unless they are eager in every way to suppress and restrain their insolence, those places especially are at once to be seized by the fisc. For in this respect provision is made both for Catholic law and for the public peace, so that their madness may be brought to rest. The reading of the proceedings, by which it is shown that the error of schism mentioned above originated with the Donatists, and that Caecilian and the others whom they had wickedly thought should be accused were cleared, will be able to instruct Your Holiness most fully.

*(In another hand.)* **LET IT BE POSTED.**

Given at Carthage, after the consulship of Varanes, vir clarissimus, on the sixth day before the Kalends of July.

Here ends no. XXXIII of the documents pertaining to the history of the Donatists.

## [Laws against the Donatists]

**326. In the Year of Our Lord 402. XXXIV. Law of the Emperor Honorius, by Which Monetary Fines Are Imposed upon the Donatists.**

*(From the Theodosian Code, title “On Heretics,” law 52.)* The Emperors Honorius and Theodosius Augusti, to Seleucus, Praetorian Prefect.

> **[Note: [Col. 1419C]**
>
> **XXXIV.** In this constitution, issued immediately after the Conference of Carthage in A.D. 412, Emperor Honorius earnestly undertakes to recall the Donatists to the Catholic faith and to cut them off. In its first section, penalties or fines are imposed upon the Donatists unless they return to the Catholic Church, notwithstanding any rescript or annotation whatsoever of the emperor. To this, I say, belongs the opening of this law, which I restore as follows: “Unless, etc., they restore themselves to the Catholic Church from which they sacrilegiously seceded.” For the word *descivere* (“they seceded”), which applies altogether to persons rather than to things taken away, clearly shows the point with which I said it deals. The entire subsequent context of the law [Col. 1419D] proves that it concerns recalling Donatists from a perverse religion; this is also stated expressly in the same place. Churches, moreover, are finally dealt with at the end of the law; and this point may be confirmed by the argument of law 54, below.
>
> The penalties, secondly, are set forth according to the several classes of persons: those holding rank, common people, and Circumcellions, of whom there will be fuller discussion later. Thirdly, it prescribes a penalty for those who conceal them, including lessees, agents, persons of the imperial household, and their wives. Fourthly, after imposing a fine upon the obstinate, it threatens confiscation of property. Fifthly, it imposes the same fine even upon Catholic masters unless they recall their slaves and tenants from the perverse religion. Sixthly, Honorius orders Donatist clerics and sacerdotal ministers to be sent, each individually, into exile through the several regions under reliable escort. In the final section, the churches, meeting-houses, and estates, if any perverse generosity of heretics has conveyed them to their churches, are ordered to be claimed for Catholic churches in accordance with previous constitutions—that is, in accordance with law 43.
>
> These, then, are the seven means by which Honorius at this time sought to bring the Donatists over to the Catholic faith and break and cut off their stubborn purpose; stronger means could scarcely be imagined:
>
> 1. Fear of financial loss.
> 2. Lessees and agents stirred up against them to expose them.
> 3. Indeed, their wives as well.
> 4. Fear of confiscation of property after obstinacy.
> 5. Masters stirred up against slaves and tenants.
> 6. Clerics sent into exile.
> 7. Churches and donations ordered to be claimed for the Catholic Church.
>
> Similar measures occur repeatedly in law 54 below, where several additional provisions are also made.
>
> Such being the general purport of this law, Augustine briefly expressed its force in Letter 50 to Boniface: “For a LAW had already been promulgated, so that the Donatist heresy, of such great savagery, toward which indulgence seemed crueller than its own savagery, should not merely be forbidden to use violence but should not be allowed to exist at all with impunity.” This is the first purport of the law. “Yet not by capital punishment, so that mercy might be preserved even toward the unworthy, but by proposed FINANCIAL LOSSES”—the second section of this law, where the word *damna* (“losses”), as in law 54, occurs likewise—“and by exile appointed for their BISHOPS and MINISTERS.” This is the third section.
>
> Although, if one considers Augustine’s order of words, he may seem to have in view another and much earlier law, it nevertheless has the same import. Augustine certainly mentions the final section of this law in the same Letter 50 to Boniface, p. 224: “Whatever was possessed in the name of the churches of Donatus’s party, Christian emperors by religious laws ordered to pass over to the Catholics along with the churches themselves,” etc.; and there he gives at greater length the justice of this measure.
>
> Augustine likewise, at the end of Tractate 6 on John, says: “Plain laws are read in which emperors commanded that those who, outside the communion of the Catholic Church, usurp for themselves the Christian name and refuse peacefully to worship the author of peace should dare to possess nothing in the name of the Church; and in the end, let them come to the Catholic Church, and with us they shall possess not only the earth but also him who made heaven and earth.”
>
> By the force of this law, and likewise of law 54 below, Augustine testifies that the property left by testament to Donatists was claimed for Catholics; he represents the Donatists as saying: “Now, as they are everywhere failing, what do they allege against us, finding nothing to say? They have taken our villages; they have taken our estates. They produce people’s wills. Look: Caius gave them an estate for the church over which Faustinus presided. Over what church did Bishop Faustinus preside? A church? What is ‘a church’? I said, the church over which Faustinus presided? But Faustinus did not preside over the Church; he presided over a party. The dove, however, is the Church.” These judgments of Augustine concern the final section of this law.
>
> Augustine’s statement concerning the exile imposed upon clerics follows; this is the third section of the law and is repeated in law 54: “The emperor has ordained milder measures against you because of Christian gentleness: he wished to inflict exile upon you, not death. Yet you, learned men, [Col. 1421C] 327 considering what is deserved by your guilt and what is less severe in punishment, add death—not from his judgment, but from your own.”
>
> The reason for enacting this law must be sought in the outcome or event of the Conference of Carthage, which had taken place in the preceding year, seven months and more before. To this also refer law 55 below under this title, where I shall speak fully, and the final law below “On Religion.” While that conference was pending, Marcellinus, tribune and notary, acting as judge in the conference, had, out of his own humanity and without an imperial command, allowed the Donatists—who had promised that they would come—to retain their churches or basilicas until the day of judgment. Indeed, he had ordered that the churches, with all their rights, which the Catholics held according to imperial command, be restored or returned to them. This is clear from his edict in the Acts of the Conference of Carthage, pp. 10–11; from the judgment, p. 405; and from Augustine’s *Brief Account of the Conference* at its beginning.
>
> At length, when the Donatists were condemned by his final decision, they were ordered again to surrender these churches to the Catholics without any delay. Moreover, the madness and insolence of the Circumcellions were ordered to be restrained. The decurions, estate owners, agents, and lessees—not only of private property but also of the imperial domain—were commanded to prohibit Donatist meetings in all cities and places. Indeed, at the end of his judgment or edict, he ordered offerings, collections, and gifts made to Donatist churches to be handed over to Catholic bishops. All these matters suit this law exactly.
>
> This imperial law in fact followed that judgment. Yet that judgment was not everywhere obeyed in this respect, as this law and law 54 attest. As for the outcome of the Conference of Carthage generally, Augustine teaches it in Letters 127, 158, 159, 160, and 169, and elsewhere. Therefore Honorius proceeded to this more severe law, in which many individual points require notice.
>
> First, we should note the highly varied classes and ranks—ten in number—of lay persons and dignities of which provincial society consisted, which Honorius here enumerates in order and pursues with so many distinct and graduated penalties. Hunneric took the whole of this material from the present law and inserted it into his edict against the Catholics, reported by Victor of Vita in Book III of *The Persecution of the Vandals*:
>
> 1. Illustres;
> 2. Spectabiles;
> 3. Senators;
> 4. Clarissimi;
> 5. Sacerdotales;
> 6. Principales;
> 7. Decurions;
> 8. Traders;
> 9. Plebeians;
> 10. Circumcellions.
>
> A fine of fifty pounds of gold is imposed upon the *illustres*; forty upon the *spectabiles*; thirty upon senators; twenty upon the *clarissimi*; thirty upon the *sacerdotales*; twenty upon the *principales*; five upon decurions; five upon traders; five upon plebeians; and ten pounds of silver upon Circumcellions. Add to these the lessees and agents, slaves and tenants who are subjected to penalties. A list of persons not unlike this one is contained in law 54 below under this title, which in other respects also resembles this law in very many particulars.
>
> Secondly, in this enumeration of persons one should observe concerning senators that they are separated not only from the *illustres* and *spectabiles* and named after them, but are also distinguished from the *clarissimi*. So also law 54 below, which agrees with this one in very many respects: after those invested with proconsular or vicariate rank, or with the rank of a count of the first order—that is, after the *spectabiles*—senators are named first among the honored persons and are described as those “not protected by any external privilege of rank.” Immediately after them come the *sacerdotales*, without any mention of the *clarissimi*. Here, certainly, one sees many points of agreement with this law.
>
> Who, then, can these senators be, distinct from the *clarissimi*? Certainly, in the Code of Justinian there is also a title concerning the civil or criminal prosecution of senators or *clarissimi*. Cujacius thought that in the present law too senators meant persons devoid of every dignity, while *clarissimi* meant those who held office; and that they were distinguished in that sense also in the title of the Justinian Code. But even in that title senators are identical with the *clarissimi* and are joined by parallelism (*παραλληλισμῷ*); and in law 1 of that title the *clarissimi* are none other than senators, as may be learned still more clearly from law 1 of this Code, “On Accusations,” from which that law was taken. Thus in this law senators are placed before the *clarissimi*, and accordingly are treated as of greater rank and subjected to a greater penalty; while conversely not only the *illustres* but also the *spectabiles* are punished more severely than senators.
>
> Thirdly, the *sacerdotales* should be observed. In this law and in law 54 they are named after senators and before the *principales*, or chief curials (*decemprimi*). The *sacerdotales* were the leading decurions who administered the sacerdotal games; they are discussed fully above under the title “On Decurions” and under the title “On Pagans.” From this we learn, incidentally, that they too were Christians, at least Donatists.
>
> Fourthly, the name Circumcellions should here be noted. They are frequently mentioned in the history of the Donatists by Optatus of Milevis; by Augustine in the Conference of Carthage, day 3, chapter 73, and in Marcellinus’s judgment; in the Code of Canons of the African Church; by Isidore, *Etymologies* VIII.5; and by Possidius in the *Life of Augustine*. These were among the Donatists something like armed retainers, wandering through market-fairs, farms, and villages and around the *cellae*—whence their name—equipped with weapons, leaving nothing unattempted, daring everything, filling all places with frenzy. In short, they raged, were violent, and committed outrages against Catholics. Augustine mentions them at this very time, both before the Conference of Carthage in Letter 122 and after it in Letters 159 and 169. Optatus, Book III, reports that Donatus called them *Agonistici*, “combatants,” and their leaders “commanders of the saints.”
>
> Fifthly, it should be observed that lessees and agents, even of the emperor’s household, provided hiding places for Donatists and Circumcellions. This too is indicated by the said judgment of Marcellinus, tribune and notary, and by law 54 below, where the three kinds of such lessees will be discussed. This can likewise be learned from Augustine in various passages. Moreover, they also commonly provided concealment for persons guilty of other crimes, as may be seen throughout the constitutions of this Code.
>
> Sixthly, this law mentions an executor, who was to search out and exact payment from the Donatists and Circumcellions, to whom they had to be presented. If this is to be understood of a particular executor, he was certainly Dulcitius, tribune and notary, since tribunes and notaries were commonly sent for such executions. See the law above, “On the Commands of Princes.” Augustine calls him, in Book I of the *Retractations*, chapter 59, the executor in Africa of imperial commands issued against the Donatists: “At that time Dulcitius, tribune and notary, was in Africa as EXECUTOR of imperial commands issued against the Donatists,” etc. Augustine’s Letter 61 to the same man survives; among other things he says: “For neither have you received by any laws or imperial enactments the power of the sword against them, whose EXECUTION has been entrusted to you, nor has it been commanded that they be killed.” In the same place Augustine testifies that this Dulcitius was appointed by imperial authority—namely, that of Honorius—to correct errors either by intimidation or by punishment, and that he had warned the Donatists by two edicts. If this is so, Baronius was wrong to assign these matters concerning Dulcitius as executor to the year 414, nos. 8–9.
>
> Seventhly, note what is added concerning wives: “Let a separate fine, distinct from the marital fine, bind their wives also.” This may seem to refer to the wives of lessees and agents who supplied concealment to Donatists and Circumcellions; or, more probably, to all wives of Donatists and Circumcellions generally. For these ruined persons were of both sexes, as Augustine attests in Letter 158, where he treats of Macrobius, bishop of the Donatists, p. 718, at the end. Honorius therefore did not wish wives to be spared under this law, but bound them by a distinct fine separate from that imposed upon their husbands—*maritali segregatim*, which I read as “separately from the marital [fine].”
>
> Eighthly, note that slaves are ordered to be recalled from the Donatist religion by their masters’ admonition, and tenants—whose condition I have discussed fully in the parallel title “On Fugitive Tenants”—by more frequent strokes of the whip; otherwise their masters themselves, even if Catholic, are to be fined. This likewise is a distinctive provision contained in law 54 below. In this connection, first, one should observe that the term *admonitio* (“admonition”) denotes chastisement, concerning which see the Theodosian Glossary. Secondly, masters are granted the same right of chastisement over tenants as over slaves—also granted in the final law of the Code “On Agricultural Workers,” in the law of the Code “On the Claudian Decree,” and in Novel 22, chapter 17. In the first law “On Fugitive Tenants,” tenants are likewise bound in irons by their masters as punishment. Nevertheless, as stated, slaves were to be chastised by admonition and tenants by strokes of the whip. Hence it appears that here *admonitio* differs from blows of the whip. Certainly the term *coercitio* (“coercion”) denotes both in law 54, which immediately says that tenants in particular are compelled by whippings.
>
> Ninthly, observe in this law and law 54 the type of exile imposed on Donatist clerics, ministers, and sacerdotal persons: namely, that they are to be sent individually, each into the several regions, under proper escort, as this law says; or, as law 54 says, that they are to be dispatched to the several islands and provinces for the purpose of exile. This kind of solitary exile was also commanded elsewhere, in order to break up persons who carried out their frenzy by force and filled everything with sedition. Examples of this same kind of solitary punishment occur elsewhere in comparable cases and for the same purpose.]

With the revocation of whatever may have been obtained by an imperial rescript or by an annotation in our own hand, and with the continued force of those provisions that were previously determined on this matter and maintained by the enactment of earlier emperors: unless, from the day on which this law is promulgated, all Donatists—priests, clerics, and laymen alike—restore themselves to the Catholic Church from which they sacrilegiously seceded, then the *illustres* shall each be compelled to pay into our fisc, by way of penalty, fifty pounds of gold; the *spectabiles*, forty pounds of gold; senators, thirty pounds of gold; the *clarissimi*, twenty pounds of gold; the *sacerdotales*, thirty pounds of gold; the *principales*, twenty pounds of gold; decurions, five pounds of gold; traders, five pounds of gold; plebeians, five pounds of gold; and Circumcellions, ten pounds of silver.

Unless they are presented to the executor for exaction by the lessees under whom they reside or by the agents, those persons themselves shall be liable to the penalty; so that not even the persons of our household shall be considered exempt from such assessment. Their wives also shall be bound by a separate fine, distinct from the marital one.

Those whom the imposition of these penalties does not correct shall subsequently suffer confiscation of all their property. The admonition of masters shall recall slaves, and the more frequent stroke of the whip shall recall tenants, from the perverse religion—unless their masters themselves, even though Catholics, prefer to be held liable to the aforesaid losses.

Their clerics and ministers, and their most pernicious sacerdotal persons, having been removed from African soil, which they have polluted by a sacrilegious rite, shall be sent individually into exile, each to the several regions, under suitable escort. Their churches, meeting-houses, and estates, if any perverse generosity of heretics has conveyed them to their churches, shall be claimed for the ownership and control of the Catholic Church, as we have long since decreed.

Given at Ravenna, on the third day before the Kalends of February, in the consulship of Honorius Augustus for the ninth time and Theodosius Augustus for the fifth time.

**328. In the Year of Our Lord 414. XXXV. Another Law of the Same Emperor against the Donatists.**

*(From the same Code, in the same place, law 54.)* The same Augusti, to Julian, Proconsul of Africa.

> **[Note: [Col. 1424C]**
>
> **XXXV.** This is now the second constitution of Emperor Honorius after the Conference of Carthage, directed against the Donatists throughout proconsular Africa. The conference had taken place three years earlier, in A.D. 411. The first was law 52, issued shortly after its conclusion, approximately seven months later. In both laws, after a long period of patience, Honorius earnestly endeavored by proposing various kinds of penalties to recall the Donatists from their error to the Catholic Church and to “cut off their purpose,” as this law says—that is, to break their stubborn design.
>
> The former law, law 52, was issued in A.D. 412 with nearly the same penalties proposed. This one, however, came in the following year, 414, more distinctly and with stricter severity, since the former had made little progress; indeed, as he himself testifies at the beginning of the law, his patience had preserved them until then. He therefore considered that they should now be struck with appropriate authority and strictness, and in this law he decrees that they are to be struck—his own express words. Again, in section 6, he says that they are to be bound by the authority of a sacred decision and fined by the authority of the promulgated command.
>
> He repeatedly pierces their heresy with harsh language: he calls their superstition “dire” in section 2; their position an “error” in sections 5 and 8; the body of Donatists a “flock” in section 3; and at the beginning of the law and at the end of section 5, a “heresy” and “heretics.” In section 6 he says that the sacred mystery—that is, baptism—is polluted by them. He also plainly indicates that no further indulgence should be shown them in future, as had earlier been done, when, in addition to what I have already said, he declares: “so that by an EVIDENT command they may recognize themselves to be incapable of making wills,” etc.; and in section 5: “We EVIDENTLY impose losses of property and financial penalties.” This is the meaning of the terms *evidens* and *evidenter* in constitutions.
>
> Finally, throughout the law he orders them to be subjected by Julian, proconsul of Africa, to the penalties established by it; indeed, there is one place where he orders a report to be made to himself concerning them. This is because Donatist madness, so far from having been extinguished after the Conference of Carthage, had instead increased immeasurably, as Augustine frequently testifies.
>
> Let us now set out these penalties in summary. There are ten in all, into which we have divided this constitution in order by sections; afterward we shall draw out certain individual matters from them:
>
> 1. Donatists generally are to be incapable of making wills; commerce is to be forbidden them; they are to be branded with infamy—the penalty of infamy imposed upon heretics having been discussed once in connection with the said law 7.
> 2. Their meeting-houses must be joined to the Catholic Church.
> 3. Their priests and ministers, after confiscation of their property, are to be deported.
> 4. So too those who conceal them.
> 5. A fine is to be imposed upon Donatists generally—men, women, persons who have joined the Donatist communion, those found in the Donatist flock, those who have preferred to remain in heresy and persist in their purpose—according to the condition and rank of each: two hundred pounds of silver upon those vested with proconsular, vicariate, or first-rank comital honors; one hundred upon senators; fifty upon chief curials (*decemprimi*); ten upon the remaining decurions.
> 6. Persons who provide a place on estates belonging to others for the celebration of mysteries—namely, lessees of the imperial private domain and emphyteutic lessees—must pay the fisc as a penalty as much as they customarily pay by way of rent or lease.
> 7. Private owners of estates are likewise liable if they do not correct their errant lessees or replace those who persist.
> 8. Officials of judges caught in this error are likewise to be fined thirty pounds of silver.
> 9. Tenants and slaves are to be restrained by whippings; if they persist, they are to be fined one third of their peculium.
> 10. Finally, everything collected from places or fines is immediately to be remitted to the emperor’s treasury.
>
> This, I say, is the sum of this law. Besides the points we noted concerning law 52, which resembles it, many distinctive matters call for observation.
>
> First, Donatists are deprived of the power to make wills, as is likewise provided in the law *Ne sanctum baptisma*, law 4; indeed, they are deprived also of commercial rights and finally branded with infamy. Thus they are deprived of the common law of Rome. This has already been discussed under other laws. Consequently, dying persons are not left even the consolation of being able to make a will concerning their property, nor do survivors have the power of entering into any contract—this, namely, must here be supplied—and, as persons infamous in perpetuity, they are to be excluded from the company of respectable persons and from public assembly.
>
> Heretics incapable of making wills have been dealt with under other laws. The African Fathers had already requested from Honorius, ten years earlier in A.D. 404, that Donatists be made incapable of making wills, as canon 93 of the African Code teaches. This was granted by Honorius at their request at the beginning of the following year, 405, in law 4, *Ne sanctum baptisma*, a law very similar to the present one.
>
> Augustine mentions the whole affair, and hence this law itself, in Book I against the Letter of Parmenian: “There are also other general commands by which they are deprived either of the ability to make wills, or of the ability to confer property upon another by donations, or of the ability to receive anything from donations or wills. For in one case, when a nobleman had petitioned the emperors because his sister, who had belonged to Donatus’s party, upon dying had bestowed very much upon I know not whom of her communion, and especially upon a certain Augustine, one of their bishops, it was commanded under that general law that everything be restored to her brother. In that case mention was also made of Circumcellions, and how they were to be repelled by what forms of help and support if they violently resisted in their usual manner.”
>
> Augustine says similarly, though ironically, in Letter 48 to Vincentius: “Certainly I ought to have opposed this provision, lest you lose the things you call yours and securely proscribe Christ: so that you might make wills by Roman law and tear apart by calumnious accusations the will made by divine law for the Fathers, where it is written, ‘In your seed all nations shall be blessed’; so that you might have free contracts in buying and selling and dare to divide among yourselves what Christ purchased by being sold; so that what any one of you had given another might be valid, while that which the God of gods gave to his children, summoned from the rising of the sun to its setting, might not be valid; so that you might not be sent into exile from the land of your body, while you attempted to make Christ an exile from the kingdom of his blood, from sea to sea and from the river to the ends of the earth? Indeed, let the kings of the earth serve Christ even by enacting LAWS for Christ.”
>
> In *On the Sheep*, chapter 13, Augustine says: “Take heed, heretics; hear from the shepherd the testament of peace; come to peace. Be angry with Christian emperors because they refused to allow your wills to be valid in your homes. See what a fitting penalty it is. What is it that a will is not valid in your house? What is it? How great is it? That pain is an admonition, not yet a condemnation.”
>
> Secondly, note that those who conceal Donatist priests and ministers are threatened with the same penalty of confiscation and deportation. Penalties were elsewhere prescribed as well for those concealing especially detestable heretics, such as the Manichaeans in Africa by law 35, and the Donatists by this law and law 52 above.
>
> Thirdly, note the list of dignities and honors, and the corresponding diversity of fines or penalties. First are those invested with proconsular or vicariate rank and counts of the first order, concerning whom see Book VI above. They are followed by other *honorati*; not those who flourished in the provinces with a falsely assumed honor, concerning whom see law 1, “On the Offices of Civil Judges,” but the following senators, unadorned and protected by no external privilege of rank, entirely without another dignity. I have also discussed them under law 52 above. Next come the *sacerdotales*, namely those who stood first among decurions, concerning whom see law 52 above, the title “On Decurions,” and below, the title “On Pagans.” These are followed by the chief decurions (*decemprimi*), treated fully under the title “On Decurions,” and finally the remaining decurions.
>
> The scale of penalties is this: a fine of 200 pounds of silver is imposed upon the first group; 100 upon unadorned senators and likewise upon the *sacerdotales*—from which it appears that the dignity of these *sacerdotales* was equal, though next in rank, to that of senators; 50 upon chief curials; and 10 upon the other decurions.
>
> Fourthly, observe that two passages of this constitution, sections 5 and 8, add a provision about a fifth condemnation: that is, persons who have fallen five times, have been fined, restrained, and fallen again are no longer to be punished with the ordinary penalty or fine, but with an extraordinary one. Five lapses are indeed to be restrained by the same fine; but upon the sixth and thereafter the matter is either to be referred to the emperor, if it concerns those holding dignities or honors, so that more severe punishment may be exacted from them; or, as with officials, they are at once to be restrained more severely by judges. This is the penalty for obstinacy in this matter after a fifth correction.
>
> Fifthly, observe the enumeration of other persons after those established in dignities and honors—persons throughout Africa who were entangled in the Donatist heresy or favored it. First come three classes of lessees: lessees of houses and estates belonging to the emperor’s private domain; emphyteutic lessees, that is, lessees of estates belonging to republics and cities, concerning whom Book X has treated; and finally lessees of private persons, or estate managers. These same three sorts of people were also accustomed to furnish hiding places to persons guilty of other crimes, as countless constitutions attest. Then come officials of judges, and finally slaves and tenants.
>
> Sixthly, note the kind of fine in sections 6 and 7: namely, that a person is to pay into the fisc as much as he customarily pays or receives annually from an estate by way of rent. This is imposed either for making an estate available for the celebration of heretical mysteries or for failing to correct or replace lessees of one’s own estates who do so.
>
> For the remaining matters, including the exile—indeed solitary exile—of Donatist bishops and ministers, see law 52 above.
>
> It may, however, appear doubtful whether, after Marcellinus’s death, of which the next law treats, Honorius sent Dulcitius, tribune and notary, to Africa as executor expressly of this law, or of law 52 above, or of both; to this question refer what Augustine writes in Book II of the *Retractations*, chapter 59. Baronius understood it of the present law. I would understand it no less of the preceding law 52, where Dulcitius himself seems to be indicated in the words: “Unless they are presented to the executor for exaction,” that is, etc.
>
> Augustine frequently mentions this edict and demonstrates from Holy Scripture that it was entirely just. In particular, he presses the point in writings expressly composed on this subject: Letter 59 to Count Boniface, entitled “On Moderately Correcting the Romans”; Letter 61 to Dulcitius; the books against Gaudentius; Letter 48 to Vincentius, “On Correcting Heretics by Force,” concerning persons who made wills under Roman law while tearing apart under divine law the testament … See Book I against Gaudentius, chapter 19, vol. 7, p. 259: “The emperor ordained milder measures against them; he wished to inflict exile upon you, not death,” etc. This law and the said law 12 brought great benefit; see Augustine, the said Letter 50 and Letter 48, and Book I against Gaudentius, chapter 29, p. 61.]

The Donatists and heretics, whom the patience of Our Clemency has until now spared, We decree shall be smitten by appropriate authority:

1. So that, by an explicit command, they may recognize that they are incapable of making a will and have no power to enter into any legal act, but, branded with perpetual infamy, are to be excluded from honorable associations and public assembly.

2. Those places, moreover, in which that dreadful superstition has until now been maintained shall be joined to the venerable Catholic Church.

3. Their bishops, presbyters, all their prelates, and ministers, stripped of all their property, shall be sent into exile, each to particular islands and provinces.

4. Whoever receives such persons fleeing the penalty imposed upon them, in order to conceal them, shall know both that his property is to be added to the revenues of Our treasury and that he himself will undergo the punishment prescribed for them.

5. We also expressly impose loss of property and monetary penalties upon men, women, individual persons, and ranks according to their respective condition. Therefore, anyone invested with proconsular, vicariate, or first-rank comital honor, unless he turns his mind and purpose to Catholic observance, shall be compelled to pay two hundred pounds of silver, to be added to the resources of Our treasury. And lest this alone be thought sufficient to cut short their obstinacy, as often as he is convicted of having joined such communion, so often shall the fine be exacted. If, after five convictions, it is established that he is not recalled from error by these losses, then the matter shall be referred to Our Clemency, so that We may judge more severely concerning his entire estate and his civil status.

We bind the remaining *honorati* likewise under conditions of this kind: namely, a senator, not protected by any special privilege of rank, if found among the Donatist body, shall pay one hundred pounds of silver; those of sacerdotal rank shall be compelled to pay the same sum; the ten leading curiales shall be assessed fifty pounds of silver; the remaining decurions shall pay ten pounds of silver, if they prefer to persist in heresy.

6. The tenants of Our estates, if they permit these practices upon lands belonging to the venerable imperial property, shall be compelled, by way of penalty, to pay as much rent as they customarily pay under their lease. The same authority of this sacred enactment shall bind emphyteutic lessees as well.

7. But tenants of private persons, if they permit conventicles to be held on those same estates, or if through their tolerance the sacred mystery is polluted, shall be reported by the judges to the knowledge of the owners. If the latter wish to escape the penalty of the sacred command, it concerns them either to correct those who resist or to replace those who persist, and to provide their estates with such managers as will observe the divine commands. If they neglect to make this provision, they too shall, by authority of the promulgated command, be fined in the amount of the rents they customarily receive, so that what might have accrued to their profit may be joined to the sacred treasury.

8. Officials of the various judges, if caught in this error, shall be liable to pay thirty pounds of silver as a penalty; and if, having been condemned five times, they refuse to desist, they shall be beaten and consigned to exile.

9. The most severe punishment shall restrain slaves and coloni from attempts of this kind. And if coloni, compelled by beatings, persist in their purpose, then they shall be fined one-third of their *peculium*.

10. And all that can be collected from persons and places of these kinds shall immediately be sent to the sacred largesses.

Given on the tenth day before the Kalends of July, at Ravenna, in the consulship of Constantius and Constans.

330. A.D. 414. XXXVI. ANOTHER LAW OF THE SAME EMPEROR, DECLARING THAT THE PROCEEDINGS AGAINST THE DONATISTS, CONDUCTED IN THE YEAR 411 UNDER MARCELLINUS AS INVESTIGATING COMMISSIONER, RETAIN FULL VALIDITY AND FORCE, ALTHOUGH HE HAD DIED AND BEEN MALICIOUSLY SLAIN.

(*Ibid.*, Law 55.) The same Augusti to Julianus, Proconsul of Africa.

[Note: [Col. 1428C]

XXXVI. By this constitution Honorius the emperor commands that the proceedings against the Donatists, conducted three years earlier under the cognizance of Marcellinus the investigating commissioner, now dead, nevertheless retain perpetual force, in accordance with the appended general rule—which deserves notice—that the death of an investigating commissioner ought not to destroy public credit. For acts done under public credit, and once entered in public records or proceedings, establish perpetual authority; and so the *Basilica*, book VI, title I, express this law: “Things brought before a court and entered in records remain firmly valid, even when the judge dies”; and Chrysostom, Homily I on Holy Pentecost, tome VIII, p. 609: “Whatever a litigant may say in court for the record is in every case entered permanently in writing, and can no longer be erased.” Thus far is the death of the investigating commissioner from being able to detract from them in any respect. Just as death does not dissolve other things, so neither does the death of an investigating commissioner dissolve public acts.

Such indeed is the meaning of this law. But three matters must be considered: namely, what these proceedings are, who this Marcellinus is, and what is the occasion for the promulgation of this law.

As to the first point: the *Acts*, or Proceedings, of the Conference of Carthage between Catholics and Donatists are here indicated. Marcellinus, tribune and notary, presided over it as investigating commissioner by Honorius’s command in June of A.D. 411, after the consulship of Varanis, that is, three years and somewhat more earlier. On this matter see Augustine, Letters 158, 139, and 160, and Possidius, *Life of St. Augustine*, chapter 2, where the Donatists were refuted by the Catholics through the production of every kind of documentary evidence.

The acts or proceedings of that conference, arranged, distinguished, and collected by Marcellus in concise form, as he himself says, were first published by Papirius Masson; afterwards they were compared with a manuscript and corrected by P. Pithou. Yet, regrettably, a large portion of the hearing on the third day is mutilated. Augustine himself, who was present at the Conference—indeed, by whom it was chiefly brought about, according to Possidius—wrote a very brief epitome of it, or *Breviculus*. And before the acts themselves were published, François Balduin issued a distinguished history of that Carthaginian Conference or disputation.

These, then, are the proceedings in question; this is that Marcellinus, of whom Augustine, Orosius, and Jerome say much. The final law below, under “Religion,” is also addressed to him. As the acts of the Conference show, that law is part of the very instructions, or imperial sanction of Honorius, by which the investigation was entrusted to him in A.D. 410, as will there be shown more fully. Although the proceedings concerning the crimes of the Donatists after the Conference of Carthage may also be understood here; these are discussed at the end of the Commentary.

As to the second point: even from this law it is clear that the death of Marcellinus himself furnished the occasion for its enactment. For after his death the Donatists maintained that the authority of the proceedings conducted under his cognizance should also perish—especially because they alleged that he had been removed from the scene as a partisan of the tyrant Heraclianus [concerning whom see Law 21, “On Punishments,” and Law 13, “On Invalidating Acts Done under Tyrants,” and Law 51 above and the following Law 56, where I shall speak]. Thus they sought to make it appear that, just as the acts of the tyrant Heraclianus had been annulled by Law 13 in the preceding year, so likewise these acts of Marcellinus ought to be invalidated.

Jerome writes in book III *Against the Pelagians* that Marcellinus was innocently slain by heretics through the odium arising from Heraclianus’s tyranny. That is, just as immediately after the Conference the Donatists launched weapons of slander against him, alleging that he had improperly rendered judgment against them by night and after being bribed with gold by the Catholics, so later, through the machinations of the same persons—for these are undoubtedly the heretics whom Jerome meant—he suffered the accusation of being a partisan of Heraclianus and was slain. Nor do I doubt that this occurred upon the occasion of Law 21, “On Punishments,” by which Honorius publicly summoned informers against Heraclianus’s attendants and accomplices. In the end, their principal aim was to assert that the proceedings conducted by him were null because he was dead and, as they alleged, a traitor.

But just as Marinus the Count, author of Marcellinus’s death, who had restored Africa to the Roman Empire and freed the commonwealth from the tyrant Heraclianus, was recalled from Africa and dismissed by Honorius—as Orosius writes, book VII, chapter 42, at the end—so by this constitution Honorius vindicated Marcellinus’s reputation. This is clear because he calls him “a man of illustrious memory” and at the same time confirms the proceedings conducted under his cognizance against the Donatists. I shall shortly show that the following law was promulgated for a similar reason.

From this we also learn in the meantime, as is otherwise established, that in matters of religion heretics sometimes seized upon the death of a judge as an occasion for annulling proceedings conducted before that judge and entered into public records. But, as this law determines, the emperors wished their authority to be perpetual; Honorius wished this by the present law. This determination or constitution applies where everything has been lawfully conducted, with the parties present face to face, as in the Conference at Carthage between Catholics and Donatists.

The case is otherwise if certain things are done unilaterally (*monomerōs*), while some persons are absent. Of this there is a passage in Athanasius, *Apology to Emperor Constantius*, written in A.D. 356, at its beginning: “Moreover, if you would deign to learn, for clear proof, that while we were present those accusing Macarius the presbyter proved nothing, but when we were absent they acted alone as they wished: things of this kind, first the divine law and then your own laws, have declared to possess no force.” And in the *Apology*, p. 578, where inquiry is made against Marcellus: “But at Mareotis he was not present, where the records are said to have been drawn up against him; and, beloved, you know that proceedings conducted unilaterally have no force, but are suspect.”

All these things belong to that equity of law: no one is to be condemned in absence; accuser and defendant alike ought to be present in court. There are other passages of Athanasius to the same effect. But the case is otherwise here, where everything was lawfully done. Undoubtedly the Donatists wished these things abolished because their frauds and sophistries, which they saw tending to their disgrace, would become known from them, and therefore they desired them removed from view. Thus also matters entered in public records for the purpose of defaming another are ordered to be removed, Law 37, “On Injuries.” But Honorius wished these proceedings to remain firm and to survive for their disgrace, just as he also wished the same rescript which the Donatists had obtained from Julianus to be posted, by public proclamation, in the most frequented places, together with the proceedings in which such an allegation had been inserted. He added that the established constancy of Catholic confidence and the despair and broken audacity of the Donatists might become more clearly known.

This, I say, was Honorius’s intention. For the same purpose, the work *On the Proceedings with Emeritus* testifies that these same acts of the Conference of Carthage were customarily read in the African churches during Lent. Marcellinus also wished the proceedings concerning Donatist crimes after the Conference of Carthage to be posted at Theoprepria, whither, it seems, a large crowd gathered, as to a most frequented place in Carthage; and Augustine, in Letter 158 addressed to Marcellinus, desired them to be read in the churches. This law too may be understood of these proceedings, as I indicated above.]

[Col. 1428C]

Those things which were done against the Donatists through the cognizance and diligence of Marcellinus, a man of illustrious memory, and transferred into public records, We desire to retain perpetual force. For public credit ought not to perish through the death of the investigating commissioner.

Given on the third day before the Kalends of September, at Rome and Ravenna, in the consulship of Constantius and Constans.

331. XXXVII. ANOTHER LAW OF THE SAME EMPEROR AGAINST THE DONATISTS.

(*Ibid.*, Law 56.) The same Augusti to Heraclianus, Count of Africa.

[Col. 1430A] [Note: [Col. 1430C]

XXXVII. By this constitution the Emperor Honorius again prohibits throughout Africa the assemblies and rites of heretics, under the penalties of proscription and capital punishment. This constitution is addressed to Heraclianus, Count of Africa, and bears the consuls corresponding to A.D. 415. Finally, it is transcribed almost word for word from Law 51. This is certainly remarkable, so that it may seem open to suspicion as erroneous. For Heraclianus, to whom it is addressed, had become a tyrant and thereafter had been defeated and slain two years before, in A.D. 413; this is shown by Law 13, “On Invalidating Acts Done under Tyrants,” and Law 21 above, “On Punishments.” Therefore Baronius judged that this law should be assigned to A.D. 412, that is, to the consulship of the Augusti Honorius IX and Theodosius V; and consequently that the consuls appear to have been put in the wrong order.

Yet, upon closer consideration, I judge that nothing should be changed. I believe that, on a similar occasion, this law was published—or rather republished—in Africa, just as I showed that Law 45 had been promulgated anew in the preceding year. Once the tyrant Heraclianus had been slain and his acts invalidated by the said Law 13, and once his memory had been ordered to be abolished both privately and publicly, the Donatists seem to have asserted that the law formerly issued against them five years earlier, in A.D. 410—that is, Law 51, addressed to Heraclianus—was likewise to be invalidated and had been invalidated. This was no different from their claim that the proceedings under Marcellinus were null after his death.

Therefore Honorius wished this law to be renewed and posted in Africa with the same address to Heraclianus, Count of Africa, so that the Donatists might understand that, although other acts conducted under Heraclianus had been invalidated and his memory ordered to be abolished privately and publicly by the said Law 13, Law 51 had not thereby been invalidated. There was a great difference between things done by Heraclianus himself, or by private persons under him, and public and imperial acts—and therefore constitutions directed to him. So likewise, by the preceding law, Honorius wished the proceedings, transferred into public records through the cognizance and diligence of Marcellinus the investigating commissioner at the Conference of Carthage, to retain perpetual force.

By this interpretation the law may be defended from emendation. It should also be observed that this law no longer deals—as Law 51 did—with invalidating an oracle by which the Donatists had stealthily introduced their rites. At this time, certainly, no oracle of that kind had arisen. This is the difference between this law and that one.

Thus far the constitutions of Emperor Honorius; those of Theodosius the Younger and Valentinian III follow.]

Let all enemies of the most holy law who have stealthily embraced their rites through the superstitions of heresy know that they are liable to the penalties both of proscription and capital punishment, if hereafter they attempt, with rashness in the public exercise of their crime, to assemble; lest any true and divine reverence be polluted by contagion.

Given on the eighth day before the Kalends of September, in the consulship of the Augusti Honorius X and Theodosius VI.

A.D. 428. XXXVIII. A LAW OF EMPEROR THEODOSIUS THE YOUNGER, IN WHICH THE DONATISTS ARE ENUMERATED AMONG THE HERETICS TO WHOM NO PLACE FOR ASSEMBLING OR PRAYING IS LEFT ANYWHERE ON ROMAN SOIL.

(*Ibid.*, Law 65.)

[Note: [Col. 1431C]

XXXVIII. This is the very extensive constitution of Theodosius the Younger against heretics and heresies, twenty-three of which it names here. It was issued at the end of May in A.D. 428. Since it repeats and expressly confirms many provisions made by earlier constitutions, there is no point in examining them individually, especially since we have already distinguished its clauses and holdings in the notes. I shall therefore pursue only some particular points in it.

First, this law is noteworthy because Theodosius the Younger says that not all heretics are to be punished with the same severity. This must be carefully observed in the question of heretics, and indeed we learn the same thing repeatedly from the constitutions in this title. Theodosius in this law certainly establishes four classes of heretics and corresponding degrees of punishment.

The first class is those to whom he denies the right of churches only within cities, not in the countryside. In this category he places three groups: Arians, Macedonians, and Apollinarians. Thus certain churches were left to them by Theodosius under this law outside the cities. We also learn this concerning the Macedonians from events occurring in the next year, A.D. 429: that is, churches were taken from the Macedonians outside the walls of certain cities, including Constantinople, on the occasion mentioned by Socrates, book VII, chapter 31, and by Marcellinus in his Chronicle. Socrates says: “Both the church at Constantinople before the old wall of the city, and the one at Cyzicus, and many others which they possessed in the estates of the Hellespont, were taken away.” Marcellinus says: “Our orthodox people took away the church of the Macedonians situated outside the city walls, because,” etc.

The second class of heretics consists of those whom he orders to be content with their own churches and not build new ones—namely, the Novatians and Sabbatians. The third class consists of those to whom he commands that nowhere on Roman soil, not even in the countryside, may they have the right to assemble or pray. In the last class are the Manichaeans, whom he also commands to be expelled from cities. Thus it is clear that the condition of the Novatians and Sabbatians was the mildest, and that of the Manichaeans the most severe. The Novatians and Sabbatians were always held in a better position among heretics; on this I have spoken fully at Laws II and 59, also from Socrates and Sozomen. But the Manichaeans were held in the worst position; accordingly Theodosius the Younger says here, in his Novel on the Jews, 3, *superest*, that they had descended to the lowest wickedness of crimes and were always offensive to God. On this I have spoken at Law 3 and at Laws 3 and 4, “On Apostates.”

Second, note that heretics, including Eunomians, are not excluded from palace service or armed military service; nevertheless Synesius, Letter 5, complains about the military service of Eunomians. Certainly the armed service of those times admitted a miscellaneous body of persons of every kind—barbarians and heretics.

Third, note that heretics had been granted the right to make gifts and wills in favor of certain persons. What persons these were is not specified elsewhere.

Fourth, note that just as heretics were permitted to have Catholics as slaves under any title, so they were subjected to the penalty of exile and ten pounds of gold if they instructed them in their own mysteries or prevented them from following the Catholic religion. But a Jew was not permitted to have a Christian slave under any title, and it was a capital offense to instruct one in his superstition, as will be shown under the title “That a Jew shall not possess a Christian slave.”

Finally, note that a judge is not permitted, without fraud, either to ignore the penalties of the law or to mitigate them. This accords with Law 8 above, “On Appeals”; the final law above, “To the Julian Law on Public Violence,” or Law VIII of the Code under the same title; and Symmachus, last book, final letter. One is the condition of magistrates, whose judgments appear corrupt if they are more lenient than the laws; another is the power of ruling princes, who ought to temper the rigor of harsh law.
