See also Justinian, Novel 82; Quintilian, Declamation 17, 345; Law XV, π, “On Municipal Affairs.”

What then is meant by Augustine’s statement in Letter 158 to Marcellinus: “I am accustomed to hear that it is within a judge’s power to mitigate a sentence and punish more mildly than the laws”? I take this to refer to laws written for deterrence, as almost all those written against heretics were. Yet this law expressly forbids judges even this.

Finally, I consider Baronius’s conjecture certain: that this law was promulgated by Theodosius the Younger at the persuasion of Nestorius, who in the preceding month, on the fourth day before the Ides of April, was made bishop of Constantinople under these consuls, as Socrates testifies, book VII, chapter 29. For not only Vincent of Lérins, writing eight years after this law, testifies that he persecuted the blasphemies of every heresy; Socrates also explicitly writes in the said chapter 29 that, as soon as Nestorius was made bishop, he addressed Emperor Theodosius the Younger and among other things said what later became common on many lips: “Give me, O Emperor, the land cleansed of heretics, and I will give you heaven in return. Help me overthrow the heretics, and I will help you overthrow the Persians.”

Although these words were welcomed even by those who hated heretics, Socrates adds in the same chapter 29 what Nestorius attempted against the Arians, Novatians, and Quartodecimans, even to the point of riot and fire; nevertheless, the emperor restrained his attack upon the Novatians. This law also bears witness to Theodosius’s moderation toward the Novatians. Socrates adds in the same book, chapter 31, that Nestorius also afflicted the Macedonians and finally persuaded the emperor to take away their churches: indeed, the church situated outside the old walls of Constantinople, another at Cyzicus, and many elsewhere which they held in the estates of the Hellespont, were taken from them. This was in accordance with the present law, which forbade them churches only in cities. Therefore the events mentioned by Socrates occurred after this law.]

1. The madness of heretics is to be restrained in such manner that, before all else, they shall not doubt that whatever churches they hold anywhere, having taken them from the Orthodox, must immediately be handed over to the Catholic Church. For it cannot be tolerated that those who ought not to have had even churches of their own should continue to retain churches possessed or founded by the Orthodox and seized through their own rashness.

2. Further, if they attach to themselves other clerics or, as they think, priests, a fine of ten pounds of gold for each person shall be imposed upon the one who did it and upon the one who allowed it to be done; or, if they plead poverty, it shall be exacted from the common body of clerics of the same superstition, or even from their offerings, and paid into Our treasury.

3. After this, since not all are to be punished with the same severity: Arians, Macedonians, and Apollinarians—whose offense is that, deceived by harmful reflection, they believe falsehoods drawn from the fountain of truth—shall not be permitted to possess a church within any city. From the Novatians and Sabbatians all license for innovation shall be removed, should they perhaps attempt any. Eunomians, Valentinians, Montanists or Priscillianists, Phrygians, Marcianists, Borborians, Messalians, Euchytes or Enthusiasts, Donatists, Audianians, Hydroparastatae, Ascodrogitae, Photinians, Paulinians, Marcellians, and Manichaeans, who have descended to the lowest wickedness of crimes, shall nowhere on Roman soil have leave to assemble or pray; the Manichaeans shall also be expelled from cities. For no place whatsoever is to be left to all these persons in which injury may be done even to the elements themselves.

No military service is to be granted to them at all, except palace service in the provinces and camp service. No right whatsoever is to be allowed them of making gifts to one another, or of making a will or final disposition. All laws formerly enacted against these and other opponents of Our faith, and promulgated at different times, shall remain in perpetual and unfading observance: whether concerning gifts made to churches of heretics; or property left in any manner by final testament; or private buildings into which, through the Lord’s permission or restraint, they may have assembled, to be claimed by the Catholic Church venerable to Us; or concerning an agent who has done this without his owner’s knowledge, and who, if freeborn, shall incur a fine of ten pounds of gold or exile, but if of servile condition shall, after beatings, be sent to the mines.

Thus they shall not be able to assemble in a public place, build churches for themselves, or devise anything for evasion of the laws, being prevented by the assistance of every civil and military authority, including curial officials, defenders, and judges, under threat of twenty pounds of gold. All provisions concerning military service, the right of making gifts, and testamentary capacity—whether wholly denied or barely granted to specified persons—and the various penalties promulgated against different heretics, shall remain in their full force; so that not even a special favor obtained contrary to the laws shall prevail.

No heretic shall be permitted to lead back to his own baptism either freeborn persons or his own slaves who have been initiated into the mysteries of the Orthodox; nor may he prevent those whom he has bought or otherwise acquired, and who have not yet joined his superstition, from following the Catholic religion of the Church. Whoever does this, or, being freeborn, permits it to be done to himself, or fails to report its commission, shall be condemned to exile and a fine of ten pounds of gold; both parties shall be denied the right to make a will or gift.

We decree that all these provisions shall be observed in such a way that no judge may commit an accusation brought before him to a lesser punishment, or to no punishment at all, unless he himself wishes to suffer what he has allowed others by overlooking it.

Given on the third day before the Kalends of June, at Constantinople, in the consulship of Felix and Taurus.

[Col. 1434A]

[FRAGMENTS OF THE ANCIENTS CONCERNING THE DONATISTS.]

333. A.D. 440. XXXIX. POPE LEO I TO THE BISHOPS OF MAURETANIA CAESARIENSIS.

(From the first letter.)

We do not remove Maximinus, though reprehensibly ordained from the laity, from the episcopal dignity which he has acquired in whatever manner, provided that he is no longer a Donatist and is free from the spirit of schismatic perversity; on condition that he too, by a written declaration submitted to Us, make clear that he is Catholic.

XL. FASTIDIOSUS THE ARIAN.

(In Fulgentius, Letter IX.)

The Donatists also preach that the good are defiled by communion with the wicked. And afterwards:

For Donatist vanity does not consider that the benefit of baptism was bestowed upon human beings so that those who are originally burdened by the errors of others, once relieved by the help of healing grace, might thereafter bear only their own burdens; and that it is not communion in the sacrament but consent that condemns each person for sin.

XLI. SAINT PETER CHRYSOLOGUS, ARCHBISHOP OF RAVENNA.

(Sermon 13.)

[Col. 1434C]

The devil betrays himself by his counsels. “Cast yourself down.” He seeks a fall; he commands precipices; and by such counsel he makes martyrs throughout Africa, saying without a cry: “If you wish to be a martyr, cast yourself down,” so that he may drive them from a height to death, not raise and lift them from lowliness to a crown.

XLII. CASSIODORUS.

(On Psalm LX.)

Let the Donatists hear the Church crying from the ends of the earth, and let them at once cease to call it local. Who can be heard against the voice of the world? It is most shameless to speak against the testimony of the three; yet they do not blush to arm themselves impudently against the universal judgment. Why do they weary souls with new inventions? Let them certainly receive what they may believe, not what they may pervert through their own wickedness.

The faithful people pray from the ends of the earth because the Lord has become their hope, and afterward they rejoice in hymnic exultation that they have been heard, because they shall continually appear before the Lord. What answer can now satisfy, if this does not satisfy? We see daily that what He promised comes to pass; we see the world coming to the rule of Christian faith. And—alas for sorrow!—falsehood strives to conceal what truth decreed to reveal.

A.D. 591. XLIII. GREGORY THE GREAT.

(Book I, Letters, Indiction IX, Letter LXXII.)

[Col. 1435B] Gregory to Gennadius, patrician and exarch of Africa.

Just as the Lord of victories has caused Your Excellency to shine brightly in this life through hostile wars, so you ought also to oppose with every energy of mind and body the enemies of His Church, so that its renown may shine ever more brightly through a twofold triumph: since you both vigorously resist in secular conflicts the adversaries of the Catholic Church and, like warriors of the Lord, fight bravely the battles of the Church.

For it is known that men of heretical religion, if—may it not be so—they have freedom to harm, rise up violently against the Catholic faith, so that they may pour forth the poisons of their heresy to corrupt the members of Christ’s body. We have learned that they lift their necks against the Catholic Church, although the Lord opposes them, and seek to overthrow the faith of the Christian name. But let Your Eminence crush their attempts and press their proud necks beneath the yoke of righteousness.

XLIV. THE SAME, TO THE SAME, IN THE SAME BOOK, LETTER LXXV.

Gregory to all the bishops of Numidia.

For through Hilary, Our chartulary, you petitioned Our predecessor of blessed memory that all the customs of former times might be preserved for you which long antiquity has maintained until now from the beginnings of the ordinances of blessed Peter, prince of the apostles. We, indeed, in accordance with the tenor of your report, grant that the custom which is recognized as assuming nothing contrary to the Catholic faith shall remain unaltered, both concerning the appointment of primates and the other chapters—except for those who attain the episcopate from among the Donatists. We absolutely forbid them to be promoted to the dignity of the primacy, even when the order of clerics puts them forward for that same place.

It is enough for them to care only for the people entrusted to them; they are not to precede, in attaining the summit of primatial rank, those bishops whom the Catholic faith has both instructed and begotten within the bosom of the Church.

A.D. 592. XLV. THE SAME, BOOK II, LETTER XXXIII.

Gregory to Columbus, bishop of Numidia.

It is known, dearest brother in Christ, that the ancient enemy, who by crafty persuasion first cast the first human being down from the delights of Paradise into this wretched life, thereby already then inflicted upon humankind the penalty of mortality. By the same craftiness he now endeavors, in order more easily to seize the flock, to infect the shepherds of the Lord’s sheep by pouring in poisons, and thus rightly to claim them for his own power.

But we, who, though unworthy, have undertaken to govern the Apostolic See in the place of Peter, prince of the apostles, are compelled by the very office of the pontificate to oppose the common enemy with all the effort in our power.

The bearers of the present letter, Constantius and Mustellus, having presented a petition, informed us and assert that the deacons of the Church of Pudentiana, situated in the province of Numidia, have allowed Maximinus, bishop of the same church, in the place where he resides, corrupted by a bribe, to be made a bishop of the Donatists under a novel license; although, even if earlier usage allowed this, the Catholic faith forbade it to remain and endure.

For this reason, by the present letter, we have judged it necessary to exhort your Fraternity that, when Hilary, Our chartulary, comes to you, you should gather a general council of bishops and investigate this matter with subtle and diligent inquiry, keeping before your eyes the terror of the coming judgment. If this charge is proved against the said bishop by suitable evidence from the bearers of this letter, he must in every way be removed from the dignity and office which he exercises, so that he may return through acknowledgement of his offense to the profit of repentance, and others may not presume to attempt such things.

For it is just that one who, as is reported, sold our Lord Jesus Christ to a heretic for received money should be excluded from handling the mysteries of His most holy body and blood. But if any dispute concerning certain losses or private affairs, apart from this crime, is pending between them, as the petition of the deacons themselves contains, let your Fraternity investigate it by private inquiry together with Our aforesaid chartulary, and let justice proceed to determine it between both parties.

Moreover, from the statement of the bearers of this letter we have learned that the Donatist heresy is daily spreading because of our sins, and that very many people, when permission is granted through venality, are after Catholic baptism baptized anew by Donatists. How grave this is, brother, we must consider with the full attention of our minds. Behold: the wolf is no longer secretly tearing apart the Lord’s flock at night, but in open daylight; we see him raging in the slaughter of the sheep, yet oppose him with no diligence and no darts of speech. What fruits, then, of the multiplied flock shall we show the Lord, if we behold with idle minds even the flock we undertook to feed being devoured by the beast? . . . .

Let us therefore keep watch lest anything perish; and if perhaps anything has been taken captive, let us bring it back to the Lord’s flock by the words of the divine oracles, so that He who is Shepherd of shepherds may mercifully deign, in His judgment, to approve that we have kept watch over His flock.

You must also diligently attend to this: if any just complaint exists against the bearers of this letter on the part of the same bishop, it too must be investigated with careful inquiry; and if perhaps they themselves must rightly be punished for their fault, we by no means judge that they should be spared.

A.D. 594. XLVI. THE SAME, BOOK III, LETTER XXXII.

Gregory to Pantaleon, prefect of Africa.

[Col. 1437A]

It is not unknown to Your Excellency how earnestly the law pursues the most abominable perversity of heretics. Therefore, since both the integrity of our faith and the severity of worldly laws condemn these persons, it is no slight sin if in your time they find freedom to spread again.

In those regions, as we have learned, the audacity of the Donatists has grown to such a degree that they not only expel, by pestilential authority, priests of the Catholic faith from their churches, but also do not fear to rebaptize those whom the water of regeneration had washed in true confession. We are greatly astonished, if indeed this is so, that while you are stationed there men of such perverse character are allowed to go to these excesses.

First, consider what judgment concerning yourself you leave to people, if those who were restrained with good reason under the administrations of others find, while you govern, a way to their excesses. Then know that our God will require at your hand the souls of the lost if you neglect, insofar as your power permits, to correct so great an abomination.

XLVII. THE SAME, *Ibid.*, LETTER XXXV.

Gregory to Victor and Columbus, bishops of Africa.

We have learned that the assaults of the Donatists have so disturbed the Lord’s flock in those regions as though it were governed by the restraint of no shepherd; and word has reached us of what we cannot mention without profound grief: that very many have already been torn by their venomous teeth. [Col. 1437C] In short, they are said, with most reckless audacity, to drive canonical priests from their churches; and, moreover, by rebaptizing many whom the water of regeneration had conferred salvation, to have slain them by their utterly wicked perversity. These things deeply grieve us, since, while you are stationed there, it has been permitted to their condemned presumption to perpetrate so great a crime. Therefore, in this letter we exhort your brotherhood that, after deliberation has been held and a council convened, you ought zealously and with all your strength to resist this disease while it is still in its growth, lest it gain force through neglect and shake the flock entrusted to you with the ravages of pestilence.

**A.D. 596. XLVIII. THE SAME, Book V, Epistle XXXVI.**

Gregory to Columbus, bishop of Numidia.

[Col. 1437D]

Furthermore, a matter altogether grievous and hostile to the true faith has reached us: namely, that Catholic and religious persons—which is worse—consent to have their children, slaves, or others subject to their authority baptized in the heresy of the Donatists. Therefore, if this is true, let your brotherhood take the greatest care [Col. 1438A] to correct it, so that the purity of your faith may remain unstained through your vigilance, and innocent souls which might have been saved by Catholic baptism may not perish through the infection of heretics. Whoever, therefore, among the persons mentioned above has allowed any of his own people to be baptized among the Donatists, must labor with every effort and all diligence to recall them to the Catholic faith. But if any such person henceforth permits this to be done to his own people on any pretext, let him by every means be excluded from the clergy.

**336 XLIX. THE SAME, ibid., Epistle LXIII.**

Gregory to Maurice Augustus.

Amid the cares of warfare and the innumerable anxieties which, with untiring diligence, you endure for the government of the Christian commonwealth, [Col. 1438B] it is a great cause of joy to me together with the whole world that Your Piety always watches with especial concern over the guardianship of that faith by which the empire of sovereigns shines brightly. Hence I am wholly confident that, just as you defend God’s cause with the love of a religious mind, so God by His grace protects and assists Your Majesty. The tenor of the commands sent forth has made it very clear how the serenity of Your Piety has been moved, by consideration of justice and zeal for most pure religion, against the most disgraceful perversity of the Donatists.

But the most reverend bishops arriving from the African province assert that these commands have been set aside through careless dissimulation, so that neither is God’s judgment there held in fear, nor have the imperial orders hitherto taken effect. They add also [Col. 1438C] that in the aforesaid province the Catholic faith is openly sold, the rewards offered by the Donatists prevailing. Conversely, the glorious man Gennadius complained to me in similar terms concerning one of those who made such complaints, and two other trustworthy persons bore witness with him on the same matter. But because the case concerned a secular judge, I judged that the same bishops should be directed to the feet of Your Piety, so that they might themselves lay before your most serene ears what they declare they have suffered for the Catholic faith.

Therefore I beseech you that the Christianity of our sovereigns, for the salvation of its soul and the life of its most pious offspring, command by a strict decree that those whom it knows to be such be punished; that it uphold with a rescuing hand those who are falling into ruin; apply to mad minds the medicine of correction; and drive out from them the diseases of their errors. [Col. 1438D] Thus, when by the remedy of your pious providence the darkness of this pestilential perversity has been driven away and the true faith has shed there the rays of its brightness, a heavenly triumph may await you before the eyes of our Redeemer: because those whom you defend outwardly from the enemy you also, more gloriously, free inwardly from the poison of diabolical deceit.

**337 APPENDIX TO THE PRECEDING MONUMENTS.**

[Col. 1439]

# HISTORY OF THE CONFERENCE AT CARTHAGE ONCE HELD BETWEEN CATHOLICS AND DONATISTS.

By François Balduin, Doctor of Civil Law.

## FRANÇOIS BALDUIN GREETS THE REVEREND LORD JEAN TILLET, BISHOP OF MEAUX.

[Col. 1439A]

When in these days I happened to reread our Optatus, whom, with the help of your manuscript, I intend to publish again in a newly corrected edition, I thought long and deeply about what he meant when he said that the commonwealth is not in the Church, but the Church is in the commonwealth. Yet when at last I seemed to have grasped the reason and ground of this most weighty statement, looking back upon the condition—or rather, the confusion—of our own times, I judged that one might also rightly say that the commonwealth is more in the Church than the Church is in the commonwealth.

For the Church itself is, as it were, the soul of the commonwealth, which is like a body; so that if the former is sound, we judge the latter to be well, but if the former is mad, the latter ill. Indeed, without a well-ordered Church no stable condition of the commonwealth can exist; nor, if any such condition can exist, is it greatly to be desired, provided we remember that there ought to be some end to human affairs. We do not deny that the difficulties of ordering the Church aright have always been greater than those of rightly ordering the commonwealth; nor, amid this accumulation of corruption in the world, do we wonder that they have always been so great, when even now there is the sharpest dispute over what and where the Church is, and which body is the Church, or what its form ought to be.

This question is greater in proportion as the matter itself is known to be of greater weight and consequence. We must acknowledge that the welfare of the commonwealth is bound up with the welfare of the Church—as its disturbance is followed by disturbance in the former—so that all who foresee what calamity otherwise threatens both will the more desire that each may be safe, and understand the means by which each is to be preserved. [Col. 1439C] Nor is there any question what, or how great, is now the disturbance, indeed the confusion, of both: for we know, more than we could wish, that it is most grievous and miserable. But the question is whether any removal of such great evils may not only be desired but also hoped for.

For I hear alarmed governors, if there are any wise ones, anxiously asking this question; otherwise this tempest and its violence not only terrifies them, but strikes them down, broken and weakened by a certain despair. Yet remembering that the waves were formerly no smaller, from which nevertheless both commonwealth and Church emerged, set free through the counsel and courage of their defenders, I do not think that counsel is lacking, provided the rulers themselves do not fail themselves and their office, to whom it has been entrusted to take care that neither the one nor the other suffers loss. [Col. 1440A]

For the history itself of the ancient Church and commonwealth furnishes an example, as it were a pattern—indeed a law—of duty and of wisdom in harmony with religion, which once composed all disturbances and can compose them now. Therefore I have always judged that wise and religious antiquity should above all be consulted. Nor do I arrogate so much to myself as to wish to pronounce my own opinion on so great a matter; nor, if I presumed so greatly, should I be tolerated.

This alone I shall say: if Gaul now had such men as Africa once had in Marcellinus and Augustine, great relief might be hoped for from the evils under which the commonwealth is now oppressed. But what those great men, those very heroes, did while the Donatists were throwing Africa into disorder, and what method they followed to overcome them, you yourself enabled me to understand more fully, by communicating to me certain unpublished records of the Conference of Carthage. The reading of these moved me to trace that history back more deeply, investigate it more carefully, and set it out more familiarly, since I perceived it to be no insignificant part of ecclesiastical history, in which I do not deny that I take an interest, and judged that its remembrance might be very useful in these times.

I did not think I ought long to deliberate to whom I should dedicate it, when you presented yourself: you who were author and helper of my giving some labor to this commentary; who are especially a suitable judge of these matters and of ecclesiastical antiquities; and who in some measure model yourself after Augustine. Finally, it came to mind that not only the commonwealth and the Church owe you very much, but that I myself privately am bound to you for many reasons: not only to you, but also to your brother the chief secretary, and to the lords de Saint-André, brothers and your relatives by marriage, men most distinguished and learned. [Col. 1440C]

Nor indeed did I judge there to be a better way of testifying to my respect for you and yours than this dedication of the present work. Nor did I think that, if I revived some idle, low, and hackneyed dispute drawn from the subtle dust either of the forum or of some lecture hall concerning our private civil law, the publication of such a gift would be more pleasing to you. Rather, I feared that I should then hear that old saying:

> This is not the time that calls for such spectacles.

Farewell. Paris, the Kalends of April, 1566.

## 339 TO THE READER.

[Col. 1441A]

Concerning Aeneas viewing the Carthaginian painting of the Trojan War, the good poet once wrote:

> His spirit feeds upon the empty picture,  
> Sighing deeply over many things . . . .

But as I sometimes reread that *Aeneid*, which I remember being read aloud to me at school when I was a boy, and compare the condition of my own misfortunes, I am variously affected, having myself been much tossed upon lands and sea. So too, in this almost desperate calamity of the Church and in the common miseries of the commonwealth, by which I am moved no less than by private afflictions, I somehow sustain my sorrowful mind by recalling ancient histories, in which many things occur that console both me and my groans.

While engaged in this, I happened upon certain records of the Church of Carthage. In them I read—not, as Aeneas did in Dido’s temple, a painted history of the Trojan War—but a most noble account of an ecclesiastical disputation concerning the Church and the Donatists. Its reading refreshed me, though at the same time I often groaned as I reflected on the conflicts of our own age. [Col. 1441B]

I remember that when Emperor Charles V held the Diet at Regensburg in Germany, in which religion was examined and debated, the old precedent of that Carthaginian conference, as it was called, was commended. And some years later, after returning to Gaul, when I came upon that assembly at Poissy, in which a not dissimilar conference was said to have been instituted anew, I did not conceal that the ancient history of the African Church contained a memorable precedent to which this age ought to look.

But what follows? Neither presidents like Marcellinus nor bishops like Augustine now appear again to deal with grammarians like Cresconius and advocates like Petilian. Therefore it is all the more necessary to have recourse to the counsel and protection of sound antiquity, whose authority is such that it often terrifies even the boldest adversaries.

I therefore most willingly examined the records of that Carthaginian conference, of which I have just spoken, which Jean Tillet, the most learned bishop of Meaux, communicated to me unpublished, and compared them with Augustine’s *Breviculus*. For in them are scattered many ornaments, as it were, of our own law; and they contain an action and disputation concerning the Church that is nearly civil in character. And just as Marcellinus is investigating commissioner and judge, a great glory of jurisprudence, [Col. 1441C] so the parties are not unskilled in forensic proceedings. Indeed, Petilian—the advocate of the bad side in this case—was a more crafty lawyer and more practiced in the cautions and evasions of the courts than the case required. For after he had entered upon the administration of the Donatist church, he could not forget his old habit and profession. As Augustine says (*Against Petilian*, Book III, ch. 17), he used to boast of his former power in forensic advocacy.

Yet it was well that such a wrangler not only encountered Marcellinus but ran into Augustine himself, who could suppress the troublesome barking of an unclean and shameless dog with a just and weighty reply; and who, even now by the same example, could restrain other gown-wearing men of that kind and order—not petty jurists, but charlatans. For such busybodies are still stirred by a similar intemperance to bark aloud; and, because their tongues are venal, we now see that they are also prostituted.

I would not dare to compare Petilian with that worthy Theodore, whom some call mad, while others report that in the skirmish at Poissy, as he himself called it, he appeared very crafty—if not an old campaigner, certainly an old deceiver. This alone I say: although in the Carthaginian arena there were many things that weakened Petilian, and in that of Poissy many that aided Theodore, it nevertheless happened that the latter stuck in the mire no less than the former when the question of the Church was reached, where Augustine again stood in the way like a rock. [Col. 1442A]

Indeed, before the first encounter, Theodore offered a confession of his faith, in his own name and in that of many Frenchmen who had nevertheless never read it. At the outset he professed that he condemned and detested all sects and heresies that had formerly been condemned in the Church by holy doctors, from the times of Hilary and Athanasius down to Ambrose and Cyril. Some in that assembly laughed to hear such a foolish statement—though one evidently long and carefully composed—produced, joining Ambrose with Cyril and implying that a great interval of time lay between Athanasius or Hilary and Ambrose. Yet Theodore himself, that wonderful chronologer, had recently written to the Poles that Hilary was **σύνχρονος** (*synchronic*, a contemporary) of Augustine.

Good hearers forgave that bearded master such solecisms, which the schoolmaster’s rod would have punished, as readily as they marveled that he spoke and wrote in such a way as not merely to seem not to condemn heresies condemned before Hilary’s time, but even to imply his approval of all the judgments of the ancient Church from Hilary’s age to Cyril’s. But those who listened calmly to that confused and disorderly confession judged it to reveal a certain alarm in men summoned, as it were, before the tribunal of religious antiquity. They wished that, once returned to themselves, they might hold so firmly to their position as simply to acknowledge that the perpetual consensus of the Church, extending from apostolic times onward wherever it is found, [Col. 1442D] possesses great authority.

Indeed, when the worthy Theodore was recalled to that consensus, the dispute might have been settled without fraud if he had acted in good faith. And, so that he might doubt less, there was produced what had been written by his master in the *Institutes*: that Augustine had rightly objected to the Donatists the continuous succession of the Church; for there was no doubt that meanwhile nothing—not even at Rome—had been changed in the doctrine itself. But when cautious Theodore saw where an admission of this would lead him, yet was not so bold as openly to deny it, he evaded the issue, muttering obscurely and confusedly something in which neither admission nor denial could be understood.

Thus Petilian too, when pressed, since he alleged that the Church had long ago fallen away through degeneration, to identify the time and define the character of that apostasy, and had nothing clear to say, claimed that he had become hoarse through the length of the discussion; and, using that excuse for silence, made his escape. Theodore is too glorious a soldier to deign to flee. But while retainers followed him in triumph, some who were less mad asked whether there was nothing Petilian could have answered to Augustine, who had brought forward the prophecies concerning the Church to be spread and extended throughout the world, applying them even to his own time.

Theodore, a more ingenious prophet, greeted this with a sneering laugh:

> Mountains will be in labor; a ridiculous mouse will be born.

His friends warned him that this Lucianic mockery was too obvious. Therefore the good poet, wishing to make some show of an answer, added like a new Sibyl: at least the Donatists, against whom Augustine had set the prophecies concerning the future Church, could have objected to Augustine the Virgilian verse:

> The fates shall show her to the lands only for a time,  
> And shall not suffer her to remain longer.

When it was said again that this was boundless and absurd, where the question is when and how the visible Church ceased to exist, acute Theodore perceived that he was pressed again. But after he had tortured himself for some time, he thought he could cleverly escape when in his latest preface he recently wrote that the Church’s succession, once so highly praised, had long ago failed; for wicked men had long since succeeded good ones. [Col. 1443C]

I said that this was no answer at all, and was a second absurdity, since he spoke as though the question concerned succession of persons rather than succession of things; although in the debate at Poissy he had professed that he cared nothing for a succession of persons, but sought a succession of doctrine and things. But what mockery again is this: when asked so often about the time of the falling away, he repeats nothing but his “long ago”? Indeed, when he could no longer restrain his bursting indignation, I hear that in that same military preface of his, which he prefixed to the Gospel in order to frighten me, he angrily cried out, among many other unworthy statements intended to slaughter the Church which we defend with Augustine, that those ancient bishops had never conceived that one must neither “Judaize” nor, as he puts it, “Gentilize”; and that for this reason the Christian religion had quickly and shamefully degenerated into empty ceremonies, theatrical liturgies, manifest superstition, and finally into **ἀθεότης** (*atheotēs*, godlessness).

I was indeed astonished that inspired—**ἔνθεος**—Theodore should write such things and turn against the ancient Church what he might have said of his own party, declaring that the Church which he had said long ago fell away had degenerated no less quickly than shamefully. But what does Lucianic impiety not dare now? Petilian with his Donatists shouted that the Church which Augustine proclaimed was apostolic, and that Catholics were regarded by them not as Christians but as pagans; Optatus and Augustine are witnesses. Yet Petilian accused only the morals of bishops, not also the doctrine and rites of that Church.

Theodore, indignant at this accuser—whom he suspected of being either foolish, too modest, or even a traitor to his cause—thought, being an honest man, that nothing should be concealed and that they must at last act more harshly. Because perhaps he had been more restrained in his skirmish at Poissy, was indulgence always to continue? Why not indeed? Thus Gaudentius himself, another advocate of the Donatists, who at the Carthaginian conference had maintained that his party was the Catholic Church, after he perceived that he could not prove what Augustine asserted for his Church, dared openly to say that everything said about the Catholic Church was a human invention. See where mad men end or return.

I for one would least of all wish, when the body of the Church is defended, that its blemishes, stains, and corruptions should also be defended or excused. On the contrary, these sins of men must be most severely condemned. But I wish that we ourselves would observe the measure which the prophets observed in their ministry, when we read those divine heralds of the Church, who were at once censors and most severe accusers of vices, as we shall also say in our exposition of the Carthaginian conference. [Col. 1444B]

Meanwhile, I confess—and know that no one can deny—what and how great is the foulness of the miserable Church, overgrown with filth; what deformity belongs to her corruption; how great the decline of one sinking utterly; and finally, what and how great the despair of one seemingly abandoned. I confess, therefore, that matters have come to such a pass that nothing remains for us but to repeat with groaning that most sorrowful complaint of Jeremiah lamenting the devastation of Jerusalem, overthrown and deserted:

> Zion has spread out her hands,  
> But there is none to comfort her.

Yet in the midst of her ruins we have not yet forgotten what the psalm says: that the servants of the Lord love even the ruins and dust of Zion and pity them. [Col. 1444C] So far are we from flattering those whom we see insulting her both at home and abroad that the words often come to mind which another prophet, Ezekiel, wrote shortly before that calamity: that he was commanded by God to break through the wall and, as through an opened window, behold what impious and wicked men were doing in the temple, so that he might abhor their abominations.

But one thing consoles me at the same time. For in that same passage, when God announces that He will exact a terrible vengeance, He also signifies that meanwhile He wishes to have mercy on those who mourned with the prophet, having turned away from that profane or sacrilegious mass. He therefore commands that the avenging angel mark the foreheads of those who groan, so that those to be spared may be more plainly recognized and distinguished when he makes a terrible slaughter of the others.

I return to the case of the Donatists. For many things now come to mind when I read in Optatus that they once asked Constantine for judges in Gaul, in whom for some reason they had greater confidence; and when I learn from Augustine what faithfulness and integrity belonged to the synod at Arles in Gaul, to whose judgment Constantine committed the second hearing of that case and of the Donatists who appealed. They immediately perceived that they had vainly and foolishly hoped there for either favor or protection. For, condemned again, they received a judgment worthy of their insolence, and they were no less disappointed then in Gaul than they were a hundred years later in the court at Carthage. [Col. 1445A]

What we ought now to think when we read such things, I leave for others to consider. For both what is now being done and the point to which matters have come are all too well known. “To such evils,” says Augustine (*Epistle* 22), “long groans are more fitting than long books.” Yet when we read that the Donatists of old, armed with force and audacity, were also learned craftsmen of lying, we marvel that their shamelessness was such that they not only always boasted that they had conquered where they had been defeated, but even at the Carthaginian conference produced the book of Optatus—which recounted their condemnation—as a witness to their victory and acquittal, having so mutilated and corrupted it that they seemed to have turned everything upside down.

What then shall we say? Is not the shamelessness of many storytellers from the mad faction even greater now, who invent whatever they please for their own advantage and for the deception of others, vending their lies and inventions as histories and truthful narratives? Surely those who foresee how greatly this imposture will pour error and darkness upon miserable posterity cannot help grieving that this is being done, so that, to use the words of the law, “the truth of events is corrupted by errors in the records.”

Augustine once said he wondered that the Donatists had blood in their bodies who never blushed, though caught so often in manifest lying. What would he have said about the pallid shamelessness of men who are both forgers and bloodthirsty? When he refuted Cresconius, the Donatist grammarian, he wondered whether he might exclaim:

> Shame has utterly vanished from the world.

But he had written concerning the Pelagians that the forehead of heretics is not a forehead. Would he have hesitated if he had seen the shamelessness of the mad heresy? Would he not also have repeated Ezekiel’s words:

> You have acquired a harlot’s forehead;  
> You refused to be ashamed.

And further, what if he saw the wide-open ears of an ignorant multitude listening to impostors? He once said that Petilian’s followers, applauding their lying master, had not ears in their heart but a heart in their ears. What heart, then, would he think remained in those who feed on nothing but filthy and insulting fables? [Col. 1445D]

Behold: not yet sated with the libelous books of their most libelous Beza, they have even corrupted the proceedings of the colloquy at Poissy, inventing in them many things which the facts themselves cry out to be utterly false. They even inserted me, although I was scarcely present, and—ridiculously—related that I had had almost the role of some **μεσίτης** (*mesitēs*, mediator), not to say the role Marcellinus himself had at Carthage.

What? Aeneas, viewing the painting which I mentioned before,

> Recognized himself also mingled with the Greek chiefs.

But with what eyes was I to read that I had almost presided over the leaders and directors of the disputation at Poissy? I suppose those witty triflers invented such tales in order to laugh and play. But they have too much leisure if they have time to be so very foolish and frivolous in a serious matter. Indeed, because they had heard that the Donatists once jestingly alleged that Marcellinus had been bribed in the conference, they also invented that I had been enriched by some unknown Navarrese liberality and munificence. [Col. 1446A] Why should I not seriously grieve here that they play and lie?

I believe that, had that excellent prince lived longer, he would not have disappointed the hope which he had given, that he would reward my greater and better labors. Now perhaps there is some reason why, after his death, our adversaries insult us—especially since at last they have accomplished, by the many snares they had long attempted, that what I thought would be the hope of my little household I have found to be its greatest calamity, compounded in these recent days by a new and almost incredible wrong, with even the resources of my studies plundered.

But I shall complain elsewhere about such reward or viperine favor. This alone I say: by such a benefit this work, to which I was giving attention when it happened, was broken off no less than another, by whose addition I otherwise intended to enlarge this one. At the same time I had happened to be asked publicly to interpret the laws concerning religion and the Church which first occur in the Code of Constitutions. I spent several days on this in the law lecture hall at Paris, especially because such was the assembly and multitude of hearers—for several thousand most learned men gathered—and such their attention and constancy, that I myself was stirred to set forth at greater length the counsels of that most wise, brave, and, above all, most religious prince, Theodosius, and his best enactments concerning the reconciliation and restoration to wholeness of the Church, counsels confirmed also by the Council of Constantinople. [Col. 1446B]

I therefore wished then, if the Davuses who throw everything into confusion had permitted it, to compare the example and policy of Theodosius the father, which saved the Church of the East, with the plan which his son Honorius adopted thirty years later for freeing the African Church. Each is an especially memorable example, which those who wish the commonwealth to be safe together with the Church should follow even now in a similar danger threatening the alarmed commonwealth.

I know that such things are now ridiculed and are even odious. But because many now ridicule virtue also as a fable or an empty name, shall we therefore trample underfoot every image and cast away every memory of virtue? On the contrary, because wicked men have never seen virtue—not even piety—it must be thrust upon them against their will and set before them all the more, as antiquity once honored it:

> Let them behold Virtue, and waste away because they have abandoned her.

At least let me be pardoned if I do not conceal my delight in laws and good examples drawn also from ecclesiastical history, and in memorials of a holier jurisprudence. In comparison with these, the other, more subtle mysteries—as they are called—of civil law now seem almost sordid to me, though they are vaingloriously celebrated under that title. [Col. 1446D]

For all I care, let jurists who wish throw themselves either into the pursuit of petty schoolroom glory from empty **λεπτολογίαι** (*leptologiai*, subtleties), or into gathering wealth in the courts, or even into pursuing offices miserably—or certainly purchasing them ruinously. Only let it be permitted me, with their good leave, to leave and concede to them entirely what they prize so highly, so that I may rather embrace what they neglect.

# 343 HISTORY OF THE CONFERENCE AT CARTHAGE.

[Col. 1447]

[Col. 1447A] In speaking of the most celebrated Conference of Carthage between Catholics and Donatists, I shall begin somewhat further back with the ancient record of the African Church. For even very learned men make various errors in listing the councils of Carthage, setting forth this part of ecclesiastical history somewhat too negligently.

Balsamon, the Greek translator of the *Nomocanon*, observes that the first council after the time of the apostles was that Council of Carthage over which Cyprian presided when the baptism of heretics was discussed. But this is said no less foolishly than the claim of the compilers of the Latin miscellany of councils, and of the Magdeburg copyists in the *Centuries of Ecclesiastical History*, that the first Council of Carthage was that Donatist synod in which Caecilian of Carthage was condemned in absentia.

If one asks which council was the first after the apostolic age, I would rather say that it was the synod at Caesarea in Palestine which debated the Paschal day in the time of Emperor Commodus. Eusebius bears witness (*Ecclesiastical History*, Book V, ch. 23; Book VI, chs. 36–37) that shortly afterward synods gathered for the same reason at Rome, in Gaul, Achaia, and Arabia. Then, before Cyprian, another Carthaginian synod on the baptism of heretics was held. Cyprian writes to Jubaianus: “It is now many years and a long time since, under Agrippinus, a man of blessed memory, many bishops assembling together decreed this,” and so forth. Augustine, however, in Book IV of *On Baptism*, ch. 6, says that this happened not many but few years before Cyprian, so that we understand the event not to have occurred so very many years earlier. [Col. 1447C]

Nor was there only one Council of Carthage on that subject in Cyprian’s time. Indeed, Cyprian indicates in his letter to Jubaianus that there were three. Concerning the most famous of these, which the Donatists especially abused, some once even said that it was false and fabricated; and Augustine at one time indicated that he was not altogether remote from their view (*Against Cresconius*, Book I, ch. 32). Yet in *Epistle* 48 he candidly admits, and confesses that the style itself makes clear, that it was not fabricated.

Besides, if an African or Carthaginian synod is to be praised in Cyprian’s time, the one rather to be commended is that which Cyprian recounts in Book IV, Epistle 8: it met against those who, abusing the example of circumcision, refused to baptize infants before the eighth day. But the African bishops who, together with Cyprian, wrote to Cornelius, pope of Rome, concerning the granting of peace to repentant lapsed persons, provided at that time the appearance of a commendable Carthaginian synod against Novatus. Eusebius likewise testifies that at the same time a Roman synod, in which Africans also took part, made a similar determination (*Ecclesiastical History*, Book VI, ch. 43). [Col. 1447D]

Before proceeding to the Donatists, it is worthwhile also to say something about the Novatians. For the Donatists succeeded them, as it were; there were many similarities between them; and many highly learned men in former times confused much here that must be distinguished. So great is the disorder in the ecclesiastical history of Africa, which is most worthy of better remembrance.

Thus Epiphanius and Theodoret say that the Donatists belonged to the Novatian heresy. Indeed, Epiphanius ignorantly attributes to the Novatians what ought properly to be said of the Donatists, when he says that the former were called “Mountaineers” at Rome. Certainly, although they agreed in rebaptism, they did not agree in baptismal ceremonies. The Donatists also used chrism; the Novatians did not. Nor were the Donatists opponents of repentance, as the Novatians were; nor did they, like the latter, condemn second marriages.

At least Cresconius himself, a Donatist, when denying that he was a heretic and listing heretics with whom he had nothing in common, also mentions the Novatians; and Augustine, replying to him, does not brand him with any mark of Novatian heresy (*Against Cresconius*, Book II, ch. 3). Yet the Novatian schism had many similarities with that of the Donatists; but the Novatians did not rage so cruelly, and held sway rather in Italy and the East than in Africa.

Just as some people formerly rashly confused Donatus the Numidian with Donatus of Carthage, so also many confuse Novatus with Novatian. Certainly Theodoret, in his *Compendium of Heretical Fables*, writes of Novatus what ought rather to have been written of Novatian; and Epiphanius says that [Col. 1448C] Novatus was at Rome during the persecution, whereas this seems rather to be said of Novatian. Finally Zonaras likewise calls Novatus, through the same error, a presbyter of the Roman Church and the founder of a heresy. But those who have read Cyprian, or even Jerome in the *Catalogue*, or Pacian’s recently published letters, readily perceive what should properly be attributed to Novatus and what to Novatian. I therefore wonder all the more that the authors of the *Centuries* of ecclesiastical history wrote that Novatian had been made a deacon of Carthage by Novatus against Cyprian’s will. They ought rather to have said Felicissimus.

Novatus was indeed a presbyter of Cyprian, bishop of Carthage. Having come to Italy, he procured the appointment at Rome of Novatian, a Roman presbyter, as a kind of antipope, [p. 344] [Col. 1448D] when Novatian was cavilling that the election of Cornelius—which he had been unable to prevent—was not legitimate. So Donatus the Numidian, when accusing the ordination of Caecilian, bishop of Carthage, procured the ordination of Majorinus, to whom the other Donatus succeeded, as Augustine testifies in his book *On Heresies*. Augustine accordingly adds that Donatus was the first in the city of Carthage [Col. 1449A] to set up “altar against altar,” just as Cyprian had earlier said in similar terms that the Novatians had done the same, but at Rome.

This is the supreme evil of schism, charged alike against the Donatists and earlier against the Novatians, rather than a charge of heresy. Dionysius of Alexandria, writing to Novatian and reminding him of his duty, says that he ought to have done anything whatever rather than divide the Church by schism; and that he ought to have fled schism even more than idolatry, because in fleeing the latter he safeguards only himself, while in fleeing the former he provides for the whole Church. Jerome in the *Catalogue* is the witness.

Indeed, had the Novatians not been guilty of schism, they might perhaps have said that their opinion concerning the lapsed and concerning the baptism of heretics was not a novel and unprecedented example. For what then? Cyprian himself writes in his letter to Antonianus that, among his predecessors, as he says, in his own province certain bishops had thought that peace was not to be granted to adulterers, and had altogether closed against adultery the place of repentance. Yet what does he add in order somehow to excuse them? “Nevertheless,” he says, “they did not withdraw from the fellowship of their fellow bishops, nor did they break the unity of the Catholic Church by the obstinacy of their severity or discipline.” Augustine too, agreeing with Cyprian, carefully observed this in Letter 48.

I pass over the fact that Tertullian himself seems long before, in his book *On Modesty*, to have defended most vehemently what Cyprian here says certain bishops before him had believed. But Tertullian broke the unity of the Church through obstinate adherence to his severity or discipline [Col. 1449C].

Moreover, because the Novatians did not regard as baptized those baptized in the Church—which they accused of being polluted and from which they had seceded as though it were profane—and therefore rebaptized them, they did what Cyprian indicates, in his letters to Jubaianus and Pompeius, and Augustine, *On Baptism*, book III, chapter 10, heretics had not previously dared to do. Yet they rested on a principle followed by most Catholic Africans and apparently confirmed by certain African councils, as I have said. Thus, as Novatus did not regard as valid baptism administered by Cyprian, so neither did Cyprian regard as valid baptism where Novatus or Novatian had been the minister.

The difference, however, was this: Cyprian disagreed with those who believed baptism should not be repeated, [Col. 1449D] yet did not on that account avoid their communion, break the bond of unity, or become the author of any schism. Augustine therefore reproves Cyprian’s error concerning baptism, but praises that charity of unity by which, he says, sin is covered. He declares that those who rebaptized in Cyprian’s time, yet did not withdraw from the bond—so he speaks—of unity, attained pardon through the same love of peace by which Cyprian himself tolerated persons admitted into the Church with no baptism other than that of heretics. Thus, just as Cyprian, for the preservation of unity, forgave those whom he otherwise thought mistaken in not repeating baptism, so Cyprian himself, who was in fact mistaken in repeating baptism, [Col. 1450A] was forgiven because of the same charity of unity, in which he nevertheless remained.

But the schismatic Novatians, who had departed from the Church while imbued with this error, were not forgiven; still less were the Donatists. For the opinion of the latter, although similar to that of the former, admitted of less excuse, because the Donatists knew that the error of that African council—which the Novatians might have pleaded—had been condemned in an ecumenical council.

Between the times of Novatus and Donatus, Sabellius the African, standing, as it were, in the middle, ventured upon something greater and attacked the very head of the Church, that is, Christ himself, whom he loudly declared to be no more than a man. In order to abolish the mystery of the Trinity, he contended that there was not only one *ousia* (οὐσία, essence) of divinity but also one hypostasis; and he taught that Father, [Col. 1450B] Son, and Holy Spirit were not persons but sounds and words. Finally, he repeated what Paul of Samosata, bishop of Antioch, was asserting at the same time.

This was a capital heresy, but it disturbed the African Church less than the faction of Donatus. Because Paul of Samosata was immediately condemned in the synod of Antioch, the African Catholics did not think it necessary to convene a new council to condemn Sabellius. Nor indeed does Sabellianism appear to have spread widely in Africa. At least Optatus writes in book I that, in his own time, not only the errors but even the names of Sabellius, Praxeas, and Marcion were almost unknown in the African provinces. I pass over the fact that Calvin writes in his *Institutes* that Sabellius came after Arius. For it is established that Sabellius [Col. 1450C] died before Arius was born. Yet it is no new thing for even highly learned men to wander ignorantly in the history of the African Church.

Pentapolis had produced Sabellius; and behold, shortly afterward, in neighboring Egypt Arius, and from Numidia—the other extremity of Africa—Donatus, caused greater commotions: the former in the Church of Alexandria, the latter in that of Carthage. As Optatus says in book III, speaking of Donatus, in Africa a conflagration was made from a spark; so Eusebius, book II of the *Life of Constantine*, says that, as a great fire is kindled from a small spark, the Arian conflagration spread even through Libya itself. But we are now concerned only with the Donatist tragedy, which was both earlier and less subtle.

Optatus carefully sets forth its origin and, as it were, its opening action in book I. Augustine likewise directs us, in book I *Against Parmenian*, chapter 3, to draw this history from Optatus, though certain matters absent from Optatus’s books must be drawn from Augustine [Col. 1450D].

First, I observe what Augustine writes in book VII *On Baptism*, chapter 7: forty years after Cyprian’s martyrdom occurred that surrender of the codices in Africa, the question of which is said to have been, if not the cause, at least the first occasion of the Donatist schism. Augustine also indicates, in book III *Against Cresconius*, chapter 27, that Diocletian was consul for the eighth time and Maximian for the seventh when they decreed that Christian books should be destroyed by fire. Eusebius describes in book VIII the tragedy of that final persecution. But concerning Africa he says only that it contained an innumerable multitude [Col. 1451A] of martyrs.

He says that at that time the Baths of Maximian were built in the city of Carthage, just as others were being built for Diocletian at Rome; many thousands of Christians labored at their construction, as though condemned to the mines. But our inquiry now concerns the Christians in Africa who fell, those guilty of surrendering the sacred codices, and the state and condition of the Church of Carthage.

Optatus relates that there was then a council at Cirta which somehow absolved those accused, though nearly the same men were both judges and defendants. This took place in Numidia, whose most famous and powerful city was Cirta: once, as Mela says, the home of the kings Juba and Syphax; later a Roman colony, which [p. 345] Pliny says was called the colony of the Sittiani; and formerly also the capital of the Masaesylians, as Livy writes in book XXX. Augustine indicates that the Council of Cirta of which I speak occurred in the same year, by naming the same consuls. Secundus of Tigisis, primate of Numidia, presided.

The very men who had met at Cirta afterward assembled, with some others of the same kind, in the city of Carthage. As mild and indulgent as they had been in the Cirtan gathering, so severe they wished to appear in this Carthaginian one. They condemned unheard and absent Caecilian, bishop of Carthage, whom they either charged with surrendering the Scriptures or loudly alleged to have been ordained by a traditor; they ordered him to abdicate, and appointed a certain Majorinus as his rival. Augustine in the *Breviculus* relates that this Carthaginian council against Caecilian consisted of seventy bishops [Col. 1451C], but was unjust and inequitable; its sentence against Caecilian was afterward annulled.

I therefore said that the Magdeburg writers were wrong to include it among ecclesiastical councils in their *Centuries*, and to represent it as the first Council of Carthage. This was the council which, as Augustine relates in the *Breviculus*, the Donatists later praised above all others at the Carthaginian Conference of which we shall speak, but without date or consuls, so that it might seem to be the first council in which they had judged a case involving surrender of the Scriptures; for the Council of Cirta, in which they had been more indulgent, was raised against them.

But whether they pronounced judgment earlier or later, they certainly ought to have allowed others the same right of judgment in the same case. They were intolerable: they punished so harshly in others an offence not even proved, while wishing it to go unpunished in themselves even when confessed. Moreover, Optatus, book I, indicates that the Carthaginian council came later than the Cirtan, saying that, “not long afterward,” those who had previously assembled at Cirta came to Carthage. Augustine uses a similar phrase in *Against the Donatists after the Conference*, chapter 33.

At the same time there must have been another and much larger Carthaginian council of Donatist bishops, since Augustine, Letter 48, testifies that two hundred and seventy Donatists—so swiftly did Donatus’s faction grow—assembled at Carthage forty years before the Macarian times. I infer from book III of Optatus that these times were those of the emperor Constans. If, then, we count forty years backward, we understand [Col. 1452A] that this occurred before Constantine obtained power, at least in Italy or Africa.

When I hear Augustine already reckoning 270 Donatist bishops at that Carthaginian council, while I recall that scarcely more than a hundred assembled against the Catholics at the Conference a century later, as I shall say, I suspect the number in Augustine to be corrupt—especially since it seems scarcely credible that so many Donatist bishops existed so quickly. I therefore suspected that two hundred might be removed, leaving only seventy, the number which, as we have said, assembled at that time against Caecilian; and someone may perhaps suppose it was the same council. But here I venture neither to affirm nor alter anything rashly.

Very memorable is Augustine’s addition that, after seventy-five days of prolonged deliberation, that Carthaginian council of so many Donatists decreed that communion should be held even with traditors who had not been rebaptized [Col. 1452B]. This accords better with what they had decreed in their Cirtan synod than with what they had done at Carthage against Caecilian.

What followed when, seven years later, the Donatists referred Caecilian’s case to the emperor Constantine must be drawn partly from Optatus and partly from Augustine. Constantine first appointed bishop-judges at Rome, then others at Arles, and finally himself judged the matter while at Milan. Optatus lacks what Augustine supplies concerning the judgment at Arles and Constantine’s sentence at Milan, by which Caecilian was finally acquitted: Letter 162 and book III *Against Cresconius*, chapter 71. Otherwise one might rashly infer from Optatus that Constantine rejected the Donatists’ appeal against the judgment of Miltiades in such a way that he would appoint no further judges; or that he simply then pronounced that an appeal was rashly made from a case already rightly decided, as someone has reported.

Rather, we should know truly that Constantine appointed judges for this appeal: not the bishop of Arles himself—Calvin rashly thought so, because he did not observe that this bishop had already been a judge at Rome with Miltiades—but other bishops who assembled at Arles.

If anyone asks when the Donatists, dissatisfied with their Carthaginian council, appealed to Constantine: Optatus’s first book says that the case was judged at Rome by those whom Constantine first appointed as judges when Constantine was consul for the fourth time and Licinius for the third [Col. 1452D]. Augustine, however, has that it occurred when Constantine was consul for the third time and Lucianus for the second. There is no doubt that “Lucianus” was mistakenly written for Licinius; but in Optatus, I in turn think, “IV” has been mistakenly written for “III,” and “III” for “II,” as scribes easily err in numbers.

Augustine supports what I have said by stating in *Against the Donatists after the Conference*, chapter 33, that in the following year Volusianus and Anianus were consuls. Diocletian, therefore, though long since abdicated, was still alive when Constantine was first appealed to by the Donatists. For Diocletian died under the consulship of Volusianus and Anianus, in the tenth year [Col. 1453A] after his edict for the destruction of Christian books.

As Donatus laid the foundations of his schism throughout that whole decade, so for nine subsequent years this case also wearied Constantine. Augustine finally relates that, while Constantine himself was consul with Crispus, he issued letters releasing the Donatists from exile and leaving their madness to God. So incapable did the Donatist faction seem of being restrained or repressed.

Three or four years after those letters, excessively indulgent toward the Donatists, had been issued, Constantine summoned the Council of Nicaea against Arius, whose suppression concerned him more deeply. The records indicate that Caecilian himself attended. Although several came there from Libya and the Thebaid, Benignus, bishop of Heraclea, also declared at the Fifth Synod—as its acts testify—that Caecilian alone was present from all Africa [Col. 1453B].

The Nicene Fathers, wholly occupied with refuting the Arians, somehow dismissed the Donatists. Yet I suspect that something concerning them was dealt with at Nicaea. Many perhaps will wonder why I suspect this, since neither the Nicene canons now circulated nor the acts commonly held mention them. But I have observed in Augustine’s books something not commonly noticed.

As regarding the Church, so concerning baptism there was a great controversy against the Donatists. They invoked Cyprian’s Carthaginian council because they did not regard as valid the baptism of their opponents, whom they judged alien to the Church, and therefore repeated it within their own communion. Ambrose testifies in *On the Surrendering of the Basilicas* that the Arians did this as well.

What of the Council of Nicaea? Augustine often indicates that what had pleased Cyprian’s Carthaginian council was reproved there. He contrasts that provincial Carthaginian [p. 346] council with a “plenary,” as he calls it, council of the whole world, of the universal Church, and of all nations. He writes in book II *On Baptism*, chapter 9, that this council met after Cyprian’s martyrdom and before Augustine himself was born; elsewhere he says more of Nicaea.

Since at Nicaea the Novatians and the lapsed were discussed, and pardon was given more readily to the former than to the latter when repentant, it seems that the Donatists and their doctrine were thereby also sufficiently dealt with, though silently. Let us now pursue the history and, as it were, tragedy of Donatus.

[Col. 1453D] The first Donatist bishop of Carthage, as I have said—the man who set himself against Caecilian and raised altar against altar—was Majorinus. He was succeeded by the other Donatus, who greatly strengthened this schism. Jerome in the *Catalogue* testifies that he wrote many works pertaining to his heresy. Gennadius, in his *Catalogue of Illustrious Writers*, also testifies that at the same time the African Vitellius was an extremely vigorous defender of this faction.

Meanwhile I have not read that any Catholic writer refuted the Donatists. I suppose that our side, as I have said, was wholly occupied with refuting the Arians. Thus the Donatists became ever more powerful in Africa. Donatus of Carthage [Col. 1454A] advanced so far that he not only arrogantly despised Roman emperors like some Hannibal, but was worshipped by his followers as though he were a god; oaths were sworn by his name as by a divinity; finally, it was believed that God answered him from heaven. Augustine and Optatus are witnesses.

Jerome nevertheless indicates in his *Chronicle* that this Donatus was eventually expelled from Carthage, although the chronological indication appears corrupt where it signifies that he flourished for thirty years. Optatus calls him a tyrant. Encouraged by such a leader, the Donatists dared everything. Arian supporters, armed with the patronage of emperors such as Constantius or Valens, dared persecute Catholics; but the Donatists immediately imitated Arian violence even though the emperors not only did not assist them but protested against them, and even though they were supported only by the audacity and frenzy of their own Circumcellions.

At some point the emperor Constans sent Macarius, his prefect, to Africa to restrain them; Macarius punished the Donatists severely. But such punishment could not remove the madness that had occupied many minds. The Catholics would have preferred the matter to be conducted without arms, and the error driving the headlong Donatists to be examined by reason and discussion, as Optatus sufficiently indicates.

Later Julian the Apostate armed Donatist audacity and restored to them the basilicas Constantine had previously taken away. Augustine is the witness, book II *Against Petilian*, chapter 92; he also often testifies that the Donatists praised the Apostate for this reason. Memorable, moreover, is the fact that the emperor Honorius decreed that the rescript which they had obtained from Julian should be published by public proclamation, so that the Donatists’ despairing, painted-over perfidy might become known to all: *Theodosian Code*, book XVI [OCR: “XXXVII”], title 5, *On Heretics*. I wish that rescript still survived. But whatever its character, the Apostate favored everyone whom he heard to be either apostates or enemies of the Church.

Thus the Donatists began to grow ever more insolent. Parmenian succeeded Donatus of Carthage and again spread and strengthened his sect through new pamphlets. At last someone of our party arose in Numidia to answer him: Optatus, bishop of Milevis. He testifies that he writes back and answers Parmenian, so that there might be, as it were, a conference between absent parties.

Many had desired a contest between the parties for the discovery of truth. But the Donatists had forbidden access, blocked the approaches, avoided permission, and refused a colloquy. Therefore it had been possible to deal with them only by letters. (Optatus calls the work he refutes Parmenian’s *treatise*. Parmenian also wrote a letter to Tychonius, which Augustine refuted in three books.)

After Parmenian, the Donatists’ Carthaginian primate was that Primianus who, accused by his own deacon Maximianus, whom he had condemned, brought it about that the Donatists, as it were, fought among themselves. Through a new schism they tore apart their own schism, and one party, as it were, rent the other, just as we have learned that the Arians were eventually divided into several sects.

Thus forty-three Donatist bishops assembled against Primianus in the city of Carthage and, as Augustine says, condemned him beforehand by their preliminary judgment. Then there was another Council of Cabarsussi, consisting of more than a hundred bishops of the same party, which condemned Primianus more fully. Augustine is the witness, book V *Against Cresconius*, chapter 6. In his exposition of Psalm 36, he quotes the complete and formal decision of that council. Augustine also says in *On Heresies* that Maximianus himself was ordained at Carthage against Primianus by a hundred bishops sharing the same error.

The year and consuls under which this occurred are less clear. Yet it may somehow be conjectured, since the contrary Council of Bagai followed shortly afterward, and Augustine indicates in book III *Against Cresconius*, chapter 56, that it met one year before Theodosius’s death. This Council of Bagai in Numidia consisted of 310 Donatist bishops. They annulled the decision rendered against Primianus in favor of Maximianus, declared that the hundred bishops—now called not Donatists but Maximianists—had judged wrongly, and restored Primianus to his former position. Augustine quotes the formula of the Bagai decision in book III *Against Cresconius*, chapter 53.

It is very necessary to know this entire affair carefully. For this is finally the matter by which Augustine proves that the Donatists had been cut down, as it were, by their own sword. At the Carthaginian Conference he accordingly pressed this point upon them above all others. Later, meeting Emeritus in Mauretania and reading the proceedings of the Conference, he earnestly entreated his hearers to learn attentively the history of the Maximianists, which he there again carefully expounds.

Since Primianus, primate of the Donatists at Carthage, is said to have been their leader and standard-bearer, I believe that he is the very man defended by the Synod of Bagai. Only sixteen years intervened between it and that Conference.

Finally, it must be observed that, in order to enforce the decision of their Council of Bagai, the Donatists produced the Theodosian law concerning heretics, by whose authority they expelled or coerced the Maximianists as heretics. Yet this law had been enacted against all Donatists, as well as the remaining heretics. But although the Donatists themselves did not obey it, they insisted that the Maximianists were subject to it, even occupying their basilicas.

The law provided that those who did not communicate with the Catholic Church should possess nothing in the Church’s name, but should rather restore it to unity, as Augustine says in Tractate 6 on John and book II *Against Petilian*. I omit other Theodosian laws against heretics, which Augustine often mentions, among which two especially notable laws had been enacted two or three years before that Council of Bagai. The earlier and extremely severe law, issued under the consulship of Titianus and Symmachus, survives in Justinian’s Code, book I [OCR: “III”], title 7, *On Apostates*. The other, issued [p. 347] in the following year—that is, under the consulship of Arcadius II and Rufinus [Col. 1456A]—concerning a fine of ten pounds of gold, survives in the Theodosian Code.

Yet although scarcely any of these laws was enforced, the Donatists bitterly and resentfully cried out that they were unjustly harassed, and that their cause was not being handled by law but crushed by force. Shortly after Theodosius’s death, Count Gildo of Africa, leader of rebels, threw everything into confusion in Africa in order to secure his tyranny. His chief henchman was a certain Optatus, notorious for brigandage, who devoted himself so completely to the Donatist cause that he seemed even to surpass the madness of the Circumcellions. Augustine often mentions this Gildonian Optatus.

By acting in this way, however, he increasingly disgraced and—using Augustine’s word—stained his sect. The Donatists therefore relied at that time rather on Petilian, who, formerly an advocate, became their bishop first at Cirta and then at Caesarea, and was a most vigorous champion of their faction. Yet it happened well: he encountered Augustine, who in the year of Theodosius’s death became bishop of Hippo, a strong and constant defender of the Catholic Church, and eventually drew the resistant opponents into a Conference, which seemed the best means of convicting them.

[But before speaking of it, something must again be recalled concerning other Carthaginian councils. I see that much is reported about them falsely, out of order, and confusedly. First, the account of the writers of the *Centuries* of ecclesiastical history appears wholly false and fabricated: they relate that a certain Carthaginian council, which they call the second, met under the consulship of Valentinian and Theodosius. These men were never consuls together, nor does any ancient writer mention any Council of Carthage in the time of Theodosius the Great except the Donatist one already mentioned.

I reject less readily their statement that some Council of Carthage met under the consulship of Caesarius and Atticus, since Balsamon indicates this; but why they call it the third, let them see to that. Certainly they are mistaken in assigning to that council canons which should rather be assigned to another, far more celebrated Council of Carthage held some years later, as may be understood from Photius’s *Nomocanon*.

Also to be rejected is their fabrication concerning another Council of Carthage, which they call the fourth and say met two years after the foregoing “third,” under the consulship of Honorius IV and Eutychianus. For although Balsamon admits that under those consuls something was decreed in the Church of Carthage regarding the dispatch of legates to the emperor, I do not know whence are drawn the many canons assigned to this council.

As I am troubled that so much is fabricated concerning Carthaginian councils of this sort, so I wonder that the Carthaginian Conference with the Donatists is passed over, though it should have been especially commemorated in their history. Soon afterward the very eminent Council of Carthage against the Pelagians met, which Augustine calls the African Council. We shall consider it later. The order now requires that we speak of the Conference.]

For nearly a hundred years the Donatists had so thrown everything into confusion that in Africa it could scarcely be discerned which was the Church, since altar against altar had everywhere been erected and each party contended for the Church’s title and possession [Col. 1457A]. Many had long desired that the issue be determined through some lawful examination; the people demanded this no less than the matter itself.

“We know,” says Augustine in his book *After the Conference*, “how many of you—and perhaps all, or almost all—are accustomed to say: ‘Oh, if only they would meet in one place! Oh, if only they would at last confer, and, while they disputed, the truth would appear!’” Yet as much as the Catholics wished to meet the Donatists, so much did the Donatists avoid the meeting.

Augustine writes in Letter 166 to the Donatists: “Your bishops, when summoned by us, have never wished to confer peaceably with us, as though fleeing from speaking with sinners.” Indeed, when it was said on one occasion that a certain Donatist bishop had declared that he was willing to confer with Augustine in the presence of good men seated together, Augustine did everything possible eagerly to meet him, and even to spur him on while he ran: Letter 47.

Finally, failing to obtain what he so earnestly wished, Augustine arranged for his clergy at Hippo to urge Januarius, the Donatists’ archbishop of Carthage. Their letter survives as Letter 68 among Augustine’s letters. It presses especially this point: since the emperor had long ago been appealed to in this cause, a public Conference should be established by his authority. For he alone, being not bound by laws already enacted, could more freely both order the Conference and determine the entire matter; governors, who serve laws already enacted, were not permitted to do so.
