Because the Donatists had refused, on the pretext mentioned, to meet our side, the clergy of Hippo lowered themselves so far as even to allege that Christ himself spoke with the devil concerning the Law, and that Paul conversed not only with Jews but also with Epicureans.

The Donatists replied that dialectical disputations did not suit Christian religion, and that Augustine was nothing but a contentious disputant, to be fled from and guarded against rather than refuted and defeated. What Augustine replied to this cavilling may be read in his first book *Against Cresconius*. In the fourth book he says: “You reproach, under the vicious name of contention and animosity, the zeal for contending for the truth, because we have often wished to confer with your people so that, error being removed, brotherly charity might be bound by the bond of peace.”

He notes that the Donatists offered this pretext because, as he says, they preferred to cover a bad cause with an excuse rather than settle it through discussion. In the same book he says: “I think that you understand quite easily that it is not from a desire to avoid contention—which does not exist when truth is sought, or when there is no litigation for empty glory—but from distrust of a bad cause, that you do not wish to confer with us.”

[Here it is worthwhile incidentally to observe that discussions concerning religion are at times good and useful, at times harmful. Certainly one must consider what the matter under inquiry is, and moderation must always be maintained. Tertullian, in *On Prescription*, denies that one should dispute with heretics. Yet the Nicene Fathers nevertheless did not refuse to debate once with the Arians.

When the case of the Arians was again to be handled at a certain assembly in Constantinople, Theodosius praised the counsel of those who said that, lest the same matter be repeatedly reopened, opponents should be pressed not so much by fresh debates as by previous decisions and authority.

Finally Augustine rightly perceived with whom, to what extent, when, and how one should debate. What he determined on this matter may be understood from what he writes in book II *On the City of God*, chapter 1; book I *On the Merits and Forgiveness of Sins*, final chapter; the *Enchiridion*, chapter 69; and Letters 111 and 121.

At last, by a most wise and religious law enacted in accordance with the decision of the Council of Chalcedon, the emperor Marcian forbade anyone publicly to treat of the Christian faith before assembled crowds, as he says, or to reopen matters already judged and rightly settled by debate and contention, lest venerable mysteries be profaned by such conflict: Justinian’s Code, book I [OCR: “III”], title 1, *On the Supreme Trinity*. But this [p. 348] edict concerned the mysteries of faith, followed four ecumenical councils, and came after the Third Council—Ephesus—had decreed that nothing was to be added to the creed of faith. Its purpose was finally to put a curb upon the innumerable debates on the subject and upon their wantonness and insolence.

But this has no bearing upon the Donatist case, nor upon Augustine’s age or person. Indeed, Augustine alone finally showed what this method of defending truth was, and how it should be used; and he had often experienced it, but never more fully than in the Conference with the Donatists of which I have now undertaken to speak.]

[Col. 1458C] Augustine’s first public encounter of this sort, while he was not yet a bishop but only a presbyter, was a two-day debate with Fortunatus the Manichaean in the city of Hippo. Notaries were present to take down and authenticate every word. The people were the audience of the disputation, but no judge was otherwise present. Although that unhappy Fortunatus was not completely converted, he was at least shaken by the encounter.

A second disputation in the same city was Augustine’s three-day debate with Felix the Manichaean, similar in kind but with a happier outcome. Sharper and more celebrated, in the same place, was his encounter with Maximinus, the Arian bishop, though with by no means the same success. The records of these conferences survive among Augustine’s works. There was another, with Pascentius, an Arian count, [Col. 1458D] in the city of Carthage; but their first meeting was more troublesome, because the opponent at first refused to allow the presence of notaries to record the proceedings, and did not abide by the agreements made. At length, however, he accepted the rules of the conference; he not only allowed notaries to be employed, but also accepted Laurentius, formerly a judge, and did not refuse to have judgment rendered by him. Augustine is witness in Letters 174 and 178.

But no conference was either more useful or more illustrious—though it concerned a question less subtle and more popular—than that with the Donatists. Augustine had already encountered, privately and incidentally, a certain Fortunius, a Donatist bishop, amid a popular crowd. Since this crowd, by its noise, disturbed even the recording notaries, [Col. 1459A] and the debate was consequently broken off, Augustine had requested, in Letter 163, that the matter be conducted in some safe and quiet retreat. Yet he obtained much more than he had hoped when the Carthaginian Conference was instituted. Possidius, who was present, writes that it was procured chiefly through Augustine, with great benefit to the Church, aided, as he says, by the most glorious and most religious Emperor Honorius, who for its accomplishment also sent from his own court into Africa, as judge, the tribune and notary Marcellinus.

That is, on Augustine’s advice the African Catholics had sent envoys to Honorius in Italy to request this. For they saw that, without the authority and protection of the prince, neither could such a meeting be convened, nor their adversaries compelled to attend it, nor could they be prevented from evading the debate. [Col. 1459B] Indeed, just as Constantine had granted to the civil councils of African cities and provinces free power subsequently to lay their wishes before the prince—Book I of the Theodosian Code, *On Envoys and Decrees of Envoys*—so Theodosius and Honorius prescribed the form of such provincial and extraordinary councils, Book XII and XIII of the Theodosian Code, under the same title. But the matter now concerned the petition of the African Church and the authority of an ecclesiastical meeting or council.

And lest anyone wonder that this ecclesiastical cause was referred to princes and that its hearing was entrusted by them to a civil magistrate, let him remember that it was an extraordinary and singular example, because of necessity, which is said to have no law; and that therefore it ought not to be drawn into precedent. Augustine himself indicates this in Book III *Against Julian*. After provincial councils of bishops, the Pelagians appealed to some so-called ecumenical synod, and had obtained letters from the emperor under that name. The Catholics refused this, understanding that it was sought no less treacherously than ambitiously. The Pelagians objected the example now under discussion. Augustine replied to them:

> “Do not deceive yourselves and others, as though you possessed against us such an argument as we possessed against the Donatists, whom we compelled by imperial commands to come to a conference with us. For their frenzy had occupied the whole of Africa; and by violent assaults, brigandage, plundering, fires, and slaughter—devastating many places and terrifying all—they did not permit the truth to be preached by Catholics against their error. [Col. 1459D] We could accomplish nothing with them before bishops whom we did not hold in common. What our forefathers had done with them nearly a hundred years earlier no longer remained in the people’s memory. Therefore this necessity compelled us, at least by completing our conference in official records, to crush their shamelessness and restrain their audacity.”

Such is Augustine’s statement. Although this kind of conference was in some way extraordinary, and more customary in Africa than elsewhere, I recall that Epiphanius wrote that the emperor Constantine granted a similar power of disputation, in the presence of notaries recording the proceedings, to the heretic Photinus, already otherwise condemned at the Synod of Sardica. Among the hearers and arbitrators of that debate [Col. 1460A] appointed by Constantine, Epiphanius counts a certain Marcellinus. That conference, between Photinus and Basil of Ancyra, concerned a question far more subtle than that debated with the Donatists. For Photinus attacked the Head—that is, Christ himself—whereas the Donatists attacked only the body—that is, the Church.

Add that, against the Donatists, there was a certain connected cause containing a civil factual question concerning Caecilian and Felix, his ordainer. The Donatists themselves had formerly first referred this matter to Constantine; and that emperor had committed it partly to his prefects in Africa and partly to ecclesiastical bishops in Gaul and Italy. Later the Donatists’ violence increased. They treated their defeat as an injury; yet they could not be brought into court or to a conference except by the magistrate’s command, [Col. 1460B] and at the conference they could not be compelled to come to the issue except by the protection and authority of that same power. Finally, their military frenzy, armed with the swords of the Circumcellions, could not be restrained except by imperial terror.

They were astonishing legal manipulators, more slippery and cunning calumniators than any advocates have ever been in their own forum. They were also gladiators more bloodthirsty than soldiers trained in any camp, who did not “join issue by hand according to law,” but rather reclaim their claim by iron, as Ennius says. Indeed, unless some Marcellinus had been present with his official retinue, there was danger that they would turn the Conference into something like that furious Synod of Ephesus held shortly after Augustine’s death, which was called the *Robber Synod* (*ληστρική*). Certainly they would not have hesitated to treat Augustine as the Nestorians treated Flavian at that synod. For what else? Possidius, an especially trustworthy authority, relates that, when the Donatists were invited to a moderated debate, they furiously cried out that Augustine ought to be crushed like a wolf and that those who killed him would easily obtain pardon from God. I believe that for these reasons Honorius wished his Marcellinus to be present at this Conference with an armed retinue.

Otherwise Augustine certainly would have wished such protection absent. For in Letter 203, when he challenges the Donatists, he says: “Let fear of temporal authorities cease on our side; let terror of assembled Circumcellions also cease on yours.” And in Letter 173, challenging the Donatist Crispinus to a conference, he says: “Let the people of Mappalia hear us both, provided that what we say is written down, and that what we have written is interpreted for them in Punic, and that, with fear of domination removed, they choose what they will.”

Finally, he foresaw what the Catholics afterwards justly reproached in that wicked and armed Ephesian council which they rejected. For this was the objection of those who later pleaded Flavian’s cause at the Synod of Chalcedon: “Where there are swords and clubs, what sort of synod is that?” Meanwhile the fathers assembled for the Chalcedonian Synod, fearing the tumults and arms of the Eutychians, asked Emperor Marcian through the envoys of Pope Leo to be present to prevent violence; otherwise, they said and protested, they would not meet without such protection, [Col. 1461A] as Liberatus of Carthage witnesses in chapter thirteen.

Lastly, this too should be observed: while the Donatists litigated their case, Marcellinus was by no means an arbiter of law, whether new or doubtful, but rather an investigator of fact than of law; a *cognitio* was committed to him rather than jurisdiction; finally, he was appointed judge with a formula, as private judges in matters of private right were formerly appointed by the praetor. Yet Marcellinus would not sit unless the conferees sat with him; whereas in a civil trial the judge sits alone and the litigants are ordered to stand. Finally, he makes a protest, as Constantine did while seated on a low bench at the Nicene Council.

Nevertheless, just as the Conference differed from a forensic trial, so too it differed from an ecclesiastical council, in which bishops are rather the judges. The proceedings themselves will show better how humbly, moderately, and modestly Marcellinus conducted himself. Nor will anyone who weighs what I have already said wonder that no mention is made here of the bishop of Rome. The Africans certainly revered and respected him, although at the councils of Milevis and Carthage, when they had referred to him in each case their judgment concerning the Pelagians, they are said nevertheless to have prohibited appeals overseas.

Nor should it be passed over that, as some observe, at the time this Conference was requested, Innocent, bishop of Rome, after the city had been captured by the Goths, had very different business at home. What if I were to say that he, as it were, endorsed the conference mandated by Honorius’s rescript? Orosius certainly relates [Col. 1461C] that he was at Ravenna when the Goths invaded Rome. If he was then at Ravenna, he was with Emperor Honorius. I shall add something that may appear even more surprising: the proceedings indicate that a certain Felix, who claimed to be bishop of the city of Rome, was present at this Conference with the Donatists, where a certain Roman nobility is also said to have attended. But I suspect that he was some Donatist pseudo-bishop who had presided at Rome over his Donatist adherents, called there the Montenses; after the capture of the city, fleeing the Goths with his people, he crossed into Africa and eagerly and ambitiously thrust himself into the Carthaginian Conference, upon which he happened to fall. For such assistance seemed seasonable to the Donatists.

Now when we hear that Marcellinus, tribune and notary, [Col. 1461D] presided over this Conference, we understand that a wise and religious man, endowed with great authority—I mean a magistrate of the rank *spectabilis* and *clarissimus* (for tribunes and notaries were adorned with these titles, and Augustine himself in Letters 159 and 160 gives them to this Marcellinus)—devoted his efforts to this investigation. Dulcitius also, of whom Augustine writes that the care of imperial laws and commands against the Donatists was later entrusted in Africa, is called tribune and notary. Ambrose, in Letter 32, says that the emperor Valentinian sent to him Dalmatius, tribune and notary, to summon Ambrose before the imperial consistory in a case of religion.

I omit that the poet Claudian, of that time, is adorned with the title of tribune and notary in an epitaph which stood at Rome in Trajan’s Forum. Book XII, title VII of the Code survives, *On the Primicerius and Notaries*, where tribunes and notaries are also discussed. In the law of Theodosius it is written: “The principal concern of our piety is directed to the office of notaries.” Then, in a law of Emperor Leo: “We believe that the distinguished and noble service of the *spectabiles* tribunes and notaries ought to be strengthened and increased by various titles of privileges.” These notaries appear to have been what are now called the secretaries of kings in Gaul. Theodosius, in Book XII of the Code, *On Exemptions from Public Duties*, says: “Let our notaries be exempt from degrading public services.”

What manner and greatness of man this Marcellinus was, how fair an arbiter and how moderate a judge, the proceedings of this Conference themselves show better. I might say what Orosius says: that he was a man above all prudent and industrious, and most eager for every kind of worthy learning. But I am content with the testimony of Augustine alone to understand that he was a great man and a jurist by no means profane. Augustine wrote to him not only the books *On the Merits and Forgiveness of Sins* against the Pelagians and *On the Spirit and the Letter*, but also those most learned books *On the City of God*, begun shortly after the capture of the city, that is, around the time of the Carthaginian Conference. He also wrote Letters 5 and 7, from which it appears that, amid the very administration of the state, Marcellinus was especially concerned about religion and understood even the most subtle questions of that kind; indeed, he was something like an *ergodiōktēs* (*ἐργωδιώκτης*), a pursuer or instigator of work, urging Augustine onward.

Add Augustine’s two Letters 158 and 159 to him, where it is also written that ecclesiastical causes were especially entrusted to his Excellency. He was not like that ridiculous Lucius Gellius in Cicero, who, when he was going to Asia and came to Athens, thought that he could at once, in passing, settle all the controversies of all the philosophers whom he summoned to himself, though he did not even understand them. Our Marcellinus was skilled in divine no less than human law. And indeed such jurists, such—yes, such—statesmen are as worthy to have this responsibility entrusted to them as the Church of Christ rightly abhors certain secular Ulpians of our time, mockers and tramplers upon religion, rather than its protectors.

Augustine, Letter 50 to Count Boniface, says: “I praise, congratulate, and admire you, most beloved son Boniface, because amid the cares of wars and arms you earnestly desire to know those things which are of God.” But how much more could he have said this of Marcellinus, a man of the toga? Jerome’s letter to this Marcellinus also survives. It witnesses that he diligently proposed the most subtle questions of the Church, such as the origin of the soul, and was more ready to learn than Jerome himself was to answer. Nor had he relaxed even this pursuit amid the disturbance of public affairs, when Jerome, writing back, confesses that, confounded by the devastation of the city of Rome, he could not devote himself to letters.

I do not wish here to pass over what Augustine himself says in the book *After the Conference*, chapter 24: that the Donatists had been summoned by their primate through a *tractoria*. *Tractoria* [Col. 1463A] is a term of Roman law, as is, in almost the same sense, *evectio*, a word Augustine also uses in Book V of the *Confessions*. It signifies a letter or diploma by which public travelling expenses are granted to those sent or summoned, and by which they may use the public post. Book XII of the Code, title *On Tractoriae*, survives; there the commentator further cites a fragment of an edict of Constantine mentioning the grant of *tractoriae* and public *evectio* to the Donatists because of the case of Caecilian.

It remains to ask in what year the Carthaginian Conference was held. The more necessary it is especially to ascertain this, the more I wonder that it is nowhere expressed or noted by Augustine. Nor was there any hope that it could be learned from elsewhere. Yet I congratulated myself all the more when, in the manuscript Acts—and indeed immediately on the first page—I read that it was held *P. C. Varanis, kal. Jun.* Thus I finally understood that it was held on the Kalends of June after the consulship of Varanes: that is, in the year of Christ 411, the year following the capture of Rome.

Certainly, in the year of Christ 410, on the Kalends of January, no ordinary consuls are said to have been created; and therefore in certain Fasti I find that year marked thus: “After the consulship of Emperor Theodosius the Younger, Augustus, for the third time, and Emperor Honorius, Augustus, for the eighth time.” Yet it is established that in that year Varanes was made consul in the East on the Kalends of February, while at Rome Tertullus was made consul around the Kalends of July. Therefore the Chronicles of Prosper and Cassiodorus record that Rome was captured by the Goths under the consuls Varanes and Tertullus. But Tertullus was remembered less frequently and more obscurely. Thus the Chronicle of Marcellinus records that the capture occurred under Varanes as sole consul. I know that this name is variously written: I hear him called sometimes Varo, sometimes Vararim, sometimes Varanus. Yet I think Varanes is more correct.

I grant that in the following year Theodosius Augustus, consul for the fourth time, is indicated in the Chronicles of Prosper, Cassiodorus, and Marcellinus. But Prosper adds that Varanes was not only sole consul of the eastern regions when Rome was captured by the Goths, but that the same arrangement was observed in the following year also. Therefore, in the Acts I mentioned, it is written *P. C. Varanis*, that is, “after the consulship of Varanes,” to indicate the year that followed his consulship.

[Col. 1463D] It is more accurate to say that Rome was captured by the Goths on the ninth day before the Kalends of September. In that same year, shortly afterward, I observed that the Carthaginian Conference was proclaimed and commanded by Emperor Honorius, because his rescript on this subject survives in the Acts already mentioned; it is said to have been given at Ravenna on the day before the Ides of October. The consul is not added, through the copyist’s negligence. But Varanes can and ought to be supplied. Thus what was chiefly sought in this history, and could not be learned from elsewhere, becomes clear concerning the date of the Conference. I investigated it all the more carefully because it is especially worthwhile to observe the time when Honorius was so urgently petitioned by the African Catholics against the Donatists’ violence.

He remained at Ravenna amid not merely the greatest disturbance but even desperation in his affairs, especially after Stilicho’s death. The Goths had captured Rome, were devastating all Italy, and threatened every province of the Roman Empire. Yet the unhappy and stunned Honorius did not therefore fail to hear the prayers of the African Church. He himself had already enacted many laws against the Donatists, following his father’s example. But he allowed both his own laws and those of his father, as it were, to be suspended when he heard that the Donatists must now be dealt with differently. Some years before, regarding their enforcement, he had decreed that the Donatists should not suppose those laws had grown cold, or even lukewarm, as he says in Law XLVI of the Theodosian Code, *On Heretics*. At that same time he had also ordered public posting of the edict on unity which he had sent into Africa, Law II of the Theodosian Code, *On Religion*. Yet he heard that the Donatist schism could not be removed by edicts alone; nevertheless, he desired by every means to restore the unity of the African Church.

Finally, he appears to have taken greater care for that Church than for Rome and Italy themselves. In this matter, anyone who remembers how great this emperor’s otherwise sluggishness, inactivity, or—as Cicero calls it—indifference was, and how great the confusion of those times, will readily recognize the admirable providence of God. God caused Honorius to listen to good men and allowed them to dictate to him the rescripts that he would issue. Thus, in the mandate for this Conference, one might think Theodosius rather than Honorius was speaking. Ambrose says that Theodosius was more concerned for the salvation of the Church than for that of his own soul. I shall not say [Col. 1464C] that Honorius the son was altogether of the same mind. Yet at least in this Donatist affair he did what his father would have done, issuing edicts full of paternal piety.

While Stilicho was alive, many used to allege maliciously that laws sent into Africa, although bearing Honorius’s name, were sent more by Stilicho than by Theodosius’s son, as Augustine relates in Letter 129. Now that Stilicho was dead, no such thing could be said. Augustine himself, in Letter 166, writes that the Donatists complained of the laws of Theodosius’s sons. But he replies that these laws do nothing but repeat and confirm the judgment of Constantine, Valentinian, Gratian, and Theodosius; and he simultaneously denounces Julian the Apostate, who, he says, granted freedom for the ruin of Donatus’s party, because he thought that the Christian name could perish from the earth if sacrilegious dissensions were allowed to remain free.

The Donatists, on the contrary, extolled that Julian by name and boasted that justice had a place only with him, for that reason. Augustine says that nothing could be more unjust, more unworthy, or more harmful. “And what,” he asks, “is a worse death of the soul than freedom of error?” Yet, so that the Donatists might not complain either that they were being wronged or that they were condemned unheard, it was decided that they should again be heard in a conference for as long as they wished, and that meanwhile they should remain free. But Honorius always judged the permission in Africa of altar against altar to be a greater deformity of the Church than Rome’s destruction and devastation then were.

[Col. 1465A] We must now come to the Acts, or—as they were called—the *Gesta*, of the Conference. These had once been diligently recorded, written, and collated, but had perished through the injury of time and the negligence of posterity. Therefore, when recently, through the kindness of Jean de Tillet, I acquired the greater and better part of them, I judged that a great treasure had been offered to me. For though the principal points may readily be recovered from Augustine, I desired many things which he omitted, and I remembered how earnestly the Church had formerly wished these Acts to be read in their entirety and their memory preserved.

For Augustine himself, in the book *On the Proceedings with Emeritus*, relates that in all, as he calls them, diligent African churches they were read annually, in order, from beginning to end, at the time when it was most convenient for the people to hear them. I admit that they may appear not merely overly minute but almost repetitious, because every quibble of the Donatists is rehearsed and not even a single word omitted. Yet it was in the interest of the Church and the commonwealth that every detail should be written and set forth in this manner. Nevertheless, lest perhaps their length discourage readers, Augustine also composed an epitome, which he called the *Breviculum*; he then wrote again on the same matter in the book *After the Conference*; and finally he repeats the same narrative from the Synod of Cirta in Letter 152. He indicates this letter when writing to Marcellinus about these labours in Letter 158:

> “My abridgment of the proceedings of our Conference was laborious enough, when I saw that no one wished to undertake the reading of so great a mass of writings; just as my letter to the Donatist laity about this same Conference of ours was also laborious.”

He writes to Marcellinus that the proceedings in the case of certain cruel Donatists convicted in court should be published. For he desires such matters to be read throughout all the churches no less than the proceedings of the Conference itself. So worthy of repeated inculcation did the history of the Donatists appear.

I note in passing that Erasmus is mistaken when, in the argument to Augustine’s letter to Marcellinus, he observes that Augustine asks Marcellinus to publish what was decreed against the Donatists in a council of bishops. Certainly what occurred before Marcellinus’s tribunal was not decreed in a council of bishops. Further, just as Augustine rejoiced that Marcellinus had been the examiner of the Conference, so he wished Count Boniface to know its history. Thus, writing to him in Letter 50, he says: “Since the proceedings are exceedingly lengthy, and since you, occupied with other matters necessary to Roman peace, have much to read, an abridgment of them may be read to you.” Why say more? He thought the Church’s victory rested in them. Thus in Letter 204 to a certain Donatist he says:

> “The mercy of God has granted that both we and your bishops should come to Carthage in so frequent and numerous an assembly and should debate between ourselves concerning the very dissension in the most orderly manner. The proceedings have been written down; our subscriptions too are preserved. Read them, or allow them to be read to you; and then choose what you will.”

Indeed, when I happened upon the Acts of the Second Council of Constantinople, held in the time of our Justinian and said to be the Fifth Ecumenical Council, and found there, by chance, a certain chapter, as it were a fragment of the Acts of the Carthaginian Conference—produced at that eastern council more than one hundred and forty years after it had been written in Africa—I judged that I had obtained something which ought by no means to be neglected in this commentary. It is as follows:

> “From the Acts transacted before Marcellinus, *vir clarissimus*, tribune and notary, chapter 188: Augustine, bishop of the Catholic Church, said: ‘The Church’s hope is not to be placed in human beings if they are good; nor, if they are evil, is God’s Church to be judged to have perished. Yet we undertake their cause as that of our brothers; and, if they can be shown to us to be guilty, today we anathematize them. Nevertheless, because of them we do not desert and abandon the Church promised and manifested by God.’”

This fragment, and chapter 187 of the Acts of the Conference, were absent even from the Tillet manuscript, which is defective and mutilated in many other ways. But while we await the eventual discovery and publication of those Acts in their entirety, let us set forth the principal part of this Conference.

First, I observe that the assembly was great and celebrated: 286 Catholic bishops and 279 Donatists met. Yet shortly before, many more Donatists had met at the Council of Bagai against their own Maximianists, another Donatist sect. So strong in Africa had become the offspring of Donatus; nor did they boast of their multitude less than at other times of their smallness. Augustine wishes to convict them of vanity because they boasted that they were more than four hundred bishops in Africa. But if they allowed their Maximianists to be joined to them, they truly were more than four hundred.

The Maximianists desired to take part in this Conference no less eagerly than the other Donatists avoided it. Yet not only did the Donatists reject them, but the Catholics excluded them as well. Augustine indicates in Book III *Against Julian* why this was done: “Wishing to console their small number at least with the name of a contest, and thus to appear something in the eyes of those to whom they were contemptible because they might be permitted to enter into examination with us, they petitioned and submitted a written request and challenge; we disregarded them. For they desired more to be named in connection with the contest than they feared defeat in it; nor did they hope for the glory of victory, but sought the reputation of a conference because they lacked numbers.”

This is Augustine’s statement. From it he proves that it does not follow that those who wish, but are not permitted, to confer in some judicial proceeding ought to be thought confident in the truth. He presses this upon the Pelagians, who, having already been condemned in a council of bishops, boasted of certain imperial letters by which they challenged the Catholics to a new conference; when the Catholics refused it, they foolishly gloried that they were victors.

Further, as the Maximianists voluntarily offered themselves and were rejected, so the remaining Donatists, who resisted, [Col. 1467A] were invited. And just as there was much trouble in summoning and compelling them, so too, after they had come, there was trouble in drawing them into the Conference, although its conditions, most equitable as they were, were proposed. It is amusing that, when Marcellinus, in his secretarium or hearing-room, respectfully asked the Donatists to sit, as the Catholics sat, they refused, replying that it was written in Psalm 36: “I will not sit with the wicked.” Our party aptly replied that they had nevertheless already done what David adds in the same psalm: “and I will not enter with the unrighteous.” But it should have been added that David says in that same psalm that he so hates the society of the impious that he will nevertheless not, because of them, desert the temple or altar of the Lord.

Certainly it is remarkable that the Donatists, with excessively foolish obstinacy, preferred to stand rather than sit, when the former is the position of defendants and the latter of judges. Indeed, when a defendant was ordered to sit, he was understood to have been acquitted; and their forefathers had used no other formula of acquittal in that first Council of Cirta already mentioned. These hypocrites undoubtedly displayed an incredible arrogance. But by God’s just judgment, they rejected the honour too generously offered to them, of which they were unworthy.

Optatus, Book I, relates that they even resented being called brothers by Catholics. Many years later, indeed in the Conference itself, they proudly rejected this humanity of ours. Augustine, Book III *Against Gaudentius*: “Are you angry because I call you brother? For you rejected this name from us even in our Conference,” etc.

[Col. 1467C] Although many things in the proceedings of this Conference deserve particular notice, this especially is memorable: the Catholics, in order to deal with the Donatists more fairly, did not refuse voluntarily to accept an unequal condition, while offering their opponents an advantageous one. They proposed that, if they were defeated in this Conference, they would resign their office, to use the Roman term; but that, if they prevailed, their defeated opponents should nevertheless remain free not to resign. Rather, the victors would share with them, should they return to their senses, the honour and rank of the episcopal office, so that two bishops might be tolerated in the same Church, as colleagues, 352 just as formerly there were consuls at Rome; but with a certain—using the term of the Greek jurists—*allēloklēronomia* (ἀλληλοκληρονομία), or mutual succession, and, as it were, a right of accrual: so that whichever died first would leave his fellow bishop as sole heir [Col. 1467D], that is, sole bishop.

Certainly, the canon of the Council of Nicaea prohibited there being two bishops in one city. For it foresaw the disadvantages of such an association; and just as at Rome there was only one chief of the senate, though there were two consuls, so it was judged that only one man should preside over the college of presbyters. But as this rule was approved for the sake of fostering peace, so too, where the prospect of reconciliation seemed to require that two should be tolerated because one could scarcely be expelled, the purpose and intent of the canon, rather than its wording, had to be considered.

Yet when Augustine allowed himself to be made colleague of Valerius, bishop of Hippo, so as to be, as it were, co-bishop, he said that the Nicene canon had been unknown to him. Possidius therefore relates that, once he was bishop, he wished the Nicene canons to be read publicly more often. But no one will deny that these matters must be assessed and measured by the Church’s practice and benefit, so that where a just cause required it, that canon should yield. Such a cause seemed to exist in offering the Donatist bishops, whom ambition held fast, some hope of honour if they returned to their senses, and in removing their fear of disgrace and a shameful resignation if they returned to the Catholic Church.

For the Nicene Fathers themselves, when dealing with the Novatians, acknowledged that this concession might be made. A similar condition was also offered to the Arians, who for some years had occupied the government of the Church in the East and were commanded by Theodosius to withdraw from that possession if they would not be healed. At that very time Meletius, bishop of Antioch, for the sake of preserving peace, offered Paulinus—who otherwise maintained his own separate congregations, under a pretext not unlike that of the Donatists—a share in his episcopate, in order that reconciliation might take place, on the condition that, when one died, the survivor should remain sole bishop.

Why delay? Augustine, in Epistle 163, relates that when Melchiades, bishop of Rome, condemned Donatus by the judgment of his fellow bishops, he dealt so leniently with Donatists willing to return to their senses that, Augustine says, “he gave them a free choice of recovering health,” prepared to send letters of communion even to those known to have been ordained by Majorinus. Thus, wherever there were two bishops, made double by dissension, he wished the one ordained first to be confirmed, while provision was to be made for the other to govern another people [Col. 1468C].

Speaking of Melchiades’ judgment, Augustine exclaims: “How innocent! How upright! How prudent and peaceable! What an excellent man! What a son of Christian peace, and father of the Christian people!” In Epistle 50 Augustine recounts the same history and also indicates that the Catholics subsequently followed this example in receiving Arians: when they returned to their senses, they remained clergy and bishops in the same rank as before. He also relates that this so displeased Lucifer that he therefore seceded from the Church, as Jerome likewise relates in *Against the Luciferians*. But our party judged this to be an unjust ground for schism.

What I now wish to emphasize is that the Nicene Fathers themselves followed shortly afterward the judgment of Melchiades when dealing with the Novatians. Although they decreed that those whom they called the lapsed should indeed be admitted after public confession (*exomologesis*) to the Church’s communion, but not to any rank of clergy or ecclesiastical ministry, they nevertheless remitted to Novatians returning to their senses not only the harsher requirement of a prolonged public confession, but also permitted them to perform the functions of ecclesiastical ministry.

There was no reason why African bishops should be harsher toward the Donatists; there was great reason why they should be even more indulgent, if perhaps on this condition they could purchase the unity and peace of the Church. I pass over the fact that Cyprian had long before written to Pope Cornelius about his own kindness toward the lapsed—although he too was an African bishop, severe and strict. I say that, in the case of heretics returning to their senses who had sinned through error, rather than in that of the lapsed, who had sinned through fear, the ancient law of the Twelve Tables was heard: “Let the same right belong to those recovering as to the sound.”

Moreover, the Catholics not only offered the Donatists the condition already described, but generously added another, which I learned from Augustine’s book *On the Proceedings with Emeritus*. There he relates something memorable that happened when the Catholics were deliberating among themselves about proposing it. At a certain assembly in Mauretania Caesariensis, a record drawn up by the Catholics at the Carthaginian Conference was read. When they came to this passage:

> “If perhaps Christian peoples are pleased with individual bishops and cannot tolerate, in this unprecedented situation, the association of two, let both sides withdraw from office; and, once the cause of schism has been condemned and the individual Churches established in peaceful unity, let individual bishops be appointed in the individual Churches, with the consent of those belonging to each Church, to the unity that has been achieved, wherever necessary”—

Bishop Augustine said:

> “I shall tell your charity, and recall, a most sweet and delightful thing which, with the Lord’s help, we experienced. Before the Conference itself, some brethren were discussing this matter among ourselves: namely, that for Christ’s peace bishops ought to be bishops—or ought not to be bishops. You must acknowledge that, looking around at all our brethren and fellow bishops, we did not readily find men who would undertake this and offer this humility as a sacrifice to the Lord. As commonly happens, we said: ‘That man can do it; that man cannot. This one consents to it; that one will not endure it’—speaking more from our suspicions, since we could not see their hearts [Col. 1469C].
>
> “But when it came to being openly discussed in a council of all, so numerous—almost three hundred bishops—it pleased everyone so much, and all were so inflamed, that they were ready to lay down the episcopate for Christ’s unity: not to lose it, but to entrust it more safely to God. There were scarcely two found there to whom this displeased. One was an aged old man, who even dared to say this rather freely; the other signified his opinion by a silent expression. But after the brotherly rebuke of all overwhelmed the one who spoke so freely, he changed his opinion—and the other changed his expression as well.”

So Augustine. These words are worth repeating all the more because they have been preserved in the records of the Conference; and because the example is memorable and especially useful whenever there is contention over the episcopal office and the ambition of the contenders causes disturbance in the Church.

I return to the proceedings of the Conference. To reach the matter more quickly and to deal with the state of the weightier case, the Catholics wished to detach and separate the case of Caecilian, and to set aside that question, which concerned fact rather than law. For it was a private and personal case and had nothing in common with the other, so to speak, real and general case—namely, that concerning the Church. Accordingly, they did not refuse voluntarily to grant what the Donatists nevertheless falsely alleged: that Caecilian had been a *traditor*, one who handed over the sacred books. For our party maintained that the Donatists ought not even then to have seceded from the Catholic Church that communicated with him.

Certainly nothing was easier than to prove that Caecilian had not been such a man and that he had rightly been acquitted [Col. 1470A], and thereby expose the Donatists’ calumnies and their almost unbelievable effrontery. 353 Yet the Donatists persisted in this quibble rather than allow themselves to be drawn to the legal question concerning the Church. By confusingly mixing together many matters, they wished to cast darkness over the issue and escape.

Though at other times they commonly had on their lips that forensic maxim, “Neither one case prejudges another case, nor one person another person,” they were indignant that this exception should be urged against them when they joined Caecilian’s case to that of the Church in such a way as to make the latter depend on the former. Augustine certainly says, in Epistle 204, that there was nothing in the proceedings of the Conference which the Donatists wished more to have erased.

It was indeed an old device of heretics: when they could not defend their doctrine, they would, in order to evade the issue, appeal to the conduct which they praised in their own party; or, when they could not refute their opponents’ teaching, they would accuse their opponents’ conduct. But such digressions belong to those who wish to evade.

Before the Conference Petilian attacked Augustine, with whom he was disputing, with many insults precisely so that discussion might turn to Augustine’s person rather than to the Church, the subject of the debate. Augustine says: “He makes me the issue when he has failed in the issue.” Again: “Leaving aside the public matter, he pursued with abusive reproaches the life of one man out of some private animosity, as if that man were the question under investigation.”

But just as Augustine indicates the purpose of his cunning adversary, so he prevents him from gaining his end by that cunning. He prefers to suffer a private injury rather than, by straying elsewhere, abandon the public cause [Col. 1470C]. Thus, replying to the Donatist Cresconius, he says: “Stop such things. I am one man; the case being dealt with between us is that of the Church, not mine.” Likewise he restrained the Pelagians, who sought in debate what the Donatists sought: “As regards our conduct, the way we live is known to those with whom we live. The question now concerns Catholic doctrine.”

The Manichees, though less educated in those rhetorical arts, nevertheless sought similar digressions. They not only accused others’ conduct, but, though themselves utterly impure, advertised their own. Thus Fortunatus the Manichee, when asked about faith, answers about the life of himself and his associates. What does Augustine say? In his book *Against Fortunatus*: “The question of faith is one thing, that of morals another.”

To be sure, Augustine elsewhere accused the conduct of Donatists and Manichees and defended that of his own party with the greatest constancy. But he did not allow the religious question to be mixed with such litigation. Likewise Jerome, in *Against Rufinus*, makes it his chief business to insist that matters which ought to be separated must not deceitfully be joined: “There is no need,” he says, “in ecclesiastical discussions to debate a case for the courts.” Again: “Which of us, leaving the case aside, has occupied himself with the superfluous bringing of accusations, which ought to be contained not in ecclesiastical documents but in judicial indictments? Or what does it matter if you lose the case but prevail in an accusation? These are the devices of heretics, so that, when convicted of faithlessness, they may resort to abuse.”

These are Jerome’s words. It is worthwhile carefully to observe such things, because even in this age we see those who contend about religion inopportunely leap to accusations against persons in order to confuse everything [Col. 1471A].

Certainly, the more I consider the proceedings of the Carthaginian Conference, the more I perceive that the Catholics wished at once to come to the principal matter, whereas the Donatists avoided it—men who, as Augustine often said, had this one aim: that nothing should be done. Indeed, they seem to have come to Carthage only in order to return home. Augustine also once said in his books against Julian the Pelagian that “the face of heretics is no face.” This could and should have been said even more strongly of the incredible shamelessness of the Donatists.

Certainly, when refuting Cresconius the Donatist grammarian, he indicates that he is almost ready to exclaim with Persius that shame has perished from human affairs. Elsewhere he says that he marvels that Donatists have blood in their bodies and yet never blush. I might say that these cruel assassins were as crafty as they were litigious. But the records of which I speak will show that their tricks were common, covered not by any learned artifice but by a kind of brazen, harlot-like insolence.

The legal books explain the words of the statute, *si calvitur*—“if he acts vexatiously.” But scarcely ever has its meaning been more plainly displayed than in the Donatists’ evasions and obstructions. Marcellinus was therefore compelled to insert almost six hundred interlocutory rulings in order to counter their mockery before he could bring them back from their resistance to the matter at hand and come to judgment on the principal case.

Indeed, he needed to be skilled in civil law no less than in divine law to perform what was necessary here. For although the Donatists pretended that they wished to conduct the case solely from the sacred writings, as befitted theologians, they nevertheless drew innumerable preliminary pleas from forensic technicalities, which could not be refuted without knowledge of civil law [Col. 1471C].

One might wonder why, while gathering from every side all the so-called declinatory exceptions, they did not plead the exception which Ambrose had earlier made when he had been summoned through the courtly deceit of Justina to the court of the younger Valentinian to debate there with Arians. But the difference is easy to see. The Donatists ought rather to have congratulated themselves that they were not now summoned to Honorius’s court or to some overseas tribunal, as they had previously contrived to have Caecilian summoned.

The records state that this Conference was held in the *Secretarium* of the Gargilian Baths, which appears to have been a distinguished hearing-room in the city of Carthage. Cyprian, when accused, is said to have been brought before Paternus, proconsul of Carthage, into a certain *Secretarium*. In the Code of Constitutions, moreover, the judges’ *Secretarium* is often mentioned, just as the emperor’s *Consistorium*. Augustine calls it the *Secretarium of the praetorium* in Book III, chapter 56, of *Against Cresconius*. In the bath at Hippo Sosn. [reading uncertain], he says in *Against Fortunatus* that he debated with Fortunatus the Manichee in the presence of the people. It is well known that the Council of Constantinople met in the Trullo, the hall of the palace. I say this so that no one may stumble over the phrase “the Gargilian Baths.” Now to the matter.

[Col. 1472A] As soon as the Donatists took their places, they quibbled, I know not what, about the appointed time having already elapsed. But Marcellinus ruled concerning an extension, and held to Ulpian’s principle: “He who takes cognizance from the tribunal sometimes extends the time for judgment,” etc., *Digest*, II, *On Judicial Matters*. I believe the Donatists would gladly also have muttered that maxim from civil law: delay cannot be excused where it has been incurred by lapse of time. But there was no room for such quibbles now.

Moreover, since the order of the Conference particularly required that definite representatives be chosen by both sides, and Marcellinus directed this and the Catholics approved it, the Donatists again protested. Though nearly three hundred had assembled, they wanted all to debate, which certainly could not happen without tumult and confusion. Marcellinus therefore ruled that the practice observed in public actions and corporate bodies must be maintained here: that all things should be done through definite, as he says, ordered and duly authorized persons, as our Ulpian writes.

Those to whom it is permitted to have a corporate body in the name of a collegium or association have, after the model of a commonwealth, the right to have an agent or syndic through whom whatever ought to be transacted and done collectively may be transacted and done; *Digest*, I, “Concerning What Is Owed in the Name of Any Corporate Body.” At last, therefore, it was agreed, 354 that seven from the Catholics and the same number from Donatus’s party should be chosen to conduct the case in the name and by the mandate of their whole body, and to carry on the debate at this Conference.

Among these seven, Augustine was, as it were, leader on one side, Petilian on the other. Previously they had contended with one another in opposing writings, and each was most eminent in his own party. Petilian, who had once been an advocate, used to boast, as Augustine says in Book III, chapter 17, of *Against Petilian*, of his former power in forensic advocacy. But the event itself showed that he was nothing but an inept pettifogger, who did not even understand how incompetently he was conducting the case concerning the Church at the Conference—like insolent and talkative advocates trained in the forum, who rashly, ignorantly, and confusedly stammer about religion.

Since the Catholics had requested the Conference from the emperor, the Donatists initially wanted the names of the envoys and the petition to be produced for them. They were looking for something to gnaw at even in this respect. Marcellinus declared that this had no bearing on the matter, replying that petitions were not customarily included in a pragmatic rescript. The Donatists did not dare altogether to condemn the request for a Conference from the emperor, because they themselves had once requested it first and had long ago referred Caecilian’s case to Constantine. Yet they muttered something secretly. “They stir up hostility against us,” Augustine says in the book written after the Conference, “because we plead the Church’s case before the emperor.”

Hence that saying of Primianus the Donatist: “They carry the sacred rescripts of many emperors; we carry the Gospels alone.” I have said something on this subject in my notes on Optatus, where I also cited another reproach of Petilian from Augustine: “What have we to do with the kings of this world, whom Christianity has never found except jealous?” Had Petilian been more learned and sharper, perhaps he might have pressed this point so as to make Augustine’s answer more difficult. What if he had objected from Tertullian the African’s *Apology*: “The Caesars would have believed in Christ if Caesars could also have been Christians”?

But the Donatists seem to have been too dull to sting and press their adversary sharply. At least they should have been less courtly, so that, if their opponents were excessively courtly, they might have reproved them on fairer grounds. For we must acknowledge that it is desirable that religion should not be entangled and defiled by courtly tricks—the very kind of tricks which were all too familiar to the Donatists themselves.

What shall I say of the African Church, which earlier had seen no emperors or kings within its own home, but shortly afterward learned what it meant to have within its bosom such rulers as the Vandals? Then, indeed—then, when summoned before their tribunal, where Arian bishops held sway—it would have endorsed the Donatists’ cry in Optatus: “What have bishops to do with the Palace?”

Now I return to the circuits and evasions by which the Donatists fled from the Conference. But who can enumerate them all? Meanwhile, it belonged to an unruffled judge patiently to hear whatever they might eventually say, even though they often repeated it idly and pointlessly. The records testify that Marcellinus did this. Their quibble was indeed astonishing: whenever an ecclesiastical council was produced with its date and consul, they alleged, because this chronological notation had been added, that the council was fabricated. Conversely, when some rescript of Constantine was produced against them to which perhaps the consular designation of the particular year had not been added, they likewise quibbled that it was false and forged.

What did Marcellinus do? He says nothing about councils, for it was far too well known and certain that the day and consul were appended to them precisely in order that they might be recognized as not fabricated. But he ruled that the truth of laws and rescripts is not impaired if this chronological notation is omitted. Augustine says: “The cognitor ruled that it had been established by most evident laws that imperial enactments, even if the consuls were not read, must not be called into doubt.”

I know that Constantine rescripted that personal privileges produced without date and consul lack authority, *Code*, IV, *On Various Rescripts*. But such privileges stand on a different footing; and Justinian himself, although he included this rescript in his Code, stated in his preface that this cannot be said of constitutions. For he insists that no doubt should arise from the fact that some enactments are read without date and consul.

Certainly, when inquiry was made concerning a certain letter or security, our Cervidius Scaevola answered that it was not therefore of no effect because it lacked date and consul, *Digest* 34, *On Pledges*. And though it is not found in the Pandects, there survives a fragment from the books of rules of our Modestinus: a will is not invalidated if date and consul are not appended. They were, however, often appended. Yet when a will was opened, Ulpian says, the praetor did not permit the date and consul to be copied or inspected, lest anything false be done, Book II, *How a Will Is Opened*.

But who would be surprised that the Donatists, in the Conference [Col. 1474A], seized upon every avenue of obstruction which not even a forensic advocate in a bad case could have discovered? Even after judgment they raised exceptions and pretended that these were derived from civil law; of these I shall say something later. Finally, more time and words were wasted here on matters not otherwise relevant to the principal case than on the one question which alone the participants in the Conference ought to have considered.

Come then, let the principal case again be examined, and let us see what its character was. In two words, the question concerned the Church: whether it belonged to the Catholics or to the Donatists. But judgment was much more difficult because nearly the same doctrine otherwise sounded on both sides and a similar outward form was visible; indeed, the same formulas were heard, as Optatus indicates in Book I. Augustine, in Book I, chapter 5, of *On True Religion*, observes this not without reason not only among schismatics but also among certain heretics, such as Arians and Photinians.

But he says that the Manichees and some others wished even to differ in sacramental rite, so that it is less surprising that the Catholic Church could tolerate these people less than the former. Since, therefore, the Donatists seemed equal in doctrine and rites, the question of identifying the Church was more difficult in their case; other marks besides doctrine and sacraments were required.

Indeed, if the Donatists communicated with the Catholic Church in doctrine of faith and in rites and ceremonies, though they did not communicate with persons whom they avoided as defiled, their schism appears to have been no more than a kind of scrupulousness. But in their argument they varied in such a way that they did not agree even with themselves and at the Conference inconsistently mingled certain contradictory claims.

Otherwise, I would say that the contest came down to this: all professed in the Creed that the Church is one, holy, and catholic; at the Carthaginian Conference this was variously debated, with our party pressing the prophecies that promise a catholic Church, while the Donatists opposed prophecies describing a holy Church. I admit that Augustine argued this case against Petilian more forcefully and clearly in the book *On Unity* than in the Conference itself, because an adversary did not interrupt writing as he interrupted speech; but the case was always the same. Let us observe, however, that the Catholics introduced no other matter that might disturb the established debate [Col. 1474D].

They might perhaps have thrown at the Donatists, to their embarrassment, some charge of Arianism. But they did not wish to stray elsewhere; rather, they chose amicably to acknowledge that their dispute with them concerned not the head—that is, Christ—but the body—that is, the Church. Indeed, they also omit here the question of rebaptism, of which the Donatists were guilty. They deal with them just as with the Luciferians, who at the same time had separate congregations from the Catholic Church even in Africa itself, and yet were not heretics but rather schismatics—though much more moderate than the Donatists.

Jerome describes a conference with them modeled in some way upon the Carthaginian conference with the Donatists [Col. 1475A]. Augustine condemns both together. For in chapter 30 of *On Christian Combat*, after discussing the Donatists, he says:

> “Let us not listen to those who, though they rebaptize no one, nevertheless preferred to cut themselves off from unity and be called Luciferians rather than Catholics. We do not disapprove that they do not rebaptize; but that they too chose to be cut off from the root—who would not recognize this as detestable? These are those of whom the Apostle says: ‘Having an appearance of godliness, but denying its power.’ They do not possess this power because they are cut off from unity,” etc.

Prosper, Augustine’s disciple, in Book II of *On Promises and Predictions*, compares the Luciferians with the Donatists and says that both persecuted Christ’s body—that is, the Church—with human calumnies, while other heretics persecuted the Church’s head—that is, Christ himself. Finally, Jerome, disputing against the Luciferians, at the same time condemns the Donatists, whom he calls “Mountaineers,” as they were then called at Rome, and declares that among them there is not Christ’s Church but the synagogue of Antichrist.

The Donatists cried out that the Catholic Church, as they put it, had apostatized, and compared it with Romulus’s asylum, as Augustine says in Book II, chapter 13, of *Against Cresconius*. The Luciferians said that the Church had become a brothel, as Jerome relates in *Against the Luciferians*. The reasoning of both was alike: those who had lapsed, or heretics who returned to their senses, were received. But the Catholics replied that this was not a just excuse for schism.

Lucifer of Cagliari, bishop in Sardinia, was an ardent defender of the Nicene faith, and for this reason was praised by Athanasius, Hilary, and Jerome. Even now we read the published books of this same Lucifer addressed to the emperor Constantius, which show how fierce an enemy of heretics Lucifer was. Yet he was no less guilty than Donatus of an unjust schism. Grieved that Arians were readily forgiven and believing that the Church was defiled by communion with them, he withdrew, abandoned Catholic communion, and finally declared that the Church survived in Sardinia alone, just as Donatus did in Africa—that is, in his own assembly. Thus the Luciferians joined the Donatists and, to come closer to them, crossed into Africa.

But I recall what Ambrose relates in his oration *On the Death of His Brother Satyrus*. He praises his brother, who, having happened to cross to Africa where there was a Luciferian Church [Col. 1475D], refused to communicate with it because it did not communicate with the Catholic Church:

> “For although Lucifer had been exiled for the faith and had left heirs of his faith, nevertheless faith is not found in schism. And although he kept faith toward God, he did not keep it toward God’s Church, whose members he allowed, as it were, to be divided and whose limbs to be torn. For since Christ suffered for the Church, and the Church is Christ’s body, faith is not shown to Christ by those through whom his suffering is rendered void and his body torn apart.”

These are Ambrose’s words.

I have not unwillingly inserted this brief discussion of the Luciferians, because it illuminates the Donatists’ condition. For whenever we hear the former condemned, we understand that the latter deserve condemnation still more. Augustine, in Epistle 48, strongly rebukes the error of those who thought it made no difference in which party a person was a Christian, provided he held the faith. He objects that it belongs to God alone to be worshipped in unity.

He also relates, in Book I of *Against Parmenianus*, that Tychonius, who among the Donatists was at once the most moderate and the most learned, frankly acknowledged that the Catholic Church was spread throughout the world, but denied the consequent point: that Donatists sinned by refusing communion with it. That saying of Christ is rightly praised as proverbial: “Wherever the body or carcass may be, there the eagles will be gathered”; so that we may understand that, when religion is in question, we must look to Christ and run to him, just as ravens or vultures fly together to a carcass [Col. 1476B].

[“I hear that Calvin has noted at this place that all who cling to Christ are outside the danger of schism. But in order to cling to the head, we must be grafted into the body. Surely the head is not without the body, just as the body is not without the head.”]

Indeed, in the same passage Christ also commends to us the glory and brightness of his body—that is, of the Catholic Church—by whose guidance, as it were, we may run to him and upon which we should look. Speaking of his new kingdom and its sudden and marvelous spread, he says: “As lightning comes forth from the east and appears as far as the west,” etc. Accordingly Augustine says in Book I, chapter 38, of *Questions on the Gospels*: “By the names East and West he intended to signify the whole world, throughout which the Church was to exist.” He then adds: “Therefore, once the authority of the Church, conspicuous and manifest throughout the world, has been established, Christ consequently warns his disciples and all the faithful not to believe schismatics, who gather secretly, as though in inner chambers, and a few in the wilderness,” etc.

To return to the proceedings of the Conference: there is now nothing that ought especially to be observed more than what Augustine writes in *On Unity against Petilian*: “Because our question with the Donatists is not about the head, but about the body; that is, not about the Savior Jesus Christ himself, but about his Church: the head himself, concerning whom we agree, shows us his body, concerning which we disagree.”

Correctly so. But if they display that head as we do, where is the body more likely to be thought to exist? Augustine warns that this is sufficiently indicated by the words of the head—that is, the sacred Scriptures [Col. 1476D]. Which words? Those that show the Church to be catholic. When the dispute was with heretics with whom the principal question concerned the head—that is, Christ, whether his essence and nature or his office and benefit—and then concerned the body—that is, the Church—as with the Arians, Catholics simply maintained that, in order to identify the body, one must look to the head, and they dealt chiefly with the head.

But where the issue was with Donatists, who agreed about that head, they maintained by another argument, as was necessary, that the body, which alone was disputed, belonged to them. This judgment was difficult amid such general similarity. But the indication already mentioned was judged sufficient.

Therefore, even if the Donatists might display along with the head some more attractive appearance or colour of a body—that is, of their own society and association—namely, rites and conduct less corrupt, the Catholics’ other proof prevailed: by it they established that Christ’s body—that is, the Church—belonged to them, and at the same time showed that it was not among the Donatists. For it is admittedly one. In vain do those glory in the head who are not of the body. For where one is absent, neither is present, since, as Augustine says, the whole Christ is head and body. 356 Hence his familiar saying against the Donatists: “Outside the Church there is no salvation.”

Paul indeed calls the Church “Christ.” And although *Jehovah* is the proper name of God, it is nevertheless attributed not only to the altar at Jerusalem but also to the new Jerusalem—that is, the Church. I say these things in passing, so that we may better understand how great a matter is at issue when the Church is in question, and remember that the Donatists’ dispute concerned a great matter—indeed, the greatest of all [Col. 1477B].

Once we understand *to krinomenon* (τὸ κρινόμενον), “the matter to be decided,” let us inquire into *to kritērion* (τὸ κριτήριον), “the criterion of judgment.” Although we have already judged this point as well, I do not wish to pass over Chrysostom’s admission in Homily 49 on Matthew chapter 24: in his time it was most difficult to know, learn, and distinguish the Church amid such confusion of resemblance, when heretics displayed what Catholics displayed. The one remaining criterion, however, was from the Scriptures. But how? Augustine explains it.

At the Conference the Donatists asked by what testimonies the case was being tried, divine or human, and by what judgment the dispute was to be resolved. Our party answered that sacred Scripture would be both their witness and their judge. But it must also be observed how they used it and what they drew from it to establish their claim.

When Augustine disputes against the Donatists concerning baptism administered by heretics—that is, outside the Church—he adduces not only Scripture, but apostolic tradition and the Church’s practice, custom, testimony, and authority, as in Book II, chapter 7; Book IV, chapter 6; Book V, chapter 23, of *On Baptism*; and Book I, chapters 31–33, of *Against Cresconius*. He knew that Optatus had wished to settle the question of the one Baptism against the Donatists from Scripture alone. But he recognized that Optatus had attempted this unsuccessfully and did not judge it honest to twist passages of Scripture.

Therefore, Optatus, who when about to speak against the Donatists on baptism had appealed to the sacred writings, and the jurists, who say that a testator’s intention must be judged from the documents of the will—Augustine applied this principle in his exposition of Psalm 21, yet said it rather in the question concerning the Church. For in this more weighty case he thought Scripture proved his claim more clearly.

Thus also in the book *On the Unity of the Church against Petilian*: “Let us not hear, ‘This is what I say; this is what you say’; but let us hear, ‘This is what the Lord says.’ Certainly there are the Lord’s books, to whose authority both of us consent, both of us believe, both of us submit. There let us seek the Church; there let us examine our case.”

The Donatists did not reject this rule; but in the particular case there was disagreement [Col. 1478A]. Although each side drew, as it were, its theses from the sacred writings, they were by no means agreed as to their conclusion, application, or interpretation. For the Catholics, since they had no doubt that their Church was catholic—that is, spread throughout the whole world—held it abundantly sufficient if they proved from the sacred writings that the catholic Church is there commended. They begin, moreover, with the books of the Old Testament. For the Donatists did not repudiate these, as the Manichaeans did. And, to begin from the beginning, they first set forth the promise made to Abraham (for whatever we afterward admire in the universal Church depends upon that covenant). Then they accumulate the prophecies of the Prophets concerning the calling of the Gentiles, which was to take place when Christ had appeared. For these also accord with the promise made to Abraham.

[Col. 1478B] It must be carefully observed that Augustine made, and solemnly and devoutly urges, an important observation in his second sermon on Psalm XXX: namely, that the Prophets spoke more openly about the Church than about Christ. This was because, as he says, they saw in the Spirit that people would make parties against the Church, and would not merely dispute concerning Christ, but would stir up great controversies concerning the Church. Therefore, that matter about which the greater disputes were to arise was predicted more plainly and openly. He offers an example from Genesis, chapter XXII, where, after Isaac is rescued from death, Abraham is promised an innumerable seed; and in this manner the Church is openly proclaimed, while Christ is proclaimed only figuratively. Finally, he concludes that Christ was preached almost everywhere by the Prophets under some veiled mystery [Col. 1478C]; but the Church openly, so that even those who were to arise against her might see her.

What did the Donatists say? Augustine, in *On Unity*, chapter 9, says that they did not indeed dare plainly to say that the prophecies drawn from the Prophets concerning the future extent of the Christian Church, spread over the whole world—that is, the catholic Church—were false. Yet they objected that these had not been fulfilled, because people had been unwilling. Here Augustine rises up all the more vehemently and cries out that this is nothing other than saying that prophecy is false and that the Prophets were false prophets. I grant that the perversity of ungrateful people has caused many promises of God—not, I say, to become void, but to be in some manner hindered—insofar as they were conditional appendages of the covenant. But as regards the principal [Col. 1478D] promise, which was unconditional—for example, the promise of the Messiah’s appearing and of the establishment and propagation of his kingdom—the Apostle declares that it could not be hindered by human unworthiness. I also grant that the Prophets foretold many things concerning the excellence and majesty of the Church which are fulfilled in heaven. Yet no one will deny that they are at least begun on earth. In Isaiah, God, speaking of the enlargement of the Church, says with an oath: “Every knee shall bow to me.” Paul refers this to the end of the world and to the final judgment, as it is called. Yet meanwhile he does not deny that it also occurs in its own manner within the Christian Church.

Since the Donatists could not deny that some catholic Church existed, they claimed this title for their own Church [Col. 1479A]. And while they denied that their opponents were what they were called, namely Catholics, they then styled themselves, at the Conference, bishops and defenders of the catholic Church and of truth. Here the question began to be one of fact rather than of law; and it was again so much more difficult because the Donatists also seemed to retain catholic doctrine of faith and were not charged with apostasy in that respect. Against other heretics, such as the Manichaeans and Arians, the decision of this question was easier. Lactantius, indeed, writes in book IV, chapter 30, that every heretical group thought its own Church to be catholic. At least they boasted this when they saw that it was the primary condition of the Christian Church. But when it came to proof, they were ridiculous. Indeed, it even happened that they ultimately conceded to our side what, in their rash ignorance, they had wished to take away from it. Augustine, *Against the Letter of the Manichaeans*, chapter 4:

> Within the bosom of the catholic Church, the very name “catholic” keeps me; not without reason has this Church alone obtained it among so many heresies, so that, though all heretics wish to be called Catholics, yet if some stranger asks where the catholic assembly meets, no heretic would dare point out either his own basilica or his own house.

The same Augustine, in *On True Religion*, chapter 7, says:

> Communion with that Church which is catholic, and is called catholic, must be maintained—not only by her own members, but also by all her enemies. For, whether they wish it or not, heretics themselves and adherents of schisms, when speaking not with their own people but with outsiders, call the catholic Church by no other name than “catholic.” For they cannot make themselves understood [Col. 1479C] unless they distinguish her by that name by which she is called throughout the whole world.

Again, in *On the Usefulness of Believing*, chapter 7, he writes that all heretics wish to appear and to be called Catholics; but that there is nevertheless one catholic Church—as all admit—more abundant in numbers, if one considers the whole world, and purer in truth than all the rest. From this, he says, it is clear to unbiased judges, whom no personal favor impedes, to which Church the catholic name ought to be given—the name which all seek. Later, moreover, we shall hear from Victor of Utica that the Arians, at a certain Conference of Carthage, made a dispute above all about this title.

I have observed in a certain letter of Pacian, bishop of Barcelona, to Sympronianus the Novatian, that the Novatians once mocked this title because, as they said, under the Apostles no one was called “catholic” [Col. 1479D]. But that same letter indicates what Pacian—once a great bishop in the Church—answered in defense of the name; and the Donatists could have read it. Further, see what the Emperor Theodosius himself decreed somewhat before Augustine on this matter, in the law issued in book I, title *On the Supreme Trinity*. Let us now see what the Donatists put forward in order to claim this title for themselves and deny it to our side.

Cresconius the Donatist loudly asserted that the Church with which Augustine communicated was not catholic, because the whole world did not communicate with it: many barbarian peoples had not yet believed in Christ, and many heresies under Christ’s name were outside Augustine’s communion. Augustine, in book III *Against Cresconius*, chapter 63, seizes upon Cresconius’s own admission that the whole world was daily turning to the Christian name; and answers that the Church was daily spreading in order to occupy what remained.

Fortunius the Donatist, hearing that only the Church spread throughout the world was catholic, dared to say that his own communion existed everywhere on earth. Augustine, in letter 163, asks, in reply, whether he could issue *formatae* letters wherever he wished. For in this way the question could be settled very easily. These were letters of communion, composed in a fixed formula, which bishops sent to and fro as testimonies and, as it were, tokens of their confession. Thus Optatus, in book II *Against the Donatists*, says that his people communicate with Damasus, with whom the whole [Col. 1480B] world agrees through the exchange of *formatae* letters.

The Donatists boasted, at least, of the great number of their sect; and to display it, so many had flocked competitively and in crowds to Carthage for the Conference. They even complained that they were wronged by those who said that they were not numerous. Yet, since they appeared few in comparison with the Catholics, they nevertheless wished their small number to count as a mark of the Church, because, as their advocate Cresconius said, truth is often found among the few, while the many err. Augustine, in book III *Against Cresconius*, chapter 66, replies that good and true Christians, who are many in themselves, are likewise few in comparison with the wicked and false. Likewise, in book II *Against the Adversaries of the Law*, chapter 12, when he heard a Manichaean commend the fewness of his party because, as he said, wisdom belongs to the few, he answered that this is common to all heretics who oppose the catholic Church, which is spread with rich fruitfulness through all lands, each in the peculiar vanity of his own position: all glory in their fewness and wish, if possible, to seduce the multitude. Socrates, indeed, *Ecclesiastical History*, book V, chapter 10, relates that the Arians first gloried in their multitude. But when they had been suppressed by Theodosius and expelled from the cities, they boasted in their deserted synagogues: “Many are called, few are chosen.”

When the Donatists perceived that they could not establish the name “Catholic” by number and multitude, they resorted to another quibble. For the acts of the Conference report Gaudentius as saying that “catholic” means that which is full of sacraments, perfect, and immaculate [Col. 1480D].
