Thus Augustine, in the *Breviculus*, writes that the Donatists replied that the name “Catholic” was established not from the universality of the nations but from the fullness of the sacraments. But this was a foolish and empty subtlety. “They seemed to themselves,” Augustine says in letter 49, “to be saying something acute when they interpret the name ‘Catholic’ not from communion with the whole world, but from the observance of all commandments and sacraments.” Augustine replies that the word has another meaning; yet he promises not to dwell upon that meaning, but to rest on the divine oracles which promise a Church spread over the whole world. And that same Gaudentius finally fell so far that, when he felt himself pressed, he indignantly exclaimed that [Col. 1481A] the catholic Church was a human invention. Augustine is witness in book II *Against Gaudentius*. They would have spoken with greater warmth had they said that the name “Catholic” is a secular and civil term used by the laws when they signify the procurator of Caesar: final law, *Code*, *On the Property of the Proscribed*.

Before Augustine, Optatus, disputing against the Donatists in book II, not only pressed the point that the Church which is spread through the whole world is catholic and is so called, but also indicated other “endowments,” as he calls them, of the Church, by which she is adorned and recognized—though he does so coldly and obscurely. I pass over what Vincent of Lérins wrote more acutely on this subject somewhat after Augustine. But I do say this: when the apostolic Church is defended, what is not being defended is an apostolic rabble of certain scoundrels, who ought rather to be called *kakolykoi* (κακολυκοί, “evil wolves”).

The Donatists finally charged the Catholics with apostasy—a charge of which they themselves were rather guilty. Augustine, *On the Christian Conflict*, chapter 29:

> When you bring against the Donatists passages of Scripture concerning the Church’s diffusion throughout the whole world, they say: “All this had already been fulfilled before the party of Donatus existed; but afterward the whole Church perished, and its remnants remained only in Donatus’s party.”

What does Augustine say to this? “O proud and impious tongue!” In *On Unity against Petilian*, he likewise relates that the Donatists at length confessed what the Prophets had predicted concerning the Church’s extent; but added that afterward the whole world, as they put it, had apostatized, and that the Christian religion had failed among all nations except the party of Donatus—just as the Church formerly remained in Enoch, Noah, Abraham, Isaac, Jacob, and the two tribes of Judah [Col. 1481C]. This was a plausible Donatist rejoinder: they alleged that even an apostasy might be called “catholic” if it spread broadly and widely and occupied the world. But they stumbled ignorantly in proving the apostasy, because they wished it to be assessed not from doctrine of faith but from people’s morals and degenerate wickedness—persons surely perverse, captious, and troublesome rather than vigorous or acute.

This controversy could not have been judged better than by succession. The Catholics therefore replied that a lawful succession from the Apostles onward supported them, while the Donatists had none. By succession I mean not merely of persons but also of things [Col. 1481D]; not merely of doctrine but also of ordination; not merely of ordination but also of religion. Certainly, where such succession exists, there is no falling away; rather, there is continuation. Thus those to whom succession is made do not even appear to have wholly departed.

Irenaeus and Origen had formerly employed this defense against the heretics of their age; and likewise Tertullian of Africa, in *On the Prescription against Heretics*. Optatus opposes the same argument to the Donatists in book II, and Augustine follows his example. Augustine also thrusts this same battering ram against the Manichaeans five or six times in the books *Against Faustus*, and in *Against the Letter of the Manichaeans*, *On the Usefulness of Believing*, and book I *Against the Adversaries of the Law*, chapter 20. But when the dispute is with the Donatists, this argument is more difficult, because the Donatists [Col. 1482A] also maintained that they agreed with the ancient and excellent Roman Church and had departed only from its degeneration. Thus there was a certain transfer of the issue: inquiry henceforth concerned not so much the African as the Roman Church, and again a complex question of fact arose.

The Donatists did not deny that the African Churches ought, as colonies, to look to the Roman Church as their mother-city. So Tertullian of Africa says in *On the Prescription*: “Let us see what the Roman Church has learned, what she has taught, with what she has exchanged the token of fellowship even with the African Churches.” The Donatists therefore had shrewdly arranged to have some Church at Rome. But they could not make it appear that they had had there a bishop of their sect from the times of the Apostles onward. Thus, when recalled to the origin, they vanished away. Tertullian himself had forewarned, in *On the Prescription*, that the origin must be examined when succession is at issue. Indeed, the acts of the Conference testify that Petilianus, by a kind of anticipation, voluntarily raised a dispute even with Augustine and his colleagues concerning origin and succession. He asked: who had ordained them? What father and founder did they have? From where had they begun? Augustine replied that Christ himself pointed out the beginning of his communion and the origin of his Church, which had spread from Jerusalem through all nations in one continuous progress. Thus Christ was his head, God his Father, and such a Church his mother. The Donatists asked who had ordained Augustine. Augustine acknowledged that it was Megalius, Primate of Numidia. The Donatists wished to note and condemn some defect in that ordination [Col. 1482C]. But their quibble was futile, for it did not compel the African Catholics to defend their communion with the Roman Church, in which they rejoiced.

Optatus, in book II, disputing against Parmenianus the Donatist, enumerates the uninterrupted succession of Roman bishops from Peter onward, with whom the African Catholics communicated. Then, taunting the Donatists, he says: “Set forth the origin of your own chair.” The Donatists, foolish as they were, replied that they too had a bishop in the city of Rome. Optatus answers first that the man whom they had there—or rather, whom they sent there—was one Victor, an African, who had not existed before Donatus. Thus Augustine, in a certain psalm against the Donatists, says: “Count the priests from Peter’s very see; and see, in the order of those fathers, who succeeded whom.” Likewise, in *Questions on the Old and New Testament*, chapter 110—a book attributed to Augustine—he says: “They disturb the order begun from the Apostle Peter and preserved to the present time through the succession of bishops, while claiming for themselves an order without origin, a body without a head.”

In order to show that the succession of Roman bishops, of which the African Catholics who communicated with them boasted, was interrupted and corrupt—and yet not appear merely to rant confusedly about it—the Donatists sometimes said that certain of the earliest bishops had indeed administered the Roman episcopate blamelessly, as they phrased it [Col. 1483A], but that others afterward had been unlike them. They pursued these with incredible calumnies, as Augustine says in *On the One Baptism*. Finally, they loudly alleged that Marcellinus, Miltiades, and Sylvester had been no less *traditores* than Caecilianus.

It is surprising that they did not rather allege a certain desertion by Liberius, and the tumultuous ordination of Damasus who succeeded him—an ordination which the Pelagians also attacked for that reason. Augustine indicates this when, in book VI *Against Julian*, he says: “You tauntingly allege the dissension of the Roman people in appointing a bishop.” From Ammianus it is known what that dissension was like and how bloody when Damasus was made bishop. Julian the Pelagian, moreover, when pressed by the authority of the Roman see, accused even Zosimus himself—“the bishop of the apostolic see, of blessed memory,” as Augustine calls him in the same place—of prevarication [Col. 1483B].

When such charges were raised, however, the Catholics answered that they were calumnies; and that even if the accusations were true, the private vices of persons did no harm to religion and the Church, which condemns such sins. The argument would have had more color if the Donatists had alleged what Tertullian of Africa himself had once noted in *Against Praxeas*: that the Roman bishop of his day was almost a Montanist. They might then have amassed the other charges which Tertullian himself brings against his own schismatic party in *On Modesty* and *Against the Psychics*. But they employed Petilianus as their advocate, who was as inept as Tertullian had formerly been keen and vehement. Had they possessed a second Tertullian on their side at the Conference, Augustine would have sweated more. As things stood, it was easy to defeat persons languid and soft. For whatever they object, what else do they do than, in the Poet’s phrase, hurl “a feeble weapon without a blow,” or, as the saying goes, threaten with a blunt leaden dagger?

See, lest they should seem to wander in the air and act without any testimony, at one time, Augustine says in letter 48, “as though lying in wait for divine testimonies,” and as though the Church had already perished from the world, they alleged a certain complaint of Hilary concerning the Asiatic provinces which followed Arius [Col. 1483C]. Had they been more learned and incisive, they could have intensified such a charge of apostasy. For Jerome, *Against the Error of John of Jerusalem*, says: “The heresy of the Arians held the whole East, except Athanasius and Paulinus.” Indeed, it had also invaded the West and broken even the bishop of Rome. What need of more? Basil, letter 60, acknowledges that he had thought the beginnings were at hand of that apostasy which Paul mentions to the Thessalonians.

The Donatists could also have alleged at the Conference that Rome had been captured by barbarians and that the Roman Empire was already collapsing. Thus Jerome himself, alluding in his day to that Pauline passage to the Thessalonians, and lamenting the ruin of the Roman Empire—which was believed to precede the reign of apostasy—writes in his letter to Gerontia *On Monogamy*: “He who restrains is removed from the midst; and do we not understand that Antichrist is approaching?” But the Donatists proceed somewhat more mildly. Nor indeed could they have drawn a plausible defense of their schism from this, since they had separated from the Church already in Constantine’s time, when both the Roman Empire [Col. 1484A] and the Christian Church were flourishing most greatly.

Nor does Augustine here labor to expound Paul’s Thessalonian passage concerning Antichrist; he did so later for our Marcellinus in book XX, chapter 19, of *The City of God*. For the present, he merely dissolves the Donatists’ objection from Hilary. Hilary’s words in *On Synods* are these:

> I have heard and seen the faults of those now present—not of laymen, but of bishops. For, apart from Bishop Eleusius and a few with him, the greater part of the ten Asian provinces do not know God. And would that they did not know him! For they would be ignorant with a more ready pardon than they malign him.

If the Donatists wished to prove from this that the Church had already perished throughout the world in 359, they foolishly took Asia for the entire world. On the contrary, in the same book Hilary admits that at least the Churches of Gaul and Britain had remained steadfast in the sincere faith. Nor had the African Churches any less rejected Arianism. Augustine, however, uses another defense. What is it? He says that Hilary had rebuked the tares of the ten Asian provinces, not the wheat itself; or even the wheat itself, endangered by some deficiency, which Hilary thought should be rebuked all the more vigorously because such rebuke was more beneficial. He says that the Donatists slander a learned man who rebuked severely in order that he might again travail in birth; and that they could in the same way say that there were then no Churches of Galatia when the Apostle said: “O foolish Galatians,” and so forth.

He says that the Church is at times obscured and, as it were, overshadowed by a multitude of scandals; but even then stands out in her most steadfast members. At times her multitude appears quiet and free in the calm of peace; at times it is covered and disturbed by the waves of temptations and tribulations [Col. 1484C]. Such, he says, was the time about which Hilary wrote. I add that, a little later, in the time of Theodosius, that Church was in some measure set free, so that it again became what it had been in Constantine’s time. I add that a similar alternation had once been seen in the kingdom of David. But an interruption which seems to break continuity does not abolish perpetuity.

But, to return to the Donatists: if they wished to bring forward something from Hilary to object to Augustine in this cause, why did they not rather produce what Hilary wrote against Auxentius concerning the Church? Why did they not press what Rufinus wrote, that the face of the Church was already then exceedingly foul? Indeed, why do they not object to the graver and terrible complaint of Basil, who gives a dreadful picture, as one might say, of a Church confused in confused disorder? Why do they not cry out that Jerome confessed that, at the time of this Conference, the dregs of the Church alone remained in place of the Church? Why do they not repeat Augustine’s own words to Marcellinus from letter 5: “In this mass of the worst morals and of ruined ancient discipline,” and so forth? But let us pursue the straightforward history of the Donatist proceedings.

When the Donatists loudly asserted that the catholic Church had apostatized, as they put it, and perished—and wished by this outcry to evade the prophecies concerning the Church’s glory, extent, and perpetuity—the Catholics asked at the Conference where it was written that she was so soon to perish [Col. 1485A]. Thus Augustine asks Petilianus in *On Unity*: when, by whom, and how were the Churches founded by apostolic labor destroyed? Likewise, in letter 161 to Honoratus, he asks how Christ lost the inheritance of the nations promised to him. This question, indeed, as it were stopped the Donatists’ mouths, since they were by no means equipped as they ought to have been for this contest. I wonder that they did not allege what Ezekiel, Daniel, or the Apocalypse is said to write concerning Antichrist, or even what is written in the letter to the Thessalonians. Did they think that the time of that Antichrist had not yet arrived in their age?

There remained another passage of Paul to Timothy concerning apostates who would arise in the last times. But Augustine himself, in *On Unity against Petilian*, as if forestalling this, says that it concerns the purgings of the Church and those who have fallen away from the Church. Thus he also turns that passage against the Manichaeans in book V *Against Faustus*, chapter 10, and book XXX; in book I *Against Felix the Manichaean*, chapter 7; and in *Against Secundinus*, chapter 2.

I come to what the Donatists pressed most strongly at the Conference. Since the catholic Church was preached, they in turn contended that it must also be holy; and they loudly asserted that their opponents’ Church—that is, the Catholic Church—was not such. The Catholics acknowledged what was lacking to them and what kind of Church she ought to be. But they admitted that she would not be perfect in this life, though she would be so in heaven; and that this work is daily being done, so that her stains may be removed and she may cease to be wrinkled [Col. 1485C]. But they denied that complete reformation exists amid this mass of human corruption. Thus Augustine answered Fulgentius the Donatist, who boasted proudly of his Church’s perfection, in letter 50 to Boniface:

> Far be it from any one of us to call himself so righteous as to dare boast that he is without sin in this life, as the Donatists said at our Conference, that they were in a Church which has neither spot nor wrinkle nor anything of the kind.

The Pelagians made a not dissimilar boast, as Augustine indicates in book IV to Boniface, chapter 7; book II *On the Gift of Perseverance*, chapter 5; and book II *Against Julian*. But how windy the vanity of heretics is, is well known.

Further, when the Catholics at the Conference distinguished the Church which is in heaven from that which is on earth [Col. 1485D], the Donatists slanderously said that they imagined two Churches and forgot that there is only one. The Catholics easily refuted this calumny when they replied and showed that the same one holy Church is now in one condition and will then be in another, as Augustine says in the third Conference, chapter 4. I would not hesitate to recognize three successive forms and kinds of the Church: the first Mosaic or Jewish; the second catholic; and the third heavenly. The second is promised by the Prophets as far excelling the first, and the third as in turn far better than the second. Yet such progress does not interrupt the continuity of the one Church; nor does it prevent that first Church—which was also a kind of prefiguration of the second [Col. 1486A]—from being highly praised. Hence Psalm LXXXVII says of Zion and Jerusalem: “Glorious things are spoken of you, O city of God.”

I return to the Donatists. Recalling that example, they plausibly boasted that they were like the two tribes which did not fall away when the other ten tribes of Israel revolted from the kingdom of Judah and followed Jeroboam. But the Catholics rightly reversed the comparison; and though they admitted that many stains and blemishes existed in their Church, they maintained that, so long as she had Christ as her head, the Donatists’ schism was impious. Augustine, moreover, in *Against Fulgentius*, when he heard Catholics called Samaritans by the Donatists, proves that the Donatists themselves were rather like Samaritans.

Upon this depended the judgment concerning the example of communion derived from the ancient Jewish Church, a matter most vigorously contested at the Conference. Yet I do not conceal that both sides seem to have exercised too little care in that dispute, since neither sufficiently observes, in the example of the Prophets which it alleges, the distinction which all the Prophets nevertheless repeatedly emphasize. So greatly does the heat of controversy sometimes indiscriminately mingle things which ought to be distinguished. Therefore this part of the Conference must now be examined all the more closely, so that, having reached the chief point at issue, we may weigh more carefully the arguments of each side.

The acts of the Conference testify that the Catholics produced their document, as they called it, and that the Donatists produced and set theirs against it, since they conducted and contested the matter more by writings than by words. In that age, *notaria*, or also *notoria*, meant a writing which made something known or indicated it; it is not otherwise so called by us or by notaries. Augustine also uses the word in the history of this Conference in the manner I have described; and elsewhere, more in the civil sense, in the history of the Donatists, he calls *notoria* or *notaria* the written report of *irenarchs* concerning Donatist defendants, in letters 159 and 160. The term is likewise used in civil law: law *Divus*, *On the Custody of Defendants*; law *Ab accusatione*, § *Accusatores*, *To the Senate under the Lex Turpilia*; law *Ea quidem*, *Code, On Accusations*; law 31, *Theodosian Code, On Bishops and Clerics*. In Vopiscus, in two places, *notoria* generally means a letter. But I return to the Catholic *notaria* or *notoria* set forth at this Conference, in which the Acts testify that this thesis was written and first proposed [Col. 1486D]:

> The Prophets rebuked with severe words the sinful people who offended the Lord with many execrable abominations; and by the lashes of correction they stirred hard and untamed minds to terrible enmity against themselves. Yet they did not separate themselves by a bodily division from that people, among whom, to be sure, good persons were also among the evil; judging it better patiently to endure the wicked than, through calumny, to abandon the good.

The Donatists’ response in those Acts is longer; but its conclusion concerning the Prophets just mentioned is this: “That they were among those whom they condemned was a matter of dwelling among them, not of communion.”

[Col. 1487A] Augustine briefly explains what the Catholics then replied in the *Breviculus of the Conference of the Third Day*, in these words:

> Concerning the Prophets, because the Donatists had said in their writings that they did not communicate with those against whom they uttered so many evils, the Catholics replied that there was one temple, used by all; and that none of the Prophets who said so much against the wicked established for himself another temple, sacrifices, or priests.

The same Augustine, in *Against the Donatists after the Conference*, chapter 20, says:

> They still dare to bring up prophetic and apostolic testimonies, to which we answered comprehensively in that Conference, showing that the holy Prophets themselves moved among the wicked in one temple, under the same priests, amid the same sacraments, yet were not defiled by the wicked, because they knew how to distinguish between the holy and the unclean—not, as these men think, by bodily separation of the people, but by sound judgment and good living.

The same author, shortly afterward, approaching the Donatist objection more closely, says that the Prophet was commanded neither to eat bread nor drink wine in Samaria, where he had been sent to rebuke those who had set up calves to be worshiped after the manner of Egyptian idols. He certainly had to do what the Lord commanded, who then chose in that manner to rebuke them, so that the Prophet whom he had sent should touch nothing there. “For does this not happen daily in the Church, when, while rebuking more sharply those whom we rebuke, even if we are on their property, we touch nothing there among them, so that they may feel how greatly we grieve over their sins? Yet must a departure of the people therefore be made, so that the weak—like tender grass—are uprooted indiscriminately, though they cannot judge from human hearts and unknown deeds, even if these are known to us? For in that very Samaria were Elijah and Elisha; and though they themselves were in the wilderness, this was not because they were avoiding sacraments, but because they suffered persecution from impious kings. For there were there, not in the wilderness, seven thousand men unknown to Elijah himself, who had not bent the knee to Baal.” Thus he speaks.

Here, however, I must candidly say what I think. When I consider more carefully what has now been quoted, both Catholics and Donatists seem to me thoughtlessly to confuse the distinction that formerly existed between Judah and Israel, and between Jerusalem and Samaria. For just as the Donatists confusedly contend that, because of human vices [Col. 1487D], the Prophets did not communicate in either the Jerusalem or the Samaritan sacrifices, so the Catholics seem no less confusedly to contend in reply that the Prophets communicated in both sacrifices; and that, although they separated themselves in morals, they remained joined to the altars.

Yet, as Augustine himself rightly said in book XVII, chapter 22, of *The City of God*, all the kings in Israel were reprobate, but not so in Judah. He should have said the same about the sacrifices: namely, that the Prophets did communicate, and ought to have communicated, in the Jerusalem sacrifices so long as their form was lawful, even though the corruption of priests and people was otherwise great and their hypocrisy condemnable. But in the sacrifices of Israel or Samaria, the Prophets neither did communicate nor ought to have communicated [Col. 1488A], since no altar outside the Temple was lawful, even if the life of priests and people had been entirely without fault.

Indeed, the Prophets rebuke Judah’s sacrifices differently from Israel’s. In the former they rebuke the hypocrisy and impiety of the persons; in the latter, also the form and substance of the sacrifices themselves. Augustine, in the book written after the Conference, says that this question had been plainly resolved at the Conference. But I, to conceal nothing, am compelled to say that there was a manifest error on both sides—an error alike of law and fact—so long as the distinction I have stated is not applied. I therefore wonder that, though so many distinguished bishops were present at the Conference of Carthage, no one noticed that distinction which the Prophets so often and so plainly emphasize.

The Donatists rightly say that Elijah and Elisha never communicated with the altars of Samaria and for that reason lived in the wilderness. I therefore wonder that Augustine answers that Elijah and Elisha were not in the wilderness in order to avoid Samaria’s sacraments. They also lived at Bethel. Yet they never either sacrificed there or communicated in that place’s sacrifices. Finally, it was singular and extraordinary that Elijah should once have sacrificed on Mount Carmel. At least, when Augustine says that Elijah or Elisha did not avoid Samaria’s sacraments, a distinction should be made between the sacraments of circumcision and the sacraments of sacrifice. Sacrifices in Samaria certainly had altogether to be avoided and shunned, because it was lawful to sacrifice only in the Temple [Col. 1488C] at Jerusalem. Circumcision, however, was not similarly tied to the Temple.

Correctly again the Donatists said of the prophets Hosea and Amos what they had said of Elijah and Elisha: since those prophets likewise dealt with the Israelites, and yet cried, “Do not go to Gilgal; do not go up to Beth-aven”—that is, do not share in the sacrifices of Israel or Samaria. Yet they would not similarly have said, “Do not go up to Jerusalem.” Therefore the Donatists wrongly add: “But how, in the city of Jerusalem, could the prophets share in the sacrifices of sinful men, which, being filled with the divine Spirit, they condemned?” In these matters the prophets condemned not so much the form of the sacrifice as the person of the hypocritical sacrificer.

And where the Donatists concluded that it was a matter of dwelling together [Col. 1488D], not communion, because the prophets were among those whom they condemned: again a distinction had to be made between Judah and Israel. Prophets, even those native to Judah, migrated into Israel, in order, while dwelling there, not to share in the altars of Samaria, but to condemn them—as Amos and Hosea did. But the Levites who lived among the tribes of Israel all fled from there to the city of Jerusalem, where alone it was lawful to sacrifice.

In order to refute what the Catholics had said at the Conference—that good persons ought to be separated from bad by their conduct, not by bodily separation—the Donatists cited that passage of Isaiah: “Depart, depart, go out from their midst. Be clean,” etc., 361 since Paul too repeats it in the Epistle to the Corinthians [Col. 1489A]. But with respect to Isaiah, it is clear that those opening words mean and seek only this: that the Jews should be ready to depart from Babylon as soon as the day of liberation comes. Meanwhile, however, he also warns them to be clean: namely, not to share in the idols of the Chaldeans. The Apostle repeats this to his Corinthians, lest they too share in things sacrificed to idols, etc. But otherwise he does not command them to leave their native land and flee from cities of idolaters. Otherwise they would have to go out of the world, as he says elsewhere. The command that the Jews should depart from Babylon had a particular rationale which must not be extended to others.

Augustine, in *On Unity*, chapter 12, relates that Petilianus loudly asserted that the ten tribes had been separated and handed over to Solomon’s servant, namely Jeroboam; but that two [Col. 1489B] had remained with Solomon’s son. Then, by inventing a comparison, he kept declaring: “Thus now the whole world has apostasized; but we, like those two tribes, have remained in the temple of God—that is, in the Church.” What does Augustine say to this? “Let them show,” he says, “that it is written that they are such as those two tribes are written to have been; and then we offer no resistance.” But the succession of which I have spoken showed rather that the Catholics were such. Their schism indicated that the Donatists rather resembled the ten tribes.

Formerly, indeed, those ten tribes of Israel claimed that the Church was with them rather than at Jerusalem. But they never proved it, nor did any prophet ever grant it to them. When they had been carried away into captivity and the Samaritans had succeeded them, the same controversy continued [Col. 1489C], so much so that a rival temple was built on Mount Gerizim, like that which had shortly before been restored at Jerusalem by the returning Jews. Indeed, the question was then also debated as to which temple was legitimate; and in the end it was referred to the judgment of Ptolemy, king of Egypt, under the terrible condition that whichever advocate lost his case should be punished by death. But after the Law of Moses had been heard, and the uninterrupted succession of the Jewish high priests established, judgment was rightly given for the temple at Jerusalem. Josephus is witness, book XIII, chapter 6.

That history is certainly memorable and an apt example to be cited here. Yet we should also wonder that the Samaritans nonetheless continued to claim for themselves what they had claimed before, even after their Gerizim temple had been destroyed [Col. 1489D], so that we hear that the controversy still endured in Christ’s time. I shall say nothing of the other apostate temple, founded in Egypt by Jews themselves after the model of the Jerusalem temple, with King Ptolemy’s connivance. For I confine myself here to the example of the ancient dissension between Samaria and Jerusalem. Nor can a more illustrious example or a history of the ancient Church be drawn upon in this argument. When we consider it, the memory of so dreadful a schism, which lasted so long, must strike us forcefully. Nor is there any doubt that Augustine, foreseeing much from it, gathered therefrom grounds on which he mournfully lamented the Donatist schism and bewailed the Church’s most grievous calamity.

[He had read [Col. 1490A] that Nazianzen, speaking and sighing in complaint about his own times and the excesses of the Arians, lamented that the Church had not only been torn apart, as Judah and Israel once were, but that the Christian people had been divided household by household. He had read that Nazianzen, turning to God, was accustomed to pray: “O Lord, let there be some end to this ecclesiastical war. Let there no longer be Judah and Israel, Jerusalem and Samaria, Rehoboam and Jeroboam.” I do not doubt that Augustine’s prayers, wishes, and sighs were similar.

But though Hosea and Jeremiah had foretold that Judah and Israel would at some time be reunited under one head—which undoubtedly happened when the Christian Church first came together—Augustine scarcely dared to hope that this would readily happen again, when he saw a new schism gaining strength in the Church [Col. 1490B]. Certainly the same Nazianzen, seeing how Theodosius was bringing about the Church’s *henōsis* (unity), joyfully at last exclaimed: “We no longer bear and carry one another; Judah and Israel set before themselves one rule; we have all become Christians.” But Augustine was not so fortunate as to see this fully, although the Carthaginian Conference contributed greatly toward restoring that unity.]

I return to the place where Augustine denies that the Donatists are what they claim to be—namely, like the tribe of Judah. He adds, by way of concession, that even if they were so, they ought nevertheless to read the prophets, who say that backsliding Israel was justified by comparison with the sins of treacherous Judah. Jeremiah certainly said this in chapter III, and Ezekiel [Col. 1490C] in chapter XIX, in order to chastise their own Jews for abusing most unworthily the title of the Church. Nor do I doubt that Augustine himself, by no means indulging the sins of his own people, often reproached them with this.

What surprises me is that, in the same book *On Unity against Petilianus*, when he treats this question, he adds that that portion of the ancient people—that is, Israel—should not be reckoned as though it had been heresy. For God had commanded those ten tribes to be separated, not in order that religion should be divided, but that the kingdom should be divided. When I read this, I confess—so that once again I may conceal nothing—that I hesitate and pause. God had indeed justly and deservedly decreed that Jeroboam should be king, in order to punish Solomon’s sin. Yet Israel nevertheless sinned when, treacherously, it adopted such a king as would lead it to revolt from the kingdom of David and from the temple [Col. 1490D].

But Augustine himself, in book I against Cresconius, chapter 31, says that the Samaritans were as it were heretics of the Jews. I hear what he says against Petilianus: that God commanded the kingdom of Judah to be divided, not religion as well. He did not command a schism to be made. “Just as,” he says, “kingdoms are often divided throughout the world, yet Christian unity is not divided, because the Catholic Church is found in both parts.” But—if I may frankly say what I think, and set forth what I take to be true, modestly indeed but freely, unimpeded by any prejudice in Augustine’s favour—I think it must be observed that the character of the Judaean or Davidic kingdom was different from that of other kingdoms. For the Church was so contained within, and so joined to, David’s kingdom [Col. 1491A] that it could not be divided without religion being divided—that is, without the person who revolted from it becoming guilty of schism. For whoever revolted from it revolted also from the Church itself. Certainly prayer was offered for that kingdom as for the Church, in Psalms LXXVII and CVIII; and David was for this reason called the firstborn among kings, Psalm LXXXIX.

“But,” you will say, “God is nevertheless said to have divided David’s kingdom.” I grant it, but for an end wholly different from the intention of the schismatic Jeroboam or of the ten tribes that followed him; their purpose was wholly other than God’s counsel. Let these remarks be made in passing. Augustine’s conclusion against Petilianus is that there were prophets also in Israel. I agree. But then I admit that the Donatists rightly said that it was a matter of dwelling together, not communion. In Judah, however, it must also be said, as I warned before, that they not only lived among them [Col. 1491B] but also shared in communion.

Here I would ask pardon for boldness if I seem to criticize Augustine and his colleagues somewhat freely for not sufficiently observing the distinction between Judah and Israel. But a fair judge devoted to truth will recognize in my act a mark of modesty rather than any trace of insolence. Certainly, as I could not honestly conceal what I thought, so I acknowledge that, in the heat of disputation and to restrain the very obstinate importunity of the Donatists, the Catholics at the Conference distinguished Judah less carefully from Israel when they wished to show that prophets, however severe their rebukes of vices, were by no means schismatics, and when they sharply censured the Donatists [Col. 1491C] for deriving an example for their schism from prophets whom they indiscriminately declared to have fled the sacrifices of their own nation—thus, in a contrary manner, confusing the distinction between Judah and Israel. Yet that Augustine otherwise did not fail to know what I have said, but indeed carefully indicated such a distinction elsewhere, is witnessed by book XVII of his *City of God*.

But to put some restraint upon today’s new Momuses, who would ridicule the entire Carthaginian Conference on account of a *mnēmonikon hamartēma* (“an error of memory”) and insult the good Fathers, I am reminded that Calvin himself, the chief of the new censors, although elsewhere in six hundred places he had noted the distinction so often indicated by the prophets, seems somehow to have forgotten it when heated in argument. Certainly [Col. 1491D], when he first wrote angrily against me, he seems even to have reversed it. He says: “That the true Church existed at Jerusalem when the priests had turned aside from the lawful worship of God is beyond doubt. But whether the authority of that Church ought to have remained vigorous and valid among the godly is clear from the prophets, who everywhere cry out that one must withdraw as far as possible from their impious faction.” Shortly afterward he says that it cannot be denied that among the Israelites who followed Jeroboam there was some Church.

I add another passage that has now occurred to me. The complaint is well known of the prophet Elijah, lamenting that he alone had been left. Augustine rightly observed and noted, in book XVII of *The City of God*, chapter 22, that this properly concerned the condition of Israel rather than Judah. Yet Calvin, in the preface to his *Institutes*, maintains from that complaint [Col. 1492A] that, generally speaking, there was no visible Church in Elijah’s time. But sacred history itself testifies that Elijah speaks only of the kingdom of Israel, where he lived; in the kingdom of Judah, meanwhile, there was at that time a distinguished Church under King Jehoshaphat, whom it also suggests was like a second David.

Indeed, in his *Institutes* itself Calvin seems confusedly to say what the Donatists said on this point at the Conference. He alleges that the prophets everywhere cried concerning the Jews and Israelites of their age that their assemblies were profane, that joining in them was no more lawful than denying God; or that, if those were Churches, Elijah, Micaiah, and the like in Israel, and Isaiah, Jeremiah, and Hosea in Judah, were alien from the Church of God. He concludes [Col. 1492B] that it was necessary to withdraw from agreement with those assemblies, which was nothing other than an impious conspiracy against God. Who does not see that this is said confusedly, where one ought to distinguish Judah from Israel?

And indeed, on the same page a little earlier, apparently contradicting himself, he said what we also maintain and say in refuting the Donatists:

> “I confess that all the prophets who were at Jerusalem, while matters there were exceedingly corrupt, neither sacrificed separately nor held meetings apart from others for prayer. For they had God’s command requiring them to assemble in Solomon’s temple. They knew that the Levitical priests, because they had been appointed by the Lord as ministers of sacred things and had not yet been deposed, still occupied that place, however unworthy of that honour they were. Nor were they compelled to engage in any superstitious worship [Col. 1492C].”

Again, a little earlier in the same *Institutes*, he says:

> “Terrible are those descriptions by which Isaiah, Jeremiah, Joel, Habakkuk, and others lament the maladies of the Jerusalem Church. Among the people, the magistrates, and the priests, everything was so utterly corrupt that Isaiah cries out that from the crown of the head to the sole of the foot there was nothing sound. Religion was partly despised, partly defiled. Everywhere in conduct are reported thefts, robberies, perfidies, murders, and like crimes. Yet the prophets did not on that account establish new churches for themselves or construct new altars on which to offer separate sacrifices. Rather, whatever men were like, because they nevertheless reckoned that the Lord had deposited his word among them and instituted the ceremonies by which he was worshipped there, they stretched out pure hands to him in the midst of an ungodly assembly [Col. 1492D]. Certainly, if they had thought that they contracted any contagion from it, they would a hundred times rather have died than have allowed themselves to be drawn there. Therefore nothing restrained them from separating except zeal for preserving unity. If it was a matter of religion for the holy prophets not to estrange themselves from the Church because of the many and most grievous crimes, not of one or two men but of almost the whole people, we arrogate too much to ourselves if we immediately dare to withdraw from communion with the Church wherever not all conduct satisfies either our judgment or even the Christian profession.

> “What, then, was the age of Christ and the apostles like? Yet the desperate impiety of the Pharisees, and the unrestrained license of life then prevalent everywhere, could not prevent them from using the same sacred rites with the people and assembling with the rest in one temple for the public exercises of religion [Col. 1493A]. Why was this? Unless because they knew that those who shared in the same sacred rites with a pure conscience were not polluted at all by association with the wicked? If anyone is insufficiently moved by the prophets and apostles, let him at least yield to Christ’s authority. Cyprian therefore speaks well: ‘Although tares or impure vessels appear to be in the Church, we ourselves have no reason to withdraw from the Church. We must make every effort and strive as far as possible to be vessels of gold and silver. But to break earthen vessels belongs to the Lord alone, to whom also the rod of iron has been given. Let no one claim for himself what properly belongs to the Son alone, as though he were sufficient to winnow the threshing floor and cleanse the chaff, and to separate all tares by human judgment. This is proud obstinacy and sacrilegious presumption which perverse madness assumes for itself,’ etc. [Col. 1493B]

> “Let both these points therefore remain established: first, that one who voluntarily abandons the Church’s outward communion where God’s word is preached and the sacraments administered has no excuse; secondly, that neither the vices of few nor many hinder us from rightly professing our faith there through the ceremonies instituted by God. For a devout conscience is not harmed by the unworthiness of another, whether pastor or private person; nor are the Lord’s mysteries less pure and salutary to a holy and upright person because they are also handled by the impure.”

These are his words, which I now willingly transcribe, in order that I may complete the case which I maintain even by the adversary’s confession [Col. 1493C], and confirm by such a subscription the conclusion of the Carthaginian Conference against the Donatists. Therefore I shall not hesitate to repeat from the same *Institutes* what is set down a little earlier. For it appears to be taken from Augustine and, as it were, cuts the Donatists’ throats. 363

> “There have always been persons imbued with a false conviction of absolute holiness who, as though they had already become certain aerial demons, scorned all association with men in whom they perceived something still human. Such were formerly the Cathari and the Donatists who approached their madness. Such today are some Anabaptists who wish to appear to have advanced beyond others. Others sin more through an inconsiderate zeal for righteousness than through that insane pride. For when they see among those to whom the Gospel is proclaimed fruit not corresponding to its doctrine, they immediately judge that there is no Church there. Their offence is indeed most just, and in this most miserable age we give more than enough occasion for it. We cannot excuse our accursed sloth, which the Lord will not leave unpunished; indeed, he has already begun to chastise it with severe scourges. Woe, therefore, to us who permit such unrestrained license of wickedness that weak consciences are wounded because of us. But those of whom we have spoken in turn sin in this: they do not know how to set a limit to their offence. For where the Lord requires gentleness, they abandon it and give themselves wholly to immoderate severity [Col. 1494A]. Since they think that there is no Church where there is not complete purity and integrity of life, they depart from the legitimate Church out of hatred for crimes, while supposing that they are withdrawing from a faction of wicked persons. They allege that Christ’s Church is holy. But that they may at the same time understand that it is mixed of good and bad, let them hear from Christ’s mouth the parable in which it is compared to a net gathering fish of every kind, which are not sorted until they are laid out on the shore. Let them hear that it is like a field sown with good seed but infected by tares through an enemy’s fraud, from which it is not cleansed until the harvest has been brought to the threshing floor. Finally, let them hear that it is a threshing floor in which wheat has been so gathered that it lies hidden under chaff until, purified by winnowing fan and sieve, it is at last stored in the barn. If the Lord has declared that the Church will suffer this evil until the day of judgment, being burdened by a mixture of wicked people [Col. 1494B], they vainly seek one unstained by any blemish.”

These are his words. If they do not yet suffice to crush the obstinacy or captiousness of our censors, I shall add what their same master wrote against the Anabaptists:

> “We have seen what vices the prophets rebuke in the Jewish Church—or rather against what abominations they cry out. Nor do those rebukes apply to one class of persons alone; rather, they openly declare that from the leaders down to the common people, from the highest to the lowest, all things had been so corrupted and depraved that scarcely a single sound member could be found. For these are their own words. But did they therefore cease to meet with the wicked and perverse people to worship God, offer sacrifices, and hear the teaching of the Law [Col. 1494C]? Did they construct a temple or altar apart, that they might possess a pure Church? If a believer is polluted by sharing with the wicked in prayers, hearing doctrine, and receiving sacraments, then all the prophets were polluted, and were like leaders who by their example led the rest to destruction.

> “Now let us come to Christ our Lord and to his apostles. First, we know what the condition of the Jerusalem Church was at that time. Yet the Lord Jesus chose to be circumcised with the rest. Then, on the day of purification, he was brought to the temple, that according to the customary rite he might be offered to God. If they allege that he was received into the hands of holy men, I answer that this was done in the name of the whole Church, which nevertheless abounded in much filth and abominable vices [Col. 1494D]. If again they object that he was an infant and that this was not properly done by him, I answer that he was so an infant in the human nature which he had received from us that he was at the same time governed by his divine providence, by which he could never know himself to be contaminated by any action contrary to the purity of God’s children. Indeed, when he had become a man—and, what is more, when he preached God’s word and discharged his office—he continued in this course to the last day of his life. If God is offended by one who enters an assembly for the purpose of prayer and confession of faith, from which wicked persons are not excluded, what did our Lord intend and what example did he give when he entered the temple at Jerusalem in order to perform sacred rites together with the scribes, Pharisees, and the people, who were then utterly corrupt? [Col. 1495A]

> “Immediately, I know, they will object that Christ went up to the temple only to rebuke the vices and crimes then committed there, not to participate in their sacrifices and other confessions of faith. But it is easy to show that this answer is false. Paul says, not without reason, that Christ was made subject to the Law in order that he might redeem all who were subject to it from its bondage. He expressly speaks of the ceremonial Law. Therefore, when Christ came to the temple, especially on feast days and solemn occasions, although he came in order to obtain a better opportunity of advancing the Gospel and correcting the wicked persons’ vices, he did not cease to show himself an observer of the Law, doing what the Law commands, coming into the temple for worship and sacrifice [Col. 1495B].

> “He himself confirmed this in his own words when he met the Samaritan woman. Speaking in the person of all the Jews, he says: ‘We know what we worship; but you do not know what you worship, because salvation is from the Jews.’ Certainly he does not separate himself from them when he speaks of worship, which includes sacrifices as well; rather, he places himself in the common order with the rest. The reason he adds confirms this even more: namely, because salvation is from the Jews. By these words he means nothing other than that the worship offered to God at Jerusalem was pleasing to God himself solely because of the covenant he had made with that people. From this we see that one who shares in sacraments instituted by God with wicked persons is not polluted by association with them, provided that he himself is free from guilt and endowed with a pure conscience.

> “The apostles [Col. 1495C] followed their Master’s example. But, that we may not be more prolix than is fitting, let us be content with Paul alone. I pass over the fact that, wherever he went, he entered without any difficulty into the Jews’ synagogue to pray to God and discourse on Scripture. I also pass over the fact that he did not scruple to appear in the temple, worship God there, and use the lawful ceremonies together with the rest, although the priests and scribes who were there at the time were extremely wicked and corrupt. Not because these matters are irrelevant, but because we have no lack of a clearer kind of proof, less capable of evasion by calumnies. Paul complains that those who ought to have helped him, setting aside Christ’s honour and the Church’s advancement, pursued their own private advantage. Yet we do not read [Col. 1495D] that he separated himself from their assembly lest he be polluted.

> “Likewise, when he rebukes those dreadful vices under which the Corinthians and Galatians suffered, he does not forbid those who are pure and free from guilt to have any communion with the rest until all things have been thoroughly cleansed; but he only exhorts them to correct the vices which he rebukes, each in its proper place, without making any mention of such separation as these fanatics wish to introduce.

> “And what need is there to argue at such length? When the Apostle himself elsewhere treats of how each person should prepare to receive the Lord’s Supper worthily, he does not command each person to examine the faults of his neighbour. Instead he speaks thus: ‘Let a man examine himself, and so let him eat of that bread and drink of that cup. For whoever eats and drinks unworthily eats and drinks judgment to himself’ [Col. 1496A]. In these words two things must be observed. First, to eat the Lord’s bread unworthily is not to share with those who are unworthy, but not rightly to prepare oneself or consider one’s own faith and repentance. Second, when the Supper is to be received, we should not begin with others in order to examine them, but should test ourselves. And certainly, if all matters are carefully considered, those who have such leisure as to investigate others are more often negligent and forgetful in their own affairs.”

Thus far he.

I have thought fit to transcribe several preceding pages from the writings of that man, by whose mouth and confession I gladly hear that the Donatists too, and similar hypocrites and busybodies, are condemned, so that the mouths of certain ill-employed disciples of his may be all the more [Col. 1496B] effectively stopped—their stern criticism, that is, their mad excess, plainly needs to be noted and restrained.

Now to return to the Conference: its acts indicate that the Donatists also adduced something from Haggai the prophet, chapter II, concerning avoiding the contagion of evil people, although Augustine writes that they cited it only after the Conference. The question concerned these words: “Whoever approaches it shall be defiled,” etc., which are found in the Septuagint translation. But if the Catholics had observed that these words appear to have been added by those translators, or at least do not occur in the Hebrew text, they could easily have spared themselves much trouble in answering.

The Donatists were not so ingenious, acute, eloquent, or vehement in accusing the Church [Col. 1496C] from which they had separated as certain others. Indeed, they seem somehow to have passed over many things which they could plausibly have alleged for their schism. At least today new censors, otherwise almost their advocates and accusers of the Church, say that they can seem to have betrayed their case, pleaded a good cause badly, and been ignorant of their right: ignorant of the condition of the Church from which they had departed, ignorant of its blemishes and vices. They say that Aerius, Jovinian, Vigilantius, Faustus the Manichaean, and the like more carefully noted what they censured; and that because the Church condemned these critics, she should again be held guilty. But there is now no point in suggesting a new accusation to the Donatists, though it would also be easy to refute it. I might likewise exaggerate the utter corruption of the Carthaginian people and the dreadful, countless crimes which Salvian, bishop of Marseilles, described in book VIII of *On Providence* [Col. 1496D]. But even these did not suffice to excuse the Donatists’ schism.

Certainly, when Augustine admitted and lamented that many things were commonly done wrongly, the Donatists had his agreement in avoiding them. But what the Church rightly approved, he stoutly defended, refuting the adversaries’ slanders. And though many accusations were brought against her, he most steadfastly maintained that she was Christ’s Church, especially because she had good authors, had been promised and praised by the prophets as she appeared after Christ and was spread throughout the whole world; nor could the Donatists show any other Church to which those prophetic predictions could be referred. Therefore he concludes that the Donatists ought not to have separated from that Catholic Church [Col. 1497A]. And—what is remarkable—this is now also the conclusion of those who otherwise most fiercely accuse even the Church of that age and thus claim permission for themselves which they deny to the Donatists.

Moreover, what the Donatists said to prove that their faction was the true Church of Christ is too stale to require lengthy refutation. Yet let us hear it. At the Conference they boasted that they were bishops and defenders of the sincere Church, which, as they said, suffers persecution and does not inflict it. For they professed that the cross and patience are certain marks of the Church. But Augustine maintains that they inflict persecution rather than suffer it; or, if they sometimes suffer anything, that they suffer justly for what they do unjustly. Indeed, in his Epistle L he proves that it does not follow that the true Church is that which suffers persecution rather than that which inflicts it; and he refutes the Donatists, who do not inquire into the reasons why anyone inflicts persecution or suffers it, but think that the mark of a true Christian is suffering persecution rather than inflicting it [Col. 1497B].

Since the prefect Macarius had once been sent by the emperor to restrain Donatist insolence, the Donatist Parmenianus, reproaching the Catholics, had enviously cried out against what he called “Macarian violence”: “It cannot be called a Church which feeds upon bloody bites and grows fat on the blood of saints.” But Optatus, in book II, had turned this back upon his adversary in a just counteraccusation: “And I shall show,” he says, “that your party fed upon bloody bites and grew fat upon the blood of Christians,” etc. Later, however, the Donatist Petilianus repeated the complaint or reproach of his Parmenianus much more offensively and verbosely. But Augustine shows that these are futile slanders and empty insults; indeed, he proves that the Donatists shamelessly charge others with what they themselves did [Col. 1497C].

The Donatists boasted of their martyrs, and Parmenianus had formerly thrown them invidiously in our faces. But Augustine had gravely refuted that boast in book I against Parmenianus, chapter 7. Nevertheless Petilianus sings the same tune. Augustine therefore repeats the same answer, showing that martyrs are made not by their punishment but by their cause. Yet he denies that the Donatists were killed. Indeed, he proves that they cast themselves down in madness and voluntarily inflict death upon themselves. Let his fiftieth Epistle to Boniface be read [Col. 1497D], and let Cyprian, Christ’s martyr, be added. Long before the Donatists’ time, Cyprian had also said that a martyr cannot exist outside the Church, nor be crowned in death. And many centuries after Augustine, Bernard himself showed that even the devil has his martyrs; elegantly observing that it is no wonder if one who can impel persons to kill themselves can persuade them to allow themselves to be killed by others. Eusebius too, book V, chapter 6, writes that the Montanists had long ago also boasted of their martyrs, and fled to this glory as to a sacred anchor in order to recommend and celebrate their sect. But the matter itself shows this to have been foolish *kenodoxia*—vain glory.

[Col. 1498A] Further, because the Donatists heard that the Catholic Church had been adorned not only with holy martyrdoms but also with illustrious miracles, they also boasted of certain supposed miracles of their party, as though they were certain signs and testimonies of the Church. But Augustine shrewdly turns these against them, so that they should rather be regarded as signs of Antichrist or false prophets.

365 What did the Donatists not dare? What did they not attempt, in order to prove that the Church was theirs? They even boasted that a heavenly angel had appeared and confirmed their case. But Augustine, in Epistle CLXV, rises to a higher ground and dares to pronounce anathema even upon that angel, if there had been one, relying on the prophecies promising the Catholic Church. “To one holding these promises,” he says, “if an angel from heaven were to tell you, ‘Abandon the Christianity of the world and hold to the party of Donatus,’ he ought to be anathema” [Col. 1498B]. At length the Donatists went so far as to say that God himself had answered Donatus from heaven—almost as though, of their founder, they said that the divine voice had been heard: “Hear him.” But Augustine now brings against them the same answer they heard when they boasted of miracles: “They are either deceived,” he says, “or they deceive. Against these, if I may so speak, miracle-mongers, my God has warned me, saying: ‘In the last times false prophets shall arise, working signs and wonders so as to lead even the elect, if possible, into error. Behold, I have told you beforehand.’ Therefore the Bridegroom has made us cautious, because we must not be deceived even by miracles.”

I return to the acts of the Conference, to hear at last what Marcellinus pronounced concerning the Donatists [Col. 1498C]. Otherwise nothing would have been accomplished. Augustine, in the *Breviculus*, says that Marcellinus pronounced that the Donatists had been refuted by the Catholics through the manifest evidence of every document. The complete judgment, which is longer and takes the form of an edict, is contained in the acts of which I speak. Most memorable in it, above all, is the command that the public guarantee given to the summoned Donatists—commonly called a safe-conduct—be observed, so that they might freely and safely return home. But meanwhile he could not postpone any longer the execution of the laws enacted against them; and he therefore commanded that their assemblies be dissolved and that the basilicas which they had occupied be restored to the Catholics.

Possidius, who was also present, says that the Donatists were branded by the judgment [Col. 1498D] of the examiner and, after their appeal, were rightly condemned among heretics by the reply of the most pious emperor. Marcellinus’s judgment, that is, was followed by an imperial law. For the constitution of Honorius against the Donatists found in the Theodosian Code, book XVI, *On Heretics*, issued at Ravenna in the consulship of Constantius and Constans, was promulgated only two years after the Carthaginian Conference. And in this way Christian emperors of old customarily confirmed the decrees of councils.

Honorius the Emperor declares at the outset that he had hitherto spared the Donatists, whom, he says, “the patience of our clemency has preserved.” This would not be sufficiently understood unless we remembered how patiently and kindly they had shortly before been heard at the Conference. [Col. 1499A] Yet what Honorius orders—that they be incapable of making wills and, as he puts it, have no power “of entering into anything whatsoever”—is not wholly new. Certainly there had also been a Theodosian law by which they were deprived of the power either to make wills, or to confer anything upon anyone by gifts, or to receive anything under gifts or wills, as Augustine himself recounts at the end of book I *Against Parmenianus*.

But this also concerns civil law; and therefore I cannot pass over what Augustine relates in the same place: when a certain nobleman had petitioned the emperors because his sister, who belonged to the party of Donatus, had, when dying, bestowed very considerable property upon certain members of her communion, it was ordered that everything be restored to the brother. Thus the Papian law concerning escheats did not apply here—the law under which the treasury received what had been left to someone incapable of receiving it. Yet even if that brother had been passed over or disinherited, he could under the common law have annulled his sister’s will, in which disgraceful and infamous persons, such as the Donatists were, had been instituted as heirs. But since this is not the place to discuss civil law, I pass over what might be said on this subject at greater length.

I nevertheless warn the reader to compare the perversion which Huneric the Vandal afterwards produced in Africa from this law, as Victor of Utica narrates in book III. Moreover, from book XVI of the Theodosian Code, title V, chapter 5, we learn [Col. 1499B] something wholly relevant here: Marcellinus died not long after the Conference, and therefore the question was raised whether the acts of the Conference were invalidated by his death. About two months after the preceding law, however, Emperor Honorius again confirmed them by this edict. For he writes thus to Julian, proconsul of Africa:

> The proceedings conducted against the Donatists by the judicial cognizance and diligence of Marcellinus, a man of distinguished memory, we wish, having been transferred to the public records, to retain perpetual validity. For public faith ought not to perish with the death of the examiner.

Given at Rome, the third day before the Kalends of September, in the consulship of Constantius and Constans.

But in order to understand the purport [Col. 1499C] of this law or rescript, the history of the Conference which I have set forth was necessary. And, to gather together fragments which, scattered and separated, are not understood: I shall now add what Orosius writes and what belongs to this place. In book VII, chapter 42, he says:

> [Col. 1499D] In these days, by the command of Honorius, peace and unity were restored throughout all Africa to the Catholic Church, and the body of Christ—which we are—was healed after its division had been made whole, when the execution of the holy command was entrusted to Marcellinus, tribune, a man especially prudent and industrious and most eager for every good pursuit. Marinus, the count at Carthage, killed him, whether, it is uncertain, stirred by zeal or corrupted by gold; he was immediately recalled from Africa, reduced to private status, and left to his conscience, whether for punishment or repentance.

Thus Orosius. These things indicate what the fruit or outcome of the Conference with the Donatists was, and what followed upon it; so that those who ask whether it achieved anything may be answered. First, indeed, I answer concerning the Donatists what Jerome said of the Luciferians, who were nearly allied with them: they could be conquered, but not persuaded.

[Col. 1500A] Nevertheless Augustine himself testifies, in *On the Proceedings with Emeritus*, that many who were capable of healing came to their senses. Speaking there of this Conference, he says: “In the name of Christ we have received the Donatists in great part into the bosom of the Catholic Church, so that we rejoice that almost all have been joined to Catholic communion.” The same Augustine, in Letter L to Boniface, says: “Especially after the Conference which took place between us and their bishops at Carthage, they were corrected in great part.” This Conference therefore accomplished what even the greatest and otherwise best councils could scarcely ever accomplish.

But I wish that it had also accomplished what Augustine desired: that the bad Catholics, whose corruption provoked the Donatists, might have been corrected and reformed by their disturbances. But how much [Col. 1500B] worse they instead became, Salvian of Marseilles is a good witness in his book *On Providence and Judgment*, where he describes the incredible madness and abandoned wickedness of the Carthaginians. Thus not long after the Conference enemies far more savage than the Donatists poured into Africa and gave a terrible example of divine vengeance against desperate depravity: they destroyed more than forty churches and finally overthrew Carthage itself. Augustine, dying amid such calamity, lamented it in such a way that, groaning, he nevertheless acknowledged in it the just judgment of God, as Possidius relates.

Meanwhile, the Donatists who were capable of healing should be congratulated that no scandal prevented them from returning to the Church which they had recognized at the Conference. Possidius, who, as I said, attended the Conference, [Col. 1500C] testifies that it was chiefly through this Conference that God gave Augustine the victory, that day by day the unity of peace and fraternity of the Church was advanced, that many Donatist bishops returned to Catholic peace, and that they suffered every kind of thing from the Donatists on that account.

Yet Possidius adds that there were not lacking people who maliciously alleged that the Donatists had not been allowed, before the authority which heard the case, to say everything on behalf of their side, because the examiner, belonging to Catholic communion, favored his own Church. Possidius shows that this evasion was empty. [Col. 1500D] Others pretended that Marcellinus had been corrupted by money. But they said this with the same impudence with which, long ago, when they had appealed to Constantine and he acquitted Caecilian and condemned Donatus, they cavilled that the emperor had been corrupted.

And, that we may understand that there was nothing they did not seize upon for slander, they even complained that Marcellinus had judged by night. They themselves had already consumed the day in cavilling during the Conference, so that they might escape in darkness. The judge, wishing by his patience to cut off from them every future occasion for a just complaint, added a water-clock and allowed them to say whatever they wished rather than interrupt the proceedings. Yet at last he delivered judgment, once they had spoken and had admitted that they had spoken; nor, because he had judged late, did he allow the adjudicated matter to be evaded.

Gellius writes in book XIV that a senatorial decree [Col. 1501A] made neither before sunrise nor after sunset was valid. Indeed, when judicial proceedings were involved, the Twelve Tables prescribed: “Sunset shall be the final limit of time.” But not all decrees were governed by the same rule, nor was that law always observed. For the Romans also often imitated the Areopagites, who judged only at night. And our Justinian himself, in Novel 82, orders his inferior judges to sit on the tribunal from earliest dawn until evening twilight, or, as he says, *eis deilēn opsian*—“until late evening”; and nothing prevents a judge, if the case requires it, from sitting still longer. Finally, the law says that there is no doubt that wills and contracts may be made at night: book XXII, final section, *On Wills*; law *Non minorem*, Code *On Settlements*. Our Augustine himself, [Col. 1501B] replying to the Donatists, cries out: “Who could endure defeated men complaining that judgment was pronounced against them at night, as though the necessity of hearing cases did not often compel judges to sit until a great part of the night? Is what is said untrue because it is said during the night?” etc.

Emeritus the Donatist had attended the Conference. But he did not candidly admit that he had been defeated there, and he spread I know not what clouds of slander in his Caesarean Mauretania. When Augustine had therefore gone there, he did not refuse, as it were, to retry the case and again to expound and defend the proceedings of the Conference. He says that he did this in the twelfth consulship of Honorius and eighth of Theodosius. It thus appears that this happened seven years after the Conference, and indeed in the very year in which the case of the Pelagians was being heard at the Council of Carthage, after it had been judged at Milevis in the preceding year.

Augustine, in book II of the *Retractions*, [Col. 1501C] simply says that, some time after the Conference, when a necessity had arisen for going into Caesarean Mauretania, he dealt with Emeritus; otherwise he does not state the reason for that journey. Likewise in Letter CCVII: “The ecclesiastical necessity laid upon us by Zosimus, bishop of the Apostolic See, led us there.” Possidius, who attended that Caesarean proceeding no less than the Carthaginian Conference, merely says that letters from the Apostolic See compelled Augustine and other bishops to go into Mauretania in order to settle other necessities of the Church. There they encountered Emeritus, the Donatist bishop of that place, and again conferred with him, so that he might freely say whatever he wished on behalf of his own side, because some kept alleging that he had been forbidden at the Conference to say everything. Augustine himself wrote what was done there, so that the proceedings of that Caesarean discussion might be joined to the Acts of the Carthaginian Conference.

[Col. 1501D] It is ridiculous that the recent compilers of the *Centuries of Ecclesiastical History* observed that the emperors Honorius and Theodosius attended that Caesarean repetition, because Augustine says it was held under their consulship.

It remains to observe that at the same time that most distinguished Council of Carthage convened against the Pelagians; yet fewer Catholic bishops attended it than had attended the Conference. For 286 are counted in the latter, but 207 in the former.

[Col. 1502A] Prosper, in his Chronicle, says that Pelagius published his doctrine in the year of Christ 415, that is, immediately after the Donatists had been suppressed at the Conference. In the year 420, however, after a council of 217 bishops had been held at Carthage, synodal decrees were sent to Pope Zosimus; once these had been approved, the Pelagian heresy was condemned throughout the world. But Prosper does not sufficiently explain the whole matter. From Augustine’s writings, however, one may recover what must especially be observed here.

Because of Pelagius, in the time of Pope Innocent, whom Zosimus succeeded, two great councils appear to have met at the same time: the Carthaginian and the Milevitan. Augustine calls the former the council of Carthage and Africa, the latter the council of Numidia, in Letters XLVII, XCII, XCIV, CVI, CX, and CLVII. I grant that, when the Pelagians wished their case to be judged [Col. 1502B] in a universal council of East and West, Augustine denied this to them and replied that heresies for the condemnation of which a gathering of a synod had been necessary were very rare. Yet when Augustine wrote this, in book IV *Against Two Letters of the Pelagians*, final chapter, he had already seen at least two provincial synods assembled to condemn the Pelagian heresy. For he writes this to Pope Boniface, and does not conceal that he wrote much later than those synods. Indeed, their prior judgment was the reason why the Pelagians were all the more denied what they further demanded maliciously.

I believe that they cavilled as a certain Arian, Palladius, is recorded [Col. 1502C] to have done in order to evade the Synod of Aquileia: he said that he rejected the synod because it was not universal. But Augustine could reply to the Pelagians as Ambrose, who presided over that council, replied to Palladius—although Ambrose had this further advantage, that the Arian heresy had been condemned at the Council of Nicaea. Moreover, it is noteworthy that Augustine further indicates that the Pelagians requested a Conference like that which had been held with the Donatists. But the Catholics rightly rejected it, lest they should retry a matter already concluded.

Yet, even if we say that Augustine attended the Council of Milevis rather than that of Carthage, since the Milevitan Council ended sooner and the Carthaginian lasted longer, we do not deny that he may eventually have attended the latter as well. It is nevertheless foolish for the writers of the *Centuries* to note that Augustine presided over it and wrote to Innocent on its behalf. They ought rather to have named Aurelius, just as he is named first in that council’s letter to Innocent, in which Augustine is not named; although the letter is included among Augustine’s letters as no. 90, and Innocent’s reply is appended as no. 91. [Col. 1502D]

Moreover, both from the Council of Milevis and later from the city of Carthage, Augustine with his colleagues wrote to the same Innocent on the same matter, in Letters XCII and XCV; Innocent’s replies to both survive as Letters XCIII and XCVI. Augustine, in book I *Against Julian*, chapter 2, simply says that Innocent answered the African councils in accordance with what the Apostolic See and Roman Church had held from antiquity together with the others.

[Col. 1503A] Furthermore, since the fathers of the Council of Carthage say in their letter to Innocent that the case of Caelestius had been debated in the Church of Carthage almost five years before, it is apparent not only that the Pelagian heresy had been published earlier than Prosper notes, but also that it was condemned there at the time when the case of the Donatists was being debated in the same place, although Augustine, then occupied in refuting the Donatists, had not yet taken up the Pelagians. Certainly, in book II of the *Retractions*, chapter 33, indicating that Caelestius, Pelagius’s disciple, was condemned there before his master, Augustine says: “Caelestius, his disciple, had already deserved excommunication on account of such disputes at Carthage in an episcopal judgment at which I was not present.”

[Col. 1503B] The fathers of the Milevitan Council—among whom Sylvanus is counted first and Augustine eighth—say in their letter to Innocent that they write to him from the council of Numidia concerning the Acts against Pelagius, imitating their fellow bishops of the Church and province of Carthage. Thus the decree of that Carthaginian Council against the Pelagian heresy had already been issued.

The reply of Pope Innocent to the Milevitan fathers is said to have been given on the sixth day before the Kalends of February, in the consulship of Honorius and Constantius. I think it should be read, “in the consulship of Constans and Constantius,” just as these consuls are joined in the manuscript. Constantius was indeed consul for the second time with Emperor Honorius, but Innocent had then died, as is evident from Prosper’s Chronicle. Prosper also indicates that Constans and Constantius were consuls in 416. Thus, if Innocent replied to the Milevitan fathers in that year, the Carthaginian Council against the Pelagians must have begun immediately after the Conference against the Donatists.

Furthermore Augustine, in Letter XLVII, speaking of the condemnation [Col. 1503C] of the Pelagian heresy, says that not only had letters been sent to Pope Innocent from the council of the province of Carthage and from Numidia, but also a somewhat more detailed letter from five bishops. These were Aurelius, Alypius, Augustine, Evodius, and Possidius, who, excepting Evodius, had also been selected for the encounter with the Donatists at the Conference. It is noteworthy that Augustine says in Letter CX that, by the two councils of Numidia and Carthage, the bishops had entrusted him with responsibility for the writings. From this one may infer how highly this bishop was then esteemed; [Col. 1503D] and yet he exceeded expectation.

But I say only this: Aurelius brought together the judgment of the Carthaginian Council, over which he had presided, and Augustine’s judgment from the Milevitan Council, which he had attended; together with three others, they again handled the same case and wrote more carefully to Innocent from the city of Carthage. This is Letter XCV, whose beginning is: “We have sent to Your Holiness letters, subscribed by no small number of bishops, from the two councils of the province of Carthage and Numidia.” That is, Aurelius had sent those from Carthage, Augustine those from the Milevitan synod.

After Innocent had died, more bishops appear to have assembled again at Carthage, [Col. 1504A] having previously gone their own ways, in order to discuss the same case. As Augustine calls the earlier Council of Carthage the council of the province of Carthage, so he calls this second council, which he says wrote to Zosimus, Innocent’s successor, the African Council, in Letter XLVII. Someone might reasonably say that it was a continuation, as he calls it, of the same council, with more persons coming together from Africa and with those who had formerly attended Milevis meeting those who had attended Carthage. Augustine likewise indicates in Letter XLVII that a later plenary council of all Africa met again for the same reason.
