The condition was not unlike that of the Council of Constantinople, which they call the Second Ecumenical Council, where the fathers were now dismissed, now recalled.

[Col. 1504B] But since historians narrate these matters confusedly and distinguish nothing, they ignorantly mix together many things that ought to be distinguished, and often deceive the credulous reader.

Prosper notes that the Council of Carthage wrote to Zosimus in the twelfth consulship of Honorius and eighth of Theodosius, in the year of Christ 420. The Acts indicate that, under those consuls, the Council pronounced against the Pelagian heresy and that Augustine attended. Augustine himself, however, relates that under the same consuls, on the twelfth day before the Kalends of October, he met the Donatist Emeritus at Caesarea in Mauretania and defended the judgment of the Carthaginian Conference with the Donatists. Thus this excellent bishop did and accomplished everything, concerned for the Church’s safety.

[Col. 1504C] Furthermore Augustine says, in Letter XLVII, that the African Council wrote to Zosimus and that Zosimus replied to all the bishops of the entire world. But neither that letter nor its reply survives. Augustine adds: “And what we briefly established against Pelagius’s error in the later plenary council of all Africa.” Yet I have nothing further to say about that plenary council, in which he indicates that he took a more active part, except that the Acts of the Council of Carthage now circulated, as they do not mention Pelagius, so indicate that another case was dealt with at the end: the case of the presbyter Apiarius, of which Augustine makes no mention. They further indicate that, in that case, the question of the right of appeal was disputed against the legates of Zosimus, that letters were written about it to Boniface, Zosimus’s successor, and finally to Celestine, [Col. 1504D] Boniface’s successor. If so, this council must have continued for many years. But I fear that many things are asserted concerning this matter both confusedly and falsely.

I do not deny that some question of this kind was debated. But it ought to be recounted faithfully and simply, not contaminated with insulting additions. Good Beza orders us to judge the matter from the Greek rather than the Latin text. But does he suppose that the African Acts were first written in Greek rather than Latin? The African fathers rightly thought that the Nicene canons should be judged from the Greek archetypes and authentic books. But by the same reasoning I shall say that the African canons should be judged from Latin archetypes.

[Col. 1505A] No less foolish is what Beza says in the same confession: he calls this Council of Carthage—at which, he angrily relates, that question of forgery was decided—the third; shortly afterwards, forgetting himself, he calls it the sixth; and, after rashly accusing Boniface in place of Zosimus, he exclaims that it was decreed at this Council of Carthage that whoever appealed to Rome should be excluded, or, as he says, deposed. But whence did he draw this decree? For not even the Acts which he cites mention it. Clearly, from his master, who with the same rashness in this matter invents that Zosimus and his successors wished what he says had been decreed at the Council of Milevis to be repealed at Carthage.

Yet the ancients do not report [Col. 1505B] that anything was decreed at Milevis against the will of the Roman bishop. Indeed, Innocent strongly praises the Acts of that council against the Pelagians which were sent to him. And shortly afterwards, Augustine, in Letter XCV, writing to him at the instruction of his colleagues about the Pelagian heresy already condemned in two councils, Carthaginian and Milevitan, nevertheless asks that Pelagius, having been summoned, be brought to the city of Rome: “He must be summoned to Rome by Your Reverence,” he says, “and carefully examined.”

But what would Beza have hesitated to assert, when in the same little book he also taught that the Council of Milevis was held twelve hundred years ago—that is, before Augustine’s time? And from his teacher’s lectures he repeats that the Council of Aquileia, over which Ambrose presided, was universal. What could be said more shamelessly?

[Col. 1505C] Finally, I shall say this concerning the Council of Carthage or Africa: something is found in its canons that pertains to the Donatists. Whatever it may be, however, being defective, mutilated, and confused, it depends upon the prior judgment of the Carthaginian Conference.

Now I should like the Carthaginian Conference of Catholics with Donatists to be compared with the other Conference, that of Arians with Catholics, held about seventy years later. It was called by Huneric the Vandal, a tyrant no less cruel than he was a frenzied Arian, as Victor of Utica describes him in books II and III. This comparison will also make clear the distinction useful to observe here.

First, the edict of Huneric summoning the Catholics, whom he calls “Homousians,” was composed with a speciousness [Col. 1505D] no less polished than the edict by which Emperor Honorius or Marcellinus had summoned the Donatists. Eugene, bishop of Carthage, hearing Huneric’s commands, replied [Col. 1506A] in his own name and that of the Catholics in Africa that they in no way refused or avoided the Conference commanded by Huneric, but requested that Catholics from overseas also be summoned, since without them they could not conduct a common cause, especially one so great and important. He advanced this pretext in order that, when the overseas Catholics were present—against whom Huneric would not dare rage, lest he offend their emperor—the discussion might be freer.

Victor himself admits that otherwise there was no wrong in provincial assemblies meeting to debate. Eugene and his companions did indeed come on the appointed day to confer with the Arians, as Huneric had commanded. But although the tyrant had promised the Catholics complete safety in his edict, he immediately broke his pledge and laid hands upon those who had come; he raged against the most learned and even put them to death. Such was the beginning of that Conference.

[Col. 1506B] Those who survived nevertheless did not disperse. Indeed, in order that the discussion might proceed without tumult, they selected some from their own order to speak for all, just as had been done in the other Carthaginian Conference. But while the Arians ought to have prepared for the discussion on equal terms, they wanted some patriarch of theirs, Cyril, to be judge; they seated him on a high platform, armed with a great body of attendants. The Catholics complained of such a form of utterly unfair judgment, but in vain. Indeed, they were accused of calling themselves Catholics and were nearly overwhelmed by the loud cries of their opponents.

[Col. 1506C] Then our party generously granted them, of its own accord, that the name “Catholic” should, as it were, be suspended until the question had been settled. In order to come to the matter, they produced a written confession of their faith, which they undertook to defend. What did the Arians do? When they ought in turn to have produced their own confession, they merely shouted that our people were seditious and inflamed their Huneric. He immediately issued against our people the very decree which Christian emperors had issued against the Donatists. Such was the catastrophe of that Conference.

But let the entire history be read in Victor of Utica, and from it let one learn what the condition of the Church of Carthage then was. There is no mention then of the Donatists. For they seem in Africa to have yielded to the Arians. Yet they had not otherwise ceased to exist, for it is apparent from Pope Gregory’s letters that many were still found in various places in his time. At last the African Church was free, when the Vandals had been expelled and it had been restored to its liberty and to Roman rule; and although the times were very barbarous and dark, it did not [Col. 1506D] cease to convene pious synods for the preservation of religion, as is evident from the Carthaginian councils against the Monothelites.

## ANALYTICAL INDEX OF THE WORKS OF SAINT ZENO

An Arabic numeral denotes the pages of the sermons printed in bold type in our edition; a Roman numeral denotes the *Prolegomena*; while the letters *adn.* followed by an Arabic numeral indicate the number of notes.

[Note: [Col. 1511] In this index, Arabic numbers refer to column numbers printed in the text in bold type between Migne’s columns 253 and 760. The letters “adn.” followed by Arabic numbers refer to the numbers of the notes.]

## A

**Abel:** a martyr because he was righteous; righteous because patient; martyrs learned from him how to suffer, 67.

**Abraham:** pleased God by faith without the Law, 5. By believing God, he earned God, 11, 104. He did not learn righteousness but begot it, 183 and notes 1, 2. Righteous because faithful, 20. He was bound by no right of the Law, yet observed above all every divine law, 177. He is praised, 67. He bore in himself the type of the two peoples: by the mark of circumcision he expressed the Jew, and by the righteousness of faith the Christian, 102. In old age he received his son Isaac as the gift of faith and belief, 174, 178. His steadfastness in the immolation of his son is described and commended, 175 ff., 181, 185.

**Abortion:** procured for the sake of avarice, 79.

**Foreskin (*acrobustia*):** 102 and note 14.

**Adam:** by sinning he left to his descendants the inheritance of death, 65, 102. Through Adam’s sin, the whole human race, ruined by hereditary condition, was perishing without exception, 93. The opinion of some concerning Adam’s sin—what kind it was—CIV, 102. *Adaeque*, 12, note 15, 119, 208.

**Worldly administration:** 128 and note 14.

**Adserit** in the sense of “defends by arguments,” 18, note 59.

**Adulter** in the sense of “adulterous,” 13, note 42, 259.

**Adulteries:** punished by capital penalties under Roman laws, 47, note 33.

**Egyptian days:** what they were, 122, note 19; why so called, same place. They were regarded as unlucky, and pagans thought that no work should be begun on those days, same place.

**Coeval (*aequaevus*):** 262.

**Air:** its bodily emptiness, 206, note 5. Spirits of the air, 206; whom the author calls by this name, same place, note 7.

**Aestivalia:** used for women’s summer dress, 193 and note 8. Summer dress was clean and untouched, 196.

**Agapes:** that is, banquets formerly held on martyrs’ feast days, 121, note 18. Having turned into lust and drunkenness, they are censured [Col. 1512] and abolished, same place. Saint Zeno excelled in abolishing this custom, same place, CXXVII.

**Aggressura (“an onset”):** 129 and note 19; 189, 199.

**Agina:** a part of a balance, 267, note 9.

**The legal lamb:** a type of Christ, 282, 283, 291. Why some believed that the Jews had to take a lamb of twofold nature, 289, note 4, 291.

**Prayers are accepted when presented, even before they are poured forth:** 52 and note 54.

**Love:** see *Charity*.

**Impure love, or desire:** its description, effects, and diversity, 27.

**The angels ascending and descending upon Jacob’s ladder:** what they signify, 190.

**Soul:** a perceptive and intelligent image of God, 93. How this is to be understood, 93, note 12. The spirit of God from its own source, 93 and note 13. It is encompassed by the features of the body, 94. Principally, it is not contained in any place, but is found in a place only through its union with the body, 372. It compels the body subject to it to fulfil, through servile offices, the desires of its ruling power, 103. It is brutish if it cares for the flesh, 103. The life of the soul is acquired through baptism, 95. The soul’s immortality is demonstrated, 127 ff. No one dares deny it, 127. Plato wrote excellently about it, 126 and notes 4–5. Philosophers spoke variously about the soul, but almost all nevertheless acknowledged it to be immortal, 127 and note 11. Epicurus, Dicaearchus, and Democritus argued against the soul’s immortality, same place and note 12. The twofold path asserted by poets confirms the soul’s immortality, same place, note 13. By libations at the tombs of the dead, the gentiles signified belief in the soul’s immortality, 127 and note 9. The author held that the souls of the righteous are daily received into heaven before the day of final judgment, CXIX.

**Calculation of years from Christ’s birth:** proved by many examples formerly to have exceeded the true reckoning by about fifty years, XLIV, XLV.

**The anonymous author of the Life of Saint Zeno and of his Translation:** in what century he wrote, CLVII; assessment of that Life, CXXVI, [Col. 1513] CLVII. The history of the Translation is published as supplemented from manuscripts, CLVII.

**The anonymous Pipinian writer on the praises of Verona:** LXVII. He described Saint Zeno’s deeds much better and more briefly than Coronatus, CXXVIII; supplemented from manuscripts, CXXVIII; restored and more fully supplemented from the manuscript of Lobbes, CXCVIII.

**Antipodes, or Antichthones:** 206, note 6.

**Apophoreta:** gifts distributed at banquets, 252.

**The apostles called heavens:** 225.

**Arbiter:** in the sense of judge or observer, 40 and note 6.

**Chest (*arca*):** the Eucharist was formerly kept in a wooden chest, 113, note 18.

**The discipline of secrecy:** violated by the Arians, 14, note 44.

**Saint Arcadius:** suffered at Caesarea in Mauretania, 211 and note 1; not under Gallienus, same place. His *Acts* were composed from Saint Zeno’s tract, same place. During a raging persecution he hid himself, 214. Soon afterward he voluntarily presented himself to the judge, 213. He was tortured by an exceedingly cruel punishment, 215. He is praised, same place and 216.

**Arcarius (“treasurer”):** 252, note 12.

**Errors of the Arians:** XLVII ff. They did not believe the Son of God to be true God, 117 and note 2. They did indeed call the Son of God “God,” but denied that he was begotten from the perpetuity of the Father’s nobility; they said that there was a time when he was not, 163, note 5. They blasphemed that the Son did not exist before he was born, 149, note 8. By crafty disputation, they despised the foundations of the Law and hastened to reduce the Father and the Son to common names of human nature, which could be grasped by arguments, 141 and note 4. They are called men of a carnal mind, 141; they are refuted, XLVII ff., 142, 143 ff. They issued various and manifold formulas of faith, XCVIII ff. Catholics detested them, same place, 8, 9 ff. Why their formulas of faith were offered for sale, 9, note 32. Sustained by the favor and effort of novel controversy, 9. Ever changing, 9, note 33. Arians abused philosophy, 70, notes 2–3, 304. Their disputations were crafty, 304, note 4. Those arguing about faith by reasonings are reproved in an entire tract, 1. They corrupted many with gold and rewards, 9. Arian faith required the patronage of kings, 12, note 38; of judges and the rich, same place, note 39; and sometimes even of pagans, 13, note 40. Shameful and slippery, 13, note 41. It prevailed through factions, 13. Adulterous, same place, note 42. Publican, 14, note 44.

**With pallid fat (*arvina pallenti*):** 212, note 12.

**Astutus** in the sense of “learned,” 6.

**A passage of Athenagoras on the eternal generation of the Son of God:** defended against Petavius’s criticism, XCII.

**Avarice:** the enemy of justice, 36. Whoever labors to have more than he had plays the part of avarice, 37. It is present in all, and is accused by all as though it were not present, 37; because it is common, it has ceased to be a crime, 79. It is natural to avarice to make a person more avaricious, 85. Its effects and the sins arising from it, 37, 79 ff., 85 ff., 90. A miser is one who seeks what he does not have and thinks that he does not have what he does have, 82. A miser is one who monopolizes the market in every commodity, 83. He grieves at sterility and at fertility, same place. A miser is not unlike a tyrant who alone possesses what can benefit the interests of very many people, 38. He watches for the time to sell, 83. He denies possessing what he intends to sell, so that he may slaughter, same place. The harshness of misers toward the poor is sharply censured, 36, 37. Misers are rebuked, 78 ff. Misers used to commit gold or silver to the earth to be hidden, 86.

**Auctor is of the feminine gender:** 65.

**Auguries:** how they were performed, 122, 210; how foreign they are to a Christian, 122.

## B

**Baiae:** 95. What was customarily called by this name, same place, note 25.

**The girded bath-attendant:** supplied what was necessary for anointing and for drying, 247.

**Baptism:** baptism of the Holy Spirit is not a seal, as circumcision once was, but a sign, 107 and note 37; its effects, 245 ff., 292. It procures life for the soul, 93. It cuts away vices of the soul and original sin, 107–108 and note 38. It washes away absolutely all sins, 233, 255, 277, 292; leads shipwrecked persons to the sweetness of life, 112, 292. One reborn through baptism ceases to be what he was and begins to be what he was not, 197; he becomes a son of the Church, 195. Baptism receives the dead and immediately makes them living, inspired by heavenly water, 233. From infancy’s very cradle to the final end of every age, it imparts its saving gift, 118. It cannot be repeated, 249, note 3. The crossing of the Red Sea was a type of baptism, 281, note 5. Promises were made in baptism, 234 and note 16. At the administration of baptism a solemn hymn was sung, 243. The water used in it was warmed at Eastertime, 246, note 3. Ever-new water flowed into the font, same place. Baptism by immersion was customary, 245, 248. Among the ceremonies of baptism in Zeno’s time, a denarius was handed over, 114 and note 21; 247 and note 5; there was a double anointing in baptism, 247, note 4; and washing of feet before or after baptism, same place. See *Catechumens*, *Neophytes*.

**Many baptisms among the Jews:** 295, note 3.

**Baptistery:** a place generally separate from the church, 241, note 1.

**Those baptized:** boys, adolescents, young men, and old people of both sexes, 262. Persons differing in origin, age, sex, and condition were baptized into one, 244, 259; and also differing in nation, 250. They differ by diverse charisms, 280, note 4. Why all baptized persons are called infants, 250, note 5.

**Gaspar Barthius:** elucidated with notes Saint Zeno’s tract on the Resurrection, 125, note 1; and another on Saint Arcadius, 211, note 1. His emendations of three tracts of Saint Zeno on Christ’s Nativity were published by Daumius, 163, note 1.

**Heavenly blessedness:** described, 84.

**Churches dedicated to Saint Zeno in the territory of Bergamo:** CL.

**Twofold nature:** 282.

**Twelvefold (*bissenus*):** 278.

**The twofold path of poets in the underworld:** indicated the soul’s immortality, 127 and note 13.

**The goods of the spirit:** set on heights, so that no one can reach them except with the greatest difficulty, 96.

**Breviatum (“an abridgment”):** 28 and note 55.

**Churches dedicated to Saint Zeno in the diocese and city of Brescia:** CXLIX.

**Foul-smelling cattle (*bromosis pecudibus*):** 119 and note 10.

**A foul-smelling banquet (*bromosum convivium*):** 290, note 6.

**Of a brutish heart (*bruti cordis*):** 294, note 2.

**Bull’s interpretation of certain testimonies of Saint Zeno:** proposed and assessed, LXXX.

**Smoking limbs on a pyre:** 61 and note 31, 212.

## C

**Cacabaeus bread:** what it was, 266, note 6.

**Muddy liquid:** 287.

**Caesena:** ancient churches dedicated to Saint Zeno, CXLVI.

**Pen:** description, 187; pens were made from reeds, 191 and note 25.

**A scholarly calumny:** 71; a calumny of curiosity, 29.

**A calumnious question:** 92.

**Camelarius (“camel-driver”):** 252.

**“Swallowing a camel, straining out a gnat”:** 79.

**The altar enclosed by railings in Zeno’s time:** 241 and note 4.

**Candidates:** neophytes so called because of the white garments they put on, 242, 248.

**“Scripture sings”:** 16, note 49.

**Capitolia:** used for temples of idols, 109 and note 3.

**Captives:** redeemed, freed from death-dealing edicts, stripped of harsh conditions by the generosity of the people of Verona, 89. When this occurred, same place and LVII.

**Capulus:** one meaning is “the hilt of a sword,” 186.

**Sacred poem:** used for Holy Scripture, 141 and note 5.

**Prophetic poem:** 73 and note 15; 228 and note 2; 230.

**Poem:** used for a festal formula, 95 and note 26.

**Carnally:** 282.

**Carnatus (“made flesh”):** 159 and note 10.

**Flesh:** cannot rule the mind, 103. It is a certain mirror pregnant with the fullness of the beholder, 139; that is, it reflects the image of the mind, same place, note 69. Carnal spoil, 140. The soul’s pleasant poison, same place. It distributes its gifts everywhere, especially to the unworthy, 97. The sins of the flesh are described, 95; all are enticed by them, same place; why people are overcome by them, 96. The old flesh, meaning the old and sinful person, is killed by saving baptism, 138. A new person rises from the sacred flood of the font, same place.

**The *Carpsi* manuscript of the Church of Verona:** cited, CXXXII, CXXXIII, CLXI, CLXII, CLXV, 261, note 1; 273, note 1. In what century Stephen, priest and cantor, wrote that work, CXXXII.

**“He pitches camp in the temple of the predestined Virgin”:** meaning, the Son of God prepared for himself a dwelling in the Virgin’s womb, 169 and note 7.

**According to John (*kata Joannem*):** 161 and note 18; **according to Luke (*kata Lucam*):** 195.

**Cataclysm:** 67.

**Catechumens:** why so called, 277, note 6. They were examined in scrutinies, 253, note 3. At what time and how often the creed was delivered to catechumens before baptism, 240, note 1. Catechumens confessed sins before baptism, 253, note 4; 256, note 6; 258. Penance was imposed upon them, 254, note 5. See *Baptism*.

**Causa** in the sense of “principle,” 205, note 3.

**The varied meaning of *cavea*:** 78, note 18.

**The wealth of charity:** is to possess everything for mercy, 29.

**Most abundant wealth:** 90.

**Chaos:** some taught that it existed in the beginning—that is, an unformed and unordered mass of hidden nature, 144 and note 1. They are refuted, 145.

**Praises of charity:** 22 ff., 28 ff. Duties of charity, 24, 25. Charity, the substance of all divine virtues and their natural teacher, 24. Whence it comes, where it resides, and to whom it is especially owed, 28. How broadly the author takes the name charity, 22, note 21; CVIII. Its praises, 28, 29.

[Col. 1515]

**The two births of Christ:** the first spiritual, without a mother; the second carnal, without a father, 164, 169. By taking flesh Christ became what he was not, yet did not cease to be what he had been before, 168. With his majesty temporarily concealed, he pitches camp for himself in the temple of the predestined Virgin; into that dwelling he secretly enters, intending to be born as a man, 169. Why he is said to have entered the Virgin’s womb secretly, 169, note 8; 173, note 3; 237, note 2. The Son is born without a father, not wholly belonging to his mother, owing to himself that he was conceived, and granting to his mother that he was born, 173 and note 6. He deigned to put on flesh so that no one might excuse himself through the flesh, 172. He tastes death in order to conquer death, 158. He enters the underworld in order to bring back its dead alive, 159. He descends pure from heaven and ascends into heaven made flesh, 159. Accomplishing and completing every mystery, he opened the path to heaven for all who follow him, 192. Why he received circumcision, 106. Christ’s resurrection brought the hope of conquering death and admitted humanity to the rewards of immortality, 94. Christ signified by the pillar showing the Jews the way, 281. What Christ’s temporal kingdom is, 160; how it differs from the eternal kingdom, 161. The heretics who maintained that Christ took his beginning from the Virgin’s womb and that he thereafter became God by reason of righteousness, rather than having been born God, L, 163, note 3; 158, note 3. See *Son of God*.

**The number of Christians in Saint Zeno’s time:** CXXV, 5. Almost the whole world was Christian, XLVI, 55.

**Unconsecrated Christians:** who they were, 60 and note 28.

**Christians called the household of the Lord:** 212, 213. In churches they stretched out their hands, bent their necks, prostrated themselves, and made confession (*exomologesis*), 87, notes 15 and 17. Marriages of Christians with pagans are disapproved, 58 ff. The foundations of Christian perfection consist in hope, faith, and charity, 19. If a Christian lacks any of these, he will not possess the perfection of his work, same place. Christians must observe God’s will, 108. A Christian cannot be saved, even though righteous, unless he makes confession and extinguishes his present sins and repels future ones, 197. In baptism, renouncing the world after making a promise, he is spiritually bound by sacred questions, 234 and note 16. Christians intermediate between the pious and impious, who are uncertain, 222. They will be judged, 223. How this is to be understood, CXVII ff.

**Circular scar:** 99 and note 3.

**Circumcision:** definition, 99. Circumcision was called a seal, not a sign, 107 and note 37. It was not necessary for Abraham, but was instituted as a designation of the Jewish people, who were to be carnal, 101 and note 13. Why a second circumcision is said to be commanded in Joshua, 105 and note 30. The first, carnal circumcision is proved to have been abolished, 104 ff. Circumcision of the heart is required, 105. This is the spiritual circumcision of Christians, 106. What it is, 107 ff.

**The power of the Church’s keys in baptism:** 256.

**Coeternity:** 146, 162.

**Heaven:** in the sense of the celestial sphere, 205, note 4.

**The heavens called apostles:** 225.

**Pillar of matronhood:** 50.

**Combinata (“joined together”):** 191 and note 24.

**“Common to all who fear God”:** in what sense this is said, 37, note 25.

**Holy communion of the faithful:** 197.

**Comedies:** censured, 123, note 4.

**“A short cut to modesty”:** 51 and note 47.

**Competentes:** who they were, 277, note 6. They were examined by the prescribed number of examinations in the scrutinies before baptism, 233, note 14. See *Catechumens*.

**Counting on the fingers:** 83 and note 19.

**“May their endeavors succeed”:** 43, note 18.

**Conciliabulum:** a joining together of walls, 110, note 6.

**A corpse over which the death-cry has been raised (*conclamatum cadaver*):** what it was, 133, note 36.

**Concubines:** pagans thought it lawful to have them, 47, notes 33–34.

**Harsh conditions:** 89 and note 23; 162, note 23; 284.

**Confession of sins before baptism:** 253, note 4; 256 and note 6; 258.

**The sacrament of confirmation:** administered in the medieval Church of Verona on Easter Monday, 261, note 1.

**Fear of conscience for guilt:** worse than other fears, because it is not erased, 75.

**Consecrated:** in the sense of baptized, 60 and note 28.

**“Books of our constitution”:** meaning, our treatises on faith, 11.

**“To observe what is commanded”:** 65.

**Contumelia:** in the sense of loss, 64 and note 12.

**Assembly of the brethren:** what it was, 257, note 1.

**Coronatus, notary:** in what century he wrote the Life of Saint Zeno, LXX, CLV. The Life written by him, CLXIII. From what source it was drawn, CXXI, CXXVIII, CLV. It is subjected to examination, LXIX, CXXVIII, CXXXIX and note, from p. CLXIII to p. CLXVIII. The story which he relates—that the daughter of the emperor Gallienus was healed by Saint [Col. 1516] Zeno—is fabulous, LXX. Whence Coronatus derived this error, LXX.

**Body:** see *Flesh*.

**Corrigit** in the sense of “directs,” 76 and note 12.

**Credulitas** in the sense of faith, 5, note 6; p. 6; 11, 102, 104, 115, 175, 196 and note 4.

**Credulus (“believing”):** 208 and note 15.

**Chrismal oil (*cremiale oleum*):** 265, note 4.

**The devil, the accuser:** 93.

**Difficulties raised by critics concerning Saint Zeno’s sermons:** set forth, XXXIII; resolved, XXXVIII ff.

**The cross:** a projecting piece of wood in the form of the letter Tau, defending against hostile attack, 113, note 17. A Christian cannot at all live or attain immortality without the sign of the Lord’s cross, 233. The cross signified by Jacob’s ladder, 191.

**How much the antiquity and dissemination of a cult contribute to knowing the merits and fame of saints:** CXLIII.

**Description of desire:** 26.

***Cura mortis*:** in the sense of “a remedy for sin,” 102 and note 19.

**Curiosity in matters of faith:** censured, XCIX, 6, 15, 71, 153, 157 and note 17, 164, 205 and note 2, 217 and note 2. Curiosity makes one guilty, not knowledgeable, 153 and note 10.

**Why Cybele is called a lover:** 100, note 6. The priests of this goddess, called Galli, cut off their genitals in honor of their goddess, 99 and note 4.

## D
### D

Loss of hair, 133. Daniel. In Daniel, the hymn of the three youths is described and praised, 300, 301. The same three youths are a figure of the Trinity, 297, 299. They were martyrs, 255 and note 2. David’s humility is commended, 72. Daumius, a Christian, inserted three sermons of St. Zeno on Christ’s Nativity, together with Barthius’s corrections, among the homilies of the Fathers, 163, note 1. “Owed” (*debitus*), 213. A legitimate gestation of ten months, 169 and note 10. *Defero* in the sense “I revere,” 301. A denarius seems to have been given at baptism in Zeno’s time, 114 and note 21; 247, note 5. Various meanings of the word *denarius*, 187, note 10. The two denarii stamped as one coin, 191 and note 26. *Denique* in the sense “a few,” 163; 201 and note 10; 279 and note 3; 289. In the sense “then,” 53. “To designate” (*denotare*), 230, 296. “To appease” (*deplacare*), 175. *Derivavit* in the sense “he turned,” 138 and note 62. “Things desired” (*desiderata*), 243. What this word means among the Fathers, ibid., note 3. God is that which He is; but whatever man judges ought to be defined does not exist, 164 and note 12. God alone is the principle of all things, 145. His attributes, ibid. and 146. God would not be perfect if there were something which, though He willed it to be, could not be, 168. It belongs properly to God to know what has passed and what is future, 226. The devil is the father of all who live corruptly, 196, note 52. It was the deacons’ duty to go in to the bishop whenever he was to proceed from his chamber to the sacred offices, 147, note 1. The Jews paid a gold didrachm to the Temple, 187, note 10. Days were divided into twelve hours, both in summer and in winter, 64, note 11. What Egyptian days were: they were considered unlucky, and why they are so called, 122, note 19. Vain observance of days displeases God, ibid. To expose every kind of sin through the Law, 6. God unfolded Himself into God, 146 and note 7. Fingers customarily used in counting, 83 and note 19. To become worthy, 67. The gods of the Gentiles were unchaste and born from unchastity, 44 ff. “It is discoloured” (*discoloratur*), 128. [Uncertain OCR reading: *dispositus tus*], 168 and note 3. *Dispunctus mortis lege*, “marked off by the law of death,” meaning “dead,” 130 and note 25. If disputation is subtle and sophistical, it uproots faith, 7. “You constrain law by law,” 16. Secular wisdom “constrains right by right,” meaning “overthrows it,” 34 and note 11. Few rich persons are holy, 116. Learned persons attended St. Zeno’s sermons, 30. Who they were, ibid., note 1. How the inner rooms of houses were decorated, 81. *Dulcia*, used substantively for sweet things, 252 and note 17.

### E

The Church is called paradise, 292 and note 5. It is figured by Nineveh, 209. Christian churches were not formerly called temples, 59, note 26. St. Ambrose was the first to use the term *templum* for a church [col. 1517], ibid. They were called sacred strongholds, 109; places of prayer, ibid. and note 4, 116; meeting-houses or assemblies, 110 and note 6. They were public in St. Zeno’s time, LI. Their buildings were by no means comparable to Gentile temples, ibid. and 109, note 4. They were narrow, so as not to hold the multitude of believers, 111 and note 8. What funerary edicts were, 89, note 22. *Effectus*: “in effect,” 43. To refuse alms to a person dying of poverty is to kill that person, 38. *Elogium*, 221. It is used both in a good and in a bad sense, ibid., note 6. An inscription of condemnation, 317. Demoniacs (*energumeni*), 128. Their condition while being adjured, 128. They were possessed by wandering and unclean spirits, 128. Sometimes the spirits themselves spoke through them, 129. Some of these spirits are said formerly to have been human beings, CXVI; 129, note 20. On the vigils of more celebrated feasts bishops read the ninth lesson, 99, note 2. How highly the ancient order of bishops is to be esteemed, LXVI, LXVII. It derives from the diptychs, ibid. The epoch of certain ancients exceeded Christ’s birth by about fifty years, XLIV, XLV. The name “Gospel” was assigned to all books of the New Testament, 91, note 1. The Eucharist is indicated by the name of a banquet, 251, or of a meal, 252; and perhaps also of milk, 244, note 7. Why it is indicated by these allegories, ibid., note 5. It was called the secret sacrifice, 60 and notes 27–28. It could not be seen by catechumens, ibid. Women formerly received it in linen cloths, men with bare hands, 113, note 18. Christians carried it home, 60 and note 29. How it was kept, 113, note 18. Christ’s body and blood foretold by the Psalmist, 197. Eucharistic communion after baptism, 241, note 4. Under both kinds, under the names of bread and must, 280; of bread and wine, 251, note 9. To offer the Eucharistic sacrifice unworthily is sacrilegious; to eat it unworthily is deadly, 124 and note 25. “Vomited” (*evomitus*), used adjectivally, 209. To make an *exagium* [a standard weight], 267 and note 9. A tangible, fleshless shadow, 97. Christians made confession (*exomologesis*), 88 and note 17; 197 and note 40. Openings were sometimes prepared by authors, 238. St. Zeno’s opening, 303, note I. *Expono* in the sense “I lay down,” 193 and note 7. *Exponit infantem* in the sense “she gives birth,” 170 and note 11. An exposed body, 55 and note 13. *Expungo* in the sense “I distribute,” 252, note 16; 279, note 2. Funeral attendants return from the tomb, 21 and note 16. Used for a funeral procession, ibid. and 216. Of displayed majesty, 155, note 11; openly, 142 and note 7. “Foreign things” (*extraria*), 164.

### F

*Fabula* in the sense “history,” 289, note 2. “They tell secrets,” 14. How the face was embellished with cosmetics, 45. A battle famous in report, 199 and note 3; a much-talked-of matter, 301. Shrines, especially on country estates: in St. Zeno’s time they smoked with sacrifices, 120 and note 14. Who the fanatics were, 61, note 32. Women’s vanity is described, 45, 56, 86. Women adorned with trappings hang the deaths of souls upon their trappings, 38. They went to church with their whole bodies covered in gold, 86 and note 12; delicate everywhere, bold beneath necklaces, 87 and note 13. Vain women insult God with prayers rather than entreat Him, 88. Women who do not fear God cannot fear their husbands, 88. At their husbands’ funerals they cut off their hair and laid it upon the corpse, 55, note 13. Old women marrying repeatedly are censured, 57. “To lend at interest upon marriages,” meaning to multiply marriages or enter several marriages, 62 and note 35. Usury censured, 82; whence the term comes, ibid., note 16. It was paid on the Kalends, ibid., note 13. See Usury. The usurer seeks not the sum he lent, but that which days, months, and fingers armed with calculation have produced for him, 82; by some chance—fraud, want, flight, or death—he wrings [it] from the debtor, 83. He rightly loses what is his who desires what belongs to another, ibid. *Fero* in the sense “I take away,” 83 and note 21. “Hastened upbringing,” in the sense “diligent,” 180. An inexperienced pregnant woman, 170 and note 12. Faith arises from the will, 4; does not depend upon the speaker’s mouth, 4; is so connected with hope and charity that each is necessary to the others, 16; is the substance of hope, ibid.; where there is no faith, there is no hope, ibid.; must be guarded by every kind of virtue, ibid.; is the immovable foundation of our life, 20. The duties of those skilled in faith, 16, note 49. What true nobility of faith is, 18; its praises, 19, 20, 21. Faith cleanses the conscience to its marrow, and how, 7. Faith joined with charity is a capable expeller of avarice, 84. Where faith is, there is no sorrow [col. 1518], 177. Whoever has it must necessarily live readily and purely, 199. Nothing is difficult to faith, which possesses as much as it believes, 184. Truth is established in believers’ faith, not in carnal eyes, 132. There is no faith where faith is sought, 7. To see the secrets of faith is not within human capacity, 15. The nature of faith does not allow itself to be subjected to the artifice of talkativeness, 8. Presumptuous faith: it prefers that its new tradition be believed rather than antiquity, 15. Ancient faith is the same in Abraham and in us, 10, note 34. What “faith” means in the author’s treatise, 8, note 27. “Many faiths” is the same as many creeds, 9, note 31; 10. How much St. Zeno recoiled from these, XCIX. To speak confidently, 52. “He fashioned man,” 93. Children compelled by their fathers’ avarice to beg for alms at crossroads, 80. The Son of God is proclaimed by Catholics as God, equal to the Father, 141. His equality with the Father is demonstrated, 142, 149, 159, 161 ff., LXX. He alone is aware of the Father’s antiquity, 283. The paternal substance and will are of undiminished Deity, 189. How the Son of God is called the executor of the Father’s heart, 143, note 13, LXXXVIII. He is subject to the Father by affection, not by condition; by charity, not necessity; not by diminishing but by religious subjection, 162. What is said by the Father, and can be said, because the Son is the Word, is not without the Son, 143 and note 12. He is the Beginning, 147; why He is so called, ibid., note 2. Before all ages the Father embraced the Son in the depth of His sacred mind, in an unfathomable mystery, 148. The Son was eternally begotten and distinct from the Father, LXXXI; but this generation is hidden, and therefore without distinction or disclosure: thus the Father is said to have embraced the Son, ibid., 148. The generation of the Son, 148 ff., 152, 155. Several formulas of Zeno concerning it are explained and defended, LXXVII ff. The Son’s manifestation in creating the world is called His birth by some, LXXXII. The decree or command concerning the creation of the world is held to be the very Son of God, LXXXIV. A certain eternal generation is attributed to the same Son in that same decree, ibid. Its visible effect was that He Himself was to make the world and visit the human race, 152, LXXXV. The three terms Word, Son, and Image properly belong to the second Person, LXXXVI. See Word. “He proceeds into birth who was before He was born, equal to the Father in all things”: how this should be understood, LXXXIX. The formulas “the Word, the Son of God, came forth from the Father’s mouth” and “was belched forth from the region of the heart”: their sources and explanation, 154, note 5, LXXXIV. The teaching of the ante-Nicene Fathers concerning the divine generation of the Word is defended, XCII; likewise that of Marius Victorinus, XCVI. The Son of God belongs to an ineffable origin; [the son] of man belongs to the mystery, 92. God and man, 158. See Christ. The ancient commemoration and cult of the holy martyrs Firmus and Rusticus in the Church of Verona, 298, note I. *Flagitat* in the sense “he defames,” 27 and note 45. The swelling of rivers amid marine tides, 202, note 8. “Foul-smelling” (*foeterosus*), 121. “Of a spring” (*fontanus*), 244. A prostitute, 193 and note 9; 198. Genuine prostitutes hate conception and always avoid it, 193. The term “fornication” is understood not narrowly but broadly of matters other than those usually meant by it, CXII. What the strength of this world is, 34. A fraudulent man excuses his thefts by specious arguments, 224. “Reins” (*frenos*), 164 and note 11. In the Church of Freising, St. Zeno has been especially venerated since the time of St. Corbinian, CLIII. A frivolous accusation, 78 and note 2; frivolous gain, 85. We are poured forth by nature, 94; a newborn child, 170. Theft in the sense “adultery,” 48, note 34; 123 and note 21.

### G

St. Gaudentius corrected, 119, note 10. Generality of a name, 137. “Nativity” (*genitura*), 262. Genesis, 263. In Zeno’s time Gentiles attended temples, LII, 59; especially on estates, 120 and note 14; hence they were called pagans, ibid. Their liberty to build new temples was taken away by Jovinian or Valentinian, LIII, 109. What was decreed concerning pagan worship from Julian’s death until 391 is set forth historically, LV ff. Gentiles are signified by the term “earth,” 226. To what extent they worshipped Christ, 304, note 6. Why they were called learned, 30, note 1. They called Christians unlearned, ibid. They attended St. Zeno’s sermons, ibid. They despised the Scriptures because of their low and unpolished style, 36 and note 19; attacked them, 91 and note 1. Although enemies of chastity, they nevertheless admired it, 39 and note 3; and worshipped it as a goddess, ibid. They had their own virgins, 57 and note 23. Among them women’s repeated marriages were ill-reputed, CXIII. Their chastity was neither fruitful nor true, 40 and note 7. Gentile philosophers and sophists thought that God’s justice resided in rhetorical powers, 31 and note 3. They asserted two forms of justice, one civil and the other natural, ibid. and note 5. Having no expectation of the future, they lost justice by their compromises and devices, 32. They prescribed penalties for widowhood and celibacy, 39, note 3. Gentiles believed it permissible to have intercourse with unmarried women, 48 and notes 33–34, p. 48. Gentile sacrifices are rebuked, 118. Their superstitious worship is recounted, 209, 212. The two-edged sword in Revelation signifies the two Testaments, 186. Of graduated age, 65 and note 14. The men of Greece wish to seem wise, 70. Hail-laden with stony showers, 207 and note 11. “Greatly” (*granditer*), 227 and note 7. “She becomes pregnant” (*gravidatur*), 139; “impregnated” (*gravidatum*), 139.

### H

Who illegitimate heirs are, 43 and note 16. Inheritances were hunted after, 88 and note 19. By what art spouses sought one another’s inheritances through legacy-hunting, ibid. The ancient monastery at Hallein in the Diocese of Salzburg, under the invocation of St. Zeno, CLIII. Hartmann, monk of St Gall, inserted St. Zeno’s name into litanies, CLIII. To be drawn apart by a hard spear, 68 and note 28. Demigods, 194 and note 19. Er, Judah’s firstborn son, a figure of the first people, 194. Hercules was overcome by unchastity in his love for Omphale, 46, note 28. Hierocles, author of Diocletian’s persecution, attacked Holy Scripture, 91, note 1. St. Zeno imitated St. Hilary, XXXIX, LVI, 70, note 1; 71, note 6; 72, notes 10 and 12; 74, note 1 ff.; 75, note 8; 205, notes 1, 3–5; 220, notes 1, 2, and 4; 222, notes 7 and 11. Why man was made by God in His image and likeness, 25. What God’s image in man is, 218, 219. Man, a mobile image, wholly ignorant of himself, 157 and note 14. He received his name from soil (*humus*), 93 and note 14. Within man a hidden war roars, while spirit strives to subdue flesh and flesh spirit, 95. Why man is especially overcome by flesh, 96. Such blindness is shown and censured, 97. To assume man, 140. Man assumed by God, 159. The man whom He assumed, 158. “To bear man,” meaning that God encloses Himself in man, 72 and note 8. About to put on man, 142. He had put on man, 197. Christ, mingled with man, 158 and note 4. These formulas, commonly used by the Fathers before the heresies, are defended, CI ff. Humility is praised and commended, 70 ff. Hymn of the three youths: see Daniel.

### I

What the image of God in human beings is, 217, note 3; 218, note 6; 219. The honour accorded to imperial images, 26, note 40; penalties for those who violated them, ibid. He falsely worships the image who does not love its truth, 297. To render truth to the image, 283, note 2; 285. *Imago* in the sense “thought,” 42, note 15; in the sense “figuratively,” 135. Immortality does not admit temporal sequence, 92. See Soul. Christians were called unlearned by pagans, note 1. Why Christians called themselves unlearned, 17, note 54. It is safer to appear unlearned than to be sacrilegious, 17. *Impiata* in the sense “defiled,” 66 and note 18. The impious, or unbelievers, will not be judged, 223. Why, 221, 223, CXVII. Impatience described and censured, 64 ff. In what sense impossibilities are said to be possible for God, 134, note 41. *Impotentia* in the sense “immoderate power,” 85 and note 4. Unchastity is a goddess among idols and a minister among Gentiles, 44 and notes 22–23. She gave birth to the gods of the Gentiles, 45. It belongs to idolatry, 46; why, ibid., note 30. Who the unchaste robber is, 41, note 7. Unchastity with concubines was unpunished and permitted among the Gentiles, 47 and notes 33–34. Effects of unchastity, 42 ff. It belongs to the unchaste to kill or expose their children, 45, note 17. The preposition *in* is here constructed with the accusative where the general grammatical rules would require the ablative, and with the ablative where they would require the accusative. “He buries [them] in a confused mass,” 199 and note 5. “He will descend into hell,” 84 and note 23. The Holy Spirit entered into the boy Daniel, 204, note 7. Unaffected, 50. The bodily emptiness of the air, 206, note 5. Prisoners, 35. [Col. 1520] The Incarnation of the Lord called a sacrament or mystery, 28, note 54; 92, note 9; 197. Incarnate, 263. Incestuous person, 256. *Inceste* in the sense “impiously,” 112 and note 11. Incomprehensible, 146, 148. Through unbelief or fear, temporal things are preferred to eternal, 97. Without hesitation, 148 and note 3; 154. Undiminished, 189. Unchangeable, 146. Ineffable, 92, 148. Inextinguishable, 65. “You measure the lower regions,” 104 and note 28. To enter into a city, 209. “By assaults” (*infestationibus*), 24 and note 29. “You heap [things] upon time,” in the sense “you thrust them in,” 165 and note 14. Injustice, veiled under the name of justice: see Justice. By laws it acts to usurp what belongs to others under the pretext of defending its own, 37. The unbegotten substance of God, 150. Veronese inscription, CXXXVII. An exposition of the Law in the sense of instruction in faith, 4, note 5. By insolent arguments, 70. Unsubjected, 207. In an unfathomable mystery, 148 and note 1. Of an unfathomable secret, 168 and note 1. Inner parts, 252. To contrive envy, 132 and note 34. With envious words, ibid. To arouse envy, ibid. and 200, note 7. Isaac: the name means “laughter,” given by the angel, 174, note 7; 180. Despaired of by his parents but conceived by God’s permission, 178. He rejoices at his father’s word concerning his own sacrifice, 176. His steadfastness in the sacrifice, 187. He was a figure of Christ, ibid. Isaiah’s coal, by which his lips were cleansed: what it signifies, 186. Isaiah’s martyrdom described by Potamius, 317.

### J

Jacob’s patience is praised, 68. He was an image of Christ, 186. What the stone and ladder seen by Jacob signify, ibid. What the ascending and descending angels signify, 190. Jacob, priest of Verona, described the miracles of St. Zeno in verse: when, CLX. During the season of fasting abstinence was maintained from marital intercourse, 52, note 53. Hence the chaste fasts of sacred expiation, 250, note 2. The book of Baruch praised under Jeremiah’s name, 166. Why, ibid., note 18. St. John called barbarous by Amelius the Platonist, and why, 36, note 19. John of Verona, author of a manuscript *Imperial History*, was a priest-mansionary of the Church of Verona, LXII. Pastrengo and Peter de Natalibus drew from him, ibid.; 3, note 1; CXCIX. He is praised, LXIII, CXXI, CXXXV, CXLI, CLV, CXCVIII; 262, note 1. Job’s patience, 68. His virtues and remarkable patience are described, 199. A figure of Christ, 201. Jonah’s shipwreck is described, 208; what it signifies, ibid. The chastity of Joseph the Hebrew is praised, 49; his patience, 67. Judah was, in one respect, a type of the prophets and, in another, of the patriarchs and fathers, 149. What his sons signified, ibid. ff. The Jews are signified by the old and sterile vine, 231 and note 1; 236. Benefits bestowed on the Jews, 226, 281, 284. What they signify spiritually, 282, 292. What the Jewish people’s flight from Egypt signifies, 280. The Jews are reproved because they despised to listen, 225. After royal dignity, they served the Roman Empire with greater disgrace, 293, 296. The rejection of the Jews is the election of other persons, 224. Their punishment is a warning to Christians not to imitate them, 236. Jews cannot celebrate the lawful Passover after the Temple’s destruction, 288, note 2; 295 ff. Jewish blindness is charged, 246; 228 ff.; 283 ff. Many Jewish baptisms, 295, note 3. Jews glory in circumcision, 100; they are censured, ibid. ff. Jews were permitted to build synagogues before Theodosius the Younger, LIII, 109 and note 2. *Judex* in the sense “governor,” 12, note 39. *Judicium* in the sense “examination of a doubtful case,” CXVIII, 221. There will be judgment concerning those intermediate between the godly and the ungodly, 223. In what sense there will not be judgment concerning others, CXVII, 221 ff. Judgment of water and judgment of fire, 281. Yokes of captives, meaning instruments by which captives are bound, 35 and note 16. The vine’s yoke, 232, note 7. What the right of the Law and divine right signify in St. Zeno, 177 and note 18. What the right of temples is, 120, note 14. *In jure* in the sense “in a state,” 137 and note 59. To discharge the last rites of a cruel funeral, 200 and note 6. Justice is the fountain and mother of virtues, 35; it is praised, ibid. Immortality is justice’s reward, 94. Christ taught this justice, 33. Justice cannot be understood without the teaching of divine wisdom, 31. True justice was called folly by the Gentiles, 36. The philosophers produced nothing certain concerning justice, 30 and note 2. Philosophers and sophists thought justice resided in rhetorical powers, 31 and note 3; they are censured, 33 and note 10. They asserted two justices, one civil and the other natural, 31. Who expounded them, ibid., note 5. What natural justice was among them, 32 and notes 7–8; 31 and note 5. It was called folly, ibid. What civil justice was, ibid. It was called wisdom, but was unjust, ibid. The Gentiles could not transform the reality, but only the names, 33 and note 9. Folly is more fitting to injustice, wisdom to justice, 33. Whoever follows justice must necessarily be tested, 197. What is falsely thought to be justice’s perfection, and what it is, 36. Who is just, 34. Whoever is not just is not wise either, 34. While he lives in this world, he is always in tribulation and always in punishment, 140.

### L

Milk was formerly given to neophytes, 244, note 7; 259, note 5. He is stripped of garments, 77 and note 16. St. Zeno imitated Lactantius, XL, LVI, 30, note 2; 31, note 5; 32, notes 6–8; 33, note 9; 34, note 14; 35, notes 15–16; 37, note 25; 92, note 12; 93, notes 13–15; 94, notes 19 and 21; 127, notes 11–13; 144, note 1; 145, note 4. Lactantius’s testimonies concerning Christ’s generation defended, XCV. Matthew Larroque criticized, 124, note 25; 195, note 32. What the shameful hiding places and underground chambers among the Romans were, 48, note 35. What the ninth lesson in the night office formerly was, 99, note 1. It was sometimes said by the bishop, ibid. To attack laws by laws through an eloquence favoring injustice, 34. To act against justice through the evasions of laws is worse than every violence, because what is taken by force can sometimes be recovered, whereas what is taken by legal evasions cannot, 37. Deceived by the unjust impunity of human laws, people do not know true justice, 48 and 49, note 34. The Julian Law on Adulteries, permitting concubines and prostitutes, was extremely unjust, 47, note 33. The Law is the indicator of God’s will, 7. It is not to be despised but revered, 24. The name Sacred Law is assigned less to Moses’ Pentateuch than to the other books of the Old Testament, and even of the New, 91, note 1; 141 and note 3; 282 and note 5. Among Jews it means the Old Testament, 164 and note 6. “Law,” meaning doctrine founded on arguments and reasonings, as used by Arians in the mystery of the Trinity, is reproved throughout an entire treatise, 3. How useful “law,” in the sense of instruction in faith, is, 6. The distinction between law and faith, 7. Presentation of the Law, 4 and 5, note 5. The freedom of man is maintained and grace commended, CV. See Will. A binding, 181; 234 and note 15. Testaments were inscribed on wooden tablets, 189 and note 14. “Made clear” (*limpidatus*), 270. “They are touched by one line,” 49, note 37. A servant of God ought not to quarrel, 18. *Litterator*, meaning one who teaches letters, 19. The serpent’s slipperiness, 65. St. Lucillus, friend of St. Athanasius, sixth bishop of Verona: in what year he was still alive, LXVIII.

### M

The Maccabean mother did not bring up her seven sons; rather, through her encouragement she herself happily put them to death, 132. “More glorious,” 41 and note 8. “Prefers more,” 15. *Magnopere* in the sense “with the greatest diligence,” 64, note 9; 86. *Non magnopere* in the sense “easily,” 64, note 9; 264. Majesty, in the sense of divine power and dignity, 172 and note 1; majesty guards, 146. *Mancipes*, meaning lictors, 214 and note 20. Description of St. Zeno’s manuscript codices, VI ff. Manuscripts cited, LXIII, LXVI, LXVII, LXXII, LXXIII, CXXII, CXXIV, CXXVIII, CXXIX, CXXXI–CXXXV, CXXXVIII, CXL, CXLIV–CLI, CLV–CLXI, CLXVII, CLXVIII, CLXXIX–p. CXCVIII; 261, note 1; 273, note 1. Sea: see Ocean. Miriam, Moses’ sister, a type of the Church, 282. The Virgin Mary knew none of the inconveniences of a ten-month pregnancy; she gave birth not in pain but in joy, 169, 173. The story of the midwife who found the Virgin to be the Mother of God, 171 and note 17; its origin, ibid. Mary’s virginity, 106; 173 and note 16. Mary: virgin after marriage, virgin after conception, virgin after her son, 54. Those who detracted from Mary’s virginity, ibid., note 5. Marital, 57. By martyrs’ praises the people are kindled toward the heavenly reward, 212; martyrs’ torments are recounted, 215. Bishops and churchmen especially were killed in persecutions, 271, note 8. The fourth-century persecutions in which many martyrs died are recounted, LIX. In some manner, it is part of martyrdom that martyrs did not shudder at punishment, 298. The three youths were martyrs although they escaped the furnace unharmed, 299, note 2. Martyrdom supplies the place of baptism, 106, note 36. Some people produced martyrs for themselves through love of drinking and luxury, 121. Some philosophers and heretics taught that matter was coeternal with God, 144, note 1. This error is attacked, 144, 145. Matter cannot be a principle, 145. Maternal guilt, 102. Matronhood, 50, note 42. Intermediate Christians: who they are, 222 and note 9. The middle sword represents [them], 185 and note 9. Moderation, 155, 226, 233. The great veneration of the Milanese Church toward St. Zeno is set forth, CXLVII ff., CLXI, CLXXXIV. “It is improved” (*melioratur*), 298. He entreats God member by member, 74 and note 17. “A measuring-out” (*metatura*), 172 and note 2. Why some called the course of human life a “carnal mime,” 97 and note 35. Christ mingled with human flesh, 169 and note 9. Man mingled, 158 and note 4. This formula’s use by the Fathers before heresy is defended, CI. *Moliti* in the sense “appointed,” 270, note 4. At every moment, 37, 54, 88, 95, 292. In one moment, 79. For a moment, 133, 136. At moments, 13, 38, 44 and note 21, 63, 67, 79, 113, 208. The monastery of virgins at Verona, the first founded in the entire West by St. Zeno, CXXVII. Those dying by departing from this world’s corruption ought not to be mourned, 133; the departed were customarily commended by God’s priests in solemn divine services, 133 and note 35. Gentiles exposed corpses in the vestibules of houses, Christians in churches, 55, note 13. They were wrapped in some garment, 88 and note 24. A cry was raised for them, 133 and note 36. Women’s customary lamentations at someone’s death are described and censured, 133. Manifold riches, 95. Those who maintained that God established and adorned the world from pre-existent matter, 144, note 1; they are refuted, 145. Another world is that inhabited by the Antipodes, 206, note 6. “Reeking of must” (*mustulentus*), 270.

### N

Among pagans, nativity was customarily carried out through the twelve signs of the Zodiac, 262. The author transfers it from profane observance to sacred [meaning], 263 ff. Nature, meaning created things, 165. Time comes from nature, ibid. What the treasury of nature is, 131 and note 29. Nature’s secret, 133 and note 39. To create nature outside nature, 134 and note 42. Nature made from nothing, 165. Natures of heaven, 205 and note 4. No one gives what he does not have, 8. Nineveh bears the image of the Church, 209. Neophytes were called flowers, 124 and note 26; the Church’s most radiant flowers, 270; new vines, 236 and note 4; infants, 250, note 5. In the West, neophytes were given milk, 244, note 7; 259, note 5. Hence they were called those being fed with milk, 244. They wore white garments, 242, note 5. Immediately after baptism they received the Eucharist, 241, note 4; 244, note 7. Noah’s patience, 67. To change names while things remain untouched, and to brand vices with the names of virtues, 33. A very bright night on the vigil of Easter, 250, note 3. Numerousness, 216. If coins are distributed, they are money; if hoarded, they are images, 86. Why, ibid., note 11. “Now they were,” 21 and note 17; 56 and note 14. *Nundinari* in the sense “to be defamed,” 228 and note 14. Second and repeated marriages are discouraged, 133. Why second marriages are called matters “almost sound,” 57, note 19. Among ancient Fathers, second and repeated marriages were ill-reputed, CIX. Yet they did not regard them as evil and unlawful in themselves, CXI. Why they rebuked them, CXII. How hateful they were also to the Gentiles [col. 1523], ibid. Marriage with unbelievers is reproved, and why, 57 and note 24, CXIII, CXV.

### O

## Z

Whence St Zeno appears to have originated, CXXII. He came from Syria to Italy, ibid. In what year and on what day he was ordained bishop of Verona, LXXII, CXXIII. It is demonstrated that he flourished in the fourth century, XLIV ff., LXV ff. He opposed the Arians, XLVI. He confronted the pagans, CXXV. Pagans heard him preaching, ibid.; 30 and note 1. He baptized very many people at once at Easter, CXXV. He cleansed Verona of errors and brought it to true religion, CXIII. He delivered a sermon at the dedication of a new church, 109, note 1. He rebuked and abolished agapē-feasts turned into lust and drunkenness, 121, note 18. The virgin Indicia was approved by his judgment and sanctified blessing, LXVI, CXXVII. He was poor, 277, CXXVII. He commends hearers in whom faith and piety remained, 84. He celebrates with exceptional praise the liberality displayed by the Veronese in redeeming captives, 88. Famous for miracles, CXXVIII. Approximately in what year and on what day he died, CXXIX. Why his feast-day is celebrated in various places on a day other than that of his death, CXXIX. The dates of his life established within definite limits, LXXI. The claim that St Zeno flourished under Gallienus is shown to be a fable, LXX. See Coronatus. Whether he died a martyr, CXXXI. Whether only a confessor, CXXXIV. The ancient church in which his body first rested, CXL, CXLI. The miracle of the Adige at his church, described by St Gregory, CXL, CXCVII. In what year it occurred, CXL. On what day, CXXIX. When the translation of St Zeno took place, CXL. History of that translation, ibid.; CLXXII ff. For some time, owing to Hungarian incursions, his body was deposited in the cathedral, CXLII. In what year, ibid. It was restored to his own church and is still reverently preserved there, ibid. Relics of St Zeno preserved in various places, ibid. How ancient and widespread devotion to St Zeno has been, CXLIII ff. The Church of Verona has never acknowledged any bishop named Zeno other than the great saint, its patron, LXIV. St Zeno’s sermons are vindicated by ancient codices, many witnesses, and the ancient tradition of the Church of Verona, LXI ff. Certain of his treatises were formerly read publicly in the liturgical offices of the Church of Verona, VII. See “In the Church of Verona.” His collection of treatises is among the most ancient of all Latin Fathers, LXXV. How useful it is for understanding ancient discipline and establishing principal doctrines, [Col. 1529] ibid. Why St Zeno’s treatises for Eastertide are brief, XLIII, 238. Some are prefaces rather than treatises, ibid. Why some contain similar sentiments, XL, 238–239. They were not published by their author, but collected from loose papers by an ancient copyist not long after his death, XVI, 239. These sermons are demonstrated to have been written in the fourth century, XLIV. Some wrongly report that he published an Easter canon, CXXVII. Whether he wrote letters, 3, note 1. His treatise on faith translated into German, ibid. Certain sermons elucidated by Barthius: see Barthius. Sermons [Col. 1530] XI, formerly wrongly ascribed to St Zeno, restored to their authors, 307, XXXVII. How explicitly St Zeno asserted the Nicene doctrine against the Arian heresy, XLVI and LXXIX. Several difficult passages of his defended and explained, LXXX ff. St Zeno was practiced in reading Virgil, 128, 138. He imitated Lactantius, XL, LVI. See Lactantius. Also St Hilary, XXXIX, LVI. See St Hilary. An uncertain author imitated St Zeno and copied several things from him, 203, notes 1 and 4.

# ANALYTICAL INDEX OF THE WORKS OF SAINT OPTATUS

> [Note: [Col. 1529] In this index, Arabic numbers refer to column numbers printed in bold type in the text.]

We have omitted from this index the names of bishops and places discussed in the Conference of Carthage, because they have their own special indices. We have carefully collected everything else. The sign *Praef.* indicates the Preface to the whole work; *Hist.*, the History of the Donatists prepared by us; *Geogr.*, our Geography; *Annot.*, the various annotations, observations, and notes at the end of Optatus; *Hist. Coll.*, the History of the Conference of Carthage by Baldwin. Where no mark is prefixed and only a page is indicated, understand that Optatus’s text itself is being cited. (The reader is referred to the numbers printed in bold type in our edition.)

## A

**ABITINIAN MARTYRS.** After their glorious confession, thrown into prison, *Hist.* p. 2.

**ADELPHIUS OF THE COLONY OF LONDONERS.** Present at the First Council of Arles, *Hist.* 7.

**AELIANUS**, proconsul of Africa. Investigates the case of Felix of Aptunga, 25 ff.; ibid., note 42. He is the same person to whom Constantine writes concerning the conveyance of bishops to the Council of Arles, *Hist.* 7; see there note 16, p. 3.

**AFRICA.** Description of Africa, *Geogr.* 23; its division, ibid., 23–24; *Annot.* 122–123. Fertility of Africa, *Geogr.* 23–24. Multitude of inhabitants, places, and bishoprics, 24–25. When and from whom it received the light of the Christian religion, *Hist.* 1. See ibid., notes 1–2. How rapidly it grew, ibid., and pp. 1–2.

**AGRIPPINUS**, bishop of Carthage. The period in which he flourished, *Geogr.* 30.

**AGROETIUS OF TRIER.** Present at the Council of Arles, *Hist.* 7.

**ALBASPINAeus**, bishop of Orléans. On the edition of Optatus’s works bearing his name, *Praef.* 9.

**ALFIUS CAECILIANUS.** See CAECILIANUS.

**ALTAR.** What is denoted by this name, *Annot.* p. 121. A mark of the true Church, note 31, p. 19. Upon altars the vows of the people and the members of Christ are borne, 90. The Holy Spirit, invoked there, descends, ibid. Hence many receive there the pledge of eternal salvation, the protection of faith, and the hope of resurrection, ibid. The altar is the seat of Christ’s Body and Blood, ibid. There Christ’s Body and Blood dwell for definite intervals, 91. Altars of unbloody sacrifice, *Annot.* 7–8, p. 90. Their notable names, *Annot.*, ibid. Wooden altars, 91–92. Altars are covered with linen cloths in the performance of the mysteries, 92. The reverence due to altars, *Annot.* p. 133. It is sacrilege to break or remove altars, 45 and 90. How grave the danger of erecting altar against altar, ibid.; 121, 122, 126.

**AMBITAUSUS OF RHEIMS.** Present at the First Council of Arles, *Hist.* 7.

**ANASTASIUS OF BENEVENTUM.** Present at the First Council of Arles, ibid.

**ANGEL.** The Church’s dowry, 36. What this means, ibid., note 84; *Annot.* 84, p. 36. The angels of the seven churches to whom John writes, 36. An angel is present at the waters of purification, and the profession of faith is made before him, 38; ibid., note 17.

**SOULS.** Redeemed by Christ’s blood, they cannot be sold, 68.

**RING.** The ring with which the Church’s fountain was sealed, 9–10. What it is: see ibid., note 91; *Annot.* 90, p. 9.

**ANULINUS.** He persecuted Christians in the proconsular province during Diocletian’s time, *Hist.* 1.

**APPEALS IN ECCLESIASTICAL CASES.** See what Baldwin thinks concerning them, p. 114.

**APOSTLES.** They do not have sees distinct from Peter’s, 31; ibid., note 28.

**WATER.** The beginning of all things, *Annot.* 24, p. 52. In what sense it was not made, ibid. We do not read that water was made, 529; ibid., note 24. More on baptismal water, 51–52; *Annot.* 21, p. 81.

**ALTARS.** Altars built over the tombs of martyrs, 60; ibid., note 77. Altars of martyrs whitewashed, notes 77–78, p. 60.

**ARIUS.** He taught that the Son was made from no substances, 75. His teaching condemned by 318 bishops at the Council of Nicaea, ibid.

**ASMODAEUS.** The demon driven from the maiden Sarah by Tobias, 52, [Col. 1530] ibid., note 18.

**Ἀτέλεστα.** What this word signifies: Wisdom III.16, p. 77, note 59.

**BIRDCATCHERS.** Excellent description of birdcatchers who catch birds with birdlime, and comparison of them with heretics, 98; *Annot.* p. 134; p. 98, notes 8–9.

**HAIL.** It must not be said to heretics, 74.

**ST AUGUSTINE.** His conferences with the Donatists, *Hist. Coll.* 347–348. His works and acts against the Donatists, ibid., 41 ff.

**AVITIANUS OF ROUEN.** Present at the First Council of Arles, *Hist.* 7.

**AURELIUS OF CARTHAGE.** The time when he held the see of Carthage, *Geogr.* 31.

**AUTUMNITANUS**, or bishop of Aptunga. Of which province he was bishop, 17; ibid., note 3.

**AXIDO.** Leader of the Circumcellions, 59–60.

## B

**BAGAI**, or Vaga, an episcopal city of Numidia, 51, 58, note 8.

**BALDUINUS (Francis).** Accused by Beza, *Hist. Coll.* 341. His poverty, ibid. His studies and professional career, ibid., 342. His plan for publishing Optatus, *Annot.* pp. 111, 124. Editions of Optatus’s works published by him, *Praef.* 4.

**BALLIS**, or Vallis, a town in Numidia, 33; ibid., note 55.

**BALUZE.** The Acts of the Martyrs and the Conference of Carthage published by him, *Praef.* 9; his learning, ibid.

**BAPTISM.** When instituted by Christ, 85. Baptismal water is God’s thing, not God, 78. There is one baptism, 79–80. Praises of baptism, 80–81. Its effects, ibid.; and *Annot.*, 8–9, p. 80. These are effected not by the minister but by the believer’s faith and the Trinity, 81. Baptism’s power rests in the names of the Trinity, 38. The faith of believers concurs with it, ibid. It has its power not from the minister but from God, ibid. Where the Trinity and faith are in accord, one who had been born to the world is spiritually reborn to God, ibid. Its necessity, *Praef.* 3. Through baptism walls are made for men as protection, 52. Ceremonies of baptism already in Optatus’s time, *Annot.* p. 121. Exorcism preceding baptism, 6. The anointing performed in baptism, ibid. In baptism there are three: the Trinity, the Believer, and the Worker, 83. The Flood and circumcision as figures of baptism, 6, 80. The unity of baptism in the Trinity, ibid. Conferred in the Trinity, *Annot.* 50–51, p. 6. Christ is the fish inserted in baptismal font-waters, 52. Singular baptism, ibid. Whether it requires the faith of the recipient in order to be valid according to Optatus, 6. Valid even if conferred by wicked persons and heretics, ibid.; *Annot.* pp. 130–131 and p. 7, notes 50 ff. On the baptism of heretics, *Annot.* 118, 125. Baptisms of heretics vain and false, 12, 80–83. What the Synod of Arles decreed concerning baptism by heretics, *Hist.* 8. Those rebaptized by the Donatists will rise without a wedding garment, 89. On the repetition of baptism, *Annot.* 80 ff., p. 8. Baptism conferred in the name of the Trinity must not be repeated, 6 and 80. Repetition of baptism prohibited, 38, 51–52. Its unlawfulness proved from Holy Scripture, 51–52, 81–82, *Annot.* 133. Repetition of baptism contrary to laws, 6–7; note 12, p. 30; 51, note 15. Repetition of baptism rejected by the canon of Carthage, 313.

**BAPTISM OF JOHN.** Different from Christ’s baptism, 84–85. John’s baptism was not complete, 85. Those baptized by John before Christ instituted baptism were saved, 85. Those baptized with John’s baptism after Christ instituted baptism were rebaptized with Christ’s baptism, ibid. Whether those baptized by John were again immersed in Christ’s baptism, 7.

**BASILICAS.** Burial is not generally allowed in basilicas, 60–61. Basilicas of heretics are unnecessary, 51; ibid., note 6. Persecutors spoke of basilicas being destroyed, 51. Catholic basilicas in Africa occupied by the Donatists, 41. They were not restored immediately after the persecution in Africa was remitted, 14. Many basilicas in Rome in the earliest period, *Praef.* 4. Forty or more basilicas in Rome at the beginning of the Donatist schism, 34; ibid., note 70.

**BEZA (Theodore).** His errors, *Hist. Coll.* 339. Compared with Petilian, 340. His errors at the Colloquy of Poissy, ibid.

**BONIFACE OF BALLIS**, pseudo-bishop at Rome of Donatus’s party, 33. Sent to Rome by the Donatists as an envoy, *Hist.* 12.

**BONIFACE OF CARTHAGE.** The time when he held the see, *Geogr.* 31.

**BOTRUS.** Sought the bishopric of Carthage, 17. Disappointed in his hope, ibid. The same account, *Hist.* 4. Baldwin on Botrus and Celestius, 126.

**BYZACENA.** A province of Africa, *Geogr.* 23. Its description and boundaries, ibid., 26.

## C
CAECILIAN, archdeacon of Mensurius in the Church of Carthage, *History*, p. 2. He kept back the indiscreet crowd approaching to visit the Abitinian Martyrs, *History*, 2. Hence the Donatists’ calumny against him, that he had ordered those who came to provide food for the Martyrs to be beaten, ibid., 2. By the vote of the people he is chosen bishop of Carthage and ordained, Felix of Aptunga laying hands upon him, 17. The same, *History*, 3 and 4. The time at which he obtained the see of Carthage, *Geography*, 30, 31. His ordination is charged with defect, 18. Secundus of Tigisis and other bishops who were traditors assemble at Carthage against him, ibid. In what sense he offered himself for re-ordination, annotations, pp. 126, 127, and notes 30, 31, p. 19. He is deposed in absentia by seventy Numidian bishops, ibid.; *History*, 4. Majorinus is ordained against him by these same men, 18 and 19. Caecilian retains his chair, ibid. He is accused of crimes by letters from the Numidians, 19. The same, *History*, 3 and 4. He did not depart from Majorinus, but Majorinus from Caecilian, annotation 1, p. 10. Letters are sent against the man condemned by the Numidians, *History*, 4. He remains in his see, 4. Judges appointed by Constantine at the Roman council acquit Caecilian, 24; *History*, 5, 6, and annotations, pp. 128, 129, 177. The judgment of Miltiades in his favor, 24. He is kept at Brescia for the sake of peace, 25. He returns to Carthage, ibid. He is acquitted again at the Council of Arles, ibid., 136, 137; annotations, pp. 128, 129, and notes 13, 14, 15, p. 24. He is again accused before the emperor by the Donatists, ibid., 19, 20. Summoned to Rome for a stated day, he does not appear, ibid., 21. The emperor pronounces him innocent, ibid., 21, 22. The Donatists again present a petition against him, calling him a scoundrel, ibid., 25. Death of Caecilian, ibid., 29. For Baldwin’s account of his history and of the proceedings conducted against or for him, see annotations 127 ff. On him, Albaspinaeus, annotations 134 and 135.

CAECILIAN, decurion of the colony of Aptunga. What he did during the persecution to extort books from the bishop and clergy of that place, *History*, 2. Witness in Felix’s case, 17; *History*, 6.

CALAMA. A town of Numidia; see p. 14, ibid., note 51.

CHALICES. Bearers of Christ’s blood, 92. To sell them is sacrilege, ibid.

CALIDIUS GRATIANUS. Witness in Felix’s case, 26; *History*, 6.

CALVIN. Called Lucanian by Baldwin, annotation 131. His errors (*σφάλματα*, “faults”) noted by Baldwin, ibid., 114, 115, 120. Other errors of his concerning doctrine, ibid., 115, 116, 118, 119; concerning discipline, ibid., 117. His testimonies concerning the Synagogue and the Church, *History of the Conference*, 362, 363.

CALVINISTS. An excellent comparison between them and the Donatists, annotations 121, 127.

CAMPITAE. A name given to the Donatists, *History*, 12.

DOG. A lowly animal among the Hebrews, unfit for sacrifices, 76, note 50.

CAPITO. Bishop of Majorinus’ party, 22. Accuser of Caecilian, *History*, 9.

CAPREOLUS OF CARTHAGE, ordained about the year 425; *Geography*, 31.

CARPI. A city of Africa, 42, ibid., note 46.

CARPOPHORUS. Whether he should be reckoned among the bishops of Carthage, *Geography*, 30.

CARTHAGE, city. History and changing fortunes of the city of Carthage, *Geography*, 28, 29. Its site according to the ancients, ibid., 29, 30.

BISHOP OF CARTHAGE. Primate of all Africa, *Geography*, 26. Privileges of this see, ibid. and p. 26. Succession of the bishops of Carthage [Col. 1532], ibid., 30 ff. Succession of certain bishops of Carthage according to Albaspinaeus, annotation 137.

CASAUBON (Méric). On his edition of the works of Optatus, Preface, 4 and 5.

DELUGE. A figure of baptism, 80.

CATAPHRYGIANS. Heretics, 8.

CHAIR. What it is, 10, 11, 31 and note 31. One chair through Peter, annotations 20, 21 ff., p. 31; annotation 79, p. 35; note 83, p. 38; notes 11 and 27, p. 104. The Church’s first endowment, 38, 31, 36 and annotation 94, p. 10. Ours through Peter, 36. Through it she also possesses the other endowments, 37. Who first sat in it, 31. The chair of Peter and Cyprian, 10 and ibid., notes 3, 4. To withdraw from the chair and establish a new one is evidence of schism, 10, 11. The chair of Peter: unity is preserved in it, 31. The pontiffs who held it, 31, 32. The Donatist bishops sent to Rome did not sit in it at all, 31.

CATHOLIC. The etymology and meaning of this word, 29, ibid., note 6.

CAUSES. Certain matters are reserved for God, 15.

COELESTIUS. He seeks the bishopric of Carthage, 17. His hope is frustrated, ibid. The same, *History*, 3. On Coelestius and Botrus, Baldwin, annotations p. 18 and 126.

CHARITY. The necessity of charity for martyrdom, 65.

CHRISM. Holy chrism from oil, 62. Before it becomes oil, its simple nature becomes fragrant when it is prepared in Christ’s name, 102. Those coming from the Donatists are not chrismated again by Catholics, 103. Effects of chrism, ibid. Its ancient use is established, annotation p. 126. Optatus mentions it as a sacred thing, Preface, 3. The ampulla of chrism, thrown down, settled unharmed among the rocks, 42.

CHRIST. Son of God, 1. God, ibid. The coming Judge of the age, 2. According to his humanity, first born, having suffered, died, and been buried, 2. He rose again, ibid.; and before ascending into heaven left peace to his own, ibid. Christ alone, the Son of God, is perfect, 44. King and bridegroom of the Church, 54. Bridegroom and wedding garment, 89. Fish, and in what sense, 52. Free from sin, annotation 70, p. 7. Christ’s flesh ought not to have been called sinful, 7, nor baptized for the remission of sins, ibid. Heretics who subtract flesh from Christ, 11. Through Christ’s flesh the world was reconciled, ibid. Concerning him the Prophet said, “Let not the oil of the sinner anoint my head”; and in what sense, 76. On his anointing and baptism, ibid.

CHRISTIAN. He cannot be called a pagan, 68.

CIRCUMCELLIONS. When they arose, 24. Who they were and whence they were named, ibid. and 59, note 70. Incited by Donatus of Bagai, 59. Their frenzy, 24, 60. Very many of them killed, 62, 63. When soldiers were punished by fines, they gave them an occasion for cruelty against themselves, 63.

CIRCUMCISION. A figure of baptism, 80.

CIRTA. A city of Africa, 14. Description of this city, *History of the Conference*, 344, 345.

CLARENTIUS, Donatist bishop. Augustine’s controversy with him, *History*, 18.

CLAUDIAN, pseudo-bishop at Rome from Donatus’ party, Preface, 1; *History*, 12. What the Italians said about him to Valentinian, and Valentinian to the Italian bishops, ibid., 12 and 13.

CLAUDIANISTS. A Donatist sect, *History*, 15.

CLAUDIUS SATURNINUS, curator of the commonwealth. Witness in the case of Felix of Aptunga, 26, ibid., note 45; *History*, 6.

KEYS. The keys of the Church given to Peter, 35. Peter received them to share with the others, 101, 102. Heretics do not possess the keys that Peter alone received, 9, 12. Against them the gates of hell shall not prevail, 35.

Immunity of CLERICS granted by Constantine to Africans, *History*, 5. Confirmed by another law, ibid., pp. 25, 26.

COCHLAEUS, first editor of the works of Optatus, Preface, 4.

SACRED BOOKS. The pretext on which Diocletian’s edict ordering their burning was issued, annotation p. 125.

CONFERENCES in matters of religion. Their usefulness, *History of the Conference*, 347, 348. Whether they may be requested from princes, ibid., 348.

CONFERENCE OF CARTHAGE of the year 411 with the Donatists. The conference is requested by Catholics, *History*, 19, and *History of the Conference*, 348. The Donatists are invited to accept a conference, *History*, 19. An embassy is sent to the emperor, ibid. It is requested by the Donatists, ibid., 20, and *History of the Conference*, 348. Summoning of the Conference of Carthage, *History*, 20. Its usefulness, *History of the Conference*, 348, 349. Marcellinus as judge, ibid. On the date of the conference, ibid., 227 and 349, 350. Names of the records, ibid., 228. Information about them, ibid., 229. Heads of the conference, ibid., 231 ff. The edict of the emperor and of Marcellinus concerning the conference, ibid., 146 ff. Advocates on each side, ibid., 228, 229. The proceedings themselves, ibid., pp. 246–317. A brief digest, from Augustine, of the missing proceedings, ibid., pp. 317–325.
