Judgment of the Cognitor, 325 and 265. Laws that followed, 365. The Catholics offer the Donatists that, even if the latter are defeated, they should nevertheless retain their bishoprics, *History of the Conference*, 351. Fortune of the manuscript codex containing the proceedings, ibid., 226. How it was corrected by Baluze, ibid., 226, 227. History of these proceedings composed by Baldwin, 350 and [Col. 1533] ff. Again, Baldwin’s history of the proceedings, pp. 353 to the end. Brief history of this Conference, *History*, 20, 21. Another conference after that of Carthage, *History of the Conference*, 365, 366.

CONFERENCE OF CARTHAGE with the Arians. On it, *History of the Conference*, 367, 368.

TO GATHER. What it means to gather a people, 34, ibid., notes 64, 65.

COMMUNION, with the whole world, 39; with the churches and memorials of the Apostles, ibid., 40 and 93. The one communion of the whole Church through the Roman pontiff, annotations 36, 37, etc., p. 32. Communion of all bishops with the bishop of Rome, and through him with one another, 32, ibid., note 37. It is one thing for bishop to communicate with bishop, another for a layman to communicate with a bishop, 105, 106. No one can be removed from communion unless accused and convicted as guilty, ibid.

AFRICAN COUNCIL. On the first councils held in Africa, *History of the Conference*, 343.

COUNCIL OF ARLES, A.D. 314. Convened by Constantine, *History*, 6, 7. How many bishops attended, *History*, 7. Who they were, ibid. President of the council, ibid., 8. Its judgment concerning Caecilian’s case, ibid. How many canons it enacted, ibid. Two of its canons explained, ibid., 8. Synodical letter, ibid., 8, 9. On this synod, Baldwin, annotations pp. 113, 114, 128, 129; and Albaspinaeus, p. 141.

COUNCIL OF BAGAI of the Primianists against the Maximianists. What was done there, *History*, 16. On it, Baldwin, *History of the Conference*, 246.

COUNCIL OF CABARSUS of the Maximianists against the Primianists, *History*, 15.

COUNCIL OF CARTHAGE. Numidian bishops, 70. Bishops against Caecilian, 18, 19; *History*, 4; *History of the Conference*, 345. By whom these bishops were called and received, *History*, 4. Caecilian, summoned by them, refused to appear, ibid. He is condemned as though ordained by a traditor, ibid. They ordain Majorinus, 19; *History*, 4. They write against Caecilian, ibid.

COUNCIL OF CARTHAGE, 270. Donatist bishops, *History of the Conference*, 345.

COUNCIL OF CARTHAGE, A.D. 249. It gives thanks to God for unity restored, *History*, 14.

COUNCIL OF CARTHAGE of the Maximianists against the Primianists, *History*, 15.

COUNCIL OF CARTHAGE against the Pelagians. On it, *History of the Carthaginian Conference*, 366, 367.

COUNCIL OF CARTHAGE, A.D. 346, under Reparatus. Its acts, *Geography*, 31.

COUNCILS OF CARTHAGE. Errors concerning the Carthaginian councils noted, *History of the Conference*, 347.

COUNCIL OF CIRTA. When held, 14. See ibid., notes 59, 62. Where, ibid. Of what bishops composed, 14, 15. See also note 73, ibid. Its acts, 15 and *History*, 3. On it, 100; annotations p. 125, notes 59, 62, p. 14; *History of the Conference*, 344, 345.

COUNCIL OF MILEVIS against Pelagius. On it, *History of the Conference*, 367, 368.

COUNCIL OF NICAEA. The 318 bishops condemn Arius, 75. Whether it determined anything against the Donatists, *History of the Conference*, 345, 346. Several observations on it made by Baldwin against Calvin, annotations pp. 114, 115. Its creed defended, ibid., 115.

ROMAN COUNCIL in Caecilian’s case. When and where held, 23; ibid., notes 90, 91; *History of the Conference*, 345. How many bishops attended, who they were, and their names, 23. Sentence passed against Donatus, ibid. Caecilian acquitted, 24. On the same matter, *History*, 5, 6; annotations pp. 113, 114, 127, 128; p. 23, notes 4, 7; and p. 24, notes 13, 14, etc. What it pronounced concerning the bishops who condemned Caecilian and those ordained by Majorinus, *History*, 6. Letter of this council to the emperor, ibid.

SACRED SERMONS. They begin in God’s name, *History*, 14. On them, annotations 18, 19, p. 73, and p. 74, note 26. They were heard while standing, ibid., note 19. Preaching belongs to bishops, ibid., note 21; p. 102; and p. 105, note 30. Whether it was allowed to deacons and others, ibid.

CONSTANS, emperor. His efforts to bring about unity, *History*, 12; *History of the Conference*, 345, 346.

CONSTANTINE, emperor. The prosperity and tranquillity of the Church under Constantine, 40. He entrusts Caecilian with distributing money in Africa, *History*, 5. He grants immunity to African clergy, *History*, 5. How Caecilian’s case was brought before him, annotations pp. 113, 114. What he did, 153, 154. The Donatists request judges from Constantine, 22. Of a just family, whose father among the emperors did not carry out persecution, ibid.; the same, *History*, 5. What he replied to the Donatists asking him for judges, 22, 23. He convenes the Council of Arles, *History*, 12, 13. Letter of the Council of Arles to him, *History*, 8. His letter to the bishops of that synod, ibid., 8. He summons Caecilian, *History*, 8, 9. He threatens the Donatists, ibid. He judges Caecilian’s case, ibid., 9. He entrusts Aelianus, proconsul, with the trial concerning Felix of Aptunga, 25, 26; *History*, 6. He enacts a very severe law against the Donatists, *History*, 10. He revokes it, *History*, 10. He commits the judgment of the Donatists to God, [Col. 1534] *History*, 10, 11. He orders a new basilica to be built for the Catholics of Constantine in place of that seized by the Donatists, *History*, 11. His actions in Caecilian’s affair according to Baldwin, annotations 123, 126, 127, 129, 130.

CONSTANTIUS, bishop of Faenza. He sits in the Roman council under Miltiades, 23.

KORAH, DATHAN, AND ABIRAM, leaders of schismatics, 20. Their punishment, 20, 21.

CORPIANS, heretics. What Optatus meant by this name, note 37, p. 74.

CRESCENS, perhaps the same as Crestus of Syracuse. He attends the first Council of Arles, *History*, 7.

CRESCONIUS, Donatist grammarian. Refuted by Augustine, *History*, 19.

CRESTUS OF SYRACUSE. Summoned to the Synod of Arles by Constantine’s letters, *History*, 6. Perhaps the same as Crescens, ibid., 7.

CRISPINUS OF CALAMA, Donatist. His actions against Catholics, *History*, 19.

CUTZUPITAE. A name given to the Donatists, 34, note 77.

CYPRIAN, bishop of Carthage, 19. The time at which he held the see of Carthage, *Geography*, 30.

CYPRIACUS, bishop of Carthage in the time of Gregory VII, *Geography*, 31.

CYRUS is not to be reckoned among the bishops of Carthage, *Geography*, 30.

## D

DAPHNUS OF VAISON. He attends the First Council of Arles, *History*, 7.

DAVID. He refuses to lay his hand upon the Lord’s anointed, 46.

SON OF GOD, distinct from the Father, 11.

DEOGRATIAS, bishop of Carthage. His ordination and fate, *Geography*, 31.

“THANKS BE TO GOD.” A customary formula of peace, 16. Spoken by bishops at the Council of Cirta, *History*, 3.

GOD. One God, 11. God’s kind is to have no kind, 52. In God everlasting majesty overflows, 77. Whatever is above human beings is already, as it were, God, 57. One swears by God alone, ibid. On the invocation of God’s name, 93, 106. Heretics who introduce two gods, 11.

DEUTERIUS, Catholic bishop, deposed by the Donatists, 48.

DEACONS. Established in the third priesthood, 13, 14; Preface, 3. They presided over the lesser clergy, annotation 36, p. 19. A deacon ordained presbyter without laying on of hands, Preface, 4.

DIGNATION. What it is, 73, note 21; annotation 20, p. 73.

DIGNUS. Bishop of Majorinus’ party, 22.

DISPUNGERE. What it means, annotations 65, 66, p. 59.

DOMINICUS, bishop of Carthage in the time of Gregory the Great, *Geography*, 31.

DONATIAN, bishop of Forum Claudii, sits in the Roman council under Miltiades, 23.

DONATISTS. Donatus’ party: what it is, 57. At first they were in the Church; they departed from it, 105. Origin and causes of the Donatist schism according to Optatus, 17, 18; *History*, 3. At what time the beginning of this schism is to be placed, *History*, 4; annotation 125; *History of the Conference*, 344. The instigators of the Donatists were guilty of handing over the Scriptures, 14, 15. The same men were authors of the schism, and how, 16, 17. Convicted of traditio and schism, 27. They make little account of emperors, 22; yet they approached Constantine and asked him to be their judge, ibid. Judgments rendered against them, *History of the Conference*, 341. Their shamelessness and insolence, ibid., 342. Appeal of the Donatists from the Roman synod, 24. They are rebuked by Constantine, ibid. They appeal to the emperor from the judgment of the Synod of Arles, *History*, 8. See ibid., note 6. Their machinations against Caecilian, ibid., 8. They withdraw from the imperial court, ibid., 9. They stir up disturbances in Africa, ibid. They seize the basilica of the city of Constantine, *History*, 10, 11. Constantine’s law against the Donatists, *History*, 10. By it they are made more ferocious, ibid. Abusing Constantine’s indulgence, they harass Catholics, ibid., 10. They present a petition to Emperor Constantine, ibid., 10. Council of the Donatists against repetition of baptism, ibid., 11, 12. Yet the Donatists dissent from it, ibid. They present petitions to Julian the Apostate and obtain liberty from him, ibid., 14, 17, 18, and notes 34, 35, p. 40. They rage against Catholics, 40, 41. Their sacrileges, 42. They send bishops to Rome, 32, 33; *History*, 12. Few Donatists are at Rome, ibid. They have neither chair nor church there, 33, 34. On the succession of their pseudo-bishops at Rome, annotation 41, p. 31; note 56, p. 33; notes 64 ff., p. 34. Entirely Africans and foreigners, note 73, p. 34. Gathering their adherents outside the city from a cave, ibid., note 74. Why they were called Montenses, 34, ibid., note 77; *History*, 12; annotations 76, 77, p. 34. Called Campitae, note 77, p. 34. Also Cutzupitae, ibid., note 77. Perhaps Rupitae, ibid. No persecution was stirred against them by Catholics, 51. They fled when unity was announced, ibid. They ought to impute to themselves the harsh measures taken against them, ibid. They stir up new disturbances in Africa after 408, *History*, 20. They convene a council, ibid., 21, 22. [Col. 1535] On judgments rendered against them, *History of the Conference*, 345. Laws against them, ibid., 46, 347, 350. Laws of Honorius against the Donatists, *History*, 17, 20, 31; of Theodosius the Younger, ibid., 22. Their condition under the Vandals, ibid. Their remnants down to Gregory the Great, ibid. They reject the conference, *History*, 19. They rage against Catholics, ibid. They are compelled into unity by Honorius’ law, ibid., 20. Condemned by Marcellinus, *History of the Conference*, 365. Laws against them after the conference, ibid., 365, 366. Their quibbles against the judgment, ibid., 366. Their obstinacy after the conference, *History*, 21, 22. Albaspinaeus at length on their schism, errors, and crimes, annotations 134 ff. In what they agreed or disagreed with the Novatians, annotation 136; *History of the Conference*, 343, 344. Whether and how they were heretics, annotation p. 120, note 68, p. 15. What they believe about the Church, *Monuments*, 313 ff. They admit that hidden guilty persons exist in the Church, ibid. Whether they held erroneous views concerning the Trinity, *History*, 10. Their doctrine, ibid., 11. They do not rebaptize after associates are found guilty of sin, annotation p. 131. Their dogmas and crimes, ibid. and p. 132. Whether the Donatists reordained, annotations pp. 140, 141. They wrongly lay hands upon persons, curse God, and rebaptize, 3, 7. They rejected the name “brothers,” 4; ibid., note 28. They avoid sitting with and conferring with Catholics, 5; *History of the Conference*, 347. They flee peace, 72. They reject the name Donatists, *Monuments*, 296. Their frenzy, 40; and their arts, annotation 132. They seek proselytes in various regions, *History*, 12; but their sect adhered to Africa, ibid., and to a few Montenses at Rome and in the estate of a Spanish woman, ibid. Their acts, 2, 3. They scrape, break, or remove Catholic altars, 90, 91. Their sacrilege in this respect, ibid. They likewise sell chalices, 92. They swear by their own people, 45. They shave priests’ heads in contempt of priestly anointing, ibid. They spare no one, but overturn the souls of all, 46. They exorcize believers, wash walls, and strip bishops, presbyters, and deacons of their honors, 44, 46, 47. They impose penance on the innocent, 48. They restored virgins consecrated to God by Catholics to their former condition, 94, 95. These women were compelled by them to receive a second veil, 96. They take divine implements from Catholics, ibid.; likewise veils, coverings, and other sacred vessels, ibid. They wash church coverings and walls with salt water, 97. The Donatists’ folly and superstition in washing Catholic walls and coverings is ridiculed, ibid. They rage against dead Catholics, not permitting their bodies to be buried, 97, 98. They are compared to bird-catchers, 98. Proudly, they falsely boast themselves holy, 44. They curse Catholics in sermons, 73, 74. Donatist speech spreads like cancer, 75. Thieves of Christians, ibid. Donatist schismatics, false prophets, 2, 66, 67. They build a ruinous wall, according to Ezekiel’s prophecy, 67. What their speeches to their neophytes are, 67, 68, 75. They are shown to be deceivers, 67, 68. Sinners whose oil must be feared and sacrifice rejected, 72. Dead flies that spoil the sweetness of ointment, 103. Their pseudo-martyrs, 61, 63.

DONATUS, Catholic bishop. At the age of seventy he is deposed and driven into penance by Felix of Idicra, 43, 48.

DONATUS, son of Ninus, deacon, killed by the Donatists at the fortress of Lemelle, 41.

DONATUS OF BAGAI, Donatist. Leader and standard-bearer of a mad multitude, 51. He stirs up the Circumcellions, 59. He leads a crowd against Macarius, 61.

DONATUS OF CALAMA. He confesses traditio, 14, 15.

DONATUS OF CARTHAGE, distinct from Donatus of Casi Nigri, *History*, 9; ibid., note 9; annotation 112. Albaspinaeus’ opinion whether he was distinct from Donatus of Casi Nigri, annotations 136 ff. What manner of man he was, *History*, 9 and ibid., note 9. About A.D. 316 he succeeds Majorinus, *Geography*, 31. Immediate predecessor of Parmenian, ibid. Author of the schism, 23. The Donatists were named from him, 58; annotation 136. His followers were called Donatus’ party, ibid. He is compared with the prince of Tyre, 57. His pride and arrogance, 57, 58. Donatus dies in the world and in the love of worldly literature, 58, 59. He rises against the authorities, 56. He rejects alms, 56, 59. Donatus’ case is judged at the Roman council, 23. Sentence pronounced there against him, 23, 24; *History*, 5, 6. He appeals the sentence of the Roman council, 24. What kind of appeal this was, ibid., note 26. He asks permission to return to Africa, and obtains it on condition that he not approach Carthage, 25. He later returns to Carthage, ibid. He challenged the making of unity, 51, 55. He was still alive in 347, *History*, 13. The pseudo-Sardican synod writes to him, ibid. He is banished into exile, ibid., 13. His death, ibid., 14. He survives until about A.D. 355, *Geography*, 31. His insults against Gregory, *History*, 12, 13. His writings, ibid. His errors concerning the Trinity, ibid., 10. His letter is refuted by St. Augustine, ibid., 13. A Donatist pseudo-martyr, 63, ibid., note 99. On him, Baldwin, annotation 132.

DONATUS OF CASAE NIGRAE. While Caecilian is still deacon, he disturbs the Church of Carthage, *History*, 4. Why he was condemned at the Roman council, annotation 11 ff., p. 128 and p. 23. He asks permission [Col. 1536] to return, ibid., notes 29, 30, p. 24. On him, Baldwin, annotation 109.

DONATUS OF MASCULA. He attends the Council of Cirta and asks pardon for the crime of traditio, *History*, 3. On him, 14; annotations 47, 48, p. 14.

DONATUS OF SABRATA. He attends the Council of Cabarsus, *Monuments*, 205, 206. Condemned at Bagai, ibid., 207.

DULCITIUS, count. Executor of Honorius’ laws against the Donatists, *History*, 21, 22.

## E

EBION. Baldwin’s observation on him, annotation 131.

EBORIUS OF YORK. He attends the First Council of Arles, *History*, 7.

CATHOLIC CHURCH. Why so called, note 5, p. 29; note 12, p. 30. What the name “Catholic Church” means, note p. 130. It consists of bishops, presbyters, deacons, and the multitude of believers, 39, 46; Preface, 3. It is shown from the Law, Prophets, Gospels, and Psalms, *Monuments*, 235. Besides the one Catholic Church there is no other, 7, 9, 28. Faith and unity of mind make it Catholic, 11, note 16, p. 11. The Catholic Church precedes heresies, 104. It cannot exist among heretics and schismatics, 28. Arguments to establish it, *History of the Conference*, 355, 356. That it is dispersed everywhere, ibid., 357; that it is established from succession, ibid., 358. Whether it can perish, ibid., 359. Whether there are two Churches, ibid., 359. Spread throughout the world, 28, 29; Preface, 3; *Monuments*, 254, 255, 302. Throughout the whole world, 29, 30, 39, 54. It contains good and bad mingled together on earth, *Monuments*, 255, 256, 316, 317; *History of the Conference*, 359–361. It does not perish through communion with the wicked, *Monuments*, 255, 256. It obtained chief place throughout the world from the Roman Empire, annotation 27, p. 54. It is in the commonwealth, not the commonwealth in the Church, 56; ibid., notes 40, 41. In what sense it is in the commonwealth, annotations p. 131, notes 40, 41, p. 56; *History of the Conference*, 337, 338. The succession of bishops is an argument for the Catholic Church, annotations pp. 118, 119, 120. Its endowments, 9, 31, ibid., note 14. The endowments of the Church are so connected that they cannot be separated, 36. In the Church is the Spirit, who blows where he wills, ibid. Communion and union of churches, 93. It retains peace and unity, 35, 36. Its holiness is inferred from the sacraments, 28. Those who belong to any party cannot belong to the Catholic Church, 58. That the Church is not among more recent heretics is proven by the same arguments as against the Donatists, annotation p. 118. The Church is a building, 67. It is compared to a building, schism to a ruinous wall, annotation 15, p. 2. The Church is Mount Zion, 54. Whether the Church is meant by “the world,” *Monuments*, 256. The Church is rightly called Paradise, and why, 39. An enclosed garden, a sealed fountain, ibid. Bride, ibid. Not only are its endowments to be mentioned, but its holy members must also be discussed, situated in the sacraments and names of the Trinity, 38; ibid., note 15; and in believers’ faith and confession, 38. How it should be defended, *History of the Conference*, 341. The Donatists boasted that it had perished and remained only in their party, *History*, 11. Petilian asserts that the Church perished through private persons’ vices, *Monuments*, 299. The Catholic Church is vindicated against the Donatist calumny that it acted cruelly against the Donatists, 39. Offering for the Church spread throughout the world, ibid.

CHURCHES OF HERETICS. Christ rejects them as unnecessary, annotations 86, 87, p. 9.

CHURCH, TEMPLE. Who have authority to sit in the Church, 73, ibid., note 18.

CHURCH ORNAMENTS AND PRECIOUS VESSELS. On them, Baldwin at length, annotations 125, 126.

ELAMITES. Called “choirs of camps,” 55; ibid., note 32; annotation 32, p. 55.

ELECTION. The people’s vote in the election of a bishop, 17.

ALMSGIVING. Alms given by emperors are not to be rejected, 56.

EMERITUS, Donatist bishop of Caesarea, author of the sentence against Maximian, *History*, 16. Augustine’s proceedings with him, *History of the Conference*, 366. Again defeated by Augustine after the conference, *History*, 21.

ENCOLPIUS, pseudo-bishop sent to Rome by the Donatists, 32; *History*, 12.

EPICTETUS OF CENTUMCELLAE. He attends the First Council of Arles, *History*, 7.

BISHOP. The name, honor, and office of a bishop, annotation 59, p. 43. Chosen by the vote of the whole people, 17. Ordained by neighboring bishops, ibid. Whether necessarily by the primate, ibid., note 1; annotation 7 ff., p. 18. Bishops are established in the first priesthood, and their superiority (*ὑπεροχή*) over presbyters, Preface, 3. Episcopal ordination is accomplished by the laying on of hands, Preface, 4. Bishops are the summits and leaders of all, 14. See note 46. Bishops are judges in the Church, 105, 106; annotation 32, p. 106. They must serve God, 57. Preaching the word of God is the bishop’s proper office, 105, 106; Preface, 4. It belonged only to them to preach, baptize, etc., *History*, 14; annotation 30, p. 105. Laying on of hands is a bishop’s act, 106. A bishop ought to be a citizen of the city, not a stranger, 34. [Col. 1537] Bishops deposed without cause, 44. Preserved amid the torments of penance, ibid. By penance bishops are reduced to the condition of laypersons, annotation 59, p. 43. Communion among bishops themselves differs from that of laypeople with a bishop and with one another, 106. What the episcopal college is, annotation 37, p. 5. The episcopal college is not shared by Catholics and schismatics, 5. Catholic bishops offer the Donatists that they may retain their bishoprics, even if defeated, *History of the Conference*, 351. Bishops’ pride censured, 58. Baldwin reproves courtly bishops, annotations pp. 126, 127.

EPISCOPATE. Multitude of episcopal sees in Africa, *Geography*, 27, 28.

FORMED LETTERS. What they are, annotations 35 ff., p. 32. By them bishops communicate with one another, 32. What Baldwin says concerning them, annotations 133, 134.

EVANDRUS, bishop of Ursinum. He sits in the Roman council under Miltiades, 23.

GOSPEL. Testament of the divine will, 81, 82. Judge of controversies, 82.

EUCHARIST. Pledge of eternal salvation, safeguard of faith, and hope of resurrection, 90. The altar, seat of Christ’s body and blood, ibid. There the body and blood of the Lord dwell for fixed intervals, 91. Chalices, bearers of Christ’s blood, 92. In the celebration of the mysteries it is said to be offered for the one Church dispersed everywhere, 39. Wine is offered to God in sacrifice, 62. How impious it is to cast away the Eucharist, 45. How grave a crime to spill it, 42. Dogs which, when it was thrown to them, tore their guilty masters with avenging teeth, ibid. Optatus acknowledges Christ’s real presence in the Eucharist, Preface, 3.

EUGENIUS OF CARTHAGE. His life and praise, *Geography*, 31.

EUNOMIUS, bishop, sent with Olympius to Carthage to pronounce where the Catholic Church was, 25. He confirms the Roman synod’s judgment, 24; *History*, 5, 6.

EVODIUS, bishop. Envoy to the emperor, *Monuments*, 305.

EXCOMMUNICATION. It can take place only against one accused and convicted as guilty, 106.

EXORCISM. What it accomplishes, annotation 43, p. 75. Before baptism it drives away the unclean spirit with which all are born, 75. The impiety of exorcizing believers, 44, 45, 75, 82. He who exorcizes a believer and one baptized is rightly said to curse God, annotation 23, p. 3. On exorcism, Baldwin, annotation 132.

## F

FASIR. Leader of the Circumcellions, 62.

FASTIDIOSUS, Arian. His testimony against the Donatists, *Monuments*, 333.

FAUSTA. Fausta’s house in the Lateran, where the Roman council was held, 23; *History*, 5.

FAUSTUS OF TUBURBO. He attends the First Council of Arles, *History*, 7.

FELICIANUS OF MUSTIS. Ordainer of Maximian, *History*, 16. Condemned by the proconsul, ibid. Nevertheless, the Church, ibid. Received by the Primianists, 17. He attends the Council of Cabarsus, *Monuments*, 205. Condemned at Bagai, ibid., 207. Petition of Peregrinus against him, *Monuments*, 207.

FELIX, deacon of Carthage. Accused because of a notorious letter against the emperor, 17. See ibid., note 92. The same, *History*, 3. On him, annotation p. 126, and note 94, p. 17.

FELIX, bishop of Aptunga or Autun. Ordainer of Caecilian, 17. Accused of traditio by the Donatists, 18. Investigation of his case before Aelianus the proconsul, 25, 26. He is proved not to have been guilty of traditio, *History*, 2. The proconsul’s judgment in Felix’s favor, *History*, 6. Judgment pronounced by Aelianus in his favor cited by Catholics, *Monuments*, 324. On Felix’s vindication before Aelianus, as reported by Baldwin, annotations 129, 130. On the day and year of his acquittal, according to Albaspinaeus, annotation 141. On his acquittal, annotations 40, 41, p. 25.

FELIX, bishop of Florence. He sits in the Roman council under Miltiades, 23.

FELIX OF IDICRA, Donatist bishop. He rages against Catholics, 43. He makes mothers of consecrated women, ibid. He violates a virgin, ibid. He drives Donatus, the Catholic bishop, into penance, ibid.

FELIX OF ROTARIUS, bishop. He attends the Council of Cirta, 15.

FELIX OF THE THREE TAVERNS. He sits in the Roman council under Miltiades, 23.

FELIX OF ZABA, Donatist bishop. He rages against Catholics, 41.

FELIX, pseudo-bishop at Rome from Donatus’ party. He attends the Conference of Carthage, *History*, 12; *History of the Conference*, 349.

FIDENTIUS, bishop of Majorinus’ party, 22. Accuser of Caecilian, *History*, 9.

FAITH. It commends to God, 1. Principal articles of faith, ibid., 2. Necessary in one receiving baptism, annotations 40 ff., p. 83. The faith of the recipient of baptism cooperates with the Trinity [Col. 1538] in regeneration, 38. On the power of faith, 87, 88.

FILUMINUS. Supporter of Donatus, 25; *History*, 5.

FIRMUS THE MOOR. He seizes tyranny in Mauretania, *History*, 15. He persecutes the Rogatists, ibid. His death, ibid.

FLORIANUS OF SINUA or CESENA. He sits in the Roman council under Miltiades, 23. On him, Baldwin, annotations pp. 127, 128.

FLORUS. He rages against Christians in Numidia in the time of Diocletian, *History*, 1.

FLUMEN-PISCENSIS. On this bishopric, see annotations 40, 41 ff., p. 41.

FOUNTAIN. An endowment of the Church, and in what sense, 37. Heretics have no fountain because they do not have the Catholic creed, 37, 38.

FORTIS, bishop of Donatus’ party. His letter to Silvanus and the Cirtensians in favor of Nundinarius, *History*, 7.

FORTUNATUS, bishop of Caesarea. He attends the First Council of Arles, *History*, 7.

FORTUNIUS, bishop of Carthage in the time of Pope Theodore, *Geography*, 31.

FORTUNIUS, Donatist. His conference with Saint Augustine, *History*, 18.

FORUM CLAUDII. An episcopal city, 23, note 97.

BROTHER. On this name among Christians, annotation 125. The name “brother” applies to schismatics, and why, 71. Brothers are those whom one mother, the Church, has brought forth from the same womb, ibid. All are brothers who have one spiritual birth, even if their acts differ, 38, 39.

FULGENTIUS OF RUSPE. A passage of Optatus cited by Fulgentius, annotation 133.

## G

GAUL. Exempt from persecution under Constantius, 22. Judges from Gaul requested by the Africans, ibid.

GAUDENTIUS, bishop of Pisa. He sits in the Roman council under Miltiades, 23.

GAUDENTIUS OF THAMUGADI, Donatist. His frenzy, *History*, 22.

GENETHLIUS OF CARTHAGE. He succeeds Restitutus, *History*, 14. He lived until A.D. 390, *Geography*, 31.

GEOGRAPHY. On our geography of Africa, Preface, 6.

GETULICUS, Catholic bishop deposed by the Donatists, 48.

GILDO, tyrant. He seizes tyranny in Africa, *History*, 16, 17. His death, ibid., 17.

GRACE. To perfect belongs to God, 44. What Optatus thought concerning grace, Preface, 3.

GRATIAN, emperor. His law against rebaptizers, *History*, 15; *Monuments*, 203.

GRATUS OF CARTHAGE. Successor of Caecilian before A.D. 347, *History*, 13; *Geography*, 31. He gives thanks to God for unity restored in Africa, *History*, 14.

GREGORY, count. He restrains the Donatists, 67; *History*, 13. Donatus’ insults against him, *History*, 13.

GREGORY, bishop of an uncertain place. He attends the First Council of Arles, *History*, 7.

GREGORY THE GREAT. His letters concerning the Donatists, *Monuments*, 334, 335, 336.

GREGORY OF PORTUS. He attends the Council of Arles, *History*, 7.

## H

**HERETICS.** Their description, note 79, 80 and following, pp. 8–9. They are rightly called adulterers, 74, 77. According to Optatus, deserters from the Creed and the faith, 11; Preface 3. They have falsified the Creed, 11. They alone possess diverse and false baptisms, 12. Among heretics there are no Sacraments held in common with Catholics, 8, 9; nor do the Church’s endowments exist among them, ibid. Heretics differ from schismatics, and in what respect, 10. They cannot administer Sacraments, 11. They must be avoided, 73, 74. Their speech spreads like a cancer, 74, 75.

**HONOR.** To deprive someone of honor is a kind of homicide, 44–48.

**HONORIUS, emperor.** His law against those who burst into churches, Hist. 17; Mon. 208. Likewise concerning publication of the rescript which the Donatists had obtained from Julian, Mon. 208, 209. Four laws against rebaptizers, Hist. 19, 20; Mon. 215–217. Edict of unity, Mon. 218. Law concerning a fine upon Donatists, ibid. 289. Laws renewed against Donatists, Hist. 19, 20; Mon. 221–224. His laws against the Donatists after the Conference, Hist. 20–22; Mon. 326 and following through p. 330; Hist. Coll. 365.

**HUMILITY,** in acknowledging sins.

## I

**Ἰχθύς (Fish).** In this name are contained the initial letters of very many names, 52; ibid., note 20; note, p. 131.

**IDOLS.** Broken cisterns, 77. They possess no power, 77, 78; note 68, p. 77.

[Col. 1539]

**IGNATIUS OF ANTIOCH.** On his letters, note, p. 131.

**IMAGE.** On the emperor’s image, notes 43, 44, p. 69. To place the emperor’s image upon the altar is sacrilegious, 69, ibid., note 43. On the image of the emperor which the Donatists falsely alleged that Macarius intended to place on the altar, note, pp. 132–133.

**EMPEROR.** How great an honor is due to the emperor, 56. Above the emperor there is no one except God, ibid.

**LAYING ON OF HANDS.** Formerly twofold, note 128: episcopal and penitential, 19. What it was in Christ’s baptism, 76, 77. Confirmatory laying on of hands, note 56, 76. The laying on of hands ought not to be imposed upon bishops and clerics, 23; see ibid., note 10. Those who wrongly lay on hands put forward a veil of overthrow, 3; ibid., note 22. The laying on of hands as a veil of overthrow among heretics, and in what sense, note 18, p. 3. Which laying on of hands is meant by the decree of the Roman council, according to Balduin, note, pp. 127–128; and according to Albaspinaeus, ibid., pp. 137–139.

**INGENTIUS, SCRIBE,** decurion of Ziqua. Witness in the case of Felix of Aptunga, 26, ibid., note 49; Hist. 6. His deceit in seeking to defame Felix with the charge of handing over sacred books, Hist. 2. He falsified Caecilian’s letter, ibid., 2, 3. He was convicted and confessed that he had falsified it, Hist. 6. For this reason he was thrown into prison, Hist. 6; sent to the imperial court, Hist. 6, 9.

**INNOCENT, bishop of Rome.** On his letters to the Africans, Mon. 219.

**INVOCATION OF GOD’S NAME.** It sanctifies and cleanses, 93. Ecclesiastical discourses begin with it and end through it, 105, 106.

**ISRAEL.** Whether true sacrifices existed in the kingdom of Israel, Hist. Coll. 359–361. That the Israelites were schismatics, ibid., 261, 362.

## J

**JANUARIUS OF FLUMEN-PISCENSE, Donatist.** He rages against Catholics, 41.

**JERUSALEM.** On its destruction, note 131.

**JUDAH.** The distinction between the sacrifices of Judah, Israel, and the Samaritans, Hist. Coll. 360–362.

**JEWS.** Ezekiel says of them: “They forsook the fountain of water and dug for themselves broken cisterns,” 77. How this is to be understood, ibid.

**TRANS-MARINE JUDGMENTS.** Bishops ought not lightly to go overseas for judicial proceedings, Mon. 219.

**JULIAN THE APOSTATE, emperor.** By his edicts he declared himself to be an apostate, 40. He favored Donatists and idolaters, 40, 41; note, p. 131. He granted liberty to the Donatists, Hist. 14. His rescript in favor of the Donatists, Mon. 201. His death, 41.

**OATH.** One must swear in the name of God alone, 45.

## L

**LAITY.** Those supported by no rank in the Church, 13.

**LAMPADIUS OF UTICA.** Present at the First Council of Arles, Hist. 7.

**READERS.** In former times they kept the sacred codices in their custody, Hist. 2.

**CASTLE OF LEMELLA.** A town of Mauretania Sitifensis, 41 and ibid., note 42.

**LEONTIUS, count.** Defender of unity in Africa, 51, 67; Hist. 13.

**SUPPLICATORY PETITION** presented by the Donatists to Constantine, 22; ibid., notes 73 and 79; Hist. 5.

**LIBERIUS OF EMERITA.** Present at the First Council of Arles, Hist. 7.

**FREEDOM.** It belongs to a human being to will the good and to run in that which he has willed well, 43, 44.

**THE CITY OF LIMATA.** See note 53, p. 14.

**WASHING OF FEET.** A figure of baptism, 82.

**LUCIAN, bishop of Carthage,** 10. Predecessor of Mensurius, Geogr. 30.

**LUCIAN, bishop of Majorinus’s party,** 22. Accuser of Caecilian, Hist. 9.

**LUCIAN, pseudo-bishop of Rome from Donatus’s party,** Preface 1; Hist. 12.

**LUCIFERIANS.** On the Luciferians, Hist. Coll. 355.

**LUCILLA.** A factious woman, 16. Rebuked by the archdeacon Caecilian because, before spiritual food, she kissed the mouth of a martyr not yet vindicated, ibid. She separated herself from communion, 17, 18. She supported the ordination of Majorinus, formerly a member of her household, 19. The same account, Hist. 3, 4. On her, Balduin, note 126; and Albaspinaeus, ibid. 134.

## M

**MACARIUS.** Sent into Africa to distribute alms, he secured unity, 51; ibid., notes 4, 55, 59; Hist. 13. Falsely accused of bringing an image to place upon the altar, 69. Things harshly done for unity ought not to be charged against him, 42, 50, 51. His action is defended against the Donatists’ calumnies by many examples, 63, 64. What he did cannot be called persecution, 64. He addressed the people and communicated, not as a bishop but as a layman, 105; Hist. 14. He ought not to have been removed from lay communion, because he was God’s minister, 106, 107. Even if he had been guilty, he could not, while the accuser remained silent, have been excommunicated, ibid. On his case, Balduin, note, p. 131. On him and Paul, ibid., note 67, p. 7.

**MACROBIUS, pseudo-bishop of Rome from Donatus’s party and writer,** 27; Hist. 12. When he held office, Preface 1.

**MAJORINUS, bishop of Carthage of Donatus’s party,** 10, 11. Grandfather of Parmenian—that is, Parmenian’s predecessor, with Donatus intervening—10 and note 99; note 98, p. 10. He went out from Caecilian and withdrew from the chair of Peter and Cyprian, ibid. and note 5. Guilty of schism, note 96, p. 10. A reader while Caecilian was a deacon, 19. A member of Lucilla’s household, ibid. Ordained against Caecilian by the *traditores* as pseudo-bishop of Carthage, 16, 19; Hist. 3, 4; Geogr. 31. On the date of this ordination, Hist. 4. On his ordination, Albaspinaeus, note 134.

**MALEDICTION.** What it is to curse God, 3.

**MAMMARIUS, Donatist presbyter.** Accuser of Caecilian, Hist. 9.

**MAMERTINUS, bishop of the Elosatii.** Present at the First Council of Arles, Hist. 7.

**MARCELLINUS, count.** Who and what kind of man he was, Hist. Coll. 348, 349. President and judge at the Conference of Carthage, Hist. 20, 21. His judgment, ibid. 21; Hist. Coll. 365. Donatist calumnies against him, Hist. 21. His death, ibid.

**MARCELLUS MEMORIALIS.** Author of the summary of the acts of the Conference of Carthage, Mon. 230. His Preface, ibid.

**MARCIANUS,** one of the bishops present at the Council of Carthage against Caecilian. His opinion, Mon. 176.

**MARCION, heretic.** Having become an apostate from being a bishop, he introduced two Gods and two Christs, 11, 74, and note 36. In Optatus’s time neither his heresy nor his name was known in Africa, 8. Balduin’s observation on him, notes 132, 133.

**MARCULUS, Donatist.** Donatist pseudo-martyr, 63; ibid., note 99.

**MARINUS, bishop of Aquae Tibilitanae,** 14. He denies that he handed things over at the Council of Cirta, Hist. 13. He confesses the handing over, 15.

**MARINUS, bishop of Arles.** He sat as judge in Rome in Caecilian’s case, 23; Hist. 5. He attended the Council of Arles, Hist. 7. President of the council, ibid. 7. On him, Balduin, note 127.

**MARTIALIS OF PERTUSA.** Present at the Council of Cabarsussi, Mon. 206. Condemned at Bagai, ibid. 207.

**MARTIANUS OF SULLECTUM.** Present at the Council of Cabarsussi, Mon. 205, 206. Condemned at Bagai, ibid. 207.

**MARTYRS.** What a vindicated martyr is, notes 87, 88, p. 17. To kiss the mouth of a martyr, notes 83, 84, p. 16. Those who, without having been arrested, offer themselves ought not to be regarded as martyrs, Hist. 2. Pseudo-martyrs who killed themselves or threw themselves down, 61. Pseudo-martyrs who were not killed in war, 64. Without confession of Christ’s name, but in vindication of God’s commandments, 65; those who do not love peace, ibid. On Donatist pseudo-martyrs, Hist. Coll. 365. Canon against pseudo-martyrs, Mon. 202.

**MASCULA, city of Numidia.** See note 48, p. 14.

**MATERNUS, bishop of Agrippina.** He sat as judge in Rome in Caecilian’s case, 23; Hist. 5.

**MATERNUS OF COLOGNE.** Present at the First Council of Arles, Hist. 7.

**MAURICE, emperor.** His rescripts against the Donatists, Hist. 22.

**THE MAURETANIAS,** Tingitana and Caesariensis, Geogr. 26. When Sitifensis became a distinct province, ibid. 34. Their description and boundaries, ibid. 26, 27.

**MAURUS OF UTICA.** Excommunicated because he had bought a bishopric, Hist. 2.

**MAXENTIUS.** He issued an indulgence to Christians, 17 and ibid., note 98. By him Christian liberty in Africa was restored, and when, Hist. 4. On him and his indulgence sent to Africa, Balduin, note 126. A notorious pamphlet against him, 16, 17.

**MAXIMIANISTS.** Origin of the Maximianists, Hist. 15. The Councils of Carthage and Cabarsussi in their favor, ibid. 15, 16; Mon. 205. Condemned at Bagai, ibid. 16. Many return to the Primianists, ibid. Catholics investigate the Primianists’ proceedings against the Maximianists, Hist. 13; Mon. 213. The case of the Maximianists cited against the Donatists, Mon. 212, 256. Balduin rebukes someone’s error concerning the Maximianists, notes 130, 131. On them, Hist. Coll. 346.

**MAXIMIANUS,** deacon excommunicated by Primian, Hist. 15; Mon. 205. Ordained bishop of Carthage after the Council of Cabarsussi, Hist. 16. Condemned at the Council of Bagai, ibid.; Mon. 207; and expelled from his see, Hist. 16.

**MAXIMIANUS, bishop of Bagai.** Converted from the Donatist schism to the Church, he surrendered his episcopate, Mon. 212, where see the note.

[Col. 1541]

**MAXIMIANUS, bishop of Pudentiana.** Corrupted by money, he ordains a Donatist bishop, Mon. 334, 335.

**MAXIMINUS.** Though a converted Donatist, because he was blameworthily ordained from the laity, Leo orders him stripped of rank, Mon. 333.

**MAXIMINUS, Donatist bishop of Sinitum.** Refuted by Augustine, Hist. 18. He requests a conference, ibid. 20. He voluntarily embraced the Catholic Church, ibid. 18.

**MAXIMUS, bishop of Ostia.** He sat at the Roman council under Miltiades, 23.

**MEMORIAL SHRINES OF THE SAINTS.** What they are, 33 and ibid., note 51. The memorial shrines of the Apostles at Rome, ibid. On communion with the Apostles’ memorial shrines, note 47 and following, p. 33; note 28, p. 40; note 95, p. 63. The meaning of Paul’s passage concerning memorial shrines of the saints, ibid. 130.

**MENALIUS.** He stirs up disturbances in Africa, Hist. 9. A burner of incense, he feigns eye pain in order not to be accused, 14. On him, note 54, p. 14.

**MENSURIUS, primate of Carthage.** The time when he held the see of Carthage, Geogr. 30. His judgment against handing over codices and concerning those who voluntarily presented themselves for martyrdom, Hist. 1, 2. He did not hand over the sacred books, but preserved them by his prudence, ibid. 2. His precaution concerning visits to confessors in prison, ibid. 2. Summoned to the palace, 17. He entrusts the Church’s property to the elders, 18. Ordered to return, he dies on the journey, 17. The same account, Hist. 3. His innocence is proved by the Catholics, Mon. 319, 320.

**MEROCLES, bishop of Milan.** He sat at the Roman council under Miltiades, 23. Present at the First Council of Arles, Hist. 7. On him, Balduin, note 128.

**METATORES.** Who they were, 61, ibid., note 87; note, p. 132 and p. 61, note 86.

**ECCLESIASTICAL METROPOLISES.** No metropolitan cities were assigned in Africa, Geogr. 25, except Carthage, ibid.

**MIGGIN OF ELEPHANTARIA.** Present at the Council of Cabarsussi, Mon. 205, 206. Condemned at Bagai, ibid. 207.

**MILEVIS, formerly MILEUM,** a city of Numidia, 1, note 1. To be distinguished from Melita, note 123. On the bishops of Milevis, ibid.

**MILTIADES, bishop of Rome.** He sat as judge in Caecilian’s case, 23; Hist. 5. Whether he was given as judge by Constantine, note 137. His judgment in Caecilian’s favor, by which the Roman trial was closed, 24. Invited to attend the Synod of Arles, he could not come, Hist. 7. He sent legates, ibid. The canons were sent to him, ibid. The council wrote him a synodical letter, ibid. 8. On Miltiades, Balduin, note 127.

**MINISTERS OF THE CHURCH.** An evil minister baptizes validly, 38. Inferior ministers, 13, 14.

**MITELLA, or MITRE.** What it is, 43; notes 55, 56, p. 43. The *mitellae* of professed virgins and matrons, 43, 94; ibid., note 54. They are a sign, not a remedy for chastity, 94, 95. They are not commanded, 95, 96. On *mitellae*, Balduin, note, p. 133 and p. 94, note 53.

**MITRE.** See *Mitella*.

**MONTENSES, or CAMPITAE.** The name given to Donatists at Rome, and why, 34 and ibid., note 77; Hist. 12; note 130.

**MONUMENTS.** Assessment of the ancient documents relating to Donatist history appended at the end of Optatus’s books, Preface 5, 6.

**END OF THE WORLD.** The ancients thought that it would come together with the end of the Roman Empire, note 131.

## N

**NAAMAN.** The leprosy of Naaman the Syrian, a figure of the leprosy of sin, 88. His washing and cleansing likewise a figure of baptism, ibid.

**NABOR, bishop of Centurionis.** Present at the Council of Cirta, 15.

**NASUTIUS, Donatist bishop.** Accuser of Caecilian, 22; Hist. 9.

**NATALIS, presbyter of the Church of Urgel.** Present at the First Council of Arles, Hist. 7.

**NAME OF GOD.** Invocation of God’s name sanctifies and cleanses, 93. Ecclesiastical discourses begin with it and end through it, 105, 106.

**NOTARY.** What rank this was, Hist. Coll. 349.

**NOTORIA, or NOTARIA.** What it is, Hist. Coll. 359, 360.

**NOVATIANS.** In what they agreed with the Donatists, Hist. Coll. 343. On the Novatians, ibid. 344, 357. On them, Albaspinaeus, note 136.

**NUMIDIA, a province of Africa.** Geogr. 23. The two Numidias, which formed only one province, ibid. 23, 24. Its description and boundaries, ibid. 26.

**NUNDINARIUS, deacon.** He disagrees with his bishop Silvanus of Cirta, Hist. 3. He proves before Zenophilus that Silvanus was a *traditor*, Hist. 10. His writings concerning the Council of Cirta, 14.

**MARRIAGE.** Marriage rites, notes 62, 63, p. 94; notes 64, 65, 70, p. 95.

## O

[Col. 1542]

**OFFERINGS OF BREAD upon the altar,** note 2, p. 90, and notes 10, 11, 16, p. 90. An offering is made to God for the one Church spread throughout the whole world, 39. Offerings for *eulogiae* (blessed gifts), notes 49, 50, p. 57.

**OCTAVUM,** a town in Numidia, 60, ibid., note 76.

**OFFICIA,** in the sense of officials, note 71.

**OIL.** On holy oil, note 65, p. 7. On avoiding the oil of sinners, ibid., note 68. In what sense the statement is to be understood: “The oil of the sinner shall not anoint your head,” note 132. Uses of oil, note 92, p. 62.

**OLYMPIUS, bishop.** Sent with Eunomius into Africa to declare where the Catholic Church was, 25. He confirms the judgment of the Roman synod, 25; Hist. 6.

**OPTATUS OF GILDO.** His character and deeds, Hist. 16, 17. On him, Balduin, note 124; Hist. Coll. 346.

**OPTATUS OF MILEVIS.** There were several men of this name in Africa, note 112. Optatus of Milevis is distinct from them, ibid. and 123. He was bishop of Milevis in Africa, not of Melita, 112, 123. African, 1; Preface 1. When he lived and wrote, ibid. and p. 2; notes 123–126, 130. Why he undertook to refute Parmenian’s book, 5. His praises, Preface 1, 2; note 112. Whether he was enrolled among the saints in the Martyrology, and by what circumstance, ibid. 2. Occasion of his work, ibid. and note 124. Division of his work and subjects of the individual books, 7; Preface 2. On his seventh book, whether it is spurious, ibid. 2, 3; notes 123, 124. Value of Optatus’s books, Preface 2; note 113. His doctrine, Preface 3. Style, ibid. 4. His method of interpreting Scripture, ibid. 4; notes 120, 121. His opinion on the baptism of heretics, note 128. He errs concerning the designation “Donatists,” 24, note 28. Assessment of his work, note 112. On him, Balduin, Hist. Coll. 346. A lacuna in his work, note 128. On its various editions and this latest edition, ibid., extensively under its own heading. Manuscript codices of Optatus’s books, Preface 4, 5. Documents formerly and now appended to this work, ibid. 5, 6. Testimonies of the ancients concerning Optatus, after the Preface. Writings of Nundinarius transcribed at the end of Optatus’s books, 14, 15.

**THE LORD’S PRAYER.** It was recited at the altar, 44.

**ORDINATION.** According to Optatus, episcopal ordination is performed by laying on of hands, Preface 4. A deacon ordained bishop, ibid. An ordination performed by *traditores* was declared valid by the Synod of Arles, Hist. 8. Whether persons baptized in schism or heresy may be promoted to orders, and African councils on this question, Hist. 17; Mon. 208, 210, 211. Whether Donatists returning to the Church were to be received with their orders, and what was decreed on the matter, Mon. 204; see the note there. When schismatics were received with their honors, ibid.; Hist. 17. Ordination of the bishop of Carthage by neighboring bishops alone, with the Numidians absent, 17. Whether Donatists reordained, notes 140, 141.

**ORESIUS OF MARSEILLES.** Present at the First Council of Arles, Hist. 7.

**EAST.** After exorcism, baptismal candidates turned toward the east, note 55, p. 86.

**ORIENTALIS, bishop of Bordeaux.** Present at the First Council of Arles, Hist. 7.

**ORNAMENTS OF THE CHURCH.** Of gold and silver, 17, 18.

**KISSES.** Signs of communion, 74.

## P

**PALLAE.** What *pallæ* were among the ancients, 96 and ibid., note 87.

**PARDUS OF ARLES.** Present at the First Council of Arles, Hist. 7.

**PARMENIAN, Donatist bishop of Carthage.** Who he was and what he wrote, note 112. He succeeded Donatus in the see of Carthage around the year 226 [an apparent source/OCR error], Preface 2. A foreigner brought by African Donatists into their sect and ordained bishop of Carthage, 36, 37; ibid., note 99 and p. 55, note 1; Preface 2; note 49, p. 6. Who and what manner of persons his ordainers were, 58. He died around the year 390, Geogr. 31. On him, note 99, p. 37; Hist. Coll. 346. He wrote against Catholics, 5. Of what kind are the matters contained in Parmenian’s book, ibid. He said much in favor of Catholics, 5, 6; other things not relevant to Catholics, 6; and some things in favor of both Catholics and Donatists, ibid. Subjects of Parmenian’s books, 7. On his works, Preface 2.

**PARTENIUS, Catholic bishop.** Deposed by the Donatists, 48.

**PAUL THE APOSTLE,** an innkeeper, and in what sense, 94, ibid., note 56.

**PAULUS OF CIRTA.** Charged with handing over sacred things, Hist. 2. His death, ibid. 3.

**PAULUS, count.** Sent with Macarius into Africa to distribute alms, he secured unity, Hist. 13.

**PEACE.** Peace was given by Christ to human beings before he ascended into heaven, 2. Peace of God and of human beings alike, ibid. If peace had not been disturbed, there would have been no schism, ibid. Peace proper to the Church, note 6, p. 2. How great the good of peace is, 35, 36. How it ought to be desired and preserved, 35. Whoever does not love peace cannot be a martyr, 65. It is disturbed by schismatics, note 8, p. 2.

[Col. 1543]

**SINNER.** Sinners must be tolerated in the Church, 101, 102. The sinner whose oil must be feared and whose sacrifice rejected, 72, 73.

**SIN.** No one is without sin except God alone, 44, 76, 100. Sins are to be buried for the good of unity, 101.

**PELAGIUS.** When he promulgated his heresy, Hist. Coll. 366, 367. Councils held against him, ibid. 367, 368.

**PERSECUTION.** Description of pagan persecution of Christians, 64, 65. What the faithful were compelled to do by pagans in persecution, 51. No persecution was stirred up by Catholics against Donatists, ibid. The Donatists were troubled only because of the fury of the Circumcellions, 59–61. They first provoked soldiers by their own wrongs, 62. What was done by the imperial commissioners ought not to be imputed to the Church, ibid. Such actions are excused by the examples of Moses, Phinehas, and Elijah, who secured unity by force, 62–64. Yet the times before the Gospel differ from those after it, 64.

**PERSECUTION OF DIOCLETIAN.** Its description, note 125. When it began, 13; ibid., note 36; Preface 1. What occurred in it, 12–14. On his edict against Christians, Preface 5. How cruel Diocletian’s persecution was against Christians, Hist. 1, especially in Africa, ibid. 1. Its particular evil was that Christians were compelled to surrender sacred codices and sacred vessels to be burned, ibid. When this persecution abated, 14 and ibid., note 58. When it was quieted and ended, 17, ibid., note 97.

**PETILIAN, Donatist bishop of Constantina.** On his letters refuted by Augustine, Hist. 19. His book on the one baptism, ibid. 19.

**PETER.** Head of the Apostles, 31; Preface 3; note 22, p. 31. Why he was called Cephas, 31; ibid., note 23; notes 121, 130. His chair, 31; note 29, p. 12 and note 20, p. 31; and his successors, 31, 32. Whether he alone received the keys, note 88, p. 9. He deserved to be set before the Apostles and alone received the keys of the kingdom of heaven to be shared with the others, 101, 102. Peter’s sin teaches that the wicked must be tolerated for the good of unity, 102. How great Peter’s sin was, ibid. Whether he went to Rome, notes 120, 121. The memorial shrines of Peter and Paul at Rome, 33; ibid., notes 51, 52; note 51, p. 33.

**PHOTINUS, heretic of Optatus’s time.** He said that the Son of God was merely human, not God, 75. When he died, Preface 1.

**PENANCE.** In penance hands are laid on, and penitents are commanded to kneel, 48. Equal periods of penance ought not to be imposed for equal crimes, 49. Penance ought not to be imposed upon bishops and clerics, 45. To do so is a kind of homicide, ibid. In time of persecution, penance was not imposed on fallen bishops, 48. That bishops and clerics could formerly be compelled to penance only with injury, Preface 4; notes, pp. 137 and following, note 21, p. 18. What Optatus thought about penance, Preface 4.

**POLLUTED.** In what sense the things touched by a polluted person are polluted, 92, 93. How human beings are polluted, ibid.

**CONFERENCE OF POSSIACUM.** On it, Balduin, Hist. Coll. 340.

**PRAETEXTATUS OF ASSURAE.** Ordainer of Maximian, Hist. 16. Condemned by the Primianists and by the proconsul, ibid. He retained his church, ibid. Received by the Primianists, ibid. 17. Present at the Council of Cabarsussi, Mon. 205, 206. Condemned at the Council of Bagai, Mon. 207. Petition against him, ibid. 207.

**PRAXEAS.** Heretic, 8. He argued that the Father suffered, 74, 80, 81. His baptism is void, 81. Balduin’s observation on him, notes 132, 133.

**PRESBYTERS.** Established in the second rank of priesthood, Preface 3.

**PRIMATES.** In Africa primates were the same as metropolitans, Geogr. 25. The senior bishop of each province was its primate, ibid. 25. Whether primacy was better attached to antiquity than to a see, ibid. 26.

**PRIMACY.** Denied to Donatists returning to the Church, Hist. 22.

**PRIMIAN, bishop of Carthage.** Bishop of Donatus’s party, Hist. 15. He succeeded Parmenian, Geogr. 31. Condemned by the Council of Carthage, Hist. 15; then at Cabarsussi, ibid.; Mon. 205, 206. Acquitted at Bagai, Hist. 206, 207. With him the succession of Carthaginian bishops of Donatus’s party failed, Geogr. 31. On him, Hist. Coll. 359.

**PRIMIANISTS.** Catholics investigate the Primianists’ proceedings against Donatists, Hist. 15, 17; Mon. 213.

**PRIMOSUS, Catholic bishop of Carthage.** Successor of Reparatus, Geogr. 31. He complained of Catholics who had been killed, 41.

**PRIMUS, son of Januarius.** Deacon killed by Donatists at the Castle of Lemella, 41.

**PRINCES.** Whether princes have the right to judge ecclesiastical causes, notes 113–115.

**PRIORIUS (PHILIP).** On his edition of Optatus’s works, Preface 4. The value of his notes on Optatus, ibid. 4.

**PROCULEIAN, Donatist bishop of Hippo.** His controversy with Augustine, Hist. 17. Persons unworthy of reception received by him, ibid. 18.

**PROPHETS.** They did not say everything with reference to our own times, 77, 78.

**PROTERIUS, bishop of Capua.** He sat at the Roman council under Miltiades, 23.

**PURPURIUS, bishop of Limata.** A murderer, 14. He threatens to strike, ibid. How he checked Secundus, Hist. 2. Charged with homicide at the Council of Cirta, ibid. 3. He accuses Secundus of handing things over, 15; Hist. 3. He threatens him with destruction, 15; Hist. 3. His counsel, full of wickedness, against Caecilian, 18, 19; the same account, Hist. 4. His letter to Silvanus and the Cirtensians in Nundinarius’s favor, Hist. 10. He removes casks and vinegar from the temple of Serapis, Hist. 10. On him, note 52, p. 14.

## Q

**QUINTASIUS OF CAGLIARI.** Present at the First Council of Arles, Hist. 78.

**QUINTIANUM.** A city of Raetia, 23, note 96.

**QUODVULTDEUS OF CARTHAGE.** His ordination and fate, Geogr. 31.

## R

**REBAPTISM.** Rebaptism of believers is unlawful, 3, 75. Donatus was condemned in the Roman synod for rebaptism, 23. Laws against rebaptizers, Hist. 19, 20; Mon. 215–217.

**KINGS.** Honor due to kings, 56.

**RELICS.** What Optatus taught concerning the veneration of relics, Preface 3.

**REORDINATION.** Whether Donatists reordained, notes 140, 141.

**REPARATUS OF CARTHAGE.** Time of his ordination, Geogr. 31. A council held by him, ibid. Deposed for defending the Chapters, ibid. Sent into exile, where he died, ibid.

**COMMONWEALTH.** The commonwealth is in the Church, 56, ibid., note 40.

**RESTITUTUS OF CARTHAGE.** He succeeds Gratus in the see of Carthage, Hist. 14. Present at the Council of Rimini in 359, Geogr. 31.

**RESTITUTUS, bishop.** Ordained by the Primianists against Salvius of Membresa, Hist. 16.

**RESTITUTUS OF LONDON.** Present at the First Council of Arles, Hist. 7.

**RETICIUS, bishop of Autun.** He sat as judge at Rome in Caecilian’s case, 23; Hist. 5. Present at the First Council of Arles, Hist. 7. On him, Balduin, notes 127, 128.

**RIGALTIUS.** His praise and his plan for publishing Optatus, Preface 4.

**ROGATISTS.** A Donatist sect deriving from Rogatus the Moor, Hist. 15. Their doctrines, ibid.

**ROMAN CHURCH.** Mother of the others, Preface 3. It possessed many basilicas in its earliest period, ibid. 4.

**ROMAN PONTIFF.** His prerogatives, notes 113, 114, 127. Succession of Roman pontiffs from Peter to Siricius, 31, 32. Their succession as an argument for the true Church, notes 118, 119 and p. 31, notes 24, 25; Hist. Coll. 357–359. Calvin’s errors concerning this subject, ibid. 119, 127, 130.

**ROMAN BISHOPS.** Donatist pseudo-bishops at Rome, Hist. 12.

**ROMAN EMPIRE.** The Church is in the Roman Empire, 56. In the Roman Empire are holy priesthoods, chastity, and virginity, which do not exist among barbarians, 56, ibid., note 43.

**RUINART (THIERRY).** The value to be assigned to his notes on the Ecclesiastical Notice of Africa, Preface 6.

**RUISSICCADE.** The site of the city, note 49, p. 14.

## S

**SABELLIUS.** Heretic, 8. He wishes the Son to be known in the person of the Father, 11. On him, Hist. Coll. 213.

**SABINUS, bishop of Terracina.** He sat at the Roman council under Miltiades, 23.

**PRIESTHOOD.** The threefold rank of priesthood is explained, notes 42, 43, pp. 13–14. Deacons are established in the third, presbyters in the second priesthood, 13, 14. Bishops hold the summit of priesthood, 14. It exists in the Catholic Church, 38.

**SACRAMENTS OF THE CHURCH.** They are by no means shared with heretics, 8, 9. They cannot be administered by heretics, 11, 12. The Donatists thought Sacraments administered by Catholics invalid, Hist. 11. Whether Sacraments exist among heretics, note 80, p. 8.

**MINISTER OF THE SACRAMENTS.** He is a worker, not the Lord; the Sacraments are holy not through him but through themselves, 83, 84. The effect of baptism must be attributed not to ministers but to the Trinity and faith, 80. Whatever the minister may be, baptism is valid, 82, 83. Though polluted and sinful, he does not pollute, 92. God is the one who baptizes, 83, not the minister, ibid. and following.

[Col. 1545]

**SACRIFICE.** Celebration of the sacrifice of the Mass according to Optatus, Preface 3. A sacrifice of wine is offered to God, 62. The sacrifice of unity is pure and holy, 69. On sacrifice, note 65, p. 7. The sacrifices of the kingdom of Judah were lawful, but not those of the kingdom of Israel and Samaria, Hist. Coll. 360.

**AGE / WORLD (*saeculum*).** Used for “world,” note 4, p. 2.

**SALVIUS OF AUSAPHA.** Present at the Council of Cabarsussi, Mon. 205, 206. Condemned at Bagai, ibid. 207.

**SALVIUS OF MEMBRESA.** Ordainer of Maximian, Hist. 15. Repeatedly accused before the proconsul by the Primianists, ibid., 16. Condemned at the Council of Bagai, Mon. 207. Expelled from the Church and treated with mockery, ibid.; Hist. 16.

**SAMARITANS.** Their dispute with the Jews concerning religion and the temple, Hist. Coll. 360, 361. Their case fails before Ptolemy as judge, ibid. 361.

**HOLINESS.** There is no perfect holiness among human beings, 43, 44.

**SCHISM.** What it is, note 61, p. 6. Separation from the root of mother Church, 11, 12. Its origin, ibid. Evils of schism, 3, 4. Who are the authors of schism, 2, note 9. How grave an evil schism and division are, 20, 35; notes 58, 61, p. 20. On the crime of schism, pp. 115, 116; how it is to be refuted, ibid. 116, 117. The distinction between heretics and schismatics, notes 43 and following, pp. 5–6. Examples of punishments inflicted upon schismatics, 20, 21. Excellent description of the African schism, 65, 66.

**SCHISMATICS.** Who are schismatics, 10, 11. Those who withdraw from a bishop and establish a new chair are schismatics, ibid. In what they differ from heretics, 11, 12, 81; notes 51 and following, p. 6. They cause tears irreconcilable to God, 2. False prophets building a ruinous wall, ibid. 66, 67. Who are the authors of schism, 2, ibid., notes 9–12. Evils introduced by schismatics, 3, 4. They can be called brothers even if they do not wish it, 4. Compared to severed branches and shoots, 37; to branches divided from a tree and to torn cloth, 65, 66. They have the same Sacraments, the same faith, and the same Lord’s Prayer as Catholics, 12, 66. They proclaim peace, and there is no peace, 66. Why Catholics seek them for unity, 99, 101. On receiving schismatics in their own ranks of honor, Hist. Coll. 352.

**SCORPIANUS, heretic,** 74, 75. Whom Optatus means by him, 74, ibid., note 39.

**SCORPIANI.** What they were; Balduin’s ignorance concerning them, notes 132, 133.

**AFRICAN WRITERS.** How highly praised, notes 111, 112.

**SCRIPTURE.** Its authority in determining controversies, note 133.

**SECUNDUS, bishop of Palestrina.** He sat at the Roman council under Miltiades, 23.

**SECUNDUS OF TIGISIS, primate of Numidia.** How vain he was, Hist. 2. His letter to Mensurius, ibid. How Purpurius of Limata rebuffed his boasting, Hist. 2. How, fearing for himself, he allowed colleagues guilty of handing things over to go free from every punishment, ibid. He presides at the Council of Cirta, 15; Hist. 3. He questions his colleagues, ibid. Charged with handing things over by Purpurius, ibid. He leaves the case of the *traditores* to God, ibid. He sends visitors to Carthage, Hist. 4. He comes to Carthage with Numidians for the ordination of a bishop, ibid. 4. He condemns Caecilian, ibid. He ordains Majorinus, ibid.

**SITTING.** Who have authority to sit in the Church, 16, ibid., note 75. Bishops who are judges sit in councils; the accused stand upright, 16. See ibid., note 75. A sign of acquittal, notes 64, 65, p. 15.

**ELDERS.** Those to whom the Church’s ornaments had been entrusted, 18; note 95, p. 17.

**SEPTIMINIUS, proconsul of Africa.** His decree against the Donatists, Mon. 214. Another decree of his concerning the drawing up of official acts, Mon. 307.

**BURIAL.** Burial ought not generally to be permitted in the house of God, 61. Burial denied in a church, notes 80, 81, p. 61.

**SILVANUS OF CIRTA.** While still a deacon, he voluntarily hands over a lamp and a silver *capitulata*, Hist. 2. How he was ordained bishop despite the protest of clergy and people of Cirta, 3, 10. He receives money to ordain a presbyter, Hist. 3, 10. His quarrels with Nundinarius the deacon, Hist. 3, 10. Records proving that he was a *traditor*, ibid. He removes casks from the temple of Serapis, ibid. He is driven into exile, ibid.

**SYLVESTER, count.** Asked to prevent Donatus from using force, 61.

**SIMPLICIANUS OF MILAN.** Consulted by Africans, Mon. 208.

**SION.** Sion is the Church, 54.

**SIRICIUS, supreme pontiff.** When he was elevated to the Roman see, Preface 1. Consulted by Africans, Mon. 208.

**SOLON, official.** Witness in the case of Felix of Aptunga, 26; ibid., note 52; Hist. 6.

**SPIRIT.** One endowment of the Church, 36; ibid., note 96.

[Col. 1546]

**UNCLEAN SPIRIT.** Everyone who is born, even though born of Christian parents, cannot be without an unclean spirit, 75. It is driven out by exorcism, ibid.

**STENNIUS, bishop from Rimini.** He sat at the Roman council under Miltiades, 23.

**SUCCESSION OF BISHOPS.** Those lacking this succession are schismatics, 10, 11. Succession of bishops is an argument for the truth of the Church, Hist. Coll. 357, 358.

**PRIDE.** Pride is to think oneself holy, 44.

**SUPERIUS, stationarius.** Witness in Felix’s case, 26; ibid., note 47; Hist. 5.

**SURGENTIUS, bishop of Procofeltum, perhaps of Vicus Biltensis.** Present at the First Council of Arles, Hist. 7.

**CREED.** All Christians have the same Creed, Preface 3. Heretics do not possess the Catholic Creed, 37.

**CREED OF THE TRINITY.** What it is, notes 113, 114.

## T
Three Taverns. Now Cisterna, 23, note 97. Taurinus, count. Agent of unity, 51. He ordered armed soldiers to go against the Circumcellions in order to restrain their frenzy, 60. Termatius, presbyter of the people of Basti. Present at the First Council of Arles, I, History 7. Tertullian. His saying concerning the blood of the martyrs, History 1. On Tertullian, note 78, p. 8. Testament. The Gospel is Christ’s Testament, which ought to be consulted in doubtful cases, note 133. Theasius, bishop. Envoy of the Catholics to the Emperor, Monumenta 305. Theodorus of Aquileia. Present at the First Council of Arles, History 7. Theodorus of Usula. Present at the Council of Cabarsussus, Monumenta 205, 206. Condemned at the Council of Bagai, ibid. 207. Theodosius the Younger. His law against the Donatists, History 22. Theophilus, bishop of Benevento. Sat in the Roman council under Miltiades, 23. Aquae Tibilitanae, or Tibilis. A city; see note 50, p. 14. Tichonius. His testimony concerning the Donatist council against repetition of baptism, History 11. Tigisis, a city of Numidia; see note 65. Tilius (John): his praise, History 337, 338, 339. Tipasa, a city of Mauretania Caesariensis, 42, note 47. Treatise. What it is, note 23, p. 74, and note 1, p. 79. Delivered in the Church by the bishop, 106. They begin with the name of God and end with the same name, ibid. Tractoria. What it is, History of the Conference 218. Tradition. On the authority of traditions, notes 116, 117. Handing over of the sacred codices. The charge of handing over sacred books, 12, 13. By whom and when it was committed, ibid. A distinctive evil of Diocletian’s persecution, History 1. It was especially prevalent in Africa, ibid. Traditores. The charge of handing over is minimized by Pseudo-Optatus, 107, 108 and following. Who the traditores were, History 2. Canon of the Council of Arles against traditores, History 7. It provided that no one should be accused of handing over except on the basis of public records, ibid.; and that an ordination performed by them should not be regarded as invalid, ibid. Traditores ought to be expelled from the Church, 107, 108; but not likewise their children, 100, 101. Those charged with and convicted of handing over are left to God, 15. Trinity. The names of the Trinity: what they are, note 14, p. 38. Baptism is performed in the Trinity, 80, 81. The Trinity works and completes all things, 81. It confers the effects of baptism, 81. The Trinity acted in creation, ibid. Three persons are indicated at the beginning of Genesis, ibid. Tripolitana. A province of Africa, Geography 23. Distinct from the others, ibid. 23. When assigned to Spain, ibid. 25. Its description and boundaries, ibid. 26. Wedding garment. On it, note 75, p. 89. Tyre. Carthage is called Tyre in Isaiah, 56, ibid. note 46.

## U

Umbilicus (“navel”). Called by Parmenian a gift of the Church, and the altar [is likewise so called], 37. Rejected by Optatus, ibid. Symbol of the Trinity in the Catholic Church, 38. Unction. A form of communion, note 52, p. 76. The holiness of priestly unction, 45, 46. It cannot be taken away, 46. On Christ’s unction, 75, 76. Unity. Of the Church, 65. How great a good unity is, and by what means it should be maintained, 35, 36. It is better to possess unity together with evil persons than to break it off because of them, 101, 102. Urbanenses, a Donatist faction, History 15. Urbanus Carisius. The Council of Cirta was held in his house, 14. Urbanus, Donatist bishop of Forma. He raged against the Catholics, 42; made mothers out of consecrated virgins, 43. [Col. 1547] Ursacius, count. Under Constantine he suppressed the Donatists in Africa, 67; History 10, 11, 12, 13.

## V

Valentinian the Elder, emperor. When elected, Preface 1. When and where he died, Preface 1. His law against the Donatists, History 15; Monumenta 202. Valentinus, heretic, 8. He denied flesh to the Son of God, 11, 74, 77. Baldwin’s observation on him, note 133. Valerius of Melzi. Condemned at the Council of Bagai, Monumenta 207. Sacred vessels, notes 94, 95, p. 17. Veil. What it is according to Optatus, 3, 4. The veil of destruction in Ezekiel, ibid. Altar-veils, 96. Venerius of Milan. Consulted by the African bishops, Monumenta 210. Victor, bishop of Carthage. In Martin’s time, Geography 31. Victor, bishop of Garba. Present at the Council of Carthage, 15. Sent to Rome as an intervener on Donatus’s side, 33, 34; History 12. First sent there by the Donatists, 34. Victor of Leges. Present at the First Council of Arles, History 7. Victor, bishop of Rusicade, 14. He confesses that he handed over [the books], 15; History 3; Monumenta 175. Victor of Utica. Present at the First Council of Arles, History 7; Monumenta 183. Victorinus of Carcabia. Present at the Council of Cabarsussus, Monumenta 205, 206. Condemned at Bagai, Monumenta 207. [Col. 1548] Victorinus, bishop of Petabium, 8. See there the variant readings, t. He wrote against heretics, 8. On him, note 75, p. 8. Vincentius the Rogatist, bishop of Cartenna. Rogatus’s successor in both see and schism, History 15. Virginity. What Optatus thought concerning virginity, Preface 4. The profession of virginity is a spiritual kind of marriage, 94, 95. Virginity is a matter of will, not necessity, 94, 95. Women professing virginity: note 54, p. 94; notes 53, 54, p. 43; and notes 50, 52, pp. 93, 94. They wear head-coverings, ibid. # INDEX OF MATTERS CONTAINED IN THIS VOLUME

## WORKS OF ST ZENO

**Prolegomena.** 9–253. Dedicatory Letter, 9. Preface of the Ballerini brothers, 11. **DISSERTATION on Zeno’s genuine treatises and on his date.** 25. Preface.—After the various critical judgments and difficulties have been reviewed, and the spurious treatises, which were the source of the principal difficulties, have progressively been separated by the sure evidence of the manuscripts, this dissertation sets forth what is to be determined concerning the remaining genuine works. Ibid.

Chapter I.—It is established that there is one author of the ninety-three treatises which we have separated from eleven supplementary ones, 33.

§ I.—Arguments drawn from manuscripts are set forth. Ibid.

§ II.—Argument from style. Examples are produced especially from those treatises which Coustant assigns to Hilary. The author is shown to have imitated him in some places, 34.

§ III.—Other objections dismissed, 38.

Chapter II.—It is demonstrated that the Author wrote in the fourth century, and that everything contained in all the treatises agrees with this, 40.

§ I.—A notable passage is examined in which the Author mentions nearly four hundred years. The arbitrary emendation of the Veronese editors is noted. Cardinal Baronius’s objection is dissolved by other examples; and the testimony of St Philastrius, likewise arbitrarily emended in Fabricius’s edition, is shown to require restoration from the authority of the manuscripts. Certain other words of the same passage are considered. Ibid.

§ II.—The Author, by arguing against the Arians and therefore to be assigned to the fourth century, is proved so by numerous testimonies. The response of the Veronese editors is refuted, 44.

§ III.—Other fourth-century heresies attacked by the Author confirm his date, 50.

§ IV.—A new argument is drawn from the public urban Church. The objections of the Veronese editors and Baronius are refuted. Further inferences are drawn from the bishop’s public sermons, attended also by Gentiles, and from the great number of catechumens baptized every year at Easter, 51.

§ V.—The prohibition on Gentiles to build temples, and yet the public worship of idolatry mentioned by the Author, define his date after the middle of the fourth century within more certain bounds. Baronius’s objection is dismissed. What was decreed concerning pagan worship from Julian’s death until the year 391, 54.

§ VI.—The Author is shown to have lived after the middle of the fourth century because he imitated not only Lactantius but also Hilary. [Col. 1548] 58.

§ VII.—A notable passage by the Author on the redemption of captives, remarkably agreeing with two other passages of St Ambrose, is shown to concern persons captured by barbarians after the Battle of Hadrianople in 378. It is established that the Author’s date cannot be extended beyond the fourth century, 59.

§ VIII.—The objection concerning persecutions and martyrs is dispelled. A brief history of fourth-century persecutions, 62.

Chapter III.—It is proved that the author of the Treatises is Zeno, bishop of Verona, 65.

§ I.—It is shown from manuscripts, ancient witnesses, and the tradition of the Church of Verona that the treatises mentioned have always been attributed to this Zeno. Ibid.

§ II.—The common preconception that St Zeno lived under Gallienus—which alone is opposed to what has hitherto been established—is reconsidered. The opinion of Baronius and Ughelli concerning two Zenos, one flourishing under Gallienus and the other, in the fourth century, the author of the treatises, is wholly novel. All documents recognize only one Zeno as bishop of the Church of Verona; consequently Baronius withdrew his opinion. The origin and basis of the preconception mentioned above, 69.

§ III.—Zeno is proved to have lived in the fourth century from St Ambrose’s letter to Syagrius. The same conclusion is established by the ancient list of bishops of Verona, which plainly derived from the diptychs, 70.

§ IV.—The narrative of the notary Coronatus, which assigns Zeno to the age of Emperor Gallienus, is examined and shown to abound in fables, 76.

§ V.—St Zeno’s date is fixed within definite limits, with which everything is shown to agree, 77.

# THE SEVEN BOOKS OF ST OPTATUS ON THE DONATIST SCHISM
## BOOK ONE

Those who were *traditores* in the persecution; the causes, place, and authors of the schism. 883

## BOOK TWO

It is explained what the one true Catholic Church is, where and among whom it remains, and that the five endowments of the Church are found more in the Catholic Church than in that party which the schismatics wished to make for themselves; also, that they impiously shaved the heads of priests with the razor of penance, that they committed murders, and that they either gave to dogs or threw away those things which had been provided for the salvation of believers. 941

## BOOK THREE

Four causes by which it came about that unity was not established without severity:

First, because the schismatics rendered the basilicas unnecessary and introduced rebaptism;

second, because Donatus at Carthage demanded that unity be established;

third, because Donatus of Bagaia gathered Circumcellions in order to hinder the workers of unity;

fourth, because nothing of those things by which some people think reproach ought to be cast upon unity was done without the will of God. 987

## BOOK FOUR

In this book it is shown by God’s judgment who are sinners at this time; that God, through Jeremiah, is angry with the Jews, not with Christians; and that the idols are the broken cisterns, [Col. 1554] not Macarius or Taurinus, as Parmenian thought. 1029

## BOOK FIVE

In baptism human beings do not act: God washes, and Christ gives what is received in baptism. That those rebaptized cannot possess the kingdom of God, and that they have lost the wedding garment. 1043

## BOOK SIX

In this sixth book it is shown that a bishop of Donatus’s party, contrary to the law, broke up altars and recklessly melted down and everywhere sold vessels of the Lord; that he washed things which ought not to have been washed; and that he exchanged the head-coverings of maidens—concerning which no Scripture is read. 1063

## BOOK SEVEN

That *traditores* who sinned through necessity rather than will did not commit a grave sin; that such persons could be received into communion for the good of unity. 1081
